# Patrologia Latina, volume 78 — English translation

# Patrologia Latina, Vol. 78

## Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal Library

A complete, uniform, convenient, economical library of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reissue of all the surviving monuments of Catholic tradition from the first twelve centuries of the Church, based on the most accurate editions, carefully collated with one another and with several manuscripts, thoroughly corrected; continuously elucidated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by all works discovered after the extensive editions produced during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume and each author of importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of every page and indicating the subject matter below; augmented by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and also by works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any theme may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it may readily be ascertained which Fathers have commented on the individual books of Scripture, and in what places in their works. An edition of the greatest accuracy, and one that can easily be preferred to all others, if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reprinted works, the extremely convenient format of the volumes, consistently alike throughout the entire work, and the low price; and especially this collection, a single, methodical, chronological gathering of six hundred fragments and minor works hitherto scattered here and there, but now for the first time assembled in our library from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.

## First Series

In which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers of the Latin Church, from Tertullian to Gregory the Great. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of the complete courses in each branch of ecclesiastical learning.

# [Complete Works of Gregory the Great]

## [Column 0009]

## Notice from the Editor of the Patrology

In the brief notice prefixed to the first volume of this edition of the works of Saint Gregory the Great (*Patrologia Latina* 75), we stated that certain additions would have to be made by us to the outstanding Benedictine recension. In this volume those additions are included: first, a certain Benedictional attributed to the blessed Pontiff by Kollarius in his *Vienna Analecta*; second, several Roman Orders—fifteen, namely—which the learned Mabillon collected and elucidated in his *Museum Italicum*.

The first half of the Benedictine volume contained the Book of the Sacraments together with other documents relating to the liturgy; the second contained commentaries on various books of the Old Testament. We retain the former in its place, but not the latter, which, as we judge, most suitably gives way to the materials to be added. These materials, together with the Book of the Sacraments and the documents that follow it, will constitute a very extensive and valuable collection of monuments preserving the tradition of the sacred rites of the early Church. The commentaries themselves will be placed more appropriately before Paterius’s Compilation, which also explains the Scriptures, in the following volume, in place of the three Lives of Saint Gregory, which, out of consideration for the reader, we placed before all the works of the holy Father.

Two catalogues of Roman Pontiffs will close the volume. One was first published by the most illustrious Mabillon from a sixth-century Corbie manuscript; the other was published by Emmanuel Schelstrat from a Vatican manuscript contemporary with the blessed Pontiff.

# [Book of the Sacraments]

## [Column 0009]

# Preface to the Book of the Sacraments

## I

We count the Book of the Sacraments among the other works of Saint Gregory the Great—not because he was its original author, since it is owed to the earlier Roman pontiffs, especially Gelasius I, but because the holy Doctor arranged it with the greatest care in a better form, as John the Deacon teaches in Book II, chapter 17. Walafrid Strabo agrees with John in *On Divine Offices*, or *On Ecclesiastical Matters*, chapter 22, as do many others who have written on this subject, as may be read in all the prefaces prefixed to the Book of the Sacraments, which has already been published so often. There is no need to repeat what has already been said.

The original Gelasian Codex was first published at Rome by Joseph Maria Thomasius, a cleric regular and highly skilled in liturgical matters. The entire difference between the Gelasian Codex and the Gregorian lies in the variety and number of the prayers that we call Collects, as our Mabillon observes in *On Gallican Liturgy*, Book I, chapter 2, no. 5.

## II

When we undertook to publish in a new edition the Book of the Sacraments collected, corrected, arranged, and enlarged by Saint Gregory, we had to determine which one, among the many printed and manuscript codices in our possession, should principally be selected for publication. We searched carefully for a long time and deliberated with mature judgment.

### 1

The first candidate was the book which Angelus Rocca arranged to have printed from a very ancient copy in the Vatican Library, as he testifies in his preface, and which has been repeatedly reprinted in collections of Saint Gregory’s works. Yet the antiquity of the praised Codex was made doubtful to us by what Hugo Menard observed in his preface, which we shall soon place below ours. Its completeness, too, is deficient in several respects, and especially the Benedictions have been omitted. This is evident from what is read on the feast of Saint Paul the Apostle: “The Preface and Benediction which appear above.” This plainly proves that Benedictions once existed in the Book of the Sacraments, although now not even one can be read in the entire volume.

### 2

We understood that the edition of Jacobus Pamelius, in volume II of the *Liturgicon of the Latin Church*, highly esteemed by learned men, was closer to the sources, provided that the additions enclosed in parentheses or brackets were omitted. In this purified form, it is said to agree with two very ancient codices formerly belonging to the library of Queen Christina of Sweden, written under Charlemagne or his son Louis the Pious.

This edition of Pamelius was collated with one of the said codices, now preserved in the Vatican Library under number 1275. From this recension we learned that it often differs from Pamelius’s printed edition—even when everything enclosed in parentheses is set aside—not merely in words, but also in Collects and other prayers, and indeed in entire offices.

### 3

We were by no means unaware that the Codex of Saint Eligius, published and illustrated with notes and observations by our Hugo Menard, possessed the greatest authority among learned men. After weighing everything fairly, we judged that no codex should be preferred to it, either on account of its antiquity or its completeness, having read the preface which the most learned author prefixed to his edition.

What moved us above all to publish this Codex before the others was that Menard’s observations and notes could be adapted to no other codex. It was important, both for sacred and literary scholarship, to reprint them in a better form. We do not doubt that, from the addition of such an abundant store of carefully prepared annotations, the diligent reader will derive considerable benefit and pleasure.

Since it was not possible, according to our usual practice, to place these notes beneath the columns because of the excessive length of many of them, we judged that they should be printed separately and distinguished by numbers. In the Book of the Sacraments, we indicated in the margin, by corresponding numbers, each item that is elucidated and adorned by those notes.

> **Note:** In this edition, the numbers are placed within parentheses inserted into the text. —Editor.

## III

Since, however, many distinguished writers on liturgical matters appeared after Hugo Menard—including the eminent Cardinal John Bona; the already mentioned Joseph Maria Thomasius; John Fronto, a regular canon of Sainte-Geneviève in Paris; our own John Mabillon, who almost brought the ancient Gallican liturgy out of darkness; and Edmund Martene, who published three volumes on the rites of the Church, in which he treats carefully and at length everything especially relating to the administration of the sacraments—we have taken care to note, in annotations attached at the foot of the columns, whatever we were able to gather from their works that Menard had omitted and that could shed some light on the subject under discussion.

## IV

We also consulted a great many manuscripts, of which we shall touch upon and briefly sample only a few here.

We collected all the variant readings of the Codex of Queen Christina of Sweden, copied eight hundred years ago, by collating it with Pamelius’s printed edition. From this we observed many differences between the two. Certainly, at the very beginning, the Codex presents the ordinations of bishops, priests, and deacons before the vigil of the Nativity of Christ; all this is absent from Pamelius, to say nothing of the other differences.

We infer that it was written for a church where the memory of Saint Chlodoald was celebrated, and indeed in the region of Paris, because in the prayer *Deliver us, we beseech you*, said after the Lord’s Prayer, after the names of the holy Apostles Peter, Paul, and Andrew have been recited, there is added: “and also your blessed martyr and bishop Dionysius, with his companions Rusticus and Eleutherius, and blessed Chlodoald.” Hence we scarcely doubt that this Codex once belonged to the church of Novigentum, commonly called Saint-Cloud, near Paris.

The Codex of Calais, or the Codex of the convent of Blessed Mary of Calais, can compete in antiquity with this royal Codex. It comes closer to our edition, but is more abridged and contains fewer feasts.

Two Codices of Saint-Thierry, or of the monastery of Saint-Thierry not far from Reims, appear to surpass all the others in age. The first, marked 62, is noteworthy for the figures with which it is adorned. It is believed to have been written at the end of the eighth century or the beginning of the ninth, since it mentions the tearing out of the eyes of Pope Leo III as an act committed not long before. It reads as follows:

> “Benediction for making the sign, etc. Mass of the Invention of Saint Stephen, when the Romans, out of envy, removed the eyes of Lord Pope Leo.”

Leo sat from 795 to 816. He is believed to have suffered violence at the hands of his rivals in 799.

In this Codex the ordinations of lector, subdeacon, deacon, priest, and bishop are placed first. There follow many more Benedictions than in the commonly used Benedictional and in Menard’s edition. After a special prayer of exomologesis, or confession, and many others, there follows a Mass of the Transfiguration. Then come the Preface, *Communicantes*, and so forth. Later one reads: “On the ninth day before the Kalends of January, at the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord,” and so on.

In the same Codex, the chants to be sung at the individual Masses are indicated in the margin, as prescribed in the Antiphoner. For example, for the first Mass of the Nativity of the Lord the following are assigned:

- Antiphon: “The Lord said to me”
- Psalm: “Why do the nations rage?”
- Responsory: “With you is princely rule”
- Verse: “The Lord said”
- Alleluia: “The Lord said to me”
- Offertory: “Let the heavens rejoice”
- Verse: “Sing to the Lord”
- Communion: “In splendoribus”

The second Codex of Saint-Thierry, marked 63, appears to be of nearly the same age. It was certainly written for the use of the monastery of Blessed Mary of Soissons, for it reads:

> “Remember, Lord … and your handmaids, the whole congregation of Blessed Mary, Mother of God, and of the holy confessors Medard and Eligius.”

It is divided into three parts, the last of which contains Prefaces.

In both Codices of Saint-Thierry there are many Masses of what are now called votive Masses, which do not exist in the printed editions—for example, Masses “On Humility,” “On Mercy,” and “On Faith, Hope, and Charity.” There are six Masses for an abbot or congregation.

In the Order for blessing an abbot, nothing is said about the mitre, pastoral staff, or ring; nor is anything said about the procession that accompanies this blessing today. Immediately afterward follows the Mass for a child on the day of his offering, that is, according to the rule of Saint Benedict. I omit the rest because it is too lengthy.

From these two highly distinguished ancient Codices it is clear that such sacred books, merely because they are more extensive, should not always be considered more recent. The most illustrious prince of the Church, Charles Maurice Le Tellier, archbishop and duke of Reims, ordered these Codices to be copied and arranged for them to be sent to us. We owe him many other things as well.

The Codex of Jumièges, which we used, is certainly later than those just praised in age, but yields to none in elegance and completeness. It was written in the year 1000 in an unknown Benedictine monastery in England, constructed in honor of the holy Mother of God and of the holy Apostles Peter and Paul, as is clear from the table of movable feasts. It was then given to the monastery of Jumièges by Robert, formerly abbot of the aforementioned English monastery and then bishop of London, later archbishop of Canterbury. After being driven from his see, he died at Jumièges on 26 May, around the year 1052, when returning from Rome, where he had gone for religious purposes.

Many things that we read in the commonly used editions are absent from this Codex. Certainly, this English book appears to deserve greater consideration than the others, because the English Church received its liturgy and sacred rites directly from Saint Gregory, whereas the Roman Order was adopted throughout the Gallican Church only later, in the time of Pepin and Charlemagne.

It was not possible, however, to present all the differences of that Codex or of the others; otherwise this work would have grown without limit. For the Western Churches arranged the Book of the Sacraments for their own uses in such a way—adding and removing various items—that scarcely two ancient Codices can be found to be completely alike.

Our Edmund Martene has supplied much more on this subject. In Book I of his work *On the Ancient Rites of the Church*, in the section on the administration of the sacrament of the Church and the celebration of the unbloody sacrifice, he presents many Orders, or ritual books, of different Churches.

## V

The place held by the Book of the Sacraments in ancient times is evident from the ivory, silver, and even golden panels with which it was covered in certain churches. Flodoard writes in Book III, chapter 9, of his *Ecclesiastical History of Reims*:

> “He also presented the Book of the Sacraments beneath ivory panels marked with gold …”

In former times, priests were required to learn it almost by heart, as may be gathered from Burchard, Book XIX, chapter 8:

> “Now therefore, brothers, whoever wishes to bear the name of priest must first, for God’s sake, take care to learn those things that are necessary … namely, the Psalter, the Lectionary with the Gospels, the Book of the Sacraments, and so forth.”

And rightly so, since nearly the entire structure of the Christian religion is drawn from this book. Hence those who once contended for the faith against heretics drew arguments from the solemn prayers contained in this Codex—for example, in controversies concerning the Incarnation against Elipandus, concerning the veneration and use of images, and concerning Christ’s body in the Eucharist. See Menard’s notes 254 and 257.

This Post-Communion prayer—“May your sacraments, O Lord, we beseech you, accomplish in us what they contain,” and so forth—used on the Saturday of the September Ember Days, is cited by Gratian in *On Consecration*, distinction 2, chapter 34, and by Lanfranc, Guitmund, and others, whether opponents or defenders of real presence. From what source, moreover, did Augustine especially defend the necessity of divine grace against the Pelagians, if not from the prayers by which the Church continually asks that his help be present to us?

To demonstrate, then, with good reason that the Roman order and rite expounded in this Book of the Sacraments ultimately prevailed everywhere, it is enough to compare it with the Gothic, Frankish, and Old Gallican Missals published by Mabillon in Book III of *On Gallican Liturgy*, and with the Gallican Sacramentary published through Mabillon’s work in part II of the first volume of the *Museum Italicum*. In those books, obscure and base expressions, barbarous language, and words corrupted beyond recognition—good heavens!—are so far removed from the gravity and majesty of the Book of the Sacraments attributed to Gregory.

Enough about the book itself. The reader must now be briefly informed about the notes and observations composed by Menard on it and here printed again.

## VI

The learned man often praises in these notes certain letters of Saint Ignatius the Martyr, which are now regarded as spurious. In this he followed the nearly universal opinion of learned men in his own age. The same must be said of the forged decretal letters of the Roman pontiffs, from which this man of extensive learning frequently adduces testimony.

We have not presumed to alter or correct these matters. Where, however, we found that something praised in the printed edition was manifestly a printer’s error rather than the author’s, and had been printed contrary to what it should have been, we did not hesitate to correct it.

Thus, on page 104, we read: “Behold, you have been immersed; you came to the priest; he said to you, ‘God,’” and so forth. We restored it as follows: “Therefore you have been immersed … what did he say to you? ‘God.’”

On page 105 of the earlier edition, the reading “of Saint Gelsinus the martyr” is found; it should be “Gelasinus,” as it now appears in this edition.

On page 115, Menard gives the passage of Deuteronomy 6:4 in this form:

> “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is.”

But now, at column 363, it reads:

> “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one.”

The booklet of Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, *On the Order of Baptism*, printed in Menard’s notes on pages 113 and following, is full of many errors. It appeared much more accurately through the care of Jacques Sirmond, and from his recension we corrected numerous errors.

We were compelled to leave untouched the corrupted passages on which Menard proposed his conjectures or attached notes, so that we might reproduce Menard’s edition with greater fidelity. A learned man must be forgiven when he encounters a corrupt Codex. Yet Menard often heals corrupted passages by conjecture and restores the genuine reading, which Sirmond later adopted.

To Menard’s notes we added those which Angelus Rocca, Camers and prefect of the apostolic sacristy, wrote in the Vatican edition of the Book of the Sacraments. These are followed by the episcopal Benedictions absent from the Codex of Saint Eligius.

Next comes the Gregorian Antiphoner, presenting the chants to be sung at the Masses. Finally, we appended the Responsorial, or Official, containing the ecclesiastical course arranged in order for both the nocturnal and daytime hours, copied from an old Codex of Compiègne.

Thus nearly everything relating to sacred matters is found collected here, with the sole exception of the Lectionary. We did not dare to add it, both because no one attributes it to Saint Gregory, but rather to Jerome and Pope Damasus, and because it has already been printed more than once—namely by Jacques Pamelius in volume II of the *Liturgicon*, and much more accurately by the most illustrious Étienne Baluze.

In this Lectionary, moreover, only the readings are indicated, both from the Apostle—with a few readings drawn elsewhere from the Old Testament—and from the Gospel. Nearly all of these are still recited in the Mass. As for the Gospel readings, they are supplied for the most part by the homilies on the Gospels in the first volume.

## VII

Although the notes and observations which Menard wrote on the Book of the Sacraments seem sufficient for his praise, something must nevertheless now be said briefly about him and about his other works.

Nicholas Hugo Menard was born in Paris in 1585 to a respectable family. From childhood he devoted himself both to piety and to learning. His memory was sharp and so retentive that he never forgot anything he had once read. Thus, having quickly and easily mastered Latin, Greek, and Hebrew, he resolved to devote himself entirely to the study of sacred literature.

Thinking no less seriously about ordering his life in holiness and piety, while still a young man he bound himself to the rule of Saint Benedict in the royal monastery of Saint-Denis. In order to fulfill more easily what he had promised to God, at the age of twenty-nine he devoted himself to stricter observance in the monastery and congregation of Saint-Vanne at Verdun, on 5 August 1614.

> **Note:** He put on the monastic habit on Sunday, 3 February 1608, and made his profession on 10 September 1612.

Sent from there to Paris, he taught rhetoric for many years at the Cluniac College. Later he spent the rest of his life in the monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, devoting himself entirely to sacred studies and regular observance in the freedom of leisure.

He lamented the waste of time more than anything else. Hence, being extremely fond of retreat and solitude, he was content with a few friends, and those carefully chosen. Among them the foremost place belonged to Jacques Sirmond, a theologian of the Society of Jesus, than whom no one was more favorably disposed either toward learning or toward learned men. Menard, a man above all of great modesty, was accustomed to submit whatever he composed to the judgment and discernment of such critics.

His first offspring was a Benedictine Martyrology illustrated with notes. He was occupied with revising and republishing this work in a second edition when death overtook him.

He recovered the *Concordia of the Rules*, by Saint Benedict, abbot of Aniane, from the Codex of Fleury and published it in Paris in 1638, enlarged with notes and observations.

Four years later he brought to light Saint Gregory’s Book of the Sacraments, together with separately printed notes and extensive observations.

In the following year, under his own name withheld, he published his dissertation on the one Dionysius, bishop of Athens and Paris, against John Launoy’s discussion of Millet’s response.

In 1645 his posthumous work appeared in public: the Letter of Saint Barnabas from an ancient version, with learned notes, as William Cave says in his *Literary History of Ecclesiastical Writers*.

In the fifty-ninth year of his life, he was seized by an almost sudden death, and indeed one that came in accordance with his own wish, on 20 January 1644, after he had lain ill for only a few hours from abdominal pains.

## [Column 0013]

# Letter of Dedication from Dom Hugo Menard to His Eminence Armand Jean, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, Duke of Richelieu and Peer of France

Gregory has filled the world sufficiently, Your Eminence, so that no one can be unaware of the greatness of the man who, while bearing a dignity of immense weight and surrounded by a multitude of affairs, seemed scarcely able to free himself from them, yet never ceased to attend to each matter, resolve difficulties, overcome dangers, and establish what was beneficial.

Among his other achievements, it is especially clear how truly he rose as “the Great” in advancing the discipline of religion and the worship and practice of sacred things. These never shone forth either with greater majesty or in a manner better suited to awaken the sense of piety than after his singular efforts. To this he certainly applied his mind and care no less earnestly than if it alone had been his task while all other matters were set aside.

Although his outstanding writings bear witness to this diligence and care, this Book of the Sacraments in particular demonstrates it with conspicuous proof. It now comes forth into public view, as though by a new birth, illuminated to some extent by my humble labors. In whose name ought it to be born into the light, if not under the auspices of your favor, Your Eminence?

If I consider its author Gregory, he who is everywhere “the Great” could come to no one except him who stands eminent among the other princes of the Church in his purple; nor should the most brilliant light of our order be conveyed to anyone except him through whose aid it awakens again to a new day of restoration.

If I turn my mind to the dignity of the work, it is owed above all to you for this reason: Gregory demonstrated how highly he valued sacred matters by this fruit of his singular providence and piety—by this, I say, Book of the Sacraments. You likewise demonstrated how highly you esteemed the same matters by the monuments of your own intellect, learning, and zeal which you once published.

If Gregory found part of his greatness in divine worship and in the ceremonies that illuminate the Christian religion—ceremonies whose dignity he raised, whose arrangement he adorned, and whose authority he secured—you have added no small portion of splendor from that same divine worship to your purple. You have restrained its enemies in more than one way; by your counsel you have advanced into the administration of ecclesiastical affairs hierarchs distinguished in learning and piety; and in the most elaborate and august buildings of the churches themselves you have entrusted your memory to eternity.

Finally, if I give even brief attention to myself, the least of the ascetics, since I am a member of that congregation which recognizes you as its restorer, which under your auspices continually receives fresh growth day by day, and whose position has thus far remained secure under your authority, it flourishes through your benevolence and hopes, through your good fortune, to be almost blessed.

To whom could I deliver this modest labor with greater right than to you, Your Eminence, who add this to your other praises: just as nothing small or unworthy of his mitre seemed to Gregory, our own Gregory, if it contributed to Christian piety, so your Eminence does not reject things that may be considered even very small if they proceed from the fountain of piety.

Therefore accept this gift favorably among the countless offerings brought to your purple—as a token of your greatness from its Great author, of your zeal from its subject matter, and of the gratitude of the Benedictine congregation from its commentator—from your most devoted servant, Brother Hugo Menard, Benedictine.

## [Column 0015]

# Preface of Dom Hugo Menard to the Book of the Sacraments

As a pledge of eternal salvation and of his perpetual love, candid reader, Christ, on the point of dying, gave his body and blood to his Church. He gave everything that he was, so that together with all his blood he might pour out upon us his entire love.

Nor did he consider it sufficient to offer himself as the price of our redemption to his almighty Father on the altar of the cross, unless he himself, both priest and victim, should offer himself daily through the ministry of priests—not indeed in one corner of the earth, but throughout the whole world, in accordance with the prophecy of Joel, whose truth and certainty daily experience makes plain.

For from the time this sacrifice was instituted, this victim has never ceased to be offered throughout the entire world. Although the rite has differed, the reality and truth itself have always remained unshaken. It is difficult for the whole world to agree upon the same rites and ceremonies, although the faith itself cannot be weakened by diversity of rites.

This diversity, however, appears to have been abolished over many past centuries and in many regions, especially in the West, which long ago adopted the Roman order for celebrating Mass.

An attempt had once been made to do this in Spain. For Profuturus, bishop of Braga, had received from the Apostolic See the method of celebrating Mass according to the Roman order. Under his successor Lucretius, at the First Council of Braga, held in the year of Christ 561 according to García, or 563 according to Baronius, it was decreed in canon 22:

> “That Masses be celebrated according to the same order: Profuturus, formerly bishop of this metropolitan Church, received a written directive from the authority of the Apostolic See.”

This was, of course, throughout Galicia, the province in which that council was held. The later constitution was nevertheless superseded by the Mozarabic Mass, which remained in use throughout Spain until the time of Pope Gregory VII, who abolished it and ordered the Spaniards to follow the order of the Roman Mass.

Gaul, on the other hand, once had its own rite for celebrating Mass, until, through the diligence of King Pepin, that rite was abolished and the Roman order was adopted. This is clear from the letter of the Emperor Charles the Bald to the clergy of Ravenna:

> “For until the time of our great-grandfather Pepin, the churches of Gaul celebrated differently from the Roman and Milanese Church.”

The same was later provided in Book V of the *Capitularies of the Emperors Charles and Louis*, chapter 219:

> “Let each priest celebrate Mass according to the Roman order, with sandals.”

Charles the Bald confirms this in the letter just cited:

> “But we are to follow the Roman Church in the celebration of Masses.”

And rightly so, for the Roman Church is the mother of the others, which all the rest ought to imitate and obey.

Accordingly, when I examined more attentively the dignity of the Roman Mass, it occurred to me that I should illuminate it to the best of my ability, especially when I had the opportunity through the excellent and most ancient Book of the Sacraments of Saint Gregory the Pope, commonly called the Missal of Saint Eligius. I was further impelled to this by the requests of a certain friend, who earnestly begged me to publish this book and not allow so great a treasure to remain hidden any longer, to the detriment of the Christian religion.

This book therefore belongs to the library of the monastery of Saint Peter of Corbie in the farthest part of Picardy. It is commonly said once to have been the Missal of Saint Eligius, bishop of Noyon. For on the back of the same Codex is written as follows:

> “Missal of Saint Eligius.”

Yet certain items found in the same Codex seem to contradict the claim that it belonged to him, such as the feasts of Saint Projectus and Saint Leo II, who flourished several years after the death of Saint Eligius.

I therefore think that the Book of the Sacraments of Saint Gregory I, the Pope, was once sent to Saint Eligius by some Roman pontiff, but that it was later copied, with a few additions made to it, and retained the name of Saint Eligius because of the exemplar from which it was taken. Or at least it must be said that this book is called Saint Eligius’s because it once belonged to the monastery of Saint Eligius at Noyon. Since this is not entirely certain, however, I would not dare assert it.

Whatever the case may be, it is certain that the manuscript Codex is extremely ancient. Its script approaches in appearance that of another manuscript Book of the Sacraments, once written by a certain priest named Rodradus, who lived in the year of the Lord 853 and of whom we shall speak below. Yet the script of the present book appears older, as does the form of the book itself.

Its antiquity is further commended by the fact that it contains fewer feasts than the other Sacramentaries and manuscript Orders in our possession, and than the printed editions based on the Vatican Codex. No one is unaware that, as time passed, feasts and solemnities increased.

The same antiquity of this Codex can be inferred from ancient writers. In the Codex of Saint Eligius there are five Sundays of Advent. The one farther from the Nativity of Christ is called the fifth; the one following it is called the fourth, and so on.

But Amalarius Fortunatus, in Book III of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 40, testifies that this was the arrangement of the Sundays of Advent in ancient Missals, so that they contained the wording:

> “The fifth week before the Nativity of the Lord.”

In the same Codex of Saint Eligius it is written:

> “Who lives and reigns with you, God.”

This sequence of words belongs to the most ancient exemplars, as the *Micrologus*, chapter 6, teaches concerning ecclesiastical observances:

> “It should be known that in the very customary conclusion, ‘through our Lord,’ the Roman Order and the most ancient exemplars explain the words as ‘who lives and reigns with you, God,’ and so forth.”

And indeed, a very learned man who recently inspected the Vatican and the more distinguished libraries of Rome testified to me that he had seen there no Book of the Sacraments of Saint Gregory that could compete in antiquity with this Missal of Saint Eligius.

It also appears that this book was written before the empire of Charlemagne, since in it there is no mention of the emperor, whereas such a mention can be found in other manuscript Books of the Sacraments in our possession, about which we shall speak immediately.

## [Column 0017]

These words commend the authority and dignity of the book: “Copied from an authentic book of the library of the Cubiculum.” They are also found in the Sacramentary of the same Saint Gregory, which was printed from the Vatican Library under Pope Clement VIII, under the care and scholarship of the Reverend and most learned Father Angelo Rocca, papal sacristan. For they indicate that this Codex was copied from a book once kept in some chamber, or secretarial archive, of the Basilica of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, together with other sacred books which the Roman pontiff used for the divine offices.

We have therefore furnished this book with notes and observations. For this purpose the following principal aids were available to us, especially several excellent manuscript Sacramentaries. The first is from the library of the distinguished monastery of Saint Remigius at Rheims. It was written by a certain Lantbert, priest and solitary, at the command of a certain Gaudelgaud, priest, monk, and dean, as Lantbert himself explains in his prologue—which I would have transcribed here had not the frequent solecisms with which it abounds prevented me. In our observations we have called it the Rheims Codex.

On the other page of the Codex, opposite the prologue, appears a portrait of Godelgaud himself, dressed in a chasuble depicted according to the ancient manner, with the middle of his head shaved and his chin circularly shaven as though close-cropped, holding a closed book in his left hand. Around his head is the inscription: “GAUDELGAUDUS PRESBYTER,” “GAUDELGAUD, PRIEST.” On the facing page stands [Note: [Col. 0017] These portraits are reproduced at cols. 559 and 560. Mabillon also gives a portrait of Gaudelgaud in *Annales Benedictini*, vol. II, p. 153.] a portrait of Pope Saint Gregory, with a chasuble and tonsure of the same form as Gaudelgaud’s, and a dalmatic with sufficiently long and broad sleeves according to the ancient style, and a white archiepiscopal pallium without crosses. He too holds a book in his left hand, and around his head is the inscription:

**ϹΚϹ ΓΡΕΓΩΡΙΟϹ ΠΑΠΑ**

that is, “Saint Gregory the Pope.”

On the following page stands a portrait of Saint Remigius, bishop of Rheims, with the same tonsure, pallium, and attire as Saint Gregory. He likewise holds a book in his left hand, and around his head is the inscription:

**ϹΚϹ ΡΕΜΙΓΙΟϹ ΕΡΚ . ΟΡΒ. ΡΕΜΡ.**

that is, “Saint Remigius, Bishop of the City of Rheims.”

At the end of the prologue he says that he began this work on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, in the sixth indiction, and placed the colophon on the tenth day before the Kalends of August, in the eighth indiction, in the thirty-first year:

“OF THE REIGN OF OUR LORD CHARLES, MOST GLORIOUS KING OF THE FRANKS.”

But since such indictions cannot correspond to Charles the Bald or Charles the Simple, I think that this book was written in the time of Charlemagne. For the sixth indiction, in which this book was begun, falls in the thirty-first year of the reign of Charlemagne, who began his reign in the year 768, as is clear from Einhard and from the Life of that same Charles preserved by Pithou. Thus the writer of this book seems to have used a hyperbaton, so that Charlemagne’s thirty-first year is to be referred to the sixth indiction in which the book was begun, rather than to the eighth in which it was completed.

At the end of this Codex are two images painted in priestly attire, without inscriptions. They appear to be portraits of the scribe Lantbert himself. The following page is written in Greek letters, though it contains not Greek but a very crude Latin composition, packed with solecisms. In the narrative itself he declares that he was the scribe and painter of this Codex, that he began it in year 29 and completed it in year 31 of the reign of Charles, king of the Franks, on the same Kalends as above, with the indictions omitted. He then discusses the difficulty of writing and finally asks for the reader’s prayers. He consistently uses the letter *O* for *V*; thus, above, in the portrait of Saint Remigius, he wrote *ORBIS* for *URBIS*. Finally, on the facing page, which is the last page of the book, these words may be found:

“This book of Saint Remigius, Pontiff of Rheims, is enjoyed by the brothers of that place to this day. Hincmar, Abbot.”

The second manuscript Codex [Note: [Col. 0017] For a specimen of this Codex’s script, see *De re diplomatica*, vol. II, p. 363.] is called the Codex of the priest Rodrad, who was its scribe. It belongs to the library of the aforementioned monastery of Saint Peter at Corbie. He flourished in the year of Christ 853, for in his preface he says that he was ordained a priest in that same year by Hilmerad, bishop. This Hilmerad was bishop of Amiens, as may be seen from the Councils held at Tours IV in 849, Soissons II in 853, and Verberie in that same year, all of which he attended.

To make the matter clearer, we shall reproduce two brief prefaces from this Codex, the first in prose and the second in verse, as follows:

> I, Rodrad, in need of the mercy of God, overcome by the commands of Bishop Hilmerad and bound by four excommunications imposed by episcopal authority, tremblingly undertook the office of the priestly ministry on the fourth day before the Nones of March, in the year 853 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the first indiction, with an epact of seven and a concurrent of seven, at the Paschal term, on the fourth day before the Kalends of April. Whoever reads this brief record of my ordination and, through this Codex, recites the consecration of the Lord’s Body, aided, I ask, by your prayers, may I be worthy to present a priesthood dedicated to Christ and to attain the prize of the heavenly vision.

The second brief preface, which is metrical, is as follows:

> I, Hrodradus, an unworthy fosterling of the saints,  
> Composed this book, to be dedicated in Christ’s honor,  
> While the victim of the Lamb worthy of the sacred offices  
> Is piously sacrificed upon the holy altar.  
>   
> Though unworthy, deprived of the endowment of good merits,  
> Base beneath the excessive burden of sin,  
> May at least the devotion of this undertaking grant me favor  
> With the King on high, before whose judgment  
> We all bear the rewards deserved according to our merit.  
>   
> You also, blessed priest of Christ,  
> Who perhaps will make use of this Codex,  
> I humbly ask to remember me  
> Amid the solemnities of the sacred rites,  
> And by your prayers reconcile God to me,  
> Whose heavenly gifts you taste in service.

This book is divided chiefly into two parts. The first contains what Rodrad himself believes to have been collected solely by Saint Gregory, except for certain passages which, he says, he struck through with virgules for the sake of distinction. The second contains material which, he says, Saint Gregory omitted and which Rodrad himself collected from works carefully written by the most approved and learned men, adding prefaces and episcopal blessings. It also includes what is absent from the aforementioned work of Blessed Gregory concerning the institution of the lower orders in the Church. Thus he speaks in his preface, after the first part of his book:

> Up to this point, the preceding little Sacramentary is acknowledged to have been issued by Blessed Gregory, except for those which the reader, through careful attention, will find struck through by virgules placed before them in Lent. For, as we have learned from the report of certain persons, the apostolic lord entirely abstains from stations on those same days, because he is wearied by observing stations on the other weekdays of the week; on those days he rests, so that, free from popular disturbance, he may more freely distribute alms to the poor and attend to external affairs. It is beyond doubt that the Mass appointed for the feast of the same Blessed Gregory, struck through by virgules placed before it, was inserted into this work by his successors out of affection, or rather veneration for him, etc.

This passage is found in Pamelius, who reports the same preface under the name of Grimold, abbot, even after the earlier portion which Rodrad says belongs to Saint Gregory.

This preface is followed by the sequence of chapters of the second part, which is precisely the same in Pamelius. Thus, in this arrangement, the book claims two authors for itself: Rodrad the priest and Grimold the abbot. Yet there is no great controversy here. For [Col. 0019] although the method of both books is the same, and one borrowed a preface from the other, there is nevertheless a considerable difference between them.

First, leaving aside the Prayers or Collects in which the books of Rodrad and Grimold sometimes disagree, in the first part of Rodrad’s Codex one finds material concerning the institution of the higher orders, except for certain rubrics of which there is no mention anywhere in Grimold’s Codex.

Second, in the second part of Rodrad’s book are all the matters concerning the conferral of the lower orders, together with their rubrics. Nothing similar to this can be found in Grimold’s Codex, although his preface contains these words: “Also that which is not found in the aforesaid Codex of Blessed Gregory concerning the institution of the lower orders in the Church.”

Third, in Rodrad’s Codex, on Holy Saturday, the rites preceding baptism are described, but more briefly than in Grimold’s Codex; the rest are relegated to the second part, though certain items are omitted toward the end.

Fourth, near the end of the first part of Rodrad’s Codex there is a baptismal rite for the sick, along with certain other material lacking in the Codex of Grimold the abbot.

Fifth, in Rodrad’s second part there are episcopal blessings for nearly all the feasts of the saints. For Sundays, however, they extend only through Pentecost, inclusively. In Grimold’s Codex, by contrast, episcopal blessings for Sundays extend through the eleventh Sunday after Pentecost, inclusively; for the solemnities of the saints there are fewer, namely, for the feast of the Holy Cross, the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, the Nativity of the apostles Peter and Paul, the Nativity of Saint Mary, the Martyrdom of Saint John the Baptist, and the Commemoration of All Saints.

Sixth, Rodrad’s second part contains prefaces absent from Grimold’s Codex, although Grimold mentions them in his own preface. Pamelius, however, who first published Grimold’s book, added many prefaces from the Sacramentary of Alcuin.

Finally, in Rodrad’s Codex, appended to the second part as though in the manner of an appendix, are many Masses with apologies and a rite for administering extreme unction; none of these appears in Grimold’s Codex.

From all this it is easily concluded that Rodrad’s book is distinct from Grimold’s Codex, and that these authors wrote separately and each compiled his own Sacramentary. But who this Grimold was is not sufficiently established. In the Life of Saint Notker the Stammerer, preserved by Henricus Canisius in volume VI of *Antiquae Lectiones*, mention is made of a certain Grimald who was abbot and canon of the celebrated monastery of Saint Gall and archchaplain of Emperor Louis the Pious; but whether this man is the same as Grimold remains to be investigated.

But, to return to the same book of Rodrad, if we trust the Micrologus, Master Albinus, commonly called Alcuin, seems to have compiled a similar book. For he says in chapter 6, *On Ecclesiastical Observances*:

> The same Albinus nevertheless produced a work in the holy Church that ought not to be despised. For he is said to have collected the Gregorian Prayers in the Sacramentary books, adding a few others which he indicated should be marked with an obelus; then he collected other Prayers, or Prefaces, which, although not Gregorian, were nevertheless suitable for ecclesiastical celebration, as the prologue testifies—a prologue which he placed in the middle of the same book, after the Gregorian Prayers.

These words clearly indicate that Albinus wrote a Sacramentary similar to the Codices of Rodrad and Grimold. For the preface noted above in both Codices is placed in the middle of the work, between the first and second parts.

Nor can there be a scribal error, as Pamelius maintains, whereby “Albinus” was written for “Grimoldus.” Since we see that Rodrad’s book differs from Grimold’s Codex, it is possible that Albinus too compiled his own.

But I am surprised that this distinction, or division, of the offices and Masses occurred to these authors, so that one part seems to belong to Pope Saint Gregory, with a few exceptions, while the other does not belong to him at all. For in the Life of Saint Gregory written by John the Deacon, when he discusses the Sacramentary collected by Saint Gregory, it is stated simply:

> But after removing much from the Gelasian Codex concerning the solemnities of the Masses, altering a little, and adding certain things, he compressed it into the volume of a single little book.

Walafrid Strabo likewise states this in book *On Ecclesiastical Matters*, chapter 22.

Nor is it likely that the Gelasian Codex, even if it required correction in certain respects, was so mutilated that it did not contain the Masses to be said throughout the entire annual cycle. Even if this were granted, it is not credible that Saint Gregory, who revised the Gelasian book by removing some things and adding others, would have left the book of Masses celebrated throughout the year so mutilated that most of the Sunday Masses—or the Masses that ought to be said on Sundays—were absent from it.

For, according to the teaching of the writers cited above, in this Codex of Gregory the Sunday Masses falling between the Nativity of the Lord and Advent, except for Septuagesima, Sexagesima, and Quinquagesima, Easter and its octave, and Pentecost, are not Saint Gregory’s. This is absurd. For it is incredible that in the time of Gelasius and Saint Gregory no Masses were customarily celebrated on those Sundays. If they were celebrated, let an explanation be given why they would not have been written in the Codices of Gelasius and Saint Gregory.

Our opinion is confirmed by the title of the Sacramentary book, both in printed editions and in our manuscript Codices, indeed even in the Codices of Rodrad and Grimold. It reads as follows:

> Here begins the book of the Sacramentary, expounded from the annual cycle by Pope Saint Gregory, concerning how the Roman Mass is celebrated.

The truth of this title cannot stand together with the opinion of our opponents, since in their Codices the greater part of the Sunday Masses is absent.

Our opinion is supported by the manuscript Codices of Saint Eligius and Rheims, which are older than the volumes of Rodrad and Grimold and do not admit such a separation of the Gregorian Codex. It is also confirmed by the manuscript Codex of Ratold, the abbot, which will be discussed shortly, although it is later than the Codices of Rodrad and perhaps Grimold. It does not recognize such a division, nor does the Sacramentary book published under Clement VIII from the Vatican Library.

The third manuscript Sacramentary [Note: [Col. 0019] A specimen of this book’s script may be seen in *De re diplomatica*, p. 367.] which we used also belongs to the library of Corbie. We designate it by the name of Ratold, abbot, because it was written at his command, as is clear from the calendar of the same book, in which, on the Ides of March, the following distich is found:

> The holy remembrance of Lord Abbot Ratold stands here,  
> The man who indeed had this book written.

Ratold was the twenty-sixth abbot of Corbie, and died in the year of the Lord 986, on the Ides of March. It is therefore clear that this book was written before that year.

This Codex is excellent and extremely accurate. It contains more ceremonies, feast days, episcopal blessings, and prefaces than the others because it is more recent.

To these Codices was added a manuscript book from the Tilius Library. It is a Roman Ordo, a copy of which was supplied to me by the distinguished John Tilius. There are nevertheless certain items in it that do not occur in the Roman Ordo, just as certain things found in the Roman Ordo are absent from this Tilius Codex.

This book lacks its beginning, since its first gathering has been torn away. It seems once to have belonged to the Church of Sées in Normandy, under the metropolitan Church of Rouen. For in this Codex, where the orders are discussed, the following words occur: “The Church of Sées and episcopal authority grant you …” The Church of Sées and the Sagiensis Church are the same, and Sées was also called *Salarium*, as is clear from Orderic Vitalis. In book VIII of his *Ecclesiastical History*, when he mentions Serlo, formerly abbot of the monastery of Saint Evroul, as bishop of Sées, he says in book XII of the same History, in the epitaph of Roger, who succeeded Serlo as abbot of Saint Evroul:

> Once Serlo had become bishop at Sées, this man  
> Took up the governance of the monastery of Saint Evroul.

And below:

> In the same month, after the venerable Serlo had governed the Church of Sées for thirty-two years, etc.

Moreover, in this Tilius Codex there is frequent mention of the illustrious martyrs Saints Gervasius and Protasius. In the Commemoration of the Saints, after the Lord’s Prayer, the words “and Andrew” are followed by:

> “and also your blessed martyrs Gervasius and Protasius.”

This was because the Church of Sées was dedicated under the title of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, as is evident from Orderic Vitalis in the cited book and from William of Jumièges, book VII of his *History*, chapters 13 and 15.

Near the end of this Codex is a succession of the Roman pontiffs, ending with Sergius III. A chronicle follows, beginning with the origin of the world. At its end are these words:

> And from Charles and Carloman until Charles there were four years; then Lord Charles alone assumed the kingdom and, with God’s protection, governs it happily up to the present year, which is the forty-second year of his reign. The total from the origin of the world to the present year is 4,761 years.

The same Codex contains a succession of the kings of the Franks, at the end of which the following is written:

> After King Robert died, his son Henry, still a young man, suffered many plots and disasters from the princes of the kingdom. Strengthened by God’s help, he subjected all his enemies to his servitude.

From this it is clear that the Codex was written while that Henry who is called the First was reigning in France. He began his reign in the year of the Lord 1032, according to Sigebert’s *Chronicle*. The form of the letters in this book also seems to support this conclusion.

We also used a very ancient manuscript Roman Ordo from the library of Corbie. But since it is torn for the most part, we were able to draw little from it.

Nor was I helped insignificantly by a certain manuscript Ordo from the library of the monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, situated near Paris, where, with God’s help, I composed this present little work. The Codex appears sufficiently ancient and to have been written five hundred years ago. At its end is an order for anointing the sick, but its script differs from that of the entire work and is not so old, since it scarcely seems to exceed three hundred years. It follows a more recent practice of extreme unction and has a deprecatory form resembling the modern one, not the indicative form recognized by the older manuscript Codices.

In addition, the most learned John Le Prevost, canon and distinguished librarian of the Church of Rouen, sent me collections from two ancient manuscript Sacramentaries or Pontificals preserved in that Church’s archive. One of them seems to be English, as he himself thinks; this is evident from the English saints frequently named in the book and from the coronation of the kings of England contained in the Codex. The other seems formerly to have belonged to the Church of Rheims, because in the litany of the coronation of kings found there, the following saints of the Church of Rheims are named: Nicasius, Remigius, Sixtus, Sinicius, and Rigobertus.

I also used a manuscript Codex given to me from the library of the monastery of Saint Remigius, founded at Rheims, written around the year 1000. Besides much other material irrelevant to our purpose, it contains two rites: one for imposing penance and the other for visiting the sick. These brought me considerable illumination for explaining these two sacraments.

The manuscript Martyrology of Saint Jerome from the library of Corbie also contributed no little assistance. To state frankly what I think of it, it does not seem pure, since it appears to contain many names of saints who lived after Saint Jerome, added by the scribe himself, who was certainly a monk of Corbie. For it records the translation of Saint Praecordius, whose body is preserved in that monastery; the death of Theofredus, the first abbot of Corbie; the death of Ratold, abbot of the same monastery; the dedication of the church of that place; and the dedication of several chapels still visible at Corbie.

Nevertheless, the Codex is ancient and seems to have been written six hundred years ago. Other manuscript Martyrologies and Calendars were also added to it, and they likewise served as guides for us in this work.

Nor should the Roman Ordo already printed [Note: [Col. 0021] On the Roman Ordo, see the preliminary commentary to it in Mabillon, *Museum Italicum*, vol. II.] be omitted here. We also carefully compared it with the Codex of Saint Eligius.

Honorius of Autun, in his book *On Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*, makes a certain Bernold, a priest of the Church of Constance, the author of the Roman Ordo. Bernold flourished under Emperor Henry IV. Honorius says:

> Bernold, priest of the Church of Constance, composed the Roman Ordo under Henry IV.

This does not seem entirely true. For this Roman Ordo is older than Bernold himself and than Emperor Henry IV. Indeed, the Roman Ordo is cited in the manuscript Sacramentary of Ratold, abbot, discussed above, on Maundy Thursday, where the reconciliation of penitents is treated, in these words:

> And let him deliver a sermon both to the people and to the penitents, as the Roman Ordo commands.

This book was written before the year 986, when Bernold had not yet been born.

Isaac, bishop of Langres, also mentions it in canon 35. He flourished in the time of Emperor Charles the Bald, long before Bernold was born:

> And there, he says, let them be reconciled by the bishop canonically and in due order, as is contained in the Sacramentary and the Roman Ordo.

Amalarius, who flourished in the time of Emperor Louis the Pious, also cites it in book I of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 12:

> One item remains in the Roman Ordo, where it is still prescribed that from Thursday until Holy Saturday the altars should be bare.

This is found in the Roman Ordo, on Maundy Thursday:

> From Vespers on this day, however, let the altars be bare until the morning of Holy Saturday.

Therefore Bernold cannot properly be called the author of the Roman Ordo, but only its restorer, who revised it by removing and adding certain things according to the practice he observed in the Church in his own time.

This is sufficiently credible, since the Roman Ordo that was printed long ago is not pure, because in many respects it falls short of the ancient Sacramentary books. Indeed, the book itself, near the end of the arrangement of the Mass for Holy Saturday, cites the Roman Ordo and then departs from its rite. It says:

> Then the deacon says, “The Mass is ended,” according to the Roman Ordo; but the custom of the Church does not permit this on account of Vespers.

On this night nothing is done among the Romans concerning the vespertine assembly, either before or after the Mass. Among us, however, one of the schola, whoever has been instructed to do so, begins the Alleluia in place of the antiphon at Vespers; and while they are receiving Communion, the psalm “Praise the Lord, all nations,” etc., is sung rapidly in place of Vespers, according to the present custom, which afterward also prevailed in the Roman Church.

I also carefully compared this Codex of Saint Eligius with the printed Sacramentary that was issued under Clement VIII from the Vatican Library. I found a considerable difference between them, although they agree in many respects.

For the manuscript Codex of the Vatican Library from which the printed copy was transcribed does not seem to be especially ancient, since it contains certain things that do not bear the marks of antiquity, such as numerous feasts that came into use long afterward. Nor are any episcopal blessings found in it, although they were still customary in the time of Honorius of Autun, the author of the book entitled *Gemma animae*, in which their rationale and method are described. He lived in the year 1120, according to Trithemius; indeed, episcopal blessings are still celebrated in certain Churches.

[Col. 0023] This is nevertheless surprising, because in that printed Vatican edition, on the feast of Saint Paul, it says: “The Preface and Blessing are as above, as in the Codex of Saint Eligius.”

Hence I believe that the manuscript Codex was indeed copied from another very ancient exemplar, but that certain things were partly removed and partly added by the copyist, according to what he saw to suit the practice of his own time. He deleted the feast of Saint Mary at the Martyrs, which had been abolished in his time. For since he includes the feast of All Saints, which was instituted long after the feast of Saint Mary at the Martyrs, this shows that he did not live before the institution of that feast but after the abolition of the former one, when only the feast of All Saints was celebrated. All our manuscript Sacramentaries establish that the latter feast had long been celebrated while the feast of Saint Mary at the Martyrs was still in force.

Although certain items found in the printed Sacramentary from the Vatican Library are absent from the Codex of Saint Eligius, the latter is nevertheless richer, as I said in the prospectus of the book; for it contains far more than the other and is of much older character.

Moreover, I recorded, illustrated, and explained in my observations the more noteworthy features of these three manuscript Sacramentaries—those of Rodrad, Rheims, and Ratold—especially those concerning the structure of the Sacramentary and the celebration of feasts. Whatever was rarer in the Tilius Codex I carefully transferred to the same observations after comparing it with the Codex of Saint Eligius.

The materials included in the appendix, extracted from our observations, I relegated to the end of the book under the title of an appendix, so that they would not lie buried within them.

In these observations I proceeded in such a way as to restore, as far as lay within my power, the practices of the present day to the ancient rites of the Church. I was nevertheless far removed from those who strive to refer all ecclesiastical institutions and rites, including more recent ones, to the age of the apostles, “with every oar and sail,” as the saying goes. I have always judged nothing more absurd than this.

Such men do not hesitate to do violence to the words and judgments of the ancient Fathers and councils, provided that they can give some color and cosmetic appearance to their follies, forged in the workshop of their own minds. They wish not to follow the mind of antiquity but to drag it toward the fogs of their own foreheads, not without grave injury to ecclesiastical antiquity and truth. They fail to observe that ecclesiastical traditions were not everywhere and at all times the same. Consequently, they confuse and corrupt everything; and in this they think they are serving the authority of the Church admirably, when by this manner of writing they utterly tear it apart.

No one so opposed to all judgment that he does not know that councils, bishops, and supreme pontiffs—whom God appointed stewards of his mysteries—can abolish certain ancient practices and establish new ones, whenever, guided by the impulse of the Holy Spirit, they judge such measures advantageous to the utility and dignity of the Church.

Finally, I carefully compared the rites and ceremonies of both Churches, Latin and Greek, with one another, and diligently noted, as far as I could, where they agreed and where they differed.

But so that no one may be offended that I said the world is full of wandering priests, I declare that I did not mean honest priests, who either have fixed sees or reside in Churches and parishes. I meant only those who wander through cities, *ἀπειρόκαλοι* (*apeirokaloi*, “uncultivated and ignorant men”), utterly unworthy of the priesthood.

No one should be offended, either, by what I noted concerning a certain rite of extreme unction in which one person anoints while another pronounces the words, when I said that this supports the opinion of those who say that baptism is valid if one person pours the water or immerses the candidate while another pronounces the words. I did not say this because I hold that opinion, which I do not fail to recognize is commonly rejected.

This is what I wished to explain to you, candid reader. If anything in these little works of mine pleases you, use it gladly; if you find any blemishes or stains, excuse them with fairness and goodwill.

[Col. 0023]

# A NOTABLE TESTIMONY CONCERNING THE SACRAMENTARY BOOK

*(From the second volume of Peter Lambecius’s Imperial Library, chapter 5, p. 298, no. 14.)*

The second Codex of the most august Imperial Library, pertaining to the life and deeds of Emperor Charlemagne, is among the manuscript Latin theological Codices, no. 360, and contains chiefly the first book of the Sacramentary of Pope Saint Gregory the Great.

I said that this Codex pertains to the history of Charlemagne’s life because it is the very book which Pope Adrian I sent as a gift to Charlemagne at his request, as may be seen from letter 82 of the collection of ancient letters prepared through Charlemagne’s own care and scholarship. There Pope Adrian mentions this Codex in the following words:

> Concerning the Sacramentary arranged by our holy predecessor, the divinely inspired Pope Gregory, Paul the Grammarian requested it from us some time ago on your behalf; and, according to the tradition of our holy Church, we have sent it to your royal Excellence through John, monk and abbot of the city of Ravenna. Since we desire the same apostle of God and your protector for your royal and unconquered Excellence, we ask and beseech him that, always accompanying you everywhere, he may make you victorious over all barbarian nations, and that, together with our spiritual daughter, the most excellent queen, and with the noble offspring of your lineage, he may grant, through his intercession, that you who reign in this world for a long age may reign without end in eternal life with all the saints. May heavenly grace preserve your Excellence unharmed.

Thus far the conclusion of the letter of Pope Adrian I, in which mention is made of the Sacramentary book of Saint Gregory the Great sent to Charlemagne.

The title of the same book in the manuscript Codex itself reads as follows:

> IN THE NAME OF THE LORD. HERE BEGINS THE BOOK OF THE SACRAMENTARY, EXPOUNDED FROM THE CYCLE OF THE YEAR, EDITED BY SAINT GREGORY, ROMAN POPE, COPIED FROM THE AUTHENTIC BOOK OF THE LIBRARY OF THE CUBICULUM.

[Col. 0025]

# THE SACRAMENTARY BOOK OF SAINT GREGORY THE GREAT, ROMAN PONTIFF

## In the name of the Lord

[Note: [Col. 0025] Hugo Menardus’s notes on the *Liber sacramentorum* have been printed by Migne as a separate document in cols. 263–582. Each number in parentheses in the text of the *Liber sacramentorum* refers to the corresponding note in that separate document.] (C,S)*

**(1 [Note: [Col. 0025] The numbers enclosed in parentheses refer the reader to the notes of Dom Hugo Menardus, placed at the end of the Sacramentary book. Editor.])** This book **(2)** of the Sacramentary [Note: [Col. 0025C] By “sacraments” are understood either all the sacraments of the New Law—in which sense theologians publish treatises on the Sacraments—or chiefly the three sacraments that were formerly received together, namely baptism, confirmation, and the Eucharist, concerning which six books *On the Sacraments* were written and included among the works of Ambrose, vol. II of the new edition—or solely the sacrament of the Eucharist, which is designated by the plural number in nearly every Mass, both because of the twofold matter of bread and wine and because it contains the body and blood of Christ. See Menardus’s note 2.] expounded from the annual cycle [Note: [Col. 0025C] In the Theoderician Codex II and in the Vallicellian Codex this title reads: “Here begins the book of the Sacramentary from the annual cycle, edited by Saint Gregory, Roman Pope.”] and edited by Saint Gregory, Roman Pope, **(3)** copied from the authentic book of the library of the Cubiculum [Note: [Col. 0025C] See Menardus’s note 3, to which may be added what is read concerning Saint Leo I in the Roman Pontifical: “He also established and added over the tombs of the apostles … [Col. 0026C] guardians called chamberlains.”], describing **(4)** how the Roman Mass is celebrated, as follows:

[Col. 0025A]

**1.** First **(5)**, at the Introit, an Antiphon, whatever has been prescribed for the appointed seasons, whether feast days or ordinary days.

**(6)** Then: “Lord, have mercy.”

It is also said, **(7)** “Glory to God in the highest.” **(8)** If the celebrant is a bishop, this is said only on Sunday or on feast days. **(9)** By priests it is not said at all, except on Easter alone. [Note: [Col. 0026C] The litany belongs to mourning. Hence Gregory reproves John, bishop of Ravenna, because during the litanies—that is, in the season of ashes and sackcloth—he wore the pallium ostentatiously. See book III, letter 2, indiction 11, formerly letter 54, now 56. The same was the reason why, during the litany, they refrained from the hymn “Glory to God in the highest” and from the Alleluia.] When the litany is being performed, neither “Glory to God in the highest” nor the Alleluia is sung.

**(10)** Afterward the Prayer is said; then follows **(11)** the Apostolic reading.

**(12)** Likewise, the Gradual, or the Alleluia.

Afterward **(13)** the Gospel is read; then **(14)** the Offertory follows, and the Prayer over the offerings is said.

When this has been completed, the priest says in a loud voice:

> Throughout all ages of ages.

**R.** Amen.

He says:

> The Lord be with you.

**R.** And with your spirit.

He says: **(15)**

> Lift up your hearts.

**R.** **(16)** We have them with the Lord.

He says: **2 (17)**

> Let us give thanks to the Lord our God.

**R.** **(18)** It is worthy and just.

> It is truly worthy and just, right and beneficial to salvation, that we should always and everywhere give you thanks, holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God, through Christ our Lord. Through him your Majesty is **(20) praised** by angels, adored by dominions, feared by powers; the heavens and the virtues of the heavens, together with the blessed seraphim, celebrate you with united exultation. With them we ask that you command our voices also to be admitted, as we say in humble confession:
>
> **(21) HOLY, HOLY, HOLY**, Lord God of Sabaoth. Heaven and earth are full of your glory. Hosanna in the highest.
>
> **(22)** Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.
>
> **(23)** Hosanna in the highest. [Note: [Col. 0026C] In the earlier Theoderician Codex, before “Therefore, most merciful Father,” and so forth, several Prayers are found. We have included only one of them after Menardus’s note 23.]

**THEREFORE**, most merciful Father, through Jesus Christ, your Son, our Lord, we humbly ask and entreat you to accept and bless these gifts, these offerings, these holy and unblemished sacrifices [Note: In the manuscripts of Theoderic and Gemeticus, three crosses are marked in this way at these words: these gifts † these offerings † these holy † unblemished sacrifices.]: first, those which we offer you for your holy catholic Church, which may you deign to grant peace, guard, unite, and govern throughout the whole world, together with your servant, our pope N., and our king N., and all who are orthodox and who cultivate the catholic and apostolic faith.

[Col. 0026B] Remember, O Lord, your servants, men and women, N. and N., and all standing around, whose faith is known to you and whose devotion is manifest. They offer you this sacrifice of praise for themselves and all their own, for the redemption of their souls, for the hope of their salvation and safety; to you, the eternal, living, and true God, they render their vows [Note: In the second Theoderic manuscript: “Remember … and all my relatives, and those whose alms we have received, or who have confessed to me, as well as those whose names are written upon your holy altar.”].

Communicating together and venerating the memory, first, of the glorious ever-virgin Mary, Mother of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ; and also of your blessed apostles and martyrs: Peter, Paul, Andrew, James, John, Thomas, James, Philip, Bartholomew, Matthew, Simon, and Thaddeus; Linus, Cletus, Clement, Sixtus, Cornelius, [Col. 0027A] Cyprian, Lawrence, Chrysogonus, John and Paul, Cosmas and Damian, Hilary, Martin, Augustine, Gregory, Jerome, Benedict, and all your saints. Grant that by their merits and prayers we may be defended in all things by the help of your protection. Through Christ our Lord.

Therefore, O Lord, we ask you graciously to accept this offering of our service and also of your entire household; and to order our days in your peace, to rescue us from eternal damnation, and to command that we be numbered among your chosen flock. Through Christ our Lord.

May you, O God, deign to make this offering, we ask, blessed, enrolled, ratified, reasonable, and acceptable in every respect, [Col. 0027B] so that it may become for us the †body and †blood of your most beloved Son, our Lord God Jesus Christ.

Who, on the day before he suffered, took bread into his holy and venerable hands; and, with eyes raised to heaven, to you, God his almighty Father, giving you thanks, † blessed it, broke it, and gave it to his disciples, saying: Take and eat, all of you, from this:

**FOR THIS IS MY BODY.**

In like manner, after supper had ended, taking also this glorious chalice into his holy and venerable hands, likewise giving you thanks, he † blessed it and gave it to his disciples, saying: Take and drink from it, all of you:

**FOR THIS IS THE CHALICE OF MY BLOOD, OF THE NEW AND ETERNAL COVENANT, THE MYSTERY [Col. 0027C] OF FAITH, WHICH WILL BE POURED OUT FOR YOU AND FOR MANY FOR THE FORGIVENESS OF SINS.**

Whenever you do these things, you shall do them in remembrance of me.

Therefore, O Lord, we, your servants, and also your holy people, remembering the blessed passion of Christ, your Son, our God, as well as his resurrection from the dead and also his glorious ascension into heaven, offer to your glorious Majesty from your gifts and endowments, a †pure victim, a †holy victim, an †unblemished victim, the †holy bread of eternal life, and the chalice of everlasting †salvation.

Upon these offerings may you deign to look with a favorable and serene countenance and accept them, just as you deigned to accept the gifts of your righteous servant Abel, and the sacrifice of our patriarch Abraham, and that which your high priest Melchizedek offered to you, [Col. 0027D] a holy sacrifice, an unblemished victim [Note: From the *Pontifical Book*, in the Life of Saint Leo I, inserted in volume III of the Councils, col. 1290 and following: Saint Leo established that “a holy sacrifice, an unblemished victim” should be said within the action of the sacrifice.].

We humbly ask you, almighty God: command that these offerings be carried by the hands of your angel to your sublime [Col. 0028A] altar, into the presence of your divine Majesty, so that all of us who, by participation in this altar, have received the most holy † body and † blood of your Son may be filled with every heavenly blessing and grace. Through Christ our Lord.

**(69) Over the diptychs.**—(70) Remember also, O Lord, your servants, men and women, N., who have gone before us with the sign of faith and sleep in the sleep of peace. For them, O Lord, and for all who rest in Christ, we ask that you grant a place of refreshment, light, and peace [Note: In the Pamelian and Swedish Queen manuscripts: “through Christ our Lord.”]. Through the same Christ our Lord.

And to us sinners, your servants, who hope in the abundance of your mercies, deign to grant some share and fellowship with your holy apostles and martyrs: with John, [Col. 0028B] Stephen, Matthias, Barnabas, Ignatius, Alexander, Marcellinus, Peter, Felicity, Perpetua, Agatha [Note: Pamelian manuscript: Agatha, as in the other printed editions.], Lucy, Agnes, Cecilia, Anastasia, [Note: In the Gemeticus manuscript the names of the holy Æthelthryth and Gertrude are inserted here.] and with all your saints. Admit us into their company, we ask, not as one who weighs merit but as one who grants pardon. Through Christ our Lord.

Through him you continually create all these good things, O Lord; † sanctify them, † enliven them, † bless them, and bestow them upon us. Through † him, and with † him, and in † him, is to you, God the almighty Father, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, all honor and glory [Note: The crosses marked here do not appear in the Swedish Queen manuscript.].

For ever and ever. Amen.

**Let us pray.**—Instructed by saving commandments and formed by divine teaching, we dare to say:

[Col. 0028C] **Our Father**, who are in heaven, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come. Your will be done, as in heaven, so on earth. Give us today our daily bread. And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors. And lead us not into temptation.

**R/.** But deliver us from evil.

Deliver us, we ask, O Lord, from all evils, past, present, and future; and, through the intercession of the blessed and glorious ever-virgin Mary, Mother of God, and of your blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and Andrew, and also of your blessed protomartyr Stephen, [Note: In the Swedish Queen manuscript is added: “and also of your blessed martyr and bishop Dionysius, with his companions Rusticus and Eleutherius, and your blessed confessor Clodoaldus, and all …” In the Pamelian manuscript: “with your blessed martyr Cyriacus and your holy confessor Martin,” which are absent from the Swedish Queen manuscript. In the second Theoderic manuscript the names of the saints Quintinus, Nicasius, Gregory, Medard, and Eligius are inserted here.] and of all the saints, graciously grant peace in our days, so that, helped by the assistance of your mercy, we may always be free from sin and secure from every [Col. 0028D] disturbance. Through the Lord.

**The peace of the Lord be always with you.**  
**R/.** And with your spirit.

**Lamb of God, who take away the sins of the world, have mercy on us** [Note: After the *Agnus* in the first Theoderic manuscript follow six prayers, of which the second is: “O Lord Jesus Christ, who said to your apostles, ‘I leave you peace,’ etc.,” which is read in [Col. 0029D] modern missals. In the Swedish Queen manuscript, before the *Agnus Dei* there is a bishops’ blessing, “Be present,” etc., as in the Roman *Pontifical*; afterward comes the consecration, “God of all good things.” Then, over the offerings, “May this victim,” etc., as in the Roman *Pontifical*; the preface, “Therefore,” etc.; for the conclusion, “May this communion,” etc. These are followed by the ordinations of a priest and a deacon.].

[Note: Here the manuscripts do not agree, except in the first two prayers.]

## 9 Kalends of January.—On the Vigil of the Lord’s Nativity

[Col. 0029A]

**At None.**—O God, who gladden us by the yearly expectation of our redemption, grant that we may joyfully receive your Only-Begotten as our Redeemer and also look upon him, when he comes as Judge, with confidence: our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you, God, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, for ever and ever.

**Over the offerings.**—Grant us, we ask, almighty God, that just as we anticipate the worshipful Nativity of your Son, so we may receive his eternal gifts with rejoicing. Through the same Christ our Lord.

**Preface** [Note: The preface is absent from the Pamelian and Swedish Queen manuscripts. In the Gemeticus manuscript the preface assigned is the one placed in the Vatican and Gussanville editions for the third Mass of the Lord’s Nativity.].—It is truly worthy and just, right and conducive to salvation, that we should always and everywhere give you thanks, holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God, through Christ our Lord: whose face we anticipate today in confession, and whom we entreat with a suppliant voice to make us so watchful during the offices of the coming night that, with sincere minds, we may be worthy to receive his coming Nativity.
