And the closer you see the clergy to the sacred altars, the more mindful you shall be to show them greater honor in the places appropriate to them, so that the Mediator of God and human beings may confirm you as mediator between clergy and people upon this throne of the kingdom, and may cause you to reign with him in the eternal kingdom: Jesus Christ our Lord, King of kings and Lord of lords, who lives with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

(1121) “The duty of a newly ordained king, elevated to the throne, is to command these three things to the Christian people subject to him. First, that the Church of God and all the Christian people, +preserving true peace, do so at all times. Second, that he forbid acts of rapacity and every form of iniquity among people of every rank. Third, that in all judgments he command equity and mercy, so that the kindly and merciful God may, in his mercy, forgive him and us; he who lives with the Father.”

Then (1122) he shall kiss all the clergy and people, and (1123) each one shall say: “May the king live happily forever!” three times: “May the king live!” as above. After the Gospel, (1124) the king shall offer the offering and wine into the hand of the archbishop, and the Mass shall proceed in its proper order. Then he shall receive communion from the archbishop with the body and blood of Christ; (1125) and thus they shall give thanks to God. Afterward they shall proceed to the table.

## (1126) FOR BLESSING THE QUEEN

263 She must be brought into the church and prostrate herself before the altar. After she has been raised from prayer by the bishops, and with her head bowed, the archbishop shall say this Prayer:

(1127) “Be present, O Lord, to our supplications, and may what must be carried out through the ministry of our humility be accomplished by the effect of your power. Through.”

(1128) Then her head must be anointed with oil.—“In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, may this anointing with oil benefit you for eternal honor and confirmation.”

Prayer following the anointing.—“Almighty and eternal God, graciously pour forth, at our prayer, the abundant Spirit of your blessing upon this female servant of yours, (1129) so that she who today is established as queen through the laying on of our hands may remain worthy and chosen through your sanctification, and may never afterward be separated, as one unworthy, from your grace. Through.”

(1130) Then the ring must be placed on her finger.—“Receive the seal of the faith of the Holy Trinity, by which you may be able to avoid all heretical perversities and, (1131) by the power granted to you, call barbarous peoples to the knowledge of the truth.”

Prayer follows.—“O God, to whom belong all power and dignity, grant your female servant N., through the sign of your faith, the prosperous effect of her dignity, by which she may always remain steadfast for you and continually strive to please you.”

(1132) Then the crown must be placed upon her head.—(1133) “Receive the crown of glory and the honor of joy, so that you may shine resplendently and be crowned with eternal exultation. Through the Lord.”

Likewise, a Prayer.—“O Lord, source of all good things and giver of every advancement, grant your female servant N. to govern well the dignity she has attained, and strengthen with good works the glory you have bestowed upon her in it. Through the Lord.”

## BLESSING OF NUPTIALS

From the Codex of Rheims.

[Col. 0261B]

263 Here begins the nuptial rite (1134) [Note: It seems worthy of observation that in the old Gallican Sacramentary there occurs a Prayer or Blessing over those who marry a second time, although such marriages were not usually blessed in the Church].—“Be present, O Lord, to our supplications, and graciously assist your institutions, by which you ordained the propagation of the human race, so that what is joined with you as its author may be preserved with your help. Through our Lord Jesus Christ.”

Likewise, another.—“We beseech you, almighty God, accompany the institutions of your providence with pious favor, and preserve in lasting peace those whom you join in a lawful union. Through the Lord.”

Over the offerings.—“Be present, O Lord, to our supplications, and (1135) graciously and kindly accept this offering [Note: Our Edmund Martene, who presents these same words from the Gelasian Missal and the manuscripts of Rheims and Gellone, in book I, *On the Ancient Rites of the Church*, chapter 9, on the sacrament of marriage, article 5, reads *famularum*—‘of the female servants.’ We shall append the other emendations made by him.] of those female servants of yours, which we offer to you for your female servant, whom you have deigned to lead to the age of maturity and to the day of marriage, so that what is sought according to your disposition may be fulfilled by your grace. Through our Lord.”

“It is truly worthy … [you], who have bound the covenants of marriage with the gentle yoke of concord and the unbreakable bond of peace, so that the chaste fruitfulness of holy marriages might serve the multiplication of adopted children. For by your grace, O Lord, your providence disposes both matters in ineffable ways, so that what generation produces for the adornment of the world, (1136) [Note: The same writer reads *regeneratio*, “rebirth,” instead.] generation may bring to the increase of the Church. Through Christ.

Within the canon.—“Therefore, O Lord, graciously accept this offering of your female servants, for whom we earnestly implore your majesty, [Col. 0261D] so that, just as you granted her to reach an age suitable for marriage, so, joined to a husband by your gift, you may complete her joy with the offspring she desires, and graciously advance, with her husband, the offered course of years. (1137) [Note: Read *optatam*, “desired,” according to the same Martene.] Through Christ our Lord. This offering, which you, O God…”

Within the rite.—(1138) [Note: In the same place, “within the rite.”] For the thirtieth or annual anniversary of a marriage.—“Therefore, O Lord, we beseech you graciously to accept this offering of your male and female servants, which they offer to you on the thirtieth day of their union, or on the annual day on which you deigned to join them by the marriage bond. For this reason, therefore, may they render their vows to you, the true and living God, for whom we pour out suppliant prayers before your awesome kindness: that they may grow old together in goodness and peace, see their children’s children to the third and fourth generation, and bless you all the days of their life. Through Christ our Lord. This offering…”

Complete the full canon, and (1139) say the Lord’s Prayer, and (1140) then bless her in these words [Note: In the same Martene, and thus he sings the Prayer of Blessing in these words]:

Prayer.—(1141) “O God, who bless the beginning of the growing world with multiplied offspring, favorably hear our supplications, and (1142) pour the help of blessing upon this female servant of yours, so that in marital partnership they may be joined in equal affection, like-mindedness, and holiness as yours [The praised writer restores: “mutual holiness”].”

Likewise, a Prayer.—“Father, creator of the world, begetter of those who are born, founder of the multiplication of origin, who added Adam’s companion by your hands, whose growing bones from his bones were marked by an equal form in wondrous diversity: from this, the commanded partnerships of the marriage bed, for the increase of the whole multitude, gathered throughout the world and bound together the covenants of the human race.

“So it pleased you, O Lord; so it was necessary: (1146) because what is far off and weak—‘what [is] like to the man, than what you had made for yourself, O God’ [the text is corrupt]—has the weaker sex added to the stronger, so that you might make one out of two, and offspring, mingled in an equal pledge, might remain. (1147) Then posterity, brought forth in due order, would proceed, so that (1148) those to come would follow those who came before, and, though mortal, would set no end for themselves within so brief a term.

“For these things, therefore, let the institutions of the law to come be given. [Note: The same source has: “let the institutions of the law to come be given.” Menard’s restoration, found in the notes, seems preferable.] Therefore sanctify the beginnings of this household of yours, Father, so that, joined in a good and prosperous union, she may keep the rights of the eternal law [Note: The same source reads *jussa*, “commands.”]; and may she remember, O Lord, that she has been joined not merely for conjugal license, but for the observance of faith and the love of holy offspring [Note: The same source reads *diligatam*, “beloved.”]. Faithful and chaste, may she marry in Christ and remain an imitator of holy women. May she be lovable to her husband like Rachel, wise like Rebecca, long-lived and faithful like Sarah. (1153) Let that treacherous author of transgression seize nothing from her; bound by faith and commandments, may she remain [The text is corrupt here] among women, serving the true God, devotedly strengthening her weakness with the firmness of discipline, joined to one marriage bed, and avoiding unlawful contacts in life. [Note: Martene reads: “May she be truly modest, grave, venerable in chastity … may she be fruitful in offspring.”]

May she be modest, grave in chastity, venerable, instructed in heavenly teachings; (1160) may she be fruitful in offspring, approved and innocent, and may she reach the rest of the blessed, even the heavenly kingdoms.”

After this say *Pax vobiscum*, “Peace be with you,” and give them communion. Then, after they have received communion, say the Blessing over them in these words:

“Holy Lord, almighty Father, through repeated rites we suppliantly entreat you: for those for whom Christ has interceded with you, (1162) deign to cherish the union of your servants, that they may deserve (1163) to receive your blessings [Note: The same source: “and may they be made fruitful in the success of children; deign to confirm their marriage as you confirmed that of the first human being. Let all the snares of enemies be turned away from them, so that they may also imitate the holiness of the Fathers.”], so that they may be made fruitful in the succession of children, just as you deign (1164) to confirm all the very many [the printed text is corrupt]. May the snares of enemies be turned away from them, O almighty One, (1165) so that (1166) they may also imitate the holiness of the Fathers in this very marriage, they who by your providence, O Lord, deserved to be joined. Through our Lord Jesus Christ.”

After Communion.—“Hear us, holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God, so that what (1167) is not administered by our ministry may rather be fulfilled by your blessing. [Note: The same source reads: “so that what is administered by our ministry may rather be fulfilled by your blessing.”] Through our Lord Jesus Christ.”

[Col. 0263]

## NOTES AND OBSERVATIONS ON THE SACRAMENTARY OF ST. GREGORY THE GREAT, BY DOM HUGO MENARD, BENEDICTINE MONK

[Col. 0263C] 273 [Note: The numbers prefixed to the notes correspond to the numbers enclosed in parentheses that occur in the text of the Sacramentary. EDITOR.] 1. “This book.” In the printed editions it reads: “Here begins the book.”

[Note: This title is found in the oldest Sacramentary books, especially in the very ancient Harlaean manuscript; a specimen of its script may be read in Mabillon, *On Diplomatics*, p. 365.]

2. **Book of Sacraments.** Thus it is designated in our manuscript codices of Rodradus, Rheims, and Abbot Ratoldus. It is so called in the Council of Rheims, cited by Burchard, book III, chapter 97:

> When the Mass has been completed, the chalice with the paten, and the Book of Sacraments together with the priestly vestments, are to be placed in a clean location under lock and key.

The same may be seen in the same Burchard, book XIX, chapter 8:

> Now therefore, brothers, whoever wishes to bear the name of priest must first, for God’s sake, consider that he should learn the things necessary before the bishop’s hand touches his head: namely, the Psalter, the Lectionary with the Gospels, the Book of Sacraments, the Baptistery, and the Computus with its cycle, etc.

Here *the Baptistery* means the method or rite of conferring baptism.

Flodoard, *History of the Church of Rheims*, book III, chapter 9, says:

> He also presented there the Book of Sacraments, enclosed beneath ivory tablets marked with silver, and a Lectionary for the Mass, a book adorned with equal elegance.

The Micrologus likewise calls it this, chapter 6, *On Ecclesiastical Observances*:

> The same Albinus accomplished a work in the holy Church that ought not to be despised; for he is said to have collected the Gregorian Prayers in Books of Sacraments, with a few others added, etc.

Abbot Berno of Reichenau, chapter 1 of his book *On Certain Matters Pertaining to the Mass*, says:

> Since Pope Gregory corrected the Book of Sacraments with the greatest diligence according to the standard of truth.

John the Deacon, in the *Life of Saint Gregory* cited by the same Berno, in the same chapter, says:

> Hence we read in his Life: “He also took the Gelasian Codex of the solemn rites of the Mass, removing much, changing a little, and adding some things, and compressed it into the volume of a single little book; this volume he entitled the Book of Sacraments.”

Thus it stands in John the Deacon. [Note: [Col. 0264D] In the manuscripts of John the Deacon, even those older than Berno, who flourished at the beginning of the eleventh century, these words are absent; nor do any traces of erasure remain.] But the final member of this passage was torn from his text by someone unknown.

Walafrid, in *On Ecclesiastical Matters*, chapter 22, says:

> Blessed Gregory took care to bring together whatever was reasonable and, excluding what seemed either excessive or ill-arranged, composed the book called the Book of Sacraments, as is most clearly demonstrated by its title.

Gennadius also uses this title, although he is speaking of another book, in *On Illustrious Men*, in the chapter on Voconius, bishop of Castellane:

> He also composed a volume of Sacraments.

And in the chapter on Musaeus, a presbyter of Marseille:

> He composed an excellent and not inconsiderable volume of Sacraments, arranged in sections according to the needs of offices and seasons, according to the sequence of readings and Psalms, yet harmonious in the solidity of its arrangement for entreating God and proclaiming his benefits.

The same title is found in the Mass edited by Illyricus:

> Here begins the order of the Book of Sacraments.

Therefore I do not agree with those who write that the title of this book is *the Sacramentary*, rather than *Book of Sacraments*. The contrary is evident from this Book of Sacraments itself, in which the Sacramentary is plainly distinguished from the Book of Sacraments. For there, on the sixth feria of Holy Week, the Sacramentary is cited:

> When he came from the sacristy and proceeded before the altar to pray, according to the order contained in the Sacramentary. As soon as he has risen, etc.

Nor is it an objection that Albinus, Amalarius, and several others called this book the Sacramentary, since the foregoing makes it sufficiently clear that *Book of Sacraments* is the true and proper title of this work. Nevertheless, I do not deny that the word *Sacramentary*, or *Sacramentarius*, is ancient, since Gennadius used it of Paulinus:

> He also composed a Sacramentary and a Hymnary.

This work is most aptly called the Book of Sacraments because it contains the liturgical offices of the Mass properly arranged. The holy Fathers formerly called these *sacraments*, as Optatus of Milevis says in book II against Parmenianus:

> For who would doubt that you could not pass over that legitimate rite in the mystery of the sacraments? You say that you offer on behalf of the Church, which is one.

And in book VI:

> Among the sacraments the veil could be touched, but not the wood; that is, in the celebration of the Mass the altar-veil could be touched, but not the altar itself, which is called wood because it was wooden. This matter will be discussed below.

Saint Ambrose, in book III *On Virgins*, says:

> What is more disgraceful than to surround the divine oracles so that they may not be heard, believed, or revealed? To drown out the sacraments with confused voices, so that prayer offered for the salvation of all may be impeded?

Saint Augustine, letter 59 (now 149), to Paulinus, says:

> We understand as “prayers” those which we make in the celebration of the sacraments, before that which is on the Lord’s table begins to be blessed.

And in *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 13:

> What, then, is said in the sacraments of the faithful—“Let us lift up our heart to the Lord”—is the Lord’s gift.

3. **Written from the authentic book of the library of the Cubiculum.** In our other manuscript codices these words are absent; yet they contribute considerably to the authority of this codex. They are found in the printed editions, except for the word *book*. The *Cubiculum* was a kind of secretarium, cell, or house beside the church of Saint Peter, in which those who kept watch over the bodies of the holy Apostles—hence called *cubicularii*—were stationed. It also contained a library of sacred books, especially those pertaining to ecclesiastical office and the performance of the divine mysteries. The same may be seen in the basilica at Nola, built by Saint Paulinus, where, on the left side of the apse, he made a secretarium suitable for storing sacred books, as the inscription itself indicates:

> If anyone possesses a holy desire to meditate on the law,  
> Here, seated, he will be able to devote himself to the sacred books.

As the same Saint Paulinus testifies, letter 12.

4. **Mass.** Ancient Fathers generally use this word in the plural number; nevertheless, it is found in the singular in Saint Ambrose, book V, [Note: [Col. 0265D] In the latest edition it is letter 20 of the first class.] letter 35, to his sister Marcellina:

> On the following day—it was a Sunday—after the readings and the homily, when the catechumens had been dismissed, I was delivering the Creed in the baptisteries of the basilica to certain candidates for baptism. There I was informed, after the matter had been discovered, that decans had been sent from the palace to the Portian Basilica and were hanging curtains, and that part of the people were going there. Nevertheless, I remained at my post and began to celebrate the Mass. While I was making the offering, I learned that a certain Castulus, whom the Arians called a presbyter, had been seized by the people. Passers-by had encountered him in the street. I began to weep most bitterly and to pray to God during the very offering, asking him to come to our aid.

The words “I make the offering” and the noun “offering” plainly show that *Mass* here must be understood liturgically of the sacrifice of Christ’s body and blood.

5. **What kind of Antiphon there was at the Introit.** Thus it appears in the Gregorian Antiphonary, manuscript of the library of Corbie, [Note: [Col. 0265D] We shall shortly publish Saint Gregory’s Antiphonary. The manuscripts of Theodorus, apart from the Collect, Prayer, Prayer over the Offerings, Preface, etc., which all the Books of Sacraments display, assign to each Mass an Antiphon, or Introit; the Psalm corresponding to this Antiphon; the Responsory with its Verse, now understood under the name Gradual; the Alleluia; the Offertory with several Verses; and the Communion with a Psalm—all of which the Antiphonary contains.] and also in the printed editions.

Walafrid Strabo, *On Ecclesiastical Matters*, chapter 22, and the Micrologus, chapter 1, *On Ecclesiastical Observances*, speak in this way:

> Meanwhile the Antiphon for the Introit is sung, which earned this name from the entrance of the priest to the altar.

It is commonly called the *Introit*, and is found in the manuscript codices of the presbyter Rodradus and Abbot Ratoldus, as well as in the printed editions. The same may be seen in Amalarius, book III *On Offices*, chapter 5:

> The office called the Introit of the Mass begins with the first Antiphon, which is called the Introit, and ends with the Prayer that is said by the priest before the reading.

There is no mention here of the Psalm; yet it is sufficiently understood, since mention is made of the Antiphon that is ordinarily placed before it in the Mass. Formerly this Psalm was sung in its entirety. Hence, in the Gregorian Antiphonaries and in the Roman Missal, the beginning of the Psalm is placed after the Antiphon. If the first verse of the Psalm is itself the Antiphon, then the second verse of the Psalm follows it, although some more recent composers of new Masses, through ignorance, observe this less carefully.

Thus formerly the Mass began with psalmody, as it does now. This is clear from Saint Dionysius, chapter 3 of the *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*. After the bishop had begun the incensation at the altar and had made the circuit of the choir with incense, he returned to the altar and “begins the sacred melody of the Psalms” (*ἀπάρχεται τῆς ἱερᾶς ψαλμῶν μελῳδίας*), while the entire ecclesiastical order joined in the sacred psalmody.

Saint Basil seems to support this in *On the Holy Spirit*, to Amphilochius, chapter 27, when he says that certain things precede the reading of the Apostle and the Gospel:

> Οὐ γὰρ δὲ τούτοις ἀρκούμεθα ὧν ὁ Ἀπόστολος, ἢ τὸ εὐαγγέλιον ἐπεμνήσθη· ἀλλὰ προλέγομεν καὶ ἐπιλέγομεν ἕτερα, ὡς μεγάλην ἔχοντα πρὸς τὸ μυστήριον τὴν ἰσχύν.

> For we are not content only with those things mentioned by the Apostle or the Gospel; rather, we introduce and append certain other things, as possessing great force in relation to the mystery.

Alcuin, however, in *On Divine Offices*, in the chapter *What the Vestments Signify*, and Amalarius, book III *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 5, write that this practice proceeded solely from Pope Celestine, who instituted the singing of the 150 Psalms before the sacrifice—a practice that had not previously existed, since the Mass had begun only with the reading of the Apostle and the Gospel.

They are correct. For in the time of Saint Justin Martyr, who was a contemporary of the disciples of the Apostles, the Mass began with readings, as he himself testifies near the end of the second *Apology for the Christians*:

> On the day called Sunday, all who live either in the towns or in the countryside gather in the same place, and the memoirs of the Apostles or the writings of the Prophets are read as long as time permits: *καὶ τὰ ἀπομνημονεύματα τῶν Ἀποστόλων, ἢ τὰ συγγράμματα τῶν Προφητῶν ἀναγινώσκεται μέχρις ἐγχωρεῖ*. Then, when the reader has ceased, etc.

In Saint Cyril’s fifth *Mystagogical Catechesis*, where the order of the Mass is reviewed, mention is first made of the washing of hands and then of the kiss of peace, for which he gives a mystical explanation. But I do not think that the Mass at that time lacked a sacred reading. For the same Cyril, in the fourth catechesis, urges that only those Scriptures which are read in the Church should be read. If he made no mention of the reading of Scripture in the fifth *Mystagogical Catechesis*, the reason is readily apparent: when Scripture was read in the assembly, its explanation was easy; the other mysteries were not so readily understood, and these he explains more fully in that catechesis.

The practice of beginning the Mass with the Scriptures continued in the Church for a long time. It was still in force in the time of Saint Ambrose, as is clear from letter 35 of book V [now letter 20 of the first class]:

> On the following day—it was a Sunday—after the readings and the homily, when the catechumens had been dismissed, I was delivering the Creed in the baptisteries of the basilica, etc.

At Carthage, in the time of Saint Augustine, the use of Psalms before the offering alone was adopted, as appears from book II of the *Retractions*, chapter 11:

> Meanwhile a certain Hilary, a man of tribunitian rank and a Catholic, irritated—I do not know how—against the ministers of God, as often happens, tore apart with malicious criticism the custom that had then begun at Carthage: that hymns should be sung at the altar from the Book of Psalms, either before the offering or while what had been offered was distributed to the people. He asserted that this ought not to be done.

Later, therefore, we see mention of the Psalms in the liturgies themselves, as is clear from Gennadius’ account of Musaeus of Marseille, who composed a Book of Sacraments distinguished by the sequence and chanting of the Psalms.

Yet this use of the Psalms was by no means received everywhere in Gaul in the time of Musaeus of Marseille or afterward. For in the time of King Theudebert the Mass still began with readings, as is evident from Saint Gregory of Tours, in the *Lives of the Fathers*, in his account of Saint Nicetius, bishop of Trier:

> Sunday arrived, and behold, the king entered the church with those whom this priest had ordered to abstain from Communion. When the readings prescribed by the ancient canon had been read and gifts had been offered upon the altar of God, the priest said: “The solemn celebration of the Mass will not be completed here today unless those deprived of Communion first depart.”

In view of these facts, it must be said that in those ancient times there was no single uniform practice: some began the Mass with psalmody, while others began it with readings.

6. **Then, Kyrie eleison.** It was plainly an ancient custom of the Roman Church to sing *Kyrie eleison* both in the Masses and in the other divine offices, as is clear from the Council of Vaison, held in the consulship of Decius the Younger, a man of illustrious rank, in the year of Christ 529, canon 3:

> Since, both in the Apostolic See and throughout all the eastern and Italian provinces, the sweet and exceedingly salutary custom has been introduced of saying *Kyrie eleison* with great feeling and compunction, it has pleased us also that, by God’s favor, this most holy custom should be introduced into all our churches, both at Matins, at Masses, and at Vespers.

It is therefore clear that certain Greeks wrongly accused Pope Saint Gregory of having instituted the singing of *Kyrie eleison* in the Roman Mass for the first time, supposedly in order to oppress the Church of Constantinople. [Note: [Col. 0267D] Now book IX, indiction 2, letter 12. Menardus, however, seems to me not to have correctly understood the words of this letter. For no one ever complained that Gregory wished to oppress the Church of Constantinople by borrowing its rite and introducing it into the Roman Church, since that would rather have been highly honorable to the see of Constantinople. But some were surprised that Gregory, at the very time when he opposed the patriarch of Constantinople for arrogating to himself the profane title “ecumenical,” and was, as his defenders wrongly cried out, striving to oppress and despoil the Church of Constantinople, nevertheless wished to subject the Roman Church to its rites. The words of the cited letter must therefore be understood thus: “He who follows the customs of the Church of Constantinople in every respect is arranging to crush it.” As though it were said: “See, he who is most hostile to the Church of Constantinople nevertheless confers upon it the highest honor by subjecting the Roman Church to its rites.”] He himself testifies to the contrary in book VII of the *Register*, letter 64, where he says that he had never borrowed this practice from the Church of Constantinople, and that the supplication was sung by the Roman Church according to a different rite:

> We have neither said nor do we say *Kyrie eleison* as it is said by the Greeks, because among the Greeks all say it together; whereas among us it is said by the clergy and answered by the people. *Christe eleison* is likewise said the same number of times, whereas among the Greeks it is not said at all.

So he writes.

As for the words “because among the Greeks all say it together,” the rite is known from the liturgies of Saint Mark, Saint James, and similar liturgies, in which the people say *Kyrie eleison*. In the liturgy of Saint John Chrysostom, however, the choir says it; here the word *choir* means the entire assembly, whether clerical or lay, just as the word *people* must be understood in the liturgies cited.

As for the words “*Christe eleison* is likewise said the same number of times,” this refers to the rite by which *Christe eleison* was formerly said as many times as *Kyrie eleison*. That practice is no longer in use, since now in the Mass *Christe eleison* is repeated only three times, and *Kyrie eleison* six times.

Thus, since in George Codinus’ Greek translation of the Gregorian Mass the modern practice is preserved concerning this prayer, this indicates that he lacked ancient and pure copies for his translation. In our three manuscript codices, however, nothing contradicts Saint Gregory’s passage, since *Kyrie eleison* is written only once in them, presumably for the sake of brevity.

When Saint Gregory writes that *Christe eleison* is not sung by the Greeks, the truth of his statement is evident from the ancient Greek liturgies, in which *Christe eleison* is not found.

7. **Likewise, Gloria in excelsis.** It is commonly stated that Pope Telesphorus instituted the singing of this angelic hymn in the Mass. This institution is attributed to him by Anastasius the Librarian in his Life; by Walafrid Strabo, *On Ecclesiastical Matters*, chapter 22; by Amalarius Fortunatus, book III *On Ecclesiastical Office*, chapter 8; and by Alcuin, *On Divine Office*, in the chapter *What the Vestments Signify*. Yet in the following chapter of the same book Alcuin says that this hymn was later enlarged and completed by Saint Hilary of Poitiers. If that is so, Alcuin does not seem consistent with himself.

But I think that in the earlier passage Alcuin was speaking only of the words of this hymn that occur in the Gospel. The Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 12, writes that the remaining words that follow were composed by ecclesiastical teachers.

In the liturgy of Saint James, the angelic or evangelical words are said three times. This gave some people an opportunity to write that the custom of saying this hymn in the Mass derived from apostolic tradition. That, however, cannot be clearly inferred from the same liturgy, because it is one thing to speak precisely of the angelic or evangelical words, and another to speak of the entire hymn—even though the complete hymn is found in the *Apostolic Constitutions*, book VII, chapter 47. All learned men know, however, that many additions were later made to works of that kind.

Formerly this angelic hymn was sung at Lauds in the morning, as we noted in our *Concordance of the Rules of Saint Benedict, Abbot of Aniane*.

8. **If he is a bishop.** Thus it appears in the printed editions and in the codices of Rodradus and Ratoldus. In some manuscripts, however, *affuerit* is incorrectly read, as the following context makes clear.

9. **But it is by no means said by presbyters except at Easter.** The same institution may be seen in Berno of Reichenau, chapter 2, *On Certain Matters Pertaining to the Mass*, although the following passage might seem contrary to it:

> Why should presbyters not be permitted to sing every Sunday, or on the birthdays of the saints, the hymn that the angels sang to the Lord born in the flesh, saying: “Glory to God in the highest”? If permission has been granted to sing it at Easter, according to the heading of the Missal, I think it is no less lawful at the Nativity of the Lord, when it first began to be heard by human beings on earth how it was sung by angels in heaven. Let those who disagree bring forward where it was forbidden by the holy Fathers, or by that most holy Pope Gregory himself.

Yet the authority of his Missal should have sufficed for him: it had been instituted formerly by the holy Fathers and revised by that most holy Gregory himself. This may also be seen in the manuscript codices of Rodradus and Ratoldus. But eventually the institution was changed.

10. **Afterward the Prayer is said.** In this codex of Saint Eligius, as in the codices of Rodradus and Ratoldus, in the printed editions, and in the Roman Order, there is a single Prayer, or Collect, in the first part of the Mass before the Gospel; only rarely are there two. In the Rheims Codex, two are found, and only rarely one.

Therefore I do not agree with those who assert that, in the Roman Church, from apostolic times it was customary to recite three Prayers in this first part of the Mass—except on double feasts—and an equal number of Prayers over the Offerings and Postcommunions.

Formerly among the Greeks five Prayers were said before the giving of peace, which was followed by the offering of the mysteries. This is evident from canon 19 of the Council of Laodicea. Since a learned man cited it in a very mutilated form, I shall reproduce almost the whole canon, so that its entire teaching may be apparent:

> Περὶ τοῦ δεῖν ἰδίᾳ μετὰ τὰς ὁμιλίας τῶν ἐπισκόπων, καὶ τῶν κατηχουμένων εὐχὴν ἐπιτελεῖσθαι, καὶ μετὰ τὸ ἐξελθεῖν τοὺς κατηχουμένους, τῶν ἐν μετανοίᾳ τὴν εὐχὴν γίνεσθαι, καὶ τούτων προσελθόντων ὑπὸ χεῖρα, καὶ ὑποχωρησάντων, οὕτως τῶν πιστῶν τὰς εὐχὰς γίνεσθαι τρεῖς, μίαν μὲν τὴν πρώτην διὰ σιωπῆς, τὴν δὲ δευτέραν, καὶ τρίτην διὰ προφωνήσεως πληροῦσθαι, εἶθ᾽ οὕτως τὴν εἰρήνην δίδοσθαι.

> It is necessary first to offer separately, after the sermons of the bishops, the Prayer of the catechumens; after the catechumens have departed, the Prayer of those undergoing penance; and when these have approached under the hand and then withdrawn, three Prayers of the faithful are to be offered—one, the first, in silence, and the second and third completed aloud. Then peace is to be given.

These three Prayers were indeed offered after the Gospel, since the catechumens and penitents were not dismissed until it had been sung.

Saint John Chrysostom, in homily 72 on Matthew, mentions only three Prayers, namely those said before the peace:

> Καὶ πρώτη ἡ δέησις ἐλέους γέμει, ὅταν ὑπὲρ τῶν ἐνεργουμένων παρακαλῶμεν, καὶ ἡ δευτέρα πάλιν ὑπὲρ ἑτέρων τῶν ἐν μετανοίᾳ πολὺ τὸ ἔλεος ἐπιζητοῦσα, καὶ ἡ τρίτη δὲ πάλιν ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν αὐτῶν.

> The first Prayer is full of mercy, when we entreat on behalf of those under the power of demons; the second, offered again on behalf of others who are undergoing penance, seeks abundant mercy; and the third is again recited on behalf of ourselves—that is, the faithful.

The same author, in homily 18 on the Second Epistle to the Corinthians, mentions the Prayers poured out in the sacred liturgical action for those under the power of demons and for penitents.

From these passages it may sufficiently be gathered that the Greeks differed somewhat among themselves in this rite, and still more from the Latins. Nor do I accept the explanation that, in the passages of Saint John Chrysostom cited above, those under the power of demons are understood to mean catechumens.

For the remaining matters concerning the arrangement of the Collects, see our observations on the *Concordance of the Rules*, chapter 15, § 8.

11. **Then the Apostle follows.** That is, a reading from the Apostle, commonly called the Epistle. This is the best reading, and it is also found in the printed codices and in those of Rodradus and Ratoldus.

The First Council of Toledo speaks in this way, canon 2:

> So that they do not read the Gospels or the Apostle.

And canon 4:

> So that he does not read the Gospel and the Apostle.

Codinus likewise says, in *On the Offices of the Palace of Constantinople*:

> Καὶ μετὰ τὸν τρισάγιον ὕμνον ἀναγινώσκεται ὁ Ἀπόστολος.

> And after the Trisagion hymn, the Apostle is read.

A little earlier he says:

> Καὶ ἡ μὲν λειτουργία ψάλλεται ἡσυχῶς, μέχρι καὶ τῆς ἀναγνώσεως τοῦ Ἀποστόλου.

> The liturgy is sung quietly up to the reading of the Apostle.

The same expression is found frequently in the Greek Euchologion. Therefore there is no need for our purer codices to be emended on the basis of certain manuscripts in which *the Epistle* is found.

The ancient custom, however, is to read the Epistles of the Apostles, especially those of Saint Paul, in the celebration of the Mass. This is established by Saint Basil, chapter 27 of *On the Holy Spirit*, to Amphilochius:

> Οὐ γὰρ τούτοις ἀρκούμεθα ὧν Ἀπόστολος ἢ τὸ εὐαγγέλιον ὑπεμνήσθη.

> We are not content with those things mentioned by the Apostle or the Gospel.

It is also established by Saint Justin Martyr, when he discusses the sacred liturgy in the second *Apology for the Christians*:

> Καὶ τὰ ὑπομνημονεύματα τῶν Ἀποστόλων, ἢ τὰ συγγράμματα τῶν Προφητῶν ἀναγινώσκεται μέχρις ἐγχωρεῖ.

> The memoirs of the Apostles or the writings of the Prophets are read for as long as time permits.

This passage, however, may also be understood of the Gospel.

12. **Gradual.** Thus it appears in the codices of Rodradus and Ratoldus. In the printed editions and in the commonly used Missals it is *Graduale*.

13. **The Gospel is read.** This follows from the ancient rite of the Church, as is evident from the passage of Saint Basil cited shortly above; the passage of Saint Justin produced shortly before may also be referred to the same practice.

The same is suggested by Saint Cyprian, letter 24:

> Let him be conspicuous to the entire people by the dignity of his office; let him read the commandments and the Gospel of the Lord.

A little later he says:

> There is nothing in which a confessor can benefit the brothers more than when the evangelical reading is heard from his mouth.

There is no mention here of the Creed after the Gospel; this will be discussed more appropriately below, in connection with the Easter Mass.

14. **Then the Offertory.** Thus it appears in our manuscript codices of Rodradus and Ratoldus, although these words are absent from the printed editions. The Offertory is an Antiphon sung while the people offered their gifts upon the altar according to the ancient custom, which will be discussed below in connection with the Easter Mass.

15. **Lift up your hearts.** Here the Preface begins; this term will be discussed below. These words do not derive from a recent institution, since they are found in the liturgies of Saints James, Basil, and Chrysostom. Saint Caesarius of Arles also mentions them in homily 12:

> Almost everyone leaves the church after the readings have been recited. To whom, then, will the priest say, “Lift up your hearts”?

Saint Augustine, in *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 13, says:

> What, then, is said in the sacraments of the faithful—“Let us have our heart lifted up to the Lord”—is the Lord’s gift.

And in *On the Good of Widowhood*, chapter 16:

> For when, amid the sacred mysteries, we are commanded to have our heart lifted up, you will be able to do this with his help.

He says the same in many other places.

Saint Anastasius Sinaita, in his sermon *On the Synaxis*, says:

> Ταῦτα διαμαρτύρεται ὁ ἱερεὺς λέγων· Ἄνω σχῶμεν τὰς καρδίας.

> The priest testifies to these things, saying: “Let us lift up our hearts.”

Saint Cyril of Alexandria, in the fifth *Mystagogical Catechesis*, says:

> Μετὰ τοῦτο βοᾷ ὁ ἱερεὺς· Ἄνω τὰς καρδίας.

> After this the priest cries out: “Lift up your hearts.”

Saint Cyprian likewise says, in *On the Lord’s Prayer*:

> Therefore, before the Prayer, the priest prepares the minds of the brothers by saying: “Lift up your hearts.”

16. **We have them lifted up to the Lord.** Besides the ancient liturgies, the Fathers mentioned above also recall these words.

Saint Caesarius, in homily 16, says:

> When the priest says, “Lift up your hearts,” let us answer with a clear conscience that we have them lifted up to the Lord.

Saint Cyril, in the same catechesis, says:

> Καὶ ἀποκρίνεσθε, Ἔχομεν πρὸς τὸν κύριον.

> And you answer: “We have them lifted up to the Lord.”

Saint Cyprian, in the work cited, says:

> So that when the people answer, “We have them lifted up to the Lord.”

Saint Anastasius Sinaita, in the sermon cited, says:

> Εἷτα τί πρὸς ταῦτα ἡμεῖς ἀποκρινόμεθα, Ἔχομεν πρὸς τὸν κύριον;

> Then what do we answer to this? “We have them lifted up to the Lord.”

And below:

> Ἰδοὺ πρὸς βράχεως συνέθεσθε· Ἔχομεν πρὸς κύριον τὰς καρδίας.

> Behold, a little earlier you agreed: “We have our hearts lifted up to the Lord.”

17. **Let us give thanks to the Lord our God.** The following words of Saint Augustine pertain to this, in *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 13:

> We are reminded by the priest, after this utterance addressed to them, to give thanks for this gift to the Lord our God.

He says the same in *On the Good of Widowhood*, chapter 16:

> Therefore it follows that, because our heart has been lifted up for so great a good, we should not attribute glory to ourselves as though this were the result of our own powers; rather, let us give thanks to the Lord our God.

And in sermon 21 *On Various Matters*:

> The faithful know where and when it is said: “Let us give thanks to the Lord our God.” But who gives thanks to God except one who has his heart lifted up to the Lord?

The same is found in the letter to Honoratus cited below.

Saint Cyril says, in the catechesis already cited:

> Εἶτα ἱερεὺς λέγει· Εὐχαριστήσωμεν τῷ Κυρίῳ.

> Then the priest says: “Let us give thanks to the Lord.”

For this reason Saint John Chrysostom, to be cited immediately below, calls this Prayer *εὐχαριστία*, that is, thanksgiving.

18. **It is worthy and just.** Saint Cyril of Jerusalem touches upon these words in the fifth *Mystagogical Catechesis*:

> Εἶτα λέγετε· Ἄξιον καὶ δίκαιον.

> Then you say: “It is worthy and just.”

Saint John Chrysostom, sermon 18 on the Second Epistle to the Corinthians, says:

> Τὰ τῆς εὐχαριστίας πάλιν κοινὰ, οὐδὲ γὰρ ἐκεῖνος (ἱερεὺς) εὐχαριστεῖ μόνος, ἀλλὰ καὶ ὁ λαὸς ἅπας· πρότερον γὰρ αὐτῶν λαβὼν φωνὴν, εἶτα συντιθεμένων, ὅτι ἀξίως καὶ δικαίως γίνεται, τότε ἄρχεται τῆς εὐχαριστίας.

> The things pertaining to thanksgiving are again common to all. For the priest does not give thanks alone, but the entire people also do so: first he receives their acclamation, and then, when they agree that this is done worthily and justly, he begins the thanksgiving.

Saint Augustine says in *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 13:

> And they answer that it is worthy and just.

And in *On the Good of Widowhood*, chapter 16:

> We are immediately reminded that it is worthy and just to remember this.

By these passages Saint Augustine proves against the Pelagians that we must acknowledge that we have received everything from God. For when the people answer that they have their heart lifted up to the Lord, and then, instructed by the priest to give thanks to God for so great a gift and benefit with their heart lifted up, immediately answer, “It is worthy and just,” they respond in proportion to the greatness of the benefit.

19. **To give you thanks always and everywhere.** Saint Irenaeus mentions this thanksgiving in book IV, chapter 34:

> The Church alone offers this pure oblation to the Creator, offering it to him with thanksgiving from his own creation.

Saint John Chrysostom, cited shortly above, says:

> Τότε ἄρχεται τῆς εὐχαριστίας.

> Then he begins the thanksgiving.

This thanksgiving was offered not only because we have our hearts lifted up, but also for all the benefits received from God, as Saint Augustine teaches in letter 120, to Honoratus:

> He bestows everything and foreknows everything; but he foretells sins, threatens punishments, and promises benefits. Therefore we are children of promise, children of benefit. This is grace, which is given freely—not on account of the merits of the one who acts, but through the mercy of the giver. Hence we give thanks to the Lord our God. This is the great sacrament in the sacrifice of the New Testament; where, when, and how it is offered, you will discover once you have been baptized.

This thanksgiving is also celebrated on account of so great a mystery and benefit, as is clear from Saint Justin Martyr, *Second Apology for the Christians*:

> Then bread and a cup of water and wine are brought to the one who presides over the brothers. When he has received them, he offers praise and glory to the Father of all things through the name of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, and he makes extended thanksgiving because he has deemed us worthy of these gifts: *αἶνον καὶ δόξαν τῷ Πατρὶ τῶν ὅλων διὰ τοῦ ὀνόματος τοῦ Υἱοῦ καὶ τοῦ Πνεύματος τοῦ ἁγίου ἀναπέμπει, καὶ εὐχαριστίαν ὑπὲρ τοῦ κατηξιῶσθαι τούτων παρ᾽ αὐτοῦ, ἐπὶ πολὺ ποιεῖται*.

The same point is repeated below, and it is expressly found in the liturgy of Saint John Chrysostom:

> Εὐχαριστοῦμέν σοι καὶ ὑπὲρ τῆς λειτουργίας ταύτης, ἣν ἐκ τῶν χειρῶν ἡμῶν δέξασθαι κατηξίωσας.

> We give you thanks also for this liturgy, which you have deemed worthy to receive from our hands.

20. **The angels praise, etc.** It is an ancient custom of the Church, in the Preface of the Mass, to mention those heavenly spirits who praise God without interruption in heaven. This is clear from the liturgies of Saints James and Chrysostom, and from Saint Caesarius, question 44 of the first *Dialogue*:

> ᾯ ἑπόμενοι οἱ τῆς θείας τελετῆς ἱερεῖς ἀναφωνοῦσι Θεῷ, σὲ ὑμνοῦσιν ἄγγελοι, ἀρχάγγελοι, θρόνοι, κυριότητες, ἀρχαὶ, ἐξουσίαι, δυνάμεις.

> Following him, the priests of the divine rite cry aloud to God: “Angels, archangels, thrones, dominions, principalities, authorities, and powers praise you.”

The same is evident from Saint Cyril, in the catechesis cited so often:

> Καὶ μετὰ ταῦτα μνημονεύομεν … ἀγγέλων, ἀρχαγγέλων, δυνάμεων, κυριοτήτων, ἀρχῶν, ἐξουσιῶν, θρόνων, τῶν χερουβίμ, etc.

> After this we make mention of angels, archangels, powers, dominions, principalities, authorities, thrones, cherubim, etc.

The same appears in Saint Isidore, to be cited shortly below.

But the Preface seems to have been abridged. For in the liturgy of Saint James mention is made also of the sun and moon, the stars, and the whole of creation. The same may be seen in the catechesis of Saint Cyril cited above, and Saint Isidore testifies to it in book I *On Ecclesiastical Office*, chapter 15:

> In it the whole assembly of earthly creatures and heavenly powers is also summoned to the praise of God.

### 21. “Holy, Holy, Holy”

The use of this hymn in the most holy mysteries is ancient, as may be seen from canon 3 of the Second Council of Vaison in the province of Vienne, held in the year of Our Lord 529. In Homily 12 of Saint Caesarius of Arles:

> For when the greater part of the people—or, worse still, almost everyone—leaves the church after the readings have been recited, to whom will the priest say, “Lift up your hearts”? Can they reply, when they depart below, into the streets, in body and in heart alike? And how will they cry out with fear and joy together, “Holy, Holy, Holy”?

In the prayer of Saint Gregory of Nyssa, *On Not Delaying Baptism*:

> I am ashamed of you, because, although you have grown old, you are still dismissed with the catechumens, etc. Join the mystical people and learn the secret utterances.  
> “Say with us those things which the six-winged seraphim, hymning together with the Christians, say.”

That is:

> Say with us those things which the six-winged seraphim say.

In the fifth mystagogical catechesis of Saint Cyril of Jerusalem:

> “Holy, holy, holy, Lord of hosts.”  
> “For this reason we utter this theology delivered to us from the seraphim, so that we may become participants with the heavenly armies in the hymn.”

[Note: What is read in the old Gallican Sacramentary appears to have been taken from the Greek: “Aios is said after Aios: You, most high God, Aios, himself holy,” etc.]

That is:

> “Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord of hosts. For this reason we utter this seraphic theology delivered to us, so that we may share in the hymn with the heavenly host.”

In the liturgies this hymn is called *epinikios* (ἐπινίκιος), that is, “victorial.” For this reason some incorrectly confuse this hymn with the *Trisagion*, which is as follows:

> “Holy God, Holy Mighty, Holy Immortal.”

That is:

> “Holy God, Holy Mighty, Holy Immortal.”

For in the liturgies they are distinguished; the Trisagion is sung when the priest first approaches the altar, as Jobius testifies in book 15, chapter 6, in Photius’s *Bibliotheca*, no. 222:

> “For this reason, as soon as the priests enter the altar, the sacred cantor cries out from above: ‘Holy God, Holy Mighty, Holy Immortal.’”

That is:

> “Therefore, as soon as the priests enter the altar, the sacred cantor cries out from the higher place: ‘Holy God, Holy Mighty, Holy Immortal’; for this is the Trisagion.”

The same may be seen in Codinus, *On the Offices of the Palace of Constantinople*:

> “Immediately they open the doors of the church, and after the Trisagion hymn the Apostle is read, and thereafter the divine liturgy is performed.”

That is:

> “Immediately they open the doors of the church, and after the Trisagion hymn has been sung, the Apostle is read, and the liturgy is performed in due order.”

But the Victorial hymn is sung after the Preface, as may be seen throughout the liturgies.

The distinction between these hymns is recognized from Saint Caesarius, brother of Saint Gregory of Nazianzus, *Dialogue 1*, question 29:

> “Neither do the holy cherubim add anything of sanctification to the divine Trinity in heaven when they cry out, ‘Holy, Holy, Holy’; nor, again, when we cry out in the Trisagion, ‘Holy God, Holy Mighty, Holy Immortal,’ does the divine being receive any addition of sanctity, strength, or immortality.”

That is:

> “Neither do the holy cherubim add anything of holiness to the Holy Trinity when they cry out without ceasing in heaven, ‘Holy, Holy, Holy’; nor, again, when we cry out in the Trisagion, ‘Holy God, Holy Mighty, Holy Immortal,’ is anything added to God—neither holiness, strength, nor immortality.”

It is no objection that Saint John of Damascus and certain others call the Victorial hymn *Trisagion*, since they speak of it outside the sacrifice of the Mass. Although it may be called *Trisagion*, it does not ordinarily receive this designation in sacred usage.

Nor does it matter that in the Ambrosian liturgy it is called the Trisagion, since, because this liturgy is not purely Ambrosian—on account of various omissions and additions—it is uncertain whether this designation came from Saint Ambrose.

But, to say something further about the Trisagion, I do not approve the opinion of those who write that it was first instituted by Proclus, Patriarch of Constantinople, so that this hymn might be sung in the sacred liturgy. They say that, when Constantinople was being punished under the reign of Theodosius the Younger by many scourges from God and was additionally shaken by a severe earthquake, the people were compelled to leave the city and withdraw into the countryside. While they were imploring divine mercy to rescue them from such evils, a certain boy was carried up into heaven in the sight of everyone, was taught this hymn by angelic ministry, and was sent back down to earth; when the whole multitude sang the hymn together, God was appeased. This is reported by Saint John of Damascus, book 3 of *The Orthodox Faith*, chapter 10; George Cedrenus, *Compendium of Histories*, in the thirtieth year of Theodosius the Younger; Theodore Balsamon, on canon 82 of the Council in Trullo; and Jobius, who reports that this hymn was then sung by the angels.

But its institution is older, for the aforementioned Saint Caesarius mentions it, as do the First Councils of Nicaea and Constantinople, according to Asclepiades, bishop of Tralles, in his letter to Peter the Fuller.

Nor was Saint John of Damascus ever of the opinion alleged by some. For he does not write that Proclus instituted the Trisagion so that it might be sung in the liturgy; rather, relying on the authority of this story and of the Council of Chalcedon, he proves only that Peter the Fuller ought not to have added to this hymn the words, “Who was crucified for us.”

For this Peter the Fuller, that is, the Antiochene bishop, added to the hymn:

> “Who was crucified for us” (ὁ σταυρωθεὶς διὰ ἡμᾶς).

That is:

> “Who were crucified for us.”

This is reported by Theodore the Reader, book 1 of the *Collectanea*; Saint John of Damascus, in the chapter cited; Asclepiades, bishop of Tralles, in the letter cited; Pope Felix, in his letter to the same Peter; and Theodore Balsamon, on the canon cited.

By this addition he intended the Trinity to have been crucified for us, as is sufficiently clear from Ephraemius, bishop of Theopolis, in his letter to Zenobius the scholasticus of Emesa, in Photius’s *Bibliotheca*, no. 228; and he was introducing a fourth person into the mystery of the Trinity, as Saint John of Damascus maintains in the chapter cited.

Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, however, in his letter to the same Peter, said that by adding *crucified for us* after “Mighty,” he was introducing two sons; and that, by adding the same words after “Immortal,” he was asserting that the Holy Spirit had been crucified, in accordance with the heresy of the Manichaeans.

The aforementioned Ephraemius says that this hymn is attributed to Christ by the Easterners; consequently, they do nothing wrong if they add, “Who was crucified for us.” But the Constantinopolitans and Westerners, applying this hymn to the Holy Trinity, altogether reject these words. In many provinces of Europe the words are indeed rejected, but the following are added:

> “Holy Trinity, have mercy on us” (ἁγία Τριάς, ἐλέησον ἡμᾶς).

But Calandio, bishop of Antioch, added to the Trisagion:

> “Christ the King” (Χριστὴ βασιλεῦ),

because of those who had added, “Who were crucified for us,” as Theodore the Reader reports in book 2 of the *Collectanea*.

### 22. “Blessed”

This is not found in the printed editions. It is nevertheless found in the Greek liturgies, and Saint Caesarius of Arles mentions it in the homily cited:

> “And with what trembling together with joy will they cry out, ‘Holy, Holy, Holy, Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord’?”

In the printed editions the following prayer follows:

> “About to commemorate the saving Victim of the whole world,” etc.,

but this is not found in our manuscript codices.

[Note: It is also absent from the Royal Swedish manuscript, from the Gemeticensis, etc. In the first Theodoric manuscript, however, in place of this prayer is read: “Prayer before Mass. Asking pardon before the altar, let him say this prayer: ‘May this service of my devotion please you, O holy Trinity, God; and grant that this sacrifice of praise, which I, unworthy, shall offer before the eyes of your Majesty, may be acceptable to you and, by your mercy, propitiatory for me and for all those for whom I shall offer it; you who live and reign, God, forever and ever. Amen.’”]

### 23. “Hosanna in the highest”

Saint Isidore mentions it in book 1, chapter 15, of *On the Ecclesiastical Offices*:

> “And ‘Hosanna in the highest’ is sung, because, when the Savior was born from the line of David, salvation reached the world even to the heights.”

### 24. “Therefore, most merciful Father,” etc.

Haymo mentions this prayer in his commentary on 1 Timothy 2.

This prayer is commonly called the Canon; this designation is found in Saint Gregory, book 7 of the *Register*, letter 64—now book 9, letter 12:

> “Because you have decreed that the Lord’s Prayer be said after the Canon.”

In the same passage he also calls it a *prayer* and says that it was composed by a certain scholasticus. Who that scholasticus was, however, is uncertain.

Some attribute it to Voconius, bishop of Castellum in Mauretania; others to Musaeus, a presbyter of Massilia, who composed books of Sacraments, concerning whom Gennadius writes in his *Catalogue of Illustrious Men*. But it can be attributed to neither, because it is older than they were: Saint Ambrose cites much from it, and Optatus of Milevis cites some passages, as will be seen below; both lived before the authors mentioned.

As we have said, this prayer is called the Canon, and also the *action*. Walafrid Strabo gives the reason for both names in chapter 22 of *On Ecclesiastical Matters*:

> “It is called the Action because the Lord’s sacraments are effected in it; but the Canon is called the same Action because in it there is the lawful and regular accomplishment of the sacraments.”

### 25. “We humbly beseech you,” etc.

These words are absent from Haymo’s commentary on 1 Timothy 2:

> “When the priest begins to consecrate the mysteries of the Lord’s body and blood, saying: ‘Therefore, most merciful Father, we ask you.’”

### 26. “These gifts, these offerings, these holy sacrifices”

This may be a case of synonymy. An old manuscript exposition of the Canon of the Mass from the Corbie library distinguishes these terms as follows:

> “Gifts are things bestowed voluntarily; offerings are things offered in return for some gift or recompense, as we offer them to God so that our sins may be forgiven; sacrifices are things which are consecrated together with prayers.”

An old manuscript treatise on the Mass from the same library distinguishes them thus:

> “A gift belongs to the giver, an offering to the recipient, because the former is named from giving, the latter from furnishing or bestowing. Yet properly ‘gifts’ are what are given to God; ‘offerings’ belong to everyone, because they are given or received by hand. Nevertheless, in this passage both gifts and offerings are offered to God. ‘Sacrifices’ means sacred things made so, because they are consecrated by mystical prayer.”

These explanations are largely taken from Saint Isidore, book 6 of the *Etymologies*, chapter 19, where he adds that offerings are called *munera* because the poor offer services to the rich in place of gifts.

Fortunatus seems to allude to this in book 4 of *The Life of Saint Martin*:

> When he placed God’s unblemished gifts upon the altar,  
> and the astonished Father consecrated the sacred rite,  
> or the priest blessed the offerings of Christ with his mouth.

Here *ceremonia* means sacrifices. The old manuscript glosses have:

> “Ceremonia: sacred things of the gods or temples.”

There, therefore, you see gifts, offerings, and sacrifices.

### 27. “Unblemished”

That is, whole and undefiled.

### 28. “Which we offer to you,” etc.

Agobard mentions these words of the Canon in his letter to the emperor Louis the Pious:

> “Finally, when the blessed Pope Pelagius was rebuking certain bishops because they omitted his name in the Action of the sacred mystery, in the solemn celebrations of the Mass—specifically at the beginning, where we customarily say: ‘In the first place, the things which we offer to you for your holy Catholic Church, which may you deign to pacify, guard, unite, and govern throughout the whole world, together with your servant, our pope’—he said to those same bishops: ‘I am greatly astonished at your division from the universal Church, which I cannot endure with any toleration.’”

### 29. “For your holy Catholic Church”

The Africans added to their Canon, “which is one,” as is clear from Optatus of Milevis, book 2:

> “For who could doubt that you cannot omit that legitimate phrase in the mystery of the sacraments? You say that you offer for the Church, which is one; this very claim is part of the falsehood, to call it one when you have made it two.”

### 30. “Pacify”

Thus in the liturgy of Saint Basil:

> “Remember, Lord, the Catholic and apostolic Church,” etc.,  
> “and pacify it” (καὶ εἰρήνευσον αὐτήν).

To this belong the words of Saint Cyril in the catechesis cited above:

> “We beseech God for the common peace of the Churches” (Παρακαλοῦμεν τὸν θεὸν ὑπὲρ κοινῆς τῶν ἐκκλησιῶν εἰρήνης).

That is:

> “We implore God for the common peace of the Churches.”

### 31. “Unite”

So that all believers may have one heart and one soul.

### 32. “Throughout the whole world”

To this belong the words of Optatus of Milevis, book 2:

> “And you say that you offer vows for the one Church, which is spread throughout the whole world.”

### 33. “For our king”

A prayer for kings, emperors, and princes is found in all the liturgies, in accordance with the ancient custom touched upon by Saint Cyril in the catechesis cited above:

> “We beseech,” etc., “for the kings” (ὑπὲρ τῶν βασιλέων).

That is:

> “We pray,” etc., “for the kings.”

Tertullian, book *To Scapula*:

> “Accordingly, we sacrifice for the emperor’s safety, but to our God, who is his as well.”

And Saint Ambrose, book 4 of *On the Sacraments*, chapter 4:

> “In what words and speeches, then, is the consecration made? In those of Jesus Christ. For all the other things that are said are offered as praise to God. Prayer is made for the people, for kings, and for the rest.”

This is in accordance with the teaching of Saint Paul in 1 Timothy 2.

### 34. “And for all the Orthodox,” etc.

These words are absent from the Rouen Pontifical manuscript on the Thursday of Holy Week. Micrologus, in *Ecclesiastical Observations*, chapter 13, writes that these words are superfluous in the Canon:

> “Likewise, after the name of the lord pope or of their own bishop, they add: ‘and for all the orthodox and worshipers of the Catholic and apostolic faith’; but this is superfluous. For the order immediately following, where it says, ‘Remember, Lord, your male and female servants,’ grants us permission to commemorate whichever living persons we wish.”

In chapter 23, when describing the Canon, he omits these words—but unjustly, for they are found in our manuscript codices, those of Rheims and Rodrada, and in this manuscript of Saint Eligius, as well as in the Greek version of George Codinus.

Micrologus’s argument is not valid. By these words, “and for all the Orthodox,” etc., a general commemoration is made of all the faithful who are living; in the following words, “Remember,” etc., the commemoration is specific: of those who offer and of certain particular persons whose names were formerly read from the diptychs.

### 35. “Those standing around”

Thus it is found in the printed editions, in the Tilianus Codex, in Illyricus’s Mass, and in all our manuscript codices. It is likewise found in the oldest manuscript exposition of the Canon of the Mass in the Corbie library, and in the very old manuscript treatise on the Mass from the same library.

So too in Burchard, book 3, chapter 68, from the Council of Nantes:

> “To whom does the Lord say, ‘The Lord be with you,’ or ‘Lift up your hearts,’ or ‘Let us give thanks to the Lord our God,’ when there is no one to answer? And in the Canon, ‘and of all those standing around,’ when there is no one?”

So also in Master Florus’s exposition of the Mass:

> “Then is added, ‘and of all those standing around.’”

And in the manuscript glosses on the Roman Order from the Thuana library:

> “and of all those standing around.”

In the commonly circulated Missals, however, it reads *circumstantium* (“of those standing around”).

### 36. “Who offer it to you”

Thus it is found in all our manuscript codices, in the printed editions, and in both of the manuscript treatises from the Corbie library cited shortly before.

So too in Micrologus, chapter 23 of *Ecclesiastical Observations*:

> “And note the devotion: ‘who offer this sacrifice of praise to you.’”

He confirms this reading in chapter 13, rejecting what is commonly found:

> “For whom we offer it to you.”

He says:

> “Likewise, after a little they add, ‘For whom we offer it to you,’ although in the older and more reliable Sacramentaries those who offer are found there only in the third person.”

Usage nevertheless established the reading in Roman and other commonly circulated Missals:

> “For whom we offer it to you,”

or:

> “who offer it to you,”

where the disjunctive particle *vel* (“or”) is used in place of the copulative *et* (“and”), as often happens, as we have observed more than once in our notes to the *Concordance of the Rules*.

### 37. “Their vows”

Saint Augustine explains what *votum* means here in letter 59 to Paulinus, now letter 49:

> “Moreover, if, as I said, εὐχή is more commonly called *votum* in Scripture, apart from the name *prayer*, it is properly understood as the prayer which we make as a vow, that is, πρὸς εὐχήν.”

Everything offered to God is vowed, especially the offering of the holy altar, by which sacrament our other great vow is proclaimed: the vow by which we promise to remain in Christ, namely, in the structure of Christ’s body.

Among the pagans also, vows are sacred prayers:

> [lacuna] you cease from vows and prayers.

### 38. “Being in communion”

Namely, with the memory of the saints, because the Church militant shares communion with the Church triumphant.

### 39. “And venerating their memory”

In all the liturgies there is a commemoration of the saints, in accordance with ancient custom. For this sacrifice cannot be offered except in communion with the saints, whose memory we share as children with their fathers and as followers with those who went before, as Alcuin teaches in chapter 1 of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*.

This custom may be seen in the fifth mystagogical catechesis of Saint Cyril of Jerusalem:

> “And we offer this sacrifice to you, so that we may remember those who have fallen asleep before us: first, patriarchs, prophets, apostles, and martyrs, so that God may receive our petitions through their prayers and intercessions.”

That is:

> “And we offer this sacrifice to you so that we may also remember those who fell asleep before us, especially the patriarchs, prophets, apostles, and martyrs, so that God may receive our prayers through their prayers and supplications.”

From this one should understand the words of Optatus, book 3, concerning Marculus and Donatus, who were killed by Macarius and whom the Donatists included in the list of their martyrs:

> “Against my will I am compelled at this point to mention even those men whom I do not wish to mention, whom you place among the martyrs, through whom, as though through the sole religion of your communion, your people swear. I would indeed prefer to pass them over in silence; but the cause of truth does not allow itself to be silenced, and from the very names themselves envy foolishly barks against the truth.”

The meaning is:

> “I would prefer to dismiss these false martyrs; but your envy foolishly barks against the Catholic Church from the very names themselves, namely, by reciting the names of these false martyrs in your sacrifices.”

### 40. “Thaddaeus’s”

Thus in the Codex of Ratoldus and that of Rodrada. In the Rheims Codex, *Tatdei*. In the printed editions, *Tatthaei*, incorrectly.

### 41. “Sixtus’s”

This term will be discussed below.

### 42. “Hilary, Martin, etc.”

In the Rheims Codex these names are added:

> “Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius; Hilary, Martin, Remigius, Augustine, Gregory, Jerome, Benedict.”

In Ratoldus’s Codex:

> “Nicasius, Hilary, Martin, Benedict, Gregory, Amandus, Remigius.”

[Note: In the Gemeticensis: “Cosmas and Damian, George, Benedict, Martin, Gregory, and all the saints.” In the first Theodoric manuscript: “Cosmas and Damian, and those whose triumph is celebrated today in the sight of your glory.” In the second Theodoric manuscript: “Cosmas and Damian, Hilary the martyr, Benedict, Gregory, Amandus, Medard, Eligius.”]

In the liturgies of Saint Basil and Saint John Chrysostom, the name of the saint whose memory or feast is celebrated on that day is added:

> “of this saint, whose memory we also celebrate” (ἁγίου τοῦδε, οὗ καὶ τὴν μνήμην ἐπιτελοῦμεν).

That is:

> “and of that saint whose memory we also celebrate.”

This was likewise formerly used at times in the Latin Church, as may be seen in the treatise *How Certain Prayers and Crosses Are to Be Made in the “Te igitur”*, in the Tilianus Codex and in Hittorp:

> “If it is the birthday of saints, let him say here: ‘And also the day of the birth of those blessed ones,’ or ‘of that blessed one.’”

But Pope Gregory III ordered the following to be added:

> “Whose solemnity is celebrated today in the sight of your Majesty, Lord our God, throughout the whole world,”

as Orderic Vitalis reports in book 2 of his *Ecclesiastical History*.

### 43. “By whose merits”

Thus in Codinus’s version; in the liturgy attributed to Saint Peter:

> “by whose intercession” (ὧν τίνων τῇ πρεσβείᾳ).

That is:

> “by whose intercession.”

### 44. “And order our days in your peace”

[Note: Bede teaches this especially in book 2, chapter 1, of his *History*.]

These words are said to have been inserted into the Canon by Saint Gregory. In the Rheims Codex it reads *dispone* (“order”).

### 45. “To rescue”

Thus it is commonly found. Alcuin reads *ereptos* (“rescued”). The Rheims Codex has *eripe* (“rescue”).

Moreover, in the Mass published by Illyricus, the Canon differs greatly in many respects from the common Canon, as follows:

#### Within the Action

> “In the first place, together with your servant, our pope N., and for all the orthodox and worshipers of the apostolic faith, bishops, abbots, governors, and rulers of the holy Church of God, and for all the holy people of God.
>
> “Remember, Lord, your male and female servants, namely all those joined to me by blood relationship, familiarity, and friendship, and all those who confess their sins to me, refresh me with good things in your name, and all those standing around.
>
> “Also receive, I beseech you, this offering of my humility and devotion, which I offer to you for the correction and forgiveness of my sins and criminal actions, for the dissolution and illumination of the blind and stony hardness of my heart. Receive it, I beseech you, Lord, in your favor, and spread over me the bosom of your mercy; enlighten me, open my understanding, grant me the Spirit for amendment, and, through the lamentation of repentance, grant me, miserable as I am, an avenue of return to you. Through Christ our Lord.
>
> “Which offering, O God, we beseech you, in all things…”

Thus far the Mass of Illyricus. Nevertheless, the phrase *Within the Action* ought to be prefixed to the words:

> “Also this offering,” etc.,

as it is found in the other Canons.

### 46. “Blessed”

That is, consecrated. To bless means to consecrate, in accordance with Paul’s words in 1 Corinthians 10:

> “The cup of blessing which we bless,” etc.

### 47. “Accepted into the number”

That is, received among the things pleasing to you, as Master Florus explains; the exposition of the Preface and Canon of the Mass from the Corbie library cited above follows him:

> “That is, assigned so that it may please you.”

The manuscript treatise cited above explains it thus:

> “Assigned to the heavenly table.”

This word is found in the printed editions and in all our manuscript codices, as in the Roman Missals and also in the Greek version of George Codinus, as well as in Saint Ambrose, book 4 of *On the Sacraments*, chapter 5.

In the liturgy believed to belong to Saint Peter it is incorrectly read as:

> “unbounded, incomprehensible” (ἀπερίγραπτον).

Hesychius gives:

> “incomprehensible” (ἀπέγραπτον, ἀπερινόητον).

### 48. “Ratified”

That is, perpetual with immovable firmness, according to Florus.

In the manuscript treatise cited above on the Mass:

> “Firmly solidified.”

And in the cited manuscript exposition of the Preface and Canon:

> “That is, judged, so that he may judge it worthy to be offered in his sight.”

Thus it is read in the printed editions and in our manuscript codices, as in the Roman Missal and in Micrologus.

[Note: This word now appears, having been restored by our editors in the new edition from several manuscripts. On the words of the Canon, read the notes in book 4 of *On the Sacraments* of Ambrose, volume 2, column 365 and following.]

Saint Ambrose does not have it.

Fortunatus called the altar gifts *ratified* in book 4 of *The Life of Saint Martin*:

> “Or the priest blessed the offerings of Christ with his mouth,  
> ratified as the body and blood placed upon another.”

In Codinus’s version it is *βεβαίαν*, that is, “firm” or “ratified.” In the liturgy commonly called Saint Peter’s it is *ἐράσμιον*, that is, “pleasing” or “lovable.” From this it is clear that the translator or author of that liturgy used a corrupt manuscript in which “pleasing” was read instead of “ratified.”

### 49. “Reasonable”

Thus in the printed editions, the Roman Missal, and all our codices. So too in Saint Ambrose, in the chapter cited.

In Codinus’s version:

> “rational” (λογικήν).

That is:

> “rational.”

In the liturgy circulated under the name of Saint Peter:

> “excusable” (εὐαπολόγητον).

The term is likewise explained in the old Greek-Latin glosses:

> “εὐαπολόγητος: excusable.”

But what this word means in that liturgy I do not sufficiently understand.

As for “rational,” the treatise cited above explains it as:

> “performed with reason.”

The exposition of the Preface and Canon cited above explains it in this way:

> “That is, may he deign to make it full in just reason.”

Some interpret it as:

> “offered with reason and discernment.”

Florus explains it as:

> “full, namely, of reason; full of mystery.”

Paschasius interprets all these terms in this way in book 12 of *On the Body and Blood of Christ*:

> “We ask that he make this offering blessed, through which we may be blessed; accepted into the number, through which we may all be enrolled in heaven; ratified, through which we may be reckoned within Christ’s inmost being; reasonable, through which we may be stripped of bestial understanding; and acceptable, so that through that by which we have displeased within ourselves we may become acceptable in his only Son.”

In this Codex of Saint Eligius, no crosses of the sort customarily drawn appear in these words or in other parts of this Canon. I nevertheless restored some of them as I found them in the printed editions.

They are found, however, in the Rheims Codex and in that of Rodrada,

[Note: Add also the Gemeticensis and the two Theodoric manuscripts. They are absent from the Codex of the Queen of Sweden.]

and also in other Canons of this Codex of Saint Eligius that occur on certain feasts, namely in the same places where they are drawn in the Roman Missal and indicated by Micrologus and certain other authors who wrote about the Mass.

And rightly so, for it is an ancient custom of the Church that the offerings be blessed by the sign of the cross, as may be seen in Saint Augustine, sermon 19, *On the Saints*:

> “By the sign of the cross basilicas are dedicated, altars are consecrated, and the sacraments of the altar are effected with the Lord’s words interposed.”

And in sermon 18, *On the Season*:

> “For by this sign of the cross the Lord’s body is consecrated.”

And in tractate 118 on John:

> “Unless this sign is applied, whether to the foreheads of believers—and shortly afterward—whether to the sacrifice by which they are nourished, none of these things is rightly accomplished.”

From this one should understand the words of Fortunatus, book 3 of *The Life of Saint Martin*:

> “When with his hands he blessed the holocausts of the sacred altar.”

The same may be seen in the letter of the bishops from the synod at Quierzy, sent to Louis, king of Germany, chapter 15:

> “For it is abominable that the hand anointed with sacred chrism—which, through prayer and the sign of the cross, makes from bread and wine mixed with water the body and sacrament of the blood of Christ—should, after episcopal ordination, touch secular sacrament in any way, whatever it may have done before ordination.”

Ivo of Chartres also mentions crosses after the consecration in letter 233:

> “When, however, with the Host already consecrated, the sign of the cross is impressed within or above the chalice, from the eastern side of the chalice to the western, and from the northern to the southern, we understand this to signify what the Lord foretold to his disciples before his Passion in commendation of his Passion: ‘And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw everything to myself.’ The Host that is signed beside the chalice ought likewise to be placed so that, by the position of itself and of the chalice, it represents Christ’s right side.”

How such crosses are to be made is taught in an ancient synod commonly attributed to Saint Ulrich, bishop of Augsburg, found in a manuscript codex of the monastery of Neresheim written in the year of Christ 1009, canon 19:

> “Sign the chalice and the offering with a straight cross. That is, not in a circle or with a movement of the fingers, as many of you do, but with two fingers held straight and the thumb folded inward, through which the Trinity is signified. Strive to make this sign correctly, for otherwise you cannot bless anything.”

### 50. “The day before he suffered”

Thus Saint Ambrose has it in the chapter cited.

### 51. “He took bread into his holy and venerable hands”

Saint Ambrose, in the chapter cited:

> “In his holy hands he took bread.”

### 52. “With eyes lifted,” etc.

Saint Ambrose, in the chapter cited:

> “He looked up to heaven, to you, almighty Father, eternal God.”

In the Roman Missal, in Codinus’s version, and in Rodrada’s Codex, the copulative conjunction is prefixed; but in the liturgy circulated under the name of Saint Peter and in our other manuscript codices, it is not.

This rite observed by Christ is found in the liturgies of Saints Peter, James, and Mark, and rightly so. For when Christ was about to give thanks to the Father, he customarily raised his eyes toward heaven, as may be seen in Matthew 14, Luke 9, Mark 6, and John 11.

Therefore there is no doubt that he did the same in this most sacred action, even though it is not found written in the New Testament.

### 53. “He gave”

Thus in the printed editions, in our other manuscript codices, and in the Mass of Saint Peter. But in the Roman Missal and in Matthew 26 it reads *deditque* (“and he gave”). The copulative conjunction is also inserted in Codinus’s version.

### 54. “From this, all”

Thus in Saint Ambrose. These words do not occur in the liturgy of Saint Peter, in Codinus’s version, or in the New Testament.

### 55. “For this is my body”

[Note: It may not be irrelevant to observe that the author of the book *On the Sacraments*, who is praised here, clearly attributes the consecration of the Eucharist and the conversion of bread and wine into Christ’s body and blood to these words: “For this is my body,” and to these: “For this is my blood.” Tertullian preceded him, for in book 4 of *Against Marcion*, chapter 40, he says: “Having taken bread and distributed it to his disciples, he made it his body, saying, ‘This is my body.’”]

The particle *enim* (“for”) is found in Saint Ambrose, in the chapter cited, and in the liturgy of Saint Mark. It is absent, however, from the other liturgies, from sacred Scripture, and from Codinus’s version.

### 56. “This”

This word does not occur in sacred Scripture, in Saint Ambrose, or in the liturgies; but it is found in Codinus’s version.

It is added to signify that the priest performs the same sacrifice that Christ performed, in accordance with Paul’s words in 1 Corinthians 10:

> “We partake of one bread and of one cup.”
