For there is one altar and one sacrifice in the Church.

### 57. “Splendid”

In Codinus’s version:

> “most splendid” (λαμπρότατον).

It does not occur in Saint Ambrose, in the liturgies, or in the New Testament. Nevertheless, the epithet is taken from Psalm 22:

> “My cup that makes me drunk—how splendid it is!”

### 58. “He gave”

Thus in the printed editions, in our other manuscript codices, and in the Mass of Saint Peter. In the Roman Missal it reads *deditque* (“and he gave”). In Matthew 26 it is *dedit* (“he gave”), as in Codinus’s version.

### 59. “This is the cup of my blood,” etc.

The particle *enim* (“for”) is found in Matthew 26. This formula of words by which the chalice is blessed, however, is not found in sacred Scripture or in the liturgies.

It is found in Codinus’s version and is excellent, because it contains the meaning of the other formulas found in the Evangelists and in Saint Paul.

In Saint Ambrose, in the chapter cited, the following form of the consecration of the chalice is found:

> “For this is my blood,”

from Matthew 26 and Mark 14.

### 60. “The mystery of faith”

These words are not found in the Roman Order. They occur in Codinus’s version:

> “the mystery of faith” (τὸ μυστήριον τῆς πίστεως).

### 61. “Therefore, remembering also”

In Saint Ambrose, book 4 of *On the Sacraments*, chapter 6, the particle *et* (“and”) is absent, although the verb *sumus* (“we are”) is present. The verb nevertheless occurs in the Rheims and Tilianus Codices, in the treatise on the Mass from the Corbie library, and in Master Florus’s exposition.

The words “of his glorious Ascension” should be enclosed by a point.

This commemoration of the Passion, Resurrection of Christ, and so forth, is found in all the liturgies. Saint Ambrose touches upon it in the chapter cited:

> “And the priest says: ‘Therefore, remembering his most glorious Passion, his Resurrection from the dead, and his Ascension into heaven…’”

### 62. “From your gifts and grants”

In the liturgies of Saints Basil and Chrysostom:

> “We offer to you your own gifts from your own” (τὰ σὰ ἐκ τῶν σῶν σοι προσφέρομεν).

That is:

> “We offer to you your own gifts from your own.”

The emperor Justinian appears to allude to this in the inscription on the table he made from all the precious things found on land and sea:

> “Your own gifts from your own we offer to you, your servants, Christ—Justinian and Theodora” (τὰ σὰ ἐκ τῶν σῶν σοι προσφέρομεν οἱ δοῦλοί σου, Χριστὲ, Ἰουστινιανὸς καὶ Θεοδώρα),

as Cedrenus writes.

### 63. “A pure victim,” etc.

In the chapter of Saint Ambrose cited above it reads:

> “This spotless victim, reasonable victim, bloodless victim, this holy bread, and the cup of eternal life.”

“Pure victim”: Saint Irenaeus, book 4 of *Against Heresies*, chapter 34:

> “And this offering the Church alone offers pure.”

### 64. “An immaculate victim”

Fortunatus appears to look to this in book 4 of *The Life of Saint Martin*:

> “When he placed God’s immaculate gifts upon the altar.”

### 65. “As you deigned to accept”

Saint Ambrose, in the chapter cited:

> “As you deigned to receive.”

### 66. “Your supreme priest”

In Saint Ambrose, in the chapter cited, the pronoun *your* is absent.

### 67. “Command that these things be carried”

Not Christ’s body itself, but the memory of the Passion, the faith, prayers, and vows of the faithful.

Paschasius understands it differently in book 12 of *On the Body and Blood of Christ*:

> “Why does it ask that these things be carried there, unless it is understood that these things take place in his priesthood?”

### 68. “Upon your sublime altar”

Saint Ambrose, in the chapter cited, has:

> “May you receive them upon your sublime altar.”

The altar is used metaphorically in this passage.

### 69. Over the diptychs

These words [Note: They are also missing in the two Theodulf manuscripts. In both of them, and in the Gemet manuscript, before “Remember also,” etc., the following prayer is read:], which were missing here, I restored from the printed editions:

> Remember me, I ask, Lord, and have mercy, although these holy sacrifices are unworthily offered to you, holy Father almighty, eternal God, by my hands—I who am not worthy even to invoke your holy and venerable name. But since they are offered in honor, praise, and memory of your most glorious and beloved Son, our Lord God Jesus Christ, may they be kindled like incense in the presence of your divine Majesty with a sweet fragrance. Through Christ our Lord.

Ancient glosses in manuscripts of the Corbie library explain *diptychs* as tablets:

> Diptychs are tablets that properly have two folds,

as Ausonius says, *Epigram* 137, “a writing-tablet open on both sides.” Sacred diptychs are tablets on which the names of living and departed faithful were written, whose commemoration took place during Mass. See our observations on the *Harmony of the Rules*, chapter 4, § 4.

### 70. Remember

This commemoration of the dead is likewise absent from this manuscript of Saint Eligius, but I restored it from the printed editions. Nevertheless, it exists in this manuscript of Saint Eligius in another Canon, appointed for the Thursday of the Lord’s Supper.

This commemoration of the dead is found in all liturgies, according to the ancient custom of the Church, which has always been concerned that prayer for the departed faithful should have its place in this liturgical sacrifice, as can be seen in the oft-cited catechesis of Saint Cyril:

> Then also for the departed holy fathers and bishops, and for all our departed generally, we pray, believing that the greatest benefit will come to their souls, for whom the supplication is offered during the holy and most awe-inspiring sacrifice set before us.

Saint Augustine likewise says in *On Care for the Dead*, chapter 1:

> In the books of the Maccabees we read that a sacrifice was offered for the dead. But even if it were nowhere at all found in the ancient Scriptures, the authority of the universal Church, which shines forth in this custom, is not slight; for in the prayers of the priest, poured out before the Lord God at the altar, the commemoration and commendation of the dead have their appointed place.

And in *Confessions*, book IX, chapter 11, Saint Monica says:

> I ask only this: that you remember me at the Lord’s altar, wherever you may be.

One may add this notable passage from Cyprian, letter 1 in the new edition, formerly letter 66:

> Our predecessors, the bishops, decreed that no brother departing this life should name a cleric for his protection or care; and if anyone did so, no offering should be made for him, nor should a sacrifice be celebrated for his repose. For he does not deserve to be named before God’s altar in the priestly prayer who wished to draw priests and ministers away from the altar, and so forth.

You see that this custom is much older than Cyprian. Indeed, Tertullian mentions it in *On the Crown of the Soldier*, chapter 3; *On the Exhortation to Chastity*, chapter 2; and *On Monogamy*, chapter 10.

### 71. And they sleep in the sleep of peace

The souls for whom prayer is offered here are said to sleep in the sleep of peace—not because they have been exempted from the punishment of purgatory, but because they are no longer troubled by any disturbance of mind, nor pierced by the goads of vices, as they await eternal life in complete security.

### 72. And all who rest in Christ

The preceding commemoration concerns those whose names have been recited from the diptychs; this one concerns those of whom there is no remembrance among human beings, whether because they lack parents or friends. Saint Augustine speaks of this in *On Care for the Dead*, chapter 4:

> Supplications for the spirits of the dead are not to be omitted. The Church has undertaken to offer them for all who have died within the Christian Catholic fellowship, even without mentioning any names, under a general commemoration, so that those whose parents, children, relatives, or friends are lacking to perform such duties may have them provided by the one common mother.

### 73. John

Here Saint John the Baptist seems to be intended. He is also mentioned in the liturgies of Saints Basil and Chrysostom after the consecration.

### 74. Stephen

Saint Stephen is placed here before Saint Matthias because he suffered martyrdom before him; Matthias too is regarded as equal to the apostles.

### 75. Alexander

This is Alexander I, pope and martyr.

### 76. Agatha, Lucy

The following passage of Saint Aldhelm, bishop of Sherborne, in chapter 25 of *On Virginity*, is relevant:

> It also seems worthwhile to me that the reports of Saint Agatha should be followed by the praises of the most chaste virgin Lucy. Our teacher and preceptor Gregory is known to have joined them together in the daily Canon, when the solemn rites of Mass are celebrated, placing them together in the catalogue of martyrs in this order: Felicity, Anastasia, Agatha, Lucy, and so forth.

[Note: The old Gallican Sacramentary likewise reads *Agathae, Agne*, though in the reverse order, for Agnes precedes Agatha in that manuscript. In the ancient Carthaginian Calendar published at the end of the *Acts of the Martyrs* by our Theodoric Ruinart, one reads: “On the Nones of February, Saint Agatha, martyr.”]

Our manuscript, however, by saying *Agatha*, follows the Greek inflection.

### 77. Agnes

Thus it appears in the Rheims manuscript; this name will be discussed below.

### 78. Anastasia

In the Tilius manuscript, Euphemia is added. In the liturgy said to be that of Saint Peter, Barbara and Juliana are also added.

In the Gemet manuscript, after Anastasia, the names of Saints Æthelthryth and Gertrude are read. The old Gallican Sacramentary, after Saint Lucy, mentions only Eugenia.

### 79. Merit

That is, demerit or sin. For immediately afterward it says, “But the giver of pardon.” This interpretation is supported by an old manuscript exposition of the Preface and Canon of the Mass in the Corbie library:

> Let him not reckon the recompense of sins, but let him himself be the giver of pardon.

Sometimes *merit* is used for sin. Saint Augustine says in *On Care for the Dead*, chapter 1:

> Whose merits are so evil.

### 80. All these good things

These are the things consecrated upon these altars, says Florus.

### 81. You sanctify

You make holy from earthly substance. Thus Bishop Firmilian, in his letter to Cyprian, spoke of sanctifying the bread; Saint Cyprian himself, in letter 63, spoke of sanctifying the chalice.

### 82. You give life

That is, you transform inanimate bread into the living body of Christ, says Odo of Cambrai in his exposition of the Canon of the Mass.

### 83. Instructed by saving precepts, and so forth

Saint Jerome touches upon this formula as a preamble to the Lord’s Prayer in book III *Against the Pelagians*:

> Thus he taught his apostles that every day, in the sacrifice of his body, believers might dare to say, “Our Father,” and so forth.

From this the antiquity of the formula is established.

### 84. Our Father, and so forth

It is an ancient and apostolic custom that the Lord’s Prayer be recited over Christ’s body, as is known from all the liturgies, from Saint Gregory, book VII of the *Register*, letter 63 [now book IX, letter 12], and from Saint Jerome, cited above.

Its use is also evident from Saint Ambrose, *On the Sacraments*, book V, chapter 4; and from Saint Anastasius the Sinaite, in his sermon *On the Synaxis*:

> What greater ruin is there than not only to lie to Christ during that fearful hour of the divine assembly, but also to retain anger against one’s brothers, although they say in prayer, “And forgive us our debts,” and so forth?

Saint Anastasius means:

> What greater destruction is there than not only to lie to Christ at that fearful hour of the divine synaxis, but also to hold a grudge against one’s brothers, even though they say in prayer, “Forgive us our debts,” and so forth?

Saint Augustine says in letter 59 to Paulinus:

> Let us understand as prayers those which we offer in the celebration of the sacraments, before what is on the Lord’s table begins to be blessed; prayers said while it is blessed and sanctified and broken for distribution. Nearly the whole Church concludes this entire petition with the Lord’s Prayer.

Optatus of Milevis says in book II *Against Parmenianus*:

> For during the intervening moments, while you lay on hands and forgive sins, immediately afterward, when you have turned toward the altar, you cannot omit the Lord’s Prayer; and certainly you say, “Father who are in heaven, forgive us our debts and our sins.”

Saint Cyprian, in his book *On Prayer*, says that, out of reverence, a preface was placed before the Lord’s Prayer; and this was certainly said only in the sacrifice of the Mass.

So too Tertullian, in *On Prayer*, after explaining the Lord’s Prayer, treats the remaining matters as pertaining to the sacrifice of the Mass. Saint Caesarius of Arles, in homily 12, speaking of the sacrifice of the Mass, says:

> Or when the Lord’s Prayer is said, who is there who humbly and truthfully cries out, “Forgive us our debts”?

It is rightly that this Prayer follows the commemoration of the dead in these Sacramentaries, because ancient custom requires this, as can be seen in Saint Cyril’s fifth *Mystagogical Catechesis*:

> After these things we say that prayer which the Savior delivered to his own disciples.

That is:

> After these things—namely, the commemoration of the faithful departed—we say that prayer which the Savior delivered to his disciples.

Accordingly, it follows the Canon in all liturgies, because, as Saint Augustine correctly observes in the passage cited, nearly the whole Church concludes the entire petition with the Lord’s Prayer.

In former times the priest added the following words to this Prayer. They are not found in this Canon, but Saint Ambrose reports them in *On the Sacraments*, book VI, chapter 5:

> Listen to what the priest says next: “Through our Lord Jesus Christ, in whom, and with whom, you have honor, praise, glory, magnificence, and power with the Holy Spirit, from ages past, and now, and always, and throughout the ages of ages.”

Observe that the formula “and now and always” follows the Greek rite, whose usage did not place before it the words “as it was in the beginning,” as we noted in our *Harmony of the Rules*.

In the liturgies of Saints James, Basil, and Chrysostom, these words are appended to the Prayer:

> For yours is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, now and always, and throughout the ages of ages.

That is:

> For yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, now and always, and throughout the ages of ages.

This explains Saint Caesarius, *Dialogue* 1, question 29:

> Following the angel, we too, as it were, strengthen Christ victoriously at the time of the divine celebration of the mystical rite, crying out, “Yours is the might, and the kingdom, and the power, and the glory.”

That is:

> Imitating this angel, we too, insofar as we can, cry out victoriously at the time of the mystical sacrifice, “Yours is the strength, and the kingdom, and the power, and the glory.”

### 85. And with the blessed

Thus in the manuscripts of Rodriguez and Ratoldus. In the Roman Missal: “with the blessed.”

### 86. And Andrew

In the Tilius manuscript, the following is added: “and also with your blessed martyrs Gervasius and Protasius.” They are the patrons of that church, to which this Tilius manuscript once belonged—namely, the church of Salaria, as we stated in the preface.

In the second Theodulf manuscript, after “and Andrew,” the following is added:

> and also with your holy martyrs Stephen, Quentin, and Nicasius, and with your blessed confessors Gregory, Medard, and Eligius, together with all…

### 87. And also with blessed Stephen

These words are not found in the printed editions. Formerly, however, after the words “and Andrew,” it was permissible to add any saints, as is clear from the Tilius manuscript.

From “Deliver us” through “Peter and Paul,” he names whichever and however many saints he wishes. Here *how many* means “as many as.” The *Micrologus*, chapter 25, likewise says:

> And Andrew. Here he names as many saints as he wishes.

### 88. Lamb of God

Pope Sergius I ordered this Prayer to be sung during Mass, as Anastasius reports in his Life:

> He decreed that, at the time of the breaking of the Lord’s body, “Lamb of God, who take away the sins of the world, have mercy on us” should be sung by the clergy and people.

Walfridus Strabo says the same in *On Ecclesiastical Matters*, chapter 22.

Here the order of the Mass ends both in our manuscript of Saint Eligius, in the manuscript of Rodriguez, and in the printed editions.

In the Swedish Royal manuscript, “Lamb of God” and the following are absent. In the Gemet manuscript, after “Lamb of God,” the Canon of the Mass ends.

In the first Theodulf manuscript the following is added:

> Lamb of God, who take away the sins of the world, grant us peace. [lacuna] May this most holy mingling of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ be salvation of mind and body for me and for all who receive it, and a saving preparation for attaining eternal life. Amen. [lacuna] After the peace, let him say inwardly: “May the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, guard our hearts and our minds.” Amen. [lacuna] For giving the peace: [lacuna] “Peace be with you.” [lacuna] After the peace: “May the peace and charity of God remain always in our hearts.” Amen. Prayer: “Lord Jesus Christ, who said to your apostles,” and so forth, as in the Missal. Four prayers follow.

Having explained these matters, it will not be inappropriate to append certain material from the Tilius manuscript concerning the ancient ceremonies used in reciting this Canon, as follows:

> “Therefore, most merciful Father,” through “have and bless these gifts”: Here he signs the offering and the chalice three times, not with one cross over both, but separately, making one cross over each.
>
> “These gifts, these offerings, these holy and unblemished sacrifices,” through “Remember, Lord”: Here the names of the living may be commemorated, if you wish, but not on the Lord’s Day, only on the other days.
>
> “And all who are standing around,” through “Cosmas and Damian”: If it is the feast of saints, here he says, “And the day of the birth of those blessed persons,” or “of that blessed person”; and “and of all the saints,” through “through Christ our Lord.”
>
> Here he bows toward the altar, saying, “We humbly beseech you, almighty God,” through “command us to be numbered among the flock,” through Christ our Lord. Here he raises himself upright.
>
> Here he blesses only the offering: “Which offering, O God, we ask you graciously to make in all respects blessed, approved, ratified, reasonable, and acceptable.”
>
> Here he signs both—that is, the offering and the chalice—“so that it may become for us the body and blood,” through “almighty,” “giving thanks to you, he blessed it, broke it, and gave it to his disciples, saying,” through “again giving thanks to you, he blessed it.”
>
> Here he sanctifies [read: signs] the offering alone four times. On the fifth occasion, making a cross over the chalice alone, he says: “A pure host, a holy host, an unblemished host, the holy bread of eternal life, and the chalice of everlasting salvation,” through “unblemished host.”
>
> Here he bows again beside the altar, saying: “We humbly beseech you, almighty God.” Here he prays privately whatever he wishes.
>
> Then he says: “Command these things to be carried by the hands,” through “in the presence.”
>
> Here he rises, saying these words: “So that all who partake of this altar,” through “through Christ.”
>
> These two Prayers are said, one over the diptychs and the other after the reading of the names, and this only on ordinary days or on days appointed for the rites:
>
> “Remember, Lord, those also whose names have preceded us with the sign of faith and who sleep in the sleep of peace.”
>
> The names are recited. Then, after they have been recited, he says:
>
> “For them, Lord, and for all who rest in Christ, we beseech you to grant a place of refreshment, light, and peace. Through the same one.”
>
> “And to us sinners,” through “but, we ask, the giver of pardon,” “admit us.”
>
> Here the archdeacon rises, comes forward, wraps the chalice in a cloth, and lifts it toward the lord pope.
>
> “Through whom, Lord, you always create all these good things.”
>
> Here he signs both—the offering and the chalice—three times, making one cross each time: “you sanctify, give life, bless, and grant them to us.”
>
> Here the lord pope raises the two offerings to the rim of the chalice and, touching it with the offerings while the archdeacon holds it, says:
>
> “Through him, and with him, and in him, to you, God the almighty Father, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, is all honor and glory.”
>
> Then he says aloud: “Throughout the ages of ages.”
>
> Then he replaces them on the altar and says aloud: “Let us pray.”
>
> Then he says: “Instructed by saving precepts,” through “but deliver us.”
>
> Then the lord pope, without any intervening sound, says this Prayer: “Deliver us,” through “Peter and Paul.” Here he names whichever and however many saints he wishes.
>
> Then he continues:
>
> “With all the saints, graciously grant peace,” through “throughout the ages of ages. Amen.”
>
> Then he says: “The peace of the Lord.”
>
> Then he gives the peace to the altar or paten, and thus gives it to himself.
>
> When the lord pope says, “May the peace of the Lord be always with you,” he does not place a portion of the Holy Sacrament into the chalice, as is customary among the other priests.
>
> While he breaks it, he says, “Lamb of God.”
>
> When the breaking is finished and the apostolic lord communicates, he bites off one portion for himself and puts the remainder into the chalice, making a cross with it three times over the chalice without saying anything. Thus he is confirmed from the chalice, while the archdeacon holds it.
>
> When the apostolic lord descends from the altar, he begins to give Communion to the people, and the Communion antiphon is said.
>
> When Communion and the antiphon are finished, the lord pope rises, comes to the altar, and gives the greeting, saying more loudly: “The Lord be with you,” and “And with your spirit.”
>
> Then he says the Prayer:
>
> “What we have received with the mouth, Lord, may we grasp with the mind; and may what is temporal in your gift become for us an eternal remedy.”

Thus far the Tilius manuscript; these same things are also found in Hittorp.

### 89. At the ninth hour

Thus in the printed editions and in the Rheims manuscript. In the manuscript of Ratoldus it reads, “At the ninth hour.” Formerly Masses during semi-fasts were held at the ninth hour. Consult our observations on the *Harmony of the Rules*.

### 90. God

That is, the Father, to whom the Prayer should be directed in the sacrifice of the Mass, according to the decree of the Third Council of Carthage, canon 23:

> When one is assisting at the altar, the prayer should always be directed to the Father.

Sometimes, however, it is directed to the Son.

### 91. Grant that your Only-Begotten Son, and so forth

These words are cited by Alcuin, book VII *Against Felix, Bishop of Urgel*:

> For in the Mass of the Nativity of this same Lord of ours, we are accustomed to sing: “Grant that your Only-Begotten Son, whom we joyfully receive as Redeemer,” and so forth.

### 92. God, who lives and reigns with you

Observe that formerly, in the conclusion of Prayers or Collects, the word “God” immediately followed the verb “reigns,” as can be seen in the Ambrosian Mass, in the Tilius manuscript, in our other manuscript codices, and in a manuscript exposition of the Preface and Canon in the Corbie library:

> When it says, “Who lives and reigns with you, God, in the unity of the Holy Spirit,” it wishes the people to believe and understand…

The *Micrologus* confirms this in chapter 6, *On Ecclesiastical Observances*:

> It should be known, however, that in the customary conclusion “Through our Lord,” the Roman Order and ancient copies insert the name “God” where it says, “Who lives and reigns with you, God.” Modern usage, however, generally adds it after the name of the Holy Spirit.

This custom has become so firmly established even among the Romans that the implementation of the ancient tradition cannot take place without causing offense. Here you see that the sequence of words found in our manuscript codices was the ancient usage.

### 93. Throughout the ages of ages

This is an ancient formula of Prayer among Christians, as can be seen in Saint Irenaeus, book I *Against Heresies*, chapter 1:

> Indeed, we too, when giving thanks, say, “Throughout the ages of ages.”

That is:

> Indeed, when we give thanks, we say, “Throughout the ages of ages.”

A similar expression is reported by Tertullian in *On Spectacles*: “through ages from an age.” No one else should say this except God and Christ.

### 94. Over the offerings

Thus in the Rheims manuscript and in those of Ratoldus and Rodriguez. In the Tilius manuscript it is called “Secret,” as in the printed editions; more often it is “Over the offerings.”

In the appendix to the manuscript of Rodriguez, “Secret” is used. Some learned men hold that *Secret* derives from the setting apart of the gifts and offerings. Thus the same Prayer, called *Over the offerings* in some codices of the sacramentary, is called *Secret* in others, as can be seen here in the Pamelian and Vatican manuscripts.

The reading in the very ancient manuscript of the Sacramentary of the Church of Tours seems to oppose this view, since it has *Arcana* instead of *Secret*. In the appendix to the Roman Order, taken from Amalarius’s excerpt on the same Roman Order, number 24, the following is said concerning the Secret:

> It is called the Secret because the bishop says a secret Prayer over the offering.

See also number 27 in Mabillon, volume II of the *Museum Italicum*, pages 558–559.

This Prayer is called “Over the offerings” because it is recited over the bread and wine offered in the Mass.

### 95. Preface

This is a Prayer, or thanksgiving, placed before the Canon, by which the priest and people are prepared for the celebration of the awe-inspiring mysteries.

Saint Cyprian mentions it in *On Prayer*:

> Therefore, before the Prayer, after the Preface has been delivered, the priest prepares the minds of the brothers, saying, “Lift up your hearts.”

It is also mentioned in the Second Council of Milevis, canon 9:

> It was also decided that prayers, or Orations, or Masses, which have been approved in the council—whether Prefaces, commendations, or impositions of hands—should be celebrated by all.

Saint John Chrysostom, in homily 3 on the Epistle to the Colossians, printed during the pontificate of Pope Clement VII, calls it *prophasis*.

In the Rheims manuscript it is called *contestada* in many places. Hence, in a manuscript exposition of the Mass in the Thuane library:

> “It is truly worthy and just,” and so forth. The priest *contests*—that is, affirms—the people’s fixed and true profession: that it is worthy to give thanks to God.

In the old Gallican Sacramentary it is called *Contestatio*, as also in the Gallican Missal and in the Gothic Missal published with the care of the most learned Thomasius and Mabillon. In the Gothic Missal it is also sometimes called *Immolatio*.

In those old Missals, the name *Preface* refers to the first part of the liturgy, which is a kind of exhortation to the people to devote themselves more attentively to entreating God, as Mabillon observes in book I of *On Gallican Liturgy*, chapter 3, number 17.

The complete common Preface of the Roman Missal is found in the Frankish Missal. The Preface is the subject of the famous canon 9 of the Second Council of Milevis:

> It was also decided that prayers, or Orations, or Masses, which have been approved in the council, whether Prefaces… should be celebrated by all.

Many Prefaces are placed here, as in the printed editions, in the Rheims and Ratoldus manuscripts, and in the second part of the Rodriguez manuscript. Nevertheless, only nine are said to have been received by Pope Pelagius II, which the Roman Church now uses, as can be seen in his letter preserved by Burchard, book III, chapter 69.

But it is well known that the decree was not observed, both from our manuscripts and from the printed editions, and also from these words of Guitmund, book II *On the Body and Blood of Christ*:

> I have inserted here the Preface which is found throughout almost the entire Latin world on a certain Sunday between Epiphany and Septuagesima, containing the following: “Eternal God, and to you we offer this sacrificial Host, which is the saving and ineffable sacrament of divine grace, which is offered by many and is perfected as one body of Christ through the infusion of the Holy Spirit. Each person receives Christ the Lord, and in each portion he is wholly present.”

Alger likewise says in book I *On the Truth of the Lord’s Body and Blood*, chapter 15:

> Ambrose, on the fifth Sunday after Epiphany: “Each person receives Christ the Lord, and in each portion he is wholly present; he is not diminished in the separate portions, but presents himself whole in each.”

These words are found in the Preface for that same fifth Sunday after Epiphany in the printed Sacramentaries and in our manuscript codices, and it is not among those excluded by Pope Pelagius. It follows that the Roman Church ceased using such Prefaces scarcely four hundred years ago. Two have been added to the nine Prefaces of Pelagius.

### 96. For completing

Thus in the manuscripts of Rodriguez and Ratoldus. Formerly the final Prayer of the Mass was called this, as Walfridus testifies in chapter 22 of *On Ecclesiastical Matters*:

> The proper time for communicating is before the final Prayer, which is called “For completing.”

It is so called because it is the completion and conclusion of the whole Mass.

Saint Augustine, in letter 59 to Paulinus, calls it “Thanksgiving”:

> When these things have been completed and so great a sacrament has been received, Thanksgiving concludes everything.

In the Rheims manuscript it is called “After Communion.” In the Roman Missal, with one word, it is called *Postcommunion*.

### 97. Through the same Lord, and so forth

The Prayer concludes through the Son because he is the mediator of God and human beings, through whom we have access to the Father, as the Apostle says. This accords with ancient custom, which Optatus mentions in book III:

> You call him a pagan who has asked God the Father before his altar through the Son.

Haymo, commenting on chapter 7 of the Epistle to the Hebrews, says:

> Hence the priests of the Church, standing at the altar, say: “Receive, holy Lord Father, the prayers of your people, through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son.”

### 98. At the Vigil of the Lord during the night

Thus in the printed editions and in the Rheims manuscript: “At the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity during the night,” which amounts to the same thing. It is said this way because of the nocturnal vigil.

The preceding vigil is at the ninth hour, which is commonly called the eve—the day before the feast itself.

In the manuscript of Rodriguez: “The Nativity of the Lord at Saint Mary Major.” In that of Ratoldus: “At night at Saint Mary’s.” In Pamel’s edition: “At midnight at Saint Mary Major.” But the word “midnight” seems to have been added by some corrector.

It is not read in the Swedish Royal manuscript or in the Gemet manuscript. It is found in the Vatican and Gussanville editions, which agree with the two Theodulf manuscripts. In those same copies it reads, as in Pamel’s edition, “At Saint Mary Major.” In the Roman Calendar illustrated by John Fronto, only “at Saint Mary” is found.

### 99. In the threefold name

Thus in the printed editions and in the manuscripts of Rodriguez and Rheims, without excluding the persons. The ancient Fathers sometimes spoke in this way.

Saint Cyprian says in letter 75:

> So that the baptized person might obtain grace, after the Trinity of names had been invoked: of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

Prudentius says in the *Psychomachia*:

> For we worship one God under a threefold name.

### 100. Benediction

Concerning the blessings that occur throughout the manuscript of Saint Eligius edited by Menard, see the notice that we shall place before the Benedictional to be published below.

In the Gothic Missal, edited by Mabillon in book III of *On Gallican Liturgy*, scarcely any Masses occur in which blessings are not read, although they are entirely different from ours. In the old Gallican Missal published in the same work, there are also some blessings, but they are altogether different and shorter.

In former times it was customary for the bishop to bless the people with certain prescribed prayers before receiving the Eucharist, as can be seen throughout this entire book of Sacraments, as well as in the manuscripts of Rodriguez, Rheims, Ratoldus, and Tilius, and also in the Roman Order and the old Roman Pontifical dedicated to Pope Leo X. These contain very many blessings.

This is established by Saint Augustine, cited shortly below, and by Haymo, commenting on chapter 2 of the First Epistle to Timothy:

> Petitions are episcopal blessings, which the bishop says over the people, invoking the name of the Lord upon them.

This accords with the meaning of Saint Augustine, cited below.

More precisely, that blessing was given at the clause of the Prayer “Deliver us, we ask,” followed by “Throughout the ages of ages,” as is plainly established by the Roman Order, in the second order of the Procession:

> When the bishop has finished the Our Father, the archsubdeacon, receiving the paten from the acolyte, should offer it to the archdeacon. When the bishop says, “Graciously grant peace,” the archdeacon, presenting the paten to him, should kiss his shoulder; and immediately, when the bishop says, “Throughout the ages of ages,” he should receive the Benedictional book, turn toward the people, and say, “Bow yourselves for the blessing.” When the clergy respond, “Thanks be to God,” he should hand the book to the bishop. When the blessing has been completed, the priest comes and receives the blessing from the bishop.

The same can be seen in the Easter Mass of the Ratoldus manuscript:

> After the Lord’s Prayer, when they have finished “Deliver us from evil,” with the bishop’s assent the deacon says, “Bow yourselves for the blessing,” and the people respond, “Thanks be to God.” The bishop says this blessing: “May he bless you,” and so forth. Then, taking a portion of the Lord’s body, he says, “May the peace of the Lord be always with you.”

The words “when they have finished ‘Deliver us from evil’” are not to be understood as though the bishop blesses immediately after those words have been said; what follows must be understood, through “May the peace of the Lord be always with you.”

The same is found in the manuscript Pontifical of the Church of Rouen for the fifth day of Holy Week:

> “Deliver us,” and so forth. “Throughout the ages of ages. Amen.” Then the deacon says, “Bow yourselves for the blessing.” And the bishop, turned toward the people, says, “May the almighty Lord bless you,” and so forth.

The same is clear from the Mass published by Flacius Illyricus:

> Let the bishop not place a portion of the offering into the chalice, as priests customarily do, but let him wait until, after the blessing has been completed, the bishop is to communicate. Then, taking the portion that he had previously broken, holding it over the chalice, he inserts it while saying, “May the mingling of the sacred blood,” and so forth.

In Spain, however, this blessing was given only after the mingling of the body and blood, as is clear from the Mozarabic Mass:

> “Deliver us, we ask, Lord.” And, beating his breast, he says, “Put an end, Lord, to sins.” When this has been completed, he places the received particle, which is called the *kingdom*, upon the chalice after saying a Prayer; then he adds another particle and puts it into the chalice. After this he says, “Bow yourselves for the blessing,” and blesses the people with certain prescribed formulas.

This is established by canon 17 of the Fourth Council of Toledo:

> But after the Lord’s Prayer and the joining of the bread and chalice, the blessing of the people should follow.

This blessing was given by the laying on of hands, as is known from Saint Augustine, letter 59 to Paulinus, question 5:

> Intercessions—or, as our manuscripts have it, petitions—are made when the people are blessed. For then the bishops, like advocates, offer those entrusted to them to the most merciful power by the laying on of hands. When these things have been completed and so great a sacrament has been received, Thanksgiving concludes everything.

Indeed, formerly the blessing was given by the laying on of hands. Saint Ambrose says in book I *On Repentance*, chapter 7:

> Why, then, do you lay on hands and entrust the work of blessing?

This is how Saint Jerome should be understood in his letter to Eustochium:

> With hand extended, so that, if you did not know better, you might think they were blessing them, they receive the price for greeting them.

I do not deny that the sign of the cross was formerly customary in blessing. Hence, in canon 12 of the Second Council of Milevis, the formulas of the blessings mentioned above are called “impositions of hands”:

> It was also decided that prayers, or Orations, or Masses, which have been approved in the council, whether Prefaces, commendations, or impositions of hands, should be celebrated by all.

Nor do these impositions concern penitents, upon whom hands were also laid during the solemn rites of Mass. Since the subject here is prayers belonging to the Mass, among which blessings are included, such impositions of hands should rather be understood as these blessings than as the impositions performed over penitents. The latter are not parts of the Mass but are performed solely for the sake of penitents; if there were no penitents, such impositions of hands would not be needed at all.

These blessings consist of three sections and a conclusion, as Honorius of Autun teaches in the *Gemma*. This is also clear from the blessings themselves, which can be seen in this manuscript of Saint Eligius, in the manuscripts of Rheims, Rodriguez, and Ratoldus, and also in Pamel. Nevertheless, a few blessings consisting of four sections are found in the Ratoldus manuscript.

There is also another Blessing, which is given at the end of Mass; concerning it, the Council of Agde, canon 47, says:

> We decree by special ordinance that secular persons are to remain for the whole of Mass on Sunday, so that no one may presume to leave before the priest’s Blessing.

For if this Blessing were not given at the end of Mass but before Communion, then, once it had been given, the people would leave and would not be present for the whole Mass, since they would depart before Communion. The words of Saint Caesarius of Arles, who presided over that council, must therefore be understood in this sense. He says in Homily 12:

> Whoever wishes to celebrate the Mass in its entirety, with profit to his soul, must remain in the church, with humbled body and contrite heart, until the Lord’s Prayer has been said and the Blessing has been given to the people.

Walafrid Strabo, in chapter 22 of his book *On Ecclesiastical Affairs*, explains the passage from the council—which he calls the Council of Orléans instead of the Council of Agde—as referring to the priest’s final Prayer, which, as we said above, is called the Prayer for Completion:

> It was decreed by the Council of Orléans that the people should not leave the Mass before the priest’s Blessing.

This Blessing is understood to be that final Prayer of the priest, of which Amalarius had plainly spoken above in the same chapter. Amalarius, in book III, chapter 36 of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, discusses this final Blessing, though he does not state the words in which it is given:

> The priest follows this custom: after all the sacraments have been completed, he blesses the people and greets them. Then he turns back toward the East, commending himself to the Lord’s Ascension, and the deacon says: “Go, the Mass is ended.”

Rabanus, in book I, chapter 33 of *On the Instruction of Clergy*, says:

> After Communion, therefore, and after the chant bearing that same name, once the priest has given the Blessing to the people, the deacon announces that the service of the Mass has been completed, giving permission to depart.

If these words are considered attentively, it will clearly appear that Rabanus was of the same opinion as Walafrid. For the chant bearing the same name as Communion is nothing other than the Antiphon or Responsory called the Communion. Since Rabanus places the Blessing immediately after this Antiphon, there can be no doubt that by the Blessing he understands the final Prayer called the Prayer for Completion. This Prayer was in use in his time and immediately follows the Antiphon or Responsory called the Communion.

Nevertheless, although no Blessing is found at the end of Mass in our ancient Masses and manuscripts, I nevertheless think that the canon of the Council of Agde is to be understood of a Blessing given at the end of Mass, distinct from the Prayer for Completion. For since the same council forbids a presbyter to impart the Blessing, it would not be reasonable to prevent him from reciting the final Collect, which, according to Saint Augustine, is a thanksgiving and certainly must not be omitted, whether it is said by a presbyter or by a bishop.

I think, however, that there were differing ecclesiastical usages concerning this Blessing at the end of Mass. As I said, it is found neither in the ancient Masses that we have published, nor in our manuscript codices, nor in the Orders of Mass edited by Melchior Hittorp. In all of these, after the Prayer for Completion, the deacon dismisses the people by saying, “Go, the Mass is ended,” just as in the Order of the Procession, when the bishop wishes to celebrate Mass on festive days. This order is found in the Tilius Codex, where we read:

> When the bishop has finished the Collect, and the deacon has said “Go, the Mass is ended,” and the clergy have said “Thanks be to God,” two deacons, taking the bishop’s hand, and so forth, are to lead him back to the sacristy with the entire procession.

But in the Amalarius passage cited above, this final Blessing appears to be at the end of Mass. It is also found in the Order of Mass instituted by Saint Peter, together with its exposition, in the Tilius Codex:

> In the morning, while the people pray, the singers chant the Post-Communion, to show that Christ remains among the people, strengthened in body and blood. Hence the priest asks for an eternal Blessing, because Christ, eating and drinking before his disciples, after rising from the dead, gave them the remnants, and, raising his hands, blessed them.

In this cited order of the Tilius Codex the earlier Blessing, which is given before Communion, is not found. That Blessing at the end of Mass was given before the deacon said, “Go, the Mass is ended,” as is clear from a manuscript treatise on the Mass in the library of Corbie:

> Then the priest performs the Prayers after Holy Communion, and the Blessing over the people, so that, having worthily received these things, we may remain steadfast in faith and pure in heart, and may believe that we possess salvation of soul and body. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father lives and reigns, God, with the Holy Spirit, for ever and ever. Amen.  
>   
> Then the deacon announces to the people, saying: “Go, the Mass is ended.”

The same is evident from manuscript glosses on the Roman Order in the library of Thou:

> After giving the Blessing, the bishop returns to his place; afterward the deacon announces, “Go, the Mass is ended.”

The episcopal Blessings mentioned above, which were given before Communion, are still in use in certain churches. Some of them are found at the end of printed editions of the Roman Pontifical produced in the time of Leo XI; they have been removed from more recent Pontificals.

### 101. Mass early in the morning

In the Ratold Codex and in the printed editions one reads: “Mass at first light at Saint Anastasia,” as also in Pamelius. In the Rodrad Codex: “At night at Saint Anastasia.” In the Rheims Codex, after the Mass at night, another Mass follows under this title: “On the feast of Saint Anastasia.”

### 102. “Grant, we beseech you, O God,” etc.

In the Rodrad Codex, [Note: In the Swedish Royal Codex, the Prayer over the Offerings for Saint Anastasia likewise precedes the Prayer for the Nativity of the Lord. The Gemetic Codex agrees with the Rodrad Codex.] the Prayers for Saint Anastasia precede the Prayers for the Nativity of the Lord, as does also the Preface for Saint Anastasia.

### 103. “Just as he was born a man, so he shone forth as God.”

Thus Corippus, book IV of *On the Praises of Justin the Younger*:

> He was born a man, yet did not cease to be the true God.

### 104. Preface: The Nativity of the Lord

In the Rodrad and Ratold Codices and in the printed editions there is added: “Preface of Saint Anastasia,” which is from the Common of Virgins.

### 105. “His”

Thus in the printed editions and in the Rodrad Codex. In Pamelius, and in the Rheims and Ratold Codices, one reads “of this one.” But I think that *his* is more correct, referring to Christ, since what follows is “whose birth.”

### 106. “Sacrament”

Here *sacrament* means the solemn feast in which some mystery of Christ—whether his Nativity, Passion, or Ascension—is represented, as Saint Augustine teaches in Letter 118 to Januarius, where he discusses unwritten sacraments:

> Those things that we preserve not as written but as handed down, and which are observed throughout the whole world, are understood to have been commended and established for preservation either by the apostles themselves or by plenary councils, whose authority in the Church is most salutary. Such are the annual solemn celebrations of the Lord’s Passion and Resurrection, his Ascension into heaven, and the coming of the Holy Spirit from heaven, together with anything of this kind that is observed by the universal Church, wherever it extends.

This is how Saint Jerome’s passage in Letter 48 to the deacon Sabinianus must be understood:

> After the basilica of the Apostle Peter, which was consecrated with Christ’s crimson garment; after the sacraments of the Cross, Resurrection, and Ascension, in which she had once again promised that she would live in the monastery.

### 107. “Nativity”

Thus in the Rheims and Rodrad Codices. In the printed editions, in the Ratold Codex, and in Pamelius, one reads “the newness of the Nativity,” which better suits the sense, both because of the paronomasia between *newness* and *Nativity* and because of the wordplay between *novitas* and *nativitas*. Nevertheless, I think that *nativity* is redundant.

### 108. “Birth”

In the Rodrad and Rheims Codices one reads *nobilitas* (“nobility”), which is not correct.

### 109. “Grant, we beseech you, almighty God, that we…”

Alcuin mentions this Prayer in book III of *Against Felix, Bishop of Urgel*:

> And on the day of the Nativity of the Lord: “Grant, we beseech you, almighty God, that the new birth of your Only-Begotten in the flesh may free us.”

### 110. “May we be carried away by love of invisible things”

Thus in the Rodrad and Ratold Codices and in Pamelius; Angelus Rocca writes that he found this reading in one manuscript Codex. In the Roman Missal one reads, “May we be carried away into love of invisible things,” a reading which the cited author says he also saw in three manuscript Codices.

### 111. “Who, just as he was an infant,” etc.

This is an excellent antithesis.

### 112. “Grant, we beseech you, almighty God”

In the Ratold Codex this Prayer is followed by another Blessing, as follows:

> O God, who restored the wounded human race in the first man by a new remedy, etc.

But this is not its proper place; it ought to follow immediately after the preceding Prayer of the same Codex.

### 113. “Who in the minds,” etc.

This is an elegant paronomasia.

### 114. “An increase of faith and security”

Thus in the Rheims and Rodrad Codices; Angelus Rocca attests that he found this reading in one Codex. In the manuscript Codex of Ratold, abbot, and in Pamelius, one reads: “An increase of faith, hope, and charity.” This reading seems more plausible; nevertheless, the former should not be rejected, since it is found in ancient Codices and is not without meaning in its own right.

### 115. “Paternal”

That is, of the father Adam.

### 116. “Having received the newness of this creation”

That is, having been transformed into a new creation, in accordance with Paul’s saying in Galatians 6:

> In Christ Jesus neither circumcision counts for anything, nor uncircumcision, but a new creation.

### 117. “O God, who human…,” etc.

The Roman Church now uses this Prayer in the mixing of wine and water, with these words inserted: “Through the mystery of this water and wine.”

### 118. “In the truth of the Body”

These words are directed against Mani, who attributed to Christ a phantom body, and against Valentinus, who attributed to him a heavenly body, as well as against other heretics of the same kind, who did not grant Christ a human and fleshly body.

### 119. “As the Passion made them glorious, so may,” etc.

In the Rodrad Codex: “Since the Passion made them glorious, and devotion [makes] us,” etc. In the Ratold Codex: “Because the Passion made them glorious, and devotion [makes] us,” etc. In the printed editions and in Pamelius: “As the Passion made them glorious, so may devotion [make] us,” etc.

[Note: In the Royal Codex of Saint Gall, *which also made* is absent. Indeed, Angelus Rocca admits in his scholia that he added the word *made*, which was lacking in the manuscript Codex. The Gemetic Codex agrees with the Rodrad Codex; but the two Theodorian Codices present our reading.]

The reading of the Codex of Saint Eligius seems preferable. In the Rheims Codex this Prayer is absent; instead there is another:

> May the gifts of today’s devotion, we beseech you, be pleasing to you, O Lord, etc.

### 120. “The first martyr entered into the glory that is eternal”

Ennodius writes admirably in hymn 4, concerning Saint Stephen:

> He was the first to enter the path  
> Untrodden by any footsteps.

### 121. “Through whom”

This is lacking in the printed editions and in Pamelius. It also appears to have been erased in the first Prayer of the Codex of Saint Eligius.

### 122. “Your Church,” etc.

Thus in the printed editions and in the Ratold, Rodrad, and Rheims Codices. In the last of these, however, it is placed second. The first is:

> O God, who through the mouth of your blessed apostle John opened to us the mysteries of your Word, etc.

[Note: In the Gothic Missal the feast of the apostles James and John is celebrated together on this day. See Mabillon’s note on this passage.]

In the Ratold Codex there are two Masses for Saint John the Evangelist, as also in Pamelius. The second is entitled, “Likewise on the day,” so that the first was said “at first light,” according to the title prefixed to it in the same Pamelius, while the second was said during the day.

### 123. “We trust”

In the printed editions *we* is lacking. In the Rheims Codex one reads “we know.”

### 124. “Carnal”

Read *carnalis* (“carnal”), so that it agrees with *genitoris* (“parent”).

### 125. “He mercifully assigned a substitute to his mother”

A similar expression occurs in Saint Ambrose’s Mass of Saint John, although the Preface is not the same:

> He mercifully assigned to his mother a son as his substitute.

### 126. “At Vespers”

Thus in the printed editions, in Pamelius, and in the Ratold Codex. In the Rodrad Codex there is added, “where mentioned above.”

### 127. “Another”

In the Rodrad Codex and in Pamelius one reads “At the fountains.”

[Note: Thus it is read in the Swedish Royal Codex.]

### 128. “Another”

In the same Codex and in Pamelius one reads “At Saint Andrew.”

### 129. “And among precious things,” etc.

This Preface is found in the Ambrosian Mass, though it varies in certain copies.

### 130. “And the confession was already clear,” etc.

Saint Augustine, Sermon 9 *On the Saints*:

> Blessed is the age that cannot yet speak of Christ, and already deserves to be slain for Christ.

### 131. “Before the Passion,” etc.

Thus Saint Augustine, in the cited sermon:

> Not yet fit for wounding, nor ready for suffering.

### 132. “Votive gifts”

Votive gifts are called the sacraments of Christ’s body and blood because everything offered to God is vowed, as we showed above from Saint Augustine.

### 133. “On the same day, Saint Fulgentius the bishop”

This is not found in our other manuscript Codices, nor in the printed editions, nor in Pamelius.

[Note: The same must be said concerning our manuscripts.]

This Saint Fulgentius, formerly a monk, became bishop of Ruspe in Africa. His Acts may be found in Surius under 1 January. There is no separate Mass here for Saint Fulgentius, because the Mass of Saint Sylvester is to be applied to him, since it suits both saints.

### 134. “During the Octave of the Lord”

Thus Corippus, book IV:

> The eighth light of Christ, newly born in light.

The eighth day of a solemnity is called by the Greeks *apólysis* (ἀπόλυσις), as may be seen in Saint Basil of Seleucia, book II, chapter 18 of *On the Miracles of Saint Thecla*:

> It was the feast of the martyr herself, and the final day of the feast, which it is our custom to call *apólysis*, since the feast has reached its conclusion.

That is:

> It was the feast of the martyr and the last day of the festival, which it is our custom to call *apólysis*, that is, “departure,” because the feast thereafter reaches its end.

Here, however, the Nativity of the Lord and his Circumcision are celebrated on one and the same day. The octave of the Nativity appears from the title of the feast in all our manuscript Codices and in the printed editions.

[Note: The feast of the Circumcision is noted in the ancient Lectionary in Mabillon, *On Gallican Liturgy*, book II, p. 112 and following. There one also reads, “The Sunday after the Circumcision.” In book III of the Gothic Missal there is a Mass “On the Circumcision of Our Lord Jesus Christ.”]

The day of the Circumcision is evident from the Preface and the Blessing. Its celebration is ancient, since it is mentioned in the Second Council of Tours, canon 17:

> And at the eighth hour, on the Kalends themselves, a Mass of the Circumcision is to be celebrated, by God’s favor.

In the Rheims Codex, on the same day, there follows a Mass entitled “Mass for the prohibition of idols.” But the particle *ad* is missing, and it should be read: “Mass for the prohibition of idols,” to which the Collects of that Mass pertain.

The reason for instituting this Mass is that formerly, on the Kalends of January, people were subject to many pagan superstitions. On these matters consult our observations on the *Concord of Rules*, chapter 50, section 13. Saint Peter Chrysologus attacks them in Sermon 155.

### 135. “Inasmuch as on the eighth,” etc.

By the eighth day, or octave, is signified the final day of the Resurrection and the ultimate age of eternal blessedness, after the week of this present age has run its course.

Saint Anastasius Sinaita, in his exposition of Psalm 6:

> A Psalm of David concerning the eighth. Scripture customarily calls “the eighth” that life which follows the seventh age of this world, which was foreshadowed by the circumcision performed on the eighth day.

That is:

> A Psalm of David for the eighth. Scripture customarily calls “the eighth” that life which follows the seventh age of this world, which the circumcision performed on the eighth day prefigured.

Saint Gregory of Nyssa, in his exposition of Psalm 6:

> Because, when the time of the sevenfold period has ceased, the eighth day will arise after the seventh: it is called “eighth” because it comes after the seventh, but it no longer admits within itself any succession of number, etc.

That is:

> Because, when the time of the sevenfold period has ended, the eighth day will follow the seventh. It is called eighth because it comes after the seventh, but it no longer admits within itself any succession of number. For one remains forever, never divided by any darkness. Another is the sun, which produces true light by its radiance; once it has shone upon us, as the Apostle says, it is not thereafter hidden by setting.

Saint Basil, chapter 27 of *On the Holy Spirit*, addressed to Amphilochius:

> But since this day appears in some way to be an image of the age to come, and since it is the beginning of days, it was called by Moses not “first” but “one”: “And there was evening, and there was morning, one day,” as though it were destined to recur often.

And then:

> Thus the same day is both one and eighth, and the eighth which the Psalmist mentions in certain titles of the Psalms manifests by itself the state that follows this present time: the unceasing day, the day without evening, the day that does not pass to a successor, that endless and ageless age.

That is:

> Thus the one day is also the same as the eighth: that singular and true eighth, which the Psalmist mentions somewhere in certain titles of the Psalms, signifying by itself the day after the state of these times—a day that never ends, knows no evening, and yields to no successor; that is, eternity, which has neither end nor old age.

Plato also appears to have possessed some knowledge of this matter, for he was not entirely unfamiliar with Hebrew affairs. He wrote that, after completing the course of this life, when holy men had remained for seven days in a most pleasant meadow, they would on the eighth day depart from there to heaven through the orbits of the seven planets.

> The journey after the wandering orbits leads to heaven—that is, to the eighth movement and day.

That is:

> The journey undertaken after those wandering orbits leads directly to heaven; for this is the eighth movement and day.

This passage occurs in Clement of Alexandria, book V of the *Stromata*.

This is said in the present Preface with reference to the Circumcision, which the Mosaic Law prescribed for every Hebrew child on the eighth day after birth. According to its allegorical meaning, it signifies the day of the Resurrection, on which the mortification of all vices and movements and disturbances of the soul will be perfected, as Saint Athanasius testifies in his sermon *On the Sabbath and Circumcision*:

> For this reason the Law also commanded circumcision on the eighth day, and the command was inviolable, signifying the regeneration of all things after the seventh.

That is:

> For this reason the Law commanded circumcision on the eighth day, and this command was never violated: it signified the regeneration of all things after the seventh day.

So also Saint Anastasius Sinaita, cited above. It should nevertheless be noted that this Preface differs to some extent from the Fathers cited. They call the seventh day the entire course of this age, whereas the Preface calls the whole of this age a period of six days, and the seventh the rest of blessed souls, who, having laid aside the body, await the Resurrection.

### 136. “May you attain joys that will remain without end”

That is, when the blessed will enjoy perfect blessedness both of soul and of body, since before the Resurrection they possessed only the happiness of the soul.

### 137. “May we be found in the likeness of that one”

That is, in the likeness of the glorified one.

### 138. “The first Sunday after the Nativity of the Lord”

In the Ratold and Rheims Codices, the office of this Sunday differs from that in our Codex of Saint Eligius. But the office of the first Sunday after the octave of the Nativity in the Ratold Codex agrees with this one both in the Preface and Blessing and in the Prayers, except for the final one, “Be favorable, merciful God,” etc., which is not found in the same Ratold Codex.

### 139. “On the Vigil of the Theophany”

*Theophany*—ἡ τοῦ Θεοῦ φανέρωσις, that is, “the manifestation of God”—says Suidas. It is also called *theophania* (θεοφάνια), neuter plural; Synesius mentions the sacred festival of the Theophanies, which was celebrated by the pagans, in his *Encomium of Baldness*. It is commonly called Epiphany.

This vigil is without fasting because, on account of the joy of Christ’s Nativity, the twelve days that formerly intervened between Christ’s Nativity and the Epiphany were exempt from fasting. The Greeks call this period the *dodecahemeron* (δωδεκαήμερον), that is, “twelve days,” except for the three days around the Kalends of January, during which, in many places and especially in Gaul, litanies were performed to trample underfoot the custom of the pagans, as decreed by the Second Council of Tours, canon 17.

This vigil is not found in the Rodrad Codex or in the very ancient Cologne Codex, as Pamelius notes.

[Note: Nor is it found in the Swedish Royal Codex.]

### 140. “On the Epiphany of the Lord”

This feast is celebrated in January according to an ancient rite, as is clear from Ammianus Marcellinus, book XXI, when he speaks of the emperor Julian while he was in Gaul:

> Meanwhile, so that these matters might be concealed, on the day of the festival which, when celebrated in January, they call Epiphany, he went into the church, solemnly worshiped the deity, and departed.

Epiphany, says Suidas, is “the incarnate dispensation of our Savior Jesus Christ” (ἡ τοῦ σωτῆρος ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ ἔνσαρκος οἰκονομία), that is, the Incarnation of our Savior Jesus Christ.

On this day the Greeks recite the service of the Great Sanctification, with everyone going to the fountains carrying lamps and incense. There the water is blessed with many prayers, both for baptism and for various Christian uses. The priest immerses the holy cross upright in the water, and from that water sprinkles the church and the people, as is described at length in the *Euchologion*.

Theodore the Lector mentions this rite in his second *Eclogue*:

> And he ordered the invocation over the waters at the Theophanies to take place in the evening.

That is:

> And he ordered the invocation over the water on the day of the Theophanies to take place in the evening.

There he is discussing Peter the Fuller, bishop of Antioch, whom he says ordered this Blessing to be performed in the evening.

### 141. “With the star as guide”

Diodore of Tarsus, bishop, in book V of *Against Fate*, chapter 53, writes that the star which appeared to the Magi at the Lord’s birth was not one among many in the sky, but:

> A certain more divine power fashioned in the likeness of a star.

The Greek is δύναμίν τινα θειοτέραν εἰς ἄστρον μὲν σχηματιζομένην, that is, “a certain more divine power formed into the likeness of a star.”

Saint Isidore of Pelusium, in Letters 377 and 378 of book I, writes that it was indeed a real star, but that it followed a course different from that of the other stars, and that the Magi, struck by it, sought the Lord.

### 142. “He restored us to the new light of his immortality”

Thus in the first Sunday after the Epiphany and in the printed editions. The sense is good. In the manuscript Codices—the Ratold Codex, the first Sunday after the Epiphany; the Rheims and Rodrad Codices; and Pamelius—one reads: “He restored us in the new light of his immortality.” From this, after the preposition was removed, there arose the reading found in the Roman Missal: “He restored us by the new light of his immortality.”

### 143. “Of the Magi”

Suidas writes that among the Persians the Magi were men who loved wisdom and loved God (φιλοσόφους καὶ φιλοθέους), that is, devoted to wisdom and lovers of God. Hesychius interprets *magus* as “theologian.”

Saint Epiphanius, in his *Exposition of the Catholic Faith*, reports that the Magi who worshiped the infant Christ were descended from the sons of Keturah. Their father had given them gifts—gold, frankincense, and myrrh—which he had received from the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah. Therefore, since they lived in the region of Magodia in Arabia, they offered those same gifts to the infant Christ.

Diodore of Tarsus, in the chapter cited above, writes that they were Persians and had been instructed by the Chaldeans through the star that the Savior of all had been born in the flesh, in accordance with the ancient prophecy of Balaam.

### 144. “As first fruits”

In the printed editions one reads “first,” which is incorrect.

### 145. “Who, together with wisdom,” etc.

Thus in the Ratold Codex. It is the common opinion of theologians that Christ was granted, from the very moment of his conception, all wisdom and all the other powers and virtues of soul due to him by reason of the hypostatic union. At the very instant of his conception he was already a comprehensor, as they call it, and never a wayfarer—that is, he always possessed the intuitive vision of God.

When, therefore, in this Blessing the pontiff prays that God may grant the faithful an increase of spiritual virtues, just as Christ advanced in wisdom, age, and grace, these words must be understood according to the measure and proportion of the persons compared. Just as Christ increased in experiential wisdom and grace, so may they grow by a new acquisition of virtues.

### 146. “During the octave of the Theophany”

In the Rodrad Codex and in Pamelius this solemnity is absent.

[Note: Thus it is found in the Roman Calendar and in the Calense Codex. But in the Gemetic Codex and in both Theodorian Codices this feast is noted. In the same Codices the feast of Saint Hilary is listed separately, with the Prayers and Preface assigned here. In the first Theodorian Codex several other feasts precede it: Saint Basil, bishop, confessor, and doctor, on the second day before the Kalends of January; on the same day, Saint Columba the virgin; Saint Genevieve on the third day before the Nones of January; Saint Remigius, bishop and confessor, on the Ides of January, on which day the feast of Saint Hilary is also announced.]

In the Ratold Codex one reads: “The octave of the Epiphany, and the deposition of Saint Hilary.” The second Prayer is there for Saint Hilary:

> O God, by whose mercy sinners are changed into those who receive pardon, etc.

The first Prayer over the Offerings is for Saint Hilary:

> Creator of all things and restorer of the human race, etc.

The Preface is for Saint Hilary, with none for the octave:

> Who chose the blessed Hilary, your confessor, to be for you a bishop of your consecrated confession, etc.

The Blessing, however, is for the octave, with none for Saint Hilary:

> O God, who have deigned to choose the present day, and to demonstrate that you chose it by so many miracles, etc.

The second Prayer for Completion is for Saint Hilary:

> O God, rewarder of the souls of the faithful, etc.

### 147. “Saint Felix”

This is Saint Felix, priest of Nola, whose deeds Saint Paulinus, bishop of Nola, wrote in elegant verse. In the Rodrad, Rheims, and Ratold Codices, and in Pamelius, “at Pincis” is added. This is a place in Rome where the church of Saint Felix was built.

[Note: Joan Fronto proves this very well in his notes on the Roman Calendar, in this passage, against Rosweyde.]

### 148. “Confessor”

Saint Felix is called this in all our Codices, not “martyr.” He is so called in the manuscript Martyrology of the library of Corbie:

> 14 January, at Nola in Campania, Saint Felix, priest and confessor.

The same designation is used by Saint Augustine, in book *On the Care to Be Taken for the Dead*, chapter 1:

> So that he might be placed in the basilica of the most blessed Felix the confessor.

The same occurs in the printed Usuard.

This is correct. For formerly those were called confessors who, after enduring many torments for the faith of Christ, were finally delivered by the will of God, survived so many struggles, and died a peaceful death, as is clear from Letter 46 of Saint Cyprian and from many other passages. Saint Felix was prominent among such men.

In the Fourth Council of Toledo, Saint Leocadia, who died not by the sword or under torture but through the squalor of imprisonment and hunger, is called a confessor.

### 149. “Heretics”

Thus in the printed editions and in our manuscript Codices. The word is improperly used in place of “pagans.”

[Note: This interpretation is by no means satisfactory to the learned Tillemont, and it is rejected in note 3 on the history of Saint Felix; consult that work. See also our Theodorus Ruinart, *Acts of the Martyrs*, p. 256. For the rest, I do not see what causes such difficulty in explaining these words of the Preface: “He could be diverted neither by heretical perversities nor by the blandishments of the world from the rectitude of his established way of life.” Were there no heretics in the time of Saint Felix? On the contrary, it is certain that there were very many. But, you will say, who could easily persuade himself that Felix, the presbyter of Nola, fought so outstandingly against heretics, and that this was either unknown to Saint Paulinus or at least omitted by him? Yet in the Preface under discussion there is not even a word about Saint Felix’s struggles against heretics.]

Saint Fructuosus, in chapter 1 of his Rule, also called certain pseudo-monks who lived according to their own will “heretics”:

> When you find such men, believe that they are not monks but hypocrites and heretics.

### 150. “We celebrate”

In the printed editions one reads “we worship.” On 19 January, in the Rodrad Codex, there follows: “The feast of Mary and Martha”; in the Rheims Codex: “The feast of Saint Mary and Martha”; in the Ratold Codex: “The feast of Saints Mary and Martha.” Here *saints* is used substantivally in the plural, and this occurs frequently in our manuscripts and in the Roman Missal.

In the cited Codices there are similar Prayers for the same saints, as follows:

> Hear, O Lord, your people, who plead with you under the patronage of your saints, so that you may grant us to rejoice in the peace of this temporal life and to find support for eternal life. Through the Lord.

Over the Offerings:

> Regard, O Lord, the Prayers and offerings of your faithful, so that they may be pleasing to you for the feast of your saints and may bring us the help of your mercy. Through the Lord.

After Communion:

> Appeased by the intercession of your saints, grant, we beseech you, that what we celebrate in a temporal action we may receive in perpetual salvation.

In these Prayers, *saints* must likewise be understood substantivally, as stated above.

In the Roman Martyrology and in that of Ado, on the same day, the feast of Saints Marius and Martha, husband and wife, is recorded. But the Mass of our Sacramentaries must be understood of Mary and Martha, the holy sisters of Lazarus, first because they are not called martyrs in it. Secondly, this is suggested by the manuscript Martyrology of Saint Jerome, where on the same day one finds:

> Jerusalem: Martha and Mary, the sisters of Lazarus.

The same appears in the manuscript Martyrology of the library of Corbie:

> Jerusalem: Martha and Mary.

The remaining words were scraped away by some—in all likelihood—a trifler, but it appears in some fashion that “the sisters of Lazarus” had been written. In the small manuscript Martyrology attached to the Rheims Sacramentary, on the same day one reads:

> Jerusalem: Martha and Mary, sisters of Lazarus.

In the Calendar of the Ratold Codex, on the same day:

> At Jerusalem: Martha and Mary.

In another small manuscript Martyrology of the library of Corbie:

> 19 January, in Africa: Quintus, Paul, Gerontius, Mary, and Martha.

In the Martyrology of Rabanus, on the same day:

> Jerusalem: the feast of Martha and Mary, sisters of Lazarus.

And in the Martyrology of Notker:

> 19 January, at Jerusalem: the birth-feast of Martha and Mary, sisters of Lazarus.

On the following day, however, in the same Martyrologies of Saint Jerome, the greater Martyrology of Corbie, Rabanus, and Notker, as also in the Martyrology of Usuard, the day of the holy martyrs Marius and Martha, husband and wife, is recorded.

From these facts it is evident how correctly the Mass of Mary and Martha is assigned in the aforementioned Sacramentaries to 19 January, and that these names are to be understood of the sisters of Lazarus.

[Note: In the Gemetic Codex, under 19 January, one reads only: “The holy Mary and Martha.” Earlier, however, the feast of Saint Maurus, abbot, is noted on 15 January, and the deposition of Anthony on 17 January.]

### 151. “Of Fabian”

In the Ratold Codex there is a single Mass for Saints Fabian and Sebastian, though with different Prayers. The Prayer of Saint Sebastian always comes first, and he has only a Preface, which does not differ from the Preface in the Rodrad and Rheims Codices.

The Blessing belongs to both saints:

> O God, who by the right hand of your power open the royal gate of the heavenly court to the martyrs who triumph for you.

Here *regia* means “door,” as in the *Rule of the Master*, chapter 83:

> Once they have been stripped of the monastery’s possessions, they are expelled through the closed royal door, without serious injury.

Consult our observations on the *Concord of Rules*, chapter 67, section 2.

### 152. “And those whom weight…”

The best reading. In the Rodrad Codex: “And because we are weight”; at the end *we* also appears in the form “may protect us.” In the Ratold Codex and in Pamelius one reads: “And because weight,” as in the Roman Missal.

### 153. “Of Saint Agnes”

In the Rodrad Codex the reading is *sanctae Agnes* rather than *sanctae Agnetis*, following the Greek form, as may be seen near the end of Theodore the Lector’s second *Eclogue*:

> The relics of the holy Stephen, Lawrence, and Agnes were deposited.

That is:

> The relics of the holy Stephen, Lawrence, and Agnes were deposited.

Saint Ambrose speaks in this way in book I of *On Duties*, chapter 41. Prudentius likewise, in the *Peristephanon*:

> The tomb of the renowned brave girl martyr Agnes is in the city of Romulus.

Below, however, he uses *Agnes* in the nominative case:

> “No,” said Agnes, “Christ is not forgetful  
> Of his own.”

And frequently farther on.

[Note: In the Gemetic Codex one reads “of Saint Agna.” In both Theodorian Codices, “of Saint Agnes.”]

### 154. “And solemnly recounts the day consecrated to the martyrdom of blessed Agnes”

The Rheims Codex has:

> For, recounting the day consecrated to the martyrdom of blessed Agnes.

### 155. “At the same time she was made conformed,” etc.

In the Ambrosian Mass one reads:

> At the same time she was made conformed to him, so that she might share in his eternity and glory.

### 156. “That she might conquer”

In the Rodrad Codex and in Pamelius: “by which she might conquer,” which should have the grave accent on *quo*, so that it means “by what means”; the sense will be the same. In the printed editions and in the Ratold Codex: “what she might conquer.” This too gives a good sense if the particle *quod* is accented.

In the Ratold Codex this Blessing is found:

> May the Lord, ruler and creator of the heavens, bless you, etc.

Furthermore, in Codex Rhemensis, on the tenth day before the Kalends of February, there is recorded the feast of the holy martyrs Merentianus and Macarius. But read *Emerentianae*, who was a virgin and martyr, the foster-sister of Saint Agnes. [Note: In the earlier Theodoricus, it reads: “On the tenth day before the Kalends of February, of Saint Emerentiana and Macarius.” In Gemeticus it is written by abbreviation: “of Saint Emerentiana and Macarius.”] In the little Martyrology sewn into the Rhemensis Sacramentary, these martyrs are also mentioned on the same day: “On the tenth day before the Kalends, of Saints Emerentianus”—read *Emerentiana*—“and Macharius, and the passion of Saint Ascla.” In the Calendar prefixed to Ratoldus’s Sacramentary: “On the tenth day before the Kalends, the feast of Saint Emerentiana the virgin and Saint Macharius, and the passion of Parmenas the deacon.” Likewise, in the manuscript Martyrology of Saint Jerome, on the same day: “And elsewhere, the passion of the holy martyrs Eugenius, Emerentiana, and Macharius, Pulvius.” Perhaps read *Publius*. Thus Macharius, for whom the present Mass is intended, since he is joined on the same day in the aforementioned Martyrology with Saint Eugenius the martyr, is that Macarius who was banished by Julian the Apostate to the town of Oasis in Arabia and was there beheaded together with Saint Eugenius, as Metaphrastes writes in his account of Saint Artemius. Rabanus also mentions Macarius and Eugenius on the same day in his Martyrology. The Mass of Emerentiana and Macarius is as follows in Codex Rhemensis: “May the blessed supplication of the martyrs reconcile us, Lord, to your Majesty,” etc. “May the feasts of your martyrs, Lord, always gladden us,” etc. Over the offerings: “May the offering of your consecrated people be acceptable to you, Lord,” etc. Postcommunion: “May the vows of your saints continually gladden us, Lord,” etc. [Note: The same Mass is assigned in the Codices already mentioned.]

**157. “O God, who taught the whole world through the preaching of blessed Paul,” etc.** Saint Paul taught the whole world through his preaching, as Saint Clement testifies in his First Epistle to the Corinthians:

> “Because of his zeal Paul received the prize of endurance; after being bound seven times, beaten, and stoned, he became a herald in both the East and the West, obtained the noble glory of faith, taught righteousness to the whole world, and reached the extremity of the West.”

And Saint Gregory of Nyssa, in his *Oration on the Encounter of the Lord*:

> “The lightning that shone from Jerusalem and around it as far as Illyricum—or rather, as far as the ends of the earth—the voice of the divine thunder, rolling through the mystical wheel of the Gospel over the whole inhabited world, a most penetrating and mighty voice.”

Here he is speaking of the holy apostle Paul. Saint John Chrysostom likewise, in Homily 13 on the First Epistle to the Corinthians, speaking of Saint Paul:

> “Consider, then, the golden statue,” etc. “But running from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum, going on to Spain, and carried everywhere throughout the inhabited world as though winged.”

That is: “running from Jerusalem to Illyricum, going to Spain, and traversing the whole world as if borne on wings.”

**158. “Which his teaching did not establish.”** In Codex Rhemensis it reads: “Who did not conform to his disciplines.” [Note: The same reading occurs in the earlier Theodoricus.] After this, the following occurs in the same Codex:

> “Whom today, made the vessel of election, the teacher and instructor of the nations to be called, you established under a changed name through Christ the Lord,”
