omitting the passages found in this Codex of Saint Eligius and in our other codices. Here it should be noted that Saint Paul is said to have had his name changed on the day of his conversion.

**159. “On the same day, Saint Projectus.”** [Note: No commemoration of Saint Projectus appears in the Calensis manuscript.] Codex Rhemensis also reads “Saint Projectus.” Commonly, *Praejectus*, as in Codex Rodradi, namely in the collection of Prefaces; in French, Saint Prix. He was bishop of Arvernia and was murdered together with the abbot Amarinus by the local nobles in the year 670, according to Sigebertus. Usuardus discusses him in his Martyrology on this day, as does the manuscript Martyrology of the Corbie library cited above. See his *Acts* in Surius under this same day.

**160. “Repeated.”** So it reads in Codex Rodradi. In Codex Rhemensis the preposition *in* is placed before it. The words “with the feast repeated” indicate a double feast of Saint Projectus, which still continues in Gaul.

**161. “And may you grant us,” etc.** So it reads in Codex Rodradi, through the end of the Preface, which is absent from Codex Rhemensis. In its place, after the words “may you continually grant sweetness,” the following occurs:

> “May you graciously grant us what we ask, Lord, so that we may love the merit of his passion, and that your martyr Projectus, ever a faithful patron, may obtain forgiveness for us. Through Christ our Lord.”

**162. “Of the Nativity.”** So reads Codex Rhemensis; this is absent from Codex Rodradi. In its place, Codex Ratoldi and Pamelio have “second.”

**163. “The Purification of Saint Mary the Virgin.”** In the Codices of Rodradi and Ratoldi: **ΥΠΑΠΑΝΤΙ**; [Note: Also in Calensis and in the two Theodorici.] in Pamelio, **ΥΠΑΝΤΙ**. Both amount to the same thing, namely “encounter.” Saint Hildefonsus gives the reason in his sermon on the Purification:

> “Since, when the Lord had been brought into the temple by his parents on this day, we believe that he was met by the saints, of whom there is no doubt that there were very many in Jerusalem.”

The name is derived from the Greeks, who designated this feast in this way. Thus Codinus Curopalates, in his book *On the Offices of Constantinople*, calls it **κατὰ τὴν τῆς Ὑπαπαντῆς ἑορτὴν**, “at the feast of the Encounter”; so also Cedrenus, in his account of Justin, and in the novella of the emperor Manuel Comnenus, which Theodore Balsamon cites in chapter 1, title 6, of Photius’s *Nomocanon*:

> **ἡ βʹ τοῦ Φεβρουαρίου διὰ τὴν τοῦ Σωτῆρος ὑπαπαντήν**  
> “The second day of February, on account of the Encounter of the Savior.”

Theophylact Simocatta, Book VIII of his *History*, chapter 4, calls this feast:

> **τεσσαρακοστὴ ἡμέρα τῆς γενεθλιακῆς πανηγύρεως τοῦ μεγάλου Θεοῦ Ἰησοῦ**  
> “The fortieth day of the festival of the Nativity of the great God Jesus.”

In Codex Rhemensis this feast is called that of Saint Simeon.

On this feast, prayers or processions are held with burning candles, according to a sufficiently ancient custom. This derives from an old superstition by which the Romans, in that month, purified the city with burning candles in honor of the god Februus, that is, Pluto; the practice was transformed into a pious and holy rite. Saint Hildefonsus mentions it in the sermon cited above; he flourished in the year 644:

> “This festival is celebrated in the month of February, which the Romans, while still pagans, called by this name from Februus, that is, Pluto,” etc.

The Christian custom appropriately and religiously transformed that practice of purification, since in the same month—that is, on this day—not only the clergy but the entire people go around the churches in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God and perpetual virgin, carrying candles and singing various hymns. Saint Eligius writes the same in Homily 2:

> “Now, therefore, Christian devotion has beautifully converted the error of vain superstition into true religion. No longer, every fifth year, nor—as formerly—around the end of February, is a single Roman city purified in honor of Februus, who was falsely considered powerful in purifications, that is, cleansings, and the god of the underworld, and on account of whose dignity the Roman earthly empire has now ceased; rather, every year, around the beginning of the same month, the whole city of God, namely the holy Church, is illumined, signifying by the light of candles the light of faith that shines in the hearts of her children, which is carried in their hands,” etc.

In Alcuin, Amalarius, and Walafrid, there is no Blessing of the Candles; Alcuin merely says that the candles are given by the bishop. But in Codex Ratoldi there is a single Blessing under this title: “Blessing over the candles,” which is found in the Roman Ordo and Missal, though it differs in some respects. It begins:

> “Lord Jesus Christ, Creator of heaven and earth, King of kings and Lord of lords,” etc.

[Note: This Blessing is found in Gemeticus, but three others precede it.]

Cedrenus reports that the solemnity of the Purification originated at Constantinople in the ninth year of Justin the Great, when Antioch collapsed in a severe earthquake. Theophanes, Book XVI of his *History*, assigns the institution of this feast to the fifteenth year of Justinian’s reign:

> “In the fifteenth year of the reign of Justinian, in the month of October, a pestilence occurred at Byzantium; and in that same year the Lord’s Hypapante began to be celebrated at Byzantium on the second day of February.”

These authors are to be understood as referring to the time when this feast first arose at Byzantium. For its institution in the Church is much older; it was celebrated in the time of Saint Gregory of Nyssa, as is clear from the sermon he composed on the Encounter of the Lord:

> **Καὶ γὰρ ὅτε κατὰ τὸν ἀρχέτυπον καιρόν, ὡς ἄν τις εἴποι, τῆς παρούσης ἑορτῆς** etc.

That is:

> “For when, so to speak, at the archetypal time of the present feast, he who possessed the divine form and had assumed the form of a servant, having become Mediator between God and human beings, was fulfilling the commandment of the Law, the eternal Word, as an infant forty days old, proceeded to the temple together with his mother, who carried the prescribed and appropriate offering,” etc.

> **Οὗ τινος ἡμεῖς τὴν ἀνάμνησιν ἑορτάζοντες σήμερον** etc.

That is:

> “Celebrating today the commemoration of this mystery,” etc.

Therefore Pope Gelasius did not open the way for the celebration of this solemnity when he abolished the Lupercalia. Nor did this feast arise on the occasion of the Lupercalia, as is shown by the Fathers Hildefonsus and Eligius cited above; rather, it arose from the purification of the city that was practiced at Rome in honor of the underworld gods, especially Februus, that is, Pluto, a superstition transformed into true religion. For although the Lupercalia were held in February, funeral rites or sacrifices to Pluto were also celebrated in the same month. This month was named from the gods of the underworld, or Pluto, not from the Lupercalia, as may be seen in Varro, Book V of *On the Latin Language*:

> “February was named from the infernal gods, because offerings are made to them.”

Ovid, Book II of the *Fasti*:

> “Either because the times are purified by appeased tombs,  
> when the days of the dead have passed.”

Macrob­ius, Book I of the *Saturnalia*, chapter 13:

> “He dedicated the second month to the god Februus, who is said to have power over purifications. For it was necessary to purify the city in that month, in which he decreed that offerings should be paid to the spirits of the dead.”

And Saint Isidore, Book V of the *Etymologies*, chapter 32:

> “February is named from Februus, that is, Pluto, to whom sacrifices were offered in that month; for they consecrated January to the heavenly gods and February to the gods of the dead.”

From all these passages it can easily be understood that the purification of the city and funeral offerings were celebrated in February, and that the month itself was named from Februus, that is, Pluto. These points accord with what Cedrenus writes under the year of the world 5281:

> **Ἀνύσιος ἐν τῷ περὶ μηνῶν, Φεβροῦον τὸν καταχθόνιον τῇ Θούσκων φωνῇ, λέγει. Ὁ δὲ Λαβέων, ἀπὸ τοῦ πένθος λέγει κληθῆναι τὸν Φεβρουάριον· φέβρους γὰρ παρὰ Ῥωμαίοις τὸ πένθος προσαγορεύεται· κατ᾽ αὐτὸν δὲ τοὺς κατοιχομένους ἐτίμων, καὶ φεβρουᾶραι τὸ καθᾶραι.**

That is:

> “Anysius, in his book *On the Months*, says that the being who is among the dead below is called Februus in the Etruscan language. Labeo, however, holds that February was named from grief, since among the Romans grief is called *februs*; during that month they honored the dead. Moreover, *februare* means ‘to purify.’”

Nevertheless, Saint Augustine, Book XVIII *Against Faustus*, chapter 5, writes that February is named from the sacred rites of the Luperci dedicated to Februus. Festus is not far from this opinion when he writes that February is named from Juno Februata, whom others call Februalis and the Romans Februlis; and that her festival is the Lupercalia, on which women were purified by the Luperci with the garment of Juno, that is, a goatskin. But the earlier opinion seems more probable.

**164. “To the Collect.”** [Note: For the various meanings of *Collecta*, see again the notes of Angelo Rocca on this passage in the Vatican and Gussanvil editions.] Some think that *Collecta* here signifies a collection of alms, and that this Mass is entitled “To the Collect” because alms were given on the more solemn days. Although I might admit this, I do not think that *Collecta* here signifies almsgiving, but rather an assembly and gathering for the performance of the divine office and the offering of common prayers, and also the divine office itself.

Saint Jerome, in the *Epitaph of Paula*:

> “By this sign they were summoned to the Collect.”

Saint Epiphanius, in his letter to John, bishop of Jerusalem:

> “When, therefore, the Collect was being celebrated in the church of the village that lies near our monastery.”

Saint Pachomius, in the Rule, according to Saint Jerome’s translation, article 107:

> “They shall offer six evening prayers according to the pattern of the greater Collect.”

Article 121:

> “If anyone takes something that is not his, it shall be placed upon his shoulders, and he shall do public penance at the Collect.”

The explanation of this passage is clear from the Roman Ordo. For it relates that, on this feast, clergy and people gather—or assemble—at Saint Adrian, awaiting the bishop:

> “The bishop, having entered the sacristy, puts on black vestments, and the schola sings *Exsurge*. Then follows the Prayer at the Collect, *Exaudi*, or *Erudi*, as it is read in some of our Sacramentaries. Afterwards the candles are blessed. When the blessing has been completed, they proceed to Saint Mary, where Mass is celebrated.”

This is confirmed by the Mass of the Nativity of Saint Mary in this Codex, in which another prayer precedes its own and bears the title “For the Procession.” Here *Procession*, at least understood according to its terminus—that is, the assembly of those proceeding when they have reached the church—is nothing other than what is called the *Collecta* in this celebration of the Purification.

**165. “Teach.”** So it reads in the printed editions, in our manuscript Codices, and in Pamelio. In the Roman Ordo and Missal it reads “Hear.” Although *hear* should not be rejected, *teach* suits this prayer exceedingly well, as though the people, instructed through external worship, might attain the inward grace signified by that external worship.

**166. “Servant.”** A servant, a subject, because Christ subjected himself to the Law as a singular example of humility; and he who had come to redeem the world at the infinite price of his blood willed to be redeemed for five small shekels.

**167. “Punishments.”** In Codex Rhemensis, “sinners,” that is, torturers, executioners, and tyrants.

**168. “Agatha.”** So it reads in our other manuscript Codices, according to the Greek form, **ἀγαθή**.

**169. “Always existed.”** In the printed editions, the word *always* is absent.

**170. “This Offering.”** Not simple bread and wine, but Christ, who is to be sacrificed under the appearances of bread and wine. These terms must not be considered in isolation, but insofar as they refer to Christ.

**171. “Through the flower of the virginal womb.”** That is, Christ, the true flower, who came forth from the Virgin’s womb. According to Isaiah, chapter 11:

> “A shoot shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root.”

**172. “With righteousness preserved,” etc.** For it was just that, since Adam’s flesh had been conquered by the devil, Christ’s flesh should conquer the devil, so that the one exalted by fallen flesh might be laid low by flesh.

**173. “Which is the saving and ineffable sacrament of divine grace.”** So it reads in Codex Ratoldi and in Guitmundus, cited below. In the Ambrosian Sacramentaries and Codex Rodradi:

> “Which is offered as the saving and ineffable sacrament of divine grace.”

In Codex Rhemensis:

> “Which is again the wondrous and ineffable grace of the sacrament.”

But I think it should be read:

> “And the ineffable sacrament of divine grace.”

**174. “And one body of Christ is perfected through the infusion of the Holy Spirit.”** Correctly so. For the ancients attribute to the Holy Spirit the production of Christ’s body and blood in the Eucharist, by a certain appropriation. Saint Cyril of Jerusalem, *Mystagogical Catechesis* 5:

> **Παρακαλοῦμεν τὸν φιλάνθρωπον Θεόν, τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα ἐξαποστεῖλαι ἐπὶ τὰ προκείμενα, ἵνα ποιήσῃ τὸν μὲν ἄρτον σῶμα Χριστοῦ, τὸν δὲ οἶνον αἷμα Χριστοῦ. Πάντως γὰρ οὗ ἂν ἐφάψαιτο τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα, τοῦτο ἡγίασται καὶ μεταβέβληται.**

That is:

> “We beseech the benevolent God to send the Holy Spirit upon the offerings set before us, so that he may make the bread the body of Christ and the wine the blood of Christ. For whatever the Holy Spirit touches is certainly sanctified and transformed.”

Theophylact, on chapter 5 of John:

> **Μεταποιεῖται ἀποῤῥήτοις λόγοις ὁ ἄρτος οὗτος διὰ τῆς μυστικῆς εὐλογίας καὶ ἐπιφοιτήσεως τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος εἰς σάρκα τοῦ κυρίου.**

That is:

> “This bread is transformed by secret words, through the mystical blessing and coming of the Holy Spirit, into the flesh of the Lord.”

Saint John Damascene writes the same in Book IV, chapter 14, of *The Orthodox Faith*. There he teaches that bread and wine are transformed into Christ’s body and blood through the descent of the Holy Spirit, just as the Word of God became incarnate in the Virgin’s womb through the infusion of that same Holy Spirit:

> “How will this happen,” says the holy Virgin, “since I do not know man?” The archangel Gabriel answers: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you.”

> **Καὶ νῦν ἐρωτᾷς, πῶς ἄρτος γίνεται σῶμα Χριστοῦ, καὶ οἶνος καὶ τὸ ὕδωρ αἷμα Χριστοῦ; λέγω σοι κἀγώ· Πνεῦμα ἅγιον ἐπιφοιτᾷ, καὶ ταῦτα ποιεῖ ὑπὲρ λόγον καὶ ἔννοιαν.**

That is:

> “And now you ask how bread becomes Christ’s body, and water and wine Christ’s blood? I too say to you: the Holy Spirit comes upon them, and accomplishes these things beyond speech and understanding.”

Saint Germanus, patriarch of Constantinople, teaches the same in his *Mystical Commentary*. Thus the Holy Spirit, by the good pleasure of the Father and the will of the Son, invisibly manifests the divine making and seals it by the priest’s hand:

> **Καὶ μεταβάλλει, καὶ τελειοῖ τὰ προκείμενα ἅγια δῶρα εἰς σῶμα καὶ αἷμα τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ.**

That is:

> “And he converts and perfects the holy gifts set before us into the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

This also appears from the old inscription on a wooden altar plated with silver, formerly built through the munificence of Roger, bishop of Oloron:

> “The gracious Spirit changes the things placed upon it;  
> From bread there becomes flesh, and from wine the substance becomes blood.”

This is found in Book V, chapter 18, of the *History of Béarn*, by the most distinguished and learned Peter de Marca.

Therefore, formerly, when certain most holy men were celebrating these sacred mysteries, the presence of the Holy Spirit would sometimes appear under a visible sign. So it happened once to Saint John the abbot, surnamed the Chozebite, who later became bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, as John Moschus reports in the *Spiritual Meadow*, chapters 25 and 27. He writes the same concerning a certain priest of a village in Cilicia named Mardardus, who would not begin Mass until he saw the Holy Spirit overshadowing the altar. In chapter 150 he writes of a certain bishop of Rumella near Rome, who customarily saw the descent of the Holy Spirit at the Prayer of the Oblation; and when he was celebrating before Pope Agapetus, after removing a certain deacon who was obstructing him, he himself and the pope saw the coming of the Holy Spirit.

**175. “He is whole in each portion.”** This doctrine agrees with what Saint Basil says in his letter to the patrician Caesaria:

> **Ταὐτόν τοίνυν ἐστὶ τῇ δυνάμει, εἴτε μίαν μερίδα δέξεταί τις, εἴτε πολλὰς μερίδας ὁμοῦ.**

That is:

> “It is therefore the same in power, whether someone receives one portion or many portions together.”

Hence Saint Caesarius says splendidly in Dialogue 3, Question 169:

> **Τὸ ἐπὶ τῆς θείας τραπέζης ἱερουργούμενον, καὶ τῷ θιάσῳ παντὶ ἀτμήτως διαιρούμενον καὶ ἀλήκτως μετεχόμενον.**

That is:

> “What is consecrated on the sacred table is divided indivisibly among the entire sacred assembly and is received without diminution.”

Guitmundus mentions this Preface in Book I of *The Truth of the Body and Blood of Christ in the Eucharist*:

> “So that no one may think that I have devised this statement from my own understanding, I have inserted here the Preface that is found throughout almost the entire Latin world on a certain Sunday between Epiphany and Septuagesima, containing the following: ‘Eternal God, and to you we offer this sacrificial Offering, which is the saving and ineffable sacrament of divine grace; it is offered by many, and one body of Christ is perfected through the infusion of the Holy Spirit. Each receives Christ the Lord, and in each portion he is whole; he is not diminished through the portions, but presents himself entire in each,’” etc.

Algerus, Book I on the same Sacrament, chapter 15, cites these words of the same Preface, which he attributes to Saint Ambrose:

> “Likewise Ambrose, on the fifth Sunday after Epiphany: ‘Each receives Christ the Lord, and in each portion he is whole; he is not diminished through the portions, but presents himself entire in each.’”

These words are also found in the Ambrosian liturgy.

**176. “In each one.”** So it reads in the Codices of Rodradi and Ratoldi, in Guitmundus, and in the Ambrosian liturgy. In the chapter of Algerus cited above it reads “through each portion.” This is not incorrect, since it may refer to “portions.”

**177. “We become one body of Christ.”** According to the teaching of Saint Augustine, *Tractate 27 on John*:

> “Therefore, by mystical words, he taught and admonished us to be in his body under the one head, as his members, eating his flesh and not abandoning his unity.”

Moreover, in Codex Rhemensis the following occurs: “On the fourth day before the Ides of February, the feast of Saints Zot­icus, Hyacinthus, and Herennius,” where one should read *Irenaeus*, as in Usuardus and in the manuscript Martyrology of the Corbie Library on this day. In the manuscript Martyrology of Saint Jerome:

> “At Rome, of Soteris, Zoticus, Jacinthus, Irenaeus, and Dionysius.”

For the last name, Usuardus and the cited manuscript Martyrology have *Amantius*. Their Mass is as follows. Prayer:

> “Lord our God, multiply your grace upon us,” etc.

Over the offerings:

> “Receive, Lord, on the feast of the holy martyrs, the offering of your people,” etc.

But *Hostias* (“sacrificial offerings”), *sacrificium* (“sacrifice”), or something similar seems to be missing.

Postcommunion:

> “May the blessing of your sacrament, Lord, which we have received, continually…” etc.

**178. “The feast of Saint Valentine the martyr.”** [Note: *Martyr* is absent in Calensis. Before this feast, Gemeticus assigns several others: Saint Vedastus the confessor, on the eighth day before the Ides of February; Saint Scholastica the virgin, on the fourth day before the Ides of February; and Saint Soteris the virgin on the same day. Finally, Saint Eormenihild the virgin, on the Ides of the same month.] So it reads in the printed editions, in Pamelio, and in our manuscript Codices, except Rhemensis, which has:

> “The feast of Saints Valentine, Vitalis, Felicula, and Zeno.”

All these saints occur on the same day in Usuardus’s Martyrology:

> “At Rome, the feast of blessed Valentine the priest,” etc.

Likewise:

> “At Rome, of Saints Vitalis, Felicula, and Zeno.”

The same is found in Notker’s Martyrology and in the manuscript Martyrology of the Corbie Library, where *Feniculae* is incorrectly written. Their Mass is as follows. Prayer:

> “Protect us, Lord, we beseech you, by the prayers of your saints,” etc.

Over the offerings:

> “As we come, Lord, to the feast of your martyrs Valentine, Vitalis, Felicula, and Zeno,” etc.

Postcommunion:

> “Protect your people, Lord,” etc.

In the same Codex Rhemensis the following occurs: “On the fourteenth day before the Kalends of March, the feast of Saint Juliana.” This is Juliana the virgin and martyr, who suffered at Nicomedia. Concerning her, the Martyrology of Saint Jerome says on the same day:

> “At Nicomedia, the passion of Saint Juliana the virgin and martyr.”

In Usuardus and in the manuscript Martyrology cited so often:

> “At Cumae, of Saint Juliana the virgin, who, after various tortures,” etc.

But they name the place of translation, not of her passion, as is known from the Martyrologies of Notker and Rabanus:

> “She suffered at Nicomedia, but after a short time, by God’s providence, was translated to Campania.”

Her Mass is as follows. Prayer:

> “Almighty and eternal God, who choose the weak things of the world to confound the strong,” etc.

Over the offerings:

> “In the precious passion of your holy martyr Juliana,” etc.

Postcommunion:

> “As we make libation, Lord,” etc.

**179. “The Chair of Saint Peter.”** [Note: This is omitted in Codex Calensis. In the Gallican Sacramentary published by D. J. Mabillon from a Codex written more than a thousand years ago in the Italian Museum, volume I, part II, there is a certain Mass called Romensis, whose first Prayer is the same as that of the feast of the Chair of Saint Peter: “O God, who, having conferred the keys upon blessed Peter the apostle,” etc., although no further mention of Saint Peter occurs in the entire Mass. In the old Lectionary of Luxeuil, readings are prescribed for this feast, and in the Gothic Missal a Mass is assigned for the Chair of Saint Peter the apostle. Mabillon proves very well, in Book II of *Gallican Liturgy*, page 120, that this feast of the Chair was once celebrated among the Gauls in January.] Without an adjunct, as in Pamelio, in Codex Rodradi, in the second part, in Codex Rhemensis, and in the little manuscript Martyrology appended to the same book. In the printed editions, “at Rome” is added. In Codex Ratoldi it reads: “At Antioch, the Chair of Saint Peter.”

Among Saint Augustine’s sermons on the saints there is Sermon 15, on the Chair of Saint Peter, in which he attacks pagan superstition as follows:

> “Although religious observance rightly introduced this solemnity into the Churches, I wonder why among certain unbelievers”—read “believers”—“such a destructive error has grown today that they bring food and wine to the tombs of the dead, as though the souls that have departed from their bodies desired bodily food.”

The Second Council of Tours, canon 22, also mentions this same feast and similar superstitions:

> “There are also those who, on the feast of the Chair of the lord apostle Peter, offer food to the dead. Returning to their homes, they revert to the errors of the pagans, and after the Body of the Lord, they receive foods consecrated to the demon.”

> “We charge both pastors and priests to exercise such care that, if they see anyone persisting in this folly, or carrying out at certain stones, trees, or springs—marked places of the pagans—practices that do not belong to the order of the Church, they should expel such persons from the holy Church by authoritative action.”

In these passages the day and month of the feast are not stated. From the words cited, however, it may sufficiently be inferred that the Chair of Saint Peter is intended, which is celebrated in February. First, mention is made of those who, according to pagan custom, made offerings to the dead and brought banquets to their tombs. This was formerly done during the Feralia, which in the ancient Roman Calendar begin on 20 February and last almost until the end of that month. During them the spirits of the dead were appeased, with food set upon their tombs for them to consume, as is clear from Ovid, Book II of the *Fasti*, which concerns the month of February:

> “Now the thin souls and bodies committed to tombs  
> wander; now the shade is fed by food set out.  
> Yet this continues no longer than the number of days  
> that remain in the month, as many as the verses of our song.”

> “Because they bring these rites, they called that day Feralia.”

Varro writes of this superstition in Book V of *On the Latin Language*:

> “The Feralia take their name from funeral offerings and from carrying, because they carry banquets to the tomb, by which they are entitled to make offerings there.”

Second, in the council cited above, those are reproved who perform at certain stones acts that do not pertain to the Church. These stones are clearly nothing other than boundary markers of fields, which the ancients worshiped under the name of the god Terminus and whose feast the pagans called the Terminalia. Like the Chair of Saint Peter at Antioch, this feast falls on 22 February, as is clear from the ancient Roman Calendar, which reads:

> “The Terminalia.”

Ovid also sings of this in the book cited above, concerning the same month:

> “When night has passed, let the accustomed honor be celebrated  
> for the god who separates the fields with his boundary.  
> Whether you are a stone or a stake buried in the field,  
> you too bear a name inherited from the ancients.”

Varro also discusses it in the book cited above. Therefore, since in this council and in the manuscript Codices cited above the Chair of Saint Peter is named without an adjunct, I think that formerly, on 22 February, the solemnity of both Chairs was celebrated, and that in the course of time it devolved upon the Chair of Antioch alone. It should also be noted that in our manuscript Codices there is no feast of the Chair of Saint Peter at Rome, nor is there one in the printed editions or in Pamelio.

**180. “Pontifical.”** Here *pontifical* means power or authority. In the *Law of the Burgundians*, title 19, section 6:

> “But if, within three months after the debt has been paid, he has not recovered his pledges, he will thereafter have no authority to reclaim them.”

And title 40, section 1:

> “We order that the authority of this action be preserved only with respect to manumitters and their freedmen.”

Likewise in Marculphus, formula 23:

> “And elsewhere, having no authority to alienate it.”

And formula 27:

> “Namely, so that we have absolutely no authority thereafter to alienate or diminish anything of whatever kind.”

And in Arnobius, on Psalm 58:

> “They receive the authority to judge and correct.”

**181. “You founded [it] upon the patriarchs.”** So it reads in all our manuscript Codices, in the printed editions, and in Pamelio. Therefore the reading *cleansed*, which some seek to defend, must be rejected. For it can rightly be said that the Church was founded upon the patriarchs, since Christ was first revealed to them and their faith was the precursor of ours. Moreover, *cleansed* cannot produce any sound meaning, since one cannot say that the Church, which did not yet exist, was cleansed in the patriarchs.

**182. “So that whatever he had established on earth.”** This explains what Christ had once said allegorically to Peter:

> “And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven,” etc.

**183. “Of Saint Matthias.”** This feast is absent from our other manuscript Codices. [Note: Nor is it found in the Swedish Royal manuscripts or in Calensis. It is contained in Gemeticus and Theodoricus.]

**184. “The sacred number.”** Namely, the number twelve, formerly signified for the apostolic college by the twelve patriarchs, the twelve springs of water, and the twelve gates of the heavenly Jerusalem.

Moreover, in Codex Rhemensis the following occurs: “On the Nones of March, the feast of Saints Perpetua and Felicity.” Concerning them, the manuscript Martyrology of the Corbie Library says on the same day:

> “In the Mauritanian city of the Tuburbitans, the passion of the holy martyrs Perpetua and Felicity, and with them Revocatus, Saturninus, and Secundolus.”

In Usuardus’s Martyrology:

> “In the Mauritanian city of the Tuburbitans, the feast of the holy martyrs Perpetua and Felicity, and with them Revocatus, Saturninus, and Secundolus, the last of whom rested in prison, while all the others were given to the beasts under the emperor Severus.”

And in the manuscript Martyrology of Saint Jerome:

> “In the Mauritanian city of the Turbitans, the passion of Saints Perpetua and Felicity.”

Above, on the same day, Saturninus, Revocatus, and Secundillus—read *Secundolus*—are also mentioned among other saints assigned to Antioch. But I think *in Africa* has been omitted, at least before *Saturninus*. See more in Baronius on this day.

Their Mass is as follows. Prayer:

> “Grant us, Lord our God, to venerate the palms of the holy martyrs with unceasing devotion,” etc.

Over the offerings:

> “Look with favor, Lord, we beseech you, upon the gifts placed upon your altars,” etc.

Postcommunion:

> “Grant us, Lord, we beseech you, through the intercession of the saints, that what we have touched with our mouth,” etc.

[Note: The same Mass is assigned in Gemeticus and Theodoricus on this very day, namely the Nones of March.]

**185. “May they grant us, Lord,” etc.** In the printed Codices of Rodradi and Ratoldi: “O God, who [—] blessed Gregory,” etc.

Moreover, in Codex Ratoldi the feast of Saint Cuthbert the bishop follows. [Note: Gemeticus agrees.] He was bishop of Lindisfarne, whose life Bede wrote in prose and verse; Bede also discusses him in Book IV of his *History of the English*. The life of Saint Cuthbert written by Bede in verse is found in Henry Canisius, volume V of *Ancient Readings*. [Note: The Mass is entirely different in Gemeticus, and in neither the Prayers nor the Preface is he ever called a martyr.] His Mass is as follows:

Prayer:

> “The holy and glorious martyr Cuthbert.”

Over the offerings:

> “By this sacred work of Christ and of all the holy martyrs,” etc.

Preface:

> “On this day of the migration to Christ of the most holy priest Cuthbert,” etc.

Blessing:

> “Lord God of all graces, look upon all this people of yours, who serve you through divine offices in your honor; and whatever benefited your holy martyr Cuthbert today for blessedness, may it benefit this Church as an example. Amen,” etc.

At the Completion:

> “Satisfied, Lord, with the gifts of your offerings,” etc.

I see no reason why Saint Cuthbert should be called a martyr in this Mass, since Bede wrote nothing of the kind about him, nor did Usuardus on this day. The manuscript Martyrology of the Corbie Library supports Codex Ratoldi, where it reads on the same day:

> “In Britain, the feast of Saint Cuthbert the martyr.”

[Note: In Gemeticus and Theodoricus this feast is celebrated with a solemn vigil.]

In the same Codex Ratoldi the following follows: “On the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, the feast of Saint Benedict the abbot.” His Mass is as follows:

> “Almighty and eternal God, who have shown us the example”—read *exemplar*—“of glorious Benedict and the triumph of humility,” etc.

Preface:

> “Celebrating the glorious day of the venerable Father Benedict,” etc.

Blessing, as in the Mass of Saint Cuthbert.

At the Completion:

> “Having received, Lord our God, the saving Sacraments,” etc.

Over the people:

> “The people subject to your name,” etc.

**186. “The Annunciation of the Angel to Saint Mary.”** So it reads in the printed edition from the Vatican; but in our other manuscript Codices it reads: “The Annunciation of Saint Mary.” [Note: This is how Codex Calensis reads, and Gemeticus and Theodoricus agree.]

At the Council in Trullo, canon 52, this feast is called:

> **ἡ ἁγία τοῦ εὐαγγελισμοῦ ἡμέρα**  
> “The holy day of the Annunciation.”

In the novella of the emperor Manuel Comnenus, cited by Theodore Balsamon in the first chapter of title 7 of Photius’s *Nomocanon*:

> **τῆς θεομήτορος εὐαγγελισμός**  
> “The Annunciation of the Mother of God.”

In the Alexandrian Chronicle, Olympiad 351:

> **ἡ ἡμέρα τοῦ εὐαγγελισμοῦ τῆς δεσποίνης ἡμῶν τῆς θεοτόκου**  
> “The day of the Annunciation of our Lady, the Mother of God.”

Codinus Curopalates, in his book *On the Offices*, simply calls it:

> **εὐαγγελισμός**  
> “Annunciation.”

**187. “In the womb of the blessed Virgin.”** So it reads in the Codex of the priest Rodradi and in Pamelio. Correctly so. For in Matthew 1:20 it reads: “what has been born in her.” In the Roman Missal it reads “of the blessed Virgin,” etc. This Prayer seems to be for the Procession or Collect, etc.; for another is marked for the Mass.

**188. “In the womb of the blessed Virgin.”** So it reads in Codex Rodradi. Correctly so. In Codex Ratoldi, in the printed editions, and in Pamelio, the preposition *in* is absent.

189. **To be incarnated.** Thus in the Codex of Rodrardus. Excellent. In the Codex of Ratoldus, in the printed editions, and in Pamel(i)us, one reads: [Note: [Col. 0305D] The same is also read in Gemet.] “to unite.” If anyone wishes to approve this reading, it is necessary to restore the preposition *in*, which has dropped out of the aforementioned Codices, reading [Note: [Col. 0305D] The particle *in* is absent from Codex Gemet.] “to unite in the womb of the Blessed Virgin,” so that the sense is: “God, who wished to unite your Word—namely, with our human nature—in the womb of the blessed [Col. 0305C] Virgin.” Otherwise the following absurd sense would result: that God wished to unite his Word to the womb of the Blessed Virgin.

190. **The present solemnity.** In the Codex of Rodrardus one reads [Note: [Col. 0306D] So also in the first Theoderic. But in Gemet one reads: “make us so to complete this day.”] “the present celebration.” In the printed editions and in the Codex of Ratoldus one reads: “Make us so to complete it.” Incorrectly.

191. **With peace granted.** Not so much external peace 314 as internal peace.

192. **Of divine grace.** This the angel in Luke 1 calls “the power of the Most High.”

193. **On Septuagesima.** Concerning Septuagesima, consult our notes and observations on the *Concordia of the Rules of Saint Benedict, Abbot of Aniane*, chapter 56, § 7.

194. **So that, freed from earthly sustenance.** For at that time the fasts of ecclesiastical persons formerly began then.

195. **And through that food, etc.** For, according to the diversity of the seasons, earthly and spiritual food is given by God: earthly food outside the fast, spiritual food during the fast; that is, when people fast, they abound more richly in spiritual food.

196. **By attainment.** To eternal life.

197. **On Sexagesima.** The Fourth Council of Orléans, canon 2, forbids priests to impose Sexagesima and Quinquagesima: “We decree this also to be observed, that Lent be kept equally by all Churches; and that no priest presume to impose Quinquagesima or Sexagesima before Easter.” But the council does not prohibit the office of such days, only the fast, because those who fasted during Sexagesima and Quinquagesima did not observe the Saturday fast in Lent, but fasted during Sexagesima and Quinquagesima in compensation for the Saturdays and Sundays. Hence the council adds: “Nor shall anyone, except on account of illness, break the Lenten fast on Saturdays, unless he eats only on Sunday.”

This Saturday fast during Lent had formerly been prescribed by the Council of Agde, canon 12: “It has also pleased us that all the children of the Churches, except on Sundays, fast during Lent, even on Saturday, by priestly ordinance and under threat of discipline.” But since this decree was observed nowhere, it was renewed at the Fourth Council of Orléans, especially on account of the Goths, who, having received the faith from the Easterners, did not observe the Saturday fast according to their custom and drew their Gallic neighbors into this practice.

198. **To its fullness.** The fullness of the sacred sacrament is the grace which the Eucharist confers fully and abundantly [Col. 0306B].

199. **So that thirtyfold.** In accordance with the words of the Gospel, Matthew 13, which Saint Jerome explains as follows in Book 1 *Against Jovinianus*, near the beginning:

“Thirty refers to marriage. For the joining of the fingers itself, as though embracing and sealing with a gentle kiss, represents husband and wife. Sixty refers to widows, since they are placed in distress and tribulation; hence they are pressed down by the upper finger. And the greater the difficulty of abstaining from the allurements of pleasures once experienced, the greater is the reward. Moreover, the number one hundred—pay close attention, I ask, reader—is transferred from the left hand to the right; and, with the same fingers but not the same hand by which married women and widows are represented on the left, it forms a circle expressing the crown of virginity.”

These matters are expressed more specifically by Bede in his book *On the Art of Counting*. The number thirty is explained from the joining of the fingers as follows: “When you say thirty, gently join the nails of the index finger and thumb in an embrace.” Sixty is formed in this way: “Carefully encircle the thumb, bent as above, with the curved index finger.” One hundred is formed thus: “You will make one hundred on the right hand as you make ten on the left.” Ten, however, is made, according to the same Bede above, as follows: “When you say ten, fix the nail of the index finger in the middle joint of the thumb.”

Saint Jerome says that one hundred is transferred from the left hand to the right because the first counting is done on the fingers of the left hand, up to one hundred; when these have been traversed, one passes to the right hand, on which the counting begins with one hundred. Hence Juvenal, in Satire 10, said of a long-lived man:

> Fortunate indeed is he who through so many ages  
> Has postponed death and now counts his years on his right hand.

When ten thousand is reached, counting begins again on the left hand, with the palm placed upon the middle of the breast, Bede says. Hence the jest of the poet Nicarchus in Book 2 of the *Anthology*, concerning a remarkably vigorous old woman:

> She, beginning again to count old age  
> With her left hand.

[Col. 0306D] That is, “she who begins again to count old age with her left hand.” [Note: [Col. 0306D] What the most learned Menardus has collected here admirably confirms what we said in note *d* on Homily 5 of Book 2 on Ezekiel, no. 12.]

200. **May he be present to us.** In the Codex of Rheims one reads: “May he be with us.”

201. **And the sacrifice to be celebrated.** Thus in the Codices of Rodrardus and Ratoldus, and in Pamel(i)us. In the printed editions and in the Roman Missal one reads: “and for the celebration of the sacrifice.” [Note: [Col. 0306D] The same is also found in the Royal Codex of Sweden.] In the Codex of Rheims there is another Prayer: “We offer, Lord, the sacrifice of the observance of Easter, etc.” Here “the observance of Easter” means the Lenten fast, because it is a kind of preparation for the celebration of the Paschal feast. [Col. 0307A]

Hincmar, Archbishop of Rheims, calls the Lenten fast the Paschal fast in a manuscript letter of the monastery of Saint Remigius at Rheims: “And you who have begun,” he says, “the Paschal fasts, keep before your eyes what the Lord Jesus said at Easter—that is, at his passage from this world to the Father—when he handed over his body and blood to his disciples, concerning the treacherous disciple.” But more on this below.

202. **And to entreat your Majesty with bowed devotion.** These words are lacking in the Codex of Rheims.

203. **Bowed.** *Cernuus* properly means “inclined,” as though one were looking at the earth, says Nonius Marcellus, chapter 1.

204. **The beginning of the fast.** It is certain that this celebration, or Mass, was added after the death of Saint Gregory, since in his time the four days before Lent were not subject to any law of fasting, as is clear from Saint Gregory himself, *Homily 16 on the Gospels*, where he writes:

“From the present day until the joys of the Paschal solemnity there are six weeks, whose days amount to forty-two. When the six Sundays of abstinence are subtracted from these, no more than thirty-six days remain in abstinence. Since the year consists of 365 days, while we afflict ourselves for thirty-six days, we give God, as it were, the tithes of our year.”

Since Saint Gregory therefore assigns here the number of days during which the Lenten fast is to be observed, and the four days preceding Lent are not included within this number, it is certain that at that time they were not subject to any fast. Nor does it matter that shortly before this he speaks, following the example of Christ, Moses, and Elijah, of forty days. For although in former times many did not fast for the full forty days but for fewer, they were nevertheless said to fast forty days and to keep Lent, as Socrates notes in Book 5 of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 21.

The Easterners and Egyptians also formerly observed this same tithing of the days, as Cassian teaches in *Conference* 21, chapters 25 and 27, and Saint Dorotheus in *Teaching* 15. They added to the aforementioned tithe half of the night of Holy Easter Sunday: for those who fasted on Holy Saturday were not permitted to break the fast before cockcrow on Sunday. Since they did not fast on Sundays or Saturdays, except Holy Saturday, they observed seven weeks.

Those among the Greeks who fasted forty complete days extended Lent over eight weeks, as Saint Dorotheus teaches in the same place. For there was formerly no single manner of observing the Lenten fast, either among Catholics or among heretics, as is evident from Socrates, Book 5 of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 21; Sozomen, Book 7 of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 19; John Chrysostom, *Homily 16 to the People of Antioch*; Photius’s *Bibliotheca*, no. 107; and Saint Leo the Pope, *Sermon 4 on Lent*.

Socrates, in the chapter cited, writes that at Rome the Lenten fast consisted only of three consecutive weeks before Easter, Saturdays and Sundays being excepted. But since he excludes Saturdays from the fast, I think that his text has been corrupted and that one should read *ἐν νέᾳ Ῥώμῃ*, that is, “in New Rome,” namely Constantinople. For formerly at Constantinople, in the time of Saint John Chrysostom, as he himself writes in the homily cited above, the entire Lent was not fasted by everyone: some fasted two weeks, others only three, and others the whole period. Thus, after the death of Saint John Chrysostom, the practice of the Lenten fast was reduced to three weeks.

Otherwise Socrates would contradict himself, since below in the same chapter he writes: *ἐν Ῥώμῃ πᾶν σάββατον νηστεύουσι*, that is, “At Rome they fast every Saturday.” And indeed the Romans fasted every Saturday, whereas the Greeks did not, except on Holy Saturday.

205. **For the collect.** Namely, at Saint Anastasia, to which the procession proceeded. On this day ashes were formerly imposed upon penitents; but more on this below.

206. **Of the sacrament.** That is, of the observance or celebration—in this case, the Lenten one.

207. **Aid.** In the Codices of Rodrardus and Ratoldus one reads “protection.” In the Codex of Rheims neither of these words is found, but one or the other must be restored.

208. **From the punishment of sin.** That is, from penance.

209. **Of the sacrament.** That is, of sacramental grace—a metonymy, with the cause standing for the effect.

210. **Of the Paschal observance.** Here “Paschal observance” means the Lenten fast. Hincmar, in the manuscript letter cited above, calls the Lenten fast the Paschal fast; and it is likewise called this by Timothy, bishop of Alexandria, in his *Questions*, as Theodore Balsamon correctly explains there, question 7:

> γυνὴ ἐὰν γεννήσῃ, τὸ Πάσχα ὀφείλει νηστεύειν;

That is: “If a woman gives birth, must she fast for Easter?”

And question 9:

> εἴ τις ἀσθενὴς, καὶ ἐκ βίας νόσου σφόδρα λελωβημένος, καὶ ἔλθῃ τὸ ἅγιον Πάσχα

That is: “If someone is ill and severely weakened by the force of disease, and Holy Easter arrives, must he fast?”

211. **They regard them as useless.** Supply: “to be performed.”

212. **To be judged.** Supply: “rationally.”

213. **His food is every good intention, etc.** These words correspond to John 4: “My food is to do the will of him who sent me.”

214. **Of the sacrament.** That is, of the mystery, the secret under whose covering something mystical lies hidden—namely, the reason why Christ wished to consecrate this number of forty days by his fast.

215. **Throughout the whole of Lent, etc.** These words are absent from the printed editions, from the other manuscript Codices in our possession, and from Pamel(i)us. [Note: [Col. 0307D] They are likewise entirely absent from our manuscripts.]

216. **He stands with his head uncovered.** This occurs during the Prayer, according to the ancient custom of Christians, which Tertullian mentions in the *Apologeticus*: “Looking up toward heaven, Christians pray with hands extended because they are harmless; with head uncovered because we do not blush; finally, without a prompter, because we pray from the heart for all emperors.” 317

The pagans, by contrast, prayed with their heads covered and veiled. Saint Cyprian, in his *Sermon on the Lapsed*, says: “Your head remained free from the impious and criminal covering with which the heads of the sacrificing captives were there veiled.”

217. **As a remedy.** In place of “for a remedy”; the sense is: “Grant that the votive sacraments may come to us as a remedy for the temporal life”—namely, so that it may be rightly conducted—and for the eternal life that is to be attained. The common reading is “remedies.”

218. **On Saturday with the twelve readings.** This first fast of the four seasonal fasts did not formerly always occur in the first week of Lent; but more on this below.

219. **Eternal remedies for us.** Eternal remedies are those which conduce to the attainment of eternal life. This is a metonymy, like “pale death.”

220. **Which, by afflicting itself in the flesh.** [Note: [Col. 0307D] This reading is confirmed by the authority of the Codices of Pamel(i)us, the Royal Codex of Sweden, Gemet, and both Codices of Theoderic.] This is the best reading, recognized by the Codex of Rodrardus: “that is, by afflicting itself in the flesh.” The common reading is “the flesh.”

221. **Of eternal redemption.** That is, of the grace which obtains eternal redemption for us. This is a metonymy, with the effect standing for the cause.

222. **External things.** That is, “alien things,” for this is an antithesis: personal sins are set against alien sins.

223. **Those who are ignorant.** That is, sinners.

224. **And which through earthly pleasure.** The passage is corrupt and, in my judgment, should be emended as follows: “And since we renounce carnal feasts for the sake of earthly pleasure, let us cut off the perverse intentions of the human will.”

225. **The effect of our redemption.** That is, the grace which Christ acquired for us by his blood. Below, in the Preface, “immediately” means “at once” or “straightaway.”

226. **May he render us acceptable to the heavenly promises.** That is, “may he render us acceptable and pleasing to you, so that we may obtain the heavenly promises.”

227. **A water jar.** The author of the ancient etymological work explains what a *hydria* is: *ὑδρία κυρίως τὸ εἰς ὕδωρ εὔθετον ἀγγεῖον*, that is, “a *hydria* is properly a vessel suitable for water.”

Saint Augustine, *Tractate 15 on John*: “There was a vessel from which water was drawn. In Greek it is called a *hydria*, because in Greek *ὕδωρ* means ‘water,’ as though it were called an aquarius.”

Saint Isidore, Book 20 of the *Etymologies*, chapter 6: “A *hydria* is called, by derivation, a kind of water vessel; for the Greeks call water *ὕδωρ*.”

It was not only a vessel for water but also for wine, as Julius Pollux testifies in Book 10 of the *Onomasticon*, chapter 20:

> ὥστε οὐ μόνον ὕδατος, ἀλλὰ καὶ οἴνου ἀγγεῖον ἡ ὑδρία ἦν.

That is: “Thus the *hydria* was a vessel not only for water but also for wine.” And rightly so, because the *hydriai* used at the wedding in Cana of Galilee, John 2, were full of wine; when these had been emptied, Christ commanded that they be filled with water so that he might turn it into wine. In this Preface, however, *hydria* is used metaphorically.

228. **Unharmed.** That is, subject to no guilt of sins [Col. 0309B].

229. **By the fourfold mass of sins.** He alludes to the four-day corruption of Lazarus. The fourfold mass of sins consists of the principal sins: pride, avarice, lust, and gluttony.

230. **And may lead them to eternal remedies.** That is, may lead them to the Paschal sacrament of Christ’s body and blood, which is rightly called an eternal remedy, because through its benefit we attain eternal life.

231. **Of the sacrament.** That is, of sacramental grace, as noted above.

232. **Whose mercy goes before us so that we may act well, etc.** Saint Augustine says the same in the *Enchiridion*, chapter 28: “He goes before the unwilling, so that he may will; he follows the willing, lest he will in vain.”

Here it should be noted that, although theologians often understand by prevenient grace precisely what they mean by exciting grace, and by subsequent grace precisely what they mean by assisting grace, nevertheless prevenient grace is often understood to include all graces—exciting, assisting, and habitual—insofar as through them we are made just. Subsequent grace, however, is also understood to include all graces, but insofar as, once justification has been received, we are strengthened, increased, and preserved by them unto the end.

Hence Saint Augustine, in *On Nature and Grace*, chapter 51: “God goes before us so that we may be healed; he follows us so that, once healed, we may be strengthened. He goes before us so that we may be called; he follows us so that we may be glorified. He goes before us so that we may live devoutly; he follows us so that we may live with him forever.”

Saint Fulgentius, Book 1 *To Monymus*, chapter 11: “He goes before the ungodly so that he may become just; he follows him lest he become ungodly. He goes before the blind man to give him light; he follows the seeing man to preserve the light he has bestowed. He goes before the fallen so that he may rise; he follows the one raised up lest he fall.”

Cassiodorus, on Psalm 22: “He follows, certainly, in order to confer justice; he precedes in order to confer grace. For if he only followed, no one would receive gifts; if he only preceded, no one could preserve what had been bestowed. The snares which the devil prepares from behind are more dangerous; and unless the Lord’s mercy follows, human frailty is very easily deceived. For when someone thinks that he has passed beyond a vice, he is then deceived by even more careless ignorance. Hence it is supremely necessary that the Lord’s grace always precede us and his mercy follow us.”

And Saint Gregory, Book 9 of the *Moralia*, chapter 29: “The Lord, by the mercy with which he goes before us so that we may live well, subsequently guards us; for unless he supplies mercy, the life he grants cannot be preserved.”

This teaching is founded on Scripture: Psalm 58, “His mercy will go before me”; Psalm 22, “Your mercy will follow me.” Therefore, when it is said here, “He goes before us so that we may act well; he follows us lest we act in vain,” it is understood that prevenient grace is given for acting well, while subsequent grace is given for preserving the good that has been granted and persevering in it. Thus the person who perseveres in the good he has begun does not act in vain, and subsequent grace is given so that he may not act in vain.

233. **Sunday of the Palms.** Codinus Curopalates, in his book *On Offices*, calls it *ἑορτὴ τῶν βαΐων*, that is, “the feast of Palms.”

234. **So that, just as he entered with palm branches, etc.** Note the antiquity of the solemnity of Palms, during which a procession is made with blessed branches of trees. It is indeed extremely ancient; Saint Cyril of Jerusalem mentions it in *Catechesis 10*:

> Ὁ φοῖνιξ ὁ ἐπὶ τῆς φάραγγος, μαρτυρεῖ τὰ βάϊα παρασχὼν πᾶσι τοῖς τότε εὐφημοῦσι.

That is: “The palm tree in the valley bears witness, supplying branches to all who then offer praise.”

Saint Aldhelm, bishop of the Eastern Saxons, also mentions this solemnity in Book 15 of *On the Praise of Virginity*, when speaking of our holy father Benedict:

“He did not without reason share the privilege of the name Benedict with our Advocate and Redeemer, concerning whom the nursing children of the Gospel, singing in harmony with one voice, proclaimed together: ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.’ Our own humble station, relying upon the authentic authority of the ancients, also celebrates this event in the most sacred solemnity of Palms, resounding with melodious voice in two choirs and exulting with two harmonies in the singing of ‘Hosanna,’ with the melody of joyful jubilation.”

The Codex of Ratoldus contains a Blessing of the Palms. Alcuin, Book 14 *On the Divine Offices*, describing the entire order of the procession, says near the end:

“When this has been completed, two singers begin certain verses:

> You are Israel’s King.

“The choir responds, looking toward, or bowing to, the holy Gospel written above:

> Glory, praise, and honor be to you.

“And the other verses follow in order.”

The holy Gospel mentioned here is the one placed upon and carried in a certain litter during that procession, as the same Alcuin writes above in the same chapter.

In the passage cited, attention should be paid to the verses “You are Israel’s King” and “Glory, praise, and honor,” which are commonly said to have been composed by Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, while imprisoned at Angers. For, as the story goes, when he had been accused of conspiracy against Emperor Louis the Pious with Bernard, king of Italy, he was imprisoned at Angers by order of that emperor. There he composed these verses. When he sang them in the prison on Palm Sunday, the emperor, who happened to be passing by, was captivated by the melody of the hymns, freed Theodulf from prison, and restored him to his see.

Certain authors who were not very ancient wrote this story. But the passage cited above from Alcuin, where these verses are mentioned, proves that they were mistaken, since Alcuin died in the year 804, long before Bernard’s conspiracy, as Oderannus, monk of Saint Peter of Viviers, testifies in his *Chronicle*: “In the year 804 Alcuin, philosopher and abbot of Saint Martin, died.”

Among the ancient writers who recorded the deeds of Emperor Louis the Pious, it is astonishing that there is no mention of such a story—or rather, fable—and what they themselves write about Theodulf and the other conspirators is wholly opposed to this tale. For in the same year, 818, after capturing the conspirators, the emperor returned to Aachen. When the Lenten fast had ended, a few days after Easter he ordered that the authors of the conspiracy and Bernard the king, having been condemned to death by the judgment of the Franks, should merely be deprived of their sight; that the bishops, deposed by synodal judgment, should be confined to monasteries; and that the others, according as each appeared more or less guilty, should either be condemned to exile or have their hair cut and live in monasteries, as Einhard writes under that year.

Thegan likewise records this in Book 22 of *On the Deeds of Emperor Louis the Pious*, mentioning only the deposition of the bishops and making no mention of their confinement in monasteries. The same is testified by an ancient anonymous writer in the *Life of Louis the Pious*, who reports that Theodulf and the other bishops were deposed and forced into monasteries, that is, into exile.

For Theodulf himself testifies that he was driven into exile, in a letter to Bishop Modoinus:

> This, Modoinus, Theodulf sends to you in exile,  
> Behold, bowed before the highest pontiffs, a song.

And in a letter to Bishop Aigulf:

> This poem, most holy bishop Aigulf, I send to you—  
> Theodulf, an exile, from exile.

In the letter cited to Modoinus he complains that he had not confessed himself justly deprived of his episcopate, and that this had been done without the authority of the Roman pontiff:

> No witness was present there, nor any suitable judge;  
> I myself had confessed to no crime.  
> Suppose I had confessed: whose judgment would have had the power  
> To impose upon me the appropriate restraints of judgment?  
> That task belongs solely to the Roman pontiff,  
> From whose hand I received the sacred pallium.

These verses may be found in Henry Canisius, volume 5 of *Ancient Readings*, part 2.

From this it is clear that, since Theodulf had already been condemned shortly after the Paschal solemnity, the emperor—who at that time was at Aachen—did not release him from chains on Palm Sunday because he was delighted by his melody.

Afterward Emperor Louis went to Lesser Brittany, that is, Armorica, [Col. 0311B] to suppress Morman, who had arrogated royal power over the Bretons to himself. Having restored order, he returned and came to Angers, where Queen Irmingard, his wife, whom he had left there sick when he departed, died two days after he arrived, her illness having worsened, on 3 October, as Einhard writes under the same year. Thegan and the anonymous writer cited above also attest this.

The emperor was therefore at Angers twice that year, on his way to Armorica and on his return. Yet he could not have released Theodulf: the emperor went to Angers only after Easter, returned in October, and departed shortly afterward.

Finally, in the year 821, that pious and merciful emperor, at the general assembly at Thionville, when the marriage of his son Lothair and Irmingard, daughter of Count Hugh, was being celebrated, summoned the conspirators, forgave the injury, and restored to them all their goods and possessions. Einhard testifies to this under that year:

“In this palace the singular mercy of the most pious emperor shone forth, which he displayed toward those who had conspired with his nephew Bernard in Italy against his person and kingdom. When he had ordered them to come into his presence, he granted them not only life and limb but also, with great generosity, restored to them the possessions which by legal judgment had been confiscated to the treasury.”

The anonymous writer cited above in the *Life of Louis the Pious* gives the same testimony. From this it is clear that Theodulf’s crime was not pardoned while he was in prison at Angers.

Indeed, Louis was very hostile toward Theodulf and was unwilling to spare him unless he first confessed his crime, as Bishop Modoinus wrote to Theodulf:

> He prefers to forgive you every crime committed,  
> If only you are willing to acknowledge that you have sinned.  
> For a sincere confession will benefit you,  
> If by your words you prove yourself guilty of the crime.

And shortly afterward:

> I think the prince’s anger can be overcome in no other way  
> Unless you prove yourself guilty of the crime.

Henry Canisius reports these verses in the book cited above. But the pious emperor later changed his sentence, as we said shortly before, and in his singular clemency spared all the conspirators.

A certain anonymous writer, who lived in the time of Philip Augustus, king of the Franks, in chapter 3 of his book *On the Translation of the Relics of Saint Mammas to Gaul*, attributes these verses to Reinald, bishop of Langres, and tells a story almost identical to the one falsely believed about Theodulf, as related above:

“In the course of time Reinald, bishop of Langres of blessed memory, was appointed to govern the city of Langres. He was the tenth bishop to sit before the venerable William, who is now our elected bishop. That man was indeed distinguished by birth, but the nobility of his lineage was enhanced by upright character and a wide knowledge of letters. He was learned not only in the liberal studies but also sufficiently instructed in the pages of both Testaments. His works themselves bear witness to the truth.

“For when he held the county of Tonnerre and the county of Bar-sur-Seine on behalf of his nephews, who were still children, the king of the Franks at that time, because of certain disputes, as the story goes, detained him in the city of Noyon, in a tower beside the gate. There, not broken by adversity but rejoicing because he understood that God scourges the son whom he loves, he composed a hymn and sang it with the boys in melodious voices on Palm Sunday, namely, ‘Glory, praise, and honor.’ He himself also translated the Life of the blessed martyr Mammas from Greek into Latin.”

This is what the anonymous writer says. I would think that he should be followed, were it not for the mention of these verses in Alcuin. (In the library of Fleury, belonging to Abbot John of Bosco.)

235. **Grant, we beseech you, almighty God, that we who in so many adversities have grown weak through our infirmity, etc.** Alcuin, in Book 2 *Against Elipandus, Bishop of Toledo*, cites this Prayer, but assigns it to the Mass of the Palms. For he says in the Mass for the Palms, in a certain Prayer: “Grant, we beseech you, almighty God, that we who in so many adversities have grown weak through our infirmity, etc.”

236. **Humility raises up.** Saint Augustine says splendidly in Book 1 *On the Creed for Catechumens*: “Man exalted himself and fell; God humbled himself and raised him up. What is the humility of Christ? God extended his hand to fallen man. We fell; he descended. We lay prostrate; he bowed down. Let us take hold and rise, so that we may not fall into punishment.”

237. **Sacraments.** That is, feasts.

238. **Which have been instituted amid medicinal fasts.** That is, which have been instituted to be celebrated during medicinal fasts.

239. **And he says the solemn Prayers.** According to the ancient custom, which may be seen in Alcuin, *On the Divine Offices*, in the chapter on the Wednesday of Holy Week: “He says the solemn Prayers, as on Good Friday.” He adds the reason: on this day the Jews took counsel concerning the arrest of Jesus.

The same is found in Amalarius, Book 1 *On the Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 11: “The aforementioned little book, the Roman Order, declares that according to Roman custom the Prayers which we ordinarily perform on Good Friday should be recited on this day before the public office.”

This may be seen in the Roman Order, in the section concerning Wednesday of Holy Week: “And he says the solemn Prayers: ‘Let us pray, most beloved, first for the Church of God,’ and the others in order; only the prayer for himself is omitted. Then he says the Prayer for the king of the Franks or for the emperor. Finally, no knees are bent for the Jews.”

This custom also seems to be found in the Codex of Tilly, which formerly belonged to the Church of Séez, as we noted in the Preface. For this Codex says, in the order for Wednesday of Holy Week:

“Awaiting the bishop, who always says the solemn Prayers himself in the principal church on that day, as they are contained in the Sacramentary, this is the order.”

And shortly afterward:

“After the Amen he says the solemn Prayers: ‘Let us pray, most beloved, first for the Church of God,’ and the others in order; only the prayer for himself is omitted; after the emperor he says the prayer for the king of the Franks. Finally, no knees are bent for the Jews.”

Prayers of this kind are also found in the printed editions for this same Wednesday, but they do not occur in the other manuscript Codices in our possession [Note: [Col. 0311] In the first Theoderic, in the office of Friday, this title precedes such Prayers: “Here begin the Prayers to be said on Wednesday and Friday.”] nor in Pamel(i)us. Nor are they now said on this Wednesday.

240. **Let us pray.** The Greeks say *τοῦ Κυρίου δεηθῶμεν*, that is, “Let us beseech the Lord,” as is clear both from the liturgy of Saint John Chrysostom and frequently from the Greek *Euchologion*. It is said by the deacon, not by the priest, as is evident from the same liturgy of Saint John Chrysostom: *ὁ διάκονος, Τοῦ Κυρίου δεηθῶμεν*, that is, “The deacon says: ‘Let us beseech the Lord,’” and likewise throughout the *Euchologion*.

It should be noted that on this Wednesday, as on the following Friday, in these Prayers the priest does not merely announce the Prayer by saying “Let us pray,” as is customary; he also states for whom and for what one should pray, as was formerly customary in the Prayers of all other Masses, when the priest exhorted the people to pray. This is manifest from Saint Augustine’s Letter 107 to Vitalis:

“Exercise your arguments against the Prayers of the Church, and when you hear the priest of God at the altar exhorting God’s people to pray for unbelievers, that God may convert them to the faith; for catechumens, that he may inspire in them the desire for regeneration; and for the faithful, that by his gift they may persevere in what they have begun to be—mock these pious words and say that you do not do what he exhorts.”

241. **Let us bend our knees.** It is an ancient ecclesiastical custom for the deacon to cry out, “Let us bend our knees.” This may be seen in Homily 34 of Saint Caesarius of Arles:

“For when I frequently and carefully observe, as I ought, I see that when the deacon cries out, ‘Let us bend our knees,’ the greater part of the people remain standing upright like columns. This is neither permitted nor beneficial to Christians when prayer is being offered in church.”

At the end of the Homily he says:

“And whenever the deacon cries out that you should bend your knees in prayer or bow your heads for the Blessing, do so obediently and faithfully with true humility.”

242. **After they have prayed.** Formerly, after the deacon had cried out “Let us bend our knees,” the people prayed. Jesse of Amiens, in his letter *On Baptism*, says: “Afterward let them be admonished by the deacon: ‘Pray, you who have been chosen; bend your knees.’ And after they have prayed, he says: ‘Rise.’”

They prayed in silence. Hence the Codex of Rheims says: “And the deacon announces: 322 ‘Let us bend our knees,’ and the people are silent.”

243. **He says, ‘Rise.’** After the Prayer had been completed, the deacon formerly cried out, “Rise.” This may be seen in the passage of Jesse of Amiens cited above: “After they have prayed, let him say, ‘Rise.’”

And in the Codex of Rheims, on Good Friday: “And the deacon announces, ‘Let us bend our knees,’ and the people are silent. He says, ‘Rise,’ and gives the Prayer.” The last words, “and gives the Prayer,” are to be understood of the bishop.

Alcuin likewise says, in *On the Divine Offices*, in the chapter on Friday, also called Parasceve: “He says, ‘Let us pray’; and the deacon says, ‘Let us bend our knees’; then the deacon says, ‘Rise,’ and the bishop gives the Prayer.”

And in the Codex of Tilly, where this Friday is discussed: “And let him say, ‘Let us pray,’ and let the deacon say, ‘Let us bend our knees’; and let him pray for a very long time; and let the deacon say, ‘Rise.’”

Today, however, *Rise* is said by the subdeacon.

It should further be noted that in the Roman Order, in the section concerning Friday, among these solemn Prayers—“Let us pray, most beloved, for the holy Church of God,” etc.—only “Rise” is said by the deacon at the end of each Prayer. Once it has been said, the priest says “Through the Lord,” in this manner:

“Almighty and everlasting God, who has manifested your glory, etc.”

“Rise.”

“Through the same.”

“Almighty and everlasting God, whose judgment, etc.”

“Rise.”

“Through the Lord.”

244. **Only the Prayer for himself is omitted, etc.** Thus Alcuin, in the chapter cited above on Wednesday of Holy Week: “Knowing this, let them commemorate there what the bishop omits for himself.”

245. **Let them not bend the knee for the Jews.** In the Codex of Tilly: “Finally, for the Jews let them not bend their knees.”

Alcuin gives this Prayer in *On the Divine Offices*, in the chapter on Friday, also called Parasceve: “And during all the other Prayers we bend our knees, so that by this posture of the body we may show the humility of our minds, except when we pray for the faithless Jews. For they bent the knee before the Lord while doing a good deed wickedly, because they did it in mockery.”

246. **For confessors.** “Confessors” here are singers and psalmists, who occupy a lower grade among the clergy, according to canon 11 of the Fourth Council of Carthage. This is sufficiently clear from the First Council of Toledo, canon 9: “Let no professed woman or widow, in the absence of a bishop or priest, perform Antiphons in her house with a confessor or with her servant.”

The sixth canon of the same council is to be understood in the same way: “Likewise, let no maiden of God maintain familiarity with a confessor.”

They were so called because in sacred Scripture “to confess” commonly means to sing the praises of God. Since, therefore, this passage of the Sacramentary mentions all persons devoted to the worship of God, it is reasonable to believe that by “confessors” it means singers or psalmists.

247. **For virgins.** Devoted or professed virgins are meant, that is, women who have vowed their virginity to God; more about them below.

248. **For widows.** Likewise, those widows are understood who have professed widowhood by solemn rite; more will be said of them below.

249. **For our most Christian king.** So the printed editions read. In the [Note: [Col. 0313D] Gemetian manuscript also reads “for our most Christian emperor,” although below it is written “look favorably upon the kingdom of the English.”] Rheims Manuscript one reads: “For our most Christian emperor, or king.” In the manuscripts of Rodrade and Ratold, and in Pamelius: “And for our most Christian emperor.” In the Roman Ordo we find: “Afterward he says it for the king of the Franks, or for the emperor.” In the Tilian Manuscript, on Wednesday, it reads: “After the emperor, however, he says it for the king of the Franks.” But no particular prayers are assigned, nor are any on Friday.

250. **Look favorably upon the empire of the Romans and Franks.** So the printed editions read. In the Rheims Manuscript: “Look favorably upon the empire of the Romans, or Franks.” In the manuscript of Rodrade and in Pamelius: “Look favorably upon the empire of the Romans.” [Note: [Col. 0314D] Thus in the second manuscript of Theodore. In the other: “Look favorably upon the empire of the most Christian.”] In the manuscript of Ratold: “Look favorably upon the empire of the Romans, or Franks.”

251. **When these things have been completed, etc.** Note that on this day these prayers were indeed formerly accustomed to be said immediately before the Mass, but with some interval.

252. **At the eighth hour.** That is, at the second hour after midday, according to the ancient method of beginning the day and numbering the hours.

253. **The schola.** In the Roman Ordo and in the Sacramentary books, *schola* is a college of singers. For formerly not all the clergy sang in church; rather, there were certain singers, distinct from the other grades of the clergy and appointed to perform this duty, as may be seen in the Council of Carthage IV, canon 10. Our theologians, however, do not usually reckon these among those who are properly initiated into the orders. Thus also in the Council of Laodicea, canon 15:

> περὶ μὴ δεῖν πλὴν τῶν κανονικῶν ψαλτῶν ἐπὶ τὸν ἄμβωνα ἀναβαινόντων etc.

That is:

> No one except the canonical singers, who ascend the ambo and sing from a written text, ought to sing in the church.

The canonical singers there are those who have been appointed canonically and lawfully to perform this duty.

In Saint Ignatius’ *Letter to the Antiochenes*, in which he lists the clerical grades, he also mentions the psalmist, or singers. The same is found in the *Apostolic Constitutions*, book VIII, in the Mass of Saint Clement, in which prayer is offered for readers, singers, virgins, and widows.

Nor should it be said that in those ancient times this grade was not distinct from the other minor grades, but that singers were taken from among them, especially from the readers. The contrary is evident from the passages cited above, and especially from the Council of Carthage IV, where a particular blessing is assigned after the others to the psalmist, or singer. This blessing clearly belongs to a distinct person who had not yet been initiated into any order, since this grade is the last of all, and we do not see, under ordinary law, that someone promoted to a higher grade is ordained to a lower one.

Moreover, the canons of the Apostles distinguish readers from singers. Thus canon 26 grants readers and singers permission to marry. Canon 43 forbids the subdeacon, reader, and singer to devote themselves to gambling and drunkenness. Canon 69 decrees that any bishop, presbyter, deacon, subdeacon, reader, or singer who does not fast during the holy Quadragesima, or on Wednesday, or on Parasceve, [Col. 0315A] is to be deposed.

Later, however, psalmists or singers were taken from among subdeacons and the other minor orders, so that they might constitute the singers’ schola mentioned here. For in the First Council of Braga, canon 29, we see readers performing the office of psalmists. And in the Roman Council under Saint Gregory I it was decreed that thereafter singers should be taken from among the subdeacons or the other minor orders, as may be seen in book IV, letter 44 of the *Register* [Note: [Col. 0315] The acts and canons of this Roman synod are now read at the end of the *Register*.]:

> For this reason, says the pope, I decree and establish that in this see the ministers of the sacred altar are not to sing, but are to perform only the office of the Gospel reading during the solemn celebrations of Mass. I judge that the psalms and the other readings should be presented by subdeacons or, if necessity requires, by members of the minor orders.

Nevertheless, it must be said that formerly certain things were accustomed to be sung by other clerics and even by laypeople, such as “Kyrie eleison,” “We have unto the Lord,” “And with your spirit,” “Amen,” and similar responses.

254. **Grant, we beseech you, etc.** Alcuin, in book II *Against Elipandus, Bishop of Toledo*, cites this prayer:

> Likewise, on Wednesday of that same week: Grant, we beseech you, almighty God, that we, who are constantly afflicted by our offenses, etc.

And in book VII *Against Felix, Bishop of Urgel*:

> Likewise, on Wednesday before Easter: We beseech you, almighty God, that through the passion of your Only-Begotten Son we may be delivered,

with the words occurring in the middle of the prayer omitted.

**324 355. The second reading follows, etc.** This rubric is absent from the printed editions, from our other manuscript codices, and from Pamelius.

256. **The Passion of the Lord.** Thus in the Tilian Manuscript, as also in the order of the books that are read, and in the manuscripts of the Corbie library concerning Wednesday through Saturday before Easter. Below, on holy Friday, Parasceve, the Passion according to John is prescribed for reading; no mention is made of the Passion according to Matthew, which is read on Palm Sunday, or of that according to Mark, which is read on Tuesday. I think these were omitted because on those days the writer of this book followed only the common arrangement of the other Masses.

The ancient use of reading the Passion in church is clear, for Saint Augustine mentions it in Sermon 144, *On the Season*:

> But because the Passion is read on a single day, it is not usually read except according to Matthew. At one time I wanted the Passion also to be read every year according to all the Evangelists. It was done, but people did not hear what they were accustomed to hear, and they were disturbed.

Here note, first, that formerly the Passion was accustomed to be read on only one day. Although he does not specify the day, it is believable that it was holy Parasceve. Second, Saint Augustine instituted that the Passions of the four Evangelists should be read annually in church, on different days, even though he does not state this explicitly, since reading all four Passions on one day would have been tedious. It is reasonable to believe that he arranged this according to the order of the week during the octave of Easter, during which, according to the same sermon, the Lord’s Resurrection is read for seven days according to all the Evangelists.

[Col. 0315D] 257. **Grant to our faculties, etc.** This prayer is cited by Alcuin in book VII *Against Felix, Bishop of Urgel*:

> And in another prayer: Grant, almighty God, that through the temporal death of your Son, which the venerable mysteries testify to,

with the conclusion omitted, and with these words:

> to our faculties.

258. **At the third hour they entered the sacristy.** Formerly the solemn celebrations of Mass were held at the third hour, that is, at the ninth hour of the morning; this is said to have been instituted by Pope Telesphorus. I do not think, however, that this institution was so ancient. For in the times of the primitive Church the solemn celebrations of Mass were held at night, as is clear from Tertullian, *On the Crown of the Soldier*:

> The sacrament of the Eucharist, received both at the time of food and by all, as commanded by the Lord, even at gatherings before dawn, and from no hand other than that of the presidents.

This took place only during the solemn celebration of Mass. Those gatherings before dawn are well known from Pliny’s letter to Trajan (book X, letter 101), cited by Tertullian in his *Apology*. Hence came the pagan slanders about infanticide and those who overturn lamps—dogs, that is, pimps of darkness who promoted the shamelessness of impious lust—in the same Tertullian, later in the same book.

Christians performed these sacred mysteries at night in order to protect their majesty and dignity against the envy and fury of the pagans.
