They did so even after the time of Pope Telesphorus, who flourished under the emperor Antoninus Pius. Therefore, the institution of celebrating Mass at the third hour was much later. Nevertheless, Masses were celebrated at the eighth or ninth hour, or in the evening, during fasts, as we have shown in the *Concordance of Rules*.

On this day, the hour is advanced because of the blessing of the oil and Chrism, the reconciliation of penitents, and the washing of feet—not because the fast is relaxed, lest either the number of thirty-six days, according to Saint Gregory, or forty days, according to the later institution, be lacking. Although formerly many did not fast on Maundy Thursday according to the rite of their own Church, as may be seen in Saint Augustine, letter 118.

The beginning of the office at the third hour on this day is likewise prescribed in an old manuscript Pontifical preserved in the sacristy of the Church of Rouen; it appears formerly to have belonged to the Church of Rheims. In the Council of Rouen, held in the year of the Lord 1072, as reported by Orderic Vitalis in book IV of his *Ecclesiastical History*, canon 1 decrees that the consecration of Chrism, baptismal oil, and anointing oil should be performed at the proper hour, that is, after None, according to the decrees of the Fathers. This consecration is performed during the solemn celebration of Mass, as is evident from all our Sacramentaries.

259. **Dalmatics.** Saint Isidore explains what a dalmatic is in book XIX, chapter 22 of the *Etymologies*:

> The dalmatic, a garment first woven in the province of Dalmatia in Greece, is a priestly tunic with purple bands.

The old Glosses say:

> *Dalmata*—read *dalmatica*—is a white priestly garment with purple bands.

The Glosses of Cyril explain what a *clavus* is:

> πορφύρα ὑφασμένη

That is, “woven purple.” *Clavus* has no plural, meaning purple sewn onto or woven into a garment. But the claim that it has no plural conflicts with the passages cited.

The *clavi*, therefore, are bands or patches, some purple strips formerly sewn onto the togas of senators. The Greeks call them *σημεῖα*. From such broad bands the senatorial garment is called *laticlavium*, or “broad band,” *πλατύσημος* and *πλατύσημον*.

The Glosses of Cyril:

> *πλατύσημον*: *laticlavium*.

The old *Onomasticon*:

> “Broad band”: *πλατύσημον*.

The old Lexicon:

> “Broad band”: *πλατύσημος*.

From narrow bands comes *angusticlavia*. The same Lexicon:

> *Angusticlavia*: *ψειχόσημα*.

For more, see the commentaries of the most learned Johannes Savaron on Apollinaris, book I, letter 9, chapter “What the garments signify.”

Alcuin describes the dalmatic differently, with the ancient rite altered, in his book *On the Divine Offices*. It is seamless, has the shape of a cross, has fringes on the left side, and has broad sleeves, or “arms,” as he calls them. Amalarius, in book II, chapter 21 of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, adds two scarlet lines at the back, likewise on the front and also on each shoulder. This may be seen in the prayer of the priest putting on the dalmatic in the ancient Mass published by Matthias Flacius Illyricus:

> Clothed in this typological garment, woven in the form of a cross with purple bands according to the rite of the ancient Fathers, I ask, etc.

I have therefore punctuated this passage so that the garment is in the form of a cross, according to the authors mentioned above, and woven with purple bands, according to Amalarius.

It was the garment of bishops and deacons, as the author of the *Questions on Both Testaments*, among the works of Saint Augustine, writes in question 46:

> As though deacons today did not wear dalmatics, just as bishops do.

Subdeacons, however, wore tunics with bands, as is clear from book VII of the *Register* [Note: [Col. 0317D] Now book IX.] of Saint Gregory, letter 63:

> From where, then, do they have it today that subdeacons proceed in tunics with bands, unless they received it from their mother, the Roman Church?

Here note that the dress of deacons and subdeacons was formerly distinct. The deacon wore a dalmatic; the subdeacon wore a tunic. This may also be seen in the ancient rite for celebrating Mass of John, Bishop of Avranches, in the appendix to this book of Sacramentaries.

260. **Ampullae.** Saint Isidore explains what an *ampulla* is in book XX, chapter 5 of the *Etymologies*:

> *Ampulla* is so called as if from *ampla bulla*, “a broad bubble.” It resembles in its roundness the bubbles that arise from the foam of water and are inflated by the wind.

The old Glosses:

> *Ampulla*: λήκυθος.

But a *λήκυθος* is, as the author of the old Etymological Lexicon says, an *ἀγγεῖον ἐλαιόδοχον*, that is, “a vessel in which oil is stored.” Hence “oil flask” in 1 Kings 17.

Oil, or Chrism, was therefore properly stored in ampullae, according to the ancient custom, which may be seen in Optatus of Milevis, book II *Against Parmenian*:

> They also threw the ampulla of Chrism through the window so that they might break it.

Formerly bishops were free to prepare holy Chrism every day, as is clear from the First Council of Toledo, canon 20:

> It is certainly established that a bishop may prepare Chrism at any time.

Later, however, the custom prevailed that it should be prepared only on Maundy Thursday, as is evident from all our Sacramentaries and from the Greek *Euchologion*. The same may be seen in Saint Eligius’ homily 8 *On Maundy Thursday*:

> And because on this most holy day many things are done in the holy Church that your diligence must necessarily know about, such as the reconciliation of penitents, the blessing of the sacred oil, the preparation of the holy Chrism, and the fraternal washing of the feet.

And in the sermon *On the Anointing of Chrism*, among the works of Saint Cyprian:

> This day is honored with many mysteries. On this day the breaking of bread was first commended to us. Today in the Church, together with the other anointings, holy Chrism is prepared for the sanctification of the people of possession, for participation in dignity and name.

The Council of Meaux, canon 46, also decrees [Col. 0317C]:

> Let no one presume to prepare holy Chrism except on Thursday of Holy Week, that is, on Maundy Thursday, which is specially called the Lord’s Day.

261. **When the balsam has been received, etc.** Chrism is not simple oil; balsam is mixed into it, as is clear from the sermon cited above *On the Anointing of Chrism*:

> Holy Chrism is prepared, in which balsam mixed with oil expresses the unity of royal and priestly glory.

Gregory the Great, in his exposition of chapter II of the *Song of Songs*:

> Balsam is produced at Engedi; when it is combined with oil by pontifical blessing, it becomes Chrism, through which the gifts of the Holy Spirit are expressed.

And in the Council of Chalon-sur-Saône, chapter 9, as quoted by Burchard in book IV, chapter 93:

> Certain brothers said that it had formerly been customary for presbyters to give two or four denarii for purchasing balsam to make Chrism, or for preparing the church lamps.

In preparing Chrism, the Greeks mix in various fragrant substances, as Saint Dionysius testifies in chapter 4 of *The Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*:

> ἡ τοῦ μύρου σύνθεσις συναγωγή τίς ἐστιν εὐπνόων ὑλῶν.

That is:

> The composition of the ointment, or Chrism, is a kind of collection of fragrant substances.

In addition to wine and oil, they mix thirty-six different kinds of aromatic substances or herbs, as is stated in their *Euchologion*.

262. **Candle stands.** *Cereostata* are candlestands used at altars. This word may frequently be seen in Anastasius the Librarian’s *Lives of the Roman Pontiffs*.

263. **Peace be with you.** This is a formula of greeting used especially by the pontiff in sacred rites. For during the sacred rites themselves the pontiff often gave peace to the people in church, whether he said *Pax vobis* (“Peace be with you”), *Pax vobiscum* (“Peace be with you”), or *Pax omnibus* (“Peace to all”).

Optatus of Milevis, book III *Against Parmenian*:

> You were not able to lead astray every household at once [read: *simul*]. Either the wife went away [namely, to your church] while the husband remained seated; or the parents were led astray and the children wanted to follow; or the brother remained while the sister departed. By your persuasions bodies and the names of piety were divided.

And you could not omit what is lawful; plainly you said, “Peace be with you,” namely, in ecclesiastical assemblies and sacrifices.

He calls that “lawful” which is sanctioned as something to be done during the sacred rites themselves. In book II *Against Parmenian*:

> For who would doubt that we cannot omit that lawful element in the mystery of the sacraments? You say that you offer for the Church.

Some people wrongly interpret this as the Canon of the Mass. If that were so, it ought to be said *illud legitimi*, not *illud legitimum*.

Saint John Chrysostom, homily 3 on the Epistle to the Colossians:

> Ἐν ταῖς ἐκκλησίαις εἰρήνην ἐν ταῖς λιταῖς, ἐν προρρήσεσιν, καὶ ἅπαξ, καὶ δὶς, καὶ τρὶς, καὶ πολλάκις αὐτὴν δίδωσιν ὁ τῆς Ἐκκλησίας προεστώς, Εἰρήνη ὑμῖν, ἐπιλέγων.

That is:

> In the churches, during the prayers and the prefaces, once, twice, three times, and often, the president of the Church gives peace, saying, “Peace be with you.”

Here, however, one should not read *ὑμῖν*, “with you,” but *πᾶσιν*, “to all.” For shortly afterward he says:

> Καὶ οὐ λέγει ὁ τῆς Ἐκκλησίας προεστώς, Εἰρήνη ὑμῖν, ἁπλῶς, ἀλλὰ, Εἰρήνη πᾶσιν.

That is:

> The president of the Church does not simply say, “Peace be with you,” but “Peace to all.”

He adds the reason: peace is not to be maintained with one or another person, but with everyone, so that everything in our own mind may also be tranquil and peaceful.

This is confirmed by homily 16 on the First Epistle to the Corinthians:

> Εἰρήνην, καὶ νῦν πᾶσιν ὁ τῆς Ἐκκλησίας προεστὼς ἐπεύχεται.

That is:

> And now the president of the Church prays for peace for all.

In the liturgies of Saints Basil and Chrysostom, the priest says:

> Εἰρήνη πᾶσιν,

that is, “Peace to all,” as also in the liturgies of Saints James and Mark and in the liturgy of the Presanctified.

This is confirmed by the *Mystical Theory* of Saint Germanus, Patriarch of Constantinople. Explaining these words, he says:

> Εἰρήνη πᾶσιν· ὁμογνωμοσύνην, καὶ ἀγάπην καὶ ταυτότητα συνάπτοντες etc.

That is:

> “Peace to all”: by joining together concord, love, and unity of mind among ourselves, let us receive an imitation of the Lord, who left and gave us his peace.

But *Pax omnibus* (“Peace to all”) is Greek, as the passages cited testify; whereas *Pax vobis* and *Pax vobiscum* (“Peace be with you”) are Latin, as is clear from the Optatus of Milevis cited above, from our book of Sacramentaries, and from the manuscript of Ratold to be cited shortly.

At one time in the West, especially in Spain, “The Lord be with you” was said, as may be seen in the First Council of Braga, canon 21 of the second constitution:

> It has also seemed good that bishops should not greet people in one way and presbyters in another, but in one manner, saying, “The Lord be with you.”

Where it later says, “The whole East retains this,” I think one should read “the West,” since the testimonies produced clearly show that a different usage existed in the Eastern Church.

Concerning this greeting, “Peace be with you,” the following points should be noted from the manuscript of Ratold the abbot:

> Afterward, “Peace be with you,” although the bishop is not accustomed to say it except on feast days.

[Col. 0318D] Before the Mass, the Rheims Manuscript contains the reconciliation of penitents, which will be discussed more conveniently below. After the Mass it continues:

> Likewise, on Thursday, the Chrism Mass. Prayer: Lord God, who in the regeneration of your peoples, etc.  
> Second prayer: Grant us, almighty God, the remedies of human condition, etc.  
> Over the offerings: We beseech you, Lord, that the power of this sacrifice, etc.  
> Preface: We humbly implore your mercy, so that for those who are to be renewed by the baptism of the spiritual bath, the creature of Chrism may be made into a sacrament, etc.  
> Within the Canon: “Communicating,” etc., as in the manuscript of Saint Eligius.

Likewise another prayer:

> Graciously receive, Lord, we beseech you, this offering of your male and female servants, which they offer to you on the day on which our Lord Jesus Christ handed over to his disciples the mysteries of his body and blood to be celebrated; and in your goodness grant that, through many cycles of years, they may remain safe and unharmed and may deserve to offer their gifts to you, Lord.

> “Which offering,” etc.

Finally it continues:

> Likewise, at the end, before “Through whom you create all these things, Lord,” he blesses the oil for the sick, or for the people, in these words, etc.

When the blessing of the oil and Chrism has been completed, and the prayers that follow have been said in the Mass:

> After Communion: Grant, Lord, that through the mystery of the new sacrament begun [read: received], etc.  
> Over the people: Grant, we beseech you, Lord, that just as concerning past things, etc.

It continues:

> Likewise, the preparation of the exorcized oil: “I exorcize you, creature of oil,” etc.

Then follows this Preface:

> You who reveal the secrets of the mysteries, etc.

Finally:

> At the late Mass: God, from whom Judas also, etc., as in this manuscript of Saint Eligius.

Thus far the Rheims Manuscript. Three Masses are to be noted on this Thursday: the first for penitents, the second for the Chrism, and the third in the evening.

Formerly, in certain Churches, two Masses were celebrated on this same Thursday: one in the morning for those who did not fast on that day but bathed and relaxed the fast, and the other in the evening for those who fasted. Saint Augustine notes this in letter 118 to Januarius, discussing this solemnity:

> And because some also observe the fast, he says, the morning Mass is offered for those who eat, since they cannot endure fasting and baths at the same time; but the evening Mass is for those who fast.

264. **By today’s handing over.** Namely, of his body and blood.

265. **He sold.** That is, “he sold.” For *distrahere* sometimes means “to sell.” Nonius Marcellus, chapter 4:

> *Distrahere* means “to sell.”

Lucilius, book XXIX:

> Let them divide, defer, scatter, sell.

The *Rule of the Master*, chapter 85:

> Whenever any craft has something completed and superfluous for the monastery’s use, or has an abundance of items to be sent as blessings, after inquiry into the value of the price, let as much as can be sold to secular people always be sold below the lesser monetary price.

See also the *Concordance of Rules*, chapter 64, section 4.

266. **Whom not even the sharing of the sacred food…** At the Last Supper, our Lord Jesus Christ extended his body and blood to Judas the betrayer together with the other apostles. [Note: [Col. 0319] A little below, where it reads, “The gentle Lord suffers,” etc., the Fécamp Manuscript has: “Thus the gentle Lord feeds.”]

Many Fathers assert this. Saint Augustine, book II *Against the Letters of Petilian*, chapter 106:

> Or did his apostolic predecessors share in Judas’ theft and crime, because they shared the most holy supper with him, who was already the seller of the Lord?

The author of the *Mixed Questions from Both Testaments*, among the works of Saint Augustine, question 102:

> Judas, therefore, although he was among the disciples, did not contaminate them by his contagion, since they disagreed with his thefts. Receiving the Eucharist among them, he did not pollute the innocent; nor did the Lord deny his body to the man whom he knew to be a robber.

Saint Leo, sermon 3 *On the Passion of the Lord*:

> You should have awaited the completion of your crime and delayed the noose of your hideous death until the blood of Christ had been poured out for all sinners. And when so many miracles of the Lord and so many gifts tormented your conscience, at least those sacraments which, at the paschal supper, you received after your treachery had been exposed by the sign of divine knowledge should have recalled you from your plunge.

Saint Eligius, homily 8:

> How many receive from the altar and die! Hence the Apostle also says: “He eats and drinks judgment upon himself.” Was not the Lord’s morsel poison to Judas?

Saint John Chrysostom, homily 27 on the First Epistle to the Corinthians:

> Καὶ οὐδὲ τοῦτον ἐξέβαλεν, καὶ ἁλῶν αὐτῷ μετέδωκε, καὶ τῶν μυστηρίων κοινωνὸν ἐποίησεν.

That is:

> He did not drive him out, but made him a participant at the table and a sharer in the mysteries.

Saint Anastasius of Sinai, sermon *On the Synaxis*:

> Οὐκ ὁρᾷς πῶς Ἰούδας ἀναξίως, καὶ δολίως τοῦ σώματος μεταλαβὼν τοῦ δεσποτικοῦ εὐθέως κατεκρίθη;

That is:

> Do you not see how Judas, having received the Master’s body unworthily and deceitfully, was immediately condemned?

Hincmar, Archbishop of Rheims, in a manuscript letter in the library of the monastery of Saint Remigius at Rheims:

> And afterward it was said: “After the morsel, Satan entered into him,” because when the holy bread entered a belly full of iniquity, the ancient enemy, who is called the Devil and Satan, entered the cruel and impious mind.

267. **In which our Lord Jesus Christ was handed over for us.** So the printed editions and our other manuscript codices read, as does Pamelius.

268. **In which our Lord Jesus Christ handed over to his disciples, etc.** So in the manuscripts cited.

269. **Then the oil is offered to the pontiff.** The consecration of the oil for the sick begins here; it takes place immediately before the words, “Through whom you always create all these good things,” as may be seen in this manuscript of Saint Eligius.

It should not be thought that the oil is consecrated immediately after the words, “He took bread into his holy and venerable hands,” even though the words “then the oil is offered to the pontiff,” etc., follow them. The writer did this because he did not wish to write out the entire Canon.

270. **Chrism.** This word is not used here in a very strict or proper sense.

271. **And facing toward the East.** It was an ancient and commendable custom of the Church, handed down from apostolic times to our own, that Christians praying should have their faces turned toward the East.

Saint Basil, book *On the Holy Spirit* to Amphilochius, chapter 27, discussing apostolic traditions:

> Τὸ πρὸς ἀνατολὰς τετράφθαι κατὰ τὴν προσευχὴν ποῖον ἐδίδαξεν ἡμᾶς γράμμα;

That is:

> What Scripture taught us to turn toward the East in prayer?

The author of the *Questions to the Orthodox*, among the works of Saint Justin Martyr, question 118, writes in his response on this matter:

> Τοῦτο δὲ παρὰ τῶν ἁγίων Ἀποστόλων

That is:

> This comes from the holy Apostles.

Saint Germanus, Patriarch of Constantinople, in the *Mystical Theory*:

> τὸ κατ’ ἀνατολὰς εὔχεσθαι παραδεδομένον ἐστὶν, ὡς καὶ τὰ λοιπὰ, ἐκ τῶν Ἀποστόλων.

That is:

> To pray toward the East has been handed down, like the other practices, from the Apostles.

Tertullian mentions this custom in his *Apology*:

> Hence arose the suspicion that it had become known that we pray toward the region of the East.

And in book I *To the Nations*:

> Others, in a more humane fashion, certainly suppose that the sun is the God of the Christians, because it has become known that we make our prayer toward the region of the East.

Saint Augustine, book II *On the Sermon on the Mount*, chapter 9:

> To signify this matter, when we stand for prayer, we turn toward the East.

Saint John Damascene discusses this matter at greater length in book IV, chapter 13 of *The Orthodox Faith*, as does the author of the *Questions to Antiochus*, among the works of Saint Athanasius.

Gregentius the archbishop also mentions it in his disputation with the Jew Herban:

> κατ’ ἀνατολὰς ἐδιδάχθημεν προσεύχεσθαι.

That is:

> We have been taught to pray toward the East.

He adds two reasons: we find that God created the human being there and made paradise there. Saint Basil, in the chapter cited, offers another reason, which nevertheless does not differ greatly from the second: we seek our ancient homeland, the paradise that God planted in Eden toward the East.

Saint John Damascene, in the chapter cited, the author of the *Questions to Antiochus* in the question cited, and Saint Germanus, Patriarch of Constantinople, in the work cited, support this view.

Saint Germanus also gives another reason: because Christ our God, the spiritual Sun of righteousness, appeared on earth in the regions of the sensible rising sun.

The author of the *Questions to the Orthodox*, in the question cited, gives another reason:

> τιμιωτέρα ἐστὶν ἡ ἀνατολὴ τῶν ἄλλων μερῶν τῆς κτίσεως,

that is:

> The East is nobler than the other parts of creation.

The author of the *Questions to Antiochus*, in the question cited, gives still other reasons: because Christ’s feet stood on the Mount of Olives, and because God is true light.

Saint John Damascene, in the chapter cited, gives further reasons: because God is intelligible light, the Sun of righteousness, and Christ is called “the East” in Scripture; because the ancient tabernacle of Moses had its veil and mercy seat toward the East; because the tribe of Judah, as the most honorable, pitched its camp toward the East; and because in the famous temple of Solomon the Lord’s gate faced East.

Because Christ was crucified facing West, we worship him by turning toward him. Finally, because when Christ was taken up into heaven he was carried toward the East, as is found in Psalm 67:

> Sing to God, who rises above the heaven of heaven toward the East.

Thus the Apostles worshiped him.

From this it came about that sacred buildings generally faced East, according to Saint Paulinus, letter 12. This may be seen in [Note: [Col. 0321D] Namely, in Sidonius Apollinaris.] Apollinaris, book II, letter 10:

> The lofty temple shines, and is drawn neither  
> To the left nor to the right; but the altar  
> At the front looks toward the equinoctial  
> Rising of the sun.

Thus formerly at Chalcedon the sanctuary in which the tomb of Saint Euphemia was kept faced the eastern region, as Evagrius testifies in book II, chapter 3 of his *Ecclesiastical History*:

> Εἴσω δὲ τοῦ θόλου πρὸς τὰ ἑῷα εὐπρεπής ἐστι σηκός, ἔνθα τὰ πανάγια τῆς μάρτυρος ἀπόκειται λείψανα.

That is:

> Inside the dome, toward the East, there is a splendid sanctuary in which the most holy relics of the martyr are deposited.

The same is also clear from Socrates, book V of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 21. He writes that the basilica at Antioch had an arrangement contrary to the others, since its altar faced not East but West. It is also clear from Stephen of Tournai, letter 105, where, speaking of the Basilica of Saint Benedict located in Paris, he says:

> The form of that church is unlike and differs from that of the other churches: on the sanctuary side it faces West, and from the entrance it faces East.

If, therefore, the church at Antioch and the Basilica of Saint Benedict located in Paris formerly did not face the rising sun, but, contrary to the other sacred buildings, faced the setting sun, this indicates that the other churches, or at least the majority of them, faced East.

Later, however, the Basilica of Saint Benedict mentioned above was arranged so that it now faces East from the sanctuary side and West from the entrance, so that it would not differ in orientation from the others.

Today the ancient practice is changing, especially in Paris. For among the great number of sacred buildings that have been built in that city during the past forty years, one would scarcely find one or two facing East. Indeed, we see some old churches that formerly faced the eastern region now, with their orientation changed, facing West.

As for the temples of the pagans—to say something about them—they too generally faced East. Vitruvius teaches that temples should be constructed in this way in book IV, chapter 5 of *On Architecture*:

> The regions toward which the temples of the immortal gods ought to look are to be determined as follows: if no reason prevents it and the choice of the site is free, the image placed in the cella should face the evening region of the sky, so that those who approach the altar to sacrifice or perform rites may face the eastern part of the heavens and the image in the temple. Thus, while making their vows, they may look toward the temple and the eastern sky; and the images themselves may appear to look upon those who petition and sacrifice as they rise. It therefore seems necessary that all the altars of the gods face East.

Saint Isidore agrees in book XV, chapter 4 of the *Etymologies*:

> The place marked out toward the East was called a temple from contemplation. It had four parts: the front faced East, the rear West, the left North, and the right South. Thus, when they built a temple, they looked toward the equinoctial East, so that lines drawn from East to West would make the right and left parts of the sky equal, and so that the person consulting and praying might look directly toward the East.

This is chiefly to be understood of the sacred buildings of the Romans. For the temples of the ancient Greeks generally had their altars turned toward the West and their doors toward the East, as Porphyry writes in his book *On the Cave of the Nymphs*.

As for the Jews, Solomon’s Temple faced toward the region of the West, as is clear from Ezekiel, chapter 8:

> He brought me into the inner court of the house of the Lord; and behold, at the door of the temple of the Lord, between the vestibule and the altar, there were about twenty-five men with their backs toward the temple of the Lord and their faces toward the East, and they were worshiping the rising sun.

Indeed, the Jews prayed to God turned toward the western region of the sun, as Archbishop Gregentius testifies in the disputation cited above, speaking to the Jew Herban:

> Ἐπὶ τὴν δύσιν γὰρ ὑμεῖς προσκυνεῖτε.

That is:

> For you worship facing toward the West.

They did this so that they would not appear, like the Gentiles, to worship the sun.

272. **At the consecration of the Chrism.** It is an ancient custom of the Church to bless and consecrate holy Chrism.

Saint Cyprian, letter 70:

> Moreover, the Eucharist and the oil with which the baptized are anointed are sanctified on the altar.

Optatus of Milevis, book VII *Against Parmenian*:

> They call it oil, namely, that liquid which is compounded from the name of Christ; after it has been compounded, it is called Chrism.

Basil, book *On the Holy Spirit* to Amphilochius, chapter 27, refers the rite to apostolic times:

> Εὐλογοῦμεν τὸ ὕδωρ τοῦ βαπτίσματος, καὶ ἔλαιον τῆς χρίσεως.

That is:

> We bless the water of baptism and the oil of anointing.

This is also confirmed by the authority of Dionysius the Great, who discusses the consecration of Chrism at length in chapter 4 of *The Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*.

### 273. He announced that peace had been restored to the earth by the olive branch.

Thus Tertullian, *On Baptism*:

> Just as, after the waters of the flood, by which iniquity had been purged, after the baptism—as I may so put it—of the world, the dove, herald of the heavenly wrath’s peace, announced peace to the earth, sent forth from the ark and returning with an olive branch—a sign which is also held forth among the nations as a token of peace—so, by the same arrangement, the spiritual effect comes upon the earth, that is, upon our flesh emerging from the washing after its former sins: the dove of the Holy Spirit flies down, bringing the peace of God, sent forth from heaven, where the Church is symbolized by the ark.

Cassiodorus, on Psalm XXII:

> But what is the reason that the very form of the holy Benediction is so frequently employed? It anointed prophets and consecrated kings. Not without reason, since the tree itself also provided an indication of peace; its particular function is known to be divine: its arboreal fluid, its fatness that gladdens, is the grace of great dignities, whose leaves continue in the beauty of their greenness. Noah also announced through the dove that health had been restored to the earth, so that what enjoys both the great beauty and the usefulness of its fruit may rightly appear capable of so great a Benediction.

Saint John Damascene, *On the Orthodox Faith*, book IV, chapter 13:

> And announcing to us the mercy of God through the Holy Spirit: “For the dove also brought an olive branch to those who had been saved from the flood.”

That is: “After the dove had also brought an olive branch to those preserved from the flood.”

Why, therefore, in the Greek *Euchologion* this branch is rightly called “a symbol of reconciliation, of salvation after the flood, and a mystery of grace.”

### 274. Whence you have anointed priests.

In Leviticus VIII, where Aaron was anointed priest by Moses. This rite is mentioned in Exodus, chapter XXIX:

> The holy garment which Aaron shall use shall belong to his sons after him, so that they may be anointed in it and their hands consecrated.

### 275. Kings.

The anointing of kings is mentioned in the First Book of Kings, chapter IX:

> And you shall anoint him as leader over my people Israel.

And in chapter X:

> Samuel then took a flask of oil and poured it over his head, kissed him, and said: “Behold, the Lord has anointed you over his inheritance as prince.”

And elsewhere repeatedly in the Books of Kings.

### 276. Prophets.

The anointing of prophets is mentioned in the Third Book of Kings, chapter XIX:

> But Elisha son of Shaphat, who is from Abel-meholah, you shall anoint as prophet in your place.

### 277. And martyrs.

By receiving the sacrament of Confirmation, through whose benefit they received from God the strength to resist the devil and his satellites.

### 278. When this has been completed, he blesses the flask of oil.

This oil is blessed for anointing the catechumen who is approaching the holy washing of regeneration, as is clear from the following Prayer and from the Codex of Ratold:

> Then the subdeacon shall receive from the acolyte the oil for baptizing.

This oil is blessed according to an ancient custom mentioned by Saint Cyril of Jerusalem, *Mystagogical Catechesis* II:

> Thus also exorcized oil receives such great power through the invocation of God and prayer.

That is: “Thus also exorcized oil receives such great power through the invocation of God and prayer.”

This anointing is discussed in the *Questions to the Orthodox*, which are extant among the works of Saint Justin Martyr, question 137. Fortunatus mentions it in poem IV of book V, concerning Jews baptized by Saint Avitus, bishop of Auvergne:

> Hence the fleece of the sheep is drenched with the oil’s unction;  
> And by the sacred sprinkling it becomes the flock’s second fragrance.

Among the Latins, the person to be baptized is anointed on the chest, the shoulders, and between the shoulders. Jesse of Amiens, in his letter *On Baptism*:

> The chest, too, is touched with holy oil, so that entry may be denied to the unclean Spirit. For the shoulders are marked with oil, so that he may be strengthened on every side by the fortification of the cross.

And shortly afterward:

> He is touched between the shoulders, so that the consecrated shoulder, together with the shoulders, may subject his entire self to the power of God.

Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, in the manuscript of the Corbie library, *On the Order of Baptism*, chapter 10, mentions only the anointing of the shoulders and chest:

> Therefore, too, the chest and shoulders of those who are to be baptized are touched with oil.

He adds the reason: so that the person may be protected behind and in front. The same is found in the Rheims Codices and in that of Abbot Ratold.

The Greeks, however, anoint the whole body, as may be seen in their *Euchologion* and in Severus, patriarch of Alexandria, in his book *On the Rites of Baptism*:

> And the priest places olive oil in the palm of his hand and anoints the entire body of the one being baptized.

In Saint Cyril of Jerusalem, *Mystagogical Catechesis* II:

> Then, after you had taken off your clothes, you were anointed with exorcized oil from the hairs at the top of your head down to your lowest feet.

The same is clear from Saint Dionysius, *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, chapter 2:

> While the ministers completely strip him, the priests offer the sacred oil. But the bishop, having begun the anointing by sealing him three times, hands the man over to the priests to anoint him over his whole body.

That is: “The bishop, having begun the anointing by sealing him three times, hands the man over to the priests to be anointed over his whole body.”

The same is attested by Saint John Chrysostom, homily 6 on the Epistle to the Colossians:

> He is anointed as an athlete entering the stadium. For he is born at once, and not like the first man, gradually, but immediately; not as the priests formerly were, on the head alone, but rather more extensively. For they were anointed on the head, the ear, and the right hand, so that he might be aroused to obedience and good works: but this man is anointed entirely. For he does not come merely to be taught, but also to compete and to be trained.

Saint Dionysius gives the same explanation in the chapter cited above.

The words of John Moschus, *Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 3, are also to be understood of this same anointing:

> He himself anointed and baptized.

And below:

> On the following day, after anointing her, he baptized Persia.

That is: “On the following day, after he had anointed the Persian girl, he baptized her.”

This girl, then, was to be anointed naked, as we see in the Latin translation:

> One day a girl came from Persia who was so attractive and of such great beauty that the presbyter could not anoint her naked with oil.

Here the translator plainly recognized the word γυμνήν, that is, “naked,” which has dropped out of the Greek edition. For the passage concerns a certain presbyter-monk named Conon, to whom the archbishop had entrusted the task of baptizing. When he suffered a grave temptation in anointing women, he repeatedly considered leaving the monastery. After he finally departed, he returned, healed by Saint John the Baptist—by no small miracle—from this temptation of the flesh.

But if such women were to be anointed only on the crown of the head, there could not have been so great an occasion for temptation; it would rather have been aroused during the immersion itself than during an anointing of the head. Moreover, in the words cited, we see that the anointing precedes baptism. Therefore these words should be understood rather of the anointing of the entire body according to the custom of the Easterners than of the anointing of the head, which follows baptism.

If the bishop baptized, the catechumen was first anointed by him with a threefold sign, and afterward was to be anointed over the entire body by the priests, as Saint Dionysius notes in the place cited above.

Finally, it should be noted that on the Lord’s Supper the bishop sanctifies three oils: the oil of the sick, the holy chrism, and the oil for those being baptized, or of the catechumens. This is clear from our Sacramentaries. Thus in the Council of Meaux, in Ivo, part I of the *Decretum*, chapter 269:

> He decreed that on the Lord’s Supper the presbyter should bring with him three flasks: one for chrism, another for anointing catechumens, and a third for the sick, according to the apostolic injunction, so that whenever someone is sick he may summon the presbyters of the Church.

### 279. Of spiritual growth.

In the printed editions and in the Rheims Codex, τὸ remunerator is added. In the Codex of Abbot Ratold, with these words omitted, we read:

> God, who by the power of your Holy Spirit strengthen the beginnings of feeble minds.

### 280. From the apostate powers.

That is, from apostate angels, or demons. For *refuga* means an apostate, a deserter. Prudentius, ode 1 of the *Peristephanon*:

> The ruler of the worldly court  
> Had ordered them to go to the altar,  
> To sacrifice to black idols,  
> To be deserters from Christ.

Saint Pacianus, in his exhortation to repentance:

> Deserters from God, or those established outside the Church, etc.

Saint Augustine, *City of God*, book XX, chapter 19:

> Since unless the deserter comes first and the man of sin is revealed.

And shortly afterward:

> There is no doubt that he said this about Antichrist and the day of judgment. For this day of the Lord will not come unless that one first comes whom he calls the deserter, certainly a deserter from the Lord God. And if this can be said of all the impious, how much more of this one?

Here note that the translator of the passage cited by Saint Augustine, from II Thessalonians II, read ἀποστάτης, that is, “deserter” or “apostate,” not ἀποστασία, that is, “departure,” as is commonly found in the Greek text and in the common version.

Saint Valerius the abbot, *On the Monastic Order*:

> And the enemies persecute and hate the Lord, whose most faithful servants they are; hateful deserters, they become outsiders.

Consult our observations on the *Concordia of the Rules*, chapter 6, § 7.

### 281. And all the people communicate in their order.

So in the printed editions. This communion of the people on this Thursday of the Lord’s Supper is also found in the Codex of Ratold. Formerly the people communicated during the three days of Easter, as may be seen in Theodulf’s *Capitulary*, chapter 41:

> On each Sunday in Lent, except for those who are excommunicated, the sacraments of the body and blood of Christ are to be received, and also on the Lord’s Supper, Good Friday, and the vigil of Easter.

In the Codex of Saint Eligius, everyone is ordered to communicate on Good Friday; on Holy Saturday, mention is made only of the communion of those who are baptized. Yet it is not determined there whether this communion applies only to those recently baptized.

### 282. And they reserve some of the sacrifice for the following day.

So in the printed editions and in the Rheims and Ratold Codices. For on Good Friday of Holy Week the body of Christ is not consecrated; rather, in the Mass the priest uses the presanctified elements—that is, hosts consecrated beforehand—both for himself and for the entire people.

The Greeks observe this throughout Lent, except on Sundays, Saturdays, and the feast of the Annunciation, on which they celebrate the sacrifice of the Lord’s body and blood according to an ancient custom found in canon 52 of the Sixth Synod:

> On all the days of the fast of holy Lent, except Saturday and Sunday and the holy day of the Annunciation, let the sacred liturgy of the presanctified gifts be celebrated.

[Displaced or defective fragment: “...let us love one another. Psalm: ‘Behold, how good.’ Antiphon.”]

The same is found in canon 49 of the Council of Laodicea, although there is no mention there of the presanctified gifts:

> For it is not permitted to offer bread during Lent except on Saturday and Sunday.

They transfer to these days the solemn celebrations of martyrs that occur during Lent, according to canon 51 of the same council:

> It is not permitted to celebrate the birthday-feast of martyrs during Lent, but on Saturdays and Sundays to make commemoration of the holy martyrs.

These practices were instituted among the Greeks because they do not fast on Saturdays and Sundays, as Theodore Balsamon notes on this canon.

Among the liturgies of the Greeks there is a Liturgy of the Presanctified, that is, of the presanctified gifts. The Liturgy of the Presanctified is mentioned in the Alexandrian Chronicle, or, as others call it, the Sicilian Fasti, Olympiad 348, year 5 after the consulship of Heraclius, where it is written that under Sergius, patriarch of Constantinople, from the first week of Lent, in the fourth indiction, after τὸ κατευθυνθείτω, that is, “Let it be directed,” while the presanctified gifts were being brought from the sacristy to the altar, and the priest had said κατὰ τὴν δωρεὰν τοῦ Χριστοῦ σου, that is, “according to the gift of your Christ,” the people began to chant:

> Now the powers of heaven invisibly worship with us.  
> Behold, the King of glory enters.  
> Behold, the mystical sacrifice, completed, is borne forth.  
> Let us approach with faith and fear, that we may become partakers of eternal life.  
> Alleluia.

This is the account of the Alexandrian Chronicle. But there is some difference in the Liturgy of the Presanctified. For in that liturgy, after τὸ κατευθυνθείτω, that is, “Let it be directed,” the priest’s words κατὰ τὴν δωρεὰν and so forth do not immediately follow; many things intervene. Second, what is sung by the people in the same liturgy is not complete: after τῆς δόξης, “of glory,” with an Alleluia, the remainder is absent. Third, in the same liturgy the priest takes up the holy gifts and transfers them to the altar after the people have sung the foregoing words, and after the priest has said, “Like the prodigal son,” and so forth. But in the Chronicle cited, the sacred gifts are transferred while the people are singing the aforesaid ode.

From this it is clear that in such a liturgy certain things were added, removed, and altered by later authorities.

In the Codex of Abbot Ratold the following follows:

> “The bells are rung, and Vespers are sung. And the cantor begins: Antiphon, ‘The cup.’ Psalm, ‘I believed.’ Antiphon, ‘With those who hated.’ Psalm, ‘To the Lord when I was in distress.’ Antiphon, ‘From unjust men.’ Psalm, ‘Deliver me.’ Antiphon, ‘Guard me from lips.’ Psalm, ‘Lord, I have cried.’ Antiphon, ‘I was considering.’ Psalm, ‘With my voice.’ Antiphon, ‘From the hand of the sons.’ Psalm, ‘Blessed is the Lord.’ Verse: ‘Christ was made for us.’ In the Gospel: ‘While they were at supper.’ Antiphon, ‘Having taken bread.’ Antiphon, ‘If I have spoken evil.’ At the conclusion: ‘Refreshed by life-giving nourishment,’ and so forth. Let the bishop say: ‘The Lord be with you.’ Response: ‘And with your spirit.’ And the deacon: ‘Go, the Mass is ended.’ Response: ‘Thanks be to God.’”

Thus far the Codex of Ratold.

Here note: first, that the evening synaxis is included in the Mass itself, as on Holy Saturday (below, in the Pontifical of Rouen); second, that Vespers itself consists of six Antiphons and an equal number of Psalms, followed by the versicle; third, that the words “in the Gospel” signify at the Magnificat; fourth, that three Antiphons are said for the canticle itself.

In the same Codex of Ratold the following continues:

> “And each person stands at the table. Then, after the meal, their feet are washed. While this is being done, these Antiphons are sung with alternating Psalms: ‘A new commandment.’ Psalm, ‘Blessed are the undefiled.’ Antiphon, ‘In those days.’ Psalm, ‘Great is the Lord.’ Antiphon, ‘After the Lord had risen.’ Psalm, ‘May God have mercy on us.’ Antiphon, ‘Before the feast-day.’ Antiphon, ‘You call me.’ Antiphon, ‘If I, the Lord and Teacher.’ Psalm, ‘Blessed are the undefiled in the way.’ Antiphon, ‘Let us love one another.’ Psalm, ‘Behold, how good.’ Antiphon, ‘By this everyone will know.’ Psalm, ‘Great is the Lord.’ Hymn on the Lord’s Passion”—which we give here with the ancient musical notation:

> Earth and heaven exult  
> At the supper of the great Prince,  
> Which cleansed the heart  
> Of the first-formed man by its food.
>
> On this night the Maker of all,  
> In a mighty mystery,  
> Changes his flesh and blood  
> Into food for the soul.
>
> Rising from the lofty banquet,  
> Offering an example to mortals,  
> Out of the grace of humility,  
> He seeks the footsteps of Peter.
>
> The servant grows pale with amazement  
> When he sees the Lord of angels  
> Carrying water in a towel  
> And lying prostrate in the filth.
>
> Allow yourself to be washed, Simon;  
> These acts signify mystical things,  
> While the highest bears the lowest,  
> And ashes serve ashes.
>
> The left hand of the torturer reclines,  
> And piles up the honeycombs of the Word;  
> Among these he marks the enemy,  
> Who broods over the treacheries of death.
>
> Savage wolf, most wicked Judas,  
> You carry kisses to the gentle Lamb,  
> Giving the royal limbs  
> To the cords that cleanse the ages of their filth.
>
> Today those bound are freed  
> From the prison of flesh and heart;  
> The chrism’s ointment is consecrated;  
> From it hope increases for the wretched.
>
> Let us compose glorious praise  
> To the victor over death,  
> With the Holy Father and the Spirit,  
> Who redeemed us by his death.

When this has been completed, the bishop shall kiss the Gospel, and all who stand around him. Then they shall say the Lord’s Prayer silently. When it is finished, the bishop shall say, “And lead us not into temptation”; “Behold, how good”; “We have received, O God”; “You commanded”; “You washed the feet of the disciples, the work of your hands”; “Be present, we ask, O Lord, to the duties of our service, who deigned to wash the feet of your disciples,” and so forth.

Saint Eligius mentions the washing of feet preserved in the Church on the Lord’s Supper, sermon 8:

> The preparation of the holy chrism, the fraternal washing of feet.

And the Master, in the Rule, chapter 43:

> On the Lord’s Supper they shall extend their hands, for the blessing, to wash the feet of the abbot, and afterward those of all the superiors, with the assistance of the brothers. Yet, beginning with the abbot, let him wash the feet of the doorkeepers as well, etc.

The same may be seen in the seventeenth Council of Toledo, canon 3, where this holy work of foot-washing on the Lord’s Supper is prescribed for all the churches of Galicia, because certain churches had discontinued it.

Saint Augustine also mentions it in letter 119 to Januarius, where he writes that many did not wash feet on that day, lest the washing appear to pertain to baptism.

Formerly at Constantinople, on the same Thursday, the emperor used to wash the feet of twelve poor men. Codinus describes the rite in *On Offices*, in the following manner:

> Before the liturgy of that same great Thursday, the foot-washing takes place as follows: Twelve poor men are prepared and dressed in undershirts or tunics, short leggings, and sandals. A washbasin having been placed in the emperor’s chamber, the protopapas, standing outside at its door, sings “Blessed,” and says the Trisagion. Then, while the same man is reading the Gospel, when he says, “He pours water into the basin,” the emperor pours water into the washbasin. Afterward the prepared poor men are brought in one by one, each carrying a lighted candle, while the protopapas, as stated, reads the Gospel and says, “Jesus began to wash the feet of the disciples,” repeating this very often, namely, until all have been washed. The emperor washes the right foot of each one; and when he has wiped the washed foot with the cloth hanging before him, he kisses it. When this has been done, the things pertaining to the rite of foot-washing are completed. Three gold coins are given to each of them. After this, the liturgy is celebrated.

Thus Codinus.

It will not be unwelcome to append the ancient order or rite formerly observed in the Church of Rouen, or Rheims, on the Thursday of the Lord’s Supper. The most learned Joannes le Prevost, canon and librarian of the same church of Rouen, sent it to me from an old manuscript Pontifical preserved in the sacristy of the church of Rouen, because it contains many things worthy of note that are not part of current practice.

### The order on the day of the Lord’s Supper begins

On Thursday of Holy Week, that is, on the Lord’s Supper.

Early in the morning, the mansionarii shall arrange everything necessary for the consecration of the chrism, placing three flasks full of the purest oil in the sacristy: one for the oil of the sick, another for the chrism, and the third for the oil for anointing catechumens. The chrism must be covered [read: “covered”] with white silk; cover the others with silk of another kind. The bishop shall provide the balsam.

At the third hour the signal shall sound, so that everyone may come to the church in which the chrism is to be consecrated. On that day the bells shall be rung for Mass and for the other hours, as is customary on feast days, and thereafter they shall remain silent until Holy Saturday.

The presbyters and the other clerics shall put on solemn vestments; the deacons, dalmatics; and the subdeacons, white silks—as in the Roman Order. Each shall stand in his proper order in the church, waiting until the bishop comes in full procession for Mass, as he customarily does on solemn days with seven deacons, censers, and incense.

The bishop and the presbyters, standing with the others in order before the altar, say: “I confess to almighty God,” and so forth.

Meanwhile, the cantor and the schola, as they have been instructed, begin the Introit for the Mass: “But as for us,” and so forth; “May God have mercy,” and so forth. And again: “But as for us,” and so forth; “Glory be to the Father.” Again: “But as for us.” Kyrie eleison three times, Christe eleison three times, Kyrie eleison three times.

Then the bishop begins the *Gloria in excelsis* with the presbyters. While the *Gloria in excelsis* is sung, the entire peal is sounded until it is finished. When it is finished, the bishop says with the presbyters: “Peace be with you.” “Let us pray.” “O God, from whom Judas…”

Another Prayer at the consecration of the chrism:

> O God, who use the ministry of priests for the regeneration of your peoples, grant us perseverance in serving your will, so that by the gift of your grace in our days your people, consecrated to you both in merit and in number, may increase.

Through…

To the Corinthians:

> Brothers, when you come together…

Response: “Christ…”

Verse: “Therefore…”

Before the Gospel, the deacon alone who is to read the Gospel ascends the ambo with the subdeacon, preceded by the cross, the candlestick, and the censer:

> The continuation of the holy Gospel according to John. At that time, before the feast of Passover…

After the Gospel has been read, the bishop says with the presbyters: “I believe in one God,” and so forth.

Then the bishop says with the presbyters: “The Lord be with you.” “And with your spirit.” “Let us pray.” Offertory: “The right hand of the Lord,” and so forth.

The presbyters and any others who wish, after the chalice with wine and water and the offerings have been brought—of these the presbyters, deacons, and the rest shall communicate, and some shall be reserved until the morning of Good Friday—bowed before the altar, the bishop and the presbyters continue the Secrets of the Mass, saying:

> In a spirit of humility and with a contrite heart may we be received by you, O Lord; and may our sacrifice today be made in such a way that it may be received by you and please you, O Lord my God.
>
> Receive, Holy Trinity, this offering which I offer to you in memory of the Incarnation, Nativity, Passion, and so forth, of Jesus Christ; and in honor of all your saints who have pleased you from the beginning of the world, and of those whose feasts are celebrated today, and whose names and relics are kept here, so that for them, and so forth, for salvation, all those whom we commemorate on earth may deign to intercede for us in heaven.

Through the same Lord of ours.

> Pray, brothers, for me to the Lord, that my sacrifice and yours may be acceptable in his sight.

Secret:

> May it itself, O Lord, and so forth.

Another Secret:

> Let us pray. May the power of this sacrifice, we ask, mercifully wipe away our old nature and increase in us newness and salvation. Through…

The Lord be with you. Lift up your hearts, and so forth.

> Whom on this night, while reclining amid the sacred banquet, he rebuked, and so forth.

“Therefore, most merciful Father, with your servant our pope N., and our bishop N. [and our king N.]. Remember, O Lord,” and so forth.

> To you they render their vows, eternal, and so forth.
>
> Likewise, after supper, he blessed and gave it to his disciples, and so forth.
>
> Therefore, O Lord, mindful servants that we are, and so forth.
>
> Of our Lord God’s most blessed, and so forth.
>
> Remember also, O Lord, your servants and handmaids N. May you graciously admit them, together with all the faithful departed, and so forth.

Through Christ our Lord.

> Then oil is offered to the bishop for anointing both the sick and the possessed. Let both he himself [perhaps read *ipse*] and all the presbyters who are present bless it.
>
> On the apostolic authority that we possess concerning the oil of the sick. We possess apostolic authority concerning the oil with which the sick are anointed, as the blessed apostle James says: “Is anyone among you sick? Let him summon the presbyters of the Church, and let them pray over him; and if he is in sins, they shall be forgiven him.” Hence it is evident that this custom was handed down by the apostles themselves to the holy Church, namely, that the possessed and all other sick persons should be anointed with oil consecrated by pontifical blessing.
>
> For it is consecrated in the very office of consecrating the Lord’s body and blood. It does not have a proper office—that is, it does not have at its beginning the words of greeting, namely, “The Lord be with you,” nor “Let us pray.” Nor is it concluded at the end, as the other Prayers are, with “Through our Lord Jesus Christ,” but only with “In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.”
>
> In the place where we customarily bless grapes, the oil for the sick is consecrated, and it is concluded with the conclusion, “Through whom you always create all good things, O Lord,” and so forth. Hence we understand that this is an insertion—that is, something inserted or interposed—into the office mentioned above.
>
> Of the same oil the Sacramentary contains the following: Before “Through whom you always create all good things, O Lord” is said, the flasks which the people offer are raised, and both the lord pope and all the presbyters bless them.
>
> It is the custom of the Roman Church—note this—that at the making of the body and blood of the Lord the presbyters are present and, together with the bishop, effect it by words and hands. In the same way the presbyters ought to make the oil together with the bishop.
>
> Exorcism of the oil for the sick and for the people. Before “Through whom you always create all good things, O Lord” is said, the oil is to be exorcized, so that it may be heard by those standing around, as follows: “I exorcize you, most unclean Spirit,” and so forth.
>
> Likewise its blessing: “Let us pray. Send forth, O Lord,” and so forth.

Then the oil is carried back and honorably reserved in its place. The bishop and the presbyters continue:

> Through whom you always create all good things, O Lord, and so forth.

“Throughout all things,” and so forth. “Deliver us,” and so forth. “World without end. Amen.”

Then the deacon says: “Bow down for the Blessing.” And the bishop, turned toward the people, says:

> May almighty God bless you, who through the passion of his only-begotten Son…

Then, turning toward the altar in the customary manner, holding the holy things, he says:

> And may his peace always be with you.

And with your spirit.

The schola sings the *Agnus Dei* three times. The peace is not given.

Prayer when he sends the holy things:

> May this most holy commingling of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ be salvation of mind and body for us and for all who receive it, and a saving preparation for attaining eternal life. Through the same Christ our Lord.

Prayer to the Father:

> Holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God, give me this body and blood of Christ, and so forth.

Prayer to the Son:

> Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the living God, and so forth.

Then the bishop alone communicates, and he does not break the offerings except the one from which he communicates. He reserves some of the blood in the chalice for the communion of the presbyters and the rest of the clergy.

Prayer when he receives:

> May the reception of the body and blood…

Another:

> May what I have taken with my mouth, O Lord, I receive with my mind, so that the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ may be an everlasting remedy for me. Through the same Christ our Lord. Amen.

Then the chalice containing the blood and the offerings are covered, and the bishop appoints presbyters and deacons to guard them carefully.

> Then the bishop goes to his seat with the deacons and waits. While the bishop is waiting in his seat, twelve presbyters and as many other clerics as are needed come to the sacristy to carry, with every mark of honor, the chrismal oil, as well as the oil of the catechumens and neophytes, into the church before the bishop.
>
> Let those presbyters be prepared, and with them the other clerics, in chasubles and solemn vestments. Then two acolytes take the two flasks that are to be consecrated for the chrism and for the oil of the catechumens, and proceed, as in the Roman Order.
>
> The presbyters and the aforementioned clerics shall arrange themselves properly and in due order, so that two acolytes walk first with candlesticks and burning candles. Then two crosses are carried, with the chrismal oil between them. After them two censers with incense are carried, with the oil of the catechumens between them. Then the Gospel is carried, so that every gift may be fulfilled.
>
> Afterward the twelve presbyters, witnesses and fellow-workers of this most holy mystery of the chrism, followed by acolytes, subdeacons, and the rest, proceed two by two. Let them stand in their order according to their rank where the ascent to the altar begins, except that the deacon is to be sixth, in the more elevated place, and beside the archdeacon who read the Gospel.
>
> Receiving the wrapped flask in order as it ascends, when it reaches the archdeacon, let him carry it, still wrapped, before the bishop. Meanwhile one subdeacon carrying a small vessel with balsam offers it to another deacon, and that deacon offers it to the bishop.

> Then the same candlesticks, crosses, censers, and Gospel, as well as the aforesaid twelve presbyters, witnesses and assistants of the same mystery, are arranged on either side around the bishop, so that the deacons stand behind the bishop. The presbyters stand on the right and left; the crosses and the other objects stand between them on either side.

The same is prescribed in the Council of Rouen, in Orderic Vitalis, *Ecclesiastical History*, book IV.

> When these things have been arranged, the bishop, or the person whom he has appointed, turns both to the clergy and to the people and gives a sermon appropriate to the consecration of the chrism.
>
> Then the bishop turns and begins the consecration of the principal chrism, mixing the balsam with the oil. Afterward he breathes three times over the flask itself and says in a low voice the exorcism of the chrismal oil.
>
> Exorcism of the holy oil: “I exorcize you,” and so forth.
>
> Then the bishop says with the presbyters in a loud voice: “Throughout all ages,” and so forth; “It is truly worthy,” and so forth; “Who in the beginning, among other things,” and so forth.
>
> When the blessing has been completed, the bishop greets the uncovered chrism, and those who are near him say: “Hail, holy chrism.”
>
> Again he descends in order as he ascended, and the chrism is carried, covered, to everyone for veneration. When this has been done, it is treated with the highest honor until the other flask ascends and descends again, so that both may return honorably to their proper place.

Concerning the fact that the flask is carried uncovered for some people and covered for others to venerate, the booklet of the Roman Order says the following in the consecration of the chrism:

> Immediately two acolytes hold the two wrapped flasks in a white silk cloth on the left arm, so that they can be seen from the middle. Before the flask comes to the bishop at the altar, one half of it is covered and one half uncovered.
>
> The flask containing the chrism in some way signifies the body of the Lord taken from the Virgin. Before it passed to the altar of the cross, it was for a certain time covered and for a certain time uncovered.
>
> At first it was covered, when he fled to Egypt as though he were not the King of kings; when he was carried into the temple as though he were not omnipotent; and when he was subject to his parents as though he were not the author of his parents. In these and similar circumstances he lay hidden, covered.
>
> It was uncovered after he began to perform miracles and at the same time to preach and to show himself to be God, as he says: “I and the Father are one.” In these and other circumstances he was uncovered.
>
> After the flask has been blessed, it returns from the altar. It is greeted uncovered and visible by the bishop and the ministers of the altar. This signifies that after Christ came forth from the altar of the cross, he granted bodily presence to those whom he wished to be witnesses of his resurrection.
>
> That it is carried to be greeted by the others invisible and covered signifies that when Christ returned to heaven he became invisible to human beings, as he himself testifies: “I came forth from the Father and came into the world; again I leave the world and go to the Father.”
>
> Although we do not see his bodily presence, nevertheless by venerating him we greet him every day.

> The exorcism of the oil with which the catechumens are to be anointed begins.
>
> As the flask containing the chrism descends, another containing the oil of the catechumens immediately ascends, just as the first did, to the bishop. He breathes into it as into the first; first he performs its exorcism and blesses it as though reading a lesson.
>
> Exorcism in Greek means in Latin an adjuration, or a speech of rebuke, directed against the devil so that he may depart. It concludes: “Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who is to come to judge the living and the dead and the world by fire.”
>
> In that oil the catechumens are anointed so that, if any stains have clung to body or mind, after they have come to the scrutiny they may depart [add the conjunction “and”]; thereafter, through this anointing, they may have a protection, so that the devil cannot return. The words of the Prayer demonstrate this, when it says:
>
> “So that if any stain of hostile spirits has clung to them, all may depart at the touch of this holy oil.”
>
> Exorcism of the same oil: “I exorcize you, creature of oil,” and so forth.
>
> Then let it be said: “The Lord be with you.” “And with your spirit.” “Let us pray.”
>
> “God of increase,” and so forth.
>
> Then the bishop and those who are near him greet the aforesaid flask, saying: “Hail, holy oil.”
>
> And it descends in order, as the other did, and is carried to everyone for veneration.

“After these things have been completed, let both women return to the sacristy in the same order and under the same guidance by which they ascended into the church. Then let the pontiff wash his hands, and let the deacons go to the altar and uncover the sacred elements; and when the pontiff comes to the altar, let him divide the offerings for breaking. Let him take from them whole offerings to be reserved for the morning of Good Friday; from these they are to communicate without the Lord’s blood. The blood, however, is to be entirely consumed on that same day. And let the schola sing the Communion: ‘The Lord Jesus,’ etc.

“When the offerings have been broken, let the priests and deacons, and all the others, communicate, and thus let the Mass be completed according to its order. Then let Vespers be said.

“Antiphon: ‘The Chalice,’ etc. Psalm: ‘I believed.’ Antiphon: ‘With these,’ etc. Psalm: ‘To the Lord.’ Antiphon: ‘From unjust men,’ etc. Psalm: ‘Deliver me.’ Antiphon: ‘Guard,’ etc. Psalm: ‘Lord, I have cried.’ Antiphon: ‘I considered at the right hand,’ etc. Psalm: ‘With my voice.’ Antiphon: ‘As they were dining,’ etc. Psalm: ‘The Magnificat.’

“Then let the pontiff turn and say: ‘The Lord be with you.’ ‘And with your spirit.’ ‘Let us pray.’

“Postcommunion: ‘Having been refreshed with life-giving nourishment,’ etc.

“Another Postcommunion. Let us pray. Grant, we beseech you, almighty God, that we may feel both in body and in mind the mystery of the new sacrament which we have received. Through our Lord, etc.

“The Lord be with you,” etc.

“The deacon: Go, the Mass is ended.” “Thanks be to God.”

“Prayer after Mass before the altar: May the homage of my service be pleasing to you, Lord God, holy Trinity; and grant that this sacrifice, which I, unworthy, have offered before the eyes of your Majesty, may be acceptable to you and, through your mercy, propitiatory for me and for all for whom it has been offered. Through the Lord.

“Then, having laid aside his pontifical vestments, let the pontiff descend into the sacristy, instructing the priests as he wishes.”

Thus far the rite of Thursday of the Lord’s Supper in the manuscript Pontifical of Rouen.

[Col. 0331C] 283. Friday. The solemnity of Good Friday is described; its ceremonies are found almost identically in Alcuin, *On the Divine Offices*, in the chapter on Friday.

284. At the third hour let all the priests assemble. So the printed editions read. But nothing similar is found in the other manuscript codices in our possession.

285. In the Sacramentary. Note the distinction between *Sacramentary* and *Book of Sacraments*. Since this codex of Saint Eligius is entitled *Book of Sacraments* and cites the *Sacramentary*, no one can fail to see that the *Sacramentary* is distinguished from the *Book of Sacraments*.

286. He ascended to the seat. The pontiff is said to ascend to the seat because the bishop’s seat, or chair, ought to be higher than the others in the church, in accordance with the ancient custom of the Church. This may be seen in Burchard, book XI, chapter 10, from a letter of Pope Urban, in which the reason for this custom is given:

“But the fact that the seats of bishops are found established and prepared on high in the church shows, by the throne, the contemplation and power of judging, loosing, and binding given to them by the Lord.”

Saint Ambrose likewise teaches this in *On the Dignity of the Priesthood*, chapter 6:

“For what else does ‘bishop’ mean except ‘overseer,’ especially since he sits on a throne in a more elevated place in the church?”

And Saint Augustine, on Psalm 126:

“For this reason a higher place has been appointed for bishops, so that they may oversee.”

This is likewise established in the Fourth Council of Carthage, canon 35:

“Let the bishop sit in the church in a higher place among the assembly of priests.”

The matter may also be seen in Eusebius, book X of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 4, in his description of that magnificent church built at Tyre by Paulinus the bishop:

“Having thus completed and perfected the temple, and having placed thrones in the highest position for the honor of the presidents of the Church,” etc.

That is: “Moreover, when this temple had thus been completed and perfected, and certain thrones had been placed in the highest position for the honor of the presidents of the Church, while the benches for the remaining ranks of the clergy had also been decently arranged in their proper order and ornamented.”

The same may be seen in Prudentius, in the *Passion of Saint Hippolytus*, where it is called a tribunal, as also in Saint Isidore, book XV of the *Etymologies*, chapter 4:

“Opposite the façade, a lofty tribunal is raised high on steps;

from it the bishop proclaims God.”

Nor do these words of Sulpicius Severus, *Dialogue* 2, stand in the way:

“Recently I saw someone—I call the Lord to witness—not without embarrassment on my part, seated on a lofty throne, as though on a royal tribunal, in an elevated seat.”

For there he condemns the arrogance of a certain bishop who exceeded proper measure in this matter, sitting in the church not as a bishop but as a king, in order to contrast him with the humility of Saint Martin, who used to sit in the temple on a lowly chair.

The same must be said of the lofty throne which Paul of Samosata had set up for himself in the church, on account of which he is reproved in the letter of the bishops. That throne exceeded episcopal modesty, since it was not fitting for a disciple of Christ, but gave him the appearance of a secret ruler of the world, as Eusebius says in book VII of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 24.

[Note: [Col. 0331D] In the edition of Henri Valois it is chapter 30.]

287. As is found on Wednesday. I added these words from the printed editions, because in this codex of Saint Eligius all these prayers are repeated here.

288. In the oratory. So the printed editions read; nevertheless, read *in orario*, as in Alcuin. It is an oblong tapestry, like an orarium, spread beneath the cross for those who are to adore it. It extends from the place where the cross has been set to approximately the middle of the choir, a practice that is still observed in certain churches.

289. Let him kiss the cross after adoring it. It was an ancient custom to adore the cross on the great Preparation, that is, Good Friday. Formerly this was done at Jerusalem, when on the same day the bishop displayed the true cross of Christ for the people to adore, as Saint Paulinus testifies in Letter 11:

“The cross of Christ, discovered and proved by the experience of the Resurrection, was soon consecrated with fitting ceremony. It was placed in a basilica whose gilded ceilings glitter, and the cross, set in a secret shrine, is preserved there. Each year, when the Lord’s Passover is celebrated, the bishop of that city himself, as leader of the worshipers, brings it forth for the people to adore. Apart from this day, on which the mystery of that cross is celebrated and it is itself the cause of the sacraments, it is not brought forth as a mark of the sacred solemnity—unless exceptionally the most devout request it, those who have traveled there for no other reason than that its unveiling might be offered to them as the reward of their distant pilgrimage.”

The words “apart from this day, on which the mystery of that cross is celebrated” sufficiently indicate that *Passover* (*Pascha*) in this passage of Saint Paulinus is used for the solemnity of Good Friday.

290. And another. So the printed editions read. In Alcuin, at the cited chapter, *the subdeacon* is added.

291. It is always sung. I restored *always* from the printed editions, since in our codex *super* was incorrectly written.

292. Psalm 118. Alcuin adds the following:

“Likewise: We adore your cross, etc. Psalm: May God have mercy. Another: While the Creator.”

But in the Codex of Ratoldus there is more, and because it deserves notice and differs considerably from present-day custom, I shall not hesitate to add it here:

“After these prayers, let two deacons proceed to the sacristy or behind the altar. They sing: ‘My people.’ The two priests, however, stand before the cross and respond to the salutation: ‘Holy God’ (*Agios o Theos*). The choir likewise: ‘Holy God, holy Strong One.’

“Let the cross be carried a little farther forward, and again let the deacons sing: ‘I indeed led you through the desert.’ The priests, however: ‘Holy God’ (*Agios o Theos*). And the choir again: ‘Holy God, holy Strong One.’

“Again let it be carried a little farther: ‘What more ought I to have done?’ ‘Holy [God].’ Likewise: ‘Holy God.’

“Let the cross be carried forward a third time before the altar, and let the two priests uncover it from the linen with which it had been wrapped. Let them say, lifting up the cross: ‘Behold the wood of the cross.’ Psalm: ‘May God have mercy.’

“Then let the pontiff come with two deacons, prostrate himself three times, and let them adore the cross in the customary manner. After these, the priests and levites follow; then all the clergy; thereafter all the people, including the women.

“Meanwhile let them sing these antiphons: ‘We adore your cross, Lord.’ Psalm: ‘Blessed are the undefiled.’ Antiphon: ‘We adore the cross.’ Antiphon: ‘While the Creator of the world.’ The hymn of Fortunatus: ‘Sing, my tongue, the glorious.’”

Thus far the Codex of Ratoldus.

Before the words “What more ought I to have done?” the following should be supplied: “And again the deacons sing”; before “Agios,” understand “the priests, however”; and before “Holy God,” understand “and the choir again.”

The words “prostrating himself three times,” etc., are corrupt and should be read: “Let them prostrate themselves three times, adoring the cross.”

293. Of the holy [bread]. So the printed editions read. In Alcuin: “It is taken from the holy bread.” The following words deserve notice and explanation:

“Wine that has not been consecrated is sanctified through the consecrated bread.”

This must not be understood as though unconsecrated wine, through such an admixture, became the blood of Christ, but rather as receiving a certain external sanctification from such a mixture. From this we should note the ancient custom, which still continues: namely, that on Good Friday the celebrant communicated under the species of bread alone.

294. Saying nothing. In Alcuin it reads “in silence,” and he adds:

“‘The peace of the Lord’ is not said, because the kisses of those standing around do not follow.”

295. And all communicate. Both clergy and laity, as was proved above from Theodulf.

Formerly, in the monastery of a certain ancient father of the monks, who is called *the Master* in his Rule and flourished not long after Pope Gregory I, the monks communicated on that same day of Good Friday, as is clear from chapter 43 of his Rule, in the *Concordia of Rules*, chapter 56, section 4:

“Let the sacraments of the altar be concluded in a larger glass paten, so that when the Jews seek Christ for his Passion on Friday, he may be revealed to our minds on that very day, in order that on Saturday he may appear to us through the Resurrection in the new sacrament. Those who are to be refreshed on Friday should therefore refresh themselves without communion, so that it may be recognized that on Friday one is unjustly refreshed without Christ.”

Formerly, however, the practice was different in Spain. On that day neither the solemnity of Mass nor communion was celebrated, as is evident from the Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 6, where the following provisions are made concerning Friday of the Lord’s Passion:

“Therefore on that day it is fitting that the mystery of the cross, which the Lord himself wished to be proclaimed to all, should be preached, and that the whole people should ask aloud for the pardon of sins, so that, cleansed by the compunction of repentance, we may deserve to receive the venerable day of the Lord’s Resurrection with our iniquities forgiven, and may receive, cleansed from sin, the sacrament of his body and blood.”

Here one sees that on the day of the Passion the pardon of sins is to be requested, so that on the day of the Lord’s Resurrection the body and blood of the Lord may be received.

The same is clear from the Sixteenth Council of Toledo, canon 8:

“Except on the day of the Lord’s Passion, when the altars remain stripped bare, no one is permitted to celebrate the solemn rites of Mass on that day.”

Let no one say, then, that it was indeed unlawful to consecrate the body and blood of Christ on that day, but that it was possible to celebrate with the presanctified elements. The words “when the altars remain stripped bare” stand against this. For Mass cannot be celebrated, even with the presanctified elements, when the altar is stripped bare. If Mass was not celebrated on that day, neither was communion, which formerly was not received in basilicas or churches outside the solemn rites of Mass.

296. And all things were completed. The printed editions add the following:

“Having done this, the pontiff says: ‘In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.’”

These words are found in none of our manuscript codices.

297. Let the altars be bare. The stripping of the altars formerly took place on this Friday, as may be seen in the manuscript Rule of the Master, chapter 43, in the *Concordia of Rules*, chapter 56, section 4. There it is prescribed that on Friday the covering of the altar, or the various ornaments of the oratory, should be removed; likewise that lamps and lanterns should be denied sight throughout the monastery. Here the particle *or* is used conjunctively.

But there was a different custom. Formerly, in certain places, the altars were also stripped on the Lord’s Supper, as now. This may be seen in the Roman Order concerning this day:

“Immediately let two acolytes, dressed in black chasubles, begin to strip the altars.”

And in Alcuin, *On the Divine Offices*, in the chapter on the Lord’s Supper:

“When these things have been finished, the altars are stripped, now near nightfall.”

This also seems to be indicated by canon 8 of the Sixteenth Council of Toledo, where, speaking of Good Friday, it says:

“When the altars remain stripped bare.”

For *remain* indicates that on that day they had not been stripped, but on the preceding day, according to the custom. This is also confirmed by the Seventeenth Council of Toledo, canon 2:

“So that unless at the celebration of the Lord’s Supper, when according to customary practice the altars ought to be divested, those same doors should be opened.”

The same is proved by the washing of the altars, which formerly took place on the same day together with the washing of the walls and pavement of the church and of the sacred vessels. We shall discuss these matters briefly here.

Above, in the same chapter of the Rule of the Master, when it treats of Friday of Holy Week, we read:

“The washing of objects and of the Paschal furnishings is to be arranged for that very day.”

This is to be understood of the washing of the altars, walls, and floors of the church, and of the purification of the sacred vessels, which, although in the homeland of the Master—and perhaps elsewhere—it may have been performed on Good Friday, was nevertheless performed at Rome on Thursday of the Lord’s Supper, as is clear from the Roman Order, where it treats of the solemnity of that day:

“On that same day the altars and walls of the church, or the floors of the church, are to be washed, and the vessels consecrated to the Lord are to be purified.”

In Gaul, as is plain from the eighth homily of Saint Eligius, bishop of Noyon, on the Lord’s Supper:

“And to commend the form of humility, he washed their feet on that day; hence it is that on the same day the altars and the walls of the church are washed, and the vessels are purified.”

In Spain, as is clear from Saint Isidore, book I of *On the Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 28, when he writes concerning the same day:

“Hence it is that on that day the altars, the walls of the church, and the floors are washed, and the vessels consecrated to the Lord are purified.”

Moreover, in the Codex of Ratoldus, the following words at the end of this solemnity deserve notice:

“After everything has been completed. Shortly afterward each person privately says Vespers, and so they go to the table.”
