The same is found in the Roman Order when it treats of this Friday. This is done today in certain churches, with the clergy or monks reciting Vespers privately and silently in the choir itself, kneeling.

298. Saturday. The solemnity of Holy Saturday is described.

299. The eighth hour. That is, the second hour after midday. The previously cited Council of Rouen gives a different rule:

“It is likewise decreed that on Easter Saturday the office should not begin before the ninth hour.”

300. Notaries. Here *notaries* are the bishop’s scribes, who for the most part were chosen from the college of readers.

Thus, in the *Library of Photius*, number 256, in the *Life of the Saints Metrophanes and Alexander*, we find Paul, a reader and notary of the Church of Constantinople, who later became patriarch of that same Church. The same appears in Ennodius, in the *Life of Saint Epiphanius, Bishop of Ticinum*. For when he wrote that Epiphanius had been admitted into the fellowship of readers, he added shortly afterward:

“Having quickly mastered the abbreviations of signs in writing and the various figures encompassing a multitude of words, he distinguished himself after being enrolled among the shorthand writers.”

Here *exceptores*—shorthand writers—are notaries, so called from those abbreviations of signs. Martial speaks of their speed in writing in book 14:

“Though the words may run, their hand is swifter than they;

the tongue has not yet completed its work, while the right hand has.”

Ausonius likewise writes in epigram 137:

“Boy, swift with signs,

skillful servant, hasten here;

unfold the two-leaved writing tablet,

on which much power of speech,

completed in individual strokes,

is brought to an end in a single utterance,” etc.

Saint Jerome, in his letter to Julian, volume I:

“And yet, with a notary placed beside him, he compelled him to dictate what the hand, receiving the words as they were rapidly uttered, could record, and the signs could seize the speed of the tongue.”

And in his letter to Principia, volume III:

[Note: [Col. 0335D] In the new edition, volume II, col. 684, the holy Doctor expounds Psalm XLIV and, on the verse, “My tongue is the pen of a scribe,” etc., says:]

“He wrote down the Gospel’s concise and compressed discourse in a certain brief system of signs, which we may understand as that of a notary.”

Hence, in the Glosses of Philoxenus:

“Notary: *semeiographos* [σημειογράφος], that is, a writer of signs.”

Synesius, Letter 61, calls such a person a *tachygraphos* [ταχύγραφος], that is, “one who writes rapidly”; and Philostratus, book I of *The Life of Apollonius*, chapter 13, calls him one who writes *eis tachos graphon* [εἰς τάχος γράφων], “writing with speed.”

Furthermore, in the Roman Order, in the Reims and Ratoldus codices, and in certain other Sacramentaries, a blessing of the Paschal candle appears here before the readings. Its prelude is:

“Let the angelic host of heaven now exult.”

This is indeed found in the Order of the Ambrosian Mass, but the remainder of the formula of blessing differs considerably from the customary one.

In the codices of Rodrada and Reims, the formula of blessing differs from the common one in two respects. First, it pursues the praises of bees at considerable length, in this manner:

“The bee surpasses the other animals subject to man [Virgil, *Georgics* IV]. Though small in bodily stature, it turns great spirits within its narrow breast; weak in strength, but strong in intelligence.

“Once it has observed the turning of the seasons, when the frosty winters have laid aside their whiteness and the cold old age of winter has been wiped away by the moderation of spring, immediately the care of going forth to work follows. Scattered through the fields, they settle upon the flowers, having balanced their wings for a little while and suspended their legs: some gather little flowers with their mouths; others, laden with provisions, return to their camps.

“There some, with immeasurable skill, construct cells with tenacious glue; others pack in liquid honey; others turn flowers into wax; others shape their young with their mouths; others enclose nectar collected from leaves.

“O truly blessed and beloved bees, whose sex is not violated by males, whose offspring are not disturbed, and whose children do not destroy their chastity—just as the holy Virgin Mary conceived, bore as a virgin, and remained a virgin.”

Then follows:

“O truly blessed night, which despoiled the Egyptians,” etc.

Second, at the end of the blessing only the pope is named, with no mention of a bishop, king, or emperor.

[Note: [Col. 0335D] The same words are found both in our manuscript codices and in the Gothic and Gallican Missals edited by Mabillon in his *On Gallican Liturgy*.]

This blessing of the candle is mentioned in the Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 8:

“The lamp and the candle are not blessed in the Paschal vigils in certain churches, and they ask why we bless them. Because of the glorious sacrament of that night, we solemnly bless these things, so that in the blessing of the holy Light we may receive the mystery of Christ’s sacred Resurrection, which arrives during this votive night.”

So reads the second edition of García; in the first, *of Easter* is absent, but this makes little difference, since what follows sufficiently indicates that the canon is to be understood as concerning the blessing of the Paschal candle.

Alcuin, *On the Divine Offices*, in the chapter on Holy Saturday, and Amalarius, *On the Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 18, attribute this institution to Pope Zosimus. Some object, asserting that it is older than Zosimus because a hymn concerning the Paschal candle exists in Prudentius, who flourished before Zosimus. But this is without justification: that hymn is not about the Paschal candle; it is an evening hymn about the light which formerly was kindled every evening in the church with a certain solemn rite, as we explained at length in section 2, chapter 24 of the *Concordia of Rules*.

Whatever the case may be, the rite is certainly ancient, since two blessings of the Paschal candle, written in a genuinely elegant style, are extant among the miscellaneous works 9 and 10 of Ennodius, bishop of Ticinum, who died in the year 521 after the birth of Christ. The Preface mentioned above, “Let the angelic host of heaven now exult,” is not prefixed to them.

[Note: [Col. 0335D] Almost the same text is read in the Calais manuscript and in two manuscripts of Theodore. In the Gemetic manuscript it is longer, beginning with the words “the bee,” or, as it reads in the manuscript, “the mother bee brought forth,” and much is added in praise of bees. In the old Gallican Sacramentary, whose antiquity may be consulted in Mabillon, *Museum Italicum*, volume I, part II, it reads: “The blessing of the holy candle of Bishop Augustine, which, while he was still a deacon, he sang, saying: ‘Let it exult,’ etc.,” as in the printed editions, though with several additions.]

The Order of the Ambrosian Mass also contains a blessing of the Paschal candle, but I have not discovered whether it was composed by the holy doctor himself.

It should additionally be noted that in the Codex of Ratoldus, above the words “of this incense,” a cross is depicted over *this*. Likewise, above the words “consecrated in honor of your name,” a cross is depicted over *consecrated*; in the codex of Rodrada it is depicted over *name*.

For the mystical meanings of the Paschal candle, consult Alcuin, Amalarius, Bartholomew Gavantus, and the others who have written about ecclesiastical offices or rites.

But the rites for blessing the Paschal candle found in the Reims and Ratoldus codices must not be omitted. In the former it reads:

“For at first, at the eighth hour in the middle of the day, they proceed to the church and enter the sacristy, and put on their vestments according to custom. The clergy begin the litany, and the priest proceeds from the sacristy with the sacred orders. They come before the altar and stand with bowed heads until they say ‘Lamb of God.’ Then the priest, coming from the prayer, goes behind the altar, takes some of the light that had been hidden on Friday, makes a cross over the candle, and lights it. These things are completed by these prayers.”

In the latter it reads as follows:

“At the sixth hour the pontiff is to enter the sacristy with the levites and ministers. They are to put on the sacred vestments and arrange themselves as is prescribed for the following day of Easter. He is to order a new fire to be obtained, either lighted from the sun with a vessel or struck from flint.

“Then let them make a cross of incense on the candle, and let the year of the Lord, together with Alpha and Omega, be written upon it. Then let the candle be carried before the bishop in procession, with candlesticks and censers, but without a flame. Thus let the bishop proceed surrounded by them in the middle of the choir, and let the candle be placed there.

“When the prayer has been completed, the bishop proceeds to the altar and sits there at the appointed hour. He is not to ascend to the seat until the time when he says, ‘Glory to God in the highest.’ Then the levite, asking the bishop’s blessing, is to go to the candle and consecrate it.

“The procession is to divide, part on the right and part on the left. Meanwhile, while seated, the bishop is to bless the fire and the incense, so that those standing around may hear. The candle is not to be lit until the deacon reaches the words, ‘The fire is kindled.’”

Thus far the Codex of Ratoldus.

The words in the Codex of Reims, “these things are completed by these prayers,” are understood of the prayers with which the bishop concludes the rite mentioned above. These are followed by the blessing of the candle, “Let it exult,” etc., which nevertheless is not found there.

The procession to the altar prescribed here in the Codex of Ratoldus, “as on the following day of Easter,” is found above, at the end of the *Book of Sacraments*. The prayer mentioned here is the first prayer of the Mass.

The procession that is to divide is the group of priests, deacons, and ministers who accompanied the same bishop from the sacristy to the altar and who are to assist him throughout the entire time of the Mass. Before “so that they may hear,” the particle *thus* should apparently be supplied.

In the Roman Order there are other rites that also differ from those of today. Among them is the following: as soon as the pontiff has proceeded from the sacristy, a certain candle is lit in a clean place, and the pontiff, or the priest, making a cross over it, blesses it in a subdued voice, while the schola sings the seven Penitential Psalms, beginning in this way:

“The Lord be with you,” etc. “Let us pray. God, creator of the world, author of light,” etc.

This blessing is also found in an old manuscript *Book of Sacraments*, a copy of which the very learned John Aubert, royal interpreter of the Greek language, made available to me. It follows the customary blessing of the Paschal candle, as though a second blessing of it.

Because it is longer than the aforementioned blessing of the Roman Order and differs from it in certain places, I have decided to append it here:

“God, creator of the world, author of light, maker of the stars; God, who have reclothed the world lying in darkness with perpetual light; God, through whose ineffable power all brightness took its beginning: invoking you in your works during this most sacred vigil of the night, we humbly offer to your Majesty, from your gifts, this candle—not polluted with the fat of flesh, nor corrupted by profane anointing, nor touched by sacrilegious fire, but constructed from wax, oil, and papyrus, and kindled in honor of your name—which we offer in the service of religious devotion.

“Therefore this great mystery and wondrous sacrament of this night must be heaped up with fitting praises. In it, through the miracle of the Lord’s Resurrection, the darkness of long age perceived that day had been introduced for it; and the delay that had formerly been condemned to eternal night, when the light of true radiance had been inserted, was astonished to find itself dragged captive in the Lord’s triumphs.

“But what had been condemned to servitude through the dark presumption of the first-created man is illumined by the splendor of freedom through the miracle of this night.

“Therefore, descending in spirit with fervor for the reverence of this festival, we present to you, God, peaceful lights shining with the brilliance of flames, as far as human devotion requires, so that while these things are performed with sound faith, the praises of your creature may also be exalted.

“For the light of the flame must be spoken of: through it the power of the Godhead deigned to appear to Moses. It provided the people departing from the land of slavery with guidance by saving light; and, when the three boys had been cast into the furnace by the tyrant’s sentence, it preserved their life with gentler caresses.

“Just as the horror of darkness is driven away by the preceding grace of this light, so, Lord, as the command of your Majesty shines forth, the burdens of sins are washed away.

“Since we marvel at the wondrous origin of this substance, we must necessarily praise the origin of bees. Bees are frugal in their expenditures and most chaste in reproduction. They build cells founded upon liquid wax, cells whose art no human skill equals as a teacher.

“They gather flowers with their feet, and no damage is found in the flowers. They do not give birth to offspring; rather, gathering with their mouths, they produce conceived offspring as swarms—just as Christ proceeded from the Father’s mouth in wondrous example.

“Virginity is fruitful without childbirth; and the Lord, in his love of virginity, deigned to have it as his bodily Mother.

“Such gifts, therefore, Lord, worthy of your sacred altars, are offered; and Christian devotion does not doubt that you rejoice in them.

“Come, therefore, almighty God, upon this incense, with a long outpouring of your blessing; and attend, invisible Ruler, to this nocturnal splendor, so that not only may the sacrifice offered this night shine through the admixture of your hidden light, but wherever something of this sanctification has been carried from its mystery, may the power of your Majesty stand present, the wickedness of diabolical deceit having been expelled. Through the Lord.”

Thus far the blessing of the candle.

Concerning it, it should first be noted that formerly papyrus—that is, the reed or cane growing along riverbanks—was used for candles, lamps, and lanterns.

Ennodius, in the first blessing of the Paschal candle:

“The water supplied papyrus as fuel for the fires.”

Saint Gregory of Tours, in *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 8:

“Lamps are continually lit in it. One of them, therefore, according to the custodian’s own assertion, continued to shine for forty days and as many nights without the help of any fuel; no papyrus was added to it, nor was a drop of oil poured in.”

In these words, in the phrase “whose human skill,” the word *industry* seems to be missing, or something similar, so that it should read: “whose industry.”

For the industry of bees in forming honey and constructing cells, and for their virginity, read Saint Ambrose, book V of the *Hexameron*, chapter 21; Aristotle, Pliny, Aelian, Virgil, and others.

The words “but wherever something of this sanctification from its mystery,” etc., are to be understood of pieces of the Paschal candle which Christians kept at home, so that through their help they might be protected against storms and diabolical attacks, as is clear from Ennodius, first blessing:

“And if anyone takes from this, let it be, while doing your command, a singular refuge against blasts of wind and against the spirits of storms; let it be a wall for the faithful against the enemy.”

And from the second blessing:

“At the time of your Resurrection, when the infancy of the reviving year blooms, grant that the piece taken from this may fight against storms and every attack.”

The Paschal lamb-candles formerly blessed at Rome by the archdeacon on Holy Saturday had the same power in place of the Paschal candle.

For formerly in the Roman Church the Paschal candle was not blessed. Rather, early on the morning of Holy Saturday, the archdeacon entered the church, melted wax in a clean vessel, mixed it with oil, and, blessing it, fashioned it in the likeness of lambs. On the octave of Easter, after communion, he distributed them to the faithful, who burned them in their homes for fumigation whenever necessity arose. This is taught by the Roman Order in its section on Holy Saturday, and by Alcuin and Amalarius in the chapters cited.

But this rite began only when the custom of blessing the Paschal candle ceased at Rome. That custom seems to have been restored by Pope Theodore. This may have given some people the opportunity to say that he was the author of the rite; how false that is is demonstrated by the blessings quoted above from Ennodius, who lived many years before that pope.

Or, if one prefers to say that Zosimus instituted the blessing of the Paschal candle throughout the parishes, as the *Pontifical of Damasus* testifies, but that Pope Theodore decreed that it should be blessed within the Roman city, or at Rome, then this may be said.

301. Into the ambo. Among the Greeks, properly speaking, “ambons are called mountainous and lofty places” [ἄμβωνες λέγονται ὀρεινοὶ καὶ ὑψηλοὶ τόποι].

And “ambo means ascent, eminence, and the summit of a mountain” [ἄμβων, προσανάβασις, καὶ ὑπεροχή, καὶ ὄρους λόφος], says the author of the ancient etymological lexicon.

For Hesychius, “ambons are the ascents of mountains” [ἄμβωνες αἱ προσαναβάσεις τῶν ὀρῶν]. Hence the name was transferred to signify the church’s pulpit or platform: the elevated place in the church from which readers read the divine Scriptures and the psalmists sang.

The Council of Laodicea, canon 15:

“Except for the canonical psalmists who ascend into the ambo” [πλὴν τῶν κανονικῶν ψαλτῶν ἐπὶ τὸν ἄμβωνα ἀναβαινόντων].

Sozomen, book IX of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 2:

“I suppose that it lay near the ambo, which is the platform of the readers” [εἰκάζω αὐτὴν κεῖσθαι περὶ τὸν ἄμβωνα, βῆμα δὲ τοῦτο τῶν ἀναγνωστῶν].

Cedrenus, in his account of Leo, son of Basil:

“When he was already entering and approaching the sacred doors, a certain man leapt out from the ambo” [ἄνθρωπός τις ἐκπεπηδηκὼς τοῦ ἄμβωνος], “and struck him on the head with a thick and heavy club. The blow would have killed the emperor had not the club, striking a hanging candelabrum while the blow was being delivered, somewhat diminished its force.”

Here one sees that the ambo is an elevated and lofty place in the church. The Latins call it a *pulpitum*, a pulpit.

The manuscript Glosses of the Library of Corbie:

“Ambo: pulpit.”

The same may be seen in Letter 34 of Saint Cyprian:

“When this man, dearest brothers, came to us with such great favor from the Lord, accompanied by the testimony and miracle of the very one who had persecuted him, where else should he have been placed than upon the pulpit—that is, upon the tribunal of the church—so that, supported by the dignity of a higher place and conspicuous to the entire people through the distinction of his honor, he might read the commandments and Gospel of the Lord, which he follows with courage and fidelity?”

302. A reading from the prophet Isaiah. “This is the inheritance.” [Note: [Col. 0337] These words are read in the Calais manuscript.] They are absent from the printed editions.

303. He came. This word is absent from the printed editions, although it is not particularly necessary.

304. The sevenfold litany. The sevenfold litany is one performed by seven choirs, as may be seen in Saint Gregory, book XI of the *Registrum*, chapter 2:

“Therefore, dearest brothers, with contrite heart and corrected works, let us come tomorrow at first light to the sevenfold litany, according to the arrangement set out below, with devout mind and tears.”

He then enumerates the seven choirs of this litany: the first of the clergy, the second of men, and so forth.

[Note: [Col. 0339D] This prayer of Saint Gregory is now found at the end of volume I, after the homilies on the Gospels.]

305. And those two candlesticks. It was an ancient custom of the Church that burning candles be carried before bishops.

Theodoret, book V of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 34, speaking of the return of Saint John Chrysostom:

“For everyone went out to meet him, carrying torches lit from wax” [ἅπαντες γὰρ ὑπήντησαν τὰς ἐκ κηροῦ λαμπάδας προάπτοντες].

That is: “For everyone went out to meet him with lighted candles.”

The bearer of a lamp before the pontiff is called a *lampadarios* [λαμπαδάριος]. See the *Greek-Barbarian Lexicon* of John Meursius.

### 306. And, standing, he blesses the fonts.

It is an ancient custom of the Church that the water of those who are to be baptized should be blessed by the bishop with solemn rite. Saint Dionysius, *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, book II:

> And having sanctified its water by sacred invocations.

Saint Basil, *On the Holy Spirit*, to Amphilochius, chapter 27:

> And we bless the water of baptism,

and he reckons this among the apostolic traditions. Saint Ambrose, *On Those Who Are Initiated into the Mysteries*, chapter 5 (rather, book I of *On the Sacraments*, chapter 5):

> Why did Christ descend first, and afterward the Holy Spirit, when both the form and practice of baptism require that the font be consecrated first, and then that the one who is to be baptized descend? For when the priest first enters, he performs an exorcism; secondly, he makes an invocation over the creation of the water; afterward he offers a prayer, so that the font may be sanctified and the presence of the eternal Trinity may be present.

[Note: That is, over the creation of the water; for this is how it is read in these blessings and exorcisms: “I bless you, creature of water. I exorcise you, creature of water.” In the latest edition this passage now reads: “He performs an exorcism beside (that is, near) the creature of water, then an invocation,” etc. See the note on this passage.]

Saint Cyprian, letter 70, to Januarius:

> Therefore the water must first be cleansed and sanctified by the priest, so that through its baptism it may wash away the sins of the person who is baptized.

Saint Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechesis* 3:

> Thus the plain water, receiving at the invocation the power of the Holy Spirit and of Christ, acquires holiness.

Saint Gregory of Nyssa, *Oration on the Baptism of Christ*:

> Hear, then, from us also how blessed water cleanses and illumines a human being.

Victor of Utica, book II of *The Vandal Persecution*:

> And at that hour when he blesses the font, so that those approaching the faith may be baptized, your eyes will be touched, and they will be opened, and you will see the light.

And shortly afterward:

> When Eugenius also perceived his shameless credulity, and since the appointed time was already pressing, he proceeded with him, accompanied by the clerical office, to the font. There, fixing his knees to the ground, beating heaven with great groaning and sobs, he blessed the rippling basin of the font.

Moreover, some refer the institution of blessed water to Alexander I, while the *Apostolic Constitutions* (book VIII, chapter 28) refer it to the holy apostle Matthew. It is also an ancient custom to place in the vestibule of a church a vessel full of blessed water for the purification of the people entering, as may be seen in Synesius, letter 121:

> For indeed the public sword is no less than the lustral water which, in the forecourts of the temples, is the city’s purification.

Here *χέρνιβον* properly means a vessel of lustral water, though here it is used by metonymy for the lustral water itself; elsewhere it is called *χερνιβόξεστον*, that is, “a polished basin.” *Χέρνιβον* is derived from *κέρνιψ*, which among the pagans, with the accent on the penultimate syllable, signifies lustral water. Athenaeus, book IX, describes the way it was prepared and used as follows:

> It is water into which they dipped a brand taken from the altar on which they had performed the sacrifice; sprinkling those present with it, they purified them.

This is also clear from Euripides, *Heracles Furens*, Act IV:

> And as he was about to carry a brand in his right hand,  
> so that he might dip Alcmena’s son in the lustral water.

That is: “And when he was already about to carry the brand in his right hand, so that he might dip Alcmena’s son in the lustral water.” And from Aristophanes, *Peace*:

> Come, then, bring the little torch; when I have taken it, I will dip it.

That is: “He brings the brand, and when I have taken it, I will immerse it.” Sophocles mentions it in *Oedipus Tyrannus*:

> … nor to distribute lustral water.

That is: “nor to partake of lustral water.” And Aeschylus, in the *Eumenides*:

> And what lustral water of the clansmen will receive him?

In the same Athenaeus, in the work cited, *ῥχένιψ* [probably *χέρνιψ*], with the acute accent, signifies a basin. *Χερνὶψ*, with the grave accent, is also *τὸ κατὰ χειρὸς ὕδωρ*, that is, “water for the hands,” as Julius Pollux notes from Homer, book II of the *Onomasticon*, chapter 2.

### 307. Whose spirit was over the waters.

So Saint Ambrose, *On Those Who Are Initiated into the Mysteries*, chapter 3.

### 308. Might conceive.

The printed editions read *reciperet*, “might receive,” incorrectly.

### 309. Who [—] the crimes of the guilty world.

So Saint Ambrose, in the chapter cited, and book II of *On the Sacraments*, chapter 1.

### 310. For the renewal of the nations.

So Lucian—or whoever else is the earlier author—writes concerning baptism in the *Philopatris*:

> Through water he renewed us.

### 311. In the form of a cross.

It is an ancient custom of the Church that baptismal water be blessed by the sign of the cross, as is established by Saint Augustine, Sermon 181, *On the Time*:

> For by this sign of the cross the Lord’s body is consecrated, and the baptismal font is sanctified.

And in *Tractate* 118 on John:

> What sign is meant, unless it is applied either to the foreheads of believers or to the water itself from which they are regenerated, etc.?

### 312. *Subripiat*, that is, *subrepat*.

[Note: In other works of Saint Gregory, as they are represented by manuscript codices, nothing occurs more frequently than *subripere* used for *subrepere*.]

### 313. At the creation of the world.

These words do not occur in the printed editions, nor in the Roman Order.

### 314. Whose Spirit was borne over you.

Optatus of Milevis, book VII against Parmenianus:

> O water, created sweet by God, over which, before the world’s own birth, the Holy Spirit was borne.

### 315. Who makes you flow from paradise.

This is not found in the printed editions.

### 316. Who [—] you, bitter in the desert.

Optatus, in the book cited:

> O water, which under Moses, so that you might lose your natural bitterness, sweetened by wood, satisfied the breasts of so many peoples with most pleasant draughts.

Saint Ambrose, *On Those Who Are Initiated into the Mysteries*, chapter 3, and book I of *On the Sacraments*, chapter 4; and Saint Gregory of Nyssa, *Oration on Not Delaying Baptism*.

### 317. Here let two candles be placed inside the baptistery.

Here *baptistery* means the baptismal water, for the Roman Order says: “Here the blessed candle is placed in the font”; and the Rheims Codex: “Here they place the candles in the fonts.” Elsewhere *baptistery* means a certain building beside a church, in which the faithful were formerly baptized; this will be discussed below.

### 318. He blows three times upon the water.

This blowing may be seen in the treatise of Severus, Patriarch of Alexandria, *On the Rites of Baptism*. Through it the coming of the Holy Spirit upon the waters is signified, just as Christ, in John 20, breathed on his disciples while giving them the Holy Spirit.

In the Rheims Codex this rite is followed by these words:

> The fullness of the font is the power of the Holy Spirit.

In the Ratold Codex:

> You breathe upon it benignly.

In the Rodradi Codex:

> Effective in purified minds.

### 319. He pours chrism into the font.

It is an ancient custom to pour chrism into the baptismal font, as is established by Saint Dionysius, cited shortly; by Saint Gregory of Tours, book I of *The Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 24:

> Then, after it had been sanctified with an exorcism, all the people devoutly drew the water sprinkled above with chrism;

and book I of his *History*, chapter 31:

> The baptistery is prepared, and balsams are poured out;

by Hincmar, in the *Life of Saint Remigius*:

> From this chrism the venerable bishop pours into the sacred font.

Moreover, in the passage cited from Gregory of Tours, we learn from book I of *The Miracles* that the people drew blessed water already infused with sacred chrism. This was afterward prohibited, as is evident from book VI of the *Capitularies* of the emperors Charles and Louis, title 77:

> If anyone wishes on Holy Saturday of Easter or on Pentecost Saturday to receive consecrated water for sprinkling in his house, let him receive it before the infusion of chrism.

### 320. In the form of a cross.

Chrism is poured into the baptismal water in the form of a cross, according to an ancient custom that may be seen in Dionysius the Great, chapters 2 and 4 of the *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*:

> Hence, as I think, the hierarch pours the myron into the cleansing baptistery in cross-shaped streams.

The Greeks and Easterners do this three times, as is established by the same Dionysius, chapter 2 of the *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*:

> And having sanctified its water by sacred invocations, he perfects it with three cross-shaped pourings of the most holy myron.

The same appears in the Greek *Euchologion*, in the rite following holy baptism:

> He makes three crosses with the oil in the water.

Here *oil* means ointment or chrism. The Fathers sometimes use the word in this sense, as will appear below from passages to be cited from Prudentius and Saint Augustine. The same rite seems to occur in the book of Severus, Patriarch of Alexandria, *On the Rites of Baptism*. The Ethiopians also customarily perform the same rite, as is clear from the baptismal order of the Ethiopian Church.

### 321. What is your name?

From this question it is clear that formerly names were given to infants or children not during baptism itself but before it. Since baptism was celebrated only on the days of Easter and Pentecost, and was often postponed for many years, it is not credible that infants then had no names—unless perhaps this should be asserted of those infants who were baptized on the eighth day of their birth or before the eighth day, concerning whom we shall have to speak below. It is indeed credible that names were given to such children during baptism itself.

Thus, when we see in Gregory of Tours, book II of his *History*, that the infants Ingomer and Clodomer, sons of King Clovis, and, in book X, Chlothar, son of King Chilperic, received their names during baptism itself, it is certain that this happened because they were baptized outside the aforementioned periods and not long after the day of their birth.

Formerly among the Romans, names were given to males on the ninth day from birth and to females on the eighth; these days were called *lustrical*, from the purification of the children. Macrobius, book I of the *Saturnalia*, chapter 16:

> There is also a Roman goddess called Nundina, named from the ninth day of newborns, which is called *lustrical*. The lustrical day is the day on which infants are purified and receive a name; for males it is the ninth day, and for females the eighth.

Festus:

> The lustrical days are called the days of infants: the eighth for girls, the ninth for boys, because on these days they are purified and names are given to them.

The Greeks gave infants names on the tenth day, as Hesychius testifies:

> “On the tenth we sacrifice.” “On the tenth day they gave names to the infants.” “Aristotle, however, says on the seventh.”

That is: “We sacrifice on the tenth. On the tenth day they gave names. Aristotle, however, says on the seventh.” This was done with the observance of certain superstitions, which some called *amphidromia*, involving circuits around the hearth, as Hesychius, Harpocration, Suidas, and the author of the ancient etymological lexicon note.

The ancient Franks gave infants a name on the ninth day, as may be gathered from the Salic Law, title 26, § 5:

> If anyone kills an infant in its mother’s womb, or after it has been born but before it has a name, within nine nights…

I therefore think that the ancient Christians followed their own customary practice in giving names, after removing all pagan superstition. Today the Greeks give infants names on the eighth day after their birth. The infants are brought by midwives before the church doors, and the priest signs them on the forehead, mouth, and breast, as may be seen in their *Euchologion*.

Some oppose us with canon 30 of the First Council of Nicaea, namely the canon translated from the Arabic language, in which the opposite of our position is asserted. But since this canon and similar ones are of doubtful authenticity and are not commonly received, they cannot weaken our position in the least.

They also object to a passage of Dionysius of Alexandria preserved by Eusebius, book VII of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 2, where he writes that infants receive from their parents the names Peter, Paul, or John. But this is futile, since that passage makes no mention of baptism.

Nor is the passage they produce from Saint Dionysius, chapter 2 of *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, of any force, where he says that a name is given in baptism. Saint Dionysius never wrote this, but rather:

> And when a certain priest proclaimed him and the sponsor from the written register.

That is: “When a certain priest proclaimed him and the sponsor from the written record.” Saint Maximus explains these words very well:

> Note also the register of the one being baptized and of the sponsor.

For formerly the *competentes*—that is, catechumens who, after spending a considerable time among the hearers, requested baptism—gave their names several days before baptism to be entered in the register.

This is clear from Saint Augustine, *On the Care to Be Taken for the Dead*, chapter 12:

> Easter was already approaching; he gave his name among the other candidates;

and *On Faith and Works*, chapter 6:

> This is done much more diligently and urgently on those days when they are called candidates, when they have already given their names in order to receive baptism.

Saint Cyril of Jerusalem, in the preface:

> The registration of names has already taken place among us.

Saint Gregory of Nyssa, *Oration on Those Who Delay Baptism*:

> Give me the names, so that I may write them in sensible books, while God may inscribe them on imperishable tablets.

The Fourth Council of Carthage likewise decreed, canon 85:

> Those who are to be baptized shall give their names.

The names of infants were also written down, as is clear from the Rheims Codex:

> When they have come to the church, the names of the infants are written down by the acolyte; and they are called in the church by their names, just as they have been written, etc.

And in the Ratold Codex:

> When they have come to the church, the names of the infants are written down by the acolyte, and they are called before the church door by their names, just as they have been written.

The same may be seen in the letter of Jesse, bishop of Amiens, *On Baptism*:

> In the third week of Lent, on Monday, at the third hour, let them come to the church; and before they enter the church, let the names of the infants and of those who are to receive them be written down by the acolyte. Then the infants themselves are called by the acolyte inside the church, etc.

From these passages it is clear that infants formerly had names before baptism and therefore did not receive them in baptism itself.

Thus, when the same Jesse later says in the same letter:

> There also the infant is named, just as John is in the Apocalypse,

this naming of the infant means nothing other than the repetition of a name previously given. This practice certainly did not prevail everywhere, for in the Ratold and Rheims Codices, in which the baptismal ceremonies are described in detail, one finds nothing similar.

The passage seems to be understood as referring to a change of name and the imposition of a new one, as these words appear to indicate: “just as John is in the Apocalypse.” Formerly, too, whenever a name was to be changed, it was changed in baptism, as Theophanes reports concerning Eudocia, wife of Theodosius the Younger, book XIV, under the year 1177. When the emperor was about to take her as his wife, Bishop Atticus made her a Christian; and in baptism, since she had previously been called Athenais, he gave her the name Eudocia.

### 322. Do you believe in God the Father, etc.?

These and similar questions follow the ancient custom of the Church, which Dionysius of Alexandria mentions in his letter to Pope Xystus, preserved by Eusebius, book VII of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 8. He speaks of someone who had been baptized by heretics and received into the Church:

> And having heard the questions and answers…

That is: “When he had heard the questions and answers, he wished to be baptized again.”

Saint Cyril likewise testifies, *Mystagogical Catechesis* 2:

> And each person was asked whether he believed in the name of the Father, etc.

That is: “Each person was asked whether he believed in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; and you confessed the saving confession, and you were immersed three times.”

Saint Cyprian, letter 70:

> The very question that is asked in baptism is also a witness to the truth. For when we say, “Do you believe in eternal life and the remission of sins through the Church?” etc.

And letter 75:

> He also baptized many, using the customary and lawful words of the interrogation, so that he might appear to differ in nothing from the ecclesiastical rule … especially since he lacked neither the Trinitarian Creed nor the lawful and ecclesiastical interrogation.

Optatus of Milevis, book V against Parmenianus:

> For when the one who believed was asked, he believed in God; and after his one “I believe,” you demand another “I believe.”

He speaks thus because, when the Donatists rebaptized those who had defected, they questioned them again about the Creed before baptism and demanded a second “I believe” from them, although they had previously answered it in the Catholic Church.

Saint Ambrose, book IV of *On the Sacraments*, chapter 7, to be cited below.

Saint Jerome, *Dialogue Against the Luciferians*:

> Moreover, since it is customary, after the confession of the Trinity, to ask in the bath: “Do you believe in the holy Church? Do you believe in the remission of sins?”

Saint Augustine, book V against the Donatists, chapter 20:

> And everywhere, when a person is baptized, he is also questioned concerning the holy Church.

And *On the Soul and Its Origin*, chapter 10:

> Therefore, when they are baptized, they also give the Creed, and they themselves answer the questions asked on their own behalf.

But if small children who had not yet attained the use of reason were baptized, the sponsors answered when questioned on their behalf. Saint Augustine, letter 23, to Boniface:

> We ask those by whom they are presented, and we say: “Does he believe in God?” Concerning that age which does not know whether God exists, they answer: “He believes.”

Tertullian, *On Baptism*, although he seems to criticize the practice:

> Thus, according to the condition and disposition of each person, and also according to age, delay of baptism is useful, especially in the case of little children. For what necessity is there to expose sponsors also to danger? They themselves may be prevented by death from fulfilling their promises, and they may be deceived by the development of an evil character.

The author of *On the Dogmas of the Church*, among the works of Saint Augustine:

> But if they are infants or dull-witted persons who do not understand instruction, those who present them should answer on their behalf according to the custom of baptism.

### 323. And I baptize you, etc.

So it appears in the printed editions, in the Roman Order, in the Ratold Codex, and in Pamelius. The conjunction *and* is added for emphasis; it is absent from the Rheims Codex, which nevertheless has the following pronoun *I*.

Here, in the printed editions, there is a single immersion. [Note: The same is so in the Gemetic and Theodulfian codices. In the Royal Codex of Sweden no mention is made either of a single or of a triple immersion. The Calais manuscript agrees with the printed editions.] But in our other manuscript codices—the Rheims and Ratold Codices—in the Roman Order, both the printed editions and the manuscript of the Corbie library, and in Pamelius, as also in Alcuin, book *On the Divine Offices*, in the chapter on Holy Saturday; Theodulf of Orléans, chapter 13 of the book *On the Order of Baptism*; and Jesse, bishop of Amiens, in the letter cited above, there is a triple immersion according to the ancient custom of the Church. This custom may be seen in canon 50 of the Apostles and in the ancient Fathers: Saint Dionysius, book *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, chapter 2; Tertullian, *On the Crown of the Soldier*, chapter 3, who counts the rite among the ancient traditions of the Church:

> Then we are immersed three times, answering something more than the Lord prescribed in the Gospel.

Saint Cyril of Jerusalem, *Mystagogical Catechesis* 2:

> And you descended three times into the water, and again you rose up.

Saint Gregory of Nyssa, *Catechetical Oration*, chapter 35:

> The descent into the water, and the fact that a person is placed in it three times, contains a mystery.

Saint Basil, *On the Holy Spirit*, to Amphilochius, chapter 27, who reckons this rite among the apostolic traditions:

> And the threefold baptism of a person—from where does it come?

That is: “And the fact that a person is immersed three times—where does it come from?”

And Saint Leo, letter 4, who, together with Saint Cyril and Saint Gregory of Nyssa cited above, writes that by this three-day immersion and rising from the waters the three-day burial of Christ and his resurrection after three days are signified.

There is also another explanation of this rite, namely the remembrance of the Persons of the Trinity, as Pope Saint Gregory states, letter 41 [Note: It is now letter 43], book I of the *Register*. Hence Eunomius, because he did not believe in the Holy Trinity, is said to have introduced a single immersion.

Others, however, think that the authors of this single immersion were Theophronius of Cappadocia and Eutychius, formerly followers of Eunomius, as may be seen in Sozomen, book VI of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 26.

The First Council of Constantinople, canon 7, orders that Eunomians baptized with a single immersion be baptized again, because they used a false form of baptism, which may be seen in Saint Epiphanius, book III, heresy 56.

Therefore the decree of that council does not concern Catholics who, holding a correct doctrine of the Trinity and using the correct form of baptism, were baptized with a single immersion. Pope Saint Gregory approved this practice among the Catholic Spaniards in the letter cited above to Saint Leander, although Alcuin strongly opposed the single immersion.

For in letter 69, to the people of Lyon, Alcuin condemns the Spaniards because they used only a single immersion in baptism. In the following letter and in letter 81 he likewise attacks this single immersion; and because he sees himself pressed by Saint Gregory’s letter, he calls its authenticity into question. Thus he says in letter 10:

> As for the letter which they say was written by blessed Gregory concerning single immersion, we have not found it in his book of letters that was brought to us from Rome; we have examined all the others in that book which he had written to the churches, bishops, and kings of the western regions. Therefore we are uncertain whether it is his, or whether it was written under his name by some author of this sect.

So he writes, but unjustly. For the style of this letter is the same as that of Saint Gregory’s other letters. And although the copy of Saint Gregory’s letters brought to Alcuin from Rome did not contain this letter, that cannot make us doubt it. John the Deacon, the author of Saint Gregory’s life, who wrote that life at Rome in the time of Charles the Bald and was therefore not very far removed from Alcuin’s age, acknowledges this same letter in chapter 53 of that life as a genuine and authentic work of Saint Gregory. Certainly, when he wrote the life at Rome, he did not have a copy brought from Spain.

The Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 5, also bears witness to this. Saint Isidore, bishop of Seville and brother of Saint Leander, to whom the letter was sent, presided over that council:

> Therefore Gregory of blessed memory, pontiff of the Roman Church, who not only illumined the regions of Italy but also instructed distant churches with his teaching, when the most holy bishop Leander requested guidance concerning this Spanish diversity, among other things wrote as follows: “Concerning the triple immersion of baptism, nothing truer can be answered than what you yourselves understand,” etc.

Moreover, in the triple immersion the formula was pronounced only once, and Alcuin, letter 81, reproves those who repeated it three times. But the Persons were named individually at the individual immersions, as is clear from the codex of Abbot Ratold:

> Then the priest baptizes under a triple immersion, invoking the Holy Trinity only once, and saying: “And I baptize you in the name of the Father”—and he immerses once—“and of the Son”—and he immerses again—“and of the Holy Spirit”—and he immerses a third time.

The same is found in the ancient manuscript Order of the Corbie library. The Roman Order and Alcuin, book *On the Divine Offices*, chapter on Holy Saturday, agree with this.

Nor does the Greek *Euchologion* differ in the rite following holy baptism:

> The servant of God N. is baptized in the name of the Father, amen; and of the Son, amen; and of the Holy Spirit, amen; now and always and unto the ages of ages, amen; at each invocation, lowering and raising him.

That is: “The servant of God N. is baptized in the name of the Father, amen; and of the Son, amen; and of the Holy Spirit, amen; now and always and unto the ages of ages, amen; at each naming—that is, of each Person—lowering and raising him.”

We see this rite clearly enough in Tertullian, *Against Praxeas*:

> And finally he commands them to dip into the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—not into one, for we are dipped not once but three times, once for each name and each Person.

Nevertheless, it was at some time customary among the Greeks to repeat the formula itself three times, as appears in Cedrenus, in his epitome of history under Marcus Antoninus:

> For the third time he poured it over his head, saying for the third time, “Theodore is baptized,” etc.

That is: “Three times he pours it over his head, saying three times, ‘Theodore is baptized,’ etc.”

In Saint Ambrose, book IV of *On the Sacraments*, chapter 17, questions are inserted between these immersions in the following manner:

> You were asked: “Do you believe in God the Father almighty?” You said, “I believe,” and you were immersed. You were asked: “Do you believe in our Lord Jesus Christ and in his cross?” You said, “I believe,” and you were immersed, etc. A third time you were asked: “Do you also believe in the Holy Spirit?” You said, “I believe,” and a third time you were immersed.

So he writes. Although he makes no mention of the formula, he sufficiently indicates it in book III of *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 18:

> How, then, does he not possess all that belongs to God, who is named by priests in baptism together with the Father and the Son?

Whether the words “I baptize you” belong to the necessity of the form of this sacrament, or whether the invocation alone of the most holy Persons of the Trinity is sufficient for the validity of the sacrament—by saying only, “In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit”—is discussed by Stephen of Tournai in letter 5.

A certain man of the diocese of Clermont, lacking a priest, had baptized (*undejassed*, as he himself calls it) his son and, immersing him while omitting the words “I baptize you,” had said only, “In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” Bishop Peter of Clermont, learning of this, consulted the venerable Maurice, bishop of Paris. When Maurice replied that such a baptism was invalid, Peter, not content with this answer, wrote to Stephen, bishop of Tournai. Stephen replied that such a form was sufficient, that the words “I baptize you” did not belong to the essence of the baptismal form, and therefore that the baptism was valid; and he strives with all his strength to prove this. Nevertheless, this opinion conflicts with the teaching of the theological schools.

The Greeks prefix these words to the naming of the three Persons of the most holy Trinity:

> The servant of God is baptized.

That is: “The servant of God is baptized,” followed by the name of the person being baptized. This is clear from their *Euchologion*, cited above. The form is indicative, as is also evident from Severus, in John Moschus, chapter 176 of the *Spiritual Meadow*:

> Theodore is baptized in the name of the Father.

That is: “Theodore is baptized in the name of the Father,” etc.

Theodore the Lector, *Eclogue* 2:

> Barbas is baptized in the name of the Father, etc.

That is: “Barbas is baptized in the name of the Father,” etc.

Cedrenus, in the passage cited above:

> Theodore is baptized, etc.

And under the emperor Anastasius:

> Barbarus is baptized.

Read *Barbas*.

[Note: Perhaps *Everate* should be read, the surname by which John Moschus was known among the Greeks.]

From these passages observe the agreement of the ancient and modern Greeks concerning this indicative form of baptism. I am therefore astonished that certain scholastics have written that the Greeks customarily say, “Let him be baptized.”

Observe further from the passages cited that the ancient Greeks did not include the words *the servant of God* in the baptismal form; these were added by later writers.

It is also worth noting Cedrenus’s error when he assigns the story of Theodore the Jew, who was first baptized in sand and afterward in water, to the time of the emperor Marcus Antoninus, although it happened many years later. John Moschus, who recounts the same story in the chapter cited, lived around the year 600 and writes that a certain Father Andrew was present at this baptism and later conversed with him.

Finally, it should be observed that the Greeks answer “Amen” at the naming of each Person of the most holy Trinity. This follows an ancient custom, which may be seen in John Moschus, in the chapter cited:

> We answered “Amen” at each name of the holy, consubstantial, and worshiped Trinity.

The same is found in the treatise of Severus, Patriarch of Alexandria.

### 324. Let him make the sign of the cross with chrism, using his thumb, on the crown of the head.

So it appears in the Rheims, Rodradi, and Ratold Codices, and in Pamelius. It was an ancient custom for those baptized to be immediately anointed with chrism on the crown of the head. Jesse, bishop of Amiens, testifies to this in his letter to priests *On Baptism*:

> After the person has been baptized, the presbyter makes the sign of the cross with chrism on his crown;

and below:

> Then his head is thoroughly anointed with chrism.

Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, manuscript book *On the Order of Baptism*, chapter 15:

> Therefore the heads of those baptized are anointed with chrism; and [read “so that”] anointed in the Church’s kingdom and priesthood, they may receive the privilege of the Christian name and become members of the one who redeemed them and is their head.

This is also clear from Fortunatus, book V, poem 4, where he speaks of Jews baptized by Saint Avitus, bishop of Clermont:

> Surpassing Ambrosian scents with sweet breath,  
> a scent exhales from the crown drenched with chrism.

Saint Ambrose, book III of *On the Sacraments*, chapter 1:

> You receive the mystery—that is, the ointment upon your head—because, as Solomon says, “The sense of the wise is in his head.”

Saint Isidore discusses this matter in book II of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapters 25 and 26; Saint Innocent in his letter to Bishop Decentius; and several others.

### 325. God the almighty Father, etc.

The same formula, at least in substance, occurs in the anointing in Saint Ambrose, book II of *On the Sacraments*, chapter 7:

> Therefore you were immersed; you came to the priest. What did he say to you? “God,” he said, “the almighty Father, who regenerated you from water and the Holy Spirit and granted you the remission of your sins—may he himself anoint you unto eternal life.”

### 326. With linen cloths in his hands.

They were used to wrap the baptized as soon as they had lifted their feet from the font, according to an ancient custom. For, rising naked from the bath, they were wrapped by the sponsor in a linen cloth, as is clear from Victor of Utica, book III of the *History of the Vandal Persecution*:

> When, with Elpidophorus seated and raging, the venerable old man had begun to be stretched out, before he was stripped, secretly and by stealth, unknown to all, he carried the sheets with which the one receiving him had formerly covered him from the font. When these had been shaken out and spread before everyone, he is said to have moved the whole city to weeping and tears with these words: “These are the linen cloths, Elpidophorus, ministers of error, which will accuse you when Majesty comes, while my vigilance guards them, as testimony to your destruction, to plunge you into the abyss of the pit. These wrapped you, spotless, as you rose from the font.”

And in Pope Paul’s letter 6 to King Pepin:

> namely, the sheet in which our sweetest and most beloved spiritual daughter, after being washed in the most sacred bath, was received.

A *sabanum* is a linen cloth. The old manuscript glosses of the Corbie library read:

> *Sabanum*: cheap linen [text incomplete].

On this word, consult our observations on the *Harmony of the Rules*, chapter 41, § 11.

### 327. So that, when they have been clothed.

That is, in white garments. For after they had been brought out of the baptismal font, they were clothed in white garments as a sign of the whiteness and purity of the mind. This is discussed by Dionysius the Great, chapter 2 of the *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*; Saint Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechesis* 4; Saint Ambrose, *On Those Who Are Initiated into the Mysteries*, chapter 7; and Saint Paulinus, letter 12, to Severus:

> Then the priest, their father, leads from the sacred font  
> infants white in body, heart, and clothing.

Fortunatus, book III, poem 7, concerning the Saxons baptized by Bishop Felix:

> A white garment also marks their shining souls,  
> and the shepherd rejoices in the flock of snow.

And book V, poem 4, concerning Jews baptized by Avitus, bishop of Clermont:

> From this comes the milky color of the garment; from this the radiance  
> is drawn, and the day is adorned with varied light.

John Moschus, chapter 207:

> When the neighbors saw her dressed in white, they said to her: “Who baptized you?”

That is: “When her neighbors saw her wearing white, they said to her, ‘Who baptized you?’”

Saint Gregory of Tours, book II of his *History*, chapter 29:

> He died in the very white garments in which he had been regenerated.

Jobius, book III of *On the Incarnate Word*, chapter 18 (in the library of Photius, no. 222):

> Therefore those who are illumined wear shining garments for seven days.

And below, in the same chapter:

> The wearing of shining garments by those who are baptized is a sign of the splendor of the angels, representing the purity of mind and separation from matter and passions that exist in them.

Theodulf, manuscript book *On the Order of Baptism*, chapter 14:

> We too are clothed in white garments after baptism, so that in our conduct we may preserve the purity that we received in regeneration, maintaining both our renewal and the beauty of angelic splendor.

Jesse, bishop of Amiens, in the letter cited:

> Then he is clothed in white garments because of the joy of regeneration, purity of life, and the beauty of angelic splendor.

Note the reasons given by the authors cited. The same may be seen in Socrates, book VII of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 17, where the baptism of a certain Jew is discussed:

> And having bought him a bright garment.

That is: “And having bought him a white garment.”

And in the *Alexandrian Chronicle*, concerning Saint Gelasinus the martyr, who was baptized amid laughter in the theater and converted to Christ:

> Having been baptized, and coming up from the basin wearing white garments, he refused thereafter to perform as a mime, saying: “I am a Christian.”

328. They are also forbidden to nurse before holy communion. So it is printed in the editions. The Rhemish Codex gives a different instruction: “Taking care, however, that after they have been baptized they are not weaned before they communicate.” Likewise in the Codex of Ratold: “It must be provided, however, for the baptized that no one take food, nor be weaned, and then communicate, except after the masses.” I do not think, however, that children and infants communicated while fasting, since the office of Great Saturday in these sacramental books begins only at the eighth hour, that is, at two in the afternoon; but it was observed in some places that, after receiving baptism, they took no food or milk before receiving the Eucharist, out of reverence. Formerly, however, the sacrament of the Eucharist was received together with baptism, as is clear from Saint Ambrose, *On Those Initiated into the Mysteries*, chapter 8; from Saint Justin Martyr, *Apology 2 for the Christians*, where he writes that on Sundays, after the baptism had been celebrated, the divine mysteries of the body and blood were performed and those present communicated; and from Origen, *Homily 4 on Joshua*, chapter XLIII:

“If, then, you come to the mystical font of baptism and, with the priestly and Levitical order present, have been initiated into those venerable and magnificent sacraments which are known to those for whom it is permitted to know them, then also, when the Jordan has receded, you will enter the land of promise through the ministry of the priests.”

Nor did only adults receive the sacrament of the Eucharist; infants themselves also received it together with baptism. This is attested by the codices of Saint Eligius, Ratold, and Rheims; and by Saint Dionysius, *On the Celestial Hierarchy*, chapter 7:

“And the hierarch makes the child a participant in the sacred symbols,” etc.

That is: “Moreover, the pontiff makes the child a participant in the sacred mysteries, so that he may be brought up in them and may lead no life other than one that always looks toward divine things.” He is speaking there of a child who lacks the use of reason, for shortly beforehand he discusses the child’s sponsor, who must guarantee on his behalf and respond to each renunciation and interrogation. Saint Paulinus, *Letter 12 to Severus*:

> From there the priest leads infants from the sacred font,
>
> White in body, heart, and clothing.
>
> Surrounding the unformed lambs at the sacred altars,
>
> He moistens their dear mouths with life-giving food.

Saint Augustine, *Letter 102 to Vitalis the Pelagian*:

“Therefore they too, as I said, if they die at that early age, certainly do so according to what they accomplished through the body—that is, during the time when they were in the body—when they believed or did not believe through the hearts and mouths of those carrying them; when they were baptized or were not baptized; when they ate the flesh of Christ or did not eat it; when they drank the blood or did not drink it.”

The author of the book *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, among the works of Saint Augustine, chapter 52:

“But if they are little children or dull-witted persons who cannot grasp instruction, let those who present them answer on their behalf according to the custom of baptism; and thus, strengthened by the laying on of hands and chrism, let them be admitted to the mysteries of the Eucharist.”

Jesse of Amiens, in the letter cited so often:

“Finally, the infant is confirmed with the body and blood of Christ, so that he may be a member of him who suffered and rose again for him, as the Lord himself testifies when he says: ‘Whoever eats my flesh remains in me.’”

329. But the adults place one foot on the foot of their godparent. Some ancient images of this rite are still to be seen.

330. *Their godparent.* Godparents are those who present the persons to be baptized and, once they have been baptized, receive them from the sacred font; in French, *parrains*. The Sixth Council of Arles, canon 9: “And the godparents who receive them from the font of the bath,” etc. The chapter of Herard, archbishop of Tours, chapter 27: “That fathers and godfathers may teach and nourish their sons and godchildren.” They are also called sponsors. Jesse, bishop of Amiens, in the letter cited: “And let the sponsors, men or women—that is, godfathers or godmothers—sign those infants on their foreheads.” They are also called guarantors. Tertullian, *On Baptism*: “For what need is there to involve sponsors in danger as well?” Saint Dionysius, *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, chapters 2 and 7, calls them *anadochoi* (ἀνάδοχοι), that is, receivers or sponsors.

331. *With his hand raised over the heads of all.* So it is printed in the editions. In the Roman Order: “With his hand raised and laid upon the heads of all.” In the Tilius Codex: “With his hand raised and composed over the heads of all.” Alcuin, in the chapter *On Holy Saturday*: “The pontiff gives a prayer over them, namely, with his hand laid upon their heads,” etc. In the Roman Pontifical: “Then, extending his hands toward those to be confirmed, he says.” These words were omitted in the *Ceremonial of Bishops* by its author Andrea Piscara Castaldo, book II, section 15. For he says:

“Then, having laid aside his mitre, he rises and, turning toward those to be confirmed, with his hands joined before his breast, says: ‘The grace of the Holy Spirit,’ etc.” Then, signing himself from forehead to breast, he says the verse “Our help,” and afterward adds the verses and the prayer: “Almighty,” etc.

I marvel at this, since through this laying on or extension of hands, accompanied by the pontiff’s prayer, the Holy Spirit is invoked and invited, as will be clear from the authorities to be cited: Tertullian, *On Baptism*: “Afterward the hand is laid on, invoking and inviting the Holy Spirit through the blessing”; and *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*: “The flesh is overshadowed by the laying on of hands, so that the soul also may be illumined by the Spirit”; Saint Cyprian, *Letter 72*: “Since it is little for them to lay hands upon them so that they may receive the Holy Spirit, unless they also receive the baptism of the Church”; and *Letter 73 to Jubaianus*:

“What is now also done among us is that those who are baptized in the Church are presented to the leaders of the Church, and through our prayer and the laying on of hands receive the Holy Spirit and are marked with the Lord’s sign.”

Saint Augustine, *On the Trinity*, book XV, chapter 26:

“Nor did any of his disciples give the Holy Spirit. For they prayed that he might come upon those on whom they laid hands; they themselves did not give him. This custom the Church still maintains in its leaders.”

These words certainly deserve notice and wonderfully illuminate this passage of the ancient Sacramentaries, the Roman Order, and the Roman Pontifical, in which we clearly see that the pontiff lays on hands and invokes the Holy Spirit by saying the following prayer: “Almighty and eternal God,” etc. Hence Saint Isidore states excellently, *On the Divine Offices*, book II, chapter 26:

“We can receive the Holy Spirit, but we cannot give him; rather, we invoke God so that he may be given.”

This is evident from Acts, chapter VIII:

“When they had come, they prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Spirit; for he had not yet come upon any of them, but they had only been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. Then they laid hands on them, and they received the Holy Spirit.”

Theodulf, however, and many others say that the Holy Spirit is given by the pontiff, but he does so not as the principal cause, but as the instrumental cause.

332. *Almighty and eternal God,* etc. This is found in the Roman Order and Pontifical, in which “Amen” is inserted after each enumeration of the gifts of the Holy Spirit. In the Codex of Rodrade this title is prefixed: “Prayer for marking infants.” In Amalarius Fortunatus, *On the Offices of the Church*, book I, chapter 27, this prayer begins only with the word “Send forth.” Saint Ambrose seems to allude to it, *On the Sacraments*, book II, chapter 3, when he says:

“Then follows the spiritual seal, which you heard read today. For after the font, perfection remains to be accomplished, when, at the priest’s invocation, the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and strength, the Spirit of knowledge and piety, and the Spirit of holy fear are poured in.”

333. *The pontiff, dipping his thumb in chrism,* etc. So it appears in Alcuin, in the chapter *On Holy Saturday*, and in the printed Sacramentaries. The anointing with chrism is mentioned by Saint Dionysius, *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, chapters 2 and 4; Saint Cyril of Jerusalem, *Mystagogical Catechesis* 3; an anonymous author, in a sermon *On Chrism* among the works of Saint Cyprian; Tertullian, *On Baptism* and *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*; Saint Augustine, *On the Trinity*, book XV, chapter 26, and in other passages cited below; the Council of Seville, canon 7, to be cited below; the author of the book *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, among the works of Saint Augustine; Pope Innocent, in his letter to Decentius, bishop of Gubbio; Saint Isidore, *On the Divine Offices*, book II, chapter 26; Jesse, bishop of Amiens: “Let the bishop confirm him on the forehead with chrism”; Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, in the work and chapter cited:

“For priests, whether bishops are absent or present, may baptize and anoint the baptized with chrism, provided that it was consecrated by a bishop; yet they may not mark the forehead with that same oil, since this belongs exclusively to bishops when they impart the Holy Spirit”; Saint Pope Gregory, *Register*, book III, chapter 26 [Note: [Col. 0349D] Now book IV, letter 26]; Saint Gregory of Tours, *History*, book II, chapter 3; and many others.

359. You therefore see here two rites of this sacrament: first, the laying on of hands; second, the anointing of the forehead with chrism, which includes marking, since the sign of the cross is impressed by anointing. Alcuin distinguishes these two acts, in the oft-cited chapter *On Holy Saturday* in *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, in conformity with the Roman Order, the Roman Pontifical, and our Sacramentaries:

“And after they have been clothed, the pontiff gives a prayer over them, laying his hand, that is, upon their heads, with an invocation of the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit. Let us pray: ‘Almighty and eternal God, who regenerates …’ When this is finished, he makes a cross with chrism using his thumb on their foreheads, saying …”

William of Paris, *On the Sacraments*:

“For after the prayer over those to be confirmed, the sign of the cross is painted with chrism on their foreheads; and, with hands laid upon their heads, it is said to them: ‘Peace be with you.’ For formerly the Holy Spirit was given at the apostles’ laying on of hands, and now he is given at the laying on of bishops’ hands.”

The Second Council of Seville, canon 7:

“Nor is it permitted to them”—that is, priests—“to impart the Paraclete Spirit to baptized believers or converts from heresy through the laying on of hands, nor to prepare chrism, nor to mark the foreheads of the baptized.”

Saint Cyprian, *Letter 73 to Jubaianus*:

“What is now also done among us is that those who are baptized in the Church are presented to the leaders of the Church, and through our prayer and the laying on of hands receive the Holy Spirit and are marked with the Lord’s sign.”

Tertullian, *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*:

“Certainly the flesh is washed so that the soul may be cleansed; the flesh is anointed so that the soul may be consecrated; the flesh is marked so that the soul may be fortified; the flesh is overshadowed by the laying on of hands so that the soul also may be illumined by the Spirit.”

Here he attributes different effects to the anointing and to the laying on of hands. From that text it should also be observed that the laying on of hands was sometimes placed after the anointing, as also seems to be the case in the passage cited above from William of Paris.

This anointing with chrism existed in the time of the apostles, as did the laying on of hands, although James of Vitry, *History of the West*, chapter 37, asserted the contrary:

“This sacrament was instituted partly by the apostles, insofar as the laying on of hands is concerned, and partly by the Church, insofar as the anointing with chrism is concerned, which we do not read that the apostles performed.”

The contrary, however, appears from Saint Pacian, a very ancient writer. For in his first letter he writes that the authority to bind and loose came down from the apostles, just as did the authority of baptism and chrism:

“Therefore”—he says—“we have built upon this what the apostles’ teaching founded. Finally, bishops are also called apostles, as Paul describes Epaphroditus: ‘My brother and fellow soldier, but your apostle.’ If, then, the power of the font and of chrism, together with the greater and more distant charisms, descended from there to the bishops, so too did the power of binding and of loosing. And shortly afterward: ‘Therefore neither chrism, nor baptism, nor the remission of sins, nor the renewal of the body was entrusted to his holy authority, because nothing was commanded by his own usurpation, and everything flowed down from apostolic right.’”

Indeed, it is shown that this practice existed in the time of the apostles, as is known from the history which Eusebius reports from Clement of Alexandria, *Ecclesiastical History*, book III, chapter 17. There, concerning a bishop who had baptized a young man commended to him by the holy apostle John, he writes:

“Having set upon him the Lord’s seal as a perfect safeguard.”

That cannot be understood otherwise than of chrismation, which, because it is performed in the form of a cross on the forehead itself, as will be said later, is rightly called the Lord’s seal. Likewise, in the extract from the *Life of Saint Athanasius* in Photius’s *Bibliotheca*, no. 258:

“Having anointed them with the seal in Christ, he perfected them.”

The passage concerns those children whom Athanasius, while still a child, baptized, and to whom Saint Alexander the pontiff later imparted the sacrament of confirmation. Hence Christians are also said to be marked in Saint Athanasius, *Letter 1 to Serapion*:

“But if creatures are anointed and marked in him”—that is, in the Holy Spirit.

And in Tertullian, *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*: “The flesh is marked so that the soul may be fortified”; and in *On the Prescription against Heretics*, where he proves that the devil is a parody of the divine mysteries:

“And, if I still remember, Mithras marks his soldiers there on their foreheads.”

This also sufficiently indicates the meaning of *to phylaktērion* (τὸ φυλακτήριον), that is, “safeguard.” For that marking is the strength and protection of the soul; hence Tertullian rightly added: “so that the soul may be fortified.” Clement also rightly added the epithet *teleion* (τέλειον), that is, “perfect,” because the function of this anointing and marking is to perfect and complete the baptized. Accordingly, Saint Dionysius calls it *teleiōtikē chrisis* (τελειωτικὴ χρῖσις), *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, chapter 4—that is, “a consummating and perfecting anointing.” And in the cited extract from the *Life of Saint Athanasius* it is said:

“By the seal in Christ he perfected them.”

The authority of Saint Augustine may also be added. He calls this rite of chrismation or marking a sacrament; therefore it came from the apostles, since it was instituted by Christ. For he teaches us as follows, *Against the Letters of Petilian*, book II, chapter 104:

“And in this anointing you wish the sacrament of chrism to be understood, which, among visible seals, is itself sacred, just as baptism is.”

And in his exposition of Psalm CXLI:

“We receive many sacraments in different ways. Some, as you know, we receive with the mouth; some we receive through the whole body; some we receive on the forehead through the sign of the cross.”

234. *He makes a cross on the forehead.* The anointing with chrism is performed on the forehead in the form of a cross, according to an ancient custom of the Church. Saint Augustine, in his exposition of Psalm CXLI:

“Let him mock the Crucified One there; let me see on the foreheads of kings the cross of the Crucified One.”

And shortly afterward:

“We receive many sacraments in different ways: some, as you know, with the mouth,” etc.

Saint Pope Gregory, *Register*, book III, chapter 26 [Note: [Col. 0351D] Now book IV, letter 26]. Bachiarius, letter to Januarius:

“Let the gate in Anathoth be rebuilt, which is interpreted as ‘responding sign.’ We suspect this to be the gallows of the forehead, where we receive the sign of our salvation and of the Lord’s holiness—the golden plate on which the pontiff is commanded to receive the name of the Lord, the Tetragrammaton. Do you wish to know why we not unfittingly take the gate of Anathoth, interpreted as ‘responding sign,’ for the gallows of the forehead? The prophet joins to this gate the places of the ointment-makers, which, through the figurative meanings of their names, are said to be rebuilt by other virtues. But what are the places of the ointment-makers except those touched by the sanctification of chrism?”

Victor of Vita, *On the Vandal Persecution*, book I:

“And they would show the forehead on which Christ had placed the standard of his cross, while the descending and roaring sinews made it wrinkled.”

Saint Gregory of Tours, *History*, book II, chapter 3:

“Accordingly, the king, confessing the almighty God in the Trinity, was baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, and, having been smeared with sacred chrism, with the sign of Christ’s cross.”

Prudentius, in the *Psychomachia*:

> After the signs on the forehead inscribed with oil,
>
> Through which the royal ointment was given, and everlasting chrism.

And in the hymn of the *Cathemerinon* entitled “For Every Hour”:

> Tell of the trophy of the Passion,
>
> Tell of the triumphant cross,
>
> Sing of the standard
>
> That shines upon marked foreheads.

And in the *Apotheosis*:

> He too, lifeless, his diadem laid aside, the prince
>
> Grows pale and looks around at those standing by: whether some fosterling
>
> Might mark his temples with the sign inscribed by chrism,
>
> Which would have confounded the Zoroastrian whispers on his forehead.

361. He is speaking of Julian the Apostate. While he was engaged in magical rites, the demons were thrown into confusion by the presence of a certain baptized young attendant and, giving no answer, fled. Jesse of Amiens, in the letter cited above:

“After this let the bishop confirm him with chrism on the forehead.”

This is the passage that must be understood in Tertullian, *On the Prescription against Heretics*:

“He himself also baptizes certain persons, clearly his believers and faithful, promises the exposition of sins from the washing; and, if I still remember, Mithras marks his soldiers there on their foreheads.”

This, then, is the rite of the Latins.

Formerly, however, the Greeks anointed not only the forehead but also the ears, nostrils, and breast, as Saint Cyril of Jerusalem teaches, *Mystagogical Catechesis* 3:

“And first you were anointed on the forehead, so that the shame which the first transgressor, man, carried everywhere might be removed from you, and also so that, with the veil removed from your forehead, you might be able to behold the glory of the Lord,” etc.

“Then the ears are anointed, so that you may have ears for receiving the divine mysteries, concerning which Isaiah said: ‘And the Lord added to me for hearing’; and the Lord in the Gospel: ‘Let him who has ears to hear, hear’ (Matthew IX, 1). Afterward the nostrils are anointed, so that, receiving the divine ointment, you may say: ‘We are the good odor of Christ among those who are being saved’ (2 Corinthians II). Then the breast is anointed, so that, clothed in the breastplate of righteousness, you may stand firm against the assaults of the devil.”

In the book of Severus, patriarch of Alexandria, on baptism, all their limbs are marked and anointed with chrism, while the forehead is anointed three times. Among the Ethiopians, nearly all their limbs are anointed: the forehead, eyes, nostrils, and lips; the ears, back, and breastbone, or pit of the stomach; the shins and forearms; the knees and all the joints; the soles of the feet and the spine, as is clear from the *Order of the Mysteries*, as it is called. Today among the Greeks the forehead, eyes, nostrils, mouth, ears, breast, hands, and feet are anointed, as may be seen in their *Euchologion*. So much concerning the anointing or marking.

Finally, it should be noted that in our Codex of Saint Eligius there are no words or formula to be spoken during the anointing, just as [Note: In the Vatican and Gussanville editions, in agreement with the manuscripts and Theodulf, the text reads: “But when he has risen from the font, the one who receives him is to present him to a priest, who is to make the sign of the cross with chrism, using his thumb, on his crown, saying: ‘Almighty God, Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who regenerated you from water and the Holy Spirit and gave you remission of all sins, may he himself anoint you with the chrism of salvation unto eternal life.’ Response: ‘Amen.’”] neither in the printed editions nor in the ancient manuscript Pontifical preserved in the church of Rouen, which is thought to be English. Formerly, however, we see that an invocation of the most holy Trinity was used in Alcuin, *On the Divine Offices*, in the chapter *On Holy Saturday*. This follows the practice of the Roman Church:
