“On this matter the Apostolic See at Rome prescribes as follows: After the pontiff has baptized, or those whom he himself has directed have baptized, they lift the infants in their hands,” etc. Further on:

“And after they have been clothed, the pontiff gives a prayer over them, laying his hand, that is, upon their heads, with an invocation of the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit. Let us pray: ‘Almighty and eternal God, who regenerates …’ When this is finished, he makes a cross with chrism using his thumb on the forehead of each, saying: ‘In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Peace be with you.’ They all respond: ‘And with your spirit.’”

Amalarius, *On the Ecclesiastical Offices*, book I, chapter 2, has the same:

“The Roman booklet, of which we have often spoken, says: When the prayer has been completed, he makes a cross with his thumb from the chrism on the foreheads of each, saying: ‘In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Peace be with you, and with your spirit.’”

In the Roman Order these words are prefixed: “I confirm you.” When the prayer has been completed and the deacons have asked the names of each person, the pontiff, dipping his thumb in chrism, makes a cross on the forehead of each, saying:

“I confirm you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.”  
**Response:** “Amen.”  
“Peace be with you.”  
**Response:** “And with your spirit.”

In the manuscript Orders of Tilius and of Saint-Germain-des-Prés it is written as follows:

“I confirm you and mark you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen. Peace be with you, and with your spirit.”

362. In William of Paris, *On the Sacraments*, this formula is found:

“I mark you, and I confirm you with the cross.”

“For since”—he says—“the pontiff, while painting the character, says, ‘I mark you and confirm you with the cross,’ the marking is to be understood.”

In Albert the Great, in a manuscript of the library of Saint-Victor in the Paris suburbs, *Sentences* IV, page 234, this form of confirmation appears:

“I confirm you with the sign of the cross and with the chrism of salvation, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.”

In another manuscript Pontifical preserved in the church of Rouen, the following is found:

“Then let him make a cross on their forehead with chrism”—read: “with *chrismate*”—saying: “I mark you with the sign of the cross and confirm you with the chrism of salvation, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen. Peace be with you [plural], or peace be with you [singular]. And with your spirit.”

Finally, in the Roman Pontifical it is written:

“I mark you with the sign of the cross and confirm you with the chrism of salvation, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, so that you may be filled with the Holy Spirit and have eternal life.”  
**Response:** “Amen.”

The Greeks, after first reciting this prayer, as it appears in their *Euchologion*,

“Master, King of all, compassionate, grant him also the seal,” etc.,

that is:

“You, Lord, King of all and merciful, grant him also the seal of the gift of your holy, all-powerful, and adorable Spirit.”

During the anointing they say:

“Seal of the gift of the Holy Spirit.”

This formula appears in canon 7 of the First Council of Constantinople, in which the council decreed that Novatians, Macedonians, Apollinarians, and certain other heretics who, after renouncing their heresy, were reconciled to the Catholic Church should be anointed on the forehead, eyes, nostrils, mouth, and ears with chrism, while saying:

“Seal of the gift of the Holy Spirit.”

In Severus, patriarch of Alexandria, *On the Rites of Baptism*, this formula may be found:

“Such a one, N., is sealed with the holy chrism of the sweet fragrance of Christ God, with the seal of the true faith, and with the completion of the pledge of the Holy Spirit, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, unto the life of the ages of ages. Amen.”

Thus far concerning the sacraments of baptism and confirmation. But since we have omitted many things that appear to pertain to the rites of baptism, it will not be out of place to append to what we have written the little book of Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, on the order of baptism. We obtained the manuscript from the library of Corbie; in it everything pertaining to the sacrament of baptism is expounded with considerable clarity, together with its mystical interpretation. To aid that explanation, we shall also append some notes.

## Theodulf’s Little Book on the Order of Baptism

“To the most reverend and dearly beloved brother John, bishop, Theodulf sends greetings.

“Your command, venerable man John, I have carried out, though not with energetic effectiveness, at least with complete obedience. For you commanded me—or rather, through you charity commanded me—to answer briefly and quickly certain questions concerning the order of baptism that had been sent to you by the lord and glorious emperor Charles. I was therefore constrained on one side by brevity, which forced me to dispatch great matters in a short discourse, and on the other by the pressure of time, since I wished to fulfill quickly what you had commanded.

“Would that this work had been completed as effectively as it was willingly undertaken! Although, then, because various occupations obstructed me, I had no opportunity to treat the subject at length or to review the volumes of the Fathers, and although charity moved me to fulfill the command, I wrote rapidly concerning each point that occurred to me and sent it to your Fraternity, so that, even if the answers should bring no benefit, obedience might at least bear fruit.

“These questions, meanwhile, as I am certain that you know, were not posed by the royal majesty out of a need to learn, but from a desire to teach; nor were they posed so that he himself, once these matters had been settled, might be instructed in things he did not know, 363 but so that others, sluggish with the sleep of bodily indolence, might be roused to the useful completion of their duties. For it has always been familiar to him to exercise bishops in the investigation of the holy Scriptures and in sound and sober doctrine; all the clergy in discipline; philosophers in knowledge of divine and human things; monks in religion; everyone generally in holiness; primates in counsel; judges in justice; soldiers in military experience; prelates in humility; subjects in obedience; and everyone generally in prudence, justice, courage, temperance, and concord.

“By such and similar works that excellent man never ceases, with God propitious to him, to increase the eminence of the holy Church; vigorous and admirable in the administration of ecclesiastical and civil affairs, he overflows with the fountain of wisdom and triumphs through the display of virtue”—read: “of virtues.”

### The Chapters Begin

“I. Why an infant is made a catechumen. II. What a catechumen is. III. Why he is exsufflated. IV. Why he is exorcized. V. Why a catechumen receives salt. VI. What the interpretation of the Symbol is according to the Latins. VII. On belief: how one should believe in God the Father almighty, and in Jesus Christ his Son, born and having suffered, and in the Holy Spirit, the holy Catholic Church, and the other things that follow in that Symbol. VIII. On the scrutiny. IX. Why the nostrils and ears are touched with spittle. X. Why the breast is anointed with oil, or the shoulders are marked or smeared. XI. What renunciation is. XII. On the renunciation of Satan and all his works and pomps—or, what the works of the devil and his pomps are. XIII. On the sacrament of baptism. XIV. Why he is clothed in white garments. XV. Why the head is anointed with sacred chrism. XVI. Why he is covered with a mystical veil. XVII. Why he is confirmed by the bishop and receives the Spirit of the sevenfold grace through the laying on of hands. XVIII. Why he is confirmed with the Lord’s body and blood.

“I. The ancient custom is maintained. For whenever believers came to the apostles to be baptized, they were instructed and taught by them; and, once instructed and taught concerning the sacrament of baptism and the other rules of faith, they received the most holy mystery of baptism. Hence the Apostle says: ‘Do you not know, brothers, that all who have been baptized in Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death?’ In these words it is shown that those who were baptized were not ignorant of the mysteries of the sacrament of baptism.

“But the Lord did not simply say, ‘Go, baptize,’ but ‘Go and teach all nations, baptizing them,’ so that we may understand that we must first instruct and teach the one who is to be baptized, and afterward baptize him. Infants, therefore, are made hearers and catechumens—not because at that age they can both be instructed and taught, but so that the ancient custom may be maintained, according to which the apostles first taught and instructed those whom they were going to baptize, as has already been said.

“II. A catechumen, however, is interpreted as ‘a hearer’ or ‘one who has been instructed.’ For the human race hears and is instructed before it comes to baptism; and what it once heard through Moses—‘Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one’—it was instructed through the Law and the Prophets in the worship of the one true God. Now, through the ministry of priests, let him become a hearer”—read: “let him become a hearer”—“and be instructed”—read: “so that he may be instructed”—“so that, having abandoned the rite by which he served the creature, he may serve God the Creator alone.

“Thus catechumens believe in Christ while still bearing their sins. I think this is what is said in the Gospel: although they believed in Jesus, Jesus himself did not entrust himself to them. Therefore, all who were taught or instructed by John, since his baptism could not erase sins, must be understood to have prefigured the catechumens [Latin *typhum*, read *typum*].”

“III. On their faces also the priest makes the sign of the cross by exsufflation, so that the devil may be driven away and a way may be prepared for Christ. The devil, who by his alluring persuasion had inhabited the human race, which at its beginning had received the breath of life, is compelled by Christ’s power and by the most sacred sign, through the ministry of priests, to depart. Christ too is read to have breathed upon his disciples and rebuked unclean spirits.

“IV. Hence that same evil spirit is also exorcized, so that he may depart and withdraw from that created form”—read: “that creature”—“which he had long possessed through the sin of the first man. And because, according to the Apostle, there is no agreement between Christ and Belial, nor any fellowship between light and darkness, the darkness went out and the true light, Christ, entered.

“He is also read to have worn filthy garments figuratively in Zechariah because of our sins, which he bore in his body; and, rebuking Satan [read: *Satanam*], he chose holy Jerusalem, namely the Church, which is the vision of peace and which he daily makes fruitful with new offspring. To her it is said through the prophet: ‘Your sons will come from afar, and your daughters will rise at your side.’

“Moreover, an exorcism is a word of rebuke. Hence exorcists are read to have existed in the Acts of the Apostles, and the holy Church includes the ministry of exorcists among the ecclesiastical orders. For it must be understood that when an exorcism is performed, the one unquestionably exorcized is he who is opposed to baptism, to the salvation of the faithful, and to all their virtues. Once he has been exorcized or expelled, the seasoning of the divine word is given to believers.

“V. Therefore those who are to be baptized receive salt in the sacrament, so that by its taste they may perceive the seasoning of wisdom, may not become foolish concerning the flavor of Christ, and may not be tasteless and foolish. For he who said to his disciples, ‘You are the salt of the earth,’ also said: ‘No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of heaven.’

“But so that those who are baptized may be fit for the kingdom of heaven, and so that they may not repeat their former sins and look back, becoming a pillar of salt and, remaining senseless, seasoning others by the example of their punishment, they ought to receive the salt of wisdom. Thus whatever is unstable and fluid in them may be healed by the salt of God’s word, and, according to the Apostle, they may remember Lot’s wife.

“And just as Elisha cured the barrenness of the water by casting in salt, so the true Elisha, our Lord Jesus Christ, by the flavor of his word brings the fluid barrenness of the human race to the sweet flavor of faith and good works. The firmness of this faith now shines clearly when the one who had heard that the worship of God alone must be maintained—and hence was called a hearer—had begun to be instructed in the worship of true religion—and hence was called a catechumen—and, through exsufflation and exorcism, had been delivered from the evil spirit, and, in the giving of salt, had begun already to possess a taste for the divine word.

“Let the Symbol be handed over to him—that is, the complete and unshaken confession of the true faith—so that the house, abandoned by its former inhabitant, may be adorned with faith; and so that, once the thorns of unbelief have been uprooted from it, the teachings of true faith may begin to be planted there. For first the thorns of the vices of unbelief must be uprooted, and afterward the beginnings of faith and good works must be planted.

“Hence the Lord crushed before the children of Israel the seven nations that bore the type [Latin *typhum*, read *typum*] of vices, and in their place established the Israelite people as a type [Latin *typho*, read *typo*] of virtues.”

“And he says to the prophet Jeremiah: ‘Behold, I have appointed you this day over nations and over kingdoms, to uproot and to tear down, to destroy and to demolish, to build and to plant.’ First he mentioned uprooting, tearing down, destruction, and demolition; afterward he added building and planting. And through the same prophet he says: ‘As I watched over them to uproot, demolish, destroy, and scatter, so I will watch over them to build and plant.’

“This is because after exorcism and exsufflation comes the handing over of the Symbol.”

[Note: On the misuse of the word *typos* in place of *typhos*, and vice versa, see what we said in book XXIII of the *Moralia*, no. 25.]

## VI. That “Symbol” Is Interpreted in Latin as “Indication,” “Sign,” or “Collection”

“Indication,” because by it the integrity of the faith is indicated; “sign,” because by retaining and understanding it rightly, the faithful are distinguished from the unfaithful; “collection,” because in it the apostles brought together the whole integrity of the faith. What they all retained in their hearts with equal sincerity of faith, they confessed with their mouths; and each, contributing his own statement, issued the Symbol—that is, the collection of the whole faith.

For, as they were about to depart from one another, they established together the rule of their future preaching 365 [Col. 0356A], lest, departing from one another into different regions, they should preach anything diverse or discordant. It was most fitting and useful that those who had one soul and one heart in the Lord, and whom the breath of the Holy Spirit enlivened, should also be adorned by one confession of faith. For those bound together by the bond of one faith could neither be, nor ought to be, divided in anything.

Meanwhile, most people [corrected from *plerumque*] wish the “abbreviated word” prophesied through Isaiah to be understood in the Symbol and in the Lord’s Prayer. In the one, the integrity of the faith is contained; in the other, the integrity of prayers—so that in the twelve words the teaching of the twelve apostles may be contained, and in the seven petitions everything belonging to the dispensation of the present and future life.

Although the word of the whole teaching may also be called “abbreviated,” because what the Law and the Prophets formerly contained in the breadth of their commandments, the Lord, coming, expressed in summary and said: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength, and your neighbor as yourself.” The whole Law and the Prophets depend upon these two commandments. In [Col. 0356B] these two utterances he clearly abbreviated the Prophets and the Law.

This has been said about the Symbol and its name.

## VII

The faith contained in this Symbol must be understood by those who are to be baptized in such a way that they believe in God the Father almighty, creator of all things visible and invisible. He alone is called “unbegotten,” because he is not from another.

They must believe also in Jesus Christ, his Son, through whom all things were made: true God, the Only-Begotten, and true Son of God—not made or adopted, but begotten, of one substance with the Father, and in every respect equal to God the Father, so that he cannot be inferior in time, rank, or power, and so that the one who is begotten is as great as the one who begot him.

They must also believe that he was born of the Holy Spirit and Mary ever-virgin—that is, that, with the Holy Spirit cooperating, the Son of God assumed a true body from the Virgin, [Col. 0356C] so that he who was the Son of God the Father in divinity became the son of a human mother in humanity.

They must also believe that, at the end of time, he descended from the Father for the redemption of the world, although he never ceased to be with the Father; and that he became truly human, so that a human being might free the human race; and that he who from the beginning possessed eternity with the Father and the Holy Spirit assumed, at the end of the ages, a complete human being of our nature, and that the Word became flesh by assuming humanity, not by changing his divinity.

They must also believe that he endured suffering and death—not in the power of his divinity, but in the weakness of his humanity; that he died by a true death of the flesh; that he rose by a true resurrection of the flesh; and that by his resurrection he bestowed upon us the hope of resurrection—namely, that just as he rose alive from the dead on the third day, so we too shall rise at the end of the ages in the same flesh in which we now live.

They must also believe that, in the same body which he assumed from the Virgin, in which he suffered and rose again, he ascended into heaven; that he is now in that same body; that he will come in it for [Col. 0356D] judgment; and that, after all have been raised, he will assign to some, because of their sins, the sentence of eternal punishment, and to others, because of the merits of their righteousness, the reward of eternal blessedness.

They must also believe in the Holy Spirit, true God, proceeding from the Father and the Son, equal in every respect to the Father and the Son in will, power, eternity, and substance; and that in this holy Trinity there are no ranks by which anyone may be called inferior or superior.

They must also believe in the holy catholic—that is, universal—Church; not “in the holy Church,” as they believe in the Trinity. They must believe that the holy Church is the house of that same holy Trinity. Those who depart from its communion are called schismatics and heretics and are placed in eternal condemnation. Those who remain in its communion are both members of Christ and receive the remission of sins, and thus belong to [Col. 0357A] eternal life [*et* corrected from *ut*].

Since, therefore, little children who do not yet possess the use of reason cannot grasp these things at all, they must, when they reach an age capable of understanding, be taught both the sacraments of faith and the mysteries of their confession, so that they may truly believe them and carefully preserve them.

We have expressly said “their confession,” because although they cannot yet speak, 366 those who receive them from the laver of the font confess and speak on their behalf. And rightly so: it is fitting that those who are liable for the sins of others should, through the mystery of baptism, receive remission of original sins through the confession of others.

## VIII

Those who are already of an age at which they can give an account of their belief must be examined with careful scrutiny, to determine whether they truly believe or whether some stain of falsehood lies concealed in them. Still less should they, whether through fear of or favor with earthly powers, or through the acquisition of certain things, come to the sacrament of baptism while the ministers of the Church are unaware; then what is holy may be handed over to dogs, pearls may be thrown [Col. 0357B] among swine, and wolves may be clothed in sheep’s clothing.

The Church has customarily observed this practice: those who are to be baptized at the solemnity of Easter are examined over a period of several days, so that the sacraments of life may be imparted to those who come instructed and taught, and with a sincere heart, to the true faith. In order that they may be found more suitable for the sacrament of baptism, and that their faith may be more credible, certain things are performed bodily which, tasted with spiritual perception, convey a mystical and spiritual meaning.

## IX

Their nostrils and ears are therefore touched with spittle, and one says, “Ephphatha.” The nostrils are touched so that they may follow Christ in the fragrance of perfumes and say, “Draw me; we will run after you”; and so that, with the Apostle, they may confess, saying, “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God”; and may become members of him to whom it is said, “The fragrance of your garments is above all perfumes.”

They will then be able to possess this fragrance rightly, like Mary—whose name is interpreted as “lady” or “enlightener”—if, taking an alabaster vessel of ointment, that is, [Col. 0357C] the purity of holy faith, they anoint the feet of Jesus, fulfilling the instructions of the apostles or of any preachers through whom Christ walks. Then the house—that is, the world, or the whole of the holy Church—may be filled with their good reputation as with a certain sweet and pleasing fragrance.

And because the sweetness of fragrance and various incense usually belong to those who are dissolute and lovers of pleasure, these people, having instead become self-controlled and lovers of Christ, should always embrace only his life-giving fragrance.

Their ears are also touched, so that, hearing the words of God and doing them, they may be like, according to the Gospel, the wise man who built his house upon rock. By spiritual hearing they should always listen to spiritual things, so that they may say with David, “I will hear what the Lord God speaks within me,” and with Isaiah, “The Lord God has opened my ear; but I do not contradict; I have not turned backward.” Thus, hearing what is spoken spiritually, they may attain the benefits of spiritual works.

When the Lord says in the Gospel, “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear,” and John [Col. 0357D] says in his Apocalypse, “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear what the Lord says to the churches,” it is not bodily ears that are being sought, but spiritual ears; and by the name of ears the hearing of the inner person is signified. For in sacred speech, the virtues of the spiritual soul are often understood through the members of the body.

Because, therefore, the divinity, in assuming humanity, made a kind of salve from the mingling of two substances in the one person of the Son of God, by which it might illuminate the human race, which had been born blind from its first parents, the ears and nostrils are now touched with spittle [corrected from *non* to *nunc*], just as, when spitting, he had touched the tongue of the mute, made mud with spittle, and opened the eyes of the man born blind; so that now, through the ministry of priests, he may grant spiritual hearing to those who have been baptized, provide the ability to speak rightly—that is, to confess the true faith—and open the nostrils by which they may receive the good fragrance of Christ.

The breast of the one who is baptized must always be filled with [Col. 0358A] the nectar of divine fragrance and steeped in spiritual anointing.

## X

Accordingly, the breast and shoulders of those who are to be baptized are touched with oil, so that, anointed with the unction of that holy oil—that is, the Holy Spirit—of which the Apostle says, “His anointing teaches us about everything,” they may be protected before and behind; that is, they may be watchful concerning all things, whether prosperous or adverse. In imitation of the heavenly living creatures, they should be full of eyes before and behind—that is, looking toward the past and the future—so that they do not lose the guardianship of their salvation.

Their breast is touched 367 so that they may say with David, “May his mercy go before me.” Their shoulders are touched so that they may say with the same man, “And his mercy shall follow me.” That is: the things in front, so that they may will what is good; the things behind, so that they may not will in vain.

To will well and to accomplish the good are given to us by God, from whom every good gift and every perfect gift comes. And since the mind is often designated by the name “heart,” as in the saying, “With my whole heart I have sought you,” and since by the name “oil” the anointing of the Holy Spirit, or works of light and mercy, is understood, the place of the heart is fortified on both sides by anointing—that is, in front and behind—so that the Christian’s mind may everywhere abound both in the richness of the Holy Spirit and in works of light and mercy.

## XI

[Col. 0358B] Those in whom these things abound do so if, by renouncing the devil and his works, they reject his dominion, and if the yoke that weighed upon them is broken by the anointing of that oil. Then the prophetic saying is fulfilled: “The yoke will rot because of the oil” (Isaiah 10).

To renounce is commonly used to mean despise, reject, oppose, or whatever else may express this meaning. Although the sense of the word *nuntio* (“announce”) is readily apparent when it is used without a prefix, and although with a prefix it sometimes does not depart far from its meaning—as in “I will tell” and “I will report”—at other times it turns to another sense, as in: “So therefore, whoever does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple.” Nevertheless, *abrenuntiare* (“to renounce”) is always customarily used in the sense mentioned above.

A person therefore [Col. 0358C] confesses that he renounces Satan, all his works, and all his pomps. This renunciation is rightly followed by the confession of the holy Trinity, so that where sin abounded, grace may abound all the more; and where the devil’s yoke has rotted through the presence of the Holy Spirit’s anointing, there may come the yoke of him who said: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls; for my yoke is easy and my burden light.”

Satan, who is also called the devil, is renounced by the faithful so that they may serve the Lord Savior more freely, because, according to the Lord’s own word, no one can serve two masters.

## XII

His works are also renounced, because his works are opposed to the works of the Savior; and because he subjected the human race to himself by his weapons—that is, by vices—the Lord conquered him with his own weapons—that is, with virtues.

In his service—that is, in our sins—we received lasting bondage and death [*servitus permanens*, read *servitutem permanentem*]; in the latter’s service—that is, in virtues—we receive eternal life.

We may therefore appropriately call the seven principal [Col. 0358D] vices with which the devil afflicts the human race the works of Satan; opposed to them are the seven principal virtues, which are unquestionably works that bring salvation.

His pomps are likewise renounced, and these too are works of Satan. Yet they seem to be distinguished from his other works because they somehow represent his pride, of which he is the author and by which he was cast down.

His pomps, therefore, are ambition, arrogance, vainglory, and other things of this kind, which are recognized as proceeding from the fountain of pride. That “pomp” should be understood as ambition, ostentation, and similar things is demonstrated by the prophetic utterance: “Woe to you who are wealthy in Zion and trust in the mountain of Samaria, distinguished men, heads of the peoples, entering the house of Israel pompously.”

[Col. 0359A] The most eloquent and most Christian poet Clemens Prudentius also used “pomp” in this sense in his book *Psychomachia*, where he says:

> The ostentatious pomp of empty splendor  
> Is stripped bare of its vain robe.

Although every sin may be called pride, because when someone sins against God, who forbade sin, he seems to oppose God, nevertheless it is one thing to sin sluggishly, another maliciously, another knowingly, another ignorantly, another negligently, and another arrogantly.

However a person may sin, if he refuses to repent, he plunges himself into the great abyss of pride. From that abyss he can emerge only through confession of his sins, amendment of his conduct, and the aid of saving repentance 368.

A human being is proud against God in two ways: either when he is disobedient to God’s commandments and commits what has been forbidden, or when he neglects to repent of what he has committed.

Therefore, whether those who are to be baptized or we who have already received the sacrament of baptism must place before our eyes the covenant made with God in baptism, in which Satan, his works, and his pomps are renounced. That covenant is made void if, while remaining in the faith, someone submits to vices, or, departing from the faith [Col. 0359B], submits to the worship of idols or the errors of heresies.

## XIII

Since, then, it is established that believers make two covenants—one in which the devil, his pomps, and all his works are renounced, and another in which they confess that they believe in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—these must be held with an unwavering intention of mind. And so that they may be preserved undefiled [corrected from *temerate* to *intemerate*], they must always seek the help of him who bestowed the sacrament of baptism for the salvation of the human race.

Its mystery was prefigured in the Old Testament through Moses, when the people were baptized in the cloud and in the sea, and was most openly demonstrated in the New Testament through the Mediator between God and human beings. For he himself says: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of heaven.” And John says of him: “I baptize you; but he will come,” and so forth: “He has baptized you” [that is, “he will baptize you”] “in the Holy Spirit and fire.”

Through this, those who are born into the world are reborn to God; and those who through sin were children of wrath become, through [Col. 0359C] grace, children of God.

By this immersion and this washing the Church is enlivened. Woman was built from the bone of the first parent; the Church was formed from the side of Christ sleeping on the cross. For blood and water flowed from his side—the two principal sacraments of the holy Church—so that through the one consecration, and through the other cleansing, might be granted to that same Church.

We are regenerated from the laver so that we may be consecrated also by the blood. Thus the people crossed the Red Sea, because the baptism of Christ is consecrated by his blood.

Since the element of water in this world is more suitable than all the other elements for cleansing, giving life, and refreshing, the dignity of baptism is not inappropriately conferred upon it. For it conceived the power of regenerating human beings when the Spirit of God moved over it at the beginning of the world, and it received the dignity of cleansing when it flowed from Christ’s side.

Through this visible element that invisible reality is signified: just as water cleanses the body outwardly, so the soul is secretly purified through its ministry by the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 0359D] After God has been invoked, the Holy Spirit descends from heaven and, sanctifying the waters, grants them the power of purification. From them the human being, restored to the image of the holy Trinity in whose image he had been created, is driven out; and he who had entered them old through the sin of the first human being emerges from them new through the grace of Christ. Changed for the better by the Spirit of grace, he becomes something altogether different from what he had been.

He had been foul through the deformity of sins; there he is made beautiful by the whiteness of virtues.

The mystery of baptism can in no way be completed except under invocation of the holy Trinity, because the Lord also said to the apostles: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.”

The same Lord confirmed this sacrament when, at his baptism, the Father was declared by the voice, the Son by the body, and the Holy Spirit by the appearance of a dove.

O splendid and wondrous sacrament, which makes children of God from children of wrath, new people from the old, and beautiful people from the foul! [Col. 0360A] In it we are regenerated, cleansed, and imitate the example of Christ’s death.

How we should imitate this example the Apostle explains: “Do you not know that whoever among us has been baptized in Christ Jesus has been baptized into his death? Therefore we have been buried with him through baptism into death, so that just as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too may walk in newness of life.”

We die to sin, therefore, when we renounce the devil and everything that belongs to him. We are buried with Christ when, under invocation of the holy Trinity, we descend into the laver of the font by a triple immersion, as into a certain tomb. We rise with Christ when, stripped of all sins, we emerge from the font, as from a tomb.

Nor is the mystery of the three days and nights during which Jesus is said to have been in the tomb passed over, when, with the holy Trinity invoked [corrected from *invoti* to *invocata*]—which is truly the light—we descend into the font. For the Father is light, and in his light, which is the Son, we see the light that is the Holy Spirit.

We also make three nights when we contradict the father of darkness and ignorance together with the falsehood [text uncertain: *una commendatio*, corrected editorially as *cum mendacio*] that was born from him, because it is a liar, as its father is. [Col. 0360B] In the third place, we destroy the spirit of error, which inspires false prophets to say, “Thus says the Lord,” although the Lord did not send them.

We destroy and trample these things if we have been buried with Christ, in accordance also with what he himself says: “Behold, I have given you power to trample upon serpents and scorpions, and upon all the power of the enemy.”

Each of these things is opposed to the holy Trinity as night is to day, darkness to light, and falsehood to truth.

The baptismal font also bears the likeness of Christ’s tomb, which is said to have been new. Whoever is buried with Christ in it and rises with him must, according to the same Apostle, walk in newness of life.

The seven steps of this font seem to signify three nights in the descent, and three days in the ascent, about which we have spoken above. The seventh, which is also [Col. 0360C] the fourth, is the one of whom someone says: “And the appearance of the fourth was like the Son of God”—the one who extinguishes the furnace of fire, who is the support of the feet and the foundation of the water, in whom, according to the Apostle, the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily.

Baptism is not repeated because Christ also dies no more than once. Sins committed after baptism are erased by tears of repentance, almsgiving, and the performance of other good works, not by repeating baptism.

Meanwhile, the body of the Lord, when it is to be buried, is treated with the purest linens and spices. Likewise, the person who desires to be buried with Christ—if his age already permits it—although he is dead through original sin, which he still bears, must nevertheless give off fragrance through the performance of good works and be clothed in clean garments. Of these the prophet asks that priests be clothed when he says: “Let your priests be clothed with righteousness.”

If, therefore, before he is reborn, cleansed of original sin, and buried with Christ, he must give off fragrance, emit a pleasing odor, and be clothed in the cleanest garments, how much more, once reborn, cleansed, [Col. 0360D] made alive together with Christ, walking in newness of life, and made a new creation, must he abound in fragrant odor and shine with the brightness of white garments!

## XIV

Therefore, so that we who die to the world may rise with Christ, let us be clothed in the splendor of good works and strengthened by hope of heavenly joys. For this reason the angel who announces his resurrection is most appropriately described as sitting in white garments; those who announce his return to the apostles appear in white garments; and after baptism we too are clothed in white garments, so that we may preserve in our conduct the purity that we received in regeneration, maintaining both our renewal and the beauty of the angelic splendor [text corrected editorially to *ut*].

Let individual white robes be given to us, namely, the hope of immortality and eternal happiness, so that with the prophet we may say: “Rejoicing, I will rejoice in the Lord, and my spirit has exulted in my God, because he has clothed me with the garment of salvation and surrounded me with the robe of righteousness.”

May he who gave us these garments [Col. 0361A] make us preserve them, so that it may be said of us what is written in the Apocalypse: “Blessed is the one who watches and keeps his garments.”

Since everything in the rite of baptism breathes mysteries and overflows with sacraments, it was fitting that the new human being should receive new garments and, cleansed of the filth of the old offense, be clothed in the brightness of white robes.

Moses first washed Aaron and his sons with water and then clothed them in linen garments. So too our true Moses, who frees the people from Egyptian slavery—that is, from the error of paganism—the Mediator between God and human beings, purifies us by the ineffable water of his sacrament and adorns us with the garments of good works.

His face—that is, the manifestation of his divinity—shines like the sun on the mountain of the Church, testified to by the Law and the Prophets; and his garments—that is, all the saints—become white 370 like the moon [corrected from *luna* to *lana*, “wool”], or like snow.

With the Apocalypse, let us give thanks to him who washed us from our sins in his blood and made us a kingdom and priests [Col. 0361B] for his God and Father, to whom be glory forever and ever.

For this kingdom and priesthood are anointed by the Lord through the ministry of priests with the visible ointment of chrism and with the invisible grace of the Holy Spirit.

## XV

The sacrament of this ointment is first recorded as having been composed by Moses at the Lord’s command in Exodus, and in the New Testament it is truly declared by the Lord, who was anointed by the Father with the oil of gladness above his companions [corrected from *tuis* to *suis*], to whom God does not give the Spirit by measure, because in him the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily.

To him the Church says: “Your name is oil poured out; therefore the young women have loved you.” For the name of Christians arose both from Christ’s chrism and from Christ.

Before his coming, only kings and priests were anointed, and they too were called “Christs.” After his coming, however, not only kings and priests but the whole Church is consecrated by this anointing, because it is established that she is a kingdom and a priesthood, and that her children are [Col. 0361C] kings and priests.

The heads of those who have been baptized are therefore anointed with chrism, so that, anointed for the kingdom and priesthood of the Church, they may receive the privilege of the Christian name and become members of him who redeemed them and is their head.

## XVI

Since, therefore, our Redeemer is both King—to whom the prophet says, “Your kingdom, Lord, is a kingdom of all ages, and your dominion is from generation to generation”—and wondrously triumphed over the devil, death, and the world—and Priest [corrected from *Sacerdotes* to *sacerdos est*], to whom the same prophet says, “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek,” and who offered himself in sacrifice to God the Father, it is most fitting that his holy Church, which is indeed his body, should be both kingdom and priesthood.

We, regenerated in her and being her members, should likewise be kings and priests: kings, so that we may fight manfully against the devil and govern the administration of our life with admirable discipline; priests, so that in the holy temple of God, which we are, building the altar of faith [Col. 0361D], we may offer him peaceful sacrifices of good works, and say with the Apostle: “Blessed be God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places.”

From this altar may the smoke of our prayers rise to him daily, according to what the prophet says: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight.”

The heads of those who are regenerated from water and the Holy Spirit are covered with a mystical veil, so that Peter may say to them: “You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for acquisition.”

By this veil both the royal diadem and the covering of the priestly head are signified. And because in sacred speech the mind is often understood by “head,” as in the saying, “Look up and lift your heads,” the mind of those who have been reborn should possess the ornaments of royal dignity and the covering of the priestly crown.

Thus it may be protected against vices by a priestly veil, spiritually [Col. 0362A] adorned with the jewels of virtues, and anointed with the unction of the most holy chrism. Through this anointing of chrism the Spirit of the sevenfold grace is also granted to them, so that they may deserve to become not only the dwelling place of the Holy Spirit, who is of one substance with the Father and the Son, but of the whole holy Trinity.

## XVII

That priests may anoint the baptized with chrism, but may not confer the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands, is an ancient practice handed down to the Church by the apostles.

For it is written in the Acts of the Apostles: “It happened that, while Apollos was at Corinth, Paul, having passed through the upper regions, came to Ephesus and found certain disciples. He said to them, ‘Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?’ But they said to him, ‘We have not even heard whether there is a Holy Spirit.’ He said, ‘Into what, then, were you baptized?’ They said, ‘Into John’s baptism.’ Paul replied, ‘John baptized with a baptism of repentance, telling the people to believe in the one who was to come after him,’ that is, 371 in Jesus.

“When they heard this [Col. 0362B], they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. And when Paul had laid hands upon them, the Holy Spirit came upon them, and they spoke in tongues and prophesied.”

Again, in another passage: “When the apostles who were in Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent Peter and John to them. When they had come, they prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Spirit; for he had not yet come upon any of them, but they had only been baptized in the name of the Lord. Then they laid hands upon them, and they received the Holy Spirit.”

Finally, it must be understood that just as the other sacraments of baptism are performed visibly through priests but consecrated invisibly by God, so too the grace of the Holy Spirit is bestowed upon the faithful through the laying on of hands and the ministry of bishops.

Although priests are indeed priests, they do not possess the summit of the episcopate. That the power either to sign or to confer the Spirit, the Paraclete, belongs to bishops alone is demonstrated not only by ecclesiastical custom but also by the passage above [Col. 0362C] from the Acts of the Apostles, which asserts that Peter and John were sent to confer the Holy Spirit upon those who had already been baptized.

Priests may baptize and anoint the baptized with chrism, whether bishops are absent or present, but the chrism must be that which has been consecrated by a bishop. They may not, however, sign the forehead with that same oil, since this belongs to bishops alone when they confer the Spirit, the Paraclete.

This Spirit, the Paraclete, is also called the Spirit of the sevenfold grace because of the mystery of the number seven, in which complete perfection is understood. Seven is composed of the entire first even number and the entire first odd number: of the entire first even number, which can be divided, and of the entire first odd number, which cannot be divided.

In the number seven there is the mystery of the Trinity in the ternary, and of the Gospel in the quaternary. For whether three is multiplied by four or four by three, the result is twelve. The mystery of the holy Trinity and the teaching of the Gospel were spread through the twelve apostles into the four parts of the world—namely, East and West, North and South.

This [Col. 0362D] number is customarily used in sacred speech to signify perfection. When God had completed his works, he rested on the seventh day. Enoch, who is the seventh from Adam, walked with the Lord, and his translation gave us hope of eternal rest.

Therefore the jubilee year, in which complete rest is signified, is completed through seven weeks of years. Seven times seven makes forty-nine, which is completed by adding the one—the unity of our union.

The prophet commends the perfection of this number when he says: “Seven times a day I have given you praise.” In another psalm, explaining this almost explicitly, he says: “His praise shall always be in my mouth.”

John too, in his Apocalypse, is believed to have written what he wrote to the seven churches generally for the whole catholic Church. Hence he himself says: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.”

“Concerning the number seven, which in some passages of Scripture signifies totality or perfection, and in others the sevenfold Spirit of grace, there are many examples in both the Old and the New Testament, whose investigation would take too long. Let us now see how the prophet Isaiah enumerates the gifts of that same sevenfold Spirit. When he prophesied about Christ, who is the rod of the Lord’s power, he said: ‘A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root, and the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and fortitude, the Spirit of knowledge and piety, and he shall be filled with the Spirit of the fear of the Lord.’ Upon this flower, which came forth from the rod of Jesse—that is, from the birth of blessed Mary, ever-virgin—the Spirit of the Lord rested. For in him it pleased the whole fullness of divinity to dwell bodily—not in parts, as in the other saints, to whom one is given the word of wisdom, another the word of knowledge, another the grace of powers, and so forth, each being given according to measure, but in the fullest manner. Hence the Apostle also says: ‘God does not give the Spirit according to measure.’ And the prophet says: ‘Behold my servant whom I have chosen, my chosen one, in whom my soul is well pleased; I will put my Spirit upon him, and he shall bring forth judgment to the nations.’

“So that the Spirit might rest in him in perpetual dwelling, it came to him, according to the testimony of John the Baptist, who says: ‘I saw the Spirit descending like a dove from heaven, and he remained upon him, and I did not know him; but he who sent me to baptize told me: Upon whomever you see the Spirit descending and remaining upon him, he is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.’ This Spirit is called the Spirit of the Lord [Note: Read *appellatur* (“is called”), as in Sirmond’s edition.] and the Spirit of wisdom [Perhaps read: “who by the Spirit … the Spirit of wisdom”], because it is written of Christ, who is the wisdom of God: ‘All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made’; and in the Psalms it is sung: ‘How magnificent are your works, O Lord! You have made all things in wisdom.’ And in another place, where the Trinity is plainly demonstrated, it is written: ‘By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their power.’ For through Christ, who is the Word of the Lord—that is, of the Father—of whom it is written, ‘In the beginning was the Word,’ the heavens, namely the holy preachers who proclaim the glory of God, were made; and through the Holy Spirit, who is consubstantial with them and proceeds from both, comes all their power. For the adornment of all the saints rests upon the inspiration of the Holy Spirit.

“The Apostle writes: ‘Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God.’ And in Proverbs it is read: ‘God founded the earth in his wisdom and prepared the heavens in his prudence.’ Just as the same Word of the Lord is called light, life, and resurrection, so it is called the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, of counsel and fortitude, and of knowledge and piety, as well as of the fear of the Lord. This does not mean that he is different according to the distinctions among the names, but that he is one and the same source and origin of all the virtues. Without Christ, therefore, no one can be wise, understanding, a counselor, strong, learned, or filled with the fear of the Lord.

“It should also be known that the Spirit of the Lord—of wisdom and understanding, of counsel and fortitude, of knowledge and piety, and of the fear of the Lord—that is, the number seven, which Zechariah calls the seven eyes in one stone [Col. 0363D], rests upon the rod and the flower that arose from Jesse, and therefore from the stock of David. This Spirit, who proceeds from the Father and the Son, the Lord himself gave to the apostles, and through the ministry of the apostles and their successors to his holy Church. Although the gifts of this Spirit proceed from one eminent source [Note: In Sirmond’s edition, read ‘from the source of one Spirit.’], they nevertheless appear in a certain way to possess distinct properties.

“For it is one thing to have wisdom and another to have understanding. Many indeed have a taste for eternal things, but are quite unable to understand them. Wisdom therefore fills the mind it inhabits with hope and certainty concerning eternal things [Note: Read “with hope and certainty”]. Understanding, because it penetrates hidden things, refreshes the heart it has touched and enlightens its darkness. Counsel, by preventing someone from being rash, fills the mind with reason. Fortitude, when it does not fear adversity, gives confidence to the trembling mind. Knowledge, when it drives away ignorance, enlightens by its light the one whom it has filled. Piety permits the one whom it has filled to abound in works of mercy. Fear, while it restrains the mind lest it grow proud of present things, strengthens it concerning future things by restoring hope.

“Thus these virtues help one another by a certain mutual support, so that while one assists another, the order and condition of life may be arranged most suitably. Wisdom is lesser if it lacks understanding, and understanding is quite useless if it does not arise from wisdom; for when it penetrates higher things without the weight of wisdom, its own lightness raises it only to make its fall more grievous. Counsel is worthless when it lacks the strength of fortitude, because what it discovers through deliberation, lacking the power to act, does not bring to completion the work it has begun. Fortitude is also greatly undermined unless it is supported by counsel, because the more it perceives itself able to do, the more disastrously virtue rushes headlong without the moderation of reason.

“There is no knowledge if it lacks the usefulness of piety, because when someone neglects to carry out the good things he has learned, he binds himself more tightly for judgment. Piety is likewise quite useless if it lacks the discernment of knowledge, because when no knowledge enlightens it, it does not know how to show mercy. Fear itself, too, if it does not possess these virtues, certainly rises to no work of good action; for while it trembles at everything, through fear of itself it remains sluggish and empty of every good thing.

“Therefore we must observe with the greatest care and implore the help of the Holy Spirit himself: that wisdom may not exalt us; that understanding, while running subtly, may not go astray; that counsel, while multiplying its considerations, may not confuse us; that fortitude, while giving confidence, may not precipitate us; that knowledge, while knowing but not loving [read: ‘and not loving’], may not inflate us; that piety, while inclining beyond uprightness, may not distort us; and that fear, while trembling more than is right, may not plunge us into the pit of despair.

“It must certainly be known that these distributions of spiritual gifts, in the body of Christ, which is the Church, are supported by these aids; but in him who is the source of light and origin of goodness they reign fully and perfectly, incomparably and ineffably. Wisdom, which built for itself a body in the Virgin’s womb and the Church in the world, possesses the Spirit of wisdom, by which it does all things wisely; of understanding, by which it searches out all the secret mysteries; of counsel, by which it accomplishes all things with great dispensation, for he is the angel of great counsel; of fortitude, because it reaches all things mightily from end to end and can be conquered by none; of knowledge, because it knows nothing by ignorance, except those to whom it will say, ‘I do not know you’; of piety, because the man whom it created through goodness, it condemned in justice and redeemed in pity [Note: In Sirmond’s edition: ‘whom he created in goodness, condemned in justice’]; and of fear, on account of those who need the fear of the Lord, because they are little ones, to whom he says through the prophet: ‘Come, children, hear me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord.’

“Since, therefore, he descended to our weakness, emptied himself, took the form of a servant, humbled himself even to death, and bowed himself down so as to raise us who were lying prostrate up to himself, it is not inappropriate that the Spirit of the Lord who rests upon him should begin with wisdom and descend through the most fitting degrees all the way to fear.

“We, however, coming from fear—which love casts out—arrive at the chaste fear that endures forever and ever, then at piety [read: ‘from piety’], so that adorned with works of piety we may come to knowledge—not the knowledge that inflates, but that which love builds up—and from knowledge to fortitude, so that adorned with the beauty of knowledge we may fight bravely against vices; from fortitude to counsel, so that we may fortify with the gravity of counsel the things we do bravely; and, with our actions obeying counsel [read: ‘properly adjusted to counsel’], entering into the secrets of understanding, we may come to that wisdom which has the fear of the Lord as its beginning. Thus, completing all things wisely and possessing good understanding through our actions, we may be admitted to that Wisdom through which all things were made, which was ineffably begotten by the Father before the ages and, at the end of the ages, deigned to assume flesh for the sake of our salvation, when he gave his flesh to his faithful to eat, saying: ‘Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves.’”

“XVIII. To obtain this life we are both baptized, and nourished by his flesh, and given drink from his blood. For we cannot pass into his body unless we are imbued with these sacraments. Thus he himself says: ‘My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink; and whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him.’ In him there is the saving sacrifice. In the Old Testament, Melchizedek, king of Salem, offered it in a type of the Lord’s body and blood [Col. 0365B]; and in the New Testament the same Mediator between God and human beings fulfilled it before he was handed over, when, taking bread and a cup, blessing them, and giving them to his disciples, he commanded that these things be done in his remembrance.

“The Church therefore celebrates this mystery, offering it in place of the former sacrifices, which have been abandoned and brought to an end: bread on account of the living bread that came down from heaven, and wine on account of him who said, ‘I am the true vine,’ so that through the visible offering of the priests and the visible [read: ‘invisible’] consecration of the Holy Spirit, the bread and wine may pass into the dignity of the Lord’s body and blood. Water is mixed with this blood, either because water flowed from the Lord’s side together with blood, or because, as the ancients wish it to be understood, just as Christ is signified by the wine, so the people are signified by the water. Wine and water are mixed inseparably in the cup because the Church also remains inseparably joined to her head.

“The Church therefore keeps the custom of receiving the Eucharist handed down by the Lord: when someone is reborn from water and the Holy Spirit, he is nourished by the Lord’s body and given drink from his blood, so that, having been transferred into the body of Christ, he may remain in it and Christ in him; and, strengthened by the power of this food, he may, following the example of Elijah, reach the mountain of God, namely Christ, who is the mountain of the house of the Lord prepared at the top of the mountains, and by his gift may advance to the glory of eternal blessedness. There his desire will be satisfied with good things, and he will be able to say with the prophet: ‘But I shall appear in your sight in righteousness; I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed.’”

Thus far Theodulphus on the order of baptism, concerning which I have wished to note a few things.

In the dedicatory letter the author calls himself Theodulphus. He is certainly none other than Theodulphus, bishop of Orléans, who flourished in learning and piety under the emperors Charlemagne—whom he mentions in this letter—and Louis the Pious. That John to whom Theodulphus dedicates the little book was bishop of Arles, Theodulphus’s contemporary under the same emperors. He is mentioned in the preface to the Sixth Council of Arles, held under Charlemagne [Col. 0365D]. Louis the Pious sent him with the aforementioned Theodulphus to meet Pope Stephen IV as he approached Rheims, as the author of the Life of Louis the Pious testifies; some think this author was Ademar. In the same letter the words ‘which you commanded’ [Note: The words enclosed above in brackets.] seem superfluous. *Primates* are the nobles, magnates, and highest men of the kingdom; see the Visigothic Law, book III, title I, law 5: ‘Whoever among the primates of our palace …’

Chapter 1 deals with catechumens. Saint Isidore explains what a catechumen is in book VIII, chapter 14, of the *Etymologies*: ‘A catechumen is so called because he is still hearing the teaching of the faith, although he has not yet received baptism; for *κατηχούμενος* in Greek means “hearer.”’ This is also clear from Lucian, in the *Philopatris*: ‘But, having become a catechumen, be persuaded by me, if indeed you desire to live forever.’ That is: ‘And, having become a catechumen, allow yourself to be persuaded by me, if you desire to live forever.’ Hence Latin Fathers call a catechumen a *hearer* and one who is *hearing*. Tertullian speaks in this way in his book *On Repentance*: ‘Let no one therefore flatter himself because he is counted among the first exercises of the hearers.’ And shortly afterward: ‘For this is the first impulse of one who hears: complete fear.’ And again shortly afterward: ‘Therefore hearers ought to desire immersion, not presume upon it.’ Saint Cyprian likewise says in Letter 13: ‘Nor should your vigilance be lacking toward hearers, if any should be overtaken by danger and placed at the point of death.’ And in Letter 24: ‘We appointed a learned teacher of hearers among the readers.’

There were also other hearers, but they were penitents, who occupied the second rank of penitents, as will be explained below.

Formerly there were two grades of catechumens. The first consisted of beginners, the untrained, and the imperfect; the second of the more advanced, who were called *competentes*. All of these—both the *competentes* and the beginners—heard the Scriptures in the Church. Beginners and the untrained were taught only in summary fashion about God’s works, the creation of the world and of humanity, and especially those things in both Testaments that are more remarkable, as well as pure and wholly sincere charity. This is clear from chapter 3 of Saint Augustine’s book *On Catechizing the Uninstructed*: ‘The narrative is complete when someone is first catechized from what is written, “God made heaven and earth,” up to the present times of the Church. Yet we should not therefore recite the whole Pentateuch, all the books of Judges, Kings, and Ezra, the whole Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles, either by memory if we have learned them word for word, or by narrating and explaining in our own words everything contained in these volumes. Neither does time allow it nor does any necessity require it. Rather, everything should be embraced in summary and general form, so that the more remarkable and more pleasing things to hear may be selected,’ and so forth.

This is also evident from Lucian, in the *Philopatris*, where Triephon the Christian teaches Critias, who desires to become a Christian, those things that he had once learned from Saint Paul, in the following manner:

‘For I shall teach you what the universe is, who existed before all things, and what the constitution of the universe is.’

That is: ‘I shall teach you what the universe is, who existed before all things, and what the structure of the universe is,’ and so forth.

And below:

**TRIEPHON:** Have you ever read the comedy of Aristophanes the comic poet, *The Birds*?

**CRITIAS:** Indeed, and very thoroughly.

**TRIEPHON:** There is something of this kind written there by him:

> ‘Chaos was, and night, and black Erebus at first, and broad Tartarus;  
> but earth was not, nor air, nor heaven.’

That is: ‘In the beginning there was chaos, and night and black darkness, and lofty Tartarus; but there was not yet any earth, air, or heaven.’

**CRITIAS:** You speak correctly. But what came afterward?

**TRIEPHON:** ‘There was an incorruptible, invisible, incomprehensible light, which dissolves darkness,’ and so forth.

That is: ‘There was an incorruptible, incomprehensible light, which dissolves darkness and drove away formlessness by a word spoken by itself, just as that slow-tongued man’—he means Moses—‘described. It formed the earth upon the waters, spread out the heavens, formed the fixed stars, and ordered their course, which you worship as God. It also adorned the earth with flowers, brought the human being from nothingness into existence, and is in heaven, looking upon the just and the unjust alike and recording each person’s deeds and actions in books,’ and so forth.

And below:

‘Good words! Do not say anything contemptuous or vile about God, who is on the right hand; but, as a catechumen, allow yourself to be persuaded by me if you desire to live forever. “If he spread out heaven like a skin, and fixed the earth upon the waters,”’ and so forth.

That is: ‘For if he spread out heaven like a skin, fixed the earth upon the waters, formed the stars, and brought the human being forth from nothing, why is it so surprising if the affairs of all things are likewise recorded in this way?’

They heard the mysteries, but did not understand them; they heard the Scriptures, but were ignorant of their meaning, as is clear from Saint Cyril in the preface to the *Catecheses*.

The more advanced, however, were those who, having completed the first grade and given their names, were enrolled as soldiers of God and taught the divine mysteries, as is clear from the same Cyril, in the preface just mentioned. The Creed was delivered to them; that is, all its articles were explained to them more fully, as may be seen in the four books of Saint Augustine *On the Creed to the Catechumens*. This is not done in the book *On Catechizing the Uninstructed*, since it was written solely for the benefit of catechumens of the first grade.

The same is clear from Saint John Chrysostom, in the first catechesis, where he writes that the more advanced, after a year of catechumenate, were initiated into the mysteries—*μυσταγωγεῖσθαι*, that is, were imbued with the mysteries of religion—during a period of thirty days.

Such catechumens were called *competentes* because they were seeking baptism, as Saint Isidore writes in book I, chapter 27, and book II, chapter 21, of *On the Offices of the Church*, and in book VII, chapter 14, of the *Etymologies*: ‘A *competens* is one who, after instruction in the faith, seeks the grace of Christ; hence he is called *competens* from seeking.’ But when he says ‘after instruction in the faith,’ this should be understood of the instruction of the more untrained catechumens, to whom it was forbidden to hear the mysteries.

Saint Augustine also mentions the *competentes* in *On Faith and Works*, chapter 6: ‘When we were seeking the sacraments of that font, and for this reason were also called *competentes*.’ Saint Ambrose mentions them in book V, Letter 33: ‘I delivered the Creed to certain *competentes* in the baptisteries of the basilica.’

Catechumens were made through the sign of the cross, with which they were marked on their foreheads, as is evident from Saint Augustine, book I, chapter 11, of the *Confessions*, cited below, and book II of *On the Creed to the Catechumens*: ‘You have not yet been reborn through holy baptism, but through the sign of the cross you have already been conceived in the womb of holy mother Church.’ And in book IV: ‘While holy mother Church received you into her womb through the most sacred sign of the cross, she will spiritually give birth to you, as to your brothers, with the greatest joy.’ In *On Catechizing the Uninstructed*, chapter 20: ‘You are to be marked with the sign of his passion and cross on the forehead, as on a doorpost; and all Christians are marked in this way.’ And in chapter 26 of the same book: ‘If he should answer solemnly, he must certainly be marked and treated according to the custom of the Church.’ Also in book II of *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, chapter 26, which will soon be cited.

In the Codex of Ratoldus the catechumen is marked on the forehead [Col. 0367C] and on the breast, as appears in the following formulas of that same Codex:

‘I place the sign of the Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, upon your forehead.’

‘I place the sign of the Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, upon your breast.’

The same appears in the Rheims Codex, in the formula for making a convert from paganism a catechumen; it is the only formula, in this form:

‘Receive the sign of the cross both on your forehead and in your heart,’ and so forth.

Besides the sign of the cross, the laying on of hands was also used, as Saint Augustine testifies in book II, chapter 26, of *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*: ‘For I think that catechumens too, in their own manner, are sanctified through the sign of the cross, prayer, and the laying on of hands.’ The same is evident from the Rheims Codex, in the making of a convert from paganism a catechumen, where mention is also made of insufflation:

‘When you receive a pagan man’—supply *τὸ vis* (“you wish”)—‘first catechize him with divine teachings and give him instructions concerning how he ought to live after coming to knowledge of the truth. After this you make him a catechumen, blow upon his face, make the sign of the cross over him, and place your hand upon his head, saying: “Receive the sign,”’ and so forth above.

This laying on of hands is not found in the Codex of Ratoldus.

Salt was also put into the catechumen’s mouth, but this matter will be treated below.

In chapter 2 of Dionysius’s *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, mention is made of the sign of the cross and the laying on of hands. These, however, are not performed there at the beginning of catechumenate, or the apprenticeship of faith, when the beginner Christian is first imbued with the elements of religion, but when he approaches baptism, as may be seen in that passage.

In chapter 3 the sign of the cross is made through exsufflation. Dionysius, in the chapter cited; Cyril, in the second *Mystagogical Catechesis*; Saint Augustine, in book IV *On the Creed to the Catechumens*; and many others mention insufflation or exsufflation.

Satan is insufflated against three times by the converted catechumen toward the western direction, as Saint Dionysius writes in the chapter cited. By this insufflation it is signified that the Christian curses and abominates Satan.

But two forms of this exsufflation appear. For in Dionysius, in the chapter cited, the catechumen is ordered by the bishop to exsufflate Satan himself: ‘He commands him to blow upon Satan three times.’ But in Alcuin, in the chapter on Holy Saturday in the book *On Divine Offices*, and in the letter to Charlemagne, in Theodulphus here, and in the Rheims Codex, the exsufflation is performed by the priest or clergy.

This is also attested by the author of the book *On Ecclesiastical Doctrines*, among the works of Saint Augustine, chapter 31:

‘We do not regard without careful attention that which holy Church uniformly does throughout the world concerning those who are to be baptized. Whether infants or young people come to the sacrament of rebirth, they do not first approach the font of life until the unclean spirit has been driven away from them by the exorcisms and exsufflations of the clergy.’

Saint Cyril seems sufficiently to imply this when he says in the catechesis cited:

‘For just as the insufflations of the saints,’ and so forth.

That is: ‘For just as the insufflations of the saints and the invocation of God’s name burn the demons like a kind of exceedingly powerful flame and put them to flight.’

The Greeks now observe both forms, as is evident from their *Euchologion*. First the priest insufflates three times into the catechumen’s face; after the third exorcism the same priest insufflates into the catechumen’s mouth, forehead, and breast; and after the renunciation the catechumen is ordered to insufflate and spit upon Satan.

In the First Council of Constantinople, canon 7, mention is made of insufflation; the catechumen is insufflated upon the face and ears.

In the same chapter of Theodulphus, in the words ‘so that it may go out,’ the word ‘so that’ is superfluous. In the words ‘who also taught his disciples,’ and so forth, the words ‘following Christ’s example,’ or something similar, should be placed before them.

Chapter 4 deals with the exorcism, which Theodulphus himself writes is a speech of rebuke, according to Saint Isidore, book II, chapter 20, of *On Divine Offices*, because exorcists assail the devil with many rebukes.

Saint Cyril, in the preface to the *Catecheses*; Saint Gregory the Theologian, in his oration *On Holy Baptism*: ‘Do not reject the healing of exorcism’; Saint Augustine, in *On Faith and Works*, book IV *On the Creed to the Catechumens*, and several other books; Saint John Chrysostom, in the first catechesis; Saint Ambrose, in book I, chapter 5, of *On the Sacraments*: ‘For as soon as the priest enters, he performs an exorcism’; and many others mention exorcisms before baptism.

There is, however, no explicit mention of them in chapter 2 of Dionysius’s *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*. Some nevertheless think that the prayer which he says is completed by the bishop together with the whole Church is an exorcism, since in the Greek *Euchologion* we see that the third exorcism is in the form of a prayer.

Those who were exorcized listened to the exorcisms with their faces covered, as Saint Cyril writes in the preface to the *Catecheses*: ‘Your face is covered.’ He gives the reason: so that, when the eyes wandered, the mind might not also wander. They stood ungirded, their clothing removed, wearing only a little tunic and barefoot, as may be seen in the catechesis of Saint John Chrysostom cited above:

‘Having ungirded you, stripped you naked and barefoot, with only the little tunic, they send you forth to the voices of those performing the exorcism.’

That is: ‘They ungird you, strip you, and, without shoes and wearing only the little tunic, send you to the voices of those performing the exorcism.’

In chapter 2 of the *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, Saint Dionysius says:

‘He ungirds him and strips him through the ministers.’

And below, in the *Theoria*:

‘He makes him stand naked and barefoot, looking toward the west.’

That is: ‘He makes him stand naked and barefoot, looking toward the west.’

Saint Augustine, to be cited below, calls this nakedness of the feet ‘humility of the feet.’ The Greeks also observe it today, as is clear from their *Euchologion*.

They were raised onto their feet, as may be inferred from Saint Basil’s exhortation to baptism: ‘Not to stand upon one’s feet.’ There he speaks of the bedridden, who, compelled by the severity of illness, received baptism; nor could they stand on their feet, as had been prescribed. They also knelt during prayer, as may be seen in the same passage: ‘Nor to bend the knee in worship.’

Something similar appears in the letter of Jesse of Amiens and in the Rheims and Ratoldus Codices:

‘And they are admonished by the deacon: “Pray, you who are chosen; bend your knees.” After they have prayed, he says again: “Rise.”’

Chapter 5 deals with the salt that is there called the sacrament of catechumens. The words ‘so that by tasting it they may receive the seasoning of wisdom and not become foolish apart from the savor of Christ’ are taken from Saint Isidore, book II, chapter 20, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*. I have restored the word *desipiant*—‘become foolish’—since in our manuscript Codex it is corruptly read *decipiantur*, ‘be deceived’; and *alieni* (“of something foreign”), or a similar word, is to be understood.

Isidore mentions this rite in the chapter cited, as does Saint Augustine in book I, chapter 11, of the *Confessions*:

‘For while still a boy I had heard of the eternal life promised to us through the humility of your Son, the Lord our God, who descended to our pride; and I was already marked with the sign of the cross and seasoned with his salt.’

Although some interpret these last words as referring to the salt of divine grace, by which he was, so to speak, seasoned, I would not readily accept that interpretation. For if the matter is carefully weighed with mature judgment, Saint Augustine is speaking there of his own catechumenate, which consisted of the three things listed here: hearing, the sign of the cross, and the reception of salt. By it is signified the salt of divine wisdom, with which the catechumen ought to be seasoned: abstaining from vices through God’s grace and embracing virtues. Augustine himself had greatly departed from this way of life because his boyhood was polluted by many vices, as may be seen in the preceding and following chapters of the same book. He had indeed received the material salt, but had withdrawn completely from what it signified, having already been made foolish by the salt of the world.

There is also mention of it in the Third Council of Carthage, canon 5:

‘It was also decided that even during the most solemn days of Easter the sacrament should not be given to catechumens except the customary salt, because if the faithful do not change their sacrament during those days, neither ought it to be changed for catechumens.’

This is how Saint Augustine should be understood in book II, chapter 26, of *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*:

‘And what they receive, although it is not the body of Christ, is nevertheless holy, and holier than the foods by which we are nourished, because it is a sacrament.’

And in chapter 26 of *On Catechizing the Uninstructed*:

‘As for the sacrament which he received, when it has been properly commended to him as visible signs of divine things, it should be understood that the visible things themselves are honored.’

Nor should it be believed that in these two passages of Saint Augustine *eulogiae* are meant—that is, blessed bread. For, according to the council cited above, there was one sacrament of catechumens, namely salt, which must never be changed, not even during the most solemn Easter days, because the faithful—that is, the baptized—do not change their sacrament during those days.

Nor did that council prohibit blessed bread to catechumens; rather, it prohibited changing their sacrament even during the Easter days, because the baptized do not change theirs on those days. Since Saint Augustine does not explain in these two passages what the sacrament of catechumens is, the passage from the council cited properly explains what the sacrament of catechumens means in Saint Augustine.

Nor should it be said that in Saint Augustine’s time it was customary to give catechumens blessed bread in place of a sacrament, since this plainly conflicts with the council in which Saint Augustine took part, where the customary salt is said to be the sacrament of catechumens. Rather, an abuse that was gradually being introduced is removed. In the passages cited, *sacrament* is not used for a sacrament properly so called, but for something that is mystical.

The Greeks lack this rite. It is found neither among their ancient Fathers nor in the book of Severus, patriarch of Alexandria, nor in their *Euchologion* in the section that follows concerning baptism.

Chapter 6 deals with Theodulphus’s explanation of the Creed and its institution, following the teaching of Rufinus’s book *On the Explanation of the Creed* and of Saint Isidore, book II, chapter 1, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*. This Creed was given to the *competentes*, that is, to those catechumens to whom it was lawful to explain the mysteries of the faith, as Saint Isidore testifies in the chapter cited.
