Saint Augustine mentions the handing over of the Creed in book II *On the Creed to the Catechumens*:

‘After the household of the Redeemer had been purified and had sung the song of salvation, it received the remedy of the Creed against the poison of the ancient serpent, so that, whenever the adversary, the devil, should wish to lie in wait again, the redeemed person might know that he must confront him with the sacrament of the Creed and the banner of the cross.’

Saint Ambrose likewise says in book V, Letter 33:

‘On the following day—it was a Sunday—after the readings and the sermon, when the catechumens had been dismissed, I delivered the Creed to certain *competentes* in the baptisteries of the basilica.’

The Creed was delivered to the *competentes* on Palm Sunday, as Saint Isidore reports in book I, chapter 27, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*. He adds the reason:

‘On this day it is delivered to the *competentes* because of the proximity of the solemnity of Easter Sunday, so that those who are already hastening to receive God’s grace may recognize the faith that they are to confess.’

Formerly nearly the same custom was observed in Gaul. The Creed was delivered to the *competentes* eight days before Easter, as was established in the Council of Agde, canon 12:

‘It was also decided that in all churches the Creed should be publicly delivered to the *competentes* on the same day, namely eight days before the Sunday of the Resurrection.’

This handing over of the Creed is nothing other than an exposition of the mysteries contained in it.

Theodulphus says that the Creed of our faith was composed by the apostles. Besides the Rufinus and Isidore cited above, this is confirmed by Saint Jerome in his letter to Pammachius against the errors of John of Jerusalem:

‘In the Creed of our faith and hope, which was handed down by the apostles, it is not written on paper and with ink,’ and so forth.

Chapter 7: Theodulphus explains the faith contained in the Creed. But when he says that Christ is not the adopted Son of God, he shows himself to be orthodox and not to agree with the heresy that arose in Spain in his time, which Elipandus, bishop of Toledo, and Felix, bishop of Urgel, defended by asserting that Christ was the adopted Son of God. Alcuin refuted them in many books.

Theodulphus says that Christ was born from the Holy Spirit because this was once written in certain copies of the Creed, as may be seen in Saint Augustine, books I and II *On the Creed*, and in Rufinus’s *Explanation of the Creed*. But Theodulphus immediately makes his meaning clear: ‘That is, with the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, the Son of God assumed a true body for himself from the Virgin.’ These words, ‘that is, the Son of God,’ are corrupt, and should read, ‘who is the Son of God.’

It should also be noted that below he writes that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. In this too he shows himself orthodox, especially since in his time a question had arisen concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit through John, a monk of Jerusalem, who denied that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. For this reason Charlemagne, in the year of the Lord 809, convened a council of bishops at Aachen and sent Bishop Bernhard and Adalard, abbot of Corbie, to Pope Leo III to settle this question, as Eginhard writes in the *Deeds of Charlemagne*, as does a certain monk of Angoulême in the *Life of Charlemagne*, an anonymous author in the *Life of the same emperor*, and the *Annals of Fulda* under the year mentioned above.”

## Chapter 8

Chapter 8 deals with the scrutiny—that is, the examination, as Saint Augustine calls it—of those who were to be baptized. In former times baptism was not administered rashly; rather, the life and intention of those seeking baptism were examined with great care, as Tertullian testifies in *On Baptism*:

> Those whose duty it is should know that baptism is not to be entrusted rashly. “Give to everyone who asks you,” has its own heading and therefore belongs to almsgiving. Rather, this should be carefully considered: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor throw your pearls before swine.”

Saint Augustine mentions the scrutiny in *On Faith and Works*, where he says:

> Their character is examined on the very days on which they are catechized and exorcized; they are examined, exorcized, examined.

See also the same author, *On the Catechizing of the Uninstructed*.

Theodulphus adds:

> For the Church has been accustomed to preserve this practice for a certain number of days, [Col. 0371A] etc.

In these words he is speaking of the *competentes*, who gave in their names on Palm Sunday and were required to undergo the scrutiny, as we have explained above. They went to the church with bowed heads, prostrate in sackcloth and barefoot; they were breathed upon and exorcized; they renounced Satan, his pomps, and his works; the Creed was handed over to them—that is, it was explained; fasts were imposed upon them, which they were to observe until the day of baptism, together with abstinence from their wives. All this will become clear from the passages of Saint Augustine quoted below, first from Book II of *On the Creed to the Catechumens*, chapter 1:

> What is it, dearly beloved, that has been celebrated in you? What is it that has been done around you this night, which was not done on the preceding nights, so that you were brought out one by one from secret places into the presence of the whole Church? There, with your heads bowed—heads that had previously been lifted up wrongly—the examination was celebrated in you amid humility of feet and the spreading of sackcloth, and the proud devil was driven out from you while the humble Most High, Christ, was invoked over you. Thus you were all humble, and humbly you asked, praying, singing psalms, and saying: “Test me, O God, and know my heart.” He tested and examined the hearts of his servants.

And in Book IV, chapter 1:

> All the sacraments that have been and are being performed in you through the ministry of God’s servants—by exorcisms, prayers, spiritual songs, breathings, sackcloth, the bowing of heads, humility of feet, and this fear, which should be sought above all security, etc.

And in *On Faith and Works*, chapter 6:

> They certainly would not have been admitted if, during those very days in which, after giving in their names, they were to receive the same grace and were being cleansed by abstinence, fasts, and exorcisms, they had declared that they intended to have intercourse with their lawful and true wives and would observe no continence during those few solemn days.

This passage mentions the handing over of the Creed. The handing over of the Creed is discussed in Book II of *On the Creed*, chapter 1:

> Thus, after the household of the Redeemer had been cleansed, it received the remedy of the Creed against the venom of the ancient serpent.

And in Book IV, chapter 1:

> You have also received the Creed, the protection of the woman in labor against the poisons of the serpent.

The renunciation of the devil is mentioned in Book I of *On the Creed to the Catechumens*, chapter 1:

> If your help is in his name, let us renounce the devil, his pomps, and his angels. You have heard this, and you too have professed that you renounce the devil, his pomps, and his angels.

Tertullian also mentions repentance before baptism at the end of *On Baptism*:

> Those who are about to enter baptism ought to pray with frequent prayers, fasts, kneelings, and vigils, together with confession of all their former sins.

The Fourth Council of Carthage, canon 85, says:

> Let those who are to be baptized give in their names, and for a long time remain under abstinence from wine and meat, etc.

Here I think *aliquandiu*—“for some time”—should be read instead of *diu*, “for a long time.”

[Note: In the latest recension and edition of the Councils, *diu* has been retained, although *aliquandiu* seems preferable.]

For Saint Augustine, in chapter 6 of *On Faith and Works*, says:

> During those few solemn days.

Saint Isidore agrees with him in Book I of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 27, when he says that the *competentes* were created on Palm Sunday. These were the persons subjected to exorcisms and similar penance, as can be seen in Saint Augustine at the same chapter. It is therefore perfectly clear that this penance was not of long duration. Tertullian sufficiently indicates this in the passage cited, when he says *τὸ ingressuros*—“those who are about to enter.”

Among the Easterners, or Greeks, this penance lasted forty days, as is clear from the preface of Saint Cyril to those catechumens who had given in their names in order to receive baptism:

> **Πολλή σοι ἡ προθεσμία, τεσσαράκοντα ἡμερῶν μετάνοιαν ἔχεις.**  
> “The period prescribed for you is long; you have forty days of repentance.”

Saint Cyril is speaking there to those catechumens who, having given in their names, were seeking baptism. He warns them with what purity of heart they ought to receive this sacrament and urges them, if they have not completely cast off the will to sin, to remove every affection for sin entirely while they have the prescribed forty-day period for repentance.

Nor should it be said that the baptism of such persons was postponed until Pentecost, so that they might learn wisdom, and that these forty days should consequently be understood as the forty days preceding Pentecost. This cannot be the meaning merely because Saint Cyril recited the preface a few days before Easter. The former interpretation is preferable:

1. Because it cannot be proved that Saint Cyril recited such a preface shortly before Easter.

2. If we reckon at least one week before Easter, fifty-seven days would intervene from the beginning of that week until Pentecost.

3. The word *προθεσμία*, meaning a prescribed or appointed period, is opposed to the contrary interpretation. For if a period of forty days was prescribed for catechumens seeking baptism so that they might be instructed and perform penance, this indicates that all those persons were subject to the prescription.

This period of forty days is further confirmed by Cyril himself. In Catechesis 1, exhorting those seeking baptism to put aside worldly things, he says:

> Put off these worldly things altogether; what you are leaving is small, but what is given by the Lord is great. Leave the present and believe in the future. You have passed through so many cycles of years, laboring vainly for the world: **Καὶ τεσσαράκοντα ἡμέρας οὐ σχολάσεις τῇ προσευχῇ** etc.  
> “And will you not devote forty days to prayer for the sake of your soul?”

In Catechesis 4, section 1, he says to the same persons:

> Before the handing over of the faith, it seems to me an excellent course to repeat briefly the principal necessary doctrines, lest the abundance of what must be said, **καὶ τὸ μεταξὺ διάστημα τῶν ἡμερῶν τῆς ἁγίας τεσσαρακοστῆς ἁπάσης**, that is, “the intervening period of all the days of the holy Quadragesima,” should bring forgetfulness of those matters of ours that are more substantial and worthy of thought.

This is confirmed by Catechesis 18, the last of those catecheses, where he writes:

> Concerning the holy and apostolic faith handed over to you for confession, we have said, as much as catechesis could contain, by the grace of God, **ἐν ταῖς διελθούσαις ταύταις τῆς τεσσαρακοστῆς ἡμέραις**, that is, “during these past days of the Quadragesima.”

A little later he adds:

> **ἐνεστώσης τὸ λοιπὸν τῆς ἁγίας τοῦ Πάσχα ἡμέρας** etc., that is, “with the holy day of Easter now approaching, and your regeneration in Christ.”

Since the preface mentioned above belongs to the catecheses just cited, it is an indication that it was recited at the beginning of those forty days that were granted to those seeking baptism for fuller instruction and the performance of penance. These days seem to have begun shortly before the Lenten fast.

Although, then, Saint Cyril makes it clear that forty days were prescribed for the Greek *competentes*, Saint John Chrysostom mentions only thirty days in his first catechesis:

> **Ἀλλ᾽ ἔτι τριάκοντα ἡμέρας.**  
> “But thirty days still remain.”

And the King of heaven, not Pharaoh, will call us to our heavenly homeland.

A little later, speaking of the same period of years, he says:

> Why, then, did the Fathers legislate that throughout the whole preceding year, **ἐν τούτῳ τῷ καιρῷ μυσταγωγεῖσθαι τὰ τέκνα τῆς Ἐκκλησίας**, that is, “at this time—the thirty days—they should initiate the children of the Church into the more secret mysteries”?

But there was not one universal practice everywhere.

During these days such *competentes* confessed all the sins of their former life, as is evident from Saint Cyril, Catechesis 1:

> **Ἐξομολόγησαι τὰ πεπραγμένα τὰ ἐν λόγῳ, τὰ ἐν ἔργω, τὰ ἐν νυκτὶ, τὰ ἐν ἡμέρᾳ.**  
> “Confess your deeds, whether in word or in action, whether by night or by day.”

We have already noted the same practice among the Latins from Tertullian. But this confession, like the penance, was not sacramental, since no sacrament is conferred before baptism, as theologians commonly teach. Both confession and penance were merely a kind of preparation for receiving baptism properly and as one ought.

There was another form of penance for catechumens—whether perfected or imperfect—if they happened to commit some capital crime during the course of their catechumenate. This is discussed in the First Council of Nicaea, canon 14, and in the Council of Neocaesarea, canon 5.

## Chapter 9

Chapter 9 explains how the scrutiny is performed, namely by touching the nostrils and ears with saliva. This is done according to the practice of the Roman Church, as can be seen in Alcuin, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, in the chapter on Holy Saturday, where he explains the Roman rite for administering baptism:

> Then he touches his nostrils and ears with spittle and says into the right ear, “EPHPHETA,” which means “Be opened”; and to the nostrils, “For the fragrance of sweetness.”

According to another practice, described by the same Alcuin in the chapter cited, only the ears and nostrils are touched, without spittle, as in Saint Ambrose, chapter 1 of *On Those Who Have Been Initiated into the Mysteries*:

> Open your ears, therefore, and draw in the good fragrance of eternal life, which has been breathed into you through the gift of the sacraments. This is what we signified to you when, celebrating the mystery of opening, we said, “EPHPHETA,” that is, “Be opened.”

He adds the reason:

> So that each person coming to grace might know what he was being asked and remember what he ought to answer.

And in Book I of *On the Sacraments*, chapter 1:

> Therefore the priest touched your ears, so that your ears might be opened to the priest’s speech and discourse.

A little later:

> Therefore, because of the grace of the work and the gift, the bishop does not touch the mouth but the nostrils. Why the nostrils? So that you may receive the good fragrance of eternal devotion, so that you may say: “For we are the good fragrance of Christ to God,” as the holy Apostle said, and so that the fragrance of faith and devotion may be full in you.

The Greeks do not have this rite, for it is not found in their *Euchologion*, nor do the Greek Fathers mention it. Theodulphus mentions only the touching of the nostrils and ears when discussing the scrutiny, as though that alone were used. But the breathing upon the candidate, exorcism, renunciation, and anointing of the shoulders and breast are also rites of the scrutiny.

There were seven scrutinies. The first began on the third Sunday of Quadragesima, according to the Roman Order and the Codex of Ratoldus, or on the fourth Sunday of Quadragesima, according to the Rheims Codex; the last was performed on Holy Saturday. They took place during the solemn celebration of Mass, but after the readings the persons to be baptized were dismissed together with the other catechumens.

Formerly in Spain this scrutiny was performed twenty days before baptism, as decreed in the Second Council of Braga, canon 1:

> If this has not been done, they must teach the uninstructed and by every means prescribe this, as the ancient canons command: that twenty days before baptism the catechumens should come together for the cleansing of exorcism, and that during those twenty days all the catechumens should be specifically taught the Creed, namely, “I believe in God the Father almighty.”

When the council orders the catechumens to come to the church for the cleansing of exorcism, it is undoubtedly speaking of the scrutiny, since exorcism must be counted among the principal scrutinies.

In the time of Saint Augustine and Saint Isidore, however, the scrutiny began on Palm Sunday, as we explained above. Among the Greeks it lasted forty or thirty days, as we noted above.

During the scrutinies the males were separated from the females, as is stated in the Codices mentioned above and in Saint Cyril of Jerusalem’s preface:

> **Ἄνδρες μετὰ ἀνδρῶν, καὶ γυναῖκες μετὰ γυναικῶν.**  
> “Males with males, and females with females.”

The males were placed on the right side and the females on the left, as the cited Codices testify.

When they were beside the fonts, those immediately about to be baptized stood trembling, with downcast faces and holding one another by the hands, as stated in the Constantinopolitan synod under Mena, session 5, in the formal document against Peter, bishop of Apamea:

> **Ἵστανται τὸ σχῆμα τοῦ ἀγῶνος ἀποπληροῦντες, κάτω νεύοντες καὶ τὰς χεῖρας συμπλέκοντες, καὶ τρέμοντες εὐκαίρως** etc.  
> “They stand, fulfilling the form of the contest, bowing downward, holding one another by the hands, trembling at the proper time, and resisting the devil’s envious cunning.”

In the Latin version it reads “not resisting,” but the negation is absent from the Greek.

In the same chapter of Theodulphus, these words should be noted:

> “By the members of the body are understood the spiritual powers of the soul.”

Thus Vincentius Victor, who correctly believed that God is not corporeal, when the names of bodily members attributed throughout Scripture to God were brought against him, rightly said that incorporeal powers were to be understood by them.

But when he said that the human soul was corporeal and supported his opinion by certain names of bodily members attributed in Scripture to the human soul, Saint Augustine, arguing against him in Book IV of *On the Soul and Its Origin*, turns the solution against him and begins:

> Since you most correctly defend the proposition that God is not corporeal, what reason is there, then, why these names of bodily members do not make God corporeal for you, but do make the soul corporeal? Or, when these things are said of a creature, are they to be taken literally, whereas when they are said of the Creator, they are figurative and metaphorical?

The following words in the same chapter should also be noted:

> “Since, therefore, the Divinity assumed man.”

He spoke similarly above, in chapter 7:

> “He assumed a perfect man of our nature.”

This follows the common manner of speech among the holy Fathers, who say that the Son of God assumed man, without thereby asserting two persons in Christ. By *man* they understand nothing other than human nature.

Accordingly, Theodulphus immediately adds in the same chapter 7:

> “And the Word became flesh by assuming humanity,” that is, human nature.

When he says “perfect man,” he does so because of Apollinaris, who, as Vincent of Lérins writes in chapter 17 of *For the Antiquity and Universality of the Catholic Faith*, said that in the flesh of our Savior there was either no human soul at all or, at any rate, one without mind and reason. Saint Paulinus writes similarly in Letter 25 that Christ had a man assumed by God, possessing a soul empty of the human mind, such as that of cattle and beasts of burden. If this were so, Christ would not be a perfect man.

Finally, in this chapter 9 it should be noted that when Theodulphus says that, from the commixture of two substances in the one person of the Son of God, a *collyrium* was made, he does not mean that the two substances in Christ, divine and human, were mixed together and coalesced into a third substance, as ordinarily happens with mixtures; that would be blasphemous. Rather, he used the word “commixture” improperly, on account of the allegory derived from the collyrium.

For above, in chapter 7, he said that the Son of God became a true man and assumed a perfect man of our nature, according to the interpretation given above, and that the Word became flesh by assuming humanity, not by changing the divinity. All these statements are opposed to a commixture of the two substances and are far removed from the heresy of the Monophysites.

Theologians do admit composition in the person of Christ, but they deny commixture. See Saint Thomas, Part III, question 2, article 4. Boethius argues at length against this commixture in *On the Two Natures and One Person of Christ*.

## Chapter 10

Chapter 10 concerns the anointing of the breast and shoulders, which we have discussed sufficiently at length above.

## Chapter 11

Chapter 11 concerns the renunciation by which the catechumen renounces the devil, his works, and his pomps.

Optatus of Milevis mentions this renunciation in Book V *Against Parmenianus*. Tertullian says in *On the Spectacles*:

> When we enter the water and profess the Christian faith in the words of its law, we publicly declare with our mouth that we have renounced the devil, his pomp, and his angels.

And in *On the Crown of the Soldier*:

> As we are about to enter the water, and somewhat earlier in the church under the hand of the bishop, we publicly declare that we renounce the devil, his pomp, and his angels.

Saint Augustine says in Book II of *On the Creed to the Catechumens*:

> You have heard this; you have professed that you renounce the devil . . . . . . . . and his angels.

Saint Cyprian, in Letter 7 and frequently elsewhere, speaks, for the sake of brevity, of renouncing the world:

> “We had renounced the world,” he says, “when we were baptized.”

In Theodulphus the renunciation is of the devil, his pomps, and his works, as also in the Rheims and Ratoldus Codices.

In Book VI of *On the Governance of God*, Salvianus speaks of renouncing the devil, his pomps, spectacles, and works:

> For what is, he says, the first saving confession of Christians in baptism? What else, namely, except that they declare that they renounce the devil, his pomps, spectacles, and works?

A little later:

> “I renounce,” you say, “the devil, his pomps, spectacles, and works.”

Here he takes “pomps” and “spectacles” as one and the same thing. Saint Augustine and Tertullian, cited above, and Saint Cyril, who will be cited shortly, interpret the devil’s pomps as spectacles—that is, the wantonness of the theater, the cruelty of the amphitheater, and the shouting and madness of the circus.

The renunciation is commonly made three times, as stated in chapter 2 of Saint Dionysius’ *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, in the Greek *Euchologion*, and in the Rheims and Ratoldus Codices.

Saint Cyril, in Mystagogical Catechesis 1, adds a fourth renunciation, namely, of the worship of the devil:

> Hear also what is said with the hand extended as though toward one who is present: **ἀποτάσσομαί σοι Σατανᾷ**, that is, “I renounce you, Satan.”

A little later:

> You are then taught to add the second part of the renunciation, **καὶ πᾶσι τοῖς ἔργοις σου**, that is, “and all your works.”

And later:

> Then you say: **Καὶ πάσῃ τῇ πομπῇ αὐτοῦ**—read *σου*—“and all your pomp.”

And further:

> You also say: **Καὶ πάσῃ σου λατρείᾳ**, that is, “and all your worship.”

By the devil’s worship he understands every honor offered to idols, omens, divination, magical arts, and wicked sacrifices.

In Saint Ambrose, Book I of *On the Sacraments*, chapter 2, there are only two renunciations:

> When he asked you, “Do you renounce the devil and his works?” what did you answer? “I renounce.” “Do you renounce the world and its works?” What did you answer? “I renounce.” Remember your pledge, and never let the sequence of your pledge slip from your memory.

These final words confirm the twofold renunciation that then existed in the Ambrosian Church.

The person making the renunciation turned toward the West, as Saint Dionysius writes in the chapter cited above, as does Saint Jerome, who will be cited shortly, and Saint Cyril in Mystagogical Catechesis 1:

> First you entered the portico of the baptistery, **καὶ πρὸς τὰς δυσμᾶς ἑστῶτες** etc., that is, “standing facing the West,” etc.

The same is found in the Greek *Euchologion*. In Dionysius, the person renouncing Satan thrusts out his hand; in Cyril and in the *Euchologion*, he extends it.

After the renunciation had been made, he turned toward the East, as is clear from the same chapter of Dionysius; from Saint Jerome, in his commentary on Amos 6:

> Hence, in the mysteries, we first renounce him who is in the West and dies for us together with our sins; and thus, turning toward the East, we make a covenant with the Sun of righteousness and promise that we will serve him.

The same is found in Saint Cyril’s cited catechesis, where he gives the reason for this rite. When the person to be baptized has renounced Satan, the prince of darkness, and broken the former covenants, he turns toward the East, where Paradise is, which God planted in the East.

Thus turned, he raised his hands upward, as Saint Dionysius teaches in the chapter cited and Saint Basil in his exhortation to baptism, where he says:

> **Χείρας ἆραι εἰς οὐρανόν**, that is, “to raise the hands to heaven.”

In this way he professed that he would serve Christ and cling to him. The Greeks call this **συντάσεσθαι**, as do Saint Dionysius, the *Euchologion*, and Saint Gregory the Theologian, who says in his Oration on Baptism:

> **Ὅλῃ θεότητι συντασσόμενος**, that is, “joined and attached to the whole Divinity.”

Saint Basil, in the cited oration, says:

> **Θεῷ συνθέσθαι**, that is, “to make a covenant with God,”

unless it should be read *συντάσσεσθαι*, whose opposite is *ἀποτάσσεσθαι*, that is, “to renounce” or “to abjure,” in the authors mentioned above and in Palladius’ *Lausiac History*.

## 384

After these rites had been duly performed, the person to be baptized recited the Creed, as stated in the Greek *Euchologion*, following an ancient practice found in Saint Cyril, Mystagogical Catechesis 1:

> Then you were admonished to say: **Πιστεύω εἰς τὸν Πατέρα, καὶ εἰς τὸν Υἱὸν, καὶ εἰς τὸ Πνεῦμα ἅγιον, καὶ εἰς βάπτισμα μετανοίας**, that is: “I believe in the Father, and in the Son, and in the Holy Spirit, and in the baptism of repentance.”

When he adds, “Concerning these matters we have discussed more fully in the preceding catecheses, insofar as divine grace permitted,” he sufficiently indicates that the entire Creed was to be recited, since above, in Catechesis 4, he expounded it in full.

The same is known from Salvianus, Book V of *On the Governance of God*:

> “I renounce,” you say, “the devil, his pomps, spectacles, and works.” And what afterward? “I believe,” you say, “in God the Father almighty and in Jesus Christ, his Son.” Thus the devil is first renounced, so that one may believe.

And from Saint Augustine, Book *On the Soul and Its Origin*, chapter 10:

> Therefore, when they are baptized, they render the Creed and answer the questions put to them.

This is how Optatus should be understood in Book V *Against Parmenianus*:

> Against us sinners, as you wish, let us question another gentile whether he renounces the devil and believes, etc., and let him say, “I renounce and I believe.”

And Rufinus, in *On the Exposition of the Creed*:

> The ancient custom is preserved there: those who are about to receive the grace of baptism publicly—that is, with the people of the faithful listening—render the Creed.

Theodulphus calls this Creed the profession of the Holy Trinity.

In the Greek *Euchologion*, after the renunciations and the answers to several questions, the person to be baptized recites the Creed.

In Saint Dionysius, chapter 2 of the *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, he makes a threefold profession, which is nothing other than the recitation of the Creed.

In the Rheims Codex the priest himself recites the Creed:

> Then you touch his breast and the space between his shoulders with exorcized oil, and, calling him by name, say to each one: “Do you renounce Satan?” Response: “I renounce.” “And all his works?” Response: “I renounce.” “And all his pomps?” Response: “I renounce.” “And I anoint you with the oil of salvation in Christ Jesus our Lord.” Then you recite the Creed, placing your hand upon their heads.

This imposition of the hand is also found in Dionysius, in the chapter cited, after the threefold profession:

> After he has professed three times, **ἐπευξάμενος εὐλογεῖ, καὶ χειροτονεῖ**, that is, “having prayed, he blesses and lays on his hand.”

## Chapter 12

Chapter 12 explains what the pomps and works of the devil are, and says that by them the seven capital sins are understood.

## Chapter 13

When chapter 13 says that the blood and water flowing from Christ’s side signify the two principal sacraments of the Church, by the blood “by which we are consecrated” it understands the Eucharist, which formerly was administered together with baptism.

Some understand the water and blood as all the sacraments; others understand them as the Church. See Cyril, Catechesis 13.

The following words occur in the same chapter:

> “For when God has been invoked, the Holy Spirit descends from heaven,” etc.

Tertullian says in *On Baptism*:

> Thus all waters, through the privilege of their original source, obtain the sacrament of sanctification when God has been invoked. For the Spirit immediately comes down from heaven and rests upon the waters, sanctifying them from himself; and thus, after they have been sanctified, they absorb the power of sanctifying.

Here these two authors say that the water is sanctified through the invocation of God—that is, through the form—and that through it the water receives the power of sanctification.

The same chapter mentions the threefold immersion, which we discussed above. Those who were baptized were formerly immersed in the font in such a way that the entire head was submerged.

Saint Jerome says in *Dialogue Against the Luciferians*:

> For they also observed many other things that are preserved in the churches by tradition, as though they had been commanded by the authority of written law—for example, immersing the head three times in the bath.

Saint Cyril sufficiently indicates this in Catechesis 17, when he says:

> **Ὥσπερ γὰρ ὁ ἐνδύνων ἐν τοῖς ὕδασι καὶ βαπτιζόμενος πανταχόθεν ὑπὸ τῶν ὕδατων περιβάλλεται.**  
> “For just as one who enters the waters and is baptized is surrounded on every side by the waters.”

## 385

Finally, what he says about the baptismal font, or baptistery, should be noted. A similar description is found in Saint Isidore, Book XV of the *Etymologies*, chapter 4:

> The font in shrines is the place of those who are regenerated. In it seven steps are formed as a mystery of the Holy Spirit: three in the descent and three in the ascent. The seventh is also the fourth; that is, it is like the Son of Man, extinguishing the furnace of fire, the support of the feet, and the foundation of the water, in which the fullness of divinity dwells bodily.

From these passages of Isidore and Theodulphus it should be noted that formerly baptisteries had seven steps: three by which one ascended to it and three by which one descended into it. The seventh was in the middle of the baptistery, where the font itself was established. There stood those whose services were necessary for the baptism; hence it is called “the foundation of the water” and “the support of the feet.”

Above the font hung a golden or silver dove representing the Holy Spirit, as can be seen in the Constantinopolitan synod under Mena, session 5, in the petition of the clergy and monks of Antioch to John the patriarch, etc.:

> He also presumed this for himself: golden and silver doves, suspended in the form of the Holy Spirit above the sacred baths and altars, he appropriated to himself along with other things.

## Chapter 14

Chapter 14 concerns the white garments with which the neophytes are clothed after the sacred bath. We have discussed these sufficiently at length above.

## Chapter 15

Chapter 15 concerns the anointing with chrism performed by priests on the crown of those recently baptized. We have also discussed this above.

Since many of the Fathers speak rather confusedly about the anointing with chrism, without distinguishing between the anointing performed by a priest on the crown and that performed by a bishop on the forehead, some report that the latter was instituted by Pope Saint Sylvester, as stated in the *Pontifical of Damasus*, so that the priest might anoint the person who had been lifted from the water with chrism.

I say that all the Fathers who spoke of the anointing with chrism before Saint Sylvester are to be understood as speaking of the anointing performed by the bishop on the forehead, which pertains to the sacrament of confirmation, even if they sometimes use the word “oil.” In those passages, whether in the Greek or Latin Fathers, “oil” is used for ointment or chrism.

Second, it should be noted that, since the Greeks lack the anointing performed by a priest on the crown, all their ancient Fathers, when they speak of the anointing with chrism, are to be understood as speaking of the anointing performed by the bishop on the forehead.

Third, because mention of the anointing with chrism performed by a priest on the crown is rare among the holy Fathers, I say that when they speak simply and without qualification of chrism or its anointing, they are to be understood as speaking of the chrism or anointing belonging to the sacrament of confirmation—especially when no circumstance indicates that they were speaking either of the anointing with chrism used by priests or of the anointing by which certain heretics returning to the Church are reconciled.

Nor do the various mystical interpretations pose an obstacle. The same interpretation is not always assigned to the same anointing; rather, the interpretations are often applied indifferently, as also happens with the anointing that precedes baptism.

To remove every ambiguity, it should be noted that formerly, when the bishop baptized—as happened very frequently, for priests and deacons baptized more rarely—he immediately administered the sacrament of confirmation, anointing the neophyte on the forehead with chrism. This can be seen in Saint Ambrose, Cyril, Dionysius, Severus, the author of the *Questions* among the works of Saint Justin, Question 137 *To the Orthodox*, and others.

The neophyte was not anointed on the crown by a priest, since this sort of anointing was instituted because of the absence of a bishop, although later it was applied to the neophyte lifted from the font, to be followed shortly afterward by the anointing with chrism on the forehead by the bishop. This can be seen in our manuscript Sacramentaries and in the Roman Order.

I have noted this because I observe that some more recent writers confuse the anointing of the crown with the anointing of the forehead in passages of the Fathers commonly cited by treatise writers.

## 386 — Chapter 16

Chapter 16 concerns the mystical veil with which the head of the newly baptized is covered after the anointing of the crown. Jesse of Amiens discusses it in his *Letter on Baptism*, as does Alcuin in Book *On Divine Offices*, in the chapter on Holy Saturday:

> Then the head is anointed with sacred chrism and covered with a mystical veil, so that the person may understand that he bears the diadem of the kingdom and the dignity of the priesthood, according to the Apostle: “You are a chosen race, a royal and priestly people, offering yourselves to the living God as a holy and acceptable sacrifice.”

But when Theodulphus says that this veil signifies the covering of a priestly head, he seems to be referring to the priests of the ancient law, since in his time the ministers of the new law did not yet use a covering for the head in sacred rites.

## Chapter 17

Chapter 17 treats the imposition of hands, the dignity of chrismation, and the significance of the number seven, especially the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit.

These words—“yet not to mark the forehead with the same oil,” etc.—clearly indicate that chrismation is distinct from the imposition of hands. Optatus of Milevis makes this sufficiently clear in Book IV *Against Parmenianus*:

> When he had been washed and was held in John’s hands, the order of the mystery followed; the Father fulfilled what the Son had requested and what the Holy Spirit had announced. Heaven was opened when God the Father anointed him; spiritual oil immediately descended in the form of a dove and settled upon his head. Hence he began to be called Christ, when he was anointed by God the Father. And lest the laying on of hands should seem to be lacking, the voice of God was added from the cloud, saying: “This is my Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him.”

What is said here about the number seven seems to have been taken from Saint Gregory, chapter 6 of his exposition of Book I of *Job*, and Homily 7 on Ezekiel.

What is said about the Jubilee on account of the number fifty, which consists of the unit and the number seven repeated seven times, is also said by Saint Augustine, Letter 119 to Januarius, and Saint Basil, Book *On the Holy Spirit to Amphilochius*, chapter 27, concerning Pentecost—that is, concerning the number fifty that lies between Christ’s resurrection and the coming of the Holy Spirit.

Finally, Theodulphus adds many excellent things concerning the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and rightly so, because it is proper to the sacrament of confirmation, in a distinctive and especially excellent manner, to confer the gifts of the Holy Spirit upon the faithful soul. Through their benefit the Christian state is brought to its fullest perfection.

The sacrament of confirmation perfects the Christian person, as we have taught above from the holy Fathers (*Roman Catechism*, Part 2, chapter 3, section 19). For confirmation is credited with perfecting the grace of baptism. Those who have become Christians through baptism are like infants newly born and still possess a certain tenderness and weakness; afterward, through the sacrament of chrism, they become stronger against all the assaults of the flesh, the world, and the devil, and their minds are completely confirmed in faith so that they may confess and glorify the name of the Lord Jesus Christ.

This sacrament received its name because, through its power, God confirms in us what he began to accomplish through baptism and brings us to the perfection of Christian maturity.

It does not merely confirm but also increases grace. Melchiades bears witness to this as follows:

> The Holy Spirit, who descended upon the waters of baptism in a saving influx, grants fullness in the font for innocence; in confirmation he bestows increase for grace.

Moreover, it does not merely increase grace but increases it in a remarkably powerful way. All these things show how great are the dignity, usefulness, and necessity of this sacrament.

Therefore those who, whenever it can conveniently be done, neglect to receive this sacrament commit a grave sin; and bishops sin more gravely if they do not exercise every diligence to ensure that those entrusted to them receive it.

But those who write that anointing or chrismation on the crown of the head by a presbyter has the same efficacy as chrismation on the forehead by a bishop are greatly mistaken. For this chrismation of the crown is not a sacrament; it cannot confer grace by the work performed (*ex opere operato*), nor can it bestow the Holy Spirit. Rather, it is given so that the baptized person may understand that from that day he is joined to Christ the Head as a member, incorporated into his body, and that for this reason a Christian is called from Christ, while Christ is called from the chrism, as is stated in the *Roman Catechism* (Part 2, chapter 2, section 72). Theodulf likewise teaches, chapter 15:

> Accordingly, the heads of the baptized are anointed with chrism so that, having been anointed for the kingdom and priesthood of the Church, they may receive the prerogative of the Christian name and may become members of the one who redeemed them and is their Head.

But enough on this subject. See more in the learned Francis Hallier’s *Defense of the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, chapter 2.

In the final chapter Theodulf discusses the body and blood of Christ, which formerly were received together with baptism, even by infants, as we have explained at length above. This is also evident from the work of Theodore of Antioch *Against Those Who Assert That Human Beings Sin by Nature, Not by Will*, in Photius’s *Bibliotheca*, no. 177, as well as from the question of mixing water in the chalice. The following words, “Therefore to offer this sacrifice from the remnants of the sacrifices,” etc., are corrupt. With the redundant word “to offer” deleted, they should read:

> Therefore the Church celebrates this mystery, after abandoning and bringing to an end the former sacrifices and victims, etc.

The text next deals with mixing water with wine in the chalice when it is consecrated. On this subject Saint Cyprian writes in Epistle 63 against those who performed the mystery of Christ’s blood with water alone, without wine. These people were later called Hydroparastatae in canon 32 of the Sixth Synod. There were others—namely, the Armenians—who used only wine in the mysteries of Christ’s blood; the same synod condemns them in the same canon. Having made these observations concerning Theodulf, let us return to our subject.

**335. “Glory in the highest.”** This is prescribed in the Council of Rouen, cited by Orderic Vitalis, *Ecclesiastical History*, book IV, where the Mass of this Holy Saturday is under discussion:

> On account of its reverence, “Glory to God in the highest” and “Alleluia” are sung.

[Note: [Col. 0379D] This angelic hymn, as it is now sung, is found in its entirety in the Gallican Sacramentary of D. J. Mabillon’s Italian Museum, volume I, part 2, column 281.]

**336. “And with your spirit.”** This is the people’s response from the ancient rite of the Church. When the pontiff invokes a blessing upon them, they in turn invoke a blessing upon him, as can be seen in the First Council of Braga, canon 21:

> And the people are to respond: “And with your spirit.”

Likewise in Saint John Chrysostom, Homily 18 on the Second Epistle to the Corinthians:

> Ἐπ’ αὐτῶν πάλιν φρικωδεστάτων μυστηρίων ἐπεύχεται ὁ ἱερεὺς τῷ λαῷ, καὶ ἐπεύχεται ὁ λαὸς τῷ ἱερεῖ· τὸ γὰρ, Μετὰ πνεύματός σου, οὐδέν ἐστιν, ἢ τοῦτο.

That is:

> In the midst of those most awe-inspiring mysteries, the priest invokes a blessing upon the people, and the people invoke a blessing upon the priest; for “With your spirit” means nothing other than this.

In the liturgies of Saints James, Mark, and Peter, this response of the people is sometimes expressed in the dative case: Καὶ τῷ πνεύματί σου, that is, “And to your spirit.” Saint Germanus, patriarch of Constantinople, also recognizes it in his *Mystical Theory*, where he explains it as follows:

> Καὶ τῷ πνεύματί σου, τουτέστι τὴν πρὸς σε ἀδιαίρετον ἕνωσιν δὸς ἡμῖν, ἵνα τῷ πνεύματι εἰρηνεύοντες, ἀχώριστοι τυγχάνωμεν.

That is:

> “And to your spirit,” that is, “Grant us indivisible union with you, so that, being at peace in spirit, we may remain inseparable.”

And Saint John Chrysostom, Homily 33 on Matthew:

> And when I say, “Peace be with you,” then you say, “Καὶ τῷ πνεύματί σου,” that is, “And to your spirit.”

**337. “O God, who has made this most sacred night.”** This is found in Alcuin, because the office of Holy Saturday looks toward the night of the Lord’s Resurrection, as is stated in the Council of Rouen, cited by Orderic Vitalis, *Ecclesiastical History*, book IV. For on Friday and Saturday of Holy Week the sacrament of the body and blood of Christ is not celebrated, as is taught in the same council from the *Book of the Office*:

> The *Book of the Office* relates that during these two days the sacrament is not celebrated.

It calls these two days Friday and Saturday, during which the mourning and grief of the apostles are commemorated. The *Book of the Office* is an antiphoner, as Agobard teaches in his letter to the singers of Lyon.

**338. “Let them not sing the Offertory.”** Alcuin gives the reason in the chapter cited:

> The fact that after the Gospel the Offertory is not sung, and that the singers remain silent during the sacrifice, recalls the sacrifice—or the silence—of the women.

Moreover, in the Codex of Ratold there is a blessing of milk and honey in the following form:

> Bless, O Lord, this creature of milk and honey, etc., as in the Roman Order.

Then follows:

> Through whom, O Lord, you always create all good things.

This was done for the newly baptized, who after the holy washing were ordered to taste milk and honey as infants newly born. By this rite it was signified that Christians, having entirely put away malice, ought to embrace the simplicity of an infant. This can be seen in the order of the Ethiopians, as it is called. After those baptized have been sacredly anointed with chrism, one reads there:

> Then the deacon gives them milk and honey and says: “Unblemished milk and honey for regeneration. Amen.” The priest, however, says: “Unblemished milk and honey for regeneration through Jesus Christ. Amen.”

In Saint Jerome, *Dialogue Against the Luciferians*:

> As though in the washing, immerse the head three times; then, after emerging, let them taste beforehand the harmony of milk and honey, as a sign of infancy.

And in Tertullian, *On the Soldier’s Crown*:

> Thereafter, having received them, we taste the harmony of milk and honey.

This is the meaning to be given to the words of the Greek Council of Carthage, canon 40:

> Ἀπαρχὴ δὲ εἴτε μέλι, εἴτε γάλα, ὡς εἴωθεν, προσφερέσθω ἐν μιᾷ ἡμέρᾳ ἐθίμῳ εἰς τὸ τῶν νηπίων μυστήριον.

That is:

> Let the first fruits, whether honey or milk, be offered on the customary single day for the mystery of infants.

For this concerns the blessing of honey and milk at the altar. The words “for the mystery of infants” signify that the baptized are to taste milk and honey because, having laid aside all malice through baptism, they ought always to preserve the simplicity of infants. Another explanation is given in the blessing itself: the baptized, having left Egypt—that is, the world—enter the Church, a land flowing with honey and milk, that is, overflowing with every spiritual delight.

**339. “Nor the Lamb of God.”** Thus it is found in Alcuin. Note, however, that Vespers are absent here, just as they are absent from the codices of Rodradi and Rheims, in accordance with the ancient custom of which Alcuin writes in the chapter on Holy Saturday:

> On this night nothing is done among the Romans concerning the evening assembly, either before the Mass or after the Mass, because, according to Augustine and other teachers, this Saturday has no evening.

Nevertheless, this is found in the Codex of Abbot Ratold. After the episcopal blessing it reads:

> Meanwhile, while the people are receiving Communion, the cantor begins the Alleluia. Psalm: “Praise the Lord, all nations.” Antiphon at the Gospel: “But in the evening.” Psalm: “My soul magnifies.” After this the bishop rises from his seat, goes to the altar, and says the Collect: “Pour into us, O Lord, the Spirit of your love, so that those whom you have satisfied with the paschal sacraments you may by your mercy make harmonious. Through the Lord.” After this the deacon says: “Go, the Mass is ended.”

**340. “On the holy day of Easter.”** It is called Holy Easter out of reverence for the day. On this matter, consult our observations on the *Harmony of the Rules*, chapter 56, section 1. In the Codex of Ratold there is a complete paschal Mass here, with its rites and ceremonies, which we have placed in the appendix.

**341. “Who … by dying destroyed our death,” etc.**

[Note: [Col. 0379D] This Preface is much longer in the two Theodulf manuscripts and differs entirely from the Preface of Holy Saturday, of which only the beginning is found in the common printed editions. The *Contestatio*, or Preface, assigned to the day of Holy Easter in the often-mentioned Gallican Sacramentary is also entirely different from the printed versions. For Holy Saturday, however, the prescribed text is precisely the one now read: “You indeed, O Lord, at all times, but especially on this night, with glorious praise, when our Passover,” etc.]

Christ’s death destroyed our death, and his resurrection restored life. Corippus, *On the Praises of Justin the Younger*, book IV:

> By dying he trampled down death, and by rising  
> He himself gave life to all who believe in him.

And Ennodius, hymn 7, admirably writes:

> He slew it before the funeral,  
> Buried, he drove death away;  
> Death fell through the force of death,  
> Sing, ages, of what has been done.  
>   
> The funeral overcame Tartarus;  
> Though slain, he conquered the end.  
> From the place where it presumed joy,  
> Pale death now mourns.

**342. “He omitted.”** That is, “he dismissed,” as below in the final *Apology*:

> If through the fault of my lukewarmness or negligence they have contracted, or are contracting, any stain, omit it.

**343. “Let them hold fast the sacrament by living.”** That is, let them preserve sacramental grace by living rightly. This is a metonymy, the cause being put for the effect. For the sacrament is the cause of sacramental grace.

**344. “May he offer himself to you as a sacred victim,” etc.** Saint Paulinus writes admirably in Epistle 5 to Severus:

> For he placed and received his soul and his flesh for us; he is priest and victim, lamb and shepherd. For his sheep he was the shepherd, and for his shepherds he was slain as the lamb. The Lord himself is the victim of all priests: offering himself to the Father as a sacrifice for the reconciliation of all, he was both the victim of his priesthood and the priest of his victim.

**345. “May it continually remain in our minds.”** Through its effect and through devout affection.

**346. “Is born.”** Because whoever receives the body of Christ has life in himself, according to the passage in John 6: “Unless you eat,” etc., “you will not have life in yourselves.” In the Roman Missal it reads “is nourished.”

**347. “And he who gives you.”** There begins the third member of this blessing; therefore the word “Amen” should be placed before these words.

**348. “That you are angry.”** That is, “by which,” or “on account of which,” you are angry. This is a Hellenism.

**349. “He alone of all priests did not need the remission of sin.”** As in Hebrews 7:

> Such a high priest was fitting for us: holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners, etc.

**350. “Rather.”** Thus in the Codex of Rheims. Read “of the whole.”

**351. “May he perfect.”** That is, “may he make.” This usage occurs frequently in Cicero.

**352. “The Sunday of the octave of Easter.”** That is, “the Sunday of Easter’s octave,” or “on the octave of Easter.” The word *octavas* is indeclinable according to the usage of those times. Thus in ancient codices one often reads *Vitas Patrum*, that is, “Lives of the Fathers.” In the Codex of Rheims it reads *octabas*, with *b* for *u*, according to the ancient spelling custom, as we noted in the *Harmony of the Rules*. In the codices of Rodradi and Ratold the title here reads:

> On the Sunday after the White Garments.

In the Ambrosian Mass it is correctly written, “Sunday in the Deposited White Garments,” because on the preceding day the baptized removed their white garments. Alcuin, *On the Office of the Church*, chapter on Saturday in White Garments:

> Today those who had been baptized on Holy Saturday, having been clothed in white, are stripped of their white garments.

Therefore, when the Roman Missal and Breviary say “Sunday in white garments,” understand the word *deposited*.

**353. “Other paschal prayers.”** The codices vary here: in some there are more prayers, in others fewer.

**354. “May he reconcile us through that which is like our own,” etc.** That is, may he reconcile us through his humanity and absolve us through his divinity. The expression “through that which” (*quod*)—that is, “through which”—is Greek in form, like Virgil’s:

> “Like a god in face and shoulders,” etc.,

which was taken from Homer, *Iliad* B:

> Ὄμματα καὶ κεφαλὴν ἵκελος Διὶ τερπικεραύνῳ.

That is:

> “Like Zeus who delights in thunder, in eyes and head.”

Moreover, in the Codices of Ratold and Rodradi, in the appendix, and in the Codex of Rheims, the following is added:

> April 13: the feast of Saint Euphemia.

[Note: [Col. 0381D] The Gemetic manuscript and the two Theodulf manuscripts agree.]

This is the famous Euphemia, virgin and martyr of Chalcedon, whose feast is recorded on the same day in the manuscript Martyrology of the library of Corbie:

> April 13: at Chalcedon, the feast of Saint Euphemia, virgin and martyr.

The same is found in the calendar prefixed to the Codex of Ratold and in the manuscript Martyrology of Saint Jerome:

> April 13: at Chalcedon, the feast of Saint Euphemia.

In the small manuscript Martyrology at the end of the Codex of Rheims:

> April 13: at Chalcedon, the feast of Saint Euphemia.

In Rabanus’s Martyrology:

> On April 13, in the city of Chalcedon, the feast of Euphemia.

And in Notker’s Martyrology, on the same day:

> At Chalcedon, Saint Euphemia.

In the Novel of the Emperor Manuel her solemnity is recorded on June 11, the day on which she suffered martyrdom, as can be seen in the Greek *Menologion*. In the Roman Martyrology it is recorded on September 16.

In the same Codex of Ratold, the Mass of Saint Euphemia is followed by the Mass of the anniversary Easter, which is also found in the Codex of Rodradi, in the appendix, and in the Codex of Rheims.

Micrologus explains what the anniversary Easter is in his *On Ecclesiastical Observances*, chapter 56:

> The Romans call anniversary Easter almost an annual Easter, because formerly those who had been baptized at the preceding Easter gathered at the Church on the same day of the following year and solemnly celebrated the anniversary of their rebirth with offerings.

So he writes. I do not, however, think that this anniversary Easter was ordinarily celebrated on Saturday, the day on which they had been baptized, since only one Mass was celebrated on that day and night. Rather, I believe that this kind of Easter was celebrated after the Sunday of the White Garments, especially since in our manuscript codices its Mass is assigned only after that day.

[Note: [Col. 0381D] On the same day, the first Theodulf manuscript and the Gemetic manuscript note the feast of Saint Leo. In both Theodulf manuscripts and in the Gemetic manuscript there is also a Mass of Saint George the Martyr. The Codex of Cales omits all these feasts, indeed even the feast of Saint Mark. The same is true of Mabillon’s Gallican Sacramentary, in which there are very few Masses of the saints; we shall indicate them in their proper places.]

In the Codex of Rheims it reads:

> April 11: the feast of Saint Leo, pope.

This is Saint Leo I. Nothing concerning him, however, is found in the codices of Saint Eligius, Rodradi, or Ratold, nor in Pamelius.

**355. “May these blessed gifts sanctify us.”** This is a hypallage; that is, “may he sanctify us through these blessed gifts.”

**356. “Gifts.”** Thus in the printed editions, in the codices of Rodradi and Ratold, and in Pamelius. In the Roman Missal it reads “by the gift.”

**357. “April 25: the feast of Saint Mark.”** Thus in the printed editions, in which there is no mention of a litany.

[Note: [Col. 0382D] In our manuscripts, except for the Codex of Cales, a litany is mentioned. In the Gallican Sacramentary there occurs a Mass to be said for the litanies, and earlier one to be read for the litanies, but immediately before the Ascension. Pamelius, who mentions the Greater Litany, agrees with the Royal Swedish Codex. Where Pamelius reads *ad Pontem Olbi* (“at the bridge of Olbi”), the codex reads *Molbi*, by which perhaps the Milvian Bridge is meant. The Theodulf manuscript likewise reads *Molvi*.]

But in certain other manuscript codices of ours, as in Pamelius, the Greater Litany is noted on this day. Its office may be found among the Rogation observances.

In the Codices of Rheims and Ratold, Masses for the second and third days follow. In the Codex of Rheims three prayers for the fourth day are added. In those same codices of Rodradi, Rheims, and Ratold there is no Mass of Saint Mark, nor are there Rogation observances before the Ascension.

**358. “Might attain the palm of martyrdom.”** From this passage we learn that Saint Mark was a martyr. Pope Gelasius teaches this in the Roman Synod, as does Saint Gregory of Tours, *History*, book I, chapter 24:

> Then James, the brother of the Lord, and Mark the evangelist were crowned with glorious martyrdom for the name of Christ.

The same is clear from the Ambrosian Mass:

> O God, who consecrated this day of your evangelist and martyr Saint Mark, drenched in the rose-red blood of your martyrdom;

and from the Ethiopian Liturgy:

> And of Saint Mark the evangelist and martyr, and of Saint Stephen the archdeacon and first martyr.

Rabanus and Notker agree in their Martyrologies, where they also describe his martyrdom.

**359. “Of Saint Vitalis.”** In the Ambrosian Mass Saint Valeria is added, and the Mass is for several martyrs.

[Note: [Col. 0383D] In our codices there is mention only of Saint Vitalis.]

**360. “B. R.”** That is, “Seek the Blessing,” namely at the feast of the holy apostles Peter and Paul.

**361. “Of Saint Alexander,” etc.** In the Codex of Rheims, on the same day, there is a Mass of Saint Juvenal, which precedes the Mass of these saints. It is also found in the appendix to the Codex of Rodradi.

**362. “The Finding of the Holy Cross.”**

[Note: [Col. 0383D] The Gallican Sacramentary presents a Mass of the Finding of the Holy Cross, but one entirely different from the common version.]

The Greeks do not have this feast. No mention of it is made in their *Menologia*, nor in the decree of the Emperor Manuel Comnenus concerning feasts, preserved by Theodore Balsamon in his commentary on Photius’s *Nomocanon*, title 7, chapter 1.

**363. “You have revived the miracles of your Passion.”** At the finding of the cross, a dead man was brought near the Lord’s cross so that the cross might be distinguished from the others, and he came back to life. Likewise, at Christ’s Passion many bodies of saints were seen in the holy city, as Saint Paulinus testifies in Epistle 11:

> Finally, resurrection revealed the Lord’s cross; at the touch of the saving wood, death recoiled, the corpse was shaken, and the body was raised upright.

Severus Sulpicius writes the same in *History*, book II:

> After two crosses had first been brought near without effect, when the cross of Christ was touched, wondrous to relate, while all were trembling, the corpse was shaken and stood among the spectators.

So too does Sozomen, *Ecclesiastical History*, book II, chapter 1.

**364. “Who through the Passion of the cross,” etc.** In the codices of Rodradi and Rheims there is another, much longer Preface:

> Especially on this day, on which the glorious triumph of your only-begotten Son, hidden by the Jews, was found, etc.

Here the word “triumph” signifies Christ’s cross. Saint Ambrose uses it in this sense in his account of the death of Theodosius:

> He found the three crosses confused together, which the collapse had covered and the enemy had hidden; but Christ’s triumph could not be obliterated.

**365. “What is the breadth of that same cross,” etc.** This is from chapter 3 of the Epistle to the Ephesians. Saint Augustine explains the passage with reference to the cross in Tractate 118 on John:

> Its breadth is in the transverse beam, on which the hands of the one hanging are extended, and it signifies good works in the breadth of charity. Its length extends from the transverse beam to the ground, where the back and feet are fastened, and it signifies perseverance throughout the length of time until the end. Its height is at the top, where the transverse beam projects upward, and it signifies the heavenly end to which all works are directed. For all things that are done well and perseveringly in breadth and length are to be done for the sake of the height of divine rewards. Its depth is in the part that is fixed in the earth; there it is hidden and cannot be seen. Yet all visible and prominent things arise from it, just as all our good works proceed from the depth of God’s grace, which cannot be comprehended or judged.

**366. “He deemed it worthy to redeem.”** In the Codices of Rheims and Rodradi the following is added:

> You who are the tree of life, restorer of paradise.

**367. “The feast of Saint John,” etc.** This feast is not found in the printed editions.

[Note: [Col. 0383D] It is found in both Theodulf manuscripts and in the Gemetic manuscript. The same codices mention Saints Gordian and Epimachus, but not Saint Cyril and Saint Domitilla; below, however, a Mass of Saints Nereus, Achilleus, and Pancratius is provided.]

**368. “Of Saints Gordian and Epimachus.”** In the Codex of Ratold it reads “of Gordian, Cyril, and Epimachus.” Yet the Mass makes no mention of Cyril. The Martyrology of Saint Jerome deals with him on the same day:

> Likewise, of Cyril and Dionysius.

In the Codex of Rheims it reads:

> The feast of Saint Gordian,

with no mention of Saint Epimachus, and the Mass is for Saint Gordian alone.

**369. “Of Saint Pancratius.”** In the Codices of Rheims and Ratold, and in Pamelius, Achilleus and Nereus are added; in the Roman Missal Domitilla is added as well. In the Codex of Ratold there are two Masses: the first of Saint Pancratius, the second of Saints Achilleus and Nereus. In Pamelius, however, the first Mass is of Saints Achilleus and Nereus, and the second of Saint Pancratius.

**370. “R. B.”** That is, “Seek the Blessing,” namely below, in the Common of One Martyr.

**371. “Salutation.”** Read “salvation.”

[Note: [Col. 0383D] Thus it is read in Pamelius and in the Vatican Edition, on which Guss’s edition was based.]

**372. “The feast of Saint Mary at the Martyrs.”** This feast is not found in the printed editions.

[Note: [Col. 0383D] The same is true in our manuscripts; in the Gemetic manuscript it reads “the Dedication of Saint Mary.”]

It is found in all our other manuscript codices. In the Codex of Rheims the title is:

> The Dedication of the Church of Blessed Mary at the Martyrs.

This feast was formerly instituted by Pope Boniface IV, when the Roman Pantheon was converted into a church of Saint Mary and All Martyrs. Paul the Deacon discusses this in *History of the Lombards*, book IV, chapter 37, and book V, chapter 11.

This Pantheon was built by Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa. It was so called either because, among the images of Mars and Venus, it contained many images of the gods, or because, crowned with a convex roof, its form displayed the likeness of heaven, as Dio Cassius says in *History*, book LIII. That there was an image of Venus in the temple is also established by Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, book III, chapter 17:

> It was cut apart, and two were made from a single pearl, and they were placed upon the image of Venus, so that it might be of monstrous size in the temple called the Pantheon.

Formerly, in a district called Bethelia near the Palestinian city of Gaza, there was also a temple situated on a man-made citadel, which was called the Pantheon, as Sozomen reports in *Ecclesiastical History*, book V, chapter 14.

[Note: [Col. 0384D] In the edition prepared by Henri Valois, the passage now reads, in chapter 15, as follows: “The Pantheon was placed upon a certain man-made hill, like a citadel.”]

At Athens there was formerly a θεοῖς τοῖς πᾶσιν ἱερὸν κοινὸν, that is, “a temple common to all the gods,” which the Emperor Hadrian built, as Pausanias writes in his *Description of Attica*.

**373. “Of Saint Urban.”** This feast is not found in the Codex of Rheims.

[Note: [Col. 0384D] It is absent from the two Theodulf manuscripts, but not from the Gemetic manuscript, where the feast of Saint Dunstan is first noted; and on May 26, that of Saint Augustine, bishop—namely, of Canterbury.]

**374. “Sacrifice.”** In the Roman Missal it reads “for the sacrifice.”

**375. “And to ask for the mercy of your gift.”** In the Codex of Rheims it reads “asking from your gift.”

**376. “With his help.”** These words are absent from the Codex of Rheims.

**377. “Blessing.”** Namely, that of the preceding Sunday.

**378. “And to entreat your Majesty with tireless prayers.”** These words are absent from the Codex of Rheims.

**379. “Let us strive to possess the paschal mystery perpetually.”** That is, let us strive to possess everlasting happiness in heaven.

**380. “Monday in the Greater Litany.”** This Greater Litany is the Rogation observance, which was instituted to be celebrated during the three days before the Lord’s Ascension by Saint Mamertus, bishop of Vienne, as Saint Gregory of Tours writes in *History*, book II, chapter 34:

> Avitus, in a certain homily that he wrote on the Rogations, relates that these very Rogations, which we celebrate before the triumph of the Lord’s Ascension, were instituted by Saint Mamertus, bishop of that same city of Vienne, who at that time was presiding there, while the city was being terrified by many portents.

[Col. 0385A]

Let us hear the very words of Saint Avitus in his sermon on the Rogations. After describing the various calamities of his city, he finally says:

> These events continued amid public rumors and private rumors until the solemn night of the approaching vigil, when annual custom demanded that the feast of the Lord’s Resurrection be celebrated. For with united hearts they awaited that hour as aid in their labors, an end to their misfortunes, and security for those who feared. That venerable night therefore arrived, a night that had opened the customary solemn observance as a vow of public deliverance. But immediately a much more violent din resounded there, the blow of a lash striking more heavily, since, once the steps had already been traversed, nothing but chaos seemed capable of following what had reached the superlative degree.  
>   
> For the public building, which the immense height of its elevated summit had raised above the city’s crown, began at twilight to burn with terrible flames. The joy of the solemnity was interrupted by the report of the danger, and the Church was emptied by a people filled with fear. Everyone feared that a fate similar to the one overtaking their own possessions or houses might come down from the height of the raging fire.  
>   
> Nevertheless, the unconquered bishop remained before the festal altars. Approaching in the warmth of his faith, he restrained the power that had been allowed to the flames by a flood of tears, and as the fire withdrew, he brought it under control. Abandoning despair, they returned to the church; when the brightness of the flames had been extinguished, the beauty of the lights shone forth. Nor was there any further delay in taking up the remedy of contrition.  
>   
> For my predecessor and spiritual father from my baptism, the priest Mamertus [Al., Mamercus], to whom, as God willed, my father in the flesh succeeded in the priesthood some years ago, conceived the Rogations in his mind throughout the whole [read: *toto*] night of the vigil that we mentioned above. Silently with God he determined what the world now proclaims with psalms and prayers. Once the paschal solemnity had passed, the question of not what should be done, but how and when it should be done, was first considered in private consultation.  
>   
> Some members of the senate of Vienne—whose court at that time flourished with numerous illustrious men—thought that nothing could be added, since it scarcely consented to submit even to what was lawful.

[Note: [Col. 0385D] That is, “added”; this is how it is read in the manuscripts.]

> But the pious and watchful shepherd, rich in the salt of wisdom, first softened the minds of the sheep by prayer, rather than their hearing by speech. He disclosed the arrangement, prescribed the order, and explained its salutary character. And it was not enough for a man [read: *viri*] of such religious and skillful intelligence merely to propose the institution to those who obeyed, unless from the beginning he also established the bond of custom.  
>   
> Therefore, with God inspiring the hearts of the contrite, it was heard by all, confirmed, and exalted. The present three-day period was chosen for the time: it was enclosed between the worship of the sacred Ascension and the Lord’s Day, as though by a particular boundary of opportunity, with solemnities marking its edges.  
>   
> A little later:

> In the period immediately afterward certain churches of Gaul followed an institution so evidently exemplary, though in such a way that it was not celebrated [read: *celebraretur*] everywhere on the same days on which it had been established among us. Nor did it matter greatly which three-day period was observed, provided that the offices of the psalms and the duties of tears were performed annually. Nevertheless, as affection for the Rogations and the concord of the priests increased, concern for universal observance yielded to a single time, namely, the present days.

Thus Avitus. I have transcribed these passages from a manuscript of the library of Fleury, although this sermon had long before been edited by Jean Gagné.

Apollinaris Sidonius gives the same testimony in book I of his letters, letter 7, to Saint Mamertus:

> Yet, through your authorship, I was touched by the help of the newly introduced Rogations, etc.

And in book VII, letter 14:

> Whatever it is that occupies you, whether leisure or business, you will nevertheless, unless we are mistaken, be recalled to the city by consideration of the Rogations. Their solemn observance was first discovered, instituted, and introduced for us by our father and bishop Mamertus, in a most reverent example and with the most useful result.

Nothing clearer could be said in these words.

Aimoinus teaches the same in book I of *On the Deeds of the Franks*. Similar material is reported by Burchard, book XIII, chapter 7, from the Council of Orléans. Other ancient writers teach the same, consistently asserting that Saint Mamertus was the author of these three-day Rogations before the Lord’s Ascension, not merely their restorer, as some more recent writers prefer on account of the following words of Sidonius:

> For previously—let this be said without offense to the faith—the supplications were wandering and infrequent, and, so to speak, drowsy.

These words in no way harm our position. Even if Rogations—that is, supplications, processions, or litanies, as they are called—existed before Saint Mamertus, they were nevertheless wandering, that is, not fixed or established for a definite day. Because of the various calamities described by Saints Avitus and Gregory of Tours and by others, Mamertus instituted them to be celebrated on the day before the Lord’s Ascension.

Therefore, “wandering” should not be understood as though formerly the people wandered around the churches on horseback during the Rogations.

Nor do the words found in Burchard, in the chapter cited, support this interpretation:

> Let no one presume to ride there; rather, let everyone walk with bare feet.

And in the Council of Mainz, chapter 33:

> It has been decided that the Greater Litany is to be observed by all Christians for three days, as we find by reading and as our holy Fathers instituted it—not riding and not dressed in costly garments.

For wandering around the churches is one thing, while riding during the procession itself is another. Moreover, such councils are later in date than Saint Mamertus.

Nor is it valid to say that Saint Augustine, in sermon 173, remembered such Rogations. For this sermon is not by Saint Augustine: it is absent from some of his codices, does not bear his style, and is in fact Saint Caesarius of Arles’s thirty-seventh sermon.

Indeed, such Rogations conflict with Saint Augustine’s teaching. This is clear from his Epistle 119 to Januarius. There he discusses fully and explicitly the exemption from fasting that occurs between Easter and Pentecost, and explains the significance of those fifty days more precisely than would be possible if that three-day fast were inserted into them and wholly weakened their character.

He says:

> The fiftieth day possesses another sacrament: seven times seven makes forty-nine, and when one returns to the beginning, which is the eighth and also the first day, the fifty days are completed after the Lord’s Resurrection, now symbolizing not labor but rest. Therefore fasts are relaxed, and we pray standing, which is a sign of the Resurrection.

For this reason Amalarius Fortunatus, thoroughly versed in Saint Augustine’s writings, says admirably in book I of *On the Offices of the Church*, chapter 37:

> There follows one variation between the octave of Easter and the vigil of Pentecost, namely, the three-day fast on the vigil of the Lord’s Ascension. I wonder how the custom of this present fast arose in our Church, since it is not observed throughout all the Eastern Churches. The holy Fathers whom we have mentioned—Ambrose, Jerome, and Augustine—say that fasts should be relaxed during the time of Pentecost, as does also the venerable presbyter Bede.

He later attributes the institution to Saint Mamertus, as does the Roman Order, which further adds that it passed from the Gauls to the Romans.

Since the discussion here concerns the Greater Litany, it will not be inappropriate to append the ancient form of the litany preserved in a manuscript of the library of Corbie, written approximately eight hundred years ago. Its title is:

> Here begins the order of prayers.

> Here begins the litany.

Kyrie eleison, three times. Christ, have mercy, three times. Christ, hear us, three times. Christ, have mercy on us.

Holy God of gods, have mercy on us. Holy Virgin of virgins, intercede for us. Holy Mother of God, intercede for us. [Col. 0387A] Holy Mary, pray. Holy Peter, pray. Holy Paul, pray. Holy Andrew, pray. Holy James, pray. Holy John, pray. Holy Thomas, pray. Holy James, pray. Holy Philip, pray. Holy Bartholomew, pray. Holy Matthew, pray. Holy Simon, pray. Holy Thaddeus, pray. Holy Matthias, pray. Holy Barnabas, pray. Holy Luke, pray. Holy Mark, pray. Holy Stephen, pray. Holy Clement, pray. Holy Sixtus, pray. Holy Lawrence, pray. [Col. 0387B]

Holy Dionysius, pray. Holy Rusticus, pray. Holy Eleutherius, pray. Holy Quintinus, pray. Holy Lucian, pray. Holy Firminus, pray. Holy Crispinus, pray. Holy Crispinianus, pray. Holy Maurice, with your companions, pray. Holy Silvester, pray. [396] Holy Hilary [read: Hilary], pray. Holy Martin, pray. Holy Cassian, pray. Holy Remigius, pray. Holy Medard, pray. Holy Vaast, pray. Holy Germanus, pray. Holy Gauricus, pray. Holy Amandus, pray. Holy Eligius, pray. [Col. 0387C]

Holy Benedict, pray. Holy Felicitas, pray. Holy Perpetua, pray. Holy Agatha, pray. Holy Lucy, pray. Holy Agnes, pray. Holy Cecilia, pray. Holy Anastasia, pray. Holy Euphemia, pray. Holy Columba, pray. Holy Genevieve, pray. Holy Aldegundis, pray. Holy Gertrude, pray.

All holy ones, pray for us.

Be merciful, spare us, Lord. Be merciful, deliver us, Lord. From every evil, deliver us, Lord. From every diabolical temptation, deliver us, Lord. From every evil thought, deliver us, Lord. [Col. 0387D]

From every iniquity, deliver us. From every uncleanness, deliver us. Through your cross, deliver us.

We sinners ask you: hear us.

That you may graciously deign to grant us peace, Lord Jesus, we ask you.

That you may deign to bestow tranquility and peace upon your Church, we ask you, Lord.

That you may deign to remove your anger from the Christian people, we ask you, Lord.

That you may deign to defend us from the dangers posed by our enemies, we ask you, Lord.

That you may deign to grant us pardon for our offenses, we ask you, Lord.

That you may deign to grant us remission of our sins, Lord Jesus, we ask you.

That you may deign mercifully to pour the grace of the Holy Spirit into our hearts, Lord Jesus, we ask you. [Col. 0388A]

That you may deign to grant us the intercession of your saints, Lord Jesus, we ask you.

That you may deign to grant us right faith, Lord Jesus, we ask you.

That you may deign to grant us firm hope in your goodness, Lord Jesus, we ask you.

That you may deign to grant us eternal life, Lord Jesus, we ask you.

That you may deign to grant us perpetual light, Lord Jesus, we ask you.

That you may grant us to offer praise of the saints to your name, Son of God, we ask you: hear us.

Lamb of God, who take away the sins of the world, have mercy.

Christ, hear us, three times. Kyrie eleison, three times. Christ, have mercy, three times. Kyrie eleison, three times. Our Father.

## Prayer after the litany

God of hosts, God of Abraham, God of Isaac, God of Jacob, God of the patriarchs, God of the prophets, God of the apostles, God of the martyrs, God of confessors, [Col. 0388B] God of virgins, God of all the saints, whom we confess to be three in persons and one in substance, from whom are all things, through whom are all things, in whom are all things, etc.

With regard to this litany, it should be observed that after “three times” (*tribus*) the word *vicibus*—“times”—is to be understood; after “have mercy” (*miserere*), *nobis*—“on us”—is to be supplied; and after “pray” (*ora*), *pro nobis*—“for us”—is to be supplied. In the petitions where “Lord Jesus” does not occur, it is to be understood.

[397] Finally, from these passages it should be noted that formerly the words “hear us” were not customarily said after “we ask you,” except in these two supplications, “Son of God” and “We sinners.” This may also be seen in the litany of Ratpertus, although it is written in verse, in Canisius, volume V of *Antiquae Lectiones*, part 2:

> Hear us sinners; we ask you, Christ.  
> Grant us peace; we ask you, Christ.  
> Forgive every sin of your own people; we ask you, Christ.  
> Grant temperate weather; we ask you, Christ.  
> Grant the fruits of the earth; we ask you, Christ.  
> Save all the people; we ask you, Christ.  
> And strengthen your Church; we ask you, Christ.  
> Son of him who sits on high, hear us; we ask you, we ask you.

Here one sees that in those petitions, “We sinners” and “Son of God,” only the word “hear” is inserted. The same could also have been done in the other petitions, with certain words removed, while preserving the integrity of both sense and meter, for example:

> Grant peace, hear us; we ask you, Christ.  
> Forgive sin, hear us; we ask you, Christ.

And similarly with the rest. Indeed, the sense is clearer when “hear us” is absent from these petitions.
