Arnoldus Wion, book IV of *The Tree of Life*, chapter 12, contains a litany which he asserts to be that of Saint Gregory the Great and which he says he found in a manuscript of the monastery of Cassino. But no one even slightly versed in the study of ecclesiastical antiquity would suppose that such a litany was his—to say nothing of the invocation of that same Saint Gregory, and of certain saints who were still living when it was composed, which it contains.

### 381. “The mind of your household,” etc.

These and similar prayers are said before Mass, at [Col. 0388D] the Collect or Procession—that is, at the place to which the clergy and people have proceeded.

### 382. *Fatigari*

That is, “to be struck.” Nonius Marcellus, chapter 4: “*Fatigare*, to strike.” Virgil, book IX:

> And with the spear we strike  
> The turned backs of the young bulls . . . .

The word is used in this sense more than once in this Sacramentary, as below, on Tuesday: “We are struck by our offenses”; that is, “we are punished for our sins.”

### 383. “Grant, we ask, almighty God,” etc.

In the printed editions, the Prayers in the Field follow; they are not found in our manuscript codices, nor in Pamelius.

### 384. “The vows of your fasting and prayers”

That is, “the devout offerings of your fasting and prayers.”

### 385. “We are struck by our offenses”

That is, “because of our sins we are reproved and struck.”

[Col. 0389A]

### 386. “With the instruments of true belief”

That is, “with the writings, books—that is, the teachings—of the true faith.” This is a metonymy of container for contained. *Instrumentum* is sometimes used for “book.” Tertullian, book V *Against Marcion*:

> How many pitfalls Marcion has especially dug in this epistle, by removing what he wished, will become clear from the integrity of our instrument.

In the *Apology*:

> The highest antiquity indicates the authority of these instruments.

And below:

> But since we have shown that this sect is supported by the most ancient instruments of the Jews.

### 387. “At the Ascension of the Lord”

*Ascensa* means “ascension.” Magister, in the manuscript *Rule*, chapter 28: “Because the Lord’s ascension occurs on that very day at all times.” This reading is found in the Rheims and Rodradi codices.

### 388. “Grant, we ask,” etc.

Alcuin, book II *Against Elipandus, Archbishop of Toledo*, cites this Prayer to prove that Jesus Christ is the true Son of God, not an adopted son:

> Likewise, at the Ascension of the Lord: “Grant, we ask, almighty [Col. 0389B] God, that we who believe that your Only-Begotten ascended to heaven on this day . . .”

[398]

### 389. “Gifts”

That is, “the Holy Spirit.”

### 390. “To his participants”

That is, “to the apostles.”

### 391. “Before the descent of the font”

That is, “before the descent into the font,” namely for the celebration of baptism, in accordance with the ancient institution of the Church, by which baptism was conferred on the solemnities of Pentecost and Easter. Tertullian teaches this in his book *On Baptism*:

> Easter provides the more solemn day for baptism.

And shortly afterward:

> From that point, Pentecost offers the broadest period for arranging baptisms.

This is also known from letters 4 and 8 of Saint Leo, from Socrates’ history, and from the councils cited shortly below. We have an eloquent testimony concerning Easter baptism in Fortunatus, book III, poem 7. Speaking of the Easter solemnity, he writes near the end of the poem:

> Behold, the sacred King’s great share in your triumph shines forth,  
> When sacred baths make pure souls blessed.  
> A radiant host comes forth from gleaming waters,  
> And washes away the ancient fault in a new stream.  
> A white garment also marks the shining souls,  
> And the shepherd rejoices in his snow-white flock.

[Col. 0389C]

The same Fortunatus, book V, poem 4, speaking of Jews baptized by Saint Avitus, Bishop of Arverna, on that very day, writes concerning baptism at Pentecost:

> Behold, the day had come when the gracious Spirit, sent from above,  
> Flowed into the mouths of apostolic men.  
> The King summons country dwellers and city dwellers to sacred rites,  
> And they hasten eagerly to the holy festivals.  
> The Jewish odor is washed away in holy baptism,  
> And a new offspring is said to have been restored from its own [reading uncertain].

The same may be seen in Saint Jerome’s letter to Pammachius, *Against the Errors of John of Jerusalem*:

> We are the ones who divide the Church, who a few months ago, around the days of Pentecost, when the sun was darkened and the whole world was already fearing the Judge who was about to come, presented forty persons of different ages and sexes to your presbyters for baptism.

And shortly afterward he mentions Easter baptism. The emperor Constantine the Great himself was baptized on the day of Pentecost, as Eusebius testifies in his *Life*, chapter 64.

Since formerly the Easter solemnity began at sunset—that is, on Saturday evening—and baptism was celebrated that very night, as is clear from the office of Holy Saturday and from the letter of Paschasius of Lilybaeum to Saint Pope Leo, it follows that, according to the ordinary manner of speaking, baptism is said to have been celebrated on Easter Saturday. Saint Gregory speaks in this way, book IV of the *Dialogues*, chapter 32:

> A certain magistrate received in baptism, on the most sacred Easter Saturday, the young daughter of one of the faithful.

The same must be said of Pentecost Saturday.

Later, some baptized people on the solemnities of the martyrs. This was finally forbidden by Saint Pope Leo, letter 80, and by the Second Council of Mâcon, canon 3. Some also baptized on the solemnity of Epiphany. When this practice had arisen in Sicily, Saint Pope Leo abolished it in letter 4. When it had likewise arisen in Gaul, at least in Neustria or Normandy, it was abolished in the Council of Rouen held in the year of the Lord 1072:

> On the vigil or day of Epiphany, we absolutely forbid anyone to be baptized except from necessity arising from illness.

[Col. 0390A]

Nevertheless, this custom continued in Africa after Saint Pope Leo, as is known from Victor of Vita, book II *On the Vandal Persecution*, in the time of Saint Eugenius, Bishop of Carthage, who flourished not long after Saint Leo. He writes:

> There was in that same city, Carthage, a certain blind man, very well known to the citizens and to the city, named Felix. He was visited by the Lord, and in a vision during the night—it was the dawn of Epiphany—he was told: “Rise, go to my servant Eugenius the bishop, and say to him, ‘I have sent you to him’; and at the hour when he blesses the font so that those who approach may be baptized, he will touch your eyes and they will be opened.”

In ancient times baptism was also celebrated in Lycia on the day of Epiphany, as may be seen in John Moschus, chapter 214 of *The Spiritual Meadow*:

> There is a certain village called Soruba at the foot of a mountain on which the city of the Caeanites is situated. In it there is a baptistery which, on the holy Epiphanies, sweats. This sweat increases continuously for three hours, then, after the baptism has been completed, begins to diminish and gradually disappears over another three hours.

That the village mentioned above is in Lycia is attested by Moschus in the following chapter.

In certain parts of Gaul, however, the celebration of baptism appears to have been customary on the Nativity of the Lord. For Clovis, the first Christian king of the Franks, was baptized on that very day, as Bishop Avitus of Vienne testifies in a letter to the same king:

> Indeed, even in the western regions the light of a new radiance shines forth in a king who is not new; its splendor was fittingly begun by the birth of our Redeemer, so that it may become evident that you were regenerated from the water for salvation on the day when the world receives the Lord of heaven, born for its redemption. Therefore, let the day on which the Lord’s Nativity is celebrated also be yours, on which you were born for Christ and Christ was born for the world; on which you consecrated your soul to God, your life to your contemporaries, and your fame to posterity.

(Jacobus Sirmond, volume I of *The Councils of Gaul*.)

This is what he says. Although Fredegar, chapter 11 of the *History of the Franks*, and Hincmar, in the *Life of Saint Remigius* cited by Herivaeus, Archbishop of Rheims, in his letter to Vitonus, Archbishop of Rouen, write that Clovis was baptized on Easter Day, the authority of Avitus is preferable, since he was Clovis’s contemporary.

This opinion is confirmed by a miracle that once occurred annually at Embrun, on the Nativity of the Lord and on Maundy Thursday, around a baptistery built by Saint Marcellinus, formerly bishop of that city. On those days each year, water divinely arose in that basin or baptistery, and water was carried from it to another basin for the purpose of baptism, as Saint Gregory of Tours writes in chapter 69 of his book *On the Glory of the Confessors*. Certainly, this miracle would not have occurred on the Nativity of the Lord if baptism ought not to have been conferred on that day. [Col. 0390D]

Likewise, once in Sicily, on an estate called Meltinus, the baptismal font was miraculously filled each year on Easter Day, as Bishop Paschasius of Lilybaeum reports in his letter to Saint Pope Leo.

If, however, the danger of death had arisen, the sick were baptized outside the aforementioned solemnities. This is clear from the letters of Saints Cornelius and Cyprian cited below, from the Second Council of Mâcon cited above, from the letter of Gregory II to the clergy and people of Thuringia, and from the Council of Auxerre, canon 8:

> It is not permitted to baptize at any time without the solemnity of Easter, except those whose death is near, whom they call *grabatarii*.

Here it should be noted that *grabatarii* are those who, because of the danger of death, were baptized in bed or on a pallet by sprinkling or pouring water. They are otherwise called *clinici*, from Greek *κλίνη*, that is, “bed.” This is evident from letter 73 of Saint Cyprian, who rightly defends this manner of baptizing, although Pope Cornelius appears to doubt it in his letter to Fabius, Bishop of Antioch, preserved by Eusebius, book VI of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 35. Nevertheless, such baptized persons were irregular, as the term is used, and could not be advanced to the clergy, as Pope Cornelius testifies in the letter cited.

The discipline of the Thessalonians, however, was more severe than it ought to have been: they baptized absolutely no one outside the Easter solemnity, with the result that, apart from a few exceptions, everyone departed this life without baptism, as Socrates writes, book V of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 21.

If the subject is infants, it was sometimes customary in those ancient times for them to receive baptism outside the solemnities of Easter and Pentecost. We learn this from Saint Cyprian, letter 59, where he argues against someone who maintained that infants should not be baptized on the second or third day of their birth, but that, as in circumcision, the eighth day should be awaited. If it had then been customary to postpone baptism for such little children until Easter and Pentecost, Saint Cyprian would have argued in vain that they could be baptized before the eighth day after their birth.

### 392. “Who [the] sacrament”

In our other manuscript codices there is a Preface: “Who, ascending above all the heavens,” etc., as in the Roman Missal.

“And anticipating the most sacred day of Pentecost.” Thus it is found in the printed editions, in the codices of Ratoldus and Rheims, and in Pamelius. In the codex of Rodradi it reads: “And celebrating the most sacred day of Pentecost.” This is excellent, because when this Mass was formerly celebrated on the very night that gives light to Sunday—that is, after Saturday Vespers—the day of Pentecost had already begun according to the custom of the Church, though not according to the usage of the world, as was said above concerning Easter.

### 394. “Who, ascending above all the heavens,” etc.

In the Rheims codex there is another Preface:

> Today we celebrate the advent of the Holy Spirit,

etc., as in the Ambrosian Mass, in which “because” (*quia*) is more correctly read. At the end of this Preface the following words are added:

> Therefore, with overflowing joys, the whole world rejoices throughout the earth,

which are lacking in the Rheims codex. [Col. 0391C]

In the same Ambrosian Mass one reads:

> The same distributor and maker of the one faith,

whereas the Rheims codex has:

> The same distributor, and one maker.

[Note: There is also a wholly different Preface in the ancient Gallican Sacramentary, where this feast is called “the Fiftieth”; but the same Preface is found in the Royal Swedish Codex and in our other manuscripts.]

### 395. “In fiery forms”

Excellent. In the printed editions, in our other manuscript codices, and in Pamelius, the reading is *innumeris* (“countless”).

[Note: In the Royal Swedish Codex it reads: “He filled the apostles and the believing people with the presence of his majesty.”]

### 396. “To pass from hope to vision”

This is a paronomasia: that is, to pass from hope to the enjoyment of eternal goods, to the contemplation of the face of God; for *species* means “face.” Nonius Marcellus, chapter 4: “*Species* means image, face.” Livius, in *Aegisthus*: “Now pleasing in the eyes, the desirable appearance of the man.” Hence, in chapter 1, he says: “As *species* comes from looking, and *figura* from forming, so *facies* comes from the making of the body.” Thus *species* in this passage means the clear vision of God. So also in Tertullian, *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*:

> Therefore, confident and knowing that while we remain in the body we are exiles from the Lord—for we walk by faith, not by vision.

### 397. “Thursday”

This weekday is absent from the codices of Rodradi and Rheims. Concerning it, the Roman Order and Alcuin give the following instruction:

> On Thursday there is no office and no Mass; therefore you must sing the Mass of Pentecost Sunday.

In the codex of Abbot Ratoldus, the Mass for this Thursday is the same as that for Friday in this codex of Saint Eligius.

### 398. “Give, we ask, to your Church,” etc.

In the codex of Abbot Ratoldus there is another Mass here, except for the Preface.

### 399. “If it has occurred during the fast”

These words are absent from the printed editions, from our other manuscript codices, and from Pamelius. They are nevertheless worth noting, since formerly the fast of the fourth month did not always fall in the week of Pentecost; concerning this, see below.

### 401 [400]. “That the light of your Spirit may pour into us”

That is, “that the light of your Spirit may be poured into us.” This is a hypallage.

[Col. 0392A]

### 401. “The Sunday of the octave of Pentecost”

In the printed editions it reads, “The Sunday during the night of Pentecost” (see Micrologus, chapter 59). But I do not adequately understand what this is intended to mean. In the codex of Rodradi it is written: “On Sunday there is no office.” Nevertheless, three Prayers are assigned in the following manner:

> Hear, we ask, O Lord, our supplication, etc.

Over the offerings:

> Sanctify, O Lord, the gifts that have been offered, etc.

At Compline:

> May this communion, O Lord, cleanse us from guilt.

In the appendix to the same codex, however, it reads: “Sunday in the octave of Pentecost.” Its Prayers are the same as those in the codices of Ratoldus and Rheims, in which there is no mention of the Most Holy Trinity. But in the series of Prefaces in the same codex of Rodradi, at the octave of Pentecost, there is a Preface of the Holy Trinity, identical with that in the Roman Missal and in this codex of Saint Eligius. It is also found in the codices of Ratoldus and Rheims.

In the blessing of the codex of Ratoldus, the first verse mentions the Most Holy Trinity in this fashion:

> May the divine majesty of the Trinity bless you, and the one Godhead, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; and may it find the days of judgment such as the font of regeneration has sent forth. Amen.

But in the blessing of the Rheims codex not even a word concerning the Most Holy Trinity is to be seen.

This diversity of the office arose because some maintained that the octave of Pentecost ought to be celebrated, while others denied it. Abbot Berno of Reichenau saw this controversy being debated in Gaul, as he himself testifies in chapter 3 of his book *On Certain Matters Pertaining to the Mass*, and at the end of the chapter finally concludes that the octave of Pentecost ought to be celebrated.

Micrologus, chapter 16 of *On Ecclesiastical Observances*, plainly denies that the feast of the Most Holy Trinity ought to be celebrated, because Sundays are assigned to its honor. He writes that the office of the Holy Trinity was composed by Stephen of Liège and was rejected by the Apostolic See. He also writes that, when Pope Alexander was asked about the day of the Holy Trinity, he replied that, according to the Roman Order, no day ought to be specially assigned to the solemnity of the Holy Trinity, any more than to the Holy Unity, especially since the memory of both is celebrated on every Sunday—indeed, every day.

Nevertheless, since this feast is found in our codex of Saint Eligius and in the Sacramentaries published from the Vatican, there is no doubt that it was once celebrated, then later discontinued, and finally restored by the Roman pontiffs. I am genuinely surprised by what the same Micrologus writes concerning the Preface of the Holy Trinity, said to have been instituted by Pope Pelagius, when he says that it was frequently used on Sundays. For in all our manuscript Sacramentaries and in those published from the Vatican, no such Preface is found on any Sunday, except the octave of Pentecost; rather, each Sunday has its own Preface. These manuscript codices are certainly older than Micrologus, who therefore seems to have considered only the practice of his own time in certain parts of Italy, without sufficiently investigating the more ancient usage.

Thus, from the observations made above, this Preface appears to have been instituted by Pelagius for the feast of the Holy Trinity.

[Note: None of our manuscripts has this Preface for the Sunday or week following Pentecost.]

[Col. 0392D]

### 402. “Who, with the Only-Begotten Son,” etc.

Corippus writes admirably, in his book *On the Praises of the Younger Justin*:

> There the power of the Father and the Begotten One  
> Is seen to remain piously undivided,  
> And the Holy Spirit is believed to be one in substance.  
> There are three persons; they subsist, and their names shine forth.  
> As the Father is God, so the Begotten is God, equal in honor,  
> And likewise the Holy Spirit is God.

### 403. “Dedication of the Basilica of Saint Nicomedes”

This Mass is absent from the printed editions, but it exists in all our other manuscript codices and in Pamelius. [Note: In the Calian Codex it reads: “The feast of Saint Nicomedes, martyr,” with the second Theodulf agreeing. In the Gembloux Codex: “The dedication of Saint Nicomedes, martyr.” In the first Theodulf Codex: “The dedication of the church of Saint Nicomedes.” In the Royal Swedish Codex: “The dedication of the Basilica of Saint Nicomedes.”]

In Pamelius, the word “basilica” is lacking. In the Rheims codex an error has crept into the title: for it reads “Nicodemus,” although that name is absent from the Prayers of the same codex, where “Nicomedes” and “Nicomede” are read.

This dedication is found on the same day in the Martyrologies of Bede, Usuard, and Ado, and in the manuscript Martyrology of the Library of Corbie:

> At Rome, the dedication of Saint Nicomedes, martyr, whose martyrdom is celebrated there on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of October.

In the Martyrology of Rabanus:

> On the Kalends of June, the dedication of the church of Saint Nicomedes, martyr.

And in the Martyrology of Notker, on the same day:

> At Rome, the dedication of Saint Nicomedes, priest and martyr, whose martyrdom is celebrated on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of October.

In the manuscript Martyrology of Saint Jerome, Saint Nicomedes is indeed mentioned on the same day, but not the dedication of the church:

> At Rome, Juvencus, Cyricus, Nicomedes the martyr, Exuperantius, Heraclia.

In the small manuscript Martyrology attached to the Rheims codex:

> On the Kalends of June, the dedication of Saint Nicomedes in Thessalonica.

The words “in Thessalonica” do not refer to this dedication. Rather, because each day in this Martyrology occupies a single line, when the end of the line was reached the remaining words belonging with these words were omitted by the scribe. This is clear from the Martyrology of Rabanus, in which immediately after the dedication of Saint Nicomedes comes:

> In Thessalonica, the feast of Octavius;

and from the Martyrology of Saint Jerome, in which immediately after Saint Nicomedes and the others have been named there follows:

> In Thessalonica, Lucia the virgin, etc.

This is so because at the beginning of these Kalends he had already named Saint Octavius:

> In Thessalonica, Saint Octavius.

This church of Saint Nicomedes is mentioned in the First Roman Council under Pope Symmachus. Moreover, in the codex of Abbot Ratoldus it reads:

> On the sixth day before the Ides of June, the feast of Saint Medard, confessor.

### 404. “The feast of Saints Primus and Felicianus”

This feast day is absent from the codex of Rodradi, as is the following one.

### 405. “And may what eternal excellence bestowed upon them”

In the Rheims codex it reads:

> And may the eternal excellence that he bestowed upon them

—that is, the merit of their passion, which bestowed eternal glory upon them—be applied to the fruits of our devotion.

Moreover, in the codices of Ratoldus and Rheims, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of July, the feast of Saint Vitus is recorded; in the Roman Missal Modestus and Crescentia are added to him.

### 406. “Through whom”

Read as in the codex of Ratoldus, “through whom,” so that it refers to “Lord”; or “through which,” as in the Rheims codex, so that it refers to “wonders.”

### 407. “Announcement of the fasts”

This announcement of the fasts was formerly made in the Mass after the words:

> The peace of the Lord be always with you.

And:

> And with your spirit.

This may be seen in the Rheims codex, in the Daily Prayers for Masses:

> The peace of the Lord be always with you, and with your spirit. After this, the people are to be reminded concerning the fast of the first, fourth, seventh, and tenth months.

### 408. “But on the Saturday,” etc.

According to Saint Pope Leo, sermon 9 *On the Fast of the Seventh Month*:

> But on Saturday let us celebrate vigils at the blessed Apostle Peter.

[Col. 0393D]

### 409. “Fourth month, Wednesday”

In the printed editions it is incorrectly read: “Wednesday of the seventh month,” that is, September.

### 410. “If it occurs after the week of Pentecost”

These words are absent from the printed editions and from our other manuscript codices. They were nevertheless written in accordance with the custom of those times, when the fast of the fourth month was celebrated in the second week of June. It therefore often happened that this fast was observed after the week of Pentecost, as may be seen in the Council of Mainz under Charlemagne, at which thirty bishops and twenty-five abbots assembled, canon 34:

> Likewise, in the month of June, let there be fasting in the second week, on Wednesday and Friday and Saturday, until the ninth hour.

This is cited by Burchard, book II, chapter 14, but in a more abbreviated form, and by Micrologus, chapters 24 and 25 of *On Ecclesiastical Observances*. He seems, however, to understand another Council of Mainz, since he says that it was held under Henry II and attended by twelve bishops.

The same is established in the Council of Rouen held in the year 1072:

> The observance of the four seasons, at the proper time according to divine institution, is to be maintained by us in common observance—that is, in the first week of March, the second of June, etc.,

as Ordericus reports, book IV of the *Ecclesiastical History*.

So much for the practice of those times. There was certainly an older custom of celebrating this fast during the very week of Pentecost, as is clear from Saint Isidore, book I *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 37, and Saint Pope Leo, sermons 1, 2, 3, and 4 *On the Fast of Pentecost*. It was eventually revived in the Church by the authority of Gregory VII, as Micrologus teaches, chapter 25, and by Urban II at the Council of Clermont, where the following was decreed:

> The second fast shall always be celebrated during the week of Pentecost,

as Ordericus Vitalis reports, book IX of the *Ecclesiastical History*.

Thus formerly the first fast of the four seasons was observed in the first week of March, as may be seen in the same canon of the Council of Mainz cited above:

> It has been established that the four seasons of the year are to be observed by all with fasting, that is, in the first month, the first week, etc.

And in the Council of Rouen cited above:

> It is to be observed by us in common observance, that is, in the first week of March.

But afterward Gregory VII transferred it to the first week of Lent, as Micrologus teaches, chapter 24. This was likewise established at the Council of Clermont cited above:

> At all times, the first fast of the four seasons is to be celebrated in the first week of Lent,

as Ordericus Vitalis reports in the book cited.

### 411. “After the blessings”

That is, after the hymn of the three boys has been recited:

> Bless the Lord, all the works of the Lord, etc.

[Col. 0394C]

### 412. “The feast of Saints Gervasius and Protasius”

In the Rheims and Ratoldus codices, on the day before this feast, there is a vigil of the same saints, with the same office in both codices. Its first Prayer and Prayer over the offerings are the same as in the Ambrosian Mass, at the vigil of those same saints.

### 413. “Of the holy martyrs,” etc.

In the codices of Rodradi and Ratoldus there is another Mass. [Note: Also in the Royal Swedish Codex. In Pamelius’s edition it is present, but enclosed in parentheses.]

### 414. “Through the intercession of the blessed,” etc.

In the Ambrosian Mass it reads:

> Protasius and Gervasius, martyrs.

Here it should be noted that Protasius is named before Gervasius, as is always done in both Masses of the Ambrosian liturgy and in the codex of Rodradi, although Saint Gervasius is commonly placed first. In the Rheims codex the words “and through the intercession” are absent.

### 415. “May it be strengthened”

In the Ambrosian Mass and in the Rheims codex it reads:

> May it be confirmed.

### 416. “The vigil of Saint John the Baptist”

[Note: Before this vigil there is the following entry in an ancient Roman Sacramentary, written at least in the ninth century and now preserved in the library of the Fathers of the Oratory at the Vallicella in Rome:

> In the month of June, on the twenty-second day, of 1,480 holy martyrs, whose vigil is to be celebrated with silence and fasting; and it has been granted to them, for that one day, to remit a year of penance.

I mention this because it provides an ancient example of an indulgence being granted.]

In the Rheims codex it reads:

> During the fast of Saint John the Baptist.

### 417. “Offering the solemn fast,” etc.

In the Rheims codex the same Preface is indeed found, but it is somewhat longer and many words have been changed.

### 418. “At the first Mass of the night”

Thus in the Rheims codex. In the codices of Rodradi and Ratoldus it reads, “in the early morning”; in Pamelius, “in the morning, first.”

The Mass is absent from the printed editions and from the Ambrosian liturgy. Alcuin, in his book *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, in the chapter on Saint John, says that three Masses are celebrated on the feast of Saint John the Baptist. Among these he lists the Mass of the vigil, which, because it was a solemn fast, was consequently said after sunset, when, according to ecclesiastical custom, feast days then began. He gives the following explanation:

> Three Masses are celebrated on the feast of Saint John because he shone forth brilliantly with three distinguished triumphs. For he came for this purpose: to prepare the way of the Lord by the example of his manner of life; this triumph is celebrated at his vigil. He became distinguished through the ministry of baptism; the triumph of this ministry is commemorated in the first Mass. He remained a Nazirite in his mother’s womb; this gift is commemorated on the day itself.

The same seems to be found in the Roman Order:

> Three Masses are celebrated, namely one at his vigil and two on the day of his nativity, because he shone forth distinguished by three triumphs: the office of Forerunner, the ministry of Baptizer, and the fact that he remained a Nazirite in his mother’s womb.

### 419. “And still enclosed in the womb,” etc.

Ennodius writes admirably in the speech delivered to Bishop Maximus:

> He whose elder was so by grace rather than by nature, while before entering the light he fulfilled the office of the devout prophet, marked the light of this life by his power.

And Prudentius, in the *Apotheosis*:

> The infant, though unborn, first announces the infant.  
> For our little one did not yet know how to cry out for himself,  
> Nor did he open his babbling lips to God, Christ.

[Col. 0395B]

### 420. “Who also [of] the mother,” etc.

Ennodius writes admirably in the speech cited above:

> For at one and the same time he made the mother noble through fertility and, as the use of speech returned, set the inarticulate lips of the father in motion toward their former utterance.

In the Rheims codex there follows the vigil of Saints John and Paul, which is absent from our other manuscript codices.

### 421. “The feast of Saint Leo the pope”

This feast is absent from the Rheims codex.

### 422. “That this offering may benefit the soul of your servant Leo”

Thus it is found in the printed editions, in the codex of Ratoldus, and in Pamelius. Understand “for the glory” or “for the honor,” as Innocent III explains, *On the Celebration of Masses*, chapter 6, section 3.

In the codex of Rodradi it reads:

> That, through the intercession of blessed Leo, this offering may benefit us.

In the Roman Missal:

> That, through the intercession of blessed Leo, etc.

### 423. “The vigil of Saint Peter”

In the codices of Rodradi, Ratoldus, and Rheims there is a double vigil. [405] The second is during the night. Amalarius notes the two vigils of this feast in book *On the Order of the Antiphonary*, chapter 69:

> From the Roman Antiphonary I placed two vigils in our Antiphonary. The Apostolic usually celebrates the first at the beginning of the night; it is held without an Invitatory, because at that hour the people are not invited to the vigils. The people are invited to the vigils at that hour of the night of which the prophet David said: “I anticipated the dawn and cried out.”

Here “dawn” is understood as midnight, as Amalarius himself explains from Saint Augustine.

424. “When the Apostolicus, etc.” These words are absent from the printed editions and from our other manuscript codices. They are appropriate to this day, on which there is a double Mass, one of Saint Leo and one of the vigil of the apostles; and the pontiff sometimes celebrated two Masses and sometimes one, according to his devotion. For formerly one priest was permitted to celebrate several Masses. Thus, as will be seen below, the pope formerly celebrated two Masses on the solemnity of the apostles Peter and Paul, one at Saint Peter’s and the other at Saint Paul’s. Nor does it constitute an objection that Saint Leo, in Letter 80, forbids the celebration of Masses to be repeated on the same day unless, because of the church’s limited capacity, the whole people could not attend the sacrifice. For such a decree seems to concern one and the same church, and this practice was no longer in use at the time when this Sacramentary was written.

425. “He does not wash his mouth.” This is not so much because of the danger that a small quantity of water might accidentally pass through as because it is altogether unnecessary. For if one were to abstain from holy communion on that account, this would often occur through Satan’s malice, as Timothy, patriarch of Alexandria, writes in his canon, question 15.

426. “You consecrated [him] through the faith and name of your apostle Peter.” Namely, when he confessed that Christ was the Son of the living God and received the name Peter from Christ, Matthew 16. In the Greek text, πέτρος is “rock”; among the Greeks, πέτρος signifies a rock, as is clear from Hesychius, and it seems to have this sense in Sophocles’ *Oedipus at Colonus*, near the beginning:

> Οὗ κῶλα κάμψον τοῦδ᾽ ἐπ᾽ ἀξέστου πέτρου.

That is: “There sit upon this rough rock.” And the Latin name *Petrus* is rightly derived from the Greek.

427. “The feast of the same Peter and Paul.” In the Codex of Rodradi it reads: “The feast of Saint Peter.” In the Codex Rhemensis: “The feast properly of Saint Peter.”

428. “Pontifical.” *Pontificium* means power. See the observations above.

[Col. 0396B] 429. “The feast of Saint Paul.” Thus in the printed editions and in our other manuscript codices, as also in the Roman Ordo. In the Roman Missal, however, it is “Commemoration of Saint Paul the Apostle.” Micrologus, chapter 42, attributes the transfer of this feast to Saint Gregory—that is, when formerly both solemnities were celebrated on Saint Peter’s day. For on that day the pope formerly performed the sacred rites twice, first in the basilica of Saint Peter and second in the basilica of Saint Paul, as is clear from Prudentius, *Peristephanon*, poem 12:

> First the vigilant priest performs the sacred rites across the Tiber;  
> then he hastens back here and doubles his vows.

There was also a frequent gathering of the people at both basilicas, as appears from the same passage of Prudentius:

> Behold, the Roman city pours through its divided streets;  
> one light burns brightly in two festal celebrations.

[406] Therefore, in the hymn of Saint Ambrose, where it is written:

> It is celebrated by three roads,  
> the feast of such great martyrs,

there is no doubt that *binis*—“two”—should be read instead of *trinis*.

430. “The Preface and blessing given above.” Thus in the printed editions, in which there is no blessing here, just as there is none in the entire volume.

[Note: Although these words are also found in the Vatican Edition and in Gussanville’s edition, in which no blessings are found, it necessarily follows that the codex from which the Sacramentary was first published under the care of Angelo Rocca was mutilated, or that, at his command, the printers omitted the blessings contained in our codex.]

431. “The octave of the Apostles, etc.” This octave is absent from the Codex of Rodradi. Moreover, in the Codex of Abbot Ratoldus, under 4 July, there follows:

[Note: The same is read in the Codex of Jumièges, but the office is different. In both Theodorus manuscripts this feast is recorded; in the second, however, it says “The feast of Saint Martin.” In that manuscript the Mass is the same as in the Jumièges codex; in the former, both Masses are included—that is, both the one found in Ratoldus’s codex and the one found in the Jumièges codex.]

“The Translation of Saint Martin,” on which day the ordination of the same saint and the dedication of his church are also celebrated, as can be seen in the calendar attached to Ratoldus’s Sacramentary: “4 July: the translation of Saint Martin, and the ordination and dedication of his basilica”; and in Rabanus’s Martyrology on the same day: “4 July, in Gaul, in the city of Tours: the ordination of the episcopate, the translation of the body of Saint Martin, bishop and confessor, and the dedication of his basilica.” This is based on the teaching of Saint Gregory of Tours, who writes in Book II of his *History of the Franks*, chapter 14, that this threefold solemnity is celebrated on this day:

> The solemnity of his basilica possesses a threefold dignity: namely, the dedication of the church, the translation of the saint’s body, and the ordination of his episcopate.

“You shall observe this on 4 July, but you shall know that his burial is on 11 November.” The same author writes this in Book IV of his *Miracles of Saint Martin*, chapter 6. It is likewise found in the Martyrology of Ado; but Usuard’s Martyrology makes no mention of the dedication of the church.

This church of Saint Martin is the one built by Saint Perpetuus, bishop of Tours, over Saint Martin’s tomb, after the earlier church had been demolished because it was too small, as the same Saint Gregory of Tours teaches in the cited chapter and in Book X, chapter 31. Sidonius, Book IV, Letter 18, also composed, at the request of the same Saint Perpetuus, an epigram to be engraved on the walls of this church, whose conclusion is as follows:

> And when Christ comes, who raises up all peoples,  
> may the roofs of Perpetuus endure forever.

The translation of the body took place when it was transferred from his tomb into the apse of the larger church by the same Saint Perpetuus, as Saint Gregory of Tours writes in Book X of his *History of the Franks*, chapter 31:

> He—Perpetuus—removed the basilica that Bishop Brictius had previously built over Saint Martin and constructed another, larger one, with remarkable workmanship; in its apse he transferred the blessed body of that venerable saint.

The Mass is given as follows in Ratoldus’s codex:

**Prayer:** “O God, who have consecrated this day’s solemnity to the honor of your confessor and pontiff Saint Martin, attend to the prayers of your family, so that by the merits of him whose feast we celebrate we may be helped by his aid.”

**Over the offerings:** “Look favorably, Lord, upon your people hastening toward the sacraments of life [read: *vitae*] in the present festival of your confessor and pontiff Martin; may what they have brought in honor of your name profit all for the remission of sins” [read: “so that what they have brought…”].

**Preface:** “It is truly worthy and just. You gladden your blessed confessor and pontiff Martin in regeneration and in eternal blessedness, so that, at the everlasting end, he may behold all things in your glory with all the saints: where there is spiritual temperance and wondrous sweetness, wondrous refreshment and indescribable joy, where there is the saving presence of your Son, our Lord, in whom the angels, always rejoicing, desire to advance [read: *prospicere*, ‘to look forward to’], and whom they adore.”

**At the conclusion:** “We give you thanks, holy Lord, almighty Father, who have deigned to restore us by heavenly healing. Grant us forgiveness for our sins, just as you gave your confessor Saint Martin the seat of the episcopate. Through him.”

432. “Of the seven brothers”—namely, the sons of Saint Felicity. In the Roman Missal Saints Rufina [Col. 0397C] and Secunda, sisters, are added; they are found neither in the printed editions, nor in Pamel’s edition, nor in our other manuscript codices.

In Ratoldus’s codex the following appears on the same day:

“Vigil of Saint Benedict, abbot.

**Prayer:** ‘Grant, we ask, Lord, that with cheerful hearts we may celebrate the solemnities of your confessor Saint Benedict,’ etc.

**Over the offerings:** ‘May the offering of your confessor Benedict in his honor…,’ etc.

**At the conclusion:** ‘Those whom you refresh, Lord, with heavenly nourishment…,’ etc.”

In the same codex, the following is found on the next day:

“11 July: the feast of Saint Benedict,” as in the Rhemensis and Rodradi codices, in which the Mass is from the common of one abbot, with the intercession and the rest as in the Roman Missal. In Ratoldus’s codex, however, this Mass is found:

“Almighty and everlasting God, who on this day raised your most holy confessor Benedict, brought forth from the prison of the flesh, up to heaven,” etc.

**Over the offerings:** “Be pleased, Lord, with the gifts offered in honor of your confessor Saint Benedict,” etc.

**Preface:** “And to entreat your glory with poured-out prayers,” etc.

**At the conclusion:** “Look graciously, Lord our God, upon the petitions of your faithful; and through the intervention of blessed Benedict, whose day of burial we celebrate,” etc.

Nevertheless, one should not therefore suppose that the feast of Saint Benedict was transferred to this day because of Lent, since in the same Ratoldus codex the feast of the same Saint Benedict is found on 21 March under this title:

“21 March: the feast of Saint Benedict, abbot.”

[Note: In our manuscripts also a double feast of Saint Benedict is assigned: his burial on 21 March and his feast, or translation, on 11 July.]

In the Preface of the Mass, his death is commemorated: “Celebrating the glorious day of the venerable Father Benedict, on which, leaving this sorrowful age, he migrated to the joys of the heavenly homeland,” etc. Likewise in the Prayer after Communion: “Having received, Lord our God, the saving sacraments, we humbly beseech you that, through the intercession of your blessed confessor Benedict and abbot, what we perform in reverence for his death may profit us for salvation.”

It should therefore be understood that formerly, on the day of the translation of relics, the day of burial was celebrated without any mention of the translation, as will be seen below in the translations of Saints Remigius and Vedastus. Consequently, the prayers or Masses cited above cannot undermine the opinion concerning the translation of Saint Benedict’s body to the monastery of Fleury, about which we have treated at length in our observations on the Benedictine Martyrology.

In the same Ratoldus codex, the fourth Sunday after Pentecost is followed by the octave of Saint Benedict, whose Mass is from the common of one abbot, as in the Roman Missal. In the same codex there follows:

[Note: Our codices also record this feast. In Theodorus there is another Mass.]

“21 July: the feast of Saint Praxedes,” who is called a martyr in the first Prayer of the Mass: “Grant, we ask, almighty God, that we who celebrate the feast of your blessed martyr Praxedes…” etc. The common opinion is otherwise. In the same codex there follows: “23 July: the feast of Saint Apollinaris.”

433. “Of Saint James the Apostle.” In the Roman Missal there is a commemoration here of Saint Christopher the martyr, of whom no mention is made in our codices, either printed or manuscript.

In Ratoldus’s codex the following appears:

“On the same day, the feast of Saint Cucuphas the martyr.” He suffered martyrdom at Barcelona in Spain. Hence Prudentius, in the *Peristephanon*:

> Barcelona, relying on illustrious Cucuphas,  
> shall rise.

The first Prayer of the Mass: “O God, through whom faith does not feel the fire and unbelief is burned up without fire, who granted your blessed martyr Cucuphas, kindled by the flame of your Spirit, to overcome the fires of torture,” etc.

**Over the offerings:** “A sacrifice of praise,” etc. This Prayer is longer than usual.

**After Communion:** “May it be for us, Lord, through the intercession of blessed Cucuphas,” etc.

From the first Prayer we learn that this holy martyr was tortured in a fire, as Notker attests in his Martyrology:

> In Spain, in the city of Barcelona, Cucuphas the martyr, who was originally from the city of Scillium. At Barcelona, under the proconsul Rufinus and Galerius Maximianus, he suffered. First he was most severely tortured and beaten; then, bound with chains, he was stretched out upon a grill and, soaked with vinegar and mustard, was ordered to be roasted. When he appeared unharmed by the fire and the balls of flame, by order of the impious judge he was led outside the city and thrown again into a great fire. When that fire had been extinguished by divine intervention, he was again bound with iron and cast into custody. There, consoled by divine splendor, he was again beaten most cruelly with iron hooks and bull-hide whips; finally, he was brought to completion by the sword that killed him.

So much for Notker. In his text, however, the words “under the proconsul Galerius, and Maximianus, and Rufinus” have been transposed; it should read: “Under the proconsul Rufinus and Galerius Maximianus he suffered.”

His body was later transferred to the monastery of Saint Dionysius, at the second milestone from Paris, where it may still be seen enclosed in a casket in the apse of that church. His Passion is preserved in the breviary and in the old lectionaries of the same monastery. Notker treats of this translation in the same passage:

> His body, buried there at that time by Christians, was later transferred from there to a place not far from the city of Paris, to the church of the blessed martyrs Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius, and was honored there with every respect up to the time of the Normans.

This martyr is mentioned in the manuscript Martyrology of Saint Jerome: “In Spain, in the city of Barcelona, the Passion of Saint Cucuphas the martyr.”

434. “Of Saint Felix.” Thus in the printed editions. In the Codex of Rodradi:

[Note: The same is found in the Calais manuscript and in the Codex Regius Suecicus. In the Jumièges codex, after the feast of Saint Felix, there is written, on the same day, “the feast of Saints Simplicius, Faustinus, and Beatrix.” This is how Pamel’s edition reads. Saint Felix is joined with the others in the Roman Calendar.]

“Of Saints Felix, Simplicius, Faustinus, and Beatrix.” The Mass, however, is only for Saint Felix and is the same as in the Codex of Saint Eligius.

In the Codex Rhemensis it reads: “28 July: the feast of Saints Simplicius and Faustinus.” Saint Beatrix’s name is also found in their Prayers. Afterwards, in the same codex, there follows:

“29 July: the feast of Saint Felix,” with his own Mass, whose first Prayer is:

“May the confession of your martyr Saint Felix, having been rehearsed, Lord, confer upon us an increase of devout faith,” etc.

**Over the offerings:** “Sacrifices for the commemoration of Saint Felix,” etc. Here it should read: “Sacrifices to you, Lord, for the commemoration…” etc.

**After Communion:** “Filled with heavenly food and drink,” etc.

In Ratoldus’s codex, however, under 29 July, there is the feast of Saints Felix, Simplicius [read: *Simplicii*], Faustinus, and Beatrix, with the same Prayers as in the Rhemensis codex. Afterwards, in the same Ratoldus codex, there follows:

“Likewise, the proper Mass of Saint Felix,” whose Prayer over the offerings is as follows:

[Col. 0399B] “May our devotion be acceptable in your sight, Lord,” etc.

The remainder is as in the Codex of Saint Eligius.

This Felix [Note: In the Roman Calendar he is called Saint Felix the pope.] is Saint Felix II, substituted for the exiled Liberius. He was pope, and because of his Catholic faith was expelled from his see by Constantius, the Arian son of Constantine the Great; he was crowned with martyrdom, as may be seen in the Roman Martyrology and those of Usuard, Rabanus, and Notker. The last two write that he was beheaded.

The manuscript Martyrology of the Corbie Library says of him: “At Rome, on the Via Aurelia, Saint Felix, bishop and martyr, under Constantine” [read: “Constantius,”] “son of Constantine.”

In Saint Jerome’s Martyrology there is no mention of him on this day, but only of a certain Felix in Africa. Contrary evidence, however, is found in excerpts from the *Life of Saint Athanasius* in Photius’s *Bibliotheca*, no. 258:

> Καὶ ἀντιχειροτονεῖται Φῆλιξ, ὃς παραχρῆμα μὲν ποινῇ θεηλάτῳ τῇ τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν πηρώσει ὑποβάλλεται· ὕστερον δὲ καὶ λοιμικῇ νόσῳ κατασχεθεὶς διαφθείρεται.

That is: “Felix is ordained in his place—namely, in place of Liberius—and immediately is punished by a divinely inflicted blindness of the eyes; afterwards, seized by a pestilential disease, he dies.”

These statements are not free from suspicion of falsehood, since the ancient ecclesiastical historians Socrates, Theodoret, and Sozomen wrote nothing similar. See Baronius, volume III of the *Annals*, under the year 357.

435. “And whom.” Very well. It should be construed thus: “And us, whom the burden of our own action…” In the Roman Missal it reads “and because.”

436. “Sennes.” This is sufficiently correct in the nominative case. In the Martyrologies of Saint Jerome, Rabanus, and Notker, it appears in the genitive as *Sennis*. Thus the name may, according to individual preference, be either declinable or indeclinable.

[Note: In the Roman Calendar it reads: “Saints Abdon and Sennes.”]

In Ratoldus’s codex there follows: “31 July: the feast of Saint Germanus.” This is to be understood of Saint Germanus, bishop of Auxerre.

437. “At Saint Peter ad Vincula.” In the Codex Rhemensis there is added: “And his chains are kissed on that very day.” In the appendix to Rodradi: “And they kiss his chains” [read: “they are kissed”]. “Also on that day, the feast of the Maccabees.”

In the Roman, Bede’s, and Usuard’s Martyrologies: “The dedication of Saint Peter ad Vincula.” In the Martyrologies of Saint Jerome and Rabanus: “At Rome, the dedication of the first church constructed and consecrated by the blessed Apostle.” In Notker’s Martyrology: “At Rome, a station at Saint Peter ad Vincula, the church which he himself first constructed and consecrated, the first in Europe.””

This is how the words of Saint Leo the pope, in his sermon on the Maccabees, should be understood:

> For there is a double reason for rejoicing, since we celebrate both the feast of the church and rejoice in the suffering of the martyrs.

In Ratoldus’s codex there is a double Mass here: the first for Saint Peter, the second for the holy Maccabees, as in the Codex of Rodradi. The Mass of the Maccabees, however, is in the appendix. In the Rhemensis codex there is one Mass, for the Maccabees, and none for Saint Peter, although the title of Saint Peter’s solemnity precedes the title of the celebration of the Maccabees.

[Note: In the Codex Regius Suecicus there is no commemoration of the Maccabees, nor in the Roman Calendar. In the Jumièges codex and the other Theodorus manuscript it reads: “The seven martyr brothers with their mother,” with the name Maccabees suppressed.]

438. “Of Saint Sixtus.” Thus it is read in the Rhemensis, Rodradi, and Ratoldus codices; and thus Saint Jerome read it in Book I *Against the Pelagians*:

> He gave the title to the book of Xystus, a Pythagorean, a pagan and a man without Christ, changing the name to that of Sixtus, the martyr and bishop of the Roman Church.

It is likewise written in the manuscript Martyrology of Saint Jerome, as well as in the manuscript Martyrology of the Corbie Library and in the Martyrologies of Rabanus and Notker. Popular usage, however, says [Note: This is how it is read in the Codex Regius Suecicus and in Pamel’s edition, as well as in the old Gothic Missal, where there is a Mass for the feast of Saint Sixtus, pope of the city of Rome.] “Xystus,” as in the small manuscript Martyrology of the Corbie Library and in Eusebius, Book VII of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 8: ξύστος.

439. “Preface of the grape.” That is, a Preface for blessing the grape, although this Preface is absent here, just as it is in the Codex of the priest Rodradi.

[Note: In the two Theodorus manuscripts “Preface of the grape” is also read, but the Preface is nevertheless absent. It is read in the same way in Pamel’s edition and in the Codex Regius Suecicus, where the Preface is likewise lacking. The cited codices, however, contain the blessing of the grape.]

Although these same words, which are absent from the Codices of Ratoldus and Rhemensis, are found in the latter.

440. “Blessing of the grape.” These words are absent from the Rhemensis codex. In Ratoldus’s codex there is added: “or of the bean.” On the same day, at the end of the Greek *Euchologion*, there is a blessing of the grape, in almost the same wording.

It was certainly an ancient custom of the Church to bless ripe grapes and beans on the altar, following the institution of Pope Eutychianus, as is clear from the *Pontifical of Damasus*: “He instituted that bean crops and grapes be blessed on the altar,” and from the Martyrologies of Rabanus and Notker.

In the Third Council of Carthage, canon 3, mention is made of grain and grapes to be blessed on the altar, according to the Greek version and the ancient codices. Likewise, in the Council in Trullo, canon 28:

> The firstfruits of grapes and grain are to be offered on the altar to be blessed with their own particular blessing.

And in canon 5 of the Apostles, according to the ancient interpretation:

> It is not permitted to offer anything upon the altar except new ears of grain or grapes.

At Constantinople, grapes are offered on the altar of the church of Blachernae by the patriarch on the feast of the Dormition of Saint Mary, as Theodore Balsamon reports in his commentary on the cited canon.

Moreover, in the Codex Rhemensis, under 7 August, there is a Mass for Saint Donatus, bishop.

441. “Of Cyriacus the martyr.” Thus in the printed editions and in our other manuscript codices. In the Roman Missal Largus and Smaragdus are added.

442. “In the first Mass at night.” This Mass is absent from the printed editions. It is nevertheless found in our other codices and in Pamel’s edition. In Ratoldus’s codex it reads only “in the first”; in the Rodradi and Rhemensis codices, “in the first Mass”; in Pamel’s edition, “in the early morning.” Therefore “at night” should not be understood too strictly.

443. “Replente.” Correct. Thus it is found in our other manuscript codices; commonly, “Repleti” is found.

444. “On the day of today’s solemnity.” In the Codex Rhemensis: “On the day of today’s solemnity, on which you received the pleasing victim of blessed Lawrence and the chaste body…” [read: “and the holocaust of the body”].

[Note: In the earlier Theodorus manuscript the same Preface is found, in which I see nothing that needs changing, for it has an excellent meaning: “You received the victim pleasing and pure in body…” But the Rhemensis codex incorrectly reads *castum*—“chaste,” neuter. From this we learn that ancient books should not readily be altered for the sake of correction.]

[Col. 0401A] 445. “He was offered.” Thus in the Codex of Abbot Ratoldus. In the printed editions it reads “She was offered,” which is less correct.

446. “Votive.” That is, devoted, offered to God, and consecrated.

447. “Of Saint Tiburtius.” In the Roman Missal Susanna is added.

448. “We beseech that the help of your propitiation may be present to us.” In the Codex Rhemensis it reads: “We obtain for ourselves the help of your propitiation.”

449. “Because we believe, etc.” In the same codex it reads: “Nor do we despair of the *venitate* which we ask through those who have pleased you.” Here *venitate* means *venia*, “forgiveness”; or, certainly, it should read: “the forgiveness which we ask from you through those who have pleased you,” so that these words were confused by the copyist.

450. “The help of the present life and of the future.” That is, help for leading the present life rightly and for attaining the future life.

451. “Of Saint Hippolytus.” In the Roman Missal Saint Cassianus, martyr of Forum Sempronii, is joined to him.

[Note: Not so in our codices.]

Prudentius speaks of him in the *Peristephanon*.

452. “And your kindness, etc.” In the Codex Rhemensis there is another Preface:

> Because you not only repay our evils with good things, but also grant more abundant gifts to the wretched, you have bestowed your saints, who can worthily intercede for us, so that the intercession of the righteous may plead by grace for what our resources lack. But these words are corrupt. First, read: “But that you may grant more abundant gifts to the wretched, [you have bestowed] your saints, who can worthily [intercede for us], etc.” Second, read *sufficientia* (“resources” or “means”) in place of *scientia* (“knowledge”).

453. “Of Eusebius the confessor.” Because he survived many torments endured for the orthodox faith, he is called a confessor, for the same reason as Saint Felix of Nola above.

454. “The vigil of the Assumption, etc.” This vigil is absent from the Rhemensis codex.

455. “May he do.” Thus in the printed editions, in the Codices of Rodradi and Ratoldus, and in Pamel’s edition. In the Roman Missal it reads “may you do.”

[Col. 0401C] 456. “The Assumption of Saint Mary.” This feast [Note: Mabillon proves very convincingly, in Book II of his *Gallican Liturgy*, p. 118, that this feast was formerly celebrated on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February—that is, 18 January. In the Lectionary of Luxeuil it is recorded after the Second Sunday after Epiphany, and in the Gothic Missal between Epiphany and the feast of Saint Agnes. Consult Mabillon’s notes and observations.] is called by Codinus, in his *Book on the Offices of the Palace*, and by Theodore Balsamon in his commentary on the third Apostolic canon, κοίμησις τῆς ὑπεραγίας θεοτόκου—that is, “the Dormition of the Most Holy Mother of God.” In the novel of the emperor Emmanuel Comnenus it is called ὑπερένδοξος τῆς ἁγίας θεοτόκου μετάστασις—that is, “the most glorious departure of the holy Mother of God.” In the Greek *Euchologion* it is called ἡ σεβασμία μετάστασις τῆς ὑπεραγίας δεσποίνης ἡμῶν θεοτόκου καὶ ἀεὶ παρθένου Μαρίας—that is, “the venerable departure of our most holy Lady, the Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary.”

457. “Venerable to us, etc.” This Prayer is for the Procession, or Collect, since afterwards the Prayer for the Mass follows.

458. “Among whom undefiled, etc.” These words are given more briefly in the Codex Rhemensis.

459. “O God, who through, etc.” Thus in Ratoldus’s codex, in which, contrary to the custom of these episcopal blessings, a fourth section is nevertheless added before the conclusion.

[Col. 0401D] The same thing occurs more than once elsewhere in the same codex.

Moreover, in the Codex Rhemensis there follows the octave of Saint Lawrence. The Prayers are as in Pamel’s edition. The Preface is:

> Recalling the feast of blessed Lawrence, from whom the fire inflicted upon him did not take away faith and confession,

etc., as in the Ambrosian liturgy. This octave is also found in Ratoldus’s codex, whose first Prayer is:

> With the feast of blessed Lawrence repeated,

etc.; the other Prayers and the Preface are as in the Rhemensis codex.

[Col. 0402A] 460. “Of your holy martyr Agapitus, etc.” In the Codices of Rodradi and Ratoldus this Prayer is found:

> Let the Church rejoice, etc.,

as in the Roman Missal.

Moreover, in the Rhemensis and Ratoldus codices there follows: “19 August: the feast of Saint Magnus.”

[Note: In the earlier Theodorus manuscript there is the feast, or feast day, of Saint Magnus the martyr, but on 24 August. In the Jumièges codex, however, it is on 19 August.]

On the same day the Roman Martyrology reads:

> At Anagni, Saint Magnus, bishop and martyr, who was killed in the persecution of Decius.

There was also another Magnus who was only a martyr, not a bishop. Peter treats of him on the same day in Book VII, chapter 76, of his catalogue, and Saint Jerome’s manuscript Martyrology says: “And the feast of Saint Magnus the martyr.”

He is also called Andrew, and suffered with many others, as may be seen in Usuard’s Martyrology:

> The feast of Saint Magnus, or Saint Andrew the martyr, with his companions, two thousand five hundred ninety-seven.

And in the manuscript Martyrology of the Corbie Library:

> The feast of Saint Magnus, or Andrew of the martyrs [read: “of the martyr”], with his companions, two thousand five hundred ninety-seven.

The calendar of Abbot Ratoldus’s Sacramentary also mentions this Saint Magnus the martyr, but suppresses the name Andrew:

> Saint Magnus with his companions, 2,597.

Although this martyr is not called a martyr here, that can nevertheless be recognized from the circumstances. In the small Martyrology attached to the Rhemensis codex, Saint Magnus is mentioned without an additional designation, as follows: “And the feast of Saint Magnus.”

I think, however, that our Sacramentaries should be understood to refer to this latter saint, since in their Collects he is called only a martyr and never a bishop. The Collects of the two codices are similar and identical.

461. “Of Saint Timothy the martyr.” Thus in the printed editions and in the Codices of Rodradi and Rhemensis. In Ratoldus’s codex, however, there are two Masses here: the first for Saint Timothy, the second for Saint Symphorianus, with no mention of Saint Hippolytus, who is joined with others in the Roman Missal.

462. “9 August: Saint Bartholomew.” This feast is recorded on this day in all the ancient Martyrologies and in our manuscript Codices of Rodradi [Col. 0402C] and Rhemensis. In Ratoldus’s codex it is assigned to 24 August, the day on which it is celebrated at Rome, because on that day his body was transferred to the island in the Tiber. On this matter, see Baronius.

I nevertheless think that an error entered Ratoldus’s codex through the omission of one character, because this feast is recorded in its calendar on 9 August.

463. “You do not abandon.” Thus in Ratoldus’s codex. In the Rhemensis codex it reads: “Not abandoning.”

Moreover, in the Rhemensis and Ratoldus codices there follows: “27 August: the feast of Saint Rufus.”

[Note: Our codices also mention Saint Rufus.]

The office is the same in both codices, and the Prayers are ordinary. In the Prayer over the offerings in both codices this Saint Rufus is called a martyr:

> Be pleased, we ask, Lord, with the gifts, and, through the intercession of your blessed martyr Rufus, etc.

This martyr was at Capua, a disciple of Saint Apollinaris, the first bishop of Ravenna. Usuard’s Martyrology says of him on this day:

> At Capua, the feast of Saint Rufus the martyr, whom the blessed Apollinaris, disciple of the Apostle Peter, taught when he was of patrician rank.

Ado’s Martyrology adds: “and baptized him.” Notker’s Martyrology says:

> At Capua, the birth of Saint Rufus the martyr, taught and baptized by Saint Apollinaris.

The manuscript Martyrology of the Corbie Library:

> At Capua, the feast of Saint Rufus the martyr.

Saint Jerome’s manuscript Martyrology:

> At Capua, Saints Rufus and Magnus.

The manuscript Calendar of Abbot Ratoldus’s Sacramentary:

> At Capua, the feast of Saint Rufus the martyr.

The small Martyrology attached to the Rhemensis Sacramentary:

> At Capua, the feast of Saint Rufinus [read: “Rufus”] the martyr.

All these agree with the Mass of the aforementioned Saint Rufus, in which he is called only a martyr, as I noted earlier, and not a bishop, although in the Roman Martyrology he is called bishop and martyr:

> At Capua in Campania, Saint Rufus, bishop and martyr, etc.

Immediately thereafter it adds:

> In the same place, the holy martyrs Rufus and Carpophorus, who suffered under Diocletian and Maximian.

But nowhere else is this Rufus said to have been a bishop, either in the *Life of Saint Apollinaris* in Surius or in the claim that there were two martyrs named Rufus from that city.

464. “Blessed Augustine, etc.” In the Codex Rhemensis there is another Preface, as follows:

> And to celebrate the glory of your omnipotence in every place and at every time; through this duty of devotion, in the commemoration of your blessed confessor and pontiff Augustine, we offer you a sacrifice of praise and adore your majesty in his death, while your power works in all things, so that, with your Spirit kindling him, he might be overcome in love neither by any enticements of the body nor by any promised power of deceptive blandishments, etc., as in our Codex of blessed Eligius.

These final words are corrupt and should be corrected as follows:

> So that, kindled by the power of your Spirit, he might be overcome in love by none of the deceptive blandishments of promises.

465. “The intercession, Lord, etc.” In the Codices of Rodradi and Ratoldus there is another Prayer:

[Note: It is found in both Theodorus manuscripts.]

> O God, who by the power of steadfastness [made] your blessed martyr Hermes, etc.,

as in the Roman Missal.

Agobardus mentions this Prayer in his letter to the emperor Louis:

> Consider, consider, brothers, how far your mind is from that petition which you are accustomed to say to God during the celebrations of Mass, not with your will but with your voice: “Grant us, for love of you, to despise the prosperity of the world and to fear none of its adversities.”

466. “Which we trust are assisted by the confession of your Saint Hermes, etc.” In the Rhemensis codex it reads:

> Which we trust are assisted by the present confession of your confessor Hermes. Through Christ.

467. “Hear us, O God, etc.” In the Codices of Rodradi and Ratoldus there are other Prayers in this Mass, and they are ordinary.

468. “Baptized by him in the Spirit.” Note that Saint John the Baptist was baptized by Christ himself.

469. “Might enjoy.” In the Codex Rhemensis it reads “might preserve.”

470. “Then he underwent the capital sentence, etc.” In the same codex this is read differently:

> Thereafter he was punished by beheading, he who was more than a prophet. For the Jews lost Christ, who is Lord and head of the prophets. But John, declared faithful, fulfilled the office of precursor, so that he might precede into the underworld by his precious death the Redeemer of the world whom he had previously pointed out with his finger.

In the same codex and in Ratoldus’s codex there follows: “1 September: the feast of Saint Priscus.”

[Note: Thus in the Jumièges and Theodorus manuscripts.]

This Saint Priscus was a martyr, as is clear from the Collects of both codices. He was one of the seventy-two disciples of Christ and suffered at Capua, on the Aquaria road. On this day he is mentioned in the Roman Martyrology, those of Usuard and Notker, the frequently cited manuscript Martyrology of the Corbie Library, the small manuscript Martyrology attached to the Rhemensis codex, and Saint Jerome’s manuscript Martyrology, which reads as follows:

> At Capua, on the Aquaria road, the feast of Saint Priscus the martyr.

471. “For the Procession.” That is, for the Collect, *synaxis*, or assembly. For here “procession” means nothing other than what above, on the Purification of the Holy Virgin Mary, is called the Collect. This is sufficiently indicated by the Prayer for the Procession, which is not said during the actual movement or procession, but in the church itself, with the people already gathered and assembled there.

This is also evident from the Council of Laodicea, canon 17:

> Do not join Psalms together in the processions.

For there “processions” are not those solemn walks or circuits that are now performed on account of some feast or public necessity, which people commonly call supplications, rogations, or processions. Rather, they are the assembly and gathering of the people in the church, as is clear from the Greek text of the same council:

> Περὶ τοῦ μὴ δεῖν συνάπτειν ἐν ταῖς συνάξεσι τοὺς ψαλμούς

That is: “That Psalms ought not to be joined together in the assemblies.”

Here one sees that in that old translation of the council, *processions* are *synaxes*, that is, gatherings or assemblies. This is also clear from what follows:

> Ἀλλὰ διὰ μέσου καθ᾽ ἕκαστον ψαλμὸν γίνεσθαι ἀνάγνωσιν

That is: “But that a reading should take place in the interval between each Psalm.” For readings take place in the church itself, not while people are walking from one place to another.

Therefore Theodore Balsamon very rightly explains this entire canon as referring to an ecclesiastical assembly in which the divine offices are performed. The passage in the eighty-first letter of Pope Leo to Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria, must likewise be understood in this way:

> Therefore, since we have given this letter to your Fraternity to be carried by our returning son, the presbyter Possidonius, who frequently attended our Processions and ordinations and, having been admitted so often, learned what we held in all matters concerning apostolic authority.

For this letter concerns the celebration of Masses and the ordination of clerics. The verb *procedere* means “to assemble at church,” according to the ancient manner of speaking. Saint Augustine, *City of God*, book XXII, chapter 8:

> From there people run to me, where I was sitting, already about to proceed—

that is, to the church. Shortly afterward he adds:

> We proceed to the people; the church was full.

Ennodius, in the *Life of Saint Epiphanius, Bishop of Ticinum*:

> He judged that all should proceed earlier, whatever the disturbance of the weather, so that the bishop, going before the readers, might provide the church with the form of a vigil.

Here one sees that *procedere* means “to go to church.” Saint Jerome, letter 22, volume I, to Eustochium:

> Let your going out in public be rare; let the martyrs be sought in your chamber. There will never be a lack of reason for proceeding, if you are always prepared to proceed whenever it is necessary.

He reproves the virgin because she went too frequently to the martyrs’ shrines, more often than was proper. For he wished her excursions to be rare, since there could be no lack of reason for proceeding to church whenever it was necessary to do so—for example, to hear the word of God or to receive the Eucharist.

Therefore the objection drawn from Tertullian, book II, *To His Wife*, is irrelevant:

> If one must proceed, never does the household’s business impose a greater obstacle.

For there the subject is not those circuits and litanies commonly called Processions, which in Tertullian’s time had not yet come into use. At that time Christians performed their sacred rites in hiding places, crypts, and concealed locations, out of fear of the pagans, who would certainly have slaughtered Christians singing through the streets; if that had happened, no histories of the martyrs would ever have remained silent about it. Rather, the explanation of the passage cited above must be sought in another passage of Tertullian, in the book *On the Apparel of Women*—which is wholly opposed to such public circuits—where, discussing the three reasons for which Christians should proceed, he says:

> For you neither go around the temples, nor seek the spectacles, nor know the festivals of the pagans. It is for the sake of those very gatherings, and of seeing and being seen by one another, that all processions are brought out into public, either so that luxury may conduct its business or so that vanity may grow insolent. For you, however, there is no reason for proceeding that is not solemn: either some weak brother is visited, or a sacrifice is offered, or the word of God is administered.

Since the latter three activities were formerly performed by Christians secretly and without display, women did not need adornment for purposes of ostentation. Thus these words of Tertullian, book II, *To His Wife*—“if one must proceed”—must be referred to those three reasons for Procession: when a sick brother had to be visited, when a sacrifice had to be offered, or when the word of God had to be heard. A Christian woman married to a pagan could scarcely undertake these duties because of the frequent demands of the household.

Nor is the objection drawn from letter 63 of Saint Basil relevant, where he writes that litanies were customary in the Church in the time of Saint Gregory, bishop of Neocaesarea. I admit this, but in that passage *litanies* means certain prayers, namely, “Kyrie eleison,” and so forth, such as are found in the Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 9:

> After these things let a reading from the Apostle follow, to be recited from memory, and a verse and the supplication of the litany, that is, “Kyrie eleison.” And thus let the nocturnal vigils conclude.

And likewise in chapter 17. They do not mean circuits and processions, which were not customary in the Church in the time of the aforementioned Gregory, for the reason stated above. Such processions first began at Constantinople under Saint John Chrysostom, in order to break the pride of the Arians, who at dawn went out through the city gates, singing certain hymns suited to their heresy, and proceeded to the places [415] where they held their assemblies, as Sozomen reports, book VI of his *History*, chapter 8.

It should nevertheless be noted that Saint Avitus, in his sermon *On the Rogations*, uses *Processions* to mean these solemn circuits and supplications.

### 472. Saint Adrian.

Thus in the printed editions. But in certain other manuscript codices of ours there is here neither a Mass nor any mention of Saint Adrian.

[Note: In the Roman Calendar this feast is recorded, and likewise in both Theodorus manuscripts and in the Gemeticensis. It is absent from Pamel’s edition, although it is contained in the Swedish Royal Codex.]

Moreover, in the printed editions and in the Codex of Ratoldus there is, on the fifth day before the Ides of September, the feast of Saint Gorgonius the martyr, which is absent from the codices of Saint Eligius and Rodrada.

### 473. Blessed Protus, etc.

Thus in all the other manuscript codices of ours. Commonly: “Of the Blessed Protus, etc.”

### 474. Exaltation of the Holy Cross.

The Greeks call this *hypsōsis* (ὕψωσις), that is, “exaltation,” as is clear from the Novel of the emperor Manuel Comnenus, in Theodore Balsamon’s commentary on Photius’s *Nomocanon*, title 7, chapter 1: *hypsōsis tou zōēphorou staurou* (ὕψωσις τοῦ ζωηφόρου σταυροῦ), that is, “the exaltation of the life-giving cross.”

In Codinus, in the book *On the Offices of Constantinople*, it is also called *staurophaneia* (σταυροφάνεια), that is, “the manifestation of the cross,” as is clear from the Alexandrian Chronicle:

> Under these consuls the dedication of the church of the Holy Cross, built by Constantine under Macarius the bishop, took place in the month of September, on the seventeenth. From this point the feast of the manifestation of the cross began.

That is:

> Under these consuls—Dalmatius and Anicius Paulinus—the dedication of the church of the Holy Cross, built by Constantine under Bishop Macarius, took place on September 17. From that time the feast of the manifestation of the Holy Cross began.

But I think there is an error in the numerical notation, and that one should read the fourteenth rather than the seventeenth. Here it is indicated that the feast of the exaltation of the Holy Cross began under Constantine the Great after its discovery. This is also clear from the Greek Menologion in Henri Canisius, volume II of the *Antique Readings*:

> The exaltation of the precious and life-giving cross under the emperor Constantine the Great.

### 475. O God, who [of] your Only-Begotten Son, etc.

In the Rhemensis Codex: “O God, who on this day of the exaltation [of the cross],” etc., as in the Roman Missal.

[Note: In the Gemeticensis and in both Theodorus manuscripts the two Orations assigned here are found. In the Swedish Royal Codex only the first appears.]

### 476. Devoted, Lord, etc.

In the Codex of Ratoldus there is no Oration over the offerings here; it was evidently omitted by the copyist, who was perhaps occupied with something else.

[Col. 0405D] In the same codex this blessing is found:

> O God, who redeemed the human race through the gallows of the blessed cross, etc.

### 477. Of Jesus Christ, etc.

In the Rhemensis Codex the following is added:

> For saluting the cross: O God, who [of] your Only-Begotten Son, etc., as above.

In Pamel’s edition, many Orations follow the Oration over the people, the last of which is of this kind:

> O God, who willed to sanctify the banner of the life-giving cross of your Only-Begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

Alcuin cites this in book II *Against Elipandus*:

> Likewise, at the elevation of the Holy Cross: O God, who willed to sanctify the banner of the cross made life-giving by the precious blood of your Only-Begotten Son.

Here *life-giving* should be read as in Pamel’s edition.

Formerly, on that day, toward the end of Mass, the cross was raised by the bishop so that it might be adored by the people. This Collect, or one similar to it, was recited, as can be gathered from the Rhemensis Codex, where toward the end of Mass there is an Oration for venerating the cross, and as is established by the passage of Alcuin cited above.

### 478. On the same day, the feast of Saints Cornelius, etc.

In the printed editions, in all the other manuscript codices of ours, and in Pamel, the feast of these martyrs is celebrated on the same day as the solemnity of the exaltation of the Holy Cross, which is the day of their passion. But it was afterward transferred to the sixteenth day before the Kalends of October, as can be seen in the Roman Missal.

### 479. Of the blessed martyrs, etc.

In the codices of Rodrada and Ratoldus:

[Note: The same reading is found in the Gemeticensis. The Theodorus manuscripts also present it, in the second position. The first Mass differs from that found in the commonly circulated books: “salutarem,” etc., as below in the appendix of Rodrada.]

> Look favorably, we ask, Lord, upon our weakness, and through the intercession of your saints avert all the evils that we justly deserve. Through [Christ].

### 480. And in your saints, etc.

In the Codex of Ratoldus this Preface is followed by another proper to Saint Cyprian:

> As we recount the birthday of blessed Cyprian, who was illustrious in your sight through the dignity of the priesthood and the palm of martyrdom, may he support us in the present age by his intercession and, as a merciful mediator, lead us to eternal mercy. Through Christ.

In the appendix of Rodrada there is a proper Mass of Saint Cyprian in the following form:

**Oration:** “Today’s feast of blessed Cyprian, priest and martyr, has produced for us, in your power, Lord, a saving joy,” etc.

**Secret:** “May our sacrifice, Lord, we ask, be made pleasing to you by the very act of its offering.”

**After Communion:** “Having been filled, Lord, with the sacred gifts, we ask that your protection be present to us,” etc.

### 481. Receiving, that is, honoring and venerating.

### 482. Offering you the sacred mysteries in reverence for the apostolic dignity.

In the Rhemensis and Ratoldus codices it is read differently:

> We offer the summit of apostolic reverence to be imbued with the sacred mysteries; grant, Lord, we ask, etc.

But I consider the reading of our Codex of Saint Eligius, which agrees with the printed editions, far superior. In the Codex of Rodrada the beginning of this Oration is different, namely:

> Grant, we ask, that of blessed Matthew, etc.

### 483. Here.

This word is absent from the Codex of Rodrada.

### 484. Of the heavenly kingdom.

That is, of the honor and worship of God, through which God reigns in the faithful soul.

### 485. Grant, we ask, almighty God, etc.

In the Rhemensis Codex:

> Let blessed Matthew the evangelist be, Lord, a helper of our frailty, etc.

This is followed by another:
