> Grant, we ask, etc.

As in this Codex of Saint Eligius.

In the Codex of Ratoldus the following appears:

> Ten days before the Kalends of October, the feast of the holy Mauricius with his companions.

[Note: The Gemeticensis likewise has “of Saint Mauritius with his companions.”]

The Mass is as follows:

**Oration:** “Grant, we ask, almighty God, that the festive solemnity of Saints Mauritius, Exuperius, Candidus, Victor, Innocent, and Vitalis, and their companions, may gladden us,” etc.

**Over the offerings:** “Look favorably, we ask, upon the gifts that we bring to your altars in commemoration of your holy martyrs Mauritius, Exuperius, Candidus, Victor, Innocent, and Vitalis, and their companions,” etc.

**Preface:** “Because we have learned how distinguished the life of the saints is in your sight,” etc.

**At the Completion:** “Filled with heavenly sacraments and joys,” etc.

In the same codex another Mass of these same martyrs follows:

> Almighty and merciful God, who granted the crown of martyrdom to your holy martyrs Mauritius, Exuperius, Candidus, and Victor with their companions, etc.

**Over the offerings:** “The victims that are solemnly to be sacrificed, Lord, we ask,” etc.

**At the Completion:** “Having received, Lord, the heavenly sacraments and the joys of rewards.”

In the first Mass, however, instead of *Innocent*, one should read *Innocentius*, as in the manuscript Martyrology of Saint Jerome, the Roman Martyrology, and several others.

[Note: Nevertheless, the Gemeticensis reads it this way.]

Ordericus Vitalis mentions Saint Vitalis in book XIII of his *Ecclesiastical History*, near the end, and writes that he was one of Saint Mauricius’s companions:

> The name Vitalis, in place of an angelic name, which the Normans considered strange, was given to me; it was borrowed from one of the companions of Saint Mauricius the martyr, whose martyrdom was then being celebrated.

### 486. O God, who [saved] the three youths, etc.

In the Rhemensis Codex:

> O God, by the power of whose adorable Majesty the blaze of the raging flame was changed into radiance for the three holy youths, etc.

In the same codex the Greek heading *to Post Benedictiones* (τὸ Post Benedictiones) is placed before this Oration, that is, “after the canticle *Benedicite, omnia opera Domini*,” etc.

### 487. Restricted.

In the Rhemensis Codex it is read *strictis*, “bound” or “tightened.”

### 488. May custody guard.

The word *custodia* is redundant.

### 489. Be present to your people, etc.

In the Rhemensis and Ratoldus codices the following is added:

> Grant us, Lord, the perpetual assistance of your mercy, etc.,

as in Pamel. In the Codex of Ratoldus this is followed by another:

> Grant us, almighty God, the aid of blessed Michael the archangel, etc.

Moreover, in the printed editions and in the Codex of Ratoldus the following appears:

> Two days before the Kalends of October, the feast of Saint Jerome.

[Note: This feast is recorded in our manuscripts.]

The Orations in the Codex of Ratoldus are different:

**Oration:** “May the glorious intercession of your Saint Jerome commend us to you, Lord, we ask.”

**Over the offerings:** “Receive our prayer favorably, Lord,” etc.

**Preface:** “And to plead for your mercy, so that in our minds the repeated solemnity of the presbyter Jerome may continually grant the sweetness of spiritual joy,” etc.

The words “repeated solemnity” suggest that formerly the Church had a double solemnity of Saint Jerome, although in this Codex of Ratoldus there is only one.

[Note: In the first Theodorus manuscript one reads: “On the Nones of October, the octave of Saint Jerome,” which may be called a repeated solemnity.]

**At the Completion:** “We have received, Lord, the votive gifts of blessed Jerome,” etc.

In the same Rhemensis Codex the following appears:

> On the day before the Kalends of October, the vigil of Saint Remigius.

[Note: The Theodorus manuscripts agree. In the Gemeticensis no vigil of the feast of Saint Remigius is assigned; instead, Saint Remigius is joined with three other holy confessors, namely Germanus, Vedastus, and Bavo. In Theodorus, likewise, another Mass of those four saints follows the office of Saint Remigius.]

**Oration:** “This solemnity of your most blessed confessor and bishop Remigius, begun for us through his merits,” etc.

**Over the offerings:** “May your mercy descend, Lord, we ask, upon this sacrifice,” etc.

**Contestada:** “It is truly right . . . therefore, through the intercession of your blessed confessor Remigius, we humbly ask the mercy of your loving-kindness,” etc.

**After Communion:** “We believe this great mystery of loving-kindness.”

It should be noted that in many manuscript codices *Remegii* is written instead of *Remigii*, as in this codex. Hence in many manuscript codices and ancient printed editions, with *g* changed to *d*, it is written *Remedii*, so that this bishop is called Remigius—and indeed this is the usual form—sometimes Remegius and occasionally Remedius.

It should further be noted that the word *Contestada*—which I do not remember having read in another codex—is used here for *Preface*, as noted above.

[Note: *Contestada* is the same as *Contestatio*, which is invariably found in the ancient Gallican Sacramentary in place of *Preface*.]

In the same Rhemensis Codex the following appears:

> On the Kalends of October, the feast of Saint Remigius, bishop and confessor.

**Oration:** “Grant, we ask, almighty God, that through the intercession of your blessed confessor Remigius,” etc.

**Over the offerings:** “That this offering may be acceptable, Lord,” etc.

**Preface:** “Always to give thanks and, with joy and exultation, to proclaim in your praises the glory of your confessor Saint Remigius; to raise praises and continually exult, whose annual feast of deposition we celebrate today,” etc.

**After Communion:** “Grant, we ask, that through the intercession of your holy bishop, whose glory of blessedness we celebrate today in the sight of your Majesty with worthy praises,” etc.

**Over the people:** “Hear us, holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God; through the merits of your holy bishop and confessor Remigius, guard this people with your customary mercy,” etc.

Although this Mass is headed “the feast of Saint Remigius,” and although the Preface contains the words “we celebrate the feast of his deposition,” while the Oration after Communion says “we celebrate the glory of his blessedness with worthy praises,” this is nevertheless not the birthday—or death day—of Saint Remigius. He died on the Ides of January, as Flodoard testifies in book I, chapter 17, of his *History of the Church of Rheims*, and as all the Martyrologies testify. Rather, this is the day of the translation of his sacred body, which was translated on the second day before the Kalends of October, though not in the same year.

The first translation was carried out by the ministry of angels into a new crypt behind the altar, as Flodoard testifies in the same book I, chapter 20. The second was carried out by Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, in the time of the emperor Charles the Bald, as Hincmar testifies in these verses preserved by Flodoard in the same book, chapter 21:

> And Charles the Third was ordering the affairs of the realm,  
> when October gave its first day.

This confirms what was said above: formerly, on the day of the translation of saints, it was not the translation itself that was celebrated, but their birthday, or day of deposition.

In the same Codex of Ratoldus, on the Kalends of October, there is the feast of Saint Vedastus. In Notker’s Martyrology, on the same day:

> At the city of Arras, blessed Vedastus, bishop,

which is the day of the translation of his relics, as can be seen in the manuscript Martyrology of the Corbie Library, on the Kalends of October:

> On the same day, the translation of the bodies of the holy confessors Remigius, bishop of Rheims, and Vedastus of Arras.

And in the Calendar of Ratoldus’s Sacramentary, on the same day:

> At the monastery of Nobiliacum, the translation of Saint Vedastus.

Consult the notes of the most learned Georgius Colvenerius on chapter 19 of book I of the *Chronicle of Cambrai*, which will be cited shortly.

In the same Codex of Ratoldus there is another Mass of Saint Vedastus on the eighth day before the Ides of February. This translation was made from the church of Saint Mary to the truly noble monastery of Nobiliacum, which is now called by the name of this holy bishop. It was carried out by Saint Autbert, bishop of Cambrai, and Saint Audomarus, bishop of Tarvanna, as Alcuin writes in the *Life of Saint Vedastus*, and Baldric in book I of the *Chronicle of Cambrai*, chapters 9 and 19.

The Mass is as follows:

**Oration:** “O God, who through the devout earnestness of your confessor and bishop, blessed Vedastus, deigned to call us to knowledge of your name,” etc.

**Over the offerings:** “We bring offerings of praise to your altars, Lord,” etc.

**Preface:** “And, humbly entreating that we may venerate the birthday of blessed Vedastus with the utmost devotion, so that he may be [our advocate] before your mercy,” etc.

**At the Completion:** “Trusting in the prayers of your confessor and bishop, blessed Vedastus, Lord,” etc.

Another:

> O God, who grant us to rejoice in the temporal commemoration of your saints, etc.

In this Mass—as was noted above concerning the Mass of Saint Remigius—one sees that, at the translation of saints, it was not the translation itself but the birthday that was celebrated, according to the custom of those times, which we discussed above under the month of July.

### 490. Of Pope Mark.

In the Roman Missal, the martyrs Sergius, Bacchus, Marcellus, and Apuleius are added. In the Rhemensis Codex the following appears:

[Note: The Theodorus and Gemeticensis manuscripts agree. In the Gemeticensis, before the Mass of Saint Mark, one finds: “On the sixth day before the Nones of October, Saint Leodegarius, bishop.”]

> On the same day, the feast of Saints Marcellus and Apuleius.

This is missing from the other manuscript codices of ours, as well as from the printed editions and Pamel.

In the same codex and in the Codex of Ratoldus there is the following:

[Note: This vigil is recorded in the two Theodorus manuscripts and in the Calensis on the eighth day before the Ides of October. In the Gemeticensis no vigil is assigned; it reads: “On the seventh day before the Ides of October, the feast of the holy martyrs Dionysius, etc.”]

> On the seventh day before the Ides of October, the vigil of Saints Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius; and on the following day, their feast.

The Masses are different in the two codices. On the eighth day before the Kalends of November, the same Ratoldus Codex has the octave of these saints.

### 491. Having taken up the shield of faith, etc.

In the Rhemensis Codex it is read differently:

> He who, taking up the shield of faith with which he might extinguish the flaming darts of the enemies, and the helmet of the hope of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is your word, resisted with courage the passions of the vices that attacked him. Therefore we pray, Lord of hosts: since after the mortification of his body you rewarded him as he bore the marks of suffering, may we be formed by his triumphant examples and aided by his merits. Through Christ.

### 492. Flowed.

Here *mano* is used transitively.

### 493. May we be formed by their examples, etc.

In the Rhemensis Codex it is read differently:

> Thus, by following what they practiced, may we celebrate their birthdays more fittingly. And therefore, with the angels, etc.

### 494. Which we may be able to do, yours, etc.

In the Rhemensis Codex:

> Which you may dare to do for us. Through Christ.

### 495. The feast of Saint Caesarius.

This feast is found in the printed editions and in our manuscript codices, the Rhemensis and Ratoldus.

The acts of this Saint Caesarius are found in Surius under the same day.

[Note: The most learned Tillemont judges these Acts unfavorably, volume II of the *Commentaries Concerning Ecclesiastical History*, page 614, note 4, under Saint Caesarius. He does not consider the other Acts of Saints Nereus, Achilleus, etc., any sounder, and therefore thinks that attempts to reconcile them are futile.]

There it is said that he suffered in the time when Claudius killed his mother. If the words are sound, no other emperor than Claudius Nero can be meant. He was an African by birth and a deacon by rank; he suffered at Tarracina together with the presbyter Julian, as the same Acts testify. The Martyrologies of Usuard, Rabanus, Ado, and the one circulated under the name of Bede say that he suffered under the emperor Claudius.

There is nevertheless a considerable difficulty in the Acts of Saints Nereus, Achilleus, and Domitilla, in which the deacon Caesarius is said to have buried at Tarracina the bodies of Saint Domitilla and her companions, who suffered under Trajan. From this some conclude that Saint Caesarius did not suffer under the emperor Claudius—whether one understands Claudius Nero, the matricide, or that Claudius whom Trebellius, who wrote his Life, praises in such extraordinary terms—because Saint Caesarius lived under the emperor Trajan. I can scarcely persuade myself of this, even to the slightest degree. For, unless I am mistaken, the authority of the Life of Saint Caesarius and of the other authors cited does not seem inferior to the Acts of Saints Nereus and Achilleus alone. If those Acts are not corrupt in this respect, one must say that two Caesariuses once flourished at Tarracina at different times.

Therefore, when Surius says that Saint Caesarius suffered at the time when Claudius killed his mother, it must be believed that this passage was corrupted by some ignorant person.

### 496. O God, who [have granted] us, etc.

In the Rhemensis and Ratoldus codices this Oration is prefaced by the title:

> At Mass.

In those codices another Oration precedes it. In the Rhemensis Codex its title is:

> At the Collect, at Saints Cosmas and Damian.

In the Codex of Ratoldus:

> Collect at Saints Cosmas and Damian.

More correctly:

> At the Collect, etc.

The Oration is as follows:

> Be present, Lord, to the supplication of your holy martyrs; and those whom you granted to suffer for your name, make intercessors for your faithful. Through [Christ].

Here the holy martyrs meant are Cosmas and Damian, in whose church this Oration was recited at the Collect, or Procession, according to the explanation we gave above.

### 497. The feast of all the saints.

Nothing concerning this solemnity appears in the codices of Rodrada and Rhemensis.

[Note: It is found in the Calensis, Gemeticensis, and Theodorus manuscripts.]

This feast was instituted by Pope Gregory III, as Usuard says in his Martyrology:

> Gregory III, the supreme pontiff, later decreed that it should be solemnly and perpetually observed by the whole Church in honor of all the saints.

In Gaul it was celebrated under Louis the Pious, as Ado testifies in his manuscript Martyrology:

> At the urging of Gregory, the most pious pontiff of holy memory, the emperor Louis, with all the bishops of his kingdom and empire in agreement, decreed that the feast of all the saints should solemnly be celebrated annually and perpetually on the aforementioned day.

This Gregory, however, is Gregory IV, as Sigebert testifies under the year of Christ 853. The decree nevertheless did not immediately take effect everywhere. In the Codex of Rodrada, which was written in the time of the emperor Charles the Bald, there is no office for this solemnity.

It must nevertheless be said that before the emperor Louis the Pious, this feast was celebrated in certain places in Gaul. For Alcuin assigns its office in his book *On the Divine Offices*. He flourished in Gaul in the time of Charlemagne, although under Charlemagne there was no decree concerning the observance of this solemnity. Indeed, in the Council of Mainz, held during Charlemagne’s reign, canon 36, which concerns the observance of feasts, contains no mention of the feast of all the saints.

### 498. The names of the Four Crowned Ones are these, etc.

Thus in the printed editions. In the other manuscript codices of ours and in Pamel this title is absent.

[Note: This title is found in both Theodorus manuscripts. In all books, both printed and handwritten, the Mass of the Four Crowned Saints is present.]

### 499. Whose birthday was neglected through carelessness, etc.

Thus in the printed editions. In the Roman Order it is read differently:

> The names of the Four Crowned Ones, neglected through carelessness, are these, as God has revealed them: Severus, Severianus, Victorinus, and Carpophorus. Nevertheless, their solemnity remained celebrated, as it had been established, under the names of the other saints—namely, the five martyrs who are named in this Mass.

Usuard’s Martyrology says nearly the same on this day:

> Since their names could not be found at all—although, after some years had passed, they were subsequently revealed by the Lord—it was decreed that their anniversary should be commemorated under the names of the five martyrs mentioned above.

The Roman Martyrology supports this:

> Since their names—which were subsequently revealed by the Lord after some years had passed—could not then be found, etc.

Ado likewise says in his Martyrology, as printed by Surius:

> Since their names could not be found, blessed Melchiades the bishop decreed that the anniversary of the Four Crowned Ones should be commemorated under the names of five holy martyrs.

But how could the names of these Four Crowned Ones have been consigned to oblivion in the time of Pope Melchiades, when their memory was then still recent in Rome? They suffered under Diocletian, during whose reign blessed Melchiades was seated as bishop; their Acts remained safe and intact, and many Christians who had known them were still alive.

Alcuin, chapter 31 of *On the Divine Offices*, gives a different account, mentioning not only the oblivion of their names but also of the day of their passion:

> The names of the Four Crowned Ones are these: Severus, Severianus, Victorinus, and Carpophorus. Their names and the day of their birthday had been so neglected through carelessness that they could not be found. Therefore it was decreed that in their church the birthday of the five other martyrs who are recited in the Mass should be celebrated—namely, of Claudius, Nicostratus, Symphorianus, Castorius, and Simplicius—so that their memory also might be commemorated together with these.

This appears to have been copied word for word from the Sacramentary. Hence the words “their names and” seem to have been inserted by some careless copyist. If they are removed, the passage will be free of its solecism. Beyond doubt, the following was also added at the end of this chapter:

> Later, however, their names were revealed, but their solemnity remained celebrated, as had been established, under the name of the other saints.

The final clause was copied from the Roman Order.

But in the old manuscript Martyrology of the Corbie Library, which appears to be Ado’s, nothing is found concerning such an oblivion of their names or of the day of their birthday:

> On this day, the feast of the four holy Crowned Ones, namely Severus, Severianus, Carpophorus, and Victorinus. When they were urged to sacrifice, they resisted and gave no assent whatever to the impious demand; they persevered in the faith. This was reported to the emperor Diocletian, who immediately ordered that they be beaten with leaded scourges before the statue of Asclepius until they died. He ordered their bodies to be thrown into the street for the dogs; they lay there for five days. Then devout Christians came, gathered the bodies of the holy martyrs, and buried them on the Via Labicana, at the third milestone from the city, in a sand-pit beside the bodies of the holy martyrs Claudius, Nicostratus, Sympronianus, Castorius, and Simplicius.

Nor is anything of the kind found in the manuscript Martyrology of the same library, which we have cited so often:

> On this day, the four holy Crowned Ones, namely Severus, Severianus, Carpophorus, and Victorinus.

Nor is it found in the manuscript Martyrology of Saint Jerome:

> And of the four Crowned Ones, Severus, Severianus, Carpophorus, and Victorinus.

From all this it is clear that the reading of our Codex of Saint Eligius and of the Sacramentary published from the Vatican is not entirely to be rejected.

Another difficulty concerning these martyrs arises from Anastasius the Librarian, who seems, in his account of Leo IV, to distinguish the Four Crowned Ones from Saints Severus, Severianus, Carpophorus, and Victorinus. For he says:

> Seeking with diligent care the bodies of the four holy Crowned Martyrs, he found them. Out of his devoted love for them, he rebuilt from the foundations, with the clemency of heavenly power granting its consent, the basilica that had been dedicated in the name of the saints and that he himself, after being raised to the summit of the pontificate, had governed with the wisest administration. Shaken by the weakness of old age through the long passage of time, and almost shattered by ruins, it had long appeared ancient and broken. He built it into a more splendid and beautiful condition, and for the praise of God placed their most sacred bodies there together with Claudius, Nicostratus, Sympronianus, Castorius, and Simplicius, as well as Severus, Severianus, Carpophorus, and Victorinus, etc.

But since this book is filled with errors, there is no reason to doubt that this passage too has been corrupted, with these last four names improperly added by someone unknown.

### 500. Claudius, Nicostratus, etc.

Thus in the printed editions and in all our manuscript codices, in accordance with the rubric of this feast:

> Therefore it was decreed that in their church the birthday of these five saints, who are recited in the Mass, should be celebrated.

### 501. Symphonianus.

In the Rhemensis Codex it is read *Simphronianus*. In the codices of Rodrada and Ratoldus, *Simphorianus*.

[Note: This is also the reading in our manuscripts, especially in the Swedish Royal Codex, which agrees with Pamel’s edition.]

In the Martyrology of Saint Jerome he is called *Symphronius*. In Anastasius, and in the manuscript Martyrologies of Usuard in the Library of Saint-Germain and of Ado in the Corbie Library, he is called *Sympronianus*.

### 502. By whose gift blessed Martin, etc.

In the Rhemensis Codex there is another Preface in the following form:

> To adore you in the praises of blessed Martin, your bishop and confessor: set aflame by the gift of your Holy Spirit, he was found so perfect in the very apprenticeship of faith that he covered Christ in the poor man, and the Lord of the world put on the garment that the needy man had received. Worthily did the fury of the Arians submit to him; worthily, out of such great love for martyrdom, he did not fear the tortures of his persecutor. How great, we think, will be the glory of his passion, when even a part of his cloak proved so glorious! What will he receive in return for the offering of his whole body, who for the small amount of a garment merited both to clothe the Lord and to see him?

The words “and the garment that the needy man had received,” etc., resemble the following passage of Ennodius, hymn 20, concerning Saint Martin:

> With the garment with which he had covered the naked man,  
> With that garment the King of the heavenly realm shone.

By the words “Worthily did the fury of the Arians submit to him,” it is meant that he overcame the torments of the Arians, by whom he was scourged. Hence Ennodius, in the hymn cited:

> He willingly endured the scourges  
> With which he wove his crown.

### 503. On the third day before the Kalends of December, the feast of Saint Saturninus.

In the Rhemensis Codex “and Chrysanthus” is added. The Collects of both martyrs are common—and rightly so. For in the manuscript Martyrology of the Corbie Library, under the third day before the Kalends of December, we read:

> On this day, at Rome, the feast of Saints Chrysanthus and Daria the virgin.

In the manuscript Martyrology of Saint Jerome:

> On the third day before the Kalends of December, at Rome, Arosonis, Saturninus, Chrysanthus, Daria, Maurus, and seventy-two others.

In Ado’s Martyrology, on the same day:

> On this day, at Rome, the feast of Saint Chrysanthus and Daria the virgin.

In the Calendar of the Codex of Abbot Ratoldus, on the same day:

> At Rome, the passion of Saints Saturninus, Chrysanthus, and Daria the virgin.

In the small manuscript Martyrology at the end of the Rhemensis Codex:

> On the third day before the Kalends of December, at the city of Nantes, the feast of Saints Saturninus, Chrysanthus, Eulalia, and Daria.

I am surprised that “at the city of Nantes” is written here. The same is found in Rabanus’s Martyrology:

> At Nantes, Saturninus, bishop and martyr.

Immediately afterward, the passion of Saint Saturninus, bishop of Toulouse, is narrated, and it occurred on the same day, as is clear from all the Martyrologies. But I think there is an error in both places, and that after “Nantes” the name of some saint belonging to this city of the Armorican region should be inserted.

It should further be noted that in all the Martyrologies mentioned, except that of Rabanus, nothing concerning Saints Chrysanthus and Daria is recorded on the eighth day before the Kalends of November, which is their commonly observed day.

As regards the office of this feast, the prayers in the Rheims Codex differ from those in the Codices of Saint Eligius, Rodrade, and Ratold. In the Codex of Ratold there is this Preface:

> By whose grace he chose blessed Saturninus for the priesthood, instructed him in doctrine for preaching, strengthened him by his power for perseverance, so that through the priestly dignity he might attain the palm of martyrdom; teaching his subjects by preaching, instructing them by the example of his life, strengthening them by his suffering, so that he might come to you to receive his crown—he who had fearlessly overcome the threats of his persecutors. Through his intercession, we ask, cleanse us from our sins, for he pleased you by so many prerogatives of gifts. Through him, etc.

This Preface also appears among the Prefaces of the Codex of Rodrade. From it, it is even clearer that the Mass numbered 423 in the Codices of Rodrade and Ratold concerns Saint Saturninus, bishop of Toulouse and apostle, also crowned with the laurels of martyrdom, since it could in no way apply to Saint Saturninus who suffered martyrdom at Rome with the deacon Sisinnius under Maximian, and who was never a priest or bishop. Although I do not deny that the Masses in the Codices of Saint Eligius and Rheims concern that Saint Saturninus who suffered martyrdom at Rome.

**504. Sacrandum.** [Note: [Col. 0412D] In the Swedish Royal Codex there is a Preface differing from these two. In Pamel’s edition there is none.] In the Codex of Abbot Ratold, *sacrificandum* is written.

**505. And humbly beseech your majesty, etc.** In the Rheims Codex there is another Preface:

> Rejoicing in the fast dedicated to your Reverence, which we anticipate for those desiring the merits of the blessed Andrew the Apostle with suitable offices, so that we may prepare ourselves to celebrate them solemnly;

but the words are corrupt and transposed, and should be corrected as follows:

> That we who anticipate the apostolic merits of blessed Andrew with the desired offices may prepare ourselves to celebrate the same solemnly, etc.

**506. Since it is present to us, etc.** The beginning of this Preface is corrupt in the Rheims Codex.

**507. Nor, hanging upon the cross, would he remain silent.** Because on the cross itself he preached the faith of Christ for two days, as is written in his Acts.

**508. On the feast.** Of the holy apostles Peter and Paul.

**509. Through whom.** Namely, through the apostles.

**510. Here begins the order for dedicating a church.** The dedication of a church is found in the Codices of Rheims and of Abbot Ratold. It is absent from the Codex of Rodrade, the printed editions, and Pamel’s edition.

**511. Let twelve candles be lighted.** Thus in the Codices of Rheims and Ratold, in the Roman Order and Roman Pontifical, and in the Tilian Codex. Peter Damian teaches the same in Sermon 1 *On the Dedication of a Church*, as does Ivo of Chartres in his Sermon *On the Dedication*:

> When a church is dedicated, twelve candles are lighted inside.

By these twelve candles the apostles are understood, for they are the lights of the Church and, according to Christ’s saying, the light of the world. The Codex of Ratold, being more recent and therefore adding more ceremonies, begins as follows:

> First, it is fitting that the bishop, together with the other ministers, go to the old church, and there, in the evening, deposit the relics and order vigils to be kept there throughout the entire night. On the following day the pontiff should go to the church that is to be consecrated and arrange in it what must be arranged; by his command twelve candles should be lighted, and everyone should be sent outside, except that the archdeacon alone should remain there with the door closed. Then the pontiff, with the sacred clergy, should return to the old church, put on the sacred vestments, and perform the litany as the hour requires. When it has been completed, he should say this Prayer: Let us pray: Go before our actions, we ask, O Lord, by your inspiration, [Col. 0413C] etc. Then, beginning the Responsory: “Lord, if your people should be converted.” Also another: “You have heard, O Lord, the prayer of your servant.” Also another: “You, Lord of all, who have need of nothing.”

From this it should first be noted that the bishop and clergy kept vigil in some old basilica before the relics were placed in the new basilica; then they proceeded to the new basilica; after it had been consecrated, they returned to the old basilica and transferred the relics taken from it to the new church in solemn procession. This may be seen in chapter 20 of Saint Gregory of Tours’ book *On the Glory of the Confessors*:

> After this had been carefully arranged and the altar placed according to custom, we spent one night keeping vigil in the holy basilica; in the morning, however, we came to the little chapel and sanctified the altar that we had erected. Returning to the basilica, we solemnly brought its holy relics, together with those of the martyrs Saturninus and Julian, and also of blessed Illidius, accompanied by shining candles and crosses.

**512. From his *cambutta*.** A *cambutta*, or *cambuta*, [Col. 0413D] is the pastoral staff of bishops. The old manuscript Glosses of the Corbie Library say: “*Cambuta*, the staff of bishops.” It is also used by abbots. The *Acts of Saint Gall the Abbot*, in Surius, say: “And also his staff, which is commonly called a *cambota*, etc.” Orderic Vitalis, book VI of his *Ecclesiastical History*, speaking of the translation of Saint Ebrulf, abbot of Utica in the diocese of Lisieux, writes:

> Herluin, since he was a priest, abbot of the canons of Saint Peter, and chief chaplain of the duke’s chapel, kept for himself the head and greater part of the bones of Saint Ebrulf, as well as the book, a small chest covered with silver, the *cambuta*, the belt, and the charters of donations.

A *cambuta* is therefore a curved staff and a support. Papias, in a manuscript Vocabulary, says:

> *Cambuta*: a support, or a curved staff, a *pedum*, or a crozier; in French, *crosse*. Also, a staff by which the lame and weak are supported.

Peter the Deacon, in the supplement to the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, chapter 70, writes: “In memory of this deed, the crutches were hung before the doors of the church of Saint Benedict.”

The staff of bishops is also mentioned in the Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 27: “If he is a bishop, [he shall have] a stole, a ring, and a staff.”

**513. Lift up the gates, etc.** In the Codex of Ratold the following is added:

> Psalm: “The earth is the Lord’s.” Then the minister inside, answering, should say: “Who is this King of glory?” And thus the entire procession should proceed around the church, singing this Antiphon three times together with the Psalm and the Gloria. After the bishop has struck the door three times and said, “Lift up the gates,” and the minister has answered three times, “Who is this King of glory?”, the pontiff should reply: “The Lord of hosts—he is the King of glory.” Then, when the door has been opened, he should enter and say three times: “Peace to this house; the cross drives away the enemy; the cross of Christ triumphs.”

Here mention is made of the circuit around the church. Ivo of Chartres, in his sermon *On the Dedication of a Church*, and a certain anonymous manuscript in the Corbie Library, also in a sermon *On the Dedication of a Church*, state that it was made three times with the sprinkling of holy water. This rite of opening a church was also customary among the Greeks and was called *ἄνοιξις* and *ἀνοίξιον*, that is, “opening,” as may be seen in Theodore Balsamon’s commentary on canon 31 of the Sixth Council and canon 7 of the Seventh Council.

**514. And when the door has been opened, let those entering say: “Peace,” etc.** In the Ratold Codex: “And when the door has been opened, let him enter and say three times: ‘Peace,’ etc.” In the Roman Order: “Then, immediately after the door has been opened, let him enter the church with two or three ministers; and with the mansionary and acolyte let him say: ‘Peace to this house.’”

**515. Or deacons.** In the Rheims Codex it reads *vel lente*, incorrectly.

**516. Bedding.** These are carpets spread beneath, from *sternere*, “to spread beneath.” Saint Benedict, in chapter 51 of his Rule, also speaks of the bedding of beds, meaning what is spread on a bed: “The bedding of the beds should consist of a mat, a blanket, a woolen covering, and a pillow.”

**517. Then let the pontiff begin from the left corner, etc.** In the Codex of Ratold the passage reads as follows:

> Then let the pontiff begin from the left corner on the eastern side, writing [Col. 0414C] these letters A, B, C on the pavement with his *cambuta*, and let him say this Antiphon: “Confirm, O God, what you have wrought in us, from your holy temple which is in Jerusalem, alleluia.” Psalm: “Let God arise,” with the Gloria. Then, going to the right western corner and beginning again at the right eastern corner, let him write A, B, C as far as the left western corner, singing another Antiphon: “Send forth your Spirit, and they shall be created, and you shall renew the face of the earth. Alleluia, alleluia.” Psalm: “Bless the Lord, O my soul; O Lord my God.”

**518. A, B, C.** Thus in the Codex of Ratold. In the Rheims Codex there is *ABCTURIUM*, which amounts to the same thing. From this it should be noted that formerly only these three letters were customarily drawn in the dedication of a basilica. Now two alphabets are written, one Greek and one Latin—that is, all the letters, both Greek and Latin—as in the Roman Order and Pontifical and in the manuscript Tilian Codex.

Some bishops formerly added the Hebrew alphabet, as is clear from the previously cited manuscript sermon of an anonymous author *On the Dedication of a Church*, in which the reason is also given:

> Nevertheless, because ecclesiastical doctrine makes use of the Hebrew, Greek, and Latin languages, some bishops therefore write these three alphabets.

Peter Damian, in the sermon cited above, writes generally:

> He writes the alphabets transversely in a quadrangular arrangement.

This must be understood, according to present usage, of the Greek and Latin alphabets, for in that sermon he refers the reader to Ivo of Chartres, who, as will be shown below, recognizes only these two alphabets in his work *On the Dedication of a Church*.

**519. Then, coming before the altar.** The word *altare* was absent from this Codex of Saint Eligius, but I supplied it from the Codices of Rheims and Ratold.

**520. Without the Alleluia.** Thus in the Roman Order, the Codices of Rheims and Ratold, and the manuscript sermon cited above, where the reason is added: “Because it is not yet the house of the Lord.”

**521. Then follows the exorcism of the water.** In the Rheims Codex it reads: “The blessing of salt and water.” In the Codex of Ratold:

> Then, blessing the salt and water with ashes, let him say this Prayer: “O God, who for the salvation of the human race,” etc., as in the blessing of water on Sundays;

and this is also found in the Rheims Codex.

**522. Depart, unclean Spirit.** This is a formula for exorcising a demon. A similar formula appears in Optatus of Milevis, book IV *Against Parmenianus*:

> You exorcise a faithful man by rebaptizing him, and you say to God who dwells within him: “Accursed one, go out.”

In the aforementioned Rheims and Ratold Codices, the following words occur in the exorcism of the water: “I exorcise you, creature of water,” etc. These correspond in a certain manner to the exorcisms used by the Church on Sundays in the blessing of water.

Here the water is blessed for use in the dedication of the church. It is an ancient custom for a church to be sanctified by the sprinkling of exorcised or blessed water. This may be seen in Saint Gregory, [Note: [Col. 0415D] Now book XI, letter 76.] book IX, letter 71:

> Let blessed water be made and sprinkled in those same shrines; let altars be built and relics placed.

The matter is mentioned in Pope Vigilius’ letter 2, although there he says that it is by no means necessary.

**523. Sacraments.** In former times, *sacraments* referred not only to the seven instituted by Christ the Lord, which are vessels of sanctifying grace, but also to any rite directed toward some degree of sanctification—what are commonly called sacramentals. Consult Saint Augustine, letter 118, to Januarius.

**524. To sanctify, etc.** This Prayer is absent from the Codices of Rheims and Ratold.

**525. Hardened into a mass.** Saint Ambrose uses the same expression in book III of *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 4:

> So that, as though the waves were freezing in the middle of the sea, a kind of wall might rise up to provide a passage for the Jews.

**526. Through you, for the dry places.** These words, up to “but you, O Lord,” [Col. 0415C] are taken from Saint Ambrose, chapter 22 of book X *On Luke*; but there they are expressed more fully, whereas here they are abbreviated.

**527. Lord God, Father, etc.** This Preface is absent from the aforementioned Codices and from the Roman Order.

**528. I exorcise you, creature of salt, etc.** This exorcism is absent from the aforementioned Codices and from the Roman Order.

**529. By the divine utterance of the mouth, etc.** Thus in the Roman Order.

**530. And through his Apostle, etc.** Thus also in the Roman Order.

**531. Gravedines.** *Gravedo* means pain, sadness, or distress. The old Glosses say: “*Gravedo*, *ἀχθηδὼν*, that is, distress, sadness, pain.”

**532. And salt and ashes are mixed, etc.** Thus in the Roman Order and in the Codices of Rheims and Ratold. But in the Rheims Codex the word *ter* is absent. Wine is also mentioned below. Peter Damian, in the sermon cited above, adds hyssop: “Then he blesses water sprinkled with salt, ashes, wine, and hyssop.”

**533. Eternal almighty God, etc.** In the Codex of Ratold, [Col. 0415D] there is another Prayer: “God, author of unconquerable power,” etc., as in the blessing of water on Sunday, which is also found in the Roman Order. In the Rheims Codex no Prayer is found.

**534. Transmitted.** That is, transmitted from the first parent to his descendants and flowing down to them.

**535. Creator.** In the Ratold Codex it reads: “God the Creator.” In the Roman Order and Pontifical: “Almighty, eternal God the Creator.”

**536. Permit.** Thus it is read in the Codices of Rheims and Ratold; in the Roman Order, *mitte*, “send”; in the Pontifical, *emitte*, “send forth.” Therefore *permitte* here has the same meaning as *emitte*; concerning this word, see below.

**537. Armed.** Thus in the Rheims Codex. In the Codex of Ratold it reads *arma*, incorrectly.

**538. Then he makes a cross with his finger, etc.** Thus in the Rheims Codex. In the Codex of Ratold the following is prefixed:

> And let him put chrism into it, and from that water let him prepare lime, and make *maltha*, with which he is to seal up the relics.

Here read *maltham*.

*Maltha* is lime worked with water, liquid pitch, and lard, in French *ciment*, for repairing walls, roofs, and similar structures. Palladius discusses it in book I *On Agriculture*, chapter 17. It is also pitch mixed with wax, as Festus writes. Hence in the Glosses of Philoxenus, *maltana*—read *maltha*—is *πισσόκηρον*, that is, “resin mixed with wax.” Julius Pollux also mentions it in book X of the *Onomasticon*, chapter 14: *ἐνὼν τῇ πινακίδι κηρὸς, ἡ μάλθα*, that is, “wax adhering to a tablet, *maltha*.” And Hesychius says: *μάλθῃ μεμαλαγμένος κηρὸς*, that is, “wax worked and softened”; in the same place, *μάλθη, ῥύπος ξηρὸς*, that is, “*maltha*, dry wax.” Here, however, it means lime worked with water.

Moreover, in the Roman Order and Pontifical, before crosses are made at the corners of the altar, a cross is made from the same water in the middle of the altar.

**539. At the four corners of the altar.** Thus in the Rheims Codex. The Codex of Ratold adds: “Singing the Antiphon, ‘You shall sprinkle me, O Lord, with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed.’”

**540. With hyssop he sprinkles the altar itself seven times.** Thus Peter Damian, in the sermon cited above:

> He sprinkles the altar seven times with the same water.

This author, in the sermon cited so often, after touching upon certain rites of dedication, finally adds:

> Who could illuminate the darkness of this abyss with the clarity of speech? Yet we would have touched upon it, however slightly, unless in our own times someone who presides over the Church of Chartres had explained everything more clearly with the keenest fire of his mind.

The bishop of Chartres whom he mentions is Ivo of Chartres, who wrote a sermon *On the Sacraments of Dedication*. It may be found with the other authors who wrote on the divine offices, published at Cologne in the year of our Lord 1568 under the care of Melchior Hittorp; he was a contemporary of Peter Damian. Both flourished under the emperor Henry IV and Gregory VII. [Col. 0416C] He was not, however, Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, who flourished under Robert, king of the Franks, in the year 1033, as Glaber writes in book IV of his *History*, chapter 4. Fulbert wrote nothing about the dedication of a church—not even in his letter to Deodatus, although some maintain the contrary.

**541. With the same Psalm.** Namely, “Have mercy on me, O God,” as appears in the Rheims Codex. In the Codex of Ratold the word *ipso* is absent.

**542. Until, coming again before the altar, etc.** Thus in the Rheims Codex. In the Codex of Ratold it appears differently, as follows:

> Then let him sprinkle water across the pavement in the form of a cross, lengthwise and breadthwise, singing the Antiphon: “God founded the foundations of this temple by his wisdom,” etc., and the Psalm “Foundations.” Then along the interior walls of the church, singing the Antiphon: “The Lord sanctified his tabernacle,” etc. Psalm: “Great is the Lord.” Antiphon: “At the dedication of this temple,” etc. Psalm: “Praise the Lord from the heavens.” Antiphon: “Precious stones,” etc. Psalm: “Praise the Lord, Jerusalem.” Antiphon: “The Lord shall be my God,” etc. Psalm: “Our God.” Antiphon: “This is the house of the Lord,” etc. Psalm: “Behold, how good.”

From this and what follows it is clear that many Psalms were sung at the dedication of a basilica, according to an ancient custom also attested in letter 16 of Saint Paulinus. He cites certain Psalms that nevertheless do not occur in our manuscript Codices or in the Roman Order. He writes:

> We confess to your revered piety—and shortly afterward: Our spirit so rejoiced in God our Savior that we seemed to be present at the gatherings of dedications, as though they were taking place before our eyes, and to sing those words of prophetic joy from the Psalms: “Rejoice in God our helper; take up the Psalm and give the timbrel.” “Offer sacrifices, and enter the courts of the Lord; worship the Lord in his holy court”; or that saying of the same Prophet: “Arise, O Lord, into your rest, you and the ark of your sanctification. Let your priests be clothed with salvation, and let your holy ones rejoice.”

**543. Or of the Church.** The particle *vel*, “or,” is used here in a connective sense.

**544. Singing the Antiphon “He has sanctified.”** In the Rheims Codex it reads: “Singing the Antiphon ‘He who dwells in the shelter of the Most High,’ with the same Psalm.”

**545. Let those outside sing the walls of the church with one voice.** The passage is corrupt. Read, as in the Rheims Codex: “Those who, singing with one voice outside the walls of the church, sprinkle them.” In the Codex of Ratold it appears as follows:

> Then let him go outside the church with the entire schola, sprinkling the walls all around three times and singing above them the Antiphon: “Bless, O Lord, this house,” etc. Psalm: “God have mercy on us.” Antiphon: “Behold, the dwelling of God with human beings.” Psalm: “Blessed are the undefiled in the way.” Antiphon: “Bless, O Lord, this house,” etc. When this has been finished, let the pontiff enter the church with the entire schola and begin the Antiphon: “O how awesome is this place,” etc. [Col. 0417B] Psalm: “My words.” Antiphon: “He who dwells in the shelter of the Most High.” Psalm: “The same.” Antiphon: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord.” Psalm: “How beloved.” Then let him place incense in the censer and say this Prayer, etc.

Thus far the Codex of Ratold.

Festus explains what an *acerra* is:

> An *acerra* is an altar that used to be placed before a dead person, on which perfumes were burned.

Some say that it is a small censer, namely, a receptacle in which incense was kept. Here it means a thurible.

**546. Making a cross upon the pavement.** It is certain that basilicas were formerly dedicated with the sign of the cross, as we see in sermon 19 among the works of Saint Augustine:

> When basilicas are dedicated with the mark of that same cross.

In some editions this sermon is numbered 75, *On Various Matters*.

**547. O God, who [have given] places to your name, etc.** After this Prayer, the Codex of Ratold continues:

> Then let him fill the entire church with the smoke of good-smelling incense, and standing in the middle let him say the Antiphon: “My house shall be called a house of prayer.” Verse: “I shall declare your name,” with the Gloria.

**548. And the Prayer follows.** In the Rheims Codex it reads: “And the Prayer of the consecration of the church follows.” In the Codex of Ratold, after this Prayer there follows:

> Preface in the middle of the church. “Lift up your hearts,” etc. “Be present to our prayers; be present to the sacraments,” etc., as in the Roman Order.

**549. When this has been completed, he begins the Antiphon, etc.** The consecration of the altar follows the dedication of the church. In the Codex of Ratold, before the altar is consecrated, a veil is spread while the Antiphon “I will go in to the altar of God” is sung.

A notable passage on the consecration of the altar occurs in Saint Gregory of Nyssa’s oration on the baptism of Christ:

> Ἐπεὶ καὶ τοῦτο θυσιαστήριον ᾧ παρεστήκαμεν, λίθος ἐστὶ κατὰ φύσιν κοινὸς, οὐδὲν διαφέρων τῶν ἄλλων πλακῶν αἳ τοὺς τοίχους ἡμῶν οἰκοδομοῦσι, καὶ καλλωπίζουσι τὰ ἐδάφη. Ἐπειδὴ καθιερώθη τῇ τοῦ Θεοῦ θεραπείᾳ καὶ τὴν εὐλογίαν ἐδέξατο, ἔστι τράπεζα ἁγία, θυσιαστήριον ἄκραντον.

That is:

> This holy altar also, before which we stand, is by nature an ordinary stone, differing in no way from the other slabs from which our walls are built and our floors adorned. But because it has been consecrated to the worship of God and has received the blessing, it is a holy table, an undefiled altar.

**550. And he pours out what remains of that water, etc.** Thus in the Rheims Codex and the Roman Order. In the Codex of Ratold it reads:

> And let him pour the water over the altars, wipe them with a linen cloth, and bless the table with holy water.

There follow there these two Prayers: “That singular propitiatory,” etc.; and another: “Almighty God, rational craftsman of all things,” etc., as in the Roman Order.

**551. Afterwards he offers incense.** The use of incensing is ancient in the Church. Saint Dionysius mentions it in chapter 3 of the *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*:

> Ὁ μὲν Ἱεράρχης εὐχὴν ἱερὰν ἐπὶ τοῦ θείου θυσιαστηρίου τελέσας, ἐξ αὐτοῦ τοῦ θυμιᾷν ἀρξάμενος ἐπὶ πᾶσαν ἔρχεται τὴν τοῦ ἱεροῦ χωροῦ περιοχήν.

That is:

> After the hierarch has completed a sacred prayer upon the divine altar and begun the incensing from it, he proceeds around the whole circuit of the sacred place.

Saint John Chrysostom, in the liturgy, says:

> Ὀ δὲ διάκονος θυμιᾷ γύρωθεν τὴν ἅγιαν τράπεζαν, καὶ δίπτυχα.

That is:

> The deacon incenses the holy table all around, as well as the diptychs.

Canon 3 of the Apostles says that nothing else may be offered on the altar except oil for the lamp, “καὶ θυμίαμα καιρῷ τῆς ἁγίας προσφορᾶς,” that is, “and incense at the time of the holy offering.”

The Council of Chalcedon, in session 3, records in the petition of Ischyrion, a deacon of the Church of Alexandria, who complained about Dioscorus, patriarch of Alexandria, that he had distributed among prostitutes and actors the money bequeathed by the most illustrious woman Peristeria for the support of the poor:

> So that, as far as he was concerned, not even incense from the offering of that most illustrious woman Peristeria, of blessed memory, would be offered to God.

Gregory of Tours, in the *Lives of the Fathers*, in the *Life of Saint Lupicinus*, writes:

> Having arranged along the route companies of singers with crosses and candles, and with the fragrance of sweet-smelling incense;

and Coryppus, book II *On the Praises of Justin the Younger*:

> Immediately, proceeding to the threshold of the angelic temple,  
> He placed pious incense upon the hearths, and offered  
> Gleaming wax candles.

Hence Chosroes, king of the Persians, sent a golden thurible among other gifts to the church of the martyr Saint Sergius, for the child received through his intercession, as Theophylact Simocatta writes in book V of his *History*, chapter 14.

**552. Making a cross in the middle and upon the four corners.** This is an ancient rite, once observed by Saint Germanus, bishop of Auxerre, when he dedicated at Encolisma in Aquitaine an altar in honor of the chief of the apostles, as Erricus reports in the manuscript supplement to the miracles of that bishop, chapter 3:

> Wherever and whenever he marked the corners and middle of the altar with the figure of a cross using the liquid of sanctified oil, the marble, melted by the pressure of his thumb, withdrew beneath it, so that at the touch of his finger one would think that snowy softness had yielded.

[Col. 0418C] That altars were formerly consecrated with the sign of the cross is also clear both from the passage just cited and from the sermon of Saint Augustine quoted above:

> When basilicas are dedicated with the mark of that cross, the altars are consecrated.

**553. Foundations.** In the Codex of Ratold: “How beloved.” In the Rheims Codex: “How lovely,” which amounts to the same thing.

**554. And with his hand he anoints the stone itself.** The use of anointing altars is ancient. It is mentioned in a letter of Pope Damasus to the bishops of Numidia:

> Neither to erect an altar, nor to anoint it, nor to consecrate it;

and in letter 88, commonly attributed to Saint Leo:

> Just as the establishment, blessing, or anointing of an altar.

The same may be seen in the decree of Felix IV, in Burchard, book IV, chapter 58:

> And the tables consecrated to the Lord and anointed by the sacred unction of pontiffs;

and in a letter of the younger Isidore to Luitfrid:

> The consecration of basilicas and the anointing of the altar belong to the bishop.

See also the supplement cited above and the other authors mentioned below, who are worthy of consultation concerning the anointing with chrism.

**555. When the Psalm has been completed, he again applies oil, etc.** Thus in the Rheims Codex, although these words are absent from the Codex of Ratold.

**556. Rising in the morning, Jacob, with the Psalm “It is good,” etc.** Differently in the Rheims Codex: “The Lord sanctified his tabernacle,” with the Psalm “Our God is our refuge.”

**557. He applies chrism.** Thus in the Rheims Codex and in the Roman Order. In the Codex of Ratold it reads as follows:

> After this let him place incense and chrism and say: “Behold the fragrance of my son, like the fragrance of a field which the Lord has blessed.” Psalm: “Behold, how good.” Antiphon: “The Lord shall be my God,” etc. Psalm: “Our God.” Antiphon: “Jacob saw the ladder.” Psalm: “Foundations.”

Here the altar is anointed with chrism according to the ancient custom of the Church, which is clear from the Council of Agde, canon 14:

> It has been determined that altars should be consecrated not only by anointing with chrism but also by priestly blessing.

From the Council of Epaon, canon 26:

> Let altars that are not made of stone not be consecrated by anointing with chrism.

And from Saint Dionysius, chapter 4 of the *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*:

> Observe this also sacredly: that law of the most sacred mysteries completes the consecration of the altar ταῖς τοῦ ἱερωτάτου μύρου τελετουργεῖ παναγέσιν ἐπιψυσέσιν,

that is:

> It completes it by the most holy outpourings of the most sacred ointment.

Peter Damian, in the sermon cited above *On the Dedication of a Church*, writes:

> He anoints the altar with a mixture of chrism and oil.

He speaks this way because the altar is first anointed with oil and then with chrism, as is evident from our Sacramentaries and from Ivo’s sermon *On the Sacraments of Dedication*.

**558. On the right, toward the right.** The particle *de* is missing here; it appears in the Rheims Codex. But it should be read: “From the right to the right.” In the Codex of Ratold it reads:

> Then, making crosses around the walls with the same chrism using his thumb, let him say the Antiphon “He has sanctified.” Another Antiphon: “Precious stones.” Psalm: “Praise the Lord, Jerusalem.” Antiphon: “Rising in the morning, Jacob.” Then, going around inside, let him place good-smelling incense and say: “Let us pray. Almighty, eternal God, pour out your grace upon this place,” etc. Also another: “O God, who from living and chosen stones,” etc.

In the Roman Order it is different:

> Then let the pontiff go around the church and make a cross upon the walls with his thumb using the same chrism at twelve places: three in the east, three in the south, three in the west, and three in the north; beginning on the right side and proceeding around, saying at each cross: “Let this temple be sanctified,” etc.

Thus the Roman Order.

It should be noted, however, from Peter Damian’s first sermon *On the Dedication of a Church*, that twelve crosses were imprinted on the inner walls of the temple and anointed with chrism by the pontiff:

> Twelve crosses, he says, are imprinted around the interior of the church.

And shortly afterward:

> He anoints the crosses with chrism, but the altar with a mixture of chrism and oil.

Ivo of Chartres likewise writes in his sermon *On the Sacraments of Dedication*:

> Hence, after the altar has been consecrated, those twelve crosses are anointed on the walls. They represent the apostles, who received the first fruits of the Spirit and strove to make the mystery of the cross known to peoples and nations.

This practice seems to have been established shortly before their time, since the Roman Order gives a different account—unless perhaps the Order itself underwent some alteration in this part.

The Greeks also anoint the temple itself with chrism, as is clear from Theodore Balsamon on canon 7 of the Seventh Council:

> Καὶ ἅπας τούτου ἀπαρτισμὸς ὑπ` ἁγίου μύρου χριομένου,

that is:

> And all its completion—that of the church—is anointed with sacred chrism.

**559. Then making a cross of incense upon the altar.** In the Rheims Codex the particle *inde* is absent. In the Roman Order it reads:

> Then let him return again to the altar and offer there a cross of incense upon it, and say the Antiphon: “Behold the fragrance of my son,” etc.

In the Codex of Ratold, without any mention of a cross, the following is found:

> Then let him go to the altar, place incense, and say: “Let us beseech the mercy of God the almighty Father,” etc. Another: “Almighty God, in whose honor this altar,” etc.

A Preface over the altar follows, as in the Roman Order. Then there follows:

> “We humbly implore your majesty, O Lord,” etc., as in the Roman Order.

**560. Under the invocation of your name.** Altars are consecrated and sanctified through the invocation of God’s name. Optatus of Milevis, book VI *Against Parmenianus*, writes:

> For if there is an invocation of the name of God, the invocation itself sanctifies even what seemed to be polluted.

There he is speaking of altars that had been scraped, removed, or broken by schismatics.

**561. Then, while they hold, etc.** In the Codex of Abbot Ratold there is added: “With holy water and incense.”

**562. Linens.** Namely, the altar linens, whose use in the Church is ancient, as appears in Optatus of Milevis, book VI *Against Parmenianus*:

> Who among the faithful does not know that, in celebrating the mysteries, the very wood is covered with linen?

Here “wood” means wooden altars, which were then customary in Africa, as is clear from the same Optatus, in the same book:

> But, as I believe, in one place he ordered them to be broken because wood was plentiful; in another he commanded them to be scraped because wood was scarce; and in some places he ordered them to be removed out of shame.

He is explaining why the schismatics had broken altars in some places, scraped them in others, and removed them elsewhere. They broke them where wood was abundant; they scraped them where wood was scarce, lest there be insufficient wood for erecting new altars; and where they merely removed them, shame was the reason. Shortly afterward he says:

> Why should I recount the hired multitude of the wicked, and the wine given as payment for crime? So that it might be drunk with unclean mouth by sacrilegious enemies, water was heated from the fragments of altars.

That is, they heated water from fragments of altars. Further on:

> Amid the sacraments—that is, amid the solemnities of the Mass—the covering could be touched, but not the wood; or, if the covering could be penetrated by touch, then the wood could also be penetrated, etc.

There he gives the reason why the schismatics ought not to have scraped the altars: they had not been touched by Catholic priests, but only the covering had been touched during the offering. If the covering could be penetrated by touch, then so could the wood; if the wood, then the earth; and therefore, he concludes, the schismatics ought to have scraped or dug up the very earth in which the altars were founded.

This is how Saint Augustine should be understood in book V of *On Baptism, Against the Donatists*, chapter 20:

> Why, then, can God sanctify the oil through words proceeding from the mouth of a murderer, but cannot do so upon an altar set up by heretics? I do not know, unless perhaps a heart deceitfully converted within does not hinder him, whereas wood deceitfully set up outside hinders him from graciously being present to his sacraments, since he is impeded by no human falsehood.

Here *wood* is used metonymically for a wooden altar.

Formerly, wooden altars were also used in certain places in Gaul. Thus the Council of Epaon, canon 26, decreed:

> Let altars, unless they are of stone, not be consecrated by anointing with chrism.

Wooden altars also existed formerly in the East, in the time of Saint Athanasius the Great, as is clear from his letter to the solitaries:

> Ἁρπάσαντες τὰ συμψέλλια, καὶ τὸν θρόνον, καὶ τὴν τράπεζαν, ξυλίνη γὰρ ἦν, καὶ τὰ Βῆλα τῆς Ἐκκλησίας.

That is:

> When they had seized the benches, the throne, and the table—for it was wooden—and the veils of the Church.

**563. Almighty and merciful God, etc.** This Prayer is absent from the Rheims Codex and from the Roman Order.

**564. To purify, sanctify, bless.** In the Codex of Abbot Ratold, a separate cross is placed beside each of these words.

**565. Almighty, eternal God, from whom all things, etc.** This Prayer is absent from the Codices of Ratold and Rheims. In its place there is the following:

> Lord God almighty, just as from the beginning you have provided what is useful for human beings, etc.,

as in the Roman Order. In that Prayer the following words deserve attention:

> These linens for the use of your altar, to cover and wrap the body and blood of your Son, our Lord Jesus Christ;

by which the corporal cloths are meant, commonly called *corporalia*. Formerly they were so large that they wrapped the body of Christ itself and the chalice. Consult our observations on the *Concordia regularum*, chapter 66, section 1.

Moreover, in the Codex of Ratold there follows:

> Blessing for all the ornaments of the Church: “Deign, O Lord God almighty, King of kings,” etc.

In the Rheims Codex there follows the order for bringing the relics into the basilica.

**566. A blessing over any offering.** Here *offering* refers to all those things offered by the faithful for the adornment of the church, as may be seen in the very formula of the Blessing, which is absent from the Codices of Ratold and Rheims and from the Roman Order. Formerly, at the very dedication of a temple, all its gifts or offerings presented by the faithful for the temple’s use were consecrated by the bishops. This was done at the dedication of the temple that the emperor Constantine built at Jerusalem, as Sozomen testifies in book II of his *History*, chapter 25.

**567. For consecrating the paten.** In the Codex of Ratold it reads: “Consecration of the paten: make a cross with oil.”

**568. We consecrate, etc.** This formula for the consecration of the paten is absent from the Roman Order.

**569. Then, making the sign of the cross with holy oil, etc.** Thus in the Codices of Rodrade and Rheims. But in the Codex of Ratold it is different:

> Also, the blessing of the paten. And make a cross with chrism. “To consecrate,” etc.

In this Codex both oil and chrism are used, whereas in the Roman Order only chrism is used.

**570. Blessing of the paten. “Lord God almighty,” etc.** These words are absent from the Codices of Ratold and Rheims and from the Roman Order.

### 571. For blessing the chalice

In the Roman Order it reads: “Preface of the chalice.” There is mention of the consecration or blessing of altar vessels in Burchard, Book III, chapter 58, from a letter of Felix IV: “And with divine prayers and holy anointings, together with the altars and vessels, as well as vestments and the other implements required for divine worship, let them devoutly and solemnly consecrate them.” Here, however, it should be noted that no anointing is used in the blessing of the chalice, as in the manuscripts of Rheims, Rodradus, and Ratoldus, whereas in the Roman Order an anointing with chrism is employed.

### 572. With the pious devotion of your servant N.

In the manuscript of Ratoldus, the words “with the pious devotion of your servant N.” are absent. After this prayer the Roman Order has: “And let him make the sign of the cross with chrism over the chalice, on its sides,” which is absent from our manuscripts of Saint Eligius, Rodradus, Rheims, and Ratoldus.

### 573. O God, who for your servant Moses, etc.

This is absent from the manuscripts of Rheims and Ratoldus. In the Rheims manuscript, however, the following appears:

“Preface of the chrismal: Let us pray, dearest brothers, that almighty God may deign, as we pray, to endow this vessel bearing the body of his Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, with the blessing, the safeguard of sanctification, and the gift of protection. Through him.”

Here *chrismalis*, or *chrismal*, or *chrismale*, means the vessel in which Christ’s body is kept. This is clear from the Roman Order, where the following title is prefixed: “Preface of the little vessel in which the Eucharist is stored.” There *vasculum* is unquestionably used for *chrismale*. The same is evident from Book VI of Halitgarius, in the manuscript of the Corbie library: “But whoever loses his chrismal, or merely the sacrifice, in any region, etc.”

It is also used for the corporal, or corporal cloth, as is known from Glaber, Book V of his *History*, chapter 1: “The chrismal also, which by some is called the corporal, has been found to provide very many remedies.” A little later he writes:

“At the monastery of Réomé, in the time of the venerable abbot William, it happened that a fire devastated the areas surrounding the monastery. The brothers of that place seized the chrismal, set upon a pole, and raised it against the flames of the fire, which were burning fiercely. Immediately the fire, recoiling upon itself, was unable to seize anything more than it had already consumed. Yet that cloth of the Lord, when a breeze arose, slipped from the pole and flew more or less two miles away, etc.”

In the same preface of the manuscript, the chrismal is rightly called a *ministerium*. For *ministerium* means a vessel; hence the golden or silver vessels of a church are called *ministerium*. In the Council of Rheims, canon 22, as reported by Flodoard, Book II of the *Ecclesiastical History of Rheims*, chapter 5:

“If a bishop—except when a grave necessity for the redemption of captives should arise—should presume to break the sacred vessels for any reason whatsoever, he shall cease from ecclesiastical office.”

In Letter 20 [Note: [Col. 0421D] Now Letter 25; formerly it was 19] of Saint Gregory, Book II of the *Register*:

“That the written inventory prepared by you may truthfully contain both the vessels of the churches and the silver used for ordinary purposes, and whatever else, after the property has been carefully inspected.”

And in Book III, Letter 15 [Note: [Col. 0421D] It is now Book IV, Letter 16; formerly Book III, indiction 12, Letter 16]: “It has come to our attention that various priests of Italy, fleeing to Sicily, carried with them many vessels of their churches.” The Council of Arvernus, canon 8: “Let not sacred vessels be supplied for the adornment of weddings.” The Third Council of Orléans, canon 23: “To alienate ecclesiastical property or sacred vessels.”

In Saint Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 22:

“And the priest himself was covered by the sea, having around his neck, together with the Book of the Gospels, his daily vessel—that is, a small paten with a chalice.”

In Fortunatus, Book I, poem 15:

> And with pious gifts you endowed Christ’s altars,  
> when your vessels carry the holy gifts of God.  
> For the blood and body of the Lord, libations of the Most High,  
> come duly in the sacred vessel through your giving.

That is: the body and blood of the Lord are placed in the vessel through your generosity. Hence Saint Paulinus, in Letter 12, uses *the splendid array of the sacred service* for all the altar vessels, whether golden or silver, which are kept in the church treasury:

[Col. 0422B]

> Here is the venerable storehouse in which is kept, and in which  
> is placed, the gracious splendid array of the sacred service.

This passage must be understood in this sense, not of the Eucharist, which is kept on the altar and not in the treasury; that altar vessels are customarily kept in the treasury or sacristy is obvious to everyone. In pagan authors too, *ministerium* is used for the golden or silver vessels required for setting a dining room, as may be seen in Lampridius, in his life of Alexander Severus: “The weight of his silver service never exceeded two hundred pounds.”

This word is mentioned in the old Glosses, but by metonymy it means the sideboard or table that holds the vessels:

“*Abacus*—read *abacus*—of Delphi, *menistērion*, as Juvenal has it.”

The passage occurs in Satire 13:

> Codrus’s bed was smaller than Procula’s; three little pitchers  
> were the adornment of the sideboard, and also, below,  
> a little cup, and Chiron reclining beneath the same marble.

[Col. 0422C] Hence in the old manuscripts of the Corbie library *abacus* means a marble table holding cups:

“*Abacus* or *abax*: part of a capital, or a gaming board, or a marble table on which the ancients placed cups.”

These words illuminate Juvenal’s expression, in which he called the *abacus* “marble”—that is, a marble table.

*Ministerium* is also used for carpets, hangings, and similar church ornaments, as may be seen in the Council of Arvernus, canon 3: “Care must be taken that the bodies of the dead not be wrapped in hangings or sacred furnishings.”

Finally, in the same Rheims manuscript the following appears:

“Also another prayer: Almighty God, inseparable Trinity, pour the aid of your blessing upon our hands, so that through our blessing this vessel may be sanctified and may, by the grace of the Holy Spirit, become a new tomb of Christ’s body. Through our Lord.”

### 574. Then they go to the place where the relics are, etc.

This describes the rite of carrying the relics into the church. It is an ancient practice of the Church to dedicate basilicas by bringing in and depositing holy relics, whose presence sanctifies the church.

Saint Ambrose, Book X, Letter 85, to his sister Marcellina:

“For when I had dedicated the basilica, many began to appeal to me as though with one voice, saying: ‘Will you dedicate a basilica in Rome?’ I replied: ‘I shall, if I find relics of martyrs.’”

Saint Paulinus, Letter 11, to Severus:

“The Lord is witness that, if we had possessed even a small amount of sacred ashes beyond what was necessary for us to dedicate the basilica that will soon be completed in the Lord’s name, we would have sent it to your community.”

A little later:

“We found something that we could worthily send both for the sanctification of the basilica and for increasing the blessing of the ashes: a fragment of the wood of the divine cross.”

And in the following letter:

“But this little basilica too they will consecrate, in the name of Christ, with the blessed relics and sacred ashes of the apostles and martyrs, of the holy saints, of the martyr, and of the lords.”

Saint Gregory, Book V, Letter 145 [Note: [Col. 0423D] Now Book VI, Letter 45]:

“We have also granted permission to dedicate the basilica of the blessed martyr Stephen, which your fraternity asserts was consumed by fire and which, as you recently reported, has now been restored; and we wish the shrines of the relics of that same blessed martyr Stephen to be placed there.”

Saint Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 20:

“Returning to the basilica, we solemnly brought his holy relics there, together with those of the martyrs Saturninus and Julian and also of the blessed Illidius, with shining candles and crosses.”

The passage concerns the dedication of an oratory.

Theophanes, in Book XVI, under the emperor Justinian:

“Later, in the month of June, the dedication of the apostles’ church was celebrated at Constantinople, and the relics of the apostles Andrew and Luke were deposited. Bishop Menas passed along with the holy relics, seated in the imperial golden carriage adorned with precious stones, holding on his knees three reliquaries of the holy apostles, and thus celebrated the dedication.”

Saint Gaudentius, bishop of Brescia, likewise, possessing many relics of the saints, especially those of the Forty Martyrs brought from Caesarea in Cappadocia, dedicated a church which he ordered to be called the Council of the Saints, as is clear from his treatise *On the Dedication of the Church*.

The same rule is laid down in canon 7 of the Seventh Synod:

> “Therefore, regarding all venerable temples that have been consecrated without the holy relics of martyrs, we decree that a deposition of relics be made in them, together with the customary prayer. But whoever consecrates a temple without holy relics is to be deposed, as one who has violated the ecclesiastical traditions.”

These relics were carried into the basilica in solemn procession, as is clear from the passage of Theophanes cited above and from the acts of Saint Virgilius, bishop of Arles, in the *Chronicle of the Saints of Lérins*.

### 575. Take away from us, etc.

This is absent from the Rheims manuscript and from the Roman Order. It is found in the manuscript of Rodradus and also in that of Ratoldus, where a litany precedes it.

### 576. Walk, etc.

So it appears in the manuscript of Ratoldus, but these words are absent from the Rheims manuscript. More material can be found in the Roman Order.

### 577. With crosses and censers, and candelabra, and many lights, etc.

So it appears in the Rheims manuscript. The manuscript of Ratoldus makes no mention of lights; the Roman Order says nothing about censers.

We see a similar procession when the relics of the saints are carried into a newly consecrated basilica in Saint Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 20:

“Returning to the basilica, we solemnly brought his holy relics there, together with those of the martyrs Saturninus and Julian and also of the blessed Illidius, with shining candles and crosses.” [The supplied *ab basilicam* has an irregular preposition and case; “to the basilica” follows the sense of the passage.] The passage concerns the dedication of an oratory.

It should be noted here that not only the candles but also the crosses are called “shining.” For formerly, during public processions, lighted candles were placed upon the crosses, as is clear from the same Saint Gregory, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 79:

“After lighting candles and candle-bearing devices upon the crosses, they raise their voices in song and go around the city through its streets.”

This practice originated with Saint John Chrysostom, as Socrates testifies, Book VI of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 8:

> “For silver crosses bearing lights from waxen lamps had been devised by him.”

That is: “Silver crosses were devised by him, upon which waxen lamps were placed.”

So too the passage of Sozomen, Book VIII of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 8, must be understood:

> “For silver images of crosses, beneath burning candles, went before them.”

That is: “Silver signs of crosses, beneath blazing candles, went before them.”

Accordingly, the translator did not express the meaning very well when he said merely “with burning torches”; and Sozomen, who relates the same history, understands nothing different from Socrates.

### 578. Your house, O God, etc.

This prayer is absent from the Roman Order and from the Rheims manuscript. In the manuscript of Ratoldus, the following is placed before it at the door of the new church:

“O God, who are present as the Dedicator in every place of your dominion, hear us, we ask, so that the consecration of this church may remain inviolate and that it may deserve the benefits of your gift, for which it pleads.”

Also another prayer with an antiphon:

“Bless, O God, this house; enter, we ask, this tabernacle, almighty and eternal God, etc.”

When this has been completed, the bishop is to receive the relics from the priest and place them upon the new altar, with a veil extended, etc.

### 579. With a veil extended between them and the people

Formerly, a veil was hung at the screens of the sacristy or choir, where the clerics stood. Saint Dionysius mentions it in his letter to Demophilus:

> “And proceeding graciously toward the places outside the divine veils.”

That is: “And proceeding benevolently toward those places that are outside the divine veils.”

Saint John Chrysostom also mentions such a veil, Sermon 3 on the Epistle to the Ephesians:

> “When you hear, ‘Let us all pray together,’ and see the curtains being drawn up, you imagine that heaven itself is being opened.”

Although I am not unaware that *amphithyra* sometimes means double doors, as Ovid uses the term in Book II of the *Metamorphoses*, the word *anelkomena* prevents that interpretation here.

Our interpretation is confirmed by Evagrius, Book VI, chapter 20, and by Theophylact Simocatta, Book V, chapter 14. In the letter of Chosroes, king of the Persians, to Saint Sergius the martyr, the gifts that the king sent to Saint Sergius are listed: a golden cross and censer, “and a Hunnic *amphithyron* adorned with gold.”

That is: “and a Hunnic veil adorned with gold.” For it is not likely that the king himself sent actual doors for closing the sacristy; rather, he sent some veil of great value.

### 580. In the place of the altar

It is an ancient custom to deposit the relics of the saints in the altar itself. Saint Paulinus, Letter 12, to Severus, concerning the dedication of a basilica:

“If their venerable ashes are placed beneath the altars without the company of the cross, this inscription will indicate what is concealed”:

> The glory of the divine table covers the saints’ relics,  
> brought forth from apostolic bodies.

And below, concerning the dedication of the basilica at Fundi:

> Behold, beneath the blazing altars, the bones of our forebears  
> are covered by a royal crust of purple marble.

In the manuscript of Ratoldus it reads: “In the confession of the altar.” The *confession* is the hollowed-out part of the altar in which the bishop deposits the relics of the saints. For another account of the meaning of *confession*, see our observations on the *Harmony of the Rules*, chapter 66, §31.

The same manuscript of Ratoldus continues:

“And let him make a cross inside, with chrism, in the four corners, saying: ‘In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Peace to you.’ Response: ‘And with your spirit,’ as in the Roman Order.”

Among the Greeks, when they deposit the relics of the saints, they pour chrism over them, as may be seen in their *Euchologion*:

> “The priest pours myron [ointment] over them—that is, over the relics.”

The same manuscript further continues:

“And let him place three portions of the Lord’s body inside, and three portions of incense.”

The relics are then enclosed while the antiphon “The saints shall exult in glory” is sung, followed by the psalm “Praise the Lord from the heavens.” Then the antiphon “You have received your seats beneath the altar of the Lord,” followed by the psalm “Blessed are the undefiled in the way.”

What is said here concerning the three portions of the Lord’s body and of incense, to be placed in the confession together with the relics of the saints, is likewise found in both dedication rites of the Roman Order.

Finally, the same manuscript of Ratoldus continues:
