“And then let the slab be placed, upon which he shall make four crosses with oil and holy chrism; and they are marked at the four corners with a knife. Then let the pontiff say this prayer: ‘O God, who from the entire joining together of the saints, etc.’”

The Roman Order has a different form:

“Then let him place the slab over the relics and say this prayer: ‘Let us pray. O God, who from the entire joining together of the saints, etc.’ Then let him coat it with the lime that had previously been prepared. After it has been coated, let him make a cross above it with chrism, saying as before: ‘In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen. Peace be with you.’ Response: ‘And with your spirit.’

“And let him pour chrism into the four corners of the altar, saying the words written above and making a cross. Then let them sing the antiphon: ‘The bodies of the saints have been buried in peace, and their names shall live forever,’ with the *Gloria*.”

This is the form in the first description of the dedication. In the second it is somewhat different:

“And taking the slab that is to be placed over the relics, let him first seal it underneath with chrism, saying: ‘In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.’ Then let him place the slab over the relics and say this prayer: ‘Let us pray. O God, who from the entire joining together of the saints …’ Then let him coat it with the lime that had previously been prepared. After it has been coated, let him make a cross above it with chrism, as above; and likewise let him make a cross with chrism above the four corners of the altar, saying as above.”

### 581. With the psalm “Praise the Lord from the heavens,” etc.

In the Rheims manuscript everything from here up to the words “Then let the pontiff return to the sacristy” is absent.

### 582. After this, let the altar be vested

In the manuscript of Ratoldus there is added: “With blessed water and incense.”

The altar is vested with linen hangings and also with silken cloths, as was done at the dedication of the temple at Jerusalem under Constantine the Great, as Theodoret writes in Book I, chapter 31, of his *Ecclesiastical History*.

And in Synesius, Letter 67, among the things necessary for dedicating a basilica, there is listed a *mystikon katapetasma*—that is, “a mystical veil.”

### 583. With an antiphon

For this, the manuscript of Ratoldus has:

“Let the bishop say the antiphon ‘They adorned the temple with golden crowns,’ etc. Antiphon: ‘Zacchaeus, hastening, come down,’ etc. While the altars are being adorned, let these things be sung, and let the pontiff say the prayer:

‘Let your Holy Spirit descend, we ask, Lord our God, upon this altar, etc.’”

### 584. Let the pontiff return to the sacristy

In place of this, the manuscript of Ratoldus has the following:

“Then let the cantor begin the antiphon ‘This place is awesome.’ Then ‘Glory to God in the highest.’ Collect for the Mass: ‘O God, who are the author of the gifts offered to you in consecration, etc.’

“Reading from the book of the Apocalypse of the apostle John: ‘In those days I saw the holy city, Jerusalem.’ Response: ‘This place was made by God.’ Verse: ‘O God, before whom the choir of angels stands.’ Alleluia: ‘I shall adore toward your holy temple.’ [Note: [Col. 0425D] That is, according to Luke.] Saint Luke. [Col. 0425D] ‘At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “A good tree is not …”’

“Offertory: ‘Lord God, in simplicity.’ Verse: ‘Majesty.’ Verse: ‘Solomon made.’

“Prayer over the offerings: ‘Almighty and eternal God, an altar dedicated to your name.’

“Preface: ‘Through whom we humbly beseech you concerning this altar, etc.’

“Blessing: ‘May almighty God bless and keep you, and illumine this house with the presence of his divinity’ [*numinis*; in the manuscript, *muneris*, “his gift”], etc.

“Communion: ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer.’

“Prayer after Communion: ‘We ask, almighty God, that in this place, etc.’

“Then proceeding to the fonts, let him consecrate them:

‘Almighty and eternal God, sanctify this baptistery, dedicated by heavenly visitation, through the illumination of your Holy Spirit, so that all whom this font will wash may, purified by the threefold washing, obtain by your gift the forgiveness of all sins. Through him.’

“Also another prayer:

‘Multiply, Lord, your blessing, and strengthen our faith through the gift of your Spirit, so that those who descend into these waters may deserve to be enrolled in the book of life. Through him.’”

This consecration of the baptistery or baptismal fonts is rather brief; for a fuller form, consult the Roman Order.

Sidonius mentions the consecration of a baptistery in Book IV, Letter 15:

“For you write that the baptistery which you were formerly constructing can now be consecrated.”

A baptistery is a building near a church in which there was a pool or font, either natural or artificial, suitable for baptizing Christians.

Prudentius, describing a baptistery in the *Peristephanon*, at a place where martyrs had once suffered:

> Christ chose this place, where tested hearts  
> may be carried to heaven by blood and cleansed by water.

Fortunatus, Book II, poem 12, on a baptistery built at Mainz:

> The lofty hall of sacred baptism gleams,  
> where Christ washes Adam’s sins in the river.

[Col. 0426B] Paulinus, Letter 12, to Severus, concerning his baptistery:

> Rich in Christ’s wealth, poor in himself, the beautiful Severus  
> established lofty halls with sacred fonts.

Ennodius, epigram 149, concerning the font of Saint Stephen’s baptistery and the water that comes through the columns:

> Behold, beneath a roof, rain falls serenely without a cloud,  
> and the pure face of heaven supplies the waters.  
> Streams flow forth over sacred marble,  
> and look—the stone gives birth again to dew.  
> For the dry pergola pours forth liquid springs,  
> and once more the heavenly water comes to the fountains thus produced.  
> Holy water flows from heavenly recesses,  
> led here by the ministry of the poet Eustorgius.

The same is clear from the Eighteenth Council of Toledo, canon 3:

“Although at the beginning of Lent the mystery of baptism is generally closed, nevertheless, as the order of ecclesiastical custom requires, it is necessary that the doors of the baptistery, sealed on that same day by the hand and ring of the pontiff, be closed.”

### 585. Let Mass be celebrated there solemnly

According to the decree of Pope Evaristus, in Ivo, Part 3, chapter 32:

“All basilicas must always be dedicated with Mass.”

Thus, at the consecration of the temple at Jerusalem under Constantine the Great, certain bishops “appeased the divine power with bloodless sacrifices and mystical sacred rites”; the Latin gloss renders this “appeased the divine power with bloodless sacrifices and mystical consecrations,” as Eusebius writes in Book IV, chapter 45, of *The Life of Constantine*.

Consult the second letter of Pope Vigilius.

### 586. Throughout the entire week, public Masses are to be celebrated there

So it appears in the manuscript of Ratoldus, where the following continues:

“And during those eight days there must be lights before the altar, either of wax or of oil; during the aforesaid eight days, until the eight days have been completed, the basilica is in no way to be without lights and the nocturnal and diurnal offices.”

Here read *Nullo modo reperiatur*, “Let it by no means be found [without lights and the night and day offices]”; supply *basilica*, “the basilica,” as the subject.

From this it should be noted that, to make the dedication more solemn, formerly the feast of the dedication was celebrated for eight complete days, both with sacred sermons and with bloodless sacrifices and other divine offices.

This is sufficiently suggested by the words of Apollinaris, Book IX, Letter 3:

“When, at the weekly festivities of the dedication of the church of Lyons, you were asked by the most holy colleagues to preach at length.”

For the weekly festivities of a dedicated church mean nothing other than that it was celebrated throughout an entire week.

### 587. On the anniversary of the dedication of the basilica

The anniversary of the dedication of a basilica is celebrated in the Church according to an ancient custom. Felix IV, in a letter preserved by Burchard, Book III, chapter 58, writes:

“The solemnities of the dedications of churches and of priests are to be celebrated solemnly each year, the Lord himself providing the example. For, when giving a model by which all were to celebrate the feast of the dedication of the temple, he came to celebrate it with the rest of the people.”

This is also clear from Sozomen, Book II of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 25, where he writes that the anniversary of the dedication of the temple at Jerusalem, formerly founded by Constantine the Great, was accustomed to be celebrated each year for eight days:

> “From that time the Church of Jerusalem celebrates this feast every year with great splendor, so that during it the initiations of sacred rites are performed, and afterward an assembly is held for eight days.”

Having made these observations concerning the dedication of a basilica, we must now append the rite for blessing the sign—that is, the bell—which is found in the manuscripts of Rheims and Ratoldus the abbot.

In the Rheims manuscript it reads:

“For blessing the sign of the church: Bless, Lord, this water with heavenly blessing, etc.”

In the manuscript of Ratoldus:

“For blessing the sign of the church: First dip it three times in the water and wash it in the water that is to be blessed, with these words: ‘Bless, Lord, this water with heavenly blessing,’ etc., as in the Roman Order.

“After this, you shall sing six psalms—that is, ‘Praise the Lord, my soul,’ to the end of the Psalter. Meanwhile wash it with water—namely, blessed water, as prescribed in the Rheims manuscript—with oil and salt. And say:

‘O God, who through Moses the lawgiver commanded silver trumpets to be made, etc.,’ as in the Roman Order.

“Then wipe it with a cloth and say the verse:

‘The voice of the Lord is over the waters; the God of majesty has thundered; the Lord is over many waters,’ to the end of the psalm.

“After this touch it with chrism seven times on the outside and four times on the inside.

“Prayer: ‘Almighty and eternal God, who before the ark of the covenant, etc.,’ as in the Roman Order.”

In the Rheims manuscript it reads as follows:

“And you shall say the antiphon with the heading: ‘The voice of the Lord,’ etc.”

“Then place incense in the *acerna* [read *acerra*, that is, a censer] and myrrh, and let it produce smoke inside and outside. Sing the verse:

‘The waters saw you, O God; the waters saw you,’ to the end of the psalm.

“‘Almighty Lord Christ, who, according to the assumption of the flesh, while sleeping in the boat, etc.,’ as in the Roman Order.”

In the Rheims manuscript it reads:

“Then place incense, perfumes, and myrrh in the censer, raise the bell, and say the antiphon:

‘O God, your way is in holiness; what god is as great as our God?’

“Verse: ‘The waters saw you, O God,’ to the end of the psalm. Then say the collect:

‘Almighty Lord Christ, etc.’”

This is what concerns the blessing of the bell.

The *clocca* mentioned in the Rheims manuscript is a church sign—that is, a *nola* or bell, called *cloche* in French. Otholonus confirms this in Book II of *The Life of Saint Boniface, Bishop of Mainz*:

“Meanwhile the church sign, commonly called a *glocca* [read *clocca*], began to sound without human action.”

It is also mentioned in Gutbert’s letter to Saint Lullus, which is Letter 89 among the letters of Saint Boniface:

“And we have taken care to send to your fatherhood a bell of the kind that I had at hand.”

### 588. On the vigil of the apostles

What they call the Common of the Saints follows. At its beginning the following is found in the Rheims manuscript:

“Announcement of the feast of a single martyr:

‘Let your devotion know, most holy brothers, that the anniversary day of that blessed martyr has arrived, on which, overcoming the devil’s temptations, he was joined to the Creator of all by a glorious passion. [The text has the corrupt *quod diaboli tentationis exuberant*; read *quo diaboli tentationes exsuperans*, “on which, overcoming the devil’s temptations.”]

“‘In the plural [that is, if the solemnity of several martyrs is to be announced]: on which, overcoming the devil’s assaults, they were joined to the Creator of all by a glorious passion. [Read *quo*, “on which,” instead of *quod*.]

“‘Therefore let us praise together the Lord, who is wondrous in his saints, so that he who bestowed upon them the crown of victory may, through their merits, grant us the forgiveness of our sins.

“‘Accordingly, in that place or in that village, on that day, let us celebrate this same feast with devoted diligence.’”

This is an ancient formula for announcing a feast before Martyrologies were publicly read in the Church. Mention of that reading occurs in the First Addition to the Capitularies of the emperor Louis, title 69:

“Let the Martyrology first be read at the chapter meeting, and let a verse be said; then let the Rule or any homily be read; then let ‘But you, Lord’ be said.”

But I scarcely believe that the reading of the Martyrology was in use before the time of Louis the Pious, as is clear from the material I have quoted from the Rheims manuscript, which was written in the time of Charlemagne. In it—let me note this in passing—there is nothing concerning the Common of the Apostles.

[Note: [Col. 0427D] In both Theodulf of Gembloux and the Calendar there are Masses for the feast of a single apostle. Also, for the feast of several apostles, and therefore from the Common. In Theodulf there are Masses both for the vigil and for the feast of a single evangelist, followed by the Mass for the feast of holy doctors.]

### 589. “Of a martyr” precedes it

In the Rheims manuscript it reads: “Of a martyr confessor precedes it.” But *confessor* is redundant.

### 590. “They are restored”

In the same manuscript it is corruptly written: “restorer.”

### 591. “With the precious Passion which we precede”

In the same manuscript it is incorrectly written: “With precious passion and solemn things.” But it should read, as in the manuscript of Rodradus: “With precious passion and solemnity.”

### 592. “Votive”

That is, devoted. Papias: “*Votivus*: devoted—that is, ready and eager for the worship of God.”

[Col. 0428B]

### 593. Another preface

This third preface is for a martyr who was a bishop.

### 594. On the vigil of several martyrs

This vigil is absent from the Rheims manuscript. But there is another Mass for the feast of several martyrs.

### 595. “Let them be set aflame”

That is, let them be inflamed.

### 596. “Of a confessor”

The Church calls those men confessors who, distinguished by piety and renowned for virtues and miracles, have rested in Christ without martyrdom, dying a peaceful and tranquil death.

Sidonius, Book IV, Letter 18:

“Perpetuus, bishop and most worthy successor to so great a predecessor, renewed the basilica of the holy bishop and confessor Martin, making it much larger than the former building, which until then had been adequate.”

And below:

> Which was not equal to its own confessor.

### 597. “After the Virgin came forth from the Virgin,” etc.

That is, after Christ, a virgin, came forth from Mary the Virgin, lust was overcome by the Virgin’s childbirth, as Prudentius beautifully sings in the *Psychomachia*:

[Col. 0428C]

> Is any right of yours still left  
> after the childbirth of the untouched Virgin?

And below:

> After Mary, you cannot break my laws.

### 598. “And in which there was the ease of sinning,” etc.

This is an elegant paronomasia.

### 599. Another Mass

This is absent from the Rheims manuscript. In the manuscript of Rodradus it reads: “Mass for the feast of a confessor-virgin.” Note here that a holy virgin who is not a martyr is called a *confessor*, just as holy men who are not martyrs are called confessors. We nevertheless find this term sometimes applied to holy women; for in the Fourth Council of Toledo, in the edition of Garcia, Saint Leocadia is called “confessor.”

### 600. “Or of a widow”

These words are absent from the printed editions. Concerning the profession of widowhood and the imposition of the garment by the bishop, the First Council of Orange, canon 27, states:

“The profession of preserving widowhood, made before the bishop in the sacristy and indicated by the widow’s garment imposed by the bishop, etc.”

### 601. Blessing of a virgin

It is an ancient custom among Christians to consecrate virgins to God. Ammianus Marcellinus, although a pagan, also touches upon it in Book XVIII, near the end:

“He nevertheless ordered that other virgins whom he found consecrated according to the Christian rite to divine worship should be kept inviolate and should serve their religion, as was customary, with no one preventing it.”

### 602. To be said by the bishop

It belongs to the bishop to consecrate virgins. Saint Jerome, in his letter to Demetrias, Book I:

“I know that, at the bishop’s invocation, the holy bridal veil covered the virginal head.”

And in Letter 83, to Oceanus, Book II:

“Yesterday a catechumen, today a bishop; in the evening in the circus, now at the altar; formerly a patron of actors, now a consecrator of virgins.”

The same is evident from the Second Council of Carthage, canon 3:

“All the bishops decreed that the preparation of chrism and the consecration of girls are not to be performed by priests.”

If priests should ever perform these rites, they must not do so without the bishop’s knowledge, as stated in the Third Council of Carthage, canon 36:

“That a priest is not to consecrate virgins without consulting the bishop.”

### 603. Which takes place at Epiphany

So it appears in the printed editions, in the Rheims manuscript, and in the Roman Order. The same is established in the letter of Pope Gelasius to the bishops of Lucania:

“Nor should they place the sacred veil upon virgins devoted to God except on the day of Epiphany, during the Easter white season, or on the feast days of the apostles.”

### 604. Or on Easter Monday

In the Roman Order: “Or during the Easter white season.” So too in the aforementioned letter of Gelasius.

In Saint Ambrose, in the very solemnity of the Lord’s Resurrection, Book *To the Fallen Virgin*, chapter 5:

“You did not remember the holy day of the Lord’s Resurrection, on which you offered yourself to be veiled at the divine altar.”

### 605. Or when the feasts of the apostles are celebrated

According to the decree of Pope Gelasius in the letter cited above.

### 606. And they wear black garments outwardly

These words are absent from the Roman Order and from the Rheims manuscript. Formerly, virgins consecrated to God were clothed in dark garments.

Saint Jerome, Letter 15, Book I, *On the Praises of Asella*:

“And she put on the darker tunic, which she could not obtain from her mother.”

And in the letter to Gaudentius, Book II:

“Some, when they have betrothed a future virgin, customarily clothe her in a dark tunic and cover her with a dusky mantle, so that from her earliest years she may grow accustomed to this kind of clothing.”

### 607. Of certain goods

Namely, of chastity, whose excellence will be more clearly perceived in heaven, as the following words sufficiently indicate.

### 608. In the new

So it appears in the Rheims manuscript and in the Roman Order. In the printed editions it reads “in this,” incorrectly.

### 609. Which offers you her devotion

That is, she offers you her purpose and her firm intention of serving you perpetually.

### 610. A vow

That is, a desire and intention.

### 611. Food in fasting

Spiritual food, namely, by which the mind is nourished while the flesh fasts. For of devoted virgins Prudentius writes in Book II against Symmachus:

> Their meals are sparse and light, and their mind always sober.

### 612. So that the hundredfold fruit, etc.

Thus Prudentius writes in the same book, speaking of virgins:

> Hence ten times tenfold fruits are gathered into the granaries.

See the notes above.

### 613. For veiling the handmaids of God

Formerly, virgins consecrated to God were veiled in a solemn rite. Besides the passages cited above, this may also be seen in Saint Jerome, Book I, Letter 48, to Sabinianus:

“After the basilica of the apostle Peter, in which you were consecrated to Christ with the bridal veil.”

And in Prudentius, in the book cited above:

> There are also most beautiful rewards for our virgins,
And modesty, and a face covered with a holy veil. This, however, was done after a prolonged testing of virginity, because in such veiling there is a particular consecration of the virgin and the strictest union with Christ the Bridegroom. Accordingly, formerly virgins were not veiled before their fortieth year, as is established in the Council of Agde, canon 19:

“Although the life and conduct of nuns may have been approved, they are not to be veiled before their fortieth year.”

And in the Council of Zaragoza, canon 8:

“It was likewise read that virgins who have vowed themselves to God are not to be veiled unless their age of forty years has been tested.”

And in a Novel of Majorian:

“We decree that daughters whom father or mother, having withdrawn them from worldly intercourse, have judged should keep the precepts of the Christian faith in continual virginity are not to be consecrated by assuming the honored veil until they have completed forty years of age and have deserved, by blameless observance, to be adorned with such fillets.”

Nor does this conflict with what Saint Basil established in Letter 1 to Amphilochius, canon 18: that the ὁμολογία of virgins—that is, their profession—should be received in the sixteenth or seventeenth year of age. For the reception of the veil is distinct from the profession or vow of virginity; nor were these ceremonies always performed at the same time, but sometimes at different times, as is clear from the Council of Zaragoza cited above, in which the vow of virginity and the reception of the veil are distinguished. The same is clear from Letter 1 of Pope Saint Innocent to Victricius, bishop of Rouen, chapters 12 and 13:

“Likewise, those who have spiritually married Christ and have deserved to be veiled by the priest, if afterward they marry either publicly or secretly violate themselves, are not to be admitted to perform penance unless the man to whom they had joined themselves has departed from this world, etc. But those who, although not yet covered with the sacred veil, have nevertheless promised always to remain in their resolve of virginity—if they should happen to marry, although they have not been veiled—are to perform penance for some period of time, etc.”

[Col. 0430B] Besides the veil, virgins commonly adorned their heads with a mitre or small mitre, which was woven of wool, gold, and purple, as can be seen in Optatus of Milevis, *Against Parmenianus*, book II:

“Meanwhile, the aforementioned Felix, amid his crimes and unspeakable offenses, did not hesitate wickedly to violate the girl whom he himself had seized and upon whom he had placed the mitre, and from whom he had shortly before been called ‘Father.’”

And in book VI:

“How foolish, how vain was that action which you wished to summon according to your will and, as it were, according to your dignity: that the virgins of God should do penance while learning; that they should later alter, at your command, the signs of their will which they had long before professed upon their heads; that they should throw away their golden small mitres and receive others.”

And shortly afterward:

“There are no accompanying prescriptions concerning what kind of wool the small mitre should be made from, or with what purple it should be colored; for virginity cannot be aided by this fabric.”

They did this in imitation of brides, to indicate that, having rejected the men of the world, they had married Christ, as is evident from the same passage of Optatus:

“Nevertheless, if virginity remains unharmed, it can be safe without the small mitre. This is a spiritual kind of marriage: by their will and profession they had already entered into the marriage of the Bridegroom, and they showed that they had renounced worldly marriages.”

Saint Isidore gives another reason in *On the Ecclesiastical Offices*, book II, chapter 17, where he also distinguishes the veil from the mitre:

“It is asked why virgins are veiled at the Benediction; the reason is this. Women are in no way assigned places or offices in the ecclesiastical ranks. For they are neither permitted to speak in church nor to teach; nor are they permitted to baptize or to offer anything belonging to a man’s ministry, or to claim for themselves any share in priestly office. Therefore, solely because she is a virgin and has resolved to sanctify her flesh, permission is granted her to enter the church conspicuous and distinguished, and to display, with her head uncovered, the honor of a sanctified body, and to wear upon her crown, as it were, the mitre of virginal glory.”

Almost all this is taken from Tertullian’s *On the Veiling of Virgins*. In Saint Isidore, *contingere* is incorrectly read here instead of *tingere* (“to dye” or “to color”).

The following statement of the same Isidore, *Etymologies*, book XIX, chapter 31, is to be understood of the mitre of virgins:

“A mitre is a Phrygian cap covering the head, such as is the head-dress of women dedicated to religious service.”

Here *devoted women* means virgins dedicated and consecrated to God, as in the First Council of Toledo, canon 16:

“A devoted woman who sins is not to be received into the Church unless she has ceased to sin.”

And canon 19:

“If the daughter of a bishop, presbyter, or deacon is a devoted woman, sins, and takes a husband, etc.”

Hence Ausonius calls a devoted virgin and devoted virginity by these names in the *Parentalia*, epigram 7:

“Emilia Hilaria, my maternal aunt, a devoted virgin,

You always hated the female sex, and from that

grew your love of devoted virginity.”

Because the mitre is called a Phrygian cap, it came about that the mitre, or tiara, of the Roman pontiff was called *frigium*, or rather *phrygium*, according to the more correct spelling. Abbot Suger of Saint-Denis, writing in the *Life of Louis the Fat*, king of the Franks, about Pope Alexander II, says:

“And when, at Tours, at Saint Martin’s, he had celebrated ‘Rejoice, Jerusalem’ while wearing the *frigium*, as is customary among the Romans.”

Here *friguum* is incorrectly read. Further on, writing about Pope Callistus II, where such a *phrygium* is described, he says:

“And there, preparing themselves according to Roman custom with rich and marvelous adornment, they placed upon his head the *fugium*—read *frigium*—the imperial ornament, like a helmet, encircled by a golden ring.”

Finally, the hair of virgins was worn loose and unbound, like that of brides, as is clear from the same Optatus, book VI:

“They had loosened their hair for the spiritual Bridegroom and had already celebrated the heavenly marriage.”

And below:

“You therefore found such virgins, who had already spiritually married, and, as though forcing them into a second marriage, you commanded them to loosen their hair again.”

For the schismatics, having carried off or enticed Catholic virgins to their party, first imposed penance upon them and then consecrated them again. From this passage of Optatus it is clear that formerly virgins did not have their hair cut. This is also confirmed by Saint Ambrose, chapter 8 of *A Book to the Fallen Virgin*:

“Let the hair be cut off which, through vain glory, provided an occasion for sexual excess.”

There he imposes upon the fallen virgin, who is to perform penance, the cutting of her hair as a punishment for the sin of her hair, according to an ancient custom. The same may be observed in book VI of Optatus; this indicates that she had worn her hair uncut before her fall. It is also confirmed by Saint Jerome’s letter to Sabinian, where he relates that a certain virgin who had made her profession at Rome came to Bethlehem and, in order to preserve the custom of the people, had her hair cut and gave it to her lover Sabinian.

The same is confirmed by canon 17 of the Council of Gangra:

“If any woman, because of the exercise that is so regarded—or, that is, on account of the monastic life—cuts off her hair, etc., let her be anathema.”

But the contrary practice prevailed in parts of Egypt and Syria. For there, formerly, nuns—whether virgins or widows—had their hair cut, as Saint Jerome teaches in the letter cited above:

“It is the custom in the monasteries of Egypt and Syria that every virgin or widow who has vowed herself to God, renounced the world, and trampled underfoot all the world’s delights should offer her hair to the mother of the monastery to be cut off.”

He also gives the reason: so that they would not be overrun by lice, since they did not visit the baths and did not anoint themselves with oil. This practice is observed among us today, and also among the Greeks, as Theodore Balsamon writes in his commentary on the canon cited.

### 614. Prayer for making an abbot

For the rite of ordaining both an abbot and an abbess, consult the Roman *Ordo*.

### 615. The second week

What follows is the *Order of the Weeks* throughout the year, from Pentecost to the Advent of the Lord. In the printed editions one reads: “The second, third, fourth Sunday,” and so forth.

### 616. After the times had been happily prolonged

That is, after a long life had been happily led.

### 617. And the priest alone, without the stain of sin

In accordance with the Apostle’s words in Hebrews 7: “For such a high priest was fitting for us: holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners, etc.”

### 618. To whom belongs everything that is best

Here *optimum* means “good”; it is a Greek idiom, using the superlative for the positive degree. For every good, in whatever degree or distinction it is considered, belongs to God and comes from God. Thus James 1, according to the Greek text, says: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above” (*Πᾶσα δόσις ἀγαθὴ, καὶ πᾶν δώρημα τέλειον ἄνωθέν ἐστι*), that is, in the common version, “every best gift,” with the superlative used for the positive, as it stands in the Greek text. Saint James very appropriately attributes the good gift and the perfect gift—that is, the best gift—to God, because every good, whatever its kind, belongs to God and comes from God.

For this reason the philosopher-emperor Marcus was accustomed to say *πάντα ἄνωθεν*, “everything is from above,” as Dio of Prusa reports.

### 619. To offer sacrifice to you

Here *litare* means “to sacrifice,” from *λιτή*, that is, “prayer,” as Festus teaches.

### 620. You have sanctified

That is, “you have made holy.” *Sancire* sometimes means “to sanctify.” Tertullian, in *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, says: “The soul is sanctified not by washing but by profession.” And in *On Fasting*, citing Joel: “Joel cried out: ‘Sanctify a fast.’”

For the sacrifices of the Old Law derive their dignity and holiness from the Eucharistic sacrifice of the New Law, as a figure derives them from its prototype.

### 621. So that what each person offered

He speaks in this way because the faithful who were going to communicate at the solemn celebrations of Mass each offered bread and wine for his own communion. More will be said about this below.

### 622. The spirit of thinking what is right

The Church rightly asks for the spirit of thinking what is right, because no good thought exists in a person without God’s help, in accordance with Paul’s words in 2 Corinthians 3:

“Not that we are sufficient to think anything from ourselves, as though from ourselves; rather, our sufficiency is from God.”

In these words, *non quod* (“not that”) is an anastrophe for *quod non* (“that not”). He gives the reason why we ought to have confidence through Christ in God: we are not sufficient to think anything right or holy from ourselves, as though from ourselves.

This is likewise defined in the Second Council of Orange, canon 7:

“If anyone asserts that, by the power of nature, a person can think, as is necessary, or choose, or consent to the preaching of salvation—that is, the Gospel—without the illumination and inspiration of the Holy Spirit, who grants all people sweetness in consenting to and believing the truth, he is deceived by a heretical spirit.”

### 623. To pertain

That is, “to reach” or “to attain.”

### 624. Of those who steal upon us

Instead of *τὸ subrepentium*, “of those who steal upon us,” a form frequently found in ancient manuscript codices.

### 625. The work of our Redemption is carried out

This is so both with respect to representation, because the unbloody sacrifice of the altar recalls the bloody sacrifice completed on the altar of the cross, and with respect to application, because through the sacrifice of the altar Christ’s merit in his Passion is applied to us.

### 626. And compel by terror

This does not mean that God uses terror to force the will and remove the exercise of free choice. Rather, these words follow the ordinary manner of speaking, as when we say to someone while threatening him: “If you do not do it willingly, you will do it unwillingly.”

### 627. And what was hidden became visible

Namely, the world. While hidden in the divine ideas, it was created by God and made visible.

### 628. You granted that your Church should grow amid adversity

This is demonstrated by the experience of so many martyrs, and Saint Justin Martyr bears witness to it in his *Dialogue with Trypho the Jew*, where he beautifully compares the Church to a vine: if someone cuts off its budding shoots, it will produce other green and fruitful branches.

Tertullian, *To Scapula*, says:

“Yet this sect will not fail; you should know that it is built up more when it seems to be cut down.”

And Saint Nilus, *Homily 2 on the Ascension of Christ*:

“*Τὰ τῆς Ἐκκλησίας κατεκόπτετο κλήματα, καὶ ὁ τῆς πίστεως μᾶλλον ἐπεδίδου καρπὸς, καὶ ἄνθος ἀμάραντον ἔφερε.*”

That is:

“The branches of the Church were cut down, yet the fruit of faith advanced all the more and produced an unfading flower.”

### 629. And he who granted you the desire to make supplication

The desire to make supplication is granted by God, because no one can supplicate God without God’s grace. This concerns the statement of the Second Council of Orange, canon 3:

“If anyone says that God’s grace can be bestowed through human invocation, but denies that grace itself causes us to invoke God, he contradicts the prophet Isaiah or the Apostle, who says the same thing: ‘I was found by those who did not seek me; I openly appeared to those who did not ask me.’”

### 630. By a gift

That is, “by grace.”

### 631. By our senses

That is, by our opinions, which are for the most part deceptive and erroneous.

### 632. So that our judgment may not be in us, etc.

That is, so that we may not be led by our desires, but by the operation of heavenly grace. “In us” means “us”; this is a Hebrew idiom.

### 633. So that what you have bestowed although we did not deserve it, etc.

That is, so that you may bring to fulfillment the good will to serve you which, through your grace, you have bestowed upon us.

### 634. Of merits

That is, “of sins.” See above in the exposition of the Canon of the Mass.

### 635. We carry out

That is, “we administer” or “we perform.”

### 636. Unharmed

That is, not subject to any condemnation on account of a crime or guilt, while patiently enduring the adversities of this world for God’s sake.

### 637. Through the venerable exchange of this sacrifice

These words are metaphorical. The meaning is: through the sacrifices—or in exchange for the sacrifices—which we offer to God, as through a kind of mutual exchange, he makes us participants in his supreme divinity.

### 638. And may he not abandon us in the mysteries of his bodily presence, etc.

The two words *deserat* and *relinquat* (“abandon” and “leave”) seem here to be used in the sense of “desert” or “deprive.”

### 639. *Reg. Ben.*

That is, consult the *Benediction*, namely, in the preceding Week.

### 640. The fifth week before the Nativity of the Lord

Thus in the printed editions. In the Rheims Codex there are also five Sundays, or weeks, of the Advent of the Lord, numbered in the same order. Concerning these, Amalarius writes in book III of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 40, under “Advent”:

“In the ancient books of the Missal and Lectionary one finds written: ‘The fifth week before the Nativity of the Lord.’ For there are as many lessons in the Lectionary, and as many Gospels, from the time mentioned through the Sundays up to the Nativity of the Lord.”

In the codices of Rodrada and Ratold, and in Pamelius, there are only four weeks and Sundays of this same Advent of the Lord.

[Note: In the old Gallican Sacramentary there are only three.]

They are numbered in reverse order, so that the one farther from the Nativity of the Lord is called the first Sunday, or week, while the one nearest to it is called the fourth.

Berno of Reichenau, in chapter 4 of his book *On Certain Matters Pertaining to the Mass*, writes that this is the arrangement of the Advent of the Lord in the Gregorian codices. I can scarcely persuade myself of this, however, since the printed codices from the Vatican, the Rheims Codex, and the Codices of Saint Eligius—which are Gregorian—contradict him.

In the Ambrosian Masses apud Pamelius, six Sundays of the Advent of the Lord may be seen, because there the first Sunday of Advent immediately follows the feast of Saint Martin. Radulphus of Tongeren also testifies to this in proposition 16:

“The Ambrosian Advent has six weeks and begins on the Sunday after Martinmas.”

This office was established out of reverence for the Nativity of the Lord, as was the fast, which varied according to time and place.

Saint Perpetuus, bishop of Tours, among other fasts throughout the year, established:

“From the burial of Saint Martin until the Nativity of the Lord, three fasts each week.”

Saint Gregory of Tours reports this in book IX of his *History*. In canon 9 of the First Council of Mâcon, held under King Guntram in the year 581, it is decreed:

“It is established that from the feria of Saint Martin until the Nativity of the Lord, fasting is to be observed on the second, fourth, and sixth days of the week.”

In book VI of the *Capitularies* of the kings Charles and Louis, title 183, a forty-day fast before the Nativity of the Lord is prescribed:

“Therefore let priests admonish the people that the three lawful fasts of the year be observed: forty days before the Nativity of the Lord, forty before Easter—when we pay the tithes of the year—and forty days after Pentecost.”

Rabanus discusses the same fast in book II of *On the Instruction of Clerics*, chapter 22:

“Accordingly, by the authority of divine Scripture the Church has adopted this custom and celebrates a universal fast according to this observance. This fast, however, beginning in the ninth month and extending into the tenth, continues until the Nativity.”

Thus, by an appropriate arrangement, the teachers of the Church established the forty-day fast here, so that before the day of the Nativity of the Lord we might discipline ourselves by fasting and abstinence.

In the calendar prefixed to the Sacramentary of Abbot Ratold, the eighteenth day before the Kalends of November is marked as the Forty-Day Fast before the Nativity of the Lord.

Saint Cuthbert, bishop of Lindisfarne, was accustomed to fast for forty days before the Nativity of the Lord, as Bede writes in his *Life*, chapter 42.

The Greeks likewise observe the same custom of fasting, as is clear from George Codinus, in his book *On the Offices of the Palace of Constantinople*. Speaking of the ceremonies of the imperial table at the Nativity of the Lord, he writes:

“*Καὶ ποιῶν εὐχὴν ἐπὶ τῆς τραπέζης διὰ τὸ τὴν τεσσαρακοστὴν παρελθεῖν, ἀρχὴν δὲ κρεοφάγον λαβεῖν, λαμβάνει ἄρτον καὶ μίνσον.*”

That is:

“And after making a prayer at the table, because the Forty-Day Fast has passed and the beginning of the season in which meat is eaten has arrived, he takes bread and *minson*.”

To distinguish it from this, the Paschal Forty-Day Fast is called by the same Codinus *ἁγία καὶ μεγάλη τεσσαρακοστή*, “the holy and great Forty-Day Fast.”

This forty-day fast before the Nativity of the Lord, however, is not very ancient among the Greeks. It did not exist in the time of the Council in Trullo, nor even in the age of Theodore Balsamon, who flourished in the year of the Lord 1191. Thus he writes in his commentary on canon 52 of that council:

“*Σημείωσαι οὖν καὶ ἀπὸ τοῦ παρόντος κανόνος, ὅτι κυρίως μία ἐστὶ τεσσαρακονθήμερος etc.*”

That is:

“Note from this canon also that properly there is one Forty-Day Fast. For if there were another, it would have been prescribed that the sacred mystery should not be celebrated in it by the full sacrifice, but by the Presanctified Gifts, just as it was also prescribed that this should not be done during the Forty-Day Fast of the Great Pascha.”

He would certainly not have written this had the Forty-Day Fast of the Nativity of the Lord then been in use among the Greeks.

Formerly the monks in Gaul followed a different practice. For in the Council of Tours, held in the year 567 under King Charibert, it was decreed that, according to ancient statutes, monks should fast every day from December until the Nativity of the Lord.

[Col. 0434C] Formerly the Romans reckoned the beginning of Advent from the Sunday after the feast of Saint Catherine, as Radulphus of Tongeren testifies in proposition 16:

“Among the Romans, the Advent of the Lord begins on the first Sunday after the day following Catherine’s feast.”

This is also to be understood of the fast. For shortly afterward he adds:

“Among the Romans too, a fast is observed during the Advent of the Lord.”

But this span of Advent is not very ancient among the Romans, since the feast of Saint Catherine is not found in the ancient Sacramentaries. Nor is the present arrangement ancient, which consists of three complete weeks and several days of the following week, and which some therefore mistakenly think was instituted in this form by Saint Peter.

The more ancient Sacramentaries cited above oppose this view, for in them the Advent of the Lord consists of five Sundays.

Nor should we listen to a certain more recent writer who, in order to prove the antiquity of the Advent of the Lord, produces this passage of Saint John Chrysostom from homily 3 on the Epistle to the Ephesians:

“If,” he says, “the solemn day of Epiphany should arrive—I add also, if the sacred season of the Advent of the Lord should arrive, much less [should one wait for] Epiphany and the Forty-Day Fast.”

But these words prove nothing, and the writer does not grasp the author’s meaning, as will be clear from the Greek text:

“*Ἂν ἐπιστῇ, φησὶν, ὁ τῆς ἁγίας τεσσαρακοστῆς καιρός, οἷος ἂν ᾖ τις, μετέχει τῶν μυστηρίων· ἂν ἐπιστῇ τῶν Ἐπιφανίων ἡμέρα. Καίτοι καιρὸς οὐ τοῦτο προσόδου· οὐ γὰρ Ἐπιφανία, οὐδὲ τεσσαρακοστὴ ποιεῖ ἀξίους τοῦ προσιέναι, ἀλλὰ ψυχῆς εἰλικρίνεια καὶ καθαρότης.*”

That is:

“If,” he says, “the time of the Forty-Day Fast arrives, whoever a person may be, he becomes a participant in the mysteries. If the day of Epiphany arrives—yet the time of approaching is not determined by this. Neither Epiphany nor the Forty-Day Fast makes those who approach worthy, but sincerity and purity of soul.”

Here he attacks those who rarely received the Eucharist and said that they would receive it at Epiphany and during the Forty-Day Fast. He answers that the time at which one approaches the sacred table is not the determining factor: people of whatever character they may be ordinarily approach communion either at Epiphany or during the Forty-Day Fast, but Epiphany and the Forty-Day Fast do not make them worthy; rather, sincerity and purity of soul do.

Thus this is a dialogue between a negligent person who delays receiving the Eucharist and Saint John Chrysostom. The sluggish person says: “When the time of the Forty-Day Fast comes, I will approach the sacred table.” The holy Doctor replies: “Whatever a person may then be, he becomes a participant in the mysteries.” The sluggish person says: “At Epiphany”—with “I will approach communion” understood. The holy Doctor replies: “The time of approaching is not the determining factor; for Epiphany and the Forty-Day Fast do not make people worthy,” etc.

### 641. Stir up your power, O Lord, etc.

In the Rheims Codex another prayer is added:

“We ask you, almighty God, daily to purify our consciences,” etc., as in the Roman Missal.

### 642. The mystery of the first Advent, etc.

In the Rheims Codex there is another Preface:

“He who will instruct us as little children with nourishment, distributing food for mind and body,” etc.

### 643. To whom it is proper and unique that you are good

Namely, by essence. In the Codex of Abbot Ratold there is the Preface of the preceding Mass.

### 644. That it may be evident to be perfect

In the same codex *proficiatur* (“may it advance”) is read instead of these words. This is corrupt. It should read *perficiatur* (“may it be perfected”).

### 645. Which had previously been promised through the oracles of the prophets

In the Rheims Codex one reads:

“Which you promised through the Gospel of the Word of God.”

### 646. May they receive the dignity of adoption, etc.

In the same codex it is read differently, as follows:

“And may the fullness of adoption possess what the testimony of truth has endured.”

In the same codex three other Masses follow, which are absent from the printed editions and from our manuscript codices.

### 647. Who by your unspeakable gift have granted, etc.

In the Codex of Ratold there is another Preface:

“To whom it is proper and unique that you are good,” etc., as above.

Likewise, in the Rheims Codex:

“To whom it is proper to grant forgiveness for sins,” etc., as in the Ambrosian Order of the Mass for the Fourth Sunday of Advent.

### 648. Of the ancient Virgin

That is, Eve, because the earthly paradise was free from every contamination of lust, as theologians commonly teach.

### 649. God, whose Advent, etc.

In the Codex of Ratold the word “God” is absent.

### 650. Another prayer for the Mass

In the Rheims Codex it reads: “After the Benedictions,” that is, after the canticle *Benedicite, omnia opera Domini* (“Bless the Lord, all you works of the Lord”).

### 651. The first Sunday before the Nativity of the Lord

In the codices of Rheims, Rodrada, and Ratold one reads:

“The Sunday is vacant.”

[Note: In our manuscripts it is read in this way.]

### 652. Prayers for Advent

There are fewer of these in the Rheims Codex than are found here. They do not exist in the codices of Rodrada and Ratold.

[Note: In the codices of Thérouanne and Jumièges there are many Advent prayers that generally differ from the common versions. We have decided to refrain from recording these differences among the manuscript codices.]

### 653. Prayers for sins

There are more of these in the Codex of the presbyter Rodrada; but none are found in the Rheims Codex or in the Codex of Abbot Ratold.

### 654. Daily prayers

These do not exist in the Rheims Codex or in Ratold’s codex. There are more in the Codex of Rodrada. I think these prayers were formerly said on ordinary weekdays.

### 655. Evening prayers

In the Codex of Rodrada one reads:

“Morning or evening prayers.”

Although that codex contains many more prayers than are found here, none of these four is present, and those it does contain differ from their title. There are none in the Rheims Codex or in Ratold’s codex.

### 656. Prayers at the cross

These are lacking in the other manuscript codices we possess.

### 657. Prayers at Compline

Nor are these found in the other manuscript codices we possess.

### 658. Morning prayers

There are fewer in the Codex of Rodrada, and none in the Rheims Codex or in the Codex of Abbot Ratold.

### 659. At Matins, as day dawns

These prayers are lacking in the other manuscript codices we possess, as is the following prayer at Prime.

### 660. For making a cleric

It is an ancient custom of the Roman Church that clerical status be conferred through the cutting of the hair. Thus Arator writes in his letter to Parthenius:

“For I, mingled with the pleasant branches

of the Roman Church, became a sheep with my head shorn.”

This was done before the reception of any order, as is clear from the *Life of Saint Germanus, Bishop of Auxerre*, by the presbyter Constantius:

“A crowd of clerics and nobles gathered around him. They laid hands upon Germanus, seized him, and, invoking the name of the Lord, cut the hair from his head; then, rejecting worldly ornaments, they clothed him in the religious habit with the dignity of advancement.”

And in the *Life of Saint Patroclus the Abbot*, by Saint Gregory of Tours:

“He went to Arcadius, bishop of the city of Bourges, and asked that the hair of his head be cut and that he be enrolled among the clerics. The bishop, God willing, completed this without delay; and not long afterward he assumed the first office of the diaconate.”

Hence the testament of Saint Remigius says:

“And if anyone in the clerical order, from presbyter down to the tonsured, etc.”

The Greeks follow a different practice. Among them, when a lector is ordained—which is now the only one of the minor orders conferred among them—the clerical tonsure is given, as can be seen in their *Euchologion* in the rite for ordaining a lector:

“*Προσαγόμενος τῷ Ἀρχιερεῖ ὁ τοσοῦτος, εἰ μὲν κοσμικός ἐστι, μετὰ ἱματίου, εἰ δὲ μοναχός, μετὰ μανδίου, καὶ σφραγίζεται τρίτον τὴν κεφαλὴν παρὰ τοῦ Ἀρχιερέως, καὶ κείρεται παρ’ αὐτοῦ σταυροειδῶς, λέγοντος etc.*”

That is:

“So-and-so is brought before the bishop; if he is a layman, wearing his garment, but if he is a monk, wearing his monastic cloak. He is signed three times on the head by the bishop and is tonsured by him in the form of a cross, while he says, etc.”

The same is also clear from the *Life of Saint Euthymius the Abbot*—in Surius, 20 January:

“After he had baptized him and cut the hair which, according to the Law, is cut from boys, he enrolled him among the lectors.”

That custom, however, does not seem to have been universal. For in the Seventh Synod, canon 14, we see that boys were admitted to the clergy by tonsure even though they had not been ordained as lectors by the imposition of the bishop’s hands. Although they read publicly in the church from the ambo, the synod forbids this and decrees that such clerics must not thereafter presume to read in the church unless they have first been instituted as lectors by a bishop.

The author of ecclesiastical tonsure was Saint Peter, Prince of the Apostles, as Saint Gregory of Tours testifies in book I of *On Miracles*, chapter 28:

“The Apostle Peter established that the top of the head should be tonsured in order to teach humility.”

This was done in the likeness of the crown of thorns of our Lord, as Bede teaches in book V of the *Ecclesiastical History of the English*, chapter 22.

A certain more recent writer, disapproving of this form of the crown and miserably distorting Bede’s passage, went so far as to write that in the time of Saint Isidore clerics had two tonsures: one at the crown of the head and another lower down around the temples; that the former signified the priestly tiara and the latter the royal diadem; and that this was stated on Saint Isidore’s authority, “and most explicitly,” as he says.

But Saint Isidore’s own words, in book II of *On the Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 2, demonstrate that writer’s error most clearly:

“As for the fact that, after the upper part of the head has been shorn, a circular crown is left below, I think that the priesthood and the kingdom of the Church are symbolized in them. For among the ancients the tiara was placed on the priest’s head. Made of fine linen, it was round, like half a sphere; this is signified in the shorn part of the head. The crown, however, is the breadth of a golden circle that encircles the heads of kings.”

Where, I ask, is there a double tonsure here? There is plainly only one: the upper part of the head is shorn, signifying the tiara—not merely the very top, as is done today—while the lower circle of hair signifies the crown.

This is indeed the ancient crown of Saint Peter and of the early clerics, representing Christ’s crown of thorns. It can also be seen in canon 40 of the Fourth Council of Toledo:

“All clerics and lectors, like Levites and priests, with the whole upper part of the head shorn, shall leave below only a circular crown.”

Not as lectors in the regions of Gaul appear to do up to the present, who, with long hair like laymen, shave only a small circle at the crown of the head, etc.

These words mean nothing other than what Saint Isidore says. They are clear and unmistakable, and they do not differ from Bede’s opinion, who recognizes a single tonsure among clerics, not a double one. Consult our observations on the *Harmony of the Rules*, chapter 62, § 10.

### 661. Prayers and petitions over the penitent who confesses, etc.

These prayers are not in their proper place, which is the Wednesday of Quinquagesima, at the beginning of the fast, as in the codices of Rodrada and Ratold and in the Roman *Ordo*. Accordingly, in the Codex of Rodrada the following is rightly added:

“Wednesday in Quinquagesima.”

On that day prayers of this kind were said over one who had confessed his sins, as can be seen in the Roman *Ordo* and in Ratold’s codex. From the latter I shall present the rite for undertaking penance:

“Wednesday, the beginning of the fast. The order for giving penance begins.

Psalm: ‘O Lord, rebuke me not in your fury,’ twice throughout.

‘Hear, O Lord, the prayers of those who supplicate you, and spare the sins of those who confess to you,’ etc.

Then he says another psalm:

‘Bless the Lord, O my soul,’ up to ‘your youth is renewed like the eagle’s.’

Prayer: ‘May the inspiration of saving grace be present, we ask, O Lord, to this your servant.’

Psalm: ‘Have mercy on me, O God,’ up to ‘restore to me the joy.’

Prayer: ‘May your servant be preceded by,’ etc.

Psalm: ‘Why do you boast in wickedness,’ up to ‘the righteous shall see.’

Let us pray: ‘Be present, O Lord, to our supplications; and may your merciful compassion not be far from this your servant,’ etc.

Psalm: ‘O God, in your name,’ throughout.

Let us pray: ‘O Lord our God,’ etc.

Then the prayer ‘Our Father,’ and the verses:

‘Have mercy on me, O Lord, for I am weak.’

‘And my soul is greatly troubled.’

‘Turn, O Lord, and deliver my soul.’

‘O Lord, behold my humility and my labor.’

‘Make your face shine upon your servant.’

‘Save your servant.’

‘Send him help, O Lord, from the sanctuary.’

‘O Lord, hear.’

Let us pray: ‘Grant, we ask, O Lord, to this your servant continual observance of his purification,’ etc.

Another prayer: ‘O God, whose indulgence no one fails to need,’ etc.

‘Now they are to rise.’

Blessing of the ashes.

‘O God, who desire not the death but the repentance of sinners, look with the greatest kindness upon the frailty of human condition,’ etc.

Another:

‘Almighty and everlasting God, spare those who fear you, show favor to those who supplicate you, and deign to send your holy angel from heaven, who may + bless and + sanctify these ashes,’ etc.

Here he places ashes upon their heads with blessed water, and they are expelled from the church.

The responsory begins: ‘In the sweat.’

And they prostrate themselves before the door.

Psalm: ‘Incline, O Lord.’

Prayer: ‘I beseech the Majesty of your kindness and mercy, O Lord,’ etc.

Afterward they go around the church singing the antiphon.”

In the Rheims Codex the following is found for the same day:

“Concerning those performing public penance on Wednesday morning at the beginning of Lent. And you cover him with sackcloth, pray for him, and enclose him until the Lord’s Supper. On that same day he is presented in the bosom of the Church, and after he has prostrated his whole body upon the ground, the bishop says a prayer over him for reconciliation on Thursday, the Lord’s Supper.”

“Prayers and petitions over the penitent”—understand, the person confessing his sins.

This assumption of penance on Wednesday at the beginning of the fast is discussed in the Council of Meaux, chapter 76, where it is prescribed that no count or anyone exercising judicial authority should presume to hold a court or assembly:

“After the Wednesday called the beginning of the fast, on which all penitents receive the imposition of hands in order to devote themselves solely to penance and the divine Offices.”

The same may be seen in Burchard, book XIX, chapter 2:

“Presbyters ought to admonish the people subject to them that everyone who feels himself wounded by the deadly wound of sin should hasten with all speed, on the Wednesday before Lent, to the life-giving mother Church. There, having confessed simply and with all humility and contrition of heart what he has done wrongly, he should receive the remedies of penance according to the measure established by canonical authorities.”

These words are cited as belonging to Saint Augustine, but falsely. They have nothing of Augustine about them, both because of their style and because in Saint Augustine’s time penance was offered at every time, without waiting for this Wednesday.

The Roman *Ordo* also contains an order for giving penance on the same Wednesday. In the manuscript codex of the monastery of Saint Remigius there is:

“Order for giving penance, as the holy Fathers established.”

It begins with questions concerning the faith:

“Do you believe in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit?” etc., as in Burchard, book XIX, chapter 4.

What is written above in Ratold’s Codex—namely, that ashes are placed on the heads of penitents and that they are purified with blessed water—derives from an ancient custom found in the Council of Agde, in Burchard, book XIX, chapter 26, and in Ivo, part XV of the *Decree*, chapter 45:

> “Then, rising from prayer, let him impose hands upon them, as the canons command; let him sprinkle blessed water over them; let him first place ashes upon them, and then cover their heads with sackcloth.”

This also appears in Optatus of Milevis, book VI *Against Parmenian*, where, speaking of the schismatics who compelled Catholic virgins to undertake penance, he says:

> “When you sprinkled those consecrated to God with unclean ashes, you also ordered their hair to be drenched with counterfeit water.”

Although they were schismatics, nevertheless in sacred rites they did not dissent from the Church. The same is evident [Col. 0438C] concerning ashes from Tertullian, book *On Penance*:

> “In the harshness of sackcloth and the horror of ashes”;

from Saint Isidore, book II *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 16:

> “But they are sprinkled with ashes, so that they may remember that they are ash and dust.”

And in the Tilian Codex:

> “Then ashes are to be placed upon the penitent’s head, saying: ‘Remember, human being, that you are dust, and to dust you will return.’”

From this arose the rite of placing ashes on Christians’ heads on Wednesday, at the beginning of the fast, saying, “Remember, human being,” etc.—if only they would receive them with true contrition of heart.

In the Rheims Codex mentioned above, the penitents are clothed in sackcloth, which is the garment of penitents. The same can be seen in the passage of the Council of Agde cited above:

> “Then let him cover their heads with sackcloth.”

And in Saint Eligius, sermon 8:

> “Why, then, have you been placed on the left side of the church? The Church’s custom has not obtained this without reason; rather, it is because the Lord will place the sheep—that is, the righteous—on his right, but the goats—that is, sinners—on his left at the judgment. For goats signify sinners. Hence sackcloths also, [Col. 0438D] which are the garments of penitents, are made from the hair of goats and kids.”

Finally, penitents used to let their hair and beards grow, as is clear from the chapter of Saint Isidore cited above:

> “But those who undertake penance accordingly let their hair and beard grow.”

From Orderic Vitalis, book VIII of the *Ecclesiastical History*, we learn that formerly penitents, captives, and pilgrims went unshorn. This is the origin of the following words in the manuscript Penitential of Saint Columbanus, abbot of Luxeuil:

> “Penitent brothers, although they perform difficult and filthy tasks, should not wash their heads except on Sunday, that is, the eighth day. Otherwise, not until the fifteenth day—or at least because of the growth of their flowing hair.”

This was done according to the custom of the ancient Romans, 451 who, in mourning, let their hair and beards grow. Saint Isidore gives another reason in the chapter cited above: that by this sign the multitude of sins is indicated.

Nevertheless, we see the opposite rite in the Council of Agde, under King Alaric, canon 15:

> “Penitents [Col. 0439A], at the time when they seek penance, are to receive from the priest the imposition of hands and sackcloth upon the head, as has been established everywhere. But if they do not cut off their hair or change their garments, let them be cast out.”

These statements, however, can readily be reconciled. What Isidore, Columbanus, and Orderic wrote was written according to the common custom of the Church; but what was decreed in the Council of Agde was established out of consideration for the Goths, in whose region the council was held. For they took pleasure, according to the custom of their people, in long hair grown for beauty and majesty, and they exulted and rejoiced in abundant locks, as is clear from Sidonius, book I, letter 2, when he describes the appearance and dress of Theodoric, king of the Goths in Gaul:

> “As is the custom of the people, they are covered by the lashes of the hair lying over them.”

From Claudian, book *On the Gothic War*:

> The long-haired fathers sat, and the fur-clad  
> Curia of the Getae . . . [Col. 0439B]

And from Jordanes, book *On Gothic Affairs*:

> “To the rest of the people they gave the name ‘long-haired.’ The Goths, accepting this name as a great distinction, still remember it in their official documents.”

Since, therefore, it was appropriate for penitents, having laid aside all bodily adornment and beauty, to lie in filth, the council decreed that they should put away from themselves their hair and every ornament of their locks.

Finally, in the same Ratold Codex, the penitents are expelled from the church while the clerics sing the responsory *In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread*, according to the ancient custom that appears in the council cited above, in the authors Burchard and Ivo:

> “And with groaning and frequent sighs let him declare to them that, just as Adam was cast out of Paradise, so they too are expelled from the church on account of their sins. After this, let him order the ministers to drive the guilty persons outside the doors of the church. But the clergy should follow them with the responsory, ‘In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread.’”

The impious and wicked are barred from the church, the temple, sacred rites, and the common society of human beings, according to the ancient custom of the Church, which was also common among the ancient pagan peoples [Col. 0439C] in many nations, such as among the Greeks, as appears in Euripides’ *Hercules Furens*, act 5:

> Οὔτε ἐμαῖς φίλαις  
> Θήβαις ἐνοικεῖν ὅσιον, ἢν δὲ καὶ μένω,  
> Εἰς ποῖον ἱερόν, ἢ πανήγυριν φίλων  
> Εἶμι

That is:

> “Nor is it permitted me to dwell  
> In my beloved Thebes; and if I remain,  
> To what temple or assembly of friends shall I go?”

There Hercules is lamenting the slaughter of his children, which he himself committed; because of it, he says that, if he returns to Thebes, he will have access neither to the temples nor to the gathering of his friends.

And in Theon the Sophist:

> Διὰ τοῦτο χερνίβων εἰργέσθω  
> σπονδῶν, κρατήρων, ἀγορᾶς, ἱερῶν

That is:

> “For this reason let the homicide be excluded by the lustral waters from libations, mixing-bowls, the marketplace, and temples.”

And in Sophocles [Col. 0439D] in *Oedipus Tyrannus*: “I forbid anyone in this land over which I rule to receive or address such a man, whoever he may be:

> Μήτε εἰσδέχεσθαι, μήτε προσφωνεῖν τινα,  
> Μήτε ἐν Θεῶν εὐχαῖσι, μήτε θύμασι  
> Κοινὸν ποιεῖσθαι . . . . .

That is:

> “Let no one receive him or address him,  
> Or make him a participant  
> In divine prayers and sacrifices.”

This custom was also practiced among the Gauls by the institution of the Druids, as Julius Caesar—or Celsus—testifies in book VI of *The Gallic War*:

> “If either an individual or a people has not obeyed their decree, they exclude them from sacrifices. Among them this is the most severe punishment. Those against whom such an interdict has been pronounced are counted among the number of the impious and wicked; [Col. 0440A] everyone withdraws from them and avoids their company and conversation, lest they suffer some harm through contagion. Nor is justice rendered to them when they request it, nor is any honor communicated to them.”

And likewise in Germany, as Cornelius Tacitus writes in his book *On the Customs of the Germans*:

> “It is not permitted, for one who is disgraced, either to attend sacred rites or to join the council.”

### 661. The second part: the penitent confessing his sins

The confession of such penitents was exceedingly extensive, varied, and included many sins, which could scarcely be found in a single person. It can be seen in the Roman Order in the following form:

> “I confess to you, Lord of heaven and earth, and to you, good and most gracious Jesus, together with the Holy Spirit, before your holy angels, and before your saints, before this altar and your priest, that I was conceived in sins, born in sins, nourished in sins, and that after baptism, down to this hour, I have lived in sins.
>
> “I also confess that I have sinned greatly through pride, empty glory, and arrogance, both of my eyes and of my clothing and of all [Col. 0440B] my actions; through envy, hatred, avarice both of honor and of money; through anger, sadness, acedia, gluttony, and sodomitical lust; through sacrilege, etc.”

A similar confession of the ancient Germans can be found in Goldast, book *On German Affairs*.

There is also the confession of Saint Isidore, bishop of Seville, recorded in writing by Redemptus, his cleric, when, as death approached, he confessed publicly in the church of Saint Vincent. He made only a general confession, specifying nothing individually.

There is also the confession of Robert, bishop of Le Mans, published by the most learned Jacob Sirmond of the Society of Jesus in volume III of the *Councils of Gaul*. When near death, he sent it by letter to the bishops who were with Emperor Charles the Bald during the siege of the city of Angers. In it he confesses no particular crime, but merely declares himself to be an abominable and detestable sinner.

In the very ancient manuscript Codex of the Corbie Library, [Col. 0440C] entitled *Order of Prayers*, there is the confession of Saint Fulgentius, which it will not be burdensome to reproduce here:

> **The confession of Saint Fulgentius, bishop, for the imposition of penance begins.**
>
> [Note: [Col. 0439D] For many observations formerly made by us on this formula of confession in the French treatise *On Confession*, against Dallaeus, part I, chapter 12, the pious and learned reader may consult the work.]
>
> “I confess to you, Lord, Father of heaven and earth, before this holy altar of yours, and the relics of this place, and before this priest of yours, all my sins and everything that God’s mercy brings back to memory: impure thoughts, idle and unclean words, and whatever I have done against God’s commandment.
>
> “I also confess all the vices of my heart and body: sacrilege [read: sacrileges], envy, slander, perjury, thefts, curses, abuse, filthy speech, buffoonery, lies, mockery, insults, dissimulation, complaints, flattery, sadness, useless vigils despised by God, and the worst carnal desires. Because of the sweetness and pleasure of my body, I set aside God’s commandments and transgressed [Col. 0440D] through pride, arrogance, idleness, and laziness. I committed [read: pleasures] impure pleasures, fornications, pollutions, lusts, drunkenness, [453] banquets, and homicides, openly and secretly, in body and soul.
>
> “I did not show the service of honor owed, according to God’s commandment and God’s will, to my father and mother, brothers and sisters, uncles and aunts, cousins, or all my relatives and kin. I listened to and obeyed my carnal superior and my friends more in evil than in good. I did not love all Christians as God commanded.
>
> “I always provided and displayed for others an example and instruction of evil, not of good. I did not regard or observe Sundays and the feasts of the saints in a worthy or God-pleasing manner, and I did not proclaim them to the ignorant [Col. 0441A]; rather, I polluted myself in them through drunkenness and lust, and incited others to do the same.
>
> “I concealed and consumed robbery [read: theft], and consented to those who concealed it. I did not visit the sick or those held in prison; I did not clothe the naked. For God’s sake I did not receive guests, nor wash their feet; I did not feed the hungry; I did not console those who were grieving and weeping. I provoked those who were at odds with one another—whether relatives or all Christians who were quarrelling—more toward anger than peace.
>
> “I confess that I have sinned greatly through sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch, and that I have thought and perpetrated many evils. I confess that in the holy Church I thought many evil thoughts and spoke disorderly and proudly; in the holy church I stood, sat, kissed, looked, walked, lay down, and consented. I touched the sacred vessels and every sacred ministry while polluted. I was polluted by a wicked kiss. Upon the holy altar, in the consecrated church, and upon the blessed cross and the holy relics I swore; I uttered perjured words [read: false oaths] and lies, and committed perjury.
>
> “I also confess that [Col. 0441B] I was disobedient to you, almighty God, and to all the saints and all good people; inwardly and outwardly I was faithless and troublesome, contentious, hateful, envious, angry, greedy, covetous, rapacious, unbelieving, and harsh.
>
> “I negligently poured out my prayer in God’s sight because of empty thoughts and a hardened heart. I knowingly and unworthily received the body of the Lord and his blood, with polluted heart and body, without confession and penance.
>
> “I did not love or cherish bishops, good abbots [read: priests], monks, canons, or all the clergy of the Church of God, nor did I offer them the service of honor, as God commanded.
>
> “I contaminated, dishonored, and destroyed myself through carnal desires, evil thoughts, evil will, and evil works, and I consented in my will to the devil.
>
> “Concerning all these things and innumerable others, which because of the multitude of my sins, crimes, and wicked deeds I cannot sufficiently recall; and concerning whatever I have done against the will of God, all the saints, [Col. 0441C] and Christian law, and have perpetrated with a hardened heart—whether unknowingly or knowingly, in evil thought, word, or deed, or through the persistence or pleasure of sin, whether by day or night, at hours and moments, awake or asleep, or from whatever cause I may have thought or wished to do something and carried it out in deed against God’s will—I confess all these things today to you, God and Lord of heaven and earth, before your holy altar, in pure and true confession, with the will to amend and henceforth abandon these sins, so that you, almighty God, who said, ‘I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live,’ may have mercy on me, spare me, forgive me, and blot out all my past, present, and future sins, crimes, deeds, and offenses, and lead me to eternal life. Amen.
>
> “I beseech you, priest of God, to be my witness concerning all these things on the day of judgment, lest my enemy rejoice over me; and deign to implore God’s mercy for me, so that he may grant me the pardon of indulgence and the remission of all my sins.”

**The priest’s response**

> “May almighty God have mercy on you and grant you true pardon for your sins; may he avenge you against all your invisible enemies; may God grant you 454 counsel in this world and lead you safely to eternal life.”

Thus far the confession of Saint Fulgentius, bishop. But of the two celebrated Fulgentiuses, it is not readily possible to say whose confession this is: whether that of Saint Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe in Africa, or that of Saint Fulgentius, bishop of Astigi in Spain, brother of Saints Leander and Isidore.

In the manuscript Codex of the monastery of Saint Remigius at Rheims cited above, there is another [Col. 0442A] confession similar to this one.

[Note: [Col. 0441D] Our fellow religious D. Edmund Martene collected similar confessions in *On the Ancient Rites of the Church in the Administration of the Sacraments*, part II, chapter 6, article 7.]

But since the same confession is found in the Roman Order, differing from it by only a very few words, I did not think it necessary to copy it here. In the same manuscript Codex it is followed by this single priestly response:

> “May almighty God have mercy on you and forgive you all your sins; may he free you from every evil work, preserve you in every good work, and lead you, through the intercession of all the saints, to everlasting glory. Amen.”

The following is found in the same manuscript Codex of Saint Remigius:

> “Likewise, when the penitent comes to the priest, let him humbly throw himself at his feet, asking pardon. When he has done this and the priest has ordered him to rise, let the priest tell him to wait a little until he enters his chamber for prayer. But if there is no room for a chamber, then the priest should say this prayer in his heart:
>
> [Col. 0442B] **Prayer.**—‘Lord almighty God, be favorable to me, a sinner, so that I may be able worthily to give you thanks,’ etc., as below in the Roman Penitential.”

Finally, the following occurs in the same manuscript Codex of the monastery of Saint Remigius:

> “Meanwhile, while the priest enters his chamber for prayer, the penitent who has come to confession should say this prayer:
>
> “My Creator and Redeemer, Christ, almighty Lord God, be favorable to me, a sinner, who redeemed me with your precious blood; and grant me, in your immeasurable mercy, fully to recognize my sins, worthily to mourn them, purely to confess them, truly to repent, to perform worthy fruits of penance, and, I beseech you, deign in your goodness to grant me the fullest pardon of all my sins, and, freed from every evil, join me to the fellowship of the saints.
>
> “Forgive also all those joined to me by familiarity and kinship, from whose alms I am sustained, [Col. 0442C] or whenever I have received anything, and for whom I have been ordered to pray or have myself undertaken to do so; and forgive all your faithful. Free them from every evil, preserve them in every good, and lead them to everlasting joys.
>
> “But to those who have been polluted by me in any way, grant perfect remission of their offenses; and, so that I may love them according to your commandment and forgive them from my heart, deign, I ask, to shape my heart by your customary kindness.
>
> “I also humbly beseech you to grant eternal life, through your mercy, to all my familiar associates and relatives, and to those by whose alms I am sustained, and whenever I have received anything, and for whom I have been ordered to pray or have myself undertaken to do so—whose names you, Lord, know, you who write their names in the book of the life of your saints—and to all who have died in your name.

**Another confession**

> “I confess to the Lord and to you, Father, with all my heart, [Col. 0442D] that I, wretched and unhappy sinner, have sinned exceedingly before God and his holy angels: through pride, disobedience, and contention; through gluttony, overeating, and drunkenness before and after the hour, without permission 455 and blessing; through fornication, adultery, and sodomitical sins; and in every way in which I could, unhappy that I am, I polluted myself through impure thought, sight, touch, kissing, and embracing.
>
> “With my own hands also I frequently polluted myself, fasting and drunk alike. On the very day on which I received the Eucharist, I fell into fornication. On Sundays and feast days, and during the principal periods of Lent, I offered an unclean offering and received communion before confession and penance for countless days and years.
>
> “Through avarice, theft, envy, anger, lies and perjury, sadness, resentment of heart and despair, weariness of heart, sleepiness and laziness in good works, empty glory, hypocrisy, discord and slander, giving and receiving contrary to the command of the rule, and through every kind of vice—by sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch; by thought, speech, and action—I, unhappy that I am, have been ruined.
>
> “My sins are many and innumerable, and I cannot recall them all: in deeds, words, and thoughts. For all of them my wretched mind is pierced and at times tormented by sharp penance. Therefore I humbly beseech your counsel, indeed your judgment, since you have been appointed as mediator and intermediary between God and the sinful human being; and I humbly ask that you stand as intercessor for these same sins of mine.”

**The priest’s response**

> “May almighty God have mercy on you and grant you true pardon, amendment, and forgiveness of your sins, and remission; may he avenge you against all your visible and invisible enemies; may God grant you [Col. 0443B] true counsel in this world and lead you safely to eternal life. Amen.”

Thus far the manuscript Codex of the monastery of Saint Remigius.

This confession, however, belongs to monks. This is evident first from the words: “Before and after the hour”—namely, the hour of the meal—“without permission and blessing.” For monks are not permitted to eat or drink outside the hour of the meal, as is clear from chapter 43 of the Rule of Saint Benedict:

> “Let no one presume to take any food or drink before the appointed hour or afterward.”

See chapter 52 of the *Concordance of the Rules*.

Secondly, these words—“in giving and receiving contrary to the command of the rule”—also testify to this. For it is forbidden for a monk to give or receive anything unless he has been permitted by the abbot, as is prescribed in chapter 33 of the Rule of Saint Benedict:

> “Let no one presume to give or receive anything without the abbot’s [Col. 0443C] order.”

See chapter 42 of the *Concordance of the Rules*.

I could add several other formulas of confession, but since they differ little or not at all from those mentioned above, and since brevity should be pursued, I shall refrain from reporting them.
