It should nevertheless be noted that these and similar formulas of confession are criticized by the author of the work *On Visiting the Sick*, book II, chapter 5, volume IX of the works of Saint Augustine:

> “Nor,” he says, “should you address the priest with a certain cunning, as some do, since such an address would be a deception of yourself. For deceitful persons approach priests, confessing in their presence as follows: ‘I, a sinner, Lord priest, have sinned by committing perjury, adultery, fornication, killing a man, lying, sacrilege, theft, and robbery. I committed all these things through my fault, either in deed or in will.’”

So much for his words.

Although the foregoing formulas of confession were not deceptive, since they had been established by the Church, they would certainly not have been very acceptable to me unless another confession had ordinarily preceded them, one in which the number of sins is declared together with the necessary [Col. 0443D] circumstances. This can be seen in the Roman Order, which says:

> “Then let the priest order him to sit opposite him and converse with him about the vices written above, or about exhortations, lest, through shame, sluggishness, or forgetfulness, some corruption remain in his heart by which the devil may again lead him back to the vomit of sin,” etc.

And shortly afterward:

> “Also concerning the nature of the sins and of the persons involved; whether the person is continent or not; whether the act was done voluntarily or accidentally or in secret; with what contrition he is to make amends; and whether it was done from necessity or voluntarily; let him distinguish places and times,” etc.

456

Finally, in the same Roman Order the priest questions the penitent about the articles of faith, whether he willingly forgives his enemies, and about certain other matters, as may be seen there. When these things have been completed, the penitent recites the formula of confession mentioned above:

> “I confess to you, Lord, Father of heaven and earth,” etc.

The same is also clear from Burchard. In his work that formula of confession is absent [Col. 0444A]; instead, after the penitent has already confessed his sins, the priest questions him in sufficient detail about many other crimes. All these questions can be seen in the same author, book XIX of the *Decrees*, chapter 5, where he says:

> “But when the priest sees him showing shame, let him continue again: ‘Perhaps, dearest son, not everything that you have done comes to your memory at this moment. I shall question you; take care lest, at the devil’s urging, you presume to conceal anything.’ And then let him question him in order:
>
> “‘Have you committed murder voluntarily and without necessity—not against an enemy, but through your own greed?’” etc.

There, the word *hostis*, or *ostis*, French *ost*, means “army,” as below in the same chapter. Consult the Glossary of Frederick Lindenbrog.

It is certain that the custom once prevailed in the Church of confessing one’s sins individually and not in a confused manner. This can be seen in Socrates, book V of the *History*, chapter 19, where, speaking of a certain noble woman of Constantinople, he writes:

> Καὶ κατὰ μέρος ἐξομολογεῖται τὰς ἁμαρτίας etc.

That is:

> “And she confesses individually the sins she had [Col. 0444B] committed after baptism.”

### 662. “Hear, O Lord, our prayers,” etc.

Thus in the Rheims and Rodradi Codices, and in the Roman Order. In the printed editions these and the following prayers are missing.

### 663. “May this servant of yours be preceded,” etc.

Thus in the Roman Order.

### 664. “Be present, O Lord,” etc.

Thus in the Rheims and Rodradi Codices and in the Roman Order.

### 665. “Lord our God,” etc.

Thus in the same codices.

### 666. “You are not overcome by our offense,” etc.

Thus in the Rheims and Rodradi Codices. In the Roman Order it reads: “You are offended by our sins.”

### 667. “But.”

This particle is absent from the Roman Order.

### 668. “That he may keep penitential vigils for you.”

In the Roman Order it reads: “That your servant may keep vigil for you in penance.”

### 669. “I beseech you, O Lord,” etc.

This prayer is also found in Burchard, book XIX, chapter 7, but not in Henry Canisius, volume V of the *Ancient Readings*, nor in book VI [Col. 0444C] of the manuscript of Halitgarius, bishop, in the Corbie Library, nor in the Ratold Codex.

### 670. “The clemency of your majesty and name.”

In Canisius and Burchard, at the places cited. In the Ratold Codex and in the manuscript of book VI of Halitgarius it reads: “The majesty of your clemency and mercy.”

### 671. “To the folds.”

In the books cited these words are absent.

### 672. “You who were appeased by the prayer or confession of the publican.”

Thus in the Rheims Codex. In book VI of Halitgarius it reads: “You who, appeased by the prayer [read: prayers] and confession of the publican, heard him.” In Henry Canisius: “You who heard the publican’s prayers, being appeased by his confession.” These words are absent from the Ratold Codex.

### 673. “Stand by.”

In the Rheims and Ratold Codices, as also in the authors cited, it reads: “Breathe upon.”

### 674. “Persisting, may he quickly implore your clemency.”

457 Thus in the Rheims Codex. In the Ratold Codex and in the authors cited it reads: “May his weeping remain, and may his petition quickly implore your perpetual [Col. 0444D] clemency.”

### 675. “Holy altars.”

In the Rheims Codex it reads: “Holy and sacred altars.” In the Ratold Codex: “Holy altars and sacred things.” In book VI of Halitgarius: “Holy altars and sacrifices.” In Canisius: “Holy altars and shrines.”

### 676. “Let him be restored.”

Thus in the Rheims Codex. In the Ratold Codex and in the authors cited it reads: “Let him be consigned.” *Reformare* means “to restore”; concerning this word, consult our observations on the *Concordance of the Rules*, chapter 38, section 3.

### 677. Prayers for reconciling the penitent

In the printed codices, the prayers for reconciling the penitent are found on Thursday in the Lord’s Supper. That is their proper place. For it was formerly the custom of the Roman Church to absolve and reconcile penitents on Thursday in the Lord’s Supper. This appears in the Roman Order and in the Rheims and Ratold Codices, in which the matters pertaining to the reconciliation of penitents [Col. 0445A] are described for that same day.

It is also known from the letter of Pope Innocent I to Decentius, bishop of Gubbio:

> “But concerning penitents who perform penance either for graver offenses or for lesser ones, if no illness intervenes, the custom of the Roman Church shows that they are to be released on the Thursday before Easter.”

The same can be seen in canon 35 of Isaac, bishop of Langres, volume III of the *Councils of Gaul*:

> “It has been established and forbidden in the holy canons that no priest should presume to reconcile public penitents without consulting the bishop. Rather, all public penitents, on the Thursday before Easter, which is the Lord’s Supper, should gather in the city before the bishop with faces prostrate, in ashes and sackcloth; and there they should be reconciled by the bishop canonically and in due order, as is contained in the Sacramentary and the Roman Order,” etc.

In Alcuin, book *On Divine Offices*, chapter on the Lord’s Supper, and in Saint Eligius’s homily 4 on the Lord’s Supper—both of whom followed Roman custom in this matter—we see penitents reconciled on that same day:

> “So, as your belovedness has heard [Col. 0445B], all this washing of the feet is the cleansing of our sins. Hence, not incongruously, on this very day, as the custom of the Church has it, the reconciliation of penitents takes place.”

This is also established from the sermon on the anointing with chrism among the works of Saint Cyprian:

> “On this day the breaking of bread was first entrusted to us,” etc.

And shortly afterward:

> “Today sinners are reconciled to the Church; those cast outside are led back to the mother’s breasts; and those excluded from the assembly of the saints return to the communion of which they had been deprived.”

And from chapter 71 of book V of the *Capitulary* of the emperors Charles and Louis:

> “For two years also they are not to be permitted in any way to offer oblations; but they are to join the people only in prayer, so that in the seventh year they may attain perfection, on the Lord’s Supper—that is, by receiving through the imposition of the hands of the bishop, or, if he is absent, of other priests at his command, the grace of Catholic communion through the absolution of priestly prayers.”

The same is attested by William of Paris, book *On the Sacrament of Penance*, [Col. 0445C] chapter 5.

Thus far concerning the day of absolution and reconciliation. It will not be useless to set forth here from the Ratold Codex its entire procedure and form:

> “After the Gospel ‘Before the feast of Easter’ has been read, etc., let the bishop afterward sit in his seat beside the altar, and let him not say, ‘The Lord be with you’; but let the archdeacon read before him and the people a small booklet containing certain instructions concerning the reconciliation of penitents.
>
> “After this, let the bishop pray before the holy altar. When this has been completed, let him proceed to the ambo 458 and ascend it, and let him preach both to the people and to the penitents, as the Roman Order commands.
>
> “Then let him return before the altar and prostrate himself; and let the entire people, including the penitents—both those who are inside and those who are outside—prostrate themselves with him, and let them sing seven psalms.
>
> “When these psalms have been completed, let him alone rise and say these prayers both for himself and for the people: ‘Be present, O Lord, to our supplications,’ etc., as in the Roman Order and Roman Pontifical.
>
> **Another.**—‘Grant, we ask, O Lord,’ etc., as in the Roman Order and Roman Pontifical.
>
> [Col. 0445D] **Absolution.**—‘As is established by the principal sentence,’ etc., as in the Roman Order.
>
> **Another.**—‘Most gracious God, creator of the human race,’ etc., as in the Roman Pontifical and in book VI of Halitgarius.
>
> **Another.**—‘I beseech your clemency, O Lord,’ etc., as in the Roman Pontifical, though it varies in certain respects.
>
> **Another.**—‘God, who by the justice of your law always moderate the multiplication of mercy, when you impose penance upon those who offend, while you do not withdraw from them the gifts of your providence and mercifully suspend punishment. Through . . .’
>
> **Another.**—‘Merciful God, gracious God, who according to the multitude of your mercies,’ etc., as in the Roman Pontifical. It is indeed found in the Order, but varies at the end.
>
> **Another.**—‘We suppliantly beseech your majesty, O Lord,’ [Col. 0446A] etc., as in the Roman Pontifical. It is indeed found in the Order, but varies in the middle and at the end.
>
> **Also another.**—‘We absolve you in the place of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, to whom the Lord gave the power of binding and loosing; and insofar as accusation pertains to you, remission pertains to us. May almighty God be your life and salvation and the forgiver of all your sins; and may he who gave you compunction of heart grant forgiveness of sins, bestow upon you a long and happy life in this world, and in the future grant you life abiding without end with Christ and all his saints. Through the same Lord of ours.’”

Thus far the Ratold Codex concerning the absolution of penitents. Several points should be noted concerning these matters.

First, this absolution is performed in the Mass immediately after the reading of the Gospel. This also appears in the Rheims Codex, in which, once the reconciliation of the penitents has been completed, the Prayer over the Offerings follows.

In ancient times penitents were also absolved during the solemn celebration of Mass, but immediately before the Lord’s Prayer, as is clear from Optatus of Milevis, book II *Against* [Col. 0446B] *Parmenian*:

> “For during those neighboring moments, while you impose hands and forgive sins, once turned toward the altar you cannot fail to say the Lord’s Prayer: ‘Our Father, who are in heaven, forgive us our debts and our sins.’”

Secondly, there are seven prayers here for reconciling the penitent, if, omitting the first two prayers—which are said for the bishop and the people—you count from the prayer entitled “Absolution.” This appears to follow an ancient rite that also prevailed in Gaul in the time of Louis the Pious, as is clear from his life:

> “And during the celebration of Mass, seven archbishops sang over him seven prayers of ecclesiastical reconciliation.”

Third, note what is written:

> “Let the archdeacon read before the people a small booklet,” etc.

The contents of that booklet are as follows:

> “Behold, venerable bishop, the acceptable time is present, the day of divine propitiation,” etc., as in the Roman Order.

[Col. 0446C] Fourth, note these words:

> “As the Roman Order commands,”

and what is written there when the sermon that the bishop delivers to the penitents is under discussion. For in the Roman Order that now exists there is no mention of this sermon. From this it is clear that although the Roman Order that now exists is ancient, certain things in it have nevertheless been partly removed, partly changed, and partly added, as we observed in the Preface.

In the Rheims Codex mention is also made of this sermon, or exhortation, in the following form:

> “After this the bishop, or another priest, admonishes him that what he has washed away through penance he should not call back by repeating it.”

Likewise in the Roman Pontifical:

> “After these words, the bishop rises and approaches the door of the church with the ministers, while the choir does not move; and standing in the middle of the doorway he gives a brief exhortation.”

459

Fifth, note this form of absolution:

> “We absolve you in the place of blessed Peter,” etc.

It is not found in this Codex of Saint Eligius, nor in the Rheims or [Col. 0446D] Rodradi Codices, nor in the frequently cited manuscript of book VI of Halitgarius, nor in Henry Canisius’s book cited above. In all these sources only prayers are employed for the reconciliation of penitents. The same can be seen in Alcuin, chapter on the Lord’s Supper.

But in the Roman Order and in the manuscript Tilian Codex this formula of absolution, or reconciliation, is found; it agrees substantially with the formula of the Ratold Codex:

> “We also, according to the authority entrusted by God to us unworthy persons, absolve you from every bond of your offenses, so that you may deserve to possess eternal life. Through him who [text abbreviated: ‘ven.’].”

It is not found in the Roman Pontifical.

I shall append here another noteworthy formula of absolution, recently discovered at Périgueux in a certain tomb of the abbey of Saint-Front, which Father John du Puy, a Recollect Franciscan, publishes in his book *On the State of the Church of Périgueux*, under William of Montebrulpho, bishop. When certain ancient tombs in the said abbey were excavated, a leaden cross was found; on one side of it the following inscription was discovered engraved:

**“He is granted baptism in the holy font; he is called Elias. He died on the Kalends of May, in the year of the Lord 1071, Philip, king of the Franks, reigning.”**

In its center these two letters were engraved: **O. N.** On the other side the following was inscribed:

**“The Lord God almighty, who gave his holy apostles the power of binding and loosing, may he himself deem you worthy to absolve, Brother Elias, from all your sins; and, insofar as is permitted by my frailty, may you be absolved before the face of him who lives and reigns forever and ever.”**

These words cannot be understood as absolution from excommunication, since no mention of such an absolution occurs there, but rather as absolution from sins. Nor can this be referred to canon 39 of the First Council of Orange: “Those who depart from the body after having accepted penance—it was decreed that they should be admitted to communion without the reconciling hand,” and so forth. For in this kind of absolution one finds nothing similar. Moreover, by the reign of Philip—the first of that name, to whom the preceding words must refer—this canon had already fallen into disuse. I therefore think that this monk, moved by a pious impulse of devotion, wished a representation of his baptism and absolution, inscribed on this cross, to be buried with him in the tomb. The words *may you be absolved* are equivalent to our formula, “I absolve you.”

In former times a dispute arose between Saint Thomas and a certain doctor concerning the form of absolution. The latter asserted that it was deprecatory, and that it was scarcely thirty years since everyone had used only this formula: “May almighty God grant you absolution and remission.” The other, by contrast, maintained that the form of absolution was enunciative or indicative, expressed in the words, “I absolve you,” and so forth, which indicate the judicial power of the priest. See him in *Opusculum* 22.

Alexander of Hales, *Question* 60, article 3, member 2, writes that the form had been either indicative or deprecatory:

“But if it should be objected that the absolution of the priest, which is made by the utterance of such words as ‘I absolve you’ or ‘May the Lord absolve you,’ expresses absolution from sin more clearly than the penitent’s confession…”

There was also once this customary form: “I forgive you your sins,” as is clear from Radulfus Ardens, sermon on the Greater Litany:

“Confession of venial sins may be made to one another and to anyone, even to an inferior, since because of venial sins a person is not separated from God, unless through negligence he exceeds the proper measure—just as under the Law no one was separated from the camp because of scabies or impetigo. This confession is made, not because one can absolve from sins, but because through our own humiliation, through the accusation of our sins, and through the brother’s prayer, we are cleansed from sins. Hence we do not say, ‘I FORGIVE YOU YOUR SINS,’ but say in prayer, ‘May almighty God have mercy on you,’ and so forth.”

Here, when he says that in the cleansing of venial sins the words “I forgive you your sins” are not pronounced, but rather “May almighty God have mercy on you” is said in prayer, this indicates that the form of absolution from mortal sins was “I forgive you your sins,” which means nothing other than our customary formula, “I absolve you,” and so forth.

The Greeks use many deprecatory formulas in absolution from sins, as may be seen in their *Euchologion*. Yet they first mention the power of absolving divinely granted to them:

**σὺ ὁ δέσποτα**, that is, “You, Lord, granted through your holy apostles to those who, in the holy Church, successively exercise the priestly office throughout the ages the power on earth to forgive sins and to bind and loose every bond of iniquity. We therefore beseech you on behalf of our brother N., who stands before you: grant him your mercy, breaking the bond of sins.”

And shortly afterward:

“Forgive all voluntary and involuntary sins.”

And shortly afterward:

“Release this servant of yours from the bondage of sins,” and so forth.

In certain copies containing canons, from whose strictness satisfactions are imposed upon penitents, a formula of this kind is found:

“Our Lord Jesus Christ, who gave his apostles the power which passed through them to us, **συγχωρήσοί σοι**, that is, ‘may he absolve you.’”

Nevertheless, besides those deprecatory formulas, they say:

**ἔχω σε συγκεχωρημένον**, that is, “I hold you to have been forgiven.”

Peter Arcudius, *On the Sacrament of Penance*, book IV, chapter 3, believes that the form of absolution from sins among the Greeks lies in these words, and proves that they signify nothing other than “I absolve you from your sins.” Christ, absolving the paralytic and the sinful woman, said in Matthew 9, Mark 2, Luke 5 and 7: “Your sins are forgiven you,” and “Your sins are remitted to you.”

Finally, it should be noted that formerly the customary absolution was not given—not only from excommunication, but also from sins—before an entire penance or satisfaction had been completed, except at the point of death, or when bishops remitted and dispensed with some portion of it in response to the pleas of martyrs or confessors. This is clear from the Roman Order, the Tilian Manuscript, the Rheims and Ratoldus Manuscripts, the sixth manuscript book of Halitgarius, and the letter of Saint Innocent quoted above to Bishop Decentius, as well as from Letter 91 of Saint Leo:

“For the mediator of God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, entrusted this power to the leaders of the Church, so that they might both assign an act of penance to those who confessed and admit those same persons, purified by salutary satisfaction, to communion in the sacraments through the gate of reconciliation.”

From Sozomen, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VII, chapter 16:

“They stand there sorrowful and as if mourning; and when God’s sacrifice has finally been completed, those who have not been made participants—although it was lawful for pure worshipers of God to become participants—throw themselves face down upon the ground with wailing and lamentation. Then the bishop, running toward them from the opposite side and lamenting, likewise falls to the ground with groaning, and at length the whole multitude of the church is drenched in tears. Afterward the bishop rises first and raises those who are lying there; and, having prayed sufficiently on behalf of those doing penance for their sins, he dismisses them. Then each person privately waits for the period appointed by the bishop, voluntarily afflicting himself with fasts, abstinence from baths and food, or with other suitable disciplines. When the appointed day has finally elapsed, and the punishment has now been discharged as though some debt had been paid, **τῆς ἁμαρτίας ἀνίεται, καὶ μετὰ τοῦ λαοῦ ἐκκλησιάζει**, that is, ‘he is absolved from his sins and joins the people in the church.’”

Sozomen says this, and he teaches above that it was in accordance with the practice of the Roman Church and of the Western churches.

This is also established by that edict of the Roman pontiff which Tertullian rashly ridicules in *On Modesty*, book [chapter unspecified]:

“I hear that an edict has been issued—and indeed a definitive one. The supreme pontiff, that is, the bishop of bishops, declares: ‘I forgive the sins of adultery and fornication to those who have performed penance.’”

Since there were five degrees of penance, as may be seen in the canonical letter of Saint Gregory, bishop of Neocaesarea, in the final canon:

1. **πρόσκλαυσις**, that is, weeping: those who stood outside the church gate and wept in the mourning of penance, and, clinging to the knees of the faithful as they came out, earnestly begged them to pray for them;

2. **ἀκρόασις**, that is, hearing: those who stood inside the gate, in the narthex, listened to the divine Scriptures, and went out with the catechumens;

3. **ὑπόπτωσις**, that is, prostration: those who lay prostrate, placed their heads beneath the hands of the bishops, and left the church with the catechumens;

4. **σύστασις**, that is, standing together: those who prayed with the faithful and did not leave with the catechumens, yet did not partake of the Eucharist. With respect to participation in prayers they were not excommunicated, but only with respect to reception of the Eucharist;

5. **μέθεξις τῶν ἁγιασμάτων**, that is, participation in the holy things: those who, having completed their penance, partook of the Eucharist. They should be called not so much penitents as persons restored to the sacraments of the Church.

The question is at which degree—whether at the third, which is prostration, or at the fourth, which is standing together—the remission of sins and complete absolution from excommunication were obtained.

I, subject to better judgment, believe that penitents obtained this absolution at the end of the fourth degree, that is, **συστάσεως** (*systasis*, or standing together).

First, in the passage of Sozomen cited above, those penitents who attended the Mass but did not partake of the Eucharist, and who, when the solemn rites of the Mass had ended, fell to the ground with lamentation and weeping, while the bishop, meeting them, likewise fell with tears and prayed for them as he raised them, and who afterward afflicted themselves privately with fasts or similar punishments, upon completion of which they obtained forgiveness of their sin, were not in the fourth degree, that is, prostration, since those in that degree left the church with the catechumens.

Second, although the prostrate received the imposition of the bishop’s hands, the bishop did not impose his hands upon those penitents of whom Sozomen is speaking. Therefore the passage must be understood as referring to those standing together, who did not leave with the catechumens but participated in prayers with the faithful, though without receiving the Eucharist—just like those whom Sozomen describes in this chapter, who, at the end of the period of standing together, were absolved, as we have said.

Although the prostrate received the imposition of hands from the bishop, this was not absolution, but only a kind of prayer and blessing. After receiving it, they departed with the catechumens. Thus the 80th canon of the Fourth Council of Carthage must be understood: “At all times during the fast, priests shall impose hands upon penitents.”

The same applies to canon 19 of the Synod of Laodicea:

**Καὶ τούτων προσελθόντων ὑπὸ χεῖρα, καὶ ὑποχωρησάντων**, that is, “and when these have approached under the hand and have withdrawn”—namely, from the church—“prayers for the faithful are to be made.”

**678. “Be present, O Lord,” etc.** These and the following prayers are found in the Rodradi and Rheims Manuscripts.

**679. “Grant, we beseech you, to this servant of yours,” etc.**

In the Rheims Manuscript these three prayers are added:

“Almighty and everlasting God, forgive this servant of yours, who confesses to you,” etc.

“Almighty and merciful God, who have placed the forgiveness of sins in prompt confession,” etc.

Here “prompt confession” means ready, prepared, and devout confession, not unwilling or compelled confession.

“Holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God, look upon this servant,” etc.

The first two of these occur in Henry Canisius and in the manuscript of Halitgarius, book VI, which is called the *Penitential* and has not yet been published. For Canisius, in volume V of the *Ancient Readings*, published only five books of Halitgarius. Mention is made of this sixth book in the preface to the same work, which is mutilated toward the end in Canisius:

“Another little sixth book,” says Halitgarius, “will also be included for penance. It is not the product of our own excerpting, but was taken from the archive of the Roman Church, in which many different things are contained that are not found in the canons; nevertheless, it ought to benefit the simpler people who are unable to grasp greater matters.”

The preface of this sixth book begins as follows:

“We add to this work of our excerpting another Roman *Penitential*, which we took from the archive of the Roman Church.”

In this little book are found, above all, matters relating to the imposition of penance and the reconciliation of penitents. All of these, except for three chapters, may be seen in Henry Canisius at the end of book V, where the learned man rightly conjectured that they belonged to Halitgarius.

This first part is followed by another, prefaced with this title:

“Here begins the judgment of the penitent, which is divided into ten chapters.”

Flodoardus agrees with this in book II of his *Ecclesiastical History of Rheims*, chapter 19:

“At the urging of this prelate, Ebbo, archbishop of Rheims, Halitgarius, bishop of Cambrai, composed six books on remedies for sins, and on the order and judgments of penance. A letter of his to him is extant.”

He then adds Ebbo’s letter, followed by Halitgarius’s response to Ebbo.

Baldricus confirms this in book I of the *Chronicle of Cambrai*, chapter 38:

“To Hildouard succeeded Halicharius—this is how he writes the name everywhere—a man apostolic in doctrine and Catholic in faith. At the request of Ebbo, archbishop of Rheims, he composed six books on remedies for sins, and on the order and judgments of penance. A letter of Ebbo to him is extant.”

He then adds Ebbo’s letter, to which he appends Halitgarius’s response, as they are found in Canisius and in our manuscript in the library of Corbie.

This Halitgarius was bishop of Cambrai, as Baldricus teaches in the chapter cited above. He lived in the time of Louis the Pious and Charles the Bald. The latter sent him to Constantinople to the emperor Michael, from which place he brought back many relics of the saints, enriching his church with them, as Baldricus writes in chapter 40 of the work cited.

We here make this sixth book available for the benefit of students, with certain corrections and notes, because several errors have crept into it. Burchard, in his work on decrees, cites several passages from the Roman *Penitential*, some of which are found here and some of which are not. From this one might conjecture either that there were once two Roman *Penitentials*, or that the one copied by Halitgarius is incomplete, unless perhaps we say that it had been mutilated. Certainly the end of the one we are publishing appears to be missing.

There were also other *Penitentials*, such as those of Theodore, bishop of the English, and of Bede, whom Burchard often cites. Since many of them were not authentic, the Third Council of Tours, canon 22, decreed:

“When all the bishops have assembled at the sacred palace, they shall determine which of the ancient *Penitentials* ought preferably to be followed.”

And in the Second Council of Chalon, canon 38, and the Third Council of Paris, canon 32, *Penitentials* circulated without a known author are forbidden, since they rather flattered penitents than cured them.

The work we are now publishing is of a different character:

> **Preface of Halitgarius**
>
> “We also add to this work of our excerpting another Roman *Penitential*, which we took from the archive of the Roman Church, although we do not know by whom it was issued. For this reason we have decided to attach it to the judgments of the canons set out above, so that, if any of those judgments should happen to seem superfluous to someone, or if he should be unable to find there what he desires concerning individual crimes, he may perhaps at least find all offenses explained in this final brief work.
>
> **Here begins how bishops or priests ought to receive a penitent.**
>
> “Whenever Christians approach penance, we impose fasts, and we too ought to share their fast with them for one or two weeks, or as much as we can, so that it may not be said to us what the Lord and Savior said to the Jewish teachers of the Law: ‘Woe to you, lawyers, who burden people and lay heavy loads upon their shoulders, while you yourselves do not touch those burdens with one of your fingers.’ No one can lift up a person falling under a burden unless he bends down to extend his hand; nor can any physician heal the wounds of the sick unless he has shared in their foul odors. Likewise, no priest or bishop can heal the wounds of sinners or remove sins from their souls without devoted care and tearful prayer.
>
> “It is therefore necessary, dearest brothers, that we be concerned for sinners, because we are members of one another; and if one member suffers, the other members suffer with it. Therefore, if we see someone lying in sins, let us hasten to call him to penance through our instruction. Whenever you give counsel to a sinner, at the same time immediately assign him penance—how long he must fast and make satisfaction for his sins—lest you forget how long he ought to fast for his sins and have to inquire of him about his sins again. He might then be ashamed to confess his sins a second time, and might already be found subject to a harsher judgment.
>
> “Not all clerics who find this writing should use or read it, but only those for whom it is necessary, namely, priests. Just as none except bishops and priests, to whom the keys of the kingdom of heaven have been entrusted, ought to offer the sacrifice, so no others ought to usurp these judgments. If necessity arises and no priest is present, let the deacon receive the penitent for holy communion.
>
> “As we said above, bishops and priests ought to humble themselves and pray with sorrow, groaning, and tears, not only for their own offenses but also for those of all Christians, so that they may say with blessed Paul: ‘Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not inflamed?’
>
> “When someone comes to a priest to confess his sins, let the priest tell him to wait a little while, until he enters his chamber to pray. If he has no chamber, the priest should nevertheless say this prayer in his heart:
>
> **“Let us pray.**—Lord God almighty, be favorable to me, a sinner, so that I may worthily give you thanks, since through your mercy you have made me, unworthy as I am, a minister of the priestly office, and have appointed me, small and humble, as a mediator to adore and intercede with our Lord Jesus Christ for sinners and for those returning to penance. Therefore, Lord and Ruler, who desire all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth, who do not desire the death of sinners but that they should be converted and live, receive my prayer, which I pour out before the sight of your clemency, for your male and female servants who have come to penance. Through our Lord Jesus Christ.
>
> “When the person who has come to penance sees the priest sorrowful and weeping over his own offenses, he himself is struck more deeply with fear of God, grows more sorrowful, and shudders at his sins. If you see each person who approaches penance standing firmly and constantly in penance, receive him immediately.
>
> “But if someone is able to fast what has been imposed upon him, do not prevent him; permit him to do so. Those who hasten to discharge the debt imposed upon them quickly are more deserving of praise, because fasting is a debt. Thus give this instruction to those who do penance: if someone fasts and completes what the priest has commanded him, he will be cleansed from his sins. But if he returns again to his former habit of sin, he is like a dog returning to its own vomit.
>
> “Every penitent must therefore not only fast what the priest has commanded him, but, after completing what has been ordered, he ought, as he sees fit, to fast either on Wednesdays or Fridays. For if he does what the priest has commanded him, his sins will be forgiven; but if afterward he fasts of his own will, he will gain a reward for himself and the kingdom of heaven.
>
> “Whoever fasts throughout the week for his sins should eat and drink on Saturday and Sunday whatever is suitable. Nevertheless, he must guard against gluttony and drunkenness, because all wantonness arises from drunkenness. Therefore blessed Paul forbade it, saying: ‘Do not become drunk with wine, in which is wantonness.’ Not because wantonness is in wine, but in drunkenness.
>
> **“The prologue ends.”**
>
> “If someone is unable to fast and has the means to pay a redemption, then, if he is rich, let him give twenty solidi for seven weeks. If he does not have enough to give that much, let him give ten solidi. If he is extremely poor, let him give three solidi.
>
> “Let no one be troubled because we have ordered twenty solidi, or less, to be given. If someone is rich, it is easier for him to give twenty solidi than for a poor person to give three. But let each person consider to whom he ought to give it: whether for the ransom of captives, for the sacred altar, or to be distributed among poor Christians.
>
> “And know this, brothers: when male or female servants come to you seeking penance, do not burden them or compel them to fast as long as the rich, because they are not their own masters. Therefore impose upon them half the penance.
>
> **“Here begins the method for assigning penance.**
>
> “First he says the entire Thirty-Seventh Psalm: ‘Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger.’ Then he says, ‘Let us pray.’ He says the One Hundred Second Psalm: ‘Bless the Lord, O my soul,’ up to ‘your youth shall be renewed like the eagle’s.’ He says the Fiftieth Psalm: ‘Have mercy on me, O God,’ up to ‘blot out my iniquities.’ After this he says Psalm 53: ‘O God, in your name.’ Then he says, ‘Let us pray.’ He says Psalm 51: ‘Why do you boast,’ up to ‘the righteous shall see and fear.’ And he says:
>
> **“Let us pray.**—O God, whose indulgence no one does not need, remember, Lord, your servant N.; and since he has been stripped bare by the slippery earth and frailty of the body, we ask that you grant forgiveness to the one who confesses. Spare the suppliant, so that we, who are accused by our merits, may be saved by your mercy. Through our Lord Jesus Christ.
>
> **“Another.**—O God, beneath whose eyes every heart trembles and every conscience quakes, be favorable to the groans of all and heal the wounds of everyone. Just as none of us is free from guilt, so may no one be excluded from forgiveness. Through the Lord.
>
> **“Another.**—O God of infinite mercy and boundless truth, be favorable to our iniquities and heal all the sicknesses of our souls, so that, having received the remission of your mercies, we may always rejoice in your blessing. Through the Lord.
>
> **“Another.**—I beseech, Lord, the Majesty of your clemency and mercy: deign to release forgiveness to this servant of yours, who confesses his sins and offenses, and pardon the guilt of his former crimes. You brought back upon your shoulders the lost sheep; appeased by the publican’s prayers and confession, you heard him. Be appeased also by this servant of yours, Lord; look favorably upon his prayers, so that he may remain acceptable in confession. May his weeping and petition quickly entreat your perpetual clemency; and, restored to the holy altars and sacrifices, may he once again be committed to the hope of eternal heavenly glory. Through the Lord.
>
> **“Prayer for the imposition of hands.**—Holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God, who through Jesus Christ your Son, our Lord, have deigned to heal our wounds, we humbly beseech and ask you—we, your humble priests—that you deign to incline the ear of your kindness to our prayers, forgive all crimes, pardon every sin, and grant this servant of yours forgiveness in place of supplications, joy in place of sorrow, and life in place of death. He has been cast down from the heavenly height; trusting in your mercy, may he be found worthy to attain good peace through the reward of your [text: “your rewards”] and the heavenly life unto eternal life. Through the Lord.
>
> **“Here begins the reconciliation of the penitent on Thursday of the Lord’s Supper.**
>
> “First he says Psalm 50 with the antiphon ‘A clean heart.’
>
> “Most kind creator of the human race and most merciful restorer, who, in the reconciliation of the fallen, have also wished me, who first need your mercy, to serve the effects of your grace through the priestly ministry, so that, when the merit of the suppliant ceases, the clemency of the Redeemer might become more wondrous. Through our Lord.
>
> “Almighty and everlasting God, in your goodness release the sins of this servant of yours who confesses to you, so that the guilt of his conscience may not harm him more for punishment than the indulgence of your mercy benefits him for forgiveness. Through the Lord.
>
> **“Another.**—Almighty and merciful God, who have placed the forgiveness of sins in prompt confession, come to the aid of the fallen and have mercy on those who confess, so that what the chain of offenses binds, the greatness of your mercy may absolve. Through the Lord.
>
> **“Prayer over a sick person.**—O God, who granted your servant Hezekiah fifteen additional years of life, may your greatness raise your servant from the bed of sickness to salvation. Through our Lord Jesus Christ.
>
> **“I. Here begins the judgment of the penitent.**
>
> “If a bishop or anyone ordained commits homicide; if a cleric commits homicide, let him do penance for ten years, three of them on bread and water. If he is a layman, let him do penance for three years, one of them on bread and water; a subdeacon, six years; a deacon, seven; a priest, ten; a bishop, twelve. If anyone consents to the commission of homicide, let him do penance for seven years, three of them on bread and water. If anyone wished to commit it but was unable to do so, let him do penance for three years, one of them on bread and water. If a layman commits homicide voluntarily, let him do penance for seven years, three of them on bread and water. If anyone suffocates an infant, let him do penance for three years, one of them on bread and water; a cleric likewise shall observe this.
>
> **“II. On fornication.**
>
> “If anyone fornicates like the Sodomites, let him do penance for ten years, three of them on bread and water. If a cleric commits adultery with another man’s wife or betrothed and fathers a son, let him do penance for seven years. If he does not father a son, and the matter has not become known among people, then, if he is a cleric, let him do penance for three years, one of them on bread and water. If he is a deacon or monk, let him do penance for seven years, three of them on bread and water; a bishop, twelve years, five of them on bread and water.

> **[Note: Almost the same things are read in the penitential judgment of the ancient Gallican Sacramentary, from which many things here seem to have been drawn.]**
>
> “If a cleric—that is, one whose rank is higher—has a wife and, after his conversion or ordination, has relations with her again, let him know that he has committed adultery; therefore let him do penance as established above. If anyone fornicates with a nun or a woman consecrated to God, let him acknowledge that he has committed adultery; according to the preceding judgment, let each person do penance according to his rank.
>
> “If anyone fornicates by himself, or with an animal, or with any quadruped, let him do penance for three years. If he has a rank or a vow, let him do penance for three years. If anyone lusts after a woman but is unable to sin—that is, because the woman did not receive him—let him do penance for half a year on bread and water, and abstain for an entire year from wine and meat.
>
> “If a cleric, after having vowed himself to God, returns to secular dress, like a dog to its own vomit, or takes a wife, let him do penance for six years, three of them on bread and water, and afterward let him not enter into marriage. If he refuses, the holy synod or the apostolic see shall separate them from the communion of Catholics. Likewise, if a woman, after vowing herself to God, commits such a crime, she shall be subject to the same judgment.
>
> “If a layman fornicates like the Sodomites, let him do penance for seven years. If anyone fathers a son by another man’s wife—that is, commits adultery and violates his neighbor’s marriage bed—let him do penance for three years, abstain from more sumptuous foods and from his own wife, and moreover give the husband of the violated wife the price of her chastity.
>
> “If anyone wishes to commit adultery but is unable to do so—that is, is not received—let him do penance for forty days. If anyone fornicates with women—that is, widows or girls—let him do penance for one year if with widows, and for two years if with girls.
>
> “If a virgin man is joined to a virgin woman, then, if the parents wish, let her be his wife; nevertheless, let him do penance for one year, and let them live as married persons. If anyone fornicates with an animal, let him do penance for one year. If he has no wife, let him do penance for half a year.
>
> “If anyone abducts a virgin or widow, let him do penance for three years. If a man has a betrothed woman and perhaps violates her sister, cohabiting with her as though she were his own, and afterward marries her—the betrothed woman—while the one who was violated perhaps kills herself, let all who consented to this deed be reduced to ten years on bread and water, according to the statutes of the canons.
>
> “If any woman who has fornicated kills what is born, or hastens to procure an abortion, the original decree forbids this until death [text materially corrupt: “* that they may obtain something more humane than what has truly been determined”]. We decree that they do penance for a period of ten years according to the ranks established.”

> **“III. On perjury.**
>
> “If a cleric commits perjury, let him do penance for seven years, three of them on bread and water; a layman, three years; a subdeacon, six; a deacon, seven; a priest, ten; a bishop, twelve. If anyone commits perjury under compulsion because of some necessity, or unknowingly, let him do penance for three years, one of them on bread and water, and make restitution for a life on his behalf—that is, free a male or female slave from servitude—and give abundant alms.
>
> “If anyone commits perjury out of greed, let him sell all his possessions and give the proceeds to the poor, be tonsured, enter a monastery, and serve there until death.
>
> **“IV. On theft.**
>
> “If a cleric commits capital theft—that is, steals a quadruped—or breaks into or breaks open a house, or steals [text: *] any valuable possession, let him do penance for seven years; a layman, five; a subdeacon, six; a deacon, seven; a priest, ten; a bishop, twelve years.
>
> “If anyone commits theft of lesser things once or twice, let him restore what he stole to his neighbor and do penance for one year on bread and water. If he cannot restore it, let him do penance for three years.
>
> “If anyone violates a tomb, let him do penance for seven years, three of them on bread and water. If a layman commits theft, let him restore to his neighbor what he stole and do three forty-day periods on bread and water. If he cannot restore it, let him do penance for one year and three forty-day periods on bread and water; an alms from his labor shall also be joined to the altar for the poor and at the priest’s discretion.
>
> **“V. On magic.**
>
> “If anyone destroys someone through magic, let him do penance for seven years, three of them on bread and water. If anyone practices magic out of love and destroys no one, then, if he is a layman, let him do penance for half a year; if a cleric, let him do penance for one year on bread and water; if a deacon, three years, one of them on bread and water; if a priest, five years, two of them on bread and water.
>
> “If by this means someone causes a woman’s birth to be lost, let each person add six forty-day periods, lest he be guilty of homicide. If anyone is a sender of storms, let him do penance for seven years, three of them on bread and water.
>
> **“VI. On sacrilege.**
>
> “If anyone commits sacrilege—that is, if he performs what the haruspices, who practice auspices, call ‘super-auspice’—or by any evil device, let him do penance for three years on bread and water.
>
> “If anyone is a diviner, one whom they call a fortune-teller, and performs any divinations, because this is demonic, let him do penance for five years, three of them on bread and water.
>
> “If anyone does what many do on the Kalends of January, and leads about the little deer [text: *duci/ducit*], or goes to an old woman, let him do penance for three years.
>
> “If anyone possesses lots, which they call [text uncertain: ‘the counter-argument of the saints’], or possesses any lots, or casts lots by any evil device, or practices divination, let him do penance for three years, one of them on bread and water.
>
> “If anyone makes or fulfills a vow at trees, springs, a railing, or anywhere except in a church, let him do penance for three years with bread and water. This is sacrilege or demonic. Whoever eats or drinks there shall do penance for one year on bread and water.
>
> “If anyone is a mathematician—that is, if through the invocation of demons he has taken away a person’s mind—let him do penance for five years, one of them on bread and water.
>
> “If anyone makes amulets or bindings, which is detestable, let him do penance for three years, one of them on bread and water.
>
> “If some people celebrate a feast together in abominable places of the pagans, bringing their food and eating it, it has been decided that they shall be subject to two years’ penance and then be received [text corrupt: ‘which ought to obey’]; after the offering, each person’s spirit must be tested and the life of each examined.
>
> “If anyone eats or drinks near a shrine, then, if he did so through ignorance, let him promise that he will never repeat it and do penance for forty days on bread and water. But if he did so contemptuously—that is, after the priest had preached to him that this was sacrilege—and has shared in the table of demons, then, if he has committed this offense only once, let him do three forty-day periods on bread and water.
>
> “But if he did this in the worship of demons and in honor of an image, let him do penance for three years.
>
> “If anyone has been forced to sacrifice a second or third time [text corrupt: *immolatus per vim*], let him be subject to three years’ penance, communicate for two years without an offering, and in the third year be fully received.
>
> “If anyone eats blood, carrion, or anything sacrificed to idols, and was not compelled by necessity, let him fast for twelve weeks.
>
> **“VII. On certain chapters.”**
“If anyone has voluntarily cut off any member of his body by any means, let him do penance for three years, one of them on bread and water. If anyone has voluntarily caused an abortion, let him do penance for three years, one of them on bread and water. If anyone has exacted usury from anyone, let him do penance for three years, one of them on bread and water. If anyone, through authority or by any device, has seized or taken another’s property in an improper manner, let him likewise do penance according to the *legal sentence, and give many alms. If anyone has taken or sent a slave, or any other person, into captivity by any device, let him do penance as above. If anyone has voluntarily burned a threshing floor or house with fire, let him do penance as above. If anyone, in anger, has struck another and shed his blood or disabled him, let him first pay him compensation and seek a physician; [Col. 0455C] if he is a layman, for forty days; a cleric, for two periods of forty days; a deacon, for seven months; a presbyter, for one year. If anyone has engaged in hunting, let a cleric do penance for one year, a deacon for two, and a presbyter for three years. If anyone has defrauded or neglected any work whatsoever belonging to the ministry of the holy Church, let him do penance for seven years, three of them on bread and water. If anyone has sinned with animals, being more than thirty years old, let him undergo fifteen years, * and then be deemed worthy of communion. * His manner of life, however, must be examined, whether he deserves something more humane, * continually toward sinning. If he persists, let him have a long penance. But those who, at a more advanced age and while having wives, entered into this sin shall undergo twenty-five years, so that after five they may be deemed worthy of communion with an offering. But if some, while having wives and being more than fifty years old, have committed this sin, let them be deemed worthy to receive Viaticum at the end of life.

[Col. 0455D] “468 VIII. Concerning drunkenness.

“Thus, if anyone becomes drunk on wine or beer, contrary to the injunction of the Savior and his apostles, then, if he has made a vow of holiness, let him atone for his fault for forty days on bread and water; but let a layman do penance for seven days. If a bishop commits fornication, let him be degraded and do penance for sixteen years. But a presbyter or deacon who commits natural fornication * before the monastic vow [the corrupt reading is uncertain] shall do penance for three years. Let him ask forgiveness at every hour and perform a superposition each week, except during the fifty days.

“IX. Concerning minor cases.

“If anyone negligently loses the sacrifice by leaving it outside, and it is devoured by someone, let him do penance for forty days; but otherwise let him do penance for one year. If anyone, unknowingly, receives communion with persons excommunicated by the Church, let him do penance for forty days. If the sacrifice falls to the ground through negligence, let there be a superposition. [Col. 0456A] We ought to offer for good things, but by no means for evil things. Presbyters, however, are not forbidden to offer for their bishops. Whoever provides the barbarians with a guide, let him do penance for three years. Whoever despoils monasteries, falsely saying that he is redeeming captives [Leg. reading: saying], let him do penance for three years, and give to the poor everything that he took away. Whoever eats the flesh of animals whose death he does not know, let him do penance for a third of a year. Let us bring forth the institutions of our former fathers [Leg. reading: let us bring forth]: boys who converse together privately and transgress the institutions of their elders shall make amends by three superpositions. Those who give a simple kiss: seven [In the Roman Penitential: five] superpositions. Let those who give a seductive kiss without defilement be corrected by eight superpositions; but with defilement, whether [Leg. without] an embrace, by fifteen [In the Roman Penitential: ten] superpositions.

“X. * Concerning offenses against the sacrifice.

“Whoever does not guard the sacrifice properly, and a mouse eats it, let him do penance for forty days. But whoever loses his chrismal or the sacrifice alone in any region, so that it cannot be found, let him do penance for three periods of forty days or for one year. If anyone spills the chalice over the altar when the cloths are being removed, let him do penance for seven days. If the sacrifice falls inside the table, let him do penance for seven days. Whoever receives the sacrifice while burdened by a full stomach, let him do penance for twenty days. If a deacon forgets to offer the oblation without a cloth, let him do penance likewise until the offerings are made. But if these little creatures are found in flour, or in some dried food, or in honey, or in milk, let what is around their bodies be thrown outside. Whoever has been negligent concerning the sacrifice, so that it is consumed by worms and becomes worthless, let him do penance for three periods of forty days. If it is found intact and there is a worm in it, let it be burned, and let its ashes be hidden beneath the altar; and let the negligent person do penance for forty days. If the sacrifice falls from the hand [Col. 0456C] of the one offering it to the ground, and something is found, let everything whatsoever that is found be burned in the place where it fell, and let the ashes be hidden beneath the altar; and let the priest do penance for half a year. If something is found, let it be cleansed as above, and let him do penance for forty days. If it has fallen only as far as the altar, let him impose a superposition. If something drips from the chalice onto the ground through negligence, let the tongue lick it up, let the board be scraped and burned in the fire, and let him do penance for forty days. If the chalice drips upon the altar, let the minister suck it up, and let the linen that the drop touched be washed * times, and let him do penance for three days. If a priest stumbles over the Lord’s Prayer, which is called dangerous, let him recite fifty Psalms the first time, and receive one hundred lashes the second time. But if he has taken his father’s or his brother’s widow, such persons cannot be judged unless they first separate from one another. If anyone kills a man without cause on a public expedition, let him fast for twenty-one weeks. But if he perhaps killed someone while defending himself, his parents, or his household, he shall not be guilty; if he wishes to fast, it is in the power of the one who did this under compulsion. If he commits homicide during peacetime, and there was no disturbance through power or because of enmity, in order to seize the man’s property, let him fast for twenty-eight weeks, and let him return the property of the one he killed to his wife or children. But if anyone comes to penance, and illness overtakes him, and he cannot fulfill what was assigned to him by the priest, let him be admitted to holy communion; and if God wishes to save him, let him fast afterward. If anyone does not repent, and perhaps falls ill, and asks to receive communion, let him not be prohibited; rather, give him holy communion, and instruct him that, if it pleases God’s mercy and he escapes from that illness, he must afterward confess everything and then do penance. But if an excommunicated person dies, having already confessed, and the priest does not arrive because death overtakes him either on the road or at home, if one of his relatives is present, let him offer something on his behalf at the holy altar, or for the redemption of captives, or in commemoration of his soul. If anyone has taken his wife’s daughter, this man [Leg. reading: these persons] cannot be judged unless they first separate. After they have separated, impose fourteen weeks on each of them, and let them never again join themselves together. But if they wish to marry, whether the man or the woman, let them have the power to do so, but not * the one who dismissed her. If anyone has taken a kinswoman, or his stepmother, or his uncle’s widow, and likewise one who has taken his father’s wife or his wife’s sister, let him be condemned by a severe canonical judgment. If anyone, while still a child, has unknowingly tasted things sacrificed to idols, or carrion, or anything abominable, let that person fast for three weeks. But concerning fornication, many do not know the number of women with whom they have fornicated; let such men fast for fifty weeks. But if anyone unknowingly ate something sacrificed to idols or carrion, pardon shall be granted him, because he did it unknowingly; [Col. 0457B] nevertheless, let him fast for three weeks. If anyone unwillingly kills a man because of his parents, let him fast for eight weeks. If anyone, out of necessity, steals food, clothing, or a four-footed animal, because of hunger or nakedness, pardon is granted him. Let him fast for four weeks. If he returns what he took, do not compel him to fast. If anyone steals a horse, ox, beast of burden, or cow, or food or cattle that support an entire household, let him fast as above. If any woman deceives her mother’s husband, she cannot be judged until she leaves him. When they have separated, let them fast for fourteen weeks. If anyone, having a lawful wife, dismisses her and takes another, the woman whom he took does not belong to him. He must neither eat nor drink nor speak at all with the woman whom he wrongly took, nor with her relatives. They themselves, however, if they consented, are to be excommunicated. If a woman persuades another woman to take a husband, let her be excommunicated from the Christians. If any Christian sees a Christian wandering or straying and sells his relative, that man is not worthy to have rest among Christians until he redeems him. But if he cannot find the place where he is, let him give the price he received on his behalf, and redeem another from slavery, and let him fast for twenty-eight weeks. If any man’s wife has died, he has the power to take another, and likewise a woman. If he takes a third, let him fast for three weeks; if he takes a fourth or fifth, let him fast for twenty-one weeks. If anyone cuts his hair, or lacerates his face with a sword, or his nails [Leg. reading: with his nails] after the death of his parents, let him fast for four weeks; and after he has fasted, let him receive communion. If any pregnant woman wishes to fast, she has the power to do so. A herbalist, man or woman, who has killed infants, when they come to the end of life, if they ask for penance with mourning and tears of lamentation, * if he ceases to receive him, let him fast for fifty weeks. If a dog, fox, or hawk kills something, whether it has been killed by a club, a stone, or an arrow without iron, all such things are suffocated animals and must not be eaten; whoever eats one shall fast for six weeks. If anyone strikes a stag or another animal with an arrow, and it is found after the third day, and perhaps a wolf, bear, dog, or fox has tasted it, no one is to eat it; whoever eats it shall fast for four weeks. If a hen dies in a well, let the well be emptied; if anyone knowingly drinks from it, let him fast for one week. If a mouse, hen, or anything else falls into wine or into any [Leg. reading: water], let no one drink from it. If it falls into oil or honey, let the oil be used up in a lamp, but let the honey be used as medicine or for some other necessity. If a fish dies in a pond, it must not be eaten; whoever eats it shall fast for four weeks. If a pig or hen eats from a human corpse, it must not be eaten or kept for breeding; rather, let it be killed and [Col. 0458A] given to the dogs. If a wolf wounds an animal and it dies, no one is to eat it; but if it survives and a man later kills it, it may be eaten. If a man has sinned with a goat, sheep, or any other animal, no one is to eat its flesh; rather, let it be killed and given to the dogs. If he wishes to give alms for his soul from this money, he who has done penance for the booty has permission to do so. It is finished. (The Roman Penitential, or Book VI of Halitgar.)

Thus far the Roman Penitential, concerning which several matters must be noted and considered.

In the preface, the word “another” deserves notice. He calls this the second Roman Penitential because earlier, in Book IV, he placed a Penitential excerpted from the canons of ancient councils.

Burchard cites the first chapter, Book XIX, chapter 33, up to the words, “For not all clerics,” somewhat more briefly from the Penitential of Theodore, bishop of the English. The words “You shall give counsel to the penitent” are to be explained thus: you shall admonish the penitent in what manner he should henceforth be more cautious in avoiding sins. He then says that penance should be imposed by the priest while he recalls the sins confessed, lest, if the penitent is unwilling to disclose his sins, he be judged more severely by the priest. The words “Let the deacon receive the penitent to communion” are to be explained in this way: when necessity presses, especially in danger of death, the deacon ought to offer holy Eucharist to a penitent whom he knows, from the outpouring of tears or similar signs, to be repentant sincerely, even though, because of the absence of a priest, he has not been absolved. Burchard quotes this passage in Book XIX, chapter 154, from the Roman Penitential. Precisely the same thing is established in the Roman Order, in the order for Wednesday, at the beginning of the fast, in exactly the same words. We read of something similar having happened in Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, Book VI, chapter 36, although not through the ministry of a deacon. It concerns a certain Serapion, who, overcome by the violence of torture, had sacrificed to idols, was expelled from the Church, and, having repented of his deed, pleaded in vain to be admitted to the communion of the faithful. At last, after being afflicted by a serious illness, he lost all use of his senses and voice for three days. When he recovered and regained the use of his voice, he sent his grandson to the presbyter at night, asking him to come to him as quickly as possible. But since the presbyter was prevented by illness from approaching the sick old man, he gave the grandson a particle of the Eucharist, instructing him to moisten it and pour it into the old man’s mouth. When the grandson returned from the presbyter and had done this, the old man immediately rested in peace.

These three words, “Bishops or presbyters ought to humble themselves,” and so forth, are also found in Burchard, Book XIX, chapter 2. Saint Ambrose did the same, as the presbyter Paulinus testifies in his Life of him: “Indeed, whenever anyone who had fallen came to him to receive penance and confessed his sins, he wept in such a way that he compelled that person also to weep. He seemed to himself to be lying with the one who was silent.” Likewise, formerly, when the solemnities of the Mass had been completed and the penitents, drenched in tears, fell at the feet of the pontiff, the pontiff himself, soaked with tears, would prostrate himself even at the feet of the penitents, as Sozomen testifies, Ecclesiastical History, Book VII, chapter 16.

Fourth, the rite “Let the priest command him,” and so forth, is also found in the chapter cited above and in the manuscript Order of the library of Saint Remigius at Reims, for the giving of penance, together with the prayer that follows. In that prayer, as in the aforementioned Order of Saint Remigius, “for adoration” is wrongly read; it should be read “for prayer,” as in Burchard.

The following chapter is found in Burchard, chapter 32, cited from the Roman Penitential; in some places it is mutilated. It is not in the cited manuscript Order of Saint Remigius. The word “Tetrads” derives from the nominative *Tetras*, that is, the fourth day of each week, just as *parasceve* means the sixth day, on which Christians, especially Eastern Christians, fast according to ancient custom, as we have explained at length in the notes and observations on the Harmony of Rules. [Col. 0459A] Below, in the same chapter, it says, “Let him eat on Saturday and Sunday.” So it is in Burchard; but “Saturday” appears to have been added by those who followed the custom of the Greeks, who did not fast on Saturdays, especially since this little book is a Penitential of the Roman Church, as is clear from Burchard, who often cites it under this name. Finally, at the end of this chapter appear the words “The prologue is finished,” but I think they should be transferred to the end of the following chapter, since that seems to be part of the preceding one.

The words “If anyone is unable to fast” up to “and know this” are cited by Burchard, chapter 22, from the Penitential of Theodore. Among the ancient Romans, a *solidus* was a gold coin whose value Cassiodorus records, Book I of the *Variae*, letter 10: “They wished a solidus to be six thousand denarii.” Formerly a Frankish solidus was counted as forty denarii, as Hincmar teaches in his Book on the Life of Saint Remigius, and as is clear from the Second Synod of Reims, canon 41. Eventually it was reduced to the value of twelve denarii.

Several Psalms for the giving of penance follow, [Col. 0459B] which are also found in Burchard, Book XIX, chapter 7, though there they are to be recited in full. There are an equal number of prayers, but the second and third are different. In Canisius, “Let us pray” is not found; instead, “Say the prayer.”

The Prayer of the Imposition of Hands follows. In Burchard it is the second among the prayers mentioned above. This prayer is called the prayer of the imposition of hands because formerly, when giving penance, the priest placed his hand on the head of the penitent while reciting this prayer or one similar to it. The Council of Agde, canon 15: “At the time when penitents seek penance, they are to receive from the priest the imposition of hands and sackcloth upon the head, as has been established everywhere.” The following prayer is not complete in Henry Canisius; you have it in full in the Roman Order, in the order for Thursday of Holy Week at the Supper of the Lord. I also restored “me,” because in our manuscript codex, as in Canisius, “also I” is wrongly read. In the third prayer, “so that what” is read, as also in Canisius; but in Burchard and in the Roman Order, “so that those whom” is read.

[Col. 0459C] In the first chapter of the second part, the words “If a cleric commits homicide” appear to be superfluous. With the words “If a layman,” supply “not voluntarily,” because shortly afterward it deals with the voluntary homicide of a layman.

In the second chapter, “a cleric whose rank is higher” means a bishop, presbyter, or deacon. With the words “If he has a rank or vow,” supply “has possessed it.” The end of the chapter is corrupt and, as I think, should be emended as follows: “If any woman who has fornicated has killed what is born, the first established rule forbids her to receive communion until the end” [supply: of the period]. “But so that, according to what has been defined, she may obtain something more humane, we establish that she do penance for ten years, according to the ranks that have been established.” These words are nothing other than canon 21 of the Council of Ancyra.

Chapter 3, concerning perjury. First, these words, “But if anyone, compelled by necessity,” and so forth, are cited by Burchard, Book XI, chapter 6, from the Roman Penitential: “Nevertheless, the Roman Penitential commands as follows: If anyone, compelled by the need to save his life, or by any cause or necessity, swears falsely, because he loved his body more than his soul, let him do penance for three Lents—others judge, three years—one of them on bread and water.”

Second, these words also, “If anyone swears falsely through greed,” and so forth, are cited by Burchard, Book XIX, chapter 7, from the Roman Penitential in this form: “Nevertheless, the Roman Penitential commands that if anyone swears falsely through greed, he sell all his possessions, distribute them to the poor, and, having entered a monastery, submit himself to perpetual penance.”

Chapter 4. After “a four-footed animal,” “has stolen” or something similar should be read. These words, “or any better protection,” are corrupt, and I think they should read: “Or any better livestock, if protection [is involved].” This [Col. 0460A] chapter 4 is cited by Burchard, Book XI, chapter 58, from the Penitential of Theodore, [472] but in a more abbreviated form. If the earlier emendation does not please someone, we shall correct it from that source. It should therefore read: “If a cleric commits capital theft, that is, takes four-footed animals, or breaks into or breaks open a house, or steals property.”

Here *praesidium* means the substance that someone possesses among his movable goods. The First Council of Orléans, canon 14: “With all property remaining under the authority of the bishops.” The Fourth Council of Paris, canon 8: “We have learned that, when an abbot, presbyter, or those who serve in the parishes are lacking, whatever property they have left behind in danger of death is seized by the bishop or archdeacon.” Gregory of Tours, Book VI of his History, chapter 4: “They attacked Lupus’s houses and, having seized all his property, pretending to store it in the king’s treasury, brought it into their own houses.” Marculfus, formula 67, concerning the division of an inheritance among relatives: “So-and-so received the estates called so-and-so, situated there, together with so many slaves, so-and-so. As for the property, consisting of cloths, manufactured goods, or every household article that can be said or named, they appeared to have divided equivalent portions among themselves.” Formula 69 likewise says: “Property of either sex.” By these words he appears to mean male and female slaves.

There follows the penalty for violators of tombs, who, in order to dig out treasures buried with the dead according to the custom of those times, violated graves, as may be seen in Cassiodorus, Book IV, letter 18, concerning a certain presbyter Laurence who had violated a tomb in order to seize the gold from it. In former times, this crime was punished under the laws by many and varied penalties. The Edict of King Theodoric, chapter 110: “Whoever destroys a tomb shall be killed.” The Salic Law, title 17, Book II: “If anyone digs up a dead man and strips him, he shall be judged guilty of eight denarii, which amount to two hundred solidi.” Book I of the Laws of the Lombards, title 12, law 2: “If anyone breaks open the burial place of a dead man and strips the body, let him pay the dead man’s relatives eighty solidi.” These and many other similar laws were enacted because of the treasures hidden in tombs and the precious clothing of the dead, concerning which more is said below.

Chapter 5. By the words “If anyone is a sorcerer for love” is meant one who draws to himself the love of women or boys by love potions or erotic incantations, as we see in the *Pharmaceutriae* of Theocritus and Virgil, and in Lucian’s *Pseudomantis*, who calls them “the graces for erotic matters,” that is, charms or graces for winning love. Most of this chapter is quoted by Ivo of Chartres, part 15, chapter 116, from the Penitential of Theodore, although it differs in certain places. At the end of the chapter a penalty is established against the one who sends storms, as in Burchard, Book X, chapter 28, from the Roman Penitential. But in chapter 8 of the same book, from the same Roman Penitential, a penalty is established against one who believes that there are storm-senders, and the two provisions appear to conflict. Agobard, bishop of Lyon, published a little book in which he condemns those who believe that there are storm-senders. The author of the *Questions* among the works of Saint Justin Martyr, question 31, writes that such things cannot be done through the activity of magicians, and says that such people are called “cloud-drivers” (*nephodiōktas*); the Latins call them *tempestarii*, as Agobard writes in the same place, and Benedict the Levite, Book I of the *Capitularies*, title 64. This storm is called a “wind raised by enchantment,” as Agobard writes.

Chapter 6. The following words deserve notice:

[Note: [Col. 0459D] In the *Judgment of the Penitential*, article 31, you find: “If anyone on the Kalends of January has appeared in the form of a young deer or a heifer, let him do penance for three years.” The very learned Mabillon conjectures that *vitola* should be read for *vitula*. See another of his conjectures in the same place, *Musei Italici*, p. 394.]

“If anyone on the Kalends of January—which many do—and goes about as a young deer, or goes about as an old woman,” words taken from the Council of Auxerre, canon 1: “It is not permitted on the Kalends of January to act as an old woman or a young deer.” Burchard mentions it, Book XIX, chapter 5: “Have you done anything of the sort that the pagans did and still do on the Kalends of January, as a young deer or an old woman? If you have, do penance for thirty days on bread and water.” Saint Pacianus, bishop of Barcelona, likewise says in his *Exhortation to Penance*: “I think that this little deer recently achieved this much: it made him more diligent because he was more sharply reproved; and that whole reproof, expressed and repeated so often, seems not to have restrained but to have educated his licentiousness. Wretched man that I am! What crime have I committed? I think they would not have known how to make a young deer if I had not shown them by reproving them.”

This was a superstition in which, on the Kalends of January, people assumed the forms of wild animals and cattle and ran about here and there with excessive wantonness, as we have explained in the notes and observations on the Harmony of Rules, chapter 50, § 4.

In the same chapter of our Penitential the following passage occurs:

[Note: [Col. 0461D] In the *Judgment of the Gallican Penitential Sacramentary*, article 26: “If anyone invokes the lots of the saints contrary to reason,” and so forth. Our Mabillon observes there that such lots are made through sacred books. What follows here hints at this plainly enough.]

“If anyone has lots which they call the lots of the saints contrary to reason.”

Burchard reports similar things, Book X, chapter 9, from the Roman Penitential, in this form: “Auguries or lots that are called false lots of the saints, or divinations—those who observe them, or those of any writings whatsoever; or whoever makes or fulfills a vow at a tree, or at a stone, or at any object whatsoever except a church—all shall be excommunicated.”

It continues: “If anyone makes a vow at trees or springs,” and so forth.

[Note: [Col. 0461D] Nearly the same is found in the aforementioned *Judgment of the Penitential*, article 27: “If anyone makes a vow at trees, or springs, or railings . . . let him do penance for three years,” and so forth.]

These words are taken from the Councils of Agde, canon 42; the Second Council of Tours, canon 22; and the Council of Auxerre, canons 3 and 4.

It continues: “If anyone is a mathematician,” and so forth. Here “mathematician” means a magician. Strictly speaking, however, it is one who, having examined the hour of birth, investigates what is destined to happen to each person. Saint Augustine, Book II of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 21: “Those who are called genethliaci because of their examination of birthdays are now commonly called mathematicians.” Spartianus, in his Life of Severus: “Then, when he had consulted an astrologer anxiously in a certain African city and had given him the hour, the astrologer saw extraordinary things.” Lampridius, in his Life of Antoninus Diadumenus: “On the days when he was born, the mathematicians, having received his horoscope, exclaimed both that he was the emperor’s son and that he himself would be emperor.” Their art is called *mathesis*. Spartianus, in his Lives of Aelius Verus and Severus: “He inquired into the horoscopes of brides; he himself was also highly skilled in astrology.”

“To take away a person’s mind” means to disturb his imaginative faculty so greatly that he believes himself to be a beast of burden or some other brute animal, like the woman mentioned by Palladius who believed herself to be a beast of burden and whom the blessed Macarius of Egypt healed, and like the daughters of Proetus and those whom Circe drove mad, as the poets once related in their fables. In Book VI of the Visigothic Law, title 2, law 3, it says: “And those who disturb the minds of men through the invocation of demons.”

There follows the prohibition of ligatures, concerning which Saint Augustine speaks, Book II of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 20: “To this class belong all ligatures as well as remedies, which the medical discipline also condemns, whether they consist in certain signs called characters, or in certain things hung up and tied.” And chapter 29: “For it is one thing to say, ‘If you drink this crushed herb, your stomach will not hurt,’ and another to say, ‘If you hang this herb around your neck, your stomach will not hurt.’” Ammianus Marcellinus mentions the matter in Book XV: “If anyone carries around his neck remedies for quartan fever or some other pain,” and so forth.
