Saint Boniface likewise writes in his letter to Pope Zachary: “They also say that they saw women there wearing, according to pagan ritual, phylacteries and ligatures on their arms and legs.” Consult what we have written about phylacteries and amulets in the Harmony of Rules, chapter 3, § 6.

What follows—“If some eat together at a festival,” and so forth—is nothing other than canon 7 of the Synod of Ancyra, where “to undergo two years” means to be in the third grade of penitents, called *hypoptōsis*, that is, prostration. In this grade penitents prostrate themselves before bishops when the bishops lay hands upon them, as was noted above. The words “and so be received” are to be explained as follows: after the grade of prostration, the person is to be received into the grade of those who stand, so that he may pray at Mass with the faithful, as was said above.

But the words “which ought to obey, and after the offering,” and so forth, are corrupt and should be emended from the same synod as follows: “And afterward, whether they are to be admitted with an offering, it is necessary to test each person’s spirit and to learn the life of each.” The words “if he has committed this fault only” are corrupt; it should read: “If he has committed this fault only through gluttony.” The words “let him communicate without an offering” are to be understood as communion in prayer and petitions: standing at the whole Mass with the faithful, but without an offering, that is, without receiving the Eucharist.

Finally, it continues: “If anyone has eaten blood,” and so forth. It is reported in Acts, chapter 15, that the eating of blood was prohibited, as also later in the Sixth Synod, canon 67, where the eating of the blood of any animal is forbidden, not only blood prepared by some technique but blood eaten in any manner whatsoever. This was customary in the Eastern Church. [Col. 0462B] It was also observed at times in the Western Church, as is clear from the letter of the Churches of Lyon and Vienne to the Churches of Asia and Phrygia, in Eusebius, Book V of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 1. In that letter the martyr Biblis, responding to the slander of the pagans, says: “How could such people eat infants, when they are not even permitted to eat the blood of irrational animals?” But it was not universally customary in the Western Church. For some interpret the passage in Acts as referring to homicide and the shedding of human blood, as Saint Pacianus, bishop of Barcelona, does in his *Exhortation to Penance*.

Chapter 7. The provision against mutilating one’s own limbs is taken from canon 23 of the Apostles, which establishes that a layman who mutilates himself is to be subject to excommunication for three years. As for a voluntary abortion, this crime is punished by capital penalty in Book XXXIX of the *Digest*, *On Penalties*, and in canon 92 of the Council in Trullo. The prohibition of usury is taken from canon 17 of the First Council of Nicaea, in which usury is prohibited. The sale of slaves—namely, the sale of another person, whether a slave or a freeborn individual—is forbidden in Book V of the Visigothic Law, title IV, laws 11 and 17. In the Penitential of Theodore, cited by Burchard, Book XIX, chapter 85, this offense is punished by three years of penance.

The words “If anyone burns a threshing floor,” and so forth, are cited by Burchard, Book XIX, chapter 86, from the Roman Penitential in this form: “If anyone voluntarily burns another’s house or threshing floor with fire, let him restore everything that was taken away or burned, and let him do penance for three years.” In the same author, Book V of the same work, in the examination of a penitent, the following is found: “Have you burned another’s house or threshing floor out of hatred? If you have, repay the damage and do penance for one year on the legally appointed weekdays.”

This decree, “If anyone, in anger,” and so forth, Burchard reports from the Roman Penitential, Book XIX, chapter 101, in this form: “Whoever, in a quarrel, makes a man disabled or deformed by a blow shall pay the physician’s expenses and do penance for half a year. If a layman sheds blood through deceit, let him repay him as much as he harmed him; and if he has nothing with which to repay, let him make payment through work for his neighbor for as long as the injured man is sick; afterward, let him do penance for forty days on bread and water.”

It continues: “If anyone from the ministry of the Church,” and so forth. Here “the ministry of the holy Church” means sacred or silver vessels. After the word “Church,” the preposition *ad* appears to be missing; it should therefore read:

[Note: [Col. 0462D] In the *Judgment of the Penitential* it is read, article 38: “If anyone defrauds or neglects anything from the ministry of the holy Church, let him do penance for seven years,” and so forth.]

“If anyone takes anything from the ministry of the Church for any work whatsoever,” and so forth.

Finally, it continues: “If anyone has sinned with animals,” and so forth. This is nothing other than canon 16 of the Synod of Ancyra, where *eikosaeteis* is read, that is, “twenty years”; here, however, “thirty years.” The rest is mutilated. In the words “may deserve communion,” “of prayers” is missing. Add afterward: “When he has persevered in communion for five years, let him be a participant in the offering.” For “of them,” read “of him.” The words “continually toward sinning” are redundant. With the words “let them undergo,” add “and attain communion in prayers.” With the word “five,” supply “years.”

Chapter 8. This provision, “If a bishop commits fornication,” and so forth, is found in canon 25 of the Apostles and in Burchard, Book XVII, chapter 39, from the Penitential of Theodore. But this passage, “before the monastic vow,” is corrupt; it should be read, from the same Penitential of Theodore, as follows: “But a presbyter, *praelato monachi voto* [with the monastic vow set aside],” that is, one who is bound by no monastic vow.

Here *superpositio* means abstinence from food for a full and complete day; *superponere* means to abstain from food for an entire day. It is also an addition or extension of the fast: *superponere* means to extend the fast, in Greek *hyperthesis*, that is, “superposition,” a word used by Saint Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechesis* 18: “Because of the labors that arise both from the extension, prolongation, and addition of the fast of Preparation and from the vigil.” And *hypertithesthai* means “to impose additionally,” “to extend the fast,” or “to add to it”; this word is used by Dionysius of Alexandria in his letter to Basilides and by Saint Epiphanius in his exposition of the faith.

Finally, the word “fifty-days” is corrupt; it should be read “of the Fiftieth,” meaning the Paschal Pentecost—the fifty days that intervene between the two solemnities of Easter and Pentecost—which, according to ancient custom, are free from fasting.

Chapter 9. If the cause is negligence: read “if the cause is negligence.” In these words, “to offer for good things,” the word *rebus* seems redundant. But more on this passage below.

There follows: “If anyone provides guidance to barbarians.” In Burchard this is worded differently, and is set forth more fully in Book XIX, chapter 103, from the Roman Penitential: “If anyone provides guidance against Christians so that they may plunder them, and no slaughter of Christians occurs, let him do penance for three years; but if it does occur, then, having laid aside his weapons, let him live dead to the world until death.” Later one is forbidden to eat the flesh of animals whose death is unknown, lest one happen to eat carrion or something strangled.

These words, “Boys conversing,” and so on, to the end of the chapter, are cited from the Roman Penitential by Burchard, Book XVII, chapter 56, where one reads, “Boys conversing alone,” namely about cinaedic fornication among themselves, as he said shortly before. After “the kiss,” the particle “not” is placed in the cited passage; the sin there is marked by five impositions [of penance].

Chapter 10 follows. Its title is corrupt and should read, “On Defects Concerning the Sacrifice.” Some of these sins concerning the sacrifice of the Mass are found in the manuscript Penitential of Saint Columbanus, abbot of Luxeuil in Burgundy. This chapter, however, is lengthy. But I think that several matters were included under a single title, and that the copyist of this Penitential used a corrupt manuscript, or at any rate lacked care in copying it.

Those matters in this chapter that concern the sacrifice of the Mass are found in Burchard, Book V, chapters 51 and 52, from the Roman Penitential, although they differ in some respects. What *chrismal* means was explained above, in the discussion of the dedication of a basilica.

These words, “So that if the mind is burdened,” are corrupt and should read: “so that, taking the sacrifice while burdened by the fullness of the stomach,” and so forth. The following words, “A deacon forgetting to offer the oblation,” are corrupt. In Burchard, chapter 51 of the cited book, one reads: “A deacon forgetting to offer the oblation until the linen cloth is offered, when the names of those at rest are recited, shall likewise do penance.”

There follows: “But if in the flour,” and so forth. Some words seem to be missing before this. Instead of *quadragenas*, Burchard reads *quadragesimas*. After *negligens*, add *fuerit*. Burchard reads: “And whoever has been negligent shall pay for his negligence with four days.”

[Note: *Judicium poenitentiale*, article 46, has this: “If a priest who is offering [the sacrifice] lets the Eucharist fall from his hands onto the ground and does not find it, let him sweep the place with a clean broom and burn it in the fire,” and so forth.]

Instead of these words, “And if something is found,” Burchard reads, “So that nothing is found.” The earlier reading is preferable, because it explains what must be done when something from the sacrifice is found.

But these words, “And if it should be found,” are otherwise read in Burchard: “But if the sacrifice should be found, let the place be cleaned with brooms, and let the straw be burned, as above, and let the ashes be stored away above,” and “let the priest do penance for twenty days”; where one should read, “let it be given to the fire.”

What follows, “If, through negligence, something from the chalice,” is found in Burchard, Book V, chapter 47, from the decrees of Pope Pius, chapter 3, where *linguabitur* is corruptly written, but one should write *lingua lambatur*, “let it be licked by the tongue.” In the following article, where *vicibus* is written, a word expressing the number is missing. In the cited chapter of Burchard, *vicibus* is absent.

The Lord’s Prayer is called dangerous here because formerly priests recited it at Mass with such reverence and caution that they believed they had committed a grave offense if, while reciting it, they stumbled even slightly.

[Note: *Judicium Poenitentiale*: “If a priest has stumbled over the Lord’s Prayer, let him spend one day on bread and water.” See Mabillon’s note on this passage. Here *tutoaverit* means the same as *titubaverit*, “has stumbled.”]

These words, “If someone does not do penance,” are understood of those who, while they are healthy, do not come to penance but seek it in illness. These three articles concerning penance are taken from the Fourth Council of Carthage, canons 76, 77, 78, and 79.

These words, “But not that woman who dismissed,” are corrupt and should read, “But not for her whom he dismissed,” that is, the woman from whom he is separated.

These words, “If someone unwillingly kills a man belonging to his parents,” should be explained as follows: if someone, against his will, kills the slave of his relatives or kinsmen. For in this passage *parents* means relatives and kinsmen, and *man* means one who is of servile status. On this word, consult Cujas, *Feudorum*, Book I, and Frederick Lindenbrog in his *Glossary* and in his notes on Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, Book IV, chapter 3.

These words, “If a woman persuades another woman [concerning] her husband,” are incomplete; *to dismiss* or *to leave*, or something similar, must be added.

These words, “If one of the Christians sees a Christian walking,” and so forth, are utterly corrupt. I conjecture that they should be corrected as follows: “If one of the Christians sees a Christian walking or wandering and does not show him the way, let him be excommunicated,” or something similar should be restored. Likewise, before the words “has sold his parent,” these words should be placed: “If someone,” so that the text reads, “If someone has sold his parent.”

This regulation, “If he has taken a third [wife],” and so forth, deserves notice. Although the Church permits men who have married twice, three times, and so forth, because such polygamy, or repetition of marriage, nevertheless indicates some lack of continence in a man, it formerly wished such persons to be subject to certain other penalties in addition to the stigma of irregularity.

Saint Basil, in his First Canonical Letter to Amphilochius, excluded digamists from the fellowship of the faithful for two years and trigamists for five. The constitution of the emperor Constantine Porphyrogenitus, issued in the year of the world V I C I C I V C X X I X [as printed], commands that quadrigamists, as long as they remain in this condition, be separated from every ecclesiastical assembly and barred from entering the temple, as Theodore Balsamon reports in his commentary on the cited letter.

What, indeed, would that emperor have decreed concerning the man who, at Rome in the time of Saint Jerome, had outlived twenty wives, and the woman who had already buried twenty-two husbands? In the end they were joined together in marriage, while the Romans eagerly waited to see which of the two would carry out the other. When this happened to the man, he, crowned and carrying the palm, went before his wife’s bier, as Saint Jerome writes in his letter to Ageruchia. The emperor Leo the Philosopher was expelled from the Church because he was a quadrigamist, as Cedrenus writes.

What follows, “If anyone cuts his hair,” and so forth, is established because of pagan superstition. For when pagans carried out and buried their dead, they hired women for pay to mourn the deceased, praise him, stir up others to do the same, cut their own hair, and tear their cheeks. These women were called *praeficae*.

Nonius Marcellus, chapter 1: “Among the ancients, *praeficae* were women who were customarily brought to a funeral to weep and praise brave deeds.”

The old glosses: “*Praefica*: the woman who, in front of the bier during the carrying out of the dead, tears herself; a dirge-singer at a funeral.” That is, she who, preceding the bier when the dead person is carried out, mutilates herself and sings a mournful song during the carrying out of the dead.

The old manuscript glosses of the library of Corbie mention these women: “*Praeficae*, leaders of the lamentation.”

Servius explains this custom for us in his commentary on Book XII of the *Aeneid*: “It was the custom among the ancients for human blood to be shed before funeral pyres, either that of captives or of gladiators; and if such persons were not available, they tore their cheeks and shed their own blood.” This also seems to be referred to in the Twelve Tables, in Cicero, *On the Laws*, Book II, where such madness is forbidden: “Let women not tear their cheeks, nor have a funeral dirge on account of a funeral.” Here *lessus* is a funeral song, otherwise called a *naenia*.

Such women also tore out their hair, as is forbidden here. This is clear from Lucilius XXII, quoted by Nonius in the cited passage: “Hired for pay, they weep profusely at another’s funeral and tear their hair.”

Cutting and shaving the hair at funerals was also customary among the Greeks as a sign of mourning. Euripides, in the *Alcestis*, Act I:

> [lacuna]
>
> ἢ τεμῶ τρίχα  
> Καὶ μέλανα στολμὸν πέπλον  
> Ἀμφιβαλώμεθ᾽ ἤδη;

That is: “Shall I cut my hair, or ought we now to put on dark clothing?”

And in Act II:

> Πένθος γυναικὸς τῆσδε κοινοῦσθαι λέγω  
> Κουρᾷ ξυρήκει, καὶ μελαμπέπλῳ στολῇ.

That is: “I command that we participate in this woman’s mourning by shaving the hair and wearing dark clothing.”

Thus formerly among the Egyptians, whenever a dog had died in any household, all the members of the household, having shaved their entire bodies, were afflicted with great mourning, as Eusebius writes, Book II of the *Preparation for the Gospel*, chapter 1.

The *ungulae* mentioned in this passage of the chapter are curved and pointed iron instruments, shaped like claws and suitable for tearing flesh. Formerly executioners used them in the punishments of martyrs; they are also called *fidiculae*, as is clear from Saint Isidore, *Etymologies*, Book V, chapter 27:

> They are called *ungulae* because they dig out; they are also called *fidiculae*, because by them criminals are tortured on the rack, so that the truth may be discovered.

The same is evident from the glosses of Cyril: “*Ὄνυχες*, those used in tortures: *fidiculae*,” that is, claws or claw-like instruments used in tortures or interrogations.

The same can easily be gathered from Prudentius, *Peristephanon*, concerning Saint Romanus the martyr:

> [lacuna]
>
> When the raging Asclepiades  
> Commands the executioner to turn his blow  
> Against the speaker’s face, and to apply his hand  
> To the cheeks with sharp furrows and claw-like hooks.

And shortly afterward:

> The wicked lictor fulfills the commands given:  
> With writing claws he scores  
> Both cheeks. [lacuna]

Here one sees that when the governor ordered the martyr’s cheeks to be torn with *fidiculae*, the poet afterward says that the martyr’s cheeks were scored by the attendants with writing claws. From this it is perfectly clear that these words have the same meaning.

Isidore derives the name from *fides*, “faith”; but it is in fact a verbal noun from the preterite *fidi* of the verb *findo*, “to split.” Such claw-like instruments were forked, or two-pronged; that is, they had two curved points, as is clear from the same hymn:

> [lacuna]
>
> Offering his naked ribs of his own accord  
> To be cut apart by the two-pronged claws.

Hence below the instrument is called a claw with a gaping point:

> The most savage soldiers split  
> The hanging side of the man  
> With a gaping point.

So much for the claws.

The *herbarius* mentioned next is a poisoner, because of the harmful herbs and herbal poisons used by a poisoner. Hence the French word *enherber*, “to kill someone with poison.” An old poet writes:

> Beneath lies the cool serpent in the grass;  
> Flee, children, for it poisons.

Before these words, “If he ceases to receive him,” some material is missing; for the words do not connect with what precedes. The word *acceptor* is corrupt; read *accipiter*, “hawk.”

Here penance is assigned for eating carrion or a strangled animal, which is also forbidden by Apostolic Canon 63 and Canon 67 of the Sixth Council.

This is relevant to the passage in Burchard, Book XIX, chapter 5: “Have you eaten carrion—that is, animals that had been torn apart by wolves or dogs and were found dead in that condition? If you have, you must do penance for ten days on bread and water. Have you eaten birds that a hawk had crushed, without first killing them with some iron instrument? If you have, do penance for five days on bread and water.”

There follows: “If a hen has died in a well,” and so forth. Almost similar provisions are reported by Burchard, Book XIX, chapter 106, from the Roman Penitential:

> If anyone gives another person a liquid in which a mouse or weasel has been found dead, if he is a layman, let him do penance for seven days; if this happens in a monastery, let him sing three hundred Psalms. Whoever later learns that he has drunk such a beverage shall sing sixty Psalms.

There follows: “If anyone [finds] a mouse or a hen,” and so forth. Not unlike this is what Burchard reports from the same Roman Penitential:

> Whoever eats or drinks something contaminated by a domestic animal, that is, by a dog or cat, and knows it, shall sing one hundred Psalms; if he does not know, let him fast for two days. Or, if he wishes to redeem the penalty, let him sing fifty Psalms.

There follows: “If a dead fish has been found in a fishpond,” and so forth. Similar is the passage in Burchard, Book XIX, chapter 5: “Have you eaten a fish that was found dead in a river? If you have, do penance for three days on bread and water.”

In these words, “Let no one eat its flesh,” *its* refers to the animal with which the man has had intercourse.

The following words, “If he wishes to give something for his soul,” are corrupt and do not sufficiently connect with what precedes. I think they should be read as follows: “If he wishes to give an alms for his soul from the money that came from the plunder, and has completed his penance, he has the power to do so.”

Up to this point is the Corbie manuscript, in which, as I think, the ending of this Penitential is missing. We have touched on these matters briefly so that we might shed some light on this Penitential. Nor shall we write more about the penance of the ancient Christians, since many learned men before us have already traversed this field, especially Gabriel Albaspinaeus, bishop of Orléans, in Book II of his *Observations*; Jean d’Artis, professor of law at the University of Paris and royal professor, in his book *On the Canonical Discipline of the Church Concerning the Sacraments*, and so forth; and Denis Petau of the Society of Jesus, in his *Annotations on Saint Epiphanius*, on heresy 59, which is that of the Novatians.

Nor is it our custom to heap together all the writings of learned men, as certain compilers of monstrous volumes do today, who by the bulk of their books adorn the Muses less than they burden libraries and booksellers’ shops. But let us return to our subject.

### 680. Mass for a Deceased Bishop

The Masses for the dead follow.

[Note: Concerning the commemoration of the dead and prayers for their repose, see Epiphanius, *On the Exposition of the Faith*, no. 23. As for the dead, they are expressly mentioned by name; prayers, sacrifices, and mysteries are regularly offered. Consult the learned Petau’s *Annotations*, volume II, p. 367. Read more on this subject in the notes on Book IV of the *Dialogues*, chapter 55. Concerning almsgiving for the refreshment of the dead, see Paulinus, Letter 33, to Alethius: “You refreshed the soul of your blessed wife, since the hand of Christ pours into her what you distribute to the poor.” And at the end of the same letter: “She is now nourished by your loaves and abounds in your resources.”]

The Masses for the dead are mentioned in the First Canon of the Council of Braga. On their account we shall say something here about the funeral rites, using two funeral offices transcribed here, one from a manuscript of Reims and the other from a manuscript of Abbot Ratoldus.

Thus the Reims manuscript:

> **Here begins the office for the dead.** First, the Psalm *In exitu Israel* is sung with an antiphon, or *Alleluia*. Then the priest sings these prayers:
>
> “With the affection of loving remembrance, dearest brothers, let us make commemoration of our beloved N., whom the Lord has taken away from the temptations of the world, beseeching the mercy of our God that he may grant him a pleasing and peaceful dwelling; that he may forgive all offenses arising from slippery presumption; and that, once the pardon of full indulgence has been granted, whatever his own error brought about in this world may be wholly compensated by his ineffable compassion and kindness. Through the Lord.”
>
> Then follows the Collect:
>
> “Struck by the novelty of a grievous wound and, as it were, wounded in our hearts, we beseech your mercy, Redeemer of the world, with faithful voices, that you may receive the soul of our beloved one,” and so forth.
>
> Then follows the Collect:
>
> “May you, Lord, deign to provide us assistance; may you grant help and mercy, and also [receive] the spirit of your servant N. and of our beloved one,” and so forth.
>
> Another:
>
> “Receive, Lord, the soul of your servant N., returning to you from the regions of Egypt and journeying to you. Send your holy angels to meet him and show him the paths of righteousness,” and so forth.
>
> Likewise the Preface of the dead:
>
> “Mindful, dearest brothers, of the ancient record by which the condition of the human race was subjected to the sin and corruption of the first man, under whose laws each person fears what he sees happen to another, let us implore the mercy of almighty God for the spirit of our beloved one, whose burial is celebrated today, that he may receive him into eternal rest and present him in a blessed resurrection. Through.”
>
> Now follows the Collect:
>
> “God, who are present to righteous supplications and deign to regard pious vows, grant your servant N., whose day of burial we honor today with pious offices, a share in the blessed gift together with your saints and elect.”
>
> Chapters are recited: *In memoria*, and so forth; *Ne tradas bestiis*, and so forth; *Exsultent sancti*, and so forth; *Pretiosa est*, and so forth; *Exsultabunt sancti*, and so forth.
>
> Likewise, a prayer before the body is carried to the tomb.
>
> Preface:
>
> “Let us beseech God, the judge of the universe, God and Lord of the heavenly, earthly, and infernal realms, for the spirit of our beloved one N., that God may deign to place him in rest and raise him in the portion of the first resurrection. Through our Lord Jesus Christ.”
>
> Then follows the Collect:
>
> “We humbly beseech you, holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God, for the spirit of your servant N., whom you commanded to be summoned to you from the origins of this world,” and so forth.
>
> Likewise now the Preface:
>
> “Let us implore the mercy of almighty God, by whose judgment we are either born or brought to an end, that eternal rest may receive the spirit of our brother N., whom the mercy of the Lord has commanded to pass from the habitation of this world; that it may present him in a blessed resurrection and deign to place him in the bosoms of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Through our Lord.”
>
> Then follows the Collect:
>
> “God, who are the creator and maker of all things, who, although you are yourself the blessedness of your saints, grant us who ask,” and so forth.
>
> Likewise, a prayer at the tomb before burial:
>
> “Let us pray, dearest brothers, for the spirit of our beloved one N., whom the Lord has deigned to free from the snare of this world, whose little body will today be handed over to burial, that the mercy of the Lord may deign to place him among his saints and elect, that is, in the bosom of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and that he may have a share in the first resurrection, for which he was made, while we pray through the Lord.”
>
> Then follows its Collect:
>
> “It is the work of your mercy, almighty Father, eternal God, to pray for others, since we ourselves are not sufficient for ourselves. Receive, Lord, the soul of your servant N.,” and so forth.
>
> Preface after burial:
>
> “Having completed, according to the custom of the faithful, the duty owed to the burial of the human body, let us faithfully beseech God, to whom all things live, that he may raise this body, enclosed by us in weakness, in the power and order of the saints; that he may command its spirit to be joined to the faithful; and that he may grant mercy at the judgment to the one whom, redeemed by death, his debt paid [read: *debito*], reconciled to the Father, carried back on the shoulders of the good shepherd, and protected by the Holy Spirit, he grants to enjoy perpetual joy in the company of the eternal King and the fellowship of the saints. Through the Lord.”
>
> “Almighty and eternal God, who deigned to breathe a soul from yourself into the human body,” and so forth.
>
> “God, Redeemer of souls, grant eternity to the departed,” and so forth.
>
> “We commend to you, Lord, the soul of our brother N.,” and so forth.
>
> “Grant safe passage to those who depart in your name from this unstable and most uncertain life into that eternal life and joy among the heavenly beings. Through our Lord.”

Thus far the funeral office from the Reims manuscript.

A few points must be noted concerning it. First, these words, “or *Alleluia*,” show that formerly this cry of joy was not omitted from the office for the dead, on account of the joy that comes to the whole Church from the death of the righteous, as can be seen in Saint Jerome’s *Epitaph for Fabiola*:

> “And now the flying report, herald of so great a mourning, was gathering the people of the entire city for the funeral; the Psalms resounded, and the gilded roofs of the temples shook the *Alleluia* aloft.”

[Note: To this may be referred what is read in Victor of Vita, *History of the Vandal Persecution*, chapter 5: “Who could endure, or recall without tears, that he ordered the bodies of our dead to be carried to burial without the solemnity of hymns, in silence?”]

The Greeks sing this cry of joy in the liturgy for the dead—*εἰς κοιμηθέντας*, that is, “for those who have fallen asleep”—after the reading of the Epistle has ended.

After the words, “The priest sings,” the word *Preface* seems to be missing, because this is not a prayer but an announcement of a prayer, just as below it is written, “Likewise, the Preface of the dead.” It is an announcement, or invitation, by which the priest invites the people to pray, as we noted above concerning the Wednesday of Holy Week.

It should therefore be noted that in sacred usage the word *Preface* is employed in two ways. First, it means the Preface, or thanksgiving and preparation for the consecration, which is customarily placed before the Canon of the Mass. Second, it means the announcement or invitation to pray pronounced by the priest, which is customarily placed before the Collect or Prayer, as can easily be observed in this office for the dead.

Afterward the *capitella* follow. These are certain verses, as is clear from the office itself. The same is evident from the Council of Agde, canon 33: “And at the conclusion of the morning or evening Masses, after the hymns, chapters from the Psalms are to be said, and the people, having gathered for the Prayer, are to be dismissed toward evening by the bishop with a blessing.”

The word is also used for a Collect or Prayer. Gregory of Tours, *On the Miracles of Saint Martin*, Book I, chapter 5:

> “For you should know that my brother Martin, the priest, had departed from the body, and that I had performed the service at his funeral; and, when the customary service had been completed, I did not finish the chapter when you were prompting me.”

Teridius, *Rule for Monks*, no. 21:

> “When the Masses are completed, say Matins: *I will exalt you, my God and King*. Then *Confitemini*. Then *Cantemus Domino*. *Praise the Lord, my soul*. *Benedictiones*. *Praise the Lord from the heavens*. *We praise you, God*. *Glory in the highest*. And every Sunday let the chapter be said in this way.”

After the words, “Before he is buried,” the word *Preface* seems to be missing. For what follows is not a prayer but a Preface.

These matters having been clarified, the funeral office from the manuscript of Abbot Ratoldus should be transcribed as follows:

> **Here begin the prayers for the office of the dead.**
>
> When the soul appears to be struggling in the agony of its departure through the dissolution of the body, the brothers, or all the other faithful, should hasten to assemble. The seven Psalms of penance are to be sung: two *Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger*, and two *Lord, hear me*; *Blessed are those*; *Out of the depths*; and *Have mercy on me, God*.
>
> A litany is also to be performed, as the time permits and as it can be perceived or judged from the circumstances of the person who is about to depart. When the names of the saints have been completed, everyone is immediately to begin the response, *Come to his aid, saints of God*. When it is finished, the priest is to say this Prayer or Commendation for him:
>
> **Prayer.** “To you, Lord, we commend the soul of your servant N., so that, dead to the world, he may live to you,” and so forth.
>
> Another:
>
> “With an affection of compassion, holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God, we are compelled to pray for others,” and so forth.
>
> But if he should survive for a time, other Psalms are to be sung, or the litany performed, until the soul is released from the body of corruption.
>
> At his departure the antiphon is to be said:
>
> “May Christ receive you, who called you, and may the angels lead you into the bosom of Abraham.”
>
> Psalm: *When Israel went out*.
>
> Then follows the Prayer:
>
> “Almighty and eternal God, who deigned to breathe a soul into the human body according to your likeness,” and so forth.
>
> Likewise the antiphon:
>
> “May the choir of angels receive you and place you in the bosom of Abraham, so that with Lazarus, once poor, you may have eternal rest.”
>
> Psalm: *I have loved*, through *To the Lord, when I was in distress*.
>
> Then follows the Prayer:
>
> “Struck by the novelty of a grievous wound and, as it were, wounded in our hearts,” and so forth.
>
> Then the priest asks that prayer be offered for him:
>
> “And lead us not into temptation.”
>
> “Eternal rest.”
>
> “His soul shall dwell among good things.”
>
> “And do not enter into judgment.”
>
> “From the gate of hell.”
>
> “May he obtain a share in the blessed resurrection and deserve to have eternal life in heaven, through you, Christ Jesus, who live and reign as God throughout all ages of ages.”
>
> Another:
>
> “God, to whom alone it belongs to provide healing after death,” and so forth.
>
> Then the body of the deceased is washed.
>
> **Prayer after washing the body, before it is carried out of the house.**
>
> **Prayer.** “Receive, Lord, the soul of your servant N., whom you have deigned to call from the prison of this world,” and so forth.
>
> Another:
>
> “Receive, Lord, the soul of your servant N., returning to you; clothe it in a heavenly garment and wash it in the holy font of eternal life,” and so forth.
>
> Then, with the response *Come to his aid, saints of God* and the other responses for the dead, the body is carried out. When they have approached the church, the Psalm *Have mercy on me, God* is sung with the antiphon *Eternal rest*.
>
> In the church the body of the deceased shall rest until Mass is sung for his soul and offered by all who see fit.
>
> **Here begin the Masses.**
>
> **Prayer.** “We beseech you, Lord, in your mercy, have pity on the soul of your servant N., and, stripped of the contagions of mortality,” and so forth.
>
> **Reading of the Epistle of blessed Paul the Apostle to the Thessalonians.**
>
> “Brothers, we do not want you to be ignorant concerning those who sleep,” and so forth.
>
> Then follows the Gospel according to John:
>
> “At that time Martha said to Jesus: Lord, if you had been here,” and so forth.
>
> **Over the offerings.**
>
> “May this offering, Lord, which, once sacrificed, took away the sin of the whole world, free the soul of your servant N. from all vices and sins of the human condition. Through the Lord.”
>
> **Preface.**
>
> “Eternal God: Although the condition imposed upon the human race by death troubles human hearts and minds, nevertheless, by the gift of your mercy, we are raised by hope of future immortality; and, mindful of eternal salvation, we are not afraid to endure the loss of this light. For by the benefit of your grace, life is not taken away from the faithful but changed; and souls freed from the bodily prison abhor mortal things while they attain immortal things. Therefore we ask that your servant N., established in the tabernacles of the blessed, may glory in having escaped the troubles of the flesh and may await the day of judgment with confidence and the desire for glorification.”
>
> [Note: The manuscript reads, “*peccata nostra contristet; tamen*” (“may our sins grieve; nevertheless”); but this is a manifest error.]
>
> **Within the Canon.**
>
> “Therefore, Lord, graciously receive this offering, which we offer to you for the soul of your servant N., whom today you have freed from bodily corruption; and remove whatever he contracted through the intrusion of human weakness, so that, purified by your remedies, he may reach everlasting joy. Through our Lord Jesus Christ.”
>
> **For the completion.**
>
> “May it profit, Lord, we beseech you, the soul of your servant N.”
>
> Finally, after the celebration of the Mass, the priest stands beside the bier and says this Prayer:
>
> “Do not enter into judgment with your servant, Lord N., for no human being will be justified before you unless forgiveness of all sins is granted through you,” and so forth.
>
> Then follows the Responsory:
>
> “Come to his aid, saints of God.”
>
> Verse: “May the choir of angels receive him and place him in the bosom of Abraham.”
>
> And three times: “Lord, have mercy.”
>
> Likewise the Prayer:
>
> “God, to whom all things live, and for whom our bodies do not perish through dying but are changed for the better,” and so forth.
>
> Then follows the Responsory:
>
> “Before I was born, you knew me.”
>
> Verse: “I tremble at my offenses.”
>
> And three times: “Lord, have mercy.”
>
> Likewise the Prayer:
>
> “Grant, we beseech you, Lord, this mercy to your deceased servant N.,” and so forth.
>
> Then the priest asks that prayer be offered for him:
>
> “And lead us not into temptation.”
>
> “Eternal rest.”
>
> “From the gate of hell.”
>
> **Prayer.** “Incline, Lord, your ear to our prayers, by which we humbly beseech your mercy,” and so forth.
>
> Thus he is carried out of the church with the antiphon, “Open to him the gates of righteousness,” and Psalm 117, namely, “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good.” [Note: The manuscript has *illi* (“to him”); the same hand writes *mihi* (“to me”) above the line.] He is carried to the tomb.
>
> **Prayer before the tomb.**
>
> “With the affection of loving remembrance, dearest brothers, let us make commemoration of our beloved one N., whom the Lord has taken from the temptations of this world,” and so forth.
>
> Then follows the antiphon:
>
> “I shall enter into the place of the tabernacle.”
>
> Psalm: *As the deer longs*.
>
> **Prayer.** “We beseech your mercy, almighty and eternal God, who deigned to create the human being in your image,” and so forth.
>
> Then follows the antiphon:
>
> “This is my rest forever and ever.”
>
> Psalm: *Remember, Lord, David*.
>
> **Prayer.** “God, with whom the spirits of the dead live, and in whom the souls of the elect, having laid aside the burden of the flesh, rejoice in complete happiness,” and so forth.
>
> Then follows the antiphon:
>
> “From the earth you fashioned me.”
>
> Psalm: *Lord, you have searched me*.
>
> The body of the deceased is then placed in the tomb.
>
> **Prayers after the body has been buried.**
>
> “Let us pray, dearest brothers, for the spirit of our beloved one N.,” and so forth.
>
> Another:
>
> “God, who are always present to righteous supplications and deign to regard pious vows,” and so forth.
>
> Likewise another Prayer:
>
> “God, giver of life and restorer of human bodies, who have willed to be entreated by sinners,” and so forth.
>
> Likewise another:
>
> “God, who are the eternal lover of human souls,” and so forth.
>
> Another:
>
> “God, who are always present to righteous supplications,” and so forth; as above, but this one is more extensive than the preceding.
>
> Likewise another:
>
> “It is indeed presumptuous, Lord, that a human being should dare to commend to you, the Lord our God, one human being, mortal one mortal, ashes ashes,” and so forth.
>
> Another:
>
> “Having completed, according to the custom of the faithful, the duty owed to the burial of the human body, let us humbly beseech God, to whom all things live,” and so forth.

[Note: In the manuscript, *fideliter* appears, but incorrectly.]

Then the priest asks that prayer be offered for him and says the chapters as above:

> “May he obtain a share in the blessed resurrection and deserve to have eternal life in heaven, through you, Christ Jesus, who, with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, live and reign as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.”
>
> Psalm: *Have mercy on me, God, according to your great mercy*.
>
> “Eternal rest.”
>
> Then follows the Prayer:
>
> “Absolve, Lord, the soul of your servant N. from every bond of sin, so that, raised among your saints in the glory of the resurrection, he may breathe again. Through the Lord,” and so forth. Amen.
>
> “May he rest in peace. Amen.”

Thus far the funeral office from the manuscript of Ratoldus.

First, it should be noted in this manuscript that *agenda* is taken to mean the divine office.

[Note: In the edition of Pamelius it reads, “Prayers in the office of the dead.” In the Swedish Royal Manuscript: “Likewise other prayers in the office of the dead.” Moreover, the most learned Quesnel holds that *agenda* in liturgical books means the same as the Mass, and that *Action* in the Canon means the consecration itself. He praises the most eminent Cardinal Bona, Book I, chapter 3, *Liturgical Matters*. Read Quesnel’s complete note 8 on Letter 11 of Saint Leo.]

Saint Benedict, chapter 13 of the Rule: “Certainly, the morning or evening office should never be omitted,” and so forth.

Second, the *commendation* is a Prayer for the dead. The Second Council of Milevis, canon 12, mentions this: “Whether Prefaces, or commendations, or impositions of hands, let all be celebrated.” And the Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 12: “Masses are composed, whether prayers or Orations, or commendations.”

There is also an office for the dead. The Third Council of Carthage, canon 29: “For if, in the afternoon, a commendation is to be made for some of the dead, whether bishops, clergy, or others, let it be done with prayers alone, if those who perform it are found already to have eaten.”

Third, the washing of the body of the deceased should be noted, according to the ancient custom of Christians, who were accustomed to provide the dead with every act of piety, especially because of the hope of the future resurrection that has come down to us from the apostles. This can be seen in Acts IX, concerning Tabitha of Joppa, who had died and was restored to life through the ministry of Saint Peter: “When they had washed her, they placed her in the upper room.”

This washing is mentioned by Eusebius, Book VII of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 17, from Dionysius of Alexandria:

> “They were not reluctant even to receive the bodies of the saints with hands raised and turned upward, to place them in their laps, to close their eyes, to shut their mouths, to cling to them, to embrace them, adorning them with washings and clothing.”

That is, they did not shrink from washing them and clothing them.

Gregory of Tours, chapter 3 of the *Book on the Lives of the Fathers*, concerning Saint Gallus, bishop of Clermont: “Afterward, having been washed and clothed, he was carried into the church.” There are many other such passages.

Nothing is said here about anointing the body of the dead, although this was formerly customary among many, as is clear from Prudentius, in the *Cathemerinon*, in the hymn concerning the funeral of the dead:

> “And sprinkled with Sabæan myrrh,  
> The body preserves itself with medicine.”

And Corippus, Book III, *In Praise of Justin the Younger*:

> “A hundred other kinds and wondrous ointments are brought,  
> Preserving the sacred body for all eternity.”

That this was also practiced in the earliest beginnings of the nascent Church is clear from Tertullian, in the *Apologeticus*:

> “We certainly do not buy incense. If the Arabians complain, let the Sabaeans know that their merchandise is expended more abundantly and at greater cost on burying Christians than on fumigating the gods.”

There was another anointing of the dead, but during the funeral rites themselves, when the divine hymns had been sung, “after the salutation the hierarch pours oil upon the departed”—that is, after the salutation the pontiff pours oil upon the deceased, says Dionysius, chapter 7 of *The Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*. This anointing was not practiced for the preservation of the corpse, but to declare that the deceased had now completed the sacred contests, just as before baptism he had been anointed with oil as a sign of the contests he was about to undertake, as the same Dionysius writes.

There formerly existed certain heretics whom Theodoret, in Book I of *The Fables of Heretics*, heresy 15, calls the Ascodrytae. They anointed their dead, but were led by a certain vain superstition, which Saint Irenaeus notes in Book I of *Against Heresies*, chapter 18:

> There are others who redeem the dead, sending oil and water upon their heads at the end of their death, or the aforesaid ointment—opobalsamum—with water, together with the aforementioned invocations, so that they may become incomprehensible and invisible to principalities and powers, and so that their inner man may ascend above the invisible things, while their bodies are indeed left in the creation of the world, but their souls are cast out to the Demiurge.

[Col. 0471D]

They clothed the anointed dead in garments, as is clear from John Moschus, chapter 78 of the *Limonarium*, concerning a certain girl who “was buried with many garments,” that is, she was buried with many clothes. Those garments were also expensive, according to the person’s rank, as Saint Jerome says at the end of the *Life of Saint Paul*:

> Why do you wrap your dead in gilded garments? Why does ostentation not cease amid mourning and tears? Do the corpses of the rich know how to decay only in silk?

Saint Augustine, Book IX of the *Confessions*, chapter 13:

> For, with the day of her dissolution approaching, she did not consider that her body should be covered expensively.

[Col. 0472A]

Gregory of Tours, Book VIII of the *History*, chapter 21:

> She was buried in the basilica of the city of Metz with great ornaments and much gold.

The body of Constantine the Great was buried adorned with purple imperial clothing and a diadem, and enclosed in a golden coffin, as Eusebius writes in Book IV of the *Life of Constantine*, chapter 66.

Corippus describes the clothing in which the emperor Justinian was buried, in Book I of the *Praise of Justin the Younger*:

> And he bore a garment woven with precious purple,  
> On which the whole sequence of Justinian’s exploits  
> Was marked in interwoven gold and gleamed with gems.  
> There the painter had represented, with necks bowed,  
> Barbarian phalanxes, slain kings, and subjected peoples  
> In ordered ranks, with a fine needle and great artistry.  
> He had also made the shining gold stand out in its colors,  
> So that everyone looking upon it might think  
> The figures were real bodies: blood was painted in scarlet.  
> In the middle of the hall he had painted him himself, victorious,  
> Treading upon the savage necks of the Vandal tyrant,  
> While Libya applauded and carried grain and laurel.  
> He added ancient Rome, stretching out her arms  
> And bearing her uncovered breast,  
> The nourisher of empire and mother of freedom.  
> The living Wisdom ordered these things to be done,  
> So that the royal funeral, adorned with its own triumphs,  
> Might lead Augustus to the tomb when the fatal hour arrived.

[Col. 0472B]

Charles the Great was buried with no less distinction of adornment, as a certain monk of Angoulême wrote in his *Life*:

> His body was embalmed and placed upon a golden throne in the curved part of the tomb; he was girded with a golden sword, held a golden Gospel in his hands, and, with his shoulders reclining in the chair and his head honorably raised, was fastened by a golden chain to the diadem. In the diadem a piece of the holy cross had been placed. They filled his tomb with aromatics, spices, balsam, and musk, and with many treasures of gold. His body was clothed in imperial garments, and his face was covered beneath the diadem with a shroud. A hair shirt was placed against his flesh, which he had always secretly worn; and over the imperial garments a golden pilgrim’s pouch was placed, which he had been accustomed to carry to Rome. A golden scepter and a golden shield, which Pope Leo had consecrated, were placed before him, hanging down. Then his tomb was closed and sealed.

Saint Gregory of Nyssa, in his letter to the bishop of Melitene, when dealing with violators of tombs, mentions the adornment of the buried. Hence formerly there were so many laws against violators of tombs.

[Col. 0472C]

Yet this custom was not so universal in the Church that the bodies of the dead were not wrapped somewhere in a white linen cloth. Prudentius suggests this in the hymn cited above:

> It is customary to spread out linen cloths  
> Gleaming with bright whiteness.

Deceased bishops were clothed in priestly or pontifical garments. Bede, cited by Amalarius in the chapter soon to be mentioned, says, concerning the burial of Saint Cuthbert, bishop of Lindisfarne:

> Clothed in priestly vestments.

Flodoard, Book IV of the *Ecclesiastical History of Rheims*, chapter 48, concerning the discovery of Saint Merolilanus the Scot:

> And, looking, he sees the body intact, crowned with priestly insignia.

[Col. 0472D]

For it is believable that this holy man was a bishop, since the wandering Scots who were clerics were for the most part bishops—namely, regional bishops consecrated without a fixed title.

The same is read concerning Saint Birinus, bishop of Dorchester, in Surius, under 3 December:

> A ring was also found, as well as a leaden cross, a small chalice, and pieces of his garments, which are plainly pontifical, as is clear from the circumstances.

And concerning Saint Gebhard, bishop of Constance, in Book I of his *Life*, chapter 22:

> When, therefore, he had been washed, clothed, as was customary, in priestly garments, and placed upon a bier, he was carried to the church.

*(In Henry Canisius, title 6, preceding chapter.)*

[Col. 0473A]

This is how Saint Gregory of Tours should be understood, in chapter 3 of the *Book on the Lives of the Fathers*, concerning Saint Gallus, bishop of Clermont:

> Afterward, having been washed and clothed, he was carried into the church.

And in chapter 4, concerning Saint Gregory, bishop of Langres:

> Nor was anything shown to have been removed from the very garment that had been placed with him.

It was also sometimes customary for the sacred body of Christ, which they call the Eucharist or the oblation, to be placed upon the breast of a deceased bishop in the tomb. Amalarius Fortunatus teaches this in Book IV of *The Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 42, from Bede:

> The Lord Bede plainly declares in the funeral rites of Saint Cuthbert how a deceased bishop ought to be clothed. For he writes as follows concerning his funeral. After Cuthbert, bishop of holy memory, having completed the Communion, raised his eyes and hands to God, commended his soul to him, and gave up his spirit, he died seated and without a groan on the road of the Fathers. He was carried by sailors to our island, his whole body lifted up, his head surrounded by a shroud, the oblation placed upon his holy breast, clothed in priestly vestments, with his shoes prepared to meet Christ, and wrapped in a waxed linen cloth, his soul rejoicing with Christ.

[Col. 0473B]

Amalarius adds that this was undoubtedly the custom of the Roman Church, since the English received the faith from it through Saint Augustine, the disciple of Saint Gregory. Yet because this passage is not found in Bede, neither in Book IV of the *History of the English*, in which he writes at length about Saint Cuthbert, nor in the *Life of Saint Cuthbert* written by him, I think that something is missing from the printed copies of Bede. For I do not believe that Amalarius was so foolish as to invent these things falsely.

The same point also seems to appear in the *Life of Saint Basil*, circulated under the name of Saint Amphilochius:

> And, dividing the bread into three portions, he received one with great fear, kept another for his own burial, and hung the third above the altar upon a silver dove.

[Note: [Col. 0473D] The same point may be seen in the previously cited *Life of Saint Birinus*.]

Nor was this forbidden by the Third Council of Carthage, canon 6:

> It was likewise decided that the Eucharist should not be given to the bodies of the dead; for it was said by the Lord, “Take and eat,” but corpses can neither receive nor eat.

Nor was it forbidden by the Council of Auxerre, canon 12:

> It is not permitted to give the dead either the Eucharist or the kiss.

For these councils are speaking of those who placed the Eucharist in the mouths of the dead for the sake of communion. Hence the Council of Carthage rightly adds: “For it was said by the Lord, ‘Take and eat,’” and so forth; and the Council of Auxerre adds “nor the kiss,” because those who were about to receive the Eucharist kissed one another.

Since, therefore, the passages cited from Bede and Amphilochius in no way concern communion given to the dead, but rather the placing of the Eucharist upon the breast of the deceased, there is nothing in them contrary to the councils cited.

Thus Saint Benedict, our holy father, who was not ignorant of the sacred canons, in order that the earth might receive back a boy monk whom it had twice vomited forth, after sudden death had snatched him away in his parents’ house—parents whom he had visited without Abbot Benedict’s blessing—immediately gave the boy’s parents the Communion of the Lord’s Body with his own hand, saying:

> Go, and place this Lord’s Body upon his breast with great reverence, and then commit him to burial.

When this had been done, the earth no longer expelled the boy, as Saint Gregory writes in Book II of the *Dialogues*, chapter 24.

## Second

In this Office of Abbot Ratold there follows the lifting of the corpse with singing. We also see this in Corippus, Book III of the *Praise of Justin the Younger*:

> … delaying no longer,  
> Augustus commands the lofty bier to be lifted at his signal,  
> And the whole people proceeded from the palace.  
> Every sex and age gathered for the funeral.  
> Who could number the wonders of so great a procession?  
> Here was the venerable order of singing Levites;  
> There the virginal choir thundered, and its voice struck the heavens.

## Third

Over the body itself, after it has been carried into the church and before it is committed to the earth, the sacred sacrifice of the Mass is celebrated, according to the ancient custom evident from Saint Augustine, Book IX of the *Confessions*, chapter 12:

[Col. 0474A]

> When the body had been carried out, we went and returned without tears; for not even in those prayers which we poured out, when the sacrifice of our redemption was offered for her, with the corpse placed beside the tomb before it was lowered, as is customary there—

From the Council of Valencia in Spain, chapter 4:

> After the sacrifice has been offered to God for his commendation, let him immediately and most carefully commit him to burial.

From Saint Gregory of Tours, in the *Lives of the Fathers*, concerning Saint Lupicinus:

> After the Masses had been celebrated, he was buried with the greatest honor and joy.

And there are many other testimonies, whose production would be tedious.

## Fourth

Note the singing of *Kyrie eleison*, according to the ancient usage, as prescribed in a certain Council of Arles, cited by Severinus Binius after the Third Council of Arles. After the council had prohibited diabolical and profane songs at the funerals of the dead, it adds:

> But if anyone wishes to sing, let him sing *Kyrie eleison*.

## Fifth

These words must be noted: “And thus it is lifted from the church”—namely, the corpse, which was to be carried outside the church. [Col. 0474B] From this it is clear that formerly it was not permitted to everyone to obtain burial in churches or basilicas.

The Council of Nantes plainly forbids this, canon 6:

> It must also be prohibited, according to the institutions of our predecessors, that anyone be buried in the church; rather, let them be buried in the atrium, or in the portico, or outside the church. Within the church, moreover, or near the altar where the body and blood of the Lord are consecrated, no one may by any means have permission to bury.

In Gratian, *Decretum*, Part II, cause 13, question 2, chapter *Praecipiendum*, the same decree is produced from the Council of Vaison:

> Let no one be buried in churches, but in the atrium, or in the portico, or in the side-chambers of the church.

Yet this decree is absent from the two Councils of Vaison.

It exists in the First Council of Braga, chapter 36:

> It was likewise decided that the bodies of the dead should in no way be buried within the basilica of the saints; but if necessity requires it, burial outside, near the wall of the basilica, is not so abhorrent.

The Council of Mainz, held under Charlemagne, canon 52, makes an exception for certain persons:

[Col. 0474C]

> Let no dead person be buried inside the church, except bishops, abbots, or worthy priests, or faithful laymen who, by the merit of their life, acquired such a place for their bodies by the way they lived.

The final words, “who by the merit of their life,” and so forth, are absent from volume II of the Councils of Gaul.

Before the First Council of Braga, however, it had been permitted for Christians to be buried within the precincts of churches. This is clear from that question of Saint Paulinus, who asked Saint Augustine whether it benefited someone after death for his body to be buried near the memorial of a saint. Saint Augustine answered him by composing the excellent book *On Care for the Dead*.

On this subject see more in Book I, part 3, chapter 14, of the *Sacred Cemeteries* of the most reverend and learned Henry Spondanus, bishop of Pamiers.

## Sixth

It should be noted that at the end of each Psalm sung before the tomb, a Prayer or Collect is inserted. This is done according to an ancient custom, which may be seen in Cassian, Book II of *The Nocturnal Prayers*, chapter 7:

[Col. 0474D]

> Among them—the monks of Egypt—it is not so; rather, before bending their knees, they pray for a short while, and, standing in supplication, spend the greater part of the time. Thus, falling prostrate upon the ground for the briefest moment, as though merely adoring the divine mercy, they rise with the utmost speed. Then, standing upright again with outstretched hands, they remain more earnestly in prayer in the same manner in which they had previously prayed standing.

And shortly afterward:

> When the one who is to collect the Prayer has risen from the ground, all rise together.

There he is speaking of the Prayers said during the intervals between the Psalms.

In the same Codex of Abbot Ratold, in the Mass for a priest or abbot, the following Prayer is to be noted after the Gospel:

> Receive, holy Trinity, this offering, which I offer to you for the soul of your servant N., that you may grant him eternal rest among your saints and elect, so that in their company he may enjoy eternal life. Through …

This is followed by the Prayer over the Offerings.

In the same Codex, after the Mass mentioned above, there follows:

## MASS FOR THE LIVING OR THE DEAD OF SAINT AUGUSTINE

Here *or* is taken conjunctively.

> Almighty and everlasting God, who rule over both the living and the dead, and have mercy upon all whom you foreknow will be yours in faith and works, I earnestly entreat you to grant that, for those on whose behalf I have resolved to pour out prayers, etc.

As in the Roman Missal, in Lent.

**SECRET:** God, to whom alone is known the number of the elect to be placed in heavenly happiness, grant, I beg you, that the book of blessed predestination may retain written the names of all those whom I have received as commended in prayer, or of all the faithful.

**AFTER THE COMMUNION:** May the sacraments which we have received purify us, we beseech you, almighty and merciful God, etc., as in the Roman Missal in the same place.

**681. Also after the reading.** Namely, of the names of the faithful departed.

**682. Or of the third, seventh, and so forth.** Consult our observations on the *Concordance of the Rules*, chapter 7, section 11.

[Col. 0475A]

**683. Here begins the order, etc.** Having now arranged matters relating to the Masses and certain other matters, the discussion turns to the ecclesiastical orders.

**684. For blessing the sacred orders.** Thus in the printed editions. In the Rheims Codex it reads: “For the blessing of the sacred orders.” Here note that all orders, both major and minor, are called sacred, because through them clerics are ordained and consecrated for that supreme worship which is offered to the divine Majesty through the sacrifice of the Mass—some to celebrate the Mass itself, others to minister or serve in some other way. Long usage has nevertheless established that some orders are called sacred and others not sacred, and that some are called major and others minor.

**685. The major orders before the Gospel, etc.** Thus in the printed editions. Today the usage is reversed, because the minor orders are conferred first and the major orders second. The same is found in the Codex of Abbot Ratold, whose sequence I shall set out here.

On the Saturday of the twelve readings of the first month—that is, March—after the Prayer “Look graciously, we beseech you, Lord, upon your people,” etc., the door-keepers are ordained. Then, after the reading from Deuteronomy has been completed, the Responsory sung, and the Prayer “O God, who have placed us in such great dangers,” etc., the ordination of lectors takes place. Afterward, when the reading from Deuteronomy has been completed, the Responsory sung, and the Prayer “Our Protector, look upon us, O God,” etc., the exorcists are ordained.

After the reading from Maccabees and the appointed Prayer, the acolytes are ordained. The reading from the Book of Wisdom, the Responsory, and the Collect “Hear mercifully, we beseech you, the prayers of your people,” etc., are followed by the ordination of subdeacons. When the reading and Responsory have likewise been completed, and the Prayer “We beseech you, almighty God, look upon the vows of the humble,” etc., has been said, the deacons are ordained.

After the ordination of the deacon, a Mass for the ordination of the deacon is inserted; yet, as I believe, it was not then celebrated. Finally, the Collect “O God, who mitigated the flames of fire for the three boys,” etc., is followed by the ordination of priests. When this has been completed, the Epistle is read, and the Mass is then concluded.

This is what the Codex of Ratold contains. In the Rheims and Rodradus Codices it is not at all clear what order is followed, because in them the arrangement of the orders is described outside the solemn celebrations of the Masses.

**686. The minor orders on Sundays.** Thus in the printed editions. But this has long since become obsolete.

**687. The major orders, however, on the Saturdays of the twelve readings.** That is, at the beginning of the night of Saturday which dawns into Sunday—namely, begins Sunday—so that formerly, at the beginning of Saturday evening, when Sunday began according to the ancient custom of the Church, the priestly and levitical orders were celebrated and received.

[Col. 0475B]

Saint Leo I, pope, established this according to ancient custom in Letter 81 to Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria:

> What, therefore, we know to have been observed by our fathers with particularly careful attention, we wish you also to preserve: that priestly or levitical ordination not be celebrated indiscriminately on every day, but that the beginnings of that night which dawns into the first day of the week after Saturday be selected—that is, that they be appointed under the rule of the divine office—and that on those occasions sacred Benediction be conferred upon those who are to be consecrated, while they are fasting and by those who are fasting.

And in Letter 89:

> Let no one consider the stability of his status secure if he has not been ordained on Saturday evening, which dawns into the first day of the week, or on the Sunday itself. For our predecessors judged only the day of the Lord’s resurrection worthy of honor, so that priests who are appointed should be conferred especially on that day.

First note that when it says “or on the Sunday itself,” this must be understood to mean that the ordination takes place on Sunday if the Saturday fast has been continued, as he wrote in Letter 81. The same observance applies if it is celebrated on Sunday morning with the Saturday fast continued.

[Col. 0476A]

This is also made clear by the Council of Clermont under Urban II, supreme pontiff, cited by Orderic Vitalis in Book IX of the *Ecclesiastical History*:

> Orders are to be celebrated at all times on Saturday evening, or on Sunday while the fast continues.

And by the Council of Rouen, under Archbishop John, in the year of the Lord 1072, following the teaching of the same Saint Leo, canon 7:

> It has also been decreed that in conferring the sacred Orders we must not be found violators of apostolic authority. For it is read in the decrees of Pope Leo that the sacred orders are not to be celebrated indiscriminately on every day, etc.; and the same observance applies if they are celebrated on Sunday morning with the Saturday fast continued, etc.

Thus in Orderic Vitalis, Book IV of the *Ecclesiastical History*.

Second, it should be noted that by “the day of the resurrection” Saint Leo does not mean exclusively Easter Day, but Sunday, which is celebrated in memory of Christ’s resurrection. Hence in Letter 81 he immediately adds:

> From that time the beginnings of the preceding night do not depart, since there is no doubt that it belongs to the Day of the Resurrection, just as is also shown on the Lord’s Pasch.

And later in the same letter, after saying, “Benedictions are never to be conferred except on the day of the Lord’s resurrection,” he writes:

[Col. 0476B]

> Finally, on this day the Holy Spirit, promised by the Lord to the apostles, came; so that we may know that it was indicated and handed down by a certain heavenly rule that the mysteries of priestly Benedictions are to be celebrated for us on that day on which all the gifts of grace were bestowed.

For there he enumerates the prerogatives of Sunday: Christ rose on that day; it is the first of the days on which heaven and earth were created; and on that same day the Holy Spirit was sent upon the apostles. For these reasons the sacred orders ought to be celebrated on that day.

These passages must be understood of the Sundays of the four seasons, whether the orders are celebrated on Saturday evening or on Sunday morning with the fast continued, as we have noted.

Pope Gelasius likewise establishes this in his letter to the bishops of Lucania:

> The ordinations of priests and deacons must not be performed except at fixed times and on fixed days—that is, during the fast of the fourth, seventh, and tenth months, as well as at the beginning of Lent and on the middle day of Lent. They should know that the ordinations are to be celebrated toward evening, with the Saturday fast.

[Col. 0476C]

The present usage, by which both major and minor orders are conferred together on the Saturdays of the twelve readings—that is, on the Ember Days—is nevertheless ancient. Chrodegang, bishop of Metz, who flourished in the times of Charles the Mayor and of King Pippin [perhaps: “and Pippin”], used to act in this way, as Paul the Deacon writes in his *Book of the Bishops of Metz*:

> He consecrated very many bishops in various cities, as well as priests and deacons and the other ecclesiastical orders, as is the custom of the Roman Church on the four Saturdays of the seasons of the year.

**688. Door-keeper.** Door-keepers are mentioned in Letter 34 of Saint Cyprian; in Saint Ignatius’ Letter to the Antiochenes; in the letter of Pope Cornelius to Fabius, bishop of Antioch, in Eusebius, Book VI of the *History*, chapter 35, where they are called *πυλωροί* (*pylōroi*); in canon 34 of the Council of Laodicea; and by Saint Epiphanius, in his exposition of the Catholic faith, where they are called *θυρωροί* (*thyrōroi*). The ordination of door-keepers is treated in the Fourth Council of Carthage, which will be cited below.

**689. After he has been instructed by the archdeacon, etc.** Thus in the printed editions and in the manuscript Rheims and Rodradus Codices, and likewise in the Fourth Council of Carthage, canon 9. In the Codex of Ratold and in the Roman Order these words are expressed in the plural. In the Roman Pontifical it reads:

[Col. 0477A]

> Then the pontiff takes the keys of the church and hands them to all; one after another they touch them with the right hand, while the pontiff says: “Act in this way,” etc.

**690. Let the bishop hand him the keys of the church.** In our other manuscript Codices the words “of the altar” are added, as in the Fourth Council of Carthage, where it reads “of the altar.”

**691. And let the deacon hand them to him.** Thus in the printed editions and in the Rheims and Rodradus Codices; but it seems that the reading should be *the archdeacon*, as in the *Order*, the Roman *Pontifical*, and the Codex of Ratold, where the following is found:

> And let the archdeacon lead them to the door of the church and say: “Through this door the ministry is entrusted to you, so that you may be doorkeepers of the temple and have the power to receive the good and reject the unworthy.”

Saint Isidore seems to allude to these words in Book II of *The Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 15:

> For they have authority both to receive the good and to reject the unworthy.

These words do not appear in the Fourth Council of Carthage.

Isidore the Younger says the following about the office of the door-keeper in his letter to Luitfrid, bishop of Córdoba:

> The keys of the church belong to the door-keeper, so that he may close and open the temple of God and guard everything that is inside and outside; he is to receive the faithful and reject the unbelieving and excommunicated.

**692. God the almighty Father, etc.** Thus in the Rodradus and Rheims Codices. In the printed editions, in the Codex of Ratold, in the *Order*, and in the Roman *Pontifical*, these words are expressed in the plural.

**693. For distinguishing the fixed hours.** The ancients observed the hours according to the courses of the stars, as we noted in the *Concordance of the Rules*, chapter 54, section 11, and also according to the shadow of the human body. This can be seen in Bede’s *Book on the Reckoning of Time*, where he composed a sundial for this purpose. The same work also exists in an old manuscript Codex of the library of Corbie, from which we recovered Theodulf’s *Book on the Order of Baptism* and the *Roman Penitential*. At the end of the latter are these words:

[Col. 0477B]

> Let the canons strive with the utmost diligence and vigilant care to observe the aforementioned hours and to perform the divine office at them humbly and devoutly. For as soon as the signal has been given, let them all hasten to the church and assemble; let the bells be rung at the appointed times.

The sundial in the said manuscript Codex is as follows:

**January and December:** hour 1 and 11, 29 feet; hour 2 and 10, 19 feet; hour 3 and 9, 17 feet; hour 4 and 8, 15 feet; hour 5 and 7, 13 feet; hour 6, 11 feet.

**February and November:** hour 1 and 11, 27 feet; hour 2 and 10, 17 feet; hour 3 and 9, 15 feet; hour 4 and 8, 13 feet; hour 5 and 7, 11 feet; hour 6, 9 feet.

**March and October:** hour 1 and 11, 25 feet; hour 2 and 10, 15 feet; hour 3 and 9, 13 feet; hour 4 and 8, 11 feet; hour 5 and 7, 9 feet; hour 6, 7 feet.

**April and September:** hour 1 and 11, 23 feet; hour 2 and 10, 13 feet; hour 3 and 9, 11 feet; hour 4 and 8, 9 feet; hour 5 and 7, 7 feet; hour 6, 5 feet.

**May and August:** hour 1 and 11, 21 feet; hour 2 and 10, 11 feet; hour 3 and 9, 9 feet; hour 4 and 8, 7 feet; hour 5 and 7, 5 feet; hour 6, 3 feet.

**June and July:** hour 1 and 11, 19 feet; hour 2 and 10, 9 feet; hour 3 and 9, 7 feet; hour 4 and 8, 5 feet; hour 5 and 7, 3 feet; hour 6, 1 foot.

But the shadow varies at different parallels.

The series of hours here is reckoned from sunrise. For the shortest shadows always occur at the sixth hour, which is noon.

**694. Benediction.** This word is commonly used in the sacred ordinations. This is how the statement of the Second Council of Seville, canon 5, is to be understood:

> And a certain priest had given them a Benediction contrary to ecclesiastical order.

And Sidonius, Book VII, Letter 6:

> If by a succeeding Benediction he does not receive an heir to the dignity.

**695. Let service render obedience.** Thus in the Rodradus and Rheims Codices. In the printed editions it reads, “Let services render obedience.” In the Codex of Ratold it likewise reads, “Let services render obedience.” In the *Order* and the Roman *Pontifical*: “Let them obey your command,” which is more correct.

[Col. 0478A]

**696. Lector.** *Ἀναγνώστης* (*anagnōstēs*).

Lectors are mentioned in canon 43 of the Apostles; in Saint Ignatius’ Letter to the Antiochenes; in the letter of Pope Cornelius to Fabius, bishop of Antioch; in Eusebius, in the chapter cited above; in the letter of Saint Cyprian soon to be cited; in the First Council of Arles under Saint Sylvester; in canon 24 of the Council of Laodicea; in the Third and Fourth Councils of Carthage, soon to be cited; by Saint Epiphanius in his *Exposition of the Catholic Faith*; in the First Council of Toledo, to be cited below; and in the proceedings of the trial of Caecilian and Felix.

In ancient times lectors were not only of mature age but also children, even prepubescent boys, since the Church considered it appropriate that boys who were teachable and of good character should become accustomed early to the ecclesiastical yoke.

This is clear from the Third Council of Carthage, canon 19:

> It was decided that when lectors have reached the years of puberty, they must either be compelled to marry or profess continence.

Victor of Vita supports this in Book IV of the *Vandal History*:

> At that time also, while Eugenius the pastor was in exile, the entire clergy of the Church of Carthage was worn down by slaughter and hunger—nearly five hundred or more men—among whom were very many little-boy lectors, who were handed over to exile rejoicing in the Lord.

Here *little boys* should not be taken to mean children so young that they lacked the use of reason and could not speak, but those who, having already passed beyond infancy, had reached childhood.

Nor should it be believed that *lectors* is being used here for psalmists, as some explain, taking the term *lector* in a broad sense and relying on these words of Victor:

> From the multitude of confessors being led away, on the information of a certain apostate former lector, Teucharius, twelve little boys were separated whom he knew to be skilled singers and vigorous in the melodies of song, and whom he had had as pupils while he was a Catholic.

[Col. 0478B]

Although those twelve little boys were skilled in the melodies of song, there is nothing to prevent their having been ordained from among the psalmists. Moreover, if those twelve were skilled singers, the others evidently were not; for besides them there were other little-boy lectors, since Victor says “very many little-boy lectors,” and therefore more than twelve.

Nor is the reading “lectors and little boys” valid, since the coordinating conjunction is not found in Victor or Usuard.

Our assertion is confirmed by the words of Pope Zosimus in the *Roman Order*:

> The following periods are to be observed for each grade. If someone has devoted himself from childhood to ecclesiastical ministries, he is to remain among the lectors through the twentieth year of his age by continuous observance.

The same can be seen in the Second Council of Vaison, canon 1, where younger lectors are placed under the care of a priest; and at the end of the canon it adds:

> When they have reached mature age, if any one of them should wish to take a wife because of the weakness of the flesh, the power to enter into marriage is not to be denied him.

Here you see that the same rule is established as in the Council of Carthage cited above.

The same is evident from Saint Paulinus, Book IV of the *Life of Saint Felix the Martyr*:

> And, from boyhood, his pious mind, giving itself to heavenly things (*edens*; read *addens*, “joining or adding itself”),  
> Trained itself to serve God; nor was grace absent (*abfuit*; read *adfuit*, “was present”) from the poor man;  
> And (*et*; read *at*, “but”), in proportion as his heart thirsted,  
> His soul, gaping for the light, drew in the gifts of God in abundance;  
> In his earliest years he served as a lector.

Sidonius, Book IV, Letter 25:

> They consecrated to themselves as a colleague Saint John, a man distinguished by integrity, humanity, and gentleness—first a lector, then a minister of the altar, and that from childhood.

And from Ennodius, in the *Life of Saint Epiphanius*, bishop of Pavia, who, under his predecessor, the most upright man Crispinus the Pontiff, having undertaken the novitiate of the heavenly army at about eight years of age, received the office of ecclesiastical lector.

It is no objection that in Africa, in the time of Saint Cyprian, as is known from his Letters 33 and 34 and several others, the office of lector was entrusted only to men of advanced age, distinguished by merit and learning. For it is one thing to speak of the age of Saint Cyprian and another to speak of the period of the authors and councils cited by us. If that usage prevailed in the earlier century, it did not prevail in the later one.

[Col. 0479A]

**697. Let the bishop address the people about him, etc.** Thus in the Fourth Council of Carthage, canon 8, and in Saint Isidore, Book II of *The Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 11:

> First, the bishop speaks to the people about their conduct. Finally, before the people he hands them the book of the divine writings, so that they may proclaim the word of God.

**698. Let him hand him the book.** In the Codex of Abbot Ratold it reads:

> Let him hand them the Book of the Prophet Isaiah.

**699. From which he is to read.** Isidore the Younger explains the office of the lector in the letter cited above:

> It belongs to the lector to pronounce the readings and to proclaim to the people what the prophets foretold.

In those ancient times of the Church, lectors read the Gospel and the Epistle in church, as is known from the authorities cited below.

Saint Cyprian, Letter 33, concerning Aurelius the confessor, ordained as a lector:

[Col. 0479B]
