> For nothing is more fitting for the voice that has confessed the Lord in a glorious confession than to resound in the celebration of the divine readings with the exalted words that have proclaimed Christ’s martyrdom, to read the Gospel of Christ, from which martyrs are made.

And in the following letter, concerning Saint Celerinus the confessor, likewise made a lector:

> When this man came to us, most beloved brothers, with so great a display of the Lord’s favor, illustrious through the testimony and miracle of the very man who had persecuted him, what else ought to have been placed upon the pulpit—that is, upon the tribunal of the church—than he, so that, supported by the height of the elevated place and conspicuous before all the people through the distinction of his honor, he might read the commandments and the Gospel of the Lord, which he follows bravely and faithfully? Let the voice that confessed the Lord be heard daily in those things which the Lord spoke. Is there, perhaps, a higher grade to which one may advance in the Church?

From the First Council of Toledo, canon 2:

> It was likewise decided that penitents should not be admitted to the clergy, unless necessity or custom should compel it; and then they are to be assigned among the door-keepers or among the lectors, so that they may not read the Apostle or the Gospel.

This prohibition would have been pointless if penitents who later advanced to the lectorate had not been permitted to read the Gospel and the Apostle—that is, the Epistle, as it is commonly called.

[Col. 0479C] The same may be seen in canon 4, where a subdeacon who has married twice is rejected among the doorkeepers and readers, so that he may not read the Gospel and the Apostle. For the bigamous subdeacon, once rejected among the readers, is not forbidden to read the Gospel so that he may be deprived of an honor which he would previously have possessed by virtue of the subdiaconate—for subdeacons never had the duty of reading the Gospel—but rather on account of the rank of reader to which he is relegated, so that he may be deprived, because of his bigamy, of the honor of reading the Gospel, an honor which he might otherwise have assumed by virtue of the readership. Thus the council says:

> But if a subdeacon, after the death of his wife, should take another wife, let him be removed from the office in which he was ordained, and let him be counted among the doorkeepers and readers, so that he may not read the Gospel and the Apostle.

[Note: [Col. 0479] This will also become clear below from Gregory of Tours and Pachymeres, to be cited in connection with the Mass of Ratoldus.]

I nevertheless write this without denying that another practice may at some time have existed, as we shall say below when discussing deacons. It was also the duty of readers to preserve the sacred books, as can be seen in the proceedings concerning the purgation of Caecilianus and Felix:

> When all the books were demanded from Mars, he denied that he had any. Then Victor gave the names of all the readers; and below: Bishop Paul said, “The readers have the Scriptures”; and below: “Bring forth the Scriptures that you have.” Catulinus and Marcuclius said, “We have no more, because we are subdeacons, but the readers have the books.”

For the pagan judges were searching out the sacred books of both Testaments in order to consign them to the fire.

700. “Receive, and be a bearer of the word of God,” etc. Thus it appears in the printed editions, in the cited canon of the Council of Carthage, and in the Rhemish and Rodradi manuscripts. In the Roman Pontifical and Ordinal, and in the Ratoldus manuscript, these words are expressed in the plural.

701. “Holy Lord, Father,” etc. This blessing is found in this form in our other manuscripts, [p. 492], and in the Roman Pontifical. In the Ordinal it varies in some copies, in which, as also in the Roman Pontifical, the following prayer or Preface is placed first: “Let us pray, dearest brothers, to almighty God,” etc.

[Col. 0480A] 702. “Distinctus” (“distinguished”). Thus in the printed editions and in the Rhemish, Rodradi, and Ratoldus manuscripts, although in the latter it is expressed in the plural. In the Roman Ordinal it is written *apti* (“fitting”); in the Pontifical, *instructi* (“instructed”).

703. “And ordained.” Thus in the printed editions. In the Ratoldus manuscript one reads “and ordained” in the plural. In the Rhemish and Rodradi manuscripts: “and adorned.”

704. “Exorcist.” It is rightly the case that the ordination of an exorcist follows the creation of a reader, according to the ancient custom, which is evident from Book IV of Saint Paulinus’ *Life of Saint Felix*, where we see that this holy martyr was first ordained a reader and then an exorcist:

> In his earliest years he served as a reader;  
> Then he assumed the rank whose duty it was, with faithful voice,  
> To adjure the evil ones and drive them away with sacred words.

Exorcists are mentioned in the letter of Bishop Firmilian to Saint Cyprian (letter 75 among the letters of Saint Cyprian); in the letter of Pope Cornelius to Fabius, bishop of Antioch; in Eusebius, Book VI of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 31; in the letter of Saint Ignatius to the Antiochenes; in the subscriptions of the First Council of Arles under Pope Sylvester; in the Council of Laodicea, canon 24; in the Fourth Council of Carthage, to be cited shortly; in Saint Hilary’s *Book on Synods*; in Saint Epiphanius’ *Exposition of the Catholic Faith*; in Sulpicius Severus, chapter 3 of the *Life of Saint Martin*; and in many others. Among pagan authors, Lucian mentions them in letter 30, although, in his customary manner as an old and crafty scoffer who despises sacred things no less than profane, he mocks them:

> A loud-speaking, foul-mouthed exorcist  
> Drove out a demon—not by the power of oaths, but of dung.

And Julius Firmicus, Book III of the *Mathesis*, chapter 5:

> They will be terrifying to all demons; at their arrival the wicked spirits of demons will flee. They will free people suffering in this way, not by the force of words, but merely by showing themselves. And although the demon may be violent, shaking the body and mind of human beings—whether it is aerial, terrestrial, or infernal—it will flee at this man’s command, because it will be terrified by his instructions with a certain reverence. These are the men whom the common people call exorcists.

This pagan author, who attributes the power of God to the constellations, grants such great power over demons to exorcists that there can be no doubt that these statements apply to Christian exorcists, not to pagans, who never possessed such authority over demons, even though they sometimes appeared to drive demons from human bodies by certain deceptive incantations. And in chapter 9 of the same book:

> In the ninth place, Mercury, situated together with the Sun and equally with the horoscope, will make exorcists, who free people suffering from demonic attack by suitable remedies; hence great wealth will accrue to them from these arts.

This word is also found in the sacred Scriptures, Acts 19:13:

> Some of the itinerant Jewish exorcists also attempted to invoke the name of the Lord Jesus over those who had evil spirits, saying, “I adjure you by Jesus whom Paul proclaims.”

705. “When he is ordained,” etc. Thus in the Fourth Council of Carthage, canon 7, and in all our other manuscript copies.

[Col. 0480D] The same may be seen in Saint Isidore, Book II of *Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 13:

> For when they are ordained, as the canon says, they receive from the hand of the bishop a little book in which the exorcisms are written, receiving the power to lay hands upon the possessed, whether baptized or catechumens.

706. “Receive and commit to memory.” Thus in the cited canon, as also in the Rhemish and Rodradi manuscripts.

493 707. “Have the power to lay hands,” etc. In the cited Fourth Council of Carthage, canon 9, it is decreed:

> Every day let the exorcists lay hands upon the possessed.

And this is their proper duty, as can be seen in Saint Isidore, in the chapter cited above and in Book VII of the *Etymologies*, chapter 12, and in the younger Isidore’s letter cited above.

708. “Preface of the exorcist.” In the Ratoldus manuscript one reads [Col. 0481A] “Consecration of the exorcists,” incorrectly, since this is a Preface, not a consecration; and in the same manuscript the blessing, that is, the consecration, follows immediately.

709. “God the Father,” etc. Thus in the Rhemish and Rodradi manuscripts. In the other copies mentioned above, these words are expressed in the plural.

710. “Holy Lord, Father,” etc. Thus in the Rodradi and Rhemish manuscripts. In the printed editions and in the Ratoldus manuscript, and in the Pontifical and Roman Ordinal, these words are expressed in the plural.

711. “Of restraining unclean spirits.” In the Ordinal and Roman Pontifical one reads: “of restraining unclean spirits.”

712. “Approved”—that is, good. A rule of a certain Father says: “Afterward, if his approved repentance is recognized, only then shall he be received within the enclosure of the monastery.” The Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 4: “He shall have proved himself in life and teaching.”

713. “The grace of healings,” etc. Thus in Book VIII of the *Apostolic Constitutions*, chapter 27, it is said that the exorcist receives the grace of healings.

714. “Acolyte.” Acolytes are mentioned by Saint Cyprian, letter 55, and in the above-cited letter of Pope Cornelius. The author of the old etymological lexicon explains the meaning of *acolyte* as follows: “Akolouthos signifies one who makes the road behind”—that is, *acolyte* signifies one who follows behind. Hesychius: “Akolouthos: a younger boy.” The old glosses: “Akolouthos: follower, attendant, one who follows behind,” from *akoloutheō*, that is, “I follow.”

As regards the Church, Saint Isidore teaches the following about acolytes, Book VII of the *Etymologies*, chapter 12:

> Acolytes are called in Greek *acolythi*, and in Latin *ceroferarii*, from carrying candles, when the Gospel is to be read or the sacrifice offered. At that time they light and carry the lamps—not to dispel darkness, since the sun is shining at that hour, but to display a sign of joy, so that under the figure of bodily light that light may be shown of which it is written in the Gospel: “That was the true light, which enlightens,” etc.

Papias agrees:

> Acolytes are called *acolythi* in Greek and *ceroferarii* in Latin, from carrying candles.

715. “First let him be instructed by the bishop.” Thus in the Fourth Council of Carthage, canon 6, in the Roman Ordinal, and in our other manuscript copies.

716. “Let him receive the candle-bearer from the archdeacon,” etc. Thus in the printed editions, in the Council of Carthage, in the cited canon, in the Roman Ordinal, and in our other manuscript copies. It is otherwise in the Roman Pontifical:

> The pontiff takes and gives to all a candlestick with an extinguished candle, which each successively touches with his right hand, while the pontiff says: “Receive the candle-bearer,” etc.

Here, I think, *ceroferarium* should be understood as neuter for “candlestick,” since *ceroferarius* in the masculine is the acolyte. Gregory of Tours calls it *ceroferale* in his *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 79.

717. “For lighting the lamps of the church.” Saint Isidore, in the passage cited above: “For then the lamps are lit and carried by them.” The younger Isidore, in the letter cited above: “The preparation of the lamps in the sacristy belongs to the acolyte.”

494 718. “Thus saying to himself.” In the Roman Pontifical [Col. 0481D] and in the Ratoldus manuscript, the pronoun “to himself” is absent.

719. “Receive this bearer of the light,” etc. Thus in the Ratoldus manuscript. But in the cited canon of the Council of Carthage and in the Rodradi and Rhemish manuscripts, as also in the printed editions, no formula of words is given here. It does appear in the Ordinal and Roman Pontifical, but in a shorter form:

> Receive the candle-bearer with the candle, so that you may know that you are appointed to light the lamps of the church.

720. “Let him also receive the little pitcher,” etc. Thus in the printed editions and in the Rhemish and Rodradi manuscripts, as also in canon 6 of the Fourth Council of Carthage. In the Roman Ordinal the following is added:

> The bishop saying to him: “Receive the little pitcher for supplying wine and water for the Eucharist of the body of Christ.”

This formula also appears in the Roman Pontifical. In the Ratoldus manuscript one reads:

> Let an empty pitcher be given to them: “Receive the pitcher for pouring”—read, “for supplying”—wine in the Eucharist of the body of Christ.

721. “For pouring.” Thus in the printed editions and in the Rodradi manuscript. But in the Rhemish manuscript and in the aforesaid council, as also in the formula of the Roman Ordinal and Pontifical, one reads “for supplying,” which agrees with the younger Isidore’s letter to Luidfredus:

> He himself supplies what is needed for the Eucharist to the subdeacons.

722. “Wine.” Thus in the printed editions and in the Rodradi manuscript, and also in the cited canon of the Council of Carthage. But in the Rhemish and Ratoldus manuscripts, as well as in the actual formula of the Roman Ordinal and Pontifical [Perhaps: “the formula in the Ordinal and Roman Pontifical,” or “the formula of the Ordinal in the Roman Pontifical”], the phrase “and water” is added.

723. “Almighty everlasting God,” etc. Thus in the printed editions and in the Rodradi manuscript. But in the Roman Pontifical three prayers are placed before this blessing. In the Ratoldus manuscript a second is added:

> Holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God, who through Jesus Christ, [Col. 0482B] etc.

This is found in the Roman Ordinal and Pontifical, and is the only one in the Rhemish manuscript.

724. “Ordination of the subdeacon.” Subdeacons are mentioned in canon 43 of the Apostolic Canons, in the frequently cited letter of Cornelius, in Saint Ignatius’ letter to the Antiochenes, in Saint Cyprian’s letter 24, in Saint Epiphanius’ *Exposition of the Faith*, in the Council of Laodicea, canons 21, 22, and 25, where they are called *hypēretai*, that is, ministers, and in the Council of Carthage, to be cited shortly.

Note here that the subdeacon is assigned a place among the minor orders, as in the printed editions, although Saint Gregory, Book IV, letter 88, distinguishes subdeacons from the minor orders.

[Note: [Col. 0481D] Now the acts of this synod, which previously stood in place of letter 44 of Book IV, have been relegated to the end of the letters.]

I think this happened because formerly the subdiaconate was not a sacred order, which is clear from the Council of Laodicea, canon 21, in which subdeacons are forbidden to touch the sacred vessels. This is confirmed by the authority of Peter the Chanter, who lived in the year 1197. In a manuscript book *On the Miraculous Word* in the library of the monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, chapter 54, he writes that it was only recently instituted that the subdiaconate should be a sacred order:

> The first imposition of hands, he says, belongs to those being ordained deacons; for it was only recently instituted that the subdiaconate should be a sacred order.

725. “As one who is invited,” etc. These words [Note: [Col. 0482D] Now Book IX, letter 105.] are found in Gregory’s Book VII, letter 110, but not continuously, since after certain intervening words the following appears: “Why did he not consider,” etc. These words are absent from the Roman Ordinal.

726. “To be removed,” etc. Thus in our other manuscript copies. In the printed editions one reads *admovendus* (“to be admitted”), as in Saint Gregory’s cited letter. This reading seems more plausible, although the former is not entirely absurd, since no one should be ordained unwillingly.

495 727. “When a subdeacon is ordained, because he does not receive the imposition of hands,” etc. Thus in the printed editions and in our other manuscript copies. So also in the Fourth Council of Carthage, canon 5; in the Roman Ordinal; in Saint Isidore, Book II of *Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 10; and in the Tilian manuscript.

728. “Let him receive the paten from the bishop’s hand,” etc. The same may be seen in the Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 27:

> If a subdeacon [receives] the paten and chalice.

For the passage concerns the restoration of a degraded man, who, according to that same council, receives at his restoration what he had previously received at his ordination.

729. “A little pitcher.” In Isidore one reads “a cup of water.” *Urceolus* is a diminutive of *urceus*. Papias: “A pitcher is a vessel for water”; hence *urceolus* is its diminutive. Here, however, it is not used for a vessel of water. It should be noted that in the cited Council of Toledo no mention is made of the little pitcher, the basin, or the towel in the restoration of a degraded subdeacon.

730. “A basin.” In the cited Council of Carthage one reads, corruptly, “water and cloth.” The old glosses: “A basin, *chernibon*,” that is, a vessel suitable for washing the hands.

[Col. 0483A] 731. “A towel.” It is a cloth suitable for wiping the hands. In Greek, *cheiromaktron*, as is clear from Julius Pollux, Book VI, chapter 14. This is also evident from Athenaeus, Book IX:

> A *cheiromaktron* is what they used to wipe their hands with, a linen cloth placed upon the shoulders.

Moschopulus, in the *Scholia*, and Hesychius mention *cheiromaktron*, “a towel.” The author of the old etymological lexicon and Suidas say: “*Cheiromaktron*, what among the Romans is called *mandylion*.” But when they say that it is called *mandylion* by the Romans, this must be understood of the Romans of the New Rome, that is, the inhabitants of Constantinople. For among them *mandylion* means a cloth, as is clear from Codinus, in the *Book of Offices*:

> The cupbearer immediately brings the little bowl of the wine vessel, also holding a cloth.

Either these Greek grammarians were mistaken, or everywhere in the cited passages *mantelion* should be read, that is, “cloth.”

732. “See whose ministry is entrusted to you,” etc. Thus [Col. 0483B] in our manuscript copies, but in the Ratoldus manuscript these words are expressed in the plural, as in the Roman Ordinal, where they are nevertheless given more briefly. The Roman Pontifical shortened the entire formula as follows:

> See whose ministry is entrusted to you; therefore I admonish you to conduct yourselves in such a way that you may be able to please God.

The rest has been transferred to the admonition which the pontiff later gives to the subdeacons. The Council of Carthage omitted all these words for the sake of brevity.

733. “The cloths that are on the underlay.” He distinguishes these cloths from the corporal cloths commonly called the corporal. Those cloths, therefore, are what we call the altar cloths, or what the ancients called *mantilia*; elsewhere they are called altar cloths, as we explained in the *Concordance of Rules*. An underlay is something placed beneath another object, such as the coarser fabrics now placed beneath the altar cloths on the altar.

734. “On another corporal cloth.” Thus in the Council of Meaux, in Burchard, Book IV, chapter 13:

> Likewise, there should be proper vessels for washing the corporal and for the altar cloths, in which nothing else is to be done.

And in the Council of Rheims, in the same author, Book III, chapter 48:

> Or when the corporal is washed by a priest, deacon, or subdeacon, it should first be washed in the church, in a place and vessel prepared for this purpose, because it has been stained by the body and blood of the Lord.

735. “Let us pray to God and the Lord,” etc. Thus in the Rodradi and Rhemish manuscripts. But in the Ratoldus manuscript and in the Roman Ordinal and Pontifical, these words are expressed in the plural.

736. “Holy Lord, almighty Father,” etc. Thus in the Rodradi and Rhemish manuscripts. But in the Roman Ordinal and Pontifical, these words are expressed in the plural, as also in the Ratoldus manuscript, where they appear as follows:

> With the Spirit of wisdom and understanding. Amen.  
> With the Spirit of counsel and fortitude. Amen.  
> With the Spirit of knowledge and piety. Amen.

In the Roman Ordinal the following comes next:

> And the bishop shall give them the small cloths, saying while they are being vested with these cloths: “We earnestly beseech you, Lord,” etc.

In the manuscript Ordinal of Saint-Germain there is a handing over of the small cloth in this form:

> Here the bishop gives them the small cloth, saying: “Receive the small cloth; fulfill your ministry. For God is powerful enough to increase his grace in you.”

The small cloth is nothing other than the maniple which the bishop places on the left arm of each subdeacon, saying: “Receive the maniple, by which the fruits of good works are signified,” as is seen in the Roman Pontifical. Formerly the small cloth was carried for wiping mucus from the eyes and nose, as Alcuin teaches in his *Book on Ecclesiastical Offices*, in the chapter on vestments.

In the same Roman Pontifical, after receiving the maniple, the subdeacons are vested in the tunic by the pontiff with the following formula: “The robe of joy,” etc. Then he takes and gives each of them the book of the Epistles; they touch it simultaneously with their right hand, and he says: “Receive the book of the Epistles,” etc.

This handing over of the book of the Epistles is absent from the Fourth Council of Carthage cited above; from the manuscript Ordinal of Saint-Germain-des-Prés; from the manuscript Pontifical kept in the sacristy of the church of Rouen, which is thought to be English; from the Roman Ordinal; from the printed Sacramentaries; from our manuscript copies; from the Tilian manuscript; from Saint Isidore; from Rabanus, Book I, chapter 8, *On the Instruction of Clerics*; and from Amalarius Fortunatus, Book I of *Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 11. From Amalarius’ words it is clear that formerly the book of the Epistles was not customarily handed to the subdeacon at his promotion:

> I wonder, he says, for what reason the practice has been introduced into our Church that the subdeacon frequently reads the lesson at Mass, since I have not found this entrusted to him among the ministry given to him at his consecration, nor in the canonical writings, nor in his name, “subdeacon,” as has been shown, because he is placed beneath the deacon, etc.

It is also absent from the Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 26, in the restoration of a degraded subdeacon.

737. “The order of how it is done in the Roman Church,” etc. Thus in the printed editions and in the Ratoldus manuscript. But in the Rhemish manuscript “of the subdeacon” is added [Col. 0484B], because in that manuscript these words are placed before the ordination of the subdeacon.

738. “Of the title of this person and that person.” Thus in the printed editions and in the Rhemish manuscript. But in the Ratoldus manuscript, in place of these words, the following appears:

> “That man as subdeacon, or deacon.”

Then he names those of the title of Saint Mary, or of Saint Peter and the others. But nothing of this kind is found in the Roman Ordinal or in the Tilian manuscript. In the Roman Pontifical this custom is antiquated.

These words seem to be understood specifically of the titles that exist in Rome, to which cardinal deacons or priests are ordained. They are so called because they are, as it were, incardinated and fixed in their titles or churches—that is, established there.

There was also formerly a custom that no cleric was ordained except to a particular church, shrine, or monastery of some city or district, as is established by canon 6 of the Council of Chalcedon. If this were observed today, when the world is full of wandering priests, to what glory and dignity the ecclesiastical order would rise cannot be expressed.

739. “A priest of the title of this person.” Thus in the printed editions. In the Ratoldus and Rhemish manuscripts these words are absent, and, as I think, more correctly. For here the question concerns only the promotion of a subdeacon to the diaconate and of a deacon to the presbyterate.

740. “If anyone has anything,” etc. Formerly the morals, character, and ability of those to be ordained were carefully investigated, as is clear from the edict of Theophilus, to be cited shortly; from Saint Leo, letter 88:

> The wishes of the citizens should certainly be awaited, the testimony of the people sought, the judgment of honorable men requested, and the choice of the clergy preserved—things which, in the ordinations of priests, those who know how to observe the rules of the Fathers customarily maintain, so that the norm of apostolic authority might be observed in all things. That norm commands that one who is to preside over the Church be supported not only by the testimony of the faithful but also by that of those who are outside.

From the Third Council of Carthage, canon 22:

> Let no one be ordained a cleric unless he has been approved either by the examination of the bishop or by the testimony of the people.

From Saint Cyprian, letter 33:

> In the ordinations of clerics, dearest brothers, we customarily consult you beforehand and, in common deliberation, weigh the conduct and merits of each individual.

The same is found in letter 68 and in Saint Basil’s letter 181, where this subject is treated more fully.

The same may be seen in Lampridius’ account of Alexander Severus:

> Whenever he wished to appoint some men as governors of provinces, prefects, or procurators—that is, financial administrators—he published their names, urging the people that if anyone knew of any crime against them, he should prove it by clear evidence; if he failed to prove it, he would undergo the penalty of death. He also said that it was a serious matter that Christians and Jews did this when proclaiming priests who were to be ordained, but that it was not done in the case of provincial governors, to whom both the fortunes and the lives of human beings would be entrusted.

For this reason clerics are also to be ordained publicly, so that the bishop may openly inquire of the people concerning them, as seems to be prescribed in our manuscript copies, in accordance with the ancient custom. This may be observed in the edict of Theophilus, patriarch of Alexandria, canon 6:

> Concerning those who are to be ordained, the following procedure shall be observed: let the entire priestly order consent and choose; then let the bishop examine, or, with the priestly order also consenting, let him ordain in the midst of the church, with the people present and the bishop addressing them, asking whether the people can bear witness on his behalf. Ordination, however, must not take place secretly.

741. “All begin the Kyrie eleison with the litany.” In the Rhemish manuscript and in the Roman Ordinal nothing of this kind appears. This litany was formerly rather brief; I shall set it out here from the Ratoldus manuscript.

> Lord, have mercy. Lord, have mercy. Christ, hear us.  
> Holy Mary, pray for us. Holy Michael, pray. Holy Gabriel, pray. Holy Raphael, pray. All holy angels, pray.  
> Holy John, pray. Holy Peter, pray. Holy Paul, pray. Holy Andrew, pray. All holy apostles, pray.  
> Holy Stephen, pray. Holy Linus, pray. Holy Cletus, pray. All holy martyrs, pray.  
> Holy Sylvester, pray. Holy Leo, pray. Holy Ambrose, pray. Holy Augustine, pray. All holy confessors, pray.  
> Saint Felicitas, pray. Saint Agnes, pray. Saint Agatha, pray. All holy virgins, pray. All saints, pray.  
> Be favorable, deliver us, O Lord.  
> Through your coming, deliver us, O Lord.  
> Through your nativity, deliver us, O Lord.  
> Through your circumcision, deliver us, O Lord.  
> Through your baptism, deliver us, O Lord.  
> Through your fasting, deliver us.  
> Through your cross, deliver us.  
> We beseech you for sinners.  
> We beseech you for our apostolic [lord].  
> We beseech you for our king.  
> We beseech you for our bishop.  
> Son of God, we beseech you. [Three times.]  
> Lamb of God, who take away. [Three times.]  
> Christ, hear us. [Three times.]

Note that the foregoing litany, which we have published, is of an older form than the present one; wherever “us” is missing, it should be supplied.

742. “Let the bishop alone, who blesses him, place his hands upon his head.” Thus in the printed editions, in the Rodradi and Ratoldus manuscripts, and in the Fourth Council of Carthage, canon 4.

[Col. 0485D] Amalarius nevertheless disapproves of this rite, Book II of *Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 12. He wants the deacon to receive the imposition of hands not only from the bishop but also from the other priests:

> There is, he says, among us a certain little book on the sacred orders, of unknown authority, which says that only the bishop ought to impose hands upon the deacon, because he is consecrated not to the priesthood but to the ministry. Was the writer of the book more learned and holier than the apostles, who placed several hands upon the deacons when they were consecrated?

This is surprising, because the Fourth Council of Carthage, the Roman Ordinal—not to mention the Pontifical—and the books of the Sacraments, both printed and manuscript, agree with that very little book. Nor is Amalarius’ reasoning compelling, since when this first ordination was performed by the apostles assembled together, it was fitting that all should impose hands, although this was by no means necessary, since one alone would have sufficed.

The great Dionysius also supports this common teaching, chapter 5 of *The Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*:

> The minister, bending one knee before the divine altar, has upon his head the right hand of the hierarch who consecrates him, and is perfected by him through the consummating invocations used for ministers.

That is:

> The deacon, with one knee bent before the altar, has upon his head the right hand of the pontiff who consecrates him, and is consecrated by him through the prayers ordinarily used for the consecration of deacons.

[Note: [Col. 0485D] The manuscript copies vary concerning this rite. Some prescribe that only the bishop impose hands upon the deacon being ordained, as do the Gemetic manuscript and the most ancient Pontifical of Egbert, archbishop of York, written in Saxon letters before the year 900. Others command the priests standing by, after the bishop’s imposition of hands, to touch the head of the person being ordained, as do the manuscripts of Noyon and our Royal manuscript of Edmund. Consult Martène, *On the Ancient Rites of the Church*, chapter 8, “On the Rites Concerning the Sacrament of Orders.”]

The manuscript Pontifical kept in the secretarium of the church of Rouen, which appears to be English, seems to favor Amalarius’ opinion. It adds:

> But let the other priests touch his head beside the bishop’s hand, because he is consecrated not to the priesthood, etc.

743. “Let us pray, beloved,” etc. Thus in the printed editions, in the Ratoldus manuscript, and in the Roman Ordinal. In the Rhemish manuscript, as in the Roman Pontifical, this prayer is somewhat longer. In both the Ordinal and the Roman Pontifical it is preceded by the following address of the pontiff:

> Our common prayer, etc.

In the Rhemish manuscript this appears after the consecration “Be present, we beseech you, almighty God,” etc., and it bears the title “For completing the office of the diaconate.” In the Ratoldus manuscript it occurs at the end of the ordination under the same title.

744. “Hear, O Lord, our prayers,” etc. Thus in the printed editions, in the Roman Ordinal, and in the Rodradi and Ratoldus manuscripts; it is also found in the Roman Pontifical.

499 745. “Be present, we beseech you, almighty God,” etc. In the printed editions the words “It is truly fitting,” etc., are prefixed, as in the Roman Pontifical. They are absent from our other manuscript copies and from the Roman Ordinal. Hence above, in this manuscript of Saint Eligius, it is written: “And ‘It is truly fitting’ is not said in the consecration.”

746. “Honors.” Thus in all our other manuscript copies [Col. 0486C] and in the Roman Pontifical. But in the printed editions, in the Tilian manuscript, and in the Roman Ordinal one reads “goods,” less correctly. For the word “honor” is used of the three higher orders: the diaconate, presbyterate, and episcopate.

Ennodius, in the *Eucharisticus*:

> You ordained that, compelled through the office of the Levites, I should be healed, and that the burden of the honor imposed upon me should remove the weight that pressed upon me.

And in the *Life of Saint Epiphanius of Pavia*:

> Afterward, raised to the insignia of the diaconate, he reached his twentieth year of age, and was troubled by the novitiate of the honor he had received.

Saint Cyprian, letter 34:

> Moreover, you should know that we designated for them the honor of the presbyterate.

Letter 65:

> You exercise toward him the power of your honor, so that you may either depose him or refrain from doing so.

And letter 68:

> To be prevented from ordination to the clergy and from sacerdotal honor.

Optatus of Milevis, Book II against Parmenianus:

> The priests were stripped of the honor of their name.

And below, speaking of the Donatists who had expelled Catholic deacons, priests, and bishops and compelled them to do penance:

> Although you could have been children of God, you chose to be children of human beings, and, to sink your teeth into the honors of others, you sharpened your tongues into swords. You fulfilled in yourselves what is written in Psalm 56: “The sons of men, their teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword.” Therefore you sharpened your tongues into swords, and used them to bring about the death not of bodies but of honors. You slaughtered not limbs but names. What does it profit that the men are alive and their honors have been killed by you? They are strong in their limbs, but they carry away the funerals of their dignity.

And below:

> You hunger for the honors of innocent priests.

And shortly afterward:

> The funerals of honors are not enough for your throats.

Saint Augustine, Book II against the Letter of Parmenianus, chapter 11:

> And although it does not seem expedient for the Church that their leaders, when they come into Catholic communion, should not exercise their honors there, nevertheless the sacraments of ordination themselves are not taken away from them but remain upon them.

The Fourth Council of Arles, canon 1:

> Let no layman receive the honor of the episcopate or presbyterate before the aforesaid conversion or before the age of thirty.

And canon 2:

> Nor should the other pontiffs presume to confer the honor of the presbyterate or diaconate, etc.

Among the Greeks also, the word *timē* means “honor” in reference to these three orders. The Council of Nicaea, canon 8:

> The one called a bishop among those called Cathari shall have the honor of a presbyter.

That is: the one who is called a bishop among those known as Cathari shall possess the honor of a presbyter.

The Council of Ancyra, canon 2:

> Deacons who have likewise sacrificed, but afterward have resisted, shall have the other honor.

That is: deacons who have likewise sacrificed, but later have resisted, shall retain the other honor.

And canon 18:

> But if they stir up sedition against those bishops who have been established there, let the honor of the presbyterate be taken away from them.

That is: if they rebel against the bishops appointed there, let the honor of the presbyterate be removed from them.

Synesius, letter 67, speaking of bishops:

> They possess the honors,

that is, they enjoy honors, wandering about wherever there is greater profit.

And below:

> For they would return more quickly if they were at risk of losing their honor.

That is: they would return more quickly to their own places if they feared the loss of their honor.

Since the diaconate is an honor in the Church and above is called a sacred order, from this we can discern the dignity of this order, which consists chiefly in the fact that the deacon stands immediately beside the priest performing the sacred rites and is his assistant in the celebration of so great a mystery. According to Saint Ambrose, Book I of *On Duties*, chapter 41, the consecration of the Lord’s body and blood is entrusted to him.

This must be understood in the sense explained by Peter the Chanter, in the manuscript *On the Miraculous Word*, chapter 41:

> Consider, then, whether you have chosen a suitable minister to whom you have entrusted the consecration of the Lord’s body and blood—not for effecting it, but for assisting. As the secretary of the altar, he participates in the making of the Eucharist—not because he receives or effects it, nor because it could not be done without him, but because the body of the Lord is made more solemnly and with greater reverence in the presence and testimony of the minister.

From Peter’s text it is evident that the passage of Saint Ambrose [Note: [Col. 0487D] Consult the new edition of Ambrose’s works at this passage, which reads as follows: “To whom you have entrusted the consecration of the Lord’s blood.” Nevertheless, ten French manuscript copies and one Vatican copy support Peter the Chanter’s reading. [Col. 0488D] On the change of the word “consecration” to “dispensation,” see the note of the learned editors, by which this passage is very clearly elucidated.] is corrupt. For in the older and more recent editions of Ambrose the word “body” is absent, and in the more recent editions “consecration” has been changed to “dispensation.” In the older editions, printed at Basel in 1492, “consecration” is present, as also in the manuscript of the library of Corbie, in which “body” is absent.

747. “To grant what is to be done.” In the Roman Pontifical the following words are inserted:

> Here the pontiff alone, extending his right hand, places it upon the head of each person being ordained, and no one else, because he is consecrated not to the priesthood but to the ministry, saying to each: “Receive the Holy Spirit for strength and for resisting the devil and his temptations, in the name of the Lord.”

The earlier words, “Here the pontiff alone,” etc., or at least similar words, are not found at this place in the printed editions, nor in the Rhemish and Ratoldus manuscripts, nor in the Tilian manuscript, nor in the Roman Ordinal. Rather, they are placed before this prayer:

> “Let us pray, beloved, to almighty God the Father,” etc.

In the Rodradi manuscript they are found nowhere, because it contains no rubrics in the ordinations of a bishop, priest, or deacon. The later words, “saying to each, ‘Receive the Holy Spirit for strength,’” etc., are found nowhere in the printed editions, nor in our other manuscript copies—that is, the Rhemish, Rodradi, and [Col. 0488A] Ratoldus manuscripts—nor in the Roman Ordinal or the Tilian manuscript.

### 748. When you put on the stole: “By this sign [may] the office of the diaconate [be signified] to you,” etc.

These words are lacking in the Codex of Rodradus. In the Codex of Ratoldus the wording of the formula is expressed in the singular. In the Roman Ordo and Pontifical the stole is put on with a different formula.

In the same Roman Ordo the handing over of the Book of the Gospels follows in this form: “Receive the power to read the Gospel, etc.,” as in the Roman Pontifical and the Codex of Tilius.

But this presentation of the Book of the Gospels, together with its formula, is absent from the printed editions and from the Codices of Rheims, Rodradus, and Ratoldus. Nor is it found in the Fourth Council of Carthage, or in Saint Isidore, Amalarius, Alcuin, or Rabanus. Nor was it formerly found in the most ancient Ordinal of the Church of Le Puy (Anicium), which Durandus used in conferring orders, as he himself testifies in *Sentences* IV, distinction 24, question 3:

> But an argument can be made against this, because that in which the character is impressed ought to be observed; [Col. 0488B] and it is probable that it is observed in every Church. But the handing over of the book in the ordination of a deacon is not observed in every Church, and perhaps formerly was not observed in any Church. Thus, according to the most ancient Ordinal of the Church of Le Puy (Anicium), over which we presided, the Book of the Gospels was not handed to the deacon at his ordination. But, wishing to conform ourselves to the other Churches, we ourselves wrote in the margin of the said Ordinal that the Book of the Gospels should be handed over with the customary formula of words.

Therefore it does not seem that the character of the diaconate is impressed through the handing over of the book. Hence there is another opinion: that the character is impressed through the imposition of hands. This is understood to mean that he is assigned to the great ministry. Canon 23 of the *Decretum*, distinction 24, seems to agree with this, where it says that, when a deacon is ordained, only the bishop lays his hand upon him, because he is assigned to the ministry.

Therefore it seems to me that the response of those who say that the Church of Le Puy (Anicium) [Col. 0488C] erred in this matter is a weak one—a response that did not even occur to Durandus—since we see a manifest conformity between this ancient Ordinal of the aforesaid Church and the Sacramentary Codices, authors, and Fourth Council of Carthage cited above.

Nor is it an objection that, according to ancient custom, deacons read the Gospel, as appears from Saint Jerome’s letter to Sabinianus: “You used to read the Gospel of Christ as though you were a deacon.” For this was not always and everywhere the practice of the Church, as is clear from what we explained above concerning lectors on the authority of Saint Cyprian and the First Council of Toledo. This is confirmed by Sozomen, *Ecclesiastical History* VII, chapter 19:

> Ταύτην τὴν ἱερὰν βίβλον (εὐαγγέλιον) ἀναγινώσκει ἐνθάδε μόνος ὁ Ἀρχιδιάκονος, παρὰ δὲ ἄλλοις διάκονοι. Ἐν πολλαῖς δὲ ἐκκλησίαις οἱ ἱερεῖς μόνοι, ἐν δὲ ἐπισήμοις ἡμέραις Ἐπίσκοποι, ὡς ἐν Κωνσταντινουπόλει κατὰ τὴν πρώτην ἡμέραν τῆς ἀναστασίμου ἑορτῆς.

That is:

> “Here [at Alexandria] only the archdeacon reads this sacred book—the Gospel; elsewhere, deacons do so. In many Churches, the priests alone read it; on solemn days, however, bishops do so, as at Constantinople on the first Sunday of the feast of the Resurrection.”

[Col. 0488D] Nor should one say that these priests and bishops were also deacons. That is by no means certain, since formerly many bishops and priests were created with the diaconate omitted.

This doctrine is also supported by the fact that, when deacons were first instituted, the Gospels had not yet been written.

Finally, in the Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 27, when a degraded deacon is restored to his dignity, he receives only the stole and alb, with no mention of the Book of the Gospels. For the council says that he receives what he had previously received at his ordination. The canon reads as follows:

> If a bishop, priest, or deacon [Col. 0489A] has been unjustly removed from his rank and is found innocent at a second synod, he cannot be what he formerly was unless he receives back his lost rank before the altar from the hand of the bishops: if he is a bishop, the stole, ring, and staff; if a priest, the stole and chasuble; if a deacon, the stole and alb; if a subdeacon, the paten and chalice. In the same way, the remaining ranks are to receive, for their restoration, those things which they received when they were ordained.

The words “unless he receives back his lost rank” should not be understood as though such a person—whether bishop, priest, deacon, or subdeacon—had been entirely deprived of his rank. The loss of rank is understood only with respect to the ability to minister in that order and to clerical communion. Thus the person removed from office could no longer exercise the ministry of his order or communicate with clerics, but only with laypeople.

Accordingly, the restoration of these instruments is not a repeated ordination, but merely a certain external rite signifying that the person so removed may now exercise his ministry and communicate with clerics. [Col. 0489B] Otherwise the imposition of hands, which is essential to these orders—apart from the subdiaconate, which is not conferred through the imposition of hands—would have had to be repeated. Yet no such repetition appears here.

In the manuscript Pontifical cited above, believed to be English, the handing over of the Book of the Gospels occurs in this form:

> “Receive this volume of the Gospel; read and understand it, hand it on to others, and fulfill it in your conduct.”

Finally, after the stole has been put on, the Roman Ordo and the Codex of Rheims contain the following:

> “The blessing follows: ‘Lord of holy faith, hope, grace,’ etc.”

In the Codex of Ratoldus:

> “Blessing after the stoles, over all: ‘In the name of the holy Trinity and the one Godhead.’ Another: ‘Lord of holy faith, hope, grace,’ etc. To complete the office of the diaconate. May our common vow endure; may our common prayer continue,” etc.

In the English manuscript Pontifical cited above, after the handing over of the Book of the Gospels, the deacon’s hands are anointed. It reads:

> “Consecration of the deacon’s hands [Col. 0489C] with oil and chrism. May these hands, we ask, Lord, be consecrated and sanctified through this anointing of yours and your blessing, so that whatever they bless may be blessed, and whatever they sanctify may be sanctified. Through [abbreviated in the source as *Per.*].”

And indeed this practice had formerly become established in Gaul, whereby the hands of deacons were anointed. This is clear from Pope Nicholas I’s letter to Rodulfus, archbishop of Bourges (*Tome III of the Councils of Gaul*):

> “Moreover, you ask whether, when they are ordained, the hands of priests alone, or also those of deacons, ought to be anointed with the liquid of chrism.”

Rodulfus would not have asked the supreme pontiff this question unless he had learned that the practice existed somewhere in Gaul as part of the ordination of deacons.

### 749. When a priest is ordained, etc.

Thus it appears in the printed editions and in our manuscripts: the Codex of Rheims, the Codex of Ratoldus, the Codex of Tilius, and that of Saint-Germain-des-Prés.

In the Roman Ordo, the Fourth Council of Carthage, canon 3, and the manuscript Pontifical believed to be English, instead of the words “let them hold [their hands] over his head,” we read: “[Col. 0489D] let them place [their hands] over his head.”

In the Roman Pontifical all these matters are presented differently, as follows:

> “The bishop, standing before the faldstool and wearing the mitre, without any prayer or chant having been said beforehand, successively places both hands upon the head of each person being ordained, saying nothing; and after him all the priests who are present do the same.”

### 750. Let us pray, dearly beloved, etc.

Thus it appears in the printed editions and in the Codex of Rodradus and the Codex of Ratoldus. It likewise appears in the Codex of Rheims and in the Roman Ordo, in which an address to the people is placed beforehand in this form:

> “Since, dearly beloved brothers,” etc.

In the Roman Pontifical this prayer is expressed in the plural number.

### 751. Hear us, we beseech you, Lord our God, etc.

Thus in the printed editions, in the Codices of Rheims, Rodradus, and Ratoldus, and also in the Roman Ordo and Pontifical. In these, the words “Let us bend our knees; arise” are placed beforehand.

### 752. Consecration

Thus in the printed editions and in the Codex of Rodradus. [Col. 0490A] In the Codices of Rheims and Ratoldus, the word *presbyteri*, “of the priest,” is added. These two words, *Consecratio presbyteri* (“Consecration of the priest”), are lacking in the Roman Pontifical. In the Roman Ordo we read: “the consecration of the same persons.”

### 753. Holy Lord, almighty Father, etc.

In the Codex of Ratoldus the following precedes:

> “The Lord be with you,” etc.  
> “Lift up your hearts,” etc.

In the Roman Pontifical, the words “World without end” precede this.

In the Codex of Rheims the following comes after this prayer:

> “May the completion of the priesthood be for us, brothers, a common prayer.”

Also:

> “Blessing: ‘God, author of sanctifications.’”

These words do not appear in the printed editions or in the Codex of Rodradus. They are indeed found in the Codex of Ratoldus, but after the anointing of the hands and head; and likewise in the Roman Ordo, but after the chasuble has been put on.

In the Pontifical, however, the words “May the completion of the priesthood be for us, brothers, a common prayer,” etc., are absent. But after the chasuble has been put on, the following is said:

> “God, author of sanctifications.”

### 754. Of honors

In the printed editions and in the Roman Ordo we read **bonorum**, “of good things,” which is not correct. See the remarks above.

[Col. 0490B] ### 755. The supreme pontiffs

That is, the bishops. For bishops were called by this name. Fortunatus, book XI, epigram 13:

> “We pray that you commend us to the supreme pontiff;  
> Bring gifts of salvation to kings and lords.”

There he means Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris. Consult our observations on the *Martyrology of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, and Jean Savaron’s notes on book IX, letter 11, of Sidonius.

In the Codex of Ratoldus, the following is added after this prayer:

> “Now let him turn the stole around his neck and put on the chasuble. Through these garments, the stole and chasuble, may you deserve to be clothed with salvation, and, with Christ ministering, may you be able to attain, together with the holy priests and with Christ ministering, the fullness of eternal perpetuity.”

The same rite appears in the Roman Ordo and Pontifical, but with a different formula:

> “Receive the yoke of the Lord,” etc.

The same rite is also found in the Greek *Euchologion* in the ordination of a priest:

> Καὶ φέρει τὸ ὄπισθεν ὀραρίου αὐτοῦ ἐπὶ τὸ ἔμπροσθεν τοῦ δεξιοῦ μέρους

That is:

> “And he brings the rear part of his orarion to the front on the right side.”

This is how the passage in the Third Council of Braga, canon 3, should be understood:

> “Namely, when a priest approaches the solemn celebration of the Mass, whether he is about to offer the sacrifice to God himself or to receive the sacrament of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, he must approach wearing the orarion around both shoulders, just as he is known to have been consecrated at the time of his ordination. Thus, pressing one and the same orarion upon his neck and both shoulders alike, he should set the sign of the cross upon his breast [elsewhere: ‘bear it before him’]. But if anyone acts otherwise, he is to be subject to excommunication.”

The **orarion** is what we commonly call the stole. On this, see Jean Meursius in his *Greek-Barbarian Lexicon*, and Isaac Casaubon in his notes on Flavius Vopiscus’s *Life of Aurelian*.

That the orarion, or stole, was given to priests at their ordination is also clear from the Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 27. In Greek it is called **ἐπιτραχήλιον** (*epitrachēlion*), as is clear from the mystical *Theory* of Saint Germanus, patriarch of Constantinople, because it is arranged around the neck.

### 756. Here you also clothe him in the chasuble. The blessing of the Father, and of the Son, etc.

Thus in the printed editions and in the Codex of Rheims. In the Roman Ordo and Pontifical we find:

> “Receive the priestly garment,” etc.

In the Codex of Ratoldus:

> “Blessing after the chasubles, over all. May the blessing of God the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, descend upon you; and, clothed and protected with these priestly garments, may you be able to remain defended and fortified against all assaults of evil spirits. May you be blessed in the name of our Lord and in the power of the Holy Spirit in the priestly order, and may you offer pleasing sacrifices for the sins and offenses of the people to almighty God, to whom are honor and glory.”

In the Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 27, the priest receives the **planeta** at his ordination; this is the same as the chasuble.

[Col. 0491A] ### 757. May these hands be consecrated, etc.

Thus in the printed editions and in the Codex of Rheims. In the Codex of Ratoldus we read:

> “May these hands, we beseech you, Lord, be consecrated with holy oil and holy chrism,” etc.

In the Codex of Tilius, the Roman Ordo, and the Roman Pontifical, the wording is:

> “Deign to consecrate and sanctify these hands, Lord.”

This anointing of the hands is absent from the Codex of Rodradus.

Concerning the anointing of a priest’s hands at his ordination, one may find the following in Burchard, book II, chapter 55, drawn from the words of Saint Augustine addressed to priests:

> “Therefore you ought always to remember such great dignity; remember your consecration; remember the sacred anointing which you received upon your hands, so that you may not degenerate from it and pollute, by sinning, hands smeared with sacred ointment.”

Amalarius says in book I of *On the Offices of the Church*, chapter 13:

> “Our bishops observe this custom: they anoint the hands of priests with oil.”

The practice is mentioned in Pope Nicholas I’s letter to Rodulfus, archbishop of Bourges. In that letter he says that it is not customary in the Roman Church and doubts whether it ever existed anywhere. This surprises me in view of the authorities cited above and of certain of our manuscript Codices, which follow Roman usage and are older than Pope Nicholas—especially since he refers Rodulfus to the letter of Innocent I written to Decentius of Gubbio. In that letter, concerning this matter and concerning ordinations, there is not even a γρῦ—“a single word”—although Nicholas nevertheless mentions it.

This anointing of the hands was performed in the form of a cross, as is clear from the Roman Ordo:

> “When the prayer has been completed, taking the holy oil, let him make a cross over both hands,” etc.

This anointing is performed differently in the Roman Pontifical.

In the Codex of Ratoldus, anointing of the head is added under the following heading and formula:

> **LET THE HEAD BE ANOINTED.**  
> “May your head be anointed and consecrated with heavenly blessing in the priestly order, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen. Peace be with you.”

The same may be seen in the manuscript Pontifical preserved in the treasury of the church of Rouen, which is believed to be English:

> **CONSECRATION OF THE HEAD WITH OIL.**  
> “May your head be anointed and consecrated with heavenly blessing in the priestly order, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen. Peace be with you.”  
> **R.** “And with your spirit.”

This anointing of the head, together with its formula, is absent from the printed editions, from our other manuscript Codices, and from the Roman Ordo and Pontifical.

The Codex of Ratoldus continues:

> **ALSO, HE BLESSES THE HANDS OF THE PRIESTS.**  
> “Bless, Lord, these hands, and sanctify the priest N. for consecrating the Hosts that are offered for the sins and negligences of the people, and for blessing the other things that are necessary for the people’s use. And grant, we beseech you, that whatever they bless may be blessed, and whatever they consecrate may be consecrated, O Savior.”

Finally, in the Roman Pontifical there follows the handing over of the paten with the Host placed upon it, and of the chalice with wine and water, in this form:

> “Receive the power to offer sacrifice to God, both for the living and for the dead, in the name of the Lord.”

In the manuscript Ordines of Saint-Germain-des-Prés and of Tilius, and in the Roman Ordo, the handing over of these instruments occurs with its formula, but it is expressed there in the plural:

> “Receive the power,” etc.

Nor is any mention of water made in those books.

But this handing over, together with its formula, is absent from the printed Sacramentaries and from the manuscript Codices of Rheims, Rodradus, Saint Eligius, and Ratoldus, as well as from the manuscript Pontifical believed to be English.

It is also absent from the oft-cited Fourth Council of Carthage, from the Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 27, and from every ancient Father who might have mentioned it. Saint Isidore does not mention it; nor Amalarius; nor Rabanus; nor the *Apostolic Constitutions*, book VIII, chapters 16 and following; nor Dionysius the Great, most ancient of all, who treated the sacred orders deliberately and expressly. Nor will one find anything similar in Sacred Scripture.

When Christ instituted the apostles as priests at that supreme Supper, he did not hand over instruments of this kind to them. Nor did he then give them bread and wine; rather, he gave them his body and blood under the appearances of bread and wine.

The Eastern, or Greek, Church agrees with this. It does not use the handing over of such instruments in the ordination of priests, as is evident from their *Euchologion*, which we shall produce below. Yet the Roman Church has never disapproved their ordinations; indeed, it permits Greek priests among us to celebrate Mass while we attend, just as in their own region we attend Mass celebrated by them. This would be intolerable idolatry if they were not truly ordained.

Nor was there ever any doubt concerning their ordinations at the Council of Florence, where the Greeks were reconciled with the Roman Church. Nor, in the union with the Armenians, did Eugenius IV, when he handed the Armenians the rite of the Roman Church to be observed in ordinations, invalidate their former ordinations. Nor did Clement VIII, when he received the Russian bishops, priests, and deacons into communion with the Roman Church—although they followed the Greek rite even in their ordinations—judge that they had to be ordained again.

Therefore it must be said that the essential matter of the diaconate, priesthood, and episcopate consists in the imposition of hands.

[Col. 0492B] Nothing else is expressed by the passage in Acts 6 concerning the ordination of the seven deacons:

> “After praying, they laid their hands upon them.”

And in 1 Timothy 4:

> “Do not neglect the grace that is in you, which was given you through prophecy with the laying on of the hands of the presbyterate.”

And in chapter 5:

> “Do not lay hands upon anyone hastily.”

And in 2 Timothy 1:

> “For this reason I remind you to stir up the grace of God that is in you through the laying on of my hands.”

This is confirmed by the authority of Dionysius the Great, chapter 5 of *The Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*. Treating expressly of the three orders mentioned above, he requires nothing for their matter apart from the imposition of hands.

This is also clear from Saint Jerome, chapter 58 of Isaiah:

> “Ordination is completed not only by the invocation of the voice but also by the imposition of hands.”

And from Saint Ambrose, *On the Dignity of the Priesthood*, chapter 5:

> “A human being lays on the hand; God bestows grace. The priest lays on his supplicating right hand; God blesses with his powerful right hand.”

And from the Second Council of Seville, canon 5:

> “At the fifth judicial inquiry, for the recognition of our examination, it was reported by Agabius the deacon that certain clerics of that Church had been involved. While one was being consecrated to the priesthood [Col. 0492C] and two to the ministry of the Levites, their bishop, who was suffering from pain in his eyes, is said merely to have laid his hand upon them, while a certain priest gave them the blessing contrary to ecclesiastical order.”

The council declares these ordinations invalid because the blessing had been pronounced by a priest.

The same is evident from Synesius, letter 66:

> Ὑπὸ τῶν ἐκείνου χειρῶν ἐπίσκοπος ἀνεδείχθη τῆς Βιθυνῶν Βασινοπόλεως

That is:

> “By his hands he was consecrated bishop of Basinopolis in Bithynia.”

And letter 76:

> Καὶ ὧν τῇ θατέρου χειρὶ πρεσβύτερος ἀπεδέδεκτο

That is:

> “And by the hand of the other he had been consecrated a priest.”

I pass over many other authorities for the sake of brevity. Yet I shall not be excessively long if I produce the authority of a more recent writer, a man of great gravity and learning, Marianus Victorius, bishop of Amelia. In his note on the letter of Saint Epiphanius, which is found among the letters of Saint Jerome, volume II, he says:

> “Ordination was performed with prayer and the imposition of hands, [Col. 0492D] just as the Church now practices,” etc.

Here, then, you see that ordination is completed through the imposition of hands, and that through the same act the grace of the Holy Spirit is conferred. It follows that the imposition of hands is not accidental to ordination, nor merely a disposition toward grace, as some maintain.

Moreover, it is not credible that councils and Fathers spoke only about matters incidental to ordination, while remaining silent about what is essential to it—especially the Fourth Council of Carthage, which describes with particular clarity everything that concerns the matter of the orders.

Nor is the answer of some valid: that the council did not set out everything because it was not writing a Pontifical. Even if the council was not writing a Pontifical, it would not have been difficult or burdensome to note the handing over of the instruments in explaining the three hierarchical orders. [Col. 0493A] This could have been done in one or two lines, just as it had been done in the lower orders.

Moreover, the Sacramentary books produced by us were Pontificals, which the bishops used in conferring orders; therefore all the essential matters are assigned in them. Yet they contain nothing beyond what is contained in the Fourth Council of Carthage. Consequently, all the essential matters of the orders are contained in that council itself.

Since the council agrees remarkably in this respect with Sacred Scripture, other ancient councils, the Fathers, and the Sacramentary books, one must necessarily conclude that, in assigning the essential matter of those three orders, it omitted nothing.

Further, if the council assigned the essential matters of the lower orders with such care, why did it not do the same for the other orders, which are of greater weight and importance? If you say that the matters were omitted because they were common and well known, the same must also be said of the matters of the lower orders, which are equally common and well known.

Finally, this doctrine is manifestly gathered from the same council, canon 5, where, speaking of the ordination of a subdeacon, it says:

> [Col. 0493B] “When a subdeacon is ordained, because he does not receive the imposition of hands, let him receive from the hand of the bishop an empty paten and an empty chalice,” etc.

If instruments are handed to the subdeacon because hands are not laid upon him, it rightly follows that the handing over of instruments is not necessary for those three higher orders, because hands are laid upon them. Consequently, the council omitted nothing concerning the matter essential to them.

Thus, just as the lower orders can be completed by the mere presentation of instruments without the imposition of hands, so those three higher orders can be completed by the mere imposition of hands without the handing over of instruments. The reasoning is parallel in both cases, by way of contraries.

To this may be added the authority of the Faculty of Theology of Paris, easily foremost among the others. This doctrine is commonly defended in its public theses, as in a thesis of 7 June 1633, produced by [Col. 0493C] the most reverend and learned Father Jacques Sirmond in chapter 8 of his *Antirrhetic*, entitled:

> “In those orders in which there is an imposition of hands, that alone is sufficient for the validity and firmness of the sacrament.”

In the theses of Jacques de Montrouge, a Parisian bachelor of the Navarre College, canon of the Church of Angers and ordinary almoner of the queen, dated 19 January 1639, presented for the ordinary major disputation in the schools of the theologians of the royal College of Navarre, under the presidency of S. M. N. Albert de Saint-Gilles, doctor of Paris and professor of theology among the Carmelites, and dedicated to the illustrious Augustin Potier, bishop of Beauvais and grand almoner of the queen, the eighth proposition reads:

> “In the ordination of ministers there is found a sign or external rite, namely the imposition of hands, which in bishops, priests, and deacons is designated as essential; the remaining elements concern only the integrity of the matter.”

In the theses of René Robeville, bachelor of theology and rector of the University, on 21 June of the same year, in the external schools of the Sorbonne, under the presidency of S. M. N. Jacques Charton, doctor of theology and fellow of the Sorbonne, canon and penitentiary priest of the Church of Paris, and dedicated to the illustrious Pierre Séguier, chancellor of France, the eighth proposition states:

> “The imposition of hands is the essential matter; the presentation of books or vessels is accessory.”

In the theses of Jean Helyes of Bayeux, a bachelor of the Navarre College, for the ordinary major disputation in the hall of the royal College of Navarre on 13 October of the same year, under the presidency of S. M. N. Jean Nicolai, professor of theology among the Dominicans, and dedicated to the illustrious Henri-Louis Habert de Montmort, marquis, count, etc., the final proposition says:

> “In bishops, priests, and deacons, the presentation of instruments is the integrating matter; the imposition of hands is the essential matter.”

In the theses of Michel de Beauharnois of Orléans, a bachelor of the Sorbonne, on 10 December 1639, for the ordinary minor disputation in the external schools of the Sorbonne, under the presidency of S. M. N. Jacques Pereyret, doctor of theology and professor at the Navarre College, and dedicated to the blessed memory of Robert de Sorbon, the fifth proposition contains the following:

> “The entire Christian people is so much a holy nation and a royal priesthood that nevertheless not every believer has the power to offer sacrifice; only the person consecrated by a divine vocation as a priest through the episcopal imposition of hands has that power. I judge this imposition of hands to be the essential matter of the hierarchical orders.”

In the theses of Antoine Arnaud of Paris, bachelor of the Sorbonne, canon of the Church of Verdun, for the ordinary major disputation on 13 January 1640 in the Sorbonne schools, under the presidency of S. M. N. Julien Joubert, professor of theology among the Dominicans of Paris, and dedicated to the true Israel who feeds on the true bread from heaven, the third proposition reads:

> “The imposition of hands appears to be essential matter for the diaconate and the other higher orders.”

I could produce many other theses of this kind, but, lest I become tedious, I shall stop here.

Nor should anyone object to us with the Bull of Eugenius IV, in which the matter of the diaconate and priesthood appears to be placed in the handing over of instruments. It should be explained as concerning accessory matter, or integrating matter, as others prefer.

Some say that the matters had been expanded. But if the pontiff makes no mention of the imposition of hands, this was because it was already in use among the Armenians, to whom he wished to transmit a distinctive rite of the Roman Church.

For more on this, see Peter Arcudius, book VI, *On the Sacrament of Orders*, whose work was approved at Rome by the authority of Pope Paul V.

These points having been established, we must ask what the hand, or the imposition of hands, is, since this is the matter under dispute.

The imposition of hands is the placing of a hand upon someone’s head. This is evident from Saint Dionysius, chapter 5 of *The Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*:

> Ἐπὶ κεφαλῆς ἔχει τὰ θεοπαράδοτα λόγια καὶ τὴν ἱεραρχικὴν χεῖρα

That is:

> “Upon his head he has the divinely transmitted oracles”—that is, the Gospel—[Col. 0494C] “and the hand of the bishop.”

A little later, concerning the ordination of a priest:

> Sacerdos, flexis genibus ante divinum altare, ἐπὶ κεφαλῆς ἔχει τὴν ἱεραρχικὴν δεξιὰν

That is:

> “The priest, kneeling before the divine altar, has the bishop’s right hand upon his head.”

Likewise, concerning the ordination of a deacon, he writes:

> Minister uno poplite flexo ante divinum altare, ἐπὶ κεφαλῆς ἔσχε τὴν τοῦ τελοῦντος αὐτὸν ἱεράρχου δεξιὰν

That is:

> “The minister, kneeling on one knee before the divine altar, has the right hand of the bishop who initiates him upon his head.”

The *Apostolic Constitutions*, book VIII, chapters 16 and following, agree with this, where it says:

> τὴν χεῖρα ἐπὶ τῆς κεφαλῆς ἐπιτίθει αὐτὸς

That is:

> “Let him himself place his hand upon the head.”

The same is clear from canon 3 of the Fourth Council of Carthage, concerning the ordination of a priest:

> “The bishop blessing him and holding his hand over his head.”

And canon 4:

> “Let the bishop alone who blesses him place his hand upon his head.”

The same is evident from the printed Sacramentaries and from the manuscripts of Saint Eligius, Ratoldus, and Rheims, from the manuscript Ordines of Tilius and Saint-Germain-des-Prés, and from the Roman Ordo and Pontifical. In all of these, there is no imposition of hands unless the hand is placed upon the head.

This is also clear from the words of Metaphrastes, when he is discussing the creation of Saint John Chrysostom as a priest:

> “When they had approached the sacred altar, he, as the law requires, ὕπεσχε τῷ ἱεράρχῃ τὴν κεφαλήν, τούτου δὲ χεῖρες ἐπετίθεντο.”

That is:

> “He submitted his head to the bishop, and the bishop’s hands were laid upon him.”

This is supported by the Syriac version of Acts 6, in which we read, “They placed their hands upon them,” whereas in the Vulgate, according to the Greek text, we read, “They laid their hands upon them” (*On the Sacrament of Orders*, book VI, chapter 7).

Since this is so, Peter Arcudius must be refuted when he writes that the actual presentation of the instruments is the imposition of hands, because the bishop, by the very fact that he hands over the instruments, lays on his hand. He says that the character is impressed not so much on account of the instruments as on account of the action and presentation performed by the bishop himself, which he calls the imposition of hands.

If this were true, it would have to be said that baptism is conferred through the imposition of hands. For the person who baptizes, whether by immersion or by pouring water, would, according to Arcudius’s understanding, necessarily lay on his hand.

The same would also have to be admitted concerning extreme unction, since the person who anoints the body lays on his hand, although no one has hitherto written that these two sacraments are conferred through the imposition of hands.

Nor is the objection concerning confirmation valid. For this sacrament has an imposition of hands distinct from the anointing, as was said above.

Moreover, from this explanation of the imposition of hands it follows very clearly that the lower orders consist in the imposition of hands. For when the bishop hands the chalice and paten to the subdeacon, the book to the exorcist and lector, and the keys to the doorkeeper, he lays his hands upon them just as he does upon the priest when he offers him the instruments to be touched. Yet this is plainly contrary to the truth, beyond dispute.

It conflicts with the Fourth Council of Carthage, the Roman Ordo and Pontifical, and the ancient Sacramentary books, in which a clear distinction appears between [Col. 0495B] the handing over of instruments and the imposition of hands: the former belongs to the lower orders, the latter to the higher orders.

Indeed, such a doctrine conflicts with ordinary understanding and common usage. It would follow that someone who hands an apple to a child or bread to a poor person lays his hand upon them—something unheard of until now.

Nor is the objection from Mark 7 valid, where, when certain people asked Christ to lay his hand upon a lunatic, he touched his tongue and ears. It does not follow that such contact is the imposition of hands required here.

Although they asked Christ, according to his customary practice, to lay his hand upon the sick man, he was not obliged to follow that procedure or method. Nor were they able to impose such a rule upon him, since, for the sake of a certain mystery, he wished to use in the healing of this lunatic a method different from the one they expected. Consequently, it does not follow that touching the tongue and ears constitutes the imposition of hands.

These points having been settled, we must briefly address those who say that the imposition of hands is [Col. 0495C] merely an election, performed by raising or extending the hands, and is not a rite of consecration. They maintain that the ancients therefore called it **χειροτονία**—that is, “election”—and used the verb **χειροτονεῖν**.

I admit that in pagan writings these words mean “to elect,” namely, to choose someone for public office. Councils and the holy Fathers sometimes use them in this way when discussing the election of bishops, but not always.

For **χειροτονεῖν** in Acts 14 means to establish bishops through the solemn rite of the imposition of hands:

> Χειροτονήσαντες δὲ αὐτοὺς πρεσβυτέρους κατ᾽ Ἐκκλησίαν προσευξάμενοι μετὰ νηστειῶν.

That is:

> “And having ordained elders for them in each Church, and having prayed with fasting.”

This is confirmed by Acts 6:

> Καὶ προσευξάμενοι ἐπέθηκαν αὐτοῖς τὰς χεῖρας.

That is:

> “And after praying, they laid their hands upon them.”

This passage explains the earlier one. For **ἐπιτιθέναι τὰς χεῖρας**, “to lay on the hands,” in no way means “to extend the hands,” or “to elect,” as we shall demonstrate below.

This is confirmed by the first Apostolic Canon:

> Ἐπίσκοπος χειροτονείσθω ὑπὸ Ἐπισκόπων δύο ἢ τριῶν.

That is:

> [Col. 0495D] “Let a bishop be ordained by two or three bishops.”

The books of the saints are full of evidence that in former times a bishop was ordinarily elected by the clergy and people, but consecrated by three bishops.

The second Apostolic Canon says:

> πρεσβύτερος ὑπὸ ἑνὸς ἐπισκόπου χειροτονείσθω.

That is:

> “Let a priest be ordained by one bishop.”

The same appears in canon 4 of the Council of Nicaea and in Synesius’s letter 67, where he discusses Siderius, bishop of Palaebisca, who had been unlawfully created by Philo, bishop of Cyrene, because he had not been ordained at Alexandria or by three bishops:

> καὶ εἰ τὸ σύνθημα τῆς χειροτονίας ἐκεῖθεν ἐδίδοτο.

That is:

> “Even if the authorization for the ordination had been given from there.”

Here **χειροτονία** does not mean election, which is presupposed to have taken place, since permission to ordain is being requested from the Alexandrian patriarch, without whose authorization this could not be done, as is established by canon 6 of the Council of Nicaea.

The same is also clear from letter 76. When a certain priest named Antonius had received the votes of all the bishops and people [Col. 0496A] who had gathered to elect a bishop for the village of Olbiatis, Synesius writes to Theophilus:

> ἑνὸς οὖν ἔτι δεῖ, τοῦ κυριωτάτου μέντοι τῆς ἱερᾶς σου χειρός.

That is:

> “One thing, therefore, is still needed—your sacred hand, which is nevertheless the decisive one.”

The same distinction seems to appear in Sozomen, book VIII of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 19. When the bishop of the small city of Geras had died, the citizens by their votes decided to appoint Nilammon as bishop of their city. Since he resisted with all his strength, the patriarch Theophilus, summoned by the citizens, approached him and:

> συνεβούλευσε καταδέχεσθαι παρ᾽ αὐτοῦ χειροτονίαν

That is:

> “Urged him to accept ordination from him.”

Here the election by the citizens and the **χειροτονία** are distinct.

The latter is otherwise called **χειροθεσία**, that is, “the imposition of the hand,” and **ἐπίθεσις τῶν χειρῶν**, “the imposition of hands,” in 2 Timothy 1; and “to lay on the hands,” **ἐπιτιθέναι τὰς χεῖρας**, in Acts 6.

Nor should one say that these expressions mean “to elect” and “election.” In the passage from Acts just cited, election and the imposition of hands are distinguished:

> [Col. 0496B] “And they chose Stephen, a man full of faith and the Holy Spirit,” etc. “They set them before the apostles, and they laid their hands upon them.”

Here one first sees the election, and afterward the ordination through the imposition of hands.

But enough has been said about the imposition of hands.

In the Roman Pontifical, the following points preceding the utterance of these words—“Receive the power to offer sacrifice to God,” etc.—deserve notice. The bishop washes and dries his hands; then, successively, he hands each man a chalice with wine and water, and a paten placed above it with the Host, and they themselves receive these between their index and middle fingers, touching the cup of the chalice and the paten simultaneously, while the bishop says to each, etc. Thus it is read correctly in the old Paris edition of 1520; for the pronoun *illa* refers to the things that are to be touched, whether mediately or immediately. But if one reads *illam*, as it is found in certain more recent editions and in Cataldus’s *Caeremoniale episcoporum*, I do not see the sense of these words, since it cannot refer only to the noun *Hostiam*. The meaning is that everything being offered should be received [Col. 0496C]; afterward the manner of reception is specified, namely, between the index and middle fingers, so that the cup of the chalice and the paten are touched at the same time.

Since this is so, those who say that contact with the Host or bread is required by the Pontifical should not be heeded, since nothing of the kind appears there—and still less should one heed those who write that contact with the bread is necessary for the sacrament, so that anyone who has not touched the bread must be ordained again. For, morally speaking, a person is said to accept what he receives—or touches—the instruments or vessels in which the things being offered are contained; thus a person truly accepts the apples offered when he receives the basket or vessel in which they are contained, without touching the apples. This opinion is followed by [509] many serious authors, apart from those who assert that contact with the instruments or vessels is not necessary for the sacrament. Among the latter is Albert the Great, in the manuscript *Sentences*, book IV, p. 313, col. 3, in the library of the monastery of Saint-Victor at Paris, in his response to objection 3:
