> It is said that nothing is required except presentation, and that touch belongs to the category of what is fitting, because in this sacrament the form signifies the transmission of power, and this is signified entirely in the presentation, provided that the person to whom it is presented does not expressly dissent. For he is understood to have accepted it when he shows no dissent, when it has been presented to him for acceptance.

Finally, in the same Roman Pontifical, after communion has been completed, etc., the bishop again lays his hands upon the heads of each of them, saying: “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive,” etc. This rite, together with its formula, is not found in the Fourth Council of Carthage, nor in our Sacramentaries, whether printed or manuscript, nor in the Tilius Codex, nor in the manuscript Pontifical thought to be Anglo-Saxon, nor in the manuscript *Ordo* of Saint-Germain-des-Prés. It was, however, later added in the margin of this Codex, by another hand. Nor is it found in Saint Isidore, Amalarius, or Rabanus, or in the Roman *Ordo*.

Finally, in the Ratold Codex, after the Benediction of the hands [Col. 0497A], the following appears:

> **Completion of the presbyters.**  
> Let us have a common prayer, brothers, for those who are chosen for the assistance and benefit of your salvation, etc.

Then:

> **ANOTHER [PRAYER].**  
> Author of all sanctifications, whose is true consecration and whose is full Benediction, you, Lord, pour the grace of your Benediction upon these servants of yours, N. and N., whom we dedicate to the honor of the presbyterate, etc.

When this Prayer has been completed, the same Codex continues:

> Now let the Epistle, the Tract, and the Gospel be read, and then let all offer the sacred offerings.

I think *sacrandas* should be read here instead of *sacras*. For in former times everyone offered upon the altar the bread and wine of which they were going to partake. This is clear from the same Ratold Codex, in the consecration of a bishop, where after the bishop’s anointing the following appears:

> Let the Gospel according to Luke be read: “At that time there arose a contention.” And then let he himself and everyone offer bread and wine.

Here *he himself* is the bishop being ordained, while *everyone* means the other assisting bishops and the rest of the clergy.

**758. When a bishop is ordained.** In the printed editions, before these [Col. 0497B] words, there is an examination or interrogation, according to Gallican usage, as the Tilius Codex and the Roman *Ordo* note; these differ from the interrogations in the Fourth Council of Carthage. In our manuscript Sacramentaries, however, there are none.

According to Saint Ambrose’s interpretation, in chapter 6 of *On the Dignity of the Priesthood*, a bishop is a superintendent—that is, an overseer and guardian. In Plutarch, in the *Life of Numa*, the phrase τῶν παρθένων ἱερῶν ἐπίσκοπος means “guardian of the sacred virgins,” and refers to the chief pontiff. Among the jurists, in the final law of the *Digest*, “On the Office and Honor of a Bishop,” it means one who presides over bread and other saleable goods. Among the Athenians it meant the prefect and guardian of a city subject to them, sent there to inspect everything done by each person; the Lacedaemonians called such a person ἁρμοστής, as Harpocration teaches. Julius Pollux mentions him in book VIII, chapter 1. By analogy with this, among us the person who presides over divine and sacred matters in each city is called a bishop.

In the Ratold Codex, certain materials precede this section. Since they are not insignificant, I thought they should be transferred here:

> **How the clergy and people elect a bishop in his own see, with the consent of the king, the archbishop, and the whole people** [read: “and of all the people”].
>
> “To the Lord N., supreme bishop, who is equal to the merits of the Lord of the Franks [perhaps: ‘to the father of the fathers’], all the clergy and the entire people of the holy Church of N. wish manifold health in the Lord.
>
> “Therefore, whenever any people subject to your authority has been deprived of its own shepherd, aid must be sought from no one other than you, whom the divine Majesty has foreordained for this purpose: not only that you might specially [510] feed your own sons, but also that you might provide shepherds for those who lack rulers and are in need of spiritual nourishment. Accordingly, we confidently pour forth our prayers to your paternal holiness, asking, namely, that you may deign to ordain as our bishop this humble servant of yours, N., a man of the highest integrity [the manuscript reads *indigemini*; read *dignemini*]. [Col. 0497D] As far as we have known his conduct and character, we praise them, and we testify that he is suitable for so worthy a task. And while we remain free from episcopal Benediction [read: ‘from the episcopal Benediction’], strengthened by his teaching and example, we believe that, by the Lord’s mercy, we shall return to the way of salvation like a lost sheep [the manuscript reads *onus*; read *ovis*] that has been found. We have resolved to send you this decree, ratified by our hands, to your Church of N. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation, of your episcopate, and of the king N., in the indiction of such-and-such a year, dated on such-and-such a day.”
>
> **Prayer to be said by the archbishop after the election, over the elect and over himself.**
>
> “Let us pray, brothers, that God and our Lord Jesus Christ may deign to enlighten us and our elect with the grace of the Holy Spirit. Through …”
>
> [Col. 0498A]
>
> **The bishop’s admonition follows** [read: “the archbishop’s admonition”].
>
> “Preserve these solid things [the manuscript reads *solita*; read *solida*] with vigilant mind and effort, and take care to make them known to those entrusted to you, so that, being of one mind and with one voice, you may praise God for his benefits toward you; to him honor and glory are due. Through all things.”
>
> **Promise.**
>
> “In the name of the high-throned Creator, the eternal King, I, N., a humble servant of Christ, although unworthy, elected to the episcopal see of the Church of N. to govern it and to serve God [read: ‘to preserve it for God’], humbly confess, with the help of almighty God, and with whatever grace heavenly wisdom may be willing to reveal to me and whatever life it may grant me in this age, that I desire always to serve and obey with devoted and faithful mind you, holy Savior of the world, and the venerable Father, Archbishop N., and his successors, whom heavenly grace provides and predestines for us as a father. I confess that I shall remain steadfast and constant, without any dissimulation or deception, all the days that my spirit remains in my nostrils and life endures; I shall never turn either to the right or to the left from that see of the Church of N., which is its head [read: ‘I shall not turn’]. Without any scruple of diabolical fraud, with humble devotion and sincere mind, I confess before almighty God that I shall serve and obey in all my strength that aforesaid Father, N., and his successors, whom divine grace has predestined as bishop of that holy see.
>
> “I humbly confess in every respect that I wish always to preserve, with all humility and obedience, both divine and human, that holy apostolic faith which our fathers worthily preserved, just as my predecessors, subject to that holy see of the Church of Christ, did. Whatever they preached and fulfilled by guarding it, here and elsewhere, to the people of God, I do not cease to preach and observe, with the favor and will of our pious Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.”
>
> **Another admonition after the promise.**
>
> [Col. 0498C]
>
> “Remember the pledge and espousal of the Church, and the love of the Lord your God, on the day when you attained this honor; take care not to forget it.”
>
> **Benediction for the bishop’s ring.**
>
> “Creator and preserver of the human race, giver of spiritual grace, bestower of eternal salvation: you, Lord, pour your Benediction upon this ring, so that, armed with the power of heavenly protection, it may benefit him [the manuscript reads *illis*] for eternal salvation. Through …”
>
> “Here let the ring be given on the finger.”
>
> “Receive, therefore, the ring of discernment,” etc., as in the Roman *Ordo*.

**511. Benediction of the staff.**

> “You are the staff and ruler of our life throughout the ages,
>
> “Sanctify this little staff by the right of your goodness,
>
> “By which evils may be struck down and by which what is always right may be guided.”

> “Here let the pastoral staff be given.”
>
> “Receive the staff of sacred governance,” etc., as in the Roman *Ordo*.

> **Another giving of the staff.**
>
> “Receive the staff of pastoral office. May you be fierce in correcting vices, holding judgment without anger in anger; and when you have become angry, remembering mercy. Through …”

> “Now they are to rise, and let the Introit begin.”

> “The Lord has chosen you for himself as a priest.” Psalm: “May the Lord hear you.” At the Response: “May he send you.” Another Antiphon: “As I was with Moses.” Psalm: “May the Lord hear you.” Antiphon: “Today God has blessed you.” Psalm: “God of gods.”

> **PRAYER AT THE MASS ON THE DAY.**  
> “Let us pray, most beloved, that for this man …,” as below in the Codex of Saint Eligius.

> **EPISTLE:** “Dearly beloved, this is a faithful saying: if anyone desires the office of a bishop.”

> **Response:** “May he remember all your sacrifice.”  
> **Verse:** “May the Lord send you.”  
> **Response:** “Offer to God.”  
> **Tract:** “Desire.”  
> **Alleluia:** “He has appointed.”  
> **Alleluia:** “Grace has been poured forth.”

> “Here the bishop being ordained is to be brought forward before the Gospel is read, after the Alleluia. Then two bishops should lead him by the hands out of the sanctuary, in the presence of the archbishop, before the altar; and he should prostrate himself, while the others perform the litany. When it has been completed, they hold the Book of the Gospel over his shoulders, and the archbishop blesses him.”

Thus far the Ratold Codex concerning the ordination of a bishop. Its heading shows that formerly, in the time of the kings in Gaul, bishops were elected by the votes of the clergy and people, with the consent of the king. The king, however, often commanded by his authority that whomever he wished should be ordained bishop, so that, because his influence so frequently prevailed, the elections were extremely weak. Gregory of Tours repeatedly attests this in his *Histories of the Franks* [Col. 0499B] and in the *Lives of the Fathers*, as do other writers of Frankish history. Finally, through the agreements between Pope Leo X and Francis I, king of the Franks, these elections were completely removed: the authority of nomination remained with the king, and that of confirmation with the pope.

In the other regions of the Western Church, the same freedom of election remained intact for the clergy and people, until, after they had shaken off the yoke of the Roman emperors, their kings claimed for themselves an authority over elections scarcely inferior to that of the Frankish kings.

Among the Greeks, or Easterners, elections do indeed continue, but, with the clergy and people excluded, the right of election has devolved upon the provincial bishops alone. Theodore Balsamon maintains that this was established by canon 4 of the First Council of Nicaea. I do not agree with this opinion, because the cited canon must clearly be understood not as referring to election but to the laying on of hands. For when it says that the appointment is to be made by the provincial bishops, it immediately calls such an appointment χειροτονία—that is, the laying on of hands—and requires it to be performed by at least three bishops if the other bishops are unable to attend because of some impediment, though they are to give their consent by letter.

This is confirmed by canon 6 of the Council of Sardica, held under the emperor Constantius after the Council of Nicaea:

> Τὰ δὲ πλήθη συναθροισθέντα παρακαλοῖεν γίνεσθαι τὴν κατάστασιν τοῦ παρ᾽ αὐτῶν ἐπιζητουμένου Ἐπισκόπου.

That is:

> “But when the multitude has assembled, let it request that the appointment of the bishop whom it seeks be made.”

For the matter there concerns an appointment—that is, the ordination—of a bishop already elected by the votes of the people. If one of the provincial bishops did not attend his ordination, the council decreed that he should be admonished by letter. Since *κατάστασις* means ordination, and the canon of the Council of Nicaea uses the same word, this indicates that the Council of Nicaea was speaking of ordination, not [512] election; consequently, it did not reject the votes of the clergy and people in the election of bishops.

Indeed, the Council of Nicaea itself explains its meaning in the synodal letter addressed to the holy Churches of God throughout Alexandria, Egypt, Pentapolis, and elsewhere, concerning the case of the patriarch of Alexandria against the Meletians:

> Μόνον εἰ ἄξιοι φαίνοιντο, καὶ ὁ λαὸς αἱροῖτο etc.

That is:

> “Only if they should appear worthy, and the people should elect them, with their own consent and with the confirmation of the bishop of Catholic Alexandria.”

The same is plainly evident from the eleventh action of the Council of Chalcedon, in which Anatolius, patriarch of Constantinople, speaking of the deposition of the bishops Bassianus and Stephen, who had been ordained contrary to the canons as bishops of the Church of Ephesus, says:

> “A bishop shown by God shall be given to the metropolis of Ephesus; καὶ παρὰ πάντων τῶν μελλόντων ποιμαίνεσθαι ψηφιζὸμενος—that is, ‘and elected by all those who are to be shepherded.’”

But there are also almost innumerable examples of elections of this kind by clergy and people, even after the Council of Nicaea.

Peter, bishop of Alexandria, previously designated by Saint Athanasius, was elected by the votes of everyone, both ecclesiastics and magistrates, as Theodoret writes in book IV, chapter 18 of his *Ecclesiastical History*. In Synesius, letter 76, Antonius the presbyter is elected bishop of the village of Olbia, not only by the votes of the bishops who were present, but also by those of the entire people who had assembled. The sixty-seventh letter of the same Synesius conveys the same meaning.

In Sozomen, book VIII, chapter 19 of his *Ecclesiastical History*, Nilammon was elected bishop by the people of the small city of Geras. When Paulinus, bishop of Antioch, died, Evagrius was appointed in his place by the votes of the people, as Socrates writes in book V, chapter 15 of his *Ecclesiastical History*. After Timothy Aelurus, bishop of Alexandria, had been sent into exile, another Timothy was substituted in his place by the votes of the citizens of Alexandria, as Evagrius writes in book II, chapter 11 of his *Ecclesiastical History*. Saint John Chrysostom was elected bishop of Constantinople by the common votes of clergy and people, with the emperor also giving his assent, as Sozomen writes in book VIII, chapter 2.

[Col. 0500B] Nor is this contradicted by canon 13 of the Council of Laodicea, which decrees that mobs should not be permitted to elect those who are being put forward for the priesthood. For that canon does not reject the votes of the clergy and honorable citizens, but rather those of people drawn from the dregs of the populace, who frequently stir up riots and seditions in assemblies of this kind.

**759. Let all the other bishops place and hold the Book of the Gospels over his head.** Thus it appears in the printed editions. In canon 1 of the Fourth Council of Carthage and in the Rheims Codex, it reads: “Over his head and neck.” In the Tilius Codex: “Over his crown and closed between his shoulders.” In the Roman *Ordo*: “Over his neck and closed between his shoulders.” In the Roman Pontifical: “Over his neck and shoulders, in accordance with the manner in which the open book ought to be held.”

The rite of placing the Book of the Gospels over the head of a bishop when he is ordained is extremely ancient. Saint Dionysius discusses it in chapter 5 of the *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*:

> Ὁ ἱεράρχης ἐπὶ τὴν ἱεραρχικὴν τελείωσιν προσαγόμενος, ἄμφω τὼ πόδε κλίνας ἔμπροσθεν τοῦ θυσιαστηρίου, ἐπὶ κεφαλῆς ἔχει τὰ θεοπαράδοτα λόγια καὶ τὴν ἱεραρχικὴν χεῖρα.

That is:

> “The hierarch, when he approaches the hierarchic initiation, with both knees bent before the altar, has above his head the divine words handed down by God and the hierarchic hand.”

Here “the divine words” can easily be understood as the Gospel, as is clear from many passages in George Pachymeres’ paraphrase of this chapter.

Saint John Chrysostom, in the homily entitled *That the Legislator of the Old and New Testaments Is the Same*, says:

> Διὰ τοῦτο ἐν τῇ Ἐκκλησίᾳ, ἐν ταῖς χειροτονίαις τῶν ἱερέων τὸ εὐαγγέλιον τοῦ Χριστοῦ ἐπὶ κεφαλῆς τίθεται.

That is:

> “For this reason, in the Church, at the ordinations of bishops, the Gospel of Christ is placed upon their head.”

Peter Damian, sermon 1 *On the Dedication*:

> “The Gospel page is also placed upon the head of the man lying there, so that by the word of life he may perceive that it surpasses reason, and that his eyes may fail before the word of the Lord.”

The same can be seen in the aforementioned Fourth Council of Carthage and in the Sacramentaries [513] and *Ordines* cited above (“In the rite for the creation of a bishop”), as well as in the Greek Euchologion:

> Ἀναπτύσσει τὸ εὐαγγέλιον ὁ ἀρχιερεύς, καὶ ἐπιτίθησι τῇ κεφαλῇ καὶ τῷ τραχήλῳ τοῦ χειροτονουμένου συνεφαπτομένων τῶν ἄλλων ἀρχιερέων.

That is:

> “The chief pontiff opens the Gospel and places it upon the head and neck of the person being ordained, while the other chief pontiffs touch it together with him.”

Amalarius, however, opposes this in book II, chapter 14 of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*:

> “A booklet says, according to whose order the ordination is celebrated among certain people, that two bishops should hold the Gospel over his head; but neither ancient authority indicates this, nor apostolic tradition, nor canonical authority.”

All these claims are sufficiently refuted by the passages cited. Indeed, although Amalarius does not at all approve this placing of the Book of the Gospels, he immediately supplies its mystical interpretation:

> “The placing of the Gospel over the head may nevertheless admonish those holding it either to pray that the Lord may firmly establish that same Gospel in his heart, or to admonish the man being consecrated to remember that he is more subject to the yoke of the Gospel than he otherwise would be.”

[Col. 0501A] Saint John Chrysostom gives other reasons in the homily cited above: that the person being ordained may learn that he is receiving the true diadem of the Gospel, and may learn that, although he is the head of all, he is nevertheless subject to the laws. Saint Dionysius adds another reason in the cited chapter: the perfecting power and knowledge are divinely granted to bishops, who are to transmit them to others.

In all our Sacramentaries and *Ordines*, in the Council of Carthage, and in the Euchologion cited above, the Book of the Gospels is placed by bishops. In Clement, however, book VIII, *Constitutions*, chapter 4, it is placed by deacons; in the Roman Pontifical, by one of the chaplains.

**760. All the remaining bishops.** Many bishops customarily assemble for the ordination of one bishop—namely, those belonging to the same province in which the bishop is consecrated—as established by canon 6 of the Council of Sardica and canon 9 of Antioch. If they cannot all be present, he must be ordained by at least three, with the others giving their consent by letter, as decreed by canon 4 of the Council of Nicaea. Canon 18 of the Fourth Council of Toledo establishes the same rule.

The first canon of the Apostles decrees that a bishop is to be ordained by two or three. Synesius, letter 67, says that Siderius of Palaebisca was not a legitimate bishop because he had not been ordained by three bishops. The same is established in canon 20 of the First Council of Arles. Canon 21 of the First Council of Orange forbids a bishop to be ordained by two bishops.

**761. Let them touch his head.** In the Ratold Codex and in the Codex believed to be Anglo-Saxon, there is neither contact with the head nor the laying on of hands. In the printed editions, the following appears:

> “When this has been done, let him receive the paten with the offerings and the chalice with the wine, and let him give it to him, saying: ‘Receive the power to offer sacrifice both for the living and the dead.’”

Since these words are absent from our manuscript Codices, from the Tilius Codex, and from the Roman *Ordo* and Pontifical, they appear to be spurious. In the Rheims Codex there follows an exhortation to the people:

> “This must be preserved, most beloved brothers,” etc.

**762. Prayer, etc.** In the Anglo-Saxon Codex it reads:

> “And let the bishops say Prayers over him.”

[Col. 0501C]

**763. “Let us pray, most beloved,” etc.** Thus it appears in the printed editions and in the Rheims Codex. It is absent from the Rodrad Codex. In the Ratold Codex it does not occur at this point, but is the first Prayer of the Mass at which the bishop is consecrated, with the plural changed to the singular. In the Roman *Ordo* and Pontifical it is placed after the following Prayer.

**764. “For the benefit to be provided for the chosen.”** In the Roman *Ordo* and Pontifical it reads: “Providing for the benefit of the Church.” In the Ratold Codex: “Advancing toward the benefit of the Church.” The reading in the Roman *Ordo* and Pontifical is indeed excellent, but differs in sense from the others.

**765. “Be present, Lord, to our supplications,” etc.** Thus it appears in the printed editions, in the Rodrad and Ratold Codices, and in the Roman *Ordo*. In the Rheims Codex there is another Prayer, but with the same meaning:

> “Hear, Lord, the prayers of your suppliants, so that what must be performed by our ministry may rather be strengthened by your power. Through the Lord.”

It is absent from the Roman Pontifical.

**766. “Be favorable, Lord,” etc.** In the Roman Pontifical, before this Prayer, the words “Receive the Holy Spirit” are found. They are absent from the printed editions, from our manuscript Codices, from the Roman *Ordo*, and from the Tilius Codex.

**767. “God of all honors.”** Thus it appears in all our other manuscript Codices. In the printed editions, “God of all good things,” etc., is read incorrectly; see the notes above. In the Tilius Codex and in the Roman *Ordo* and Pontifical, it reads: “God, honor of all.”

**768. “God of all dignities.”** Thus it appears in the printed editions and in the manuscript Rodrad and Ratold Codices. In the Rheims Codex, the word *Deus* is absent.

**769. “And now the pontifical glory is not commended to us by the honor of garments,” etc.** Fortunatus attests this in book II, epigram 10, concerning Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris:

> Germanus, the bishop, stands amid the honor  
> who rules the young on one side and raises up the old on the other.  
> The Levites go before; a solemn order of singers follows;  
> by his walking he moves some, by his governance he leads others.  
> Yet he proceeds gently, like another Aaron,  
> not shining through his garment, but pleasing through his devotion.  
> No stones, scarlet, bright gold, purple, or fine linen  
> adorn his shoulders; holy faith flashes forth.

In the printed editions *cidarim* is read, but this makes no sense. In the manuscript Codex of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, *Cidar* is found, but above it, in the same writing, *Clar* is written; a line is drawn beneath the word *Cidar* to mark the error. Therefore, from *Clar* I produced *clarum*, “bright,” and the sense is clear.

**770. “Because those things which then pleased carnal eyes demanded rather those things which were to be understood in them.”** This is found in all the Codices cited so often above. I think the word *quam* is missing, so that the passage should read:

> “Because those things which then pleased carnal eyes demanded those things rather than the things that were to be understood in them”—

that is, that carnal people took greater delight in the splendor of the garments than in the mysteries signified by that splendor.

**771. “Of the highest priesthood.”** The highest priesthood is the episcopate, so that the highest priest is the bishop, as noted above.

**772. “So that whatever those coverings, in the splendor of gold, etc.”** The aforementioned Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris, exemplified this admirably, as Fortunatus sang in the poem cited above:

> This priest is far better than the one under the old Law,  
> because he truly honors what was formerly a shadow.

**773. “Here you receive chrism.”** These words are absent from the printed editions.

**774. “To sanctify with the flower of heavenly ointment,” etc.** The bishop is anointed in the form of a cross, as appears to be shown in the Rodrad Codex.

In our other manuscript Codices, crosses are not depicted—not only in the ordination of a bishop, but also in the conferral of the other grades. Yet formerly they were used in all the grades, as they are also today, as appears from the [515] Roman Pontifical and the Greek Euchologion. This is made clear by Saint Augustine, sermon 181 *On Time*:

> “For by this sign of the cross the Lord’s body is consecrated, the baptismal font is sanctified, and presbyters and the other ecclesiastical grades are also initiated.”

Saint Dionysius attests the same concerning the bishop, presbyter, and deacon in chapter 5 of the *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, since he wrote about the consecration of these three grades alone:

> Ἑκάστῳ δὲ αὐτῶν ἡ σταυροειδὴς ἐνσημαίνεται πρὸς τοῦ τελοῦντος Ἱεράρχου σφραγίς.

That is:

> “Upon each of them the cross-shaped seal is impressed by the consecrating hierarch.”

Saint John Chrysostom speaks more generally in homily 55 on Matthew:

> Κἂν ἀναγεννηθῆναι δέῃ, σταυρὸς παραγίνεται, κἂν τραφῆναι τὴν μυστικὴν ἐκείνην τροφήν, κἂν χειροτονηθῆναι.

That is:

> “For the Lord’s cross is present when we must be regenerated, when we must be nourished with that mystical food, and when we must be ordained.”

**775. “Here you pour upon his head.”** Namely, chrism. In the Ratold Codex it reads: “Here let oil be placed upon his head.” In the Tilius Codex and in the Roman *Ordo* it reads:

> “Here let him put chrism upon the bishop’s head in the form of a cross; let him be anointed and consecrated,” etc.

This anointing of the head in the ordination of a bishop follows an ancient custom, which can be learned from Amalarius, book II *On Offices*, chapter 14, where he discusses the ordination of a bishop:

> “Oil is also poured upon his head for his consecration.”

Optatus of Milevis, in book II *Against Parmenianus*, speaking of the schismatics who degraded Catholic bishops and cast them down into penance, writes:

> “And you do not admit the voice of God into your ears, who says in Psalm 104: ‘Touch not my anointed, and do not lay your hands upon my prophets.’ The books of Kings show that kings and priests are anointed; and David says in Psalm 132: ‘Like the ointment that ran down into Aaron’s beard.’ Yet you have striven with the same force to despise the commandments by which those who fear the Lord strive to fulfill his commands. Show us where you were commanded to shave the heads of priests, when, on the contrary, so many examples have been given showing that this must not be done. Saul deserved to be anointed before he sinned; after his anointing he gravely offended. When God saw this, wishing to provide an example that the oil was not to be touched, he declared his repentance; for the Lord is read to have said: ‘It repents me that I have anointed Saul as king.’ Certainly God could have taken away the oil he had given; but when he wished to teach that even the oil given to a sinner ought not to be touched, he himself, who had given it, repented. Therefore, if God, in order to teach you, could not take away what he had given because he did not wish it taken away, who are you to take away what you did not give? You who ought to have prepared your ears to hear prepared a razor for wrongdoing.”

Optatus is there complaining that the schismatics laid sacrilegious hands upon the heads of bishops in order to remove the sacred oil or chrism—that is, to degrade them and cast them down from episcopal honor by shaving their heads—setting against them God’s example: he did not take away from the wicked king Saul the oil he had given him.

Therefore such shaving here is not for penance but for degradation. Although the Catholic bishops were cast down into penance by the schismatics, it is also clear that they were degraded and stripped of their honor; for above he says:

> “The priests were stripped of the honor of their name.”

And below:

> “Therefore you sharpened your tongues into swords, which you moved toward the deaths not of bodies but of honors. You found deacons, presbyters, and bishops; you made them laymen.”

Peter Damian teaches the same in his sermon *On the Dedication of a Church*, speaking of the consecration of a bishop:

> “His head is anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions, in the likeness of him who, poured forth more abundantly with spiritual balm from a virginal bridal chamber, caused the oil of Benediction to drip upon the sons of men.”

Here also belongs the passage of Saint Gregory, book IV of his *Commentary on the First Book of Kings*, chapter 5:

> “This anointing certainly expresses what is now also materially exhibited in the holy Church: the one who is placed at the summit receives the sacraments of anointing. But since the anointing itself is a sacrament, the one who is promoted is rightly anointed outwardly if he is strengthened inwardly by the power of the sacrament.”

Likewise, this [516] passage of Saint Gregory of Nazianzus, in his oration in praise of Basil the Great:

> Νέος ἐπάνεισιν, εὐσθενὴς ἄνω βλέπων, ῥωσθεὶς ἐκ χειρὸς καὶ τῆς χρίσεως.

That is:

> “The young man returns, strong, looking upward, strengthened by the laying on of hands and by anointing.”

The same should be understood of this passage of Symeon Metaphrastes in the *Life of Saint John Chrysostom*:

> Τῷ ἱερατικῷ χρίσματι τελειοῦται, καὶ τῷ τῆς Ἐκκλησίας ὕψει στηρίζεται.

That is:

> “He is initiated by the priestly chrism and established in the exalted position of the Church.”

For this reason Pacian, in letter 3 to Sympronianus, calls the priest—that is, the bishop—“the anointed one”:

> “From where does the Spirit come to your people, whom the anointed priest does not sign?”

**776. “Sincerity of peace.”** From these words up to “grant him, Lord,” many passages are inserted in the Ratold and Rheims Codices, and also in the [514] Roman *Ordo* and Pontifical. They are absent from this Codex of Saint Eligius, from the Rodrad Codex, and from the printed editions.

**777. “Grant him, Lord, the episcopal chair,” etc.** Amalarius touches upon this passage in book II, chapter 14 of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*:

> “The words of his consecration mean this: ‘Grant him the episcopal chair for governing your Church and the entire people.’”

In the Ratold Codex, this consecration is followed by another under the title:

> **Another prayer over the bishop.**

The consecration runs as follows:

> “Holy Father, almighty God, who through our Lord Jesus Christ created all things from the beginning, and afterward, at the end of time, according to the promise which our patriarch Abraham had received, founded also the Church through the congregation of the saints,” etc.

This is absent from our other manuscript Codices, as well as from the printed editions and from the Roman *Ordo* and Pontifical.

In the same Ratold Codex, the anointing of the hands with oil and chrism follows in this form:

> “Then he ought to anoint his hands:
>
> “‘Let these hands be anointed and sanctified, and let them be ordained in you, God of gods. I anoint these hands with sanctified oil and with chrism purified by anointing, just as Moses anointed with the word of his mouth the hands of holy Aaron, his brother; and just as the Holy Spirit, through his breath, anointed the hands of all priests; and just as Jesus, the Savior of us all, anointed the holy hands of his apostles. So let these hands be anointed, sanctified, and consecrated, so that in all things they may be perfect in your name, Father, Son, and eternal Holy Spirit, who are one and supreme God of all the living and the dead, remaining throughout the ages of ages.’”

The same passage is also found in the manuscript Pontifical believed to be Anglo-Saxon.

This same anointing of the hands occurs in the Rheims Codex, and in the Roman *Ordo* and Pontifical, and in the Tilius Codex, in the following, shorter formula. In the Roman Codex it reads:

> “Let these hands be anointed with sanctified oil and with the chrism of sanctification, just as Samuel anointed David king and prophet. So let them be anointed and completed” [thus in the *Ordo*; the Pontifical reads “confirmed,” and the Tilius Codex “consecrated”], “in the name of God the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” [thus in the Roman *Ordo* and Tilius Codex; but in the Pontifical crosses are added to each person], “making the image of the holy cross of our Lord and Savior, who redeemed us from death and brought us to the kingdoms of heaven. Hear us, merciful Father, almighty and eternal God, and grant what we ask and pray.”

In the *Ordo* and Pontifical and in the Tilius Codex it reads:

> “And grant that we may ask for what we entreat you.”

In the manuscript Pontifical preserved in the sacristy of the church of Rouen and thought to belong to the church of Rheims, there is also an anointing of the hands. William of Paris also mentions it. It is absent, however, from the Codex of Saint Eligius, from the printed editions, and from the Rodrad Codex.

This anointing is mentioned in the letter of the bishops at the synod held at Quierzy to Louis, king of Germany, chapter 15:

> “For it is abhorrent that the hand anointed with sacred chrism—which, from bread and wine mixed with water, through Prayer and the sign of the cross, makes the sacrament of the body and blood of Christ—should touch [517] secular things in any way after episcopal ordination, whatever he may have done before ordination.”

The same can be seen in blessed Peter Damian, sermon 5 *On Saint Severus, Bishop of Ravenna*, where he speaks of a dove flying over him at his ordination:

> “And what else,” he says, “was it to touch that same dove while driving it away from him, except to receive in those very hands, according to the order of ecclesiastical institution, the oil of holy anointing? For when the dove descended and settled upon the head of the most holy man, it fulfilled the office of the laying on of hands; but when it allowed itself to be touched by the sacred hands, it marked those hands with the anointing of the Holy Spirit.”

And in sermon 1 *On the Dedication of a Church*, when he speaks of the ordination of a bishop:

> “The hands are also rubbed with oil, so that whatever they bless may be blessed and accepted in the sight of the divine Majesty.”

This anointing is alluded to in the *Life of Saint Aquilinus, Bishop of Évreux*, in Surius, under 19 October:

> “With whose hands anointed by priestly grace,” etc.

Some people formerly added an anointing of the thumb, which can be seen in William of Paris, in the book *On the Sacraments*, in the chapter on extreme unction:

> “Just as in the consecration of pontiffs perfection and fullness are signified by the anointings of the head, hands, and thumb, so too is the richness of inward anointing.”

This anointing was performed on the thumb of the right hand, as is clear from the manuscript Pontifical preserved in the sacristy of the church of Rouen and apparently belonging to the church of Rheims:

> “And let him confirm the thumb of the right hand, saying with chrism: ‘God and Father of the Lord,’” etc.

Furthermore, in the Pontifical believed to be English there is a double anointing of the head: the first with oil and chrism, the second, after the anointing of the hands, with oil alone:

“Here let oil be poured upon his head; let him be anointed,” etc.

And in the Codex of Ratoldus, where the following comes next:

“Then he ought to anoint his head: Let your head be anointed and consecrated with heavenly Benediction in the pontifical order, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Peace be with you.”  
**Response:** “And with your spirit.”

These words are absent from the printed editions and from our other manuscript codices. This second anointing of the head is peculiar to these codices; it is followed by this Prayer:

[Col. 0505A]

> Lord Jesus Christ, you chose your apostles beforehand so that they might preside over us in teaching; so also may you deign to appoint bishops, in the place of the apostles, to teach, bless, and instruct, so that they may preserve an immaculate and unblemished life, in order that the sevenfold Holy Spirit may come upon them and upon us all, and that the power of the Most High may guard us all together without sin; and that every Blessing written in the Holy Scriptures may likewise come upon us and strengthen us: God the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit, so that we may have eternal life forever and ever.

This Prayer is found neither in the printed editions nor in our other manuscript codices, nor in the Roman Order and Pontifical, nor in the Codex of Tilius. In the same Codex of Ratoldus the following comes next:

“And then let the Gospel according to Luke be read: ‘At that time there arose a dispute.’ And then let he himself, and everyone, offer bread and wine. Offertory: ‘I have found David my servant.’ ‘May the Lord remember.’ Offertory: ‘With glory and honor.’”

Such is the account of the ordination of a bishop according to the rite of the Latins, who also, according to them, is ordained on Sunday, as is clear from the Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 18:

[Col. 0505B]

“Or certainly he shall be consecrated a priest by three men on Sunday.”

### 778. If the pope is to be ordained

These words are absent from the printed editions and from our other manuscript codices, nor are they found in the Roman Pontifical. Concerning the rite of ordaining the pope, I shall here add what I read in a very ancient manuscript Roman Order from the library of Corbie.

> **ORDINATION OF THE ROMAN PONTIFF**
>
> They shall sing psalms according to custom. The elected man proceeds from the sacristy with seven candle-bearers and comes to the confession. After the litany, the bishops and priests ascend together to the seat. Then the bishop of Albano gives the first Prayer; afterward the bishop of Porto gives the second Prayer. Next the Gospels are brought, opened, and held over the head of the elected man by deacons. Then the bishop of Ostia consecrates him as pontiff. After this the archdeacon places the pallium upon him; then he ascends to the seat, [518] and gives the peace to all the priests; and he says: “Glory to God in the highest.”

[Col. 0505C]

Thus far the manuscript Codex of Corbie.

The same account is found in the published Roman Order, in which the Prayers are noted, as in the ordination of a bishop. Here observe, first, that the confession is a kind of tabernacle adorned with varied workmanship, in which the bodies of the holy apostles rest. For this term, see Onuphrius Panvinius, Julius Caesar Bulengerus, in their short works, and our observations on the *Concordia of the Rules*.

Second, observe that the Book of the Gospels is not held by a bishop, as happens in the ordination of other bishops, but by deacons, just as in the *Apostolic Constitutions*, in the ordination of other bishops.

Third, observe that the pope is consecrated by the bishop of Ostia, according to the ancient custom by which the bishop of Ostia ordinarily ordains the Roman pontiff. Saint Augustine bears witness to this in the conference of the third day with the Donatists, chapter 16:

[Col. 0505D]

> And that Caecilianus did not wait to be ordained by a superior as a superior, since the Catholic Church has another custom: that not the bishops of Numidia, but the bishops who are nearer, should ordain the bishop of the Church of Carthage; just as no metropolitan bishop ordains anyone for the Roman Church, but the bishop of Ostia, as the nearest.

### 779. “And the primate of all,” etc.

Note the distinguished encomium of the Roman pontiff, to whom primacy over the universal Church is owed. Hence Cassiodorus says admirably in Book XI of the *Variae*, letter 2:

> For you preside as watchmen over the Christian people; in the name of a father you love all. The security of the people, therefore, depends upon your reputation, to whom their guardianship has been divinely entrusted. Accordingly, it is fitting that we guard some things, but that you guard all things.

And below:

> May that See, admired throughout the whole world, shelter its own devoted worshipers with affection. Although it has been granted to the world as a whole, it is also known to have been locally assigned to you.

I omit the other encomia of the Fathers and of the councils.

### 780. “And the sacrifice to be celebrated”

So it stands in the Codex of Ratoldus; this was also noted above in the same Prayer. In the Roman Missal it reads: “And to the sacrifice,” etc.

### 781. “Therefore, this offering,” etc.

The same words are found in the Codex of Ratoldus and in the Roman Order. In the Codex of Ratoldus the following comes next:

[Col. 0506A]

> Episcopal Blessing for the day: “O God, who in showing mercy to peoples console them” (or “care for them”), “and rule them in love, grant the spirit of wisdom to those to whom you have entrusted the governance of discipline.” Amen, etc., as in the Roman Order.

In the latter, however, this Blessing varies in some respects. In the same Codex of Ratoldus the following comes next:

“And then all the bishops receive Communion at the hands of the archbishop.”

But in the Roman Order the following points are to be noted:

[Col. 0506B]

> When he has come to receive Communion, the Lord pontiff extends to him the *formata* and the consecrated offering in its entirety. The bishop receives it and himself communicates from it upon the altar; whatever remains, however, he shall keep for himself, in order to communicate again from it each day until forty days have been completed. Afterward, at the command of the Lord pontiff, he communicates the people together with the other bishops.

Here *formata* means a diploma or letter of the archbishop, by which he testifies that he has ordained the bishop in question for the church in question. A specimen is appended there:

> To our most beloved brothers and sons, the priests, deacons, honored men, clerics, and possessors, or to the whole people of the church of N., N.  
> We, N., archbishop of the holy Catholic See of N., with the Lord’s help, approving your election as most acceptable to God, have consecrated for you the venerable man N. as a priest in the first order, etc.

Saint Pacianus mentions this in Letter 2 to Sympronianus—and calls it a letter when speaking of Novatianus:

> I recognize the root of the ancient law, the source of the ancient people, as having left behind Cornelius, envying him, and having lent itself to the madness of Novatianus, who was made a bishop without legitimate consecration; and therefore he was not made so by the letter of those who pretended to be confessors.

You will learn what a *formata* is from Marculfus, near the end of his formularies. You will also learn that this document, although drawn from the Roman Order, is not properly a *formata*.

In it, however, one point should be noted: in the first order, “priest” means bishop, just as in the second order “priest” means presbyter. This is clear from Letter 25 of Sidonius, Book IV, where, discussing the election of John as bishop of Chalon-sur-Saône, he writes:

[Col. 0506C]

> Later, as time and labors passed, the archdeacon—who, whether in rank or ministry, had been retained for a long time because of his diligence, and who could not for a long period be advanced in dignity lest he be released from his authority—nevertheless, now already a priest of the second order, etc., was consecrated their colleague.

Nor can it be inferred from these words, as some wish, that the archdeacon was a priest of the second order on account of the phrase “nevertheless, now already a priest of the second order.” For if that were so, the words would seem superfluous, since Sidonius had already sufficiently explained John’s rank above, and the word “nevertheless” plainly shows that the priest of the second order must be distinguished from the archdeacon.

For, when Sidonius sets forth John’s merits, he says first that he had been a reader and minister of the altar almost from infancy, and afterward an archdeacon, remaining for a long time in that office because he was highly suitable for it. “Nevertheless,” since he was already a priest of the second order—that is, a presbyter—he was ordained a bishop. Otherwise the sense of these words would be less fitting: John was retained for a long time in the ministry of the archdeaconate; nevertheless, this man, already an archdeacon, was made a bishop.

[Col. 0506D]

Our interpretation is sufficiently clarified by this passage of Optatus, Book II:

> Why should I mention deacons established in the third priesthood, or presbyters established in the second priesthood?

Here one sees that a presbyter is established in the second priesthood, not an archdeacon, who is established only in the third priesthood, because he is a deacon.

Finally, it should be noted that the ordained bishop is said to receive from the hand of the pontiff the sacred offering from which he is to communicate immediately and for forty consecutive days from what remains of that same Host. Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, writes the same concerning priests or presbyters in his letter to Finardus:

[Col. 0507A]

> A few days ago, as you may remember, you came to me in the evening and disturbed me with a sudden inquiry concerning the Host which, shortly before, when you had been promoted to the priesthood, you received from the hand of the bishop: namely, what the rule was for consuming it daily until the fortieth day.

And below:

> All our provincial bishops agree to this rite. Moreover, in our time a certain man, admitted among the others to the priestly rank, also received a Host from the hand of the bishop, as did the others. He wrapped it in parchment prepared for this purpose and, at each daily celebration, took a small portion calculated according to the number of days then at hand.
>
> It happened, however, that one day, after the sacred rites had been completed, while he was carelessly gathering up the vestments together with the altar cloth, he forgot about the sacred Host and, failing to take proper care, unhappily lost the heavenly treasure. Arriving at his lodging, he attended to what was necessary; the day passed, and on the following day the celebration was repeated.
>
> When the hour of Communion approached, that brother, greatly troubled and dismayed, ran back and forth but could not find even a trace of it.

[Col. 0507B]

And below, explaining the reason for this rite, he writes:

> For the bishop, who holds the place of Christ, when sending priestly men to the people entrusted to them, distributes the Eucharist of the sacred Body to be consumed over forty days, so that, while they are daily refreshed by the nourishment of the heavenly bread, they may keep in mind that period during which, for forty days, the Lord appeared to his disciples and ate with them, refreshing them with the satisfaction of the desired vision.

In the same Codex of Ratoldus the following comes next:

“And then all the bishops receive Communion at the hands of the archbishop.”

Communion: “We shall rejoice in your salvation, and in the name of the Lord our God we shall be magnified.”

Communion: “Blessed is the servant.”

Here note the two Communions.

### 782. “May this Communion, Lord,” etc.

In the Codex of Ratoldus:

> We ask, Lord, work fully in us the remedy of your mercy, etc., as in the Roman Order.

In the same Codex of Ratoldus the following comes next:

[Col. 0507C]

> [520] Then he must be placed in the cathedra, and this Prayer must be said:
>
> Almighty Holy Father, God eternal, you have deigned to arrange every order in the heavenly seats, as the Psalmist says: “Lord, your Word remains forever in heaven.” You ordained that angels and archangels should be enlisted in your service according to their order; under the privilege of the Old Testament, you appointed Moses, Aaron, and Samuel among your priests, who call upon your name; you ordained patriarchs and prophets. In the New Testament, through your Son Jesus Christ, you chose the holy apostles according to their orders: first Peter the apostle in the cathedra of honor, and Matthias, his companion, to the apostleship; you also counted him in the cathedra of honor and called him into the number of all the holy apostles, so that, as the Holy Spirit says through the prophet, “In the assembly of the elders let them praise the Lord.” By divine will, the same things happened to others among them.
>
> And you, Lord, in your immeasurable mercy, grant in our own times a similar grace to our brother N., after the example of your holy apostles seated in the cathedra of honor and dignity, so that he may appear worthy of honor in the sight of your Majesty. Through the same [Lord].

[Col. 0507D]

From this it should be noted that formerly it was customary, once a bishop’s consecration had been completed, to place him solemnly in the episcopal seat or throne. This may be seen in Fortunatus, Book I of the *Life of Saint Martin*:

> He is chosen, drawn forth, consecrated, and placed in the citadel.

Here “in the citadel” means “in the throne.” Likewise, above, in the consecration of the Roman pontiff:

> Then the bishop of Ostia consecrates him as pontiff; the archdeacon places the pallium upon him; then he ascends to the seat.

In the *Apostolic Constitutions*, Book VIII, chapter 5, an ordained bishop is placed in his seat.

In the same Codex of Ratoldus the following comes next:

[Col. 0508A]

> Prayers to be said by the lord pope over the archbishop before the pallium:
>
> Almighty God the Father, who, without the support of personal merits, etc., as in the Roman Order.

Likewise another:

> God, restorer and lover of innocence, direct this servant of yours, N., by the fervor of your Spirit, etc., as in the same Order.

Here the pallium is given.

Consecration after the pallium:

> Holy Lord, Almighty Father, King of kings and Lord of lords, we humbly beseech your clemency, etc., as in the Roman Order.

Thus far the Codex of Ratoldus.

Innocent III describes the pallium in Book I of the *Mysteries of the Mass*, chapter 63:

[Col. 0508B]

> The pallium is made of white wool. It has above a circular band encircling the shoulders, with two strips or bands of the same cloth hanging down on either side; it has four purple crosses, front and back, on the right and on the left. On the left the pallium is double, on the right single. Since it is cut into three parts, three needles—others call them pins—are inserted into it, by which it is sewn together.

The Greeks call it an *omophorion* (ὠμοφόριον), but its form and that of the pallium are not entirely the same. Nor did crosses formerly appear on the pallium, as may be seen in the most ancient images of Saint Gregory and Saint Remigius, which I have had printed in this book.

For more about the pallium, see what the learned men Andreas du Saussey wrote in his book *On Mystical Writers*, rite 4, and in his short work *On the Sacred Pallium*, and what Franciscus Florens, former official of Orléans, wrote in relation to title 8, *On the Use and Authority of the Pallium*.

### 783. “On the feast of the Pope”

The day on which he was promoted to the supreme pontificate of the whole world. For formerly the supreme pontiffs and bishops were accustomed to celebrate solemnly the anniversary of the day of their ordination. On this matter consult Baronius in his notes on the Roman Martyrology, 18 January.

### 784. “On the day of his ordination”

Understand: “the anniversary of his ordination.” This is sufficiently indicated by the words of the Prayer over the offerings: “Repeating the annual festivals of the beginning of the priesthood.”

This ordination, however, is to be understood as that of a bishop, not the initiation of a pope, as is clear from this Mass.

Thus far concerning the conferral of orders according to the norm of the Latin Church. It will not be unwelcome to append the rite of the Greek or Eastern Church in conferring orders, from the Greek *Euchologion*. The first order encountered is that observed in the appointment of a reader and psalmist, since they ordinarily do not confer the other minor orders.

The candidate, therefore, is presented before the pontiff. If he is a secular candidate, he is presented in his garment; if a monk, in his monastic pallium. The pontiff signs his head three times with the sign of the cross and tonsures him in the form of a cross, saying, “In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit,” while those assisting at each invocation acclaim, “Amen.”

Then someone else tonsures him completely according to the clerical form. He is presented again to the pontiff, who, after receiving the *phaenolium*, clothes him in it. The pontiff signs his head three times with the cross, lays his hand upon him, and prays:

> Lord Almighty God, choose this servant of yours and sanctify him, etc.

After the exclamation—namely, “Amen”—he gives the reader the apostolic book. The reader reads briefly and receives the peace from the pontiff.

If the person being ordained is a cantor, he recites something from the Psalter. If several are being ordained as readers, they are ordained together, and the invocation is recited in the plural.

This concerns the ordination of a reader and psalmist.

[Col. 0508D]

The order to be observed in the creation of a subdeacon follows.

The pontiff sits at the Beautiful Gate. Before he begins the liturgy, the man who is to be ordained subdeacon is brought to the pontiff. If he is a secular candidate, he comes in the *phaenolium*, that is, the *penula*; if he is a monk, in the monastic pallium.

The pontiff orders him to remove the *penula* and to put on and gird himself with the *sticharion*, that is, the close-fitting tunic. An ewer and towel are then brought.

The pontiff signs his head three times with the cross and lays his hand upon him. When the deacon says, “Let us pray to the Lord,” the pontiff says this Prayer:

> Lord our God, who through one and the same Spirit distribute various graces to each of those whom you have chosen, etc.

After the response “Amen,” the pontiff takes the towel and places it upon the left shoulder of the man being ordained. He likewise gives him the ewer. The man receives it, kisses the pontiff’s hand, pours water over the pontiff’s hands, which are washed, while saying three times, “All you who are faithful” (ὅσοι πιστοί, τρίς).

Having thus received the Blessing, he stands before the sacred doors, etc. If several are to be ordained, the Prayer is expressed in the plural.

The order for the creation of a deacon follows.

After the pontiff has said this exclamation:

> And may the mercies of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ be with you all.

Two deacons leave the sanctuary, take the deacon being ordained, who is standing in the *solea*, and introduce him into the sanctuary. They go around the holy table three times, singing:

> Holy martyrs, who fought the good fight.

Then he approaches the pontiff, who signs his head three times with the cross, orders him to remove his girdle, and orders the towel to be taken away.

The candidate rests his forehead upon the holy table, bends his right knee, and, when the archdeacon has exclaimed, “Let us attend,” the pontiff, laying his hand upon the head of the man being ordained, exclaims:

> Divine grace, which always heals the infirm and completes what is lacking, promotes this most devout subdeacon to the diaconate. Let us therefore pray for him, that the grace of the most holy Spirit may come upon him.

Immediately “Kyrie eleison” is sung three times, both by those within the sanctuary and by those outside. The pontiff signs the candidate’s head three times with the sign of the cross. When the deacon says, “Let us pray to the Lord,” the pontiff, keeping his hand laid upon him, prays:

> Lord our God, who in your foreknowledge send the help of your holy Spirit, etc.

When “Amen” has been said, the archdeacon, in a low voice so that the deacons present may hear and respond, recites this litany:

> In peace let us pray to the Lord for heavenly peace . . . for the servant of God N., who is now being promoted to the diaconate, and for his salvation let us pray to the Lord, etc.

The pontiff, keeping his hand laid upon him, prays:

> God our Savior, who by your incorruptible voice established the law of the diaconate for the apostles, etc.

After “Amen” has been said, he places the orarion around the ordained man’s left shoulder, saying, “Worthy.” According to custom, “Worthy” is sung three times by those in the sanctuary and three times by the cantors.

Then the bishop gives him the flabellum, likewise saying, “Worthy.” All the deacons greet him. He, having received the flabellum, stands on the right side of the holy table, etc.

At the time of Communion, the man who has been ordained communicates first and recites the litany, etc.

The order for the ordination of a presbyter follows.

When the Cherubic Hymn has been completed, [522] the candidate for the presbyterate stands in the *solea*. Two deacons come out, take him on either side, and lead him as far as the sacred doors. There the deacons leave him, and two priests, the first and the second, take him. They go around the holy table and sing:

> Holy martyrs, who fought valiantly.

When they have completed the circuit, they bow before the pontiff, who stands before the holy table in his throne. The candidate kisses the pontiff’s knee above the *humerale*.

Then the pontiff rises, and the candidate is presented to him. The pontiff signs him three times on the head with the cross. Bringing his forehead to the holy table, the candidate bends both knees.

When the deacon exclaims, “Let us attend,” the priest immediately exclaims, also laying his right hand upon the candidate’s head:

> Divine grace, which always heals the infirm and completes what is lacking, promotes this most devout deacon to the presbyterate. Let us therefore pray for him, that the grace of the most holy Spirit may come upon him.

Those within the sanctuary, and likewise the cantors, say “Kyrie eleison” three times.

Then, again signing him three times and keeping his hand laid upon him, the pontiff says this mystical Prayer when the deacon says, “Let us pray to the Lord”:

> O God, without beginning and without end, etc.

When “Amen” has been said, the protopapa, in a low voice so that those present may hear and respond, recites this litany:

> In peace let us pray to the Lord for heavenly peace . . . for the servant of God N., who is now being ordained presbyter, and for his salvation let us pray to the Lord, etc.

The pontiff, keeping his hand laid upon him, prays:

> O God of great power and inscrutable wisdom, etc.

When “Amen” has been said, he raises him and moves the back portion of his orarion to the front on the right side, saying, “Worthy.” Then he clothes him in the *phaenolium* and again exclaims, “Worthy.” The same is sung by those within the sanctuary and by the psalmists.

He then greets the pontiff and the priests and, departing, stands among the priests, reading the *kontakion*. The deacon stands in the customary place, saying:

> Let us complete our prayer to the Lord.

When the sacred rites have been completed, and the pontiff is about to say, “Let them be for those who receive,” he gives the sacred bread to the approaching ordinand, saying:

> Receive this deposit, and preserve it until the presence of our Lord Jesus Christ, when he must ask it back from you.

The candidate receives it, kisses the pontiff’s hand, and returns to his former place. Placing his hands upon the holy table, he says privately:

> Lord, have mercy; and have mercy on me, O God.

When the pontiff is about to say, “Holy things for the holy,” the ordained man returns the sacred bread, communicates first among the other priests from the hand of the pontiff, and recites the Prayer customarily said after the ambon.

Finally, the order to be observed in the creation of a bishop follows.

When the Trisagion has been completed, the pontiff ascends to the step before the holy table. The man to be ordained is presented before him by three bishops on the right. The chartophylax, on the left, gives him a document on which the following is written:

If the ordaining bishop is a patriarch:

> With the suffrage and approval of the most holy metropolitans and archbishops, and of the bishops;

but if he is a metropolitan:

> With the suffrage and approval of the bishops beloved of God and of the most devout priests, divine grace, which always heals the infirm and completes what is lacking, promotes N., the priest most beloved of God, as bishop of the city N., saved by God. Let us therefore pray for him, that the grace of the most holy Spirit may come upon him.

Those within and outside the sanctuary sing “Kyrie eleison” three times.

When this document has been given to the archbishop, and the chartophylax or archdeacon says, “Let us attend,” the bishop reads the letters aloud while those standing around listen and all cry “Kyrie eleison,” as has been explained.

The bishop opens the Gospel and places it upon the head and neck of the candidate, while the other bishops touch it at the same time. Then, making three crosses over his head and keeping his hand laid upon him, he prays:

> Master Christ, our God, who through your glorious apostle Paul prescribed for us the series of ranks and orders, etc.

When “Amen” has been said, one of the ordaining bishops, in a low voice so that the assembled bishops may hear and respond, recites this litany:

> In peace let us beseech the Lord for heavenly peace [523] and salvation . . . for the servant of God N., who is now being promoted to the episcopate; and for his salvation let us beseech the Lord, that God who loves mankind may grant him an immaculate and irreproachable episcopate; let us beseech the Lord, etc.

The pontiff, keeping his hand laid upon the crown of the candidate’s head, prays:

> Lord our God, because human nature cannot bear the essence of divinity, in your providence you appointed teachers subject to a condition like ours, etc.

When “Amen” has been said, he lifts the Gospel and places it upon the holy table. He then puts the *humerale* upon the ordained man, saying, “Worthy”; the clergy likewise say, “Worthy.”

Then the ordaining bishop greets the man who has been ordained. After the customary favorable acclamation, they ascend together to their thrones. The ordained man sits first and gives the peace to the apostle—that is, after the apostolic reading has been recited, he says, “Peace be with you.” He becomes the first among the others to partake of the Lord’s Body and Blood, and he extends them to the ordaining bishop and to the others.

This concerns the ordinations according to the rite of the Eastern Church. It is worthwhile to make several observations about them.

First, therefore, it should be noted what the *phaenolium* is. *Phainolēs* (Φαινόλης), or *phelonēs* (φελόνης), is a kind of pallium, *penula*, or outer garment worn over the *sticharion*, that is, the close-fitting tunic, as may be seen in Codinus:

> Wearing his customary *sticharion*, and wearing over it his *phelonion*.

The author of the old *Etymologicum* says: “Φαινόλης χιτὼν· οἱ δὲ παλαιοὶ ἐφεστρίδα· παρὰ τὸ φαίνεσθαι ὁλον,” that is:

> *Phainolēs*: a tunic; the ancients called it an *ephestris*, from its appearing all over.

That is correct, since it is an outer garment, like an *ephestris*. A little later he says, “φελόνης, χιτώνιον,” that is:

> *Phelonēs*: a little tunic.

Moreover, the patriarchs’ *phaenolium* was white and scattered with many crosses; for this reason it was called *polystaurion* (πολυσταύριον), “having many crosses,” from the multitude of crosses. Consult the *Greek-Barbarian Glossary* of the learned John Meursius.

### 2.

Note that a reader is ordained through the laying on of hands, according to the *Apostolic Constitutions*, Book VIII, chapter 22, and the Seventh Synod, chapter 14. There the synod censures boys who, having been tonsured, read in church, “μήπω παρ᾽ Ἐπισκόπου χειροθεσίαν λαβόντας,” that is, as not yet having received the laying on of hands from a bishop.

### 3.

Note that the hypodeacon is also ordained through the laying on of hands. This may likewise be seen in the *Apostolic Constitutions*, Book VIII, chapter 21.

### 4.

It should be noted that the subdeacon, after receiving the Blessing, immediately stands before the sacred doors. The guardianship of these doors, which was formerly entrusted to deacons among the Greeks, as is known from Saint Dionysius, chapter 5 of the *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, is now believed to be entrusted to subdeacons. This was also customary in the time of Saint Maximus, as is clear from his scholia on Saint Dionysius: “Σημείωσαι, ὅτι οἱ Διάκονοι τότε τὰς θύρας εἶχον, νῦν δὲ οἱ ὑποδιάκονοι,” that is:

> Note that at that time the deacons had charge of the doors, but now the subdeacons do so.

The sacred doors here are the doors of the screen enclosing the sanctuary, as may be gathered from the ordination of a presbyter.

### 5.

Note that the deacon, at his ordination, bends his right knee, according to Saint Dionysius, chapter 5 of the *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*. Whether the other knee should also be bent there, however, is not expressly stated.

### 6.

It should be noted that *diaconica* are certain verses which we call prayers and which are sung by deacons. They are also called *eirenika* (εἰρηνικά), that is, “peace-prayers.” In the Liturgy of the Presanctified, after the words “and to them also,” the following is said: “λέγονται καὶ ταῦτα τὰ διακονικὰ, ἤγουν εἰρηνικὰ,” that is:

> These diaconica, that is, peace-prayers, are also recited.

That the peace-prayers are customarily said by deacons is clear from the Liturgy of Saint John Chrysostom. Below, in the ordination of a bishop, the diaconica are said by bishops, because they pertain to the ordination of a bishop.

### 7.

It should be observed that the word “worthy” is also proclaimed at the coronation of the emperor, according to Codinus in his *Book on the Offices of the Court*.

### 8.

The flabellum is given to the deacon because, among the Greeks, while the sacred mysteries are celebrated, the deacons move over them flabella fashioned from feathers, as a symbol of the six wings of the holy seraphim.

Jobius, Book V, chapter 25, adds that those attending the sacred ministers “ῥιπίδας πτερῶν πεποιημένας τοῖς προκειμένοις φρικτοῖς ἐπικινεῖν,” that is:

> Moreover, when the Lord’s Body has been placed upon the holy table, those who stand on either side assisting at the sacred rites move over the dreadful mysteries set before them flabella made of feathers, as a symbol of the six-winged beings, so that they may not allow the initiated to linger over things seen, etc.

This is in the *Bibliotheca of Photius*, no. 222.

Saint Germanus of Constantinople, in his *Mystical Theory*, says: “Ριπίδες εἰς τύπον εἰσὶ τῶν χερουβὶμ,” that is:

> The flabella are figures of the cherubim.

And below: “Τὰ δὲ ῥιπίδια καὶ οἱ διάκονοι ἐμφαίνουσι τὰ ἑξαπτέρυγα Σεραφὶμ,” that is:

> The flabella and the deacons signify the six-winged seraphim and the many-eyed likeness of the cherubim, etc.

John Moschus, chapter 96, speaking of certain shepherd boys in a village called Thorax, in the region of Apamea in the second Syria, who imitated the celebration of the divine mysteries, writes:

> One of them, acting in the office of priest, stood in the middle; two others stood on either side like deacons. The first recited the words of the holy offering, while the others “οἱ δὲ τοῖς φακιολίοις ἐῤῥίπιζον,” that is, made a breeze with little strips of cloth, as though they were flabella.

In chapter 150, speaking of a certain bishop celebrating the divine mysteries before Saint Agapetus, the Roman pontiff, he says:

> “Πλὴν τὸν διάκονον τὸν κατέχοντα τὸ ῥιπίδιον”: But remove from the altar the deacon holding the flabellum, etc.

Here note that the use of this flabellum once existed at Rome.

The *Life of Saint Epiphanius*, in Metaphrastes, says:

> “Πρῶτον ἐπέχει τῷ ἐξ ἀριστερῶν διακόνῳ τῷ ῥιπιστήριον διακρατοῦντι τὸ λειτουργικὸν”: First he watches the deacon on the left, who holds the liturgical flabellum.

The *Alexandrian Chronicle* mentions the matter under Olympiad 351:

> In this year, in the month of Artemisius, which is May among the Romans, in the twelfth indiction, under Sergius, patriarch of Constantinople, singing began after they had received the sacred mysteries, “ἐν τῷ μέλλειν τοὺς κληρικοὺς ἐπὶ τὸ σκευοφυλάκιον ἀποκαθιστάναι τὰ τίμια ῥιπίδια,” that is, while the clergy were about to return the venerable flabella to the sacristy.

The practice appears in the Liturgy of Saint John Chrysostom:

> “Καὶ ῥιπίζει ἐπάνω τῶν ἁγίων μετὰ ῥιπιδίου εὐλαβῶς”: And he reverently fans the holy things with the flabellum.

Note here that the deacon is understood.

### 9.

It should be determined what the *solea* is in the ordination of a presbyter and deacon: ἡ σωλέα, ὁ σωλέας, τὸ σωλέον, and σολείον. This name is written in various ways. Some explain it as the more elevated pavement of the church; some as the choir; others as the throne.

I, however, think it is the pavement of the church before the doors of the sanctuary, between the choir and the sanctuary in which the altar stands.

[Col. 0512B]

This is apparent from the following passage of the *Euchologion*: two deacons come out from the sanctuary and lead the man who is to be ordained presbyter, standing in the *solea*, as far as the sacred doors. From there two priests take him and, together with him, go around the holy table.

In Codinus, in the *Book on the Offices of the Court*, it is said that the emperor descends from the ambon on the side that leads toward the *solea* and the holy altar.

It is a more elevated pavement of the church, raised and adorned with beautiful stones. In the great church of Constantinople it was paved with onyx stone, as is clear from Cedrenus.

### 10.

It should be determined what the *protopapa* is. According to Codinus, he is the *ekdikos*, “the defender,” and the first of the *bēma*, “the altar,” and he “holds the second place after the high priest”:

> The defender, the first of the altar, and holding the second place after the high priest.

He is the protopapa of the Church. For the emperor also had his own protopapa, as Codinus teaches in his *Book on the Offices of Constantinople*:

> For the emperor has a protopapa for his clergy, and the Church also has one.

Sometimes, however, one protopapa presided over both clergies, says the same Codinus.

### 11.

It should be determined what the *kontakion* is. Arcudius interprets *kontakion* as the liturgy recited by the newly ordained man together with the other priests who are present.

But *kontakion* has two meanings. First, it means a tome or volume. Manuel Moschopulus, in his *On Notes*, says:

> *Tomos*: a volume, the *kontakion*.

Hence Codinus, in his *Book on the Offices of the Court*, speaking of the hieromnemōn, says:

> The volume in which the ordinations are contained.

Second, it is a certain kind of hymn, as is clear from the same book of Codinus:

> Singing afterward the *kontakion*: “The Virgin today,” etc.

### 12.

As regards the ordination of a bishop, no position is assigned to the candidate—whether he should sit, stand, or bend his knees. In former times he bent both feet, as is clear from Saint Dionysius, chapter 5, *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, and from Saint Gregory Nazianzen, in the funeral oration for his father. Speaking of his father’s baptism, Gregory says that many observed an omen of his future episcopal dignity in the fact that, according to the custom of those being baptized, he did not stand at all but bent his knees, as bishops customarily do when they are ordained.

But the ancient custom has changed. Saint Maximus also observes this in commenting on Saint Dionysius’s words, “both feet,” when he says:

> Now it is performed differently.

But the ancient custom has changed. Saint Maximus also observes this in commenting on Saint Dionysius’s words, “ἄμφω τὼ πόδε,” that is, “both feet,” when he says, “νῦν ἑτέρως ἐπιτελεῖται,” that is:

> Now it is performed differently.

Therefore I am surprised that Peter Arcudius added to his translation the words “bringing his forehead to the sacred altar, he bends both knees,” since they are not found in the Greek text that he cites, nor in the old Venetian edition that we used.

[Col. 0513A]

### 13.

From Codinus, in the book cited, near the beginning, one should learn what the chartophylax is:

> The chartophylax, who holds the ecclesiastical paper documents relating to rights, etc.

That is, he has the written records pertaining to ecclesiastical rights; he is judge of all ecclesiastical cases, hears matrimonial cases, and is the defender in the other cases of clerics, “ὡς δεξιὰ τῆς Αρχιερέως χεὶρ,” that is, “like the right hand of the high priest.”

14. What the *ὠμοφόριον*, or shoulder-vestment, is must be considered. It is an ornament common to all bishops, whatever their rank, resembling elongated towels. Among patriarchs and archbishops it signifies the stole of Aaron, arranged around the left shoulder, and the yoke of Christ’s commandments. Among bishops, however, it signifies the lost sheep whom the Lord carried back upon his shoulders. It bears crosses because Christ carried the cross upon his shoulders; and those who wish to imitate Christ take up the cross upon their shoulders, which signifies endurance of adversity. Thus teaches Saint Germanus, patriarch of Constantinople, in his *Mystical Theory*. Saint Isidore of Pelusium mentions it in Book I, Letter 136: “The bishop’s *ὠμοφόριον*, being made of wool but not of linen, signifies the skin of the wandering sheep,” that is, it signifies the skin of the wandering sheep whom the Lord lifted upon his shoulders. It is mentioned in the Synod at the Oak, in Photius’s *Bibliotheca*, no. 59, where Saint John Chrysostom is accused of having summoned the three deacons Acacius, Edaphius, and John on the charge that they had “stolen his *ὠμοφόριον*.”

15. It should be observed that formerly, when a bishop-elect was signed, it was customary to say: “N. is signed from presbyter as bishop, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” Likewise at the ordination of a presbyter and deacon, as Saint Maximus teaches in his scholia on chapter 5 of Saint Dionysius. These words, however, do not occur in the *Euchologion*. Saint Maximus calls them an *αὐάρρησις*, that is, a kind of proclamation made in the person’s name. Such signings are taken from Saint Dionysius, in the chapter cited.

16. These words should be noted: “The divine grace,” etc. Their use is sufficiently ancient, since Saint Maximus mentions them in the chapter of Saint Dionysius cited above. He calls this a recitation, when during the ordination he pronounces: “ἡ θεῖα χάρις προχειρεῖται τόνδε εἰς τόνδε”—that is, “Divine grace promotes this man who is being ordained to this rank.”

17. These words should be noted: “for the servant of God.” Formerly the wording was different, as is clear from the same Maximus in the chapter cited. He describes the declaration made during ordinations, for example, at the ordination of a bishop: “For this holy father,” namely, the bishop. For a presbyter: “For this presbyter.” For a deacon: “For this our brother, the deacon.” That is: “For the holy Father, Bishop N.; for Presbyter N.; for our brother N., the deacon.”

18. Note that the greeting frequently mentioned here, [p. 526], is not an ordinary greeting, but one made with an embrace as an expression of friendship. For *ἀσπάζεσθαι* does not simply mean “to greet,” but “to be joined through friendship,” with an embrace, as the old etymological lexicon says. Therefore, as Saint Dionysius says in chapter 5 of the *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, from which this greeting has been borrowed, such a greeting signifies sacred communion and the loving joy of minds harmoniously united.

19. It should be observed that this *Euchologion* contains no anointings in the ordinations of a bishop or presbyter. I believe this occurred because it follows Saint Dionysius very closely: in the chapter repeatedly cited, he makes no mention of anointing in these ordinations. Nevertheless, anointing seems formerly to have been used even among the Greeks, since the Saint Gregory Nazianzenus and Saint John Chrysostom cited above mention it—unless one prefers to say that they were speaking according to the mystical sense.

785. *Prayer for making an abbot.* In the blessing of an abbot, the imposition of hands is not used, but only a simple prayer, as Ivo of Chartres teaches in Letter 57: “What, then, is there to dispute about in the blessing of an abbot, from whatever bishop he may have received it, in which there is neither imposition of hands nor consecration, but only a simple prayer,” etc. This does not differ from the Roman rite, although that rite adds certain ceremonies, which may be seen there; in that context, however, “consecration” is understood more broadly as “blessing.”

Thus it is in the Latin Church; it is otherwise in the Greek Church. There the abbot is appointed through the imposition of the bishop’s hands, as appears from canon 14 of the Seventh Synod: “The imposition of hands upon a reader may be performed in his own monastery even by the head of each individual monastery alone, if the head himself has received from a bishop the imposition of hands for the presidency or dignity of an abbot,” etc.—that is, provided that it is established that he is a presbyter.

786. *Apologies begin.* Here “apology” means an excuse and a purification, by which the priest excuses himself because he approaches mysteries so venerable and awe-inspiring while unworthy. The old manuscript glossaries say: “*Apologia*, or *apologesis*: excuse.” Hence *apologeticus* means “excusing.” The old Greco-Latin glossaries give *ἀπολογία*: “excuse, purification, satisfaction.” “Satisfaction” here means “excuse,” as in Saint Ambrose, Sermon 46: “Therefore Peter burst into tears, praying nothing in words. I find that he wept; I do not find what he said. I read his tears; I do not read his satisfaction.
