Peter rightly wept and remained silent, because what is ordinarily mourned is not ordinarily excused; and what cannot be defended can be washed away.” These words clearly show that “satisfaction” is taken for “excuse.” For Adam, who excused himself, is contrasted there with Saint Peter, who did not excuse himself but wept. The verb *ἀπολογοῦμαι* is likewise glossed: “I excuse myself.”

Accordingly, in the Codex of Rodrade the term is sometimes *apologia* and sometimes *excusatio*. The priest used to say these and similar apologies during the Mass before the Offertory and Consecration, and more rarely afterward, while the choir was singing, as may be seen above in the Mass of the Tilian Codex.

In the published codices and in Rodrade’s Codex several apologies are found, but fewer than in this Codex. The first in Rodrade’s Codex bears this title: “The blessed Ambrose composed this prayer; and before celebrating Mass he used to sing it while asking pardon for his sins, as follows,” beginning: “Before the sight of your divine Majesty I stand guilty,” etc., as in the Tilian Codex, although some readings vary. There it is also recited before the Offertory. This is how Rodrade’s title should be understood when it says that this prayer was customarily recited by Saint Ambrose before Mass. For the Mass properly begins with the Offertory, as is clear from Saint Ambrose himself, Book V, Letter 33, to Marcellina:

“On the following day (it was Sunday), after the readings and the tract, when the catechumens had been dismissed, I was delivering the Creed in the baptisteries of the basilica to certain candidates for baptism. There I was informed that, having learned that the Arians had sent decans from the palace to the Porciana basilica and were hanging curtains, and that part of the people were going there, I nevertheless remained at my post and began to celebrate Mass. While I was offering, I learned that a certain Castulus, whom the Arians called a presbyter, had been seized by the people.”

Here you see that the Mass begins after the catechumens have been dismissed and the Creed has been delivered to them; yet they were dismissed only after the Gospel had been read. The candidates are those catechumens who were seeking baptism, concerning whom the preceding discussion was held.

787. *The duty of ministering impels me*, etc. This apology, in the Mass published by Matthias Flacius Illyricus, is recited by the bishop together with several others while the choir sings the Gradual, Alleluia, and Sequence. There it reads: “The sinner impels me.”

788. *A saving victim.* The passage is corrupt. Read it, as in Illyricus’s Mass: “to offer a saving victim”; the sense is then clear.

789. *Peripsema.* This is how it appears in Illyricus’s Mass; it is an *antiptosis*, for it should read *peripsemate*. He explains what *peripsema* is. Hesychius gives these words: “*περίψημα*, *περικατάμαγμα*, *ἀντίλυτρα*, *ἀντίψυχα*, or what is beneath everyone’s feet”—that is, refuse or filth, the price of redemption, an expiatory offering, or that which lies beneath everyone’s footsteps and is trampled under all feet. The old manuscript glossaries of the Corbie Library say: “*Peripsema*: metal filings, fruit refuse, household rubbish, and shavings of anything.” Here it is used, as formerly by Saint Paul, for something worthless and despised.

790. *Lest I be unworthy.* In Illyricus’s Mass it reads: “lest I be unworthy.”

791. *Suspend the axe.* In the same Mass it reads: “I beg you, by the intercession of these and by the merits of all the saints, suspend *securum*”; but read *securim* (“axe”) in both places.

792. *Clearly.* Read *propitious*, as in Illyricus’s Mass.

[Col. 0515B] 793. *While the confessor is on the cross, the possessor.* This is a *paronomasia*.

794. *So that because.* In Illyricus’s Mass it reads: “but because.”

795. *Before your eyes, O Lord*, etc. This apology occurs in the Mass of the Tilian Codex. There it is said by the priest or bishop after the Gospel has ended, while the altar is being prepared, before the priest receives the offerings of those presenting them. It occurs twice in Matthias Illyricus’s Mass. The first time it is recited between the Epistle and the Gospel, together with certain other prayers; the second time, after the altar has been prepared and before the priest receives the offerings of those presenting them. It is found in Rodrade’s Codex and in the published editions.

796. *I scarcely dare.* In Illyricus’s Mass it reads: “I do not dare.”

797. *For you, O Lord, know everything that is done in us.* In Illyricus’s Mass it reads: “You know, O Lord, what is done in us.”

798. *We are ashamed to confess*, etc. Ovid has the same thought in the *Epistles*:

> What it delights us to have done, we are ashamed to report.

799. *Through us.* This is absent from Illyricus’s Mass and from the Tilian Codex.

800. *To admit.* In Rodrade’s Codex it reads: “to be admitted.”

801. *Spare, O Lord, those who confess*, etc. In the Tilian and Illyrican Masses it reads: “But spare, O Lord, those who confess; forgive sinners; have mercy on those who ask you.” In the first of Illyricus’s versions, however, *confidentibus* (“those who trust”) is found instead of *confitentibus* (“those who confess”), and *praying* instead of *sinners*.

802. *He is infirm.* In the Tilian and Illyrican Masses these words are added: “And before you sinners have no words free from guilt.”

803. *So that whoever is from us.* In the aforementioned Masses it reads: “We who are among the unworthy and sinful.” In the first Illyrican version, *and sinful* is lacking.

804. *Through you for us.* In Illyricus’s Mass it reads: “through yourself, forgiveness,” etc. In the Tilian Codex: “through yourself for us,” etc.

805. *Through the Lord.* In Illyricus’s Mass: “Who live and reign,” etc. In the Tilian Mass: “Who live and reign, O God, now and forever, and world without end.”

806. *Trembling in conscience*, etc. In Illyricus’s Mass this prayer is recited after the altar has been prepared, before the priest receives the offerings of those presenting them. It is absent from the Tilian Mass, the Mass of Abbot Ratoldus, Rodrade’s Codex, and the published editions.

807. *But if we withdraw.* In Illyricus’s Mass it reads: “Yet if we withdraw,” which seems to be the better reading.

808. *For which reason deign to*, etc. In Illyricus’s Mass it reads: “For which reason, almighty God, may you, in paternal goodness and with a gracious countenance, deign to cleanse the inner places of our hearts.”

809. *Although we are burdened by the guilt of sins*, etc. In Illyricus’s Mass this is contracted and corruptly written: “We also pray that, although we are guilty, our mysteries nevertheless pleasing to you may be consecrated.” For *our* is redundant there, and *consecrated* is not correctly read, since when this prayer is recited by the bishop the mysteries have not yet been consecrated but are still to be consecrated.

810. *Forgive, O Lord, forgive.* In the Tilian Codex this prayer is recited by the priest after the Collect, from the altar until the Gospel, according to his preference. In Illyricus’s Mass it is recited while the people are receiving Communion: “Meanwhile, while they communicate, let him say: ‘Forgive, O Lord.’” In the aforementioned Masses, *forgive* is not repeated. This apology is found in Rodrade’s Codex.

811. *When I am compelled to ask.* Thus in Illyricus’s Mass. In the Tilian Codex: “when I am compelled to ask you.”

812. *And with shameful deeds.* In the Tilian Mass it reads: “So that with shameful deeds,” etc. In Illyricus’s Mass: “and with unclean deeds.”

813. *I have nothing before you, not even words free from guilt.* In the Tilian Codex it reads: “For I have before you,” etc. In Illyricus’s Mass the particle *not even* is absent.

814. *And of thoughts.* In Illyricus’s Mass it reads: “you, of thoughts.”

[Col. 0516B] 815. *Through our Lord Jesus.* In Illyricus’s Mass it reads: “Savior, have mercy on me.” In the Tilian Mass: “Savior of the world, who lives”; read *you live*. In Rodrade’s Codex: “Savior of the world, who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, live and reign forever and ever. Amen.”

816. *I beseech you, God of Sabaoth*, etc. This apology is absent from Illyricus’s Mass, the published editions, the Tilian Codex, and our other manuscript codices.

817. *Uti.* That is, *ut* (“so that”).

818. *Before the presence of the eternal King*, etc. This apology too is absent from Illyricus’s Mass and from the other codices cited above.

819. *He is tormented by envy.* That is, “he wastes away.”

820. *May he deliver us*, etc. This apology and the next two occur in the published editions, under the same titles. This first one, however, is absent from Illyricus’s Mass, the Tilian Codex, and our other manuscript codices.

[Col. 0516C] 821. *By the goads of a biting conscience*, etc. This apology is said in Illyricus’s Mass during the Gradual, Alleluia, and Sequence. It is absent from the Tilian Codex and from our other manuscript codices.

822. *You.* In Illyricus’s Mass, omitting the pronoun *you*, it reads: “the Lord.”

823. *It is a sin.* In the same Mass it reads: “we have sinned.”

824. *Committed.* In the same Mass it reads: “we have committed.”

825. *May he deign to release and forgive.* In the same Mass: “May he deign to loose and pardon.” After this, the following words occur in the same Mass: “So that, with you, O Lord, giving assent, we may be able to avoid what is evil and consequently accomplish what is good. And because you have made us belong to your sacraments, mercifully perform their gift in us, and forgive all who have gone astray according to the greatness of your mercy.”

826. *Me, unworthy, O Lord*, etc. This prayer is recited in Illyricus’s Mass, together with several others, after the bishop has completed the Confession at the altar. It is also found in Ratoldus’s Mass, where it is recited as soon as the bishop has approached the altar.

827. *What I [am] you with flattering [words].* Thus in Ratoldus’s Codex. In Illyricus’s Mass it reads: “For he who approaches you with flattering words.”

828. *You thrust yourself upon me.* In Illyricus’s Mass and in Ratoldus’s Codex, *the sick man* is added.

829. *To my health.* In Illyricus’s Mass *unceasingly* is added.

830. *I withdraw.* In Illyricus’s Mass the following is added: “As though I were worthy, I display myself in the eyes of men; but in your sight, which hidden things do not deceive, I am defiled and filthy with various crimes. But it is yours, O Lord God, to give the sinner a contrite heart and a fountain of tears, by which I may worthily wash away the multitude of my crimes.”

831. *To erase that cloud quickly.* Thus in our manuscript Codex of Saint Eligius, but between *that* and *quickly* there appear traces of two erased letters *M*. In the published editions it reads: “to erase the cloud quickly.” In Illyricus’s Mass, more correctly: “to erase it quickly as a cloud.” In Ratoldus’s Codex: “to erase it quickly as snow,” which is excellent.

832. *So that I, who have lost this palm*, etc. In Ratoldus’s Codex it reads: “and although I have lost the palm.” Thus also in Illyricus’s Mass, in which, however, *of innocence* is added.

833. *May I at least attain forgiveness*, etc. In Ratoldus’s Codex it reads: “may I arrive.” In Illyricus’s Mass: “May I at least, through confession, deserve forgiveness, by your mercy.”

834. *For to you, God, belongs*, etc. In Illyricus’s Mass it reads: “So that glory, praise, and honor may belong to you, who rule all things, forever and ever. Amen.”

835. *With us prostrate*, etc. This apology, together with many others, is recited by the bishop or priest in Illyricus’s Mass during the Gradual, Alleluia, and Sequence—that is, between the Epistle and the Gospel.

836. *Because it belongs to you.* In Illyricus’s Mass the conjunction *and* is placed before it, more correctly.

837. *We bear.* In Illyricus’s Mass it reads: “we have borne,” more correctly.

[Col. 0517B] 838. *Let there be in us, O Lord*, etc. In Illyricus’s Mass this is worded differently: “Grant that in us confession may not be only of the lips but also of the heart.”

839. *For chaste*, etc. In Illyricus’s Mass it reads: “since chaste.”

840. *Pure.* This word is absent from Illyricus’s Mass.

841. *Conduct.* In Illyricus’s Mass it reads: “conduct is.”

842. *Anxiety of the flesh.* In Illyricus’s Mass it reads: “earthly anxiety.”

843. *Give forgiveness for past things*, etc. In Illyricus’s Mass it reads: “And give forgiveness for past evils, amendment for present ones, and caution for future ones, you who live,” etc.

844. *Thus, O Lord, guilty of an immense crime.* This apology is absent from the published editions, the Masses of Illyricus, Ratoldus, and the Tilian Codex, and from Rodrade’s Codex.

845. *Nor from your face.* Read: “not from your face.”

846. *Whatever.* Read: “whomever.”

847. *Another one in tribulation.* This apology is recited by the bishop or priest in Illyricus’s Mass during the Gradual, Alleluia, and Sequence. It was recently published by order of Pope Urban VIII, but is approximately half as long. It is absent from the published Sacramentaries, the Tilian Codex, and our other manuscript codices.

848. *If before your eyes*, etc. Thus in Illyricus’s Mass. In the published edition it is worded more fully as follows: “Before your eyes, O Lord, we set forth our faults; and we compare the wounds we have received, if we consider the evil we have done,” etc.

849. *And let us compare the wounds that we suffer.* In Illyricus’s Mass it reads: “Let us compare the wounds, however severe, that we can suffer in this life.”

850. *What we deserve.* In the published edition the following is added: “What we have committed is more serious; what we endure is lighter.”

851. *It is broken.* In the published edition it reads: “it is worn away.”

852. *And in deed.* In Illyricus’s Mass it reads: “and yet in deed.”

853. *Does not amend.* Thus in Illyricus’s Mass, and this phrase occurs more than once in the Rule of Saint Benedict. In the published edition it reads: “does not amend himself.”

854. *If you await.* Thus in the published edition. In Illyricus’s Mass it reads: “if we are awaited.”

855. *In correction.* Thus in Illyricus’s Mass. In the published edition it reads: “in correction.”

856. *If you have impressed [it].* Thus in Illyricus’s Mass. In the published edition it reads: “if you have extended.”

857. *If you spare.* In the published edition it reads: “if you have spared.” In Illyricus’s Mass: “if you spare.”

858. *We provoke you.* Thus in Illyricus’s Mass. In the published editions the pronoun *you* is absent.

859. *If troubles come*, etc. Thus in Illyricus’s Mass. In the published edition this passage is absent up to the words: “You have, O Lord, those who confess themselves guilty.”

860. *We do not fear to observe.* The particle *not* appears redundant. In Illyricus’s Mass it reads: “we do not fear to neglect,” which is correct.

[Col. 0518A] 861. *We know.* In Illyricus’s Mass it reads: “we have vowed,” incorrectly.

862. *May you punish us.* Thus in Illyricus’s Mass. In the published edition it reads: “may you not destroy”; but read “may you punish us.”

863. *From nothing.* This is absent from Illyricus’s Mass.

864. *Who might ask.* In Illyricus’s Mass it reads: “to whom they might ask,” which is not as correct. In the published edition: “who might ask you”; the text ends with this word.

865. *Suppliants for your help.* From here through the words “raise us up, O Lord,” this passage is absent from Illyricus’s Mass.

866. *What you are asked to receive.* That is, “what they ask to receive from you,” namely, the remission of sins.

867. *From your justice.* They fear it greatly because of the gravity and multitude of their sins. Or certainly one should read: “from their own justice.”

868. *Of those ruling all things.* The passage is corrupt; read: “of all nations,” as in Illyricus’s Mass.

869. *Forgive, O Lord*, etc. This apology occurs in Illyricus’s Mass and is recited by the bishop or priest after the altar has been prepared and before he receives the offerings.

[Col. 0518B] 870. *With the filth of a stained conscience.* In Illyricus’s Mass it reads: “Whom the conscience of a stained life made fearful and the confusion of my crimes made captive.”

871. *Who deserve nothing by which to obtain anything for me.* In Illyricus’s Mass it reads: “who am unable to obtain forgiveness for me.”

872. *The distresses of the poor.* These words are absent from Illyricus’s Mass.

873. *The lamentations of widows.* In Illyricus’s Mass *the desolations of churches* is added.

874. *And since in the same*, etc. In Illyricus’s Mass it reads: “But since the same chain of sin binds me, as it does the people.”

875. *I mourn the sufferings we share.* In Illyricus’s Mass it reads: “Therefore I mourn all sufferings.” The earlier reading, however, seems preferable.

876. *A vow.* That is, a sacred and divine prayer.

877. *God, to whom one approaches*, etc. This apology is absent from Illyricus’s Mass and from the Tilian Codex, as well as from the published editions and our other manuscript codices.

878. *Forgive, O God*, etc. This apology is recited in Illyricus’s Mass by the bishop or priest between the Epistle and the Gospel—that is, during the Gradual, Alleluia, and Sequence. It is prefaced there by the title: “Prayer of the shepherd, to be said for himself and for his subjects.”

879. *God.* In Illyricus’s Mass it reads: “Lord God almighty.”

880. *Everlasting.* Here *perennare* is used transitively, that is, “to perpetuate,” or “to cause something to endure forever.” Alcimus’s epitaph reads:

> Whom piety, whom generous faith, whom fame makes everlasting.

Elsewhere it is used intransitively. Tertullian, in *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, says: “But also to make the teeth endure incorrupt.” Here there is a hypallage, for “May the proclamation of truth in my mouth be everlasting.” In Illyricus’s Mass it reads: “by weapons,” but the earlier reading is preferable.

881. *May you justify.* In Illyricus’s Mass it reads: “may you sanctify,” which amounts to the same thing.

[Col. 0518D] 882. *You look upon.* In Illyricus’s Mass the word *is* is found. The earlier reading, however, seems preferable, since *you inspect* follows, producing an elegant *paronomasia*.

883. *If any*, etc. In Illyricus’s Mass it reads: “If any offenses have arisen through the fault of my lukewarmness or negligence, graciously receive them.” But *receive* is corrupt and should read *omit*, that is, “forgive,” as in our Codex. For *omitto* means “I forgive,” as noted above. Alternatively, one should read *amitte*, that is, “remove, drive away, banish,” as in Terence.

884. *Or having known.* Read: “or knowing.” In Illyricus’s Mass it reads: “or knowing.”

885. *Forgive.* In Illyricus’s Mass it reads: “Take it away from there by the hand of your mercy.”

886. *And the rebuke itself.* In Illyricus’s Mass the words *and itself* are absent.

887. *Mortals.* This is an apparent solecism. In Illyricus’s Mass it reads: “to mortals.”

[Col. 0519A] 888. *Of both parties.* Both those to whom I gave an occasion for sin and those whom I subjected to the laws of repentance.

889. *And who.* In Illyricus’s Mass it reads: “and because.”

890. *Flaming.* In Illyricus’s Mass it reads: “to flame.”

891. *So that they may also profit from disciplines*, etc. In Illyricus’s Mass it reads: “So that they may gain profit from the discipline of our governance.”

892. *Let us rejoice.* In Illyricus’s Mass it reads: “we rejoice.”

893. *Cleanse us, O God*, etc. In Illyricus’s Mass it reads: “Cleanse us, almighty God, from both another’s offense and our own.”

894. *Prayers for visiting the sick.* The visitation or anointing of the sick, which they call extreme unction, is the final sacrament of Christian law. By its benefit the soul is fortified against the attacks of the evil demon in its final struggle, sins are forgiven, and sometimes bodily health is restored. It is proclaimed by Saint James, in chapter 5 of his Epistle: “Is anyone among you sick? Let him bring in the presbyters of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord,” etc.

Formerly Christians showed the greatest care in visiting the sick. Tertullian lists such visitation among the three reasons for going out in public, in Book II of *On the Apparel of Women*: “For you there is no reason for going out that is not solemn: either some brother who is weak is being visited, or a sacrifice is being offered, or the word of God is being proclaimed.” He also recalls it in Book II *To His Wife*: “The sick person is visited freely; the needy person is supported.”

Innocent I discusses this anointing in his letter to Decentius of Gubbio, where he notes that the sacrament is not conferred upon penitents, because, as he teaches, no sacrament is given to penitents. Later, however, the practice changed, as is clear from Ivo of Chartres, Letter 257: “For the anointing of the sick is a sacrament of public penance.” Ivo nevertheless wrote these words according to the custom of his own time.

Burchard, in Book XVIII, chapter 2, discusses this sacrament on the authority of a decree of Pope Callixtus. But the citation is corrupt. For this decree cannot be understood as belonging to Callixtus I, since Innocent I is mentioned there, who flourished long after Callixtus I; nor can it belong to Callixtus II, who lived approximately a hundred years after Burchard. For Burchard was made bishop of Worms in the year 1008, as Sigebert teaches in his *Chronicle*, whereas Callixtus II was elected supreme pontiff in the year 1120, as Abbot Anselm teaches in his supplement to Sigebert. Therefore, in Burchard, instead of the words “from the decree of Pope Callixtus,” one should read “from Bede”; for what is cited here may be found in Bede’s commentary on the Epistle of the holy apostle James.

895. *Let them sprinkle it.* As soon as the priest approaches to visit the sick person, he sprinkles him and the house itself with holy water, as appears in the Council of Nantes, canon 4: “When the priest hears that someone in his parish has fallen ill, let him go to him as quickly as possible, and upon entering the room let him sprinkle blessed water over him and throughout the room.” The same is found in Burchard, Book XVIII, chapter 1.

This is also sufficiently clear from Alcuin’s words, in the chapter on the sick: “Whenever someone falls ill, the brothers enter to the sick person with blessed water and with candles or incense before the holy oil.” It is likewise clear from Rodrade’s Codex: “First, let the priests prepare blessed water and sprinkle it over the sick person and his house, with an antiphon and prayer. Then let the priest say this prayer: ‘O Lord God, who spoke through your apostle,’” etc. In Ratoldus’s Codex there are other ceremonies, which we shall present below.

896. *With an antiphon and prayers.* Namely: “Sprinkle me, O Lord, with hyssop,” etc.; Verse: “Let God arise,” etc. Then he says the prayer “O God, who have granted such great grace to your priests,” as it appears in the council cited and in Burchard, in the same chapter. There, as soon as the priest enters the sick person’s house, he must say: “Peace to this house and to all who dwell in it.”

897. *Exorcism of salt.* The salt is exorcised so that it may be mixed with blessed water, as noted above: “First, let the priests make blessed water after salt has been sprinkled into it.” The following prayers for the exorcism and blessing of salt and water are also found in the second part of Rodrade’s Codex. In them, as here, the customary crosses are not added. This surprises me, since it is an ancient custom of the Church to bless water with the sign of the cross, as appears in Saint Epiphanius, Book I *Against Heresies*, volume II, in the section on Joseph the Count: “And when he had ordered water to be brought, and had taken a vessel of water before everyone, that man, having placed the sign of the cross upon the vessel with his own finger and having invoked the name of Jesus,” etc. Theodoret likewise says in Book V of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 21: “Having spoken these and similar words, and having marked the water with the form of the cross.”

898. *Blessing of a grape.* See what was noted above.

899. *Favae.* This is written for *fabae* (“beans”); in older manuscript codices *v* is often written in place of *b*.

900. *Blessing of bread.* Concerning blessed bread, see our observations on the *Concordia of Rules*, chapter 71, section 1.

901. *For the cutting of the hair.* Supply “to be cut,” a phrase found in the Roman Order. This tonsure is not the clerical tonsure discussed above, but that of boys, when their hair was cut for the first time. For the Sacramentaries contain other prayers for the clerical tonsure.

902. *Almighty and eternal God*, etc. Thus in the codices of Rodrade and Ratoldus. In the Roman Order two other prayers precede this one.

903. *And to be a fellowship of heavenly gifts, of commandments.* Thus in Rodrade’s Codex. In the first part, I think one should read *perceptorem* (“recipient”). In Ratoldus’s Codex and in the Roman Order it reads: “And to attain a share in heavenly gifts.”

904. *Prayer for cutting the beard.* That is, at the first cutting of a young man’s beard. This same prayer occurs in the Rheims and Ratoldus codices and in the Roman Order.

905. *Prayer for anointing a sick person.* This prayer is repeated below; nor does this seem to be its proper place.

906. *O God, who [did something for] your servant Hezekiah*, etc. This prayer and those that follow occur in Burchard, Book XVIII, near the end, after the anointing has been administered. The published Sacramentaries contain only the first three.

907. *O God, who spoke through your apostle.* This prayer is found in Rodrade’s Codex.

908. *And thus let him bend the knee.* Thus in the codices of Rodrade and Tilianus. In the manuscript Roman Order of the Corbie Codex it reads: “Then let the sick man stand at the priest’s right and bend his knees.”

909. *The Lord has spoken.* Thus in Rodrade’s Codex. In the Tilian Codex certain other words precede it. In Rodrade’s Codex the following comes afterward: “Here let all the priests and their ministers lay their hands upon the sick person. Verse: ‘God of gods,’” etc.

This imposition of hands also seems to occur in the Tilian Codex: “Let all the priests lay their hands upon the sick person, at the command or at least with the permission of the bishop, because the canonical order teaches this.”

Note here that several presbyters are present in the administration of this sacrament, in accordance with Saint James: “Let him bring in the presbyters of the Church.” This, however, is not so necessary that the sacrament cannot be conferred by a single priest. The practice of this appears to be found in the Council of Nantes cited above, chapter 4, in Burchard, Book XVIII, in the published Sacramentaries, and in Ratoldus’s Codex, which will be cited below. Simeon of Thessalonica nevertheless opposes this view; Peter Arcudius refutes him in Book V of *On Extreme Unction*, chapter 3.

910. *To the Lord, when I was in distress.* In Rodrade’s Codex the following is added: “And let it be repeated as before.” The prayer then follows: “O God, who [did something for] your servant Hezekiah,” etc.

911. *And thus let him anoint the sick person with consecrated oil, making crosses on the neck, throat*, etc. Thus in the Rodrade and Tilian codices.

“And while the sick person is being anointed, let one person say this prayer while supplicating.” Thus in Rodrade’s Codex. It should be noted that the priest who performs the anointing has the formula pronounced by another person. This supports the opinion of those who say that a baptism is valid if, while one person pronounces the words, another immerses the candidate or pours in the water.

### 912

“I anoint you with holy oil,” etc. Thus in the Codex of Rodrade. Formerly the form of this sacrament was indicative, as appears here (although it is called a “prayer,” improperly—for in truth it is not a prayer); this is also clearly established by the manuscript Codices of Ratoldus and of Tilianus, of the monastery of Saint Remigius, and by the printed Manual of the Church of Soissons, which have the indicative form and know nothing of the deprecatory form, as will be seen below. It is likewise established by the Ambrosian form cited by Saint Bonaventure, *In IV Sententiarum*, distinction 23, question 4:

“I anoint you with sanctified oil in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, so that, prepared for combat like an anointed soldier, you may be able to overcome the aerial powers.”

This form is also found below in the Codices of Ratoldus and Tilianus. Richard of Mediavilla, *In IV Sententiarum*, distinction 23, article 1, question 4, does not reject it, but merely says that the deprecatory form is more fitting because of the text of Saint James. Nor does he reject it in his response to the second objection, just as Bonaventure does not reject it in his response to the second objection, where he says:

“It is objected that the form is not the same. It must be answered that, insofar as what is necessary and essential to the sacrament is concerned, it must be the same; but the form of the word is not necessary by reason of the external utterance, but insofar as it expresses the interior word.”

Accordingly Durandus, using the same distinction, question 3, defends both forms problematically. After asserting the deprecatory form, he finally adds:

“If anyone wished to maintain that the indicative form, which Saint Ambrose—one of the early teachers—is said to have used, is valid, one could answer the arguments of the opposing side. For blessed James, when speaking of prayer, perhaps did not intend the sacramental form, but the supplication made through the preceding or following prayer, by which the sick person is commended to God and raised up before him.”

Paludanus likewise approves the same form, *In IV Sententiarum*, distinction 23, question 1:

“If certain Churches possess only the indicative form, as the Ambrosian Church did, at least in the time of Ambrose, as is said, it must not be asserted that nothing was accomplished.”

Aureolus too, *In IV Sententiarum*, distinction 23, article 1, although he does not mention this form, “I anoint you with holy oil,” etc., says that it may be indicative in this manner:

“Through this holy anointing the Lord spares you,” etc.

But concerning the form there is a question: why is it optative? I answer that in certain Churches the form is indicative, for example, “Through this holy anointing the Lord spares you.” In others it is imperative. But James’s words seem to have an optative form, for he says, “And the prayer of faith will save the sick person,” as though the form were expressed by an optative prayer. Therefore it must be said that the form of the words may indifferently be indicative or optative, just as the form of the baptismal words is indicative among the Latins but optative among the Greeks. Consequently custom must be observed in such matters, and anyone who changed the custom would sin gravely. Thus far Aureolus.

To this may be added the authority of the *Book of Sacraments* published from the Vatican Library, in which this single form may be found:

“I anoint you with holy oil, just as Samuel anointed David as king and prophet. Work, creature of oil, in the name of God the almighty Father, so that the unclean spirit may not lurk here, neither in your limbs, nor in your marrow, nor in any joining of your limbs, but that the power of Christ Most High and of the Holy Spirit may dwell in you. Through him.”

Nor does the theological faculty of Paris reject this form, as is clear from the theses of Louis de Machault, bachelor of the Sorbonne, prior of Saint Peter of Abbéville, debated on 13 February 1635 in the external schools of the Sorbonne for the major ordinary disputation, under the presidency of S. M. N. D. Stephen Tonnelier, doctor of Navarre, pastor of Saint-Eustache in Paris, and dedicated to His Eminence Cardinal de Richelieu, duke and peer of France. In their seventh proposition one reads:

“Even by a single anointing with oil in a case of necessity, and with indicative words uttered, it seems possible for it to be effected.”

The same is clear from the theses of Master Jacques Helyes, cited above, in which it is maintained that the form of extreme unction is indicative or deprecatory. For in the eighth proposition he says:

“The sacrament of extreme unction has as its matter a sacred anointing; its form is either indicative or deprecatory.”

Therefore the response of Peter Ledesma, chapter 3, concerning the form of this sacrament, is not valid when he says that the indicative form is merely a preamble to the sacrament of extreme unction. For the theologians cited, when they wrote these things, were not so foolish as to be unaware that, besides the indicative form, the Ambrosian Church had another, deprecatory form.

Moreover, just as no one would say that, when the person pouring the water says, “I baptize you,” etc., this form is a preamble to the sacrament of baptism, so it is absurd to say that, when the sick person is anointed with sanctified oil and the words “I anoint you,” etc., are uttered, such a form is merely something preliminary to extreme unction. Accordingly Durandus, in the question cited above, when he reports the rite of certain Churches that use both the indicative and deprecatory forms, did not say that the indicative form was a preamble to this sacrament. Later, when he reported the form of the Ambrosian Church, he did not reject it.

Nor does this doctrine conflict with the Council of Trent, when it says, Session 14, chapter 1, that the form consists of the words, “Through this anointing,” etc. The council does not establish the deprecatory form in such a way as to reject the indicative form, whose former use is clearer than daylight. Nor does it establish the words “through this anointing” in such a way as to destroy the form of the Greeks, which, although deprecatory, does not contain those words.

Finally, before I withdraw my hand from this subject, it should be noted that no form is found in Burchard, in the book cited. After the sick person’s responses to the priest’s questions, he adds:

“Afterward let him be anointed. After the confession, the profession of faith, and the anointing, let the antiphon *In veritate tua exaudi me, Domine* be said. Psalm: *Domine, exaudi orationem meam, auribus percipe.* Then *Kyrie eleison*, with the *Pater noster* and prayers,” etc.

### 913

“Lord God, our Savior,” etc. In the Codex of Rodrade this prayer is divided into two, and the second begins with these words: “Heal also, we beseech you, O physician of all.”

### 914

“May the Lord show favor,” etc. Thus in the Codex of Rodrade.

### 915

“Then let him communicate in the body and blood of the Lord.” Thus in the Codices of Rodrade, Ratoldus, Tilianus, Saint Remigius, and Saint-Germain-des-Prés, in which the Eucharist is given after the anointing itself. This is highly noteworthy, because formerly the sick person was anointed before receiving the viaticum of the Lord’s body and blood. This may be seen in the decree of Pope Eusebius in Burchard, Book XVIII, chapter 11, and in Ivo, Book XV, chapter 35:

“Let the priest carry out everything as it is written above concerning the penitent sick person; that is, let him say the prayers, anoint him with holy oil, and give him the Eucharist.”

It also appears from Theodore’s *Penitential* in Burchard, the same book, chapter 14, and Ivo, Book XV, chapter 36:

“And therefore, according to canonical authority, so that the door of mercy may not seem closed to them, let those who have been strengthened by sacred anointing with oil, according to the statutes of the holy Fathers, be refreshed by the communion of the viaticum through prayers and consolations.”

This practice seems to appear in the *Life of Charlemagne*, from Pithoeus’s edition:

“After Emperor Charles had been anointed with holy oil by the bishops, received the viaticum, and arranged all his affairs, he commended his spirit to the Lord and died in peace.”

In the *Life of Saint Otto, Archbishop of Bamberg*, Book III, chapter 45:

“Meanwhile the illness pressed ever more heavily upon his struggling spirit. After he had duly arranged everything that he could provide for those who would live after him, and had first made a humble and pure confession, he received the propitiatory viaticum, the body of the Lord, after being anointed with that gentle and sacred anointing of holy oil.”

Arnold of Lübeck, *History of the Slavs*, Book III, chapter 3, concerning the death of Saint Henry, Bishop of Lübeck:

“Thus strengthened in the Lord, he summoned the brothers and said that he was already being dissolved. Receiving the anointing of holy oil, he himself extended his hands and his feet, and sang with those who were chanting. After receiving the viaticum of the Lord’s body, he said: ‘O King of glory, come in peace.’”

Theodoricus, *Life of Saint Elizabeth, wife of Louis, Landgrave of Thuringia*, Book IV, chapter 5, likewise says of the death of that Landgrave:

“Seeing, therefore, that the danger of death threatened him, he summoned the patriarch of Jerusalem and received from him the sacrament of sacred anointing. To perform this solemn office, the patriarch took the bishop of the Holy Cross as his assistant. When the anointing had been completed, they gave him the viaticum of the most holy body of our Lord Jesus Christ, which he received with Catholic faith and sincere devotion.”

—Henry Canisius, volume IV, *Antiquae Lectiones*.

In the *Life of Saint Adelaide*, Book I, chapter 16:

“Having somewhat recovered her bodily strength, she asked that she be more carefully fortified with the mysteries of the Church. Then, after she had been anointed with sacred oil, she received the sacrament of the Lord’s body, adoring it humbly and most devoutly.”

—Henry Canisius, the same volume.

The same may be seen in the *Life of Saint Hugh, Abbot of Cluny*, in Surius, 29 April, where the vision of Saint Godefrey, Bishop of Amiens, is discussed:

“The brothers asked that he anoint Abbot Hugh with holy oil; and, vested in the episcopal mitre, while celebrating Mass, that he administer to him the viaticum of the Lord’s body and blood.”

This is also prescribed by the Constitutions of Riculfus, Bishop of Soissons:

“Likewise, priests ought to anoint their sick with holy oil after confession and reconciliation, and then give them communion.”

The same is clear from the *Life of Saint Adalard, Abbot of Corbie*, in that same Surius, 2 January: “After being strengthened by holy anointing, he was nourished by the sacred viaticum the next morning.”

Perhaps some obstacle had intervened that prevented him from receiving it on the same day. For formerly the three sacraments—penance, extreme unction, and the Eucharist—were administered to the sick together, as is clear from the manuscripts of our own collection cited above.

### 916

“And thus let them do this for seven days, if necessity requires it, both with regard to communion and to the other office.” Thus in the manuscript Codex of the monastery of Saint Remigius.

Observe the care that priests formerly exercised toward the sick. The phrase τὸ *de alio officio*—“with regard to the other office”—means the anointing, which Matthew Galen, in the *Theological Promptuary*, catechesis 182, restricts to the afflicted parts, because, as he holds, the sacrament was not repeated. He says:

“Moreover, it was not performed perfunctorily or hastily; rather, when the sick person did not recover, the priests returned for seven days, anointing him—not indeed repeating the sacrament so many times, but treating the afflicted members with the appointed prayers and anointing, and providing the holy Eucharist.”

Thus far he.

But his statement that the sacrament of extreme unction was not customarily repeated in the same illness does not seem probable, because the words “both with regard to the other office” are general and cannot be restricted to the anointing of the afflicted members. And although today this sacrament is not repeated during the same illness, if the ancient practice were valid, that would not be absurd. Since the illness had not ceased and the person still remained in sins—at least venial sins, which daily creep upon us, since “the righteous falls seven times a day”—this sacrament could rightly be repeated more than once during the same illness, while the very causes remained for which the sacrament is ordinarily conferred.

Moreover, if that anointing of the diseased parts were not a sacrament, it could not confer healing, and therefore it would be applied in vain. Nor did they use any oil other than that sanctified by the bishop.

### 917

“Priests and ministers of the holy Church must also,” etc. Thus in the Codices of Rodrade and Saint Remigius. Observe the care and diligence of the ancient priests toward the sick.

### 918

“Christ, the heavenly medicine of the Father.” Thus also in the Codex of Rodrade.

### 919

“For many of the priests,” etc. Thus in the Codex of Rodrade. The particle *enim* here has the force of *vero* or *autem*, “but” or “moreover.”

The manuscript *Rule of the Master*, chapter 82: “For this must not be found in anyone; the superiors must frequently examine everyone.”

In the sixth book of Halitgarius, near the beginning: “For not all clerics ought to use or read this writing.”

Here another method or custom of anointing the sick is described, namely, that of certain priests who anointed the sick in the five senses.

### 920

“Let them anoint.” In the Codex of Rodrade, *perungant*, “let them anoint.” But I think it should be read *perungunt*, “they anoint.”

### 921

“In the nostrils.” Read “in the ears,” as in the Codex of Rodrade. For afterward he says, “at the tip of the nostrils or within them.” Otherwise there would be no mention of the anointing of the ears, which is nevertheless necessary, since he wrote above that they also anointed the five senses of the body.

### 922

“Saying, ‘In the name of the Father,’” etc. Thus in the Codex of Rodrade, and there is no mention of the familiar form, “Through this holy anointing,” etc.

### 923

“Almighty and eternal God, who come to the aid of those in danger,” etc. Thus in the Codex of Rodrade.

To make the ancient method of this extreme unction more clearly known, I shall here append three ancient rites of this sacrament: the first from the Codex of Abbot Ratoldus, the second from the Codex of Tilianus, and the third from the Codex of the monastery of Saint Remigius.

## Ancient rite for conferring extreme unction, from the manuscript Codex of Abbot Ratoldus

### The order of anointing the sick begins

Here the priest says to the sick person: “Why did you summon me, brother?”

He answers: “So that you may give me anointing.”

The priest says to him: “May our Lord Jesus Christ give you a true and easy anointing. [Note: [Col. 0523] Read ‘nevertheless,’ as in the manuscript Roman Order of Corbie; cf. Burchard, Book XVIII, chapter 4.] If God regards you and heals you, will you keep it?”

He answers: “I will keep it.”

Then the priest makes a cross of ashes mixed with water upon his chest and places a hair shirt over it, saying:

“If anyone is sick, let him do penance, even under necessity, because God is merciful; for God’s mercy has neither measure nor time, as the Spirit of God says through the prophet [read: “by the prophet”]: ‘When you have turned and groaned, then you will be saved’; and elsewhere: ‘First declare your iniquities, so that you may be justified.’”

Antiphon: “Come to the aid, O Lord, of this sick person, and heal him with spiritual medicine, so that, restored to his former health, he may render thanks to you.”

Psalm: “O Lord, rebuke me not in your anger,” with *Gloria*.

Antiphon: “For with God there is mercy, and with him abundant redemption; and the manifold mercy of God likewise comes to the aid of fallen human beings, so that human hope of life may be restored not only through the grace of baptism and completion, but also through the medicine of penance and anointing.”

Antiphon: “A contrite and humbled heart God does not despise.”

Psalm: “Have mercy on me, O God,” entirely, with *Gloria*, and let the antiphon be repeated [perhaps read “repeated” or “completed”].

Seek the collect.

Antiphon: “May God bring help to this sick person upon his bed of pain; may he himself strengthen and restore him to life.”

Psalm: “Blessed is he who understands.”

Seek the collect.

Antiphon: “The Lord spoke to his disciples: ‘In my name they will cast out demons; lay your hands upon the sick, and they will be well.’”

Psalm: “God of gods.”

Antiphon: “Save your servant, my God, who hopes in you; guard his soul, because he has hoped in you.”

Psalm: “Incline, O Lord.”

Antiphon: “A thousand shall fall at your side and ten thousand at your right hand, but no evil shall come near you.”

Psalm: “He who dwells.”

Antiphon: “May God be reconciled to your iniquities and heal all your diseases, and may your youth be renewed like the eagle’s.”

Psalm: “Bless.”

First antiphon: “O Lord, deliver my soul from lying lips and from a deceitful tongue.”

Psalm: “To the Lord when I was troubled.”

### Prayer

“Almighty and eternal God, who through your apostle James commanded that the priests of the Church be introduced and that the sick be anointed with oil, grant, we beseech you, that through our hands you may deign to anoint and bless this servant of yours, N., who is sick, with sanctified oil.

“May that which we faithfully perform outwardly, embracing your gifts, be inwardly accomplished spiritually by divine power, and may the power of your greatness work wondrously. Through our Lord.”

“I anoint your eyes with sanctified oil, so that whatever sin you have committed through unlawful sight may be expiated by the anointing of this oil. Through our Lord Jesus Christ.”

### Another

“I anoint these ears with the liquid of consecrated oil, so that whatever was admitted through harmful delight in hearing may be removed by spiritual medicine. Through our Lord.”

### Another

“I anoint these nostrils with sacred oil, so that whatever has been harmfully contracted through excessive smell, this medicine may cleanse.” [The printed text is corrupt.]

### Another

“I anoint these lips with the remedy of consecrated oil, so that whatever you have sinned by idle or criminal speech may, through the mercy of divine clemency, be expiated by this anointing. Through him.”

### Another

“I anoint your chest with holy oil, so that, protected by this anointing, you may be able to contend bravely against the aerial hosts. Through the Lord.”

### Another

“I anoint these shoulders, or the middle of the shoulders, with sacred oil, so that, fortified on every side by spiritual protection, you may bravely despise the arrows of the devil’s assault and drive them far away with the strength of help. Through the Lord.”

### Another

“I anoint these hands with consecrated oil, so that whatever they have done through unlawful or harmful work may be removed by this anointing. Through the Lord.”

### Another

“I anoint these feet with blessed oil, so that whatever they have committed through excessive or harmful walking, this anointing may erase. Through the Lord.”

“I anoint you with sanctified oil in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, so that, prepared for combat like an anointed soldier, you may overcome the aerial hosts. Through him.”

### Another

“I anoint you with sanctified oil in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, just as Samuel anointed David king and prophet, so that the unclean spirit may not lurk in you, neither in your limbs, nor in your marrow, nor in any joining of your limbs. But may the power of Christ Most High and of the Holy Spirit dwell in you, so that through the working of this mystery, through this anointing with sacred oil, and through our prayer, healed or refreshed by the power of the Holy Trinity, you may deserve to receive your former and improved health. Through him, the same Lord.”

### Another

“I anoint you with holy oil, invoking the great majesty of the Creator, who commanded the prophet Samuel to anoint David king. Work, creature [read: “creature of oil”].”

### Another

“In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, may this anointing of sanctified oil be for you the purification of mind and body, and a protection and defense against the arrows of unclean spirits. Amen.”

### Here let him communicate

“May the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ lead you to eternal life and raise you on the day of judgment to holy rest.”

### Another

“Confessing with one accord the one God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, we pray that, with grace assisting, his will may be accomplished [the word *vita*, “life,” appears to be intrusive] in you. Through him.”

### Another

“May the Lord Jesus Christ be with you, to defend you; within you, to refresh you; around you, to preserve you; before you, to lead you; behind you, to justify you; above you, to bless you. He who, with the Father…”

Antiphon: “God of all virtues, who drive diseases from human bodies, have mercy on your servant, and visit him with your salvation, and grant him the medicine of heavenly grace.”

Psalm: “Blessed is he who understands.”

Thus far the Codex of Ratoldus concerning the anointing of the sick. The following points should be noted:

1. In the prayer beginning “Almighty and eternal God,” the words “and wondrously the power of your greatness” appear to be superfluous.

2. The priest’s questions to the sick person and the sick person’s responses to the priest are noteworthy; they are also found in the old manuscript Roman Order of the Corbie Library.

3. The sign of the cross made of ashes mixed with water upon the sick person’s chest, together with the placing of the hair shirt, is also found in the Order cited, in these words: “Then the priest makes a cross of ashes mixed with water upon his chest and places a hair shirt over it, saying, ‘If anyone is sick, let him do penance,’” etc., as in the Codex of Ratoldus. The only difference is that at the end of these words the Order adds: “The sick person answers: ‘Thanks be to God.’” In this Order there are no formulas for the anointings, because one or two leaves have been torn away.

4. In the third anointing the words “whatever has been harmfully contracted through excessive smell” are corrupt. It should be read, as in the Codex of Tilianus, “whatever has been harmfully contracted through smell,” or “through excess.”

5. In the fifth anointing “may you be able to provide bravely” is incorrectly read; it should be “may you contend bravely,” as in the same Codex of Tilianus.

6. In the sixth anointing, where it reads “with the strength of help,” it should read, as in the Codex of Tilianus, “with the strength of heavenly help.”

7. It should be noted that the eighth formula, “I anoint you with sanctified oil,” etc., is the same as the Ambrosian formula.

8. It should be observed that the ninth formula, “I anoint you with sanctified oil in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, just as Samuel anointed David,” etc., appears to be for the anointing of all the joints of the limbs. For in the Codex of Tilianus, in the formula for this anointing, these words are found, and they are also contained in this formula of the Codex of Ratoldus: “So that the unclean spirit may not lurk in you, neither in your limbs, nor in your marrow, nor in any joining of your limbs.”

9. In the tenth formula, after the words “Work, creature,” the word τὸ *olei*, “of oil,” seems to be missing, as it appears in the printed editions and in the Codices of Saint Eligius and Tilianus.

10. In the communion prayer, in the words “and to holy rest,” the conjunction “and” seems superfluous, just as in the following prayer, in the words “may life be accomplished in you,” the word *vita*, “life,” appears to be superfluous.

## The second rite for conferring extreme unction, from the Codex of Tilianus

### The order of anointing the sick

“Before the sick person is anointed, let him confess all his sins in every respect, purely, to God and to his priest, and receive full reconciliation from him, so that, cleansed of the ulcers of vices through confession [printed *purtus*; read *purgatus*, ‘cleansed’], he may worthily benefit from the spiritual anointing, by its healing of the inwardly hidden rottenness of wickedness. [Note: [Col. 0525D; 0526D] Read rather *purius*, ‘more purely,’ as in our Edm. Martenne, vol. II, *On the Ancient Rites of the Church*, p. 166. There it is very well read: *purius adapertis, dignius proficiat ei unctio spiritalis, medendo*, etc.—‘when he has opened himself more purely, may the spiritual anointing benefit him more worthily, by healing,’ etc.]

“And then first let the priests have salt and blessed water sprinkled, and let them sprinkle him with the antiphon *Asperges me, Domine*, ‘You will sprinkle me, O Lord,’ and *Miserere mei, Deus*, ‘Have mercy on me, O God.’

“Lord God, who spoke through your apostle: ‘Is anyone among you sick?’” etc.

“And thus let the sick person bend his knees and stand at the priest’s right hand, and let this antiphon be sung:

“Heal, O Lord, this sick person, whose bones are troubled,” etc.

“Lord, rebuke me not in your anger.”

### It follows

“Let us pray to our Lord Jesus Christ, and with every supplication let us ask,” etc.

“The Lord spoke to his fellow disciples: ‘In my name cast out demons, and lay your hands upon the sick, and they will be well.’

“God of gods: Let all the priests lay their hands upon the sick person, at the command of the bishop or merely with his permission, because the canonical order so teaches.

“God, who do not desire the death of sinners,” etc.

Antiphon: “Come to the aid, O God, of this sick person, and heal him with spiritual medicine, so that, restored to his former health, he may render thanks to you.”

“To the Lord when I was troubled,” with *Gloria*.

“Let us pray to our Lord Jesus Christ for our brother N., whom the harshness of his present illness afflicts severely, that the Lord’s mercy may deign to heal him with heavenly medicines, so that he who gave life may also give health. Through the Lord.”

“God, who have bestowed upon the human race the remedy of salvation and the gifts of eternal life, preserve in your servant the gifts of your virtues, and grant that he may feel your healing not only in body but also in soul. Through him.”

“And thus let each priest anoint the sick person with sanctified oil, making crosses upon the neck, throat, chest, and between the shoulders, or wherever the pain is greatest; and upon the five senses of the body; upon the eyebrows of the eyes; within and outside the nostrils; externally or internally at the upper part of the ears; externally upon the lips; and externally upon the hands—that is, on the outside—so that, if any stain has adhered to the five senses of mind and body, it may be healed by spiritual medicine and the Lord’s mercy obtained.

“While the priest is anointing the sick person, let him say this prayer, taking his time as he anoints:

“Be present, O Lord, we beseech you, to the services of our humility, and mercifully cooperate with them,” etc.

### Anointing with sacred oil at the head

“I anoint your head with sanctified oil in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, so that, prepared for combat like an anointed soldier, you may overcome the aerial hosts. Through him.”

### At the eyes

“I anoint your eyes,” etc., as above in the Codex of Ratoldus.

### At the ears

“I anoint these ears with the liquid of consecrated oil in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, so that whatever sin was committed through harmful hearing,” etc., as above.

### At the nostrils

“I anoint these nostrils with holy oil in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, so that whatever has been harmfully contracted through smell or excess, this medicine may cleanse.”

### At the lips

“I anoint these lips,” etc., as above in the Codex of Ratoldus; here, however, it reads “may be cleansed” instead of “may be expiated.”

### Another

“In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, may this anointing of sanctified oil be for you the purification of mind and body, and a protection and defense against the arrows of spiritual enemies. Through him.”

### At the throat

“I anoint you at the throat with holy oil in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, so that the unclean spirit may not lurk in you, neither in your limbs, nor in your marrow, nor in any joining of your limbs; but may the power of Christ Most High and of the Holy Spirit dwell in you, so that through the working of this mystery, through this anointing with sacred oil, and through our prayer, healed or refreshed by the power of the Holy Trinity, you may deserve to receive your former and improved health. Through him.”

### At the chest

“I anoint your chest,” etc., as above in the Codex of Ratoldus, where “to provide bravely” is incorrectly read instead of “to contend bravely.”

“I anoint the region of the heart with oil divinely sanctified, bestowed upon us as a heavenly gift, in the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, so that it itself, healing you inwardly and outwardly, may bring you to life—the Trinity that preserves its entire creation lest it perish. Through him.”

Here τὸ *conditionem*, “condition,” should be τὸ *creaturam*, “creature.”

### At the shoulders

“I anoint these shoulders, or the middle of the shoulders, with sacred oil, in the name of the Father,” etc., as in the Codex of Ratoldus, in which, however, τὸ *superni*, “heavenly,” is missing before τὸ *juvaminis*, “help.”

### At the hands

“I anoint these hands with sacred oil, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit,” etc., as in the Codex of Ratoldus.

### At the feet

“I anoint these feet with blessed oil, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit,” etc., as in the same Codex.

### Where the pain is greatest

“I anoint you with holy oil, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, beseeching the mercy of that one Lord of ours, Jesus Christ, so that, all the pains and bodily ailments of your body having been driven away, the power and health of life may be restored; and so that, through the working of this mystery, through this anointing with sacred oil, and through our prayer, healed by the power of the Holy Trinity, you may deserve to receive your former and stronger health. Through him.”

### At all the joints of the limbs

“I anoint you with holy oil, invoking the majesty of the great Creator, who commanded David the king to be anointed through the prophet Samuel. Work, creature of oil, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, so that the unclean spirit may not lurk here, neither in the limbs, nor in the marrow, nor in any joining of the limbs; but may the power of Christ Most High, the Son, and the sanctification of the Holy Spirit dwell in you.”

But the ending here is corrupt. It should read: “the power of the Most High, the Son, and the sanctification of the Holy Spirit,” or, as above and in the Codex of Ratoldus, “the power of Christ Most High and of the Holy Spirit.”

### Another anointing

“I anoint you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, with holy and consecrated oil, so that through the power of the Holy Spirit this sacred anointing may grant you health of soul and body, for the remission of all sins and eternal life.”

### Imposition of hands

“God our Savior, who are true salvation and medicine, and from whom all health and healing come; who instruct us through the voice of your apostle to touch the sick with the liquid of oil and ask for your merciful kindness,” etc.

### Then the prayers written below for the sick

“After this, let the priest communicate him with the body and blood of the Lord; and thus let them abstain for seven continuous days, unless necessity intervenes, both from communion and from the other office; and the Lord will raise him up to salvation, and if he is in sins, they will be forgiven him, as the Apostle says.”

In this rubric certain things appear corrupt. First, in the words “and thus seven,” one should read, as in the Codex of Saint Eligius, “and thus let them do this for seven.” In the following clause there is no sense, and in that Codex the words “unless necessity intervenes, let him abstain” are absent. But I think it should be read:

“And thus let them do this for seven continuous days, both with regard to communion and to the other office—that is, the anointing—unless necessity intervenes, so that he may abstain,” namely, from this repetition.

### Prayer at the reception of the Eucharist

“May the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ guard your soul unto eternal life. Amen.”

“May the peace and communion of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ guard your soul unto eternal life.”

### After receiving the Eucharist

“Lord Jesus Christ and our Savior, hear us as we pray for our brother N., that your holy Eucharist may be for him the protection of soul and body and the attainment of eternal life, you who live.”

### Absolution of the hands

“Ministers of the holy Church of God must also, with the greatest reverence, sing over the sick every day and night the evening and morning praises in full, as is customary in the Church.”

The words “absolution of the hands” appear superfluous; or one should read “washing of the hands.”

### Prayer over the sick person before absolution

“Holy Lord Father, maker [read: ‘author’] of the universe, almighty and eternal God,” to whom all things live, who bring the dead to life and call into existence things that are not as though they were, kindly exercise your customary help upon this creature of yours, you who are the great craftsman; we ask this.”

### Absolution with the imposition of hands

“God, who commanded sinners, those burdened with crimes and wounded, to show themselves to your priests; God, who commanded your disciples to lay hands upon the sick so that they might be well,” etc.

“Almighty and eternal God, forgiver of crimes and pardoner of sins, who said to your apostles and to the successors of the apostles: ‘Without me you can do nothing,’” etc.

## Episcopal blessings

“May the Lord Jesus Christ, who deigned to say to his disciples, ‘Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven; and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven’—although I am unworthy and bound by the chains of sin, he willed in his graciousness that I should be one of their number—may he himself, through the abundant gift of his mercy and through the ministry of my own littleness, deign to absolve you inwardly and outwardly from all the excesses of your frailty contracted in human weakness.”

**Response:** Amen.

“And just as he deigned to cleanse the sins of the whole world through his self-delivery and the shedding of his immaculate blood,” so may he mercifully not disdain to cleanse the stains of your sins through the intervention of that same blood, which was poured out for the remission of sins.”

**Response:** Amen.

“May he also not disdain henceforth to strengthen your devotion through the assistance of his grace, so that in this age you may be able to escape the snares of sins that creep upon you, and in the age to come possess without faith the eternal life purchased by Christ’s blood.”

**Response:** Amen.

“With the assistance of that same Lord Jesus Christ, who made us when we did not exist and redeemed us when we were lost, to the praise and glory of his name, world without end.”

**Response:** Amen.

## Prayers from above

“God, who mercifully raised up the world lying in the pit of sin; God, who commanded lepers to be cleansed,” etc.

### Another

“Almighty and eternal God, creator of the human race, who created all things from nothing and deigned to form humanity in your likeness,” etc.

### Another

“God, who purify the hearts of those who confess to you and absolve those who accuse their consciences from every bond of iniquity,” etc.

### Another

“Holy Lord Father of heaven and earth, protect your servant and forgive him all his sins,” etc.

### Another

“May the Lord be your helper and protector, and the forgiver of your sins. And may the God of mercy and compassion grant you correction for your sins; and, granting you a place for repentance, may he worthily give you the grace to mourn the evils you have committed and happily attain the joys of eternal life. Through him.”

When these things have been completed, the priests shall say the Prayers and Blessings over the sick person, each one his own. But if a bishop is present, this shall be his office.”

Thus far the Tilian Codex concerning the visitation of the sick, or extreme unction. There follows a third rite from the manuscript Codex of the monastery founded at Rheims in honor of Saint Remigius, which begins as follows:

> **Order for anointing the sick person.**

> “When the priest enters the sick person’s house, after the blessed water has been prepared, those entering shall first say, *Peace to this house*, three times; and blessed water shall be sprinkled, with the fragrance of incense or another aromatic offering, saying the Antiphon: *Bless, O Lord, this house.* Psalm: *May God have mercy on us.* Prayer: *Bless, O Lord God almighty, this place, so that for those dwelling in it there may be health and holiness, strength and chastity, victory and sanctity*, etc. Another: *Hear us, O holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God, and deign to send your holy angel from heaven, who may guard, cherish*, etc. Another: *Be present, O Lord, to our supplications, and illuminate this house with the serene eyes of your mercy*, etc. Another: *Be present, O Lord, to our supplications, and to your servants whom, called by charity, we visit in its duties*, etc. Another: *Grant, O Lord, to us your servants, through this creature of sacred sprinkling*, etc. Another [printed “Alla”]: *Hear us, O holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God, so that if there are any adversities*, etc. *Hear us, almighty Father, eternal God, and deign to mingle the grace of your visitation with the services of our humility*, etc.

> “Prayers to be said for those arriving within the house: *God, visitor of the humble*, etc. *God, who manifest to us your servants the signs of your presence*, etc. Then the priest shall say to the sick person: *You called.* The sick person shall say: *I desired to speak with you, so that you might grant me penance and the remission of sins.* The priest shall say: *May the Lord Jesus Christ grant you pardon; but if God has looked upon you, will you keep it?* The sick person answers: *I will keep it.* Then the priest shall hear his confession, as he is best able to inquire into it, whether in writing or in words. Then he makes a cross from ashes upon the sick person’s breast and places a hairshirt upon his head.

> “After this follow the seven penitential Psalms, namely: Psalm, *O Lord, rebuke me not in your fury*; *Blessed are those*; *O Lord, rebuke me not in your fury*, twice; *Have mercy on me, O God*; *O Lord, hear*; *Out of the depths*; *O Lord, hear*. Prayer: *Spare, O Lord, spare your servant N., whom you have redeemed, O Christ, with your blood; do not be angry with him forever—you who are to come to judge the living and the dead and the world by fire.*

> **The litany begins.**

> “Lord, have mercy, three times. Christ, have mercy, three times. Holy Mary, pray for us. Holy and perpetual Virgin, come to the aid of one placed in distress. Holy Mary, Mother of God, pray for your servant. Holy Michael, pray for him. Holy Gabriel, pray for him. Holy Raphael, pray for him. All holy archangels, pray for him. All holy patriarchs, pray. All holy prophets, pray. Holy John, pray. Holy Peter, pray. Holy Paul, pray. Holy Andrew, pray. Holy James, pray. Holy John, pray. Holy Thomas, pray. Holy James, pray. Holy Philip, pray. Holy Bartholomew, pray. Holy Matthew, pray. Holy Simon, pray. Holy Thaddeus, pray. Holy Mark, pray. Holy Luke, pray. Holy Barnabas, pray. Holy Timothy, pray. All holy apostles, pray. Holy Stephen, pray. Holy Clement, pray. Holy Dionysius, pray. Holy Rusticus, pray. Holy Eleutherius, pray. Holy Maurice with your companions, pray. Holy Gereon, pray. Holy Xystus, pray. Holy Lawrence, pray. Holy Quentin, pray. Holy Tiburtius, pray. Holy Valerian, pray. Holy Gervasius, pray. Holy Protasius, pray. Holy Quiricus, pray. Holy Salvius, pray. Holy Nazarius, pray. Holy Sebastian, pray. Holy Nicasius, pray.

> **545** All holy martyrs, pray.

> **[Note: In the litanies for anointing the sick that are read in the Gemetian Codex, after “all holy martyrs” one reads: “Holy Benedict, holy Martin, holy Hilary, holy Sylvester, holy Gregory, holy Augustine, holy Birinus” (he was bishop of Dorchester), “holy Cuthbert” (he was bishop of Lindisfarne), “holy Eudocius, holy Remigius, holy Columbanus.” From the place that Saint Benedict occupies in this order of saints, it is clear that the Gemetian Codex was written for a monastery where the Rule of Saint Benedict was observed. Nevertheless, the commemoration of Saint Benedict, even in the canon of the Mass, does not prove that the Sacramentary books in which it occurs belonged to Benedictine monks, since it is also found in the oldest books of cathedral churches, as in the canon of the Church of Milan copied before the year 600; indeed, it occurs even in the published Missal reformed under Saint Charles. Consult Mabillon, in the preface to the Gallican Sacramentaries, no. 9.]**

> “Holy Hilary, pray. Holy Martin, pray. Holy Sylvester, pray. Holy Augustine, pray. Holy Jerome, pray. Holy Remigius, pray. Holy Medardus, pray. Holy Vedastus, pray. Holy Amandus, pray. Holy Eligius, pray. Holy Bavo, pray. Holy Cassian, pray. Holy Benedict, pray. Holy Paul, pray. Holy Antony, pray. Holy Gregory, pray. Holy Eusebius, pray. Holy Ultan, pray. Holy Acharius, pray. Holy Richarius, pray. Holy Goar, pray. Holy Arsenius, pray. Holy Bertinus, pray. All holy confessors, pray. Holy Felicity, pray. Holy Perpetua, pray. Holy Agatha, pray. Holy Agnes, pray. Holy Lucy, pray. Holy Anastasia, pray. Holy Thecla, pray. Holy Savina, pray. Holy Susanna, pray. Holy Christina, pray. Holy Justina, pray. Holy Juliana, pray. Holy Praxedes, pray. Holy Prisca, pray. Holy Columba, pray. Holy Scholastica, pray. Holy Eugenia, pray. Holy Aldegundis, pray. Holy Gertrude, pray. Holy Eusebia, pray. Holy Godoberta, pray. Holy Amalberga, pray. Holy Radegund, pray.

> “All holy saints from the beginning of the world until the present, pray for us and for this sick person. Be favorable, spare us and him, O Lord. Be favorable, deliver him, O Lord. From every evil, deliver him, O Lord. From the evil enemy, deliver him, O Lord. From the snares of the devil, deliver him, O Lord. From torment and everlasting death, deliver him, O Lord. From dreadful anger, deliver him, O Lord. From unclean thought, deliver him, O Lord. From every iniquity, deliver him, O Lord. From uncleanness of heart and body, deliver him, O Lord. From all errors, deliver him, O Lord. From the bonds of the devil, deliver him, O Lord. From the power of darkness, deliver him, O Lord. Through your annunciation, deliver him, O Lord. Through your coming, deliver him, O Lord. Through your incarnation, deliver him, O Lord. Through your nativity, deliver him, O Lord. Through your circumcision, deliver him, O Lord. Through your manifestation, deliver him, O Lord. Through your passion, deliver him, O Lord. Through your cross, deliver him, O Lord. Through your resurrection, deliver him, O Lord. Through your ascension, deliver him, O Lord. Through the coming of your Holy Spirit from the Father, deliver him. Through the coming of your judgment, deliver him, O Lord. Through your teaching, deliver him, O Lord. Through your power, deliver him, O Lord.

> “Sinners, we ask you: hear us. That you may grant him perpetual peace, we ask you: hear us. That you may grant him compunction of heart, we ask you: hear us. That you may grant him a fountain of tears, we ask you: hear us. That you may deign to remove evil thoughts from him, we ask you. That you may deign to cut off unlawful pleasures from him, we ask you. That you may grant him a period of penance, if it can be done, we ask you. That you may deign to pour the grace of the Holy Spirit into his heart, we ask you: hear us. That you may grant him hope, faith, and charity, we ask you. That you may cut away murmuring and impatience from him, we ask you. That you may deign to grant him your grace, we ask you. That you may deign to assist him in his present danger, we ask you. That you may drive away from him all the princes of darkness, we ask you. That you may deign to lead him to eternal joys, we ask you. That you may deign to hear us, we ask you: hear us. Son of God, we ask you: hear us.

> “Lamb of God, who take away the sins of the world, spare us and him, O Lord. Lamb of God, who take away the sins of the world, have mercy on us and him, O Lord. Lamb of God, who take away the sins of the world, forgive his sins, O Lord. Christ, hear us, three times. Lord, have mercy, three times. Christ, have mercy, three times. Lord, have mercy, three times. Our Father.

> **Prayers.**

> “Save your servant, my God, who hopes in you.

> “May the Lord preserve him, give him life, and make him blessed upon the earth, and may he not hand him over to the soul of his enemies.

> “May the Lord bring him help upon his bed of pain; you have transformed his entire bed in his sickness.

> “Make his steps firm, O Lord, in your paths, so that his footsteps may not be moved.

> “Command your angels concerning him, that they may guard him in all his ways.

> “Send him help, O Lord, from the sanctuary, and protect him from Zion.

> “May the enemy accomplish nothing against him, nor the son of iniquity.

> “Do not remember, O Lord, the sins of his youth and his ignorances; remember him according to your great mercy.

> “Be for him, O Lord, a tower of strength in the face of the enemy.

> “Turn your face away, O Lord, from his sins, and blot out all his iniquities.

> “Create a clean heart in him, O God, and renew a right spirit within him.

> “Do not cast him away, O Lord, from your presence, and do not take your Holy Spirit from him.

> “Restore to him the joy of your salvation, and strengthen him with a sovereign spirit.

> “Add days to his days, and his years until the day of generation and generation.

> “May he remain forever in your sight; we seek your mercy and truth.

> “Turn, O Lord—how long?—and be entreated on behalf of your servants.

> **547** “O Lord, do not remember our ancient iniquities; may your mercy quickly anticipate us, for we are poor, etc.

> “Help us, O God our Savior; for the glory of your name deliver us, and this sick person, O Lord.

> “Be favorable to our sins and to his, for your name’s sake.

> “Arise, O Lord, help us and him, and deliver us and him for your name’s sake.

> “Then the entire Psalm *Inclina, Domine* [*Incline, O Lord*].”

> **Prayer.**

> “Almighty and merciful God, we beseech your immense goodness, that at the entrance of our humility you may deign to visit beneficially this servant of yours, N., lying exhausted in this tabernacle, etc.”

> **The sick person’s confession follows.**

> “Lord, minister of Christ our Lord, no skill is able to comprehend how many accursed deeds I have contracted at various times from the days of my youth; for by their multitude they exceed the bounds of number, since, compared with my sins, no wicked person can be found. Indeed, no kind of sin can be found to which I have not subjected myself and by whose fires and bonds I have not been surrounded. Now, too, the days of my dissolution are at hand, by which I am compelled to leave [perhaps *lay aside*] my humanity; now I tremble and lament before the final day of my calling, because I fear that what I have perpetrated by consenting wickedly to the flesh will be punished with fitting vengeance. And unless I were sustained by God’s clemency, avenging retribution would already justly avenge me for my crimes.

> “Therefore, with my limbs exhausted and the foundations of my body dissolved, having lost all the strength of my entrails [read: *all*], I do not cease to implore the mercy of your goodness with interrupted sobbing, so that, by the power granted to you from heaven, you may loosen the bonds of my sins and, through the earnestness of your prayers, cleanse my offenses, so that I may not be led to Tartarus with the rejected, but rather, through your intercession, may deserve to be raised to the heavenly joys everlasting.”

> **Absolution.**

> “Since the principal judgment declares that we have all offended in many things, from which we groan, so by the principal judgment we are consoled: for if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just—[the source has an asterisk here]—because Jesus Christ, our creator, redeemer, and savior, whom we have as a just advocate with the Father, is the propitiation for our sins and faithfully intercedes for us who confess, forgives us our sins, and cleanses us from every iniquity.

> “Therefore, our brother, to you confessing your sins, through the ecclesiastical authority of the apostolic power that our Lord Jesus Christ entrusted to his disciples and apostles, saying, ‘Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them’; and through those same apostles, to their successors, whose place we, although unworthy, occupy; and although not by merit, nevertheless by name and by the assumption of office, he granted the same power, and faithfully said to one who believes in him, ‘Let it be done for you according to your faith’: by his grace and power, through the virtue of the Holy Spirit, who is the remission of all sins, may he forgive you all your sins, free you from every evil, preserve you in every good work, and lead you to eternal life and to the fellowship of the saints, the heavenly citizens. Amen.

> **The priest’s exhortation to those standing around.**

> “Let us pray to our Lord Jesus Christ, dearest brothers, and let us ask with every supplication that he may deign to visit, gladden, and strengthen this servant of his, N., through his holy angels—he who lives and reigns.
