> “The Antiphon follows: *Come to the aid of this sick person, O Lord, and heal him with spiritual medicine, so that, restored by you to his former health, he may, being well, render thanks to you.* Psalm: *To the Lord, when I was in distress.* Prayers: *O God, who [healed] your servant Hezekiah*, etc. Another: *Most gentle almighty God, look favorably upon our prayers*, etc. Another: *O God, who enlighten every person coming into this world*, etc. Another: *Look, O Lord, upon your servant N., laboring under the sickness of his body*, etc. Another: *O God, who always rule your creation with devoted affection*, etc. Another: *O God, who have bestowed upon the human race both the remedy of salvation and the gifts of eternal life*, etc. Another: *God of the heavenly powers, who by the authority of your command drive every illness and every sickness from human bodies*, etc. Another: *Holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God, who strengthen the frailty of our condition through the infusion of your bestowed power*, etc. Another: *Look, O Lord, from heaven, and see, and visit your servant N.*, etc. Another: *Forgive, O Lord, our sins, and grant us your mercy*, etc.

> **548** “When these things have been done, the priest, the sick person’s confessor, shall ask the other priests to say the Prayers that concern the reconciliation of a penitent at the point of death.

> “Merciful and gracious God, who according to the multitude of your mercies blot out the sins of the penitent*, etc. Another: *We suppliantly beseech your Majesty, O Lord, that you may grant to your servant N., worn down by the long squalor of penance*, etc. Another: *We beseech your Majesty, holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God, who always seek not the death but the life of sinners*, etc.

> “Then the entire Psalm *O Lord, how they have increased*, with *Glory*, *Our Father*, and prayers. *Shine your face upon your servant; save him in your mercy, O Lord, so that we may not be confounded, because we call upon you.* Prayer: *We beseech your clemency, O Lord, that you may deign to grant pardon for his sins and crimes to this servant of yours, N., who confesses them, and to release the guilt of his former offenses*, etc.

> “Antiphon: *You shall be justified, O Lord.* Psalm: *Have mercy on him, O God, according to your great mercy, and according to the multitude of your mercies blot out his iniquities. Wash him more and more, O Lord, from his iniquity, and cleanse him from his sin. For he himself acknowledges his iniquity, and his sin is always against him. Against you alone he has sinned and done evil before you, so that you may be justified, O Lord, in your words and prevail when you are judged. For behold, he was conceived in iniquities, and his mother conceived him in sins. For behold, you have loved truth; you have revealed to him the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom. You shall sprinkle him, O Lord, with hyssop, and he shall be cleansed; you shall wash him, and he shall be made whiter than snow. You shall give joy and gladness to his hearing, and the humbled bones shall rejoice. Turn your face away from his sins, and blot out all his iniquities. Glory to the Father.*

> “Lord, have mercy, Our Father, and prayers.

> “*Why, O Lord, have you withdrawn far away? Do you despise us in times of opportunity, in tribulation? Look upon your servants and your works, and direct their children, and may the splendor of the Lord our God be upon us*, and the rest. Prayer: *Let us pray to the Lord our God for brother N., whom the present evil of illness has cruelly embittered [read: Burch. *dure*, “harshly”; Burg. *affligit*, “afflicts”]*, etc.

> “Likewise, Antiphon: *A contrite and humbled heart, O God, you shall not despise.* Psalm: *Have mercy on me, O God.* Glory to the Father. Our Father and prayers: *Deliver him from bloodguilt, O God, our God, so that our tongues may rejoice in your righteousness. Deal kindly, O Lord, in your good will, so that the walls of Jerusalem may be built up.* Prayer: *O God, who do not desire the death of a sinner*, etc.

> “Prayer before he is anointed: *O God, who spoke through your apostle, “Is anyone among you sick?”*, etc.

> “Then the Creed is said in full, namely, *I believe in God the Father*, through *life everlasting*. Then the priest shall say to the sick person: *Brother, do you believe the Creed that we have recited?* When he has answered, or indicated by a nod, *I believe*, he is anointed by the priest, or by several priests, with sanctified oil. They make crosses, each one on the right temple and the left, not on the forehead or crown of the head, saying:

> “*I anoint your head with sanctified oil, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, so that, like a soldier who has been anointed and prepared for combat, you may be able to overcome the aerial armies. Through the same Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father—*

> **549** “Likewise, on the eyebrows and beneath the eyebrows beside the corners of the eyes, saying:

> “*I anoint your eyes with sanctified oil, so that whatever you have sinned through unlawful sight may be expiated through the anointing of this oil. Through the same one who with the Father—*

> “Likewise, the ears, inside and outside, shall receive the sign of the cross at their upper part, saying:

> “*I anoint these ears of your body, so that through these windows you may receive the hearing of the grace of Christ’s remission unto eternal life. Through the same one who with the Father—*

> “Likewise, the nostrils shall be anointed at the top and underneath in the manner of a cross.

> “*I anoint these nostrils with sacred oil, so that whatever harmful thing has been contracted through them by excessive smelling, this remedy may cleanse away. Through the same one who with the Father—*

> “Likewise, the lips, saying this, and making a cross externally over the chin and throat:

> “*I anoint these lips with the remedy of consecrated oil, so that whatever you have sinned by idle or even criminal speech may, by the mercy of divine clemency, be cleansed through this anointing. Through the same one who with the Father—*

> “Likewise, over the two shoulders, that is, the shoulder blades—not on the breast nor between the shoulder blades:

> “*I anoint these shoulder blades with sacred oil, so that, fortified on every side by spiritual protection, you may bravely despise the arrows of the devil’s assault and repel them far away with the strength of heavenly assistance. Through the same one who with the Father—*

> “Likewise, over the hands; and if he is a presbyter, not below them; otherwise both below them and over the feet and beneath the soles crosses are made, saying:

> “*I anoint these hands with blessed oil, so that whatever they have done by an unlawful or harmful work may be emptied away through this anointing. Through the same one who with the Father—*

> “Likewise, over the feet and beneath the soles crosses are made, saying:

> “*I also anoint these feet with consecrated oil, so that whatever they have committed through excessive or harmful walking, this anointing may erase through the intercessions of the saints [the source reads* oboleat*; read* aboleat*, “may abolish”]. Through the same Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father—*

> **Conclusion of the anointings.**

> “*In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, may this anointing with sanctified oil be for you unto the purification of mind and body, and for protection and defense against the arrows of unclean spirits. Amen.*

> “Then the entire Psalm *O Lord, I have cried*. Glory. Lord, have mercy. Our Father. Prayer. Then the other priests, or laypeople, shall be invited. Another priest or the confessor shall say: *The Lord be with you.* Response: *Let us pray.*

> **Absolution by the brothers.**

> “O God, who commanded sinners and those wounded by the burden of crimes to reveal themselves to your priests; who commanded your disciples, so that they might be well, to lay hands upon the sick; who taught your apostles to pray for the sick; and who desired that, through the laying on of priests’ hands with invocation of your holy name, sins should be forgiven: hear our prayers, and grant this servant of yours, N., found afflicted by the guilt of illness, through this sacred ministry which you have taught us, your unworthy servants, to perform, remission of all sins. Thus, through this anointing with sacred oil and through the laying on of hands, may all his crimes be forgiven by the grace of the Holy Spirit; and may the remedies of your healing also fill him inwardly and outwardly and make him whole, so that the consciousness of guilt may not harm him unto punishment as much as [the source has an asterisk here] your indulgence, reconciliation, and remission benefit him unto pardon. You who live and reign.”

> “From this point another anointing follows.

> **Prayer.** “Through this anointing of God, through our ministry, and through God’s blessing, may your head and your senses—sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch—be cleansed and sanctified from every filth and contagion of sin, so that whatever you have sinned in your shoulders, hands, feet, or entire body, in thought, speech, and deed, may be expiated by the mercy of our Savior; so that you may be made fit to invoke the Lord, bless, sanctify, and offer sacrifice in the name of that same Lord Jesus Christ. May he restore to you the joy of his salvation, strengthen you with a sovereign spirit, renew the Holy Spirit within your entrails, and not take him away from you. Rather, may the blessing of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit descend upon you, flow abundantly over your head, descend to the extremities of your entire body, fill and surround you inwardly and outwardly, and always be with you. Amen.”

> **Another, to be said by another priest.**

> “*I anoint you with holy oil, invoking the majesty of the great Creator, who commanded the prophet Samuel to anoint David as king; may the creature of oil work*, etc.,” as above in the Codex of Saint Eligius.

> **Another.**

> “*I anoint you with sanctified oil, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit*, etc.,” as above from the Tilian Order.

> “After the sick person has been anointed, each of the priests may say one of these prayers.

> **Prayer after the anointing.**

> “*Lord Jesus Christ, who are our salvation and redemption, and who are true salvation and medicine, from whom all health and healing come*, etc.

> **Reconciliation follows before Communion on the same day.**

> “Merciful God, gracious God, who do not confine your forgiveness by any law of time, but open the door of your mercy to the one who knocks, and do not repel penitents even at the very end of this life: look favorably upon your servant N., who with complete confession of heart asks you for the remission of all his sins. Renew in him, most merciful Father, whatever has been corrupted by deed, by word, and finally by thought itself through the devil’s deception, and join him, a member of the body of the Church, to the unity of redemption. Have mercy on his groans; have mercy on his tears; and admit him, who has confidence in nothing except your mercy, to the sacrament of your reconciliation, because for you the healing of no soul established in this body is difficult or slow. For you are faithful in your words: you said that the sinner who has turned back should not be delayed for long periods of time, but that as soon as he has groaned, he is saved. Through. Another: *We suppliantly beseech your Majesty, O Lord*, as above. Another: *We beseech your Majesty, holy Lord, Father*, as above.

> “Then the hairshirt that had been placed upon the sick person’s head shall be removed, and the following shall be said:

> “Antiphon: *Alas for me, because my sojourning has been prolonged.* Psalm: *To the Lord, when I was in distress.* Antiphon: *From where will help come to me?* Psalm: *I lifted up my eyes.* Antiphon: *We shall go rejoicing into the house of the Lord.* Psalm: *I rejoiced.* Antiphon: *You who dwell in heaven, have mercy on us.* Psalm: *To you I lifted up my eyes.* Antiphon: *Do good, O Lord, to those who are good and upright of heart.* Psalm: *Those who trust.*

> “Then the priest shall say:

> “*May the Lord be propitiated toward all your iniquities*, etc.,” as above in the Codex of Saint Eligius.

> “He shall give Communion to the sick person, saying:

> “*May the Body of our Lord Jesus Christ preserve you unto eternal life.*

> “*May the Blood of our Lord Jesus Christ redeem you unto eternal life.*

> **551** “*May the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ and the communion of the saints be with you and with us unto eternal life. Amen.*

> **Prayer at the completion.**

> “*Almighty and eternal God, who come to the aid of those in dangers and pressing needs*, etc.,” as in the Codex of Saint Eligius.

> “And for seven days, or many more if necessity requires, let the services both of Communion and of the other offices for the sick person be performed; so that, as the apostle says—or rather, as the Holy Spirit says through him—‘If he has been in sins, they shall be forgiven him.’ The ministers of the holy Church should also arrange [read: *ut*, “that”] that the canonical hours be sung around him, namely, Matins, Prime, Terce, Sext, None, Vespers, and Compline. If a bishop is present, he shall give the Blessing; if not, the individual priests shall each say one of these Prayers:

> “*May the Lord Jesus Christ be with you, to defend you; within you, to preserve you; before you, to lead you; behind you, to justify you; above you, to bless you—he who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God.*

> **Blessing.**

> “*May God the Father bless you; may the Son of God heal you; may the Holy Spirit enlighten you*, etc.

> **Another.** “*May God the Father bless you; may Christ, the Son of God, help you; may he cause your body to be guarded and preserved in his service*, etc.

> **Another.** “*May God the Father bless you, who in the beginning created all things; may God the Son bless you, who descended for us as Savior from the heavenly dwellings; may God the Holy Spirit bless you, who rested in the likeness of a dove upon Christ in the river Jordan*, etc.

> “May the almighty Lord, in the visitation of his mercy, be favorable to you and, by lifting you from the illness with which you are held, have mercy on you. Amen. May he deign to enlarge your will according to his good pleasure, and, reconciling you to himself, accept your prayers and good works [read: *your prayers and your good works*]. Amen. May he also grant that, through the intercessions of all the heavenly powers and the remaining saints, you may be guarded amid all worldly anxieties, and that, having been released from the prison of the flesh, you may deserve to be admitted among their fellowship. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, who for the liberation of human beings deigned to become human, God and our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns through immortal ages of ages. Amen.

> **Another.** “*May God the Father bless you; may Jesus Christ guard you; may the Holy Spirit enlighten you throughout all the days of your life. Amen. May the power of Christ strengthen you; may the Lord forgive you all your offenses. Amen. May the glorious intercession of blessed and ever-virgin Mary, Mother of God, and of all the saints together, we beseech you, protect you and lead you to eternal life. Amen.*

> **552 — Mass for the sick person.**

> “Antiphon: *God of all powers, who drive sickness from human bodies, have mercy on your servant, visit him with your salvation, and grant the medicine of heavenly grace.* Psalm: *O Lord, hear.* Likewise, Antiphon: *You are just, O Lord.* Psalm: *Blessed are the undefiled.* Prayer: *Almighty and eternal God, eternal salvation of those who believe, hear us on behalf of your servant N., for whom we implore the help of your mercy*, etc.,” as in the Roman Missal.

> “Reading from the Epistle of blessed James the Apostle. *If anyone among you is sad, let him pray with an even temper and sing psalms*, etc.

> “Gradual: *Arise, O Lord; come to the aid of this sick person, heal him, and cure his illness.* Verse: *In times of opportunity, in tribulation, grant your help graciously to the sick person.* Alleluia: *Send him help, O Lord, from the sanctuary, and protect him from Zion.* Verse: *Hear with your ears.* Alleluia: *Out of the depths*, etc.

> **The continuation of the holy Gospel according to Luke.**

> “At that time: *Jesus entered Capernaum. Now the servant of a certain centurion, who was seriously ill*, etc.

> “Offertory: *O Lord, who were appeased by the prayers and prayer of the publican, who freed Peter’s mother-in-law from a severe fever, be present with merciful compassion to us who supplicate you for the sick person, O Lord.*

> “Likewise, offertory: *O Lord, make him wondrous according to your word, so that he may know your testimonies.* Verse 1: *Deal with your servant.* Verse 2: *Give him understanding, so that he may learn your commandments, and make the voluntary offerings of his mouth pleasing to you, O Lord.*

> “Over the offerings: *O God, at whose commands the moments of our life pass*, etc.

> “Preface: *Eternal God, who therefore chastise your servant bodily so that he may progress in mind, powerfully showing what the splendid salvation of your mercy is, while you grant that even illness itself may work salvation for us. Through Christ our Lord.*

> **Communion:** *Come to the aid of this sick person, O Lord, and heal him with spiritual medicine, so that, restored by you to his former health, he may, being well, render thanks to you.*

> “Likewise, Communion: *Redeem him, God of Israel, from all his anxieties.*

> “For the completion: *O God, the singular protection of human weakness*, etc.

> **Prayer for restored health.**

> “*Holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God, who, by pouring the grace of your blessing into sick bodies, govern your creation with manifold goodness*, etc.

> **Mass for a sick person who is near death.**

> “Antiphon: *The groans of death surrounded me.* Psalm: *I will love you, O Lord.* *Almighty and eternal God, preserver of souls, who chastise and receive those whom you love, gently discipline them for correction*, etc.

> “Reading from the prophet Isaiah: *In those days the prophet Isaiah spoke, saying: Seek the Lord while he may be found.*

> “Gradual: *Have mercy on me, O Lord, for I am weak.* Verse: *My bones are troubled.*

> “Likewise, gradual: *My helper and my deliverer.* Verse: *Let them be confounded and ashamed*, etc.

> “According to Mark. At that time, Jesus, looking upon his disciples, said: *Have faith in God*, etc.

> “Offertory: *Have mercy on me, O Lord, according to your great mercy.*

> “Likewise, offertory: *Hear my prayer, O God, and do not despise*, etc.

> “Over the offerings: *Be present, O Lord, in your goodness to our supplications, and receive the Host that we offer to you for your servant N., lying upon a bed*, etc.

> “Preface: *It is truly fitting . . . eternal God, as we implore the mercy of your Majesty, that you may deign to grant your servant N. pardon for his sins, so that, freed from all the bonds of the enemy, he may cling to your commandments with his whole heart, always love you alone with all his strength, and at some time deserve to attain the vision of your blessedness. Through Christ.*

> “For the completion: *We give thanks for your manifold gifts, by which you customarily satisfy the souls of those who hope in you*, etc.

> “Let reconciliation likewise be performed.

> “*Merciful God*, as above. Another: *We suppliantly beseech your Majesty*, and the rest. Then also the Creed, as prescribed above, and Communion of the Body.

> **Likewise, an abbreviated form.**

> “When the illness begins to grow worse, to bring assistance, after blessed water has been prepared, this Prayer shall be said:

> **553** “*Holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God, who are the way, the truth, and the life, hear us and preserve this servant of yours, N., whom you have given life and redeemed by the price and great gift of the blood of your Son, who lives and reigns with you.*

> “Then he shall be anointed with oil.

> “*I anoint you with sanctified oil, so that you may be saved eternally, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.*

> **Collect.**

> “*Grant, O Lord, to us your servants that, praying with confidence, we may deserve to say: Our Father; deliver us from every evil, guard us always in what is good, you who reign through ages of ages.*

> “He shall receive Communion, saying:

> “*May the Body and Blood of our Lord Jesus Christ preserve your soul unto eternal life. Amen.*

> “After this the following shall be said:

> “*Let us give thanks to our almighty God, who, by the gift of his sacrament, has given us, creatures and beings of earthly origin, life in a heavenly dwelling; he who with the Son and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns.*”

Thus far the manuscript Codex of the monastery founded at Rheims in honor of Saint Remigius concerning the visitation of the sick, or extreme unction. A few points concerning it should be noted.

1. The cross made from ashes upon the breast should be noted; this is found in accordance with certain Orders and Sacramentaries cited above.

2. Concerning the litany, it should be noted that it is sufficiently ancient when compared with those in use today. Nevertheless, the first litany, which we transcribed above from the book entitled *Order of Prayers*, is older.

3. The confession of the sick person should be noted. It is not unlike the confessions transcribed above. Nevertheless, it was not the sick person’s only confession; it was preceded by a more detailed confession, which brought forward the number of sins and the necessary circumstances, as we taught above when discussing penance. This is also confirmed by the same Codex of Saint Remigius, in which, shortly before the litany, the following is found: “Then the priest shall hear his confession, as he is best able to inquire into it, whether in writing or in words.” These words clearly require a confession other than the one mentioned, and wonderfully illuminate the teaching that we established above.

4. The priest’s exhortation to those standing around follows. This exhortation is elsewhere called the preface; through it the priest moves those present to prayer, according to the ancient custom discussed above.

5. The profession of faith that the sick person must make before the anointing is to be noted. It appears in Burchard, book XVIII, as follows:

“Do you believe in God the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit?”  
Response: “I believe.”

“Do you believe that these three persons are one God?”  
Response: “I believe.”

“Do you believe that in this very flesh in which you now are, you will rise on the day of judgment and receive either the good or the evil that you have done?”  
Response: “I believe.”

6. The anointing of the temples is to be noted, for it is not found in our other [Col. 0540A] codices. But since the anointing of the head is prescribed in the published Sacramentaries and in the Tilian Codex, I think that the temples are to be anointed. Anointing the forehead and crown of the head is forbidden, because anointing of the forehead pertains to the sacrament of confirmation, while anointing of the crown pertains to the ceremonies of baptism.

7. It is to be noted that the sick person is anointed by many priests. This also seems to be found in the Tilian Codex: “And let each priest in turn anoint the sick person with consecrated oil.”

8. The words “not on the chest” are to be noted. For in the codices of Saint Eligius, Ratoldus, Rodrada, and Tilianus, and in the Suessionian Manual, the chest is anointed. John Altenstaig, to be cited below, also testifies that this is done in certain churches. The Greeks do the same, as Peter Arcudius testifies, book V, *On the Sacraments*, chapter 7.

9. The words “nor between the shoulder blades” are to be noted. For the practice is different in the codices of Rodrada and Tilianus, where it says: “I anoint these shoulders,” or “the middle of the shoulders.”

10. Also the words “and if he is a priest, not below” are to be noted, for [Col. 0540B] they are not found in our other manuscript codices.

11. This formula is to be noted: “Through this anointing,” etc. It is absent from our other manuscript codices and is ordinarily said in the anointing of a priest, because of these words: “For invoking the Lord, blessing, sanctifying, and offering sacrifice in the name of that same Lord Jesus Christ.”

12. Communion after the anointing has been completed is to be noted; it is also found in our other manuscript codices.

13. The continuation of the anointing for seven or more days is to be noted. This is also found in the Sacramentary of Saint Eligius, together with the recitation of the divine office before the sick person, which likewise appears in that Sacramentary and in the Codex of Abbot Ratoldus.

14. This prayer, “Almighty Lord, by the visitation of your mercy,” etc., together with the following prayer, is an episcopal blessing. It is also found in the Codex of Saint Eligius, though in a different verbal form. The second blessing lacks its conclusion.

15. In the Mass for the sick, note the two Antiphons, or Introits, with two Psalms; the double Gradual; the double Offertory; and the double Communion. In the Mass for the sick person who is near death there are a double Gradual and a double Offertory without Communion.

16. The words “also, let reconciliation be made,” etc., are to be noted as constituting a shorter form for administering extreme unction to the sick person who is near death.

17. The words “also, the abbreviation,” etc., are to be noted. This is a somewhat shorter form for administering extreme unction, used when the sick person appears so gravely afflicted that there is justifiable fear that he may die during the administration of the sacrament. Hence a single anointing is used, confirming the opinion of those who say that in such danger one anointing is sufficient.

18. The formula “The body and blood,” etc., is to be noted. Because of the imminent danger, the body dipped in the blood was offered to the sick person; this matter will be discussed below. Nevertheless, the Eleventh Council of Toledo decrees that those who, because of excessive weakness, are unable to swallow the body of Christ are to be content with receiving the blood alone.

19. It is to be noted that there is no anointing of the kidneys here, just as there is none in the Tilian Codex, in our other manuscript codices, among the Greeks, or in the Suessionian Manual. Richard of Mediavilla nevertheless mentions it in the question cited above, as does John Altenstaig of Mindelheim in his *Vocabulary of Theology*. He also mentions anointing of the navel:

“Some,” he says, “add the chest, kidneys, and navel, in which there is venereal pleasure, although this ought not to be done.”

In the Sacramentaries published from the Vatican, the head is anointed, while the other anointings are unspecified. The Greeks anoint the forehead, chin, both cheeks, then the chest, then the hands on both sides, and finally the feet, as Peter Arcudius testifies, book V, *On the Sacraments*, chapter 7. In the codices of Saint Eligius and Rodrada, in the description of the first rite, the sick person is anointed on the neck and throat, between the shoulder blades, on the chest, and wherever the pain is more severe; [Col. 0541A] in the second description, the five senses are anointed. In this Codex of Saint Remigius, the temples and the place above the chin are anointed, in addition to the other places. Note the difference.

To this may finally be added the method of anointing the sick according to the practice of the distinguished Church of Soissons, taken from the old *Manual*, or *Instruction Book for the Pastors* of that church, which was commissioned or printed approximately eighty years ago; the year is not recorded in the book itself. It does not differ from the codices of Ratoldus and Tilianus. Omitting the many prayers that precede it, I have copied only the following.

“Afterward let the sick person be anointed. First, make a cross + at the right ear, saying:

“‘In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, may this anointing of the oil of sanctification be for you unto the purification of mind and body and unto eternal life. Amen.

“‘In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, receive health in the name of the Lord. Amen.’

[Col. 0541B] “‘At the left ear:

“‘In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, I anoint your ears with the liquid of consecrated oil, so that whatever harmful sin was committed through the pleasure of hearing, this spiritual medicine may remove. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.’

“‘At the eyes:

“‘In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, I anoint your eyes with consecrated oil, so that whatever sin you have committed through illicit sight may be expiated by the anointing of this oil. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.’

“‘At the nostrils:

“‘In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, I anoint these nostrils with holy oil, so that whatever harm has been contracted through excessive smelling, this medicine may remove. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.’

“‘At the lips:

[Col. 0541C] “‘In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, I anoint these lips with the remedy of consecrated oil, so that whatever you have sinned through idle *sus*, or even through criminal speech *sus*, may, by the mercy of divine clemency, be cleansed by this anointing. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, who [you …], etc. Let us pray.

“‘Prayer.

“‘May the Lord Jesus Christ be with you, so that he may defend you.’  
Let him respond: “Amen.”

“‘May he be in you +, so that he may restore you.’  
“Amen.

“‘May he be around you +, so that he may preserve you.’  
“Amen.

“‘May he be behind you +, so that he may guard you.’  
“Amen.

“‘May he be above you +, so that he may bless you.’  
“Amen.

“‘He who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.’

“‘At the chest:

“‘In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, I anoint your chest with holy oil, so that, anointed *ta* with this anointing, you may be strong enough to fight against the aerial hosts. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.’

[Col. 0541D] “‘At the shoulders:

“‘In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, in each place, I anoint these shoulders, or the middle of the shoulders, with holy oil, so that, fortified *ta* on every side by spiritual protection, you may be able to despise courageously the arrows of the devil’s assault and drive them far away with the strength of heavenly aid. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.’

“‘At the hands:

“‘In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, I anoint these hands with consecrated oil, so that whatever they have done through illicit or harmful work may be removed by this anointing. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.’

“‘At the feet:

“‘In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, receive health in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ; rise and walk. In the name of the Lord, I anoint these feet with blessed oil, so that whatever they have committed through excessive or harmful walking, this anointing may wipe away. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.’

[Col. 0542A] “‘Another prayer.

“‘I anoint you with blessed oil, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, so that, strengthened *ta* by this anointing, you may be able to overcome the aerial hosts. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.’

556 “‘Another prayer.

“‘I have anointed you with consecrated oil, just as Samuel anointed David as king and prophet, with the creature of oil working [or: work, as an alternative reading], in the name of God the almighty Father, so that the unclean spirit may not remain hidden, either in your limbs or in your marrow, etc., as in our other manuscript codices.’”

[Col. 0542B] Several other prayers, seven Psalms, and a Litany follow, with many intercessions. These words are added:

“Afterward let him give him Communion with these words, if the sick person wishes to receive Communion; but if not, omitting the following four prayers, let him say these two: ‘May God bless you,’ etc. ‘May the Lord have mercy. May the body of our Lord Jesus Christ preserve your soul unto eternal life. Amen,’ etc.”

Thus far the *Manual of the Church of Soissons*, in which, however, I do not sufficiently understand what the particles *sus* and *ta*, written in red letters, signify.

[Note: [Col. 0541D] It undoubtedly means that when a male is anointed, *otiosus* should be read; when a female, *otiosa*. Likewise, in the anointing of a male, *perunctus* and *munitus* should be read; in the anointing of a female, *peruncta* and *munita*. [Col. 0542D]]

924. “We beseech you, almighty God, for your servant N., etc.” This Mass was celebrated at the coronation of Charles the Bald as emperor. Before each of these three prayers, however, a prayer for Saint Gorgonius the martyr is prefixed, because Charles the Bald was crowned at Metz on the same day, namely 9 September, as may be seen in his *Capitularies*.

925. “Of all.” This word is absent from the Mass cited.

[Col. 0542C] 926. “And N., our king.” In the Mass cited it reads: “And Charles, our king,” because it is said at his coronation.

927. “And the appointed office is to be completed.” Thus in the Codex of Abbot Ratoldus. These words are absent from the Mass cited.

928. “Prayer.” In the Mass cited from the *Capitularies of Charles the Bald*, it reads “Communion,” more correctly, as I believe.

929. “The way of the saints,” etc. This prayer is recited in certain churches after the Sunday Procession.

930. “These interceding.” Here, “believing in you,” as in certain printed books.

931. “Arms.” That is, ornaments or vestments.

932. “Secretaries.” That is, sacristies.

933. “Minister.” By “minister” he means someone initiated into the minor orders.

934. “Sandals.” Alcuin mentions these in his book *On the Divine Offices*, in the chapter on vestments, as does Leo of Ostia, who will be cited below.

[Col. 0542D] 935. “Over the shoulder garment.” Alcuin mentions it in the chapter cited. The Greeks call it *ὠμοφόριον* (*omophorion*); see what was noted above. But this shoulder garment, as is clear from the *rationale* attached to it below, is not like the *omophorion*.

936. “The alb.” The *talare* is a linen garment called *poderis*. Alcuin, in the chapter cited. The alb is mentioned in the Fourth Council of Carthage, canon 4: “Let the deacon wear the alb only at the time of the offering or of the reading.”

937. “Let the evil of the cheek be erased.” It seems that one should read: “Erase, then, the evil of the cheek.”

938. “Belt.” Alcuin mentions the belt in the chapter cited.

939. “Military belt.” Properly, this is a military belt, discussed by Varro in book IV of *The Latin Language* and by Saint Isidore in book XIX, chapter 33, of the *Etymologies*.

940. “Tunic.” 557 This is what Alcuin and Amalarius, book II, chapter 17, call the dalmatic. The Mass published by Illyricus calls it *palmatica*, but one should read *dalmatic*.

941. “With little bells.” In imitation of the Aaronic priest.

942. “Myrice.” Read *mirifice*—“wondrously.”

943. “Sleeves.” These are gloves. For later in the same Paschal Mass it says: “And let him remove the gloves and wash his hands.” In the Mass published by Illyricus it reads: “For putting on the gloves.” Leo of Ostia mentions them in book II, chapter 82, of the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*.

944. “Let a ring be given to him.” In the Mass of Illyricus: “For the ring.” In the Codex of Ratoldus, as also in the published Sacramentaries, a ring is given to the bishop at his ordination. This may also be seen in the Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 27: “If he is a bishop, an orarium, ring, and staff.” Mention is made of it in the Life of Saint Birinus, bishop of Dorchester, in Surius, 3 December, in the account of the discovery of his body: “A ring was also found, as well as a leaden cross.” It is nevertheless surprising that Alcuin, Amalarius, and Rabanus are silent about it; [Col. 0543B] this sufficiently indicates that the rite formerly varied according to time and place.

945. “Chasuble.” Concerning the chasuble, Hugh of Saint Victor, book I, *On the Sacraments*, chapter 50, writes:

“The chasuble, which is called the planeta, is placed over all the vestments; through it charity is understood, which appears superior to all the virtues. It is raised over the right arm, so that friends may be loved in God, and folded over the left, so that enemies may be loved for God’s sake.”

For the rest, see our observations on the *Concordance of Rules*.

946. “Rationale.” This is a certain breast ornament, modeled on that which the ancient legal priests used.

947. “Maniple.” Alcuin calls it *mappula*, while Rabanus calls it *phanon*. These are the pontifical ornaments, which are listed here with sufficient accuracy, though no mention is made of the miter. The same silence is remarkable in our manuscript Sacramentaries, in the Roman and Tilian Orders, in the manuscript pontifical preserved in the sacristy of the church of Rouen and thought to be Rheims-made, in the Mass published by Illyricus, and in Alcuin, Amalarius, Rabanus, and the other ancient writers who treated the divine offices and listed the pontifical ornaments. I therefore think that the use of the miter in the Church scarcely existed before the year 1000 after Christ. Later, however, we clearly find it mentioned by Peter Damian, sermon 1, *On the Dedication*; Saint Bernard, letter 40; Hugh of Saint Victor, book I, *On the Sacraments*, chapter 55; and many others who flourished afterward.

For this reason I do not agree with those who say that the use of the miter came down from the apostles themselves and that ancient bishops wore crowns, an argument they attempt to support from Ennodius’s epigram 77, *On the Life and Character of Saint Ambrose*:

“Garlanded, he bore bright wreaths upon his brow,

And with his mouth he produced a work distinguished by gems.”

It should instead be read as follows: everyone can see that these lines are spoken metaphorically of the modesty, decorum, restraint, dignity, and similar virtues that shone in the mouth of this most holy bishop and that were especially radiant when he preached because of the divine eloquence of the man. This is sufficiently clear from the words:

“And with his mouth he produced a work distinguished by gems.”

It is also evident from the preceding couplet:

558 “Whose tongue shone with dewy royal purple,

Painting in its own spring the buds it willed.”

Nor, indeed, would it have been a great subject of praise for Ambrose to wear a gem-studded crown on his head. Even if this might have suited other bishops of Milan whom Ennodius praises later, he attributes nothing similar to them.

Nor do the passages cited from Eusebius, book X, chapter 4, of *Ecclesiastical History*, in the panegyrical oration, prove the contrary:

“Friends of God and priests, clothed all around with the sacred *poderis*, a heavenly garment, a crown of glory, divine anointing, and the holy stole of the Holy Spirit.”

Nor does the passage in the *Apology* of Saint Gregory of Nazianzus:

“For this reason you anoint me as bishop, gird me with the *poderis*, place a tiara upon my head, and bring me near the altar of the spiritual burnt offering.”

These expressions are used in reference to the ancient priesthood. Nor are we troubled by those golden plates which Saints John and James are said to have worn on their foreheads, since they are neither crowns, nor tiaras, nor miters; and since their use began with them, so it ended with them.

As for the objection drawn from Ammianus Marcellinus, book XXIX, where he writes that Firmus, after being defeated in Africa, restored to the emperor Theodosius, in order somehow to win his favor, the military standards and a priestly crown, together with the other spoils that he had seized while ravaging that region, as he had been commanded, I say that the passage must be understood as referring to the crown of some pagan priest, since paganism had not yet been entirely uprooted.

Everyone knows that pagan priests formerly wore crowns during sacred rites. This is clear from Tertullian, in the book *On the Crown of the Soldier*:

“Finally, the doors themselves, the victims themselves, the altars themselves, their ministers and priests themselves are crowned.”

And in the book *On Spectacles*:

“Will that charioteer, the disturber of so many souls, the minister of so many furies, crowned as though he were the priest of so many statues, be pleasing to God?”

It is also clear from Saint Cyprian, in his *Discourse on the Lapsed*:

“A brow pure with the sign of God could not bear the devil’s crown.”

There the subject is the worship of idols. It is also clear from the Council of Elvira, canon 55:

“Priests who merely wear the crown of those making sacrifice, but neither sacrifice nor contribute anything of their own expense to idols, are, it was decided, to receive Communion after two years.”

Formerly, in the rites of Ceres, the hierophants, hierophantesses, and the *daduchus*, that is, the torchbearer, as well as the other female sacrificers, were girded with a myrtle crown, as the scholiast of Sophocles reports from Istros in his notes on *Oedipus at Colonus*.

Indeed, Tertullian himself, in the book cited, *On the Crown of the Soldier*, entirely denies that the apostles, evangelists, and bishops were crowned, which is contrary to the opposing view:

“Finally,” he says, “neither patriarch, nor Levite, nor priest, nor archon. Who afterward is found crowned, whether apostle, evangelist, or bishop?”

Was so ancient a teacher ignorant of apostolic tradition? Thus some point in vain to miters supposedly belonging to certain ancient bishops, since it cannot be proved that they belonged to them. Indeed, in some cases there appear indications that detract from their alleged antiquity.

The nature of the ancient miter is explained by the author of an old etymological work:

“*Μίτραι κυρίως οἱ ἀπὸ φασκιῶν καὶ ὠαρίων γινόμενοι στέφανοι, ἐν καταχρήσει δὲ πᾶς στέφανος μίτρα λέγεται.*”

That is:

“Miters properly are crowns made from bands and *oraria*; by misuse, however, every crown is called a miter.”

Here the word *ὠαρίων* is corrupt; one should read *ὡραρίων*, as it is found in Eustathius on the *Iliad*, book Δ:

“*Φάμενοι ὅτι μίτραι κυρίως οἱ ἀπὸ φασκιῶν καὶ ὡραρίων στέφανοι*,”

that is:

“saying that miters are crowns composed of bands and *oraria*.”

The *oraria* are certain elongated woven textiles. See how different these are from the miters of bishops today.

948. “Flamineate.” That is, clothed in sacred vestments. To make what has been said above clearer, we give here an old image of Saint Remigius [Note: [Col. 0543D] We have also brought in here the old image of Saint Gregory, which Menard had arranged to have drawn from a manuscript codex at the beginning of his edition, both so that what has been said might receive additional clarity from the image itself and because the more elegant likeness of the holy doctor placed at the beginning of the first volume of his complete works prevents this one from being engraved at the beginning of this volume, since it is less elaborate and was drawn solely for purposes of explanation.] from the Codex of Rheims.

559 949. “Procession.” This is an assembly of clergy accompanying the pontiff himself to the altar and assisting him.

950. “Although not a priest and deacon.” That is, although some are neither priests nor deacons.

951. “With the bishop’s assent he begins the Antiphon.” Note that in these Masses nothing is begun by the cantor unless the bishop commands it.

952. “Receive my confession,” etc. This formula of confession is also found in the most ancient manuscript Codex of the library of Corbie, entitled *The Order of Prayers*, in the Tilian Codex, and in the Mass published by Illyricus. In another Mass of Illyricus there is the following alternative:

“I confess my sins to you, eternal Pontiff, minister of the saints, and Priest of the true tabernacle,” etc.

Its beginning is worth noting, because formerly confessions of this kind began with the word “I confess,” and those who uttered this word struck their breasts, as may be seen in Saint Augustine, sermon 8, *On the Words of the Lord according to Matthew*:

“The sound of striking the breast also followed, when, having heard the Lord say, ‘I confess to you, Father,’ at the very sound of the words ‘I confess,’ you struck your breasts. For what does striking the breast mean except to accuse what lies hidden in the breast and, by a visible blow, to chastise hidden sin? Why did you do this, unless because you heard, ‘I confess to you, Father’? You heard ‘I confess,’ but you did not attend to the one who confesses. Now consider: if Christ said ‘I confess,’ from whom all sin is far removed—[it is] not only the word of the sinner, but also of the one who praises. For, from the long-established custom of striking the breast when they uttered this word in confession, as soon as they heard it they struck their own breasts.”

To this pertains the same Augustine’s statement in the treatise *On Christian Discipline*, chapter 20:

“Let us at least be ashamed, confess, and strike our breasts—not so as to pave a firm floor over our sins. 560 For whoever strikes his breast and is not corrected makes his sins firm rather than removing them. Let us strike our breast, beat ourselves, and be corrected by ourselves.”

[Col. 0546A] 953. “Psalm: Lord, you have searched me,” as above.

954. “Meanwhile, let him also kiss all those gathered around him.” In the Tilian Mass and that of Illyricus, he kisses only the priests and deacons; in Roman Order 1, the priests or deacons kiss the hands of the pontiff.

955. “On the left.” That is, from the left.

956. “On the right.” That is, from the right.

957. “The bishop by the sign of his finger.” The passage is corrupt and mutilated. Read: “With the bishop giving assent by a sign of his finger.”

958. “Me, unworthy,” etc. This apology is also found in the Mass published by Matthias Illyricus, where the pontiff recites it at the altar after the confession.

959. “And then let him begin, ‘Glory in the highest.’” Note that the hymn *Gloria in excelsis* is begun by the pontiff, according to ancient custom, as we see in the Life of Charlemagne by a certain monk of Saint Gall, chapter 20, concerning a certain bishop:

“And when, after the preceding melodies, he ought according to his office to introduce the angelic hymn…”

The same may be seen in the First and Third Roman Orders. This custom continues today.

[Col. 0546B] 960. “Let him read the Epistle.” Formerly, in many churches, a prophetic reading preceded the reading of the Epistle, as may be seen in Saint Gregory of Tours, book I of the *Miracles of Saint Martin*, chapter 5:

“When he celebrated the festivals of the Lord’s day, it was his custom that, when the reader came with the book, he would not presume to read before the saint gave the command by a sign. It happened that on that Sunday, after the prophetic reading had already been read, while the one who would deliver the reading of blessed Paul was standing before the altar,” etc.

This is also clear from the paraphrase of George Pachymeres. Explaining this passage of Saint Dionysius, *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, chapter 3, “the reading of the tablets of the sacred writings” (*ἁγιογράφων δέλτων ἀνάγνωσις*), he writes:

“*Ἐξῆς δὲ διὰ τῶν ἀναγνώστων (τούτους γὰρ λέγει λειτουργούς) τῶν θείων γραφῶν, τῶν προφητειῶν, τοῦ ἀποστόλου, τοῦ θείου εὐαγγελίου ἡ ἀνάγνωσις γίνεται.*”

That is:

“Then, through the readers—for he calls these liturgists—the reading of the divine Scriptures, the prophecies, the Apostle, and the divine Gospel takes place.”

These two passages confirm what we said above: that formerly it was the readers’ responsibility to read the Epistle and the Gospel at Mass.

961. “Response: This day.” The Responsory in this place is the Gradual. Formerly the Psalm was sung, as is clear from Saint Augustine, sermon 10, *On the Words of the Apostle*:

“We learned this from the apostolic reading; then we sang a Psalm, exhorting one another, saying with one heart: ‘Come, let us adore and fall down before him, and let us weep before the Lord who made us, and let us come before his face in confession, and let us sing joyfully to him in Psalms.’ After this came the Gospel reading.”

In sermon 33, *On the Words of the Lord according to Luke*:

“In the apostolic reading thanksgiving is given for the faith of the nations; in the Psalm we said: ‘God of hosts, restore us; show your face, and we shall be saved.’”

In sermon 7, *On the Words of the Apostle*:

“We heard the Apostle, we heard the Psalm, we heard the Gospel; all the divine readings are in agreement.”

In sermon 49, *On Time*:

“We heard the apostolic reading.”

And shortly afterward:

“Hear the Psalm speaking inwardly: ‘Against you alone have I sinned.’ You also heard the Gospel agreeing with these readings.”

962. “Command, Lord, that I bless.” That is, “be willing to bless,” or “bless.” For *to command* sometimes means *to be willing*, as Nonius Marcellus notes in chapter 4.

Just as formerly the Gospel was read at the nod of the bishop or of the celebrating priest, as the custom continues today, so formerly the Epistle was not read except at the nod of the bishop or priest celebrating the Mass. This is evident from book I of Saint Gregory of Tours, *On the Miracles of Saint Martin*, chapter 5:

“When he celebrated the festivals of the Lord’s day, it was his custom that, when the reader came with the book, he would not presume to read before the saint gave the command by a sign. It happened that on that Sunday, after the prophetic reading had already been read, while the one who would deliver the reading of blessed Paul was standing before the altar,” etc.

And shortly afterward:

“They stirred him, saying: ‘The hour has already passed; let the Lord command the reader to read the lesson.’”

963. “To the announcer.” Read: “For announcing.”

964. “Mary Magdalene.” This custom continues today: on the first day of Easter the Gospel according to Mark is read. Formerly, however—that is, in the time of Saint Augustine, at least in Africa—the Gospel according to Matthew was read on the first day, that according to Mark on the second, and that according to John on the third. Throughout that entire octave, as is also done today, the Resurrection was recounted according to all the Evangelists. Saint Augustine testifies to this in sermon 144, *On Time*:

“The Resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ has also been recited today, but from another book of the Gospel, which is according to Luke. For on the first day it was read according to Matthew; yesterday, according to Mark; today, according to Luke. This is the order of the Evangelists. For just as his Passion was written down by all the Evangelists, so these days, lasting a period of seven or eight, are arranged so that the Resurrection may be recited according to all the Evangelists.”

[Col. 0547D] 965. “And all after him.” Namely, the clergy. Note that no Creed is sung here. There is no mention of it in our Sacramentaries, either published or in manuscript, nor in the Tilian Order, nor in Alcuin, Amalarius, or Rabanus, who wrote in detail about the order of the Mass, nor in Remigius of Auxerre. For he says in chapter 4, *On the Celebration of the Mass*:

“After the Gospel has been recited, the priest again greets the people.”

The Creed was indeed used in the churches of the ancient Greeks, as is clear from Saint Dionysius, chapter 3 of the *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*. Presenting various opinions concerning the hymn sung during the sacred mysteries, he says:

“*Τὸν ὕμνον δὲ τοῦτον, οἱ μὲν ὑμνολογίαν καλοῦσιν, οἱ δὲ τὸ τῆς θρησκείας σύμβολον, ἄλλοι, ὡς οἶμαι, θειότερον, ἱεραρχικὴν εὐχαριστίαν.*”

That is:

“But some call this hymn a song of praise; others, the Creed of religion; and others, in my opinion more divinely, the Hierarchical Eucharist.”

In the Roman Church, however, it was not used before the year 1014 after Christ, as Berno of Reichenau testifies in chapter 2 of his book *On Certain Matters Pertaining to the Mass*:

“For if, as has often been said, we are forbidden to sing that angelic hymn on feast days because the Roman priests are not accustomed to sing it, we can similarly omit the Creed after the Gospel, which the Romans up to the time of the emperor Henry of blessed memory had in no way sung. But when they were asked by him why they acted in this way, I, who was present, heard them give the following answer: that the Roman Church had never been infected by any taint of heresy, and therefore those who at some time had been stained by a heresy had greater need to repeat that Creed frequently by singing it. But the lord emperor did not desist until, with the consent of all, he persuaded the lord Benedict, the apostolic pontiff, that they should sing it at the public Mass.”

Thus Berno speaks.

Nor should anyone respond that Berno’s words must be understood of the Constantinopolitan or Nicene Creed. For if any Creed had then been used at Rome, Berno would have been obliged to say which Creed the emperor had asked the Roman pontiff to use.

Nor does the objection drawn from Rufinus in his *Exposition of the Creed* have force:

“In the Church of the city of Rome, however, this is not found to have been done. I believe the reason is that no heresy originated there, and the ancient custom is preserved there: those who are about to receive the grace of baptism publicly—that is, with the people of the faithful listening—recite the Creed.”

For this does not concern the recitation of the Creed at Mass, but the recitation of the Creed by catechumens while the people listened; he also gives the reason why the Roman Church added nothing to the Apostles’ Creed.

Our opinion is confirmed by the codices and authors cited at the beginning, and by two Roman Orders in Hittorpus. In the Third Order:

“When the Gospel has ended, the pontiff says: ‘Peace be with you.’ ‘The Lord be with you.’ ‘And with your spirit.’”

And in the Fourth:

“When the Gospel has ended, the pontiff says: ‘Peace be with you. The Lord be with you’; the response follows: ‘And with your spirit.’”

In the Second Order in the same author, however, it says that the Creed is sung only when the pontiff does not wish to preach. I therefore think that Walafrid should not be heeded when, in chapter 22 of *On Ecclesiastical Matters*, he writes that the custom of singing the Constantinopolitan Creed at the Roman Mass came from the Greeks.

The Spaniards began to sing it at Mass at the Third Council of Toledo, canon 2, in the decrees of the council under King Reccared, where the Goths renounced the Arian heresy.

966. “Let us pray.” Then let him begin the Offertory. Here the Pontiff invites the people to prayer, although he himself does not say the prayer, as Alcuin notes in his book *On the Ecclesiastical Office*, in the chapter on the celebration of Mass:

“And he invites him likewise to prayer with himself, saying, ‘Let us pray.’”

Although among us the Collect is not then said between the Offertory and the Gospel, among the Greeks it is said. What Alcuin says about the Greeks appears in the liturgy of Saint John Chrysostom, in which several prayers are said by the pontiff between the Offertory and the Gospel.

967. “The earth trembled.” Formerly, before the Offering, a Psalm was sung in Africa. This began at Carthage in the time of Saint Augustine, as he himself testifies in book II of the *Retractions*, chapter 11:

“The custom that had then begun at Carthage, namely that hymns should be said at the altar from the book of Psalms, either before the Offering,” etc.

968. “After the offering has been received.” This is the offering that the priest is about to consecrate for his own Communion.

563 969. “With the whole Procession.” That is, with the priests, deacons, subdeacons, and the other clergy who assist him at the altar.

970. “The gloves.” That is, the gloves.

971. “And let him wash his hands.” After the readings have been completed and the offering has been made, the pontiff, about to perform the divine mysteries, washes his hands according to an ancient custom. This may be seen in Fortunatus, in the Life of Saint Marcellus, bishop of Paris (in Surius, 1 November):

“Accordingly, while he was serving in the ministry of subdeacon, on the day of Epiphany, drawing water from the river Seine, when he was offering it to blessed Bishop Prudentius for washing his hands, the elements were changed and the taste of wine was found. At this sight the astonished pontiff ordered it to be poured from that pitcher into the sacred chalice, from which, after Mass had been celebrated, the entire people received it in Communion.”

And below:

“Accordingly, once, when the most holy man, in the service of his office, had offered water for the hands to the venerable bishop, balsam immediately began to give off its fragrance from it.”

Among the Greeks, not only the bishop but also the priests standing around the altar wash their hands, as is clear from catechetical lecture 5, the *Mystagogical Catecheses* of Saint Cyril, bishop of Jerusalem:

“*Ἑωράκατε τοίνυν τὸν διάκονον τὸν νίψασθαι διδόντα τῷ ἱερεῖ, καὶ τοῖς κυκλοῦσι τὸ θυσιαστήριον τοῦ θεοῦ πρεσβυτέροις.*”

That is:

“You have therefore seen the deacon offering water for the washing of the hands to the pontiff and to the priests standing around the altar.”

And in Saint Dionysius, chapter 3 of the *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*:

“*Καὶ νιψαμένων τὰς χεῖρας ὕδατι τοῦ ἱεράρχου καὶ τῶν ἱερέων.*”

That is:

“After the pontiff and the priests have washed their hands.”

This was done as a symbol of the purity of the soul required for handling such great mysteries.

### 972. And let every procession offer its offering.

Formerly, those who were about to communicate at Mass—whether clerics or laypeople—offered their offering at the altar, that is, bread and wine for their own communion. This is clear from the Second Council of Mâcon, canon 4:

> Therefore we decree that on all Sundays the offering of the altar be offered by all men and women, so that through these sacrifices they may be freed from the burdens of their sins and may be found worthy to be companions of Abel and the other righteous offerers.

John the Deacon, in the *Life of Saint Gregory the Pope*, book II, chapter 41, writes:

> A certain matron had offered the customary offerings to the blessed Gregory while he was celebrating the solemnities of the Mass at the public stations. When, after the mysteries, he was about to give them to her, he said, “May the Body of our Lord Jesus Christ preserve your soul.” She smiled wantonly. But he turned his right hand away from her mouth and placed that portion of the Lord’s Body upon the altar. When the solemnities of the Mass had been completed, he asked before the people why she had dared to laugh when she was about to receive the Lord’s Body. After remaining silent for a long time, she finally burst out: “Because I knew that the bread which I had made with my own hands was what you were calling the Lord’s Body.”

This is also known from Saint Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 65. He reports that a certain woman always supplied a sextarius of *gazetum* wine as a sacrifice for the repose of her deceased husband to a holy basilica. But a wicked subdeacon, reserving the *gazetum* for his own appetite, offered exceedingly strong vinegar in the chalice, since the woman did not always come forward to receive communion. At last, after the subdeacon’s fraud had been revealed by the husband, who warned the woman in a vision during the night:

> She awoke, amazed at the vision, and, not consigning it to oblivion, rose according to custom for Matins. When these had been completed and the Masses celebrated, she approached the saving cup and drank such burning vinegar that she thought her teeth would be knocked out.

You see, therefore, clearly that wine was offered as a sacrifice for the holy communion of the blood of Christ.

The same is to be understood of the passage in Saint Cyprian, *On Works and Almsgiving*:

> You are wealthy and rich, and you think that you celebrate the Lord’s Day, yet you pay no attention at all to the collection; you come to the Lord’s Day without a sacrifice; you take a portion from the sacrifice that a poor person has offered.

This is how the passage is commonly explained. I therefore do not agree with a certain learned man who wrote that this passage should be understood of things offered at the altar for the use of the poor, and of the *eulogiae* sent to Christians throughout the various parishes, which they received as a sign of communion in the one same faith with their bishop. He attempts to establish this interpretation by the words that follow shortly afterward:

> Since everything that is given is contributed to orphans and widows,

which nevertheless contradicts his opinion. For if everything that is given is contributed to widows, orphans, and the poor, how could such things be blessed for use as *eulogiae*, which are sent to be distributed throughout the whole diocese to all the faithful?

Moreover, those words are spoken about the widow praised by Christ, who had once put two small coins into the treasury, as is evident both from what precedes and from what follows:

> She gives what she ought to receive.

Thus, in the passage cited above from Saint Cyprian, a twofold offering appears: one to be consecrated into the Body of Christ, the other to be blessed for the use of the poor. This is indicated by the words:

> You pay no attention at all to the collection.

To demonstrate the rich man’s greed still further, he reproaches him not only for putting nothing into the collection for the use of the poor, but also for communicating from the poor man’s offering.

The passage in Saint Augustine, sermon 215, *On Time*, is likewise to be understood in this way:

> Offer the offerings which are to be consecrated upon the altar. A person of means ought to be ashamed if he has communicated from another’s offering.

This doctrine is also evident from canon 6 of the Sixteenth Council of Toledo. Condemning those who offered with wine and water a round piece of bread taken from loaves prepared for their own use, it decrees as follows:

> Therefore, wishing to put an end to this rashness or ignorance, our assembly has determined that bread to be sanctified on the altar of the Lord by priestly blessing must not be presented in any other form than whole and clean bread, which has been specially prepared for this purpose; nor must anything large be offered, but only a small offering, in accordance with what ecclesiastical custom has retained.

That bread was round and circular in form is clear from Epiphanius, in the *Ancoratus*, around the middle of the work:

> For this is round in form,

he says, speaking there of the bread that is sanctified on the altar. The same is clear from Isone, chapter 3, *On the Miracles of Saint Othmar*:

> The small round loaves, which are called offerings.

### 973. And finally, incense.

Supply: “let it be offered by the bishop,” according to the ancient custom mentioned by Saint Hippolytus in *On the Consummation of the World and the Antichrist*:

> The Churches too will mourn with great mourning, because neither offering nor incense is performed.

That is: “The Churches too will mourn with great mourning, because neither offering nor incense is made.”

Saint Ephraem says in his testament:

> I also ask you, dearest ones, not to bury me with spices.

And shortly afterward:

> Give off the vapor of sweet-smelling smoke in the house of the Lord; accompany me with your prayers, and offer spices to God.

Saint Ambrose, in his commentary on chapter 1 of Luke, says:

> Would that an angel might stand beside us too, when we burn incense at the altars and bring forward the sacrifice—or rather, that he might make himself visible to us.

### 974. Receive, we beseech you, O Lord, etc.

Primasius, in his commentary on Hebrews 4, appears to have this prayer in view when he writes:

> Hence the priests of the Church, standing beside the altar, say: “Receive, O Lord, the prayers of your people. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son.”

This prayer is said before the Preface according to the ancient custom mentioned by Saint Augustine, sermon 83, *On Various Subjects*:

> First, he says, after the Prayer you are admonished to lift up your hearts.

### 975. The deacon.

That is, *of the deacons*: from the nominative singular *diacon*, in the dative plural *diaconibus*.

### 976. God, who desire not death, etc.

This is the *Apologia* which, in the Mass published by Matthias Illyricus, is also said by the bishop at this point:

> Then let him begin the Secret; when it has been completed and the Preface has been said, while the others sing “Holy, Holy, Holy,” this prayer is to be recited rapidly by the priest: “Lord God, who desire not the death but the repentance of sinners,” etc.

### 977. The blessing of flesh.

It is found in the Roman *Ordo*, where it is preceded by the blessing of the lamb. On the same day of Easter, the Greek *Euchologion* also contains a blessing of flesh, followed by a blessing of cheese and eggs.

[Col. 0549] **Note:** In the old Gallican Sacramentary one reads: “Blessing for blessing the lamb at Easter”; this is followed by “Blessing of every creature of fruits,” perhaps in place of “of all.”

### 978. Therefore taking care that.

It seems that it should be read: “Therefore taking care when.”

### 979. And let it precede itself.

It seems that it should be read: “And let it precede there”—namely, at the words: “Through whom, O Lord, you always create all good things,” etc., as is clear from what follows.

### 980. Lifting the chalice in the sight of the Lord.

According to the ancient custom, the chief deacon, or archdeacon, when the bishop had said the words “through him, and with him,” lifted the chalice and held it raised before the bishop. This may be seen in the First Roman *Ordo*:

> When he has said “Through whom, O Lord, all these things,” the archdeacon alone rises; and when he has said “Through him and with him,” the archdeacon lifts the chalice by its handles together with the offering and holds it raised beside the bishop.

The same appears in the Third and Fourth *Ordines*:

> When he has said “Through whom, O Lord, all things,” the archdeacon alone rises; when he has said “Through him and with him,” the archdeacon lifts the chalice by its handles together with the offering, etc.

For the rest, see below in the notes on the rite of celebrating the Mass of John of Avranches.

At present, however, in the Latin Church, as soon as the bread and wine have been consecrated, they are lifted up on high so that they may be adored by the surrounding people. I do not think that this rite is especially ancient, since nothing similar is found in our manuscript and printed Sacramentaries or in Pamelius, nor in the ancient Roman *Ordines*, nor in Alcuin, Amalarius, Walafrid, or Rabanus, who treated the order of the Mass in detail. Nor is it found in Micrologus, who devoted excellent attention to the same subject. This is clearer than daylight from chapter 15 of the book he wrote *On Ecclesiastical Observances*:

> Then the bread is taken into the hands and, before it is put back on the altar, is blessed; likewise the elevated chalice is blessed before it is set down. For the Lord himself is also read in the Gospel to have blessed both before he released them from his hands. For, having received them in his hands, he blessed them and afterward gave them to the disciples.

He also says, where it is stated:

> A pure victim, a holy victim, etc.

These are his words. Certainly, if this rite had been in use in his time, he would never have omitted it, since afterward he mentions the elevation of the Body, which takes place together with the chalice before the Lord’s Prayer is recited:

> And when we say “world without end,” we lift the Body together with the chalice.

The same will appear still more clearly from chapter 23 of the same author.

The Mozarabic Mass must be excepted—if, indeed, nothing has been added to it—in which there is a twofold elevation of the Host: the first immediately after the consecration, and the second follows the words:

> Let us speak with our mouth the faith which we believe in our heart.

The Greeks and the other Eastern peoples raise the Body of Christ after the Lord’s Prayer and other prayers, with communion following immediately. This is evident from the liturgy of Saint James:

> The deacon says, with the fear of God: “Let us attend,” while the priest, raising the gift, says privately, “Holy,” etc.

That is: “The priest, raising the gift, says privately, ‘Holy,’ etc.”

It is also evident from the liturgy of Saint John Chrysostom:

> When the deacon sees the priest extending his hands and touching the holy bread in order to perform the elevation, he cries out, “Let us attend”; and the priest says, “The holy things for the holy.”

That is: “In order to perform the elevation he cries out, ‘Let us attend’; and the priest says, ‘The holy things for the holy.’”

All these things follow the Lord’s Prayer and several prayers there. The same is clear from Saint Anastasius of Sinai, in his sermon *On the Holy Synaxis*. After mentioning the Lord’s Prayer, he adds:

> Let us say these things—that is, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive,” etc. Let us pray these things daily while we stand at the dread synaxis. Knowing this, the priest, after the consecration of that unbloody sacrifice, raises up the bread of life and displays it to everyone. Then the deacon cries out and says, “Let us attend.”

That is:

> And he raises the bread of life on high and displays it to everyone. Then the deacon cries out and says, “Let us attend.”

This is confirmed by the words that follow:

> Then the priest immediately adds and says, “The holy things for the holy.”

That is: “Then the priest immediately follows and says, ‘The holy things for the holy.’”

For Saint Cyril of Jerusalem, in catechesis 5, *Mystagogical*, writes that these words are pronounced by the bishop after the Lord’s Prayer has been completed:

> Then, having completed the prayer, he says “Amen,” sealing by the Amen—which means “let it be”—the whole prayer that we learned from God. After this the priest says, “The holy things for the holy.”

That is: “Afterward the priest says, ‘The holy things for the holy.’”

The same may also be gathered from these words of George Codinus, in his book *On the Offices of the Court of Constantinople*:

> Returning again to the platform, the emperor sits, rising only during the reading of the holy Creed, during the prayer of “Our Father who art in heaven,” and during the elevation of the Lord’s holy Body. When the elevation has taken place, etc.

That is:

> Rising only during the reading of the Creed, during the Lord’s Prayer, and during the elevation of the Lord’s holy Body. After the elevation has taken place, if the emperor is not prepared for communion, he sits on his throne until the end of the holy liturgy; but if he is prepared, the two deacons whom we mentioned earlier summon him, and he enters the holy altar with them.

Thus far Codinus. Note first that here the elevation of Christ’s Body is placed after the Lord’s Prayer; second, that as soon as Christ’s Body has been elevated, the emperor—if he is prepared for communion—is summoned by two deacons and enters the holy altar for sacred communion.

The Ethiopians imitate the same custom in their liturgy. Since the priest and the people are about to communicate immediately, the deacon says:

> Let us look.

The priest says:

> Give the Holy One to the holy ones.

The people say:

> One is the Holy Father, one the Holy Son, one the Holy Spirit.

The priest says:

> The Lord be with you.

The people say:

> And with your spirit.

The priest, elevating the Sacrament, says aloud:

> Lord Jesus Christ, have mercy on us.

Immediately the priest and the people communicate. In that Mass there is only one elevation of Christ’s Body, as in the liturgies just cited.

The same may be seen in the *Life of Saint Basil* by Amphilochius:

> After the end of the prayers, he exalted the bread, praying at length and saying, “Attend, Lord Jesus Christ, from your holy dwelling place,” etc.

This is as in the liturgies of Saint Basil and Saint Chrysostom, in which this prayer is said shortly before the words “The holy things for the holy,” after the Lord’s Prayer.

Some, however, think that formerly there were two elevations: the first, which was also performed by the priest immediately after the consecration according to the modern rite; and the second, mentioned above. They try to establish this from these words of Saint Dionysius, chapter 3 of the *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*:

> And having hymned and praised the sacred works of God, the hierarch performs the divine mysteries, brings the things that have been hymned before the eyes through the sacred symbols set forth, displays the gifts of the divine works, and then himself approaches their sacred communion.

That is:

> When the priest has sung and praised the sacred works of God, he consecrates the mysteries, brings what has been celebrated before the eyes through the sacred symbols set forth, and, having displayed the gifts of the divine operation, himself then approaches their divine communion.

Those words are to be understood of the display which, as we have said, took place shortly before communion, as Saint Dionysius indicates in his own words and Saint Maximus explains admirably in his scholia:

> “Before the eyes.” At that time the divine gifts remained concealed until the time of holy reception; and this he explains shortly afterward. Certainly, it is clear that, when the hierarch lifted up the holy bread, he displayed the blessing, saying, “The holy things for the holy.”

This accords with the liturgies of Saints James, Basil, and Chrysostom and the other Greek liturgies, in which no elevation of the Host immediately after its consecration is found. In the cited passage of Saint Dionysius there is a single elevation; and if it follows the consecration, this is because Saint Dionysius omitted the things intervening between the consecration and the elevation, which may be seen in the liturgies and in the authors cited.

The priest, when lifting the Host, also made the sign of the cross three times with it in the air, as Saint Germanus, patriarch of Constantinople, teaches in his *Mystical Theory*:

> The elevation on high of the venerable Body represents the elevation of the cross, the death upon it, and the resurrection itself. But that the priest lifts up the bread and makes the sign of the cross three times in the air with the venerable and life-giving bread signifies this.

The elevation of the Host in the Mass is mentioned in the fifth response of the Constantinopolitan synod under Patriarch Nicholas.

### 981. Or the names of the living.

This is as in the Greek liturgies and in the catechesis of Saint Cyril cited above, where, after the consecration, the living and the dead are commemorated together.

### 982. Let the deacon say, etc.

The deacon’s duties include warning the people before communion to humble themselves, or to bow in order to receive the episcopal blessing. This is clear from homily 34 of Saint Caesarius of Arles:

> I likewise admonish you, dearest brothers: whenever the deacon cries out that you ought to bow for the blessing, bow your bodies and heads faithfully.

And near the end:

> Whenever the deacon cries out that you ought either to bend your knees in prayer or bow your heads for the blessing, do so obediently and faithfully, with true humility.

In the Roman *Ordo*, this is done by the archdeacon.

### 983. Humble yourselves for the blessing.

Thus in the Roman *Ordo* and in the Mozarabic Mass. See above what we have observed concerning these episcopal blessings. Their use still survives in certain Churches.

### 984. May he bless you, etc.

I have not copied out this blessing in full, since it is found above in the Easter solemnity of the book of Sacramentaries.

### 985. May the peace of the Lord be always with you.

Formerly, “Peace be with you” was said at this point, as is clear from Saint Augustine, sermon 83, *On Various Subjects*:

> Behold, when the sanctification has been completed, we say the Lord’s Prayer, which you received and returned. After it is said, “Peace be with you,” and Christians kiss one another with a holy kiss.

### 986. Meanwhile let him kiss the archdeacon and the others.

The bishop, about to communicate immediately, gives the kiss of peace according to the rite of the Roman, or Latin, Church, if the ancient Hispanic rite is excepted. Pope Innocent I, in his letter to Decentius, bishop of Gubbio, writes of this:

> You now assert that before the mysteries have been completed some command the people to give peace, or that the priests give it among themselves, whereas peace must necessarily be announced after all the things which I ought not to disclose have been completed. Through it it is established that the people have given their consent to all that is done in the mysteries and celebrated in the Church, and the kiss of peace demonstrates that everything has been completed.

This is how Tertullian is to be understood, near the end of his book *On Prayer*:

> Another custom has now prevailed: those who fast, after prayer with the brethren, withdraw the kiss of peace, which is the seal of prayer.

The words of Pope Innocent wonderfully illuminate this passage.

It is confirmed by the authority of Saint Augustine, sermon 83, *On Various Subjects*:

> Behold, when the sanctification has been completed, we say the Lord’s Prayer, which you received and returned. After it is said, “Peace be with you,” and Christians kiss one another with a holy kiss, which is the sign of peace, etc.

Also, in book II *Against the Letters of Petilian*, chapter 23:

> To whom you joined the kiss of peace among the sacraments, into whose hands you placed the Eucharist, and to whom you extended it when he in turn gave it.

The Greeks use another rite. Among them, after the hands have been washed, the kiss of peace is given before the Preface, the mystical prayers, and the consecration. This is clear from Saint Cyril of Jerusalem, catechesis 5, *Mystagogical*:

> Then the deacon cries out, “Receive one another; let us kiss one another.”

That is: “Then the deacon cries out, ‘Embrace one another; let us kiss one another,’ etc.”

After explaining the mystery of the kiss, he adds:

> Afterward the priest cries out, “Lift up your hearts,” etc.

Saint Dionysius, in book 3 of *The Celestial Hierarchy*, says:

> And after everyone has kissed one another, the mystical recitation of the sacred books takes place.

Saint Justin Martyr, *Second Apology for the Christians*, says:
