> We greet one another with a kiss.

He then explains how bread and a cup of water and wine are offered to the bishop for consecration.

The same is also established by canon 19 of the Council of Laodicea:

> The prayer of the catechumens must first be performed separately after the discourses of the bishops; and after the catechumens have gone out, the prayer of those doing penance must be made; and when they have approached under the hand—that is, when the bishop’s hand has been laid upon them—and have withdrawn, the prayers of the faithful must then be made: the first in silence, but the second and third must be completed aloud; then peace is to be given.

That is: “Then peace is to be given.”

Shortly afterward it says:

> And thus the holy offering is to be performed.

That is: “And thus the holy offering is to be celebrated.”

Saint John Chrysostom, in homily 18 on Paul’s Second Epistle to the Corinthians, after describing the prayers said for the possessed, penitents, and others who do not communicate, adds:

> When it is necessary again to partake of peace and to give it in return, we all greet one another equally.

That is: “When peace must again be given and received in return, we all likewise kiss one another.”

Finally, he adds that the bishop prays for the people, and the people in turn pray for the bishop when they answer him, “And with your spirit”; and that they assent to the bishop’s giving of thanks by answering, “It is worthy and right.” Only then does the bishop begin the thanksgiving, that is, the Preface.

The following words of Timothy, patriarch of Alexandria, in response to question 8, are relevant here:

> In the oblation, before the kiss, the deacon proclaims, “Those who do not communicate, depart.”

Note here that, since the catechumens are excluded from the sacred rites before the salutation—that is, before the kiss of peace—it can easily be concluded that this salutation among the Greeks takes place before the consecration of the divine mysteries. For if it took place after the consecration, as among us, the catechumens could have been expelled before the salutation even though they would have been present at the consecration, contrary to the decrees of the Church.

Timothy therefore wishes the catechumens to be expelled before the salutation because, once it has been completed, the priest immediately girds and prepares himself for the sanctification of the mysteries.

Ancient Spain once followed the Greek rite, as is clear from Saint Isidore, book I *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 15. There he writes that a fourth prayer was said for the kiss of peace, followed by a fifth, which according to his text is the Oblation and the Preface.

### 987. May this most holy commixture, etc.

In the Roman Missal and in Micrologus, chapter 23, the words “and consecration” are added.

In the Mass of Illyricus, the second prayer reads:

> May there be a commixture and consecration of the Body and Blood,

in accordance with what is decreed in canon 17 of the First Council of Orange:

> The chalice must be offered, and it must be consecrated by the admixture of the Eucharist.

This is to be understood of a certain external consecration, since it had already been consecrated previously through the words of Christ. Therefore the word “consecration” does not signify the preceding consecration performed through Christ’s words, as some incorrectly explain it.

This commixture of the Body and Blood is also found in the liturgy of Saint James and in canon 17 of the Fourth Council of Toledo:

> The joining of the bread and the chalice, etc.

### 988. May it be for all who receive, etc.

The Roman Missal has it differently.

### 989. Let them communicate.

The word *se* is redundant.

### 990. And after it has been communicated, let him say these prayers.

In the Roman Missal these two first prayers precede communion, and in some versions they vary.

### 991. And let the bishop communicate the priests, etc.

The bishop gives communion according to the ancient custom, as may be seen in Tertullian, *On the Crown of the Soldier*:

> We receive the sacrament of the Eucharist, ordained by the Lord both at the time of meals and in all assemblies, even before dawn, from no hand but that of the presiding ministers.

This custom was not universal. For in the time of Saint Justin Martyr, who lived before Tertullian, deacons gave the Body and Blood of the Lord to the faithful, as is evident from his *Second Apology for the Christians*:

> Those who are called deacons among us give to each of those present a share of the bread, wine, and water over which thanks have been given.

That is: “Those who are called deacons among us give consecrated bread, wine, and water to all who are present.”

There is an important passage concerning the giving of the chalice by a deacon in Saint Cyprian’s *Letter on the Lapsed*:

> When the solemn rites had been completed and the deacon began to offer the chalice to those present, when her turn came, the little girl, prompted by the divine Majesty, turned her face away, closed her mouth by pressing her lips together, and refused the chalice. Nevertheless, the deacon persisted and, despite her resistance, poured some of the sacrament of the chalice into her.

Nor did the First Council of Nicaea prohibit this. It merely abolished the wicked custom of certain places where deacons gave the Eucharist to presbyters, since it is absurd that those who do not offer the Eucharist should give it to those who do offer it.

In canon 38 of the Fourth Council of Carthage, a deacon is forbidden to distribute the Eucharist to the people when a presbyter is present, unless necessity commands him to do so.

### 992. With a separate sacrifice.

That is, with the Body of Christ given separately from the Blood.

### 993. Yet with a mixed sacrifice.

That is, with the Body of Christ mixed with his Blood.

For formerly in many places the custom had arisen of giving the Body of Christ dipped in the sacred Blood. This is clear from the many decrees issued at different times to abolish this custom.

Pope Julius I, in Ivo of Chartres, part II of the *Decree*, chapter 85, writes:

> As for what some give to the people as a completion of communion, namely the Eucharist dipped in the Blood, they have not found this testimony in the Gospel, where the Lord entrusted his Body and Blood to the apostles. For the giving of the bread and of the chalice is mentioned separately.

The Third Council of Braga also prohibits this in canon 1, because, as it notes there, Christ gave his Body and Blood separately to the apostles.

The same was decreed by the Council of Clermont celebrated by Urban II, as reported by Orderic Vitalis, book IX of his *Ecclesiastical History*, under the year 1095. It decreed that the Lord’s Body and Blood should be received separately, in these words:

> Let the Lord’s Body and the Lord’s Blood be received separately.

As Orderic reports it, this canon is clear and presents no difficulty. But it creates a problem as reported by the very learned Baronius in the *Ecclesiastical Annals*, volume II, from the papers of Antonius Augustinus, bishop of Tarragona:

> Let no one communicate from the altar unless he receives the Body separately and the Blood likewise, except in case of necessity and precaution.

Those final words—“except in case of necessity and precaution”—do not occur in Orderic Vitalis. Nevertheless, they mean nothing other than that the species may be given mixed together if some necessity or precaution intervenes. This is the case when the people communicate during a solemn Mass, so that, because of the multitude, the Blood may not be spilled, as appears in the ancient rite of the Mass celebrated by John, bishop of Avranches:

> With the exception of the people, whom it is permitted to communicate with dipped bread—not by authority, but under the pressing necessity of fear that Christ’s Blood might be spilled.

This is also the case with those sick persons whose strength has entirely failed, who can scarcely receive the Lord’s Body because of their weakness and cannot receive the sacred chalice without danger of spilling it. In such circumstances, according to the intention of the council, the Lord’s Body could be given to such sick persons dipped in the Lord’s Blood on a spoon, so that they might easily swallow it. This may be seen in the visitation of the sick in the manuscript codex of the monastery of Saint Remigius founded at Reims.

There, when a sick person communicates after anointing, if the force of the illness has not reduced him to such weakness, both formulas are said:

> May the Body of our Lord Jesus Christ preserve you unto eternal life.  
> May the Blood of our Lord Jesus Christ redeem you unto eternal life.

These indicate separate reception.

But when a sick person communicates who has begun to grow worse, only one formula is recited, in this form:

> May the Body and Blood of our Lord Jesus Christ preserve your soul unto eternal life.

For in this case the Lord’s Body, dipped in the sacred Blood, is given to the sick person on a spoon.

### 994. Communion: “Our Passover.” Psalm: “O Lord, you have searched me,” etc.

In this communion there are an antiphon and a psalm which are sung.

Formerly a psalm was sung during communion, as is clear from Saint Augustine, book II of the *Retractations*, chapter 11:

> So that hymns might be sung at the altar from the book of Psalms, either before the Oblation or while what had been offered was distributed to the people, etc.

Among the Greeks, after the clergy have communicated, when they carry back the *muscaria*, or fans, the disks, chalices, and other sacred vessels, they begin to sing certain chants. After these have been put away, the final verse of the Communion begins, followed by the *troparion*, or verse:

> Let our mouth be filled with praise, O Lord, etc.

That is:

> Let our mouth be filled with praise, O Lord, so that we may sing your glory, because you have deemed us worthy to partake of your holy mysteries. Preserve us in your sanctification as we meditate upon your righteousness throughout the day. Alleluia.

This occurred in the year 351 of the Olympiad, in the month of May, in the twelfth indiction, under Sergius, patriarch of Constantinople, as the *Alexandrian Chronicle* reports.

This does not appear in the present-day liturgies, except that the *troparion* beginning “Let our mouth be filled” is sung in the liturgy of Saint John Chrysostom when the holy gifts are carried to the prothesis.

### 995. Go, the Mass is ended.

In the Greek liturgies there are other formulas: “Go in peace,” “Let us proceed in peace,” and “Let us go in the peace of Christ.” These are also pronounced by the deacon.

### 996. May it please you, O holy Trinity, etc.

This prayer is also found in the Mass of the manuscript Tilian Codex and in the Mass of Illyricus, with a few variations.

### 997. Here begins the bishop’s order, etc.

We have added this second Mass—or rather, this order of the Mass—from the manuscript Tilian Codex, which we have cited so often above.

Although the preceding Mass, drawn from the Codex of Abbot Ratold, appears to be older, I considered it a serious fault to omit this one, since it contains many things worth remembering and knowing—especially because it is extremely similar to the ancient Mass published by Matthias Illyricus, a man of the Lutheran sect, from the Palatine Library. This will become clear from the comparison of the two which we shall provide in these observations, once we have first answered certain objections raised by Illyricus in his preface, in which he attacks the Roman Mass.

[Col. 0555] **Note:** Concerning this Mass, consult the very learned Mabillon, book I of the *Gallican Liturgy*, chapter 3.

First, he traces the antiquity of his Mass back to the time of Gregory I, and says that it was in use in the Church during Gregory’s lifetime, or some years afterward. I certainly cannot persuade myself of this, both because it contains many elements instituted long after Gregory, and because features absent from the preceding Mass of the Codex of Ratoldus—written several years before 986—are found in the Mass of the Tilian Codex, which was written many years after Ratoldus’s Codex, namely during the reign of Henry I, king of the Franks. Nevertheless, I do not deny that many features of the Mass edited by Illyricus bear the mark of antiquity.

Second, in order to prefer the Mass he edited to the Roman Mass, he says that formerly there was only one way of celebrating Mass, as among the Greeks, and that his own Mass was composed for every need; he also says that formerly there were no Masses for saints and feasts. But the falsity of this opinion can be demonstrated from Illyricus’s own Mass. In it, the Introit, Epistle, Gradual, Gospel, Offertory, Secret, Preface, Communion, and Postcommunion are mentioned only in general terms, not individually or specifically, without the specification or assignment of any particular Introit, Epistle, or similar item. This is confirmed by these words of the same Mass:

“When the angelic praise has ended, let the priest say the Missal Prayer; then let the reading be recited.”

Here “Missal Prayer” can be nothing other than the prayer that follows the angelic hymn. If this is so, why are no particular Introit, Epistle, Gospel, and so forth assigned? Why, although so many complete prayers, or apologies, are found in that Mass, is no Missal Prayer, no Secret, and no Postcommunion Prayer described there? No explanation can reasonably be given for this except the variety of feasts and the solemnity of the saints, which, according to their diversity, require different Missal Prayers, Epistles, Gospels, Secrets, and similar items appropriate to the feast or the saint’s solemnity. If all these were placed within the order of the Mass, the celebrant would be entangled in many labyrinths of confusion. To avoid this, the ordinary order of the Mass is set out separately—as may be seen in the Illyrican Mass, whose title is as follows: “Here begins the order of the sacraments,” and at the end: “Here ends the order concerning the office of the Mass.” The remaining items, however, are arranged in an elegant order according to the variety of feasts and seasons, as is customary in sacramentaries and missals.

Surely the apostles and those ancient pontiffs who have shone before us in holiness and learning did not celebrate the feasts of the Nativity of the Lord, the Epiphanies, Easter, and Pentecost while omitting the commemoration of the great benefits that the all-good and all-great God bestowed upon us on those days. These feasts were instituted precisely so that those benefits might be remembered and gratitude toward God expressed—just as formerly God commanded the Jews to observe the feasts of Passover, Pentecost, Tabernacles, and similar festivals. Saint Isidore of Pelusium notes this admirably, book II, letter 116:

[The opening Greek is corrupt; perhaps read: “Do not be unaware, however.”] “Do not be unaware, however, that God, both formerly and now, has attached the remembrance of his benefits to the feasts, so that those who celebrate them, keeping their memory sounding in their ears, may turn not toward drunkenness but toward thanksgiving and virtue.”

That is:

“Do not fail to understand that God has joined the remembrance of his benefits to the feasts, both formerly and now, so that those who celebrate the festal days, having the memory of them resounding in their ears, may turn not toward drunkenness but toward thanksgiving.”

An ancient practice is evident from Saint Augustine, in the prologue to the First Epistle of John:

“Your Holiness remembers that we are accustomed to treat the Gospel according to John in the order of the readings. But because now the solemnity of the saints’ days has intervened—days on which certain readings from the Gospel must be recited in the Church, readings that recur annually and therefore cannot be replaced by others—the order we had undertaken has, by necessity, been interrupted for a short time, not abandoned.”

In Treatise 9 on the Epistle of John:

“Certain solemn readings proper to the feast days intervened, and they could not but be read and explained; thus they caused us to interrupt the text of this epistle.”

And in Sermon 144, *On the Season*:

“The resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ has been recited today, but from another Gospel book, the one according to Luke. First it was read according to Matthew, yesterday according to Mark, and today according to Luke. This is the order of the evangelists. Just as his Passion was written by all the evangelists, so these days extend over a period of seven or eight days, so that the resurrection may be recited according to all the evangelists. But because the Passion is read on one day, it is ordinarily read only according to Matthew. At one time I wanted the Passion also to be read each year according to all the evangelists. It was done; the people did not hear what they were accustomed to, and they were disturbed.”

From Gennadius, *Catalogue of Illustrious Men*, concerning Musaeus, presbyter of the Church of Massilia:

“He composed an excellent and substantial volume of Sacraments, divided into sections according to the requirements of offices and seasons, and distinguished according to the text of the readings and the sequence and chanting of the psalms.”

From Sidonius, book IV, letter 11, concerning Claudianus Mamertus, brother of the bishop of Vienne:

> This arranger of psalms and master of song,  
> before the altars, while his brother rejoiced,  
> taught the ordered choirs to resound.  
> He prepared for the annual solemnities  
> what should be read at each appropriate time.

And from Pope Vigilius’s letter 2:

“We do not at any time, or on any feast, indicate that the order of prayers in the celebration of Masses is divided; rather, we always consecrate the offerings made to God in the same manner. Whenever the feast of the Lord’s Passover, Pentecost, or Epiphany, or of God’s saints, is to be celebrated, we join together the individual sections appropriate to those days, so that we may commemorate the holy solemnity or those whose anniversaries we celebrate; the rest we continue according to the customary order.”

Here “the order of prayers” means the manner of celebrating Mass, not the Canon of the Mass, as is clear from the cited passage; that Canon is subsequently called the text of the canonical prayer in the same place.

If we consider the canonical hours, variety according to the diversity of solemnities and feasts can also be seen in them. For, as Gennadius reports, the aforementioned Musaeus:

“Selected from the holy Scriptures readings suitable for the feast days of the entire year, as well as responsories and sections of the Psalms appropriate to the season and the readings.”

This is also evident from the rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 14:

“On the feasts of the saints, or on all solemnities, it is to be done as we have said for Sunday, except that the Psalms, Antiphons, or readings proper to that day are to be recited.”

Nor is Illyricus’s claim valid that the Greeks even today have only one form of Mass. Although the Greek liturgies that we now possess are, as it were, common forms of Mass, nevertheless different Masses according to the diversity of feasts, solemnities, and seasons are found in their *Euchologion* and in their other ritual books.

Finally, the manuscript Codex from which Illyricus copied his Mass is not so ancient, since the letter N occurs three times in it, a letter commonly used in place of a proper name. This form began to be used shortly before the year 1000 after Christ. For in older manuscript codices, in place of this letter N, the following sign is used: Ill., with a transverse line, as may be seen in our oldest manuscript sacramentary books of Saint Eligius, the Rheims and Rodradi books. The same practice appears in the formulas of Marculf and in certain other books recently printed from very ancient manuscript codices.

Illyricus also says that before the age of Charlemagne Masses for the dead were not in use. But this is easily refuted [Note: In the old Gallican Sacramentary, copied from the Bobbio Codex a thousand years ago, several Masses for the dead are found, as may be seen in *Musei Italici*, volume I, pages 384 and following.] by canon 43 of the Second Council of Vaison, where the contrary is evident:

“In all Masses—whether Matins, Lenten Masses, or those celebrated for the commemoration of the dead—the Sanctus, ‘Holy, Holy, Holy,’ is always to be said in the same order in which it is said at public Masses.”

In canon 16 of the First Council of Braga:

“But whoever, following the sect of Priscillian, celebrates the feast of that day—the Thursday of the Lord’s Supper—from the third hour by Masses for the dead, after breaking the fast, let him be anathema.”

There it is forbidden to celebrate Masses for the dead on the Thursday of the Lord’s Supper, at the third hour, after breaking the fast. This indicates that on that day such Masses could be celebrated after None, without the fast having been broken. And in canon 10 of the Second Council of Braga, it is decreed that no one should dare to celebrate Masses for the dead even after receiving unmixed wine and the offering, so that Masses may be celebrated by those who are fasting.

Nor can the question of Saint Boniface, which Illyricus adduces, oppose our position. Saint Boniface’s question concerns only offerings for the dead within the Mass, not Masses for the dead of the kind we now celebrate. Illyricus’s argument concerning Communion and offerings does not make his Mass any more ancient than the others, since these things are also found in the Mass of the Tilian Codex, which was written in the time of Henry I, king of the Franks, as has been said.

### 998. When he washes his hands

This washing of the hands is also found in the Mass edited by Illyricus, with the same prayer: “Grant to our senses,” and so forth.

### 999. Afterwards he puts on the sandals, etc.

In Illyricus’s Mass the pontiff is clothed in pontifical vestments, but the order of vesting is different and the prayers are different. More vestments are also found in Illyricus’s Mass, namely: alb, girdle, subcinctorium, stole, subtile, dalmatic, chasuble, maniple, gloves, ring, and rationale.

### 1000. Then let him sing with those standing around him, etc.

In Illyricus’s Mass it is prescribed:

“In the meantime, while the bishop is being prepared, let the clergy standing around him sing these Psalms: ‘How lovely are your tabernacles’; ‘You have blessed your land, Lord’; ‘Incline your ear, Lord.’”

In place of the prayers, four other Psalms follow.

### 1001. Let him kiss two presbyters, etc.

In Illyricus’s Mass:

“Then, in the same place, let him give the kiss of peace to the presbyters and deacons who escort him.”

### 1002. Beginning by himself, etc.

I have corrected it in this way. In Illyricus’s Mass it reads:

“When he reaches the altar, let him himself intone the Antiphon: ‘I will go in to the altar of God,’ etc., with the Psalm ‘Judge me, O God,’ etc.; and other prayers follow.”

### 1003. Take away from us, etc.

In Illyricus’s Mass this prayer precedes the Antiphon “I will go in to the altar of God.” After *mentibus*, read *mereamur*.

### 1004. Almighty God, who [me] a sinner, etc.

This prayer is indeed found in Illyricus’s Mass, but it is recited at the kissing of the altar.

### 1005. Then, when he kisses the Gospel, etc.

In Illyricus’s Mass:

“Then he greets the Gospel, saying: ‘The peace of Christ,’ etc.”

### 1006. The priest’s confession before the altar

In Illyricus’s Mass:

“After this, let him say this Confession secretly: ‘Receive my Confession, my only hope of salvation,’ etc.”

Then ten prayers, or apologies, follow in the same Mass. The tenth is as follows:

“God, be merciful to me, a sinner,” etc.,

as it appears in this Tilian Mass, where it is said before the altar, before the priest begins Mass.

### 1007. Likewise, the prayer in the meantime, etc.

In Illyricus’s Mass:

“Let the following prayer be said by the bishop in the meantime, until the angelic hymn is finished.”

But another prayer, or apology, is found there:

“God, who are justly angry,” etc.

### 1008. From after the Collect to the Gospel

In Illyricus’s Mass the following is found:

“When the angelic praise has ended, let the priest say the Missal Prayer; then let the reading be recited. Between the reading and the Gospel—that is, during the Gradual, Alleluia, and Sequence—let the bishop say these prayers.”

But the prayers are different, sixteen in number, some of them quite lengthy.

The Prayer of the Tilian Mass, “God, who make the worthy out of the unworthy,” etc., is recited by the pontiff in Illyricus’s Mass while the Offertory is being sung.

### 1009. When incense is brought before the Gospel is read, etc.

In Illyricus’s Mass:

“When incense is placed in the thurible before the Gospel is read, let the priest say: ‘By the fragrance of his heavenly inspiration,’ etc.”

The blessing of the same incense follows:

“In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, let this incense be blessed and become acceptable as an odor of sweetness.”

### 1010. Then, as the deacon bows, let the priest say, etc.

In Illyricus’s Mass:

“Then, as the deacon bows for the blessing of God”—add *ad*—“let him say: ‘May the blessing of God the almighty Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, descend upon you; and may Christ the Lord open your mouth to pronounce his holy Gospel worthily and suitably. May the Lord God be in your mouth,’ etc.”

But the earlier Blessing is absent from the Tilian Codex.

The following comes next in Illyricus’s Mass:

“As he receives or kisses the Gospel, let the deacon say: ‘Give me, Lord, a right and well-sounding word in my mouth, so that my words may please you and all who hear them, for the sake of your holy name, unto eternal life. Amen.’”

After the Gospel has been read, let the deacon say:

“Through these words of your holy Gospel, Lord, forgive me all my sins,”

and the others say:

“Peace be with you.”

### 1011. After the Gospel has been read, etc.

In Illyricus’s Mass it is somewhat different:

“Then, when incense and the Gospel have been brought together for the greeting, let them say: ‘Through these words of the Lord’s Gospel,’ etc.”

Then in the same Mass follows:

“When incense is offered, let each one say: ‘Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight, Lord.’”

Then the priest begins the Creed, that is, “I believe in one God.” This Creed is the Constantinopolitan Creed, which is given there in full.

The following then appears in the same Mass:

“When the Apostles’ Creed has been finished, the priest says: ‘The Lord be with you.’ Then he washes his hands, saying this prayer: ‘Grant to our senses,’ etc., as above in the Tilian Mass.”

### 1012. When the altar has been adorned, etc.

In Illyricus’s Mass:

“When the altar has been adorned, before he receives the offerings, let him say the following prayers with the greatest humility, tearfully accusing himself before the altar: ‘Before your eyes, Lord,’ etc.”

Six other apologies or prayers follow this. After them the same Mass of Illyricus continues:

“Then, approaching the altar and kissing it, let him say: ‘I beseech you, Lord, almighty God, that through the merits of your saints, whose relics are contained here, and through their intercession, you may graciously forgive me all my sins; you who live and reign,’ etc.”

Note that here the altar is adorned after the Gospel has been said—that is, it is spread with linens and coverings.

### 1013. Then let him turn, etc.

In Illyricus’s Mass:

“Then let him turn to receive the offerings of the presbyters and others.”

### 1014. And let each one say this prayer

When someone offers his offering, as in Illyricus’s Mass:

“When someone offers an offering into the hand of the bishop or presbyter, let him say: ‘To you, Lord, my Creator,’ etc.”

At the end, “of the living and the dead” is added. Then follows:

“For himself and for all the Christian people: ‘To you, Lord, I offer a sacrifice of appeasement,’ etc.”

“For our king and bishop, and for all the clergy and all the Christian people: ‘To you, Lord, my Creator, I offer a sacrifice of appeasement and praise,’ etc.”

The bishop or presbyter, receiving the offerings, says:

“Receive, holy Trinity, this Offering which your servant N. offers to you; and grant that, pleasing to you, it may ascend into your sight; you who live,” etc.

After receiving the offerings from the clergy or people, let the deacon take the offering from the hand of the subdeacon, saying:

“May your sacrifice be acceptable to almighty God and to all his saints.”

Then, coming before the bishop, the deacon says this Offertory:

“Receive, Lord, holy Father, this Offering,” etc.

The bishop, receiving the offering from the deacon, says:

“May your offering be acceptable to almighty God.”

Then, with a pure heart, let him offer the offering to the Lord, saying:

“Receive, holy Father, almighty and eternal God,” etc.

Another prayer:

“Receive, most merciful Father, sacrifices of appeasement,” etc.

### 1015. Let him first accuse himself tearfully

Above, in Illyricus’s Mass:

“Let him tearfully accuse himself.”

### 1016. Before the presence of your divine Majesty, etc.

This is found above in Illyricus’s Mass as the fourth among the apologies or prayers recited there by the priest when the altar has been adorned, before he receives the offerings.

### 1017. Then, with a pure heart, let him offer to the Lord, etc.

In Illyricus’s Mass it is written:

“These prayers are to be said when the offerings are presented at the altar. This is the first daily general prayer: ‘Receive, holy Trinity, this Offering which I offer to you in memory of the incarnation, birth,’ etc.”

### 1018. Receive, holy Trinity, etc.

This is the fifth Offering Prayer in Illyricus’s Mass.

### 1019. Receive, holy Trinity, etc.

This second Offering Prayer is the first in Illyricus’s Mass.

### 1020. Receive, holy Trinity, etc.

This third Offering Prayer is the eighth of the Illyrican Mass.

### 1021. Soul

In Illyricus’s Mass, *salute*—“salvation”—is read.

### 1022. Receive, holy Trinity, etc.

This fourth Offering Prayer is the tenth of the Illyrican Mass, although it is for a single deceased person.

### 1023. To be joined

In the Illyrican Mass, *coadunari*—“to be united”—is read.

Finally, in Illyricus’s Mass, after the fourth Offering Prayer, or offering, comes the priest’s apology:

“Receive my confession, my only hope of salvation,” etc.,

as above in the Tilian Mass.

The same Mass of Illyricus continues:

“Then let him place the offering on the altar and say: ‘Sanctify, Lord, this Offering, so that it may become for us the body of your Only-Begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ.’”

Then the deacon receives wine mixed with water in a chalice from the subdeacon, saying:

“God, who bestowed dignity upon human substance,” etc.

### 1024. Then let the deacon offer the chalice, etc.

In Illyricus’s Mass:

“Then let the deacon offer the chalice on the altar and say to the bishop: ‘Offer to the Lord,’ etc.”

### 1025. As the bishop offers the chalice to the Lord, let him say

In Illyricus’s Mass:

“And the priest, offering the chalice, says this Offertory: ‘We offer you, Lord, the chalice of salvation, and we implore your mercy,’ etc.,”

as in the Roman Missal.

### 1026. Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

In the Illyrican Mass:

“Lord Jesus Christ, who, in the passion of your cross,” etc.

The following comes next:

“When the chalice has been placed on the altar, let the priest say: ‘Sanctify, Lord, the chalice offered to you, so that it may become for us the blood of your Only-Begotten, our Lord Jesus Christ. Who with you,’ etc.”

### 1027. For mixing wine with water

“God, who,” etc.

In Illyricus’s Mass:

“Then let the deacon receive from the subdeacon,” etc.

“God, who bestowed dignity upon human substance,” etc.

### 1028. You deemed it worthy, etc.

In Illyricus’s Mass it reads:

“Jesus Christ deemed it worthy to become a participant.”

We have already discussed above the mixing of water with the wine to be consecrated. When Communion is about to take place, the Greeks pour hot water into the sacred Blood, as may be seen in the liturgies of Saints Basil and Chrysostom. They do this both because hot water came out from Christ’s side and because they wish the heat of the water to signify the fervor of the Holy Spirit, as taught by Germanus, patriarch of Constantinople, in the *Mystical Theory*, and by Theodore Balsamon in his commentary on canon 31 of the Sixth Council.

### 1029. Then, raising his hand, let him bless both

In Illyricus’s Mass:

“Then, raising his hand, let him bless both and say.”

But another Blessing is given in this form:

“In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, may this new sacrifice be marked, ordered, sanctified, and blessed.”

Then follows:

“Let him add”—supply: “the following Blessing”—“Almighty and eternal God, Sanctifier, come; bless this sacrifice prepared for you. You who live and reign forever and ever.”

### 1030. Afterwards, taking incense, let him place it in the thurible and say: Through the intercession of the holy archangel Gabriel, etc.

In Illyricus’s Mass:

“Afterwards the bishop, receiving incense from the deacon, places it in the thurible, saying: ‘Through the intercession of the holy archangel Gabriel,’ etc.”

In the Roman Missal, “Michael” is found here.

The same Mass of Illyricus continues:

“This prayer is to be said while, after the incense has been placed in the thurible, the thurible itself is moved around over the bread and chalice: ‘We remember, eternal God, almighty Father, the most glorious passion of your Son, and also his resurrection and his ascension into heaven,’ etc.”

### 1031. Then let him place incense over the sacrifice, etc.

In Illyricus’s Mass the incensation of the offerings has just been mentioned. Then follows:

“While going around the altar with incense, let the bishop or priest say: ‘May this incense,’ etc.”

Then follows:

“Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight, Lord.”

### 1032. When the fragrance of that incense, etc.

In Illyricus’s Mass:

“When the fragrance of the incense is presented to the priest, let each one say: ‘May he kindle in us,’ etc.”

### 1033. Then let the priest turn with the greatest humility, etc.

In Illyricus’s Mass:

“Then let the priest turn with the greatest humility toward those standing around him, saying: ‘Pray for me, brothers and sisters, that my sacrifice and yours may be acceptable to almighty God in his sight.’”

### 1034. Then let each one say, Let them pray for you, etc.

In Illyricus’s Mass:

“Then let each one answer: ‘May almighty God receive the sacrifice from your hands, and may your prayers rise as a memorial before the Lord; and may he himself hear you, who appointed you intercessor for our sins. May the saints and elect of God pray for you,’ etc.”

“Offer to the Lord a sacrifice of praise and pay your vows to the Most High.”

“May the Lord hear you as you pray and have mercy on you,” etc.

Then the priest turns toward the altar and pours out this Prayer for himself before the Secret:

“Lord Jesus Christ, our faith and confidence,” etc.

Then he begins the Secret. When these and the Preface have been completed, while the others sing “Holy, Holy, Holy,” the priest is to say quickly this prayer:

“Lord God, who do not desire the death but the repentance of sinners,” etc.,

as above among the Apologies.

When this prayer has been completed, before the sacraments begin, he again commends himself to the Lord, saying:

“About to make remembrance of the saving Host of the whole world.”

Here τὸ *Secreta*, in the plural, means the Prayer that we commonly call the Secret, formerly *Super oblata* (“over the offerings”). From this term it may also be inferred that the manuscript Codex from which Illyricus copied this order of the Mass is not extremely ancient.

### 1035. After the priest begins “Te igitur,” the deacons and subdeacons, etc.

In Illyricus’s Mass:

“Then, with the greatest reverence, let him begin ‘TE IGITUR,’ while the ministers standing on the steps sing these Psalms until ‘TE IGITUR’ has been completed.”

“May the Lord hear you,” etc.

Then the prayers:

“Save your servant,” etc.

Prayer for the priest:

“May your servant rejoice, we beseech you, Lord.”

Another common prayer:

“By our prayers, we beseech you, Lord,” etc.

Then, within the Action:

“First, together with your servant, our pope N., etc.”

“Remember, Lord, your male and female servants, namely all those related to me by blood,” etc.

“This Offering of my humility and devotion, which I offer to you for my sins,” etc.

“And this Offering, O God, we beseech you, Lord, in all things,” etc.

Insert this in the same Canon when a council or some deliberative matter is being conducted, after you have said “To the eternal, living, and true Lord”:

“This Offering which we offer to you, according to the nature of this matter presently being discussed in the proceeding of our deliberation,” etc.

“Sharing communion and venerating the memory.”

For himself:

“Remember me, Lord, and have mercy on me, for my illnesses are many and grievous,” etc.

“And us sinners.”

For the salvation of the living and the dead:

“Remember also, Lord, your male and female servants,” etc.

Here recite the names of those whom you wish.

“To these and to all who rest in the Catholic faith, grant, we beseech you, a place of peace and rest. Through Christ our Lord.”

“And us sinners.”

“Remember also, Lord, your male and female servants N., who have gone before us with the sign of faith,” etc.

“And us sinners.”

In this order of the Illyrican Mass, the recitation of the pope’s name should be noted. It is likewise found in all our sacramentaries, both manuscript and printed, in accordance with the decree of canon 4 of the Second Council of Vaison:

“And this also has seemed just to us: that the name of the Lord Pope—whoever presides over the Apostolic See—be recited in our Churches.”

### 1036. When the Secret has been completed

Here “Secret” means the mystical Prayer “Te igitur,” etc. This is how the order of the Illyrican Mass speaks: “When the Secret has been completed.”

This Prayer, together with the consecratory words, was formerly pronounced in a loud and clear voice in certain places, as John Moschus attests in chapter 396 of the *Spiritual Meadow*:

“But because in certain places the presbyters were accustomed to pronounce the prayer aloud, it happened that the children learned the prayer of the holy offering.”

That is:

“Because in certain places the presbyters were accustomed to pronounce the Offering Prayer in a loud voice, the result was that the children learned it.”

This is also evident from the liturgies of Saints James and Mark, and of Saints Basil and John Chrysostom, in which the consecratory words are pronounced in a raised voice. In the former liturgies the people respond “Amen”; in the latter, the choir does so.

This also occurred formerly in the Ambrosian Church, since Saint Ambrose mentions the same response, “Amen,” to the consecratory words in chapter 9 of *On Those Initiated into the Mysteries*:

“Before the blessing of the heavenly words, another kind is named; after the consecration, the body of Christ is signified. He himself says that it is his blood. Before the consecration, one thing is said; after the consecration, it is called blood. And you say ‘Amen’—that is, ‘It is true,’” etc.

### 1037. The Lord’s Prayer, etc.

In Illyricus’s Mass:

“And after the Lord’s Prayer, when he has said, ‘The peace of the Lord be always with you,’ let the body be mixed with the Lord’s Blood, and let it be said: ‘May this most holy commixture of the body and blood,’ etc.”

Then follows:

“May the commixture and consecration of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ become for all who receive it—and for us—life everlasting.”

### 1038. After the episcopal blessing has been completed, etc.

In the Illyrican Mass:

“Let the bishop not place a portion of the offering into the chalice, as presbyters are accustomed to do; but let him wait until, after the Blessing has ended, the bishop is to communicate. Then, taking the portion which he had previously broken, and holding it over the chalice, let him place it in while saying: ‘The commixture of the sacred Blood,’ etc.”

The following Prayer comes next:

“Grant, Lord Jesus Christ, that just as you have given these sacraments of your body and blood to your faithful for healing,” etc.

After these words, let him kiss the altar, saying:

“Lord Jesus Christ, who said to your apostles, ‘I leave you peace,’” etc.

Then let him turn toward those standing around him and bring peace, saying:

“Hold fast the bond of peace and charity, so that you may be fit for the most holy mysteries.”

And they, making peace with one another, say:

“May the peace of Christ and of the Church abound in our hearts.”

### 1039. When he takes the Lord’s Body into his hands, etc.

In Illyricus’s Mass:

“When he takes the Lord’s body into his hands, let him say: ‘The heavenly Bread,’ etc.”

### 1040. The reception of your body, etc.

In Illyricus’s Mass the following Prayer comes next:

“The reception of your body, Lord Jesus Christ,” etc.

Another:

“May this sacrament of yours, I beseech you, become for me,” etc.

When the body is received:

“May the body of our Lord Jesus Christ be for me an everlasting remedy unto eternal life.”

### 1041. When he receives the chalice, etc.

In Illyricus’s Mass:

“When the priest takes the chalice into his hands, let him say: ‘What shall I render to the Lord?’” etc.

The Prayer, “Communion and strengthening of the body,” follows.

### 1042. Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

In Illyricus’s Mass:

“After Communion has been received: ‘Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the living God,’ etc.,”

as in the Roman Missal, with one or two words changed.

Another prayer:

“May your body, Lord, which I have received, and the chalice which I have drunk, cling to my inward parts; and grant that no stain of sin may remain there, where your holy sacraments have entered.”

Then, when the presbyters and deacons receive the body into their hands and communicate, each one is told:

“Peace be with you.”

Response: “And with your spirit.”

Another:

“The Word became flesh and dwelt among us.”

When the chalice with the most holy Communion is given, let him say to each person:

“May the reception of the Body and Blood of our Lord Jesus Christ sanctify your body and soul unto eternal life. Amen.”

In these matters, first note that the Lord’s body is given into the hands of presbyters and deacons who are to communicate, in accordance with the ancient custom of the Church. This may be seen in the Roman Order, in the order of procession, when the bishop wishes to celebrate Mass on feast days:

“The presbyters and deacons, after kissing the bishop, receive the body of Christ from him into their hands and communicate on the left side of the altar. The subdeacons, after kissing the bishop’s hand, receive the body of Christ from him with their mouths.”

But in the ancient periods of the Church all the faithful placed the body of Christ, once received into the hand, into their mouths. This is clear from Eusebius, book VII of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 8:

“And having stood beside the table and extended the hands for the reception of the holy food.”

That is:

“Having stood at the table and extended the hands to receive the sacred food.”

It is also clear from Saint Cyril of Jerusalem, to be cited shortly; from Saint Basil, letter 289, to Caesaria the Patrician:

“For even in the church the priest gives the portion, and the one receiving it takes hold of it with complete freedom and thus brings it to his mouth with his own hand.”

From Saint Augustine, book II against the letters of Petilianus, chapter 23:

“To whom you gave the kiss of peace among the sacraments, into whose hands you placed the Eucharist, and to whom you in turn extended it when giving it.”

From Codinus, in the book *On the Offices of Constantinople*:

“But after the patriarch has received Communion of the precious Body, he gives the emperor a portion of the Lord’s Body into his hands.”

That is:

“After the patriarch has communicated in the precious Body, he gives the emperor a portion of the Lord’s Body into his hands.”

Saint Cyril of Jerusalem gives the manner of receiving it in the fifth Mystagogical Catechesis:

“When you approach Communion, do not come with your palms spread out, nor with your fingers separated; but, making the left hand a throne for the right, as though it were about to receive a king, and hollowing out the palm, receive the body of Christ.”

That is:

“Instead, place the left hand beneath the right as a kind of throne for it, since the right hand is about to receive the King; and with your hollowed hand receive the body of Christ.”

Women received it not with a bare hand but with a linen cloth placed beneath it. Saint Augustine says in Sermon 25:

“All the women bring clean linen cloths on which to receive the body of Christ.”

They either immediately placed this body of Christ in their mouths or carried it home to communicate there, as is clear from Tertullian, near the end of his book *On Prayer*:

“Having received the Lord’s body and reserved it, both things remain secure: participation in the sacrifice and fulfillment of the duty.”

Saint Basil, in the letter cited above, says that the custom of communicating in one’s own home existed among his people only during the time of pagan persecution, and that in his own age it was customary in monasteries, in Alexandria, and in Egypt. Nevertheless, this custom continued at Seleucia around the year 550 after Christ, as is evident from John Moschus, chapter 79 of the *Limonarium*. There it is related that a certain servant, on the Thursday of the Lord’s Supper, after taking the Eucharist in the church, had shut it in a chest in his master’s house; and it appeared to him transformed into green ears of grain.

It was also customary at Rome in Saint Jerome’s time, as is clear from his *Apology to Pammachius*:

“I know that this is the custom at Rome: that the faithful always receive the body of Christ. I neither condemn nor approve it; let each person abound in his own judgment. But I reproach the consciences of those who, having had intercourse on the same day, communicate. As Persius says, *Satire* 2:

> … They cleanse the night in the river.  
> Why do they not dare go to the martyrs?  
> Why do they not enter the churches?  
> Is Christ one in public and another at home?  
> What is not permitted in the church is not permitted at home.  
> Nothing is closed to God, and even darkness shines before him.”

Indeed, this was the custom of the Romans: those polluted by nocturnal intercourse, whether illicit or licit [Note: “One should also read ‘licit,’ as is clear from the two testimonies of Jerome and Gregory.”], did not enter the church on the following day, because divine vengeance awaited them, as may be seen in Saint Gregory, book I of the *Dialogues*, chapter 10.

Second, it should be noted that in this Mass of Illyricus not only the Blood is given to presbyters and deacons, but the Blood mixed with the body of Christ.

### 1043. With the cooperation of the Saints

The passage is corrupt; read: “With the cooperation of the Holy Spirit.”

### 1044. Lord, holy Father, etc.

Above, in Illyricus’s Mass:

“Another prayer for both: ‘Lord, holy Father, almighty and eternal God, grant me to receive the body and blood of your Son in such a way,’ etc.”

When the blood is received:

“May the Blood of our Lord Jesus Christ preserve me unto eternal life.”

### 1045

Then, when he begins to give Communion to the clergy and the people, let him say to each: “The reception…” etc. In the Illyrian Mass: “When giving Communion to the people, let him say: May the Body and Blood of our Lord Jesus Christ profit you unto the remission of all sins and unto eternal life. Amen.” Then, while they communicate, let him say: “Forgive, O Lord, that I am compelled to ask…” etc. This Apologia is found above, among the other Apologias of the Codex of Saint Eligius. The priest recites it while the clergy and people communicate—that is, while they eat what has been placed in their mouths by the priest. For the priest could not have recited this Prayer or Apologia while at the same time saying individually to each, “The Body and Blood…” etc.

It follows: “After Communion has been received: May we grasp with the mind what we have taken with the mouth…” etc. In the Roman Missal it says, “with a pure mind,” etc. In the Illyrian Mass the following Prayer occurs: “I beseech you, most merciful helper of all…” etc. Another: “May your gifts, O Lord, preserve us and grant us eternal life. Through…” Another: “Keep within us, O Lord, the gift of your glory, so that, through the strength and power of the Eucharist which we have received, we may be fortified against all the evils of the present and future age. You who live…” Another: “Grant, Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the living God, that we who eat and drink your own Body and Blood, given for us unworthy ones, may receive it for our salvation and as an everlasting remedy of redemption from all our sins. Through…”

### 1046

“The reception of the Lord’s Body…” etc. This is a formula for giving Communion, which varied according to the circumstances of the times. In the time of Saint Gregory I, the customary formula was: “May the Body of our Lord Jesus Christ preserve your soul,” as can be seen in John the Deacon, *Life of Saint Gregory*, book II, chapter 41: “When he was about to give him the mysteries, he said: May the Body of our Lord Jesus Christ preserve your soul.”

In Alcuin, in the chapter on Holy Saturday, this is found: “May the Body of our Lord Jesus Christ preserve you unto eternal life, amen,” as it appears in the manuscript Codex of the monastery of Saint Remigius, in the rite for visiting the sick.

In the Codex of Ratoldus, in the section concerning the visitation of the sick, the following is found: “May the Body and Blood of our Lord Jesus Christ lead you unto eternal life and raise you on the day of judgment to holy rest.”

In the Tilian Codex, in the rite for visiting the sick, this is found: “May the Body and Blood of our Lord Jesus Christ preserve your soul unto eternal life, amen.” This is our customary formula, if the words “and Blood” are removed.

There was another formula formerly used in Gaul in the time of King Robert, namely: “May the Body of our Lord Jesus Christ be salvation to you in soul and body,” as is evident from Helgaudus in his *Life*. Speaking of a certain bishop who held erroneous views about the Lord and who sought, for certain reasons, a trial through the Body of our Lord Jesus Christ, he writes:

“The king, a lover of goodness, took offense. Since you possess the light of knowledge, and the light of wisdom shines in you, I am amazed that, on account of your most wicked commands and the bitter hatred of God which you bear toward God’s servants, you should seek an examination through the Body and Blood of the Lord. And since this is what the priest giving Communion says: ‘May the Body of our Lord Jesus Christ be salvation to you in soul and body,’ why do you, with rash and polluted mouth, say: ‘If you are worthy, receive it’?”

But among the ancient Fathers formulas of this kind were not customary. Rather, the priest, offering the Eucharist, would say, “The Body of Christ,” and the recipient would answer, “Amen,” as is clear from Saint Ambrose, *On the Sacraments*, book IV, chapter 5:

“Therefore, when you receive it, you do not say ‘Amen’ without reason. The priest says to you, ‘The Body of Christ,’ and you say, ‘Amen,’ that is, ‘True.’ Let what the tongue confesses be held by the heart.”

From Saint Augustine, sermon to the infants, *On the Sacrament*:

“You are the Body of Christ and its members; your mystery is placed upon the Lord’s table; you receive the mystery of the Lord. To what you are, you answer ‘Amen,’ and by answering you subscribe to it. You hear, therefore, ‘The Body of Christ,’ and you answer, ‘Amen.’”

From book VIII of the *Apostolic Constitutions*, chapter 13:

“And let the bishop distribute the offering, saying: **Σῶμα Χριστοῦ**, καὶ ὁ δεχόμενος λεγέτω, ἀμήν—that is, ‘The Body of Christ,’ and let the recipient say, ‘Amen.’ But let the deacon hold the chalice and distribute it, saying: **Αἷμα Χριστοῦ ποτήριον ζωῆς**, ὁ δὲ πίνων λεγέτω, ἀμήν—that is, ‘The Blood of Christ, the cup of life,’ and let the one who drinks say, ‘Amen.’”

From Cyril of Jerusalem, *Mystagogical Catechesis* 5:

“Καὶ κοιλάνας τὴν παλάμην δέχου τὸ σῶμα Χριστοῦ, ἐπιλέγων ἀμήν,” that is: “And, hollowing your palm, receive the Body of Christ, adding, ‘Amen.’”

The same may be seen in the letter of Pope Cornelius to Fabius, bishop of Antioch, concerning the schismatic Novatus, in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VI, chapter 35. For, as it is related there, when Novatus offered the Eucharist to his followers, he used to exact from them an oath that they would never desert him or go over to the party of Cornelius:

“Καὶ ἀντὶ τοῦ εἰπεῖν λαμβάνοντα τὸν ἄρτον ἐκεῖνον, τὸ Ἀμήν, Οὐκ ἔτι ἀνήξω πρὸς Κορνήλιον, λέγει,” that is: “And the one who receives that bread, instead of saying ‘Amen,’ which he ought to say, says: ‘I will no longer return to Cornelius.’”

### 1047

“When the Mass has ended…” etc. In the Illyrian Mass: “After the deacon has said, ‘Go, the Mass is ended,’ let the priest come before the altar and, kissing it, say: ‘May it please you, Holy Trinity…’” There it also reads, “may it be pleasing to you,” instead of “may it be acceptable to you.”

### 1048

Another Prayer: “By the merits…” etc. In the Illyrian Mass: “When the Mass has ended, let him approach the altar, saying: ‘Through the merits and intercessions of blessed Mary ever-virgin, and of these and all the saints, may almighty God, who lives and reigns, have mercy on us.’”

### 1049

“When all things have been completed, the bishop…” etc. In the Illyrian Mass: “When all things have been completed, the bishop, returning from the altar to the sacristy with the deacons and with whatever others he wishes, shall sing the hymn of the three boys: ‘Bless, all works. Praise the Lord, all nations. Praise the Lord in his holy places.’”

### 1050

“Then the prayers: ‘Let them confess…’” In the Illyrian Mass, the prayers are also found:

“Let all your works confess to you, O Lord. The righteous shall exult in glory. Let the righteous exult. Not to us, O Lord, not to us. Let your priests be clothed with righteousness. Do not enter into judgment with your servants. O Lord, Lord God of hosts…” etc.

### 1051

“Then the Prayer: ‘O God, who [didst …] for the three boys…’” In the Illyrian Mass the following Prayer follows:

“O God, whom all your works bless…” etc.

Another: “O God, who didst mercifully allay the flames of fire for the three boys, grant through their intercession and the merits of all your saints that the flame of vices and torments may not consume us, your servants. Through…”

Another: “Go before our actions, we beseech you, O Lord, by your inspiration…” etc.

These, then, are the points that needed to be noted concerning the Tilian Mass and its comparison with the Illyrian Mass. From this it is clear that, apart from several Apologias and a few rites, the Tilian Mass is exceedingly similar to the Illyrian Mass.

### 1052

“To the venerable Maurilius…” Saint Maurilius, archbishop of Rouen, was born at Rheims. He devoted himself to letters at Liège and served God under the Rule of Saint Benedict at Florence in Italy. Because of the envy of certain monks, who could not bear his holiness with equanimity, he withdrew to Normandy to escape their plots. There he was received as a brother by the monks of Fécamp and was eventually ordained archbishop of Rouen. He died in the year of Christ 1067. Guillelmus of Jumièges discusses him in book VII, chapters 26 and 36, of his *History of Normandy*; Orderic Vitalis, in books IV and V of his *Ecclesiastical History*; and William of Malmesbury, in book V of *The Deeds of the Kings of England*.

### 1053

“John of Avranches.” This John, bishop of Avranches and later archbishop of Rouen, was the son of Ralph, count of Bayeux, the uterine brother of Richard the Elder, duke of the Normans. “A man highly distinguished by nobility of character, happily imbued with spiritual wisdom, and endowed in the highest degree with secular prudence,” says Guillelmus of Jumièges.

He was first bishop of Avranches; afterward, upon the death of Saint Maurilius, he became archbishop of Rouen, having governed the see of Avranches for seven years and three months. He presided over the Council of Rouen, held in that city in the year of the Lord 1072, and died in the year of the Lord 1079. Guillelmus of Jumièges discusses him in book VII, chapters 38 and 44, of his *History of Normandy*, and Orderic Vitalis in books III, IV, and V of his *Ecclesiastical History*.

### 1054

“In the vestry.” A *vestiarium* is a place suitable for storing clothing. Properly, however, it is the place in which the clothing of a king or emperor is kept. Manuel Moschopulus, in his book *On Schedes*, writes:

“βέστια παρὰ Ῥωμαίοις τὰ ἱμάτια· ἐξ οὗ τὸ βεστιάριον κυρίως, ἐν ᾧ τὰ βασιλικὰ ἐνδύματα φυλάσσονται,” that is: “Among the Romans, *vestes* are garments; hence properly *vestiarium*, in which royal garments are kept.”

But in this passage *vestiarium* means the sacristy or secret chamber, in which not only sacred vessels but also the Church’s sacred vestments are stored. Thus, in the restoration of Ebbo, archbishop of Rheims:

“The aforesaid bishop Ebbo was also led into the vestiarum and clothed in episcopal vestments; likewise the other bishops proceeded with him to celebrate the Mass.”

In former times, just as the emperor’s clothing was kept in the *vestiarium*, so too were the gold and silver vessels used at Mass, as is clear from Codinus, in his book *On the Offices of the Court*.

### 1055

“The priest shall kiss the deacon and subdeacon.” The same may be seen above in the Tilian and Illyrian Masses.

### 1056

“Rising.” Namely, the priest.

### 1057

“To the priest kissing the middle of the altar.” The kissing of the altar appears in the Illyrian Mass.

### 1058

“The bishop’s seat according to the decrees of Pope Urban…” See above, in the Observations.

### 1059

“But the candle-bearers…” From this it may be inferred that other candle-bearers were present, since in the bishop’s procession to the altar only one candle-bearer went ahead.

### 1060

“And thus, with the candle-bearer preceding…” Here there is a single candle-bearer who goes before the Gospel; yet shortly afterward it says: “Let the candelabra be extinguished.” Therefore either *ceroferariis*—“the candle-bearers”—should be read, or *candelabrum*—“the candelabrum”—should be extinguished.

According to an ancient custom of the Church, lights are kindled for the reading of the Gospel during Mass. Saint Jerome testifies to this concerning the Eastern Church, in book II *Against Vigilantius*:

“For even without relics of martyrs, throughout all the Churches of the East, when the Gospel is to be read, lights are kindled while the sun is already shining brightly—not, of course, to dispel the darkness, but to signify joy.”

Alcuin mentions this rite in *On the Divine Offices*, in the chapter “What the Vestments Signify.”

### 1061

“Offerenda.” This is the Antiphon that we commonly call the Offertory. Alcuin uses the term in the chapter cited above.

### 1062

“Let the Verses follow.” Above, in the Mass for the sick, after the visitation of the sick in the manuscript Codex of the monastery of Saint Remigius, two Verses follow the Offertory.

To this pertains what Alcuin says in *On the Divine Offices*, in the chapter “On the Celebration of the Mass”:

“Then follows the Offerenda, which received this name because at that time the people offer their gifts. The Verses follow, called ‘averting’ because, during the Offerenda, they return when the Offerenda is repeated.”

### 1063

“Through water mixed with wine the people are united to Christ.” From Saint Cyprian, letter 63:

“When water is mixed with wine in the chalice, the people are united to Christ; and the multitude of believers is joined and united to the one in whom it has believed.”

### 1064

“The priest shall arrange the Oblation in this manner…” Thus Ivo of Chartres, letter 233:

“The host, which is marked beside the chalice, should likewise be placed so that, by the position of the host and of the chalice, it represents the right side of Christ, from which flowed the blood of redemption and the water of baptism.”

### 1065

“Then, with the priest alone bent before the altar…” He is saying one of the Apologias. In the Illyrian Mass this Apologia, or Prayer, is found:

“Lord Jesus Christ, our faith and confidence…” etc.

But it is said by the priest after he has admonished the people concerning the Prayer.

### 1066

“Let him touch the four parts of the chalice with the Oblation…” Ivo of Chartres, in the letter cited above:

“When, with the consecrated Host already present, the sign of the cross is impressed within or above the chalice, from the eastern side of the chalice to the western, and from the northern to the southern, we understand this to represent what the Lord foretold to his disciples before his Passion: ‘And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself.’”

### 1067

“Also, when the Prayer has ended.” The same occurs in other Orders, as was noted above in the Mass of Ratoldus, in these words: “through him and with him,” etc., spoken by the Pontiff.

### 1068

“Let both raise the chalice.” The chalice is raised by the priest and deacon together and then set down. In fact, it is not the chalice alone that is raised, but also the Host placed upon the paten over the chalice, as is clear from Ivo of Chartres, in the letter cited above:

“When the bread and chalice are raised with the assistance of the deacon, the raising of Christ’s body upon the cross is commemorated.”

And below:

“But when, with the assistance of the deacon, the chalice is set down and the Host is returned to its place,” etc.

In the Mass of Ratoldus and in the Roman Orders cited above, this raising is performed by the deacon alone, or by the archdeacon. In the second Order, however, it is raised by the pontiff and the deacon.

### 1069

“Joseph is represented by the deacon…” Ivo of Chartres expresses this very briefly in the letter cited above:

“This commemorates the fact that Joseph and Nicodemus, having received permission from Pilate, took Christ’s body down from the cross and reverently committed it to burial.”

### 1070

“Let him complete the office of consecration.” Here *consecration* does not mean the consecration of the offerings—that is, of the bread and wine—for they have already been consecrated. Rather, it means the liturgical mystery itself, which is to be completed through fraction, commixture, and Communion. The word is used in this sense when it is repeated shortly afterward.

### 1071

“Who, clothed in a cloth, had held it.” The passage is corrupt. The word *patenam*—“the paten”—seems to be missing, as is evident from what follows.

### 1072

“Let the commixture take place.” The word *consecratio*—“consecration”—is missing, as in the Masses of Ratoldus and of the Tilian rite.

### 1073

“Viaticum.” This refers to the sick who are in danger of death, as is clear from what follows: “The third portion that remains on the altar the holy Church calls the viaticum of the dying.”

### 1074

“According to the definition of the Council of Toledo.” I think there has been a lapse of memory here, for I do not remember ever having read this in any Council of Toledo. The prohibition is found in the Third Council of Braga, as I noted above.

### 1075

“Except for the people, to whom it is given in dipped bread…” This is understood of a solemn Mass, which in those times was almost the only kind celebrated. Because of the multitude of people receiving Communion, and because there was danger that the Blood of Christ might be spilled, the Body dipped in the Blood, rather than separated from it, was given to the people.

It is said that this was done from necessity, not by authority, because no earlier council had permitted it when such a necessity arose. The Council of Clermont, which according to the copy of Antonius Augustinus appears to permit this, had not yet been held: John of Avranches, bishop, died in the year of Christ 1079, whereas the Council of Clermont was held in the year 1095.

### 1076

“Finally, let him take the particle that remained in the chalice…” The meaning is that, after Communion has been given to the people, the priest should take the particle that he had placed in the chalice, but not the whole of it, so that the deacon and subdeacon may take the remaining part after dividing it between themselves.

### 1077

“For consecrating the king, or for blessing him.” Such was the ancient piety of Christian emperors and kings that, when they were about to assume an empire or kingdom, they wished to inaugurate it auspiciously by having themselves publicly blessed and crowned in the church by sacred pontiffs in a holy and solemn rite.

The first of the emperors to be inaugurated by a pontiff in a holy and solemn rite was Theodosius the Younger, the best and most holy of the emperors of Constantinople. He was crowned by Proclus, patriarch of Constantinople, as Theodore testifies in *Eclogue* 2, near the end:

“Στεφθεὶς ὑπὸ τοῦ αὐτοῦ Πατριάρχου,” that is, “crowned by that patriarch.”

For, so far as I judge, nothing similar concerning Christian emperors is recorded before his time.

Justin the Younger was crowned by the patriarch Eutychius, as Theophanes writes in book XVI, under the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 558. Corippus writes of this coronation in book II of his praises of Justin:

> After he saw all things completed according to the ancient rite,  
> The chief of pontiffs, handsome in the fullness of his years,  
> Blessed him as he stood before him, and, beseeching  
> The Lord who rules heaven, ordered that the Augustus’ head  
> Be consecrated with the sacred diadem; and, placing a crown  
> Upon his head, happily…

Yet before this he had been raised upon a shield according to the ancient rite, as Corippus sings above in the same book:

> Four young men, lifted higher, raise the huge sphere  
> Upon four shields; and, lifted by their hands,  
> He himself stood above the attendants, upright,  
> Like his own letter, which never bends  
> From its fixed sign, consecrated to three names,  
> Who with equal strength ruled their empire…

By “the letter” he means J, which is the first letter of Justin’s name; it is “consecrated to three names,” namely Justin the Elder, Justinian, and Justin the Younger.

So much for the coronation of Justin the Younger. After him, the emperor Tiberius was also crowned by the patriarch Eutychius, as the aforementioned Theophanes teaches in book XVII, under the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 571.

Likewise the emperor Maurice and his wife, the Augusta, were crowned by John, patriarch of Constantinople, on their wedding day, as Theophylact Simocatta writes in book I, chapter 10, of his *History*:

“Καὶ δῆτα καὶ τὰς κορυφὰς τῶν βασιλέων τοῖς στεφάνοις καθίδερυσε,” that is: “And he placed crowns upon the heads of the king and queen.”

The emperor Heraclius was crowned by the patriarch Sergius in the oratory of Saint Stephen located in the palace. On the same day his bride Eudocia was crowned Augusta, and each received from the patriarch Sergius the crowns of marriage. “On one and the same day,” says Theophanes, book XVIII, under the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 602, “the emperor and bridegroom was displayed together.” He adds:

“In the third year of Heraclius’ reign, Epiphania, the daughter of Heraclius, was crowned by the patriarch Sergius in the palace oratory. In the same year, in the first indiction, Heraclius the Younger, son of Heraclius, who was also called Constantine, was crowned by the aforementioned patriarch.”

And so with many others thereafter, whom the Christian kings imitated—especially the kings of the Franks. The first of these was Clovis, as is clear from the testament of Saint Remigius, in Flodoardus, book I of the *History of the Church of Rheims*, chapter 18. Ivo of Chartres, letter 79, writes that after Clovis his grandsons Charibert and Guntram were consecrated by the bishops of their provinces.

### 1078

“We ask to be pardoned by you…” Thus in the manuscript Order of Saint-Germain-des-Prés near Paris; it is also found in the coronation of Louis II among the capitularies of Charles the Bald, though in a fuller form.

It likewise occurs in the coronation of Henry IV, called the Great, king of the Franks, described by the most reverend Nicholas Thou, bishop of Chartres, who anointed that same Henry king at Chartres.

*Perdonari* means “to be granted pardon.”

When we say here that the coronation of Henry IV was described by Nicholas Thou, bishop of Chartres, we do not mean that he composed the formulas, the consecratory Prayers, and similar texts, which he took from some ancient manuscript Codex. Rather, he composed the booklet containing all the rites observed at the coronation of the aforesaid king.

### 1079

“According to right.” *Right* means the rectitude of the kingdom, which is given below at the end of the consecration.

### 1080

“The king’s response: ‘I promise and pardon you…’” Thus in the manuscript Order of the monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés and in the aforementioned coronation of Henry IV.

In the coronation of Louis II, which can be found among the capitularies of the emperor Charles the Bald, the formula is fuller. In the Roman Order the king makes a profession of faith; likewise the emperor of Constantinople, in Codinus, in the book *On the Offices of the Court of Constantinople*.

### 1081

“Then let two bishops address the people in the church, asking…” This address of the bishops to the people in the church, in which they ask for the people’s consent, may be seen in the Roman Orders and in that of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, in the second consecration of Charles the Bald, which was celebrated at Metz, and in the coronations of Henry II and Henry IV, kings of the Franks.

This address of the bishops to the people also occurs in the coronation of Hermitrudis, wife of Charles the Bald, in the *Capitularies* of that same Charles, near the end, though in a different formula.

The same consent is found in Peter Damian, sermon 1, *On the Dedication*:

“But before he is clothed in imperial garments, the will of the clergy and the people is sought concerning him.”

### 1082

“Let them give thanks to God.” Thus Hincmar, near the end of his address to the people at the second coronation of Charles the Bald, in the *Capitularies* of that same ruler, chapter 35:

“It does not seem unfitting to these venerable bishops, if it pleases your community, that, in obedience to the kingdom, for which you have willingly assembled before him, he should be crowned by priestly ministry before this altar and consecrated to God by sacred anointing. If this pleases you, let your voices join together.”

When everyone had shouted his assent, the same bishop said: “Let us therefore give thanks to God with one accord, singing, ‘We praise you, O God.’”

### 1083

“Singing, ‘We praise you, O God.’” Note the custom of singing the hymn *Te Deum laudamus* in public thanksgivings.

In the coronation of Charles the Bald cited above: “Let us therefore give thanks to God with one accord, singing, ‘We praise you, O God.’”

In the *Life of Louis the Pious*, when Pope Stephen was received at Rheims by the same Emperor Louis:

“The emperor went out a mile from the monastery of Saint Remigius the Confessor and received him, as the vicar of Peter, with the greatest honor. When he descended from his horse, he welcomed him and personally supported him as he entered the church, while, in such great rejoicing, the various orders of the Church sang beforehand, ‘We praise you, O God.’”

And in the restoration of Ebbo, archbishop of Rheims:

“When these things had been accomplished, while the bells again resounded and the whole Church cried out, ‘We praise you, O God,’ the aforesaid bishop Ebbo was led into the vestiarum.”

Formerly, in thanksgivings, the hymn *Gloria in excelsis Deo* was sung in place of this hymn. Saint John Chrysostom, homily 3 on chapter I of the Letter to the Colossians, writes:

“Διὰ τοῦτο εὐχαριστοῦντες λέγομεν, Δόξα ἐν ὑψίστοις θεῷ, καὶ ἐπὶ γῆς εἰρήνη, ἐν ἀνθρώποις εὐδοκία,” that is: “For this reason, giving thanks, we say: ‘Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, goodwill among men.’”

Victor of Utica, near the end of book III, *On the Passion of the Holy Martyrs who suffered at Carthage under King Hunneric* on the sixth day before the Nones of July:

“They therefore went forward confidently to punishment, as though rushing to a banquet, singing to the Lord in a loud voice through the streets: ‘Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good will.’”

Gregory of Tours, book I, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 63, concerning the discovery of the body of Saint Mallosus the martyr:

“When he had dug almost seven feet, his nose encountered the scent of an immense fragrance, and he said: ‘I believe in Christ, who showed me his martyr when this sweetness surrounded me.’ Digging further, he found the body intact; and, uttering in a loud voice, ‘Glory to God in the highest,’ he caused all the clergy to sing together. When the hymn had been said, he carried the holy body into the basilica.”

Anastasius the Librarian, in his account of Leo III, describing the meeting of that pontiff and Charlemagne:

“They embraced one another and kissed each other with tears. When the aforesaid pontiff began, ‘Glory to God in the highest,’ and all the clergy joined in, the Prayer over the entire people was given.”

Alcuin, letter 71, to the brethren in the province of the Goths:

“And sing to your God, in the harmony of peace and the unity of everlasting charity, a song of praise; and with the heavenly host praise God and say: ‘Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good will.’”

The hymn *Te Deum laudamus* succeeded this hymn, as is known from the authors cited above. Nevertheless, in certain parts of Gaul it appears to have been customary in solemn thanksgiving during the time of Duke Pippin, who was afterward made king of the Franks. For, at the translation of the body of Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris, which occurred under the rule of this Pippin, this hymn was solemnly sung in thanksgiving, as is evident from the account of this translation printed by Surius under July 25—provided, that is, that the author of the account is reliable in every respect.

The common tradition attributes this institution to Saints Ambrose and Augustine, who are said to have composed and sung this hymn extemporaneously at the baptism of Saint Augustine. The alleged author and proponent of this opinion is Saint Dacius, bishop of Milan, in his *Chronicle*. He flourished during the reign of the emperor Justinian, and Saint Gregory mentions him in book III of the *Dialogues*, chapter 4.

But whatever may be the truth of this story, it is certain that this *Chronicle* is not by Dacius. It cannot be proved that he wrote any chronicle, much less that he wrote the one cited here. Its style does not resemble that of those times, and its contents include a falsehood: namely, that Saint Augustine, hearing Saint Ambrose teaching and preaching to the people about the Incarnation, trembled and grew pale before all who were present, became rigid, and that, when blessed Ambrose had finished the exhortation that he was delivering to the people, Augustine was the first to approach him, and so forth.

This contradicts the writings of Saint Augustine and Possidius, and such a story could not have entered the mind of any learned and wise man such as Dacius was. Therefore, before Saint Benedict and Teridius, a disciple of Saint Caesarius, bishop of Arles, who spoke of this hymn in their Rules, none of the ancient writers mentioned it.

### 1084

“Invocation over the king: ‘We call upon you, O Lord…’” In the coronation of Charles the Bald, which took place at Metz before the altar of Saint Stephen, seven bishops each pronounced a separate Benediction, or invocation, over the king before the anointing itself.

In the Roman Order, when the emperor is ordained, three Prayers are pronounced: the first by the bishop of Albano, the second by the bishop of Porto, and the third by the bishop of Ostia, while he anoints the emperor’s left arm and the space between his shoulders.

In the coronation of the emperor of Constantinople, as described by George Codinus in his book *On the Offices of the Court*, only the patriarch of Constantinople reads the prayers before the anointing, partly in a clear voice and partly quietly.

This invocation over the king is also found in the office for appointing a duke, which the most learned André Duchesne published at the end of the *Normannici*.

### 1085

“That he may possess the throne of supreme rule.” In the office for appointing a duke, it reads “the throne of his dukedom.” I would think that *summi* should be read instead of *suum*.

### 1086

“O God, who [rule] your peoples…” This Prayer occurs in the coronation of Louis II and of Charles the Bald, one or two lines shorter than here. It also occurs in the aforementioned office.

### 1087

“In his times.” In the said office, *temporibus*—“times”—is missing, incorrectly.

### 1088

“Let him diligently learn about himself.” That is, although he has been placed at the highest summit of power, let him nevertheless remember the human condition and how many adversities royal sublimity is subject to.

For, according to Euripides in *Ion* and Seneca in *Oedipus*, the face of kingship is pleasing—**πρόσωπον ἡδύ**, that is, “a pleasant face”—and can easily deceive a king who does not know himself well.

### 1089

“The consecration of the king: ‘Almighty and everlasting God…’” This Prayer occurs in the consecration of Henry IV, king of the Franks, and in the coronation of Louis II, though in a much shorter form; it is entitled “The Infusion of the Sacred Oil.” Properly so, since this Prayer is said when the king is anointed.

It is also found in the Roman Order, up to the words “with virtues,” with certain words subsequently altered. It also occurs in the Roman Pontifical, though in a much shorter form. There, however, it is not recited during the infusion of the oil, nor is it recited then in the Roman Order.

### 1090

“Into the kingdom of N., of all Albion.” And shortly afterward:

“And henceforth let him so nourish and teach the Church of all Albion, together with the peoples attached to it…” etc.

These words clearly indicate that at that time some king of the Franks had been anointed king of the English. This is nevertheless difficult to determine, since I have found nothing of the kind in the ancient historians, whether Frankish or English, through whom someone might shed light on the difficulty.
