No one, however, doubts that Albion, which is mentioned here, is Great Britain. All the ancient and more recent geographers testify to this.

As for the consecratory formula, it is believable that the first person inaugurated under this formula had previously been adorned with the dignity of the kingdom of the Franks, in these words:

“And henceforth let him so nourish, teach, fortify, and instruct the Church of all Albion, together with the peoples attached to it, and let him govern it powerfully and royally by the rule of your strength against all visible and invisible enemies, so that he may not abandon the royal throne—namely, the scepters of the Franks—but, with your aid, may restore their minds to the harmony of their former faith and peace.”

Who among the kings of the Franks was anointed king of the English under this formula is obscure.

[Note: Perhaps this consecration was used at the inauguration of Louis IV, called “from Overseas,” son of Charles the Simple. Since, through his mother Ogiva, he was descended from the royal line of England, he could have been summoned in hope of that kingdom and anointed king of England and France at the same time. Those who do not approve this conjecture should supply a better one and show which king of Gaul, before the death of Abbot Ratoldus, who died in 986, could with greater right have been anointed and consecrated king of England.]

From this, however, it appears that the kings of the Franks possessed an ancient right to the kingdom of England. This also seems to be indicated in the coronation of Henry IV, king of the Franks. For in the formula cited above the following is found:

“So that he may not abandon the royal throne—namely, the scepters of the Saxons, Mercians, and Northumbrians…” etc.

This is confirmed by the manuscript Order of the monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, in the coronation of the king of the Franks, where these same words are found. That the Saxons are called English, and that the Mercians and Northumbrians are peoples of England, is well known to everyone.

In the same consecration, the letter N. appears to have been transposed and should be connected with the words “this servant of yours, N.”, so that it is placed where the proper name ordinarily occurs.

### 1091

“So that he may not abandon the royal throne—namely, the scepters of the Franks.” As was noted above, these words imply that the person who is anointed king of Albion under this formula had previously been elevated as king of the Franks.

### 1092. “Let him be anointed with oil.”

The word *oil* (*τὸ oleo*) is not to be understood of ordinary, common oil, but of sacred oil consecrated by episcopal blessing, with which kings formerly used to be anointed. Hence, in the coronation of Louis II cited above, these words are prefixed to this prayer or consecration: “The pouring out of sacred oil” [Col. 0572C]. The same may be seen in the Roman Order, in the ordination both of a king and of an emperor, and in Peter Damian, *Sermon* 1, *On the Dedication of a Church*:

> And then he is stripped of his garments and sprinkled with the oil of sanctification, so that, drenched with the symbolic dew, he may glory in the fullness of heavenly ointment.

For “oil of sanctification,” according to Hebrew idiom, means “sanctified oil.” Accordingly, Eginhard, in the *Annals* under the year 750, most appropriately calls this anointing sacred:

> In this year, in accordance with the decree of the Roman pontiff, Pepin was called king of the Franks, and, for the dignity of this honor, was anointed with sacred anointing by the hand of Boniface, bishop and martyr of holy memory.

Indeed, it is certain that the kings of the Franks were anointed with sacred chrism, as is found in the testament of Saint Remigius preserved by Flodoard, book I of the *History of the Church of Rheims*, chapter 28:

> I chose and established for perpetual rule only the royal family, whom, for the honor of the holy Church and the defense of the poor, together with my brothers and all the bishops of Germany, Gaul, and Neustria, I had destined for the summit of royal majesty; I baptized them, received them from the sacred font, marked them with the sevenfold Spirit, and, through the anointing of that same sacred chrism, ordained and established them as kings, sparing them, etc.

The same is found in the letter of the synod sent at Carisiacum to Louis, king of Germany, chapter 15:

> Above all, it is necessary for us to speak with those archbishops and bishops who, with the consent and will of this kingdom, anointed our lord, your brother Charles the Bald, king with sacred chrism, according to divine tradition.

In the *Book of Complaint of Lord King Charles against Wenilo, Archbishop of Sens*:

> But afterward, by his own election and that of the other bishops, and by the will, consent, and acclamation of the other faithful of the kingdom, together with the archbishops and bishops, Wenilo consecrated me as king according to ecclesiastical tradition in his diocese, in the city of Orléans, in the basilica of the Holy Cross, and anointed me with sacred chrism for the government of the kingdom.

[Col. 0573A] In the letter of Arthold, archbishop of Rheims, to the synod of Engilenheim, preserved by Flodoard, book IV of the *Ecclesiastical History of Rheims*, chapter 35:

> After I had blessed Louis as king, with Hugh and all the princes of the kingdom favoring him, and had likewise blessed Queen Gerberga and drenched her with sacred chrism.

The same is found in the second coronation of Charles the Bald, when he was crowned at Metz in the kingdom of Lothair, in the year of the Lord 869. At the words “May the Lord crown you,” Hincmar anointed him with chrism.

The passage of an anonymous author on the anointing with chrism, among the works of Saint Cyprian, is to be understood in the same way:

> Yet, although those practices that had grown up according to the ancient rite had not ceased, and although circumcision appeared blameworthy among the Christian people and sacrifices were attributed to idolatry, the Christian religion did not despise the mystery of anointing. Rather, while the other practices were condemned by the general agreement of the saints, the honor of anointing not only remained among kings and priests, but the fullness of this grace was poured out upon the whole Catholic people.

For this sermon concerns anointing with chrism: priests—that is, bishops—are anointed with chrism at their ordination, and the rest of the Catholic people at confirmation. For this reason, the sacred oil sent from heaven, with which Clovis, the first Christian among the kings of the Franks, and many of his successors were anointed, is called chrism.

Thus, in the capitularies of Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, concerning the second coronation of Charles the Bald:

> On the vigil of Easter, in the metropolitan church of Rheims, he was baptized and anointed with the chrism received from heaven, which we still possess, and was consecrated king.

William the Breton likewise used this designation in book I of the *Philippid*, where he describes the coronation of Philip Augustus:

> And now the long-desired day had arrived,  
> the first day of November,  
> which, already long ago sanctified for all by the saints,  
> now stood far holier still,  
> on which the great-hearted king, girded with the honor  
> of the scepter, shone resplendent,  
> drenched with sacred olive oil.  
> God, having prepared it by angelic hands  
> through divine power, granted our kings  
> to use it, so that only those might be consecrated with it  
> who successively assume the scepters of the Franks.  
> Thus our king is truly more worthy than every other king,  
> whom the metropolitan of Rheims  
> with his fellow bishops has the right to consecrate  
> with that sacred chrism,  
> which heavenly olive alone pours forth for this purpose.  
> With this, and with no other liquid,  
> our bishop William anointed the limbs  
> of our Carolingian prince in the city of Rheims,  
> following the custom preserved from his fathers;  
> and he placed a venerable diadem upon his sacred head,  
> with the clergy and people joining in their favor.  
> Such a special distinction the favor of Christ grants  
> to us, who rejoice together in the honor of the Franks.  
> Thus the heavenly King clothes our king with honor;  
> thus he exalts him above the kings of the earth,  
> whom he makes the only one to be consecrated  
> with heaven’s sacred anointing,  
> while the others are consecrated with material oil.

In the consecration of Henry II, king of the Franks, that heavenly liquid once brought by an angel to Saint Remigius was mixed with the sacred chrism [Col. 0573D]. Henry IV, king of the Franks, was anointed at Chartres with another heavenly liquid, once brought down from heaven by an angel to Saint Martin, bishop of Tours. This liquid was mixed with sacred chrism by Nicholas of Thou, bishop of Chartres, who performed the consecration, as is recorded in the frequently cited account of that coronation.

It was also formerly customary among the Greeks for the emperors of Constantinople to be consecrated not with ordinary oil, but with ointment—that is, sacred chrism—as will be clear from George Codinus, cited shortly. Commonly, kings are anointed not with chrism but with oil, as is seen in the chapter *Cum venisset*, *On Sacred Anointing*. Today the emperor is anointed with exorcised oil, while the king is anointed with the oil of catechumens, as stated in the Roman Pontifical.

### 1093. “May its most sacred anointing flow down upon his head.”

From these words it is clear that the head is the part that is to be anointed [Col. 0574A]. Formerly, at his consecration, the emperor of Constantinople was anointed on the head in the form of a cross, as Codinus testifies in his book *On the Offices of the Court of Constantinople*:

> **Ὁ δὲ Πατριάρχης χρίει σταυροειδῶς τὴν κεφαλὴν τοῦ βασιλέως τῷ μύρῳ**

That is:

> The patriarch anoints the emperor with divine ointment in the form of a cross.

Meanwhile, the patriarch pronounces **ἅγιος**, that is, “holy,” which is repeated three times both by those who are in the ambo and by the rest of the multitude.

In the second coronation of Charles the Bald, celebrated at Metz, he was anointed at the right earlobe, across the forehead to the left earlobe, and on the head, as is stated in the capitularies of that same Charles:

> At the words “May the Lord crown you,” Archbishop Hincmar anointed him with chrism at the right earlobe, across the forehead to the left earlobe, and on the head.

In the Roman Order the breast, shoulders, the inner joints of the arms, and the hands are anointed. In the consecration of the kings of the Franks two further anointings are added: on the crown of the head and between the shoulders, as may be seen in the consecrations of Henry II and Henry IV [Col. 0574B].

Constantine Manasses, in the *Chronicle Synopsis*, writes that Charlemagne was anointed by Leo III from the crown of his head to his feet:

> **Οὐ μὴν ἀλλὰ χρησάμενος καὶ νόμοις Ἰουδαίων,  
> Κακκεφαλῆς μέχρι ποδῶν ἐλαίῳ τοῦτον χρίει.**

That is:

> Rather, following the laws of the Jews, he anointed him with oil from his head to his feet.

Theophanes gives the same testimony in his *Chronicle*:

> **Ἔστεψεν αὐτὸν εἰς βασιλέα Ῥωμαίων ἐν τῷ ναῷ τοῦ ἁγίου ἀποστόλου Πέτρου, χρίσας ἐλαίῳ ἀπὸ κεφαλῆς ἕως ποδῶν**

That is:

> He crowned him king of the Romans in the church of the holy apostle Peter, anointing him with oil from head to feet.

But in the Roman Order the Roman emperor is anointed only on the right arm and between the shoulders.

The anointing of a prince is similar in the chapter *Cum venisset*, *On Sacred Anointing*:

> But when Jesus of Nazareth—says Innocent III in that passage—whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit, as it is written in the Acts of the Apostles, was anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions, he who, according to the Apostle, is the head of the Church, which is his body, the anointing of the prince was transferred from the head to the arm, so that thereafter the prince would not be anointed on the head but on the arm, shoulder, or upper arm, in which the principate is appropriately signified, etc.

For the same signification Samuel also had the shoulder placed before Saul, to whom he gave the place at the head before those who had been invited.

But the anointing on the head of a pontiff has been preserved, because in the pontifical office he represents the person of the head. The anointing of a pontiff differs from that of a prince because the pontiff’s head is consecrated with chrism, whereas the prince’s arm is smeared with oil, so that the great difference between the authority of a pontiff and that of a prince may be shown.

This is what he says. Here we should note what he said about the shoulder or upper arm. For among the pagans also that part of the victim was considered more honorable and especially fitting for a king. Thus, in former times, when Eteocles and Polynices were sacrificing, they were accustomed to send their father Oedipus the victim’s shoulder as to a king and superior person. But once, by some accident, they sent him the victim’s thigh instead of the shoulder. Thinking that they despised him, he became excessively enraged and cursed them with dreadful imprecations, as the scholiast on Sophocles’ *Oedipus at Colonus* reports, drawing on the author of the cyclic *Thebaid*:

> **Ἰσχίον ὡς ἐνόησε, χάμαι βάλεν, εἶπέ τε μῦθον,**  
> **Ὡμοὶ ἐγὼ, παῖδές με ὀνειδίζοντες ἔπεμψαν.**  
> **Εὖκτο Διὶ Βασιληῖ, καὶ ἄλλοις Ἀθανάτοισι**  
> **Χερσὶν ὑπὸ ἀλλήλων καταβήμεναι ἄϊδος εἴσω.**

That is:

> When he realized that the thigh had been sent to him, he threw it on the ground and said: “Alas for me! My sons, despising me, have sent me this.” He prayed to Zeus the King and the other immortal gods that, slain by one another’s hands, they might descend into the underworld.

In the Roman Pontifical the emperor is likewise anointed, but in the form of a cross; the king, however, is anointed between the joints of the hands and elbow and also between the shoulders, likewise in the form of a cross. From these facts it is clear that the rite was not always the same.

### 1094. “God, the strength of the elect and the exaltation of the humble,” etc.

This prayer appears in the coronation of Judith, daughter of Charles the Bald, who married Æthelwulf, king of the English. There it serves as a preface and extends only to these words: “Therefore, we beseech you, almighty Father, through the richness of this creature.” The rest is different. It also appears in the coronation of Henry IV, king of the Franks.

### 1095. “And make him in the likeness of a dove,” etc.

In the aforementioned coronation of Judith, these words are slightly altered to suit what follows:

> So that through the richness of this creature you may make her beautiful with the peace, simplicity, and chastity of a dove.

### 1096. “With your help,” etc.

Read, as in the coronation of Henry IV: “and, with your help, your blessing to the whole people.”

### 1097. “God, Jesus Christ, Son of God,” etc.

This prayer appears in the coronation of Henry IV. It is absent from the office for constituting a duke and from the Roman Order.

### 1098. “Here let the ring be given.”

This presentation of the ring appears in the coronations of Henry II and Henry IV, kings of the Franks, and also in the Roman Order, but there after the girding with the sword.

### 1099. “Receive the ring,” etc.

This formula appears in the office for constituting a duke and in the coronation of Henry IV, king of the Franks. Another formula appears in the Roman Order.

### 1100. “For perseverance.”

Thus it stands in the office for constituting a duke.

### 1101. Prayer after the ring

It appears in the office for constituting a duke. It is absent from the Roman Order.

### 1102. “Here let the archbishop gird him with the sword.”

The girding with the sword appears in the Roman Order, in the coronations of Henry II and Henry IV, kings of the Franks, and in the office for constituting a duke. It also seems to be found in the *Life of Louis the Pious*, when he was restored to the kingdom in the church of Saint-Denis:

> But on the Sunday that followed, he wished to be reconciled by episcopal ministry in the church of Saint-Denis, and consented to be girded with weapons by the hands of the bishops.

Peter Damian, in the sermon cited above, makes no mention of the girding with the sword, but says:

> The sword is also carried before his eyes, so that he may recognize that he has been appointed as the avenger of God’s wrath for this very purpose.

This agrees with the coronations of Henry II and Henry IV, in which the sword was likewise carried before them.

### 1103. “Receive the sword,” etc.

Another formula appears in the Roman Order. In the office for constituting a duke, the following formula precedes the formula in our codex:

> N., be strong and be a man, and observe the charges of the Lord your God, etc.

### 1104. Prayer after the sword

It appears in the office for constituting a duke. It is absent from the Roman Order.

### 1105. “For our most Christian king”

The designation “most Christian” is proper to the kings of the Franks and is certainly very ancient. Thus Anastasius the Librarian calls Pepin, king of the Franks, “most Christian” in his account of Stephen III:

> When this had been done, and when, by the Lord’s favor, he had joined the aforesaid most Christian Pepin in the venerable monastery, after a few days that same most Christian Pepin, king of the Franks, was anointed king by the same most holy pope, by the grace of Christ, together with his two sons.

In his account of Stephen IV, when he speaks of Charles and Carloman:

> For these most Christian kings sent twelve bishops from the same regions of the Franks.

The same may be seen in the capitularies of Charles the Bald, chapter 35, § 3:

> So that from his mouth we may hear what a most Christian king and a faithful and unanimous people in his service ought to hear, each according to his order.

In a letter of Carloman written at the palace of Verneuil:

> Especially those measures that had been promulgated by the holy Fathers against the evil of robbery and plunder, and confirmed by the authority of the most Christian kings.

### 1106. “Here let him be crowned.”

There is no imposition of the crown in the office for constituting a duke.

### 1107. “May God crown you with a crown of glory,” etc.

This formula does not appear in the Roman Order. It is found in the coronations of Louis II and Henry IV, kings of the Franks. It also appears, in a more abbreviated form, in the consecration of Charles the Bald.

Peter Damian mentions the imposition of the crown in the sermon cited above:

> A golden crown is also placed upon his head, expressing the sign of holiness, the glory of honor, and the work of strength.

It belongs to the metropolitan to impose the crown, as may be seen in the Roman Order and Pontifical. Thus William, metropolitan of Rheims, places the crown on the head of Philip Augustus, king of the Franks, as William the Breton teaches in the passage cited above:

> With this, and with no other liquid,  
> our bishop William anointed the limbs  
> of our Carolingian prince in the city of Rheims,  
> following the custom preserved from his fathers,  
> and placed a venerable diadem upon his sacred head.

At Rome, Pope Leo III placed the crown upon Charlemagne when he was created emperor, as Theophanes testifies in his *Chronicle*:

> **Ἔστεψεν αὐτὸν εἰς βασιλέα Ῥωμαίων ἐν τῷ ναῷ τοῦ ἁγίου ἀποστόλου Πέτρου**

That is:

> He crowned him king of the Romans in the church of the holy apostle Peter.

A little later:

> **καὶ περιβαλὼν βασιλικὴν ἐσθῆτα καὶ στέφος**

That is:

> And having clothed him in royal garments and placed a crown upon him.

Constantine Manasses gives the same testimony in his *Chronicle*:

> **Καὶ στέφος περιτίθησιν, ὡς οἱ Ῥωμαίων νόμοι.**

> And he encircles him with a crown according to Roman custom.

Formerly, at the coronation of the emperor of Constantinople, if the father of the new king or emperor was present, the father and the patriarch together placed the diadem upon him; if the father was absent, the patriarch alone did so, as Codinus testifies in his book *On the Offices of the Court*:

> **εἰ οὖν ὡς προείπομεν, πάρεστιν ὁ βασιλεὺς καὶ πατὴρ αὐτοῦ, αὐτός τε καὶ ὁ Πατριάρχης λαβόντες τὸ στέμμα, ἐπιτιθέασι τῇ κεφαλῇ τοῦ νέου βασιλέως etc.**

That is:

> If, then, as we said, the emperor and his father are present, the father and the patriarch, taking the diadem, place it upon the head of the new emperor, etc.

And the patriarch pronounces the word “Worthy.” If his father is not present, the patriarch alone does this. Just as, earlier, those in the sacred ambo and the rest of the multitude responded three times to the word “Holy” at the application of the ointment, so they likewise acclaim this word “Worthy” three times [Col. 0576C].

Codinus also explains above, in the same book, what the *stemma* is:

> **Δεῖ δὲ γινώσκειν ὅτι ὅπερ καλεῖται νῦν στέμμα, ὠνομάζετο πάλαι διάδημα. Τοῦτο δὲ ἦν βλατίον μετὰ λίθων καὶ μαργάρων κατὰ τὸ τοῦ βασιλέως μέτωπον κείμενον μὲν, δεδεμένον δὲ ὄπισθεν περὶ τὸν ἐγκέφαλον, διὸ καὶ ἐκαλεῖτο διάδημα, ὅπερ ἐκ τοῦ κατὰ μικρὸν ἀμειφθὲν ἐγένετο οἷον ὁρᾶται τοῦ σήμερον, καὶ ὀνομάζεται στέμμα.**

That is:

> It should be known that what is now called the *stemma* was formerly called a *diadem*. It was a purple textile adorned with small stones and pearls, laid across the emperor’s forehead and tied behind around the back of his head; for this reason it was called a diadem. Little by little it was changed into what is seen today and is called a *stemma*.

From these final words it may be understood that the *stemma* is not altogether the same as the diadem, but that it underwent some alteration. In this text the translator rendered **βλατίον** as “golden textile,” but I render it “purple textile.” For *blata* or *blatta* is a purple color. The old manuscript glosses of the library of Corbie have: “*Blata*, purple”; hence *blatea*, a linen shirt. Sidonius, poem V:

> Pontus supplies castoreum, Tyre purple, Corinth bronze.

And poem XI:

> Such honor and distinction in the hair, compared with crimson—  
> the pale purple lies concealed.

Hence, in the same author’s final letter-poem of book IX, the senate is called *blattifer*, “purple-bearing.” It is a kind of extremely exquisite purple.

But, to return from this digression, in the second coronation of Charles the Bald, celebrated at Metz in the kingdom of Lothair, the crown was placed upon his head by the bishops, as is stated in his capitularies:

> At the words “May the Lord crown you,” the bishops placed the crown upon his head.

In the coronation of Henry IV, performed at Chartres, the crown was placed upon him by Nicholas of Thou, bishop of that city, who completed the whole ceremony because the archbishop—or metropolitan—was unavailable, the see of Sens being vacant at that time. Reginald of Beaune, archbishop of Bourges, had been nominated by the king to the see of Sens and claimed that this consecration belonged to him; but because he had not yet been confirmed by the pope, he was compelled to yield to the bishop. Nor could the king, for this reason, go to Rheims, since the city was then occupied by factions.

### 1108. “Receive the scepter of royal majesty,” etc.

This formula appears in the coronation of Louis II and in the coronation of Henry IV, king of the Franks. But it does not appear in the Pontifical or Roman Order; instead, the following is found: “Receive the rod of strength,” etc., as in the Codex of Ratoldus at the presentation of the rod.

### 1109. “Receive the rod of strength,” etc.

This formula appears in the frequently mentioned coronation of Henry IV. In the Roman Order it is pronounced at the presentation of the scepter and staff.

It should be noted that the presentation of the rod is distinguished here from the presentation of the scepter. The same distinction may be seen in the coronations of Henry II and Henry IV, and in the coronation of Louis, son of King Philip I, in the continuation of Aimoinus, book V, chapter 5:

> On the day of the Invention of the Holy Protomartyr, having anointed the king with the liquid of the most sacred anointing and celebrated a Mass of thanksgiving, he set aside the sword of secular warfare, girded him with an ecclesiastical sword for the punishment of evildoers, and gladly crowned him with the diadem of the kingdom. He also most devoutly delivered to him, with the approval of clergy and people, the scepter and rod, and through these the defense of the Churches and the poor, together with all the insignia of the kingdom.

This is the rod that we call the “hand of justice.” It is so called in the coronation of Henry II and Henry IV, and the palm of a hand is fixed to it. This seems to be indicated by the words of this formula:

> Teach the way to the one who wanders, and extend your hand to the fallen.

But in the coronation of Charles the Bald the rod is not presented to him; instead, a palm together with the scepter is given, as is stated in the capitularies of that same Charles:

> At the words “May the Lord grant you the will,” they gave him the palm and the scepter.

This signifies the sign of persevering victory by which he may attain the palm of everlasting glory, as is expressed in the formula for this presentation:

> May the Lord grant you the will and the ability to do what he commands; and, advancing in the government of the kingdom according to his will, may you arrive, with the palm of persevering victory, at the palm of everlasting glory, through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives.

For the palm of the hand is not the symbol of persevering victory, but the palm tree, as everyone knows.

Another rite remains, which is not found in this Codex of Ratoldus: the king or emperor is stripped of his garments and clothed by the pontiff in royal purple, as is known from Theophanes’ *Chronicle*, where he discusses Charlemagne’s coronation as emperor by Leo III:

> **Καὶ περιβαλὼν βασιλικὴν ἐσθῆτα**

That is:

> And having clothed him in royal garments.

Peter Damian likewise says in the sermon cited above:

> Finally, he is clothed in purple, which is the insignia of royal majesty.

### 1110. “May almighty God extend,” etc.

This blessing appears in the manuscript Order of the monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés in the coronation of Henry IV and in the coronation of Charles the Bald, celebrated at Metz. In the latter, however, this clause is inserted:

> May the Lord crown you with a crown of glory, etc.

At these words he was anointed by Archbishop Hincmar. At the end of the blessing this clause is added:

> The clergy and people whom he has wished, by his own aid, to subject to your authority, etc.

Another blessing appears in the Roman Order.

The first section here appears in the blessing for the coronation of Louis II. Its opening is “The almighty Lord God,” with only a few words altered in accordance with the blessing cited above that appears in the coronation of Charles the Bald.

### 1111. “And of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles”

These words are absent from the aforementioned coronations of Charles the Bald and Louis II.

### 1112. “And of Saint Gregory”

Thus it stands in the aforementioned Order of the monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés. The words are absent from the coronations mentioned above. In the coronation of Henry IV, the following is read in their place:

> Of Saint Denis, blessed Martin, and Remigius.

### 1113. “Of the apostle of the angels”

Read “of the apostle of the English,” because Pope Saint Gregory was called the apostle of the English, to whom he sent preachers of the faith, Augustine and certain other monks of his monastery.

### 1114. “And may he grant you grace,” etc.

In the coronations of Charles the Bald and Louis II, this section begins with the preceding words:

> May the Lord forgive you all the evils that you have committed.

### 1115. “May he turn your enemies toward the kindness of peace and charity”

Thus it stands in the aforementioned blessings. In the office for constituting a duke it is corruptly written:

> May he turn your enemies and the kindness of charity.

There this blessing begins with this section and consists of this section and the two final ones.

### 1116. “Bless, Lord,” etc.

This blessing appears in the manuscript Order of the monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés [Col. 0578B]. It is also found in the coronation of Henry IV, king of the Franks, but in a more extended form in the coronation of Judith, queen of the English and daughter of Charles the Bald.

The first section of this blessing is the opening section of the blessing for that same queen, in this form:

> Bless, Lord, your handmaid, you who from eternity govern the kingdoms of kings. Amen.

### 1117. “This prelate-prince”

In the coronation of Henry IV, “our king” is read in place of these words.

### 1118. “Stand and retain from this time onward,” etc.

This designation of the condition of the kingdom appears in the aforementioned manuscript Codex of the monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés and in the coronation of Henry IV. It is somewhat shorter in the Roman Pontifical, with certain words altered, and is pronounced when the king is placed upon the throne.

It also appears in the Roman Order. Before these words, “on this throne of the kingdom,” the following is found:

> Here the metropolitan should make him sit upon his throne, saying: “On this throne of the kingdom,” etc.

### 1119. “From this time onward”

Add **τὸ locum**, “the place,” as it appears in the Roman Order.

### 1120. “At the suggestion”

Read “in succession,” as in the Roman Order.

### 1121. “The rectitude of the king,” etc.

These words lack a title. They are nothing other than a summary of what the king must perform in the proper administration of the kingdom. They appear in the manuscript Order of the monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés; they are absent from the coronation of Henry IV.

They are found in the office for constituting a duke, but in the form of an oath, as follows:

> I swear these three things, in the name of Christ, to the Christian people subject to me. First, that I will always maintain true peace, by my own authority, for the Church of God and for all the Christian people. Second, that I will forbid robbery and every kind of injustice to all ranks. Third, that in all judgments I will command equity and mercy, so that the gracious and merciful God, who lives and reigns, may grant mercy to me and to you.

Here **ut**, “that,” is used with each oath in place of **quod**.

### 1122. “And then let him kiss all the clergy and the people”

The kiss of peace is given in imitation of Samuel, who kissed Saul after anointing him, in the First Book of Kings, chapter 10. It also seems to be found in the Roman Order:

> And afterward let him give him the kiss of peace;

namely, the metropolitan, as is stated there, with no mention of the clergy and people.

In the coronation of Henry IV, the king kisses only the pontiff and the peers of France. The manuscript Order of the monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés agrees with the Codex of Ratoldus.

### 1123. “And let everyone say: ‘Long live the king!’”

Thus it appears in the manuscript Order of the monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, in imitation of ancient practice. For at the elevation of Solomon to the kingdom of Judah the cry was raised, “Long live King Solomon!” in the Third Book of Kings, chapter 1.

A similar acclamation is found in the coronation of Justin the Younger, in Corippus, book II of *The Praises of Justin*, when he was first crowned by the patriarch of Constantinople:

> Suddenly the roar of the fathers resounded; then the cries of the attendants  
> grew louder, and the sea echoed back their cries.  
> With countless praises they raised the names of the rulers.  
> With three hundred voices they wished Justin life.  
> The lofty people likewise acclaimed Augusta Sophia  
> with as many voices; a thousand sang a thousand praises.  
> They declared Justin and Sophia to be two equal lights of the world:  
> “Reign as equals forever,” they said.  
> They prayed for happy years for their fortunate rulers.  
> That voice continued to resound for a long time, and at last fell silent.

The same may be observed in the coronation of Philip Augustus, king of the Franks, in Rigord’s *Life of Philip*:

> When all the archbishops, bishops, and the other princes of the kingdom, together with the entire clergy and people, were crying, “Long live the king! Long live the king!”

Similar acclamations appear in the coronations of Henry II and Henry IV, kings of the Franks.

### 1124. “The king offers the Oblation to the archbishop’s hand”

Bread and wine, namely for communion. The same appears in the manuscript Order of the monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés.

### 1125. “And thus let them give thanks to God”

Thus it stands in the frequently cited manuscript Order of the monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, namely by singing the hymn *Te Deum laudamus*, as in the Roman Order.

### 1126. “Likewise, for blessing the queen”

In this same Codex of Abbot Ratoldus, the blessing of the queen follows the coronation of the king.

### 1127. “Be present, Lord, to our supplications,” etc.

This prayer appears in the coronation of Queen Claude of France, the first wife of Francis I.

### 1128. “Then her head must be anointed with oil”

This anointing of the head of the queen appears in the manuscript Order of the monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés; in the coronation of the aforementioned Queen Claude; in the coronation of Eleanor, the second wife of the aforesaid Francis I; and in the coronation of Catherine de’ Medici, wife of Henry II.

In the Roman Pontifical, however, the queen’s head is not anointed. Rather, her right arm is anointed between the junction of the hands and the elbow, and at the joint of the arm, as was observed above concerning the anointing of kings from that same Pontifical.

### 1129. “Who today is established queen through the laying on of our hand”

These same words appear in the aforementioned manuscript Order of Saint-Germain-des-Prés. It is credible that this laying on of hands was customarily performed after the anointing had been completed, when this prayer was recited:

> Almighty and everlasting God, pour out your abundant Spirit upon your handmaid, etc.

This is certainly highly noteworthy, because nothing similar is written above in the ordination of kings.

Nevertheless, the practice was formerly observed in the coronation of Aidan, king of Ireland, as Adamnan testifies in book II of the *Life of Saint Columba, Abbot*:

> The saint, obeying the Lord’s word, crossed over to the island of Iona. There he ordained Aidan, who arrived in those same days, as king, just as he had been commanded; and during the words of the ordination he prophesied concerning his sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons, and, placing his hand upon his head, ordained and blessed him.

### 1130. “Then the ring must be placed on her finger”

The placing of the ring on the finger appears in the coronations of the queens mentioned above. But nothing concerning it is found in the Roman Order [Col. 0579D] or Pontifical.

### 1131. “And by the strength granted to you summon barbarian peoples to the knowledge of the truth”

These same words appear in the coronation of the aforementioned Queen Claude of France. They signify that it is the queen’s role to care for the conversion of unbelievers, while their husbands fight for the safety of the fatherland. The records of ecclesiastical history are full of devout queens who labored with no little effort to spread the Christian faith.

### 1132. “Then the crown must be placed upon her head”

The imposition of the crown follows. In the Roman Pontifical it is imposed by the metropolitan, whether upon a queen or an emperor.

Formerly, the diadem was placed upon the head of the empress of Constantinople by her husband, the emperor, after he had received it from the hand of the patriarch and it had first been blessed by him, as Codinus reports in his book *On the Offices of the Palace of Constantinople*:

> **Κατερχόμενος οὖν τοῦ ἀμβωνος ὁ βασιλεὺς καὶ ἀνὴρ αὐτῆς λαμβάνει ἀπὸ τῆς τοῦ πατριάρχου χειρος τὸ στεμμα εὐλογηθὲν πρότερον παρ᾽ αὐτοῦ, καὶ ἐπιτίθησι τῇ κεφαλῇ τῆς ἑαυτοῦ γυναικός.**

That is:

> Descending from the sacred ambo, the emperor, her husband, receives from the patriarch’s hand the diadem, previously blessed by him, and places it upon his wife’s head.

### 1133. “Receive the crown of glory”

In the Roman Order and Pontifical there are other formulas for the imposition of the crown.

In the capitularies of Charles the Bald, Judith, daughter of that same Charles and wife of Æthelwulf, king of the English, is crowned with the following formula:

> May the Lord crown you with glory and honor, and place upon your head a crown of precious spiritual stone, so that whatever is signified by the gleam of gold and the varied brilliance of jewels may always shine forth in your character and actions. May he deign to grant this, to whom belong honor and glory forever and ever.

In the Roman Pontifical the scepter is presented to the queen. But this presentation of the scepter is found neither here nor in the Roman Order or that of Saint-Germain.

### 1134. “The nuptial rite”

That is, the celebration of the wedding, which takes place during the solemnities of Mass, according to an ancient custom that may also be seen in Tertullian, book II *To His Wife*, near the end:

> How could we sufficiently recount the happiness of this marriage, which the Church brings together, the offering confirms, the blessing seals, the angels announce, and the Father ratifies?

### 1135. “This Oblation of your handmaids”

Read “of your handmaid,” singular.

### 1136. “Generation for the Church,” etc.

I think **regeneration** should be read, namely that which takes place through baptism for the growth of the Church, just as natural generation occurs for the adornment of the world.

### 1137. “Offered”

This word is corrupt and disturbs the sense. Read “for joy.”

### 1138. “Below: the rite at the thirtieth, or annual, anniversary of the marriage”

I corrected it in this way, since in the aforementioned manuscript Codex of Rheims it reads: “Below, the thirtieth,” etc.

Note the devotion of our ancestors, who celebrated the thirtieth and annual anniversary of marriage by the offering of the unbloody sacrifice and participation in the same sacred mystery.

### 1139. “And you say the Lord’s Prayer,” etc.

This blessing of the bride takes place after the Lord’s Prayer, and in former times everything else was blessed during the solemnities of Mass, as is clear from our sacramentaries. Nevertheless, Judith, daughter of Charles the Bald, when she married Æthelwulf, king of the English, was blessed before the Preface.

### 1140. “You bless her”

The blessing of marriage in the Church is not a recent institution but an entirely ancient one, as is clear from the passage of Tertullian cited above:

> What the Church brings together, the offering confirms, and the blessing seals.

From the letter of Pope Soter, chapter 5:

> Let the bridegroom and bride be blessed by the priest with prayers and offerings.

From the letter of Pope Hormisdas, chapter 6:

> Let no believer, whatever his condition, marry secretly, but let him marry publicly in the Lord after receiving the blessing from the priest.

From the Council of Valence, in Burchard, book IX, chapter 5:

> When the bridegroom and bride are to be blessed by the priest, let them be presented to the priest in the church by their parents or by the bridesmen; and after they have received the blessing, let them remain in virginity that same night out of reverence for the blessing.

From Hilary the Deacon, on chapter 4 of the First Epistle to Timothy:

> For God appointed one wife for a man, with whom he is to be blessed; no one is blessed with a second wife.

From Saint Isidore, book II *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 19:

> For the fact that they are blessed by the priest at the very union of marriage was instituted by God at the first union of man.

John, patriarch of Constantinople, was asked by the emperor Maurice to bless his marriage in the palace, as Theophylact Simocatta testifies in book I of his *History of Maurice*, chapter 10:

> **Ὁ δὲ ἱερεὺς τὸ βασιλικὸν ἐθεράπευσε βούλημα, τῇ περὶ τὸ θεῖον ἱκετεία, καὶ τῶν χειρῶν τῶν βασιλέων ἑλόμενος, συνῆπτεν ἀλλήλαις εὐκτοῖς τε προσφθέγγμασι τὸν τοῦ αὐτοκράτορος κατευφήμησεν γάμον.**

That is:

> The priest dutifully fulfilled the emperor’s wish, offering prayers to God; and, taking the hands of the emperor and empress, he joined them to each other and blessed the emperor’s marriage with supplicatory words.

The same may be seen in book VII of the *Capitularies of Charles and Emperor Louis*, title 363:

> And at the proper time let him be blessed by the priest, according to custom, with prayers and offerings.

And in the capitularies of Charles the Bald, where the nuptial blessings are those of Judith, daughter of Charles the Bald, and Queen Hermintrude.

### 1141. “God, who made the growing world,” etc.

This prayer appears, in a longer form, in the nuptial blessing of the aforementioned Judith.

### 1142. “And upon this handmaid of yours, that woman”

In the aforementioned prayer it reads:

> And upon this male servant of yours, and upon this female servant of yours.

### 1143. “Holiness such as yours”

The passage is corrupt. Read, as in the aforementioned prayer, “in mutual holiness.”

### 1144. “Established”

Read “Establisher.”

### 1145. “Between the world”

Read “Between one another in the world.”

1146. *Ut quia longe est*, etc. These words are extremely corrupt and should be emended thus: “Since that which is like a human being is far weaker than that which you had made like yourself, God, the stronger sex is added to the weaker, so that you might make one out of two.”

1147. *Mista.* Read *Mistum*.

1148. *Ut in prioris.* The word *locum* is missing. Read, therefore, “so that it may take the place of the former.” For marriages are found to be remedies for necessary succession,” that is: “For marriages are remedies devised for necessary succession,” says Lucian in *Lovers*.

1149. *Data sint legis instituta ventura.* Read: “The ordinances of the law to come have been given”; that is, of the new law, which brought the bonds of marriage to a more perfect state.

1150. *Sanctorum pignorum diligata.* The passage is corrupt. I think it should be read: “And that she has bound herself diligently to the upbringing of holy offspring,” so that the whole period coheres as follows:

“May she remember, Lord, that she is bound not only to marital intercourse, but also to observance of the faith and to the diligent upbringing of holy offspring.”

1151. *Fidelis et casta nubat*, etc. These words, through the end, occur in the *Roman Ordo*, in the blessing of Queen Hermintrude, and in the Capitularies of Charles the Bald cited above.

1152. *Sit amabilis ut Rachel viro suo*, etc. These words follow the example of those elders who prayed well for Ruth the Moabite when she married Boaz, the great-grandfather of David, as is related in Ruth, chapter 4.

1153. *Nihil ex hac.* In the *Roman Ordo* and in the blessing of Queen Hermintrude one reads: “May there be nothing in her derived from her deeds.”

1154. *Subdolus ille.* These words are absent from the *Roman Ordo* and from the blessing of Queen Hermintrude.

1155. *Mandatisque.* Thus it appears in the *Roman Ordo*; the particle *-que* is absent from the blessing of Queen Hermintrude.

1156. *Feminarum.* This word appears redundant, and it does not occur in the *Roman Ordo* or in the blessing of Queen Hermintrude. Alternatively, one might read: “after the manner, or custom, or likeness of these women,” namely Rachel, Rebecca, and Sarah.

1157. *Serviens Deo vero devota.* These words are absent from the aforementioned blessings of the *Roman Ordo* and of Hermintrude.

1158. *Muniat infirmitatem suam robore disciplinae.* In those blessings these words are placed after the following: “Where, joined to the marriage bed, let her avoid illicit contacts.”

1159. *Verecunda.* Read *Verecundia* (“with modesty”), as in the aforementioned blessings.

1160. *Sit fecunda sobolem.* Read, “May she be fruitful in offspring,” as in the *Roman Ordo*. These words are absent from the blessing of Queen Hermintrude.

1161. *Sit probata et innocens.* These words too are absent from the blessing of Queen Hermintrude.

1162. *Conjunctionis.* Read *ut conjunctionem*.

1163. *Benedictiones.* Read *ut Benedictiones*.

1164. *Plurimi omnes.* Read *plurimorum* (“of very many”); the word *omnes* is redundant.

1165. *Omnipotens.* This word appears redundant.

1166. *Ut sanctitatem Patrem.* Read *ut te sanctitatum Patrem* (“[that] you [are] the Father of sanctities”).

1167. *Ut quod non ministrentur officio.* The passage is corrupt. It appears that it should read: “So that what is not supplied by our ministry may rather be fulfilled by your blessing.”

These are a few remarks about marriage and its rites, although Saint Isidore reports many more things in book II, chapter 19, of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*. First he discusses the veil with which brides are veiled at weddings:

“But the reason,” he says, “that these same women are veiled when they marry is so that they may know by this that they are subject and humble toward their husbands.”

And below:

“Hence married women are also called *nuptae*, because they veil their faces; for *obnubere* means ‘to cover.’ Hence clouds are also called *nubes*, because they cover the sky.”

The same point is clear from Saint Ambrose, in his *Exhortation to Virgins*:

“Thus they are clouds—and heavy clouds—who have married. For I think that the word for those who marry is derived from clouds. Finally, they are covered like clouds when the women who are about to marry receive the veils.”

This was the custom of the ancient Romans, as is clear from Festus:

“Because the head of the bride is wrapped in a *flammeum*, which the ancients called *obnubere*.”

And below:

“*Obnubit*: she covers the head; hence *nuptiae* is derived from the covering of the head.”

Since this custom is civil rather than superstitious, it was easily transferred to Christians.

Second, Saint Isidore writes that after the blessing, brides were joined by a band of white and purple color, and he gives the reason in these words:

“But the reason that after the blessing brides are joined to one another by the bond of a band is evidently so that they may not break apart the structure of marital unity. As for the fact that the same band is mingled with white and purple: white is used for purity of life, purple for the succession of blood, so that by this sign both parties may for a time be admonished to observe the law of continence, and afterward not refuse to render the marital debt. For what the Apostle says to married people—‘Abstain for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer’—that is signified by the whiteness of the band; but what he adds, ‘and return again to the same,’ is shown by that purple color.”

Third, he discusses the ring given by the bridegroom to the bride, and adds the reason:

“This is done, clearly, either as a sign of mutual faith, or rather so that their hearts may be joined by the same pledge.”

This rite appears in the marriage of Judith, daughter of Charles the Bald, in the Capitularies of that same Charles:

“Receive the ring, the sign of faith and love and the bond of marital union, so that no one may separate those whom God joins.”

This rite is certainly most ancient in the Church, for Tertullian mentions it in book *On Idolatry*:

“Neither the ring nor marital union derives from the honor of any idol.”

# SCHOLIA ON THE BOOK OF THE SACRAMENTS OF BLESSED GREGORY, WRITTEN BY FATHER ANGELO ROCCA OF CAMERINO, PREFECT OF THE APOSTOLIC SACRISTY

## 599. On the Title and Author of the Book

Before we begin the scholia on the book of the Sacraments of Gregory the Great, two matters in particular seem worthy of knowing, and especially this first one: why a codex of this kind, a book containing prayers and orations, is called a Book of the Sacraments, or rather a Sacramentary, or Sacramentary Book.

Formerly, as Pamelius testifies, not only the sacrifice of the Mass but also the Orations of the Mass were called *sacramenta*—those which principally concern the sacrament of the Eucharist and which are also called Collects, for reasons to be assigned in their proper place. Hence the codex we have before us is usually entitled the Book of the Sacraments, or rather—and perhaps more correctly, subject to better judgment—the Sacramentary, as may be seen in the works of ancient and highly authoritative Catholic writers.

Among these are Albinus Flaccus Alcuin, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, in the chapter on the Saturday before Palm Sunday and on Good Friday; Amalarius Fortunatus, book I, more than once in the second preface, and in chapters 1, 9, 12, and 23, as well as book III, chapter 40, and book IV, chapters 23, 30, and 42; and the *Micrologus*, chapters 13, 24, 25, 31, 42, 49, and 55. In all these places they consistently use the word *Sacramentary*, not “Book of the Sacraments.”

Among more recent writers, likewise highly authoritative, I find that J. Francis de Pavinis, in the canonization of Saint Bonaventure, before article 1, part 1, volume 7; J. Stephen Durandus, book II of *On Ecclesiastical Rites*, chapter 17, no. 8; Cardinal Caesar Baronius of the Holy Roman Church, in the *Martyrology* under January 18; and Jacobus Pamelius, in his preface to the *Micrologus*, used the name *Sacramentary*.

Although Pamelius, in the second volume of his *Liturgicon*, in the prolegomena concerning the Codex of the Sacraments of blessed Gregory, asserts that “Book of the Sacraments” is more correct than “Sacramentary,” in the place cited he nevertheless called that book simply the Sacramentary.

Thus, although only Walafrid Strabo seems in his writings to oppose this manner of writing, and although manuscript copies—which generally depend on the discretion of scribes—seem to favor Walafrid, nevertheless, at least to avoid ambiguity, it appears that the work should more correctly be entitled the Sacramentary rather than the Book of the Sacraments.

For if a work of this kind, written by blessed Gregory, is entitled the Book of the Sacraments, someone may immediately suspect that the seven Sacraments of the Church are contained in it. But if it is called the Sacramentary, or Sacramentary Book, anyone may reasonably judge that it contains not the sacraments themselves, but sacramentals, which concern the sacrament of the Eucharist.

Whatever the case may be, the work of which we speak has not without reason been entitled the Book of the Sacraments, on account of the Vatican manuscripts, which bear the title “Books of the Sacraments,” and especially the one, more distinguished than the others, which we have printed.

600. It remains for us to explain the second point proposed. I find that a codex of this kind was first published under the name of Pope Gelasius; afterward it was revised by Gregory the Great and finally enlarged by others in certain respects, as Walafrid Strabo testifies in book *On Ecclesiastical Matters*, chapter 22, in these words:

“Pope Gelasius is said to have arranged prayers composed both by himself and by others, and the Churches of Gaul used prayers of their own, which are still retained by many. And because many things seemed to have been inserted by uncertain authors and did not possess integrity of meaning, blessed Gregory took care to gather together whatever was reasonable and, after removing what seemed excessive or inelegant, composed the book called the Sacramentary, as is made perfectly clear by its title. If anything is found in it that falters in this sense, it should be believed to have been added later, not inserted by him, by others who were less careful.”

These are Walafrid’s words, which we have quoted here verbatim, so that we need not repeatedly reproduce them in these scholia, where they frequently serve to clarify certain passages.

There is also an exceptionally clear testimony on this matter from John the Deacon, in book II, chapter 17, of his *Life of Gregory the Great*, where he says:

“But he also abridged the Gelasian Codex of the solemn rites of the Mass, removing much, changing a little, and adding some things, and compressed it into a single volume for the exposition of the Gospel readings.”

This is what may be said about the title and author of the Book of the Sacraments, in response to the doubts that might occur to anyone.

# SCHOLIA

*[Note: [Col. 0583] The reader is referred back to the numbers printed in heavier type in the text. EDITOR.]*

**Column 1.** “The Gloria in excelsis Deo is also said,” etc. If it is a bishop, some manuscripts read *adfuerit* (“has been present”). But the former reading seems more consistent with the following words: “But it is not said at all by priests except on Easter alone.” There is now, however, a different practice.

In the same place one reads: “Then the Apostle follows.” Other manuscript codices have: “Then the Epistle is read.” This reading explains and corrects the former.

**Column 2.** In the first part of the Canon, which begins with the words “Therefore, Lord,” several signs of the cross, now made within the Canon, are absent between the words “These gifts, these offerings, these holy and unblemished sacrifices” and the other words “Blessed, enrolled, ratified,” as well as in other places. Perhaps they were omitted through the negligence of scribes.

For all these signs of the cross are ancient and full of mysteries. They are missing in the places mentioned and elsewhere because they are repeated so many times not only before the consecration, to sanctify what has been offered, but also after the consecration, to represent the passion and death of Christ the Savior. This is clearly taught by Saint Augustine, in his book *On the Holy Spirit*; the *Micrologus*, *On Ecclesiastical Observances*, chapter 15; 601 Amalarius Fortunatus, book III of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 24; Ivo of Chartres, sermon *On the Agreement of the Ancient and New Sacrifice*; Saint Thomas, part III, question 83, article 5; Saint Bonaventure, in his *Exposition of the Mass*; Gabriel Biel, in his *Canon of the Mass*; William Durandus, book IV of *On Divine Offices*, in his exposition of the Canon; Stephen Durandus, *On Ecclesiastical Rites*; and many others.

Nevertheless, these signs have not been restored to their proper places, so that the text may be displayed faithfully as it stands, with its very evident and countless errors—errors concerning punctuation, orthography, and the words themselves—except for those that had to be corrected without any hesitation.

**Column 3.** In the Vatican manuscript codices one reads *Tathaei* instead of *Thaddaei*. We may suspect that the word *Tathaeus*, by the grammatical figure of aphaeresis, derives its origin from a Hebrew source—namely, from the name *Mattathias*, meaning “Given by the Lord” or “Gift of the Lord.” For this word is composed of *Matthat*, meaning “gift” or “giving,” and *Ia*, “God” or “Lord”; it is therefore interpreted as “Gift of God” or “Gift of the Lord.”

*Matthias* has the same meaning by the figure of syncope, with the middle syllable removed, as does *Matthaeus*, meaning “Given.” For the Greeks convert *ia* into the diphthong *ai* when transferring something from other languages into their own; Latins customarily pronounce this Greek diphthong as *ae*. Thus, borrowing something from the Greeks in the formation of words, they combine alpha and iota into the diphthong *ae* and say *Matthaeus*.

Hence *Tathaeus* is formed by aphaeresis, as though from *Mattathaeus* or *Mattathias*, with the syllable *Mat* removed. Since, therefore, the word *Thathaeus* corresponds so well to the Hebrew word, I decided that this form, not the other, should be retained.

Add also that Pamelius, in the Book of the Sacraments that he printed under the name of Gregory the Great, found and retained the word *Tathaei* in this passage, although in the margin he added *Tatdaei* with an asterisk.

*Thaddaeus*, however, is said in Latin to mean “Praising” or “Confessing.”

**Column 3.** “Who, on the day before he suffered.” Two particles now found in the Missal are missing here, but their omission appears not to have been accidental. For one reads *Elevatis* without the conjunction *et* (“and”); likewise *Dedit* without that enclitic particle *-que*.

**Column 4.** *Super diptycha.* The text incorrectly read *Dyptitia*. *Diptychum*, or Greek *δίπτυχον* (*diptychon*), means “folded double” in Latin, from *δὶς* (“twice”) and *πτὺξ* or *πτύχη* (“fold”).

Here *diptychum* refers to two tablets, one containing the names of the living and the other those of the dead, which were publicly recited during the Mass. The names of the living were recited in that part of the Canon beginning “Remember, Lord,” after the words “your servants and handmaids,” etc.; those of the dead were recited after the words “who have gone before us with the sign of faith and sleep in the sleep of peace.”

The ancient custom in the holy Church of commemorating both the living and the dead in the sacrifice of the Mass, whose names were written on tablets, is mentioned by Pope Gelasius in his letter to the Emperor Anastasius, as may be seen in volume II of the Councils, well after the middle of the letter; by Innocent I, in his letter to Decentius, bishop of Gubbio; and it is read in *On Consecration*, distinction 1, chapter 73. Saint Cyprian, in letter 10, volume I, says that a name was offered, and in letter 66 that it was named in the priests’ prayer during the recitation of the tablets. Saint Augustine, in his letter to the clergy of Hippo, letter 137, also speaks of it; the matter is found in *Decretum* 2, question 1, chapter 12, “The Name,” and 11, question 3, chapter 50, “What harm does it do?” Gregory likewise mentions it in the *Register*, book III, letter 37, along with many others.

There are also authors who write explicitly about diptychs. Dionysius the Areopagite, in book *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, chapter 3, expressly mentions the mystical recitation of sacred tablets. For although the Latin text reads “the mystical recitation of the saints,” with no mention at all of sacred tablets, the Greek text has *ἱερῶν πτυχῶν*, that is, “of sacred tablets.” This was omitted by the translator either because the word *πτυχῶν* was absent from his copy or because he thought Dionysius was speaking only about the recitation of saints customarily performed in the sacrifice of the Mass, as Pamelius believes.

Innocent likewise, in his letter to the Emperor Arcadius, 602 and the Empress Eudoxia, in her letter to the same Innocent, expressly mention diptychs. These letters may be seen in Gregory, archbishop of Alexandria, in his *Life of Chrysostom*, as Stephen Durandus reports.

Pope Vigilius also mentions diptychs in the condemnation of Theodore, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, as is read in volume II of the Councils among that pope’s decrees.

They are also mentioned by Theodore in the ecclesiastical history called the *Tripartite History*, book X, chapter 25, where one reads concerning Chrysostom:

“That pontiff was therefore the first to insert the name of John the Great in the ecclesiastical diptychs.”

Alcuin too mentions diptychs in *On the Celebration of the Mass*, well after the middle:

“After those words in which ‘in the sleep of peace’ is said, it was the custom of the ancients—and the Roman Church does so even today—that the names of the dead should immediately be recited from the diptychs, that is, from the tablets.”

Much the same is read in Florus the Master, in his *Exposition of the Mass*.

Sacred diptychs are also mentioned in the liturgy of Saint Mark and in the synodical letter of Proclus, archbishop of Constantinople, to Domnus, bishop of Antioch, near the middle of the letter, which appears in volume II of the Councils, act 14 of the Council of Chalcedon.

In the Fifth General Synod, the Second Council of Constantinople, volume II of the Councils, session or conference 1, in the letter of the Emperor Justinian written to the synod concerning Theodore, who was bishop of Mopsuestia, one reads:

“His name has been erased from the sacred diptychs of the Church of which he was bishop.”

And below:

“We also urge them to discuss that other matter which is falsely put forward by those who say that heretics ought not to be anathematized after death, and who follow in this the teaching of the holy Fathers. For they not only condemned heretics while living, but also anathematized them after death, as having died in their impiety; just as they restored after death those who had been unjustly condemned and wrote them in the sacred diptychs. This was done in the case of John—namely Chrysostom—and Flavian, bishops of Constantinople, of revered memory.”

Almost all of this appears in Gratian’s *Decree*, 24, question 2, chapter 6, beginning “Certainly it is put forward by some who say that it is necessary,” etc.

This passage, taken from Justinian’s letter, has the same sense as the passage found in that letter. But it seems foolish and mutilated, with some words removed by the compiler and others changed. For the word *sane* (“certainly”), placed in place of the adverb *vane* (“vainly”) and with the negation removed, does not mean “well and wisely,” as the Gloss interprets the passage; it is merely an affirming word. Unless one reads, “Certainly it is well put forward,” etc., or “It is sufficiently vainly put forward by some who say that it is not necessary,” etc., with the negation restored to its proper place.

But enough of this. Let us return to the diptychs, from which our digression was prompted by the occasion.

This passage concerning diptychs formerly stood corrupted in Gratian’s *Decree*, but in Rome it was corrected in recent years from the said council. Previously, instead of *diptychis*, the reading was *dicticis*.

Hence the Gloss, explaining that corrupted word *dicticis*, says that *dicticae* are tablets, so called from *dico, dicis* (“to say”). Thus the Gloss responded corruptly to a corrupt text.

For the author of this verse, using a false word in place of the true one and lengthening the middle syllable, wrote:

> Cleric, never remove the *dictica* from your side.

I have not been able to find this corrupted verse, which the Gloss attributes to Martial, in Martial’s works. I think it should be restored as follows:

> Cleric, never remove the *diptychium* from your side.

For the verse cited by the Gloss does not correspond to the text now corrected. Restored in this way, however, it preserves the correct etymology, the genuine sense, and the quantity of the syllables. The word *diptycha*, or *diptychium*, with the syllable *pty* shortened, as was explained at the beginning of this scholium, has another etymology, derived from the folding together of two tablets.

As everyone interprets them, diptychs were tablets made of any material—whether sheets or columns—on which the images of the Fathers were placed in their catalogue. Since *diptychum* in Greek means “folded double” in Latin, as stated above, those double ecclesiastical tablets, 603, one containing the living and the other the dead, perhaps acquired this name by a transferred usage from the double shells of oysters. Blessed Ambrose calls these *diptychum* quite aptly in book V, chapter 8, of the *Hexaemeron*, volume I, because those double tablets perhaps resembled oyster shells, folded together so that one closed over the other.

By this same transfer, letters issued by any ruler and sealed with seals are believed, according to Brissonius, to have been called *diplomata*, from the folded tablets. Such letters include letters patent or papal bulls; they say that these letters were folded or doubled and sealed by means of wood passed through them. For what the Greeks call *διπλοῦν*, the Latins call *duplum* (“double”).

Hence folded tablets are called *diplomata* and *diptycha*.

For the same reason, writing tablets—or *pugillares*, that is, wax, wooden, or other tablets on which one writes with a stylus—were called by various names among the ancients. Some were fivefold, or *pentaptycha* (*πεντάπτυχα*); others threefold, or *triptycha* (*τρίπτυχα*); others twofold, or *diptycha* (*δίπτυχα*).

Thus, just as Suetonius calls double tablets *diplomata* or *diptycha* in his *Augustus*, so Ausonius called the diptych a “two-leaved writing tablet.” In the *Th.* Codex, as the learned Brissonius reports in book IV of *On the Meaning of Words*, double tablets are called the emperors’ *diptycha*. I think they may also quite properly be called *diptychia*, persuaded by the authority of Saint Father Augustine. For in book XV, chapter 1, *Against Faustus the Manichaean*, Augustine, speaking in the person of Faustus and then replying to him, repeatedly called those two stone tablets of Moses—a first tablet containing three commandments relating to God and seven relating to one’s neighbor—a “stone diptych.”

Those double ecclesiastical tablets, therefore, one of which contained the names of the living and the other those of the dead to be recited in the sacrifice of the Mass, were rightly called *diptycha*, not *diptycia*, as the Vatican copy mistakenly reads through the carelessness of scribes.

Nor should we pass over in silence something that frequently occurs in this Book of the Sacraments, concerning the places where the names of the living and the dead, or even of the saints, are to be recited. Wherever the commemoration of certain persons is customarily made by name, the older Vatican Codex does not contain the letter *N.*, the sign indicating that a name is to be supplied, but the letters *ILL.*, which have been preserved to represent the antiquity of the Codex.

**Column 4.** In the section beginning “To us also, sinners,” one reads *Agathe* and *Agne* in the sixth case, retaining the Greek form of declension, instead of *Agatha* and *Agnete*—that is, *Agathe, -es*, and *Agne, -es*. This was in use among many Latins, and especially, indeed frequently, among Saint Ambrose.

Hence Prudentius, in the *Peristephanon*, uses the Greek declension in this way:

> Agnes’ tomb is in a Roman house,  
> Of a brave girl, a renowned martyr.

Here *Agnes* is used for *Agnetis*. Some manuscripts, however, have *Agnis sepulcrum*. But *Agni, Agnis* is an entirely Greek declension, with the letter eta pronounced as iota, not as e, as in *γραμματικὴ, -ῆς* and *ῥητορικὴ, -ῆς*. When translating such words into their own language, Latins say *grammatice, -es* and *rhetorice, -es*, and so forth.

Thus *Agathe* is used for *Agatha*, and *Agne* for *Agnete*. This may also be seen, in greater detail, in the feasts of these same saints.

**Column 3.** In the same Sacramentary there are manuscripts that read *Agna, Agnae*, as appears in Pamelius’s annotations.

**Column 8.** In the Preface, one manuscript has: “Through him may we be seized by love of invisible things.” But three manuscripts agree with the Roman Missal, which reads: “Through him may we be seized by love for invisible things.” Since this reading is clearly more fitting than the former, I judged that it should be restored in this Book of the Sacraments.

**Column 8.** In the Oration “Grant, we beseech you,” one manuscript alone read: “an increase of faith, hope, and security.” The others have: “an increase of faith, hope, and charity.” Since the former reading is suspect as an error, I judged that the latter should be retained.

604 **Column 9.** In the Secret one read: “Receive, Lord,” etc., “so that what passion made glorious in them, devotion may render harmless in us.” In the first clause the verb *fecit* (“made”) is missing. I restored it so that the sentence would not remain mutilated, especially since the Missal reads *efficit* (“makes”), and Pamelius’s annotations have *fecit*, which is also found in another manuscript.

**Columns 21, 23, 24, and 25.** One may see the Mass of the holy virgins and martyrs Agnes and Agatha, whose names are plainly declined in the Greek manner, as was extensively shown above at the beginning of this column.

**Column 24.** After the Orations “at the Completion,” which is now called the Postcommunion in the Missal, there is placed an Oration that in the Vatican Codex printed by us is entitled “Collect.” It resembles the Oration customarily said over the people.

It is called a Collect because, as Saint Bonaventure says in his *Exposition of the Mass*, chapter 2, volume VII, all those standing at Mass should gather themselves together devoutly and pray faithfully with the priest. Others say that it is called a Collect because the Orations of the Mass are customarily celebrated when the people have been gathered.

This latter opinion does not please me, because by that reasoning everything said in the Mass could be called a Collect. Therefore, with Walafrid Strabo, chapter 22, we shall say:

“We call them Collects because we gather together, or conclude, the necessary petitions of the prayers in concise brevity.”

Or they are called Collects because the priest, who acts as an ambassador for the people before the Lord, gathers together and concludes all their petitions in these prayers, as the *Micrologus* judges in chapter 3 of *On Ecclesiastical Observances*. In the same place it explains which prayers are more properly called Collects, in these words:

“Those, however, seem to be called Collects more specifically that are made among the Romans over the Collect of the people, when the people are gathered so that they may proceed from one church to another to celebrate the station. Thus, on the first day of the fast, the Oration ‘Grant us, Lord’ is said over the Collect of the people at Saint Anastasia, while the station is to be celebrated at Saint Sabina.”

This is what the *Micrologus* says.

The Oration mentioned is found today in the Missal after the blessing and distribution of ashes, before the Mass. In ancient times, on Ash Wednesday, the people were gathered at Saint Anastasia, where the said Oration was recited; afterward they proceeded to Saint Sabina to celebrate the station.

Likewise, on the feast of the Assumption of blessed Mary ever-virgin, the following Oration, “Venerable to us, Lord,” was read during the station, when, as is recorded in the *Roman Ordo*, page 84, the procession proceeded with the image of Christ from Saint Mary the Less—which is in the Cattle Market by the Arch of Vespasian and is now called the church of Saint Mary the New—to Saint Adrian, where the station was held; the Mass, however, was celebrated at Saint Mary Major.

On the feast of the Nativity of the same Virgin, the Oration “The Supplication of your servants,” etc., was recited when the litany went out from Saint Adrian to Saint Mary, according to the custom of blessed Pope Gregory the Great, as Radulphus of Tongeren says in *On the Observance of the Canons*, proposition 13, and more fully proposition 23, where he discusses these three Collects and stations.

**Column 29.** On February 22, when the Chair of Saint Peter at Antioch is customarily celebrated, the title of the Mass reads as follows: “The Chair of Saint Peter at Rome.”

*[Note: [Col. 0587D] See Hugh Menard, notes 179 and 180.]*

I think the passage is corrupt through the error of scribes, since “Rome” has been written in place of “Antioch.” The Antiochene Chair, celebrated on February 22, is mentioned by the *Roman Ordo*, page 24; by the Antiphonary of blessed Gregory; by the *Micrologus*, chapter 48; and by Ivo, bishop of Chartres.

The Roman Chair, now celebrated on January 18, is found neither in the Antiphonaries, nor in the Lectionaries, nor in either manuscript or printed Sacramentaries. Nor is there any mention of it among the ancient writers on ecclesiastical rites, because the divine office of the Roman Chair was instituted by Paul IV through a bull dated January 18, 1557, at Rome, on the eighth day before the Ides of January, in the third year of his pontificate.

Hence, as far as I know, the Roman Chair celebrated on January 13 is not found in the old Breviaries printed before the pontificate of Paul IV. It does, however, occur in Martyrologies, which provide very clear testimony concerning this Chair.

There are also many other testimonies on this matter, which Cardinal Caesar Baronius of the Holy Roman Church—a truly learned man and extraordinarily versed in ecclesiastical history—reviews extensively and impressively in his annotation 605 on the Roman Martyrology under January 18. In Gaul and parts of Spain, however, this feast of the Roman Chair was observed before the decree of Paul IV, as is recounted in the bull itself.

Concerning the Mass of the Chair found under February 22 in the Vatican manuscript codices, Cardinal Baronius mentions it and cites it under January 18 in the same annotation in the Roman Martyrology as the Mass of the Roman Chair, because the Collect found in another Mass of that same day also appears to belong to the Roman Chair.

Nevertheless, the Antiochene Chair appears under the name of the Roman Chair on February 22 in the more distinguished manuscript Sacramentary. Cardinal Baronius recites the Preface of that Mass almost word for word, except for the word *mundasti* (“you cleansed”) in place of *fundasti* (“you founded”).

For in the Vatican manuscript copies it reads as follows:

“Which Church”—that is, the Church—“you founded in the patriarchs, prepared in the prophets, established in the apostles,” etc.

**Column 1339.**

*[Note: [Col. 0589D] Editor Guss. These words are absent from our copy.]*

In the Oration beginning “Almighty and eternal God,” etc., much is missing that is found in another copy, as may be seen in Cardinal Baronius, volume I of the *Ecclesiastical Annals*, page 328, D. To make this clear, it seemed appropriate to set out the Oration itself here.

In the Vatican copy it stands as follows:

> Almighty and eternal God, who by an ineffable mystery placed the primacy in the citadel of the Roman name in your apostle Peter, grant that what he began throughout the world by his preaching may be followed by the whole Christian community in devotion. Through [Christ our Lord], etc.

This is from the Vatican manuscript.

Baronius reads it as follows:

> Almighty and eternal God, who by an ineffable mystery granted your apostle Peter the primacy of the city of Rome, so that evangelical truth might spread from there throughout all the kingdoms of the world, grant, we beseech you, that what has flowed throughout the world through his preaching may be followed by the whole Christian community with devotion.

This is from Baronius, who testifies that he found these prayers in the ancient ritual books, or Breviaries, of the holy Roman Church, both in the first volume of his *Annals* and in the *Martyrology*.

**Column 29.** In the first Oration of the Mass of the Chair of Saint Peter: “You entrusted him with the pontifical authority to bind and loose souls.”

These words occur in the more distinguished Vatican manuscript codex, but in other manuscripts of the same library, as well as in the *Liturgicon* printed by Pamelius, the word *animas* (“souls”) is absent. Even without that word, however, the reading can still have the same meaning as the form found in the Roman Missal.

At the same place, in this Mass, the question presents itself for consideration why, at the end, after the Prayer “for the Conclusion,” which is now called the Postcommunion in the Roman Missal, a Collect over the People is added. This Collect is now said only on weekdays of Lent, up to and including Wednesday of Holy Week, as may be seen in the Missal. On this rite the Micrologus, *On Ecclesiastical Observances*, chapter 51, gives the following explanation:

“The Prayer after Communion is ordinarily offered for those who have communicated alone. But although the people assemble daily during Lent, they do not communicate daily, as they ought. Therefore, lest the people should be deprived of the Prayer as well as of Communion, the Prayer over the People was added; in it prayer is offered specifically not for Communion, but for the people’s protection. On Sundays, however, it is not said, because kneeling is avoided—the people formerly performed genuflection during this Prayer; or rather because, according to the testimony of Saint Ambrose, everyone ought to communicate on Sundays, and on those days the Prayer after Communion could suffice as a Blessing.”

This is what the Micrologus says. He also answers the tacit objection that follows: namely, why the Prayer over the People was added on Sundays and feast days, when genuflection is not ordinarily permitted—as may be seen in this Sacramentary—and why this practice subsequently became established, as the Roman Missal clearly demonstrates. The Micrologus therefore says as follows:

“Our most blessed Fathers, Ambrose, in Book V of *On the Sacraments*, chapter 4, and in *On Consecration*, distinction 2, chapter 56, and Augustine, sermon 28, *On the Words of the Lord*, volume X, exhort us to daily Communion. But since this practice is observed neither by all priests during Lent, much less by the laity, the Prayer over the People was appropriately added, so that at least during that season the people would not be deprived of the final Blessing, even though they might not ordinarily communicate. Hence that custom among moderns, which was not found among the ancients, also seems to have arisen: namely, that at other times as well priests bless the people after the end of Mass, lest they allow the people to depart deprived both of the Blessing and of Communion.”

This concerns the Prayer entitled “for the Conclusion,” because the Mass is completed by it. The same prayer is called the Postcommunion because it is ordinarily said after Communion for those who have communicated alone, just as in ancient times only those who communicated ordinarily remained present at the divine mysteries. The catechumens and penitents, since they had not yet prepared themselves to communicate, were ordered to leave before the Oblation, as the same Micrologus attests in the passage cited.

**Column 30.** Here stands the Mass of Blessed Pope Gregory. From this it is plainly discerned that many things, as was stated in the Preface, were added to this Sacramentary after the time of Gregory the Great. Grimoldus said almost the same thing about this Mass in the Preface to his own Sacramentary.

**Column 39.** In the Preface the Vatican Codex reads: “Faith is added” (*Fides additur*). But in the Codex printed by Pamelius one reads: “Faith is nourished” (*Fides alitur*). Since reason shows this reading to be more appropriate, I judged that it should be retained. For the passage reads:

“In which” [that is, in Christ] “the faith of those who fast is nourished, hope is advanced, charity is strengthened: Jesus Christ our Lord.”
