These words are not found in the Vatican Codices, but they make the reading clearer and more appropriate to the words that follow. The former reading, however, is not unacceptable, especially since it seems consonant with what is found in the Gospel: “Lord, increase our faith.”

**Column 41.** “On Saturday with twelve readings of the first month,” that is, of March. Each Ember Saturday in this Sacramentary is entitled “Saturday of twelve readings,” or “with twelve readings,” because on every Ember Saturday twelve readings of Holy Scripture were customarily read, as is now done on Holy Saturday of Holy Week, if the number of readings is observed. At that time, however, only six readings were read; but those six were called twelve because in the Roman Church they were read in both Latin and Greek by twelve readers, for the reasons assigned by Alcuin in his chapter on Saturday.

Concerning the twelve readings, see Amalarius, Book II, chapter 1; Berno, *On the Mass*, chapter 7; and the Micrologus, chapter 28. At present, twelve Latin readings are read on Holy Saturday of Easter; on the other Ember Saturdays, only six Latin readings are likewise ordinarily read.

**Column 51.** One Vatican Codex reads: “And our Lord of all” (*Nostroque omnium Domino*); another reads: “And Lord of our [things]” (*Nostrorumque Domino*). Since both readings yield a good sense, we have retained the former.

**Column 57.** *On the Secret.* In this Prayer there are two readings. One is:

“May they gladden us with temporal consolation, so that we may more confidently not despair of the eternal promises” (*Quae temporali nos consolatione laetificent, ut promissa certius non desperemus aeterna*).

The other is:

“May they signify temporal consolation” (*Quae temporalem consolationem significent*).

The Codices vary. For this reason I judged that the former reading, as clearer and more suitable, should be retained.

**Column 58.** In the final Collect for the Conclusion there are two readings. One is:

“May they be infected by no adversities” (*Nullis inficiantur adversis*).

The other is:

“May they be afflicted by no adversities” (*Nullis afficiantur adversis*).

Both yield a good sense, but I considered that the former, which appears in the more distinguished Vatican manuscript, should be retained.

**Column 62.** On this day, which is Wednesday of Holy Week, Prayers “for every condition” are appointed, and the same prayers are read on Thursday; in the other Codices they are found only on Friday. Nothing certain is known about this matter. We may conjecture, however, that the practice of praying for every condition twice during Holy Week was older in the holy Church, since Prayers of this kind are now recited only on Friday.

**607 — Column 65.** Although the Preface is not without variant readings in the various manuscript Codices, I did not wish to include them here, since they are of little importance. I did, however, judge that one variation of wording should be recorded, concerning Judas the betrayer and Christ’s final supper. According to the Vatican Codices, it reads:

“The gentle Lord suffers the harsh Judas and endures the cruel fellow-diner” (*Patitur mitis Dominus immitem Judam, et sustinet pius crudelem convivam*).

But the Codex printed by Pamelius reads:

“The gentle Lord therefore feeds the harsh Judas” (*Pascit igitur mitis Dominus immitem Judam*), etc.

Both readings are good, although the latter appears more probable, since this Preface is speaking about a supper, or banquet, as may be seen there. Nevertheless, we have retained the former reading as the more common and accepted one, so that no alteration might rashly be made where necessity does not require it.

At the same place: from the word “released” (*relaxavit*) exclusively to the end of the Preface, many passages are not found in the other Codices, except the larger and more celebrated Vatican Codex.

**Column 67.** In the Prayer for the blessing of oil, the final wording appears mutilated:

“From which you anointed priests, kings, prophets, and martyrs, your perfect chrism, O Lord, blessed by you,” etc.

This is how it stands in the Vatican Codex. But the Codex printed by Pamelius reads:

“From which you anointed priests, kings, prophets, martyrs, your perfect chrism, O Lord, and blessed by you, remaining in our inmost parts, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

This reading also appears truncated and mutilated, since some word is missing at the end.

**Column 69.** On Friday of Holy Week, in the first and second rubrics, several words are so obscure because of the writing itself and their sense that, even if some of them are expanded—that is, if the abbreviations, which the Italians call *breviature*, are explained—nothing certain can be extracted that yields a coherent reading. The abbreviated forms are these: *Sacrâmrio* and *Pbrôrum*. If these are taken as abbreviations for *Sacramentario* (“Sacramentary”) and *Presbyterorum* (“of the priests”), it is not sufficiently clear what they mean here, especially in the case of *Sacramentario*. This would be understandable only if another abbreviated Sacramentary were being cited, from which this text had been copied, and if “of the priests” were taken to mean “for churches,” that is, for churches that were not cathedrals, as may be seen in the Roman Order concerning the office of Good Friday.

If this is how the passage must be understood, the punctuation also appears to require alteration, as may be seen in its proper place.

**Column 69.** “With an oratory placed before it,” that is, before the cross, etc. I have not yet been able to discover what *oratorium* is intended to mean here; and if it is understood in its ordinary sense, it still does not seem appropriate to the matter. An *oratorium* is a place in which prayer is offered, but such a place is not ordinarily set before the cross on Good Friday, while the cross is being adored.

Alcuin, when discussing the rite of adoration on Good Friday, recites the same words that are read in the Sacramentary, but instead of *oratorium* he reads *orarium*. The same reading is found in the Roman Order when the rite of adoring the cross on Good Friday is described.

*Orarium*, derived from *orare* (“to pray”), is ordinarily taken to mean the stole that those who speak—or, that is, preachers—wear around the neck, as Alcuin, Rabanus, and Bede state. This, however, does not suit the present passage unless *oratorium*, likewise derived from *orare*, is taken to mean a curtain or carpet spread before the cross, upon which prayer is offered with knees bent and the cross is finally adored.

**Column 111.** The Prayer called the Secret on the feast of Blessed Leo has been changed. Whereas formerly the ancient Sacramentary read:

“Grant us, O Lord, that this Oblation may benefit the soul of your servant Leo,” etc.,

the Missal now reads:

“That this Oblation may benefit us through the intercession of Blessed Leo.”

This Secret is in fact read today in the Mass of Saint Gregory the Pope.

This alteration appears to have been made for a clearer expression and understanding of the matter, since the saints do not need our Prayers; rather, we need their intercession. Indeed, whoever prayed for the saints would do them an injury, as Augustine and other teachers affirm. See Augustine, sermon 17, *On the Words of the Apostle*, volume X.

This alteration is mentioned in the *Decretals*, Book III, title 41, *On the Celebration of Masses*, chapter 6, *Cum Marthae*, section “Thirdly.” There Innocent III, responding to the archbishop of Lyons concerning an alteration of this kind formerly made, says:

“Therefore, when it is contained in many Prayers that an Oblation of this kind may benefit or advance this saint or that one, this must be understood to mean that it benefits him in the sense that he may be more greatly glorified by the faithful on earth. Although many consider it not unworthy that the glory of the saints should increase until the Judgment, and therefore that the Church may meanwhile rightly desire an increase in their glorification.”

This is what Innocent says.

It is therefore sufficiently clear that the Prayer now under discussion should not be altered, both because it is not lacking in a good sense and, above all, because the antiquity of this exemplar is confirmed by the matter. For the reading that we find in this Sacramentary was in use before the time of Innocent, who lived around the year 1208.

Although I had understood the solution to this difficulty as soon as it first presented itself to me, and had demonstrated it in reality to my former colleagues living at the Vatican printing house, Franciscus Toletus, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, a man learned in every field, recalled to my memory the passage of the Canon that wonderfully illuminates the solution.

**Column 122.** Concerning the Vigil of the Assumption of Blessed Mary: in the first Prayer, which is addressed to God Christ concerning Blessed Mary the Virgin, one reads as follows:

“Grant, we ask, that she”—namely, the Blessed Virgin—“may make us joyful in taking part in her feast.”

It seems that *faciat* (“may she make”), not *facias* (“may you make”), should be read, subject nevertheless to better judgment.

**Column 138.** In the first Prayer for the Nativity of All Saints one reads *multiplicatis intercessionibus* (“with multiplied intercessions”). Although the Roman Missal reads *intercessoribus* (“with intercessors”), the former reading should not be rejected.

**Column 139.** The Mass of the Four Crowned Saints is present, as the rubric states. The rubric also explains why five saints are mentioned in the Prayer—namely, Claudius, Nicostratus, Simphorianus, Castorius, and Simplicius—whereas the title names only four: Severus, Severianus, Victorinus, and Carpophorus.

Evidence supporting this is supplied by the title of the church that is called in Rome by the name of the Four Saints, and in which the feast of the Four Crowned Saints is celebrated on 8 November. The rubric of the Sacramentary reads as follows:

“The names of the Four Crowned Saints are these: Severus, Severianus, Victorinus, and Carpophorus. Their birthday could not be found, because it had been entirely neglected through carelessness. Therefore it was decreed that in their church the birthday of these five saints, who are recited in the Mass, should be celebrated, so that their memory might also be kept together with theirs.”

This rubric speaks of ignorance concerning the birthday of the Four Crowned Saints. But in the Roman Breviary, the ignorance concerns the names of those same saints, and the passage is worded as follows:

“There exists in the City a church of the Four Crowned Saints, whose names, long unknown, were later revealed by divine providence. There not only the bodies of those four, but also those of five martyrs, are honorably buried, and their feast is celebrated on the sixth day before the Ides of November, on the same day.”

Bede, Usuard, Ado, Surius, Baronius, and others speak of the Four Crowned Saints and the five others, affirming that the names of the Four Crowned Saints were long unknown. For that reason, it was decreed that their anniversary should be commemorated together with the five others under the name of the Four Crowned Saints.

Surius, drawing from the Martyrology of Ado, says the following about the Four Crowned Saints:

“Severus, Severianus, Carpophorianus, and Victorinus were buried three miles from the City, in the Sand-Pit, near the bodies of the holy martyrs Claudius, Nicostratus, Simphorianus, Castorius, and Simplicius. They suffered on the sixth day before the Ides of November, but two years after the suffering of those five martyrs. Since their names could not be found, Blessed Melchiades the bishop decreed that the anniversary of the Four Crowned Saints should be commemorated under the names of the five holy martyrs. In the intervening years, however, their names were also revealed to a certain holy man. Their feast, nevertheless, remained celebrated, as it had been established, together with the feast of the other martyrs, and the place remained distinguished by the name of the Four Crowned Saints.”

This is what Surius says.

Pope Honorius built the church of the Four Crowned Saints and, according to Baronius, restored it. Leo IV discovered the bodies of all the saints mentioned above; and, as the stone tablet fixed to the high altar of that same church also shows, he placed their remains there in a repository.

**Column 226.** In that part of the sacred Canon which begins with *Communicantes* and is commonly entitled *Infra actionem*, the title here is *Intra Actionem*. Although *Infra Actionem* is always read as far as column 247 of the Vatican edition, from this point to the end of the Sacramentary the title or rubric is *Intra Actionem*, and more correctly so.

For the sacred Canon—which some divide into five parts and others into fifteen—begins with the words “Therefore, most merciful Father” (*Te igitur, clementissime Pater*), etc., and ends at the passage “Remember also, O Lord” (*Memento etiam, Domine*). According to others, it continues as far as “Let us pray, instructed by saving commands” (*Oremus, praeceptis salutaribus moniti*). According to still others, and more correctly, it extends to the words “Deliver us, we ask, O Lord” (*Libera nos, quaesumus, Domine*).

According to Biel, in lecture 15 on the Canon of the Mass, it bears four names. It is called the Canon—that is, the rule ordered toward the consecration of the venerable Eucharist—or, as Walafrid Strabo says in chapter 22 and the Micrologus in chapter 12, because in it the sacrament is confected in a lawful and regular manner.

It is also called the Secret, because, as Biel says, it signifies the most sacred mysteries of the faith, and in it the most sacred operations are performed, incomprehensible to every created intellect; and because the Canon is said secretly.

It is also called the Sacrifice, because the supreme Sacrifice is offered to God the Father: namely, the Only-Begotten Son hidden beneath sacramental form.

Finally, it is called the Action, because, as Walafrid says, the Lord’s sacraments are confected in it, or because it contains a thanksgiving. For almost the whole sacred rite of the Mass is a thanksgiving, as may be inferred from Irenaeus, Book IV, chapter 34.

Or, as Biel says, it is called the Action because in it the most sacred mystery of Christ is enacted: Christ himself, out of his immeasurable charity, bestows his flesh upon the faithful as food and his blood as drink, under the veil of the appearances of bread and wine, for their spiritual nourishment.

Since these things are accomplished only through God’s mercy and free will, this part is rightly called the Action insofar as, as Biel says, it is distinguished from *faction*—that is, from an act produced by human agency.

It is also called the Action, according to the same Biel, because in it our cause is pleaded before the supreme Judge, Christ God, through the priest as a messenger mediating between him and his bride, namely Christ and the Church.

Since, therefore, the Canon is called the Action, it seems more correct to say *Intra Actionem* (“within the Action”) than *Infra Actionem* (“below the Action”). Accordingly, from the middle of this Sacramentary to the end, I judged that this title, *Intra Actionem*, should be retained exactly as I found it written.

**[Note: Column 593C]** Since those Prayers are missing from our edition, we have decided to add them here.

**Common Mass of Saint Augustine**

“Almighty and eternal God, who rule over the living and the dead alike, and have mercy upon all whom you foreknow will be yours in faith and works, we humbly beseech you that, through the intercession of all your saints, those for whom we have resolved to pour out our Prayers—and whom either the present age still retains in the flesh or the age to come has already received after they have been stripped of the body—may by the clemency of your mercy obtain forgiveness of their sins. Through the Lord.”

**Postcommunion.** “May the sacraments which we have received, we ask, almighty and merciful God, purify us; and grant that this sacrament of yours may not be guilt leading us to punishment, but a saving intercession leading to forgiveness; may it be the abolition of crimes, the strength of the weak, a firmament against the dangers of the world, and the remission of all sins of the living and the dead. Through our Lord.”

There exists a Common Mass of Blessed Augustine, which is now recited on each individual day of Lent. In the Prayer that is sometimes called the Postcommunion and sometimes “for the Conclusion,” because it is the Prayer at the end of the Mass, in addition to other variant readings, one reads “the abolition of crimes” (*Abolitio scelerum*), whereas the Missal now reads “the cleansing of crimes” (*Ablutio scelerum*).

At the end one reads:

“May it be the remission of all sins of the living and the dead,”

without the word *fideles* (“the faithful”), which is found in the Missal.

**[Note: Column 593D]** This Mass is also omitted from our edition, and for that reason we give it here.

**Mass for the Dead Who Desired Penance but Did Not Obtain It**

“If someone, while asking for penance, should be deprived of the use of speech when the priest arrives, it has been established that, if suitable witnesses attest to this and the person himself gives satisfaction by certain movements, the priest should perform everything for the penitent according to custom.”

**For the Mass.** “Almighty and merciful God, in whose power the human condition rests, absolve the soul of your servant N. from all sins, so that, because of the intervention of death, he may not lose the fruit of the penance which his will desired. Through our Lord.”

**Secret.** “May the Oblation of this present Sacrifice, we ask, O Lord, make satisfaction to you on behalf of the soul of your servant N.; may he find the forgiveness of sins which he sought; and may he receive, by compensation through the penance he desired, what he could not fulfill by the use of speech. Through the Lord.”

**Within the Action.** “Therefore, O Lord, we ask that you graciously accept this Oblation, which we offer to you for the soul of your servant N., whose day of burial we commemorate on N.; and in your ineffable mercy grant that what, forestalled by mortal condition, he was unable to carry out through the ministry of speech, he may obtain through everlasting indulgence. And our days, etc.”

**For the Conclusion.** “O God, from whom all that is good for the human body is hoped, grant, we ask, through these holy things, that just as you granted the soul of your servant N. the desire for penance, so, in your mercy, you may grant the forgiveness he desired. Through the Lord.”

The title “Mass for the Dead Who Desired Penance but Did Not Obtain It” may cause some scruple for those unfamiliar with sacred theology. For this passage does not concern those who departed this life without the virtue of penance or without charity and who are not capable of Prayers or suffrages—also because the Church does not intend to pray for such persons, just as she does not pray for those who died in heresy or excommunication.

Rather, it concerns those who, at the point of death, desired and requested the sacrament but could obtain it only in desire, as both the rubric and all the Prayers of this Mass clearly indicate.

Nor does this passage concern forgiveness of penance sought through true contrition, as is read in chapter 12 of the Epistle to the Hebrews concerning Esau, who, according to the Apostle, “found no place for repentance,” although he had sought it with tears; nor does it concern Antiochus in 2 Maccabees, chapter 9, who, as Scripture relates, although wicked, prayed to the Lord but was not going to obtain mercy from him.

In both of these passages there is no discussion of true contrition, which arises from love of justice, but of the kind that arises from grief over temporal loss. For God rejects no one who turns to him with a right intention: “Who,” as it is read in chapter 20 of Ecclesiasticus, “called upon God, and he despised him?”

The title of the Mass must therefore be understood in the sense explained at the beginning of this note.

**[Note: Column 594D]** This Preface is not contained in the Codex of Saint Eligius, which we published after Menardus. It may, however, be seen in the edition of Gussanville, column 1551 and following. Angelus Rocca also took from this Preface the material illustrated in the two subsequent notes.

In the Preface for the exorcism of water to be blessed, many variant readings are found in the manuscript and printed Codices. For the sake of brevity we shall omit them, but we shall bring forward three matters for consideration.

The first is:

“The highest Salvation itself has known you, and the perpetual Observer” (*Ipsa te cognovit altissima Salus, et Respector perpetuus*), “to whom we humbly pray that you may hear us,” etc.

This is an excessively harsh expression and not free from difficulty if the construction of the words is carefully considered. For the speech is addressed to water, and in these few words there is an abrupt transition, without any intermediary, to God in the second person. This can hardly be maintained except with excessive license.

The printed Codex, namely the book entitled the *Sacerdotal* of the holy Roman Apostolic Church and issued by the authority of Leo, reads instead:

“Therefore we humbly beseech you, almighty God, highest Salvation and perpetual Observer, that you may hear us,” etc.

Although this reading is good, suitable, and clear, it seemed preferable to leave the former reading unchanged, lest so great an alteration be made.

At the same place one reads:

“He who commanded you to rain through secret and limpid, swift winds,” etc.

This expression is likewise sufficiently obscure. It is found not only in the Vatican manuscript Codex but also in the printed *Sacerdotal* mentioned above, except that the word *limpidis* (“limpid”) is absent there.

At the same place one reads:

“Drive out every shadow, every Satan, and all the machinations of unclean spirits, whether *Bithonatum* or those wandering through the invocation of magical art,” etc.

This expression is addressed to the water for the purpose of driving out demons and overturning their machinations. But the word *Bithonatum* seems entirely incapable of conveying any meaningful sense unless it is said to be corrupt and to consist of two Greek elements, namely *Biathanaton* or *Biathanatorum*. For *Biathanatos* or *Biathanatus* is one who has died a violent death, derived from βία (*bia*), “violence,” and θάνατος (*thanatos*), “death.”

I was unable to compare this passage with the other Vatican manuscript Sacramentaries, since this Preface concerning exorcism is not found in them. I did, however, see it in the *Sacerdotal* cited above, at the scholium on page 243 of the Vatican edition. There, instead of *Bithonatum*, I found *Biotanatorum*, without the aspirate.

Since the etymology of this word did not seem to satisfy the sense of an exorcism against unclean spirits and against the invocation of magical art—even with the aspirate added—and since there was little time available during printing, the word *Bithonatum* was left in this passage, which requires more mature consideration.

Although my conjecture concerning the word *Biathanatorum* is consonant with reason and, so to speak, close to certainty, I did not dare to insert it in that passage without the authority of some writer or exemplar. This was especially because writers frequently use the word *Biothanatorum* for those who have died violently, contrary to the etymology of the word. For *Biothanatus*, derived from βίος (*bios*), “life,” and θάνατος (*thanatos*), “death,” signifies “mortal life.”

In the Passion of Saint Andrew the Apostle, in Surius under 30 November, volume VI, written by the priests and deacons of the Churches of Achaea, I find that the proconsul Aegeas, who ordered Saint Andrew to be fastened to the cross, was immediately seized by a demon through this decree, thrown about in the middle of the city forum, and died.

Thereupon Stratocles, the brother of Aegeas, having been converted to Christ, ordered his servants to bury him among the *Biothanati*. This is what Surius says at the end of the aforementioned Passion.

Cassian likewise, in *Conferences*, conference 2, chapter 5, uses the word *Biothanatos* of those who died a violent death. For the elder Hero, after spending fifty years in the desert in an exceptionally strict life of continence, was finally deceived by a demonic illusion and threw himself headlong into a well. He was drawn out unharmed but almost bloodless by the brothers; then, persisting in the obstinacy of his deception, he died on the third day.

Cassian therefore says of Hero:

“The priest and abbot Paphnutius could scarcely be prevailed upon not to judge him—though not counted among the *Biothanati*—unworthy even of the commemoration and Oblation of those who rest.”

Lampridius, writing in *The Life of the Emperor Heliogabalus* about that most impure youth, who was killed by buffoons in the sixteenth year of his age, writes of him as follows:

“And it had been foretold to him by the Syrian priests that he would become a *Biothanatus*.”

Julius Firmicus also used this word in the same sense in his works concerning astrology, and indeed used it very frequently.

Since I was therefore perplexed in this matter—whether the expression *Biothanatorum* or *Biathanatorum* should be restored in place of the printed word—I happened, while consulting Tertullian’s book *On the Soul* for another purpose, upon chapter 33, not far from the end of the book. There the question is discussed whether souls remain here after death or travel from the underworld; and especially I came upon a passage where the invocation of magic and the antiquity of exorcisms are discussed.

In that passage Tertullian twice mentions those carried off by violent death. He does not call them *Biothanatos* or *Biathanatos*, but *Biaeothanatos*, that is, “those who have died violently,” from the Greek adverb βιαίως (*biaiōs*), “violently.” He uses these words:

“Thus *Abori* and *Biaeothanati* are indeed invoked under that principle of faith which makes it seem credible that those souls most especially inflict violence and injury which a savage and premature end has wrested away through violence and injury—as though demons perform their work in return for the offense under the pretext of those souls,” etc.

This is what Tertullian says.

Since the Tertullianic reading appears to be proper and genuine, I think that the word *Biaeothanatorum* should be restored in all the passages mentioned—or *Biathanorum*, as my own opinion suggests.

If, however, it is judged that *Biothanatorum* should be restored, one must say that it was written and pronounced through syncope, with the diphthong removed.

**Column 233.** In the exorcism of salt, as may be seen both in the title and in the exorcism itself, mention is made of the ancient custom of scattering salt to drive away every harmful thing.

**612 — Column 234.** Among the Blessings of new fruits there is a Blessing of the grape or bean. In accordance with ancient usage, *fava* is written instead of *faba*.

For those ancients—namely, those who lived in the age of Blessed Gregory—were accustomed to use *v* for *b* and *b* for *v* at will. Sometimes they imitated the usage of the Greeks, though ineptly; sometimes they imitated the writing, pronunciation, and barbarism of the Goths, Lombards, and other foreign nations, as learned men and very many others affirm, acknowledging the loss of this sort in the Latin language.

Contrary to the usage of venerable antiquity, they wrote *lavor* for *labor*, *veneficium* for *beneficium*, *vonum* for *bonum*, and many other forms of this kind. Likewise they wrote *vivere* for *bibere*, and *bibere* for *vivere*, as well as *bita* for *vita*.

This manner of writing and pronunciation has in fact remained in Spain, especially in the Province of Castile, and elsewhere among many people down to the present day.

Among several examples supplied earlier, the clearest testimony is provided by the rather large stone tablet fixed at Rome, at San Sisto—or in the portico of Saint Peter—to the wall of the church and appended at the end of the scholia. It lists many olive groves which Blessed Gregory dedicated to the holy Apostles and for preparing lights for those same holy Apostles. On that tablet one finds *olibetum* for *olivetum*, and always likewise *parba* for *parva*, *silbula* for *sylvula*, *uveribus* for *uberibus*, and *devitorem* for *debitorem*.

For this reason, to confirm the antiquity of the Vatican Codex, we judged that the word *favae* should be retained instead of *fabae*. It is clear that Pamelius did the same, since he retained this reading and wrote in the margin:

“I judge that, according to the custom of the ancients, *favae* should be read instead of *fabae*.”

This varied practice of writing and pronunciation may perhaps have originated from a varying practice in writing and pronouncing the second letter of the Greek alphabet.

For that Latin age which affected Greek ways—that is, sought to imitate the language of the Greeks—was accustomed to write many words deriving their origin from the Greek source in Greek letters, and frequently in this manner:

“IHC XPC,” that is, “ΙΗΣ ΧΡΣ.”

They also tried to pronounce certain Latin words in imitation of the Greeks, as is evident from the examples given above, in which they used the letter *b* for *v* and *v* for *b*.

This variation arose from differing opinions, as has been said, concerning the letter beta, the second letter of the Greek alphabet.

The ancient Latins, like many people down to the present day, thought that *b*, the second letter of the Greek alphabet, had the force and character that the letter *v* has among the Latins. They therefore expressed it by *v* and called it *vita*. They may perhaps have been led to this conclusion because Greek writers, when writing certain Latin names such as Valerius and Virgilius, sometimes use β and sometimes οὐ, as in Βαλέριος and Οὐαλέριος, and Βιργίλιος and Οὐιργίλιος.

They do this because necessity compels them, since, as Adolphus Mekerchus, a learned man, rightly says, they have no letter with which to render our consonant *v*, because among us the vowel *u* and the consonant *v* have one name and one written form.

For this reason Ptolemy, in all Latin names beginning with *v*, such as Verona—Οὐήρονα—Vicentia—Οὐικέντια or Οὔκεντα—and other names of the same kind, writes Οὐ, which sounds like the Latin *v*, not β.

Suidas likewise, when he wishes to pronounce *v*, does so not with β but with οὐ, as in Οὐάλης, “Valens,” the Roman emperor; Οὐαλεντινιανὸς, “Valentinianus,” likewise a Roman emperor; and Οὔαρος, “Varus,” the sophist of Laodicea. Other names of this kind are always written by him in the same manner.

In the same way, the interjection of one who grieves, “woe,” is found written in Matthew 18, which says:

“Οὐαί τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ ἐκείνῳ, δι᾽ οὗ τὸ σκάνδαλον ἔρχεται”

That is:

“Woe to that man through whom the scandal comes.”

The same occurs elsewhere in that evangelist and more than once in the other evangelists, as well as in other passages of the New Testament.

For this reason, some Latins—though very few, and more correct in their judgment—thought that Greek β had the same force and pronunciation as Latin *b* and Hebrew *beth*. They demonstrate that in Greek one should actually say Βῖτα (*bita*), or in Latin *beta*, approximately according to the Hebrew pronunciation *beth*, which the Greek took over from the Hebrew without alteration, rather than *vita*.

Among these are Juvenal, satire 24, and Martial, Book V of the *Epigrams*. In these passages they left *beta* written instead of *vita*.

Plautus held the same opinion. In the *Pseudolus*, he retained the Greek interjection of astonishment βάβαι, for which the Latins say *papae*, writing:

“Babae, now at last my mind is in a safe place.”

And in the *Asinaria*, instead of what the Latins say, “he proceeds” or “he goes,” he used the word *badizat*, saying:

“I shall certainly take it away from the barley, if you do not *badizas* all the way through.”

That Greek *b* has the same sound as Latin *b* can be recognized not only from the verb *badizo*, but also, with the greatest clarity, from the actual bleating of sheep. Learned men—namely, the Englishman John Cheke and Adolphus Mekerchus of Bruges—in their commentary *On the True and Correct Pronunciation of the Greek Language*, when reporting the opinion of Eustathius concerning Homer, cite the opinion of Cratinus that *b* imitates and signifies the voice or sound of sheep. They also cite from the same Eustathius the following verse of Cratinus and interpret it:

**Ὅδ᾽ ἠλίθιος ὥσπερ πρόβατον βῆ βῆ λέγων βαδίζει**

That is:

[Col. 0597D] This fool, like a sheep, sounds “be be.” For nature has given sheep the habit of expressing their bleating—which the Latins, changing *e* into *a*, call *balatus*—not with the sound “ve, ve,” but with “be, be,” opening their lips through the force of the breath and opening their mouths; and this most clearly demonstrates the Latin *b*. Hence Pierius Valerianus says, in Book XLVI of his *Hieroglyphics*, in the chapter on the seven letters, that the Latin *b* can be represented by a painted sheep. In the same way, those words that the Latins borrowed from the Greeks are written and pronounced [Col. 0598A] with Latin *b*: *brachium*, *balneum*, *boo*, *bos*, *barbarus*, *baptizo*, and countless others of that kind—not *vrachium*, *valneum*, *voo*, *vos*, *varvarus*, or *vaptizo*. From all this it is plainly established why *b* is found for *v*, and *v* for *b*, among the ancients.

[Note: [Col. 0597D] Namely, in the Gussanville edition. We have read many such Benedictions, both in printed editions and in various manuscripts, but our Eligius Codex does not admit them, which is evidence of its antiquity.] Columns 1554 and following. One may see Benedictions for many things that are not now in frequent use. But on page 1558 there are Benedictions “in the larder” and “in the fireplace.” *Lardarium*, they say, is a word taken from the French, who commonly call the thing itself *lardier*. *Caminata*, however, is used by the same French for a fireplace; they write it *cheminée*, entirely omitting the pronunciation of the aspiration.

[Note: [Col. 0597D] Namely, in the same Gussanville edition. The prayer in which this occurs [Col. 0598D] is the second prayer over a demoniac: “And God, creator and defender of the human race, who formed man in your image and likeness ÷ with your holy hands and with the proper mouth of your divinity.”] Column 1559. A sign of this kind, ÷, is found, which scribes formerly used for *est* (“is”), and indeed very frequently, as may be seen in manuscripts from five hundred years ago. I once saw this sign in many ancient manuscript codices; most recently, however, in the Vatican Library, where there is a very ancient book entitled *The Signs of Cicero the Grammarian and of Seneca*. In that book, among many kinds of different signs, the very sign now under discussion is found, devised for writing various forms of the substantive verb, sometimes with only one point written below, sometimes with only one point above, or with the sign placed at the end of a line. This manner of writing by signs—what they call writing through the signs themselves, or through substituted letters, or through an alteration in the position of letters, that is, *a* after *b*, and so forth—was invented both among Cicero and Seneca and among others, and is still practiced in many ways, so that written communications would not be understood by others if letters sent to absent persons were intercepted. Both notaries—so called from the signs themselves—and secretaries and scribes used this abbreviated form of writing in order to write rapidly. Martial’s poem clearly indicates this speed of writing by a notary, secretary, or scribe who took down in pen the words dictated:

614 “The tongue has not yet completed its work; the right hand has.”

[Col. 0598C] Although in this passage the sign of this kind cannot have the meaning of the said verb, it was nevertheless left there to confirm the antiquity of the Codex—unless we say that this sign indicates an addition. For the words marked with this sign, ÷, up to but excluding the verb *formasti* (“you formed”), are read in the other manuscript codices and are not found in the printed ones. Blessed Jerome also testifies that this sign was once used for this purpose, writing to Paula and Eustochium, and to Sunia and Fretella; he calls a sign of this kind an *obelus*. This mark is called by the Latins a *veru* (“spit”), by which it is shown that what is not found in the authentic books ought to be cut down and pierced.

In the same place, in a very lengthy prayer, there are various readings that are omitted for the sake of brevity. Yet it must not be passed over in silence that *urgueo* was formerly used for *urgeo*, and *contremesco* for *contremisco*; thus, as we have found them written more than once in the Prayer and elsewhere, we have retained *unguo* for *ungo* [Col. 0598D] for the same reason already assigned. For the first form there is an inscription carved in marble at Parma, in which one reads *urguente fato* (“with fate pressing”). And Caper, a sufficiently ancient grammarian, in *On the Authority of Latin Verbs*, asserts that one should say *tinguere*, not *tingere*, since the verb is *tinguo, uis*; and, as he himself says concerning usage in his own age, he maintains that *unguentum* (“ointment”) and *unguentarius* (“ointment-maker” or “apothecary”) are derived from the verb *unguo*. *Unguentarius*, however, is derived from the verb *ungo, ungis*, as it is read in inscriptions on stone. Conrad likewise says this in *On the Latin Language*. As for the second matter—that is, the use of the letter *e* for *i*—many examples exist [Col. 0599A] on stones, as may be seen in the Aldine *Orthography*. In antiquity, *sene* was said for *sine*, *sebi* for *sibi*, and *pertenet* for *pertinet*, along with countless examples of the same kind.

[Note: [Col. 0599D] See these matters in the Gussanville edition, at the place indicated.] Column 1562. In the Prayer for women, much is lacking that is found in the manuscript of the Royal Mountain Library at Palermo and in the printed Roman *Sacerdotale*. In the Vatican Codex the text stands as follows: “God of Abraham, God of Isaac, God of Jacob, who admonished the three Israelites and freed Susanna from a false charge,” etc. In the Royal Mountain Codex: “God of Abraham, etc.; God, who freed the three Israelite boys from Egyptian slavery, admonished them through Moses your servant concerning the keeping of your commandments in the desert, and freed Susanna from a false charge,” etc. In the Royal Mountain Codex, the word *(pueris)* (“boys”) is superfluous, since it is sufficiently clear that *tribus* is an accusative, and the word *(pueris)* cannot stand with the verb *monuisti* (“you admonished”). In the recently printed Roman *Sacerdotale*, however, this Prayer is read in the order for baptizing as follows: “God of Abraham, etc.; God, who freed the three [Col. 0599B] Israelites from Egyptian slavery, and through Moses your servant admonished them in the desert concerning the keeping of your commandments, and freed Susanna from a false charge, we suppliantly beseech you that,” etc. Although this Prayer is complete and clear, we retained the Vatican reading, even though mutilated, so that so great a change would not be made in a Codex that cannot serve for public reading in the Church.

[Note: [Col. 0599D] Seek this in the indicated place in the Gussanville edition, as well as the words *excarpsatum* and *adscendo*, concerning which the following two notes are written.] Column 1562. “Whom he deigned to call to the baptismal font as a gift.” This passage seems corrupt in the Vatican manuscript Codex, and has been corrected from the printed Roman *Sacerdotale* as follows: “Whom he deigned to call to the baptismal font by the gift of his grace” (namely, Christ). This correction is certainly not foreign to the Codex of Pamelius.

Column 1564. In the rubric the word *excarpsatum* occurs; what it means could not be determined, but the word is judged to be corrupt through a scribal error. The words of the rubric are these: “And the remainder, as it has been *excarpsatum* in that preceding order,” etc. But it seems probable that *enarratum* (“explained”) or *exaratum* (“written out”) should be read in place of *excarpsatum*; in this way the expression itself has a suitable meaning. Or perhaps—and indeed better—*exorcizatum* (“exorcized”) should be read, since the manner of exorcizing is being discussed there. We have nevertheless left the erroneous passage as it stands, since we have no certain conjecture. Let the more learned therefore judge this matter. Or it ought to be read *charaxatum*, from the verb *charasso*, that is, “I write,” which blessed Gregory also used in the *Register*, Book V, Letter 40. *Charasso* is derived from the word *character*, as Huguition and Papiensis hold. Hence *characatus* and *charaxatus*, from the Greek *kárax* (κάραξ) and *karáttō* (καράττω), that is, “I carve” or “I shape.”

Column 1568. *Adscendo* is read with *d*, in the manner of the ancient Latins, as is also *adscisco*, so that the second letter of the preposition *ad* may not wholly disappear; in composition it either remains, as in *adficio*, or is changed, as in *afficio*, *affluo*, and similar forms. Pamelius, however, reads it with double *s*, *assensio* and *assensa Domini*; in this form, the *d* appears to have been changed into *s*.

[Col. 0599D] Column 201. [Note: [Col. 0599D] In our edition it reads *trophaeum*.] “Tropaeum of the cross,” in place of “*Trophaeum* of the cross,” has been left without the aspiration. For the ancient Latins, imitating the Greeks, who say Τρόπαιον (*tropaion*), wrote it without aspiration. For, as Cicero testifies in Book III of *On the Orator*, well beyond the middle of the work, they used aspiration only with a vowel, saying *triumpus* and *tropaeum*, and other words of that kind, as may be seen in ancient inscriptions. This was particularly read on the ancient base of the obelisk now seen at Saint John Lateran; but the base that I saw no longer exists.

Column 228. “The Apologies begin.” There are certain Prayers on the stated page and the following page that are found entitled “Apologies” in the Vatican manuscript Codex, [Col. 0600A] [Note: [Col. 0600D] Differently in our Codices, where it reads as follows. See the indicated place and consult Menard’s notes.] but in the other manuscript Codices the title “Apologies” is found neither here nor elsewhere. Although the force of an apology consists only in defense or excuse, in this passage the Prayers themselves, as I think, under the title “Apologies,” comprise only the sinner’s accusation, which before God has the force of an excuse. For whoever accuses himself before the divine Majesty, by revealing his faults, according to Augustine deserves, in place of accusation, excuse or acquittal, receiving the name of one justified; for, as the Wise Man says, the just person is first the accuser of himself. This is exemplified by the Gospel publican, who after his accusation returned to his house justified, in accordance with Proverbs XVIII and Matthew IX: “Whoever accuses himself when he has sinned is just.” And Isaiah XLIII: “First declare your iniquities, so that you may be justified.” This seems to be the subject of Saint Ambrose’s book *On David’s Apology*, which is the accusation of the sinful David before God, and an accusation directed against his detractors.

In the same place one reads *peripsima* for *peripsema*, and *neglegentia* [Col. 0600B] for *negligentia*, according to the practice of the ancients. For among the Greeks *peripsema* means the refuse of iron or fruit, and anything discarded from any material so that it may be rendered clean. The words of blessed Paul in 1 Corinthians IV have this sense: “We have been made as the refuse of this world, the offscouring of all things, until now.” In antiquity *peripsema* was said in the Greek manner; the Greeks write περίψημα, although among the Latins the Greek *η* is ordinarily changed into a long *e*. *Neglegentia*, for *negligentia*, was also said among the ancient Latins, as may be seen from stones and manuscript books.

[Note: [Col. 0600D] Seek this also in the Gussanville or Vatican edition. Understand the same statement concerning the three notes immediately following.] Column 1572. In the Mass for one suffering from fever, mention is made of Saint Sigismund, martyr and king of Burgundy, through whom, Sigebertus of Gembloux, a monk, testifies in his *Chronicles* that health was restored to those suffering from fever. Bede, Usuard, Ado, Gregory of Tours, and Baronius write about him. In the first Prayer of this Mass one reads: “Quartan and quotidian fever,” apparently referring to a certain term for a fever that seizes a person according to a particular pattern or rule, as though one were assigned to it, [Col. 0600C] or to a certain term or order called a *type*. For Galen, speaking of a *type* in Chapter 1, says: “A type is the order of intensifications and remissions.” Or thus: “A type is the ordered return of intensifications and remissions.” Or: “A type is an affection in which onset and remission occur according to a certain order.” Galen, in *Definitions of Medicine*. Hence typical fevers are those in which onset and remission occur at fixed intervals; and directly opposed to these are erratic fevers, which observe neither a fixed time nor any order of onset and remission. Such are those that arise from black bile, which in some parts moves, in others remains still, and in others decays or begins to boil, according to Galen, Book III of the *Prognostics*, commentary 29. From this work I have taken these words verbatim, in order to explain this passage of the Sacramentary.

Column 1578. In the first Prayer one reads: “So that you may mercifully and favorably breathe upon our devout prayers, just as you also grant mercy to him.” The Vatican text stands thus, [Col. 0600D] and perhaps is not free from error, unless *aspiras* is read for *aspirans*, just as *elegas* is read for *elegans*, and *mesa* for *mensa*, not without reason, as is found on ancient stones; or perhaps *aspires* should be read. However it is read, the construction of the words does not seem sufficiently clear.

In the same place. The Prayer called “For Completion” is wholly mutilated, and the sense does not appear to be coherent; nor could another copy be obtained to clarify the matter, as has likewise happened to us in other matters. For many things are found in this exemplar that we printed which do not exist in either manuscript or printed Codices; above all, from column 1573 to the end, nothing at all is found in the other copies.

Column 1580. In the Mass for the pope, blessed Sylvester is mentioned, and the Prayers are those recited in the Mass for the pope. They appear to have been used in the time of blessed Sylvester, since they bear his name—unless we say that this was done by a scribe or someone else to suggest the papal majesty, which assumed its power in the time of blessed Sylvester.

[Col. 0602A] [Note: [Col. 0601] Namely, the Vatican edition. In ours, you will find them in the appendix to the Antiphonary.] In the same place I arranged for the hymns of blessed Gregory to be printed in Volume V, so that nothing from the works of that same saint would be missing from the Vatican Edition. Although Clichtoveus, in his *Ecclesiastical Elucidatory*, attributes only four hymns to blessed Gregory—namely, “First of all the days,” “Rising in the night,” “Behold, night is now,” and “Creator of light, most excellent”—eight were nevertheless printed under the name of the same saint in this edition, because others have formed different opinions on the matter.

[BENEDICTIONS.]

[Col. 0601]

NOTICE.

[Col. 0601] In certain manuscript Codices of the Sacramentary, there is appended the Benedictional of Saint Gregory, or the order and series of solemn Benedictions to be pronounced by bishops. Lambecius especially testifies to this concerning the aforementioned Codex of the Caesarean Library, in the following words at the place already cited: “In the same Codex of venerable antiquity, after the already mentioned book of the Sacramentary, there is also the Benedictional of the same Saint Gregory the Great, or a collection of the solemn sacred Benedictions used in the holy Catholic Church one thousand and sixty years ago. Since this is lacking both in the Antwerp and in the Roman edition of the works of Saint Gregory the Great, I think I shall do a worthwhile service if I insert it here in its entirety, so that so rare and fruitful a monument of the primitive Christian Church may no longer remain hidden.”

Lambecius considered this little work unpublished when he contemplated bringing it to light. Later, however, after seeing the book of the Sacramentary published under the care of our Menard, he corrected his error; in that book, those Benedictions—at least most of them—occur scattered in their proper places. Thus it seemed sufficient to us, in the place of an appendix, to append the remainder omitted in Menard’s edition and in ours. But because the Codex of Saint Theodoric near Rheims, said to have been written nearly nine hundred years ago, supplied us with a more abundant harvest of such Benedictions, we judged it not inappropriate to add them as an appendix. (See our Preface to the *Book of the Sacramentary*.)

Furthermore, concerning the Benedictions and their use in solemn Masses, read the hundredth note of our Menard on the *Book of the Sacramentary*, and the prolegomena of Jacobus Pamelius to the second volume of the *Liturgicon*. In that same volume he published a booklet of episcopal Benedictions for the yearly cycle, which he thinks were collected by Abbot Grimald; they differ almost always from ours. In the Gothic Missal published first by Joseph Thomasius and subsequently through the work of our Mabillon, there are Benedictions for nearly every solemnity, but they are entirely different. The Sacramentary of Ratold, copied in the tenth century, contains more Benedictions than the others because it is more recent, says Menard in his preface. We nevertheless do not at all concede to him that a greater number of Benedictions is evidence of lesser antiquity; otherwise it would have to be said that the Gothic Missal, of such venerable antiquity, and the Theodoric Codex bear the mark of a more recent age. In certain ancient Codices of the Sacramentary, Benedictions are indeed lacking, as in the Codex of the Queen of Sweden, in the Calian, Gemetian, and Theodoric Codices, etc., often cited in the notes to the *Book of the Sacramentary*. But the reason they are absent is no other than that they were contained in another separate volume, which the archdeacon presented to the bishop for reading whenever necessary. This is clear from the Theodoric manuscripts: neither contains such episcopal Benedictions, but they are displayed in a separate Codex marked on the back with the number 62. In the Gemetian Codex, approximately nine hundred years old, which contains everything to be recited by the bishop—and is therefore called a Pontifical—the Benedictions scattered through the *Book of the Sacramentary* are also displayed, along with many more than those found in the printed editions. We shall speak of this often below. Here, however, we are not dealing with the Benedictions of water, iron, and so forth, by which it was once customary to test the innocence of those accused of crimes. Many of these are contained both in the Pontifical mentioned above and in others; they may be read in Book III, Chapter 7, of *On the Ancient Rites of the Church*, by our author D. Ed. Martene. For the remaining matters relevant to this subject, read Menard’s extensive hundredth note, in which, following his custom, he discusses the subject most fully and learnedly.

[Col. 0601]

BENEDICTIONS Lacking in the Book of the Sacramentary.

From the Benedictional published by LAMBECIUS. (C)*

[Col. 0601]

[Col. 0601B] [Note: [Col. 0601B] This Benediction is found in the Theodoric Manuscript and in Pamelius’s Edition.] Benediction for the Annunciation of Saint Mary.

May the Lord Jesus Christ, who came forth from the Virgin at the end of the ages, glorify your hearts with the crown of uncorrupted virginity. Amen.

And may he who entered the Virgin’s womb when the angel announced it both instruct you and protect you through the sacrament of that ministry. Amen. And may you who devoutly celebrate today the Conception of the Virgin arrive, with exultant spirits and pure hearts, at the Nativity of our Redeemer. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, etc.

Benediction for Septuagesima.

[Note: [Col. 0601B] This too is lacking in the aforementioned Codex, which contains several other Benedictions for Septuagesima. [Col. 0602B]] May almighty God, who through his Apostle commanded each of us to run so that we might obtain the prize, pour the Spirit, the Paraclete, into your hearts, so that you may be able to complete your course most happily and, although laboring in his vineyard under different callings, may deserve to receive the coin of the promised reward from him. Amen. Enlightened by the grace of that same Holy Spirit and strengthened by his mercy, may you abandon and lament your past offenses, avoid those of the present, and worthily complete the coming abstinence of the most sacred Lent. Amen. Thus, as you properly carry out the season of Lent, may you, with your minds purified from every stain of vice, deserve to come in purity to celebrate the paschal feast. Amen.

Benediction of the Holy Eucharist.

[Note: [Col. 0602B] This Benediction too is not found in the Theodoric Codex.] Almighty God, maker of the whole structure of the world, who in the beginning established all his works in the perfection of the number six, may he deign through his ineffable grace to grant you that throughout all the time of your life you may deserve to be protected by the continual shelter of his Benediction. Amen. May he also grant you to perform those works throughout the six-day cycles by which, on the seventh day, you may obtain such great and such a kind of grace from him that you may both delightfully devote yourselves to his praises and, with the most sincere devotion and without sin, communicate in the sacred body and blood of the Lord for your healing. Amen. Refreshed by that spiritual nourishment and protected by his desirable guardianship, may you please him forever, completely freed from every servile work and likewise cleansed from every crime. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, etc.

Benediction on the Resurrection.

[Note: [Col. 0603D] The same should be said of this one.] May almighty God bless you, who created you through gratuitous mercy and, in the Resurrection of his only-begotten Son, granted you the hope of rising again. Amen. May he raise you from the tombs of vices, he who raised him from the dead. Amen. So that you may live happily without end with him whom you truly believe to have risen from the dead. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, etc.

Another.

God, who through the Resurrection of his only-begotten Son bestowed upon you both the good of Redemption and the honor of adoption, may he grant you the rewards of his Benediction. [Col. 0603B] Amen. And through the one by whose redemption you received the gift of perpetual freedom, may you, by his generosity, become sharers in an eternal inheritance. Amen. And may you who rose with him in baptism through faith deserve to be joined to him in the heavenly region by living well. Amen. May he himself grant this, etc.

Benediction for the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist.

May almighty God bless you, who through blessed John at last announced on earth the coming of his only-begotten Son, taking pity on us. Amen. May the Holy Spirit himself, who filled him while he was enclosed in his mother’s womb and loosed his father’s tongue from its bond, cause you to be filled with his Benediction and to abound abundantly in spiritual gifts. Amen. May the voice of the supplicating Forerunner rise to the ears of the most merciful Father; may he who knew and confessed the world’s Redeemer before he was born, and who with his sacred hands baptized the author of baptism in the font, mercifully cleanse the stains of your sins through his intercession and make you fruitful with an abundance of virtues. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, etc.

[Col. 0603C] Benediction for the Assumption of Saint Mary.

God, who on this day willed to summon the most blessed Virgin Mary, the most glorious mother of our Lord Jesus Christ, to heaven and to exalt her sublimely above the choirs of angels, may he deign, through her intercession and merits, to enrich you with the grace of his Benediction in such a way that you may deserve to pass from vices to virtues. Amen. May he grant you, from this world onward, to grow strong in faith, rejoice in hope, and abound in charity; to shine continually with the excellence of chastity and to gleam also with the distinction of humility, so that, adorned in every respect with good works, you may be able to please him. Amen. And may he cause you to expiate all your past offenses and crimes day and night with groans and tears, and so salutarily avoid those of the present and the future, that with her you may shine eternally in the heavenly places. Amen. May he himself grant this, etc.

Another, for Advent.

[Col. 0603D] May the ineffable grace and mercy of the living God bless you, and may he grant you, through the wondrous and saving Advent of his Son, not to remain—God forbid—captive under the dominion of sin. Amen. May he deign so powerfully to free you from every misery and so mercifully and steadfastly to confirm you in his mercy that he may make you serve him in the present age in such a way that you may deserve to reach him joyfully in the future. Amen. And may he who for our sake willed that his only-begotten Son become incarnate in the first Advent himself cause you in the second to be separated from the company of the unjust and gathered with himself to remain forever in the fellowship of the just. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, etc.

[Col. 0604A] Another.

May almighty God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, Savior and Redeemer of the world, bless you, and, by blessing you, justify and sanctify you through the illumination of the first Advent of that same only-begotten Son, so that in the second you may not appear unclean before him. Amen. May his grace so firmly establish you in true humility and so steadfastly strengthen you in sincere charity that the things of the world may displease you in such a way, and the things of God continually please you, that you may abide together with the saints in heavenly blessedness. Amen. And may he who for the salvation of his servants willed that same Son to humble himself so greatly that, by joining our nature to the unity of his person, he deigned to be united within the maternal womb, cause you in this first Advent to be illumined by the splendor of his visitation and indwelling, so that in the second you may deserve to glorify forever with him. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, etc.

Benediction for the Nativity of one apostle.

[Col. 0604B] [Note: [Col. 0603D] It is in second place in the Gemetian Codex.] God, who has granted you to stand upon apostolic foundations, may he deign to bless you through the interceding merits of his blessed apostle N. Amen. May he defend you from every adversity with apostolic protections, he who willed you to be adorned and fortified by their examples and teachings. Amen. So that through their intercession you may reach the inheritance of the eternal homeland, through whose teaching you preserve the integrity of the faith. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, etc.

Benediction on the anniversary of the dedication of a church.

Almighty God, who willed this holy temple to be dedicated to his most glorious name in honor of his blessed apostle N., may he himself, through that apostle’s prayers and merits, cause you to be justified by his Benediction and sanctified by the illumination of his visitation and indwelling. Amen. So that you, who once were, like all the others, dwelling places of the ancient enemy and captives under his dominion, may each deserve to become most pleasing temples of the living God, having been made by his grace adopted sons instead of servants. Amen. [Col. 0604C] May he himself deign to grant this, etc.

On the anniversary of the consecration of a bishop.

Almighty God, who, although I am unworthy, through the abundance of his immense mercy deigned to appoint me among the bishops to minister at his altar by offering sacrifices of praise, and ordained me to distribute to his people both the sacraments of the heavenly table and the nourishment of eternal life, may he deign to enrich you with an abundance of Benediction and mercifully strengthen your hearts with the sanctifying grace of the Holy Spirit. Amen. May he also deign mercifully to cleanse you from every kind of wickedness and powerfully confirm you in the excellence of his mercy. Amen. May he also grant you to advance daily from evils to good things and from good things to better things, and, after the end of this life, to pass happily to the joys of eternal rewards. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, etc.

[Col. 0604D] Benediction [Note: [Col. 0603D] In the Gemetian Codex, Benedictions are noted for each weekday. For Monday: “May almighty God [with] his …,” as below. For Tuesday: “May he incline …”; for Wednesday: “Devotion”; for Thursday: “May almighty God grant, or give, you …”; for Friday, two are assigned that have not been published. The one placed for Saturday is likewise absent from the printed editions.] for the weekdays.

May the Lord bless you and keep you. Amen. May he shine his face upon you and have mercy on you. Amen. May he turn his countenance toward you and give you peace. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, etc.

Another.

May almighty God bless you with his mercy and pour into you a wise understanding that brings salvation. Amen. May he nourish you with the teachings of the Catholic faith and make you steadfast in holy works. Amen. May he turn your steps away from error and show you the way of peace and charity. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, etc.

[Col. 0605A] Another.

May the Lord incline his ear to the prayers of your humility, and grant you the grace of his Benediction and the reward of eternal salvation. Amen. May you always and everywhere have the Lord as your gracious protector and exult in his praises. Amen. May he loose the bonds of all your sins and cause you to reach eternal glory. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, etc.

624 Another.

May the Lord multiply within you the abundance of his Benediction and confirm you in the hope of the heavenly kingdom. Amen. May he correct your actions, amend your life, order your conduct, and lead you to the inheritance of heavenly Paradise. Amen. May you be able to be filled with such an intention that you may please him forever. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, etc.

Another.

May the Lord graciously regard your devotion and grant you the gifts of his Benediction. Amen. May he protect you in the present age with such assistance that in the future he may make you inhabitants of Paradise. [Col. 0605B] Amen. Thus may he bless your hearts by sanctifying them, and sanctify them by blessing them, so that he may delight in dwelling continually with you, indeed within you. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, etc.

Another.

May almighty God give you the grace of his Benediction and fill you with the spirit of truth and peace. Amen. So may you run along the way of salvation with devout minds that you may salutarily escape the snares of encroaching sins. Amen. Thus may you become devout in his supplication and sincere in mutual love, so that you may be able to reach the heavenly kingdom in safety. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, etc.

Another.

May almighty God, who knows your weakness, grant you the gift of his Benediction. Amen. And may he who has granted you the desire to supplicate grant you the help of consolation. Amen. So that you may receive from him the support of both the present and the future life, from whose goodness you believe yourselves to have been created. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, etc.

Another.

May almighty God forever surround you with the help of his right hand and fill you with the gift of his Benedictions. Amen. May he defend you from every wickedness and grant you to abound in heavenly gifts. Amen. So that, cleansed in body and mind, you may render him such service that you may be able to attain his favor. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, etc.

Another.

May almighty God purify the secrets of your hearts and grant you increases of his Benediction. Amen. May you be stripped of all the dangers of the present life and clothed with the ornaments of spiritual virtues. Amen. So that, supported by his help, you may serve him on earth in such a way that you may be able to be joined to him in heaven. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, etc.

Another.

May almighty God exclude every adversity from you and, in his favor, pour upon you the gifts of his Benediction. [Col. 0606B] Amen. May he make your hearts intent upon sacred teachings, so that they may be filled with everlasting benefits. Amen. So that, both understanding what must be done and doing what you have understood, you may be found unharmed amid the adversities of the world and may become fellow heirs of the blessed Spirits. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, etc.

Another.

May almighty God order your days in his peace and grant you the gifts of his Benediction. Amen. May he free you from all disturbances and consolidate your minds in the tranquillity of his peace. Amen. So that, adorned with the gems of faith, hope, and charity, you may pass through the present life unharmed and reach the eternal one safely.

May he himself deign to grant this, whose kingdom and dominion remain without end for ever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0605]

ANOTHER SUPPLEMENT OF EPISCOPAL BENEDICTIONS.

From the very ancient Codex of Saint Theodoric near Rheims. (C)*

[Col. 0605C] Benediction concerning the Most Holy Trinity.

[Note: [Col. 0605D] In Pamelius’s Edition, Volume II, pp. 508 and following, many Benedictions concerning the Most Holy Trinity are read; this one is not among them.] 625 May the Holy Trinity and the one undivided Deity—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—bless you and grant you remission of all sins. Amen. May it grant you health of mind and body and free you from every adversity. Amen. So that, cleansed from every vice and fortified by its protection, we may deserve to reach heavenly glory. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, whose kingdom and dominion remain without end for ever and ever. Amen. May the Benediction of God the Father, who is three in persons and one in the essence of divinity, fill you.

Another.

May God fill our hearts with the teachings of the sacred faith and shape us for a life of eternal salvation. Amen. And may he who declared that he is in the Father and the Father in him deign to grant us the gifts he promised to those who love him. Amen. So that, with the grace of the Holy Spirit cooperating, we may deserve to carry out the words of the Triune Majesty in such a way that, for receiving the rewards of eternity, we may deserve to be blessed by the right hand of his power. Amen. [Col. 0605D] May he himself deign to grant this, etc.

Benediction for the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord.

Almighty God, etc., as in the printed edition.

Benediction for the Nativity of the Lord at night.

God, who appeared in the flesh for this reason, so that he might enroll his chosen ones in eternity, may he, sanctifying you by his Benediction, write your names in the book of life. Amen. [Col. 0606C] And may he who deigned to be born of the Virgin Mary in the city of Bethlehem cause you after death to reach the heavenly Jerusalem. Amen. So that there you may sing the glory of God in the highest with the angels and may be able to enjoy the heavenly peace of every good will. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, etc.

Another Benediction.

May Christ, the Child and God, whose manger the shepherds admired, on this day of his Nativity fill your minds with the splendor of his Benediction. Amen. And may you who today believe that God and man was born for you always experience his saving protection. Amen. So that, following the example of the blessed Virgin Mary, you may preserve all the words and commandments of Christ in your heart, and, praising and glorifying him, may exult like good shepherds. Amen. May he himself grant this, etc.

Benediction for the first morning.

[Note: [Col. 0605D] In the Pontifical of Gemet it reads as “Blessing at cockcrow”: “Your people,” etc.] We ask you, Lord, to favor your people with loving kindness, for whom you have deigned on this most sacred day to manifest your presence to the world. Amen. In your fatherly compassion, guard them from every adversity, for whom at this time you deigned to be born from a Virgin into the world. Amen. Grant that they may always acknowledge you as their Redeemer and truly comprehend your grace. Amen. May he deign to grant this, etc.

### Another Blessing

626 [Note: [Col. 0606D] It is found in the Pontifical of Gemet together with another commonly used blessing for the day of the Lord’s Nativity: “May almighty God bless you.”] O God, who willed not only to create the human race but also, by your birth, to make the human being pass from earth to the stars, look upon the prayers of your suppliants, who today, after long darkness, acknowledge you as the light born among them. Amen. Embrace within the bosom of the Church this people: you who came forth for us from Mary’s bridal chamber. Amen. May this people be pleasing in obedient submission to your commands, just as the Virgin’s birth is singular in its origin; so that, when the day of your splendor shines forth, you may find in them something to store in the granary, for whose sake you deigned to come from heaven in the flesh. Amen. May he deign to grant this, etc.

After this follows: “Blessing on the day of the Lord’s Nativity. May almighty God bless you, both …,” etc., as in the printed editions.

### Blessing on the Nativity of Saint Stephen the Martyr

O God, who … the blessed one, etc., as in the printed editions and in the Gemet manuscript and others.

### Another

Open, we ask, Lord, your heavens; open our eyes. From there may your gifts descend to us, and from here may our hearts look toward you. Amen. May your dwelling be open to us in receiving the benefits for which we pray. May our mind be open to you in rendering the services that we are commanded to offer. Amen. May this devout people have your holy Stephen as its patron, whom even that impious man had as his advocate. Amen. May that voice interceding for the people draw near to you—the voice that prayed for its enemies in the very martyrdom—so that, with him obtaining and you rewarding, the people acquired by grace may reach that place where, with the heavens opened, he himself saw you in glory. Amen. May he deign to grant this, etc.

### Blessing on the Nativity of Saint John the Evangelist

May almighty God deign to …, etc., as in the printed editions, and in the Gemet codex and other manuscripts.

### Another

O God, who prepared your apostles as precious lights for the nations, who, to illumine souls, set James and John forth among the vessels of the Church as lampstands of faith, grant that your people may imitate what one formed by entreaty and the other poured forth by evangelizing. Amen. May what this one sowed by the word and that one planted by martyrdom bear fruit among the people. Amen. Through their intercession, may this throng be refreshed by the sweetness of the one upon whose breast the beloved John reclined out of love. Amen. May he deign to grant this, etc.

### Blessing on the Nativity of the Innocents

Almighty God, for whose Only-Begotten Son’s venerable infancy the Innocents …, etc., as in the printed editions, with the Gemet manuscripts and others agreeing.

### Another Blessing

Grant, we ask, Lord, to your people the grace of the Innocents, who consecrated to you the firstfruits of the martyrs from the innocence of little children. Amen. 627 Preserve here, purified by baptism, this people whose innocence you made pleasing to yourself in blood. Amen. Through their intercession, may this flock approach there after its washing, where the blessed little ones, bathed in the dew of blood, rejoice forever. Amen. May he deign to grant this, etc.

### First Sunday after the Nativity of the Lord: Blessing

[Note: [Col. 0607D] In Gemet: “O God, who sent his Only-Begotten into the world in order to save it,” etc.] O God, who sent your Only-Begotten to save the world, etc., as in the printed editions.

### Blessing on the Vigil of the Lord’s Octave

[Col. 0607D] Almighty and everlasting God, who through your incarnate, Only-Begotten Word gave light to the age, we humbly implore his mercy, that he who made the holy Church fruitful from the nations within the flock may release her from every error of paganism. Amen. And he who on the following day, in order to remove the yoke of the Law, was circumcised bodily according to the Law, may graciously circumcise the hearts of this people spiritually and cut away all vices at the root, so that they may pursue zeal for sobriety and not the harmfulness of drunkenness. Amen. May all always be saved by your protection, and while they desire bodily circumcision, may they be strengthened by your blessing, so that they may escape the poisons of the crafty serpent and, with you going before them, happily reach eternal blessedness. Amen. May he deign to grant this, etc.

### Blessing on the Octave of the Lord’s Nativity

Almighty God, etc., as in the printed editions.

### On the Second Sunday after the Nativity of the Lord

O God, who made the temporal chastity of your Son wondrous, may you deign to enlighten and instruct your hearts with the Spirit of wisdom. Amen. And he who willed that he be temporally subject to his parents, may he, in mercy, form you through the gifts of humility and piety. Amen. And he who willed that he advance in wisdom, age, and grace, may he graciously bestow upon you growth in spiritual progress. Amen. May he deign to grant this, etc.

### Blessing on the Theophany

O God, the light, etc., as in the printed editions.

### Blessing on the Third Sunday after the Nativity of the Lord

[Col. 0608B] O God, who by your wondrous power changed water into wine, may you transfer those whom you have withdrawn from oldness into the newness of blessed life. Amen. And he who willed to be present at the wedding in order to affirm its goodness by his presence, may he grant you the gift of perpetual chastity and sobriety. Amen. May he grant you spiritual understanding of the holy Scriptures, who, by changing water into wine, willed to signify this very thing. Amen. May he deign to grant this, etc.

### Blessing on the Octave of the Epiphany

O God, who deigned to choose the present day and demonstrated your choice by so many miracles: on this day a new star led the Magi to adore you, and the Jordan deserved to be sanctified by your baptism; moreover, the pallor of water at Cana of Galilee produced wine. We ask you: be yourself the light of the way for your household, you who, with the star as herald, were glorified as the King of salvation. Amen. Grant your people a full knowledge of the splendor of their Redeemer, so that through his increase they may reach everlasting brightness. [Col. 0608C] Amen. Grant your people a full knowledge of the splendor of their Redeemer, so that through his increase they may reach everlasting brightness. Amen. Turn the hearts of the faithful to seek you, so that, joined with the angels on high, your devoted people may sing glory to you, God. Amen. And you who today deigned to descend from the spring of the Jordan—the fountain of living water—and to sanctify it by your baptism, grant your peoples to rejoice in perpetual peace and always kindle their hearts with the splendor of your grace. Amen. May he deign to grant this, etc.

### Blessing on the Fourth Sunday after the Nativity of the Lord

[Note: [Col. 0607D] In Gemet it is assigned to the Third Sunday, namely, after the Epiphany. The one assigned above to the Third Sunday after the Nativity of the Lord [Col. 0608D] is for the Second Sunday after the Epiphany.] May almighty God cleanse you from the stains of every sin. He who deigned by his own touch to cleanse the supplicating leper, may he mercifully deign to enter the dwelling of your hearts. Amen. And may he thus form you in the fullness of his faith that he may grant you to recline with his saints in the kingdom of heaven. Amen. May he deign to grant this, etc.

### Blessing on the Purification of Saint Mary

[Col. 0608D] Almighty God, who …, etc., as in the printed editions.

### Blessing on the Fifth Sunday after the Nativity of the Lord

[Note: [Col. 0608D] In Gemet it is assigned to the Fourth Sunday after the Epiphany, and the following one to the Fifth Sunday.] May the Lord remove from you the dangers of every temptation and, in mercy, exclude the storms of every disturbance. Amen. May he dissolve the deceits and schemes of the tempter and make you cautious and invincible against him. Amen. May he grant you the gifts of continual peace and, in his favor, establish you in the harbor of tranquility and security. Amen. May he deign to grant this, etc.

### Blessing on the Sixth Sunday after the Nativity of the Lord

[Note: [Col. 0608D] In Gemet: *bonorum semen*, “the seed of good things,” rather than *bonum semen*, “good seed.”] May God, who is accustomed to sow good seed in his Church, never cease to preserve and multiply it in you. [Col. 0609A] May he drive far from you the one who sows weeds over it, and continually refresh you with the nourishment of his word. Amen. Thus, when the day of judgment comes, may you be separated from the rejected and stand at the Judge’s right hand, and be placed in his most blessed kingdom. Amen. May he deign to grant this, etc.

### Blessing on the Seventh Sunday after the Nativity of the Lord

[Note: [Col. 0609D] It is found in Gemet for the Sixth Sunday after the Epiphany.] O God, who made the sea passable beneath your feet, may he himself lay beneath you whatever is harmful. Amen. May he restrain the opposing movements of unclean spirits and confirm you in his peace. Amen. May he steer you in the ship of his cross amid the waves of the world and lead you to the shore of blessed eternity. Amen. May he deign to grant this, etc.

### Blessing on Septuagesima
