Thus may you be able to offer him, in place of turtledoves, gifts of chastity or charity, and, in place of young pigeons, may you abound in the gifts of the Holy Spirit. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, etc.

### Blessing on the Annunciation of Saint Mary

May the Lord Jesus Christ, who came forth from the Virgin at the end of the ages, glorify your heart with the crown of incorrupt virginity. And may he who, when the angel announced it, entered the Virgin’s womb both instruct and protect you through the sacrament of that ministry. Amen. And may you who today celebrate the Virgin’s conception with the greatest devotion reach the Nativity of our Redeemer with exultant hearts and a pure mind. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, who, with the Father, etc.

### Blessing on Septuagesima

Almighty God, who through his apostle commanded each of us to run in such a way that we may obtain the prize, may he pour the Paraclete Spirit into your hearts, so that you may successfully complete your course and, although laboring in his vineyard under diverse callings, may deserve nevertheless to receive from him the promised coin as your reward. Amen. Enlightened by the grace of that same Holy Spirit and invigorated by his clemency, may you abandon and lament your past crimes, avoid those of the present, and beware of those to come, so that the abstinence of the most holy approaching Lent, which you ought rightly to observe, may be worthily begun by you here and completed still more worthily. Amen. Thus, properly observing the Lenten season itself, and with minds purified from every stain of vice, may you deserve to come cleansed to celebrate the Paschal feast solemnly. Amen.

### Blessing of the Most Holy Eucharist

Almighty God, maker of the whole structure of the world, who in the beginning established all his works in the perfection of the number six, may he graciously grant you through his ineffable grace that throughout all the days of your life you may deserve to be protected by the continuous shelter of his blessing. Amen. And may he grant you to perform during the course of six days those works through which, on the seventh, you may obtain such and so great a grace from him that you may both delightfully devote yourselves to his praises and, with the most sincere devotion and without sin, receive the most holy body and blood of the Lord for your healing. Amen. Thus, refreshed by spiritual nourishment and protected by his desirable guardianship, may you please him forever, entirely freed from every servile work and likewise cleansed from every crime. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, etc.

### Blessing in Lent

May divine goodness and his eternal Majesty bless you—he who through Moses the lawgiver, his servant, commanded the Jewish people that in the year of Jubilee there should be remission for the land and also freedom for slaves. Amen. May he free you from the yoke of diabolical servitude, and, adding to you the strength of your former salvation, may he mercifully pour out upon you the spirit of service. Amen. Thus may you deserve to leave the body cleansed from every contagion of crimes, just as you were mercifully purified by the redemption of Christ’s rosy blood. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, etc.

### Blessing at the beginning of Lent

May almighty God, who consecrated the number forty through the fasts of Moses, Elijah, and likewise our Mediator, bless you; and may he grant that you so pass through the dispensation of the present life that, having received the denarius of reward from the master of the household, you may arrive at forgiveness of all sins and at the glorious resurrection with all the saints. Amen. May he give you the invincible weapons of spiritual virtues, by which, following the Lord’s example, you may conquer the most cunning temptations of the ancient enemy. Amen. Thus, taking spiritual nourishment not from bread alone but from every word that proceeds from his mouth, may you, through the observance of fasts and the performance of other good works, deserve to receive the unfading crown of glory. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, etc.

### Blessing for the second week of Lent

Almighty God, author and lover of fasting and of the other virtues, may he sanctify you with his blessing. Amen. May he kindle within you the affection of pious devotion and grant his kindly hearing to those who entreat him. Amen. Thus, when your minds have been cleansed by sincere fasts, may they abound in the increase of every good thing. Amen. May he himself grant this, etc.

### Blessing for the third Sunday in Lent

May almighty God mercifully receive the sacrifices of your fasts and make you worthy of his blessing. Amen. May he so fortify your minds against vices through the good of moderation, instruct them with the teachings of his commandments, and fill them with the gift of charity, that he may grant you to please him in all things. Amen. Thus, as you devoutly celebrate the days of the present Lent, may you be able to approach the Paschal feasts with purified hearts. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, etc.

### Blessing for the fourth Sunday in Lent

O God, who have deigned to bring you to the midpoint of the Lenten days, may he himself deign to bless you through his mercy. Amen. May he accept your past abstinence and make your future abstinence so pleasing to him that, just as he grants you to abstain from unlawful foods, so also he may grant you to abstain from every vice. Amen. Thus, giving thanks to him for the fruits of spiritual gifts, both past and future, may you be able to reach holy Easter unharmed. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, etc.

### Blessing on the fifth Sunday in Lent

May the Lord kindle within you the power of his love, and through the observance of fasts pour into you the gift of his blessing. Amen. May you offer him the sacrifices of moderation in such a way that you please him by the sacrifice of a contrite and humbled heart. Amen. Thus may your prayer, borne upward on the wings of fasting and almsgiving, rise to the ears of your Creator in such a way that he may make you heirs of eternal blessedness and companions of the citizens above. Amen. May he himself grant this, etc.

### Blessing on Palm Sunday

May almighty God bless you, whom you strive to please both by the mortification of fasts and by the observance of the present days. Amen. May he grant you that, just as you have striven to present yourselves to him with palms and other leafy branches, so after death you may be able to appear before him with the palm of victory and the fruit of good works. Amen. And may you who believe with a pure heart in the passion of his only-begotten Son and strive to venerate it with devout mind, supported by his protection, come to the feasts of his Resurrection and to the rewards of your own recompense. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, etc.

### Another blessing on the Passion

Almighty God, who through the passion of his only-begotten Son has granted you an example of humility, may he grant you through that same humility to receive the ineffable gift of his blessing. Amen. Thus may you share in the resurrection of him whose lessons of patience you venerate. Amen. And may you receive from him the gift of eternal life, through whose temporal death you believe that you escape eternal death. Amen.

### Blessing on the Lord’s Supper

May God bless you, who through the passion of his only-begotten Son willed that the old Passover should be changed into the new, and may he grant you that, when the contagion of the old leaven has been purged away, the new mixture may continue in you. Amen. And you who have gathered with devout mind to celebrate the supper of our Redeemer, may you carry away with you a feast of eternal foods. With his merciful help, may you also be cleansed from the filth of sins—he who, to impress upon us an example of humility, willed to wash the feet of his disciples. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, etc.

### Blessing on Holy Saturday

O God, who, bringing forth new peoples from the undefiled womb of your Church, continually make her fruitful with new offspring while her virginity remains intact, fill you with the gift of faith, hope, and charity, and pour upon you the gifts of your blessing. Amen. And may he who willed to illumine this most holy night by the Resurrection of our Redeemer make your minds, cleansed from the darkness of sins, shine with an abundance of virtues. Amen. Thus may you strive to imitate the innocence of those who have just been reborn, and illumine the vessels of your minds after the example of the present lights, so that with the lamps of good works you may be able to enter with the wise virgins the bridal chamber of this Bridegroom whose Resurrection you celebrate. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, etc.

[Col. 0631B] ### Blessing on holy Easter Day

May almighty God bless you as the Paschal solemnity of this day intervenes, and in his mercy deign to defend you from every wickedness. Amen. And may he who restores you to eternal life in the Resurrection of his only-begotten Son clothe you, at his coming, with the joys of immortality. Amen. And you who, having completed the days of fasting or of the Lord’s Passion, celebrate the joys of the Paschal feast, may, with his help and exultant hearts, come to those feasts that are not annual but perpetual. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, etc.

### Blessing on the octave of Easter

O God, whose only-begotten Son today deigned to appear to his disciples when the doors were closed, may he deign to enrich you with the gift of his blessing and open to you the gates of the heavenly kingdom. Amen. And may he who removed the wound of doubt from their hearts by the touch of his body grant that, through the faith by which you believe that he rose again, you may be free from every stain of sin. Amen. And you who, with Thomas, believe him to be God and Lord, behold him, and invoke him with your voices, may you be able to be protected by him from every evil in this age and to be admitted among the assemblies of the saints in the age to come. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, etc.

### Blessing on the Resurrection

May almighty God bless you, who created you through gratuitous mercy and, in the resurrection of his only-begotten Son, granted you hope of rising again. Amen. May he who raised him from the dead raise you from the tombs of vices. Amen. Thus may you live happily without end with him whom you truly believe to have risen from the dead. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this.

### Another

O God, who through the Resurrection of your only-begotten Son bestowed upon you both the good of Redemption and the glory of adoption, may he bestow upon you the rewards of his blessing. Amen. And by him through whose redemption you received the gift of perpetual freedom, may you, through his generosity, become companions in an eternal inheritance. Amen. And as you rose with him in baptism by believing, so may you deserve to be joined to him in the heavenly region by living well. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, etc.

### Blessing for fasting

May almighty God graciously attend to your devotion and grant you the gifts of his blessing. Amen. May he forgive all the evils you have committed and grant you the pardon that you ask from him. Amen. May he receive the vows of your fasting and prayers in such a way that he turns away from you every adversity that you deserve as repayment for sins, and pours into you the gift of the Paraclete Spirit. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, etc.

### Blessing on the day of the Lord’s Ascension

May almighty God bless you, whose only-begotten Son today penetrated the heights of heaven and opened for you the way of ascent to where he is. Amen. May he graciously grant that, just as after his Resurrection he appeared visibly to his disciples, so, when he comes for judgment, he may appear to you as one who is favorable. Amen. And you who believe that he sits with the Father in his majesty, may you perceive him, according to his promise, remaining with us until the end of the age. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, etc.

### Blessing on the vigil of Pentecost

May almighty God bless you, for whose Paraclete Spirit you prepare your minds today through the observance of fasting and honor the present day with solemn praises. Amen. May you possess, like infants newly reborn, such innocence that, by his gift, you may be able to become a temple of the Holy Spirit. Amen. And may that same Holy Spirit today make you worthy of his dwelling in such a way that tomorrow he may pour himself into your minds, to dwell perpetually with you, and, when the course of the present life has been completed, lead you to the heavenly kingdoms. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, etc.

[Col. 0632B] ### Blessing on Pentecost

O God, who today deigned to illumine the minds of the disciples through the outpouring of the Paraclete Spirit, may he cause you to be filled with his blessing and to abound in the gifts of that same Spirit. Amen. May that fire which appeared over the disciples cleanse the filth of your sins and, through the outpouring of its light, illuminate your hearts. Amen. And may he who deigned to unite the diversity of languages in the confession of one faith make you persevere in the constancy of that same faith, and through it come from hope to vision. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, etc.

### Blessing on the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist

May almighty God bless you through the intercession of blessed John the Baptist, whose nativity you celebrate today, and may he grant that you experience the patronage of him whose solemn feast you honor. Amen.

Through his intercession may you be protected from every adversity and enjoy every good thing—he who, though not yet born, recognized the coming of the Redeemer of the world; by being born removed his mother’s barrenness; and by being born loosed his father’s tongue. Amen. Thus may you be clothed in the wool of virtues and be able to imitate innocence, so that you may be joined in the blessedness of the eternal homeland to that Lamb whom he pointed out with his finger and by whose sacrifice you have been redeemed. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, etc.

### Another

May almighty God bless you, who through blessed John at last mercifully announced on earth the coming of his only-begotten Son. Amen. May the Holy Spirit himself, who filled John while he was enclosed in his mother’s womb and released his father’s tongue from its bond, cause you to be filled with his blessing, so that you may abound richly in spiritual gifts. Amen. May the voice of the interceding Forerunner rise to the ears of the most merciful Father—he who knew to confess the Redeemer of the world before he was born, and who with his holy hands baptized the author of baptism in the font—and may that Father through John’s intercession mercifully cleanse the stains of your sins and make you fruitful with an abundance of virtues. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, etc.

### Blessing on the feast of the Holy Cross

May almighty God bless you, who through the passion of his only-begotten Son, Jesus Christ our Lord, and the gibbet of the cross redeemed the human race. Amen. May he grant you, with all the saints, to comprehend with devout mind the length, breadth, height, and depth of that same cross. Amen. Thus, denying yourselves and carrying the cross, may you be able to follow our Redeemer in the course of the present life in such a way that after death you may deserve to be admitted among the choirs of angels. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, etc.

### Blessing on the Nativity of the apostles Peter and Paul

May almighty God bless you, who has founded you upon the firmness of ecclesiastical faith through the saving confession of blessed Peter. Amen. And may he protect with his most gracious defense those whom the most holy preaching of blessed Paul has instructed. Amen. Thus may Peter with the key, Paul with his word, and both through their intercession strive to lead you to that homeland which they deserved to reach today, one by the cross and the other by the sword. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, etc.

### Blessing on the Assumption of Saint Mary

O God, who today willed to summon the most blessed virgin Mary, the most glorious Mother of our Lord Jesus Christ, to heaven and exalt her sublimely above the choirs of angels, may he deign through her intercession and merits to enrich you with his blessing’s grace in such a way that you may deserve to pass from vices to virtues. Amen. May he grant you in this age to flourish in faith, rejoice in hope, and abound in charity; continually to shine with the excellence of chastity and also to gleam with the excellence of humility, so that, adorned in every way with good works, you may be able to please him. Amen. And may he cause you to expiate all past crimes and offenses by groans and tears, day and night, and to avoid present and future evils so healthfully that you may shine eternally in the heavenly places with her. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, etc.

### Blessing on the feast of Saint John’s martyrdom

O God, who has granted you to frequent the solemn feast of blessed John the Baptist, grant you also to celebrate it with devoted minds and to receive the gifts of his blessing. Amen. And may he who for proclaiming his law was confined in the darkness of a prison free you through his intercession from the incitements of dark works. Amen. And may he who did not hesitate to lose his head for the truth, which is God, cause you through his intervention to reach your head, who is Christ. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, etc.

### Blessing on the Nativity of Saint Mary

O God, who through the birth of blessed Mary the virgin deigned to redeem the human race, may he deign to enrich you with his blessing. Amen. And may you always and everywhere experience the protection of her from whose undefiled womb you were granted to receive the author of life. Amen. And you who have gathered today with devoted minds to celebrate her Nativity, may you carry away with you gifts of spiritual joys and eternal rewards. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, etc., as above.

### Blessing concerning the Advent of the Lord

Almighty God, whose only-begotten Son’s coming you both believe to have occurred in the past and await in the future, may he sanctify you through the illumination of that same coming and enrich you with his blessing. Amen. May he defend you from every adversity in the course of the present life and show himself favorable to you in judgment. Amen. Thus, freed from every contagion of sins, may you await without fear the day of that dreadful examination, by whose blood you have been redeemed. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, etc.

### Another

May almighty God look upon you with a favorable countenance and pour into you the gift of his blessing. Amen. And may he who made these days solemn through the Incarnation of his only-begotten Son render you unharmed by every adversity of the present and future life. Amen. Thus, you who rejoice with devout mind in the Advent of our Redeemer according to the flesh, may you, at his second coming, when he arrives in his Majesty, be enriched with the rewards of eternal life. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, etc.

### Another

May ineffable grace, and the goodness of the living God, bless you; and, through the admirable and saving Advent of his Son, may he grant you not to remain—God forbid—captive under the dominion of sin. Amen. May he deign so powerfully to free you from every misery and so mercifully and steadfastly confirm you in his mercy that he may cause you to serve him in the present age in such a way that in the future you may deserve to reach him rejoicing. Amen. And may he who willed his only-begotten Son to become incarnate for you at his first Advent himself, at the second, separate you from the company of the unjust and gather you with himself, to remain forever in the fellowship of the just. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, etc.

Item, another.

May almighty God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Savior and Redeemer of the world, bless you, and, by blessing you, justify and sanctify you through the illumination of the first Advent of that same Only-Begotten Son, so that at the second Advent you may not appear unclean before him. Amen. May his grace establish you so firmly in true humility and strengthen you so steadfastly in sincere charity that the things of the world may displease you in such a way, and the things of God continually please you, that together with the saints you may remain united in heavenly blessedness. Amen. And may he who willed that same Son to be humbled for the salvation of his servants, so that he might graciously be united to our nature within the maternal womb by joining it to the unity of his person, cause you during this first Advent to be illumined within by the splendor of his visitation and indwelling, so that at the second Advent you may deserve to glorify eternally with him. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, who, with the Father, etc.

### Blessing on the nativity of one apostle

May God, who has granted you to stand upon apostolic foundations, deign to bless you through the merits of blessed N., his apostle, interceding. Amen. And may he defend you from every adversity by apostolic protections, who willed that you be adorned and fortified by their examples and teachings. Amen. May you, through their intercession, attain the inheritance of the eternal homeland, through whose teaching you preserve the integrity of faith. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, who, with the Father, etc.

### Blessing on the nativity of one martyr

May the Lord bless you through the intercession of his blessed martyr N., and defend you from every evil. Amen. May he who received him through the sufferings of his passion extend over you the right hand of his favor. Amen. May you deserve to share in heaven with him whose triumph you celebrate on earth with devoted hearts. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, etc.

### Blessing on the nativity of several martyrs

May the Lord bless you through the suffrages of his blessed martyrs NN., and deliver you from every adversity. Amen. May their glorious intercession commend you, whose death is precious in his sight. Amen. Just as they obtained the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom through various kinds of torments, so may you deserve to share in their fellowship through the practice of good works. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, etc.

### On the feast of one confessor

May almighty God grant you an abundance of blessing, he who took blessed N. to himself through the strength of confession. Amen. And may he who made him shine with miracles adorn you with an increase of good works. Amen. Enlightened by his examples and fortified by his intercession, whose day of deposition you celebrate, may you be able to be joined to him in the heavenly realm. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, whose, etc.

### Blessing on the nativity of several confessors

May the Lord cause you to be blessed through the merits of his holy confessors NN., and fortified against every adversity by their intercession. Amen. May he make you happy through their suffrage, whose feast day you celebrate with rejoicing. Amen. Imitating their examples, may you be able to attain the promises of heaven. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, whose kingdom, etc.

### Blessing on the nativity of one virgin

May the Lord bless you, who granted blessed virgin N. both the beauty of virginity and the glory of martyrdom. Amen. Through whose aid she deserved to overcome both the frailty of her sex and the fury of her persecutors; may you likewise be able to overcome both the allurements of your bodies and the devices of the ancient enemy. Amen. Just as she, though of the frailer sex, ventured to undertake a manly contest and, after the contest, to triumph over her enemies, so may you, living in this mortality, be able both to conquer the ancient enemy and to reach the heavenly kingdoms. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, etc.

### On the nativity of several virgins

May almighty God, through the intercession of his holy virgins, deign to bless you—he who willed to triumph over the ancient enemy not only through men but also through women. Amen. And may he who willed to grant them the fruit a hundredfold through the beauty of virginity and the struggle of martyrdom deign both to cleanse you from the filth of vices and to adorn you with the lamps of virtues. Amen. May you be able to fill the lamps of your hearts with the oil of virtues in such a way that, with them, you may be able to enter the bridal chamber of the heavenly Bridegroom. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, etc.

### Blessing on the anniversary of the dedication of a church

Almighty God, who willed that this holy temple be dedicated to his most glorious name in honor of blessed N., his apostle, may he himself cause you to be justified by his blessing through that apostle’s prayers and merits, and sanctified through the illumination of his visitation and indwelling. Amen. Although you were once, like the others, dwellings of the ancient enemy and captives under his domination, may each of you deserve to become a most pleasing temple of the living God, made by his grace from servants into adopted sons. Amen. May he grant you that, as you celebrate the anniversary festival of the dedication of this tabernacle of his, you may proceed joyfully with the holy angels to the everlasting celebration of the heavenly temple. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, etc.

### On the anniversary of the consecration of a bishop

Almighty God, who, although I am unworthy, through the overflowing abundance of his immense compassion has deigned to appoint me among the number of bishops to minister at his altar by offering sacrifices of praise, and has also destined me to distribute to his people both the sacraments of the heavenly table and the nourishment of eternal life, may he deign to enrich you with an abundance of blessing and mercifully invigorate your hearts with the sanctifying grace of the Holy Spirit. Amen. May he also deign graciously to cleanse you from every kind of wickedness and powerfully confirm you in the excellence of his compassion. Amen. May he further grant you to advance daily from evil to good and from good to better, and, after the end of this life, to pass happily into the joys of eternal rewards. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, etc.

### Blessing for ordinary days

May the Lord bless you and keep you. Amen. May he make his face shine upon you and have mercy on you. Amen. May he turn his countenance toward you and give you peace. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, etc.

### Another

May almighty God bless you with his mercy and pour into you the understanding of saving wisdom. Amen. May he nourish you with the teachings of the Catholic faith and make you steadfast in holy works. Amen. May he turn your steps away from error and show you the way of peace and charity. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, whose, etc.

### Another

May the Lord incline his ear to the prayers of your humility and grant you the grace of his blessing and the reward of eternal salvation. Amen. May you always and everywhere have the Lord favorable to you, and may you exult in his praises. Amen. May he loosen all the bonds of your sins and bring you to eternal glory. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, whose, etc.

### Another

May the Lord multiply within you the abundance of his blessing and confirm you in the hope of the heavenly kingdom. Amen. May he correct your actions, reform your life, order your conduct, and lead you to the inheritance of the heavenly paradise. Amen. May you be able to be filled with such an intention that you may please him forever. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, who, with, etc.

### Another

May the Lord graciously regard your devotion and grant you the gifts of his blessing. Amen. May he fortify you in the present age with such assistance that in the future he may make you inhabitants of paradise. Amen. May he bless your hearts by sanctifying them, and sanctify them by blessing them, so that he may delight in dwelling continually with you—indeed, within you. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, etc.

### Another

May almighty God grant you the grace of his blessing and fill you with the spirit of truth and peace. Amen. May you run along the way of salvation with such devoted hearts that you may healthfully escape the snares of creeping sins. Amen. And may you become devoted in supplication to him and sincere in mutual love, so that you may be able to reach the heavenly kingdom securely. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, whose command, etc.

### Another

May almighty God grant you the gift of his blessing, he who is aware of your weakness. Amen. And may he who has granted you the desire to pray also grant you the help of consolation. Amen. May you receive support both for the present life and for the life to come from him whose goodness you believe created you. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, etc.

### Another

May almighty God surround you with heavenly protection and enrich you with the gift of his blessing. Amen. May he grant that, as you rely upon the sole hope of heavenly grace, you may also be fortified by heavenly protection. Amen. Thus may you receive the consolations of mortal life in the present age and be able to attain eternal joys. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, etc.

### Another

May almighty God perpetually surround you with the help of his right hand and fill you with the gift of his blessings. Amen. May he defend you from every depravity and grant you to abound in heavenly gifts. Amen. Thus, purified in body and mind, may you offer him such service that you may be able to obtain his favor. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, etc.

### Another blessing

May almighty God purify the hidden places of your hearts and grant you an increase of his blessing. Amen. And may you be stripped of all the dangers of the present life and clothed with the adornments of spiritual virtues. Amen. Supported by his help, may you serve him on earth in such a way that you may be able to be joined to him in heaven. Amen.

### Another

May almighty God exclude every adversity from you and, in his mercy, pour upon you the gifts of his blessing. Amen. May he make your hearts intent upon sacred teachings, so that they may be filled with eternal benefits. Amen. Understanding what must be done and doing what you understand, may you be found unharmed amid the adversities of the world and become fellow heirs of the blessed spirits. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this. Amen.

### Another

May almighty God order your days in his peace and grant you the gifts of his blessing. Amen. May he free you from every disturbance and make your minds firm in the tranquility of his peace. Amen. Adorned with the jewels of hope, faith, and charity, may you pass through the present life unharmed and reach the eternal one securely. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, whose kingdom and dominion remain without end forever and ever. Amen.

# [THE ANTIPHONARY.]

[Col. 0637]

## PREFACE TO THE ANTIPHONARY OF ST. GREGORY

649 What we have already said about the book of the Sacraments—namely, that its collector and corrector was rather St. Gregory than its author—is also to be understood of the Antiphonary, which bears his name. This seems to be indicated by John the Deacon when, in Book II, chapter 6 of the Life of St. Gregory, entitled “Compiling the Antiphonary,” he says that Gregory “established a school of singers” and, “in the manner of the wisest Solomon, because of the sweetness of musical compunction, compiled with great diligence and great usefulness an anthology for the singers.” What John the Deacon reports there about the school of singers established by that most holy pontiff, the couch on which he composed melodies while reclining, the whip with which he threatened the boys, and his authentic Antiphonary, preserved at Rome with great veneration, may be read in that place.

When the author of Gregory’s Life calls the Antiphonary an anthology and at the same time asserts that it was compiled, he sufficiently indicates that it did not have a single parent, but was in part the offspring of many who had preceded him, perhaps Roman pontiffs. Ecclesiastical song is certainly much older than our Gregory; indeed, Socrates, Book VI, chapter 8, and others have shown that it was received almost from the beginning of the Christian commonwealth. On this subject one should consult those who formerly wrote about the divine offices: Isidore, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*; Rabanus, Book II of *On the Instruction of Clergy*; and others; in our own age, Cardinal Bona, *On Divine Psalmody*, and Jean Mabillon, in his inquiry *On the Gallican Course*, § 1.

Some things were formerly sung in the Church antiphonally, as is still done; others were sung simultaneously by united choirs. The ancients called the first manner of singing **ἀντίφωνος ὑμνῳδία**, “antiphonal hymn-singing,” and the second **σύμφωνος**, “consonant.” Socrates mentions the former manner in the passage cited; St. Gregory Nazianzen mentions both in his iambic poem *On Virtue*, near the end [Note: See the preface of P. Gussanvillaeus, which we have appended to this one.]. Hence the name *Antiphon* was transferred to the Latins, and from *Antiphon* the book was called the *Antiphonary*. Our Hugh Menard also observes, from Agobard, that it was called the *Official*, in note 337 to the Book of the Sacraments.

Although the Roman, or Gregorian, Antiphonary embraces not only the Antiphon but also whatever the choir sings at Mass, it nevertheless took this name from the Antiphon that is sung beforehand, which we now call the Introit because it precedes the entrance. At the very beginning of the Book of the Sacraments: “First, at the Introit, what sort of Antiphon there is, at the appointed times.” Almost everything else retained its former name, except the Gradual, which was formerly called the Responsory. It was, however, sometimes also called the Gradual, as is clear from the beginning of the Book of the Sacraments: “Afterward the Prayer is said; then follows the Apostle, and also the Gradual.” Hence we observe that the Antiphonary itself was called the Gradual by the *Micrologus*, as is evident from the notes on the feast of St. Paul and on the office of St. Apollinaris.

The most holy Father’s disciples spread throughout the West the method of singing established by our Gregory, especially those who joined themselves as companions to Augustine as he traveled to Britain, as John the Deacon teaches, Book II, chapter 8. We possess a particularly clear testimony concerning the English in the venerable Bede, Book V of his *History*, chapter 21. Concerning Bishop Acca he says:

“He also summoned to himself, for the instruction of himself and his people, an outstanding singer named Maban, who had been taught the sounds of singing in Kent by successors of the disciples of the blessed Pope Gregory.”

The same point emerges no less clearly from St. Wilfrid, bishop of York, who, according to Eddius, the author of his Life, boasts 650 that after the death of the first nobles directed by St. Gregory, he had taught the entire people of the Northumbrians “how, according to the custom of the primitive Church, with harmonious modulation of the voice, standing in two choirs, they should leap through Responsories and alternate Antiphons” (*Acts of the Saints of the Order of St. Benedict*, fourth century, part I).

Ecclesiastical song, corrupted among the English, Gauls, and other Western peoples through the passage of time, was restored by a certain Roman singer named John, who had followed Theodore, sent to Britain by Pope Vitalian, and appointed over the Church of Dorobernia, otherwise Canterbury, the metropolitan church of all England (John the Deacon, Book II, chapter 8). Thus, when we read that the use of the Roman Antiphonaries was brought from the Roman Church into the Gallican Church through Pepin (Mabillon, *On the Gallican Course*, p. 398), to whom Pope Paul sent an Antiphonary and Responsary from the city, this should perhaps be understood rather as the restoration of that practice than as its original establishment. Nevertheless, we do not deny that many churches in Gaul retained their ancient usages until the time of Charlemagne.

That emperor, offended at Rome by the discord between Roman and Gallican song, and seeing Romans and Gauls disputing with one another, settled the quarrel after examining Gregory’s authentic Antiphonary, judging the Roman method of singing far preferable to the Gallican. Therefore he left two industrious clerics of his own with Hadrian, then bishop; when they had finally been adequately instructed, he restored the metropolitan church of Metz to the sweetness of its former melodies and, through it, corrected all his Gaul, says John the Deacon, Book II, chapter 9.

The fame of the Metz Antiphonary continued until the time of St. Bernard, as is clear from his treatise *On the Song or Correction of the Antiphonary*, volume II, work XIII, p. 693 of the latest edition. Since the earlier Cistercian Fathers considered nothing more important than singing in the divine praises what was found to be most authentic, they sent people to transcribe and bring back the Antiphonary of the Church of Metz—for it was said to be Gregorian—as St. Bernard reports. But they found that manuscript corrupted and disordered both in its song and in its writing.

We have again reviewed this Roman and Gregorian Antiphonary, already edited by Pamelius in volume II of the *Liturgicon*, later inserted into the Vatican edition of St. Gregory’s works, and reprinted in the Gussanvillaeus edition, against two manuscript Codices of Thérouanne, in which it is contained concisely together with the Book of the Sacraments, against the Codex of Clairvaux, and especially against the Compendian exemplar of St. Cornelius, magnificently painted and adorned with purple and golden letters through royal munificence. In it many passages occur that have been prepared for singing with musical notes written above them.

Its title reads:

“Gregory, the prelate worthy in merit and name, ascending to the highest honor, renewed the memorials of the earlier Fathers and composed this little book of the musical art for the school of singers throughout the cycle of the year. It begins with the First Sunday of Advent of the Lord.”

The age of that notable Codex may be investigated both from its script and from a certain prose piece about blessed Mary that we have presented in the appendix. The script certainly belongs to the ninth century; from the prose, copied in the same hand, it is clear that the Normans were then ravaging Gaul—events that indicate the time of the emperor Charles the Bald, founder of the monastery of Compiègne. From the same Codex we shall append the Antiphons, Verses, and Responsories belonging to the ancient ecclesiastical course. We shall say no more about St. Gregory’s Antiphonary, because we have judged it appropriate to append to this work the preface of the most learned Peter Gussanvillaeus, from which those who delight in abundance and variety may draw much worthy of knowledge.

[Col. 0639]

## PREFACE OF PETER GUSSANVILLAEUS

651 John the Deacon, writing almost three hundred years after St. Gregory, attributes this Antiphonary, which we are publishing, to St. Gregory in Book II of his Life, chapter 6; he testifies that Gregory’s Codex—whether an autograph or a copy, I do not know—is found at Rome in the Lateran patriarchate. Let the matter rest upon his faith and that of his followers; I would not dare contradict him, although this assertion may seem to some capable of being obscured by certain clouds.

It is one thing to compose Antiphons and another to arrange, distinguish, and revise them, adding some new elements. Most authors continually thrust upon us many things gathered here and there about Antiphons, taking no care to explain the ambiguous word or to separate the various rites that, concealed beneath the covering of this word, are ineptly confused. I shall therefore make a few observations both about the word and about its use.

The word is Greek in origin: **ἀντίφωνος**, “sounding in response,” from **ἀντιφωνέω**, “to sound in response.” The poet Anacreon, Ode 1:

> Κᾀγὼ μὲν ᾖδον ἄθλους  
> Ἡρακλέους· λύρη δὲ  
> Ἔρωτας ἀντεφώνει.

That is:

> I was singing the labors of Heracles;  
> but the lyre was sounding back the loves.

Among Greek and Latin ecclesiastical authors, this word did not always have the same use. Originally, **ἀντιφωνεῖν** meant to sing Psalms, prophecies, or Hymns in alternation, as though one choir were answering another. Thus in Isaiah, chapter VI: “The angels cried out one to another.” Thus in Psalm LXVII, 18, where we commonly read *millia laetantium schinan*, Rabbi Solomon and Eugubinus interpret *schinan* as “alternating,” from the root *shanah*, which means “to repeat” or “to double,” as though the angels were praising God with alternating songs. In accordance with our practice, we still sing the Psalms of David and whatever Hymns are inserted in our Breviaries, and the Proses in our Missals, in concert.

Philo, as quoted by Eusebius, *History*, Book II, chapter 17, and by Nicephorus, Book II, chapter 15, says that when one person rose from among all and sang the psalm, the others sang along at the end. But it is better to read Philo himself, in *On the Contemplative Life*. From the *Tripartite History*, Book X, chapter 9, and Nicephorus, Book XIII, chapter 8, it appears that St. Ignatius received this custom of alternation from the angels.

Those who have written about Antiphons have not sufficiently considered Theodoret, *History*, Book II, chapter 24. I point to the passage rather than transcribe it; the histories would need to be reconciled before anything certain could be asserted. For my part, I think that an Antiphon was not the words that were sung, but the very manner of singing—whether Psalms, prophecies, Hymns, Responsories, or something similar. In Sozomen, Book VIII, chapter 8: **Κατὰ τῶν ἀντιφώνων τρόπον ἔψαλλον**, “they sang in the manner of the Antiphons.” He is speaking of the Arians, whose deceptions St. John Chrysostom dispelled by prudent imitation.

Haimo, on Psalm VII, notes that Antiphons are sometimes joined from different Psalms or praises. John Cassian, speaking of Antiphons among monks in Book II of the *Institutes*, recognizes and almost condemns their ancient custom: in chapter 2 he accepts it; in chapter 8 the subject concerns Matins. The Second Council of Tours, canon 18, in the year 567, establishes certain rules concerning Antiphons that are obscure to us; and canon 23 concerns Ambrosian Hymns.

From St. Augustine, *Retractations*, Book II, chapter 11, it is clear that at Carthage the custom then began of singing Hymns from the Book of Psalms at the altar, either before the Offering or while the Offerings were being distributed to the people. His Letter 119 to Januarius, chapter 18, also discusses the singing of Hymns and Psalms. We also read in *Retractations*, chapter 19, of a Psalm and a Hypopsalm composed by the holy man against the Donatists.

Whether anyone has yet clearly explained the difference among Psalms, Hypopsalms, Hymns, Responsories, Tracts, Offertories, Graduals, Introits, Ephymnia, Typica, Troparia, and Antiphons, I do not know; many, however, have wrongly confused them. In the *Typikon* of Saba one can observe the distinction between Antiphon and Typica. The liturgy of St. John Chrysostom likewise presents it, almost 652 saying: **μετὰ τὰ εἰρηνικὰ ὁ χορὸς ψάλλει τὸ πρῶτον ἀντίφωνον, ἢ τὰ τυπικά, εἰ ἐστὶ κυριακή**, “after the petitions of peace, the choir sings the first Antiphon, or the Typica, if it is Sunday,” etc.

In the Mass of the Mozarabs and in the mysteries of the Presanctified, Antiphons 1, 2, and 3 occur, as they do in St. Germanus of Constantinople, *On Ecclesiastical Matters*. He mentions Antiphons 1, 2, and 3; shortly before, he says that an Antiphon consists of the predictions of the prophets, etc. They were generally taken from the sacred Scriptures. Thus the Councils of Laodicea, final canon, and Braga I, canon 30. But the Fathers of the Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 12, legislate less strictly concerning Hymns; and much relevant to the matter under discussion can be found both in that canon and in canons 12, 13, 14, and 15, provided that we do not measure the ancient custom by our own. For modern Antiphons are not sung antiphonally as they were in antiquity.

Most people make St. Ambrose the first Latin author of Antiphons. I do not object, provided they first explain what they mean by *Antiphon*: Hymns such as he published, or the poems about which he bears witness in Letter 32. For my part, I would interpret the praises mentioned by the Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 11, and the Hymns mentioned by Theodoret in *Publius*, chapter 5 of the *History of the Saints*, and the Psalms and Hymns mentioned by Tertullian, *To His Wife*, Book II, chapters 6 and 9, and the Psalmody mentioned by St. Basil in Letter 63 to the Neocaesareans, as Antiphons if the singing was alternating.

I would say the same of the passage of St. Gaudentius, treatise 4, *On the Reading of Exodus*, where he explains what St. Paul says in Ephesians V and Colossians III about Hymns and spiritual songs. Concerning Antiphons, Collections, Capitella, and so forth, one should read canon 30 of the Council of Agde, in the year 506, when St. Gregory had not yet been born.

Thus the Antiphonary was not newly invented at that time; indeed, even then people were abusing the word, contrary to its original institution, without always observing the principle of alternating song. Augustine treats this mystically in the title of Psalm LXXXVII, and St. Gregory Nazianzen historically, speaking of the Nazarenes in his iambic poem *On Virtue*, shortly before the end:

> Ὁρᾷς ἀγρύπνους πρὸς Θεὸν ψαλμῳδίας  
> Ἀνδρῶν, γυναικῶν, φύσεως λελησμένων,  
> Οἵων θ` ὅσων τε καὶ ὅσον θεουμένων,  
> Σύμφωνον ἀντίφωνον ἀγγέλων στάσιν·  
> Δισσὴν ἄνω τε καὶ κάτω τεταγμένην  
> Θείας ὑμνῳδὸν ἀξίας καὶ φύσεως.

That is:

> Do you see the wakeful psalm-singing to God—  
> of men and women forgetful of their nature?  
> How many, and how holy! You see the angelic choir,  
> which now sings in unison, now in alternating turns,  
> partly set below and partly above,  
> singing without end the praises of the highest Father?

Perhaps Cassian had not seen this passage; I would like those who, guided by his authority, maintain that this practice was received in monasteries only later to be advised of it.

[Col. 0641]

# THE ANTIPHONARY OF ST. GREGORY THE GREAT, ROMAN PONTIFF, ARRANGED THROUGHOUT THE CYCLE OF THE YEAR

653 [Note: In the Compendian manuscript is added: “Station at St. Andrew’s, at the manger.” The same appears in a six-hundred-year-old Codex of the Angelica Library, except that instead of *at the manger* it reads *after the manger*. At this passage Angelus Rocca of Camerino, formerly bishop of Tagaste, from the Augustinian order and prefect of the Apostolic Sacristy, a patron of that library, added the following note: “After careful inspection in the year 1601, this little chapel, formerly dedicated to St. Andrew the Apostle, now within the atrium of the church of St. Anthony near the Basilica of St. Mary Major, is seen to have been desecrated and converted to human use.” The same scholar, especially devoted to sacred antiquity, observes that the apse of that ancient chapel, in which images once made in mosaic work could be seen, had also been desecrated. In Angelus Rocca’s time those images were seen half-ruined and collapsed; but now, says Mabillon, *Italian Journey*, p. 93, nothing at all remains of that mosaic.]

## First Sunday of Advent of the Lord

[Col. 0641A]

**Antiphon.** To you, O Lord, I have lifted up my soul; my God, in you I trust; I shall not be put to shame, nor shall my enemy mock me. Indeed, none who await you shall be confounded.

**Psalm.** Make your ways known to me, O Lord, and teach me your paths.

**Responsory.** None who await you shall be confounded.

**Verse.** Make your ways known to me, O Lord, and teach me your paths.

**Alleluia.** Show us, O Lord, your mercy, and grant us your salvation.

**Offertory.** To you, O Lord, I have lifted up my soul; my God, in you I trust; I shall not be put to shame. Let not my enemies mock me, for none who await you shall be confounded.

**Verse 1.** Guide me in your truth and teach me, for you are God my Savior, and I have waited for you all day long.

**Verse 2.** Look upon me and have mercy on me, O Lord; guard my soul and deliver me. I shall not be confounded, for I have called upon you.

**At Communion.** The Lord will give goodness, and our land will give its fruit.

**Psalm.** You have blessed, O Lord.

## Second Sunday of Advent

**Antiphon.** People of Zion, behold, the Lord will come to save the nations, and the Lord will make the glory of his voice heard in the joy of your hearts.

**Psalm.** Give ear, you who rule Israel, you who lead Joseph like a sheep.

**Responsory.** From Zion comes the beauty of his splendor; God will come manifestly.

**Verse.** Gather his saints to him, those who have established his covenant above sacrifices.

**Alleluia.** I rejoiced at the things that were said to me: “We shall go into the house of the Lord.”

**Verse 1.** Our feet were standing in your courts, Jerusalem.

**Verse 2.** Our king, Christ, will come, whom John proclaimed to be the Lamb who was to come.

**Offertory.** O God, once turned toward us, you will give us life, and your people will rejoice in you. Show us, O Lord, your mercy, and grant us your salvation.

**Verse 1.** You have blessed your land, O Lord; you have turned away the captivity of Jacob; you have forgiven the iniquity of your people.

**Verse 2.** Mercy and truth have met one another; truth has sprung from the earth, and righteousness has looked down from heaven.

**At Communion.** Jerusalem, arise and stand in a high place, and see the joy that will come to you from your God.

**Psalm.** Give ear, you who rule Israel.

## On the feast of St. Lucy

**Antiphon.** You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions.

**Psalm.** My heart has uttered a good word; I speak of my works to the king.

**Responsory.** You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity.

**Verse.** Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions.

**Alleluia.** Grace has been poured upon your lips; therefore God has blessed you forever.

**Offertory.** Virgins will be offered to the king; her companions will be offered to you in joy and exultation; they will be led [Note: In the Compendian manuscript: “into the temple of the King.”] into the temple to the king, the Lord.

**Verse 1.** My heart has uttered a good word. [Note: In the same Codex this verse is completed with the following: “My tongue,” and then *they will be led* is resumed.]

**Verse 2.** [Note: Instead of this verse, the Compendian manuscript assigns: “Grace has been poured out … therefore God has blessed you forever.”] In your beauty.

**At Communion.** Grace has been poured upon your lips.

**Psalm.** As above.

[Note: The Compendian manuscript adds: “At St. Peter’s,” with “station” understood.]

## Third Sunday

**Antiphon.** Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice. Let your moderation be known to all people. The Lord is near; have no anxiety, but in every prayer let your requests be made known before God.

**Psalm.** [Note: After this verse the Compendian manuscript reads, in golden letters, **AR**, perhaps meaning “otherwise”; then it adds, “Show us,” etc.] You have blessed your land, O Lord; you have turned away the captivity of Jacob.

**Responsory.** You who sit above the cherubim, O Lord, stir up your power and come.

**Verse.** Give ear, you who rule Israel, you who lead Joseph like a sheep.

**Alleluia.** Stir up your power, O Lord, and come, that you may save us.

**Offertory.** You have blessed your land, O Lord; you have turned away the captivity of your people. [Note: The Compendian manuscript reads: “of your people.”]

**Verse 1.** You have covered all their sins; you have calmed all your anger. [Note: In the cited Codex is added: “You have forgiven,” etc.]

**Verse 2.** Show us, O Lord, your mercy, and grant us your salvation.

**At Communion.** Say: “You fainthearted, take courage, and do not fear. Behold, our God will come and will save us.” [Note: The Compendian manuscript reads: “You fainthearted one.”]

**Psalm.** You have blessed your land, O Lord, as above.

[Note: In the same place is written: “At St. Mary’s, at the manger.”]

## Wednesday

**Antiphon.** Drop down dew, you heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain down the Just One; let the earth be opened and bring forth the Savior.

**Psalm.** The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the work of his hands. [Note: In the Compendian manuscript: **AR**, “In the sun he has set,” etc.]

**Responsory.** Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, you everlasting gates, and the King of glory shall enter.

**Verse.** Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord, or who shall stand in his holy place? He who is innocent in hands and pure in heart.

**Responsory.** The Lord is near to all who call upon him, to all who call upon him in truth.

**Verse.** My mouth shall speak the praise of the Lord, and all flesh shall bless his holy name.

**Offertory.** Take courage, and now do not fear; for behold, our God will render judgment. He himself will come and save us.

**Verse 1.** Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall hear; then the lame shall leap like a stag, and the tongue of the mute shall be clear.

**Verse 2.** Hear, therefore, O house of Jacob [Note: In the same place: “House of David”]: Is it a small thing for you to offer battle to men, since the Lord offers battle? Therefore the Lord will give you a sign. Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb [Note: In the same place: “shall receive”] and shall bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel.

[Note: The words enclosed in brackets are absent from the manuscript. In Pamelius they are given as this two-part Offertory.]

> **Offertory.** Hail, Mary, full of grace; the Lord is with you; blessed are you among women.  
> **Verse 1.** How shall this happen to me?  
> **Verse 2.** Therefore the holy one who will be born from you shall be called the Son of God.

**At Communion.** Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel. [Col. 0643C] [Note: In the editions of Pamelius and others: “Psalm as above.” The same words noted above are read at the end of the Mass both for the feast of St. Lucy and for the Third Sunday, and with excellent sense; this means that during Communion the entire Psalm from which the Antiphon was taken was customarily sung. But on Wednesday this Antiphon at Communion is taken from the Gospel; therefore “Psalm as above” entered the edition by error, contrary to the evidence of the manuscripts.]

**Psalm.** The heavens declare.  
**Responsory.** In the sun he has set.

## Friday

**Antiphon.** You are near, O Lord, and all your ways are truth; from the beginning I learned from your testimonies that you are forever.

**Psalm.** Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord. [Note: In the manuscript, before this Responsory is written: **AR. You have commanded.**]

**Responsory.** Show us, O Lord, your mercy, and grant us your salvation.

**Verse.** You have blessed your land, O Lord; you have turned away the captivity of Jacob. [Note: In the same place is added Verse 2: “Mercy and truth.”]

**Offertory.** O God, once turned toward us, you will give us life, and your people will rejoice in you.

**At Communion.** Behold, the Lord will come, and all his saints with him, and on that day there will be a great light. [Note: In the printed editions of Pamelius and others: “Psalm as above.” We have corrected this from the manuscript. See note *e* above.]

**Psalm.** Blessed are the undefiled.

**Responsory.** You have commanded.

[Note: In the manuscript: “At St. Peter’s.” But what “in the twelve lessons” signifies, see again in the Book of the Sacraments, on Saturday of the first month, or the Ember days of Lent, col. 41.]

## Saturday in the Twelve Lessons

[Col. 0644A]

Antiphon: “Come and show us your face, O Lord, who are seated above the cherubim, and we shall be saved.” Psalm: “O Shepherd of Israel, give ear, you who lead Joseph like a sheep.” [Note: [Col. 0644D] The manuscript adds: “AR. Stir up.” Something of this kind is always inserted in the manuscript Compendium between the Psalm that follows the Antiphon—which we call the Introit—and the Responsory, now better known by the name Gradual. That it was formerly also occasionally designated by this name is clear from the Sacramentary. At almost the very beginning: “Then follows the Apostle. Likewise the Gradual.” See note 12 to the Sacramentary.]

Responsory: “Lord God of hosts, turn us, and show us your face, and we shall be saved.” Verse: “Stir up your power, O Lord, and come, that you may save us.”

Responsory: “Stir up your power, O Lord, and come, that you may save us.” Verse: “O Shepherd of Israel, give ear, you who lead Joseph like a sheep; you who are seated above the cherubim, appear before Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh.” [Col. 0644B]

### Hymn of the Three Youths

“Blessed are you, O Lord, God of our fathers;  
and worthy of praise and glorious forever.

“And blessed is the name of your glory, which is holy;  
and worthy of praise and glorious forever.

“Blessed are you in the holy temple of your glory;  
and worthy of praise and glorious forever.

“Blessed are you upon the throne of your holy kingdom;  
and worthy of praise and glorious forever.

“Blessed are you upon the holy seat of your divinity;  
and worthy of praise and glorious forever.

[Col. 0644C] “Blessed are you upon the scepter of your divinity;  
and worthy of praise and glorious forever.

“Blessed are you who sit above the cherubim, gazing into the depths;  
and worthy of praise and glorious forever.

“Blessed are you who walk upon the wings of the winds;  
and worthy of praise and glorious forever.

“Let all your angels and saints bless you; and let them praise and glorify you forever.

“Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit;

“and praise, and honor, and power, and dominion.

“As it was in the beginning, is now, and ever shall be, world without end. Amen.

“And praise, and honor, and power, and dominion.”

### Sunday after the Nativity of the Lord

Antiphon: “While all things were held in deepest silence, and the night was halfway through its course, your almighty Word, O Lord, came from heaven, from the royal seats.” Psalm: “The Lord reigns; he is clothed in beauty; the Lord is clothed with strength and has girded himself with power.”

Responsory: “You are beautiful beyond the sons of men; grace has been poured upon your lips; therefore God has blessed you forever.” Verse: “My heart has uttered a good word; I speak my works to the king; my tongue is the pen of a swift-writing scribe.”

Alleluia: “The Lord reigns; he is clothed in beauty.”

Offertory: “For God established the world.” [Col. 0649C]

Communion: “Take the child and his mother, and go into the land of Judah, for those who sought the child’s life are dead.” Psalm: “As above.”

[Note: [Col. 0650D] It is absent from the Compendium and Val. Cl. It is noted in Theoderic, but the Mass “While all things were held in silence” is assigned, as above, on Sunday.]

### Vigil of the Epiphany

Antiphon: “The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you.” Psalm: “Why did the nations rage?” 661

Responsory: “With you is the beginning on the day of your power, in the splendors of the saints; from the womb, before the morning star, I begot you.”

[Note: [Col. 0650D] It is absent from our manuscripts on the holy day. In the Compendium and Theoderic, the station is at Saint Peter.]

### Epiphany of the Lord: On the holy day, at Mass

Antiphon: “Behold, the Lord the ruler has come, and the kingdom is in his hand, and power and dominion.” Psalm: “Give the king your judgments, O God, and your righteousness to the king’s son.”

Responsory: “All shall come from Sheba, bringing gold and frankincense and proclaiming praise to the Lord.” Verse: “Arise and shine, Jerusalem, for the glory of the Lord has risen upon you.”

Alleluia: “We saw his star in the East, and we came with gifts to adore the Lord.”

Offertory: “The kings of Tarshish and the islands shall offer gifts; the kings of Arabia and Sheba shall bring presents; and all the kings of the earth shall adore him; all nations shall serve him.” Verse 1: “Give the king your judgments, O God, and your righteousness to the king’s son; judge your people with righteousness and your poor with judgment.” Verse 2: “In his days righteousness shall arise, and abundance of peace, until the moon is lifted up; and he shall rule from sea to sea.” Verse: “Let the mountains receive peace for your people, and the hills righteousness.”

Communion: “We saw his star in the East, and we came with gifts to adore the Lord.” Psalm: “Give the king your judgments,” as above.

### Sunday after the Epiphany

[Note: [Col. 0650D] Alternatively, “after the Theophany,” as it is read in Val. Cl.]

Antiphon: “Upon a lofty throne I saw a man seated, whom a multitude of angels, singing together, adores; behold, the name of whose empire is eternal.” Psalm: [Col. 0650B] “Shout joyfully to God, all the earth; sing a psalm to his name; give glory to his praise.”

Responsory: “Blessed is the Lord, the God of Israel, because he alone has done great wonders from eternity.” Verse: “Let the mountains receive peace for the people, and the hills righteousness.”

Alleluia: “Shout joyfully to God our helper; sing joyfully to the God of Jacob; sing a psalm with the harp.”

Offertory: “Shout joyfully to God, all the earth; serve the Lord with gladness. Enter into his presence with exultation, for the Lord himself is God.” Verse 1: “He made us, and not we ourselves.” Verse 2: “Praise his name, for the Lord is gracious.”

Communion: “Son, why have you treated us so? Behold, your father and I, in sorrow, were seeking you. And why were you seeking me? Did you not know that I must be in the things that belong to my Father?” Psalm: “Shout joyfully to God, all the earth; sing a psalm to his name; give glory to his praise,” as above. [Col. 0650C]

[Note: [Col. 0650D] It is not listed in the Compendium and Val. Cl.]

### The octave of the Epiphany, as on the day

### The Nativity of Saint Felix in Pincis

[Note: [Col. 0650D] In the Compendium and Val. Cl., “of Saint Felix the priest and confessor” is absent.]

Antiphon: “The mouth of the righteous shall meditate wisdom, and his tongue shall speak judgment; the law of his God is in his heart.” Psalm: “Do not be jealous of the wicked; do not envy those who commit iniquity.”

Responsory: “The Lord has sworn, and he will not repent: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.” Verse: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand.” 662

Alleluia: “The righteous shall not be disturbed.”

Offertory: “You crowned him with glory and honor, and established him over the works of your hands, O Lord.”

Communion: “You placed upon his head, O Lord, a crown of precious stone.” Psalm: “Psalm 20.”

### Second Sunday after the Epiphany

[Col. 0650D]

Antiphon: “Let every land adore you, O God, and sing to you; let it sing a psalm to your name, O Most High.” Psalm: “Shout joyfully to God, all the earth; sing a psalm to his name; give glory to his praise.”

Responsory: “The Lord sent his word and healed them, and rescued them from their destruction.” [Col. 0651A] Verse: “Let them confess to the Lord’s mercies and his wonders to the children of men.”

Alleluia: “Praise the Lord, all his angels; praise him, all his powers.”

Offertory: “Shout joyfully to God, all the earth; sing a psalm to his name. Come and hear, and I will tell you, all you who fear God, how great things the Lord has done for my soul.” [Note: [Col. 0651D] Compendium: “To all of you . . . alleluia, alleluia.”] Verse 1: “I will pay you my vows, which my lips have uttered distinctly.” Verse 2: “My mouth spoke in my tribulation; I will offer you burnt offerings rich in marrow.”

Communion: “The Lord says: Fill the jars with water and take them to the master of the feast. When the master of the feast had tasted the water made wine, he said to the bridegroom: You have kept the good wine until now. Jesus performed this first sign before his disciples.” Psalm: “As above.”

[Note: [Col. 0651D] In the manuscripts: “The seventeenth day before the Kalends of February, Saint Marcellus, pope.”]

### The Nativity of Saint Marcellus

[Col. 0651B]

Antiphon: “The Lord established a covenant of peace with him, and made him a prince, so that the dignity of the priesthood might belong to him forever.” Psalm: “I shall sing the mercies of the Lord forever.”

Responsory: “I have found David my servant,” etc. Verse: “The enemy shall profit nothing against him, and the son of iniquity shall not add to harming him.” [Note: [Col. 0651D] Compendium: “shall not harm him.”]

Alleluia: “I have found David my servant.”

Offertory: “My truth and my mercy are with him, and in my name his horn shall be exalted.” Verse 1: “I have placed my help upon the mighty, and exalted the chosen one from my people; for my hand shall help him, and my arm shall strengthen him.” Verse 2: [Note: [Col. 0651D] Compendium: “I shall not remove my mercy from him; his seat is in my sight.”] “My mercy.”

Communion: “Lord, you delivered five talents to me; behold, I have gained five more. Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much, says the Lord.” [Note: [Col. 0651D] The same source: “Enter into the joy of your lord.”] [Col. 0651C] Psalm: “The mercies of the Lord,” as above.

[Note: [Col. 0651D] Namely, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February, as is noted in the manuscripts. On this day the feast of the Chair of Saint Peter is now celebrated, but it is not recorded in our manuscripts, nor in the Sacramentary, nor in the Roman Calendar of Fronto, nor in Bede’s Martyrology, nor in many other similar records. It is nevertheless marked in Usuard and Ado; indeed, also in an ancient Martyrology bearing Jerome’s name, and in another nine-hundred-year-old one mentioned by Mabillon in *On Gallican Liturgy*, p. 121. We readily agree with those who think that formerly the Chair, or episcopate, of Saint Peter was not accustomed to be celebrated on one and the same day, but in January in Gaul and in February at Rome. Hence arose the occasion for celebrating two solemnities of the Chair of Saint Peter. Since some celebrated that same Chair, that same episcopate, in January and others in February, afterward 18 January was consecrated to the memory of the Roman Chair, and 22 February to the Antiochene. From this it is clear that Paul IV did not so much institute the feast of the Roman Chair on 18 January as restore it, as he himself declares in the letters of this restoration, dated 1558. In the constitutions of Saint Perpetuus, bishop of Tours, concerning vigils, one reads: “On the nativity of Saint John, at the basilica of Lord Martin. On the nativity of Saint Peter’s episcopate, at his own basilica.”]

### The Nativity of Saint Prisca

Antiphon: “I spoke of your testimonies before kings, and I was not ashamed; I meditated on your commandments, which I loved exceedingly.” Psalm: “Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord.”

Responsory: “In your beauty and your splendor, give heed; proceed prosperously, and reign.” Verse: “Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions.”

Alleluia: “Grace has been poured upon your lips; therefore God has blessed you forever.” 663

Offertory: “The daughters of kings are in your honor.” Verse 1: “My heart has uttered a good word.” Verse 2: “In your beauty.”

Communion: “I have done judgment and righteousness.” Psalm: [Col. 0651D] “As above.”

[Note: [Col. 0652D] Assigned in the manuscripts to the thirteenth day before the Kalends of February.]

### The Nativity of the holy martyrs Fabian and Sebastian

[Col. 0652A]

Antiphon: “Let the groaning of the prisoners enter into your presence, O Lord; repay our neighbors sevenfold in their bosom; avenge the blood of your servants that has been shed.” Psalm: “O God, the nations have entered into your inheritance; they have defiled your holy temple; they have made Jerusalem a place for keeping fruit.”

Responsory: “Glorious is God in his saints, wondrous in his majesty.” Verse: “Your right hand, O Lord, has been magnified in strength; your right hand has broken the enemy.”

Alleluia: “Your saints, O Lord.”

Offertory: “Rejoice in the Lord and exult.” Verse 1: “Blessed are those whose.” Verse 2: “For this every holy person shall pray to you at an opportune time.”

Communion: “The multitude of the sick and those troubled by unclean spirits came to him, because power went out from him and healed them all.” [Col. 0652B] Psalm: “O God, the nations have entered into your inheritance.”

[Note: [Col. 0652D] In the manuscripts: the twelfth day before the Kalends of February, the Nativity of Saint Agnes.]

### The Nativity of Saint Agnes

Antiphon: “Sinners waited for me in order to destroy me; I understood your testimonies, O Lord; I saw the end of all perfection; your commandment is exceedingly broad.” Psalm: “Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord.”

Responsory: “Grace has been poured upon your lips.” Verse: “Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions.”

Alleluia: “In your beauty and your splendor; therefore God has blessed you forever.”

Offertory: “Virgins shall be brought to the king after her; her companions shall be brought to you.”

Communion: “The five wise virgins.” Psalm: “As above.”

### Third Sunday after the Epiphany

[Col. 0652C]

Antiphon: “Adore God, all his angels. Zion heard and rejoiced, and the daughters of Judah exulted.” Psalm: “The Lord reigns; let the earth exult; let the many islands rejoice.”

Responsory: “The nations shall fear your name, O Lord, and all the kings of the earth your glory.” Verse: “For the Lord has built Zion, and he shall be seen in his majesty.” [Note: [Col. 0652D] In the Compendium: “Alleluia. The Lord reigns; let the earth exult; let the many islands rejoice.”]

Alleluia: “Exult in God our helper; shout joyfully to the God of Jacob; sing a psalm with the harp.”

Offertory: “The right hand of the Lord has shown strength; the right hand of the Lord has exalted me; I shall not die, but live, and recount the works of the Lord.” Verse 1: “In tribulation I called upon the Lord, and he heard me in an open place, because the Lord is my helper.” Verse 2: “I was thrust and shaken so as to fall, but the Lord received me and became my salvation.” [Col. 0652D]

Communion: “All marveled at the things that proceeded from the mouth of God.” [Col. 0653A] Psalm: “The Lord reigns; let the earth exult.”

[Note: [Col. 0653D] In the manuscripts: the eleventh day before the Kalends of February, Saint Vincent. Val. Cl. adds: “deacon and martyr.”]

### The Nativity of Saint Vincent

Antiphon: “The righteous shall rejoice in the Lord, shall hope in him, and all the upright of heart shall be praised.” Psalm: “Hear, O God, my prayer when I entreat you; rescue my soul from fear of the enemy.”

Responsory: “You placed upon his head, O Lord, a crown of precious stone.” Verse: “You granted him the desire of his soul, and did not deprive him of the will of his lips.”

Alleluia: “Blessed is the man who fears the Lord; he greatly desires his commandments.” 664

Offertory: “You crowned him with glory and honor, and established him over the works of your hands, O Lord.” Verse: “O Lord, our Lord.”

Communion: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.” [Col. 0653B] Psalm: “Hear, O God.”

[Note: [Col. 0653D] Namely, the fifth day before the Kalends of February. In Val. Cl. it reads: “The octave of Saint Agnes, of the Nativity.”]

### Saint Agnes, the second time

Antiphon: “All the rich among the people shall entreat your face.” Psalm: “My heart has uttered a good word.”

Responsory: “In your beauty.” Verse: “Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions.”

Alleluia: “Grace has been poured upon your lips; therefore God has blessed you forever.”

Offertory: “Grace has been poured.”

Communion: “The kingdom of heaven is like.” Psalm: “As above.”

[Note: [Col. 0653D] In the Compendium: “The fourth day before the Nones of February, the Purification of Mary; Collect at Saint Adrian.” In Val. Cl.: “The Nativity of Saint Simeon; collect at Saint Adrian, station at Saint Mary.” In Theoderic: “Hypapante, station at Saint Mary; collect at Saint Adrian.”]

### The Purification of Saint Mary, at the Procession

Antiphon: [Note: [Col. 0653D] The Greek words read here are absent from the manuscripts.]

Χαῖρε κεχαριτωμένη — “Hail, full of grace,”  
θεοτόκε παρθένε — “Virgin Mother of God,”  
ἐκ σοῦ γὰρ ἀνέτειλεν — “for from you has arisen”  
ὁ ἤλιος τῆς δικαιοσύνης — “the Sun of righteousness,”  
φωτίζων τοὺς ἐν σκότει — “illuminating those who are in darkness”;  
εὐφραίνου καὶ σὺ — “rejoice also, you,”  
πρεσβῦτα δίκαιε — “righteous elder,”  
δεχόμενε ἐν ὠλέναις — “receiving in your arms”  
τὸν ἐλευθερώτην — “the liberator”  
τῶν ψυχῶν ἠμῶν — “of our souls,”  
χαριζόμενον ἡμῖν — “granting us”  
καὶ τὴν ἀνάστασιν — “the resurrection.”

Verse:

Κατακόσμησον τὸν θάλαμόν σου, Σιὼν — “Adorn your bridal chamber, Zion,”  
καὶ ὑπόδεξαι τὸν βασιλέα Χριστὸν — “and receive the King Christ,”  
ἁσπάζου τὴν Μαρίαν — “greet Mary,”  
τὴν οὐράνιον αὐλὴν — “the heavenly court” [Latin: “the heavenly gate”];  
αὐτὴ γὰρ βαστάζει τὸν βασιλέα τῆς δόξης — “for she herself carries the King of glory,”  
νεοφύτου φωτὸς ὑπάρχει παρθένος — “the Virgin is of ‘newly planted’ light” [wording uncertain],  
φέρουσα ἐν χερσὶν υἱὸν πρὸ ἑωσφόρου — “bringing in her hands the Son before the morning star,”  
ὃν λαβὼν Σιμεὼν ἐν ὠλέναις αὐτοῦ — “whom Simeon, receiving in his arms,”  
[Col. 0653D] ἐκήρυξεν τοῖς λαοῖς — “proclaimed to the peoples”  
δεσπότην αὐτὸν εἶναι — “to be the Lord”  
ζωῆς καὶ θανάτου — “of life and death,”  
καὶ σωτῆρα τοῦ κόσμου — “and the Savior of the world.”

Verse: “Simeon received an answer from the Holy Spirit that he would not see death unless he had first seen the Christ of the Lord.”

### At the Introit

[Col. 0654A]

Antiphon: “We have received your mercy, O God, in the midst of your temple; according to your name, O God, so also is your praise to the ends of the earth; your right hand is full of righteousness.” Psalm: “Great is the Lord and exceedingly worthy of praise, in the city of our God, on his holy mountain.”

Responsory: “We have received your mercy, O God.” Verse: “As we have heard, so we have seen in the city of the Lord of hosts, in the city of our God; God founded it forever.”

Alleluia: “I will adore toward your holy temple and confess your name in fear of you.”

“Virgins shall be brought to the King.”

“If it falls after Septuagesima.” [Note: [Col. 0654D] No Tract is assigned in the Compendium. In Val. Cl. it reads: “If it falls during Septuagesima, the Tract ‘Shout joyfully’.”]

The following Tract shall be said:

“Grace has been poured upon your lips; therefore God has blessed you forever. In your beauty and your splendor, give heed; proceed prosperously, and reign. Because of truth and meekness and righteousness, your right hand shall lead you wondrously. [Col. 0654B] You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions. Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear; forget your people and your father’s house. And the King shall desire your beauty, for he himself is the Lord your God, and they shall adore him. Virgins shall be brought to the king after her; her companions shall be brought to you. They shall be brought in joy and exultation; they shall be brought into the temple to the King and Lord.” 665

Offertory: “Grace has been poured.” Verse 1: “My heart has uttered a good word.” Verse 2: “In your beauty and your splendor.”

Communion: “Simeon received an answer from the Holy Spirit that he would not see death unless he had seen the Christ of the Lord.” Psalm: “As above.”

[Note: [Col. 0654D] In the Compendium: “The Nones of February, the Passion of Saint Agatha, virgin and martyr.” In Val. Cl.: “The Nativity of Saint Agatha, virgin and martyr.” In Theoderic, she is called simply a martyr.]

### The Nativity of Saint Agatha

[Col. 0654C]

Antiphon: Let us all rejoice in the Lord, celebrating the feast in honor [Note: [Col. 0654D] In the Compendium: “in honor.”] of the martyr Agatha, at whose passion the angels rejoice and praise together the Son of God. Psalm: My heart has uttered.

Responsory: God will help her with his countenance; God is in her midst, she will not be shaken. Verse: The force of the river makes glad the city of God; the Most High has sanctified his dwelling.

Tract: Those who sow in tears [Note: [Col. 0654D] In the Compendium: “will reap in joy.” And below, “carrying their seed” instead of “casting their seed.”] will reap in exultation. Going, they went and wept, casting their seed; but coming, they will come with exultation, carrying their sheaves.

Offertory: Virgins will be brought to the King after her.

Communion: He who deigned to heal me from every wound and to restore my breast to my own body—I call upon him as the living Lord. Psalm as above.

## Feast of Saint Valentine

[Col. 0654D]

Antiphon: In your power, O Lord, the righteous man will rejoice, etc. Psalm: He asked for life. [Note: [Col. 0654D] In the same source: “Psalm: O Lord, in your power,” etc.] Responsory: Blessed is the man who fears the Lord; he greatly desires his commandments. Verse: His offspring will be mighty upon the earth; the generation of the upright will be blessed.

Tract: You granted him the desire of his soul; you did not deprive him of the request of his lips, etc.

Offertory: In your power, O Lord, the righteous man will rejoice.

Communion: Great is his glory.

Psalm XX.

[Note: [Col. 0655D] This is absent from the Vallicellian and Compendium manuscripts; but after “the feast of Saint Valentine” one reads: “The fourth day before the Ides of March: the feast of Saint Gregory.” The feast of the Chair of Saint Peter appears in Theoderic, where seven Sundays after Epiphany and before Septuagesima are also assigned.
