Religion is indeed next to divine faith: by established signs and ceremonies instituted through common agreement, it worships and venerates the supreme Majesty whom faith believes and reveres. And just as most, not to say all, of the Churches of the West trace the origin of their faith to the Roman Church, so it is fitting that from the same source they should derive the manner and form of divine worship.

Certainly, when I reflect upon the various rites that the piety of our ancestors established in the principal Churches of Gaul, and that it has transmitted to us, for the most part unimpaired, I seem to see [II] a certain image of the Roman rites—such, of course, as we observe in the ancient books.

It is therefore not without reason that devout and learned men—as Cassander observed—judge that “nothing of this kind can be found more excellent than the Roman Order itself, which all who have written about ecclesiastical rites and divine offices acknowledge as their prince and head, and to which they grant the highest authority, so that all writings of this kind are nothing other than commentaries on this book.” Those who are less informed should not therefore be heeded if they think that this subject is not worthy of the dignity that would merit its treatment with such apparatus. If anyone is persuaded of this, let him remember that this labor and reflection are not unworthy even of the wisest men under the New Law, since under the Old Law—where the gravity of our mysteries was only sketched—God himself did not consider it beneath him to describe the sacred rites by which he wished to be worshiped and honored.

Indeed, men of great reputation did not so disdain this kind of subject that they failed to devote their studies to it. To pass over Cassander, Hittorpius, Ralph, dean of Tongeren, and others of the same sort for the moment, Onuphrius Panvinius illuminated this ritual subject in his writings; and we would possess a study by Salmasius on the matter, if his death had not forestalled his plan. I call Salmasius himself as witness, for in the preface to his work on Solinus he says that he had resolved to devote himself to illuminating this author, setting aside for a time the commentaries on the ritual history of the whole ancient Church that he had in mind and in hand. Whether these commentaries were completed and finished by him, I confess that I do not know.

[Col. 0852A] As for Onuphrius, his complete work survives in manuscript in the Vatican Library, and a copy of it is kept in the royal library. This work, however, presents not so much a commentary by Onuphrius as a collection of the ancient ritual books of the Roman Church. The collection is preceded by a dedicatory letter from Onuphrius to Alessandro Farnese, cardinal bishop of Sabina and chancellor of the supreme Apostolic See. That letter contains an extensive preface designed to elucidate, from ancient sources, the action of the sacred assembly.

There follow four little books on the Roman Order, as published by Hittorpius; then the Micrologus; next, an interpretation of ecclesiastical words that seem obscure or barbarous [III]; and after these, an index of the stations celebrated in our own time throughout the year in the individual churches of the City. All this is followed by the Ritual Book of Cardinal Censius, chamberlain of the Holy Roman Church, which Onuphrius divides into three parts, changing the author’s arrangement. Finally, the whole work is concluded by an exposition of the Mass, which he himself composed from the sayings and opinions of the Fathers, proceeding through commonplaces that others later pursued.

There were also others among the ancients who had the same plan and purpose, namely, to illuminate the Roman rites. Melchior Hittorpius gathered most of them into a single body; his edition is in everyone’s hands, so that it is unnecessary to list the names of those authors here. To these must be added Rupert, John Beleth, and both Durands, followed by a great host of more recent writers, among whom the most distinguished is the late Cardinal Bona. Among those ancient authors, Amalarius and the man who chose to conceal himself under the humble name of Micrologus examined the books of the Roman Order with particular diligence, and from them either corrected or illuminated the rites of other Churches.

[Col. 0852C] Amalarius, apparently a cleric of the Church of Metz, was chorepiscopus of Lyon. For this judgment we have as authority Florus, a deacon of that same Church, who in an earlier letter against Amalarius himself, still unpublished, mentions three of his works: first, a large Codex extending through four volumes—that is, books—which he called the *Official*; next, an Antiphonary that he claimed to have arranged and corrected; and finally, a new volume, which he called the *Embolus* of his little works, and which he had handsomely bound at Lyon and distinguished with silk ribbons.

These details come from Florus’s first letter against the false inventions of Amalarius, formerly chorepiscopus of Lyon, concerning the tripartite body of the Lord. In this letter Florus attacks Amalarius rather harshly, as do Agobard and the bishop of Lyon himself. For although Amalarius perhaps went too far in seeking mystical meanings in the sacred rites used by the Church, he should not nevertheless have been treated with such bitterness—a man learned for his time, who was certainly guided by devout religion and by zeal to illuminate sacred matters.

The first two of his little works have been published, namely, the *Official* and the book on the Antiphonary; but we believe that the *Embolus* still lies in darkness [IV]. Students of ecclesiastical matters use those two published works with benefit, reading them with eyes very different from those of Florus and Agobard. Amalarius called the *Official* a little book after the Fathers of the Fourth Council of Toledo, in canon 26.

Three books of Agobard survive, written against Amalarius. The first is a book on Psalmody, in which he accuses Amalarius as though he were a foolish and wicked slanderer because he introduced certain fabrications of human ingenuity into the nocturnal offices. He explains the same matter in a second book on the correction of the Antiphonary, in which he criticizes certain corrections to Antiphons and Responsories made by Amalarius. Agobard himself was corrected by the most modest Joseph Maria Thomasius in his notes on the Roman Responsorials and Antiphonaries, where certain restorations by Amalarius are defended on the authority of ancient codices of the Roman Church. Thus rigid censors sometimes call down upon themselves the just censure of others. Finally, Agobard’s third offspring is directed against the four books of Amalarius the abbot—that is, against his *Official*, in which Agobard mocks certain moral interpretations.

Florus the deacon, and finally priest of the Church of Lyon, was no less hostile to Amalarius. Amalarius was challenged by him at the synod of Quierzy, and accused by him at the council of bishops held at Theodone’s Villa of having said that the body of Christ was threefold and of everywhere translating sacred rites into mystical meanings.

Florus himself explains what took place at both synods, both in the letter just mentioned, in a subsequent little work, and in another letter to the Fathers of the council assembled at Theodone’s Villa. The first letter is addressed to Drogo, master and most illustrious pontiff of the sacred council; to Hetti, bishop of Trier; to Aldric, most reverend bishop of Le Mans; to Rabanus, venerable abbot; and, from the province of Lyon, to Alberic, bishop of Langres.

The first and principal head of the accusation is that Amalarius himself, the distinguished teacher, taught that the body of Christ was threefold and tripartite in such a way that there were three bodies of Christ: the first, which he himself assumed; the second, in us who walk upon the earth; and the third, in those who lie buried. Therefore, he said, three parts ought to be made in the sacrifice of the Mass: one in the chalice for Christ, another on the paten for the living, and a third on the altar for the dead.

The second head of the accusation is that the same Amalarius transferred most of the rites of the sacrifice to moral and figurative meanings, as I have just said. The third and final charge is that he regarded the book of the Roman Order as possessing such authority that he attempted to explain it almost word for word, even though he admitted that this book had been unknown to the Roman archdeacon whose traditions he claimed as his authority.

[Col. 0853D] Yet far from having harmed the Church by explaining the book of the Roman Order, the Church is, on the contrary, greatly indebted to him, because he alone among the ancient authors has confirmed for us the antiquity and dignity of this book.

Besides the works mentioned above, Amalarius composed an eclogue on the Roman Order, which the most learned Baluze published in an appendix to the *Capitularies*. In the title of this little work Amalarius is called an abbot both in the Codex of Saint Gall, on which the Baluze edition was carefully based, and in the Einsiedeln manuscript, as also in the title of the third little book that Agobard composed against Amalarius. What has just been said about him is sufficient.

[Col. 0854A] The knowledge we possess of the Micrologus is more obscure than his date. In some copies the book is inscribed *Micrologus of John*, and in others *of John the Bishop*; but who that John was is uncertain. The conjecture that he was a Gaul arises from chapter 11, in which he mentions a Prayer according to the Gallican Order. It is certainly inferred that he was not a German from the fact that he makes little of the decree of the Council of Mainz concerning the designation of the four Ember fasts.

Guido of Arezzo also gave this same title to his work on Music. But this Micrologus, whoever he may be, is undoubtedly another person, understood from chapters 14 and 17 to have lived during the time of Gregory VII and Anselm of Lucca. He praises and interprets the Roman Order in many places, for example in chapters 9, 10, 11, and 17, as well as elsewhere.

George Cassander was the first to arrange for the Roman Order to be printed at Cologne in 1561; seven years later Melchior Hittorpius reprinted it there together with other ancient writers on ecclesiastical matters. Before both of them, however, Christophorus Marcellus, elected archbishop of Corcyra, had published at Venice three books of *Ecclesiastical Rites, or Sacred Ceremonies of the Holy Roman Church*, and had done so with the pontifical privilege of Leo X, granted toward the end of 1516.

[Col. 0854B] Paris de Crassis, then master of ceremonies in the City, took this edition very seriously, believing that such secret rites of the Church ought not to be brought before the general public, lest they eventually fall into contempt. Accordingly, he lodged complaints about the edition with the pope, before whom he accused the archbishop of Corcyra of plagiarism, because he had published under his own name the work of Augustinus Piccolomineus on sacred ceremonies.

Paris tells the story as follows in his *Ceremonial*:

“The reverend elected archbishop of Corcyra this year, when he had delivered a ceremonial book to be printed at Venice—or rather, so to speak, had prostituted it to the public—perhaps because, if I may say so with his permission, he is exceedingly ignorant of ecclesiastical rites, having only a few days earlier been transferred from the profession of a Venetian merchant to the clerical state, and perhaps not yet capable of such doctrines, sent the books thus printed to various places in Italy and beyond it, as merchants customarily do, even to the City, for sale.

“When I learned of this, I immediately went to the pope, expressed my distress, and begged him, in the interests of justice, to deign to prevent so great a sacrilege, lest he allow the ceremonies of his Most Holy Apostolic See—which had always been preserved in the more secret Palatine library—to be polluted under his pontificate by their publication.

“When his Holiness had rightly and graciously assented, certain fellow countrymen of the Corcyran, who happened to be present, dared to intervene on the other side, because this would result in a loss to their trade. They asked for what reasons sacred ceremonials also could not be published, like Missals and Pontificals. Since at that time it was not permitted to do so in a few words, I finally thought that I had satisfied both the reasoning stated above and their request in the more extended manner that follows.

“But he himself also satisfied me on behalf of the honor of my colleague—or rather my teacher—the bishop of Pienza, the true author of this *Ceremonial* book. After erasing his name and title, this Corcyran did not blush to claim for himself a false title and the name of the author.”

[Col. 0854D] What followed is not found in the manuscript codex, from which someone removed several quires.

From the diary of the same author, however, certain further details—though not all—can be supplied, and these should be briefly sampled here. When Paris learned that the *Ceremonial* book of Bishop Augustinus of Pienza had been published at Venice by the elected archbishop of Corcyra with the true author’s name suppressed, he first referred the matter to the cardinals. Many of them were disturbed that the sacred ceremonies and their mysteries had been made public.

The complaints were then brought before the pope. At first disturbed by what he heard, he said that he would do whatever pleased the cardinals. [VII] But because the cardinal of Santa Croce had perhaps been responsible for having the book printed, he said that it was not a bad thing. Nevertheless, he took care that no copy of it should be sold until a decision on the matter had been made in the next consistory.

[Col. 0855A] These events took place in the year 1517, on 11 March. In the following month, after the feast of Saint Mark, Paris read in consistory a lengthy letter that he had written on the subject. In it he attempted to refute those who thought that the ceremonies of the Christian religion ought to be published for the public benefit of mortals. He said that, if this permission once prevailed, the veneration owed to the supreme pontiff would be greatly diminished. For since, on account of these sacred secrets—which by their greatness and variety seemed to display a kind of divinity—the pope was regarded and believed to be like some god on earth, once these matters were published he would necessarily fall from that opinion and be returned to the class of other mortals.

He therefore declared that the elected archbishop of Corcyra deserved severe punishment because he had stolen the book of the ceremonies of the Holy Roman Church and rashly brought it to light, suppressing even the name of the true author; indeed, because he had introduced a thousand or more corruptions into the printed books. Finally, Paris requested that the recently printed book of ceremonies be completely burned together with its false author, or at least that the author himself be corrected and punished.

The pope, however, ordered Paris’s petitions to be communicated to three cardinals so that they might examine them. [Col. 0855B] I have thought it worthwhile to report these matters briefly; they will be understood more fully from Paris’s own letter and narrative, which are to be printed at the end of this volume.

As for the demands of Paris, certainly that elected archbishop of Corcyra deserved correction because he had attributed to himself an alien work, taking it away from its true and genuine author. But he did not deserve such rage for having published a book of ceremonies, as though he were guilty of violating papal majesty. For those who think correctly within the Christian religion do not measure the veneration due to the supreme pontiff by such secret ceremonies, but by the fact that he is the head of the Catholic Church and the successor of blessed Peter in the chief see—especially when he adorns that supreme dignity with a corresponding holiness of life, as we now perceive in the most blessed Pope Innocent XI.

Nor did Paris’s request in fact succeed according to his wishes, since neither the published book nor its editor suffered the punishment of fire. Why should both have been burned, when the pope had protected them by privilege? Are there such angers in heavenly minds?

## II. On the Roman Order and on the various authors and books that treat the rites of the Holy Roman Church

[Col. 0855C]

We possess no book older concerning the rites of the Roman Church than the one commonly entitled the *Roman Order*. Most people assign its antiquity to the eighth century, and it is clear that it cannot be dated later than that, since Amalarius, an author of the ninth century, frequently praises little books on the Roman Order and composed commentaries on them.

Nevertheless, I believe that the Roman Order is older than the eighth century and should be traced back either to the time of Pope Gelasius or at least to that of Gregory the Great. Certainly, the rubrics prescribed for Holy Week in the Gregorian Sacramentary occur word for word in the first Roman Order that we are about to publish.

Moreover, the reason we should not defer it to the pontificate of Innocent I is that it contains no mention of the *fermentum*—the Eucharistic bread sent to the titular churches of the City—although Innocent prescribed this in his letter to Decentius. Nevertheless, in our first Roman Order the Eucharist itself is [Col. 0855D] given the name *fermentum*.

We understand from Amalarius that there were formerly not one but several booklets of the Roman Ordo. He writes as follows in chapter 52 of his *Antiphonary*, where he discusses the Office of Easter Week:

> It is solemnly known that our mother, the Roman Church, sings three psalms before the Gospel hymn, and two after the hymn, at various altars in different places, most often, however, at the Cross and at the fonts, as we learn from the writings that contain the Roman Ordo in various booklets.

These booklets differed not only according to their various subjects—for example, the booklet on the pontifical Mass, the booklet on the episcopal Mass according to the rite of the Roman Church, the booklet on baptism, the booklet on sacred orders, and so forth—but also with respect to one and the same subject. This is evident from the passage of Amalarius just cited, where he cites different booklets for one and the same Office of Easter Week. [Col. 0856A] Hence, following the judgment of the ancients, we distinguish as many booklets of the Roman Ordo as are the writings on the same or different subjects concerning Roman rites that we cite.

[Col. 0856A]

[IX] First we present three exceedingly ancient booklets on the pontifical Mass; these are followed by two others on the episcopal Mass according to the rite of the Roman Church. After them come booklets on the order of baptism and on sacred ordinations. All these writings were composed before the ninth or tenth century. They are followed by authors from the twelfth century: Benedict the canon of Saint Peter under Innocent II; Cencius de Sabellis, cardinal under Celestine III; also the *Ceremonial* published by order of Gregory X; the *Ordinary* of Cardinal Jacobus Gaietanus; and finally the book of ceremonies of Peter Amelius, bishop of Senigallia. This entire collection will be completed by various fragments from the history of John the Deacon concerning the Lateran Basilica, from the diaries of the Roman pontiffs, and from other ancient documents.

At present it is of no use to preface our edition of the various booklets of the Roman Ordo with anything further, since individual introductory notices have been placed before each of them to inform the learned reader. [Col. 0856B] The judgment that should be formed both of these works and of the published Roman Ordo is taught us by Joseph Maria Thomasius, most skilled in these matters, in his scholia on the Responsories:

> The Roman Ordo, he says, was not circulated in ancient times in the form in which it has been published among us. For it was contained in separate booklets, in which the more important offices throughout the year were explained. Moreover, that Roman Ordo published by Hittorp is rather a mixture of various rites according to differing customs, so that, amid such great diversity, it is almost impossible to distinguish the more ancient and more genuine rites without the assistance of those booklets.

Nevertheless, it must be acknowledged that Hittorp’s edition is not to be dismissed and is not entirely without the recommendation of antiquity. For, with certain additions and omissions, it is found both in the Roman Codex of the Vallicellian Library and in our Vendôme manuscript, except for those portions belonging to the first part of Hittorp’s work—that is, to the rite of the pontifical and episcopal Mass. [Col. 0856C] The Vallicellian Codex was written in the time of the Ottonian emperors; the Vendôme manuscript, on the other hand, was written nearly six hundred years ago, during the time of Goffrid, abbot of Vendôme, who perhaps brought this exemplar from Rome. Although many corrections could be made to the printed editions from those two manuscripts, we did not think it worthwhile to reprint the entire work. It has been sufficient for us to present the ancient booklets dealing with the Mass, baptism, and sacred ordinations, either previously unpublished or corrected against the authority of the [X] manuscripts.

We shall refrain here from discussing Benedict the canon, Cencius, and the other authors whom we place after those earlier booklets; we shall treat them in their proper places. Let the preface of Cencius himself to the book of the revenues of the Holy Roman Church be read in Baronius, toward the end of the year 1192, under the following title:

> Here begins the book of the revenues of the Holy Roman Church, composed by Cencius the chamberlain according to the registers of the ancient Fathers and various memoranda, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1192, in the second year of the pontificate of Pope Celestine III.

[Col. 0856D] And shortly afterward:

> I, Cencius, formerly chamberlain of blessed memory of Pope Clement III, but now chamberlain of the lord Pope Celestine III, canon of Saint Mary Major, etc.

So much concerning Cencius. We intended to add to the authors mentioned above the little work of Peter Mallius on the Basilica of Saint Peter in the Vatican, dedicated to Alexander III. But since it contains little of a ritual nature, we shall cite from it only certain fragments relevant to our purpose.

The Roman *Ceremonial* of Augustine Patricius, addressed to Innocent VIII, certainly deserved a place among these ritual books. But since it has already been published, with a few alterations, by the bishop-elect of Corcyra, and has been reprinted many times, we leave the care of a new edition to others. For the present we are content to publish the author’s dedicatory letter to Innocent VIII, which both gives the date of the composition—namely, 1488, on the Kalends of March [March 1]—and vindicates the work for its genuine author, apart from what we reported above from Paris.

[Col. 0857A] Augustine Patricius, previously called Piccolomini through adoption, was appointed bishop of Pienza in 1483 after having served as master of ceremonies to Innocent VIII, and died in 1496, during the pontificate of Alexander VI. We read this recorded in the Chigi Codex, which contains the works of Lactantius. Augustine himself also records certain matters about his own life in his work. In particular, he served Pius II for four years, from whom he received the surname Piccolomini. He was present at the pope’s death and reports his final words.

Worth mentioning is what he writes in book 3, chapter 13, concerning the reverence bishops should show toward cardinals. He says:

> I have heard that some cardinals permit bishops to speak before them while kneeling and, at table, while they wash their hands, to offer the towel in a servile manner. This seems to me utterly absurd. Although, he says, I have often been present at banquets with many most reverend lords, both before and after I was, unworthy though I am, enrolled among the bishops, [Col. 0857B] I have never seen this practice observed. This should be attributed—let me say it with their indulgence—to the laziness and stupidity of those prelates who do such things and who do not recognize the supreme episcopal dignity in the Church of God; or else to their ambition and flattery, by which, in their pursuit of the cardinals’ favor, they disregard the dignity of their own office and servilely disgrace it. As for the cardinals who tolerate such conduct, whether through inattention or for some other reason, I beg them, in the charity of God, to reject such immoderate flattery and to remember that the supreme pontiff is honored by no other title than that of bishop. When he publicly washes his hands, even during a sacred service, it is not a bishop but his chaplain, an auditor of the Rota, who offers the towel. If they happen to see some men like myself, unworthy of such eminence, let them honor in them not the person but the sacred dignity, and let them employ their services in matters appropriate to the dignity of both offices.

The same author adds:

> Nevertheless, it is fitting that bishops, in all matters, publicly and privately, insofar as their dignity permits, honor and revere the most reverend lords the cardinals and, to the best of their ability, assist, obey, and serve them. It is equally fitting that the cardinals themselves receive bishops kindly and [Col. 0857C] honor those whom the supreme pontiff calls “brothers,” not as servants but as fellow servants.”

Thus speaks this religious author with admirable appropriateness.

[Col. 0857D]

## III. On the ancient basilicas and titular churches of the City, the deaconries, and the seven ecclesiastical regions; including the form of the ancient basilicas

Those who first published booklets of the Roman Ordo prefaced them, as though by way of a necessary foundation, with the assertion that there were seven ecclesiastical regions in the city of Rome and with an account of the order that each class occupied within them—presbyters, deacons, and the other sacred ministers. Following in the footsteps of these authors, we have thought it worthwhile to make certain preliminary observations here concerning the ancient basilicas and the Roman clergy, so that the reader may proceed more clearly when reading these rites.

To begin with the churches, four classes may be distinguished in the City. Some were patriarchal, some titular; some were deaconries, and some were oratories or cemeteries. The patriarchal churches had no title because they belonged properly to the supreme pontiff. They did not have a defined people assigned to them but were regarded as belonging to everyone. Such were the Lateran Basilica, the Vatican Basilica, the basilicas of Saint Mary Major, Saint Paul, and Saint Lawrence in the Verano district.

Other major churches were also counted among the patriarchal churches; these likewise lacked a title, such as the basilicas of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, Saint Agnes Outside the Walls, Saint Mary of the Martyrs, and several others of the same kind. In his rescript to Symmachus, prefect, against Eulalius, Honorius Augustus distinguishes between titular churches and places frequented by a notable gathering. Before him, Arcadius, when by law he forbade heretics all the places of the City, says that they were forbidden all places, “whether they are held under the name of churches, or are called deaconries, or even decaneries.” [Col. 0858A] What is meant by the word *decaneries* in this passage is not sufficiently clear; for here, as elsewhere, it is hardly credible that prisons are intended.

Titular churches were called parish churches to which the care of souls was entrusted. At first each had a single presbyter responsible for that care; later there were several, the principal one of whom was called the cardinal presbyter. The titular churches had dioceses or parishes assigned and defined for them. Onuphrius Panvinius, in his book on the bishoprics, titular churches, and deaconries of the City of Rome, asserts that their number gradually increased to twenty-eight and was completed around the time of Innocent I or Zosimus. He also asserts that this number continued almost to his own time—a matter that deserves closer examination.

[Col. 0858B] Pope Cornelius, in his letter to Fabius, bishop of Antioch, as reported by Eusebius, testifies that “in his own time, that is, in the middle of the third century, there were in Rome forty-six presbyters, seven deacons, an equal number of subdeacons, forty-two acolytes, fifty-two exorcists and readers together with doorkeepers, and finally more than fifteen hundred widows, sick persons, and needy people, whom the grace and kindness of God supplied with food.” Thus Eusebius, book 6, chapter 43.

From this passage the highly learned Henri Valois concludes that there were then forty-six basilicas in Rome. Since each presbyter at that time governed his own basilica, if there were forty-six presbyters, it must be said that there were the same number of basilicas. Optatus indeed—as Valois himself observes—in book 6, when discussing the basilicas existing in Rome during the persecution of Diocletian, at which time the Donatist Macrobius arrived there, reports that there were forty or more basilicas. The Donatists were not permitted to enter them and had no place among those forty and more basilicas where they might assemble.

[Col. 0858C] If this passage is compared with Cornelius’s letter, which reports that there were forty-six presbyters in Rome, one will understand from Optatus that an equal number of basilicas existed there in the time of Diocletian—that is, about forty years after Cornelius. Hence Cyprian, in his letter to Cornelius, which is number 58 in the new edition, not without reason calls the Roman clergy exceedingly flourishing.

Those basilicas, then, each of which had its own presbyter, were undoubtedly titular churches. For titular churches are nothing other than basilicas to which particular priests and ministers are assigned and attached. Therefore, well before the time of Innocent I, there were far more than twenty-eight titular churches in the City. This is clearly demonstrated both by the ordination of Pope Boniface I, carried out in 419 with the signatures of approximately seventy presbyters, apart from the others who had tumultuously elected Eulalius during the sedition; and by the Roman synod held under Symmachus in 499, to which sixty-six Roman presbyters subscribed, all of them titular presbyters.

[Col. 0858D] Yet not so many titular churches existed in the City at that time. The practice had already become established whereby several presbyters were assigned to one titular church. Thus, in that synod, one, two, three, or even four presbyters of the same title are sometimes found subscribing. Two presbyters belonged to each of the following titles: Saint Cecilia, Pudentiana, Cyriacus, Pammachius, Nicomedes, Julius, Saint Clement, Saint Sabina, Saint Cyriacus, Tigrida, Gaius, Lucina, Lawrence, and Marcellus. Three belonged to each of the following: Vestina, Saint Chrysogonus, Aequitius, Aemiliana, Crescentia, Eusebius, Anastasia, the Apostles, and Mark. Four belonged to the title of Fasciola.

Since these subscriptions are of some importance for learning the ancient titular churches of the City, it is useful to reproduce them as we transcribed them from the Vallicellian Codex, placing before each the number of the title, except where a title with several presbyters must be repeated.

[Col. 0859A]

1. Caelius Laurentius, archpresbyter, of the title of Praxedes, subscribed here.

2. Januarius, presbyter of the title of Vestina.

3. Marcianus, presbyter of the title of Saint Cecilia.

4. Gordianus, presbyter of the title of Pammachius.

5. Peter, presbyter of the title of Saint Clement. [XIV] Urbicus, presbyter of the title of Saint Clement.

6. Paulinus, presbyter of the title of Julius.

7. Valens, presbyter of the title of Saint Sabina.

8. Peter, presbyter of the title of Chrysogonus. Seranus, presbyter of the title of Vestina.

9. Asterius, presbyter of the title of Pudentiana. Justinus, presbyter of the title of Pudentiana.

10. Felix, presbyter of the title of Aequitius. Redemptus, presbyter of the title of Chrysogonus.

11. Projectitius, presbyter of the title of Damasus.

12. Jobinus, presbyter of the title of Aemiliana.

13. Bonus, presbyter of the title of Crescentiana.

14. Paschasius, presbyter of the title of Eusebius. John, presbyter of the title of Pammachius.

15. Sebastianus, presbyter of the title of Nicomedes.

16. Martinus, presbyter of the title of Cyriacus. Epiphanius, presbyter of the title of Cyriacus.

17. Andreas, presbyter of the title of Saint Matthew. Servant of God, presbyter of the title of Saint Clement. Opilio, presbyter of the title of Vestina. Peter, presbyter of the title of Chrysogonus.

18. Romanus, presbyter of the title of Tigrida.

19. Marcellinus, presbyter of the title of Julius. Domninus, presbyter of the title of Crescentina. Abundantius, presbyter of the title of Sabina.

20. Marcellinus, presbyter of the title of Romanus.

21. Asellus, presbyter of the title of Bizas. Sebastinus, presbyter of the title of [Col. 0859B] Aequitius. Valentinus, presbyter of the title of Eusebius.

22. Anastasius, presbyter of the title of Anastasia. Genesius, presbyter of the title of Nicomedes. Dionysius, presbyter of the title of Aemiliana.

23. Epiphanius, presbyter of the title of the Apostles. Paulinus, presbyter of the title of Fasciola. Adeodatus, presbyter of the title of Aequitius.

24. Dominicus, presbyter of the title of Prisca. Severus, presbyter of the title of Gaius. Crescentius, presbyter of the title of the Apostles. Septimus, presbyter of the title of Julius. Epiphanius, presbyter of the title of Fasciola.

[XV] 25. Peter, presbyter of the title of Praxedes.

26. Hilarus, presbyter of the title of Lucina.

27. Laurentius, presbyter of the title of Saint Lawrence. Julianus, presbyter of the title of Anastasia. Vincemalus, presbyter of the title of Crescentia.

28. Venantius, presbyter of the title of Mark. Paulus, presbyter of the title of Saint Lawrence. Acontius, presbyter of the title of Fasciola. Agapitus, presbyter of the title of the Apostles. Benedictus, presbyter of the title of Gaius. Redemptus, presbyter of the title of Tigrida.

29. Stephanus, presbyter of the title of Marcellus. Julianus, presbyter of the title of Anastasia. Cyprianus, presbyter of the title of Mark. Bonifacius, presbyter of the title of Cecilia. Timotheus, presbyter of the title of Marcellus. Victorius, presbyter of the title of Sabina. Eutyches, presbyter of the title of Aemiliana.

30. Marcus, presbyter of the title of Lucina. Abundius, presbyter of the title of Mark. Stephanus, presbyter of the title of Eusebius.

[Col. 0859C] Sixty-six presbyters subscribed.

Among so many subscribers, only thirty titles are counted, evidently because the presbyters of the others were absent or the titles themselves were vacant. The five patriarchal churches are not included among these titles—not even the intramural ones, the Lateran and the Liberian churches, much less the extramural ones, the Vatican, Saint Paul’s, and Saint Lawrence in the Verano district.

Also missing are the titular basilicas of Saint Sylvester, Saint Susanna, Saint Xystus, Saint Balbina, Saints Marcellinus and Peter, and the Four Holy Crowned Martyrs. The presbyters of these titles were witnesses at the Roman synod under Gregory the Great, where the title of Pammachius is called that of Saints John and Paul. Also missing are the titles of Saint Prisca, Saint Potentiana, and Saint Mary, which appear with subscriptions at another synod under Pope Zachary.

[Col. 0859D] The titles were established for two reasons: for the baptism and penance of those who were converted from paganism to the Christian faith, and for the burial places of martyrs. This is what the commonly received text of Anastasius says in his life of Pope Marcellus XXXV, where Marcellus is said to have established twenty-five titles in the City, as though they were dioceses. Although this final statement does not possess sufficient authority to command firm belief, the twofold reason for establishing the titles can nevertheless be accepted.

Accordingly, not all the titles were perhaps parish churches; some were established to honor the burial places of martyrs. Thus, at the Council of Chalcedon, *martyria*—that is, basilicas of martyrs—are counted among the titles. The archpresbyter was the presbyter who was first in ordination among the presbyters of those titles which Anastasius, in the acts of Benedict III, calls the Catholic churches.

But since Innocent I, in his letter to Decentius, clearly distinguishes titles from cemeteries—that is, from churches built over the tombs of martyrs—stating that the titles had a people assigned to them, whereas the cemeteries did not, and that the *fermentum*, or Eucharist, was sent to the titles but not to the cemeteries of the martyrs, it is permissible to assert that there were two kinds of titles: the greater, namely parish churches, and the lesser, which belonged to the isolated basilicas of martyrs.

[Col. 0860A] Public Masses were sometimes celebrated in all these churches, and indeed sometimes in others that were not distinguished by the name of a title, whenever the gathering of the people, because of relics or the cult of martyrs, required it. Thus, on Sundays, the people gathered in the Basilica of Saint Pancras to hear the solemn celebration of Mass, although it was not a titular church before the time of Leo X. Gregory the Great bears witness to this in book 3, letter 18; he also preached a homily there to the people, which is homily 27 in his *Homilies on the Gospels*.

Panciroli observes that this basilica was not granted the honor of a title from the beginning because it lay outside the City; titular status was not granted to extramural basilicas, nor were stations assigned to them unless they were patriarchal churches. Hence stations are frequently recorded as being held at Saint Peter’s, at Saint Paul’s, and at Saint Lawrence Outside the Walls. Concerning these churches, Pope Simplicius decreed that presbyters should remain there for one week on account of penitents and baptism.

[Col. 0860B] Nevertheless, stations were held not only at titular or patriarchal churches but also—as will become clear from what follows—at deaconries, which must now be discussed briefly.

“Among the Romans,” says Sozomen in book 1, chapter 15, “there are no more than seven deacons, in imitation of those who were first ordained by the apostles. Among other peoples, however, the number of deacons is by no means fixed.”

This is certain concerning the Roman deacons who were called *regionarii*, or regional deacons. But there were other deacons in those churches that were distinguished by the name of titles. The regional deacons were regarded as the principal ones. Unlike the others, they were subject not to the titular presbyters but to the archdeacon, who was first among the seven.

Each of them had under his care those deaconries that lay within the region assigned to him. [Col. 0860C] In the deaconries there were hospitals and shelters for the poor, where widows and other needy persons were supported from ecclesiastical charity. Each hospice had a church attached to it, presided over by the Father of the deaconry. He is mentioned in the first Roman Ordo published here and in our *Italian Journey*, page 151, where Ustathius, duke, bequeaths certain estates to the deaconry of Saint Mary in Cosmedin on the condition that the presbyter who at the time was to celebrate the daily Masses should receive three solidi from the Father.

That Father had charge of temporal affairs under the regional deacon. He was sometimes a member of the clerical order and sometimes a layman. Among these was Theodatus, formerly duke and then *primicerius* of the apostolic see—that is, chief of the notaries—and Father of the deaconry of Saint Angelo in Piscina under Gregory II, as is read in an ancient inscription cited by Torrigius in his work on the Vatican crypts.

In the course of time such deaconries were transformed into colleges of clergy, and their resources were reduced to such an extent that they provided no assistance to the poor, for whose benefit they had originally been established. They are now called the titles of cardinal deacons, although when cardinal deacons subscribe their names, they refrain from using the word “title” and express only the church, omitting the region.

[Col. 0860D] When the ancient regional deacons placed their names on the acts of councils, they did not observe the order of the regions but that of their ordination. This is clear from the Roman synod under Symmachus: Cyprian, deacon of the Holy Roman Church of region 7, subscribed first; Anastasius of region 1, second; Citonatus of region 5, third; John, deacon of region 2, fourth; Tarrensis, deacon of region 1, fifth; and Tertullus, deacon of region 4, sixth.

When we find two deacons of the first region, Anastasius and Tarrensis, this indicates that one was a regional deacon and the other a titular deacon of that same region. At first there were only seven regional deacons, corresponding to the seven ecclesiastical regions. [Col. 0861A] Later, namely from the time of Honorius II, their number increased to eighteen, and two further deaconries eventually brought the total to twenty. In this increase of deacons, some were called regional deacons, twelve in number; others were palatine deacons, six in number, placed over the regional deacons.

Cencius includes eighteen deaconries in all, on page 173; Peter Mallius enumerates them here, on page 160.

An old booklet cited by Baronius under the year 1057 distinguishes the subdeacons into three orders, in the following words:

> The subdeacons are twenty-one in all: seven regional subdeacons, who chant the Epistles and lessons at the stations; seven palatine subdeacons, who perform the same service in the Lateran church; and seven others, called the schola cantorum, who sing only when the supreme pontiff is accustomed to celebrate.

Among the first group was that John, subdeacon of the first region, who is said to have removed the pallium from the neck of Pope Silverius and, after stripping him, clothed him in a monastic habit. This was reported to the clergy by Sixtus, subdeacon of the sixth region.

[Col. 0861B] Finally, there were also regional acolytes and titular acolytes, of whom we shall say more after making certain preliminary observations concerning the division of the ecclesiastical regions, knowledge of which is necessary at this point.

The division of the City into seven ecclesiastical regions is well established, since it had previously been divided into fourteen regions by Augustus’s decree. Yet the ecclesiastical division—though much later and now obsolete—is far more obscure than the civil division, which has continued to be maintained.

Of all writers, Nardini most accurately assigned the location and boundaries of each ecclesiastical region, using Anastasius, who places Mount Aventine in the first, the Mamertine Way in the second, the Basilica of Saint Lawrence above Saint Clement in the third, and the head of the Bull in the fifth. The same author identifies the others by conjecture.

To these we may add the title of Vestina in the fourth region, from an ancient inscription read in *Subterranean Rome*, volume 2, or book 4, chapter 25. There Abundantius is praised as an acolyte of the fourth region and of the title of Vestina. This title was later called that of Saints Gervasius and Protasius, or of Saint Vitalis.

[Col. 0861C] Paul Aringhus observes at this point that there were formerly three classes of acolytes in Rome: palatine acolytes, who served the supreme pontiff in the apostolic palace and the Lateran Basilica; station acolytes, whose principal duty was to minister to the same pontiff in the churches where stations were customarily held; and finally regional acolytes, who diligently assisted the deacons in carrying out the sacred functions in the titular churches of their respective regions. Abundantius, mentioned above, belonged to this last group.

Yet it is clearly understood from the first and third Roman Ordines that in those early times there were only two classes of acolytes: regional and titular acolytes. The former served the regional deacons and the pontiff; the latter served the titular presbyters. The palatine acolytes were Lateran acolytes, while the station acolytes were selected from among the regional acolytes.

[Col. 0861D] The Roman Ordo published by Hittorp calls them “parish clergy,” page 31. In discussing their ordination, on page 89, it plainly declares that each was ordained to a title; and it says the same concerning the subdeacons, deacons, and presbyters, page 91.

Gregory the Great, as reported by John the Deacon in book 2, chapter 11, of his *Life*, removed laymen from his chamber and chose clergy and monks as his advisers and intimate associates. With them Gregory, spending his days and nights, left nothing of monastic perfection in the palace and nothing of pontifical discipline in the church.

After the titles and deaconries, the subject requires us to make certain observations here concerning the oratories. These were of two kinds: some were assigned to a cardinal presbyter, while others were attached to no presbyter.

In his letters, when he discusses the dedication of oratories, Gregory the Great regularly requires five conditions: that no body be buried in the place; that a sufficient endowment be assigned; that no baptistery be established there; that there be no cardinal presbyter; and consequently that no public Masses be celebrated there, [Col. 0862A] since only cardinal presbyters were permitted to celebrate them. Thus, if sacred rites were ever to be performed in such oratories, permission had to be obtained from the bishop for a presbyter to do so, so that no other priest might presume to undertake anything of the kind. All this is found in book 2, letter 9, indiction 10, and elsewhere.

There were, however, certain oratories in which it was permitted to have a cardinal presbyter—not as parish priest but as a kind of chaplain. Of this sort was the oratory that the same pontiff permitted Passivus, bishop of Fermo, to dedicate, in book 10, letter 12:

> We also wish you to establish there a cardinal presbyter, so that whenever the aforementioned founder wishes Masses to be celebrated for himself, or whenever the gathering of the faithful requires it, there may be nothing to prevent the solemn celebration of the Mass.

Such titles may be called lesser titles, while others were greater titles, to which the care of souls was attached. In the latter there was one presbyter, sometimes several, together with other ministers; in the former there was a single presbyter incardinated there. [Col. 0862B] Gregory uses this term in book 1, letter 81.

Pope Leo IV, in the acts of the Roman synod published by Holstenius, calls Anastasius—who was restored to order in that synod because he had abandoned his parish, that of the city of Rome—“one of our cardinal presbyters” (*presbyter cardinis nostri*). Similarly, Gregory the Great later deprived of communion Peter, an acolyte of the Roman Church whom he had assigned as companion to the deacon Sabinianus on a mission, when Peter became a fugitive; this is related in book 7, letter 7, indiction 1.

At this point it would appropriately be possible to discuss the churches of the City and their number. Cencius counts 310; anyone who wishes may consult him here, beginning on page 190. Nor should we omit what Arnold, a monk from Regensburg and formerly a count, writes on this subject in the eleventh century. [Col. 0862C] Discussing the religious worship then flourishing in the City, he says:

> Religious worship has grown to such an extent, he says, that in place of ruined walls and ancient temples countless buildings of churches and monasteries arise every day. Of their astonishing number, as I heard from an old man who said that he had been raised in that same city, twenty are possessed by nuns and forty by monks, apart from those situated outside the city and from the other churches or chapels that abound in the same city.

From the enumeration of Cencius and Peter Mallius, however, it is possible to conclude that there were not then so many monasteries of men or so many colleges of canons, since they count no more than twenty-two abbeys of men.

In that same eleventh century there was a community of canons in the Lateran church. Hence Peter Damian, writing to Peter, archpresbyter of the Lateran canonical community, calls him the rector of the holy congregation. This perhaps should be understood of regular canons. The same author elsewhere praises the canonical community of Saint Cecilia.

Although there were regular canons at the Lateran at that time, they did not occupy the titles of that church in such a way that other clergy, or even monks, were excluded from such titles. [Col. 0862D] For Oderisius, a monk of Monte Cassino, was made a deacon of the Lateran church by Nicholas II, as Leo of Marsica testifies; and Alexander II likewise appointed Todinus, also from Monte Cassino and summoned to Rome, as a Levite in the Lateran patriarchate, according to the same author. Other examples could be cited, but these would take us too far afield.

Before proceeding farther, it is useful to place before the reader, in passing, the form of the ancient basilicas of the City.

Most faced east, while some faced west. The nave was supported by columns, or terminated by a painted ceiling, or by the structure of the roof itself. In it the men sat on the south side and the women on the north. Next came the schola cantorum, which we call the choir. Its enclosure or barrier was made of marble and was approximately the height of a man.

One or two ambos, or lecterns, were attached to it, each having four or five double steps on either side for ascent and descent. From this one may see how different the form of those ambos was from that of our *odea*, whose position was also different: those ambos were generally placed toward the north, whereas our *odea* stand on the side that separates the choir from the nave.

[Col. 0863A] Those Roman ambos resembled the structure described by Gregory, bishop of Tours, in his book *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 94. There, speaking of the most blessed Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, he says that in his basilica there was an *analogium*—that is, a lectern on which the book placed above it is sung or read—which was wonderfully constructed:

> It is said to have been carved entirely from a single block of marble. It has a table above, reached by four steps. There are screens all around, and columns beneath, because it also has a pulpit, beneath which eight persons can be accommodated.

Such is the account of Gregory, bishop of Tours. It agrees with the ninth Roman Ordo published by us, in which those being ordained are said to have stood beneath the steps of the *pogium* or ambo, numbers 2 and 8, while the lessons were being read.

Cyprian calls the pulpit—the church’s tribunal—in his letter to the presbyters and deacons of the church. That letter is number 34 in Pamelianus’s edition and number 39 in the Oxford edition. I say nothing of canon 14 of the Fourth Council of Toledo, whose canon 39 distinguishes between a double choir, the first and the second, as among the Romans.

[Col. 0863B] After the choir of singers, the steps of the sanctuary rose gradually. The sanctuary was separated from the choir by screens. The term *rugae*, or “royal gates,” referred either to the entrances or doors of the screens, or to the screens themselves. The acolytes watched over them, as is read in our first booklet, where the pontiff’s return to the secretarium after Mass is described. More will be said about the *rugae* below, in chapter 20.

The altar stood beneath a ciborium. Beneath the altar was the confession, and behind the altar the presbyterium, or choir of priests, was arranged in the form of a circle. The bishops sat on the right, the presbyters on the left, and at the head was the pontiff’s throne, generally made of marble. It had two couches or benches, stood somewhat higher than the other seats, and was adorned with linen. Hence Pacianus speaks of a “linen-covered seat”; Pontius also suggests that this was already in use in Cyprian’s time.

In the Basilica of Saint Mary at the Cradle, the pope’s throne stood on the women’s side, [Col. 0863C] so that the women, standing near the pontiff for the solemn celebration of Mass, appeared to be standing close behind the pontiff’s seat. [Col. 0863D] But Paschal I placed it in the higher position according to custom, as Anastasius testifies.

Below the screens of the presbyterium was the senators’ enclosure on the southern side, nearer to the screens, where senators and princes stood; on the opposite side stood the matrons.

The presbyterium was therefore situated beneath the apse, which was customarily furnished with a vault and mosaic paintings. From it hung chalices, crowns, and other objects of that kind as ornaments. The altar was adorned by a ciborium resting on four columns, which Anastasius sometimes appears to call a *propitiatorium*. The published Roman Ordo calls it the altar’s canopy, page 122.

Beneath the ciborium was the confession, the place where the relics and bodies of the saints were preserved. There were curtains at the doors of the basilica and also at the altar, in sets of four; Anastasius calls these *tetravila*.

The secretarium, commonly called the sacristy, was placed in the lower part of the nave on the south side, that is, on the men’s side. Thus, in the old Vatican basilica and in the Lateran basilica [Col. 0863D], the secretaria were to the left of those entering them, because the basilicas themselves faced east and therefore had the south on their left. By contrast, the old sacristy of the diaconia of Saint Mary in Cosmedin stood to the right of those entering, because the south side of that church was on the entrants’ right. In those secretaria there was also an oratory: in the Lateran, that of Saint Thomas; in the Vatican, that of Saint Gregory, which is now called the oratory of Saint Mary of the Fever. Neither, however, now serves as a secretarium. In these secretaria the Roman pontiffs put on the vestments that they were to use in the sacrifice, and from there proceeded ceremonially to the altar.

Councils were also customarily held there, sometimes in the sanctuaries or presbyteries, which are occasionally also called secretaria. To this refers canon 15 of the Second Council of Arles [Col. 0864A]: that a deacon may not sit among the presbyters in the secretarium, nor presume to administer the body of Christ in the presence of a presbyter. Furthermore, it is clear that these secretaria, like many other things, were adopted in imitation of the ancient Romans, from the fact that an old inscription, carved into the apse of the ancient basilica of Saint Martina [XXIII], testifies that it had been the secretarium of the Roman Senate, in these words:

> With our lords Honorius and Theodosius, most victorious princes, preserved, the secretarium of the most distinguished Senate, which an illustrious man had founded and which a fateful fire consumed, Flavius Annius Eularius Epiphanius, vir clarissimus, prefect of the City by sacred delegation, in the indiction, repaired and restored to its former appearance.

Likewise, by imitating the pagans, who customarily painted the walls and vaulted ceilings of temples, as Pliny bears witness in Book XXXV, chapter 3, our people too took care that the apses and walls of the basilicas should be adorned with paintings. Concerning the basilica of Saint Hippolytus, read Prudentius’s hymn 11, “On the Crowns.”

[Note: [Col. 0863D] Pages XXIV, XXV, and XXVI present a rough specimen of the basilica of Saint Clement in the Caelian district [Col. 0864D], near the amphitheater. Since this specimen is entirely foreign to our purpose, we have deliberately omitted it. EDIT.] [XXVII]

## IV. On the Roman clergy and the ancient rite of celebrating the divine offices in the Roman Church

[Col. 0864B]

During the first nine centuries of the Church, there were few clerical colleges in the City, and perhaps none except in the Vatican basilica. In the titular churches, as we saw above, one, two, or three presbyters, together with approximately the same number of sacred ministers, performed the divine service. In the patriarchal churches, mansionarii, or church custodians, were employed to adorn and clean them and to perform whatever other necessary services were required; the titular clergy appointed by the pontiff ordinarily carried out the remaining functions of divine worship in the other basilicas. By the ninth century the ministers, that is, the clergy, were already attached to the basilica of Saint Peter. Amalarius says in the second preface to his books *On Ecclesiastical Offices* that he asked them how many Orations they were accustomed to celebrate before the Epistle of the Mass on feast days.

Yet one should not suppose that during this period the divine offices were lacking in the Roman Church. Indeed, we understand that they were celebrated daily from chapter 13 of the Rule of Saint Benedict, which assigns for each weekday, on ordinary or non-festal days, a particular prophetic canticle at [Col. 0864C] Matins, that is, at Lauds, “as the Roman Church chants.” The commonly received text of Anastasius also says that Gregory III established an abbot and a congregation of monks in the church of Saint Chrysogonus to offer praise to God in that titular church by day and by night, arranged according to the pattern of the offices of the Church of Blessed Peter the Apostle. He adds that the aforementioned abbot and his congregation [XXVIII] were separated, or exempted, from the jurisdiction of the presbyter of that title.

That the Vatican Church provided the example for the Lateran basilica may be inferred from the subsequent words of the same author. There it is recorded that the same pontiff renewed the monastery of Saints John the Evangelist, John the Baptist, and Saint Pancratius, which had been established beside the church of the Savior in ancient times but had been left utterly neglected by every monastic order. In it he established a congregation of monks and an abbot to perform daily the sacred offices of divine praise in the basilica of the Savior [Col. 0864D], which is called Constantinian, beside the Lateran, by day and by night, arranged according to the pattern of the Church of Blessed Peter the Apostle.

The monks of our order had therefore disappeared from that place at that time. After the monastery of Cassino had been destroyed by the Lombards, Pope Pelagius had established them at the Lateran. Its abbot was Valentinian when Gregory the Great was preparing to write the second book of the *Dialogues*. Gregory says that he learned certain things about Saint Benedict from Valentinian, who had presided over the Lateran monastery for many years. The third person to govern the congregation of the Lateran monastery after him was Theodore, whom the monk Faustus mentions in the preface to his booklet on the life of Saint Maurus, abbot. There was another monastery, that of Honorius, attached to the Lateran basilica, which Adrian I restored in the same manner.

I return to the basilica of Saint Peter, in which [Col. 0865A] monks from four monasteries performed the divine offices. These were the monasteries of Saint Martin and of the lesser Saint Stephen, on the right side of the basilica; and those of the greater Saint Stephen and of Saints John and Paul, on the left. The monastery of the greater Saint Stephen was also called Catafarfara, or Catagalla Patricia; that of the lesser Saint Stephen was called Catabarbara Patricia. Gregory III is recorded by the commonly received text of Anastasius to have issued a decree concerning three of these monasteries. Anastasius also testifies that one of them, namely that of Saints John and Paul, had been founded by Leo the Great.

The basilica of Saint Paul, the third patriarchal basilica, was governed by provosts in the time of Gregory the Great, as is clear from Book X, Letter 9. But it was granted, or rather restored, to monks by Gregory II [Col. 0865B]. For he renewed the monasteries beside the basilica [XXIX] of Saint Paul, which had been reduced to desolation, and, having arranged for monks as servants of God, after a long interval he established a congregation there, so that they might render praise to God day and night.

The same was done by that pontiff in the basilica of Saint Mary at the Crib, where he established a monastery out of a gerontocomium; and the same was instituted by other pontiffs in the basilica of Saint Lawrence Outside the Walls. An old inscription exists on a marble tablet in the basilica of Saint Mary at the Crib, carved in the marble in the time of Gregory IV. It briefly records a donation made to that basilica by Flavia, daughter of Xanthippus, formerly imperial *a secretis*, for the benefit of the mansionarii who then lived in that church. Among the subscribers are Theodore, *adorator* of the Theodosian military unit; Gregory Optius, of the military unit; Epiphanius the goldsmith; and Theodore, acolyte of the Holy Roman Church. The date of the donation was omitted by the abridger.

In these subscriptions, *numerus* is used for a legion. Accordingly, *Adorator* may perhaps be the same as a tribune or count. This is the conjecture of the most illustrious Ciampini and Fabretti, with whom the learned and excellent Father Thomasius communicated this inscription before transmitting it to us. Thus, the mansionarii cared for that Liberian basilica [Col. 0865C]; but neighboring monks, as in the other patriarchal churches, performed the divine praises by night and by day.

As for the Masses, in the Lateran basilica they were celebrated by seven suffragan bishops of the Roman pontiff; in the others, by weekly presbyters drawn from the titular churches. That this was an ancient custom is clear from the acts of Pope Stephen IV, who decreed that every Sunday the sacred rites should be celebrated upon the altar of Blessed Peter by the seven cardinal bishops serving by turns each week, who observed the solemn Masses in the church of the Savior, and that the *Gloria in excelsis Deo* should be sung.

Thus, by that time, the practice had already become established that those seven cardinal bishops should perform the sacred rites in the Lateran church, each during his assigned week. Because of this prerogative, Peter Damian greatly exalts the Lateran church, which, just as it is distinguished by the name of the Savior—for he is the head of all the elect—is likewise the mother and a certain summit and crown of all the churches throughout the world. “It has seven cardinal bishops, and to them alone, after the apostolic pontiff, is it permitted to approach that most holy altar [Col. 0865D] and celebrate the mysteries of divine worship.” [XXX] Thus Peter writes in Book II, Letter 1, addressed to the holy bishops who were cardinals of the Lateran Church.

These bishops were the bishops of Ostia; Portus; Saint Rufina and Saint Secunda, otherwise Silva Candida; Sabina; Praeneste; Tusculum; and Albano. Which presbyters from the urban titular churches served the other patriarchal churches is explained in our appendix to the eleventh Roman Order, below, p. 160.

Moreover, on certain feast days the Roman clergy assembled with the pontiff in those basilicas where stations had been appointed, and there celebrated the sacred rites; indeed, on occasion they held nocturnal vigils for the solemnity of the feasts. Furthermore, on the vigil of Easter the suburban churches appeared at those assemblies. Evidence for this is found in our appendix to the first booklet on the Roman Order, pp. 34–35.

On the other feasts and Sundays [Col. 0866A], the titular presbyters celebrated Vespers in their own titular churches with the acolytes of the regions, as is stated in the same appendix, concerning Easter Week, p. 38. On those same days the same presbyters also celebrated the public Mass with their people. For that reason, no clerical college or school of singers was necessary; the ministry of the deacons and subdeacons was sufficient, and, apart from the Epistle and Gospel, they could easily perform the rest, perhaps omitting the Introit antiphon, the Offertory, and the Communion antiphon.

What the Roman Church’s nocturnal and diurnal office was before the ninth century can be understood from Amalarius’s *Antiphonary*. The number of readings at the vigils is assigned by the *Liber Diurnus* in the bishop’s pledge. The Roman practice at that time was that, if the time of the vigils had elapsed through negligence, the nocturnal office was omitted or shortened and Lauds began at dawn.

We have a clear witness to this in Amalarius, *Antiphonary*, chapter [Col. 0866B] 4, where he strongly praises this custom:

> The Roman Church itself, whenever it sees morning—that is, dawn—approaching, whatever the order or number of the readings may be, dismisses the nocturnal office, as I have heard, and begins the morning office. For it is dangerous to transgress the bounds established by the Fathers, and so forth.

Moved by the same religious principle, the holy Father Benedict prescribed in chapter 11 of his Rule that, if the brothers happened to rise late, which he says must be especially guarded against, something should be subtracted from the readings or responsories, so that Matins, or Lauds, which are to be sung at the beginning of dawn, might be completed at the proper time [XXXI].

Would that this religious discipline were restored after its long absence in most of the churches of Italy, where nocturnal vigils, while the sun of the preceding day is still shining, are not so much sung as recited.

What we have said about the custom of the City—that the cardinal bishops and the presbyters of the titular churches came on assigned weeks to the patriarchal churches to celebrate the sacred rites—was not without an example in the Gallican Churches. This practice existed at Verdun in the seventh century, as we learn from the [Col. 0866C] Acts of Bishop Paul, who ordered that the rural presbyters should come at fixed turns to the cathedral church to perform the divine offices.

But the most distinguished example is that of the Church of Auxerre. There, by the institution of Bishop Tetricus, who died at the beginning of the eighth century, abbots, archpresbyters, and even the rectors of rural churches performed the divine office in turn, each in his appointed rotation, on the condition that they should receive a sufficient stipend from the church’s common storehouse through the steward. I quote these very words from the Acts of the bishops of that church. In those Acts it is expressly explained which of them was to serve during each week of each month. What is lacking there for September in Labbe must be supplied from the second part of the fourth century of the Benedictine work, p. 575. We omit similar customs of other churches.

## V. On the collects and stations, and on the Roman litanies

The word *station* is ambiguous: it is sometimes used for voluntary fasting and at other times for the posture of those praying. [Col. 0866D] It occurs in both senses frequently in Tertullian and other authors. Here it means the gathering of the people at an appointed place, that is, at a church where the procession of the clergy comes to a halt on appointed days to offer appointed prayers.

For it is an ancient custom in the City that on certain days the Roman clergy gather in one particular church for a supplication, where the sacred rites and the other divine offices are performed.

The procession of the Roman clergy to those stations is of two kinds, solemn or private. A private procession occurs when each person goes individually to the appointed place; a solemn procession occurs when the pontiff and all the others go there according to solemn custom, singing litanies and other prayers.

Solemn processions are preceded by a *collecta*, that is, the gathering of the clergy in one church, so that from there they may proceed to the station as though in an organized column [XXXII]. It is so called because at that place the clergy and people gather [Col. 0867A] to make the solemn procession. And because at the place where the collecta is held a prayer is poured out over the people before the procession, it follows that such prayers are also called *Collectae*, since they are said over the *collecta* of the people while they are gathered to proceed from one church to another and make the station, as the *Micrologus* says in chapter 3.

Thus, on the first day of the fast, the prayer *Concede, quaesumus* is said at Saint Anastasia over the *collecta* of the people who are about to celebrate the station at Saint Sabina. Such collects were held especially during Lent and on each of the three-day periods of the four Ember seasons, because solemn processions were celebrated on those days. Since, however, the procession was perhaps private at other times, no collects are assigned for those periods in the old register of collects and stations, which we shall present below in its proper place.

Of the collects that were in use in the twelfth century, Benedict, canon of Saint Peter, writes as follows:

> The collecta is held on Monday, Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday throughout all Lent, and in the four Ember seasons of the entire year [Col. 0867B], and on Thursday at Saint Mary across the Tiber and at Saint Apollinaris.

Gregory the Great established in his Sacramentary the stations that had previously been mobile or had not been assigned in writing to particular churches, and arranged them by basilicas or cemeteries of the blessed martyrs, as John the Deacon testifies in Book III, chapter 18, of his *Life*.

Originally, those stations had been instituted either for the anniversaries of the saints, or for public procession days, or for Masses to be celebrated at the proper time. Stations held for the anniversaries of the saints took place at their memorials or in their cemeteries—that is, in churches built over their tombs—which for that reason are sometimes called cemeteries.

Since the feasts and memorials of the saints were well known, it was not necessary to assign the day and place of these stations in the Sacramentaries, in which all the proper Masses of the saints were included and which formerly required public stations. But the stations of other days—for example, of Lent, the four Ember seasons [Col. 0867C], Advent, Christmas, Easter, and similar periods—were uncertain and therefore had to be designated, so that no doubt might arise about which church one should proceed to for the public station.

Accordingly, Gregory assigned them to particular days in his Sacramentary, so that they might be known by everyone [XXXIII]. He established them generally in the principal basilicas, namely, the patriarchal and titular churches; but sometimes in diaconiae and oratories as well, such as the oratory of Saint Pancratius, in which the same holy pontiff delivered a homily.

Gregory II supplied several vacant days of Lent, namely the Thursdays, and assigned those stations to other churches so that they would not be repeated in the titular churches. This is what the author of the book *On the Deeds of the Pontiffs* intended to signify by these words:

> He established that during Lent, on Thursdays, fasting—that is, the station—and the celebration of Masses should take place in the churches, where this had not previously been done.

Nevertheless, the *Micrologus* states in chapter 50 that all the Thursdays of Lent had been festive like Sundays even before Gregory II.

[Col. 0867D] Although the stations were fixed and established in the Sacramentary, it was nevertheless customary to announce them to the people. This was done by the archdeacon at the preceding public Mass. For after the pontiff had communicated, the archdeacon came with the chalice to the side of the altar and announced the station. These words are found in the first booklet of the Roman Order, no. 19.

There is no doubt that the collecta too was announced whenever circumstances required it. Sometimes, however, a notary performed this duty in place of the archdeacon. A notable example occurs in the Acts of Leo III. On a certain day, when he was proceeding according to the customary rite in the litanies that everyone calls the Major Litanies, at which the people were supposed to come out to meet him and, according to the annual custom, celebrate the litanies and the solemn Mass with the priests, and when, according to ancient tradition, the litany itself had been proclaimed by a notary of the Holy Roman Church in the church of Saint George the Martyr on his feast day, everyone, men and women alike, [Col. 0868A] came devoutly in crowds to the church of Saint Lawrence, the martyr of Christ, called Lucina, where the aforementioned collecta was also held.

A collecta was therefore also held during the Major Litanies, although none is assigned to this occasion in our register. The *Book of the Pontiffs* continues its account of Leo III. When he had gone out from the patriarchium, the unjust man who should not be called Paschal, the primicerius, met him without a chasuble and hypocritically asked his pardon, saying, “I am ill, and therefore I have come without a chasuble.” From this it is clear that the sacred ministers came to meet the pontiff at those collects wearing chasubles.

Sacred vessels were carried from the Lateran patriarchium to the station churches. A processional cross went before, and it was customary for the pontiff to be carried there in a portable chair. Sometimes, however, he rode a horse.

[XXXIV] Leo IV restored the golden cross of the predecessor pontiffs, which, as Anastasius says, was carried in a subdeacon’s hands “as was the ancient custom.” *Presbyteria*, that is, distributions, were also made, both for the services of the ministers [Col. 0868B] and for the praises and acclamations. Indeed, the pontiff sometimes settled cases along the way, or at least, at his direction, the nomenclator and treasurer did so, as in the first Roman Order, no. 2. The rest is explained in our booklets, in which one may see what stations formerly took place at the Lateran and which took place at Saint Peter’s.

Furthermore, such processions are often called *litanies* by ancient authors. Among the earliest examples is the emperor Arcadius, who, in a rescript against the heretics addressed to Clearchus, prefect of the City, forbade them all to gather within the city for the making of a litany, whether by night or by day, in profane assemblies. There *litany* appears to be used for a supplication or procession.

Although, in the course of time, it became customary for the prayers and petitions made in such supplications to be more properly designated by the term *litanies*, especially the invocations of the saints, Walafrid Strabo appropriately writes in chapter 28:

> It should be noted that litanies do not refer only to that recitation of names by which the saints are called upon for assistance in human weakness [Col. 0868C]; all the petitions made in supplications are called rogations.

At first, however, the name *litanies* referred only to the beginning of our litanies, so that *Kyrie eleison* was repeated many times. It is in this sense that the term is used more than once in the Rule of Saint Benedict.

The word is used in the same sense in an ancient Ritual of the Roman Church preserved for us in the Cassinese Codex. There, for the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin, a supplication is prescribed with three hundred repetitions of our initial litany. I quote the actual words here:

> On the Assumption of Saint Mary, at the very evening of the vigil, a certain portable shrine is prepared at Saint Lawrence beside the Lateran. A panel bearing an image of Christ our Lord is placed beneath it. From midnight onward, as the people gather, they go out with the litany to Saint Mary the Lesser, the streets having been cleansed along the way and lamps hung from the houses. There, after the icon has been placed for a while on the steps of Saint Mary, the entire choir of men and women, humbly kneeling before it [Col. 0868D] and even beating their breasts with their fists, say with one voice, in the prescribed number: one hundred times, “Kyrie eleison”; one hundred times, “Christe eleison” [XXXV]; and likewise one hundred times, “Kyrie eleison.” After pouring forth tears and prayers, they go by the straight road through Saint Hadrian to Saint Mary Major. After hearing the solemn Mass, they return to the palace.

Accordingly, when a certain man was present, he broke out in amazement:

> Holy Mary, what is this? If you climb the regions of heaven,  
> Be gracious to your own.

And after several verses, the time when the poem was written is indicated by these lines:

> Otto the Third, relying on the support of your palm,  
> May he stand ready for pardon.  
> Whatever he possesses, he offers you here  
> With devoted heart; he does not hesitate to scatter it.  
> Let every man rejoice, for Otto the Third reigns.

Thus far the Cassinese Codex.

In the Lateran basilica there are only eight stations [Col. 0869A], two of them very ancient—namely, the First Sunday of Lent and the Sunday *in albis*—while the station on the Tuesday before the Ascension is more recent. In the basilica of Saint Peter there are twenty stations, most of them very ancient; in the basilica of Saint Paul Outside the Walls, five; in the basilica of Saint Mary Major, twelve; and in the extramural basilica of Saint Lawrence, three.

A separate booklet will present below these and the ancient stations of the other churches. Onuphrius, in his *History of the Vatican Basilica*, lists forty-four churches in which stations are held today, and eighty-seven stations on eighty-three days. So much for these matters; let us now proceed to greater ones.

## VI. Particular rites of the pontifical Mass according to the Roman Order; first, from the beginning to the Canon

Passing over the common ceremonies of the most holy sacrifice of the Mass, since these have been explained by commentators—especially by the cardinal Giovanni Bona, of pious memory—we shall pursue here only the [Col. 0869B] particular rites of the pontifical or episcopal Mass according to the Roman Order, lest we seem to repeat what has already been done. We shall treat the subject in this way: if anything occurs to us that may illuminate these particular matters, we shall present it briefly; otherwise, it will be enough for us to state the matter as it is.

### 1.
