[XXXVI] First of all, there is a notable indication of venerable antiquity in the eighth section of our first booklet of the Roman Order. During the pontiff’s procession to the altar, two acolytes carry open boxes containing the Holy Things, while the following subdeacon, holding his hand at the mouth of the box, displays the Holy Things to the pontiff or to the deacon who has gone ahead—that is, to the deacon as well.

Then, with bowed head, the pontiff or deacon salutes the Holy Things and inspects them, so that, if there should be an excess, he may order it to be placed in the *conditorium*. What these Holy Things are, no one, so far as I know, has yet explained. Let the reader consider whether what we are about to present proves that this term signifies the Eucharist.

In the first place, whenever the name *Sancta* occurs alone in the plural, especially in these books [Col. 0869C], it signifies the Eucharist either always or almost always, following the example of the Greeks, who call it τὰ Ἅγια (*ta Hagia*, “the Holy Things”). Tertullian likewise uses *Sanctum* absolutely, both in his book *On Prayer* and in another, *On Prescription Against Heretics*.

The same Roman Order says, no. 17:

> When he has said, “The peace of the Lord be always with you,” making the sign of the cross three times over the chalice with his hand, he puts the Holy Things into it.

No one will doubt that this passage must be understood of the Eucharist. It seems to me, however, that it refers to nothing other than a consecrated particle taken from those Holy Things that were displayed to the pontiff in the box as he proceeded to the altar, and which he adored together with the deacon.

For this particle, placed in the chalice in this way, cannot easily be explained as part of the Host consecrated in the Mass then being celebrated, since immediately afterward the text says that the pontiff breaks the offering and places in the hands of the archdeacon a portion of the Holy Thing that he has bitten off, saying, “May there be a commixture in the chalice,” and so forth.

Thus two particles were placed in the chalice: one before the breaking of the offering, and another after the breaking, taken from the offering [Col. 0869D] itself. Accordingly, the first seems to have been nothing other than a particle of Eucharist consecrated earlier, which the pontiff had adored as he proceeded to the altar and which had been displayed in the box. From it he had ordered whatever was in excess to be stored in the *conditorium*, that is, in the place where the Eucharist was customarily kept.

In the second booklet, too, a double commixture of the sacred particle in the chalice is prescribed, but both particles come from the sacrifice then being offered. This differs from the first booklet, where, in my judgment, the first commixture comes from the preceding sacrifice and the second from the present one.

And lest anyone doubt that a double particle was placed in the chalice, Amalarius explicitly noted this. After reporting the rite, he comments as follows in Book III, chapter 31 [XXXVII]:

> If this is done in the Roman Church, from them one may learn what the twice-placed bread in the chalice signifies. For nothing performed in the office according to the constitution of the Fathers is without a mystery.

It is therefore established that a double particle of the Eucharist was placed in the chalice [Col. 0870A], one from an earlier consecration, as I believe, and the other from the present one. Why, however, was a particle from the reserved Eucharist placed in the chalice? Perhaps so that the unity and perpetuity of the sacrifice might be impressed upon us by this rite.

This may be inferred from another very similar rite that follows in the same first booklet, no. 21. It concerns the case in which, in the pontiff’s absence, a bishop celebrates Mass at the place where the station is being held:

> Sixth, when it is to be said, “The peace of the Lord be always with you,” the subdeacon who carries the offering brings a particle of the *fermentum* consecrated by the apostolic pontiff and gives it to the archdeacon; he in turn gives it to the bishop. Then, making the sign of the cross three times and saying, “The peace of the Lord be always with you,” he places it in the chalice.

This passage is especially important for proving what we have said elsewhere: that the *fermentum* discussed by Innocent I in his letter to Decentius was the consecrated Eucharist itself, not *eulogiae*, or blessed bread.

Furthermore, this rite of the episcopal Mass celebrated in the pontiff’s absence illuminates the similar rite of the pontifical [Col. 0870B] Mass. In the latter, we observed that a particle of previously consecrated Eucharist was carried to the altar and afterward placed in the chalice. Finally, this rite commends the unity of the sacrifice, as well as the union of the pontiff with the priest who had previously consecrated the Holy Things, and the union of the bishop with the pontiff by means of the particle of the *fermentum*—that is, of the Eucharist—previously consecrated by the pontiff and placed in the chalice.

From these points we conclude clearly enough that the Holy Things carried before the pontiff as he proceeded to the altar were the Eucharist. A similar rite was observed on Good Friday in the fourteenth century, as James Gaetani testifies in chapter 92 of his *Ordinary*. After describing the pope’s procession with his clergy from the Lateran Church to the basilica of the Holy Cross, carrying the Lord’s body, he adds:

> The priest who carries the Lord’s body shall place it in the secretarium while the lord pope prepares himself. Once he has prepared himself, the priest shall carry it back before the pope in procession to the altar.

What we have said above on this subject can thereby be clarified and confirmed.

### 2.

[XXXVIII] Concerning the *fermentum* that was sent to the titular churches every Sunday [Col. 0870C], Innocent I writes in Letter 29 to Decentius:

> As for the *fermentum* that we send on Sunday to the titular churches, you have wished to consult us unnecessarily, since all our churches within the city are established there. Their presbyters cannot assemble with us on that day because of the people entrusted to them. Therefore they receive through the acolytes the *fermentum* prepared by us, so that they may not regard themselves as separated from our communion, especially on that day.

Thus one sees that the *fermentum* was a symbol of ecclesiastical communion, as we said just above. The pontiff adds:

> I do not think this should be done for the parishes, since the sacraments do not have to be carried far, nor do we send them through the various cemeteries to presbyters established there, since their presbyters have the right and permission to consecrate them.

That *fermentum* was therefore sent every Sunday to the titular churches, that is, to the titular churches of the City, but not to the parishes, or suburban churches; nor to the cemeteries, that is, to churches erected over the tombs of martyrs [Col. 0870D].

It is said that Innocent’s decree was preceded by a constitution of Miltiades, according to which consecrated offerings were to be sent through the churches from the consecration performed by the bishop, which was called the *fermentum*. A similar constitution is circulated under the name of Pope Siricius: no presbyter was to celebrate Mass throughout the week, or on Sunday, unless he received the consecrated offering of the designated bishop, which was called the *fermentum*.

We have already observed above that this *fermentum* was nothing other than the Eucharist. This is established by the very ancient Regensburg Codex, which contains glosses on the decretal letters of the pontiffs. Its words, already reported in our *German Journey*, are as follows:

> Concerning the *fermentum* of which he speaks: it is the Roman custom that from the Mass celebrated on the Lord’s Supper, and on Holy Saturday, and on the holy day of Easter, and at Pentecost, and on the Nativity of the Lord, a portion of the Holy Thing [this should be read, “of the Holy Thing,” not “on the holy day”] should be preserved throughout the entire year. [Col. 0871A] And whenever there are stations, if the pope himself is not present at the Mass, a portion from that Mass [perhaps, “the Holy Thing”] is placed in the chalice when it is said, “The peace of the Lord be always with you.” And this is called the *fermentum*.

This clarifies what we noted above: both that *fermentum* was used for the Eucharist, as was *Sancta*, and that the Eucharist from a previous sacrifice was reserved so that a consecrated particle might be placed in the chalice at subsequent Masses [XXXIX]. It also clarifies the rite used in an episcopal Mass when a station was held in the pontiff’s absence.

I add immediately the words of the same gloss:

> Nevertheless, on Holy Saturday of Easter no presbyter communicates anyone in the baptismal churches until some portion of the Holy Thing that the lord pope offered has been sent to him.

In fact, this was done not only on Holy Saturday but also every Sunday, as we understand from the testimony of Innocent quoted above. The practice was different in the cemeteries—that is, in the churches erected over the tombs of the martyrs. There the presbyters were permitted to celebrate the sacred rites without waiting for the pontiff’s *fermentum*, just as in the parishes, that is, in the suburban churches.

[Col. 0871B] A similar rite was observed in the ordination of bishops and presbyters, as we shall see later. The ordinand was given by the ordaining bishop an entire consecrated offering, from which he communicated for a certain number of days after his ordination, placing a particle from the previously received offering into the chalice that he himself had consecrated. In this way he testified to his communion with his ordainer and to the unity of the sacrifice.

These were the two reasons why the pontiff sent the Eucharist to the titular churches of the City every Sunday through the acolytes. A third may be supplied from the words of Innocent just quoted: namely, that the titular presbyters might thereby be given the authority to celebrate Mass, unlike the presbyters of the parishes, or suburban churches, and of the cemeteries, since the presbyters of those churches had the right and permission to consecrate the Eucharist themselves.

“But why,” you may ask, “was the *fermentum* carried by acolytes, if it was the Eucharist itself, and not by higher ministers? Or why, finally, was the Eucharist given the name *fermentum*? Was it because the bread [Col. 0871C] from which it was made had been fermented?”

To the first question: it was the duty of the acolytes to carry little bags for breaking the consecrated offerings during Mass and to present them to the priests who were to break them, as is clear from the booklets of the Roman Order. For this reason, in their ordination they anciently received such bags from the bishop as a sign of this responsibility and office. This is demonstrated by the eighth booklet edited here, on sacred ordinations. Accordingly, at a pontifical Mass, when the pontiff proceeded to the altar, two acolytes carried cases containing the Sancta—that is, the Eucharist—and held them open while the pontiff had adored the Sancta and ordered that a particle be taken from them for use in the sacrifice that he himself was about to celebrate. Perhaps this is related to what is read in the *Propyleum* to volume I of the *Acta Sanctorum* for April, in the Bollandists [XL], concerning Pope Zephyrinus, who is said to have established that ministers should carry glass patens before the priests in church while the bishop celebrated Mass.

Certainly the martyr Tarsicius belonged to the number of those acolytes. One day, while he was carrying the sacrament of Christ’s body [Col. 0871D], and refused to disclose it to the pagans who were examining him, they beat and stoned him until he breathed his last, as Usuard testifies under 18 Kalends of September.

As for the reason why the Eucharist was given the name “ferment,” whether because it was made from fermented bread or rather for some mystical reason, it is not easy to determine. It does, however, seem certain that in all antiquity the Eucharist was given the designation “ferment” on this one occasion alone. There was therefore a special and distinctive reason for this name in the act itself. What if it was intended to conceal the sacred mystery from outsiders, as was customary in those times? What if this term was thought especially suitable for designating communion and the bond of unity? For, as we have seen, the Eucharist was sent to the titular churches on this occasion so that the titular priests—who, on Sundays, could not assemble with the pontiff because of the people entrusted to their care—would not appear to be separated from his communion. No word could have been brought forward more suitably as a sign of this than “ferment.” For just as a small amount of leaven, as Josephus Thomasius rightly observes in the most illustrious Ciampini, leavens the whole mass of flour into which it is put, so that one divine ferment of the pontiff, sent to the titular churches, united the faithful of one city as though they were one mass and one body. This passage therefore contributes nothing toward proving the use of fermented bread in the Latin Church. Whether that bread was unleavened or fermented, the Eucharist was designated by the name “ferment,” not because of the material of which it consisted, but because of a moral and mystical cause: it produced in Christ’s mystical body what ferment produces in material bread.

Moreover, we gather from the booklets of the Roman Order that this custom of sending the ferment, or Eucharist, to the titular churches of the City had fallen into disuse before the ninth century. No memory of such a sending remains in them, nor does one occur in Alcuin or in the other commentators on the Roman Order [Col. 0872B].

From this it may be conjectured that the more recent custom of carrying the Eucharist before the pontiff when he goes somewhere perhaps arose not only from the common practice of the first Christians, who were accustomed to carry the Eucharist with them when traveling, but also from the ancient custom of carrying the sacred mysteries before the pontiff when he proceeded to the altar to celebrate the solemnity of the Mass. That rite, however, is prescribed only in the first booklet of the Roman Order, not in the others. For the second booklet orders that, when the pontiff has reached the altar, he should first adore the Sancta; consequently, they must already have been present there beforehand.

### 3.

Gregory the Great explains the order of the Mass briefly at the beginning of his *Sacramentary*:

> First, at the Introit, the antiphon appropriate to the appointed times, whether feast days or ordinary days; then, “Kyrie eleison.” Likewise, “Glory to God in the highest” is said if the celebrant is a bishop, but only on Sunday or feast days; priests do not say it at all, except on Easter. When a litany is held, neither “Glory to God in the highest” nor the Alleluia is sung. Afterwards the Collect is said. Then follows the Apostle. Likewise the Gradual, or the Alleluia. Afterwards the Gospel is read; then the Offertory; and the Prayer over the Offerings is said.

This Prayer is almost invariably so called in the ancient books; in the editions, and by Amalarius, it is called the Secret. When it has been completed, the priest says in a loud voice, “For ever and ever,” and so forth. Compare chapter 23 of the *Micrologus*, where a brief description of the Mass is given.

Many matters in Gregory’s words above would deserve notice, but we leave these to others, intending to observe only the more important points.

First, the *Kyrie eleison* was repeated as many times as the pontiff indicated by some gesture that it should end. Thus Paris de Crassis observes that at pontifical Masses the *Kyrie* was prolonged for as long as the cardinals’ reverence toward the pope lasted. In those Masses, however, which followed litanies, it was customary to omit the *Kyrie eleison*, as is clear from our booklets, because it had already been sung in the litanies [Col. 0872D].

When “Peace be with you” is to be said, the pontiff turns toward the people where the church is oriented toward the east. The practice is different when it faces west—as in the Lateran Basilica, the Vatican Basilica, and similar churches—where the pontiff, while celebrating the sacred rites, faces the people and does not turn toward the clergy, who are opposite him. See the *Ordinarium* of Jacobus Gaietanus, p. 415.

Furthermore, during the Mass the pontiff did not sit before the Prayer that precedes the Epistle had been completed. While he was seated and giving his assent, the bishops and priests sat, but not the deacons, subdeacons, or other ministers. Jerome refers to this in Letter 85 to Evagrius:

> Moreover, in the Church of Rome the priests sit and the deacons stand, although gradually, as vices increased, I have seen a deacon sit among the priests in the bishop’s absence, and at private banquets give blessings to priests. Let those who do this learn that they are not acting rightly.

An ancient author cited by Augustine writes that this arose from pride:

> But because they are ministers of the Roman Church, they are thought more honorable than those in the other Churches, on account of the magnificence of the city of Rome, which seems to be the head of all cities.

For the same reason, Jerome rightly concludes that the priests of the Roman Church ought to claim even more for themselves; in the same passage he attributes this rashness of the deacons to their small number:

> The small number of deacons makes them honorable; the multitude of priests makes them contemptible.

See more on this subject in Baronius under the year 402 [Col. 0873A].

Before the pontificate of Gregory the Great, moreover, the Alleluia was not said at Mass outside Pentecost—that is, outside the fifty days extending from Easter to the feast of the Holy Spirit. The witness is Book VII, Letter 64, indiction 2, to John, bishop of Syracuse. Compare what we shall say below concerning the rites of Holy Saturday.

If the commonly circulated book on the Roman pontiffs is trustworthy, Pope Anastasius I established that whenever the holy Gospels were recited, the priests should not sit but stand bowed. This bears upon what Sozomen reports as an unusual practice in the Church of Alexandria: namely, that at the Gospel the bishop did not rise. When certain Roman priests attempted the same thing, Anastasius corrected it by his decree.

After the Gospel, Gregory makes no mention in the rubric above either of the Creed or of a sermon. Most people indeed believe that the Creed was not recited in the Roman Church before the time of Emperor Henry I. To prove this, they cite the authority of Berno, abbot of Reichenau, an eyewitness, who explicitly asserts it and adds that, when the Romans were questioned by the emperor about the matter, they replied that the Roman Church had never been infected by any heresy. Nevertheless, they say that the emperor obtained from Pope Benedict that the Creed should thereafter be sung at the public Mass; this occurred in 1014.

Yet long before that time it was customary for the Creed to be sung at a pontifical Mass, as the second booklet on the Roman Order makes clear. And lest anyone allege that the passage is an interpolation, Amalarius comments on this same passage in his *Eclogue* on that booklet. Moreover, in booklets V and VI on the episcopal Mass according to the Romans, as it was celebrated before the ninth century, the Creed is assigned after the Gospel. Therefore it must be said that, during the interval extending from the ninth to the eleventh century, the Romans discontinued the recitation of the Creed at Mass.

The same very probably happened with the Lord’s Prayer, since Gregory the Great ordered it to be recited at Mass after the Canon, according to Book VII, Letter 64, indiction 2. Certainly Walafrid Strabo says in chapter 22 that the custom of singing the Creed is believed to have come from Constantinople to the Romans, while among the Gauls and Germans the same Creed began to be recited more widely and more frequently in the offices of the Mass [Col. 0873D]. Among others, this is attested by Aeneas, bishop of Paris, in Book I of his work *Against the Greeks*, where he calls the Catholic faith that which the universal Church of Gaul sings at Mass on Sunday.

Finally, Cencius asserts that the following was written for the Lord’s Supper in the book of Gelasius: “Let them not say the Creed.” This indicates that it could have been said on other days under Pope Gelasius I, which is how we think this passage should be understood. But since nothing of the kind is read in the Gelasian Sacramentary published by Thomasius, judgment concerning the recitation of the Creed during Gelasius’s pontificate must for the moment be suspended—especially since the Fathers of the Third Council of Toledo, in canon 2, introduce the practice of reciting the Creed in the sacred rites according to the form of the Eastern Churches. Had this rite already been customary among the Romans, they would have said “according to the Roman Church”; this was in the Spanish era 627 [i.e. A.D. 589].

After the Gospel or the Creed, the pontiff sometimes delivered a sermon to the people. It may be inferred that this first began under Leo the Great both from the fact that no homilies of Roman pontiffs before him survive and from Book VII, chapter 19, of Sozomen, where, speaking of Rome, he says:

> In that city, neither the bishop nor anyone else teaches the people in church; but among the Alexandrians only the bishop of the city of Alexandria preaches. They say that this practice, which had not previously been established, was introduced from the time when Arius the presbyter, discussing the doctrine of faith, introduced new teachings.

The same author makes several other observations there that may be reported here:

> This too is unusual in Alexandria: at the Gospel the bishop does not rise. There the archdeacon alone reads the Gospel; elsewhere deacons do so; in many places, priests; and in some places the bishop, on the principal feasts—as at Constantinople on holy Easter.

Nevertheless, Prudentius, who was earlier than Leo the Great and Sozomen, testifies in hymn 11, *On the Crowns*, where he describes the Roman basilica of Saint Hippolytus, that the pontiff was accustomed to address the people from the tribunal [Col. 0874B]:

> Opposite the façade, a lofty tribunal  
> Rises on steps, from which the bishop preaches God.

This may perhaps have happened less frequently. Certainly, after Gregory the Great we possess only a few homilies of the Roman pontiffs, although some did preach at times, among them Innocent III, and after him Clement VI, who delivered many sermons.

It is worth noting what Optatus writes in Book III: every episcopal exposition or preaching sermon was furnished with a double greeting.

> For, he says, a bishop does not begin to say anything to the people unless he has first greeted the people in the name of God. The endings resemble the beginnings. Every exposition in the church begins in the name of God and ends in the name of that same God.

For several centuries the beginning has been made with the angelic greeting. This practice was already established in the fifteenth century, as is clear from the *Ceremonial* of Peter Amelius, chapter 42 [Col. 0874C], which is included here as order 15.

### 4.

Everyone made his own offering at the pontifical Mass—not only laypeople of both sexes, but also priests and deacons. The booklets on the Roman Order explain individually the manner in which this was done. The offerings of the princes—that is, the bread—were received by the pontiff in the senatorial area, which had been assigned to them on the southern side; the archdeacon, after the pontiff, received the wine-flasks from the same persons. The offerings of the other laymen were received by the weekly-duty bishop, and the deacon received the wine-flasks, which he poured into a large vessel. The same was done by both the Pontiff and the deacons on the women’s side. The priests and deacons offered bread alone, without wine.

Concerning the form of the offered bread, Onuphrius reads the following in John the Deacon’s exposition of the Roman Order, an exposition that we have been unable to locate [XLV]:

> Although the form and measure of the offerings seem in ancient times to have been determined by each person’s zeal and devotion in divine worship, we can nevertheless gather more certain indications of the matter from the writings of blessed Gregory. In Book IV of the *Dialogues*, chapter 55, he writes: “A certain priest brought two crowns of offerings to a certain person, such crowns as Christian devotion at that time used to offer to God for itself and for all its own.” A little later he says: “It is evident what measure and form the priests’ offerings ought to have: they are ordered to be made from a handful of fine flour and in the shape of a crown.”

The story is well known of that Roman matron who, when she received communion from Gregory from bread that she herself had offered, laughed at the statement that it was Christ’s body, since, as she said, “it was made from that offering which I made with my own hands and offered to you.” At that time it was customary for each person to make his or her own offering—the one they called their own—with his or her own hands. Hence the emperor Valens is said to have offered to the divine table gifts that he himself had made—“of which he was the maker” (*ὧν αὐτουργὸς ἦν*)—as Gregory of Nazianzus relates in his funeral oration for Basil the Great.

Nor should we omit here what Cardinal Humbert writes in his book against Michael Cerularius [Col. 0875A]: that the deacons with the subdeacons, or the priests themselves, clothed in sacred vestments, brought forth from the sacristy, accompanied by the melody of psalms, leavened bread prepared there for the sacrifice. The *Customs of Cluny* should be consulted concerning this matter.

As for the wine, the archdeacon poured the offered wine-flasks into the chalice used by the pontiff for the consecration. When it was completely filled, he emptied it into another ministerial chalice, which one of the acolytes held. In our booklets this chalice is called a *scyphus*; besides it, a larger chalice is assigned in the third booklet. This observation is necessary for clarifying what we shall later say about the communion of laypeople under the other species. The cantor offered water covered with a linen cloth to the deacon, who mixed it with the wine in the chalice, pouring it in the form of a cross.

John III established that offerings, wine-flasks, or lights should be supplied from the Lateran to the cemeteries on every Sunday [Col. 0875B]. Gregory III likewise established that, in the cemeteries situated all around Rome, on the anniversaries of the saints buried there, lights for keeping vigils and offerings from the patriarchal treasury should be transported by the offering-bearer so that Masses might be celebrated, by whichever priest the pontiff in office at the time should appoint.

A diploma of Gregory III survives concerning the daily offerings he made at Saint Paul’s: at the first Mass, one offering at the body; at the second Mass, one offering at Saint Timothy; at the third Mass, one offering at the image of the Savior, which is also called the image of the Apostles; at the fourth Mass, one offering at Saint Gregory at the doors; and then, at the fifth Mass, two offerings at the high altar. From this one can see that already then six Masses were customarily celebrated in that basilica each day, and indeed at different altars. The pontiff concludes the diploma as follows:

> We have given this high altar to the monks for this reason: so that all these things may be done at all times.

Compare the *Typicon* of the empress Irene Doukaina, chapter 34, which orders that seven loaves be offered each day in the divine liturgy, in the first volume of the *Greek Analecta*, recently brought to light through our efforts [Col. 0875C].

For more than four hundred years the laity have ceased to offer the material of the sacrifice. But Augustine Patrizi, in his *Ceremonial*, describes the procedure that was to be observed two hundred years earlier in the offering at a pontifical Mass:

> After the Gospel has been read, the deacon of the Gospel takes one Host from the three that are on the paten; with it he touches the other two Hosts, and gives it to the sacristan to eat. Then he takes another Host from the two that remain, and with it touches the paten and the chalice all over, inside and out; and likewise gives it to the sacristan to eat. This is done to avoid the danger of poison, which by this procedure would fall upon the head of the sacristan, who has to prepare everything. After this, for the same reason, he gives the wine and water from the cruets into a cup for the sacristan to taste. Then, taking the paten with the Host, he places it in the pope’s hands; the pope, offering it to God, says: “Receive, holy Father,” and so forth.

This is taken from Augustine in his account of the principal Mass on Christmas Day, which he repeats for Holy Saturday.

Here we ought to discuss the sacred vessels used by the Romans in the sacrifice of the Mass. On this subject, however, Cardinal Bona of pious memory should be consulted before all others. I should like to add here one detail concerning the sacred vessels of the Vatican Basilica, which are mentioned by Orosius. Speaking of the sack of the city of Rome by Alaric, in Book VII, chapter 39, he says that an Arian soldier tried to extort the sacred vessels from a certain virgin to whom they had been entrusted [XLVII]. When the vessels’ riches had been displayed, the barbarian was struck with astonishment at their size, weight, beauty, and even the unfamiliar quality of the vessels. The virgin said to him:

> These are the furnishings of the apostle Peter.

Among the various instruments used for sacred purposes must be counted the fan for driving away flies. It was held by the person who attended to the pontiff’s mitre, as James Gaietanus testifies, p. 297. The same author mentions two such fans on p. 305: one for cooling the air, the other for driving away flies. Although our older booklets make no mention of these fans, their antiquity is nevertheless demonstrated by the *Life of Fulgentius, Bishop of Ruspe*, who, when he was a monk, very often wove fans from palm leaves. The monk Cyril calls it a liturgical fan, *λειτουργικὸν ῥιπιστήριον*, in his book on the life of Abbot Euthymius, volume I of the *Greek Analecta*, p. 60. But let us proceed to other matters.

### 5.

In Letter 29, Innocent I censures two practices in the sacred mysteries that, as he considered them, were performed in the wrong order. The first was that some gave the peace before the mysteries had been completed:

> After everything that I ought not to disclose—for at that time they concealed those sacred mysteries—peace must necessarily be proclaimed, by which it may be established that the people have given their consent to everything celebrated in the mysteries and performed in the church, and that the rite has been completed may be demonstrated by the seal of the concluding peace [Col. 0876B].

The second was that the names of those making offerings were recited before the priest made the prayer—that is, before the Prayer over the Offerings had been made, indeed before the Canon, which Pope Vigilius also designates below by the name “prayer.” Therefore, says Innocent, the offerings should first be commended; then the names of those to whom the offerings belong should be announced, so that they may be named amid the sacred mysteries—that is, after the consecration—not among the other things that we put first, by which we open the way for the prayers that will follow in the mysteries themselves.

The Gallican and Hispanic Churches observed both rites that Innocent here condemns; Justin Martyr in his *Second Apology* in fact confirms the former. Innocent’s regulation was accepted by the Gauls in 789, in the *Capitulary of Aachen*, chapters 53 and 54.

### VII. Continuation of the distinctive rites in the pontifical Mass, from the Canon to Communion [XLVIII]

Passing over the Preface, in which nothing distinctive occurs, we proceed to the Canon. The priest did not begin it before the choir had completed the singing of the Trisagion. This is prescribed by our booklets and, after them, by Herard, bishop of Tours, chapter 16:

> Let priests not begin the Secret before the Sanctus has ended.

He calls the Canon the Secret because the priest recited it in a subdued voice and alone. It is called the same thing in the old Gallican Missal, p. 335, where the Collect after the Secret is the prayer said immediately after the consecration. This proves that the Canon of the Mass was also recited in a subdued voice in the Gallican Order. The same was true in the Roman rite; hence in the second Roman Order it is written that the pontiff secretly enters upon the Canon.

The ancients called it “the Prayers” and “the canonical prayer,” especially Pope Vigilius, in his letter to Profuturus, bishop of Braga:

> We do not at any time or on any feast indicate that the order of the prayers in the celebration of Masses is different; rather, we always consecrate the gifts offered to God in the same manner. Whenever the feast of Easter, the Ascension of the Lord, Pentecost, the Epiphany, or one of God’s saints is to be celebrated, we add individual sections appropriate to the days, in which we commemorate the holy solemnity or those whose anniversaries we celebrate; we continue the rest in the customary order. For this reason we have also sent below the text of the canonical prayer itself, which, by God’s favor, we received from apostolic tradition.

The variation of which Vigilius speaks is still preserved in that part of the Canon which begins with the word “Communicantes.”

Gregory the Great was the first, or among the first, to call this prayer absolutely “the Canon.” In Book XI, Letter 59, he notes that Bishop Januarius, when celebrating the sacrifice, frequently suffered such severe distress that he could scarcely return, after long intervals, to the place in the Canon that he had left. As a result, many wondered whether they ought to receive communion from his consecration [Col. 0877A]. Gregory says that they should be warned not to fear at all, but to communicate with complete faith and confidence, because illness in the person neither changes nor defiles the blessing of the sacred mystery; indeed, neither does the priest’s sin, as Optatus of Milevis attests in Book VI. It is therefore plainly evident that something can be sanctified by the invocation of God’s name, even if the person invoking God is a sinner.

A very ancient author, in Book IV *On the Sacraments*, transmitted by Ambrose, reports nearly the whole Canon, though with its wording altered somewhat. In the most ancient Codex of Queen Christina of Sweden, no. 1454, the words of the consecration of Christ’s body are missing. In some Churches the people said “Amen” after the words of consecration; but neither our booklets nor the Gregorian Sacramentary says anything about this, although Augustine mentions the practice in his letter to Januarius.

Throughout the entire Canon, the bishops, deacons, and subdeacons serving the pontiff, together with the priests in the presbytery, remained bowed down, except that at the words “And to us sinners” the deacons rose. By this inclination of their bodies they adored the sacred Action and the sacred mysteries, which the commonly circulated Anastasius, in his life of Pope Martin, calls the Host to be adored.

In those earliest times the Host and the chalice were not immediately raised high by the priest after the consecration. Rather, this occurred toward the end of the Canon, when the priest said, “Through whom you create all these things,” and so forth. At that point the archdeacon alone stood up; and when “Through him, and with him” was said, he lifted the chalice by its handles with the offertory and held it raised beside the pontiff. The *Micrologus*, in chapter 15, says that the body was then raised together with the chalice, and makes no mention of any other elevation after the consecration. [Note: [Col. 0877D] See the *Life of Abbot Euthymius*, vol. I of the *Greek Analecta*, p. 62.]

The Easterners perform this shortly before communion. The elevation after the consecration seems to have begun in Gaul after the middle of the eleventh century; I do not know whether it began somewhat later in the Roman Church, although in both places the sacred mysteries were adored at the consecration. This relates to the letter of Ivo, bishop of Chartres, no. 142, to Matilda, queen of the English, in which he thanks her for the bells granted to his church. He says that the sound of them renews the queen’s memory, especially when that saving Host, offered for our redemption on the altar of the cross, is consecrated daily on the Lord’s table by ministers of the new priesthood. There is no mention there of an elevation, nor is there any in the *Usages of the Cistercians*, chapter 53.

Likewise, in the *Institutions of the General Chapters*, chapter 25, distinction 3, it is recorded that in the general chapter of 1215 it was decreed that, once the consecration had been completed, the Host should be elevated. At approximately the same time William, bishop of Paris, and in Germany Cardinal Guido established that a little bell should be rung at the elevation. Here one is reminded of the sacred chalice of Saint Malachy, primate of Ireland, preserved in the treasury of Clairvaux; several little bells hang from its rim, so that, when the chalice was moved, those present would be summoned to adore.

Finally, in the thirteenth century, the *Ceremonial of Gregory X* published here, p. 235, prescribes that at the elevation of Christ’s body they should prostrate themselves on the ground and adore reverently, falling forward on their faces; they should remain prostrate until “For ever and ever.” The Carthusians still do this today. Add the *Ordinarium* of James Gaietanus, in which elevation and adoration are also mentioned, here on p. 285 [Col. 0877D].

In the Canon there were two commemorations, as there still are today: the living before the consecration and the dead after it. In both, the names of the apostolic Churches were recited, together with the names of the living bishops in the first commemoration and of the dead in the second. We gather this from Augustine’s Letters 43, 52, and 53.

> We recite not only the names of our own codices, he says in Letter 43, no. 21, but also those of theirs—that is, of the Donatists—the Churches whose names they read today, although today they do not communicate with them. When these names are recited in their assemblies, they say to their readers, “Peace be with you,” although they do not communicate with the congregations to which those letters were written.

These names of the apostolic Churches—that is, of those to which the apostles wrote—had been written in the holy books, in the sacred codices, namely in the books of the Sacraments. By this name they customarily designated books containing the rite of the most holy sacrifice [Col. 0878A].

The Lord’s Prayer is appended to the Canon. Some Greeks or Latins from Sicily complained that, following the example of the Greeks, the Roman pontiffs had ordered it to be said immediately after the Canon. Gregory replies:

> We say the Lord’s Prayer immediately after the prayer—that is, the Canon—because it was the custom of the apostles to consecrate the Host of the offering by that prayer alone.

Gregory suggests in the words that follow that he himself was the author of this regulation:

> It seemed highly inappropriate to me that we should say over the offering the prayer composed by a scholar, while remaining silent over Christ’s body and blood concerning the very tradition that our Savior composed.

He finally adds that the practice differed from that of the Greeks in the Roman Church: among the Greeks the Lord’s Prayer is said by the entire people, whereas among us it is said by the priest alone. From the words “It seemed highly inappropriate to me,” it may be inferred that Gregory was responsible for introducing the Lord’s Prayer into the Roman Mass, or rather for restoring it. It is not plausible that this divine prayer—which is known to have been used in the sacred rites of all the other liturgies, both Eastern and Western, Gallican, Hispanic, and Milanese, and indeed on the example of the apostles—was originally omitted by the Roman Church alone, which has always followed apostolic tradition more closely than the others.

Certainly, in Augustine’s time nearly every Church concluded the entire petition of the sacrifice with the Lord’s Prayer, as is clear from his Letter 149 to Paulinus. In Sermon 351, which appears in volume V of the new edition, he likewise teaches, in section 6, that bishops standing at the altar were accustomed to strike their breasts together with everyone else. He indicates below that this was done during the recitation of the Lord’s Prayer:

> For if we have no sins, and while striking our breasts say, “Forgive us our sins,” then by this very act we certainly sin gravely, with no one doubting it, since we lie amid the sacraments.

Here he uses “sacraments” to mean the consecration of the sacred mysteries of the body and blood of the Lord Christ, which elsewhere too he calls “sacraments” in the plural. Therefore, as I had begun to say, before Gregory’s time it was the custom of the universal Church for the Lord’s Prayer to be said at Mass.

But perhaps the Roman priests omitted this prayer as something otherwise common [Note: [Col. 0877D] Thus the Fathers of the Council of Basel complain that the Lord’s Prayer is omitted at Mass in certain Churches. (Title 16, concerning those who do not complete the Mass.)]. Gregory brought the Romans back to a uniform rite by his decree, just as the Hispanic priests omitted it outside Sunday in the divine offices, according to canon 9 of the Fourth Council of Toledo. Certainly, in the Mass of the Presanctified, which is celebrated every year on Good Friday according to the primitive rite, the Lord’s Prayer is recited [Col. 0878D].

After the Lord’s Prayer, the consecrated bread is broken, and one of the three particles is placed into the chalice. In ancient times, however, there were two commixtures at a pontifical Mass: one before the *Agnus Dei*, from the preceding sacrifice, as we saw above; the other after the pontiff’s communion, from the sacrifice then being celebrated. For many centuries now, only one commixture has been made—namely, the latter, from the portion of the Eucharist remaining between the pontiff’s fingers after communion.

### [LII]

In the Gallican and Hispanic Churches, before “The peace of the Lord be always with you” was said, it was an ancient custom for the bishop celebrating the sacred rites to impart a blessing to the people standing around him. This is clear both from the most ancient books of the Gallican Order and from canon 18 of the Fourth Council of Toledo. This blessing was bestowed on the people through three prayers, of the kind that have more than once been printed.

I do not find these blessings, however, adopted in the pontifical Mass; indeed, Pope Zacharias seems strongly to disapprove of them. I understand the following words of his letter to Boniface to refer to them:

> As for the blessings that the Gauls give, as you know, brother, they vary in many ways through numerous abuses. For they do this not from apostolic tradition but through empty glory, bringing condemnation upon themselves … Therefore proclaim to everyone the rule of Catholic tradition, which you have received from the holy Roman Church, which by God’s authority I serve.

If Zacharias is speaking of these blessings, as I believe he is, his words are harsher than the cause—which might otherwise be considered praiseworthy—deserves.

Some words concerning such blessings have been inserted into the second Roman Order:

> After the pontifical blessings have been given, as is customary in these regions, when he has said, “The peace of the Lord be always with you,” he places into the chalice some of the holy offering.

It is sufficiently clear that the words “as is customary in these regions” were added with consideration for the place where this Roman Order was written. The *Benedictionale* therefore ought not to have been inserted into the new edition of Gregory’s works, since it is alien to the rite of the Romans and consequently to Gregory’s own intention, even though it is found attached to the Gregorian Sacramentary in a codex of the Imperial Library, having been copied for the use of another Church rather than the Roman [Col. 0879B].

### VIII. Distinctive features of sacred communion at the pontifical Mass

Since many distinctive features occur in the communion as it was formerly administered at the pontifical Mass, and since they may more easily be observed if this is stated beforehand, it should be noted that in those solemn celebrations—even after Masses began to be multiplied somewhat—all who were present, not only laypeople and those outside the priestly order but also priests and bishops, partook of holy communion.

We observe this rite among the Easterners in the case of Nestorius, patriarch of Constantinople. When he did not merely fail to rebuke Bishop Dorotheus for pronouncing an anathema on those who called the Virgin *Theotokos* [“God-bearer”] [LIII], but immediately admitted him to the mystical communion and made him a participant in it, this is reported in Cyril of Alexandria’s letter to those who complained about him.

The same rite was observed among the Romans at the pontifical Mass, as is explained in the following booklets of the Roman Order. They do not explain, however, whether the priests celebrated the sacred rites together with the pontiff. Amalarius supplies this information in Book I, chapter 12:

> It is the custom of the Roman Church that priests be present at the making of Christ’s oblation and, together with the pontiff, accomplish it by word and hand.

From this it is clear that the custom is ancient. James of Vitry is a witness to it in chapter 38 of his *History of the West*:

> The cardinal priests are accustomed to assist the supreme pontiff in the sacrament of the altar, to celebrate together with him, and indeed also to communicate.

Innocent III teaches both points in Book IV of *On the Mysteries of the Mass*, chapter 25, where he says that the cardinal priests were accustomed to surround the Roman pontiff and celebrate together with him; and when the sacrifice had been completed, to receive communion from his hand.

It is now worthwhile to explain the rites of this communion individually.

1. First of all, after “The peace of the Lord be always with you” had been said, the Agnus Dei was not sung immediately; rather, the pontiff placed into the chalice the Sancta, or a portion from the Sancta, or, as the second book has it, from the consecrated offering. This particle does not seem to have come from the present sacrifice, since the offering had not yet been broken; it must therefore have been taken from the preceding one. Having done this, the pontiff gave the peace to the archdeacon.

2. The archdeacon, having received the peace from the pontiff, gave it to the first bishop, then to the others in order, and to the people, so that the bishop gave it to the first person standing beside him, and that person to the next, and so in order; men and women separately.

3. The pontiff broke the offering at the right side and left the particle he had broken upon the altar; the remaining offerings [Col. 0880A] he placed upon the paten held by the deacon. This genuinely obscure passage is clarified by the Micrologus, chapter 17:

> When he says “Through our Lord,” he breaks the Host at the right side, according to the Ordo, to signify the striking of the Lord’s side. Then he breaks the larger portion into two, so that he may make three portions of the Lord’s body. For he must put one into the chalice, making a cross . . . . . but the other the presbyter himself necessarily consumes, and so forth.

According to this interpretation, the other offerings that the pontiff placed upon the paten were the two remaining particles from that breaking. As for why the first particle remained upon the altar, the first of our books on the Roman Ordo gives one reason, and the Micrologus another; yet the reasons are not altogether opposed. Our first book on the Roman Ordo teaches that this was done because they observed the practice that, while the solemnities of the Mass were being performed, the altar should not be without a sacrifice—a consideration that perhaps also led to the Eucharist’s being carried before the pontiff as he proceeded to celebrate the sacred rites [Col. 0880B]. The Micrologus, however, says that the particle was left for those who were to receive Communion, or for the sick. Yet at that pontifical Mass the communicants were given other consecrated offerings. After the aforesaid breaking, the pontiff returned to his seat.

4. In only the first Roman Ordo it is then read that the nomenclator (whose duty was to invite those who were to dine at the banquet and to record their names), the treasurer (who was in charge of the treasury or fisc), and the notary of the vicedominus, or steward, after saying the Agnus Dei among themselves, went up to the altar before the face of the pontiff, so that he might authorize them to write down the names of those who were to be invited—either to the pontiff’s table by the nomenclator, or to that of the vicedominus by his notary. After they had recorded the names, they went down to invite them and then returned to the seat where the pontiff was standing.

5. Meanwhile the archdeacon lifted the chalice from the altar [Col. 0880C] and gave it to the regional subdeacon, or archsubdeacon, to hold beside the right-hand corner of the altar.

6. The other subdeacons then approached with acolytes, who carried small bags, on the right and left sides of the altar. The acolytes extended their arms with the bags, while the subdeacons standing in front opened the mouths of the bags to receive the offerings from the archdeacon, who dropped them into the bags.

7. When the altar had been emptied of the offerings, the archdeacon signaled to the choir that they should sing the Agnus Dei, which Pope Sergius I is said to have established as being sung by clergy and people during the breaking of the Lord’s body. Certainly, in the Mass of Holy Saturday—which is still celebrated according to the ancient custom—the Agnus Dei is omitted, together with the Antiphons at the Offertory and at Communion; Walafrid Strabo and others observed that these were not part of the original institution. In the [LV] rubrics of the Gregorian Sacramentary, however, the Agnus Dei is assigned to the customary Masses, though perhaps only by the singers, as our more ancient books prescribe [Col. 0880D]. At that time it was customary for it to be sung by the clergy and people, as Sergius ordered, so that, while the Lord’s body was being prepared for distribution, those who were to receive it might pray that he who had been offered innocently for them would enable them to receive, for their salvation, the pledges of eternal salvation, as the same Walafrid writes above in chapter 22.

8. The acolytes, having received the offerings into the bags, divided into two groups: one went to the bishops who were on the pontiff’s right, the other to the presbyters who approached on his left. They were preceded on either side by two regional subdeacons, each carrying his own paten, so that, at the pontiff’s signal, the offerings might be broken over those patens, both by the bishops and by the presbyters and deacons. The patens were therefore exceedingly large. Anastasius states that one given by Pope Sergius I weighed twenty pounds; I believe that this is why they were sometimes called simply *communicales*. Augustine mentions the Eucharist being broken into small pieces for distribution in Letter 149 to Paulinus, section 16.

9. When the breaking had been completed, the Antiphon at Communion was sung with its psalm. Then the junior deacon received from the subdeacon the paten on which the two particles remaining after the pontiff’s breaking of the Host had been placed, and carried it to the pontiff’s seat, so that he might receive the Lord’s body—standing, and turned toward the East, as we learn from our fifth book. Innocent III says only “standing,” below.

10. After receiving the Eucharist, the pontiff placed the particle of the Sancta from which he had bitten, between the hands of the archdeacon, into the chalice held by the subdeacon, saying: “Let there be a commingling and consecration,” and so forth. “Amen.” Here *consecrate* means “to make sacred together”; these are the words of Pope Pelagius I in his letter to John the Patrician, in Holstenius’s Roman collection. The words of canon 17 of the First Council of Orange likewise refer to this. [Col. 0881B] Thus there were two comminglings in the chalice during the pontifical Mass: one immediately after the first breaking performed by the pontiff, and the other after his Communion. Amalarius mentions both, as we saw above, although only one is mentioned in the third book. In the first book, however, where the first commingling was made from the preceding sacrifice, as it seems to me, another was made from the present one, according to what has been said.

[LVI] 11. After these words, “Let there be a commingling,” and so forth, the two earlier books add: “Peace be with you.” Response: “And with your spirit.” Then, in the first book, the pontiff is “confirmed” by the archdeacon—that is, he receives the blood as the completion of Communion, in the language of the Micrologus. What this invocation of peace signifies is not apparent from these books. Perhaps it should be referred to what Innocent III reports in book VI, chapter 9, where he explains the Communion of the pontiff and ministers as follows:

> But so that no deception can arise in the reception of Christ’s body and blood, and so that the truth of the reception may clearly appear in both, the supreme pontiff does not immediately drop the particle of the Host into the chalice. Rather, after making the threefold sign of the cross, he places it upon the paten. After the kiss of peace, he ascends to his seat and, standing there in full view of everyone, takes the larger part of the offering from the paten presented to him by the subdeacon; dividing it in full view of them, he consumes one particle and places another into the chalice, which the subdeacon holds before him, and from it he drinks the blood through a tube. Then, with a kiss, he gives one particle to the deacon, and another, without a kiss, to the subdeacon; the deacon, ministering at the altar, kisses him as he gives him the chalice.

I have no doubt that, when the pontiff gave the Eucharist to the deacon, kissing him as Innocent says, he pronounced the preceding words, “Peace be with you,” while the archdeacon replied, “And with your spirit.”

Indeed, in ancient times the faithful, after receiving the Eucharist, customarily kissed the bishop or priest from whom they had received it, both in the East and in the West. Jerome, in Letter 62 against John of Jerusalem, writes:

> Does anyone communicate with you unwillingly? Does anyone turn his face away with outstretched hand and offer Judas’s kiss amid the sacred banquet?

Paul, deacon of Mérida, in *The Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 7, speaking of Bishop Fidelis, says:

> “Go,” he said, “receive Communion, and give us a kiss.”

Finally, in a certain treatise of the Friars Preachers, published by Stevartius:

> The Greeks do not complete participation in Holy Communion in the same way as we do; rather, they say that the priest celebrating Mass kisses the person wishing to receive Communion.

After the foregoing Innocent III adds:

> The deacon and those who belong to the higher orders, when they receive the Eucharist, receive a kiss from the bishop. The acolyte and those who belong to the lower orders do not receive one. The subdeacon, however, because this rank was formerly counted among the non-sacred orders but is now reckoned among the sacred orders, does not receive a kiss from the pontiff when receiving the body; but when receiving the blood, he receives a kiss from the deacon.

[LVII] 12. On certain feasts, when celebrating the sacred rites, the pontiff received Communion at the altar—namely, on Good Friday. Jacobus Gaietanus and Petrus Amelius add that this also occurred at the first Mass on Christmas Day; Augustine Patricius adds Ash Wednesday. On these days he drank the most holy blood of Christ not from a tube but from the chalice. Nicholas III ordered that the psalm “I rejoiced,” with several verses and the Collect for Peace, be sung before Communion, to obtain peace among Christian princes; John XXII instituted the same practice in his own time. The same rite continued under Urban VI, according to the Ceremonial of Petrus Amelius.

13. After the pontiff’s Communion had been completed, the archdeacon announced the station that would follow. Thus it is stated in the first two books of the Roman Ordo; but one Benedict, a canon, explains the procedure while discussing Ash Wednesday, in section 33 of the tenth book:

> Before Communion the regional subdeacon stands beside the altar, saying in a loud voice: “Tomorrow, when the day has come, the station will be at the church of Saint George the Martyr at the Golden Veil.” The choir responds: “Thanks be to God.”

The same author explains there how, after the Mass had ended, the greeting from that day’s station was offered to the pontiff. After the pontiff’s Communion, the announcement of the Ember fast was also made; the most eminent Cardinal Bona gives the formulas for this.

14. After the pontiff had been “confirmed,” the archdeacon poured a little from the chalice—that is, from the consecrated blood—into a bowl held by the acolyte. This is the ministerial bowl or chalice, into which, as we noted above, the wine offered had been poured from the larger chalice. Accordingly, the blood poured into that bowl was mingled with the wine already poured into it, in order to confirm the people, as we shall shortly explain. In other places and churches, wine was not poured in with the consecrated blood unless the ministers noticed that the pure blood would not suffice for those receiving Communion.

We have an example of this in chapter 53 of the Cistercian Usages:

> While the brothers are receiving the blood, wine is to be poured into the chalice by the deacon, when necessary, from the flask prepared beforehand by the subdeacon beside the altar. If any of that blood remains, he is to drink it together with the chalice, and so forth.

Thus the term “blood” was used absolutely even after that addition of wine. [LVIII] The Ceremonial of Saint Benignus at Dijon states the matter still more clearly and explicitly:

> Wine must always be present in a flask beside him—that is, beside the deacon—so that, whenever he sees it to be necessary, he may augment the Lord’s blood with that wine.

This Ceremonial is approximately six hundred years old, and the first Cistercian Usages differ from it by scarcely any length of time. Somewhat more recent is the Ordinarium of the Abbey of Saint Victor at Paris, which says:

> Meanwhile, while they are receiving Communion, the subdeacon must stand beside the deacon with a wine flask and, whenever necessary, pour wine into the chalice, and so forth.

The same practice was observed by Nicholas, Abbot of Palermo, in certain places where, after the reception of Christ’s body and blood, some of the blood itself was reserved in the chalice and pure wine was poured over it, so that other communicants might receive from it. For it would not be seemly to consecrate so much blood, nor would a sufficiently capacious chalice be found. Finally, William of Lindwood, official of the Church of Canterbury, writes in his *Collection of the Provincial Constitutions of his Church*:

> The priest who holds the chalice containing the blood, seeing that the quantity of blood would not suffice for all the brothers, puts a little wine into it.

Thus writes William, who lived at the beginning of the fifteenth century. But we shall return to this matter below; for now let us return to the Roman rites.

15. The bishops and presbyters then immediately approached to receive Communion from the pontiff. The bishops stood at the pontiff’s seat, while the presbyters knelt at the altar, as is clear from the Ceremonial of Gaietanus, pages 312 and 313—a practice contrary, at least, to the ancient rite of the Greeks, about which Valesius writes in his notes on Eusebius, page 145. The archdeacon “confirmed” both groups with the Lord’s blood; the bishop confirmed the following orders while standing at the corner of the altar. The presbyters and deacons received the Eucharist by hand, the subdeacons [Col. 0883A] by mouth, according to the sixth book. In the fifth, however, the subdeacon offers the chalice to the first presbyter receiving Communion, who gives it in turn to the next, and so successively to the others.

16. After this, the archdeacon received the chalice from the bishop’s hand and poured the remaining blood into the acolyte’s bowl mentioned above, or at least into the larger chalice, which likewise contained wine from the offering. This second pouring is expressly described in the first two books, but only one pouring appears in the third, whose words deserve to be noted:

> The pontiff himself is confirmed by the archdeacon from the holy chalice, from which the archdeacon pours a little into the larger chalice, or into the bowl held by the acolyte, so that the people may be confirmed from that same sacred vessel; for wine, even if unconsecrated, when mingled with the Lord’s blood, is sanctified in every respect.

From this inference—which is not found in the other books and may perhaps have been inserted by later hands—it is understood that the larger chalice or bowl contained wine from the offering, [Col. 0883B] poured into it before Christ’s blood was poured in. Why the people were “confirmed” not with pure blood but with blood mixed with wine, we shall consider later. Once the sacred chalice had thus been emptied, it was first handed to the subdeacon, who immediately gave the tube to the archdeacon so that he could confirm the people; then it was handed to the acolyte, who stored the same chalice in his *paratorium*, or case.

17. After this second pouring, the pontiff descended from his seat into the senators’ area, where he refreshed the nobles with the Eucharist. Then he went to the opposite side, where the matrons stood, to give them Communion; the archdeacon followed with the aforesaid bowl to confirm both groups. In the earliest times the Eucharist was also given to laypeople in the hand. Augustine is an important witness to this, both in book II against the letter of Parmenian, chapter 7, and likewise in book XI against the letters of Petilian, chapter 23. Among the Romans, however, even before the pontificate of Gregory the Great, the priest placed it into the mouth, as is proved by book III of the *Dialogues*, chapter 3, where Pope Agapitus is said to have placed the Lord’s body into the mouth of a certain mute and lame man.

18. Meanwhile, with the primicerius’s approval, the bishops and presbyters on either side made the people participants in Holy Communion, while the deacons confirmed them from the bowl.

19. The pontiff returned to his seat and gave Communion in order to the regional clergy, to those who had been standing in a line, and, on feast days, to twelve members of the choir. The regional clergy are the deacons, subdeacons, and acolytes who on other days received Communion in the presbytery, wherever they could.

20. After all these people had returned, the nomenclator, the treasurer, the acolyte who held the paten, the one who held the towel, and the one who supplied the water received Communion at the seat; after the pontiff, the archdeacon confirmed them.

21. Finally, after all these people, the psalm that was sung with the previously mentioned Antiphon at Communion was completed with the concluding verses “Glory be to the Father” and “As it was,” while the regional subdeacon assented by making the sign of the cross upon his forehead. The Micrologus says in chapter 18:

> It should be known that the same Antiphon always has the same psalm as the Introit, if it does not have its own psalm from which it appears to have been taken.

Thus far we have presented the order and sequence of the general Communion as it was observed in the Roman Church before the ninth century. If anything in this rite remains obscure, it must be attributed to the remoteness of the period and the disuse of the rites.

Someone might then ask whether, when the pontiff celebrated the sacred rites with this solemn ceremony and thus gave Communion both to the bishops and to the presbyters, several Masses were celebrated in Rome on the same day; and, further, whether sometimes several were celebrated in one and the same church.

The answer to both questions is easy. Since there were either individual presbyters assigned singly to the titular churches, or several assigned to each, not all of them were present at the pontifical celebration [Col. 0884A]; consequently, they celebrated Masses in their own titular churches to satisfy their people. Indeed, if the multitude of faithful who had gathered required it, the sacrifice was repeated in one and the same church. Thus Pope Leo the Great ordered in Letter 7 to Dioscorus, Bishop of Alexandria:

> So that our observance may agree in all respects, we also wish this to be maintained: when a more solemn feast has summoned a larger gathering of the people, and so great a multitude of the faithful has assembled that one basilica cannot contain them all at once, the offering of the sacrifice must unquestionably be repeated. Otherwise, if only those who arrived first were admitted to this devotion, those who later gathered might appear to have been rejected, although it is entirely in keeping with piety and reason that, whenever the presence of a new congregation has filled the basilica in which the rite is being celebrated, the ensuing sacrifice should be offered again, and so forth.

Whether this repetition of the sacrifice was performed by one priest or by several is not sufficiently clear. Yet in those times the same priest sometimes doubled the solemnities of the Masses. Among these was that holy man Severinus [Col. 0884B], about whom Gregory of Tours writes in *The Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 50. For this Severinus—or Severus, as he is read in a very ancient manuscript—after building two churches, when Sunday arrived, celebrated the Masses in one place and then went to the other. But the Council of Auxerre forbade one priest to say several Masses at one and the same altar.

[LXI] IX. When, and how, Communion under both kinds ceased in the Roman Church.

Since the Communion of laypeople in the Roman Church was by no means administered from pure blood, the transition to the more recent practice—by which laypeople were admitted to participation under only one kind—was not especially difficult. This custom had already been accepted in the thirteenth century. The writers of that period prove it, among them Alexander of Hales:

> It must be said that, because Christ is received whole under both kinds, it is rightly permitted to receive Christ’s body under the appearance of bread alone, as is done almost everywhere by laypeople in the Church.

Yet it is clear from the authors who flourished at the beginning of the twelfth century—Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury, William of Champeaux, Hugh, canon of Saint Victor, and others—that Communion under both kinds was then in force. I published William’s previously unedited testimony in the first preface to the third Benedictine century, section 75; it is useful to bring here what bears upon our subject:

> The fact that each kind is received separately serves to preserve more closely, and as though to present, the remembrance of the body that visibly hung upon the cross and the remembrance of the blood that flowed from his side with water. Nevertheless, it must be known that whoever receives one kind receives the whole Christ.

And below:

> Therefore, to say that both kinds must be received is plainly heretical . . . . And so, although the whole Christ is received under either kind, nevertheless, for the reason stated above, the sacrament under both kinds is unalterably retained by the Church.

These writings were composed before the year [Col. 0884D] 1120; consequently, at that time Communion under both kinds was still unalterably retained by the Church. Hugh of Victor confirms the same in chapter 7 of the *Speculum Ecclesiae*; he lived until the year 1142. We have evidence of this in the ancient Chartulary of the Abbey of Absie among the Pictons, where we read that a certain William of Barges invested Rainier, abbot of Absie, with certain estates, together with the chalice with which he had received Communion, approximately around the year 1150.

Robert Pulleyn, cardinal presbyter of the Holy Roman Church, outlived Hugh of Victor by scarcely ten years; in his writings the opposing practice had already begun to prevail. There is a passage concerning this in part VIII, chapter 3, of his *Sentences*:

> First the body, then the blood, is to be received from the presbyters. Christ’s institution must not be changed . . . . But he entrusted to the judgment of his bride how the Eucharist ought to be received by laypeople; by her counsel and practice it is appropriately done that Christ’s flesh be distributed to laypeople. It would plainly be dangerous to distribute the blood under its liquid appearance to a multitude of the faithful in church; far more dangerous if it were carried throughout the parish to the sick.

Thus already at that time laypeople had begun to receive Communion under one kind, according to Pulleyn, who disapproves of giving the Eucharist dipped into the blood but approves of administering blood to someone who is extremely ill, so that it may be consumed more easily. In some places, however, Communion under both kinds continued longer; it was abolished not by any particular decree but gradually and little by little.

Several causes, not one alone, provided the occasion for this change, without any decree of the universal Church preceding it. Hence in the time of Saint Thomas, and even of Paludanus, certain churches, including Latin ones, retained the ancient practice. The danger of spilling the blood, the prohibition of intinction, examples involving the Communion of the sick and of infants, and the heresy of those who believed that one kind was ineffective without the other gradually led the pastors of the Church to give laypeople Communion under one kind.

After his coronation in the Vatican basilica, Urban VI communicated all the cardinal deacons with his own hand, giving them the precious body and blood of Christ, as had always been the custom of the supreme pontiffs. This is recorded in the letter concerning Urban’s election, published in volume IV of the *Spicilegium*, page 306; the event occurred in 1378. Yet, according to the Ordinarium of Jacobus Gaietanus—who flourished at the end of the thirteenth and the beginning of the fourteenth century—even presbyters were not granted the other kind by the Roman pontiff at their ordination. This privilege is attributed only to bishops, who did not kneel when receiving Communion. These facts are evident from chapters 57 and 58 of that Ordinarium.

Nevertheless, before the Hussite heresy, Communion under both kinds was given by the pontiff to the king and emperor, according to chapter 107 of the same Ceremonial, but not to the queen, according to chapter 109. Pope Clement VI, as Odorico Rainaldo reports, granted John, Duke of Normandy, and his wife Communion under both kinds, provided that it was done privately; he granted the same privilege to the Duke of Burgundy, just as he had granted it to the king and queen of France. [Col. 0885C]

But when Frederick, the third emperor of that name, had gone to Rome during the pontificate of Paul II, [LXIII] the supreme pontiff received the sacrament of the altar under bread alone together with the emperor, deacon, and subdeacon. As for the chalice, although it is customary for those who communicate with the pontiff to share in it, no one except the pontiff drank from it because of the rising condemned heresy of the Hussites and Bohemians, who considered drinking from the chalice necessary for salvation. This was written by the eyewitness Augustine Patricius in his booklet on the emperor’s arrival in the City, which we included in the first volume of the *Museum*.

We shall not burden the reader by relating from the diary of Paris de Grassis, who was then master of ceremonies, the rite by which Clement VII gave Communion to Emperor Charles V shortly before his coronation. On Christmas Day in the year 1529:

> After the Agnus Dei had been said in the Mass, Cardinal Farnese, the assisting cardinal, received the peace from the pope and distributed it to the others, having first kissed the altar, and then the pope himself on the face and breast, and then the emperor. When the emperor wished to kiss the altar at the sacristan’s urging, I expressly forbade him, Paris says, because neither the emperor nor the cardinal deacons are permitted to kiss the altar in such a case, but only bishops and cardinal presbyters. When these things had been done, the pontiff, with his head uncovered, came from the altar to his throne, where he stood and devoutly awaited the sacrament. The cardinal of the Gospel, kneeling at the altar, took the sacrament with the paten, carried it around the altar at the height of his eyes, and gave it to the subdeacon of the Epistle, who was kneeling and awaiting it at the Gospel corner. The subdeacon rose and carried it to the pope, while another master lifted the fringes; he stationed himself at the pope’s left, that is, he stood there with the sacrament. Then the same cardinal, kneeling, took the chalice with the blood and carried it around in the same manner; while I lifted the fringes, he carried it to the pope’s right, where he stationed himself. Then the pontiff, after reading the Prayers as in the book, consumed a portion of the sacrament [Col. 0886A] and then a portion of the blood from the chalice with a golden tube. Caesar and the other princes wished to receive Communion. The pontiff broke another portion of the sacrament and gave one particle to Cardinal Cibo and another to the subdeacon, after first kissing the pope’s hand and face. They then withdrew to the altar, where each consumed a portion of the blood, with the particle placed inside it, as is customary.

To certain persons, however, Communion under both kinds has been granted by privilege: to the kings of France at their coronation; to the deacon and subdeacon of the church of Saint-Denis near Paris on Sundays and solemn feast days; and to the ministers of the altar at Cluny on every Sunday and feast day. This prerogative was approved by the Council of Trent.

X. Special rites on the Saturday before Palm Sunday and on Palm Sunday itself.

Having explained certain distinctive ceremonies that formerly came generally into use in the pontifical Mass, we must now briefly touch upon other special rites that occur on particular days of the year [Col. 0886B]. We begin with the Saturday before Palm Sunday, for which the ritual books display great diversity. This diversity concerns chiefly three matters: the station, the pope’s alms, and the *fermentum*.

In the books of the Gregorian Sacramentary that Amalarius saw in his own time, no station is assigned, as is clear from book I of the *Officialis*, chapter 9, where the following is read concerning the Saturday before Palm Sunday:

> In our Sacramentary and Antiphonary it is entitled: “Saturday is vacant.” The Lord Pope gives alms—as if it said that this Saturday was vacant from the station, and therefore from its proper office, because on that day the pope was occupied with distributing alms.

Indeed, to this day the office of the Mass, except for the Collects, Epistle, and Gospel, is repeated on that Saturday from the preceding Friday; the Micrologus long ago observed that this was customary on days vacant from a station and office. Nevertheless, in our list of Collects and stations, a Collect is assigned on this Saturday to Saint Xystus, and the station to Saint John at the Latin Gate. The Sacramentary of the Pamelian edition agrees: omitting mention of the Collect, it indicates the station at Saint John before the Latin Gate.

By contrast, in the manuscript of Queen Christina, written in capital letters in the eighth century, these words are read:

> Saturday at Saint Peter’s, when alms are given.

Here the station is placed at Saint Peter’s, whereas in the preceding sources it is placed at Saint John at the Latin Gate. Both are combined in the Vatican Manuscript:

> Saturday at Saint Peter’s, when alms are given. Collect at Saint Xystus; station at Saint John at the Latin Gate.

But in the *Capitulare* of Epistles and Gospels, which the learned John Fronto published under the title *Roman Calendar*, another variation occurs for the same day: [LXV]

> On Saturday the *fermentum* is given in the Lateran consistory.

What accounts for such diversity?

Perhaps in Gregory’s time those alms were not given at Saint Peter’s, and consequently the station could be held at Saint John at the Latin Gate. This may be proved by the fact that Pope Zacharias decreed that, on frequent days, the cost of provisions—which is still called alms—should be carried from the venerable patriarchate by the vice-chancellors to the poor and pilgrims staying at Saint Peter’s and distributed to them. Whether this also applied to the Saturday before Palm Sunday, others may judge. They may also decide whether what is read about Hadrian I can be referred to this matter: he repaired the structure called the Sabbatine, through which water flowed for the benefit of the poor who annually came to receive alms at the Paschal feast and to wash themselves.

Yet, if what we said above about the station at Saint Peter’s is properly weighed, it may perhaps appear that it was not an ordinary but a discretionary station—namely, one held when alms were given, which perhaps depended upon the pontiff’s will.

There is no less difficulty concerning the *fermentum* that is ordered to be given in the Lateran consistory [Col. 0887A].
