It is inferred that this *fermentum* was something different from the alms mentioned above, not only from the difference in the word but also from the difference of place: alms were distributed at Saint Peter’s in the Vatican, while the *fermentum* was distributed in the Lateran palace. But if we interpret this *fermentum* as the Eucharist, which every Sunday was sent to the titular churches from the consecration performed by the pontiff, why is it mentioned specifically in connection with the Saturday before Palm Sunday rather than another day? Was it because, since the titular presbyters would be occupied on the following Sunday, the distribution of the *fermentum*, or Eucharist, was made not on Sunday itself as usual but on the preceding Saturday, and was therefore recorded because of its extraordinary character?

I confess that I have not ascertained this matter adequately, but I have nevertheless thought it worthwhile to record it and leave it for examination by others.

As for the alms of that Saturday, other churches also, following the example of the Roman pontiff, were accustomed to wash the feet of the poor on that very day. Among them was the province of Rouen, as witnessed by John, Bishop of Avranches, whose words are these:

> On the Saturday preceding Palm Sunday, the ecclesiastical Ordo orders the bishop or the senior official of the church to wash the feet of the poor, and each of the brothers, if he can, to wash the feet of one poor person—indeed, in imitation of Mary, who washed the Lord’s feet.

There is no doubt that alms were likewise given to those poor people themselves.

On Palm Sunday a bier was customarily carried with the text of the Gospels, so that the honor offered to Christ the Lord on that day might, in his place, be bestowed upon the most holy Gospel. Concerning this Cencius writes in chapter 9:

> On Palm Sunday a certain portable bier is prepared with the greatest dignity, into which the holy Gospel is placed, signifying Christ; it is set in the church before the altar from which the clergy are to proceed.

The same was formerly done in other churches and monasteries as well. Thus it is read in a manuscript book of the Customs of the Monasteries of Germany:

> In the morning on Palm Sunday, the keepers should carefully prepare a certain portable bier in the form of a coffin, into which small cases, or the text of the Gospels, are to be placed. Reliquaries, or reliquary boxes, should also be hung above it. They should secretly carry it before Prime to the church, to the place from which they are to proceed, together with crosses, candlesticks, the thurible, holy water, the Gospel book, albs, flowers, palms, and everything appropriate to that procession.

In certain places, instead of the Gospel, the holy Eucharist was placed in the bier; this practice formerly prevailed in the monasteries of Normandy even before the heresy of Berengar. Lanfranc, Berengar’s opponent, describes the order of this rite in his Statutes:

> When the cantor begins the Antiphon “The crowds approach,” two priests dressed in albs should go out carrying the bier, which shortly before that day should have been brought there by those same priests and in which Christ’s body should have been placed. Immediately before the bier should go those carrying banners and crosses, together with the other things mentioned above. While those who carry the bier are standing, they too should stand on the right and left as they came.

And below:

> When these things have been done in this manner, with the abbot or cantor beginning the Antiphon “Hail, our King,” let the bearers of the bier pass through the middle of the station, preceded by those carrying the banners and by the other bearers mentioned above, with everyone maintaining on the return the order they had on the outward journey. As they pass, they should bend their knees—not all together, but individually on either side, as the bier passes before them.

The same rite is described in our *Book of the Usages of Bec* and in the *Customs of the Monastery of Lyre* in the same province. In them various genuflections before the sacred bier are prescribed, clearly demonstrating veneration of the most holy Eucharist [LXVII]. It is not useful to report these at greater length, since all these matters will be treated more accurately in the work on monastic rites which one of our number, Edmund Martène, has under preparation for the press. I add here only that this solemn carrying of the most holy sacrament long preceded the institution of Urban IV, who [Col. 0888A] was the first to institute the feast of that same most holy sacrament and the annual carrying of the sacrament during that feast. Moreover, the same rite which we described above from Lanfranc is, as I hear, still observed in the Church of Rouen; its special zeal in combating the nascent heresy of Berengarius is clearly demonstrated by what we reported in the second volume of the *Analecta*. That this was an ancient rite of the Church of Rouen is evident from the Acts appended to the book on ecclesiastical offices by John of Avranches, although no mention of any such rite occurs there.

### XI. Singular rites during the three days before Easter, especially on Maundy Thursday and Good Friday

On Maundy Thursday it was customary for penitents who had been confined on the preceding Ash Wednesday to be absolved; for new chrism to be consecrated; for a new fire likewise to be blessed; and for the Eucharist to be reserved for the following day. Also—and this was instituted approximately four hundred years ago—general processes, as they are called, or excommunications, were pronounced against certain criminals [Col. 0888B]. These processes were also customarily carried out on the Ascension of the Lord and at the dedication of the basilica of the apostles. All these matters are treated at length in the course of the following books; here certain observations must be made about them.

First of all, what is read concerning Thursday of Holy Week in the very ancient *Book of the Sacraments of Egbert, Bishop of York*, preserved in the church of Évreux, seems worth reporting.

“On Maundy Thursday, at the sixth hour, Mass is celebrated at the Lateran. Thus beginning, the Pontiff says, ‘Let us pray.’ Then the Holy Things are placed upon the altar, and the altar is hollow. When everything has been duly arranged upon the altar—the oblation and offerings—and a few lights have been kindled throughout the church, the deacons dressed in dalmatics, with nine candelabra set before the altar, while the pontiff stands before the altar and says in a raised voice, ‘Lift up your hearts,’ the people respond, ‘We have them with the Lord.’ After the Pontiff has finished ‘It is truly worthy,’ all the clergy and people say, ‘Holy.’ Thus he proceeds through the Mass as far as ‘Whom, we beseech you, O Lord, the giver, graciously admit’ [Col. 0888C]. Then the cardinal deacon, taking the oil for the sick, carries it to the Pontiff. The latter, turning slightly away from the altar and standing on his step, makes the sign over the oil in the deacon’s hand, silently saying the Prayer above it. When the Prayer is finished, the oil is placed upon a certain column. The priest celebrates the Mass in its proper order and says, ‘Through whom you make all these things,’ etc. After the Lord’s Prayer, the Pontiff silently makes the sign over the chalice with the consecrated oblation, with no one responding. The deacons cover the sacraments. Then the archdeacon, ascending with the chrism, offers the Pontiff for blessing a golden ampulla, veiled with a white cloth, in his hand. When the Prayer of consecration is finished, it is brought forward by the acolytes for veneration and placed in the sacristy. While the clergy and all the people are receiving communion, the Pontiff says to all communicants, ‘Jesus took bread. Let us pray.’ After thanks have been given, all the people respond, ‘Amen.’”

Thus far the *Codex of Egbert of York*, who flourished in the middle of the eighth century.

Several points in this passage require fuller explanation. First, before Mass the Holy Things are placed upon the altar [Col. 0888D]. By this name, I believe, the Eucharist reserved from the preceding sacrifice is meant, so that it might be mingled in the chalice together with a fragment of the newly consecrated Eucharist, according to the solemn rite which we explained above. For the miraculous blood preserved in the hollow stone, which on this day of Maundy Thursday was brought onto the altar—as we shall soon see—does not seem to be of such great antiquity.

Second, the altar of the Lateran church is hollow. Thus the Pontiff, after removing the table that closed access to its interior, performed the sacred rites within the altar itself on this day. The Roman Order edited here from the Maffaean Codex, Order 10, explains the matter as follows:

“The table is removed from the altar, with the coverings folded above it, and with reverence and complete devotion it is carried back by those same men to the chapel of Saint Pancratius beside the canons’ cloister, because that is the place of preservation; and with every precaution it is guarded until Saturday. Then [Col. 0889A] the Pontiff comes to the altar, taking a glass vessel which contains within it a certain golden container; in the container is a precious hollow stone, and in the hollow of the stone Christ’s blood is carefully enclosed. It is said to have flowed miraculously from a certain image of Christ that had been struck. Each year it is taken out and placed back there in the hollow of the stone of the chest [LXIX]. Then the Pontiff lifts it up and displays it, so that the entire crowd may see it with fear and complete devotion. Afterwards it is entrusted for safekeeping to the prior and canons of that church until Saturday. Then the Pontiff enters alone within the chest in order to sacrifice, signifying what is written in the Old Testament: that the high priest alone entered the Holy of Holies once a year, etc.”

Innocent III gives the same explanation of this action in his sermon on Maundy Thursday; William Durand also agrees with him in Book VI, chapter 75.

After the blessing of the chrism, the Pontiff washed his hands and returned to the altar, where he received communion, and after him all the people in their proper order. These are the words of the first Roman Order [Col. 0889B]. The Holy Things were preserved until the following day. On that day, at the ninth hour, they caused fire to be struck from a stone in a place outside the basilica, so that a candle could be lit from it. The light was kept until Holy Saturday, to illuminate the candle which was to be blessed on that same day. Now this blessing of the new fire is deferred until Holy Saturday itself.

In the commonly circulated Roman Order it is prescribed that, after the blessing of the chrism, the Pontiff return to the altar and the deacons uncover the Holy Things. The Pontiff then divides the oblations for breaking, and all the people receive communion in their proper order. He takes from them whole oblations to be preserved until the morning of Good Friday, from which they are to receive communion without the Lord’s blood. The blood, however, is to be entirely consumed on that same day. The same is also read in the Vendôme Codex. A little later it says:

“When the oblations have been broken, the priests shall receive communion first, then the deacons and all the others. Thus the Mass shall be completed entirely in its proper order.”

In the Maffaean Order mentioned above, it is said that only the Pontiff received communion on this day [Col. 0889C], when he celebrated the sacred rites at the Lateran.

The Corbie Codex must not be passed over here. It contains a Roman Order for the three days before Easter, adapted to monastic usage eight hundred years ago. What it says about communion on Maundy Thursday seems worthy of attention:

“When the priest has broken the Holy Things, he shall put one part into the chalice and receive communion from another. He shall leave a third part upon the altar, and the deacon shall communicate him from the chalice, and on that day only. After he has communicated the priest, he shall place the chalice upon the altar. The deacon shall take the larger paten, place whole oblations from the Holy Things upon it, and set it beside the chalice on the left [LXX]. Then two subdeacons shall come, one with a paten and the other with a chalice, both empty. The deacon shall take from the larger paten as much of the oblations as may suffice for the communion of the people, and likewise from the chalice; he shall place these in the paten and chalice held in the hands of the subdeacons. Immediately what remains upon the altar [Col. 0889D] shall be covered by two deacons, each with a clean cloth. From the other portion beside the altar they shall make the fraction, and return to the priest so that they and the others may receive communion in order. After the Prayer has been said following communion, the deacon shall not say, ‘Go, the Mass is ended’; rather, everything shall be concluded with that Prayer itself. The oblations which remained covered upon the altar shall be preserved for the following day according to custom.”

Thus far the Corbie Codex, no. 663, to which we shall return below. The words “The deacon shall communicate him from the chalice, and on that day only” are somewhat obscure. They can be clarified from other books, in which it is prescribed that the Pontiff suck the blood from the chalice with a tube or reed, except on Maundy Thursday, the only day on which he formerly drank the blood directly from the chalice.

Finally, in the ancient Missal of the most illustrious Bishop of Riez, written nearly six hundred years ago, almost the same words as those in the Roman Order are reported as follows:

“Then only the priest or bishop shall receive communion, and the deacon [Col. 0890A] covers the Holy Things with a cloth upon the altar. Afterwards the priest washes his hands, and the deacon goes to the altar and uncovers the Holy Things. The priest comes before the altar, divides the oblation for breaking, and all the people receive communion in their proper order, etc. The Lord’s body is most carefully reserved for the following day. When the choir has sung Vespers, it is reverently carried by the priest and deacon, together with the other ministers, to the place where it is to be reserved, while they hold a very clean cloth above it. This is done without the blood, with incense and lights preceding, until it is placed where it is to be placed; and it must never remain without a light.”

Thus far the ancient Missal that belonged to the use of the same Church of Riez, which consequently at that time followed the Roman Order, with only a few additions reflecting the circumstances of time and place.

As for the penitents, they were reconciled to the Church before Mass. The general processes against criminals, however, took place after Mass, before the *mandatum*, or washing of the feet. Jerome discusses this reconciliation of penitents in his letter to Oceanus on the death of Fabiola. She had put on sackcloth [Col. 0890B] in order publicly to confess her error; with the whole city of Rome looking on, she stood in the order of penitents in the basilica once belonging to Lateranus, who had been struck down by Caesar’s sword, before Easter Day [LXXI], while the bishop, priests, and all the people wept with her. Sozomen gives a lengthy description of the same rite in Book VII, chapter 16, which it will be worthwhile to consult. The solemn form for absolving penitents on this day is found in the commonly circulated Roman Order.

Moreover, so that the basilica of Saint Peter might not be deprived of honor on Maundy Thursday, John XIX established by a special diploma that the Bishop of Silva Candida should consecrate the chrism in that basilica on that very day and perform the other duties expressed in the papal letter that will be published here in its proper place.

On Friday, called Good Friday, after the customary Prayers had been said for each order of the Church and for all people—for these Prayers are mentioned in the booklet appended to the letter of Pope Celestine I, containing [Col. 0890C] the authorities of earlier bishops of the Apostolic See concerning grace and free will against the Pelagians, chapter 8—and after the adoration of the cross, the two senior priests, who had first venerated the cross, entered the sacristy, or the place where the Lord’s body that had remained from the preceding day had been deposited, and placed it on a paten. A subdeacon held before them a chalice with unconsecrated wine, while another subdeacon held a paten with the Lord’s body. While these men held them, one of the senior priests took the paten and the other the chalice, and they carried them onto the stripped altar. This is how it is written in the first Roman Order and its appendix.

The very ancient Sacramentary granted by Charlemagne to the monastery of Gellone has it somewhat differently:

“After the Prayers written above have been completed, the deacons enter the sacristy and proceed with the Lord’s body and blood, which had remained from the preceding day, and place them upon the altar. The priest comes before the altar, adoring the Lord’s cross, etc.”

Here it is not priests but deacons who carry from the sacristy the Lord’s body, which is called the Lord’s body and blood even though it had been reserved under only one species. The Gelasian Sacramentary has the same wording for this day [Col. 0890D]. This testimony is supported by Augustine Patricius in his *Ceremonial*, according to which, before John XXII, the deacon carried the sacrament before the altar; the common rubric also has this. “After those times,” he says, “the Pontiff carries it back, and this is better.” Indeed, even now the Pontiff, although he may not himself celebrate the divine mysteries, customarily carries the most holy sacrament on Maundy Thursday into the chapel where it is to be reserved, and from there [LXXII] brings it back to the altar on the following day.

In the aforementioned appendix to our first Roman Order the following is then read:

“After the cross has been venerated and returned to its place, the Pontiff descends before the altar and says, ‘Let us pray. Instructed by saving precepts,’ etc., together with the Lord’s Prayer. Then follows, ‘Deliver us, we beseech you, O Lord.’ When they have said ‘Amen,’ he takes from the Holy Things and places it in the chalice, saying nothing. All receive communion in silence. And everything is completed.”

The same words occur in the first Roman Order, in which the following is added:

“And the Pontiff says, ‘In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Peace to you.’ They respond, ‘Amen.’ Shortly afterward each person says Vespers privately, and thus they go to the table.”

In both texts all are said to receive communion on Good Friday, just as they did on Maundy Thursday. The Gellone Codex also testifies to this. The commonly circulated Alcuin, however, teaches the opposite. Concerning Maundy Thursday he says:

“There are some who wish to receive the Eucharist daily. Since the Lord’s body is not confected on Good Friday, it is necessary that those who wish to receive communion have a sacrifice from the preceding day; yet the Romans do not do this.”

This passage is found word for word in Amalarius, Book I, chapter 12, except for the clause “yet the Romans do not do this.” In chapter 15, however, he presents the matter itself, after quoting the passage above from the Roman Order:

“In the book mentioned above I found it written that, after the veneration of the cross, two priests should bring the Lord’s body, reserved from the preceding day, and a chalice with unconsecrated wine, which was then to be consecrated, and from these the people should receive communion. Concerning this practice I questioned the Roman archdeacon, and he replied: ‘At that station where the Apostolicus venerates the cross, no one there receives communion.’”

Therefore, the rite prescribed in the older booklets of the Roman Order had by then ceased. The Roman archdeacon could not have been ignorant of the custom of his own time, since he was an eyewitness; and Amalarius, who was precise in such matters, should be regarded as far removed from any suspicion of error, and even more from any suspicion of falsehood. Certainly, in the tenth booklet of the Roman Order which we publish here (p. 101, line 19), it is recorded that only the Pontiff received communion on Maundy Thursday and Good Friday, even excluding the ministers, although general communion continued on those days elsewhere.

What that station was in the tenth century, where the Pontiff performed the sacred offices on Good Friday [LXXIII], we learn both from the same booklet and from Benedict, canon of Saint Peter’s:

“On Good Friday,” says Benedict, “the hebdomadary bishop performs the office in the basilica of the Savior. The Lord Pope descends from the palace and dresses behind the altar there with the other orders; barefoot, he proceeds with the Procession, and everyone with him, singing the Psalter, as far as the Holy Cross. A certain cardinal honorably carries the Lord’s body from the preceding day, preserved in a container for the corporals, while the regional subdeacon carries at his breast the covered stational cross. When the Pontiff arrives at the church of the aforementioned basilica, he washes his feet, puts on shoes, and ascends to the altar, where he first prays and then sits. A basilican cleric goes to the lectern and begins to read; thereafter the entire office proceeds as it is written in the book. After the Lord’s Prayer, etc., he takes the Lord’s body that the cardinal had brought and communicates from the wine poured into the chalice. When the office is finished, dressed in this same manner they return by the same Procession as before, but shod, to the palace, singing the remaining Psalms.”

Yet we cannot doubt that in the eighth century the station on Good Friday took place neither in that location nor with those same rites. For in the first Roman Order and its appendix it is prescribed that on that very day, at the third hour, all the priests—both those of the city and those from the suburbs—and all the clergy with the people should assemble in the designated church within the City, though not in the greater church. There they were to await the Pontiff, or whoever acted in his place. After the priests’ Prayers, the priests of the churches, whether from the City or the suburbs, went to their own churches, so that everything might be done in this order until Vespers.

In the most ancient book of stations no place is assigned for Good Friday. Only this rubric is read:

“On Good Friday we sing the daytime course separately, and at the ninth hour we enter the church with the lord bishop or cardinal priest. Dressed in black garments, without any singing, we proceed to the altar; and the lector ascends the lectern.”

The station, therefore, was formerly determined at discretion. Nevertheless, since the station on the preceding day had been at the Lateran basilica, where one species of the Eucharist had consequently been reserved, the station on the following day could not be far away, lest it become necessary to carry the Eucharist too great a distance [Col. 0892A] for the Mass of the Presanctified to be celebrated on Good Friday.

That the station at the Lateran basilica was extremely ancient may be inferred from Jerome’s letter to Oceanus on the death of Fabiola [LXXIV]. He says that she stood in the order of penitents before Easter Day in the basilica of the Lateran, once belonging to Lateranus, who had been beheaded by Caesar’s sword. This reconciliation of penitents was then performed at Rome on the Thursday before Easter, as Innocent I explicitly reports in his letter to Decentius.

Before concluding this chapter, it is worthwhile to investigate whether, in the earliest centuries of the Church, the Mass of the Presanctified was customary on Good Friday; whether this rite was universal; then why a solemn Mass was not celebrated on that day, nor on the following Saturday—for the Mass now said on that day belonged to the following night; finally, why wine and water were placed in the chalice according to custom, and why a particle of the Eucharist was at last put into the chalice.

The first question is not easily answered. According to the tradition of the Church, as Innocent I testifies, during those two days—Good Friday and Holy Saturday [Col. 0892B]—the sacraments, that is, the sacred mysteries of the Eucharist, were not celebrated at all. But whether this testimony should be extended to the Mass of the Presanctified is unclear. If what we noted above from the commonly circulated Gelasian Sacramentary is not an interpolation, it must be asserted that this custom was already in existence in the fifth century. At least no one can rightly deny that it was practiced in the age of Gregory the Great.

Yet among the Latins this rite does not seem to have been universal before Gregory’s pontificate. From the African Church we learn only this from Augustine’s Sermon 218, which appears in the new edition under the title *On the Passion of the Lord*: the Passion was then read solemnly and celebrated solemnly. What this solemnity consisted in is not clear, except that, according to Sermon 232, because the Passion was read on a single day, it was customarily read only according to Matthew. Augustine therefore wished at one time that it should be read each year according to all the Evangelists. When this was done, people did not hear what they were accustomed to hearing [Col. 0892C], and they were disturbed. But neither in these passages nor elsewhere, so far as I know, does Augustine say anything about the Mass of the Presanctified.

The fathers of the Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 7, criticize the abuse of certain churches in Spain where, on the Friday of the Lord’s Passion, the doors of the basilicas were closed, neither was the office celebrated nor the Lord’s Passion preached to the people. They therefore decree that on that day the mystery of the cross—which the Lord himself wished to be announced to all—must be preached, and that the whole people must ask aloud for the remission of sins [LXXV], so that, cleansed by penitential contrition, they might be worthy to receive the venerable day of the Lord’s Resurrection with their iniquities forgiven and to receive the sacrament of his body and blood cleansed from sins.

Communion, therefore, was deferred until the day of the Resurrection. At that time, on Good Friday, only the preaching or recitation of the Lord’s Passion together with the divine office was customary, accompanied by a solemn granting of forgiveness to sinners. The Mozarabic Missal accurately presents the ancient rite on this very day [Col. 0892D]; in its printed editions a Mass of the Presanctified appears to have been added. Certainly, that general communion was not then customary among the Spaniards is confirmed by canon 8 of the same council. Those who had not honored the day of the Lord’s Passion by abstinence—as certain people customarily did, breaking their fast at the ninth hour on that very day—were excluded from paschal joy, or communion.

If the author of the rule published in Gaul under the name of the Master lived there, it may be inferred from him that in the seventh century the Mass of the Presanctified was practiced in Gaul on Good Friday. For in chapter 53 the Master prescribes that on that day the sacraments of the altar should be completed in a large glass paten—that is, reserved—so that, when on Friday the Jews sought Christ for his Passion, he might be revealed on that day in our minds, namely through communion, and, as he says, might appear to us on Saturday through the Resurrection in the new sacrament.

He deprives those of communion who have tasted any food on Good Friday. “Those who will eat on Friday,” he says, “should eat without communion, so that it may be recognized who unjustly eats on Friday without Christ.” Since, therefore, the Master commands that those who had eaten should abstain from communion on that day as a punishment, it follows that communion was granted to those who had remained fasting throughout the entire day. But whether this can be attributed to the Gallican churches is uncertain, especially since in the most ancient liturgical books that were in use among our Gallic peoples before the Roman Order was received, nothing concerning this is prescribed.

Why the solemn sacrifice—the second question—was omitted on Good Friday and the following Saturday is also a considerable difficulty. Expositors of ecclesiastical rites commonly give a moral reason for Good Friday: on that day the Lord offered himself, and that offering is sufficient for the salvation of believers. This is the explanation of Amalarius and the commonly circulated Alcuin.

More probable is the reason indicated by Innocent I: during those two days the apostles, being in sorrow, remained fasting, so that, for this reason, the tradition of the Church holds that during those two days the sacraments were not celebrated at all. Hence the first Christians, out of a desire to imitate the apostles, likewise abstained from all food during those two days, and from the offering of the sacrifice itself, and perhaps also from communion from the Presanctified, although I do not know whether this was omitted in the earliest times.

But whether this Mass and communion from the Presanctified were instituted from the very beginnings of the nascent Church or during the following early centuries, another difficulty arises: why were water and wine poured into the chalice in such a Mass, and why also a previously consecrated particle of the Eucharist? The reason is evidently that communion has the character of a sacred banquet and must consist of food and drink. Since, however, the other species of the Eucharist did not seem to be reserved for the following day, and custom did not permit the sacraments to be celebrated during those two days, it followed that the second part of the banquet—namely, the drink—was supplied by pure wine mixed with water but sanctified by a particle of the Eucharist [Col. 0893C]. These are our conjectures, which we submit to the judgment and criticism of those more learned than ourselves. Let us now proceed to other matters.

### XII. On the sanctification of an unconsecrated chalice through contact with a consecrated particle

This passage requires us, for a fuller understanding of the subject, to examine whether the chalice in the Mass of the Presanctified celebrated by the Latins on Good Friday was truly and properly consecrated by the insertion of a consecrated particle, and whether the cup used for the communion of the people in the pontifical Mass was likewise consecrated by the pouring in of consecrated blood.

In examining this twofold question, which is almost reducible to one, we must distinguish authors who lived before the heresy of Berengarius from those who lived after it. We must then inquire whether their opinion was private or common. Finally, if some of them believed that consecration took place through contact, we must ask whether this opinion was contrary to the Roman Church’s conviction concerning the true body and blood of Christ in the Eucharist [Col. 0893D].

#### 1.

To begin with the Mass of the Presanctified, nothing earlier on this matter is found than the Gelasian Sacramentary. For the canon 22 of Orange, which some introduce here, must unquestionably be understood only of the mingling of the Eucharist in an already consecrated chalice. Nothing, I say, is earlier than the Gelasian Sacramentary, whose edition was prepared at Rome in 1680 by Joseph Maria Thomasius, a man deserving well of the Church. In that Sacramentary the following is read under Maundy Thursday:

“When this has been completed”—that is, the blessing of the chrism—“you shall come before the altar and place some of that host in the mouth of the chalice. You shall not say, ‘The peace of the Lord,’ nor shall they exchange the peace. They shall reserve some of that sacrifice for the following day, from which they may receive communion.”

For the following Friday:

“When all these things have been completed, all adore the holy cross and receive communion.”

A somewhat later document is the Roman Order, whose words in the printed books, under Good Friday, are as follows:

“After it has been venerated”—that is, the cross—“and returned to its place, two subdeacons and the two senior priests shall enter the sacristy, or the place where the Lord’s body has been placed, which remained from the preceding day. They shall place it upon a paten. Let one subdeacon hold before them a chalice with unconsecrated wine, and another subdeacon a paten with the Lord’s body. While they hold these, let one senior priest take the paten and the other the chalice, and let them carry them onto the bare altar, singing the Communion, ‘This body, which is for you.’ When the Communion has been finished, let the bishop begin, ‘In a spirit of humility,’ bowing before the altar; and when he has risen, let him say: ‘Instructed by saving precepts,’ and the Lord’s Prayer, and ‘Deliver us, we beseech you, O Lord,’ through ‘World without end.’ When they have said ‘Amen,’ he takes from the Holy Things and places it in the chalice, saying nothing, unless perhaps he wishes to say something secretly. He does not say, ‘The peace of the Lord,’ because no kisses of those standing around follow. But he shall sanctify the unconsecrated wine through the sanctified bread. All shall receive communion in silence, and thus everything is completed.”

Thus far the Roman Order, as it is read in the excellent Vendôme Codex. In that codex the words enclosed in brackets are absent from the printed editions; this passage also varies there. Where the printed editions have, “The unconsecrated wine is sanctified through the sanctified bread,” the aforementioned codex reads, “Let him sanctify,” and so forth, without any difference in meaning.

Yet whatever the meaning of these words—which will be discussed later—they appear to have been inserted by later writers for purposes of explanation into the original booklet of the Roman Order. For these words are absent from our first booklet, no. 34. They are also absent from its appendix. In both places, with this gloss omitted, the reading is:

“He takes from the Holy Things and places it in the chalice, saying nothing; and all receive communion in silence, and everything is completed.”

This is how it stands in the extremely ancient Vatican, Corbie, and Colbertine Codices, the last two of which approach eight hundred years in age. It is also how it stands in the Gregorian Sacramentary.

After the Roman Order comes Amalarius, Book I, chapter 15:

“In the book mentioned above I found it written that two priests should bring, after the veneration of the cross, the Lord’s body, which had been reserved from the preceding day, and a chalice with unconsecrated wine, which was then to be consecrated, and from these the people should receive communion . . . Whoever, according to the order of the booklet, consecrates the wine through the mingling of bread and wine does not observe the tradition of the Church, concerning which Innocent says that during those two days the sacraments are not celebrated at all . . . The proper order is that we should wait until our Lord consecrates the sacraments of his body and blood on the cross, and makes them new through his Resurrection, and then at last we may eat and drink that most health-giving sacrament.”

The commonly circulated Alcuin uses nearly the same words as the published Roman Order:

“When they have said ‘Amen,’ he takes from the holy bread and places it in the chalice in silence. He does not say, ‘The peace of the Lord,’ because no kisses of those standing around follow. The unconsecrated wine is sanctified through the sanctified bread.”

We shall see later that these words were taken from the first edition of Amalarius.

These are the authors whom we have found to mention this consecration or sanctification before the condemnation of Berengarius. Shortly after the death of Gregory VII, who finally imposed silence upon Berengarius, the *Micrologus* was written. It discusses the matter in chapter 19:

“It is not an authentic practice for some people to dip the Lord’s body and distribute it dipped to the people as the completion of communion. For the Roman Order contradicts this, since on Good Friday it commands the unconsecrated wine to be consecrated with the Lord’s Prayer and the insertion of the Lord’s body, so that the people may be able to receive communion fully.”

In the booklets of Benedict, canon of Saint Peter’s, and of Cardinal Cencius, no mention is made of consecration through contact. Indeed, Benedict says that after taking the body of the Lord Christ, the Pontiff is confirmed by wine poured into the chalice, not by consecrated or sanctified wine. James Gaetanus, however, says in chapter 92 that the unconsecrated wine is sanctified by the body of the Lord that has been inserted. Peter Amelius says the same, “through the placing (*immissio*) of the Lord’s body” [Col. 0895A].

Finally, to conclude with the Roman ritual books, Augustine Patricius simply calls it wine. In Book II, chapter 51, he says:

“He takes wine and water with the particle existing in the chalice”—that is, the bishop celebrating the divine mysteries in the presence of the Pope.

In chapter 54 he says:

“The Pontiff himself does not suck the wine with a reed, but drinks from the chalice.”

There is greater difficulty in the tenth booklet of ours published here. In the section concerning Viaticum for the sick, it prescribes that the Eucharist of the Lord’s body, dipped in wine, should be given to them, and that the wine, sanctified by such dipping, is transformed into Christ’s blood, while saying:

“Receive, brother, the Viaticum of the body and blood,” etc.

Here the word “transformation” leaves no room for doubt about the meaning. Yet in the Roman Ritual preserved in the library of Santa Croce at Florence, the same rite is reported in the same words, except for “transformed into Christ’s blood.” This is evidence that the same thing happened to this Ritual as to the Roman Order: these words were inserted as a commentary by some private author, expressing not the common opinion of the Roman Church but the private opinion of a certain individual.

Certainly Cardinal James of Vitry, who could not have been ignorant of the teaching of that Church, unequivocally declares that those who say that on Good Friday Christ’s body changes wine into blood through contact are lying. Therefore no one should say that this was then the doctrine of the Roman Church, but at most the opinion of certain glossators of ritual books.

#### 2.

The second question that must be discussed here is whether the authors and books just mentioned require us to understand their statements as referring only to true and proper consecration—that is, whether it was their opinion that wine is truly and properly changed into Christ’s blood through contact with a consecrated particle—or whether they believed this consecration or sanctification to be merely accidental and metaphorical.

Concerning the Gelasian Sacramentary and the first booklet of the Roman Order, together with its earlier appendix, nothing certain or established can be offered [Col. 0895C], since they mention only the mingling of the particle and say nothing about a consecration or sanctification resulting from contact. The commonly circulated Roman Order explicitly does mention this sanctification on Good Friday, and the Vendôme Codex agrees with the printed books, except that where the printed editions have, “The unconsecrated wine is sanctified through the sanctified bread,” the aforementioned codex reads, “Let him sanctify,” and so forth, without any difference in meaning.

But whether this clause was written in the original exemplar of the Roman Order may rightly be doubted. For it is found neither in the Gelasian nor in the Gregorian Sacramentaries [LXXX], nor in the older booklets of the Roman Order. The clause has the appearance of a gloss by an interpreter, not of a rite instituted by the original author himself.

But granting that this clause is proper to the Roman Order itself—the third one that we publish—and not an interpolation, what finally is its meaning? Certainly, although Cyprian in his letter to Epictetus equates the sanctifying and consecrating of the offering [Col. 0895D], here the only apparent meaning is that unconsecrated wine receives an incidental sanctification through contact with the particle that has been inserted, but not a true and real consecration by which the wine is actually changed into Christ’s blood. This will seem unclear to no one who carefully considers the passage from the office for the Lord’s Supper as it appears in the printed editions:

> The Pontiff, coming to the altar, shall divide the offerings and take from them whole offerings to be kept until the morning of Good Friday; from these they shall communicate without the blood of the Lord. But the blood shall be entirely consumed on that same day.

From these words it is clear that the meaning of this passage is that on Good Friday Communion takes place without the blood of the Lord, because the blood was entirely consumed on the preceding day. Therefore the author’s intention is that wine by no means truly and properly becomes blood through contact with the particle injected into the chalice; otherwise Communion would not take place without the blood of the Lord. Accordingly, when in the office for Good Friday one reads, “But unconsecrated wine is sanctified [Col. 0896A] by the sanctified bread,” if these words have not been inserted into the commonly received Roman Order, they must be understood only of incidental sanctification, and not of true and real consecration.

This interpretation is supported by the tradition of the Church, which Pope Innocent I mentions in his letter to Decentius. That tradition holds that during the two days preceding Easter the sacraments are not celebrated at all; but this would be false if the consecration of the wine were truly effected by whatever means. For one could not say that the sacraments were not celebrated at all if consecration took place even in part. Thus, if the Church’s tradition is to remain consistent, on Good Friday one must admit only such sanctification as excludes every kind of celebration or consecration of the sacraments—namely, the sanctification of the wine that comes externally from contact with a particle previously consecrated. Certainly, if the Church had wished on Good Friday to have a complete Communion under both species without a celebration, it would have been easy to reserve the Lord’s blood from the preceding sacrifice [LXXXI] for the following day, without danger [Col. 0896B] or injury to so great a sacrament.

There is greater difficulty concerning Amalarius’s opinion. To make it easier to understand and clarify, it is useful to observe that Amalarius made not one but several editions or revisions of the book *The Ecclesiastical Office*, in which he discusses this matter. For around the year 820 he composed this work, which consists of four books, and dedicated it to Emperor Louis. Later, when he had been sent by the same emperor to Rome after ten years and had observed many things concerning ecclesiastical rites firsthand, he revised his work again, correcting and altering some points. He prefixed to it a second preface, which mentions this revision in the following words:

> After I had written the little book which, because of my smallness, is called *On the Ecclesiastical Office*, I came to Rome and questioned the ministers of the Church of Saint Peter, etc.

From these inquiries Amalarius gained much that enabled him to polish and correct *The Ecclesiastical Office*. Hence there is considerable variation in it, since some copies preserve the earlier reading and others the later. This is especially evident from Book I, chapter 15, which exists in two entirely different editions. In those copies that lack the second preface mentioned above, the chapter reads as follows:

> After this the Order commands that the priests bring the body of the Lord that remained from the preceding day, and a chalice with unconsecrated wine.

After several intervening words concerning moral significance:

> When these things have been placed on the altar, the priest says the Lord’s Prayer and what follows it, up to “For ever and ever.” When this has been done, he takes some of the holy body and places it silently in the chalice. “The peace of the Lord be always with you” is not said, because the kisses of those standing around do not follow. For the unconsecrated wine is sanctified by the sanctified bread. Afterwards everyone communicates.

This is found in the Colbertine Codex, no. 224, which contains only the first three books and omits the later preface. It is also found in three other copies seen by Hittorp, although in Hittorp’s edition the aforementioned chapter 15 is entirely different within the text of the work [Col. 0896D]. From that version we extract the following:

> In the book mentioned above I found it written that two priests should bring, after the greeting of the cross, the body of the Lord that had been reserved from the preceding day, and a chalice with unconsecrated wine, which was then to be consecrated, and that the people were thereafter to communicate. Concerning this practice I questioned the Roman archdeacon, and he replied: [LXXXII] “At that station where the Apostolicus greets the cross, no one communicates. Whoever, in accordance with the Order of the little book, consecrates the wine through the commingling of bread and wine does not observe the Church’s tradition, of which Innocent says that during these two days the sacraments are not celebrated at all.”

When Hittorp noticed this great discrepancy in this chapter and in another that we shall discuss shortly, he attributed it to a different edition of the same work made by the author. He judged the earlier reading of this chapter to belong to the first edition, and the later one to the revised work. The evidence is that Amalarius begins the chapter in its revised form with the question addressed to the Roman [Col. 0897A] archdeacon during his Roman mission, after which he corrected his work. Hence, in the Colbertine Codex, where the earlier reading of this chapter appears, the second preface to the work—prefixed to the revision—is omitted.

There is another, no lesser, variation in the same work, in Book IV, chapter 26. After reporting Gregory the Great’s letter to John of Syracuse concerning certain rites of the Roman Church, Amalarius gathers several observations from it. Among them was the following, which appeared in the first edition of the work but was removed in the revision and reported by Hittorp at the end of the work with various other readings:

> And the doubt concerning Good Friday is removed: some are uncertain whether the body of the Lord is consecrated on that day or not. On the same day the apostolic practice is recalled, which used to say only the Lord’s Prayer over the body and blood of the Lord.

That is, because it was the practice of the apostles—as Gregory relates in that letter—to consecrate the sacrificial Host by saying only the Lord’s Prayer. The passage continues:

> Therefore, unless it had been commanded by the Roman Order that the body of the Lord be reserved from Thursday until Friday, it would not have been necessary to reserve it, since the Lord’s Prayer alone would suffice to consecrate the body, just as it suffices to consecrate the wine and water. For what Innocent says—that during these two days the sacraments are not celebrated at all—is to be understood as meaning that, according to the custom of our Church, they are not celebrated.

With these points established, we must investigate what Amalarius’s opinion was in these two passages of the first edition concerning the consecration of the wine on Good Friday, and what he finally corrected in revising his position. In the earlier passage he says that unconsecrated wine is sanctified by sanctified bread. In the later passage, as though he had realized that this sanctification through the commingling of the consecrated particle was not sufficient, he went further in Book IV, chapter 26, believing that the consecration of the wine was effected by the Lord’s Prayer alone. To make it clear that he was speaking of true and properly so-called consecration, he explains his meaning as follows:

> Unless it had been commanded by the Roman Order that the body of the Lord be reserved from Thursday until Friday, it would not have been necessary to reserve it.

Why not?

> Because the Lord’s Prayer alone would suffice to consecrate the body, just as it suffices to consecrate the wine and water.

Here it is manifest that the author is speaking of the true and properly so-called consecration of the Lord’s body, which, according to him, would be effected by the Lord’s Prayer alone on Friday if nothing had been reserved from the earlier consecration. It follows that, in Amalarius’s view, the same Lord’s Prayer suffices to consecrate the wine and water by a consecration that is not merely incidental but true and real.

What, then, did the author correct in the second revision of his work at these two points? The solution is easy in the first passage, from the comparison we have just made between the first and second editions, where everyone can see that the words, rather than the meaning, were changed. In the first edition he concludes that unconsecrated wine is sanctified by sanctified bread; in the second, according to the Order of the Roman little book [Col. 0897D], the wine is consecrated through the commingling of bread and wine. And lest anyone think that this should be understood as a metaphorical consecration, he adds that whoever does this fails to observe the Church’s tradition, concerning which Innocent says that during these two days the sacraments are not celebrated at all. But Innocent is speaking of the true consecration of the mysteries; consequently, Amalarius, who believed that this commingling violated the aforementioned tradition, attributed true consecration to that commingling.

Since, however, in the later passage of the first edition he had attributed that consecration not to the commingling but to the Lord’s Prayer, he removed the entire passage in order to remain consistent with himself and to attribute the whole power of consecrating the wine to the commingling. These observations may reasonably be expected to displease no one, since they seem to contribute something toward clarifying a very obscure question.

Above we added to Amalarius a passage from the commonly printed Alcuin, which we shall not discuss at length, since it is drawn in almost the same words from Amalarius, Book I, chapter 15, as that chapter was formulated by the author in the first edition [Col. 0898A]. We add only that the book *On the Divine Offices*, which in the printed editions bears Alcuin’s name, is [LXXXIV] a patchwork stitched together from various genuine excerpts of Amalarius and Alcuin, along with passages from other authors later than Alcuin. For chapter 40 is nothing other than the little work of Remigius, a monk of Auxerre, *On the Explanation of the Mass*; and chapter 18 reports a letter from the monk Helpric to Saint Gall toward the end of the tenth century. Further, to omit many other points, the author says that *Pascha* is a Greek word, contrary to Alcuin’s explicit opinion in Book VI on John, chapter 32, where he writes:

> Easter (*Pascha*), brothers, is not, as some think, a Greek name, but a Hebrew one.

Finally, that spurious compiler says in chapter 36 that the word *sacerdos* is Greek, an error wholly foreign to Alcuin’s teaching. But these matters lie outside our purpose.

### 3.

It is now easy to see how well Amalarius’s opinion, as we have just explained it, agrees with the Catholic faith concerning the true and real presence of Christ in the Eucharist. If he had admitted only a metaphorical and figurative consecration, there would have been no reason to reflect so carefully on the manner in which the wine is consecrated on Good Friday—whether through the contact of the inserted particle or through the Lord’s Prayer. Once the consecration of one species had been effected metaphorically, it would have been obvious that an incidental consecration resulted from contact with it. But because Amalarius believed that the change was true and substantial, he anxiously investigated how it could take place. What is surprising, then, if Amalarius believed that the true consecration of the wine was effected through contact and admixture with the other species, long before Berengar’s time, when after Berengar’s heresy had been condemned not a few Catholic authors held the same opinion, as we shall later see?

In the meantime, it is worth citing the *Micrologus*, who, in chapter 17, where he praises Gregory VII of blessed memory, gives sufficient indication that he wrote after Gregory’s death. Discussing the avoidance of intinction, he says in chapter 19:

> It is not authoritative that some people dip the body of the Lord and distribute what has been dipped to the people as the completion of Communion. For the Roman Order contradicts this practice: on Good Friday it commands that unconsecrated wine be consecrated with the Lord’s Prayer and the insertion of the Lord’s body, so that the people may communicate fully. It would plainly give this command unnecessarily if the body of the Lord, dipped on the preceding day, were preserved and what had been dipped were thought sufficient for the people’s Communion.

These words [LXXXV] leave no room for doubt that the *Micrologus* believed true consecration to be effected by the Lord’s Prayer and the insertion of the Lord’s body. This is clear both because he thinks that the completion of Communion is supplied from the chalice consecrated in this manner and because he considers such consecration equivalent to intinction from the true blood. Hence Hittorp believes that he was led to this opinion by a mistaken interpretation of the Roman Order’s words and by Amalarius’s judgment: Amalarius first believed that the wine was truly consecrated through the Lord’s Prayer, and later, after retracting that opinion, through the insertion of the consecrated particle. The *Micrologus*, however, admitted both positions and therefore should not be regarded as having departed from Amalarius.

### XIII. What Other Churches and Other Authors Thought about This Commingling

Before we leave this subject, it is useful to investigate the position of other Churches on the matter, especially the Latin Churches. Since all of them either followed the Roman Order or had it before their eyes, it is not surprising that its older interpreters, Amalarius and the *Micrologus*, were approved in their handling of obscure expressions. Their approval was not, however, so harmonious and unanimous, nor so constant, that some Churches did not think it permissible to depart from the interpretation of Amalarius and the *Micrologus. We shall therefore first review those Churches that followed these authors, and then the other Churches that did not accept their authority.

Beginning with the Gallican Churches, the first that comes to mind is Rheims. In its old Missal for Good Friday it is prescribed that a particle be placed from the sacrifice into the chalice, with the words:

> Let there be effected the union and consecration of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ for those who receive them, unto the remission of sins and unto eternal life.

These words seem to have no meaning if one does not believe that the chalice is changed into blood through contact. For how otherwise would the union of the body and blood take place? Support is provided by the Pontifical of the Church of Noyon, where the following is clearly written:

> The commingling of the body and the consecration of the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

Here the commingling is distinguished from the consecration of the blood, which takes place through that commingling.

Other Churches of the same ecclesiastical province, Soissons and Amiens, also followed the same path [LXXXVI]. The Soissons book has these words [Col. 0899B]:

> Meanwhile, taking a portion of the Holy, the bishop places it in the chalice without saying anything; having made the sign of the cross over it, he communicates himself and all who wish to do so. Thus unconsecrated wine is sanctified by sanctified bread.

These are the words of the commonly received Roman Order, reproduced in the old Missal of Soissons, which seems to belong to the twelfth century. But another Missal of the same Church, from the century before our own, expresses the matter more clearly:

> Without saying anything, the priest shall place one part of Christ’s body in the chalice. Having done this, he shall communicate himself without saying anything and receive the Lord’s blood. For the wine is consecrated through the commingling made in the chalice from Christ’s body.

The definition of the Church of Amiens in its Ordinal is somewhat less explicit:

> The wine and water in the chalice are sanctified when the body of the Lord is mingled with them.

So much for the metropolitan Church of Rheims.

The same words are also found in the Viennese Ordinal. But the Verdun Missal says:

> Here the wine is consecrated [Col. 0899C] through the body of the Lord.

Finally, to conclude briefly, the Pontifical of Mende, in its section on Communion for the sick, says:

> Let the priest give him the Eucharist of the Lord’s body dipped in wine, and wine sanctified by this dipping and changed into the blood of Christ the Lord, saying, “Receive, brother, the viaticum of the body and blood of the Lord,” etc.

The same words appear below in our tenth little work.

The same opinion also prevailed in most Gallican monasteries. The Ceremonial of Saint Benignus at Dijon, written five hundred years ago, prescribes the following for Good Friday:

> He takes a portion of the Holy and places it in the chalice, and the unconsecrated wine is sanctified by the sanctified bread.

Here “sanctified” has the same meaning as “consecrated,” since the bread and the wine are equally called sanctified.

The Ordinal of Saint Aper at Toul contains certain distinctive provisions for the Lord’s Supper, which it seemed appropriate to reproduce here:

> After the last “Lamb of God,” the one who is first in the choir shall say the *Confiteor*, and the brothers shall answer, “May he have mercy on you.” Then they too shall say the *Confiteor*, and the one who is first shall say, “May he have mercy on you”; he shall also say the *Indulgence*. When all have answered “Amen,” the brothers shall approach for holy Communion. A portion of Christ’s body shall be placed in the chalice and carried by the deacon to the altar of blessed Aper. He shall keep the chalice there, and one boy shall hold a flask containing wine, which is to be poured into the chalice whenever necessary, until all the monastic brothers have drunk. For the wine is sanctified by the body of Christ, consecrated and placed in the chalice, when the words “Let this commingling be effected” are said. The sacristan, however, shall have another chalice and a pitcher with wine at the altar of Saint Christopher; there the male and female conversi who have received the Lord’s body shall drink.

Here the monks attached to the choir communicate in one way, while the male and female conversi communicate in another. The monks, after receiving the Eucharistic species of bread, drink from the chalice in which the consecrated particle had been mingled in order to sanctify [Col. 0900A] the wine; the conversi, male and female, drank wine from another unconsecrated chalice.

Nor should the Missal of the monastery of Elnon, or Saint-Amand in Belgium, be omitted. For Good Friday it says:

> Here the wine is consecrated through the body of the Lord; the unsanctified is sanctified by the sanctified.

The Vicoigne Missal says:

> Here the wine is consecrated through the body.

In the Rotomagus Missal of 1531, this consecration is expressed in the priest’s own words:

> When the priest has divided the Host into three parts, he shall place a part of the consecrated bread in the chalice, saying these words: “Through this sanctified and consecrated bread, may this unconsecrated wine be sanctified and consecrated.” Afterwards the priest shall communicate himself in the usual manner.

So much for the Gallican Churches.

As for the Churches of other kingdoms, the two Salisbury Missals from the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries reproduce the same words that we shall cite below from the Rouen Missal. The Oxford Missal, in its section on Communion for the sick, says:

> Here the sick person shall communicate, and the sacrifice shall be placed in wine without water, with the words: “Let there be effected the commingling [Col. 0900B] and consecration of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ,” etc.

The Bamberg Missal likewise says:

> Unconsecrated wine is sanctified by sanctified bread.

In both places the same word is used to designate the consecration of the bread and wine, as we noted above concerning the Ceremonial of Saint Benignus.

Finally, in the Mozarabic Missal, in the section for Good Friday, we read:

> The particles “Kingdom” and “Glory”—as two of the nine consecrated particles are called, into which the Host is broken—are placed in the chalice. According to some, this particle consecrates the wine in the chalice.

Although the rubric does not approve this opinion, neither does it reject it, as appears from the following precaution:

> He shall take the paten and clean it over the chalice with his thumb; having cleaned it, he shall place it beneath his chin. When it has been placed there, he shall take wine from the chalice with its particle, because according to some it consecrates the wine in the chalice.

From this it is clear that this opinion was proposed, at least as a matter of doubt, in the Hispanic Churches.

[Col. 0900C] Thus far we have presented the arguments that can establish consecration through contact. We must now set forth those that support the contrary position. One is supplied by the Missal of the Church of Paris, written in later centuries, where the following words occur:

> The wine is not consecrated through the insertion into it of a portion of the consecrated Host, which is what the Church does on Holy Friday.

Then it adds:

> Let him take the greatest care not to say, “This most holy commingling of the body and blood,” or anything else in which the blood is mentioned.

The old Dionysian Ritual confirms the same opinion.

A certain Pontifical of the Church of Rheims says:

> For this reason the wine did not become consecrated, but only blessed . . . . . Prayers are to be said without mention of the blood . . . . . Nor should the blood be mentioned, because on this day the blood is not consecrated.

The Missal of Saint Remigius in the same city, published in the middle of the preceding century, points in the same direction, as do the Rouen Missals published in that century. Yet the Missal of 1513 is inconsistent with itself, since on Good Friday it distinctly says of the priest:

> Afterwards he shall receive the body of the Lord, saying, “The body of the Lord,” etc.; then the chalice, saying, “The body and blood,” etc., in the usual manner; and whoever wishes shall communicate, as on the preceding day.

Why distinctly say “body and blood” for the chalice if the wine is not consecrated through contact—a position that the same Missal maintains?

Besides these, two further arguments are available to us in support of the negative position. One comes from the Corbie Ritual, which is at least five hundred years old and prescribes the following for Good Friday:

> “The peace of the Lord,” “Lamb of God,” and “This most holy commingling” are not to be said; but a fragment of the fraction shall be allowed to fall inside the chalice, without saying anything. “Lord Jesus Christ” and “The body of the Lord, which we have received with our mouth” are to be said, but the blood shall not be named. “May it please you” shall not be said. When all have communicated, each person shall take wine through a tube and then drink from the chalices prepared before the high altar.

Although the wine is customarily taken through a tube or reed, it is nevertheless expressly [Col. 0901A] commanded that mention of the blood be avoided. The Fontesbrald Missal of 1534 likewise stipulates this. Finally, the Cluniac Missal of 1530 rejects this consecration in explicit terms, saying:

> The wine is not consecrated by contact with the sacred Host, but is sanctified and made worthy of reverence.

So much for the Ritual books. In collecting them, I admit that I benefited considerably from the observations supplied to me by the religious and learned Claude de Vert, a Cluniac theologian.

If we now consult the authors on this subject, we shall also find their opinions in conflict. We shall not repeat here what we said above about Amalarius, the *Micrologus*, and several others. Some of the Greeks appear to support the affirmative position. Among them was Michael Cerularius, Patriarch of Constantinople, who lived six hundred years ago and is cited by Allatius in his treatise *On the Presanctified*. He believes that through the admixture of presanctified bread the wine is changed into the blood of the Lord. The same is held by Symeon of Thessalonica, who lived three hundred years after Michael, in the same work of Allatius.

A certain Eucharistic miracle may also be referred to the same opinion. Abbot Helmold reports that it occurred in his own time, that is, toward the end of the twelfth century. It happened to a girl in Thuringia who, after receiving viaticum from a priest, noticed that a small portion of the Eucharist had fallen into a cup in which the priest had washed his hands after giving Communion. She asked that it be brought to her to drink and discovered that all the water had been changed into blood, while the small portion itself had become bloody flesh. Baronius reports this event under the end of the year 1192 and concludes the account as follows:

> This concerns the transubstantiation of water into blood of Christ, divinely effected through the commingling of Christ’s body—a thing that antiquity believed always occurred in wine whenever commingling took place. Hence the statement of the Roman Order: “Wine, even if unconsecrated,” etc.

What Baronius attributes to antiquity must not, however, be understood as though this had been the general conviction of all antiquity. To say nothing of the first eight centuries, in which no trace of this opinion appears—in fact, in which that change was always and everywhere believed to occur only through the words of Christ pronounced by the priest—certainly in subsequent centuries, when this opinion began to gain ground among some people, many authors, and very authoritative ones, adopted the contrary position; others, proceeding along a middle path, left the matter undecided.

[XCI] [XC] Among the authors of the negative position, Saint Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, should be regarded almost as the chief. In Letter 69 he says that, through the insertion of a particle into unconsecrated wine, the wine became sacred but was not truly and properly consecrated. The occasion was provided by the case of a certain priest who, having rashly pronounced the words of consecration over only water that had been placed in the chalice, later noticed the mistake, poured in wine, and inserted a particle of the consecrated Eucharist into the chalice [Col. 0901D] to supply what was lacking in the consecration. He consulted Bernard about what he thought should be done and received this reply:

> In so grave a matter, let us not think that it could have been done better, judging that the liquid, although not changed into blood through its own proper and solemn consecration, was nevertheless sacred through contact with the sacred body.

When Bernard says that the wine was not changed into blood through its own proper and solemn consecration, take care not to suppose that he believed a transmutation had occurred through a less proper and less solemn consecration effected by contact with the sacred body. For it is clear that he believed the liquid to have been merely made sacred by this contact, not consecrated.

The same opinion is confirmed most clearly by James of Vitry in chapter 38 of his *History of the West*:

> We do not say, he declares, that the wine used for ablution is changed into blood through contact with the blood; rather, it remains pure wine, although through contact with a sacred thing it is sanctified, just as river water mixed with blessed water is said to be sanctified.

After this he adds words that bear even more directly on our subject:

> Therefore those who say that on Good Friday Christ’s body changes wine into blood are lying. On that day the body, but not the blood, is received; yet neither is made, because on that day the Host was truly sacrificed, and therefore is not sacrificed figuratively.

James could not have stated the position more emphatically.

Someone might say that James lived after the middle of the thirteenth century, when Communion under the other species had almost ceased; consequently, he may not have thought the other species necessary—even if consecrated through contact—to complete Communion, which was what led earlier authors to devise this consecration. But in James’s time Communion under the other species had not yet been abolished everywhere. Moreover, this objection does not apply to Saint Bernard [XCI], in whose time Communion under both species continued, as we have shown [Col. 0902B]. The same must be said of Hugh of Saint-Victor, who asks why the blood of Christ is not received on Good Friday, just as the flesh is. That would be contrary to the practice if wine were changed into blood through contact. In addition, many authors of Ritual books after James of Vitry, although they did not accept the necessity of Communion under the other species, nevertheless rejected this consecration through contact.

John Beleth preceded James of Vitry by approximately a century. He too follows the negative position and confirms it by an argument in chapter 99:

> If someone asks whether the wine received on that day, namely Good Friday, is consecrated through contact with the Lord’s body, although the writings of many seem to assert this, nevertheless, following the truth more closely and adhering to what the holy Fathers have handed down, we say that the wine is not consecrated at all through that contact, but is sanctified.

The same author then supplies the reasons for this position, and William Durandus repeats them in almost the same words in Book VI, chapter 75, of his *Rationale*:

> But is the wine that is received on Good Friday together with the reserved body of the Lord consecrated on the altar and made Christ’s blood through the insertion of that body into the chalice and through its contact? On this subject some say—among whom he undoubtedly means Amalarius and the *Micrologus*—that through the Lord’s Prayer, which is said then, the consecration or change of the wine into blood takes place. For Gregory, assigning the reason why the Lord’s Prayer is said by the priest on that day, says that in the primitive Church the apostles used only the Lord’s Prayer in the consecration. Yet we do not say this. For if that were so, it would not be necessary to reserve the Lord’s body for that day, since bread and wine would equally be consecrated by the Lord’s Prayer. Furthermore, from what precedes the Lord’s Prayer in the Canon it is sufficiently clear that transubstantiation does not occur at the utterance of that Prayer. At no time was Mass celebrated without those words, “This is my body,” etc.; these alone were spoken by the apostles at the beginning of the nascent Church, and only later did they add the Lord’s Prayer. We therefore say that the wine is not consecrated but sanctified. The difference between these is this: to consecrate is to transubstantiate through consecration; to be sanctified is, through contact or admixture with a sacred thing, to be made worthy of reverence and holy, as is evident in the case of blessed water, etc.

We thought it appropriate to reproduce Durandus’s arguments—which are also those of Beleth—in full, because they rest on solid foundations relevant to our purpose.

From everything we have said both in this and in the preceding chapter concerning the argument in question, several conclusions may be drawn that should not be passed over lightly:

1. The opinions of the authors and Ritual books concerning consecration through contact were varied and inconsistent: some affirmed it, others denied it, and others left the matter undecided. Consequently, this kind of consecration was not received as a dogma.

2. The affirmative position was in no way handed down or defended by the Roman Church, nor was it certainly asserted in the little books of the Roman Order. Indeed, the words “For the unconsecrated wine is sanctified,” etc., which provided the foundation for the affirmative opinion, appear to have been inserted by some glossator.

3. Beleth is justified in saying that the affirmative position conflicts with what the holy Fathers handed down. Their harmonious and unanimous opinion is that the true consecration of both species can be accomplished only through the words of Christ the Lord pronounced by the priest. Finally, Jerome’s argument against deacons who exalted themselves above priests—that at the prayers of priests Christ’s body and blood are made—falls to the ground if true blood could be consecrated through contact, a power that could also have been attributed, and in fact was attributed, to deacons and even to laypeople in domestic Communion.

From all this collapses the argument of the heterodox, who contend that Communion under the other species is supplied through the commingling of a particle with unconsecrated wine. This presumption was forcefully refuted in a separate little work by the most illustrious Bishop of Meaux, and after him by Louis Thomassin, the learned priest of the Oratory, in the second volume of *On the Unity of the Church*.

### XIV. The Sanctification of the Chalice through the Commingling of Consecrated Blood

Once the preceding controversy has been settled, the question we have just proposed may seem superfluous: namely, whether the wine in the ministerial chalice, which we previously observed to be offered for the Communion of the laity at a pontifical Mass, is truly and properly consecrated through the infusion of a portion of the most sacred blood of Christ. But if one considers the matter more closely, one will easily notice that something different remains in this question [XCIII]. For a liquid poured into another liquid insinuates itself into it and permeates all parts of the liquid receiving it much more readily than a thicker and denser particle of bread, which touches only one part of the liquid into which it has been inserted [Col. 0903C].

This commingling of blood and wine took place one way in the Roman Church and another way in certain other Churches. In the Roman Church, the blood was poured from the consecrated chalice into the ministerial chalice, in which there was wine. In certain other Churches, when the supply of consecrated blood was insufficient for communicating the people, as much wine as was needed to complete Communion was poured into the chalice to be mixed with the remaining blood. The first type of commingling is presented by the first three little books of the Roman Order; the second by the Ritual of Saint Benignus, the Cistercian Usages, those of Saint Victor, and the English Constitutions reported by William Lyndwood. We presented the testimony of all of these in chapter eight above.

This latter rite continued in certain Churches toward the end of the thirteenth century, as William Durandus attests in chapter 42, section 1, of his *Rationale*:

> In certain places, he says, after the body and blood [Col. 0903D] of Christ have been received, some of the blood itself is reserved in the chalice, and pure wine is poured over it, so that the communicants may receive from it. For it would not be fitting to consecrate so small an amount of blood, and no sufficiently large chalice would be found.

The same author, in what follows, denies that a true consecration of the wine is effected by contact of this kind. The arguments he brings forward here are common to both forms of mixture; the chief is that there is never a true conversion of bread or wine in the Eucharist except through the solemn words of consecration instituted by Christ. Nevertheless, there is a particular difficulty concerning wine and consecrated blood, since they can more readily be converted into one another. For wine can be poured into the blood in such a quantity and of such a quality that, if the wine in both cases were pure, one would be completely absorbed by the other; for example, if a little weak wine were poured into a large chalice of the finest wine, why should it not be converted into that wine itself? [Col. 0904A] Yet even if the weak wine were penetrated and thoroughly suffused by the stronger, there would still be no true conversion of substance. For intimate mixture is one thing; transformation of substance is another. Thus nearly all Catholic authors hold [XCIV] that even if a little water is poured into the chalice and the water loses its taste and other qualities, its substance nevertheless remains water and is not changed together with the wine into the blood of Christ. The same must be said of a small quantity of wine poured into a larger quantity, even if no distinction between one and the other can be made by taste or any other sense.

Someone may ask why communion was not given to the people from the pure blood of the chalice. There was not one reason for this, but several. The first was that some prerogative might be granted to the priest and the other sacred ministers, to whom pure blood was given, over the laity; this reason applies especially to the rite of the Roman Church. The second reason was that it would be difficult to consecrate accurately as much blood as would suffice for communicating the laity, so that the supply of blood neither exceeded nor fell short of what was needed by those receiving communion. Hence in some churches a smaller quantity of blood was consecrated, so that when it began to run short it could be increased by adding wine. The third reason, closely related to the one just mentioned, is that where there was a large gathering of people, scarcely any chalice could be found large enough to contain a quantity of blood sufficient for so great a multitude; this is the reason given above by William Durand. Finally, at least for the Roman rite, one may add the reason that the danger of spilling the blood could be avoided with less inconvenience.
