For it was far less troublesome if some liquid from the wine mixture dripped from the chalice during communion than if pure blood were spilled.

For the same reason, in certain churches the Eucharist was administered dipped in liquid, specifically to avoid the danger of spilling it. It frequently happened, as Ernulf, bishop of Rochester, relates, that bearded men and those with long “grains”—that is, with scattered hairs—while taking the cup during the meal, first stained their hairs with the liquid before pouring the liquid into their mouths. [Col. 0904C] Moreover, if beardless men without such hairs, or women, came to receive Holy Communion, what priest could minister so prudently and distribute the Lord’s chalice so carefully that he could divide it among many people one by one, pouring it into their mouths in such a way that nothing was spilled while he poured? Thus that author argues in support of the rite of his own age, namely the eleventh century; the letter is reproduced in the second volume of the *Spicilegium*. For the same reason, therefore, the Roman Church perhaps instituted that the pure blood should not be distributed from the chalice to the people [XCV], but should be mixed with a larger quantity of wine: on the one hand, to lessen the danger of spilling it, and on the other, to ensure that the people were not entirely deprived of communion from the sacred chalice.

## XV. Concerning certain rites of Holy Saturday

Holy Saturday included twelve readings from Scripture, formerly customarily recited in the Roman Church, both in Greek and in Latin; then the Blessing of the Font, and the baptism of those who, through the various scrutinies conducted during Lent, had been prepared for this sacrament.

After Matins had been celebrated at midnight, at the third hour those to be baptized proceeded into the Lateran church; there the candidates stood in order, the males on the right and the females on the left. Then the priest, imprinting a cross on each person’s forehead, completed the rites of exorcisms and renunciations.

At the ninth hour the pontiff, with the priests and other ministers, came out of the sacristy without singing, wearing the sacred vestments, preceded by one or two candles, which were placed in a candlestick before the altar. Then, after the Blessing of the Paschal Candle had been performed, a lector, having removed his chasuble and ascended the ambo, recited a reading from the book of Genesis in Greek; immediately afterward another did so in Latin, and then others in succession likewise. When these had been completed, the Psalm *As the deer longs* was sung in Greek, followed by another psalm in Latin.

[Col. 0905A] After this they proceeded, singing the litany, to the baptistery of Saint John; there the Blessing of the Font took place. When it was finished, the presbyters, deacons, and, if necessary, acolytes entered the fonts themselves barefoot, as is read in the first book of the *Roman Order* that we have published. The Gregorian Sacramentary likewise records this in exactly the same words in the Gellone Codex, which we have judged to have been written in the eighth century. The commonly circulated *Roman Order* does not differ from it.

Our older books do not state how many infants the pontiff ordinarily baptized. Book VII suggests one, or two, or as many as he wished. The tenth *Order* assigns only three; the bishops of other churches followed this practice. For in the Acts of Udalric, bishop of Augsburg, who flourished in the tenth century, we read that on Holy Saturday the holy bishop, after baptizing three boys with the sevenfold litany, withdrew into the sacristy to prepare himself for Mass. The Council [XCVI] of Limoges of 1031 gives the same number. After describing the rite of baptism customarily celebrated each year in the monastery of Saint Martial, it states that on Easter and Pentecost no fewer than three infants were baptized there, and adds that a greater number was baptized at the mother church: after the baptism of only three infants by the bishop, the remainder, if there were more, were baptized by another priest. Our books also testify that deacons baptized together with presbyters at Rome, as we shall explain below. The rest were baptized by whichever deacon the pontiff commanded.

After receiving baptism, each infant was presented to a presbyter; the presbyter himself impressed the sign of the cross with chrism on the infant’s crown. Immediately afterward the sponsors, holding linens in their hands, received the infants from the presbyters and deacons who had baptized them and presented them to the seated pontiff. He gave each of them a stole, a chasuble, and a chrismal containing ten siliquae, clothed them all in white garments, and, after reciting a prayer over them, made a cross with chrism on each one’s forehead while invoking the Holy Trinity. In this way he bestowed on them the sevenfold grace [Col. 0905C] of the Holy Spirit—that is, he conferred on them the sacrament of Confirmation.

Our books, which deal with the rite of baptism, prescribe this double anointing, one performed by the presbyter and the other by the pontiff. The Gelasian Sacramentary likewise says:

> Afterward, when he has risen from the font, the infant is signed by the presbyter on the crown of the head with chrism, with these words: “Almighty God,” and so forth. Then the sevenfold Spirit is given to them by the bishop. To seal them, he lays his hand upon them with these words: “Almighty God,” and so forth. Afterward he signs them on the forehead with chrism, saying: “The sign of Christ unto eternal life.” Response: “Amen.”

In our seventh book of the *Roman Order* the wording is different:

> “In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Peace be with you.” Response: “Amen.”

Amalarius cites this passage. Innocent I discusses both anointings in his letter to Decentius, as everyone knows; but he does not dare to state the actual words by which the Holy Spirit was given by the bishop to the baptized, evidently because they were still secret:

> “Lest I should seem,” he says, “to disclose more than to answer the inquiry.”

[Col. 0905D] Furthermore, the *Roman Order* teaches that by this pontifical anointing every legitimate baptism is confirmed in the name of Christianity. This does not mean that the later anointing is [XCVII] an appendage of baptism, but that it strengthens and confirms baptismal grace. Augustine briefly expresses the entire rite of baptism at the end of Sermon 324: “He was baptized, he was sanctified, he was anointed, hands were laid upon him, and, all the sacraments having been completed, he was received.” Cyprian, before Augustine, expresses the same sequence in the synodal letter that is now numbered 70.

The baptized, clothed and confirmed, were arranged in a circle. The infants were held in the arms, as the commonly circulated *Roman Order* states; the older candidates, however, placed one foot upon the foot of their godfather, as is also stated in the Maffaean *Order*, which we shall publish here as the tenth.

Meanwhile, at the pontiff’s command, the schola began the litany before the altar, first the sevenfold, then the fivefold, and finally the threefold litany. The commonly circulated *Roman Order* explains the rite as follows:

> Meanwhile the schola, as commanded, performs the litany at the font before the altar, first the sevenfold litany; and after an interval they perform another, the fivefold litany, for this is how it is begun. One primicerius stands in the right choir and says *Kyrie eleison* together with that choir; the secundicerius responds with the left choir, *Kyrie eleison*, up to three times; then *Christe eleison*, up to three times. This is repeated seven times, and therefore it is called the sevenfold litany. After this, *Christe, hear us*, is said seven times, and so forth in order. After an interval, following this order, they proceed, as stated above, with the fivefold litanies—that is, repeated five times.

Afterward, when the *Agnus Dei* was being sung, the master of the schola ordered the lights to be lit. Once this had been done, the pontiff proceeded from the sacristy to the altar to celebrate the sacred rites of the night, for the ancient rite did not permit these celebrations to be held during the daytime on Holy Saturday.

At this Mass the *Alleluia* was sung for the first time with great solemnity. Sozomen remembers this in Book VIII, chapter 15, where he states that at Rome the *Alleluia* was sung only once each year, on the first day of the Paschal feast, to such an extent [Col. 0906B] that many Romans were accustomed to use an oath that they would live to hear and sing this hymn. Victor of Vita refers to the same custom in Book I:

> A single lector, standing on the pulpit, sang the melody of the *Alleluia*—namely, on Easter Day. At that moment, having been struck in the throat by an arrow, he fell dead, the Codex dropping from his hands.

There is a difficulty in the passage cited above from Sozomen, since he asserts that at Rome the *Alleluia* was sung only once each year, whereas during the entire fifty days extending from Easter to Pentecost the Romans frequently sang it before Gregory the Great, who even ordered that the *Alleluia* be sung outside Pentecost [XCVIII]. For this reason, when certain people in Sicily complained that he had borrowed this rite from the Greeks, he replied in a letter to John, bishop of Syracuse—Book VII, Letter 64, indiction 2:

> That the *Alleluia* should be said here is reported to have been brought from the Church of Jerusalem, through the tradition of blessed Jerome, in the time of Pope Damasus of blessed memory. Therefore, in this see we have all the more removed that custom which had been introduced here by the Greeks, perhaps those who had introduced this expression into the funerals of the dead and into Lent.

That the *Alleluia* was once sung among the Romans at the funerals of the dead is clearly attested by Jerome in the epitaph of Fabiola:

> Now flying rumor, herald of so great a grief, was gathering the people of the entire city for the funeral. The psalms resounded, and the gilded roofs of the temples trembled aloft with the *Alleluia*.

Menardus also infers this from the Codex of Ratoldus; to these witnesses may be added the Mozarabic Missal. Indeed, certain Spanish churches even sang the *Alleluia* during Lent before the Fourth Council of Toledo, whose tenth canon abolished this practice. Gregory abolished a similar practice and decreed that the *Alleluia* should be sung even at Masses after Pentecost, though not at Masses for the dead or during Lent. Amalarius correctly infers from the letter cited above, in Book IV, chapter 33, that at some time—that is, before Gregory the Great—Mass was celebrated in the Roman Church without the *Alleluia*, specifically at Masses after Pentecost.

I return to Sozomen, who may have fallen into the same error as Michael Cerularius [Col. 0906D]. Among the latter’s other accusations against the Romans was this: that they did not sing the *Alleluia* during Lent, but only once, at Easter. The last assertion is demonstrably false for the eleventh century, in which Cerularius wrote.

Concerning the communion of infants, the first book of the *Roman Order* gives the following instruction:

> Provision must be made concerning the little ones that, after they have been baptized, they should receive no food and should not be nursed before they have communicated in the sacrament of the body of Christ; and that on every day of Easter week they should proceed to Masses, and their parents should offer on their behalf, and all should communicate.

The same rite was observed at the vigil of Pentecost.

John the Deacon, in a letter to Senarius that we published in the first volume of the *Museum*, answers a question put to him concerning why milk and honey were put into the most sacred chalice and offered with the sacrifices on Holy Saturday. He replies [Col. 0907A] that this kind of sacrifice was offered to the baptized [XCIX] so that they might understand that they themselves, not others, who became participants in the body and blood of the Lord, would receive the promised land; and that, among those who are beginning, they are nourished like infants with milk and honey.

But concerning this rite—namely, the putting of milk and honey into the chalice—we find no mention in the ancient Roman books. The commonly circulated *Roman Order* does indeed contain a Blessing of Milk and Honey on Holy Saturday, but it was performed outside the chalice, and the milk and honey were given separately to the little ones. Perhaps, however, in the ninth century some people mixed both in the chalice, which occasioned this question. Relevant here is the prohibition enacted by the African Council, that nothing except bread and wine mixed with water should be offered in the sacrifice. The first fruits, however—or the honey and milk—which are customarily offered on one particularly solemn day in the mystery of the infants, though offered on the altar, have their own distinct Blessing, so that they may be distinguished from the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood.

The Greeks criticized another rite of the same day, not greatly different, as Aeneas, bishop of Paris, reports: namely, that the Latins placed a lamb on the altar together with the body of Christ and offered it in the manner of the Jews. But this Blessing of the lamb was performed separately, as is clear from the commonly circulated *Roman Order*, not so that the lamb might be offered to God, but so that its flesh might afterward be eaten with the Church’s blessing. The same book therefore also contains a Blessing of other kinds of meat.

After Mass the Romans omitted Vespers, because the rite of baptism and the following Mass continued far into the night. Thus the commonly circulated *Roman Order* states:

> On this night nothing is done among the Romans in the evening assembly, either before Mass or after Mass. Among us, however, one member of the schola, whoever has been commanded, begins the *Alleluia* as an antiphon at Vespers.

From this passage anyone can see that the commonly circulated *Roman Order* has been interpolated where it reads, “Among us, however,” and so forth. In fact, not only on the vigil of Easter, but also during the preceding two days, the daily offices were not publicly recited in the Roman Church, as is clear from our books.

At this point we should recall what we stated above concerning baptism, from the ceremonial of Benedict, canon of Saint Peter. Namely:

> “When the readings had been completed, the pontiff, as we said, descended to the font with the regional deacons and subdeacons, while the litany was being sung meanwhile, and the Psalm *As the deer longs* continued as far as the portico of Saint Venantius, where the pontiff sat for a short time. [C] Meanwhile, the cardinals who had remained in the choir of the Lateran basilica went out through the small door behind the apse and proceeded through the portico of Saint John to the oratory of Saint Venantius. Then, at the archdeacon’s command, two cardinals, with the senior cardinal between them, approached the pontiff, followed by the other cardinals. After the senior cardinal had asked three times and, on the third occasion, received the Blessing on behalf of them all, the pontiff said: ‘Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.’ Having received this commission, the cardinals [Col. 0907D], riding on horseback, returned to their own titles, each to baptize the children of his title.”

The first book of the *Roman Order* adds, in section 3, that on Easter Day, when the pontiff was proceeding to Saint Mary Major, a regional notary met him at the Merulana and, after greeting the pontiff, said:

> “In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, last night at Holy Mary, Mother of God, so many male infants and so many female infants were baptized.”

To these words the pontiff replied, “Thanks be to God.”

Furthermore, deacons also administered baptism in the presence of the pontiff, with the assistance of subdeacons and acolytes, as is stated in our books, especially the first, section 43. But in the commonly circulated Anastasius, Boniface V is said to have established that at the Lateran an acolyte should not baptize with a deacon, but that the subdeacons should follow. Book VII designates only a deacon; this was preceded by the Roman Council under Innocent I, canon 7.

[Col. 0908A] The ancient Missal of the Church of Riez, which we have already mentioned above, after reproducing the words of the *Roman Order*—

> “Provision must be made concerning the little ones that, after they have been baptized, they should receive no food and should not be nursed before they have communicated in the sacraments of Christ; and that on every day of Easter week they should proceed to Masses and an offering should be made on their behalf”—

adds in the same place:

> “And if they are such that they can knowingly eat, we judge, by the authority of the canons, that they should receive communion. Otherwise they are to communicate only by drinking the Lord’s blood. The same should be done at their death.”

Here we have a clear example of communion under the single species of blood; it is also established elsewhere by the testimony of Cyprian, Hugh of Saint Victor, and others.

John the Deacon, in the letter to Senarius cited above, suggests another distinctive rite of Holy Saturday: it was customary to celebrate and arrange—that is, adorn—seven altars in the city of Rome on Easter Saturday. Ambrose uses the term “arranged” for the most sacred altar in his *On the Mysteries*, chapter 8 of the new edition, section 43; Optatus says that the altars were solemnly prepared in Books III and VI. John admits that he himself has no idea what this rite meant. Yet it is surprising that, so far as I know, no trace of this rite is found in any other author, much less in the books of the *Roman Order*.

Nor should we pass over here the fact that the year of the Lord’s Passion was customarily inscribed on the Paschal Candle among the Romans. A number of ancient writers attest this, although our books contain nothing on the subject. Such an inscription was attached to a tablet on the Paschal Candle. According to Udalric, in Book I, chapter 14 of the *Customs of Cluny*, the precentor wrote on it the year of the Lord’s Incarnation, the indiction, the concurrent, and the epact. Nor should this rite be considered recent, since the Venerable Bede, in *On the Reckoning of Time*, chapter 45, says that the Roman and apostolic Church bears witness, through the little notes it customarily writes annually on its candles, to the time of the Lord’s Passion—namely, a number of years always thirty-three fewer than the number Dionysius assigns from his Incarnation.

Finally, he says, in the year 701 from his Incarnation according to Dionysius, in the fourteenth indiction, our brothers who were then at Rome reported that they had seen and copied the following inscription written on the candles of Saint Mary at the Nativity of the Lord:

> “From the Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ: 668.”

From this it may be understood either that this inscription was placed at the Nativity of the Lord to designate the new year, which the Romans began on that very day, or, if the inscription was used at Easter, that it was kept until the Nativity of the Lord.

We shall not linger over proving the antiquity of blessing the candle on Easter Saturday. The hymn of Prudentius concerning the lighting of the lamp is wrongly cited for this purpose, since it is clear that it should be understood not of the Paschal Candle but of the candle that was lit each day in the church according to a certain solemn rite. The authority of Ennodius, deacon of Ticinum, is especially decisive on this matter, for he composed two Blessings of the Paschal Candle. Such a Blessing, however, was not accepted everywhere, as is evident from the Fourth Council of Toledo, whose ninth canon contains these words:

> “The lamp and the candle are not blessed in the Easter rites in certain churches, and they ask why they are blessed by us. Because of the glorious mystery of that night we solemnly bless these things, so that in the Blessing of the sanctified light we may receive the mystery of Christ’s sacred resurrection, which arrives at the time of this votive night.”

Finally, we must cite the response of Pope Adrian I to the questions of the monks of Corbie. We read it in the very ancient Corbie Codex, which we have already mentioned once; it contains the *Roman Order* adapted to monastic practices for the three days before Easter. On Holy Saturday, after these words of the *Roman Order*—

> “Before the Gospel they do not carry lights on that night itself, but incense; they do not sing the Offertory, the *Agnus Dei*, or the Communion”—

the Codex continues:

> “Nevertheless, in accordance with your instructions, we asked the apostolic lord Adrian whether on Easter Saturday the knees ought to be bent while the readings are being recited. He himself replied that this ought by all means to be done. When we said to him, ‘How can priests, ministers, or the clergy prostrate themselves on the ground while wearing stoles and chasubles?’ he added that priests, ministers, or the clergy should not first be clothed in stoles and chasubles, but only afterward, when the new light is introduced so that the candle may be blessed. We asked again at what hour on the Saturday of Pentecost it would be appropriate to enter for the office of the readings. He told us that this should be done at the sixth hour.”

Thus far the Corbie Codex. Where it asks whether the knees should be bent while the readings are recited on Easter Saturday, I think this should be understood not of the readings themselves, but of the prayers that are customarily inserted among the readings, with the deacon’s admonition to bend the knees omitted. But enough on this subject.

## XVI. Concerning the sacred ordinations of the Roman Church

Although we do not read that the Roman pontiffs, who at the Easter vigil were occupied with the rites of baptism and other ministries, formerly performed any ordinations, the sequence of events nevertheless requires us at this point to note something concerning the sacred ordinations that were once performed in the Roman Church after baptism and Confirmation. We publish only two books on this subject, content to indicate others that have appeared both in Morinus’s book *On Sacred Ordinations* and in our Menardus’s *Book of Sacraments*, in addition to the published *Roman Order*.

“The first apostolic bishops,” says Amalarius in Book II, chapter 1, “always administered consecrations in the month of December, in which the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ is celebrated, down to Simplicius, who was the forty-ninth after blessed Peter. He was the first to consecrate in February.” The *Micrologus* gives the same testimony from the *Roman Pontifical*, by which name it understands a book concerning the deeds of the Roman pontiffs.

Why the Roman bishops more frequently held ordinations in December rather than at other times is not easy to determine. Amalarius offers a moral reason, namely, that they might signify that those advanced through the sacred ministry were to be joined more closely to the body of Christ. A clearer practical reason may be given: the season was more suitable for easing the labor of the ordaining bishop and those being ordained. In summer the heat is everywhere extremely oppressive in the City, and autumn is occupied with the vintage festivals. Travel for those arriving during Lent was likewise not so suitable, since at that time the Roman pontiffs and their ministers were occupied with celebrating stations each day and with the scrutinies of those being baptized. Indeed, among all the pontiffs who performed ordinations down to the end of the ninth century, only Leo II held ordinations in May, and Gregory the Great held one in September. After Simplicius, all the others ordained either in December or in the first or middle week of Lent; none, so far as we know, did so on Easter Saturday.

Leo the Great teaches when ordinations were celebrated in the earliest centuries in his letter to the bishop of Alexandria, which is Letter XII in Quesnel’s edition:

> “What we have learned was preserved by our fathers with particular care, we wish to have preserved by you also: priestly or levitical ordination should not be celebrated indiscriminately on every day, but the days should be selected after the Sabbath, during the night whose beginning dawns into the first day of the Sabbath, and on these days the sacred Blessing should be conferred upon those who are to be consecrated while they are fasting and while those who confer it are fasting. The same observance will be maintained if it is celebrated in the morning of the Lord’s Day itself, with the fast of the Sabbath continued; for the beginnings of the preceding night do not depart from that day. It is beyond doubt that this night belongs to the day of the Resurrection, as is also declared at the Lord’s Pasch.”

Leo approves this practice by the authority of custom, which, he says, we know to derive from apostolic teaching, and by the authority of Sacred Scripture [CIV]—specifically, the action of Paul and Barnabas recounted in Acts 13. Finally, he concludes that the form for ordaining priests ought to be preserved in such a way that those who are to be consecrated should never receive the Blessing except on the day of the Lord’s Resurrection, whose beginning is clearly assigned to the evening of the Sabbath.

The learned Quesnel makes several observations on this letter. First, by “the Resurrection of the Lord” is meant not the feast of Easter itself but any Sunday, as also in Gregory, bishop of Tours, and other ancient authors. Second, so far from the consecration of the Church’s ministers having been performed only on Holy Saturday or the following Sunday, it seems rather never to have been performed on those days because of the solemnity of baptism, to which that time was devoted. Third, ordinations were celebrated on any Sunday, with a fast first observed by the ordaining bishop and those being ordained. Fourth, this fast was prolonged from the preceding Saturday into the morning of Sunday, when the ordination took place. Since this exhausted both the ordaining bishop and those being ordained, the ordination gradually moved backward from Sunday morning to the beginning of the night, then from the beginning of the night to the evening of the preceding Saturday, afterward from the evening to midday, and finally from midday to the morning hours, as it is done today.

The first pontifical constitution that has come down to us which recalls ordinations to the seasons of solemn fasts is that of Gelasius I, in a letter sent to the bishops established throughout Lucania and Bruttium:

> “Ordinations of presbyters and deacons should not be performed except at fixed times and on fixed days: namely, during the fast of the fourth month, the seventh, and the tenth, and also at the beginning and middle of Lent, and on the Saturday fast, toward evening.”

In the time of Urban II, ordinations were also held toward evening, as is clear from the Council of Clermont, where it is recommended that the fast be prolonged until evening and, if possible, until the following day, so that it might more clearly appear that the orders were conferred on Sunday. This is why the Sundays that fall within the solemn seasons of ordination are all without their proper Mass offices: the Mass for those being ordained supplied the office and sacrifice of the Sunday. Consult chapter 29 of the *Micrologus*.

I return to our books, in which many matters deserve notice. In the first place, the ordination of only the acolyte among the minor orders is explicitly described [CV] in the eighth book we publish, entitled *How Acolytes Are Ordained in the Holy Roman Church*. The rite of ordaining an acolyte is described as follows:

> “When Mass has been celebrated, they vest that cleric in a chasuble and an orarium. When the bishop, or the apostolic lord himself, comes to receive communion, they bring him to the bishop, and he places a little bag in his arms over the chasuble,” and so forth.

It is surprising that the chasuble and orarium are assigned to the acolyte being ordained. More surprising still is that no mention is made of the ordination of the doorkeeper, lector, or exorcist; nor is there any such mention in the later book, except that boys of this kind are said first to have been raised in the singers’ school, then to have become the pope’s chamberlains, before being appointed acolytes.

The first letter of Pope Siricius largely agrees with this. It mentions only the lector, acolyte, and subdeacon:

> “Whoever has devoted himself to the service of the Church from infancy ought to be baptized before the years of puberty and joined to the ministry of lectors. Whoever, from the beginning of adolescence until the twentieth year of life, has lived respectably and has been content with one wife ought to be an acolyte and subdeacon.”

Gelasius speaks somewhat differently in his letter to the bishops established throughout Lucania and Bruttium. After the grades of lector, notary, or defender, he mentions the acolyte and subdeacon, preceded by a reference to the doorkeeper. Yet in the commonly circulated *Roman Order*, in the Codex of Vendôme, and even in the Gregorian Sacramentary, the ordination of the doorkeeper, lector, and exorcist is placed before that of the acolyte. This shows how ancient our books are.

The same antiquity is also established by the fact that acolytes are ordained by the presentation not of a candle-bearer or candlestick with a candle, as is soon noted in the *Roman Order* and the Sacramentary, but of a little bag. Acolytes evidently used such bags at pontifical Mass to receive the consecrated offerings: both those broken at Mass for the communion of the faithful and those sent to the titular churches under the name of the fermentum. We discussed this matter above. Justin assigns this duty to deacons in his *First Apology*, namely, to carry the Eucharist to those who were absent.

Furthermore, the later book states that the acolytes received their first Blessing from the archdeacon, as though indicating that they were ordained by the archdeacon. For immediately afterward the ordination of the subdeacon follows, with no other ordination of the acolyte mentioned.

[Col. 0911B] The same book then adds that acolytes could be ordained to the office of subdeacon whenever and wherever it pleased; the situation was otherwise with deacons and presbyters, who could not be ordained except in a public ordination—that is, on the solemn fast days assigned for ordinations. From this it is understood that, at the time when these books were in use, the subdiaconate had not yet been counted among the sacred orders.

Hence the vow of continence was then first prescribed for the deacon, as the first letter of Siricius testifies. The matters we have said here concerning the conferral of the minor orders should not, however, conflict with the received opinion that attributes this authority to bishops by ancient right. For from the letters of Cyprian we learn that Aurelius and Celerinus were ordained lectors by Cyprian—and, for the moment leaving others aside—by his colleagues who were present. Here we are merely presenting a specimen from our books, without any prejudice against venerable antiquity. The Roman synod under Sylvester mentions all the minor orders.

I come to the deacons. In their ordination no anointing is performed, either in our books or in the commonly circulated *Roman Order*. The English therefore adopted this rite from the practice of another church: the hands of the deacon were anointed with holy oil and chrism, accompanied by the solemn words customarily used in the consecration of a presbyter. This anointing in the ordination of deacons is prescribed not only by the Anglican Codex cited by Menardus, but also by the *Book of Sacraments* of Egbert, bishop of York, which, as we have just said, now belongs to the church of Évreux in Gaul.

Gregory decreed at a Roman synod that deacons, who ought appropriately to devote themselves to preaching and the distribution of alms, should not thereafter undertake the office of singers, while singers themselves were employed in sacred ministries because of the sweetness of their voices. Thus it usually happens [Col. 0911D] that, while a pleasing voice is sought for the sacred ministry, a suitable life is neglected; and the singing minister provokes God by his conduct while delighting the people with his voice. Concerning this matter, he says:

> “By the present decree I establish that in this see the ministers of the sacred altar should not sing, but should perform only the ministry of reading the Gospel during the solemn celebrations of Mass. I judge that the psalms and the other readings should be performed by subdeacons or, if necessity requires, by those in the minor orders.”

Here observe in passing that the subdiaconate is distinguished from the minor orders, although in Gregory’s time it was not yet counted among the sacred orders. There were seven subdeacons assigned to the singers’ school [CVII], concerning whom we spoke above, page XVIII.

In the ordination of presbyters, the archdeacon’s testimony concerning those being ordained is customarily requested. That this is a very ancient rite is attested by Jerome’s Letter 85 to Evagrius. “But,” you say, “how is a presbyter ordained at Rome upon the testimony of a deacon? Why do you bring me the custom of a single city?” From this it is understood that this practice was peculiar to the Roman Church and has continued to the present day in the Latin Church.

The books we possess concerning the ordination of bishops provide material for two inquiries: first, whether bishops were once consecrated by a single Roman pontiff, with the other bishops excluded; second, whether those chosen for the episcopate from among the deacons were ordained by advancement over an intermediate grade, omitting the presbyterate.

As for the first point, in our earlier treatise priests—that is, bishops together with presbyters—are said to participate in the present ordination and to confer the Benediction upon the elect together with the pontiff. For thus we read, no. 8:

> The apostolic lord, together with the priests and the elect himself, having prostrated himself on the ground before the altar, shall rise when the litany has been completed, and then they shall bless him. When the Benediction has been completed, the apostolic lord gives him the kiss; and the archdeacon, holding him, carries him away, and thus he gives the kiss to the bishops and presbyters. Then the apostolic lord commands him to sit above all the bishops.

It is doubtful, however, whether the reading should be in the singular number, [Col. 0912B] “and then he shall bless him,” namely, the apostolic lord. Certainly, in Morinus, p. 326, where this rite is adapted to a metropolitan, it reads: “They rise, and he blesses him.” This conjecture is confirmed by the fact that in our later treatise mention is made of one pontiff laying on his hand, no. 4:

> And they sing the litany. Then the elect approaches nearer to the altar with his head bowed. The pontiff, however, shall place his hand upon his head and say one Prayer in the manner of a Collect, and another in the melody in which the “contestatio” is customarily sung; and the pontiff sits in his chair. The elect himself kisses his foot and is received to peace, and thus his consecration is completed.

The same things are read in the published Roman Ordinal, p. 97. [Col. 0912C] There you see complete silence concerning the other bishops who might assist at the consecration; consequently, at that time one Roman Pontiff completed the episcopal ordination without the ministry of other bishops.

This opinion is supported by Fulgentius Ferrandus’s *Breviatio canonum*, chapter 6:

> That one bishop should not ordain a bishop, except in the Roman Church, according to the Council of Zell and from a letter of Pope Siricius.

By this exception, a special prerogative is attributed to the Roman pontiff—namely, to ordain a bishop without fellow bishops. But the learned Johannes Cotelerius, held in good memory among scholars, thinks that a twofold error lies beneath this passage in his notes on the *Apostolic Constitutions*, p. 217: first, that the first two decrees of Siricius’s fourth letter have been improperly conflated; and second, that the apostolic see of the primate or metropolitan has been changed into the Roman apostolic see—not through Ferrandus’s fault, as the learned man suspects, but through the fraud of some later person.

Here are Siricius’s words:

> 1. Let no one dare to ordain outside the knowledge of the apostolic see, that is, of the primate. For a judgment is complete when it follows the opinion of the majority.  
> 2. Let no single bishop presume to ordain a bishop, on account of arrogance, lest the benefit conferred appear furtive.

In these words of Siricius, the exception of the Roman Church is indeed lacking. But what if Ferrandus, taking account of the circumstances of his own time, added it from his own resources? That it was written by Ferrandus himself, and not through the fraud of some later person, is made certain to us by the very ancient Corbie Codex, written a thousand years ago, containing various councils together with Ferrandus’s *Breviatio*. In it this passage occurs in exactly the same words as in the printed editions. It therefore cannot be asserted without foundation that, on account of his pre-eminent dignity, the Roman pontiff was granted the privilege of conferring the episcopal character alone, without other bishops.

[Col. 0912D]

Whether, then, those elected to the episcopate from among the deacons were ordained among the Romans by a leap over the intervening grade is a question of no small importance. Our earlier treatise appears to support the affirmative position. The consecration of one ordained from the diaconate and that of one ordained from the presbyterate are described in the same way. This may perhaps be because, as Jerome holds in Letter 85, the presbyter is contained in the bishop. This opinion is confirmed by Photius’s objection against the Romans: why were levites made bishops without first receiving the grade of presbyter?

[Col. 0913A]

Ratramnus says that this objection arose from slander, and turns it back against his adversaries, who, contrary to ecclesiastical regulations, suddenly made bishops from laymen who had been tonsured. But Aeneas, bishop of Paris, does not deny the truth of the matter. He replies that perhaps those who approve this kind of ordination intend the following: that whoever receives pontifical Benediction should also be adorned with the honor of the other Benedictions, and that in the eminence of the greater pontiff there is also the honor of the lesser priest.

He then adds:

> Perhaps, however, those who ordain a bishop from a deacon, omitting the presbyteral Benediction, appear in part to entrust themselves to the assertion of blessed Jerome in his letter, where he says, in his discussion of Titus, that the office of presbyter participates in some degree in the episcopal ministry.

[Col. 0913B]

From this it is clear that Aeneas admitted what Photius had objected—namely, that at Rome a deacon was often consecrated bishop by a kind of leap, without receiving the presbyteral Benediction. This was Photius’s seventh objection. Here a broad field for learned discussion would open before us, but these remarks suffice for our purpose.

It will nevertheless not be irrelevant to note what Alexander II decreed concerning a certain cleric who, having omitted the grade of subdeacon, had hastily—not ambitiously, but negligently—climbed to the honor of the diaconate and presbyterate. When consulted on this matter, he replied that he had found no canonical precept concerning the question. He nevertheless gave the same advice that he had given to Grimoald, bishop of Constance, in a similar case: namely, that the man so ordained should be suspended from the office of priest and levite until, at the proper time, he could be present with those who were to receive the Benediction for the honor of the diaconate and receive the Benediction of the subdiaconate together with them. See this more fully in Baronius, under the year 1069. From this it is understood that such ordinations had long before that time not been approved in the Roman Church, since no memory of similar cases then remained.

## XVII. On the Various Forms of the Creation of the Roman Pontiff

[Col. 0913C]

Scarcely any other matter was subject to so many and such great changes as the creation of the Roman pontiff. The very learned Onuphrius Panvinius treated this subject in ten books and dedicated them to Carlo Borromeo, then a cardinal. In them he enumerates eighteen different methods of creating a pontiff. The final one was that by which, once not only the votes of the people but also those of the clergy had been removed, the right of creating the pontiff was transferred to the cardinals alone.

It is useful to compress this entire history of papal election into a brief account, insofar as it can contribute to the explanation of Roman rites. To present it in order, I have thought it appropriate to distinguish six periods of this election: the first, from Saint Peter to the emperor Constantine; the second, from Constantine to Justinian; the third, from Justinian to Charlemagne; the fourth, from that point to the creation of Formosus; the fifth, from Formosus to Otto the Great; and the sixth, from that Otto to Frederick Barbarossa, [Col. 0913D] or to Pope Alexander III, in whose time and through whose efforts the election devolved upon the cardinals alone.

[Col. 0913D]

Apart from Clement, whom tradition records as designated by blessed Peter as his successor, the election of the Roman pontiff after Peter rested with the clergy and the body of the faithful. When the pontiff died, all the bishops of the neighboring cities were immediately informed by the presbyters and deacons of the Roman Church of the death of the Roman bishop and were summoned to the election. The same death was also announced by letter to other, especially more distinguished, Churches; several letters of Cyprian bear witness to this above all.

At this assembly, presbyters, deacons, subdeacons, acolytes, and the other clergy, together with the rest of the faithful Roman people, could be present. Their votes were then collected by spoken declaration, and the man whom they preferred from among the presbyters or deacons was considered elected [Col. 0914A] Roman pontiff. He was immediately consecrated by the bishop of Ostia and the other bishops present, through the laying on of hands before the entire council.

Then came the praises and acclamations of the clergy and people. Such was the acclamation of the confessors who, after initially opposing Cornelius and adhering to Novatian, finally joined Cornelius’s party with these words:

> We know that Cornelius has been elected by almighty God and our Lord Jesus Christ as bishop of the most holy Catholic Church.

This acclamation is found in Cornelius’s own letter to Cyprian and differs little from that which prevailed in later centuries, in Cencius and others.

Other Churches also observed this form of election, following the example of the apostles, who, when they were about to substitute Matthias in the place of Judas the betrayer, carried it out in a large gathering of the faithful. Finally, once consecrated, the pontiff immediately sent letters of communion to the apostolic Churches and received letters from them in return—such as the letters Cornelius sent to Cyprian and Cyprian sent to Cornelius.

If disturbances had arisen on the occasion of the election, the other bishops attempted to settle them. [Col. 0914B] Cyprian did this in the case of Novatian against Cornelius. Such letters were carried by presbyters, commonly by deacons and subdeacons, and sometimes even by acolytes.

[CXI]

In addition to those communion letters, after hearing of Novatian’s faction Cyprian requested other letters from the bishops who had participated in Cornelius’s election. He explains the unusual nature of this action to Cornelius in these words:

> As for our having desired the written testimonies of our colleagues who had been present there at your ordination, we were not seeking something new because we had forgotten ancient customs. It would indeed have been enough for you to announce by letter that you had been made bishop, had there not been a contrary faction . . . . . For this reason we thought it necessary to obtain from there the firm and solid authority of our colleagues who were writing to us.

This seemed necessary because it was the first division in the election of a Roman pontiff and therefore the first precaution raised against schism.

Once peace had been restored to the Church, and the Roman episcopate had begun to be regarded with envy even by pagans, [Col. 0914C] the election of a new pontiff subsequently caused various disturbances. It became the practice that, in the election of the pontiff, the votes of the clergy and Roman people were joined first by the authority of the Roman emperors who ruled in the West and then, after the emperors had been expelled, by that of the Gothic kings.

This does not mean that the emperors or kings themselves took part in the election, but that they sent representatives to Rome to participate in their name. Or, at least, when two men claimed the pontificate amid a disputed election, they used their influence to favor whichever one they wished. This occurred in the cases of Damasus and Ursinus, Boniface and Eulalius, and Symmachus and Laurentius.

The more religious emperors, however, did not approve either of the two claimants but favored the one who had been created through a new election. Honorius Augustus held this view, as his letter to Pope Boniface proves. Boniface had appealed to him to establish that no bishop should ever be ordained in the City through canvassing.

The representatives chiefly took care that concord [Col. 0914D] should be preserved in the election of the bishop, so that the city might not be thrown into doubt through the occasion of a sedition, as Flavius Basilius explains. He had been sent by Odoacer after the death of Pope Simplicius to support the election of Hilary.

To this also pertains Pope Symmachus’s decree that the opinion of the majority should prevail in an election, but in such a way that a man who had decided the election through a promise rather than sound judgment should be deprived of the priesthood.

Nor was the decree of Boniface II, by which he himself chose Vigilius as his successor, any more acceptable. When it was later rejected by the priests who had assembled, Boniface burned his own decree.

[CXII]

What the communion letters of the new pontiff were like at that time is attested by a letter of Gelasius I to all the bishops established throughout Dardania.

Moreover, that in the creation of the pontiff at that time three days were awaited after the death of his predecessor—a practice later established by law—is proved by the report of the prefect Symmachus to Honorius Augustus concerning what happened in the creation of the successor after the death of Pope Zosimus. [Col. 0915A] There we read that Eulalius, the rival of Boniface, was led by the people and clergy to the Lateran Church after the funeral of the previous bishop. He remained there for two days so that the customary day might be awaited on which he could be solemnly ordained, that is, elected.

Because this three-day interval was not observed in the election of Gregory VII, who was created on the very day of Alexander II’s death, Cardinal Benno and other adversaries later brought this charge against Gregory. Baronius, however, considers that at that time the three-day period had not yet been established by any law and rejects Benno’s accusation at this point.

After the Goths had been completely expelled from Italy by the patrician Narses, the general of Emperor Justinian, and after Italy, together with the city of Rome, had been incorporated into the eastern empire, a significant change took place in the election of the pope, lasting until Charlemagne.

Secundinus, a servant of God living in seclusion, asked Gregory the Great about this change. Gregory replied in these words:

> Your Charity asks whether anything was added to the ordinations of the pontiffs of the apostolic see after the most blessed [Col. 0915B] man Hormisdas. But you should know that until the time of Pope Vigilius the ordinations of the bishops were open—that is, conducted publicly—whereas in Vigilius’s time some were carried out through the hidden tunnels of ambitious men. Among these, even the election of Vigilius himself was not free from fault.

From that time onward, affairs were conducted as follows. When the pontiff died, responsibility for the vacant apostolic see was entrusted to the three principal ministers of the clergy: the archpriest, the archdeacon, and the first notary.

They immediately informed the exarch of the pope’s death—the exarch whom the emperor had established at Ravenna after expelling the Goths. Once the proper funeral rites had been performed for the deceased and the three-day fast had been completed, discussion began concerning the election of a pontiff.

The clergy, the nobles, the people, and the soldiers took part in this election—that is, the military units stationed chiefly at Rome and Ravenna to defend the remaining part of Italy against the Lombards.

The result of the election was then reported to the emperor, from whom approval of the election was requested and awaited. The same matter was also written about [Col. 0915C] [CXIII] to the exarch, the judges, the archbishop, and the *apocrisiarius* at Ravenna, so that they might support the election.

After the emperor’s approval had been given, the elected man was finally ordained at the confession of blessed Peter. There he professed his faith and immediately sent a confession of his faith to all the Churches.

All these details are established by the *Liber Diurnus* of the Roman pontiffs, whose formulas began to be used from that time, namely, from the middle of the sixth century.

The elected man did not, however, conduct himself as pontiff before receiving confirmation. This is clear from the letter to the bishops and presbyters of Scotland reported by Bede under the heading:

> To the most beloved and most holy brothers Thomianus, etc., Hilary the archpriest and keeper of the place of the holy apostolic see, John the deacon and, in the name of God, the elect, likewise John the first notary and keeper of the place of the holy apostolic see, etc.

Although John had been elected Roman pontiff, he is nevertheless listed second. Nor do the others abandon the title that belonged to them before the election—namely, that of those who kept the place of the apostolic see.

Yet they address the bishops as “brothers,” just as the presbyters and deacons of Rome call Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, “brother” in Letter 36 of the new edition and elsewhere.

[Col. 0915D]

The emperor’s confirmation was not gratuitous, but was granted in return for a fixed payment. Emperor Heraclius abolished this payment under Pope Agatho and also granted the privilege that the elected pontiff could be consecrated without awaiting the emperor’s approval. Constantine, Heraclius’s great-grandson, likewise confirmed this. See what is said about the election of Adrian I in volume I of the *Museum*.

[Col. 0916A]

After Charlemagne had subdued Desiderius, king of the Lombards and the bitterest enemy of Pope Adrian, and had secured for the apostolic see the exarchate of Ravenna and the portion of Umbria and Picenum that Pippin had granted to it, Adrian, according to Anastasius, mindful of so great a benefaction, summoned a synod of 153 bishops at Rome. Together with the entire synod, he granted to Charles the right and power of electing the pontiff and of governing the apostolic see, in addition to the dignity of patrician, which he had granted him together with the investiture of bishoprics.

By this decree of Adrian, which Gratian and Ivo reported, it was established that the true Roman pontiff would be the man whom Charles, king of the Franks, and his successors, the Frankish kings, elected for consecration.

[CXIV]

Whether the right of electing the pontiff was thereby transferred from the clergy and people to one king, or whether “election” is here understood to mean confirmation, may be debated. The term is used in the same way when the kings of the Franks, who succeed to the kingdom by hereditary right, are nevertheless often said by ancient writers to have been elected by the people—that is, accepted and acknowledged.

But whether the word “election” is understood in this or another way, after Adrian’s death Charlemagne left the clergy and people free to elect his successor. He and his son, the emperor Louis, likewise asserted this freedom for each Church in the creation of bishops, through an enactment reported by others.

[Col. 0916B]

Nevertheless, this freedom was granted to the Roman Church on the condition that the confirmation and approval of the elected pontiff would be given by the emperors or their representatives, in whose presence the consecration of the new pontiff was customarily performed.

Thus, after the death of Gregory IV, when Sergius II had been elected and ordained without awaiting imperial authority, Lothair sent his son Louis together with Drogo, bishop of Metz, to ensure that thereafter, upon the death of a pontiff, no one should ordain a bishop there without the emperor’s command and the presence of his representatives. This is recorded in the Bertinian Annals under the year 844. Had Baronius read this passage, he would certainly have treated Sigebert more mildly, since Sigebert records the same event, though in a different manner.

This rite continued until Adrian III, who issued a decree providing that thereafter the emperor’s authority should not be awaited in approving and ordaining the pontiff.

From this it is clear that the commonly circulated sanction of Louis the Pious is suspect: it remits this practice and restores to the Roman clergy and people the unrestricted [Col. 0916C] power of electing and consecrating the pontiff. This is sufficiently refuted by the decree of Stephen IV, which required the elected man to be consecrated in the presence of the imperial representatives.

After Adrian III, the election of the pope was generally tumultuous until the rule of Otto the Great, who claimed supreme authority for himself and his successors in papal elections.

Peter Damian, under Pope Alexander II, says in Book I, Letter 20, that the principal decision in the election should be made by the cardinal bishops, so that the clergy should lawfully give their assent in second place and popular favor raise its applause in third place. The matter should then be suspended until the authority of the royal majesty had been consulted, unless danger threatened that might compel the matter to be hastened.

No one is unaware how many disturbances this imperial authority caused under Gregory VII [CXV] and his successors.

Finally, after many and prolonged disputes, Alexander III prevailed in establishing that the pontiff should be elected by the cardinals alone—a provision that Nicholas II had already made, [Col. 0916D] but had been unable to enforce—provided that two-thirds should agree upon one candidate.

It was not difficult for Alexander to remove the clergy from the election, once those who had been foremost among the clergy had been incorporated into the cardinalate or their offices had been completely abolished.

Thus the following were made cardinals: the prior, or archpriest, of the Lateran; the archpriests of Saint Peter and Saint Mary Major; and the abbots of Saint Paul and Saint Lawrence Outside the Walls.

Seven bishops of the City were added to these, as well as an equal number of the principal officials of the Roman Church: the *primicerius* (chief notary), *secundicerius* (second notary), *protoscrinarius* (head of the chancery), *saccellarius* (treasury officer), *arcarius* (cashier), *adminiculator* (assistant), and *primicerius defensorum* (chief of the defenders). Their offices had either become wholly obsolete or, under changed names, had been incorporated into the college of cardinals.

Once the heads of the clergy had been removed or elevated, it was easy to deprive the ordinary clerical multitude of this electoral right. And when the clergy had yielded, the people too gave up their ancient right without great difficulty.

[Col. 0917A]

This is substantially Onuphrius’s account. It should not be understood as though under Alexander III the dignity of the cardinals first rose to this summit of authority, but rather that the dignity’s increase in this manner easily deprived the clergy and people of their right.

Certainly Peter Damian, in the letter just cited, exalts the cardinal bishops who principally elected the Roman pontiff to such a degree that he asserts that they surpassed not only the rights of ordinary bishops but also those of patriarchs and primates.

Indeed, from the time of Gregory VII onward, it may be inferred that the cardinals played the leading role in the creation of the Roman pontiff from the formula of the oath of Henry, the elected patriarch of Aquileia. In it he pledges his faith to Gregory and to his successors who shall enter through the better cardinals. Baronius reports this under the year 1079.

Nevertheless, not only the cardinals but also the other clerics—acolytes, subdeacons, deacons, and presbyters—participated in Gregory’s own election. Abbots and monks were also present, while crowds of both sexes gave their consent and raised acclamations. [Col. 0917B]

Finally, to conclude briefly, under Gregory X the cardinals’ conclave was instituted for the election of a new pontiff. The three forms of election that thereafter prevailed were also devised: by scrutiny, by compromise, or by the Holy Spirit. All these matters are explained at length in our books [CXVI], especially in treatises XIII and XIV.

## XVIII. The Rites Formerly Observed in the Consecration of the Pontiff

The pontiff’s election is followed by his installation, which is carried out in two ways: namely, by ordination and by enthronement. The ordination was customarily performed in the Vatican, in the basilica of Saint Peter; the enthronement, in the Lateran.

The order was not constant. Although consecration usually preceded enthronement, enthronement was sometimes performed first, as will be clear from what follows. We learn from Anastasius and from the treatises of the Roman Ordinal what rites were observed in enthronement and ordination before the eleventh century.

[Col. 0917C]

Concerning the creation of Conon, which took place in the year 686, Anastasius records the following:

> The priests and clergy unanimously elected Conon at the Lateran. Immediately all the judges, together with the leaders of the army, came to greet him and acclaimed his praises. When the army saw the unanimity of the clergy and people, they agreed to the election that had been made and subscribed the decree together with them. Finally, together with the clergy and people, they sent their representatives to the exarch, as was customary.

The election was therefore first conducted by the clergy; then came the greeting and acclamation by the judges and military leaders. The army’s consent followed, and finally everyone subscribed the decree, which was sent to the exarch and the emperor.

Anastasius adds, in his account of the creation of Stephen III, which took place in the church of Blessed Mary at the Praesepe:

> Stephen was then carried to the basilica of the Savior, which is called the Constantiniana, and, once brought inside to the patriarchium, was enthroned according to custom.

[Col. 0917D]

What greeting was given to the new pontiff is explained more distinctly by the same author in his account of the election of Valentinus, which took place in the Lateran palace. The elected man is said to have been led to the Lateran patriarchium with fitting praises of glory and magnificence of honor. He was placed upon the pontifical throne, and the entire Roman senate kissed his feet. The same custom was observed in the case of Leo IV.

Anastasius calls this the “greeting.” On the following day Valentinus was consecrated in the basilica of Saint Peter, as the same author relates. Thus enthronement preceded consecration, as it also did in the case of Benedict III.

[CXVII]

The same author describes the rite by which Valentinus was consecrated in these words:

> On the day of his consecration, when the serene light of day had already begun to shine, all the Romans together led the aforesaid bishop from the palace to the church of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. With divine Majesty assisting, they consecrated him as supreme pontiff upon the high throne. Soon ascending the lofty seat [Col. 0918A] of the blessed apostle Peter, key-bearer of the heavenly kingdom, and having piously offered divine praises and sacrifices to God, he returned with a great and magnificent assembly of Romans to the palace, namely, the Lateran, with immense joy. After partaking of sumptuous banquets, he richly endowed the sacred people, the senate, and the Roman people with many and varied gifts.

The rites of the consecration were therefore these: the consecration itself of the new pontiff at Saint Peter’s; his placing upon the seat of Saint Peter; the offering of the sacrifice by the new pontiff; a banquet; and gifts distributed to the senate and people, which in common usage were called *presbyteria*.

The Roman Ordinal and the *Liber Diurnus* of the Roman pontiffs explain that ancient rite of consecrating the pontiff more fully.

> They sing the Psalm according to custom—that is, they sing the Psalm which was customarily chanted after the Antiphon had been prefixed for the Introit. The elect proceeds from the secretarium with seven candle-bearers and comes to the confession, namely, of Saint Peter. After the litany—that is, after “Kyrie eleison” and “Christe [Col. 0918B] eleison” have each been said at least nine times—the bishops and presbyters ascend together to the seat. Then the bishop of Albano gives the first Prayer over the pontiff, *Attend to our supplications*. Next the bishop of Porto gives the second Prayer, *Be favorable, Lord, to our supplications*. Afterward the Gospels are brought, opened, and held over the head of the elect by deacons. Then the bishop of Ostia consecrates the pontiff with the prayer *God of all good things*. In this Prayer the following words must be added at the place beginning, “And therefore to your servant N., etc.” After this the archdeacon fastens the pallium upon him. Then he ascends to the seat, gives peace to all the priests, and says, “Glory to God in the highest.”

In the consecration of a bishop, the Gospels are held over the head of the elect not by deacons but by two bishops, while the other bishops present lay their hands upon his head. The commonly circulated Alcuin asserts that this is found neither in ancient nor in recent authority, nor in Roman tradition, although the Gregorian Sacramentary expressly prescribes it.

Nothing of this kind [CXVIII], however, is read in our two treatises, in which certain things beyond those already mentioned can be observed in the ordination of the pontiff. It is unnecessary to report them, since they are presently at hand.

Innocent III adds one point: only the Roman pontiff—who is consecrated before the angelic hymn and afterward, once consecrated, begins and completes the solemnities of the Mass—is permitted to celebrate ordinations on the day of his consecration. We shall see below that Paschal II did this.

At this point three questions arise. First, was it at some time assigned to the bishop of Ostia alone to consecrate the pontiff, with the other bishops excluded? Sigonius writes that this occurred before Leo II, under the year 682. Second, was the man elected to the pontificate from the diaconate ordained immediately as pontiff, omitting the grade of presbyter, as we proved above had occurred with bishops consecrated by the Roman pontiff? Third, is there any mention before the eleventh century, in the enthronement of the pontiff, of that seat which the common people call the “dung seat”?

[Col. 0918D]

The first question is decided against Sigonius by one of our two treatises on ordination, in which, as in the Roman Ordinal, three bishops are mentioned in the ordination of the pontiff:

> One bishop approaches and gives a Prayer over him, then withdraws; another does likewise. A third approaches and consecrates him.

This treatise was unquestionably written before the pontificate of Leo II. If Leo’s ordination is carefully considered, as it is described in the *Deeds of the Pontiffs*, it will also yield a suitable argument against Sigonius:

> The most holy man written about above was ordained by three bishops, namely Andrew of Ostia, John of Porto, and Placentius of Velletri, because the Church of Albano had no bishop.

When the author gives the reason why the bishop of Velletri was substituted for the bishop of Albano, whose see was vacant, this indicates that previously the custom had been for the bishop of Albano, together with the bishops of Ostia [Col. 0919A] and Porto, to assist in the ordination of the Roman pontiff.

Certainly, we infer that episcopal ordinations had been performed at Rome by three bishops even before the Council of Nicaea from the case of Novatus. He compelled three drunken bishops, summoned to Rome and shut in at the tenth hour, to confer the episcopate upon him through a sort of simulated and empty laying on of hands. Pope Cornelius writes this in his letter to Fabian of Antioch, reported by Eusebius [CXIX] in Book VI, chapter 43. If one bishop had then been sufficient to consecrate the Roman bishop, Novatus would have been content with one.

Perhaps Sigonius was led into error by misunderstanding Augustine’s authority. In the *Brief Account of the Conference against the Donatists*, Augustine writes that it was customary for the Roman pontiff to be ordained not by some metropolitan bishop but by the nearby bishop of Ostia.

This should not be understood as though he alone was present, but as meaning that he was the principal consecrator, acting in place of a metropolitan.

I do not know whether some light can be brought to this question from the case of Eulalius, who after the death of Zosimus contended with Boniface for the [Col. 0919B] pontificate. As we read in the letter of the Roman clergy to Honorius Augustus, he circumvented a very few presbyters and, with the bishop of Ostia also brought in together with others, rushed through canvassing into an office not owed to him, with the order of religion neglected.

When you hear that the bishop of Ostia was summoned together with others to ordain Eulalius, it is extremely likely that the other bishops also assisted at his ordination. This concludes what concerns the first question.

What we prefaced in the preceding chapter concerning the ordination of bishops by a leap over the intervening grade constitutes a kind of preliminary judgment on the second question: namely, that an elect of the Roman see, if he had been chosen from among the deacons, was ordained pontiff with the presbyteral grade omitted.

This is inferred from another of our treatises, where, in the discussion of the pontiff’s election, we read:

> One of the cardinals is elected, whatever his title may have been, provided only that he has been ordained by his predecessor the pontiff, whether as a presbyter or a deacon; for he cannot be a bishop.

[Col. 0919C]

But in the consecration of this same elect there is no distinction between an elected deacon and an elected presbyter. One and the same ordination is prescribed for both.

This conjecture is strengthened by the example of Constantine, who opposed Stephen III—elsewhere called IV—and acted as pontiff. Constantine had been elected by a faction from among the laity. George, bishop of Praeneste, first made him a cleric, then on the following day a subdeacon and deacon; finally, when Sunday arrived, he was consecrated pontiff by the same George together with two other bishops, Eustratius of Albano and Citonatus of Porto. Anastasius reports this without making any mention of the presbyterate.

If someone thinks that this cannot be demonstrated very legitimately from the example of an intruded pontiff, we can offer two other examples of legitimate pontiffs, Valentinus and Nicholas I. The former was elected from the archdiaconate, [CXX] the latter from the diaconate, and both were made pontiffs without any other ordination, as is clear from Anastasius.

Immediately after his election, Valentinus was led to the Lateran patriarchium with fitting praises of glory [Col. 0919D] and placed upon the pontifical throne. Then, when the day of his consecration dawned, all the Romans together led him from the palace to the church of blessed Peter and consecrated him as supreme pontiff upon the high throne. Soon ascending the heights of blessed Peter and having piously offered the sacrifices, he returned to the palace.

Nicholas, however, after being placed upon the apostolic throne in the Lateran basilica, was afterward led to the basilica of blessed Peter. In the presence of the Caesar he was consecrated, exalted upon the apostolic seat, and made pontiff; and he celebrated the solemnities of the Mass over the most sacred body of the apostle.

You see that in both cases no mention whatsoever is made of the conferral of the presbyterate.

It is not sufficiently clear at what time this custom was changed. By the eleventh century an opposite practice had prevailed: at that time Hildebrand, an archdeacon elected after the death of Alexander II, was ordained to the priesthood within the week of Pentecost, [Col. 0920A] and was consecrated Roman pontiff on the feast of the Apostles. Hence, at the beginning of the twelfth century, Gelasius II, likewise elected from the diaconate, was not consecrated pope until after he had been ordained priest. The event is related by an eyewitness named Pandulf in his book on the Roman pontiffs. After Pandulf has described the arrival of the elected pope at the port of Gaeta and the approach of many bishops to him, he adds:

“In their presence the same lord pope, through the hands of Lambert of Ostia, Peter of Porto, and Vitalis of Albano, bishops, with many archbishops and bishops assisting, together with other religious men, and with William, duke of Apulia, Robert, prince of Capua, Richard of Aquila, and very many other barons, who then all swore fealty to him, while an innumerable clergy and people were present, the Holy Spirit directing him, was made a priest; and within the Kalends of March he was consecrated as Pope Gelasius. There he promoted Peter Rufus, cardinal deacon, Baro, a subdeacon, and me, Pandulf, the doorkeeper who wrote this, to the offices of lector and exorcist, and ordained many others in the minor orders.” [Col. 0920B]

From this it is clear that Gelasius—as we have just observed concerning Gregory as well—received the priestly rank separately before the pontificate, and that during the intervening period between Nicholas I and Gregory VII ordination by skipping ranks [CXXI] had been abolished in the Roman Church. It is moreover likely that this occurred because of Photius’s objections, one of which was that the Romans ordained bishops by skipping ranks. From Pandulf’s testimony above, it is also proved that which we previously observed from Innocent III: namely, that the Roman pontiff conferred the Orders on the very day of his consecration.

It remains to investigate at what time the use began, and at what time it ceased, of that stone seat which the common people call the *stercoraria*. Those who trace the origin of this seat to the false pope Joan are easily refuted by the fact that no mention of any such seat is found before the twelfth century. For a better understanding of the matter, it is useful to note that for several centuries the following custom had ordinarily been observed at the installation of new pontiffs. After the elected pope had been introduced into the Lateran church, he was first placed upon the pontifical throne that formerly stood in the apse of that basilica. There, as Cencius says, he admitted all the bishops and cardinals to the kiss. Then he was led to the stone seat called the *stercoraria*, situated in the portico of the same basilica between two doors, and sat upon it while this verse from Psalm 112 was sung:

> He raises the needy from the dust  
> and lifts the poor from the dungheap.

Afterward he was conducted to the chapel of Saint Sylvester near the Lateran palace. There were two pierced porphyry seats. He first sat on the right in one of them, and then received the keys of the basilica from the prior of Saint Laurence as a sign of government and correction. Finally, placed on the left in the other seat, he returned the same keys to the prior.

I have thought it worthwhile to report these details briefly from the book of Cencius, here published, so that everyone may understand that the seat called *stercoraria* was not so called because it was pierced—for it was not pierced, as we ourselves established by inspection—but because, while the pontiff stood upon it, these words of Psalm 112 were sung: “He raises the poor from the dungheap.” This seat is made of marble; the other two are of porphyry. All three remain, discarded together with superfluous furnishings, in the Lateran peristyle, as we stated in the *Italian Itinerary*. [Col. 0920D]

I have found no one who mentioned these seats before the Pandulf cited above. For in the installation of the pontiffs elected after Leo IV—the man whom they absurdly say was succeeded by that false pope—all are reported to have been placed upon the patriarchal throne set within the basilica, not upon these seats, [CXXII] which stood outside the basilica. Thus, when the electors had led Benedict III, the successor of Leo, to the Lateran patriarchium, they placed him upon the pontifical throne, as is the custom of pontiffs and as ordinary practice demonstrates. From this it is understood that nothing had yet been changed. The same happened with Nicholas I, whom they introduced into the Lateran patriarchium and placed upon the apostolic throne. [Col. 0921A]

Pandulf, as I was just saying, is the first to mention these seats, in the case of Paschal II. He records Paschal’s installation in the following manner:

“While he long resisted, the chief notaries and regional scribes, changing his name, acclaimed to him the response: ‘Saint Peter has elected Pope Paschal.’ When these and other praises had been solemnly completed, he was clothed by the fathers in a scarlet cloak and a tiara was placed upon his head. Accompanied by a crowd with singing, he was carried to the Lateran and brought before that portico which leads from the southern quarter to the basilica of the Savior, which they call the Constantinian basilica. He dismounted from his horse and was placed upon the seat that is there, and afterward upon the patriarchal throne. Ascending the palace, he came to two curule seats. Here he was girded with a belt from which seven keys and seven seals hung. From this he was to understand that, according to the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, he ought to provide for the government of the holy Churches over which, by God’s authority, he presides—in locking and unlocking—with as much deliberation as the solemnity of the undertaking demands. Having been seated in both places, and having been given a staff in his hand, he fulfilled the manner of his election as master, whether seated or passing through the other parts of the palace reserved for the Roman pontiffs. On the following day, the sixth month, the fourteenth day, the pontiffs, with a great multitude of people and commoners, entered the basilica of blessed Peter, first to consecrate him pontiff, and to consecrate the pontiff…” [Col. 0921B]

These details suffice for the present purpose, though many matters worthy of notice arise in them.

First, the elected pontiff was then clothed in a scarlet cloak and tiara. The same author mentions this custom in the cases of Callistus II and also Honorius II; before him, Peter Damian mentions it in Book I, Letter 20, addressing the antipope Cadalus:

> You perhaps now have a mitre; you have, according to the custom of the Roman pontiff, a red cloak.

In this dress the pope is usually depicted in the splendid chartulary of Casauria, which is preserved in the royal library.

Next, after the pontiff had been carried on horseback to the Lateran, he dismounted at the southern gate, which is the principal gate, and was placed upon the seat that was there, and afterward upon the patriarchal throne. Here you see that the seat which stood in the portico of the Lateran basilica was distinguished from the patriarchal throne, which we have said was situated beneath the apse of the basilica. [Col. 0921C]

The elected pope was then led to the Lateran palace and came to the two curule seats, in which he sat in turn. He received a belt with seven keys and an equal number of seals. These were the two porphyry seats—indeed, pierced ones—which we saw in the cloister of the Lateran canons together with the aforementioned *stercoraria*, the name by which Cencius is the first known to have called it.

The same Pandulf, in his account of Honorius II, without mentioning this seat, states that the elected pontiff was arranged in the *syrni* situated before the church of Saint Sylvester. By this term Pandulf means those two porphyry seats. James, cardinal priest, gives a full description of the same rite in the life of Celestine V, where he discusses the coronation of Boniface VIII. Furthermore, in the letter of Pileus of Prata, archbishop of Ravenna and cardinal, to Louis, count of Flanders—printed in volume IV of the *Spicilegium*, and concerning the election of Urban VI—after Urban’s coronation in the Vatican basilica, where, according to custom, he personally communicated all the cardinal deacons with the precious body and blood of Christ, it is stated that he was conducted in solemn procession to the Lateran church and there enthroned in seats arranged according to the form of the Roman Church. [Col. 0921D]

From these facts it is reasonable to understand that the use of the aforementioned seats was introduced into the installation of the pontiff long before the fable of the false pope—of which Martin of Troppau was the author—arose, although the reason for the rite is unknown. The same rite continued until Leo X, who, after being carried to the Lateran according to custom, sat upon a little seat lying beside the right-hand door of the church, as Paris de Grassis writes in his diary.
