Afterward they went to the chapel of Saint [Col. 0922A] Sylvester:

> First the pope sat, as though lying down, and received from the prior of the canons the keys and then the staff. Then the pope immediately rose and went to another seat, and lay down; and from the same prior of the canons he received a red belt with a purse containing twelve glass stones, which are still shown. Immediately the pope rose and handed the staff and keys back to the same prior; but he retained the belt until the chamberlain had taken the silver money and thrown it three times from his hand or lap, while he said: “He has scattered; he has given to the poor,” and so forth. Then the pope removed the belt and purse and went to the chapel of the Savior.

Thus far the diary of Paris.

There are several details in Paris’s account that differ somewhat from Pandulf’s narrative. Pandulf mentions a belt with seven keys and an equal number of seals; Paris, however, joins the belt with a purse containing twelve small stones. Censius agrees with Paris, saying that the elected pope was girded with a red silk belt from which hung a purple purse containing twelve seals of precious stones and musk. Cardinal James gives the same account in verse when discussing the coronation of Boniface VIII:

> And there the Father is girded with a belt,  
> to which a purple purse is attached, bearing  
> twice six precious little stones, engraved seals,  
> and musk—great omens marking great things.

But at last the entire rite of these seats was completely abolished after Leo X, when the Romans began to be ashamed of a fable so poorly devised yet so readily believed. The origin of the rite, however, preceded that fable by one or two centuries. [Col. 0922B]

It may appropriately be added here that which is read in the *Accusations of the Greeks against the Latins*, volume III of Cotelerius’s *Greek Monuments*, p. 498, article 16:

> “The successor of the dead pope is appointed in this way. They elect the one whom they make part of their synod, and bring him while alive to the dead body. They take the hand of the one who is without consciousness and place it upon the neck of the living man, and they consider this to be the successor’s anointing and consecration. He then, as the first act, celebrates the sacred rites for the funeral of the deceased man who anointed him, and thereafter, as one most perfectly anointed, vigorously performs the pontifical duties.”

It is easy for anyone to judge, however, that this accusation is false and was borrowed from an event in the Church of Alexandria.

The pontifical ornaments are discussed in various parts of our little books, the oldest of which is the *Roman Ordo*, here numbered fifth in sequence. The supreme pontiffs do not use the *cambuta*, or pastoral staff; nor do the cardinal bishops in the Roman Curia, as James Gaetani notes in chapter 48 of his *Ordinary*.

It will not be irrelevant to note that in our older books the pontiff is ordinarily designated not by *domini* but by *domni*. That this usage was current even in Peter Damian’s time is proved by the following verse of his concerning Alexander II and Hildebrand, then an archdeacon. Because Hildebrand wielded very great authority with the pontiff, Peter calls him the pontiff’s master:

> I serve the pope more as *domino* than as *domno*.

This is why, wherever the pontiff is concerned, we have generally retained the form *domni* according to the old usage, which was once also transferred to the saints.

As for the stations which the pontiffs frequented on fast days, they often proceeded barefoot; on other, more solemn processions, they were accustomed to ride a white horse. To this point may be referred what Gregory the Great wrote to Peter, subdeacon of Sicily, in Book XII, Letter 30:

> Moreover, you sent us one wretched horse and five good asses. I cannot ride the horse, because it is wretched; but I cannot ride the good ones, because they are asses. Yet we ask that, if you intend to keep us—that is, to make us content—you send us something worthy of us. [CXXV]

And certainly this is what pontifical dignity requires.

## XIX. An examination of the passage of Socrates Scholasticus concerning the omission of the sacred mysteries on Saturdays among the Romans; concerning the midweek and middle Sunday, and various rites briefly explained

[Col. 0923A]

After having discussed at length the matters pertaining to the three days before Easter, and consequently to the sacred Ordinations, we must now touch briefly upon certain rites that occur at other times, so that we may approach our Ritual books better prepared and more readily equipped.

First there presents itself a passage of Socrates Scholasticus in Book V, chapter 22, where he says:

> “Although all the churches throughout the world celebrated the sacred mysteries every week on Saturday, the Alexandrians and Romans, preferring an ancient tradition, refrained from doing so.”

This seems no more consistent with the truth than what the same author asserts in the same place concerning Lent: “Those who are in Rome fast for only three continuous weeks before Easter, except on Saturday and Sunday.” For it is certain from Cassian and from Leo the Great—authors contemporary with Socrates in time, though superior in authority—that the Romans then fasted for six weeks before Easter. It is no less certain that among the ancient Romans there was a fast on Saturdays during Lent, indeed throughout the entire year, as the learned Quesnel proves in his Sixth Dissertation on Saint Leo.

I am completely convinced that Socrates made an error of the same kind when he writes that the sacred mysteries were omitted on Saturdays among the Romans. First, no trace of such a practice appears among the ancient authors. On the contrary, in the oldest liturgical codices proper Masses are assigned for the Saturdays of Lent, with one or two exceptions made for particular reasons. Thus it is in the Gelasian Sacramentary, thus in the Gregorian, and thus in the *Book of Comes*, which contains the readings of the Epistles and Gospels for the entire year. Although it is falsely attributed to Jerome, it is undoubtedly the work of a very ancient author. [Col. 0923C]

Moreover, this opinion of Socrates seems to conflict with another statement of his, when he says that the Romans fasted during Lent for only three weeks, except on Saturday and Sunday. For this exception of Saturday from the fast implies a certain solemnity, which certainly ought to have been celebrated with the sacred mysteries. Further, Innocent I, in his letter to Decentius, excepts only Holy Saturday from the celebration of the mysteries, for a particular reason—a reason that would have been improperly introduced if the mysteries had also been omitted on all the other Saturdays of the year.

From what source, then, did Socrates derive the occasion for his error? Perhaps from a misreading of the letter of Innocent I to Decentius, which he may have seen. In that letter, explaining why one must fast on Holy Saturday as well as on Good Friday, the pontiff says that this was done on account of the sorrow of the Apostles, who remained fasting during those two days. “That they fasted during the aforesaid two days,” he says, “is certainly beyond doubt, so much so that the tradition of the Church holds that during those two days the Sacraments were not celebrated at all.” [Col. 0923D] He then adds:

> “This form, moreover, must be observed every week, because the commemoration of that day must always be celebrated.”

These last words could easily lead an incautious reader into error, as though Innocent intended to assign not only a fast but also abstention from the mysteries to every Saturday of the year. Yet he must be understood as speaking solely of the fast; that a fast was observed among the Romans on every Saturday of the year is clear from Augustine, Leo the Great, and other authors cited by Quesnel.

There is greater difficulty concerning the fast of Thursday during Lent among the Romans themselves. For if we trust the commonly circulated Acts of the pontiffs, Pope Miltiades decreed that no one should fast on Sunday or on Thursday during Lent. Hence the *Micrologus*, in chapter 50, infers that Saint Gregory, when arranging the offices, left Thursday within Lent vacant, so that, because it was festive like Sunday, it might also be honored with the Sunday office. But because that same weekday was later assigned to fasts, like the others, Gregory the Younger—that is, Gregory II—decreed that it should be solemn, with offices gathered from various sources, especially from the summer Sundays. Hence antiphons from the Sunday Gospels are still found assigned to Thursdays, and so forth. [Col. 0924A]

Since Lent has again been mentioned here, it seems appropriate to say a few words about the middle week, which immediately follows the fourth Sunday of Lent, and about Passion Sunday, which the Apostolic See chose to call “middle,” as we read in our little books.

The distinguished scholar Henri Valois, investigating the origin of this designation in Book V, chapter 22, of Socrates, draws from it an argument in support of Socrates’s opinion that the Romans fasted during only three weeks before Easter in Lent. He says that he can find no other reason why Passion Sunday was called “middle” than that, of the three weeks during which the Romans fasted in Lent, it was the second Sunday and therefore the middle one. But, with due respect to the great man, this explanation cannot be accepted. For it is established from Leo the Great and Cassian that the Romans then fasted for six weeks before Easter. Moreover, the week preceding Passion Sunday—which, according to Socrates’s view, would have been the first week of the Roman Lent—was likewise called “middle” by the ancients, as in Pope Pelagius I, in Holstenius’s *Roman Collection*:

> “When the middle week of Easter arrives, do not delay promoting each person through the offices which we have mentioned.”

And before him, Gelasius I, in Letter 9, chapter 11:

> “Ordinations of priests and deacons should not be performed except at prescribed times and days, namely during the fast of the fourth, seventh, and tenth months; and they should also know that those of the beginning of Lent and of middle Lent are to be celebrated on the Saturday evening of the fast.”

Here you see that the Saturday of the beginning of Lent is distinguished from the Saturday of middle Lent; otherwise, according to Socrates’s view, they would have been one and the same. [Col. 0924B]

“Why, then,” you ask, “was the fourth week of Lent called ‘middle,’ and why was Passion Sunday designated by the same term?” I think it was for this reason: since the six weeks of Lent can be divided into two equal parts, the week of the second part may be called “middle,” as though it were the first week after the midpoint of Lent. And because Lent began on Monday, the Sunday following the middle week was likewise called “middle.”

### 1.

Leaving these matters aside, so that we may proceed to certain other rites, the following words concerning the reading of the passions of the saints deserve particular notice. They occur in the Roman Ordo of the Vallicelliana and Saint Gall libraries:

> “The passions of the saints, or their deeds, were read there only up to the time of Hadrian, and only where the church or title of that saint existed. But from his own time onward he ordered a change—that is, he ordered them to be read in the church of Saint Peter.” [CXXVIII]

Thus, before Hadrian I, the passions of the saints were not read in the Vatican basilica, nor in the Lateran. This is evident for the time of Gelasius I from his decree concerning the canon of the sacred books. See Thomasius, *Antiphonalia*, p. 495. [Col. 0924D]

### 2.

The same author observes in the same place, p. 12, that in ancient times the Roman Church did not admit hymns into the divine offices. This is clear both from Amalarius’s *Supplement* and from the books of Benedict the canon and Cencius the chamberlain, published here; from them it appears that this custom continued into the twelfth century. The Churches of Lyons and Vienne retained nearly the same practice. In them, until now, there have been no hymns at the night Vigils or at Morning Lauds, and not even at Vespers or the other hours, except Compline. The Roman Church also first admitted hymns at Compline several centuries ago, and later introduced others into the individual offices.

Read Radulfus, dean of Tongeren, *Propositions*, 13. Thomasius objects at this point that Udalric, in Book II, chapter 52, of the *Customs of Cluny*, mentions hymns of the Roman Church. But the learned man interprets this as referring to certain particular churches of the city, although Saint Benedict, in his Rule, praises the Ambrosian hymns and orders them to be sung. Here it is worth recalling in passing what Leo of Monte Cassino writes in Book II, chapter 97, of the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino: namely, that at that time—that is, during the pontificate of Stephen X—the singing of the Ambrosian chant was entirely forbidden in that Cassinese Church by the same Stephen, who had formerly been abbot of Cassino under the name Frederick. The same Radulfus, dean of Tongeren, mentioned above, explains in Proposition 12 how the Ambrosian chant differed from the Roman. [Col. 0925A]

### 3.

At the night Vigils, when each reading was to be concluded, the deacons sang beforehand, “But you,” as Benedict the canon and Cencius prescribe here, on pages 123 and 174. This indicates that even then the readings were extended at the discretion of those presiding. Charlemagne, according to the monk of Saint Gall, signaled their conclusion with a hiss of the tongue. In the Church of Rheims even in our own time, the longer reading delivered before Compline during Lent is concluded by a priest singing “But you” beforehand; the cleric who is chanting the reading then continues and finishes it.

### 4.

When the pontiff is incensed, if he is standing, he is incensed by someone standing; if he is seated, by someone kneeling. The reason for this difference may be given as follows: according to the Second Roman Ordo published here, no. 9, the thuribles are brought to people’s noses, and the smoke is drawn toward the mouth by the hand. This could scarcely be done if incense were brought to a seated pontiff by someone standing.

### 5.

The Lateran Church, as John the Deacon reports in the work published here, preserving the apostolic institution, uses only the Lord’s Prayer in its offices on Sunday, since other prayers were added afterward—namely, those which we call Collects. William Durandus noted this custom in Book IV, chapter 14. The same rite once prevailed in the Church of Poitiers, as is proved by Letter 79 of Fulbert, bishop of Chartres:

> “When the readings have been completed after the Lord’s Prayer, where it says, ‘Lord, hear my prayer,’ the prayer that is recited from the Sacramentary should immediately follow.”

Nevertheless, allow the Church to retain its own practice to the present day. Saint Benedict, in his Rule, orders Masses to be celebrated after the Lord’s Prayer—that is, a dismissal or permission to depart, as many interpret it—although some commentators, including certain older ones, think that this dismissal was made together with the Collect.

### 6.

Concerning the aforementioned Lateran Church, the following statement of Peter Abelard, in Letter 5 to Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, deserves remembrance:

> “Certainly not even the city itself observes the ancient custom of the Roman See, but only the Lateran Church, which is the mother of all. It preserves the ancient office, with none of its daughters following it in this matter—not even the basilica of the Roman palace.”

If this is so, anyone who wishes to investigate the ancient rites of the Roman Church accurately ought to read with particular diligence those matters that pertain to the Lateran Church. [Col. 0925D]

### 7.

Peter Amelii has several observations about Easter communion in chapter 85. Since we did not mention them above, it will be worthwhile to touch upon them briefly here. First, he says that at the pontifical Mass celebrated on Easter Day, all and each of those who had truly confessed, were penitent, and were contrite in heart could receive Holy Communion from the pope without the permission of a bishop, parish priest, or any other superior. Next, to all who had communicated, a deacon handed a tube through which they drank the blood of Christ. Thus it is established that toward the end of the fourteenth century, at least Easter communion at the pontifical Mass was celebrated under both kinds. This observation should be referred to what we said above on this subject in chapter 9. Finally, after receiving the blood, each person drank a little wine from a cup held by the sacristan or acolyte. [CXXX]

### 8.

Finally, in the burial of the bodies of distinguished dead, it was once customary among the Italians—not only at Rome—for coffins to be placed in elevated positions. This may be observed at Milan in the portico of the church of Saint Nazarius. But in 1561 Pius IV decreed—as John Francis Firmanus reports in his diary—that the coffins of the dead which had been raised high in the walls of the church should be lowered. The ordinaries were instructed to carry this out in their churches, and it was executed in many places, not without grief among the living. Thus at Milan Charles Borromeo, that most holy bishop and nephew of Pius, had the bodies of the Trivulzio family, which had been placed in elevated positions in the aforementioned portico of Saint Nazarius, buried in the ground, leaving the burial niches empty at the top.

### 9.

On this occasion it is worth observing that even the earliest Christians of old considered it unlawful for the bodies of their own people to be buried together with the corpses of pagans in a common tomb. When a certain Spanish bishop named Martial had attempted the contrary, Cyprian complained bitterly about the matter in his synodal letter against the same Martial and Basilides, bishops who had purchased certificates of sacrifice:

> “Martial also, besides the shameful and filthy banquets of the pagans, the clubs which he long frequented, and the sons whom he deposited in the same association according to the custom of foreign peoples near pagan tombs and buried together with foreigners…”

From this it is understood how far from the truth are those who think that the Roman cemeteries in which the bodies of Christians were first buried were also shared with profane persons and pagans. How great the multitude of the faithful, indeed of the saints, buried there was in the age of Prudentius, Prudentius himself teaches in his hymn on Saint Laurence:

> Scarcely known by hidden fame  
> is how full of saints Rome is,  
> how richly the urban soil  
> flourishes with sacred tombs.

Moreover, that the bodies of saints were long accustomed to be removed from those cemeteries is attested, among others, by Gregory III in a letter that is number 116 among the Bonifatian letters, addressed to Otgar, bishop of Mainz. It is useful to quote the words of the letter:

> “As for the holy body which your prudence humbly asked us to send, we did not have one, because our predecessors brought with them all the bodies of the saints collectively, and with the greatest veneration deposited each one in newly dedicated churches. Therefore we ask your benevolence to grant us time to search more diligently, so that we may be able to find a holy body and fulfill your request. If one is found, may your diligence deign to believe us: we shall immediately accomplish what you have asked. At present we have not sent it, because although we searched, we were in no way able to find one.” [Col. 0926C]

If the same religious care and diligence were now applied to searching for and distinguishing the bodies of the saints, it would be far more difficult—after nearly all the more celebrated cemeteries had been emptied—to find the bodies of saints with certain and indisputable evidence of holiness, much less of martyrdom. Perhaps, however, Gregory is speaking of saints known by name, because at that time the custom had not yet arisen which prevails in our own day: that the bodies of baptized persons, whom people call saints, should be distributed as genuine and indisputable sacred relics. But enough of this. [Col. 0926D]

## XX. Concerning the confession of blessed Peter in the Vatican basilica; what *rugae*, *regiae*, and *regulares* mean among ecclesiastical writers; concerning the various ways of preserving the Eucharist among the Romans; what *capsa* means in the Council of Arausio; what *turris* means in Gregory and Venantius Fortunatus

Since these books frequently mention the confession of blessed Peter, we have thought it worthwhile to make a few brief observations about it here. First, among Latin ecclesiastical writers the term “confession” in this context means nothing other than what the Greeks call a *martyrion*—that is, a place in which the relics or bodies of martyrs were preserved. Why the tomb of the blessed Apostle Peter was first given the name “confession,” Onuphrius derives from the Acts of the Eighth Council of Constantinople, session four. He says that no pilgrim was admitted into the basilica of Saint Peter unless he had first presented a statement of his faith, and affirms that this was customarily done at the confession of blessed Peter. But since the confession itself was located in the innermost part of the basilica, visitors were admitted into the basilica before they made their profession of faith. It is simpler to say that it was called a confession because it was the place of a confessor or martyr. Others offer other explanations, which do not belong here. [Col. 0927A]

That no one was admitted to the confession of blessed Peter—or rather, to his basilica—unless he had first demonstrated his own faith, we gather from Optatus, Book VI, where, speaking of Macrobius, the Donatist pseudo-bishop living at Rome, he says:

> “Finally, if Macrobius is asked where he sits there, can he say, ‘In the chair of Peter’? I do not know whether he has even seen it with his eyes, and he does not approach the memorial of Peter, as though he were a schismatic.”

But the following words of Optatus prove that this must also be understood of any Catholic church in the city of Rome:

> “Behold, the memorials of two Apostles are present there. Say whether he was able to enter these places in such a way as to offer there, where it is established that the memorials of the saints are located.”

Hence Polycarp did not first celebrate the sacred rites in the Roman church until he had received permission for this from Bishop Anicetus.

On this occasion we must not omit what escaped us above: that a particular custom existed at Rome whereby adults who came from paganism to the Christian faith, at the hour appointed for professing the faith, recited the Creed before baptism from an elevated place in the sight of the faithful people, using fixed words learned and retained by memory. Augustine reports in Book VIII of the *Confessions*, chapter 3, that this practice was preserved by Simplicianus.

I return to the confession of Saint Peter, which Gregory, bishop of Tours, describes in Book I of *The Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 28:

> “This tomb, placed beneath the altar, is considered very exceptional. But anyone who wishes to pray, after the barriers surrounding the place have been opened, approaches above the tomb. Then, when a small window has been opened and he has inserted his head within, he asks for whatever necessity demands. The request is not ineffectual if only a just prayer is offered. If he wishes to take away blessed relics, he throws inside some little cloth weighed on a steelyard, and then, keeping vigil and fasting, most devoutly begs that apostolic power may support his devotion. Wonderful to say! If the man’s faith has prevailed, the cloth lifted from the tomb is so filled with divine power that it weighs much more than it had weighed before; and then the one who lifts it knows that by the saint’s grace he has received what he asked. Many also make golden keys for opening the barriers of the blessed tomb; those who carry them receive the earlier ones as a blessing, by which they may heal the infirmity of the afflicted. For perfect faith accomplishes all things. There are also four columns of elegant appearance and snowy whiteness, which are said to support the canopy over the tomb.”

Thus far Gregory of Tours. [Col. 0927D]

There were not one but two small windows at the tomb of blessed Peter, an upper and a lower one, called *cataracts* in a petition of the legates Germanus and John, bishops, sent in the name of Count Justinian to Hormisdas. It contains these words:

> “Therefore, if it also seems good to Your Beatitude, command that sacred tokens of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul be granted to him according to custom; and, if it can be done, it is yours to decide that the sacred tokens themselves be lowered to the second *cataract*.”

For it was considered a much greater privilege if cloths were brought onto the sacred tomb from the second window, since access from that point was evidently closer to contact with the sacred body. A window of this kind existed at the Memorial, or oratory, of blessed Stephen in the city of Uzalis, as Evodius testifies in Book I of *The Miracles of the Same Holy Martyr*, chapter 12. A certain citizen of Utica, afflicted with paralysis of the feet and tongue, came there and, having recovered the use of his feet, removed the sleeve of his tunic because he had no handkerchief (*orarium*). He inserted his hand through the window of the memorial and sent the sleeve into the inner place of the sacred relics; then, withdrawing his right hand again, he brought it to his mouth, and by touching his tongue gradually loosened the knots of speech through the power of faith. [Col. 0928A]

Such windows were called *cataracts* because they were closed by strong little gates—for stronger gates are called by that name.

As for the cloths that were placed over the body of the blessed apostle with prayers and fasts, Gregory the Great calls them *brandea*. By the same rite, pallia for archbishops were customarily consecrated; these were said to have been taken from the body of blessed Peter. The same is read concerning the *oraria* of those being ordained in our ninth booklet. Nor is the example that Bishop Gregory of Tours cited above without relevance: he says that cloths of this kind were customarily weighed on a small balance or steelyard before being placed over the sacred tomb, so that, from the greater weight subsequently acquired, the grace of the virtue received might be perceived. The same practice was carried out at the tomb of Saint Martin, according to the same author, in Book I *On the Miracles of that Saint*, chapter 11 [Col. 0928B]. There he tells of Callaeci Suebi who placed a weighed portion of a silk pallium upon the blessed man’s tomb, saying:

“If we have found favor [CXXXIV] before the patron whom we seek, what we have placed will weigh more on the following night, and what has been placed will be a blessing for us, sought through faith.”

Accordingly, after keeping vigil for one night, when morning came they weighed what they had placed. So great was the grace of the blessed man infused into them that they raised the bronze balance aloft for as far as the small steelyard could rise. Finally, the sword with which the new emperor was to be girded at his solemn inauguration was taken from above the confession of Saint Peter, by a singular privilege not granted to kings, as we read in the *Ordinary* of James Gaetanus.

At the same confession, the expiation of sins was also carried out through the sacrament of penance. This is clear from Peter Damian’s Letter or Opusculum 55, addressed to the Empress Agnes, to whom Peter writes as follows [Col. 0928C]:

“But so that those who flock to the threshold of the apostles may imitate the example of your holy devotion with salutary effect, you also made me sit beneath the hidden confession of blessed Peter, before the sacred altar; and through mournful groans and bitter sighs, beginning with the very first five years of your life, when you were still tender and recently weaned, you unfolded in faithful accounts whatever subtle or minute thing might have touched the innermost parts of your humanity, whatever was vain in your thoughts, and whatever superfluous matter might further have crept into your speech—as though the blessed apostle himself were bodily presiding there. For this reason it seemed to me that I ought to impose no other burden of penance upon you as you confessed than to repeat that saying of divine commission: ‘Do what you are doing; carry out what you are carrying out,’ and so forth.”

This, incidentally, does not seem to agree sufficiently with Peter’s own judgment in Opusculum 13, chapters 6 and 7, where he censures certain heads of monasteries who imposed no other penance upon anyone coming from the world, even if he had fallen gravely, than that he should observe the monastery’s common order. You will read much about the confession of blessed Peter and its customs in the appendix to Order 11 [Col. 0928D].

Something more ought to be added concerning the manner of administering the sacrament of penance in the Roman Church. But since we have already proceeded at considerable length, it seems preferable to refer the reader to the study of the following booklets, especially to the Roman Order, which is here number ten, where many excellent prescriptions are given concerning the sacrament of penance and communion for the sick. According to the tenth booklet, this communion followed the anointing that we call extreme unction [CXXXV]; but the contrary practice gradually became established from the beginning of the thirteenth century. We have explained the origin and rationale of this change in the preface to the first Benedictine century.

Since obscure terms sometimes occur in these booklets and in the writings of the ancient ecclesiastical authors, Anastasius and others, it will be useful to explain them here in advance.

The first term that presents itself is *rugae*, whose meaning is disputed among scholars. Caesar Bullingerus, considering the Latin meaning of the word, interprets *rugae* as lines in marble or metal, or as little channels and furrows resembling the wrinkles drawn together on the forehead of old men; alternatively, he understands them as tablets of gold and silver that were wrinkled and striated. Most others, tracing the same word *rugae* to a Gallic origin, believe that it means roads, paths, or little ways of the sort that we Gauls call *rues*. Among these, the most learned Cangius says that *ruga* seems to mean the way within the sacred building before the presbytery, along which the bishop proceeds into it to celebrate the sacred rites. The most illustrious Ciampinus departs little from this opinion in chapter 14, *On Unleavened Bread*, where he carefully explains both the various passages concerning *rugae* and the various opinions of authors concerning the word. It is unnecessary to repeat them here.

Yet, in order to reach a firm conclusion about this term, several matters must first be considered.

1. The *rugae* consisted of something solid and of solid material, chiefly silver; indeed, they were adorned with gold and gems. This is clear from various passages of Anastasius, for example in his account of Leo III [Col. 0929B]:

“He made in the basilica of blessed Andrew, at blessed Peter the apostle, silver *rugae* weighing eighty pounds.”

And in his account of Paschal I:

“He made in the church of the blessed Mother of God, called the Domnica, silver *rugae* weighing sixty-six pounds.”

From these and other passages, which we omit for the sake of brevity, it is clear that the name *rugae* cannot signify roads or paths if it is being used for the space occupied by the paths themselves, since the *rugae* were evidently not something empty and vacant but something solid. For the same reason, the *rugae* cannot be explained as the actual entranceway of the doors leading to the presbytery.

2. Some *rugae* were larger and others smaller; the latter are also called *rugulae*. The same Anastasius says of Paschal I:

“He also made before the vestibule of the altar larger silver *rugae*, weighing seventy-eight pounds.”

3. The same author mentions six pairs of *rugae* made of brass in his account of Sergius II [CXXXVI]; and, evidently in the same sense, twelve larger *rugae* before the secretarium in his account of Leo III. This can be applied to paths even less plausibly [Col. 0929C].

4. The *rugae* were located at the entrance to the presbytery, both on the men’s side and on the women’s side; they were also at the head of the presbytery before the confession, and at the vestibule of the altar. Anastasius, in his account of Stephen IV, says:

“He made *rugae* in the presbytery, on the men’s and women’s sides, of the purest silver, weighing one hundred and thirty pounds, and also other *rugae* at the head of the presbytery before the confession.”

In his account of Leo III:

“He adorned the *rugae* before the entrance to the altar with the purest silver.”

And in his account of Paschal I:

“He also made larger silver *rugae* before the vestibule of the altar.”

5. There were also smaller *rugae*, or *regulae*, within and outside the confession. Anastasius, in his account of Paschal I, says:

“He most beautifully adorned the confession, enclosing it within and without with its *rugulae*.”

The same author repeats this later in another passage.

6. The *rugae*, or *rugulae*, were inserted into grilles that enclosed and supported them. In his account of Leo IV:

“He made cast-silver *rugulae* with grilles at the entrance to the presbytery and the confession.”

And in his account of Nicholas I:

“Moreover, on the purple marbles that hold the silver *rugae* before the body of blessed Peter the apostle, he placed two silver crosses, one on the right and one on the left” [Col. 0929D].

7. Finally, *regulares* were placed upon the *rugae*, from which curtains and images hung before the *rugae*, as we shall see shortly.

From all these facts we conclude without doubt that *rugae* or *rugulae* were nothing other than doors, small gates, or little windows, located at the entrance to the presbytery, at the vestibule of the altar, and below and outside the confession, and also interspersed among the grilles [Note: [Col. 0929D] See the *Sanctuarium Capuanum*, p. 48, where *regulae* are called doors.]. From this, the Italian word *ringuieres*, which even today signifies the little windows of ciboria, also appears to have been derived. All the features mentioned above can readily and suitably be applied to such doors, small gates, and little windows, as will immediately be apparent to anyone who compares the evidence. Pairs of *rugae* were double-leaved doors or gates, as is frequently the case with grilles. The *rugulae* that we have said were inside the confession were nothing other than those little windows of which we spoke in the preceding chapter. Indeed, Torrigius interprets *rugae* as doors in the Vatican crypts. Accordingly, in our First Roman Order, where the acolytes are said to watch the *rugae*, the Colbertine Codex reads *regiae*, a word meaning doors.

Although the term *regiae* seems at times to have a somewhat broader scope, so that it designates not only doors but also the leaves or grilles attached to them. James Gaetanus, in chapter 79 on Ash Wednesday, writes:

“It should be noted that the pope’s chamberlain exits through the *regiae*, that is, the grilles, and distributes ashes while standing to those who are outside.”

Peter Amelius has the same words. He writes again in chapter 18 that the bull granting the cardinal permission to celebrate the sacred rites at the altar of Saint Peter remains suspended all day before the *regiae*; and in chapter 21 that the bishop goes to the *regiae* to distribute candles. Furthermore, in chapter 56, concerning the distribution of palms:

“He goes as far as the *regiae* of the chapel on the right side, and there throws branches and olive leaves to the people through the openings of the *regiae*, that is, the grilles.”

Finally, and decisively, the same author mentions the door of the *regiae* in chapters 76 and 78. In these passages it is necessary, as everyone can see, to interpret *regiae* as grilles [Col. 0930B].

There were grilles not only between the presbytery and the choir of singers but also between the presbytery and the altar. Thus there were *rugae* before the entrance to the altar—that is, small gates—as Anastasius says in his account of Leo III, or before the vestibule of the altar, as he says in his account of Paschal I. Consequently, according to our eighth booklet, the deacon being ordained stood before the *rugae* of the altar; and the man being promoted to the priesthood was likewise led outside the *rugae* of the altar.

The grilles separating the presbytery from the choir of singers were sometimes called the *pogium* and sometimes the *pectoralia*. Thus, in the Appendix to our First Roman Order, number 11:

“As the deacons ascend to the *pogium*, the bishops and priests are stationed in their places, and the schola, that is, the singers, stands before the altar.”

These were the seats of the individual orders during the sacred rites. Thomasius aptly explains *pogium* in his scholia on the *Responsorialia*:

“Here *pogium* means those marble grilles or panels by which the sanctuary is separated from the choir and the church. In the ancient basilicas of the City they are constructed in such a way that, on their rear side, the steps of the sanctuary or presbytery rise gradually, so that those who are in the area of the same sanctuary and lean against them up to breast height can conveniently look out from there over the entire congregation of the church. Writers of a later age called these *pectoralia*; they would more properly be called *maeniana*. This seems to have been the proper place of the Levites. Since, according to the ancient canons, they were forbidden to sit in the presbytery, they decently occupied this position, where, situated between the bishop together with the priests on the one hand and the choir of singers and the people on the other, they could readily minister to the former and preside over the latter as inspectors and monitors. For the bishop sat opposite the altar in the middle beneath the apse, with the bishops seated on his right and the priests on his left; while the choir of singers, together with the other subdeacons and the lesser clergy, stood before the sanctuary and altar in the body of the church—that is, in the choir or *maenianum*” [Col. 0930D].

Thus far the learned and devout author.

At these enclosures, therefore, or *maeniana*, which scarcely exceeded the height of half a man, sacred communion was distributed; ashes and palms were handed out; and other things of this kind were provided to the laity, since the religious practice of those times did not permit such things to be done within the sanctuary. Concerning communion, Augustine says in Sermon 392 of the new edition, number 5:

“Let those abstain from communion who know that I know their sins, lest they be thrown out from the grilles.”

Pope Leo IV, as Anastasius reports, decreed by canonical authority, in accordance with ancient custom, that while the solemn rites of Mass were being celebrated, no layperson should presume to stand, sit, or enter in the presbytery, except the sacred people who appear to be assigned to the administration of the sacred office. Would that this decree were still in force among everyone!

[Col. 0931A] Third, we must investigate what the *regulares* were that were placed above the *rugae*, and from which curtains and images hung. Evidence for this occurs in Anastasius’s accounts of Stephen IV, Hadrian I, Leo III, and Paschal I. Some wish this term to designate cast grilles, which the Greeks call κιόνια (*kionia*, “little columns”); others, wooden or bronze rods by which the curtains were drawn and redrawn. We approve the latter opinion. Anastasius proves in various passages that images hung from these *regulares*. In his account of Stephen IV:

“He made three silver *regulares* above the *rugae* through which they enter to the altar, where images are set in the frontispiece.”

And in his account of Hadrian I:

“He placed the aforesaid three images upon the same *regularis*.”

Curtains were also hung there. In his account of Leo III:

“Four small curtains of *stauracium*, which hang on the *regularis* before the images.”

Everyone knows that curtains were accustomed to be hung on doors. In order that they might easily be drawn and redrawn, they required these *regulares*, which were sometimes made of iron or bronze and sometimes of silver.

Besides these *regulares*, there were also beams for supporting the curtains; these beams were sometimes made of silver, as in Leo III’s account, and some were placed above the altar columns, as in Paschal I’s account [CXXXIX]. Gregory IV mentions curtains surrounding the sacred altar.

Before I finish this chapter, it will be useful to note the various ways in which the Romans preserved the Eucharist, as we learn from our booklets.

The older practice seems to have been that it was kept in the *secretarium*, or sacristy. From there, a small container holding the Eucharist was carried before the bishop as he approached the altar. This practice seems to have continued in Gregory XI’s time, at least in the Lateran basilica, as is suggested by the constitutions of that pontiff published here, number 18, where it is prescribed that the old furnishings of that church should be kept locked in the sacristy, where the Lord’s table is located.

Another practice was to keep the Eucharist on the altar, either the principal altar or a separate one. The latter practice is now generally followed in the City.

[Col. 0931C] The third practice, which is followed only in the basilica of Santa Croce, is to keep the Eucharist behind the high altar, against the farthest wall of the basilica, without an altar beneath it, in an open vessel, with ornaments placed around it. This work was undertaken by Cardinal Francesco Quignonius.

The object containing the Eucharist is called by various names in our booklets: *conditorium*, *cophinum*, and *armarium*. Peter Amelius treats the last two as one and the same thing. The First Roman Order uses the word *capsa*, but with a slightly different meaning: it denotes a chest used to carry the Eucharist before the bishop who is about to celebrate the sacred rites, whereas the other terms designate an object fixed in place.

The word *capsa* seems to be used in the same sense in canon 17 of the First Council of Orange:

“The *capsa* and the chalice are to be offered, and the chalice is to be consecrated by the admixture of the Eucharist.”

This somewhat obscure passage requires us to pause briefly in order to explain it. The meaning seems to me to be that, together with the *capsa* in which the sacred vessels—and perhaps also the Eucharist—were carried to the altar at the beginning of Mass, the chalice was likewise to be brought; and that this chalice, after being consecrated, should contain both consecrated species together, once a particle of the Eucharist had been customarily placed in it, and should thus have been consecrated, as it were, by one and the same consecration. The canon therefore has two parts. The first is that the chalice should be carried to the altar together with the *capsa*. The second is that both species of the Eucharist should be joined together in the chalice. The heading of the later chapter corresponds only to the latter point: “That the sacramental offering should be consecrated into one.”

Gregory, Bishop of Tours, calls such a *capsa* by another name, *turris*, in Book I *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 86. There he tells how an impure deacon, when the time had come to offer the sacrifice, took a *turris* containing the ministry of the Lord’s body and began carrying it toward the doorway through which access from the *secretarium* to the basilica was provided. When he entered the church in order to place it upon the altar, the *capsa* slipped from his hand and fell into the pavement [Col. 0932A]. There is no doubt that the sacred vessels are designated by the expression “the ministry of the Lord”; but Saint Odo, abbot of Cluny, judged that the Eucharist was also contained in it. In his *Collation*, Book II, chapter 32, he substitutes *capsa* for Gregory’s *turris*: “When he was carrying the *capsa* with the body of the Lord,” and so forth.

This interpretation is supported by a poem of Venantius Fortunatus concerning the *turris* of Felix, Bishop of Bourges. No one can deny that this tower was of the same kind as Gregory’s. Felix’s tower served to contain the Eucharist, as the following distich from Book III, poem 13, proves:

“How aptly they will call the things joined together, so that the great golden gifts may bear the pearl of the sacred Body of the Lamb!”

Therefore Saint Odo was not without foundation when, explaining the story of the deacon related by Gregory, he understood by the name *turris* a *capsa* containing the body of the Lord. Thus the same rite was in use among our fellow Gauls and among the Romans: at the beginning of Mass, the sacred Eucharist was carried in a *capsa*. The canon of the Council of Orange mentioned above evidently refers to this rite. Accordingly, the *turris* was a portable *capsa*, not a fixed repository for the Eucharist.

I return to the Romans, among whom the objects they call tabernacles are now almost the only things in use. The Eucharist is nowhere suspended—not even, so far as I know, throughout Italy. Yet in the church of Bobbio we saw a bronze dove formerly intended for preserving the Eucharist. This practice may perhaps have been introduced into the monastery of Bobbio from Gaul under the influence of Columbanus. But enough of this; let us return to our own rites.

[CXLI] XXI. Are ancient rites always to be preferred to new ones? Are all rites to be reduced to a single form? Recent masters of ceremonies criticized. What should be thought of the Illyrian Mass?

There are three things that can be considered in sacred rites: antiquity, uniformity, and stability. The antiquity of sacred rites is nearly the same as that of religion itself, but their diversity is equally ancient in different churches. “Many things vary according to the diversity of places and peoples,” says Firmilianus in his letter to Cyprian, “yet on that account there has been no departure from the peace and unity of the Catholic Church.” This diversity existed from the beginning even among the Romans, not only concerning the days on which Easter was celebrated but also concerning many other mysteries of divine worship. Firmilianus asserts that not everything observed at Jerusalem was observed there in the same way. On this subject one should read Socrates, Book V, chapter 22, where he says that no religious sect observes the same ceremonies, even though it embraces the same opinion concerning God.

This diversity of rites arises partly from the different customs of peoples, who do not take pleasure in the same ways of acting and cannot become accustomed to the same institutions; and partly from the different founders of the churches, who established a matter indifferent by its nature and open to different arrangements in different ways, according to the diversity of times and places. Consequently, those who try to reduce everything to one and the same form seem to me to act as though they were attempting to reduce all peoples to the same customs and precisely the same institutions [Col. 0932D]. They also fail to make sufficient allowance for the first founders of the churches, whose established or permitted practices they so easily overturn. Indeed, such attempts have never been made without endangering ecclesiastical peace, as could be demonstrated by many examples if this were not already evident to everyone.

That diversity of rites must therefore be tolerated, above all for the sake of peace, and also for the sake of the Church, which is adorned by this variety. For I do not know how it is that what is ornamented with varied worship tastes sweeter. This is the first thing that must be guarded against in those who hold the office of masters of ceremonies [CXLII]: some of them never cease until they have compelled everyone, even unwillingly, to adopt their rites.

The second error belongs to those who always insist that either ancient rites should be preferred to new ones or new rites to ancient ones. Neither position is pleasing without discrimination. Where ancient rites prevail, they should be retained steadfastly; where new rites have prevailed over ancient ones, it is proper to praise the ancient without rejecting the new. For it scarcely ever happens that what has once been accepted and established by custom can be changed without disturbance. Indeed, just as the diversity of rites was introduced by the diversity of places, so the diversity of times has sometimes persuaded people to change them in the same places.

Constancy in such matters is therefore praiseworthy, provided that the other conditions are present: the peace and harmony of the Church, and Christian charity, to which all rites must yield and lend their support. If antiquity can be preserved without harm to peace and charity, no genuinely wise person will deny that it should be preferred to novelty.

It is astonishing how much authority those who have written new books of sacred rites in recent times have attributed to themselves in overturning venerable antiquity. They were entirely ignorant not only of the reasons for ancient institutions but even of the institutions themselves. Because they imagined that whatever they saw being done in their own time had always been practiced throughout all preceding centuries, they devised plausible reasons for established novelty—reasons that often directly contradict the judgment of the ancients. To make this clear to everyone, I should like to bring together here several examples in proof.

1. As we have seen, it was formerly the custom in the Roman Church for the sacred Eucharist to be carried before the bishop as he proceeded to the altar and to remain there until communion, at which time a particle of the Eucharist consecrated earlier was lowered into the chalice. Then, from the offering of the new sacrifice, one particle was reserved and the same particle remained on the altar until the end of Mass. Amalarius testifies to this in Book III, chapter 35, and the First Roman Order says the same here, on page 14:

“They observe this practice, so that while the solemn rites of Mass are being celebrated, the altar may not be without a sacrifice.”

Thus throughout the entire Mass the Eucharist was never absent from the altar, whether the Eucharist was kept on the altar itself as a viaticum or was kept in the *secretarium* [Col. 0933C].

By the time of Pope Leo X, a contrary rite had already been introduced. Paris de Crassis, who was master of ceremonies, sought the reason why the sacrament of Christ’s body, which is ordinarily preserved in churches, should first be removed from its place before solemn celebration could take place there. He says:

“Our ancestors prescribed this, not because they thought one ought to shrink from the sight of the saving Host, but because during the sacrifice not everyone could perform all the ceremonies properly and correctly. For in the presence of the sacrament itself, neither the pope nor the celebrating bishops could suitably sit there, retain the mitre on their heads, or receive incense, except after the sacrament itself had been incensed—especially since they themselves would have to incense it so many times, and not the deacon of the Gospel, whose proper ministry this is. Add,” he says, “that whenever and as often as the celebrating prelate must incense, he must each time adore the sacrament on his knees before he incenses the altar cross, the offerings, and the altar itself. Finally, it is extremely discordant that in the same chapel or oratory in which the sacrament being adored is already present, another sacrament should there newly be made, lest uncertainty arise as to which of the two sacraments ought to be adored” [Col. 0933D].

In those earlier times, however, it was sufficient to have adored the Holy One once, whether the Eucharist was carried before the altar, as in the First Roman Order, or was preserved on the altar itself, as in the Second. Those holy Fathers were persuaded that no injury at all was done to the Eucharist by whatever sacred ceremonies were performed, provided that they were carried out religiously; indeed, they thought that by such actions God was honored all the more. Nor did they have any uncertainty about which consecrated species ought to be adored, since their attention was directed solely to the sacrifice then being offered. Moreover, adoration of one species rather than the other ought to cause no scruple, since it is directed toward the same object.

2. Another example can be drawn from the same Paris, concerning the deacon singing the Gospel. Since the use of ambos for singing the Gospel and Epistle has ceased, the question is which way the deacon should turn: should he stand beside the altar, or should he face the altar, as in the palace chapel and similar places where the altar does not face toward the rising sun?

Paris replies that, as a general rule, the Gospel should be recited by a deacon standing toward the north, from which, according to the Prophet, all evil is spread. The situation is different in the palace chapel. There, because of the position of the place, the Gospel corner does not face north but south, the direction in which the bishop who is present at the sacrifice always sits. Therefore, when the deacon sings the Gospel there, he does not turn his back and shoulders toward the bishop remaining on his throne; instead, he sings it facing directly toward the Gospel corner, with his left shoulder turned toward the bishop. In the bishop’s absence, however, so that the deacon may satisfy universal custom and the rite, he should stand beside the altar but turned toward the bishop’s throne, which is situated to the south. It is less objectionable, after all, for him to stand in this way than to turn his back toward the bishop’s throne and have the altar, which is the holy of holies, beneath and to his left [Col. 0934B]. In churches whose high altar does not face east, the deacon should sing the Gospel not standing beside the altar but facing the altar itself, that is, directly toward it.

How much more simply the ancient booklets of the Roman Order prescribe that, when the deacon is to sing the Gospel in the ambo, he should stand facing north but turn his face toward the southern side, where the men stood, not toward the north, where the women stood. Paris notes only this point: the right corner of the altar in the expression “Gospel corner” must be understood with reference to the altar itself, as the more honored body, not with reference to the celebrant. For the right side of the cross and of the crucified figure standing upon the altar is likewise turned toward the aforesaid Gospel corner. The rubrics of the Missal, however, especially those for Good Friday, must be interpreted differently, so that “right corner” and “left corner” are understood with reference to the priest [Col. 0934C].

3. It would be endless to go through every feature that differs from the rites of today. Nevertheless, it will be useful to gather several matters here for the benefit of the reader’s studies. According to our First Booklet, the priest used to intone the angelic hymn while turned toward the people; by contrast, he sang the final greeting preceding the Collect after communion while turned toward the altar. Moreover, he did not begin the Canon until the singing of the *trisagion* had been completed, so that, while the priest recited the Canon in a subdued voice, clergy and people might remain silent, as though struck with awe in contemplation of so great a mystery. Furthermore, the antiphon called the Communion was sung, together with its Psalm, not after communion itself, as is now done in many churches, but during the communion. This rite was observed in the African Church when the people came forward to communion, as Augustine provides abundant testimony in Book II of his *Retractations*, chapter 11 [CXLV]. Finally, the priest did not recite what was being sung by the choir or read by the ministers; he was wholly occupied either with meditating on the matters being proclaimed or with performing other rites. The prayers found in the Illyrian Mass for this interval are certainly not part of the ancient Roman institution, as we shall see later.

We do not report these matters with the intention of restoring such ancient rites by private authority or, God forbid, of encouraging contempt for more recent practices. Rather, we wish to invite those entrusted with such offices to consult antiquity, which is more venerable the nearer it is to the source; and we wish to warn them not to prefer such common and worn-out little explanations, as though they believed that our ancestors, when establishing contrary rites, had been entirely devoid of reason. If sacred rites are ever to be reformed, the reasons of the ancients should indeed be taken into account, and every effort should be made to remain as close to them as possible.

This was the aim proposed by the Church of Cambrai and the Church of Arras when they wished to restore the order of sacred rites to a better form, as is read in the most ancient Order of both churches, recently published from the papers left by Pierre Pithou in the appendix to the *Code of the Canons of the Roman Church* [Col. 0935A]. The reformers of that Order preface it by saying that they wished to regulate those things that seemed to have deviated from the state of correctness or to differ from the Roman Order. They did so, however, in such a way that no new Order would be instituted, lest their enemies accuse them of violating in any way the most sacred Roman Order that they desired to imitate.

In the same Order, certain points are emphatically reaffirmed from the Roman Order itself; it will not be tedious to mention them here. One is that the morning office, which we call Lauds, is to be sung slowly, though the Psalms themselves are to be sung more loudly than the nocturnal Psalms. This is how it is done in the Roman Church. A little farther on:

“We wish Mass to be celebrated in the morning on Sundays, because the Lord rose very early. This is also the practice at the holy see of the Roman Church.”

But in the titular churches located in the city or outside it, Mass should not be sung before it has been sung in the public church in the city; nor should their bells be rung, so that the whole people may proceed to the public church, except perhaps on account of the sick or for travelers [CXLVI]. Nor should the prescription concerning the nocturnal vigils be omitted:

“With all due decorum, let the lessons be read slowly and the responsories sung. The ninth lesson, however, should be from the Gospel, taken from the homilies of the Fathers. The homily on the Gospel itself should be read in its entirety by the deacon, priest, or bishop, unless the intervening dawn should have postponed it.”

Thus in the Roman Church, when dawn appeared, it was customary for the nocturnal office of the breviary to be shortened, as we saw above. These provisions come from that ancient Order of Cambrai, which was written before the twelfth century [Col. 0935B].

Someone may ask why in former times the bishop intoned the angelic hymn, or *Gloria in excelsis*, turned toward the people, whereas he pronounced the final greeting after communion—and not the other greetings—turned toward the altar. It is not our purpose to answer these questions; it is enough for us to have explained the ancient Roman rites. I approve the rule of John the Deacon in his letter to Senarius:

“I firmly hold this in mind: the Church would not preserve anything handed down from its ancestors unless a certain reason for it had required it; nor can we say that such things appear empty and frivolous merely because we have not learned their reason.”

If, however, conjecture may be permitted, the bishop turned toward the people when intoning the angelic hymn in order to invite them to praise God. He pronounced that final greeting facing the altar because he was then directing his words to the faithful, who had been refreshed by communion, or by the body and blood of the Lord Christ; and consequently, in that greeting, he was not speaking as one making a prayer or a wish, but as one expressing congratulations and declaring that the Lord was present [Col. 0936A].

Finally, it should be observed that the Latin Mass once published at Strasbourg by Matthias Flacius Illyricus is not a Roman Mass interpolated with various prayers for the priest to recite while the choir was occupied with singing. Those prayers do not agree with the original institution of the Roman Church; indeed, some of them are directly opposed to it. An example is the instruction concerning the Canon:

“Then, with the greatest reverence, let him begin *Te igitur*; and let the ministers standing on their steps sing the Psalms themselves until *Te igitur* is finished.”

By contrast, our more ancient booklets prescribe that, while the bishop recites the Canon, the choir should maintain the strictest silence; the ministers should remain bowed and silent throughout the entire Canon; and the subdeacons should do so until the words “To us also, sinners” [CXLVII]. Add that this Mass prescribes at the beginning the verse *Introibo* with Psalm *Judica*, which was not used among the ancients; that the same Mass mentions the *Sequentia*, which others call the *Prosa*, an institution attributed to Notker Balbulus, who died in the year 912; and finally that the litanies appended to the Mass invoke Saint Adalbert, who is known to have suffered martyrdom at the end of the tenth century.

The next subject ought to be the various additions made to the Gregorian Sacramentary by Grimold the abbot and others. Grimold seems to have been abbot of the monastery of Saint Gall among the Swiss. He is also called Grimaldus and the chaplain of Louis Augustus, surnamed the Pious. He added five episcopal blessings to the Gregorian Sacramentary, which, as we observed above, were not of Roman institution. But these discussions are carrying us too far; let us finally come to the booklets of the Roman Order.

## [ROMAN ORDER I]

[Col. 0935]

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FIRST ROMAN ORDER

1. We showed above that there were various booklets of the Roman Order, three of which, pertaining to the pontifical Mass, we shall now present. The first of these, which appears to be the oldest, is frequently cited by Amalarius and is found in the very ancient Codices of Monte Cassino, Saint Gall, Einsiedeln, and Colbert. It was first published at Cologne by Georg Cassander in 1561 and reprinted there seven years later by Melchior Hittorp. In those editions more than half of this booklet is missing. We have supplied the missing portion from the Codex of the distinguished Abbey of Saint Gall, beginning at number 21.

2. The antiquity of this same booklet is proved especially by the bringing of the Eucharist to the altar before the pontiff at the beginning of the Mass; by the term *fermentum* (“leaven”), used for the Eucharist as in the letter of Innocent I to Decentius, no. 22; and then by the rubrics (as they are called) that are found in the Sacramentary of Gregory the Great for Holy Week, expressed here in exactly the same words, as will be clear to anyone who compares them. Hence it is extremely probable that Gregory transferred the aforesaid rubrics from this booklet into his Sacramentary. Certainly the authority of Amalarius proves that this first Order, whose words he frequently quotes and explains, is earlier than the ninth century; and, in my judgment, the entire rite of the pontifical Mass prescribed in this Order bears the mark of Gregory’s age. Some new material was nevertheless inserted in the course of time, such as what is reported in no. 24 concerning the rite instituted by Pope Adrian, namely, that prayer should be made for King Charles—that is, Charlemagne—and in no. 28, that the Prayer for the King of the Franks should be said. From this, someone might perhaps remain uncertain whether this supplement, which we obtained from the Codex of Saint Gall, was later attached to the following booklet. It is preferable, however, to admit that these few items just mentioned were inserted—as commonly happens—in the most ancient booklet.

I should not conceal, nevertheless, that Onuphrius considers the Order edited here in second place to be older, because in the procession to the altar the pontiff is there said to give the peace to two priests, whereas in our first and third Orders it is given to one of the weekly bishops, namely, the bishop of the Lateran Church, whom a learned man believes to have succeeded the priests eight hundred years ago. In fact, both arrangements can have existed at the same time: the peace might be given to one of those bishops when Mass was celebrated in the Lateran church, whose weekly ministers they were; otherwise, to two priests when it was celebrated in another church. Moreover, at what time those weekly bishops were instituted at the Lateran is unclear, although it is evident from the Acts of Stephen IV that they had been instituted before that pontiff, as we stated in the preliminary commentary.

3. The Colbertine exemplar, no. 416, which contains the following Order, is approaching eight hundred years in age [Col. 0937] and bears this title: *Order of the Ecclesiastical Ministry of the Roman Church, or How Mass Is Celebrated*; in the Codex of Saint Gall it is entitled *Ecclesiastical Order of the Roman Church*, etc. We have adopted the latter title.

4. After this booklet, which ends at no. 21, the Colbertine Codex contains an appendix *On the Offices at Night from the Lord’s Supper to Easter*. The same appendix is found in the Vatican Codex, no. 487, and therefore it appears that this appendix should be joined to the complete booklet of this first Roman Order. Amalarius cites it under the name of the Roman booklet, in book I, chapter 20. The booklet mentioned also adds *Another Candle*, where it says: “And then two candles are lit, held by two notaries,” and so forth. These same words are read in the said appendix, no. 10, and demonstrate its antiquity.

[Col. 0937]

# FIRST ROMAN ORDER (C)

Here begins the Ecclesiastical Order of the Roman Church, describing how pontifical Mass is to be celebrated.

[Col. 0937A]

1. First of all, it must be observed that there are seven regions of the ecclesiastical Order of the city of Rome. Each region has its own regional deacons, and the acolytes of each region are assigned, through the agency of the regional subdeacon, to the deacon of their region for the purposes of his office. If one of these deacons should die, then, until another is substituted in his place, the acolytes of that region obey the archdeacon, because all acolytes, whatever their religious affiliation, belong to his ministry for the sake of ecclesiastical office.

The same is to be understood of the Orders that follow, with each archdeacon’s prerogative in the ministry of his own rank preserved over those subject to him. Thus, for example, if someone suffers violence, whether from an ecclesiastical person or from any military person, and the matter cannot be brought to a conclusion by the first official of his own rank, the archdeacon—that is, the pontiff’s vicar—shall have jurisdiction, so that he may resolve the complaints of his subjects without the pontiff’s knowledge; other matters, however, are to be settled through the minor Orders.

For one must first know, after learning the number of ecclesiastical regions, the number of days in the week and the order in which they serve in rotation: on the first day, the third region, that is, Easter; on the second day, the fourth region; on the third day, the fifth region; on the fourth day, the sixth region; on the fifth day, the seventh region; on the sixth day, the first region; on Saturday, the second region.

Each is bound to perform its proper duties, both in procession and in church, or wherever ancient ordinance, by reason of its rank, has compelled it to go or minister [Col. 0937B]. No one may fail in the pontiff’s service without incurring the disciplinary judgment of excommunication or punishment. Their ministries are initially divided each day in a simple twofold manner: into the procession of the Apostolic to the station, and from the departure from the sacristy until the completion of the Masses.

2. On solemn days, such as Easter, all the acolytes of the third region and the Defenders of all the regions assemble at dawn in the Lateran patriarchate and precede the pontiff on foot to the station. Lay horse-guides ride on his right and left [Col. 0938A], so that he may not stumble anywhere. Those who precede him on horseback are the deacons, the *primicerius*, two regional notaries, the regional Defenders, and the regional subdeacons. They proceed in separate groups, leaving space between themselves and the Apostolic.

Those who ride behind the pontiff are the *vicedominus*, the *vestararius* [sic], the *nomenculator*, and the *saccellarius*. One of the station acolytes precedes the pontiff’s horse on foot, carrying the holy chrism, wrapped in a small cloth together with its flask. The acolytes do not proceed without their bags, linen cloths, and chrism; the station acolyte arranges these.

If anyone wishes to approach the pontiff, then, if he is on horseback, as soon as he sees him he must dismount and wait at the side of the road until he can be heard by him [Col. 0938B]. After requesting his blessing, his case is examined by the *nomenculator* or *saccellarius*. They report it to the pontiff and settle it. [Note: Thus cases were sometimes settled in the procession itself. Hence some learned men suppose that the term *processus* in our French language derived from a lawsuit.] The same procedure is observed if anyone encounters him without having made a petition. Anyone who is on foot merely stands in his place so that he may be heard or blessed by him.

[Note: The *nomenculator*’s office was to invite guests and record their names, as we shall see below, no. 18. The *saccellarius* was the same as the treasurer, from *saccus* or *saccellus*, “bag.”]

3. On the day of the Lord’s Resurrection, as the pontiff proceeds to Saint Mary, the regional notary stands at a place called [Note: [Col. 0938C] This place is on the Esquiline Hill, not far from the Basilica of Saint Mary Major, where there is the church of Saint Matthew, called “at the Merulanas.”] Merolanas. After greeting the pontiff, he says: “In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, last night at the holy Mother of God Mary, so many male infants and so many female infants were baptized.” The pontiff replies: “Thanks be to God.” The notary receives one solidus from the *saccellarius*, while the pontiff proceeds to the station.

[Col. 0938C] On Monday, toward [Note: [Col. 0938C] Thus the Codex of Saint Gall; Colbertine: “toward the returned place also”; printed editions: “toward the Mass likewise.” The passage is obscure and perhaps corrupt.] the return, simply. On Tuesday, at the turning of the portico of Saint Paul, only those who attend on foot do likewise.

On the day of holy Easter itself, all the acolytes of the third region together with the Defenders of all the regions assemble at first light in the Lateran patriarchate, so that, when the pontiff sets out, they may precede his horse. The acolytes who are assigned there take care to carry the chrism before the pontiff, and the Gospels, linen cloths, and bags, as well as the water vessel, behind him, as we have said above. The subdeacon who is to read will have the Apostle under his care; the archdeacon will have the Gospel.

They take from the church of the Savior, through the hands of the first mansionary, the water vessel, the daily paten, the chalice, cups, and [Col. 0939A] small vessels [Note: [Col. 0939D] Here *pugillaris* means a reed or tube by which the Lord’s blood was drawn from the sacred chalice. The *scyphi* were the acolytes’ ministerial chalices, discussed below. The *colatorium* was a small vessel perforated with holes at the bottom, through which wine purified from the *amulae* or flasks was poured into the chalice. Onuphrius suspects that the *gemelliones* were ewers, used to pour water over the hands of the pontiff and perhaps his ministers; the water was received in the basin below, here called the *aquamanus*, that is, the *aquamanile*. Anastasius, in his account of Gregory IV, joins together *amae*, *scyphi*, and *gemelliones*, making it clear that the latter must be distinguished from *amae* or *amulae*.]—some silver and others gold—silver *gemelliones*, a silver and a gold strainer, another larger silver vessel, silver *amae*, the cantatorium, and the other gold and silver vessels, as well as gold and silver candleholders. The bearers carry them.

On feast days they obtain the larger chalice and paten and the larger Gospels from the papal vestuary under the seal of the *vestararius* [sic], checking them by the number of their gems so that they are not lost. A lay chamberlain who precedes carries the pontiff’s chair, so that it may be ready when he comes into the sacristy.

4. On feast days, early in the morning, all the apostolic clergy first precede the Apostolic to the announced station, to the church where the station had previously been announced [Col. 0939B], except those who accompany him in attendance, as we have said above. They wait for the pontiff in the church together with the supplementary ministers, the bearers, and the others who carry crosses, seated in the presbytery: the bishops on the left of those entering, and the priests on the right. Thus, when the pontiff sits and looks toward them, he sees the bishops on his right and the priests on his left.

When the pontiff has come near the church, the acolytes and Defenders from the region whose day it is for service go out to await him at the appointed place, before he reaches the place where he will dismount. Likewise, the priest of the title or of the church where the station is located, together with the senior officials of the Roman Church or the Father of the *diaconia*—if that church is a *diaconia*—comes out to attend him, accompanied by the priest and mansionary subject to him, carrying the censer, bowing their heads when he arrives.

First the acolytes with the Defenders, then the priests with their attendants, after requesting a blessing and dividing into groups on either side according to their offices, precede the pontiff to the church. The advocates of the church stand with the senior officials, but do not precede them. They merely follow the pontiff’s chair with the acolyte who carries the water vessel. The latter must always follow the pontiff until he ascends to the altar, ready beneath the shoulder in the presbytery whenever the regional subdeacon calls him to give the water.

5. When the pontiff has entered the church, he does not immediately ascend to the altar. Instead, he first enters the sacristy [Col. 0939D], supported by the deacons who receive him as he dismounts from the chair. When he has entered, he sits in his chair. The deacons greet the pontiff, leave the sacristy, and change their vestments before its doors [Col. 0940A]. The one who is to read prepares the Gospel, the seal having been opened at the archdeacon’s command, upon the *planeta* of an acolyte. If the larger Gospels require it, two acolytes hold their *planetae* and the Gospel is prepared upon them.

When this has been done, the acolyte carries the Gospel into the presbytery, as far as before the altar, preceded by the following subdeacon, who receives it from above the acolyte’s *planeta* and honorably places it upon the altar with his own hands. When the deacons have left the sacristy, the following remain with the pontiff: the *primicerius*, the *secundicerius*, the *primicerius* of the Defenders, the regional notaries, and the following subdeacon, who holds the pontiff’s pallium on his arm over his *planeta*, on his left arm with its pins.

6. The pontiff changes his vestments through the hands of the regional subdeacons [Col. 0940B] in the following order. A tonsured chamberlain brings them folded, having received them from the doorkeeper beside the head of the bench. The regional subdeacons, according to their order, take the vestments to dress the pontiff: one the linen garment, another the girdle, another the [Note: [Col. 0940D] The printed editions have *anabolagium*, a reading defended by the learned Cangius in his *Glossary*. Nevertheless, not only the extremely ancient Codex of Saint Gall at this point, but also another equally ancient manuscript, in which the *Ordo Missae episcopalis* is given below, provided no reason for changing it; there we read *anagolai* and *anagolagi*. Observe that in these passages *anabolagium*, or *anagolagium*, that is, the *amictus*, is placed over the alb and girdle, as is still customary among Maronite priests.] *anagolaium*, that is, the *amictus*; another the linen dalmatic; another the larger dalmatic; and another the *planeta*. Thus they dress the pontiff in order. The *primicerius* and *secundicerius* arrange his vestments so that they sit properly.

Finally, whichever deacon or subdeacon the lord pontiff chooses, and to whom he gives the command, takes the pallium from the hand of the following subdeacon, places it upon the pontiff, and fastens it with pins to the *planeta* behind and in front and at the left shoulder. He then greets the lord pontiff and says: “Command, lord, a blessing.” He replies: “May the Lord save us.” The other replies: “Amen.”

7. Then the regional subdeacon, holding the pontiff’s small cloth over his left arm, folded across the *planeta*, goes out to the royal [Alternative: door] of the sacristy and says: “Schola.” [Alternative: “He calls the school.”] The response is: “I am here.” He asks: “Who will sing?” The response is: “This one and this one.”

The subdeacon returns to the pontiff, presents him with the small cloth, bows to his knees, and says: “Servant of my lord, such-and-such a regional subdeacon will read the Apostle, and such-and-such a person from the school will sing.” After this, no one may replace another in the place of reader or cantor. If this is done, the archiparaphonista is excommunicated by the pontiff [Note: [Col. 0940D] That is, as it may be interpreted, he is suspended from office.]—that is, the fourth member of the school, who always reports to the pontiff concerning the singers.
