When this has been reported [Col. 0940D], the subdeacon standing before the pontiff immediately follows, until the pontiff gives him a sign that they should sing. When he has received the sign, he immediately goes out before the doors of the sacristy and says: “Light them.” When they have lit them, the following subdeacon, carrying the golden censer, immediately places incense before the doors, so that it may proceed before the pontiff. The fourth member of the school reaches the presbytery and, with bowed head, says to the first, second, or third member of the school: “Lord, command.”

8. Then they rise and proceed in order before the altar. Only two ranks are formed: the *paraphonistae* outside, on either side, and the boys in order within, on both sides. Immediately the first member of the school begins the antiphon for the Introit [Col. 0941A]. When the deacons hear their voice, they immediately enter the sacristy to the pontiff.

The pontiff then rises, gives his right hand to the archdeacon and his left to the second deacon, or to whichever deacon is next in rank. They kiss his hands and proceed with him, supporting him. The following subdeacon goes before him with the censer, placing incense upon it. Seven acolytes of the region whose day it is, carrying [Note: [Col. 0941C] Namely, corresponding to the number of the seven ecclesiastical regions.] seven lit candleholders, precede the pontiff until they reach the altar.

Before they arrive at the altar, the deacons remove their *planetae* in the presbytery. The regional subdeacon receives them and hands them to the acolytes of the region to which those deacons belong. Then two acolytes, holding open cases containing the Holy Things [Note: [Col. 0941C] The Colbertine has *Sancta*, by which we understand the Eucharist, as is clear from nos. 17, 18, 30, and 34. See below, no. 41, in the booklet of Benedict, canon of Saint Peter, and chapter 6 of the preliminary commentary. The *conditorium* was therefore the place or vessel in which the Eucharist was then customarily stored.], together with the following subdeacon, who holds his hand at the mouth of the case, show the Holy Things to the pontiff or to the deacon who has preceded him.

The pontiff or deacon, bowing his head [Note: [Col. 0941D] Thus the Colbertine. Others have “to the pontiff or deacon,” but incorrectly.], greets the Holy Things and examines them, so that, if there is an excess [Note: [Col. 0941D] Thus the Colbertine. The printed editions have “above,” but with the same sense.], he may order it to be placed in the *conditorium* [Col. 0941C].

As he approaches, before reaching the school, the candleholders are divided: four to the right and three to the left. The pontiff passes to the head of the school, bows his head toward the altar, rises and prays, makes the sign of the cross on his forehead, and gives the peace to one of the weekly bishops [Note: [Col. 0941D] Namely, one of the seven weekly bishops of the Lateran patriarchate, mentioned above in the preliminary commentary.] and to the archpriest, and to all the deacons.

Looking toward the first member of the school, he signals to him to say the *Gloria*. The first member of the school bows to the pontiff and begins it. The fourth member of the school precedes the pontiff in order to place the *oratorium* before the altar [Note: [Col. 0941D] Later writers call it the *faldistorium*. The Colbertine reads incorrectly, “the oratory upon the altar.”]. The pontiff approaches and prays over it until the repetition [Note: [Col. 0941D] That is, of the antiphon for the Introit. Compare no. 21.] of the verse.

The deacons rise when “As it was in the beginning” is said, so that they may salute the sides of the altar, first two and then two in turn, returning to the pontiff. The pontiff rises, kisses the Gospels and the altar, approaches his chair, and stands facing east.

9. When the school has finished the antiphon, it begins the *Kyrie eleison*. The first member of the school watches the pontiff, so that he may signal him if he wishes to change [Note: [Col. 0941D] This relates to what Paris de Crassis says: in papal Masses the *Kyrie* is said as long as the cardinals’ reverence toward the pope continues. The Colbertine reads, “he should bow to the pontiff.”] the number of invocations, and bows to the pontiff.

When they have finished, the pontiff turns toward the people [Note: [Col. 0942C] Now with his face turned toward the east, or altar, as Amalarius proves in *On the Offices*, book III, chapter 8], begins “Glory to God in the highest” [Col. 0942B], and immediately turns again toward the east until it is finished. After this he turns again toward the people and says, “Peace to you” [Note: [Col. 0942C] The same Amalarius, near the end of the second preface to his *Official Book*, lists among the things he received from the Roman See: “The first greeting to the people, he says, is pronounced ‘Peace to you,’ not ‘Peace be with you.’ See also his book III, chapter 9.]. He then turns again toward the east, says “Let us pray,” and the Prayer follows. After it has been completed [Note: [Col. 0942C] The same author, at the beginning of book III, chapter 5, says that the custom had arisen of not sitting in church before this Prayer was finished. On this subject, see the third booklet that follows here.], he sits; the bishops or priests likewise sit.

10. Then the regional subdeacons ascend to the altar and station themselves on its right or left. The pontiff signals to the bishops and priests to sit. The subdeacon who is to read, as soon as he sees the bishops and priests seated behind the pontiff, ascends the ambo and reads.

After he has read, the cantor ascends with the cantatorium and says the [Note: [Col. 0942D] What the cantatorium is may be learned from Amalarius’s preface to the *Antiphonary*. “The volume,” he says, “that we call the *Antiphonary* has three names among the Romans. What we call the *Gradual*, they call the *Cantatorium*.] Responsory [Note: [Col. 0942D] Amalarius himself, in book III, chapter 11, says: “The reading that is read after the sitting is followed by a chant called the Responsory.” The same Italians mentioned above transmitted the Responsories, which are called responsorial chants because, when one has ended, another responds to it. Hence the responsorial psalm in Gregory of Tours, book VIII, chapter 3: after one verse has been sung by the cantor, the same verse is repeated by the choir or people, and so successively with the others. Later writers called it the *Gradual* or *Graduale* because it was sung on the steps or in the ambo, as Amalarius’s testimony records.]. If it is the proper time for the *Alleluia*, that is sung; otherwise, the Tract; if neither, only the Responsory.

11. Then the deacon kisses the pontiff’s feet silently, and the pontiff says to him: “May the Lord be in your heart and on your lips.” He then comes before the altar, kisses the Gospels, and lifts the Codex into his hands. Two regional subdeacons proceed before him, lifting the censer from the hand of the following subdeacon and placing incense upon it. Two acolytes carrying two candleholders go before them [Col. 0943A].

When they reach the [Note: [Col. 0943D] The Romans have had no further use for the ambones since the time of Paris de Crassis.] ambo, the acolytes divide before it, while the subdeacons and the deacon carrying the Gospel pass between them. The one without the censer turns toward the deacon and extends his left arm, upon which the deacon places the Gospel, so that the subdeacon may open it to the place where the reading mark has been placed.

The deacon inserts his finger at the place of the reading, ascends to read [Note: [Col. 0943D] When reading the Gospel, the deacon turns toward the south according to the Roman Order, as is clear from chapter 9 of the *Micrologus*, not toward the north, where the women stand.], and the two subdeacons return to stand before the step by which one descends from the ambo.

When the Gospel has been completed, the pontiff says [Note: [Col. 0943D] This is found in the Second Roman Order.]: “Peace to you.” Then he says: “The Lord be with you.” The response is: “And with your spirit.” He says: “Let us pray.”

As the deacon descends, the subdeacon who had first opened the book receives the Gospel and hands it to the following subdeacon, who stands in line [Col. 0943B]. Holding it before his breast over his *planeta*, he presents it to be kissed by all standing according to the order of their ranks.

After this, an acolyte is prepared on the step near the ambo with a case [Note: [Col. 0943D] There is no mention here of the Creed after the Gospel, though it does occur in the following Order. See chapter 6 of the preliminary commentary. Amalarius, in another preface to his books *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, testifies that after the Gospel they do not bring incense onto the altar. The *Micrologus*, chapter 20, agrees.], into which the same subdeacon places the Gospel so that it may be sealed. The acolyte of the same region as the subdeacon takes the Gospel back to the Lateran [sic].

12. Then, as the deacon proceeds to the altar, an acolyte stands with the chalice and corporal upon it. He lifts the chalice on his left arm, presents the corporal to the deacon, takes it from above the chalice, and places it on the altar to the right, with one end extended toward the second deacon so that they may spread it out.

Then the *primicerius*, the *secundicerius*, and the *primicerius* of the Defenders ascend to the seat, together with all the regional officers and notaries. The subdeacon, carrying the empty chalice, follows the archdeacon.

13. The pontiff descends to the *senatorium*, with the first notary holding his right hand and the *primicerius* of the Defenders holding his left, and receives the offerings of the princes in the order of the principal arches [Note: [Col. 0943D] Thus the Colbertine. Some manuscripts have *arcuum*, “of the arches”; others omit the word. The reading of the Colbertine Codex should apparently be retained, indicating the principal or chief order.].

The archdeacon follows him, receives the flasks, and pours them into the larger chalice, which is held by the regional subdeacon. An acolyte follows him with a cup over his *planeta*, into which the filled chalice is poured. The regional subdeacon receives the offerings from the pontiff and hands them to the following subdeacon; the following subdeacon places them in a linen cloth held by two acolytes.

The weekly bishop receives the remaining offerings after the pontiff, so that he may place them with his own hand in the linen cloth that follows him. After him, the deacon who follows the archdeacon receives the [flasks] and pours them with his own hand into the cup.

Before the pontiff passes into the women’s section, he descends before the confession and receives the offerings of the *primicerius*, *secundicerius*, and *primicerius* of the Defenders [Col. 0944A]. On feast days they offer after the deacons at the altar. Likewise, when the pontiff ascends into the women’s section, he completes everything in the order described above. The priests likewise, if necessary, perform these actions after him or in the presbytery.

14. After this, the pontiff returns to his chair, with the *primicerius* and *secundicerius* holding his hands, and washes his hands. The archdeacon, standing before the altar, having completed the receiving of the offerings, washes his hands. Then he looks into the pontiff’s face and signals to him; the pontiff returns the greeting and approaches the altar.

The regional subdeacons lift the offerings from the hand of the following subdeacon onto their arms [Col. 0944B] and hand them to the archdeacon, who arranges the altar. The subdeacons hand them over from either side.

When the altar has been adorned, the archdeacon takes the pontiff’s flask from the offering subdeacon and pours it through the strainer into the chalice; then he pours in the deacons’ [Alternative: “the deacon’s”] offerings and, on a feast day, those of the *primicerius*, *secundicerius*, and *primicerius* of the Defenders.

Then the following subdeacon descends to the school, receives the water [Note: [Col. 0944D] That is, water. See below, the Roman Order for episcopal Mass. John, bishop of Avranches, writing to our Menard, p. 275, shows that the same rite was observed in Gaul: “At feasts, the cantor is to bring water covered with a cloth to the deacon, and the deacon is to mix it with the wine.”] from the hand of the archiparaphonista, and carries it to the archdeacon. The latter pours it into the chalice, making a cross [Note: [Col. 0944D] Not over the vessel or water, as is done now, but by pouring the water into the chalice in the form of a cross.].

Then the deacons ascend to the pontiff. When the *primicerius*, *secundicerius*, and *primicerius* of the regional Defenders, the regional notaries, and the regional Defenders see them, they descend from their ranks in order to stand in their proper place.

15. Then the pontiff rises from his chair, descends to the altar, greets the altar, and receives the offerings from the hand of the weekly priest and from the deacons. The archdeacon receives the pontiff’s offerings from the offering subdeacon and gives them to the pontiff. When the pontiff has placed them on the altar [Col. 0944C], the archdeacon lifts the chalice from the hand of the regional subdeacon and places it on the altar beside the pontiff’s offering, on the right [Note: [Col. 0944D] This is what Amalarius reports as having been received from the Romans, at the end of the second preface to his *Official Books*: “The chalice is arranged beside the offering, not behind it.” The same is stated in chapter 10 of the *Micrologus*.].

With its handles wrapped in the *offertorium*, he places it at the corner of the altar and stands behind the pontiff. The pontiff inclines slightly toward the altar, looks toward the school, and signals that they should be silent [Note: [Col. 0944D] What the *Offertorium* was at that time will be read below, no. 26.].

16. When the Offertory has ended, the bishops stand behind the pontiff, the first in the middle and the others in order. The archdeacon stands on the bishops’ right, the second deacon on their left, and the others in order in a line.

When the Offertory has ended, the regional subdeacons go behind the altar, looking toward the pontiff, so that whenever he says “For ever and ever,” or “The Lord be with you,” or “Lift up your hearts,” or “Thanks,” they may be ready to respond [Col. 0945A], standing upright until they begin the Angelic Hymn, that is, the *Sanctus*. When they have completed it, the pontiff alone rises and enters the Canon. The bishops, deacons, subdeacons, and priests remain in the presbytery, inclined [Note: [Col. 0945C] Concerning this inclination, Amalarius says in book III, chapter 23: “They remain standing behind him, inclined, until the entire present Prayer, which they call the Canon, has ended.”].

When the pontiff says “To us also, sinners,” the subdeacons rise. When he says “Through whom you create all these things, O Lord,” the archdeacon alone rises. When he says “Through him and with him,” the archdeacon lifts the chalice by its handles together with the *offertorium* and holds it up beside the pontiff. [Note: [Col. 0945C] At this point too, most Greeks and Easterners first elevate the chalice together with the consecrated Host.]

The pontiff touches the chalice with the offerings at its side and says “Through him and with him” through “For ever and ever. Amen.” He places the offerings in their proper place, and the archdeacon places the chalice beside them, leaving the *offertorium* on its handles [Note: [Col. 0945C] Amalarius observes this rite near the end of the second preface to the *Official Book* and in book III, chapter 26 of the same work.].

17. What we omitted concerning the paten: when the pontiff begins the Canon [Note: [Col. 0945D] Amalarius quotes this article, in exactly the same words, from the Roman booklet, in book III, chapter 27.], an acolyte comes, carrying a linen cloth beneath his shoulder, tied around his neck, and holding the paten before his breast on the right side until the middle of the Canon. Then the following subdeacon receives it upon his *planeta*, comes before the altar, and waits until the regional subdeacon receives it.

18. When the Canon has ended, the regional subdeacon stands with the paten behind the archdeacon. When he has said, “and safe from all disturbance,” the archdeacon turns [Note: [Col. 0945D] The *Micrologus* records this from the Roman Order, chapter 17.] and, after kissing the paten, gives it to the second deacon to hold when he says, “May the peace of the Lord be always with you.” He makes the sign of the cross three times with his hand over the chalice and places the Holy Things into it [Note: [Col. 0945D] The Colbertine, after “May the peace of the Lord be always with you,” omits the rest and adds: “He will place some of the Holy Things into the chalice.” Amalarius has the same in book III, chapter 31: “The aforesaid booklet, namely the Roman one, says: ‘When he has said, “The peace of the Lord,” etc., he places some of the Holy Things into the chalice.’ These Holy Things appear to be the same as those mentioned above, no. 8, and as the particle of *fermentum* below, no. 22—namely, that which had been consecrated earlier and reserved for the sacrifice to come; the other kind occurs below, no. 19. Amalarius also quotes immediately afterward these words from the said booklet: ‘But the archdeacon gives the peace,’ etc.]. But the archdeacon gives the peace to the first bishop, then to the others in order, and to the people.

19. Then the pontiff breaks the offering on the right side, and leaves upon the altar the particle which he breaks there; he places his remaining offerings in the paten held by the deacon, and returns to his seat.

[Note: Amalarius reads thus in Book III, chapter 31, better than the printed editions and the Saint Gall manuscript; the latter read, “the particle which he breaks, he leaves a portion upon the altar.” The Colbert manuscript, “the particle which he had broken he takes up, [and] leaves another portion upon the altar,” is also more correct.] Immediately the first chancellor, the second chancellor, and the first chancellor of the defenders, together with all the regional subdeacons and notaries, ascend to the altar and stand in their order on the right and left.

When the nomenclator, the treasurer, and the notary of the deputy steward have said “Lamb of God,” they then come and stand before the pontiff, so that he may give them permission to write down the names of those who are to be invited—either to the pontiff’s table by the nomenclator, or to that of the deputy steward by his notary. When they have completed the names, they go down to issue the invitations.

For the archdeacon lifts the chalice and gives it to the regional subdeacon, whom he keeps beside the right-hand corner of the altar. The following subdeacons then approach with the acolytes who carry the pouches, on the right and left sides of the altar. The acolytes extend their arms with the pouches, while the following subdeacons stand in front, so that they may open the mouths of the pouches for the archdeacon to place the offerings in them, first on the right and then on the left.

Then the acolytes go to the right and left around the bishops, circling the altar; the others go down to the presbyters, so that they may break the Hosts.

[Note: Colbert: “They go to the left of the bishops.”] The paten goes ahead near the seat, carried by two regional subdeacons to the deacons, so that they may break them. But the deacons look into the face of the pontiff, awaiting his signal to break them. When he has signaled, they return his greeting and break them. And when the archdeacon has emptied the altar of the offerings, except for the particle which the pontiff left upon the altar from his own broken offering—for they observe this so that, while the solemnities of the Mass are being celebrated, the altar may not be without a sacrifice—he looks toward the schola, gives them a signal to say “Lamb of God,” and goes with the others to the paten.

[Note: Colbert has “the offerings, and looks toward the schola,” with the rest omitted. In the printed editions only the words enclosed in parentheses are absent; they are found, however, in the manuscript of Saint Gall, which should certainly not be disregarded, and to which Amalarius referred in Book III of *The Office*, chapter 35: “The particle remains upon the altar until the end of the Mass.” Micrologus, in chapter 17, thinks that it was reserved for those about to receive Communion, or for the sick. But the reason given here seems preferable.]

When the breaking has been completed, the lesser deacon takes the paten from the subdeacon and carries it to the seat, so that the pontiff may receive Communion.

[Note: That is, while standing, and indeed turned toward the East, according to the Fourth Roman Order concerning the bishop’s Mass, no. 10, and according to other later booklets.]

When he has received Communion, he places from the Holy Sacrament which he has bitten into the hands of the archdeacon, saying into the chalice: “May there be a commingling and consecration of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ for us who receive them unto eternal life. Amen. Peace be with you.” “And with your spirit.” And the pontiff is confirmed—that is, receives the chalice—from the archdeacon.

[Note: That is, by taking the Lord’s blood as the completion of Communion, as Micrologus says in chapter 19. This is surely a remarkable example of general Communion, including that of priests and bishops.]

20. Then the archdeacon comes with the chalice to the corner of the altar and announces the station. Having poured a little from the chalice into a bowl held by an acolyte, the bishops first approach the seat, in order to receive Communion from the pontiff according to their rank; and the presbyters likewise approach, to receive Communion after them.

[Note: The Colbert manuscript varies here: “But let all the presbyters approach, so that they may receive Communion at the altar.” This reading agrees with the other two booklets below. A little later Colbert has: “Then the archdeacon, receiving the chalice from his hand, pours it back into the bowl,” and so forth. This is clearer, but has the same meaning.]

The first bishop receives the chalice from the hand of the archdeacon and stands at the corner of the altar in the next rank, as far as the first chancellor of the defenders. Then the archdeacon receives the chalice from his hands, pours it back into the bowl mentioned above, and hands the chalice to the regional subdeacon, who gives him the *pugillaris* (communion tube), with which he administers the chalice to the people. The following subdeacon takes the chalice and gives it to the acolyte.

[Colbert: “from the acolyte.”]

The acolyte carries it back to the dressing room. When he has given Communion to those whom the pope communicates, the pontiff descends from the seat with the first chancellor of the notaries and the first chancellor of the defenders, who hold his hands, so that he may give Communion to those who are in the senatorial section; after him, the archdeacon gives them Communion.

After these things, the bishops give Communion to the people, with the first chancellor giving them a signal with his hand beneath the pontiff’s cope, after asking the pontiff. After them, the deacons administer the chalice to them. Then they cross to the left side, to do the same.

The presbyters, with the first chancellor’s permission and by order of the pontiff, give Communion to the people, and in turn administer the chalice. For as soon as the pontiff begins to give Communion in the senatorial section, the schola immediately begins the Communion antiphon, alternating with the subdeacons, and they sing psalms until, after all the people have received Communion, the pontiff gives a signal for them to say “Glory be to the Father”; then, after repeating the verse, they stop.

[Note: From this it is clear that the antiphon now called the Communion was formerly preceded by the singing of a psalm; Micrologus explicitly says so in chapter 18. Compare the Gallican Liturgy, Book I, chapter 5, no. 27. In the Colbert manuscript it reads: “Immediately the schola begins the Communion antiphon, and they sing psalms until all the people have received Communion. For as soon as the pontiff has given Communion in the women’s section,” and so forth.]

As soon as the pontiff has given Communion in the women’s section, he returns to the seat and gives Communion in order to the regional subdeacons, to those who had stood in line, and on feast days to the twelve from the schola. On other days they receive Communion in the presbytery.

[Note: Colbert has: “For on other days the presbyters should give Communion wherever they can.”]

After all these people, the nomenclator and treasurer return, together with the acolyte who holds the paten, the one who holds the towel, and the one who gives the water; they receive Communion at the seat, and after the pontiff the archdeacon administers the chalice to them.

21. The regional subdeacon stands before the pontiff, awaiting his signal. The pontiff looks over the people to see whether they have already received Communion, and gives him a signal. The subdeacon goes to the shoulder, looks toward the first member of the schola, makes the sign of the cross on his own forehead, and signals him to say “Glory.” The latter returns the greeting and says “Glory,” “As it was,” and the verse.

[Note: Colbert has: “And he looks toward the first member of the schola.”]

When the antiphon has ended, the pontiff rises with the archdeacon, comes before the altar, and gives the Prayer at the Dismissal, facing East.

[Note: Colbert omits these words and has simply: “He gives the Prayer at the Dismissal.” When it is finished, the archdeacon commands one of the deacons, and so forth. At this point the priest, turned toward the people, says “The Lord be with you,” as he does here.]

For at this point, when he has said “The Lord be with you,” he does not turn toward the people. When the Prayer has ended, the deacon whom the archdeacon has instructed looks toward the pontiff for his signal, and says to the people, “Go, the dismissal is made.” They answer, “Thanks be to God.”

Then seven candle-bearers precede the pontiff, and the regional subdeacon with the censer goes to the sacristy. When he descends into the presbytery, the bishops first say, “Command, lord, that we bless.” The response is: “May the Lord bless us.” Response: “Amen.” After the bishops come the presbyters; then the monks; then the schola; then the dragon-bearers, that is, those who carry the standards; after them the bearers; after them the candle-bearers; after them the acolytes who watch the passageway; after them, outside the presbytery, those carrying crosses; then the junior attendants; and he enters the sacristy.

[Note: The reading of the Colbert manuscript must not be overlooked: instead of *rugam* it has *regiam*, that is, the passageway or door of the screens, which the acolytes customarily guarded. The duty of the bearers is described above, no. 3.]

II. If, however, the supreme pontiff should happen not to be present at the station, the following things are done differently by another bishop.

22. First, the deacons, not the pontiff, precede with the candle-bearer or censer.

Second, he does not sit in the seat behind the altar.

Third, he does not say the Prayer behind the altar, but on the right side of the altar.

Fourth, not the bishop himself but a deacon makes the sign at that point where it is customary.

[Possibly: “signs.”]

Fifth, after the Canon has ended, when “Through whom, Lord, you create all these things” is said, the chalice is not lifted by the archdeacon.

Sixth, when “May the peace of the Lord be always with you” is to be said, the offering-bearer subdeacon carries the particle of the leaven which has been consecrated by the apostolicus and gives it to the archdeacon; he in turn presents it to the bishop. The bishop, making the sign three times and saying “May the peace of the Lord be always with you,” places it in the chalice.

He also does this differently: the apostolicus does not break the offering; the bishop himself breaks it upon the cloth called the corporal on the altar. Then everyone except the bishop receives Communion, since he does not communicate himself with his own hand. If he places the portion in his own hand, he communicates himself with his own hand. A presbyter does the same for a presbyter, and a deacon for a deacon. Everything else is done in the same way as by the supreme pontiff.

The same is also done by a presbyter when he celebrates Mass at a station, except for “Glory to God in the highest,” since a presbyter says it only at Easter. Bishops who preside over cities perform everything in the same way as the supreme pontiff.

III. Wednesday: The Beginning of Lent

23. Everyone gathers at the church of Saint Anastasia around the seventh hour. The pontiff enters the sacristy and puts on the vestments. The schola sings the Entrance Antiphon.

24. Then the pontiff arrives and ascends to the altar. When the antiphon has ended, the pontiff, standing on the right side of the altar and facing the people, says, “The Lord be with you.” Then he turns back toward the East and says, “Let us pray”; the deacon says, “Let us bend the knee,” and then, “Arise.” The Prayer follows.

Then the antiphon “By the way” is begun. When they have come near the church, they begin the litany. When they have entered the church, the pontiff enters the sacristy. The schola continues singing until the altar. When they have finished the litany, after a short interval they begin the Entrance Antiphon. Then the pontiff comes and ascends to the seat, says “Let us pray,” and the deacon says, “Let us bend the knee,” and “Arise.” Then, after the Prayer, the reading is read, and Mass is celebrated in the customary manner.

After he has said the Communion, the deacon says, “Bow your heads before God.” The clergy respond, “Thanks be to God,” and the Prayer over the People is said. When the Prayer has ended, the deacon says, “Go, the dismissal is made.”

[Note: From this point throughout Lent, except on feast days, “Let us bless the Lord” is said. See Micrologus, chapter 46, and compare chapter 34.]

The same is done on Monday, Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday throughout Lent. For on Saturday, in the time of Hadrian, it was established that prayer should be made for King Charles; previously this had not been customary.

[Note: That is, Charles the Great; these words imply that this is a later institution. See no. 28.]

25. On Tuesday, or Thursday, when they have entered for the Masses, he says, “The Lord be with you,” and the deacon says, “Let us bend the knee,” and “Arise.” When the Mass has ended, the deacon says, “Bow your heads before God.”

[Note: On this rite, see Amalarius in the second preface to *The Office*, near the end of the preface.]

Everyone bows toward the East. The pontiff says the Prayer over the People, and the deacon says, “Go, the dismissal is made.” The other bishops or presbyters who do not conduct a collect, or where the station has not been in that church, do throughout the week in the same way as these do on the two days.

Likewise, concerning “Glory to God in the highest”: it is sung on Sundays until the beginning of Lent.

[The printed column reference appears here as Col. 0949D.]

But presbyters do not sing “Glory to God in the highest” except at Easter. Bishops, however, sing it at all times on Sundays or feast days. When the litany is performed, neither “Glory to God in the highest,” nor “Lord, have mercy” after the Entrance, nor “Alleluia” is sung, except at the great litany.

26. Likewise, concerning the gradual Responsory: it is sung from its beginning to its end, and the verse likewise. On ordinary days, “Alleluia” is treated in the same way. On ordinary days, if they wish, only the first part is said.

Candlesticks are held in the hands until they begin the repetition; afterward they are placed on the pavement. After the first Prayer of the Mass has been given, they are carried before the altar. “Glory” is divided, but only on feast days. At the repetition, whether on feast days or ordinary days, it is always begun. Only once during a single Mass is the Offertory, or its verse, sung twice for the lord pope.

[Note: Two things are distinguished in the Offertory: the Offertory itself and the verse. Such Offertories are found in ancient books with two or three verses. See Amalarius, Book III, chapter 19, at the end.]

IV. Here begins the Order from Mid-Lent Sunday to the Octave of Easter

27. From the Sunday which the Apostolic See wished to be called “Mid-Lent Sunday,” we believe that the customary observance should be explained. The words said on that day themselves indicate the number of days, as in: “On the fourteenth day, in the evening,” and shortly afterward: “On the fifteenth day you shall celebrate the solemnity.”

[Note: Thus the published Roman Order calls Passion Sunday “Mid-Lent Sunday”; it contains much more detail than is found here, on page 41.]

From that day until the vigil of holy Easter Sunday, “Glory” is sung neither in any Responsory nor in “Come”; and from the Lord’s Supper onward, “Glory” is sung neither in the Psalms nor anywhere else until Easter.

On Palm Sunday, when the Gospel is read, the deacon says, “The Lord be with you.” Response: “And with your spirit.” He also says: “The Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ according to Matthew.” Response: “Glory to you, Lord.”

28. On Wednesday, which is the day before the Lord’s Supper, at the third hour the pontiff proceeds with the clergy and his order to the altar in the greater church, and says the solemn Prayers in this order: “Let us pray.” He gives the Prayer, “O God, from whom Judas…” After the Amen, he continues and says the solemn Prayers as they are contained in the Sacramentaries; only for himself he omits the prayer. He says the Prayer for the king of the Franks, then the remaining prayers in order; finally, for the Jews, they do not bend the knee.

[Note: Amalarius, in Book I, chapter 11, observes a fifth variation on this day, namely, the addition of one reading and one Responsory with five verses, as well as the Passion of the Lord and, as we find written in the booklet called the Roman Order, a genuflection. He then adds: “The aforesaid booklet declares, according to Roman custom, that on the same day, before the public office, the Prayers that we customarily perform on Friday should be recited.” These words refer to the present passage. On the genuflection, see Micrologus, chapter 52.]

When these have been completed, he kisses the altar and goes out. Then, at the eighth hour, they enter for the Masses in the following order. The schola says the Entrance Antiphon, and the pontiff gives the Prayer. One reading is read, as it is contained in the *Capitulare*.

[Note: The *Capitulare* is the index of Epistles and Gospels for the Masses; in ancient times these were designated in the sacred books by their first and last words. See volume II of the *Capitularies*, column 1310.]

The Gradual “Do not turn away” follows, and another reading is read. After it, the canticle “Lord, hear” is sung with its verses. The Gospel is proclaimed in this way: “The Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ according to Luke,” and he begins to read. When it has been read through, the Mass is completed in its proper order.

V. Thursday: The Lord’s Supper

29. They are to rise at midnight, and the signal is sounded. After this, there is no rising except on the night of holy Easter for Matins. The church, however, is decorated with every light. In the customary manner they do not say “O God, come to my aid,” nor “Glory,” nor the Invitatory; rather, the cantor begins the antiphon in the Psalms, as it is contained in the Antiphoner.

Nor does the presbyter complete the Prayer at the end.

[Note: That is, at the end of the Prayer “Look upon us, we beseech you, Lord,” and so forth; he does not add, as usual, “Who lives with you,” and so forth.]

They are to rise silently, and the reader is not to ask for a blessing. When he finishes, he is not to say, “But you, Lord”; he is commanded to end with the words of the reading.

Three readings are to be read from the Lamentation of the prophet Jeremiah, where it says, “How solitary sits the city,” through “The Lord has planned to destroy the wall of the daughter of Zion.” Three are from the treatise of Saint Augustine on the Psalm “Hear, O Lord, my prayer,” beginning with its first words. Three are from the Apostle, where he says to the Corinthians, chapter 57: “For I received from the Lord what I also handed on to you.”

Nine Psalms, nine readings, and nine Responsories. When everything has been completed, Matins follows.

[Note: By “Matins” are meant Lauds, as we call them, just as in the Rule of Saint Benedict.]

When Matins has been completed, neither “Lord, have mercy” nor “And lead us not into temptation” is said.

30. At the third hour they enter the sacristy and put on dalmatics, both the pontiff and all the deacons, or they put on the entire vesture, while the pontiff sits in his chair. Two flasks of oil are prepared. The better one is carried to the pontiff, so that, after receiving balsam and mixing it with the oil, he may fill it with his own hand; the other ministers hold it full. Then, having washed his hands, the pontiff proceeds with the seven candle-bearers to the Masses.

After the Entrance Antiphon has been said, he says “Glory to God in the highest” and the Prayer. The reading from the Apostle is read: “Brothers, when you come together,” through “so that we may not be condemned with the world.” The Gradual “Christ became obedient for us” follows.

The Gospel according to John, chapter 13, is read: “At that time, Jesus, knowing that his hour had come,” through “just as I have done for you, so you also should do.” Before “Through whom you create all these things” is said, the oil for the sick which the people bring is blessed; thereafter the Mass proceeds in its proper order. When it has been completed, the bishop alone receives Communion before the altar, and the deacon administers the chalice to him.

31. On that day alone, after he has received Communion, he places the chalice upon the altar. Then, having received the paten from the subdeacon, he places it beside the chalice on the left side. Immediately two deacons cover both with a clean linen cloth, which they had previously prepared at the edge of the altar opposite the pontiff, after the corporal had been spread.

[Note: Amalarius reports these words and others in Book I, near the middle of chapter 12: “The booklet of the Roman Order says concerning the consecration of the chrism: Immediately two acolytes,” and so forth. At the beginning of the same chapter he also says that the oil is consecrated together with the body and blood of the Lord, and that it has no separate office, but is blessed at the place where, he says, “we customarily bless the grapes.” From this we understand that it is an insertion into the office described above.]

Immediately two acolytes hold the flasks wrapped in a white silk cloth, so that they can be seen from the middle, on their left arms, with the cloths thrown over their left shoulders and extending to the right shoulder, so that they can more securely hold the hanging ends. From these men, standing beneath the shoulder, the subdeacon comes and takes one of the mixed flasks together with its cloth. He gives it to the archdeacon, who carries it before the pontiff at the altar.

Then the pontiff looks toward the East, while the deacon holds before him the flask wrapped in cloth on his left arm, as we have said above. Here he breathes three times into the flask of chrism, and the pontiff says, “Lift up your hearts.” Response: “We have them with the Lord.” Then he begins the consecration of the chrism in a loud voice. Before it is blessed, however, he breathes three times into the flask.

When this has been completed, he blesses the flask of oil brought in the manner described above. He likewise breathes into it, but silently. As soon as the flask containing the chrism has been blessed, it is covered, so that no one may see it uncovered. The acolyte holds it, and everyone greets it in order, while the bishop and the deacon first greet it uncovered.

When this has been completed and the pontiff has washed his hands, he comes before the altar, and all the people receive Communion in their order. He preserves some of the Holy Sacrament until the next day.

32. On that day, at the ninth hour, they make fire by striking a stone outside the basilica.

[Note: It is worth recalling what Amalarius reports that he learned from Theodore, archdeacon of the Roman Church, in Book IV, chapter 44: “I, Theodore, am accustomed to be with the apostolicus at the Lateran when the office of the Lord’s Supper is celebrated. Nothing there is observed that night concerning the extinction of lights. On Friday no lamp or candlelight is kept in the church in Jerusalem while the lord apostolicus performs the solemn Prayers there, or while the cross is greeted; nevertheless, on that day a new fire is kindled, from which a light is reserved until the nocturnal office.”] If they have no oratory there, they strike it at the gate; otherwise, they do so at the place chosen by the superior, so that a candle may be lit from it. The candle is to be placed on a reed and carried by an attendant of the church in the presence of the congregation or people.

From that fire, immediately, in the same church or place where it is kindled, one lamp is to be kept until Holy Saturday, to light the candle which is to be blessed on that same day according to the order contained in the Sacramentaries.

[Note: Pope Zacharias gives a somewhat different account in Letter 12 to Boniface: namely, that on the Thursday of Easter, that is, before Easter, when the sacred chrism is consecrated, it is customary for three lamps to burn in a more secluded place of the church until the third day, that is, Saturday.]

On that day they sing the entire daytime office together. From Vespers onward, the altars are to remain bare until Saturday morning.

[Note: Amalarius, near the end of chapter 12: “One thing still remains in the Roman Order, where it commands that from Thursday until Holy Saturday the altars should be bare.”]

VI. Friday

33. On Good Friday they are to rise at midnight. Nine Psalms with Responsories are said; three readings from the Lamentation of Jeremiah, beginning where he says, “The Lord has planned to destroy,” through “The mercies of the Lord are many”; three from the treatise of Saint Augustine on Psalm 63; and three from the Apostle, where he says to the Hebrews, chapter 5: “Let us therefore hasten to enter.”

Then Matins follows. The lamps are extinguished. The lights of the church begin to be extinguished (Latin *tutare*, “to extinguish”) from the beginning of the nocturnal singing, in this order: beginning at the entrance of the church, they are gradually extinguished, so that, for example, after the first nocturn, a third of them may be seen to have been extinguished; during the middle nocturn, another third; and when the third has been completed, no light remains except seven lamps. These are extinguished during Matins in the following manner.

At the beginning of the first Psalm, a custodian is always prepared at the place on the right side of the church near the lamps. When he hears the antiphon, he holds a reed in his hand and extinguishes one lamp. At the end of that Psalm he extinguishes another on the left side. Thus one on one side and another on the other are extinguished, until the Gospel. During the Gospel, the central lamp is extinguished.

34. At the third hour all the presbyters, both those of the city and those from the suburbs, and all the clergy with the people, are to gather in the church appointed within the city, though not in the greater church. They await the pontiff or whoever is acting in his place.

When he comes from the sacristy and proceeds before the altar to pray at the oratory, as is customary, as soon as he rises he silently ascends to the seat. When he is seated, the subdeacon immediately ascends to read, and after the reading the canticle “Lord, I heard” is sung with its verses.

The pontiff says, “Let us pray,” the deacon says, “Let us bend the knee,” and he says, “Arise.” He gives the Prayer, “O God, from whom Judas…” Then another reading follows, after which comes the Tract “He who dwells,” or “Rescue me.”

[Note: Amalarius also assigns this psalm in Book I of *The Office*, chapter 13, near the middle, and in Book IV, chapter 34.]

When it has ended, the deacon proclaims: “The Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ according to John,” and begins to read. When it has been completed, two deacons immediately strip the altar of the linen cloth which had previously been placed beneath the Gospel, in the manner of a thief.

[Note: Amalarius quotes these words from the Roman booklet near the middle of the aforementioned chapter 13 of Book I.]

Then the pontiff comes before the altar and says: “Let us pray, dearly beloved, first for the Church of God,” and the rest in order, as we said on Wednesday. When they come to the Jews, they do not bend the knee. When he has finished these prayers, everyone silently goes outside.

The presbyters of the churches, whether from the city or from the suburbs, go to their own churches, so that they may perform everything in this order until Vespers, changing only this: where the pontiff mentions the apostolicus, they name their own bishop.

35. After the Prayers, a cross is prepared before the altar, with a space placed between it and the altar. It is supported on either side by two acolytes, and an oratory is placed before it.

[Note: Amalarius likewise says in Book I, chapter 14: “After this, the aforementioned booklet commands that a cross be prepared before the altar, which everyone greets and kisses.”]

The pontiff comes and, after adoring the cross, kisses it; then the presbyters, deacons, subdeacons, and the others in order, and then the people. The pontiff sits in the seat until everyone has greeted it.

The two senior presbyters, as soon as they have greeted the cross, enter the sacristy, or the place where the Lord’s body had been placed, which remained from the preceding day. They put it on a paten. A subdeacon holds before them a chalice with unconsecrated wine, and another subdeacon holds the paten with the Lord’s body. While they hold these, one presbyter takes the paten and the other the chalice, and they carry them onto the stripped altar.

The pontiff remains seated while the people greet the cross. Whenever the pontiff or the people greet the cross, the antiphon is always sung: “Behold the wood of the cross, on which hung the salvation of the world; come, let us adore.” Psalm 118 is said, that is, “Blessed are the undefiled.”

When the cross has been greeted and returned to its place, the pontiff descends before the altar and says: “Let us pray. Instructed by saving commandments: Our Father.” Then follows: “Deliver us, we beseech you, Lord.”

When they have said “Amen,” he takes some of the Holy Sacrament and places it in the chalice, saying nothing. Everyone receives Communion in silence, and everything is completed.

[Note: Amalarius himself says in the aforementioned chapter 15: “He who, according to the order of the booklet, consecrates the wine by the commingling of bread and wine does not observe the tradition of the Church, concerning which Innocent says that during these two days the Sacraments are not celebrated at all. But whether this commingling is a true consecration, we have examined in our commentary.”]

The pontiff says: “In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, peace be with you.” They answer: “And with your spirit.” After a short interval, each person says Vespers privately, and thus they go to the table.

VII. Saturday

36. They are to rise at midnight. Nine Psalms with Responsories are said. Three readings are taken from the Lamentation of Jeremiah, beginning where he says, “The mercies of the Lord are many,” through the end. Then homilies of the holy Fathers pertaining to that day are read. Concerning the lighting and extinguishing of the candles, the procedure is as stated above.

[Note: The often-cited Amalarius, in chapter 17, says: “The Roman booklet relates that on this same day wax mixed with oil was blessed, and that from it lambs were made and preserved until the Octave of Easter”; this is not found in the present booklet. The same is found in the published Roman Order, in the section concerning the Octave of Easter, and in the book attributed to Alcuin.]

37. After the third hour on Saturday, those who are to be baptized proceed to the church and are arranged in order, as written: the males on the right, the females on the left.

The priest makes the sign of the cross on each person’s forehead. Then, placing his hand upon each person’s head, he says: “Nor is it hidden from you, Satan.”

When this has been completed, he touches each person’s nostrils and ears with spittle and says to them: “Ephphatha,” which means “Be opened,” for the fragrance of sweetness. But you, devil, flee; for the judgment of God is approaching.

Then he touches their shoulders and breasts with holy oil and says: “Do you renounce Satan?” Response: “I renounce him.” “And all his works?” Response: “I renounce them.” “And all his pomps?” Response: “I renounce them.” “I anoint you with the oil of salvation in Christ Jesus our Lord, having been made propitious unto eternal life. Peace be with you.”

38. When this has been completed, he walks around them, placing his hand upon their heads, and says only in a loud voice, “I believe in God.” He turns toward the women and does the same.

Afterward the archdeacon says to them: “Pray, chosen ones; bend the knee.” After a short interval he says: “Arise. Complete our prayer together, and say, Amen.” They all answer, “Amen.”

Again they are admonished by the archdeacon in these words: “Let the catechumens depart. If anyone is a catechumen, let him depart. Let all the catechumens go outside.”

Again the deacon says: “Dearest children, return to your places, awaiting the hour when the grace of God may effect baptism around you.”

39. At the ninth hour the pontiff, the priests, and the others enter the sacristy and put on the vestments in which they are to celebrate the vigil. After a candle has been lit, they all proceed together from the sacristy into the church in silence, carrying the same candle and singing nothing; it is placed in a candlestick before the altar.

One deacon asks one of the priests or levites who stand there vested to pray for him. When he has risen, the deacon himself says, “The Lord be with you.” Response: “And with your spirit.” He says the Prayer as it is contained in the Sacramentaries.

Afterward the pontiff and the priests sit in their seats; the deacons remain standing. When this has been completed, he says, “The Lord be with you.” Response: “And with your spirit.” Then: “Lift up your hearts.” Response: “We have them with the Lord.” Then: “Let us give thanks to the Lord our God.” Response: “It is worthy and just.”

Then he proceeds to the consecration of the candle, chanting as though it were a canon. After this, two candles are lit in two candlesticks, and from that fire they light candles in every house, because all the former lights are to be extinguished.

[Note: Amalarius differs in Book I, chapter 20. The aforementioned booklet also adds another candle, where it says: “Then two candles are illuminated, held by two notaries,” and so forth. These words are absent here but are present in the appendix which we shall immediately append.]

40. Then the lector removes his chasuble; ascending the ambo, [Col. 0955D] he does not announce, “A reading from the book of Genesis,” but begins thus: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth”; for all the other readings likewise begin in this way. First the Greek is read, and immediately afterward the Latin by another reader. [Col. 0955D]

> **Note:** Amalarius cites these words in chapter 21: “The booklet of which we have often spoken, which contains the Roman Order, says: ‘The reading from the book of Genesis is not announced,’” and so forth.

> **Note:** Appropriately concerning this passage, the same Amalarius mentioned above says at the beginning of Book II: “The six readings were read by the ancient Romans in Greek and Latin”—a custom that is still observed at CP, if I am not mistaken—for two reasons: first, because Greeks were present for whom the Latin language was unknown; second, on account of the concord of both peoples. Compare the *Micrologus*, near the end of chapter 28, and Berno, abbot of Reichenau, chapter 7, where he cites Amalarius’s words under the name of the Fathers. [Col. 0955D–0956D]

Then the pontiff first rises and says, “Let us pray,” and the deacon, “Let us kneel,” followed by, “Arise.” The pontiff gives the Collect, and the reading is read in Greek: “It came to pass in the morning watch”; and he himself sings this canticle in Greek: “Let us sing to the Lord.” After this another reader ascends and reads the aforementioned passage in Latin, and sings the aforementioned canticle in Latin. [Col. 0956A]

Then the pontiff rises and says, “Let us pray,” and the deacon responds as above; and the Collect is given. After this the reading is read in Greek: “Seven women shall take hold”; and he himself sings the canticle in Greek, “The Vineyard.” Then another reader ascends to read the aforementioned passage in Latin; [26] he sings the aforementioned canticle in Latin.

The pontiff says, “Let us pray.” The deacon responds as above; and again the reading is read in Greek: “Moses wrote this song.” Another reader ascends and reads it in Latin. Then the pontiff or deacon proceeds as above. After this the Psalm “As the deer longs” is sung in Greek, and another reader sings the same Psalm in Latin.

41. After this the pontiff, facing the people, says, “The Lord be with you,” and they respond, “And with your spirit.” He says, “Let us pray,” and, facing east, gives the Collect. [Col. 0956B] When it has ended, he says, “The Lord be with you.” Immediately one minister comes, holding ampullae in his hands, and stands at the right corner of the altar; then he goes ahead of the pontiff to the fonts.

Next the schola descends to the fonts to perform the litany, waiting prepared for the pontiff. The second member of the schola holds a golden vessel in his left hand over his chasuble, from which the pontiff is to pour the chrism into the font; and, when instructed, they perform the litany three times. Then the pontiff proceeds with all due ceremony, supported by two deacons; and the two candle-bearers that had previously been lighted continually proceed before him until everything has been completed. [Col. 0956B–C]

42. When the litany is finished and silence has been made, the pontiff says, “The Lord be with you.” They respond, “And with your spirit.” He says, “Let us pray,” and gives the Collect, “Almighty and everlasting God.” Likewise another: “O God, whose invisible power …” Here he makes the first cross at the fragment, “*Qui hanc aquam*” (“Who [—] this water”), while dividing the water with his hand in the form of a cross. The second is made at, “Therefore I bless you.” Likewise the third, at, “I bless you, and through Jesus Christ.” [Col. 0956C]

When all this has been completed, he pours the chrism from the little vessel into the font over the water itself in the form of a cross; with his hand he mixes the chrism with the water and sprinkles it throughout the font, or over all the people.

After this, anyone among the people who wishes may take a blessing from this water in his own vessels, before the children are baptized there, in order to sprinkle it in their houses, vineyards, fields, and on their produce.

43. Then the presbyters or deacons, and, if necessary, the acolytes also, barefoot and putting on other clean or white garments, enter into the fonts, into the water. [Col. 0956D]

> **Note:** The same rite is found in the Gellone Codex—indeed, also in the common Roman Order.

First the males are baptized, then the females, with these questions: [27]

> Do you believe in God the almighty Father, creator of heaven and earth?  
> **Response:** I believe.  
> Do you also believe in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord, who was born and suffered?  
> **Response:** I believe.  
> Do you believe in the Holy Spirit, the holy catholic Church, the forgiveness of sins, the resurrection of the flesh, and eternal life?  
> **Response:** I believe.

Then, having received the infants from their parents, they baptize them with three immersions, invoking the Holy Trinity only once, saying:

> I baptize you in the name of the Father—and he immerses him once—  
> and of the Son—and he immerses him again—  
> and of the Holy Spirit—and he immerses him a third time.

> **Note:** This is the handing back of the Creed, which Amalarius says is performed on Holy Saturday according to the Roman Order; elsewhere, in Book I of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 12, near the beginning, he says that it is performed on Maundy Thursday. [Col. 0956D–0957A]

44. When the infants have been lifted up in their hands, let them be presented to a presbyter. The presbyter, making a cross of chrism with his thumb on the crown of their heads, with an invocation of the Holy Trinity, says:

> Almighty God, Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has regenerated you from water and the Holy Spirit, and who has given you the forgiveness of all sins: may he himself anoint you with the chrism of salvation in Christ Jesus our Lord unto eternal life. Amen. [Col. 0957B]

Those who are to receive them should stand ready, with cloths in their hands, and receive the infants from the presbyters or deacons who baptize them.

> **Note:** The seventh booklet mentions only the deacon for the ministry of baptism, number 12. [Col. 0957D]

The pontiff then leaves the font, having a prepared seat in the church wherever he wishes, and sits there. The infants are brought before him, and he gives each of them a stole, a chasuble, a chrismal, and ten siliquae; and they are clothed.

> **Note:** The seventh booklet says the same. In most other sources only a white garment and a chrismal are mentioned. The same rite is described more fully in the following appendix. [Col. 0957D]

When clothed, they are arranged in the prescribed order in a circle, and the pontiff gives a Collect over them, making a cross with chrism on their foreheads, with an invocation of the Holy Trinity, and bestows on them the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit.

> **Note:** Amalarius says near the end of chapter 27: “The Roman booklet of which we have often spoken says: ‘When the Collect has been completed, he makes a cross,’” and so forth. These words are found in the appendix that follows. [Col. 0957D]

They take every precaution that this not be neglected, because then all baptism is confirmed as legitimate in the name of Christianity. [Col. 0957C]

45. Meanwhile, at the command, the schola performs a litany before the altar: first seven petitions; after an interval, another five; and after another interval, three. [Col. 0957D]

> **Note:** Amalarius, at the end of the second preface to his book *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, mentions this rite of litanies after baptism, according to the numbers seven, five, and three. See chapter 15 of the preceding commentary.

While the *Agnus Dei* is being said, the master of the schola says, “Light them,” and then the church is illuminated. [Col. 0958D]

The pontiff leaves the sacristy with the two candle-bearers, which, as we said above, stand as before on the right and left sides of the altar. When the litany is completed, the pontiff says, “Glory to God in the highest.” Then the Epistle is read, followed by “Alleluia,” “Give thanks to the Lord,” and the Tract, “Praise the Lord, all nations.” They do not sing the Offertory, the *Agnus Dei*, or the Communion. Before the Gospel, they do not carry a light during that night, but incense. [Col. 0957D–0958D]

> **Note:** Amalarius, near the middle of chapter 31, says: “In my opinion, because of the imitation of the women, the Roman booklet says that on this night nothing is carried before the Gospel except incense,” and so forth.

46. Provision must be made concerning the infants: after they have been baptized, they are to receive no food and are not to nurse before they have received the sacrament of the Body of Christ. On every day of Easter week they are to proceed to the Masses, and their parents are to make an offering for them, and all are to receive Communion. [Col. 0958A]

The order of baptism described above is to be celebrated in every respect on this Easter Saturday, and likewise on Pentecost Saturday.

47. On that same day they separately sing the full office at night, after cockcrow. When daylight begins to break through the darkness, they rise, come into the church, and, kissing one another in mutual charity, say, “O God, come to my assistance”; the Invitatory follows with *Alleluia*.

Three Psalms follow, with the antiphons “Blessed is the man,” “Why have they raged?” and “Lord, why have they increased?” Then three readings follow with Responsories. The first reading is from the Acts of the Apostles; the second and third are from the homilies of Saint Augustine. Matins follows with *Alleluia*. [Col. 0958B]

During the Easter White Days, over *Venite*, they sing, “The Lord has truly risen, alleluia,” and three Psalms over the nocturn. These are assigned for each night until the octave of Easter:

- Monday: “When I called,” “My words,” “O Lord, rebuke me not in your anger.”
- Tuesday: “O Lord my God, in you I have hoped,” “O Lord our God,” “In the Lord I trust.”
- Wednesday: “Save me, O Lord,” “How long, O Lord?” “The fool has said.”
- Thursday: “Lord, who shall dwell?” “Preserve me, O Lord,” “Hear, O Lord, my justice.”
- Friday: “The heavens declare,” “May the Lord hear you,” “O Lord, in your strength.”
- Saturday: “The earth is the Lord’s,” “To you, O Lord, I have lifted up,” “Judge me, O Lord, for I have walked in innocence.” [29]

From Easter until the octave, at all the offices no Responsory is sung and no reading is recited. Instead of the Verse and Responsory, the Gradual “This is the day” is sung, but only at the first office. [Col. 0958C]

> **Note:** Amalarius observes much concerning this Roman rite in Book IV, chapter 52. [Col. 0958D]

After the octave of Easter, *Alleluia* is sung over *Venite* and over all the Psalms. On Monday, at *Venite*, and throughout the entire week, they sing, “The Lord has truly risen, alleluia.”

## VIII. The following is found in the same manuscript codex, but separated from the preceding material by half a folio. [Col. 0959]

48. On the feast days—that is, Easter, Pentecost, Saint Peter’s Day, and the Nativity of the Lord—during these four solemnities, the cardinal presbyters have offerings to collect, each holding a corporal in his hand. The archdeacon comes and presents three offerings to each of them.

When the pontiff approaches the altar, they surround it on the right and left, and together with him they recite the Canon, holding the offerings in their hands, not on the altar, so that the pontiff’s voice may be heard more powerfully. Together they consecrate the Body and Blood of the Lord, but only the pontiff makes the sign of the cross over the altar, to the right and left. [Col. 0958D–0959A]

> **Note:** Amalarius’s words in Book I, chapter 12, near the middle, belong here: “It is the custom of the Roman Church that presbyters be present at the making of Christ’s sacrifice and that, together with the pontiff, they consecrate it by word and hand.”

When the acolytes have received the Hosts from the archdeacon at the altar, they go to the presbyters, taking the first three chalices.

> **Note:** That is, ministerial chalices, which are otherwise called cups. Otherwise Gregory II, in Letter 9 to Boniface, bishop of Mainz, would not have written that it was not appropriate to place two or three chalices on the altar when the solemn rites of the Mass are celebrated. [Col. 0959D–0960D]

While the deacons break the offerings into the paten, the archdeacon turns toward the schola so that they may begin the *Agnus Dei*. It is sung for as long as they continue the breaking. If necessary, the archdeacon may summon anyone to perform the breaking into the paten.

Where the pontiff is not present, however, as soon as the deacons have broken the offerings and, with their hands shaken out, have placed them in the paten, the first member of the schola looks toward them, immediately gives a signal with his hand, and they finish.

49. When he has said, “Safe from every disturbance,” the deacon who is junior in rank turns, receives the paten from the subdeacon, kisses it, and holds it on his arm. When he has said, “World without end,” he breaks the offering on the right side; and the portion he has broken he places in the chalice when he says, “The peace of the Lord,” making the sign of the cross three times. [Col. 0959B]

50. This is done when the pontiff is not ill. The pontiff stands before the altar. The deacon places the paten on the altar. The pontiff places on the paten the offerings that he alone is to break, and breaks them.

Then the deacons stand on the right, and on the left the archpresbyters, together with the second, fourth, or whichever others the pontiff wishes; and he gives each of them one offering, and they break them with him on the altar, upon the corporal. [Col. 0960A]

The remaining offerings, which are in excess, the bishop, archdeacon, or whichever deacon is present places in the small bags held by the acolytes; and they carry them to the other presbyters, who stand below to perform the breaking.

If the pontiff is ill, the order by which he is to act has been written above.

51. Therefore, when the deacon has said, “World without end,” after “Glory to God in the highest,” they lift their chasubles onto their shoulders and stand beside the pontiff. The subdeacons likewise lift theirs, but with a fold or pouch. The subdeacon from the schola, as soon as he has imposed the antiphon for the Introit, lifts his chasuble with its fold. [Col. 0960B]

At the completion of the *Alleluia* or Responsories, the deacon prepares to read the Gospel. If no deacon is present, a presbyter stands beside the pontiff like a deacon, but without lifting his chasuble. When he reads the Gospel, he does not prepare himself in the place where the deacon does; instead, immediately, dressed in his chasuble, he comes before the altar and adorns the altar as the deacon does.

# APPENDIX

## I. Concerning the offices at night from Maundy Thursday until Easter

1. Therefore, beginning with the Sunday that the Apostolic See wished to call *Mediana*, we believe that the established practice should be made known. The words said on that day themselves indicate the number of days, as in the passage, “On the fourteenth day, at evening,” and shortly afterward, “On the fifteenth day you shall celebrate a solemnity.” From that day until the vigil of the Lord’s Resurrection, “Glory” is not sung in any Responsory. From Maundy Thursday, “Glory” is sung neither in the Psalms nor in any other place until Easter. [Col. 0959C]

On that same night they rise for the vigils at the eighth hour of the night, and then the church is adorned with every light. They do not say, as usual, “O God, come to my assistance,” nor the Invitatory, nor “Glory”; instead, the cantor begins the antiphon in the Psalms, as it is contained in the Antiphoner.

At the end of the nocturn, the lector does not ask for a blessing, nor does the presbyter complete the blessing as usual. When the lector finishes, he does not say, “But you, O Lord”; rather, he is instructed to make an ending from the words of the reading. [Col. 0959D]

2. The light of the church begins to be extinguished (*tutari*, that is, “to extinguish”) from the beginning of the nocturn chant, in this order: it begins at the entrance of the church and is gradually extinguished—for example, after the first nocturn, a third of the lights should appear to have been extinguished; during the middle nocturn another third; and when the third has been completed, no light remains except seven lamps.

At Matins these are extinguished in the following order. At the beginning of the first Psalm, the custodian should always be ready on the right side of the church, near the lamps. When he hears the antiphon, holding a reed in his hand, he extinguishes one lamp; at the end of that Psalm he extinguishes another on the left side. [Col. 0960B–C]

In the second Psalm, when he hears the antiphons, he extinguishes another on the right. Thus one on one side and another on the other are extinguished until the Gospel; during the Gospel the central lamp is extinguished.

> **Note:** That is, until the canticle *Benedictus*, taken from the Gospel according to Luke. The same method is used below to designate the canticle *Magnificat*. [Col. 0960D]

On Maundy Thursday, at the ninth hour, they cause fire to be struck from a stone outside the basilica. If there is an oratory there, they strike it at its door; otherwise, at a place chosen by the prior, so that a candle may be lit from it. This candle must be placed on a reed and carried by the church’s mansionarius in the presence of the people. From this fire one lamp is immediately lit in a secluded place in the same church, and it is kept until Holy Saturday to light the candle that is to be blessed on that day, according to the order contained in the *Sacramentary*. This order for blessing the candle is practiced in the suburban cities. [Col. 0960D]

3. In the Catholic Church within the city of Rome, on Holy Saturday at Prime, the archdeacon comes into the Lateran church, pours wax into a larger clean vessel, mixes oil into it there, and blesses the wax. From it he pours figures in the likeness of lambs and keeps them in a clean place.

On the octave of Easter, the archdeacon gives these lambs to the people in the church after the Masses and Communion. From them they make incense in their houses for fumigation, for whatever need may befall them. The same is done with wax in the suburban cities. [Col. 0961A]

4. When this has been completed, the chief mansionarius takes the aforementioned candle, already lit, in his hand on a reed. The people follow him in reverent silence, so that the illuminated tip of the candle, inclined toward the altar, faces the church into which they are about to enter. That church is still without light, except that seven lamps have been prepared before the altar and arranged so that, without any obstruction or delay, the mansionarius can light them with the same candle; thereafter, with custodians prepared, the church is adorned with every light.

They enter for the Masses as prescribed in the *Sacramentary* or the Antiphoner. When the Mass is completed, they receive Communion in the appointed order, and they preserve a portion of the Holy Sacrament until the following day according to custom. [Col. 0961B]

The church itself is to remain illuminated until the vigils. As we have prescribed for this day, so it is also to be done on Friday; likewise on Saturday, with this one provision: at the ninth hour they strike fire from a stone, as we have said. On Thursday the mansionarius carries it; on Friday the archdeacon; on Holy Saturday the junior bishop carries it.

If this order is practiced in monasteries, on Thursday the fire is carried by the church custodian, on Friday by the provost, and on Holy Saturday by the abbot.

## II. Wednesday, the day before Maundy Thursday

5. At the third hour all the presbyters, both from the city and from the suburbs, and all the clergy with the people assemble in the appointed church within the city, awaiting the pontiff. He always completes the solemn prayers for that day by himself in the major church, as prescribed in the *Sacramentary*. [Col. 0961C]

When he comes from the sacristy and proceeds before the altar to pray over the oratory, as soon as he rises he says, “Let us pray,” and the deacon says, “Let us kneel,” followed by, “Arise.” The pontiff [variant: presbyter] says, “Let us pray, dearly beloved, first for the Church of God,” and the remaining prayers in order. He omits only the prayer for himself. Finally, at the prayer for the Jews, they do not kneel.

When these prayers have been completed, he kisses the altar and departs. The presbyters of the churches, whether from the city or the suburbs, go to their own churches so that they may do everything in this order on Friday at the third hour. They know that where the pontiff omitted himself, they are to name him. [Col. 0961D]

Then, at the eighth hour [variant: ninth], they enter for the Mass in this order. The schola sings the antiphon for the Introit, and the pontiff gives the Collect. One reading is read, as listed in the *Capitulary*. The Gradual “Do not turn your face away” follows.

Another reading follows, after which comes the canticle “O Lord, hear,” with its verses. The Gospel is announced as follows: “The Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ according to Luke.” When it has been read, the Mass is completed in its proper order.

## III. Thursday, Maundy Thursday

6. At the third hour they enter the sacristy and put on dalmatics—the pontiff as well as all the deacons—or all the proper vestments, while the pontiff sits in his chair. Two ampullae containing oil are prepared. The better one is brought to the pontiff, so that, after receiving balsam and mixing it with the oil, he may fill it with his own hand. The ministers retain the other one, full.

After washing his hands, the pontiff proceeds with seven candle-bearers to the Mass. After the antiphon for the Introit has been sung, he gives the Collect. The Apostle’s reading is read: “Brothers, when you come together,” through “so that we may not be condemned with this world.” The Gradual follows: “Christ became for us.” The Gospel according to John, chapter XII [variant: XVII], is read: “At that time, Jesus, knowing that his hour had come,” through “as I have done for you, so you also should do.” [Col. 0962A–B]

The Mass is then celebrated in its proper order. When it is completed, the pontiff alone receives Communion before the altar, and on that day only the deacon confirms him with the chalice.

After he has received Communion, he places the chalice on the altar. Then, having received the paten from the subdeacon, he places it beside the chalice on the left side. Immediately both are covered by two deacons with a clean linen cloth, which they had previously prepared at the edge of the altar opposite the pontiff.

7. After the corporal has been spread, two acolytes immediately hold the ampullae, wrapped in a white silk cloth, so that they can be seen. They hold them at the middle on an arm extended outward, with the cloths thrown over the left shoulder so that they reach the right shoulder and the hanging ends can be held. [Col. 0962B–C]

From beneath their arms the subdeacon comes and receives one ampulla, together with its cloth, and gives it to the archdeacon, who carries it to the pontiff before the altar.

Then the pontiff, facing east, [34] and the deacon [variant: archdeacon] holds before him the ampulla, wrapped in a cloth around his left arm, as described above. The pontiff says, “Lift up your hearts.” The response is, “We have them with the Lord.” He begins the consecration of the chrism in a loud voice. Before it is blessed, however, he breathes three times into the ampulla.

When this has been completed, he silently blesses the ampulla of oil, brought in the order described above, and likewise breathes into it three times.

> **Note:** The word “silently” is absent from the preceding Order, number 30. In the Colbertine manuscript: “He blesses the ampulla of oil for the chrism, brought in the order described above; likewise he breathes into it, but silently blesses the ampulla containing the chrism. As soon as it has been blessed,” and so forth. [Col. 0961D–0962D]

As soon as the ampulla containing the chrism has been blessed, it is covered so that no one sees it uncovered. While the acolyte holds it, everyone venerates it in order. The bishop and deacons, however, first venerate it uncovered.

When this has been completed, the pontiff washes his hands, comes before the altar, and the entire people receive Communion in due order.

From Thursday evening the altars are to remain bare until Saturday morning, and on that day no Responsory is sung at Vespers.

8. On Friday at the third hour, the pontiff, or whoever acts in his place, proceeds to the appointed church within the city, but not to the major church.

> **Note:** Colbertine manuscript: “On Friday, at the third hour, let all the presbyters, both of the city and of the suburbs, and all the clergy with the people assemble in the appointed church within the City, though not in the major church, and await the pontiff or whoever holds his place. When he comes from the sacristy,” and so forth. [Col. 0962D–0963D]

When he comes from the sacristy and proceeds before the altar to pray over the oratory [variant: to adore], as is customary, as soon as he rises he silently ascends to the seat. When he is seated, the subdeacon immediately ascends to read. After the reading, the canticle “O Lord, I have heard,” is sung with its verses.

The pontiff says, “Let us pray”; the deacon says, “Let us kneel,” followed by, “Arise.” He gives the Collect, “O God, from whom Judas …” Another reading follows, after which comes the Tract “He who dwells.”

> **Note:** In the Colbertine manuscript: “Deliver me, O Lord”; in the preceding Order: “He who dwells,” or “Deliver me.” [Col. 0963D]

When it is finished, the Passion of the Lord according to John is read. When it has been read as far as “They cast lots for my clothing,” two deacons immediately strip the altar of the linen cloth that had previously been placed beneath the Gospel, in the manner of a thief.

When the Gospel has been completed, the pontiff comes before the altar and says, “Let us pray.” The deacon says, “Let us kneel,” and he prays for a very long time; then he says, “Arise.” He continues, “Let us pray, dearly beloved, first for the Church of God,” and the remaining prayers in order, as we said above for Wednesday.

When he has finished them, everyone silently goes outside.

> **Note:** These words are absent from the Roman Codex up to “At evening, however,” and so forth. [Col. 0963D]

The presbyters of the churches, whether from the city or the suburbs, go through the churches and carry out all these things in this order at Vespers, changing only this: where the pontiff mentions the apostolic see, they name their own.
