At Vespers, both in the church where the pontiff says the prayers and in the other churches of the presbyters, after the prayers a cross is prepared before the altar, with an interval between it and the altar, supported on either side by two acolytes. An oratory is placed before it [variant: it is placed before the oratory].

The pontiff comes and venerates and kisses the cross; then the bishops, presbyters, deacons, and the others in order, followed by the people. The pontiff sits in his seat until everyone has venerated it.

As soon as the two senior presbyters have venerated it, they enter the sacristy, or the place where the Body of the Lord, left over from the previous day, had been placed. They put it on a paten, while a subdeacon holds before them a chalice with unconsecrated wine, and another subdeacon holds the paten with the Body of the Lord.

While these are being held, one of the senior presbyters takes the paten and the other the chalice, and they carry them onto the bare altar. The pontiff remains seated while the people venerate the cross.

Whenever the pontiff or the people venerate the cross, the antiphon is always sung:

> Behold the wood of the cross, on which hung the salvation of the world; come, let us adore.

For repetition, Psalm 118 is sung.

When the cross has been venerated and returned to its place, the pontiff descends before the altar and says, “Let us pray.” Then follows, “At the command of the Savior,” and “Our Father.” This is followed by, “Deliver us, we beseech you, O Lord.”

When they have said “Amen,” he takes a portion of the Holy Sacrament and places it in the chalice without saying anything. All receive Communion in silence, and everything is completed.

9. On Holy Saturday everyone comes into the church. Then two candles are illuminated, held by two notaries: one at the right corner of the altar and the other at the left. [Col. 0964A]

> **Note:** Amalarius reports these words verbatim from the Roman booklet in Book I, chapter 20, as stated above. [Col. 0963D–0964D]

The lector ascends the ambo. He does not announce, “A reading from the book of Genesis,” but begins simply, “In the beginning.” The other readings are handled in the same way. Before “In the beginning,” he does not say a Collect.

After the Collects and readings have been completed, one of the ministers immediately comes, holding ampullae in his hands, and stands at the right corner of the altar. He then goes ahead of the pontiff to the fonts.

Next the schola descends to the fonts to perform the litany, waiting for the pontiff to make his preparations. They do not finish the litany, but continue saying the *Agnus Dei* until the pontiff arrives and signals them to be silent. [36]

The second member of the schola holds a golden vessel in his left hand over his chasuble, from which the pontiff is to pour the chrism into the font.

Then the pontiff proceeds with all due ceremony, supported by two deacons. The two candle-bearers that had previously been illuminated proceed continually before him until everything has been completed [variant: until everything has been completed].

As soon as he arrives before the fonts, he stands and blesses them as customary. Here he first makes the cross at the fragment, “*Qui hanc aquam*” (“Who [—] this water”), dividing the water with his hand in the form of a cross; second, at “Therefore I bless you”; and likewise third, at “I bless you through Jesus Christ.”

After the fonts have been blessed, he pours in the chrism with the golden vessel and sprinkles [variant: spreads] the water with his hand over the people. Then he baptizes and returns to the sacristy, waiting to confirm the infants after they have been clothed.

10. Then, at the command, the schola performs a litany before the altar: first seven petitions; after an interval, another five; and after another interval, a third group of three.

While the *Agnus Dei* is being said, the master of the schola says in a loud voice, “Light them,” and then the church is illuminated.

The pontiff leaves the sacristy with the two candle-bearers, as we said above, and they stand as before on the right and left sides of the altar.

When the litany is completed, the pontiff says, “Glory to God in the highest.” Then the Apostle is read, followed by “Alleluia,” “Give thanks to the Lord,” and the Tract, “Praise the Lord, all nations.” They do not sing the Offertory, the *Agnus Dei*, or the Communion. Before the Gospel, they do not carry lights during that night, but only incense. [Col. 0964C]

> **Note:** Walafrid Strabo appropriately comments on this passage in chapter 22. He believes that in ancient times the holy Fathers offered or received Communion in silence, which, he says, we still observe on Holy Saturday of Easter. [Col. 0964D]

When the bishop pours the chrism on the infants’ foreheads, he must say:

> In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Peace be with you.

The response is:

> And with your spirit. [Col. 0964D]

11. From Easter until the octave of the Lord, at all the offices no Responsory is sung and no reading is recited. Instead of the Verse and Responsory, the Gradual “This is the day that the Lord has made” is sung only once. [Col. 0964D]

> **Note:** In some manuscripts “first” is read. In my opinion, the copyists incorrectly rendered this sign, “1,” which signifies “one,” “first,” or “once,” according to the circumstance.

On Easter Sunday, at *Venite*, *Alleluia* is said before “Let us go before his face,” and *Alleluia* is sung throughout all the Psalms. [Col. 0965A]

On Monday, at *Venite* and throughout the entire week, they say the antiphon, “The Lord has truly risen,” *Alleluia*.

## 12.

At the vespers of Holy Easter Day, the schola, having assembled somewhat earlier[Note: [Col. 0965C] Compare the published Roman Ordo, p. 80, where many things reported here—and indeed the Greek material altogether—are found.], together with the bishops and deacons in the greater church, at the place of the crucified one,[Note: [Col. 0965C] That is, at the place where a statue of the Crucified was placed upon a transverse beam in the basilica; this rite is still observed among us today, though scarcely among the Romans.] begin the *Kyrie eleison* and proceed as far as the altar. When the deacons ascend into the *pōgium*,[Note: [Col. 0965D] By *pōgium* here understand the place of the screens by which the sanctuary is separated from the choir; it was so called because it gradually rose by steps.] the bishops and priests are stationed in their places,[Note: [Col. 0965D] That is, behind the altar, around the apse, where the presbyterium was; it still exists at Rome in the more ancient basilicas.] and the schola before the altar. When the *Kyrie eleison* is finished,[Note: [Col. 0965D] The same is read in the published Roman Ordo, p. 80, col. 1. Although this seems contrary to Amalarius, whose words in Book IV, chapter 23, are: “We have it written in the Roman Ordo that *Kyrie eleison* or *Christe eleison* is not to be said at any office on the days mentioned, but without interruption we sing ‘This is the day,’ etc.” Compare no. 12 below. The Roman numerals after the verses occur only in the Colbertine manuscript.] the archdeacon gives a signal to the first member of the schola; and he, bowing to him, begins the *Alleluia* with the Psalm, “The Lord said to my Lord.” After this he gives a signal to the second, or to whomever he wishes; and he gives this instruction to all who begin in the same manner. He therefore says the *Alleluia* with Psalm 110.

After him the first member of the schola follows with the child *paraphonists*, singing *Alleluia*; and the *paraphonists* respond. The subdeacon follows with the children, singing *Alleluia, The Lord reigns*, and the rest; and the *paraphonists* always respond. He announces Verse 2 to the children: “Your throne, O God, is established.” Likewise Verse 3: “The rivers have lifted up, O Lord.” After these verses the first member of the schola greets the archdeacon; with his signal, he begins the *Alleluia* with the children’s melodies. When this has been completed, the *paraphonists* respond once. After this the third *Alleluia* begins, with Psalm 111. It is followed by:

*Alleluia. Christ our Passover has been sacrificed.*  
*Verse: Let us feast on the unleavened bread.*

When this order has been completed as above, the archdeacon begins in the Gospel[Note: [Col. 0965D] Here and in what follows, “Gospel” is used in place of the canticle *Magnificat*.] the antiphon, “I know that you seek Jesus,” or, “Jesus whom you seek.”[Col. 0965C]

After these things the priest says the Prayer, and they descend to the fonts with the antiphon, “On the day of my resurrection.” When they have finished it, the first member of the schola says the *Alleluia* with Psalm 112. It is followed by:

*Alleluia. The Lord has reigned.*  
*Verse: For he also established the inhabited world,[Greek: καὶ γὰρ ἐστερέωσε τὴν οἰκουμένην, ἥτις οὐ σαλευθήσεται.] which shall not be shaken.*

When the order has been completed as above, the second deacon follows in the Gospel with the antiphon, “Come and see the place where the Lord was laid. Alleluia, alleluia.” Then the priest says the Prayer, and they go to Saint John at the Vestment,[Note: [Col. 0966C] Some manuscripts omit “at the Vestment.” In the published text of Alcuin: “to Saint John at the Fonts, or at the Vestment.” There still exists the oratory of Saint John the Baptist at the Lateran Fonts, built by Pope Hilary; because perhaps those who were to be baptized put their garments there, and those already baptized resumed them there, it was called Saint John “at the Vestment.”] singing the antiphon, “The stone which the builders rejected”; then the *Alleluia* with Psalm 113.

Then the first member of the schola says with the boys:

*Alleluia. Come, let us rejoice in the Lord.*  
*Verse 2: Let us go before his face.*  
*Verse 3: Today, if you hear his voice.*

After this the deacon follows with the antiphon, “Go quickly and tell his disciples.” Then the Prayer is said, always without *Kyrie eleison*, and they go to Saint Andrew at the Cross.[Note: [Col. 0966D] The church of Saint Andrew, built by Pope Symmachus, was near the Vatican basilica.] They sing the antiphon, “I saw water flowing out from the temple on the right side,” followed by: “And all those to whom this water came were saved.” Then they say *Alleluia, alleluia*.

After this they say the *Alleluia* with Psalm 114. When it is finished, the schola begins, “Come, let us rejoice in the Lord,” and the rest as above. Then the antiphon, “Go quickly,” is said, followed by the Prayer.

Then the principal clergy of the church go down to the couches, at the invitation of the notary and *vicedominus*, and drink three times: once from the Greek,[Note: [Col. 0966D] The published texts read: once from the Greek, a second time from Pactis, and a third time from Procovia. In the Vatican manuscript: once from the Greek, once from Pactis, and once from Procoma; but in the Colbertine distinctly: “from the Greek once,” that is, once; “from Pactis once”; “from Procoma once.” Finally, in the Vendôme manuscript: once from the Greek, a second time from Pactis, and a third time from Procovium. Pactis and Procoma, or Procovium, were places where this kind of wine was produced. In the printed editions and in the Colbertine manuscript these words are lacking: “they drink what is given by the priest,” though they are found in the Vatican manuscript.] once from Pactis, and once from Procoma. After all the priests, and all the deacons or subdeacons, or all the acolytes from the several *tituli*, have drunk, they return to perform Vespers, and drink what is given by the priest. This arrangement is observed throughout the entire week, up to the Sunday in White.

## 13.

On Monday at Vespers they again enter the Lateran in the order given above, changing the following *Alleluia* after Psalm 111:

*Alleluia. O Lord, you have become our refuge from generation to generation.*  
*Verse 2: Before the mountains were made, or the earth and the world were formed, from eternity to eternity you are God.*

In the Gospel the deacon says the antiphon:

*Was it not necessary that Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory? Alleluia.*

After the Prayer has been given, they descend to the fonts with the antiphon:

*The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner. This was done by the Lord, and it is wonderful in our eyes. Alleluia, alleluia.*

Then, after Psalm 112, there follows the *Alleluia*:

*O shepherd of Israel, attend; you who guide Joseph like a sheep. You who sit upon the cherubim, appear before Ephraim and Benjamin and Manasseh.[Greek: Ὁ ποιμαίνων τὸν Ἰσραὴλ πρόσχες, ὁ ὁδηγῶν ὡς ἐπὶ πρόβατον τὸν Ἰωσήφ. Ὁ καθήμενος ἐπὶ τὰ χερουβὶμ ἐμφάνηθι ἐναντίον Ἐφραῒμ καὶ Βενιαμὶν καὶ Μανασσῆ.] (Psalm 79:1–2.) You brought a vine out of Egypt; you drove out the nations and planted it. You made a path before it, and it filled the land.[Greek: Ἄμπελον ἐξ Αἰγύπτου μετῇρας· ἐξέβαλες ἔθνη καὶ κατεφύτευσας αὐτήν. Ὡδοποίησας ἔμπροσθεν αὐτῆς, καὶ ἐπλήρωσε τὴν γῆν.] (Ibid. 9–10.)*

After this, in the Gospel, the antiphon is said:

*They recognized the Lord. Alleluia.*

At the breaking of the bread:

*Alleluia.*

After the Prayer has been given with an antiphon—whatever one you wish according to the place—they go down to Saint Andrew. After Psalm 113 has been said, there follows:

*Alleluia. When Israel went out of Egypt, the house of Jacob from a barbarous people.*  
*Verse 2: It was made.*  
*Verse 3: The sea saw.*

In the Gospel the antiphon is:

*The Lord has truly risen. Alleluia, and he appeared to Peter. Alleluia.*

The Prayer follows.

## 13.

On Tuesday, at evening, they again go to the Lateran. After Psalm 111:

*Alleluia. My heart is ready, O God; my heart is ready. I shall sing and chant a psalm to the Lord.*  
*Verse 2: Awake, my glory.*  
*Verse 2: That your beloved may be delivered.*

In the Gospel the antiphon is:

*Jesus stood in the midst of his disciples.*

After the Prayer has been given, they descend to the fonts with the antiphon. After Psalm 112 there follows the *Alleluia*:

*Attend, my people, to my law; incline your ear to the words of my mouth.[Greek: Προσέχετε, λαός μου, τῷ νόμῳ μου· κλίνατε τὸ οὖς ὑμῶν εἰς τὰ ῥήματα τοῦ στόματός μου.] (Psalm 77:1.)*  
*Verse: I will open my mouth in parables.[Greek: Ἀνοίξω ἐν παραβολαῖς.]*

In the Gospel the antiphon is:

*See my hands.*

After the Prayer, likewise at Saint Andrew, after Psalm 113, he says:

*Alleluia. I will confess to you, O Lord, with my whole heart, in the sight of the angels.*  
*Verse 2: I will worship toward your holy temple.*  
*Verse 3: Because of your mercy.*

In the Gospel the antiphon is:

*These are the words that I was speaking to you.*

## 15.

On Wednesday, after Psalm 111:

*Alleluia, alleluia. Praise is fitting for you, O God, in Zion.*  
*Verse: We shall be filled with the good things of your house.*

In the Gospel the antiphon is:

*Cast the net on the right side of the boat.*

After the Prayer has been given, they go to the fonts. After Psalm 113:

*Alleluia. Give thanks to the Lord and call upon his name.*  
*Verse 2: Sing to him and chant psalms to him.*  
*Verse 3: Glory in his holy name.*

In the Gospel the antiphon is:

*That disciple whom Jesus loved said to Peter, “It is the Lord.” Alleluia.*

After the Prayer has been given, likewise at Saint Andrew, after Psalm 113, they begin:

*This is the day.*

All respond:

*Which the Lord has made.*

Without an antiphon. In the Gospel the antiphon is:

*This he has now manifested for the third time.*

Only at the *tituli* do they say the Psalm with the *Alleluia*, or the Gradual:

*This is the day which the Lord has made.*

The antiphons are:

*They have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have laid him.*  
*I am ascending to my Father.*  
*Likewise, Mary came announcing it to the disciples.*

## 16.

On Thursday, after Psalm 111 [another reading: 112]:

*Alleluia. I rejoiced.*  
*Verse 2: They were standing.*  
*Likewise, Verse: Pray for the things that make for peace.*

In the Gospel the antiphon is:

*The eleven disciples.*

After the Prayer has been given, they descend with the antiphon to the Cross, to the chamber of Rigodem.[Note: [Col. 0967C] So it is found in both the Vatican and Colbertine manuscripts.] After Psalm 113, the Gradual is sung:

*This is the day which the Lord has made.*

The antiphon is:

*All things have been given to me.*

Then, after the Prayer, they go to the fonts. After Psalm 113:

*Alleluia. Those who trust in the Lord.*  
*Verse: The mountains surround him.*  
*Likewise, Verse 3: So that the righteous may not stretch out their hands.*

In the Gospel the antiphon is:

*Go and teach all nations.*

Likewise the antiphon:

*Jesus said to his disciples, “Bring”[sic; the supplied text reads *afferte*.]*

Likewise the antiphon:

*Behold, I am with you, alleluia, all days, alleluia.*

## 17.

On Friday,[Note: [Col. 0967C] Amalarius had another Roman Ordo before his eyes when he wrote in chapter 52 of the Antiphonary: “On Friday the Responsory ‘This is the day . . .’ is inserted between two Alleluias . . .” Concerning these things it is written in the Roman Ordo: “Up to the eighth day of Easter, according to Roman custom, we celebrate the aforesaid office,” etc.] after Psalm 115 [another reading: 111]:

*Alleluia. Sing to the Lord a new song, because he has done wonders.*  
*Verse: The Lord has made it known.*

In the Gospel the antiphon is:

*The disciples rejoiced. Alleluia.*

After the Prayer has been given, they descend to the fonts. After Psalm 111 [another reading: 115], the *Alleluia* is:

*The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the work of his hands.[Greek: Οἱ οὐρανοὶ διηγοῦνται δόξαν Θεοῦ, ποίησιν δὲ χειρῶν αὐτοῦ ἀναγγέλλει τὸ στερέωμα.] (Psalm 18:1–2.)*  
*Verse: Day pours forth the word to day, and night announces knowledge to night.[Greek: Ἡμέρα τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ἐρεύγεται ῥῆμα, καὶ νὺξ νυκτὶ ἀναγγέλλει γνῶσιν.]*

In the Gospel the antiphon is:

*Receive the Holy Spirit.*

## 18.

On Saturday, after Psalm 111 [another reading: 110]:

*Alleluia. Come, let us rejoice in the Lord; let us shout aloud to God our Savior.[Greek: Δεῦτε, ἀγαλλιασώμεθα τῷ κυρίῳ, ἀλαλάξωμεν τῷ θεῷ τῷ σωτῆρι ἡμῶν.] (Psalm 94:1.)*  
*Verse: Let us go before his face with confession, and let us shout aloud to him with psalms.[Greek: Προφθάσωμεν τὸ πρόσωπον αὐτοῦ ἐν ἐξομολογήσει, καὶ ἐν ψαλμοῖς ἀλαλάξωμεν αὐτῷ.]*  
*Verse: For the Lord is a great God, and a great King over all the earth.[Greek: Ὅτι θεὸς μέγας κύριος, καὶ βασιλεὺς μέγας ἐπὶ πᾶσαν τὴν γῆν.]*

And in the same church there follows the antiphon:

*Because you have seen me, Thomas, you have believed; blessed are those who have not seen and have believed.*

Psalm:

*Blessed is the man who fears the Lord.*

After this:

*Alleluia. All nations, clap your hands.*  
*Verse 2: For the Lord Most High is terrible.*  
*Verse 3: God has ascended amid jubilation.*

In the Gospel the antiphons are:

*Put out your hand and recognize.*

Likewise:

*I have put my finger.*

Likewise:

*Now these things have been written.*

After the Prayer has been given, the service ends in the name of the Lord.

*This concludes successfully, with God’s help. Amen.*

# [ROMAN ORDO II]

## ADMONITION CONCERNING THE SECOND ROMAN ORDO

### 1.

The Roman Ordo that follows here was first published by Cassander and Hittorp. Onuphrius Panvinius thinks that it is the Gelasian Ordo, corrected by Gregory the Great. Nevertheless, the Ordo presented above seems to contain more elements of an older rite, such as the practice whereby the *Sancta*, that is, the Eucharist, are carried at the beginning of the pontifical Mass—namely, in the procession to the altar—from the *secretarium*, or sacristy; and whereby they are put into the chalice, apart from a particle taken from a Host freshly consecrated.

In the following Ordo, however, when the pontiff reaches the altar he adores the *Sancta*, which therefore must already have been on the altar, not in the *secretarium*, as in the other Roman Ordo. Nor is there any mention except of a single particle placed in the chalice.

### 2.

Nevertheless, this Ordo is extremely ancient, since Amalarius explained it in sections in the *Egloga* composed on this Ordo, which the distinguished Stephanus Baluzius published from a very ancient manuscript of Saint Gall in the appendix to the *Capitularies*. It seemed appropriate to reproduce it here among the *Probationes* of the ritual books. Micrologus also had this very Roman Ordo before his eyes in chapter 9, where he notes three features from the Roman Ordo that are found only here: namely, the sign of the cross on the forehead and breast during the reading of the Gospel; the laying aside of staffs; and the deacon’s station while reading, facing south rather than north.

In the printed editions it is entitled: “The Order of the Procession to the Church or to Mass.” The following title seems more suitable.

# ROMAN ORDO II: CONCERNING THE PONTIFICAL MASS (C)

## 1.

When the station has been announced on feast days, early in the morning the entire clergy precedes the pontiff to the church, except those who accompany him in his service and who are listed in their proper order, awaiting the pontiff in the church.

But when the pontiff has come near the church, the acolytes and *defensores* from that region whose day is assigned to service go out and await him at the appointed place, before he arrives at the place where he will dismount. Likewise, the priest of the *titulus* or church where the station is to be held, together with the principal officers of that city, or the Father of the *diaconia*—if that church is a *diaconia*—with the priest and *mansionarius* subject to him, carry censers in his service and bow their heads when he arrives.

The acolytes with the *defensores* first, and then the priests with their attendants, having requested a blessing, proceed before the pontiff, divided on either side according to the assignments under which they serve, all the way to the church.

## 2.

When the pontiff has entered the church, he does not immediately ascend to the altar, but first enters the *secretarium*, supported by the deacons who received him as he descended from the saddle. When he has entered, he sits in his chair.

The deacons, having greeted the pontiff, leave the *secretarium* and change their vestments before its doors. The one who is to read the Gospel prepares it, having broken the seal at the archdeacon’s command, over the chasuble of the acolyte.

The pontiff, meanwhile, changes his solemn vestments with the assistance of the regional subdeacons. The *primicerius* and *secundicerius* arrange his vestments in proper order so that they sit well. Finally, through the deacon or subdeacon whom he himself has commanded, the pallium is placed upon him and fastened with pins to the chasuble at the back, front, and left shoulder. Then the regional subdeacon presents him with the *mappula*, bowing toward his knees.

## 3.

When these things have been arranged, the aforementioned subdeacon invites the schola to the royal entrance of the *secretarium*. The fourth member of the schola, who always announces the singers to the pontiff, stands before the pontiff’s face and awaits his signal to chant. As soon as he signals to him, he goes out before the doors of the *secretarium* and says, “Light them.”

When they have lit them, the following subdeacon immediately places incense in the golden censer before the doors, so that he may proceed before the pontiff. The fourth member of the schola, bowing his head to the first, second, or third, says, “Command, lords.”

Then two lines are arranged in the choir in due order, one on each side, and immediately the first member of the schola begins the Introit antiphon. The subdeacons from the schola lift the chasubles by their folds; when the deacons hear their voice, they immediately enter the *secretarium* to the pontiff.

## 4.

Then the pontiff rises and gives his right hand to two priests. After kissing his hands, they proceed with him, supporting him; seven deacons go before them.

Then the ministers with censers and thuribles—no more than three—proceed before him, scattering incense. Seven acolytes carrying seven candleholders, lit outside the church,[Note: [Col. 0969D] Amalarius, in the *Egloga*: “The candles are first lit by the acolytes outside the church,” etc.] go before the pontiff as far as the choir. After the thuribles, the Gospel book is carried nearer to the bishop.

This procession proceeds from south to north. Then the pontiff advances, and before he reaches the schola the candleholders are divided, four to the right and three to the left. The pontiff passes to the head of the schola and, on the higher step, bowing his head toward the altar, first adores the *Sancta*,[Note: [Col. 0969D] That is, the Eucharist. Amalarius’s *Egloga* says at this point: “The bishop, coming before the altar, first adores the *Sancta*, and afterward gives the peace to the priests,” etc.] and remains bowed until the prophetic verse.[Note: [Col. 0970D] That is, until the repetition of the Verse or antiphon of the Introit, which antiphon is always taken from the Prophet’s Psalms.]

## 5.

Then he rises, makes the sign of the cross on his forehead, and gives the peace to two priests and to all the deacons who are on the right and left: from the higher step, to the smaller number; from the lower, to the larger. Looking toward the first member of the schola, he signals to him to say, “Glory be to the Father.” The first member of the schola bows to the pontiff and gives glory to the Trinity.

The pontiff is then led by the aforementioned priests to the higher step, but not all the way to the altar. He must keep his step fixed there until the priests first, then the deacons two by two, kiss the horns of the altar, and finally the archdeacon alone. The Gospel book, immediately after they reach the altar, is placed upon it.

The subdeacons, stretched out as though in a single line, proceed as far as the altar; they bow together before it and, after the Gospel has been placed upon it as stated, return to the choir, four standing on the right and three on the left.

The deacons, as before, stand behind the bishop, bowed. When “As it was in the beginning” is said, they rise to greet the sides of the altar first—that is, before the bishop[Note: [Col. 0970D] By this term the pontiff is often designated absolutely.]—two by two in turn, and return to the bishop.

Finally, the bishop kisses the Gospel book and the altar, proceeds to the right side of the altar to his seat, and stands upright facing east. The deacons stand upright behind him, one behind another, more on the right side and fewer on the left side of the altar.

At the deacon’s signal, the schola imposes the litany: *Kyrie eleison, Christe eleison*, and the rest. Immediately the acolytes place the candleholders on the floor of the church, four on the right side and three on the left,[Note: [Col. 0970D] Or, as others prefer, in a line from south to north.]

## 6.

When the litany is finished, the pontiff alone begins in a clear voice the hymn *Glory to God in the highest*, if the season permits. Then the entire choir responds, “And on earth peace to men.” The bishop does not sit before they say “Amen” after the first Prayer.

Afterward, greeting the people, the pontiff says:

*Peace be with you,* or, *Peace to you.*[Note: [Col. 0971D] The printed editions add: “But the priest: The Lord be with you.”]

Response:

*And with your spirit.*

Then he says:

*Let us pray.*

The first Prayer follows, which they call the Collect, up to:

*Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you, God, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages.*

Response:

*Amen.*

Then the candleholders are removed from the place where they had previously stood, so that they may be placed in a single line from east to west through the middle of the church.

After the first Prayer has been given, the pontiff sits facing the people, with the priests beside him at his signal, while the deacons stand before the pontiff. The subdeacons ascend to the altar, taking their positions on the right or left.

## 7.

As soon as the subdeacon who is to read sees the priests seated behind the pontiff, he ascends the ambo to read—but not to the higher step, which only the one who is to read the Gospel customarily ascends.

After he has read, the cantor with the *cantorium*, without any necessity,[Note: [Col. 0971D] Perhaps: “without any pause.” Nevertheless, the *Egloga* suggests that the cantor could ascend higher without distinction.] ascends—not higher—but stands in the same place as the reader. He alone begins the Responsory; everyone in the choir responds, and he alone sings the Verse of the Responsory.

If the season permits the *Alleluia* to be said, so be it; otherwise, the Tract; if neither, only the Responsory. The cantor who begins the *Alleluia* alone sings its Verse. He again says the *Alleluia*, standing on the same step, that is, the lower one.[Note: [Col. 0971D] The printed editions insert: “The jubilus follows, which they call the Sequence.” But there is nothing about this in the *Egloga*. Certainly the “Sequences”—that is, the rhythmic chants sometimes inserted by us between the *Alleluia* and the Gospel—were not in use before Notker Balbulus, who is said to have been their author and died in 912.]

## 8.

Then the deacon kisses the pontiff’s feet and, having requested a blessing, comes before the altar. After kissing the Gospel book, he lifts into his hands the Codex from which he is to read, places part of it on his right shoulder, and goes to the ambo.

Two subdeacons proceed before him with two thuribles, or one. They take the censer from the hand of the following subdeacon and put in incense. Two acolytes carrying two candleholders come before the ambo and separate from one another. The subdeacons and the deacon with the Gospel pass between them.

The two subdeacons with the thuribles ascend into the ambo before the Gospel from one side and immediately descend from the other. They return to stand before the step by which one descends from the ambo.

The one without the censer turns toward the deacon and extends his left arm. The deacon places the Gospel book upon it, so that the place where the reading mark has been set may be opened for him by the hand of the subdeacon. Once the place of the reading has been found, he ascends to the higher step of the ambo and says:

*The Lord be with you.*

Everyone responds:

*And with your spirit.*

When he hears this, the pontiff and the entire priestly order—or the entire faithful people—turn toward the east.[Note: [Col. 0971D] The frequently cited *Egloga* observes this.]

After he has said:

*The continuation of the holy Gospel according to Luke,* or *according to Mark*, and the rest,

the same deacon makes the sign of the cross on his forehead and breast. Likewise the bishop and all the people do so.[Note: [Col. 0971D] The *Egloga* makes no mention of the breast, but only of the forehead. Micrologus, however, has both in chapter 9.[Col. 0972D]] Then they turn back toward the Gospel.

The staffs of all are also laid down,[Note: [Col. 0972D] The author of the *Egloga* says: “After this the staffs are laid down from their hands,” etc. These were staffs on which people leaned while standing for prayer, so that the station would be less burdensome. He continues: “Nor do they at that hour hold a crown or any other covering upon their heads.” More concerning the pontifical crown appears below.] and at that hour neither crowns nor any other covering are worn on their heads.

The deacon himself stands facing south, the direction toward which the men customarily gather; otherwise, toward the north.[Note: [Col. 0972D] Amalarius notes this in the *Egloga*. The following words, “otherwise, toward the north,” seem to have been inserted here. Compare chapter 9 of Micrologus.]

The candles also are set down on the floor beside the ambo, out of the acolytes’ hands, while he proclaims the Gospel, until the Gospel reading is finished.

When the Gospel has been read, the people hasten to fortify themselves again with the sign of the holy cross. As the deacon descends from the ambo, the subdeacon who stands in line receives the Gospel book. Holding it before his breast over the chasuble, he presents it to be kissed first by the bishop[Note: [Col. 0972D] The printed editions add: “or by a priest”], then by all who stand according to the order of their rank, and by the entire clergy, as well as by the people. Then it is put away in its proper place.

## 9.

After the Gospel has been read,[Note: [Col. 0972D] Amalarius in the *Egloga*: “After the Gospel has been read, the candles are extinguished.”] the candles are extinguished in their proper place, and the bishop sings:

*I believe in one God.*[Note: [Col. 0972D] From Amalarius’s *Egloga* we understand that this passage concerning the Creed has not been interpolated, although Berno of Reichenau says otherwise, stating that the Creed was not sung in the Roman Church before the reign of Saint Henry. Micrologus, who followed this Ordo, says nothing about the Creed.]

The thuribles are carried around the altars, and afterward brought to the noses of the people; the smoke is drawn toward the mouth by the hand.

Then the bishop greets the people, saying:

*The Lord be with you.*

Afterward he says:

*Let us pray.*

The Offertory is then sung with its Verses.

The subdeacon comes carrying a paten on his right arm and a chalice on his left, into which the people’s small vessels are emptied. A corporal—that is, a linen cloth—is placed over the chalice. The deacon takes it and places it on the altar to the right, with one end extended toward the second deacon, so that they may spread it out.

Then the priest proceeds to receive the offerings. Meanwhile the singers sing the Offertory with its Verses, and the people present their offerings, that is, bread and wine. They offer with white cloths: first the men, then the women. Finally the priests and deacons offer, but bread only, and this before the altar.

The subdeacon with the empty chalice follows the archdeacon. As the pontiff receives the people’s offerings, the archdeacon receives the small vessels behind him and pours them into the larger chalice, which the subdeacon holds. An acolyte follows him with a bowl over the chasuble, into which the filled chalice is emptied.

The subdeacon receives the offerings from the pontiff and places them in the linen cloth that follows him, held by two acolytes.

Then, with two priests holding his hands, the bishop returns to his seat and washes his hands. The archdeacon looks into the pontiff’s face and gives him a signal. The pontiff returns his greeting and, while the singers are still singing, approaches the altar.

The subdeacons lift the offerings from the hand of the following subdeacon and present them to the archdeacon, who arranges the altar. When the altar has been adorned, the archdeacon takes the pontiff’s small vessel containing wine from the subdeacon and pours it through the strainer into the chalice.

Then the following subdeacon descends to the schola, receives the water from the chief *paraphonist*, and carries it to the archdeacon. The archdeacon pours it from the small vessel into the chalice, making the sign of the cross. The deacons ascend to the pontiff.

Then the pontiff rises from his seat and, while the singers are still singing, descends to the altar. He prays, greets the altar, and receives the offerings from the hands of the priests and deacons who are permitted to approach the altar.

Then the archdeacon receives two offerings from the offering-bearer and gives them to the pontiff. When the pontiff has placed them on the altar, the archdeacon lifts the chalice from the hand of the subdeacon and places it on the altar to the right beside the pontiff’s offerings, with its handles wrapped in its offertory cloth. He also places the cloth at the right horn of the altar.

After the offering, incense is placed on the altar. The pontiff bows slightly toward the altar, looks toward the schola, and signals them to be silent. Then he turns toward the people and says:

*Pray.*

## 10.

When the Offertory is finished, the priests arrange themselves behind the pontiff, the archdeacon to their right, the second deacon to their left, and the rest in order in a line.

After the Offertory, the subdeacons also go behind the altar, looking toward the pontiff and standing upright until the Prayer over the offerings, the Secret, has been said. When the bishop begins in a loud voice, *Throughout all ages of ages*, after the greeting and exhortation, and the Preface has been completed, they begin to say the angelic hymn, that is:

*Holy, holy, holy*,

in which *Hosanna* is repeated twice.[Col. 0974A]

When they have completed this,[Note: [Col. 0973D] Bishop Herard of Tours gives a corresponding instruction in chapter 16: “Let priests not begin the Secret—that is, the Canon—before the *Sanctus* has been completed.”] the pontiff alone rises and silently enters the Canon.[Note: [Col. 0973D] Therefore the Canon was not recited in a raised voice, as among the Greeks. See the *Egloga* and Remigius of Auxerre.] The deacons, subdeacons, and all the priests in the presbyterium remain bowed.

Six orders of crosses are observed in this Canon.[Note: [Col. 0973D] When Bishop Boniface asked about these signs of the crosses, Pope Zachary answered in a letter numbered 142 among the Bonifacian letters.]

The first is at the words:

*That you may accept and bless these gifts, these offerings, these holy and unblemished sacrifices.*

The second is at:

*Which offering, O God, we ask you in all respects to bless, approve, ratify.*

The third order of the cross is at:

*And taking bread into his holy and venerable hands, he blessed it.*

Likewise:

*Giving you thanks, he blessed it.*

The fourth is where it continues:

*A pure Victim, a holy Victim, an unblemished Victim, the holy Bread of eternal life and the Chalice of everlasting salvation.*

The fifth is at:

*Through whom, O Lord, you always create all these good things, sanctify them, give them life, and bless them.*

The sixth order follows when:

*Through him, and with him, and in him*

is pronounced, at which point the chalice is touched with the offering.

During the same rite, the deacons, still bowed, wash their hands with the assistance of the acolytes. When the priest says:

*We humbly beseech you*,

he bows before the altar with his head lowered.

When he says in a loud, open voice:

*To us also, sinners*,

the subdeacons rise, stand in the place where they had stood before, and look upward into the pontiff’s face.

When he says:

*Through whom, O Lord, you always create all these good things*,

the archdeacon alone rises.

When he says:

*Through him, and with him*,

the archdeacon lifts the chalice by its handles with its offertory cloth and holds it raised beside the pontiff.

The pontiff touches the side of the chalice with the offerings, making two crosses and saying:

*Through him, and with him*, through *Throughout all ages of ages.*

The pontiff places the offerings in their proper place, and the archdeacon places the chalice beside them, leaving the offertory cloth on its handles.

## 11.

The Preface of the Lord’s Prayer follows aloud, together with the Lord’s Prayer and its embolism,[Note: [Col. 0973D] That is, with the prayer that follows it, “Deliver us, we beseech you, Lord,” etc.] in which three divisions of the Prayer are found.

When the subdeacons have seen the chalice containing the Lord’s Blood surrounded by the offertory cloth, and have heard:

*But deliver us from evil*,

they go behind the standing deacons and prepare clean chalices or linen cloths in which they may receive the Lord’s Body, lest it fall to the ground and be turned into dust.[Note: [Col. 0974D] Namely, through the breaking, discussed in the preceding Ordo. What the *Egloga* says here is obscure: “Afterward, that is, after the Lord’s Prayer, the Lord’s Body mixed with the wine, and peace having been announced, the Lord’s Body is taken from the altar.” And below: “And therefore, because the whole human being has risen, it is right that immediately the Lord’s chalice also be removed from the altar with the offering”—apparently for the purpose of giving Communion to the pontiff, who customarily received Communion at his seat.]

The matter concerning the paten, which we omitted, is as follows. When the Canon begins, an acolyte comes with a linen cloth tied around his neck beneath his shoulder, holding the paten before his breast on the right side until the middle of the Canon.

Then the following subdeacon receives it over the chasuble and comes before the altar, awaiting the regional subdeacon’s reception of it.

When the Canon has been completed, the regional subdeacon stands with the uncovered paten behind the archdeacon. When he has said:

*And secure from every disturbance*,

the archdeacon turns, kisses the paten, and gives it to the second deacon to hold.[Note: [Col. 0975C] The printed editions add after this: “After the pontifical blessings have been given—as is customary in these regions—when he has said,” etc. I have no doubt that this addition is by a Gallican or German scribe, since such blessings were not customary among the Romans, as we noted above, and nothing about them is found in the *Egloga*.[Col. 0976C]]

## 12.

When he has said:

*The peace of the Lord be always with you*,

he places a portion of the consecrated offering into the chalice. The archdeacon gives the peace to the senior bishop; then the others in order, and the people, men and women separately.

Then the pontiff breaks the offering at the right side and leaves the particle he has broken upon the altar. He places the remaining offerings on the paten held by the deacon and returns to his seat.

## 13.

Now the archdeacon lifts the chalice and gives it to the chief subdeacon, who holds it beside the right horn of the altar.

The subdeacons then approach with the acolytes carrying bags, on the right and left. The acolytes extend their arms with the bags and stand in front, so that they may open the mouths of the bags for the archdeacon to place the offerings in them, first on the right and then on the left.

Then the acolytes go to the right and left behind the bishops, around the altar. The others descend to the priests in order to break the Hosts.

The paten goes first beside the seat, carried by two subdeacons to the deacons so that they may break the Hosts. But they look toward the pontiff’s face, awaiting his signal to break them. When he has signaled, they return his greeting and break them.

The archdeacon, having emptied the altar of the offerings, looks toward the schola and signals them to say:

*Lamb of God.*

Then he goes to the paten with the others.

When the breaking has been completed, the junior deacon takes the paten from the subdeacon and carries it to the seat so that the pontiff may receive Communion. After he has received Communion, he places in the chalice, between the hands of the archdeacon, a portion of the *Sancta* from which he had bitten, making the sign of the cross three times and saying:

*May this commingling and consecration of the Body and Blood of our Lord Jesus Christ bring eternal life to us who receive it.*

Response:

*Amen.*

*Peace be with you.*

Response:

*And with your spirit.*
14. Then the archdeacon comes with the chalice to the corner of the altar and announces the station. After pouring a little from the flagon into the chalice held by the acolyte, the bishops first approach the seat to receive Communion from the pontiff’s hand, in order. All the presbyters likewise ascend to receive Communion at the altar. The first bishop receives the chalice from the archdeacon’s hand and stands at the corner of the altar to administer Communion to those following in order. Then the archdeacon takes the chalice from his hand, pours its contents back into the flagon mentioned above, and hands the chalice to the regional subdeacon, who gives him the small vessel with which he is to administer Communion to the people. The subdeacon then takes the chalice and gives it to the acolyte, who carries it back to the sacristy.

When he has administered Communion to those whom the pope communicates, the pontiff descends from his seat, supported by those who had led him there, to communicate those who are in the senatorial area; afterward the archdeacon administers Communion to them. Then the bishops communicate the people at the pontiff’s signal, and after them the deacons administer Communion. The presbyters, at the pontiff’s command, communicate the people and themselves in turn administer Communion.

As soon as the pontiff begins to communicate the people in the senatorial area, the schola immediately begins the Antiphon for Communion and sings until all the people, including those in the women’s section, have received Communion. The pontiff returns to his seat, and when the Verse has been repeated, they cease. After all these, he communicates the regional officials at the seat in order, as well as those who had stood in the line, the treasurer, the acolyte holding the paten, the one holding the towel, and the one supplying the water. After the pontiff, the archdeacon administers Communion to them.

15. When the pontiff sees that the people have received Communion, he signals through the subdeacon to the first member of the schola. The first member of the schola, after again saluting the pontiff, says, “Glory to the Father,” and “As it was,” and the Verse. When the Antiphon is finished, the pontiff rises with the archdeacon, comes to the altar, and gives the Prayer after Communion. When it is finished, the deacon whom the archdeacon has instructed looks toward the pontiff for his signal and says to the people, “Go, the dismissal is made.” Response: “Thanks be to God.”

Then seven candle-bearing stands precede the pontiff, and the subdeacon with the thurible accompanies him to the sacristy. When he descends into the presbytery, the bishops first say, “Command, lord, a blessing.” Response: “May the Lord bless you.” Response: “Amen.” After the bishops come the presbyters, then the monks, then those of the schola, then all the processional officers and the mansionarii, and he enters the sacristy.

[Note: At the time when this was written, monks lived at the Lateran and at Saint Peter’s, as stated above in chapter 4 of the Commentary.]

[ORDO ROMANUS III.]

[Col. 0975]

ADMONITION ON THE THIRD ROMAN ORDER.

[Col. 0975] 52 I cannot easily say at what time the following Roman Order was written. It contains almost the same things as the two preceding orders. The Eucharist is not carried to the altar before the Mass, and there is not a twofold but a single commingling of the consecrated particle before Communion. We noted above that both of these are also absent from the Second Roman Order, unlike the First.

The use of the word *monastery* for the principal church, as it is found in the following Order, no. 3, does not seem to have been current before the ninth century. I find no distinctive passage of this Order cited either by Amalarius or by the Micrologus. Hence it may be conjectured that this Order is not as ancient as the other two, which were cited by both authors.

Moreover, we have not been able to find a copy of this Third Order by which we could distinguish any interpolated passages it may contain. It is doubtful whether such are the words found in no. 18: “For wine, even when not consecrated but mingled with the Lord’s blood, is sanctified in every way.” For nothing similar occurs in the two preceding booklets, although the same occasion presents itself. We discuss this matter more fully in our commentary.

After this Third Order we shall append a fragment of a Fourth Pontifical Order from a manuscript that once belonged to Constantine Cajetanus.

[Col. 0977]

ROMAN ORDER III (C)

[Col. 0977A] In the name of the Lord, the book of the Roman Order begins: How the office of the Mass is to be celebrated.

53 1. First of all, it must be observed that there are seven regions of the ecclesiastical order in the city of Rome, and that each region has its own regional deacon. The acolytes of each region are subject, through the regional subdeacon, to the deacon of their own region for the performance of their duties. The higher orders, both of deacons and of subdeacons, must obey the archdeacon, who is the pontiff’s deputy, while he preserves for each its proper ministerial order according to its rank.

2. Whoever wishes to know the number of the ecclesiastical regions must also know the number of the weekdays on which, in a circular order, they serve according to the ancient arrangement. On the first day of the week—Easter Sunday—the third region shall minister; on the second day, the fourth region; on the third day, the fifth region; on the fourth day, the sixth region; on the fifth day, the seventh region; on the sixth day, the first region; and on Saturday, the second region.

Thus each region shall have its own ranks both in procession and in church, or wherever the established order of its rank requires them to go or minister on its proper day according to the ancient constitution. No one assigned to a particular region may be absent from the pontiff’s ministry without a sentence of excommunication or disciplinary penalty.

3. When the station has been announced on feast days, early in the morning the entire clergy ought to precede the Apostolicus to the church, except for the official ministers who accompany him in attendance according to his pontifical dignity: namely, the station deacons, the subdeacons, and all the acolytes of the region whose duty it is to minister to the pontiff that day.

The lay chamberlain, however, is charged with ensuring that the pontiff’s chair is ready in the sacristy until he arrives to celebrate the divine mysteries. The bishops and presbyters, awaiting the pontiff in the presbytery together with those preparing the ecclesiastical vestments and the church vessels, shall sit according to this local arrangement: as one enters the church, the bishops shall be on the left and the presbyters on the right, so that when the pontiff sits and looks toward them, he sees the bishops on his right and the presbyters on his left.

4. The pontiff is received by the presbyters of the title or of the church where the station has been proclaimed, together with the leading clergy of that church. A censer of incense is offered for his service, with the heads of those offering it bowed. After they have requested and received his blessing, they precede the pontiff on both sides to the church, each according to the order in which he happens to serve.

The acolytes, however, are responsible for ensuring that the vessels of the sacred ministry are carried. They receive them through the hands of the first mansionarius, who is the custodian of the Lord’s wardrobe, and have them carried by porters from the principal [Note: [Col. 0977] Here “monastery” means “church,” according to the usage current from the ninth century onward.] church to the place where the station is to be celebrated. These vessels are the *aquamanile*, that is, the hand-washing vessel; patens; chalices and flagons; small vessels; golden or silver vessels; silver flagons prepared for pouring wine; a golden or silver strainer; and the chant book.

The subdeacon who is to read shall have the Apostolic Epistle in his keeping, and the archdeacon shall have the Gospel.

5. When the pontiff has entered the church, he does not immediately ascend to the altar. He first enters the sacristy, supported by the deacons, who meet him as he descends from the sedan, receiving him, as they say, with outstretched hands. When he has arrived there and sat in his chair, the deacons, after saluting the pontiff, leave the sacristy in orderly formation and change their vestments before its doors.

When the deacons leave the sacristy, the first secretary and the notaries of the station remain with the pontiff, as do the subdeacons already prepared for their duties. One of these holds the pontiff’s pallium, with its pin, over the chasuble on his left arm. Through the hands of the regional subdeacons, the pontiff himself changes into his solemn vestments, just as the Levites do on the other side.

6. The regional subdeacons, according to their order, take the vestments with which to clothe the pontiff: one the linen garment; another the *ambolagium*, that is, the amice, which is called the shoulder garment; another the linen dalmatic, which we call the alb; another the girdle; another the dalmatic; another the orarium; and another the chasuble. Thus they clothe the pontiff in order.

The first and second secretaries arrange the pontiff’s vestments so that, through their dignified arrangement, a spectacle of reverent rank may be presented to those standing nearby.

Finally, the deacon whom the lord pontiff has ordered takes the pallium from the hand of the next subdeacon, puts it on the pontiff, fastens it with its pin to the chasuble at the back, the front, and the left shoulder, salutes the lord, and says, “Command, lord, a blessing.” He replies, “May the Lord save us. Amen.”

7. Then the regional subdeacon reports to the pontiff who are to read or sing. With a disciplined inclination toward the pontiff’s knees, he places a small cloth over the pontiff’s left arm above the chasuble and announces that such-and-such regional subdeacon is to read the Epistle, and such-and-such is to sing the Responsory and such-and-such the Alleluia. Afterward it is not permitted to substitute another person in the place of reader or singer. If this is done, the archiparaphonista—that is, the fourth member of the schola, who must always report the singers to the pontiff—shall be excommunicated.

Two lines are arranged in order, with four paraphonistae outside, on either side; the boys stand below them in order on both sides. After the pontiff has signaled to the archiparaphonista to begin the singing, he says either to the acolytes standing before the doors of the sacristy with the candle-bearing stands, or to the regional subdeacon who is to carry the censer before him in the procession: “Light them.”

8. The fourth member of the schola arrives in the presbytery, where the choir stands in four groups, as stated above, arranged with reverent order. After he has said, with bowed head, to the first, second, or third member of the schola, “Lord, give the command,” the first member of the schola immediately begins the Introit Antiphon.

When they hear its voice, the deacons enter the sacristy to the pontiff. After the archdeacon and the second deacon have received and kissed the pontiff’s hands on both sides, the deacons proceed with him, supporting him. The remaining ranks proceed in their order, except that one of the regional subdeacons must precede with the censer.

Seven acolytes of the region whose day it is follow him, carrying seven lighted candle-bearing stands before the pontiff until he reaches the altar. Before the procession reaches the schola, however, the candle-bearing stands are divided: four on the right and three on the left.

In this reverent ceremony the pontiff is to come to the tribunal of the church and bow his head toward the altar. After rising, he makes the sign of the cross on his forehead, gives the kiss of peace to one of the weekly bishops, to the archpriest, and to all the deacons. Then, looking toward the first member of the schola, he signals him to say the Gloria.

The first member bows to the pontiff and begins the Hymn by which glory is given to the Holy Trinity. Meanwhile the pontiff silently concelebrates the Prayer, bowed before the altar, until the repetition of the Verse. When “As it was in the beginning” is said, the deacons rise from their inclination and, saluting the sides of the altar, return two by two to the pontiff, each retaining his place according to his order.

At the repetition of the Verse, the pontiff rises from the Prayer, as stated above, kisses the Gospel and the altar, then approaches the seat and stands facing east.

9. When the schola has finished the Antiphon, it begins the “Kyrie eleison.” The first member of the schola must watch the pontiff for the signal to change the number of the litany, and at his signal he bows.

When this has been completed, the pontiff begins “Glory to God in the highest,” if the season permits. The pontiff ought not to sit before they say “Amen” after the first Prayer.

Then the regional subdeacons are to ascend and station themselves on the right and left of the altar. The subdeacon who is to read, after seeing the bishops or presbyters sit behind the pontiff—whom the pontiff himself causes by a nod to sit with him—ascends the ambo and reads the lesson.

After the reader has read, the cantor ascends with the chant book and sings the Responsory. Then, through another cantor, the Alleluia is sung if the season permits; otherwise only the Responsory is sung.

10. Then the deacon kisses the pontiff’s feet and receives from him this blessing: “May the Lord be in your heart and on your lips.” He comes before the altar, kisses the Gospels, and lifts the Codex in his hands.

The first of the two subdeacons who are merely to precede the deacon puts incense into the censer; the other receives it through the next subdeacon of the station in order to carry it.

Two acolytes with two candle-bearing stands proceed before them. After these acolytes have divided before the ambo, the subdeacons and the deacon carrying the Gospels pass through the middle between them.

The subdeacon who is without the censer extends his left arm so that he may receive the Gospel book from the deacon and open for him the place where the reading marker has been placed. When the deacon ascends to read, these two subdeacons return to stand before the steps of descent.

When the Gospel has been completed, the pontiff says, “Peace to you,” or “The Lord be with you.” The response follows: “And with your spirit.”

When the deacon descends, the subdeacon who had earlier opened the Gospel book receives it. Returning to the presbytery, he hands it to one of the subdeacons, so that he may offer it for kissing to all who have stood in the ordered ranks. After the Gospel reading, the Gospel book is placed in some repository or in the sacristy.

11. The acolyte holding the chalice on his left arm offers the corporal laid over it to the deacon. The deacon takes the chalice from above and spreads the corporal over the altar, throwing the other end toward the next deacon.

[Col. 0980C] 12. The pontiff, supported on his right and left by the first secretary of the notaries and the first secretary of the defenders, descends to the senatorial area, which is the place of the leading persons, to receive their offerings.

The archdeacon follows him and receives the flagons. He pours their contents into the larger chalice, which the next regional subdeacon carries, empty. When it has been filled, it is poured into the ministerial chalice held there by the next acolyte.

The regional subdeacon receives the offerings of the leading persons from the pontiff and hands them to the next subdeacon, who places them in the linen cloth held by two acolytes.

The weekly bishop receives, after the pontiff, the offerings of the others; he himself places them by hand into the linen cloth that follows him. After him, the next deacon receives the flagons and pours them by hand into the flagon after the archdeacon.

The pontiff likewise passes to the women’s section and completes everything as above.

13. Then he returns to the seat, with the first secretaries holding his hands. After the reception of the offerings has been completed, the archdeacon, standing before the altar, washes his hands. After this he looks toward the pontiff. When the pontiff signals to him, he salutes him with a humble inclination and approaches the altar.

Then, receiving the offerings from the subdeacons who extend them from both sides, he places upon the altar as many as will suffice for the people. When the altar has been arranged and adorned, the archdeacon takes the pontiff’s flagon from the subdeacon responsible for the offerings and pours it into the chalice through the strainer; then he pours in those of the deacons, and afterward those of the first and second secretaries.

The next subdeacon then descends to the schola, receives the water from the hand of the archiparaphonista, brings it to the archdeacon, and he pours it into the chalice, making the sign of the cross.

When the deacons ascend to the pontiff, the first and second secretaries, the notaries, and the regional defenders descend and take their places.

14. Then the pontiff rises from his seat, descends to the altar, salutes the altar, and receives the offerings from the hand of the weekly presbyter, the deacons, and the first secretaries.

The archdeacon then receives the pontiff’s offerings from the official responsible for the offerings and gives them to the pontiff. When the pontiff has placed them on the altar, the archdeacon lifts the chalice from the hand of the regional subdeacon and places it on the altar beside the pontiff’s offering, on the right. With the offertory cloth placed at the corner of the altar, he wraps it around the chalice by its handles and stands behind the pontiff.

The pontiff inclines slightly toward the altar, looks toward the schola, and signals that they are to be silent.

15. When the offertory has ended, the bishops stand behind the pontiff, the first in the middle and the others in order. The archdeacon stands on the right of the bishops, the second deacon on the left, and the others in ordered ranks.

When the offertory has ended, the regional subdeacons go behind the altar, looking toward the pontiff and standing upright until they begin to say the Angelic Hymn, that is, the “Sanctus.” When they have completed it, the pontiff alone rises and enters the Canon.

The bishops, deacons, subdeacons, and presbyters remain bowed in the presbytery. When he has said, “To us also, sinners,” the subdeacons rise. When he has said, “Through whom you create all these things, O Lord,” the archdeacon alone rises.

When he has said, “Through him, and with him,” the archdeacon lifts the chalice with the offering by its handles and holds it raised beside the pontiff. The pontiff touches the side of the chalice with the offerings and says, “Through him, and with him,” until “for ever and ever.”

The pontiff places the offerings in their proper place, and the archdeacon places the chalice beside them, leaving the offertory cloth on its handles.

16. When the Canon has ended, the regional subdeacon stands before the altar behind the archdeacon with the paten. During the middle of the Canon the next subdeacon receives it through the acolyte.

This acolyte, when the pontiff begins the Canon, comes with a linen cloth tied around his neck beneath his shoulder and holds the paten on his right side before his chest.

When the pontiff says, “And protected from all disturbance,” the archdeacon turns, receives the paten, kisses it, and gives it to the second deacon to hold.

When the pontiff says, “The peace of the Lord be always with you,” he places a portion of the Holy Sacrament into the chalice, adding these words: “May this mingling and consecration of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ bring eternal life to us who receive it.”

Meanwhile the archdeacon gives the peace to the first bishop, who gives it in turn to the person standing next to him, and then the others do so in order. The people also kiss one another with the kiss of Christ.

Then the pontiff breaks the offering on the right side and leaves on the altar a particle of the Holy Sacrament that he has broken from it. He places his remaining offerings on the paten then held by the deacon.

The archdeacon lifts the chalice and hands it to the regional subdeacon to hold at the right corner of the altar. The following subdeacons then approach with acolytes carrying suitable bags on the right and left sides of the altar. The subdeacons, while the acolytes extend their arms with the bags, stand in front and prepare the openings of the bags for the archdeacon to place in them the offerings, first on the right and then on the left.

Then the acolytes go to the right and left behind the bishops or presbyters around the altar, so that the priests may begin breaking the Hosts. The paten precedes them; two regional subdeacons carry it to the deacons for the breaking, so that they too may break the Hosts when the pontiff signals to them.

The archdeacon, after clearing the altar of the offerings, looks toward the schola and signals them to say “Lamb of God.” Then he goes to the paten held by the two regional subdeacons, so that he too may break the Host with the other deacons at the corner of the altar.

When the breaking has been completed, the junior deacon takes the paten from the subdeacon and carries it to the pontiff, so that he may receive the Lord’s body.

The pontiff himself receives the sacrament from the archdeacon in the holy chalice. From it the archdeacon pours a little into the larger chalice or into the flagon held by the acolyte, so that the people may receive the sacrament from the same sacred vessel, “because wine, even when not consecrated but mingled with the Lord’s blood, is sanctified in every way.”

[Note: [Col. 0981D] Three chalices are assigned in this Order: the larger one, into which the offerings of wine were first received; the flagon or ministerial chalice mentioned above, no. 12; and the sacred chalice, in which the consecration took place.]

17. The bishops first approach in order to receive Communion from the pontiff’s hand. After them all the presbyters ascend to receive Communion at the altar.

When the archdeacon has received Communion, the first bishop meanwhile holds the chalice.

[Note: [Col. 0982D] The material that follows these words, “After receiving the chalice,” appears to have been inserted.]

Just as bishops minister to the supreme pontiff in the Roman Church, so presbyters ought to minister to bishops in the other churches. After receiving the chalice, the archdeacon administers the Lord’s blood to all whom the pontiff has communicated with the Lord’s body.

When this service has been completed at the altar, and the small vessel with which the people are to receive Communion has already been received by the regional subdeacon, the archdeacon hands the chalice to that same subdeacon, who carries it to the acolyte to be returned to the repository.

Then the pontiff descends with the first secretary of the notaries and the first secretary of the defenders to communicate the leading persons and their wives. Just as the archdeacon administers the sacrament to those whom the pontiff communicates, so the other deacons administer it to those whom the bishops or presbyters communicate after the pontiff.

18. When the pontiff begins to communicate the clergy or the people, the schola begins to sing the Communion Antiphon. Then, at the pontiff’s signal, “Glory to the Father, as it was in the beginning, is now and always” is said, while the subdeacon makes the sign of the cross on his forehead. By this sign the first member of the schola understands when, after Communion, he is to say glory to the Holy Trinity, prepared also to add the Verse of repetition.

When the Antiphon, which is repeated at the repetition Verse, has ended, the pontiff gives the Prayer after Communion at the altar. When this too is finished, the deacon whom the archdeacon has instructed looks toward the pontiff for his signal and says to the people, “Go, the dismissal is made.” The people respond, “Thanks be to God.”

When the bishops, presbyters, or the following orders say, “Command, lord, a blessing,” the pontiff responds, “May the Lord bless us. Amen.” Seven candle-bearing stands then precede the pontiff, and the regional subdeacon with the censer accompanies him to the sacristy.

[Col. 0983]

ROMAN ORDER IV, OR A FRAGMENT OF THE ANCIENT ROMAN ORDER CONCERNING THE PONTIFICAL MASS

[Col. 0983B] 61 [lacuna] counted among the flock. Through Christ our Lord.

Here he raises himself upright. Here he blesses only the offering: “Which offering, O God, we ask that you graciously make blessed, approved, ratified, reasonable, and acceptable.” Here he makes the sign over both, that is, over the offering and the chalice: “that it may become for us the body and blood,” up to the words, “giving thanks to you, he blessed, broke, and gave it to his disciples, saying,” and onward.

Likewise, “giving thanks to you, he blessed.” Here he signs only the offering four times; on the fifth time he makes the sign of the cross over the chalice alone: “a pure offering, a holy offering, an immaculate offering, holy bread of eternal life, and the chalice of everlasting salvation,” up to “the immaculate offering.”

Here he inclines again beside the altar, saying, “We humbly beseech you, almighty God.” Here he prays privately whatever he wishes. Then he says, “Command that these things be carried by the hands,” up to “into your presence.”

Here he straightens himself and says these words: “That as many as, from this participation in the altar,” up to “through Christ.”

These two Prayers are said, one over the diptychs, the other after the reading of the names; and this is done only on ordinary days or on days appointed for such rites:

“Remember also, O Lord, those who have gone before us with the sign of faith and sleep in the sleep of peace.” And the names are recited.

Then, after they have been recited, he says:

“To them, O Lord, and to all who rest in Christ, we ask you to grant a place of refreshment, light, and peace, through the same Christ.”

“Also to us sinners,” up to “but admit us, we ask, as the giver of forgiveness. Through him.”

Here the archdeacon rises and comes forward, wrapping the chalice in a small cloth. He lifts it toward the lord pope and says, “Through whom, O Lord, you continually create all these good things.”

Here he signs both the offering and the chalice three times, making one cross each time: “You sanctify, enliven, bless, and bestow these things upon us.”

Here the lord pope lifts the two offerings to the rim of the chalice and, touching it with the offerings while the archdeacon holds it, says:

“Through him, and with him, and in him, to you, God the Father almighty, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, is all honor and glory.”

Then he says aloud, “For ever and ever.” Then he replaces the offering on the altar and says aloud, “Let us pray.”

Then he says, “Instructed by saving commands,” up to “but deliver us from evil.”

Then the lord pope says this Prayer without any intervening sound:

“Deliver us, we beseech you, O Lord,” up to “Peter, Paul, and Andrew.”

Here he commemorates by name whatever saints, or as many saints, as he wishes. Then he continues:

“With all the saints, graciously grant,” up to “for ever and ever.”

The response is, “Amen.”

Then he says, “The peace of the Lord be always with you.”

He does not place a portion of the Holy Sacrament into the chalice, as is customary among other priests.

While the offering is being broken, “Lamb of God” is said. When the breaking has been completed, as the lord Apostolicus receives Communion, he bites off a portion for himself and puts the remainder into the chalice, making the sign of the cross over the chalice with it three times, saying nothing. Thus he receives Communion from the chalice, which the archdeacon holds.

When the lord Apostolicus descends from the altar, he begins to communicate the people, and the Communion Antiphon is sung. When Communion and the Antiphon have ended, the lord pope rises, comes to the altar, and gives the greeting in a louder voice, saying, “The Lord be with you.” The response is, “And with your spirit.”

Then he says the Prayer:

“What we have taken with our mouth, O Lord, may we receive in mind, and may the temporal gift become for us an eternal remedy. Through him, and so forth.”

[Note: [Col. 0983D] This is to be understood of those who had been enrolled in the sacred diptychs, whose names it was formerly customary to recite.]

[Note: [Col. 0983D] Here there is one difference not found in the first two Roman Orders: there the lord Apostolicus places into the chalice a portion of the Holy Sacrament previously consecrated. Amalarius praises this rite from the Roman booklet in Book II, chapter 31, and after him the Micrologus does so in chapter 18.]

[Note: [Col. 0984D] Here there is another difference: the lord Apostolicus receives Communion at the altar, not at his seat, as in the preceding Orders. From these two observations it may be inferred that this Order is later than the others. We received the preceding fragment from a very ancient codex that once belonged to Constantine Cajetanus, abbot, and was later transferred to the Roman Library of Wisdom.]

[ORDO ROMANUS V.]

[Col. 0985]

ADMONITION ON THE FIFTH ROMAN ORDER.

[Col. 0985] 63 The following Roman Order, of great antiquity, follows in the very ancient Codex of Saint Gall the booklet on the Grades of the Roman Church, which we shall append below. After first listing the sacred vestments of the pontiff and the other ministers, it presents the rite of the episcopal Mass according to the custom then received in the Roman Church.

That this Order belongs to the Roman Church is understood from the designation made at the beginning of the Roman bishop, distinct from the pontiff, and likewise of the Roman presbyter. The rites of the Mass contain many details worthy of observation. The Creed of Constantinople is assigned after the Gospel, as in the Second Roman Order. This conflicts with the opinion of Berno, abbot of Reichenau, who believed that this had not been customary in the Roman Mass before the reign of the holy Emperor Henry.

This book on the episcopal Mass is followed by another Order on the same subject, already published but now collated anew with ancient manuscript codices.

[Col. 0985]

ROMAN ORDER V, FIRST ORDER OF THE EPISCOPAL MASS

64 I. On the pontifical vestments.

[Col. 0985A]

1. First, the *cam.* [Note: [Col. 0985C] That is, the *camisia*, namely the linen garment, specifically the tighter and inner one. According to the commonly cited Alcuin, the broader linen garment with the *cotta* is worn over it; by this name Romans even now call the undulating surplice.] is put on and girded above. Then the linen garment with the *cottas*, made of silk, and the girdle. After this the *anagolagium* is put on [Note: [Col. 0985C] Above we have already seen *anagolagium* used for the amice or shoulder garment.] ; next the smaller dalmatic, then the larger dalmatic, and over it the orarium. After this the chasuble, and over it the pallium is placed.

On the days of the Nativity of the Lord, Easter, Saint Peter, and the day of his ordination, a chasuble of another color is worn.

He carries a *sestace* in his hand [Note: [Col. 0985C] I believe that by the name *sestace* the towel is meant, which ancient priests and ministers carried with their fingertips.], and likewise the footwear: perhaps, in addition, the *odhones* [Note: [Col. 0985C] Perhaps the reading is “in addition, *odhones*.” The same word occurs again below [Col. 0986C], perhaps signifying sandals. The Roman Order, in the ordination of a bishop, distinguishes sandals from *campagi*, which covered the lower leg. Stockings reaching to the knee are called *caligae* in Menard’s Sacramentary, p. 260.], then the *campagi*.

II. Likewise, on the vestments of the other Roman bishop.

2. First, the *cam.* and girdle; afterward the white tunic; then the orarium. After this the chasuble; and the *sestace* in his hand, the footwear, the *odhones*, and the *campagi*.

3. The Roman presbyter likewise, except only for the *subtalaria*, which the presbyter and deacon put on.

First, the *cam.* and, over it, the girdle. Then the white tunic and girdle; afterward the *anagolagium*; after this the armlet on the right hand [Note: [Col. 0986C] This is distinct from the sleeves or gloves discussed in the published Roman Order, p. 99, col. 2, and in Menard’s Sacramentary, p. 260. Thus the *brachiale* here was an ornament for the right arm.]; the smaller and larger dalmatic, and the chasuble, until he comes to the presbytery. There it is removed by an acolyte.

His footwear is like the pontiff’s.

The subdeacons wear the *cam.* and girdle; then the *anagolagium* and white tunic, the orarium, and the *sestace* in the left hand.

The acolytes wear the *cam.* and girdle, with the *sestace* hanging from the left side at the girdle, the white tunic, the orarium around the neck, and the chasuble. When they sing in the rank, the chasuble is removed and they carry the orarium in the hand. Their footwear consists of shoes, *odhones*, and *subtalaria*, like that of the subdeacons.

The other lower orders of the church who sing in the rank are dressed like the acolytes. Those who do not sing in the ambo are similarly vested if they have the means; but if they cannot, [lacuna].

4. Likewise, how the pontiff is vested on ordinary days.

First, the *cam.* and girdle; then a silk tunic, the orarium, the chasuble, and the pallium, with the *sestace* in his hand. The footwear of the pontiff and of all the others, both on feast days and on ordinary days, is put on in the same manner.

Likewise, the deacons.

III. Further details concerning the foregoing.

5. First the bishop is to be vested, together with all the presbyters who are found to be present, and seven, five, or three deacons, with the same number of subdeacons, and as many acolytes as there are deacons.

When the cantor begins the Invitatory, the presbyters shall all stand in their places, that is, on both sides of the choir. When the cantor has raised the Verse of the Invitatory, the procession begins. Two acolytes carrying censers precede it.

After them come seven, five, or three acolytes with candle-bearing stands, according to the number of deacons or subdeacons, as stated above. Then the subdeacons proceed two by two, followed likewise by the deacons two by two. Two of them lead the pontiff, supporting him on either side: the archdeacon on the right, that is, the one who is to read the Gospel, and any other deacon on the left.

When they have reached the front of the singing choir, the subdeacons immediately go to their places in the choir. The deacons and the acolytes carrying the candle-bearing stands and censers divide on either side of the pontiff. If there are seven, four stand on the right and three on the left; if five, three on the right and two on the left; if three, two stand on the pontiff’s right and one on the left.

The two acolytes carrying censers also divide and stand before the line of presbyters.

When he has completed a short Prayer, the pontiff turns to the right, signals to one presbyter standing before the others, and kisses him. Then he turns to the left, signals to another presbyter, and likewise kisses him.
