Then he signals to the last deacon standing on the right and kisses him; afterward he signals to the last one standing on the left and likewise kisses him. Thus, turning alternately, he kisses all the deacons, but lastly the one who is to read the Gospel.

6. When this has been completed, let him signal to the cantor to say the *Gloria*. He himself, led by the deacons, shall proceed before the altar; when all have bowed for the Prayer, the acolytes shall stand with the candlesticks and censers in the place where he had previously prayed. When the Prayer is nearly completed, let him signal to the two deacons at the ends—one on this side and the other on that—to go and kiss one the right and the other the left horn of the altar. Thus let him signal to all the deacons that they should do this in pairs, and finally to the one who is to read the Gospel. The bishop himself shall rise from the Prayer, proceed, and kiss the Gospel lying upon the altar. He shall go to the right side of the altar, while four, or three, or two deacons stand on that side, and three, or two, or one on the other. The bishop shall signal to the cantor when the *Kyrie eleison* or *Christe eleison* is to be sung in a higher voice. When this has been completed, the bishop shall say the *Gloria in excelsis Deo*, and the acolytes shall remove the candlesticks and put away or suspend the censers.

7. When the *Gloria in excelsis Deo* has been sung in full, the bishop shall say the Prayer, as is customary; and, sitting down, shall signal to the presbyters to sit. When the reading has been read, the subdeacon shall kiss the bishop’s knee. The cantors who have sung the Gradual or Alleluia shall likewise kiss the bishop’s knee if they have been ordained to any rank; but if they are outside the clerical order, they shall prostrate themselves at his feet. The bishop shall signal to the master of the school when the Gradual or Alleluia is to be repeated by the cantors. When the deacon must go to read the Gospel, he shall kiss the bishop’s knee. Approaching, he shall lift up the Gospels, preceded by two acolytes with candlesticks and, before them, by two other acolytes with censers. When the Gospel has been read, the bishop shall say, “Peace be with you,” and shall raise the *Credo in unum Deum*. The acolytes shall extinguish the candlesticks and place them behind the altar. Of the acolytes carrying censers, one shall go to the altar to offer incense around it, as well as to the bishop, the presbyters, the deacons, and the entire clergy; the other shall go to the people. The subdeacon who read the lesson shall stand ready beside the ambo, so that, when the Gospel has been read, he may receive the Gospels from the deacon and present them to the bishop to be kissed. After they have been kissed, the censer shall also be presented to him.

8. After the *Credo in unum* has been sung, the bishop shall say, “The Lord be with you. Let us pray.” Supported by two deacons and followed by the others, the bishop shall go first to the men making an offering with wine, then to the women. One acolyte, holding before him a linen cloth made in the customary fashion, shall receive from the bishop the offerings; another, carrying a reed into which any deacon receiving a libation of wine may pour it, shall do likewise. On returning from the people, the bishop shall receive the offering of the choir (*schola*) without wine [Note: [Col. 0987D] Namely, water; concerning this, see above in the first book. The matter is clearer below: “The cantor, through his junior, shall send to the subdeacon a reed wrapped in a small cloth, with water” [Col. 0988D].], proceed to his seat, and sit; water shall be offered to him, and he shall wash his hands. At that time the subdeacon shall have in place a chalice with wine, with a folded corporal upon it, and the acolyte a paten with the offerings. The deacon, taking the corporal, shall go to the right side of the altar and cast it by unrolling it toward the other side of the altar; another deacon shall receive it and spread it out upon the altar.

The deacon who read the Gospel shall return, kiss the bishop’s knee, and approach the altar. He shall signal to the acolyte carrying the offering of the people and of the school in the cloth, receive from those offerings as much as seems appropriate to him, and place them upon the altar, on the corporal they had spread. He shall pour a libation of wine from the reed into the chalice. Then he himself, together with another deacon, shall go and lead the bishop to the altar, supporting him by the arms. The presbyters shall approach, offering; then the deacons, without one [Perhaps: “without wine”]. When this has been completed, the deacon shall receive the paten from the acolyte and hand it to the bishop. After taking away the offerings lying upon it, he shall return it to the acolyte. The cantor, through his junior, shall send to the subdeacon holding the chalice a reed wrapped in a small cloth, with water; the subdeacon shall pour that same water into the chalice and return the chalice to the deacon, who, with the bishop’s signal, shall place it upon the altar.

9. While the *Sanctus* is being sung, the subdeacons shall go and stand behind the altar, turned toward the deacons standing behind the bishop. Behind those deacons, two acolytes shall stand with two patens. During the Canon, water shall be given to the presbyters so that they may wash their hands. When the bishop says, “To us also, sinners,” water shall be given to the deacons, and the subdeacons shall return to their places [Note: Amalarius, Book III, chapter 25: “In the same office the deacons wash their hands.”].

10. One of those who read the lesson shall stand behind the deacons beside the acolytes, so that, when the bishop says, “Graciously grant peace,” he may receive the patens from the acolytes, kiss them, and give them to the deacon; the deacon shall kiss them between his hands and present them to the bishop to be kissed. Having received them, the bishop shall divide the consecrated holy Body among them, break one offering, place one particle from it upon the corporal and another into the chalice, saying: “The peace of the Lord be always with you.” Two presbyters shall come, one from this side and one from that, and make peace with him; then the archdeacon shall do so, and return to his seat.

The archdeacon—that is, the one who had read the Gospel—shall approach the altar, lift up the patens, and give them to the acolytes. He shall order one to be held before the presbyters and the other before the deacons, so that they may break the offerings placed upon them. He shall also lift up the chalice and give it to the subdeacon. When the offerings have been broken, the deacon shall order the acolyte to carry one paten to the seat, before the bishop. Rising, the bishop shall turn toward the East and communicate. The deacon shall take the chalice received from the acolyte, offer it to the bishop, and administer it to him; then the chalice shall be returned by the deacon to the subdeacon.

11. The presbyters shall also approach and communicate. The bishop shall give them the holy Body into their hands; they shall go to the left horn of the altar, kiss it, and communicate. The subdeacon shall follow them with the chalice and give it to the first communicant, who shall give it to the next; thus, in order, one shall give it to another until all have been administered the sacrament. Likewise, after them, the deacons shall communicate and be administered the sacrament. Then the clergy shall receive Communion from the bishop and be administered the sacrament by the deacon.

One, two, three, or four presbyters, as necessary, shall receive another paten and distribute portions from it among the remaining patens. They shall administer the sacrament with the holy Blood and thus communicate the people, while the school sings the *Agnus Dei* and the Communion. All who wish shall receive Communion.

On solemn days—that is, days having a principal feast—when the solemnity of the Mass has been completed, the bishop shall proceed, and the cantor with the school shall meet him and say: “Command, lord, that we bless.” The bishop shall respond: “May God bless us,” and the entire school shall say loudly, “Amen.” The same procedure shall be followed when he must enter the secretarium.

[Col. 0989]

# ROMAN ORDER VI, THE SECOND ORDER CONCERNING THE EPISCOPAL MASS

[Col. 0989B] The Order of the Procession, whenever the bishop wishes to celebrate Mass on feast days, is here set down as it was established by the institution of the ancient Fathers of the Western Church.

1. After Prime has been celebrated in the community of the brothers—called by some a chapter—the dean or cantor shall assign each person to the ministries they are to perform at Mass. When the bell has sounded for Terce, all the brothers must gather together in the choir in orderly fashion, dressed in humerals and albs, though in some places in chasubles. Those who are to perform the procession before the bishop shall receive their vestments from the church custodian in the sacristy: capes for the two presbyters who are to lead the bishop, stoles and dalmatics for the deacons, and suitable garments for the subdeacons, which in some places are called subdeaconal vestments. Cloths shall be carried in the left hand; chasubles shall be provided for the acolytes who are to carry candlesticks and censers.

When they have put these on, the acolytes carrying the candlesticks shall stand in orderly formation behind the subdeacon carrying the Gospel for the archdeacon, in the middle outside the sacristy—or inside it, wherever the bishop is preparing himself. The two presbyters, dressed as they are for Mass except that they wear capes, shall serve before the bishop together with seven deacons, singing with him the seven Psalms with the litany.

2. When the brothers have completed Terce, the deacons shall come out of the sacristy and divide into two groups, four on the right and three on the left. Then the bishop shall proceed and stand so near the choir that he can signal to the cantor with his hand. The cantor must remain silent until the bishop orders him to sing. At the bishop’s signal, the Introit shall be sung.

The bishop shall receive incense from the church custodian, who must be dressed in an alb, place it in the censer, and kiss the Gospel brought by the archisubdeacon in folded form. Since most people unfold it, however, he kisses the Gospel that is to be read on that day. When this has been done, while the Psalm is being sung, the bishop shall signal for the acolytes with candlesticks to proceed: first one, then two and two, and likewise the subdeacons. The deacons shall follow immediately.

The priest shall thus proceed into the choir, led by the two presbyters whom we have already said are dressed in capes—or, as others prefer, by deacons. In some places during this procession, with other subdeacons preceding, the one who is to read the lesson, carrying the Gospel, precedes the bishop behind the deacons; before him two acolytes with candlesticks and one with a censer proceed. We wish this practice to be followed here.

3. When the entire procession has entered the choir, the acolytes with candlesticks shall divide: four on the right and three on the left; the deacons shall do likewise. As soon as the subdeacons have entered the choir, they shall proceed toward the altar, extended as though in a line, bow together before it, and, after the Gospel has been placed upon it, stand four at its right horn and three at its left.

After the bishop has been led to the middle, with the presbyters who led him—or the deacons—kissing his hands and returning to their proper places, he shall bow and beseech God for his sins. Then, having risen, he shall first give the kiss of peace to the two presbyters and then, in order, to all the deacons.

In some places there is a custom that, when these things have been completed, a minister with a censer precedes the subdeacon carrying the Gospel to the altar, placing incense before it; the subdeacon then deposits the Gospel upon it and returns. In other places incense is not brought to the altar before the offerings have been placed upon it.

4. When these things have been done, and the *Gloria* is sung at the bishop’s signal, he is to be led by the aforementioned presbyters to the upper step, but not all the way to the altar. He must remain at that spot until the presbyters first, then the deacons two by two, kiss the horns of the altar, and finally the archdeacon alone does so.

As soon as the bishop begins to ascend to the higher steps, the subdeacon who had previously stood beside the altar shall return to his proper place while the choir sings “Glory be to the Father”; four shall stand in the right side of the choir and three in the left. When this has been completed, the verse shall again be sung by the choir, and the bishop shall be led to the middle of the altar. There, bowing to the altar, he shall kiss the Gospel, and then finally kiss the right horn of the altar, where his seat has also been prepared.

One presbyter shall return to his proper place; another shall hand the book to the bishop and turn it over; and four deacons shall stand at the right horn of the altar and three at the left.

5. When the Introit has been completed, the *Kyrie eleison* must be sung at the bishop’s signal; without his indication the cantor may sing nothing. The acolytes shall then place the candlesticks on the lower step, either in a straight line, like a thread, or, as some prefer, in the form of a cross.

When the *Gloria in excelsis* is sung in full and the bishop turns toward the people to say, “Peace be with you,” the deacons shall turn with him. When he has finished the Collect, the lesson shall be read. While the bishop is seated, the archdeacon shall approach, kneel before him, arrange his garments, present himself at his feet, and return. When the lesson has been completed, those who are to sing the Gradual and Alleluia shall stand beside the ambo on the lower step.

6. When everything up to the Gospel has been completed, the principal officer of the church shall approach the bishop carrying in his hand a pyx containing incense, followed by an acolyte carrying a censer. After the bishop has placed incense in it, and the subdeacon is awaiting the deacon on the right side of the altar, the deacon shall approach the altar to adore the Lord with these words: “Lord, open my lips, and my mouth shall proclaim your praise.”

After adoring the altar, kneeling before the bishop, he shall receive his blessing. Presenting himself at the bishop’s feet, with the bishop extending his hand, he shall kiss it. Then proceeding immediately to the altar, he shall take the Gospel that he is about to read.

Those carrying the candlesticks must stand below the ambo opposite the deacon. The one holding the censer shall stand beside him on the left until the Gospel has been completely read. When the deacon begins to read, two acolytes, having received sacred vessels from the church custodian in the sacristy, shall carry them into the choir: one shall be on the right with a chalice covered by a corporal and filled with wine mixed with water; the other shall be on the left with a paten.

7. When the Gospel has been read, the subdeacon shall receive the cushion and the Gospel from the deacon and precede him. Before him, one acolyte with a censer and seven acolytes with candlesticks shall proceed to the altar. When he has arrived there, the bishop, having received the fragrance of the incense and kissed the Gospel, shall be led by the presbyter and the archdeacon to preach.

While he is preaching to the people, the subdeacon shall carry the Gospel around to the brothers, so that all may kiss it in order. If the bishop does not wish to preach, he shall begin to sing loudly, “I believe in one God,” and the entire choir, beginning with “the almighty Father,” shall continue it to the end.

As soon as the deacon has ascended from the ambo to the altar, he shall receive the corporal from the acolyte and, with another deacon assisting him, spread it upon the altar. This cloth must be woven of pure linen, because it is written that the Lord’s body was wrapped in a clean linen cloth in the tomb; and it must be large enough to cover the entire surface of the altar [Note: It is now much smaller, as is obvious to everyone. It is of the same size as in the preceding books.].

8. When the archisubdeacon has placed upon the altar the Gospel after it has been kissed by all the clergy, he shall take the chalice from the acolyte and bring wine to the archdeacon to be filtered through a strainer. The Roman Order instructs the archisubdeacon to carry this strainer in his left hand, suspended from the little finger [Note: Printed editions have *colum* or *colatorium*, through which it was customary to pour the wine into the chalice so that nothing impure might fall in. This addition is taken from the Roman Order; I do not find it in our books.].

This vessel, made of some metal for that purpose, displays in its middle a great number of small holes, almost like those of a needle, for filtering the wine. The archisubdeacon is to carry it throughout the entire office of the Mass in his left hand, suspended from the finger mentioned above by a ring.

9. When these things have been completed and the Creed has ended, the bishop shall say to the people, together with the deacons who, as stated above, have turned with him, “The Lord be with you,” and “Let us pray.” At his signal, the choir shall sing the Offertory. He shall then be led by the presbyter and archdeacon to the place where the offerings are presented by the faithful laity, whether men or women, so that he may receive them. Before him shall proceed the subdeacon with the chalice and the acolyte with the paten.

When he has arrived there, the deacon shall receive the chalice from the subdeacon. After receiving the offerings from all who presented them and placing them in the paten, he shall offer his hand with the chalice to be kissed, and then give it again to the subdeacon to carry. The deacon, together with the presbyter, shall lead the bishop back to the altar in the same way as before, preceded by the subdeacon and acolyte with the chalice and paten.

When they have arrived and the bishop has sought his seat, two acolytes shall precede him with a towel. Kneeling before him, they shall cover his entire lap with it, so that when he washes his hands the water will not splash his chasuble. A third acolyte, who is to provide him with water, shall kneel in the middle of the two.

This is said to have been decreed by the ancient Fathers so that the bishop, who is about to receive the heavenly bread, may cleanse his hands by washing them from the earthly bread that he has already received from the laity.

After washing his hands, the bishop shall rise to receive the offerings from the two presbyters, the deacons, and all the clergy—offerings which the institutions of the Fathers command less than personal judgment urges him to sacrifice. When he has received them and placed them upon the altar, the archdeacon shall bring him offerings on a paten that no one has sacrificed. He shall take from them as much as seems sufficient for him and return the rest to the archdeacon, who shall entrust them to the church custodian for safekeeping.

10. When the offering has been placed upon the altar, the deacon shall receive the chalice from the archdeacon and immediately place it upon the altar. Then the bishop, blessing the offerings, shall say:

“Come, almighty eternal God, sanctifier; bless this sacrifice prepared for you, who live and reign forever and ever.” [Note: [Col. 0993C] Micrologus, chapter 11, says that this prayer is recited according to the Gallican Order.]

He shall turn, receive incense from the church custodian, place it in the censer, offer it to the altar, and give it to the archdeacon. After entrusting it to the acolyte, the archdeacon shall go to his place, namely, the middle of the deacons, all of whom must stand in a straight line before the altar behind the bishop.

Then the bishop shall turn toward the people and say, “Pray for me.” When he has said this, the subdeacons shall go behind the altar and stand there to sing the fifteen Gradual Psalms; the deacons shall likewise stand before the altar. In some places the custom has prevailed for the subdeacons to stand in the choir until the *Sanctus* is sung; when it has been completed, they stand before the altar, behind the deacons, several steps below them, and behind the subdeacons the acolyte carrying the paten and reed stands below.

11. When the *Sanctus* has been said, three acolytes shall come to provide water for the deacons. When they have washed, the archdeacon has lifted the chalice with the bishop, and he has said, “Forever and ever,” in some places the deacons remain there while the subdeacons return to their former place until the *Pater noster* is sung; only then do all return.

When the bishop has finished the *Pater noster*, the archisubdeacon shall take the paten from the acolyte and offer it to the archdeacon. When the bishop says, “Graciously grant peace,” the archdeacon shall adjust the paten to him and kiss his shoulder.

Immediately, when the bishop says, “Forever and ever,” the archdeacon shall take the book of blessing. Turning toward the people, he shall say, “Bow yourselves for the Blessing.” When the clergy respond, “Thanks be to God,” he shall hand the book to the bishop.

12. When the Blessing has been completed, the presbyter shall come and receive peace from the bishop, to offer it to the others. The deacon, taking the chalice and paten from the altar, shall hand the paten to the subdeacon, who shall present it to the acolyte to hold.

The deacon himself, holding the chalice and reed, shall stand before the bishop until the bishop has received as much as he wishes of the Blood and Body of Christ. He shall then entrust the chalice and reed to the subdeacon. The subdeacon shall immediately go to the left horn of the altar, where the acolyte shall stand with the paten before the bishop.

The presbyters and deacons shall kiss the bishop and receive the Body of Christ from him in their hands, to communicate on the left side of the altar. The subdeacons, kissing the bishop’s hand, shall receive the Body of Christ from him with their mouths [Note: This differing manner of communicating should be observed: presbyters and deacons receive the Eucharist in their hands, while subdeacons receive it with their mouths.].

After the deacons have communicated from the Blood of Christ at the left horn of the altar, the subdeacons shall come in order and receive the Blood from the archdeacon, kissing his hand. The archdeacon must take the greatest care that nothing of the Blood or Body of Christ remains in the chalice or paten.

13. When these things have been completed, two deacons shall fold the corporal and place it over the chalice, with the reed still remaining in it. Meanwhile the *Agnus Dei* and the other things appointed to be sung shall be sung.

Then, when all have communicated, the acolyte carrying the paten shall go to the left side of the altar and stand there with the subdeacon. While the bishop is seated according to the order described above, three acolytes shall kneel before him and provide water for his hands. After he has washed his hands, the bishop shall rise, turn toward the people, and say, “The Lord be with you.” The subdeacon with the chalice, the acolyte with the paten, and the deacons shall turn with him.

When the bishop has finished the Collect, the deacon has said, “Go, the Mass is ended,” and the clergy have said, “Thanks be to God,” two deacons shall take the bishop’s hands; the subdeacon with the chalice and the acolyte with the paten shall precede him. As we described his entrance, so they shall lead him out with the entire procession and return him to the sacristy.

# [ROMAN ORDER VII]

[Col. 0993]

## ADMONITION CONCERNING THE SEVENTH ROMAN ORDER

[Col. 0993] After the old books of the Roman Order, three ancient little books follow: one concerning baptism and two concerning sacred ordinations. The first of these was supplied to us by the learned Joseph Maria Thomasius, and we compared it with the very ancient Colbertine Codex, no. 416. The same little book, with many interpolations, is found in the published Roman Order beginning at page 61. Its antiquity is demonstrated even by its wording. Many similar matters occur in the Gelasian Sacramentary beginning at page 47 of the Thomassian edition.

[Col. 0993]

# ROMAN ORDER VII

Here begins the Order of the Scrutiny of the Elect: how it ought to be celebrated. (C)

[Col. 0993C] Announcement of the Scrutiny, which begins in the third week of Lent, on Monday.

1. “Know, beloved brothers, that the day of the Scrutiny is approaching, on which our elect are to be divinely instructed. Therefore, with earnest devotion, please assemble on the following Wednesday, around the third hour [All.: the sixth hour of the day], so that, with God’s help, we may perform without blame the heavenly mystery by which the devil with his pomp is destroyed and the gate of the heavenly kingdom is opened. Through [Christ our Lord].”

When they have come to the church, as we have said, on Wednesday at the third hour, the acolyte shall write down the names of the infants or of those who are to receive them [Note: Thus they already had names before baptism, although names were often assigned at that time. See Menardus, *Sacramentary*, p. 98.]. The acolyte shall call the infants in the church by name, or in the order in which they are written, saying, “That boy,” and so with each one. The males shall be placed separately on the right side and the females on the left.

Then first the presbyter shall make the sign of the cross on each person’s forehead with his thumb, saying, “In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.” Placing his hand upon their heads, he shall say this Prayer:

“Almighty, eternal God, Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

He shall do the same over the females. Afterwards he shall bless the salt in this manner:

“I exorcise you, creature of salt.”

He shall place some of that salt in the mouth of each infant, saying:

“Receive, N., salt of wisdom, made acceptable for eternal life.”

After the salt has been given, he shall say this Blessing:

“God of our fathers, God, creator of all truth.”

2. From there they shall go outside the church, awaiting the hour when they are to be called back. Then the clergy shall begin the Introit Antiphon, “When I have been sanctified among you.” When it has been completed, the priest shall ascend to the altar and say the Prayer:

“Let us pray. Grant, we ask, O Lord, to our elect…”

Afterwards he shall sit in his seat, and the deacon shall call the infants, saying: “Let the catechumens come forward.” The acolyte shall call the infants by name, or in the order in which they are written, and they shall be placed as before, the males on the right and the females on the left.

Then the deacon shall admonish them:

“Pray, elect ones; bend your knees.”

After they have prayed, he shall say:

“Rise. Complete your Prayer together and say, ‘Amen.’”

They shall all respond, “Amen.”

The deacon shall also say:

“Sign them; approach for the Blessing.”

The godfathers or godmothers shall sign the infants on their foreheads with their thumbs, saying, “In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.” Then the acolyte shall come again, making the sign of the cross on each forehead and saying, “In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” He shall place his hand upon them and say over them in a loud voice the Prayer beginning with these words:

“God of Abraham…”

When it has been completed, he shall turn to the females, make the sign of the cross on each of their foreheads, and say:

“God of heaven, God of earth.”

The deacon shall announce:

“Pray, elect women,”

and the rest as above. The godparents shall sign them as before.

Another acolyte shall follow, making the sign of the cross over the males as the first had done. He shall place his hand upon them and say:

“Hear, accursed Satan.”

He shall likewise make the sign of the cross over the females and place his hands upon them, saying:

“God of Abraham, God of Isaac.”

The deacon shall again tell the elect to pray, and the rest as before; the godparents shall sign them as before.

Then a third acolyte shall make the sign of the cross on the children’s foreheads as the preceding acolyte had done and place his hand upon their heads, saying:

“I exorcise you, unclean spirit.”

He shall likewise make the sign of the cross over the females and place his hand upon their heads, saying:

“I exorcise you, unclean spirit.”

Again the deacon shall admonish them: “Pray, elect women,” and the rest as before; the godparents shall sign them as before.

Then the presbyter shall approach, make the sign of the cross on each person’s forehead as before, place his hand upon their heads, and say this Prayer:

“Your eternal and most just mercy…”

He shall do the same over the females, likewise saying the same Prayer.

When all these things have been completed, the deacon shall again admonish them:

“Pray, elect ones; bend your knees.”

After a short while he shall say:

“Rise. Complete your Prayer together and say, ‘Amen.’”

Again he shall say:

“Sign them; stand with discipline and silence.”

The godparents shall sign them as before.

3. From there the priest shall return to his seat, and the reading from the prophet Ezekiel shall be read:

“Thus says the Lord: I will pour clean water over you, and I will save you from all your impurities…”

The Gradual follows [All.: Responsory], “I will look upon you and make you increase.”

Then the deacon shall admonish them:

“Let the catechumens depart. If anyone is a catechumen, let him depart. Let all the catechumens go outside.”

The elect themselves shall go out and wait at the doors until the solemnities of the Mass have been completed.

Next the Gospel according to Matthew shall be read:

“At that time, Jesus answered and said: I confess to you, Father of heaven…”

up to:

“For my yoke is easy and my burden is light.”

Offerings shall be presented by the parents or by those who are to receive the infants. The priest shall place them upon the altar and say the Secret Prayer:

“Your mercy, O God, for receiving these mysteries…”

When he says, “Remember, O Lord, your male and female servants,” the names of the men and women who are to receive the infants shall be recited. Likewise, during the Canon, at *Hanc igitur*, the names of the elect shall be recited. When they have been recited, he shall say:

“These, O Lord, are to be renewed in the font of baptism.”

When the solemnities of the Mass have been completed, all shall communicate except the infants. Then the presbyter shall announce that they are to return to the Scrutiny during that same week, saying:

“Come on Saturday; gather yourselves early at that church or that one.”

4. When they have all come on the appointed day, as had been announced to them, they shall perform the Scrutiny and the Mass in the entire order written above.

Again the presbyter shall announce whatever day he wishes in the following week, which is the fourth from the beginning of Lent, saying:

“When that day comes, gather yourselves early at the church which he has announced.”

When they have come to the church on the day announced to them, the deacon shall call out:

“Let the catechumens come forward.”

The acolyte shall call the infants by name, or in the order in which they were written, as before. They shall perform the Scrutiny in every respect as the earlier ones did, up to the point where it says:

“Sign them; stand with discipline and silence.”

Then two readings shall be read for the opening of the ears.

A reading from the prophet Isaiah:

“Thus says the Lord: Listen, listening to me, and eat what is good…”

up to:

“To the Lord our God, for he is abundant in forgiveness.”

The Gradual follows: “Come, children.”

Then another reading from the Letter to the Colossians:

“Brothers, strip off the old man with his deeds…”

up to:

“And indeed their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.”

The Gradual follows: “Blessed is the nation.”

5. From there four deacons shall come out of the sacristy with four books of the Gospels. Two candlesticks with a censer and incense shall precede them. They shall place the Gospels at the four corners of the altar. Before any of them reads, the presbyter shall explain with these words:

“Beloved children, we are about to open the Gospels for you—that is, the divine deeds—and so forth.”

When this has been completed, the deacon shall announce:

“Stand in silence; listen attentively.”

Then one deacon shall take the Gospel book from the first left-hand corner of the altar. Two candlesticks with a censer shall precede him as he ascends to read. He shall read:

“The beginning of the holy Gospel according to Matthew…”

up to:

“For he himself will save his people from their sins.”

After he has read, the subdeacon shall receive that Gospel from him upon a cloth and carry it to the sacristy. The presbyter shall explain with these words:

“Beloved children, let us not detain you any longer.”

When this has been completed, the deacon shall again announce:

“Stand in silence; listen attentively.”

Again the deacon shall take another Gospel book from the other left-hand corner of the altar, preceded by candles and a censer as above. Again he shall say:

“The beginning of the holy Gospel according to Mark…”

up to:

“I baptize you with water; he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit.”

Afterwards the presbyter shall continue with these words:

“Mark the evangelist, bearing the figure of a lion.”

When this has been completed, the deacon shall again announce:

“Stand in silence; listen attentively.”

The deacon shall take the third Gospel book from the third, right-hand corner of the altar, the Gospel according to Luke, and read up to:

“To prepare a perfect people for the Lord.”

The presbyter shall explain with these words:

“Luke the evangelist, and so forth.”

When this has been completed, the deacon shall again make the announcement as above. The deacon shall take the fourth Gospel book from the fourth, right-hand corner of the altar, the Gospel according to John:

“In the beginning was the Word…”

up to:

“Full of grace and truth.”

The presbyter shall again continue with these words:

“John the evangelist, and so forth.”

6. Then he shall give the preface of the Creed:

“Beloved, you are about to receive the sacraments of Baptism…”

When it has been completed, the acolyte shall hold one of the male infants in his left arm, and the presbyter shall ask him:

“With what language do they confess our Lord Jesus Christ?”

He shall respond:

“In Greek.”

“Announce their faith, how they believe.”

The acolyte shall chant the Creed in Greek with these words:

“Πιστεύω εἰς ἕνα …” — “I believe in one …” [the supplied text is incomplete].

When this has been completed, he shall turn to the females and do the same.

Again another acolyte shall take one of the Latin-speaking infants in his left arm, place his right hand upon the infant’s head, and the presbyter shall ask him:

“With what language do they confess?”

As before, he shall respond:

“In Latin.”

The presbyter shall say to him:

“I believe in one God, the almighty Father, of visible things…” [The supplied formula is abbreviated here.]

When this has been completed, he shall turn to the females and do the same.

Then the presbyter shall continue with these words:

“This is the summary of our faith, beloved…”

When this has been completed, the deacon shall announce:

“Stand in silence; listen attentively.”

Then the priest shall give the preface of the Lord’s Prayer:

“Our Lord and Savior…”

When this has been completed, the deacon shall admonish them:

“Stand in silence; listen attentively.”

The presbyter shall say:

“You have heard, beloved, the Lord’s Prayer.”

When this has been completed, the deacon shall announce:

“Let the catechumens depart. If anyone is a catechumen, let him depart. Let all the catechumens go outside.”

7. After the parents have gone out with their infants, they shall leave the infants outside in custody. Then both the parents and those who are to receive the infants enter the church again, with their offerings, and the offerings are made on behalf of the infants. The infants themselves wait outside the doors until the solemnities of the Mass have been completed. When the Mass is finished, everyone receives Communion except the infants themselves.

8. The priest again announces which day of the following week, the week beginning Lent, he wishes them to return for the scrutiny. When they have come, that scrutiny is celebrated throughout according to the whole rite, just as the first two were before the opening of the ears. Afterwards the priest announces which day, or to which church, he wishes them to return during that week for the fourth scrutiny. When they have come, he performs that scrutiny in every respect as he did the preceding one. When this is completed, he again announces to them, as above, that they are to return for the sixth scrutiny in the following week, the final week before Easter, on whichever day or at whichever church he wishes; and he completes that scrutiny, or all its parts, just as he did previously. It must nevertheless be conducted in such a way that from the first scrutiny—which begins in the third week of Lent—until Holy Saturday, the vigil of Easter, there are to be seven scrutinies, corresponding to the form of the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, so that when the number seven has been fulfilled sevenfold, the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit may be granted to them.

9. The priest also announces that on Holy Saturday itself, at the third hour, they are to return to the church. Then they are catechized, recite the Creed, are baptized, and their seven offerings are completed. The rite of their catechization is as follows. After the third hour on Saturday they proceed to the church and are arranged in order as they have been enrolled: the males on the right, the females on the left. The priest makes the sign of the cross on each person’s forehead, then lays his hand upon each head and says: “Satan, it is not hidden from you.” When this has been completed, the priest touches each person’s nostrils and ears with the spittle of his mouth and says into the ear of each: “Ephphatha,” which means “Be opened,” “in the fragrance of sweetness,” and the rest. When this has been completed, he walks around them, laying his hand upon their heads and chanting in a loud voice: “I believe in one God,” and the rest. Then he turns to the women and does likewise.

Afterwards the archdeacon says to them: “Pray, elect ones, and bend your knees.” After a short interval he says: “Rise. Complete your prayer together and say, ‘Amen.’” They all answer: “Amen.” Again the archdeacon admonishes them in these words: “Let the catechumens withdraw. If anyone is a catechumen, let him withdraw. Let all the catechumens go outside, awaiting the hour at which the grace of God may work baptism upon you.” Afterwards the Benediction is performed. Then the readings follow in order, with the chants pertaining to that day.

10. When this has been completed, the bishop proceeds from the church with the entire order of priests, singing the litany—that is, “Kyrie eleison”—until they reach the fonts. Before him go the notaries with two burning candles, each as tall as a man, together with censers and incense vessels. They begin the litany, followed by “Christe, audi nos,” and the rest. When the procession around the font has been completed, with all the clergy and the entire people standing there amid many lights, silence is made, and the bishop says: “The Lord be with you.” All reply: “And with your spirit.” He says: “Let us pray,” and gives the Benediction: “Almighty and everlasting God.” Then another: “O God, who by your invisible power,” and the rest. Then another: “To us who keep these commandments,” and the rest.

When all these things have been completed, he pours chrism from a golden vessel into the fonts, over the water itself, in the form of a cross. With his hand he mixes the chrism into the water and sprinkles it over the entire font and the people standing around it. After this, everyone who wishes receives a blessing from that water in his own vessels, before the children are baptized there, so that it may be sprinkled in their houses, vineyards, fields, or upon their crops.

[Note: In the Colbertine manuscript: “Let each take some of that water in his own vessels before … or upon their crops.” When the priest asks the Creed, those who are to receive them hold them, and he says: “Do you believe in God the almighty Father?” R. “I believe,” and so forth. The bishop baptizes one, etc.]

11. Then the bishop baptizes one, two, or as many of the infants as he wishes; the rest are baptized by the deacon to whom he has given the order.

[Note: The first booklet, no. 42, assigns priests or deacons as ministers of baptism.]

They lift the infants in their hands and present them to a priest.

[Note: In the Book of Sacraments published by our Menard: “And indeed, holding the infants in their right arms; but the older ones place a foot upon their godfather’s foot.”] The priest makes the sign of the cross with chrism using his thumb upon their crowns, saying: “Almighty God, Father of our Lord Jesus Christ,” and the rest.

[Note: It is remarkable that infants—this was the customary term for those newly baptized, including adults—are first anointed on the crown by the priest and then on the forehead by the bishop. This practice, customary among the Romans, is observed by the received text of Alcuin, p. 64.]

Those who are to receive them should be ready with linens in their hands, and they take them from the bishop or from the deacons who baptized them. The bishop then leaves the font. He has a prepared seat in the church wherever he wishes, and sits there. The infants are carried before him, and he gives each one a stole, a chasuble, a chrismal, and ten sicli, and they are clothed.

[Note: In the First Roman Order, above, no. 44, “ten siliquae” is read.]

12. Once clothed, they are arranged in order, as they have been enrolled, around the font. The bishop gives a Prayer over them, confirming them with the invocation of the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit. When the Prayer has been completed, he makes the sign of the cross with his thumb and chrism on the forehead of each, saying: “In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Peace be with you.” The response is: “Amen.”

Every precaution must be taken that this not be neglected, because then every baptism is confirmed as legitimate in the name of Christianity. Afterwards they enter for Mass, and all the infants receive Communion. Care must be taken that after they have been baptized they take no food and are not nursed before receiving Communion. Afterwards, throughout the entire week of Easter, they must come to Mass each day, and their parents must make offerings on their behalf. This rite of baptism, described above, is to be celebrated in every respect not only on Holy Saturday of Easter but also on the Saturday of Pentecost.

# [ROMAN ORDER VIII]

## ADMONITION TO THE EIGHTH BOOK OF THE ROMAN ORDER

This booklet is joined continuously in a very ancient Vatican Palatine manuscript, marked no. 487, to the preceding fragment concerning the offices during the nights from the Lord’s Supper until Easter. There is no doubt that the following booklet contains a purer Roman Order for the ordination of sacred ministers than the one found in the received texts, as anyone will easily understand by comparison.

Amalarius further observes, in book II, chapter 1, that the first apostolic, or Roman, pontiffs always performed ordinations in December, until Simplicius, who was the forty-ninth after blessed Peter and was the first to ordain in February. Add the Micrologus, chapter 28, which cites here the authority of the Roman Pontifical, by which title it undoubtedly understands a book concerning the deeds of the Roman pontiffs. More on these matters may be found in chapter 15 of the preliminary commentary.

2. It seemed worthwhile also to append to this Order another booklet, likewise concerning sacred ordinations according to the custom of the Roman Church, taken from an ancient manuscript of Saint Gall, so that the matter might be further clarified through mutual comparison. This second Order agrees more closely with the received Roman Order, though the latter is much fuller. It did not seem worthwhile to reprint here the other Ritual books published by our Menard and by Morinus.

# ROMAN ORDER VIII (C)

## I. How acolytes are ordained in the holy Roman Church

1. When Mass has been celebrated, they vest that cleric in a chasuble and orarium. When the bishop, or the apostolic lord himself, comes to receive Communion, they bring the cleric to him, and he extends a small bag over his arms, outside the chasuble. He prostrates himself on the ground with the bag and gives him this Prayer:

“Through the intercession of blessed and glorious Mary, ever virgin, and of blessed Peter the apostle, may the Lord save you, guard you, and protect you.” Amen.

[Note: Such a bag was used to receive and carry the Eucharist; as we have seen above, this was once the duty of acolytes.]

2. If he wishes to summon him to the office of subdeacon, he is brought to the middle and swears before the holy Gospels concerning the four chapters according to the canons.

[Note: These four chapters are explained below in no. 5 and concern four kinds of carnal vice.]

Then the archdeacon or bishop places the holy chalice in his arms, outside the chasuble. He prostrates himself on the ground, and the bishop gives him the Prayer mentioned above.

3. If he wishes to summon him to the order of deacons, when the Introit of the Mass begins, the subdeacon, vested in a white tunic and holding his orarium in his hand, stands before the steps of the altar. “Kyrie eleison” is not said at that point. Once the Introit has been completed, the bishop gives the Prayer, and the Epistle to Timothy is read:

“Brothers, deacons must be temperate, not double-tongued,” and so forth, to the end: “which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.”

The Gradual is sung. Then the deacon removes the chasuble from the subdeacon. The bishop says:

“Let us pray, dearly beloved, to God the almighty Father, that he may mercifully pour out upon this servant of his, whom he deigns to assume into the sacred Order, the grace of his blessing, and grant him the gift of consecration, through which he may lead him to eternal rewards.”

Then the schola begins “Kyrie eleison.” The bishop prostrates himself before the altar, and after him the subdeacon. When the litany has been completed, they rise from the ground, and he immediately gives him the Prayer of consecration. Once he has been consecrated, he kisses the bishop and the priests and stands at the right hand of the bishops, now clothed in a dalmatic.

4. If he wishes to consecrate him there as a priest, the archdeacon takes him by the hand and leads him outside the steps of the altar. He removes the dalmatic from him, clothes him in a chasuble, and leads him back to the bishop. The bishop then gives him another Prayer and consecrates him as a priest. He kisses the bishop and the other priests, stands in the order of priests, and “Alleluia,” or the Tract, and the Gospel are said, together with what follows; the Mass is completed according to its order.

## II. How a bishop is ordained

5. When the bishop of a city and place has died, another is chosen by the people of the city. He is appointed by the priests, clergy, and people, and they come to the apostolic lord, bringing with them a petition—that is, letters of request—that he consecrate the man as their bishop.

[Note: A formula for such a decree is found in the Book of the Roman Pontiffs’ Diurnal.]

The petition is carried with them. Then the apostolic lord orders the sacellarius or the numinculator to send him to the archdeacon, who is to examine him concerning the four chapters according to the canons: namely, arsenochita, that is, with a male; a consecrated handmaid of God, called nonnata by the Franks; with four-footed beasts; and with a woman joined to another man; or whether he had a wife after another husband, which the Greeks call deuterogamy.

When the man is conscious of none of these matters, the elected candidate is brought before the Gospels and swears to the archdeacon. Afterwards, handed over to the subdeacon, he goes with the aforementioned candidate to the hall of the blessed apostle Peter; there, before his most sacred body, he confirms that he had not committed the chapters named above. On the following day the matter is announced by the archdeacon as it occurred.

6. Then the apostolic lord puts on the pallium and sits in his seat. He calls the bishops or priests to him and orders them to sit with him. While all the clergy remain standing, he orders his sacellarius to have the city’s people enter.

As the sacellarius goes to bring them in, he selects from among them—that is, from the priests—a person who will give the account when questioned. When they have entered, the apostolic lord questions them:

“What is it, brothers, that has wearied you?”

They answer: “So that you may grant us, lord, a patron.”

The apostolic lord replies: “Do you have your man?”

They answer: “We do.”

“What office does he hold?”

They answer: “Deacon, priest, or whatever it may be.”

They are asked: “How many years has he been a deacon or priest?”

They answer how many years and in what manner.

The apostolic lord says: “Is he from this Church or from another?”

They answer: “From this one.”

If they say “from another,” the apostolic lord says: “Does he have a letter of dismissal from his bishop?”

They answer: “He does,” and immediately present it.

The apostolic lord says: “Has he had a wife? Has he settled his household?”

They answer: “He has settled it.”

The apostolic lord says: “What pleased you about him?”

They answer: “His chastity, hospitality, kindness, and all the good qualities that have been reported about him.”

The apostolic lord says: “Take care, brothers, that he has not made you any promise; you know that this is simony and contrary to the canons.”

They answer: “Far be it from us.”

The apostolic lord says: “You will see to it.”

Again he says: “Do you have the decree?”

They answer: “We do.”

When they present it, he orders the sacellarius to have it read. When it has been read, the apostolic lord orders the elected candidate to be brought in.

7. When the elected candidate has been brought in, and the subdeacon has prostrated himself at a distance on the ground for the third time, the apostolic lord says this Prayer:

“May the Lord protect us.”

All reply: “Amen.”

The apostolic lord asks him: “What has wearied you, brother?”

He replies: “My fellow servants have brought me to what I am not worthy of.”

He says: “What office do you hold?”

He replies: “Deacon, priest, or whatever it is.”

The apostolic lord asks him: “How many years have you been a deacon or priest?”

He replies with the number.

Again the apostolic lord asks him: “Have you had a wife, and have you settled your household?”

He replies whether he has or has not, and that he has settled his household.

The apostolic lord also asks him whether he has made any payment or promise.

He replies: “Far be it from me.”

Again the apostolic lord asks him: “What books are read in your church?”

He replies: “The Octateuch, the Books of Kings, the Prophets, the Acts of the Apostles, the Gospel, and the Apostolic Epistles.”

The apostolic lord asks: “Do you know the canons?”

He replies: “Teach us, lord.”

The apostolic lord says:

“If you perform an ordination, do it at the proper times, that is, in the first, fourth, seventh, and tenth months.

Do not promote bigamists or curiales to the sacred orders. Nevertheless, an edict will be given to you from the archive explaining how you ought to conduct yourself.”

Then the apostolic lord orders the archdeacon to read again the petition that the elected candidate had presented to the apostolic lord on behalf of the people. When it has been read, the apostolic lord says:

“How do all the people’s votes converge upon you? Today you shall abstain, and tomorrow, if it pleases God, you shall be consecrated.”

The archdeacon replies: “You have commanded it, lord.”

The apostolic lord kisses the elected candidate, and they go outside.

[Note: These words are found in the published Roman Order, p. 104, but in a much fuller form.]

8. On the following day, which is Sunday, the apostolic lord proceeds into the church. The bishops and priests are there with him, and the other orders of the clergy stand in their places. The apostolic lord enters the sacristy and orders the schola to sing. He proceeds from the sacristy into the church with every form of splendor, as is customary.

When the Introit has been completed, “Kyrie eleison” is not said at that time, but the apostolic lord immediately gives the Prayer. Then the Epistle to Timothy is read:

“Dearest brother, this saying is trustworthy: if anyone desires the office of bishop, he desires a good work,” and the rest.

While the Gradual is being sung, the archdeacon goes out with the acolytes and subdeacons, clothes the candidate in a dalmatic, chasuble, and campagi [read: campagi], and brings him in.

When he has been brought in, the apostolic lord calls him and says:

“The clergy and the consenting people of the city of such-and-such, together with its neighboring parishes, have chosen this deacon or priest, such-and-such a man, to be consecrated bishop. Let us therefore pray for this man, that God and our Lord Jesus Christ may grant him an episcopal chair to govern his Church and all his people.”

Then the schola begins “Kyrie eleison” with the litany. The apostolic lord, together with the priests and the elected candidate, prostrates himself on the ground before the altar. When the litany has been completed, they rise, and then he blesses him.

[Note: It may perhaps be read “they rise, and then he shall bless him,” as we noted in chapter 15 of the preliminary commentary.]

When the Benediction has been completed, the apostolic lord gives him a kiss. The archdeacon takes him by the hand and carries him, and he likewise kisses the bishops and priests. The apostolic lord then orders him to sit above all the bishops. When he has sat down, “Alleluia” is said, followed by the Gospel, and the Mass is completed.

9. When he comes to receive Communion, the apostolic lord offers him a prepared and consecrated oblation. The bishop receives it and communicates from it upon the altar; he reserves the remainder for himself to receive Communion for forty days. Afterwards, by order of the apostolic lord, he gives Communion to all the people.

# ROMAN ORDER IX

## On the grades of the Roman Church

1. First, wherever boys who sing well are found in any school, they are taken from there and brought up in the singers’ school; afterwards they become chamberlains. If they are sons of noblemen, they are immediately brought up in the chamber.

From this office they receive their first Benediction from the archdeacon, so that they may be permitted to sit upon a woolen cloth, as is customary to place upon a horse’s saddle. Then, as the Book of the Sacraments contains, whenever and wherever it may be desired, they are ordained up to the office of subdeacon. Deacons and priests, however, are ordained only in a public ordination.

A gathering of the people and assembly of the districts is held first at Saint Adrian’s. From there the bishop proceeds with the people, preceded by the customary procession—crosses, censers, and the like—until they reach Saint Mary at the Crib.

When the bishop approaches the altar, the singers’ schola repeats the litany, then the Introit. The bishop says: “Let us pray,” and the deacon says: “Let us bend our knees.” After the Collect, the lector ascends the ambo and reads aloud the lesson for Wednesday, followed by the Gradual.

Then the bishop says: “The Lord be with you.” The deacon responds as above. After the Collect, the lector ascends the ambo and reads aloud a brief announcement before the ears of the people, containing the following:

“Let your fraternity know that such-and-such and such-and-such are being called to such-and-such an office. If anyone has any complaint against these men, let him come forward confidently for God’s sake and according to God’s will, and speak. Let him nevertheless be fully mindful of his own communion.”

If no opponent appears, the Lesson and Responsory follow.

2. Afterwards they are summoned forward and stationed on the left side of the altar until the bishop has completed the Mass. Then on Friday they are summoned to the Church of the Holy Apostles in the same manner as above.

On Saturday the bishop goes out to Saint Peter, and all the districts go with him, singing the litany. When the pope enters the sacristy, they await his arrival in the presbytery. The singers’ schola sings the Introit, and the bishop gives the Prayer. The subdeacons read the lesson, and the Gradual is sung. Those who are to be blessed wait beneath the ambo until the five lessons have been completed.

Then the apostolic lord himself reads the brief announcement of their appointment before the people. The ministers of each are standing ready with the vestment until the archdeacon comes and gives each person his own vestment with his own hand.

Afterwards, at the bishop’s signal, the archdeacon descends and takes one of them by the hand. The others follow him, and they ascend to the altar. The bishop prostrates himself with them in prayer while the clergy sing the litany.

When they rise from prayer, the bishop stands in his seat and lays his hands individually upon their heads, blessing them. The archdeacon approaches and takes the oraria from the confession.

[Note: That is, from the tomb of Saint Peter. This passage is clarified by no. 8.]

The oraria had been placed there the preceding day. He lays them upon the candidates, and the bishop clothes them in chasubles. They stand clothed.

Those who are to be deacons take the deacon’s vestments from among them, and the Benedictions of those being ordained priests are completed. Then they descend into the presbytery, and immediately one of the newly ordained deacons reads the Gospel. At that Mass each ministers according to his office.

The bishop takes the whole oblations and gives one to each of the newly ordained priests; from it they receive Communion for eight days.

[Note: Bishop Fulbert of Chartres gives forty days in his second letter to Einard, where he discusses this matter explicitly.]

3. When everything has been completed and the Mass has been properly concluded, the districts belonging to the individual titular churches stand ready with candlesticks and censers to receive their own priest. The bishop gives them priestly vestments and the instruments for Mass, as well as gold or silver, wine, grain, and oil.

As they leave the basilica of Saint Peter, thirty candlesticks with censers precede each of them. He sits upon a white horse; the people before and behind him sing his praise.

Likewise the deaconesses and priestesses, who are blessed on the same day.

[Note: This passage concerning the time for ordaining deaconesses and priestesses should be observed.]

The streets of the city through which they are to pass are crowned with laurel and hangings. With such magnificence they lead each priest to his appointed titular church, and on that day the bishop himself gives them a banquet.

4. Bishops are blessed at all times; now, however, it is customary for them to be blessed at night. At the second incision—that is, at the sixth lesson—the bishop leaves the church of Saint Peter and ascends to the monastery of Saint Martin, situated beneath the roof of that church. He proceeds simply with the rest of the clergy and stands outside the door of the oratory.

The singers’ schola begins the Introit. Afterwards the bishop says: “Glory to God in the highest.” The Prayer follows. One priest and another deacon come out from the altar and vest him in pontifical garments: first the linen garment and belt, then the large anagolagium, afterwards the smaller dalmatic and belt, the armlet, and the short orarium, and then the larger dalmatic.

Meanwhile the clergy sing the Responsory “Offer to God,” the Tract “He who sows,” and the Gospel “He sent them two by two before his face.”

Then he is summoned into the basilica, with the priest at his right and the deacon at his left. With his head bowed, he walks between them until he comes before the altar. Then he is stripped of the chasuble, and the bishop vests him with a planeta. He reads a brief containing the following:

“Our citizens,” he says, “have chosen this man for themselves as pastor. Let us therefore pray for this man, that almighty God may pour into him the grace of his Spirit and deem him worthy to govern the episcopal chair.”

The schola responds: “Christ, hear us,” and sings the litany. Then he approaches more closely to the altar, his head supported and bowed. The bishop lays his hand upon his head and says one Prayer in the manner of a Collect, and another in the melody in which the Contestation is customarily sung.

[Note: In the published texts, Contestatio—the term by which the Preface, as we call it, was formerly designated, especially among the Gauls.]

The bishop sits in his seat. The newly ordained bishop kisses his foot, is received into the kiss of peace, and thus his consecration is completed. On that same day, wherever the apostolic lord celebrates Mass, he is to receive Communion from his hand.

5. When the supreme pontiff himself is blessed, one of the cardinals is chosen, from whichever titular church he may be, provided that he was ordained by his predecessor as either priest or deacon; he may not be a bishop.

The entire clergy or people go with him to the basilica of Saint Peter. When he enters the sacristy, he is clothed in pontifical vestments. Coming to the confession of Saint Peter, he prostrates himself in prayer while the schola sings the Introit “The Lord has chosen you.”

Rising, he ascends to the altar and prostrates himself in prayer, and all the clergy do so with him. Afterwards the bishops raise him and place him between the seat and the altar. They hold the Gospel over his head or neck.

One bishop approaches and gives a Prayer over him, then withdraws; another does likewise. A third approaches and consecrates him. The archdeacon places the pallium upon him, and then he is raised between the archdeacon and the deacon and placed in the seat.

Standing on the steps of the seat, he says in a loud voice: “Glory to God in the highest.” Afterwards, once the peace has been given, the singers’ schola sings his praise, and the patrons of the districts do likewise.

He celebrates Mass according to the rite and gives Communion to everyone. When the solemnity of the Mass has been completed, the entire apostolic procession goes before and behind him, and ranks are formed on the right and left. He himself proceeds in the middle, surrounded by a dense company of priests. All the scholae ask a Benediction from him; as he blesses them, they all answer him with a loud “Amen.”

6. Having entered the sacristy, he now sits in the apostolic seat. When he leaves it and descends to the lower steps of Saint Peter, a horse or the predecessor’s saddle is standing there, prepared for him to sit upon.

The patrons of the districts approach. One begins, and the others respond, singing his praise in this manner:

“Lord Pope Leo, whom Saint Peter chose to sit upon his seat for many years.”

This is said three times. Then the master of the stable approaches and places upon his head the crown, which is made in the likeness of a helmet from white material. Only then does he mount the horse. He is surrounded by judges, and the streets are crowded with immense masses of people awaiting him and singing his praise.

[Note: This passage may perhaps be understood of Leo III, in whose time this book may have been written.]

## The Order of the Four Ember Times

7. The fasts of the first, fourth, seventh, and tenth months are as follows. In the first month, the first fast is celebrated in the first week of that month, on Wednesday and Friday or Saturday. In the fourth month, the fast is completed on Wednesday and Friday or Saturday of that month.

The third seasonal fast occurs in the seventh month, that is, September, and is completed in the third week of that month, on Wednesday and Friday or Saturday.

The fourth seasonal fast occurs in the tenth month, that is, December, on Wednesday and Friday or the Saturday immediately before the Nativity of the Lord. If the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity falls on Saturday, the fast prescribed above is to be celebrated on the preceding Saturday.

[Note: Compare chapter 33 of the Micrologus.]

8. At the third hour, or at whatever hour he wishes, the bishop and the levites enter the sacristy and put on the religious vestments in which they are to celebrate the solemnity of the Mass. Meanwhile the clergy sing the Antiphon pertaining to that day for the Introit.

When it has ended, they say “Kyrie eleison.” Then the bishop says: “Let us pray”; the deacon says: “Let us bend our knees”; and when they have risen, he says: “Rise.”

The priest continues with the first Prayer, as it is contained in the Book of the Sacraments. The reading follows. The lector then announces the reading from the book, and it is read in the manner of the reading, as Paul’s Epistles are on Sundays. Then comes the Responsory.

The priest says: “Let us pray,” and the deacon responds as above. He says the Prayer after the first reading, and after each reading in the same way as above.

When the reading from the prophet Daniel has been completed, he sings the Benediction.

[Note: That is, the Song of the Three Children.]

While the Benediction is being sung, those who are to be ordained stand in the boio beneath the steps.

[Note: Read in poio or pogio, a word that here signifies the ambo. This follows from no. 2 above: “Those who are to be blessed wait beneath the ambo”; consequently it must have been hollow. See chapter 3 of our commentary.]

Then the archdeacon descends to them and re-vests them. If deacons are to be ordained, he gives them oraria and dalmatics; if priests, oraria and chasubles.

The oraria that are to be given are first placed upon the altar throughout the entire night. The archdeacon takes them from the altar, and the bishop places them upon the candidates’ necks.

When the Benediction has been completed, the clergy begin the litany. While it is being sung, those who are to be ordained lie prostrate before the altar, while the bishop stands over them with his head bowed toward the altar. When the litany has ended, the bishop rises, ascends to the seat, turns toward the East, and consecrates them.

### On the Saturday of Pentecost: station at Saint Peter’s with twelve readings

9. If this week falls in the fourth month, they fast on Wednesday and Friday and on Saturday until the ninth hour, and they read the lessons written for the fourth month, together with four Responsories and the Benediction.

If it falls earlier, it is conducted at its proper time. When the lessons are read, the lector does not announce the reading from the book but begins it directly. If it is conducted at its proper time, however, he announces it, and the readings are read in the manner of the reading, like Paul’s Epistles.

The same applies to the other three seasonal times.

The following is written in the margin:

“Twelve readings are said because of the twelve readers, not because of twelve variations in meaning.”

# [ROMAN ORDER X]

## ADMONITION TO THE FOLLOWING BOOK

1. The following little work is found in the old manuscript of the Roman knight Maffaeus. It contains the Roman Order for the three days before Easter, as well as the Order for assigning penance, anointing and giving Communion to the sick, and burying clerics.

The first part, concerning the Lord’s Supper, is also found in the Roman manuscript used by Onuphrius in writing the History of the Vatican Basilica.

2. There is no certain evidence showing when this book was written. It is older than the thirteenth century and seems to belong to the eleventh. It prescribes triple immersion in baptism. The laws concerning penance are also preserved in this book, as is the form of absolution received before the age of the scholastics, the anointing of the sick before the viaticum, their Communion from a particle dipped in wine, and ashes and sackcloth for the dying. All these things breathe a good antiquity.

The form of anointing the sick is deprecatory, not indicative, the latter having succeeded it.

3. Above all, the rite for burying the clerics of the Roman fraternity is an outstanding one. The same rite was transferred by another author into another Ritual book of the Roman Church, which we saw in Florence in the library of Santa Croce. In that Ritual, however, the Order of the viaticum has been changed, with the anointing placed afterward. We have reported certain fragments of this Ritual in the *Italian Journey*.

4. Amalarius, in chapter 69 of the *Antiphonary*, reports that he found in the Roman and Metz Antiphonaries an Order describing how one should perform the office concerning those at the point of death and concerning their burial. I would not dare to assert that this corresponds to the following Order. For it does not appear to me to be of such great antiquity. In the Vindocinian Codex, which contains the commonly transmitted Roman Order, after the Order of Penance—and also in Morinus, at the end of his books *On Penance*, p. 22, where it is published from the Sicilian Codex—there is an *Office for the Dying*, or *How one should proceed with a sick person detained by death*. This office begins as follows:

“Once they have seen that the sick person is approaching his end, he is to receive Communion from the holy sacrifice, even if he has eaten that very day; [96] and they are to perform a litany. Before the soul leaves the body, the priest says the Antiphon: ‘His spirit will go forth and return to his earth; on that day he will see God his Creator.’ ‘Merciful God, gracious God, who by the multitude of your indulgences …’ Then the priest gives the viaticum, and afterward says the Prayer: ‘May our prayers ascend to you, Lord, and may the eternal joys receive the soul of your servant, so that the one whom you made a participant in adoption you may command to be a sharer in your inheritance.’ Through … After this Prayer has been completed, let everyone begin this Responsory: ‘Come to his aid, saints of God,’ etc. But if anything of life should remain, let the Psalms be sung, or let a litany be performed; and after it this Prayer is said: ‘Almighty, eternal God, who fashioned the soul of the human race in your likeness,’ etc. Likewise, the Antiphon after the soul’s departure: ‘May the choir of angels receive you,’ etc. Psalm: ‘I have loved,’ through ‘To the Lord’; and so in order through ‘By the rivers’; and, if more is needed, through the end of the Psalms. Then the Prayer: ‘Struck by the novelty of a grievous wound,’ etc. Then the priest asks everyone to pray for him, and he and everyone say: ‘Lord, have mercy,’ etc.; ‘To you, Lord, we commend him,’ etc., almost as in the printed editions.”

When the body has been carried into the church, the Office at the vigil of the deceased is said, with the Antiphon “Direct, Lord,” etc., as in our books, as are also the first five lessons. The sixth, however, is: “My spirit will grow weak,” etc. Three lessons frequently taken from the *Enchiridion* of Saint Augustine follow; the seventh is: “Therefore, dearly beloved, when the sacrifice of the altar, or alms of any kind, are offered for all baptized deceased persons,” etc.; the eighth: “Let us therefore console one another in these words of ours,” etc.; the ninth: “For he is an outstanding consoler,” etc. Lauds follow, then Vespers. When these have been completed, those who are to watch over the body itself are appointed, until Masses are celebrated for the soul with offerings, while the body meanwhile lies in the church. I pass over the manner of burial, which in many respects agrees with ours. After each of the priests has given the Blessing over the grave, the same priests say: “May the sign of Christ be upon you. Amen.”

[Col. 1009]

## ROMAN ORDER X

[97] How one should proceed on Thursday in the Lord’s Supper—Station at Saint John Lateran.

[Col. 1009A]

### 1

On this day the celebration of the sacrifice of the holy Body and Blood took its beginning from our Lord Jesus Christ himself. On this day the holy chrism is prepared throughout the whole world. On this day also assistance is given to penitents for their pardon. In the morning of this day, first of all, the *mansionarii* (church attendants) should prepare everything necessary for the consecration of the chrism: three flasks filled with the purest oil, but the largest flask, which is to contain the chrism, is to be covered with white silk cloth, while the others are covered with other silk. The cloth should be so fine that the flasks can be seen through it.

At the third or sixth hour the signal is to be sounded, and everyone is to come to the church in which the chrism is to be consecrated. Then the penitents are to leave the place in which they have performed their penance, so that they may be presented to the bosom of the Church by the pontiff, who is to sit before the church doors and reconcile them with the Antiphons and Prayers, which you may consult. When these have been completed, the bells are to be rung as is customary on solemn days, and from that time the bells are to remain silent until Holy Saturday.

[Note: [Col. 1009C] The formula that was in use in the time of Gelasius for receiving penitents is found in Morinus, *On Penance*, p. 696.]

### 2

Before the lord pope leaves his chamber, he says Terce. At the sixth hour the lord pope leaves the palace with the bishops and cardinals and with the entire apparatus of the curia, proceeding to the larger palace, where the residence of the bishop of Albano is customarily located. Standing there in an elevated place, he addresses the people as is customary; afterward the sentences are recited. After the confession has been made by the cardinal deacon and absolution has been given by the pope, an indulgence is granted to the people.

[Col. 1009B] When all this has been completed, he descends to the Lateran church, enters the church of Saint Thomas, and says None there with his chaplains. But if he is at Saint Peter’s, he descends to the aforesaid church, comes before the secretarium to the chapel of Saint Gregory, and says None there.

### 3

Then the pontiff, as well as the bishops, priests, deacons, and other clerics, each puts on the vesture of his order. The pontiff puts on white vestments, the bishops copes, the priests chasubles, and the deacons dalmatics in reverence for the chrism. The pontiff, already vested in the dalmatic and having his hand at his neck, sits in his seat. The larger flask is presented to him by the acolytes, together with the balsam. The pontiff mixes and prepares the balsam with the oil, rolling between his palms a staff inserted into the flask. All the flasks are to remain there and be carefully guarded until they are carried to the altar.

### 4

Afterward, having washed his hands and put on the chasuble, the pontiff proceeds with the bishops, priests, deacons, subdeacons, acolytes, and all the orders. In the procession they are to carry the cross, the Gospel book, seven candlesticks, and a thurible with incense. [Col. 1010B] Thus they proceed processionally to the altar with the flask. After making the confession and reverence, the pontiff ascends to his seat.

Meanwhile the singers chant the Introit without “Glory be to the Father”; when the first verse has been completed, the Introit is repeated. Then the pontiff says in a loud voice: “Glory to God in the highest.” After the Prayer has been said, the Epistle and Gospel read, and—if he wishes—a sermon delivered to the people, and after “I believe in one God” has been sung, the Mass proceeds in its proper order. [Note: [Col. 1009C] The words enclosed in brackets are not read in the Maffean Codex, but only in the Codex of Onuphrius. This is to be understood when the pontiff celebrates outside the Lateran church, where he alone communicates; see below, no. 9.] He prepares two Hosts: one to be consumed, and the other to be reserved for the following day, as well as as many as are necessary for those who are to receive Communion today.

### 5

After the lord pope enters to offer the sacrifice, the acolyte leads the junior cardinal deacon, together with several subdeacons. One of these subdeacons carries the cross, preceded by the acolyte with the thurible and incense. Thus they proceed processionally to the church of Saint Thomas or Saint Gregory, where the flasks containing the chrism and oil are kept.

[Col. 1010C] The cardinal deacon takes the flask containing the chrism. Two other subdeacons take the two flasks containing the exorcized oil and the oil of the sick, carrying them on their left arms; and they return in the same manner in which they came. When they arrive at the altar, before the lord pope says “Through whom you make all these things,” the subdeacon carrying the flask of the oil of the sick presents it to the supreme pontiff for blessing.

The pontiff, all the bishops and cardinal priests, and the others present say in an unadorned voice:

“I exorcize you, most unclean spirit,” etc., “and by the name of his beloved Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, who is to come to judge the living and the dead and the world by fire.”

**Blessing of the oil of the sick.**

“Send forth, we ask, Lord,” etc., “remaining in our inward parts, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is to come.”

### 6

When these Blessings have been completed, he returns to the altar and says: “Through whom you make all these things,” etc., through “For ever and ever. Amen.”

“Let us pray: Instructed by saving commandments,” etc., through “May the peace of the Lord be always with you.” The *Agnus Dei* is not sung, and the peace is not given.

### 7

Nevertheless, we should know that if the pontiff is at the Lateran, after “I believe in one God” has been sung and before he enters to offer the sacrifice, the altar table is lifted by the deacons and subdeacons, with the cloths folded over it. [Note: [Col. 1011D] This rite of lifting the altar table at the Lateran is mentioned in the book both of Benedict the canon and of Cencius the chamberlain below.
