See chapter 10 of the preliminary commentary.] With reverence and complete devotion they carry it back to the chapel of Saint Pancratius beside the canons’ cloister, because that is the place of reservation, and there it is guarded with every precaution until Holy Saturday.

### 8

Then the pontiff comes to the altar and takes a glass flask containing within it a small golden vessel. In that vessel is a hollow precious stone, and in the hollow of the stone the precious Blood of Christ is carefully enclosed. Each year it is removed and placed in the hollow of a chest. The pontiff then lifts it and displays it, so that the entire crowd of the people may see it with fear, reverence, and complete devotion. Afterward it is entrusted to the prior and canons of the same church until Holy Saturday.

Then the pontiff enters alone beneath the ark to offer the sacrifice, signifying [100] what is written in the Old Testament: that the high priest alone entered once a year into the Holy of Holies. Only the cross and a linen cloth are placed beneath him, while a bishop or cardinal, with a priest as chaplain, ministers to him.

### 9

After the sacrifice has been completed, the pontiff alone receives Communion at the altar without ministers. On that day, and on Good Friday, he is to receive not with a reed but with the chalice alone, and he places that fourth part in the chalice.

[Col. 1011D] After he has communicated, he places the chalice on the altar and the paten beside it, with the reserved Body of the Lord, because on Good Friday he takes again from that sacrifice. Both are covered with a clean cloth.

### 10

Having received the Body and Blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, the pontiff ascends to the wooden seat. Immediately two acolytes bring the flasks, wrapped in white silk cloth and carried on the left arm, so that they can be seen from the middle. The deacon assisting the lord pope takes one flask mixed with balsam and presents it to the supreme pontiff, holding it wrapped on his left arm.

[Col. 1012A] Then the pontiff breathes three times upon it. All the bishops assisting there, the cardinal priests, and the others likewise breathe upon it, and they say without singing and without “The Lord be with you”:

“I exorcize you, creature of oil,” etc., “so that you may become, for all who are to be anointed from you, adoption as sons through the Holy Spirit [+ on *sanctum*, ‘holy’], in the name of God the almighty Father and of Jesus Christ, his Son, our Lord, who with him reigns and lives as God in the unity of the same Holy Spirit.”

Then he says in a loud voice, while the bishops and priests say quietly:

“For ever and ever. Amen.”

“The Lord be with you.”

“And with your spirit.”

“Lift up your hearts.”

**Response:** “We have them with the Lord.”

“Let us give thanks to the Lord our God.”

**Response:** “It is right and just.”

“It is truly right and just, fitting and salutary, that we should always and everywhere give you thanks, holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God, who in the beginning, among the other works of your goodness,” etc., “so that for those who have been reborn from water and the Holy Spirit it may be the chrism of salvation, and that you may make them participants in eternal life and sharers in the heavenly kingdom, through the same one,” etc.

### 11

Then the bishop greets the unveiled chrism, and all the others do likewise. When this has been completed, he blesses the flask of oil brought in the order described above. The pontiff likewise breathes upon it three times, but silently; and all the bishops and cardinal priests besides him, as well as the other bishops, breathe upon it three times.

Then he says without singing and without “The Lord be with you”:

“I exorcize you, creature of oil, in the name, etc., sanctified for the reception of every spiritual grace,” etc., “through the same one,” etc.

The pontiff says: “The Lord be with you.”

“And with your spirit.”

“Let us pray.”

**Prayer.**

“God, giver of spiritual growth and progress,” etc., “which they are to obtain in the sacrament of baptism, through the same Lord our,” etc.

After this Blessing, all the bishops, cardinal priests, and other bishops greet the holy chrism and the oil, three times for each, bowing their heads as they greet them and saying: “Hail, holy chrism,” three times for each. They kiss the flask only once. The flask of oil is then carried by a subdeacon. The supreme pontiff greets the oil and kisses the flask, just as he did with the chrism, and all the others in turn greet the flask by kissing it.

Afterward the flasks are carried back processionally, just as they were brought, to the sacristy or the place where they are to remain. From there they are distributed to each person, as is proper and as opportunity requires.

[Col. 1012D] The pontiff, in his seat, gives Communion to those who wish to communicate. Nevertheless, the offerings consisting of the intact Body of the Lord are to be reserved for Good Friday; but the Blood of the Lord is to be entirely consumed. The kiss of peace is not given. The *Agnus Dei* is said, and the Communion Antiphon is “The Lord Jesus Christ.”

### 12

But before the pontiff returns to the altar to complete the Mass, the junior of the cardinal priests carries the Body of the Lord, placed in a pyx, to the prepared place. He is preceded by the cross and lights, with a canopy above.

Then the pontiff returns to the altar and says this Prayer:

“Refreshed with life-giving nourishment,” etc.

When it has been completed, the deacon says: “Go, the Mass is ended.”

When the Mass has therefore been solemnly completed, the pontiff, still vested, ascends to the palace, accompanied by the bishops, priests, and deacons, all vested according to their order. The pontiff enters the basilica of Saint Laurence [Note: [Col. 1013] The Codex of Onuphrius adds: “or of Saint Nicholas, if he is at Saint Peter’s”], and, without the chasuble, sitting in his seat, performs the *mandatum* (foot-washing) for the twelve subdeacons. Meanwhile the singers chant Vespers before him, as is customary. When everything has been completed, the prepared participants come to the table.

## 102 Good Friday

### 13

At the sixth hour everyone gathers at the Lateran church or another church and says the seven Psalms. Then the lord pope puts on only his Lenten vesture; the bishops put on copes, and the priests, deacons, and subdeacons chasubles.

Then the junior of the cardinal priests carries the decorated box containing the Lord’s Body reserved from the preceding day. Thus, with the subdeacon carrying the papal cross preceding the procession, everyone proceeds barefoot and without singing, reciting the Psalms, to the church of the Holy Cross, which is Jerusalem, where the station is to be held. They are to proceed in orderly fashion when the lord pope is at the Lateran.

When they have arrived there, they enter the church without singing and, prostrate in the middle of the church, pray for a long time. The priest carrying the Body of Christ places it in the secretarium while the lord pope prepares himself. When he is ready, the priest brings it back in procession before the lord pope to the altar.

Rising from prayer, the lord pope enters the secretarium with the clergy. Having removed the chasuble and cope, he sits in his seat; after his feet have been washed, the ministers put his ordinary shoes on him. Coming to the faldstool, he says None. After a short while, having put on the chasuble and cope again, they proceed in ordered silence to the altar, preceded by the cross and Gospel book, without lights or incense. Then everyone prostrates himself and prays for a long time.

### 14

Meanwhile the ministers spread only one towel over the stripped altar. When the Prayer has been completed, he says nothing else and does not make the confession.

After kissing the altar, the pontiff ascends to his seat as usual—not to the decorated and solemn seat, however, but to the faldstool on the right of the altar, as though before the steps where the subdeacon stands during Mass. The subdeacon immediately proceeds to read, beginning without a title:

“Thus says the Lord: In their tribulation.”

The lessons are read in the tone of a reading, without reverence or kissing of the feet. When the lesson has been completed, the Tract “Lord, I have heard your report” is sung.

When the Tract has ended, the pontiff says: “Let us pray,” and the deacon: “Let us bend our knees.”

**Response:** “Arise.”

He says the Prayer: “God, from whom Judas …”

When it has been completed, the subdeacon similarly reads without a title:

“In those days the Lord spoke to Moses.”

The Tract “Deliver me, Lord” follows. When it has ended, the deacon, having made a reverence and without giving a Blessing, proceeds with the Gospel, [103] without torches or incense. Ascending the bare ambo, he likewise begins:

“The Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ according to John.”

With no one responding, he reads:

“At that time, Jesus went out across the brook.”

[Col. 1014A] When it has been completed, he says the Prayers: “Let us pray, dearly beloved.” Someone other than the lord pope says these Prayers at the altar.

When they have been completed, the pontiff venerates the cross. Then he presents it to the people, singing the Antiphon: “Behold the wood of the cross.” After the cross has been venerated, the deacon spreads the corporal over the altar. On it the Body of the Lord is placed, together with the chalice containing wine and water. The pontiff says in a full voice, as usual, without “For ever and ever. Amen”:

“Let us pray. Instructed by saving commandments,” etc.

“Our Father.”

In the same voice:

“Deliver us.”

“Let us pray. We ask, Lord.”

When the Prayer has been completed, “The peace of the Lord” is not said. The *Agnus Dei* is not sung, the kiss of peace is not given, and the postcommunion is not sung.

### 15

The pontiff alone receives Communion without ministers—not solemnly at the seat, but only there, before the altar, on that day, out of humble reverence for God and for the Passion of Christ.

On the preceding Friday [perhaps: “on the present Friday”], and when Mass is celebrated for the dead, he makes a pouring into the chalice and consumes it himself; afterward he washes with water in basins.

Then, returning to his seat, he removes his vestments and says Vespers of the preceding day with his clerics, not singing but reciting.

## On Holy Saturday

### 16

At the sixth hour everyone gathers at the church. A new fire is struck from crystal or stone, from which the candle is to be lit by the deacon. The Blessing is to be performed by the junior cardinal priest.

**Prayer:** “God, who through your Son, the cornerstone,” etc., “may we be able to reach the feasts, through the same,” etc.

**Another Prayer:** “Lord God, almighty Father, unfailing light,” etc., “that we may deserve to attain eternal life and light.” Through.

**Another Prayer:** “Holy Lord, almighty Father,” etc., “and help us, who live and reign with the same Only-begotten Son and Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen.”

**Blessing of the incense:** “May there come, we ask, almighty God,” etc., “may the power of your Majesty assist us.” Through.

When the fire has been blessed, it is sprinkled with blessed water and incense is burned. Then they proceed to the Blessing of the candle.

### 17

While the candle is being blessed, the pontiff, with the cardinals [104] and the other schools, proceeds to the altar. Having made a reverence, he ascends to the decorated seat.

When the Blessing of the candle has been completed, the subdeacon ascends the ambo and begins to read without a title:

“In the beginning God created heaven and earth.”

When this has been completed, if the lord pope wishes, the Greek subdeacon reads the same lesson again in Greek. When it has been completed, the pontiff says: “Let us pray”; the deacon: “Let us bend our knees”; and after a short while: “Arise.”

The deacons, if there are several, say alternately: “Let us bend our knees,” and “Arise.” Then a Prayer follows. In this manner twelve lessons in Latin and twelve in Greek are read alternately, as the lord pope wishes.

When they come to the lesson concerning Nebuchadnezzar, at the Prayer that follows it they say: “Let us pray,” but not “Let us bend our knees,” because that king had compelled the entire people under his rule to bend their knees before the golden statue he had erected. The Church, judging that deed to have been done in contempt of almighty God, does not bend its knees after that lesson.

### 18

Meanwhile, while the lessons are being read, seven subdeacons carrying the cross, preceded by acolytes, reverently descend for the Blessing of the fonts. There they perform a sevenfold, fivefold, and threefold litany.

One of the canon priests catechizes the infants presented to him at a suitable place. Making the sign of the cross with his thumb on each of their foreheads, he says:

“In the name of the Father + and of the Son + and of the Holy Spirit [+ on *sancti*, ‘holy’]. Amen.”

Then, placing his hand upon their heads, he says this Prayer:

“Let it not be hidden from you, Satan,” etc., “through the water of regeneration,” etc., “in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is to come.”

### 19

After this he touches each person’s nostrils and ears with spittle and says:

“Ephphatha,” which means “Be opened,” “for the fragrance of sweetness. But you, devil, flee, for the judgment of God has drawn near.”

Then, invoking each person by name, he says:

“Do you renounce Satan?”

**Response:** “I renounce him.”

“And all his works?”

**Response:** “I renounce them.”

“And all his pomps?”

**Response:** “I renounce them.”

Afterward he touches the breast and the space between the shoulders with holy oil, making a cross with his thumb, and says:

“And I anoint you with the oil of salvation in Christ Jesus our Lord unto eternal life. Amen.”

Then, placing his hand once more upon their heads, he is to recite the Lord’s Prayer and the Creed.

### 20

After the infants have been catechized, and the lessons, Prayers, [105] and songs have been completed, the pontiff, with the entire school of clerics, descends to bless the fonts. The subdeacons precede him with the cross and candle and the other things necessary for the Blessing of the fonts. The *primicerius* and singers chant the Tract “As the deer longs for the springs of water,” while the subdeacon and the rest of the clergy perform the litany.

Before entering for the Blessing, he says this Prayer beside the font:

“Almighty, eternal God,” etc., “may he sanctify soul and body.” Through.

Then he ascends the steps, with ministers standing on either side holding candles. After silence has been made, he says:

“The Lord be with you.”

**Response:** “And with your spirit.”

“Let us pray.”

“Almighty, eternal God, be present,” etc., “may it be filled with the effect of your power. Through the Lord.”

### 21

**Preface.**

“For ever and ever.”

**Response:** “Amen.”

“The Lord be with you.”

**Response:** “And with your spirit.”

“Lift up your hearts.”

**Response:** “We have them with the Lord.”

“Let us give thanks to the Lord our God.”

**Response:** “It is right and just.”

“It is truly right and just,” etc., “almighty and eternal God, who by invisible power,” etc., “incline the ears of your mercy.”

“God, whose Spirit was over the waters,” etc., “might conceive the nature of the waters.”

“God, who,” etc., “of the guilty world,” etc., “the grace of the Holy Spirit.”

Here he divides the water with his hand in the form of a cross:

“May he corrupt this water by infecting it,” etc.

Here he touches the water with his hand:

“May this holy and innocent creature be,” etc., “may they obtain pardon.”

Here he makes the sign of the cross over the font:

“Therefore I bless + you,” etc., “whose Spirit was borne over you.”

Here he divides the water into four parts, saying:

“He who brought you forth from the fountain of Paradise,” etc., “and produced water for the thirsty people from the rock.”

Here he makes the sign of the cross again:

“I bless + you through Jesus Christ,” etc., “baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.”

Here he changes his voice, as though reading a lesson:

“These commandments have been given to us,” etc., “and are effective for purifying minds. Through our Lord Jesus.”

Here he places the candles in the water and says in the former tone:

“May the power of the Holy Spirit descend into the fullness of this font.”

Here he blows into the water three times in this manner:

“And may it make the whole substance of this water fruitful for the work of regeneration.”

Here the candles are removed:

“Here may the stains of all sins be wiped away,” etc., “may a new infancy be reborn. Through our Lord,” etc.

Here water is taken from the blessed water for sprinkling wherever and whenever he wishes.

Afterward he pours chrism into the font in the form of a cross over the water, saying:

“May this font be sancti + fied and made fruitful in the name of the + Father and of the + Son and of the Holy + Spirit. Amen.”

Then he mixes the chrism with the same water and sprinkles it with his hand throughout the entire font.

### 22

When the Blessing has been completed, he withdraws for a short while into the secretarium beside the fonts. After removing his chasuble and cope, the acolytes prepare him as is customary.

When he is ready, he returns to the fonts. When the infants have been presented to him—John, or Peter and Mary—he asks the one presenting the child:

“What are you called?”

**Response:** “John.”

He continues and says:

“John, do you believe in God the almighty Father, creator of heaven and earth?”

**Response:** “I believe.”

**Question:** “Do you also believe in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord, born and having suffered?”

**Response:** “I believe.”

**Question:** “Do you also believe in the Holy Spirit, the holy catholic Church, the communion of saints, [Col. 1016C] the forgiveness of all sins, the resurrection of the flesh, and eternal life?”

**Response:** “I believe.”

**Question:** “John, do you wish to be baptized?”

**Response:** “I do.”

Then he baptizes him with a threefold immersion, invoking the Holy Trinity only once in this manner:

“And I baptize you in the name of the Father”—and he immerses him once—“and of the Son”—and he immerses him a second time—“and of the Holy Spirit”—and he immerses him a third time—“so that you may have eternal life.”

**Response:** “Amen.”

Peter and Mary are treated in the same manner.

After these three have been baptized, the pontiff, wearing a mantle over the dalmatic, goes to the chrismarium, while the junior cardinal deacon and the canon priests baptize the remaining children.

The priest anoints the baptized on the crown of the head with the holy chrism, saying:

“Peace be with you.”

**Response:** “And with your spirit.”

**Prayer:** “Almighty God,” etc., “may he himself anoint you with the chrism of salvation in Christ Jesus our Lord unto eternal life.”

**Response:** “Amen.”

### 23

Then the infant is clothed in garments, while the priest says:

“Receive this holy and spotless garment, which you are to carry before the tribunal of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that you may have eternal life.”

**Response:** “Amen.”

Afterward he gives the child a candle, saying:

“Receive this blameless lamp. Keep your baptism, so that when the Lord comes to the wedding you may be able to meet him in the heavenly hall.”

**Response:** “Amen.”

## Order for Signing Children or Infants

### 24

Here, when the infants are held on the right arms, while the older children place one foot upon the foot of their sponsor, all arranged in order before the pontiff, the pontiff places his hand upon the head of each and says over them the Prayer invoking the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, as follows:

“The Lord be with you.”

**Response:** “And with your spirit.”

“Let us pray.”

“Almighty, eternal God, who regenerate,” etc., “the Holy Paraclete from heaven.”

**Response:** “Amen.”

“The Spirit of wisdom and understanding.”

**Response:** “Amen.”

“The Spirit of counsel and fortitude.”

**Response:** “Amen.”

“The Spirit of knowledge and piety.”

**Response:** “Amen.”

“Fill them with the spirit of your fear, and, being propitious, sign them with the sign of Christ’s cross unto eternal life. Through [lacuna] in the unity of the same.”

Then the pontiff dips his thumb in the chrism and, after asking each person’s name, makes a cross on each forehead, saying:

“John”—or, invoking whatever other name they have—“I sign you with the sign + of the cross, and I confirm you with the chrism of salvation in the name of the + Father and of the + Son and of the Holy Spirit [+ on *sancti*, ‘holy’].”

“Peace be with you.”

**Response:** “And with your spirit.”

When all have been signed, he says these Verses:

“Behold, thus shall the man be blessed who fears the Lord. May the Lord bless you from Zion, and may you see the good things of Jerusalem all the days of your life. Glory be to the Father,” etc.

“Peace be with you.”

**Response:** “And with your spirit.”

“Let us pray.”

“God, who gave to your apostles,” etc., “may perfect them by dwelling within them. Who with God the Father …”

Then he makes the sign of the cross over them, saying:

“May almighty God + bless you, the Father + and the Son and the + Holy Spirit.”

**Response:** “Amen.”

## Order for Giving Penance

### 25

When someone wishes to confess his sins, the priest says this Prayer privately:

“Lord God almighty, who do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live, be gracious to me, a sinner, and receive my prayer, which I pour out before the sight of your mercy. May you thereby strip both me and this person of all sins, and make us take care not to sin thereafter. Through the Lord.”

### 26

For this purpose he questions the penitent, saying:

“Brother, for what reason have you come to this church?”

The sinner replies:

“I have come to do penance for my sins.”

Then the sinner places his hands between the hands of the priest and says three times to God:

“Into your hands, Lord, I commend my spirit.”

Then the priest says:

“We have received your mercy, O God, in the midst of your temple.”

Psalm: “Great is the Lord and greatly to be praised.”

“Glory.”

Verse: “As we have heard.”

“Kyrie.”

“Our Father.”

And the capitula as written above. Then he says:

“The Lord be with you.”

**Response:** “And with your spirit.”

“Let us pray.”

“God, whose proper work is always to have mercy and to spare, receive our supplication; may the compassion of your mercy free your servant, bound by the chain of offences and moved to compunction by the inspiration of your goodness unto confession, penance, true amendment, and forgiveness. Through.”

**Another Prayer.**

“Merciful God, gracious God, God of forgiveness, God of mercy and peace, who for love of the human race stretched out your hands on the cross, who called the Canaanite woman and the tax collector to penance, deign to convert your servant, who confesses his guilt before your holy altar, acknowledges himself to be humble, and asks forgiveness for all his crimes. Mercifully grant him time for repentance, worthy fruits of penance, and a fruitful penitential end. Through.”

**Another Prayer.**

“God, under whose eyes every heart trembles and every conscience is afraid, be gracious to the groans of your servant N., and govern all his weaknesses and those of everyone, so that, just as no one is free from guilt, so no one may be excluded from pardon. Through.”

### 27

After these things, he carefully questions him whether he believes correctly, whether perhaps he harbors anger or hatred toward anyone, whether he wishes to forgive those who have sinned against him, whether he wishes to abstain from the sins he has committed up to now, and whether he wishes to make restitution for anything he has taken.

When he has promised to do all these things, the priest immediately warns him to confess his sins to God and to himself. After he has confessed, he asks what occupation he practices.

If he is a count or judge, he is to be told not to accept rewards and not to judge unjustly. If he is a provisioner, he is not to withhold the household’s grain. If he is a moneyer or merchant, he is not to oppress anyone in business or in exchange. If he has a father or mother, he is to honor them and provide them with what they need. If he tends animals, he is not to cause harm to others. If he is a *massarius*, he is not to defraud his lord in his labor. [Note: [Col. 1017] That is, a tenant or cultivator who manages some estate or farm.] If he has a widow or orphans, he is to show them mercy. If he is a slave, he is to be faithful to his master and work as much as he can; and he is to correct those who do evil. If he has a wife, he is not to have intercourse with her on feast days or during Lent until the octave of Easter. If he is a monk, nun, priest, deacon, or cleric, he is to keep what he has promised.

Then he is to consider whether the person is rich or poor, master or slave, healthy or ill, married or unmarried, young or a child. He is to consider everything and impose penance according to what the person is able to do. On one to whom he cannot impose fasting, he is to impose almsgiving or prayer, and require him to bend his knees by day and by night.

Before imposing penance, however, he must show how great the evil is and for how many years the person ought to repent. Nevertheless, he must admonish him not to despair, because the Lord is merciful and will forgive him all his sins, provided that he amends his life.

### 28

Then the priest tells him during which years, seasons, and days he must observe penance.

These are the days that are not counted as part of the penance: the Nativity of the Lord through Epiphany; Easter through Pentecost; the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist; Saint Laurence; the Assumption of Saint Mary; the feast of the twelve apostles; the feast of All Saints; and all Sundays, or the feast days of those saints whose relics they possess.

The penitential days, however, are: the greater Lent; the Saturday of Pentecost; the Ember days; the vigil of Saint John the Baptist; the vigils of the apostles; the vigil of Saint Laurence; the vigil of Saint Mary; the vigil of All Saints; and other days—namely Monday, Tuesday, and Friday—on which the Lord grants assistance for the contest of fasting.

29. Then the priest shall hear his confession. Thereafter [Col. 1019A] he shall say the prayer:

> Hear, O Lord, we beseech you, the prayers of those who entreat you, and pardon the sins of those who confess to you, so that those whom the guilt of their conscience accuses may be absolved by the indulgence of your compassion. Through [Christ our Lord].

Another prayer:

> Almighty God, who gave blessed Peter the apostle, and the other apostles, and thereafter bishops and priests, the power of binding and loosing: may he himself absolve you from all your sins and set you free. Through [Christ our Lord].

Absolution:

> We absolve you in the place of blessed Peter the apostle, to whom the power of binding and loosing was granted by God. Although unworthy, we nevertheless exercise his place in name, though not in merit; and we pray that, insofar as your accusation deserves it and the remission of guilt pertains to us, almighty God may be the gracious pardoner of all your sins. He who lives [and reigns].

Another prayer:

> By the authority of almighty God, may blessed Peter, the keeper of the keys of the heavenly kingdom, who has the power of binding and loosing in heaven and on earth—and whose place, although unworthy, we nevertheless exercise with the help of divine grace—himself absolve you from all your sins. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son.

## 110. Order for reconciling a Penitent

30. The priest says the capitula:

> Turn your face away from my sins.

**Response:** And blot out all my iniquities.

> Create in me a clean heart, O God.

**Response:** And renew a right spirit within me.

> O Lord, hear my prayer.

**Response:** And let my cry come to you.

Prayer:

> We humbly beseech your majesty, O Lord, that you would deign to grant the forgiveness of your compassion to this servant of yours, N., worn down by the long squalor of penitence, so that, having received the wedding garment, he may be found worthy to enter the royal table from which he had been cast out.

Another prayer:

> Almighty God, God from God, who have the power to forgive sins; who forgave the thief already hanging on the cross and led him to the delights of paradise; who gave holy Peter the power of binding and loosing in heaven and on earth; and who said to the other disciples, “Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain, they are retained”: may he himself, according to his great mercy, absolve you from all your sins, and cause you to perform true penitence and thus persevere to the end in good works, so that he may say to you, “Now I shall not condemn you; go, and do not sin again.” He who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, [lives and reigns] etc.

The blessing follows:

> +May the Lord bless you and always keep you. May the Lord show his face to you and have mercy on you. May the Lord turn his countenance [Col. 1019D] toward you and grant you true peace, he who lives [and reigns].

Another blessing:

> +May almighty God bless you, and through the abundance of the Holy Spirit strengthen your heart, sanctify your mind, enlarge your life, adorn your chastity, and confirm your understanding in all works; may he grant you prosperity, bestow peace, confer health, grant rest, fortify you with charity, and always defend you by his protection and power from all diabolical and human snares; and whatever you justly ask, may he mercifully grant. May he remove all the evils you have committed; may he grant you the grace for which you have always prayed, he himself assisting and going before us to the kingdoms of heaven, he who, with the Father [and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns].

Another blessing:

> +May God the Father bless you, +may the Son of God keep you, and +may the Holy Spirit [Col. 1020A] enlighten you; may Christ, the Son of God, keep your body, save your soul, and lead you to everlasting life, he who lives with you, etc.

## 111. Order for visiting the sick

31. The priest shall be dressed in sacred vestments, and the ministers shall take holy oil for the sick person, blessed water, a cross, sacred vine-ash, and two candleholders. They shall proceed to the sick person’s house, singing this Psalm: “Have mercy on me, O God.” As he enters the house, the priest shall say: “Peace to this house.”

**Response:** “Our help is in the name of the Lord.”

Then the priest says: “The Lord be with you.”

**Response:** “And with your spirit.”

Prayer:

> May eternal happiness, divine prosperity, serene joy, fruitful charity, and everlasting health enter this house, O Lord Jesus Christ, at the entrance of our humility. May the approach of demons flee from this place; may angels of peace be present, and may discord, driven away, depart from this house. Magnify your name over us, O Lord, and +bless our way of life; sanctify the entrance of our humility, you who are holy and merciful and remain with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ever and ever.

Prayer:

> Let us pray and beseech our Lord Jesus Christ that, by blessing, he may +bless this dwelling and all who live in it, give them a good guardian angel, and make them serve him by contemplating the wonders of his law. May he turn away from them all hostile powers, rescue them from every disturbance, and deign to keep them safe and sound in this dwelling. You who live [and reign].

Another prayer:

> Hear us, holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God, and deign to send your holy [Col. 1020C] angel from heaven, who may guard, cherish, protect, visit, and defend all who dwell in this house. Through Christ.

Another prayer:

> Almighty and merciful God, who, in your immeasurable kindness, [lacuna], deign to visit this servant of yours, N., for our saving benefit in answer to our humble prayers, just as you visited Tobias, Sarah, Peter’s mother-in-law, and the centurion’s servant; so that, having received again his former bodily and spiritual health, he may render due praises to your Majesty in the church. Through [Christ our Lord].

Another prayer:

> God, who powerfully granted your servant King Hezekiah fifteen additional years of life, we beseech you mercifully to raise this servant of yours from the bed of sickness to health. Through our Lord.

Another prayer:

> God, who sent blessed Peter the apostle to your servant Tabitha so that she might be raised to life through his prayers, hear us, we beseech you, and may the desired remedy of your mercy come to the aid of this servant of yours, N., whom our frailty visits in your name.

## 112

> We pray to you, Lord Jesus Christ, and with every supplication we ask that you would deign to visit, gladden, strengthen, deliver, and heal this servant of yours through your holy angel, you who live and reign.

32. Then the priest shall make the sign of the cross over the sick person with blessed water and sprinkle water throughout the house, saying:

> Sprinkle me, O Lord, with hyssop, and I shall be clean,

together with “Have mercy on me, O God.”

Then he shall say:

> Why have you called me, brother?

The sick person answers:

> So that I may confess my sins to God and to you, so that you may pardon them to me in God’s place, impose penance upon me, and pour into me the anointing of the Holy Spirit.

The priest answers:

> May the Lord Jesus Christ pardon you all your sins and grant you a healing anointing. Yet, if God has regarded you favorably and the Lord heals you, will you preserve it?

He answers:

> I will preserve it.

Then the priest shall make a cross over his breast with water and ash, placing a haircloth upon him, and say:

> With the Lord there is mercy, and with him abundant redemption. For thus does he aid fallen human beings, so that the human spirit may be restored to eternal life not only through the grace of baptism and confirmation, but also through the medicine of penitence and anointing.

The sick person answers: “Thanks be to God.”

Then, after the confession has been received and penance imposed, the seven penitential Psalms and the litany follow. Thereafter are said:

> Kyrie, Christ, have mercy; Kyrie. Our Father.

**Verse:** And lead us not into temptation.

**Response:** But deliver us.

**Verse:** Save your servant.

**Response:** My God.

**Verse:** Send him, O Lord, help.

**Response:** And from Zion.

**Verse:** Be for him, O Lord, a tower.

**Response:** From the face of the enemy.

**Verse:** Let the enemy accomplish nothing.

**Response:** And the son of iniquity.

**Verse:** O Lord, hear my prayer.

**Response:** And let my cry [come to you].

Prayer:

> Almighty and eternal God, who through your blessed apostle James commanded the priests of the Church to be brought in and the sick to be anointed with oil: grant, we beseech you, that you would deign through our hands to anoint this sick servant of yours with sanctified oil and +bless him; and may your divine power invisibly accomplish inwardly, spiritually, what we faithfully ask for and outwardly embrace.

Another prayer:

> Lord God, who spoke through your apostle: “Is anyone among you sick? Let him call for the priests of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with holy oil in the name of the Lord; and the prayer of faith will save the sick person, and the Lord will raise him up; and if he is in sins, they will be forgiven him”: heal, we beseech you, our Redeemer, by the grace of the Holy Spirit, the infirmities of this sick person; heal his wounds; forgive his sins; drive away from him all the pains of heart and body; and mercifully restore to him complete health, inwardly and outwardly, so that, restored by the aid of your mercy, he may be renewed for his former duties. Through [Christ our Lord].

## A concise and consequent order for anointing the sick

33. Dipping his thumb into the oil for the sick, the priest shall make the sign of the cross on the sick person’s body in seven places, or in several places, saying the following at the head:

> In the name of the +Father and of the +Son and of the +Holy Spirit, may every power of the devil be extinguished in you through the laying on of our hands—indeed, through the invocation of all the holy angels, archangels, patriarchs, prophets, apostles, martyrs, confessors, virgins, and all the saints together.

**Response:** Amen.

Another prayer:

> Through this holy anointing and his most merciful compassion, may the Lord pardon you whatever you have sinned through the fault of your eyes.

**Response:** Amen.

At the ears:

> Through this holy anointing and his most merciful compassion, may the Lord pardon you whatever you have sinned through the fault of your ears.

**Response:** Amen.

At the nostrils:

> Through this holy anointing and his most merciful compassion, may the Lord pardon you whatever you have sinned through the fault of your nostrils.

**Response:** Amen.

At the mouth:

> Through this holy anointing and his most merciful compassion, may the Lord pardon you whatever you have sinned through the fault of your tongue or mouth.

**Response:** Amen.

At the hands:

> Through this holy anointing and his most merciful compassion, may the Lord pardon you whatever you have sinned through the fault of touch, walking, the loins, or the flesh.

**Response:** Amen.

After this the priest shall say:

> Regard, we beseech you, O Lord, this servant of yours, exhausted by the infirmity of his body, and refresh the soul that you created, so that, corrected by chastisements, he may know himself saved by your medicine. Through [Christ our Lord].

Another prayer:

> Holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God, who, by pouring the grace of your blessing into sick bodies, preserve your creation with manifold kindness: graciously assist us at the invocation of your name, so that, having freed your servant from sickness and restored him to health, you may raise him up with your right hand, strengthen him with your power, protect him with your authority, and restore him, with every desired prosperity, to your Church and your holy altars. Through [Christ our Lord].

Another prayer:

> May the Lord Jesus Christ be with you, to defend you; within you, to refresh you; around you, to preserve you; before you, to lead you; behind you, to guard you; above you, to +bless you—he who is in the Trinity.

## 114. Order for communicating the sick

34. The priest washes his hands and throws the water used for washing into a pool or fire. Then he causes the sick person to adore and kiss the cross, and says:

> May the Lord Jesus Christ, who said to his disciples, “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven”—among whose number, although unworthy, he willed us to be—himself absolve you through our ministry from all your sins, whatever you have negligently committed in thought, word, or deed, and, having freed you from the bonds of sins, deign to lead you to the kingdoms of heaven, he who, with the Father, [lives and reigns], etc.

Then the priest gives him the Eucharist of the Lord’s body, dipped in wine, and the wine sanctified by such dipping [Note: In the Roman Ritual preserved in the library of Santa Croce at Florence, these words being omitted, it reads as follows: “Sanctified by such dipping,” saying: “Receive, brother, the Viaticum,” etc. See chapter 11 of the preceding commentary.], transformed into the blood of Christ, saying:

> Receive, brother, the viaticum of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, who may keep you from the evil enemy and lead you to eternal life.

After communion the following prayer is said:

> Holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God, we faithfully beseech you that the holy body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, which our brother has received, may be for the everlasting remedy of both body and soul. Through the same Lord.

Blessing of the haircloth:

> Almighty and merciful God, who granted mercy and forgiveness to sinners clothed in this garment while seeking the mercy of your compassion, we pray your clemency: deign to +bless and +sanctify this garment called haircloth, so that whoever is clothed in it for his sins and implores mercy may obtain the forgiveness and pardon of your mercy. Through [Christ our Lord].

[Col. 1023A] Blessing of ashes:

> God of compassion, God of pardon and mercy, who came to the aid of the Ninevites clothed in ash and haircloth and crying out for your mercy, graciously hear us, so that you may deign to +bless this creation of ash, which sinners use while imploring the pardon of your mercy, and to pour over it the grace of your +sanctification, so that whoever is sprinkled with its dust may deserve to receive from you, the merciful Lord, pardon and remission of all offenses. Through [Christ our Lord].

35. Then the haircloth shall be spread on the ground, and the priest shall make a cross upon it with blessed ash and sprinkle it with blessed water. The sick person shall be placed upon it. Likewise a cross and sprinkling shall be made upon his breast, and the priest shall say to him:

> Remember that you are ash, and to ash you shall return.

Again the priest says to him:

> Does the ash and haircloth please you as a testimony of your penitence before the Lord on the day of judgment?

**Response:** It pleases me.

## Order for burying the clerics of the Roman fraternity

36. First, the announcement is made at night by messengers throughout all the churches of the city of Rome, by order of the rectors. When morning has come, after the bells have been rung, the clerics from all the churches assemble, according to the arrangement of the prelates, in the church where the dead cleric is to be buried. Each priest, with his clerics, sings the vigil of nine lessons.

Meanwhile, unless Sunday is at hand, a bishop or cardinal, or any notable among the archpriests, celebrates Mass for the deceased by order of the rectors. When Mass has ended, all the clerics gather around the bier in the form of a circle, and, by order of the rectors, the clerics of the church assigned by the rectors sing the responsory “Come to his aid.”

**Verse:** “May he receive.”

When the responsory has ended, one of the rectors says, “Pray, all of you,” and all silently sing the Lord’s Prayer. Then the aforementioned rector commands one of the senior clergy to give absolution. He says:

> And lead us not [into temptation].

**Verse:** In everlasting memory.

**Verse:** From the gate of hell.

**Verse:** May he rest.

**Verse:** O Lord, hear [our prayer].

**Verse:** The Lord be with you.

Prayer:

> Absolve,

as above.

37. When the prayer has ended, the aforementioned rector commands one church to sing the antiphon “Eternal rest.” Psalm: “To you praise is due.” Afterwards he commands another church to sing the antiphon “My soul thirsted.” Psalm: “As the deer.” When the antiphon has ended, they sing:

> Kyrie, Christ, have mercy; Kyrie, have mercy; Our Father.

While these are being sung, four bishops or cardinal priests, or archpriests, dressed in sacred vestments with copes and four thuribles, ascend to the altar and incense it. Then the senior of the four absolves in a loud voice and says:

> And lead us not [into temptation].

**Response:** But deliver us.

The capitula are as above. Only the first says the capitula. The prayers are said in the tone of the prayers of the Mass.

Prayer:

> Do not enter into judgment, etc., with the sign of the Holy Trinity. You who live and reign for ever.

When the prayer has ended, the man positioned opposite begins it again, saying:

**Verse:** The Lord be with you.

**Response:** And with your spirit.

Prayer:

> Do not enter into judgment.

Then the one placed subordinate opposite him repeats the aforementioned prayer in the same manner. Afterwards the fourth does so.

When the prayer has ended, at the command of the aforementioned rector, the choir of another church begins to sing the responsory “Be present to our sorrow.”

**Verse:** “She has been turned into mourning.”

While the responsory is sung, the four ascend to the altar, as stated above, and do as stated above. Nevertheless, the one who is first in saying the following prayer must be the first to incense.

When they have returned to the bier, the one who was last in the aforementioned prayer begins:

**Verse:** The Lord be with you,

without capitula.

Prayer:

> God, to whom all live, etc., wash away [sins] by forgiving. Through Christ the Lord.

They perform with this prayer as with the first.

When the prayer has ended, by order of the aforementioned rector, the choir of another church begins the responsory “Do not remember.”

**Verse:** “Do not enter”; “Eternal rest” is repeated.

While the responsory is sung, the four, with incense, ascend to the altar and do as the first did. The one who was second in the first prayer must incense first and begin:

**Verse:** The Lord be with you.

**Response:** And with your spirit.

Prayer:

> Grant, we beseech you, O Lord, etc., that he may join the angelic choirs. Through our Lord Jesus Christ.

This is said four times, as were the first and second prayers.

38. Afterwards, by order of the aforementioned rector, the spiritual father [Note: This is the testimony rendered by the *sanctulus*, referred to in the office for deceased clerics in Thomasius’s *Responsoriale*, p. 211. The Romans still call a godfather a *sanctulus*.] comes into the midst and gives testimony concerning the deceased: whether he had been anointed, whether he had confessed, and concerning his life.

When the testimony has been heard, the aforementioned rector asks the entire clergy, saying:

> Does it please you that this deceased brother be absolved?

**Response:** It pleases us.

Then the rector asks, with everyone’s consent, the senior among them, or the one who was first in the prayer, to absolve him. The one to whom this is assigned says:

> Pray, all of you.

The Lord’s Prayer.

**Verse:** And lead us not [into temptation].

**Response:** But deliver us.

**Verse:** In memory,

as above.

Prayer:

> Absolve.

When the prayer has ended, the aforementioned rector orders the subdeacon and deacon to take up the bier. Taking it, they carry him to the tomb, singing the antiphon “The choir of angels.” And the prayer is said:

> God, who founded the earth, etc., with all the saints, grant true resurrection through the same Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

39. When these things have been done, the antiphon “Open the gates for me” is said on behalf of the deceased, and the tomb is immediately opened.

Psalm: “Give thanks to the Lord.”

Likewise, on behalf of the same deceased, the antiphon “I shall enter into the place” is said, and he is buried.

Psalm: “As the deer.”

After he has been buried, again on behalf of the same deceased, the antiphon “This is my rest for ever and ever” is said.

Psalm: “Remember, O Lord, David.”

Antiphon:

> From the earth you formed me, O Lord, and clothed me in flesh, my Redeemer; raise me up on the last day.

Psalm: “O Lord, you have searched me.”

Antiphon:

> Do not enter into judgment.

Psalm: “O Lord, hear [my prayer].”

Second antiphon:

> Let every spirit praise the Lord.

Psalm: “Praise the Lord from the heavens.”

Antiphon:

> I am.

Psalm: “Blessed.”

Prayer:

> Let us pray, dearest brothers, for the spirit of our brother, etc., that he may cause him to rise again. Through Christ our Lord.

**Response:** Amen.

Prayer:

> God, to whom all live, etc., which you have prepared for those who love you. Through our Lord.

**Response:** Amen.

Prayer:

> It is indeed presumption, O Lord, etc., to be crowned on the right hand. Through Christ our Lord.

Prayer:

> It is a work of mercy, holy Lord, etc., that he may be transferred into the bosom of Abraham. Through Christ our Lord.

**Response:** Amen.

Another prayer:

> The debt of the human body, etc., and may he deserve to enjoy everlasting happiness. Through Christ.

Prayer:

> Almighty and eternal God, who command the human body, etc., to be joined to eternal dwelling places. Through our Lord Jesus Christ.

40. Likewise, for absolution, after he has been buried, he is sprinkled with holy water before the people depart, and the priest says:

> Our Father.

**Verse:** And lead us not [into temptation].

**Verse:** Do not enter into judgment.

**Response:** For no one [living is righteous before you].

**Verse:** From the gate [of hell].

**Verse:** Deliver, O Lord.

**Verse:** O Lord, hear [our prayer].

**Response:** And let my cry [come to you].

**Verse:** The Lord be with you.

**Response:** And with your spirit.

Prayer:

> To you, O Lord, we commend, etc.; wipe away [his sins] through your most merciful compassion. Through the Lord, etc.

For the cemetery:

Psalm: “Have mercy on me, O God.”

The Lord’s Prayer.

**Verse:** And lead us not [into temptation].

**Verse:** Eternal rest.

**Verse:** From the gate of hell.

**Verse:** O Lord, hear [our prayer].

**Response:** And let my cry [come to you].

**Verse:** The Lord be with you.

**Response:** And with your spirit.

Prayer:

> God, by whose compassion, etc., may they rejoice with you without end. Through the Lord.

Finally the prayer is said:

> Absolve, O Lord.

And the following is added:

> May his soul and the souls of all the faithful departed rest in peace.

Amen.

Then they return to the church, singing the seven penitential Psalms with the prayer “Absolve.”

# [ROMAN ORDER XI]

[Col. 1025]

## ROMAN ORDER XI, OR THE BOOK PROMISED BY BENEDICT, CANON OF BLESSED PETER

By Benedict, canon of blessed Peter, addressed to Guido of Castello, then cardinal of San Marco, who later became Celestine II.

[Col. 1025C] 118

### 1

To Guido of Castello, master of clear learning and profound wisdom [Note: Accordingly, this book was written before the year 1143, in which that Guido was raised to the pontificate and called Celestine II.], by divine providence cardinal priest of the holy Roman Church of the title of Saint Mark: Benedict, unworthy canon of the blessed apostle Peter and cantor of the Roman Church, sends the affection of intimate love and an unfading crown among the ranks of holy prelates.

Reverend Father, I give immense thanks for divine piety’s mercy, insofar as my limited knowledge permits, because I see that you take care for your salvation and concern yourself with the ecclesiastical order. Therefore I humbly implore the great mercy of God and the abundant goodness of his manifold compassions, that he may establish and strengthen you in this excellent purpose until he himself comes to remove the lampstand from its place.

Moreover, concerning the request regarding the ecclesiastical order of the whole year, and especially the apostolic dignity and the entire curia, about which your illustrious wisdom and outstanding prudence have been pleased to ask your servant for a little work describing how, with God’s favor, the apostolic lord with his curia, the whole Roman Church, may conduct itself in the principal solemnities and in the daily offices, I shall undertake to explain, insofar as God has granted me ability, even though the matter is difficult and not inappropriate to the duty of my profession.

But it is exceedingly astonishing that you ask me, an ignorant man and virtually without knowledge, to disclose and unfold what I do not possess in the storehouse of my heart, to investigate what I cannot discover, and to pour out what, as a thirsty cupbearer, I desire to draw from you. For who can know what the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys does as it crosses mountains and leaps over hills, except one whom he has given to drink from the torrent of his delight [Col. 1026C] and intoxicated with the abundance of his house?

Nevertheless, as I said, moved by your affection and continual urging, I shall endeavor to write, for perpetual remembrance, what I saw over many periods of time concerning the dignity of the Roman pontiff, the cardinal priests, the deacons, and the other orders of the curia, as well as concerning the ecclesiastical office of the whole year, and what I heard from the wise men of the curia, together with what other teachers have left in their writings.

### 2

In Advent, when each year the office and the books read in the Church are recapitulated, on Saturday, the vigil of the Advent of the Lord, at Vespers the antiphon “On that day the mountains shall drip” begins. Under this antiphon all the Psalms of this Vespers are sung.

When the antiphon has ended, the verse is said:

> Show us, O Lord, your mercy.

At the Magnificat:

> The Holy Spirit descended upon you, Mary.

When the antiphon has ended, the prayer [or, according to another reading, prayers] is said.

### 3

At Matins: the invitatory “The King who is to come,” with its “Come.” When this has ended, the first antiphon begins:

> The angel Gabriel was sent.

Psalm: “Blessed is the man,” through “O Lord, rebuke me not in your anger,” and the antiphon is said.

Then the second antiphon is said:

> Hail, Mary, full of grace.

Psalm: “My God, in you I have hoped,” through “In the Lord I trust.”

When the antiphon has ended, the third antiphon is said:

> Do not be afraid, Mary.

Psalm: “Save me, O Lord, for the holy one has failed,” through the Psalm “O Lord, who shall dwell?”

When the antiphon has ended, the verse is said:

> Show us, O Lord.

Three lessons are read from the prophet Isaiah.

First lesson: “The vision of Isaiah.”

Responsory:

> Looking from afar.

When this has ended, the verse is said:

> And all you earthly-born,

in full; then “Go to meet him and say” is repeated.

Verse:

> Attend, you who rule Israel,

in full; “Tell us whether you are he himself” is repeated.

Verse:

> Lift up your gates, princes,

in full; “You who are to reign over the people of Israel” is repeated.

> Glory be to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit.

“Looking from afar” begins again from the beginning.

In the second lesson, the second responsory is:

> I was looking in a vision of the night,

with the two verses “Behold, the Lord who rules” and “His power is an everlasting power,” together with their repetitions, as above; then “Glory be to the Father,” and the responsory from the beginning.

In the third lesson the responsory is:

> The angel Gabriel was sent,

with the two verses “Hail, Mary” and “The Lord God will give him.” The first “Do not be afraid, Mary” is repeated; the second “And he shall be called,” and the rest, is repeated. “Glory be to the Father.” When this has ended, the responsory is sung from the beginning.

These three responsories are to be sung in assemblies as follows: the first and second sing the first responsory before the altar with all its verses and repetitions through the end; the third and fourth sing the second responsory in the same way; the fifth and sixth sing the third responsory.

In the second nocturn, the antiphon begins:

> Behold the handmaid of the Lord.

Psalm: “Preserve me, O Lord.”

Another antiphon:

> The angel of the Lord.

Psalm: “Hear, O Lord, my justice.”

Third antiphon:

> Before they came together.

Psalm: “I shall love you, O Lord.”

When the whole Psalm and the antiphon have ended, the verse is said. Three lessons are read from a sermon of Saint Augustine and Saint Leo, and three responsories are sung as is customary.

In the third nocturn:

> Blessed are you, Mary, who believed the Lord;

and:

> All generations shall call me blessed;

and:

> The Lord will give him,

with their Psalms:

> The heavens declare,

> May the Lord hear you,

and:

> O Lord, in your strength.

The verse and two lessons are from the epistle [Note: Namely, from the epistle of Leo the Great to Flavian, which explains with great dignity the mystery of the Incarnation against the error of Eutyches; it is discussed below, no. 9.]; the third is from the homily.

When these have ended, “We praise you, O God” is sung. When it has ended, the morning Lauds begin, with the antiphon “On that day” and all the other antiphons and Psalms.

When these have ended, the verse is said. When it has ended, the antiphon begins:

> The Holy Spirit descended upon you, Mary,

and:

> Blessed is the Lord God of Israel,

etc.

### 4

Then Prime is said, and the second antiphon of Matins begins:

> Rejoice,

with the Psalms.

When these have ended, the lesson from the Epistle, the verse, and the prayer of the day are said.

In the morning there is a station at Saint Mary Major, to which the lord pope comes with all the orders. There, honorably and according to custom, he celebrates Mass with “Glory to God in the highest,” as on the other Sundays until the Nativity of the Lord, and he is crowned.

At Terce the third antiphon is sung; at Sext the fourth antiphon; at None the fifth antiphon; at Vespers all the antiphons are sung, but neither “The angel Gabriel was sent” nor “Behold, the Lord will come” is said, unless it occurs during the week; only the prayer is said.

### 5

During the week, the office of Advent at Matins has the invitatory:

> The King who is to come.

The nocturn has an antiphon from the Psalmist. The verse is from Advent, and a lesson is read from the prophet Isaiah.

At morning Lauds one antiphon is sung:

> On that day the mountains shall drip,

under which all the Psalms are sung.

Prime is sung with a lesson from Advent and the capitula, as the Church is accustomed to do, kneeling.

At Terce, Sext, and None, with the Advent antiphons, they lie prostrate on the ground, with the capitula, Psalms, and prayer, as is customary.

At Vespers all the ferial Psalms are sung under one antiphon:

> On that day the mountains shall drip.

At the end these antiphons are sung:

> The angel Gabriel was sent;

> Hail, Mary, full of grace, the Lord is with you,

with the prayer:

> God, who from the womb of blessed Mary the virgin,

and the antiphon:

> Behold, the Lord will come, and all his saints with him.

**Verse:** The saints shall rejoice in glory.

Mass is of Advent through Thursday.

On Friday the Mass of the Cross is sung, which is not appropriate during Advent.

On Saturday it is of Saint Mary, unless there is a feast of nine lessons. If there is such a feast, the entire office belongs to the feast. If there is a feast of three lessons, at Vespers on the vigil the Psalms of the day are sung under one Advent antiphon.

When they come to the Magnificat, a verse from the feast is said, with the saint’s antiphon and prayer; and a commemoration of Advent is made:

> The angel Gabriel was sent,

etc.

All Matins is of the saint, but with the nocturn of the day.

At morning Lauds, if they have proper antiphons, they are sung; otherwise all the Psalms are sung under one common antiphon.

Prime is sung with one antiphon of the feast and the lesson of the day; the entire office is sung not prostrate but standing.

Terce and Sext are of the feast; None and Vespers are of Advent.

### 6

On the second Sunday, three lessons are read from the same prophet Isaiah, and three lessons from a sermon; two lessons are from the Epistle, the third from a homily, and material from its history is sung.

In the morning, at Mass, there is a station at Jerusalem, in the Susurrian palace, where the lord pontiff with the whole curia must sing Mass, receive the crown, and celebrate it, as is customary.

### 7

On Gaudete Sunday there is a station at Saint Peter.

When the lord pope comes with all the scholae to Vespers, and the lord remains there, the lord pontiff receives twenty solidi from the offering, together with the expenses of the curia and of his horses.

The cardinals and deacons, the primicerius with the schola, the basilicarian and regional subdeacons, and the acolytes receive five solidi of Papiensian denarii, which is called the *coenaria* [another reading: *cenatica*]. The archdeacon receives eighteen denarii for the responsories, which are spent through his hands; and the canons of the church are to receive twelve solidi from the presbytery from the same offering.

The aforementioned sacred-palace orders lodge in the house of Agulia [another reading: Augulia]. The master of the lodging must prepare beds with his own good linens, receive their horses in his stables, and guard them.

If it is necessary to prepare the supper for that day, it is to be done from the prescribed denarii called *coenatica*, not only at stations but throughout the whole year, whenever the cardinals come to sing Mass with the primicerius and the singers or other palace clerics.

The master of the lodging is to receive as a benefit every day one coin from the offerings of the Mass, as well as the wax drippings that remain from the Mass offering.

This aforementioned arrangement is to apply at all the nocturnal stations of Saint Peter. At the daytime stations only five solidi are given; but the lord pope receives twenty solidi at both the nocturnal and daytime stations, as stated above.

### 8

At midnight, when he has risen upon hearing the signal, the lord pope must come with all the orders to Saint Leo. There the mansionarius prepares the thurible for the bishop, and the bishop for the pontiff, all dressed in their proper vestments.

The chamberlains, with two lighted torches, and the *camerarii*, with two candleholders and lighted torches, must go before the pontiff.

The pontiff first incenses the altar of Saint Leo. Then, proceeding in procession through the pontifical portico to Saint Gregory, he first incenses his altar, then the altar of Saint Sebastian and the altar of Saint Tiburtius. Afterwards he incenses the two altars in the middle, at the crucifixes, where we have heard from the ancient fathers that the apostles Simon and Jude rest.

Then he goes to the sweat-cloth of Christ, which is called the Veronica, and incenses it, and likewise the altar of Saint Mary.

Afterwards he ascends to Saint Pastor beside the triumphal arch and incenses it. Then, descending to the body, he incenses the altar over the tomb of Saint Peter, and thus sits on the bench with the candleholders before him.

The *paraphonista* with the schola begins the vigil:

> From Egypt I called my son.

Psalm: “Blessed is the man.”

Second antiphon:

> Behold, the Lord will appear upon a white cloud.

Psalm: “Why have the nations raged?”

Third antiphon:

> Behold, the Lord will come, whom John proclaimed.

Psalm: “O Lord, why are they multiplied?”

Then two basilicarian subdeacons say the verse. The acolytes hold the station book, and the chamberlains hold the torches. The basilicarians read the lessons:

> Rejoicing, I shall rejoice in the Lord.

The deacon intones:

> But you, Lord.

The primicerius with the schola sings the responsories.

When the three lessons have ended, the primicerius says:

> We praise you, O God.

The regional subdeacon hands the Sacramentary to the bishop, and the bishop holds it before the pontiff. The basilicarians hold the candleholders, and the pontiff says the prayer.

The deacon says:

> Let us bless the Lord.

And the lord pope gives the blessing.

[Col. 1029D] **9.** Then, going out from there, he ascends to the high altar and incenses it; he descends to the *pectoral* [*pectorale*] before the altar, with the vested deacons around him.

**Note:** This is their name for the railing, like the *stēthea* (στήθεα), as the Greeks call the small columns arranged in a row and joined to the upper architrave; the most learned Cange notes this from Goar on Cedrenus [Col. 1029D–1030D]. The bishops stand at another *pectoral*, the cardinals in the choir with the canons of the church. The chamberlains and treasurers place torches before the pontiff.

The pontiff begins Matins: “O Lord, open my lips” (*Domine, labia mea aperies*). The singers sing the Invitatory. When it is finished, the *primicerius* begins “Out of Egypt I have called my Son” (*Ex Aegypto vocavi Filium*) [Col. 1030A]; Psalm: “Blessed is the man” (*Beatus vir*), and all the psalms of the first nocturn with their antiphons.

When the first nocturn is finished, the canons of the church read three lessons, “I shall rejoice greatly” (*Gaudens gaudebo*), and sing three Responsories; the remaining ones are sung by the singers and the *basilicarii*. Then the bishops read the fourth and fifth lessons from a letter of Pope Leo to Bishop Flavian, concerning the incarnation of the Lord and against the heretic Eutyches; the cardinals read the sixth and seventh. The prior *basilicarius* reads the eighth, from the exposition of the Epistle, “Rejoice in the Lord always” (*Gaudete in Domino semper*). The pontiff himself reads the ninth, at the point where he enters, from a homily, and says, “Command, Lord, that I be blessed” (*Jube, Domine, benedicere*). No one blesses him except the Holy Spirit; everyone merely replies, “Amen.”

When the pontiff’s lesson is finished, the *primicerius* says “We praise you, O God” (*Te Deum laudamus*), and the others respond. He then begins the antiphons [Col. 1030B] for the Matins Lauds. When these are finished, the *basilicarii* sing the verse before the altar. The *primicerius* announces to the pontiff the antiphon for “Blessed is the Lord God of Israel” (*Benedictus Dominus Deus Israel*). The bishop presents the book to the pontiff, having received it from the regional subdeacon. The pontiff says the prayer; the deacon says, “Let us bless the Lord” (*Benedicamus Domino*).

The pontiff celebrates Mass. “Glory to God in the highest” (*Gloria in excelsis Deo*) is said, and praise is rendered by the deacons, subdeacons, and notaries. He is crowned at Saint Peter [124] and proceeds through the middle of the city to the palace with all the orders, as is customary.

From the feast of Saint Nicholas until the feria before the Nativity of the Lord, these antiphons are sung at Matins: “O Wisdom” (*O Sapientia*) at the Benedictus, and all the others in their proper order at the four Ember seasons.

**Note:** Here there is an evident distinction between the Vigils and Matins: a twofold office was said on the Third Sunday of Advent at Saint Peter’s. Something seems to be missing here to indicate the day.

**10.** On Wednesday the station is at Saint Mary Major. [Col. 1030C] The Collect is made at Saint Peter ad Vincula, at the Eudoxian church. The *primicerius* with the schola, the regional subdeacons, and the acolytes with Saint Peter’s processional cross [Col. 1030D] lift the cross from there with the Collect “For the procession,” singing as far as Saint Mary Major.

There the Lord Pope, prepared, sings Mass according to the Lenten rite, and announces whom he intends to ordain in the following manner: “With the help of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, we have chosen this deacon for the priesthood. If anyone has anything against him before God, let him come forward confidently and say so.” Nevertheless, let him remember his own condition.

**Note:** The processional cross, which was customarily carried to the stations and used to be placed upon the altar; see below, no. 29.

**11.** On Friday the station is at the Holy Apostles, with a procession.

**12.** On Saturday the station is at Saint Peter, where ordination is to be carried out by the pontiff, and where he is to celebrate Mass. While the office is being sung with great solemnity by the schola, and the hymn of the three youths, “Bless the Lord, all the works of the Lord” (*Benedicite omnia opera Domini Domino*), the pontiff descends from the altar and goes to Saint Andrew. There he performs the consecration.

After the consecration he returns to the altar, because no consecration is to be performed at this altar except that of the Roman pontiff. And so it is to be done in all four Ember seasons.

[Col. 1031A] **13.** On the Sunday of “Blow the trumpet” (*Canite tuba*), a reading is taken from the prophet Joel, “Blow the trumpet in Zion” (*Canite tuba in Sion*), as well as from a sermon, the Epistle, and a homily. When the ferial antiphons occur, let them all be sung in order at Matins. At Vespers let all the psalms be sung under the first antiphon. At the Magnificat let the proper antiphon be sung.

**14.** At Matins on the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord, the Invitatory is “Christ will come to us; come, let us adore” (*Christus adveniet nobis, venite adoremus*).

Antiphon: “The Lord said to me” (*Dominus dixit ad me*); Psalm: “Why do the nations rage?” (*Quare fremuerunt gentes*).

Antiphon: “He has set his tabernacle in the sun” (*In sole posuit tabernaculum*); Psalm: “The heavens declare” (*Coeli enarrant*).

Antiphon: “Lift up, eternal gates” (*Elevamini portae aeternales*); Psalm: “The earth is the Lord’s” (*Domini est terra*).

Verse: “Today you shall know that the Lord will come” (*Hodie scietis quia veniet Dominus*), followed by five lessons and five Responsories. The fourth lesson is a sermon of Saint Augustine, “You, I say, I address, O Jews” (*Vos, inquam, convenio, o Judaei*). In the fourth lesson the Sibylline verses are sung: “The sign of Judgment: the earth is drenched with sweat” (*Judicii signum, tellus sudore madescit*). The fifth lesson is from a homily.

On that day “We praise you, O God” (*Te Deum laudamus*) is not said. Instead, only “O God, come to my assistance” (*Deus, in adjutorium meum intende*) is said, with the antiphons of the vigil, and Psalm “The Lord reigns” (*Dominus regnavit*), with the other psalms.

At Prime, with the vigil antiphon, and the lesson “Paul, servant of Jesus Christ” (*Paulus servus Jesu Christi*), with the Verse, without the Kyrie, only the prayer of the day is said. Terce, Sext, and None are celebrated with their antiphons. The prayers are said not while prostrate, but only while standing.

On this day the station is at Saint Mary Major, where the Lord Pope is to sing Mass with the schools of clerics and the palace household. The Bishop of Albano is to provide an excellent dinner for the entire curia and is to send to the curia two excellent sides of pork. At [Col. 1031C] Vespers and for the vigil the pontiff is to remain there throughout the whole night.

**15.** At the first vigil the canons of the church read three lessons from the prophet Isaiah and sing three Responsories: “At the first time the land of Zebulun was made light” (*Primo tempore alleviata est terra Zabulon*), “Be comforted” (*Consolamini*), and “Arise” (*Consurge*). Thus the office is performed by the cardinals, bishops, and singers, as at the nocturnal stations of Saint Peter.

At the second vigil, readings are taken from sermons. At the third, from the same sermons and from a homily. At the manger he is to sing Mass, say “Glory to God in the highest” (*Gloria in excelsis Deo*), and one prayer only, together with “I believe in one God” (*Credo in unum Deum*).

The *primicerius* with the schola performs the Mass. When it has been completed, the *primicerius* returns to the choir, singing “Behold, Mary has borne us the Savior” (*Ecce Maria genuit nobis Salvatorem*), with the psalms and antiphon, as it is written in the Antiphoner.

When these Matins Lauds have been completed in this manner with the prayer, the pontiff begins Matins. [Col. 1031D] The schola says the Invitatory, and Matins is performed in the same order as the vigil.

**Note:** Observe here that the Vigils are distinguished from Matins, although the office is the same: the Vigils were celebrated in the depths of the night, divided into nocturns as if into several vigils, while Matins was celebrated in the morning. See below, nos. 60 and 63. Amalarius indicates this distinction in chapter 15 of the Antiphoner: “I found,” he says, “in the Roman Antiphoner two nocturnal offices placed in one and the same night, namely at the Nativity.”

**16.** In the morning he celebrates Mass at Saint Anastasia. When it is finished, he descends with the procession by the road beside the portico of the Gallators, before the temple of the Sibyl, and between the temple of Cicero and the portico of the Cimmerians [variant: Crinians]. Proceeding between the basilica of Jupiter and the Flaminian arch [Col. 1032A], he then goes beside the Severine portico; passing before the temple of Craticula, and before the Milicenan island [126] and the dragon-bearers, he descends on the left to the major road of Arenula, passing through the theater of Antoninus and the palace of Cromatius, where the Holomitrium [variant: Oloritrium] was located, and under the arch of the emperors Gratian, Theodosius, and Valentinian.

Entering by Hadrian’s bridge before his temple, and beside Nero’s obelisk and the monument of Romulus, he ascends through the portico into the Vatican to the basilica of Saint Peter, where the station is held. There Mass is sung honorably with all the palace orders, as is fitting. He is to receive the crown upon his head there and return crowned through the middle of the city with the procession to the palace, completing the festival of the crown.

**17.** But because of the shortness of the day and the difficulty of the route, he holds the station at Saint Mary Major and goes into the secretarium. The chamberlains guard the secretarium. The senior bishop serves with the book; the archdeacon with the Gospel; the senior regional subdeacon with the *mappula*; the prior *basilicarius* with the Epistle; and the *primicerius* and the schola with the singing.

Thus supported by two deacons, the archdeacon proceeds alone, without a companion, before the pontiff, and so enters the procession. Every order proceeds in its place, two by two: the acolytes with candlesticks, and the cross of the Lord Pontiff before the procession.

At the entrance to the church, the chamberlains carry the *mappula* high above the pontiff’s head. When he enters the presbytery, the church’s mansionary presents him with a reed bearing a lighted candle. The pontiff takes it and places the fire in the tow laid upon the capitals of the columns, symbolizing the end of the world by fire.

Advancing into the middle of the presbytery, he halts. The *primicerius* removes his mitre and kisses the pontiff’s right shoulder, and the pontiff blesses him. When he comes before the altar, the chamberlains offer the *mappula* above the pontiff’s head. [Col. 1032D] The pontiff himself gives the kiss of peace first to the senior bishop who is to serve him, then to the two cardinals, the first and the second.

**Note:** Below, no. 40, “with a linen cloth extended over his head.” Hence the name *mappularii* for those entrusted with this duty; they are discussed in the following little book of Cencius.

**18.** Ascending first to the altar, he makes his confession, kisses the Gospel which the subdeacon holds before him, and enters the altar area. Bowing his head, he says the prayer. When it is completed, he kisses the altar, rises, and gives the kiss of peace to the archdeacon and all the deacons.

The acolyte presents the censer and the box of incense to the archdeacon who is to read the Gospel. [127] The pontiff takes the box, places incense in the censer, and incenses the altar, while the archdeacon holds back his chasuble so that it will not impede him.

After the incense has been placed, he ascends to the seat. The cardinals descend to the choir, to their places, and the bishops to the right, to their places beside the pontiff. Meanwhile the *paraphonista* with the schola sings the Introit and “Lord, have mercy” (*Kyrie eleison*).

The pontiff begins “Glory to God in the highest” (*Gloria in excelsis Deo*), and the schola responds, “And on earth peace to people of good will” (*Et in terra pax hominibus bonae voluntatis*), through to the end. The pontiff says, “Peace be with you” (*Pax vobis*); the schola responds, not in the former tone but loudly, “And with your spirit” (*Et cum spiritu tuo*). One prayer is said.

**19.** Meanwhile the archdeacon, with the deacons and subdeacons standing in a line to the right beside the altar, and the notaries standing below in the choir, vested in copes, says in a loud voice with all the others: “Hear us, O Christ” (*Exaudi, Christe*).

The notaries respond: “To our Lord Innocent, by God’s decree supreme pontiff and universal pope, life!” (*Domino nostro Innocentio, a Deo decreto summo pontifici et universali papae, vita*). The archdeacon and his assistants say this three times; the notaries respond three times.

The archdeacon says, “Holy Mary” (*Sancta Maria*); the notaries respond, “Help him” (*Tu illum adjuva*). “Holy Mary”; they respond in the same manner from each of the three choirs. “Holy ones” (*Sanctos*)—so the text reads—twice. At the end of the Kyrie, the archdeacon with the deacons and subdeacons says it three times, and they receive three solidi as payment for the praise.

**Note:** This book was written while Pope Innocent II was alive and seated on the pontifical throne; these praises are therefore adapted to him.

**20.** The senior Latin subdeacon and the Greek subdeacon carry books before their breasts, accompanied by two subdeacons and one acolyte vested in a white tunic. An *oblationarius* [variant: *blacionarius*] goes before them, making a way with his hand.

On this day and on the day of Holy Easter, the two singers, the first and the second, descend into the ambo, and an acolyte stands before them in the ambo.

When the praise is finished, the Latin subdeacon reads the Latin Epistle; then the Greek subdeacon reads the Greek Epistle. They return to the altar giving thanks and kiss the pontiff’s feet.

The singers then begin the Gradual and the Alleluia [Col. 1033C], and the *primicerius* with the schola sings the Responsory.

The archdeacon and the Greek deacon, carrying the book before their breasts with four subdeacons, remain before the pulpit. The acolytes carry candlesticks before them and stand with the lighted candlesticks. The archdeacon and the Greek deacon read the Gospels.

When they descend, they bring the Gospels to meet the pontiff. The pontiff kisses them, ascends the pulpit, and preaches the Gospel. At the end he makes his confession, [128] gives a blessing, returns to his seat, and says “I believe in one God” (*Credo in unum Deum*). The *basilicarii* respond and sing.

The *primicerius* with the schola sings the Offertory (*Offerenda*). Then seven cardinals ascend to the altar with books, three on one side and four on the other. The pontiff, supported by a deacon, enters the altar area into the Canon to sacrifice the Host with the cardinal.

When the Preface has been completed, the *basilicarii* sing “Holy, holy, holy” (*Sanctus, Sanctus, Sanctus*), and so forth.

**21.** When Mass is finished, the pontiff, crowned by the archdeacon, mounts his horse and proceeds with the procession to the palace in the following manner.

Behind him is the prefect, dressed in a costly cloak and wearing one golden shoe and one red one. Around him are judges vested in copes. Before the pontiff are the archdeacon and deacon with the *primicerius*, two by two; then the subdeacons; before them the cardinals; before the cardinals the notaries, singing before them; before the notaries the bishops; before the bishops the cross of the Lord [Col. 1034A] Pope; before the cross the dragon-bearing soldiers, carrying twelve banners called *bandora*.

The Lord Pope’s horse is ornamented but empty. The *dirungarii* surround the procession.
