Two naval prefects, called *dilungarii* [variants: *dirungarii*], wearing copes and carrying staffs, accompany it. The *majorentes*, wearing silk mantles and carrying staffs, called the “spur school,” guard the procession so that no one may intrude.

**22.** When the pontiff comes to the basilica of Pope Zacharias, before he dismounts the cardinals descend to perform the praises.

Then the senior cardinal of Saint Lawrence Outside the Walls, having removed his mitre, says: “Command, lord, that I be blessed” (*Jube, domne, benedicere*). The pontiff blesses him. He says in a loud voice: “To the supreme, excellent, and thrice-blessed Pope Innocent, life!” The cardinals all respond: “May God preserve him” (*Deus conservet eum*), three times.

“ Savior of the world” (*Salvator mundi*). The cardinals respond: “Help him” (*Tu illum adjuva*), three times.

“Holy Mary, help him” (*Sancta Maria, tu illum adjuva*); throughout the entire choir, three saints are named. At the end: “All you saints, help him” (*Omnes sancti, adjuvate illum*), three times. The Kyrie is said three times. They receive three solidi as payment for the praise.

The judges then present themselves, and the *primicerius* says: “Command, lord, that I be blessed.” The pontiff blesses him and says in a loud voice: “This day” (*Hunc diem*). The judges respond: “For many years” (*Multos annos*), three times. “May you have good times” (*Tempora bona habeas*). The judges respond: “May we all have good times” (*Tempora bona habeamus omnes*).

Then the Lord Pontiff dismounts from his horse. The *primicerius defensorum* and the *secundicerius* take him by the hands and lead him into the chamber. [129] There he gives the *presbyterium* to all the orders.

On this day, the Nativity of the Lord, and on the day of Holy Easter, he gives all the priors the *manus*, that is, double *presbyterium*: to the prefect, twenty solidi, and the *manus*; to the *primicerius* of the judges, four solidi and the *manus*; to each judge, four solidi; to the senior bishop, four solidi and the *manus*; to each bishop, three solidi; to the senior cardinal, four solidi and the *manus*; to each cardinal, three solidi; to the archdeacon, three solidi and the *manus*; to each deacon, three solidi; to the *primicerius* of the singers, three solidi and the *manus*; to the *secundicerius* of the singers, two solidi; to the prior *basilicarius*, two solidi and eight denarii as an honorarium; to each singer, two solidi; to the prior *basilicarius*, two solidi and the *manus*; to each subdeacon, two solidi; to the senior regional officer, two solidi and the *manus*; to each of them, two solidi; to each acolyte, two solidi; to the two *dilungarii*, eight solidi; to the record-keepers, ten solidi; to the *majorentes*, five solidi; to the dragon-bearers, five solidi; and to the other orders according to custom.

**Note:** I believe that from this usage the familiar word *mancia*, meaning a gift made to dependents, derives.

**23.** After the *presbyterium* has been given, they enter the prepared dining hall. The bishops and cardinals sit on the right; the archdeacon, the deacon, the *primicerius*, the prior *basilicarius*, and the senior regional officer on the left. Every order is in its place.

The doorkeeper places a lectern with the book of homilies in the middle. About halfway through the meal, at the archdeacon’s command, the deacon rises and reads a lesson; the archdeacon himself brings it to an end.

Then the pontiff sends [Col. 1035A] an acolyte to tell the singers to rise and sing the Sequence (*Sequentia*) in melodious tones. They rise and carry out the command.

When the Sequence is finished, they go and kiss the pontiff’s feet. They receive one bezant from the sacristan, and the Lord Pope gives them a cup full of drink from his own mouth; they drink.

When the meal is finished, everyone returns to his own home; the cardinals are customarily sent to their own residences.

**Note:** This was the Sequence beginning with the word *Laetabundus*, from the Ceremonial of Urban VI.

**Note:** This manner of speaking still survives among us: *du vin de sa bouche*—“wine from his mouth.”

**24.** On the feast of Saint Stephen there are three lessons from the Acts of the Apostles, “But Stephen, full of grace and power” (*Stephanus autem plenus gratia et fortitudine*), and three from a sermon of Saint Stephen, with their antiphons and Responsories.

In the third nocturn there is material from the Nativity of the Lord, with three psalms, the Verse, lessons, and their antiphons. The Matins Lauds are of Saint Stephen.

After Saint Stephen’s prayer, the antiphon “Today the faithful Virgin” (*Virgo hodie fidelis*) is said, with the prayer of the Nativity. Terce, Sext, and None are of Saint Stephen; Vespers is of the Nativity of the Lord. The antiphon and prayer are of Saint Stephen and Saint John; likewise for the other feasts.

At first light the Lord Pontiff, crowned, leaves the palace and proceeds honorably with the procession to Saint Stephen, where the station is held. There they sing Mass as on the Nativity of the Lord, with the praise. When it is completed, he returns crowned to the palace, receives the praises from the cardinals and judges, gives the *presbyterium* or *manus*, and celebrates the banquet as written above. Then everyone departs.

**25.** On the feast of Saint John the Evangelist there are three lessons from the Apocalypse and three from a sermon of Saint John, with their antiphons, psalms, and Responsories. Some wish to read his Passion.

In the third nocturn there are antiphons and three psalms, and three lessons from the Nativity, with their Responsories. The Matins Lauds are of Saint John, with the commemoration as above; Prime is of Saint John; the prayer is of the Nativity.

**26.** On the feast of the Holy Innocents, at Matins, there are three lessons from the Apocalypse and three from a sermon. In the third nocturn the office returns to the Nativity of the Lord.

The *Te Deum* is not sung; the Matins Lauds begin instead. Prime is sung as above. At Mass “Glory to God in the highest” and the Alleluia are not sung, unless the feast falls on a Sunday; rather, the entire office is Lenten.

On this day the Romans eat neither meat nor fat, unless it falls on a Sunday.

**27.** On the vigil of the Epiphany, the office is that of the Nativity of the Lord.

On the Epiphany the station is at Saint Peter, where the Lord Pope with the entire curia sings the Verses as on the Sunday of “Rejoice” (*Gaudete*), on the day noted above.

At midnight he rises, and all the orders gather with him at the altar of Saint Leo. From there, with the procession as previously described, incensing the altars along the way, they proceed to the body, where he celebrates a vigil of three lessons. When these are completed, he ascends to the high altar and incenses it. He descends to the *pectoral*, and all the orders take their places.

He signals to the *primicerius* to begin the vigil. The latter begins the antiphon “Bring to the Lord, sons of God” (*Afferte Domino filii Dei*), and so forth.

Then three lessons are read from the prophet: “Arise, shine” (*Surge, illuminare*), [Col. 1036A] “Jerusalem,” and other lessons from a sermon, except for the ninth lesson, the homily, which belongs to the Lord Pope, [131] in the same order as on the Sunday of “Rejoice.”

He is to sing Mass honorably with the praises, receive the crown, return crowned to the palace, and conduct himself as at the other crown ceremonies.

During the Octave, each day at Matins there are three psalms and three lessons from a sermon, with their antiphons and Responsories, except on Sunday, when there are nine lessons. After the Octave, Paul’s Epistles are read. Some read from an exposition of the Psalter.

**28.** On the First Sunday after the Octave of the Epiphany, Paul’s Epistles are read, and the history from the Psalmist is appointed: “He will meditate on the law of the Lord” (*Qui meditabitur in lege Domini*), through Septuagesima.

At the first and second nocturns of Matins, antiphons are sung from the same psalms: “Serve the Lord in fear” (*Servite Domino in timore*), and so forth. In the third nocturn, Alleluia is sung in place of the antiphons.

At the Matins Lauds, Alleluia is sung in the tone “The light has dawned upon us” (*Lux orta est super nos*), and the other antiphons are sung as contained in the Antiphoner. At Prime, Terce, Sext, and None, Alleluia is sung. Vespers is from the Psalmist.

On all the Sundays of the entire year mentioned above, this is sung at the aforesaid Hours, except on the Sundays from Septuagesima through the Octave of Pentecost, from Advent of the Lord through the Octave of the Epiphany, and on the feasts of Sundays.

On ferial days, if there is no feast, this antiphon is sung at Prime: “Blessed are you, O Lord; teach me your statutes” (*Benedictus es, Domine, doce me justificationes tuas*).

At Terce: “Incline my heart to your testimonies, O God” (*Inclina cor meum, Deus, in testimonia tua*).

At Sext: “Give me life, O Lord, according to your word” (*Domine, vivifica me secundum verbum tuum*).

At None: “Look upon me, O Lord, and have mercy on me” (*Aspice in me, Domine, et miserere mei*).

**29.** On the Purification of Blessed Mary, sermons of that feast are read.

In the morning the station is at Saint Mary Major. Eighteen images [Col. 1036D] come out, carried by deacons, and proceed with the clerics and people to Saint Adrian, where the Collect is made.

But the Lord Pontiff goes down to Saint Martina with the bishops, cardinals, and the other schools. There he and all the other orders vest. Some cardinals bless the candles brought by the curia and the chamberlains.

The pontiff then comes out and ascends the seat before the church, where he distributes the candles as follows: first to the bishops, then to the cardinals, afterward to the deacons, the other orders, and the people.

Then he goes to Saint Adrian, where the processional cross is. The archdeacon signals the schola to sing. The *primicerius* begins and sings “Arise, O Lord, help us” (*Exsurge, Domine, adjuva nos*).

When the antiphon is finished, the pontiff says, “Let us pray” (*Oremus*); the deacon says, “Let us bend the knee” (*Flectamus genua*); another deacon [Col. 1036D] says, “Rise” (*Levate*); and the pontiff says the prayer.

**Note:** Not another, but the same deacon who said “Let us bend the knee” added “Rise” in those early times, as we saw above.

The deacon says, “Let us proceed in peace” (*Procedamus cum pace*). The schola responds, “In the name of Christ” (*In nomine Christi*).

Then the regional subdeacon lifts the processional cross from the altar, carrying it plainly in his hands to the church. When he comes outside, he raises it aloft and carries it before the pontiff in the procession as far as Saint Mary Major.

The *primicerius*, guiding the pontiff’s pallium from behind with his left hand, sings with the singers the antiphon “Adorn your bridal chamber, O Zion” (*Adorna thalamum tuum, Sion*). The pontiff and the others recite psalms.

Proceeding barefoot before the arch of Nerva, they enter Trajan’s Forum. Coming out through the arch of the Golden [Col. 1037A] Portico, they ascend in a straight line—variant: “house”—beside Eudoxia. Passing over the paved road, they go by the house of Orpheus, ascend through the title-church of Saint Praxedes, and reach Saint Mary Major.

There, when the schola has finished the antiphon, the regional subdeacon carries the cross to the altar as usual and performs the Litany, with the schola and acolytes responding. The Lord Pope sings Mass, but the Kyrie is not sung because of the Litany.

**Note:** See below, no. 33, concerning these images.

**Note:** The paved road is mentioned below, no. 52, where Simon Magus fell.

**30.** On the Saturday of Septuagesima, Alleluia is silenced at Vespers, and “Praise to you, O Lord” (*Laus tibi, Domine*) is said. Under the one antiphon “Call the laborers” (*Voca operarios*), all the psalms are sung.

When Vespers is finished, at Saint Peter the Pentateuch is read in three lessons until Matins.

At Matins, Genesis is appointed, from which six lessons are read: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (*In principio Deus creavit coelum et terram*). The seventh and eighth are from an exposition of the Epistle; the ninth is from a homily.

Thereafter the *Te Deum* and “Glory to God in the highest” are silenced, unless there is a feast of nine lessons.

At the Matins Lauds, all the antiphons are sung in order. At Mass, “Glory to God in the highest” is not said. During the week, the Gradual and Tract are read from Leviticus through Tuesday of Lent.

On this Sunday of Septuagesima the station is at Saint Lawrence Outside the Walls, where the Lord Pontiff is to sing Mass and, in his preaching, expound the Introits of this Sunday and of the Sundays that follow.

“The groans of death surrounded me” (*Circumdederunt me gemitus mortis*), says the sinner, and placed in such affliction [Col. 1037C] he cries: “Arise; why do you sleep, O Lord?” (*Exsurge, quare obdormis, Domine?*). When he can no longer endure so much suffering, he says: “Be for me, O Lord, a protector” (*Esto mihi, Domine, in protectorem*).

Now, trusting in God’s mercy, he says: “Have mercy on me according to your great mercy” (*Miserere mei secundum magnam misericordiam tuam*).

But the Lord, struck by such great lamentations, says: “He called upon me, and I will answer him” (*Invocavit me, et ego exaudiam eum*).

The sinner, breathing again after recognizing God’s mercy, says: “The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?” (*Dominus illuminatio mea et salus mea, quem timebo?*)—“My eyes are always toward the Lord, for he will draw my feet out of the snare” (*Oculi mei semper ad Dominum, quoniam ipse evellet de laqueo pedes meos*).

He is to join this Tract to the Gospel.

**31.** On the Sunday of Sexagesima, the reading is from Noah; on Quinquagesima, from Abraham; on Quadragesima, from sermons; on the Third Sunday, from Jacob and Esau; on the Fourth, from Joseph; on the Fifth, from Moses.

At the Chair of Saint Peter, the office is read as on the day of his Nativity. Nevertheless, at Vespers and the Matins Lauds “Behold, a great priest” (*Ecce sacerdos magnus*) is sung. The station is at his basilica.

The Lord Pope is to sit in the chair at Mass.

**Note:** That is, in the very chair of Saint Peter, which the Vatican basilica still preserves today.

**32.** On the Annunciation of the Blessed Virgin Mary, at Vespers:

Antiphon: “The angel Gabriel was sent” (*Missus est angelus Gabriel*); Psalm: “The Lord said” (*Dixit Dominus*).

Antiphon: “Hail, Mary” (*Ave, Maria*); Psalm: “Praise, children” (*Laudate, pueri*).

Antiphon: “Do not be afraid” (*Ne timeas*); Psalm: “When we rejoiced” (*Laetatus sum*).

Antiphon: “The Lord will give him” (*Dabit ei Dominus*); Psalm: “Unless the Lord” (*Nisi Dominus*).

Antiphon: “Behold the handmaid” (*Ecce ancilla*); Psalm: “Praise the Lord, Jerusalem” (*Lauda, Jerusalem*).

Verse: “Hail, Mary” (*Ave, Maria*).

At the Gospel: “The Holy Spirit will descend upon you” (*Spiritus sanctus in te descendet*); Psalm: “My soul magnifies” (*Magnificat*).

At Matins: “King of virgins” (*Regem virginum*), with its *Venite*.

In the first nocturn:

Antiphon: “Gabriel was sent” (*Missus est Gabriel*); Psalm: “O Lord, our Lord” (*Domine, Dominus noster*).

Antiphon: “Hail, Mary” (*Ave, Maria*); Psalm: “The heavens declare” (*Coeli enarrant*).

Antiphon: “Do not be afraid, Mary” (*Ne timeas, Maria*); Psalm: “The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness” (*Domini est terra et plenitudo ejus*).

Verse: “Hail, Mary” (*Ave, Maria*).

In the second nocturn:

Antiphon: “The angel of the Lord announced” (*Angelus Domini annuntiavit*); Psalm: “My heart overflows” (*Eructavit*).

Antiphon: “Before they came together” (*Antequam convenirent*); Psalm: “O Lord, our Lord” (*Domine, Dominus noster*).

Antiphon: “The Lord God will give him” (*Dabit ei Dominus Deus*); Psalm: “Its foundations” (*Fundamenta*).

Verse: “Blessed are you among women” (*Benedicta tu in mulieribus*).

In the third nocturn:

Antiphon: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord” (*Ecce ancilla Domini*); Psalm: “Sing to the Lord,” first (*Cantate Domino*, first).

Antiphon: “You are blessed, Mary” (*Beata es, Maria*); Psalm: “The Lord reigns” (*Dominus regnavit*).

Antiphon: “All will call me blessed” (*Beatam me dicent omnes*); Psalm: “Sing,” second (*Cantate*, second).

Verse: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord” (*Ecce ancilla Domini*).

These are the Responsories: “Gabriel was sent” (*Missus est Gabriel*), “Before they come together” (*Antequam veniant*), “Receive the word” (*Suscipe verbum*), “Behold, a virgin” (*Ecce virgo*), “We await the Savior” (*Salvatorem exspectamus*), “Let the heavens rejoice” (*Laetentur coeli*), “A star will rise” (*Orietur stella*), “All will call me blessed” (*Beatam me dicent*).

A sermon and a homily of Saint Ambrose are read.

**33.** In the morning the Collect is made at Saint Adrian, where the Lord Pope assembles with all the palace orders. After the blessed candles have been distributed, they proceed barefoot in procession, with the eighteen images of the deacons, to Saint Mary Major, as described for the Purification. There he sings Mass and Vespers, as stated for the vigil.

**34.** On Wednesday, the beginning of Lent, the station is at Saint Sabina, and the Collect at Saint Anastasia [Col. 1038C], where the Lord Pope comes with the entire curia. There he and all the other orders vest and ascend to the altar.

There the Lord Pontiff distributes ashes, and the *primicerius* with the schola sings the antiphon “Hear us, O Lord” (*Exaudi nos, Domine*).

After the Collect, the pontiff, barefoot, and all the others proceed with the procession to Saint Sabina. The *primicerius* with the schola sings from behind, “Let us change our clothing” (*Immutemur habitu*).

When he comes to the church, the regional subdeacon, having laid down the cross with the Litany, goes to the altar, with the schola and acolytes responding. There the Lord Pontiff sings Mass without the Kyrie because of the Litany.

**Note:** That is, because *Kyrie eleison* was said in the preceding Litany; see below, no. 35.

Before Communion, the regional subdeacon stands beside the altar and says in a loud voice: “Tomorrow, when the day comes, the station will be in the church of Saint George the Martyr at the Golden Veil.” The schola responds, “Thanks be to God” (*Deo gratias*). Then the *primicerius* sings the Communion.

When Mass is finished, the acolyte is to remove the wick [Col. 1038D], dip it in the oil of the candle, wipe it carefully, and carry it to the palace before the pontiff, saying: “Command, lord, that I be blessed” (*Jube, domne, benedicere*). The pontiff blesses him.

He then says: “Today the station was at Saint Sabina, who greets you.” The pontiff responds: “Thanks be to God.” The acolyte presents him with the wick. Out of devotion to the saint, the pontiff kisses it and gives it to the chamberlain. The chamberlain stores it and carefully preserves it until the pontiff’s death.

And so it is done at all the stations. At the pontiff’s death, a cushion is made from them and placed beneath his head in the tomb.

**Note:** Thus the ancients called the *ellychnium*, the wick used in lamps and candles. See Cangius’s Glossary under *Papyrus*.

**35.** When a Collect is made, the Kyrie is not sung at Mass, because the regional officer has said it in the Litany.

Throughout Lent the Gradual is repeated during the week, unless there is a Tract.

The Collect is made on Monday, Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday throughout Lent; during the four Ember seasons of the whole year; and on Thursday at Saint Mary across the Tiber and at Saint Apollinaris.

**36.** On the Sunday “Rejoice, Jerusalem” (*Laetare, Jerusalem*), the station is at Jerusalem, in the Sessorian palace, where the Lord Pontiff sings Mass honorably, holding in his hand a golden rose with musk.

After the Gospel he ascends the pulpit and preaches about the flower, the redness, and the fragrance of the rose, displaying it to the people. Then he expounds the Gospel.

After the praises have been performed and Mass has ended, he receives the crown there and returns crowned with the procession to the palace, as is customary.

Long before the pontiff’s descent, the prefect descends and walks beside him to the place where the pontiff is to dismount. There he gives him the rose, and the prefect kisses his feet.

After the praises have been received and the crown ceremony celebrated according to custom, everyone returns to his own place.

**Note:** Concerning this rose, see the observations in Cangius’s Glossary.

**37.** On the Sunday of the Passion, the prophet Jeremiah is appointed. There are three lessons from that prophet, three from a sermon, the seventh and eighth from an exposition of the Epistle, and the ninth from a homily; the rest of the office is entirely as written.

**Note:** Perhaps from the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 11: “Christ, appearing as high priest,” and so forth.

From this day until Holy Saturday, “Glory to the Father” (*Gloria Patri*) is sung in no Responsory, no *Venite*, and no Introit.

**Note:** That is, the Matins Lauds and the other daytime Hours.

**38.** On Palm Sunday at Matins there are three lessons from Jeremiah, three from a sermon on the Passion, two from the Epistle, and the ninth, the Gospel of the Passion.

The Matins Lauds are sung with their antiphons, as contained in the Antiphoner; the remainder of the office is as the church customarily performs it.

In the morning the station is at the Lateran. The palms have been gathered by the acolytes in the basilica of Saint Sylvester. From these the acolytes give palms to the basilica of Saint Peter [variant: palms are given to the acolytes of the basilica], and receive eight [variant: two] solidi from the altar.

One of the cardinals of Saint Lawrence’s basilica in the palace blessed the palms of the aforementioned basilica of Saint Sylvester. The doorkeepers carry them to the Leonine basilica for the pontiff.

When all the palace orders have vested, the pontiff distributes the palms. Afterward he leaves there with the procession. The *primicerius* with the schola sings “The children of the Hebrews” (*Pueri Hebraeorum*) and the other antiphons as far as the entrance of the church of the Holy Savior.

There a seat is placed upon the steps, and the pontiff sits. The *primicerius* with the schola begins “Glory, praise, and honor” (*Gloria, laus et honor*).

The prior *basilicarius*, standing with the subdeacons at the closed door, responds and sings the Verse “To whom belongs the honor of children” (*Cui puerile decus*). To every two verses the schola responds and says “Glory, praise, and honor.”

When these have been finished, the door is opened and they enter the church singing “When the Lord entered” (*Ingrediente Domino*).

In the secretarium the pontiff vests and enters for Mass without the *mappula*. The *primicerius* sings the Introit without “Glory to the Father.”

The deacon says the Gospel in this manner: “The Lord be with you” (*Dominus vobiscum*). The schola responds: “And with your spirit” (*Et cum spiritu tuo*). He says: “The Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ according to Matthew” (*Passio Domini nostri Jesu Christi secundum Matthaeum*). The schola responds, “Glory to you, O Lord” (*Gloria tibi, Domine*) [Note: omitted at this time].

Then the Gospel is read, and it is not preached.

On Wednesday and Friday alone, the Gospel of the Passion is read with its recitation, without the greeting and without a response.

39. From the Lord’s Supper until Holy Saturday: “O God, come to my assistance” is not said, nor the Invitatory, nor “Glory be to the Father” in the Psalms; rather, “Zeal for your house” begins, as it is contained in the Antiphonary. Nor does the priest say “Let us pray”; the reader does not ask for a blessing; [Col. 1040B] when he finishes, he does not say “But you, O Lord,” but is instructed to end with the words of the reading. Nine readings are read: three from the Lamentations of the prophet Jeremiah, and the others from an exposition of the Gospel; nine Psalms and eight responsories. Matins follows with its Antiphons and Psalms. When it has been completed, “Kyrie” is not said, but “Christ became obedient for us” is sung, “even unto death,” and they depart in silence. On Good Friday they extend the text with “even death on a cross”; on Holy Saturday, similarly, with “Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name.”

40. For the Mass, the supreme pontiff descends to the sacristy. After vessels filled with oil have been prepared, he mixes balsam with the oil. Then he vests himself with all the others, and has seven candelabra lit before him; [Col. 1040C] with a procession he proceeds to the altar, with a cloth stretched over his head. The primicerius kisses the pontiff’s shoulder and sings the Introit with “Glory be to the Father” and the Kyrie. The pontiff begins: “Glory to God in the highest.” The primicerius and the schola respond. When this has ended, the pontiff says only one Prayer. The subdeacon reads the Epistle from the ambo. Two cantors begin the Gradual: “Christ became obedient for us.” The primicerius and the schola respond, and the two cantors repeat the Gradual. The deacon reads the Gospel.

On that day, 137 while the lord pontiff preaches, the cardinals remove the table from the altar [Note: [Col. 1040D] What it means to remove the table from the altar, which is also mentioned in the following book of Cencius, no. 19, is clear from the preceding Tenth Roman Order, no. 7], strip the altar, and place the table in a secure location. After the preaching has been completed, he grants remission, blesses the people, and descends to the seat, where he announces “I believe in one God.” The Offertory is not said; only the pontiff enters the altar for the sacrifice, and he preserves some of this sacrifice for the following day, Good Friday. He sanctifies the chrism and the oil, as was stated in the Episcopal Order. The primicerius and the schola sing the Agnus Dei three times, “Have mercy on us,” and he says the Communion: “The Lord Jesus, after he had supped with his disciples.”

41. When the Mass is finished, the lord pontiff, still vested in this manner, returns to the palace in the basilica of Saint Lawrence, and there removes his vestments down to the dalmatic. After a fur [Col. 1041A] [Note: [Col. 1041D] Thus some people placed what they call an almutia around the neck against the cold] has been placed around his neck, he sits down. The chamberlains place a basin before him and a clean cloth. Twelve subdeacons remain outside the basilica; two ostiarii take the prior in their arms and carry him before the pontiff. The pontiff washes his feet with warm water, dries them with a cloth, kisses them, and gives him five solidi [Alt. II: two]; he does the same for each of the twelve.

Meanwhile, the primicerius, together with the cantors, cardinals, and deacons, sing Vespers. When this is finished, they sing “The Lord Jesus, after he had supped,” and the lord pope gives each bishop four solidi, each cardinal three solidi, the primicerius three solidi, and each cantor two solidi. When this has been completed, they go to supper in the basilica of Theodore, which is the Panetaria, where a subdeacon gives a continuous reading. After supper has been completed, he returns to his chamber, where he removes his vestments.

[Col. 1041B] 42. On Good Friday the weekly-duty bishop performs the office in the basilica of the Savior. The lord pope descends from the palace, vests himself there behind the altar with the other orders, and proceeds barefoot with the Procession; everyone goes with him, singing the Psalter, as far as the Holy Cross. A certain cardinal honorably carries the body of the Lord, preserved from the previous day in a case of corporals [Note: [Col. 1041D] This passage concerning the case of the corporals must be observed: the Eucharist was kept in it from the Lord’s Supper until the following Good Friday. Compare the beginning of the First Book of the Roman Order, no. 8]. A regional subdeacon carries at his breast the covered stational cross.

When the pontiff comes to the church of the aforementioned basilica, he washes his feet, puts on his shoes, and ascends to the altar; 138 he first prays and afterward sits down. A certain basilicarius goes to the pulpit and begins to read; thereafter the rest of the office is conducted as it is written in the book. After the “Our Father who art in heaven” has been completed, he takes the body of the Lord that the cardinal had brought and confirms it with wine poured into the chalice [Note: [Col. 1041D] He does not say “with wine consecrated by the insertion of a particle of the Eucharist into the chalice” [Col. 1042D]]. When the office is finished, they return in the same Procession, vested as before but wearing shoes, as far as the palace, singing the remaining Psalms. In the chamber the lord pope removes his vestments; the others, having removed theirs, depart.

43. On Holy Saturday, in the morning, the archdeacon rises and mixes oil and the previous year’s chrism into clean wax. The acolyte prepares and strains it, and makes from it figures resembling lambs, which the lord pontiff distributes on the Saturday of the White Garments. At Sext on Holy Saturday a new fire is made and the candle is blessed. Twelve readings are read in Latin and twelve in Greek, and three canticles are sung: “Let us sing gloriously to the Lord,” “The vineyard was planted,” and “Give ear, O heaven” [Col. 1041D].

When this office has been completed, the lord pontiff descends to the font with the regional deacons and subdeacons, singing the litany. The primicerius and the schola sing “As the deer longs,” as far as the portico of Saint Venantius. There, after a faldstool [Alt.: facistorium] has been prepared, the pontiff sits. The cardinals who remained in the choir go out through the small door behind the apse and enter through the [Col. 1042A] portico of Saint John, proceeding into the church of Saint Venantius.

Then the archdeacon orders two men to go to the door of Saint Venantius. They obey, take the prior of the cardinals by the hands, escorting him on either side until he is before the pontiff, with all the cardinals following him. The prior bows and says: “Command, lord, that I be blessed.” The pontiff blesses him. Advancing a little, he does the same, and the pontiff blesses him. The third time he does likewise, and the pontiff blesses him and says: “Go, baptize all the nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” [Note: [Col. 1042D] This is the sending of the cardinals to baptize infants in the baptismal churches, of which there were quite a few at Rome—especially the church of Saint Mary Major, discussed below, no. 45. See Cencius below].

The cardinals, thus vested, return to their titular churches on horseback [Note: [Col. 1042D] That is, with horses, as certain people of old used to do]. Then the pontiff enters for the baptism. When it is finished, he returns to the chrismal place, chrismates the infants, and washes his hands. Then he returns to the altar with a litany made by the regional subdeacon. 139 The primicerius [Col. 1042B] and the cantors sing the Kyrie; the lord pontiff begins “Glory to God in the highest.” The primicerius and the schola respond. When it has ended, he says the Prayer; the subdeacon reads the Epistle, and the pontiff announces the Alleluia. The primicerius sings it from the pulpit, and the schola responds. When this singing has ended, the primicerius descends and goes to the pontiff; he kisses his feet, and ought to give him one excellent cope.

On that day the Creed is not sung, nor the Offertory, nor the Agnus Dei, nor the Communion. Rather, at Vespers the following are said: “Alleluia”; the Psalm “Praise the Lord, all nations”; the Antiphon “But on the evening of the Sabbath”; the Magnificat; and the Prayer and “Go, the Mass is ended,” with the Blessing.

44. On the day of the holy Resurrection, at Matins, “Alleluia” is sung over “Come.” Some say “The Lord has truly risen” [Col. 1042C]. There are three Antiphons and three Psalms: “Blessed is the man,” “Why do the nations rage?” and “Lord, why have they multiplied?” In place of these three Antiphons, “Alleluia” is sung, as it is written in the Roman Antiphonary. The Verse “This is the day that the Lord has made” is sung like a Gradual. There are three readings from the Gospel with their Responsories. When these are finished, “We praise you, O God” is sung.

The Matins Lauds are performed with their Antiphons and Psalms. When the Antiphons have been completed, the Gradual “This is the day that the Lord has made” is sung in place of the Verse; the Antiphon is “The Lord has risen from the tomb,” the Psalm is “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel,” and only the Prayer of the feast is said. Prime is performed without an Antiphon, with three Psalms. When these have been completed, the Gradual “This is the day” and the Prayer of the day are sung.

[Col. 1042D] 45. At the Mass only one Prayer is said. On this day the station is at Saint Mary Major. In the morning the lord pontiff rises, goes to, and enters the basilica of Saint Lawrence. After a chapel and a bench have been placed there, he first prays; afterward he is vested by the regional deacons and subdeacons down to the dalmatic. He rises and enters to the Savior, unveils the image, and kisses its feet, saying aloud in song three times: “The Lord has risen [Col. 1043A] from the tomb, he who for us hung upon the wood, alleluia.” The others respond, and he returns to the bench.

First he gives the kiss of peace to the archdeacon, who returns to his place; then to the second deacon, who returns and gives the kiss of peace to his own archdeacon, and returns to the line. The other deacons do the same. Then the primicerius 140 and the cantors receive the kiss of peace and likewise return in line. Then the prior basilicarius and the subdeacon receive it and return in line; then the acolytes and the other palatine orders.

When the peace has been completed, the lord pontiff puts on the white chasuble, and from this day until the Octave of Easter does likewise; he also puts on the pallium and the mitre. With all these orders he descends from the palace. After horses have been prepared with white cloths on their saddles, he is crowned and rides in procession to Saint [Col. 1043B] Mary Major.

When he has arrived at Merulana, a notary stands there and says aloud: “Command, lord, that I be blessed.” The pontiff blesses him. The notary says: “In the church [Note: [Col. 1043D] The same rite occurs above in the earliest Roman Orders] of Saint Mary, on this night, so many males and so many females were baptized.” The pontiff responds: “Thanks be to God.” The notary receives one bezant from the treasurer. The same is done on the second day of the week at Saint Peter’s, and likewise on the third day at Saint Paul’s.

46. When the lord pontiff has arrived at Saint Mary’s, where the station is held, he dismounts; he removes the crown from his head and gives it to the stratores, so that they may guard it carefully. The church’s canons receive him with a thurible, incense, and holy water, in procession and singing. The pontiff places incense in the thurible and sprinkles water over the people.

[Col. 1043C] Then he enters the church, prays, and goes to the sacristy. When all the orders have assembled there, he first gives the kiss of peace to the prior bishop who is to serve him, and the bishop returns to his place. Then he gives it to the second bishop, who, returning, gives the kiss of peace to his own prior and returns to the line; and similarly to the others. Then likewise to the cardinals; afterward to the prefect and judges, to the delungarii—that is, the naval prefects—and to the majorentes, who are called the Schola Stimulata, and to the other lay officials.

Then two basilicarii subdeacons rise and take the prior regional subdeacon by the hands, escorting him on either side from the entrance of the sacristy before the pontiff. He says aloud: “Command, lord, that I be blessed.” The pontiff blesses him. Then they bring him forward a little, and he says again: “Command, lord, that I be blessed,” and he blesses him. [Col. 1043D] He advances farther and says: “Command, lord, that I be blessed.” The Lord blesses him and says:

“Servants of our Lord Jesus Christ; servants of our Lord Jesus Christ; servants of our Lord Jesus Christ: G., the archdeacon, shall read the Gospel; Hyacinthus, the subdeacon, shall read the Epistle; G., the primicerius, and the other cantors shall sing.”

141 47. Then the lord pontiff rises, supported by two men, and proceeds in procession, as is customary. At the entrance of the church the chamberlains hold a cloth stretched out, which they carry over his head as far as before the [Col. 1044A] altar. When he enters the presbytery of the church, the mansionarius prepares a reed with a lighted candle. He takes it and places the flame in the tow on top of the columns standing there.

When he comes to the first candle, the primicerius removes the mitre and kisses the pontiff’s right shoulder, and the pontiff blesses him. When he comes before the altar, the chamberlains remove the cloth from over his head. Thereafter he performs the office as the Church is accustomed to do.

The primicerius and the cantors sing the Introit “I have risen, and I am still with you.” The lord pontiff announces “Glory to God in the highest.” When this has been completed, the pontiff says the Prayer. The archdeacon, with the deacon and subdeacon, stands in ordered fashion beside the altar, while the notaries, in choir wearing copes, stand below. The archdeacon, with his companions, says aloud:

[Col. 1044B] “Hear, O Christ.”

The notaries respond:

“Life to our lord Pope Innocent, appointed by God supreme pontiff and universal pope.”

The archdeacon and deacon again say: “Hear, O Christ.” The notaries respond in the same way. This is said three times, and so forth, with what follows in the praise.

When the praise has been performed, the prior basilicarius subdeacon reads the Latin Epistle, and the Greek subdeacon reads the Greek Epistle. Two cantors sing the Gradual from the pulpit: “This is the day that the Lord has made.” The primicerius and the schola respond. When the singing has ended, the archdeacon reads the Latin Gospel, and the Greek deacon reads the Greek Gospel.

In the secret prayer, two deacons descend before the altar, together with two subdeacons, standing in ordered silence. When the pontiff says “For ever and ever,” no one responds to him; instead he begins and says “Our Father who art in heaven,” and what follows, etc.

48. When the Mass has ended, he is crowned and returns in procession to the palace by way of Mount Esquiline. He enters beneath the arch where the Lunanan [Alt.: Eumanan] market is said to be, proceeds before the temple of Marius, which is called Cimbrum, passes through Merulana, and ascends to the palace beside the Fullery [Note: [Col. 1044D] Another manuscript has: “which is called the Arch of Gallienus, now Saint Vitus in the Macellum of Nardini,” passing through Merulana and ascending to the Cimbrum palace beside the Fullery].

At the entrance of the basilica of Pope Zacharias, after receiving the praises from the cardinals and judges, as at the other coronations, he dismounts. He is received by the primicerius, and the secundicerius of the judges removes the crown and gives it to a chamberlain, who carefully stores it in a chest. The judges lead him that day into the great Leonine basilica, to the chamber where eleven benches have been prepared, [Col. 1044D] together with one bench around the table of the lord pontiff, and his bed, well prepared in the form of the twelve apostles around Christ’s table when they ate the Passover.

There five cardinals, five deacons, and the primicerius recline at table for the meal, after the presbyterium has first been given in the chamber with the hands, as on the day of the Nativity of the Lord. From there he rises and comes to the place called the Cubita, where the roasted lamb is blessed. He blesses it and returns to the prepared table-bed. The prior basilicarius sits on the bench before the [Col. 1045A] bed.

Then the lord pontiff takes a small portion of the lamb and first offers it to the prior basilicarius, saying: “What you do, do quickly; as he received it for condemnation, so receive it for remission.” He puts it into the man’s mouth, and he receives and eats it. He gives the remainder of the lamb to the eleven who recline at table and to others whom he wishes, and so everyone eats.

At the midpoint of the feast, by order of the archdeacon, a certain deacon rises and reads a lesson. The cantors, by order of the lord pontiff, sing a Sequentia appropriate to Easter, with instruments playing. When it is finished, they go and kiss the pontiff’s feet; he gives them a cup filled with a drink. They drink and receive one bezant from the treasurer.

49. When the feast is over, he descends into the basilica of the Savior, to the sacristy, where he rests briefly. Rising, after None has first been said, he enters for Vespers in the order written in the Antiphonary. When the three Vespers have been completed—in the basilica of the Savior, at the Fountains, and at the Holy Cross—the lord pontiff returns to the prepared portico. A faldstool [Alt.: facistorium] is placed there, and he sits, with the other orders around him.

The chief steward, together with the other young men, prepares a drink in an orderly manner before the lord pontiff. He himself drinks wine, and all the others drink as well. Meanwhile the cantors rise and sing this Greek Sequentia: Πάσχα ἱερὸν ἡμῖν σήμερον—“A holy Passover for us today.” When the Sequentia has ended, they go and kiss the pontiff’s feet, and he gives them a cup of the drink to drink. Thus everyone departs joyfully.

50. On the second day of the week the station is at Saint Peter’s. At Matins, over “Come,” “The Lord has truly risen,” alleluia. [Col. 1045C] “Come, let us rejoice.” In place of the three Antiphons, “Alleluia” is sung, and the three Psalms are “When I called,” [Alt.: “In the Lord”], “Hear my words,” and “O Lord, rebuke me not in your anger.” The Verse is “This is the day that the Lord has made”; there are three readings from the homily and two Responsories of the day; then “We praise you, O God.”

The Matins Lauds are sung with their Antiphons, Psalms, and Verses of the preceding day. When morning has come, all the palatine orders assemble at the palace with the pontiff. They descend from the palace, and the lord pontiff rides. He enters across the field beside Saint Gregory in the Campus Martius; descends to the main road beneath the arch of the aqueduct, and, keeping Saint Clement’s on his right, turns left beside the Colosseum. Passing through the Golden Arch [Alt.: Nervian] before Trajan’s Forum as far as Saint [Col. 1045D] Basil, he ascends by the hill around the Tiberian military quarters; he descends past Saint Abbacyrus, and, passing before the Church of the Holy Apostles, descends with the left hand along the Via Lata, turns through the Quirinal Way, and proceeds to Saint Mary in Aquiro at the Arch of Piety.

From there he ascends to the Campus Martius, passing before Saint Tryphon beside the small doors, as far as Hadrian’s Bridge. He enters by the bridge and exits through the Colline Gate [Alt.: Colina], before the temple and fortress of Hadrian. Proceeding before Nero’s obelisk, he enters through the portico beside the tomb [Col. 1046A] of Romulus. He ascends to the Vatican, to the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter, and there, with all the Roman people, sings Mass.

51. When this has ended, he is crowned before Saint Peter’s basilica, at the place where he mounted his horse. Crowned, he returns in procession to the palace by this Sacred Way, through the portico and over the aforementioned bridge. He enters beneath the triumphal arch of the emperors Theodosius, Valentinian, and Gratian, and goes beside the palace [Note: [Col. 1045D] Another manuscript has “commentarii,” as I suppose, instead of “before the palace of Saint Stephen in the fishpond of Bachi”] of Cromacius, where the Jews perform the praise.

Leaping forward through the Parion, between Alexander’s Circus and Pompey’s Theater, he descends through Agrippa’s portico [Note: [Col. 1046D] The same manuscript adds, for clarification, “of Saint Mary Rotunda, the Pantheon”]. He ascends by the Pinea beside the Palatine; proceeding before Saint Mark, he ascends beneath the Arch of the Fleshly Hand by the Silverers’ Slope, between the island of that name [Col. 1046B] and the Capitol. He descends before the private property of Mamertinus, enters beneath the triumphal arch between the Temple of Fate and the Temple of Concord, and proceeds between Trajan’s Forum and Caesar’s Forum. He enters beneath the Nervian Arch, between the temple of that goddess and the Temple of Janus; he ascends before the asylum by the paved road, 144 where Simon Magus fell, beside the Temple of Romulus.

He proceeds beneath the triumphal arch of Titus and Vespasian, which is called the Arch of the Seven Lamps. He descends to the Sweating Meta before Constantine’s triumphal arch, turns left before the amphitheater, and by the Sacred Way beside the Colosseum [Alt.: Colliseum] returns to the Lateran. There he is honorably received, and, after the praises of the cardinals and judges have been performed, ascends to the palace. He gives the presbyterium without the hands and celebrates a feast in the same Leonine basilica. When the feast is finished, he descends for Vespers and performs the office as it is written.

52. During the days within the White Garments of Easter, at Matins, the Invitatory is “The Lord has risen,” with its “Come.” On the third day of the week: the three Psalms “O Lord my God, in you I have hoped,” “O Lord, our Lord,” and “In the Lord I trust.” The Verse is “This is the day”; there are three readings with their Responsories. The Matins Lauds are as befits the day, as is the other office.

On the fourth day of the week: the Psalms “Save me, O Lord,” “How long, O Lord?” and “The fool has said.” In place of the Antiphons, “Alleluia” is sung, with the Verse “This is the day,” and with three readings and Responsories. The Matins Lauds and the other office are as above.

On the fifth day of the week: the Psalms “O Lord, who shall dwell?”; “Preserve me, O Lord”; and “Hear, O Lord.” There are [Perhaps: instead of] three Antiphons, “Alleluia,” with the Verse “This is the day,” and with three readings and Responsories. The Matins Lauds and the other office are as above.

On the sixth day of the week: the Psalms “The heavens declare”; “May the Lord hear you”; and “O Lord, in your strength.” The Verse is “This is the day”; there are three readings with their Responsories of the day. The Matins Lauds are as above, as is the other office.

53. On the Saturday of the White Garments, at Matins, the three Psalms are “The Lord is my shepherd”; “The earth is the Lord’s”; and “Judge me, O God.” In place of the three Antiphons, “Alleluia” is sung; the Verse is “This is the day”; there are three readings with Responsories. [Col. 1047A] The Matins Lauds and the rest of the office are as above.

In the morning the station is at the Lateran, where the apostolic lord sings Mass. There the Gradual is changed into an Alleluia, and two Alleluias are sung with their Verses. While the primicerius and the schola sing the Agnus Dei, the lord Apostolic distributes the lambs among the people, for this reason: just as the children of Israel, when they were in Egypt, by the Lord’s command wrote the sign T on the doorposts of their houses with the blood of the spotless Lamb, so that they would not be struck by the angel, so we too ought, through faith, to write this sign on the threshold of our houses with the blood of the passion of the spotless Lamb, Christ, so that we may not be struck by the devil and by vices, and may be freed from the devil’s power.

Another reason concerns the newly baptized infants, who, in the church, lay aside their old [Col. 1047B] tunic and announce “Alleluia,” that is, the glory of the blessed heavenly homeland. A third reason is that whoever possesses some of the wax of the aforementioned lambs and has made a cross from it in his house, or carries it with him, will not be harmed by any phantom spirit or by thunder.

From Easter until Saturday at Sext, at all the Verses of the office no Responsory is said at Prime, Terce, Sext, None, or Compline, nor is a reading recited at those Hours. Instead of a reading, Verse, and Responsory, the Gradual “This is the day” is sung, and the Verse is said as on the other days to come.

54. In the morning the station is at Saint Pancratius. At Vespers the lord pontiff ought to be at Saints Cosmas and Damian, with all the scholae. There he is to sing Vespers honorably, as on Easter Day, [Col. 1047C] and to have a meal supplied by the church, for himself and all the palatine orders—namely, bread, wine, milk products, and lettuce.

55. From Easter until the vigil of the Ascension, three Psalms of each nocturn of the particular weekday are to be sung, and three readings in place of the Antiphons. Among the Romans there are only three Alleluias, on Sundays, weekdays, and feast days alike; so that by the aforementioned term the Psalter may be completed without genuflection in any office. An Antiphon is not sung; instead of an Antiphon, “Alleluia” is sung, except when there are Sunday Antiphons with “Alleluia,” and likewise a feast-day Antiphon with “Alleluia.”

During the week, at Matins, the Invitatory is “Alleluia,” with its “Come.” At Lauds, one “Alleluia” is used. All the Psalms are sung to the tone “Do not weep, Mary”; the same is done at Vespers, except on Sundays and feast days. At all Matins Lauds and at the evening Hours, a commemoration is made of Christ’s Passion and Resurrection: the Antiphons “He underwent the holy cross” and “Do not weep, Mary,” with their Verses and Prayers.

On the second day of the week after the Octave of Easter, the Apocalypse is begun, together with the history “I am the vine,” continuing until the Sunday “A little while.”

56. On the Major Litanies, all the crosses of the city of Rome proceed honorably in procession, with the clergy and people, to Saint Mark’s. First they sing the Antiphon “O Lord, our Lord, who with our fathers”; then the Psalm “Blessed is the man,” and the remaining Psalms. When they have come to the church, the Responsory “Servant of God, Mark” is sung.

When the Responsory has ended, they make the Collect: “People of Zion, turn back to the Lord.” When the singing has ended, they say: “Let us bend our knees”; “Arise”; and the Prayer “Let us proceed in peace.” They respond: “In the name of Jesus Christ.”

Leaving the church, they return to the Procession and proceed along the road, singing Antiphons and Psalms, and at the appointed places the litanies, as is customary, as far as Saint Peter’s. They receive from the court of the lord pope the presbyterium according to the custom of this day.

57. Meanwhile, all the canons of the patriarchal churches, with their crosses, assemble in the basilica of the Savior, which is called the Constantinian basilica. There the lord pontiff vests behind the altar of that church with the bishops, cardinals, and other orders of the sacred palace. Then the primicerius and the cantors sing “People of Zion.”

When the singing has ended, the lord pontiff says “Let us pray”; the archdeacon says “Let us bend our knees”; another responds “Arise”; and the pontiff says the Prayer. The schola responds “Amen.” The archdeacon announces “Let us proceed in peace”; the schola responds “In the name of Christ.”

The regional subdeacon raises the stational cross from the altar and carries it fully extended on his arm, so that everyone may kiss it, in procession before the pontiff as far as the church’s exit; then he raises it upright. The primicerius, with the schola behind the lord pope, holding the pallium with his left hand, first begins the Antiphon “O Lord, our Lord.” Then the Lateran sings the same Antiphon; afterward Saint Mary Major; fourth, Saint Peter’s.

When the patriarchal churches have finished, the primicerius again begins the same Antiphon. In this order the other Antiphons are sung along the entire route while the pontiff sings the Psalms.

When the Procession comes before the Colosseum, the regional subdeacon begins the sevenfold litany [Note: [Col. 1047D] Note here the sevenfold, fivefold, threefold, and simple litany. Gregory the Great instituted the sevenfold litany, which was distributed among seven choirs [Col. 1048D]. Read Menardus in his notes on the Sacramentary, p. 94. Compare also the First Roman Order above, no. 43]. The basilicarii respond with the same words through the seventh repetition.

When they have come before Saint Mary the New, the lord pontiff rests on the prepared bed with the bishops, cardinals, and deacons until the litany is finished. When it has ended, the lord pontiff rises and says “Let us pray”; the deacon says “Let us bend our knees”; the response is “Arise.” 147 The pontiff says the Prayer; [Col. 1048D] the deacon says “Let us proceed in peace,” and everyone returns in procession along the Sacred Way to the previously mentioned Silverers’ Slope.

The subdeacon begins the fivefold litany in the same order as before, as far as the bed before Saint Mark’s, where the Lord rests, as at the first station. Then they return in procession as far as the triumphal arch of the emperors Theodosius, Valentinian, and Gratian, where the threefold litany begins and continues to the bed on Hadrian’s Bridge.

Coming to Saint Lawrence in the greater portico, the simple litany begins and is sung as far as the bed before Saint Mary in Virgari [Alt.: Virgariorum], at the end of the curtain.

58. When the litany and the other offices have ended, he ascends to the basilica of Saint Peter, where the station is held; there the lord pontiff sings Mass. At this station the lord pontiff receives twenty Pavia-denarii solidi; the cardinals, deacons, and the primicerius with the cantors receive forty Lucchese solidi; the prior basilicarius and the scrinarii write all the crosses and receive one Lucchese for each. Of these, the acolytes receive half and the basilicarii half; the [deacons receive] ten solidi, and the regional subdeacons six solidi.

59. On the Sunday “A little while,” the canonical Epistles are begun and continue until the third Sunday: “Father, while I was with them.” On this Sunday the Acts of the Apostles are begun [Col. 1049B] and continue until the vigil of the Ascension. From the aforementioned history, “If I forget,” is sung. Three readings from this book are read at the Ascension of the Lord, three on the Sunday of Roses, and two at Pentecost.

60. On the Ascension of the Lord the station is at Saint Peter’s, where the lord pontiff, with the bishops, cardinals, deacons, and the other scholae, ought to sing Vespers and, as at the nocturnal stations, rise at midnight and incense the altars. First he celebrates vigils at the body, then begins the same vigils in the choir before the high altar. There are three readings from the Acts of the Apostles; five from sermons for the feast; and the ninth from the homily, in the order stated above.

At the Mass, praises are performed by the archdeacon, deacons, subdeacons, and seven notaries. While the praises are being performed, [Col. 1049C] the pontiff stands. When they have ended, the rest of the Mass office is sung; when it has ended, he is crowned and returns to the palace in more glorious fashion.

During the week until the Saturday of Pentecost, on each weekday three Antiphons 148 and three Psalms of the aforementioned feast are sung, and three readings from sermons are read.

61. On the Sunday of the Rose, the station is at Saint Mary Rotunda, where the pontiff ought to sing Mass and, in his preaching, speak of the coming of the Holy Spirit, because roses are sent down from the height of the temple in the form of that same Spirit.

62. On the Saturday of Pentecost, for the baptismal office, six Latin readings and six Greek readings are read, and the rest of the office is as it is written in the Sacramentary.

[Col. 1049D] 63. On Sunday the station is at Saint Peter’s, to which the lord pontiff comes at Vespers of the vigil with all the orders; at night, for Matins, he does as at the nocturnal stations. He performs a vigil of three readings at the body; afterward, Matins at the high altar.

The Invitatory is “Alleluia,” as on the day of the Resurrection, with its “Come.” Others sing “Alleluia: the Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world; come, let us worship, alleluia.” Antiphon: “Alleluia.” Psalms: “Blessed is the man”; “Why do the nations rage?”; “Lord, why have they multiplied?” Others say “Suddenly there came a sound from heaven.” “Confirm this, O God.” “Send forth [Col. 1050A] your Spirit and they shall be created,” with their Psalms.

Three readings are read. The canons of the church read the first reading, “They were all filled,” and sing the first Responsory. The cardinals read the second reading from sermons; the cantors and basilicarii sing the Responsory. The pontiff reads the third reading. The remaining office is performed by the primicerius with everyone.

The pontiff sings Mass, with the praises. After the Mass, he returns crowned to the palace, as is customary. During the week, readings are taken from sermons. On the Saturday of the Four Times, the knees are not bent for the readings on account of Easter; instead of the Graduals, “Alleluia” is sung with its Verses. The Kyrie is not said on account of the litany of the procession, in which the Kyrie was said. Rather, when the hymn of the three boys has ended, the pontiff alone begins the Mass: “Glory to God in [Col. 1050B] the highest,” and the remainder.

64. It is called the “previous year’s Easter” because it occurs on the anniversary of the preceding Easter.

65. On the eighth Sunday of Pentecost, the Book of Kings is begun and continues until the Kalends of August. Then the nocturnal Psalms and the chapters are performed with genuflection, as circumstances require. At Prime, at all times, the Prayer of the day does not change, except during the days of Easter and on the great feasts of the saints, when only the Prayer of the feast is said, and during the octave.

66. On the vigil of Saint John the Baptist, at Matins, the Invitatory is “The Lord, the King of the Forerunner,” with “Come.” There are three histories of the feast and three readings concerning the saint. “We praise you, O God” is not said; rather, the Matins Lauds begin: “O God, come to my assistance” [Col. 1050C]. One Antiphon of Matins is announced, under which all the Psalms are sung.

At Prime there is an Antiphon, three Psalms, and a reading for the vigil of the feast, with the Verse and Prayer. He performs Vespers and the night vigil in the basilica of Saint John at the Fountains; the Greeks, however, do so in the basilica of the Savior. At Matins the Greeks perform the office at the Fountains, while the court is in the basilica of the Savior. The pontiff sings Mass there where the station is held.

At the vigil of Saint Peter, the vigil of Saint Lawrence, the vigil of Saint Mary, the vigil of Saint Andrew, and the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord, this office is performed at Matins, as we stated above concerning the vigil of Saint John the Baptist. At Prime, Terce, Sext, and None, material concerning the saint is sung and read. At the Mass, “Alleluia” is not sung because of the fast; only the Gradual is sung.

[Col. 1050D] **67.** On the feast of Saint Peter, the members of the papal household assemble in the basilica of that apostle, with the lord pope, where Vespers is sung. The antiphons are “The Lord has sworn and will not repent,” and other antiphons with their psalms. At the *Magnificat*: “The Lord made known to Peter.” In the first nocturn [Note: [Col. 1049D] Here again, as above at the Nativity, the Vigils are distinguished from Matins. Amalarius, in chapter 60 of his *Antiphonary*, calls these two Vigils. “From the Roman Antiphonary,” he says, “I placed two Vigils in our Antiphonary, namely, for the feast of Saint Peter.”] the *primicerius* begins the antiphon: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth”; Psalm: “The heavens declare,” and other nocturnal antiphons of the apostles with their psalms. The canons read three lessons from the Acts of the Apostles: “Peter and John were going up into the temple,” and they sing three responsories. [Col. 1051A] Then the judges read two lessons from sermons of the apostles Peter and Paul; the bishop reads the sixth, the cardinal the seventh, the prior of the basilica the eighth, and the lord pope reads the ninth, from an exposition of the Gospel. The cantors and basilicarii sing the responsories. When the lord pope’s lesson has been completed, the *primicerius* says, “Te Deum,” and the pope says the Prayer and gives the blessing.

At Matins the cantors sing the Invitatory: “Lord, King of the apostles,” and *Venite*. The antiphon is: “If you love me, Simon Peter”; the psalm, “Blessed is the man,” [150] and other antiphons with their psalms, as is written in the Antiphonary. The lessons are read in the order followed at the Vigil or on Sundays. Three psalms are sung, as before. The Morning Lauds are sung with the antiphon “Peter and John,” and with the remaining antiphons [Col. 1051B] and psalms. In the morning, at the lord pope’s Mass, praises ought to be given and he ought to be crowned on so great a feast, whose vicar he is.

**68.** During the Octaves of Saint John, Saint Peter, Saint Laurence, Saint Mary, the Nativity of the Lord, and the Epiphany, this office is performed: three psalms and three lessons, and the entire office of the feast, unless one of these days is itself a feast with nine lessons.

**69.** On the feast of Saint Paul, the pontiff goes there with all the schools; he celebrates Vespers and has supper with all of them at the church. When supper is finished, he enters for the Vigils. The monks of the church read three lessons: “Saul, still breathing threats”; they sing three responsories. For each responsory they receive two denarii from the archdeacon, out of the eighteen denarii which the archdeacon had received from them. [Col. 1051C]

After the responsory following the fourth lesson, the lord pontiff rises and enters the altar-chest of Saint Paul, where there is an opening in the bottom of the chest above the apostle’s body. After uncovering it, he reaches his hand downward, grasps a thurible full of coals and incense from a hook, and draws it out. He gives the incense and coals to the archdeacon, and the archdeacon distributes them among the people, in this manner: whoever is feverish and drinks of them devoutly in faith in the Apostle is healed.

Again he fills the thurible with coals, places upon them a glass candle filled with incense, lights the coals, and the candle begins to boil [Al., *bollire*]. He replaces the thurible on the aforementioned hook, and the pontiff covers the opening of the chest above the apostle’s body.

At the fourth lesson each year, as at the Vigils of Saint Paul, the bishops read two lessons; the cardinals two; the subdeacon the eighth; the pontiff the ninth. The cantors and basilicarii sing the remaining five responsories and receive eighteen denarii from the archdeacon. [Col. 1051D] The rest of the office is performed according to custom. In the morning the pontiff celebrates Mass with the greatest solemnity, and the schools receive four solidi in coins from the church as the benefit of the feast.

**70.** On the Kalends of August the Book of Solomon is begun and continues until the Kalends of September. On the feast of Saint Laurence, the lord pontiff celebrates Vespers in his basilica in the field of Verano, where he rests, with all the schools, and performs the office throughout [Note: [Col. 1051] In the Gregorian Sacramentary the first Mass for this feast is assigned to the night, p. 120 in Menard.] the night. In the morning he celebrates Mass for the Roman people, and the schools receive eight solidi in denarii from the church as the benefit of the feast.

**71.** On the vigil of Saint Mary, in the morning, the lord pope, with the cardinals and barefoot, makes seven genuflections, opens the image, kisses the Lord’s feet, and lowers himself downward [that is, *deorsum*], singing *Te Deum laudamus*. Pope Leo IV established this practice.

**72.** On the Assumption of Saint Mary, the lord pope, with the entire papal household, celebrates Vespers and a Vigil of nine lessons in the church of Saint Mary Major. When these are finished, he returns to the Lateran. The cardinals and deacons take the image of Jesus Christ and bring it out from the basilica of Saint Laurence with all the people, carrying it across the Lateran field beside the basilica [Col. 1052B] of Saint Gregory. The *regionarius* carries the processional cross behind it. After the cross, the procession of the papal household proceeds in orderly fashion, singing psalms; the *primicerius*, with the schola, sings a responsory for the same feast.

The prefect, with twelve men, receives twelve torches from the papal household. The doorkeepers carry another twelve, burning, before the image. While the image passes across the field, the chamberlains stand on the summit of Saint George, holding two burning torches, which they extinguish after the image has passed.

When the image has come to Saint Mary the New, they set it down before the church and wash its feet with basil. Meanwhile the schools perform Matins in the church, consisting of three lessons. The people, praising and blessing the Lord, then lift it from there and carry it to Saint Adrian; there too they wash its feet. After leaving the church, they return by the road on which they came and carry it through the arch at the Lathone, because in ancient times there was there a great persecution by the devil.

Then they pass beside the house of Orpheus because of the basilisk that at that time lurked there in a cavern; by its stench and hissing the people who passed that way became ill and died. Therefore Pope Sergius established this procession on so great a feast, so that through the praises of so many people and the intercession of the most holy virgin Mary with God, the Roman people might be freed from these persecutions.

Ascending to Saint Mary, [152] the lord pontiff, prepared for the occasion, celebrates Mass and blesses the weary people; all depart.

[Col. 1052D] **73.** On the first Sunday of September the Book of Job, Tobit, Judith, and Esther is begun and continues until the first Sunday of October. In that month is the Nativity of Saint Mary, which the pontiff celebrates with the greatest solemnity at Saint Adrian, where the assembly takes place, as at the Purification and Annunciation of Saint Mary.

**74.** On the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, the station is at the Lateran. The assembly is held at Saint Mary Major, where the processional cross, the schola, the *regionarii*, and the acolytes gather with the cross of Saint John and its canons, and with the cross of Saint Mary and its canons. The *primicerius*, with the schola, sings the collect; the regional subdeacon carries [Col. 1053A] the processional cross. The cantors lead the procession, and they proceed in procession as far as the Lateran.

The *primicerius*, with the schola, first sings the antiphon: “But we ought to glory.” Then the canons of Saint Mary, coming into the field near the Fullery, wait there with all the people for the pontiff and for [Note: [Col. 1053] That is, relics, as is clear from what follows. These words, “and the relics from the Palace,” are absent from two manuscripts.] the relics from the palace.

The vested pontiff, barefoot, descends from the palace with the other orders. The cardinals carry the relics in procession—namely, wood from the Lord’s cross, the sandals of Jesus Christ, and his Circumcision—to the basilica of the Savior, where the station is held. There the pontiff celebrates Mass; when it has been sung, all depart joyfully with the Blessing.

**75.** On the first Sunday of October the Book of the Maccabees is begun and continues until the first Sunday of [Col. 1053B] November. In the middle of October, on the Sundays that follow, at Morning Lauds, when “Bless the Lord, all the works of the Lord” is said, these antiphons are sung: “While they continue,” “I see three men,” and others found in the Antiphonary.

On the first Sunday of November the prophet Daniel is begun and is read on Sundays until the Advent of the Lord. During the weeks, Ezekiel and the Twelve Prophets are read.

**76.** On the feast of Saint Andrew the lord pontiff ought to be with all the schools at Saint Andrew in the Vatican, and there to celebrate Vespers and the Vigils honorably, as on the feast of Saint Peter. Matins, however, he should celebrate at his brother’s place—that is, at the altar of Saint Peter. In the morning Mass is sung at the altar of blessed Andrew, so that all the people may depart joyfully with the Blessing.

The prefect, with the assistance of the tithe, illuminates the church and prepares the papal household’s meal. Thanks be to God.

[Col. 1053]

## Addition from the Vallicellian Manuscript

[Col. 1053B]

These are the feasts on which the lord pontiff ought to be crowned: namely, the feast of the Four Crowned Saints; the feast of Saint Martin, where the title of Equitius is mentioned; the feast of Saint Clement; the Sunday of Advent; Jerusalem Sunday; Gaudete Sunday; the feast of the Lord; the feast of Saint Stephen; the Epiphany; Laetare Sunday, “Jerusalem”; Easter; Monday at Saint Peter; “I am the Good Shepherd” Sunday; the Ascension; Pentecost; the feast of Saint Peter; its anniversary; and the feast of Saint Sylvester.

These are the nocturnal stations of Saint Peter: Gaudete Sunday, the Epiphany, the Ascension of the Lord, Pentecost, the feast of Saint Peter and its Octave, and the feast of Saint Andrew. At each of these stations the schools of the papal palace—namely, cardinals, deacons, subdeacons, regional cantors, and acolytes—ought to receive five solidi in Papiensian denarii from the altar of Saint Peter for their meal allowance. [Col. 1054B] The archdeacon receives eighteen denarii for those who sing; the canons, twelve solidi; and at Mass half of the altar’s income, divided between them and the lord pope’s chaplains until the end.

If the lord pontiff is absent and a cardinal alone comes to sing Mass, at whatever station it may be, the aforesaid schools receive the entire half of the altar. The cardinal who sings Mass receives one-third of the offerings. But if he has a cardinal companion, this does not happen; rather, the offering is divided communally among the schools, as is customary.

[Col. 1054C]

These are the daytime stations of Saint Peter: all the Saturdays of the Ember seasons; Quinquagesima Sunday; Passion Sunday; the Monday after Easter; “I am the Good Shepherd” Sunday; the Greater Litanies; the Dedication; and the Chair of Saint Peter.

At each of these stations they receive five solidi and the offering. But the lord pontiff receives twenty solidi [154] at the nocturnal stations, when the *retia* are lit, and at the daytime stations, when the candles are lit.

[Note: [Col. 1053] They are called *phara* by another name—that is, a circular lamp with a fixed number of lamps or candles.]

# Appendix

[Col. 1053]

## Diploma of Pope John XIX [Note: [Col. 1053] The John who is called John XX by us, whose third year coincides with the year 1026, the third indiction beginning in September.]

By which he grants the bishop of Silva Candida the right to celebrate the divine offices on appointed days in the church of Saint Peter in the Vatican.

[Col. 1053D]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Peter, by the grace of God bishop of the Church of Silva Candida, and through you to that venerable bishopric and to your successors forever.

It is fitting for apostolic governance to come to the aid, with kindly compassion, of those distinguished by devout religion, and to grant the requests of those who petition with eager devotion. And shortly afterward:

Again, we grant and confirm to you forever the church of Saints Rufina and Secunda, situated at Rome beside our palace, with everything belonging to it; and we grant and confirm to you forever the church of Saint Mary, with all its appurtenances within this Roman city, not far from the hill called Augusta.

[Col. 1055A] Likewise we grant and confirm to you and to your successors forever, just as they were granted and confirmed by the aforesaid holy pope or by our other predecessors, pontiffs—namely, five monasteries: those of Saint Stephen, Saint Mary, Saints John and Paul, blessed Martin, and Jerusalem, situated beside the great church of Saint Peter, with all their appurtenances; and all consecrations that take place there, whether in the aforesaid church of Saint Peter or in the other churches established throughout the Leonine City.

If it should be necessary to consecrate them, no other bishop may presume to undertake such a ministry or consecration, except you and your successors, bishops of the holy Church of Silva Candida, forever. We grant and confirm to you and to your successors forever Holy Saturday for celebrating the sacrament of baptism and performing the entire office in the church of the apostle Saint Peter and above the great altar.

Upon this venerable altar, or in the confession, whatever gold or silver, pallium or wax, or other objects may have been placed, offered, or thrown down, or offered to you—from the third hour of the day, namely, when we wish you to enter the church to ordain and perform the divine office, until you have completed the Mass of the holy Lord’s Day—shall come, through your stewards, into the possession of you and your successors, without any opposition.

And because until our time, in the aforesaid church [Col. 1055C] of Saint Peter, from which almost all the churches received instruction as from a teacher and mistress, Palm Sunday, the day of the Lord’s Supper, and Good Friday were celebrated so irreverently that neither was a procession with palms held there on that Sunday, nor on the day of the Lord’s Supper was “Glory to God in the highest” said [Note: [Col. 1055] For formerly, it was not said by ordinary priests in the Mass except on Easter alone, according to the Gregorian Sacramentary.], and on Good Friday the office was not performed there with the reverence that was fitting, we grieved over this. Desiring to improve it through you and your successors, we decree that every year on Palm Sunday you shall go out in procession from the church of Saint Mary in the Tower, and, coming to the great altar of Saint Peter, celebrate Mass.

Likewise, every year on the day of the Lord’s Supper, we wish you and your successors to celebrate Mass upon the same altar of Saint Peter, say “Glory to God in the highest,” prepare the holy chrism, and perform whatever pertains to a bishop. And every year on Good Friday we wish you and your successors to perform the entire office reverently, as is fitting, upon that same great altar of Saint Peter.

In these three Masses—namely, the Palm Sunday Mass, the Mass of the Lord’s Supper, and the Good Friday office—whatever gold or silver, pallium or wax, or other objects may have been placed or thrown down upon the aforesaid sacred altar of blessed Peter or in the confession, or offered to you from the hour at which that Mass and office begin until their completion, shall likewise come through your custodians into the possession of you and your successors, without any opposition.

On these five days, if it should seem useful to you and your successors, we wish you to request that one of our deacons minister, out of honor for Saint Peter and reverence for you. We grant and confirm to you and your successors the authority over the same church of Saint Peter, over the aforesaid monasteries belonging to it, and over all their ecclesiastical judgments, as well as those of the entire Leonine City.

In like manner, for anointing and consecrating the emperor, we first summon the fraternity of you and your successor bishops, so that he may first be blessed by those to whom the governance of the whole church of Saint Peter and of the Leonine City has been entrusted. [Col. 1056B]

Moreover, we decree by apostolic authority that all sacred offices and mysteries which we and our successors ought to perform, if we are unable to perform them because of illness or some other concern, shall be performed by you and your successors, both in the aforesaid church of Saint Peter and its monasteries and throughout the entire Leonine City.

We grant and confirm to you and your successors forever, as stated above, the consecrations of the altars of the church of Saint Peter and of the other monasteries, as well as the consecrations of the churches, altars, priests, clerics, deacons, and deaconesses of the entire Leonine City.

Moreover, the churches of Saints Rufina and Secunda, over which by God’s authority you preside, we give, bestow, grant, confirm, and perpetually establish for you and your successors in the same venerable bishopric, for its use and benefit and for that of those who in due course hold that church.

By apostolic censure, under the threat of divine judgment and the prohibition of anathema, we decree that none of our successors who are pontiffs, nor anyone who has held public office, nor any other person, great or small, shall ever dare or presume to act against this our pontifical privilege in any of the matters contained above, or to alienate or remove anything; rather, we decree that all these provisions remain firm and stable forever, just as they have been established and confirmed by us.

But if anyone—which God forbid—should presume in rash boldness to act in any way against this our apostolic privilege, to become a transgressor, or dare to break it, and presume to be disobedient and fail to observe it in every respect, let him know that by the authority of almighty God and of our lord Peter, prince of the apostles, whose place we, though unworthy, nevertheless by some divine favor occupy, he is bound by the bond of anathema, excluded from the kingdom of God, and shall share in hell with Judas, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ, and with all the impious.

But whoever, moved by pious regard, proves to be the guardian and observer of this our privilege, may, through the merits and prayers of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and of the holy martyrs Rufina and Secunda, deserve to receive and find in the heavenly citadels rewards, the grace of blessing, and mercy from the just judge, the Lord our God, and eternal life forever and ever. Amen.

Written by the hand of Gregory, regional notary and archivist of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of December, in the aforesaid tenth indiction.
