Theobald, bishop of the Church of Velletri, subscribed. Peter, bishop of the holy Church of Ostia. Stephen, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Cecilia. Peter, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Damasus. John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Mark the Pope. John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Callixtus across the Tiber. Rudolph, unworthy priest and abbot of the monastery of Saint Laurence, which is situated at the Clausura. John, cardinal priest [Col. 1058A] of the title of Saint Chrysogonus. Benedict, archdeacon. Hugh, deacon. Crescentius, deacon. John, deacon by the grace of God. Crescentius, deacon. Franco, deacon. Rainerius, deacon. John, subdeacon. John, subdeacon of Mira.

Given on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of January, by the hand of Boso, bishop of the holy Church of Tibur and librarian of the holy Apostolic See.

Given on the day before the Kalends of January, through the hands of Benedict, bishop of Porto, and in the place of Peregrine, archbishop of Cologne, librarian of the holy Apostolic See, in the year of the pontificate of our lord John, supreme pontiff and universal pope, nineteenth of that name, seated in the most holy See of blessed Peter the apostle, *ill.* [abbreviation unexpanded], in the month of December, in the tenth indiction.

[Col. 1057]

## Extracts from the Book of Peter Mallius, Canon of Saint Peter, addressed to Alexander III

[158] **On the feasts on which the lord pope was crowned. Chapter XXVII**

[Col. 1057B]

These are the feasts on which the lord pope customarily was crowned: namely, the feast of the Four Crowned Saints; the feast of Saint Martin the pope, which is called the title of Equitius; the feast of Saint Clement; the Sunday of Advent at Saint Mary at the Crib; Jerusalem Sunday at the Holy Cross; Gaudete Sunday at Saint Peter; the Nativity of the Lord; the feast of Saint Stephen; the Epiphany of the Lord at Saint Peter; “I am the Good Shepherd” Sunday; the Ascension of the Lord; Pentecost; the feast of Saint Peter; the feast of Saint Sylvester; and his anniversary.

### Nocturnal and daytime stations

[Col. 1057C]

These are the nocturnal stations of Saint Peter: the third Sunday of the Advent of the Lord, which is called Gaudete Sunday; the Epiphany of the Lord; the Ascension of the Lord; Pentecost; the feast of Saint Peter and its Octave; and the feast of Saint Andrew.

These are the daytime stations of Saint Peter: all the Saturdays of the four Ember seasons; Quinquagesima Sunday; Passion Sunday; the Monday after Easter; “I am the Good Shepherd” Sunday; the Greater Litanies on the feast of Saint Mark; the Dedication of the churches of the apostles Peter and Paul; and the Chair of Saint Peter.

At each of these stations the schools receive five solidi in Papiensian denarii, specifically from the offering, and the lord pontiff receives twenty solidi [Col. 1057D] in Papiensian denarii. The same applies at the nocturnal stations, when the *retia* are lit, and at the daytime stations, when four candles are lit in each *capitulum*.

**159. When the lectern of blessed Peter was adorned. Chapter XXX**

In memory of posterity, we, the canons of the basilica of Saint Peter, write down on which nights the lectern of that basilica is customarily adorned with a small cloth and a two-pound torch supplied from the confession: namely, Gaudete Sunday; the Nativity of the Lord; the Epiphany of the Lord; Septuagesima Sunday; “Sunday of lifting the flesh” [Note: [Col. 1057] Perhaps *de carne levanda*, for Quinquagesima Sunday, which among the ancients was sometimes called “Sunday for taking away or lifting up the flesh.”]; the Chair of blessed Peter; the Dedication of the altar performed by Pope Callixtus; Passion Sunday; Palm Sunday; the Wednesday after Palm Sunday; the Lord’s Supper; Good Friday; Holy Saturday; Easter; the Monday after Easter; “Good Shepherd” Sunday; the Ascension of the Lord; Pentecost; the feast of Saint Peter; its Octave; the Assumption of blessed Mary; the Greater Litanies; the dedication of the basilicas of Peter and Paul; and the feast of All Saints.

It is certain that we, the canons of blessed Peter, on account of other reasons and customs which we have concerning the offering of the Mass at the great altar of blessed Peter, have, by the most ancient custom, always received the tenth week out of the nine weeks of the entire year—which are divided as follows.

The first seven weeks are received by the seven cardinals of Saint Peter. The cardinal deacons receive seven weeks, apart from the Sundays of the entire year that belong to them, with the exception of Palm Sunday and Easter, and unless it happens to be a station. The ninth week belongs to the cantors; the tenth week to the canons of the church; and the eleventh week to the basilicary schola. When it has ended, the aforesaid cardinals of Saint Peter begin again from the beginning, and this continues throughout the year.

The offering belonging to a week is the offering that comes into the cardinal’s hand after the Gospel has been sung. The offering that comes to the altar, after the chalice has been placed there, is divided in half: one half belongs to the altar, and the other half to the person whose week it is.

The person whose week it is first gives three *capita*, that is, three coins, from the common fund to the *mansionarii* who serve at the altar. Then, according to the amount of the offering, he gives a share to the deacon and subdeacon and to those who serve in the cope. Afterwards, [Col. 1059A] after fish have been given to the lord cardinal, he gives one-sixth to the cantors, [160] and two of the better torches.

### On the cardinal bishops arranged according to the patriarchates. Chapter XXXI

The seven cardinal priests who ought, in their respective weeks, to celebrate the solemn Masses at the most holy altar of blessed Peter are these: Saint Mary across the Tiber; Saint Chrysogonus; Saint Cecilia; Saint Anastasia; Saint Laurence in Damasus; Saint Mark; and Saints Martin the Pope and Sylvester, which is called the title of Equitius.

The cardinals of Saint Paul are these: Saints Nereus and Achilleus; Saint Xystus; Saint Marcellus; and Saint Susanna.

The cardinals of Saint Mary Major are these: the Holy Apostles; Saint Cyriacus at the Baths; Saint Eusebius; Saint Pudentiana; Saint Vitalis; Saints Marcellinus and Peter; and Saint Clement.

The cardinals of Saint Laurence outside the Walls are these: Saint Praxedis; Saint Peter in Chains; Saint Laurence in Lucina; the Holy Cross in Jerusalem; Saint Stephen on Mount Caelius; Saints John and Paul; and the Four Crowned Saints.

### Deaconries

There are eighteen deaconries: Saint Mary in Domnica, where the archdeacon ought to be; Saint Lucy in the Circus beside the Sun’s Enclosure; Saint Mary the New; Saints Cosmas and Damian; Saint Adrian; Saints Sergius and Bacchus; Saint Theodore; Saint Gregory; Saint Mary in the Greek Schola; Saint Mary in Portico; [Col. 1059C] Saint Nicholas in Prison; Saint Angelo; Saint Eustace; Saint Mary in Aquiro; Saint Mary on the Via Lata; Saint Agatha at the Marble Horse; Saint Lucy at the head of the Subura; Saint Quiricus; [Saints Vitus and Modestus].

### Abbeys

These are the abbeys: Saint Caesarius in the palace; Saint Gregory on the Clivus Scauri; Saint Mary on the Aventine; Saint Alexius; Saint Sabas, where it is called the New Cell; Saint Pancratius on the Via Aurelia.

Within the district of the Ravenna people, namely across the Tiber, is the abbey of Saints Cosmas and Damian in the Golden Street. Within the city is the abbey of Saint Sylvester between the two gardens, which Pope Stephen II began to build, but Pope Paul completed; these two apostolic men rest [Col. 1059D] in the church of blessed Peter.

There is the church of Saint Mary in the Chapterhouse (*in Capitulo*), where the altar of the Son of God is located; Saint Basil beside the palace of the emperor Trajan; Saint Agatha the virgin, which is on the mountain of the Subura; Saint Laurence in Panisperna, where he was placed upon the gridiron; Saint Thomas beside the Claudian aqueduct; Saint Basil in the Holy Field; and the Most Holy Trinity of the Scots.

Outside the city, on the Via Flaminia, is the abbey of Saint Valentine. On the other side of Rome, on the Ostian Way, are the abbey of Saint Paul and the abbey of Saint Anastasius. Again, within the city are the abbey of Saint Mary at Pallara, where Saint Sebastian was shot with arrows; Saint Mary in the monastery at Saint Peter in Chains; and Saint Mary in the Golden Fortress.

### How many lamps should burn daily in the church of blessed Peter. Chapter XXXVII

[Col. 1060A]

For the lights at the altar of blessed Peter: eight lamps in the body, day and night; three lamps before the breastwork; one in each chapel; and one candle in each crown, to be lit throughout the night until Mass is finished. There are at least thirty-four of these chapels, extending to the crucifixes. Thus all the lamps from the altar of blessed Peter to the crucifixes number fifty every night.

At the stations, four candles are placed in each chapel; in the *rete* in the church atrium, twelve; on the pole, eighteen; before the Veronica, ten, day and night; before the image of blessed Mary, which is made of mosaic and stands behind the Veronica, one; at Saint Processus, one; at Saint Mary of the Cancels, three.

In the great arch, where we have heard that the body of blessed Matthias the apostle rests, one, night and day; throughout the night, eight; at the Holy Cross, one. At Saint John at the Fountains, one; at Saint Lucy, one; at Saint Pastor, one; at Saint Gregory, one, night and day, in each of these places; in the Vatican, one; at Saint Mary in the Oratory, one; at Saint Leo IV, one; at Peter and Paul, one; at Saint Bartholomew, one; before the crucifixes, two; in the *rete*, four; on the pole, three; before the outer doors of the church, five; in each of the porticoes, three; at Saint Petronilla, two; and at Saint Andrew, one.

Thus all the candles that burn daily in the church of blessed Peter number at least 115 every night; at the stations, however, there are 250. At the Dedication, the Ascension, and the feast of Saint Peter and its Octave, the *retia* are lit; but the great one, which is in the atrium [Col. 1060C] of the church—namely, before the Silver Door—is lit only on the feast of Saint Peter and its Octave.

Besides these, according to ancient custom, four ropes are stretched in the atrium of the same church, that is, in the paradise, in the form of a cross, on the feast of Saint Peter and its Octave. They are fastened from the porticoes to the bronze pine tree in the paradise, and six candles are suspended from each rope.

On the steps, namely before the church of Saint Mary in the Tower, one large rope is stretched from the portico above the steps of the dead to the house of Peter John of Pampano, where by right it ought to be fastened according to the terms of the lease; eighteen candles are suspended from it.

### On the customs of the confession. Chapter XXXVIII

These are the things that the lord pope is customarily to receive from those who purchase the confession of blessed Peter for three parts; the canons receive the fourth part.

First, chasubles, albs, tunics, amices, stoles, maniples, girdles, a cross, a gold thurible suitable for singing Mass, books, and other vessels belonging to the altar service; candlesticks; fringed and covered cloths that cover the entire altar without fringe, whether merely fringed cloths, small or large; three denarii by weight of balsam; ten pounds of wax for the torch of Holy Saturday; three larger ampullae and three smaller ones; three *fanones*; oil for the chrism; and twelve Papiensian denarii for the palms of the canons of blessed Peter; six solidi [Col. 1061A] at six stations, six at each; six solidi on the feast of Saint Andrew; and two *aquariciae* of oil for the same feast.

When roofs are repaired and beams replaced, two Papiensian denarii are given to each master and laborer for every day until the work is completed. When the *sandialarii* receive the beams, two solidi in Papiensian denarii and four pounds of wax are given.

When the lord pope goes to Saint Peter for the stations, twenty solidi in Papiensian denarii and three *aquariciae* of claret are given to the cardinals and the pope’s chaplains. The other schools receive half of the altar’s income from the time when the altar cloth is spread over the altar.

At each station one pair of two-pound torches is provided for Vespers [163] and Matins, as well as candles for the lessons. At Mass likewise, one pair of torches. To the cardinals, five solidi in Papiensian denarii at the station, and three Lucensian solidi for the responsories.

At the four Ember seasons, on each Saturday, five Lucensian solidi are given to the cardinal deacon, the subdeacon, the cantors, and the acolytes.

From the feast of Pope Gregory until the feast of Pentecost, twelve Papiensian denarii are given each day to the lord pope; and one thousand pounds of wax each year; and each month, one *aquaricia* of oil and one pound of incense, if he is in the city or near the city, for one day.

By custom, during Holy Week the lord bishop of Saint Rufina has the right, namely, to the altar-table and altar, from when the bell is rung for Matins until the office is completed, and from when it is rung for Mass until the end, while preserving the half belonging to the canons and cantors, which they hold at the altar with the lord bishop.

For the entire half of the offering that comes to the altar belongs to the altar of the lord bishop; the other half is to be divided equally between the aforesaid lord bishop, the canons of the church, and the cantors. One share belongs to the lord bishop, another to the canons, and another to the cantors, if they are present for the appointed offices. If they are not, it belongs to the canons, while the prior custom of those serving at the altar is preserved; their share is to come from the common fund of all parties—the bishop, the canons, and the others.

On Thursday, from the time the signal is given for the Matins office and for Mass until the end of the offices; likewise on Good Friday; and likewise on Holy Saturday, from the signal for the Matins office and from the signal for the baptismal office, they possess their right throughout the entire night and day, and until the end of the principal Mass [Col. 1062A] on Easter.

The canons of the basilica of Saint Peter also receive ten pounds of wax for the torch of Holy Saturday; three denarii by weight of balsam; three larger ampullae and three smaller ones; three *fanones*; and oil for the chrism.

Likewise, the lord pope receives ten pounds of wax for the lambs at Saint Laurence of the Palace. One *aquaricia* of oil, one pound of wax, and half a pound of incense per month; and each week, when the lord pope is not at Rome, two Lucensian solidi for the doorkeepers.

At the Purification of Saint Mary, five pounds of wax and four denarii [164] for [Note: [Col. 1061D] Thus it is read in both the Vatican and Royal Manuscripts. The conjecture *pro mineis* had been proposed. But what relevance would that have? In Cencius, chapter 5, it reads: “The church of Saint Peter gives fifteen pounds of wax for these candles.” Yet that does not adequately fit this passage.] *vincis*; at the Annunciation, the same amount.

On Palm Sunday, twelve denarii for palms to the acolytes; the same amount to the mansionarii of Saint Peter [Col. 1062B] for palms.

At the major litanies, twenty-seven Lucchese pounds for the presbyteral allowance of the crosses, lecterns, and *lobi*; for the bishops and cardinals; and for all the schools of the palace.

For the alms of Saint Rufina, of the Four Saints, of Saint Clement, and of Saint Pancras: one *aquaricia* of oil, five pounds of wax, and half a pound of frankincense; and each week, for the alms of the poor, eleven Lucchese solidi; and while the *strata* procession is proceeding, additional payments beyond what is given to those cast out. And they are to serve blessed Peter abundantly with frankincense, and observe all the other customary rights.

To the prefect’s court officials, if they hang someone, five solidi; when they behead someone, likewise; when they blind someone, twelve denarii for each eye; [Col. 1062C] when they cut off any limb, likewise.

At each of these stations, the schools of the palace—namely, the cardinal-presbyters and cardinal-deacons, the subdeacons, the regional singers, and the acolytes—are to receive five Pavia denarii from the altar of blessed Peter as their food allowance. The archdeacon is to receive eighteen Pavia denarii for those who sing the Responsories, and half the altar-offering at Mass. The aforesaid schools share these payments among themselves and the pope’s chaplains until the end of Mass. The canons of Saint Peter formerly received twelve solidi, but now they receive six for each station.

If the pontiff is absent and the cardinals come solemnly to sing Mass, at whatever station it may be, the aforesaid [Col. 1062D] schools receive the entire half of the altar-offering. The cardinal who sings Mass receives one third of the offering; but if he has an associate, this is not done; rather, the offering is divided communally among the schools, as is customary.

## [ROMAN ORDER XII.]

[Col. 1061]

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING BOOK OF CENCIUS

[165]

Who Cencius, the author of the following book, was, no one has explained better than Onuphrius Panvinius in the preface that he prefixed to the same book in the great work on ancient rituals, which is preserved in Rome in the papal Palatine Library and in Paris in the royal library. His preface runs as follows.

### Brother Onuphrius Panvinius to the devout reader, greeting.

As I was examining the books of the old Palatine Library, the most fully equipped of all, in order to find something that might assist me in writing [Col. 1063] ecclesiastical history, I happened by chance upon a very ancient codex entitled *The Census Register*. It had been compiled roughly four hundred years earlier and reduced to a single corpus by a certain Cencius, cardinal-deacon of Saint Lucia in Orpheo and chamberlain of the Holy Roman Church under Pope Celestine III—who, after the death of Innocent III, was elected Roman pontiff and named Honorius III.

In it, together with all the revenues, taxes, and census payments of the Holy Roman Church, gathered by that same Cencius with the greatest diligence and accompanied by the public documents of each item, there is also transcribed this most ancient book of Ritual, or Ceremonial. In it one can see the purity and sincerity of that holy and venerable antiquity, as well as the utmost care and observance of the Roman Church in conducting sacred rites and celebrating divine worship. Many further things, not unworthy of knowledge and suitable for discerning the beginnings of the present condition of the Church, can be drawn from it.

Since I judged this book most worthy of human reading, I published it in this shortened form, to be handled by students of ecclesiastical antiquity, because I do not permit anything that I believe may assist such studies to remain obscure, insofar as it lies within my power.

Thus far Panvinius’s preface. From it we understand that he reduced Cencius’s book to a form different from that which its author had established. [166] This new form is as follows.

The whole work is divided into three parts. The first part, consisting of twenty-eight chapters, contains all the rites customarily used in the Roman Church from Advent of the Lord through the Exaltation of the Holy Cross. The second part concerns the presbyteral allowances customarily distributed throughout the year and the various officials of the pontiff; it contains twenty-three chapters. The third concerns the election and consecration of the pontiff and the coronation of the emperor.

We, however, considered it preferable to present Cencius’s book in its pure and unaltered form. Felix Cantelorius, formerly keeper of the secret Vatican Archives, states in a letter to Cardinal Barberini, when he presented him with a transcript of the aforesaid book, that this most ancient Ritual, used in the Roman Church before the year 1192, had been inserted by Cencius into the *Book of Censuses*. Nevertheless, Cencius must be considered the book’s author, as appears from no. 72, even though he transmitted a rite received and observed before his own time. He was likewise chancellor under Celestine III and was surnamed Sabellus.

The most illustrious Fabretti supplied us with the following information about our Cencius:

> “Beneath the walls of Ardea, the most ancient city of the Rutuli, stands a church dedicated to Saint Marina. On the upper threshold of its door there can be seen, on either side, two disks a palm in diameter, in which two hooded monks are carved in relief, looking at one another. The first disk bears the inscription *Abbot*; the other, *Father of Saint Marina*. Beneath the threshold, on the side facing the ground, are these two verses:
>
> *Cencius, then chancellor of the lofty city,*  
> *offered this doorway to you, virgin Martina.*
>
> “Finally, in the impluvium of the monastery of Saint Bartholomew on the Tiber Island there is a fragment bearing these verses:
>
> *Cencius, chancellor of the lofty city for you,*  
> *commends himself to you, most illustrious virgin Jesse,*  
> *Cencius, who was born from the lineage of the Benedictines . . . .*  
>
> *Grant him forgiveness of sins . . . .*  
>
> *Cencius, and his good father and mother . . .*  
>
> *Looking upon . . . with the words . . . . .”*

[Col. 1063]

## ROMAN ORDER XII: ON THE CUSTOMS AND OBSERVANCES OF THE PRESBYTERAL OR SCHOLARLY BODY AND OF OTHER MEMBERS OF THE ROMAN CHURCH AT THE PRINCIPAL SOLEMNITIES

By Cardinal Cencius de Sabellis.

[167] 1. What the Lord Pope ought to do during Advent and on the Nativity of the Lord.

[Col. 1063A]

### 1.

From the Sunday of Advent until the Nativity of the Lord, the Lord Pope does not wear the gold-fringed mitre, except on the Sunday when *Canite tuba* is sung, when he goes to the Church of the Apostles for the feast. Nor is *Te Deum laudamus* sung, except on the principal feasts. On that same day of Advent the same Lord Pope proceeds to the station of Saint Mary Major. In the Lectionary of Saint Jerome, [Note: [Col. 1063B] This is called the *Book of Comes*, published by Pamelius. See the appendix to Baluze’s *Capitularia*.] “At Saint Mary’s, at night, at the first cockcrow.”

### 2.

On the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord, in the morning the Lord Pope goes to the basilica of Saint Mary Major to sing Mass, and in the evening to celebrate Vespers. He remains there that night, celebrates the vigils there, and [Col. 1063B] after the vigils celebrates Mass at the manger. Whatever is offered there while the Lord Pope is celebrating Mass—whether into his hands, at his feet, or upon the altar—belongs to the chaplains, except for the bread, which belongs to the acolytes if they wish to receive it.

The same [Col. 1064A] should be understood of the Mass that he celebrates at Saint Anastasia. At dawn he goes to Saint Anastasia and celebrates a second Mass there. When it is finished, he returns to the basilica of Saint Mary Major and enters the sacristy with the bishops, cardinals, deacons, subdeacons, and the remaining orders; they say Terce. When it has been said, they vest and proceed [168] to the altar, as is customary.

It should be noted that seven torches must be on the altar during Mass, and the curia must provide them. The Lord Pope then begins Mass. After the first Prayer, the cardinal-deacons, subdeacons, and the other orders, together with the *scrinarii*, [Note: [Col. 1064B] Here the reading is clearly *scriunrii*, not *scriniarii*.] perform the acclamation for the Lord Pope in the following manner.

The archdeacon, together with the other vested deacons and subdeacons, stand beside the altar in two rows, while the *scrinarii* [Col. 1064B] stand below in the choir wearing copes. Then the archdeacon, with the deacons and the others, begins the acclamation in a loud voice: “Hear, O Christ.” The *scrinarii* respond: “Life to our lord the pope.” Again the archdeacon says, “Hear, O Christ,” and the *scrinarii* respond likewise. A third time the archdeacon says, “Hear, O Christ,” and the *scrinarii* respond as before.

Again the archdeacon says “Savior of the world” three times, and the *scrinarii* answer him three times, “Help him.” The archdeacon says “Holy Mary” twice, and the *scrinarii* answer twice, “Help him.” Then the archdeacon says “Saint Michael” twice, and the *scrinarii* answer twice, “Help him.”

In the same way are said: “Saint Gabriel, Saint Raphael, Saint John, Saint Peter, Saint Paul, Saint Andrew, Saint Stephen, Saint Lawrence, Saint Vincent, Saint Sylvester, Saint Leo, Saint Gregory, Saint Benedict, Saint Basil, Saint Sabbas, Saint Agnes, Saint Cecilia, Saint Lucy.”

When these have ended, the archdeacon says “Lord, have mercy,” and the *scrinarii* likewise respond, “Lord, have mercy.” Again the archdeacon says “Lord, have mercy,” and the *scrinarii* respond, “Lord, have mercy.” A third time the archdeacon, together with the deacons, subdeacons, and *scrinarii*, say with one voice, “Lord, have mercy.”

When the acclamations have ended, the Latin epistle is read first, and afterward the Greek one. When Mass has been completed, the Lord Pope is crowned at the gate of the church by the archdeacon with one deacon, and returns with the procession to the palace.

Then the judges and advocates come to meet him beneath the steps in the portico. There the senior cardinal of Saint Lawrence Outside-the-Walls, together with the judges and advocates, performs the acclamation for him. The Lord Pope then dismounts, removes the tiara, and receives the mitre.

Next the judges lead him to the place where the presbyteral allowance is distributed. [Col. 1065C] There they remove his chasuble; with the mantle placed upon his shoulders, he sits in the *fonslatorium* [*fosteslorium*], or chair, and distributes the presbyteral allowance [169] to all the orders with his own hand, as follows.

### 3.

On the same day of Advent, the same Lord Pope proceeds to the station of Saint Mary Major. On the second Sunday of Advent the pope goes to the station of the Holy Cross. On Gaudete Saturday he goes to Vespers at Saint Peter’s. There, when announcing the antiphon *Juste et pie vivamus*—“Let us live justly and piously”—to the primicerius, the Lord Pope gives him one marabotinus, throwing it.

Wherever the Lord Pope is required to officiate, attend the vigils, and perform all the other duties, he does and receives everything there with the chamberlain and chancellor, as will be said below concerning the Dedication of Saints Peter and Paul and certain other [Col. 1065D] feasts.

## II. How the presbyteral allowance is distributed

### 4.

To the senior bishop of the Roman Church, the Lord Pope gives a double presbyteral allowance: namely, four melequins and four Pavia solidi in denarii. To all the bishops and other members of the curia he gives two marabotini and two Pavia solidi, to each in the same way.

If some foreign archbishop happens to be present at that time, he receives a presbyteral allowance at the discretion of our Lord Pope; but from the portion he is to receive only as much as the aforementioned senior bishop: namely, four melequins and the same number of solidi. If a foreign [Col. 1066A] bishop is present, he is to receive one melequin and twelve Pavia denarii.

To the senior of the cardinal-presbyters the Lord Pope gives two melequins and the same number of solidi for his seniority. To the senior of the presbyters of Saint Lawrence Outside-the-Walls, for the acclamation, likewise two melequins and the same number of solidi. To all the other cardinal-presbyters, individually, one melequin and twelve Pavia denarii.

To the senior of the cardinal-deacons he gives four melequins and the same number of solidi for the seniority, presbyteral allowance, and acclamation of the deacons and subdeacons. To all the other deacons, individually, one melequin and twelve Pavia denarii.

To the Greek deacon, one melequin and twelve Pavia denarii. If a mitred abbot happens to be present, he is given one melequin [Col. 1066B] and twelve Pavia denarii. To the primicerius . . . he gives one melequin and twelve Pavia denarii.

To the senior of the subdeacons, one melequin; to all the other subdeacons likewise. Even if there were one hundred of them—namely, five, or more or fewer—they are to receive [170] twelve melequins. To the Greek subdeacon, one melequin.

To each school of singers, one melequin. To each school of the Cross—of which, by right, there should be at most four and no more—one melequin. To the senior of the chaplains, who are two and no more, one melequin; to each of the pope’s chaplains, one melequin.

To the prefect of the city, forty Pavia solidi in denarii. The prefect, clothed in a precious mantle and shod with one golden *zanca* [Note: [Col. 1065] The form of these shoes and of the other ornaments of the urban prefect can be found in Felix Contelorius’s book on the prefect of the city.]—that is, one greave, the other red—proceeds on that same day and the following day, and also on the two days of Easter and when the pope is elected, riding beside the Lord Pope without anyone between them, from the church of the holy Virgin Mary to the palace.

Half of the senators who then govern the city attend for the presbyteral allowance and to dine with the Lord Pope. To one of them—or to two on behalf of all the others—the Lord Pope gives, as the presbyteral allowance for each senator, one melequin. The Lord Pope gives each of the city judges one melequin and twelve Pavia solidi in denarii, except the senior, who is to receive one additional melequin for his seniority and one melequin for the acclamation.

To each advocate, one melequin and two Pavia solidi in denarii. To all the *scrinarii*, however many there are, six melequins and six Pavia solidi [Col. 1066D] in denarii. To the prefect of the naval forces, who is called the *Sangarius*, two melequins and four Pavia solidi in denarii.

Let posterity know that the Lord Pope ought to give the presbyteral allowance with his own hand to no one else except those named above. The Lord Pope gives the presbyteral allowance as stated above.

### 5.

Thus dressed, he is led by the master seneschal and by the master to the table in the basilica of Pope Leo III. At table, one of the cardinal-deacons reads while wearing a cope. Near the end of the meal, the school of singers must sing the Sequence.

## III. What the Lord Pope ought to do on the feast of Saint Stephen

[Col. 1067A]

### 6.

On the day of Saint Stephen, very early in the morning all the orders listed above, both clergy and laity, assemble in the basilica dressed in silk garments, except for the cardinal-deacons and [171] subdeacons, who, having vested, lead the Lord Pope from his chamber to the basilica itself. There all the cardinals show him reverence, and there he puts on a white chasuble.

As he descends from the palace to the small portico, he finds there a caparisoned horse covered with new scarlet cloth, except that, according to the ancient custom, the Lord Pope’s horse itself must not have a caparisoned neck. He mounts the horse and, receiving the tiara from the hand of the attendants, puts it on. Thus [Col. 1067B] crowned, he proceeds to the church of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill.

### 7.

So that it may be clear to everyone, present and future, how the aforesaid orders proceed in procession with the Lord Pope, it should be known that they proceed in the order described below and return with the same Lord Pope to the palace in a similar manner.

The prefect of the city, dressed as stated above, proceeds beside the Lord Pope, with judges dressed in copes around him. Somewhat apart in front of the Lord Pope proceeds the senior regional subdeacon with a towel, so that, whenever the Lord Pope wishes to spit, he may wipe his mouth with it.

The cardinal-deacons walk nearest to the pope, two by two. After them come the basilica subdeacons, preceded both by the regional subdeacons and by the school of singers with the Greeks, who are accustomed to read the Gospel and Epistle.

The *scrinarii* and advocates precede these; before them are the cardinal-presbyters; before these, the cardinal-bishops and the abbots of the city; and before them, if there are any, foreign bishops or archbishops.

Before these are two naval prefects dressed in copes. Before them are the bearers of twelve banners, called *bandora*, and one of the Lord Pope’s caparisoned horses, but riderless. Before all of them is the junior basilica subdeacon with the pope’s cross.

The archdeacon and the senior of the basilica must arrange the processions with their staffs, as has been written. So that no one interrupts the procession, they must move about and frequently return to their proper places. The archdeacon is between the Lord Pope and the cardinal-deacons; the senior of the basilica is beside the primicerius, between the cardinal-deacons and the subdeacons.

### 8.

When they have thus reached the aforesaid church of Saint Stephen, the pope removes the tiara and enters the church. After saying the Prayer, he goes to the sacristy, removes the white chasuble, puts on a red one, and celebrates Mass in every respect as on the preceding day.

When Mass has ended, [172] he resumes the white chasuble and puts on the tiara. Everything else is done as on the first day, except for the distribution of the presbyteral allowance, which is as follows.

To each of the bishops of the curia the Lord Pope gives two melequins and two Pavia solidi; to each of the cardinal-presbyters one melequin [Col. 1068A] and twelve Pavia denarii, except the presbyter of Saint Lawrence, who receives two, one for the acclamation and one for the presbyteral allowance.

To each cardinal-deacon one melequin and twelve Pavia denarii, except the senior, who receives one additional one for the acclamation. To each archbishop two; to each foreign bishop one melequin and twelve Pavia denarii; and to all the others as on the previous day, except that all the subdeacons together receive only twelve melequins, including the senior, and the prefect likewise receives only twelve Pavia solidi in denarii.

After the presbyteral allowance has been distributed, the Lord Pope is led to the table as on the first day.

## IV. That the Lord Pope ought to go to Saint Peter’s on Epiphany

### 9.

It should nevertheless be known that on Epiphany the Lord Pope goes to Saint Peter’s for Vespers and there does and receives everything with the chamberlain and chancellor, as is noted for the feast of the Ascension and the Octave of Saint Peter.

## V. What the Lord Pope ought to do on the Purification of the Blessed Virgin Mary

### 10.

On the Purification of the Blessed Virgin Mary, the Lord Pope goes in the morning with the cardinals to Saint Martina, where he sings Terce. Then in that church he vests up to the dalmatic; after putting on the mantle, he places the mitre on his head. All the cardinals vest, and there the *vastararii*, together with the doorkeepers of the basilica of the sacred palace, present the candles for blessing. The junior cardinal-presbyter blesses them in due order.

It should be noted that the church of Saint Peter gives fifteen [Col. 1068C] [Alt.: ten] pounds of wax for these candles. When this has been done, the Lord Pope leaves the church with the cardinals and ascends the seat that is before the doors of that church; there he distributes the candles to the people with his own hand.

Then he goes through the portico to the church of Saint Adrian and ascends the seat that is behind the altar. There he sings Sext. After it has been sung, he receives a lit torch from the senior of the bishops; if he is not present, from the senior of the presbyters. The school sings the hymn *Lumen ad revelationem*—“A light for revelation”—with the Psalm.

After the distribution of the candles, the regional subdeacon stretches out a towel; the Lord Pope washes his hands and puts on his gloves, chasuble, and pallium. To each cardinal, and to the chamberlain alone, he gives two candles; to the subdeacons and to the others, both clergy and laity, he gives them according to his will.

[Col. 1068D]

### 11.

It should be noted that there are eighteen diaconates in the city. After their clergy have celebrated Masses in them, receiving images from each of the deacons, they come with these images and with the people in procession, singing, to the church of Saint Adrian.

When they have assembled in that church, the primicerius with the school begins the antiphon *Exsurge, Domine*—“Arise, O Lord.” Meanwhile the Lord Pope removes his shoes, and all who are vested go with him in the procession; the Lord Pope puts his *planelli* back on. [Note: [Col. 1067] By the name *planelli*, the shoes that the pontiff had previously removed are meant here. This is clear from the following section.]

When the primicerius has completed the antiphon, the Lord Pope says “Let us pray,” the deacon says “Let us kneel,” the other deacons say “Rise,” and the Lord Pope [Col. 1069A] says the Collect prayer, namely [Note: [Col. 1069D] Another Collect prayer is assigned in the Gregorian Sacramentary, namely *Erudi, quaesumus, Domine, plebem tuam*—“Teach, we beseech you, O Lord, your people.” The Collect prayer is the one said at the place where the *collecta*, or gathering for the procession, takes place; on this matter, see above in our commentary.] *Preces populi tui*, “The prayers of your people,” etc.

When the Prayer has ended, the deacon says “Let us proceed in peace,” and the entire choir responds, “In the name of Christ.”

### 12.

When these things have been completed, the images precede the Lord Pope in procession, singing, all the way to the church of Saint Mary Major, and the Lord Pope follows the procession.

When he has come to the gate of that church, he removes his *planelli* and proceeds barefoot with the others in procession to the aforesaid church of Saint Mary Major. It should nevertheless be known that in all processions in which the Lord Pope walks on foot, he proceeds barefoot, with only one exception: the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, in the month of September.

When the Lord Pope has come to the church [Col. 1069B] of Saint Mary, the primicerius with the school of singers sings *Te Deum laudamus* at the entrance of the church. Then the Lord Pope enters the sacristy and removes his chasuble. There the school of the *mappularii* and *cubicularii* has warm water prepared for washing the Lord Pope’s feet. After his feet have been washed, the Lord Pope puts on stockings and sandals for singing Mass, and dons a white chasuble and a gold-fringed mitre.

The cardinal-deacon and the subdeacon, having removed their chasubles, put on dalmatics. Thus, with the procession, they go to the high altar, and Mass is celebrated there in the customary manner. When the sung Mass has ended, everyone returns to his own place.

## VI. What the Lord Pope ought to do on the Annunciation and Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary

### 13.

On the Annunciation and Nativity of the same holy [Col. 1069C] Mary, the Lord Pope rides with the cardinals to Saint Mary and does there, and at the church of Saint Adrian and of the holy Virgin Mary Major, everything that has been prescribed above for the Purification of the same holy Mary.

## VII. What the Lord Pope ought to do on the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary

### 14.

On the Assumption of the same Saint Mary, the following is done. The Lord Pope goes with the cardinals to Vespers. When Vespers has been sung, the Lord Pope remains there and sleeps; he must personally attend the singing of the vigils during the night.

It should be known that the junior of the deacons must say *Benedicamus Domino*—“Let us bless the Lord.” It should also be noted that wherever the Lord Pope goes to Vespers, the church in which the station is located must provide all the torches, both for Vespers and for the night.

The vigils [Col. 1069D] are celebrated in the following order. The canons of that church read the first three lessons and likewise sing the three Responsories. As they read the lessons, the Lord Pope gives the blessing, and the same cardinal-deacons preface him with *Tu autem*, etc.

To each of those three readers, the senior deacon gives two denarii from the Senate. In addition, at each lesson the Lord Pope approaches the high altar and manger with the thurible. [Col. 1070A] Before him the *mappularii* carry two torches placed upon the Lord Pope’s candlesticks. The same church provides the torches.

The fourth lesson is read by the *scrinarii*, the fifth by the senior of the bishops, the sixth by the senior of the presbyters, the seventh by the senior of the [175] deacons, the eighth by the senior of the subdeacons, and the ninth by the Lord Pope.

For carrying the thurible to the altar, the Lord Pope orders each cardinal to do so according to his will. At the Lord Pope’s lesson no one gives the blessing; nevertheless, he himself says *Jube, Domine*, etc.—that is, the blessing “May the Lord bless him” is said, and those standing around respond “Amen.”

The other Responsories are sung by one subdeacon and another singer, and each of them receives two denarii from the person assisting the Lord Pope; all the denarii must come from the church. [Col. 1070B] The four denarii that remain belong to the acolytes.

As long as the lessons are being read, two torches with the candlesticks of that church must be on the lectern; the remainder belongs to the acolytes. Whatever remains of the torches carried by the *mappularii* belongs to those same *mappularii*.

When these things have been celebrated in order, the Lord Pope says the Prayer of the vigil and enters his bed. Very early in the morning the Lord Pope says the Prayer and celebrates Mass. When it is finished, he returns to the palace.

It should be noted that, as stated above, this is how the vigils of all the solemn feasts of the city’s patriarchal churches are celebrated.

## VIII. What the Lord Pope ought to do on Ash Wednesday

### 15.

On Ash Wednesday, [Note: [Col. 1069D] Here Onuphrius indicates the old Ceremonial Book published under the name of Charlemagne, which now circulates under the name of Alcuin. Compare it with the commonly circulated Roman Order, most of whose prayers pertaining to this day are absent from the Codex Vindocinensis.] [Col. 1070C] around mid-Terce, the Lord Pope rides with the bishops and cardinals to Saint Anastasia. Received in procession by the clergy of that church, he enters the sacristy and vests with the cardinals and the other orders.

Meanwhile the ashes are blessed by the junior cardinal-presbyter. Then the Lord Pope goes with the cardinals and the school of singers to the seat behind the altar. When the ashes have been presented to him, the senior of the bishops places ashes upon him, saying these words: [Note: [Col. 1070D] These words were omitted in the time of Urban VI when addressed to the pope, according to the Ceremonial of Peter Amelius, below.] “Remember that you are dust, and to dust you will return.”

Afterward the Lord Pope places ashes upon the bishops, cardinals, and the other orders. When this has been completed, the primicerius with the school of singers begins the antiphon *Exsurge, Domine, adjuva nos*—“Arise, O Lord; help us.”

When it has been completed, the Lord Pope says “Let us pray” [176], the deacon says “Let us kneel,” and another deacon then says “Rise.” The Lord Pope says the Collect prayer, namely *Preces populi tui*—“The prayers of your people.” When it has ended, the junior cardinal-deacon says *Procedamus cum pace*—“Let us proceed with peace”—and the entire choir responds, “In the name of Christ.”

It should be known that from Septuagesima until Easter the Lord Pope does not wear the gold-fringed mitre, nor sing *Te Deum laudamus*, except on the principal feasts and on *Laetare, Jerusalem*, on which day the cardinal-deacons wear short chasubles.

Then, with those preceding in their proper order, the Lord Pope follows the procession barefoot with psalmody to Saint Sabina. His own cross, carried by one of his subdeacons, precedes him, as does the cross of Saint Peter, carried by the senior regional subdeacon.

When he has entered the church, he enters the sacristy. The school of the *mappularii* and *cubicularii* has warm water prepared there for washing his feet.

### 16.

It should be known that at the entrance of the church the acolytes must receive the cross of Saint Peter and carry it to the altar with the regional subdeacons while performing the litany.

After his feet have been washed, the Lord Pope, prepared, approaches the altar. When Mass has been sung in the customary manner, [Col. 1071B] he mounts his palfrey and returns to the palace.

### 17.

On the Sunday when *Laetare, Jerusalem* is sung, the chamberlain presents the Lord Pope in his chamber with a golden rose containing musk and balsam. The Lord Pope carries it in his own hand to the Holy Cross, where he must celebrate Mass that day. On his return he carries it likewise to the place where he dismounts. The prefect must be there, and the Lord Pope then gives the rose to him.

On that same day he wears the gold-fringed mitre. It should be known that at the very moment when the chamberlain presents the rose, the Lord Pope must take the gold-fringed mitre.

## IX. [Note: [Col. 1071D] Nothing is said here about the Saturday before Palm Sunday, on which day especially the pontiff distributes alms in memory of the deed of Mary, the sister of Lazarus, who anointed the Lord’s feet six days before Easter. Therefore this Saturday is free from the public station, as the commonly circulated Alcuin has it, though not from the celebration of Mass, which is repeated from the preceding weekdays. On the distribution of the fermentum on the same day, see our commentary. We found this chapter and the following one only in the Royal Codex.] On Palm Sunday

### 18.

On Palm Sunday a certain [Note: [Col. 1072D] This portable shrine or bier is discussed in the preceding commentary.] portable shrine is prepared with great dignity, [177] and the [Col. 1071C] holy Gospel—which is understood as Christ—is placed inside it. It is set in the church before the altar from which the clergy will proceed.

Then palms and flowers, together with various kinds [of branches], are gathered. The Prayer *Omnipotens Deus, qui antequam Filium tuum Dominum nostrum pro nobis mortem perpeti sineres*—“Almighty God, who before allowing your Son, our Lord, to suffer death for us”—is said.

The blessing of the palms, or branches, follows: *Omnipotens Deus Christe*—“Almighty God, Christ.” When these things have ended, the custodians distribute the palms. The people take branches of olive trees or flowers, and the antiphon *Pueri Hebraeorum*—“The children of the Hebrews”—is begun.

Then the deacons receive the aforesaid portable shrine with the Gospel, carrying with immense rejoicing the yoke of Christ, which is easy, and his burden, which is light. Holy water precedes it, together with candlesticks and thuribles and other ornaments. In addition, the school of the laity goes far ahead with banners and *fanones*.

As the clergy or people leave the church, the antiphon *Cum appropinquaret Jesus*—“When Jesus drew near”—is begun. When it has ended, the school begins the antiphon *Coeperunt omnes*—“They all began”; likewise *Cum audisset*—“When he had heard”; likewise *Appropinquante*—“As he drew near.”

When they have entered the church’s atrium, the Responsory *Ingrediente Domino*—“As the Lord entered”—is said; likewise *Collegerunt*—“They gathered”; likewise *Unus etiam*—“One also” [perhaps *autem*, “but”].

### 19.

When these things have ended, in front of the church atrium, or in a suitable place, [Col. 1072A] the school stops with its staffs and remaining ornaments. The clergy or people wait in the atrium, beginning the antiphon *Occurrunt*—“They meet him.” The school responds with the antiphon *Cum angelis*—“With the angels.”

When this has ended, two singers begin a certain Verse over the holy Gospel written above:

> “Glory, praise, and honor be to you, O Christ the King, Redeemer.”

The other Verses follow in the same order.

### 20.

When these things have ended, the school, with its staffs, begins the antiphon *Pueri Hebraeorum*. Then all the people strew branches or flowers on either side, singing the antiphon *Hosanna Filio David*—“Hosanna to the Son of David”—as far as the altar, and thus they enter for Mass.

The ministers hold the palms until the completion of Mass. Some omit the greeting during the Passion, namely *Dominus vobiscum*—“The Lord be with you.” This is not read in the Orders, but only on Good Friday, where the priestly office is omitted.

## X. On Wednesday of Holy Week

### 21.

On Wednesday of Holy Week, at the third hour, the apostolic pontiff proceeds with all the clergy or people to the church and says the [178] solemn Prayers, as on Good Friday. When these have been completed, he kisses the altar and departs.

The urban presbyters of the churches and those of the suburbs return to their titular churches. They are to complete the same rite on Friday, knowing that wherever the pontiff omits something on his own behalf, they are to commemorate him there.

### 22.

Afterward, at the eighth hour, they enter for Mass in the customary manner. These Prayers are therefore celebrated today because on this Wednesday the Jews took counsel to kill Christ.

The Mass of this day [Col. 1072C] has two lessons and two Responsories with the Passion, which is recited without the greeting. For the three successive days that follow—Thursday, Friday, and Saturday—we celebrate the Lord’s three-day burial. *Gloria Patri* is not said; the bells are silent.

## XI. What the Lord Pope ought to do on the Lord’s Supper

### 23.

On Thursday of the Lord’s Supper, at the sixth hour, the Lord Pope descends to the church of Saint John Lateran wearing a mitre without a fringe. After saying the Prayer before the crosses, he proceeds to the sacristy of the church of Saint Thomas with the bishops, cardinals, and other orders, and there sings None.

Then he vests up to the dalmatic. The cardinal-deacons put on dalmatics; the presbyters put on chasubles and mitres. Then [Col. 1072D] they are presented to the Lord Pope.

It should be known that the acolytes must receive from the altar of Saint Peter one *aquaritia* of oil, together with *fanones* and ampullae, and the chamberlain must provide three denarii by weight of balsam.

The senior deacon presents the large ampulla containing the oil; while the Lord Pope is seated in his chair, he puts the balsam into that ampulla and mixes it with the oil using certain small palm branches.

Afterward the ampulla is placed back upon the altar of Saint Thomas. When this has been done, the Lord Pontiff puts on a [Col. 1073A] chasuble and a gold-fringed mitre. He proceeds to Mass, preceded in procession by seven candles in seven candlesticks, as is customary on the other festive days.

24. It should be noted, however, that the curia must provide the torches and candlesticks. The Introit, *Gloria Patri*, *Kyrie eleison*, and *Gloria in excelsis Deo* are all said. They do not say the Creed. Thus it is found in the book of Pope Gelasius [Note: [Col. 1073D] Nothing of this kind is read in the Gelasian Sacramentary which the learned Thomasius published]. But we say the Creed 179 because of the consecration of the chrism. They do not exchange the peace; what has been offered is to be preserved; the blood is to be consumed completely. Irenaeus: “Far be it that discord should corrupt the harmony of charity and unity appropriate to the feast.”

All the bells are to be rung for the *classicum* more continuously than usual. The *Gloria in excelsis Deo* is sung without the Creed, and the *Agnus Dei* is said without the kiss. After the preaching of the lord pope, the cardinal deacons remove the table from the altar and, after stripping the altar, place it in a secret place. Having taken out two ampullae containing the blood and water of Christ, they cover the altar with a cloth, and after Mass it is sealed at its four corners.

When the Preface begins, the cardinal deacons go with the subdeacons and acolytes to bring the ampullae for blessing, preceded by the cross, the thurible, and two candles. Before *Per quem haec omnia* is said, the pontiff blesses the oil for the sick, as is contained in the *Ordo*. After he has said, “The peace of the Lord be always with you,” the pontiff alone communicates before the altar, and the deacon communicates him with the chalice on that day only.

Then he places the chalice on the altar and the paten beside it, and immediately covers both with a clean linen cloth after the corporal has been spread. At once two acolytes hold the wrapped ampullae with white silk linen on their left arms, so that they may be visible from the middle. One of the deacons comes, takes one ampulla mixed with balsam, and carries it to the archdeacon; he bears it before the pontiff at the altar.

Then, facing east, with the deacon holding the ampulla before him on his left arm, wrapped in linen, the pontiff breathes three times into the ampulla, so that it may enter into the consecration of the chrism. He says in a loud voice, “Lift up your hearts”; the response is, “We have them with the Lord,” followed by “Let us give thanks,” and so forth, as contained in the *Ordo*.

When the blessing has been completed, he blesses the ampulla of oil, which has been brought in the order described above, and likewise breathes into it, but silently. He says, “The Lord be with you.” The prayer is, “God of increase,” and so forth.

As soon as the ampulla containing the chrism has been blessed, it is to be covered so that no one may see it. While the deacon holds it, the lord pope salutes it and says three times, “Hail, holy chrism,” and kisses it. The acolyte receives the ampulla; while he holds it, everyone in order—bishops, presbyters, and deacons alike—salutes it uncovered.

When this has been completed, the pontiff, having washed his hands, comes before the altar and communicates the people in their proper order. He preserves some of the Sacrament [Col. 1074A] until the following day in the corporal. 180 On that day itself the schola, together with the others, sings the entire divine office without the organ.

### 25. 

When Mass has finally ended, the pontiff, vested with the others, returns to the palace in the basilica of Saint Lawrence. There he strips down to the dalmatic. A red cloak having been placed on him, it is fastened around his neck.

The chamberlains prepare warm water for washing the feet of the subdeacons and place a basin before him. The cardinal deacon who serves him places a towel, which the chamberlain provides for this service, upon the knees of the lord pope.

Twelve subdeacons remain outside the basilica barefoot with the prior. The schola of the doorkeepers and *mappularii* take the prior of the basilica and the other eleven subdeacons in their arms; [Col. 1074B] thus, in order, they carry them one after another before the lord pope. The pontiff washes their feet, wipes them with a linen cloth, then kisses them, and gives each two Papiensian solidi.

### XII. How the presbyterium is given on Maundy Thursday

### 26. 

According to ancient custom, the prior of the basilica is to receive one marabotinum without denarii. Meanwhile the *primicerius*, with the cantors and the other orders, sing Vespers. When this has ended, they sing *Dominus Jesus postquam coenavit*.

While these things are being done, the supreme pontiff distributes the presbyterium as follows. To each of the bishops of the Roman Church, two marabotini and two Papiensian solidi. If an archbishop happens to be present, the same amount. To each foreign bishop, and to the cardinal presbyters and cardinal deacons, one marabotinum and twelve Papiensian denarii. The *primicerius* is to receive one marabotinum without denarii; each cantor, twelve Papiensian denarii.

It should be noted that neither the schola of the Cross nor any other cleric or layperson receives a presbyterium on that day. The hands [Note: [Col. 1074D] “Hands” means a double presbyterium, from the preceding book of Benedict the canon, no. 21.] of the priorate are given to no one. At the exit from the basilica, each person distributes to the doorkeepers and chamberlains two Papiensian denarii for every solid received, except the priors, who give nothing.

### 27. 

Thus the lord pope, vested, goes with all the others mentioned above to the basilica of Zacharias, which on these days is now called the Bakery. There, vested in the dalmatic and cope, the ordained persons sit with mitres and wash their hands over the table, as is customary. [Col. 1074D] But the lord pope alone is at the table.

If an archbishop is present, he is to sit first on one side; then the bishops and cardinal presbyters; on the other side, the cardinal deacons with the *primicerius*. On another side an acolyte presents the book, and the junior of the deacons reads two verses at the table.

When the meal has ended, the lord pope enters the chamber and immediately performs the *Mandatum*, washing the feet of thirteen poor men, wiping them, and then kissing them. The chamberlain is also there, prepared to hand the lord pope individual marabotini for distribution to each poor man [Col. 1075A]. When this has been done, the lord pope gives them drink with his own hand.

When these things have been completed, everyone hastens to return home, and the lord pope enters his bedroom. It should be understood that the towel with which the lord pope, while washing the feet of the subdeacons in the basilica, is girded belongs to the cardinal deacon who serves him; the other towel, with which he wipes the feet of the subdeacons, belongs to the chamber of the chamberlains.

### XIII. What the lord pope must do on Good Friday

### 28. 

On Good Friday, at dawn, the lord pope summons all the chaplains into his presence and sings the Psalter in a moderate voice. When it has been sung, the chaplains withdraw.

At the sixth hour the lord [Col. 1075B] pope enters the basilica of Saint Lawrence with all the cardinals [Note: [Col. 1075D] This basilica of Saint Lawrence adjoins the Lateran palace]. After saying the Prayer, he approaches the altar. When the altar has been opened, he takes from it the heads of the apostles Peter and Paul and two crosses. After the lord pope and the cardinals have kissed all these objects, he replaces them in the same place. Taking one cross, and after the altar has again been sealed, one of the cardinal presbyters takes the cross, and thus they proceed as far as the Lateran church, without any singing or psalmody. After saying the Prayer there, he ascends the chair behind the altar.

Then the lord pope puts on the Lenten vestments and removes his shoes. The bishops put on copes; the cardinal presbyters, deacons, and subdeacons put on chasubles.

The junior cardinal presbyter then receives the body of Christ, reserved in a small box [Col. 1075C] before his breast since the preceding day; another receives the aforementioned cross; and the regional subdeacon with his people leads the way. All proceed barefoot with the lord pope and the *primicerius*, reciting the Psalter without singing, to the Holy Cross.

The weekly bishop remains behind to perform the office in the Lateran basilica. When the pontiff has arrived at the church, entered it without singing, and prayed for a long time before the crosses, he enters the cloister with all the others and goes to the sacristy. After removing his chasuble and cope, the *mappularii*, who have warm water ready, wash his feet. While he sits on his chair, the ministers put shoes on him—not sandals, but ordinary footwear—and dress him in the chasuble and cope. Thus he approaches the altar in procession, preceded by the cross and the Gospel, without lights or incense and in silence.

### 29. 

It should be noted, however, that the lord pope, with the procession, is not to go to the altar before the crosses in the usual manner, but by the path at the head of the choir, beside the altar steps.

One of the ministers places only one linen cloth upon the stripped altar. After kissing the altar, the lord pope ascends the seat. Immediately the subdeacons ascend the pulpit and read the prophecy in the manner of a lesson, without a title. The rest is performed as contained in the *Ordo*.

Afterward the cardinal deacon, without kissing the feet, makes the reverence, ascends the bare pulpit, and there, without torches [Col. 1076A] or incense, begins the Passion in this manner: “The Passion of our Lord,” and so forth.

When the deacon reaches the passage that says, “After these things Joseph asked Pilate,” and so forth, the acolytes customarily present the thurible with incense and carry it to the Gospel. When the Gospel has ended, the subdeacon presents the Gospel to the lord pope for kissing. This done, the lord pope says the Prayers.

When he comes to the Prayer for the Jews, *Flectamus genua* is not said, because on that day they bent their knees while mocking the Lord. The Church, horrified by their crime, does not bend the knee in prayer for them.

When the Prayers have ended, the pontiff proceeds to the altar and adores the cross with the others, as contained in the *Ordo*. It should nevertheless be understood that, according to ancient custom, whatever is offered upon the cross belongs to the schola of the Cross.

After the clergy and people have kissed the cross, the lord pope returns to the altar. Having made the confession, without the chapter, without incense, and without kissing the Gospel, he communicates from the body of Christ, which the cardinals bring. It should be noted that today *Pax Domini* is not said, the *Agnus Dei* is not sung, the kiss of peace is not given, and the postcommunion is not sung.

It should also be understood that the acolytes present incense at the chalice. The pontiff does not communicate at the seat, but before the altar, out of humble reverence for God and the Passion of Christ.

When the office has been completed, he removes his vestments with the other orders and sings there the Vespers recited on Maundy Thursday. Then he returns to the palace. Upon entering the basilica of Saint Lawrence, he replaces the cross he had taken from the altar [Col. 1076C], and from there proceeds to his chamber.

It should be noted that on that day the lord pope gives no one of his household wine to drink or cooked food to eat. He gives them only bread and water, and the customary herbs. On this day the church of the Holy Cross does not provide torches.

### XIV. What the lord pope must do on Holy Saturday

### 30. 

On Holy Saturday, at the sixth hour, a new fire is made in the courtyard before the doors of the Lateran church and is blessed by the junior of the cardinal presbyters, with incense and holy water.

Then they proceed into the church with the new fire placed in a reed, and the deacon says *Lumen Christi* three times. Afterward the candle is blessed by the same deacon.

Twelve Latin lessons and twelve Greek lessons are read, and three canticles are sung: *Cantemus Domino gloriose*; *Vinea facta est*; *Attende, coelum*.

When this office has ended, the lord pontiff descends to the font with the regional deacons and subdeacons, singing the litanies. The *primicerius*, with the schola, sings *Sicut cervus* as far as the portico of Saint Venantius. There the faldstool having been prepared, the pontiff sits.

The cardinals who have remained in the choir leave through the small door behind the apse, enter through the portico of Saint John, and come into the presence of the lord pope. The prior vests and says, “Command, lord, to bless.” The pontiff blesses him.

Proceeding a little farther, he does the same and blesses him a second time. A third time the pontiff blesses him and says, “Go, baptize all nations.” The cardinals, thus vested and mounted, return to their titles.

Then the pontiff rises and goes to the church of Saint John the Evangelist, where he rests for a short while. He then proceeds to the fonts and blesses them.

After this, he returns to the same church, 184 where he removes his pallium and chasuble and puts on waxed breeches (*bracalia*) [Note: [Col. 1077D] Panvinius also reads this. Could it be waxed *femoralia*? See Anastasius, in the Life of Pope Hadrian, where it is said that when Charlemagne entered Rome on the Saturday, he remained in the basilica of the Savior beside the Lateran until the pontiff had completed the sacrament of baptism, as Onuphrius noted. See the same Anastasius there concerning the following days.].

He returns to the fonts and baptizes three children; the junior deacon baptizes the others with the Lateran canons.

Afterward the pontiff returns to the place of chrismation and chrismates three infants. Having then washed his hands, he returns with the litany performed by the regional subdeacons to the altar before the church of Saint Pancratius. There he rests briefly [Col. 1077B] and puts on the chasuble.

### 31. 

Meanwhile the cardinal deacons bring back the altar table and set it upon the altar as it had previously been. The pontiff goes to the altar with the procession and litany and celebrates Mass.

It should be noted that at Mass there are seven torches with seven candlesticks. But he does not say *Credo in unum Deum*, nor the offertory, nor the *Agnus Dei*, nor the communion.

After the Epistle, the pontiff himself announces *Alleluia*. The *primicerius* with the schola sings it from the pulpit. No lighted torches go to the Gospel.

At Vespers, *Alleluia* is said, followed by the Psalm *Laudate Dominum, omnes gentes*, the Antiphon *Vespere autem Sabbati*, the Prayer, and *Ite, Missa est*.

### XV. What the lord pope must do on Easter Day

### 32. 

On Easter morning, after Prime, the Roman pontiff, dressed in a white cope, goes to the basilica of Saint Lawrence with the vested cardinal deacons, the subdeacons, and the other minor orders, dressed in dalmatics, mitres, and tunics, together with his chaplains.

The cardinal presbyters put on chasubles; the bishops put on copes in the place called the basilica of Saint Gregory. After the Prayer, he is vested down to the dalmatic and, rising, enters to adore the Savior.

He opens the image and kisses the Savior’s feet, saying three times in a loud voice, “The Lord has risen from the tomb.” Everyone responds to him, “He who for us hung upon the wood. Alleluia.”

Then the acolytes place the cross of the chapel upon the altar, and the lord pope adores it. After kissing the Savior, he returns with all the others to the seat [Col. 1077D] and gives the peace to the archdeacon, who returns from kissing the feet of the image, saying, “The Lord has truly risen.” He responds, “And has appeared to Simon.”

The second deacon likewise kisses the Savior’s feet, approaches for the peace of the supreme pontiff and the archdeacon, and takes his place in line. The other cardinal deacons do the same.

Then the *primicerius* with the cantors goes for the peace in the same manner and takes his place in line. The prior of the basilica likewise, with the deacons; afterward the regional subdeacons [Col. 1078A] with the acolytes and chaplains, and the other palatine orders, make the peace in the same manner.

Meanwhile the schola sings *Crucifixum in carne* and *Ego sum alpha et omega*.

### 33. 

When the peace has been completed, the pontiff puts on the white chasuble, cope, and solemn mitre. Descending from the palace as far as the exit of the little portico, where a white palfrey has been solemnly prepared by the master seneschal and the attendants, with a scarlet saddlecloth placed upon it and a silver bridle, he is given the crown by the archdeacon.

Thus crowned, he mounts the palfrey and proceeds on horseback, preceded in their proper order by the *bandularii*, archbishops, bishops, cardinal presbyters, abbots, subdeacons, and cardinal deacons, and followed by the prefect and the other Roman nobles [Col. 1078B], as far as Saint Mary Major, just as is described above for the feast of Saint Stephen.

When he has passed through the Merulana, the *scrinarius* meets him at the anciently appointed place and says in a loud voice, “Command, lord, to bless.” The pontiff blesses him, and the *scrinarius* says: “In the church of blessed Mary, on this night, so many male children and so many females were baptized.” The pontiff replies, “Thanks be to God.”

Then the *scrinarius* receives from the chamberlain one marabotinum for the announcement. The same is done at Saint Peter’s on the second day.

When the pontiff arrives with the procession at the portico of Saint Mary, he descends to the Papal Stone, at the anciently appointed place. After the crown has been removed, he is led by the judges into the church. The canons of that church receive the procession, and after the Blessing he goes to the sacristy.

Removing his cope and chasuble, and placing a cope upon his shoulders, he begins Terce. When Terce has ended, the senior of the bishops who is to serve him at Mass is led before the pontiff by two bishops. Having requested the Blessing a third time, he approaches for the pontiff’s peace, rises, and takes his place in line on the pontiff’s right.

Then the second bishop approaches for the pontiff’s peace, gives the kiss to his predecessor, and stands in line on the other side of the pontiff. The other bishops do likewise, approaching for the pontiff’s peace and taking their places in line.

The senior of the cardinal presbyters is also led before the pontiff by two presbyters. Having requested the Blessing a third time, he approaches for the peace of the pontiff and the bishops and takes his place in line.

The other cardinal presbyters follow. The prefect, judges, prefects of the naval forces, advocates, *scrinarii*, senators, *majorentes*—who are called the schola of the *Stimulati*—and the other greater and lesser laymen follow in their proper order to receive the peace.

Afterward two basilica subdeacons rise, take the prior regional subdeacon, and escort him by the hands from the entrance of the sacristy to the middle of the courtyard before the pontiff. He says in a loud voice three times, “Command, lord, to bless.” Having received the Blessing from the pontiff a third time [Col. 1079A], he adds three times, “Servants of our Lord Jesus Christ,” and says: “Let the lord archdeacon read the Gospel; let the subdeacon read the Epistle; let the *primicerius* and the other cantors sing.”

### 34. 

When these things have been completed, the pontiff rises, resumes the chasuble, cope, and mitre, and proceeds in procession to the altar, beginning Mass in the customary manner.

After the Prayer, before the Epistle is read, the archdeacon descends with the deacon and subdeacon, and they stand in due order beside the altar in two lines, while the *scrinarii* stand in copes.

Then the archdeacon, with the deacon and subdeacon and the other orders, begins the laudes in a loud voice, and the others respond, as was written above for the feast of blessed Stephen.

When the laudes have ended, the Latin Epistle is read first, and afterward the Greek one; likewise the Latin and Greek Gospels.

In the Secret, when the Preface begins, two deacons with two subdeacons descend below and stand in due order silently at the front of the altar. When the pontiff says, “The peace of the Lord be always with you,” no one responds to him. Then the deacon and subdeacon return above.

### 35. 

When Mass has ended, he is crowned and returns with the procession to the palace, as stated above for the aforementioned feast of Saint Stephen. After receiving the laudes from the cardinal of Saint Lawrence, he is led by the *primicerius* and *secundicerius* and the judges, with the mitre, into the great Leonine basilica, called the Major House.

There eleven benches are prepared around the pontiff’s table for the presbyters, 187 deacons, and the *primicerius*. The pontiff’s couch is also solemnly prepared there in the form of the eleven apostles reclining around Christ’s table.

Passing through that basilica, the pontiff enters the chamber. There, after receiving the presbyterium from the chamberlain in a silver bowl, and distributing it as on the Nativity of the Lord, he rises and is led by the master seneschal and the cupbearer to the place called the Dining Chamber.

There the roasted lamb is blessed by the junior cardinal presbyter. From there he returns to the prepared dining couch. The same pontiff takes a little of that lamb and presents it to the prior basilicarius, seated on a bench before his couch, saying: “What you do, do quickly; just as he received it for condemnation, so receive it for remission.”

He distributes the remainder of the lamb to those reclining and to the others standing around. In the middle of the banquet one of the cardinal deacons rises at the command of the archdeacon [Col. 1079D] and reads at the table.

When the banquet has ended, the cantors sing a sequence appropriate to Easter, at the command of the pontiff.

Afterward he descends into the Lateran church for Vespers, as contained in the Antiphoner. Having celebrated three Vespers services—in the basilica of the Savior, at the Font, and at the Holy Cross—he returns to the portico of Saint Venantius.

There he sits with the bishops, cardinals, and other orders, and with other lay and clerical persons, seated on the ground upon carpets. Then mulled wine is served to him [Col. 1080A] and to all standing around by the archdeacon and the other cupbearers.

### 36. 

Meanwhile the *primicerius* with the cantors rises and sings the following Greek sequence:

[Note: [Col. 1079D] Literal translation: “A sacred Pascha has been shown to us today, a new Pascha, a holy Pascha, a mystical Pascha, the most venerable Pascha of Christ the Redeemer, an undefiled Pascha, a great Pascha, the Pascha of the faithful. Pascha has opened to us the gates of paradise; Pascha renews all mortals. Christ, preserve the new pope.”]

> A sacred Pascha has been shown to us today: a new Pascha, a holy Pascha, a mystical Pascha, the all-venerable Pascha of Christ the Redeemer; an undefiled Pascha, a great Pascha, the Pascha of the faithful. Pascha has opened to us the gates of paradise; Pascha renews all mortals. Christ, preserve the new pope.

When this has been sung, everyone returns to his own place.

### XVI. What the lord pope must do on the second day of Easter

### 37. 

On the Monday after Easter, very early in the morning, the lord pontiff assembles all the palatine orders in the palace. Descending through the portico and finding a horse without ornamental trappings, but equipped as is customary, he proceeds to Saint Peter’s.

There, after celebrating Mass in the customary manner and completing all the laudes and solemnities as on the preceding day, he is crowned at the steps of the basilica and returns to the Lateran.

When he begins to ride, the seneschal, following behind him, makes one throw of coins, so that the crowd obstructing the lord pope may be dispersed by attending to the collection of the coins.

When the lord pope reaches the tower of Stephen Serpetri, which is at the head of the Parione, one of the lord pope’s curials who is in that tower makes one throw there for the reason stated above.

When the lord pope arrives at the palace of Cencius Musca in Punga [Alt.: Perunga], on the Via de Papa, one of the curials likewise ascends the palace and makes one throw for the aforementioned reason.

When he reaches Saint Mark’s, one of the curials similarly makes a fourth throw there for the same reason.

When he reaches Saint Adrian’s, another of the curials ascends the palace of Saint Martina and makes a fifth throw there for the aforementioned reason.

### 38. 

It should nevertheless be understood that before the first-mentioned tower the Jews meet the lord pope, present their law to him, and sing laudes. For these laudes they receive from the chamberlain a presbyterium of twenty *provesini* solidi.

It should further be noted that from Saint Peter’s to the lord pope’s palace the Romans construct honorable arches along the road by which he passes [Col. 1080D]. All the Roman clergy come out to meet him, vested as far as they are able, with a thurible. In recompense for this honor, the Romans receive for the arches a presbyterium of thirty-five and a half *provesini* pounds; the clergy receive thirty-three *provesini* pounds for the thuribles, as will be explained more fully below.

When the lord pope has reached the palace, and the laudes have been performed by the cardinal of Saint Lawrence and the judges, he descends, lays aside the crown, and is led into the palace [Col. 1081A] by the *primicerius* and *secundicerius*. Entering the chamber, he gives the presbyterium without manual distribution, as on the feast of Saint Stephen. He is then led, as on the preceding day, to the banquet.

Today, however, it is celebrated in the Leonine basilica, which is beside the chamber. When the banquet has ended, he descends to the Lateran church. After celebrating three Vespers services, and after the serving of mulled wine and the other observances as on the preceding day, everyone returns to his own place.

### XVII. The presbyterium given for the arches: how and to whom it is given

### 39. 

The presbyterium of thirty-five pounds mentioned above is given to those who construct the arches, and is distributed in the following manner.

## XIX. Which guilds receive the presbyterium, and how much

42. This is the presbyterium of the city’s guilds, which is given to those guilds at the feasts of the Nativity of the Lord and Easter, through the chamberlain, in the following amount or number. At the feast of the Lord’s Easter and at his Nativity, and conversely each year, it is granted without reduction. [Col. 1086B]

To the Adextratores: 10 Provençal solidi and 1 solidus for the royal power. To the Ostiarii: 10 Provençal solidi. To the Mappularii: 5 Provençal solidi and 12 denarii for the towel. To the Majorentes: 5 Provençal solidi. To the Cubicularii: 4 Provençal solidi. To the Vastararii: 4 Provençal solidi. To the Fiolarii: 5 Provençal solidi. To the Ferrarii of the Column: 4 Provençal solidi. To the Calderarii: 4 Provençal solidi. To the Bandonarii of the Colisaeus: 10 Provençal solidi. To the Cospalarii: 4 Provençal solidi. To the Mandatarii: 10 Provençal solidi. To the masons of Saint Peter: 8 Provençal solidi. To the charcoal-burners: 8 Provençal solidi. To the other masons: 5 Provençal solidi. To the Bandonarii of the Cacabarius: 10 Provençal solidi. 196 To the Jews: 20 Provençal solidi.

It should be noted that the aforesaid presbyterium is granted to the aforementioned guilds because of the service they render to the Roman curia, as will be set out below. [Col. 1086C]

## XX. Concerning the Adextratores

43.
