The Adextratores [alternative: Addextratores], whenever the lord pope is crowned, guard the royal power and escort him as far as the churches to which he must ride, both on the outward journey and on the return. For this reason, on every coronation day, and also when the lord pope enters, all members of that guild eat in the lord pope’s presence, receiving a meal. Moreover, at every station to which the lord pope rides, they escort him. For this reason, on that same day four members of the guild eat with the same lord pope—neither more nor fewer, even if they themselves should wish it.

By right, all those who come to the lord pope for consecration, whether archbishops, bishops, or abbots, must be escorted by them within the city, but not outside it. Therefore they must receive the riding-fee due from the person being consecrated, and four members of that guild must eat with the consecrated person and with the lord pope, except when the lord pope consecrates in the chapel. In that case, all eat with the persons being consecrated.

Since it is burdensome for the consecrated persons to provide mounts, the ancient and original custom is that the chamberlain, in place of a mount, has the Adextratores themselves supplied with money by the persons being consecrated, according to the rank of those persons. The Adextratores themselves must receive this, though not in so great an amount, even if the consecrated bishops do not ride at all. It should nevertheless be understood that they must receive it if the person is consecrated in the city by anyone other than the lord pope. [Col. 1086D–1087A]

## XXI. Concerning the Ostiarii

44. The Ostiarii receive from the lord pope each day, for guarding the palace, a meal for two members of their guild. When the lord pope is crowned, however, all of them must come to the palace at the chamberlain’s discretion and guard the palace. For this reason, on that day they must receive a meal from the lord pope.

Two Ostiarii must always go with the lord pope to the stations whenever he rides, in order to guard the secretarium; and on that day, besides the two mentioned above who serve daily, they eat with the lord pope. Whenever the chamberlain calls them, or some of them, to guard the palace, they must come when summoned. Moreover, all of them must swear an oath to the lord pope, as will be described more fully below.

The chamberlain must give these men one sheep at Easter and one small pig at the Nativity of the Lord. It should also be noted that they must prepare all the olive branches that the lord pope gives to the Roman people on Palm Sunday, and must carry them into the palace before the chamber and afterward behind the lord pope as far as the church.

It should further be understood that, when the lord pope is not in the city, they must receive 12 Papiensian denarii each week at the altar of Saint Peter for guarding the palace. [Col. 1087B]

## XXII. Concerning the Mappularii and Cubicularii

45. The Mappularii and Cubicularii, who perform almost the same office, must come to the lord pope’s palace when the lord pope is crowned and at every station. They must take the carpet, tapestry, footstool, cushion, and predella and carry them to the mount. They must carry all these things, together with the chapel chests, conveyed by the marshals, as far as the place to which the lord pope has decided to ride.

When the chapel is set down there, the aforesaid guilds must be present and take up everything mentioned above as before, carrying it to the secretarium. There, when the lord pope removes his mantle, stole, and mitre, they must guard them with the greatest care until the service has been celebrated.

They must also carry the carpet and the other objects mentioned above as far as the altar, making a canopy from a certain cloak over the lord pope’s head. They carry it in this manner: [Col. 1087D] two at the front and two at the rear, attached at the top to four poles and stretched as far as the altar. The acolytes assign this cloth to them from the lord pope’s chests and afterward receive it back from them.

As long as the lord pope celebrates or preaches, they perform the office belonging to them. Furthermore, when the lord pope departs, they must again carry the carpet, tapestry, and all the other objects mentioned to the steps where the mount is. These are carried as far as the palace, 198 where they must remain ready and return the aforesaid objects to the place where they received them.

46. It should be noted that all the members of these guilds must eat with the lord pope on the day of his coronation; but on the days of stations, four members of each guild, and no more, must do so.

When someone is consecrated by the lord pope, in return for the service they render to the person consecrated, they must receive his cope, basins, and towel; but the basins and towel are divided between them and the acolytes. Since it seemed burdensome for the consecrated person to give them the cope, the chamberlain has them supplied with money by the person consecrated, according to his rank and means.

Two members of each guild eat with the person consecrated, and none with the lord pope if he has consecrated in the chapel. If he has consecrated outside the chapel, two members of each guild eat with the lord pope.

It should nevertheless be understood that they must receive the things mentioned above even if they were consecrated in the city by someone other than the lord pope. If outside the city, the chamberlain gives and has him escorted according to his own wishes; and both they and the Adextratores must swear to the lord pope whenever they are required to do so.

It should be noted, however, that if, when the lord pope is in the secretarium and after Mass has been celebrated, something is offered at the pope’s feet, it belongs to them by right, except for gold and worked silver, as well as cloths or towels, all of which belong to the treasury, with the exception of the guild’s banner, which it must retain.

I say the same concerning the Adextratores. If, when they are escorting the lord pope, something is offered at his feet along the way, it belongs to them, except for the things mentioned above.

With this addition: neither the guild of the Mappularii and Cubicularii nor that of the Adextratores may eat with the lord pope, or perform any office, when the lord pope rides to a church where there is no station on that same day.

It should be understood that the Mappularii, as was explained above, must always prepare warm water for the lord pope during the Procession, and on Holy Thursday they must receive half the hand-washing fee belonging to the subdeacon. [Col. 1088A–B]

## XXIII. Concerning the Majorentes, who are called Stimulati

47. The Majorentes must not come to the curia to perform any service or for any other reason, except on the day of the lord pope’s coronation. While he is riding, they carry staffs in their hands and clear the way by removing the crowd. For this reason, on that day they must eat with the lord pope. These same Majorentes are also called the guild of the Stimulati. [Col. 1088C]

## XXIV. Concerning the Vastararii

48. At all the solemnities of Saint Mary, except the Assumption, the Vastararii make candles from living vine-shoots, preparing paper for the candles. For this reason they eat with the lord pope on the day of his coronation, and for all the vine-shoots they receive four Provençal solidi from the altar of Saint Peter for those vine-shoots.

It should be understood that, in return for this service, they receive half the hand-washing fee of the major charter [alternative: chest] on Easter Day.

[Note: [Col. 1087] This may clarify the obscure passage above, on p. 164, where *vineis* should perhaps be read.]

## XXV. Concerning the Fiolarii

[Col. 1089A]

49. According to ancient custom, the Fiolarii must provide from their own resources lamps and candles for illuminating the palace whenever necessary. For this reason they eat with the lord pope on the day of his coronation.

## XXVI. Concerning the Ferrarii of the Column and of Saint Angelo

50. The Ferrarii of the Column must make the hoops of the cauldron, whenever the lord pope’s chief cooks request them, and likewise tripods. For this reason they too must eat with the lord pope on the day of his coronation.

For the labor mentioned above, they are given food from the curia when they work, four denarii each; they are also given charcoal and iron for the work.

## XXVII. Concerning the Ferrarii of Saint Angelo

51. The Ferrarii of Saint Angelo must do and receive the same in every respect. [Col. 1089B]

## XXVIII. Concerning the Bandonarii

52. When the lord pope is crowned, the Bandonarii of the Colisaeus and of the Cacabarius go before him with banners on both the outward and return journeys. 200 They are, as it were, a single guild; and on that same day they must eat with the lord pope.

## XXIX. Concerning the Calderarii

53. The Calderarii must make new cauldrons and repair the old ones, and make new basins and repair the old ones, whenever the chief cooks request it. When they work, food is given to them from the curia—namely, four denarii to each man—and iron and charcoal are also provided to them.

## XXX. Concerning the Scopalatii

54. On the day of the lord pope’s coronation, the Scopalatii must clean the guild’s steps and the portico as far as the place where the lord pope dismounts. [Col. 1089C]

## XXXI. Concerning the Carbonarii

55. On the day of the lord pope’s coronation, the Carbonarii provide charcoal for the kitchen and for repairing the cauldrons.

## XXXII. Concerning the Jews

56. On the day of his coronation, the Jews present the law to the lord pope on the road and offer him acclamations; they also bring to the treasury three pounds—one of pepper and two pounds of cinnamon.

## XXXIII. Concerning the presbyterium of the chamberlain’s treasury officials

57. This is the presbyterium given to the officials of the chamberlain’s treasury, to other officials, and to members of the court.

To each member of the court, who are called Courtiers, two marabotini are given; to the treasury scribe, two melechini; to the money-changer, two melechini; to the treasury tailor, two Saracen coins; to the treasury guard, two Saracen coins; to the lord pope’s seneschal, six melechini. The latter also receives one small pig at the Nativity of the Lord and one sheep at Easter.

To each cook, one melech. To each embroiderer, some blessing [that is, an unspecified gift]. It should be noted that the cooks and broth-makers must receive *sticchae* at Easter and the Nativity of the Lord. 201 To each baker, two melechini and the cloth they bought for the feast. To each butler, two melechini. To the marshal of the white horses, three melechini and a *naccus*; to the other marshal, two melechini. To each of the lord pope’s doorkeepers, four melechini.

For the squires, chaplains, subdeacons, and acolytes of the chapel, the meal must be doubled, and likewise at the Nativity of the Lord. To the prior of the subdeacons, one sheep at Easter and one small pig at the Nativity.

To the marshals and the other members of the household, the chamberlain gives according to his own discretion. Nevertheless, the marshals must receive one pig and, at Easter, one sheep.

It should also be noted that, when the marshals go for green fodder, straw, or hay, they must receive a *mistum* and forks. It should further be understood that the meal of the chancery must be doubled on these two days, and likewise at the Nativity of the Lord. [Col. 1089D–1090A]

## XXXIV. What the master Seneschal must receive and do

58. The senior Seneschal, who serves the lord pope at the final coronation, at Easter and the Nativity of the Lord, and at the consecration of the lord pope, must receive, at each of the festivals mentioned above, if he is crowned, a silver bowl weighing three and a half marks.

He must receive provisions for fifteen men on each coronation day. He must eat in the bakery with his companions before the lord pope returns from Mass. He must receive from the cupbearer one vessel of claret and one of wine. At his own house he must have six prepared pig’s heads and six small vessels of claret on each coronation day. At each coronation he must receive half the onions and half of all the hides of the animals that come to the lord pope’s table during the feast. [Col. 1090B]

## XXXV. What the master Cupbearer must receive and do

59. The master Cupbearer, who serves the lord pope at table on the day of his coronation, must receive one silver cup weighing three and a half marks.

On that same day the Cupbearer must give the lord pope’s daily butlers one silk belt. He must also eat before the lord pope returns 202 from Mass, receiving a meal for fifteen companions. He must have six prepared pig’s heads and six vessels of claret sent to his house, and at his meal one vessel of claret and another of wine.

On Easter Day and on the Monday after Easter, after Vespers at Saint John at the Fountain, he must provide one full barrel of wine and one good vessel full of claret, to give to the lord pope and to all those present. [Col. 1090C]

## XXXVI. What the Senators must receive

60. When they eat, the Senators must receive half a *lavina* of wine and half a *lavina* of claret on each coronation day.

The bakers also give them a towel where they eat; afterward it is returned to them. They receive a meal for forty men on each coronation day.

[Note: [Col. 1089] Onuphrius rendered this as *psalma* or *salma*, a term meaning the pack-saddle, load, or burden of a horse or another beast of burden.]

## XXXVII. What the Prefect of the City must receive

61. The Prefect of the City must receive, for a meal for fifteen companions, one iron-bound barrel of claret and another of wine.

## XXXVIII. What the lord pope must do on the Saturday following Easter

[Col. 1091A]

62. On Saturday in White [Easter] Week there is a station at Saint John Lateran. There the lord pope celebrates the solemn Mass on that same day, and the *Agnus Dei* is sung by the Primicerius and the schola cantorum.

The lord pope distributes lambs made of chrism and wax through the bishops, cardinals, and others, both clergy and laity, according to this meaning: just as the children of Israel, when they were in Egypt, wrote this sign, T, on the lintels of their houses by the Lord’s command with the blood of an immaculate lamb, so that they would not be struck by the angel, so we too must write this sign on the lintel of our houses through faith in the blood of the passion of Christ, the immaculate Lamb, so that we may not be struck by the devil and by vices and may be freed from the devil’s power.

Alternatively, this is done for infants newly baptized in the church, who have laid aside the old garment and proclaim “Alleluia,” that is, the glory of the blessedness of the heavenly homeland. Or it is because anyone who has some wax from the aforesaid lambs and has made a cross from it in his house, or carries it with him, will not be harmed by any spectral spirit or by thunder.

It should be noted that the lord pope’s acolytes must make the aforesaid Lambs of God at the altar of Saint Peter, receiving ten pounds of wax, and present them to the lord pope at the appointed hour. They must also present the lord pope, while he is eating, with a full silver bowl of the aforesaid Lambs of God, and another to be distributed by the chamberlain among the household. [Col. 1091B]

## XXXIX. How the lord pope proceeds in the Greater Litany on the feast of Saint Mark

63. On the feast of Saint Mark, during the Greater Litany, the most holy lord pope descends with all the bishops, cardinals, and other orders to the Lateran church.

When he arrives behind the altar and Terce has been sung, they all vest themselves in chasubles. Barefoot, they are arranged in the Procession by the basilica’s archdeacon, subdeacon, and prior of the subdeacons, holding rods in their hands, as was explained above concerning the other Processions. The Primicerius is present with his schola and performs his office, as is appropriate in the collect.

Thus they leave the church in procession, with the cross of Saint Lawrence outside the Walls going first, followed by the cross of Saint Mary Major, which by custom on such a day must be brought to the Lateran church. The third cross carried is that of the Lateran church itself. After these comes the lord pope’s daily cross. In this order they are carried as far as Saint Mark. [Col. 1091C–D]

64. When the lord pope arrives with the Procession at the church of Saint Clement, he rests there on a bed covered with a carpet and surrounded by herbs, which are nevertheless prepared by the clergy of that same church of Saint Clement.

After he has rested, he rises and proceeds in the aforesaid manner as far as the church of Saint Mary Nova. While he rests there in the aforesaid manner, one member of the Cross guild sings the litany.

He rises and proceeds in the aforesaid manner as far as the church of Saint Mark, where, as was written above, he rests. After he has paused, he rises and proceeds in the manner mentioned as far as the place called Parione, with the cross of Saint Peter—which by custom on that day must be brought to Saint Mark—following the cross of Saint Lawrence [Col. 1092A] and preceding the cross of Saint Mary Major in the established order.

There the lord pope rests in the manner stated above. After resting, he proceeds, as previously described, as far as the bridge of Saint Peter. There he rests in the manner already mentioned. Rising from that place, he proceeds in the prescribed manner as far as the place called Cortina, and rests there on a bed prepared by the guild of the rods in the manner described above.

He rises and approaches the steps of the church of Saint Peter. Bending over on the steps and turning his face toward the east, he first enters the church, while the Primicerius with the schola cantorum sings *Te Deum laudamus*. After the singing of *Te Deum laudamus*, a prayer is said. After the prayer following *Te Deum laudamus* has been sung over the wheel at the entrance, as it were, of the church, he proceeds to the secretarium. There he washes his feet and, having vested himself, as is customary and is written elsewhere, approaches the altar to sing Mass. [Col. 1092B]

65. It should indeed be noted that one of the subdeacons and another of the acolytes, according to the direction of the basilica’s prior, must go early in the morning to Saint Peter. There, together with one of the scriniarii, they must write down all the names of the churches that came with crosses in procession to that same church.

It should further be understood that every church that proceeds in procession to Saint Peter on that day shares in the presbyterium of 25 pounds of denarii, which are taken from the altar of Saint Peter for this purpose.

All the mitred clergy receive 40 solidi as a presbyterium, likewise taken from the aforesaid altar and divided among all according to an equal proportion.

The mitred cardinals alone, together with the Primicerius and his schola cantorum, the subdeacons, the Cross guild, and the acolytes, receive 10 solidi on that day from the aforesaid altar. These are divided by the prior cardinal deacon, into whose hands they are delivered.

First he gives 22 denarii to the cardinal priests; then 22 denarii to the cardinal deacons; afterward 22 denarii to the subdeacons; then 22 denarii to the Primicerius together with the schola; 22 denarii to the guilds of the crosses; and finally 10 denarii to the acolytes.

In addition, the lord pope receives 40 solidi on that day from the same place.

It should be noted that at every station at Saint Peter’s the lord pope receives 40 solidi from the altar when he celebrates Mass. The cardinals, subdeacons, the Primicerius with the schola cantorum, the Cross guild, and the acolytes likewise receive the aforesaid 10 solidi, divided in the manner stated above, at every station—even if the lord pope is present and a cardinal celebrates there; they must receive them from the same altar.

If the lord pope is outside the City, and a vicar, or some cardinal, [Col. 1092D] or an outsider bishop attends by the lord pope’s command and celebrates the divine offices there, 10 solidi must likewise be given from the same place. The person who then celebrates, as I have said, by the lord pope’s command, receives 10 solidi from that altar—the amount the lord pope would receive if he were celebrating the divine offices at that time.

The aforesaid 10 solidi that are given to the mitred clergy are supplied to them from the same place if they are present, even when the lord pope is outside the city. If he is in the city but does not proceed in the Procession or participate in the celebration, they nevertheless receive them.

The clergy of the City, however, always receive the aforesaid 25 pounds, whether the lord pope is in the City or outside it, and whether he sings or does not sing; these are distributed as will be described below. [Col. 1093A]

66. This, indeed, must by no means be omitted: if, from the moment the cloth is displayed by the chaplains upon the altar, anything should be offered to the pope, it belongs to those chaplains, with no one else sharing in it; and this continues until the lord pope approaches the altar to sing Mass. Whatever, however, is offered upon the altar after the lord pope has approached, until he has pronounced *Ite, missa est*, shall be divided as follows.

First, twelve denarii are given to the marshals. It should be noted that at every station where the lord pope celebrates the divine mysteries, at Saint Peter’s, they are to receive the same amount from the altar offerings. At all the other stations of other churches where the lord pope celebrates the divine mysteries, if any offerings are made from the altar after the lord pope’s Gospel, six denarii are given to the aforementioned marshals. If it should happen that there is no offering except the one that belongs to the *mappularii*, the marshals themselves receive six denarii from that offering. If no offering is present, the almoner gives them six denarii from the alms.

Whenever the lord pope sings, and wherever he sings when it is not a station, the almoner must give those same marshals twelve denarii from the alms, to the marshals, as was stated above. The better coinage is given to the *primicerius*; thereafter, from what remains, one-sixth is given to the *primicerius* and the school of singers. Half of the remaining portion is given to the cardinal deacons and subdeacons, while the other half is given only to the chaplains.

When Mass has been sung according to custom, the lord pope returns to the palace. If the chamberlain wishes, he distributes twenty-five pounds among the aforementioned clergy. Otherwise, he entrusts the distribution to the prior of the basilica and the rectors of the city, with those who were present for the writing added to their number.

67. From this clerical distribution the following are given first: twenty solidi to Saint Peter; six solidi to Saint John Lateran; five solidi to Saint Mary Major; five solidi to Saint Lawrence Outside the Walls; three solidi to each cardinal, except those who prepare the aforementioned litters in the Procession, who receive sixteen additional denarii for this; two solidi to each deacon, except Saint Mary the New, which receives an additional twelve denarii for the litter, and except the church of Saint Theodore, which is to receive twelve *proves* for the lance.

Beyond these, three solidi are given to each monastery outside the City.

The following monasteries within the City receive three solidi: the monastery of Saint Caesarius; the monastery of Saint Agatha; the monastery of Panisperna; the monastery of Pallara; the monastery of Saints Cosmas and Damian across the Tiber; the monastery of Saint Sylvester in Capite; the monastery on the Capitoline; the monastery of Saint Alexius; the monastery of Saint Sabas; the monastery of Clivus Scaurus; the monastery of Saint Basil; the monastery of the Holy Cross; and Saint Mary in the Monastery.

The following monasteries and churches receive two solidi: the monastery of Julia; the monastery of Saint Bibiana; the monastery of the Campus Martius; the monastery of Lady Rosa; the monastery of Tempoli; the monastery of Saint John at the Latin Gate; the monastery of Maxima; the monastery of Biberatica; the monastery of Saint Thomas de Formis; the monastery of Miranda; the monastery of the Holy Trinity; the monastery of Saint John on the Island; the monastery of Saint Leo; the monastery of Saint Caesarius of the Monks; and the monastery of Saint Cyriacus.

The following churches receive eighteen denarii: Saint Mary of Monticello; Saint Thomas of the Brotherhood; Saint Mary; Saint Tryphon; Saint Mary Rotunda; Saint Apollinaris; and Saint Celsus.

The following chapels receive twelve denarii: Saint Vincent; Saint Michael; Saint Mary in Saxia; the Staircase Chapel; Saint Mary Synodochia; Saint Mary in Catenara; the Savior of the Campus; Saint Paul of Aureola; Saint Anastasius of Areola; Saint Quiricus; Saint Abacyrus; Saint Mary at the River; Saint Stephen of Pinea; Saint Macutus; Saint Mary the Virgin of Canella; Saint Lawrence in Piscinula; Saint Lawrence of Mundesarii; Saint Mary in Petrochia; Saint Mary the Virgin of the *Secundicerius*; Saint Valentine outside the City; the hospital; Saint Blaise of the Market; and Saint Mary in Transpadina.

All the other churches of the City are individually to receive eight denarii.

### XL. Concerning the *Virgarii*

68. The *virgarii* are to receive ten solidi *proves* for the litter. The school of standard-bearers is to receive ten solidi. The *scrinarii* are to receive nine solidi. The scribes are to receive twelve denarii.

The rectors of the fraternity are to receive twelve solidi from the rectors; yet they have appropriated this to themselves only for a few years. For although this clerical distribution is sometimes distributed as stated, they ought not to receive anything from it—nor should the school of singers, the *mappularii*, chamberlains, attendants, doorkeepers, or any other school or person—except the prior of the subdeacons with the acolytes. When the clerical distribution of the churches is given, he receives his share, as is fully recorded in the ancient accounts of Innocent, Eugenius, Hadrian, and many other Roman pontiffs.

### XLI. What the lord pope must do on the Ascension of the Lord

69. On the Ascension the lord pope goes to Vespers at Saint Peter’s, and there he must lie down; he does and receives everything with the chamberlain and chancellor, as is written under the festival and dedication.

On the feast of Pentecost the lord pope goes to Vespers at Saint Peter’s, and there he must lie down; he does and receives everything with the chamberlain and chancellor, as is stated under the festival and dedication of Saint Peter.

### XLII. What the lord pope must do on the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist

70. On the Nativity of Saint John, the lord pope descends to the Lateran church to celebrate Vespers with the cardinals, the school of singers, and the others, as is written above under the Assumption of the Blessed Mary. There they carry out such a solemnity, both at Vespers and during the night, according to ancient custom, as at the aforementioned Assumption of the Blessed Mary, except that the canons of that church do not attend the vigils of the lord pope. Everything else is done as at the aforementioned feast of the Blessed Virgin Mary.

### XLIII. What the lord pope must do on the feast of the apostle Saint Peter

71. On the feast of blessed Peter the lord pope goes to the church with the cardinals,

[Note: Leo IV established, as Anastasius testifies, that Vespers should be sung in the basilica of Saint Peter by all the clergy and the school on the day of his nativity.]

the school, and the others, to celebrate Vespers there, as was related above. He remains there and carries out such a solemnity, both at Vespers and during the night, as at the aforementioned Assumption of the Blessed Mary; and he acts similarly concerning the torches at Vespers and during the night, the *mappularii*, the school, and everything else.

It should be noted that immediately after Vespers the lord pope is to receive two *aquariciae* of claret and two of wine, so that he may drink with the cardinals and others, and two loads of *mortula*.

[Note: To Onufrius, two loads of *mortella*. The *salma* has been discussed above; what *mortella* or *mortula* is, I leave others to determine. Below, no. 75, we read of six bundles of *mortula* for his chamber; for Onufrius, *mortella*.]

For filling the lord pope’s sack he is to receive eighteen *proves*, and the chamberlain is to receive one *aquaricia* of claret; and, if the chancellor remains, he is to receive another *aquaricia*. Otherwise, the lord pope receives it himself. All these things are taken from the altar of Saint Peter.

Concerning the altar offering and the lord pope’s feet, it shall be done as written under the feast of Saint Mark in the Greater Litany. This, however, must by no means be omitted: after the fourth lesson of the vigil, the lord pope descends to the area of the altar and takes from there the thurible with the candle that had been placed there by the lord pope on another feast, together with coals and incense. Afterwards he replaces the thurible there with a similar candle.

### XLIV. What the lord pope must do on the feast of Saint Lawrence

72. On the feast of Saint Lawrence the lord pope goes to Vespers with all the orders, as stated above under the Assumption of the Blessed Mary, and according to ancient custom carries out there such a solemnity, both at Vespers and during the night, as at the aforementioned Assumption of the Blessed Mary, except that the *primicerius* of the schools does not attend. Everything else is done as at the aforementioned feast of Saint Mary.

### XLV. What the lord pope must do on the feast of the apostle Saint Paul

73. On the feast of blessed Paul the lord pope goes with the cardinals to celebrate Vespers there. After it has been sung, he eats there with all the cardinals, the chaplains, and the other orders. They carry out there such a solemnity, both at Vespers and during the night, as was described under the Assumption of the Blessed Mary. Everything else is done as at the aforementioned feast.

It should be known that during the octave of Saint Peter everything is done as on the feast of that same Saint Peter, except for what was said concerning the thurible.

### XLVI. What the lord pope must do on the Exaltation of the Holy Cross

74. On the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, in the month of September, the most holy lord pope enters the basilica of Saint Lawrence in the morning with the cardinals. There he draws out the relics of the apostles Peter and Paul and the wood of the Holy Cross;

[Note: Anastasius relates how Pope Sergius I found this cross.]

after kissing them, he hands them to a cardinal to carry to the church of Saint Sylvester. In the basilica, the lord pope sings *Te Deum laudamus* with the cardinals and chaplains.

The *primicerius* with the school remains outside the basilica of Saint Sylvester, singing the antiphons from the Lauds with the Psalms and the *Benedictus*, while the lord pope says the Prayer. Before the door, on a certain board placed by the doorkeepers and honorably covered with cloths or sheets as appropriate, they set down the relics. After the pope and cardinals have first venerated them, all the people then venerate them in the same place.

Meanwhile the pope and cardinals sing Prime there. After the lord pope and the cardinals have venerated them, equipped as was stated above for the other Processions, the younger cardinal priests carrying the relics ascend the steps of the staircase; then they proceed in procession along the common way to the church of Saint John Lateran.

75. It should be noted that the canons of the Lateran come to meet the lord pope as far as the steps of the staircase, with the cross and the *primicerius* singing with the school of singers.

When the bearers have placed the relics upon the altar, the lord pope proceeds to the sacristy and sings Terce. After vesting, he proceeds to the altar and celebrates the divine mysteries. After the celebration, he returns with the relics to the basilica through the palace.

It should be noted that in all the other Processions, except this one, the lord pope and the cardinals proceed barefoot. It should also be known that a Procession is held only on this day, and not on the Finding of the same Holy Cross, which occurs in May.

### XLVII. What the lord pope must do at the Dedication of the churches of Saints Peter and Paul

76. At the Dedication of the churches of Peter and Paul, the lord pope goes with the cardinals to Vespers at Saint Peter’s. After Vespers has been sung, the lord pope remains and lies there, and in person must attend the singing of the Vigils during the night. He carries out there such a solemnity, both at Vespers and during the night, as at the aforementioned Assumption of the glorious Virgin Mary.

In addition, the lord pope is to receive from the altar two *aquariciae* of claret and two of wine; the chamberlain is to receive one, and the chancellor a fourth. Concerning the altar offering at the feet of the lord pope, it shall be done as written under the feast of blessed Mark. The pope is to receive four bundles of *mortula* for his chamber, four for the chamber of the chamberlain, twelve denarii for filling the lord pope’s sack, and three solidi for wood in the lord pope’s chamber. As was stated above under the feast of that same Saint Peter, all these things are taken from the altar.

### XLVIII. How the supreme pontiff is to be elected; and what is subsequently to be done whether he is elected in the City, or, having been elected and consecrated—or elected and not consecrated—he comes to the City

77. When the Roman pontiff has died and been buried, all the cardinals return to their own places according to ancient custom. On the second day they assemble in the church; after the Mass for the dead has been sung, they likewise depart according to ancient custom.

On the third day, all again assembled in the church, and the Mass of the Holy Spirit first celebrated there, they deliberate concerning the election. After the will of all the cardinals has been examined by some of their number, the one upon whom the greater and better part of the cardinals has agreed is clothed by the prior of the deacons in a red mantle and given a name by him. Then two of the senior cardinals lead him by the arms to the altar. There, prostrate, he adores while the *primicerius*, the school of singers, and the cardinals sing *Te Deum laudamus*. When this has ended, he is led by the cardinal bishops to the seat behind the altar and placed upon it as is fitting.

While the elected man sits there, he receives all the bishops and cardinals, and whomever else he wishes, first to his feet and afterwards to the kiss of peace.

78. Rising from the seat, he is led by the cardinals to the stone seat called the *stercoraria*, which stands before the portico of the basilica of the Savior of the Lateran patriarchate. The cardinals honorably place the elected man upon it, so that it may truly be said: “He raises the needy from the dust and lifts the poor from the dungheap, to seat him with princes and grant him a throne of glory.”

After standing for a little while beside that seat, the elected man receives from the chamberlain’s lap three handfuls of coins and throws them down, saying: “Silver and gold I do not have for my delight; but what I have, this I give you.”

Then the elected man is received by the prior of the basilica of the Savior of the Lateran patriarchate, together with one of the cardinals or one of his brothers. As they come through the same portico beside the basilica of the Savior, the cry is raised: “Saint Peter has chosen the lord Celestine.”

[Note: From this it is evident that this book was written in the time of Celestine III.]

Thus he is led by them to the steps of the gate—that is, the gate at the entrance to the palace for those coming from the church to the palace itself. There the judges receive the elected man and lead him through the palace to the basilica of Saint Sylvester.

[Col. 1097D] 79. When they have arrived before that basilica, above whose arch, supported by two porphyry columns, there is an image of the Savior which once emitted blood from its forehead when struck by a certain Jew, as can be seen today, the elected man sits on the right in a porphyry seat. There the prior of the basilica of Saint Lawrence gives him from the palace a staff, which is a sign of governance and correction, and the keys of that basilica and of the sacred Lateran palace, because the power of closing and opening, binding and loosing, was specially given to Peter, prince of the apostles, and through that apostle to all the Roman pontiffs.

With the staff and keys he approaches another similar seat, made of the same stone, and then returns both the staff and the keys to that prior. While he rests there for a short time, the same prior girds him with a red silk belt, from which hangs a purple purse containing twelve seals of precious stones and musk.

The elected man must sit in those two seats as though he were seen to lie between two couches—that is, to recline between the primacy of Peter, prince of the apostles, and the preaching of Paul, teacher of the nations. The belt signifies the preservation of chastity; the purse signifies the treasury from which Christ’s poor and widows are to be nourished. In the twelve seals the power of the twelve apostles is signified. Musk is enclosed so that its fragrance may be perceived, as the apostle says: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God.”

While the elected man sits in this second seat, he receives all the officials of the palace first to his feet and afterwards to the kiss. Then, still seated there, he receives from the hand of the chamberlain silver coins worth ten solidi *proves* and throws them over the people. He does this three times, saying: “He has scattered; he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures forever and ever.”

80. When these things have been completed, he is led through the same portico beneath the images of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, which came to Rome by sea without any guide, and enters the basilica of Saint Lawrence. After he has completed a lengthy Prayer before his own special altar, he proceeds to the papal chamber. When he has rested there at his pleasure, he goes to the table.

81. On the next Sunday the elected man goes with all the orders of the sacred palace and the Roman nobles to the church of blessed Peter. There, at the high altar, as is contained in the *Ordo*, he is consecrated by the bishop of Ostia in particular and by the other bishops of the curia. In addition, if the bishop of Ostia is not present, the archpriest of Ostia or of Velletri must take part in the consecration.

When the consecration has ended, the prior of Saint Lawrence of the sacred palace places the pallium upon the altar; the prior himself must prepare it with his own hand. Immediately the archdeacon and the second deacon place it in the pontiff’s hand, and the archdeacon alone says to the pontiff:

“Receive the pallium, that is, the fullness of pontifical office, to the honor of almighty God, of his most glorious Virgin Mother, of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and of the holy Roman Church.”

Nothing else is said.

Immediately the archdeacon, together with the basilica’s prior, adjusts the pallium upon the pontiff. Three golden pins are inserted in front, at the back, and on the left side; at their heads are set three hyacinth stones. Thus adorned, the pontiff approaches the altar and celebrates Mass there honorably.

It should be noted that the Lauds are then performed by the archdeacon with the cardinals, subdeacons, and *scrinarii*; the Epistle in Latin with the Greek, and the Gospel in Latin with the Greek, together with all the other solemnities, are performed as on the Monday after Easter.

82. After Mass has been celebrated, he returns to the palace crowned, with a Procession and the honor of arches, the representation of the Law by the Jews, and censers carried by Roman clerics, together with throws made in equal number and quantity to those on the aforementioned Monday after Easter.

It should be known that all the Greek cardinals, the *primicerius* with the school of singers, the prefect, senators, judges and advocates, *scrinarii*, naval prefects, the school of the crosses, and the chaplains receive such a clerical distribution and in such a manner as they receive the one named above for Easter Day.

The subdeacons, however, each receive one *melequinus*, although this is not done at any of the aforementioned solemnities. For, as is more fully written there, they are not given twelve *melechini*, even if they number thirty or more.

All the schools of the palace—the Roman clerics for the censers, the Jews for the representation of the Law, and the Roman laymen for the arches—receive such a clerical distribution, and in such a manner, as is given at the other coronations of the lord pope.

Moreover, the cupbearer and the marshal are likewise rewarded both with food and with other gifts, except that they do not receive prepared pigs’ heads or claret. The household and the courtiers also receive a clerical distribution according to the chamberlain’s will.

83. If the election has taken place in the church of Saint Peter, after the nomination the elected man is led by two cardinals, singing *Te Deum laudamus*, to the altar. There, after he has prostrated himself and adored, he is placed in the seat behind the altar; there he receives the bishops and cardinals, and whomever else he wishes, first to his feet and afterwards to the kisses of peace.

On the following Sunday he is consecrated there, after Mass has been sung with the solemnities named above. Crowned, he returns to the palace, everything else being done in due order as related above.

Before he enters the palace, he descends to the *stercorated* seat. Sitting there according to custom and making the threefold throw, as was stated above, he is received by the cardinals and led through the same portico to the church of the Lateran basilica. Ascending the seat behind the altar, he receives the canons of that church first to his feet and then to the kiss of peace.

After this he proceeds through the palace to the seat of Saint Sylvester. There he sits and performs everything in that place and thereafter as was stated above, in due order.

84. If he has been elected outside the City and not consecrated, everything is done in the order stated above, whether the descent and consecration of the elected man take place in the church of Saint Peter or the elected man descends in the Lateran church.

If the elected man has been elected and consecrated outside the City, and comes to the City by the Lateran Gate, all the Roman clerics go out to meet him, vested and carrying crosses and censers in Procession. Thus he enters the Lateran church, and everything else is done as related above, except that, when he has descended to the *stercorated* seat and entered the Lateran church through the portico, he does not immediately ascend to the altar or the seat. Instead, coming farther inside from the great choir before the crosses, after *Te Deum laudamus* has ended, he says:

“Our help is in the name of the Lord,” etc.

“The blessing of God the Father and the Son,” etc.

“May the blessing of almighty God, the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, descend upon you and remain always.”

After this he is led to the altar and prays prostrate. When he has prayed, he ascends the greater seat, where he receives the canons of that church first to his feet and then to the kiss of peace.

If he has descended to the church of Saint Peter already consecrated, everything is done as in the Lateran church, except that there is no *stercorated* seat there.

On the following day, after Mass has been celebrated, he returns to the palace without being crowned. Before he enters the church, he descends to the *stercorated* seat. Sitting there according to custom and making the throw, as related above, he is received by the Lateran prior together with one cardinal and led through the portico to the church. Everything is done as noted above.

85. It should be known, however, that the clerical distribution of the schools is not given in the same manner as when he has been consecrated in the City. Half of their distribution is then cut away, except for the Jews, the clerics of the City, and the attendants.

Furthermore, the senators of the City must attend the lord pope by the arm, whether he comes consecrated or unconsecrated, from the city gate to the place where his descent will take place, whether he descends to the Lateran church or to the church of blessed Peter. In recompense for this service they are to receive ten solidi for the horse. Nevertheless, the school of attendants is to receive twenty solidi.

### Oath of the senators of the City

86. “I, N., senator of the city of Rome, from this hour forward shall be faithful to you, my lord Pope Urban. I shall not act, advise, or consent in such a way that you lose life or limb, or are taken in an evil captivity.

“The counsel which you entrust to me, whether personally or by letter or messenger, I shall reveal to no one who, to my knowledge, would use it to your harm. If I learn of certain harm to you, I shall prevent it to the best of my ability. If I cannot prevent it myself, I shall report it to you personally, or by letter or messenger, or through such a person as I firmly believe will faithfully convey it to you.

“I shall be your helper, according to my ability and knowledge, in retaining and defending the Roman papacy and the regalia of blessed Peter which you possess, and in recovering those which you do not possess, and, once recovered, in retaining and defending them, against all men.

“In particular: Saint Peter; the Roman city; the Leonine City; Trastevere; the Island; the Crescentius fortress; Saint Mary Rotunda; the senate; the mint; the honors and dignities of the City; the port of Ostia; and the territory of Tusculum; and, generally, all the regalia within and outside the City.

“I shall provide full and true security to the cardinals, your households, and those belonging to them who come to the Roman Church, remain with it, or depart from it.

“All these things I swear to observe in good faith. So may God help me and these holy Gospels of God.”

87. When a provision is granted, if the chancellor is from the cardinals’ party, he is to receive from two cardinals, whether it is given in money or in provisions. If there is no chancellor, from the entire provision jointly, on the part of the lord pope and the cardinals, the chancery is to receive for two cardinals if it is given in provisions. But if it is given in money, the chancery is to receive for only one cardinal, and only from the cardinal’s share.

### XLIX. The Order for blessing the emperor when he receives the crown

[Note: The *Ordo* in Onofrio Panvinio is fuller and more distinct; nevertheless, it seemed preferable to present our codex as it stands.]

88. “In the name of Christ I, N., emperor, promise, pledge, and declare before God and blessed Peter that I am his protector and defender,” etc.

[Note: Thietmar, at the beginning of Book VII, reports nearly the same words as spoken by Emperor Henry I.]

89. Then the bishop of Albano is to say the first Prayer before the silver door of the basilica of Saint Peter.

**Prayer.**—O God, in whose hand are the hearts of kings, incline the ears of your mercy to the prayers of our humility, and place upon our emperor N., your servant, the kingdom of your wisdom, so that, having drawn counsel from your fountain, he may please you and excel all kingdoms, etc.

The bishop of Porto is to recite the second Prayer between the church of blessed Peter, in the middle of the circle.

**Prayer.**—O God, ineffable author of the world, creator of the human race, governor of empire, confirmer of kingship, who from the womb didst choose our faithful friend, the patriarch Abraham, as king for ages to come: enrich this present king with his army through the intercession of all your saints by abundant blessing, and fasten him securely upon the throne of the kingdom.

Visit him as you visited Moses in the bush, Joshua in battle, Gideon in the field, and Samuel in the temple; and endow him with blessing [lacuna] and with your wisdom, which blessed David received in the Psalter, and Solomon his son received from heaven at your command. Be to him a breastplate against the armies of his enemies, a helmet in adversity, [lacuna] in prosperity, and an everlasting shield in protection.

Grant that the nations keep faith with him; that his nobles possess peace, love charity, refrain from greed, speak justice, and guard truth; and that this people, united by the blessing of eternity, may always remain rejoicing, victorious, and at peace. May he himself deign to grant this.

90. Then he goes before the confession of blessed Peter the apostle and prostrates himself face down upon the ground; the archdeacon performs the litany. When it has ended, the bishop of Ostia anoints his right arm and the space between his shoulders with exorcised oil, and says this Prayer:

“Lord almighty God, to whom belongs all power and dignity, we beseech you with suppliant devotion and the most humble prayer to grant this servant of yours a prosperous exercise of imperial dignity, so that, being appointed to govern your holy Church, neither present circumstances may hinder him nor future ones impede him. Rather, inspired by the gift of the Holy Spirit, may he be able to govern the people subject to him with the just balance of justice, and in all his works always fear you and strive continually to please you. Through the Lord, etc.”

Another Prayer follows:

“O God, Son of God, Jesus Christ our Lord, who was girded by the Father with the oil of gladness above your companions: through the present outpouring of sacred anointing, may he pour the blessing of the Spirit, the Paraclete, upon your head, and cause it to penetrate into the innermost parts of your heart. Thus may you deserve to receive the invisible through this visible and tangible gift, and, having attained an earthly kingdom through righteous mercies, may you reign eternally with him who alone lives and reigns without sin with God the Father in the unity of the Spirit, etc.”

91. Finally, the Roman pontiff places the diadem upon him above the altar, saying:

“Receive the sign of glory, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, so that, having spurned the ancient enemy and rejected the contagions of every vice, you may love judgment and justice and live so mercifully that you may deserve to receive from our Lord Jesus Christ, in the company of the saints, the crown of the eternal kingdom. He lives with the Father and the Holy Spirit, etc.”

---

## In the name of Christ, amen

[Note: Onofrio extracted this from the codex of Cencius, and we in turn from Onofrio.]

A brief record of the custom of the altar of the holy Savior: namely, what belongs to the clerics of that church, or to the church itself, from the half belonging to the bishops.

[Note: This apparently means that the church is fumigated with incense and fragrances.]

First, at the Nativity of the Lord, the church is to be perfumed, and two pairs of torches are to be provided: one before the altar and the other in the reading stand; and four denarii are to be given to the *mansionarii*.

On the feast of Saint John the Evangelist, the church is to be perfumed; one *aquaricia* of oil is to be provided for the fonts, and what remains belongs to the church; twelve Papienses denarii are to be given to the clerics, together with wine to drink before the vigil; and three pairs of torches: one for the clerics and another for the acolytes. If there are no acolytes, they belong to the clerics of the church; the third pair is for Mass.

On the First Sunday of Lent, the church is to be perfumed; four denarii are to be given to the *mansionarii*, and a pair of torches for Mass. The remainder belongs [perhaps: “to the clerics,”] if an acolyte is absent.

From the First Sunday until the octave of Pentecost, the *mansionarii* are to receive one *caput* from the common fund each day; on Saturday, however, they receive three *capita* for the cleansing of the church.

[Note: Above, Peter Mallius interprets three *capita* as three coins.]

On the Wednesday of the fourth week, when the clerics go with the cross through the cemeteries to Saint Paul and Saint Anastasia, the entire altar belongs to the clerics until the cross goes out and is carried away. Or, if the clerics prefer, they may receive from it bread, wine, and fish for the evening meal.

[Note: Here “supper” refers to that one meal which was to be taken during Lent at Vespers.]

On Palm Sunday the church is to be perfumed; four denarii are to be given to the *mansionarii*, and a pair of torches for Mass.

On Maundy Thursday likewise, four denarii are to be given to the *mansionarii*, and one for washing the vessels and other preparations.

On Holy Saturday, a pair of torches is to be provided for Mass, together with the cost of cleaning the paradise and the chrism, and of the closed portico; and the church is to be perfumed.

On Holy Easter Day, a pair of torches is to be provided for Vespers. On Monday likewise. On Saturday in White Week the church is to be perfumed; a pair of torches is to be provided for Mass; and four denarii are to be given to the *mansionarii*.

During the Greater Litany, until the cross goes out and returns, the entire altar belongs to the clerics. From it they are to receive fish on Tuesday, and bread and wine, eggs, and cheese.

On Holy Saturday of Pentecost, a pair of torches is to be provided for Mass; one denarius is to be given to those who throw flowers over the lord pope; and the church is to be perfumed in the customary manner.

On the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, the church is to be especially perfumed; twelve denarii, one pound of incense, one roll of Greek candles, eighteen denarii for the singers, one *aquaricia* of oil for the fonts, and seven pairs of torches are to be provided, together with one pound for each pair: one pair for the acolytes, another for the Greeks, another before the altar at the fonts, and the rest for Mass. All these belong to the clerics if the curia is absent. Four denarii are also to be given to the *mansionarii*, together with wine for all the clerics, Greek and Latin, to drink before the vigil.

[Note: Thus wine is commonly given at vigils before the vigil, as a kind of preliminary to our little supper.]

At the vigil of Saint Peter, wine is to be provided for the clerics to drink before the vigil. At the vigil of Saint Paul likewise. At the vigil of the holy martyrs Pancratius and Venantius, and of the holy women Rufina and Secunda, likewise.

At the Assumption of Saint Mary, the church is perfumed; wine is provided for the clerics before the vigil, together with six pairs of torches and four denarii for the *mansionarii*.

At the vigil of Saint Lawrence, wine is provided before the vigil.

On the Beheading of Saint John, the church is to be perfumed, and wine provided before the vigil.

On the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, the church is to be perfumed; a pair of torches is provided for Mass, four denarii for the *mansionarii*, and wine for the clerics. From this feast until the octave of Saint Martin, the *mansionarii* receive two *capita* each day.

At the solemnity of the holy Savior, the church is to be perfumed; six pairs of torches are to be provided: one for the chamberlains, another for the acolytes, another before the altar, another in the reading stand, another for Mass, and another for the clerics. Twelve denarii are to be given to the clerics and four to the *mansionarii*, together with one *aquaricia* of wine before the vigil. All the remaining torches from the night and from Mass belong to the clerics if the acolytes are absent.

Throughout the entire year the church must receive from the bishops’ half of the altar enough oil each day for fifteen lamps: one at the apse, seven before the altar, one before the large image above the bronze columns, five in the lattice, and one before the image of Saint Mary, which is above the clock. Also [it must receive] ropes for hanging the candles, bronze bells, and incense daily for the Masses; at night, candles for the lessons and Psalms, and for lighting the lamps; and [whatever is needed] to illuminate the church sufficiently [the reading *quaerendum* is uncertain]. At all station churches, whenever the lord pope descends to celebrate Mass, wine for the sacrifice and for Communion is supplied from the altar. At that time the altar offering above belongs to the *scholae*, and that below to the clergy of the church. All [Col. 1104B] belts—of both the altar and the images—belong to the clergy.

[Note: [Col. 1104D] “Cinctures?”—for those ornaments with which they gird the images.]

220. It is also the custom of the clergy that, whenever they take care of the altar, they are provided for according to the season and receive from it one Pavia denarius. For washing or mending the church’s cloths or curtains, and for the keys and doors, payment is made from the bishops’ half of the altar. All lamps and basins belong to the canons. Of all offerings that come into the hands of the weekly bishop of the high altar, one half belongs to that bishop and one half to the canons, except for bread and wine, which belong to the canons.

At Christmas, from the bishops’ half, two *laumae* [perhaps *saumae*] of blackbirds are provided for the church; and likewise at Easter, on the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, and on the feast of the Holy Savior.

### Another, more recent text

In the name of the Lord, amen. In the year 1232, indiction 5, the following agreement was made between the Lateran church and the first cantor and the singing school: namely, that the said first cantor should come on the feast of Saint John the Baptist with ten singers—so that he himself would be the eleventh—and that they should officiate in the church at the Vigil, Matins, and Mass. They and two of their servants were to be provided decently and honorably with those foods with which the community would be served on that day; and as his remuneration he would receive one sixth of the offerings of the high altar, specifically those falling upon it during the period in which Mass was celebrated.

Moreover, the first cantor himself receives from the church two Provisian soldi of the Senate as remuneration, and each of the canons twelve denarii, the present sum including the denarii given to the singers for the responsories. Both parties are bound to observe this in all those feasts which the Lateran church wishes to celebrate according to the aforesaid arrangement and for which it has decided to invite the first cantor with the school. But at all station churches the first cantor and the school, even if not invited, must come to serve at the Mass alone; they are to receive no other remuneration except one sixth of the offerings of the high altar, only, as written above.

[Col. 1105]

# ROMAN ORDER XIII, OR THE ROMAN CEREMONIAL

Published by order of GREGORY X

[Col. 1105A] 221

1. Since life is short for every ruler, it often happens that the Roman pontiffs, who hold primacy in the subcelestial hierarchy, finish their lives within a brief span of time and pass from this prison of the flesh [Col. 1105B] to the freedom of the heavenly realm. And since such a great and eminent hierarchy ought not to be headless, like a monster, the holy Fathers therefore decreed that, once the body of the deceased ruler had been entrusted to ecclesiastical burial, another should canonically be substituted for the deceased ruler, to preside over so great a burden and honor.

Yet because there has frequently been doubt concerning the procedures and forms by which the church ought to conduct itself toward those to be substituted in this way—since at times persons established in different major ecclesiastical orders have been assumed to this burden—the most holy Father and common lord, our lord Pope Gregory X, who had formerly been constituted in the order of the diaconate before attaining the summit of the dignity of the same pontificate, wishing to cut off such doubts by means of what had been done in his own case, caused the following matters to be reduced to writing and set down in brief style, as a precaution for the present and a memorial for the future.

2. First of all, when the Roman Church is vacant of a pastor, whoever has been elected pope unanimously by all the cardinals, or by two-thirds of them, is to be regarded by the universal Church as the Roman pontiff. If he is absent, or is not from the college of cardinals, he must come when summoned to the place where the cardinals are in consistory; and, in their presence, he gives his consent to his own co-election.

The senior deacon strips him of the cape or cloak that he is wearing and puts on him, if he does not have them, the Roman alb, the camisia, and the orarium, in the manner of a priest: over the shoulders if he is a priest, or over the left side if he is a deacon [Col. 1105D] and has not been constituted in the priestly order. Afterwards he puts the mantle on him and says: “I invest you with the Roman papacy, so that you may preside over the City and the world.” He also hands him the ring customarily used by his predecessors and places on his head a mitre suitable for him. He asks him by what name he wishes to be called, and they will call him by whatever name pleases him.

Having done this, he makes him sit on the chair or faldstool. After his ordinary shoes have been removed, if red papal footwear is available, it is put on him. Then all the cardinals come before him in order—first the bishops, second the priests, and third the deacons—with knees bent. The elected man receives them in due order at his foot and to the kiss of peace, as well as all his other chaplains and the other clergy and laypeople who come to pay him reverence, the lowest, middle-ranking, and highest alike.

When these matters have been completed, with the papal cross leading, he is conducted in procession by the cardinals and the entire curia to the cathedral or another larger church of the place in which the curia is situated, if the place where he is elected is not a city. In that church he is led to the altar, and before the altar he prays for a long time, prostrate. While he prays, all the clergy sing *Te Deum laudamus* (“We praise you, O God”). When it has been sung, the senior bishop says the *Pater noster* and the customary suffrages, together with the prayer *Omnipotens sempiterne Deus nuper electo nostro* (“Almighty and everlasting God, [grant your aid] to our newly elected [pontiff]”). When this has ended, the elected man rises from prayer, says *Sit nomen Domini benedictum* (“Blessed be the name of the Lord”), and gives the blessing.

3. When this has been completed, he returns, kisses the altar, and, just as he came in due order to the church, so he returns to his chamber, continually making the sign of the cross as he goes and returns. After he has returned to his chamber, he removes the cope and mitre and assumes a red mantle. He must have leggings of red cloth without foot coverings and with *stafili*, and a red scarlet cap. Afterwards he puts on small shoes of the same cloth and religious shoes of red leather reaching halfway up; tunics and garments of scarlet; and over these cloth garments, a white camisia. He will be girded with a red silk belt over the camisia, and the camisia will be so long that, when raised, it can be suitably folded back over the belt.

4. If the same elected man, whatever his order may be, writes any letters to anyone before his consecration, he shall have those letters sealed with the side of the bull on which the apostles’ heads appear on one face; the other face shall be flat, since he has not yet been consecrated pope. In the salutation he writes his name as follows: “G., elected servant of the servants of God, to the beloved …, etc., greetings and apostolic blessing.”

At the end, before the date of the letters, he adds: “Nor should it be wondered at that the bull expressing our name is not attached to the present letters, since before the solemn ceremonies of our consecration and blessing it is not sent.” Thus far, those elected as Roman pontiffs have customarily had a bull before the office of their consecration; they are to observe this intermediate practice. After the date, in such a place, etc., [he writes]: “By the hand of such-and-such, in the first year of the apostolic office undertaken by us.” The penitentiaries, in dating their letters, say: “Given also in the first year of the prelacy of the lord bishop, the pope-elect in the Roman pontificate.”

5. The same elected man, whatever order he may hold, shall be promoted to the major orders according to the form by which others are ordained. This exception is observed: if he is a subdeacon, the elected man, dressed in amice and alb and girded with a belt, with manipule only, shall sit in his faldstool, holding his mantle, with the cope not worn but placed behind his neck, and with a suitable mitre on his head. If he is a deacon, he shall have the stole over the left side. Thus he is to be ordained.

The ordaining minister comes before him and says the prescribed prayers and performs the other acts customarily performed in the order that he is conferring. Note that while the elected man is being ordained, the cardinal deacon and the chaplain subdeacon assist him by washing his hands and clothing him, as is customarily done when the pope celebrates. They shall be dressed in the appropriate sacred vestments. Afterwards, two cardinal deacons must assist the elected man who has been ordained and serve him, as is customary; they too shall be clothed in suitable sacred vestments, even if the other cardinals of whatever order are not vested. The ordaining minister, however, shall have his own ministers, who serve him in the habit of a subdeacon and deacon. This concludes the matter of the order.

6. Once the elected man has been ordained to the order, after receiving the order and the appropriate vestments for that order, he resumes the mantle or cope behind his neck, as stated above. When the time for crowning arrives, the man who has been ordained comes to the ordaining minister at the altar, and the minister reverently crowns him. When everything has been completed and Mass has been reverently concluded, the elected man says *Sit nomen Domini* (“Blessed be the name of the Lord”) and gives the blessing. After it has been said, the ordaining minister says to the elected man three times, *Multos annos* (“Many years”), bending his knee three times before him, as is customary, and each time saying it in a louder voice.

The elected man performs no service at the altar for the ordaining minister; he neither sings the Epistle nor the Gospel. Before he receives the order of the diaconate, the customary petition *Postulat mater ecclesia nostra* (“Our mother Church requests …”) is not said. That petition is not necessary in the case of a pope, because we know him to be fully worthy in every respect. Nor is the same petition said when he is promoted to the priestly order.

When he is to be ordained to the priesthood, he is vested with the solemnity described above: he has the stole over his shoulder and the manipule on his arm. He does not, however, have the tunicle or dalmatic; he is not shod with sandals; he does not have a pectoral or a fanon, but only the amice and alb. The litany is performed as usual. Finally, the ordaining minister, standing before him, ordains him according to the customary manner used for others and anoints his hands with holy oil, placing his own hand on them first; all the assisting cardinal priests do likewise.

He puts the chasuble on him, first folding the orarium back over both shoulders, as is customary. When all the rites contained in the ordination of priests have been completed, and the chasuble has been spread down his back by the ordaining minister and arranged by the ministers, the elected man washes his hands with a crumb of bread, as is customary.

After this, he receives all the cardinal bishops, priests, and deacons, as well as the other prelates who are present, in their order, at his foot and to the kiss. Then the Gospel is sung. When it has been sung, the elected man kisses the Gospel brought to him, as is customary. After the ordaining minister has said *Dominus vobiscum* (“The Lord be with you”) and *Oremus* (“Let us pray”), the same minister comes before the elected man and receives from his hand two large loaves, two vessels of wine, and two torches, kissing his hand.

After this, the ordaining minister and the ordained man return to the altar, and one cardinal priest serves the newly ordained elected man with the book at the altar during Mass, teaching and instructing him. At the appropriate time, after the ordaining minister has crowned him, the aforesaid elected man is crowned on the altar by the hand of the ordaining minister, and everything is performed properly to the end of Mass. When it is finished, the ordaining minister says *Multos annos*, as stated above. The elected man himself sings *Sit nomen Domini benedictum* (“Blessed be the name of the Lord”), as specified above. After this, the same elected man is reverently divested, as is customary, while the prescribed Psalms are said: *Benedicite* and *Laudate Dominum*, [with] the Antiphon of the Three Children.

He receives these orders in the presence of all the priests, from whichever bishop he prefers, whether cardinal or otherwise. All this is done on Saturday. On the following Sunday he is consecrated, if he wishes. If he does not wish to be consecrated, or if he postpones the consecration for some reason, he shall sing Mass neither publicly nor privately until he has been consecrated.

6. When an elected pope who is a priest is to be consecrated, the following order must be observed. First, while the elected man is saying the Psalm *Quam amabilia* (“How lovely …”), he is shod with sandals and leggings. After washing his hands, he is vested in all his ornaments: first the alb and belt with the subcinctorium, then the pectoral, next the fanon, then the stole, thereafter the tunicle, and finally the dalmatic.

Next he receives the gloves and finally the chasuble and mitre on his head, without the pallium and pastoral ring, which he will receive later in their proper place. The vestments shall be of the color appropriate to the season. All the cardinals—bishops, priests, and deacons—as well as the subdeacons and other prelates, shall be dressed in vestments suitable to the season. With the papal cross leading, together with seven torches and incense, they all proceed in procession from the place where he has been vested to the altar.

The customary first and second examinations made at the consecration of other bishops, beginning *Antiqua* (“Ancient …”), are not performed. The elected man goes to the altar and makes his confession while the choir or school sings the Introit and *Kyrie eleison*. After this, he comes before the altar and kneels there on the prepared faldstool, and all the other prelates do likewise. The two cardinal deacons who assist him on his right and left to serve him stand there, and the chaplain subdeacon sings the litany, with the other chaplains responding.

When the litany reaches the passage *Ut consecrandum* (“That he may be consecrated …”), it is repeated twice, and each prelate, together with the ordaining minister, signs the elected man. When the litany has been said, the ordaining minister comes before the elected man and says what is contained in the bishops’ Pontifical. When this has been said, they return behind the altar.

Then one of the cardinal bishops comes and says the prayer *Adesto* (“Be present”). Afterwards another cardinal bishop comes and says the prayer *Oremus, dilectissimi* (“Let us pray, dearly beloved”), and the phrase “for the benefit of the universal Church” is added to it.

Finally, the ordaining or consecrating minister comes and places an open Book of the Gospels over the elected man’s head, toward his neck. The open book is held in this position by two cardinals, while all the prelates stand around in a circle, each vested and with his own book. The ordaining minister begins and proceeds as contained in the book, all the other prelates saying the words with him in a subdued voice, and the ordaining minister singing *Deus homini* (“God [has given] to man …”), as in the book. The exception is that, in its proper place, the passage *Et idcirco* (“And therefore …”), which is specifically included in the consecration of a pope, is inserted.

When this is finished, the ordaining minister removes the gloves and places a thin *capiturgium* in the form of a shield over the elected man’s head, with the ends of the *capiturgium* hanging behind his neck. In this manner he pours chrism over his head in the form of a cross and says the prayer *Ungatur* (“Let him be anointed …”). He adds another prayer, *Hoc, Domine* (“This, O Lord …”), and in its proper place the words *Illud tribue* (“Grant that …”) are added.

When this is finished, he anoints the elected man’s hand with chrism and says the prayer *Deus* (“God …”). When this is finished, no staff is given to him, nor is the prayer *Accipe baculum* (“Receive the staff”) said. Instead, the ring is given to him, and the prayer *Accipe* (“Receive …”) is said, with the words “the holy universal Church” added.

Again, the Book of the Gospels is given to him, and *Accipe* (“Receive …”) is said, with the words “I entrust the universal people to you” added.

When all these things have been completed by the consecrator, the supreme pontiff sits on the faldstool and washes his hands with a crumb of bread and water. One cardinal bishop comes before him and wipes his head, which had been anointed, lightly with a crumb of bread and with the crust [the reading is abbreviated or uncertain], and then wipes it with a linen cloth or fine towel. When this is finished, the supreme pontiff receives the consecrator and all the cardinal bishops, priests, and deacons to the kiss on the mouth.

7. When a bishop is elected pope, he is not consecrated in any other manner. Everything contained in this book under this number is performed, from “First, the elected man” up to the words “processionally to the altar.” After the confession has been made at the end, he ascends the prepared seat. There the cardinal bishops come before him and say the three prayers that are in the Ordinary, in the order written in the Ordinary.

When this is finished, he sits on the seat and receives those cardinals and the other prelates, performing what is contained here from the words “All the other prelates at his foot and to the kiss.” After receiving them, he comes to the altar and takes from above it the pallium prepared by the senior of the chaplain subdeacons or by the prior of the Basilica of the Holy of Holies. The two senior cardinal deacons hold the pallium, and then the senior of those two alone gives the pallium to the supreme pontiff with these words:

“Receive the pallium, the fullness of pontifical office, for the honor of almighty God; of the most glorious Virgin Mary, his mother; of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul; and of the holy Roman Church.”

After the pallium has been fitted over him with three golden pins, as is customary, the supreme pontiff ascends to the altar and incenses it. Finally he returns to the elevated seat and says *Dominus vobiscum* (“The Lord be with you”), or *Pax vobis* (“Peace be with you”), as the day requires. Afterwards he says the prayer of the Sunday aloud and another prayer for himself privately.

When this prayer is finished, the lord pope sits again on the seat. The senior cardinal deacon, carrying the ferula in his hands, descends before the altar with the deacons, subdeacons, recorders, and judges, all solemnly vested, and forms two lines, one on each side, dividing them equally. He places the deacons first beside the altar, the subdeacons second, the judges third, and the recorders fourth, in order.

The senior deacon begins the praise in a loud voice, though as if reading: *Exaudi, Christe* (“Hear us, O Christ”). The judges and recorders likewise proceed in a chant resembling recitation: “For our lord pope, by God’s decree the supreme pontiff and universal pope, life.” The same senior deacon then says a second time, *Exaudi, Christe*, and the judges and recorders say the Antiphon as before; and he does this a third time.

The same senior deacon says, *Salvator mundi* (“Savior of the world”), and the judges and recorders respond with the Antiphon, *Tu illum adjuva* (“Help him”), and the rest follows. Again, the senior deacon says twice, *Sancta Maria* (“Holy Mary”), and they respond with the Antiphon, *Tu illum adjuva*. In the same manner, but only once, he says: *Sancte Gabriel, sancte Raphael, sancte Joannes Baptista, sancte Petre, sancte Paule, sancte Andrea, sancte Stephane, sancte Leo, sancte Gregori, sancte Benedicte, sancte Basili, sancte Saba, sancta Agnes, sancta Caecilia, sancta Lucia* (“Holy Gabriel, holy Raphael, holy John the Baptist, holy Peter, holy Paul, holy Andrew, holy Stephen, holy Leo, holy Gregory, holy Benedict, holy Basil, holy Saba, holy Agnes, holy Cecilia, holy Lucy”), while the others respond, *Tu illum adjuva*.

When these things are finished, the senior deacon says *Kyrie*, etc., and they respond, *Kyrie, eleison*, etc.; this is done three times. Afterwards all likewise say *Kyrie* aloud and with one voice.

When the praises are finished, the Latin Epistle is read, followed by the Greek one from the pulpit; the same is done with the Gospel. The cardinal bishop who consecrates him, dressed in all the pontifical vestments except the pastoral staff, consecrates the supreme pontiff. When the consecration has been completed, he removes all the aforementioned ornaments and, having taken a cope with a surplice, serves the supreme pontiff at the altar, as is customary.

Thus Mass proceeds in its proper order to the end. He performs the consecration solemnly, not at the altar but at the seat. After Mass the same supreme pontiff says, *Sit nomen Domini benedictum* (“Blessed be the name of the Lord”). The consecrator, however, does not say *Multos annos* (“Many years”).

8. When everything has been duly completed, the supreme pontiff, all the cardinals, and the other prelates and subdeacons, each vested according to his rank in precious white garments, proceed as follows: the bishops in copes, the priests in chasubles, the deacons in dalmatics, the subdeacons in tunicles, and the acolytes in surplices.
