The other chaplains, bishops, archbishops, abbots, and patriarchs are also in copes; likewise the judges, recorders, prefects, and advocates are dressed in copes.

The pope himself, in cope and mitre and solemnly in surplices, has all the precious ornaments, the pallium, the finest mitre, gloves, and pastoral ring. Thus he comes with everyone to the gate or steps of the church.

There the senior cardinal deacon removes his mitre and places on his head the crown called the *regnum*, while the entire people cry out, *Kyrie*, etc. Then, in full vesture, each cardinal and prelate rides a horse covered with white cloth. The subdeacons, chaplains, recorders, and others ride richly dressed, but their horses are not covered.

The pope rides a large horse furnished with trappings and covered only at the rear with scarlet cloth; the front is not covered.

9. Once everyone has mounted his horse, the senior of the deacons arranges the procession in this manner. First comes the pope’s horse, furnished with trappings. Second comes a subdeacon with the cross. Third come twelve standard-bearers with twelve red banners, and two others with two cherubim bearing lances. Fourth come two naval prefects dressed in copes. Fifth, the recorders. Sixth, the advocates. Seventh, the judges. Eighth, the singers. Ninth, the deacons and subdeacons who read the Epistle and Gospel in Greek. Tenth, the foreign abbots. Eleventh, the bishops. Twelfth, the archbishops. Thirteenth, the abbots of the City. Fourteenth, the patriarchs and cardinal bishops. Fifteenth, the cardinal priests. Sixteenth, the cardinal deacons. Seventeenth, the lord pope, the subdeacons with a towel, and the servant who carries the canopy.

Thus he comes to his palace or to a church beside his palace. When he dismounts there, he removes the *regnum* from his head and receives the mitre. A cardinal priest then performs the praises there with the notaries and judges. When these have been completed, he removes only the pallium, chasuble, and gloves, and resumes the cope behind his neck.

He comes to a suitably prepared place, where he gives each cardinal and prelate a ceremonial gift. Then the pope sits on his seat, and each cardinal and prelate comes before him. Kneeling, the cardinal or prelate removes his own mitre and holds it open before the pope. The pope throws into it the money that the chamberlain gives him in a silver bowl, according to the chamberlain’s book, which is called the *Politicus* [read: *Polyptycus*]. The recipient of the money in the mitre kisses the pope’s knee.

The chamberlain has a large table before him, covered with a towel, on which such items are placed. Only a clerk and two riders assist the chamberlain; the chamberlain himself and the clerk of the chamber are in surplices.

After the ceremonial gifts have been distributed, the lord is solemnly led by two cardinal deacons to a richly prepared table. There he sits, with a cardinal bishop giving him water and two deacons holding a towel. Everyone then goes to sit in that place. The pope alone sits at one elevated table, with various large golden and silver vessels. At another table sit the bishops; at another, behind them, the priests. On the other side, to the left, sit the cardinal deacons, followed by the tables of all the other prelates and nobles.

Note that while eating the pope remains standing, vested and shod as stated above, and wearing his mitre. All the cardinals have surplices with camisiae and mantles, and simple white mitres on their heads. All the prelates likewise eat wearing their mitres. The senior and nobler laymen who are present serve before the pope.

When the feast is over, the pope washes his hands as before, and each cardinal likewise washes while seated, with an attendant pouring water for the cardinal who is washing. The assisting cardinals hold the towel, one on each side of the person washing, and thus serve one another mutually.

When all have washed and thanks have been returned, the pope is led by two cardinals back to his chamber and chapel. They remove his shoes and undress him, after which the pope rests. The cardinals and other prelates return to their lodgings riding with their mitres, dressed and prepared as they had been during the meal.

Note also that when he comes crowned, he must make money scatterings in four places—that is, throw various mixed coins over the people.

10. If the pope has been ordained and consecrated at Saint Peter’s in Rome, when he is to be consecrated he is led to the chapel of Saint Gregory and proceeds in procession to the altar. The remaining rites are performed as stated above. When they have been completed, he is crowned at the steps and returns to the Lateran by the pope’s road.

After he has ridden on, a scattering of money is made there in the same place by the seneschal or another person three times, and the scattering is made behind the pope. Likewise, when he reaches the tower of Stephen of Saint Peter, which is in the Parione and is today called the Tower of Campo, one of the pope’s household makes another scattering there, standing in some elevated place. The lord pope stands there, and the Jews come to him with the Law, praising him and offering him the Law for him to venerate.

Likewise, when he has reached the palace [Note: [Col. 1111] Cencius, in chapter 14, has: “to the palace of Cencius Musca in Punga.” Compare chapter 20 of Jacobus Caietanus.] … in Punga, one of the pope’s household makes a scattering from the said palace. He makes another scattering when he reaches Saint Mark’s, and another when he reaches Saint Adrian’s, standing at the window of the palace of Saint Martina. Thus he comes to the Lateran square and is led to the portico that goes to the church of Saint John Lateran.

There the prior of the Lateran and the canons, with their company, solemnly dressed and carrying the processional cross, receive the pope when he dismounts. After the pope has dismounted, they make him sit there on a certain marble seat called the *stercoraria*. All the cardinals come and honorably lift him up, so that they may truly say: “He raises the needy from the dust and lifts the poor from the dungheap, to seat him with princes and give him the throne of glory.”

The lord pope himself, standing beside that seat, takes three handfuls of coins from the chamberlain’s lap and throws them among the people, saying: “Silver and gold I do not have; but what I have, this I give you.”

Afterwards, with the prior and canons leading, he is conducted through the portico into the church of the Lateran basilica while they sing. There he prays and says, *Sit nomen Domini* (“Blessed be the name of the Lord”). He removes the *regnum*, assumes the mitre, and sits in the great seat behind the altar, where he receives the aforesaid prior and the Lateran canons at his foot and to the kiss.

After this, he is led to the palace. When he reaches the palace gate through which the palace is entered by way of the church, a faldstool is placed there. While the pope sits on it, the prior of the cardinal priests, having arranged the judges and recorders in a line, performs a praise there, just as the cardinal deacons had done at Mass before the Epistle after the prayer.

Afterwards the same cardinals lead him through the palace to the gate of the church of Saint Sylvester, where there are two porphyry seats. First he sits on the one to the right. There the prior of the Basilica of Saint Lawrence gives him the ferula, which is a sign of correction and governance, and the keys of that basilica and of the Lateran palace, signifying the power to close, open, bind, and loose.

With that ferula and the other keys he approaches the other similar seat, which is on the left. He then returns the ferula and keys to the same prior and begins to sit on the second seat.

After he has sat there for a while, the same prior girds the lord pope with a red silk belt, from which hangs a purple purse containing twelve precious stones with a seal and musk. While sitting on that seat, he receives the officials of the palace at his foot and to the kiss. Sitting there, he receives from the chamberlain silver denarii worth ten soldi and throws them over the people. He does this three times, saying each time:

“He has scattered; he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures for ever and ever.”

The pope conducts himself on these two seats in such a way that he appears to be lying rather than sitting. None of these seats, not even the *stercoraria*, is covered or prepared; they are bare.

Finally, he is led to the Holy of Holies, where he enters. Before the altar he says his prayer. Afterwards he is led back to the chapel of Saint Sylvester, which he enters, and sits in the prepared place, where he gives the ceremonial gift described above.

Then he returns to his chamber, removes the chasuble and pallium, assumes the mantle, and goes to eat, as stated above. First, however, he receives the oath from the senator according to the form: “I, such-and-such,” etc.

11. If the lord pope is consecrated or elected outside the City, when he comes to Rome, to the chapel of Saint Mary Magdalene at the foot of Mount Malo, he dismounts and enters that chapel with the cardinals. There he receives the cope and mitre. Afterwards he mounts and proceeds.

The Jews meet him with the Law and praises, and all the churches of the City honorably come out to meet him in procession. All the clergy come vested, with crosses and banners, a thurible, and a vessel containing incense. Each church meets the pope with a thurible and that vessel. The lord pope places incense from it into the thurible with a spoon, and they incense the pope with it. All the churches do likewise.

Thus he is led through the portico to the steps of Saint Peter, where the procession is prepared. The archpriest and canons of Saint Peter receive him reverently. As the canons sing, the prior of the canons introduces him into the church, holding the pope on one side and the prior of the cardinals on the other; thus he is brought into the church while they hold him.

The prior releases him before the gate of the basilica itself, and another cardinal takes him on that side. When they reach the middle of the church, the cardinal priests sing before him: *Protector noster aspice Deus, et respice in facie Christi tui* (“Look upon us, O God, our protector, and regard the face of your Christ”).

When this has been said, he is led to the altar and prays there. While he prays, the canons sing *Te Deum laudamus* (“We praise you, O God”). When it has been sung, the pope rises from prayer and says *Sit nomen Domini* (“Blessed be the name of the Lord”). Afterwards he kisses the altar of blessed Peter, offering upon the altar a precious golden cloth. The pope always offers a silk cloth upon the altar of whatever church he first ascends to its altar.

Finally, he is led to the great and elevated seat behind the altar of blessed Peter, where the senior cardinal deacon enthrones and seats him. Sitting there, he receives all the cardinals in order at his foot and to the kiss on the mouth, as well as all the canons of Saint Peter.

After this, he is led to his chamber to rest. When he later comes to the Lateran, he is received the first time as stated above concerning the seats and everything else, except the praises; and he makes an offering at the altar as described.

Having passed briefly over all these matters that are performed concerning the lord pope, let us now briefly consider how the same lord pope ought to conduct himself in the offices, whether in the church or outside it.

### 12.

First, it must be noted that the lord pope has three different mitres, which he uses at different times: namely, one entirely white; one with gold embroidery on the band but without a circlet; and a mitre embroidered with gold both on the circlet and on the band. He uses the mitre embroidered with gold on the circlet and on the band during services on feast days and other occasions, except from Septuagesima until Easter, from Advent until Christmas, and when he sings the office for the dead. The reason is that it represents the crown and the course of the active and contemplative life.

He uses the mitre with gold embroidery on the band but without a circlet when he sits in consistory and gives judgment; hence it represents the royal crown. He uses the white mitre on Sundays and other non-feast days, from Advent of the Lord until Vespers on the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord, except on the third Sunday of Advent, which is called “Gaudete Sunday.” On that day, at Lauds, the fifth antiphon is *Juste*, because on that day the lord pope performs a certain solemnity, as follows.

Since the station is at Saint Peter on that Sunday, on the Saturday evening vigil of the same Sunday the pope and the cardinals assemble at Saint Peter. There all of them—the pope and the cardinals—wear only episcopal vestments on account of the feast of the station, and begin Vespers of the day, without saying anything of the Blessed Virgin, since the office is for the feast of the station. At Vespers the antiphons from Lauds are said, and the *primicerius* sings with the schola.

The *primicerius* announces the first antiphon to the pope; the schola singers announce the other three; and the canons of Saint Peter announce the fifth, which is *Juste*, to the pope. After this announcement the lord pope receives a gold coin from the hand of the chamberlain and places it in the mouth of the person making the announcement, while that announcer holds his mouth open. When this has been done, the pope himself solemnly begins *Juste*, and then the Sunday psalms, with the last psalm, *Laudate Dominum omnes gentes*. Everything else is done as in the office for Sundays. When Vespers has been said, everyone returns.

### 13.

On the morning of that third Sunday the pope rides to Saint Peter. He wears the mitre embroidered with gold both on the journey there and on the return. At Mass he uses silk cloths of a violet color, woven in relief work, and the chasuble is ornamented with pearls. He uses these only on this Sunday and during Lent. On other Sundays and ferial days he uses violet-colored cloths at Mass, and the deacon and subdeacon likewise, unless it is a feast on which they use cloths of the color required by that feast.

It should also be noted that seven days before the vigil of the Nativity, excluding Sunday, seven great antiphons are sung at the *Magnificat*, almost jubilantly, and are sung both before and after the psalm. The *Kyrie, eleison* (“Lord, have mercy”) and the suffrages are not said; rather, *Dominus vobiscum* (“The Lord be with you”) is begun directly, and the Lord’s Prayer is said, even on ferial days if it is available.

Observe also that whenever the office is sung for the dead, or for a ferial day from Advent until Christmas, from Septuagesima until Easter, and on the four Ember Days and the vigils of the saints on which fasting is observed, and the ministers use the little cap, except on the vigil of Pentecost—and on the Ember Days of that feast the pope does not perform the office, as is contained in the Breviary—the office of the day and of the Blessed Virgin is said, one episcopal office extending from that Saturday until Vespers on the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord. The office of the Blessed Virgin is not said at Matins or at First Vespers; on the other days it is said by reading. From the first Sunday of Advent until the feast of the Nativity, fasting is observed in the manner of Lent.

### 14.

On the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord the pope comes, together with all the cardinals, the prelates summoned by the couriers, the chaplains, and the others likewise, to Vespers. The pope is vested in a precious red cope and a precious mitre; all the others wear white vestments: the bishops and cardinal deacons, as well as the other prelates, wear copes, while the presbyters wear chasubles. Thus they solemnly celebrate Vespers, and the pope begins Vespers in his prepared place, while the chaplains, in suitable attire, sing before him.

If he is in Rome, the *primicerius* of the schola announces the antiphons, according to the schola’s chant. If he is elsewhere, another chaplain of the pope, the weekly celebrant, announces them. They are announced in this order: the pope himself begins the first; the prior of the bishops, the second; the prior of the presbyters, the third; the prior of the deacons, the fourth; and another deacon after the prior, the fifth.

Then the pope offers incense, censing only the altar that has been prepared, as has been stated. After censing it, he returns to his place, and the cardinal who assists him with the book receives the thurible and censes the pope, the cardinals, all the vested prelates, and the chaplains in due order.

A chaplain says the chapter. The hymn and the antiphon for the *Magnificat* are announced to the pope, and two cardinal deacons assist him: the senior on his right and the junior on his left. The cardinal bishop or cardinal presbyter who assists with the book is present when the lord pope says the collect. When he says it, two chaplains hold large silver candlesticks with candles before him. After *Dominus vobiscum* (“The Lord be with you”), the junior deacon says *Benedicamus Domino* (“Let us bless the Lord”), and the pope says, “May the name of the Lord be blessed.”

When this is finished, they return to the pope’s hall, where many different wines, spiced wine, and spices have been prepared.

### 15.

If the pope is in Rome, after dinner has been eaten at midday [Note: Thus at that time dinner, or the principal meal, was held at midday on fast days], he goes with his household to Saint Mary Major. There he says solemn Vespers with the whole curia, as stated above, and spends the night there. He sings Matins in that church, assisted by three cardinal bishops, two deacons, and one junior presbyter, and the office is performed as contained in the order of the Breviary.

There the lord pope sings the Mass of the night at the altar called the Manger. While he divests himself, the chaplains sing the morning Lauds before him. After these have been said, he goes to rest.

And at first light, before sunrise, he goes with the whole curia to the church of Saint Anastasia and sings Mass there. After it has been said, he returns to the aforesaid church of Saint Mary Major and sings a third Mass there at the high altar. At all the Masses he uses the white color. After this Mass he returns to the Lateran and says his Vespers in the chapel with his chaplains.

On the same day all the penitentiaries, with their servants, and the weekly almoner and vice-chancellor with the entire chancery come to see the pope, and the pope gives everyone spices and wine.

### 16.

On the feast of Saint Stephen the office is performed as contained in the Ordinary.

### 17.

On the feast of Saint John the office is likewise performed as found in the Breviary, and the white color is used.

### 18.

On the feast of the Innocents the office is performed as contained in the book. At Mass, however, the violet color is used; the subdeacon and deacon wear folded chasubles (*planetae*), and the pope wears a simple mitre.

During their Octave he uses the red color at Mass, as on feast days. On the other subsequent feasts—whether the feast of confessors or of virgins—he uses the white color; red is used on Sundays from the Nativity until the Octave of Epiphany. If the office is for Sunday rather than for a particular feast, he uses white.

From the Octave of Epiphany until Septuagesima, on Sundays and ferial days, he uses the green color.

### 19.

From Septuagesima until the first day of Lent he uses the black color. He makes a procession from Saint Anastasia to Saint Sabina; the pope and the others go barefoot, and the pope removes his shoes at the church door. For this reason he is vested in the sacred vestments but does not put on sandals.

After they arrive there, the pope enters the sacristy, washes his feet, puts on his shoes, and then sings Mass. On the way, the same lord pope, together with the chaplain-deacon and the others accompanying him, goes reciting the Psalter. The schola singers sing, and the other things are done as contained in the Roman Order.

However, during Lent until Easter, from the Octave of Pentecost until Christmas, and from the Octave of Epiphany until Lent, on ferial days, whenever collects are said—whether in the office of the day, of the dead, or of the Blessed Virgin—we must kneel at all the Hours. Likewise at Mass we must remain kneeling during the collects before the Epistle and after the chant at the elevation of Christ’s body.

At the elevation of Christ’s body, after they have first risen slightly, they prostrate themselves on the ground and reverently adore, falling upon their faces [Note: Observe the rite of adoring the Eucharist at Mass; the Carthusians retain this rite to the present day]. Remaining prostrate in this manner, they stay until *Per omnia* (“Through all [ages]”), before the *Agnus Dei* (“Lamb of God”). They give the peace, prostrate themselves again, and remain prostrate until the priest receives the body and blood.

After he has received them, while the ablution is being poured, they sit; but from the elevation of Christ’s body until the reception they must stand bareheaded. Again, while the collects after Communion are being said, they must kneel and remain so until the end of Mass.

During Lent they rise and stand when the prayer over the people is said. Then they uncover their heads and bow while that prayer is being said. When Mass is finished, the pope says, “May the name of the Lord be blessed,” as is customary.

### 20.

From the first day of Lent until Easter, if the pope sings, he customarily says publicly only one collect. The chaplains say five: the first of the day; the second, *A cunctis* (“From all [dangers]”); the third, *Omnipotens sempiterne Deus, qui vivorum* (“Almighty everlasting God, who [art the God] of the living”); the fourth, *Exaudi quaesumus, Deus, supplicum* (“Hear, we beseech thee, O God, [the prayers] of thy suppliants”); and the fifth, for the pope. This is done on ferial days until Passion Sunday.

From Passion Sunday in the Mass until Easter, only the collect of the day, *Ecclesiae tuae*, and the collect for the pope are said.

The other offices are performed until Laetare Sunday, *Laetare, Jerusalem* (“Rejoice, Jerusalem”), as contained in the Order. On that Sunday the pope wears a mitre with gold embroidery and goes to sing at the Holy Cross, if he is in Rome. If he is elsewhere, he goes wherever he wishes.

He carries in his hand a golden rose made with marvelous workmanship, containing musk and balsam inside. He holds it in his hand while saying Terce. When he puts on his shoes and vestments, the chamberlain keeps it; today the deacon keeps it beside him.

If the pope does not celebrate, he wears the precious vestments used on Gaudete Sunday and holds the rose while preaching. During Mass the subdeacon who assists with the towel keeps it beside him. After Mass, he carries it in his hand and gives it to the prefect of the city, or to whomever he wishes. The recipient escorts the pope by holding the bridle of his horse, walking on foot to the place where the pope dismounts, and then precedes and follows him to the chamber. The pope gives him the rose, and he kisses the pope’s hands and feet; then he returns suitably to his own house with the rose . . . .

If the pope celebrates, he gives the rose after dismounting; if he does not celebrate, he gives it in his chamber. What this rose, the gold, the musk, and the balsam within it signify, and what is signified by its being carried on that day, is reserved for the diligent investigator.

### 21.

On Palm Sunday the office is performed as contained in the Order, with this exception: while the Passion is being sung, the lord pope holds his palm in his hands, as does everyone else.

The reason is that these two things represent the praise and the reproach of the Church. The former is expressed in palms and flowers, the latter in the Epistle and the Passion of the Mass. Although the Gallican Church uses red vestments [Note: The Gallican Church now observes the Roman rite], the Roman Church uses violet ones. The remaining rites until Holy Thursday are performed as set out in the Order.

### 22.

On Holy Thursday, at night and during the day, everything is said as contained in the Order, with this exception: on that day they read three psalms. Three junior chapel clerks read the lessons from the Lamentations; in the second nocturn, three seniors; and in the third, priest-chaplains.

At the sixth hour of that day the pope comes with the whole curia. All the cardinal bishops wear copes, the presbyters chasubles, the deacons dalmatics, the subdeacons tunicles, and all the prelates white copes. The other chaplains who are to serve wear surplices. The lord pope himself wears a precious cope and a mitre with gold.

There the lord pope delivers a sermon. When it is finished, the pope sits on the faldstool, and the excommunications are read by a chaplain. The cardinal deacon explains them, as with every legal process.

After they have been read and explained, many lighted candles are brought in. The pope holds some of them, and each cardinal and prelate holds one. They place them on the ground and extinguish them, saying, “We excommunicate all the aforesaid.” Then the bells are rung all together without order.

One might ask why the lighted candles are thrown down in this manner. The answer is that, just as a lighted candle is extinguished when it is thrown down, so through excommunication the grace of the Holy Spirit, signified by the light, is removed from those persons. And just as the Church gathers the faithful through orderly ringing, so through disorderly ringing it scatters the unbelieving.

It may also be asked why such excommunications are made in the Church of God today, on the Ascension of the Lord, and on the feast of the Dedication of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles, since on those days they might rather seem to be omitted, as judicial acts ought not to be carried out on feast days.

The answer concerns the reason for these three feasts. First, on this Thursday the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood had its beginning, in which all the faithful communicate. To show that the excommunicated do not communicate in it, they are shown excluded from the church on that day.

At the Ascension it is read that God prayed for the faithful; hence the Church sings, “Holy Father, keep them,” and so forth. Therefore the Church shows that he did not pray for these people and declares them to be such.

At the feast of the Dedication, the place appointed for the faithful to adore is displayed; and because that place is not open to unbelievers, they are expelled from the church on that very day.

All this is done for the benefit of the excommunicated, so that, seeing themselves excluded from so many benefits on such great days, they may more readily submit to the grace of reconciliation.

As for the feast day, the answer is that this is not the pronouncement of a sentence, but the public display of exclusion—not by way of judicial process, but by material admonition and correction.

When this preaching and excommunication have been completed, confession is made, followed by the granting of indulgence, as follows: one year and forty days are granted to natives; two years and two quadragins to outsiders; three years and four quadragins to those from beyond the Alps; and four years and four quadragins to those who have crossed the sea.

Absolution is given by the pope. After this has been done, he goes to the church and performs everything contained in the rite: the Mass, the preparation of the chrism, the washing of the feet in their appointed places, and the distribution of the presbyterate, which is done as follows.

The prelates come before the pope, as stated in the account of the coronation, and so forth. Then he eats.

### 23.

On Good Friday the office is said at night and during the day as contained in the Ordinary.

At the first hour of this day all the chaplains assemble in consistory before the pope’s bed, dressed in their capes and round albs, neither lined nor precious but simple, and in silence. They sit on the ground with sorrowful faces.

Then the lord pope comes, assisted by two chaplains. He is dressed in his simple scarlet cape, without lining, and sits neither on a chair nor on a faldstool but on a stool. The entire Psalter is said continuously by the choirs.

This is excepted: if the lord pope rises to absolve pilgrims or for other reasons, the prelates remain silent; when he returns, one of them resumes what was interrupted.

When this is finished, the pope himself, with the others as contained in the Ordinary, says the litany, if he wishes, and the collects. On this day and on the first day of Lent he himself customarily says the litany; but he always says the collects and blessings unless prevented.

Then, at the appointed hour, a procession is made in black vestments, and everything else is done as contained in the Ordinary. The exception is that the pope returns wearing his cape, not a cope, and wearing a cap if he is a knight, or a simple mitre.

### 24.

On Saturday everything is done as contained in the Ordinary.

### 25.

On Easter Sunday the pope rises for Matins, and all the chaplains wearing surplices assemble in the chapel, which is said to be richly decorated with many candles and large torches.

Then the pope comes wearing a white cope, which he must wear every day until Saturday at Mass and at the other Hours. Led by two chaplains, he comes to the chapel and performs the office. The other rites of that day and throughout the Octave until Saturday Vespers are performed likewise. At Vespers he resumes the red cope, as contained in the Order.

All the offices are continually performed until the Ascension, as set out in the Ordinary.

Observe, however, that on Monday and Tuesday the curia does not eat meat, but cheese and eggs. On Wednesday, the vigil of the Ascension, it fasts, eats early, and rests only briefly. Afterwards the pope goes with the whole curia to Saint Peter and there solemnly sings Vespers, with the cardinals and prelates assisting in solemn vestments.

The white color is used at this feast and throughout its Octave, unless another feast intervenes. The chaplains likewise all wear surplices. For at Easter, on the two following days, at the Ascension, at Pentecost and the two following days, and at all double feasts from Easter until All Saints, they must wear surplices at First and Second Vespers, at Matins, and at Mass whenever the office is for the feast in the chapel.

That night the pope spends the vigil with his chaplains at Saint Peter. He says Matins in his chapel with his chaplains, and in the morning sings Mass at Saint Peter. Before Mass he says Terce and vests himself in the customary manner.

When vested in full ornament, he, the cardinals, all the prelates, and the others ascend the prepared pulpit. He preaches, and everything concerning excommunication is done as on Holy Thursday. When these things are finished, Mass continues. After Mass he returns to the Lateran.

Observe also that whenever on double feasts the pope goes to First Vespers, he always incenses the altar at the third psalm. If he is at Saint Peter, he incenses the high altar, another altar below in the confession, and a third outside at the exit from the confession, where the relics of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul have been displayed.

At Second Vespers, whether he is in Rome or elsewhere, the singers of the schola customarily sing, in place of the hymn, the prose *Rex omnipotens* (“Almighty King”), with melodies.

### 26.

From the day of the Ascension until its Octave, and also on the vigil of Pentecost, the office is performed as on the day of the Ascension. Feasts are celebrated during the Octave, and the office of the Blessed Virgin is said.

On the vigil of Pentecost the pope, the cardinals, and the other prelates assemble for Vespers, since they are solemn and double. Everything is done as on the other double feasts. The red color is used that evening and throughout the entire Octave. If the pope is in Rome, he goes to Saint Peter.

Observe that when he is at Saint Peter, at Vespers the pope himself begins only one antiphon, after it has been announced to him by the prior of the schola, and at Matins he begins the last antiphon. The other antiphons are announced alternately by the canons of Saint Peter and the singers of the schola who sing them. The other prelates do not sing; no one else begins an antiphon there.

At night and throughout the week three lessons are said at Matins, as during Easter Week. The reason is the newly baptized, so that they may not become weary from the lengthy office and look back.

On that day and throughout the week Terce is said; this is because of the hymn *Veni creator Spiritus*, which is said at Terce. At Mass each day *Alleluia, Veni sancte Spiritus* (“Alleluia, Come, Holy Spirit”) and the prose *Sancti Spiritus adsit nobis gratia* (“May the grace of the Holy Spirit be with us”) are sung. The other offices are said as contained in the Ordinary.

On the Wednesday of that week two lessons are said. Therefore, after *Kyrie, eleison*, the priest says *Oremus*, without *Flectamus genua*, and then the collect is said. When it is finished, a lesson is read. After it has been read, *Alleluia* is said with its verse. When these have been said, the priest says *Gloria in excelsis Deo* and proceeds with the Mass in the customary order.

### 27.

On Saturday five lessons are said, and *Alleluia* is sung with its verse, as stated in the Ordinary, together with the collects. When these have been said, *Gloria in excelsis Deo* is sung, and the Mass proceeds in the proper order.

Although these three days are Ember Days, red vestments are nevertheless used, together with the tunicle and dalmatic, because of the solemnity of Pentecost, as on Pentecost and the two following days, on Easter and the two following days, and on the Nativity and the two following days.

If the lord pope sings, all the subdeacons must wear tunicles at Mass. Twelve subdeacons must be prepared on Holy Thursday so that their feet may be washed, as contained in the Ordinary. They must carry seven candlesticks with torches and the cross in the procession. They must also sing *Patrem omnipotentem* (“[I believe] in the Father almighty”) from the Creed and the *Sanctus* (“Holy”) at that Mass. The cardinal deacon accompanies the pope when he goes to read the Gospel. At the vigil of Easter they must read the lessons, go to the fonts, and perform the litany.

If it is asked why the subdeacons sing certain things in this manner and afterward do not sing, the answer is that they represent the state of the primitive Church. For this reason three languages are sung at Mass: Latin, Greek, and Hebrew. Latin is used in the Introit, the Epistle, the Gospel, and the collects; Greek in *Kyrie, eleison* (“Lord, have mercy”); Hebrew in *Hosanna* (“Save, we pray”).

In ancient times two languages existed in the Church of God: Greek and Latin. Each of them sang in the Creed and also in the praises of the saints. But afterward Greek did not endure; therefore, after the *Sanctus*, the subdeacons are silent.

### 27.

On the first Sunday after Pentecost, which has no Octave, from Saturday at the vigil of that Sunday until the first Sunday of Advent of the Lord, the office is performed by day and by night as contained in the Ordinary, and the Church uses the green color.

# [ROMAN ORDER XIV]

## NOTICE REGARDING THE FOLLOWING ORDINARY

In the copy made by the most illustrious Ciampini, from which our exemplar was taken, no author’s name is prefixed to the following Ordinary. But since, in the Ceremonial of Peter Amelii, which follows this one immediately, if the place permits, the book of James Gaietanus is cited in many places—namely, in chapters 24 and 25, 52, 57, 58, 76, and 85—and since all these passages are found in the Ordinary below, I have no doubt that the aforesaid James Gaietanus is the author of this Ordinary.

James was a cardinal deacon of Saint George in Velabrum, created by Boniface VIII, whose nephew he also was. He flourished under the pontificates of Benedict XI, Clement V, John XXII, Nicholas V, Benedict XII, and Clement VI, under whom he died.

Let chapter 117 of the following Ordinary be read. It contains much concerning the creation of certain cardinals who were created by the pontiffs just mentioned, in the presence of and, as it seems, under the observation of the author. We shall therefore call him James Gaietanus. Besides Amelii, this identification is supported by Augustine Patricius, who cites the same James Gaietanus in Book II, chapter 60, concerning the Greek reading of the first prophecy on Holy Saturday, discussed here in chapter 93.

Nor is it an obstacle that the following Ordinary contains certain material from the Ceremonial of the cardinal of Rouen, Stoutavilla, who was created by Eugenius IV. These passages were added later from the Ceremonial of Peter Amelii, bishop of Senigallia; the author of the aforesaid additions used the copy that had formerly belonged to Cardinal Stoutavilla.

Likewise, some material was inserted into Peter Amelii’s Ceremonial by Peter of Oloron, a bishop who lived under the pontificate of Martin V. That the work repeatedly cited here under the name of the cardinal of Rouen is in fact the aforesaid Ceremonial of Peter Amelii is clear from the final addition to Ciampini’s copy. In it, the material found in Peter Amelii, chapter 143, concerning a sick pope, is said to come from the Ceremonial of the lord cardinal of Rouen, Stoutavilla, which was edited by the lord Peter, bishop of Senigallia. All the marginal notes placed above in various places are taken from that book.

Thus no doubt remains that most of those additions were excerpted from the Ceremonial of Peter Amelii—that is, from the copy of it which had formerly belonged to the cardinal of Rouen.

# ROMAN ORDER XIV, OR FIFTH ORDINARY OF THE ROMAN CHURCH, APPARENTLY BY JAMES CAIETANUS, CARDINAL

### I. The procedure customarily observed by the lords cardinals when they undertake the election of the supreme pontiff and choose to proceed by way of compromise

In the name of the Lord, amen. In the year of the Lord one thousand, etc., on Thursday the sixth day, on such a day of the month.

We, the bishops, presbyters, and deacons who are cardinals of the Holy Roman Church, all and individually present in consistory—namely, I, the bishop of Ostia; I, the bishop of Albano; and so forth, with each bishop named individually. The same is then done in order for the presbyters, naming each individually; and afterward for the deacons, in order.

The cardinal deacons, deliberating concerning the election of the pontiff, have chosen and do choose to proceed by way of compromise. Unanimously and harmoniously, with no one dissenting, we have chosen as compromissaries the venerable fathers, the lords N., bishop, etc.; brother N., presbyter, etc.; and L., cardinal deacon of Saint Angelo. To them we grant full power to provide a pastor for the Roman and universal Church, in the following form: two of them may choose a third from among themselves, and all three, acting unanimously, may provide a pontiff for the Roman universal Church from within the college or from outside it.

We wish this power to last until the candle or torch lit by the agreement of all has been consumed. We promise that we shall regard [another reading: “look upon”] as Roman pontiff the person whom the aforesaid compromissaries shall choose in the manner stated above.

### II. How the election of the supreme pontiff proceeds by scrutiny

If, in the election of the Roman pontiff, the cardinals wish to proceed by scrutiny, three scrutineers of the college and three other scrutineers of the scrutineers are customarily chosen.

The procedure for conducting the scrutiny and depositing the vote in the scrutiny is as follows.

We choose three scrutineers of the college, as the cardinals shall agree: for example, Brother Nicholas, bishop of Ostia; Brother N., presbyter of the title of Saint Eusebius; and Neapoleo, cardinal deacon of Saint Hadrian.

Immediately afterward three other scrutineers of the scrutineers are chosen: for example, the lord Berengarius, bishop of Tusculum; Arnaldus, presbyter of the title of Saint Prisca; and N., cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in Carcere Tulliano.

### III. Concerning the scrutineers of the scrutineers

First, the aforesaid scrutineers of the scrutineers remain in consistory. Sitting, they examine secretly and individually the votes of the scrutineers of the college and commit them to writing: first those of the bishops, second those of the presbyters, and third those of the deacons among the scrutineers. The deacon customarily writes down these votes.

After the votes of the scrutineers of the college have been examined as stated above, the scrutineers of the scrutineers leave the consistory, secretly carrying with them the aforesaid written deposits of the scrutineers of the college. Only the scrutineers of the college remain in consistory—for example, the aforesaid Nicholas of Ostia and Neapoleo.

The other cardinals then follow according to seniority as regards their cardinalatial rank: first the bishops, second the presbyters, and third the deacons. Secretly and individually they deposit their votes. The scrutineers of the scrutineers also deposit their votes, like the others, in their proper order and place. A cardinal deacon, one of the scrutineers of the college—for example, the lord Neapoleo—customarily writes down the votes of the cardinals.

It should be noted that the scrutineers, both of the college and of the scrutineers, and the cardinals deposit their votes while seated and holding the *buretrum*, if they wish. Unless, perhaps out of devotion or reverence, a cardinal should wish to stand with the *buretrum* laid aside while depositing his vote.

### IV. The manner of depositing the vote

I, James, cardinal deacon of Saint George in Velabrum, name and elect the venerable father, the lord Matthew, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Portico, as supreme pontiff.

It should be noted that, as a matter of prudence and propriety, the scrutineer gives the written vote in full to the person depositing it, so that no error may be made through carelessness.

Since each person may name one or several candidates in the scrutiny, he may say:

“I, James, cardinal deacon of Saint George in Velabrum, name and elect the lord Matthew, etc., and the lord Nicholas, bishop of Ostia, as supreme pontiff.”

Or:

“I, James, cardinal deacon of Saint George in Velabrum, name and elect the lord Matthew, etc., and the lord Nicholas, bishop of Ostia, from within; and from outside, the venerable father, the lord Pampanianus, bishop of Parma, as supreme pontiff.”

Thus the person depositing the vote may name one or several candidates, whether from within or from outside, or some from within and some from outside, as many and of whatever kind as he wishes.

Nevertheless, it is a matter of propriety and perhaps expediency that not many candidates be named by one person in a scrutiny, although today some observe the contrary and name a very large number.

When the deposits of all have been completed, all the lords cardinals are recalled to the consistory. After they have taken their customary seats in their respective places and orders, the scrutineers of the college ask whether it pleases everyone that the scrutiny be opened and made public in common.

When they answer that it does, the deacon scrutineer of the college—for example, the lord Neapoleo—reads what has been written:

“In the name of the Lord, amen. I, Berengarius, bishop of Tusculum, name and elect, etc.,” as above, and likewise with the others.

So that the individual cardinals may better understand the deposits of their brothers, the same deacon reads them twice or several times.

After the deposits of the individual members of the college have been read, the scrutineers of the scrutineers ask whether it pleases everyone that the deposits of the scrutineers of the college be opened and publicly read in common.

When they answer that it does, the deacon scrutineer of the scrutineers—for example, the lord Aemilius—reads what has been written:

“In the name of the Lord, amen. I, Brother Nicholas, bishop of Ostia and Velletri, name and elect, etc.,” as above, and likewise with the other scrutineers of the scrutineers.

So that the individual cardinals may better understand the deposits of their brothers, the same deacon—for example, the lord Aemilius—reads them twice or several times.

After this, there is no comparison of merit with merit or zeal with zeal, but only of number with number.

Another cardinal deacon writes on a sheet of paper all the names of the lords cardinals individually, in the following manner, so that the comparison of number with number may be made correctly:

“The lord N., bishop of Ostia and Velletri, has . . . .”

“The lord N., bishop of Tusculum, has . . . .”

And so all the bishops are listed according to their seniority.

“The lord Nicholas, cardinal presbyter of the title of Saint Eusebius, has . . . .”

“The lord Arnaldus, cardinal presbyter of the title of Saint Prisca, has . . . .”

And so all the presbyters are listed in order.

“The lord Neapoleo, cardinal deacon of Saint Hadrian, has . . . .”

“The lord Aemilius, cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in Carcere Tulliano, has . . . .”

And so all the deacons are listed in order. Thus the comparison of number with number is made as follows.

For one of the scrutineers of the college—for example, the lord Neapoleo—begins again from the beginning and reads the scrutiny in order, as it was written:

“I, Berengarius, bishop of Tusculum, name and elect the venerable fathers, the lords N., bishop of Ostia; N., presbyter of the title of Saint Eusebius; N., cardinal deacon of Saint Hadrian; etc.,” as above.

The other cardinal deacon who had written the names of the cardinals on the sheet, as stated above, adds, where it was said:

“The lord bishop of Ostia and Velletri has the lord Berengarius, bishop of Tusculum.”

“The lord Nicholas, cardinal presbyter of the title of Saint Eusebius, has the lord bishop of Tusculum.”

“The lord Neapoleo, cardinal deacon of Saint Hadrian, [has] the lord bishop of Tusculum.”

The deacon, namely the lord Neapoleo, then continues and reads the scrutiny:

“I, Arnaldus, bishop of Sabina, name and elect the venerable fathers, namely the lord bishop of Tusculum, Arnaldus, presbyter of the title of Saint Prisca, Aemilius, cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in Carcere Tulliano, etc.,” as above, “and Arnaldus, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary Nova.”

The aforesaid deacon who had written the names on the sheet, as above, adds, where it was said:

“The lord Berengarius, bishop of Tusculum, has the lord bishop of Sabina.”

“The lord Arnaldus, cardinal presbyter of the title of Saint Prisca, has the lord bishop of Sabina.”

“The lord Nicholas, cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in Carcere Tulliano, has the lord bishop of Sabina.”

And further the deacon Lord Neapoleo continues and reads the scrutiny, while another deacon adds the names of the cardinals in their proper places, according as they were named by various persons.

When these matters had been completed, the aforementioned deacon, Lord Franciscus, cardinal deacon of Santa Maria in Cosmedin, who had subscribed the names and added the material indicated above, read the aforesaid document with his additions in the following manner.

## VIII. Certain Particular Matters Observed in the Election of the Roman Pontiff, as Written Below

Those who are absent and outside the territory are not usually summoned, as are two parts of the college; but the others who are nearby may declare that they will begin proceedings concerning the business of the election on a certain day. That day may be communicated to the absent men by one or more of their friends. [Col. 1125B]

Three scrutineers of the college are usually elected, as well as three other scrutineers of the scrutineers. Two parts of the college possessing a vote in the election are required, not counting the elected man.

The form of the decretal *Quia propter* is not observed in all its chapters.

It is sufficient that, at the same certain time, two parts concur in the same person, that person not being counted, and that he be elected by two parts and accepted.

A common election is also usually made by the agreement of two parts, although perhaps this is not essential, so that a common election follows once the elected man has been named by two parts and accepted through the agreement expressed in the scrutiny or through accession.

There is no comparison of merit with merit or zeal with zeal, but only of number with number, even if the person nominated by the greater part of the college is thereby established.

Each person may name one or several men in the scrutiny; similarly, he may accede to one or to several.

If, by an arrangement made in the scrutiny, two or more men are elected by two parts—whether the elected men probably have two parts, or whether among those two parts one has more votes than the other, or whether they are equal—none of those elected in this manner acquires anything; rather, the process must begin again from the beginning, as though absolutely nothing had been done. [Col. 1125D]

Similarly, if in the same concurrence, through imperceptible accession or through confusion of voices, two principal parts were obtained, neither man would be elected.

If several men are named by someone in the scrutiny, one first, another second, a third third, and so forth, all are understood to have been named at the same moment, and none acquires a greater right from the order of writing.

## IX. Concerning the Method of Compromise

The method of compromise is not pursued if even one person wishes to use scrutiny, since the method of scrutiny is the more ordinary procedure.

A compromise is not valid unless everyone consents, since it belongs to propriety rather than necessity.

The compromisers usually hold discussions both about themselves and about the other persons making the compromise, but differently. When they discuss one of themselves, the person under discussion withdraws to one side; but when they discuss the persons making the compromise, they may speak about the absent person both collectively and among themselves. [Col. 1126A]

These commendations, praises, and *verialia* words [the reading is uncertain], which the compromisers use when they speak about their brothers or others, are to be regarded as a confession. To avoid the dangers that might follow, the compromisers usually stipulate and protest among themselves that nothing they say is to be regarded as an effective consent unless each one of them commits his consent to writing. Once this has been done—so that each has written his own consent—it is usually said that they can no longer revoke their consent; and the college understands the matter in this way, namely, that they stipulate and protest, provided that they do not contradict or protest against it.

Compromises are generally made without a written document, but it is safer when a document is used.

Whether compromisers, after they have been elected, can revoke their decision, and so forth: I answer that they can, so long as the matter remains untouched, by two parts of those making the compromise—that is, before the pope has been made.

Whatever is said here that is not a matter of law shall remain firm during this vacancy until the whole college and each individual member, or two parts of the whole college possessing a vote in the election, decide to alter it. Today, in the consistory, although the cardinal of Tusculum was absent and was not summoned, these observances were read. It was agreed that they ought to be observed. One man added, however, that they should remain as they had been until now and according to a sound understanding, without fraud; nevertheless, no circular consultations were requested, nor do I know that everyone consented. [Col. 1126C]

## X. Concerning the Investiture of the Papacy, to Be Performed by the Prior of the Cardinal Deacons after the Election of the Man Elected Pope

When the Roman Church is vacant of a pastor, the man who has been elected pope unanimously by all the cardinals, or by two parts, or by the universal Church, is to be regarded as Roman pontiff. If he is absent, or is not from the college of cardinals, he must come, once summoned, to the place where the cardinals are in consistory. When he has given his consent to the election made of him, the prior of the deacons removes from him the cappa or cloak that he is wearing and, if he does not already have them, puts upon him an alb, rochet, and shirt, and places the vestment in the manner proper to a priest upon his shoulders if he is a priest, or over his left side if he is a deacon and has not been constituted in the priestly order. He then puts the mantle upon him and says:

“I invest you with the Roman papacy, so that you may preside over the city and the world.”

He also gives him the ring customarily used by his predecessors and places upon his head a mitre appropriate to the season. After asking him by what name he wishes to be called, they call him by whatever name he chooses. This done, he causes him to sit upon the seat or faldstool. After his ordinary shoes have been removed, if red papal footwear is available, he is shod with it. [Col. 1126D]

Thus all the cardinals come before him in order—first the bishops, second the priests, third the deacons—with bended knees. The elected man receives them properly at his foot and for the kiss of peace, as well as all his other chaplains and the other clergy and laity who come to pay him reverence, the lowly, the great, and those of intermediate rank. When these matters have been completed, he is led processionally by the cardinals and by the entire curia, with the papal cross preceding, to the cathedral or to another greater church of the place in which the curia is located, if the place of election is not a city. In that church he is led to the altar, and, prostrate before it, he prays for a long time. While he prays, all the clergy solemnly sing *Te Deum laudamus* (“We praise you, God”). When it has been sung, the prior of the bishops says the *Pater noster* (“Our Father”), the customary suffrages, and the prayer:

“Almighty and eternal God, have mercy upon our elected one.”

When this has been completed, the elected man rises from prayer and says:

“May the name of the Lord be blessed” (*Sit nomen Domini benedictum*),

and gives the blessing. When it has been completed, he reverently kisses the altar and returns to his chamber in the same orderly manner in which he came to the church, continually making the sign of the cross as he goes and returns. [Col. 1127A]

After he has returned to his chamber, he removes the cope and mitre, assumes a red mantle, and must have leggings of red cloth without foot coverings or *constaphilia* [a technical garment or ornament; the reading is uncertain], a red scarlet cap, and thereafter small shoes of the same cloth, together with religious shoes of red leather reaching to the middle of the leg. He must also have tunics and garments of white scarlet, with white cloths over them, and be girded over the shirt with a belt of red silk. The shirt must be so long that, when raised, it can be suitably folded back over the belt.

## XI. Concerning the Pronouncement to the People of the Name Assumed by the Man Elected Pope, with the Prior of the Cardinal Deacons Relating the Manner of the Election

When provision has been made for the pastor of the aforementioned Roman Church, the prior of the deacons announces the election to the people, saying:

“If it pleases you, hail; I announce to you great joy,”

or another theme, as may be appropriate. He then relates how, unanimously or by two parts of the cardinals, through the method of scrutiny, compromise, or the Holy Spirit, the cardinals elected the man from within or outside the college, naming and praising the elected person and announcing the name newly assumed by him. [Col. 1127C]

## XII. Concerning a Bishop Elected Pope, and His Blessing and Coronation

A bishop who has been elected pope is not consecrated again, but is blessed on a Sunday, on which day he is also crowned. Descending from his palace at Saint Peter’s, he enters the church in the customary manner, wearing a red cope and the mitre in its usual place. After the prayer has been said, and after he has received all the cardinals and prelates in reverence, he says:

“May the name of the Lord be blessed” (*Sit nomen Domini benedictum*),

and the response is:

“From this time forth and forever” (*Ex hoc nunc et usque in saeculum*).

After the blessing has been given, he goes to the sacristy, namely the chapel of Saint Gregory. There he is served by the cardinal bishop and cardinal deacon appointed for this purpose, and by the prior of the deacons or the prior of the basilica, who carries the mitre and the ring and holds the staff. There the man elected pope is vested in all the precious and solemn vestments suitable to the season and the day. [Col. 1127D] The most precious mitre is placed upon his head, and the pontifical ring is given to him by the same bishop. The chamberlain first places the ring on the Supreme Pontiff’s finger.

While the lord pope receives the dalmatic, the bishop himself puts on a surplice, amice, and cope of the color proper to the day, and carries a simple mitre. When the lord pope puts on the chasuble, the same bishop comes to the side of the Supreme Pontiff. Taking the ring from the hand of the acolyte, he places it in the hand of the lord pope, who is vested in all the solemn vestments and mitre; the chamberlain places the first ring.

The bishop, having received the boat with incense from the hand of the acolyte, presents it to the pope and kisses his hand. After the pope has placed incense in the thurible, the bishop goes to the place where the other cardinal bishops are arranged processionally, the customary services and honors having been performed and rendered when Roman pontiffs are vested, except that at that time he does not carry the pallium in the procession, since, as will follow below, he will receive it at the altar. The archdeacon or the prior of the deacons arranges this procession in the manner written below. [Col. 1128A]

## XIII. How the Procession Is to Be Conducted

The subdeacon proceeds with the cross, wearing a tunicle because of the solemnity. Abbots, bishops, and archbishops follow him. After them go the cardinal priests, followed by the cardinal bishops according to their precedence. After them go the acolytes with the boat, thurible, and incense. After these come seven subdeacons in tunicles, carrying seven candlesticks with candles. In their midst goes the one who is to read the Epistle, carrying the Book of the Gospels, and with him the one who is to read the Greek Epistle; after them comes the one who is to read the Greek Gospel.

The cardinal deacons follow in their order. Among them is the one who is to read the Gospel. At the end, or together at the end, two cardinal deacons—one on the right and the other on the left—lead the aforesaid pope. Around them is the subdeacon who serves with the mitre, carrying a towel. [Col. 1128C]

## XIV. Concerning the Blessing Given by the Pope in the Procession

As the lord pope proceeds processionally through the church in this manner, he continually gives blessings. When he reaches the choir, three cardinal priests meet him and arrange his chasuble. He receives them for the kiss of peace, and they reverently kiss his breast.

Proceeding from there, he goes processionally as far as the altar, but does not ascend the altar. Then, after the confession has been made, he ascends the prepared seat—not the higher seat—but sits on a faldstool placed on the level ground between the altar and the higher seat. There Albanensis, Portuensis, and Ostiensis, or the archpriest of Ostia if he is not a bishop, come before him. Albanensis gives the first prayer, namely:

**Let us pray.**—O God, who do not disdain to be present wherever you are invoked with a devout mind, be present, we ask, to our invocations, and pour out upon this servant of yours, N., whom the common judgment of your people has chosen for the summit of apostolic authority, an abundance of heavenly blessing, so that he may recognize that he has reached this height by your gift. Through, etc. [Col. 1128D]

The bishop of Portus gives the second.

**Prayer.**—Almighty God, grant to our supplications the effect of your customary mercy, and pour out the grace of the Holy Spirit upon this servant of yours, N., so that he who is established at the head of the Churches in the mystery of our service may be strengthened by the firmness of your power. Through.

The bishop or archpriest of Ostia gives the third.

**Prayer.**—O God, who willed your apostle Peter to hold primacy among the other co-apostles, and placed upon him the whole burden of Christianity, look favorably, we ask, upon this servant of yours, N., whom we raise from a lowly seat, forcibly exalted, to the throne of that same prince of the apostles. May he be increased in proportion to the advancement of so great a dignity and likewise enriched with the merits of the virtues, so that, with your help, he may worthily bear the burden of the ecclesiastical community and receive from you, who are the blessedness of your own, his deserved recompense. You who live.

The primicerius (chief cantor), with the schola, after the pope has first arrived before the altar, will sing the Introit and the *Kyrie eleison* in the Roman chant. Standing in the faldstool placed on the level ground, the lord pope receives all the cardinals—deacons, priests, and bishops—and the prelates at his foot and for the kiss. [Col. 1129B]

## XV. Concerning the Giving of the Pallium to the Pope by the Prior of the Cardinal Deacons

After he has received them, he comes to the altar, where the pallium has been prepared above it by the prior of the deacon chaplains or by the prior of the Basilica of the Holy of Holies. Two cardinal deacons hold the pallium. Then the prior of those two alone gives the pallium to the pontiff, saying:

“Receive the pallium, that is, the fullness of pontifical office, in honor of almighty God, the glorious Virgin Mary, his mother, the blessed Peter and Paul, and the holy Roman Church.” [Col. 1129C]

After the pallium has been fitted upon him with three golden pins, as is customary, the Supreme Pontiff ascends to the altar and performs the incensation. Then he returns to the higher seat and receives all the cardinals for the kiss of the foot and mouth. He says *Dominus vobiscum* (“The Lord be with you”), or *Pax vobis* (“Peace be with you”), or *Gloria in excelsis Deo* (“Glory to God in the highest”), as the day requires. He says the Lord’s Prayer aloud and another prayer secretly for himself. When the prayer has been completed and the response *Amen* has followed, the pope sits again in the seat.

The prior of the cardinal deacons, carrying the staff in his hands, descends before the altar with the deacons, subdeacons, scriveners, and judges, all solemnly vested. He forms two lines, one on one side and one on the other, dividing them equally, so that in each line there are members of every order. First he places the deacons near the altar, second the subdeacons, third the judges, and fourth the scriveners, in that order. [Col. 1129D]

## XVI. Rubric Concerning the Praise to Be Begun by the Prior of the Cardinal Deacons

Then the prior of the deacons himself begins the praise in a loud voice, almost as though reading:

“Hear us, O Christ” (*Exaudi, Christe*).

The judges and scriveners respond in the same manner, in chant almost as though reading:

“Life to our lord N., by God’s decree, Supreme Pontiff and universal pope.”

This is said and answered three times.

The same prior then says:

“Savior of the world” (*Salvator mundi*),

and the judges and scriveners respond:

“Help him” (*Tu illum adjuva*).

They do this three times.

The same prior then says twice:

“Holy Mary” (*Sancta Maria*),

and they respond:

“Help him.”

In the same manner he says only once:

“Saint Michael,” and the response is, “Help him.”

“Saint Gabriel,” response: “Help him.”

“Saint Raphael,” response: “Help him.”

“Saint John the Baptist,” response: “Help him.”

“Saint Peter,” response: “Help him.”

“Saint Paul,” response: “Help him.”

“Saint Andrew,” response: “Help him.”

“Saint Stephen,” response: “Help him.”

“Saint Leo,” response: “Help him.”

“Saint Gregory,” response: “Help him.”

“Saint Benedict,” response: “Help him.”

“Saint Sabbas,” response: “Help him.”

“Saint Agnes,” response: “Help him.”

“Saint Cecilia,” response: “Help him.”

“Saint Lucy,” response: “Help him.”

“Saint Basil,” response: “Help him.”

He says *Kyrie eleison* three times, and the response is likewise three times: *Kyrie eleison* (“Lord, have mercy”). [Col. 1130B]

## XVII. Concerning the Latin and Greek Epistle and the Latin and Greek Gospel to Be Sung from the Pulpit

Afterward all together say in a loud voice:

*Kyrie eleison* (“Lord, have mercy”).

When the praises have ended, the Latin Epistle and then the Greek Epistle are read from the pulpit; likewise the Latin Gospel and the Greek Gospel. [Col. 1130C]

## XVIII. Concerning the Vestments of the Cardinal Bishop

The cardinal bishop who serves the pope must be dressed in a surplice, amice, and cope, and must have a simple mitre. The Mass then proceeds in its proper order to the end, and he receives Communion solemnly—not at the altar, but at the higher seat.

## XIX. Concerning the Crown Called the *Regnum*, to Be Placed upon the Pope by the Prior of the Cardinal Deacons

After Mass the same Supreme Pontiff says:

“May the name of the Lord be blessed” (*Sit nomen Domini benedictum*),

and the response is:

“From this time forth and forever” (*Ex hoc nunc et usque in saeculum*).

The bishop who serves does not say *Multos annos* (“Many years”). After everything has been duly completed, the Supreme Pontiff, all the cardinals, the other prelates, and the subdeacons, each in his own rank, put on precious white vestments: the bishops, copes; the priests, chasubles; the deacons, dalmatics; the subdeacons, tunicles; the acolytes, surplices; and the other chaplains likewise. The archbishops, bishops, abbots, and patriarchs wear copes; the judges, scriveners, and advocates likewise wear copes. The first singer wears a cope and mitre, and the singers wear surplices.

The pope has all the precious ornaments, as well as the pallium, the finest mitre, gloves, and the pastoral ring. Thus he comes with everyone either to the gate or to the steps of the church. There the prior of the cardinal deacons removes his mitre and places upon his head the crown called the *regnum*, while the whole people acclaim:

*Kyrie eleison* (“Lord, have mercy”).

Then, in full vesture, each cardinal and prelate rides a horse covered with white cloth. The subdeacons, chaplains, scriveners, and others ride elegantly dressed, but their horses are not covered. The pope rides a horse equipped with trappings, uncovered at the front but covered with scarlet at the rear. [Col. 1131A]

## XX. Concerning the Order of the Procession after Mass, Belonging to the Prior of the Cardinal Deacons

When everyone has mounted his horse, the prior of the deacons arranges the procession in the following manner. First goes the pope’s horse, equipped with trappings. Second goes the subdeacon with the cross. Third go twelve standard-bearers with twelve red banners, and two others with two cherubim in *cameri* [perhaps *camurinis*] on spears. Fourth are two men who are not present today, the naval prefects, dressed in copes. Fifth are the scriveners; sixth, the advocates; seventh, the judges; eighth, the singers; ninth, the deacons who read the Epistle and Gospel in Greek; tenth, the foreign abbots; eleventh, the bishops; twelfth, the archbishops; thirteenth, the abbots of the City; fourteenth, the patriarchs and cardinal bishops; fifteenth, the cardinal priests; sixteenth, the cardinal deacons; seventeenth, the lord pope, with the subdeacon carrying the towel and the servant carrying the canopy.

Thus he proceeds processionally as far as the Lateran, to the “dung seat” (*sedes stercoraria*). When he dismounts from his horse, he removes the *regnum* and assumes the mitre.

As he proceeds processionally from the steps of Saint Peter’s, after riding as far as the aforementioned dung seat by the Sacred Way, or the papal way, three distributions or throws of money are made in the same place of the ride behind him by the seneschal or another person, just as distributions are made in three other places.

The first is at the Tower of Campo, where one of the pope’s household makes another throw while standing in some more elevated place. There the lord pope stops, and the Jews come there with the Law, offering him praise and presenting the Law to him so that he may adore it. The pope then commends the Law but condemns the observance or interpretation of the Jews, because the one whom they say is to come, the Church teaches and preaches, has already come: the Lord Jesus Christ.

Likewise, when he reaches the palace of Cencius Musca at Punga, one of the pope’s household makes one throw. He makes another throw when he reaches Saint Mark’s. Similarly, when he reaches Saint Adrian’s, another throw is made by a man standing in the window of the palace of Saint Martina. Thus he comes to the Lateran square and is led to the portico that goes to the church of Saint John Lateran.

There, before the portico now destroyed, the Lateran canons immediately receive the pope, with their retinue solemnly dressed and with the processional cross, when he dismounts. He dismounts at the aforementioned dung seat, removes the *regnum*, and takes the mitre. After the pope has dismounted, he sits on the marble seat called the dung seat. All the cardinals come and honorably lift him up, so that he may truly say:

“He raises the needy from the dust and lifts the poor from the dung heap, to make him sit with princes and hold the throne of glory.” [Col. 1132A]

The same lord pope, standing beside that seat, takes three handfuls of coins from the lap of the chamberlain and throws them among the people, saying:

“Silver and gold I do not have; but what I have, this I give you.”

Then two cardinals serve him, and, taking him, lead him to the church of the Holy Savior by the road where the portico mentioned above stood.

As they come from the dung seat, the acclamation is made:

“Saint Peter chooses our lord.”

Thus he is led by the aforementioned cardinals to behind the altar, where he prays. When he has entered and is praying, the canons sing:

*Te Deum laudamus* (“We praise you, God”).

After he has prayed, he says over the altar and over the people:

“May the name of the Lord be blessed” (*Sit nomen Domini benedictum*),

and the response is:

“From this time forth and forever” (*Ex hoc nunc et usque in saeculum*).

Afterward he is led to the higher marble seat, where he receives the Lateran canons at his foot and for the kiss. This done, he is led by the cardinals to the palace of Pope Zacharias, commonly called the Casa Major, and comes to the palace gate.

From there he enters the palace through the church. Between the gate by which one ascends to the said palace and the gate of the palace itself, a faldstool is placed. The lord pope sits there, namely on those steps where he usually sits when *Gloria, laus*, and so forth are sung.

While the pope is sitting there, the prior of the cardinal priests, having arranged the judges and scriveners in a line, performs the praise there, just as the cardinal deacon had done at Mass before the Epistle after the prayer in the basilica of Saint Peter.

Afterward the same cardinals lead him through the palace as far as the gate of the church of Saint Sylvester, where there are two porphyry seats. The pope sits in the one on the right. There the prior of the Basilica of Saint Lawrence gives him the staff, which is a sign of correction and governance, and the keys of that basilica and of the sacred Lateran palace, signifying the power of closing and opening, binding and loosing.

With that staff and those keys he approaches the other similar seat on the left. He then returns the staff and keys to the same prior and begins to sit in the second seat.

After he has sat there for a little while, the same prior girds the lord pope over his chasuble with a belt of red silk. A purple purse is to hang from it, containing twelve precious stones with seals, and musk. While he is sitting in that seat, he receives the officials of the palace at his foot and for the kiss.

While sitting there, he takes from the hand of the chamberlain silver coins worth ten Provençal solidi and throws them over the people. He does this three times, saying each time:

“He has scattered; he has given to the poor; his righteousness remains forever and ever.” [Col. 1132D]

In these two seats the pope must conduct himself in such a way that he seems rather to be lying than sitting. Neither of these seats, nor the dung seat, is to be covered or prepared; they are to remain bare.

## XXI. When the Pope Is Led to the Holy of Holies

Then he is led to the Holy of Holies through the same portico, beneath the images of the holy apostles that came by sea without anyone conducting them. He enters the aforementioned Basilica of Saint Lawrence, commonly called the Holy of Holies, and says his prayer before the altar, while the prior and the canons of that basilica sing:

*Te Deum laudamus* (“We praise you, God”).

Afterward he is led back to the chapel of Saint Sylvester. He enters it and sits in the prepared place with his ornaments, holding the mantle over his shoulders and the mitre over the *fanon* or orarium. He gives the *presbyterium* (the customary gift to the clergy).

Afterward he returns to the chamber, where he removes the chasuble and pallium, assumes the mantle, and goes to eat. At that time he used first to receive an oath from the senator according to the form, “I, such-and-such,” and so forth; but the reception of this oath has long been omitted.

## XXII. Rubric Concerning the Office of the Senators of the City in This Solemnity

It should also be noted that, after the lord pope has dismounted from the horse equipped with trappings beside the dung seat, the senators receive that horse and lead it away, courteously returning it to the chamberlain, as is customary.

It should also be noted that from Saint Peter’s to the Lateran triumphal arches are made for the lord pope, and the Roman clergy come out to meet him, dressed along the Sacred Way wherever they can, with thuribles and incense. In the accounting, thirty-five pounds are given to the Romans for the arches, and thirteen and a half pounds to the clergy for the thuribles.

## XXIII. How the Lord Pope Is Led to the Table, and Concerning the Order of Sitting There

When he goes to eat, two cardinal deacons lead him to the table. When he is seated, the cardinal bishop gives him water, while two cardinal deacons hold the towel; he is not to hold the mantle. After the blessing has been given there, they go to the table.

On the right side sit the cardinal bishops and priests; on the left, the deacons. Note that while the lord pope is at table he is dressed in all the table vestments, except that he holds the mantle at his shoulders and the *fanon*; on his head he wears the mitre above them. All the cardinals have surplices with mantles and simple mitres.

When they are to wash, the bishop and the two cardinal deacons rise and give the water as before. After it has been given, they return to their places at the tables. After the drink has been received and *Tu autem* (“But you”) has been said, the deacon rises and holds the tunic while thanks are rendered.

When these things have been completed, he enters the chamber with the two deacons at his right and left, where the chaplains remove all his vestments. All the cardinals return to their own places, as at table, but they go dressed.

It should be noted that at the final washing the cardinals must be washed while sitting at the table, one holding the towel for another, while the page pours the water.

## XXIV. Concerning the Coronation of the Pope outside the City, and the First Reverence to Be Paid to Him by the Cardinals and Other Prelates

First, early in the morning at the appropriate hour, the lord pope, dressed in a red cope with a Phrygian mitre, enters the church of Saint John, where the coronation is to be celebrated. When he has entered that church, he prays in the middle of the church at a faldstool prepared for him.

After the prayer has been said, he receives all the cardinals and prelates in their proper order while standing, and says:

“May the name of the Lord be blessed” (*Sit nomen Domini benedictum*),

and the response is:

“From this time forth,” and so forth.

After the blessing has been given, he turns to the place where he is to be vested. After Terce has been said with the chaplains, the cardinal bishop assisting him holding the book, and after the pope has said the prayer at the end of Terce, the subdeacon and one of the acolytes put leggings and sandals on him, while the chaplains alternately recite the Psalms, namely *Quam amabilia* (“How lovely”), together with the others that are customarily said.

When these things have been completed, with the customary prayers, he washes his hands while the cardinal bishop who is to assist him pours the water. After the washing, and after the cardinal bishop has returned to his place, he is vested in all the green, precious, and solemn ornaments that the Roman pontiff customarily uses in the solemn celebrations of Mass, since the Sunday requires this. The cardinal deacon and subdeacon vest him, with the acolytes supplying what is needed.

When the cardinal bishop has returned to his place, as stated above, he is vested in a surplice, amice, and green cope with a simple mitre. [Col. 1134B]

## XXV. Concerning the Mitre to Be Placed upon the Pope by the Cardinal Deacon, and the Pontifical Ring to Be Given by the Cardinal Bishop

Afterward the cardinal deacon places the precious mitre upon the lord pope. The pontifical ring is given to him by the same bishop who serves him, with one of the chamberlains placing the aforesaid ring on the pope’s finger.

Then the bishop who ministers to him receives the boat from the hand of the acolyte, presents it to the lord pope, and kisses his hand. After the lord pope has placed incense in the thurible, the bishop goes to his place, where the other cardinal bishops have been arranged processionally.
