When all the aforesaid matters have been duly completed—the things customarily done and performed when Roman pontiffs are vested and prepared—except that in the procession which follows he will not carry the pallium, but will receive it, the said procession will otherwise be arranged by the prior of the cardinal deacons in the manner written below. [Col. 1134C]

## XXVI. Order of the Procession before the Introit of Mass

First the subdeacon proceeds with the cross, wearing a tunicle. After him follow the abbots, bishops, and archbishops, dressed in copes and simple mitres. Then follow the cardinal priests, dressed in chasubles with simple mitres. Next come the cardinal bishops, dressed in copes with simple mitres, each in his proper order. After them follow two candle-bearing acolytes and another with the boat, thurible, and incense, dressed in surplices.

After these acolytes, seven subdeacons are arranged in tunicles, carrying seven candlesticks. In the midst of these seven is the subdeacon who is to read the Epistle, carrying the Book of the Gospels before his breast. Beside that subdeacon goes another subdeacon who is to read the Greek Epistle.

After the aforementioned subdeacons follows the deacon who is to read the Gospel in Greek. Next proceed the cardinal deacons in their order, dressed in dalmatics. Among them is the cardinal who is to read the Gospel, at the end.

Then two cardinal deacons—one on the right and the other on the left—lead the lord pope, with an extended cloth held over his head, as is customary. Finally comes the subdeacon who serves with the mitre, carrying a towel before him.

The lord pope continually gives blessings as he proceeds processionally through the church. When he reaches the throne, three cardinal priests meet him. He receives them for the kiss of peace, and they reverently kiss his breast. The last of them arranges the pope’s chasuble. [Col. 1135A]

## XXVII. Concerning the Confession Made at the Altar, the Introit of Mass, and the Prayers Said over Him near the Altar

Proceeding afterward, he goes processionally as far as the altar, but does not then ascend the altar. The cardinal deacon removes his mitre, and he makes the confession, as is customary.

While the confession is being made, the singers begin the Introit, followed by *Kyrie eleison*.

After the confession has been made, the lord pope receives the mitre and goes to his seat—not the higher seat—but sits on a faldstool placed on the level ground between the choir and the altar because of the arrangement of the church, although with his face turned toward the altar.

While the lord pope is sitting in this manner, three cardinal bishops come before him, namely those of Albano, Porto, and Ostia. While they stand before the pope, the bishop of Albano says the first prayer, namely:

“O God, who deign to be present,” and so forth, as above.

The bishop of Porto, or his substitute, says the second:

“With our supplications,” and so forth, as above.

The bishop of Ostia says the third:

“O God, who willed your apostle Peter,” and so forth, as above. [Col. 1135C]

## XXVIII. Concerning the Second Reverence of the Prelates

It should nevertheless be understood that, when the aforesaid prayers are said, the lord pope does not sit but stands without the mitre. Afterwards the lord pope, sitting on the faldstool placed on the level ground, receives all the lords cardinal and prelates at his foot and for the kiss.

## XXIX. Concerning the Giving of the Pallium by the Prior of the Cardinal Deacons

After he has received them, he comes to the altar, where the pallium has been prepared by the prior of the subdeacon chaplains. Two priors of the cardinal deacons hold the pallium. Then the prior of those two cardinal deacons alone gives the pallium to the pontiff, saying:

“Receive the pallium, that is, the fullness of pontifical office, in honor of almighty God, the glorious Virgin Mary, his mother, the blessed Peter and Paul, and the holy Roman Church.” [Col. 1135D]

## XXX. Concerning the Pope’s Ascension to the Altar, the Incensation of the Altar, and the Third Reception of the Cardinals and Prelates for Reverence while He Is in the Higher Seat
And when the pallium has been fitted over him with the three golden pins by the cardinal deacon and the subdeacon, as is customary, the lord pope ascends to the altar and incenses the altar. When it has been incensed, he ascends to the eminent seat; and, seated in that seat, vested with the pallium, he receives all the cardinals and prelates again for the kiss of the foot and mouth [Col. 1136A]. When this reception has ended, he begins the *Gloria in excelsis Deo* (“Glory to God in the highest”) while standing. When this Angelic Hymn has been sung by the singers, he says in the same seat, “Peace be with you” (*Pax vobis*), and, after the response “And with your spirit” (*Et cum spiritu tuo*), he begins the Sunday Collect aloud. When that Collect has been completed and the response “Amen” has followed, he may say another Prayer secretly for himself, if he wishes. The Prayer, however, is to be expressed in full; afterward he will sit in the seat.

### XXXI. Concerning the arrangements of the ranks to be made by the prior of the cardinal deacons, and the praises to be begun by him before the Epistle

While the lord pope is thus seated in his seat, the prior of the deacons, carrying the staff in his hands, together with the deacons and subdeacons, the scriveners, and the judges—all solemnly dressed in copes—will descend [Col. 1136B] before the altar and form two lines, one on one side and the other on the opposite side, dividing them equally so that each line contains members of every order. He will place first the deacons next to the altar, who may hold their mitres if they wish; second, the subdeacons; third, the judges; and fourth, the scriveners.

When these lines have been arranged in this way, the prior of the deacons begins the praise in a loud voice, as though reading, and stands without a mitre: “Hear, O Christ” (*Exaudi, Christe*). The judges and scriveners likewise respond in chant, as though reading: “Life to our lord N., by God’s decree the supreme pontiff and universal pope” (*Domino nostro N. a Deo decreto summo pontifici et universali papae vita*). This is said three times by the aforesaid cardinal prior, and the judges and scriveners respond three times.

Next the same prior of the deacons says, “Savior of the world” (*Salvator mundi*), and the judges and scriveners respond, “Help him” (*Tu illum adjuva*). This is said three times, and the response is made three times. The same prior of the deacons then says, “Holy Mary” (*Sancta Maria*), and those mentioned above respond twice, “Help him.” In the same manner the same prior says only once, “Saint Michael,” and so forth, as above.

When these things have been completed, the prior of the deacons says, “Lord, have mercy” (*Kyrie, eleison*), and the judges and scriveners mentioned above respond, “Lord, have mercy.” This is said three times, and the response is made three times. Afterward all together say in one loud voice, “Lord, have mercy” (*Kyrie eleison*).

### XXXII. Concerning the Latin and Greek Epistle, the Gospel, the Gradual, and the Alleluia

When the praises have thus ended, the Latin Epistle is read, and afterward the Greek one, from the elevated lectern. When these have been read, the Gradual and the Alleluia are sung. Afterward the Latin Gospel is read, and afterward the Greek Gospel, from a high and suitable lectern, as is customary, with seven subdeacons carrying seven candles preceding the deacons mentioned above, and with a thurible containing incense, as is customarily done. Thus the Mass proceeds in its proper order to the end.

### XXXIII. Rubric concerning the pope’s communion, to be received at the eminent seat

The lord pope shall nevertheless receive Communion at the appropriate time with solemnity—not at the altar, but at the eminent seat. The solemnity of this Communion shall be observed which is customarily observed in other solemn Masses. When the Mass has been completed, the lord pope says, “Blessed be the name of the Lord” (*Sit nomen Domini benedictum*) [267], and the response is made, “From this time forth and forevermore” (*Ex hoc nunc et usque in saeculum*), and he gives the Blessing. When the Blessing has been given, the bishop who served shall not say to the lord pope, “Many years” (*Multos annos*).

### XXXIV. Concerning what is to be done after the Mass, and the vestments of the lord pope, the cardinals, the prelates, and the others

When everything has been duly carried out as stated above, the lord pope himself, all the cardinals, and the other prelates, subdeacons, judges, and scriveners—each according to his rank—will remove their green vestments and put on white garments of precious quality, if they possess them: the bishops, copes; the priests, chasubles; the deacons, dalmatics; the subdeacons, tunicles; and the acolytes and other chaplains, surplices. The patriarchs, archbishops, and abbots will wear copes; the judges and scriveners will be dressed in copes; and the singers in surplices.

### XXXV. Concerning the coronation of the lord pope, to be performed by the prior of the deacons

[Col. 1137B]

The lord pope will have all the precious vestments, the pallium and a precious mitre, gloves, and the pontifical ring. Thus adorned, he will come with everyone to the door or steps of the church and ascend the wooden platform or pulpit, where he will find his seat solemnly prepared. When he is seated, the prior of the cardinal deacons will remove his mitre and place upon his head the crown called the *regnum*, while the entire people shout, “Lord, have mercy” (*Kyrie, eleison*).

### XXXVI. Concerning the indulgence to be granted to the people

There, by the authority of the lord pope, the prior of the cardinal bishops will grant an indulgence to the people, [Col. 1137C] as the lord pope wishes.

### XXXVII. Concerning the adornment of the horses in the Procession

When this has been done, they will descend from the pulpit, and each cardinal and prelate will ride, with all his adornment, a horse covered with a white cloth. The subdeacons, chaplains, judges, scriveners, and others will ride elegantly dressed, but their horses will not be covered [268]. The pope, however, will ride a large horse caparisoned at the rear with scarlet.

### XXXVIII. Order of the solemn Procession after the lord pope’s coronation

When everyone has mounted his horse in this way, the prior of the deacons, carrying the staff in his hands, will arrange the Procession as follows.

First proceeds the lord pope’s caparisoned horse; second comes the subdeacon with the cross; third follow twelve standard-bearers with twelve red banners, and two others with two cherubim and lances; fourth, two naval prefects dressed in copes; fifth, the scriveners; sixth, the advocates; seventh, the judges; eighth, the singers; ninth, the deacons and subdeacons who read the Epistle and Gospel in Greek; tenth, the abbots; eleventh, the bishops; twelfth, the archbishops; thirteenth, the patriarchs and cardinal bishops; fourteenth, the cardinal priests; fifteenth, the cardinal deacons; sixteenth, the subdeacon with the tablecloth, and the attendant with the canopy—these two proceeding somewhat apart from the pope; seventeenth, the lord pope.

### XXXIX. Concerning the throwing of money five times in different places

[Col. 1138A]

When the Procession has been arranged in this manner, the lord pope mounts his horse. At that same place, after him, the marshal or another person will make three distributions or throws of money. When he has reached the square before the church of Saint Nicetius, one of the lord pope’s household, standing in an elevated place, will make another throw of money, and there the lord pope will pause for some time.

### XL. Concerning the law offered by the Jews, and the pope’s response

The Jews will come with their Law, offer him praise, and present the Law to him for him to adore. Then the lord pope will commend the Law and condemn the observance—or interpretation—of the Jews, because the one whom they say is to come, the Church teaches and preaches, has already come: the Lord Jesus Christ [Col. 1138B].

Likewise, when he reaches the square where D. P. de Columna resides, one of the lord pope’s household—or the same member of the household—will make a throw of money. Similarly, when he reaches the crossroads where the elected bishop of Viterbo resides, the same member of the household will make another throw of money. Next, when he reaches the entrance of the palace, the same member of the household will make another throw.

### XLI. Concerning what is done after the Procession, both the praises to be made by the prior of the deacons and the distribution of the presbyterium

When the journey has thus been completed and they have reached the entrance of the palace, or the house of the Preachers, the Dominican friars, solemnly dressed and carrying a cross, incense, and blessed water, will reverently receive the lord pope in procession, singing *Te Deum laudamus* (“We praise you, God”).

When the lord pope has reached the church, before he descends from his horse, the prior of the cardinal priests, having arranged the judges and scriveners in a line, will make the same praise as the cardinal deacon had made at Mass before the Epistle, after the Prayer. After he has descended from his horse, the prior of the cardinal deacons who leads him removes the *regnum* from his head and places a mitre upon him. The same prior will be on his right and lead him to the altar, while another will be on his left, where he will pray at the faldstool prepared for him.

After the Prayer has been made, he will give the Blessing, saying, “Blessed be the name of the Lord” (*Sit nomen Domini benedictum*), and the response is made, “From this time forth and forevermore” (*Ex hoc nunc et usque in saeculum*). After this, he will be led to the eminent seat and will sit in the prepared place with his ornaments, having removed his chasuble, pallium, and gloves, with the mantle held upon his shoulders [Col. 1138D], and the mitre upon the *fanon* or orarium.

He will give each cardinal his presbyterium in the following manner. The lord pope himself, seated in the seat, and each cardinal and prelate, having removed his own mitre and carrying it in his hand, goes before him. Kneeling, he holds the open mitre before the pope, who places in it the money which the chamberlain will present to him in a basin, according to what is found in the chamber’s book. Those who receive the money in the mitre will kiss the lord pope’s knee.

### XLII. Concerning the pope’s being led to his chamber and table

The chamberlain himself and the clerics of the chamber, wearing surplices, will attend the lord pope [Col. 1139A]. After the presbyterium has been given, the lord pope will be led by two cardinal deacons to his chamber and will be led to the table solemnly prepared for him. When he is seated, the cardinal bishop—namely, the prior—will give him water, while two cardinal deacons hold the tablecloth; they must not hold the mantle.

### XLIII. Concerning the solemnities, garments, and vestments of the lord pope, the cardinals, and the prelates at table

At that place, after the Blessing of the table has been made, they go to the table. On the lord pope’s right sit the cardinal bishops and priests, while the deacons sit on his left. Observe that, while at table, the lord pope is dressed in all the liturgical vestments except the chasuble, pallium, and gloves [Col. 1139B]. He will wear the mantle at his shoulders and the *fanon* on his head, with the mitre above it.

All the cardinals will wear surplices with mantles and simple mitres, and all the prelates likewise. The nobler laymen who are present will serve before the lord pope, and behind the cardinals’ tables will be the tables of all the prelates and other nobles.

After the meal has been taken, the lord pope will wash his hands as before, assisted by two cardinal deacons, while a cardinal bishop pours water for him. Likewise, each cardinal will wash his hands, with a page pouring water for the cardinal who is washing. The assisting cardinals will hold the tablecloth, one on the side of the person washing and the other on the opposite side; thus they serve one another mutually.

When all have washed and thanks have been given, the lord pope will be led back to his chamber by two cardinal deacons, having put on his mantles. There, after removing the sacred vestments and having his sandals taken off by a subdeacon, he rests.

### XLIV. Concerning the cardinals’ and prelates’ return to the lord pope

The cardinals and other prelates will return mounted (sic) to their lodgings with their mitres, dressed as they stood at the meal, but on uncovered horses. It should be noted that the nobler laymen, even if they were kings, customarily ride beside the mounted pope. They divide the places among themselves in turn, as they wish and as has been arranged, so that when the first riders beside him withdraw, two others take their place.

[271] At table, one of the chief nobles, even if he were a king, places the first dish before the pope [Col. 1139D]. After placing it, the king goes to sit at the table. Other great nobles, even if they were sons of kings, serve the pope at table: one from the cup, another with the knife for cutting; others stand beside him as he eats; and others follow the person carrying the dishes, themselves carrying cutting knives for the pope and the cardinals, as has been arranged.

Whether any of the noblemen serving the pope mentioned above—for example, sons of kings or persons of similar rank—should sit at table or not, and where and how they should do so, we shall for now leave unsaid.

It is to be remembered that no oppression is to be inflicted upon the Jews when they offer the Law.

### XLV. Here begins the order according to which the Roman pontiff is to be consecrated at the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter. Rubric

[Col. 1140A]

First, the man who is to be consecrated shall come in the morning of the Lord’s Day to the basilica of the blessed Peter, where he will be received in procession by the canons. When reverence has been shown to him by the cardinals and prelates, as is customary for the Roman pontiff, he shall stand in the midst and say, “Blessed be the name of the Lord” (*Sit nomen Domini benedictum*), with the response, “From this time forth,” and so forth.

Then he shall go to the chapel of Saint Gregory, where, after Terce has been said, he will put on stockings and sandals, saying the Psalms beginning “How lovely” (*Quam amabilia*), and the others customarily said. Then, having washed his hands, he shall be dressed in all the ornaments ordinarily used by the Roman pontiff in solemn Masses, except only the pallium and the pontifical ring. The vestments shall be of a color appropriate to the season.

Then, after a solemn Procession has been arranged, in which there are to be seven candlesticks with seven torches, as is customary on the principal feasts—namely, of cardinals, prelates, and the other orders, all of whom are to have garments of a color appropriate to the season—the man to be consecrated, with a cloth spread over him, shall proceed, making the sign [of the cross], as is customary, to the high altar, and, standing behind that altar, shall make his confession.

It should be noted that at the consecration of the Roman pontiff the examination given above for the consecration of other bishops is omitted, beginning, “The ancient [tradition] of the holy Fathers,” and so forth. After the confession has been made, the man to be consecrated shall sit on his prepared faldstool between the altar and the steps of the pontifical seat, and the schola shall sing the Introit and “Lord, have mercy” (*Kyrie, eleison*) [272].

[Col. 1140C]

Meanwhile, the bishop of Ostia, who is to consecrate the Roman pontiff, shall put on stockings and sandals in a suitable place near the altar, saying the Psalm beginning “How lovely,” and so forth. He shall also receive all the pontifical ornaments, as though he were going to celebrate Mass solemnly, except the pastoral staff. He shall also receive a simple or precious mitre according to the requirements of the season. When the Introit and “Lord, have mercy” have been sung, the consecrator and the other cardinal bishops, as well as the other archbishops and bishops, and those priests who are present, approach to carry out the office of consecration.

It should be known that at the consecration of the Roman pontiff the statement “A bishop ought,” and so forth, is not pronounced, nor is the Prayer “Let us pray, most beloved,” [Col. 1140D] which are said at the consecration of other bishops. Instead, the man to be consecrated, with his face turned toward the altar and assisted by two cardinal deacons, must lean upon the faldstool prepared between the steps of the pontifical seat and the high altar.

The consecrator and the other cardinal bishops, as well as the other bishops, must prostrate themselves on their faldstools to the right and left; or, if they do not have them, upon carpets. The prior of the basilica, or another prior chaplain of the subdeacons, shall begin and continue the Litany with chant, while the other chaplains and the rest of those assisting respond.

When they come to the words “That you may bless this man to be consecrated,” and so forth (*Ut hunc consecrandum benedicere*), this must be said twice; and both the consecrator and all the other bishops assisting, raising a hand toward the man to be consecrated, make the sign of the cross over him twice.

When the Litany has ended, everyone shall rise, and the consecrator shall stand on the lowest step beneath the papal seat, which is behind the altar, with his face turned toward the altar itself. The man to be consecrated shall stand beneath the aforementioned step, facing the consecrator, assisted by the cardinal deacons and acolytes.

Beside the bishop of Ostia, on the right and left, shall stand the bishop of Albano and the bishop of Porto, dressed in copes and wearing oraria, that is, stoles. All the other bishops shall stand around them like a crown, each holding a pontifical book in which the office of consecration is written, which each is to say in a low voice.

Then the bishop of Albano gives the first Prayer [Col. 1141B] with its musical notation, saying:

**Prayer.**—“Be present to our supplications, almighty God, so that what is to be performed through the ministry of our humility may be fulfilled by the effect of your power. Through [Christ our Lord].”

Then the bishop of Porto gives his Prayer, saying it with its musical notation:

**Let us pray.**—“Be gracious, Lord, to our supplications, and, bending over this servant of yours, N., pour into him the power of your priestly Blessing’s grace. Through [Christ our Lord].”

After this, the bishop of Ostia places an open Gospel Book upon the neck of the man to be consecrated, as is done in the consecration of other bishops, with two cardinals holding it there until the consecration is finished.

When the book has been placed in this manner, the consecrator lays his right hand upon the head of the man to be consecrated, saying nothing. All the cardinal bishops, and the other archbishops and bishops who are assisting, do likewise.

After this, the bishop of Ostia says in a raised voice, in the manner of a preface, “World without end” (*Per omnia saecula saeculorum*), and the response “Amen” is made. He continues that preface, “Honor of all dignities,” and so forth, which was set out above in the consecration of other bishops [Col. 1141D]. [Note: That is, in the ancient Roman Order, not in this book of Gaetano.] Except that where it says, “And therefore to this servant of yours, N.,” in the consecration of the Roman pontiff the following elegant addition is made, and it is said thus:

“And therefore, Lord, grant, we ask, this grace to this servant of yours, N., whom you have appointed bishop of the apostolic see, chief of all priests who are in the world, and teacher of the universal Church, and whom you have chosen for the supreme ministry of the priesthood,” and so forth, through the words “May he attain advancement for all.”

Next, where it says, “Grant him,” and so forth, in the consecration of the Roman pontiff it is said as follows:

“Grant him, Lord, the pontifical chair to govern your Church and the whole people of your portion within the boundaries of the world. May authority be granted him,” and the rest.

When the consecration of the hands has been performed, the consecrator places the ring on the ring finger of the right hand of the consecrated pope, saying:

“Receive the ring, namely the seal of faith, so that—concerning the bride of God, namely the holy universal Church, etc., as above—…”

Then he gives him the Gospel Book according to the prescribed form, saying:

“Receive the Gospel, and go, preach to all the people. For powerful is he,” and so forth, as above.

After this, the archdeacon places the pallium upon him, saying:

“Receive the pallium, that is, [the sign] of the pontifical office, for the honor of almighty God, and of the most glorious Virgin Mary, his mother, and of the blessed Peter and Paul, and of the Holy Roman Church.”

Then the pope ascends to the seat and receives all the cardinal bishops, priests, and deacons, and the other prelates, for the kiss of the foot and mouth. When this has been done, he says, “Glory to God in the highest” (*Gloria in excelsis Deo*), or “The Lord be with you” (*Dominus vobiscum*), as the time requires.

The cardinal bishop who consecrated the pope, once the consecration is finished, removes his pontifical ornaments and, having put on a surplice, cope, and simple mitre, serves him at Mass, as is customary.

After “The Lord be with you,” and “Glory to God in the highest,” if it is to be said, the pope says the Sunday Collect aloud [Col. 1142B] and another Prayer secretly for himself. When these have been said, he sits in the seat. The prior of the cardinal deacons, carrying the staff in his hands, together with the deacons, subdeacons, scriveners, and judges, all solemnly dressed, descends before the altar and forms two lines, one on one side and one on the other, dividing them equally. He places first the deacons next to the altar, second the subdeacons, third the judges lower down in the choir, and fourth the scriveners in order.

When this has been done, the prior of the deacons begins the praise in a loud voice in chant, as though reading: “Hear, O Christ” (*Exaudi, Christe*). The judges and scriveners respond likewise in chant, as though reading: “Life to our lord N., by God’s decree the supreme pontiff and universal pope” (*Domino nostro N., a Deo decreto summo pontifici et universali papae, vita*).

The same prior of the deacons then says “Hear, O Christ” a second time, and the judges and scriveners respond, “Help him” (*Tu illum [Col. 1142C] adjuva*), and this is done a third time. The same prior of the deacons says, “Savior of the world” (*Salvator mundi*), and the judges and scriveners respond, “Help him”; and this is done three times. The same prior says, “Holy Mary” (*Sancta Maria*) twice, and the response is made, “Help him.” In the same manner he says only once, “Saint Michael,” and so forth, as above.

When these things have ended, the prior says, “Lord, have mercy,” and they respond, “Lord, have mercy”; and they do this a second time in the same manner. Afterward all together—the prior of the deacons, the subdeacons, and the others—say “Lord, have mercy” a third time in one loud voice.

When the praises have thus ended, the Latin Epistle is read and afterward the Greek one from the pulpit; the same is done with the Gospel. Thus the Mass proceeds in its proper order to the end, and the pope receives Communion with solemnity—not at the altar, but at the seat.

[Col. 1142D]

After the Mass the pope says, “Blessed be the name of the Lord” (*Sit nomen Domini benedictum*), and the response is made, “From this time forth,” and so forth; and he gives the Blessing.

When these things have been duly performed, the pope himself, all the cardinals, and the other prelates and subdeacons—each according to his rank—will put on precious garments of white color [275]: the bishops, copes; the priests, chasubles; the deacons, dalmatics; the subdeacons, tunicles; and the acolytes and other chaplains, surplices. The patriarchs, archbishops, bishops, and abbots will wear copes; likewise the judges, scriveners, prefects, and advocates will be dressed in copes, and the members of the schola in surplices.

The pope, however, will wear all the precious ornaments together with the chasuble, as well as the pallium, an excellent mitre, gloves, and the pontifical ring [Col. 1143A]. Thus adorned with everyone, he comes to the door or steps of the church and sits there in the seat prepared for him. The prior of the cardinal deacons removes his mitre and places upon his head the crown called the *regnum*, while the entire people shout, “Lord, have mercy” (*Kyrie, eleison*).

When this has been done, each cardinal and prelate rides a horse covered with a white cloth. The subdeacons, chaplains, scriveners, and others ride elegantly dressed, but their horses are not covered. The pope rides a large caparisoned horse, covered only at the rear with scarlet.

After he has mounted, at that same place the seneschal or another person makes a throw of money—six distributions—three times, and afterward the pope throws money.

When everyone has mounted his horse in this way, the prior of the deacons, with the staff, arranges the Procession as follows: first proceeds the lord pope’s caparisoned horse; second comes the subdeacon with the cross; third, twelve standard-bearers with twelve red banners, and two others with two additional cherubim and lances; fourth, two naval prefects dressed in copes; fifth, the scriveners; sixth, the advocates; seventh, the judges; eighth, the singers; ninth, the deacons and subdeacons who read the Epistle and Gospel in Greek; tenth, the abbots from outside the city; eleventh, the bishops; twelfth, the archbishops; thirteenth, the abbots of the City; fourteenth, the patriarchs and cardinal bishops; fifteenth, the cardinal priests; sixteenth, the cardinal deacons; seventeenth, the lord pope, together with the subdeacon bearing the tablecloth and the attendant carrying the canopy.

When the Procession has been arranged in this way, the lord pope proceeds with it along the pope’s road and returns to the Lateran. When he reaches the Tower of Stephen, which is in the Parione and is today called the Tower of Campo, one of the pope’s household makes another throw of money while standing in an elevated place. There the lord pope stops, and the Jews come there with the Law, offering him praise and presenting the Law to him for him to adore.

Likewise, when he reaches the palace of Cinta Musca at Punga, one of the pope’s household makes a throw from that palace. Similarly, he makes another throw when the procession reaches Saint Mark’s. Likewise, when it reaches Saint Hadrian’s, he makes another throw of money from the palace of Saint Martina [276].

When they have reached the Lateran square, the apostolic lord is led to the portico that goes to the church of Saint John Lateran [Col. 1143D]. There the prior of the Lateran and the canons, solemnly dressed with their retinue and with the processional cross, stand before the portico. When the pope descends, they receive him and make him sit there on a certain marble seat called the *stercoraria*.

When all the cardinals come to it, they honorably lift him up, so that he may truly say: “He raises the needy from the dust and lifts the poor from the dungheap, to seat him with princes and grant him a throne of glory.”

The lord pope himself, standing beside that seat, takes three handfuls of coins from the chamberlain’s lap and throws them among the people, saying: “Silver and gold have I none; but what I have, this I give you.”

Then, with the prior and canons following behind, he is led in procession through that portico, with singing, to the church of the Lateran basilica, where he prays and gives the Blessing, saying, “Blessed be the name of the Lord,” with the response, “From this time forth,” and so forth. He removes the *regnum*, puts on a mitre, and sits in the great seat behind the altar, where he receives the aforementioned prior and the Lateran canons to kiss his foot and [receive] a kiss.

After this he is led to the palace. When he reaches the palace gate, the palace is entered through the church. A faldstool is placed there, and while the pope is seated, the prior of the cardinal priests, with those priests and with the judges and scriveners arranged in a line, makes the praise as the prior of the cardinal deacons had made it at Mass before the Epistle, after the Prayer.

Afterward the pope is led by the cardinals through the palace to the door of the church of Saint Sylvester, where there are two porphyry seats [Col. 1144B]. First he sits in the one on the right. There the prior of the basilica of Saint Lawrence gives him the staff, which is a sign of correction and governance, and the keys of that basilica and of the sacred Lateran palace, signifying the power of closing and opening, binding and loosing.

With that staff and the other keys he approaches the other similar seat, which is on the left. Then he returns the staff and keys to the same prior and begins to sit in the second seat.

After he has sat there for a while, the same prior girds the lord pope with a red silk belt, from which a purple purse is to hang. In it are twelve precious stones with seals and *muscae* [a term of uncertain precise meaning]. While he sits in that seat, he receives the officials of the palace to kiss his foot and [receive] a kiss.

Afterward he also receives from the chamberlain silver coins worth ten *solidi* of Provins [Col. 1144C] and throws them over those standing by. He does this three times, saying each time: “He has distributed; he has given to the poor. His justice endures forever and ever” (*Dispersit, dedit pauperibus; justitia ejus manet in saeculum saeculi*).

In these two seats the pope must sit in such a way that he appears rather to be lying than sitting. Neither of these seats, nor the *stercoraria*, shall be covered or prepared in any way, but shall remain bare.

Then, rising, he is led to the basilica of Saint Lawrence, called the Holy of Holies (*Sancta Sanctorum*), where he enters and makes his Prayer before the altar. Afterward he is led back to the chapel of Saint Sylvester, which he enters. There, having removed the pallium, chasuble, and gloves, and having taken the mantle upon his shoulders, he sits in the prepared place and gives each cardinal and prelate the customary presbyterium in the following manner.

The pope sits in the seat, and each cardinal [Col. 1144D] and prelate, having removed his own mitre and carrying it in his hand, goes before him. Kneeling, he holds the open mitre before the pope, who places in it the money which the chamberlain gives him in a silver cup, according to the chamber’s book called the *Polyptych*. The person who receives the money in the mitre kisses the lord pope’s knee.

The chamberlain himself has before him a large table covered with a tablecloth, on which such coins are placed. A clerk of the chamber and two merchants assist the chamberlain. The chamberlain and the clerk of the chamber are to be dressed in surplices.

After the presbyterium has been given, the same lord pope is led by two cardinal deacons to the solemnly prepared table and sits there. A cardinal bishop gives him water, while two deacons hold the tablecloth. After he has washed and the Blessing of the table has been given, everyone goes to sit.

The pope sits alone in an eminent seat, with various large golden and silver vessels placed on the table. At another table on the right sit the bishops, and behind them the cardinal priests; on the left sit the cardinal deacons. Behind the cardinals’ tables are the tables of all the prelates and other nobles.

Observe that the pope will stand while he eats, dressed and shod as stated above, with his mitre. All the cardinals will wear surplices with shirts, mantles, and simple white mitres; they will eat in this attire, and all the prelates likewise [278]. The elder and nobler laymen who are present will serve before the pope.

After the meal has been taken, the pope will wash his hands as before. Each cardinal likewise washes while seated, with an attendant pouring water for the cardinal who is washing. The assisting cardinals shall hold the tablecloth, one on the side of the person washing and the other on the opposite side, and thus serve one another mutually.

When all have washed and thanks have been given, the pope is led by two cardinals to the chamber, where he rests after removing the sacred vestments. The cardinals and other prelates return mounted to their lodgings with their mitres prepared, as they stood at the meal.

An item concerning the pope’s Blessing made by the bishop, which is to be performed in the same place. This consecration appears to be performed between the final “Lord, have mercy” of the Mass and “Glory to God in the highest,” or “The Lord be with you”—that is, after all the other things preceding the consecration have first been completed, as above. In addition, the pope must have the pontifical ring along with the other ornaments.

While this Blessing is being read, both the pope and the bishop who gives the Blessing, as well as the other cardinals and bishops, shall stand, in the manner and order prescribed above for the consecration.

The bishop of Albano gives the first Prayer: “God, who does not disdain to be present,” and so forth, as above in the coronation of the lord pope.

The bishop of Porto gives the second Prayer: “Almighty God, be gracious to our supplications,” and so forth.

The bishop of Ostia, or the archpriest if the bishop is absent, gives the third Prayer, saying: “God, who [chose] your apostle Peter,” and so forth.

When this Blessing has been completed, the pallium is placed upon the apostolic lord, and the other things belonging to the pope’s consecration that are to be said and done after the pallium has been placed are said and done in the order stated above.

### XLVI. The following are the things that the lord cardinals and other prelates of the curia, the chamberlain, and the pope’s other household members must do when he is crowned

[Col. 1145D]

First, each bishop and lord cardinal shall have or put on, over his shirt, a surplice, amice, stole, and cope of a color appropriate to the season. In the Procession they shall have a white cope. Each shall also have his ordinary and a mitre, and a horse covered with a white covering. At table, after removing the cope, he shall receive a mantle and eat in the hall with the lord pope, with the mantle and mitre on his head.

Each of the lord cardinals shall have at table a chasuble of a color appropriate to the season in which the consecration and coronation happen to be celebrated, or a cope according to what the season requires [Col. 1146A]. In the Procession he shall have precious tunicle and dalmatic of white color, and a horse covered with a white covering. At table with the lord pope he shall be as described above for the other lord cardinals.

Each bishop or prelate found in the curia shall have a shirt, surplice, amice, stole, and cope of a color appropriate to the season for the Mass. He shall also have his ordinary and a mitre; in the Procession, a white cope, a mitre, and a horse covered with a white covering. When he has come to the palace with the lord pope, where preparations have been made for eating, he shall remove the cope and receive a mantle, and shall eat with the lord [Col. 1146B] pope with his mitre on his head.

The lord chamberlain must precede the lord pope with the cross, accompanied by chaplains, as far as the church where the consecration and coronation are to take place; at Mass he shall stand in the customary place. When it has ended, he shall go to the place in the church appointed for him, and the presbyterium shall be distributed. Thus prepared, together with one of the clerks of the chamber and the merchants, he shall provide the lord pope with the various coins to be distributed as the presbyterium to the lord cardinals, prelates, and others for whom this is customary.

The chamberlain and clerk shall be dressed in surplices. After this, the chamberlain will remain with the lord pope until the lord pope is at table. Then he shall go or return to the chamber to eat with all the chaplains of the lord pope who are in the curia, with the penitentiaries, and with many other good men who are invited on the chamberlain’s behalf.

Each chaplain of the lord pope who is not a subdeacon of the lord pope shall have a surplice. Thus he will ride in the Procession and shall take care to proceed elegantly with the companion assigned to him.

Two Greeks from the monastery of Grottaferrata—or, even if there are other Greeks at the Curia, provided that the Curia is in a place from which they can be obtained from that monastery; otherwise, others, as can be arranged—are to take part in the Mass. One of them, dressed in an alb and tunicle, shall read the Epistle appropriate to the day; the other, dressed in a vestment and dalmatic, shall sing the Gospel appropriate to the day. They are to have horses ready after Mass and shall come with the Procession as far as the lord pope’s palace.

[Col. 1146D] **280.** The treasurers are to have precious vestments ready for the lord pope, suitable to the season, when he is consecrated, as well as an alb for the Mass to be celebrated and for the Procession, a mitre, the papal crown, seven candlesticks with candles, a towel, a head-cloth, chrism, and the other things specified to them.

They are also to have twelve banners and two cherubim on spears, which shall be given to fourteen runners so that they may carry them beside the pope. When the lord pope is crowned, one of these treasurers, once the crown has been handed over, shall receive the mitre, go ahead, and wait at the church door; he shall give the mitre and receive the crown. He shall also stand ready to receive the pallium and chasuble when the pope receives the mantle. After the meal he shall receive the garments and sandals that the pope removes.

Brother N., marshal of the marshalcy, shall have ready the horses, with trappings and the other things necessary for the horse that the pope will ride, with a scarlet covering at the rear; and he shall carry out the other customary duties assigned to him.

The white-clad attendants shall be ready to lead the horse and to carry the parasol and spurs, the hat and the rain-cape against rain, and the mitre-case.

The black-clad attendants shall carry the chapel, head-coverings, faldstools, stools, and the other customary items when the lord pope goes to sing on solemn feasts. They shall also carry a morsel from three loaves; four pieces of bread on one towel for washing the hands; and cold and hot water for washing the hands. [Col. 1147B] They shall also arrange in the church the place where he is to vest and the place behind the altar where he is to sit. A faldstool shall be ready before the altar, on which he may lean when the litany is sung.

A place for sitting shall also be prepared in the church, where the presbytery (presbyterium) is to be, and where there shall be a faldstool for sitting. The pope’s subdeacons, both chaplains and others, are to be dressed in tunicles; they shall serve and sing the laudes with the senior cardinal deacon, and perform the services assigned to them. They shall have horses and shall come mounted with the Procession alongside the pope. One of them shall be ready to carry the cross, another to conduct the litany, and a third to serve with the towel. The deacon who sang the Epistle shall carry the Gospel book in the Procession, and their senior [Col. 1147C] shall carry the pallium to the altar at the proper time.

**281. XLVII. Rubric: On the ministry of the cardinal bishop or cardinal priest who serves the pope celebrating the solemn Mass in the office of chaplain**

It should be known that a cardinal bishop customarily serves the Roman pontiff when he celebrates the solemn Mass, in the office of chaplain, on the days called processional days. On these days the pontiff, vested in sacred garments far from the altar and accompanied by an ordered Procession, proceeds to the sacred altar with a cloth spread over his head. On the other days, when such a solemn Procession does not take place, a cardinal priest customarily serves. From Ash Wednesday, however, although the aforesaid Procession is ordinarily held, a cardinal priest must serve. When the pontiff entrusts a sermon at Mass to a cardinal bishop or priest, the one who is to preach must serve, even if the service would otherwise appear to belong to someone else.

When the pontiff has come to the church in which he is to celebrate, and has turned aside to the place where he is to vest in the sacred garments, the cardinal bishop or priest who is to serve him must assist him while he says Terce or another Hour that is to be said before Mass according to the requirements of the time. When the pontiff is about to say the Prayer or Collect of that Hour, the cardinal, with his head uncovered, extends his left hand through the front opening of the cope in which he is dressed; he extends his right hand beneath the edge of the cope; and, taking with both hands the book handed to him by one of the attending chaplains, in which the Prayer to be said is written, he holds it above his head before the pontiff while the pontiff says the Prayer.

If it is a weekday on which the pontiff must say the Prayer while leaning upon the faldstool, the same cardinal, kneeling before the pontiff, holds the book against his chest, or in whatever manner seems most convenient for the pontiff to read the Prayer. After the Prayer has been said, the cardinal returns the book to the person from whom he received it and remains with the pontiff until the office of the Blessed Mary is completed, if it is to be said; in that office, however, the book for the Prayer is not ordinarily held. When the Hour is finished, the aforesaid cardinal withdraws to some nearby place. If the cardinal bishops are sitting, he may sit with them not far from the pontiff, whether he himself is a bishop or a priest. He is to sit in the place belonging to him according to his rank until the pontiff has put on his sandals. Then he is summoned by one of the acolytes serving the pontiff to minister water for the pontiff’s hands.

At this point the cardinal approaches the pontiff and extends both hands outside the cope in the manner described above. From one of the pope’s attendants, who is to hand the basins with water to the cardinal, he takes the upper basin in his left hand; kneeling before the pontiff, he places it beneath the pontiff’s hands. Taking the lower basin in his right hand, he pours water over the pontiff’s hands for as long as the pontiff wishes to receive it. He then returns the basins to the person from whom he received them and returns to the place to which he had previously withdrawn.

When the pontiff has taken the chasuble, the cardinal who serves him likewise removes his cope and takes a cotta or surplice, an amice, and a cope of a color suitable to the season. If the serving cardinal is a cardinal priest, he must nevertheless put on a cope and then take his mitre. After this, when one of the acolytes has handed him the pontifical ring, he approaches the pontiff, upon whose head a cardinal deacon has placed the mitre. Removing his own mitre, he places the ring on the ring finger of the pontiff’s right hand and kisses that hand.

Finally, taking from the acolyte’s hand the boat containing incense and the spoon, he presents it to the pontiff so that he may place incense in the thurible, which the same acolyte must hold. When the pontiff takes the spoon, the aforesaid cardinal must kiss his hand; he must do the same when the pontiff replaces the spoon in the boat. For this is regularly observed whenever any cardinal hands something into the pontiff’s hands or receives something from his hand: he must reverently kiss that same hand.

After this, if a Procession is to take place, once the Procession has been arranged by those responsible for it, the cardinal himself proceeds first. If he is a bishop, he goes with the other bishops, holding the place that he ought otherwise to hold; but if he is a priest, he proceeds ahead of all the cardinal priests, as though he were one of the junior cardinal bishops. Thus the serving cardinal proceeds with the other cardinals until they reach the altar, and waits beside the right-hand corner of the altar until the pontiff himself arrives at the altar.

If it is not a processional day, but one on which the pontiff is vested in sacred garments near the altar, then, after the cardinal has given the ring to the pontiff, he immediately comes to the right-hand corner of the altar and waits for the pontiff, as stated above. When the pontiff comes to the altar, with two deacons standing beside him, one on either side, the cardinal bishop or priest who is serving must stand beside the deacon who is at the pontiff’s right until the pontiff has completed the confession and absolution.

At the end of the absolution, the cardinal receives from the acolyte’s hand the boat with incense and offers it to the pontiff, so that he may place the incense in the thurible, according to the manner described above. The cardinal then goes and waits beside the seat prepared for the pontiff, on his right. When the pontiff comes to that seat, the cardinal goes up and, assisting him on his right, says with him, while reading, the Introit of the Mass and the Kyrie eleison. He then goes to sit in his own place.

It should be known that if the cardinal who serves in the office of chaplain is a bishop, he must have his faldstool on the right side of the aforesaid seat, above the other cardinal bishops sitting on that side. If he is a priest, he must not have a faldstool; rather, he shall have a place before the pontiff’s feet on the right, beside the two cardinal deacons assisting the pontiff.

When the pontiff is about to begin the Angelic Hymn, the serving cardinal rises, assists the pontiff, and continues the aforesaid Hymn with him; he then sits in his own place. When the pontiff is about to say “Peace be with you” or “The Lord be with you,” the same cardinal rises and receives the Missal handed to him by a chaplain or another cleric to whom the book has been entrusted. He holds it open above his head, or in another decent manner as the space permits, before the pontiff until the pontiff has said all the Prayers that are to be said. The cardinal ought to know these Prayers beforehand, search for them carefully in the book, and present them to the pontiff in the proper order.

When the Prayers are finished, the cardinal returns the book to the person from whom he received it and sits until shortly before the Gospel is to be read. Then he rises, takes from the acolyte’s hand the boat with incense, and presents it to the pontiff in the manner described above, so that the pontiff may place incense in the thurible, which is to be carried to the Gospel. After this has been done, the cardinal sits again until the Gospel begins. While it is being read, he assists the pontiff, sitting on his right.

When the Gospel is finished, the cardinal receives the thurible from the hand of the acolyte returning from the place where the Gospel was read and incenses the pontiff. It is appropriate that, while incensing him, he bring the thurible three times before the pontiff’s breast.

When this has been done, if the pontiff himself is to preach, the serving cardinal goes to the place where the sermon is to be delivered and remains on the pontiff’s right while he preaches: standing if the pontiff is standing, or sitting in a suitable place if the pontiff is seated. When the sermon is finished, he returns with the pontiff to his seat, preceding him.

If the serving cardinal himself is to preach, after incensing the pontiff he kneels before him, kisses his foot, and asks for his blessing, saying, “Bid me, lord, bless.” After receiving the blessing, he respectfully asks the pontiff what indulgence he wishes to grant. Having heard the pontiff’s pleasure, he goes to the place where he is to preach and continues with his sermon.

When it is finished, he remains in the same place until the confession has been made by the cardinal deacon. Then, before the pontiff gives absolution, the cardinal who has preached announces the indulgence in these or similar words:

“By the authority of almighty God, of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and by his own authority, the supreme pontiff grants an indulgence of one year and forty days—or more, as it may please the pontiff—to all who are truly penitent and have confessed.”

After the pontiff has given absolution, the cardinal returns to him. Saying “I believe,” if it is to be said, he assists him and continues the Creed with him; then he sits. When the Creed has been sung, he rises and assists the pontiff as he says, “The Lord be with you.”

Afterward, when he has sat down, the acolyte is to spread a towel or cloth over his lap and remove his gloves, after the aforesaid cardinal has first removed the pontifical ring from the pontiff’s finger. The cardinal must keep the ring by placing it on one of his own fingers. Kneeling on the pontiff’s right, he must hold the towel neatly wrapped around the joint of the pontiff’s right arm and hand; the subdeacon holds it similarly on the left. One of the chamberlains slightly raises the towel before the pontiff’s breast, lest, while the pontiff washes his hands, drops of water should leap out and stain the sacred vestments.

Then the senior cardinal bishop among those seated around the pontiff rises, receives the basins handed to him by one of the pope’s attendants entrusted with this duty, and ministers water for washing the pontiff’s hands, as was stated above concerning the first washing.

When the pontiff’s hands have been washed and dried, the aforesaid serving cardinal places the ring on the pontiff’s finger and, rising, stands beside the pontiff’s seat until the time approaches for the pontiff to proceed to the altar. He then goes ahead and prepares the Missal on the left side of the altar, placing beneath it the folded towel with which the pontiff dried his hands. The cleric who serves the cardinal with the mitre must receive this towel from the acolyte when the pontiff rises to come to the altar.

The aforementioned cardinal must carefully search the aforesaid book for everything that the pontiff is to say, whether in offering the paten and chalice, incensing, continuing the Secret Prayers, or performing the other things belonging to the office of the Mass. When necessary, they must turn the pages attentively and discreetly and point out with a finger to the pontiff what is to be said, whenever appropriate. He is thus to assist the pontiff attentively and reverently beside the book until the Agnus Dei. At the elevation of the Lord’s Body, however, he may briefly bend his knees; he shall do likewise at the elevation of the chalice, adoring the consecrated Body and Blood.

After he has said the Agnus Dei with the pontiff, and the pontiff has begun to say the Prayer “Lord Jesus Christ, who said,” etc., which is said before the kiss of peace, the frequently mentioned cardinal leaves the book on the left side of the altar and moves to the right. When the pontiff turns to give him the peace, the cardinal bows deeply before him, but does not kneel. Rising quickly, he reverently receives the peace from the pontiff and then kisses the cross of the pallium on the pontiff’s breast.

Next, as he judges appropriate, he adjusts the pontiff’s chasuble, first over the right arm and then over the left; he may also pull it from the front. He then adjusts the pallium as follows. He neatly fits the part of the fanon that hangs before the pontiff’s breast beneath the aforesaid cross of the pallium. Then he places the fingers of his right hand over that same cross, draws the pallium down with his left hand, and places it in its proper position over the pontiff’s right arm. Afterward, placing the fingers of his left hand on the same cross, he draws and adjusts the left part of the pallium with his right hand. The proper position of the pallium over the arms is such that it should not rise so high as to approach the elbow, but should be, as it were, midway [lacuna]; “the elbow and the final portion” [syntax uncertain]. The front part of the pallium, which hangs lower, should certainly hang through the middle of the chasuble. **286** The manner of adjusting the chasuble and pallium described above can be understood better from the example of the cardinal deacons, who frequently perform this task at Mass, than it can be conveyed in writing.

When these things have been done, the aforesaid cardinal turns to the senior of the cardinal deacons assisting around the altar and gives him the peace. If the one who read the Gospel is the senior, however, he is not to receive it; rather, the peace is to be given to the one senior to him. Then the aforesaid cardinal goes to the cardinal bishops and gives the peace to the senior on the right and to the other senior on the left. Next he goes to the cardinal priests and gives the peace to the senior on the left. Finally, he goes to the other prelates dressed in sacred vestments and gives the peace to the one holding the first place, or to several of them if perhaps they have not all been seated in the same order. One of the acolytes and one or more of the pope’s runners must precede the cardinal as he goes to give the peace.

After giving the peace, he returns to the pontiff, whom he finds withdrawn from the altar and seated in his place, and assists him as he communicates. He need not be excessively concerned with the book during Communion; rather, the person entrusted with the book must hold it before the pontiff, with his right hand suitably placed upon it, so that the pontiff can read what is to be said at that time.

The cardinal himself receives from the acolyte’s hand a cloth with which the pontiff is to wipe his mouth and fingers after Communion and the ablution, together with a reed with which the pontiff is to receive the Lord’s Blood. When the pontiff has consumed the portion of the Host appointed for him and is to receive the Blood, the cardinal presents him with the reed, kissing his hand.

When the pontiff has sat down after giving holy Communion to the cardinal deacon and subdeacon, the cardinal, holding the aforesaid cloth in his right hand, kneels on the pontiff’s right and holds in his left hand the towel to be spread by the acolyte over the pontiff’s lap, in the same manner as described above.

Then the bishop who had ministered the water takes from the acolyte, in his right hand, a small jug with wine and, in his left hand, a vessel in which the ablution is to be received. He places the vessel beneath the pontiff’s fingers and pours wine slowly and modestly over them from the jug. After him, another senior cardinal bishop receives the basins handed to him by one of the pope’s attendants and then pours water over the same fingers in the manner prescribed above for the washing of the hands.

When the fingers have been washed, the frequently mentioned serving cardinal presents the aforesaid cloth to the pontiff for drying his fingers. The bishop who poured the wine, returning the jug to the acolyte, carries the vessel containing the ablution to the altar, to the cardinal deacon who read the Gospel. The latter must drink the ablution and return the vessel to the bishop; the bishop then hands the vessel to the acolyte and returns to his place.

The serving cardinal waits in the same kneeling position until the subdeacon offers the pontiff the chalice with wine and the pontiff drinks from it to wash his mouth. Then the cardinal again presents him with the aforesaid cloth to wipe his mouth. After this, returning the cloth to the acolyte, the cardinal must rise, since the time is approaching for the pontiff to return to the altar.

The cardinal precedes him and stands on his right, with the Missal there and the towel beneath it, as stated above. When the pontiff comes to the altar, the cardinal assists him while he says the Prayers to be said after Communion, which he must carefully find and present to the pontiff in the proper order.

When, after all the Prayers have been finished, the pontiff says, “Through our Lord Jesus Christ,” etc., the aforesaid cardinal first kisses the altar and then the cross of the pallium over the pontiff’s right arm. He then withdraws from the altar and goes to the place where he had sat, standing there until, after the pontiff has given the Blessing, the pontiff returns to his seat. Beside it, the cardinal assisting him removes the ring from the pontiff’s hand and returns it to the acolyte.

Then, withdrawing, he removes the sacred vestments and puts on his ordinary garments. He returns again to the pontiff, assists him, and serves him at the Hour to be said after Mass, as was stated above concerning the Hour preceding Mass. If, after the pontiff has removed his sacred vestments, a mitre is to be placed on him, the cardinal is to be present; and if no cardinal deacon has arrived, the frequently mentioned cardinal places the mitre on the pontiff. When the aforesaid Hour is finished, the cardinal may withdraw, his ministry having been completed.

**288. XLVIII. On the matters to be observed concerning the rite when a cardinal bishop celebrates the solemn Mass; the ministers he must have; and the vestments or ornaments of the pontiff and of those ministers**

When a cardinal bishop is about to celebrate the solemn Mass in some church, his clerics, to whom the care of the chapel is entrusted, must go ahead to that church with the chapel itself and carefully ensure that they bring everything necessary for the ministry, both for the pontiff and for his ministers, and for the sacred altar.

The ministers whom the pontiff must have at all times are these: a chaplain, a deacon and subdeacon, and at least four acolytes—namely, one who is to keep the mitre, one who is to serve as thurifer, and two who are to serve as candle-bearers. When necessary, some other clerics of the celebrant, dressed in surplices, may likewise assist him together with the aforesaid ministers.

The vestments or ornaments to be brought for the pontiff are these: stockings, sandals, amice, alb, cincture with the subcinctorium, which resembles a maniple and must hang from the cincture on the left side; pectoral cross, stole, tunicle, dalmatic, gloves, chasuble, and maniple; pallium with three golden pins, if the pontiff uses a pallium; mitre; and pontifical ring. The supreme pontiffs do not use the crozier or pastoral staff, nor do cardinal bishops in the Roman Curia.

For the pontiff himself there must also be a comb and a towel to be placed around his neck when he is combed; basins and a towel for drying his hands; a faldstool with a stool and cushions to be placed beneath the faldstool; and a cloth with which to wipe it.

The chaplain must have a linen shirt over his ordinary clothes, a surplice or cotta, an amice, and a cope. The deacon must have an amice, alb, cincture, stole, dalmatic, and maniple. The subdeacon must have an amice, alb, cincture, tunicle, and maniple. All the acolytes must be dressed in cottas according to the custom of the holy Roman Church.

It should be noted that on days when violet or black is customary, the deacon and subdeacon must have not dalmatics and tunicles but priestly chasubles.

The aforesaid clerics are also to ensure that they bring with the chapel a portable altar, unless they know that the altar on which Mass is to be celebrated is consecrated; a silk cloth called the dorsal, and an orphrey for adorning the front of the altar; a cross to be placed on the altar; an altar-covering, corporal, chalice, paten, a small cloth for wiping the chalice, cruets for the wine and water of the sacrifice, a vessel containing the Hosts, a barrel or vessel from which the wine for the sacrifice is carried, and another vessel for the water required in the ministry.

They are also to bring a thurible and boat with incense and spoon; and books, namely the Missal, Gospel book, and Epistle book. They must also bring towels, one of which the chaplain or another minister holds out to the pontiff when necessary for wiping his mouth or nose. The one who serves the mitre is to have towels for holding the mitre, and another to spread over the pontiff’s lap when he sits.

They must nevertheless have several other towels ready, as well as another cloth or silk cloths, which they may use for the other rites mentioned above if necessary—for example, to adorn the ambo or the rear part of the altar, if its arrangement requires it, or for some other ornament.

In summer they are also to bring fans to drive flies away from the ministry. In addition, they are to bring several carpets to be spread beneath the faldstool, before the altar, and over the seats on which the ministers are to sit. Moreover, the aforesaid clerics of the chapel are to foresee which vestments are suitable for the pontiff and the ministers, and ensure that they are of a color appropriate to the season.

**XLIX. On the variety of colors that the Roman Church customarily uses in sacred vestments at different times**

It should be known that the holy Roman Church uses five colors in sacred vestments: white, red, green, violet, and black. Some, however, count the last two as one.

It uses white from Vespers on the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord through the Octave of Epiphany, inclusive, except for the feasts of martyrs when they occur. Also on Maundy Thursday. Also from Holy Saturday in the office of the Mass through the Octave of the Ascension of the Lord, inclusive, whenever the office is of the season, except on the Rogation days and in the Mass celebrated on the day of Saint Mark for the office of the litany. Also on all feasts of holy Mary, Mother of God. **290** At the reception of candles on the feast of the Purification of the Blessed Virgin Mary, however, violet is used, and afterward white is used at Mass. White is also used on the feast of All Saints; on the feasts of the Angels; on the feast of the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist; on the principal feast of Saint John the Evangelist; on the Conversion of Saint Paul; on the Chair of Saint Peter; on the feasts of all confessors and of all holy women who are not martyrs; at the Dedications of churches; and during the Octaves of the aforesaid feasts that have Octaves, whenever the office is of those Octaves.

**L. On the color red**

Red is used from the vigil of Pentecost at Mass through the Saturday following that feast, inclusive. It is also used on the feasts of the Holy Cross; on the feast of the Beheading of Saint John the Baptist; on the feasts of all the apostles and evangelists, except the principal feast of Saint John the Evangelist, and except the feasts of the Conversion of Saint Paul and of the Chair of Saint Peter; and on the feasts of all holy men and women who are martyrs, except the feast of the Holy Innocents when it falls outside a Sunday.

If the feast of the Holy Innocents falls on a Sunday, red is used, and red is used on its Octave, whichever day it falls on. If it falls outside a Sunday, violet is used; but red is to be used on its Octave. Red is also used during the Octaves of the aforesaid feasts that have Octaves, whenever the office is of those Octaves.

**LI. On the color green**

Green is used between the Octave of Epiphany and Septuagesima, and between Pentecost and Advent, whenever the office is of the Sunday.

**LII. On the color violet**

Violet is used from the First Sunday of Advent through the Mass on the Nativity of the Lord, inclusive, and from Septuagesima through the office of the Mass on the vigil of Easter, exclusive, whenever during the aforesaid periods the office is of the season, except on Maundy Thursday and Good Friday.

It is to be understood that on Holy Saturday violet is to be used throughout the entire office celebrated before Mass. The exception is that the deacon who sings the Blessing of the Candle is dressed in a dalmatic, while the subdeacon or subdeacons serving that day are dressed in white tunicles. After the Blessing of the Candle has been sung, the deacon removes the dalmatic, takes a violet chasuble, and keeps it until the office of the Mass begins; the subdeacons do not change their vestments.

Violet is also always used on the Ember Days; on the vigils of saints on which there is a fast, when the Mass is of the vigil; on the Rogation days; and in the Mass celebrated on Saint Mark’s day for the office of the litany. It is also used on the feast of the Holy Innocents when it falls outside a Sunday, and on the feast of the Purification of the Blessed Virgin at the reception of the candles in the Procession.

**LIII. On the color black**

Black is used on Good Friday, in Masses for the dead, and in Processions that the Roman pontiff makes barefoot. It should nevertheless be known that on days when black is customary, it is not inappropriate to use violet.

When, therefore, the aforesaid clerics responsible for the chapel have arrived at the church with the chapel, they are to provide a suitable place where the pontiff is to vest in sacred garments. If there is in the church a suitable secretarium or sacristy where the pontiff customarily vests for celebrating, they are to have the chapel deposited there; carpets are to be spread; and a faldstool with a cushion, a covering cloth, and a stool are to be prepared.

They are also to display, in a suitable place and as best they can, the sacred vestments in which the pontiff and the ministers are to be dressed, together with the other things required for the rite, so that they may be readily available. If there is no suitable secretarium or sacristy in the church, the chapel is to be deposited so that the aforesaid arrangements can be made in some suitable place near the altar. If it happens to be customary in that church for the pontiff to vest far from the altar and proceed to it in an ordered Procession, that custom is to be observed.

Moreover, the aforesaid clerics are to spread one or more carpets before the sacred altar and ensure that the altar itself, before the pontiff approaches, is decently adorned, whether with cloths that they bring or with those belonging to the church. They are also to place upon the altar a cross positioned opposite the pontiff when he stands in the middle of the altar. This provision concerning the adornment of the altar may be postponed until after the Gospel or after the sermon when the crowd of people is too large. The clerics dressed in cottas are to handle the sacred ornaments at the altar.

When the pontiff comes to the church, after bowing and praying briefly before the altar, he withdraws to the place where the chapel has been prepared. Standing, he says Terce or another Hour that is to be said before Mass according to the season, together with his clerics. When he says the Prayer, his chaplain, if necessary, holds before him the book in which the Prayer is written.

While he says the aforesaid Hour, the deacon and subdeacon vest themselves in all the sacred vestments except the maniples, except on days when those ministers customarily use chasubles; on such days they must not put on the chasubles until the hour when the pontiff is to proceed to the altar. The chaplains and the other ministers are to be dressed in cottas so that they may serve the pontiff while he is vesting.

After the pontiff has completed the aforesaid Hour, he sits in the faldstool and begins and continues the Psalms “How lovely,” etc., with the Prayers customarily said while the pontiff is putting on his footwear. Meanwhile, one of his attendants approaches and removes his ordinary shoes. The subdeacon, carrying the stockings and sandals, kneels before him and puts them on him, first on the right foot and then on the left; one of the acolytes assists him in putting them on.

After putting on his footwear, the pontiff rises and, standing on the stool, removes his cope. He remains in his linen shirt, which he must always wear over his woolen garments when he goes to celebrate, even if he is a religious.

When the pontiff is seated on the faldstool, the deacon and subdeacon receive his towel and comb from the acolytes. They spread the towel around his neck and lightly and decently comb his head: first the deacon on the right and then the subdeacon on the left. If the deacon and subdeacon are not trained for this, the chaplain shall do it in their place.

After this, an acolyte spreads another towel over the pontiff’s lap. The pontiff removes the ring that he ordinarily wears and hands it to the chaplain for safekeeping. The chaplain receives from the acolyte the basins with water and, holding the lower basin in his left hand and the upper basin in his right, pours water over the pontiff’s hands on bended knees. Meanwhile, the deacon assists the pontiff on the right and the subdeacon on the left, both kneeling and holding the aforesaid towel.

### 293

When the pontiff has washed and dried his hands, he rises and stands upon the footstool. The ministers then vest him reverently and carefully: the acolytes bring the vestments, while the deacon on the right and the subdeacon on the left receive these vestments and put them on him. The chaplains and other clerics of the pontiff, vested in surplices and standing nearby, may assist them as appropriate.

First, therefore, the acolytes bring the amice. The deacon places it over the pontiff’s head; the deacon takes the left cord of the amice, and the subdeacon the right, and they draw them behind the pontiff and bring them forward again over the cincture. The pontiff himself may tie them together. Next they vest him in the alb, fitting it carefully around his neck and hands. Then they gird him with the cincture and subcinctorium: one of the ministers lifts the front of the alb around the chest, and the deacon ties and tightens the cords of the cincture together; alternatively, the pontiff himself may tighten them as he wishes. The ministers arrange the alb around the hems, so that the hems do not touch the ground but remain evenly distant from it. They also arrange its sleeves, folding them decently between the shoulder and the elbow.

Next the pontiff takes the pectoral cross, kisses it, and hangs it around his neck so that it rests before his breast. Then he takes the stole, kisses it at its middle, and places it around his neck. He should not draw its two sides together before his breast in the form of a cross, but should allow them to hang down as they fall from the neck; the ministers fasten both sides with the cincture so that they cannot slip down. After this the ministers vest him in the tunicle, fitting it around his neck and hands. Then they vest him in the dalmatic, fitting it around his neck and folding back its sleeves so that the sleeves do not touch the pontiff’s hands but remain away from them by about half a palm’s breadth.

After this the pontiff sits down again and receives the gloves offered to him by an acolyte. The deacon puts one onto his right hand and the subdeacon one onto his left. Having received them, he rises, and the aforesaid ministers place the chasuble upon him. If the pontiff uses a pallium, immediately after the chasuble has been put on, an acolyte offers it to him, holding it with a fine cloth and outstretched hands: with his right hand he holds the pallium near the left cross, and with his left hand near the right cross. The pontiff himself kisses the pallium at the rear cross. Then the ministers place the pallium upon him, the deacon lifting the part that is to hang at the back. The ministers must take care that the doubled part of the pallium comes over the left shoulder.

After the acolyte carrying the pallium comes the person who is to keep the mitre, carrying it in his right hand by means of a cloth, and in his left the pins to be inserted into the pallium. Once the pallium has been placed, the ministers insert these pins: the deacon one at the front cross, the subdeacon another at the cross over the left shoulder, and one of the other ministers a third at the rear cross. The pins are to be inserted in such a way that each passes three times through the cross into which it is inserted, and on the fourth pass the point of the pin is inserted into the pallium beyond the cross. Care must be taken that a pin never pierces through the pallium, and that its point in no way touches the chasuble. It must also be ensured that the head of each pin, in which the gem is set, is on the right side of the person inserting it.

Subsequently the deacon on the right and the subdeacon on the left neatly fold the chasuble over the pontiff’s arms. If the pontiff is vested near the altar, the subdeacon places—and as it were conceals—the pontiff’s maniple in the fold of his left arm, after receiving it from the acolyte. But if the pontiff is vested far from the altar, the subdeacon should not then put on the maniple; instead, he should carry it with the Gospel book and, when the pontiff reaches the altar, put on and arrange the maniple in the manner described above.

When the chasuble has been folded as stated above, the deacon removes the amice from the pontiff’s head and arranges it around his neck. He must see that the chasuble lies smoothly over the shoulders, and he draws it forward from the front. Then he arranges the pallium so that the front cross is before the breast, over the gold border of the chasuble. Placing the fingers of his right hand, extended together, upon that cross, he draws the pallium over the pontiff’s right arm toward the elbow with his left hand. Next, placing the fingers of his left hand upon the same cross, he draws the pallium over the pontiff’s left arm with his right hand, taking care that the pallium descends over the arms to approximately the midpoint between the shoulder and the elbow. The pallium is to be arranged in this manner whenever necessary.

Then the deacon receives the mitre from the person who keeps it and places it upon the pontiff’s head. Meanwhile the chaplain vests himself in a cope. Once the mitre has been placed on the pontiff, the chaplain inserts the pontifical ring onto the ring finger of the pontiff’s right hand, kissing it. He must always do this whenever he puts the ring on or removes it. After the pontifical ring, a second, smaller ring may also be inserted to hold the pontifical ring firmly in place; this is to be arranged episcopally.

After the ring has been inserted, the chaplain takes from the thurifer the boat containing incense and the spoon. The thurifer presents it to the pontiff together with fire, which he must prepare while the pontiff is being vested. The chaplain offers the pontiff the uncovered boat.
