The pontiff takes the spoon with incense in his right hand, places the incense upon the fire, and returns the spoon to the boat; he then blesses the incense placed upon the fire with the sign of the cross. The chaplain must kiss the pontiff’s hand both when he receives the spoon and when he returns it. After the pontiff has returned the spoon, the chaplain gives the boat back to the thurifer.

What has been said concerning the placing of incense is to be observed when the pontiff is vested far from the altar. If he is vested beside the altar, however, incense need not be placed until after the confession has been made.

Once the pontiff has been vested in the manner described, the deacon and subdeacon take their own maniples and put on their chasubles, if the season requires it. When this has been done, if they are far from the altar, they proceed toward it, preceded by the thurifer, followed by two candle-bearers, and then by the subdeacon with the Gospel book. The pontiff follows them, accompanied by the chaplain on his right and the deacon on his left. The person who keeps the mitre and the other clerics vested in surplices follow behind the pontiff.

When the pontiff reaches the steps before the altar, the deacon removes his mitre, taking it with one hand by its front horn and smoothing the pontiff’s hair with the other if necessary. The person who removes the mitre must always do this. Once the mitre has been removed, the deacon gives it to the person who keeps it. The latter must always receive it from the hand of the deacon or chaplain who removes it, and return it to that person when it is to be put on again.

If the pontiff is vested beside the altar, such a procession need not take place. When the pontiff approaches the altar, accompanied by the chaplain and deacon, the candle-bearers should already be standing beside the altar and should take the candlesticks with lighted candles from it. The thurifer should likewise be ready on the left with the thurible containing fire and with the boat.

The pontiff, bowing slightly before the altar, makes the confession, with the chaplain assisting him on the right and the deacon on the left. If the subdeacon is to put it on, he places the maniple on the pontiff. While the pontiff makes the confession, the subdeacon stands with the Gospel book beside the altar step on the left, and the candle-bearers stand around the altar, one on the right and the other on the left. The other ministers may stand behind the pontiff.

After the confession has been made and the pontiff has given the absolution, but before he says “Deus, tu conversus” (“O God, turn again”), the chaplain takes from the thurifer the boat containing incense, which the thurifer should offer him between the pontiff and the altar. The pontiff places the incense in the thurible, while the chaplain offers him the boat and the thurifer the thurible, as stated above.

Having done this, the pontiff says “Deus, tu conversus” and ascends to the altar. Bowing before it, he says the prayer “Aufer a nobis” (“Take away from us”). When this has been said, he kisses the altar. Afterwards he kisses the Gospel book, which the subdeacon must offer him open at the place where the Gospel is to be read at Mass. After the pontiff has kissed it, the subdeacon leaves it closed upon the altar, unless for some reason it seems necessary to place it elsewhere.

After kissing the book, the pontiff makes the sign of the cross over himself, and then the choir may begin the Introit. When the pontiff has signed himself in the manner described, he turns toward the right side of the altar. The deacon takes the thurible from the hand of the thurifer and gives it to the pontiff. The pontiff incenses the altar, beginning at its middle opposite his face. He first incenses the right side and then the left. Next he returns from the left side to the right, incensing the front side of the altar.

When the incensing is finished, he gives the thurible to the deacon. The deacon must kiss the pontiff’s hand both when he gives him the thurible and when he receives it back. Having received the thurible from the pontiff, the deacon incenses the pontiff himself, then the altar all around. Afterwards he gives the thurible to the thurifer and goes to the pontiff’s seat.

After the pontiff has incensed as described, he goes to his seat, accompanied by the chaplain and subdeacon. This is the faldstool prepared on the right side of the altar, or behind the altar itself, according to the character and custom of the place. Where it is customary for the pontiff to sit on a higher stone or wooden seat, that custom is to be observed.

When the pontiff reaches his seat, he stands upon the footstool and says, without singing, the Introit and “Kyrie, eleison” with his ministers. Meanwhile the chaplain arranges his vestments: he folds the dalmatic sleeves into the proper pleats, similarly arranges the chasuble over his arms, spreads it over his shoulders, and draws it forward from the front; he also arranges the pallium according to the method described above. The chaplain or deacon must always make these adjustments to the pontiff’s vestments whenever necessary, and especially when the pontiff rises.

When the vestments have been arranged, the pontiff sits down. The deacon places the mitre upon him, and one of the acolytes spreads a fine cloth over his lap. The pontiff must always have such a cloth while he is seated. If it seems appropriate, the person who keeps the mitre may stand beside the pontiff holding a fan and drive flies away from him.

Whenever the pontiff is to rise, the deacon—or, if he is unable, the chaplain—takes up the same cloth, extends his hands, and, by means of the cloth, reverently takes hold of the pontiff’s hands and helps him to rise. He then returns the cloth to the acolyte. What has been said about spreading the cloth over the pontiff’s lap must always be observed whenever the pontiff sits; and whenever he is to rise, he must be assisted in the manner described, either by the deacon or by the chaplain. While the pontiff remains seated as stated, the ministers sit around him wherever they can most conveniently do so, according to the nature of the place.

### [Col. 1160C]

When the choir has sung the Introit and “Kyrie, eleison,” the pontiff rises, and the deacon arranges his vestments as necessary. The pontiff, standing upon the footstool, has the mitre removed by the deacon. He raises his hands to approximately shoulder height, so that the right hand is before the right shoulder and the left before the left; the fingers of both hands are extended but not separated. With his hands raised in this way, he begins “Gloria in excelsis” (“Glory in the highest”), if the day requires it. When he says “Deo” (“to God”), he joins his hands before his breast and continues the Angelic Hymn without musical notation with his ministers.

When it has been said in this manner, he sits down and the deacon places the mitre upon him. After the choir has sung the same Hymn, he rises again. The deacon removes his mitre, and with his hands raised as described above he says “Pax vobis” (“Peace be with you”). Then he continues with the Prayer or Prayers according to the requirements of the season. The chaplain holds the Missal before his face and presents to him the Prayers to be said, while the deacon on the right and the subdeacon on the left support him.

When, after the last Prayer, he says “Per omnia saecula saeculorum” (“World without end”), he joins his hands before his breast. After he has sung the Prayers to be said, he may say in a low voice two additional Prayers: one for himself, namely “Suppliciter” (“We humbly beseech you”), or “Omnipotens sempiterne Deus, qui me peccatorem” (“Almighty and everlasting God, who me, a sinner”), or another Prayer suitable for a priest to say for himself; and another Prayer for the living and the dead, namely “Omnipotens sempiterne Deus, qui vivorum” (“Almighty and everlasting God, who [are the God] of the living”). These two Prayers may nevertheless be omitted on solemnities.

But if “Gloria in excelsis” is not to be said, after “Kyrie, eleison” has been sung the pontiff rises and, raising his hands in the manner stated above, says “Dominus vobiscum” (“The Lord be with you”), and continues with the Prayer or Prayers as described.

It should be noted that whenever the pontiff says “Pax vobis” or “Dominus vobiscum” at Mass, he must always have his face toward the people. The exception is that when he says “Dominus vobiscum” before the Preface—whether the people are before him, or before or behind it—he must not turn around. When he says “Gloria in excelsis,” the Prayers, or the Creed, he should face the direction toward which he ought to look while continuing the Mass at the altar, according to the arrangement of the altar.

After the Prayers have been said, the pontiff sits down. While the pontiff is saying the Prayer or Prayers, the subdeacon goes at the appropriate time with the Epistle book to the place where the Epistle is to be read, preceded by one of the acolytes. One of the other ministers then supports the pontiff in place of the subdeacon. When the Prayers that the pontiff says with musical notation have been completed, the subdeacon begins and continues the Epistle. When it is finished, he returns with the same book to the pontiff and, genuflecting before him, presents the book closed. The pontiff places his right hand upon it; the subdeacon kisses that hand, and the pontiff blesses him with the sign of the cross. Those who read the prophecies must do the same when prophecies are read at Mass.

After the Epistle, if preaching is not to take place at Mass, the subdeacon washes his fingers and prepares the chalice in a suitable place near the altar. He puts wine into it, places the paten with the Host on top, and covers both with a small cloth. If there is no suitable place near the altar, the chalice is prepared on the altar itself. The subdeacon then sits with the other ministers. If preaching is to take place, this preparation may be postponed until after the preaching.

At the proper time, before the things that are to be sung before the Gospel have been completed, the deacon genuflects before the pontiff and kisses his hand without saying anything. Then he approaches the altar, kneels, and says “Munda cor meum” (“Cleanse my heart”). Rising, he takes from the middle of the altar the Gospel book, which an acolyte must have placed there before that time. Holding the book before his breast, he turns toward the pontiff and, standing with bowed head, asks for the blessing in a low voice, saying “Jube, domne, benedicere” (“Command, lord, to bless”). The pontiff signs him with the sign of the cross, saying “Dominus sit in corde tuo” (“May the Lord be in your heart”), and so forth.

When the deacon approaches the altar to pray as stated, the thurifer, carrying the thurible with fire, kneels before the pontiff and gives the boat with incense to the chaplain, who likewise genuflects. The pontiff places the incense in the thurible and blesses it in the manner described above for the first placing of incense.

After receiving the blessing, the deacon carries the Gospel book before his breast and proceeds to the place where the Gospel is to be read. He is preceded first by the thurifer and second by the candle-bearers; the subdeacon follows him. When all that is to be sung by the choir before the Gospel has been completed, the deacon begins “Dominus vobiscum” and continues with the Gospel. The subdeacon holds his left hand beneath the Gospel book.

It should be noted that the Gospel is to be read from an ambo or elevated pulpit. The candle-bearers and the thurifer stand below, in front of the pulpit, with their faces turned toward the deacon. If the Gospel is read in a lower place, the candle-bearers and the thurifer must nevertheless stand before the deacon, the thurifer between the two candle-bearers. While the Gospel is being read, the pontiff, with his mitre removed and his vestments arranged by the chaplain, stands upon the footstool with his face turned toward the place where the Gospel is being read.

When the Gospel has ended, if preaching is not then to take place, the pontiff raises his hands as described above and begins the Creed, if it is to be said. When he says “Deum” (“God”), he joins his hands at his breast and continues the Symbol without musical notation with those assisting him.

If the Creed is not to be said, after the Gospel has ended the pontiff says “Dominus vobiscum. Oremus” (“The Lord be with you. Let us pray”). After reading the Gospel, the deacon kisses the book. He then returns to the pontiff’s office, preceded by the thurifer and candle-bearers in the same order in which they went, and immediately preceded by the subdeacon, who carries the Gospel book open.

When they have returned, the chaplain takes the thurible from the thurifer and incenses the pontiff. Then the subdeacon presents the open Gospel book to the pontiff, who, standing with his head uncovered, kisses the Gospel that has been read. After incensing the pontiff, the chaplain returns the thurible to the thurifer.

When the pontiff sits down, the deacon places the mitre upon him. If the Creed is said, after the choir has sung it the pontiff rises again; the deacon removes his mitre, and he says “Dominus vobiscum. Oremus.” Then he sits down.

But if the pontiff is to preach, he should not begin the Creed or “Dominus vobiscum”; instead, he should wait until the deacon returns. After kissing the Gospel as described above, he approaches before the altar, bows, and prays briefly with his head uncovered. If the place where the Gospel was read is far from the pontiff’s seat, the pontiff may approach for the aforesaid Prayer before the deacon returns, and afterwards receive incense and kiss the book.

Then, after the deacon has placed the mitre upon him, he proceeds to the place where he is to preach. There the deacon arranges his vestments as necessary, and the pontiff preaches wearing the mitre.

After the preaching has ended, the deacon makes the confession, and the pontiff grants or announces the indulgence. Then the deacon removes the pontiff’s mitre, and the pontiff gives the absolution in a clear voice, with musical notation, saying “Precibus et meritis” (“By [your] prayers and merits”), and “Indulgentiam” (“Pardon”), and so forth. Finally he gives the blessing, saying “Et benedictio Dei omnipotentis” (“And may the blessing of almighty God”), and so forth, signing the people all around.

When this has been done, he resumes the mitre, returns to his seat, and begins the Creed, or “Dominus vobiscum,” as stated above.

But if, while the pontiff is celebrating, someone inferior to him is to preach, the preacher approaches the pontiff after the Gospel and, kneeling, asks for the blessing, saying “Jube, domne, benedicere.” The pontiff makes the sign of the cross over him, saying:

“May the Lord be in your heart and on your lips, so that you may worthily and fruitfully proclaim the holy words, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.”

Then the preacher proceeds to the place where he is to preach and continues with the preaching. When it is finished, the deacon, standing beside the pontiff, makes the confession. After the deacon has completed it, the preacher, standing in the place where he preached, announces the indulgence, if it is to be announced. Afterwards the pontiff gives the absolution, and then begins the Creed or “Dominus vobiscum,” as stated.

The preacher may return to his place after announcing the indulgence.

### 301

When the pontiff has begun the Creed, or has said “Dominus vobiscum” and the Prayer when the Creed is not said, the acolytes spread a cloth over the altar and place the Missal on a cushion at its left side. After the pontiff has said “Dominus vobiscum. Oremus,” one of the acolytes brings a cloth, spreads it over his lap, and removes his gloves, after the chaplain has first removed the pontifical ring.

Then the deacon on the right and the subdeacon on the left, kneeling, wrap the sleeves of the pontiff’s tunicle around his hands with the aforesaid cloth and raise it before the pontiff’s breast. The chaplain takes the basins and, kneeling before him, pours water over his hands in the manner described above. If the deacon is occupied at that time with preparing the chalice, the person who keeps the mitre serves in his place.

When the pontiff has washed his hands, the deacon, having washed his fingers, approaches the altar and spreads the corporal over the cloth.

The pontiff dries his hands with the cloth, resumes the pontifical ring—the chaplain inserting it onto his finger—and rises. The same chaplain arranges his vestments, and he proceeds to the altar, accompanied by the chaplain and the subdeacon, or by the person serving as keeper of the mitre.

When he reaches the altar, the deacon, standing on the right, removes his mitre, which may then be placed upon the altar or in another suitable place. The subdeacon takes, in his right hand by means of a small cloth, the chalice with the paten and Host placed upon it, and in his left hand the small vessel containing the water to be mixed with the wine. Standing on the right side of the altar, he presents the chalice and paten to the deacon.

The deacon takes the paten with the Host using the four fingers of both hands, placing his maniple between the edge of the paten and the upper fingers with which he holds it. In this way he offers the paten with the Host to the pontiff, kissing his hand. The pontiff raises the paten with the Host, saying the Prayer “Suscipe, sancte Pater” (“Receive, holy Father”). The chaplain ensures that the pontiff can read this Prayer and the following one in the Missal.

Near the end of the aforesaid Prayer, the pontiff places the Host upon the corporal, not directly opposite his face but slightly toward the left. He sets the paten down on the right, outside the corporal.

After it has been set down, the subdeacon, holding the chalice, offers the vessel containing water to the pontiff. The pontiff turns and pours the water into the chalice, saying the Prayer “Deus, qui humanae substantiae” (“O God, who wonderfully fashioned human nature”), and so forth.

Then the deacon receives the chalice from the subdeacon’s hand. Holding it in his right hand, he makes with it the sign of the cross over the corporal, and places it upon the same corporal, not exactly in the middle opposite the pontiff’s face but slightly toward the right. Taking the corporal—which is not unfolded [Alternative: “which is not spread out”]—with the fingers of both hands, he covers the chalice with it.

While the deacon places it upon the altar in this manner, the pontiff says the Prayer “Offerimus tibi, Domine” (“We offer to you, O Lord”), and afterwards “In spiritu humilitatis” (“In a spirit of humility”). Then, making one sign of the cross over the chalice and the Host together, he likewise says the Prayer “Veni, sanctificator” (“Come, Sanctifier”), and so forth.

[Note: Thus also the Carthusians still perform the rite today.]

After the deacon has placed the chalice, he takes the paten and gives it to the subdeacon. The subdeacon receives it with his right hand by means of a small cloth, the end of which must hang down behind his right shoulder. He holds the covered paten raised, standing behind the pontiff until after the Lord’s Prayer.

After the paten has been given to the subdeacon, the thurifer brings the thurible with the boat to the deacon on the right side of the altar. The deacon places incense in the thurible, having first asked the pontiff’s blessing.

After the pontiff has said “Veni, sanctificator,” he turns and makes the sign of the cross toward the thurible, saying the Prayer “Per intercessionem” (“Through the intercession”), and so forth. The deacon takes the thurible and gives it to the pontiff, kissing his hands.

The pontiff receives the thurible with his right hand and, standing in the middle of the altar with his face turned toward the altar itself, raises it slightly, saying the Prayer “Incensum istud” (“May this incense”), and so forth. Then with the thurible he makes the sign of the cross three times over the chalice and the Host together, saying three times the verse “Dirigatur, Domine” (“Let my prayer, O Lord”), and afterwards continuing with the verses “Elevatio manuum” (“The lifting up of my hands”), through the end of the verse, “Ut non declines cor meum” (“That you incline not my heart”), and so forth. He then circles the chalice and the Host three times with the thurible.

Next he incenses the entire altar, beginning in the middle opposite his face and proceeding toward the right side. Returning to the middle, he proceeds from there toward the left side. Then from the left side of the altar he proceeds while incensing its front side, as far as the right side.

When the incensing has been completed in the manner described, he gives the thurible to the deacon, saying the Prayer “Accendat Dominus” (“May the Lord kindle”), and so forth. The deacon kisses the pontiff’s hand, receives the thurible, and incenses the pontiff himself. Then he gives the thurible to the thurifer for safekeeping and arranges the pontiff’s vestments as appropriate.

When the vestments have been arranged, the deacon takes the thurible back from the thurifer and incenses the altar all around, first on the right and then on the left. Afterwards he incenses the chaplain serving the pontiff. He may also incense prelates and persons of greater dignity, if any are present at the Mass. Then he returns the thurible to the thurifer, who incenses the deacon himself, the other ministers, and the remaining bystanders as seems appropriate.

After the pontiff has returned the thurible to the deacon, he may, for greater cleanliness, wash his fingers on the right side of the altar while the chaplain pours water with the basins, although this is not ordinarily observed in the Roman Church.

He must take care that, from that moment, he touch nothing else with the two fingers of each hand—namely, the thumb and forefinger—with which he must handle the sacred Host, until after Communion. He should touch the chalice, paten, and other things that he may need to touch with his remaining fingers.

After washing and drying his fingers, he bows before the middle of the altar, saying the Prayer “Suscipe, sancta Trinitas” (“Receive, holy Trinity”), and so forth. When it has been said, he kisses the altar over the corporal, near the left side of the Host.

Then, rising and turning his face toward the people, he says “Orate, fratres” (“Pray, brethren”), and so forth. It should be noted that whenever the arrangement of the altar requires the pontiff, standing upon the altar, to turn toward the people, he must turn from the right side and turn back toward the altar by the same route. The exception is that when he has said “Orate, fratres,” he must turn back toward the altar from the left side.

Standing in the middle of the altar with his face turned toward the book and his hands raised as stated above, he says the Secret Prayers corresponding to those he said earlier, whether chanted or in a low voice.

[Note: They are now always said quietly.]

After the deacon has returned the thurible to the thurifer, he stands immediately behind the pontiff, between him and the subdeacon, ready for whatever service is required. The person who keeps the mitre may stand beside the deacon on the right; and, if the season requires it, he may hold a fan. The chaplain, or one of the other ministers, may likewise hold another fan to drive away flies. The acolytes and other clerics vested in surplices may stand around the subdeacon, ready to serve as necessary.

After the pontiff has said the Secret Prayers, he places his hands upon the altar and, raising his voice, says “Per omnia saecula saeculorum” (“World without end”).

### 304

When he says “Sursum corda” (“Lift up your hearts”), he raises his hands upward and continues the Preface. When it has been completed, he joins his hands at his breast and says “Sanctus, Sanctus” (“Holy, holy”), and so forth, in a low voice with the ministers assisting him.

Then, after the chaplain has presented him with the Missal, he kisses the images that ought to be depicted in that book before the Canon of the Mass. Afterwards, with his hands joined, he bows before the altar and begins quietly “Te igitur” (“Therefore, most merciful Father”), and so forth.

When he says “Ut accepta habeas” (“That you may graciously accept”), he rises and kisses the altar on the left side near the Host. Then he continues the Canon itself as it appears in the book, making the sign of the cross over the chalice and the Host together when he says “Haec dona” (“These gifts”), again when he says “Haec munera” (“These offerings”), and again when he says “Haec sancta sacrificia illibata” (“These holy, unblemished sacrifices”).

When he says “Memento, Domine, famulorum famularumque tuarum” (“Remember, O Lord, your servants, men and women”), he pauses briefly in the utterance of the words and holds before God in his mind the memory of the living for whom he intends to pray. After a short interval he resumes the text, “and of all those present,” and so forth.

When he reaches “Quam oblationem” (“Which offering”), and so forth, he makes the sign of the cross over the chalice and the Host. He does the same when saying “Benedictam” (“Blessed”), again when saying “Ascriptam” (“Enrolled”), and a third time when saying “Ratam” (“Approved”), and so forth. When he says “Ut nobis corpus” (“That it may become for us the Body”), he makes the sign over the Host alone.

Similarly, when he says “Sanguis” (“Blood”), he makes the sign of the cross over the chalice alone. When saying “Dilectissimi Filii” (“Most beloved Son”), and so forth, he joins his hands at his breast and looks upward briefly.

Then, saying “Qui pridie” (“Who, on the day before”), and so forth, he wipes the thumb and forefinger of each hand slightly over the corporal. With these fingers he takes the Host and does not raise it far above the altar. When saying “Elevatis oculis in caelum” (“With eyes lifted to heaven”), he raises his eyes. When saying “Benedixit” (“He blessed”), he makes the sign of the cross over the Host with his right hand, holding it in his left.

After this he again holds the Host with the fingers of both hands and pronounces the words of consecration distinctly and devoutly. When they have been said, he first adores the sacred divine Body, bowing his head. Then he reverently and attentively raises it high for the people to adore, and places the sacred Host, after it has been adored, in its proper place.

He must take care that from this point onward he keeps the thumb and forefinger of each hand joined together and does not separate these fingers until after Communion, except when he must touch the sacred Host itself or make signs.

[Note: This was already in use in the eleventh century, when the *Micrologus* imposes this rite in chapter 16: “Therefore the fingers are not to be drawn together, as some do out of excessive caution.”]

### 305

After placing the Host, as has been said, and saying “In like manner,” etc., he takes the chalice uncovered, as before, holding it with both hands for a short while slightly raised above the altar. When he says “He blessed,” he places the chalice on the altar and makes the sign of the cross over it with his right hand, holding it with his left. Then, taking it again with both hands and raising it slightly above the altar, he continues the words of consecration up to the words “for the remission of sins.” When these are finished, he bows his head slightly and adores the sacred blood of the Lord; then he raises it for the people to adore, as was said above concerning the Body. He should not hold either the Body or the Blood raised for a long time, but after a brief pause he should put it down, nevertheless making the elevations and depositions with due reverence and deliberation. [Col. 1166D]

As he puts down the chalice, he says: “As often as,” etc. After placing the chalice in its proper place, he continues, with his hands raised as before: “Therefore, mindful,” etc. When he says “a pure Host,” he makes the sign of the cross over the chalice and the Host together; he makes it again when saying “a holy Host,” and again when saying “an immaculate Host.” When he says “the holy Bread of eternal life,” he makes the sign over the Host alone. Similarly, when he says “and the chalice of everlasting salvation,” he makes the sign [Col. 1167A] over the chalice alone.

When he says “We humbly beseech you,” etc., with his hands crossed before his chest, so that the right arm is above the left, he inclines before the altar. When he is about to say “From this participation in the altar,” etc., he rises and kisses the altar on the left side near the Host. Then, saying “the most holy,” etc., he makes the sign of the cross over the Host, and another over the chalice when saying “and the Blood.” When he says “with every blessing,” etc., he signs his face.

When he says “Remember,” etc., he makes commemoration for the dead, just as was said above concerning the living. When he reaches “To us also, your sinful servants,” etc., as he says “To us,” he raises his voice slightly, without musical notation, and strikes his breast with the fingers of his right hand—not with the thumb and index finger, but with the other fingers. [Col. 1167B] He then continues what is written up to “Through whom you make all these things,” etc. As he says “You sanctify,” he makes the sign over the chalice and the Host alike; he makes it again when saying “You enliven,” and a third time when saying “You bless.”

After this, the deacon uncovers the chalice by removing the corporal covering it, and holds the chalice firmly by its stem with the fingers of his right hand. At that point the same pontiff reverently receives the Lord’s Body with his right hand and makes with it the sign of the cross over the mouth of the chalice, from lip to lip, saying “Through him.” He makes the same sign a little beside the chalice, saying “And in him.” When he says “To you, God,” etc., he makes with the same Host the sign of the cross between himself and the chalice, toward the lip of the chalice; then he makes the sign again toward the base [Col. 1167C] of the chalice, saying “In the unity of the Holy Spirit,” etc. After this, he places the Host in its proper place. The deacon covers the chalice with the corporal, kisses the altar and the pontiff’s right shoulder, and thus returns to his place behind the pontiff.

The pontiff, remaining in his place, then lowers his hands and says in a raised voice, “World without end.” He continues, “Let us pray. Instructed by saving precepts,” etc.; and when he begins “Our Father,” he raises his hands, as above.

When, after “Our Father,” he says the prayer “Deliver us,” etc., the deacon takes the paten from the subdeacon’s hand and gives it to the pontiff, kissing his hands. The pontiff receives it with his right hand; when he says “Through the intercession of blessed Mary, Mother of God,” etc., he makes the sign of the cross over himself with the paten. When he says “Graciously grant peace,” he kisses the upper part of the paten.

After this, while continuing the prayer, he takes the Host with his left hand and places the paten beside the chalice, where the Host had been. Holding the Host over the chalice with the fingers of both hands, he divides it in half. He places the half remaining in his right hand upon the paten, beside the previously mentioned half of the Host. Meanwhile, the deacon places the fingers of his right hand on the base of the chalice and holds it firmly.

The pontiff holds in his right hand the part of the Host remaining there, while keeping two joined fingers of his left hand over the chalice. He begins in a raised voice, “World without end.” When he says “May the peace of the Lord be always with us,” he makes with that part of the Host three signs of the cross inside the chalice. Then he places it in the chalice, saying “May this commixture,” etc.

After this, the deacon covers the chalice as before, and the pontiff, with his hands joined before his chest, says “Lamb of God” in a lowered voice together with the assisting ministers. He then says the prayer “Lord Jesus Christ, who said,” etc. After saying it, he kisses the altar on the left side near the chalice and Host.

While the pontiff says this prayer, the chaplain approaches the right side of the altar. After kissing the altar, the pontiff turns toward him and gives him the kiss of peace, saying “Peace be with you.” Before receiving it, the chaplain first bows reverently before the pontiff without genuflecting. After receiving the peace, he replies, “And with your spirit.” He then kisses the pontiff’s breast and adjusts his vestments as he sees fit.

Afterward he gives the peace to the deacon; the deacon gives it to the subdeacon; the subdeacon to the one serving the mitre; that man to one of the acolytes; and that acolyte to the others. Thus the peace is spread among those present.

After giving the peace to the deacon, the chaplain carries it to any bishops, other prelates, or princes present. If they are standing together, it is sufficient for him to give it to the one holding the first place; if they are standing in different places, he approaches them as he deems expedient. After giving them the peace, he returns to the pontiff. It must be observed that if there are communicants who will receive Communion at the end of the Mass, they must not receive the peace when it is given to the others.

After giving the peace to the chaplain as described above, the pontiff turns toward the altar, inclines before the Host and chalice, and, with his hands joined, reverently says the prayers “Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the living God,” etc., and the other prayers to be said before receiving the Body, as they are found in the book.

[Note: [Col. 1167] Micrologus, in chapter 18, considers this prayer to derive not from the Roman Order but from the tradition of religious.]

Then, taking with the fingers of his left hand the two parts of the Host lying on the paten, he receives them with complete devotion and reverence. While he has the sacred Body of the Lord in his mouth, he keeps his hands joined before his chest in the manner of one praying.

After the deacon uncovers the chalice, he may wipe the paten slightly over it with his right thumb, so that if any fragment of the Host remains on it, it may fall into the chalice. He then says the verses “How shall I repay,” etc., “I will take the chalice,” etc., and the other words to be said before receiving the Blood, as they are found in the book.

Finally, he receives the Blood together with the part of the Host in the chalice, with complete reverence and caution. After receiving it, he takes a little wine from the chalice, poured in by the subdeacon, and drinks it to wash his mouth.

Then, while saying the prayers “What we have received with the mouth,” etc., and “Your Body,” he holds over the chalice the fingers of both hands with which he touched the Host and washes them slightly, while the subdeacon again pours in wine. Before drinking it, he washes those fingers again with water, which the chaplain pours over them with the basins; and the water is poured out in a clean place.

[Note: In this period water was mixed with the wine in the chalice for what is called the purification, and the priest drank both together.]

After washing his fingers in the manner described, the pontiff dries his mouth with a wiping cloth, which is handed to him by the one serving the mitre. Afterward, having drunk the wine that was in the chalice, he wipes his mouth with the same cloth. Meanwhile, the deacon, having washed his fingers, folds the corporals and puts them away in the receptacle where they are to be kept.

After Communion has been completed, the deacon adjusts the pontiff’s vestments as necessary. The subdeacon washes the chalice with clean water, which is to be poured out in a clean place; afterward he dries it and wraps it decently, together with the paten, and gives it to the acolyte to put away. The acolytes remove the altar covering and put it away folded.

Finally, after the choir has sung the Communion, the pontiff says the prayers to be said after Communion. If at the beginning of Mass he said, in a low voice, prayers for himself, for the living, and for the dead, he says the corresponding prayers before saying the principal prayer. After saying these in a low voice, he kisses the altar near its center and, raising his hands, says in a raised voice, “The Lord be with you.” If the arrangement of the altar requires him to turn toward the people, the deacon and subdeacon also turn with him.

Before the pontiff turns toward the altar, the deacon turns and slightly draws the pontiff’s chasuble at its front. The pontiff, having turned toward the altar and standing near its right corner, continues the prayers that are to be said. When, after the final prayer, he says “Through our Lord,” etc., he returns to the center of the altar, and the chaplain kisses the altar and the pontiff’s right shoulder.

After the final prayer, when the pontiff says “World without end,” he joins his hands before his chest. Then, after again kissing the altar and raising his hands, he says “The Lord be with you.” If the arrangement of the altar requires him to turn toward the people, the deacon and subdeacon likewise turn.

After saying “The Lord be with you,” the pontiff turns back toward the altar, and the deacon says “Go, the Mass is ended,” or “Let us bless the Lord,” according to the season. If, according to the arrangement of the altar, the pontiff turned toward the people while saying “The Lord be with you,” the deacon also turns while saying “Go, the Mass is ended”; but if he says “Let us bless the Lord,” he must not turn.

After the choir has replied “Thanks be to God,” the pontiff says, with musical notation, “Blessed be the name of the Lord,” etc., and gives the blessing, signing the people and turning as he signs, according to what seems suitable to the character of the place. Finally, inclining before the altar, he says quietly the prayer “May it please you,” etc.

After saying this, he proceeds, accompanied by the chaplain and deacon, to the place where he is to remove his vestments, saying with the ministers the antiphon “The Three Children,” together with “Bless the Lord,” and “Praise the Lord in his holy places,” repeating the aforementioned antiphon, as well as the Lord’s Prayer with its versicles [Col. 1170A] and the prayers to be said after Mass.

If the pontiff is to remove his vestments beside the altar, he must not take the mitre when departing from the altar. If he is to go to the treasury or sacristy to disrobe, he goes there wearing the mitre, preceded by two candle-bearers and the subdeacon, and accompanied by the chaplain and deacon.

When he reaches the place where he is to disrobe, he stands before the faldstool upon the step. If he is wearing the pallium, the acolytes remove its pins; and the deacon removes the mitre from his head, if he has been wearing it. The chaplain removes the pontifical ring and gives it to an acolyte to put away.

Then the deacon and subdeacon, removing only their own maniples, divest him of all his other vestments in an orderly and modest manner, while the acolytes receive the garments. If the pontiff is wearing the pallium, when it is removed from him he kisses its cross on the back. Likewise, he kisses the stole and the pectoral cross when they are removed from him.

Finally, after the alb has been removed, he receives his ordinary cape, which one of his attendants should have ready. The chaplain, or another person who keeps his everyday ring, returns the ring to him.

When he has finished the prayers to be said after Mass, he begins Sext or another Hour that, according to the season, is to be said after Mass. Continuing it with the ministers, he sits on the faldstool. The vested subdeacon, as he was at Mass but without the maniple, together with one of the acolytes, removes the sandals and stockings he used in the ministry. An attendant assists and puts ordinary footwear on him. Once shod, he rises to finish the Hour.

Meanwhile, the deacon and the other ministers remove their vestments, except the acolytes, who must not remove their cottae until they have gathered and folded the sacred vestments. After the pontiff has finished the Hour, he may depart, while the acolytes remain with the chapel until they have it carried away.

### LIV. Rubric concerning the use of chasubles by the deacon and subdeacon

Concerning the foregoing, it should be known that when the deacon and subdeacon wear chasubles as required by the season, their use should be as follows.

The deacon, vested in alb and stole, and the subdeacon, in alb, serve the pontiff while he is vesting. Once he is vested, they take their maniples and chasubles. They do not fold the chasubles on the right or left, as priests do, but raise them over their arms from the front [Col. 1170D], [Note: From this one can see why these were called “folded chasubles.”] so that they can minister as necessary.

When the subdeacon is to go to read the Epistle, he removes the chasuble and reads the Epistle in his alb and maniple. On returning to the altar, he puts the chasuble on again and wears it until after the end of Mass.

Likewise, when the appointed time comes for the deacon to go to read the Gospel, he removes the chasuble. The acolytes fold it properly and place it over his left shoulder, fastening it under his right arm as well as they can, so that it descends from the left shoulder to the right side, as the deacon’s stole does. The deacon wears the chasuble in this manner while reading the Gospel and until the final prayer after Communion has been said.

Then, with the assistance of one of the acolytes, he removes the chasuble from his shoulder and puts it on as it was at the beginning of Mass. After Mass is finished, both he and the subdeacon come with the pontiff to the place where they are to disrobe, remove their chasubles, and serve the pontiff as he removes the sacred vestments. Everything else that the deacon and subdeacon do when wearing chasubles they should also do when wearing the dalmatic and tunicle.

### LV. Concerning the office of the chaplain who serves the mitre

It should also be known that on the principal feasts another minister may be added to the ministers mentioned above, one who serves the mitre and is vested in a cope like the chaplain. He should then accompany the pontiff on the left side together with the chaplain wherever the pontiff proceeds, and he should assist the pontiff on the left while the pontiff makes his confession.

He should always remove and replace the mitre for the pontiff, except that when the mitre is first placed on the pontiff’s head, the deacon must put it on; and the deacon must remove it when the pontiff approaches the altar, both at the beginning of Mass and after the Gospel, and when the pontiff returns to the secretarium wearing the mitre.

When the one serving the mitre accompanies the pontiff in the manner described, the deacon should precede the pontiff immediately. When the same minister serving the mitre stands beside the pontiff as he makes his confession, or while he is seated in his own chair, the deacon should stand on the right, behind the chaplain.

The one serving the mitre, when vested in a cope, should also offer his hands to the pontiff when the pontiff rises from his seat, and help him to rise. While the pontiff stands at the altar, he should stand behind him on the right side of the deacon; and, if the season requires it, he should hold a fan to drive away flies. He should also keep and offer the wiping cloth to the pontiff after Communion.

It should be understood, however, that when the one serving the mitre wears a cope, there must nevertheless be another person vested in a cotta who keeps the removed mitre and hands it over when it is to be put on.

On the days mentioned above, when the deacon and subdeacon wear chasubles, and when the one serving the mitre wears a cope, the clerics of the chapel should provide attendants to carry these vestments for them.

All the ministers should take care in these matters that each promptly, orderly, and reverently performs what belongs to his ministry—not slowly, disorderly, or rashly. If any of them is less experienced in the ministry assigned to him, those who are more experienced should teach him how to act, or even take his place.

For example, if the deacon does not know how to put on the mitre or adjust the pontiff’s vestments, the learned chaplain should do these things in his place. Likewise, if the subdeacon does not know how and when to prepare the chalice [Col. 1172A], the chaplain or deacon, if learned in the matter, should take his place. If the subdeacon does not know how to put the pontiff’s shoes on him, one of the acolytes should do this in his place, and so in other cases.

Whatever is assigned to the acolytes may be done by any clerics wearing cottae.

### LVI. Concerning the Communion of those who are ordained

In addition to the matters already mentioned, it should be noted that if the pontiff celebrates ordinations, those promoted to holy orders should receive Communion as a matter of propriety. They should be instructed beforehand to prepare themselves worthily. The acolytes should inquire which of them will receive Communion and announce this to the subdeacon when he is to prepare the chalice, so that he may prepare the Hosts that will be needed.

When, near the end of Mass, the pontiff has received the Blood, after his first ablution and before washing his fingers, those who are to receive Communion should approach him: first the priests, second the deacons, and third the subdeacons.

Two of the ministers extend the cloth covering the chalice, or another suitable cloth, and hold it stretched between the pontiff and the communicants. The pontiff takes the paten with his left hand, placing upon it a moderate number of consecrated Hosts. He then turns toward those who are to communicate and gives each the sacred Communion with his right hand, saying:

“May the Body of our Lord Jesus Christ preserve your soul unto eternal life. Amen.”

The one receiving Communion, kneeling, first kisses the pontiff’s hand and then receives the Host. If he is a priest or deacon, the pontiff, after giving him the Host, immediately receives him to the kiss of peace.

The subdeacon pours wine into the chalice and offers it to those who have received Communion, so that they may drink from it and wash their mouths. If there are many communicants, the deacon or another minister may hold another chalice containing wine and offer it to the communicants.

[Note: Thus the use of the sacred chalice in Communion had already ceased, even for the sacred ministers.]

### LVII. Concerning the Communion of bishops who are consecrated and abbots who are blessed

Moreover, if the pontiff is at some time to consecrate one or more bishops, the subdeacon should at the proper time prepare one or more Hosts for the person or persons to be consecrated. He should also ensure that only as much wine is placed in the chalice for making the Lord’s Blood as will suffice for the pontiff and for the person or persons being consecrated, who are to receive Communion from the Blood.

When the pontiff receives from the Blood, he should not consume it all, but should take part of it together with the part of the Host that was left in the chalice; he should leave the remainder in the chalice.

He gives the sacred Host to the consecrated person or persons who are to receive Communion, as was said above concerning ordained priests, except that they do not genuflect. If there are only one or two consecrated persons, and the arrangement of the place permits them to receive Communion while standing around the corners of the altar, as they stood while concelebrating the Mass, they should communicate there while standing. Otherwise, they should approach the pontiff himself and receive holy Communion.

Afterward, with the deacon offering them the chalice, they receive from the same Blood. They may take it with a reed, if one has been prepared; otherwise they should drink from the chalice itself.

The pontiff then washes his fingers with wine over the chalice and again washes his mouth with that wine. The consecrated person or persons should also take some of it to wash their mouths, using the aforementioned reed. However, the one who receives last, whether the Blood or the wine, after taking through the reed as much as he can, should drink the remainder without the reed, so that nothing remains in the chalice. He should nevertheless suck both ends of the reed in case anything has remained inside it. Finally, the subdeacon wipes the same reed with the cloth used to wipe the chalice.

When the pontiff blesses one or more abbots, Hosts should be prepared for them. At the proper time they approach the pontiff and receive Communion in the manner described above, but they do not receive from the Blood.

### LIX. Concerning Masses for the dead

When the pontiff celebrates solemnly for the dead, the following should be observed.

After the deacon has incensed the pontiff after the Offertory, he must not incense anyone else. Likewise, the Epistle and Gospel must not be read from the ambo or from a higher pulpit, but in the presbytery itself near the altar.

After the Gospel has been read, the Gospel book is not to be carried to the pontiff for him to kiss, as is done at other Masses.

After the pontiff has said “Lamb of God,” he must not say the prayer “Lord Jesus Christ,” etc., nor kiss the altar at that point, because the peace is not given.

“Blessed be the name of the Lord” is not to be said after Mass. Let everything else be done as at other Masses.

### LX. If a cardinal bishop celebrates in the pope’s presence

If a cardinal bishop celebrates in the pope’s presence, the following is chiefly to be observed.

First, after the pontiff, vested in the sacred vestments, has come to the altar with his ministers, he should look toward the lord pope, who, on arriving, should stand in the middle opposite the altar. The pontiff who is to celebrate, standing to the pope’s left, begins the Introit, etc., and continues in the usual manner with the Psalm “Judge me.” After it has been said, the lord pope says “Our help,” etc., makes his confession, and gives the absolution. After giving it, he goes to his seat, while the pontiff, saying “You will turn again,” etc., ascends to the altar.

The lord pope himself places incense in the thurible whenever it is to be placed there—that is, after the confession, before the Gospel, and after the Offertory. The thurifer carries the thurible with the boat to the lord pope, who should hand it to the assisting cardinal priest; after the lord pope has placed the incense in it, the cardinal priest returns the boat to the thurifer.

After the confession, when the pontiff has incensed the altar, and then the deacon has incensed the pontiff and altar, the thurifer receives the thurible from the deacon’s hand and carries it to the aforementioned cardinal. The cardinal incenses the lord pope and then returns the thurible to the thurifer. No others are to be incensed at the beginning of Mass.

After reading the Epistle, the subdeacon must not make a reverence to the celebrating pontiff, but should go to kiss the foot of the lord pope.

The deacon who is to read the Gospel should also go to the pope’s foot; after taking the book from the altar, he should ask the pope’s blessing.

After the Gospel has been read, the thurifer carrying the thurible should hand it to the aforementioned cardinal, who incenses the lord pope. Then the subdeacon approaches with the Gospel book and presents it open to the lord pope to kiss, unless the Mass is for the dead.

When the lord pope places incense in the thurible after the Offertory, the celebrating pontiff should omit the prayer “Through the intercession,” etc.

After the pontiff has incensed the offerings after the Offertory, the deacon takes the thurible and incenses the celebrating pontiff, then the altar. He then gives the thurible to an acolyte, who carries it to the cardinal assisting the lord pope, so that he may incense the lord pope, who alone is to be incensed if the Mass is for the dead.

At other Masses, after the lord pope has been incensed, the others are incensed in the following manner. After the cardinal has incensed the lord pope, he gives the thurible to the thurifer. The thurifer first incenses that same cardinal, then the cardinal deacon assisting the lord pope on the right, and afterward the deacon assisting on the left. He then incenses the other cardinals on the right of the lord pope, then those on the left, and afterward the other prelates and the rest of those present, as he deems expedient.

After the aforementioned cardinal assisting the lord pope has said “Lamb of God” together with the lord pope, he proceeds to the altar. When the celebrating pontiff turns to give the peace, the cardinal receives it from him and carries it to the lord pope. The lord pope gives it first to the deacon assisting on the right and afterward to the deacon assisting on the left. These two give it to two of the other cardinals assisting on either side, and they give it to the others. Thus the peace is spread among those present.

After Mass, unless it is for the dead, the lord pope himself says “Blessed be the name of the Lord.”

If the celebrating pontiff preaches, then after the sermon has ended, the deacon has said “I confess,” and the celebrant has given the indulgence, the lord pope says “By the prayers and merits,” etc., “The indulgence,” etc., “The blessing,” etc.

### LXI. Concerning Masses celebrated by the cardinal’s chaplain before the cardinal in his chapel

The following are the practices specially observed at Mass when it is celebrated in the presence of a cardinal in his chapel.

After the priest has vested in the sacred vestments, the cardinal approaches the center of the altar. The priest, standing to his left, begins the Introit and the other parts, and continues in the usual manner with the Psalm “Judge me.” When it is finished, the cardinal says “Our help,” etc., and makes his confession. After the absolution has been given, he goes to his place, and the priest ascends to the altar.

The acolyte serving at Mass carries the thurible, and one of the attending chaplains carries the boat with incense before the cardinal. The cardinal places incense in the thurible. The person holding the boat should kiss the cardinal’s hand when receiving the spoon and when returning it.

After the incense has been placed in the thurible, the acolyte carrying it brings it to the priest, who incenses the altar. After incensing it, he returns the thurible to the acolyte. The acolyte incenses the priest, then, standing beside him, says the Introit and “Lord, have mercy” with him. When these have been said, he incenses the altar around it, beginning near its center on the front side, proceeding to the right, and returning to the left. No others are to be incensed on this occasion.

After making his confession and coming to his place, the cardinal says the Introit and “Lord, have mercy” without music, standing with those attending him. When these have been said, he may sit. He does the same when the “Glory” and the “Creed” are said.

When the priest says “The Lord be with you,” the cardinal rises. If it is a weekday Mass or a Mass for the dead outside the Easter season, or outside the octaves of feasts that have octaves, he stands with his knees bent while all the prayers are said. On other days he stands upright, unless he wishes out of special devotion to kneel for a particular prayer. After the prayers have been said, he sits until the Gospel.

After the Epistle has been read, the reader approaches the cardinal with the Epistle book and kisses his hand, and the cardinal blesses him with the sign of the cross.

When the Gospel is to be read, the cardinal places incense in the thurible according to the procedure described above. Those who carry the thurible and boat with incense to him should take care that, if the cardinal is seated, they genuflect before him while he places the incense in the thurible. The acolyte should do likewise while incensing him. If the cardinal is standing, they must not genuflect.

The priest who is to read the Gospel, standing beside the altar and facing the cardinal, bows his head and asks for the blessing, saying quietly, “Command, lord, to bless.” The cardinal gives it, making the sign of the cross toward the priest and saying “May the Lord be,” etc. The priest then continues with the Gospel, while the acolyte stands with the thurible near the left side of the altar, where the Gospel is read.

After the Gospel has been read, the acolyte incenses the priest and the Gospel book together, moving the thurible toward both. Then he approaches the cardinal and incenses him alone. The aforementioned chaplain who carried the boat with incense brings the open Gospel book to the cardinal, who, standing with his head uncovered, kisses the book, unless the Mass is for the dead.

When the priest says before the Offertory, “The Lord be with you” and “Let us pray,” the cardinal stands. After these have been said, he may sit until the Preface.

While the Offertory is being sung, the cardinal again places incense in the manner described above. Once it has been placed, the acolyte brings the thurible to the priest. After incensing the offerings and the altar, the priest returns it to the acolyte. The acolyte first incenses the priest, then the altar, then the cardinal, and finally the other persons present, unless the Mass is for the dead. In that case, no one is to be incensed except the celebrating priest.

When the priest says “World without end” before the Preface, the cardinal rises. After the Preface has been said, he says “Holy,” etc., without music, with those attending him. If it is not a weekday Mass or a Mass for the dead, he remains standing until the elevation of the Lord’s Body.

When the elevation itself begins, he kneels and remains kneeling until after the consecration of the Blood; or, if he wishes, until “World without end” before “Our Father.”

If it is a weekday Mass or a Mass for the dead outside the Easter season, after the choir has sung “Holy,” he remains kneeling until “World without end,” which is said before “Lamb of God.” Nevertheless, with his head uncovered, he raises his face at the elevation of the Lord’s Body; keeping his face raised, he remains kneeling until after the consecration of the Blood, and he reverently adores both the Body and the Blood.

When the priest says “The peace of the Lord,” etc., the cardinal rises and says “Lamb of God” without music with those attending him. If it is not a Mass for the dead, the chaplain who carried the Gospel to the cardinal for him to kiss, after the priest has said “Lamb of God” quietly, approaches the altar, receives the peace from the priest, and draws back the front of his chasuble. He then approaches the cardinal, bows before him, and gives him the peace.

The cardinal gives the peace to the person attending him who is nearest. The chaplain gives it to the acolyte, and that acolyte gives it to the other acolyte, if there are two. Through the person who receives the peace from the cardinal, and finally through the chaplain and the acolyte or acolytes, the peace is spread among those present.

After giving the peace to the person attending him, as described, if it is a weekday Mass, the cardinal again prostrates himself until the priest has received the Lord’s Blood. He does the same after saying “Lamb of God” if it is a Mass for the dead; otherwise he remains standing.

After the priest has received the Blood, the cardinal may sit until the priest says “The Lord be with you.” Then he rises. At weekday Masses or Masses for the dead, he kneels while all the prayers after Communion are said; at other Masses he remains standing upright until the end of Mass.

When Mass is finished, if it is not a Mass for the dead, the cardinal says “Blessed be the name of the Lord” and gives the blessing. After giving it, unless the Mass of the Blessed Virgin Mary is being celebrated, the priest who celebrated, returning to the cardinal while still vested in the sacred vestments, kisses his hand, and the cardinal blesses him. If the aforementioned office is being celebrated, the priest may remove his vestments and, after doing so, come to kiss the cardinal’s hand and receive his blessing.

It should nevertheless be known that if a prelate is present at Mass whom the cardinal wishes to honor, then, at the cardinal’s indication, that prelate makes the confession. All the reverences ordinarily made to the cardinal are to be made to that prelate, and he is to give the blessing.

Some of the observances mentioned above may be omitted as the cardinal sees fit, especially at Masses celebrated with less solemnity or in haste.

### LXII. Concerning the ministry of the assisting cardinal priest to the supreme pontiff when Mass is celebrated before him in the chapel or hall

[Col. 1177A]

First of all, the aforementioned priest assisting him on the right side for the celebration is to lead the supreme pontiff from his chamber, or from his seat, to the altar. If two cardinal deacons are present, they alone are to lead him, while the cardinal priest always assists on the right at the beginning. When the supreme pontiff is before the altar, the cardinal priest himself—if no cardinal deacon is present—is to remove the mitre from his head and reverently hold it in his right hand. Then the priest who is to celebrate begins, “I will go in” (*Introibo*), and the Psalm “Judge me” (*Judica me*), etc. After these have been said, the supreme pontiff says, “Our help” (*Adjutorium*), etc., and makes his confession. [Col. 1177B] Subsequently, the cardinals present, the celebrating priest, and the attendants make their confession; when this has been done, the supreme pontiff gives the absolution, “May he have mercy” (*Misereatur*), etc.

The assisting cardinal priest, on the right side and holding the mitre in his right hand, is to take the mantle or cope around the middle with his left hand and hand it to the pope’s assistant on the left, so that the front part of the pope may be covered. When these things have been completed, while the celebrating priest begins to say, “You, O God” (*Deus tu*), etc., the cardinal returns the mitre to the pope. Then the supreme pontiff is led back in the prescribed manner to his seat. There, before the Introit is said by the pope, the cardinal priest offers the boat of incense that has been handed to him to the supreme pontiff.

Carefully observe that the spoon is always on that side of the boat which faces the cardinal priest. When the pope takes the spoon from the boat in order to place incense in the thurible held by the acolyte, the cardinal priest kisses his hand; likewise, he kisses his hand when the pope replaces the spoon in the boat. After the cardinal priest has returned the boat to the acolyte, the acolyte goes to the altar with the thurible. The celebrating priest receives the thurible offered to him by the acolyte and incenses the altar in the prescribed manner. After returning the thurible to the acolyte, the acolyte incenses the altar all around. He then goes to the supreme pontiff, and the cardinal priest, receiving the thurible from the acolyte, incenses the supreme pontiff, swinging the thurible three times before his breast—standing if the pope is standing, and kneeling if the pope is seated. After he has been incensed in this manner, the cardinal returns the thurible to the acolyte, who returns with it to the altar. Then, or shortly beforehand, the Introit of the Mass is said before the supreme pontiff. The cardinal priest, together with the lord pope and the attendants, continues the Introit and the “Lord, have mercy” (*Kyrie, eleison*), etc.

When the Epistle has been read, while the Gradual and the other appointed texts are being said, especially when the Alleluia before the Gospel is begun, the acolyte is to offer the cardinal priest the boat containing incense and the spoon. He receives it and offers it to the supreme pontiff, and the pontiff places incense in the thurible in the prescribed manner. The acolyte then returns to the altar with the boat and thurible, without any incensation. [Col. 1178A]

When the celebrating priest is about to proclaim the Gospel, the cardinal priest—if no cardinal deacon is present—is to remove the mitre from the pope’s head. When the priest says, “The continuation of the holy Gospel according to …” (*Sequentia sancti Evangelii secundum*), etc., while the response “Glory to you, O Lord” is being made, the acolyte incenses the priest, and the incensed priest continues the Gospel. After the Gospel has been said, he returns the mitre to the pope in the prescribed manner.

Then the acolyte returns from the altar with the thurible to the supreme pontiff. The cardinal priest again receives from the acolyte the thurible offered to him and incenses the pope, swinging it three times before his breast—standing if the pope is standing; but if he is seated, kneeling before him. After he has been incensed in this manner, the cardinal priest rises and returns the thurible to the acolyte, who returns with it to the altar. The celebrating priest then receives the thurible from the acolyte and incenses the altar. After returning it to the acolyte, the acolyte again incenses the altar all around. [Col. 1178B]

When the altar has been incensed in this manner, the acolyte again returns with the thurible to the supreme pontiff. The cardinal priest again receives from the acolyte the boat containing incense and the spoon, offers the boat to the supreme pontiff in the prescribed manner, and the pope again places incense in the thurible. After the incense has been placed in it, the cardinal priest receives the thurible offered to him by the acolyte and again incenses the supreme pontiff in the prescribed manner. After incensing him, he returns the thurible to the acolyte and returns to his place.

The acolyte then incenses the cardinal priest and the other cardinals present there, as well as the other attendants, in due order. After this incensation has been completed, the acolyte returns to the altar and hands the thurible to the cleric or sacristan of the chapel. From that cleric he receives basins with water and brings the water to the celebrating priest for washing his hands. After the hands have been washed, the subdeacon offers the priest a towel with which to dry them.

When the elevation of the Body of Christ is to take place, the supreme pontiff descends from his seat to the faldstool. The cardinal priest—if no cardinal deacon is present—removes the mitre from his head in the prescribed manner. Assisting on the right, he kneels during the elevation of the Body of Christ and remains kneeling until the elevation of the Blood has been completed. When this elevation has taken place and the pope has risen, the cardinal priest returns the mitre to him, and the pontiff returns to his seat. [Col. 1178D]

When the celebrating priest has finished the prayer “Deliver us, we beseech you, O Lord” (*Libera nos, quaesumus, Domine*), etc., and has performed the fraction—before he begins to say, or at least when he begins to say, “For ever and ever” (*Per omnia saecula saeculorum*), etc.—the cardinal priest removes the mitre from the pope’s head and, assisting him, says the “Lamb of God” (*Agnus Dei*) three times. When this has been said, he hands the mitre to the pope’s assistant on the left side, goes to the altar, and kisses it on the right side. After making a slight bow to the celebrating priest, he receives the kiss of peace from him, draws the chasuble slightly downward at the front, and then returns to the supreme pontiff. Having made a profound inclination before him, but without kneeling, he gives the *prex* to the pontiff. Receiving the mitre from the person to whom he had handed it, he returns to his place. There he gives the peace to the subdeacon who read the Epistle, and that subdeacon gives it to the others. The supreme pontiff gives the peace to all the cardinals standing there, and after the peace has been given, the cardinal priest returns the mitre to the pope. [Col. 1179A]

After the celebrating priest has said the Communion and the postcommunions or prayers, and “Go, the Mass is ended” (*Ite, Missa est*) or “Let us bless the Lord” (*Benedicamus Domino*), the cardinal priest removes the mitre from the pope’s head. When the pope begins to say, “Blessed be the name of the Lord” (*Sit nomen Domini benedictum*), etc., the chamberlain, kneeling before the standing pope, receives the mantle on the right side and covers the front of the pope as far as the portion of the mantle on the left. [Col. 1179B] After the pope has given the Blessing, said the Lord’s Prayer secretly, and said, “Bless” (*Benedicite*) and “May the Lord bless us” (*Dominus nos benedicat*), etc., the cardinal priest returns the mitre, kissing the pope’s hand in the prescribed manner.

It should be understood that whenever a cardinal deacon is present, he always removes the mitre from the pope’s head and returns it. It should likewise be understood that whenever a cardinal bishop is present for the office described above, that bishop performs the office or ministry assigned above to the cardinal priest.

It should also be understood that whenever the cardinal priest returns the mitre to the pope, he kisses his hand. Furthermore, whenever the pope uses a cope or mantle bearing gold embroidery with pearls during such a Mass, the cardinal serving him always places the mitre on the pope’s head with his own hands. When he does not have such gold embroidery with pearls, the cardinal serving him hands the mitre to the pope in the prescribed manner. [Col. 1179C]

### LXII. The occasions on which and the times when the mitre is removed from the pope’s head while he celebrates

From what has been said above it is clear that the cardinal priest removes the mitre from the pope’s head five times.

First, when the pope has been led to the altar so that the confession may be made; the mitre is returned to him when, after the confession has been made, he is led back to his seat.

Second, it is removed when the Gospel is to be said; it is returned after the Gospel has been said, the pope has been incensed, and the Gospel book has been kissed.

Third, it is removed during the elevation of the Body of Christ; it is returned when, after the elevation of the Blood has been completed, the pope is led back to his seat.

Fourth, it is removed when the “Lamb of God” is to be said; it is returned after the peace has been given to the supreme pontiff. [Col. 1179D]

Fifth, it is removed when, after the office has been completed, the pope is to say, “Blessed be the name of the Lord” (*Sit nomen Domini benedictum*), etc.; it is returned after the pope has given the Blessing and said, “May he bless” (*Benedicat*), etc.

### LXIII. The incensation of the pope during Mass

It is likewise clear from what has been said above that the cardinal priest offers the pope the boat containing incense and the spoon, which have been handed to him by the acolyte, three times, and incenses the pope three times.

First, after the confession has been made and the pope has been led back to his seat, the altar is incensed first in the prescribed manner, and then the cardinal priest incenses the pope.

Second, he brings forward the boat before the Gospel; at that time the pope is not incensed, but only after the Gospel has been said.

Third, he offers the boat after the celebrating priest has incensed the altar, likewise after the prayer “Come, O Sanctifier” (*Veni, sanctificator*), etc. The cardinal priest then incenses the pope in the prescribed manner; afterward the cardinal priest and the other attendants are incensed.

### LXIV. The use of the mitre

The Roman Church does not use the gold-embroidered mitre from Advent until the feast of the Nativity of the Lord, except that the lord pope uses it on Gaudete Sunday. Nor does it use it from Septuagesima until Holy Thursday, except that the lord pope uses it on the Fourth Sunday of Lent, when “Rejoice, Jerusalem” (*Laetare, Jerusalem*) is sung. Nor is it used on any of the vigils on which a fast is observed, on any of the Ember Days, on the Rogations, in the litanies, [Col. 1180B] or in offices for the dead.

### LXV. On which days “Glory to God in the highest” and the Creed are said

From Advent Sunday until the Nativity of the Lord, “Glory to God in the highest” (*Gloria in excelsis Deo*) is not sung except on a feast with nine lessons. From Septuagesima until Easter it is likewise not sung except on feasts with nine lessons, apart from Holy Thursday. On all other Sundays and feast days it is generally sung.

Note also that if, during the week, a Mass of Sunday, of the Cross, or of the Blessed Virgin is sung, “Glory to God in the highest” is not said. Note also that from Easter until the Octave of Pentecost, “Glory to God in the highest” is said. If a feast with nine lessons falls on a Sunday and the feast is observed, we say “I believe in one God” (*Credo in unum Deum*) not because of the feast, but because it is Sunday. Note that the Gloria is always said at Mass when *Te Deum laudamus* is said at Matins, as “Go, the Mass is ended” is said according to the custom of the Roman Church.

The Creed, “I believe in one God” (*Credo in unum Deum*), is sung on the following days: on every Sunday throughout the year; on Epiphany and for eight days thereafter; on the Conversion of Saint Paul; on the Purification of the Blessed Mary; on her Annunciation; on the Chair of Saint Peter; on Holy Thursday; on the feast of the Resurrection and for eight days thereafter; on the octave of Saint John that falls within the octave of the Apostles; at Pentecost and for eight days thereafter; on the feast of Saint John before the Latin Gate; on the feast of the Apostles Peter and Paul and for eight days thereafter; on the feast of Saint Peter in Chains; on the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin [Col. 1180D] and for eight days thereafter; on the octave of Saint Lawrence, because it falls within the octave of the Blessed Virgin; on the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin and for eight days thereafter; on the feasts of the Angels; on the feast of the Holy Cross; on the feast of All Saints; on the feasts of the Apostles and Evangelists and of Saint Barnabas; and at all consecrations of churches, altars, and pontiffs.

### LXVI. On the office of the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord in the office of the priest

On the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord, the station is at Saint Mary Major. Until now the Roman pontiffs have been accustomed to go to Saint Mary Major, sing the Mass of the vigil there, dine there, and sing Vespers after dinner. When Vespers had been completed, refreshments were served in the hall; the lord pope remained and spent the night there, with the entire apparatus of the curia stationed there. First, the bishop or cardinal priest who assists the lord pope on Christmas night is to accompany the lord pope, as is customary, wearing a white cope. He is then to hold the mitre while “O Lord, open my lips” (*Domine, labia*), etc., and “O God, come to my assistance” (*Deus in adjutorium*) are begun, and to stand there for the office as is customary.

When the third antiphon is sung for the last time, he takes a box of incense from the hand of the acolyte and incenses the lord pope, as is customary. He then goes to the altar and incenses it, and afterward the lord pope, and returns the thurible to the acolyte. He does the same in the second and third nocturns. One cardinal priest is to read the fourth lesson.

If he is to sing Mass at cockcrow or in the morning, he first puts on all the white vestments and goes to the altar. Standing to the pope’s left, he begins by saying “I will go in” (*Introibo*) and the Psalm “Judge me” (*Judica*). Then “I will go in” is repeated, and after those standing around have responded, “To God” (*Ad Deum*), etc., the lord pope says the versicle “Our help” (*Adjutorium*), etc., and makes the confession and absolution. Then the priest says the versicle “You will turn again, O God” (*Deus tu conversus*), etc., and, before the Introit is begun, incenses the altar. He then returns to his seat, says the Introit and “Lord, have mercy,” and continues the Mass in its proper order.

At the first nocturn, three clerics of the same church read the three lessons, and the singers of that church sing the three Responsories. One of the cardinal priests reads the fourth lesson; a judge or hebdomadary reads the fifth; a deacon of the Roman curia reads the sixth; a cardinal deacon who serves the pope on the left reads the seventh lesson, the homily; the other cardinal deacon reads another homily. The lord pope reads the ninth lesson, in which he says, “Bid us, lord, give a blessing” (*Jube, domne, benedicere*); no one gives him a blessing, except that everyone responds in a loud voice, “Amen.” When the lesson has ended, *Te Deum laudamus* is said. When it has ended, the lord pope says the prayer, namely, “Grant, we beseech you” (*Concede, quaesumus*).

From the ancient Ceremonial of the lord [Note: [Col. 1181D] That is, from the example of the Ceremonial of Peter Amelius, bishop of Senigallia, which once belonged to William [Col. 1182D] de Stoutville, archbishop of Rouen and cardinal] of Rouen, de Stoutville.

At these Matins the pope comes wearing a red scarlet woolen cape, closed to the middle of the breast, with a knotted cap beneath the chin on account of the cold. [Col. 1181D] He sits without a mitre during these Matins, which he begins in the customary manner. The cardinal deacons do not stand before the altar but sit in their capes according to their order.

The first two lessons are read by acolytes or chapel clerics; the third is read by a junior cleric of the treasury chamber; the fourth by the junior cardinal priest; the fifth by the most distinguished person by birth who is then in the curia; the sixth by the prior of the subdeacons; the seventh by the junior cardinal deacon who stands to the pope’s left; the eighth by the senior cardinal deacon who stands to the pope’s right; and the ninth by the pope. In the ninth he says only, “Bid us, lord, give a blessing,” and the singers respond, “Amen.”

Note that the cardinals who read the lessons on this night do not come to kiss the pope’s foot. Note also that the Matins are not assigned, but all three Masses are said, or are to be said, by the pope: “nor is there …,” etc. [Col. 1182A]

### LXVII. On the Mass of the night of the Nativity of the Lord

When all these things have been completed, the lord pope prepares himself to sing Mass at the Crib. Whatever is offered during the time the lord pope celebrates—whether into his hands, at his feet, or upon the altar—belongs to the chaplains, except for the bread, which belongs to the acolytes if they wish to receive it.
