At this Mass the lord pope uses the Phrygian mitre.

The Roman Church does not use the Phrygian mitre from Advent until the feast of the Nativity of the Lord, except that the lord pope uses it on Gaudete Sunday. Nor does it use it from Septuagesima until Holy Monday, except that the lord [Col. 1182B] pope uses it on the Fourth Sunday of Lent, when “Rejoice, Jerusalem” (*Laetare, Jerusalem*) is sung. Nor is it used on any vigils on which a fast is observed, on the Ember Days, on the Rogations, in the litanies, or in offices for the dead. At the Mass of the night, “Glory to God in the highest,” the Creed, the Preface “For through the mystery of the incarnate Word” (*Quia per incarnati*), etc., and the *Communicantes* are said.

In the Ceremonial of the lord cardinal of Rouen, de Stoutville, it is recorded as follows.

At the present Mass the pontiff alone receives Communion, and he does so at the altar. He drinks the Blood without a reed and nothing else, because he has to celebrate the Mass of the third hour. He nevertheless wipes the chalice carefully with his fingers and washes his fingers with water, as is customary at private Masses. Those who wish receive Communion. On the night of the Nativity of the Lord [Col. 1182C] the station is at the Crib. When the Mass office has been completed, Lauds are sung, and then he goes to rest.

If an emperor or king is in the curia on this night, the sacristan and the clerics present him with the book of readings. In it he is to read the fifth lesson, and they courteously instruct him concerning the ceremonies to be observed when asking for the Blessing, when lifting the sword in its scabbard, drawing it, and brandishing it, as well as concerning the cope, cap, and other matters.

The sacristan and the chamber clerics are also to prepare a sword with scabbard, belt, and cap in accordance with the prince’s rank. During the singing of the fourth Responsory, if he is an emperor or king, the chamberlain, sacristan, and chapel clerics prepare a beautiful white cope. They remove his hood before the lectern and put the cope on him like a cloak, so that the opening is at his right hand; they gird him with the sword, and he himself draws it and brandishes it. They place the cap on his head. He inclines his head toward the pope and asks for the Blessing, then reads the lesson before those standing there. After it has been read, they lead him, so dressed, with the cap on his head and the drawn sword in his hand, to kiss the pope’s foot, and each returns to his place.

It should also be noted that if the pope is in Rome, he is to celebrate this Mass at the Lord’s Crib, sing Vespers there in the evening, and take refreshments in the hall with the clerics and nobles of the City. [Col. 1183A]

### LXVIII. How Matins and Mass are conducted before the pope on the night of the Nativity of the Lord: rubric

First, the bishop or cardinal priest who assists the lord pope on the night of the Nativity of the Lord is to accompany the lord pope to the altar, as is customary, wearing a white cope. He is then to hold the mitre while “O Lord, open my lips” (*Domine, labia mea aperies*) and “O God, come to my assistance” (*Deus, in adjutorium*) are begun, and to stand before him for the office, as is customary.

When the third antiphon is sung for the last time, he takes a box of incense from the hand of the acolyte who ministers to the lord pope, as is customary. He then goes to the altar, incenses the altar, and afterward the lord pope, and returns the thurible to the acolyte. He does the same in the second and third nocturns. One cardinal priest is to read the fourth lesson.

If he is to sing Mass at cockcrow or in the morning, he first puts on all the white vestments and comes to the altar. Standing to the left of the lord pope, he begins “I will go in” (*Introibo*) and the Psalm “Judge me” (*Judica me*), etc. He then repeats “I will go in,” and after those standing around have responded, “To God” (*Ad Deum*), etc., the lord pope says “Our help” (*Adjutorium*), etc., and makes the confession and absolution. Then the priest says “You will turn again, O God” (*Deus, tu conversus*), etc.; before he begins the Introit, he incenses the altar, then returns to his seat, says the Introit and “Lord, have mercy,” and continues the Mass in its proper order.

### LXIX. On the Mass in the morning of the Nativity of the Lord

At the very earliest morning, wearing the Mass vestments, [Col. 1183C] he goes to Saint Anastasia to celebrate the second Mass there, with the Gloria and the Creed, and uses the Phrygian mitre. The station is at Saint Anastasia. After the Mass has ended, he returns to Saint Mary Major and enters the sacristy with the cardinal bishops, cardinal deacons and subdeacons, and the remaining orders, and they say Terce. When it has been said, they solemnly put on the white vestments and go processionally to the altar, as is customary.

Note that whenever the pope celebrates solemnly, seven candles are always to be placed on the altar, except on a few days; the curia is to provide them. Then the lord pope begins the Mass, and after the first prayer his praises are made, as they are found in the *Polyptych*. When the praises have ended, the Latin Epistle is read first and afterward the Greek; likewise, the Latin Gospel and the Greek Gospel are read. After the Gospel has been said, the cardinal deacon returns to the altar and does not wait for the Greek deacon, although they went together with the cardinal, following him; he continues the pope’s Mass in its proper order. [Col. 1183D]

### LXX. On the last Mass on the day of the Nativity of the Lord

On the day of the Nativity of the Lord the station is at Saint Mary Major. When the Mass has been completed, at the door of that church he receives the *regnum* from the prior of the cardinal deacons or from the chief marshal, and wears it on his head as far as the steps of the palace. Then the judges and advocates come to meet him beneath the steps in the portico and offer him their praises, as is written in the book of the *Polyptych*. There the lord pope descends, removes the *regnum*, and takes the mitre. Finally, the judges lead him to the place where the presbyterium is given.

There they remove the chasuble from him. After a mantle has been placed over his shoulders, he sits in the consistory or on the chair and, with his own hands, gives the presbyterium.

It should be understood that on that day the chaplains receive one gold *malachinus* as the presbyterium, and only that much at each coronation. After giving the presbyterium, he goes, so dressed, to the table. On that same day a cardinal deacon wearing a cope is accustomed to read at table. Near the end of the Mass, the schola cantorum is to sing the sequence. [Col. 1184B]

From the ancient Ceremonial of the lord cardinal of Rouen, de Stoutville.

If he is in the City, the Roman pontiff is accustomed to celebrate the Mass at dawn. Leaving Saint Mary Major very early, wearing the Mass vestments, he goes to Saint Anastasia and celebrates there. At this Mass the Creed “in God” (*Credo in Deum*) and “Glory to God in the highest” are said; *Laetatus sum* is not said. The offerings are as at the other Mass of midnight. The pope alone also receives Communion, as at the first Mass. When it has ended, he returns, still dressed in the vestments, to Saint Mary Major and, after removing the vestments, rests briefly in his chamber.

At the appropriate hour he enters the sacristy or vesting room with the bishops, cardinal priests, cardinal deacons, chaplains, subdeacons, and the remaining orders. They sing Terce. When it has been said, they solemnly dress him in the sacred white vestments, and each proceeds in his proper order to the altar with the cross and seven candles; the curia is to provide them, etc. [Col. 1184C]

If the pope is not in the City, the cardinal who holds the title of Saint Anastasia is accustomed to celebrate this Mass. In his absence, if the pope is not celebrating, the prior of the cardinal priests does so, etc.

It should be noted that if the pope wished to celebrate these two Masses, he could celebrate both without removing the sacred vestments. But for the sake of propriety and because of the fatigue of the night, it is reasonable that there should be some interval between them, according to what the time permits and as the brevity of the time and day requires.

[Note: [Col. 1183] This passage concerning the propriety of an interval between the Christmas Masses should be noted.]

Note that if the pope stands at Lauds clothed in the sacred vestments, the cardinal who serves him is to incense the altar.

At this second Mass he gives Communion to all the cardinal deacons, protonotaries, table companions, and auditors, and to all attendants who have not been constituted in episcopal dignity, since those who have such dignity are required to celebrate separately. At this Communion, and at the Mass on Easter Day, three large chalices are prepared: one for the consecration, another from which the pope drinks the wine, and another for those receiving Communion. After receiving the Eucharist, they take wine from the hand of one of the acolytes. The offerings are divided as is noted elsewhere, folio 49.

At Second Vespers the pope comes in a red cope of … and a gold-embroidered mitre; the subdeacon gives the chapter, the singers give the hymn, and the pope gives the prayer. [Col. 1185A]

### LXXI. On what is to be observed concerning the Introit of the Mass while the pope celebrates, and on the second Mass of the Nativity of the Lord: rubric

The lord pope, dressed in all the pontifical vestments, says before the altar the versicle, “I will go in to the altar of God” (*Introibo ad altare Dei*); the response is, “To God, who gives joy to my youth” (*Ad Deum qui laetificat juventutem meam*). Then the pope begins Psalm 42, “Judge me, O God” (*Judica me, Deus*), and it is completed both by him and by those standing around. Finally, he repeats, “I will go in to the altar of God”; the response is, “To God,” etc.

Afterward the pope says, “Our help,” etc.; the response is, “Who made,” etc. Finally the pope says:

“I confess to almighty God, to blessed Mary ever-virgin, to blessed Michael the archangel, to blessed John the Baptist, to the holy Apostles Peter and Paul, to all the saints, and to you, brother, that I have sinned exceedingly in thought, delight, consent, word, and deed: through my fault, through my fault, through my most grievous fault. Therefore I ask blessed Mary ever-virgin, blessed Michael the archangel, blessed John the Baptist, the holy Apostles Peter and Paul, all the saints, and you, brother, to pray for me to the Lord our God.”

Then those standing around say:

“May almighty God have mercy on you, and, having forgiven your sins, may he lead you to eternal life.”

The response is, “Amen.”

Next they say the Confession as above. Finally the pope says:

“Through the prayers and merits of blessed Mary ever-virgin, of blessed Michael the archangel, of blessed John the Baptist, of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul, and of all the saints, may almighty God have mercy on you, and, having forgiven your sins, may he lead you to eternal life.”

The response is, “Amen.”

Next the pope says:

“May almighty and merciful God grant you indulgence, absolution, and remission of your sins.”

The response is, “Amen.”

Afterward the pope places incense in the thurible. Finally he says the following versicles:

“Turn again, O God” (*Deus tu conversus*), etc.

“And your people” (*Et plebs tua*), etc.

“Show us” (*Ostende nobis*), etc.

“And your salvation” (*Et salutare tuum*), etc.

“O Lord, hear” (*Domine, exaudi*), etc.

“And let my cry” (*Et clamor*), etc.

“The Lord be with you.”

The response is, “And with your spirit.”

Next the pope says, “Let us pray,” and says the prayer:

“Take away from us, we beseech you, O Lord, all our iniquities, that we may be worthy to enter with pure minds into the holy of holies, through Christ our Lord.”

The response is, “Amen.”

Then, bowing, he says the following prayer silently:

“Lord, we pray you, by the merits of your saints whose relics are here, and of all the saints, that you may deign to forgive all my sins.”

Finally, he kisses the altar in the middle, and afterward the Gospel, which is to be sung that day and is offered to him by the subdeacon on the left side of the altar. Having done this, he turns to the cardinal deacon who serves him, receives the thurible from that cardinal’s hand, and incenses the altar. After it has been incensed, he returns the thurible to the cardinal deacon. Finally, he receives all the cardinal deacons for the kiss of peace.

Then he goes to his seat and, sitting, begins the Introit: “Today light will shine upon us, for the Lord has been born for us” (*Lux fulgebit hodie super nos, quia natus est nobis*), etc. Psalm: “The Lord reigns; he is clothed with beauty” (*Dominus regnavit, decorem*), etc. [Col. 1186A] Versicle: “Glory to the Father” (*Gloria Patri*), completing it, and “Lord, have mercy,” together with the cardinals assisting him.

Then he sits in his seat. After the choir has sung the Introit and “Lord, have mercy,” he says “Glory to God in the highest.” When the choir has sung it, he says while standing, facing the people, “Peace be with you” (*Pax vobis*). Then he says the prayer:

“Grant, we beseech you, almighty God, that what we are illumined by the new light of your incarnate Word may shine forth in our works, which by faith shines in the mind, through the same [Lord].”

Another prayer for Saint Anastasia:

“Grant, we beseech you, almighty God, that we who celebrate the solemnity of blessed Anastasia, your martyr, may experience her patronage with you, through [Christ our Lord].”

Afterward he pauses in his seat.

“Reading of the Epistle of blessed Paul the Apostle to Titus. Dearly beloved, the kindness and humanity of our Savior God has appeared,” etc.

After the Epistle has been said and the subdeacon has kissed the pope’s foot, the pope signs the Gradual for him:

“Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (*Benedictus qui venit in nomine Domini*).

“God is the Lord, and he has shone upon us” (*Deus Dominus, et illuxit nobis*).

“From the Lord it has been done, and it is marvelous,” etc.

“The Lord reigns; he is clothed with beauty,” etc.

After the choir has sung the Gradual and the first Alleluia, he gives the Blessing to the cardinal deacon who is to read the Gospel as he goes to the pope’s foot, signing him and saying:

“May the Lord be in your heart and on your lips, so that you may worthily and suitably proclaim his Gospel.”

Then he places incense in the thurible, signing it once with the sign of the cross after he has placed the incense in it. Again, when the same deacon asks the pope for the Blessing at the altar, the pope signs him while seated. But when the Gospel is begun, the pope stands with his head uncovered.

“The Gospel according to Mark. At that time the shepherds were speaking to one another,” etc. [Col. 1186C]

When this has been said, he kisses the Gospel that the subdeacon offers to him.

Then he says, “I believe in one God” (*Credo in unum Deum*), etc. After the choir has said it, he says, “The Lord be with you”; the response is, “And with your spirit.” Then he says, “Let us pray,” and pauses in his seat.

“Offertory: God has established the world’s foundation” (*Deus firmavit orbem terrae*), etc.

While the choir sings the Offertory, he washes his hands while seated. When his hands have been washed and the Offertory has been sung, he goes to the altar and there receives the paten with the Host, which the cardinal deacon offers to him. Raising it slightly, he says this prayer:

“Receive, holy Father, almighty and eternal God, this spotless Host, which I, your unworthy servant, offer to you, my God,” etc.

Then he places the Host with the paten on the corporal on the left side, and places the paten on the right beside the corporal. [Col. 1186D]

Afterward he receives the cruet with water from the hand of the subdeacon and pours water into the chalice, saying:

“O God, who wonderfully formed the dignity of human nature,” etc.

Then he returns the cruet to the subdeacon. He next signs once over the chalice. While the cardinal deacon places the chalice on the corporal in its proper place, the pope says:

“We offer you, O Lord, the chalice of salvation,” etc.

“May the gift ascend with the fragrance of sweetness.”

When the aforementioned cardinal covers the chalice, the pope says the antiphon:

“In a spirit of humility” (*In spiritu humilitatis*), etc.

Next he says:

“Come, O Sanctifier” (*Veni, sanctificator*), etc.,

signing over the Host and chalice. Then he turns to the cardinal deacon and blesses the incense, signing it and saying:

“May you be sanctified by him in whose honor you will be burned.”

Then he receives the thurible from the hands of the cardinal and incenses the chalice and Host in the form of a cross, saying:

“May this incense, +blessed by you, ascend to you, +O Lord, and may your mercy descend +upon us.

“Let my prayer be directed,” etc.

“The lifting up of my hands,” etc.

“Set, O Lord, a guard over my mouth,” etc.

“And let not my heart incline,” etc.

Continuing, he incenses the crosses and images standing upon the altar, and the upper surface of the altar itself. [Note: [Col. 1187D] The same applies to the crosses below in the Mass of Saint Stephen. There were therefore several crosses upon the altar, namely the processional cross mentioned above, and those which were otherwise required to be placed upon the altar.] Then he again incenses over the Host and chalice.

Afterward he returns the thurible to the cardinal mentioned above, saying:

“May the Lord kindle in us the fire of his love and the flame of eternal charity. Amen.”

Then, bowing before the altar, he says this prayer:

“Receive, holy Trinity, this offering,” [Col. 1187B] etc.

Next he rises and kisses the altar in the middle. Then, facing the people, he says:

“Pray, brothers” (*Orate, fratres*), etc.

Those standing around respond:

“May the Lord receive the sacrifice,” etc.

Next he says the Secret:

“Our gifts, we beseech you, O Lord,” etc.

Another Secret:

“Receive, we beseech you, O Lord, these gifts,” etc.

From the Ceremonial of the cardinal of Rouen.

Whatever is offered, whether at the feet or upon the altar, is to be paid to the chamber chaplains, except for the bread and wine, which belong to the acolytes; and so with everything that comes upon the altar throughout the Mass. This procedure is always to be observed in all papal Masses, as is contained in the book of the *Polyptych of the Saints*, which is called that of James Gaetani.

The priests, together with the chaplains, receive twelve denarii from the pope, and this is called the presbyterium; half of it belongs to the sacristan according to the ordinance of Urban. On this day and the following day the cardinals are not accustomed to come to show reverence to the pope, since they are not obliged to do so twice in one day. But what has been observed elsewhere you will find there, except that those three junior cardinal priests, etc., never fail to come.

The lord Urban VI ordained the contrary. But at the second Mass, the Mass at dawn, they do not come; they come at the first and third Blessing.

For ever and ever; the response is: Amen. The Lord be with you. And with your spirit. Lift up your hearts; response: We have them lifted up to the Lord. Let us give thanks to the Lord our God; response: It is fitting and right. It is truly fitting and right, just and salutary, that we should always and [Col. 1187D] everywhere give you thanks, holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God, because through the mystery of the incarnate Word, etc.

Therefore, most merciful Father, through Jesus Christ your Son, our Lord, we humbly pray and ask you: here he rises, kisses the altar, and, raising his hands, says: That you may deign to accept and bless; here he signs three times both over the Host and over the chalice:

These + gifts, these + offerings, these + holy and unblemished sacrifices, which first of all we offer to you for your holy catholic Church; may you deign to grant her peace, guard her, unite her, and govern her throughout the whole world, together with your servant N., our pope, and N., our bishop, and all orthodox believers, [Col. 1188A] 333 and all who uphold the catholic and apostolic faith.

### Commemoration for the Living

Remember, O Lord, your servants N. and N., and all those present, whose faith is known to you and whose devotion is manifest; for them we offer you, or who themselves offer you, this sacrifice of praise for themselves and all who belong to them, for the redemption of their souls, for the hope of their salvation and well-being; and they render their vows to you, the eternal, living, and true God.

### Within the Canon

In communion and celebrating the most sacred day on which the inviolate virginity of blessed Mary brought forth the Savior for this world, and venerating first of all the memory of the same glorious ever-virgin Mary, Mother of the same God and our Lord Jesus Christ, and also of your blessed apostles and martyrs Peter and Paul, Andrew, James, John, Thomas, James, Philip, Bartholomew, Matthew, Simon, Thaddeus, Linus, Cletus, Clement, Sixtus, Cornelius, Cyprian, Lawrence, Chrysogonus, John and Paul, Cosmas and Damian, and of all your saints, grant that by their merits and prayers we may in all things be defended by the help of your protection. Through the same Christ our Lord. Amen.

### Another Prayer within the Canon

Therefore, O Lord, we ask you graciously to accept this offering of our service and also of your whole household; order our days in your peace, command that we be rescued from eternal damnation, and numbered among the flock of your elect. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

Then he says: This offering, O God, we ask you to deign in every respect—here he signs three times together both over the Host and over the chalice—to make + blessed, + inscribed, + ratified, reasonable and acceptable, so that it may become for us. Here he signs once separately over the Host and afterward over the chalice, saying: + the Body and + the Blood of your most beloved Son, our Lord Jesus Christ.

Here, reverently taking the Host with joined hands, he raises it without moving his hands from the altar, saying: Who, on the day before he suffered, took bread into his holy and venerable hands; and, with his eyes raised to heaven, to you, God, his almighty Father, giving you thanks; here, holding the Host in his left hand, he signs once above it with his right, saying: + blessed it, broke it, and gave it to his disciples, saying: Take and eat of this, all of you, for this is my body.

Here he reverently raises the Host for the people to adore, and reverently sets it down where he raised it. Then he uncovers the chalice and holds it with both hands, saying:

In like manner, after supper, taking also this noble chalice into his holy and venerable hands, likewise giving you thanks; here he holds the chalice in his left hand, and with his right, signing, blesses the blood, saying: + blessed it and gave it to his disciples, [Col. 1189A] saying: Take and drink from it, all of you. For this is the chalice of my blood, of the new and eternal Testament, the mystery of faith, which will be poured out for you and for many for the forgiveness of sins.

Here he raises the chalice for the people to adore and reverently returns it to its usual place, saying: Whenever you do these things, you shall do them in remembrance of me. Here he extends his hands and arms.

Therefore, remembering, O Lord, we, your servants, and also your holy people, the blessed Passion of this same Christ your Son, our Lord, and likewise his Resurrection from the dead, and also his glorious Ascension into heaven, offer to your sublime Majesty from your gifts and endowments. And here, drawing his hands and arms back toward himself, he signs three times over the Host and chalice, a fourth time over the Host alone, and a fifth time over the chalice, saying: A + pure Host, [Col. 1189B] a + holy Host, an + immaculate Host, the + holy bread of eternal life, and the + chalice of everlasting salvation. Then he says:

Deign to look upon these offerings with a favorable and serene countenance, and accept them, just as you deigned to accept the gifts of your righteous servant Abel, and the sacrifice of our patriarch Abraham, and that which your high priest Melchizedek offered to you, a holy sacrifice, an immaculate victim.

Finally, he bows and places his arms in the form of a cross.

We humbly beseech you, almighty God: command that these offerings be borne by the hands of your holy angel to your sublime altar, in the presence of your divine Majesty. Here he rises and kisses the altar, saying: That all of us who, through this participation at the altar, receive the most holy Body + and Blood + of your Son—here he signs first over the Host and then over the chalice—may be filled—here he signs himself—with every heavenly blessing and grace. Through the same Christ our Lord.

Afterward he says the commemoration of the dead: Remember also, O Lord, your servants N. and N., who have gone before us with the sign of faith and sleep in the sleep of peace. To them, O Lord, and to all who rest in Christ, we ask you to grant a place of refreshment, light, and peace, and that you forgive them. Through the same Christ our Lord. Amen.

Here, striking his breast and saying somewhat more loudly: To us also, your sinful servants, who hope in the multitude of your mercies, deign to grant some share and fellowship with your holy [Col. 1189D] apostles and martyrs, with John, Stephen, Matthias, Barnabas, Ignatius, Alexander, Marcellinus, Peter, Felicity, Perpetua, Agatha, Lucy, Agnes, Cecilia, Anastasia, and all your saints; admit us into their company, we ask you, not weighing our merit but granting forgiveness. Through Christ our Lord.

Through him, O Lord, you always create all these good things. Here he signs once over the Host and chalice three times, saying: You + sanctify, you + enliven, you + bless, and grant them to us.

Here, with the chalice uncovered by the cardinal deacon, he takes the Host in his right hand and with it signs three times over the chalice and the blood, saying: Through him + and with him + and in him +. Here, with the Host itself, he signs twice between it and the chalice, saying: To you, almighty Father, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, be all honor and glory. Here he replaces the Host in its usual place; and, after the chalice has been covered by the cardinal deacon, with the pope’s hands placed on the altar, he says:

For ever and ever. Amen. Let us pray. Instructed by saving commandments and formed by divine teaching, we dare to say:

Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done, on earth as it is in heaven. Give us this day our daily bread, and forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors. And lead us not into temptation;

the response is: But deliver us from evil. Amen.

Then he says the Prayer:

Deliver us, we ask you, O Lord, from all evils, past, present, and future; and, through the intercession of blessed [Col. 1190B] Mary, ever-glorious Virgin and Mother of God, and of your blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and Andrew, together with all the saints, graciously grant peace in our days, so that, aided by the help of your mercy, we may always be free from sin and secure from every disturbance.

Here he takes the paten, signs himself with it, and, holding it beneath the Host, places the Host on the paten. After the cardinal deacon has uncovered the chalice, he takes the Host and reverently breaks it in half over the chalice and the blood; he places the half from his left hand on the paten, and from the portion in his right hand he takes a particle. The portion remaining in his left hand he joins to the particle on the paten, saying:

Through the same Lord our Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy [Col. 1190C] Spirit, God.

Here he holds the portion remaining in his right hand above the blood and chalice, and says: For ever and ever; response: Amen. Here, with that particle, he signs three times over the chalice, saying: May the + peace of the Lord be + always + with you; response: And with your spirit.

Here he joins that particle to the other particles on the paten. Finally, with both hands joined, he says twice: Lamb of God, who take away the sins of the world, have mercy on us. And the third time: Grant us peace. At the end of each he strikes his breast. Then, bowing, he says this Prayer:

Lord Jesus Christ, who said to your apostles: I leave you peace, I give you my peace; do not look upon my sins, but upon the faith of your Church, and deign to pacify and unite her according to your will; you who live.

Here he rises and kisses the altar, giving the kiss of peace to the bishop or cardinal presbyter who serves him, saying: Peace be with you; response: And with your spirit.

Here the pope leaves the entire sacrament on the altar and goes to his seat. Standing with uncovered head, he awaits the subdeacon with the paten and Host, and the cardinal deacon with the chalice and blood. While they stand before him with these things as appropriate, he says this Prayer:

Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the living God, who by the will of the Father and through the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, by your death gave life to the world, deliver me through this your sacred Body and Blood from all my iniquities and from every evil; and make me always obey your commandments, and do not permit me ever to be separated from you; you who live and reign with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen.

Another Prayer:

May the reception of your Body, Lord Jesus Christ, which I, unworthy, presume to receive, not bring me judgment and condemnation, but by your goodness may it be for me a safeguard of mind and body and a remedy to be received; you who live and reign with God the Father in the unity of the same Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen.

Here he reverently takes the greater portion of the Host from the paten and says: I will receive the bread of heaven and call upon the name of the Lord.

Here, holding the aforesaid portion of the Host with four fingers above the blood and chalice, he reverently says three times: Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof, but only say the word, and my soul shall be healed.

[Col. 1191B] Then he signs himself with that Body and reverently consumes all that is outside the aforesaid fingers. What remains beneath his fingers he places in the chalice with the blood, saying: May this commingling and consecration of the Body and Blood of our Lord Jesus Christ be for those who receive it unto eternal life. Amen.

337 Then he says: May the Body of our Lord Jesus Christ preserve my soul unto eternal life. Amen.

Finally, he takes the reed from the hand of the cardinal bishop and, holding it with both hands, places it in the chalice, saying: What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me? I will receive the chalice of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord. I will call upon the Lord with praise, and I shall be saved from my enemies.

Here he takes some of Christ’s blood by sucking it through the aforesaid reed. Then [Col. 1191C] he says: May the Blood of our Lord Jesus Christ preserve my soul unto eternal life. Amen.

Afterward he gives the aforesaid reed to the cardinal deacon without removing it from the chalice. Having wiped his fingers with the washing vessel offered there by the cardinal bishop, after he has communicated, he says the Prayer:

May we receive with a pure mind, O Lord, what we have taken into our mouths, and may what is temporal become for us an everlasting remedy.

Then another Prayer:

May your Body, O Lord, which I have received, and the Blood which I have drunk, cling to my inmost being; and grant that no stain of sin may remain in me, whom these pure and holy sacraments have refreshed. You who live and reign with God the Father in the unity of the same Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen.

Then he takes one portion of the Host [Col. 1191D] that is on the paten and places it in the mouth of the aforesaid cardinal deacon, saying: May the Body of the Lord Jesus Christ preserve your soul unto eternal life. Amen.

Then he receives from him the kiss of peace. Afterward he takes another particle of the Host remaining on the paten and places it in the mouth of the subdeacon, saying: May the Body of our Lord Jesus Christ [preserve your soul unto eternal life], as above.

Finally, he sits in his seat and pours over the golden cup. Then he washes his hands and, sitting, awaits the subdeacon, who brings him the chalice with wine. The pope receives the chalice with both hands and drinks from the wine in the chalice as much as he wishes to wash his mouth.

[Col. 1192A] Communion: Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion, etc. After the Communion has been sung by the choir, he rises and goes to the altar, and then says: The Lord be with you. Response: And with your spirit.

Then, after Communion, this Prayer: May this sacrament, O Lord, etc.

Another Postcommunion: You have satisfied your household, O Lord, etc.

After the aforementioned cardinal deacon has sung: Go, the Mass is ended, without leaving the altar he blesses the people:

May the name of the Lord be blessed. Response: From this time forth, etc.

Our help is in the name of the Lord. Response: Who made heaven and [338] earth.

May almighty God bless you, the + Father and the + Son and the + Holy Spirit. The response is: Amen.

Afterward he says this Prayer secretly: May it please you, holy Trinity, etc.

After Mass, while removing his pontifical vestments, the pope says this Antiphon:

Let us sing the hymn of the three young men, which they sang in the furnace of fire while blessing the Lord.

Psalm: Bless the Lord, all the works of the Lord, the whole psalm.

Praise the Lord in his holy places.

Then he repeats the Antiphon: Let us sing the hymn of the three young men.

Kyrie, eleison. Christe, eleison. Our Father. And lead us not into temptation, etc. Response: But deliver us from evil.

Verse: Let your works confess to you, O Lord. Response: And let your saints bless you.

Verse: The saints shall exult in glory. Response: They shall rejoice in their dwelling places.

Verse: Not to us, O Lord, not to us. Response: But to your name give glory.

Verse: O Lord, hear my prayer. Response: And let my cry come to you.

Verse: The Lord be with you. Response: And with your spirit.

O God, who granted this to the three young men, etc.

Our actions, etc.

## LXXII. On the Feast of Saint Stephen: Introit

The princes sat and spoke against me.

[Col. 1192C] Psalm: Blessed are the undefiled in the way.

Glory to the Father.

Having completed it, and the Kyrie, eleison, with the cardinals standing beside him, he then sits in his seat. After the Introit has been sung, he says: Glory to God in the highest.

When the choir has sung it, he says while standing: Peace be with you, facing the people.

Prayer: Grant us, we ask you, O Lord, to imitate what we honor, etc.

Commemoration of the Nativity: Grant, we ask you, etc.

Reading from the Acts of the Apostles: Now Stephen, etc.

After the Epistle has been read and the subdeacon has kissed the pope’s foot, the pope signs him.

Gradual: The princes sat, etc.

Alleluia. Verse: I see the heavens opened, etc.

After the choir has sung the Gradual and the first Alleluia, he gives a blessing to the cardinal deacon who is to read the Gospel. The deacon goes to the foot of the pope, who signs him and says: May the Lord be in your heart and on your lips, [Col. 1192D] etc.

Then he places incense in the thurible, signing it once with the sign of the cross after he has placed it there. Again, when the same deacon asks the pope for a blessing, the pope signs him while seated. But when the Gospel begins, the pope stands with uncovered head.

According to Matthew: At that time Jesus said to the crowds of Jews and to the chief priests: Behold, I send to you prophets, etc.

After the pope has kissed the book of the Gospels, a sermon is delivered either by him or by some cardinal whom the pope has commissioned to deliver it. After the sermon, followed by the confession by the cardinal deacon, if the pope has preached, the pope himself pronounces the indulgence as he wishes:

By the authority of almighty God, the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit, of his apostles, blessed Peter and Paul, and of our own authority, we grant to all who have come today and who are in a state of true repentance an indulgence of one year and forty days, or more, according to his will.

Afterward he says:

Through the prayers and merits of blessed Mary, ever-virgin, blessed Michael the archangel, blessed John the Baptist, the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and all the saints, may almighty God have mercy on you and, with your sins forgiven, lead you to eternal life. Amen.

Then he says:

May almighty and merciful Lord grant you indulgence, absolution, and remission of your sins. Amen.

Then, signing the people in the form of a cross, he says:

And may the blessing of almighty God, the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit, descend upon you and remain always.

But if a cardinal has preached, when he goes to the foot of the pope, he asks the pope for a blessing on bended knees, kissing him, saying: Command, lord, that you bless.

The pope, while seated, gives the blessing, signing him and saying:

May the Lord be in your heart and on your lips, so that you may worthily and fittingly proclaim his holy word.

Then the said cardinal reverently asks the pope how much indulgence he wishes to grant. Once it has been pronounced, the pope gives absolution as above, and the pope grants whatever he wishes; the cardinal himself pronounces that indulgence.

Then the pope, standing on the footstool before his seat, begins: I believe in [Col. 1193C] one God.

When this has been said and sung by the choir, he says: The Lord be with you. Response: And with your spirit. Let us pray.

Then he sits in his seat.

Offertory: The apostles chose Stephen, a Levite, etc.

While it is sung by the choir, he washes his hands while seated. After washing his hands and after the Offertory has been sung, he goes to the altar. There he receives the paten with the Host, which the cardinal deacon offers him; raising it slightly, he says: Receive, holy Father, etc.

Finally, he places the Host on the corporal, with the paten on the left side, and places the paten on the right beside the corporal. Then he receives the cruet with water from the hand of the subdeacon and pours water into the chalice, saying: O God, who [concerning] human nature, etc.; and he returns the cruet to the subdeacon.

Finally, he signs over the chalice once, [Col. 1193D] and while the chalice is placed in its proper place on the corporal by the said pope, he says: We offer you, O Lord, etc.

When the said cardinal covers the chalice, he says the Antiphon: In a spirit of humility, etc.

Then he says: Come, O sanctifier, etc., signing over the Host and chalice. Afterward he turns toward the cardinal deacon and blesses the incense, saying: May you be blessed by him in whose honor you will be burned.

Finally, he receives the thurible from the hands of the said cardinal and reverently incenses the chalice and Host in the form of a cross, saying:

May this incense, blessed by you, + ascend to you, O Lord +, and may your mercy descend + upon us.

Let my prayer be directed, etc.

Continuing, he incenses the crosses and images standing upon the altar, and the upper surface of the altar itself. Then he incenses [Col. 1194A] the Host and chalice again. Finally, he returns the thurible to the said cardinal, saying: May the Lord kindle in us the fire, etc.

Then, bowing before the altar, he says: Receive, holy Trinity, etc.

Afterward he rises and kisses the altar in the middle. Then, facing the people, he says: Pray for me, brothers, etc.

Those standing around respond: May the Lord receive the sacrifice from your hands, etc.

Then he says secretly the Prayer: Receive, O Lord, these gifts, etc.

Another Prayer: Having received, O Lord, the gifts, etc.

The Preface and the other prayers are said as above.

### From the Ceremonial of Cardinal of Rouen

When Mass has been completed, if the pope is in the City, he receives the tiara from the hand of the chief marshal and carries it [Col. 1194B] as far as the steps of the palace. Then the judges and advocates come to meet him beneath the steps in the portico and again offer him acclamations, as it is written in the Polyptych; there the lord pope dismounts and, setting aside the tiara, takes the mitre.

Then the judges lead him to the place where the presbyterium is given. After removing the chasuble and placing the mantle over his shoulders, he sits in the chair and with his own hands gives the presbyterium to the chaplains, as at the coronation.

After the presbyterium has been given, he goes in this attire to the table, etc., and the cardinal deacon reads at the table wearing a cope. At the end, the singers sing the sequence *Laetabundus*.

But if the pope does not celebrate, the cardinal presbyter of the title of the aforesaid Saint Stephen customarily celebrates before the pope on that [Col. 1194C] day.

On that day, the household chaplains, acolytes, auditors, and penitentiaries eat splendidly with the pope, and at the collation the presbyterium is given.

At Second Vespers the pope comes wearing a cope and mitre.

## LXXIII. On the Office of Saint Stephen

Station at Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill.

The Mass and sermon are assigned [Note: [Col. 1193] What follows up to chapter 78, with a few exceptions, agrees with the Ceremonial of Peter Amelius.].

On Saint Stephen’s Day, early in the morning, all orders, both clerical and lay, assemble in the basilica, dressed in silk garments, except for the cardinal deacons and subdeacons, who, dressed in the proper attire, lead the lord pope to the basilica itself. There all the cardinals and prelates [Col. 1194D] come out to show him reverence. There he puts on a white chasuble; and, descending from the palace as far as the small portico, he finds there a caparisoned horse—though not its neck—with a scarlet covering [nacta?, uncertain]. Mounting the horse, and receiving the tiara from the hand of the deacon who stands at his right, he puts it on.

Thus crowned, he goes with the orders in procession to the church of blessed Stephen on the Caelian Hill, as it is written in the Polyptych. When he has reached the aforesaid church of Saint Stephen, where the station is held on that day, he sets aside the tiara, enters the church, and, after praying, goes to the sacristy. Removing the white chasuble, he puts on a red one and celebrates Mass, in every respect as on the preceding day at Mass.

When Mass is finished, he resumes the white chasuble, puts on the tiara, and returns to the palace. All the other things [Col. 1195A] are done as they are written in the Polyptych.

## LXXIV. On Saint John’s Day

The Mass and sermon are assigned, and some cardinal customarily delivers the sermon. For this occasion the pope comes wearing a red scarlet cope and a gold-fringed mitre, with the presbyters, as at a consistory.

The same is done at Second Vespers, at which all the acolytes must wear surplices: first the household members, auditors, and subdeacons; then the acolytes and the chaplains belonging to these groups.

## LXXV. On the Office of the Feast of the Innocents

On this feast there customarily are a Mass and sermon; but this is no longer observed, nor does the pope come to the chapel for Second Vespers.

On the Nativity of the holy Innocents, the station is at Saint [Col. 1195B] Paul’s. At Mass, the *Gloria in excelsis* is not said, nor is the Alleluia; instead, the Tract is sung. The Creed, however, is sung because of the Octave of the Lord’s Nativity. The vestments are to be violet, and the Preface is of the Nativity. Nor is *Ite, missa est* said, since *Ite, missa est* always follows the *Gloria in excelsis*. These things are nevertheless said during their Octave.

If this feast falls on a Sunday, *Te Deum laudamus* is sung at Matins, and the vestments are to be red. At Mass, *Gloria in excelsis Deo* is sung, as is the Alleluia, together with the Creed and the Preface of the Nativity.

## LXXVI. On the Circumcision of the Lord

Only the Mass and sermon are assigned.

Although in ancient times the Roman pontiffs customarily came solemnly at First Vespers of this day, dressed in a precious white cope and solemn mitre, and this practice is still maintained, rightly, nevertheless in modern times it is not observed. The pope comes only wearing a samite cope and a gold-fringed mitre. All this depends upon the pope’s will.

Also, if the pope is in the City on this day of the Circumcision and does not celebrate, but has a cardinal celebrate in the church of Saint Peter, before the cardinal is vested, a bull is presented explaining how the pope dispenses him to celebrate over the altar of blessed Peter. It hangs before the doors throughout the day, and likewise in all other Masses celebrated over that altar.

## LXXVII. On the Epiphany

The Mass and sermon are assigned, and Vespers are customarily assigned, but not the sermon. At both Vespers the pope is present wearing a red scarlet cope and a gold-fringed mitre.

The bishop of the City also customarily celebrates this Mass, and they always perform the ordinary course, unless prevented by illness or excessive cold.

343 Also, in the year of the Lord 1389, in the tenth year of the pontificate of the lord Urban VI, the feast of Saint Antony fell on the first Sunday after Epiphany. We did nothing for the feast of Saint Antony, but the entire office was for Sunday; and we were in the City.

During the Octave of Epiphany, every day at Mass the first Prayer is said, whether the day is a feast or a weekday. The second is a commemoration of Saint Mary, namely: O God, who are the salvation of the eternal, etc.; the third is of Saint Peter: O God, whose right hand, etc.; the fourth: Your Church; the fifth: O God, shepherd of all the faithful.

This is observed until the Purification of blessed Mary. From the Purification until the Wednesday that is the beginning of the fast, the first Prayer is of the day; the second is: From all; the third: O God of all.

Let the hebdomadary begin.

If the period from the Sunday after the Octave of Epiphany until Septuagesima is so short that the Sunday offices cannot be said on their proper days—namely, the Introits and Prayers, Epistles and Gospels—he should distribute them so that those Sundays that cannot be observed on their weekdays within the week are sung usefully, if they can be fitted in, so that they are completed in the final week.

The same is observed concerning the Sundays after the Octave of Pentecost [Col. 1196B] until Advent.

## LXXVIII. On the Blessing of Candles, Which Takes Place on the Day of the Purification of Blessed Mary

Only the Mass is assigned. No preceding Vespers are assigned; nevertheless, at First Vespers the cardinals come and begin the Antiphons.

If this feast falls in Septuagesima or Sexagesima, it is transferred to Monday. At First Vespers the pope comes wearing a simple samite cope and a gold-fringed mitre.

On the feast of the Purification of blessed Mary, the candles are blessed by the junior cardinal presbyter. He is to be dressed in a white rochet, amice, stole, and white cope, and a simple garnello mitre, [Col. 1196C] with holy water and incense, accompanied by assistants wearing surplices and by two candle-bearers with lighted torches. He blesses the candles as prescribed in the Missal and Roman Pontifical.

When the blessing has been completed, the candles are sprinkled with holy water and incensed by the same cardinal presbyter. Then the candles are distributed as follows. 344 The pope, dressed in a red mantle and wearing a garnello mitre on his head, comes with two deacons to the place prepared for this purpose according to custom.

Then, after the customary reverence has been made by the cardinal presbyters, and after everyone has put on the appropriate violet vestments—including the cardinals and others, the deacons in cotta, amice, and chasuble; the cardinal presbyters likewise with chasubles; the bishops likewise with copes; and the other prelates likewise with violet copes [Col. 1196D]—the senior of the cardinal bishops, having removed his mitre, stands before the pope, who is seated on the faldstool and wearing his mitre. He gives him an unlit torch, larger than the others, saying nothing, and kisses the pope’s hand.

Then the same senior cardinal bishop, or the junior, kneeling, receives the unlit torch from the pope’s hand and kisses the lord pope’s right knee.

All the cardinals then do likewise: first the bishops, second the presbyters, third the deacons. All the prelates who are vested do so as well, having removed their mitres, kissing the knee, in the manner in which a cardinal bishop or presbyter celebrates before the pope. Once vested, before coming to receive the candle, he does not remove his chasuble.

The chamberlain, notaries, auditor of contentious cases, and corrector—even if some of them are bishops, because they are not vested—and also the chaplains, both household chaplains, who are to wear cottas, and other chaplains and their associates, as well as the penitentiaries—in short, all the pope’s other familiars, even laymen, and any others who may come there who are not familiars—receive the torch from the pope’s hand and kiss not his knee but his foot.

It should be understood that the torches given both to the pope and to the others are unlit; immediately after they have been received, they are lit.

It should nevertheless be noted that when a king is present, immediately after the cardinals and before all other prelates, even those vested in the manner described above, he receives the candle from the pope’s hand in the aforesaid manner. After receiving the candle, he kisses the foot, not the knee.

In modern times, however, the king customarily receives it while seated, after the senior cardinal bishop; the same is done on Palm Sunday and on Ash Wednesday.

If the emperor were present, he would receive the candle after the senior cardinal bishop and kiss the foot, not the knee.

345 It should also be noted that after the senior cardinal bishop, if a patriarch is present, he receives a candle from the pope’s hand.

If a king is present, after the king the junior cardinal bishop receives the candle; in his absence, the senior cardinal presbyter receives it. Then the patriarch—and, even if several patriarchs are present, each one—receives it after the cardinals who precede him.

Patriarchs must always stand between two cardinals, even [Col. 1197C] in processions and at Masses.

The procession is arranged by the senior cardinal deacon, who says in a loud voice, with his face turned toward the procession: Let us proceed in peace. The choir responds: In the name of Christ. Amen.

Then the procession moves. Our lord the pope, dressed in a red cope with pearls and gold fringes, having set aside the other cope after the distribution of the candles—or of the palms on their appointed day—wears a gold-fringed mitre, which he carries in the procession, and holds the lighted torch, or the palm on its appointed day, in his left hand, while he signs with his right.

The pope proceeds for a short distance through the chapel in procession beneath a canopy carried by four soldiers bearing mappulae (cloths), if they are in the City, or, in their absence, by four of the more noble men of the City or by arms-bearing retainers. Thus he proceeds to the doors.

First toward the right side, then toward the left as he comes, he throws candles to the people. Afterward he returns to his seat. While he is seated there, one towel is spread over his knees by two chaplains, who hold it while kneeling, one on the right and the other on the left; and thus he washes his hands while a nobleman pours the water.

Some say that the pope never changes his cope in these processions, but only his gold-fringed mitre, without pearls, because he must always wear the cope in processions and on weekdays. This is certainly what I believe wherever it is without pearls.

Therefore there are two copes and three mitres: a white, gold-ornamented one with pearls, and [Col. 1198A] another without pearls, gold-fringed, which he wears on weekdays.

When these things have been completed, his gold-fringed mitre is removed and he receives a simple, white, plain garnello mitre.

After the Antiphons and the Psalm *Nunc dimittis* have been sung, the pope rises in his seat. The cardinal deacon standing at his right removes his mitre; while singing, the pope says: Let us pray. Immediately the deacon on his right says while singing: Let us bend the knee. The cardinal assisting on the left says while singing: Rise.

Then the pope says while singing the Prayer: Hear, we ask you, O Lord, etc. 346 Then, if the pope celebrates, he goes to the vesting room, if there is one; if there is not, he goes to his chair, prepared far from the altar on the left side of the altar. After removing the white, plain mitre [Col. 1198B] together with the cope and stole, he is vested in the sacred and precious white vestments, following the order indicated elsewhere.

It should also be noted that on this feast of the Purification, at the reception of ashes, and at the reception of palms, the cardinals and prelates, as stated above, whether the pope is going to celebrate or not, must be vested when they receive the candles, ashes, or palm. But after the Introit has been said with the pope, if he is not celebrating, the cardinals remove their vestments and resume their woolen cappas; the prelates, however, remove their vestments immediately after receiving the ashes. When the Gospel is read, all hold lighted candles or palms in their hands, standing upright in their cappas, not vested for Mass. On Palm Sunday, during the Gospel and the Passion, the pope likewise holds a lighted candle or palm; but after the Gospel or Passion has been said, he entrusts the candles and palms to the servants. If, however, the pope celebrates on these three days—the Purification, Ash Wednesday, and Palm Sunday—the cardinals and prelates do not remove their violet vestments until the Procession has taken place, if it takes place. In the Procession, if it takes place, the lord pope, dressed in the red mantle as stated above and wearing a garnello mitre, holds a lighted candle in his left hand, or a palm on Palm Sunday, because he walks while making the sign with his right hand. All the others likewise hold lighted candles or palms in the Procession, vested in violet vestments and wearing garnello mitres on their heads.

The Procession is arranged by the prior of the deacons. Once it has been arranged, the last of the cardinal deacons says in a loud voice, with the chant, “Let us proceed in peace,” turning his face toward the procession; and the response is made, also in a loud chant, “In the name of Christ. Amen.” After the Procession, they entrust the candles or palms to the servants. Then, on the feast of the Purification, everyone—the lord pope as well as the others—is vested in white in the customary manner. On Ash Wednesday and Palm Sunday, however, they retain the violet vestments until the Mass has been completed. At the Gospel the lord pope and everyone else take up the candles again, or, during the Passion, the palms; and after the Gospel or Passion they entrust them to the servants.

The same is observed, in its proper manner, on Palm Sunday in receiving the palms, in the kissing of the knee or foot, in the Procession, and in the other matters that will be described below. It should be noted that if such Processions were held at Rome by the pope, solemnly and in places where the pope was going to celebrate on these three days, the pope would also be solemnly vested in the Procession in pontifical vestments and with the pallium, and he himself, together with all the cardinals and prelates, would go barefoot in the Procession—at least on the feast of the Purification, from the church of Saint Adrian to Saint Mary Major, and on Ash Wednesday from the church of Saint Susanna to Saint Sabina, where the station is held.

At the Chair of Saint Peter, neither a Mass nor a sermon has customarily been ordered, because these are not in accordance with modern practice, although in antiquity they were customary. Pope Urban VI ordered them to be held in his first year and again in his second year. In the first year the cardinal of Grado preached; in the second, Cardinal Bonaventure of Padua, an Augustinian, preached in the church of Saint Peter in Rome, while Urban celebrated Mass in that church.

It should be remembered that “Lumen ad revelationem gentium” (“A light for revelation to the Gentiles”) is to be sung.

## LXXIX. Concerning the office of Ash Wednesday, the beginning of the fast

On Wednesday, the beginning of the fast, the office of the Ashes must not be omitted. On that day, if the pope is in Rome, everyone assembles at Saint Anastasia. Before the lord pope arrives, ashes are made there from the palms of the preceding year and are blessed by the junior cardinal priest, with ministers vested only in white. Then the lord pope goes to the aforesaid church, accompanied by the entire Curia, and says Sext; for before descending from the palace he must say Terce. Afterwards the blessed ashes are imposed upon him by the prior of the bishops, if he is present; otherwise, by the subprior of the priests. Finally, the lord pope himself imposes the ashes upon their heads, saying, “Remember, man,” and so forth.

Afterwards the Procession is arranged by the prior of the deacons. [Note: [Col. 1199D] The same is found in Peter Amelius, chapter 37.] If the lord pope wishes to go on foot, he must vest in the Mass vestments up to and including the dalmatic. After the imposition of the ashes he must remove his shoes, put on a black chasuble, and proceed in procession as far as Saint Mary of the Greeks and then to Saint Sabina, where the station is held, going barefoot. Meanwhile the members of the schola sing an antiphon along the way; finally the litanies follow. When these have been completed, the lord pope, after having his feet washed at Saint Sabina in the sacristy and putting his shoes back on, says None; 348 then he proceeds to the altar for the celebration of the divine offices.

The lord pope customarily sings only one Collect at the Mass on this day [Note: [Col. 1199D] In the ceremonial of Peter Amelius: “It should be noted that, according to the lord James Gaietani, only one Collect should be said at this Mass, although in modern times it has been customary to say three.”], and likewise on all Sundays. On ferial days, however, when he celebrates in the chapel, he says three Collects: namely, the Collect of the day, the Collect “A cunctis” (“For all”), and the Collect “Omnipotens sempiterne Deus, qui vivorum” (“Almighty and everlasting God, who are the…”). When he comes to the Prayer over the People, he says, “Per omnia saecula saeculorum. Amen” (“For ever and ever. Amen”). Afterwards he says, “Oremus. Humiliate capita vestra Deo” (“Let us pray. Bow your heads before God”); then the Prayer over the People.

[Col. 1200A] At this Mass the Lenten preface is said: “Qui corporali jejunio” (“Who by bodily fasting”), and thereafter until Palm Sunday, both on ferial days and on festal Sundays, the preface proper to the occasion is said. [Note: [Col. 1200D] From Passion Sunday the Preface of the Cross is said.] Once the Mass has been completed, he does not say Vespers, because throughout that entire week he does not say Vespers after Mass, but in the evening, as on the other preceding days.

It should be noted that from the beginning of Ash Wednesday, the beginning of the fast, each day has its own Collects, prophecies, Gospel, and antiphons for the Benedictus and the Magnificat. The Collects said at Mass over the people are said at Vespers, except on Saturday; on Saturday, at Vespers, the Collect of Sunday is said. It should be understood that from this day until the Lord’s Supper, according to Roman custom, [Col. 1200B] we do not say “Flectamus genua” (“Let us bend the knees”) except when several prophecies are read at Mass. When one prophecy is read, it is said in the manner of an epistle, and “Dominus vobiscum” (“The Lord be with you”) is said. It should be noted that when two prophecies are read at Mass, the first is read in the manner of a lesson, and “Flectamus genua” is said; the second is read in the manner of an epistle, and “Dominus vobiscum” is said.

According to the custom observed up to the present, whenever a feast with three lessons occurred during the days of Lent—that is, from Ash Wednesday through the Wednesday of Holy Week—we did nothing from the feast except its commemoration; but this is no longer observed. Thus, if the feast of Saint Scholastica occurs during Lent, we say the Mass of the feria, with a commemoration of the feast; likewise, Terce, Sext, and None are said from the feast, unless another feast follows, in which case they are said from the feria. It should be noted that the pope’s chamberlain goes out [Note: [Col. 1200D] That is, outside the screen. See Peter Amelius, chapters 21 and 35.] from the royal apartments and, standing, gives ashes to those who are outside; in his absence, another prelate does so, to whom the pope gives the order. 349

Before the Collect he does not say “Pax vobis” (“Peace be with you”), but only “Dominus vobiscum” (“The Lord be with you”); and this is likewise done on all ferial Sundays, both of Lent and of Advent, except on Gaudete Sunday and Laetare Sunday.

It should also be noted that in the Tract sung on this day, when they reach the verse “Adjuva nos” (“Help us”), the said lord pope, having removed his mitre, stands kneeling in his seat for as long as that verse is sung. If the pope is not celebrating, but someone else is celebrating in his presence, he must go to the chair prepared before the altar with a footstool and remain there for as long as that verse is sung, having removed his mitre. When it is finished, he must return to his own seat and put his mitre back on. Likewise, after the “Sanctus” has been said, if he is not celebrating, he must immediately go to the same chair and remain there until the “Agnus Dei,” wearing his mitre. When “Per omnia” begins, he returns to his seat.

The non-celebrating pope does the same whenever the first and last Collects are said in Masses of a feria, vigil, or Ember Day, whether the celebration is solemn or ferial. For as long as the Collects are being said, he always stands with knees bent, as above, with his mitre on his head, unless he wishes to remove it out of special devotion. When the Collects are finished, while “Per Dominum” (“Through our Lord”) is being said—or whenever he wishes—he rises and returns to his chair.

It should be noted [Note: [Col. 1201D] The same observance is found in Peter Amelius, chapter 39.] that in the year of the Lord 1395, Boniface IX gave ashes at Perugia. After giving them, he removed the cope and took the mantle; thus he stood at Mass without a mitre because of the cold. Nor did the cardinal deacons sit before him, but in their own places. The lord cardinal of Bologna said the Mass and gave ashes to the pope; immediately afterwards the pope gave him ashes before all the cardinals. At that time, however, there was no cardinal bishop, and the aforesaid lord pope ordered that this method should always be observed: that the one who celebrates should impose the ashes on the pope. This occurred in the fifth year of his pontificate, on the feast of Saint Matthias. On that occasion they observed the feria rather than the feast; but on the following Thursday the feast was observed.

It should be noted that whenever a cardinal performs the office before the pontiff, all the cardinals ought to wait for him until he has removed the sacred vestments and resumed his ordinary clothing. They then go with him to the pope’s chamber, together with the two deacons who precede the pope; or, if they do not wish to wait for everyone, at least two must wait.

If the lord pope is not in Rome, everyone assembles at the church of Saint Sabina. After Terce has been said, the ashes are blessed by the pontiff or by the priest who is to sing the Mass in the customary manner, as stated above. When the blessing has been completed, ashes are imposed upon the pontiff or priest who is to celebrate Mass by another pontiff or priest, if one is present. Otherwise, that same pontiff or priest imposes the ashes upon himself, and then upon the clergy and people, saying, “Remember, man,” and so forth. Meanwhile “Immutemur habitu” (“Let us change our clothing”) and “Juxta vestibulum” (“Beside the vestibule”), and so forth, are sung. After the imposition of the ashes has been completed, the Collect “Concede, quaesumus” (“Grant, we beseech you”), as above, is said. Afterwards he proceeds to the altar for the celebration of the divine offices. The same is observed in the pope’s chapel when the pope is not celebrating, except that he imposes ashes upon himself and upon everyone present.

## LXXX. The First Sunday of Lent

On the First Sunday of Lent, a sermon and Mass are ordered. On this Sunday and thereafter on the Sundays up to Palm Sunday, when Mass is celebrated in the presence of the pope and the cardinals, the pope is dressed in a red mantle with gold embroidery without pearls, wearing a plain white garnello mitre without pearls, except on the Fourth Sunday, as will be stated below.

According to James Gaietani, on this Sunday, and likewise on the other Sundays of Lent, only one Collect should be said. Nevertheless, in modern times the priests have been accustomed to say one for the day, a second, “Ecclesiae tuae” (“For your Church”), a third, “Deus omnium fidelium” (“God of all the faithful”), and a fourth, “Omnipotens sempiterne Deus, qui vivorum” (“Almighty and everlasting God, who are the…”).

The man who is to preach kisses the pope’s right foot and asks the pope’s blessing. After receiving it, the pope entrusts him with announcing, on his behalf, to those who truly repent and have confessed, who are or will be in a state of grace, three years and as many quarantines of indulgence within eight days. It should nevertheless be noted that on these Sundays five years and five quarantines have customarily been granted; on the Fourth Sunday, Laetare Sunday, seven have been granted. These seven years are never customarily granted unless the pontiff celebrates on Laetare Sunday and on Gaudete Sunday. Apart from this, the sermon and Mass on the other three Sundays of Lent, and so forth, were as stated above.

## LXXXI. Concerning the office of the Fourth Sunday of Lent, called Rose Sunday, and concerning the Annunciation

The Fourth Sunday of Lent is the station at the Holy Cross. On this Sunday the lord pope wears a noble fringed mitre when he goes to celebrate Mass at the church of the Holy Cross, called Jerusalem. On that day he also carries a golden rose, presented to him in his chamber by the chamberlain, containing balsam and musk. He carries it while going from that chamber to the Holy Cross, and when he preaches he holds it in his hand; he carries it back on his return as far as the Lateran.

When the pope mounts or dismounts his horse, the prefect of the city, dressed in scarlet or purple, with one red stocking and the other gilded, holds the stirrup for him; and when the pope dismounts, he gives the prefect the golden rose.

On this Sunday, after Mass has ended, the lord pope carries the rose to his chamber—or, if he is in Rome, to the Lateran palace. As he returns, all the nobles present in the Curia follow him. When he has returned to his chamber, if he is outside Rome, he gives the rose to the noblest person, or to anyone he especially favors. That person immediately bends the knee and kisses the pope’s foot, even if he is a king. Then the pope receives him to a kiss on the mouth. Afterwards the man withdraws, accompanied by the two senior cardinal deacons; and they ride with him for a short distance, as far as the pope wishes.

In the fourth year of Boniface IX’s pontificate, at Perugia, the rose was sent on this day to the great chapel, and all the cardinals attended the sermon, but not the pope, because he was ill. The rose was carried to the altar for Mass and brought back by the junior chamber clerk; the pope gave the rose in his chamber.

It should be noted that before the pope gives the rose, he must say a few brief words about the rose’s qualities and properties: it has a joyful color, a strengthening fragrance, and a delightful appearance, as stated in the book *Rationale divinorum officiorum*.

On the feast of the Annunciation of the Blessed Virgin Mary, a Mass and sermon are ordered. If this feast occurs during Lent, the pope does not come to First Vespers with cope and mitre, nor do the cardinals customarily come, because Vespers are sung before dinner—unless the feast falls on a Monday, for then the papal Vespers are held on Sunday evening and the cardinals begin the antiphons.

It should also be noted that, whenever this feast occurs, at Mass only the Collect of the Blessed Virgin Mary is said, and nothing from the feria. After Mass has been said and the blessing immediately given, the pontiff, standing in his seat without a mitre, begins Vespers, which are solemn. Once the first antiphon has begun, he removes his vestments and resumes the red cope; all the cardinals and prelates remove their vestments and take woolen cappas. The cardinals do not begin the antiphon at these Vespers.

The cardinal bishop who served the pope at Mass does not remove his vestments, because at the appointed hour he must carry the boat with incense to the pope, cense the altar and the container in which the Body of the Lord is reserved, and likewise cense the pope. He must also hold the book before the pope when the pope says the Collect. Two Collects are to be said: one for the feast and the other for the feria, if the feast occurs during that season. When these have been completed, the pope gives the blessing.

In antiquity, at Second Vespers of every feast, the cardinals used to say the antiphons, and no one else ever did so at Second Vespers. Yet in the time of Lords John XXII, Benedict XII, and Clement VII this was never observed.

On Passion Sunday, which is the Fifth Sunday of Lent, a sermon and Mass are ordered; all other matters are carried out as was customary on the other Sundays of Lent.

## LXXXII. Concerning the order or office on Palm Sunday, and so forth

On Palm Sunday, at the middle of the second hour of the day, the junior cardinal priest [Note: [Col. 1203D] In Peter Amelius: “According to the lord James Gaietani, the junior cardinal priest ought to bless the palms.”] and the entire clergy assemble in the church of Saint Sylvester in the Lateran palace, dressed in Mass vestments. Palm branches, olive branches, or branches of other trees having been set out in the middle, the cardinal or priest blesses salt and water. Then the antiphon “Hosanna Filio David” (“Hosanna to the Son of David”) follows. For the Gradual, the response “Collegerunt” (“They gathered together”) is sung, with the verse “Unus autem” (“But one…”); or the response “In monte Oliveti” (“On the Mount of Olives”), with the verse “Vigilate” (“Keep watch”). After the Collect has been said, the palms are spread out. While the clergy and people sing, the blessed palms are carried in this manner through the Lateran palace to the chapel, if the Curia is there.

As the lord pope comes out, he gives each bishop and cardinal a palm branch, and gives them to others as well if palms remain. Then he throws palm or olive leaves over the people and gives some to others by hand; the cantor begins the antiphon.

“On this day there has customarily been no sermon, nor have the Roman pontiffs customarily performed the office; rather, early in the morning they celebrate their Mass in the private chapel. Nevertheless, they go and distribute palms, although in modern times they sometimes celebrate.

“It should also be noted that if the pontiff does not perform the office, whoever else says the Mass—as long as he is a cardinal—blesses the branches, and not the junior priest. The same is to be observed concerning candles and ashes. In all matters pertaining to this solemnity of the palms, refer back to what is noted for Candlemas and Ash Wednesday.”

“If the pope celebrates on this Palm Sunday, he ought to wear violet or green vestments without pearls, and sandals without pearls; a simple garnello mitre, gloves without pearls, and a palm. It is true that in modern times they have been accustomed to wear a solemn and precious mitre and precious gloves, with everything else simple.

“It should be noted [Note: [Col. 1203D] These words are read verbatim in Peter Amelius, [Col. 1204D] chapter 59.] that in the year of the Lord 1388, the lord Urban VI did not perform the office with the Palm Sunday branches because he had not yet been crowned. He did, however, give palms and branches and attended Mass dressed in a red cope and white mitre. The Mass was said by the cardinal of Florence in the great chapel. Thus, in the presence of the lord cardinals, those Masses of Holy Week were also celebrated, as stated above.

“On Monday there is no papal Mass. Likewise, on Tuesday Our Lord heard a solemn Mass in his small chapel, celebrated by one of the cantors, who read the Passion.

“The same is observed on Holy Wednesday. It should be noted, however, that if pilgrims are present, the pope customarily gives an indulgence to the people after Mass as a special favor; at that time he is dressed in [lacuna]. [Note: [Col. 1204D] Peter Amelius supplies the remainder in chapter 61: “dressed in a red cope without pearls, and with a simple white mitre.”]

“It should also be noted that on Holy Wednesday evening, at the appropriate hour, the pope comes to hear the office in the chapel simply dressed in a red mantle, with a hood over his head—not folded back, as is customary on the other days, but merely extended 354 over his eyes. On these three days, after the office, the pope must give the blessing. On these three days the cardinals customarily come in the evening to hear the office in the pope’s chapel, not because they are summoned, but freely, out of devotion.

“It should also be noted that on these three days the Roman pontiffs have not been accustomed to say the office with their bishops and table companions when Matins are being said, but to hear the office devoutly and afterwards say it in their chamber with their chamberlains.”

## LXXXIII. Concerning the office of Holy Thursday, the Lord’s Supper

Holy Thursday is the station at Saint John Lateran. On this day the sacrifice of the sacred Body and Blood, instituted by Our Lord Jesus Christ himself, began. On this day holy chrism is prepared throughout the whole world; on this day also penitents are assisted through indulgence.

Early in the morning of this day the first mansionarii prepare everything necessary for the consecration of the chrism: three ampullae filled with the purest oil, with the largest ampulla—the one intended for the chrism—covered in white silk cloth, and the other two covered in another kind of silk. The cloth should be so fine that the ampullae can be seen through it.

At the third hour the signal is sounded, and everyone comes to the church in which the chrism is to be consecrated. Then the penitents come out from the place where they have performed their penance, so that they may be presented in the body of the church by the pontiff, who must sit before the doors of the church and reconcile them with antiphons and Collects. When these have been completed, the bells are rung as is customary on solemn days; from then onward the bells remain silent until Holy Saturday.

Before the lord pope leaves his chamber, he says Terce and Sext. At the sixth hour the lord pope leaves the palace with the bishops, cardinals, and the entire apparatus of the Curia, proceeding to the larger palace, where the lodging customarily is. The bishop of Albano, standing in an elevated place there, preaches to the people and conducts the Processions, if they are to be held, according to custom. When all these things have been completed, he descends to the Lateran church. He enters the church, coming before the sacristy at the church of Saint George, and says None there.

Then the pontiff, the priests, the deacons, the other clerics, and everyone else put on the vestments proper to their order. The pontiff puts on white vestments; the bishops, copes; the priests, chasubles; and the deacons, dalmatics, out of reverence for the chrism. The pontiff, already dressed in the dalmatic, sits in his seat. The better ampulla, containing oil, is presented to him by the acolytes; he mixes the balsam with the oil without saying anything and prepares the chrism. All the ampullae remain there and are carefully guarded until they are carried to the altar.

Afterwards the pontiff washes his hands, puts on a chasuble, and proceeds with the priests, deacons, acolytes, and all the orders. In the Procession they carry the cross, the Gospel book, seven candlesticks, and the thurible with incense. Thus they proceed in procession to the altar with the small cloth. After making the confession and reverence, he ascends to his seat.

Meanwhile the cantors sing the Introit without the “Gloria Patri”; when the verse is finished, the Introit is repeated. Afterwards the cantors sing “Kyrie eleison.” When this has been completed, the lord pope says in a loud voice, “Gloria in excelsis Deo” (“Glory to God in the highest”). After the Collect “Deus, a quo,” and so forth, has been said, the Epistle and Gospel have been read, and, if he wishes, a sermon has been given to the people, and “Credo in unum Deum” (“I believe in one God”) has been sung, he continues the Mass according to its order. It should nevertheless be understood that no sermon is given unless there has been a Procession.

“It should be noted that there is customarily no sermon at this Mass unless the pope wishes to conduct a Procession. If the pope does not wish to give that sermon, the sacristan, acting on his command, assigns it to one of the lord cardinal bishops or priests—for deacons never preach before the pope—or to some other prelate or master of theology.

“It should be noted that abbots have never customarily preached, nor have doctors of decretals or of law, but only prelates and masters of theology. Nowadays, however, abbots preach.”

After the lord pope enters to celebrate the sacrifice and has consecrated two Hosts, the acolyte leads the junior cardinal deacon, together with several subdeacons. One of these subdeacons carries the cross, preceded by the acolyte with the thurible and incense. Thus they proceed in procession to the church of Saint John or Saint George, where the ampullae containing the chrism and oil are kept.
