The cardinal deacon takes the ampulla containing the chrism. Two other subdeacons take the other two ampullae, containing exorcised oil and oil of the sick. They return in the same manner in which they came. When they reach the altar, before the lord pope says “Per quem haec omnia” (“Through whom you continue to make all these good things”), 356 the subdeacon carrying the ampulla of the oil of the sick presents it to the supreme pontiff for blessing. The pontiff says in an ordinary voice, “Exorcizo te, immundissime” (“I exorcize you, most unclean…”). After these blessings have been completed, he turns to the altar and says, “Per quem haec omnia,” and so forth.

We should understand that if the pontiff is at the Lateran, after “Credo in unum Deum” has been sung and before he enters to celebrate the sacrifice, the deacons remove the table from the altar, folding the cloths laid over it. With reverence and complete devotion they carry it back to the chapel of Saint Pancratius beside the canons’ cloister, where it is kept. It is guarded there with every precaution until Holy Saturday.

Then the pontiff comes to the altar and takes a glass ampulla containing within it a small golden vessel. In that vessel is a hollow precious stone, and in the hollow of that stone the precious Blood of Christ is carefully enclosed [Note: [Col. 1205D] In John, canon of the Lateran church, the following is read in chapter 3, where he discusses the relics in the basilica of the Savior: “Two ampullae of the Blood and Water from the Lord’s side.” The same is stated above, p. 99.]. Each year it is removed and placed again in the hollow of the reliquary; then it is lifted up by the pontiff and displayed so that the entire crowd of the people may see it with fear, reverence, and complete devotion. Afterwards it is entrusted for safekeeping to the prior and canons of that church until Holy Saturday.

Then the pontiff enters alone to celebrate the sacrifice and enters the ark, signifying what is written in the Old Testament: that the high priest would enter the Holy of Holies once a year. Nevertheless, a cross and cloth are placed over him, and a bishop or cardinal, assisted by a priest chaplain, ministers to him.

When the sacrifice has been completed, the pontiff alone receives Communion at the altar without ministers. On that day and on Good Friday he communicates himself not with a reed, but with the chalice alone, and he places that fourth part in the chalice. After he has received Communion, he places the chalice on the altar and the paten beside it, with the reserved Body of the Lord, because he will receive from it on Good Friday. Both are covered with a clean linen cloth.

After receiving the Body and Blood of the Lord, the pontiff ascends a wooden seat. Immediately two acolytes carry the ampullae, wrapped in white silk cloth, on their left arms, so that they can be seen from the middle upward. The deacon assisting the lord pope takes one ampulla, mixed with balsam, and presents it to the pontiff, 357 holding it wrapped on his left arm. The pontiff then breathes over it three times. Afterwards all the bishops assisting there and the cardinal priests also breathe over it, and he says without chant: “Dominus vobiscum” (“The Lord be with you”), “Exorcizo te, creatura olei” (“I exorcize you, creature of oil”), and so forth.

After this blessing, all the bishops and cardinals salute the holy chrism in order. As they salute it, they bow their heads and say, “Ave, sanctum chrisma” (“Hail, holy chrism”), and kiss the ampulla. Once the chrism has been saluted by the bishops and priests, the same men must immediately salute the oil, in the following manner.

The lord pope salutes the chrism and immediately afterwards the oil, saying, “Ave, sanctum oleum” (“Hail, holy oil”); each individual must do the same. Afterwards the ampullae are carried back in procession, as they were brought, to the sacristy or to the place where they are to remain. Then they are distributed to each person according to what is due and appropriate.

The pontiff, seated, gives Communion to those who wish to receive it. The intact offerings of the Body of the Lord are nevertheless reverently reserved until Good Friday; the Blood of the Lord is entirely consumed. The kiss of peace is not given. “Agnus Dei” is said, followed by the Communion chant, “Dominus Jesus Christus,” and so forth. Then the pontiff returns to the altar and says the Collect “Refecti,” and so forth. When it has been completed, the deacon says, “Ite, missa est” (“Go, the Mass is ended”).

## LXXXIV. The rubric concerning the Mandatum on Holy Thursday

After the solemn Mass has been completed, the pontiff, dressed as he was when he sang the Mass, ascends to the palace, accompanied by the bishops, priests, and deacons, everything having been carried out according to its proper order. The pontiff enters the basilica of Saint Lawrence in the Palace, or the chapel of Saint Martin if he is at Saint Peter’s. He removes his chasuble and has a mantle placed over his shoulders. With the fanon and mitre placed on his head, he performs the Mandatum, with twelve subdeacons wearing rochets together with surplices.

The chamberlains place a basin before him. He girds himself with a linen cloth and has a clean towel before him. According to the lord James [Note: [Col. 1207D] From this it is clear that this is not the completely pure Ordinary of James Gaietani, but has been interpolated in certain places by someone else, especially, apparently, in the places where the word *rubrica* is added in the title.] Gaietani, one deacon who serves him girds the pope himself, carrying on his arms a small sleeve brought for this purpose and holding a clean towel before him. All these things must be prepared by the treasurer or by the brothers of Prognota [Alternative: Pignotta]. The twelve subdeacons remain outside the basilica barefoot. Two doorkeepers take the prior in their arms and carry him before the pontiff.

The pontiff, using warm water, which the chamberlains are to pour, washes the prior’s feet, dries them with a towel, kisses his right foot, and gives him two solidi. He does the same for each of the subdeacons and gives each twelve denarii. Meanwhile the cantors, standing before him, sing Vespers, with the Vesper antiphon “Calicem salutaris” (“The cup of salvation”), and so forth. After these have been said, no lesson or verse is read, but the antiphon “Coenantibus autem” (“While they were dining”), and so forth, is sung. When everything has been completed, the pontiff says the Collect while reading: “Respice, quaesumus, Domine, super hanc familiam tuam” (“Look, we beseech you, Lord, upon this family of yours”), and so forth, as is customary and as is more fully contained in the Vesper office of this day.

## LXXXV. Concerning the distribution of the presbyterium

After Vespers have been said and the Mandatum has been performed by the pope, as stated above, the supreme pontiff distributes the presbyterium to the cardinals and legates. Dressed in vestments up to and including the dalmatic, wearing a red mantle over his shoulders, the fanon on his head, and the gold-embroidered mitre over it, he is led by two cardinal deacons to the chapel of Saint Sylvester. He enters it and, so vested, sits in his faldstool. He gives each cardinal and prelate individually the customary presbyterium: first to the cardinal bishops, second to the cardinal priests, and third to the cardinal deacons, according to the order of seniority of each in the rank of cardinalate in which he then stands; afterwards he gives it individually to all the other prelates.

Each cardinal and prelate, having removed his own mitre and carrying it in his hands, goes before him on bended knees. He holds the open mitre before the pope, who places in it the money given to him by the chamberlain in a silver bowl, according to the chamber book called the *Polyptychus*. The person who receives the money in his mitre kisses the lord pope’s knee.

The same chamberlain has before him a large table covered with a tablecloth, on which these coins are placed, and two chamber clerks and two merchants assist him. The chamberlain and the clerks alone wear surplices or albs. 359

## LXXXVI. Concerning the meal on the Lord’s Supper

After the presbyterium has been given [Note: [Col. 1208D] This and the following chapters through chapter 91 are found, almost word for word, in Peter Amelius, from chapter 69 onward.], the lord pope, dressed as we have said, is solemnly led by two cardinal deacons to a table prepared for the occasion. There he sits, with a cardinal bishop giving him water and two cardinal deacons—one on his right and the other on his left—holding the towel; the one on his right also holds the ring while the pope washes.

It should be noted that these three cardinals, at the first and second washings of the hands and at the blessing of the table, minister to the pope without their mantles, having removed their mitres while they minister. During the thanksgiving, however, they resume their mantles and replace their mitres. After the first washing of the hands and the blessing of the table—of which more will be said below—they all go and sit down. Once seated, all the cardinals wash their hands and serve one another, as will be described below in the account of the other washing.

## LXXXVII. The order of seating at table

The pope sits alone at one elevated table, with various large golden and silver vessels placed upon it. At another table, to the pope’s right, running lengthwise through the hall, sit the cardinal bishops. Among them, if they are present, sit the four patriarchs of the principal patriarchal churches, according to the order of precedence and subsequent rank of their churches. Each patriarch must nevertheless sit between two cardinal bishops. After them, at another table, sit the cardinal priests.

In the part on the left, which likewise extends lengthwise [Col. 1209A] along the hall, sit the cardinal deacons, all according to the order of precedence of each in the rank of cardinalate in which they stand. For the senior ones sit first at the table; and beyond the tables of the cardinals will be the tables of all the other prelates and nobles.

And note that the pope will stand while he eats, dressed as described above, namely, through and including the dalmatic, with a red mantle reaching to his shoulders, a fanon on his head, an auriphrygiate mitre over the fanon, a precious but non-pontifical ring on his finger, and sandals on his feet. All the cardinals, both secular and religious, will wear cottae with [lacuna], without white shirts, simple mitres of garnello on their heads, and mantles reaching to their shoulders. The secular cardinals will have a mantle of rose-brown brunetto; the religious [Col. 1209B] cardinals will have a mantle in the color of their religious order. Thus dressed they will eat, and all the other prelates likewise, though a distinction is to be made between secular and religious persons with respect to the color of their mantles, as was said concerning the cardinals.

### LXXXVIII. On the servers at the pope’s table

Before the pope, the laymen who are older and more noble among those present serve according to the offices assigned to them by the master of the household.

It should nevertheless be noted that at table one of the principal nobles places the first course before the pope, even if he is a king. Once it has been placed, if he is a king, he goes to sit at the table on the left, between the first two cardinal deacons. Thus did Lord Charles I, king [Col. 1209C] of Sicily, and the kings descended from him act, especially since the emperor of Constantinople, who at that time was at the Curia, sat on the right between the first two cardinal bishops; he had perhaps placed the first course before the pope, while the king of Sicily placed the second.

Other senior nobles also, even if they are sons of emperors or kings, serve the pope at table: one, namely, from the cup; another, with the knife for cutting. Others stand beside the pope while he eats; others follow the courses, themselves carrying carving knives for the pope and the cardinals, as shall be arranged.

### LXXXIX. On the second washing of hands on Maundy Thursday

After the meal, the pope washes his hands, with a bishop and two cardinal deacons serving him as before. These three cardinals, having resumed their mantles and mitres [Col. 1209D], return to sit with the other cardinals at their tables.

Then each of them, and every cardinal likewise, while seated washes his own hands, with a server pouring water for the cardinal who is washing. The assisting cardinals hold a towel, one on one side of the person washing and the other on the other side; and thus they serve one another mutually.

When all have washed, spices and wine are given. At the end, when the tables have been removed, the lord pope and everyone else rise. While he stands on his footstool, with two deacons and a bishop serving him, thanks are given to the cardinals, as follows below.

After these have been given, the pope [Col. 1210A] is led by the two aforementioned deacons to his chamber or antechamber, where he sits on the faldstool with only the cardinals, his brothers, dressed as he and they had been at table. Then, having removed his sacred vestments and taken off his sandals, he rests.

The cardinals and other prelates return to their lodgings, still wearing their mitres [Note: [Col. 1209] Peter Amelii adds: “a horseman, though the horses are not equipped, but covered.”] [lacuna], as they stood during the meal. It should be remembered that all the pope’s chaplains, both table-companions and non-table-companions, ought on that day to eat splendidly with the chamberlain.

It should also be noted that no woman ever ate in the presence of the Roman pontiff, even if she was an empress or queen. This was observed in the time of Lords Clement V, John XXII, Benedict XII, Clement VI, and [Col. 1210B] Innocent VI; nor was it ever heard that the contrary had been done at any time, including in the time of Lords Urban V, Gregory XII, or Urban VI.

It should be noted that if the pope does not make the holy chrism, the ceremonies described above do not take place.

Likewise, if the cardinals do not eat with the pope himself, these solemnities do not take place.

### XC. The blessing of the table on Maundy Thursday

On Maundy Thursday, when blessing the table, the verse is said absolutely, without musical notation: “Christ became obedient for us unto death.” Then the Lord’s Prayer is said immediately and silently. When it has been completed, the lord pope, without any spoken formula, signs both his own table and the others. Neither “Jube, domne” [“Command, lord”] [Col. 1210C] nor “Tu autem, Domine” [“But you, O Lord”] is said.

At the end of the meal, the verse “Christ became obedient,” etc., is repeated as above. Then the Psalm “Have mercy on me, O God” is said alternately, without “Glory be to the Father.” Afterwards the Lord’s Prayer is said silently. When it is finished, the pope says absolutely the prayer “Look, we beseech you, O Lord, upon this family,” etc.; it is not announced. “Who with you,” nor “May the souls of the faithful,” is said; but, without any alteration, the lord pope simply signs himself and everyone devoutly.

Then, having resumed the fanon and mitre on his head, with his mantle reaching to his shoulders, he is led, as stated above, by two cardinal deacons to his chamber or antechamber.

### XCI. Also concerning the Mandatum and the matters mentioned above when the pope is not in the City

After the lord pope has said the final prayer, the deacon has said “The Mass is ended,” [Col. 1210D] and “May the name of the Lord be blessed,” as is customary, the lord pope, dressed in all the vestments in which he celebrated, goes with all the cardinals, bishops, priests, and deacons according to their order to a prepared place, in order to perform the Mandatum.

Sitting, therefore, on the faldstool, having removed the chasuble and pallium and taken a mantle onto his shoulders, with the fanon on his head and the mitre over it, he is girded with a linen cloth. One deacon who serves him girds the pope, wearing armlets prepared for this purpose on his arms. A basin is placed before him by the chamberlains. He washes the feet of twelve deacons [Col. 1211A] or chaplains, in their [lacuna] and cottae, who, dressed in tunicles and barefoot, must wait in a separate place.

Then two ushers or attendants take the first of those subdeacons and carry him before the pontiff, and do the same with each one. The supreme pontiff washes the feet of each person brought before him with warm water, dries them with a linen cloth, kisses their feet, and gives each one two solidi of denarii.

Meanwhile the singers sing Vespers, and the chapel sings before the pope with musical notation. The pontiff says the prayer “Look, we beseech you, O Lord,” without musical notation. When this has been done, the supreme pontiff gives the presbyterium and goes to the table, as described more fully above.

Concerning the blessing of the oil of the sick, the exorcised oil, and the consecration of the chrism, it was said above [Col. 1211B] in the office of the aforementioned Thursday of the Lord’s Supper.

### XCII. How and on what days General Proceedings are conducted

General Processions, according to approved custom, are held three days each year: namely, on Thursday of Holy Week, on the Ascension of the Lord, and on the Dedication of the basilicas [of the] apostles Peter and Paul. On these three days certain special proceedings are also conducted as appropriate, whether against communities or notable persons, even if they are kings or emperors, against whom their [lacuna] might proceed, by admonition, citation, suspension, excommunication, interdict, deprivation, or other spiritual and temporal penalties and sentences. In the proceedings [Col. 1211C] all the cardinals and the aforementioned officials of the Curia are dressed in white. The lord pope, however, wears a red cope, and the other observances are as follows below.

On Thursday of Holy Week the following order is observed. After the lord pope has said Terce and Sext in his chamber without musical notation, wearing the stole around his neck in the customary manner and dressed in a red cope with a solemn pearl-studded auriphrygium, and wearing a pearl-studded mitre, with two deacons serving him dressed in their customary woolen copes, at the third or sixth hour he proceeds to a solemn and elevated place prepared for preaching and for conducting whatever proceedings are to be conducted. Cardinal deacons and chaplains and others precede him with the cross.

[Col. 1211D] On reaching the place, he sits on the faldstool and receives the cardinals and prelates who are not yet vested in formal dress as they come to pay reverence, although sometimes they come already vested, fearing the proceedings. After this reverence has been made, the lord pope addresses the people in the vernacular, though assuming authority in Latin, and briefly, since much must be done that day; or he entrusts the sermon to another person, namely, to a bishop or cardinal priest. In the sermon, if desired, mention may be made of the solemnity of the day and something may also be said about the Processions to be carried out.

If the lord pope himself preaches, while he is preaching [Col. 1212A] everyone is vested, both cardinals and prelates, each in his own habit: deacons in dalmatics and tunicles, priests in chasubles, bishops in copes, and chaplains in surplices and cottae. The pope’s subdeacons may wear tunicles; there ought to be twelve of them that day.

If a bishop or cardinal priest preaches, the preacher himself must be vested; but the other cardinals and prelates may postpone receiving their vestments until the proceedings begin, or until the cardinal deacon begins to render them in the vernacular.

364 But in any event the two deacons who serve the lord pope, the deacon who is to render the Processions in the vernacular, and at least one of the bishops—the one who preaches—may receive their vestments immediately after the reverence has been made [Col. 1212B], so that they may be better prepared to carry out their ministry.

The customary order, therefore, is as follows: when the lord pope comes to the place of the proceedings, he sits on the faldstool and people come to pay reverence; a brief sermon is given to the people by the pope or by one of the cardinals; and the lord pope returns to his seat.

If one or several chaplains preach, if there are several proceedings, standing in a cotta and scutum [scutis] facing the people, they quickly and intelligibly read the proceedings in vero [perhaps “in Latin”] [Note: [Col. 1211] Perhaps “in Latin,” as in Peter Amelii, chapter 63.] in the manner in which lessons are read in church. One of the deacons, dressed in white vestments and holding the mitre on his head, facing the people, renders in the vernacular the proceeding read by the chaplain, at least in substance. Then, after the second proceeding has been read, the same deacon renders it in the vernacular. He does the same in the same order if there are more proceedings.

It should be known that the common proceedings, which are conducted against heretics, against sea pirates, against those imposing new tolls, against falsifiers of papal bulls, against those carrying prohibited goods to the Saracens, and against those obstructing persons going to or returning from the Curia, are not customarily omitted.

When these things have been completed, the lord pope ascends the pulpit facing the people, assisted by two deacons, one on his right and the other on his left, and by one bishop on his right. The other bishops and cardinal priests, as the space permits, stand on the right; the deacons on the left; and the other prelates, whether on the right or the left, wherever they can. All, however, face the people with their mitres on their heads.

[Col. 1212D] Then the lord pope, standing facing the people, may say something about the proceedings that have been read and explained, as he wishes—namely, that he approves and ratifies them and makes them as they have been read and as the deacon has explained them. Toward the end of his words, holding some lighted torches in his hand, the lord pope throws them onto the ground toward the people. Each of the cardinals and prelates does the same, holding only one torch in his hand and saying nothing. When the candles are thrown down, the church bells must be rung in disorderly fashion.

When the proceedings have been completed, the deacon serving the supreme pontiff, on the left, having removed his own mitre [Col. 1213A] and interlacing the fingers of both hands before his chest in opposite directions, says aloud “I confess to God,” with musical notation in the customary manner. When this is finished, the lord pope briefly addresses the people again, especially if he himself preached, saying that just as the disobedient and wicked ought to receive punishments and severe proceedings for their wickedness, so the good and obedient ought to obtain thanks and rewards. He grants an indulgence to all who have attended the preaching and the proceedings, or either of them, according to the customary formula: to natives, one year and forty days; to foreigners, two years and two quarantines; to those from beyond the Alps, three years and four quarantines; and to those who have crossed the sea, four years and four quarantines.

Then the deacon serving on the right removes the mitre from the lord pope. With his hands raised, as when he says the prayer at Mass, the pope gives the absolution, saying aloud, as is customary, “Blessed be the name of the Lord,” namely, “By the prayers and merits,” etc. When “Amen” has been answered, he likewise says, “Absolution, indulgence,” etc. When “Amen” has been answered, he finally gives the blessing, saying and signing the people:

“May the blessing of almighty God, the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit, descend upon you and remain always.”

After the deacon has replaced the mitre on his head, the pope goes to the church, the cross preceding him, with the other cardinals and prelates, subdeacons, and chaplains vested and preceding after him. There, whether he says or omits “Blessed be the name of the Lord,” as he wishes, he performs everything as contained in the Ordinary and stated above.

### XCIII. On the office of Good Friday

[Col. 1213C] On Friday everything is said in order. At the first hour of the day all the chaplains are summoned to recite the Psalter, while the lord pope sits before his bed. All the chaplains also sit near his feet, and they complete the entire Psalter by turns. When it is finished, the priest with the others says the antiphon “Do not remember,” then privately the litany, “Our Father,” “Have mercy on me, O God” without a chapter, and “The Lord be with you”; the prayer “O God, whose characteristic is to have mercy,” and all the others customarily said on the days of Lent; and at the end the prayer as in the other offices.

On Good Friday itself, after Prime has been said with its prayer, “Look, we beseech you, O Lord,” and the psalm has been read, Terce is said at the appropriate hour. At the sixth hour everyone assembles at the Lateran basilica [Col. 1213D], or at another church, and says Sext. Then the pontiff dresses himself only in the complete Lenten vesture; the bishops in copes, and the priests, deacons, and subdeacons in chasubles.

“On this day the cardinals do not come to pay reverence to the pope, but immediately in the very chair they remove their scarlet capes.

“And it should be known that on this day, before going to the church or chapel to perform the office, the lord pope comes twice to the window to grant the indulgence to the people in the customary manner: once in the morning, and a second time when he wishes to go to the chapel to perform the office. Each time he wears a red cope and a plain garnello mitre without auriphrygium. After the indulgence has been granted the second time, he goes to his chamber, removes the cope there, and puts on a red scarlet cope, open from the middle of the chest to the feet. Wearing on his head the same white, plain garnello mitre without auriphrygium or pearls, he enters the chapel with the cardinals to perform the office.” [Col. 1214A]

Then the junior cardinal priest [Note: [Col. 1213D] The following words of Peter Amelii, chapter 76, belong here: “According to Lord James Gaetani, the junior cardinal priest anciently used to carry the body of Christ to the altar.”] carries the decorated casket containing the Lord’s body, reserved from the previous day. The subdeacon with the people’s cross precedes the procession; all proceed in orderly fashion, barefoot and without singing, reciting psalms, to the church of the Holy Cross, which is in Jerusalem and where the station is to be held, when the lord pope is at the Lateran. When they have arrived there [Col. 1214B], they enter the church without singing and pray for a considerable time, prostrate in the middle of the church.

The priest carrying the Lord’s body places it in the sacristy while the lord pope prepares himself. Once he is prepared, the priest brings it in procession before the pope to the altar. Rising from prayer, the lord pope enters the sacristy with the clergy. Having removed his chasuble and pallium, he sits in his seat; after his feet have been washed, the ministers put on him not sandals but his ordinary shoes.

Coming to the faldstool, he says None. After a short while, having again put on the chasuble and pallium, and preceded [Al., “preceding”] by the cross and the Gospel, without lights but with incense, they proceed in orderly silence to the altar. Then all, prostrate on carpets spread out, pray for a considerable time.

Meanwhile, while the ministers [lacuna], the chaplains spread a single sindon towel [Col. 1214C] over the bare altar, without auriphrygium. When the prayer has been completed, he says nothing else, nor does he make the confession. Instead, after kissing the altar, the pontiff ascends the middle seat in the customary manner. The subdeacon immediately proceeds to read; without title, reverence, or kissing of the feet, he begins in the manner of a reading:

“Thus says the Lord: In tribulation,” etc.

All the lessons, both today and on Holy Saturday, are read in the manner of a reading. When it is finished, the Tract “O Lord, I have heard” is sung. At the end of the tract, the pontiff says “Let us pray,” and the deacon, namely the senior of the deacons, says “Let us bend the knee”; then the other deacon assisting the pope says “Arise,” and says the prayer “O God, from whom,” etc.

When it is finished, the deacon likewise reads, without title, another Epistle: “In those days the Lord spoke to Moses,” etc. [Col. 1214D] When the reading has been completed, the tract “Deliver me,” etc., is sung.

Before the Tract has ended, the deacon who is to proclaim the Passion must remove his chasuble and take it over his left shoulder in the manner of a stole, so that its ends are fastened at the right side, almost behind him.

It should be noted that at the beginning of the Passion the pope rises from the cathedral seat, removes his mitre, and stands with his feet facing the altar, near the middle. Supporting himself against it behind his shoulders, he looks toward the person reading the Passion, with his hands joined before his chest. He remains standing in this way until he reaches the passage of the Passion where it says, “And he bowed his head,” etc. Then the pope kneels there, facing the altar, and remains kneeling for as long as the Lord’s Prayer could be said once. Afterwards he rises and stands as before. All the others do likewise.

When this has been completed, the deacon, having made reverence before the altar, proceeds with the Gospel, without blessing or kissing the feet, without torches and without incense. Ascending the bare pulpit, he does not say “The Lord be with you,” but simply says:

“The Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ,” etc.

With no one responding, he reads: “At that time [he] went out,” etc. When they have reached the place where it says, “He gave up his spirit,” the deacon immediately kneels before God, and all do likewise, remaining on their knees for as long as the Lord’s Prayer could be said. Then the deacon and the others rise, and he continues the Passion as he had begun.

When they reach the place where it says, “After this, Joseph of Arimathea asked Pilate,” the acolytes bring forward the thurible according to custom; the pontiff places incense in it, and the acolytes carry it to the Gospel and also carry lighted torches. When the Gospel has ended, the book, with the incense, is brought back to the pontiff for him to kiss.

368 Afterwards, according to modern custom, a sermon is given by a master of theology or a prelate. The person giving the sermon, kneeling before the pope, asks for his blessing, but does not kiss his foot. Having received the blessing and the indulgence to be announced in the sermon, he goes to the customary place to preach.

When the sermon is given, the pope sits on a bare cathedral seat before the altar, wearing his mitre on his head. When the sermon has ended, the Confession is not said; instead, the preacher immediately announces the indulgence by the pope’s mandate and authority, for example, of seven years and seven quarantines.

It should be noted that the senior cardinal deacon who assists the pope on the right says “Let us bend the knee” in these prayers, and the second says “Arise”; afterwards the second says “Let us bend the knee,” and the third deacon says “Arise”; then the third deacon says “Let us bend the knee,” and the fourth answers “Arise,” and so on to the last. If it is necessary to repeat the formula, it returns to the first deacon.

Then the pontiff rises and says these solemn prayers: “Let us pray, most beloved,” etc. In the prayer for the Jews, “Let us pray” is said, but “Let us bend the knee” is not said, because on this day they bent their knees in mockery of the Lord. Therefore, abhorring their crime, the Church does not bend the knee for them in the prayer “Almighty,” etc.

When the prayers have ended, the pontiff proceeds to the altar. Standing at the right horn of the altar, he receives from the ministers the cross prepared for him and covered with a clean sindon. Uncovering it from the top, with his hands raised, he alone begins the antiphon:

“Behold the wood of the cross,”

with those assisting him helping in the singing. When they have sung “Come, let us adore,” all prostrate themselves and adore reverently, bowing down to the ground. [Col. 1216A] The cantors in the choir repeat the antiphon, “Behold the wood,” etc.

Again the pontiff proceeds a little farther and uncovers the cross halfway. With his hands raised higher and his voice exalted, he alone begins the same antiphon, assisted in the singing by those around him. The cantors repeat the antiphon a second time.

A third time the pontiff proceeds before the altar, uncovers the entire cross, raises his hands upward, and begins “Behold the wood of the cross” in a higher voice. The cantors repeat the antiphon a third time; and a third time, while “Come, let us adore” is sung, everyone adores it.

Then the pontiff, still wearing his gloves, places the cross with his hands on a spread pall and very clean linen cloths at the foot of the altar. Barefoot, he alone prostrates himself a third time and adores the cross. When this [Col. 1216B] has been done, he returns to his seat and there receives his shoes, which had been removed.

“ It should be noted that Lords Gregory XI and Urban VI, Roman pontiffs, never wished to remove their shoes in the cathedral seat near the altar. It is believed that this was out of reverence for the altar, since both were devout; instead, they did so in another large, bare cathedral seat far from the altar, where they customarily vested on solemn occasions.

“Afterwards all the cardinals, barefoot in their places, go in pairs, led by their attendants, to adore the cross according to their order, and they do not kneel. Likewise, all the other persons present adore the same cross in the same manner.”

Afterwards the entire choir adores it in orderly fashion. Meanwhile the cantors sing the “Agios” antiphonally, repeating “Holy [Col. 1216C] God, holy mighty one,” etc.; the antiphon “My people, because I led you out of the land”; “What more ought I to have done?” with the entire reproach; and the other antiphons, “We adore you, O Christ,” “Your cross,” and “Save us, O Christ, save us”; and the psalm “May God have mercy on us,” and the hymns “Sing, my tongue,” “Faithful Cross.”

“After the adoration of the cross has ended, the sacristan or another person appointed for this purpose places the cross in its proper place on the altar, lights the lamps on the altar, and the sacristan alone receives the money offered during the adoration of the cross on this day, since it belongs to him; on other days it belongs to the chaplains.

“Once the cross has thus been placed, the chamberlain, or the person acting in his place, carries another cross outside the gates, accompanied by the clerics of the chamber and chapel, so that the others may adore it.

“It should be noted [Note: [Col. 1215D] This appears in Peter Amelii, chapter 76.] that in the time of the Roman pontiffs John XXII, Benedict XII, Clement VI, Innocent VI, Urban V, Gregory XI, and Urban VI, it was observed that when the pope returned to the cathedral seat, as stated here, he stood there and resumed the black chasuble and pallium with clasps from the hand of the cardinal deacon who had proclaimed the Passion. He then proceeded to the altar without mitre and without the customary confession, assisted by two cardinal deacons. Afterwards he went with the cross, lights, and incense to the small cupboard or chest in which the body of Christ had been reserved with the chalice on the previous day.

“And it was observed up to the present that the Roman pontiff himself went to the small cupboard or chest and carried the body of Christ to the altar, covered with that silk towel, with one end and with the other hanging over his left shoulder.” [Col. 1216D–1217A]

“When these things have been completed, the pontiff removes his gloves, which he does not resume, and washes his hands. With the cross placed between the torches on the altar, he either enters the altar [Note: [Col. 1217D] Perhaps: “he proceeds to the altar,” namely, where the body of Christ had been placed, as follows from the preceding.] or proceeds to the altar.

“The cardinal priest carries the body of Christ and places it on the altar. The lord pope opens the casket, takes the body with his hand, and places it on the paten. The deacon receives the paten from the subdeacon and holds it in his hand; the deacon offers the Lord’s Body, which had been reserved the previous day, to the pope on the paten. Receiving it, the pope places it on the corporal previously spread over the sindon by the same deacon.

“The deacon offers him the chalice likewise with pure wine, and the subdeacon offers a cruet with water, which the pontiff mixes with the wine, to represent that on that day the sacraments of the Church flowed from the body, namely blood and water.” [Col. 1217B]

“It should be noted that at this Mass, in the office of chaplain, one cardinal priest serves the pope, either the one whom the pope has appointed or the one whom the senior deacon, by the pope’s command, has commissioned to do this.”

In certain churches [Note: [Col. 1217D] Peter Amelii writes, in chapter 76: “In certain churches, according to Lord James Gaetani, pure wine without water is offered, so that in pure and strong wine, etc.”] pure wine is offered today without water, so that the cruelty of the Jews and the harshness of Christ’s Passion may be represented in pure and strong wine.

When the deacon has customarily placed the chalice beside the Lord’s Body, he offers incense to the pope. The pontiff censes both, as is customary. Then he bows before the altar in prayer, saying, “In a spirit of humility.” Having risen, the pontiff turns toward the people and says, “Pray, brothers.”

Then he says in a low voice, as is customary, “For ever and ever. Let us pray. At the Savior’s command. Our Father,” etc. After the Lord’s Prayer has been completed, he says this prayer in the same tone:

“Deliver us, we beseech you, O Lord, from all evils,” etc.

When “Amen” has been answered, he breaks the Host according to custom and places part of it in the chalice, saying nothing. For the unconsecrated wine is sanctified by the Lord’s Body being placed in it.

The “Peace of the Lord” is not given. The “Lamb of God” is not sung, nor is the kiss of peace given, nor is the Postcommunion sung. The pontiff alone receives Communion without the ministers, not solemnly at the cathedral seat, but there, on that day, before the altar alone, out of humble reverence for the day and Christ’s Passion. [Note: [Col. 1217D] Peter Amelii supplies here: “And not with a reed, but with the chalice he takes the blood, and after the blood has been received, the sacristan pours wine into the chalice.”] He performs the ablution in the chalice and consumes it himself, and afterwards [washes] with water in basins.

Then, returning to his seat, he removes his vestments and with his clerics says Vespers of the preceding day, not by singing but by recitation. The antiphon “The cup of salvation” is said to the end, without a lesson, hymn, or versicle. At the Magnificat: the antiphon “When he had received the vinegar.” Another antiphon is said at the Magnificat: “The thief said to the thief.” In all the others, “Glory be to the Father” is not said.

When these things have been completed, “Christ became obedient for us,” etc., is said in full. Afterwards, without “Lord, have mercy,” the Lord’s Prayer is said silently; then the psalm “Have mercy on me, O God” [Col. 1218A] and the prayer “Look,” etc. When all these things have been completed, each person returns peacefully and without conversation with the others to his own place. The lord pope does not dine with the chaplains that day, nor the chaplains with him; but anyone who wishes to dine eats with whomever he wishes and whenever he wishes.

Also, in the evening, for the office of Matins, the pope comes to the chapel in a closed scarlet cope lined with ermine, closed from the middle of the chest upward and open below. He always keeps the cowl over his head and sits without a mitre in the bare cathedral seat. The cardinal deacons neither sit before his feet at those three Matins nor give the blessing at their end.

### XCIV. The order of the office for Holy Saturday

On Holy Saturday, at the sixth hour, the ministers of the church strike fire from crystal or stone [Note: [Col. 1218D] Pope Zacharias does not approve this in Letter 12 to Boniface. Nevertheless, the same is read in Peter Amelii, chapter 77.] and kindle it.

The junior cardinal priest, vested in sacred garments, blesses the new fire with the cross, holy water, and incense. The prayers are:

“O God, who through your Son, the cornerstone,” etc.

“O Lord God, almighty Father, unfailing light,” etc.

“O holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God, bless us,” etc.

“Come, we beseech you, almighty [God],” etc.

When the fire has been blessed, it is sprinkled with holy water, and incense is placed in a thurible and burned from that fire.

Then the junior of the cardinal deacons, dressed in a dalmatic, comes and receives from the ministers a reed three cubits and a half a cubit long, bearing a triple candle. Having lit it from the new fire, he places it on the reed. He is accompanied by the subdeacons, cantors, and the rest of the clergy, with the people, while the ministers carrying the cross and incense precede.

Standing at the church door, with his hands raised slightly, he says in a loud voice:

“The light of Christ.”

The others respond:

“Thanks be to God.”

He proceeds to the door of the choir and, raising his hands higher, says more loudly:

“The light of Christ.”

They again respond:

“Thanks be to God.”

He proceeds to the middle of the choir and, raising his hands still higher, says a third time in a still higher voice:

“The light of Christ.”

All respond:

“Thanks be to God.”

He ascends to the decorated pulpit. After the great candle has been lit and the book incensed, he begins the blessing of the candle without any preface:

“Now let the angelic trumpet of heaven exult,” etc.,

as it is found in the books. All the lights must be extinguished, so that they may be lit from the new fire.

Meanwhile, while the candle is being blessed, the pontiff says Terce and Sext in his chamber [Col. 1218D], but says None in the church. After these have been said, he puts on his shoes and all his Lenten vesture; the bishops put on copes, and the priests and deacons chasubles. The subdeacons, however, are vested not in chasubles but in tunics, so that they may be properly and suitably dressed while remaining more ready to read the lessons.

Then the pontiff, leaving the sacristy with everyone else, proceeds in procession to the altar, preceded by one subdeacon with the cross and another subdeacon with the Gospel, though in silence. Having made reverence before the decorated pulpit, he ascends the seat, while everyone sits around him on both sides according to his order.

When the blessing of the candle has ended, the subdeacon ascends the ambo and begins to read the lesson without title:

“In the beginning God created heaven and earth.”

When he has completed it, if the lord pope wishes, the Greek subdeacon reads the same lesson again in Greek. When it has been completed, the pontiff says “Let us pray”; the deacon on the right says “Let us bend the knee”; and after a short while the other deacon, on the left, says “Arise.” Then the prayer follows, along with the others, as they are contained in the Ordinary.

It should be understood that throughout the entire office on Holy Saturday, before the Mass, the color violet is to be used, except that the deacon who sings [Col. 1219B] the blessing of the candle is dressed in a dalmatic. The subdeacon or subdeacons who are vested that day wear white tunicles. But after the blessing of the candle has been sung, the deacon removes the dalmatic and takes a violet chasuble, which he wears until the office of the Mass begins; the subdeacons do not change their vestments.

### XCV. The office on the day of the holy Easter resurrection of the Lord
On Holy Sunday of Easter, the station is at Saint John Lateran. Very early in the morning, after saying Prime, the lord pope goes to the basilica of Saint Lawrence, which is called the Holy of Holies. There, after the chapel has been placed before the faldstool, he first prays; afterward he is vested by the deacon and subdeacon up to the dalmatic. Then he rises and [Col. 1219C] enters to the Savior, opens the image of the Savior, and kisses the feet of that image.

Then he comes to the altar and takes the cross . . . [lacuna] which has been placed there by the chaplains. Holding it in his hand, he sings in a suitable voice the antiphon, “The Lord has risen from the tomb, who for us hung upon the wood, alleluia.” The chaplains who assist him and help him sing repeat the same antiphon two further times, each time raising the pitch, just as he began it the first time. Then he returns to the faldstool.

All the cardinal deacons must be present there, as well as the prior of the subdeacons with all the chapel subdeacons, and all the other chaplains. The aforesaid deacons are vested in dalmatics, the subdeacons in tunics, and the other chaplains in white togas.

Then, while the lord pope is seated on the faldstool, the prior of the deacons [Col. 1219D] kneels before him and gives him the kiss of peace—but first he kisses his foot. Then, as the lord pope gives the peace, he says, “The Lord has truly risen”; the one who receives it responds, “And has appeared to Peter.” That deacon then returns to the file beside the pope, to his place.

After this, all the deacons and subdeacons, the other chaplains, and the remaining orders of the curia receive the peace from the supreme pontiff; in turn they give and receive the peace, beginning with the first and proceeding to the last.

Then the lord pope puts on a white chasuble. Girded with the mitre, he descends from the palace with all the other orders. The horses have been prepared with white saddlecloths over the saddles; crowned, he rides in procession [Col. 1220A] to Saint Mary Major.

When he has come to the Merulana, a notary, chosen by all the notaries of the City, says in a loud voice, “Command, lord, that I be blessed.” The pontiff blesses him. The notary then says, singing in this voice, “In the church of Saint Mary, our Lady, so many males and so many females have been baptized.” The pontiff responds, “Thanks be to God.” The same is done on the second feria at Saint Peter’s, and on the third at Saint Paul’s.

When the lord pope has come to Saint Mary’s, the station is held there. He immediately dismounts, removes the crown from his head, and gives it to the grooms so that they may guard it carefully. The canons of the church receive him in procession, carrying a thurible with incense and holy water and singing. The pontiff places incense in the thurible and sprinkles water over [Col. 1220B] the people. Then he enters the church and prays; he goes to the prepared place, ascends his seat, and says Terce.

When Terce is finished, while the lord pope remains seated and vested up to the dalmatic, the prior of the bishops approaches him, receives the peace from him, and returns to his place. Then the second bishop approaches; on returning, he gives the peace to his own prior and stands beside him in the file. All the cardinal bishops and cardinal priests do likewise. Afterward come the prefect, the senators, and all the orders.

When this has been done, two basilica subdeacons rise and take the prior of the religious subdeacons, supporting him and escorting him on his right from the entrance of the secretarium to the middle of the secretarium, before the pontiff. He says in a loud voice, “Command, lord, that I be blessed.” The pontiff blesses him. Then they lead him forward a little, and again [Col. 1220C] he says, “Command, lord, that I be blessed”; and again the pontiff blesses him. He advances farther, says, “Command, lord, that I be blessed,” and again the pontiff blesses him.

Then that subdeacon says three times, “The servants of our Lord Jesus Christ,” raising his voice on each occasion. He immediately adds: “The lord N., cardinal deacon of Saint Hadrian, will read the Gospel. The lord John, subdeacon and chaplain of the lord pope, will read the Epistle. J., the first singer, and the other singers, will sing.”

Then the lord pontiff rises, supported by two deacons, and proceeds in procession, as is customary. At the entrance of the church the mappulary attendants hold out a mappula, which they carry over his head as far as the altar. When he enters the presbytery of the church, the mansionary prepares for him a reed with a lighted candle. He takes it and places it in tow above the capitals [Col. 1220D] of the columns that stand there.

When he comes to the first singer, the first singer removes the pope’s mitre and kisses his right shoulder; when he has come before the altar, the pope blesses him. The mappulary attendants remove the mappula from above his head. Then he celebrates the office as is customary, and the lauds are delivered as they are contained in the Polyptych.

During the secret prayer, two deacons descend before the altar, [375] and two subdeacons stand there in due order and silence. When the pontiff says, “For ever and ever,” no one responds “Amen”; instead, “Our Father” begins, together with what follows.

When Mass is finished, he is crowned and returns to the palace.

It should be known that when the lord pope does not go on such a day to Saint Mary Major, the [Col. 1221A] bishops and cardinal priests receive the kisses of peace in the portico before the basilica of Saint Lawrence of the palace, where the examinations of bishops-elect for Mass are held.

### XCVI. The First Saturday within Easter

On this Saturday the station is at Saint John Lateran. On this day the lord pope ought to sing Mass there, and the Gradual is changed into the Alleluia, with its verses.

While the school sings the Agnus Dei, the lord pope distributes the lambs. First he gives them to the bishops, second to the priests, and third to the deacons vested in their proper vestments; he places the lambs in their mitres, and they kiss his knee. The other prelates do the same if they are vested.

If they are not vested, however, and likewise those who come to receive the lambs, they kiss his foot—even if it were a king who came immediately after the cardinals to receive the candles, holding both the palm and the lambs. [Col. 1221B] Two are given to each prelate, and one to the others.

It should nevertheless be noted that before the prior of the cardinal priests receives the vestments, he receives the peace from the prelate who is celebrating before the pope. After receiving it, he goes to vest himself, as do the other cardinal priests. No sermon is given on that day; but if the pope himself were celebrating, the same arrangement would be followed.

When Mass is finished, the lord pope returns to the palace. On coming to the house where he is to eat, he ascends his seat. After washing his hands and giving the blessing, with the table set before him, the acolyte whose week it is to serve takes a towel. Holding the basin full of those lambs with both hands beneath it, he comes to the door of the house and says in a loud voice:

[Col. 1221C] “Lord, lord, these are the newborn lambs that proclaimed the alleluia; now they come to the springs, they are filled with brightness, alleluia.”

And he bows. Then, proceeding a little farther, he says the same thing in a louder voice. A third time, advancing and standing before the supreme pontiff, he reports it in a still louder voice: “Lord, lord, these are the lambs,” and so forth.

After this he places the basin on the table. The lord pope distributes those lambs among his household; but first [376] he gives them to the priests, chaplains, and acolytes, and to all the others.

### XCVII. How the wax Agnus Dei are made, and so forth

Let us learn how these lambs are made. The acolytes receive pure wax from the altar of the most blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. They prepare that wax with the chrism left over from the previous year, and place the seals in molds devised for this purpose.

[Col. 1221D] Octave Sunday of Easter. The prayer, “Grant, we beseech you, almighty God,” and so forth.

On the days that remain after the Octave of the Ascension—namely, Friday and Saturday—if a feast occurs, we perform the entire office of the Mass from the feast, with a commemoration of Sunday. If it is not a Sunday feast, we perform the entire office of the Mass, and the preface “Who, ascending above all the heavens” is said, but the Creed is not said. If, however, a feast occurs on that Saturday, we perform the entire office from the feast, while the Mass is said from the vigil, with a commemoration of the feast. On that Saturday everyone ought to fast devoutly.

At the ninth hour everyone gathers in the church, and we ought to perform the entire office or order just as we do on Holy Saturday at the [Col. 1222A] Easter vigil, except that neither the candle nor the fire is blessed. When everything has been prepared, the subdeacon proceeds to read and begins the reading without a title: “God tested,” and so forth. When it is finished, the pontiff or priest says the prayers without “Let us kneel”: “O God, who [to] Abraham …”

When the readings, Tracts, and prayers have been completed, and all the lamps of the church have been lit, the pontiff or priest descends to the fonts, preceded by the clergy singing the litany and the Tract “As the deer.” When these have been completed, before entering for the blessing, he says this prayer: “Grant, we beseech you, almighty God,” and so forth. When the prayer is complete, the blessing of the font follows, as it is found on Holy Saturday.

[Col. 1222B] After the celebration of the baptism, the pontiff and clergy enter the sacristy. Then, solemnly vested in red vestments with all the ceremonial apparatus, he proceeds in procession to the altar. When the reading and the “Kyrie, eleison” are finished, immediately after the confession the pontiff ascends his seat and solemnly says, “Glory to God in the highest.” When it is finished, he says, “Peace be with you”; then [377] the Mass follows in its proper order.

The Creed is not said. The Offertory is said, and likewise the Agnus Dei; the kiss of peace is given, and the Postcommunion is said. The prayer: “Grant, we beseech you,” and so forth.

Urban V sent the emperor one lamb as a great gift, with these verses:

“Balsam and pure wax with liquid chrism

Form the lamb, which I give you as a great gift,

As though born from the font, sanctified through sacred mysteries.

[Col. 1222C] It drives away lightning from above and every evil thing.

The pregnant woman is kept safe, and the birth is delivered without woe.

When carried in purity, it preserves [one] from the effects of the flood;

It breaks sin, as does Christ’s blood, and restrains it;

It brings gifts to the worthy and destroys the powers of fire.”

### XCVIII. On the days and solemnities when Roman pontiffs customarily celebrate the solemnities of Mass in person

On the days and solemnities listed below, Roman pontiffs customarily celebrate the solemnities of Mass in person. On those same days and solemnities, however, they customarily preach in person whenever they wished, and have someone preach before them, as follows. No one other than cardinals preaches before the lord pope when the lord pope celebrates.

[Col. 1222D] On the First Sunday of Advent, and a sermon is preached.

On the Second Sunday of Advent, and a sermon is preached.

On the Third Sunday of Advent, called Gaudete Sunday, and a sermon is preached. It has solemn papal Vespers sung beforehand in the church, and a drink is served afterward in the hall. Papal Vespers are said when the lord pope, cardinals, and all the prelates are required to be vested. In the church, however, cardinals and prelates are not vested at Vespers unless Vespers are said in the church.

At the Nativity of the Lord, at three Masses. It has only solemn papal Vespers beforehand, and it has papal Matins. No sermon is preached today, [Col. 1223A] although in ancient times one was preached at Mass; but all the cardinal deacons and officials of the curia receive Communion from the hand of the supreme pontiff.

At the feast of Saint Stephen, protomartyr, and a sermon is preached.

At the feast of Saint John the Evangelist, and a sermon is preached.

[378] At the feast of the Innocents, and a sermon is preached.

At the Circumcision of the Lord, and a sermon is preached.

At the Epiphany, and a sermon is preached. It has solemn papal Vespers beforehand, and so forth.

On the First Sunday after the Octave of the Epiphany, called the Sunday of the Marriage, when the pope is at Rome; a sermon is preached before Mass.

At the Conversion of Saint Paul, and a sermon is preached.

At the feast of the Purification, and a sermon is preached before Mass.

[Col. 1223B] At the Chair of Saint Peter, and a sermon is preached.

At Septuagesima, and a sermon is preached.

At Quinquagesima, and a sermon is preached.

On Ash Wednesday, and a sermon is preached.

On the First Sunday of Lent—and all the Sundays of Lent are papal, especially the Sunday on which “Rejoice, Jerusalem” is sung. It is that Sunday on which the solemnity of the golden rose takes place—and sermons are preached on them, except on Palm Sunday, on which, although it is papal, no sermon is preached.

On Passion Sunday, and a sermon is preached.

On Palm Sunday no sermon is preached; but before Mass blessed palms are given to the vested cardinals and prelates, and to others, both clerics and laypeople, and the procession takes place.

[Col. 1223C] On Holy Thursday, and a sermon is preached before Mass. General processions take place, and also certain special ones, as appropriate. In the processions all the cardinals and prelates of the curia are vested in white.

On Good Friday no sermon is preached.

On Holy Saturday no sermon is preached.

At Easter no sermon is preached today, although in ancient times one was preached. But all the cardinal deacons and officials of the curia receive Communion from the hand of the supreme pontiff, and before Mass certain solemnities take place, both the adoration of the cross and the kiss.

On Easter Monday, and a sermon is preached.

On the Tuesday after Easter, and a sermon is preached.

On White Saturday, the prior of the cardinal bishops, or another cardinal, customarily celebrates before the lord [Col. 1223D] pope, although in ancient times the pope celebrated. After the Agnus Dei has been said, the cardinals are prepared according to the custom of their order, and the pope himself gives the Agnus Dei to the cardinals and the other prelates, as well as to [379] others. Then Mass is concluded. Afterward the pope eats with the chaplains, certain solemnities take place, and the Agnus Dei are given to them by the lord pope.

At the Annunciation of the blessed Virgin, and a sermon is preached.

On the Sunday on which “I am the good shepherd” is sung, and a sermon is preached.

At the feast of Saint Mark—that is, at the Greater Litany—a sermon is not preached at Rome. Today the papal Mass is not observed; rather, one cardinal celebrates in the pope’s presence, with the cardinals.

[Col. 1224A] At the Ascension of the Lord, and a sermon is preached before Mass. It has solemn papal Vespers beforehand, and so forth. General processions take place, as well as certain special ones, as appropriate. In the processions all the cardinals and prelates of the curia are vested in white. The processions take place before Mass.

At the feast of Pentecost, and a sermon is preached. It has solemn papal Vespers beforehand, sung in the church, and a drink is served afterward in the hall.

On the Monday after Pentecost, and a sermon is preached.

On the following Tuesday, and a sermon is preached.

At the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, and a sermon is preached. It has solemn papal Vespers beforehand, [Col. 1224B] and so forth.

At the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul, and a sermon is preached. It has solemn papal Vespers beforehand.

At the Commemoration of Saint Paul, and a sermon is preached. At Rome it has solemn papal Vespers beforehand, and so forth.

At the feast of the Snows, which is on the fifth of August, and a sermon is preached.

At the feast of Saint Lawrence, and a sermon is preached. At Rome, and also elsewhere, it has papal Vespers beforehand. If the lord pope were staying near the church of Saint Lawrence, solemn Vespers would be sung in the church, and a drink would be served to the prelates in the hall.

At the feast of the Assumption of the blessed Virgin, and a sermon is preached. It has solemn papal Vespers beforehand, [Col. 1224C] and so forth.

On the anniversary of the supreme pontiffs and cardinals, which is on the fifth day of September, no sermon is preached.

At the feast of the Nativity of the blessed Virgin, and a sermon is preached.

At the Dedication of Saint Michael in September, and a sermon is preached.

At the feast of All Saints, and a sermon is preached. It has solemn papal Vespers beforehand.

[380] On the anniversary of All Souls, which is on the day after All Saints, no sermon is preached.

At the Dedication of the basilica of the Savior, which is on the fifth day before the Ides of November, and a sermon is preached. At Rome it has solemn papal Vespers beforehand.

At the Dedication of the basilicas of the apostles Peter and [Col. 1224D] Paul, which is on the Octave of Saint Martin, a sermon is preached before Mass. It has solemn papal Vespers beforehand, and so forth. General processions take place, as well as certain special ones, as appropriate. In the processions all the cardinals and prelates are vested in white. The processions do not take place before Mass.

On the anniversary of a Roman pontiff’s predecessor, only once—that is, only in the first year—no procession is held.

### XCIX. Addition [Note: [Col. 1223] Therefore this Ordinary was written before the pontificate of John XXII.] made in the time of Pope John XXII

On the anniversary of the consecration or coronation of the Roman pontiff, that same Roman pontiff celebrates a papal Mass throughout his entire tenure from the feast that [Col. 1225A] occurs on that anniversary day, with the cardinals and the other prelates vested in the customary manner. A sermon is preached in the presence of the lord pope, not by [Note: [Col. 1225] Formerly this was done by the pontiff himself, as is clear from the sermon of Saint Leo.] the pope himself, but by a cardinal. After the prayer of the feast, the lord pope says a certain prayer for himself, which ought to be written in the papal book.

Although the anniversary in question does not have papal Vespers—that is, the cardinals are not summoned to be vested in silk for Vespers—I say that in his chapel the lord pope sings the Vespers of the feast, and certain solemnities take place afterward. For, after the prayer of the feast has been said, “Glory be to the Father,” “As it was,” and so forth, are solemnly repeated, and the verse “The Lord has chosen you as his priest,” and so forth, is said. Afterward the pope says the prayer for himself, which ought to be written in the book.

[Col. 1225B] It should nevertheless be observed that if the anniversary of our lord occurs on a Monday, since that same Monday is the anniversary of the supreme pontiffs and cardinals, which is also papal, the pope ought to celebrate and the cardinals ought to be vested, although no sermon is preached, and they are vested in violet or black. The aforesaid anniversary of the popes and cardinals may be postponed to the following day if it pleases the lord.

[381] These practices are customarily observed; nevertheless, it belongs to the lord to do what pleases him.

At the feast of Saint Andrew, and a sermon is preached. At Rome it formerly had papal Vespers and Matins, although this is not so observed today.

Moreover, besides the solemnities listed above, there were certain ancient solemnities on which Roman pontiffs [Col. 1225C] celebrated solemnly; but today this is not generally observed.

Whenever a Roman pontiff confers orders or consecrates bishops, he celebrates, but no sermon is preached at the Mass.

Furthermore, on the principal feasts of the cities in which he is staying, and on other feasts, as devotion moves him, he celebrates and a sermon is preached.

Although Roman pontiffs have been accustomed to observe the solemnities listed above, if they are prevented by weakness or another reasonable cause, they may omit them. They have also sometimes been accustomed to commission a bishop or cardinal priest to celebrate and preach in the church whose feast it is. If he wishes, he may likewise commission a bishop or cardinal priest to celebrate [Col. 1225D] in the cathedral church of the city, or elsewhere, as he pleases, and to preach.

### C. Ordinance of Pope Alexander IV concerning suffrages to be offered for deceased supreme pontiffs and cardinals

Since it is fitting that faithful souls of the dead, unable by their own efforts to procure a means of salvation, should be aided through the suffrages of prayers, the most holy lord father Alexander, pope IV, with the unanimous counsel and assent of his brothers, decreed that the anniversary of the deceased pontiffs and cardinals of the holy Roman Church should be celebrated each year on the Nones of September [Col. 1226A] with Vespers and vigils for the dead, with nine readings, solemnly sung with musical notation.

The Roman pontiff himself, with the cardinals assisting him according to custom, shall solemnly celebrate the Mass for the dead on that day. He shall feed two hundred poor people, and each cardinal shall feed twenty-five; moreover, the lord pope shall have two hundred Masses sung.

He also decreed, with the counsel and assent of the aforesaid brothers, that whenever a Roman prelate dies, [382] the cardinals shall solemnly celebrate the day of his death, with musical notation, for the dead. Each cardinal shall provide food for fifty poor people for the soul of the deceased cardinal, and afterward they shall have the same number of Masses for the dead sung.

[Col. 1226B] He also decreed that when a cardinal dies, both the supreme pontiff and the cardinals shall solemnly sing for the dead, with musical notation, in their chapels. The Roman pontiff shall feed two hundred poor people for his soul, and each cardinal twenty-five. Moreover, the lord pope shall have two hundred Masses for the dead celebrated, and each cardinal twenty-five afterward.

### CI. On the days and solemnities when Roman pontiffs customarily abstain from consistories

It should be noted that on the days and feasts listed below Roman pontiffs customarily abstain from consistories as a general rule, as experience has partly taught and the report of our predecessors has partly made clear.

[Col. 1226C] First, it should be known that no consistory is held on any Sunday throughout the year.

Likewise, no consistory is held on any Thursday throughout the year, even if there is a feast during the week.

From the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord, inclusive, through the feast of the Epiphany, inclusive, no consistory is held. Sometimes, however, after the Circumcision, the cardinals are summoned on a certain day to a consistory, not to conduct business, but to review matters, if it pleases the lord pope.

On the first day of Lent, namely Ash Wednesday, no consistory is held. Nor is a consistory held on the two preceding days, namely Monday and Tuesday in Carnival, if the curia is in the City, because of the disturbances customarily occurring on those days. If the curia is elsewhere, however, a consistory is held, especially on the two preceding Carnival days.

[Col. 1226D] From Palm Sunday, inclusive, through the Sunday after Easter, inclusive, no consistory is held, with this exception: if processions are to take place on Holy Thursday, there is customarily a consistory on Holy Wednesday, or on some other day of Holy Week, to review the processions that are to be held. This is so even though the lord pope may previously have consulted several times with his brothers about the processions to be held.

There is also this exception: if the creation of cardinals is to take place, a consistory may properly be held on several days of Holy Week. Sometimes, however, on the Friday immediately after Easter, the [Col. 1227A] cardinals are summoned to a consistory, not to conduct business, but to review matters, if it pleases the lord pope, as was said concerning Christmas.

On the day of the Ascension of the Lord, on the preceding day, and on the Octave of the Ascension, no consistory is held. On the vigil, solemn papal Vespers are sung in the church, and a drink is served in the hall. Nevertheless, on the preceding day of the Ascension, the lord pope sometimes confers with the cardinals before Vespers, if necessary, concerning the processions that are to take place on the day of the Ascension, although the lord pope may previously have consulted several times [383] with his brothers about the processions to be held.

From the vigil of Pentecost, inclusive—on which vigil solemn papal Vespers are sung in the [Col. 1227B] church and a drink is served—through the following Tuesday, inclusive, no consistory is held. On the following Wednesday or Friday, however, the cardinals are customarily summoned to a consistory.

On the four feasts of the blessed and glorious Virgin Mary—namely, the Nativity, Annunciation, Purification, and Assumption—no consistory is held. Nor is one held on the vigil of the Assumption or on its Octave. In recent times there has also not customarily been a consistory on the day before the Nativity of the blessed Virgin or on the Octave of that feast, nor on the day before the Purification.

On the feast of the Snows, which is the feast of the blessed Virgin and falls on the fifth of August, no consistory is held.

On the vigil and feast of the Nativity of Saint John [Col. 1227C] the Baptist no consistory is held, nor on its Octave.

On the feasts of all the apostles, and also on the feasts of the evangelists, both principal and nonprincipal, and especially on the feasts of the apostles Peter and Paul, no consistory is held. Nor is one held on the vigil of the apostles Peter and Paul or on their Octave.

On the feast of Saint Lawrence and on its Octave no consistory is held. Nor is one held on the vigil of the feast at Rome; nor elsewhere on the present vigil, provided that the lord pope is staying near the church of Saint Lawrence.

[384] On the two feasts of Saint Michael—namely, the Apparition and the Dedication—no consistory is held.

[Col. 1227D] On the two feasts of the Holy Cross—namely, the Invention and the Exaltation—no consistory is held.

On the feast of All Saints no consistory is held.

On the anniversary of All Souls, which is on the day after All Saints, no consistory is held.

On the anniversary of the consecration or coronation of the reigning Roman pontiff no consistory is held.

On all double feasts no consistory is held.

On certain other non-double feasts no consistory is held, as listed below.

On the principal feasts of the cities in which [Col. 1228A] the lord pope is staying, especially when he celebrates, no consistory is held; but this is for the bishop to arrange.

Whenever there are solemn papal Vespers in honor of a feast, there is no consistory. Papal Vespers are said when the lord pope and the prelates are required to be vested in the church. Cardinals and prelates are not vested, however, unless Vespers are said in the church.

It should also be noted that some of the feasts mentioned above have papal Vespers, as listed below for each month.

To make the general points stated above clearer, the individual feasts on which Roman [Col. 1228B] pontiffs customarily cease holding consistories as a general rule will be set out month by month.

#### January

On the Circumcision of the Lord no consistory is held.

On the Octave of Saint Stephen no consistory is held.

Likewise, on the Octave of Saint John no consistory is held.

Likewise, on the Octave of the Holy Innocents no consistory is held.

On the vigil of the Epiphany no consistory is held.

On the Epiphany of the Lord no consistory is held.

On the Octave of the Epiphany no consistory is held.

On the feast of Saints Fabian and Sebastian no consistory is held.

On the feast of Saint Agnes no consistory is held.

On the feast of Saints Vincent and Anastasius no [Col. 1228C] consistory is held.

On the Conversion of Saint Paul no consistory is held.

[385] #### February

On the vigil, or the day immediately preceding the Purification, no consistory is held.

Likewise, on the feast of the Purification no consistory is held.

Likewise, on the feast of Saint Agatha no consistory is held.

Likewise, on the Chair of Saint Peter no consistory is held.

Likewise, on the feast of Saint Matthias no consistory is held.

#### March

On the feast of Pope Saint Gregory no consistory is held.

Likewise, on the feast of Saint Benedict no consistory is held.

[Col. 1228D] Likewise, on the feast of the Annunciation of the blessed Virgin Mary no consistory is held.

#### April

On the feast of Saint Mark no consistory is held.

#### May

On the feast of the apostles Philip and James no consistory is held.

Likewise, on the feast of the Invention of the Holy Cross no consistory is held.

Likewise, on the feast of Saint John before the Latin Gate no consistory is held.

Likewise, on the feast of the Apparition of Saint Michael no consistory is held.

[Col. 1229A] #### June

On the feast of the apostle Saint Barnabas no consistory is held.

Likewise, on the vigil of Saint John the Baptist no consistory is held. Solemn papal Vespers are sung in the church, and a drink is served.

Likewise, on the feast of the Nativity of that saint no consistory is held.

Likewise, on the vigil of the apostles Peter and Paul no consistory is held. Papal Vespers are sung in the church, and a drink is served.

Likewise, on the feast of the holy apostles Peter and Paul no consistory is held. If the pope is at Rome, solemn papal Vespers are sung in the church on that feast day, and a drink is served.

[Col. 1229B] Likewise, on the Commemoration of Saint Paul no consistory is held. From that time until the Octave of the Nativity of the blessed Virgin, or thereabouts, vacations are sometimes held in accordance with various arrangements, [386] as the lord pope orders in consistory with his brothers.

#### July

On the Octave of Saint John no consistory is held.

Likewise, on the Octave of the apostles Peter and Paul no consistory is held.

Likewise, on the feast of Saint Mary Magdalene no consistory is held.

Likewise, on the feast of the apostle Saint James no consistory is held.

#### August

[Col. 1229C] On the feast of Saint Peter in Chains no consistory is held.

Likewise, on the feast of the Snows, which is on the fifth of August, no consistory is held.

Likewise, on the vigil of Saint Lawrence, at Rome and also elsewhere if the lord pope is staying near the church of blessed Lawrence, no consistory is held. Solemn papal Vespers are sung in the church, and a drink is served at Rome and also in the place where the lord pope is staying near the church, as stated above.

Likewise, on the feast of blessed Lawrence no consistory is held.

Likewise, on the vigil of the Assumption of the blessed Virgin no consistory is held. Papal Vespers are sung in the church, and a drink is served.

On the feast of the Assumption of the blessed Virgin no consistory is held.

[Col. 1229D] Likewise, on the Octave of blessed Lawrence no consistory is held, as I think.

Likewise, on the Octave of the Assumption no consistory is held.

Likewise, on the feast of Saint Bartholomew no consistory is held.

Likewise, on the feast of Saint Augustine no consistory is held.

Likewise, on the feast of the Beheading of blessed John no consistory is held.

#### September

On the anniversary of the holy pontiffs and cardinals, which is on the fifth day of September, no consistory is held.

[Col. 1230A] Likewise, on the vigil, or the day immediately preceding the feast of the Nativity of the blessed Virgin, a consistory is not customarily held.

Likewise, on the feast of the Nativity of the blessed Virgin no consistory is held.

Likewise, on the feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross no consistory is held.

Likewise, on the Octave of the Nativity of the blessed Virgin no consistory is held.

[387] Likewise, on the feast of the apostle and evangelist Saint Matthew no consistory is held.

Likewise, on the feast of the Dedication of Saint Michael no consistory is held.

Likewise, on the feast of Saint Jerome no consistory is held.

[Col. 1230B] #### October

On the feast of blessed Francis a consistory is not customarily held, for Roman pontiffs grant this out of reverence for the saint.

Likewise, on the feast of the apostles Simon and Jude no consistory is held.

Likewise, on the vigil of All Saints no consistory is held. Solemn papal Vespers are sung in the church, and a drink is served.

#### November

On the feast of All Saints no consistory is held.

Likewise, on the anniversary of All Souls, which is on the day after All Saints, no consistory is held.

Likewise, on the anniversary of the Roman pontiff’s predecessor, once only—that is, only in the first year—no consistory is held, for then [Col. 1230C] the lord pope celebrates.

Likewise, on the Dedication of the basilica of the Savior, which is on the fifth day before the Ides of November, no consistory is held. At Rome solemn papal Vespers are sung in the church on the preceding day, and a drink is served. Consequently, there is no consistory on the day preceding the aforesaid Dedication of the basilica of the Savior.

Likewise, on the feast of Saint Martin, bishop and confessor, no consistory is held.

Likewise, on the anniversary of the consecration or coronation of the reigning Roman pontiff no consistory is held. Although it does not have preceding papal Vespers, the pope nevertheless hears Vespers in his chapel, and certain solemnities take place.

Likewise, on the Dedication of the basilicas of the apostles Peter [Col. 1230D] and Paul, which is on the Octave of Saint Martin, no consistory is held. Solemn papal Vespers are sung in the church, and a drink is served on the preceding day. Consequently, there is no consistory on the day preceding the aforesaid Dedication of the apostles. Nevertheless, the lord pope sometimes confers with the cardinals before or after Vespers if there is discussion of the processions that are to take place on the following day.

Likewise, on the feast of Saint Cecilia no consistory is held.
