[388] Likewise, on the feast of Saint Clement no consistory is held.

Likewise, on the feast of Saint Andrew no consistory is held.

#### December

On the feast of Saint Nicholas no consistory is held.

[Col. 1231A] Likewise, on the feast of Saint Ambrose no consistory is held.

Likewise, on the Saturday immediately preceding the Third Sunday of Advent, called Gaudete Sunday, no consistory is held. Papal Vespers are sung in the church, and a drink is served.

Likewise, on the feast of Saint Lucy no consistory is held.

Likewise, on the feast of the apostle Saint Thomas no consistory is held.

Likewise, on the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord no consistory is held. Solemn papal Vespers are sung in the church, and a drink is served.

On the day of the Nativity of the Lord no consistory is held.

Likewise, on the feast of Saint Stephen, protomartyr, no consistory is held.

[Col. 1231B] Likewise, on the feast of Saint John the Evangelist no consistory is held.

Likewise, on the feast of the Holy Innocents no consistory is held.

Likewise, on the vigil of Saint Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, no consistory is held.

Item: On the feast of the aforesaid Saint Thomas there is no consistory.

Item: On the feast of Saint Sylvester there is no consistory.

Item: As was said above at the beginning, on the principal feast days of cities—especially if the pope celebrates—and on Ash Wednesday, Easter, certain days before and after Easter, the Ascension, Pentecost and certain following days, vigils, and certain other days, the Roman pontiffs customarily abstain from consistories. [Col. 1231C]

Sometimes, moreover, there are summer recesses from the feast of Saint Peter until, or approximately until, the octave of the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin, according to different arrangements. Then no consistory is held unless they are summoned, or unless particular days have been appointed for a consistory. Sometimes, too, there are sudden holidays, either because of movement of the curia, or according to other business that arises and pleases the lord pope. Then the curia sometimes abstains from consistories for several days; and before departure and after arrival at a place, for a longer or shorter time according to what the lord has ordered. It is customary for the consistory to regulate the recesses and their arrangements; it is also customary for it to be announced to members of the curia when the recess begins, [Col. 1231D] 389 and when and where the audience is to resume, so that they may make suitable preparations and cannot be circumvented by adversaries.

Item: When cardinal legates, cardinal ministers, or those who have been absent for a longer time depart from or return to the curia, or when emperors, kings, or their sons come to or depart from the curia, the cardinals customarily accompany them. Thus, when they accompany those departing, there is customarily no consistory. When they accompany those arriving, there is no ordinary consistory for conducting business. Rather, after the aforesaid arrivals have been received in public—for they are customarily received publicly by the lord pope at the foot and with a kiss, and their other attendants at the foot, and prelates at the foot and with a kiss, [Col. 1232A] and other important persons at the foot and with a kiss, whom the lord pope wishes to honor—all others are excluded from the consistory. Only the cardinals, together with the supreme pontiff and the aforesaid emperors, kings, and their sons, remain for a short while in certain friendly and courtly conversations.

Afterward, when they depart from the lord’s presence, they ought to be accompanied by two cardinal deacons as far as the door, or until they reach their household. Sometimes, also, on the first arrival they accompany the arriving person as far as his house. Ordinarily, whenever the aforesaid emperors or kings come or return while the lord pope is sitting in consistory with the cardinals, they ought to be accompanied by two deacons as far as the door of the chamber, or as far as their attendants. Sometimes the same practice is observed if the sons of emperors or kings do not come too frequently. It should also be noted that, when there has been a long interruption of the consistory, although it is certain on which day it ought regularly to be held, the cardinals nevertheless customarily receive a special summons to the consistory.

It should also be noted that, if the lord pope ever orders the cardinals not to come to the consistory on a day when they would otherwise regularly be required to come, they do not thereafter go to the consistory unless they have been specially summoned, or unless the lord pope tells them, in the consistory or elsewhere, on which day they are to come to the consistory.

It should further be observed that before Christmas, and, if necessary, sometimes before Carnival, before Easter, [Col. 1232C] before lengthy recesses if there are to be any, before movement of the curia, and when consistories are resumed after lengthy delays or interruptions caused by the matters mentioned above or by other causes, the lord pope customarily holds certain public consistories. He hears advocates and others making petitions, regulates the business, and puts it into a settled condition, as his holiness may deem appropriate. 390

### CII. On the proclamation of prelates

[Note: These practices are not observed today; rather, they are carried out at the creation of cardinals, and more things are done than are contained here.]

Item: Ordinarily, whenever he proclaims prelates of certain churches—especially if he proclaims several, and even if only one prelate of some solemn church—the pope customarily goes out into the public consistory and proclaims the prelate or prelates to be promoted in their absence. After the pope has made some commendation of the prelates in the absence of those to be promoted, the persons to be promoted later come into the lord’s presence. After the pope has spoken a few brief words to them, they go to the lord’s foot, but not to kiss it. When one of the chaplains begins the *Te Deum laudamus*, the supreme pontiff nevertheless remaining seated in his chair, the promoted persons are led to the altar prepared there. Before it they must pray kneeling and prostrate. Each is led, according to the order of his proclamation, by two cardinal deacons, according to the order of their precedence.

When the *Te Deum laudamus* has been said, and afterward the two Orations have been recited with chant by the senior of the cardinals present, and he has pronounced the Blessing over them in a lower voice, the elected persons rise and kiss the altar. They are then received by every cardinal individually with a kiss: the bishops first, the priests second, and the deacons third. They are led back by the cardinal deacons, in the order stated above, to the feet of the lord. Each is first received at the foot and then with a kiss by the lord pope. After this, if he wishes, the lord returns to the chamber.

It should also be observed that, when major public business is to be presented—whether by ambassadors of the emperor, kings, provinces, or solemn counties [perhaps “communities”], or other important business by which the curia is often renewed—the lord pope customarily hears it in a public consistory. This is especially so with the initial propositions concerning elections brought before the apostolic see, lest some should fraudulently claim that they had been elected unanimously when in fact the election had been conducted amid disagreement. Also, when the supreme pontiff greatly wishes to honor ambassadors or solemn envoys who have arrived, even if they are presenting nothing important at that time, he customarily receives them in the public consistory. 391

Memorandum concerning feasts that are transferred.

Item: When the summons has been issued for a long time, someone should be sent for the cardinals.

### CIII. On the ordination of a cardinal deacon

On the Saturday of the Ember Days, the lord pope goes to the church. The customary reverence is made, which the person to be ordained performs with the others if he wishes; then he immediately withdraws to the place where he will receive the vestments at the appointed time. Terce, Sext, and None are said.

The lord pope is vested in Lenten vestments and proceeds toward the altar. The three priests make the reverence, kissing and touching the breast. *I will go in* is said, and so forth. He enters at the altar; the deacons make the reverence, kissing and touching the breast. The Mass proceeds in its order up to the final verse of the Tract. At this Mass there are five prophecies, and at each one *Let us kneel* and *Rise* are said.

Before the final verse of the Tract, the person to be ordained cardinal deacon, vested in the manner of a subdeacon—that is, with a [scuta; uncertain vestment], cotta, a small amice on the shoulders, a camisia or alb, girdle or maniple, dalmatic, [Col. 1233D] and, over it, stole—is led without a mitre to the pope’s presence by the senior of the deacons and another cardinal deacon. [Note: [Col. 1233] Perhaps “carried by the senior of the deacons and another cardinal deacon by the hands and arms.”] He kneels before the pope.

Then the senior of the deacons says:

“Holy Mother Church asks that you ordain this reverend present father, the lord N., subdeacon and cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, to the burden of the diaconate.”

The pope, wearing the mitre, says:

“Do you know him to be worthy?”

The presenter replies:

“To the extent that human frailty permits, and as I know it, I testify that he is worthy of this burden of office.”

The pope, seated and wearing the mitre, says:

“A deacon ought to offer,” and so forth, while the person to be ordained kneels. 392

Then the pope, reading while seated and wearing the mitre, says: “With God’s help,” and so forth. The Litany is said, with the pope lying on the faldstool and wearing the mitre, and the person to be ordained prostrate before the altar. Meanwhile, if desired, the dalmatic and stole are assigned to someone else. When the Litany is complete, the pope returns to his seat.

The person to be ordained stands reverently before him. The pope, standing and wearing the mitre, says: “The common prayer,” and so forth. Then, while the person to be ordained stands inclined before him, the pope says in the form of a Preface: “Let us pray, beloved,” and so forth. The pope says: “Let us pray.” The deacon says: “Let us kneel.” The deacon on the left says: “Rise.” The pope says: “Be present, we beseech you,” and so forth, in the form of a Preface, although some say it while reading. When this is complete, the pope alone places his hand upon the head of the person to be ordained, saying, while wearing the mitre: “Send forth,” and so forth.

To complete the office of the deacon, the lord pope takes the stole that the person to be ordained had been holding over the dalmatic and says without chant: “Receive the stole,” and so forth. He places it over the person’s shoulder and ties it on the left beneath the right side. Then the lord pope gives the book of the Gospels into the hands of the person to be ordained, saying without chant: “Receive the power,” and so forth. Then he gives the Blessing or Oration, saying with chant: “Hear, Lord,” and so forth.

After the aforesaid Oration has been said, the cardinal who has then been ordained is vested by the ministers in a white tunicella. Immediately the same person to be ordained is vested in a white dalmatic; the pope touches the dalmatic on the shoulder and says to him without chant: “May the Lord clothe you with a garment,” and so forth. Finally, the ordained person kisses the foot of the lord pope. The pope receives him with a kiss; immediately afterward the ordained person is received with a kiss by all the cardinal deacons, and also by all the cardinal bishops and priests.

When this has been done, he takes the maniple on the left arm over the tunicella and puts the mitre on his head. After removing the mitre, he goes to make the customary reverence to the lord pope. He also kneels before the altar, saying quietly: “Cleanse my heart,” and so forth. He takes the book of the Gospels from the altar; with inclined head he asks the lord pope’s Blessing, saying quietly: “Command, lord, to bless.” After receiving the Blessing, he goes with the book to the pulpit and begins, saying: “The Lord be with you.” “And with your spirit.” “The continuation of the holy Gospel,” and so forth, signing the book and himself. “Glory to you, Lord.” “At that time,” and so forth. 393

When the Gospel has been said, he kisses the beginning of the Gospel. In all else he ministers as a deacon and performs what pertains to him.

When the Offertory is said, he offers in the customary manner two large burning torches, two loaves, and two amphorae of wine; as he offers each item, he kisses the pope’s hand. The pope lightly touches the offerings.

In the Oration over the people, the pope says: “Let us pray.” The ordained deacon says: “Bow your heads before God.” At the end, when the Oration of the Mass is complete, the ordained deacon says: “Let us bless the Lord,” with his face turned toward the altar. The pope says: “May the name of the Lord be blessed,” and so forth. The ordained deacon, standing at the right corner of the altar without the mitre, says three times: “Many years,” each time more loudly, and each time kneeling before the pope, who is standing and wearing the mitre. At the end, the ordained person kisses the pope’s foot and is received with a kiss by the pope.

### CIV. The order observed in the celebration of a general council

[Note: [Col. 1235D] This Order differs from the one assigned in the commonly circulated Roman Order, p. 150.]

Before sunrise, everyone is expelled from the church. After all the doors have been closed except one, through which the priest must enter, doorkeepers stand there. All the bishops then assemble and enter together, and take their seats according to the time of their ordination. After all the bishops have entered and taken their seats, the priests whom the matter requires to enter are then summoned; no one should insert himself among those whom the order of proceedings requires to be present.

After a circle has been formed from the bishops’ seats, the priests sit behind them. The metropolitan chooses which of them will sit with him; these may also judge and determine certain matters with him. [Note: [Col. 1236D] This passage concerning the votes of priests in a council should also be observed in a provincial council.] The deacons stand in the sight of the bishops.

Then the laymen who have deserved to take part by election of the council enter.

The notaries whom the proceedings require for reading or receiving documents also enter.

After the doors have been closed, while the priests sit in prolonged silence with their whole hearts directed toward God, the archdeacon, who is about to speak, says: “Pray.” Immediately all prostrate themselves on the ground, bishops and priests alike, and pray silently for a long time with tears. 394 Then one of the senior bishops rises and openly pours forth an Oration to God while all still lie on the ground, saying this Oration:

**Oration.**—“We are present, holy Lord Spirit; we are present, indeed held captive by the enormity of sin, but gathered together especially in your name. Come to us, be with us, and deign to enter our hearts. Teach us what we should do and by what path we should proceed; show us what we ought to accomplish, so that, with your help, we may be able to please you in all things. Be the salvation, adviser, and accomplisher of our judgments, you who alone possess the glorious name with God the Father and his Son.

“Do not permit us to be disturbers of justice, since you love perfect equity. Let ignorance not drag us to the left, favor not bend us, and acceptance of a gift or person not corrupt us. Rather, join us effectively to yourself by the gift of your grace alone, so that we may be one in you and deviate from the truth in nothing. Thus, gathered in your name, may we uphold justice in all things with a moderation informed by compassion, so that here our judgment may dissent from yours in nothing, and in the future we may obtain eternal rewards for what we have rightly done.”

The *Our Father* is not said within this Oration. When the Oration has ended and all have answered “Amen,” the archdeacon again says: “Rise.” Immediately all rise, and bishops and priests alike sit with complete fear of God and discipline. When everyone has silently taken his place, a deacon dressed in white brings forth the Codex and announces the Chapters concerning the conduct of councils, namely:

“From the Third Council of Toledo, era 18. Also from the Fourth Council of Toledo, era 3. Also from the Chapters of the Eastern Fathers, which Bishop Martin translated from Greek into Latin, era 18. Concerning the holding of a synod. Also from the Council of Chalcedon, era 18. Also from the Council of Agde, era 25, or another matter from the canons that the metropolitan considers more suitable to be read.”

When the titles have been completed, the metropolitan bishop addresses the council with an exhortation, saying:

“Behold, most holy priests: after prayers have first been offered to God, I address your brotherhood with a pious exhortation, and I adjure you by the divine Name to receive with all devotion whatever we say to you concerning God and the holy orders or holy conduct, and to intend to carry it out with the greatest reverence.

“If perhaps one of you understands matters differently from what has been said, let him bring without any scruple of contention the very matters about which he has doubts back into our common deliberation, so that, with God’s help, he may either be taught or teach. 395

“Then I earnestly ask you with a similar adjuration that none of you, in judging, accept a person, or, moved by any favor or gift, knowingly turn away from a just judgment. Rather, with complete devotion reconsider whatever is brought before our assembly for judgment, so that neither contentious disagreement may find a place among you for the overthrow of justice, nor, in seeking equity, the vigor or diligence of our order grow slack.”

After this exhortation, all the priests, deacons, and religious persons who are present enter to hear the teaching. The archdeacon then reads the canon of the Eleventh Council of Toledo, era 1: “Let the council not be disturbed by tumult.” When this canon has been read, the Council of Ephesus is read in order.

Afterward, a discussion and instruction are likewise held concerning the mystery of the Holy Trinity, and also concerning the orders of offices, namely whether unity is maintained in all the sees when the same rites are celebrated. For these matters, as the length of the day permits, the letters of Pope Leo to Bishop Flavian concerning the errors of Eutyches and the mystery of the Trinity are also to be read, as are the canons concerning the unity of offices. No other matter is to be proceeded to before all these matters have been explained.

Nevertheless, during the entire three days of litanies nothing else is to be done or reconsidered except the mystery of the Holy Trinity and the sacred orders or institutions of the offices. These matters are to be distributed throughout those three days, so that, as has been said, no other question is considered except the question of the matters mentioned above, and so that the reading always appropriate to the order of the matter and to what is being investigated precedes it.

After this, on the fourth day, the remaining matters are admitted in order. All the religious persons who were present at the council on the preceding days for spiritual instruction are to go outside, while certain priests remain in the council, whom the metropolitan has judged worthy of honor. On each of those three days of Rogations and litanies, the bishops or priests, together with the admonisher, first prostrate themselves in prayer. Then, after the metropolitan has collected the Oration, they rise and hold discussion only concerning divine matters, as has been said.

On the remaining days, with all standing by, the Oration is to be collected; then, seated, they are to take up the business of cases justly and devoutly. 396 No tumult is to occur either among those seated or among those standing.

Every day all are to enter the council in the same manner and order that has already been set out above.

For if any of the remaining priests, or deacons, clerics, or laymen who have remained outside believe that the council should be appealed to concerning any matter, they are to make their case known to the archdeacon of the metropolitan church, and he is to announce it to the council. Permission is then to be granted to them to enter individually and present their case. None of them may withdraw from the common assembly before the general hour of departure arrives.

No one may dissolve the council unless everything has been determined, and whatever is concluded by common deliberation must be subscribed by the hand of each bishop. Nevertheless, two or three days before the council is dissolved, all are to reconsider carefully all the constitutions they have issued, lest they have offended in any respect.

Also, on the day when the council is to be concluded, the canons established in the holy synod are publicly reread before the church. When they have been completed, “Amen” is answered in the choir. Then, returning to the place where they sat in council, they subscribe the canons themselves. The metropolitan must also admonish them concerning the coming Easter, on what day it will occur. They must also be admonished when they are to come in the following year to hold the council. Bishops are also to be chosen who will celebrate the feasts of the Nativity of the Lord and Holy Easter with the metropolitan.

After this, when the archdeacon says: “Pray,” all together prostrate themselves on the ground. After praying for a very long time, one of the senior members says this Oration:

**Oration.**—“There is no virtue of the human conscience, Lord, that can carry out the judgments of your will without offense. Therefore, we ask you to reckon as perfection what your eyes have seen to be imperfect in us—what we earnestly desire to bring to completion with a perfect end of equity. At our beginnings we asked you to come to meet us; at the end of our judgments we also pray that you be present to our excesses: that you spare ignorance, forgive error, and grant perfect efficacy of action to perfect vows.

“And if . . . has drawn us into error, or perhaps rash will has driven us to turn aside from justice, for this reason we ask and beseech you: if we have incurred any offense in this celebration of the council, deign to pardon it or make it remissible, so that in what we are about to dissolve, the assembled council may first be absolved by you from all the guilt of our sins. Thus may forgiveness follow transgressors, and eternal recompense those who confess to you.” 397

The Oration *Our Father* is to be added to this Oration. While all still lie prostrate, this Blessing is to be pronounced:

[Note: [Col. 1237D] The same Blessings occur in the commonly circulated Roman Order, p. 157.]

“May Christ, the Son of God, who is the beginning and the end, grant you the completion of charity.”  
Amen.

“May he who brought you to the completion of this council make you absolved from every gathering of sin.”  
Amen.

“May you, made freer from every guilt and absolved also through the gift of the Holy Spirit, return unharmed and happily to the dwellings of your sees.”  
Amen.

“May he himself deign to grant this, whose kingdom and empire endure for ever and ever.”  
Amen.

“In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, let us all go in peace.”

Immediately rising together, while the metropolitan remains seated and begins the rite himself, they give one another the kiss. Thus, after peace has been given to one another, the assembly of the council is dissolved.

**Oration of the second day.**—“Bending the knees of our hearts before you, Lord, we ask that we may accomplish the good that you require from us: namely, that, walking with you in ready diligence, we may exercise the subtle judgment of lofty discernment, and, loving mercy, may be able by our efforts to please you.”

**Oration of the third day.**—“To you, Lord, we unanimously cry out with the voices of inward prayer and ask that, strengthened by consideration of your grace, we may become fearless heralds of virtue and may be able to speak your word with complete confidence.” Amen.

### CV. Here begins the order for blessing the emperor when he is crowned

[Note: [Col. 1238D] This differs greatly from the published form in the Roman Order, p. 136, apart from certain Orations.]

When the king elected as emperor reaches the Collina Gate, which is beside the fortress of Crescentius, he is honorably received by the clergy of the City with crosses and censers and is led in procession as far as the steps of the basilica of Saint Peter, while all sing: “Behold, I send my angel.” His chamberlains scatter largess before him, and the prefect of the City carries a sword before him.

When he has reached the square before the basilica that is called Cortina, senators escort him on his right as far as the aforesaid steps. When he dismounts there, the horse on which the king had been riding is to be handed over to them.

Meanwhile, the supreme pontiff, with all his orders, prepares himself in the sacristy as though he were about to celebrate the divine offices. He proceeds in procession as far as the platform of the ark (*arca*) at the head of the steps and sits there on the faldstool. The bishops and priests sit on the steps to his right; the cardinal deacons to his left; on the nearer step are the subdeacons and acolytes. The first cantor and the singers stand around them, together with the nobles, officials, and aristocrats, and the servants of the papal court.

Then the king, ascending to the supreme pontiff with the archbishops, principal bishops, and his nobles, reverently kisses his feet. Offering him as much gold as he wishes, he is kindly received by him with a kiss and an embrace.

When the supreme pontiff has finally risen, the king at his right and the senior of the deacons at his left lead him as far as the church of Saint Mary in Turrets. There, before the altar, with a subdeacon holding the Gospel text, the king makes the following oath over it bodily:

“I, N., king of the Romans, with the Lord’s consent destined to become emperor, promise, pledge, undertake, and swear to God and blessed Peter that henceforth I will be the protector and defender of the supreme pontiff and of the Holy Roman Church in all their needs and interests, guarding and preserving their possessions, honors, and rights, insofar as I am supported by divine assistance, according to my knowledge and ability, in upright and pure faith. So may God help me and these holy Gospels of God.”

Then the supreme pontiff, with all his orders, proceeds to the altar and, having said an Oration there, ascends to his seat. The king remains in the church of Saint Mary in Turrets with his attendants and three bishops, namely the bishops of Ostia, Porto, and Albano. There, having been received as a brother by the canons of Saint Peter, he is vested in the imperial insignia, his pallium being given by the lord pope’s chamberlain.

When, preceded by those canons singing “Peter, do you love me?”, he reaches the door of the basilica of the Prince of the Apostles, called the Silver Gate, he is led on either side by the count of the Lateran palace and the primicerius of the judges of the canons. Before that Silver Gate, the bishop of Albano pours this Blessing over him:

**Oration.**—“O God, in whose hand are the hearts of kings, incline the ears of your mercy to the prayers of our humility, and place the guidance of your wisdom upon our emperor, your servant N., so that, having drawn counsels from your fountain, he may please you and excel above all [kingdoms]. Through.”

When he has entered the church and reached the middle of the circular pavement, the bishop of Porto chants this Oration over him:

**Oration.**—“Unutterable Author of the world, Creator of the human race, Governor of the empire, Confirmer of the kingdom, who from the womb of your faithful friend, our patriarch Abraham, chose beforehand a king who would benefit the ages: enrich this present king and his army through the intercession of all the saints with abundant +Blessing, and bind him firmly to the throne of the kingdom.

“Visit him as you visited Moses at the Red Sea, Joshua son of Nun in battle, Gideon in the field, and Samuel in the temple. Mark him with that starry +Blessing and drench him with the dew of your wisdom, which blessed David received in the Psalter and his son Solomon received from heaven through your gracious reward.

“Be for him a breastplate against the battle lines of his enemies, a helmet in adversity, patience in prosperity, and an everlasting shield in protection. Grant that the nations keep faith with him, that his nobles have peace, love charity, abstain from greed, speak justice, and guard the truth. May this people, united by the +blessing of eternity, flourish in such a way that they always remain triumphant in peace. Through.”

When he reaches the shrine (*confessio*) of blessed Peter, he prostrates himself face down on the ground, and the senior of the deacons performs the Litany over him. When it is finished, the bishop of Ostia gives the announcement, and the senior of the priests says the *Our Father*.

Verse: “And lead us not …”  
Verse: “Save your king.”  
Response: “My God, [the one] trusting in you.”  
Verse: “Be for him, Lord, a tower of strength.”  
Response: “From the face of the enemy.”  
Verse: “May the enemy accomplish nothing against him.”  
Response: “And the son of iniquity.”  
Verse: “Lord, hear my prayer.”  
Response: “And let my cry come to you.”  
Verse: “The Lord be with you.”  
Response: “And with your spirit.”

**Let us pray.**—“Stretch forth, we beseech you, Lord, the right hand of heavenly assistance to your servant, so that he may seek you with his whole heart and deserve to attain what he worthily asks. Through.”

“Go before our actions, we beseech you, Lord, by your inspiration, and accompany them by your help, so that all our prayer and work may always begin from you and, begun through you, be brought to completion. Through.” 400

After this they proceed to the altar of Saint Maurice. There the bishop of Ostia anoints his right arm and the space between his shoulders with exorcised oil, saying this Oration:

**Another Oration.**—“Lord God almighty, to whom belong all power and dignity, we beseech you with suppliant devotion and the humblest prayer to grant this servant of yours, N., a prosperous outcome of imperial majesty. Since he has been established by your disposition to govern your holy Church, may things present not hinder him and things future not obstruct him. Rather, inspired by the gift of the Holy Spirit, may he be able to govern the people subject to him with equitable justice . . . and in all his works may he always fear you and continually strive to please you. Through . . . in the unity of the same.”

The following Oration is then said:

**Oration.**—“God’s Son, Jesus Christ our Lord, who was anointed by the Father with the oil of exultation above his companions, may he himself, through the present pouring out of sacred ointment, pour upon your head the +Blessing of the Spirit, the Comforter, and make it penetrate to the innermost parts of your heart, so that through this visible and tangible gift you may deserve to perceive invisible things, and, having carried out your temporal kingdom with just moderation, to reign eternally with him who alone is without sin, the King of kings, who lives with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit. Through.”

When these things have been completed, the king ascends to the altar of blessed Peter, where the supreme pontiff receives him with a kiss as one of the deacons. He then proceeds to the pulpit or ambo, where a platform constructed of wood and adorned with hangings is to be prepared for him. Together with his archbishops and bishops, princes, and magistrates, he stands there according to the capacity of the place.

The first cantor and the schola of singers sing the Introit in the choir before the altar. After the *Kyrie, eleison* and the Angelic Hymn have been sung, the supreme pontiff says the Oration appropriate to that day, and this Oration for the emperor:

**Oration.**—“O God, protector of all kingdoms and especially of the Christian empire, grant your servant N., our emperor, to cultivate knowingly the triumph of your power, so that he who by your ordinance is prince may always be powerful by your gift. Through.”

**Secret.**—“Receive, Lord, the prayers and offerings of your Church for the salvation of your servant N., who is supplicating; for the protection of the faithful peoples, work the miracles of your ancient arm, so that, having overcome the enemies of peace, Christian liberty may serve you securely. Through.” 401

**After Communion.**—“O God, who prepared the Roman empire for proclaiming the Gospel of the eternal kingdom, extend heavenly weapons to your servant, our emperor N., so that the peace of the Church may not be disturbed by any storm of wars. Through.”

When the Epistle has been read and the Gradual sung, the emperor proceeds in procession to the altar. There the supreme pontiff places a clerical mitre on his head and, over the mitre, an imperial diadem, saying as follows:

“Receive the sign of glory, the diadem of the kingdom, the crown of the empire, in the name of the Father +, and of the Son +, [Col. 1241B] and of the Holy + Spirit, so that, having despised the ancient enemy and the contagions of all vices, you may love justice, mercy, and judgment, and live justly, mercifully, and piously, so that from our Lord Jesus Christ himself, in the fellowship of the saints, you may receive the crown of the eternal kingdom; he who lives with the Father, and so forth.”

Then he gives him the scepter and the golden orb.

It should be known that, after Communion has been completed with him, at the imposition of the diadem, if the apostolic lord should wish, he may say Orations of this kind:

“The Lord be with you.”  
“And with your spirit.”

**Oration.**—“Look, we beseech you, almighty Lord God, with serene eyes upon this glorious servant of yours, N., so that, just as you blessed Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, so you may bestow upon him the spiritual Blessings of grace, and deign to water and drench him with the fullness of your power. Grant him from the dew of heaven and the richness of the earth an abundance of grain, wine, and oil, and an opulence of every crop; and from the abundance of your divine gift grant him long years, so that while he reigns there may be bodily health in the land, inviolate peace in the kingdom, and the glorious dignity of the royal palace may shine before the eyes of all with the greatest splendor of royal power, appearing to glitter and gleam with the brightest light, as though drenched with the greatest radiance of the most splendid brilliance.

“Grant him, almighty God, to be a most powerful protector of his country and a consoler of churches and holy monasteries through the greatest piety of royal generosity; to be the strongest of kings, triumphant over enemies, for crushing rebels and pagan nations; and to be sufficiently terrifying to his enemies through the greatest strength of royal power.

“May he be magnificent, lovable, and compassionate toward his nobles, exalted princes, and the faithful of his kingdom; may he be feared and loved by all; and after glorious and happy times and the joys of the present life, may he deserve to dwell in perpetual blessedness. Through.”

“Bless, + Lord, we beseech you, this prince of ours, N., whom we believe has been entrusted to us by you for the salvation of the people. Make him abundant in years, vigorous with sound bodily strength, and, after old age, bring him to the desired health.

“May we have confidence in obtaining grace for the people, as Aaron obtained it in the tabernacle, Elisha at the river, Hezekiah on his bed, and aged Zechariah in the temple. May we have authority to rule such as Joshua received in the camp, Gideon assumed in battle, Peter received in the chalice, and Paul exercised in teaching.

“And thus may he prosper among the shepherds around your fold [the Latin is textually uncertain], as Isaac prospered in harvest and Jacob was enlarged in his flock. May he himself deign to grant this.”

**Another Oration.**—“May God the Father of eternal glory be your helper and protector, and may the almighty one +bless you, hear your prayers in all things, and fill your life with length of days. May he continually strengthen the throne of your kingdom, preserve your nation and people forever, clothe your enemies with confusion, and make the sanctification of Christ flourish over you, so that he who grants empire on earth may himself bestow the reward in heaven. He lives.”

Therefore, after the chant has been interspersed, he is presented before the altar of blessed Peter to the lord pope, who is seated in the lofty tribunal [Col. 1242B]. The pope then ascends to that altar, takes from it the unsheathed sword, and hands it to him, signifying that the care of the whole empire is in the sword, saying:

“Receive the sword taken from above the body of blessed Peter and, through our hands—although unworthy, yet consecrated in the place and authority of the blessed apostles—granted to you in imperial fashion; and by the office of our Benediction divinely appointed for the defense of the holy Church of God, for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of the good. Remember what the Psalmist prophesied when he said: ‘Gird your sword upon your thigh, O most mighty one,’ so that by it you may exercise the force of equity, powerfully destroy the mass of iniquity, and champion and protect the holy Church of God and its faithful. Detest and scatter those who are false in the faith no less than the enemies of the Christian name. Mercifully assist and defend widows and orphans; restore what is desolate and preserve what has been restored; avenge what is unjust and strengthen what has been rightly ordered, so that, glorious in the triumph of virtues, an outstanding cultivator of justice, you may deserve to reign without end with the Savior of the world, whose type you bear in name. Who lives with God.”

403 After these words have been completed, he girds him with the sword, repeating the saying: “Gird your sword upon your thigh, O most mighty one, and observe that the saints conquered kingdoms not by the sword but through faith.”

It should be known, however, that in some books the sword is given first and the diadem afterward; but once the sword has been given, this rubric is placed: “As soon as the one who is to be crowned has been girded with the sword, he draws it from the sheath, brandishes it manfully three times, and immediately returns it to the sheath.”

[Col. 1242D] Thus girded, and marvelously made a soldier of blessed Peter, the apostolicus next takes the diadem from the altar and places it on the head of the one being crowned, saying:

“Receive the sign of glory, the diadem of the kingdom, the crown of the empire, in the name of the Father +, and of the Son +, and of the Holy + Spirit, so that, having spurned the ancient enemy and rejected the contagions of every vice, you may love justice, mercy, and judgment; and so live justly, mercifully, and piously that from our Lord Jesus Christ himself you may receive, in the fellowship of the saints, the crown of the eternal kingdom. Who lives with the Father.”

Immediately proceeding, the newly crowned man kisses the feet of the apostolicus. After these glorious rites have been performed, the apostolicus returns to the elevated tribunal of the platform, and the emperor ascends to the faldstool prepared for him on a broad step beneath the right hand of the apostolicus. As he proceeds, the crowned emperor carries the orb in his right hand and the scepter in his left. He then returns to the chamber, and, while he remains there with his princes, the senior subdeacon, with the subdeacons of the Roman Curia and the chaplains of the imperial court, says the following acclamation in a loud voice at the right-hand railing before the silver crucifix:

[Note: [Col. 1243] Here the term pectorale is understood to mean a railing. Consult Cangius’s Glossary.]

“Exaudi, Christe” (“Hear us, O Christ”).

The city scriveners, dressed in silk copes and standing in the choir before the railing, respond:

“May there be salvation and victory for the most invincible lord N., ever august emperor of the Romans.”

After this acclamation has been repeated three times, the senior subdeacon with his companions says three times:

“Salvator mundi” (“Savior of the world”),

and the scriveners respond each time:

“Tu illum adjuva” (“Help him”).

Then the senior subdeacon with his companions says twice:

“Sancta Maria” (“Holy Mary”),

and they respond each time:

“Tu illum adjuva” (“Help him”).

And so thereafter: “Sancte Michael” (“Holy Michael”), and so forth, as above.

When these things have been completed, they sing “Lord, have mercy” twice, and then all together say “Lord, have mercy.” After this, once the Gospel has been sung, the emperor lays aside his crown and mantle, approaches the supreme pontiff, and offers at his feet as much gold as he wishes. When the pontiff descends to the altar to complete the mysteries of the Mass, the emperor, in the manner of a subdeacon, offers the chalice and cruet and remains there until the pontiff, having returned to his seat, receives Communion. After the Communion has been made, he receives Communion from the pontiff’s hand with the kiss of peace. He then returns to the chamber and, in the ambon, resumes both mantle and crown.

When the Mass has ended, he reverently receives the pontifical Benediction [Col. 1243C], and immediately proceeds to the place where the supreme pontiff is to mount his horse. When the pontiff has mounted, the emperor holds the stirrup of his saddle and, taking hold of the bridle, guides him a short distance. Then, mounting his own horse, he proceeds beside the supreme pontiff as far as the church of Saint Mary in Transpadina. There, after they have exchanged a kiss—not in heart but in body—they separate.

### CVI. On the Coronation of a Queen

If a queen is to be crowned, a chamber should be prepared above the reading desk opposite the imperial chamber. She is to sit there with at least two maidens and with some of the princes of the empire, both ecclesiastical and secular.

The Benediction of a queen or empress is as follows. At the entrance to the church, the following prayer is said:

“Almighty and eternal God, fountain and source of all goodness, who do not reject or turn away from the weakness of the female sex, but rather graciously approve and choose it; who also determined, by choosing the weak things of the world, to confound all that is strong; and who once willed to place in the hand of a woman the triumph of your glory and power over a most savage enemy for the sake of the Jewish people: look, we beseech you, upon the prayers of our humility, and upon this your handmaid N., whom in humble devotion we choose as queen or empress. Multiply upon her the gifts of your + Benedictions, and always and everywhere surround her with the right hand of your power, so that, firmly protected on every side by the gift of your grace, she may triumphantly overcome the wickedness of visible or invisible enemies. May she, together with Sarah, Rebecca, Leah, and Rachel, blessed and revered women, deserve to be made fruitful in the fruit of her womb and to rejoice, for the adornment of the whole kingdom or empire and for the governance and protection of the state of the holy Church of God. Through Christ our Lord, who, from the womb of blessed and undefiled Mary the Virgin, deigned to be born, visit, and renew this world. Who with you lives and is glorified, God, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, throughout immortal ages of ages.”

405 And after the coronation of the empress, she is led to the altar before the supreme pontiff, clothed in royal garments. The supreme pontiff gives her this Benediction, saying:

[Col. 1244B] “God, who alone possess immortality and dwell in inaccessible light, whose providence is not deceived in its ordering; who made the things that are to come and call the things that are not as though they were; who by an even-handed moderation cast the proud down from authority and graciously raise the humble to the heights: we humbly implore your ineffable mercy, that just as you caused Esther, for the sake of Israel’s salvation, to pass from the fetter of her captivity, once freed, into the chamber of King Ahasuerus and into a share of his kingdom, so you may mercifully grant that this your handmaid N., by the + Benediction of our humility and for the salvation of the Christian people, may pass into a worthy and exalted union with our king or emperor and into the beginning of his kingdom or empire. Grant also that, remaining always chaste in the bond of an imperial or royal marriage, she may be able to preserve the palm of chastity next to virginity, may desire always to please you, the living and true God, in all things and above all things, and, by your inspiration, may accomplish wholeheartedly what pleases you. Through.”

At the anointing with the sacred oil:

“May the grace of the Holy Spirit descend in abundance for life through the ministry of our humility, so that, just as, by our hands—although unworthy—you are externally enriched when you are smeared with material oil, so you may deserve to be inwardly enriched when you are anointed with its invisible unction. May you always be perfectly imbued with its spiritual anointing, and may you learn and be able, with your whole mind, to avoid and reject what is unlawful, and may you be able and willing continually to think about, desire, and perform what is useful for your soul, with the assistance of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives with the Father and the Holy Spirit.”

[Col. 1244D] Then the supreme pontiff places the mitre on her, with the horns of the mitre facing to the right and left, and places the crown over the mitre, saying:

“Having been solemnly blessed as queen or empress through the office of our unworthiness, receive the crown of royal or imperial excellence, which, although placed upon your head by unworthy hands, is nevertheless placed there by episcopal hands. Therefore, just as you shine outwardly adorned with gold and gems, so strive to be adorned inwardly with the gold of wisdom and the gems of virtues. As queen of this world, worthily and laudably going to meet the eternal Bridegroom, the Lord Jesus Christ, with the prudent virgins, may you deserve to enter the gate of the heavenly court, with the help of that same Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with God the Father and the Holy Spirit throughout infinite ages of ages.”

The crowned queen is then led back to the chamber. After the Gospel she is led to present the offering to the supreme pontiff, and stands on the steps beside the apse, facing the altar of Saint Leo, until she receives the sacred coronation from the hand of the supreme pontiff after the emperor. She is then led back to the chamber, where she remains until the end of the Mass.

It is customary for the emperor to distribute generous gifts to all the orders, which the supreme pontiff bestows when he is crowned: to the bishops, priests, and cardinal deacons; to the first chorister and singers; to the subdeacons, basilicarii, and regionarii; to the entire Roman clergy; to the chaplains and other officials; to the court ministers; to the prefect of the City [Col. 1245B], senators, judges, advocates, and scriveners; and to the commanders of the naval stations.

It is customary for the king, when he descends from Monte Gaudio and comes to the Ponticello, to swear this oath to the Romans:

“For I, N., the future emperor-king, swear that I shall preserve for the Romans their good customs. So may God help me, and these holy Gospels of God.”

The rubric placed below was arranged by order of Pope Clement V by certain cardinals to whom this matter had been entrusted in consistory, when Robert, king of Sicily, sought anointing and coronation at Avignon, where the Roman Curia was then residing. For nothing had been handed down in writing concerning how kings and queens ought to be anointed and crowned, since the Roman Pontifical contains nothing except the anointing and coronation of an emperor and empress. Therefore this rubric was extracted from the aforementioned Pontifical, with certain things added, removed, and altered that do not apply to other kings but ought to be observed in the anointing and coronation of an emperor.

### CVII. Rubric concerning the Anointing and Coronation of a King

In the anointing and coronation of a king, the procedure that follows may suitably be observed. For those things which are observed for the emperor appear to be required, except for certain matters known to pertain to the emperor alone.

[Col. 1245D] First, therefore, our lord the supreme pontiff, having entered the church and there been vested in sacred vestments of a color appropriate to the season—at present, as is customary, green—should ascend to the altar with his ministers and sit there. Before the Introit of the Mass begins, the king, having entered the church, when he reaches the confession of blessed Peter, or when he reaches the area before the altar, should prostrate himself face down upon the ground. One of the pope’s subdeacons should perform the litany over him, while the other subdeacons and chaplains respond in the litany, as is customarily done elsewhere.

When it has ended, the senior of the cardinal priests should say the “Our Father,” with the other Versicles and Responses and the two Prayers, namely “Praetende, quaesumus” and “Actiones nostras,” up to “Through our Lord” in the second Prayer, as stated above concerning the emperor. When these have ended, the king should rise. What has been said concerning the litany, Versicles, and Prayers could also be performed by the cardinal bishop who anoints him beside some altar, and he could then continue there with the rite of anointing and the other matters assigned to him. Nevertheless, the Ordinal says concerning the emperor that the “Our Father,” the aforementioned Versicles, and the Prayers are said by the senior of the cardinal priests.

After this, beside some altar—provided that, if possible, it is a different altar from the pope’s altar—the bishop of Ostia should anoint him with exorcized oil on the right arm and between the shoulders. If he wishes, he should also anoint his hands, chest, both shoulders, and the joints of his arms, saying the following Prayer: “Almighty God,” and so forth, as follows, changing “of imperial dignity” to “of royal dignity,” and changing “to govern your holy Church” as follows. Another Prayer is also said, beginning “God the Son of God,” and continuing to the end. Immediately thereafter the queen ought to be anointed.

After these things have been performed, the king, clothed in precious royal garments, ascends to the altar, where the supreme pontiff receives him with a kiss on the mouth and the breast, as one of the cardinal deacons—namely, after the first cardinal deacon. The king then proceeds to the pulpit or ambon, where the chamber has been constructed, as stated above in the rubric concerning the emperor. All the foregoing is to be done before the Introit.

After the Introit has been sung, and after the “Kyrie, eleison” and the “Hymn of the Angels” have been sung, the supreme pontiff says, with chant, the Prayer appropriate to that day, and says this Prayer for the king on the same throne: “God, protector of all kingdoms, give to your servant N., our king,” and so forth. In the Prayer, “and of the Christian empire” and the word “emperor” are removed; where it says “he is prince,” it should say “he is king.” This applies to the Secret. The Prayer “Receive, O Lord” is said as it stands above. After Communion, instead of the Prayer “God, who for preaching,” as above, the following Prayer is said:

“Almighty and eternal God, extend heavenly arms before your servant N., our king, so that the peace of the Church may not be disturbed by any storm of wars. Through the Lord,” and so forth.

When the Epistle has been read and the Gradual sung, the king proceeds ceremonially to the altar upon which the supreme pontiff is to celebrate the solemn Mass. The king is presented before the altar to the lord pope, who is seated in the lofty tribunal. When this has been done, the lord pope approaches the altar, takes the unsheathed sword from its sheath, and gives it to the king, saying, “Receive the sword,” and so forth, to the end. The following exception is made: where it says “taken from above the body of blessed Peter,” it is either omitted or changed to “taken from the sacred altar”; and where it says “imperially,” it should say “royally.” When these words have been completed, he girds him with the sword, repeating the aforesaid “Gird yourself,” and so forth, to the end.

As soon as the one to be crowned has been girded with the sword, the king draws it from the sheath, brandishes it manfully three times, and immediately returns it to the sheath. Thus girded, and marvelously made a soldier of blessed Peter, the apostolicus next takes the diadem from the altar and places it on the head of the king being crowned, saying, “Receive the sign,” and so forth, to the end, as above. Where it says “the crown of the empire,” however, this may be omitted. The king should be kneeling when the diadem is placed upon him, or he should kneel during its imposition.

Then he gives him a golden scepter and orb. The king should be kneeling when he receives them, or should kneel during their reception.

It should be known that, during the imposition of the diadem, the apostolicus may, if he wishes, say Prayers of the following form:

“The Lord be with you.”

“And with your spirit.”

Prayer: “Look down, we beseech you, O Lord,” and so forth, as above. Where it says “May he be the strongest of kings,” it should say “May he be the strongest king”; and where it says “to crush rebellious and pagan nations,” that phrase should be omitted.

The Benediction of the King, which the apostolicus gives.

[Note: [Col. 1247D] In the Diary of Alexander VI by Johannes Burchard, the coronation of Alfonso, king of Naples, is described at greater length. It was performed at Naples in the year 1494 by Johannes, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Susanna and legate. [Col. 1248D] The ambassador of the Turkish emperor attended the Mass until the Preface of the Mass. When it began, the said ambassador withdrew from the church by order of the king, at the suggestion of the master of ceremonies.]

“Bless, O Lord,” and so forth, to the end, as above. Where it says “this our prince,” it should say “this our king.” Another Prayer, “God the Father,” and so forth, as above; where it says “who grants empire on earth,” it should say “who grants a kingdom on earth.”

Immediately after these rites have been completed, the king, proceeding forward, kisses the feet of the apostolicus, who receives him to the kiss. He is also received to the kiss by all the deacons, and afterward by the cardinal bishops and then by the cardinal priests.

After these glorious rites have been performed, the apostolicus returns to the elevated tribunal of the platform, and the king ascends to the faldstool prepared for him beneath the apostolicus’s right hand, where he remains for a short time.

It should be noted that the crowned king carries the orb in his right hand and the scepter in his left. Finally, before the Alleluia and Verse begin, the king returns to his chamber, which has been set up in the pulpit or ambon. While the king remains there with his magnates and nobles, the queen is crowned at the altar by the supreme pontiff, as set out below. Then the Alleluia is sung and repeated, and the Gospel is sung by a cardinal deacon.

After this, when “I believe in one God” has been said, and while the Offertory is being sung and the lord pope washes his hands in the usual manner, the king comes from his chamber to the altar. When the pontiff descends to the altar to complete the mysteries of the Mass, the king, having laid aside his crown, scepter, and golden orb, takes his place among the cardinal deacons, so that the deacon who sang the Gospel stands directly in the middle behind the pope, while the king is on that deacon’s right. To prevent the usual order of the deacons from being confused, the senior of the other deacons should be on the king’s right, with the king second; after him, the senior should be on the left of the deacon who sang the Gospel; and so thereafter, according to seniority, they should stand on the right or left in the usual manner until the number of deacons is complete.

The king remains there among the deacons until the pontiff, having returned to his seat, receives Communion, and until the deacon who sang the Gospel and the subdeacon who sang the Epistle have received Communion from the hand of the lord pope and taken the precious blood of our Lord Jesus Christ at the altar, as is customary. Then the king, kneeling, receives sacred Communion from the hand of the seated pope, who is wearing the mitre on his head, with the kiss of peace. Beforehand, however, he kisses the pontiff’s hand, and then reverently receives the Host. Returning to the altar, the same king receives the most sacred blood of our Lord Jesus Christ from the chalice through the ministry of the deacon, using a reed. When these things have been completed, he returns to the chamber and resumes the crown, scepter, and orb.

When the Mass has ended, he reverently receives the customary pontifical Benediction used in papal Masses. He then immediately proceeds to the place where the supreme pontiff is to mount his horse. When the pontiff mounts, the king, wearing the crown on his head, holds the stirrup of his saddle and, taking hold of the bridle, guides him a short distance. Then, mounting his own horse, he proceeds as far as the place where the supreme pontiff will dismount from his horse at his palace. There he likewise dismounts briefly and, as before, takes hold of the bridle and guides him a short distance; he holds the stirrup of his saddle when the lord pope dismounts.

The king, mounting his own horse dressed in royal garments and wearing the crown on his head, carries the golden orb in his right hand and the royal scepter in his left—unless custom requires something else to be observed, namely, that the orb be carried in the left hand and the scepter in the right. He then returns to his own house, if it is distinguished, or to the place where he is to provide the banquet. The king’s horse should be caparisoned.

### CVIII. On the Anointing of a Queen

After the king has been anointed and returned to his chamber, as explained above, the queen is likewise anointed immediately before the Introit with exorcized oil by the bishop of Ostia, beside the same altar at which the king was anointed. The anointing is performed either on the breast or according to the practice formerly observed for Queen Mary, mother of King Robert.

The following Prayer is first said—not at the entrance to the church, but beside the altar where this anointing is performed—by the bishop of Ostia; or it may be omitted, as he wishes:

“Almighty and eternal God,” and so forth, as above. If it is said, the words “or empress” are omitted, as is “or empire”; and where it says “for the governance and protection of the state of the Roman Church,” it should say only “for the defense of the state of the holy Church.”

During the queen’s anointing with the sacred oil, the Prayer “The grace of the Holy Spirit,” as above, is said to the end. When the anointing has ended, the queen proceeds to the pulpit [Col. 1249A], where a chamber has been prepared for her, with at least two ladies or maidens of her kingdom, both ecclesiastical and secular.

### CIX. On the Coronation of a Queen

After the king has been crowned and returned to his chamber, as explained above, the queen is immediately crowned beside the altar by the supreme pontiff. She is dressed in royal garments and wears no veil on her head, but has her hair spread out and unbound. The supreme pontiff either says or omits the following Prayer, “God, who alone,” as above. If it is said, the words “or emperor,” “or empire,” and “imperial” are omitted.

The supreme pontiff then places the crown on the queen’s head, saying “Through the office of our unworthiness,” and so forth, to the end, as above, omitting the words “or imperial” and “or of an empress.” When these words have been said, the queen kisses the feet of the lord pope. The queen should be kneeling when the crown is placed on her head, or should kneel during the placing of the crown. The crowned queen is then led back to her chamber.

### CX. On the Communion of the Eucharist Received by the Queen from the Pope’s Hand

After the king and queen have been crowned, the Alleluia and Verse are sung, and the Alleluia is repeated by the choir. The Gospel is sung by the cardinal deacon. After the Gospel, “I believe in one God” and the Offertory are said. After the pope’s Communion, and after the king has received Communion and taken the sacred blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, the queen, kneeling, reverently receives the consecrated Host from the hand of the Roman pontiff, who is seated and wearing the mitre on his head. She then returns to her chamber.

At the end of the Mass, having received the Benediction customarily given by the pope in papal Masses, she is dressed in royal garments and, as stated above, wears no veil on her head, but has her hair spread out and unbound. Wearing the crown on her head and seated on horseback with her retinue, she proceeds before the king, while the king follows, dressed royally as described above.

### CXI. On the Canonization of a Saint

[Note: [Col. 1249D] Another, more detailed rite is given below in chapter 115.]

On the morning of the day of canonization, when the pope descends to the church, a procession meets him. After this, as is customary, the lord pope receives the cardinals and prelates in the middle of the church for the act of reverence and says, “Blessed be the name of the Lord.” He ascends the pulpit with the cardinals alone. There the cardinals are vested in white, and likewise the prelates; they stand below, at the sides of the nave of the church.

The lord pope, wearing the mitre and clothed in the mantle, preaches either standing or seated. At the end of the sermon, he announces that he will pray and exhorts them to pray. He begins “Come, Creator” with its chant, kneels, and immediately afterward rises; the others continue, if he wishes. The deacon on the right says, “Let us kneel,” and the lord pope and the others pray quietly and secretly. After a short interval, the deacon on the left says, “Rise,” and the lord pope and everyone else rise.

Standing with the mitre, the lord pope decrees that the person is to be entered in the catalogue of the saints and venerated by all as a saint. He enters him in the catalogue of the saints, determining that throughout the universal Church, on the day of his death, his feast is to be devoutly and solemnly celebrated as that of a confessor bishop. Moreover, for those who come annually to his tomb on the day of his death, he mercifully remits one year or forty days of the penance imposed upon them.

Without the mitre, he begins “We praise you, O God” in song, and the others continue it. The deacon on the left says, “Pray for us,” and so forth, “alleluia”; the others respond, “That we may be worthy,” and so forth, “alleluia.” The lord pope says, “The Lord be with you,” and the response is, “And with your spirit.” “Let us pray,” and he says the Prayer, concluding it, “Through Christ our Lord. Amen.”

Then the deacon on the left says “I confess,” and so forth, as is customary, making mention of blessed N., the confessor, in the appropriate places. When the confession has ended, the lord pope gives a gracious indulgence in the customary manner. After the indulgence has been given, the lord pope, having laid aside the mitre, gives the absolution in the customary manner, “By prayers and merits,” and so forth, making mention in its proper place of blessed N., the confessor: “Indulgence,” and so forth.

Finally, he announces that he will celebrate Mass in the customary manner. In the appointed place he will receive the vestments and, God willing, celebrate the Mass solemnly. The form of the solemn proclamation is as follows:

“To the honor of almighty God, the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, and for the exaltation of the faith and the growth of the Christian religion, by the authority of almighty God himself, the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, of the blessed Peter and Paul, and of our own authority, with the counsel of our brothers, we decree and define that the late N., of blessed memory, formerly bishop … [lacuna] is to be entered in the catalogue of the saints and venerated by all as a saint. We enter him in the catalogue of the said saints, determining that throughout the universal Church, on the day of his death, namely … [lacuna], his feast and office are to be devoutly and solemnly celebrated as that of a confessor bishop. Moreover, by the same authority, to all truly penitent and confessed persons who devoutly visit his tomb annually on the day of his death, we mercifully remit one year and forty days; but to those who visit his tomb annually during the Octave of the said feast, we mercifully remit forty days of the penance imposed upon them.”

### CXII. When the Pope Hears Mass on Feast Days

When he comes, he goes before the altar, lays aside the mitre, and the priest on the left begins “I will go in.” After the “Confiteor,” when the confession has been made, the deacon replaces the mitre on the pope. Standing in the place of the seat, the pope says the Introit with all the cardinals, and “Lord, have mercy.” Meanwhile incense is placed in the thurible, with a bishop or priest ministering.

The pope then sits, and the priest receives the incense from the acolyte. After he has incensed the altar, the acolyte carries away the thurible, and the bishop or cardinal priest who is ministering incenses the pope alone, kneeling if the pope is seated; no one else is incensed.

On feast days the pope does not remove his mitre except in the “Confiteor” before the altar; when the Gospel is said, until “I believe in one God” has been said and the book has been kissed; after he descends at the elevation of the Body of Christ, after which he replaces the mitre when he returns to the seat and holds it; when the priest says aloud the second “Throughout all ages of ages,” at which point he remains bareheaded until the priest begins to receive the wine of the ablution; and finally at the end of the Mass, when he is about to say “Blessed be the name of the Lord,” he removes the mitre. Once “Blessed be the name” and the Benediction have been said, the mitre is replaced.

414 After the Epistle has been said, the subdeacon kisses the pope’s foot, and not before. While the subdeacon says the Epistle, an acolyte accompanies him, standing on the subdeacon’s left. When the Verse “Alleluia” is said, the pope places incense in the thurible, with the bishop ministering as before. The pope is not incensed, but only the Gospel.

After the Gospel has been said, the subdeacon carries the Gospel book and offers it to the pope. The pope kisses the Gospel that has been read. Then the pope alone is incensed by the bishop and the cardinal priest, as at the beginning of Mass.

After this, when the Offertory is said, the acolyte carries the boat on the left and the thurible on the right. The bishop or priest, as before, offers the boat with the spoon, and the pope places incense in the thurible. The pope is not incensed; rather, the priest incenses the altar and the acolyte incenses the priest. Then, as before, the pope is incensed by the bishop or cardinal priests.

The acolyte then incenses everyone in the following order: first the bishop or priest who is ministering; then the two deacons; then the cardinal bishops and priests; then the deacons; then the chancellors; then the archbishops and other prelates; then the chaplains; then the thurifers; then the doorkeepers; and finally the others who are present at the Mass.

Thus the pope places incense three times and is incensed three times: after the Introit, after the Gospel, and when the Offertory is said. He places incense in the thurible three times: at the Introit, at the Gospel, and when the Offertory is said. At the Introit the altar and the priest are incensed first; at the Offertory the pope is incensed; after the Gospel, only the pope is incensed.

### CXIII. On Masses Said before the Pope during Ferias

During Lent, on ferial days, at the first Prayers of the Mass, and immediately after “Holy” has been said with the cardinals through the post-Communion, and at the final Prayers, the pope descends from the seat and leans upon the faldstool with the mitre. He removes the mitre when the priest begins to make the sign of the cross over the offerings, and resumes it after the sacred elevation of the blood. He then leans upon the faldstool; at the second “Throughout all ages,” the deacon removes the mitre from him until the wine of the ablution. After receiving the peace, while standing beside the faldstool, from the priest, and after giving it to the serving deacons, he leans upon the faldstool.

The deacon gives it first to the foremost among the other cardinals, bishops, and deacons. At the final Prayers, the pope, wearing the mitre, leans upon the faldstool and does not rise, although some say that he does; the former practice is more dignified. When he says, “Humble yourselves,” and so forth, he removes the mitre and leans upon the faldstool without it. At the end he returns to the seat wearing the mitre. The mitre is white and without a fringe.

This same practice is always followed during Advent, even on Sundays, and during Lent, unless there is a feast, except on the Sunday of “Gaudete” and “Laetare, Jerusalem.” On Sundays in Lent, however, he follows the customary procedure used at other times and does not lean upon the faldstool.

If “Let us kneel” is said in the ferial rite, the pope kneels wearing the mitre; at “Rise” he rises, and when the Prayer has begun he again leans upon the faldstool with the mitre. This practice is observed whenever this occurs while he is hearing Mass.

If there is a feast during Lent, he wears a mitre with a gold fringe at the Mass of the feast; at the Mass of the feria on the same day, he wears a white mitre. After Mass he resumes the mitre with the gold fringe, and at Vespers of the feast he wears a fringed mitre.

If no cardinal bishop or priest is present, the deacon assisting at the pope’s Mass performs the duties concerning incense and the other matters just as a bishop or priest would perform them if present.

If a vigil Mass is said, the same procedure is followed regarding kneeling, the mitre, and the other matters as on a feria.

During Lent, at the Tract, when “Help us, God our Savior” is said, while the pope is hearing Mass he descends to the faldstool. The deacon removes the mitre from him, and he leans upon the faldstool. As soon as the chant has been said through the phrase “Our Savior,” inclusive, he resumes the mitre with the deacon’s assistance and returns to the seat. The same is done when he himself celebrates during Lent and the same Tract is to be said.

[Col. 1252C] In the ferial rite, the same practice described above is observed at all times as during Lent and at vigils; the same also applies at all times concerning kneeling and the other matters.

When “Go, the Mass is ended” is said, the deacon turns toward the people until he has said the whole formula. In other places, the deacon looks toward the altar, as at Saint Paul’s and in similar places.

[Note: [Col. 1251] This is because, when the pope celebrates in these places, his face is turned toward the people and his back toward the tribunal or apse, where the choir of priests is located.]

At “Let us bless the Lord,” the deacon always looks toward the altar, both there and elsewhere.

At Saint Paul’s and in similar places, when the pope begins “Glory,” he turns toward the tribunal. When he says “The Lord be with you” or “Peace be with you,” he looks toward the people while standing in the seat facing the altar. But when he says “Let us pray,” and the Prayers, and when he begins “I believe,” he looks toward the tribunal, although he continues reading the Creed facing the altar together with the others. When he says “Blessed be the name,” he always begins from the middle of the altar, facing the altar.

The deacons, however, conduct themselves in looking toward the people or the altar just as the celebrating pope does at Saint Paul’s and in similar places. In the final prayers after Mass, when the pope, standing at the altar, says, “The Lord be with you,” he turns toward the people, and so do the deacons; but the deacon who sang the Gospel, with his face turned toward the pope, prepares the pope’s vestments at the beginning of the recitation. When the Confiteor is said, the deacon on the left and the deacon on the right meanwhile prepare the fanon and the pope’s other vestments.

If there is a special feast for which the Mass is being celebrated, a commemoration is made in the Confiteor in this manner: “To the holy apostles Peter and Paul, [Col. 1253A] and to blessed George the martyr.” Likewise: “To the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and to James.” Likewise: “To the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and to John the Evangelist,” although some have said, “To blessed John the Baptist and Evangelist,” or: “To the holy apostles Peter and Paul and to John the Evangelist.” But the first form is more pleasing and more reasonable.

In the church of Saint Lawrence outside the walls, if the feast is being celebrated there, likewise: “To the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and to the blessed martyrs Stephen and Lawrence,” although someone has designated Stephen in this way, but incorrectly . . . . “with us,” not otherwise, “The Lord be with you,” which is said in the final prayer. For then the deacon must be ready to say either “Go, the Mass is ended” or “Let us bless the Lord,” as the time requires.

## When the Apostolic See Is Vacant

[Col. 1253B] When the Apostolic See is vacant, the bishops sit on the right, and after them the priests; on the left, however, the cardinal deacons, all in their proper order, rank, and place, just as they did when the pope was present. The following exception is observed: sometimes the middle place between the bishops and the deacons is not left empty. In that case also the bishops sit on the right, as stated, and the priests behind them; on the left, but immediately next to the bishops, sits the senior of the deacons, and the others after him.

There is, however, a difference in this respect: while the pope is alive, in councils the order and sequence of votes mentioned above is observed for the bishops and priests, but it is changed for the deacons. For the first vote after the priests is that of the first deacon, and so one proceeds downward to the youngest deacon, whose vote is last when the See is vacant.

[Col. 1253C] The same order and procedure is observed among the deacons while the pope is alive when the deacon announces auxiliary councils, at which the ordination of a cardinal is discussed, or the dispatch of a cardinal legate, or if the pope should request some other auxiliary council.

If a cardinal arrives late, while the other cardinals are seated, whether in consistory or elsewhere, when the pope is present, all those sitting on the same bench where he is to sit rise when he arrives, after he has shown reverence to the pope, and sit down afterward with him. Later, if a cardinal rises, whether because he has been sent somewhere or for another reason, and then returns, only the two cardinals nearest to him in rank rise for him.

The same is observed when the See is vacant. While the cardinals are seated in consistory, they hold their birettas. During conferences they remove their birettas and remain without them while they confer, whether with the pope or among themselves; and each of the parties conferring, if they confer or dispute with one another, is without a biretta. When the See is vacant, however, the person beginning to confer removes his biretta, but the others immediately do not allow this, and then the person conferring replaces his biretta.

No one should interrupt a person giving counsel, except the pope, if he wishes to do so; the person giving counsel immediately removes his biretta. But when, after resuming his counsel, he confers again, he replaces his biretta.

When the pope is conferring and giving a decision, he wears the mitre. But when he first begins to give his decision, while he is stating the preliminary matters, the cardinals wear their birettas. When he gives a decision in consistory, they remove their birettas; when he confers with someone, that person is without a biretta.

## CXIV. Rubric Concerning Masses for the Dead Celebrated in the Presence of the Pope

[Col. 1254A]

It should be noted that the pope is not accustomed to celebrate solemnly a Mass for the dead, no matter how great a king the deceased may have been; rather, he has it celebrated solemnly and preached before him by a bishop or cardinal priest, with all the cardinals summoned. When a cardinal celebrates for the dead, the pope, assisted by the two senior cardinal deacons at that time and throughout the whole Mass, makes the confession before the Introit of the Mass in the customary manner together with the celebrant.

After this confession has been made, the cardinals and prelates do not come that day to pay reverence to the pope, because he does not wear a cope when vested there, but a scarlet cappa, or a plain white mitre without pearls and gold embroidery, according to whichever he prefers.

It should be noted that at all the prayers of the Mass, [418] if it is celebrated outside the Easter season or outside the octaves of feasts that have octaves, the pope must kneel before the altar, where a chair with a footstool has been prepared, while wearing the mitre on his head. The Epistle and Gospel should not be read from an ambo or pulpit, but in the presbytery itself near the altar. After the Gospel has been said, the book is not brought for the pope to kiss. After the celebrant has incensed the altar following the Offertory, only the pope is incensed by the senior cardinal priest assisting him at the Mass, and no one else.
