It should also be noted that immediately after the pope has said, “Holy, Holy, Holy,” and so forth, he descends from his seat and goes to the chair before the altar, [Col. 1254C] where he remains kneeling until the celebrant begins, “World without end,” before the Agnus Dei. Then the pope returns to his seat and remains standing there until the celebrant says, “The peace of the Lord,” and so forth. His mitre is then removed, and he stands bareheaded until the celebrant himself has received the body and blood of the Lord.

After the Pater noster, the Psalm “I rejoiced” is not said, nor are prayers for peace made. Likewise, after saying “Lamb of God,” the celebrant should not say the prayer “Lord Jesus Christ, who said,” and so forth, nor then kiss the altar, because the peace is not given. Nor should “Blessed be the name of the Lord” be said after Mass, nor should an indulgence be granted.

The sermon delivered for the dead before the pope takes place immediately after Mass. It should be known that the person giving the sermon, kneeling and bowing before the pope, asks for the blessing. When the Mass and the sermon have been finished, immediately and without “Let us bless the Lord”—and “Blessed be the name,” and so forth, is not said—the pope withdraws inside to his chamber. The prayers, absolutions, and customary chants performed for the dead are not done after Mass. Everything else is performed as in other Masses by the person celebrating before the pope, by the pope, and by those belonging to the pope.

## CXV. Rubric Concerning the Customary Procedure in the Canonization of a Saint

When our lord the pope has heard the reputation of some saint, and the matter has been reported to our said lord pope by certain reputable and authoritative persons, who have repeatedly and insistently petitioned him for the canonization of this saint, our lord the pope is accustomed to propose the matter among the brethren, namely the cardinals. With their advice, he entrusts to certain bishops of the country of the person said to be a saint, or to other authoritative, reputable, prudent, and incorruptible persons, the task of investigating the reputation and the devotion of the people toward the person said to be a saint, as well as the miracles and other matters reported to our lord the pope.

Those to whom the task has been entrusted must investigate and report generally, not specifically, on the reputation and devotion of the people and on the other things they have discovered concerning the miracles of the person said to be a saint; and they must report concerning reputation, not concerning truth. They must also report whether it seems to them that an investigation concerning the truth and the specific details should be commissioned.

If they write back matters such that an investigation of the truth ought to be commissioned, our lord the pope again seeks the advice of the cardinals. With their advice, he decides in consistory whether, in accordance with what has been reported, the aforesaid investigation concerning the truth should be commissioned or not. If it seems that it should be commissioned, our lord the pope writes again to the same persons, or to others whom he deems appropriate, that they investigate the truth of the matters mentioned above—namely, the faith, excellence of life, miracles, and performance of miracles of the person seeking canonization—exactly, diligently, faithfully, and prudently, according to the articles and interrogatories that he sends to them and others under his seal. After conducting this investigation, those to whom it has been entrusted must faithfully return it to the said lord pope, enclosed under their seals.

[Col. 1255C] After this investigation has been returned, the pope is accustomed to entrust its examination within the curia to certain of his chaplains, or to other authoritative and prudent persons experienced in such matters, who arrange and formulate rubrics concerning the aforesaid investigation. Once these rubrics have been arranged and formulated with exact diligence, the pope entrusts the examination of the rubrics themselves and of the entire investigation to three cardinal lords: one bishop, another priest, and the third a deacon.

After seeing and diligently examining the contents of the commissions, rubrics, and investigation mentioned above, these cardinal lords must report fully to the pope in consistory, in general terms, everything stated above and everything they have found in them. They must make this exception: concerning the life, miracles, and depositions of the witnesses produced regarding them, they do not then report anything specifically. Instead, later, in consistory, in the presence of the pope and [420] the other cardinal lords, the depositions of the witnesses produced concerning the life and miracles are read individually and one by one.

First, the depositions of the witnesses concerning the life are read. After the pope and the cardinals have read and carefully heard them, and before proceeding to anything else, the pope, with the advice of the cardinals, determines whether the excellence of the life of the person in question has been fully proved or not. After this determination has been made, they proceed in the aforesaid manner to the reading of the miracles and of the depositions of the witnesses produced concerning those miracles.

[Col. 1256A] It should nevertheless be noted that, after the deposition of each witness concerning each article—or at least of the witnesses who provide the better proof—has been read in consistory, the pope, with the advice of the cardinals, decides whether those witnesses fully prove the article in question or not, or whether . . . . These matters must be written down there by one of the cardinal lords, whichever the pope prefers.

When all these things have been done and carefully examined by the pope and the cardinals, the pope must seek the advice of the cardinals and ask them whether it seems to them that such matters have been proved as would make canonization rightly appropriate. If it seems appropriate, the pope then secretly decides in consistory among the cardinals that the canonization should be carried out.

After this decision has been made by the pope, all the prelates then present in the curia must be summoned. The pope publicly recounts to them in consistory what has been done and proved, while suppressing the aforesaid secret decision already made, and seeks the advice of those prelates.

Then the pope assigns a definite day and a suitable place for the matter, where our said lord pope, the cardinals, and the other prelates of the curia, together with the clergy and the people, are to assemble. Meanwhile, outside the consistory, the pope appoints at least eight or seven prelates, as he deems appropriate, who on the assigned day are to preach publicly. Our said lord pope also arranges the order among the prelates who are to preach, so that one is to preach first, another second, and so on with the others.

The assigned day is customarily set one month in advance, or at least three weeks, so that the aforesaid prelates may diligently prepare their conferences, which on the assigned day they must deliver publicly in a concise and brief form. The conclusions of these conferences must be such as to show by arguments that the canonization in question ought rightly to be carried out, and they must petition our said lord pope to deign to carry it out.

After the aforesaid secret decision has been made by the pope, the prelates have been summoned, and a definite day has been assigned to them for delivering their conferences as stated above, the pope is accustomed meanwhile, in consistory, secretly to entrust two cardinal lords—preferably religious men learned in Sacred Scripture—with the following tasks: one of them is to arrange the lesson or lessons concerning the life of the saint, reciting in those lessons some of the proved miracles; the other is to arrange the Responsories, Antiphons, and Prayer. The two cardinal lords must read everything they have arranged in consistory at the appropriate times.

When the assigned day has arrived, in the morning, at the hour of the consistory, our lord the pope, in the customary consistorial manner—that is, with a red mantle or cope and a gold-embroidered mitre with pearls—must assemble at the appointed place, together with all the cardinals and prelates in all their vestments, namely woolen copes; the clergy and people must also assemble there.

As our said lord pope comes to the appointed place, he is accompanied by the cardinals then present, with two cardinal deacons assisting him on his right and left, as is customary. At the appointed place a faldstool or chair with a footstool must be prepared, in which the said lord pope can sit. When he has taken his seat in that chair, only the cardinal lords pay him the customary reverence. After this reverence has been made, they sit in their proper order in the customary consistorial manner. The cardinal lords and the pope’s two cardinal deacons assist him, as stated above. The other prelates stand opposite the pope, on the right and left, as the space permits.

When they have taken their seats, the procurator of this matter, standing opposite the pope, must rise. Assuming a certain degree of authority, he must recount something concerning the matter and petition our said lord that his holiness deign to hear certain prelates who intend to preach concerning the matters mentioned above. He must also ask that it please his holiness to define the person in question as a saint, to inscribe him in the catalogue of the saints, to have him venerated by the faithful as a saint, and to have his feast celebrated every year in perpetuity on a certain day, as seems appropriate to our said lord.

After this petition has been made by the procurator, the prelate who is to preach or deliver his conference first, according to the order already established, rises and begins his conference, delivering it concisely and briefly. When he has finished, the second rises and does likewise, and so with the others.

When all the aforesaid conferences have been completed, our lord the pope rises, and the cardinal deacon assisting him on the left says the Confiteor in the customary manner. After it has been said, our lord the pope grants an indulgence of one or two years and the same number of forty-day periods, or more, as he pleases. After granting the indulgence, the pope removes his mitre, performs the absolution, and gives the blessing. Then one of the cardinal lords proclaims the indulgence. When these things have been completed, the pope returns to his chamber.

After this, in consistory, a definite day is arranged for a certain church, where the pope, the cardinals, the other prelates of the curia, the clergy, and the people are to assemble for the solemnity of this canonization. When that day arrives, the church is spread with carpets, prepared, and illuminated with many candles. In the morning, when our said lord pope descends to the same church, the procession of the clergy of that church meets him.

When he is in the church, he prays for a while before the altar. Then he ascends his seat prepared in the middle of the church, and there receives the cardinals and other prelates in the customary manner for the reverence. After this reverence has been made, the cardinals and the other prelates put on white vestments.

When they are vested, the pope, as he has come from his chamber—that is, with a red cope and a gold-embroidered mitre with pearls—goes to the elevated chair prepared before the altar with a footstool. Sitting there, he delivers a sermon, wearing the mitre on his head as is customary, reciting the Process and the matters proved, and urging the people to pray that God not permit him to err in this matter.

When this sermon has ended, the pope announces that he will pray and exhorts the others to pray likewise, namely that God not permit him to err in this matter. Then, with knees bent, a devout prayer is made, and the pope himself must begin by singing the hymn “Veni, Creator Spiritus.” After beginning it, he kneels; at the end of the first verse he must rise, and all the others continue singing the entire hymn.

When the hymn has been sung, if the pope wishes, the cardinal deacon assisting him on the right says, “Let us bend the knee”; and the pope and all the others, kneeling, pray quietly and secretly. After the devout prayer has been made, following a short pause the cardinal deacon on the left says, “Rise,” and then everyone rises.

When they have risen, the pope, wearing the mitre on his head, publicly declares the person in question to be a saint, to be inscribed in the catalogue of the saints, and to be venerated by all as a saint. He inscribes him in the catalogue of the saints and decrees that throughout the universal Church, on such-and-such a day, his feast and office are to be celebrated devoutly and solemnly.

Our said lord pope may make this declaration as follows:

> “To the honor of God almighty, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and for the exaltation of the Catholic faith and the increase of the Christian religion, by the authority of that same almighty God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and by our own authority, with the advice of our brethren, we decree and define that N., of blessed memory, is a saint and is to be inscribed in the catalogue of the saints. We inscribe him in the catalogue of the said saints and decree that throughout the universal Church, every year, on such-and-such a day, his feast and office shall be celebrated devoutly and solemnly, as for one confessor if he is a confessor, or as for one martyr if he is a martyr.”

If the pope wishes, he may add these words:

> “Furthermore, by the same authority, we mercifully remit one year and forty days of the penances imposed upon all truly penitent and confessed persons who, every year, devoutly visit his tomb on such-and-such a day; and to those who every year, during the octave of the said feast, visit his tomb, forty days.”

When the pope has pronounced these words, he removes his mitre and begins by singing the hymn “Te Deum laudamus,” which the others continue singing. When it is finished, the cardinal deacon assisting the pope on the left says the versicle, “Pray for us, blessed N., alleluia”; and the others respond, “That we may be made worthy of the grace of God, alleluia.”

If this solemnity takes place from Septuagesima until Easter, the Alleluia is omitted in the aforesaid versicle. Then the pope says while singing, “The Lord be with you”; after the response, “And with your spirit,” he says, “Let us pray,” and then the Prayer appropriate to that saint, ending the Prayer, “Through Christ our Lord,” to which the response is “Amen.”

When this Prayer has ended, the cardinal deacon assisting the pope on the left says the Confiteor, and so forth, as is customary; at the proper place, immediately after the apostles, he makes mention of the said saint. When this confession has ended, the pope grants a gracious indulgence of seven years and seven forty-day periods. After the indulgence has been granted by our lord the pope, and his mitre has been removed, he performs the absolution and gives the blessing in the customary manner, saying, “By the prayers and merits,” and so forth, making mention of the canonized saint at the proper place.

When these things have been done, our lord the pope proceeds to the customary place, where he receives the pontifical vestments, namely the white ones. Then, in the customary manner, he solemnly celebrates Mass in honor of the said canonized saint.

When this Mass has ended, and an indulgence of seven years and seven forty-day periods has again been granted at the end of the Mass, he removes his vestments and returns to his chamber or palace wearing the cope and mitre, just as he first came to the church.

## CXVI. The Ceremonies and Solemnities Customarily Observed in the Creation of New Cardinals

The ceremonies and solemnities customarily observed in the creation of new cardinals follow, as well as in the giving of the ring and the assignment of a title to them, and when a cardinal priest who has not been newly created is provided with a cardinal episcopal title, and concerning the arrival at the curia of new cardinals who are absent from the curia at the time of their creation.

### First, Concerning Those Who Take Part in the Creation of New Cardinals

It should be known that the following procedure is customarily observed in the creation of new cardinals.

On the Wednesday of the Ember Days, the pope is accustomed in consistory to ask the cardinals whether it is expedient to create new cardinals, first delivering there a very brief conference to the effect that it is expedient to create new cardinals. The cardinals then customarily respond and give their advice one by one, each according to his order, as to whether it is expedient or not.

After this, the pope is accustomed to say: “We follow the advice of those who say that they should be created,” or “that they should not be created,” according to what seems best to him. When he chooses the course of creating them immediately, he asks the cardinals what number they think should be created. After they have given their response as above, the pope says: “We follow the advice of those who say that they should be created up to such a number.” Then he says there: “We will think, and you should think, about the persons to be named, and on the coming Friday, God willing, we shall act concerning them.”

This is the procedure when all the cardinals are present in consistory. If some are confined to their homes by illness, it is customary for the pope in consistory to instruct two cardinals to go to the absent cardinals and request and obtain their advice concerning the two questions mentioned above. After their report has been made to the pope in consistory, in the hearing of all the cardinals, by the cardinals appointed for this purpose, the pope then chooses in consistory whether he wishes to follow the advice of the cardinals who have said that a new creation of cardinals should be made, and what number should be created.

On the following Friday, the pope likewise instructs two cardinals in consistory to go and request and obtain the advice of the absent cardinals concerning the persons to be newly created as cardinals. After obtaining this advice, they come to the consistory while the pope hears the cardinals’ confidential counsels, and they report to him separately the advice of the absent cardinals while he is seated in his chair.

[Col. 1260B] On that Friday, after the cardinals have first paid reverence to the pope, the pope orders that the chair be brought without its covering. When this has been said, all the cardinals leave the consistory and place themselves at the end of the hall or chamber where the consistory is held, except the senior cardinal bishop, who remains there and takes his seat upon the uncovered chair, which must be prepared at the pope’s right side.

The pope is accustomed to say to that cardinal, and to the others who come after him in their order: “We are considering such-and-such persons,” naming them there; “say what you think should be done concerning these or others.” Then that cardinal, and the others successively coming afterward in their order, respond with what seems appropriate to them, according as God has inspired them. When all the cardinals have responded successively according to their order, they all return to sit in consistory according to their order.

After this, the pope is accustomed to say to them: “Thanks be to God, we have the agreement of all our brethren concerning the persons,” or “of the fewest,” or “of the greater part,” according to the circumstances, without specifying anything further about this agreement. Immediately there he creates the cardinals, both those present in the curia and those absent, saying:

> “By the authority of almighty God, of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and our own, we absolve N., if he is a prelate, from the bond by which he was bound to his church, and we take him as a cardinal priest of the holy Roman Church.”

If the person is not a prelate, he says:

> “We take N. as a cardinal priest” or “as a cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church,” according to what our said lord pope decides to order in this matter.

When these cardinals have been created, the pope goes to his chamber, and there the cardinals publicly announce the provision of the new cardinals to whomever they wish. After the pope has returned to his chamber, he sometimes has the creation of the new cardinals announced to them there by his page, and sometimes does not.

On the following Saturday, after the cardinals have paid reverence to the pope in consistory, he orders the doors of the hall where the consistory is held to be opened to everyone wishing to enter. The pope must come there to the consistory, and inside the consistory the chamberlain, notaries, the pope’s chaplains, the palace auditors, and the clerks of the pope’s chamber must sit; the others must stand outside the consistory.

All the new cardinals must at that time be outside the consistory, in the nearby hall or chamber, until the pope orders them to be summoned.

The pope delivers a brief sermon there in the presence of everyone. At the end of the sermon he proceeds in order to name the cardinals whom he has created, both those present in the curia and those absent, commending each of them for learning, fidelity, prudence, and other qualities, as the merits of each require.

At the end of the commendation he says to each of the new cardinals:

> “We absolve N. from the bond by which he was bound to his church, and we have taken and do take him as a cardinal priest of the holy Roman Church.”

If they are not prelates, no mention is made of absolution; instead he says:

> “We have taken and do take him as a cardinal priest” or “as a cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church.”

After this, the pope has the new cardinals summoned. They must come to him according to the order in which the pope named them, stand behind the consistory, and position themselves behind the bench opposite the seat of the pope’s chair, where the other cardinal lords sit.

The pope must then say something to the new cardinals for their instruction, concerning the kind of men they should be in councils and in other matters. After saying this, he calls them to come to him. At the entrance to the consistory, the two senior cardinal deacons receive the new cardinal first named by the pope; the other two senior cardinal deacons after the first receive the cardinal named second; and so the other cardinal deacons proceed in their order if several cardinals have been newly created. They lead them to kiss the pope’s foot.

When they have been received by the pope for the kissing of his foot, all the older cardinals and the others mentioned above immediately rise. Coming into the pope’s chapel, they begin “Te Deum laudamus” in a loud voice. The older cardinals, in their order, proceed two by two first to the altar, which at that time must be prepared in the hall where the pope holds consistory, but without a cross. After them, the two senior cardinal deacons lead to the altar the new cardinal first named by the pope; the other two cardinal deacons lead another; and so the other two cardinal deacons proceed if several new cardinals have been created, according to the order stated above.

When they reach the altar, the new cardinals must remain kneeling and prostrate before the altar for as long as “Te Deum laudamus,” and so forth, is sung.

When it has been completed, the senior of the cardinal bishops must say quietly, “Our Father.” Then the versicle is sung, “And lead us not into temptation,” to which the response is, “But deliver us from evil.”

**Versicle:** Save your servants.  
**Response:** My God, those who hope in you.

**Versicle:** Send them help from the sanctuary.  
**Response:** And defend them from Zion.

**Versicle:** Lord, hear my prayer.  
**Response:** And let my cry come to you.

**Versicle:** The Lord be with you.  
**Response:** And with your spirit.

**Let us pray.** Almighty and eternal God, have mercy on your servants and direct them, according to your clemency, on the way of eternal salvation, so that, by your gift, they may desire what pleases you and accomplish it with all their strength.

**Another Prayer.** Lord, we ask you to go before our actions by your inspiration and accompany them with your help, so that all our work and prayer may always begin from you and, begun through you, may be brought to completion. Through Christ our Lord. **Response:** Amen.

The aforesaid prayers must nevertheless be said by the bishop mentioned above from the book that must be prepared on the altar.

When these things have been completed, the pope’s chaplains, two by two, receive the new cardinals and have them kiss the altar. Then they lead them according to their order to kiss the mouths of the older cardinals. First they come to the bishops, second to the priests, and afterward to the cardinal deacons, kissing each of them according to his order.

After this, the older cardinals return two by two to the consistory to sit according to their order. The senior cardinal deacons then lead the new cardinals again, two by two, according to the order stated above, to kiss the pope’s foot and mouth. Afterward they lead them to the seat where they are to sit in consistory, according to the order assigned to them by the pope when he named them.

Then all the non-cardinals withdraw. After they have withdrawn, the pope imposes silence on the new cardinal lords until he himself, with the advice of the older cardinals, has decided to open their mouths. He then tells them how they should speak respectfully in consistory when speaking with the other cardinals, and so forth; when they speak, whether in giving advice or in conference, they should not contradict or attack the statements of the other cardinals, but should say other things prudently and respectfully, as the Lord will provide for them.

He also instructs them how they should honor the other cardinals, and how, when giving counsel, they should keep God before their eyes and at that time maintain holiness and purity in mind and speech, removing every partiality of love, hatred, or favor.

Sometimes, however, he is accustomed to impose silence on them at that time and to tell them the other matters just mentioned while he has decided to open their mouths.

When these things have been said, the pope rises and goes to his chamber. All the cardinals customarily remain in the pope’s residence until the tables have been prepared for lunch, and on that day all the cardinals eat in the hall with the pope.

When the pope leaves his chamber and comes to lunch, the two senior cardinal deacons accompany him to the table, preceding him. After lunch they accompany him in the same manner as far as his chamber.

The cardinals sit at table first according to their order: on the pope’s right, the cardinal bishops and priests, both older and new; on the left, both the older and the new cardinal deacons sit according to their order, following the arrangement of the consistory.

After lunch they observe the same order in seating, both older and new cardinals. When it is time to depart, the pope, seated in his chair, gives the red hat to the new cardinals according to the order he assigned them when naming them. He places each person’s hat on his head while the new cardinal stands before him kneeling. Immediately, a member of the pope’s household, who must be ready, takes the hat from the cardinal’s head.

Then, after the aforesaid placing of the hat, each of them immediately kisses the pope’s foot according to his order. Afterward the pope receives each of them to kiss his mouth, in the order stated above. Each new cardinal, after receiving the pope’s kiss, returns to his seat there.

After this, the pope rises, and all the cardinals also rise. Then, if the cathedral church is nearby, the new cardinals are sometimes accustomed to go there immediately to pray and afterward return to their homes.

On the following day the new cardinals must together begin visiting all the older cardinals, visiting each one in the house he inhabits. In visiting the older cardinals, they are not to take account of which cardinals were or are the more senior, but are to proceed according to whatever arrangement seems most pleasing to the new cardinals. At that time the older cardinals must privately instruct the new cardinals in their chambers how they ought to honor and revere the pope and the older cardinals in word and deed, and also what manner they should observe when speaking with the pope or the cardinals in consistory or elsewhere—whether in giving advice, in conversations, or in other matters—and when sitting.

After the new cardinals have visited the older cardinals in their houses, the older cardinals must visit the new cardinals individually, each one in the houses of the latter. Sometimes, by special favor, some newly created cardinals are visited immediately in their own houses.

At the second consistory which the pope holds, or at the latest at the third, he customarily opens the mouths of the new cardinals, with the advice of the older cardinals. He then exhorts them concerning how they ought to speak reverently in consistory, and at that time tells them the other good things mentioned above.

It must nevertheless be noted that, while the aforesaid advice is being sought, the new cardinals must leave the consistory and remain in some nearby chamber until, after the older cardinals have given the aforesaid advice, they are subsequently summoned by the junior older cardinal, by the pope’s command, to return to the consistory. When they have returned, the pope customarily opens their mouths.

On the day when he opens their mouths, the pope customarily gives each new cardinal his title and ring in consistory, at the end of the consistory. At that time each new cardinal, while the pope places the ring on his finger, customarily kneels; immediately after receiving the ring, he kisses the hand and foot of the said pope, and, after receiving the pope’s kiss, returns to his own seat.

The new cardinals must not wear rings, even if they had been prelates before becoming cardinals, until the pope gives them their titles and rings, as stated above. Nor may they give a blessing in their chapels or private houses until they have received their title and ring, as stated.

The rule formerly customarily observed in the opening of the mouths of new cardinals, the assignment of titles, and the giving of rings is written below. After both the older and the new cardinals have taken their places in order in the consistory, when it pleases the pope, he tells the new cardinals to sit apart. In their absence, the older cardinals hold a private consultation as to whether the mouths of the new cardinals should be opened. If they advise that they should, the absent cardinals are recalled to the consistory and sit in their places.

Then the pope, having proposed some authoritative text, if he wishes, with a brief or short explanation and without any further exposition of it, opens their mouths, saying:

“We open your mouth” — or “your mouths,” if there are several — “in deliberations, counsels, and in the election of the Roman pontiff, and in all acts, both within the consistory and outside it, which pertain to cardinals and which they are accustomed to exercise.”

They do not answer what has been said to them.

After this, at the end of the consistory, or there immediately after the aforesaid opening, according to the pope’s judgment, each new cardinal, one after another, kneels before the pope. The pope then takes one of the rings prepared for this purpose and places it on the new cardinal’s finger, saying these or similar words:

“For the honor of almighty God, of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and of Saint Prisca—or of another holy woman [Col. 1264D] or holy man, for whose honor the church entrusted to the new cardinal has been founded—we entrust to you the church of Saint Prisca, with its clergy, people, and chaplains, if he has been appointed a cardinal priest”; and similarly in other cases. Sometimes the following is added: “According to the form by which it is customary to entrust churches to cardinals who have held that same church as a title at the relevant time.”

If he has been appointed a cardinal deacon, it is said: “For the honor, etc., as above, we entrust to you the church of Saint N., with its clergy and people,” and “with its chaplains” is omitted.

The cardinal who receives the ring kisses the pope’s hand and foot, and the pope then receives him with a kiss on the mouth. The same procedure is observed successively with the other new cardinals. When these things have been completed, the aforesaid new cardinals go and sit in their places. At that time, too, the new cardinals do not respond by any of the aforesaid words or actions.

It must also be noted that at that time, in the presence of all the cardinals, the pope determines which titles the absent new cardinals are to have, so that uncertainty may be removed.

It must further be noted that the foregoing ceremonies, concerning the opening of the mouth and the giving of the ring and title, are sometimes performed outside the consistory, when the pope summons all the cardinals to his chamber to consult on certain business. All the aforesaid solemnities are then observed in every respect according to the previously stated procedure, as was done in the year 1339 from the Nativity of the Lord [Note: [Col. 1265D] Onufrius assigns this creation to the year 1337, specifically to 18 December, on which day Bertrand of Deucio, archbishop of Embrun, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Mark; Brother Guillaume Curti of Divano, abbot of Monte Oliveto, cardinal priest of the title of the Four Crowned Saints; and Guillaume Albus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill, are said to have been announced together with three others. But the authority of this Ceremonial is to be preferred.]—on 16 January, at Avignon, by Pope Benedict XII, for the persons of the lords the cardinals of Embrun, to whom the title of Saint Mark was then assigned; of Albus, to whom the title of the Four Crowned Saints was likewise then assigned; and of Monte Oliveto, to whom the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill was likewise then assigned, in the chamber of the aforesaid Pope Benedict.

It should be known that when a new cardinal who is outside the curia has been created together with others who were present in the Roman curia, on the day when he is to enter the curia all the cardinals and the pope’s chamberlain, together with the clerks of the chamber and the armed servants of that same pope, go out to meet him beyond the town. At the meeting, the other cardinals, having removed their hats and birettas, receive him with a kiss.

This done, they turn back and go to the consistory, while only two junior cardinal deacons remain with the new cardinal and accompany him as far as the hall where the pope holds the consistory. When he has arrived there and the pope subsequently comes from his chamber to the consistory, the older cardinals, except for the two junior cardinal deacons, remain with the new cardinal outside the consistory at the end of the hall where the consistory is held. They make the customary reverence to the pope.

After this, the two senior cardinal deacons who come to meet the new cardinal receive him at the entrance to the consistory. The two junior cardinal deacons who had accompanied him leave him, approach to make the customary reverence, and, after doing so, return to sit in their customary places in the consistory. The aforesaid two senior cardinal deacons then lead him to the pope, who receives him with a kiss of the foot and afterward of the mouth. The same two senior cardinal deacons then lead him to the proper seat assigned to him by the pope according to the rank and order of his creation.

After all the cardinals have taken their seats, with the others having been dismissed, the pope, after making some address and discourse for his instruction, as has been related above concerning cardinals newly created in the Roman curia, imposes silence upon the new cardinal until, after consultation with the other cardinals, he causes his mouth to be opened.

Subsequently, when it is time to depart, the pope, seated in his chamber, gives the new cardinal a red hat; or he gives it before dinner if he is not in a position to hold a solemn dinner that day. The remaining matters that the pope must say, do, and observe in the opening of the mouth and the giving of the title and ring, and that the new cardinal must carry out in visiting and in the other matters mentioned above, are to follow the procedure already described for new cardinals created in the curia and present there when the pope speaks and acts toward them and when they speak and act.

It should likewise be known that if the apostolic see is vacant when an older or newly created cardinal who has been a legate or nuncio returns to the curia, the other cardinals do not go out to meet the arriving cardinal, even if they are not in conclave for the election of the future supreme pontiff. The reason is that, while the see is vacant, they in a certain manner represent the person of the pope.

It should be known that if, on the day when a new cardinal who was absent at the time of his creation enters the curia, the pope, for whatever prudent reason, does not hold a consistory, he gives the new cardinal a red hat in his chamber, in the presence of the cardinals. On that day his mouth is not closed; this is customarily done at the first consistory that follows.

[Col. 1266C] As a rule, however, the pope does not send a red hat to an absent new cardinal. Sometimes, nevertheless, by special favor, the pope customarily sends one when the cardinal had previously been sent as legate or nuncio by the pope to negotiate and also conclude peace between kings, or between a king and princes, so that the cardinal might be held by them in greater reverence and they might thereby be induced more readily and easily to peace.

It should also be noted that a newly created cardinal, before receiving his title, if the pope celebrates solemnly or hears solemn Vespers, comes to pay reverence to the pope according to his rank. He then receives and wears his vestments like the other cardinals of his rank, if he has received the order to which he was appointed; otherwise he does not.

[Col. 1266D] It should be noted that when a cardinal whom the pope has appointed a cardinal priest or cardinal deacon is not a priest or deacon, if he has been appointed cardinal priest, he does not wear at Vespers or Mass, which the pope solemnly celebrates and says in the presence of the other older cardinals, the vestments that the other older cardinals wear at that time, until he has received the priestly order from the pope’s hands. If he has been appointed cardinal deacon, likewise he does not wear the vestments of a deacon until he has received the order of the diaconate from the pope’s hands. Instead, he stands last among the cardinals of his rank, wearing a scarlet cappa.

The minor orders are customarily conferred upon the aforesaid new cardinals by a cardinal bishop commissioned by the pope, outside the Ember seasons. The minor orders, however, are regularly conferred by the pope during the Ember seasons, and sometimes outside the Ember seasons and secretly, with only three older cardinals present, together with their vestments, one bishop or priest, and two deacons. The pope also customarily confers all the major orders upon the aforesaid cardinals at the same time.

## CXVII. The customary ceremonies observed in the creation of cardinal priests when an episcopal title is assigned to them: rubric

[Col. 1267B]

When the title of a cardinal bishop becomes vacant at the time when new cardinals are created by the pope, the pope sometimes customarily provides for it by assigning it, in the manner that follows, to one of the older cardinal priests present in the Roman curia. On Friday, when he announces the persons who are to be newly created cardinals, the older cardinals come in their order to the chair prepared beside the pope’s chair for the older cardinals, to give counsel. The pope individually asks them which older cardinal priest they think should be provided with the vacant church mentioned above, without naming any cardinal to them.

After they have answered in order, and after all the cardinals have subsequently returned to the consistory to sit according to their order, the pope provides the older cardinal priest, whether present or absent, with the vacant episcopal church mentioned above, before creating the other new cardinals.

Some of the most recently appointed cardinal priests are nevertheless preferred, on account of their legations, to older cardinal priests in the provision of an episcopal title. This happened in the time of Pope John XXII, when Bertrand of Poitiers was a legate and, while remaining in his legation, was made bishop of Ostia, although Lord Santelmus [Al.: Santelinus] John, who later became bishop of Albano, and P. of Roblayo, who had been chancellor of France, were cardinal priests senior to him.

In the provision of the said episcopal title, even the most recently appointed cardinal priests who, before their promotion to the cardinalate, had been archbishops or consecrated bishops are preferred to other older cardinals who had not been consecrated bishops before their promotion to the cardinalate. Thus, in the time of the aforesaid Pope John, Lord Peter of Prato, then a cardinal priest, who had been consecrated archbishop of Aix, was made bishop of Palestrina, although the aforesaid Lords Santelmus John [Col. 1268A] and P. of Roblayo, cardinal priests, preceded him and were senior to him in the cardinalate.

This also occurred in the time of Pope Clement VI, when Lord Dalbia, who had been bishop of Rodez, was made bishop of Porto; Lord Cardinal of Bologna, who had been consecrated archbishop of Lyon, was made bishop of Porto; and Lord Cardinal of Clermont, who later became Pope Innocent VI, was made bishop of Ostia, although Lord Cardinal of Monte Oliveto preceded them and was senior to them in the cardinalate.

In the time of Pope Innocent VI, Lord the cardinal priest of Arras was made bishop of Ostia, and Lord the cardinal priest Spaniard, who was then legate in Lombardy, was made bishop of Sabina, although Lord of Monte Oliveto, who had been a Benedictine abbot of Monte Oliveto, and Cardinal of Sées, created by the said Pope Clement VI, who had been elected bishop of Sées but had not been consecrated, preceded them all. The pope subsequently created the other new cardinals in the manner stated above.

[Note: [Col. 1267D] For the first occasions on which certain cardinal deacons, to the exclusion of cardinal priests, were promoted to episcopal titles, see Augustine Patricius, title 8, chapter 17, where he gives several examples from Gregory XI, who promoted the cardinal deacon of Limoges to the bishopric of Palestrina; and from Pius II, who promoted John Carvajal, of Saint Angelo, to the bishopric of Porto, and so forth.]

[Col. 1268B] On the following Saturday, the older cardinal to whom an episcopal cardinalial title was assigned on the preceding Friday must remain outside the consistory with the other new cardinals created on the preceding Friday, until he is summoned on the pope’s behalf to come to him with the newly created cardinals. He must then come first with them and stand first, on his feet, among the new cardinals, and perform with them all the other things which new cardinals must perform according to the procedure related above.

There is one exception: when all the aforesaid solemnities have been completed, he is led first by the two senior cardinal deacons to sit in the consistory immediately beside the last cardinal bishop among the older cardinals. Silence is not imposed upon him, as is customary for new cardinals; nor is a ring afterward given to him by the pope; nor does the pope exhort him concerning how he should conduct himself in consistory and outside it; nor is a red hat given to him by the pope.

He nevertheless visits all the cardinals, as has already been stated above concerning the new cardinals. If he is absent from the curia when the pope provides him with the title, then, when he returns, he must visit all the cardinals individually in their houses.

[Col. 1268D] It should be known, however, that an episcopal cardinalial title is not customarily assigned to any cardinal unless he has first been consecrated bishop, provided that, when such an episcopal title becomes vacant, he is the first among the cardinal priests who was not consecrated bishop before his promotion to the cardinalate.

This was the procedure when Lord Cardinal of Bologna was made bishop of Porto. He was the second-ranking cardinal priest, and before becoming a cardinal he had been consecrated archbishop of Lyon. Lord Cardinal of Monte Oliveto was the senior cardinal priest; but Lord of Monte Oliveto had not been consecrated bishop before his promotion to the cardinalate, and for that reason the aforesaid episcopal title was not assigned to him.

It must nevertheless be noted that in the time of the aforesaid Pope John, Lord Santelmus John, cardinal priest, although he had not been elected or consecrated bishop or archbishop, was made bishop of Albano.

In the time of Benedict XII and Lord Clement VI, after receiving the kiss on the mouth, the pope customarily gave noble rings to bishops newly created as cardinals when they were present in the curia; but it was not customary to give them to absent cardinals when they later returned to the curia.

This was observed by Pope Clement VI when Lord Cardinal of Périgueux was made bishop of Albano and Lord Cardinal of Rodez was made bishop of Porto. The aforesaid pope gave them rings as stated, because they were present in the curia. Lord Cardinal of Embrun, however, who was absent from the curia when he was made bishop of Sabina, was not given a ring by the pope upon his return.

When Lord Cardinal Albus was made bishop of Tusculum, he was given a ring because he was then present in the curia, by the aforesaid Pope Clement, in the manner and at the time stated above. The same was done for Lord Cardinal of Bologna when the pope provided him with the bishopric of Porto.

Sometimes, however, the pope customarily provided an older cardinal priest present in the Roman curia with an episcopal title, outside the Ember seasons and without creating new cardinals, according to the procedure fully described above. On that day all the cardinals customarily dined with the pope. On the following day that cardinal was required to visit all the cardinals individually in their houses, as stated above.

If that cardinal was absent from the Roman curia, the aforesaid solemnities were omitted, except that the pope sought private consultations from the cardinals present in the Roman curia according to the procedure stated above. After they had given their advice and had subsequently returned to the consistory, the pope then made the aforesaid provision for the absent cardinal according to the procedure previously described.

It should also be noted that, although as a rule all the aforesaid cardinals come to pay reverence to the pope when the pope comes to the consistory, nevertheless, if the pope holds a consistory either in his usual place, or in his chamber, or elsewhere, wearing a mantle and biretta or a cappa, but not wearing his customary vestments—as sometimes happens because of the cold or for some other reason—then, when he is not wearing the customary vestments, the cardinals do not come to pay the customary reverence.

It should be known that when our lord the pope creates cardinals, whether deacons or priests, after the creation and assignment of the churches to which they are given titles by our said lord the pope, he customarily grants them a private dispensation so that the said cardinals may retain all the benefices they held before the aforesaid creation, together with the churches assigned to them.

It should also be known that when our lord the pope provides a cardinal priest with a cardinalial bishopric, our lord does not say, “We entrust to you,” but rather, “We provide you with such-and-such a bishopric,” and so forth. Once this provision has been made, our said lord the pope privately—not publicly—dispenses that cardinal bishop so that he may retain, together with the said bishopric, the benefices he held before the aforesaid provision.

It should also be noted that the cardinals who are sent as nuncios or legates, on the day when they are to undertake the journey of their legation, go together with their servants first to the principal church of the city or town where the curia is located; afterward they must undertake and continue the journey of their legation.

All the other cardinals who are to remain in the curia go ahead of the legates and wait for them about half a league outside the city. There they receive their leave from the legates. After all have received this leave, the legates continue their journey to its destination.

It should also be known that cardinal nuncios or legates, when departing from and returning to the curia, must visit all the cardinals who remain in the curia. The nuncios or legates themselves, however, are not visited on those departures and returns unless this is done out of special affection, although according to the custom of the present day they are visited by almost everyone.

It should likewise be known that a cardinal legate or nuncio is not accustomed to return to the Roman curia without first obtaining special permission from the pope.

## CXVIII. The creation of cardinal legates or nuncios

It should be known that when the pope wishes to appoint one or more cardinals as a legate or legates, or as a nuncio or nuncios, and send them to some region or regions, he first publicly asks the cardinals in consistory whether it is expedient to send them, mentioning certain reasons why it appears that they should be sent.

If it seems expedient to send them, he also publicly determines in consistory whether one, two, or more are to be sent. Once the decision to send them has been made, private consultations are held concerning the persons to be sent, as is customary in the creation of cardinals. The pope then privately asks each cardinal which person or persons he thinks it would be good to appoint and send.

When the consultations have been completed, the pope sometimes first cites an authoritative text, though he gives it little further exposition; ordinarily, however, he does not cite one. There, or on the following day, according to the pope’s pleasure, he says:

“All, or the greater part, of our brothers agree” — or “agrees” — “on one person, or on two persons or more, if two or more are to be sent; and with the advice of those same brothers of ours, we appoint that you, such-and-such a person” — or “you, such-and-such persons,” if there are two or more — “go to such-and-such regions and prepare yourselves to depart,” and so forth.

Sometimes the pope customarily adds after the word “We appoint”: “And we enjoin.”

After the pope has said this, the cardinal who is to be sent customarily cites some authoritative text and excuses himself to some extent, saying that he is not capable of undertaking what the pope has appointed him to do. But when the pope does not accept his excuse, the cardinal comes to kiss the pope’s foot and mouth, with the senior cardinal deacon first uncovering the pope’s feet.

When this has been done, the pope rises and goes to his chamber. No other solemnities are performed or words spoken, except that if a cardinal is absent because of illness, two cardinals are sent to him to obtain his advice, according to the procedure observed in the creation of new cardinals.

On the day when a cardinal or cardinals are thus appointed as a legate or legates, or nuncio or nuncios, all the cardinals do not customarily dine with the pope. Only the one or those who have been appointed legate or legates, nuncio or nuncios, dine with him.

It must also be noted that if, by chance, two legates or nuncios have been appointed and, in the course of time, one of them excuses himself, or the pope excuses him, the question whether another legate or nuncio should or should not be joined to the one who remains is decided by a private consultation concerning the person to be added, as before. This is done for the sake of the one first appointed, who has not excused himself and remains nuncio or legate; he must not know merely the votes of the cardinals in this matter.

This was observed in the time of Pope Clement VI, in the fourth year of his pontificate, when the said pope excused Lord Cardinal of Bologna, who had been chosen by him as legate together with Lord Cardinal of Embrun for the regions of Italy and the kingdom of Sicily.

It should also be noted that the pope ought to appoint and commission such legates or nuncios in consistory, as stated above. Sometimes, however, he customarily appoints and commissions them in his chamber, after summoning all the cardinals.

If the pope happens not to be wearing a cope and mitre at that appointment, nevertheless, when announcing the legates or nuncios, he must wear a gold-embroidered cope and the consistory mitre. If the weather is extremely cold, the pope may, during the same announcement, wear a fur-lined samite cope and a hood of the same material. After putting on this cope and before announcing the legates or nuncios, all the cardinals must come to pay reverence to the pope, as is customary.

It should also be noted that a cardinal or nuncio, before departing from the curia, must visit every cardinal individually in his house. He must do the same upon his return. The legate or nuncio himself, however, is not customarily visited by them except by certain persons especially attached to him.

On the day of his departure, all the cardinals must wait for him outside the town in a suitable field, and first receive a kiss from him, having removed their hats and birettas. If there are two or more legates or nuncios, they must meet early in the morning at the principal church of the city or place where the pope and cardinals reside, undertake their journey together, and come to the cardinals waiting outside the town, as stated above, to receive their leave.

When such legates or nuncios return from their legation and wish to enter the curia, all the cardinals of the curia must go outside the town to meet them and wait for the legates or nuncios in a suitable field, as was stated above concerning their departure.

Then all the cardinals, together with the said legates or nuncios, must ascend to the palace. There the aforesaid legates or nuncios are received in consistory by the pope with a kiss of the foot and mouth. If there is only one legate or nuncio, he is accompanied from the place where the cardinals received him outside the town to the pope’s palace by two junior cardinal deacons.

If there are two legates or nuncios, the one senior in the order of the cardinalate is accompanied from that place by two junior cardinal deacons, while the other legate or nuncio is accompanied in the aforesaid manner by the next two junior cardinal deacons, each proceeding according to his order of seniority.

When the pope has received the legates or nuncios with a kiss of the foot and mouth, the legates or nuncios go to sit in their places according to their order. The cardinal deacons who accompanied them then come to pay reverence to the pope, as is customary, and afterward go to sit in their own places.

When they have taken their seats, the pope selects some theme and gives a discourse in their praise and commendation, as seems appropriate to him. During this discourse the legates or nuncios sit in their places with their heads entirely uncovered, even without their birettas, and remain so for as long as the pope’s praise and commendation are directed toward them.

When the discourse has ended, all the cardinals remain that day to dine with the pope. The discourse given by the pope upon the arrival of nuncios or legates was introduced by Pope Benedict XII and observed by Clement VI. It was not observed, however, in the time of Clement V and John XXII.

At the first consistory that follows, the said nuncios or legates report, or give an account, of what they accomplished in their legations. They do this in the form of a discourse, selecting an appropriate theme. This procedure is observed even if there are two or more legates or nuncios, for whom the report is made in the form of a discourse.

If the legates or nuncios are not prepared to give their report at the first consistory after their arrival, the pope customarily assigns them a definite day on which to report.

It should also be noted that when a cardinal legate travels to his legation, as soon as he leaves the territory of the city or place where the pope and cardinals reside, he immediately removes his ordinary cappa and receives a scarlet-red cappa and a red biretta, which he uses throughout his legation.

When he enters the aforesaid territory, he immediately ceases to display the cross, removes the red cappa and red biretta, and assumes an ordinary cappa and a biretta of the sort worn by the other cardinals. He then enters the curia in the manner most recently described.

These customs concerning the assumption and removal of the red cappa and biretta, and the carrying of the cross, do not apply to nuncios but only to legates.

Note, however, that a cross is not carried before either a legate or a nuncio.

It should be known that after a cardinal legate has departed from the curia, and until he has returned from his legation to the curia, he receives nothing from the revenues of the Church, from the services of prelates made by the pope during the intervening period, or from other sums owed to the pope’s chamber during that period, from which the cardinals present customarily receive and collect one-half.

The exception concerns the rings of cardinals who die during that period: absent cardinal legates receive these rings just as though they were present. A nuncio who has been sent receives in his absence as much of the aforesaid revenues as he would receive if he were present in the curia.

It should also be noted that cardinals who are to go as legates or nuncios are customarily allowed a period of one month in which to prepare themselves and undertake their journey. Nevertheless, because of the great danger that threatened and was feared [lacuna], especially in the kingdom of Majorca, which the king of Aragon had entered with armed forces and whose city of Majorca he had already captured, while he was approaching Perpignan and attempting to seize it, Lord Cardinal of Rodez, appointed legate to those kingdoms, undertook his journey toward them on the twelfth day after the announcement of his legation.

It should also be noted that on their return from their legation, cardinal legates or nuncios customarily give the cardinals who have remained in the curia various gifts, as they see fit.

It should also be noted that when the lords the cardinals are in the presence of the pope and must speak or answer there on some matter, the first cardinal bishop speaks first, followed successively by the other cardinal bishops; after them, the cardinal priests; and finally the junior cardinal deacon, followed in order by all the cardinal deacons up to the senior cardinal deacon, who speaks or answers last.

When the apostolic see is vacant and the lords the cardinals assemble and speak together, this procedure is not observed. Instead, the senior cardinal deacon speaks immediately after the last cardinal priest, and then the cardinal deacons speak individually in succession up to the junior cardinal deacon, who, while the see is vacant, speaks last of all.

[Note: [Col. 1273] Certain material had been added here in another hand, word for word from the following Ceremonial of Peter Amelii; it seemed best to omit it.]

## [ROMAN ORDER XV]

[Col. 1273]

### NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING BOOK
1. Although in the old Codex which the eminent Cardinal Casanata, in his kindness, granted us for use, no author’s name is prefixed to the following book, it is nevertheless clear from various passages of the same book that its author was Peter Amelius, a Frenchman of Electe (*Electensis*), an Augustinian hermit, sacristan to Urban V, and afterward penitentiary and librarian to Gregory XI; later Bishop of Senigallia, Archbishop of Taranto, then Patriarch of Grado and Alexandria, and administrator of the Church of Aix. He himself plainly identifies himself in chapter 79 of the following book: “Thus I, Brother Peter Amelius, Bishop of Senigallia, saw it observed.” Likewise, in chapter 141 he calls Augustine “our Father”; and in chapter 90 he testifies that, as sacristan and Bishop of Senigallia, he made the *Agnus Dei*—as it is called—in the year 1378. In addition, in chapter 158 he says that, as Patriarch of Grado together with the Patriarch of Constantinople, he pronounced the general proceedings against criminals on Maundy Thursday in the year 1393. Finally, according to chapter 165, he was still alive in 1398, when the death of Boniface IX was imminent. Those who say, therefore, that he died in 1368 are mistaken, since ten years afterward he made the *Agnus Dei* as sacristan and Bishop of Senigallia. He sat as patriarch among the cardinal bishops in 1391, according to chapter 153. He sang in verse Gregory XI’s journey from Avignon to Rome; he mentions this work in chapter 142 below: “Seek in my itinerary concerning Pope Gregory XI.” This *Itinerary* is found in Masson and Ciacconius, in their works on the supreme pontiffs, under Gregory XI. From these facts it is evident that no one other than Peter Amelius was the author of the following little book, concerning whom Augustine Patricius writes in Book II, chapter 60.

2. Some additions, however, have been scattered here and there by other authors, namely in chapter 61, where certain matters concerning the time of Eugene IV are recorded, and in chapter 63, where the funeral rites of the Cardinal of Novara, who died in 1434, are reported. From chapter 85 one may conjecture that the author of these additions was Peter, Bishop of Oloron: “And thus I, Peter, Bishop of Oloron, saw it observed in the time of Lord Boniface IX, Innocent VI, Gregory XI, John XXIII, and Martin V.”

[Col. 1273]

# ROMAN ORDER XV, OR BOOK ON THE CEREMONIES OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH

By Peter Amelius, Bishop of Senigallia

448

## I. On the First Sunday of Advent: Rubric

[Col. 1273B]

On the First Sunday of Advent a sermon and Mass are appointed. On this day the pope’s chamberlain customarily celebrates the High Mass, unless some cardinal or prelate were to preach a sermon; for then that person must celebrate the entire office. At this Mass the supreme pontiff, wearing an alb, stole, and a simple red cope without pearls, together with a white mitre, comes to Mass; and likewise on the Sundays of Advent and Lent. Before he leaves his chamber, the two junior cardinal deacons who are present—or presbyters if no deacons are present—come to kiss his hand, with the gold-worked border of the pope’s cope placed over the right hand; and they precede him as far as the chapel. At this Mass he descends from his own chair and goes to another chair before the altar when *Hanc igitur* is said, and only to *Laetatus sum*.

[Note: [Col. 1275D] The Psalm *Laetatus sum* was said before Communion, below, in chapter 43.]

## CHAPTER II. On the Second Sunday

On the Second Sunday of Advent a sermon and Mass are appointed, as above. It should also be known that on the Sundays of Advent, and likewise during Lent, the Roman Curia, even if a double feast falls on one of those Sundays, has never customarily celebrated the feast on that day; rather, it is transferred to the following weekday. Nor is a commemoration made, because these Sundays have their own proper offices.

## CHAPTERS III AND IV. On the Third and Fourth Sundays

On the Third Sunday of Advent both Mass and a sermon are appointed. If the chamberlain does not say Mass on the First Sunday, he must celebrate it on this day, unless a cardinal or some prelate preaches a sermon; for then that person will perform the entire office. On this day the prelate wears a mitre with pearls and costly violet vestments. The lord pope also wears a cope of silk or satin with pearl-worked borders, and uses a gold-worked mitre with pearls. At the first Collect, *Pax vobis* is said, not *Dominus vobiscum*.

[Col. 1275C]

On the Fourth Sunday of Advent a sermon and Mass are appointed. Everything, in every detail, is as above for the First Sunday.

## CHAPTER V. On Christmas Eve

On Christmas Eve there is neither sermon nor Mass. Vespers are announced.

[Note: [Col. 1276D] That is, they are announced to the cardinals, and so forth.]

A meal is held in the hall after Vespers.

At First Vespers the pope’s sacristan has a costly white cope prepared at an early hour, with images and pearls, together with an eagle and a costly mitre set with large sapphires, or another according to the pope’s wishes. Dressed in these, the pontiff comes to Vespers. Before he leaves his chamber, the two deacons show him reverence by kissing his hand, with the gold-worked border of the pope’s cope covering it. This is always observed in the same manner whenever the pope leaves his chamber in vestments.

After reverence has been made on bended knees before the altar, the mitre is first removed from his head on the chair by the senior deacon; but the two junior deacons remain with the pope in woolen copes. All the other cardinals, after removing their copes, receive the sacred vestments—namely amice, broad surplice, and cope—and in this manner the two senior cardinals return. When he rises from prayer, the two senior cardinal deacons receive the edge of the cope on his right, and the others on his left; with the other hand they hold the rear fringe. Thus they lead him to the solemn chair prepared far from the altar. When he is seated, the senior stands at his right and the junior at his left, with their heads uncovered.

Then all the cardinals come in their proper order to pay reverence to the pope in the customary manner: first the senior of the cardinal bishops; after him the patriarch, if one is present; in second place the junior of the cardinal bishops; after him another patriarch, if one is present; and so forth according to their order.

## CHAPTER VI. The Order for Announcing the Antiphons

When this has been done, the pope rises and remains there. The mitre is removed by the person standing at his right. Facing the altar and making the sign of the cross, he begins, *Deus, in adjutorium meum intende*. After *Gloria Patri* has been said, the pope’s subdeacon, standing with bowed head and in a low voice, begins *Rex pacificus*. He then kneels before the pope, and the pope begins the Antiphon again. When it has been said, he sits.

Immediately the choir begins again. One cardinal deacon who stands at his right places the mitre on him, while another, behind him, arranges the tails. The second Antiphon is begun by the deacon standing at the pope’s right; the third by the cardinal bishop serving in the office of presbyter; the fourth by the senior of the cardinal presbyters; the fifth by the cardinal deacon standing at the pope’s left. This order is observed whenever there is papal Vespers.

450

The subdeacon, together with one of the acolytes, announces the Antiphon to the pope and the cardinals. The subdeacon says the Chapter. One of the senior auditors or acolytes begins the Hymn, and immediately the pope begins the same Hymn again. His mitre is always removed when he sings. The subdeacon begins the Antiphon of the *Magnificat*, and immediately the pope begins it again.

After the singers begin the *Magnificat*, the pope descends from his seat and goes to incense the altar. Having done this, he returns to his seat and is incensed there by the cardinal bishop. Then that bishop, the two deacons standing at the right and left, and afterward all the cardinals wearing copes are incensed by one of the acolytes. The pope then says the Collect.

It should be noted that Matins are not appointed, but all three Masses are; nor is there a sermon.

## VII. On Matins

At Matins the pope comes wearing a woolen cappa. In modern times it is of crimson velvet, lined with ermine. Boniface IX introduced this. It is a woolen cappa of red scarlet, closed as far as the middle of the chest, with a cap tied beneath the chin because of the cold. He sits at the said Matins without a mitre, which he begins in the customary manner. The cardinal deacons do not stand before him or at his sides; rather, they sit on their benches according to their order.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the Readings

The first two readings are read by acolytes or clerics of the chapel. The third is read by the junior cleric of the treasury; the fourth by a junior cardinal presbyter; the fifth by the most distinguished person by rank who is then present in the Curia; the sixth by the senior subdeacon; the seventh by the junior cardinal deacon standing at the pope’s left; the eighth by the senior of the cardinal deacons standing at the pope’s right; the ninth by the pope. In the ninth reading he says only, *Jube, Domine, benedicere*, and the singers respond, *Amen*.

It should be noted that the cardinals who read the lessons on this night do not come to kiss the pope’s foot after the reading. Other persons who read the lessons go to kiss the pope’s foot, but the cardinals do not. When they read the lessons, everyone wears surplices except the cardinals, who stand in their cappas while reading.

When the pope has read the lesson, the subdeacon begins before him, *Te Deum laudamus*, and the pope takes up *Te Deum* again; the singers complete it all.

While *Te Deum* is being sung, the sacristan has white vestments prepared on the altar: first the chasuble, second the dalmatic; on the left side the tunicle; on the right side the breast stole, gloves, rings, pallium, three pins or brooches, and sandals; the maniple below the Gospel book; on the left side the mitre; in the middle of the altar a simple alb; on one side a girdle with a cincture, toward the mitre; and the fan on the right side. The same sacristan then successively and orderly, with due decorum, gives and distributes these items to the chaplains, table companions, auditors, and acolytes, to be carried to the supreme pontiff according to their order.

When *Te Deum* is completed, two acolytes carry candlesticks with candles before the pope, and one of the bishops attending him carries the Missal. He places it on the head of the senior presbyter who is to serve him at this Mass, and the pope says the Collect. When it is finished, no blessing is given, but the acolytes sing, *Benedicamus Domino*.

Meanwhile, while the pope is standing, the two cardinal deacons remove his garments down to his shirt or Roman alb, and vest him in the sacred vestments as written and noted above, in reverse order. First the alb is handed to him by the person who is to read the Gospel, who must also be dressed as a deacon and stand at the pope’s right; the subdeacon stands at the left. Both vest the pope together. Second comes the girdle with its cincture; care must be taken that it hangs at the left side. Third comes the breast cross; fourth the fan; and so forth.

## CHAPTER IX. On the First Mass of Christmas

At this Mass, as the pope descends from his chair, three junior cardinal presbyters come to meet him, wearing rochet, amice, surplice, and planeta or chasuble. The same occurs at all solemn papal Masses, as is noted in their order and contained at the end of the book.

After the incensing of the altar, while the pope is standing or sitting in his chair, all the cardinals pay reverence to the pope; they do not do so at Matins.

After Mass has been said, the papal blessing given, and the indulgence of seven years and seven quarantines announced by the cardinal serving him in the office of chaplain, the pope returns to the great chair. The mitre is removed by the cardinal standing at his right. He begins the Lauds, *Deus, in adjutorium meum intende*, and returns to the robing room, where he must always vest.

If the pope wishes to celebrate the second Mass without an interval, he does not undress; after saying the Collect and giving the blessing, he goes to the altar. If it is celebrated immediately by someone else, he removes not the cappa but the cope, and receives the gold-worked mitre. If he is within the chapel, he removes the sacred vestments there while reading Lauds with his chaplains. There he says only the Collect and gives the blessing again, after the singers have sung *Benedicamus Domino*. If there is no robing room, these things are done in his chair.

He resumes the closed cappa which he had previously removed and returns to his chamber, if he wishes, until it is time to begin the Dawn Mass.

[Col. 1278B]

It should be noted that neither at this Mass nor at the second is *Laetatus sum* said. At the present Mass the pontiff alone communicates, and does so at the altar. He drinks the Blood without a reed and nothing else, because he is to celebrate the Mass of the Third Hour. He nevertheless carefully wipes the chalice with his fingers and washes his fingers with water, as is customary at low Masses.

[Note: [Col. 1277D] The rubric of the Gregorian Sacramentary for the vigil of the Apostles Peter and Paul pertains here: when the apostolic celebrant celebrates two Masses in one day, he does not wash his mouth until after the office.]

It should also be noted that if the emperor or king is in the Curia late on this night, a cleric of the chapel brings him the book of readings, in which he is to read the fifth lesson, and courteously instructs him in the ceremonies to be observed when asking for the blessing, girding on the sword with its scabbard, drawing it, and brandishing it, as well as concerning the cap and other matters.

It should also be noted that the chamberlain and the clerics prepare the sword with its scabbard, belt, and cap according to the prince’s rank.

While the fourth Responsory is being sung, if an emperor or king is present, the chamberlain, sacristan, and clerics of the chapel prepare a beautiful white cope. Before the pulpit they remove his hood and put the cope on him over the middle of his cloak, so that the opening is at his right hand. They gird him with the sword, and he himself draws it and brandishes it. They place the cap on his head. He bows his head to the pope, asks for the blessing, and reads the lesson while those specified stand beside him.

[Note: [Col. 1277D] Emperor Frederick III did not permit this; see *Musei Italici*, vol. I, p. 263.]

When it has been read, they lead him, so vested with the cap on his head and the drawn sword in his hand, to kiss the pope’s foot. Each then returns to his place.

It should also be noted that if the pope is in Rome, he must celebrate this Mass at the Lord’s manger, sing Vespers there in the evening, and hold a meal in the hall with the clerics and nobles of the City.

Whatever is offered either into the pope’s hands or at his feet, or upon the altar, belongs to the chaplains and table companions, except for the bread and wine, which belong to the acolytes, and whatever comes onto the altar throughout the Mass. This practice must always be observed at all papal Masses, as is contained in the book called the *Politicus*, according to what James Gaetani says.

[Note: [Col. 1278D] That is, in the book of Cencius the chamberlain, edited above, which in this Ceremonial is commonly called *Politicus*, more correctly *Polyptychus*, and sometimes *Camerarius*.]

The presbyters, together with the chaplains, receive twelve denarii from the pope, which is called the presbyterium; half of it belongs to the sacristan according to the order of Urban.

At this Mass and the following one the cardinals do not customarily come to pay reverence to the pope, since they are not obliged to do so twice in one day—but elsewhere you will find that this was observed—except only for the three junior presbyters; those never fail. Lord Urban VI ordered the contrary. At the second, Dawn Mass, they do not come, but they do at the first and third. Good.

## X. On the Second Mass

The Dawn Mass is appointed, which the Roman pontiff customarily celebrates if he is in the City. Leaving Saint Mary Major early in the morning, dressed in the Mass vestments, he goes to Saint Anastasia and celebrates there.

At this Mass the *Credo in unum Deum* and *Gloria in excelsis* are said. *Laetatus sum* is not said, and the offerings are as at the other, Midnight Mass. The pope alone also communicates at the altar, as at the first Mass, and so forth.

When it is finished, he returns to Saint Mary Major still vested. After removing the vestments, he rests briefly in his chamber. At the proper hour he enters the sacristy or robing room with the cardinal bishops, presbyters, and deacons, chaplains, subdeacons, and the remaining orders; and they sing Terce.

When Terce has been said, they solemnly vest him in white sacred vestments, each person according to his order. They then proceed in procession to the altar with a cross and seven torches. The Curia must provide the presbyterium, and so forth.

[Col. 1279C]

If the pope is not in the City, the cardinal who holds the title of Saint Anastasia customarily celebrates this Mass; in his absence, if the pope does not celebrate, the senior of the cardinal presbyters does so.

It should be noted that if the pope wished to celebrate these two Masses, he could say both without removing the sacred vestments. Nevertheless, for propriety and because of the fatigue of the night, it is reasonable that some interval be made, in keeping with the suitable time and with what is expedient because of the shortness of the time and the days; this too should be noted.

After *Te Deum laudamus* has been said, two candle-bearers approach the pope with candlesticks and lighted candles. The pope says the Collect, and they sing *Benedicamus Domino*. The pope does not give the customary blessing, but gives it after Lauds.

[Col. 1279D]

It should be known that if he wishes to celebrate the second Mass after celebrating the first, he does not remove the sacred vestments, but says Lauds in them. When Lauds has been said, he gives the blessing and begins the second Mass again.

At the proper hour, therefore, the supreme pontiff, solemnly vested, begins the Mass in procession with the chaplains, subdeacons, and acolytes, accompanied by seven torches, the cross, and incense. Three junior cardinal presbyters come to meet him to kiss his mouth and breast.

It should be known that after the Collect has been read, his praises are customarily sung, as is found in the *Politicus* and noted in the account of his coronation.
