When those praises are finished, the Epistle is sung first in Latin and afterward in Greek. The Latin subdeacon waits for the Greek subdeacon. Then both go to kiss the pope’s foot, led by the master of ceremonies.

The Gospel is likewise read in Greek and Latin. After saying the Gospel, the cardinal deacon returns to the altar and does not wait for the Greek deacon, although they went together; the Greek deacon follows him. For the Latin Gospel seven candlesticks are carried; immediately afterward the Greek Gospel is said with two lighted candlesticks, while the other five are carried to the altar.

On this day the pope is accustomed to introduce certain innovations into the Mass. See the additions.

It should be noted that if the pope remains in the sacred vestments during the Lauds, the cardinal serving him must incense the altar.

## XI. On the Third Mass

At this Mass all the cardinal deacons, protonotaries, table companions, and auditors communicate, as do all who truly serve Christ and are not established in episcopal dignity, since such persons are bound to celebrate for the people themselves.

454

It should be noted that for this Communion, and on Easter Day, three large chalices are prepared: one for the consecration, another from which the pope drinks the wine, and a third for those communicating after receiving the Eucharist. They take the wine from the hand of one of the acolytes. The offerings are divided as at the first Mass.

## XII. On Second Vespers

At Second Vespers the pope comes wearing a red satin cope and a gold-worked mitre.

When Mass is completed, if he is in the City, he receives the tiara from the hand of the chief marshal and carries it as far as the steps of the palace. Then the judges and advocates come to meet him beneath the steps in the portico and again sing his praises, as written in the *Politicus*. There the lord pope descends, removes the tiara, and takes the mitre.

The matters contained here are not observed in modern times.

Then the judges lead him to the place where the presbyterium is given. After removing the chasuble and placing a mantle over his shoulders, he sits in the chair and, with his own hands, gives the presbyterium to the chaplains, table companions, and others, as at the coronation.

After the presbyterium has been given, he goes to the table still so vested. The cardinal deacon reads at table wearing the cope, and at the end the singers sing the Sequence, *Laetabundus*.

## XIII. On Saint Stephen

[Col. 1280D]

On the day of Saint Stephen a Mass and sermon are appointed. At times the Roman pontiffs have customarily celebrated on this day. Therefore note whether the pope is in the City.

Early in the morning all the orders—clerical and lay—assemble in the basilica, dressed in silk garments, as do the cardinal deacons and subdeacons, except those who are dressed in similar garments in the pope’s chamber and bring him from there to the basilica. There the cardinals and all the prelates come out to pay reverence to the pope. He then puts on a white chasuble.

Descending from the palace as far as the little portico, he finds a caparisoned horse there—not its neck, however, but its hindquarters are covered with scarlet. He mounts the horse and receives the tiara from the hand of the deacon standing at his right, and puts it on. Thus crowned, he goes with the orders in procession to the church of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill, as written in the *Politicus*.

When he reaches the said church, he removes the tiara, enters the church, and after prayer goes to the sacristy. There he removes the white chasuble, puts on a red one, and celebrates Mass, in all respects as on the preceding day. When it is finished, he resumes the chasuble, puts on the tiara, and returns to the palace. He performs the remaining ceremonies as contained in the *Politicus*.

If the pope does not celebrate, the cardinal presbyter holding the title of Saint Clement customarily celebrates the Mass of Saint Stephen before the pope on that day.

455

On this day the chaplains who are table companions, the acolytes, auditors, and penitentiaries dine splendidly with the pope, and pepper is served at the collation. But on these two days, of Saints Stephen and John, they do not customarily celebrate Vespers, and this is wrong.

## XIV. On Second Vespers

At Second Vespers the pope comes wearing a red cope and mitre.

## XV. On Saint John

On the day of Saint John a Mass and sermon are appointed; some cardinal customarily celebrates it. The pope comes to it wearing a red satin cope and a gold-worked mitre with pearls, as in consistory.

The same applies at Second Vespers, at which all the acolytes must wear surplices: first the table companions, auditors, and subdeacons, then the acolytes and honorary chaplains.

[Note: [Col. 1281D] From this passage the reading of James Gaetani above, p. 341, final line, must be corrected, and it should read, as here, “honorary chaplains.”]

## XVI. On the Holy Innocents

[Col. 1281C]

On the day of the Holy Innocents there was customarily a Mass and sermon; but this is no longer observed, nor does the pope come to the chapel at Second Vespers.

It should be noted that if the feast falls on a Sunday, *Te Deum laudamus* is said at Matins, and at Mass *Gloria in excelsis* and *Credo in unum* are said, with red vestments. If it does not fall on a Sunday, neither *Te Deum*, nor *Gloria*, nor *Credo* is said, and the vestments must be violet.

## XVII. On the Circumcision of the Lord

On the Circumcision of the Lord only a Mass and sermon are appointed. Although in ancient times the Roman pontiffs customarily came on the First Vespers of this day solemnly vested in a costly white cope and solemn mitre, in modern times he comes solemnly in a costly cope, and properly so.

[Note: [Col. 1281D] It seems that one should read “does not come.” Compare the Ceremonial of Peter Gaetani, chapter 77.]

The Roman pontiffs have always customarily celebrated this Mass, and no commemoration of the saints is made because of the rubric of Clement VI.

It should also be noted that if the pope is in the City on this day and does not celebrate, but has a cardinal say Mass in Saint Peter’s, before the cardinal vests, a bull is presented stating that the pope dispenses him so that he may celebrate upon Saint Peter’s altar. It hangs throughout the entire day before the railings.

[Note: [Col. 1281D] Although among other authors this word, *regiae*, often signifies the doors of the basilica, in these books it commonly means the altar railings, as below, chapters 21 and 35. See above, James Gaetani, chapter 76, and chapter 20 of our preliminary Commentary. Certainly a bull of this sort is still accustomed to be hung there; we saw this done on the feast of Saint Peter in the Vatican Basilica, where the bull had been placed on one of the columns supporting the ciborium. See our *Italian Journey*, p. 56.]

And the same is done in all the other Masses celebrated upon that altar.

456

## XVIII. On the Epiphany of the Lord: Rubric

On the Epiphany of the Lord a Mass and sermon are appointed, and Vespers have not customarily been appointed. Nowadays, however, Vespers are appointed, and the pope wears a costly white cope. The Antiphons are begun by the pope and the cardinals. At both Vespers the pope is present wearing a red satin cope and a gold-worked mitre.

The bishops of the City have also customarily celebrated this Mass, and ordinarily always do so unless prevented by illness or excessive cold. On this day they have sometimes proclaimed new cardinals, as at the Third Mass of the Nativity of Christ.

It should also be noted that in the year of the Lord 1389, in the tenth year of the pontificate of Lord Urban VI, the feast of Blessed Anthony fell on the First Sunday after the Epiphany of the Lord. We did nothing concerning Saint Anthony, but retained everything concerning the Sunday in the City.

## XIX. On the Purification of the Blessed Virgin Mary: Rubric

On the day of the Purification of the Blessed Virgin Mary only Mass is appointed. There is no appointed preceding Vespers; nevertheless, the cardinals are to be present at Vespers and begin the Antiphons, wearing white vestments.

It should be known that if this feast falls in Septuagesima or Sexagesima, it is transferred to Monday.

[Col. 1282C]

At First Vespers the pope comes wearing a simple satin cope and a gold-worked mitre.

## XX. On the Blessing of Candles

It should be known that on the day of the Purification of the Blessed Virgin Mary the candles are blessed early in the morning by the junior cardinal presbyter. He must be dressed in rochet, alb, amice, stole, and a white cope, and wear a simple garnello mitre. With holy water and incense, assisted by companions wearing surplices and by two candle-bearers with lighted torches, he blesses the candles as prescribed in the Roman Missal and Pontifical.

When the blessing has been completed, our lord the pope vests in the vesting chamber in an alb or Roman shirt, stole, and a red satin cope with gold-worked borders or pearls, together with a white garnello mitre. When he reaches the chapel, he prays before the altar, reclining somewhat upon the chair and footstool prepared for that purpose. If there is no chapel there, he goes to his own chair and sits there.

Afterward the cardinals and prelates, not vested, come to pay reverence to the pope, as is customarily done on other occasions. After making reverence, the cardinals and the other prelates go to receive their violet or indigo-colored vestments. The cardinal presbyters and deacons put on surplice, broad amice, and chasuble; the bishops put on copes, and the other prelates likewise receive violet copes.

When they are vested, the sacristan spreads a linen cloth over the pope’s knees. Two chaplains hold it on either side, or two acolytes kneeling, one at the right and the other at the left.

Then the senior of the cardinal bishops—or, if he is absent, the junior—descends in this manner, removes his mitre, and, standing before the pope seated in his chair, receives a candle from the hand of the chamberlain or of one of the bishops attending the pope. Standing, he gives the pope the said candle, made of whiter and thicker wax than the others and larger, unlit and without saying anything, while kissing the pope’s hand. He gives the pope another in the same manner. The person who hands the unlit candles to the pope then kisses the pope’s right knee.

In this way all the cardinals proceed: first the bishops, second the presbyters, third the deacons, followed by the attending prelates. All the vested prelates kiss the knee. But the chamberlain, notaries, auditor of pleas, and corrector, even if some of them are archbishops or bishops, do not customarily come vested, but in woolen cappas. The same applies to the chaplains, both the table companions, who must wear surplices, and the other chaplains, as well as the penitentiaries—in short, all the pope’s household, laymen, and any others who are not members of his household, even if one were a king. Kneeling, they receive the candle from the pope’s hand, and after receiving it they kiss his foot, not his knee.

It should also be known that in modern times the king customarily receives it while seated after the senior cardinal bishop; the same is done on Palm Sunday and Ash Wednesday.

It should be known that if the emperor were present, he receives the candle after the senior cardinal bishop and kisses the foot, not the knee.

It should also be noted that after the senior cardinal bishop, if a patriarch is present, he receives the candle from the lord pope’s hand. If the king is present, after the king the junior cardinal bishop receives the candle, and in his absence the senior cardinal presbyter, and then the patriarch. If several patriarchs are present, each receives it after the cardinal who precedes him.

The patriarchs must always stand between two cardinals; likewise, in processions and at Masses, the patriarchs must stand in this manner.

It should be noted that all the candles, both the pope’s and the others’, are given unlit; but as soon as they have been received, they are lit.

Meanwhile, the procession is arranged by the senior of the cardinal deacons, who, facing the procession, says in a loud voice, *Procedamus in pace*; and the choir responds, *In nomine Christi. Amen*.

## XXI. On the Procession

It should be noted that immediately before the distribution of the candles and ashes, before he receives another cope and a gold-worked mitre, he washes his hands.

458

Then the procession begins. The lord pope, dressed in a red cope with pearl-worked borders, having removed the other cope after the distribution of the candles or palms on their respective days, wears a gold-worked mitre during the procession of the candles or palms, which he removes during that procession. He holds a lighted torch—or, on the appropriate day, a palm—in his left hand, and makes the sign with his right as he goes.

All the others in the procession likewise hold lighted torches or palms. They are vested in violet and walk wearing mitres on their heads. The pope proceeds somewhat behind the chapel in procession beneath a canopy, if he is in the City, with four soldiers carrying the canopy with *manipulariis* [perhaps *mappulariis*, “napkin-bearers”].

In their absence, four of the more distinguished men or armed retainers carry it. Thus he proceeds to the railings. First toward the right, then toward the left, he throws candles to the people. He then returns to his chair.

There, while he is seated, a linen cloth is spread over his knees by two chaplains holding it while kneeling, one on the right and the other on the left. He then washes his hands by having water poured over them by the more distinguished person, and so forth.

Some say that the pope never changes his cope in these Processions, but only his gold-fringed mitre without pearls, which he should always wear in Processions and on such days. I certainly believe that this is the case wherever it is without pearls. Therefore there are two copes and three mitres: a white, gold-fringed one with pearls, and another gold-fringed one without pearls, which they carry on weekdays. When these things have been completed, his gold-fringed mitre is removed, and he receives a simple, white, plain garnello mitre. After the Antiphon and Psalm *Nunc dimittis* have been sung, the pope rises in his seat, and, after his mitre has been removed by the cardinal deacon assisting him on [Col. 1284C] the right, the pope sings the Collect; immediately the deacon on the right says, singing, “Let us kneel,” while the cardinal assisting on the left says, singing, “Rise.” Thereafter the pope says, singing, the Collect, “Hear, we beseech you, O Lord, your people.” Then, if the pope is celebrating, after saying the Collect he goes to the vesting room, if there is one; otherwise he goes to his chair, prepared far from the altar on the left side of the altar, and removes the white, plain mitre, and likewise the cope with the stole. He remains in the alb as before, while *Quam dilecta* and the prescribed Collects are read; and while they are being said, he is shod with sandals.

When these things have been completed, he washes his hands and is vested in the sacred and precious white vestments. Likewise all the cardinals and the other prelates, according to their rank: namely, the bishops receive copes, [Col. 1284D] the priests chasubles, and the deacons tunicles and dalmatics, as is customary, and they use them throughout the entire Mass. After the pope has received his vestments, a noble and solemn mitre is handed to him, which he uses throughout the Mass; afterward he comes to the altar. As he approaches, three junior cardinal priests should come to meet him to kiss his mouth and breast, according to their order. Then, before the altar, he makes the confession in the customary manner. Before he makes the confession, his mitre is removed by the deacon on the right; after the altar has been incensed, it is replaced, with the chaplain assisting on the right and the deacon on the left. The subdeacon, meanwhile, should return the maniple to the pontiff while the pontiff makes the confession, kissing his hand.

When this has been done, he should receive the Book of the Gospels and stand beside [Col. 1285A] the step of the altar on the left side. The other ministers should stand behind the pope. After the confession, he says, “O God, turn to us.” The cardinal serving in the office of chaplain should receive from the thurifer the boat with incense, which the thurifer must offer to him between the pontiff and the altar; and the pontiff places incense in the thurible, while the chaplain offers the boat and the thurifer offers the thurible to the pontiff.

After this the pontiff says, “O God, turn to us,” etc., and thus approaches the altar, with two acolytes lifting the front of his vestments slightly. Bending before the altar, he says the Collect *Aufer a nobis*, and kisses the altar and the Book of the Gospels, which the subdeacon should offer to him opened at the place where the Gospel is to be read in the Mass. After the pontiff has kissed it, he leaves it closed upon the altar. After kissing it, the Pontiff signs himself with the sign of the holy cross.

Then the choir begins the Introit of the Mass, and the pontiff turns toward the right side of the altar. Receiving the thurible from the hand of the deacon who will read the Gospel, he incenses the altar, beginning at its middle opposite himself. He first incenses the right side, then the left; afterward, returning from the left side to the right, he incenses the front part of the altar. When the altar has been incensed, he returns the thurible to the deacon, who should kiss his hand both when giving and when receiving it.

The pope is not incensed at the altar, but at his seat by the assisting bishop or cardinal priest, after all the cardinals have first paid him reverence. The deacon, after incensing the pontiff, then incenses the altar all around. First, however, the pope receives the aforesaid deacon to kiss his mouth and breast; afterward he receives all the deacons according to their order. The last deacon prepares the pallium and, beneath it, the front part of the *fanum*; and thus the chaplains and the other deacons lead the pope to his seat. Then the deacon incenses.

After this, he reads the Introit of the Mass upon the altar with the sacristan, if the sacristan is a bishop, or with another bishop who serves him in the office of archpriest. When the pontiff has come to his seat, standing upon the footstool, he says without singing, together with the cardinal, the Introit, “Kyrie, eleison.” The rest is done as it is prescribed when the pope celebrates.

## XXII. Serving the Pope

A note concerning the person who serves the pope whenever he celebrates. It should be noted that in the Mass mentioned above the dean of the cardinal bishops serves the pope in the office of chaplain. In all Masses celebrated by the pope, that same lord cardinal serves the pope in this office. That bishop should sit upon his own faldstool on the right side of the pope’s seat, above the other cardinal bishops, who should also sit on that side.

But note that when a sermon is given, when the Gospel is sung, when the Preface begins—at the words “Throughout all ages”—or when another prelate performs the office before the pope, he goes to sit in his own order and place, unless [Note: [Col. 1285] The expression *papamet*, that is, “the pope himself,” is also used by the author below more than once; so too *pontifexmet* in the preceding book, p. 369.] the pope himself were giving the sermon. In that case he would sit in the order of the cardinal deacons, namely before the one who assists the pope on the right, because [Col. 1286A] the pope would then be seated upon a small chair, almost before the middle of the altar, leaning against the altar.

### 460. How and where the pope should sit when he gives the sermon

If the pope is not celebrating that day, immediately after the candles have been distributed and he has finished the Collect “Hear, we beseech you,” etc., he goes before the altar to make the customary confession, beginning, “I will go in to the altar of God,” together with the one who is celebrating. The celebrant stands on the left, facing the pope, with hands joined, together with his ministers; two cardinal deacons assist the pope, one on the right and the other on the left. The pope also faces the celebrant and is without a mitre.

After the confession has been made and absolution given to the pope, the pope goes to his seat and, standing, says the Introit of the Mass with the cardinals, who always remain before him in the form of a semicircle, with two deacons beside him. Alternatively, one of the assisting non-cardinal bishops may hold the book between his hands. After the *Kyrie* has also been said there, the pope sits in his seat.

If the pope is not celebrating that day, before the confession the cardinals and prelates remove their sacred vestments; afterward all the cardinals remove their vestments, etc., and resume their woolen cloaks. Likewise all the subdeacons, auditors, and chaplains, etc.; the prelates, according to the ancient custom, should remove their vestments after receiving the candles. In modern times, however, they have become accustomed always to accompany the pope in Processions, clothed in sacred vestments and following him, with the cardinals preceding. When the cardinals remove their vestments, they too should remove theirs. [Col. 1286C] It is more proper for the prelates to remain vested throughout the entire Mass if the pope celebrates; if he does not, they should at least remain vested as long as the cardinals retain their vestments.

It should be known that when the Gospel has begun—even if the pope is celebrating—the cardinal deacon assisting on the left receives a lighted candle from the hand of the pope’s soldier or esquire, who likewise stands on the left, and places it in the pope’s hand, kissing that hand when giving and receiving it. The pope holds it lighted, as do the cardinals and all the others, who hold their own lighted candles in their hands until the Gospel has been sung.

When the Gospel is finished, the aforesaid deacon receives the candle from the pope’s hand and returns it, still burning, to the esquire or soldier. The cardinals and the other prelates likewise hand their candles to their attendants to be held [Col. 1286D] until the end of the Mass, just as they held them before the Gospel was read. There is one exception: when the sermon is about to begin, if one is given—which is not customary in modern times—all the candles should be extinguished. Immediately after the sermon has ended, they should be lighted again and held by the pope’s soldier or esquire, and by the attendants of the cardinals and other prelates, until the end of the Mass.

It should nevertheless be known that thicker and larger candles are given to the cardinals than to the others, and also to the prelates; those given to the prelates are smaller than those of the cardinals, though made of the same wax. All the others present at the Mass receive candles of suitable size; [Col. 1287A] afterward the pope’s officials receive somewhat larger ones. The rest is done as is customary in other Masses.

## XXIII. Rubric concerning the Chair of Saint Peter

On the Chair of Saint Peter, neither a sermon nor a Mass is customarily ordered, because they are not in accordance with modern practice, although formerly they were customary. Nevertheless, in the first and second years, Lord Pope Urban VI ordered that they be performed. In the first year the cardinal of Grado gave the sermon; in the second, Cardinal Bonaventure of Padua, an Augustinian, gave it in Saint Peter’s church in the City, while Urban celebrated the Mass at Saint Peter’s.

## XXIV. Concerning the first day of Lent, or Ash Wednesday

On Ash Wednesday, the Wednesday at the beginning of the fast, that is, the first day of Lent, a sermon and Mass are ordered.

On this day ashes are made from the palm and olive branches of the preceding year by the sacristan or by his clerk who has charge of the chapel. According to Lord James Gaetani, they are blessed by the junior cardinal priest, who is vested only in white vestments; vested in a cope, with incense and holy water, he blesses them before the pope leaves his chamber.

Afterward, if the pope is not in the City, Lord Pope, dressed in a red mantle or cope without gold fringes or pearls, and also wearing a white, plain garnello mitre without gold fringes or pearls, comes from his chamber to the chapel and prays in the customary manner before the altar, where a chair with a footstool should be prepared. Then [Col. 1287C] he goes to his seat, decorated with violet velvet cloth by the *primicerius* or *folcarius*. He sits there, and the cardinals then come to pay reverence.

After the customary reverence has been paid to the pope by the cardinals and other prelates, all the cardinals and the other prelates go to receive their vestments: the cardinal deacons receive a cotta, a broad amice, and a chasuble; the cardinal priests likewise receive these and a chasuble; the cardinal bishops and all the other prelates likewise receive violet-colored copes.

After the cardinals and all the other prelates have received their vestments, a linen cloth is spread, which the sacristan should offer, by two chaplains over the pope’s knees. They hold it kneeling, one on the right and the other on the left. A third chaplain or the dean of the subdeacons [lacuna] [Col. 1287D] in a violet-colored chasuble receives a basin with ashes from the hand of the sacristan. Kneeling on the pope’s right, he holds before the pope the aforesaid silver basin containing the ashes to be given to the pope. Two deacons assist in the customary manner, one on the right and the other on the left, both vested.

After the pope’s mitre has been removed by the cardinal deacon assisting him on the right, the dean of the cardinal bishops, if present—or the subdean of the bishops, or the dean of the priests, and so on down the order—standing and saying nothing, places ashes in the form of a cross upon the pope’s head, while the pontiff bows his head and remains seated. Then the same dean, kneeling, places his head between the pope’s knees, and the pope likewise places ashes upon his head, saying, “Remember, man.” He then kisses the pope’s right knee.

It should be noted that if an emperor or king is present, he receives the ashes after the dean, and kisses the pope’s foot rather than his knee. Then all the cardinals—first the bishops, second the priests, third the deacons—and all the other vested prelates kiss the pope’s knee when receiving the ashes; the patriarchs come afterward. But the pope’s chamberlain, notaries, auditors of petitions, and corrector—even if any of them is a bishop or prelate, since they do not customarily come vested but in woolen cloaks—as well as the chaplains, both table-companions and other regular chaplains, who should wear cottas, and the penitentiaries—in short, all the other members of the household, even if one were a king, duke, or count—receive the ashes from the pope kneeling; after receiving them, they kiss the pope’s foot rather than his knee.

It should be known that if a king is present, he receives the ashes after the dean of the cardinal bishops, as stated above. But the sons of kings, if present, receive the ashes in the same manner in which they sit among the cardinals; the patriarchs likewise receive them, as will be said below in its proper place.

After the ashes have been given and the pope’s hands washed, another linen cloth is spread by the acolytes and chaplains. Our lord the pope rises from his seat and, standing there with his mitre removed, says, singing, “The Lord be with you.” Note that “Let us kneel” is not said; rather, he immediately says the Collect, “Grant, we beseech you, O Lord, your protection.” After this Collect has been completed, the pope withdraws and goes to receive his vestments in the vesting room, solemnly prepared by the sacristan and his clerks in black or violet *Indius* color. In modern times the Roman Church uses these three almost as a single color; on this day, however, the pope uses violet or *Indius*-colored vestments.

After receiving them and having his mitre replaced, he comes before the altar. As he approaches, three junior cardinal priests, vested, should come to meet him; he should receive them, according to their order, to kiss his mouth and breast. Then, before the altar, he makes his confession in the customary manner. Afterward he goes to kiss the altar and the book; receiving the thurible from the dean of the cardinal bishops who serves him, he incenses the altar.

After this, and after his mitre has been replaced, the subdeacon stands behind him and holds him by the shoulders with both hands. Then he turns toward the cardinal deacons, [Col. 1288D] who pay him reverence there in the customary manner; and he receives them, according to their order, to kiss his mouth and breast. Everything is then done as is customary in other Masses. Subsequently he goes to his great seat, where, standing with the cardinals, he says the Introit of the Mass and the *Kyrie eleison*.

## XXV. Concerning the Mass and the Collect

It should be noted that, according to Lord James Gaetani, only one Collect should be said in this Mass, although in modern times it has become customary to say three. Also, in the first Collect “The Lord be with you” is said, and not “Peace be with you.”

It should also be noted that in this Mass the Tract *Domine, non secundum peccata nostra* is said. When the verse *Adiuva nos, Deus salutaris noster* is reached, the lord pope, after removing his mitre, kneels in his seat for as long as that verse is sung.

But if the pope is not celebrating and another person is celebrating before him, he should go to the chair prepared before the altar with a footstool; there he remains as long as that verse is sung, with his mitre removed. When it has ended, he should return to his seat with his mitre replaced. Also, after the *Sanctus* has been said, if he is not celebrating, he should immediately go to the same chair and remain there, with his mitre, until the *Agnus Dei*. When “Throughout all ages,” etc., begins, he returns to his seat.

It should be known that in this Mass the Preface of Lent is also said, namely *Qui corporali ieiunio*, and it is said in the ferial tone.

It should also be noted that at the end the Collect over the people, *Inclinantes se*, etc., is said. After the final Collect has been completed and the response “Amen” given, the pope says, “Let us pray”; and the one who read the Gospel, facing the pope, says in a loud voice, “Bow your heads before God.” After the Mass has ended, he again faces the pope and says, “Let us bless the Lord.”

There, before the middle of the altar and facing the people, the lord pope gives the blessing in the customary manner; afterward he goes to his seat and removes his vestments, as is stated for other Masses.

## XXVI. Serving the pope on Processional Days

It should be known that when candles are distributed on this day of Ash Wednesday, on Palm Sunday, and always on Processional days, the dean of the cardinal bishops serves the pope while he distributes them. But [Col. 1289C] after the ashes have been given, the dean of the bishops goes to his seat, after the pope’s hands have first been washed. Then the dean of the priests comes and serves the pope throughout this Mass in the office of chaplain or archpriest.

## XXVII. Concerning Indulgences

It should also be noted that in this Mass, assuming that the pope is not celebrating, seven years and seven quarantines are customarily granted, although some say that they should be granted only when he himself celebrates. Nevertheless, for the sake of greater devotion, seven years are granted.

## XXVIII. Concerning the prelate who serves the pope

Note also that the prelate who serves the pope, both in the present Mass and in solemn Masses in the office of archpriest from the Missal, should be incensed by the subdeacon immediately after the cardinal and all the pope’s assistants. The clerks should afterward give incense immediately after the cardinals and before the ambassador and the patriarch.

## XXIX. Concerning the office of the cardinal deacon when he reads the Gospel on Ash Wednesday

The duties of the cardinal deacon who is to read the Gospel on this day should be noted. While the pope is reading Terce with his chaplains, the deacon goes to his seat and receives a cotta, an amice [Perhaps a broad one], [lacuna] and an alb with cincture, and the stole over his left shoulder. Together with him, the subdeacon, also vested in an alb and maniple, vests the prelate as is customary.

When he has been solemnly vested, before he descends from the chair in the customary manner, the deacon and subdeacon receive chasubles, as do the other cardinals. They should lift them at the front over their arms up to the middle of the chest, so that they hang slightly below the chest in front.

It should be noted that the subdeacon removes his chasuble before reading the Epistle; [464] after saying the Epistle, he receives it again and carries the Missal before the pope, first kissing his foot.

When the singers begin to sing *Domine, non secundum peccata*, the cardinal deacon, having first received the maniple on his left arm from the hand of the chaplain serving him in the aforesaid Mass, rises and removes the chasuble. His ministers and clerks fold it for him in the manner of a stole. He then wears it over his left shoulder, and its ends are fastened on the right side between the cincture. He wears it in this manner [Col. 1290B] throughout the Mass, until he and the subdeacon have received Communion from the pope’s hand and have taken the blood upon the altar, as is customary. Immediately after Communion, he puts on the chasuble in the manner of the other cardinal deacons, and likewise wears it until the pope has given the blessing. After the blessing has been given, he removes the chasuble, and the subdeacon does likewise; they remain in their albs as they were when they vested the pope, and thus they divest the pope. When this has been done, they remove their own vestments.

It should be known that if the pope is not celebrating that day, but another person is celebrating before him, the procedure and all the rites observed in the Procession for receiving the ashes, and the other matters noted above, are to be observed.

## XXX. Concerning the reception of the ashes

It should be noted that if the person who performs the office before the Roman pontiff on this day is a bishop, but not the dean of the cardinal bishops, he should receive the ashes from the pope’s hand after the dean of the cardinal bishops, even if a king is present; the king follows him immediately. The bishop should be dressed in sacred vestments through the chasuble, inclusive, and not in a cope; he receives the ashes wearing a simple white mitre.

## XXXI. When the king receives the ashes

Note that if a king receives the ashes, he should be dressed in sacred vestments and a white mitre.

It should also be noted that if the person who performs the office on this day, on the day of the Purification, and on Palm Sunday is a cardinal, he himself blesses the candles, ashes, and branches, and not the junior cardinal priest. He is vested [Col. 1290D] in sacred vestments through the chasuble, inclusive.

It should also be noted that if that person is not a cardinal but another person—a primate, archbishop, or bishop—he should receive the candles, ashes, and branches before the cardinal deacon, vested in sacred vestments, by reason of the office and the person of the pope whom he represents.

## XXXII. How the patriarch should sit

It should also be noted that if there is a patriarch, who should always sit among the cardinal bishops, he should receive the candles and ashes after the dean of the cardinal bishops. If a king is present, he receives them immediately afterward, before all the others.

It must nevertheless be observed, as the ancient rubric says—and it is correct—that the person who performs the office before the pope, [Col. 1291A] whoever he may be, whether cardinal or not, represents the person of the pope. Therefore, by reason of his office, he should receive the ashes before all the cardinals, immediately after the dean of the cardinal bishops. This rule is now observed only among religious. The cardinal who sits after the king [lacuna]. But what the customary practice is in this matter I shall note in the additions, at least as it has existed in my time.

## XXXIII. How the king should sit

It should be noted that if a king is present, he sits between the dean of the cardinal bishops and the one who serves the pope in the office of chaplain, upon his own bare and low chair.

## XXXIV. Rubric for when the pope does not celebrate on this day

It should also be known that if the pope is not celebrating, after the ashes have been given, his hands washed, and the Collect “Grant us, we beseech you, your protection” completed by him, the pope goes before the altar to make the customary confession with the one who is celebrating. The celebrant stands inclined, with hands joined before his breast, at the pope’s left side, assisted by the two senior deacons, one on the right and the other on the left.

The pope begins, “I will go in to the altar of God.” After the confession has been made, the pope returns to his seat and, standing and without his mitre, says the Introit of the Mass with the cardinals in the customary manner. When it has ended, the pope sits in his seat. All the cardinals then remove their vestments and receive their woolen cloaks; the other prelates, immediately after receiving the ashes, remove their vestments.

## XXXV. Concerning the person who celebrates before the pope

It should be noted that when someone celebrates before the pope on this day, and also at another time when the Mass is that of a weekday, vigil, or Ember Day—whether it is celebrated solemnly, ferially, or privately—the pope, while the priest says the first and last Collects, descends from his great chair and goes to the low chair prepared for him with a footstool. There he remains kneeling, with his mitre on his head, unless for reasons of devotion he wishes to remove it; and he remains thus until the Collects have been said. When they have ended, at the words “Through our Lord,” etc., or “Who live,” he rises and returns to his seat.

It should also be noted that, after he has said the *Sanctus*, he immediately goes to the chair before the altar and remains kneeling there [Col. 1291D] until the *Agnus Dei*.

It should also be noted that when the Collect over the people is said, after “Bow your heads before God” has been said, the cardinal deacon assisting him on the right removes his mitre. When the Collect has been completed, he returns to his seat, and the same cardinal replaces his mitre.

It should also be noted that when the Tract verse *Adiuva nos, Deus salutaris noster* is said, [466] the pope descends from the chair and goes before the altar, as noted above.

It should be noted that while the celebrant says “Throughout all ages” before the *Agnus Dei*, the pope rises and returns [Col. 1292A] to his seat. There he stands on his feet until the celebrant says, “The peace of the Lord”; then his mitre is removed, and he remains bareheaded until the celebrant has received the blood and body. The rest is done as noted above.

It should also be observed that the cardinal who celebrates before the pope on this day does not remove his chasuble when receiving the ashes from the pope. Rather, fully vested, he receives the ashes in the manner described above, although when distributing the candles he should come in a cope, and not merely in a chasuble, by reason of the Procession.

It should also be noted that the chamberlain goes out to the gates and, standing, gives ashes to those who are outside; in his absence, another prelate to whom this has been entrusted does so.

## XXXVI. When the pope is in the City

It should be known that if the pope is in the City on Ash Wednesday, everyone gathers at Saint Anastasia. Before our lord arrives, ashes are made there from the palms of the preceding year and are blessed by the junior cardinal priest, with ministers vested only in white. Then the lord [Note: [Col. 1291] In the title of the following chapter the pope is likewise called *antistes*, and in the text *dominus antistes*.] pontiff goes to that church, accompanied by the entire Curia, and says Sext there, since before descending from the palace he must say Terce.

Afterward blessed ashes are placed upon him by the dean of the cardinal bishops or by the subdean. Then the lord pope himself places ashes upon their heads, saying, “Remember, man.” Afterward the Procession is organized by the dean of the cardinal deacons.

## XXXVII. When the pontiff wishes to proceed on foot

It should be noted that if the lord pontiff wishes to proceed on foot, before receiving the ashes he should put on the Mass vestments through the dalmatic, inclusive. After the imposition of the ashes, he should have his shoes removed by his chamberlains and put on a black or violet chasuble, and proceed in Procession as far as Saint Mary of the Greek School and as far as Saint Sabina, where the station is held, barefoot.

Meanwhile the *schola*, or singers, sing Antiphons along the way; afterward the litanies follow, as they are found in the *Politicus*. When these have ended, the lord pope has his feet washed secretly at Saint Sabina in the sacristy by his chamberlains, subdeacons, and table-companions, with warm water prepared with fragrant herbs by the aforesaid chamberlains; the rugs, benches, and other necessities for this are supplied by the *febrarius* with the couriers.

After his feet have been washed, he is shod with violet sandals without pearls while reading None and *Quam amabilia tabernacula tua, Domine, Deus virtutum*. He is then vested in sacred violet vestments, without pearls; [467] and thus he proceeds to perform the divine offices, as is customary. On this day, and on all the days of Lent, the lord pope is accustomed to sing only one Collect at Mass.

## XXXVIII. Rubric for when the pope is not in the City

But if the lord pope is not in the City, all the clergy and people should gather at the church of Saint Sabina. After Terce has been said, the ashes are blessed by the pontiff [Col. 1293A] or by the priest who is to sing the Mass, in the customary manner, as contained in the Missal.

After the blessing by the pontiff or priest has ended, when the ashes are placed upon the person who celebrates the Mass by another bishop or priest, if one is present, he receives them; otherwise he imposes them upon himself. Then he imposes them upon the clergy and people, saying to each, “Remember, man,” etc. Meanwhile *Emendemus in melius*, etc., is sung.

After the imposition of the ashes has ended, the Collect *Quaesmumus*, etc., is said, as above. Thereafter he proceeds to the altar to perform the divine offices. The same practice is observed in the pope’s chapel when the pope is not celebrating, except that the ashes are imposed upon him and everyone else by another person.

Therefore it should be noted that the pope should never impose ashes upon himself. In the absence of a cardinal, the person who is celebrating should then impose ashes upon himself alone, and the pope should then impose them upon the others.

## XXXIX. Concerning the manner in which the Roman pontiff proceeds

A note concerning the manner in which the Roman pontiff proceeds on penitential and Processional days, in its proper place. In the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Boniface IX, he himself gave the ashes at Perugia, dressed in a cope and mitre without pearls. After giving them, he removed the cope and mitre and resumed his mantle without a mitre; he remained thus throughout the Mass because of the cold.

It should be noted that in the year 1395 Lord Boniface IX gave the ashes. After they had been given, he removed the cope and received the mantle; thus, without a mitre, he stood at Mass because of the cold. Nor did the cardinal deacons sit before him, but in their own places.

The Lord Cardinal of Bologna [Col. 1293C] said the Mass and gave ashes to the pope; immediately afterward the pope gave ashes to him, before all the cardinals. At that time there was no cardinal bishop, and our aforesaid lord pope decreed that this practice should always be observed: that the one who celebrates should impose ashes upon the pope. This occurred in the fifth year of his pontificate, on Saint Matthias’s Day. At that time we observed a weekday, not a feast; but on the Thursday immediately following, a feast was observed.

## XL. Rubric concerning the First Sunday of Lent

On the First Sunday of Lent, a sermon and Mass are ordered. It should be noted that on this day and thereafter, on Sundays through Palm Sunday, Mass is celebrated before the pope only in the presence of the cardinals.

The pope, dressed in a red mantle [Col. 1293D] with gold fringes but without pearls, carries a white, plain garnello mitre without pearls, except on the Fourth Sunday, which will be discussed below. Thus he comes to the chapel and prays in the customary manner before the altar, where a chair with a footstool should be prepared.

After the Collect has been said, the aforesaid chair and footstool are first removed by a clerk or servant of the chapel, and the pope makes the confession with the one who is celebrating. The celebrant should stand on the left beside the cardinal deacon, assisted by two cardinal deacons, one on the right and the other on the left, chosen from the senior members. After the mitre has been removed, the pope begins, “I will go in to the altar of God,” etc.

After the confession has been made, he goes to his seat and says the Introit of the Mass and the *Kyrie eleison*. First all the cardinals pay him reverence [Col. 1294A] before he begins; afterward he sits, and then all the other prelates pay him reverence in the customary manner.

## XLI. That on the Sundays of Lent the dean of the cardinal priests serves the pope in the office of chaplain

It should also be noted that on these Sundays of Lent the dean of the cardinal priests serves the pope in the office of chaplain. He should stand upon the footstool before the deacon who stands on the right, as is noted in its proper place.

It should be noted that, according to Lord James Gaetani, on this Sunday, and on the other Sundays of Lent, only one Collect should be said in the Mass. The Collect *Ecclesiae tuae* should never be said in the pope’s chapel. The reason is that *Deus, omnium fidelium* is always said. These two should not be said together unless they are joined together. Nevertheless, in modern times several have become customary: the first, that of the day; the second, *A cunctis*; the third, *Deus omnium fidelium*; the fourth, *Omnipotens sempiterne Deus, qui vivorum*, etc.

It should also be noted that while the aforesaid first and second—or final—Collects are being said, the pope does not descend from the chair but stands on his feet in his seat; nor is his mitre removed except for reasons of greater devotion.

It should also be noted that the Roman pontiff never descends from his chair while Collects are being said in the Mass, except on vigils, during litanies, and on ferial days.

It should also be noted that when the celebrant begins the first Collect in Lent and Advent, he should always say, “The Lord be with you,” and not “Peace be with you,” except on the Sundays of *Gaudete* and *Laetare*, on which “Peace be with you” is said—even if the pope himself is celebrating.

## XLII. Rubric concerning the removal of the mitre

During the Gospel, the mitre is removed from the pope’s head by the cardinal deacon assisting him on the right. After the Gospel has been said, it is replaced by the same deacon, always with the assistance of the one standing on the left.

The person appointed to do this comes and kisses the pope’s right foot and asks the pope’s blessing. After receiving it, [469] the pope entrusts him with announcing, on the pope’s behalf, to all who are truly penitent and have confessed, who are or will be in a state of grace within eight days, an indulgence of three years and three quarantines.

When the sermon has ended, the deacon who read the Gospel says the *Confiteor* before the pope in the customary manner. After this has ended, the preacher immediately announces the Indulgence. After it has been announced, if the celebrant is a prelate, he quickly descends from the chair or ambo and goes to his low chair, with his mitre replaced. Whether he is a prelate or not, he goes to his place; and the pope, after removing his mitre, says, as though reading, “May he have mercy upon you,” etc., and gives the blessing, signing. The chamberlain or another of the pope’s attendants and household lifts the hem of the pope’s mantle with both hands. Then the celebrant says, “I believe in one God.”

It should nevertheless be noted that in Sunday Masses five years and five quarantines of Indulgence are customarily granted, and on the Fourth Sunday, *Laetare*, seven.

## XLIII. Concerning Indulgences granted at Mass

It should also be noted that the Roman pontiff has never been accustomed to grant seven years except when he himself celebrates the Masses, apart from the Sundays of *Gaudete* and *Laetare*.

After the mitre has been removed, the pope says *Credo in unum* with the cardinals. While he and the singers sing the words “And he was incarnate by the Holy Spirit,” etc., the pope kneels, and his mitre is always removed. The same is done when “Hail, Mary” is said at the beginning of the sermon. [Note: [Col. 1295D] From this it is clear that by the fifteenth century the practice had already become established of prefacing the sermon or discourse with the Angelic Salutation. This may be understood absolutely as referring to the beginning before the exordium, as is still done today in certain places in Italy [Col. 1296D] and Germany, which seems more convenient and appropriate; or as referring to the beginning after the exordium, as among us.]

## XLIV. Concerning the removal of the mitre
[Col. 1295B] The pope’s mitre is also removed while the Sanctus is being said. When it has been said, it is put back on him. It should also be noted that, when the celebrant begins to make the sign of the cross over the bread and wine to be consecrated, the pope goes to the throne prepared before the middle of the altar, with a footstool. When the body of Christ is to be elevated, his mitre is removed. After it has been elevated, he rises and returns to his seat, where he stands with the mitre on his head until the Pater noster is said—“And lead us not [into temptation],” and so forth. Then he descends and goes to the lower throne prepared before the middle of the altar, together with its footstool; there, kneeling on the footstool with the celebrant, he says Laetatus sum. While the celebrant says the three prayers, he always has the mitre on his head. Then, rising, he returns to his seat. When the celebrant says “The peace of the Lord,” and so forth, the mitre is removed from him, and with the cardinal he says Agnus Dei. He then remains without a mitre until the celebrant has consumed the body and blood. After this, the mitre is put back on him, and he keeps it on his head until the end of Mass, when he sings “Blessed be the name of the Lord,” and so forth; and, singing, gives the blessing. Before he says “Blessed be the name of the Lord,” his mitre is removed, and the subdeacon holds the cross before him, so that the crucifix is before the pope’s face. The chamberlain, kneeling before the hem of the pope’s cloak—if he is not a cardinal—gives the blessing. After it has been given, the mitre is put back on him, and he thus returns to his chamber, attended by two cardinal deacons who, as usual, precede him immediately.

It should also be noted that at the end of these Masses the deacon who read the Gospel says Benedicamus Domino, with his face turned toward the altar.

It should also be noted that when a cardinal performs the office of the Mass before the pope, all the cardinals must wait for him until he has removed his sacred vestments and resumed his ordinary dress; then they go with him, following him, to the pope’s chamber. Thereafter, apart from the two deacons who precede the pope, if everyone is unwilling to wait, at least two must wait.

### XLV. On Double Feasts Occurring during Lent

[Col. 1296A]

It should be noted that if any double feast whatsoever—even if it is the feast of a cardinal’s titular church—falls on a Sunday of Lent or Advent, each of which has its own proper history, the feast is in no way celebrated; rather, the Sunday is celebrated, without even a commemoration. The feast is transferred to the following Monday. Regarding other feasts that fall on those Sundays throughout the yearly cycle, observe the rubric of the Breviary noted there at the beginning: “If any feast of nine lessons should occur,” and so forth.

### XLVI. On the Second Sunday of Lent

The sermon and Mass are prescribed for the Second Sunday of Lent; everything else is to be done as above.

### XLVII. On the Third Sunday of Lent

[Col. 1296B]

The sermon and Mass are prescribed for the Third Sunday of Lent; everything else is to be done as above.

### XLVIII. On the Fourth Sunday of Lent, Which Is Called Rose Sunday

The sermon and Mass are prescribed for the Fourth Sunday of Lent, which is called Rose Sunday, or Laetare, Jerusalem. The station is at the Holy Cross. If the pope is in Rome, early in the morning he celebrates his private Mass quietly, unless he wishes to preach; for in that case he would also say Mass. Note this carefully: whenever the Roman pontiff preaches, he must also celebrate Mass, and every other prelate likewise. When the Mass is finished, he enters his chamber [Col. 1296C] and prepares to go to the great Mass.

If the pope is in Rome, he prepares himself in his chamber as usual, with a noble but not costly mitre decorated with gold embroidery; otherwise he would wear a simply gold-embroidered one. But for the procession he wears the noble one with images. Once he has put it on, the chamberlain comes with the golden rose, presents it to the pope while kneeling, and kisses his hand. The sacristan presents balsam and musk, which one of the pope’s chamberlains is to receive; the pope then pours the balsam and musk over the rose. Carrying the rose, he leaves the chamber and goes to his chapel, or, if he is in Rome, to the Holy Cross in Jerusalem. He holds it in his left hand and makes the sign of the cross with the other; he holds it in this way when he makes his confession, even if he is not celebrating. For then, when he begins the Confiteor, he hands the rose to the cardinal deacon who serves him on his right. After the altar has been kissed and incensed, he receives it again from the hand of the aforementioned deacon, after the Introit of the Mass has first been said, and holds it in the same way. If someone else is celebrating before him, he does not release it during the whole Mass, except when he bends his knee before the middle of the altar, at the elevation of the body of Christ, and when Laetatus sum is said; he also releases it while he says those prayers.

Note that whenever he receives and gives the rose, the cardinal deacon must kiss the pope’s hand.

Note that at this Mass, if a king were present and the pope were not celebrating, the king would sit between the first two cardinal bishops. If the pope were performing the office, the king would sit on the pope’s right, near the cardinal bishop who serves the pope, on a low, bare throne without a footstool, as though between that bishop and the subprior of the bishops.

It should be noted that at this Mass, provided that the pope is not celebrating, it is customary to grant seven years and seven forty-day periods of indulgence. When the Mass is finished, the lord pope carries the rose in his hand to his chamber, or, if he is in Rome, to the Lateran palace. As he returns, all the nobles present at the curia follow him. When he has returned to his chamber, if he is outside Rome, the lord pope gives the rose to the noblest person, or to the one he most prefers. That person immediately kneels and kisses the pope’s foot—even if he is a king. The pope then admits him to a kiss on the mouth. After this, the recipient withdraws, accompanied by the two senior cardinal deacons, and rides with them for a short distance through the city, as far as he wishes.

The same practice applies if the recipient is a king or emperor: some of the other cardinals customarily accompany him for a short distance on horseback. He then returns to dine with the pope; after the meal, he rides through the city with his own people, without the cardinals, accompanied by his nobles and princes.

[Col. 1297C] If the pope is in Rome, he carries the aforesaid rose as far as the steps of the Lateran palace, where he had to spend the preceding night. As he dismounts, the prefect of the city, dressed in scarlet or purple and wearing one boot and the other gilded, holds the pope’s stirrup. When the lord pope dismounts, he gives him the golden rose. The prefect, kneeling, kisses the pope’s right foot, and the pontiff admits him to a kiss on the mouth. After this, the pope ascends into the palace, while the prefect immediately rides through Rome in great triumph with the Roman nobles.

It should be noted that the cardinals do not customarily accompany the prefect in Rome, since he has a sufficient retinue.

It should be noted that, before giving the rose, the pope must say a few brief words about the rose’s qualities and properties, since it has a joyful color, a strengthening fragrance, and a pleasing appearance, as stated in the book *Rationale of the Divine Offices*.

In the fourth year of the pontificate of Pope Boniface IX, at Perugia, on this day the rose was carried into the great chapel, and everyone attended the sermon except the pope, because he was ill. A junior cleric of the chamber carried the rose to the Mass and carried it back, and the pope gave the rose in his chamber.

### XLIX. On the Feast of the Annunciation of Blessed Mary at First Vespers

On the day of the Annunciation of the Blessed Virgin Mary, the sermon and Mass are prescribed.

[Col. 1298A] It should be known that when this feast falls during Lent, the pope does not come to First Vespers wearing a cope and mitre, because on the vigil, once Mass has been said, the singers immediately begin Vespers, and the pope remains there dressed as he was while hearing Mass. The cardinals likewise do not customarily come, because Vespers are sung before dinner, unless the feast falls on a Monday. In that case, the papal Vespers are held on Sunday evening; the cardinals begin the antiphons.

It should also be noted that when the feast falls within Holy Wednesday, nothing of the feast is celebrated at that time; rather, it is transferred to the Monday after Quasimodo geniti. On that day the office is celebrated solemnly, and the pope comes to First Vespers wearing a red cope and a gold-embroidered mitre with pearls. The cardinals come, but are not vested.

### L. On the Mass on the Same Day

At this Mass everyone must be vested in white garments. If the feast falls during Lent, early in the morning the pope hears the Mass of the feria. After it has been said, he prepares himself in his chamber as usual; then he goes to the great chapel, where he is vested in sacred white vestments.

It should also be noted that at this Mass, whenever the feast occurs, no prayer is said except one concerning Blessed Mary the Virgin; nothing is said concerning the feria.

### LI. On the Rubric Concerning Collects

For this reason it should be understood that the Roman pontiff has never customarily said more than one collect at great and pontifical Masses, although this is contrary to the rubric, which says that those commemorated at Vespers and Matins must also be commemorated at Mass. Although the pope himself makes commemorations at both Vespers and Matins, he nevertheless never does so at great Masses.

Note that at this Mass the senior of the cardinal bishops serves the pope in the office of chaplain.

When Mass has been completed by the pope and he has given the blessing, he returns, still vested, to his great throne. Standing without a mitre, he begins Vespers by singing Deus in adjutorium meum intende. After the Gloria Patri has been said, the subdeacon begins the first antiphon before him by singing, and the pope also resumes it in song. The same is done before him with the antiphon of the Magnificat. Everything else is begun by the singers up to the prayer, which the pope must say. Once the first antiphon has begun, he removes those vestments and resumes the red cope. All the cardinals and prelates remove their vestments and take up woolen cloaks; the cardinals do not begin the antiphons at Vespers.

The cardinal bishop who serves the pope at Mass does not remove his vestments until Vespers has been said, because at the appointed time he must carry the boat with incense to the pope. The pope is to take a spoonful of incense from it and place the incense in the thurible presented to him by one of the acolytes. The same cardinal must then incense the altar, the chest in which the Body of Christ is kept [Note: [Col. 1299D] See below, chapter 131, on Second Vespers of All Saints, where the chest containing the Body of Christ is incensed; and the Lateran Constitutions below, no. 18.], and afterward the lord pope. He must also hold the book before the pope while he says the aforementioned prayer.

When Vespers has ended—at which two prayers are to be said, one of the feast and the other of the feria, if it falls within the period mentioned—the pope gives the blessing.

It should also be noted that if the cardinals have vestments at Second Vespers of this feast when it is celebrated during Lent, they begin the antiphons, since they did not begin them at First Vespers; nor should such a feast be omitted without solemn Vespers.

Note carefully that the cardinals never begin the antiphons at Second Vespers before the pope, except when the present feast is celebrated during Lent.

The foregoing is done in the manner described when the cardinal deacons do not have copes prepared there. If they do have them, they put them on. Yet in the time of Popes John XXII, Benedict XII, and Clement VI, the cardinal deacons did not customarily put on those vestments at the said Second Vespers, nor did they begin the antiphons, as is customary at First Vespers of other feasts. Instead, the second antiphon was begun by the cardinal deacon on the pope’s right; the third by the cardinal bishop serving at the aforementioned Vespers in those vestments; the fourth by the cardinal priest who sits in his place according to his order; and the fifth by the cardinal deacon assisting the pope on his left. [Col. 1299C] The subdeacon, together with an acolyte, always begins these antiphons before them by singing [Note: [Col. 1300D] That is, by singing them as a prelude for them, as has hitherto been customary.].

### LII. On Passion Sunday, the Fifth Sunday of Lent

On Passion Sunday, which is the fifth Sunday of Lent, the sermon and Mass are prescribed. Everything else is done as is customarily done above on the other Sundays of Lent.

### LIII. On Palm Sunday

On Palm Sunday, Mass and the office are prescribed. No sermon is given on that day, because, according to Lord James Gaetani, the junior cardinal priest must bless the palms and branches of olive trees and other trees, vested as on Ash Wednesday, with blessed water and incense. After they have been blessed, he removes his vestments if he is not to celebrate.

The lord pope celebrates his Mass early in the morning in his private chapel. After it has been said, dressed in a red cope without pearls and a simple white mitre of *garnello*, without gold embroidery or pearls, he enters the chapel or place where the palms are to be distributed. A throne with a footstool should be prepared there, and he sits on it. Then all the cardinals and the other prelates, not yet vested, come to pay reverence as is customary elsewhere: they kiss the hand covered by the cope’s gold embroidery, but neither the knee nor the foot, as above during Lent.

[Col. 1300A] Note that before the pope distributes the branches, all the cardinals and prelates wearing woolen cloaks come to pay reverence to the pope, kissing the hand covered by the cope’s gold embroidery, but neither the knee nor the foot.

It should be known that on this day the Roman pontiffs do not customarily perform the office, although they do give and distribute the branches. Note that the subdeacon must wear a tunicella throughout the entire office, and there is no procession. In modern times, however, there is a papal Mass.

It should also be noted that the person who is to celebrate Mass, if he is a bishop and the pope is not celebrating, first blesses water with salt, as is done on Sundays; then he blesses the branches. While sprinkling the branches with holy water, he says Asperges me, Domine. If the pope is celebrating, the junior cardinal priest performs the blessing.

### LIV and LV. On the Blessing of the Palms

[Col. 1300B]

Note that whoever says the Mass, if he is a cardinal, blesses the branches himself, and not the junior cardinal priest; the same applies to candles and ashes.

It should be known that on this day, if the senior cardinal bishop celebrates before the pope, after the customary reverence has been made by all the cardinals, he, dressed in a cope, gives the pope a palm and immediately receives it back from the pope; then he goes and prepares himself to celebrate. Two palms are given to the pope.

It should also be noted that if a king were present, immediately after him—that is, after the senior cardinal bishop—he receives a palm from the pope’s hands while kneeling, kissing the pope’s right foot and not his knee. After this reverence has been made by the cardinals wearing woolen cloaks [Col. 1300C] and by all the prelates, as on Candlemas, the cardinals and all the prelates put on violet vestments: the cardinal bishops put on surplices, broad amices, and copes; the cardinal priests likewise put on the aforementioned vestments and planets, not copes; and the other prelates likewise put on violet copes, but not planets.

Once these vestments have been received, a cloth is prepared, which the sacristan is to provide. It is spread over the pope’s knees by two chaplains assisting at his sides, one on the right and one on the left, who hold the cloth while kneeling; the two senior cardinal deacons also assist the pope in the customary manner.

Then the senior cardinal bishop—or, if he is absent, the subprior of the cardinal bishops—removes his mitre and, standing on his feet while the pope sits on his throne wearing his mitre, gives the pope another, more beautiful palm branch, saying nothing, and kisses his hand. The pope immediately hands it to one of his household servants for safekeeping. The senior or junior bishop then kneels there, receives the palm branch from the pope’s hand, and kisses the pope’s right knee. The same is done successively by all the cardinals in their order; then all the vested prelates, with their mitres removed, kneel, receive the palm branch from the pope’s hand, and kiss his knee, dressed in violet copes.

The pope’s chamberlain, notary, auditor of disputed cases, [Col. 1301A] and corrector—even if any of them are bishops or archbishops, since they are not accustomed to be vested but only wear woolen cloaks—and all other unvested prelates, as well as the chaplains, both table companions and the pope’s other chaplains, who are specifically to be table companions, wearing *cottas*; also the penitentiaries; in short, all other members of the household, including laymen, and anyone else not belonging to the household, even if he were a king, kneel and receive palms and branches of other trees from the pope’s hand. After receiving them, they kiss the pope’s right foot, not his knee.

It should be noted that only one prayer is said at this Mass. When the lord pope is about to begin it, he says Dominus vobiscum, not Pax vobis; afterward he says the prayer.

It should also be noted that if the pope celebrates, the senior cardinal bishop serves him at this Mass in the office of chaplain, holding the book. If the pope does not celebrate, the senior cardinal priest serves him in the office of chaplain.

It should also be noted that if patriarchs are present, they receive a palm branch after the first cardinal, provided that they are wearing copes. If a king is present, they receive palms after the cardinal who stands and after the king, so that one cardinal always precedes the patriarch, successively in this manner.

Note that after the branches have been distributed, the pope removes his cope and mitre and receives another cope with pearls and a gold-embroidered mitre with pearls.

[Col. 1301C] Note that if the pope were to celebrate today, he ought to wear sacred vestments of violet or indigo, without pearls, sandals without pearls, a simple, plain mitre of *garnello*, and gloves without pearls. The fact is, however, that in modern times they customarily wear a solemn and costly mitre and costly gloves; everything else is simple.

### LVI. Here the Singers Begin to Sing “Hosanna to the Son of David”

It should be known that after the first cardinal has received the palm from the pope’s hands, the singers sing Hosanna Filio David together with all the other antiphons, as they appear in the Missal. Meanwhile the procession is arranged by the senior cardinal deacon. Once the procession has been arranged as above on Candlemas, the cardinal deacon assisting the pope on the left says in a loud voice, Procedamus cum pace, and the choir responds in a loud voice, In nomine Christi. Amen.

### LVII. Here the Procession Moves

The procession then moves forward. First come the armor-bearers with their rods, before the subdeacon carrying the cross. The subdeacon must be dressed in a violet or indigo tunicella; around him are two candle-bearers with lights and one acolyte with the thurible and incense.

Note that when the pope rises from the throne, the four most distinguished nobles present raise a cloth over him with poles and with the poles’ corners at the top [Note: [Col. 1301D] We call it an umbrella or canopy.]. The pope always remains beneath the cloth until he reaches the collect, which he says after the distribution of the palms. A cardinal according to his order, and the patriarchs, always go before him.

When the pope has left the dining hall or chapel and is in the portico leading to the great chapel, he goes to a window overlooking the palace’s great square. There he throws palm branches, olive branches, and branches of other trees to the people.

When he reaches the chapel entrance, the singers outside sing Gloria, laus, and so forth, while those inside respond. The door must then be closed, and all sing as prescribed in the Roman Missal. The lord pope does not strike the door with the cross, as secular people customarily do; rather, once the office just described has been completed, the door is opened.

Then the lord pope, with the cardinals and prelates, enters the chapel in procession and, as usual, prays briefly before the altar, where a throne with a footstool should be prepared. After praying, he rises and goes as far as the chapel screen on the right-hand side. There he throws olive branches and leaves to the people through the openings in the screen. Afterward he goes to the great throne prepared far from the altar, which should be covered with violet cloth. With his mitre removed, standing facing the altar and with a cardinal bishop holding the book before him, he says the prayer appointed in the Missal.

### LVIII. On the Pope’s Going to the Altar and the Cardinals’ Meeting Him

He then goes to the throne prepared far from the altar and there, as usual, receives violet vestments. The cardinal deacon who is to recite the Passion prepares the pope. While preparing him, that cardinal deacon wears only a surplice, amice, white silk garment, girdle, and stole; but once the deacon himself has been prepared, the pope receives a violet planet in the manner of the other cardinal deacons.

Once the pope has been prepared and the aforementioned mitre has been put back on him—a simple white mitre of *garnello*, not a noble one—he proceeds to the altar in procession, attended as usual by the two senior cardinal deacons. As he goes, three junior cardinal priests meet him midway, and he receives them according to their order with a kiss on the mouth and breast. At times, if he himself celebrates, the pope customarily wears the precious mitre during this Mass.

Before the altar he then makes his confession as usual. When he says Misereatur, the subdeacon [Col. 1302D] hands him the maniple, kissing his hand, before he says Deus tu conversus, and so forth. The cardinal bishop who serves him presents the incense to him as customary; the pope kisses the altar and the Gospel book. He then turns to the cardinal deacons and receives them in their order with a kiss on the mouth and breast. The last of them places the fanon (fanum), beneath his pallium, for him, as is regularly done at other Masses.

He then goes to his seat. Standing there, he says the Introit with the cardinals, except for the one who is to say the Gospel, who remains at the altar with the sacristan and subdeacon. Everyone reads the Introit and Kyrie eleison at the altar, [Col. 1303A] and thereafter the pope proceeds with the Mass as is customarily done elsewhere.

Note that on 15 April in the year of Our Lord 1375, on the aforementioned Palm Sunday, the lord Pope Gregory XI performed the office and wore all the vestments described above. He also wore gloves and a precious mitre. It should also be noted that a footstool is placed before him while the Passion is read; on it the palm is placed if he does not wish to hold it in his hands.

### LIX. On the Subdeacon’s Wearing a Tunicella in the Procession

It should also be noted that the subdeacon wears a tunicella in the procession, not a planet. It should further be noted that after he has incensed the altar, but before he receives the cardinal deacons with a kiss, the mitre is put back on him by the person who is to recite the Passion or Gospel. He must wear it until he is solemnly vested; he then immediately removes it and receives a violet planet, which he removes before the Epistle and puts on again after the Epistle has been read.

It should also be noted that the pope does not give his palm to anyone, but carries it to his chamber and has it kept there.

Note that if the pope does not perform the office today, he must kneel before the altar when Et incarnatus est, and so forth, is said, before the elevation of the body of Christ, and when Laetatus sum is said. He must always hand the palm branch to the cardinal deacon assisting him on his right, and that deacon must always kiss the pope’s hand both when receiving and when handing it back.

[Col. 1303C] It should be noted that all the foregoing was restored by the lord Pope Gregory XI in Rome, at Saint Peter’s, in the year of Our Lord 1377. It should be known that today the Preface Qui salutem humani generis is said. It should also be known that all the foregoing was observed by the lord Pope Urban VI in Rome, at Saint Peter’s, in the years 1381 and 1382. On that occasion it was determined that whatever comes upon the altar belongs to the chaplains, as the rubric concerning the manger on the night of the Lord’s Nativity says.

### LX. When the Cardinal Deacon Sings the Passion

When the Tract is being sung before its last verse, the cardinal deacon who is to recite the Passion first receives the maniple from the hand of the chaplain serving him at Mass, rises, and removes his planet. He is then given a planet folded in the manner of a stole, which he wears over his left shoulder. The ends of the planet are fastened at the right side, almost behind him. He holds the planet in this manner while reciting the Passion and throughout the whole Mass, until he and the subdeacon have received Communion. Immediately after Communion, he himself puts on the planet in the manner of the other cardinal deacons.

When the Tract has ended, the aforementioned cardinal deacon who is to recite the Passion kisses the pope’s foot as usual. Returning to the altar, he kneels before it and says quietly Munda cor meum, and so forth. Rising, he takes the Gospel book from the altar and carries it before his breast, so that the panel of the book bearing the crucifix can be seen by the people. He does not ask the pope’s blessing but goes directly to the pulpit, covered with a cloth, and there, without lights or incense and without Dominus vobiscum, begins absolutely: “The Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ.” The response Gloria tibi, Domine is not given; he then continues the Passion in the customary manner.

When that deacon says in the Passion the words “he gave up the spirit,” the pope, the deacon himself, and everyone else immediately kneel facing God toward the altar. They remain kneeling for the length of time in which the Pater noster could be said once. Then he rises and the deacon continues the Passion in his manner.

When he reaches the passage “On the following day,” the cardinal deacon turns toward the pope at that same place and, standing with his head deeply bowed, but not kneeling, quietly asks him for the blessing, saying Jube, domne, benedicere. Once the pope has given the blessing, two candlesticks with lighted candles are carried to the cardinal deacon by acolytes or auditors, as is customary for the Gospel. Incense is also brought, previously blessed by the pope and presented by the cardinal bishop who serves him in the office of chaplain, together with an acolyte. The same acolyte presents the thurible to the deacon, who incenses the book. After incensing it, he returns the thurible to the acolyte and makes the sign of the cross with his thumb over the Gospel and, as usual, over himself on his forehead, lips, and breast.

He then continues the remainder of the Passion, namely, from the aforementioned passage “On the following day,” and so forth, to the end of the Gospel. When this remainder has been completed, the same cardinal deacon kisses the aforementioned passage. The book is then carried by the subdeacon to the pope for him to kiss. After this, the cardinal serving him in the office of chaplain incenses the pope with three swings, kneeling on the first step if the pope himself is celebrating; otherwise he incenses him while standing and bowing deeply. Afterward, the pope begins Credo in unum Deum and proceeds as is regularly customary at other Masses.
