It should be noted that as soon as the Passion begins, the cardinal deacon assisting the pope on his left receives the palm branch from the hand of the pope’s knight or household servant and places it in the pope’s hand, kissing that hand. The pope holds it, while the cardinals likewise hold their own branches and the other prelates hold palm branches and branches of other trees in their hands, until the Passion has been completed.

The aforementioned cardinal deacon receives the palm branch from the pope’s hand and hands it to the pope’s aforesaid knight or household servant. The cardinals and the other prelates likewise hand their branches to their servants to hold until the end of Mass.

It should be known that there is no sermon at this Mass. When the Passion has ended, Credo in unum Deum begins, after the book has first been kissed. At the end of Mass, the cardinal deacon who read the Passion says Benedicamus Domino, with his face turned toward the altar. After the pope has given the customary blessing, the senior cardinal bishop who serves him at Mass in the office of chaplain announces the indulgence by the pope’s mandate and authority, namely, seven years and seven forty-day periods. While the indulgence is being announced, the cardinal deacon who recited the Passion removes his planet and, dressed in white like a deacon, goes to the pope to undress him, that is, to remove his vestments and then put on him the stole, cope, and mitre.

The deacon then removes his own vestments, and all the other prelates likewise remove theirs and resume their woolen cloaks. The pope, after removing his sacred vestments, dressed in a red mantle and with the aforementioned mitre put back on him, goes to his chamber, attended as usual by the two senior cardinal deacons, one on the right and the other on the left.

Note that in the year of Our Lord 1388, in Rome, the lord Pope Urban VI did not perform the office on Palm Sunday because he had not yet been crowned. He did, however, give palms [Col. 1305B] and branches and attended Mass wearing a red cope and white mitre. The Florentine cardinal said that Mass in the great chapel. Thus those three Masses of Holy Week were also celebrated by the cardinals in the lord pope’s presence, as described above.

### LXI. On Monday and Tuesday of Holy Week

On Monday there is no papal Mass.

On Tuesday our lord hears the great Mass in his small chapel. One of the singers celebrates it and reads the Passion.

### LXII. On Wednesday

The same observance is followed on Holy Wednesday.

It should be noted, however, that if pilgrims are present, the pope customarily grants the people an indulgence by special favor after Mass. At that time he is dressed in a red cope [Col. 1305C] without pearls and a simple white mitre. The place where he gives the blessing, or the antechamber, is prepared for him.

First he comes wearing a scarlet cloak with its hood on his head, without a mitre. He thus comes to Matins and remains with the hood not extended over his forehead but folded back. This occurred at Florence in the time of Eugene IV. The same is done on Thursday for the blessing.

It should also be noted that in the evening, at the appointed hour, he comes to hear the office in the chapel simply dressed in a red cloak with the hood over his head—not doubled back as on other days, but merely extended over his eyes.

Note that on these three days, after the office, the pope must not give the blessing, and the cross is not carried before him.

It should also be noted that on these three days the cardinals customarily come in the evening to hear the office in the pope’s chapel, not because they are commanded to do so, but freely and voluntarily, out of devotion.

It should also be noted that on these three days the Roman pontiffs do not customarily recite the office with their bishops and communities while Matins is being said. They must nevertheless recite the office devoutly and afterward say it in their chamber with their chamberlains.

On Wednesday evening, at the appointed hour, the lord pope comes to the office of Matins wearing a scarlet cloak with its hood extended over his forehead, not folded back, and without a mitre.

[Col. 1306A] It should be known that on these three days, and whenever the pope comes to the chapel in a cloak and hood, the cross is not carried before him.

In the evening, for the office of Matins, the lord pope comes to the chapel wearing a closed cloak of red scarlet, lined with ermine, closed from the middle of the breast upward and open below. He always keeps the hood over his head. Without a mitre, he sits on a bare throne. The cardinal deacons do not sit at his feet during these three Matins services, nor does he give the blessing at the end of Matins.

### LXIII. On Holy Thursday: The Mass and the Office of the Chrism

On Holy Thursday, the day of the Lord’s Supper, only Mass is prescribed; there is no sermon today. [Col. 1306B] By right, the Roman pontiffs customarily first give the people an indulgence, but by favor this is done on Wednesday after Mass.

It should be known that in the first year after their coronation, the Roman prelates customarily prepare the sacred chrism, perform the Mandatum, and make the Agnus Dei. [Note: So below, in chapter 88, on the Saturday in Albis, when Agnus Dei are given; and in the following chapter, two Agnus Dei, and shortly afterward three Agnus Dei. Add chapter 90.] Note each matter in its proper place; this is never done more frequently than once every seven years, since many observances must then be carried out.

In the year, therefore, in which the sacred chrism is actually prepared, very early in the morning, around sunrise, our lord the pope comes to the iron screen to give the people an indulgence. He is dressed in a red cope with gold embroidery and pearls, [Col. 1306C] a mitre, and a stole with pearls in the consistorial manner. After giving the indulgence, he removes his vestments and hears Mass privately. When it is finished, he confesses his sins.

[Col. 1306C] When the short Mass has ended, he resumes the aforementioned vestments. All the cardinals, dressed in sacred white vestments according to their order—namely, bishops in copes, priests in chasubles, deacons in tunicles and dalmatics—and the other prelates in copes, receive seven candles if there are general processions, so that the holy chrism may be consecrated. Otherwise, the holy chrism, accompanied by two candles and a processional cross, is carried to the place where processions are customarily proclaimed. There he sits on a throne prepared with a noble white cloth; and all the cardinals and prelates sit in their places wearing mitres, although beforehand the cardinals make a reverence.

It should also be noted that each cardinal and prelate who is vested holds a lighted taper of ordinary wax, which the master of ceremonies gives him; and the pope [Col. 1306D] holds two pounds of almost-white wax, which they throw down at the anathemas.

### LXIV. On the Reading of the Process

It should also be noted that the subdeacon reads the Process in Latin, dressed in a deacon’s vesture, while the junior cardinal deacon repeats the same words clearly and intelligibly in the language spoken in that place. When these have been read, the pope makes the sign [of the cross] and says, “We anathematize,” or, “Let us do so.” He throws his candle downward, and all the others throw down their candles, but not the candle-bearers or acolytes, who remove them from the candelabra, since they return in procession as they came. Finally the papal sacristan receives them. Immediately there, the cardinal deacon [Col. 1307A] who stands at the pope’s left says, “I confess to God,” etc. The pope gives the customary blessing. After it has been given, the junior cardinal deacon announces, from the pope’s hand, an indulgence of seven years and seven quadragenas. Thus all proceed in procession to the great chapel, or wherever the office is to be celebrated that day. After making a prayer before the altar, he goes to the vesting room and puts on sacred white vestments and a solemn mitre, also adorned with pearls. He then proceeds to Mass in the customary manner.

Thus, on Thursday in the Lord’s Supper, the sacrifice of the sacred body and blood of Jesus Christ our Lord is celebrated.

### LXV. On the Ampullae

Early on this day, the mansionarii, the sacristan, and the chapel clerics assigned for this purpose prepare everything necessary for the consecration of the chrism, [Col. 1307B] namely three silver ampullae, though not of equal size, since the largest must be for the holy chrism. They are filled with the purest oil. The largest ampulla, which is to contain the chrism, is covered with the finest white silk cloth; the other two are covered with a different silk cloth. Nevertheless, the cloth must be so thin that the ampullae can be seen by the pope and the others.

At the third hour, the lord pope, dressed in a red mantle and wearing a mitre embroidered with gold and also adorned with pearls, leaves his chamber and goes to the chapel. [482] Before the altar there must be a throne with a footstool prepared, where he prays for a while, as is customary. Then he goes to another throne prepared far from the altar. There he receives the white vestments, and all the cardinals and prelates receive their vestments according to custom: the bishops copes, the priests chasubles, [Col. 1307C] and the deacons tunicles and dalmatics, out of reverence for the chrism. The pope, now dressed in a dalmatic, sits on his throne. The larger ampulla, containing oil, is presented to him by the acolytes, and the balsam by the chamberlain or the sacristan. The pope mixes the balsam with the oil without saying anything; it is thoroughly mixed and prepared. All the ampullae—that is, the other two—remain there, covered, on the table and are carefully guarded until they are carried to the altar. After the reading, the pope receives the chasuble, gloves, and all the other vestments, as is customary. There must be twelve vested subdeacons, without the senior subdeacon.

Afterward, having washed his hands, the pope, dressed in the chasuble and wearing the solemn mitre on his head, proceeds with the bishops, priests, deacons, acolytes, and all the orders. [Col. 1307D] There must be seven candelabra in the procession, together with the cross, the Gospel book, and the ampulla containing the chrism; the others remain there.

Note that if the holy chrism were not consecrated today, there would be only two candelabra in the procession. It should also be noted that every year the holy chrism must be consecrated with the purest and cleanest olive oil, and that three drops of the finest balsam are added. The bishop must not mix these with the oil himself; rather, this is to be done by others, and not by the pope except once every seven years, nor by anyone else in his presence, as noted above.

The thurible, always with incense, is carried, and they proceed in procession to the altar with the ampulla. After the confession and reverence, as customary, the pope ascends his throne. When the altar has been incensed, the ampulla is returned to its place between the other two. Meanwhile the singers sing the Introit of the Mass without “Gloria Patri”; when the verse has ended, the Introit is repeated. Then “Lord, have mercy” is sung. When this has ended, the lord pope begins “Glory to God in the highest.” In the prayer the pope says, “Peace be with you.” In this Mass “I believe in one God,” etc., is also said, and the Mass continues in its proper order.

Note that ordinarily there is no sermon at this Mass, unless the pope wishes to conduct a Process against someone in particular. General Processes may also be held then. If the pope does not wish to preach that sermon, the sacristan, at his command, assigns it to one of the cardinal bishops or priests, since deacons never preach in the pope’s presence, [Col. 1308B] or to another prelate or a master of theology.

Note that abbots do not ordinarily preach, nor doctors of decrees or of law, but only prelates and masters of theology; nowadays, however, abbots do preach.

After the lord pope enters to celebrate the sacrifice, he consecrates two Hosts, one for himself and the other for Good Friday. After the elevation of the body of Christ, or after the Sanctus if convenient, one of the acolytes leads the junior cardinal deacon, together with several subdeacons. One of these subdeacons [483] carries the cross, preceded by an acolyte with the thurible and incense, without lights. Thus they proceed in procession to the chapel of Saint Thomas, or Saint Gregory, or wherever the ampullae containing the chrism and the oil are kept. The aforementioned cardinal [Col. 1308C] deacon takes the ampulla containing the chrism, and two subdeacons take the other two, containing the exorcized oil and the oil for the sick, carrying them on their left arms. They return afterward in the same manner in which they came.

The lord pope, or the one who consecrates the holy chrism or celebrates on that day, before saying “Per quem haec omnia,” descends to the seat or throne prepared before the altar, facing the altar. The subdeacon carrying the ampulla of the oil for the sick presents it to the supreme pontiff for blessing. The pope says in a clear voice, “I exorcize you, most unclean one,” etc. When these blessings have been completed, the pope returns to the altar and says, “Through whom [you make] all these things.”

Note that when this sacrifice has been completed, only the pontiff receives Communion at the altar, without ministers and not with a reed; rather, on that day and on Friday of the Passion he receives himself only with the chalice, and places that fourth part in the chalice. After he has communicated, he places the chalice on the altar and the paten beside it, with the body of our Lord Jesus Christ; reserving it until Friday, he is to receive from that sacrifice, and both are covered with a clean linen cloth.

After receiving the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ from the chalice and without a reed, but before washing his hands, the papal sacristan presents to him, with great reverence, the chalice containing the reserved body of the Lord—not the chalice in which he celebrated, but only a large gold one—covered with a linen cloth and [Col. 1309A] with gold clasps. One end hangs from his left arm, and in his right hand he carries the chalice covered with the other end. Reverently he places the aforementioned chalice near the pope, about the middle of the altar, with another silk cloth, with which the chalice containing Christ’s body is covered.

Note that before the lord pope washes his fingers, he places Christ’s body with great reverence inside the aforementioned chalice, then puts the corporal cloths over the chalice—the smaller part of the corporals—and places the paten upon the corporal, and over the paten the end of that linen cloth. Immediately afterward he washes his fingers inside the chalice with which he celebrated and drinks what is in it. Before he washes his hands in the pope’s large basins, the pope himself, or the cardinal bishop who serves him at Mass, takes the aforementioned chalice containing Christ’s body, covered in this manner, with another end of the cloth hanging over his [Col. 1309B] left shoulder. Holding the chalice with both hands around its middle, he carries it to the small cabinet in which it is kept until the following day. Lights, the cross, and incense precede it in procession and devotion. After it has been placed there, he kneels and incenses Christ’s body. This done, he returns to the altar and washes his hands as usual.

### LXVI. On the Office of the Chrism

Afterward, if the pope is consecrating the holy chrism, he ascends the throne prepared before the altar, facing the altar. Immediately two acolytes carry the wrapped ampullae on their left arms, enclosed in a fine white silk cloth, so that they can be seen through the middle of the cloth, that is, through its central portion and above it. The junior cardinal deacon assisting the pope takes one ampulla, mixed with balsam, and presents it to the pope, holding it wrapped in silk on his left arm. Then the pope breathes upon it three times. All the bishops assisting there, dressed in sacred vestments, and the priests as well, whether cardinals or not, also breathe upon it. This done, the pope says without chant: “The Lord be with you. I exorcize you, creature of God,” etc.

After this blessing, all the cardinal bishops and priests salute the holy chrism after the pope, according to their order. The following order must be observed: first, on the pope’s right side, the cardinal bishops, followed by the cardinal priests; the patriarchs among the cardinal bishops; the cardinal deacons at the pope’s sides, here and there, according to their order, on the left side; then the archbishops, bishops, and cardinal priests, vested according to their order, breathing upon and saluting it after the cardinal bishops. The archbishops and bishops must precede the cardinal priests, since the consecration of the holy chrism belongs or pertains only to bishops. The cardinal priests salute after the bishops. In saluting, each bows his head and says three times, “Hail, holy chrism”; after the salutation, each immediately kisses it once.

When the bishops and priests have saluted and kissed the chrism, the pope blesses the ampulla of oil brought forward in the order given above. The pontiff likewise breathes upon it three times, but silently; all the cardinal bishops and priests, as well as the other bishops, breathe upon it three times. Here the order between the cardinal priests [Col. 1310A] and the non-cardinal bishops is changed. While the others breathe upon the ampullae, the pontiff sits; but when he salutes, all the others stand as well. Then, rising, he says without chant: “The Lord be with you,” etc. “I exorcize you, creature of oil,” etc.

After this blessing, all the cardinal bishops and priests salute the holy chrism in their order. In saluting, they bow their heads, saying, “Hail, holy chrism,” and kiss the ampulla. When all the bishops and priests have saluted the chrism, they must immediately salute the oil in the same manner. The pope salutes the chrism and immediately afterward the oil, saying, “Hail, holy oil.” Each of the others must say the same.

Afterward the ampullae are carried back in procession, as [Col. 1310B] they were brought, to the sacristy or to the place appointed by the sacristan, where they are to remain. Then the same sacristan distributes to each person whatever is due and appropriate. The pope communicates in his great throne those who wish to receive Communion. Nevertheless, the intact offerings are reserved by the cardinal deacon, as is customary; likewise, the entire body of the Lord is reserved for Good Friday. The blood of the Lord is consumed; only the pope drinks it from the chalice and without a reed. Those who receive Communion do not drink it.

Note that neither the deacon nor the subdeacon receives Communion today, unless perhaps they wish to communicate out of devotion; in that case, they communicate before the others, but do not drink the blood. Nevertheless, this is not customary. The kiss of peace is not given. “Agnus Dei” is sung, and the Communion is “Dominus Jesus Christus.” [Col. 1310C] [485] Then the pope returns to the altar and says this prayer: “Refreshed.” When it has been completed, the deacon says, “Go, the Mass is ended.”

### LXVII. If the Pope Does Not Wish to Perform the Mandatum

Note that if the pope does not wish to perform the Mandatum, as follows below, or if the cardinals do not dine with him on this day, then immediately at the end of Mass, after the pope has given the blessing and the cardinal bishop who served him at Mass has announced the indulgence, the pope and all the cardinals there in the chapel remove their vestments. Meanwhile the singers sing Vespers. At the end of Vespers, while the psalm “Miserere mei, Deus” is being said, the pope goes to the throne prepared before the altar with a footstool. There, kneeling, he says the aforementioned psalm by reading it with the others, together with the prayer “Respice,” [Col. 1310D] etc., reading it without “qui tecum,” etc. Then he rises and goes to his chamber.

### LXVIII. On the Selection of the Poor When the Mandatum Is Performed

On the same day after dinner, the pope was unable to wash the feet of the poor. Instead, the patriarch of Grado, the confessor, at the pope’s command, washed the feet of the poor in the small chapel. He was dressed in a rochet, amice, surplice, and cope, with a white mitre. He heard the Gospel, which was sung with lights, the cross, and incense, according to custom. When it had been sung, the singers began to sing; and he, having removed the cope, girded with a linen cloth and wearing a mitre on his head, began to wash the feet. When this was finished, he said the prayer, and the cardinal chamberlain gave florins together with a carlino. He refused to give the pieces of cloth for wiping the poor men’s feet, except two in all, but took everything back with him; and this was wrong, says the gloss.

Note what is done when the holy chrism is consecrated and the Mandatum of almsgiving is performed. After everything mentioned above has been completed in its proper order and Mass has ended, as stated earlier, the pope, dressed in the vestments in which he celebrated, goes to a place adjoining the chapel or church in which he celebrated. All the cardinals accompany him according to their order, as do the other chaplains and subdeacons who attended Mass, vested as they were. In the place just mentioned the pope removes his pallium and chasuble, then sits on a faldstool, keeping his feet on a footstool. He puts a maniple upon his shoulders, with the fanon placed on his head and a white mitre set upon it. The sacristan spreads a cloth over his knees, which two acolytes must hold, one on the right and the other on the left.

According to Lord Jacobus Gaietani, the pope’s cardinal chamberlain must then hand the pope, in a large silver bowl or in basins, the grossi and coin designated for the clerical allotment (presbyterium). The chamberlain must have before him a large table covered with a cloth, on which such coins are placed, and clerks of the chamber and two merchants must assist him. The chamberlain and the clerks of the chamber must wear surplices and cassocks.

Afterward the cardinals come, each according to his order, alone, carrying their mitres in their hands, though with the mitres open. They kneel before the pope, and the supreme [Col. 1311C] pontiff gives and places in the mitre of each of them, as the presbyterium, thirteen silver Tournois grossi. [486] Immediately after each cardinal has received the presbyterium from the pope in his mitre, he kisses the pope’s right knee. Thus each proceeds according to his order.

### LXIX. On the Mandatum Performed by the Pope on That Day

After the presbyterium has been given by the pope as stated, the pope himself performs the Mandatum, with twelve subdeacons wearing rochets and surplices. The chamberlains carry a basin or tub and place it before him. The pope himself is girded with a linen cloth; according to Lord Jacobus Gaietani, the pope has in his hands a small arm-rest prepared for this purpose, with a clean linen cloth before him. All these things must be prepared by the treasurer or by the brothers of the Pignotta. [Col. 1311D] The twelve subdeacons remain barefoot in some remote place.

The pope’s two ushers, or armor-bearers, carry each of the subdeacons before the pope. The ushers or servants customarily hold their feet upon their hands while they are carried. The pope, sitting, washes each one’s feet with warm water, which the chamberlains must pour. He immediately dries the feet with the linen cloth and kisses each man’s right foot. According to the statement of Lord Jacobus Gaietani, he gives each of them two solidi. After the pope has washed their feet, they must be carried back in the same manner by the same ushers or servants to their places—that is, wherever they were taken from.

The singers do not sing Vespers afterward. Rather, the pope’s chaplains say Vespers by reading them before the pope, beginning the antiphon “I will take the cup of salvation,” etc. After the psalms have been said, the Chapter is not said; instead, the pope begins the antiphon for the Magnificat to be sung, namely, “While they were at supper,” if they have completed the Mandatum at that time. Otherwise, the singers do everything.

Note also that in modern times it is not observed that the pope begins that antiphon for the Magnificat, nor any other, except at the Vespers of the Mandatum. When everything has been completed, the pope says by reading, kneeling, “Respice, quaesumus, Domine,” etc., as is more fully contained in the Roman Breviary’s office for this day.

When these things have been completed, the pope, dressed in the manner described above, [Col. 1312B] proceeds in procession to his chamber, accompanied by all the vested cardinals who are to attend the Mandatum, dressed as they were at Mass and seated in their places according to their order while the pope performs the Mandatum. The aforementioned chaplains of the pope also carry lighted candles with the cross before the pope and before the cardinals.

### LXX. Rubric on Eating at the Lord’s Supper

On the day mentioned above, the lord pope, prepared as noted earlier, is solemnly led to a richly prepared table by the two senior cardinal deacons. He sits there, with a cardinal bishop giving him water, while the two aforementioned cardinals, one on his left and the other on his right, hold a cloth. The one on the right also holds the pope’s ring while he washes.

[Col. 1312C] It should also be noted that the aforementioned three cardinals, during the first and second washing of hands and the blessing of the table, must be without mantles and mitres while they serve the pope. During the thanksgiving they resume their mantles and mitres in their proper places. After the pope has performed the first washing of his hands and the blessing of the table, which will be discussed more fully below, at the second washing all go to sit down. Then all the cardinals, once seated, wash their hands over the table in their little dishes, and serve one another, as will be said below regarding the other washing.

Note that while the pope eats, he remains dressed as stated above, including the dalmatic. He has the red mantle over his shoulders, the fanon or orale on his head, and the mitre embroidered with gold over the fanon; he wears a precious non-pontifical ring on his finger and sandals on his feet, as at Mass, except for the gloves, pallium, and chasuble.

All the cardinals, both secular and religious, wear cassocks without surplices, with only subtile garments or rochets, simple garnello mitres on their heads, and brunetto mantles over their shoulders. The secular cardinals wear rose-colored brunetto mantles; the religious cardinals wear mantles of the color of their order. Thus dressed they eat, and all the other prelates are similarly dressed, with the distinction between secular and religious being maintained among them in the color of their mantles, as stated concerning the cardinals.

But note the form of all the mantles, both secular and religious. Behind, between the shoulder blades, the two parts of the cloak are joined. They are gathered for about the breadth of a palm and remain open at that point. The sewn portion joining the two parts of the cloak lies over the neck. The cloak hangs before the breast on both sides down to the ground, and also behind down to the ground, but without a train, in a circular and spherical form. The front parts of the cloak are not joined before the breast.

### LXXI. On the Order of Seating at the Table

The pope himself sits alone at an elevated table, with various large gold and silver vessels placed upon it, or situated in the sideboard or serving table beside the table, on the pope’s left.

[Col. 1313B] At another table, on the pope’s right, extending the length of the hall or dining room, sit the cardinal bishops. The patriarchs sit among them, if present, belonging to the four principal patriarchal churches, according to the order of precedence and posteriority of their churches. The first patriarch sits between the first and second cardinal bishops, unless a king is present; in that case, the king sits between the two bishops, the patriarch between the second bishop, the third after the third, and so on. Nevertheless, each patriarch always sits between two cardinal bishops. The same applies at Mass.

At a second table on the same side, or at the same sufficiently long table, the cardinal priests sit after the cardinal bishops and patriarchs. On the left side, [Col. 1313C] which likewise extends the length of the hall or dining room, all the cardinal deacons sit according to their order and the precedence of each, that is, according to the status they hold in the cardinalate: the senior ones sit first at the table. Behind the cardinals’ table are the tables of all the other prelates and nobles.

The older and nobler laymen who are present serve before the pope, according to the offices assigned to them by the master of the household.

It should nevertheless be noted that at the table the first course is initially placed before the pope by one of the chief nobles, even if he is a king. Once it has been placed, if he is a king, he goes to sit between the first two cardinal bishops—unless he is the Roman emperor. In that case he goes to his own table, prepared on the pope’s right, with a canopy, on a step lower and smaller than the pope’s. The king carries the second course. After placing it, he goes to sit at the table on the pope’s left, between the first two cardinal deacons.

Thus did Lord Charles, the first king of Sicily, act, as did all the kings descended from him.

Note that at that time the emperor of Constantinople was at the Curia and sat between the first two cardinal bishops; he was the one who first placed the first course before the pope. The king of Sicily, who was then present, placed the second; other nobles placed the remaining courses. If these were sons of emperors or kings, they served the pope at table: one from the cup, another from the tucelli to begin; others stood beside him while he ate, and others followed [Col. 1314A] those carrying the dishes. They themselves served the dishes of the pope and the cardinals, as had been arranged.

### LXXII. On the Second Washing of the Hands

After the meal, the pope washes his hands, served as before by the bishop and the two cardinal deacons. These three cardinals, having resumed their mantles and their attendants, return to sit with the other cardinals in their places at the table. Then each of the bishops, each cardinal, and everyone else likewise washes his hands while seated; a servant pours water again for the cardinal who is washing. The assisting cardinals hold one cloth on one side of the person washing and another on the other side. Thus they serve one another mutually.

When all have washed, spices are distributed. At the end, when the tables have been removed, the lord pope rises, and while he stands with his feet on his footstool, thanks are given as follows, with the two deacons and the bishop ministering to him. After these have been given, the aforementioned two deacons lead the pope to his chamber or antechamber. There he sits on a faldstool with only the cardinals, his brothers. He and they remain dressed as they were at table; afterward he removes his garments and rests barefoot in his sandals. The cardinals and other prelates return to their lodgings wearing their mitres, mounted, but with their horses neither saddled nor otherwise covered. They depart as they stood at the meal.

It should be remembered that all the chaplains of our lord the pope who dine with him, or almost all of them, must dine splendidly with the lord chamberlain on that day.

### LXXIII. On the Blessing of the Table and the Thanksgiving

At the Lord’s Supper, for the blessing of the table, the verse “Christ for us became obedient unto death” is said absolutely, without “Gloria Patri,” and no further words are added. Then “Pater noster” is said silently. When it has been completed, without any spoken announcement, the lord pope makes the sign of the cross over both his own table and the others. Today “Jube, domne, benedicere” and “Tu autem” are not said. After the tables have been signed as stated, they go to sit down according to the order given above.

At the end of the meal, in the thanksgiving, the verse “Christ became obedient” is repeated as above; “Pater noster” is said immediately. When it has ended, the pope says absolutely the prayer “Respice, quaesumus, Domine,” etc. He does not say “Qui tecum,” nor “Fidelium animae,” but, without saying anything, the lord pope simply makes the sign of the cross devoutly over himself and all the others. Then, after the fanon and mitre have been placed upon his head, with the mantle over his shoulders, he is led, as stated, by the two cardinal deacons to his chamber or antechamber, which is called the vestment chamber.

It should be noted that if the pope does not consecrate the holy chrism, the ceremonies described above do not take place.

It should likewise be noted that if the cardinals do not dine with the pope, the solemnities described above do not take place.

### LXXIV. No Woman May Be Present at the Supreme Pontiff’s Meal

[Col. 1315A]

It should also be noted that no woman ever eats in the presence of the Roman pontiff, even if she is an empress or queen. This was observed in the time of the lord Clement V, the lord John XXII, the lord Benedict XII, and Clement VI; nor has it been heard that it was ever done at any time.

Nevertheless, the contrary occurred in the time of the lord Urban V, the lord Gregory XI, and Urban VI. The contrary of that, however, was also observed in the time of Boniface IX and John XXIII, supreme pontiffs; and [Note: [Col. 1315D] Someone added in a more recent hand in the Codex: “Indeed, it is very good to observe this. For Christ also ate with women. Therefore Innocent, Alexander, and [Col. 1316D] the others acted rightly.” Jacobus strongly disapproves of this in the case of Alexander, the author of Alexander’s Diary.] it was wrong.

### LXXV. On the Office on Good Friday

On Friday, that is, Holy Friday, so that everything may be said in order, at the first hour of the day, according to Jacobus Gaietani, all the chaplains are summoned to say the Psalter, while the lord pope sits before his bed. The chaplains, also positioned near his feet in turn, complete the entire Psalter. [490] When it is finished, the priest with the others says the antiphon “Ne reminiscaris.” Then the litanies and “Pater noster” are said privately, together with the psalm “Miserere mei, Deus,” without “Gloria,” etc. Then the Chapters are said, and, without “Dominus vobiscum,” the prayers “Deus, cui proprium est misereri” and all the others customarily said in Lent are said absolutely. At the end the prayer “Respice, quaesumus” is said.

It should be known that on this day, before going to the church or chapel to celebrate the office, the lord pope comes twice to the window to give the indulgence in the customary manner: once in the morning and once in the evening, when he wishes to go to the chapel for the office. Each time he wears a red cope and a plain garnello mitre without gold embroidery or pearls.

After the indulgence has been given in the evening, he goes to his chamber, removes the cope, and takes a red scarlet cape, open from the middle of the breast down to the feet. Wearing on his head the same plain white garnello mitre without gold embroidery or pearls, he enters the chapel with the cardinals to celebrate the office. When the pope is in the chapel, he immediately goes to the altar, where a bare throne with a footstool has been prepared. There he kneels, and the cardinal deacon standing on his right removes his mitre; he prays for a while. Then he rises and the mitre is replaced on him. He then goes to another bare throne, prepared far from the altar with a footstool.

Nevertheless, it should be noted that on this day the cardinals do not come to pay reverence to the pope. Instead, immediately, at the aforementioned scarlet throne, after the scarlet cape has been removed, the cardinal deacon who is to recite the Passion—dressed in surplice, alb, amice, and broad stole, without a chasuble—dresses the pope in sacred vestments of black or violet, as he prefers.

It should also be known that on this day the pope does not wear sandals, but ordinary shoes.

[Col. 1316A] The lord pope himself being vested, the same cardinal receives a black chasuble. Likewise all the cardinals receive vestments: the bishops cottae, broad amices, and copes; the priests and deacons likewise, but not copes; rather, they receive black chasubles, like the pope. After receiving these vestments, the pope proceeds to the right side of the altar at the front, where there is a low, bare throne without a footstool. There he sits facing the left end of the altar. All the others also sit in their places, as customary.

It should nevertheless be noted that if a king were present at that office on this day, he would not sit in the customary place, that is, when the pope performs the office; rather, he sits among the cardinal bishops, namely [Col. 1316B] between the first two cardinal bishops. As soon as all are seated, a chaplain, absolutely and without a title, says the prophecy in the manner of a reading: “Thus says the Lord: In tribulation.” When it is finished, the Tract “Domine, audivi” is sung.

When the Tract has ended, the pope rises and, facing the altar there, says, “Let us pray.” The senior cardinal deacon standing on the pope’s right says, “Let us kneel,” and immediately the cardinal deacon on the pope’s left says, “Rise.” Then the pope says the prayer “Deus, a quo,” etc., and at the end “Amen” is answered.

[491] When it has ended, the subdeacon removes his chasuble and reads, without a title, the prophecy “In those days the Lord spoke to Moses.” When it is finished, the Tract “Deliver me,” etc., is sung.

Before the aforementioned Tract has ended, the cardinal deacon who is to recite the Passion must remove his chasuble and receive it folded like a stole over his left shoulder, so that its ends are fastened on the right side, almost behind. When the Tract has ended, the cardinal deacon makes a reverence, kneels before the altar, without a blessing or a kiss of the foot, and proceeds with the Gospel book, without candles or incense, to the bare pulpit. Absolutely, without “The Lord be with you,” he begins: “The Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ according to John.” Without any response he says, “At that time, Jesus went out,” etc.

At the beginning of the Passion the pope rises from his throne, and after his mitre has been removed he stands with his feet toward the altar, about the middle of it, as though supporting himself against it behind his shoulders, looking toward the one reading the Passion, with his hands joined before his breast. He stands thus until the passage of the Passion is reached that says, “And he bowed his head,” etc. Then the pope kneels toward the altar and remains kneeling for as long as it would take to say “Pater noster” once. Afterward he rises and stands as before; all the others do likewise.

It should be known that the pope himself reads the Passion while it is being sung by the cardinal deacon. But when it is read by someone other than the pope—namely, by the deacon—and the passage is reached that must be said in the Gospel tone, namely, “After these things, he asked Pilate,” the cardinal deacon bows and, in a lowered voice, asks the pope there for a blessing. The acolytes bring forward the thurible with incense in the customary manner, and the pope places in it blessed incense, which the acolyte carries to the deacon for incensing the Gospel. Two other acolytes or chaplains carry lighted candles.

When the Passion has ended, the book itself is brought back with the Gospel, as usual, for the pope to kiss, namely at the aforementioned passage, “After these things,” etc. From that point, according to modern custom, a sermon is given by a master of theology or a prelate. The one who gives the sermon, kneeling before the pope, asks for a blessing but does not kiss the foot. After receiving the blessing [Col. 1317B] and the indulgence to be announced after the sermon, he goes to the customary place for delivering the sermon.

When the sermon is given, the pope, wearing his mitre on his head, sits in the bare throne before him, as stated above. When it has ended, the Confiteor is not said. Instead, the one who gave the sermon immediately announces, by the command and authority of our lord the pope, an indulgence of seven years and seven quadragenas.

Having completed these things, the pope rises and, with the chair removed there and the mitre laid aside, says the solemn Prayers, namely, “Let us pray, dearly beloved,” and all the others, as they are set out in the Ordinary or Roman Missal. But at the end of these Prayers, when the pope says “Let us pray,” the aforementioned cardinal deacon who stands at the pope’s right and left—who at the first bending of the knee had said “Rise”—now says “Let us bend the knee,” and the penultimate deacon says “Rise.” At the fourth Prayer, the penultimate cardinal 492 says “Let us bend the knee,” and the third cardinal deacon says “Rise.” Thus all the cardinal deacons proceed according to their order and precedence until all the Prayers have been completed. If there happen to be more Prayers than cardinal deacons, as soon as the last deacon in his order has said “Let us bend the knee,” the aforementioned first deacon says “Rise,” and thereafter they proceed as before until the end of the Prayers.

It should nevertheless be noted that in the Prayer said for the Jews, “Let us bend the knee” is not said, because on this day the Jews bent their knees while mocking the Lord. [Col. 1317D] Therefore, on their behalf the Church does not bend the knee in the Prayer that is said for them.

When these Prayers have ended, the pope, standing there at the altar, removes the *spinelli*, the pallium, the chasuble, and the mitre, and goes to the right-hand corner of the altar on the rear side. There the sacristan, if he is a bishop, or another familiar bishop—though not a cardinal—vested in a black cope, who also serves the pope at Mass, hands the pope the cross. Holding it in his hands, with his face turned toward the people, and wearing gloves, he uncovers the left side of the cross.

### LXXVI. On the first, second, and third showing of the cross

When that side has been uncovered, the pope alone begins, singing, the Antiphon *Ecce lignum crucis* (“Behold the wood of the cross”); as soon as he begins, those standing by assist him in the singing until the Antiphon itself has ended. The singers chant *Venite, adoremus* (“Come, let us adore”).

When this is finished, the pope advances a little farther, approximately toward the corner of the altar, and uncovers another part of the cross, namely, the right side. Once it has been uncovered, the pope again raises his voice and alone begins the aforementioned Antiphon, *Ecce lignum*, with those standing by assisting him as above.

When the Antiphon has ended, the pope advances farther, approximately to the middle of the altar, uncovering the entire cross and raising his voice still higher as he begins for the third time the aforementioned Antiphon, *Ecce lignum crucis*, those standing by assisting him in the singing as above.

Meanwhile the *fulcarius* places a carpet with a cushion and a clean cloth before the altar. When this has been done, without removing his gloves, the pope descends the steps of the altar and, kneeling, places the cross upon the aforementioned very clean cloth and upon the one decorated with silk, which the sacristan has placed before the altar on the ground, spread over the cushion, together with the cloth with which the cross had been covered. When the pope has placed the cross there, the subdeacon immediately kneels on the right side of the cross, holding the foot of the cross with one hand and its upper end with the other, together with the silk cloth.

After the pope has placed the cross, he goes to the aforementioned bare, low chair prepared without a footstool. Sitting there, he removes his shoes, as his chamberlains customarily remove them, while one of the bishops covers them with his cope. Barefoot, and with his mitre removed but his gloves still on his hands, [Col. 1318C] he goes toward the gate of the chapel, accompanied by the two aforementioned senior cardinal deacons, one on his right and the other on his left. Turning his face toward the altar, he kneels there, bowing his head to the ground with his hands joined. He does this three times, 493 before reaching the cross, rising and advancing little by little until he comes to the place where he had placed the cross. There, prostrate on the ground, he adores the cross by kissing it. Then he rises and returns to the aforementioned chair. Sitting there, he is shod by the aforementioned chamberlains—not with sandals, but with ordinary shoes.

Note that Lord Gregory XI, as well as Lord Urban VI, Roman pontiffs, never wished to remove their shoes in the aforementioned chair near the altar, I believe out of reverence for the altar, since both were devout; rather, they did so in the large chair, also bare, far from the altar, where they customarily vested on solemn occasions.

### LXXVII. On the adoration of the cross on that day, and on Communion

Afterward all the cardinals, having had their shoes removed by their attendants in their respective places, go barefoot two by two, in the manner described above, to adore the cross according to their order. They bend the knee three times. Likewise, all the others present there adore the same cross in the same manner.

Meanwhile the singers chant *Agios* (“Holy”), and so forth, alternately repeating *Sanctus Deus, Sanctus fortis* (“Holy God, Holy Strong One”), and *Popule meus, quid feci* (“My people, what have I done?”), and the other Antiphons, as contained in the Roman Missal. The pope too reads the aforementioned Antiphons and everything mentioned above while seated in the chair, while the cardinals and others adore the cross.

When the adoration of the cross has ended, the sacristan or another person appointed for this purpose replaces it in its place upon the altar. A cleric of the chapel receives the money offered during the adoration of the cross on this day alone, since it belongs to him; on other days it belongs to the chaplains. Once the cross has been placed on the altar between the torches or candles, the chamberlain, or the person acting in his place, carries another cross outside the chapel gates, accompanied by the clerics of the chamber and chapel, so that the others may adore it.

After the adoration has taken place in the chapel, while those outside adore the other cross, the pope washes his hands and [Col. 1319B], having removed his gloves, which he does not put on again, rises from the chair. Standing there, he resumes the aforementioned black chasuble and pallium with *spinelli* from the hand of the cardinal deacon who said the Passion. Thus he proceeds to the altar without a mitre and without the customary Confession, assisted by the two aforementioned cardinal deacons.

Then he goes with the cross, lights, and incense to the cupboard or chest in which the chalice containing Christ’s body had been reserved on the previous day. This has hitherto been observed in the time of John XXII, Lord Benedict XII, Lord Clement VI, Lord Innocent VI, Lord Urban V, Lord Gregory XI, and Lord Urban VI, Roman pontiffs. The pope himself goes to the cupboard or chest and carries Christ’s body to the altar, covered with that silk cloth, with one end over it and the other hanging over his left shoulder.

According to Lord James Gaietani, the junior cardinal priest, Christ’s body was anciently customarily carried to the altar [Note: [Col. 1319] This is evident from the more ancient booklets of the Roman Order, which we cited above.]

The pope therefore takes the chalice in his hands, after it has first been incensed or censed while he kneels, covered with a noble cloth of linen or silk, and carries it to the altar. Having uncovered the chalice, he takes the body from it with his hand and places it upon the paten, which the deacon who said the Passion holds in his hand. That deacon offers Christ’s body with the paten to the pope; the pope receives it and places it upon the altar, on the corporal spread there.

Afterward the sacristan presents the chalice to the pope without washing or wiping it, on account of the Sacrament, lest any fragments remain inside, and, saying nothing, the sacristan places [an unspecified item] in the said chalice. Then the aforementioned cardinal deacon offers the chalice with pure, unmixed wine, and the subdeacon offers a cruet with water, which the pope mixes with the wine while saying nothing. He is to reckon that on this day the Sacraments of the Church flowed forth—namely, blood and water—from Christ’s body.

In certain churches, however, according to Lord James Gaietani, pure wine without water is offered, so that in the pure and strong wine the cruelty of the Jews and the harshness of Christ’s Passion may be represented.

After the chalice has been placed in the customary manner beside the Lord’s body by the aforementioned cardinal deacon, [Col. 1320A] that cardinal deacon offers the pope the thurible, kissing the pope’s hand both in giving and receiving it. The pope, as is customary, incenses both Christ’s body and the chalice.

Then the pope goes to the corner of the altar and washes his fingers a little with water in two basins, brought by one of his soldiers or household attendants, or by the most distinguished person present, assisted by the senior bishop who serves in the office of chaplain. After this washing, the pope goes before the middle of the altar without the Confession, as stated above. He bows while praying and says, *In spiritu humilitatis* (“In a spirit of humility”); then, rising, he turns toward the people and says, *Orate pro me, fratres* (“Pray for me, brothers”), and so forth.

Next, in a low voice, as is customary, without *Per omnia saecula saeculorum* (“World without end”), and without *Te igitur*, he begins directly by singing, *Oremus, praeceptis salutaribus moniti* (“Let us pray; instructed by saving commands”), and so forth, followed by the *Pater noster* (“Our Father”), and so forth. When he reaches the place where it says, *Sicut in caelo et in terra* (“As in heaven and on earth”), the celebrant takes Christ’s body and raises it so that it can be seen by those standing around; immediately he replaces it where it had been.

At the end of the *Pater noster*, *Sed libera nos a malo* (“But deliver us from evil”) is answered. The priest silently says “Amen,” and immediately, in the same tone and without *Oremus*, says this Prayer: *Libera nos, quaesumus, Domine* (“Deliver us, we beseech you, Lord”); at the end “Amen” is answered.

Then the deacon offers the paten to the pope, and the pope breaks the consecrated Host according to custom, placing one third of it in the chalice while saying nothing. For unconsecrated wine is sanctified by the sending of the Lord’s body into it.

*Pax Domini* (“The peace of the Lord”) is not said; the *Agnus Dei* is not sung; the kiss of peace is not given; and no post-Communion is said.

The pope alone receives Communion, without the ministers, not solemnly at the usual seat, but only there before the altar on that day, out of humble reverence and in remembrance of Christ’s Passion. He does not receive the blood with a tube, but with the chalice. After he has received the blood, wine is poured into the chalice by the sacristan or another bishop who serves him at Mass. He takes it with the chalice at the corner of the altar, and there washes his hands with water in basins brought by one of the soldiers or household attendants.

Then, having removed from the altar the *spinelli* with which the pallium and chasuble are fastened, he goes to the high, bare seat. There he removes his vestments and, with the ministers, chaplains, and his clerics, says Vespers of the preceding day—not singing them, but reading them—including the Antiphon *Calicem salutaris* (“The chalice of salvation”), with the following items and Psalms, as they are marked in the Roman Breviary, always without *Gloria*, without a Chapter, and without a Verse.

The pope himself does not begin the Antiphon at the *Magnificat*, but everything is said by reading. When these things have been completed, *Christus factus est pro nobis* (“Christ was made for us”), and so forth, is said; without *Kyrie, eleison*, the *Pater noster* is said silently.

Note that after *Christus factus est*, and so forth, the pope immediately descends from the large chair and goes to the chair before the middle of the altar, which is bare and has a footstool. There, kneeling, he says the Psalm *Miserere mei, Deus* (“Have mercy on me, O God”), and when it has been completed, without *Gloria Patri*, he says, *Oremus. Respice* (“Let us pray. Look”), and so forth.

[Col. 1321A] It should be understood that on this day one cardinal priest serves the pope in the office of chaplain, namely the one to whom the pope has assigned this duty, or to whom the senior of the cardinal deacons has entrusted it by the pope’s command. A cardinal bishop serves if the pope celebrates on this day.

When all the aforementioned things have been completed, the pope, wearing a red cope and the aforementioned plain mitre, accompanied by all the cardinals dressed in woolen capes, with the two senior cardinal deacons assisting him, one on his right and the other on his left, goes to the aforementioned window at which he customarily gives the indulgence. There, in the presence of the cardinals, he gives absolution and the blessing in the customary manner. Then he grants the indulgence to the people and all those assisting—namely, seven years and seven quarantines. The junior cardinal deacon, or the one to whom the pope has entrusted the task, proclaims this indulgence by the pope’s command.

Afterward he enters his chamber, where he removes the cope and mitre and resumes his customary clothing. The cardinals return to their own places without conversation.

### LXXVIII. On the office of Holy Saturday

It should be noted that on Holy Saturday, the vigil of Easter, before the lord pope comes to the chapel or church to perform the office, he comes twice to the window to grant the indulgence to the people in the customary manner: once in the morning, and once in the evening, when he wishes to go to the chapel to perform the office. Each time he wears a red cope and a plain white mitre of *garnello*, [Col. 1321C] without gold embroidery and pearls.

On this same day a new fire is drawn from crystal or another stone and is blessed in the chapel, in the presence of the lord pope, by the junior cardinal priest, vested in sacred garments, with the cross, holy water, and incense, reading the Prayers without musical notation. The fire is blessed before the pope comes to the chapel.

At the appointed hour, after all the aforementioned things have first been completed, the pope, dressed in a red mantle and wearing the aforementioned mitre, comes to the chapel with the cardinals who are present with him there in the chamber, accompanied by the two senior cardinal deacons assisting him as usual, one on his right and the other on his left. The cardinal deacon on his right removes his mitre, and the pope kneels and prays for a short time before the altar, where a chair with a footstool and cushion has been prepared.

After the Prayer he rises and goes to his large seat, covered with a noble cloth. His mitre having been replaced, he sits down. Then the cardinals come, as usual, to pay reverence to the pope.

When this reverence has been made, the junior cardinal deacon who is to bless the candle, dressed in white vestments—namely, amice, narrow surplice, alb, stole, tunicle, dalmatic, and maniple—leaves the chapel gates. Ministers with the cross go before him; chaplains, singers, and the rest of the clergy and people accompany him. He goes approximately to the far end of the chapel and receives from an acolyte or minister a reed three and a half cubits long, bearing a three-branched candle lit from the newly kindled fire.

There, kneeling toward the reed and raising his hands slightly with the reed, he says in song, *Lumen Christi* (“The light of Christ”). When all the others answer, *Deo gratias* (“Thanks be to God”), he goes approximately to the gate of the chapel, kneels there a second time, and, raising his hands more than before and lifting his voice higher, says, *Lumen Christi*. When all answer, *Deo gratias*, he proceeds to the altar, kneels there a third time, and, raising his hands still higher and lifting his voice further, says, *Lumen Christi*. When all answer, *Deo gratias*, he then ascends to the decorated ambo and begins directly the Blessing of the Candle. Singing, he says as follows: *Exsultet iam angelica turba caelorum* (“Let the angelic host of heaven now rejoice”), continuing the Blessing to the end.

At the proper time the cardinal deacon places five grains of incense in the candle in the form of a cross. Then, at the appointed time, the candle is lit from the aforementioned new fire, as prescribed and commanded in the rubrics set out in that Blessing.

After the Blessing of the Candle, the pope descends from that seat and goes to the vestry prepared far from the altar, if there is one. Otherwise, if there is none, he puts on his sandals there, reading *Quam dilecta* (“How lovely”), which are to be white with pearls, since he does not change them.

Then he puts on all his Lenten vestments of violet color: the alb without vestments, a white girdle and subgirdle, the pectoral, the *fanon*, and the stole with pearls—which he does not change—the tunicle, the violet dalmatic, and, through the cardinal deacon who gave the Blessing of the Candle, the violet chasuble. That cardinal deacon stands only in an alb with a stole.

Sometimes Roman pontiffs, to avoid the weariness of removing and putting on these two garments, have customarily worn them in white; nevertheless, the whole matter remains at their discretion.

After the pope has put on his gloves, all the cardinals receive their vestments: namely, the bishops [receive] the cotta, broad amice, and copes, while violet chasubles are received. Likewise, the cardinal deacon who vests the pope, once the pope has been vested, puts on a violet chasuble for himself, as do the other cardinal deacons. The subdeacon, however, uses not a chasuble but a white tunicle throughout the office and at Mass, so that he may be more composed and free to read the lessons and perform the other duties incumbent upon him that day.

When all the vestments have been received, the aforementioned cardinal deacon replaces the pope’s mitre, and the pope receives his rings—the pontifical ring and the smaller ring—from the hand of the bishop or cardinal priest serving him from the book in the office or at Mass.

Then the pope proceeds in procession in silence to his aforementioned large seat, far from the altar, assisted by the two aforementioned senior cardinal deacons. This is to be understood also if he vests in the sacristy or vestry: he proceeds there in the same way. If the pope vests in the chair itself rather than in the vestry, he also sits there, with the two cardinal deacons and the cardinal priest serving him in the office and at Mass seated before him on stools, as is customary. The other cardinal deacons sit before the altar in their customary place. Likewise all the other cardinals sit in their respective places, as usual.

Afterward one of the clerics of the chapel or the acolytes goes to the bare ambo, where the Book of Epistles should be ready for reading the lessons. Directly, without a title, he begins and reads the lesson, *In principio Deus creavit caelum et terram* (“In the beginning God created heaven and earth”), and so forth. When this lesson has ended, if the pope wishes, the Greek deacon reads it in Greek.

When it has been completed, the pope, standing in the aforementioned seat, has his mitre removed by the cardinal deacon assisting him on his right and says, *Oremus*. The cardinal deacon immediately at the pope’s right says, *Flectamus genua* (“Let us bend the knee”); then the other, on the left, says, *Levate* (“Rise”). Afterward the pope says the appropriate Prayer, and the remaining actions are performed and read as they are marked in the Missal or Ordinary.

### LXXIX. If the pope wishes to confer orders or consecrate cardinals

It should be noted that if the pope wishes to confer certain orders and consecrate some of the cardinals on this day, the following procedure is to be observed.

After the first prophecy has been read, the minor orders are conferred in the aforementioned seat. After the second prophecy has been read, the order of acolyte is conferred, as contained in the Pontifical of Lord William Durand.

Nevertheless, the Roman Church has customarily observed the following practice: after the twelve prophecies have been read, the minor orders are distributed; after *Kyrie, eleison* has been said nine times with the litanies, as contained in the Missal, and *Gloria in excelsis Deo* has been sung, the order of subdeacon is conferred before the first Collect. [Col. 1323C] The last person ordained reads the Epistle.

After the minor orders and the subdiaconate have been conferred, and the Prayers, Epistle, Gradual, through the final Verse or Alleluia have been read, as everything is marked in the ordination of the deacon and cardinal priest, the archdeacon presents them to the pope. Seek the rest in its proper place.

It should nevertheless be known that the cardinal deacons, according to their order, say *Flectamus genua* and also *Levate* at the beginning of the Prayers to be said by the pope, according to the procedure explained yesterday in the rubric.

All the other lessons are read by the pope’s chaplains, wearing only surplices over their *rochetts*. When they have been read, the reader, after the end of his lesson, goes to kiss the pope’s foot.

### LXXX. On the cardinal priest serving the pope

Regarding the cardinal priest who serves on this day in the office of chaplain, it should be known that throughout the entire office of this day one cardinal priest serves the pope in the office of chaplain—namely, the one to whom the pope has assigned the duty, or to one of the senior cardinal deacons to whom, by the pope’s command, he has entrusted it.

He serves from the book when the pope says the aforementioned Prayers, holding the book above his head after each lesson. At the altar, also, after the vestments have been received, he gives the pope the rings—the pontifical and smaller rings—on the same finger. When the pope removes his vestments, this cardinal priest receives the aforementioned rings from the pope’s hand. Whenever he gives or removes them, he kisses the pope’s hand.

Note that in this rubric, in modern times, the senior bishop, or the senior priest, or the deputies in the absence of the seniors, always serve the pope in the said office of chaplain. I, Brother Peter Amelii, bishop of Senigallia, saw this observed in the time of Lords Urban V, Gregory XI, and Urban VI, Roman pontiffs.

When the Prayers, lessons, and Tracts have been completed, the subdeacon, dressed in the white tunicle mentioned above, goes to the ambo where the lessons were read. There, singing, he says the litany, and all answer him each time, repeating his words in the same tone.

At the beginning of the litany, the pope removes the pallium, *spinelli*, and chasuble and descends from the aforementioned seat. He goes to the chair prepared before the altar, with a footstool and cushion, wearing the aforementioned mitre on his head. There he remains kneeling until the place is reached where it says, *Peccatores, te rogamus, audi nos* (“Sinners, we beg you, hear us”).

Then the pope rises and goes to another chair prepared far from the altar, or to the vestry, if there is one. Having removed the aforementioned violet vestments, he is vested in white and solemn vestments by the cardinal deacon who is to say the Gospel. That deacon is to be vested in white garments when he dresses the pope, as he was at the Blessing of the Candle.

Likewise all the other cardinals receive white vestments: the cardinal bishops receive the cotta, broad amice, and cope; the cardinal priests likewise receive the amice, but not copes—they receive chasubles; the cardinal deacons receive the narrow amice, tunicle, and dalmatic; and all prelates receive copes.

After the pope has received these vestments, a noble and solemn mitre is placed upon him, and he receives both rings from the cardinal priest, as above. Assisted by the two aforementioned senior cardinal deacons, one on his right and the other on his left, he proceeds in procession to the altar.

As he comes, three vested cardinal priests meet him. As is customary, he receives them according to their order for the kiss of the mouth and breast. Then he goes to the altar and makes his Confession in the customary manner. Afterward he kisses the altar and the Gospel book at the beginning of the Gospel to be said at Mass.

He turns toward the cardinal deacons, who make reverence to him as usual, and the pope receives them in order for the kiss of the mouth and breast. Thereafter he receives the thurible from the hand of the deacon who is to say the Gospel that day.

The cardinal of France introduced the custom that the cardinal who serves the pope presents the thurible with the boat. The pope places in the incense, and after the altar has been incensed his mitre is replaced. Then he receives the cardinal deacons for reverence and incenses the altar as usual.

Afterward he goes to his seat, where, standing and without an Introit, he says *Kyrie, eleison*, and then sits. When the singers have completed the ninefold *Kyrie, eleison*, the pope rises; the cardinal deacon standing on his right removes his mitre, and the pope solemnly begins *Gloria in excelsis Deo*. The great bell is then rung.

When it has been sung, he rises, and, with his mitre removed as above, says, *Pax vobis* (“Peace be with you”). When all answer, *Et cum spiritu tuo* (“And with your spirit”), he says, *Oremus. Deus, qui hanc sacratissimam noctem* (“Let us pray. O God, who on this most holy night”), and so forth.

When this Prayer has ended, the subdeacon says the Epistle. Immediately after the Epistle has ended, that same subdeacon, bowing slightly before the pope, says in a clear singing voice: *Annuntio vobis gaudium magnum, videlicet Alleluia* (“I announce to you great joy, namely, Alleluia”), and no response is made to him. He goes to kiss the pope’s feet.

After this has been done, he immediately rises, and that subdeacon or the pope’s chaplain begins *Alleluia* once only before the pope, singing it aloud. The pope, standing with his mitre removed, begins singing the *Alleluia* three times: the second time with a higher voice, and the third time raising his voice still higher. Each time, immediately after the pope, the choir repeats the *Alleluia* in song.

When the *Alleluia* has been sung three times as stated, two singers solemnly sing the Verse *Confitemini Domino* (“Give thanks to the Lord”). Then the Tract *Laudate Dominum, omnes gentes* (“Praise the Lord, all nations”) is sung.

When it has ended, the cardinal deacon, having first received the maniple from the hand of the chaplain serving him and having laid aside the mitre, goes to kiss the pope’s foot. Then he returns to the altar, where, according to custom, he receives the Gospel book, kneeling and kissing the middle of the altar.

After he has received the book, the side on which the crucified figure is shown is held facing the altar toward the pope. Standing there and bowing slightly toward the pope, he holds the book before his breast and asks the pope in a low voice for the Blessing. Having received it, he goes to proclaim the Gospel.

On this day lights are not carried for the Gospel, but incense alone. When the Gospel has ended, the Gospel book is carried by the subdeacon for the pope to kiss, as usual. Standing, the pope says, *Dominus vobiscum* (“The Lord be with you”), and so forth; the deacon returns to the altar.

### LXXXI. That neither the Creed nor the Offertory is said

It should nevertheless be noted that *Credo in unum* (“I believe in one …”) and the Offertory are not said in the Mass being celebrated, nor is a sermon given.

After removing his gloves, the pope washes his hands and then goes to the altar as usual. The cardinal deacon who says the Gospel removes the pope’s mitre. A gold cloth having been spread over the altar by the acolytes and sacristan, the same deacon spreads the corporals in the middle of the altar.

The bishop who is not a cardinal but is the sacristan brings the chalice with a pyx of hosts and a small spoon, covered with a silk veil. He prepares the chalice with three Hosts, one for the Sacrament and two for testing. In the pope’s presence he tests the wine and bread, pours into the chalice as much wine as the small host-cup holds, and, after blessing the water, adds three drops of water with the spoon. Then he tests it, and places the paten with the Host upon the chalice.

The aforementioned cardinal deacon then receives the paten with the Host by the end of the maniple and offers it to the pope without saying anything, but kisses the pope’s hand. Afterward he offers the chalice, making the sign of the cross three times with it over the altar, holding it with both hands at its middle and saying nothing.

### LXXXII. On incensation and Communion

[Col. 1326A]

Afterward he receives the thurible with incense from the hand of the acolyte and offers it to the pope. The deacon himself places the incense into the thurible, kissing the pope’s hand, and hands the aforementioned thurible to the pope, again kissing his hand. He should always hold the handle of the thurible, where the rings are, in his right hand and grasp it near the fire with his left. Thus the pope receives it and incenses the altar, as usual.

Thereafter the cardinal deacon himself receives the thurible from the pope’s hand, always kissing his hand when giving and receiving it. Having received it, he incenses the pope three times. After handing the thurible to the acolyte, he arranges the pope’s chasuble and pallium with the *fanon*.

Then he incenses the altar and the cardinal priest who serves the pope on that day; afterward the two senior cardinal deacons who assisted the pope at Mass; then the other cardinal deacons; then the king, if he is present; and afterward the cardinal bishops, cardinal priests, and other vested prelates, as is customary at other Masses. Then he incenses the pope, as is customary only [Alternative: nevertheless] at this Mass.

The Preface *Te quidem, Domine, omni tempore, sed in hac potissimum nocte* (“Indeed, Lord, at all times, but especially on this night”) is said, and the other parts are said as contained in the Missal.

When the pope says at the appointed place, *Pax Domini sit semper vobiscum* (“May the peace of the Lord be always with you”), the response is, *Et cum spiritu tuo*. But the *Agnus Dei* is not said, and the kiss of peace is not given.

Nevertheless, the pope says that Prayer, *Domine Jesu Christe, qui dixisti apostolis tuis: Pacem* (“Lord Jesus Christ, who said to your apostles: Peace”), and so forth. The Communion is not said. Instead, the pope immediately descends from the altar and goes to his seat, accompanied by the two deacons.

The cardinal deacon, having made three circuits—turning twice before the middle of the altar, with the paten holding Christ’s body raised before his forehead on the right side, and the third time on the left—then gives the Host with the paten, kneeling, to the subdeacon to carry it to the pope in the customary manner.

Afterward the same deacon customarily receives the chalice with the blood, makes three circuits, and carries it to the pope’s seat. Standing there, he solemnly gives the pope Communion.

After the deacon, the bishop-s sacristan brings the empty chalice, covered with a noble silk cloth, in his right hand; in his left he carries the canopy with the tube and three points, which he hands to the cardinal priest serving the pope. After him comes the acolyte with the wine vessels [*vinateriis*] [Col. 1326D] and two *taxae* [vessels; the term is uncertain]. [Note: [Col. 1325D] The same word occurs below, more than once, in chapter 85.]

The pope sucks the blood through the tube. Immediately the deacon receives Christ’s body from the pope’s hand, and after him the subdeacon receives it. Having received it, the aforementioned cardinal deacon carries the chalice with the blood to the altar and there sucks some of the blood through the same tube. Then he gives the remaining blood to the subdeacon. Afterward he receives the pope’s ablution from the hand of the cardinal carrying it, according to the custom followed elsewhere.

It should nevertheless be noted that when the pope places Christ’s body in the mouth of the cardinal deacon who communicates with him, the pope should not receive him with a kiss on the mouth, as is customary on other days when he communicates at his seat. Nor should the cardinal deacon himself kiss the subdeacon after receiving the blood, because at this Mass the kiss of peace is not given, as stated above.

After Communion has been administered and all the aforementioned actions have been completed, the pope replaces his mitre and sits. The singers chant the Antiphon *Alleluia, alleluia, alleluia*. When it has been sung, the Psalm *Laudate Dominum, omnes gentes* (“Praise the Lord, all nations”), and so forth, is sung with *Gloria Patri*, and so forth; at the end the aforementioned Antiphon is repeated.

The Chapter, Hymn, and Verse are not said. Instead, the subdeacon, standing before the pope, immediately begins to sing the Antiphon *Vespere autem Sabbati* (“But in the evening of the Sabbath”). Once he has begun it, the pope removes his mitre and begins the same Antiphon in song, and the singers sing it through to the end.

Afterward the Psalm *Magnificat* is sung in full with *Gloria Patri*, and so forth; at the end the singers repeat the said Antiphon. All the aforementioned things the pope should say standing at his seat, reading them with the ministers.

When these things have been completed, the pope rises from his seat and goes to the altar. There his mitre is removed. Turning his face toward the people, he says, *Dominus vobiscum*; the response is, *Et cum spiritu tuo*. Then he says, *Oremus. Spiritum nobis, Domine* (“Let us pray. Grant us your Spirit, Lord”).

Afterward, turning his face toward the people, he says, *Dominus vobiscum*; when *Et cum spiritu tuo* has been answered, the pope turns toward the altar. The cardinal deacon who said the Gospel, turning his face toward the people, says, *Ite, Missa est* (“Go, the Mass is ended”), with a double *Alleluia*. The response is likewise a double *Alleluia*: *Deo gratias* (“Thanks be to God”).

Then the pope gives the customary blessing. After the Blessing has been given, the cardinal priest who served at Mass proclaims, by the pope’s command and authority, an indulgence of seven years and seven quarantines.

Here note that if the pope performs the office as described above, when the Psalm *Magnificat* has begun he descends from the chair and, without a mitre, incenses the altar. He does not return afterward to the aforementioned chair, but says the Prayer *Spiritum nobis, Domine* there at the altar.

When all these things have been completed, the pope, with his mitre replaced and fully vested, together with all the cardinals also vested and wearing mitres on their heads, proceeds in procession according to their order. The two senior cardinal deacons assist him, one on his right and the other on his left. Before him go the vested subdeacon with the cross and all the chaplains dressed in surplices, with lit candles. He goes to the window [Col. 1327D] at which the indulgence is customarily given to the people.

There, with all the vested cardinals present, after the pope has given the customary Blessing and granted the indulgence to the people, it is proclaimed, in the presence of all the cardinals and other prelates as above, as an indulgence of seven years and seven quarantines by one cardinal as above. Just as they came in procession, so too they all return.

Then the pope enters his chamber with the cardinals. Only the deacon who said the Gospel remains with him to assist the lord pope in removing his vestments; the others remove theirs outside the chamber. When these have been removed, the pope receives the white woolen garments customarily worn on this day.

The sacristan folds the vestments cleanly and properly. The cardinals, having removed their vestments and resumed their woolen capes, return to their own homes.

### LXXXIII. When the pope does not celebrate on that day
Moreover, if on Holy Saturday itself the pope does not perform the office—for Roman pontiffs have not been accustomed to perform the office—the following procedure is to be observed. First, therefore, the lord pope goes to give the indulgence to the people, and on his return hears a low Mass privately, in which the Alleluia is not said, since it is customarily a votive Mass, unless the Mass of the day is said. When this Mass has ended, he goes meanwhile to give the indulgence. Meanwhile all the lights are extinguished, and a new fire is struck from the stone by the master of the chapel. The junior cardinal priest, vested in sacred vestments—namely amice, stole, alb, maniple, and cope with a plain white mitre—blesses this fire with his ministers, vested in surplices, as is prescribed in the Missal. [Col. 1328B]

It must nevertheless be understood that if the person performing the office is a cardinal, he blesses the fire and must be vested in sacred vestments up to but excluding the chasuble; in place of the chasuble he wears a cope. With the cross, holy water, and incense, he reads all those prayers without singing them. After reading them, he removes the cope and takes the chasuble, whether he is a cardinal or not.

It should nevertheless be noted that whoever performs the office must be vested in violet vestments or in vestments of indigo color; the deacon and subdeacon, however, wear white. Sometimes prelates also wear a white tunicle and [Col. 1328C] dalmatic, and an indigo-colored chasuble. The sandals must be white, and are not changed, nor are the stole or maniple. Thus vested, the prelate who performs the office sits upon his chair, covered with a faldstool. After the pope has given the indulgence to the people, the pope comes to the chapel for the second time.
