Having made a prayer of some sort before the altar, he rises and ascends to his chair, dressed as he was when he gave the indulgence to the people. There he sits with his mitre; before him are two cardinal deacons, and the priest and the person who serves him.

The prelate, vested together with his ministers as above, sits; the deacon who is to read the Gospel carries a three-cubit reed with candles newly lit from the new fire, accompanied by two acolytes with candlesticks and burning torches. The subdeacon precedes [Col. 1328D] them, carrying the cross. Thus they all proceed almost to the end of the chapel; there the deacon says in a loud voice, “The Light of Christ,” and the choir replies, “Thanks be to God,” and kneels. He then approaches more closely to the chapel doors, kneels again, and intones “The Light of Christ” more loudly, while they reply, “Thanks be to God.” He enters the chapel and goes with the ministers just mentioned to the Paschal candle. There, upon the lectern, he begins, “Let the angelic host now exult” (*Exsultet iam angelica turba*), etc., first asking the pope’s blessing.

When the blessing of the candle has been completed, as prescribed in the Roman Missal, the deacon removes the white dalmatic, and one cleric or one of the singers reads the first lesson. All the others are then read by [Col. 1329A] clerics or singers, while the prelate reads them all seated in his chair with his mitre.

The prelate reads the prayers from his chair while singing them, not at the altar’s horn, and without his mitre. One of his clerics holds the book before him, and, turning his face toward the altar, he reads the prayers. After the twelve prophecies have been read, the pope rises and goes before the middle of the altar and kneels. The prelate reclines upon his faldstool, where prelates customarily stand when they perform the office before the pope. I have sometimes seen them descend from that place to a lower position on the pope’s right side. There is no legal basis for this.

While they are prostrate, the subdeacon goes to the lectern where the lessons were read and sings the litany. When the words “We sinners beseech you, hear us” are reached, the person performing [Col. 1329B] the office rises, removes the violet vestments, and his ministers likewise put on white vestments and the precious mitre. The pope remains reclining upon his chair before the middle of the altar. When the singers begin the first “Kyrie, eleison,” the pope rises and, there with the two cardinal deacons and the prelate performing the office—the latter standing on the pope’s left with his ministers—makes the confession in the customary manner. After the confession, the person performing the office ascends to the altar, and the pope returns to his chair, placing incense in the thurible. After the altar has been incensed, he himself is incensed, and the prelate proceeds to the Mass.

When “Glory to God in the highest” is begun, the pope removes the red cope, stole, and mitre, all of which must be without pearls; the subdeacon, or the person who keeps [Col. 1329C] these items, takes the consistory mitre with pearls. The sacristan or his assistant brings a white samite cope with pearl orphreys and cords. The deacon standing at the pope’s right dresses the pope. When “Glory to God in the highest” is begun, the small bells must be rung, as well as the great consistory bell. The pope says “Glory to God in the highest” with the cardinals assisting him, standing before him in a semicircle. Everything else is done as prescribed in the Roman Missal.

It should be noted that, after the Epistle has been read, the subdeacon who read it must come to the prelate performing the office. Facing him, he says in a loud voice, “I announce to you tidings of great joy, namely, Alleluia.” Immediately the prelate rises, removes his mitre, and says “Alleluia,” beginning it three times and raising his voice higher on each occasion. [Col. 1329D]

After receiving the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, the person performing the office remains at the right horn of the altar. The pope’s subdeacon begins before the pope the antiphon “On the evening of the Sabbath,” etc. The supreme pontiff begins this antiphon, having removed his mitre, and places incense in the thurible. The person performing the office incenses before the altar. After it has been sung by the singers, the person performing the office says the Collect at the aforesaid horn of the altar, not the pope; and while the Collect is being said he always stands without his mitre in his seat. Some Roman pontiffs have been accustomed to stand without their mitres throughout the *Magnificat*. Note that at this Mass “I rejoiced” is not said.

[Col. 1330A] After the pope has given the blessing, he goes to give the indulgence to the people, accompanied by the cardinals. He then returns to his chamber, removes his vestments, and takes a white scarlet cloak with a hood, which he wears throughout the Octave, inclusively, or at least until the Sunday *in albis* after dinner. It is better, however, that he wear it throughout the day; in it he also goes to the table and to Mass in his chapel.

### LXXXIV. The rubric concerning the office of the Mass on Holy Easter Day

On Sunday, the feast of Easter, only a Mass is prescribed, and there is no sermon. After hearing a low Mass early in the morning, the lord pope, vested in a white cope with a pearl-trimmed mitre, goes to give the indulgence [Col. 1330B] to the people. He then comes to the chapel, accompanied by the cardinals then present, who walk before him in their proper order. Two senior cardinal deacons assist him, one on his right and the other on his left; the subdeacon carries the cross before the pope and the cardinals.

When the pope is in the chapel, he immediately goes before the altar, where a chair prepared with a cushion must be placed. The deacon on his right removes his mitre; he kneels and prays there for a little while, as is customary.

Then, with his mitre replaced, he goes to another chair prepared far from the altar, and sits there. After the cardinals and other prelates have made the customary reverence to him, the pope begins Terce aloud in the customary manner. He himself says it by reading, while the chaplains and singers sing it before him. When it is finished, the pope says the prayer, and the prior of the cardinal bishops holds the book over his head. Two acolytes sing “Let us bless the Lord, alleluia, alleluia,” etc. The pope then sits, and the subdeacon, with one of the chamberlains, puts on his sandals. Meanwhile the pope himself reads *How lovely*, with those prayers, etc. He then washes his hands, as customary, and puts on the other sacred vestments. Likewise, all the cardinals, in their proper order and according to what is appropriate to them, also put on white vestments.

When these vestments have been put on, the solemn mitre is placed upon the pope. Then, assisted by the two aforementioned cardinals, one on his right and the other on his left, and accompanied by the prior of the bishops, who on that day must serve him with the book and the other things pertaining to him in the office of chaplain, he proceeds in procession to the altar with the cross, incense, and seven torches. Three junior cardinal priests, vested, come to meet him. As customary, he receives them according to their order for the kiss of the mouth and breast.

He then makes his confession before the altar in the customary manner, along with the other things customarily done at other solemn Masses. He then goes to his seat, where, standing, he says the Introit of the Mass and “Kyrie, eleison” with the cardinals. [505] He then sits, and the Mass proceeds according to the regular custom observed at other times.

It should be noted that at this Mass, after the Alleluia and the verse “Give thanks,” [Col. 1331A] have been sung by the singers, the same singers—not the pope—begin the Sequence “Praise the Paschal Victim” (*Victimae paschali laudes*), and Alleluia is repeated at the end.

It should be noted that on this day there is no sermon. Immediately after the Gospel has ended, the deacon who was assisting on the left says, “I confess to God,” etc., and the pope gives the blessing in the customary manner without announcing the indulgence. The blessing must be given at the end of the Mass whenever there is no sermon. After giving the blessing, the pope says, “I believe in one God,” etc.

It should also be noted that I found in an additional section of the book that, although there is no sermon, the *Confiteor* is nevertheless said and the indulgence given. It should further be noted that today the sacristan places the precious and solemn mitres on the left horn of the altar, and always does so on those processional days.

[Col. 1331B] It should also be noted that shortly before the beginning of the Preface, the two most recently elected cardinal deacons go behind the altar, in representation or likeness of the angels guarding the tomb. They remain there standing, facing the people, until the intonation of the *Agnus Dei*. When this begins, they return to their former places, and not before.

It should be noted, however, that when the pope says before the beginning of the Lord’s Prayer, “For ever and ever,” “Amen” is not answered; instead he immediately says, “Let us pray,” “At the command of the Savior,” “Our Father,” etc. At the end, “But deliver us from evil” is answered, and “The peace of the Lord” is said, along with everything else ordinarily said at another time. “I rejoiced” and the Lord’s Prayer are also said. On this day the pope solemnly receives Communion in his seat, as is customary.

It should also be noted that today the sacristan [Col. 1331C] must bring three chalices: a large one for the Mass, another from which the pope drinks wine, and a third for Communion. He also prepares a gilded container and as many small Hosts as are necessary.

### LXXXV. The Communion of the Cardinal Deacons and Other Prelates

Concerning the Communion of the cardinal deacons and of the other prelates, clerics, and laypeople, it should be understood that on this day, if the lord pope celebrates, all the deacons receive Communion in the pope’s chapel, as do his notaries and chaplains, as well as clerics and laypeople.

A note concerning the giving of the peace follows immediately after the pope. The contrary order is found in the *Ceremonial of Lord Jacopo Gaetani*, but I prefer this arrangement. Namely, after the pope has given the peace to the prior of the cardinal bishops who serves the pope at Mass, the pope immediately gives the peace to the cardinal deacons, except the one who read the Gospel. That deacon receives it immediately after he has received the body of Christ in his mouth from the pope.

After giving the peace, the pope ascends the great chair, accompanied by the cardinal deacons in their proper order. The one who recites the Gospel kneels and receives the paten containing the body of Christ while standing on his feet. He raises it, holding it elevated with both hands almost at eye level, and turns toward the right as though he were about to say, “The Lord be with you.” By the same route he returns and turns similarly toward the left. He then kneels and hands it to the subdeacon, who also kneels and carries it to the pope with the body of Christ. [Col. 1332A]

He receives the uncovered chalice and makes a similar circuit, then carries Christ’s blood to the pope.

After receiving the body of Christ and receiving the kiss of peace from the pope, he returns to the altar with the chalice. There he draws a little of Christ’s blood through the tube and gives some also to the subdeacon and kisses him. After this, the text continues uncertainly: “he receives it when he descends, because the bishop-sacristan who serves the pope places the consecrated Hosts inside the cup, not the cardinal deacon, using tongs.”

Thus I, Peter, bishop of Oloron, saw the practice observed in the time of Lords Boniface IX, Innocent VI, Gregory XI, John XXIII, and Martin V, and at the time when [lacuna] with golden tongs the consecrated Hosts and [Col. 1332B] places them in the large gilded cup dedicated for this purpose. He made a circuit in the same way and handed it to the subdeacon, both of them kneeling. The subdeacon carries it to the pope and always holds it before the pope until everyone has received Communion.

The deacon remains at the altar, holding the chalice with his left hand over the right horn of the altar and the tube in his right hand. With it he gives to drink of Christ’s blood to all who have received Communion from the pope, saying to each one: “May the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ preserve my [read: your] soul unto eternal life. Amen.” He kisses each one.

It should be noted that the cardinal deacons first receive Communion two by two according to the order of their priorate, namely after the deacon and subdeacon. Second come the chaplains, auditors, and acolytes, wearing cottas and surplices, two by two. Note that the pope kisses only the cardinals who receive Communion today, and no one else in that Communion.

Third come the notaries in woolen copes and the penitentiaries. Fourth come the barons and knights according to their order, after removing their mantles and hoods. Finally, anyone who wishes, provided he has truly confessed and is penitent.

It should also be noted that everyone who receives Communion customarily offers something upon the altar after receiving Communion; all of it belongs to the sacristan and chaplains. It should further be noted that after receiving the blood of Christ, each person must drink a little wine from the chalice held by the sacristan or by an acolyte holding the chalice.

It should be noted that on this day our lord the pope is not accustomed to wash his fingers with wine, nor to drink wine, as he customarily does, after giving Communion to the subdeacon. Instead he does so only after everyone has received Communion, and not such a small amount. The subdeacon likewise does not drink wine until everyone has received Communion.

If anything of the body of Christ remains on the paten, the pope alone must consume it; and if anything of Christ’s blood remains in the chalice, the subdeacon must consume it.

After everyone has received Communion, the pope’s confessor comes, if he is a bishop. If he is not, another bishop from the pope’s household brings the covered chalice, with one end of a gold cloth over its top and the other end hanging over his left shoulder, as is customary. The senior acolyte follows the bishop carrying the cruets [Col. 1333A] of wine and water and two small basins, covered with the cloth with which the pallium is covered.

The aforesaid bishop proceeds with the acolyte before the pope, and the subprior of the bishops washes a small gold basin with wine. He then pours wine over the pope’s fingers, and the same subprior carries this washing of the fingers to the altar; the cardinal deacon drinks it with the subdeacon, as customary.

The confessor, after washing the chalice, pours wine into it, and the acolyte adds water, both kneeling before the pope. The lord pope washes his mouth and drinks the wine from the aforesaid chalice. If anything remains, the subdeacon consumes it at the altar.

The pope then washes his hands in large gold basins. After washing them, he approaches the altar and thus completes his Mass.

Note that every person, whatever his condition or status, who has truly confessed and is truly penitent and contrite in heart, may today receive the body of Christ from the pope’s hands without the permission of the bishop, [Col. 1333B] parish priest, or another superior.

[Note: [Col. 1333D] This was observed because of the law requiring Paschal Communion to be received in each person’s own church.]

It should be noted that the pope’s butlers must bring three or four large measures of pure and excellent wine for Communion. The wine that remains, both from the great Masses and from the small papal Masses, always belongs to the sacristan.

When all communicants have received the blood, the lord deacon gives the tube or reed to the subdeacon to suck from both ends, and afterward gives him the chalice so that he may consume what remains of Christ’s blood. When this has been done, the deacon folds the corporals and also removes the cloth placed upon the altar.

Then, when the pope comes to the altar, the same deacon removes his mitre, returns afterward to his place, and the pope completes his Mass. The deacon says, “Go, the Mass is ended,” with a double Alleluia.

After the pope has given the blessing in the customary manner, the cardinal bishop who served the pope with the book at Mass announces, by the pope’s command and authority, an indulgence of seven years and seven quarantines.

After this indulgence has been announced, the pope, fully vested as he was at Mass, goes to the window to give the people an indulgence of seven years and seven quarantines. His chaplains carrying burning candles precede him, followed by the cross and all the cardinals vested as they had been at Mass. Their ministers proceed before him two by two in their proper order, with the junior cardinals preceding according to their order, while the two cardinal deacons who assisted him at Mass remain with him as his assistants. [Col. 1333D]

He then proceeds in the manner described above to his chamber, where a chair with a footstool should be prepared. When the pope arrives, the deacon who served him first hands the rings to the cardinal bishop who served him with the book, then removes from the lord pope all the vestments he had put on for the Mass. In order, he gives the pope the stole, the fan, and the pastoral cross to kiss.

When he has removed all the vestments, the said cardinal deacon removes his own vestments, and all the cardinals put on their ordinary clothing and return to their own residences. [Col. 1334A] The pope takes the white scarlet hood and cloak, which he wears throughout the Octave, and thus goes to the table.

The acolytes, clerics, and sacristan fold those vestments. Today they eat with the pope: on the right side, first one auditor, second one penitentiary, and so on in order; on the left side, first the subdeacon, second one table companion who is the master of the palace or another person, third one acolyte, and so forth. Pepper is served at the collation after dinner.

### LXXXVI. On Second Vespers on the Same Day

At Second Vespers the pope comes in a white cope and a consistory mitre with gold ornament.

### LXXXVII. On Easter Monday and Tuesday

On Easter Monday and Tuesday there is no sermon, no papal Mass, and the pope does not come to Vespers on those two days, as he does at the Nativity of the Lord, because there is no papal Mass. He neither comes to Vespers nor gives a sermon.

### LXXXVIII. Rubric for the Saturday *in albis*

On the first Saturday after Easter, called *in albis*, it was formerly customary for the prior of the cardinal bishops, or another cardinal, to celebrate before the pope, although in the ordinary course the pope himself was accustomed to celebrate on this day.

The Mass is completed, however it may be said, up to the *Agnus Dei*. When it has been said, the cardinals are vested according to their rank, if the pope does not celebrate, and in the proper order in their white vestments. The *Agnus Dei* is said by the lord pope together with the other cardinals, both prelates and others; afterward the Mass is served in the customary manner. [Col. 1334C]

It must be understood that this solemnity is held only when the *Agnus Dei* are distributed, namely in the first and seventh years.

[Note: [Col. 1334D] See above, chapter 61, at the beginning.]

If the pope celebrates, then all the cardinals and prelates put on their white vestments at the beginning of Mass, as is customarily done at other papal Masses. If someone else celebrates before the pope, whether a cardinal or a prelate, no one should vest until peace has been given to everyone and Communion has been performed at the altar by the celebrant.

It should also be noted that this Mass is not customarily accompanied by a sermon; only the Mass is prescribed, and it has no preceding papal Vespers.

### LXXXIX. What Is to Be Done on the Same Saturday When the Pope Does Not Celebrate

It should nevertheless be understood that when the pope does not celebrate, after hearing a low Mass on that day, he comes vested in a plain white cope with only gold ornament and in a white consistory mitre with pearls.

On that day the prior of the cardinal priests serves the pope wearing a surplice, broad amice, and cope; the priest likewise wears a surplice, but a chasuble rather than a cope; the cardinal deacons wear a tight amice, surplices, tunicle, and dalmatic; and [509] all the other prelates likewise wear copes.

Thus they come to the pope with their mitres. After removing their mitres, they kneel before the pope, and he places two *Agnus Dei* in the mitre that each holds in his hand. After receiving them, they kiss the pope’s right knee and return to their places, removing their vestments and putting on woolen copes.

The other prelates likewise come vested to receive the *Agnus Dei*, but not with their mitres on their heads: they carry them in their hands, and they do not kiss the pope’s right knee. Others who are not vested kiss his foot. The remaining prelates and all others who come to him to receive the *Agnus Dei* kiss the pope’s right foot, not his knee.

Even a king comes immediately after a cardinal to receive candles, ashes, palms, lambs, and wax candles, and other objects belonging to such or similar rites. Two *Agnus Dei* are given to each prelate; to the others, both clerics and laypeople, one.

It should nevertheless be noted that before the prior of the cardinal priests receives his vestments, he receives the peace from the prelate celebrating that day before the pope, and gives the peace to the pope. After it has been given, he goes to vest as described.

It should be understood that Pope Clement VI, in the seventh year of his pontificate, in the year of the Lord 1350, gave three *Agnus Dei* to each cardinal, although in the time of Pope John XXII and Benedict XII it was not customary to give more than two to cardinals and prelates and one to others.

After all those present within the chapel doors have received them, the pope washes his hands a little in his chair. The singers then sing the Postcommunion, and the Mass ends.

After the pope has given the blessing, the prelate performing the office of the Mass that day announces, by the pope’s command, an indulgence of seven years and seven quarantines, since there is not customarily a sermon on that day.

### XC. When the Pope Celebrates

[Col. 1335C]

It should also be noted that if the pope were to celebrate—although in modern times this is not customary—the *Agnus Dei* are distributed in the place, at the time, and in the manner stated above.

Furthermore, it should be understood that Roman pontiffs have not been accustomed to perform this solemnity on this day, either personally or through another, except in the first year of their creation and in the seventh year, and thereafter every seven years. It is indeed true that in the first year they are bound to perform the office on this day in person.

Popes Urban V and Gregory XI did the same at Avignon, and Lord Urban VI did so at Rome in Saint Mary across the Tiber. The latter also gave an *Agnus Dei* after dinner to everyone who wished one, and sent them to the district leaders and officials of the City in the year of the Lord 1378.

[Col. 1335D] It should be understood that in the year of the Lord 1378, Lord Urban VI, at Rome in the church of Saint Mary across the Tiber, gave them in the second year of his creation, since he could not do so in the first year because he had been elected only three weeks earlier. He gave them on Sunday *in albis*, not on Saturday, and celebrated in pontifical vestments. There was no sermon at the Mass, in which he maintained and observed this rite.

After the *Agnus Dei* had been said, [the altar or the chalice] had been covered with a single beautiful and exceedingly thin silk veil. [Note: [Col. 1335D] Supply “the altar” or “the chalice.”] He then proceeded to about the middle of the church. Before him went the subdeacon with the cross, and candle-bearers or acolytes with candlesticks and burning candles. There the subdeacon began to sing this [Col. 1336A] verse:

> Most holy Father, these are the newborn lambs who have announced Alleluia to us; just now they have come to the fountain and have been filled with radiance, Alleluia.

The choir replied, “Thanks be to God, Alleluia.”

He repeated the same procedure a second time when he reached the doors of the chapel or choir, beginning more loudly. A third time, when he reached before the pope’s altar, he followed the same procedure, beginning more loudly, while the pope always sat in his great chair; and each time he knelt.

A cloth having been spread over the pope’s knees, the aforesaid subdeacon, kneeling, always held before the pope a small tray containing the *Agnus Dei*. The pope gave three to each cardinal, two to each prelate, and one to the other clerics and laypeople.

After these had been distributed, he washed his hands and completed his Mass. Having removed the large sacred vestments, he put on a cope and a consistory mitre with gold ornament, sat in consistory inside the chapel enclosure, and kept one foot outside the chapel doors. He gave one *Agnus Dei* to everyone who came, and each person kissed one of his feet; the cardinals and prelates were vested as on the feast of the Candles.

After dinner, the chamberlains came with a large tray containing *Agnus Dei*, and the pope gave two *Agnus Dei* to each of his servants and household members. Twenty-four were made that year by Brother Peter, bishop of Senigallia, the sacristan.

It should be explained how the said Brother Peter, bishop, made those *Agnus Dei*. First, pure and very white wax was placed upon the altar of Saint Peter the Apostle. It was then handed over to him by the clerics of the chamber and by the master of the pope’s waxworks. After receiving it, he prepared it that day with the old chrism remaining from the preceding year.

He also mixed it with new chrism, however, for greater devotion, and impressed it in the seals or molds assigned for this purpose. Then he blessed it, just as candles are blessed on the feast of the Candles, with the words changed. Finally, he immersed them in holy water.

It should further be understood that the pope is accustomed always to wear a white chasuble without vestments and without any gold ornament, whether at Mass, at Vespers, or otherwise, whenever there is a principal Mass and Vespers, and whenever there is a procession and he comes into public.

Moreover, on Holy Thursday, on Easter Day, on the vigil, on the Saturday *in albis*, and on the feast of the Nativity of the Lord, there is customarily no sermon; nor is there one on the Purification of the Blessed Virgin Mary or on Palm Sunday.

### XCI. Rubric for the Feast of the Ascension of the Lord

On the day of the Ascension of the Lord, a sermon and Mass are prescribed, but not Vespers, although the pope comes in a red samite cope and a consistory mitre with gold ornament. The cardinals must also come in white copes, and they begin the antiphons as at other Vespers.

It should be noted that on this day general and particular processions may be held, and are customarily held according as necessity requires, in the morning before the pope comes to Mass. [Col. 1337A]

### XCII. Rubric for the Mass on the Vigil of Pentecost

On the vigil of Pentecost, if the pope wishes to celebrate his Mass privately and quietly, he himself reads all the lessons as they are written in the Roman Missal, and makes the confession before the first lesson in the customary manner.

At the great Mass, after making the customary reverence before the altar, the pope ascends to the great chair and sits. The first lesson is then read, followed by all the others. During the litanies the pope kneels before the altar. When “Sinners” is said, he rises and makes the confession, and he does not descend to the prayers in order to kneel, as described below.

Vespers are also prescribed, as is a drink in the hall. At these the pope comes in a beautiful red cope with pearls and images, and with a precious and solemn mitre. When he comes to Second Vespers, the cardinals simply come to First Vespers in red copes. Mass and a sermon are also prescribed.

### XCIII. On First Vespers and Matins

At First Vespers the lord pope begins the first antiphon, the hymn, and the antiphon at the *Magnificat*. The cardinals begin the other antiphons.

A chaplain always begins *Come, Creator Spirit*, before the pope; the pope repeats *Come, Creator Spirit*. When it has begun, the pope descends from his seat and goes before the chair prepared before the altar. There he kneels and remains kneeling without his mitre for as long as the first verse of the hymn begun by him is sung. When the first verse is finished, he returns to his seat. Everything else is done as is customary at other solemn Vespers.

At Matins, which are sung in the evening at a suitable hour, the lord pope comes without a mitre and without a cope. He begins Matins, gives the blessings at the beginning of the lessons, and says the prayer, and nothing more.

It should be noted that the prelates stand near him, and the senior one serves him with the book and with the incense to be placed in the thurible, provided that no one of higher rank than he—whether protonotary or another—is present.

### XCIV. Rubric for the Office on the Feast of Pentecost

On the feast of Pentecost, if the lord pope celebrates, he begins Terce by singing, “O God, come to my assistance.” Before receiving the pontifical vestments, he begins the hymn and the antiphon, after which [Col. 1337D] the acolyte sings, with the chaplains and singers. The pope, after the cardinal deacon assisting on his right has removed his mitre, says the prayer while singing it. [512] When it has been said, the same cardinal deacon replaces the mitre on his head, and, sitting, he says *How lovely*, etc., together with those prayers, while meanwhile the sandals are put on him.

### XCV. On the Procession and Mass on the Same Day

It should be noted that there are seven candlesticks in the procession. The Mass then begins.

After the Alleluia, namely the second one, when the singers are to begin *Come, Holy Spirit*, the pope descends from his seat and goes to the chair prepared before the altar. There he kneels, and his mitre is removed. He remains there until “of your love” is said.

Then, when the sequence of the Holy Spirit is to begin, the pope rises from his seat and, standing there without his mitre, one of the chaplains begins it again before him while singing. The pope sings, “Holy Spirit,” and then sits until the sequence has been said. The other things are done as customary.

On this day the prior of the cardinal bishops serves the pope in the office of chaplain.

It should be understood throughout this entire Octave that red vestments are used, including on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday at Masses, no matter how much is done from the seasonal liturgy.

On that Saturday itself, if the pope celebrates his Mass privately and quietly, before making the confession and before taking the chasuble, he reads at the horn of the altar [Col. 1338B] all those lessons together with the litanies, as they are contained in the Roman Missal. After reading them, he puts on the chasuble, makes the confession in the customary manner, and says “Glory to God in the highest.”

### XCVI. On the Feast of the Most Holy Trinity

On the day of the Holy Trinity, which falls within the Octave of Pentecost, white vestments are used. A sermon and Mass are prescribed.

It has preceding Vespers, though these are not prescribed, even though the cardinals are vested in white and the pope wears a red samite cope and a consistory mitre with gold ornament.

### XCVII. On Matins and Mass

At Matins the pope customarily comes in the evening with his prelates, hears them, and does the other things as at other times. If [Col. 1338C] the lord pope celebrates on that day, the prior of the cardinal bishops serves him in the office of chaplain.

At Mass there is no commemoration of Sunday, although at First Vespers and Matins there is a ninth lesson, a commemoration at the blessing, and a commemoration at Second Vespers. This feast has no Octave.

Nevertheless, if it falls on the feast of Saint Barnabas, we celebrate the Trinity and make no commemoration of Saint Barnabas.

It should be noted that this passage is corrupt. The text reads: “In the year of the Lord 1312, in the pontificate of Lord Boniface VIII, on the day of the Holy Trinity, [he] celebrated before [the pope] in the great chapel, [Col. 1338D] because the pope was not feeling well”; and there was a sermon. [Note: [Col. 1337D] This corrupt passage appears to require the following restoration: “In the year of the Lord 1390, the first year of the pontificate of Lord Boniface IX, on the day of the Holy Trinity, Cosmas, namely the cardinal of Bologna, celebrated,” concerning whom see chapter one hundred.]

### XCVIII. Rubric for the Feast of Corpus Christi

On the day of Corpus Christi, a sermon and Mass are prescribed. [Col. 1338D] Preceding Vespers are customarily prescribed by special favor for the sake of devotion, and then the pope comes in a beautiful cope and a precious and solemn mitre. If they are not prescribed, he comes in a simple cope of samite.

In either case, the cardinals come and are vested in white vestments, and begin the antiphons.

### XCIX. On Matins and Mass

Matins are also sung in the evening, and the pope attends wearing a cloak without a mitre.

If processions are held, the cardinal bishops wear [Col. 1339A] copes, the cardinal priests chasubles, and the cardinal deacons dalmatics.

In the Mass we use white vestments. If the pope celebrates, the first among the cardinal bishops serves him in the office of chaplain. If he does not celebrate, the first among the cardinal priests serves him.

## C. On the feasts that occur within the Octave of Corpus Christi

Of the feasts that occur within the Octave of Corpus Christi, nothing is done, except for the feasts of the Blessed John the Baptist; of John and Paul; and of the apostles Peter and Paul. If the feast of Saint John the Baptist falls on the day of the feast of Corpus Christi, nothing is done for it on that day, but it is celebrated on the following day; and the Octave of the Blessed John the Baptist, falling within the Octave of Corpus Christi, is celebrated on the following day, and on the third day a commemoration of Saint Paul is made.

It should also be noted that in the year of our Lord 1382, the fifth year of the most holy father in Christ, Lord Urban VI, the feast of the Blessed Barnabas the Apostle fell on a Wednesday within the Octave of Corpus Christi. We did nothing for it—neither a commemoration nor anything else—and there was no consistory; rather, we celebrated the Octave, and continued in this way throughout it. On Friday we celebrated Saint Barnabas after the Octave. The same was done in the year 1389. If the feast of the Blessed John falls on the day of the Octave of Corpus Christi, the office is celebrated for Saint John with a commemoration of the Octave, and on Friday [Note: [Col. 1339D] This rite is not in use in our time; nor is the Octave ever deferred to the following day.] the Octave is celebrated.

On the day of Corpus Christi, the aforesaid pope was not present at First Vespers, because he was suffering from stones, nor were the cardinals [Col. 1339C]; but the patriarch of Grado, his Holiness’s confessor, had the cantors sing Vespers in the great chapel. When these had been said, they immediately also solemnly sang Matins, in the year of our Lord 1392.

The lord cardinals also wished to hear a high Mass with a sermon in the great chapel on the day of Corpus Christi, with the pope absent, contrary to the customs of the Roman Church. For cardinals ought not to assemble either in councils or at Masses without the pope’s permission. The said Mass was celebrated by Cardinal Cosmas of Bologna. Take care not to turn this into a custom, since it is contrary to the status and honor of the Roman pontiff.

## CI. On the rubrics that occur in the month of January, and first on the Circumcision of the Lord

On the Circumcision of the Lord no commemoration is made, either of the Octave or of Saint Martina. This rubric is upheld by an Extravagant of Lord Clement, Pope VI, who decreed that no commemoration should be made of the saints even on double feasts, but that each feast should have its own day, just as the other saints do.

It should also be noted that from the Nativity of the Lord until the Sunday of Lent there are at least six Sundays in the office.

From the Octave of the Epiphany until Septuagesima Sunday there are five Sunday offices, or five Gospels; nevertheless, there is only one proper history, which cannot be transferred to the following Sundays. Therefore, it should be observed that in a year in which there is only one Sunday between the Octave of the Epiphany and Septuagesima, we can by no means celebrate the feast of any saint on that Sunday, however solemn and double it may be, as though that Sunday were placed in the middle of the week.

It should also be known that when there are three or four, five or six Sundays, and so forth, between the Octave of the Epiphany and Septuagesima, if the feast of Saint Sebastian or of Saints Vincent and Anastasius falls on a Sunday, we customarily celebrate the saints with a commemoration of the Sunday at both Vespers, and with nine lessons at Matins. The same applies to the feast of Saint Antony.

## CII. On Saint Agnes

On the feast of Saint Agnes, if it falls on a Sunday, the office is celebrated for the saint with a commemoration of the Sunday and nine lessons, when there are that many Sundays; in the Octave, however, the office is celebrated for the Sunday with a commemoration of Saint Agnes.

## CIII. On the Conversion of Saint Paul

It should also be known that if the Conversion of Saint Paul falls on a Sunday, the office is celebrated for Saint Paul with a commemoration of the Sunday, unless it falls on Septuagesima Sunday, for then the office is celebrated for the Sunday without a commemoration of Saint Paul.

It should also be known that those Epistles of Paul which cannot be read on Sundays because those Sundays are impeded by feasts or because of the brevity of the weeks [Col. 1340C] ought to be read and distributed throughout the weekdays.

## CIV. On the month of February: the Purification of the Blessed Virgin Mary

It should be known that if the feast of the Purification of the Blessed Virgin Mary falls on a Sunday, the feast is celebrated with a commemoration of the Sunday. It should nevertheless be noted that if the feast is transferred to Monday, and the office is celebrated for the Sunday because it is a Sunday having a proper history, which cannot be sung and transferred to the following Sunday. Therefore, it should be noted that all Sundays from Septuagesima until and including the Sunday in albis have a proper history; consequently, no feast is celebrated on those Sundays.

It should be known that in the year of our Lord 1381, from the Nativity, in the time of the most holy Lord Urban VI, in the fourth year of his pontificate, the feast of the Purification fell on Septuagesima Sunday. Because of the gathering and devotion of the Romans and those asking for candles, it was ordered that candles be given and that the office be celebrated for the Sunday, not for the Blessed Virgin. But, with due reverence, this ought not to have been done, since the feast yields to the Sunday, and the candles are worth as much on Monday as on Sunday [Note: [Col. 1339D] In the year of our Lord 1483, during the pontificate of Sixtus IV, the pontiff ordered the solemnity of the Purification, which fell on Sexagesima Sunday [Col. 1340D], to be transferred to the following day; and on that day the old custom concerning the candles was maintained, as James Maffei testifies in his Diary.].

It should be known that in the year from the Nativity of the Lord 1352, on the feast of the Chair of Saint Peter, which was the first day of Lent, namely Ash Wednesday, Lord Clement VI, in the tenth year of his pontificate, at Avignon, in the great chapel of the apostolic palace, established and ordered to be proclaimed, for perpetual remembrance, in a sermon delivered on that day before the said Lord Pope, the cardinals, and other prelates: whenever any feast should fall on that first day of Lent, however double it might be, that feast was to be transferred to the following day, and thereafter the office was to be celebrated for the weekday of Ash Wednesday.

In the year 1388, during the pontificate of Lord Urban VI … in the church of Saint Mary across the Tiber, funeral rites were held for the emperor. The pope attended the Mass wearing a closed woolen scarlet cloak and a white mitre. There were eighty tapers, supplied by the Camera, and two cloths of gold. The lord pope gave judgment that everything belonged to the sacristy and was its legal property. He therefore took all the candles and the aforesaid cloths, but left the wax because of the poverty of the Camera.

It should also be noted that in the same year … on Wednesday, 9 February, all the cardinals who were then in the august City received Communion at Saint Mary across the Tiber, in the small chapel and privately, at their Mass, from his hand: first, the lord Cardinal of Alençon; then the Cardinal of Grado Minor, the Cardinal of Chieti, the Cardinal of Corsica, Agapitus of Colonna, the Cardinal of Aversa, the Dominican Cardinal of Tiberias, the Cistercian Cardinal, the Cardinal of Nocera, the Cardinal of Rieti, Desangro, the Cardinal of Petramala, the Neapolitan Cardinal, the Dominican Cardinal Mesquinus, the Paduan Cardinal [Col. 1341C], and the Augustinian Cardinal.

## CV. On the month of March: the Annunciation of the Blessed Virgin Mary

If the feast of the Annunciation falls in Lent, consult the proper rubric in its place.

It should be noted that this feast fell on the Thursday before Rose Sunday in the year of our Lord 1389. It did not have First Vespers; but on that day, after Mass had been celebrated at Saint Peter’s, our most holy lord Urban VI, dressed in this manner, seated on the stone cathedra, solemnly began Vespers. He began the first Antiphon and the Antiphon at the Magnificat, and incensed the altar, remaining throughout in sacred vestments as at Mass. He ordered the cardinals to remain dressed in the same way as they had been at Mass. When Vespers had been said, the pope and the cardinals removed their sacred vestments; but the pope, seated on the wooden cathedra, and the cardinals, each in his own place, began the Antiphons.

It should be noted that this feast fell on the Monday after Passion Sunday in the year of our Lord 1300 [99], in the eleventh year of Pope Boniface’s pontificate. It had no preceding Vespers because of the severe cold; but they were sung on Monday immediately after Mass. The cantors began the Antiphons, and the pope wore a red cope as at Mass. The Cardinal of Naples said the Mass.

## CVI. On the month of April: the rubric concerning Saint Mark

It should be known that if the feast of Saint Mark or another feast falls on the Sunday in albis or within the Octave of Easter [Col. 1342A], nothing is done for the feast on that day; rather, it is transferred to Monday.

## CVII. On the month of May: the Finding of the Holy Cross

It should be noted that the Finding of the Holy Cross is a double feast and has a proper office. No commemoration of the saints is made; the entire office is for the Cross. If the aforesaid feast falls on any Sunday, the entire office is celebrated for the feast with a commemoration of the Sunday, since it is a double feast. Its history may be transferred to the following Sunday.

## CVIII. On the month of June: the Sundays that occur between Pentecost and Advent

The rubric concerning the Sundays that occur between Pentecost and Advent [Col. 1342B] is explicit, and their number is fixed.

## CIX. On Saint Barnabas the Apostle

As for Saint Barnabas, when his feast falls within the Octave of Corpus Christi, nothing is done for him.

## CX. On the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist

On the Nativity of the Blessed John the Baptist, a Mass and a sermon are ordered. At First Vespers the pope comes in a red cope and a consistorial mitre; the cardinals come in white copes and begin the Antiphons. In the evening the lord pope is present at Matins. At the Mass of the Blessed John the Baptist no commemoration is made, even if it falls on a Sunday [perhaps: “provided that it does not”]; nor is the Creed said unless it falls on a Sunday.

In the year 1389, the feast of the Blessed John the Baptist fell within the Octave of Corpus Christi. On that day we celebrated Saint John with a commemoration of the Octave at both Vespers, at Matins, and at Mass, notwithstanding the constitution of Lord John the Pope to the contrary, which the canons of Saint Peter’s display.

Then, on the following feast of the apostles Peter and Paul, while the pope was celebrating at Saint Peter’s, after *Ite, Missa est*, before he withdrew from the altar, the ancient Banderenses came barefoot from the Capitol to the altar of Saint Peter, without hoods, with straps around their necks, and wearing only a single simple jupon, with candles in their hands. They sought pardon from the pope because they had been excommunicated for refusing to receive the senator whom the pope had appointed. The pope did not wish to hear them, but entrusted them to the supreme penitentiary who was present there, so that he might absolve them. At the pope’s command, the penitentiary ascended the stone cathedra of Saint Peter at the head of the church, stood there holding a staff in his hands, and, saying “Have mercy on me, O God,” and so forth, publicly absolved them before the pope had departed from his place.

In the same place he had the feast of the Visitation of the Blessed Mary announced by the man who had preached.

On 2 July the same lord pope celebrated the first Mass of the said office of the Visitation at Saint Mary Major, where on that day he granted, for all future time, seven years and seven quadragenas of indulgences.

## CXI. On the rubric concerning the Vigil of the apostles Peter and Paul

On the vigil of the Blessed Apostles Peter and Paul [Col. 1343A], we celebrate Saint Leo. The Mass is said for the Vigil with a commemoration of Saint Leo, as the rubric states. Vespers and Mass are ordered.

At First Vespers, therefore, Our Lord comes in a precious red cope and a solemn mitre, and the cardinals in red copes; they begin the Antiphons. Refreshment is to be served in the hall in the evening. The pope is present at Matins. At Mass only one Prayer is said. Terce is sung, and there are seven candlesticks. Let everything else be done as on the other occasions. The first of the cardinal bishops serves the pope at Mass.

## CXII. On the month of July: the Visitation of the Blessed Virgin Mary

On 2 July the feast of the Visitation of the Blessed Virgin Mary is to be celebrated as a totally double feast, with a commemoration of the apostles. There are preceding Vespers and a Mass, which were said by the Cardinal of Bologna in the year of our Lord 1392 by order of our most holy lord, Pope Boniface VIII, as is recorded under 3 Kalends on that date.

## CXIII. On Saint Martial

We celebrate Saint Martial on the second day after the Octave of the Blessed Apostles Peter and Paul. On the following day there is to be a Mass for the dead for the brothers and Roman pontiffs [Note: [Col. 1343] That is, for the cardinals, who in former times were simply called “brothers.”].

## CXIV. On the office for deceased brothers and Roman pontiffs

It should be noted that on the eighth day of this July the office for the dead is to be celebrated for the brothers and Roman pontiffs.

## CXV. On Saint James

On the day of Saint James the Apostle no commemoration is made of Saint Christopher [Col. 1343C].

## CXVI. On the feast of Saints Processus and Martinian

If the feast of Saints Processus and Martinian falls on a Sunday, it is not celebrated on that day, because there is no proper office for them; it is therefore transferred to Monday. On Saturday at Vespers we celebrate the office of the Octave of Saint John up to the Chapter. The Chapter, however, is to be said from the Common of Apostles; the Hymn is *Exsultet*; the Antiphon at the Magnificat is *Gloriosi*. Afterwards a commemoration is made of Saint John and of the Sunday, if there is an appropriate place for it.

This rubric is stated more clearly in the common rubrics, in the paragraph that begins: “When a feast is celebrated within an Octave on a Sunday.”

## CXVII. On Saint Anne

It should also be noted when the Roman pontiffs customarily celebrate Saint Anne, mother of the glorious Virgin Mary [Col. 1343D].

## CXVIII. On the month of August: the Maccabees

The feast of the holy Maccabees is to be celebrated separately, because the entire office is for the Chains of Saint Peter.

## CXIX. On Saint Eusebius

Saint Eusebius is likewise to be celebrated as a separate feast.

## CXX. On the Assumption of the Blessed Mary

It should be noted that on the feast of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary, Vespers, the sermon, and Mass are ordered, and refreshment is served in the hall.

At First Vespers the lord pope comes in a beautiful white cope and a precious mitre. The cardinals likewise come in white copes and begin the Antiphons. When the pope has begun the Hymn, he remains there in his cathedra, kneeling, for as long as the first verse is said. Matins are sung without a mitre, and the pope customarily attends. At Mass the first of the cardinal bishops serves the pope in the office of chaplain. Let everything else be done as on the other solemn occasions. In the second year, Lord Urban VI had the bishops of Cremona and Senigallia sit before him in the place of the deacons at First Vespers, because there was no one except the Cardinal of Saint Peter’s.

## CXXI. On Saint Augustine

At the feast of the Blessed Augustine, our father, the Creed, “I believe in one God,” is said at Mass; and this is also done at all the feasts of the four holy doctors, Gregory, Augustine, Jerome, and Ambrose, by a constitution of Lord Pope Gregory XI and Urban VI. At Second Vespers we celebrate the entire office for Saint Augustine with a commemoration of the Beheading of Saint John the Baptist, because it is a double feast by a decretal of Lord Boniface VIII, in the Clementines of Boniface.

## CXXII. On Saint Hermes

On the day of the Blessed Augustine no commemoration is to be made of Saints Hermes and Julian; rather, each feast is to be celebrated separately.

## CXXIII. On Saint Sabina

No commemoration is to be made of Saint Sabina on the Beheading of Saint John; rather, she is to be celebrated separately, according to the form I gave at the beginning of this book concerning a saint or holy woman who is neither a virgin nor a martyr.

## CXXIV. On the month of September: the rubric concerning the histories to be placed

In the year of our Lord 1389, in the twelfth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Urban VI, 1 September was a Wednesday, and the Beheading of Saint John fell on the Sunday in question. According to certain ancient rubrics, some said that we ought then to celebrate the Sunday and place Job, since it was the first history, and not celebrate Saint John. Our lord the pope ordered that Saint John be celebrated, because the history of Job could be transferred to the following Sunday.

According to that rubric, whenever a double feast of an apostle or evangelist, or a feast having certain proper Responsories, falls on the Sunday on which the first history is placed, and that history can be transferred to the following Sunday [Col. 1344D], the office is then celebrated for the saint and not for the Sunday. Thus we acted: on the third Sunday we placed Tobit, and in the four Ember Days.

## CXXV. On Saint Giles

On the first day of September, in the province of Provence, the office is celebrated for Saint Giles. Therefore, note that both in Provence and elsewhere the Roman Ordo customarily celebrates his feast separately, and also celebrates the feast of the Twelve Brothers separately.

## CXXVI. On the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary

On the feast of the Nativity of the Virgin Mary, a sermon and Mass are ordered. At First Vespers the lord pope comes in a red cope and a consistorial mitre ornamented with gold fringe; the cardinals come in white copes and begin the Antiphons. Matins are sung in the evening, and the pope attends. At Mass only one Prayer is said, and the first of the cardinal bishops serves in it. Nowadays the lord pope comes at First Vespers with a solemn and precious mitre, and he has a Vigil composed by Lord Gregory XI in the city of Anagni in Campania.

## CXXVII. On Saint Adrian

Saint Adrian is to be celebrated as a feast, not merely commemorated.

## CXXVIII. On the Exaltation of the Holy Cross

On the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, the entire office is to be for the Cross, because it is a new office; the saints are to be celebrated on another day. As for the history to be placed, let it be done according to the proper rubric. It should also be noted that, concerning all the commemorations throughout the year mentioned in these places, by a certain Extravagant of Lord Pope Clement VI, a special feast is celebrated.

## CXXIX. On the month of October: Saints Sergius and Bacchus, and Saint Mark the Pope

On the day of Saints Sergius and Bacchus there is the feast of Saint Mark the Pope; his feast is celebrated separately.

## CXXX. On the month of November: the feast of All Saints

On the feast of All Saints, the sermon, Mass, and preceding Vespers are ordered; refreshment is to be served in the hall. At these First Vespers, therefore, our lord the pope comes in a beautiful white cope and a solemn and precious mitre. The cardinals likewise come in white copes and begin the Antiphons. At Mass only one Prayer is said. Neither at Vespers nor at Matins is a commemoration made of Saint Caesarius or of the Sunday; the feast of Saint Caesarius is transferred. Terce is said. At Mass there are to be seven candlesticks in the procession.

## CXXXI. On Second Vespers

At Second Vespers the pope comes in a red cope and a consistorial mitre. The cardinals do not vest themselves or begin the Antiphons as at First Vespers. This is always observed at Second Vespers of every feast. Consequently, neither the acolytes, nor the auditors, nor even the subdeacon stand in surplices, but in woolen capes.

When Vespers have ended and the pope has given the Blessing, he removes the aforesaid cope and mitre there, and puts on a scarlet samite cape, open from the middle of the chest down to the feet, a red biretta, and a simple white garnello mitre. Meanwhile the cantors sing *Placebo*.

In the year 1428, in the eleventh year of the pontificate of Lord Martin, on the day of All Saints at Second Vespers, the pope did not come to the chapel, where the following order was observed. The lord Cardinal of Saint Marcellus celebrated Vespers, began *Deus, in adjutorium meum intende*, and said the Prayer of the feast with a commemoration of Saint Caesarius. He remained in the office of Vespers wearing a white cope and a mitre with pearls. When Vespers had been said, he gave the Blessing. After it had been given, he removed the said cope and took up his everyday cloth cape; wearing that cape, he stood in the place where he had previously stood.

Meanwhile, the cantors began to sing Vespers for the dead and continued those Vespers, while the said lord cardinal stood or sat in the said cape on the faldstool and without a mitre. When the cantors had completed those Vespers up to the Magnificat, the cardinal said the Prayer, and two of his acolytes held two candlesticks with lighted candles for him. When these had ended, Matins for the dead began. The aforesaid cardinal always stood as at Vespers, with the said candlesticks. The altar was incensed at the Magnificat and at the Benedictus.

The two cardinals and the first among the cardinal priests who had stood before the pope stand and sit as before, before the pope, on their stools. At the Magnificat the pope approaches the altar, and the altar and the vessel in which the Body of Christ is placed are incensed [Note: [Col. 1345D] The same vessel was discussed above in chapter 1.]. After returning to his cathedra, incense is given to him alone and to no one else. He says the Prayer, namely, “God, creator of all the faithful.”

It should be noted that during the office for the dead incense is used at the Magnificat and at the Benedictus. First the altar is incensed, and then the pope; no one else is incensed.

It should be noted that the pope gives the Blessing after the said Prayer.

It should also be noted that, if the pope wishes, he may remove the scarlet cape there after Vespers and put on the cope again. In fact, the customary practice, for the sake of propriety, is for him to return to his chamber wearing the aforesaid cape. Nevertheless, Roman pontiffs have sometimes, after the completion of Vespers for the dead, listened to all of Matins for the dead sung by the cantors, standing in the said cape and wearing a white mitre. When the Antiphons for the dead have been completed, the pope rises and stands for a short time, until the cantors begin the lessons. Everything else is done in order concerning the Prayer, incensing, and candlesticks, as at Vespers for the dead.

## CXXXII and CXXXIII. On the office for the dead

At the Mass for the dead he comes in the aforesaid cape and with a simple white mitre. On this day the deacon and subdeacon use a tunicella and dalmatic, not chasubles; and the subdeacon carries the cross before the pope. Lights are carried at the Gospel, but not incense. After the *Sanctus* has been said, he immediately descends from his cathedra and goes before the altar, where he remains kneeling until the *Pater noster*. At this Mass no Blessing is given after Mass or at the Gospel; neither the book nor the pope’s foot is kissed. No one receives incense except the pope; the altar is incensed only at the Offertory, and then only the pope is incensed. One Prayer is said. The cardinals have always customarily celebrated this Mass.

When the Mass has ended, the prelate performing the office immediately removes the chasuble and takes a large cope. Meanwhile the cantors sing *Libera me, Domine, de morte aeterna*. The aforesaid prelate performs the absolution as it is contained in the Missal, and only one Prayer is said, namely, “God, creator of all the faithful,” and so forth.

It should be noted that gloves and sandals are never worn at Masses for the dead; no Blessing is given, and the book is not kissed. If the pope celebrates, neither the deacon nor the subdeacon receives Communion from the pope’s hands. Nor is it customary for Roman pontiffs to celebrate pontifically for the dead; rather, they celebrate privately.

## CXXXIV. On the sermon at Masses for the dead

It should be noted that there is no sermon at this Mass, nor should one ever be given before the Roman pontiff for the dead; nor does he ever celebrate pontifically for the dead, but privately.

It should also be known that the Roman Curia does not customarily have a sermon at Masses for the dead whenever corpses are present, however noble they may be. In modern times the contrary of this rubric is observed.

It should also be known that at Masses for soldiers, barons, dukes, counts, kings, and emperors celebrated before the pope, there is never a sermon; nor is there one in the pope’s absence when cardinals are present. But if there are no cardinals, a sermon may be given.

It should be noted that if the Roman emperor should die in the Roman Curia, whether in the City or outside it, a sermon ought to be given after the Mass. It is to be delivered by a cardinal, and the cardinals are then present.

It should also be noted that a sermon ought to be given only for a Roman pontiff or a cardinal on the day of burial, and only in the presence of the cardinals, except in the case of the emperor.

It should be noted that at the funeral rites of Lord Urban VI they wished to have a sermon every day throughout the novena, and they did so contrary to custom.

## CXXXV. On Saint Martin and Saint Clement: rubric

On the day of Saint Martin no commemoration is made of Saint Mennas. If the feast of Saint Martin or Saint Clement falls on the fourth Sunday of November, on which the twelve Minor Prophets are appointed, the office is celebrated for the saint, because he has three Responsories and the Minor Prophets are read throughout the week. This is not a proper history.

## CXXXVI. On the rubric concerning the mitre

Take careful note, and note it well, as it appears in the rubric concerning the wearing of the mitre: whenever the pope, vested, wears a mitre on his head during the office, two deacons stand before him, together with one cardinal priest.

## CXXXVII. On the wearing of the cape

But note that on Good Friday, when the pope stands in a woolen cape, open from the middle of the chest down to the feet, they do not stand before him, since he does not customarily wear a mitre, nor a folded hood over his head. The same applies on the night of the Nativity.

## CXXXVIII. On the wearing of the cape and mitre in the offices for the dead

On the day of the dead, at Vespers and at Mass [Col. 1348A], he wears that cape and the white mitre on his head, with the cape around his neck. Then two sit before him without stools, and the cardinal priest sits on a stool. At that time the cardinal bishop does not customarily serve him. It should also be noted that if the pope does not wish to wear the mitre on that day or on those days, they do not stand before him.

## CXXXIX. On the cape at the Nativity of the Lord

At the Nativity of the Lord, at Matins, he comes in a woolen cape and does not wear a mitre. Therefore, the deacons do not sit before him during the office of Matins. Roman pontiffs have sometimes also customarily attended Matins of the Nativity of the Lord, and Matins on those three days of Holy Week, at the Vigil of Easter, the Vigil of Pentecost, Corpus Christi, the apostles Peter and Paul, the Assumption of the Virgin Mary, and the Vigil of All Saints. He never wears a mitre or cope at those Matins, nor do the cardinal deacons sit before him in their places.

## CXL. On changing vestments at Vespers of All Saints

It should also be known that on the day of All Saints, after the day’s Vespers have been said and the Blessing given, the pope removes his mitre, cope, and stole there. He takes a stole without pearls, a red biretta, and a closed, ermine-lined cape, open from the chest down to the feet. Thus he sits, while two cardinals sit before him without stools and the first of the cardinal priests sits there as well.

At the Magnificat the pope incenses the altar and says the Collect for the dead, as it appears in the Breviary. No Blessing is given after these Vespers. When they have ended, the cantors begin Matins for the dead, and the pope, having removed his mitre, sits there in his red biretta. He keeps the hood of the cape over his head without folding it back, as on Good Friday. The aforesaid three cardinals go to sit in their places. At the Benedictus the pope incenses the altar; incense is given to him alone and to no one else. When he says the Collect, the aforesaid three cardinals return to him in the customary manner.

It should also be known that in the year from the Nativity of the Lord 1389, on Thursday, 8 April, our most holy lord Urban VI, in the twelfth year of his pontificate reckoned from his election, heard a Mass for his election after the ferial Mass. He came in a red cloak, as he had been at the ferial Mass, and without a cross. He remained in this manner in the great chapel throughout the Mass, which was said by the lord Cardinal of Naples.

Immediately afterward he entered the public consistory wearing a cope and a mitre ornamented with gold fringe and pearls. The master of the Sacred Palace proposed the feast of the Visitation under this theme: “How is this to me, that the master of my Lord should come before me?” After the sermon, our lord reassumed the same cloak and delivered an address there. In that address, with a bull, he granted the following:

First, that the feast of the Visitation of the Blessed Mary should be celebrated within the Octave of Saint John the Baptist.

Second, that on the day of Corpus Christi it should be celebrated throughout the world, with the doors open, notwithstanding any interdict whatsoever. He granted one hundred days of indulgence in addition to the former ones.

Third, he granted a Jubilee year every twenty-four years.

Fourth, he placed the church of Saint Mary Major among the four churches, since the first church was Saint Peter’s, the second Saint Paul’s, the third Saint John Lateran, and the fourth is now Saint Mary Major, namely, Saint Mary of the Snows.

Fifth, he confirmed the privileges of all churches in the City without exception, as is set out more fully in the bull.

## CXLI. The new rubrics and their explanations, which are imperfectly found in the books

First, it should be known that no history is called “proper” unless it has at least nine lessons and nine Responsories.

It should also be known that those Sundays which have three or six Responsories and the remainder … [the text requires *retro* or *ante*] are not called proper histories. The reason is that a thousand imperfect things do not make a perfect one; therefore, a history is called proper when nothing is lacking. Accordingly, note that on such Sundays as do not have a complete history, the Roman Church customarily celebrates a current double feast, but only on such Sundays and not on others, unless it can be transferred to the following Sunday.

It should also be noted that all four Sundays of the Advent of the Lord have a proper history. Therefore, they are not moved from their places, except for the fourth Sunday, when the feast of Saint Thomas falls on the fourth Sunday.

## CXLII. On feasts during the weekdays of Advent or Lent that have proper Lauds

Concerning the feasts celebrated on those weekdays of Advent that have proper Lauds, know that after the Prayer of the day a commemoration of the weekday is made. When everything for the feast has been completed, Lauds of the weekday are said again with five Antiphons and five Psalms, as ordered, without a Chapter, Hymn, Blessing, or Prayer. After *Laudate Dominum de caelis*, with its Antiphon, Lauds conclude.

This appears to be what the rubric means that begins: “It should be known that the Roman Church does not customarily make a commemoration of the weekdays, except only in Advent and Lent, when the office is celebrated for a feast.”

**Lord Boniface, Pope VIII.**

In the year 1389, on 2 November, the reverend Lord Peter de Thomacellis, cardinal priest, was unanimously and concordantly elected pope in the City. What he did at Rieti and Perugia is recorded in my Itinerary concerning my lord Pope Gregory XI and concerning him.

## CXLIII. On the pope when ill

It should be known that the following procedure is customarily observed in the Roman Curia when the Roman pontiff is ill. When the physicians caring for him know that death is approaching and that he cannot escape it [Col. 1350A], they are bound to tell him privately that, whatever happens, he should think about his soul, beginning with his deeds. They themselves, insofar as they can, will attend to the health of his body.

They are then bound to reveal this privately to his confessor, so that the confessor may direct him to think about the salvation of his soul, exhorting and admonishing him generally and specifically according to the confessor’s knowledge and discretion. Above all, he should be reminded that he is the light of the whole world and therefore ought to give an example to all kings and princes, lay and clerical, who in illness turn to God and put their consciences in order. He, who is the head of all Christendom, ought to do the same. He is also bound to confess, receive the Lord’s Body, and ask for an indulgence at the point of death, which the same confessor ought to grant him. He should pardon all his household and remit to them ill-gotten goods and thefts up to the sum of one hundred florins, as it may please His Holiness, just as Pope Gregory remitted up to six hundred florins.

He should also grant all his household an indulgence at the point of death under the seal of some prelate of his household.

Finally, the same pope, or his chamberlain, ought to summon his cardinals two or three days before his death, before he loses the power of speech. In their presence he ought to make his testament and choose his burial place.

He ought to declare that he is dying and wishes to die in the unity of the faith; that he believes in one Catholic Church and in all the articles of faith, for which he is prepared to die.

He should also declare that he did not conduct himself well in the government of the papacy and that he offended in certain matters; the cardinals should spare him, as should all those whom he offended improperly or unjustly, if he offended any [Note: [Col. 1349D] In the margin the following is written: “Pope Nicholas V did this, so that all the cardinals departed in tears.”].

He should also commend all his household to them.

He must disclose to them the debts he incurred for the Church of God, so that his successor may satisfy them.

He must also disclose who the creditors are, and to whom he and the Roman Church are indebted; and where his treasures, jewels, and goods are, as well as those of the Church.

He must grant the cardinals certain favors in the court of conscience.

He must commend the Church to them, and urge them to provide a good shepherd in peace and tranquility; and, if it should seem good to them, that such a person or persons would be suitable for governing it, according to their conscience.

Finally, he gives them his blessing and tells them to depart in peace.

As he approaches death, the chamberlains must always be ready to serve him, and they must summon his confessor and the prelates of his household to administer the ecclesiastical Sacraments to him. These are to be given according to the form given on page 527 of the *Polyptych* and in the *Roman Pontifical*; afterward, the commendation of the soul is to be made, as contained in that *Pontifical*. While he is in his agony, a prelate or priest must hold before his eyes the consistorial cross, without tail or staff, and frequently have him kiss it, continually bringing the Passion of Christ back to his memory.

Then the chamberlain must be instructed to have all the pope’s goods gathered into a definite and secure place against assault. All officials must hand over and assign to him whatever they have in their custody, and the chamberlains likewise whatever had been entrusted to them. The sacristan, however, is to retain the things in his own possession, since his office is perpetual; he will render an account during the vacancy of the see to the three senior cardinals, and must again have the account reviewed by those three and hold the goods from them.

## CXLIV. On the Pope Once Dead

When the pope has died—or, preferably, while he is in his agony—the penitentiaries are summoned at once. They read before him the Office of the Dead, the seven Penitential Psalms, and whatever is contained in their book. Meanwhile, together with the brothers of the Bull, if they are present, or with those of the Pignotta, they wash the body with water and good herbs, which the chamberlains must prepare. The barber shaves his head and beard.

After he has been washed, the apothecary and the aforesaid brothers of the Bull thoroughly block all his orifices with cotton or tow—anus, mouth, ears, and nostrils—with myrrh, incense, and aloe, if these can be obtained. The body is also washed with white wine warmed with fragrant herbs and with good vernaccia, which the chamberlains or the pope’s cupbearers must supply to the men performing the washing. His throat is filled with aromatics and spices, together with cotton, and his nostrils likewise with musk.

Finally, his face and hands are rubbed and anointed with good balsam. The chamberlain or the chamberlains who guard the balsam, or the sacristan, if they have it, shall provide it.

Then the penitentiaries dress him in breeches, a shirt, leggings, and a tunic. They raise him into an almost seated position and dress him completely in sacred vestments of red: first white sandals, girdle, fanon, stole, tunicle, maniple, dalmatic, gloves, chasuble, and the pallium taken from the body of blessed Peter. They fold the fanon over his head and wrap it around his shoulders, as though he were about to celebrate Mass, and place on his head a white biretta with a white mitre, without pearls and without gold.

The crosses of the pallium contain three pins, as is customary. At least two large torches must always burn before him, together with a sufficient number of small candles.

When he has thus been prepared, the penitentiaries place him on a new bier or litter, on which there must be a good mattress covered with red silk. Above it there must be two connected cloths of gold. Around it they must place and hang his arms and those of the Church, on black or hyacinth-colored silk cloth.

Under his head there shall be a pillow covered with cloth of gold; and behind his feet, on the same bier, another similar pillow with silk fringes and gold cords. Upon it the pope’s two caps or hats are to be placed. The pillows must be as wide as the bier.

It should be understood that the litter is to be placed in the pope’s chamber, where the body has been laid. After the washing, he is lifted into the private chamber and dressed in the sacred vestments, as stated above.

It should be noted, however, that before he is washed and dressed, the lord cardinals, one after another or all together, must visit him. Each absolves him upon arriving and then immediately withdraws.

Once he has been placed on the litter with the cross, a subdeacon dressed in a cope—or in a black cope, if he has one, or another consistorial cope—goes ahead and proceeds to the chapel.

The penitentiaries carry the body while singing *Subvenite, sancti Dei* (“Come to his aid, saints of God”), together with the chapel singers, preceded by at least twenty-five lit torches. These should be carried by the deceased’s nobles, household gentlemen, or squires; if they are unavailable, at least by his armed retainers, and finally by the couriers, if there are no others.

The chamberlain and the other household prelates, together with the entire household, accompany the body with their faces covered by their hoods, and sit in the chapel. Then the singers and penitentiaries sing Vespers of the Dead and the entire Office until the parish churches, canons, and religious of the four orders and of the other orders and monasteries arrive. Each church must sing at least one nocturn with one Collect, namely *Deus, qui inter apostolicos* (“O God, who among the apostolic…”), and sprinkle the funeral bier with holy water and incense it.

On that day the penitentiaries must eat splendidly in the pope’s dining hall, on account of the labor and vigils they have endured. During that night they must keep watch before the bier, either in the pope’s chamber or in the chapel: half of the penitentiaries until midnight and the other half until daybreak, always praying for him. The cupbearers and bakers must always be ready to supply them abundantly with the necessities of life. The master of wax must provide as many candles and torches as they require. If they need confections, the chamberlains must supply them abundantly.

It should be noted that if the chamberlain is a cardinal, he customarily does not accompany the funeral while the body is being washed and carried to the chapel. If he is not a cardinal, he must supervise and arrange everything and accompany the body with the other prelates; his train is carried for him whether he is a cardinal or not.

It should also be noted that as soon as the body has been taken out of the chamber, the chamberlain must receive all the keys to the chambers of the pope’s chamber and summon the three senior cardinals, namely the senior cardinal bishop, cardinal priest, and cardinal deacon. He must assign to them all the pope’s jewels, with inventories in writing only, and give them copies if they request them.

If they wish to inspect everything with their own eyes, he must not oppose them. Instead, all inventories are to be renewed in the presence of the chamberlain and the clerks of the chamber, so that each of the three has a copy and the chamberlain has another, lest fraud be possible.

## CXLV. When the Pope’s Funeral Rites Are Held

It should also be noted that when the funeral rites are held in the chapel, if any cardinals wish to attend, they should sit on the benches without ceremonial vestments, wearing woolen copes not of red color. Throughout the entire novena they should use a color other than the one specified. The benches must not be covered, nor should the chapel be dressed or spread with cloths.

There must be before and around the chapel at least twenty-five torches or brands, each of at least six pounds of wax. Many altars are to be erected in the palace, in the large chapel, and in the small one. The treasurer shall give each celebrating priest five papal grossi for the pope’s soul. Nothing is given from the Church’s treasury, which is wrong.

The lord chamberlain should take care, together with the treasurer, that black cloths are obtained in great quantity and in good time, so that the household members are dressed in them before the funeral leaves the palace. In that procession the pope’s subdeacon must always carry the cross before the bier, and everyone must proceed behind the body in procession, two by two.

First comes the chamberlain himself, dressed in a black cope if he is not a cardinal. In that case his train is not carried, either then or throughout the novena during the funeral rites. If he is a cardinal, he does not dress in black, red, or green, but in other colors; nor may the other cardinals use those colors throughout the novena.

On the first day of burial there must be at least two hundred torches, each of six pounds of wax. At the four corners of the catafalque there is to be one of the aforesaid brands, with another above in the middle, and an abundance of candles around it. These must be lit before Mass begins. Around the catafalque there must be household members dressed in black, including the chamberlain if he is not a cardinal. If he is a cardinal, he stands with the other cardinals in the choir.
