Each cardinal must be given at least one torch of four pounds of wax during the Mass, which one of his squires must hold before him; the same applies to the prelates. The torches of the other prelates are to be of three pounds of wax; those of the penitentiaries and other nobles, one pound; and those of the canons and other priests, one quarter-pound, as the chamberlain sees fit.

The chamberlain must nevertheless ensure that every day there are at least forty torches around the bier or catafalque. Above it there should be no candles except on the first day. During the novena the catafalque is to be surrounded by silk cloth bearing the arms of the pope and the Church. Beneath it there must be a bier covered with two cloths of the finest gold, also bearing the arms. At each end there is to be a pillow covered with the same cloth, one at the head and the other at the foot; and on each pillow there must stand a handsome papal cap throughout the novena.

## CXLVI. On the Masses Throughout the Novena

Each day candles are given to the prelates dressed in black who stand around the bier, as on the first day. If they wish, they may take them away with them. Candles are also given to the penitentiaries and to the canons of the church in which the service is held. After the absolution, however, all lights are extinguished, and then the sermon is preached.

The vested cardinals do not approach the bier; they wait for the four men who absolve the body. It should also be understood that on the first day the senior cardinal bishop must celebrate the first Mass and preach the sermon, or entrust the sermon to a prelate or a master of theology. He may not entrust the Mass to another: if he cannot celebrate, it must be celebrated by the second cardinal bishop, or the third, and so on.

At this Mass only one Collect is said, namely *Deus, qui inter apostolicos* (“O God, who among the apostolic…”). When the Mass has ended, the cardinal who celebrated it, together with the deacon, subdeacon, and assistant dressed in sacred vestments, goes to the place where the other cardinals are standing. The sermon is then preached, and the preacher is not given a blessing.

When the sermon has ended, all the cardinals put on an amice, surplice, black cope, and a simple white mitre of garnello. They go to the body, if it has not been buried, approaching beneath the aforesaid catafalque two by two according to their order, with mitres on their heads. The cardinal who performed the service goes first, whoever he may be.

The singers then sing *Subvenite, sancti Dei* (“Come to his aid, saints of God”). When this is completed, the cardinal, having removed his mitre, incenses the bier, sprinkles it with holy water, and says the aforesaid Collect. The singers then sing *Memento mei, Deus* (“Remember me, O God”), and another cardinal bishop incenses the bier in the same manner and says another Collect.

Third, after another responsory, the senior cardinal priest says another Collect in the same manner. Fourth, the entire clergy sings *Libera me, Domine* (“Deliver me, Lord”), and the second cardinal priest says the final Collect.

All these things are done as they are contained in the *Pontifical*. When they have been completed, everyone returns to his own place after removing the ceremonial vestments.

It should nevertheless be understood that every day there must be a Mass, celebrated by the cardinals in their order, and a sermon by them, unless they entrust it to prelates or masters of theology, and to no others.

## CXLVII. On the Cloth to Be Distributed after the Pope’s Death

It should also be understood that the following custom is observed concerning the distribution of cloth. First, the chamberlain, if he is not a cardinal, together with two chaplains and two squires; likewise the treasurer; likewise the confessor, if he is a prelate: these three lords receive cloth of the same good and noble quality.

The referendaries receive cloth of the same kind. The chamberlains receive another, inferior cloth, as do the clerks of the chamber. The physicians, together with the pope’s squires, receive cloth like that of the chamberlains.

The masters of the cupbearers, bakers, water office, wax, and kitchen receive another, inferior cloth. The ushers, doorkeepers, clerks of the chapel, masters of ceremonies, and armor-bearers all receive similar cloth to that given to the masters of the cupbearers.

All are to be clothed according to the will of the chamberlain; everything depends upon his decision.

The pope’s two cooks receive the same cloth as the officials. Those of the first and second gate receive the same or similar cloth. Couriers and servants of the stable, bakery, cupbearers, wax office, and kitchen all receive one inferior cloth, with at least two from each office. The stablemen receive according to their number, and the couriers according to the will of the chamberlain.

The marshal of the Curia, the advocate of the poor, the master of the Sacred Palace, the fiscal procurator, and the pope’s advocate all receive one cloth. The purchaser, the *guardavessalla*, the chief guard—that is, the keeper of provisions—and the keeper of the sacred chapel, who is under the authority of the sacristan, all receive the same cloth. The bell-ringer, the sweeper of the pope’s chamber, and the sweeper of the palace receive another cloth.

If the pope dies in Rome, six *banderenses*, three rectors, and two counselors customarily make a request. The heads of the regions and the *manipularii* likewise customarily request black garments, and received them at the death of Urban VI. All these are officials of the City. If they make the request, it remains at the discretion of the chamberlain whether he wishes to give them anything or not.

The Senator of Rome, on account of his office, neither uses nor wears such cloth, unless he wishes to do so himself out of affection for the pope.

It should be noted that three cannae of cloth are given to each person.

On the first day the penitentiaries and all the pope’s household eat in the palace throughout the novena, and sometimes until a new pope has been created; the new pope receives and retains those whom he wishes.

Immediately, great alms are distributed for the pope’s soul by the treasurer, at the chamberlain’s command. First, to the four mendicant orders equally: fifty florins, or twenty-five, or at least ten, together with bread, wine, and meat for one day. Then alms are given to hospitals and other poor people according to the chamberlain’s will and according to the resources of the chamber.

Immediately after the second Mass, the celebrant goes to the bier beneath the catafalque, having removed the chasuble and wearing a cope with his ministers. The pope’s singers always sing the Mass and the responsories at the absolution; the canons must help them sing the responsories. When the absolution is finished, the cardinal removes his sacred vestments and returns to the other cardinals.

They hear the sermon, and after it has been preached they all go to the palace to arrange matters concerning the conclave. Places are assigned to them there by the chamberlain. Everyone is given at least an equal amount of space, including the spaces where they must construct their chambers at their own expense, if they are wealthy and senior cardinals.

Every day after Mass and the sermon they must hold a council, considering and discussing the future bishop or pope.

Throughout the entire novena only one Collect is to be said, namely *Deus, qui inter apostolicos* (“O God, who among the apostolic…”). At the absolution they may change it if they wish and say *Inclina, Domine, aurem tuam* (“Incline your ear, O Lord”) in its place.

The chamberlain must take great care that the order of celebrating the Masses is not interrupted, since each day one cardinal must celebrate the Mass for the dead and preach the sermon there. If he does not wish to do this, he should assign it to a prelate or a master of theology; for if the order is interrupted, it could not be restored.

It would not be lawful or proper for the Mass to be celebrated by a prelate or bishop. But if one of the cardinals should fall ill or be unable to celebrate Mass, another cardinal shall celebrate it, proceeding successively through the order until the end.

## CXLVIII. On the Pope’s Novena

During the novena the catafalque is decorated with candles as on the day of burial, and at least eighty or one hundred brands are to be placed there that day.

It should be understood that the pope’s barber does not retain the box containing the razors and its contents, nor the silver basin. Later, the new pope has ten or twelve florins given to the barber. The basin, however, always remains in the pope’s chamber with the razors and towels.

If the bakers and cupbearers ask for towels or bottles—*bottas* [Note: That is, flasks, commonly called *botte* by Italians]—they are to be given to them, since they are their proper equipment. If they were not given to them, they would have grounds for requesting the towels from which the pope last ate and the bottles from which he was then last drinking wine.

The chamberlains may ask each for one of the pope’s garments. If they wish, however, all such garments are customarily given for the love of God and for the pope’s soul.

## CXLIX. Rubric on the Conclave

Concerning the conclave, the following must be said. First, the chamberlain must take careful charge of the arrangement and preparation of the place: the doors must be walled up, as must all windows low and near the ground or roof, to a height of at least four cannae, and all openings, however small or moderate, at the expense of the chamber.

There must be one chapel whose doors and windows are all closed with good masonry, except for the door leading into the conclave and the windows looking into the conclave; these are to remain open.

In this chapel the cardinals must hear Mass every day together, not sung but spoken quietly. If there is no chapel adjoining the conclave, one is to be established within the conclave in some corner, or a portable altar is to be provided for the conclave. They are to hear Mass there every day. In the same chapel they may meet to elect and to hold council, or wherever they consider more suitable.

They must take care to put everything in writing. In that chapel the body of Christ must always be present, with a candle burning for every contingency. The chamber pays for this candle and for all the others consumed in the Masses held there during the vacancy of the see.

It should be understood that in modern times each of the cardinals must enter with a priest and one servant. The lords must have their chambers prepared with their curtains and bed furnishings, without straw, unless the weather is cold. They may have a table and a bench, but not a chest, unless it is completely open at the top.

They may have a vessel for holding water, wine, or meat (*cannes*; alternative reading *carnes*) that falls from their hands, and other wooden utensils, spits or bars upon which the curtains are to be placed. The chamber pays for these items and for the surrounding arrangements.

It should be understood that the three senior cardinals, the senior one acting with the chamberlain and on the advice of the others, must, before they enter the conclave, choose four distinguished men to guard the conclave from outside with armed men. They must take great care that these men are suitable. They may be two prelates and two knights, or one knight and one *banderensis*.

The aforesaid guards must carefully observe, under penalty of perjury, that they open and inspect everything carried to the cardinals for eating. If pasties are brought to them, they must open them.

Under penalty of perjury, they must give the cardinals no letter, permit them to receive none, and receive none from them, no matter how great the necessity. Whatever they wish to obtain from outside, they must state orally to the guards.

No one may enter to see them while they are in the aforesaid council, except that a cardinal who comes from outside from his legation may enter alone with one priest and one clerk.

Every morning and evening they must have cooked food and other necessities of life brought from their households.

Their chaplains are to celebrate in the common place where all assemble, as stated above.

At the door of the conclave there must be at least three keys with three locks; each of the guards must have his own. The door must be firmly closed with bars, bolts, and a chain. In the middle there must be an opening through which food may be passed to them, one and a half palms in length and of sufficient height, and it must also be capable of being closed with a key.

It should be understood that the chamberlain’s household must sleep in the chamber in order to preserve the goods. The chamberlain himself, if he is not a cardinal, and those prelates who have charge of the conclave must also sleep there with some of their own household.

Everyone must live at the chamber’s expense until a pope has been created and for as long as they perform the guard duty.

In the towers there must be guards in at least four places, and in each tower at least three couriers; the chamber supplies them with the necessities of life. They must keep watch day and night.

Outside, appointed guards must protect the conclave on behalf of the three senior cardinals and the chamberlain. They are to be given at least bread and wine in addition to their wages. They must take care not to allow anyone to enter the palace, armed or unarmed, except with the permission of the guards.

It should be noted that the partition must have at least four palms of width between the wall and the cardinal’s bed. It is to be closed with boards only to the height of the curtains, or at least ten palms. All this was done at the expense of the apostolic chamber when Lord Urban died, because the cardinals were extremely poor. Its length was as great as the length of the chambers. Behind the cardinals, wood, coal, and other necessities of life were to be kept within that space.

In the conclave, one clerk of the Audience who serves the chapel by reading the Epistles must enter and write down everything that happens from day to day. Each day he must arrange the Mass to be celebrated before the cardinals, keep one lamp burning in the chapel and another in the middle of the conclave, and guard the vestments, chalice, book, and the cloak of Saint Peter together with the consistorial mitre.

It should be understood that after the death of Pope Gregory XI, the cardinals wished to hear Mass of the Holy Spirit in the hospital of Santo Spirito. This occurred on the day after the novena because they wished to consult with the Romans before entering the conclave, for the preservation of the conclave.

After the death of Lord Urban VI, following the ninth Mass and the sermon, the cardinals wished to hear Mass of the Holy Spirit there, with a sermon, which Lord Pisanus delivered. From the apostolic chamber, eleven large candles and two brands were supplied to him as wax. They entered the conclave that same day in the evening, after Vespers.

Four prelates were appointed to guard the conclave: two on behalf of the chamberlain, who carried staffs in their hands, and two on behalf of the college. The chamberlain did not allow these latter to carry staffs, nor afterward any of his own, except one, who was the one who carried it. Outside, two *banderenses* were assigned to preserve the conclave, each with four servants; six [lacuna].

When the pope has been elected, he is dressed in other cloths. The garments he removes are to belong to the clerk of the chapel, as has always been observed.

During the novena the catafalque was decorated with candles as on the first day. Brands stood all around the bier as before; at each corner of the catafalque there was one brand, and at the top above it one very large brand of white wax, perhaps twenty-five pounds, since it was a paschal candle. The first circle of candles around the catafalque contained twenty-four candles on each side; the space between one candle and the next was approximately one palm.

## CL. How Pope Boniface IX Attended Vespers on the Vigil of the Nativity of the Blessed Mary

It should be noted that on Thursday, 7 September, the vigil of the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary, at first Vespers, Lord Pope Boniface IX attended Vespers in a red cope and a gold-fringed mitre, though not the solemn mitre. He began Vespers and said only the Collect; he did not begin the antiphon. The cardinals began it, but did not remove their woolen copes. The singers performed the entire service.

The auditors and acolytes wore surplices. The cardinal of Todi performed the office in the morning, in the year 1391, the second year of the pope’s pontificate.

## CLI. On the Wednesdays, Thursdays, Fridays, and Saturdays of Holy Week

Take note that on Holy Wednesday, at Matins, the pope came wearing only a red cloak and without a mitre. The chair was prepared. The cardinal deacons did not sit before him, but in their own places. Nor did the bishop or priest who served him with the book sit before him on a stool; all sat in their proper places.

On Thursday everything was done in the same manner.

On Good Friday the pope came to the service wearing a cope open from the middle of the chest downward, lined with ermine, and a simple white mitre of garnello or with gold embroidery.

In the evening, at Matins, he came in the same cope with only a red biretta on his head; throughout the entire service he kept it on his head without a mitre.

On Holy Saturday, at Mass, he came in a red cope without pearls. In the evening, at Matins, he came in a white cloak without pearls.

## CLII. On the Reception of a Cardinal Entering the Roman Curia

It should be noted that if a cardinal has been outside the Curia for some time on his own business or for recreation—but not as a nuncio or legate—when he returns and enters the city where the Roman Curia resides, the other cardinals should not go out to meet him. They send their household members to accompany him instead.

If some cardinals, out of affection, nobility, or kinship, go to meet him, and one cardinal is entering while several others go out to meet him, those meeting him should be equal in number on each side. The cardinal who has newly arrived must go alone in front; the others follow behind him two by two, then the patriarchs, then the protonotaries, and then the others according to their order.

## CLIII. On the Canonization of Saint Bridget

The canonization of Saint Bridget follows. In the year of Our Lord 1391, on Saturday, 7 October, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Boniface IX, the canonization of blessed Bridget took place in the large chapel of the Sacred Palace at Rome, near Saint Peter. The following procedure was observed.

First, on Friday, the patriarch of Grado, the said lord’s confessor and referendary, by order of His Holiness, commanded the general consistory to announce the canonization of Saint Bridget, so that everyone should come to the solemnity. He also ordered that the bells of all the churches should be rung at the hour of Compline and, on the following day, at the hour of Terce.

The chapel was decorated all around with cloths and strewn with green branches. The master of the foliage office carried this out.

Throughout the chapel there were torches or brands, each of eleven pounds of wax, eighty-six in all. I found the arrangement of those candles and the order of the brands.

On Saturday morning the pope heard a solemn Mass of the Holy Spirit in his chamber.

After the solemn Mass he came to the large chapel, accompanied by all the cardinals and the Roman nobles, wearing a red consistorial cope and a consistorial mitre of pearls. After making a slight reverence before the altar, he ascended another chair prepared far from the altar. There he received all the cardinals and prelates for the customary reverence, wearing their woolen copes.

When this reverence was finished, he went to another chair prepared with a stool before the middle of the altar, leaning against the altar with his face turned toward the people. The two senior deacons sat before his feet on stools; the other cardinals also sat in their places wearing woolen copes.

When silence had been made and the lights had been lit, the pope, seated with the mitre on his head, delivered his address and sermon under the following theme: “I will bless her widow, and my sanctification shall flourish over her” (*Viduam ejus benedicam, et florebit super ipsam sanctificatio mea*).

When the sermon and an exhortation that everyone should pray to God not to permit him to err had been completed, he also made a protestation that he did not intend to act against the most holy Roman Church. Then he rose from his seat, removed his mitre, and began to sing *Veni, creator Spiritus* (“Come, Creator Spirit”). Kneeling, he remained without a mitre until the third verse, and thereafter continued standing there until the singers had finished the hymn.

When it was complete, without the verse, he said *Dominus vobiscum* (“The Lord be with you”) and the Collect *Deus, qui corda fidelium* (“O God, who hast taught the hearts of the faithful”), which he concluded with “through Christ our Lord.”

Putting his mitre on again, he then announced while seated that blessed Bridget was to be a saint and enrolled in the catalogue of the saints, as is set out in the book of the papal secrets of Pope Clement VI.

After making this pronouncement, he granted in his own words an indulgence for that day and the following day to those who visited the churches of Saint Peter and Saint Lawrence in Panisperna, and to those who took part in that divine service, the indulgence of the jubilee and many other indulgences in the lands.

After this, the procurators of the said saint requested public instruments concerning the matter, and the pope likewise, concerning his authority just mentioned, [lacuna]. Then all the cardinals and prelates put on white vestments: the bishops, copes; the priests, chasubles; and the deacons, tunicles and dalmatics. They again came to offer reverence to the pope.

Afterward, having removed the red cope, he received precious gloves and the pontifical ring, and a precious white cope with a solemn mitre. Removing the mitre, he began to sing *Te Deum laudamus* (“We praise you, O God”).

Then two large torches of white wax were given to him, each of eight pounds of wax; to each cardinal and patriarch, another torch of seven pounds of wax, not white; to all prelates, torches of two pounds; and to the other clerics, singers, auditors, nobles, and others, torches of one pound of wax.

The procession then began. Everyone held his lighted candle in his hands, each in his proper order. The two patriarchs went with the cardinals. The pope went beneath a canopy, while knights carried his lighted torches outside the canopy.

Thus they proceeded through the entire chapel to another chapel, and then returned in procession to the large chapel. The supreme pontiff ascended the chair before the middle of the altar, where he had previously preached his sermon.

Standing there, the deacon on the right sang, “Pray for us, blessed Bridget, alleluia.” The pope said *Dominus vobiscum* (“The Lord be with you”) and another Collect for Saint Bridget.

After the singers had sung *Benedicamus Domino* (“Let us bless the Lord”), the deacon on the left said *Confiteor* (“I confess”). The pope then gave the blessing in the customary manner, and the senior cardinal bishop proclaimed the indulgences.

Everyone returned home with his candle. The chamberlain had all the other candles from the altar and the torches from the chapel collected for the pope . . . . by six cardinals, all of whom were to be sacristans. The first was Lord Philip of Alençon; the second was Lord Adam of England; another was the cardinal of Rieti.

That day the pope was unable to celebrate the solemn Mass of the saint because of illness, as he should have done. On the following day, however, he celebrated and observed the following order.

On Sunday, 8 October, early in the morning, after the small Mass, the pope, dressed in a cope and a consistorial mitre with pearls, descended to the church of Saint Peter with all the cardinals, two patriarchs—namely, the patriarch of Constantinople—and the prelates and the entire clergy.

At the door of the church all the canons of Saint Peter came to meet him with the cross, copes, a canopy, and a processional bell. Singing *Te Deum laudamus* (“We praise you, O God”), they led him to the high altar.

After making a slight prayer before the altar, he withdrew to the chair where the Roman prelates customarily vest. While seated, he received the cardinals and all the prelates as they came to offer reverence. He wished Terce to be sung.

The Mass was for Saint Bridget, with a commemoration of Sunday. On that occasion I first began, by command, to sit among the cardinal bishops. The Mass proceeded according to its order.

After the Gospel, the deacon on the left said *Confiteor* (“I confess”). After the recitation of *Credo in unum Deum* (“I believe in one God”) and the Offertory, the pope sat on a low chair with a stool before the pope’s iron gates, where the Gospel had been read, facing the chair in which he had vested.

Then the three cardinal commissioners for the canonization of this saint came out of the sacristy of Saint Peter with their offerings.

First, the lord cardinal of France, with two large lighted torches covered with gold, offered them while kissing the pope’s foot and hand.

Second, the lord cardinal of England, with two loaves covered with cloths bearing the arms and shields of Saint Bridget and of the three cardinal commissioners, kissed the pope’s foot and hand.

Third, the lord cardinal of Bari, with two large basins of wine and malmsey, called in Rome gilded cups, bearing the arms and shields of the lady and of the aforesaid cardinals, kissed the pope’s foot and hand.

Finally, five procurators of the saint came with an advocate, and each offered one large candle of one pound of white wax, modestly worked with roses and flowers in green, white, and red.

Also one small basket, entirely painted green, in which there were two white doves and two turtledoves.

**538.** Note that the canons, in the Procession, ought to have had large wax candles in their hands, supplied by these executors [Col. 1362A]; and because they did not have them, the pope was disturbed.

There were also in this Mass, upon the iron screens and the stone columns near the aforesaid screens, about eighty burning torches, and seven at the elevation of the Body of Christ. Each could have been of four pounds of wax. Neither the pope nor the cardinals nor anyone else held a candle during this Mass; nor was there a sermon.

Note that, when the Mass was completed, the lord pontiff, dressed as he had been at Mass, and all the cardinals and prelates dressed in the sacred vestments in which they had been at Mass, went with mitres to the windows near the bell tower, in the ambulatory where the Roman bishops were accustomed to grant indulgence to the people. There the pope granted a true indulgence on that day, as at a jubilee, out of reverence for Bridget [Col. 1362B], and at Saint Peter’s and at Saint Lawrence in Panisperna, where Saint Bridget was said to have been buried; and whoever visited the aforesaid churches of Saint Peter and Saint Lawrence seven times throughout the present month would have the jubilee indulgence.

Note that the canons wished to have the wax from the church of Saint Peter that had been burned; but the chamberlain took all of it, so that neither the pope nor they nor the acolytes nor the singers nor the clerics had any.

Note that each singer received three ducats from the executors.

The aforesaid executors sent the pope a small gold vessel worth one hundred ducats, and one calf, twenty-four capons, twenty-four chickens, twenty-four pigeons, and two barrels of wine.

[Col. 1362C] Note that there were Vespers beforehand, but not afterward.

Note that on this day, although the Mass was for Saint Bridget, throughout the entire day we performed the office of Sunday, and we made no commemoration of that saint at Vespers or at Matins.

Note that all the cardinals, dressed in the sacred vestments, accompanied the pope as far as the chamber.

On this day no cardinal ate with the pope, except only the household prelates and the singers.

Note that the entire chapel ought to be prepared inside and outside with hangings.

On the altar there ought to be six candles, each of one and a half pounds; likewise, above the chapel screen, six torches, each of eight pounds of wax.

[Col. 1362D] Outside the screen, or chapel, perforated wooden supports should be placed all around in the wall to hold the torches, extending as far as the chapel does; and in each piece of wood there shall be six torches, each of four pounds of wax.

At the far end of the chapel, opposite the altar, the same arrangement should be made.

As for the other small candles, of an ounce or half an ounce, or a pound, twenty should be placed along the wall and distributed to laypeople and clerics.

[Col. 1361]

## ADDITIONS

**539. CLIV. On Ash Wednesday**

[Col. 1361D]

The additions: on Ash Wednesday the Lord Boniface IX descended on that day to the solemn Mass in the great chapel at Perugia, wearing a cope and a mitre without pearls, and thus gave the ashes. After they had been given, [Col. 1362D] he removed the cope and mitre and, having taken up his mantle again, stood thus throughout the entire Mass without a mitre. The lord of Naples said the Mass. The pope was affected by the cold. In the year of the Lord 1393, in the fourth year of his pontificate.

**CLV. On Rose Sunday**

[Col. 1363A]

On Rose Sunday Mass was celebrated in the great chapel, the pope being absent, in the presence of all the cardinals. The Rose was carried from the pope’s chamber to the chapel by the junior chamber cleric, and remained upon the altar throughout the entire Mass. Afterward it was carried back by the same man to the pope’s chamber. In that chamber of vestments, as the pope was leaving another chamber of his own, he carried it in his hands and, in his seat in the chamber of vestments, gave it to Hostregius of Faenza in the aforesaid year.

**CLVI. On the Annunciation of the Blessed Virgin**

Note that on the Annunciation of the Blessed Virgin Mary, the lord Boniface IX, in the fourth year of his pontificate, being confined by illness, did not attend the Mass, which was celebrated [Col. 1363B] in the great chapel at Perugia by the bishop of Ancona. The man who had been supposed to preach on the preceding Sunday, because he had not done so, preached on this day about the aforesaid Sunday, with additional words about the Blessed Virgin. It was Tuesday, 1393.

**CLVII. On Palm Sunday**

On the following Sunday, Palm Sunday, the same lord Boniface gave the branches in the small chapel in the customary manner, after the great Mass had been celebrated in the chamber. When they had been given, the lords cardinals, dressed in the sacred vestments, went to the great chapel; after removing their vestments, they heard another great Mass, at which the pope was not present. It was said by the bishop of Naples.

**CLVIII. On Holy Thursday**

Also in the same year, on Holy Thursday, after the great [Col. 1363C] Mass had been celebrated in the pope’s chamber and the Body of Christ had been reserved in a chalice upon the altar of the private chapel, the lords cardinals and all the prelates went to the great chapel and there heard another great Mass in the customary manner, which was said by the lord patriarch of Constantinople. After the Body of Christ had been reserved in the chalice and incensed in the customary manner, it remained upon the altar. After Vespers had been sung, the lords cardinals, not vested, stood before the altar in a circle, with two patriarchs among them—namely, the aforesaid patriarch of Constantinople and I, the patriarch of Grado—and by order of our lord the pope they pronounced the general legal processes in the pope’s absence. The lord patriarch of Constantinople read them. The candles were not thrown down, because they did not have any; only one taken from the altar [Col. 1363D] was used.

**CLIX. On the meal held on the same day**

Also on the same day, after the meal, the pope was unable to wash the feet of the poor. The patriarch of Grado, his confessor, therefore, by order of the pope, washed the feet of the poor in the small chapel. He was dressed in a rochet, amice, surplice, and cope, with a white mitre. He heard the Gospel, singing it with lights, cross, and incense in the customary manner. When it had been sung, the singers began to sing; and he, having removed the cope, girded with a linen cloth and with the mitre on his head, began to wash the feet. When this was finished, he said the Prayer, and the cardinal chamberlain gave florins together with a carleno. He refused to give the pieces of cloth for drying the poor men’s feet—only two in all—but carried everything back with him; and this was bad, says the gloss.

**CLX. On Good Friday and Holy Saturday**

On Good Friday and Holy Saturday the prelates performed the office in the great chapel, the pope being absent and all the cardinals present.

**CLXI. On Easter Day, the Ascension, Pentecost, and Trinity**

On Easter Day he performed the office on account of the cardinals’ Communion. Likewise on the Ascension. But on Pentecost, Trinity Sunday, and Corpus Christi there were no papal Vespers because of the pope’s illness. The Masses were said by non-cardinal prelates in the pope’s absence, with all the cardinals present, and with a sermon.

**CLXII. On Saint John the Baptist**

[Col. 1364B]

The same on the feast of Saint John the Baptist.

**CLXIII. On the holy apostles Peter and Paul**

Also on the feast of the blessed Peter and Paul there were Vespers in the pope’s absence. The cardinal of Bologna performed the office. He alone began Vespers, dressed in a cope and mitre; he began the Antiphon at the *Magnificat* and said the Prayer. He did not give the Blessing for the following day in the church of Saint Peter at Perugia, where the pope resided. He then said Mass in the pope’s absence, with all the cardinals present, and with a sermon.

**541. CLXIV. On the Purification of the Blessed Virgin Mary**

Also in the year of the Lord 1392, on the feast of the Candles, at First Vespers, Vespers had not been ordered, because our lord did not wish it; but late in the day he himself wished to hear them with a few cardinals and courtiers. They said that they ought not to be sung solemnly because there was no vigil. In the morning he gave the candles. Mass was said at Saint Peter’s by the lord cardinal of Naples. Two cardinal deacons stood before him, and the senior of the cardinal priests also stood at his side.

**CLXV. Note concerning the Nativity of Christ**

In the year of the Lord 1398, in the City, the Lord Pope Boniface IX began to fall ill on Monday, the vigil of the Nativity of Christ. Vespers were sung by the singers in the great chapel. The lord Cardinal Pileus of Ravenna began Vespers, dressed in a cope and mitre, standing at the side of the altar’s horn on the chair where the prelates stand when they celebrate before the pope. He alone [Col. 1364D] said the Prayer and did not give the Blessing.

All the cardinals attended at midnight. The cardinals did not attend either Matins or the Masses; but the lord Conrad, archbishop of Nicosia and chamberlain, and [Note: [Col. 1363] This is Peter Amelii, the author of this book, who above, in chapter 158, called himself patriarch of Grado.] Peter, patriarch of Grado, attended the entire office, with four other prelates; nor did the courtiers come. The singers read the lessons, Antiphons, and Psalms; and the hebdomadary gave the Blessing.

The lord chamberlain said the first and second Masses without an interval. He made a commemoration of the pope at both Masses and did not give the Blessing at the end of Mass, but announced an indulgence on the pope’s behalf of seven years and seven forties. [Col. 1365A] At the third Mass the lord cardinal of Ravenna said Mass. Seven cardinals attended. He did not give the Blessing after Mass, and this was wrong, because he ought to have done so.

At the meal the lord chamberlain held the table with the auditors and penitentiaries. There was no Second Vespers. On the feast of Saint Stephen the lord cardinal of Naples performed the office; on the feast of Saint John, the lord cardinal of Bologna did so.

**CLXVI. On the funerals of cardinals**

Note concerning the funerals of deceased cardinals. In the evening, the funeral rites are performed by religious and parish churches in the dining hall, with the corpse present and at least four burning torches. The cardinal ought to lie in a bier prepared with cloth of gold and black fringes, bearing his coat of arms, and with his household dressed in black. They ought to sit around near the bier, weeping.

If the cardinal is a bishop, he ought to be entirely dressed in sacred vestments of black or violet, entirely as a pontiff, [Col. 1365B] with a white mitre; gloves and sandals with the pontifical ring, his face covered with a silk veil. If he is a priest, the same arrangement applies. If he is a deacon, likewise, but in the dress of a deacon and not with a chasuble, gloves, or pontifical rings, but with the other tunics, small gloves, and a small ring.

At the funeral rites one cardinal must always say Mass. A master of theology gives the sermon, which ought to take place after Mass and before the absolution. After the sermon, the four senior cardinal priests vest themselves over the alb with an amice, white girdle, stole, and cope, with rings, but without gloves and sandals. Then the one who said Mass goes first, and the other three follow. They go near the *castrum doloris*, and the singers sing *Libera me, Domine* (“Deliver me, O Lord”). When it has been sung, the one who said Mass sprinkles the body, or the bier, with holy water and incenses it, saying *Pater noster* (“Our Father”), etc. He performs the first absolution; then the other three do the same in their order, as it is contained in the book. The other cardinals and the entire clergy remain in the choir.

If the sermon has not been given after the Gospel, as is done in some places—for the Roman Church, however, is not accustomed to this—the cardinals wait; and after the absolution the sermon is given. Some, nevertheless, are accustomed to give the sermon before the absolution, and this occurs when the altar is joined to, or roofed together with, the choir, because the one who performed the office remains vested there.

Nevertheless, wherever Mass is said, whether near the choir or far away, the one who said it remains vested with his clergy before the altar until the sermon has ended. Therefore the preacher ought to stand in an elevated place where even the one who said Mass can hear him. In this sermon neither a Blessing nor an indulgence is given.

At Mass all the cardinals and all the prelates remain in their seats; and each must have a torch of at least four pounds—the cardinals and patriarchs. The others are to have one pound or two pounds, as the executors please.

The Mass must be celebrated by a cardinal, and the sermon must be given after Mass and the absolution. He must also make a *castrum doloris* with candles. Around it there must also be at least one hundred torches, and more according to the will of the executors; and the same number when the body is carried to the church.

Under the *castrum doloris* the members of the household sit. In the bier there must be a large, long black cushion beneath the cardinal’s head, and another at his feet, upon which the cardinal’s two hats are placed.

When Mass is finished, the one who performs the office, having removed the chasuble with his ministers and carrying the thurible and holy water, approaches near the head of the deceased outside the *castrum*; with his mitre removed, he begins without intonation: *Non intres in* (“Enter not into ...”), etc. After the Prayer has been said or completed, the singers sing *Subvenite, sancti* (“Come to his aid, saints”). When it has been sung, he says *Kyrie, eleison* (“Lord, have mercy”), incenses and sprinkles the corpse with holy water, as is contained in the Ordinary.

[Col. 1366B] Then four cardinal priests are present, dressed in copes and white mitres and wearing stoles. After *Ne recorderis* (“Do not remember”) has been sung, the senior says the Prayer that he wishes after the *Pater noster* (“Our Father”), as above, and incenses, etc. Afterward *Memento mei, Deus* (“Remember me, O God”) is sung. When it has been said, another cardinal, who is the second from last, incenses in the same manner and says another Prayer.

Immediately afterward another cardinal, who stands on the other side and is second in order, says the Prayer; he likewise incenses as the others have done and says the Prayer he wishes. Then the last cardinal does likewise. When these things have been completed, *Libera me, Domine* (“Deliver me, O Lord”) is sung. When it has been sung, the one who performs the office likewise incenses as before and says the final Prayer, namely *Absolve* (“Absolve”), etc. Then each person withdraws, and the sermon is given.

[Col. 1366C] Observe that in the year 1434, at the funeral rites of the lord cardinal of Novara, the lord cardinal of Saint Mark celebrated Mass; and immediately after Mass a sermon was given. After the sermon, the lord cardinal of Orsini, the lord cardinal of Saint Marcellus, the lord of Venice, and the lord cardinal of Saint Mark, dressed in copes, came to the bier.

First came two cardinal priests, namely the lord of Saint Marcellus and the lord of Venice; then the lord of Orsini, a cardinal bishop, and the lord of Saint Mark, a cardinal priest who had celebrated that morning. Two of them stood on one side of the bier and two on the other side.

The first Prayer, *Non intres in judicium* (“Enter not into judgment”), was said by the lord of Saint Mark, who had celebrated. After that Prayer had been said, the singers sang *Subvenite* (“Come to his aid”); and after they had said *Kyrie, eleison* (“Lord, have mercy”), the lord of Orsini said *Pater noster* (“Our Father”), sprinkled the holy water, incensed, and said the second Prayer, namely *Deus, cui omnia vivunt* (“O God, to whom all things live”).

After that Prayer had been said, the singers said *Ne recorderis* (“Do not remember”); and after *Kyrie, eleison* (“Lord, have mercy”), the lord cardinal of Saint Marcellus, from the other side, sprinkled and incensed, and said the third Prayer, namely *Inclina, Domine* (“Incline, O Lord”), which Prayer is in the Missal.

After that Prayer had been said, the singers said *Qui Lazarum* (“You who [raised] Lazarus”). The same lord cardinal of Saint Mark, who had celebrated Mass and was on the other side, as above, took the place of a cardinal priest who was absent, sprinkled and incensed, and said the Prayer *Fac, quaesumus, Domine, hanc cum servo* (“Make, we beseech you, O Lord, this [one] with [your] servant”), etc. [Col. 1367A]

After that Prayer had been said, the singers said *Memento mei, Deus* (“Remember me, O God”); and after *Kyrie, eleison* (“Lord, have mercy”), the lord cardinal of Venice said *Pater noster* (“Our Father”), sprinkled and incensed, and said the Prayer *Absolve, quaesumus, Domine, animam famuli tui* (“Absolve, we beseech you, O Lord, the soul of your servant”). This Prayer is in the Missal.

After that Prayer had been said, the singers said *Libera me, Domine, de morte* (“Deliver me, O Lord, from death”), etc. After *Kyrie, eleison* (“Lord, have mercy”) had been said, there was no incensing; but at the end the lord cardinal of Saint Mark said the Prayer, namely *Absolve* (“Absolve”), which Prayer is in the Office of the Dead.

**CLXVII. When King Ladislaus of Naples entered Rome**

Note that in the year of the Lord 1393, on Saturday, 18 April, the vigil of Easter, the lord Ladislaus, king of Naples, entered Rome. All the cardinals went out to meet him at Saint Paul’s. The Romans received him at the gate near the *meta* with a canopy; beneath it he rode alone through the entire City as far as the steps of Saint Peter’s.

[Col. 1368A] Two cardinal deacons who accompanied him rode before the standard-bearers, and the Roman standard-bearers rode immediately before the king. Immediately behind the king came the patriarch of Grado, and after him Count Lawrence, together with other knights and prelates.

On Easter Day, during Mass, the king always served the pope with water and always sat between the first two cardinal bishops. Then came the patriarch of Constantinople, after the senior cardinal priest, who was third in that seat; then the subprior; then the patriarch of Grado; and so all the others. At the meal the said king likewise sat at table between the first two cardinal bishops.

Note that in the year of the Lord 1400, in the twelfth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Boniface IX, on the second Sunday of Advent, because of the cold he did not come wearing a cope and mitre. Since he was not dressed in the customary manner, the lords cardinals did not wish to pay him reverence at the beginning of Mass in the customary way, nor did the cardinal deacons wish to stand before the pope [Note: [Col. 1367B] The Acts of the Council of Lyon under Innocent IV, and another under Gregory X, followed in the Codex, almost as continuations of this book; but since these have been published elsewhere, we deliberately omitted them, as they do not belong to the author’s purpose.].

[Col. 1367]

# ROMAN ORDER XVI, OR INDEX OF THE SOLEMN COLLECTS AND STATIONS OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH

From two Vatican parchment codices.

[Col. 1367C] First Sunday of Advent: station at Saint Mary Major.

Second Sunday: station at the Holy Cross.

Third Sunday: station in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter.—Wednesday: station at Saint Mary Major.—Friday: at the Apostles.—Saturday: at Saint Peter.

Fourth Sunday: at Saint Eugenia.—The first Mass in the morning at Saint Anastasia.

On the day of the Nativity of the Lord: station in the basilica of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles.

On the Epiphany of the Lord: station in the basilica of the prince of the Apostles.

Sunday in Septuagesima: at Saint Lawrence Outside the Walls.

[Col. 1367D] Sunday in Sexagesima: at Saint Paul.

Sunday in Quinquagesima: at the blessed apostle Peter.—Wednesday at the beginning of the fast: Collect at Saint Anastasia; station at Saint Sabina. Blessing of the ashes: *Almighty and everlasting God, spare those who fear you*, etc. *O God, who desire not death but repentance*, etc. Another: *O God, who are moved by humility*, etc. Another Prayer: *Almighty and everlasting God, who, for the Ninevites in ashes*, etc.

Meanwhile ashes are to be placed upon each person’s head, saying: *Remember, human being, that you are dust, and to dust you shall return.*

Antiphon for the Collect: *Hear us, O Lord, for your mercy is kind.* Psalm: *Save me, O God, for...* [Col. 1368C] The priest says, *Let us pray*; the deacon, *Let us bend our knees*; *Arise*. Prayer at the Collect: *Grant us, O Lord, to begin the defenses of Christian warfare with holy fasts, so that, as we prepare to fight against spiritual wickedness, we may be fortified by the help of self-restraint. Through...*

*The Lord be with you.* *And with your spirit.*

The deacon says: *Let us proceed in peace.* Response: *In the name of Christ, amen.*

Antiphon through the *paradisus* (“forecourt”): *Let us change our clothing.* *Kyrie, eleison* (“Lord, have mercy”). *Kyrie, eleison* (“Lord, have mercy”). *Kyrie, eleison* (“Lord, have mercy”). *Our Father.* *And lead us not...* *In memory.* *From the gate of hell.* *May they rest in peace.* *O Lord, hear my prayer.* *The Lord be with you.* *Let us pray.*

*O God, by whose mercy the souls of the faithful rest, mercifully grant forgiveness of sins to all your servants, men and women, who rest in Christ here and everywhere, so that, freed from every guilt, they may rejoice with you without end. Through the same...*

After this Prayer has been said, we enter the church, singing *Peter, do you love me?*, with the verse *Simon, son of John*. When the Responsory has ended, the deacon begins the litany.

Note that on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday we do not say *Kyrie, eleison* (“Lord, have mercy”) at Mass, because we say nine invocations of *Kyrie, eleison* (“Lord, have mercy”) in the litany: three *Kyrie* (“Lord [have mercy]”) and *Kyrie* [perhaps *Christe*, “Christ”] at the beginning, and three *Kyrie* at the end.

Thursday: Collect at Saint Nicholas in Prison; station at Saint George.

Friday: Collect at Saint Lucy in the Seventh District; station at Saints John and Paul.

Saturday: Collect at Saint Lawrence in Lucina; station at Saint Tryphon.

[Col. 1369A] First Sunday in Lent: at Saint John Lateran.—Monday: Collect at Saints Cosmas and Damian; station at Saint Peter in Chains.—Antiphon for the Collect: *Rise up, O Lord; help us.* Psalm: *With our ears, O God...* *Gloria Patri* (“Glory be to the Father”). Verse: *The work that you have worked.* Let us pray. Let us bend our knees. The deacon says: *Arise.* Let us pray.

*Mercifully hear, we beseech you, O Lord, the prayers of your people, so that we who are justly afflicted for our sins may be mercifully delivered for the glory of your name. Through...*

*The Lord be with you.* *And with your spirit.*

The deacon says: *Let us proceed in peace.* Response: *In the name of Christ, amen.*

Antiphon for the procession: *Our sins are many.* The rest is said in the order given above. *Convert us, O God our Savior*, and *that for us*, etc.

Tuesday: Collect at Saint Nicholas in Prison; station at Saint Anastasia.

Wednesday: Collect at Saint Peter in Chains; station at Saint Mary Major.

Thursday: Collect at Saint Agatha in the Monastery; station at Saint Lawrence in Panisperna.

Friday: Collect at Saint Mark; station at the Apostles.

Saturday: Collect at Saint Mary in Trastevere; station at the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles.

Second Sunday in Lent: station at Saint Mary in Domnica. In another codex: Sunday is vacant. Station at Saint Mary in Domnica.

Monday: Collect at Saints Cosmas and Damian; station at Saint Clement.

Tuesday: station at Saint Balbina. In another codex: the Collect is lacking; station at Saint Balbina.

Wednesday: Collect at Saint [Col. 1369C] George; station at Saint Cecilia in Trastevere.

Thursday: Collect at Saint George; station at Saint Mary in Trastevere.

Friday: Collect at Saint Agatha in the Monastery; station at Saint Vitalis.

Saturday: Collect at Saint Clement; station at Saints Marcellinus and Peter.

Third Sunday: station at Saint Lawrence Outside the Walls.

Monday: Collect at Saint Hadrian; station at Saint Mark.

Tuesday: Collect at Saint Sergius; station at Saint Pudentiana.

Wednesday: Collect at Saint Balbina; station at Saint Sixtus.

Thursday: Collect at Saint Mark; station at Saints Cosmas and Damian.

Friday: Collect at Saint Mary Rotunda; station at Saint Lawrence in Lucina.

Saturday: Collect at Saint Vitalis; station at Saint Susanna.

Fourth Sunday: station at the Holy Cross.

Monday: Collect at Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill; station at the Four Crowned Saints.

[Col. 1369D] Tuesday: Collect at the Monastery of Lady Rosa; station at Saint Lawrence in Damasus.

Wednesday: Collect at Saint Menas; station at the apostle Paul.

Thursday: Collect at Saint Quiricus; station [Col. 1370A] at Saint Martin in the Hills.

Friday: Collect at Saint Vitus Magellum [reading uncertain]. In another codex, *in Macello*; station at Saint Eusebius.

Saturday: Collect at Saint Angelo of the Fish-Seller; station at Saint Nicholas in Prison.

Fifth Sunday: Also called Passion Sunday; station in the basilica of the prince of the apostles.

Monday: Collect at Saint George; station at Saint Chrysogonus in Trastevere.

Tuesday: station at Saint Cyriacus in the Baths. In another codex: the Collect is absent; station, etc.

Wednesday: Collect at Saint Mark; station at Saint Marcellus.

Thursday: Collect at Saint Mary on the Via Lata; station at Saint Apollinaris.

Friday: Collect at Saints John and Paul; station at Saint Stephen on the [Col. 1370B] Caelian Hill.

Saturday: Collect at Saint Sixtus; station at Saint John at the Latin Gate. In another codex: Saturday at Saint Peter, when alms are given; Collect at Saint Sixtus, etc.

On Palm Sunday we say Terce at Saint Mary [Note: [Col. 1369D] This oratory was at the towers of the Vatican basilica, as can easily be understood from what precedes. I note this here because of Baronius, who thought that the church of Blessed Mary at the Towers was the Pantheon in the year 1087.] in the Tower, where the palms are to be blessed. In another codex: station at Saint John Lateran.

In the procession through the *paradisus* [commonly, *le Parvis*]: Antiphon, *The children of the Hebrews, carrying...*, etc. *The children of the Hebrews, their garments...* Antiphon: *The crowds come to meet...* *Christ became obedient for us*, etc. We sing this Antiphon only once and without the organ.

Monday: Collect at Saint Balbina; station at Saints Nereus and Achilleus.

Tuesday: Collect at Saint Mary of the Portico; station at Saint Prisca.

Wednesday: Collect at Saint Peter in Chains; [Col. 1370C] station at Saint Mary Major.

Thursday, the Lord’s Supper: station at Saint John Lateran.

On Good Friday we sing the daytime office separately, and at the ninth hour we enter the church with the lord bishop or cardinal priest. Dressed in black vestments and without any singing, we proceed before the altar, and the lector ascends the pulpit, etc.

Holy Easter Sunday: station at Saint Mary Major.

Monday after Easter: station at Saint Peter.

Tuesday: station at the apostle Paul.

[548] Wednesday: at Saint Lawrence Outside the Walls.

Thursday: at the Apostles.

Saturday [Col. 1370D]: at Saint John Lateran.

On the day of the Ascension of the Lord: station in the basilica of the prince of the apostles.
