# APPENDIX TO THE BOOKLETS OF THE ROMAN ORDER

[Col. 1371]

## I. EXCERPTS OF AMALARIUS, ABBOT, ON THE ROMAN ORDER

[Col. 1371B] **549** We announce beforehand the chapters of the following little work, so that, if someone happens to be ignorant of the lowliness of this work and undertakes it as though it were worthy, then later discovers it to be worthless, he may not, moved to regret, say to himself or to those standing nearby: “If I had known the rusticity of this work, I would never have devoted the labor of my eyes to it.” Let him now see at the beginning what follows through to the end. And if, for the sake of reading, he should fall into some nausea, let him not be ungrateful only toward the one who arranged it, but also toward himself, who, having recognized its lowliness, nevertheless chose to examine it to the very end, etc.

## On the Roman Order

**1.** Males stand on the southern side and females on the northern side, so that it may be shown that, through the stronger sex, the stronger saints are always placed amid the greater temptations of the heat of this world, and that, through the weaker and more fragile sex, the weaker are placed in the more suitable location, etc.

**550 2.** The bishop enters from the left and passes to the right. For we are all the Body of Christ. [Col. 1371C] Therefore it is fitting that the bishop, entering the church, imitate his head, Christ, entering the world. Our Savior touched the left side because he assumed what is temporal, etc.

**3.** No more than seven deacons enter with him, an equal number of subdeacons, and an equal number of acolytes, carrying no more than three thuribles. It is often written, and made clear in many places, that the number seven signifies the universality of the Church, etc. Although I had said nothing about the seven deacons ordained by the apostles, from that time the apostles, or the apostles’ successors, decreed seven deacons throughout all the churches, who would be of a higher rank than the others and would stand near the altar, like the columns of the altar: seven on account of the seven perfect men, five on account of the five books of Moses, and three on account of hope, faith, and charity.

**4.** As many candlesticks are carried as there are deacons, because joy of eternal life and perpetual light are promised to the whole Church laboring and imitating Christ, etc.

**5.** The thurible is also carried, signifying the Body of Christ, as it is written in the same Apocalypse: “Another angel came and stood before the altar, holding a golden thurible,” etc.

**6.** When the bishop comes before the altar, he first adores the Holy Things and afterward gives the kiss of peace to the priests and deacons, because he imitates the one of whom the prophet wrote: “His dominion shall be multiplied, and there shall be no end of his peace.” First the bishop adores the Holy Things because mercy must first be bestowed by him from whom peace and harmony come and in whom the kingdom of Christ reigns within us.

He kisses two priests because he himself is the cornerstone, who joined two into one wall coming from opposite sides and gave peace to those who had been far away and to those who were near.

[Col. 1372B] **7.** After the peace has been given, the cantor gives glory to the Holy Trinity, as though saying: “We return glory to God the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, because the peace that he foretold through his holy prophets he has deigned to show us in the latter times.”

When he says *As it was*, the deacons proceed to the altar and return again to the bishop, and stand upright. This signifies that they—or, implicitly, the apostles—gave themselves over to death for this reason: so that they might be united to the Body of Christ.

In this verse the variety of many times is demonstrated: that is, *as it was in the beginning*—the past; *and is now*—the present; *and ever shall be*—the future and the eternal; and *world without end*—a great length of time. Hence Origen: “Whenever ‘world without end’ is mentioned, perhaps, although unknown to us, some limit of duration is nevertheless indicated by the Lord,” etc.

When the prophetic verse is said, the bishop goes to the altar and kisses it, because through the mouths of the prophets Christ came into the world and proceeded to his Passion.

**8.** The deacons first stand bowed before the altar with the bishop until *As it was*, because the choir of the holy martyrs remains in the valley of tears before the final tribulation. Afterward, crowned by martyrdom, they stand upright, liberated and now secure from every persecution; God has wiped their eyes from every tear, and from every pain and hunger. Therefore they stand forever before the Lord.

**551 9.** The bishop, however, always remains bowed until the prophetic verse, because Christ did not anticipate the time in which he had been foretold through the mouths of the prophets. At the time when the prophets had predicted it, he came into the world for his Passion.

Therefore, with the prophetic verse, he goes to the altar because he imitates Christ, to show the people that everything the prophets had foretold about Christ’s Passion was true and was accomplished in its proper time. As is plainly read in the prophecy of Daniel: “Seventy weeks,” he says, “have been shortened over your people,” etc.

**10.** After the bishop has adored the Holy Things, he proceeds to the right side of the altar and stands upright, facing east; and the deacons stand behind him, one after another, more on the right and fewer on the left.

The bishop stands on the right side of the altar because Christ preached the kingdom, in which everything is right and there is nothing left. He stands upright because he came to rule his own with an iron rod, that is, with inflexible justice. He stands facing east because, as he himself indicates, he did not seek to do his own will but the will of the one who sent him, as it is written: “He came down from heaven not to do his own will,” and what follows.

He never looks backward, but always looks upon the Father’s face. Hence the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “I know where I came from and where I am going.” Thus Christ ought to preach the heavenly kingdom, trample sins beneath his feet, look toward eternal things, and leave temporal things behind.

The deacons stand behind him because, as we have said, they can rightly be likened to the choir of martyrs, who also minister at the holy altar; and they wear dalmatics, which military custom used to wear. These deacons went before the altar because martyrs existed in the Old Testament; and now they stand behind because after the Nativity of the Lord they are nevertheless worthily crowned by martyrdom.

Some of them stand on the right and some on the left, because many who have come from the contemplative life have been crowned through martyrdom, and many from the active life proceed to the crown of martyrdom, etc.

11. The candles are first lit outside the church and are carried into the church by the acolytes. First the candles proceed, and once they have reached the altar, they are placed behind them. Both arrangements signify that the teachers of the Church—that is, the illuminators—existed before the Lord’s birth and afterward. For acolytes are called “kindlers of lights.” They are carried in the hands because those whom they fill with knowledge must never cease to raise up through good example.

These same candles are held in the acolytes’ hands until the *Kyrie, eleison*; then they are placed on the pavement and stand with fixed position. Thus teachers ought never to abandon the uneducated people from their hands before the people subject to them have learned to say, “Lord, have mercy on me, a sinner.” This is to say in deed, according to what I have been taught by my teacher: “I acknowledge myself wretched, and therefore I ought to implore God’s mercy.”

Then they stand by themselves in the church and illuminate the church, since it is proper that one who has already been taught by a teacher should teach the church in the teacher’s place. As we said concerning the deacons, more of them stand on the right and fewer on the left; and we understand this to signify the same thing that we explained above concerning the deacons.

After the first Prayer, the candles are placed before the altar, no longer on either side as before, but mixed together in an orderly line, each following the other until the last. For some abandon everything and devote themselves wholly to the contemplative life, while many lead an active life and care for earthly affairs; nevertheless, as far as they can, by giving alms and keeping vigils, they strive to hasten to the church. Our Church holds both groups together in a mixed order.

This arrangement may also be understood to mean that the candles are placed in order before the altar so that the ministers may readily run to the ambo and minister around the altars. The Gospel that is carried nearer to the bishop shows that it itself is the way by which we go to the kingdom of God.

### 12. Concerning the bishop’s seat

This signifies the rest of souls after the Prayer has been completed; it also explains what it signifies that the presbyters sit with him, and what is signified by his facing the people: namely, that he has been given authority to examine their deeds.

After the first Prayer, which we call the *precation*, the bishop sits facing the people, and the presbyters sit with him. In that *precation* itself we understand a good wish for the Church, as though he were saying to the people: “I have wished good for the Church, and therefore I sit. If you indeed take delight in possessing the rest of souls, seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and necessary things will be added to you; afterward you will find rest.”

To stand is to remain in the contest and to pray; after victory, however, comes sitting and judging. The presbyters sit with him, because their ministry is to proclaim the same thing. Concerning them Paul says: “Let the presbyters be held worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in the word of God.”

After the first Prayer, he stands facing the people to show that, after he has manifested himself and his deeds to God, prayed for himself and his own, prayed good things for the people, and rendered praise to God, he has the ministry of examining the works of his people, determining who among them is considered worthy and who unworthy.

### 13.

For this reason a higher place has been assigned to bishops: so that they may oversee and, as it were, guard the people. In Greek, indeed, the word *episcopus* is rendered in Latin as “overseer” (*superintentor*), because he watches over and superintends. Just as a higher place is given to a vinedresser for guarding the vineyard, so a higher place has been made for bishops. From this dangerous and elevated place a dangerous account must be rendered, unless we stand here with such a heart that, through humility, we are beneath your feet and pray for you.

### 14.

For the bishop was the minister who said: “I did not come to be ministered to, but to minister.” John likewise is a subordinate minister, who said: “This was he of whom I said, ‘After me comes a man who was made before me.’” He does not ascend to the higher step, which the one who is about to read the Gospel alone customarily ascends, in order to show that he is a subordinate minister; for John is not worthy to untie the strap of the sandals of the one whose words are read in him.

The cantor, however, may ascend indiscriminately. He ascends higher because Christ was placed above John. He stands at the same level because John is esteemed. He stands lower because Christ came to be baptized by John. The one who sings the Responsory does not ascend higher than the one who reads the lesson, but stands in the same place; and if he ascends higher, it is understood according to the modes described above.

The Responsory is so called because, while one sings, the others respond. One—Christ—sang, that is, he called Peter and the other apostles; they responded because they imitated Christ. Therefore the Responsory corresponds to the calling together of the apostles. He alone sings the Verse, because Christ, spending the night apart, prayed alone, as it is written in the Gospel: “But he was spending the night in prayer.”

The deacon, when he ascends to read, asks the bishop’s blessing and receives the Gospel from the altar. Two candelabra precede him, and two thuribles, or one. What this signifies has been stated. The deacon stands facing south, toward which men customarily gather.

First he asks the bishop’s blessing; the bishop gives it to him: “May the Lord be in your heart and on your lips.” The incense placed in the thurible signifies the prayer of the saints. Hence the Prophet says: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight.”

The deacon says: “The Lord be with you.” The people turn toward the east and pray to God that they may rightly understand what they are about to hear. Each person makes the sign of the holy cross on his forehead, so that through the sign of the holy cross they may be armored, lest any fantasy of diabolical deception find an entrance into their hearts and be able to snatch the seed of the Gospel from their hands.

After this, staffs are laid down from their hands. The Jews gave Jesus a reed in his right hand, placed a crown of thorns on his head, saluted him, and, bending their knees, worshiped him in mockery. We, however, avoiding agreement with them, should lay down the staff that they raised through pride. At that same hour we should hold neither a crown nor any other covering on our heads.

If someone suddenly enters the church at that hour, we do not salute him or kneel in prayer until the Gospel has been read. We may understand the staff otherwise, and so forth.

### 15.

The deacon, when proclaiming the words of the Gospel, stands facing south, because he speaks to those of whom Paul said: “We speak wisdom among the perfect.” When the sun inclines toward the south, it is customarily hotter and higher. This signifies that the Church, fervent in spirit and elevated in the love of God, has been raised to the great height of virtues.

Indeed, when we customarily sit to hear the reading of teachers, the face of our teacher is directed more intently toward the one who is able to learn more perfectly than toward those who learn less perfectly. This is not because he wishes his teaching for those alone, but because he wishes those of slower understanding to be taught again by one who can more quickly discover the true meaning in the teacher’s instruction.

We do not say this to mean that those who are behind are excluded from the holy Gospel, but so that the less educated may be educated through the more learned, and so forth.

### 16.

After the Gospel has been read, the candles are extinguished. The candles signify the teachers of the Church. What else does their being extinguished after the Gospel mean except that none of the teachers can surpass the words of the holy Gospel? It is also plainly shown that, when the holy Gospel has been closed, the teaching of the teachers has been extinguished.

### 17. Concerning “I believe in God”

After Christ has spoken to his people, it is fitting that they profess their faith more sweetly and attentively. Thus it is appropriate for the people, after the Gospel, because they have heard Christ’s words, to express the intention of their faith with splendid speech. For the Christian religion to remain safe, one believes with the heart unto righteousness, while confession is made with the mouth unto salvation.

### 18.

After the Gospel has been read, the subdeacon comes carrying on his left arm a chalice into which the people’s small vessels are to be received, and a corporal over the chalice. The deacon takes this and places it on the altar. Likewise, he places the chalice there after the small vessels have been received. The Lord Jesus himself is both deacon and subdeacon, and so forth.

### 19. Concerning the offering

Christ the Lord is priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek, who was king of Salem—that is, king of peace—and who offered bread and wine as a prefiguration of the true priesthood of Christ. Christ offered to the Lord the Father true bread, that is, his immaculate body, and wine, that is, his blood.

In his type, our Church today offers bread and wine in remembrance of the Lord’s body and blood. Those who disdain to offer offerings disdain, although not with living voice, to confess that they have been redeemed by Christ’s passion and to commit that same passion to memory—provided, however, that there is no circumstance that temporarily prevents them.

[Note: *Fanon* has various meanings. Sometimes it means the cloth that sacred ministers wore; others called these *mappulae*, which were succeeded by the *maniple*. Sometimes it means the veil carried over the pontiff’s head like an umbrella; see above, p. 270, and p. 281, where the cloth over the head is called a *mappa*. Finally, sometimes it means an oblong cloth for offering or receiving offerings, as here.]

They offer with *fanones*, because we read that a cloth was used in the Lord’s Passion. In another sense, *fanones* are made of linen; and linen is used in many ways in Holy Scripture as an exhortation concerning the Passion. Therefore they hold the offerings with clean *fanones*, to show that they have accepted, in holy and catholic religion, the willingness to lay down their life for the brethren—not only their lives, but pure lives, so that they may not be polluted by any heresy, but cleansed by charity.

Hence the Apostle says: “And if I deliver my body to be burned, but have not charity, it profits me nothing.”

Finally, the priests and deacons offer, but only bread. The archdeacon alone customarily completes the offerings of those who have gone before, pouring water into the chalice and into the pontiff’s small vessel, to show that Christ’s body is one and that what this man did, he did for all.

Thus, when the Lord asked his disciples in the Gospel, “Who do you say that I am?”, Peter alone answered on behalf of the whole company of the disciples: “You are Christ, the Son of the living God.” What all had answered in their hearts, Peter alone expressed with living voice.

The fact that the presbyters offer last is not without mystery. When John saw in his Apocalypse one like the Son of Man in the midst of seven candelabra, he saw in him the condition of the whole present Church and what it would be. After describing this, he says: “His feet were like burnished bronze, as though refined in a burning furnace.” By the fiery feet he means the Church of the final time, which must be examined and tested more fully through tribulations.

The ministry of the presbyters is to be strong in the Church, so that they may pray both for themselves and for the people. Since they are stronger in the Church, they offer last, signifying that, in the final age, the Church will have the Antichrist and will endure far more injuries than the present Church.

If one also wishes to hear why men offer before women, let it be said that the primitive Church, in its tribulation, when Christians were not yet fully established, endured more injuries than the present Church now endures. Women offer in the middle because, as is plainly evident, there is great silence in the Church. Thanks be to God, Christianity—especially in these times—is flourishing above all, since Christian power is exalted.

The ministry of the presbyters and deacons is to minister at the altar and around the altar. Therefore they alone approach the altar, since their ministry is concerned with the altar.

### 20.

At the time when Mass is celebrated, the deacons stand behind the bishop, and the subdeacons before his face. For it is known that Christ said to his disciples: “You will all be scandalized because of me on this night.” Just as Christ foretold, they abandoned him that same night and fled.

In the same way, at that hour the second ministers of the altar withdraw from the face of the bishop, signifying that the apostles were absent for a time, yet waiting behind, because after the Passion they followed him. What does “to stand behind” mean? Without doubt, it means to follow the one who is in front.

The subdeacons, however, after the Angelic Hymn, stand bent over until the words are said: “To us also, sinners.” Then they first straighten themselves and stand in the place where they had stood before, because the disciples and the women followed the Lord as far as the place of the crucifixion—not only following, but also mourning.

Jesus turned and said: “Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep over me, but weep over yourselves and over your children.” The women wept as though for a sinner; but the Lord himself showed that they ought not to weep over him, but over themselves.

And what kind of ministry do you suppose the subdeacons have when they stand bent over, if they do not pray and weep for their own sins? Tropologically, the subdeacons are bent over because they have turned aside. They stand upright through confession and look upward into the face of the pontiff after he says, “To us also, sinners.”

How could the disciples and women close their eyes so as not to see the Lord hanging on the cross, whom they loved so greatly? The subdeacons remain in that sight until the chalice is surrounded with the *fanon*. Then at last they withdraw to prepare the chalices [Editor's note: rather, the patens which the subdeacons carry for the breaking of the Hosts] in which the Lord’s body may be honorably kept.

You will hear how long they stood above on the day at the cross. Luke says: “This man went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus, and, having taken it down, wrapped it in a linen cloth. The women who had come with him from Galilee followed and saw the tomb and how his body had been placed; and returning, they prepared spices and ointments. On the Sabbath they rested.”

The women prepared spices and ointments with which the Lord’s body might be embalmed, lest it be reduced to dust. The subdeacons, after they see the chalice surrounded with linen, go to prepare the chalice—or clean cloths—in which they may receive the Lord’s body, lest it fall to the ground and turn to dust.

The women kept silence on the Sabbath; that is, the subdeacons wait until the Lord’s Prayer has been completed and until what depends upon that Prayer has been accomplished. The Sabbath is appropriately fitted to the Lord’s Prayer, in which there are seven petitions. For through the seventh [petition] the sevenfold Spirit is understood.

The silence of the Sabbath, which is adapted to the Lord’s Prayer, signifies the rest of the mind that is given through the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit; and we ministers ask for these gifts in the Lord’s Prayer. Therefore the churches rest at that same hour.

The deacons plainly remain bent over until the Lord’s Prayer has been completed, while the subdeacons straighten themselves when they hear, “To us also, sinners.” Through them are signified those to whom Christ said: “But you, sit in the city until you are clothed with power from on high”—namely, the apostles.

Their continuing inclination signifies their perseverance in prayer, so that they might receive the Lord’s promise. He expressly commanded them to await the promise of the Holy Spirit in Jerusalem until Pentecost.

They stand bent over until the seven petitions of the Lord’s Prayer have been completed; and concerning them it is read above that they ministered to him as far as the tomb, and afterward prepared the spices. Those who bear their type withdraw from the altar to prepare the ministry when they hear: “For ever and ever. Amen.”

### 21. Concerning “Te igitur,” and why it is sung secretly

The custom of our fathers was that those who prayed should render praise to God. Therefore what we say in a loud voice before *Te igitur* belongs to the praise of our Creator, so that it may be openly demonstrated to all who can distinguish it. There we are also reminded that we ought to give thanks to God, and the angelic creation is declared to praise its Creator, each in the ministry suited to it.

Afterward comes *Te igitur*, the Prayer—namely, the special prayer of the priests—in which the priest prays, particularly for certain persons, as he does for the apostolic lord. Then comes the passage where he says, “Of your servants and handmaids.” Immediately after he has poured out a prayer for his own people, he turns generally to pray for all, adding: “And all who stand around,” and other similar words.

Since this Prayer pertains especially to the priest, the priest alone enters into it and sings it secretly. He follows the command of his teacher, who says: “But when you pray, go into your room,” and so forth.

This custom remains in our Church to this day: if anyone makes a prayer, he should make it specifically. He raises his voice in such a way as to admonish himself concerning what he ought to ask in the secret of his heart.

Nor is it without reason that this custom is maintained among Christians: without doubt, because Christ prayed alone. Hence Matthew says: “And having dismissed the crowd, he went up the mountain alone to pray.”

### 22. Concerning the crosses in “Te igitur”

The crosses in this Prayer are made six times, so that, just as God’s works are perfect, the perfect body of that same God and our Lord Jesus Christ may also be understood. The number six is perfect when reckoned by its parts.

This is signified by the fact that the final cross is made with the offering: the one who came to suffer for the whole Church, whose body submitted to the Passion even to the touch of the cross.

The five series of crosses made before the sixth, when the chalice is touched with the offering, signify the five ages of the world before the Lord’s birth. The sixth signifies the time remaining from the Lord’s birth until the end of the world.

The single touching of the chalice with the offering signifies that the Lord ascended the cross once, so that the suffering that had been taking place through the five ages of the world might come to an end.

By the offering raised in the hand the prophets are signified, for they raised the true bread, Christ, in their hands when they openly proclaimed his incarnation. Hence Isaiah says: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son.”

When the deacon sees the bishop make the cross and begin to raise the chalice, he goes and holds the chalice, raised together with the bishop, until he says, “For ever and ever.” Then he places the chalice on the altar and wraps it in a cloth.

Joseph, having received the body of Jesus, wrapped it in a clean linen cloth and placed it in his own tomb. We therefore place the deacon present here, on account of the ministry that corresponds to it, in the type of Joseph, or more generally in the type of those who receive Christ’s mysteries with a pure heart.

The deacon who holds the chalice raised with the pontiff places it on the altar, because Joseph took the Lord’s body down from the cross and placed it in the tomb. As we said, the deacon wraps the chalice with a cloth, just as Joseph wrapped the body in a clean linen cloth.

On the altar—that is, in the tomb—the corporal lies. By it is understood the larger linen cloth with which the whole body was covered in the tomb. By the cloth that covers part of the chalice we understand the cloth that covered part of the Lord’s head and did not cover another part, according to the custom of the Jews.

This action remains on the altar—that is, in the tomb—until three sections have been completed: the prologue concerning the following Prayer, the *Pater noster*, and *Libera nos, Domine*. For the Lord rested three days in the tomb.

Afterward, when the Lord’s body has been mixed with wine and peace has been proclaimed, the Lord’s body is taken from the altar, just as, on the third day, the soul that had descended to the underworld to free the righteous returned to the body to give life to its members; and the Lord’s body was no longer found in the tomb.

Therefore, since the whole human being rose, it is fitting that the Lord’s chalice also be immediately taken from the altar together with the offering.

### 23. Concerning the names of the four Prayers of the bishops or the people

The first Prayer is sometimes called a *Prayer* and sometimes a *Collect*. It is plainly called a Prayer because they pray good things for the people; it is called a Collect because the people are gathered together as one.

May it please your fraternity, dearest brother, to make use of the authority of Saint Augustine in this little work. He divides this service into four kinds: petitions, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings. He recalls them as follows:

“Whatever is done in the service of the Mass before the offerings are placed on the altar is called a petition.” He distinguishes *precation*, *deprecation*, and *imprecation* in this way: *precation* occurs when one wishes good for the people; *deprecation*, when one prays that evil may be avoided and that one may cease from sins; *imprecation*, when one wishes evil, that is, curses.

The first Prayer said by the bishop is called a *precation*, that is, a good wish for the people. We said that the Introit belongs to the service of the prophets, because through the mouths of the prophets Christ entered the world. He not only entered, but also assumed flesh and became human, deriving his human origin from the holy patriarchs. One of them greatly desired and commended the expectation of him to the people, saying: “The scepter shall not be taken from Judah,” and so forth.

### 24. Concerning the Secret

It is called the Secret because the bishop offers a secret Prayer over the offering, asking that God look upon the offering that has been set forth and appoint it for future consecration. It is known that the Secret is made over the offering so that the Lord’s body may be made from it.

### 25.

The breaking of the offerings signifies the breaking that the Lord performed for the two disciples at Emmaus. For this reason some bishops, when they communicate with one another, customarily make three portions from one offering, as a type of these three: Christ, Cleopas, and, as they say, Luke.

Just as there are many Churches throughout the whole world because of their different locations, yet there is one holy catholic Church because of the one faith, so there are many offerings because of the vows of those who offer, yet there is one bread because of the unity of Christ’s Body.

If you ask why the offering is not placed whole in the chalice, since it is certain that the Lord’s whole body rose: part of it will rise, part already lives so as never to die again, and part is mortal, yet is in heaven. Hence the Apostle says: “But our citizenship is in heaven.”

### 26. Concerning the peace proclaimed before the Lord’s body and blood are mixed

The peace spoken by the bishop or priest before the Lord’s body is placed into the blood can be understood in two ways.

First, that peace may be understood by this peace which was given to the righteous at the time when Christ’s soul descended into hell and brought out all the faithful, and so forth.

Or certainly, that peace may be understood by this peace which was given to Christ’s body when the soul returned to it. Just as the soul was never troubled by its death, so the body should no longer be troubled by its transformation; rather, both should enjoy that peace, so that they may always rejoice in eternal immortality.

Nor is it irrelevant if, through the touch by which the lips of the chalice are touched, we understand at the same time that passage of Scripture: “And he breathed into his face the breath of life.” In this way the restoration of life is understood in the member to which life was first given, as we read.

It is also consistent with reason that, since there are four senses in the head, the lips of the chalice should be touched at the four quarters of the world, and so forth.

Certain Gentiles who did not yet belong to God sought through Philip, who was the mouth of the lamp, to see Jesus. This signified that the Gentiles would become the Lord’s body through faith.

In the same way, when this bread is first placed on the altar, it is understood that the Lord’s body will be made from it. Let us hear what the Lord answers concerning those Gentiles just mentioned: “Unless a grain of wheat falling into the earth dies, it remains alone.”

By this it is plainly shown that unless he himself dies, the Gentile peoples do not become his body. Thus pure bread could not previously become his body unless the priest’s sacrament of the Lord’s Passion were recalled and the sign of the cross were celebrated on its behalf.

### 27. Further concerning the Secret

Christ sought solitude in prayer. How much more ought we to seek it, surrounded as we are on every side by the turmoil of vices and by worldly custom?

It is useful that every special Prayer of the priests be secret, so that we may not consider how the sound of our voice and the arrangement of our speech might please the earthly people, but only how the mind may agree with the God alone to whom it prays.

From the place where the bishop says the Secret until the *Agnus Dei*, Augustine calls the whole passage *Prayers*.

### 28. Concerning the Preface

The Preface is so called as though it were a prelude (*praelocutio*). This Prayer, called the Preface, is the prelude to the whole Prayer that follows, which begins before *Te igitur* and continues to the *Agnus Dei*.

This Prayer follows the custom of the Prayer of our fathers, who were accustomed to render praises to God in prayer. Thus Daniel prayed: “Lord our God, who brought your people out of the land of Egypt,” and so forth.

### 29. Concerning the Blessing after Communion

Augustine calls this Prayer after Communion an intercession. It is called “after Communion” because it follows after the people have communicated; it is called “over the people” because the people are then blessed, so that they may accord with our holy Gospel.

After the Prayer and Communion, the Blessing follows, because after Christ had prayed on the cross, eaten before his disciples, given them the remnants, and blessed them with raised hands, “it came to pass, while he blessed them, that he withdrew from them and was carried up into heaven.”

Our Blessing is an intercession before God, asking that he deign to bless. After giving the Blessing, the bishop returns to his own place.

Then the deacon announces: “Go, the dismissal is made.” He speaks to the people in the type of the angels, who said to the apostles: “This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven,” and so forth.

What is “Go, the dismissal is made,” my brother, except: “Go in peace to your homes”? A Prayer has been offered to the Lord on your behalf, and through the angels, who are called messengers, it has been brought into the presence of the divine Majesty.

The people respond: “Thanks be to God.” Augustine calls this response “thanksgivings.” The holy Church does this according to apostolic custom: the apostles worshiped Jesus and returned to Jerusalem with great joy.

Hear how the apostles render thanks to God: “And they were continually in the temple, praising and blessing God, who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.”

## How certain Prayers and crosses are to be performed in “Te igitur”

“Therefore, most merciful Father, through Jesus Christ your Son, our Lord, we humbly beseech and ask that you may accept and bless.”

Here he signs the offering and the chalice three times—not under a single cross, but making a separate cross for each one.

“These + gifts, these + offerings, these + holy sacrifices, unblemished.”

“First, those which we offer to you for your holy catholic Church: may you deign to grant her peace, guard her, unite her, and govern her throughout the whole world, together with your servant, our pope, N.”

“Remember, Lord, your servants and handmaids.”

Here the names of the living may be mentioned, if you wish, but not on the Lord’s Day, except on certain days.

“And all who stand around, whose faith is known and whose devotion is recognized by you, who offer you this sacrifice of praise for themselves and all their own, for the redemption of their souls, for the hope of their salvation and safety, and who render their vows to you, the eternal, living, and true God.

“Communicating together and venerating the day … [lacuna] … Cosmas and Damian.”

If it is the feast day of the saints, he says here:

“And also celebrating the feast of blessed N., or of blessed N. and N., and of all the saints, by whose merits and prayers grant that in all things we may be fortified by the help of your protection, through Christ our Lord.”

Here he bows down to the altar, saying:

“Therefore, this offering of our service … and command that we be numbered among the flock of your chosen, through Christ our Lord.”

The rest may be found above, p. 61.

## II. JOHN THE DEACON’S BOOK CONCERNING THE LATERAN CHURCH

### Here begins the prologue to the book concerning the Holy of Holies

To the most blessed lord and most reverend father Alexander, by divine grace supreme pontiff of the Catholic Church and of the apostolic see, John, an unworthy deacon, canon of the basilica of the Savior in the Lateran patriarchate: a book concerning the Holy of Holies, renewed from the archive.

Since, according to the proclamation of the wise man, “it is the glory of kings to conceal a word, and the glory of God to investigate a matter,” it is all the more commendable for the adherents of each to render diligent and devoted service for the pleasure and honor of each, insofar as a worthy reward is hoped for from the fullness of the grace of each and is confidently believed to be forthcoming, and so forth.

Accordingly, with this consideration in view, I have taken care, by the authority and command of Your Holiness and by the mandate and will of the venerable prior John and the brothers of the same Church, to renew, for the honor of the Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, the little book containing the record of the Holy of Holies. It has been preserved in the archive of this most holy basilica by our predecessors down to our own times, but has now been almost effaced by the age of antiquity. Since this has seemed pleasing and welcome to Your Beatitude, and because its publication was most necessary, I have done so lest the memory of sacred things so celebrated, carefully preserved and handed down to us by our predecessors, should fail to reach our descendants through forgetfulness caused by our negligence; it is to be preserved by posterity and to benefit their devotion.

Since we shall undoubtedly render an account, not only for falsehoods but also for idle words, before the tribunal of the living God, into whose hands it is dreadful to fall, I wish Your Paternal Benevolence—revered before God and human beings for the fullness and sincerity of its merits—and all who take delight in the record of this little book, to know that I have inserted no presumptuous novelties for the sake of superstition.

Rather, I have simply preserved the ancient sequence by writing it down. If I add anything else, these are certainly matters that either I myself, living for the span of five lustrums in this most holy basilica in the canonical way of life, have seen with my own eyes, or have learned through truthful report from our predecessors—namely, matters concerning the translation of the saints Chrysanthus and Daria, or the discovery of the holy Rufina and Secunda, and of the saints Cyprian and Justina; or matters drawn from the histories and authorities of the saints to dispel the uncertain opinion held by some concerning the concealment of the tabernacle and the ark, and the things contained in it, or concerning the altar of incense.

To make these matters plainly clear, I have taken care in what follows to set out more explicitly the names and books of the historians, their dates, and the names and volumes of the teachers, and so forth.

## IN THE NAME OF THE HOLY AND UNDIVIDED TRINITY

### Here begins the writing concerning the supreme sanctuary of the holy Roman Church of God—that is, the Lateran Church

This work has been composed from the archives and the ancient deeds of the Roman pontiffs. That Church, patriarchal and imperial by the privilege and prerogative of the holy apostolic see, possesses, by the gift of the grace of God the Savior Jesus Christ, dominion and primacy over all the Churches of the whole world. By divine will it also bears the glorious name of the apostolic dignity and of the Roman Empire.

Since the whole world ought to render this mother Church the service of due submission, many envoys from different regions gather here. Because they do not know how great and how precious the sanctuary of God hidden in this aforementioned Church is, we wish it to be recorded through the disclosure of these writings—at least when they gather here to entreat God, the Son of God, Jesus Christ our Lord and Savior of the saints: for the peace of the holy Church, for the remission of all sins, for acquiring the glory of the eternal vision of God, and for fellowship with the eternal citizens and holy souls.

Therefore, after the blessed and saving passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, his glorious resurrection from the dead, and his wondrous ascension into heaven, having received the consolation of the most glorious coming of the Holy Spirit, the apostles set out on their journey to the portion assigned to their preaching. By the disposition of God’s ineffable mercy, those eminent senators of the heavenly kingdom, namely Peter and Paul, the heads of the whole world, entered this city of Rome. There they faithfully established the foundation of the catholic faith upon the Rock—that is, upon Christ—in honor of our Lord Jesus Christ. [Col. 1381C] For the advancement of its construction they fought even unto death; for love of it they shed their glorious blood, finally undergoing the death of the cross and the temporal sword, and crowned with laurel they sought the court of the heavenly King.

These are the holy men whose teaching makes the Church shine, 562 which the ancient enemy first through Nero and then through successive rulers attacked and shook for three hundred years and more, but was wholly unable to overthrow. When it pleased him who allowed his faithful to be tested in the fire of suffering, Constantine Augustus, son of Constantius and Helena, assumed the imperial dignity and for a time exercised the tyranny of the preceding rulers against the servants of Jesus Christ. But God’s immense pity, sympathizing with the sorrow and distress of his elect who cried out to him, did not delay to put an end to the calamity and misery of so great a persecution.

What more need be said? For, as we read in the Life of Saint Sylvester, the aforesaid Emperor Constantine was struck by God with elephantiasis, or leprosy; [Col. 1381D] and the priests of the Capitol gave him this advice: that he should descend naked into a pool filled with the blood of slaughtered infants, and, thus cleansed from his leprosy, recover his former health, etc.

Then he conferred upon the pontiff of the Roman Church the privilege that, throughout the Roman world, priests should regard him as their head and prince, just as all judges were accustomed to regard the king. Among other things, this privilege reads as follows:

“We have judged it beneficial, together with all our satraps, the entire senate, the nobles also, and the whole people subject to the glory of Rome, that just as blessed Peter appears to have been established on earth as the vicar of the Son of God, so also the pontiffs of that prince of the apostles, exercising authority in the place of the prince, should possess greater power than the earthly imperial mildness of our serenity appears to have,” etc.

For, as we read in the Deeds of Blessed Sylvester—which blessed Pope Gelasius recalls having been read by Catholics in a council of seventy bishops—[Col. 1382A] on the second day of his procession the aforesaid Emperor Constantine promulgated a law which concluded in these words:

“Let it be known to all that we have become worshipers of Christ in such a way that within our palace we shall construct a temple bearing this name,” etc.

Afterward, when this church had been built and completed, blessed Sylvester solemnly consecrated it publicly—which had not previously been done—on the fifth day before the Ides of November. That is the most celebrated festival in the City to this day: on it the first church was publicly consecrated, and the image of the Savior, fixed upon the walls, first appeared visibly to the entire Roman people. It is called the Dedication of the Basilica of the Savior.

Hence every church throughout the City and throughout the world that is specially designated by the name of the Savior recalls and venerates, on the aforesaid day, the memory of that celebration. Apostolic authority decreed that the solemnity of this dedication should be celebrated for eight days, because on the tenth day after the solemnity of this dedication the basilicas of the holy apostles Peter and Paul were subsequently dedicated.

[Col. 1382B] Hence the Roman pontiff of that same Savior Jesus Christ, who is gentle and abundant in mercy toward all who return to him, relying upon the certain mercy of almighty God, salutarily ordained that, at the dedication of this most holy basilica—which has received the name “of Mercy”—a great remission of sins should be granted to all who came to share in the joy of this festival, provided that they were known to have confessed their sins worthily to God and the Church and to have undergone penance, or that they confessed them with true and God-pleasing contrition of heart up to the eighth day.

This remission, by apostolic provision, is divided into three parts: a remission of 1,000 years for Romans and those living nearby; 2,000 years for Tuscans and Lombards; and 3,000 years for those known to have crossed the seas.

A similar and identical institution of remission is demonstrably made in this first and most holy basilica on the fifth day of the week, Maundy Thursday, when the apostolic lord consecrates the sacred [Col. 1382C] chrism, and when obstinate heretics and those who exalt themselves against this holy catholic and apostolic Church are, by apostolic judgment and the curse of public excommunication, handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that finally, by God’s mercy, when they have come to their senses and escaped the devil’s snares, their spirit may be saved on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.

## I. On the mystical names of this most holy basilica

This Church, I say, has been distinguished by the holy Fathers, as is found in their writings, by several mystical names. It is principally called a basilica because, since it has been dedicated to the King of kings, the Savior Jesus Christ—to him who on earth is the supreme king and priest—it is shown to have been entrusted to him.

It is also called the Golden Basilica, or the Constantinian Basilica, because, as is said, Constantine had it entirely decorated with golden mosaic. It is also called the Temple of Mercy because, as can be seen to this day, although it had many entrances, it was closed neither by day [Col. 1382D] nor by night, except with hangings, so that it might always lie open as another asylum to all offenders, in order that they might no longer be punished by secular laws.

It is also called the Apostolic Church, because it is instructed solely by the teachings of the apostles; the Apostolic See, because no one dares to sit there except the apostolic pontiff; the First See, because the second is Antioch and the third Alexandria; and the See of Peter, because Peter himself sits there through his vicar.

It is also called the Roman Church, after the City; and, after its location, the Lateran Church, the Lateran Basilica, the Lateran Episcopium, and the Lateran Patriarchate.

It is called the Universal Church because its bishop has the power to judge concerning everyone, while no one has power to judge concerning him. For this reason it is called the head of the Churches, the mother of the Churches, and the teacher of the Churches, because all receive nourishment and instruction from it. It provides for everyone and watches over everyone; and for the sake of its faith, so that it may never fail [Col. 1383A] but confirm its brethren, the Savior himself prays.

By these and many other names this hall of God is nobly adorned and honored in the divine writings.

## II. That Helena the mother carried to her son everything found in the Temple after its destruction

This most holy basilica, therefore, reverenced by the whole world, was enriched by the most blessed Helena, Constantine’s mother, after she had received the sacrament of holy baptism, with an incomparable treasure of sacred objects.

At the request of her August son she transported these things from the regions of Jerusalem: they had been stored away by the ancients before the Lord’s Incarnation, and after the destruction said to have been carried out by Titus and Vespasian, Roman emperors, whatever remained of them was kept there.

The almighty God deigned to open so many bowels of his mercy to this Roman Church when the aforementioned queen brought from the holy city of Jerusalem, by God’s will, the sanctuary she had carried with her to her son, and transferred its dwelling into this most holy [Col. 1383B] basilica, 564 which is both priestly and royal.

Since this has not yet been designated by its proper name, and although I am unworthy to disclose its name, I shall nevertheless not delay naming it reverently in honor of its praise.

Likewise, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1260, Pope Alexander IV, on the day of the dedication of this most holy Church, strengthened and confirmed all indulgences granted by any supreme pontiffs, at whatever time; and especially those which blessed Sylvester had abundantly established and granted. At the entreaty of the just prayers of the humble and most Christian Constantine, Alexander extended them, by his special mercy and grace, up to the day of the dedication of the apostles Peter and Paul.

## III. On the ark and the holy things of holy things in the Basilica of the Savior

In this most holy Lateran Basilica, therefore, dedicated to the Savior Jesus Christ God, which is the head of the world, [Col. 1383C] which is patriarchal and imperial, and which is the see of the apostolic pontifical chair, the ark of the Lord’s covenant is located on the principal altar of that same Church. Or, as they say, the ark is below, while an altar corresponding to the ark in length, breadth, and height has been built above it, between four columns of red porphyry beneath a beautiful ciborium.

In it, they assert, there is a great quantity of sacred treasure, but they do not know what it is, since they do not know its name.

On the altar above, which is wooden and covered with silver, and beneath it below, there is the following sacred treasure: the seven lampstands that were in the former tabernacle. Hence the apostle Paul says:

“The tabernacle was made first, in which were the lampstands, the table, and the presentation of the loaves, which is called the Holy Place; and the golden censer; and the golden urn containing manna. The second tabernacle had what is called the Holy of Holies. And there was there the rod of Aaron that had blossomed; and the tablets of the covenant; and the rod of Moses with which he struck the flint twice, and waters flowed.”

[Col. 1383D] There are also there relics from the Lord’s manger; some of the five barley loaves and two fishes; the Lord’s table; the cloth with which he wiped the feet of his disciples; and the seamless tunic which the Virgin Mary made for her son, our Lord Jesus Christ. At his death the soldiers cast lots for it rather than tearing it apart. As long as the Savior preserves it there, heresy or division of the faith will not long remain within it.

There is also the purple garment of that same Savior and Redeemer; two ampoules of the blood and water from the Lord’s side; the Lord’s circumcision; the sudarium that was over his head, one of the five linen cloths in which the most holy body of that same Lord of ours was wrapped; something from the place of Christ’s ascension into heaven; some of the blood of Saint John the Baptist; some dust and ashes from the burned body of that same precursor of Christ; his hair shirt made of camel’s hair; and an ampoule full of the manna of the burial of Saint John the Evangelist.

There is also the tunic of that same [Col. 1384A] apostle and evangelist. When it was placed beneath the bodies of three young men, they rose again, for they had died because of the poison they had drunk.

565

## IV. An explanation concerning those who object that the tabernacle, the ark, or the altar of incense was concealed

Yet very many people, investigating less wisely the profound mysteries of the sacred books and histories, and understanding neither what they say nor the matters about which they make assertions, because the Second Book of Maccabees contains a passage concerning the concealment of the tabernacle and the ark, or also the altar of incense, form the superfluous opinion that the tabernacle, the ark, or the altar has remained hidden up to the time of the future judgment—and they do not know, etc.

## V. That in the time of Titus and Vespasian the things that had been in the Temple were transferred to Rome

At what time, then, and by whom the vessels and utensils of the Temple, or all its offerings, were brought to Rome, [Col. 1384B] and where they were deposited, the aforementioned doctor Jerome—whose constant concern was to investigate new matters and clarify what was hidden—testifies in his exposition of the prophet Joel.

He says that Titus and Vespasian, Roman emperors, after the Lord’s ascension, destroyed the city of Jerusalem and the Temple, and carried away with them, as a victory trophy and monument to the Roman people, everything of special value and beauty that the Jews had possessed in the Temple; indeed, they ordered the Jews themselves to carry these things away. After building the Temple of Peace at Rome, they magnificently stored them there as objects of worship. Greek and Roman history recounts this.

There is no doubt that what so great a man taught should be accepted as confirmed by what Greek and Roman history wished to establish. The same thing can still plainly be discerned on the triumphal arch called the Arch of the Seven Lamps. It is proved to have been constructed in memory of the aforesaid emperors and the entire Roman people beside the Church of Saint Mary the New. On it the lampstands that had been in the former tabernacle, and the ark with its garments, which had been in the second tabernacle within the veil, can visibly be seen sculpted with manifest and marvelous workmanship. [Col. 1384C]

The eloquent doctor Pope Leo also seems to declare this with still clearer evidence in his sermons on the Lord’s Passion, when, arguing against Jewish unbelief concerning the veil torn in the Temple at the very time of Christ’s passion, he protested that all the elements of the world had given more evident proof against the blindness of the Jews. In the sermon that begins, “While Jewish impiety was struggling in many ways,” he wrote as follows:

“If neither the heavenly nor the infernal things suffice to refute you, and if rocks and tombs were able to perceive Christ’s cross more than your hearts, at least pay intelligent attention to what happened in the Temple. The veil by which the Holy of Holies was shut off was torn apart from top to bottom, and that sacred and mystical secret, into which only the high priest had been commanded to enter, was opened,” etc.

Beneath this most sacred altar of which we are now speaking [Col. 1384D] is an image made entirely of gold, dedicated to the Lord Jesus Christ and to the blessed Virgin Mary; 566 and there are images of Saint John the Baptist and of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, made of gold and silver electrum, as well as images of the other apostles made entirely of silver.

The Emperor Constantine, servant of God, who took care to have these images made in honor of the Savior Jesus Christ and his disciples, contrived to store them in a certain women’s chamber in such a way that no craftsman, by any ingenuity whatsoever, could gain access to it.

## VI. That it is festively rung every day at Matins, Mass, and Vespers

Because this Church represents the heavenly Church, it is festively rung day and night every day at Matins, Mass, and Vespers. Hence at Masses there is not sung in it the Agnus Dei, “who takes away the sins of the world, grant us peace,” because there the supreme peace of the righteous will itself be Christ, in whom it will be perfected and completed among the elect; neither petition nor increase will then be necessary.

## VII. On the Lord’s Prayer, which is frequently used in every office

[Col. 1385A] This Church, preserving the apostolic institution, uses the Prayer only on Sundays in its offices, since the other prayers were added later. It is fitting and appropriate that the first and chief of all other Churches should frequently use the first and chief of all other prayers; and that the Church consecrated under the Savior’s name should always hold above all others the Savior’s Prayer, which he taught his disciples to pray.

There are also certain other collects designated for Matins or Vespers, which may be said in this Church solely by the apostolic pontiff or by his seven associated bishops, and absolutely not by anyone else.

## VIII. On the seven weekly bishops and the other officials of the same Church

[Col. 1385B]

No one dares to approach this solemn and most holy altar to offer sacrifice—where, as we have said, the unsplit garment is kept, together with another abundant and incomparable sacred treasure, which we shall refrain from naming here in its entirety—except the apostolic lord and the seven cardinal bishops of that Church, who celebrate Mass in this most holy basilica in their appointed weeks.

Whatever offering they receive at that Mass, from the beginning of the office to its end, whether in gold or silver or in any other offerings, including at ordinations and consecrations, they divide equally with the canons of the same Church assisting them in the ministry of the altar and in the offices, except for the offering of bread and wine, which belongs only to the canons.

Their seven official names should be recorded here: the bishop of Ostia, who above all others ought to consecrate and bless the apostolic pontiff; 567 [Col. 1385C] the bishop of Santa Rufina, second; the bishop of Porto, third; the bishop of Albano, fourth; the bishop of Tusculum, fifth; the bishop of Sabina, sixth; and the bishop of Palestrina, seventh.

On certain Sundays and feast days, and on the principal solemnities of the saints, the priest is sometimes a royal and imperial bishop, indeed a patriarch; and the same apostolic pontiff ought to celebrate Mass at the aforementioned most sacred altar of the Savior in this Lateran Basilica.

When the lord pope, the vicar of Saint Peter, celebrates, his aforementioned vicars and associates must also assist him: namely, the seven bishops together with twenty-eight cardinals, each presiding over one of as many churches within the walls of the city of Rome. They possess the power to exercise judgment over all the bishops of the whole Roman Empire in every council or synod at which they have been present or to which they have been sent as legates.

The archdeacon must also be present there, together with the six palatine deacons, who ought to read the Gospel in the palace and in the Lateran Basilica; [Col. 1385D] and the twelve regional deacons, who customarily read the Gospel at the station churches established in Rome.

These eighteen deacons have an equal number of churches within the walls of the city. Nevertheless, all are canons of the patriarchal Lateran Basilica.

There must also be present seven palatine subdeacons and the schola cantorum—that is, another seven subdeacons called regional subdeacons. These are to read the lessons and epistles at the stations established in Rome.

Another seven, namely the schola cantorum, must sing the office while the lord pope celebrates Mass in the Lateran Basilica and elsewhere. The other seven, namely the palatine subdeacons, must read the Epistle in the palace at the apostolic pontiff’s Mass, and also in the same patriarchal Lateran Basilica, as well as at the Masses of the apostolic pontiff.

[Col. 1386A] Acolytes, chaplains, lectors, exorcists, and doorkeepers are also present there, each of whom strives to fulfill his office as it was established there by the holy Fathers.

In the aforementioned Lateran Basilica there are also altars of certain saints, whose names are as follows.

In the canons’ choir is the altar of Saint Mary Magdalene, in which her body, without the head, was deposited by the hands of Pope Honorius III, who consecrated that altar.

Behind the apse is the altar of Saints Chrysanthus and Daria, in which their precious bodies had formerly been deposited. But when it had been desecrated by schismatics, they were removed from there again and transferred to the Church of the blessed Mother of God Mary and of Saint Pancratius the Martyr, which is on the right side of the basilica. They were deposited in the altar of that church, which was consecrated by the hands of Pope Innocent II. In it he deposited the precious relics of the saints—namely, those of Pancratius; the apostle James; the apostle Matthew; [Col. 1386B] the apostle Thaddeus; Timothy, Paul’s disciple; the protomartyr Stephen; the Holy Innocents; some of the Lord’s linen cloth; some of his sepulcher; some of the unburned thorn bush; and some of Blasius, Nicomedes, Vitalis, Gervasius and Protasius, Nazarius and Celsus, Saint Felix, and the Forty Holy Martyrs.

In the same part are the tombs of the apostolic pontiffs, among them that of Pope Lucius II of blessed memory. 568 He had lived for a long time in this Church according to the canonical way of life, and from here he was taken and ordained cardinal priest in the Church of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem. He renewed that church from its foundations, rebuilding it from its ruins with splendid and admirable workmanship; he endowed it with many processions before his pontificate, and fashioned it according to the standard of religious life and the rule of blessed Augustine.

He also loved this Church in every way, remembering his appointment from it and his former way of life, and honored it with great benefactions. On the eighth day after his consecration, he offered upon the altar a [Col. 1386C] Gospel book covered with gold plates and adorned with enamel and many precious stones in the most beautiful workmanship. Then, not long afterward, [Note: [Col. 1385] Below, *tarantasmum* is mentioned as an altar covering; a little farther below, *sarantasmum*, which appears to be the genuine reading.] an excellent *sarantasmum* for the adornment of the altar; and also two large ampoules, finely wrought, of gilded silver, for the ministry of the sacrifice, weighing four pounds.

He also drew up a privilege in which he granted to this basilica the Church of Saint John before the Latin Gate, with everything belonging to it, as well as the hospital beside the gate.

Nearby lies Pope Leo V, and Pope Agapitus II beside his tomb. From there, directly to the right, lies Pope Paschal II, who, with salutary foresight and zeal, renewed the canonical order in this Church. Beside him lies Pope Callistus II, who restored peace with the Emperor Henry. Next to him rests Pope Honorius II, and then beside him Pope Celestine II.

From there, in the portico, are many burials of bishops of this Church. In the same portico lies Gerbert, [Col. 1386D] archbishop of Reims, who, having become pope, was called Sylvester. His tomb often visibly emits drops of water, even in perfectly clear weather, although it is not in a damp place—a phenomenon sufficiently astonishing to human beings.

From there is the altar of the Forty Holy Martyrs, near this altar.

In the nave of the Church lies Pope Innocent II in a porphyry sarcophagus that had been the tomb of the Emperor Hadrian. He renewed the roof of this basilica at his own expense, using new beams which the glorious and powerful Roger, king of Sicily, sent to that Church at his request. The roof fell during his pontificate and was restored during his pontificate.

He also ordered the tower before the Church, which appeared close to ruin, to be renewed. During his lifetime he offered many gifts to the Church for the adornment of the altar: [Col. 1387A] namely, a very fine *cyclas* woven with gold, from which afterward a vestment for the adornment of the altar and a chasuble for the celebration of Mass were made; a *tarantasmum* for covering the altar; a silver censer weighing two pounds; and 100 pounds of Lucchese currency for purchasing estates to support the canons.

Later, Lord Bernard, prior of this basilica—who afterward became cardinal of Saint Clement and then bishop of Porto—bought, with salutary zeal and foresight, estates not far from the City, beside the aqueducts near the Church of Saint Helena.

Likewise, in the same part beside the doors of the Church, there rests a certain pope who had been called Sergius from Peter [i.e. formerly Peter]. Beside him lies Pope Alexander II, 569 who had been bishop of Lucca. He also drew up an excellent privilege for the aforesaid basilica and renewed the common life of the regular canons there. In that privilege he granted those canons half of all the offerings of the principal altar, the houses surrounding this basilica, and many [Col. 1387B] other estates situated in various cities and places, as the worthy testimony of that privilege recounts to us.

Between the two doors is another pope who has no epitaph. Again, in this part, beside the doors of the Church:

> Here rest the limbs of the supreme pontiff John.

He renewed this same basilica.

Again, between the two doors of the Church in this part:

> Here is seen the tomb said to be that  
> of the supreme John, who was also called by that name.

This was Pope John XVII.

Before the doors of the Church rests a certain prelate who was called Peter. Above the inner side of the doors of the Church was written:

> The pious Pope Sergius himself, who began this hall  
> from its foundations, the third, copying this house  
> which you behold.

In the atrium of the same basilica there is also a beautiful oratory, and in it is the altar of Saint Thomas the Apostle. In this oratory, which Pope John [Col. 1387C] built when he renewed the Church, the pontiff put on the sacerdotal and pontifical vestments whenever he was to celebrate Mass at the stations of this basilica.

For, leaving this oratory in procession, he enters the basilica and proceeds to the most holy dominical altar, which alone among all the altars holds primacy.

Pope Celestine III lies beside Saint Mary of Repose. Pope Alexander III lies before the pulpit of the Church, or beside the road when one goes to the curia. Pope Clement III lies before the canons’ choir.

On the left side of the basilica is the altar of blessed Mary of Repose. Beside it lies Pope Anastasius IV, who had been bishop of Sabina, in a splendidly wrought porphyry mausoleum in which Helena, the mother of the Emperor Constantine, had formerly lain. The same pope had this mausoleum transported from the church which that emperor had built outside the City in honor of his mother.

While he was still a bishop, Anastasius had loved this Church uniquely and most devoutly above all others; after being elevated to the apostolic office, he [Col. 1387D] honored it with many benefactions. He solemnly drew up two privileges for the canons of the aforesaid basilica, in which he both confirmed what they then possessed and, out of his kindness and grace, added many further gifts.

In these privileges he granted this Church the Church of Saint Gregory in Marcio, together with the palace in which it is situated and everything belonging to it, as well as land with a mill outside the gate at the head, where there had once been a settlement.

While still a bishop, he also offered many gifts for the adornment of the most holy dominical altar; afterward, elevated to the apostolic dignity on the most holy apostolic see, he offered one *cyclas* to the dominical altar on the eighth day after his consecration.

Then, on the fifteenth day, he offered a white and excellent chasuble, bordered with precious gold embroidery, 570 for the celebration of Mass. After some interval of time he offered, for the adornment of the altar, two excellent candlesticks made by casting, one splendid and excellent *sarantasmum*, [Col. 1388A] and three pounds of silver for the support of the brothers.

On the anniversary of the dedication of this most sacred basilica he also offered a fairly large and remarkable chalice, notable both for the great weight of its material and for the variety of its admirable workmanship. It was marvelously fashioned with sculptural work on every side and adorned with various scenes and verses; it weighed twenty-eight pounds.

> “In the name of the Lord, amen. In the year of the Incarnation 1297, on the … day of the month of February, the Chapter altar was consecrated in honor of God and blessed Mary Magdalene, by order of Lord Pope Boniface VIII, through Lord Gerard of Parma, bishop of Sabina. In this altar he deposited the body of blessed Mary Magdalene without the head, the arm of blessed Zacharias, and relics of many other saints.”

Some judges are palatine, whom we call ordinary judges; others are consular, distributed among the jurisdictions; others are subordinate judges appointed by the consuls.

In the Roman Empire [Col. 1388B] and in the Roman Church even to this day there are seven palatine judges, who are called ordinary judges. They appoint the emperor and, together with the Roman clergy, elect the pope.

Their names are as follows. The first is the *primicerius*; the second is the *secundicerius*. They receive these names from the offices themselves. Surrounding the emperor on the right and left, they appear in a certain manner to reign with him; without them the emperor cannot establish anything important.

In the Roman Church, however, at all processions they lead the pope by the hand, while the bishops and other magnates yield before them; and on the greater solemnities they read the eighth lesson above all the bishops.

The third is the *arcarius*, who presides over the tributes. The fourth is the *saccellarius*, who distributes pay to the soldiers; at Rome, on the Saturday of the scrutinies, he gives alms and distributes *presbyteria* to the Roman bishops and clergy and to the ordinary judges.

The fifth is the *protoscrinarius*, who presides over the *scrinarii*, whom we call notaries. The sixth is the first *defensor*, who presides over the defenders, [Col. 1388C] whom we call advocates. The seventh is the *adminiculator*, who intercedes for orphans and widows, for the afflicted and captives.

They do not judge criminal cases, nor do they pronounce a sentence of death upon anyone; and they are clerics of Rome, never to be promoted to any other orders.

The others, who are called consuls, govern the jurisdictions, punish the guilty according to the laws, and pronounce sentence upon offenders according to the nature of the crime.

## XII. On the Oratories at the Fountains, and on their Sanctuaries and Gifts

Behind the Basilica of the Savior there are four oratories. One of them has two apses. Beneath one is the altar of the holy virgins Rufina and Secunda, beneath which their precious bodies were deposited. They were discovered by Pope Anastasius IV of blessed memory before he was elevated to the apostolic dignity. After their discovery, he built an altar in their honor and consecrated that altar with his own hands, while we were all present, together with the canons of the Basilica of the Savior and very many others, both from the City and from outside the City.

Beneath the other apse is the altar of Saint Andrew the Apostle and Saint Lucy the Virgin. The aforementioned Pope Anastasius also consecrated it and deposited in it relics of both: namely, of the Apostle Andrew and of the Virgin Lucy.

[Col. 1388D] On the feast of Saint Cyprian, bishop and martyr, and of Saint Justina the Virgin, he placed their bodies in a marble sarcophagus and deposited them beneath the same altar. He had found them in the altar of the aforementioned virgins Rufina and Secunda, when he had ordered us to search and dig for the bodies of Rufina and Secunda.

Another oratory is contiguous with this one. It has only one altar beneath an apse, beneath which the precious bodies of the following saints have been deposited: Saint Venantius, [Col. 1389A] Saint Domnio, Saint Anastasius, Saint Maurus, Saint Asterius, Saint Septimius, Saint Jelius, Saint Antiochianus, Saint Paulinianus, and Saint Gaianus.

The third oratory is farther on, where the fountains lie between two altars. One is dedicated to Saint John the Baptist and the other to Saint John the Evangelist.

The fountains are round, set among porphyry columns in the middle of the Church, which is beautiful and circular and where the Emperor Constantine’s chamber once stood. The oratories themselves, namely those of Saint John the Baptist and blessed John the Evangelist, arranged opposite one another on either side, were constructed by Pope Hilary [Al., Hilarus], who adorned everything with silver and precious stones.

He made the confession of Saint John the Baptist of silver, weighing 100 pounds, together with a golden cross; and in both oratories he installed bronze doors covered with silver.

Before the confession he placed a silver crown weighing twenty pounds and a *farum* with dolphins weighing twenty-five pounds. Likewise, inside the shrine of Saint John, he placed a golden lamp with ten [Col. 1389B] lights, weighing five pounds; a silver tower with dolphins, weighing sixty pounds; and a golden dove weighing two pounds.

He also built there, nearby, the monastery of Saint Stephen in the Lateran baptistery. In the same place he made two libraries. He placed all these things in the Constantinian Basilica at Saint Mary.

## XIII. On the Oratory of the Holy Cross and its Ornaments

The fourth oratory, built later, is that of the Holy Cross, in which there is a great quantity of sacred treasure from that same Holy Cross. There, at the dictation of an angel, blessed Pope Gregory wrote the Antiphonary and many other works.

This oratory is exceedingly beautiful, made in the form of a cross and decorated with mosaic. It was established by the aforementioned Pope Hilary, who likewise offered many gifts there.

He made the confession in which he placed the wood of the cross, together with a golden cross and gems, weighing twenty pounds. In the confession he installed silver doors weighing 50 pounds. [Col. 1389C] Above the confession was a golden arch weighing four pounds, carried by onyx columns; upon it stood a golden lamb weighing two pounds.

He placed before the confession a golden crown and a *farum* with dolphins, the latter weighing five pounds; four golden lamps weighing two pounds; and a nymphaeum and a three-portico structure before the Oratory of the Holy Cross.

There are *exatopentalaic* columns there, together with two fluted basins with perforated, ray-patterned porphyry columns pouring out water; and in the middle a porphyry basin with a handled shell in its center pouring out water. It is surrounded on the right and left in the middle by bronze grilles, columns with pediments and small architraves, and is everywhere decorated with mosaic, with Aquitanian, Tripolitan, and porphyry columns.

Very near this oratory there is another, that of Saint Pope Gregory, where to this day [Note: [Col. 1389D] Anastasius mentions another bed of Gregory toward the end of the life of Stephen VI, when he praises the Oratory of blessed Gregory, where his bed is kept, beside the Church of the Prince of the Apostles. There, however, the word “bed” is understood to mean a tomb.] a little bed on which that saint used to rest appears to remain beside the altar.

## XIV. On the Church of Saint Lawrence in the Palace
[Col. 1389D] For in the sacred palace there is an oratory of Saint Laurence, in which three most holy altars are counted. In the first, in a cypress chest which Pope Leo III founded, there are three reliquary chests. In one is a cross of the purest gold adorned with gems and precious stones—that is, hyacinths, emeralds, and green stones. In the middle of the cross is the navel of our Lord Jesus Christ; above it the cross is anointed with balsam, and each year the same anointing is renewed when the lord pope, with the cardinals, makes a procession on the Exaltation of the Holy Cross from that church of Saint Laurence to [Col. 1390A] the Basilica of the Saviour, which is called the Constantinian Basilica. In another silver and gilded chest decorated with scenes is a cross painted in enamel; and beneath that chest is a cross of our Lord Jesus Christ. In the third chest, which is silver, are the sandals—that is, the footwear—of our Lord Jesus Christ.

There is also there another gilded chest containing wood from that Holy Cross which Heraclius, after conquering Chosroes, brought with him from Persia, together with the body of Saint Anastasius the martyr. It is in the altar of Saint Laurence there, which is made of marble. There are also there the arm of Saint Caesarius the martyr, two bones of Saint John the Baptist, one bone of Saint Jerome, the shoulder blade of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite, a bone from the leg of Pope Saint Stephen, relics of Saint Damasus, and of Saints Primus and Felicianus, the head of Saint Praxedes, and relics of Saint Anastasia, together with many others, and of the holy virgins Agape, Chionia, Irene, Pistis, and Elpis; of Nereus and Achilleus; and of Prisca and Aquila. There are also relics from the knee of Saint Tiburtius, son of Chromatius. In this same cypress chest [Col. 1390B] there is one loaf from the Lord’s Supper, thirteen lentils from that same Supper, and some of the reed and sponge with vinegar that were placed at the Lord’s mouth, as well as wood from the sycamore tree that Zacchaeus climbed.

Above this altar is an image of the Saviour, wondrously painted on a certain panel, which the evangelist Luke designed, but which the Lord’s power completed through angelic workmanship; 573 beneath whose feet, in a line of precious stones, the relics of this sanctuary are kept.
