Their names are these: the stone on which Saint Mary sat; a stone from the holy Jordan, where the Lord sat while he was being baptised; a stone from holy Bethlehem; a stone from the Mount of Olives, where the Lord prayed to the Father; the holy rock on which the angel sat at the tomb; a piece of the holy column to which the Lord was bound and scourged; a piece from the Lord’s tomb, where he rested dead in body; a piece from the lance with which the Lord’s side was pierced; a piece of the wood of the Lord’s cross; a piece from the place called the Lithostrotos; a piece from the place of Calvary; the holy flint where [Col. 1390C] the Lord was laid; a stone from Mount Zion; the stone on which the Lord was transfigured on the mountain; wood from the Lord’s holy manger, in which the newborn child was placed; a stone from Mount Sinai, where the law was given; and a stone from the tomb of Saint Mary.

In another altar of the same oratory are the heads of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and the heads of the holy virgins Agnes and Euphemia.

In the third are coals sprinkled with the blood of Saint Laurence and with the fat of his body. In the same oratory there are also relics of the Forty Holy Martyrs and of many others.

## XV. On the church of Saint Mary Major and its sanctuary

The church of Saint Mary Major, which the younger Pope Sixtus built, and which Pope Paschal restored, has as many columns in its structure as there are days in the revolution of a single year.

[Note: [Col. 1389D] That is, Sixtus III, as the *Book of the Popes* testifies. [Col. 1390D] Before him, however, Liberius had built that basilica beside the market of Libia or Livia; according to the same book, it was therefore first called the Basilica of Livia.]

The dedication of this church is celebrated on the Nones of August. Furthermore, this venerable church of Saint Mary has seven cardinal priests, who, in their assigned weekly turns, ought to celebrate Masses at its holy altar. At the altar of this venerable church are kept relics of the hair of Saint Mary, the Mother of the Lord; of the milk of that Virgin; of the veil of her head; and of the cloth of her garment. There is also the Lord’s cradle, in which the child lay. There are relics from the Lord’s manger; relics of the apostle Matthias, who, having been added to the apostles in the place of Judas, is called “the Little One of God.” Some say that he rests beneath this altar of Saint Mary Major; others say [Col. 1391A] that he is enclosed within the altar. Some believe that he rests beneath a huge marble stone buried in the ground, which stone is before the altar window. For this window is beneath the altar in the same way as the chest is beneath the altar of Saint Peter. Many assert that in his church the body of the aforesaid holy apostle Matthias is in the wall above the great arch, which runs through the middle of the church from one wall to the other.

In the apse of Saint Mary is the pontifical chair in the middle beneath a glass window; there are five such windows in the apse. This apse has been made extraordinarily beautiful with mosaic. For many people see fish among flowers there, and beasts with birds, between the choir and the altar.

574. ## XVI. On the bishops and cardinals arranged by patriarchates

The seven cardinal bishops of the first see, who ought daily to celebrate in weekly rotation, in place of the apostolic celebrant, at the most holy principal altar in the Basilica of the Saviour, [Col. 1391B] are these: the bishop of Ostia, the bishop of Porto, the bishop of Santa Rufina, the bishop of Albano, the bishop of Sabina, the bishop of Tusculum, and the bishop of Palestrina.

The cardinal priests of Saint Mary Major are these: the cardinal of the Holy Apostles, of Saint Cyriacus at the Baths, of Saint Eusebius, of Saint Pudentiana, of Saint Vitalis, of Saints Marcellinus and Peter, and of Saint Clement.

The cardinal priests of Saint Peter are these: of Saint Mary across the Tiber, of Saint Chrysogonus, of Saint Cecilia, of Saint Anastasia, of Saint Laurence in Damaso, of Saint Mark, and of Saints Martin and Sylvester.

The cardinal priests of Saint Paul are these: of Saint Sabina, of Saint Prisca, of Saint Balbina, of Saints Nereus and Achilleus, of Saint Sixtus, of Saint Marcellus, and of Saint Susanna.

The cardinal priests of Saint Laurence are these: of Saint Praxedes, [Col. 1391C] of Saint Peter in Chains, of Saint Laurence in Lucina, of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill, of Saints John and Paul, and of the Four Crowned Saints.

There are eighteen deaconries: Saint Mary in Domnica, where the archdeacon is; Saint Lucy in the Circus, near the Seven Halls; Saint Mary the New; Saints Cosmas and Damian; Saint Hadrian; Saints Sergius and Bacchus; Saint Theodore; Saint George; Saint Mary in the Greek Schola; Saint Mary in Portico; Saint Nicholas in Prison; Saint Angelo; Saint Eustace; Saint Mary in Aquiro; Saint Mary on the Via Lata; Saint Agatha at the Marble Horse; Saint Lucy at the head of the Subura; and Saint Quiricus.

These are the abbeys: Saint Caesarius in the Palace; Saint Gregory on the Clivus Scauri, where the upper part of the arm of the apostle Saint Andrew is; Saint Mary on the Aventine, where there is part of the body of Saint Sabinus the bishop; Saint Alexius, where his body is, and that of Saint Boniface the martyr; [Col. 1391D] Saints Prisca and Aquila, where part of their bodies is; Saint Saba at the New Cell, where the head of Saint Tiburtius the martyr is; and Saint Pancratius on the Via Aurelia.

Within the city, across the Tiber, in the district of Ravenna, are Saints Cosmas and Damian in the Golden Street; Saint Sylvester between the two gardens, which Pope Dionysius built and where he also rests; Saint Mary on the Capitol, where the altar of the Son of God is; Saint Basil beside the palace of the Emperor Trajan; Saint Agatha the virgin, which is on the Subura hill; Saint Laurence in Panisperna, where he was placed in the small oratory; Saint Thomas beside the Claudian aqueduct; Saint Blaise between the Tiber and the bridge of Saint Peter; the Holy Trinity of the Scots; Saint Valentine beside the bridge; Saint Mary in the Golden Fortress; Saint Mary in Pallara, where Saint Sebastian was shot; and Saint Mary in the monastery beside Saint Peter in Chains.

575. ## XVII. On the fall and restoration of this basilica, when it was carried out by Pope Sergius III, and on the gifts and ornaments which he offered in it, as is written here and there in the inscriptions on the walls beside the bronze columns

[Col. 1392A]

In the year in which the most pious Emperor Constantine Augustus was baptised by the most blessed Sylvester, pontiff of the holy apostolic see, and cleansed from leprosy through the washing of holy baptism, he built this basilica in honour of the Saviour, our Lord Jesus Christ, and in commemoration of Saint John the Baptist.

It remained from that time onward, although the separation of its walls and the curvature of its roofs already showed its ruin, for several years, until the time of Stephen of pious memory, the sixth of that name. In his time it collapsed and was scattered and reduced to ruins, until the lord Sergius the presbyter was recalled, chosen from exile, and consecrated as the third bishop of the Romans.

In those days, [Col. 1392B] when invaders held the apostolic see, they removed from this basilica all its treasures and every golden and silver ornament, together with all the vessels that had been offered here from the beginning. Divine services were not celebrated in it; rather, it lay abandoned, almost like a bathhouse overgrown and covered with shrubs and thorns.

After his ordination, therefore, Pope Sergius III grieved exceedingly over the desolation of this most noble temple. There was no human hope or consolation for its restoration. When everyone alike despaired of its revival and human assistance was lacking, he turned to the help of divine mercy, in which he had always placed his trust. Beginning the work with the ancient foundations, he completed it to the end and adorned it with golden and silver ornaments, as is read below—and with more besides, for the most holy Pope Sergius III added further things there during his lifetime.

After the aforesaid Pope Sergius III had rebuilt this basilica, laid in ruins, from its foundations, in honour of your name, Saviour of the world, and in commemoration of you, Saint John the Baptist, through many struggles and labours and from your gifts—since all its golden, silver, and bronze ornaments had been removed by the invaders—he diligently undertook, with devout mind, to repair it and offer you other gifts. Although he was beset by many troubles, he nevertheless did not cease to serve your Majesty.

He made and offered to your omnipotence this most beautiful image, which he adorned with five pounds of gold; and a ciborium of marvellous beauty, made of silver and the purest gold with gems, whose completion amounted to 250 pounds in number and weight; a golden cross with a Crucifix; two silver crosses, one having an entire Crucifix of gold, and a golden lamb with gems; a golden crown with two crosses, and two others made of mixed metals; a golden clasp with gems; two gilded silver purses with five gems; ten silver crowns with their dolphins; thirty-nine silver baskets; twenty-five silver bowls; [Col. 1392D] four silver crosses on which the bowls hang, and one small silver cross likewise; three silver chalices, one of them gilded; a silver paten; three silver thuribles; three silver images, 576 one of them having a right hand of gold and a clasp on the breast with gems; six silver arches; a silver crossbeam; six small silver columns; twelve silver apples; two garments woven with gold; one covering with gold, and another plain one; and fifty-two silk veils.

All these things the devout Pope Sergius III prepared for you, and, so long as his spirit guides his limbs, he will not cease to prepare and offer them to you.

If anyone, grieving, should perhaps wonder why these ornaments, and the others noted above as having been offered by the Emperor Constantine, do not now appear, let him read and examine the *Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs*, and he will find when and how they were wickedly taken away from here by the invaders.

[Col. 1393]

# III. LATERAN CONSTITUTIONS

[Col. 1393A] Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, for perpetual remembrance of the matter.

Although we have sometimes rightly judged that acts performed prudently and laudably by others ought to be confirmed—especially those which, when we were constituted in a lesser rank, we usefully ordained for the praise of God and the observance of divine worship—afterward, having been raised to the summit of the supreme apostolate, we ought all the more to strengthen them by the protection of an apostolic document, the more certainly we have been informed about them, and the more disgraceful it would be if they were not observed at all.

Some time ago, when we were Peter, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary the New and archpriest, administrator and commendatory of the Lateran Church, for the reverence of God and for the healthy condition of that Church, in spiritual and temporal matters, with divine grace, both in the future and perpetually to be preserved, we issued certain constitutions in that church, both by the apostolic authority which we exercised in this matter and by our own authority. Under the penalties contained in them, we ordered that they be observed perpetually and inviolably.

Therefore, so that those constitutions [Col. 1393B] may be observed with all the greater force, insofar as they have been strengthened by the protection of apostolic approval and confirmation, we approve, ratify, confirm, and strengthen them by the privilege of the present document—whose text is inserted below word for word—with certain corrections, modifications, and ordinances recently made by us and noted below after that text. We order that they be observed inviolably under the penalties contained in them.

Since we are certain of our action, we wish and decree that this approval, ratification, confirmation, strengthening, and command have the same force and validity as if the text of the authentic instrument of the said constitutions, formerly sealed with the hanging seal of our cardinalate, had been inserted here, notwithstanding any contrary custom of the Roman Curia.

The text of the said constitutions is as follows.

577 Peter, by divine mercy, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary the New, archpriest, administrator [Col. 1393C] and commendatory of the Lateran Church, to our beloved in Christ, the chapter and canons, prebendaries, chaplains, and acolytes of the said Lateran Church, and also to all others serving in it, eternal greetings in the Lord.

Although human nature, formed by the operation of the heavenly hand, before the Fall possessed such a lucid intellect, almost equal to that of the angelic creature and illumined by the sharpness of supernal light, that it had no need whatever of human statutes or laws, nevertheless after the Fall it became so infected by the cloud of worldly darkness, and the human race brought forth from that deadly disaster so many wounds of corruption, while the ancient enemy sought to break the charity of human beings created from earthly matter and drove the sweetness of good works into the gall of envy and afflicted it with the snares of cunning, that human sensuality more readily inclines toward evil and the forbidden from its youth.

For this reason it was necessary, for wholesome and peaceful government, to order the office of those who preside. Following the example of the lawgiver Moses, they are to present to their subjects the abundance of laws granted to them from heaven and, through constitution, ordinance, the deposition of subjects, and the penalties imposed on those wandering through crooked paths, direct the structure of justice by a guiding light—removing ambiguities, taking away disputes, uprooting vices, and planting virtues.

This applies especially to those subjects who serve almighty God in that principal house of the Lord, namely the Lateran, first among all churches and enjoying among the others the prerogative of pre-eminence in divine offices. They, placed as though at the head through the example of their lucid conduct, ought by their radiant affections to be a wholesome fragrance to others.

Recalling these matters, therefore, to the focus of due consideration, we, the aforesaid cardinal, both by the authority granted to us by the vicar of the true God and by the duty of our office—which we recognise binds us, since we preside over that Church—have issued the constitutions written below. They clearly express the reform of the Church, both in spiritual and in temporal matters.

Therefore, beloved sons, incline your ears unanimously to them and apply to them a ready understanding. If, with the diligent care of cultivation—which we hope for—they bear fruit and produce the benefits expected from laborious work, you will gather the fruits of the seeds which paternal foresight scatters in the field of your devotion.

For we command and order you and each of you to observe them under the penalties contained in them.

## I. Rubric concerning divine offices

[Col. 1394B]

### 1

So that the members may conform themselves to the head, by this present enactment we decree that both the nocturnal and diurnal office in the Lateran Church be sung with musical notation according to the rubric, order, or custom of the holy Roman Church or the chapel of our lord pope. The office of the blessed Virgin Mary, however, shall be recited without notation, though clearly and at a measured pace.

In the same Church, two Masses shall also be celebrated each day with musical notation. The first shall be a Mass of the blessed Virgin on Saturdays, Sundays, and the other days on which, according to the rubric of the Roman Church, it is not customary to sing a Mass for the dead. 578 On the remaining days of the week, the first Mass shall be celebrated with the preceding vigils for the dead; the second Mass shall be that of the feast occurring on the day.

We exempt the following days: the Nativity of the Lord and the eight days following it; the Epiphany of the Lord; from Wednesday of Holy Week through Tuesday of the Lord’s Resurrection, inclusive; the feast of the Ascension; Pentecost [Col. 1394C] with the two following days; the feast of Corpus Christi; the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist; the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul; the solemnity of All Saints; and the four feasts of the blessed Virgin.

On these days, because of their solemnity, they shall celebrate only one Mass with musical notation. On the other days when, by ancient ordinance and observance, it has been customary in that Church to celebrate two other Masses solemnly, those Masses shall then be solemnised which have until now been customarily solemnised.

### 2

A distinct order ordinarily adorns solemn offices, especially divine ones. Therefore, by this statute we decree that the first Mass, as has hitherto been customary, with musical notation, shall be celebrated by that prebendary who is hebdomadary that week, immediately after Prime has been sung.

The second Mass, commonly called the High Mass, shall be solemnised by the weekly canon with a deacon and subdeacon, unless the cardinal who is archpriest of the Lateran at the time—or, in his absence, his vicar—judges that, because of the scarcity of clergy or for another reason, a dispensation should be granted allowing the canon to substitute for himself one of the priest-prebendaries of that Church.

But because most of the canons have not been promoted to orders, we grant that the High Mass may, for one year, be sung by prebendaries.

### 3

Similarly, in the months of July, August, and September, during which the climate in Rome is usually oppressive, we do not wish the canons to be bound to this duty. Instead, we order that the second Mass also be sung with its solemnity by prebendaries, except on Sundays, double feasts, and throughout the octave of Saint John the Baptist. On those days, as in the other months of the year, the canons are bound to celebrate the second Mass.

The priest canon who celebrates at double feasts shall receive eighteen denarii, and the deacon and subdeacon nine denarii, from the treasury of the aforesaid Church, in addition to what they would otherwise have received. On other days, while celebrating there, they shall receive half of the aforesaid sums.

### 4

Since we judge it fitting that bodily lights should serve the worship of the divine majesty, we decree that the vicar and chamberlains in office at the time diligently ensure that the Lateran Church suffers no deficiency in the necessary lights.

The mansionarii shall also ring the bell at the proper hour for the other hours and for Mass, and shall light the lamps. If they do not do so, they shall be punished by twelve denarii for each hour or occasion.

Until the bell is rung for Mass, before the end of that ringing, the priest, deacon, and subdeacon who are to celebrate Mass that week, 579 shall prepare and vest themselves, together with the acolytes who serve them.

If any of them is so slow that waiting for him becomes burdensome to those waiting, but nevertheless performs, after arriving, what his order requires, he shall be punished in double the amount that would have come to him from the distributions for that Mass. If he does not celebrate or minister at all, a canon shall be irreversibly punished with five solidi, a prebendary with thirty denarii, and an acolyte with fifteen denarii; these sums are to be assigned that day to those celebrating and ministering in their place.

### 5

When a canon is to celebrate Mass in the Lateran Church on double feasts, two prebendaries in copes shall be vested with him both at First and at Second Vespers. If the feast is especially solemn, there shall be four prebendaries in copes.

Anyone who acts otherwise shall forfeit three solidi if he is a canon, and two if he is a prebendary, for each occasion. [Col. 1395C] Half of the penalty shall be assigned to the treasury and half to those celebrating and ministering in their place. The chamberlains shall be bound to compensate them from the fruits of those who acted contrary to the rule, or from the fruits of the chapter itself if those fruits have otherwise devolved upon the chapter.

### 6

So that due honour may be paid to prelates, we decree that, whenever any prelate—especially a cardinal—celebrates pontifically in that Church, no priest shall presume to celebrate with musical notation in the same Church. Anyone acting contrary shall be punished at the discretion of the lord cardinal’s vicar.

### 7

We decree and ordain that four acolytes shall perpetually be present in the same Church. While the solemn celebrations of Mass are being performed, they shall assist the canons, prebendaries, or other ministers in those offices and in the other preparations, as has hitherto been customary.

### 8

By his own oath, the sacristan is bound every Saturday to make a schedule of the canons and prebendaries who are to celebrate in the coming week, of the singers in the choir by rotation, of those who are to wear copes, and of all others who are to serve during that week.

Any singer who does not obey shall incur a penalty of two solidi on each occasion.

### 9

In the choir we order the following method and order to be observed: one half of the canons, prebendaries, acolytes, and chaplains who are bound to serve the choir shall be on one side of the choir, and the remainder on the other.

Everyone shall enter the choir before the ringing for Mass or an Hour has ended, or at least before the first psalm of the Hour or the Introit of the Mass has been completed. Everyone shall sit devoutly in his place, without any conversation, murmuring, or noise. No one shall wander from one side of the choir to the other, nor presume to depart or go out before the office has ended, unless a matter of the Church or bodily necessity requires it. In that case he shall proceed honorably to the chapter house or residence.

The celebrating priest, the deacon and subdeacon, the acolytes who minister, and the singers who serve in the choir shall remain in their places to perform the divine offices assigned to them.

If anyone acts contrary to any of these provisions during that Mass or Hour, he shall be counted entirely as absent. If he makes a habit of this, he shall be reported by the writers of the absences [*scriptores fallarum*] 580 to the vicar of the lord cardinal who is archpriest of that Church at the time, to be punished with due correction as he sees fit.

### 10

With deliberation consonant with both laws, we decree that the clerics of the Lateran Church—in the choir, in the chapter, and in other assemblies—shall stand, sit, and respond according to the order of due precedence: first the priests, second the deacons, third the subdeacons. Regard shall be paid to dignity and precedence, not to the power or nobility of any privilege.

In processions also they shall proceed according to the aforesaid order, in an honourable place.

### 11

No one is unaware how greatly the word of God nourishes the soul. It is indeed a seed that takes root, grows wonderfully, bears fruit abundantly, and restores the inner person through nourishing instruction.

For this reason those who strive to obstruct the preaching of the word of God commit a greater sin: they neither receive its fruit themselves nor allow others to receive it, since their insolence hinders the preachers.

Therefore, whoever in any way, either personally or through another, obstructs the preaching of the word of God, whenever it happens to be delivered in the Lateran Church, shall incur a penalty of ten solidi on each occasion.

Nevertheless, until the preaching takes place during the solemn celebration of Mass, the clerics of the said Church may withdraw from the choir. The priest, deacon, and subdeacon who are ministering are strictly forbidden to withdraw; they must return before the end of the preaching or immediately afterward, lest their absence impede the continuation of the solemn Mass.

They are nevertheless forbidden, under the aforesaid penalty, to engage in business, other idle activities, or idle speech.

### 12

No canon, prebendary, chaplain, or anyone else shall presume to hear confessions in the Lateran Church without the special permission of the cardinal, his vicar, or the chapter. Whoever acts contrary shall be punished at the discretion of that person or persons.

### 13

So that divine worship may especially enjoy the dignity of seemly attire, we decree that, while divine offices are being sung in the Lateran Church, no canon or prebendary shall presume to enter or walk in that church without the prescribed habit.

Those acting contrary shall, on each occasion and by that very fact, incur excommunication and a penalty of ten solidi. Until such an excommunicated person has been absolved by the cardinal’s vicar alone, the chamberlains shall provide him nothing from fruits or other revenues. If they act otherwise, they shall be bound to restore to the treasury from their own property an equal amount.

He may not be absolved unless he has first actually paid the said penalty to the treasury and whatever he received from the said chamberlains during the period of the aforesaid excommunication.

### 14

And lest anyone afterward be able to doubt what is meant by the habit, we have decided to specify it in the present constitution.

From the hour on the feast of All Saints when Vespers begin for the commemoration of the faithful departed, until the vigil of the Lord’s Resurrection, every canon shall remain dressed in a *sajetta* or rochet, a black cope, and an almuce of grey or variegated material. 581 The prebendaries and chaplains who are bound to serve in the choir shall wear black copes with a surplice or white cotta, [Col. 1397A] and almuces of black *squalla* material.

But if the aforesaid canons and prebendaries prefer to wear small black hoods without points, or round almuces of black colour beneath their copes instead of the other almuces, we grant this to them.

At the vigil of Easter, as soon as the Alleluia, the word of joy, is sung, they shall remove the black copes that signify the mournful times of penance and put on surplices or white cottas, signifying the joys of eternal life. They shall wear these, together with the aforesaid almuces, until the feast of All Saints.

### 15

We likewise decree that all the chaplains of the chapels of Saints Peter and Paul, James, and the other chapel of Saint James, who are now or in the future will be in the said Church, shall, from the day of publication of these provisions until fifteen days thereafter, attend in the choir of the said Church during the daytime and at night, just as the other prebendaries do. They shall receive distributions from the chapter, in addition to the revenues of their chapels, like the acolytes.

Nevertheless, they shall celebrate in their chapels as they are bound to do by their foundations. The cardinal or vicar may compel them to this by ecclesiastical censure, including deprivation of the revenues and of the chapels themselves, according to the degree of their disobedience and as the lord cardinal or vicar judges should be done.

### 16

Since certain goods have been bequeathed, and are daily bequeathed, to the Lateran Church so that Mass may be celebrated at a particular altar for the souls of the testators, we therefore, pursuing the pious wishes of the departed with their due effect, decree that the vicar in office at the time shall effectively arrange for that altar to be served by prebendaries and chaplains, priests, and acolytes.

We likewise wish anniversary observances to be celebrated on the days established by the testators who bequeathed something to the Church for this purpose, with vigils and Mass.

If anyone fails to obey the vicar in these matters, a priest shall be punished with five solidi and an acolyte with two for each occasion. Since, however, as disobedience increases, the penalty ought also to increase, if anyone persists in such disobedience, he shall, in addition to the aforesaid penalty, be punished at the discretion of the cardinal or his vicar.

## II. Rubric concerning the relics, sacred objects, and other movable property of the Lateran Church, and their custody

[Col. 1397C]

### 17

Relics shall not be displayed at all except at the appointed times and with the consent of the vicar and chapter, unless they are being shown to a cardinal, prelate, or king.

No one shall presume to give any of the said relics away without the permission of our lord pope or of the cardinal who is archpriest of the Lateran Church at the time. Whoever violates this constitution at any time shall by that very fact incur the penalty of excommunication.

### 18

Things whose loss would cause great harm must be guarded with the greatest diligence. Therefore, by this statute we order that the statutes, privileges, inventories, seals of the Church and of the chapter be kept under lock and key within the reliquary and sacristy grilles, where the Lord’s table is located—that is, where the Eucharist is preserved for viaticum. 582

[Note: [Col. 1397] That is, where the Eucharist is kept for viaticum; for at that time the Eucharist was kept in a basket, according to chapter 50 and chapter 131 of the *Ceremonial of Peter Amelius*.]

All these things shall be closed under three different locks and keys. The vicar shall retain one, the chamberlain another, and the senior canon the third. They shall thus be kept by the vicar, chamberlain, and senior canon in such a way [Col. 1397D] that neither one nor the other of them may open or seal them without all the others.

### 19

We likewise decree that the chamberlain or sacristan shall in no way presume to allow cloths, books, vestments, or other sacred vessels to be carried outside the Church by anyone without first obtaining the permission of the vicar or chamberlains.

The chamberlains and writers shall then record the carriers in their books. Otherwise they shall by that very fact incur the sentence of excommunication, from which they may not be absolved except by the lord cardinal or his vicar, and only after satisfaction has first been made for the offence.

### 20

Every year the vicar and chapter shall make an inventory of all the things existing in the sacristy.

No one shall attempt to remove privileges, statutes, or instruments from the place where they are deposited without the permission of the lord cardinal—or, in his absence, of his vicar and the chapter—except for an evident reason concerning the Church itself or someone serving in it.

In that event, the item shall be returned to the chamberlains by the hands of the vicar or chamberlains within the period fixed by the vicar and chamberlains. Anyone acting contrary shall know that he is bound by the sentence of excommunication, from which he may not be absolved unless he first returns the item to the place in the sacristy from which he received it.

## III. Rubric concerning canons, prebendaries, and acolytes, and their number and rank

### 21

In the Lateran Church there shall perpetually and successively be eighteen canons and an equal number of prebends, apart from the prebend of the lord cardinal.

Of these prebends, eight are priestly: the prebend of Laurence de Argeleriis, Francis de Veneriis, John of Viterbo, Oddo of Saint Eustace, Francis of Utriculum, Angelo Picciardelli, Oddo Colonna, and Romanus de Micardis.

Five are diaconal: those of Marcellus Colonna, Philip de Philippis, James de Papaluccis, Thomas de Monte Nigro, and Stephen Normandis.

Five are subdiaconal: those of John Lessi, Matthias of Saint Eustace, Peter Colonna, Camillus Paulus Colonna, and John de Barattis.

22. And let every canon who holds a prebend and is henceforth to be received into that church have himself promoted, within one year calculated from the time he has obtained possession, to the order required by his prebend. If he does not do so, he shall thereby be deprived of his canonry and prebend. If, after the aforesaid year, one so deprived receives anything, he shall immediately incur the penalty of excommunication and shall be bound to restore such revenues; he shall be excluded from all fellowship with the canons and from the chapter. From that time onward, moreover, nothing shall be provided to him by the chamberlains or by anyone else. Whoever knowingly provides him with anything contrary to the tenor of this constitution shall be bound to restore an equal amount from his own property to the Church, under penalty of the aforesaid oath. [Col. 1398C]

583. 23. We likewise decree and ordain that the prebendary canons who have already been received into that church shall, within one year calculated from the time of publication of these statutes, have themselves promoted to the sacred orders required by their prebends. If they do not do so, they shall thereby be deprived of their canonries and prebends, except those who have not yet reached the lawful age for receiving orders. Such men shall be bound to receive those orders within one year calculated from the time at which they complete the age required for orders; otherwise they shall incur the same penalty of deprivation.

Meanwhile, both those men and others who, by apostolic dispensation or for another just cause, are not bound to be promoted, as well as those who, although promoted, are absent—or, if present, are unwilling to perform the duty incumbent upon them according to the tenor of these statutes—shall have their deficiencies supplied by other canons, [Col. 1398D] so that there may be no failure in the Church concerning the duties assigned or to be assigned to them. If anyone refuses to do this, the chamberlains shall deduct thirty soldi for each week from the revenues of the prebend of the canon to whom the duty belongs; from the revenues of the man to whom the duty of deacon or subdeacon belongs, they shall deduct twenty soldi, which they shall provide to the person or persons performing the duty in his place, or from their distributions, as the vicar and chamberlains shall determine. If such men have neither gross revenues nor such distributions, the chapter to which those revenues then belong shall, without any delay, pay those serving in their place; and the chamberlains shall be bound to do this by their own oath.

## IV. Heading concerning the number of beneficiates, and which of their prebends are presbyteral, which diaconal, and which subdiaconal

[Col. 1399A]

24. Concerning the beneficiates of the Lateran Church, by this present constitution we have deemed it necessary to ordain that there shall perpetually be twenty-two beneficiates in that church, fourteen of them priests, namely: Petrus de Palliano, archpriest of Utriculum; Laurentius Rusciolus de Pandolphis; Jacobus de Leolis; Joannes de Campo Floris; Joannes de Catino; Nucius [perhaps Mutius] Petri Bertae; Stephanus de Sublacu; Joannes Serleonis, archpriest of Arcula; Joannes de Civita; Nucius de sancto Marco; Dominicus de Campanea; Ganfredus de Antissiodoro; and Nucius Amici. Thus their benefices shall perpetually be presbyteral.

Four shall be deacons, namely: Nicolaus Procerti; Jacobellus de Campo Florum; Silvester Ricciardelli; and Nucius de Tibure. Thus their benefices shall perpetually be diaconal. [Col. 1400A] The remaining four beneficiates shall be subdeacons, namely: Tutius Salmenicii; Angelus de Gallicano; Antonius de Frascato; and Manardus, son of D. Antuinus. Thus, from now and forever, their benefices shall be considered subdiaconal.

25. Therefore, lest the Lateran Church henceforth suffer any deficiency in the divine offices, we command by this constitution that all and each of the beneficiates named above who presently possess their benefices shall, within one year calculated from the time of publication of these statutes, 584 each, however, to … [lacuna]; otherwise they shall be deprived of the said benefices. If, after being so deprived, they thereafter receive revenues, they shall thereby incur the sentence of excommunication and shall be excluded from all fellowship with the beneficiates and canons. Nothing shall be provided to them by the chamberlains; and if the chamberlains knowingly provide anything, those who provide it shall be bound to restore an equal amount from their own property to the treasury, under penalty of the oath they have sworn.

[Col. 1399]

## IV. Letter of Augustinus Patricius Picolomineus, bishop of Pienza [Note: [Col. 1399D] See the commentary, col. 999], to Innocent VIII, concerning the book of the Sacred Ceremonies customarily used by the Roman pontiffs

[Col. 1399B] To our most holy lord Innocent VIII, supreme pontiff of the universal Church: Augustinus Patricius Picolomineus, unworthy bishop of Pienza, sends greetings.

Having recently, by divine favor, completed with sufficient success the emendation of the Pontifical, I now undertake, at your command and under your auspices, most blessed Father, the explanation and arrangement of the sacred ceremonies customarily used by the Roman pontiffs. This task is certainly more laborious than the former [Col. 1399C] and much more difficult, both because the discipline of the matter is uncertain and scattered widely across many topics, and also because ceremonies have frequently been added, removed, altered, and repeatedly changed according to circumstances. Your most circumspect Holiness rightly judged that much belongs to the propitiation of divine mercy if it is worshiped with pure, chaste, and appropriate ceremonies; and that it likewise contributes to preserving and increasing the majesty of the Apostolic See and the authority and veneration of the sacred senate if everything is performed in due order and with fitting ritual; if regard is paid to circumstances, times, and persons; and if each person receives the honor and reverence due to him. All these things are contained, prescribed, and administered by this single discipline.

It would take too long to recount how great has been the care for sacred things among all peoples and nations. I shall pass over the vain and hidden rites of Eleusinian Ceres, the frenzied and shameful orgies of Dionysus, the laughable and monstrous trifles of the Egyptians, [Col. 1399D] and the superstitious religion of the Romans. Among the latter, no magistracies were considered legitimate, no expeditions by sea or land were undertaken, and nothing was decreed by the senate or the people unless the will of the heavenly powers had first been investigated through proper ceremonies. 585 Certainly, almost the whole sacred history of the Pentateuch is concerned with handing down divine rites, so that it is clear that nothing was more carefully attended to by Moses—or indeed by God himself—than that the divine Majesty should be worshiped by human beings through established and appropriate ceremonies; and there the precepts, ceremonies, and judgments are commanded to be observed in the same manner.

Our ancestors, the leaders and teachers of the Christian people, from the beginning of the nascent Church, inspired by divine power, handed down sacred rites to us. Thereafter, as the multitude of the faithful increased, their successors, the Roman pontiffs, [Col. 1400B] preserving the substance of the matter, enlarged, adorned, and wonderfully expanded those rites, and continue to add to them day by day. Many things are altered and varied—not so much because they conflict with ancient institutions as because they are suitable and becoming to the time and to the matters being conducted.

As a result, since very little can be found, on account of the antiquity of the matter, concerning the observances of our predecessors, and since what was later committed to writing by their successors appears to be of little use and benefit in our own times [Col. 1400C]—both because the Roman curia has frequently traveled among foreign peoples and because the opinions of writers are various and confused—we have hitherto used ceremonies not so much written down as long established by custom. Hence there have sometimes arisen differing opinions among the Fathers concerning the performance of sacred rites, and at times unbecoming disputes among the ministers of the ceremonies, since human memory is unstable and fleeting, and one thing often takes the place of another, while no fixed rule can be displayed showing what must certainly be observed.

Considering these matters prudently, as I believe, your Holiness, most blessed Father, and desiring that dignity and order be properly maintained in all things, both divine and human, and that everything be performed without tumult, quietly and peacefully, with gravity and dignity, instructed me to arrange in order all the ceremonies customarily used by the Roman pontiffs in our time. I was to draw upon the books of our ancestors, many of which I extracted from the archives of the Roman Church, and upon the daily practice of the Apostolic Chapel, in which I have been engaged for more than twenty years with constant labor; while omitting what was superfluous and obsolete. [Col. 1400D]

I would gladly have avoided and refused this task and thrown off a burden wholly unequal to my shoulders, if it had been permissible not to obey the supreme pontiff. But knowing that obedience is more excellent than sacrifices, and that he is guilty of death who does not obey the supreme pontiff, I preferred to be judged inexperienced and ignorant rather than insolent and disobedient.

My failing spirit was first uplifted and wonderfully strengthened by the supreme kindness and clemency of your piety toward all, which will measure not so much my inadequacy as my good intention and readiness to obey. It was also strengthened by the prudence, diligence, and keen and incorrupt judgment of those most reverend Fathers whom you appointed as examiners and revisers [Col. 1401A] of this work of ours, and by their profound learning in all divine and human matters. They will certainly admit nothing that is inconsistent with the gravity and dignity of the Apostolic See and of so great a senate. I willingly submitted these books for many days to their exact scrutiny, 586 judging that, if they were approved by such men, no one could justly condemn them.

We have divided the entire work into three books. The first and largest will contain matters pertaining to the supreme pontiff and the sacred senate outside the ordinary course of the divine office—for example, the election and consecration of the Roman pontiff, the coronation of the Caesar, the canonizations of saints, the creations of cardinals, and other matters of this kind.

The second will encompass the order and ritual for celebrating sacred solemnities throughout the entire cycle of the year, as well as matters pertaining to the divine office in Vespers, Masses, and the other hours. In this second book, since it contains many small details that no one could easily remember without continual practice, we employed as an assistant [Col. 1401B] Joannes Burcardus of Strasbourg, provost of Haselach and minister of the sacred ceremonies. We also used his skill in correcting the Pontifical. He collected everything with the utmost diligence and recorded it with the greatest accuracy, so that arranging the book required little labor.

We have added a third [Col. 1402A] book containing certain general matters, rules, and summary instructions for each office. At the beginning of each book we have placed a table of the matters contained in it, so that each person may more easily find what he seeks.

Many eloquent men and critics of the Latin language will perhaps be astonished that we have not everywhere preserved the force and propriety of Latin words, and that we have introduced several new terms that could have been expressed in more purely Latin form. To them we shall frankly confess our ignorance. Yet we shall affirm that many expressions occur there which, if stated otherwise, would not easily be understood by everyone. In these matters we followed the terminology used by earlier writers on these subjects and still current today among ministers of sacred things. We judged that your Holiness and the sacred senate would demand from us not verbal embellishment but the order and explanation of the matters themselves.

If we have satisfied you, we give [Col. 1402B] everlasting thanks to the all-good and all-great God, the giver of every good, who most mercifully granted us the means by which we could satisfy you. If not, we earnestly and repeatedly beg you to pardon our weakness and inexperience and kindly accept our desire to obey.

Farewell. Rome, the Kalends of March, in the year of salvation 1488.

[Col. 1401]

## V. From the diary of Paride de Grassis. 587 Against the elected Corcyran, who published the aforesaid book of Augustinus under his own name

[Col. 1401B] Today, namely 11 March 1517, when I had been told that our ceremonial book, by which our ecclesiastical commonwealth is governed and administered, had been printed at Venice and sent back to Rome for sale to everyone, I was deeply distressed. Before saying anything to the pontiff, I complained about this to the cardinals, who on the day of the annual papal creation were awaiting the pontiff’s arrival for Mass. Some of them—or rather many—were [Col. 1401C] moved and scandalized that the sacred ceremonies and their mysteries had been made public, so that our ceremonies, which had been something sacred, should become something public, and so forth. In the end they sorrowfully spoke to the pope.

At first the pope appeared disturbed and said that he would do whatever pleased the cardinals. Since the cardinal of Santa Croce had perhaps been responsible for having the book printed, he said that it was not a bad thing. Finally, the pope instructed Cardinal de Grassis, protector of the office of ceremonies, together with the auditor of the Camera, to see that no further volume was sold until the day of the consistory, because at that time the matter would be settled after the votes of all the cardinals had been carefully sought. And so it was done.

Afterward, when I had compared the printed book with ours and discovered that many things had been added arbitrarily and many others likewise deleted, I reported this to the pope in the presence of the cardinals at the following consistory. The pope saw the matter and was even more deeply moved. He summoned the auditor of the Camera again and ordered him to keep all the printed volumes in his possession and retain them there until he should give further instructions. [Col. 1401D]

As I said above, on 11 March I wrote that the elected archbishop of Corcyra had published the ceremonial book contrary to law and right. The pope charged me to examine the book carefully and compare it with the original; if anything had been added or diminished, I was to mark and report it. After examining and marking the whole book, I composed this letter, which I placed before it as an invective against that Corcyran, the tamperer with the sacred book, and I delivered it into the pope’s hands. He read and approved it and ordered me to recite at the first consistory the reasons that had moved me; and, in the presence of the senate, he would hear my petitions, which are set out here word for word in the letter itself, as follows:

[Col. 1402B] To our most holy lord Leo X, pope: Paris de Grassis, bishop of Pesaro and master of ceremonies.

Most blessed pontiff, since my youth I have been engaged in the sacred and solemn ceremonies of the Roman Church through the favor of you and of your predecessor, and for nearly sixteen years I have been placed in charge of them. I seem to be committing a grave offense, full of calumny and disgrace, if I pass over in silence and, with eyes closed, allow them to be corrupted and published in contempt of the Apostolic See through books of sacred rites recently printed under the name of a certain false and reckless author. [Col. 1402C] Nor could I calmly endure that my predecessors, who presided over these same ceremonies and handed them down to me as if from hand to hand through their labors, vigils, and studies, should be defrauded of their rights and laws under the most fortunate pontificate of your Holiness.

Through long experience we have all learned the gifts of your mind, so that I no longer doubt that, if you understand the nature of these matters, your devotion toward God, your regard for the majesty of the holy Apostolic See, and your innate justice will lead you not merely to refuse to tolerate them but, as I cannot pass over them without condemning them in words proportionate to the magnitude of the crime, to punish them severely.

For just as it belongs to every just prince to ensure that no one is deprived of his right, so, if we examine the matter carefully, it concerns no one more than the Roman pontiff that his sacred ceremonies should not be stained or altered in any respect, and especially that they should not be corrupted. [Col. 1402D] It also concerns every prince to ensure that pontifical sacred rites, once brought before the public like prostitutes, do not diminish the esteem in which they are held, cause them to be treated as worthless, or bring them into contempt.

Since, therefore, this matter concerns you above all, and concerns the sacred Apostolic See, most blessed pontiff, I beg you not to disdain to read through these materials, whatever their quality, which we have hastily gathered in the short time available. You will certainly find in them not verbal constructions pleasing and agreeable to the ear, but matters that bear most directly and necessarily upon your own affairs.

Before beginning with the point that these sacred ceremonies should by no means be disclosed to the public, [Col. 1403A] I shall answer the opinion of those who believe that the ceremonies of the Christian religion ought to be made public for the benefit of mortals, perhaps moved by the argument that the very account of the divine ordering and the other sacraments of the Church have been printed and published in the Pontifical books. Those things concern all churches and every priest and could not altogether be concealed. These matters, however, concern the Roman Church alone, its supreme pontiff, and only those ministers called to this work.

Would that even the matters I have just mentioned were more secret and more deeply hidden! For we would not see them daily falling into profane hands, to the contempt of the priesthood, nor into the hands of alien sects, to the mockery of our religion. But since what has been done can more readily be blamed than corrected, let us return to our own matter while it is still intact, lest it too be undermined by this evil example.

Your Holiness has long known that all the authority and majesty of the Roman pontiffs and of this most sacred See depend upon the thoughts and opinions of princes and prelates. For while they regard and believe the supreme pontiffs not as mortal men but as gods on earth, [Col. 1403B] they voluntarily subject themselves to them, obey them, look up to and venerate them, and even worship them. They are affected by an incredible admiration when they sometimes hear or see that, through the ceremonies of which we are speaking, someone is enrolled among the saints by a work surpassing human power; that pontiffs are elected and consecrated with such solemnity and exact observance; that emperors are crowned, kings anointed, cardinals created, patriarchs, archbishops, and bishops consecrated; and that other things are carried out which, both in the greatness and in the variety of the matters involved, seem to display a certain divinity.

But if the secrets of sacred things are disclosed and the sacred ceremonies made public, all that opinion will immediately be diminished, and pontifical authority must necessarily grow weak. The supreme pontiff will at once be subjected to the judgment of every common person. One man will accuse rites established by our ancestors of having been improperly ordered; [Col. 1403C] another will object that traditions have not been observed; another will interpret the custom and worship of sacred things incorrectly; another will ridicule and mock the gestures. Since your predecessors have been accustomed to change ceremonies at times according to time, place, and necessity, the supreme pontiffs will no longer be free to act on their own judgment, nor will they be able to carry out such changes without the murmuring of the populace, however much the matters may be brought into contempt through ordinary familiarity.

To prevent this, we who are enlightened by the light of true faith must take no less care than the pagans once took concerning their superstitions. Among them it was an established custom that no one wished or dared to publish the mysteries of ceremonies, since they asserted that it was not lawful for the profane to know the mysteries of the gods; among them no greater obligation existed than faithfulness to silence.

To pass over countless other matters reported concerning these subjects by Macrobius, Apuleius, Valerius, Plutarch, and other ancient authors, tradition records that King Tarquinius [Col. 1403D] ordered M. Tullius to be thrown into the sea on the island of Colso because he had given a book containing the secrets of the civil rites to a certain Sabine for copying. If among them the mere copying of a book was punished with so severe a penalty, what punishment should be imposed among us upon one who has not only copied sacred rites but has also corrupted what he copied and published what he corrupted?

Moreover, that triumvir presided over those very rites, and he was permitted to read and handle the same book. Our man, however, being entirely alien to all the ceremonies, can readily be believed to have stolen this book from the sacred inner chambers. For when Innocent VIII, having collected the ceremonies for this book with the greatest industry and knowing how much the secrets of sacred things had to be retained and concealed, had deposited them with great care in the palace sacristy and inner library, so that from there they might be drawn without corruption only by those in charge, and when this practice had been observed down to the present, it is not sufficiently clear how the book came into this man’s hands.

This much is absolutely certain: [Col. 1404A] this new man, only recently initiated into sacred matters, was found to be the one person who dared to do what no one else, even among those trained in the sacred ceremonies, had ever dared to do—not only to publish this book into profane hands but also to remove many things, add some, and alter and corrupt very many others.

But let him tell us, I beg, where he learned the ceremonies that he altered. On whose authority, under what teacher, and with what license did he proceed? For if the ceremonial book itself, approved by the Apostolic See, establishes law and right, as is decreed in the Clementines, title “On Oaths,” and if no one except the prince is permitted to alter matters of law, with what audacity shall we say that he was moved to suppose this alteration of the law permissible?

According to the constitutions, he did not yet even know his own name—for everywhere he called himself “elected archbishop,” although he ought to have called himself merely “elected,” since no one was permitted to be called an archbishop before receiving the pallium—and yet he thought that he was entitled to alter the law in this way. The good man was plainly copying what he understood least of all.

For if he had not been ignorant of these matters and had not walked in darkness, [Col. 1404B] he would not have put the left in place of the right, the “faithful” in place of the “filial,” or sometimes omitted negative or disjunctive particles that would pervert or corrupt the meaning. He would not have passed over the *fanones*, banners, colors, and colleges, nor altered oaths, blessings, anointings, and the other things that belong to the substance of the rites and imprint their characters, which in no way ought or can be altered.

But why should I linger over these matters? Most blessed Father, we have counted more than a thousand corruptions in this book of his, recently printed, when we compared it with the protocol exemplar of the bishop of Pienza, the true author. Let your Holiness not take our word for it; inspect the book itself, which I have brought forward. The places are marked either with an asterisk, a line, or an erasure. There is absolutely no page free from error.

Your Holiness ought to reject and repudiate all these things no less out of your devotion toward God than, in accordance with your justice, to ensure that no violence or injury is done to that same deceased bishop of Pienza, [Col. 1404C] a most learned man who deserved well of the Apostolic See; that he is not stripped of his labors and his name, and deprived of his honor.

After he had commendably and skillfully exercised the office of master of ceremonies for many years, Innocent VIII, your predecessor and kinsman, granted him leave from that office and nevertheless sent him to Siena, as to a retreat for literary work, to collect the ceremonies of the Roman Church into this book. The serious man of supreme experience labored for three years. At last, with incredible zeal and exact diligence, he completed the book and dedicated it to the name of that same pontiff, placing his own letters before it. He was content with the possibility that posterity might call him not the author but something like the collector or compiler of the sacred ceremonies.

That good father never imagined that anyone would be so hostile as to claim the work under his own name. But, O the morals of men! Under your pontificate that elected Corcyran was not ashamed to erase the name and letters of that Father, whose memory he ought rather to have honored, and to insert his own in such a way that posterity would believe him to be the author of this ceremonial book. [Col. 1404D]

For who is named in the recently printed book except one Christophorus Marcellus? What name of the bishop of Pienza, the author, or of anyone else is to be read? Indeed, this man, who so shamelessly claims for himself the labors of others, even removed the words of that excellent Father with which, in the chapter on the ministers of the ceremonies, he excused his own imperfection, saying among other things: “Would that I had known how to discharge my office as well when I held it as I know my own imperfection.”

Let him go, then, even if he maintains that he did not do this deceitfully or fraudulently; let him say that he appended his letters merely as an ornament and not to appropriate another’s praises. But let him be asked, I beg, whose work that is which he requests from your Holiness in such forceful words in the first letter: whether he means the work of his brief letter or the work of the entire compilation. Let him be asked, I say, [Col. 1405A] by whom the greater part of the work could be seen to have been completed, when he had accomplished so many and such great things in the first book that, in the words of the second letter, the work itself was “pompous”; or by whom the final book was completed, to use his own words.

Did the simple man suppose, while transcribing another’s work word for word, that he would never be caught in the theft? Or did he perhaps consider it more ingenious to render mute or conceal the person through whom he had made progress? Did he think that such a great work could be made his own by changing only a very few words and rubrics, so that the true author’s name would be entirely erased?

First of all, he records that he was the first to make these things available for common use and enjoyment. O excellent work! O laborious polishing! He “properly corrected” the *exsequias* (“funeral rites”); made *albam* (“white,” feminine) into *album* (“white,” neuter), *genuflexum* (“kneeling”) into *supplicandum* (“to be supplicated”), *officiales* (“officials”) into *magistratus* (“magistrates”), and *pileum* (“cap”) into *galerum* (“hat”). In place of *lignis* (“wood”) he inserted *tignis* (“beams”); for *cusino* (“cushion”), *pulvino* (“pillow”); for *bacili* (“basin”), *vase* (“vessel”); for *perfectis* (“completed”), *peracta* (“performed”); for *platea* (“street”), *aream* (“court”); for *armis* (“arms”), *insignia* (“insignia”); and for *rubeo* (“red”), *purpureum* (“purple”). [Col. 1405B] These and similar changes are indeed trivial and empty, yet this man boasts that he polished them with his sesquipedalian words, as though religion did not demand what is pure, plain, clear, and simple more than such verbal embellishments.

But if he intended to polish the work, why did he not polish everything? Why did he not everywhere replace *papa* with *pontifex*, or make *supplicationes* out of *processiones*? At times he left the same words untouched, as though he had grown weary even of the lengthy polishing of those books whose author he wished to be considered.

What of the fact that he erased everywhere the author’s name, defense, and letters? He did not erase this: “The emperor Frederick III, who still reigns, took this oath while he was at Siena.” Why did he leave that untouched as well? In the Pontifical, which we recently corrected, we fully recorded the ceremonies to be observed in crowning kings—so that in the one book, since the emperor had long been dead, the deceit and lie might appear, and in the other the theft might be confessed—unless he preferred to duplicate that Pontifical book, attributing it to himself just as he did these books. [Col. 1405C]

Beyond these matters, he passed over many others no less significant, either through negligence or in order to confuse everything alike. For he shamelessly claims that he attended the coronation of that same emperor, saw Cardinals of Nice and Arras, served Pius II for many years, and that in his own time no Roman pontiff except Sixtus IV was consecrated—as though he were saying that neither Pius III nor you, Leo X, were consecrated in our time.

Just as all these statements suited the original author perfectly, so they deprive this counterfeit author and his book of all credibility. Either those passages should not have been removed, or these too should have been erased along with them, so that the work would appear polished throughout.

But if the bishop of Pienza, the actual author, should return and now demand his rights, would not this industrious polisher, like Horace’s crow, stripped of all another’s feathers and left only with his own corruptions, become a laughingstock to everyone?

Perhaps he will think that these things are permitted to him because he sent his letters, together with the work he had polished, to your Holiness and concealed his offense beneath your most sacred name, imitating those who, to steal with impunity, offer their stolen goods to magistrates.

But this ingenious author in another’s work [Col. 1406A] did not see how deeply he would offend your Holiness. By inserting you into the place of the erased names as though you were excessively desirous of empty glory, he sought to make you participate in his crime. He not only gives envious and malicious people a reason to attack you, but also leaves your successors an opportunity to erase the most holy name of Leo, bringing disgrace upon you, while restoring the names of the authors to their own praise.

If these matters, which ought most to move your Holiness, do not move you, most holy pontiff, and if contempt for the Apostolic See and pontifical dignity, which will immediately arise from this publication of the secrets, does not affect you, then I beg you to let your devotion toward God move you, and do not permit it to be corrupted, together with the ceremonies themselves, by this insolent boaster.

Let the empty labors and vigils of the bishop of Pienza [Col. 1406B] move you, demanding the restoration of his rights. Finally, let the memory of your predecessor and kinsman Innocent VIII move you, to whom you owe so much that perhaps no one owes him more. He asks that his rights be restored to you both by the law of kinship and gratitude and by equity and justice. He demands that his book be preserved whole and uncorrupted and kept secret, as he established while alive.

Obey their shades, most blessed Father, since they make such just, pious, and holy requests. In accordance with your justice, reject and condemn, even under anathema, this shameless usurper together with his corruptions, and restore the books to their authors. Your Holiness will gain more true praise and glory by restoring their names than if any outstanding work were dedicated to you by its true author.

When I had delivered this letter into the pope’s hands, and he had read it willingly and eagerly and accepted the reasons and arguments I had presented in it, he turned to certain cardinals who perhaps supported him [Col. 1406C] and said that I had a case concerning my petitions. He said that the recently printed ceremonial book ought to be burned entirely together with its false author, as I had requested, or at least that the author himself ought to be corrected and punished in whatever manner seemed appropriate to those present.

Accordingly, he deferred the matter and the case to the first consistory, so that I might propose it there, as I did, with everyone listening. Finally, the pope instructed three cardinals—namely, the Reverend Lord Antonio de Monte, cardinal-priest of Santa Prassede; Lord Pietro de Accoltis, cardinal-priest of Sant’Eusebio, of Ancona; and Lord Achille de Grassis, cardinal-priest of San Sisto, of Bologna, protector of the office of ceremonies and my brother—to investigate my petitions more fully and to settle my case as justice and their judgment required, both concerning the burning of the book and the punishment of its author, as well as summoning him personally to Rome and requiring his appearance.

I shall therefore also record here, in due succession, what follows.

[Col. 1405]

## Back matter of the volume

[Col. 1407]

## INDEX OF MEMORABLE SUBJECTS AND WORDS CONTAINED IN THE BOOK OF THE SACRAMENTARIES, ETC., AND IN THE NOTES

That is, from col. 25 of this volume through col. 849. In this index the reader is referred to the numbers expressed in heavier type in the text. [Note: [Col. 1408] In this index, Arabic numbers refer to column numbers printed in the text in bold type.]

## A

**Abacus** is called marble, that is, a marble table, 433. *Abacus* is also used for a marble table holding chalices, ibid. The rite for ordaining abbots and abbesses, 443, 526. In the Greek Church an abbot is created through the laying on of the bishop’s hands, 526. There too an abbot may appoint a lector by the laying on of hands in his own monastery, if he is a priest, ibid. In the Latin Church the laying on of hands is not used in the blessing of an abbot, but only a simple prayer, ibid.

**A, B, C.** These three letters alone were formerly painted by the bishop at the dedication of a basilica, 425. Now the bishop, with his crozier, paints two complete alphabets, one Greek and the other Latin, ibid. What *abcturium* is, 425.

**Abdon (Saint), martyr**, 116, 704.

**Ablution of sins** is said in the postcommunion during Lent; in the Mass of Saint Augustine, *abolition of sins* is read, 609. —Ablution of the body of the deceased according to the ancient custom of Christians, 482. Why the bodies of the dead are washed, ibid. The body of the deceased Tabitha of Joppa was washed, ibid. The tradition of this washing and of the other duties of piety toward the bodies of the dead is affirmed, ibid. The washed bodies of the dead were formerly customarily anointed, 483. Why bodies were anointed during the funeral rites themselves, ibid.

**To renounce** (*abrenuntiare*) is commonly used for “to despise, reject, contradict,” 367. The person to be baptized confesses that he renounces Satan and all his pomps, ibid., 383. Why this renunciation is followed by a confession of the Holy Trinity, ibid. The faithful renounce Satan in order to serve the Lord more freely, ibid. The baptized are said to have renounced the devil and his angels, or to have renounced the world, 383. To have renounced the devil, his pomps, spectacles, and works, ibid. Ordinarily the renunciation is made three times; Saint Cyril adds a fourth, ibid. In the Ambrosian Church only two renunciations were customarily made, ibid. The person renouncing turned toward the west, ibid. Why, after the renunciation, he turned toward the east with his hands raised upward, ibid.

**Form of absolution** by which penitents were reconciled to the Church on Thursday of Holy Week, at the Lord’s Supper, 458. At what part of the Mass absolution was formerly given to penitents, ibid. Only prayers are used for the reconciliation of penitents, 459. A noteworthy formula of absolution found in a tomb, ibid. Controversy between Saint Thomas and another doctor concerning the deprecatory or declarative form of absolution, ibid. Alexander of Hales accepts both indifferently, ibid. Various forms of absolution, ibid., 460. This formula is valid: “I forgive you your sins,” ibid. In absolution from sins the Greeks use many deprecatory forms, ibid. To these they add: “I have you forgiven,” ibid. Formerly absolution, whether from excommunication or from sins, was not ordinarily given before complete satisfaction had been performed, except at the point of death, ibid. Sometimes, at the prayers of martyrs or confessors, bishops remitted some part of it, ibid. This was the practice of the Roman Church and of the Western churches, 461. Penitents obtained absolution at the end of the fourth degree of penance, which was called “standing,” ibid. Absolution of a sick person who has confessed, 547. Absolution by brothers, 549.

“Receive the power to offer sacrifice to God,” etc., is not found in the ancient Sacramentaries, 508. “Receive the Holy Spirit,” etc., the formula which the bishop pronounces while laying his hands on the heads of the individual priests, 509. This rite too, together with its formula, is absent from the ancient Sacramentaries and early authors, ibid.

**Acclamation “Long live the king”**, customarily made at the coronation of a king, 594.

**Acerra** is an altar that used to be placed before the dead, on which perfumes were burned, 428. It is also used for a censer, ibid., 438.

**Achilleus (Saint), martyr**, 87, 392, 694.

**Ἀκολουθός (*akolouthos*)**, “acolyte,” that is, one who follows behind, or an attendant, 493. In ecclesiastical usage, acolytes in Greek are called *ceroferarii* in Latin, from carrying candles, ibid. Ancient mention of acolytes in the Church, ibid. At what point in the Mass acolytes are ordained, 487. Ordination of an acolyte, 221. It is their duty to light and carry the lamps, ibid. To bring wine and water for the Eucharist of the body of Christ, 494. They provide the subdeacons with the vessels used for the Eucharist, ibid.

**Ἀκρόασις (*akroasis*)**, “hearing,” the second degree of penitents, 461.

**Action** in the canon is the consecration itself; *agenda* means the Mass in liturgical books, 482.

**Adalard**, abbot of Corbie, sent with Bishop Bernhard by the emperor Charlemagne to Pope Leo III, 379. Anointed with sacred unction and nourished with the sacred viaticum, 536.

**Adalheis (Saint)**, when at the point of death, after the anointing with sacred oil had been performed, humbly and devoutly received the viaticum, 536.

**Adauctus (Saint), martyr**, 127, 709.

**Ad complendum**: the prayer is said at the end of the Mass; it is the completion and conclusion of the whole Mass, 295. It is now called the postcommunion, ibid.

**Admonition of the archbishop**, 510.

**Adoptive Son of God**: Christ is not an adoptive but a natural Son, 365, 378. Elipandus, bishop of Toledo, together with Felix of Urgel, asserted that Christ was the adoptive Son of God, ibid.

**Adoration of the cross** takes place at vespers on Good Friday, 69. The ancient custom of adoring the cross on Good Friday, 341. See *Adoration of the cross*.

**Hadrian**, the emperor, built at Athens a temple common to all the gods, 393.

**Adultery**: by what canonical penalty it should be punished, 465.

**To unite** (*adunare*): in the canon it is requested that all believers may be of one heart, 284.

**Advent of the Lord**: five weeks, or Sundays, are counted, 136, 445. Elsewhere four are counted, 186, 445. In Ambrosian Masses there are six Sundays of Advent, 445. There the first Sunday of Advent immediately follows the feast of Saint Martin, ibid. The fast of the Advent of the Lord formerly lasted forty days, 445. The Advent fast varied according to place and time, ibid. In Gaul the monks fast every day from December until Christmas, 446. Formerly the Romans began Advent and its fast on the Sunday after the feast of Saint Catherine the virgin, ibid.

**Sacred buildings** are turned toward the east, 329.

**A very weak sick person** was given only the blood of Christ as viaticum, 554. A mixed sacrifice was given, ibid., 570.

**Egyptian virgins**, tonsured, 443.

**Egyptians** formerly, when a dog had died in a house, afflicted themselves with great mourning, all the members of the household shaving their entire bodies, 477. The Egyptian practice in observing Lent, 315.

**Age of a consecrated virgin**, 441.

**Names of Aetheldrytha and Gertrude** are recited in the canon after Anastasia, 4, 290.

**Ethiopians**: when they elevate the body of Christ in the Mass, 566. The Ethiopian rite in the blessing of baptismal fonts, 350; in the anointing of chrism, 361.

**Addition of the Africans** in the canon, 283.

**Agapetus (Saint), pope**, 310.

**Agapitus (Saint), martyr**, 118. On the fifteenth day before the Kalends of September, of Saint Agapitus the martyr, 123, 705, 707.

**Agatha (Saint)**, according to the Greek declension, 290, 308, 665. Her name in the canon, 4, 25.

**Agenda** is the divine office, 482. It is called the *agenda of the dead*, ibid. *Agenda* in liturgical books is the same as the Mass, ibid.

**Ἅγια τὰ ἁγίοις**, “the holy things for the holy,” 566.

**Ἅγιος**, 311.

[Col. 1410] **Agnes (Saint)**: *Agne*, Agnes, retaining the form of Greek declension, 603. *Agna, Agnes, Agnetis*, 4, 21, 304. Her name in the canon, 290. Deposit of her relics, 304. The feast of Saint Agnes, called the feast of her nativity, or the second feast, on the fifth day before the Kalends of February, 23, 664.

**Wax lambs** were formerly blessed in Rome by the archdeacon on Holy Saturday, in place of the Paschal candle, to be distributed to the people, 346, 565. When this rite began and when it ceased, 347.

**Agnus Dei**, etc. Pope Sergius I ordered it to be sung by clergy and people in the Mass, 292. The *Agnus Dei* is not sung in the Mass of Holy Saturday, 388.

**Agrippa Vipsanius** built the Pantheon at Rome, 392. Why that temple was called the Pantheon, ibid. Pope Boniface IV converted this temple into a church of Saint Mary, ibid.

**Aldanus**, king of Ireland, received the laying on of hands at his coronation, 595.

**Alba talaris** is a linen garment called *poderis*, 556.

**The bishop of Albano** is present with the bishop of Ostia in the rite of the pope’s consecration, 517. In the consecration of the emperor, three prayers are delivered by three bishops, of which the first is delivered by the bishop of Albano, 586.

**Albion** is Great Britain, 259, 586. Which king of the Franks was anointed king of the English before the year 986? He appears to have been Louis IV, surnamed “from Overseas,” ibid.

**Those brought out of the baptismal font** were clothed in white garments, 356. What the white garments of the reborn and of the angels announcing Christ’s resurrection signify, 369. Sunday *in albis depositis*, 390.

**Alcuin**, philosopher and abbot of Saint Martin, died in 804, 319. Alcuin refuted concerning the single immersion of the Spaniards in baptism, 353.

**Alexander (Saint), first pope**, is named in the canon, 4, 290. —Alexander (Saint), bishop of Alexandria, after anointing boys baptized by the boy Athanasius, completed them with the sign of Christ, 359. —Alexander, Eventius, and Theodosius (Saints), 693. Saints Juvenalis, Alexander, and Eventius, 694. —The emperor Alexander Severus complained that no inquiry was made concerning the appointment of provincial governors, although among Christians inquiry is made concerning the ordination of priests, 497.

**Alleluia** is not said when the litany is being performed, 1. Why this word of joy was formerly not omitted in the office of the dead, 480. This word of joy is also sung by the Greeks in the liturgy for those who have fallen asleep, after the reading of the Epistle has ended, ibid.

**Address of the bishops to the people** in the church at the coronation of kings, 584. With explicit consent, they give thanks to God, 257, 585. This address was delivered at the coronation of Charles the Bald and his wife Hermentrude, and of Henry II and Henry IV, kings of France, ibid.

**Two alphabets**, one Greek and the other Latin, are painted complete by the bishop on the pavement, with the crozier, at the dedication of a church, 425. Formerly some added a Hebrew alphabet, ibid. The bishop traces the alphabets transversely in a quadrangular pattern, ibid.

**Stripping of the altars** formerly took place on Good Friday, 342. Formerly in some places they were also stripped on Holy Thursday, ibid. Formerly the altars, walls, and floors of the church, and the sacred vessels, were purified by washing, 343. With hyssop the bishop sprinkles the altar itself seven times with the same water, 427. The consecration of the altar follows the dedication of the church, 428. Formerly altars were customarily consecrated with the sign of the cross, 429. The use of anointing altars is ancient, ibid. The altar is anointed with chrism according to the ancient custom of the Church, 429–430. It is first anointed with oil, then with chrism, 430. Altars are consecrated and sanctified through invocation of the name of God, ibid. Wooden altars were formerly in use in Africa, in certain churches of Gaul, and in the East in the time of Saint Athanasius, 431. The altar is adorned with the Gospel, that is, it is spread with linens and coverings, 249, 574. See *Relics; Confession*.

**Amalarius Fortunatus** refuted concerning the ordination of a deacon. He has several ancient codices supporting his opinion, which state that the hands both of the bishop and of the attending priests are to be laid upon the deacon, 498.

**Amandus (Saint)**: his name is recited in the canon of the Mass, 285.

**Amantius (Saint)**: his feast is on the fourth day before the Ides of February, 310.

**Ἀμβών (*ambōn*)**. *Ambones* are called mountainous and elevated places, 347. The ambo is the pulpit or reading stand of a church, that is, an elevated place in the church from which readers read and psalmists sang, ibid.

**Ambrosian form of Extreme Unction**, 534.

**Ambrosian Advent** has six weeks, 445. It begins on the Sunday after the feast of Saint Martin, ibid.
