**Ambrose** compelled penitents confessing their sins to him to weep through his own tears, 470. Saint Ambrose used to recite this prayer, “Before the presence,” etc., before Mass, that is, before the Offertory, 526. What sort of crown or mitre Saint Ambrose used, 557. The holy bishops commended divine virtues through eloquence, ibid. The passage concerning Saint Ambrose restored in the office of Saint Lawrence, 500.

**Amen** was formerly the response to the words of consecration, 577; when receiving communion, 580; to each of the persons of the Trinity in the baptismal formula, 354.

**To remove** (*amittere*), that is, to take away, send away, or banish, 531.

**Ἀμφιδρόμια (*amphidromia*)** is said by some to derive from certain superstitious circuits made around a place, 350. *Amphidromia* took place on the seventh day after birth, when names were given to infants, ibid.

**Ἀμφίθυρον (*amphithyron*)** means a veil hung at the railings of the sanctuary or choir, 435.

**Ampulla** is a vessel in which oil is stored, 325. Oil or chrism is stored in ampullae according to the ancient custom, ibid. An ampulla full of sacred oil was sent from heaven; with this oil, or chrism, the kings of the Franks are accustomed to be anointed, 588.

**Ἀνάδοχοι (*anadochoi*)**, that is, sponsors and godparents, are those who receive the baptized from the sacred font, 357.

**Ἀνάρρησις (*anarrhēsis*)** is a kind of proclamation derived from the name, 525.

**Anastasia (Saint)**: her name is recited in the canon, 4, 290. The first Mass on the morning of Christmas is celebrated at Saint Anastasia’s, 7, 298.

**Support of Anatolius**, patriarch of Constantinople, in the eleventh session of the Council of Chalcedon concerning the ordination of the bishop of Ephesus, 512.

**Andrew (Saint), apostle**: mention is made of him in the canon, 3, 4. His feast is celebrated with a vigil and fast, 143, 713. The acts of his passion are approved, 143, 423. His office, 836. Another office for him, perhaps for the translation of his body, 840. The basilica of Saint Andrew was near the Vatican basilica, 786.

**Angels and all heavenly spirits** are mentioned according to the ancient custom in the preface of the Mass, 280. The angels praise God in alternating chants, 651. Saint Ignatius the martyr learned this practice of alternation from the angels, ibid.

**Angusticlavia**: garments whose stripes are narrow are so called, 325. See *Clavi*.

**The soul** is incorporeal, 382. The soul in Christ is perfect, ibid.

**Animal**: intercourse with animals is punished by severe and lengthy canonical penalties, 467, 474. In this matter the person’s age is taken into account, and whether or not he has a wife, ibid.

**Anniversary** of the dedication of a basilica, 154, 438; of a marriage, 596; of the ordination of a pope or bishop, 520.

**Anniversarial Pascha** is the anniversary of baptism, on which day the baptized celebrate the remembrance of their baptism, 390. This Pascha appears to have been celebrated after the Sunday *in albis*, ibid., 791.

**Ring of discretion**, blessed, is given to the bishop on his finger, 510. A ring is placed on the finger of the queen at her coronation, 557, 595. What the ring given by the bridegroom to the bride signifies, 598. This rite is extremely ancient in the Church, ibid.

**Announcement of the archbishop**, 510. —The angel’s announcement to Mary, 31. The Annunciation of Saint Mary, 665. The holy day of the Annunciation. The Annunciation of the Mother of God, 313. This feast is ordered to be celebrated on the eighth day before Christ’s Nativity, 31, 621. —Announcement to prayer, 321. —Announcement of feasts, 439.

**Ἄνοιξις, ἀνοίξιον**, that is, “opening,” or the rite of opening a church at its dedication, customary among the Greeks as among the Latins, 424.

**Christian gatherings before dawn** in the primitive Church, for the celebration of the sacred mysteries, 324. Hence the calumnies of the pagans against Christians, ibid.

**Basilica at Antioch**, facing west, 329.

**Antiphon** is interpreted as “sounding in response.” Among churchmen it means singing by turns, 651. In the time of Gregory Nazianzen this manner of singing was already common in monasteries, 652. A psalm always follows an antiphon, 275. Hence the name *antiphon*, 649. The antiphon sung before the Mass is called the entrance antiphon, 275. Double in certain Masses, 554. The antiphon at the Gospel, that is, the one placed before the canticles *Magnificat* or *Benedictus*, taken from the Gospel, 735. Antiphons concerning the apostles, that is, taken from the Epistles of Paul, 763.

**Antiphoner**, a book named from the antiphon, 649. It is also called the *Official*, from the office, ibid. The antiphoner was not instituted by Saint Gregory but embellished by him, 652. Saint Ambrose is said to have been the author of antiphons among the Latins, ibid.

**Antony (Saint), confessor**: his deposition is recorded on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of February, 304. —Antony, bishop of Olbia, elected by the common suffrage of all, people and clergy, requests the laying on of hands from Theophilus of Alexandria, 508, 512.

**Ἀπερίγραπτον (*aperigraphon*)**, that is, “uncircumscribed, incomprehensible,” in place of the word *ascriptam* in the canon, 286.

**Opening of a basilica** at its dedication, 424.

**Opening of the ears**, customarily performed for catechumens: what it signifies, 366. By what rite it should be performed, ibid., 381. The blessing customarily pronounced at the opening of the ears, 630. See *Ears*.

**Ἀποτάσσεσθαι (*apotassesthai*)**, that is, to renounce or abjure, 383.

**Apollinaris (Saint)**: his feast is on the tenth day before the Kalends of August, 407, 116, 704. —The Apollinarian heresy: what it consisted in, 382.

**Apologia** is the excuse and purification by which the priest excuses himself for approaching the awesome mysteries unworthily, 526, 615. *Apologia*, purification, satisfaction, that is, excuse, ibid. At what points in the Mass the priest recited apologias, ibid. An apologia published by order of Pope Urban VIII, 530.

**Ἀπολογοῦμαι (*apologoumai*)**, that is, “I excuse myself,” 526.

**Ἀπόλυσις (*apolysis*)** is what the Greeks call the eighth day of a solemnity, that is, the dismissal, because the feast reaches its end, 300.

**Ἀποστάτης (*apostates*)**, that is, a renegade and deserter, 332. Saint Augustine reads *apostates*, not *ἀποστασία* (*apostasia*), that is, “departure,” in chapter 2 of the Second Epistle to the Thessalonians, ibid.

**Apostle** is used for the Epistle of Saint Paul or of the apostles, 1, 278, 491, 600.

**Apuleius (Saint), martyr**, on the Nones of October, 418.

**Extended praises of bees** in the blessing of the Paschal candle, 344. The industry and virginity of bees, 346.

**Water** is solemnly blessed at the feast of the Epiphany, the holy cross being immersed in the water, for baptism and for various Christian uses, 302. Blessed water was drunk by the people, 418. Baptismal water, according to the ancient custom of the Church, is to be blessed by the bishop with a solemn rite, 348. This custom is counted among the apostolic traditions, ibid. It is an ancient custom of the Church that baptismal water be blessed by the sign of the cross, 349. Through the invocation of God, that is, through the baptismal formula, the water is sanctified and receives the power to sanctify, 384. In a certain town of Lycia the water of the baptistery was miraculous at the Epiphany, 399. Likewise in the baptistery at Ebredunum water arose divinely on Christmas and Holy Thursday, ibid. Water from this baptistery used to be carried to another basin for the purpose of baptism, ibid. Formerly in the town of Melitine in Sicily the font of the baptistery was filled every year with water by divine power on Easter Day, ibid.

The institution of blessed water is attributed to Pope Alexander I, or even to Saint Matthew the apostle, 318. It is an ancient custom to place a vessel of blessed water in the vestibule of a church for the purification of the people entering, ibid. It is an ancient custom of the Church that water be blessed with the sign of the cross, 533. Sprinkling of blessed water in the house of a sick person, 532.

The rite for blessing water at the dedication of a church, 146, 425. It is an ancient custom that a church be sanctified by sprinkling with blessed water, 425. In this blessing the water is sprinkled with salt, ashes, wine, and hyssop, 148, 426.

The preparation of lustral water among the pagans, 348. **Χέρνιβον (*chernibon*)** is a vessel for lustral water, ibid.

A small amount of water accidentally flowing into the mouth does not prevent communion, 405. What is signified by the blood and water that flowed from Christ’s side, 384. Why water is mixed with wine in the chalice, 373, 582, 551. What water mixed with wine signifies, 374. Saint Cyprian wrote about mixing water with wine in the chalice being sanctified, 387. Why the Greeks, when communion is imminent, pour hot water into the sacred blood, 575.

**Aquamanile** is a vessel suitable for washing the hands, 495.

While the freedom of our will remains intact, God compels us through fear and leads us through love, 173, 444.

**Prayer of the archbishop over the elected bishop**, 510. His admonition, ibid. His warning after the promise, ibid. How the archbishop receives the pallium, 520.

[Col. 1413] **Burning of threshing floors**: by what penalty it is punished according to the canons, 474.

**Processions of the Arians**, 414.

**Ariolus**, one who is commonly called a diviner: by what penalties he is to be punished according to the canons, 467.

**Arms** are called ornaments or garments, 241, 556.

**Armenians** used only wine in the mysteries of the blood of Christ, 387.

**Shoulder of the victim** was given to kings, 589. Samuel ordered it to be placed before Saul, ibid. Why the shoulder, or upper arm, of a victim was regarded among the pagans as the more honorable portion, ibid. —Anointing of the shoulder in kings, 589.

**Bodies of the dead** were embalmed with spices, 483. See *Dead; Funeral rites*.

**Aroson**, martyr: his feast is on the third day before the Kalends of December, at Rome, 422.

**Haruspices**: by what penalties they are to be punished according to the canons, 467.

**Citadel**. To place the bishop in the citadel, that is, in the episcopal seat or throne in the church, 520.

**Ascension of the Lord at Saint Peter’s**. The Sunday after the Ascension, 88.

**Ascensa**, that is, the Ascension of the Lord, 397.

**Assensa**, or *assensio*, from the verb *assendo* or *ascendo*, 615.

On the vigil of the Ascension it was formerly customary to fast, 695.

**Asclas (Saint), martyr**, 305. His passion is commemorated on the tenth day before the Kalends of February, ibid.

**Ascodrytae** were formerly heretics who anointed their dead with a certain vain superstition, 483. They clothed the anointed in precious garments according to the rank of the person, ibid.

**Ascriptam** in the canon, that is, “received into the number of those pleasing to you,” 286.

**Τὸ Ἀσπασμός (*aspasmos*)** is a greeting made with an embrace as a sign of friendship, 526.

**Assumption of Blessed Mary**, 122. Vigil of the Assumption of Saint Mary, ibid. On the fifteenth day of August, the solemnity of the repose of Saint Mary, 122. The Dormition of the Most Holy Mother of God, 411. The glorious departure of the holy Mother of God, ibid. This feast was formerly celebrated on January 18, 411. Office of the Assumption of Saint Mary, 817.

**Athanasius**, as a boy, baptized boys, 359. Saint Alexander the pontiff administered to them the sacrament of confirmation, ibid.

**Athenais**, the name given to the wife of the younger Emperor Theodosius. Bishop Atticus gave her the name Eudocia at baptism, 352.

**Pantheon at Athens**, that is, a temple common to all the gods, which the emperor Hadrian ordered to be built, 393.

**“Hear us”** (*Audi nos*) was formerly not customarily said with “we beseech you,” except concerning the Son of God and sinners, 397.

**Hearer**, or auditor, is what a catechumen is called, 363, 374. Others are called “hearers” in the second degree of penitents, ibid. Hearing was the second degree of penance, 461. Penitents of this degree heard the divine Scriptures inside the door in the narthex of the church, ibid.

**Audoenus (Saint)**, bishop of Rouen, on the sixth day before the Kalends of September, 124.

**Audomarus (Saint)**, bishop of Thérouanne, together with Saint Autbert, bishop of Cambrai, transferred the body of Saint Vedast to the monastery of Nobiliacum, 418.

**Augustine (Saint)**: his name is recited in the canon of the Mass, 3, 285. He describes his catechumenate, through hearing, the sign of the cross, and reception of salt, 377. On the fifth day before the Kalends of September, the feast of Saint Augustine, 125, 412, 708. The Mass of Saint Augustine for the living and the dead, 486. —The feast of Saint Augustine the Younger, bishop of Canterbury, on the seventh day before the Kalends of June, 104, 393. Through Augustine, the disciple of Saint Gregory the Great, the English received the faith, 485. From Augustine they learned the Roman custom by which the Eucharist was placed upon the breast of a deceased bishop in the tomb, ibid.

**Levitative aura** is a storm said to be sent by magicians, 472.

**Anointing of the ears in confirmation** among the Greeks, 361.

**Ears of catechumens** are touched with spittle and are said to be opened through the word *Ephphatha*, 366. According to the ancient usage of the Roman Church, this opening of the ears takes place in the scrutiny, 381. The blessing at the opening of the ears is pronounced, 630. The ears, inside and outside at the top, are anointed with the sign of the cross in Extreme Unction, 549. Both ears are anointed under two distinct formulas, 555.

**Autbertus (Saint)**, bishop of Cambrai, 418. See *Audomarus (Saint)*.

**Abortion** (*avorsus*) voluntarily procured is punished by capital penalty, 474. According to the canons, the person guilty of this crime is to do penance for three years, one of them on bread and water, 467.

## B
## B

**Bacchus (St.)**, martyr, on the Nones of October, 418. The staff of sacred governance, or pastoral office, is given to a bishop, 511. Balsam mixed into chrism, 326, 338. Properly, *balteus* is a military belt, 242, 556. It is called the belt of chastity, 242.

Baptism is prefigured by the Flood of the world, 330; and by the water flowing from the side of Christ sleeping on the cross, 368, 384. The power and effect of baptism, ibid. The baptismal font bears the likeness of a tomb, 369. Why baptism is not repeated, ibid.

—The form of baptism, 352, 353. It was sometimes repeated three times among the Greeks, 354. Among the same people it is not supplicatory, ibid. The mystery of baptism cannot be completed except under the invocation of the most holy Trinity, 368. Through the form of baptism, which is called the invocation of God, the water is sanctified and receives the power to sanctify, 384.

—In baptism there is a triple immersion, according to the ancient custom of the Church, 352. Sometimes there was a single immersion, ibid. The rite of triple immersion is reckoned among the apostolic traditions, 353. What the triple immersion and emergence signify, ibid. Who were the authors of single immersion, ibid. Those baptized by a single immersion are ordered to be baptized again, ibid. Baptism conferred by a single immersion and the legitimate form is valid, ibid. The immersion was performed in such a way that the entire body, including the head itself, was submerged, 384.

—In former times priests and deacons baptized rarely, bishops very frequently, 385. Immediately after baptism the bishop conferred the sacrament of confirmation by anointing the neophyte on the forehead, ibid. At that time the neophyte was not anointed on the crown of the head, ibid. Whether baptism is valid if one person pronounces the form while another immerses the candidate or pours the water, 534.

—Baptism was conferred during the vigils of Easter and Pentecost, according to the ancient institution of the Church, 398. In former times these solemnities began at sunset itself—that is, on Saturday evening, 400. Baptism took place during that night, and it was said that baptism was celebrated on the Saturday itself, 398. Some baptized people during the solemnities of the martyrs, but this was eventually forbidden, ibid. Others baptized on Epiphany, ibid., 730. This custom continued longer in Africa, ibid. In certain parts of Gaul the celebration of baptism appears to have been customary on the Nativity of the Lord, 399. A miracle formerly used to occur each year around the baptistery built by St. Marcellinus at Embrun, on the Nativity and the Lord’s Supper [Col. 1414], ibid. If danger of death arose, the sick were baptized on any day, ibid. The baptism of infants was excepted from the rule requiring baptism at Easter and Pentecost, 400. These were baptized on whatever day from the time of their birth, ibid.

A baptistery is the means by which baptism is conferred, 273. The term *baptisterium* also denotes baptismal water, 73, 349. It also denotes a building beside a church in which the faithful were formerly baptized, ibid., 437. It also denotes the baptismal font, 385. What the seven steps of the baptistery signify, 385. The consecration of a baptistery, 437. The form of a baptistery, 385. An elaborate baptistery in the church of St. Stephen, ibid. According to the custom of the Church, at the beginning of Lent the doors of the baptistery were closed with the hand and the pontifical ring, 437. Miracles customarily occurring each year in baptisteries, 399.

Among the Latins the person to be baptized is anointed on the chest, shoulders, and between the shoulders, 331. Among the Greeks the whole body is anointed, ibid. If the person was to be baptized by a bishop, he was anointed by the bishop with a triple sign and was then to be anointed over the whole body by priests, 332.

Those preparing for baptism were taught by the apostles the secrets of baptism and the other rules of faith, 363. Why those preparing for baptism receive salt in the sacrament, 364. Why the nostrils and ears of those preparing for baptism are touched with spittle while *Epheta* is said, 366. Penance to be performed by those preparing for baptism before baptism, 379. What kind and how much penance was imposed upon them, ibid. Among the Greeks it lasted forty days, 380. These days appear to have originated shortly before the Lenten fast, ibid. The practice of this penance was not uniform everywhere, 381. During these days of preparation they confessed all the sins of their past life, ibid. This confession, like the penance, was not sacramental, ibid.

The names of those preparing for baptism were recorded, 351. Questions were put to them, 352. Their position and reverence before the fonts, 382. According to ancient custom, those baptized were immediately anointed on the crown of the head with chrism by a presbyter, 355. What this anointing signifies, ibid. According to ancient custom, those baptized, rising naked from the bath, were wrapped in a linen cloth by the sponsor, ibid. Those baptized in bed were irregular, 399. See *Clinici*. Those brought out of the baptismal font were clothed in white garments, 356. What these white garments signify, ibid. Those baptized—even infants—immediately after baptism received the sacrament of the Eucharist, 73, 356. Care was taken that infants should consume no food, not even milk, before Holy Communion, ibid. Infants appear to have received Communion without fasting where the office of Holy Saturday began at the second hour after midday, ibid.

**Beard.** At the first cutting of the youthful beard, a special prayer was formerly said, 235, 533.

The name of **Barbara (St.)** is recited in the canon, 290. Anyone who provided the barbarians with leadership against Christians is punished by canonical penalties, 468, 475. **Barbas the Arian**, 354.

The name of **Barnabas (St.)** is mentioned in the canon of the Mass, 4. The nativity of St. Barnabas is on the third day before the Ides of June, 104.

**Bartholomew (St.)** is commemorated in the canon of the Mass, 3. The nativity of St. Bartholomew the apostle, and his Mass, 124, 412. The feast and translation of St. Bartholomew, 412.

The rite for blessing basilicas, 145, 423. It is an ancient custom that a church be sanctified by the sprinkling of exorcised or blessed water [Col. 1415], 425. Many psalms are sung at the dedication of a basilica, according to ancient custom, 427. It is certain that formerly basilicas were dedicated with the sign of the cross, 428. It is an ancient institution of the Church that basilicas be dedicated by the bringing in and placement of holy relics, 434. Formerly it was forbidden to be buried in basilicas, 486. Later Christians were permitted to be buried within the precincts of churches, ibid. See **Dedication**, **Burial**.

**Basilides (St.)**, martyr, 105, 699.

When **Basil (St.)**, bishop of Caesarea, was dying, he divided consecrated bread into three parts, one of which he kept so that it might be buried with him, 485.

**Bassianus**, bishop of Ephesus, was ordained contrary to the canons and was deposed at the Council of Chalcedon, 512.

**Bavo (St.)**, on the day before the Kalends of October, 417.

The nativity of **Beatrice (St.)** is on the fourth day before the Kalends of August, 408, 704.

“To bless” means the same as “to consecrate,” 286. *Benedictam* in the canon means the same as “consecrated,” ibid.

The name of **Benedict (St.)** is recited in the canon, 3, 285. It is found even in the most ancient Missals of cathedral churches, 546. The nativity of St. Benedict is celebrated on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, 313, 703. His feast is celebrated with a solemn vigil, ibid., 665. On the sixth day before the Ides of July is the vigil of St. Benedict the abbot, 407. On the fifth day before the Ides of July is the nativity of St. Benedict, ibid., 810. On the day of the translation of the relics, the day of burial was formerly celebrated without any mention being made of the translation, ibid. This does not invalidate the opinion that St. Benedict’s body was translated to the monastery of Fleury, ibid. The octave of St. Benedict, ibid. The office of this feast is recorded, 115, 810. St. Benedict gave the Lord’s Body to be placed upon the breast of a buried monk, 485. The basilica of St. Benedict located at Paris formerly differed in its position from the other churches of that city, 329.

The blessing of candles, 307, 308. The blessing of the Paschal candle, 344. See **Candle**. The blessing of ashes, 449. The blessing of a ring, 510; of a staff, 511; of beans, grain, and grapes, 409, 410. The blessing in sacred ordinations, 489. The blessing of meat, cheese, and eggs, 565.

—The episcopal blessing: what it is, by what rite, with what words, and at what part of the Mass it was customarily performed by the bishop, 295, 296, etc. The formulas of these blessings: why they are called impositions of hands, 296. These blessings consist of three sections and a conclusion, ibid. There is another blessing given at the end of Mass, ibid. Whether this blessing is distinguished from the prayer for Compline, 297. After this blessing had been given by the priest, the deacon said: “Go, the Mass is ended,” 298. It is the deacon’s duty to exhort the people before Communion to bow for the episcopal blessing, 567. The use of episcopal blessings still continues in certain Churches, ibid.

—Blessings over a sick person are to be said either by the bishop himself or, if he is absent, by the individual presbyters, 551.

—The nuptial blessing is given at Mass after the Lord’s Prayer, 596. This is the ancient custom in the Church of blessing marriages, ibid. Judith, daughter of Charles the Bald, was blessed before the Preface when she married Æthelwulf, ibid.

Emperor Henry II persuaded **Pope Benedict VIII** to order the Creed to be sung at Mass in the Roman Church, 562.

“Blessed is he who …,” etc., is found in the Greek liturgies, 282.

**Bernard**, king of Italy, 319 [Col. 1415].

**Bernharius**, bishop, sent to Rome by Charlemagne to question Pope Leo III about the procession of the Holy Spirit, 379.

**Beta** is the second letter of the Greek alphabet, 612. Some think it should be pronounced *vita*, ibid. The reason for this controversy is the reciprocal use among the ancients of *b* for *v* and *v* for *b*, ibid., 734. Why the Greeks express the consonant *v* in Latin by οῦ, ibid. Greek beta has the same force and pronunciation as Latin *B* and Hebrew *Beth*, ibid. The correct pronunciation of the second Greek letter is asserted, 613.

**Biaeothanati**, or **Biothanati**, or **Biathanati**, are those who died a violent death, 611.

The canonical punishment for drinking near a shrine, 467.

The **library of the chamber** was a library of sacred books in a chamber, or cell, situated beside the church of St. Peter, 274. St. Paulinus added one of the same kind to the basilica at Nola, 275.

**Birinus (St.)**, bishop of Dorchester, 484, 545, 557. A ring, a leaden cross, a small chalice, and other objects were found in his tomb, 484.

The church of Blachernae, 410.

**Βλατίον**, that is, a gold textile or a purple textile, 592.

**Blatta**, or **blata**, is a purple color, or a kind of exceptionally fine purple dye, 592. The purple-bearing Senate, ibid.

**Boniface (St.)**, Pope IV, after converting the Roman Pantheon into a church of St. Mary and All Martyrs, established the feast of St. Mary of the Martyrs, 392.

The anointing of the arms at the coronation of kings, 589.

A **brief** containing the ministries of the churches, ordinary silver, and whatever else is recorded, 433.

The office of **Briccius (St.)**, 835.

## C
Caecilia (Saint): her name is recited in the canon of the Mass, 4. The feast of Saint Caecilia, with vigil, is on the tenth day before the Kalends of December [22 November], 140, 713. Office of Saint Caecilia, 838.

Ceremonies are sacrifices, 283.

Caesarius (Saint), a martyr, African by nationality and a deacon by rank, suffered at Tarracina, 419. The feast of Saint Caesarius the martyr is on the Kalends of November [1 November], 138, 419, 712. Under which emperor he suffered, ibid.

Καὶ τῷ πνεύματί σοῦ, that is, “And to your spirit,” instead of “And with your spirit,” is found in the liturgies of the Apostles, 387.

Calandio, bishop of Antioch, added Χριστὲ βασίλιῦ, “Christ the King,” after Ἀθάνατος, “Immortal,” in the Trisagion, 282.

The chalice to be offered, with the admixture of the Eucharist, must be consecrated, 568. Form for blessing the chalice, 151. In the Roman Order, anointing with chrism is used for the blessing or consecration of the chalice; elsewhere it is not, 432. A cross is made with chrism upon the chalice, along its sides, ibid.

The chalice is lifted by the priest and deacon, together with the host placed upon the paten over the chalice, after the words “Through him,” etc., 582. What this ceremony signifies, 256, 582, 583. The lifting of the chalice in the Mass derives from ancient custom, 565. When and how it was formerly performed, ibid. The modern rite of lifting it after the consecration is not ancient, ibid.

Calixtus (Saint), both the first and the second pope, 532. The feast of Saint Calixtus the pope is on the day before the Ides of October [14 October], 135, 711.

Cambuta, or cambutta, is the bishop’s pastoral staff, 424. It is a curved staff and a support for the feet, or one by which the lame and weak are supported, ibid.

Caminata is used by the Gauls for “chimney,” [Col. 1416] 613.

A bell is a sign, a nola, or a clocca, 438. Order for blessing a bell, ibid. Bells are to be rung on the very day of the Lord’s Supper for Mass and the other hours, as is customary on feast days, 336. While the Gloria in excelsis is sung, the entire peal is sounded, ibid. Bells are not to be rung from the Lord’s Supper until Holy Saturday, ibid.

A candelabrum is called a ceroferarium and ceroferale, 493. It is also called a bearer of light, 221.

The twelve candles within a church being dedicated signify the twelve apostles, 423. Blessing of candles, 307, 308.

Candidus (Saint), martyr. See Mauricius (Saint), 416.

The canon of the Mass is a rule arranged for the consecration of the venerable Eucharist, 609. Why it is called the secret, ibid. It is also called the sacrifice, ibid. Why it is called the action, 283, 609. One should say intra actionem rather than infra actionem, 609.

The canon is the prayer beginning “Te igitur,” etc., composed by a certain scholastic, 282. Why it is called the canon, 283. The canon of the Mass published by Illyricus differs in many respects from the common one, 286. The canon is called the text of the canonical prayer, 572. Some divide the canon into five parts, others into fifteen, 609. It begins with “Te igitur,” etc., and ends at “Libera nos,” etc., ibid.

Canonical singers: who are so called, 323. Formerly not all clerics sang in the church, ibid. Singers or psalmists have a place among the clerical orders, 323. They have their own prescribed blessing, ibid. Singers are distinct from lectors, ibid. They are free to marry, ibid. They are forbidden, like subdeacons and lectors, to devote themselves to dice-playing and drunkenness, ibid. A lector or singer who has not fasted during Holy Lent, on Wednesday, or on Good Friday is to be deposed, ibid. They are taken from among the subdeacons and the other minor orders to form the school of singers, ibid. Certain things were formerly sung by other clerics and even by laypeople, such as “Kyrie eleison,” ibid.

The rite of ordaining a singer among the Greeks, 521. In Masses a singer begins nothing unless ordered by the bishop, 559.

The antiquity of ecclesiastical chant in the Church, 649. There are two methods of singing: in alternating turns and with united choirs, ibid. The method of singing instituted by Saint Gregory the Great was spread throughout the West by his disciples, 649; especially among the English, ibid., 650. The Gallican method of singing was conformed to the Roman under the care of Charlemagne, ibid. The reputation of the Metz Antiphonary’s restoration to the Roman method continued until the time of Saint Bernard, ibid. The care of the Cistercian Fathers for the authentic chant of the divine office, ibid.

Prayer for the cutting of boys’ hair when they were tonsured for the first time, 234, 533. The cutting of hair at the funerals of pagans, 476. The hair of penitents was sometimes vowed and sometimes cut, 450, 451.

Capitella are certain little verses, 480. Capitellum is also used for a collect or prayer, ibid.

The beginning of the Lenten fast, that is, the Wednesday of Quinquagesima, began in the Church after the time of Saint Gregory the Great, 315. On that Wednesday ashes were formerly imposed upon penitents, 316.

Anointing of the head in the ordination of a priest, 504; in the coronation of the kings of France, 589. In the case of the sick, how the anointing of the head is to be understood in extreme unction, 553.

No cleric stands in church with his head covered unless he is ill, 38, 316. Christians pray with uncovered heads, according to ancient custom; pagans, however, prayed with their heads covered and veiled, 317.

Cardinals are called at Rome deacons and priests from the titles, or churches, to which they are ordained and incardinated, 496.

Why those who eat the flesh of animals whose death they do not know are punished with canonical penalties, 468.

Blessing of meat, 565.

Pope Leo III anointed Charlemagne from the crown of his head to his feet, 589. He placed a crown upon him and clothed him in royal dress, 591. Anointed with holy oil by the bishops and having received viaticum, he died in peace, 536. What clothing, ornaments, and weapons he wore and with which he was buried, 484.

The emperor Charles the Bald was crowned a second time at Metz by Hincmar of Reims on the ninth of September, 556. In the Mass celebrated at his coronation, the first collect was “Quaésumus, pro rege”; the second was for Saint Gorgonius the martyr, ibid. He was anointed with chrism, 588. He was anointed on the right ear, on the forehead as far as the left side, and on the head, 589. He is called “Most Christian King,” 591. A crown was placed upon his head by the bishops, 592. The hymn “Te Deum” was solemnly sung in thanksgiving, 585. At his coronation a staff was not given to him, but a palm together with the scepter, 592.

Charles the Bald had previously been anointed king with sacred chrism at Orléans by Wenilo, archbishop of Sens, 587.

Carpophorus (Saint), martyr, 139, 412, 420. See the Four Crowned Martyrs.

The bishop of Carthage was ordained, according to the custom of the Catholic Church, by the neighboring bishops, 518.

Blessing of cheese, 565.

Cassianus (Saint), martyr of Forum Sempronii, 410.

Castorius (Saint), martyr, 139, 421, 608.

The chasuble, or planeta, is the priestly garment with which the priest is clothed at his ordination, 503. What it signifies, 557.

Κατάστασις means the ordination or establishment of a bishop already elected by the votes of the people, 511.

Catechumenus is interpreted as “one who hears,” “hearer,” or “instructed person,” 363, 374. Formerly there were two grades of catechumens: first, beginners; second, competentes, 374. The prayer of the catechumens is performed after the bishop’s sermon, and they are dismissed, 278. Catechumens were made by the sign of the cross, with which they were marked on their foreheads, 375, 527; and on the breast with a definite formula of words, 376. Hands were also laid upon them, with blowing upon their faces, ibid. Salt was put into the catechumen’s mouth, ibid. Satan was blown upon three times when the catechumen had turned toward the west, ibid. There were two forms of exsufflation: one performed by the catechumen, the other by the priest or clerics, ibid. Among the Greeks the priest blows three times into the catechumen’s face, 376. After the third exorcism the same priest blows into the catechumen’s mouth, upon the forehead, and upon the breast, ibid. Likewise, after the renunciation, the catechumen is ordered to blow upon and spit at Satan, ibid.

The first scrutiny of the catechumens was celebrated on the Wednesday of the third week of Lent, 48. The beginning, or imperfect, catechumens were instructed concerning certain matters, 374; concerning the matters in which the perfect, or competentes, were instructed, [Col. 1417] 375, 527. They were called competentes because they were seeking baptism, ibid. There is one sacrament of the catechumens, namely salt, 377.

A catechumen approaching the holy bath of regeneration is anointed, 331. Among the Latins the person to be baptized is anointed on the breast, shoulders, and between the shoulders, ibid. The Greeks anoint the whole body, ibid. Why catechumens are anointed, 339, 366, 367.

The catechumen, instructed through exsufflation and exorcism and freed from the evil spirit, begins, after receiving salt, to acquire a taste for the divine word, 364.

Catechumens were ordered to leave the Mass before the offering, 606. The penitence of catechumens lasted forty days, 380. This penitential custom was not the same everywhere, 381. See Those to Be Baptized.

The coronation of Catherine de’ Medici, wife of Henry II, king of the French, 595. Her head was anointed with oil, ibid.

The Chair of Saint Peter, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of March [17 February], 29, 665. “At Rome” is not added there, nor “at Antioch,” ibid., 311. The ancient observance of the Chair of Saint Peter, celebrated in February, is discussed, 311, 604. Formerly, on 22 February, the solemnity of both chairs was celebrated; later only the Antiochene observance remained, 312. The feast of Saint Peter’s Chair at Rome appears to be more recent, 29, 312. Paul IV established the office of this Chair, 604. In Gaul and Spain, before Paul IV’s decree, the feast of the Roman Chair was celebrated, 605. Formerly the Chair, or Episcopate, of Saint Peter was customarily celebrated in January in Gaul and in February at Rome, 662. From this arose the occasion for celebrating a double solemnity of the Chair of Saint Peter, ibid. Paul IV did not so much institute as restore the feast of the Roman Chair on 18 January, ibid.

The hundredfold fruit: what it signifies, 314. By what sign the number one hundred is reckoned, ibid.

Burning tapers placed on crosses, 435. Burning tapers carried in the procession of the Purification, 306. Tapers placed in the baptismal water, 349. Burning tapers carried before bishops, 347.

The blessing of the Paschal candle occurs before the readings of Holy Saturday, 344. The rite of blessing this candle, whether it belongs to Pope Zosimus or to someone else, is ancient, ibid. The mystical meanings of the Paschal candle, ibid. Various descriptions of the rite of blessing this candle, 345. By keeping pieces of the Paschal candle at home, Christians protected themselves against demonic attacks, 346. The custom of blessing the Paschal candle at Rome, having been interrupted, appears to have been restored by Pope Theodore, 347.

Cereostata are candelabra whose use is at the altars, 326, 517. Cereostata, that is, candle-bearers, 71, 347.

Cernuus properly means “inclined,” as though from looking at the earth, 315.

Ceroferarii are acolytes, so called from carrying candles, 493. It was an ancient custom of the Church that burning candles be carried before bishops, 347. Ceroferarium in the neuter is a candelabrum, 493.

Cervulus. “To lead the Cervulus,” or “to go to the Vetula” (Vicola, Vitola, or Vegula), is said of those who, assuming the forms of wild animals or cattle, roamed about with excessive wantonness, 472, 473. This was customarily done on the Kalends of January, ibid. What canonical penalties were imposed upon those who committed this crime, 467.

The magi who worshiped the infant Christ were descended from the sons of Cetura, 302.

Charaxatum, charaxatus, characatus, [Col. 1418] 615. Characo, that is, “I write,” is said from the word character, ibid.

King Charibert and Guntramnus, grandsons of Clovis, were consecrated by the bishops of their provinces, 584.

A chartophylax is one who possesses paper documents concerning ecclesiastical rights, 525. He is judge of all ecclesiastical cases, ibid. He hears matrimonial cases, ibid. He is defender in the other cases of clerics, ibid. He is, as it were, the right hand of the high priest, ibid.

Κειρόμακτρον, chiromactron, is the name for a linen cloth placed upon the shoulders with which they wiped their hands, 495.

Κειροτονία among the ancients means election; Κειροτονεῖν means “to choose someone for office,” 507. Κειροτονεῖν in Acts 14 means to establish a bishop by solemn rite and the laying on of hands, 508. Κειροτονία in the Fathers and in ecclesiastical matters signifies not election but ordination, ibid.

Κέρνιβον properly means a vessel of lustral water, 348. Κερνίψ signifies lustral water, ibid. Κερνιβόξεστον is a polished basin, 348.

Why Clotarius II, son of King Chilperic, received his name at the very time of baptism, 350.

Chorus sometimes signifies the whole assembly, whether ecclesiastical or lay, 277.

Chrismal, or chrismale, is a vessel in which the body of Christ is kept, 432, 468. It is also used for a corporal, or corporal cloth, ibid. Chrismale is also called a ministry, ibid. It is likewise called a chrismal Mass, 327.

Chrismation on the forehead, 358. It is distinct from the laying on of hands, 359. It was handed down by the apostles, ibid.

The blessing of chrism and oil takes place during the solemn celebration of Mass on the Lord’s Supper, 324, 325. Formerly bishops were free to prepare sacred chrism on any day, 325. Later the custom prevailed that it should be prepared only on the Lord’s Supper, ibid., 326. Chrism is not simple oil, but balsam is mixed with it, 326. Among the Greeks, the composition of chrism is a collection of fragrant substances, ibid. Thirty-six kinds of spices are mixed in chrism with wine and oil, ibid.

It is an ancient custom of the Church to bless and consecrate the sacred chrism, 330. This rite is traced back to the time of the apostles, ibid. The solemn rite of consecrating chrism and the oil of the catechumens, 338. Twelve priests serve as witnesses and assistants in the same mystery, ibid. The ampulla with chrism signifies the body of the Lord taken from the Virgin, 339.

It is an ancient custom to pour chrism into the baptismal font, 350. The people are forbidden to draw water that has already been infused with sacred chrism, ibid. According to ancient custom, chrism is poured into the baptismal water in the form of a cross, ibid. The Greeks, Orientals, and Ethiopians do this three times, ibid.

Christians are anointed with chrism because through baptism they become kings and priests, 370. The anointing with chrism performed by a priest on the crown of the head must not be confused with that performed by a bishop on the forehead, 385. The former is not a sacrament, 355, 386. The Fathers who wrote about the anointing with chrism before Pope Saint Sylvester are to be understood as referring to the anointing on the forehead, 385. The Greek Fathers are likewise to be understood as referring to that anointing, ibid. The Greeks lack the anointing performed on the crown of the head, ibid. The Latin Fathers sometimes speak of the anointing performed on the crown of the head, sometimes of the anointing by which heretics are reconciled, ibid. How it is to be determined which of these three anointings they are discussing, ibid.

The anointing with chrism is perfective, 360. It is performed in the form of a cross, ibid.

“Christe, eleison” was formerly said in the Mass as many times as “Kyrie, eleison,” 277. The Greeks do not say “Christe, eleison,” ibid.

Christians are named from Christ; Christ is named from chrism, 386.

Formerly Christians showed the greatest care in visiting the sick, 532.

The title “Most Christian” is proper and most ancient for the kings of the French, 591.

The feast of Saint Christopher the martyr, 407.

Christ increased in wisdom, age, and grace, 17, 303. Christ is called the flower of the virginal womb, 27. He was poured forth from the Virgin’s womb, 308. Christ assumed flesh in the womb of the blessed Virgin Mary, 31. In the womb of the blessed Virgin, God the Word united himself to human nature, 313.

What Christ’s weapons and warfare are, 367. The seven chief virtues, Christ’s saving works, opposed to the works of Satan, ibid.

The Spirit of the Lord rested upon Christ according to the whole fullness of divinity, 371. In Christ the effects of the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit were present, 373.

Christ was both the victim of his priesthood and the priest of his victim, 389. Christ was accustomed to raise his eyes toward heaven while giving thanks, 288. Christ is not the adopted Son of God, 365, 378. By his death our death was destroyed, 388.

Christ wished to become the minister of the Law, 24. Christ, by the singular example of humility, subjected himself to the Law, 308. Christ’s humanity gathers us, his humility raises us, and his tradition frees us, etc., 61, 320.

In Christ there is a composition of natures in the divine person, but not a mixture, 382.

Chrodegang, bishop of Metz, flourished in the time of Charles the Elder and King Pepin, 488. He conferred orders on the Saturdays of the four Ember seasons of the year, according to the custom of the Roman Church, ibid.

The feast of Chrysantus and Daria, holy martyrs, at Rome, on the third day before the Kalends of December [29 November], 422.

Chrysogonus (Saint), martyr: mention is made of him in the canon, 3. The feast of Saint Chrysogonus the martyr is on the eighth day before the Kalends of December [24 November], 142, 713.

A hairshirt is the garment of penitents, 450. A hairshirt is woven from the hair of kids and goats; what it signifies, ibid. A hairshirt is placed upon the sick person to be anointed, 537, 539. After the anointings have been performed and the sick person reconciled before communion, the hairshirt is removed, 550.

The origin of the rite of imposing ashes upon the heads of Christians on Wednesday at the beginning of the fast, 450. In antiquity the Roman people’s collect was held at Saint Anastasia, from which they proceeded to the station at Saint Sabina, 604, 667. Blessed ashes were imposed upon the heads of penitents, 449.

Alcuin mentions a girdle with which the bishop is girded over the alb, 556.

The feast of the Circumcision coincides with the eighth day of the Nativity of the Lord, 300. The ancient celebration of the Circumcision, ibid. The office of the Circumcision pertains for the most part to the blessed Virgin, 14. What the circumcision performed on the eighth day prefigures, 300, 301.

The coronation of Queen Claude, first wife of Francis I, 594. She was anointed with oil on the head, ibid.

Claudianus, brother of Mamertus, bishop of Vienne, 572.

The feast of Claudius (Saint), martyr, on the sixth day before the Ides of November [8 November], 139, 421, 608.

Claudius Nero, matricide, and another Claudius, emperors, 419.

Who ought to keep the keys of the Church, 489.

Clavus is purple sewn onto or woven into a garment, 325. Clavi are strips of purple formerly sewn onto the tunics of senators, ibid.

The feast of Clement (Saint), bishop and martyr, on the ninth day before the Kalends of December [23 November], 141, 713, 840. Saint Clement the pope is mentioned in the canon of the Mass, 3.

The agreement of clergy and people in the coronation of a king, 585.

Clerical dignity is conferred by the cutting of the hair, according to the ancient custom of the Roman Church, 213, 448. This is done before receiving any of the orders, ibid. Among the Greeks clerical tonsure is given in the ordination of a lector, ibid. See Tonsure.

No cleric stands in church with his head covered unless he is ill, 38, 316.

Formerly no cleric was a vagus, that is, one not assigned to a particular church or title, 496.

Cletus (Saint) is mentioned in the canon of the Mass, 3.

Clinici are those who, compelled by the severity of illness, received baptism while lying in bed, 377, 399. They were irregular and could not be enrolled among the clergy, ibid.

Clocca is a sign, nola, or bell, 438.

The name of Clodoaldus is recited in the prayer said after the Lord’s Prayer in the Mass, beginning “Libera nos,” etc., 4.

Why the infants Clodomer and Ingomer, sons of King Clovis, received their names at the very time of baptism, 350.

Clovis, the first Christian king of the Franks, was baptized on Christmas Day, 399. He was inaugurated and crowned by Saint Remigius, 584. He was anointed with oil fallen from heaven, 588. In the office of Saint Vedastus he is called Louis, 827.

Clotarius II, son of King Chilperic, received his name at the very time of baptism, 350.

The Lord’s Supper. On Thursday of Holy Week, why the hour for celebrating Mass is anticipated, 324. Nevertheless, the fast was not relaxed, ibid. Formerly many did not fast on the Lord’s Supper, according to the custom of their own church, ibid. On this day the oil and chrism are blessed, penitents are reconciled, and the feet are washed, ibid., 325. Three Masses are celebrated on the Lord’s Supper: the first for penitents, the second of the chrism, and the third in the evening, 327. In Africa two Masses are celebrated on this Thursday, the first in the morning and the second in the evening, 327. Three things were formerly sanctified by the bishop on the Lord’s Supper, 332. The rites formerly observed on the Lord’s Supper in the Church of Rouen, or Reims, 336.

Formerly, as now, the altars were stripped on the Lord’s Supper, 79, 342. The altars, walls, floors of the church, and sacred vessels were cleansed by washing on that Thursday or on Good Friday, 342, 343.

It was formerly an established custom of the Roman Church to reconcile penitents, 457. This reconciliation was customarily performed in the Mass immediately after the Gospel, 458. In ancient times penitents were absolved immediately before the Lord’s Prayer, ibid. “Ad mandatum”: antiphon and responsories, 877.

How God is said to compel us through fear without prejudice to the freedom of our will, 175, 444.

There is no good thought in a human being without God’s help, [Col. 1420] 174, 443. Therefore the Church rightly asks for the spirit of thinking what is right, ibid.

Collecta signifies the gathering of alms, 308. Collecta also signifies an assembly and synaxis for performing the divine office, ibid., 316, 397. A prayer for a procession, or collecta, 411, 413. The Latins are not accustomed to say a collect in the Mass between the Gospel and the offertory, whereas the Greeks say several, 562. The Latins did not agree with the Greeks, nor the Greeks among themselves, concerning the number and order of the collects to be said in the Mass, 278, etc. The collect for Saint Leo explained, 404. Collects interspersed among psalms, 486. Why it is called a collect, 604. Collects and stations formerly customarily held, ibid., 664.

Collyrium: in what sense the term is applied to the commixture of two substances in the one person of the Son of God, 382.

A dove suspended from the dome of a baptistery, 385. What the dove sent forth from the ark signifies, 330.

Commendatio is a prayer for the dead, 482. Commendatio is also called the office for the same dead, ibid.

“Venerable exchanges of the sacrifice”: in what sense they are so called, 182, 445.

The commixture of the body and blood of the Lord in the chalice is called consecration, 568.

“Communicantes,” etc., is said because the Church militant communicates with the Church triumphant, 285.

Formerly the people communicated during the three days of Easter, 333, 342. An ancient custom by which the celebrant communicates on Good Friday under the single species of bread, 341. It is clear that in the Rule of the Master the monks formerly communicated on that same Good Friday, 342. In Spain neither Mass nor communion was celebrated on that day, ibid. Formerly communion was not received in churches outside the solemn celebration of Mass, ibid.

Formerly the sacrament of the Eucharist was received together with baptism, 356. The faithful, clerics, and laypeople who were going to communicate at Mass each offered bread and wine for their own communion, 174, 443, 509, 563. To communicate without an offering means to attend the entire Mass with the faithful but without receiving the Eucharist, 474.

The bishop gives communion according to ancient custom, 569. This custom was not universal, ibid. Deacons sometimes gave communion to the faithful, ibid.

Communion was customarily given on Sundays, 605. Daily communion, 606. The prayer over the people in place of communion, ibid. In antiquity only those who communicated used to remain for the divine mysteries, 606. Catechumens and penitents who were not going to communicate were ordered to leave before the offering, ibid.

Communion of the sick after extreme unction, 539, 542, 550, 553, 554.

Communion in one’s own home with the Eucharist received in church, 578. Various formulas for giving communion, 579.

Communion given with a dry sacrifice: what it is, 247, 569. Communion given with a mixed sacrifice, that is, with the body of Christ mixed with his blood, ibid. Many decrees prohibit giving the body of Christ dipped in the sacred blood, ibid., 583. The body and blood of the Lord are to be received separately, ibid., 256. The mixed species may be given together if some necessity or precaution intervenes, ibid., 583. The body of the Lord dipped in the sacred blood is given to a very weak sick person in a spoon, 570.

At communion a psalm was formerly sung, ibid. The bishop gives the body of the Lord into the hands of the priests and deacons who are going to communicate, according to the ancient custom of the Church, 578. Subdeacons receive it in the mouth, ibid. In the earliest times of the Church all the faithful placed the body of Christ, once received, into their mouths with their hands, ibid. The positioning of the hands for receiving the body of the Lord, ibid. Men received it with bare hands; women received it with a linen cloth placed beneath, ibid. They either immediately placed the body of Christ in their mouths or carried it home to communicate there, ibid. When, where, and for how long this custom prevailed in the Church, 579. Those who communicate at home on the same day after nocturnal intercourse, even if lawful, are censured, ibid.

The ancient formula used among the Fathers was this: the minister, offering the Eucharist, said, “The body of Christ”; the recipient answered, “Amen,” 580.

All the joints of the limbs are anointed in extreme unction, 541.

Competentes are catechumens of the second grade, 574. The Creed was handed over to the competentes on Palm Sunday, 378. The handing over of the Creed is an exposition of the mysteries contained in it, ibid. On that same Sunday the competentes gave their names and were required to undergo scrutiny, 379. With what rites and laborious offices this examination was customarily conducted, ibid. What it means for the competentes to be created on Palm Sunday, 380. The competentes performed penance, some for forty days, others for thirty, ibid. During these days the competentes confessed all the sins of their past life, 381. See Catechumens, Those to Be Baptized, Confession.

A priest to be ordained must know the computus together with the cycle, 273. The method of counting on the fingers, 314.

The conclusion of a prayer is made through the Son because he is the Mediator of God and human beings, etc., 295.

A non-martyr holy virgin is called a confessa, 440.

Confessio signifies a hollowed-out place in an altar in which the bishop deposits the relics of the saints, 435. Confessio in the rite of consecrating a pope is a tabernacle decorated with varied workmanship in which the bodies of the holy apostles rest, 518.

The confession of sins made by the competentes was not sacramental, 381. Various confessions of penitents encompassing many sins that could scarcely be found in a single person, 452. A formula of confession attributed to Saint Fulgentius—whether Fulgentius of Astigi or of Ruspe—ibid., 454. Observations on this formula, 451. The formula of confession for monks, 454. These confessions of sins in detail were customarily preceded by another confession according to the number and proper circumstances of the sins, 455, 553. The custom formerly prevailed in the Church of confessing one’s sins individually and not indiscriminately, 456, 544, 553.

Confessio is called celer, that is, prompt, ready, devout, 461. A penitent must not be compelled to confess the same sins again, 463. Confession preceding extreme unction, 540, 547. No one except bishops and priests ought to hear confessions, just as no one except they ought to offer the sacrifice, 463. If necessity arises and a priest is absent, let the deacon receive the penitent for holy communion, ibid. The priest who is going to hear the penitent’s confession should first say a prayer, ibid.

Confessors are those who, having survived tortures for the faith of Christ, undergo a peaceful death, 303, 411. The Church also calls confessors men distinguished by piety, holiness, and miracles, who have died peacefully in Christ, 439. The name confessor was also given to holy women, for example Saint Leocadia, 440.

Singers and psalmists are called confessors, 322. To confess is to sing the praises of God, ibid.

Confirmation was formerly given by the bishop immediately after baptism, 357, 385. The rite of giving confirmation, 73, 357. The bishop does not give the Holy Spirit but prays that he may come upon those upon whom he lays hands, 358.

This sacrament has two rites: the laying on of hands and the anointing of the forehead with chrism, 359, 507. Sometimes the laying on of hands was performed after the anointing, ibid. The minister of this sacrament is the bishop, 358, 359. Priests may anoint the baptized with chrism consecrated by the bishop, but they may not sign their foreheads with the same chrism, 358, 361, 371.

The apostles used anointing with chrism and the laying on of hands to confirm the baptized, 359. This rite of chrismation and signing is called a sacrament, as is baptism itself, 360. According to the ancient custom of the Church, the anointing with chrism is performed on the forehead in the form of a cross, ibid.

Formerly the Greeks anointed not only the forehead but also the ears, nostrils, and breast, 361. They anointed all the limbs, but the forehead three times, ibid. The Ethiopians anoint all the limbs when confirming, ibid. Today the Greeks anoint the forehead, eyes, nostrils, mouth, ears, breast, hands, and feet, ibid.

What the form of this sacrament is, or whether there formerly was any form, 361, 362. What this form is among the Greeks, ibid.

Priests may anoint the baptized with chrism, but they may not impart the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands, 370, 371. This custom of the Church was handed down by the apostles, ibid. A priest did not anoint on the crown of the head one baptized and confirmed by a bishop, 385.

The sacrament of confirmation perfects the Christian person, 386. How great is the dignity, usefulness, and necessity of this sacrament, ibid. Those who neglect to receive this sacrament when they can commit a grave sin, ibid. Bishops commit a still graver sin if they do not use every diligence so that those entrusted to them may receive this sacrament, ibid.

The distinction between the anointing performed on the forehead and that performed on the crown of the head, 386.

The form of this sacrament: “I confirm and sign you with the sign of the cross, in the name of the Father,” etc., 646. “Whose forehead we have anointed with sacred chrism and confirmed with the sign of the cross,” etc., ibid.

Conon the monk, while discharging the office of baptizing, was divinely freed from a grave temptation that afflicted him, 332.

The form of the consecration of the chalice is ancient and excellent, 3, 288. Formerly, in certain places, the words of consecration were pronounced in a loud and clear voice, and the choir and people answered “Amen,” 577.

Consecration is called the commixture of the body and blood of the Lord in the chalice, 568. The office of consecration means the liturgical office completed through fraction, commixture, and communion, 256, 583. Whether the consecration of the body and blood should be entrusted to the deacon, 500. Whether in Saint Ambrose one should read “consecration” or “distribution,” ibid.

Counsel restrains one from acting rashly and fills the mind with reason, 372. Counsel is useful to one who lacks the strength of fortitude, ibid.

Consistentia is the fourth grade of penitents, who shared in prayer with the faithful but not in the Eucharist, 461.

Constantinople was freed from calamities after the Trisagion was sung, 282. What observance of Lent formerly prevailed at Constantinople, 316.

Constantine the Great was baptized on Pentecost, [Col. 1422] 398. He built a church in Jerusalem, 432. At the dedication of this church the bishops consecrated for its use all the gifts offered by the faithful, ibid. The anniversary of this dedication was customarily celebrated splendidly every year for eight days, 438. The dead body of Constantine the Great, adorned with purple clothing and a diadem, was enclosed in a golden coffin and buried, 483.

The law of Constantine Porphyrogenitus concerning those married four times, 476.

The Arian emperor Constantius ordered Felix II, who had been removed from the see because of the Catholic faith, to be beheaded, 408.

Many additions were made to the Apostolic Constitutions, 277.

Contacium signifies a tome or volume containing ordinations, 524. It is also a certain kind of song, ibid. Some hold contacium to be the liturgy recited by a priest newly ordained, 522, 524.

Contact between the chalice and paten in the ordination of a priest, without contact with the host, is sufficient, 508. Someone accepts, through contact with the vessels, what is contained in the vessels, ibid.

Contact of the nostrils and ears, 366, 381.

Contestata is the name given to the preface that precedes the canon, 294, 417. It is also called contestatio and sometimes immolatio, ibid.

Contraratio sanctorum denotes lots, or counterfeit forms of saints’ lots, made through sacred books, 473. What canonical penalties are imposed for this crime, 467.

Cornelius and Cyprian, holy martyrs, are mentioned in the canon of the Mass, 3. On the day of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross is the feast of Saints Cornelius and Cyprian, bishops and martyrs; it is the day of their passion, 129, 415, 710. Their feast was later transferred to the sixteenth day before the Kalends of October [16 September], 416. The six weeks following the feast of Saint Cyprian take their name from him, 129. The proper Mass of Saint Cyprian, 416.

The clerical crown, 448. See Clerical Dignity, Clerical Tonsure.

The Christian emperors and kings wished to be crowned by sacred pontiffs in the Church with solemn rite, 583. By what rite the emperor of Constantinople is crowned, 591. This emperor formerly placed upon the empress’s head a crown blessed by the bishop, 595. In the West the bishop places a crown upon the queen’s head, ibid.

The apostles, evangelists, and bishops were crowned until the time of Tertullian, 558. Pagan priests were crowned during sacred rites, ibid.

The feast of the Four Crowned Martyrs is on the sixth day before the Ides of November [8 November], 139, 712. A church of the Four Crowned Saints exists in the City, 608. Pope Honorius built it; Leo IV restored it, ibid. The names of the Four Crowned Martyrs are Severus, Severianus, Victorinus, and Carpophorus, ibid., 420, 421, 608. Their names were long unknown, ibid. Five other martyrs are venerated together with them, ibid.

Corporals, 431. See Chrismal.

How we become the body of Christ, 310. The conversion of bread and wine into the body and blood of Christ takes place through the force of the words of both formulas, 287. The Church confesses that Christ was truly born from the Virgin Mother in our bodily nature, 299. The body of Christ is brought to perfection through the infusion of the Holy Spirit, 27. To the Holy Spirit ...

The ancients attribute the production of Christ’s body and blood in the Eucharist, 309. Each person receives the whole body [Col. 1423] of Christ through communion, 27, 310. In each portion of the host, Christ is wholly present, ibid. By receiving communion, we become one body of Christ, 27, 310. Christ’s body is not consecrated on Good Friday of Holy Week, 333. It is the custom of the Roman Church that the presbyters, together with the celebrating pontiff, consecrate the body and blood of the Lord simultaneously by word and by hand, 337. Christ’s body was given into the hands of presbyters and deacons, 578; and to all Christians, ibid. It was once customary for the sacred body of Christ, which they call the Eucharist or the offering, to be placed upon the bishop’s breast in the tomb, 484. The councils did not condemn this custom, 485. The councils forbade that the Eucharist be placed in the mouths of the dead for the sake of communion, ibid. Saint Benedict ordered that the Lord’s body be placed upon the breast of a deceased monk as a sign of reconciliation, ibid. “The Body of Christ” is said by the priest when he gives communion, 580.

—The bodies of dead Christians were embalmed with aromatics, 483. They were carried into the tomb with singing, 485. The feast of Cosmas and Damian is observed on the fifth day before the Kalends of October [27 September], 134, 711, 825. They are mentioned in the canon of the Mass, 3. King Chosroes of Persia, among the gifts he sent to the Church of Saint Sergius the martyr, gave a golden censer in gratitude for the child received through the latter’s intercession, 429. He also gave a Hunnic veil adorned with gold, 435. All creatures are summoned to praise God in the preface of the Mass, 280. Crescentia (Saint), 402. The office of Saints Crispin and Crispinian, with three nocturns, 829. Round wafers were forbidden for the Eucharist, 564.

The true cross of Christ was recognized through miracles, 391. The Exaltation, elevation, and adoration of the holy cross, 415. On Good Friday the bishop presented the true cross of Christ to the people for adoration, 341. Once a year, when the Lord’s Pascha is celebrated, the true cross of Christ is revealed, ibid. The Resurrection makes known the Lord’s cross, 391. Christ’s triumph—that is, Christ’s cross—could not be obliterated, ibid. The four dimensions of the cross are explained, ibid. The immersion of the cross in water, 302.

—Crosses and candles in a solemn procession are called radiant, 435. Saint John Chrysostom devised silver crosses on which wax candles were placed, ibid. A leaden cross was found in a tomb, 459. A cross made of ash and water was placed upon the breast of a sick person, 539, 544, 553. Crosses made with chrism on the walls of a church, 430. Crosses used in the consecration of an altar, ibid.

—The Exaltation of the Holy Cross, 128, 709. The feast of the Exaltation of the holy cross began after its discovery, during the reign of Constantine the Great, 415. See Discovery of the holy cross.

—The adoration of the holy cross takes place at vespers, after the prayers, 69. An oblong carpet, resembling a stole, was spread out for those who were to adore the cross, 340. It was an ancient custom to adore the cross on Good Friday, 341. The rite for adoring the cross, ibid. Formerly, on the very day of the Exaltation of the holy cross, near the end of the Mass, the pontiff raised the cross so that it might be adored by the people, 415. Near the end of the Mass there is a prayer for greeting the cross, ibid. The width of the cross, etc., 392.

—Offerings are blessed with the sign of the cross, according to an ancient custom of the Church, 287. Basilicas and altars are dedicated [with it], ibid., 428, 429. How the sign of the cross should be made when blessing, ibid. It is an ancient custom of the Church that baptismal water be blessed by the sign of the cross [Col. 1423], 349. Extreme Unction is administered while making the sign of the cross, 548. What the sign of the cross with the host signifies, 582. The sign of the cross was used in ordinations, 515. Water is blessed with the sign of the cross, 533.

Cubicularii were called the guardians of the bodies of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, 274. What a cubiculum is, 274. Saint Cucufas suffered martyrdom at Barcelona in Spain. His feast is celebrated on the eighth day before the Kalends of August [25 July], 407. From the first prayer of the Mass it is evident that the holy martyr was tortured by a conflagration of flames, 408. The account of his martyrdom, ibid. His body was later transferred to the monastery of Saint Denis near Paris, ibid. “With whom is honor,” etc., was added to the Lord’s Prayer, 291. Saint Cuthbert, bishop of Lindisfarne, 545. In his Mass he is called a martyr, 313. His death and funeral rites, 484. His body was raised from the tomb; the offering—that is, the Eucharist—was found upon his holy breast, ibid. It [the body] was clothed in priestly vestments, etc., ibid. The feast of Saint Cyprian, bishop and martyr, 129, 415, 710. He is mentioned in the canon of the Mass, 3. See Cornelius. Cyriacus the martyr, 4, 118, 705. Saint Cyril the martyr, 392. Saint Cyrinus the martyr, 105, 700.

# D

Dacius, bishop of Milan, wrote no chronicle, 586. He flourished during the reign of the emperor Justinian, ibid. The myrtle crown of the Daduchi, 558. *Daduchus*, that is, “torchbearer,” ibid. By what power of exorcists demons are expelled from human bodies, 492. Pagans were sometimes seen, through certain deceptive incantations, to drive demons from human bodies, ibid. The dalmatic is a white priestly vestment with purple bands, 325. Description of the dalmatic, ibid. The priest’s prayer when putting on the dalmatic, ibid. The dalmatic was the vestment of bishops and deacons, ibid. Damian (Saint). See Cosmas. Food placed upon tombs, 311. Daria (Saint). See Chrysantus, 422.

It was said that the tithe of the year was offered to God by the fast of Lent, 315. On the tenth day a name was given to children among the Greeks, 350. Dedication of the basilica of Saint Mary at the Martyrs, 694. At Rome, the dedication of the first church built and consecrated by the blessed apostle Peter, 409. Order for dedicating a church, 145, 423. Night office of the feast of the Dedication, 145. The threefold circuit of the church to be dedicated, with the sprinkling of blessed water, 424. The pontiff impresses twelve crosses with his thumb on the inner circuit of the church and anoints them with chrism, 430. Mass of the dedication, 152, 436. All basilicas are to be dedicated with a Mass, 437. Formerly the feast of the dedication was celebrated for eight days, 438, 153. The anniversary of the dedication of a basilica, according to ancient custom, is celebrated for eight days, 154, 438. It is an ancient institution of the Church that basilicas be dedicated by the bringing in and depositing of holy relics, 434. A bishop who consecrates a temple without holy relics is to be deposed, ibid.

The bodies of the dead were customarily washed, according to the ancient custom of Christians, 482. They were also anointed, 483. They were wrapped in white linen, 484. Deceased [Col. 1424] bishops were clothed in priestly or pontifical vestments, ibid. The lifting of the corpse with singing, 485. See *Anointing*, *To be anointed*.—Office for the dead, 478. Prayer for the faithful departed was always a concern of the Church in the liturgical Mass, 289, 577. Those who are called the souls of the faithful departed sleep in the sleep of peace, ibid. Why, in the canon, the remembrance of the faithful departed is followed by “and all who rest in Christ,” etc., 290. Masses for the dead, and prayers for their repose, together with funeral rites and almsgiving for their refreshment, 215, 478. Masses for the dead were in use before the time of Charlemagne, 572. See *Mass*, *Funeral rites*.

Clerics who have been degraded lose their rank only with respect to the ability to minister in that order and with respect to clerical communion, 501. They are restored to their ranks by receiving what they had received at ordination, ibid. Catholic bishops degraded and deprived of honor by the Donatists, who shaved their heads, 515. External offenses, that is, alien offenses, opposed to each person’s own offenses, 46, 317. To make a person demented is to disturb his imaginative power so that he thinks himself to be an animal, 473. Whoever, through invocation of demons, has taken away a person’s mind is to be punished by what canonical penalty, 467.

## Deus

Formerly, in the conclusion of the collects, *Deus* (“God”) was immediately added to the verb *regnat* (“reigns”), 293. “You, Triune Godhead,” is said in the office of All Saints, 832.

The *devotae* are virgins dedicated and consecrated to God, 442. *Devotion*, that is, the resolve and firm will to serve God perpetually, 441.

The devil, who had conquered Adam in fragile flesh, was himself conquered by God in the flesh assumed, 27. The devil is renounced by the faithful, so that the Lord may be served more freely, 367. Why those being baptized renounce the works of the devil, ibid. What the devil’s weapons and warfare are, ibid. The seven principal vices with which the devil assails human beings are called the works of Satan, ibid., 384. What is meant by the worship of the devil that is renounced in baptism, 383.

*Diacon* is the nominative form, from which *diaconum*, that is, “of deacons,” is derived. *Diaconibus*, etc., 564. How great is the honor of the diaconate, and how great the dignity of this order, 499. It is priestly in the third degree, 519. Its functions, 500. *Diaconica* are certain verses that we call prayers, which are sung by deacons, 523. At the ordination of a bishop, the *diaconica* are said by bishops, ibid. At what point in the Mass the deacon is ordained, 487. When the deacon is ordained, why only the bishop lays hands upon him, 223, 498, 500. Several old codices prescribe that, at the ordination of a deacon, hands are to be laid on him by the bishop and by the priests standing around, ibid. The ordination of a deacon according to the Greeks, 521. What is meant by saying that the consecration of the Lord’s body and blood was entrusted to the deacon, 500. Formerly the book of the Gospels was not presented to the deacon, ibid. According to ancient custom, deacons read the Gospel at Mass, 501. This custom did not always prevail, nor everywhere in the Church, ibid. An unjustly degraded deacon recovers his lost rank through the stole and alb, ibid. Formerly a custom had arisen in Gaul whereby the hands of deacons were anointed with chrism at ordination, 501. The deacon is called a priest of the third order, 519. The stole is placed around his left shoulder at his ordination, 521. The formula [Col. 1425] that the bishop then pronounces, 223. The fan is presented to the deacon, ibid., 523.

In the time of Saint Justin, deacons presented holy communion to the faithful, 569. The Council of Nicaea judged it absurd for deacons to present communion to priests, ibid. A deacon is forbidden to distribute the Eucharist to the people when a priest is present, except in urgent necessity, ibid. In necessity and in the absence of a priest, a deacon ought not to receive a penitent for confession of sins, but may receive him for holy communion, 463, 470, 630. Among the Greeks, deacons in the sacred rites admonish the people to pray, 321. The deacon formerly cried, “Arise,” 321. It is the deacon’s duty to admonish the people to humility, 567.

Formerly *diadem* was said; now it is called *stemma*, 592. What a diadem is, ibid. A *stemma* is not altogether the same as a diadem, ibid. The days on which virgins are veiled, 440. The day on which sinners are reconciled, 457. Bigamists marked by the Church, 476.

“It is worthy and just.” From these words Saint Augustine infers that we ought to refer all things received back to God, 280. *Dignus* (“worthy”), by what rite it is sung by the Greeks at the ordination of a deacon and priest, 521, 522. This word is also proclaimed at the coronation of the emperor, ibid., 591. “I forgive you your sins”: an ancient form of absolution, 459.

The names of Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius (Saints) are recited in the canon of the Mass, 285. They are also mentioned in the prayer that follows the Lord’s Prayer and begins “Deliver us,” etc., 4. On the seventh day before the Ides of October, the vigil of Saints Dionysius, etc., 711, 827. Their feast, ibid.; on the eighth day before the Kalends of November, their octave, 419.—The feast of Dionysius (Saint), martyr, on the fourth day before the Ides of February, 310.

A *diploma* is called a letter issued by a prince and folded, 603. Papal bulls and letters patent, because they are doubled, are called diplomas and diptychs, ibid. Diptychs are tablets with two folds, 289, 601. Sacred diptychs are tablets on which the names of the living and the dead were written for recitation at Mass, ibid. The custom of diptychs in the Church is very ancient, 601. The ancient Fathers mention these tablets, 601. So too do ancient liturgies and councils, 602.—Diptychs, or a *diptychion*, were tablets made of any material, on which images of the Fathers were placed in their catalogue, 602. *Diptychum* means “doubled,” ibid. The double shells of oysters are elegantly called a *diptychum*, 603. Among the ancients there were pentaptychs, triptychs, etc., and writing tablets, ibid. The two stone tablets of Moses were called a stone diptychion, ibid.

*Distrahere* sometimes means “to sell,” 327. Whoever practices divination, because it is demonic, is to do penance for five years, three of them on bread and water, 467. Communion formerly received at home, 578. The burning of a house: what penalty was imposed for it by the canons, 467, 474.

Why the Second Sunday in Lent is said to be vacant, 43. Why the office of this Sunday is not read, although collects and other prayers belonging to the Mass are assigned, 672. The twenty-seventh Sunday after Pentecost, 186. Elsewhere the twenty-fourth after Pentecost. Elsewhere, 25. After the Octave of Pentecost, etc., 185. Sunday is sometimes called the day of the Lord’s Resurrection, 487, 488. The twenty-eighth Sunday [Col. 1425] after Pentecost is followed by the fifth Sunday before the Nativity of the Lord, 636. The First Sunday before the Nativity of the Lord is called the Sunday that immediately precedes the Nativity of the Lord, 637. Sunday in the *Alibi*, 390. Palm Sunday, 60, 318. The order of the Sundays before Advent, 186, 445.

“The Lord be with you,” 327.

Domitilla (Saint), 392.

## Dona

What distinction is made between “these gifts,” at the beginning of the canon of the Mass, and offerings and sacrifices, 283. “The gifts of the Holy Spirit,” that is, the Holy Spirit, 398. The gifts of the Holy Spirit are conferred in a special and excellent manner through the sacrament of confirmation, 386.

Mass of Donatus (Saint), bishop, 410. Donatus, a pseudo-martyr, and Marculus were venerated by the Donatists, 285. The Donatists laid sacrilegious hands upon the heads of bishops, shaving them in order to remove the chrism, 515.

Every good gift is from God, 443. What it means for the souls of the faithful departed to sleep in the sleep of peace, 289. The Dormition of the holy Virgin Mary, 411, 707. See *Assumption*.

*Δωδεκαήμερον*—that is, “a period of twelve days”—is the span of twelve days between the Nativity of the Lord and his Epiphany, 302. These days were formerly free from fasting, ibid.

The Druids excluded the profane from sacred rites, 452. The feast of Dunstan (Saint), 104, 393. Why the number twelve is called sacred, 312. Durandus’s opinion concerning the presentation of the book of the Gospels at the ordination of a deacon, 500.

## Dux

The form of the oath to be pronounced by a duke when he is installed, 594.

# E

Ebbo, archbishop of Rheims, was restored amid resounding signs while the hymn *Te Deum* was being sung, 585. A miracle at Ebredunum concerning the baptistery, customarily occurring every year at the Nativity of the Lord and on the Lord’s Supper, 399.

Drunkenness, whether it occurs among laypeople or among those who have undertaken a vow of holiness, is punished by canonical penalties, 468. The Church is said to have been founded in the patriarchs, 312, 605. It is also said to have been prepared in the prophets and established in the apostles, 29, 605. It was prefigured by Noah’s ark, 330. The Church is quickened by the washing of baptism, 368. The Church was formed from the side of Christ sleeping on the cross, ibid., 384. It is fitting that the Church, which is Christ’s body, should be a kingdom and a priesthood, 270. The children of the Church, regenerated in it, are likewise kings and priests, ibid. What the duties of the kings and priests of whom the Church consists are, ibid. It was given by God to the Church that, like a vine, it should grow amid adversity, 177, 444.
