The impious and wicked are excluded from the Church, the temple, sacred rites, and the common society of human beings, according to the ancient custom of the Church, 451. A church sanctified by the sprinkling of blessed water, 425. It was the custom of the Romans that those polluted by nocturnal intercourse, even when lawful, did not enter the church on the following day, 579. Churches facing east, 329. The protopope of a church, 524.

Judith, daughter of Charles the Bald, married Æthel­wulf, king of the English, 590.

*Εἰρήνη πᾶσιν*, that is, “peace to all,” 326. *Εἰρηνικά*, that is, “peaceful things,” also called *diaconica*, are certain verses sung by deacons, 523. *Εἰς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων*, that is, “for ages of ages,” 294.

The election of bishops is distinguished from their ordination, 507. Formerly the election was made by [Col. 1426] clergy and people, and the ordination by three bishops, 508. The elections of the bishops Siderius, Antonius, and Nilammon are distinguished from their ordinations, ibid. In Acts 6, “to choose” and “to lay hands upon” are different, ibid. Formerly the elections of bishops in Gaul were made by the votes of the clergy and people, 511. The authority of the king was required and then often weakened the elections, ibid. Elections were abolished by concordats, ibid. The nomination of bishops belonged to the king, while confirmations through concordats belonged to the supreme pontiff, ibid. In time, the elections of bishops in the other kingdoms of the Western Church became nearly the same as those in Gaul, 511. Among the Greeks, elections made by neighboring bishops continue, with the votes of clergy and people excluded, ibid. This discipline was not established by the First Council of Nicaea, ibid. Many examples of elections by clergy and common people after that council are reported, 512. The Council of Laodicea excluded only the votes of the lowest class of people from elections, ibid.

The Lord the pope gives alms on the Saturday before Palm Sunday, which is therefore vacant, 59. On Saturday leavened bread is given in the Lateran consistory, ibid. The coronation of Eleonor, queen and second wife of Francis I, 595. She was anointed with oil on the head, ibid.

The baptism and absolution of a certain Elias, found in his tomb, 459. Elig(ius) (Saint) is mentioned in the canon of the Mass, 4, 285. The Sacramentary of Saint Eligius. See Preface.

Elipandus, bishop of Toledo, and Felix of Urgell defended, against the faith, the claim that Christ was the adoptive Son of God, 378. Elisabeth (Saint), wife of Louis, landgrave of Thuringia, after receiving extreme unction, received the viaticum of the Lord’s body from bishops, 536. What Elisha’s curing of the barrenness of water by casting in salt signifies, 364. Elpidophorus, deserter from the faith, 355.

An *embolus* is something inserted or interposed, 337. Emerentiana (Saint), foster-sister of Saint Agnes, 22. Her feast is recorded on the tenth day before the Kalends of February, 305.

The *energumens*, for whom the first prayer was formerly made at Mass among the Greeks, 278. See *Exorcists*.

*Enherber*, that is, “to kill someone with poison,” 478. *Enim* is sometimes used in place of “indeed” or “but,” 237, 537. The feast of Eormenhild (Saint), on the fourth day before the Ides of February, 310.

An *ephestris* is an outer garment, which is called by the Greeks *φαινόλης* (*phainolēs*), or *phenolium*, 523. *Ephphatha* was said at the touching of the ears, 366. Epimachus (Saint), 694.

*Ἐπινίκιος ὕμνος*, that is, “the hymn of victory,” is the *Sanctus*: “Holy, holy,” etc., 281.

Epiphania, daughter of the emperor Heraclius, was crowned by Sergius, patriarch of Constantinople, in the palace chapel, 584.—The feast of the Epiphany is celebrated in January according to an ancient rite, 302, 661. The Epiphany is the Incarnation, or dispensation, of our Savior Jesus Christ, ibid. At the fountains, the solemn blessing of water by immersion of the cross, ibid. In ancient times the custom prevailed in many places of baptizing on the Epiphany, 398. See *Theophany*.

Episcopal blessings, 625. The episcopate is called the supreme priesthood, 225, 514. The honor of the episcopate, 499. *Ἐπίσκοπος* means “overseer,” “chief overseer,” “watcher,” or “guardian,” 509. For this reason he sits in the church on a higher throne, 254, 340, 581. The pride of certain bishops, who sit in the church in the manner of kings, is condemned, 340. It was an ancient custom of the Church that burning candles be carried before bishops, 347. Formerly a bishop used to baptize and immediately confer the sacrament of confirmation upon those baptized, 385. Bishops are called supreme pontiffs, 502. At their ordination bishops kneel on both knees, 525. The ordination of a bishop according to the Greeks, 522. A bishop is clothed in a dalmatic, 325. It belongs to a bishop to present the Eucharist, 569, and to consecrate virgins, 167, 440. He is called the guardian of sacred virgins, 509.

*Ἐπίσκοπος* is one who presides over bread and other things offered for sale, 509. The prefect and guardian of a city was called an *episcopus*, ibid. Among Christians, the bishop is the one who presides over divine and sacred matters in each city, ibid. Form of the petition presented by clergy and people to the king and archbishop on behalf of an elected bishop, 509. Form of the promise to be made by an elected bishop, 510. When a bishop receives the staff, he is admonished to exercise judgment without anger even in anger, 511. Rite of ordaining a bishop, ibid. The rite of placing the book of the Gospels upon the head of a bishop at his ordination is most ancient, 512. What this rite signifies, ibid., 513. The book of the Gospels is placed upon him by bishops, ibid. How many bishops ought to assemble for the ordination of one bishop, 513. The ordination of a bishop is judged invalid if it was not performed by three bishops, ibid. Whether the bishops present ought to touch the head of the bishop being ordained with their hands, ibid. The anointing of the head at the ordination of a bishop is performed according to ancient custom, 515. Other anointings of the bishop—the hands, the right thumb, and a repeated anointing of the head—according to various codices, 516. The ordination of a bishop ought to take place on Sunday, 517. A bishop is a priest of the first order, 519. The ordaining bishop gives the one ordained a whole offering, that is, a consecrated host, of which he communicates upon the altar, 518. From this he reserves a portion for his own communion during the following forty days, ibid. What this host, to be consumed in portions by the bishop who has been ordained, signifies, 519. Formerly, once the consecration had been completed, the bishop was solemnly enthroned in the episcopal seat, 520.

Formerly a prophetic reading preceded the reading of the Epistle, 560. It is an ancient custom to read the epistles of the apostles, especially those of Saint Paul, at Mass after the prayers, 278. Formerly the Epistle was not read, just as the Gospel is not now read, except at the command of the bishop or the celebrating priest, 561. Formerly the Epistle was read at Mass by lectors, 491.—Formerly the book of the Epistles was not given to the subdeacon at his ordination, 496, nor did it belong to his duty to read the Epistle at Mass, ibid.

*Ἐπιτραχήλιον* is the *orarium*, that is, the stole given to priests at their ordination, 503. *Ἐπιτραχήλιον* is so called because it is arranged around the neck, ibid. A priest is forbidden to celebrate Mass or to communicate without the stole hanging from his neck, ibid.

One who has strayed from his way must be brought back under penalty of excommunication, 469, 476. “And,” a conjunction placed before the baptismal formula, 352. “And with your spirit”: this is the people’s response [Col. 1427], according to the ancient rite of the Church, in which the people return a blessing to the pontiff who has blessed them, 387.

Eteocles and Polynices, when they sacrificed, were accustomed to send their father Oedipus the shoulder of the victim as to a king, 589.

The consecration of the Eucharist takes place through the force of the words of both formulas, 287. Why the paschal sacrament of Christ’s body and blood is called an eternal remedy, 317. Formerly the sacrament of the Eucharist was received together with baptism, 73, 356, 384. These two sacraments are signified by the blood and water that flowed from Christ’s side, 384. Formerly the Eucharist was given to the sick after extreme unction, 536, 554. The consecration of the Eucharist was performed simultaneously by the pontiff and the priests, 337. Formerly the Eucharist was placed into the hands, 578. Penitents in the fourth degree of penance were not admitted to participation in the Eucharist, 461. Once this degree had been completed, they were restored to participation in the Eucharist, ibid. If, through negligence, the sacrifice falls to the ground, a *superpositio* is to be observed, 468. See *Superpositio*. If, through the same negligence, the person loses it and someone devours it, he is to do penance for forty days, ibid.

*Εὐχή*, that is, “a vow,” or “the prayer that we make for a vow,” 284. The empress Eudocia received the name Eudocia in baptism; previously she had been called Athenais, 552. Eudocus (Saint) is invoked in the litanies for the anointing of the sick, 545. Eugenia (Saint), 290. Eugenius (Saint), a martyr exiled with Macarius by Julian the Apostate; afterward both were struck with the sword, 305.—Eugenius, bishop of Carthage, 348.

Eulalia (Saint), martyr, on the third day before the Kalends of December, 422. *Eulogiae* were offered at the altar to be sent to Christians in various parishes as a sign of communion, 563. Eunomius introduced a single immersion in baptism because he did not believe in the Holy Trinity, 353. The First Council of Constantinople orders that those baptized by the Eunomians with a single immersion be baptized again, ibid. Euphemia (Saint) is mentioned in the canon of the Mass, 290. On the Ides of April is the feast of Saint Euphemia, 390. This is not the famous virgin and martyr of Chalcedon, ibid. Her feast is recorded on 11 June in the Greek *Menologion*, the day on which she suffered, and in the Roman Martyrology on 16 September, ibid., 130, 710.

Euplus (Saint), 121. The feast of Eusebius (Saint), priest and confessor, on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of September, 411, 121, 707. He suffered much for the orthodox faith and, surviving, rested in peace, ibid. Eustachius (Saint), or Eustochius, 134.

Pope Eutychian instituted the blessing of ripe grapes and beans at the altar, 410. Eutychius, patriarch of Constantinople, crowned Justin the Younger emperor, 583.—Eutychius, the heretic and follower of Eunomius, was the originator of a single immersion in baptism, 353.

Eve is called the ancient virgin because, while in paradise, she was free from every pollution of lust, 188, 447. Evagrius was substituted for Paulinus as bishop of Antioch by the votes of the people, 512.

According to an ancient rite, the Gospel is read at Mass, 1, 279. Formerly there was not one common custom among all the Churches as to who should cause the Gospel to be read at Mass [Col. 1428], 491, 500, 501. The Gospel read at Mass by lectors, 491. According to ancient custom, the Gospel is not read except at the command of the bishop or the celebrating priest, 561. According to an ancient institution of the Church, lights are kindled for the reading of the Gospel at Mass, 582. Formerly the Gospel of the Resurrection was read throughout the octave of Easter, 561. Formerly the Gospel of the Resurrection according to Matthew was read on Easter Day, ibid.—Formerly the book of the Gospels was not presented to the deacon at his ordination, 500. The book of the Gospels is placed upon the head of a bishop at his ordination, 512. It is placed upon the head of the pope who is to be consecrated by deacons, 518. After the Gospel has been read, the bishop kisses the book, and all the clergy after him, 561.

*Εὐαγγελισμός*, that is, “Annunciation,” 213. *Εὐαπολόγητος*, that is, “excusable,” 286. Eventius (Saint), 693, 694. The Exaltation of the holy Cross, 128, 709. Office of the Exaltation of the holy Cross, 823. See *Exaltation of the Cross*.

The examination of those to be baptized: a more careful inquiry into their life and intention, 379. What *excarpsatum* signifies, 614. *Exceptores* are notaries, so called from taking down abbreviated notes, 343.

If someone unknowingly communicates with persons excommunicated from the Church, he is to do penance for forty days, 468. How an excommunicated person who has been overtaken by death and had previously confessed is reconciled to the Church, 469. The impious and wicked are excluded from the Church, the temple, sacred rites, and the common society of human beings, according to the ancient custom of the Church, 451.

The priest’s exhortation, elsewhere called the preface, addressed to those standing around the sick person to be anointed, 547, 553.

In Greek, *exorcism*; in Latin, *conjuration*, or a speech of rebuke, is directed against the devil so that he may depart, 339, 364, 376. The evil spirit is exorcised so that it may leave the creature whom it had long possessed through the sin of the first human being, 364. Exorcisms before baptism, 363, 376, 377. The ancient form for exorcising a demon, 425. Exorcists are read of in the Acts of the Apostles, 364. The holy Church also has the ministry of exorcists among the ecclesiastical orders, ibid. Exorcists assail the devil with many rebukes, 376. At what point in the Mass the ordination of exorcists takes place, 487. According to ancient custom, the ordination of an exorcist follows the institution of a lector, 492. Among the ancient Fathers there is mention of exorcists in the Church, ibid., and even among the pagans, ibid. The proper duty of exorcists is to lay hands upon the possessed, 493. The exorcist is said to receive the grace of healings, 221, 493. One who is opposed to baptism, the salvation of the faithful, and all its virtues is to be exorcised, 364. Those being exorcised heard the exorcisms with veiled faces, 377. They stood ungirded, with their outer garments removed, clothed only in a tunic, and barefoot, ibid. They faced toward the West, ibid. They stood upright, ibid.

The expulsion of a penitent from the church, 451. The office of the funeral rites, 478. Why *Alleluia*, a word of joy, was not omitted in the office for the dead, 480. Another office of the funeral rites, ibid. The lifting of the corpse with singing, 485. After the body had been carried into the church, the sacrifice of the Mass was celebrated before it was buried, according to ancient custom, ibid. *Kyrie, eleison* is sung at funeral rites [Col. 1429] according to ancient custom, 485. At the end of each psalm sung before the tomb, a prayer or collect is inserted, according to ancient custom, ibid. See *The dead*.

Exsufflation (blowing) is performed on the face of the person being baptized by the priest through the sign of the cross, so that the devil may be driven away and a way prepared for Christ, 363.

Three rites for administering extreme unction are reported, 235, 236, 532, 534, 537. Several priests administered this sacrament, 237, 534, or were present with the one administering it, 543, 553. They laid hands upon the sick person, ibid., 548. This sacrament can be conferred by a single priest, ibid., 534. Sometimes one anointed the sick person while another pronounced the formula, 236, 534. Formerly the form of this sacrament was indicative, ibid., 538, 539, 540, 549. The opinions of the ancient and more recent theologians of the Paris school on this matter, 534, 535. The formula “Through this anointing,” etc., customarily said in an anointing performed by a priest, 554.

Formerly the sick person was anointed before receiving the viaticum of the Lord’s body and blood, 237, 536, 554. Formerly the three sacraments of penance, extreme unction, and the Eucharist were conferred upon the sick person together, 536. Extreme unction was not conferred upon penitents to whom no sacrament was given, 532. Formerly, when necessity required, the sick received extreme unction and the viaticum for seven consecutive days, 237, 537, 543, 551, 554. This sacrament could be repeated more than once during the same illness, unless the present practice of the Church prevented it, ibid.

The sick were anointed on the five senses, without any mention being made of the customary formula, 237, 537. The priest who is about to anoint the sick person makes the sign of the cross from ashes mixed with water upon the person’s breast, together with the imposition of a hair shirt, 537, 539, 544. The priest is to hear the sick person’s confession, either in writing or orally, ibid. The profession of faith that the sick person must make before the anointing, 553.

When anointing of the head is prescribed, only the temples are to be anointed, not the forehead or the crown of the head, 548, 553. The anointing of the breast is prescribed in several codices and forbidden in others; among the Greeks it is customary, 553. An anointing between the shoulders was also performed by some and not by others, ibid. The ancient codices make no mention of anointing the loins; nor is it customary among the Greeks, 554. Some add anointings of the breast, loins, and navel, ibid. The Greeks anoint the forehead, chin, both cheeks, breast, both sides of the hands, and feet, ibid. A single anointing suffices in urgent danger of death, 554.

The conclusion of the anointings, 549. The method of anointing the sick person when the illness begins to worsen, 552. Reconciliation is a shorter method of administering anointing to a sick person who is near death, 550, 554. The method of anointing the sick according to the ancient practice of the Church of Soissons, 554. In this form, which is indicative, only the left ear, the breast, and the shoulders, together with the other customary parts, are anointed, 555. In the presence of the sick person, the divine office was recited after extreme unction, 542, 554. In the Mass for a seriously ill person and for one who is near death, the introit, gradual, offertory, etc., are doubled, ibid. See *Visitation*, *Anointing*.

Exuperius (Saint), martyr, 416. See Mauritius (Saint).

# F
F

Ripe beans, or fava beans, are blessed on the altar, by institution of Pope Eutychianus, 234, 410. [Col. 1429] The feast of Fabian (St.), martyr, 20, 663. The Mass of Fabian and Sebastian is one Mass, with different prayers, the prayer of St. Sebastian preceding, 304. Exorcised persons with veiled faces, 377. *Fatigare* means the same as “to strike”; *fatigari*, that is, “to be struck,” 397. “We are wearied by our offenses,” that is, “we are rebuked and struck on account of our sins,” ibid. The feast of Faustinus (St.), on the fourth day before the Kalends of August, 408, 704. Periodic fevers, erratic fevers, 616. “Quartan” and “quotidian” signify the pattern or rule by which a fever, as though predetermined for itself, attacks a person, ibid. In the month of February the Romans purified the city in honor of the god Februus, with burning candles, 306. Hence the origin of the month’s name, 307, 308. February seems to derive its name from pain, ibid. Juno is called *Februlis*, or *februata*, by the Romans, 308. To the Romans, *Februs* means pain, 308. *Februare* means the same as “to cleanse,” ibid. Pluto was called the god Februus, 306. In the Etruscan language, *Februus* means one who is among the dead, 308. The feast of Felicianus (St.), martyr, 699. The feast of Felicissimus (St.), martyr, 118, 705. The feast of Felicitas (St.), martyr, on the ninth day before the Kalends of December, 141. See Perpetua (St.). The feast of Felicula (St.), on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of March, 28, 310. Felix (St.), Pope Felix II, was substituted for Liberius during his exile; afterward, by the Arian emperor Constantius, he was himself driven from his see and beheaded on account of the Catholic faith, 408. The feast of St. Felix on the fourth day before the Kalends of August, 116, 704. — The feast of Felix (St.), presbyter and confessor of Nola, on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of February, with its Mass, 18, 303, 661. “Saint Felix in Pincis”: this is a place in Rome where a church was built for St. Felix, ibid. — Felix and Adauctus (SS.), martyrs, on the third day before the Kalends of September, 127, 709. — Felix, bishop of Urgell, together with Elipandus, bishop of Toledo, defended the heresy that Christ was the adoptive Son of God, 378. Women were separated from men during exorcisms, 382. Men were placed on the right and women on the left, ibid. Feral days: why they are so called, 307. The *Feralia* formerly began on the twentieth of February and lasted almost until the end of that month, 311. During the *Feralia* the spirits of the dead were appeased by placing food on their tombs for them to eat, ibid. The Wednesday after Quinquagesima Sunday was not the beginning of Lent in the time of St. Gregory the Great, 315. Wednesday was a day for penance to be imposed and received at the beginning of the fast, 449. — On the Wednesday of Holy Week, solemn prayers are said as on Good Friday, according to ancient custom, 62, 321. — On Maundy Thursday the reconciliation of penitents takes place, 457. — The offices for Thursdays throughout Lent are said to have been instituted by the younger Gregory, that is, by Pope Gregory II, and to have been collected chiefly from the summer Sundays, 36, 668. On the Thursday within the Octave of Pentecost there is no office or Mass; therefore the Mass of Pentecost Sunday is sung, 400. — On Good Friday, the adoration of the cross, 69. On that day the Eucharist is not consecrated, 387. The ancient formula for announcing any feast, before Martyrologies were publicly read in church, 439. [Col. 1430] For what purpose the Church commands feasts to be celebrated, ibid. The ancient custom of the Latin and Greek Churches concerning the celebration of feasts occurring throughout the year, 571, 572. Formerly, as now, there was variation in the canonical hours according to the diversity of solemnities and feasts, ibid. The king makes a profession of faith at his coronation, as does the emperor of Constantinople, 584. Before extreme unction the sick person makes a profession of faith, 553. *Fidiculae* are iron claws, called *fidiculae*, because by them criminals are tortured on the rack, so that their “faith” may be discovered, 477. Yet *fidiculae* is also said to derive from the verb *findo, fidi*, etc., ibid. Firmus, defeated in Africa, among other spoils restored to the emperor Theodosius a priestly crown, 558. The monks of Fécamp received St. Maurilius as a brother, 581. Fans made of feathers, and moved by deacons while the mysteries are celebrated: what they signify, 523, 524. Fans are called *muscaria*, 570. A fan is handed to the deacon at his ordination; it is his duty to move it over the sacred mysteries, ibid. Why fans are moved over the awe-inspiring mysteries set before the people, 523. The use of the fan formerly existed at Rome, 524. The pontiff in the *flamineate*, that is, clothed in sacred vestments, 558. “Let us bend the knee” is, according to ancient ecclesiastical custom, the deacon’s command, 321. Formerly, after the deacon had cried, “Let us bend the knee,” etc., the people prayed in silence, ibid. Weeping is the first stage of penitents, who stood outside the church gate and remained there in the mourning of penance, 461. The dedication of baptismal fonts, 437. The seven steps of the baptismal font, 385. It is an ancient custom for the water of the baptismal font to be solemnly blessed by the bishop, 348. This blessing is counted among the apostolic traditions, ibid. The rite of this blessing, 72, 348. Above the baptismal font there was a golden or silver dove representing the Holy Spirit, 385. A miraculous fountain in the baptistery of Embrun, 399. “To the fonts,” or “to the garment,” that is, to the place where those being baptized laid aside their clothes or put on the white garment, 785. See Baptistery; Baptism. The sacred doors are the doors of the screens of the sanctuary, 523. Guarding them is the duty of subdeacons, ibid. Formerly among the Greeks it was the duty of deacons, ibid. Whether the baptismal formula, “I baptize you,” etc., is necessary for the validity of baptism, 354. Whether immersion with these words—“In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit”—is sufficient, ibid. The formula used by the Greeks is indicative and is valid, ibid. The ancient Greeks did not add “servant of God” to their formula, ibid. At the naming of each person of the most holy Trinity, the Greeks, following ancient custom, add “Amen,” 355. See Baptism. — The formula of chrismation and reconciliation of heretics among the Greeks, 362. — Various forms of confirmation, 361, 362. See Confirmation. — The formula for the consecration of the chalice is not found in Scripture, 288. See Eucharist. — The formula of extreme unction is indicative, 534, 538, 539, 540, 549. The Ambrosian form, 534. See Extreme Unction. *Formata* is a diploma or letter of an archbishop by which he testifies that a bishop ordained by him belongs to a particular church, [Col. 1431] 518. A model of a *formata*, ibid. The formula for exorcising a demon, 425. The form of a queen’s coronation, 595. Various formulas for administering communion, 579. The canonical penalty for fornication, according to each person’s status and the circumstances of the crime, 465. A bishop who commits fornication is to be degraded and do penance for ten years, 468, 474. A presbyter or deacon who commits natural fornication, while not bound by any vow of monasticism, is punished by canonical penalties, ibid. Fortitude does not fear adversity and gives confidence to a trembling mind, 372. Fortitude is destroyed unless it is supported by counsel, ibid. An emended reading of *Fortunatus*, 514. The Franks: the day on which they gave names to infants, 351. The rite formerly observed in the anointing of Frankish kings, 257. Their first king, Clovis, was inaugurated and crowned by St. Remigius, 584. At their coronation they make a profession of faith, ibid. The origin of the ancient right of the Frankish kings over the kingdom of England, 587. They are inaugurated with chrism, 587. They are anointed with sacred oil sent from heaven, 588. The coronation formula of the Frankish kings asserts their right over the Saxons, Mercians, and Northumbrians, 587. The sacred oil sent from heaven with which they are anointed is called chrism, 588. The heads, breasts, shoulders, spaces between the shoulders, joints of the arms, and hands of the Frankish kings are anointed, 589. The title “Most Christian” is proper and extremely ancient to the Frankish kings, 591. In the solemn prayers of Wednesday and Friday of Holy Week: “Look favorably upon the empire of the Romans and Franks,” 63, 322. Between Francis I, king of the Franks, and Pope Leo X, the elections of bishops by clergy and people were abolished by concordat, 511. The feast of the seven martyr brothers, 115, 407, 703. *Frigium*. See Phrygium. The anointing of the forehead in the form of a cross, 360. Three times, 361. Why the forehead of the sick is not anointed, 553. Presbyters are not permitted to anoint the forehead with chrism, 358, 361, 371. See Confirmation. The blessing of grain takes place on the altar, by institution of Pope Eutychianus, 410. Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, flourished under Robert, king of the Franks, 427. The confession of Fulgentius (St.), 452. Which Fulgentius—of Ruspe or of Ástigi—, 454. Fulgentius of Ástigi, a holy bishop in Spain, was the brother of Saints Leander and Isidore, ibid. — Fulgentius (St.), formerly a monk and afterward bishop of Ruspe in Africa, 300, 454. His feast coincides with that of Pope St. Sylvester, 13. The office for the dead, 478, 479, etc. See Exequies; The Dead. The canonical penalties by which thieves are to be punished, 466, 472. The penalty for a thief of ecclesiastical property, 467. Theft of food and clothing is excused in case of necessity. Nevertheless, one is to fast canonically, 469. If the stolen goods are returned, the person is not bound to fast, ibid.

G

The name of the archangel Gabriel in the offering of incense, 576. The Gauls were the authors of the solemnity of the Rogation rites, 395. If a hen has died in a well, etc., 469. Gallus (St.), bishop of Alvernia: after his death he was washed and clothed and carried into the church, 484. Gaudentius (St.), bishop of Brescia, dedicated a church which he ordered to be called “the Church of All Saints,” because many relics of saints had been brought into it, 434. *Gazetum* is an excellent wine, 563. Gebhard (St.), bishop of Constance, 484. After his death he was washed, clothed in priestly vestments as customary, and placed in a coffin, ibid. Gelasinus (St.), martyr, who was baptized in jest in the theater, then seriously converted to Christ and thereafter refused to act as a mime, 356. Pope Gelasius is the author of the book *Sacramentary*, Preface III. The Gemeticus Codex, Preface V. Geminianus (St.). See Lucia, 130, 710. The tearing of the cheeks at pagan funerals, 476. The feast of Genesius (St.), 708. No genuflection is made in the prayer for the perfidious Jews, 322. The genuflection of exorcised persons, 377. In the ordination of a deacon, 523. The human race, condemned through its transgression at the very root of its origin, 27. See Original Sin. George is commemorated in the canon of the Mass, 285. The feast and Mass of St. George, on the ninth day before the Kalends of May, 84, 689. The feast of Germanus (St.), bishop of Auxerre, on the second day before the Kalends of August, 409. His miracle at the consecration of an altar, 429. The law of the Germans, 452. Germanus (St.) of Paris is called by Fortunatus “the supreme pontiff,” 502, 514. His feast on 28 May, 731. — Germanus (St.), on the day before the Kalends of October, 417. The feast of Gerontius (St.), on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of February, 304. The feast of Gertrude (St.), 4, 290. The names of Gervasius and Protasius (SS.) in the canon of the Mass, 292. Their feast, with a vigil, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July, 108, 700. The girding with a sword at the king’s coronation, 590. “Glory to God in the highest”: by whom this hymn was composed, 277. Pope Telesphorus is commonly said to have ordained that it be sung at Mass, ibid. Formerly this hymn was sung at the morning praises, ibid. In the litany it is omitted, 1, 2. It was not said by presbyters except at Easter; by the bishop on Sundays and feast days, 1, 600. Formerly, instead of the hymn *Te Deum*, *Gloria in excelsis* was sung in thanksgiving, 585. According to ancient custom, the hymn *Gloria in excelsis* is begun by the pontiff, 560. It is sung at the Mass of the Lord’s Supper, while the entire trumpet call is sounding, 336. And at the Mass of Holy Saturday, 387. It is begun by the bishop and presbyters, with the entire trumpet call sounding, 336. “Glory and praise,” etc.: by whom this hymn was composed, 319, 320. Its author is older than Theodulf of Orléans and Reginald of Langres, but is unknown, ibid. Alcuin, who died in 804, is mentioned in connection with this hymn and procession, 319. The feast and Mass of Gordianus and Epimachus (SS.), 87, 392, 694. The feast of Gorgonius (St.), martyr, on the fifth day before the Ides of September, 415, 128, 709. The Goths, in accordance with the custom of their people, took pleasure in letting their hair grow long for beauty and dignity, 451. The Council of Agde decreed that Gothic penitents should remove all adornment from their hair, ibid. The Goths did not fast on Saturday, 314. *Grabatarii*, or *clinici*, were those who, because of danger of death, were baptized in bed—on a couch—by sprinkling or pouring water, 399. *Gradale* is the same as *graduale*, 1, 279, 649. Formerly the gradual was an entire psalm, 561. It was called a responsory, 649. The gradual antiphoner, ibid. There were seven steps in the baptistery: three descending and three ascending, 385. What these steps signified, ibid. Why the seventh was called “the support of the feet” and “the foundation of the water,” ibid. — The five stages of penitents, 461. — Those who flee the ecclesiastical orders are to be admitted to the sacred altars, while those who seek them ambitiously are to be rejected, 221. The Greeks do not celebrate Masses involving consecration on days when they fast, 333. They use the Presanctified throughout Lent, ibid. By ancient custom they do not fast, and they consecrate, on Sundays, Saturdays, or the feast of the Annunciation during Lent; if feasts of martyrs fall during Lent, they transfer them to those days, ibid. The Roman Church has never disapproved the ordinations of Greek presbyters, which are performed without the handing over of instruments, 504. The Greeks confer no minor orders other than those of lector and psalmist, 521. The customary rite of conferring orders among the Greeks, ibid. The Greeks do not sing “Christ, have mercy,” 277. They do not have a single form of Mass, 572. In baptism they lack the anointing of the crown of the head, 385. Which parts they anoint in extreme unction, 554. Their virgins are tonsured, 443. Their baptismal formula is indicative, 354. Their formula of absolution, 460. — The pagan Greeks had temples facing west, 330. Grace is used metonymically for eternal redemption, 317. It is called the effect of our redemption, ibid. Prevenient grace is arousing grace, 318. Sometimes it includes all graces—arousing, assisting, and habitual—insofar as by them we are made righteous, ibid., 59. Grace is necessary for us to supplicate God, 444. — Subsequent grace is called assisting grace, 318. Sometimes all graces are also understood by “subsequent grace,” insofar as through them the righteousness received is strengthened, increased, and preserved to the end, ibid., 59. “Let us give thanks to the Lord,” etc. These admonitory words of the preface were familiar to St. Augustine; St. John Chrysostom calls the Eucharist “thanksgiving,” 279. This thanksgiving is made for all benefits received from God, 280, 295. — “Thanksgiving” is the prayer after communion, or postcommunion, 295. *Gravedo* means pain, sadness, or distress, 426. Gregory the Great (St.) was unjustly criticized by the Greeks, 276. The *Book of Sacraments* is attributed to him, 273. See Preface. His name is recited in the canon of the Mass, 3, 4, 285. His feast is celebrated on the fourth day before the Ides of March, 30, 665. Why St. Gregory is called the apostle of the English, 593. Which hymns were composed by St. Gregory, 616, 878. St. Gregory is neither the author of the Sacramentary nor of the Antiphonary, but their compiler, 649. His letter to St. Leander vindicated, 353. — Pope Gregory III instituted the feast of All Saints, 420. This feast began to be celebrated in Gaul under Louis the Pious, at the urging of Pope Gregory IV, ibid. The constitution of Pope Gregory VII concerning the Ember-day fast, 403. — What the *cidaris* placed on the head of Gregory (St.) of Nazianzus was, 558. — Gregory (St.), bishop of Langres, was found in his tomb with the garment in which he had been buried intact, [Col. 1433] 484. William, archbishop of Reims, consecrated and crowned Philip Augustus, king of the Franks, 588, 591. King Guntram, grandson of Clovis, was consecrated by the bishops of his provinces, 584.

H

H. What the use of this aspiration was among the ancients, 615. “We have [our hearts] toward the Lord.” These words of the preface occur in ancient liturgies and are commended by the ancient Fathers, 299. “Heretic” is improperly used for a pagan, just as pseudomonks are called heretics, 303. Certain heretics restored to the Church were anointed, 362. Halitgarius, bishop of Cambrai, lived in the time of Louis the Pious, 462. He was sent by Charles the Bald to Constantinople to the emperor Michael, ibid. From there he brought many relics of saints, with which he enriched his church, ibid. Halitgarius’s penitential book is the sixth Roman penitential, ibid. The translation of Helena (St.), queen, 28. Henry II, king of the Franks, was consecrated with heavenly liquid once brought by an angel and mixed with sacred chrism, 589. He received a ring and was girded with a sword by the bishop, 590, ibid. — Henry IV, king of the Franks, surnamed “the Great,” was anointed and crowned king at Chartres by Nicholas Thouin, bishop of Chartres, 584. The aforesaid bishop first addressed the people concerning their consent, ibid. He was anointed with the heavenly liquid once brought from heaven to St. Martin, 589. Why Henry IV was not anointed and crowned by the bishop of Sens or by the bishop of Bourges, 592. The ancient right of the kings of France over the kingdom of England is noted in the coronation of Henry IV, 587. He received a ring and was girded with a sword by the bishop, 590. A crown was placed upon him by the same bishop of Chartres, 592. Since factions occupied Reims, the king was consecrated at Chartres, ibid. — The emperor Henry II persuaded Pope Benedict VIII to order the Creed to be sung in the Roman Church at Mass, 562. — Henry (St.), bishop of Lübeck, when at the point of death, after receiving extreme unction, received the viaticum of the Lord’s Body, 536. The emperor Heraclius was crowned by Sergius, patriarch of Constantinople, and his wife was crowned Augusta by the same man, 584. Heraclius the Younger, also called Constantine, was crowned by that patriarch in the third year of his father’s reign, ibid. *Herbarius* means a poisoner, so called because of evil-working herbs and the poisons of herbs, 478. Sorcerers who kill infants may obtain penance at the end of life if they seek it with mourning, 469. The feast of Hermes (St.), martyr, 125, 413, 708, 822. Irmengard, wife of Charles the Bald, is crowned, 585. At that coronation the bishops addressed the people in the church, asking their consent, ibid. The nuptial blessing of Queen Irmengard, 596. Hero, an old anchorite, deceived by a demon, was counted among those who died by violence, 611. The feast of Hyacinthus (St.) on the fourth day before the Ides of February, 310. Jerome (St.) is commemorated in the canon of the Mass, 3, 285. The feast of St. Jerome on the second day before the Kalends of October, [Col. 1433] 417. The feast of St. Jerome seems formerly to have been repeated, or his octave may have been celebrated on the Nones of October, ibid. Hierophants and hierophantesses formerly wore myrtle crowns in the sacred rites of Ceres, 558. Hilary (St.) is commemorated in the canon of the Mass, 3, 285. The concurrence of the Octave of Epiphany and the feast of St. Hilary, 303. The Mass of St. Hilary, with a commemoration and blessing of the Octave, ibid. Some attribute the Angelic Hymn to Hilary, 277. Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, carried out the second translation of the sacred body of St. Remigius, 418. He crowned Charles the Bald emperor at Metz, 556. The feast of Hippolytus (St.), martyr, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of September, 121, 412, 706. The Spaniards use a single immersion in baptism, 353. When episcopal blessing was formerly given among them during Mass, 296. At what point in the Mass they gave the kiss, 568. On Good Friday they neither received communion nor celebrated Mass, 342. A cleft blade. See Claws; *Fidiculae*. How much and for how many years homicide is to be assigned penance, with due regard to the circumstances, 465, 468. Whoever killed someone while defending himself, his parents, or his household is not guilty and is not required to fast, because he did it under compulsion, 468. “Man” is used for “humanity” when the Fathers say that the Word assumed a complete man, 382. They say “complete” against the heresy of Apollinaris, ibid. “Honor” is used of the three superior orders: the diaconate, presbyterate, and episcopate, 499, 502, 514. The eighth hour, that is, the second hour after midday or midnight, 70. The ancients observed the hours according to the movements of the stars, 489. Also according to the shadow of the human body, ibid. The ninth hour, 5. Formerly, during half-fasts, Masses were held at the ninth hour, 293. — Formerly, as today, there was variation in the canonical hours according to the diversity of feasts in the Church, 572. The canonical hours recited before the sick, 551, 542. A sundial based on the shadow of the human body, 489. The sequence of hours on it is reckoned from sunrise, ibid. The host is not simply bread and wine but Christ, who is to be offered under the species, 26, 308. The work of our redemption is carried out whenever the commemoration of this host is celebrated, 175, 444. How the host and chalice ought to be arranged with respect to one another on the altar, 255, 582. Touching the host, or bread, in ordination is not necessary, 508. The host is round in form, 564. A portion of the host set aside for the viaticum, 583. Christ is both the host and the priest, 389. The host placed on the paten over the chalice is lifted by the priest together with the deacon after the words, “Through him,” etc., 582. *Hostis*, or *ostis*, French *ost*, means an army, 426. Irmengard, daughter of Count Hugh, married Lothair, son of Emperor Louis the Pious, 320. — Hugh (St.), abbot of Cluny, anointed with holy oil by St. Godefrid, bishop of Amiens, received the viaticum of the Lord’s Body and Blood, 526. — Hugh Menard, Preface VI, VII. The *humerale* is not like the Greek *omophorion*, 556. The shoulders are to be anointed—that is, the shoulder blades—not the breast or the space between the shoulders, in extreme unction, 549. [Col. 1434] The people’s humbling for a blessing, 567. Christ’s humility in subjecting himself to the law, 308. His humility in bending toward a fallen human being and extending a hand to him, 320. The humility of the feet: what it is, 377. Hyacinthus (St.), 128, 709. A *hydria* is a vessel suitable for water, or a water jar, 317. A *hydria* was a vessel not only for water but also for wine, ibid. *Hydroparastatae* are those who perform the mystery of Christ’s blood with water without wine, 387. Hymns written by St. Gregory the Great, 878. The office of Hippolytus (St.), with three nocturns, 815. Hyssop used with the blessed water with which the consecrated altar is sprinkled, 427.

I

Ignatius (St.), bishop and martyr, is commemorated in the canon of the Mass after the consecration, 4. “The ignorant,” that is, sinners, 47, 317. *Ill.* This abbreviation, with a transverse line in place of a proper name, was customarily written in manuscripts produced before the year 1000 of salvation, 572. Later the letter N. came to be written, ibid., 603. The monk Elias, named *Illiante*, died in 1071 and wished the formula of his baptism and absolution, engraved on a cross, to be buried with him, 459. “Unspotted,” that is, whole and undefiled, 283. The immaculate host, that is, the immaculate gifts of God, 289. The canonical penalty for one who eats food sacrificed to gods, 467. On Maundy Thursday the emperor of Constantinople customarily washed the feet of twelve poor men, 335. The rite by which he did so, 336. After the washing of their feet, three gold coins were given to each of the poor men, ibid. According to ancient custom the emperor of Constantinople was consecrated with sacred chrism, 589. Who has the right to place the crown upon him, 591. He was anointed on the head in the form of a cross, 589. His chief priest, 524. — When the Roman emperor is ordained, three prayers are said, 586. The bishop of Albano recites the first prayer, the bishop of Porto the second, and the bishop of Ostia the third, while anointing his left arm, ibid. Today the Roman emperor is anointed with exorcised oil, whereas the king is anointed with the oil of catechumens, 589. The Roman emperor is anointed on the right arm and only between the shoulders, ibid. The anointing is performed in the form of a cross, 590. By whom the crown is placed upon the empress of Constantinople, 595. The imposition of hands in confirmation is distinguished from chrismation, 359, 386. What the imposition of hands is, 506. It is not mere election, 507. See Confirmation; Chrismation; Ordination; Election. The canonical penalties for arsonists, 467, 474. Incense is offered by the pontiff at the offertory of the Mass, according to ancient custom, 245, 564. The bishop is to offer a cross of incense upon the altar at a dedication, 430. “Unharmed,” that is, subject to no guilt of sins, 52, 182, 317, 445. The ancient use of indulgences, 404. How infants become catechumens, 363. On what day names were given to infants, 350. Their communion immediately after receiving baptism, 357. Those baptized are not to be nursed before holy communion, 356. Where the office of Holy Saturday began at the second hour after midday, those who were not fasting received communion, ibid. Baptized infants immediately received confirmation and the Eucharist, 357. When infants reach the age of understanding, they are to be taught what they ought truly to believe and carefully preserve, 365. The sponsors confess and speak on their behalf, 366. It is fitting that those who are bound by the sins of others should receive, through another’s confession, remission of original sin through baptism, ibid. See Original Sin; Baptism. Infants were customarily baptized outside the prescribed days of Easter and Pentecost, 400. On any day from their date of birth onward, ibid. Infants, or little children, are sometimes also called those who have reached childhood, 490. Funerary rites celebrated by pagans in February, 307. Responsibility for the conversion of unbelievers belongs to the queen in the kingdom, 595. The confession of the sick before extreme unction, 540, 547. The absolution of the sick, ibid. The visitation of the sick, 532. The anointing of the sick as a sacrament, ibid. Questions put to the sick before the anointing, 537, 539, 544, 553. See Extreme Unction; Visitation; Mass for the Sick, 551, 554. The Mass for the sick person who is near death, 552, 554. The canonical hours are to be recited before the sick, 542, 551. Prayer for anointing the sick, 235. The sale of free persons is prohibited, 474. Ingomer and Clodomer, sons of King Clovis, received their names at baptism itself, 350. Innocent (St.), or Innocentius. See Mauritius (St.). The feast and Mass of the Holy Innocents, martyrs, on the fifth day before the Kalends of January, 12, 659. That day seems to be spent as though in grief, ibid. The handing over of instruments must not be confused with the imposition of hands, 507. *Instrumentum* is sometimes used for a book, 397. “Instruments” are the objects customarily handed to those being ordained in ordinations, 504. The handing over of instruments in the ordination of a presbyter is not mentioned in the ancient writings of the Fathers, councils, or Scripture, ibid. The Greek Church to this day knows nothing of this handing over of instruments, ibid. Christ did not ordain the apostles as presbyters by the handing over of an instrument, ibid. “With the instruments of true belief,” that is, with the writings of the true faith: “books,” that is, teachings, by metonymy, 397. A person became a catechumen by breathing upon the face, 376. Satan was thrice breathed upon by the catechumen turned toward the west, ibid. Two forms of breathing, ibid. What kinds and how many breathings are performed by the Greeks, ibid. See Catechumen. Understanding is useless unless it rests upon wisdom, 372. To understand is one thing, to have wisdom another, 372. The questions customarily asked in baptism, according to the ancient custom of the Church, 352. The priest’s questions to the sick person being anointed and the sick person’s answers to the priest, 537, 539, 544. The Introit is the antiphon sung while the priest enters to the altar, 275. Of what parts the Introit consists, ibid. Invaders of other people’s property, acting unlawfully, are subject to canonical penalties, 467. [Col. 1435] The Finding of the Holy Cross, on the fifth day before the Nones of May, 86, 693. The Greeks lack this feast, 391. “May we be seized by the love of invisible things,” in place of “May we be seized into the love of invisible things,” 298. The invocation over the king consists of the bishops’ prayers, or blessings, poured over him at the king’s coronation, 586. The feast of Irenaeus (St.), on the fourth day before the Ides of February, 310. The death of the empress Irmengard, 319. — The marriage of Irmengard, daughter of Count Hugh, and Lothair, son of Emperor Louis the Pious, 320.

J
Mention is made of both apostles named James in the canon of the Mass, 3. The feast of James, the brother of the Lord, and of Philip the apostles, with Mass and vigil, 85, 693. The feast of James, brother of the apostle John, on the eighth day before the Kalends of August, 115. Formerly, on the Kalends of January, people were subject to pagan superstitions, 300. On this day a Mass is assigned to prevent [people] from [turning] to idols, ibid. During the three days before the Kalends of January, litanies were held to trample down the custom of the gentiles, 302. Pagan men ran about wantonly in various shapes of wild animals and domestic beasts, 472. This was called “leading the little deer” (*in cervulo ducere*) or “going as an old woman” (*in vetula vadere*), ibid. Saint John the Baptist seems to be understood in the latter part of the canon, together with John and Stephen, 290. His feast is celebrated with a vigil and fasting, 108. Three Masses are sung: the first, of the vigil, after sunset; the second, during the night; the third, during the day, 404, 701. Why these three Masses are assigned to this feast, ibid. Praise of Saint John the Baptist, 404. “His seniority is due more to grace than to nature,” ibid. Saint John the Baptist is said to have been baptized by Christ, 126, 413. The Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, on the eighth day before the Kalends of July, 107, 109, 701, 803.

The saints John and Paul are mentioned in the canon of the Mass, 3. Their feast and Mass, 110, 701, 805.

Saint John the Evangelist is mentioned in the canon of the Mass, 3. The Nativity of Saint John, on the sixth day before the Kalends of January, and the Mass, 10. His Nativity before the Latin Gate, 87, 392. Two Masses are assigned to the feast of this apostle: the first, early in the morning; the second, during the day, 299, 659. On the cross the Lord gave John as a son in place of himself to his Mother, 11, 299. John is believed to have written to the universal Church when he wrote to the seven churches, 371.

Saint John Chrysostom devised silver crosses on which wax candles were placed, 435. With the common votes of clergy and people, and with the emperor’s agreement, John Chrysostom was elected bishop of Constantinople, 512. He was anointed with sacred chrism at his ordination, 516. He was placed in a high position, ibid. He was called “the anointed priest,” ibid.

John, bishop of Avranches and later of Rouen: when he died, 581. A summary account of the acts of his life, ibid.

John of Arles, to whom Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, dedicated a short work on the order of baptism, 374. He lived under the emperors Charlemagne and Louis the Pious, ibid. These two bishops were sent by Louis the Pious to meet Pope Stephen IV as he approached Reims, ibid.

[Col. 1436] For John Chozebita, abbot and later bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, the presence of the Holy Spirit used to appear by a visible sign when he celebrated the divine mysteries, 309.

John, patriarch of Constantinople, crowned the emperor Maurice and his wife Augusta, 584.

The heresy of John the Monk of Jerusalem concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit, 379.

Joseph of Arimathea signified by the deacon, 582.

“Command, Lord, to bless” (*Jube, Domine, benedicere*), that is, “may you wish to bless”; and *jubere* sometimes means “to wish,” 561.

The Jubilee year, in which complete rest is signified, 371. It is composed of seven weeks and a unit, ibid., 386.

Judas the apostle, 137, 712. See Simon.

Christ presented his body and blood to Judas the betrayer at the Last Supper, 328. Judas, receiving the Eucharist unworthily among the disciples, did not defile the innocent, ibid.

The Jews worshiped facing west, 329. Why “Let us bend the knee” (*Flectamus genua*) is not said when the solemn prayer for the faithless Jews is offered, 322.

Judith, daughter of Charles the Bald, married Æthelwulf, king of the English, 590, and was crowned, ibid. The nuptial blessing of Queen Judith, 596.

The name of Saint Juliana is recited in the canon of the Mass, 290. On the fourteenth day before the Kalends of March is the feast of Saint Juliana, virgin and martyr, 311. She suffered at Nicomedia and shortly afterward was transferred to Campania, ibid.

Saint Julian, priest and martyr, 419.

Julian the Apostate, on the feast of the Epiphany, entered the church and, after solemnly worshiping the deity, departed, 302. When a Christian attendant of Julian, who practiced magical rites, was present, he drove away the demons, 361.

Juno was called by the Romans *februata*, *februlis*, or *februalis*, 308. Her festival was called the Lupercalia, ibid.

The funeral of the younger emperor Justin, and the carrying forth of his corpse with chant and pomp, 485. He had been crowned by Eutychius, patriarch of Constantinople, 583.

How the emperor Justinian was dressed when he was buried, 483. The table of the emperor Justinian, made entirely of precious materials, 288.

Saint Juvenal, 694.

To fast on the *tetrads*, or *Parasceves*, that is, on a weekday—either Wednesday or Friday, 463, 470. Christians, especially Eastern Christians, according to ancient custom, usually fast on Wednesday and Friday of every week, 470. When people fast, they must be refreshed with spiritual food, 168, 314, 441. The ancient custom of not fasting from Easter to Pentecost, 395. What penance is to be imposed on one unable to fast, 464. The Lenten fast is called the Paschal fast, and the Paschal observance, 315. Formerly the fast of Lent varied, ibid., 316. Just as bodies are fattened by food and drink, so souls are nourished by fasts and virtues, 39. See Lent.

Formerly the first fast of the Ember seasons did not always occur in the first week of Lent, 317. Nor did the fast of the fourth month always fall in the week of Pentecost, 400. The announcement of the fasts of the first, fourth, seventh, and tenth months, 105, 402. Formerly that announcement of the fasts was made in the Mass after the words “The peace of the Lord be always with you,” 402. Formerly the fast of the first month fell in the first week of March, 403. The fast of the fourth month fell in the second week of June, ibid. On Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday, fasting is to continue until the ninth hour, ibid. Gregory VII and Urban II restored these fasts to the first week of Lent and the week of Pentecost, ibid. A fast imposed during the three days of the Rogations, 395. If a rich penitent cannot fast for seven weeks, he may redeem the obligation with twenty solidi in alms, 464. If he cannot give that much, let him give ten; but if he is very poor, let him give three solidi, ibid. Formerly some did not observe a fast on Maundy Thursday, 327.

## K

The Roman Calendar, 7, in the notes. It was published by John Fronto, preface IV.

“Kyrie, eleison,” according to ancient usage, is sung at the funerals of the dead, 485. “Kyrie, eleison” is sung at Masses and in the other divine offices, according to the ancient custom of the Roman Church, 276. Also in the Office of the Dead, 485. Formerly “Christe, eleison” was said as many times as “Kyrie,” 277. Among the Greeks all sing “Kyrie, eleison” together, and “Christe” is not sung, ibid. *Κυρίου δεηθῶμεν*—“Let us beseech the Lord”—is said by the deacon, 321.

## L

At Extreme Unction the lips are to be anointed, and externally a cross is to be made over the chin and throat, 549.

Milk and honey are blessed at the Mass of Holy Saturday because of the newly baptized, 388. Why the baptized were ordered to taste milk and honey after the sacred washing, ibid. Newly baptized infants were permitted to receive milk before receiving the Eucharist; elsewhere this was prohibited, 356.

What were the golden plates that Saints John and James wore on their foreheads? 558.

*Λαμπαδάριος*, that is, “the bearer of a lamp before the pontiff,” 348.

What a *lardarium* is, 613.

Saint Largus, martyr, 410.

The *laticlave*, or *latus clavus*, 325. A senator’s garment is called a *laticlave*, ibid.

“Angels praise …” It is an ancient custom of the Church, in the preface of the Mass, to mention the heavenly spirits who continually praise God in heaven, 280.

Morning and evening praises ought to be sung for the sick each day and night, 542, 551.

Saint Lawrence is mentioned in the canon of the Mass, 3. His feast is celebrated with a vigil, 119. Two Masses are celebrated: the first at night, that is, early in the morning; the second during the day, ibid., 410, 706. The Office of Saint Lawrence the Martyr, 812. The octave of Saint Lawrence, 411, 707. The deposition of the relics of Saint Lawrence, 304.

Laurentius, the violator of a tomb, 472.

Twelve lessons at the Ember fasts, 42. Six of these are said twice, that is, once in Greek and once in Latin, ibid.

A prophetic reading preceding the reading of the Epistle, 560. Those about to read the Epistle used to ask permission, 561.

Readers hold a place among the clerical orders, 323. Readers are distinct from singers, ibid. Readers are allowed to marry, ibid. Readers are forbidden to occupy themselves with games of chance and drunkenness, ibid. Readers who have not fasted during Lent, on Wednesday, or on Friday are to be deposed, ibid. Readers sometimes perform the office of psalmists, ibid.

Among the Greeks, the readership is the only one of the minor orders that is conferred, 448. The ordination of readers among the Greeks, ibid. At what point in the Mass the ordination of readers takes place, 487. The ancient mention of readers in the Church, 490. Formerly readers were not only mature in age but also sometimes children, when this seemed good to the Church, ibid. In the early periods of the Church, readers read the Gospel and the Epistle at Mass, 491, 561. It was the duty of readers to preserve the sacred books, 491. Among the Greeks readers are ordained by the laying on of hands, according to the Apostolic Constitutions, 521, 523. The Seventh Synod disapproves of tonsured boys reading in church who had not yet received the laying on of hands from the bishop, ibid.

That is called legitimate which is sanctioned as to be done in the sacred texts themselves, 326.

Saint Leocadia, who died not under torture but through the squalor and hunger of imprisonment, is called a confessor, 303, 440.

The feast of Saint Leodegarius, bishop, on the sixth day before the Nones of October, 418.

The concordats of Pope Leo X and Francis I, king of the French, 511. By these the election of bishops was removed from the clergy and people, ibid.

Saint Leo I, pope, established that during the action of the sacrifice the words “holy sacrifice, unspotted victim” should be said, 3. His decree concerning the celebration of only one Mass per day, 405. The feast of Saint Leo I, pope, on the third day before the Ides of April, 390.

The feast of Saint Leo II, pope, on the fourth day before the Kalends of July, 111, 404. The translation of Saint Leo the pope, 112. His Collect is explained, 404.

Pope Leo III placed the crown on Charlemagne when he was made emperor, 591.

The emperor Leo the Philosopher was expelled from the church because he was a quadrigamist, 476.

A *lessus* is a funeral song, otherwise called a *naenia*, 477.

Formerly the deacon cried “Arise” (*Levate*) when the prayer was completed, 322. Today “Arise” (*Τὸ Levate*) is said by the subdeacon, ibid. According to the Roman Order, “Arise” is said by the deacon at the end of the prayer, before “Through the Lord,” etc., ibid.

*Λήκυθος* is a flask, or vessel in which oil is stored, 325.

The official book is the Antiphoner, 387.

Various Penitential Books, 462. Pontifical Books, 505.

What the Book of Sacraments is, preface III, 273. Why it is so called, 274. The Book of Sacraments is distinguished from the Sacramentary, ibid., 340. See the preface.

The sacred books were kept at Rome in the library of the Bedchamber, 274.

After Christ, a virgin born from the Virgin Mary, had appeared, lust was overcome by the Virgin’s childbirth, 439.

Whoever has made ligatures—a detestable act—is to do penance for three years, one of them on bread and water, 467.

Saint Linus is mentioned in the canon of the Mass, 3.

The use of altar linens is ancient in the Church, 430. The altar linens are blessed by the bishop with holy water and incense, ibid. The newly baptized are wrapped in linens by their sponsors, 355.

A litany pertains to mourning, 2. The sevenfold litany—that is, the one performed by the seven choirs on Holy Saturday—is sung at the fonts, 71, 347.

The Greater Litany: a Mass is to be said during the litany, 391, 689, 695. The Greater Litany is that of the Rogations, which are to be celebrated during the three days before the Ascension, 393. Its author is Saint Mamertus, bishop of Vienne, ibid. What occasion gave rise to the institution of these Rogations, ibid. Before Saint Mamertus there were litanies, rogations, and processions, but they were not fixed on a definite day, 394. According to what rite the Rogations instituted annually by Saint Mamertus were to be celebrated, ibid. The old formula of the Greater Litany, 395. A certain litany falsely attributed to Saint Gregory the Great, 397.

The litany of the anointing of the sick, 544. The antiquity of the litanies said before Extreme Unction, after the seven psalms have been recited over the sick person, 553. The litany to be said by the clergy at the dedication of a church, with the priests and deacons prostrate before the altar together with the pontiff, 145. The shorter litany to be said at the ordination of clerics, 497. Litanies do not always mean the public litanies performed in procession, the Rogations; sometimes they mean prayers such as those in chapter nine of the Rule of Saint Benedict, 414.

*Litare* means “to sacrifice,” 443.

*Λιτή*, that is, “prayer,” ibid.

The offering of abstinence is called *litatio*, 634.

The marriage of Lothair, son of Louis the Pious, and Irmingard, daughter of Count Hugh, 320.

The washing of feet customarily performed on Maundy Thursday, 335. Prayers are to be sung during the washing of feet, 334, 877. According to what rite and at what hour the washing of feet was customarily performed, 335. At Constantinople the emperor used to wash the feet of twelve poor men on this day, ibid.

The washing of the dead has come down to us from the apostles, 482.

After the offering has been made, the pontiff washes his hands before performing the divine mysteries, according to ancient custom, 563. Among the Greeks, the presbyters assisting him also wash, ibid. What that washing of the hands signifies, ibid.

The feast of Saint Luke the Evangelist, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November, 135.

The feast of Saints Lucia and Geminianus, martyrs, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of October, 130, 710.

The name of Saint Lucia, virgin and martyr, is recited in the canon of the Mass, 4, 290. The feast of Saint Lucia on the Ides of December, 144, 654, 635. The Office of Saint Lucia, virgin and martyr, 842.

The emperor Louis the Pious inflicted various punishments on the conspirators together with Bernard, king of Italy and his nephew, 319. He afterward pardoned the injury of all the accused, 320. He went to Brittany Minor to restrain Mormanus, 319. During the celebration of Mass, seven archbishops sang seven prayers of reconciliation of the Church over him, 458. He wished to be reconciled by the bishops in the church of Saint Denis and to be girded with arms by the hands of the bishops, 590.

The coronation of Louis II, king of the French, is included among the Chapters of Charles the Bald, 584. He was anointed with sacred oil at his coronation, 587.

Louis IV, called “from Overseas,” seems to have been anointed king of England and France, 587. Archbishop Artold of Reims anointed Louis and his wife Gerberga with sacred chrism, 588.

Why lights are kindled in the church while the sun is shining, 493, 582. Lights kindled for the Gospel, 582. Lights carried before the holy relics, 434, and before bishops, 347. See Candles.

The Lupercalia were held in February, 307. The Lupercalia were abolished by Pope Gelasius, ibid. February is named from the sacred *februa* of the Luperci, 308. The festivals of Juno *Februata* are the Lupercalia, ibid. Women were purified by the Luperci with Juno’s covering, that is, a goatskin, ibid.

Saint Lupicinus, after the Masses had been celebrated, was buried with the highest honor and joy, 485.

The *lustrici* days were so called from the purification of children, 350. The *lustrici* days are the ninth day from the birth of males and the eighth from that of females, ibid.

[Col. 1439]

## M

Saints Macarius and Emerentiana, martyrs, 22.

Saints Macarius and Eugenius, martyrs, were banished by Julian the Apostate to the Oasis and there struck with the sword, 305.

The feast of the holy Maccabees on the Kalends of August, 409. On that same day there are two Masses: the first of Saint Peter, the second of the holy Maccabees, ibid.

Among the Persians, the Magi are devoted to wisdom and lovers of God, 302. A Magus is called a theologian, ibid. The Magi are said to have arisen from the sons of Keturah, to whom Abraham gave gifts, ibid. The Magi were taught by the Chaldeans that a Savior born in the flesh would be announced by a star, ibid. Magodia, a region of Arabia, 302. Magodia, the homeland of the Magi, ibid.

The feast of Saint Magnus, bishop and martyr, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of September; he was killed in the persecution of Decius, 411.

The feast of Saint Magnus, or Andrew the martyr, with his companions, 411.

How sorcery is punished by canonical penalties according to the circumstances of the person or crime, 466. Who is called a sorcerer on account of love, 472.

The discovery of Saint Mallos the martyr and the translation of his body to a basilica, 585.

*Maltha* is lime mixed with water, liquid pitch, and lard—called *ciment* in French, 426—or pitch mixed with wax, ibid.

Saint Mamertus, or Mamercus, bishop of Vienne, was not the restorer but the author of the Rogations, 393.

The spirits of the dead were appeased by food placed on their tombs, 311.

Gloves, that is, the *chirothecae* of the celebrating bishop, 557, 563.

The heresy of the Manichaeans, which attributed a phantom body to Christ, is proscribed, 299.

The maniple, otherwise called the *mappula* and *phanon*, 557.

The laying on of hands for making someone a catechumen, 376. The laying on of hands is performed on the person being baptized while he recites the Creed, or after the threefold profession—that is, the recitation of the Creed, 384. See Catechumen.

The pontiff laid hands on penitents lying prostrate, 461. This laying on of hands was not absolution but a kind of prayer and blessing, ibid. Why the prayer is called “laying on of hands” in the Penitential Book, 471. Without the laying on of hands and sackcloth on the head, penance was not imposed, ibid. See Penance.

The laying on of hands alone is the essential matter of the diaconate, priesthood, and episcopate, 504, 506. The laying on of hands and the placing of a hand upon someone’s head, 506. The presentation of instruments is not considered the laying on of hands, 507. Christ healed the lunatic in Mark VII by touching the tongue and ears, not by laying on of hands, ibid. The laying on of hands is really distinct from election, 508. Election was customarily made by clergy and people, while ordination was performed by bishops through the laying on of hands, ibid. Among the Greeks, readers and subdeacons are ordained through the laying on of hands, 521, 523. See Ordination. In the ordination of an abbot among the Greeks, the episcopal laying on of hands is employed, 526. Formerly episcopal blessing was performed through the laying on of hands, 296. The laying on of hands is used in Confirmation, 359. It is distinct from chrismation, ibid., 507. In the coronation of a king and queen, the laying on of hands takes place, 595.

The hands of deacons are anointed at ordination, 501; those of priests, 503; those of bishops, 516. In Extreme Unction, the hands are anointed above and below, 549. If the person is a priest, his hands are not anointed below, ibid.

[Col. 1439] The Hand of Justice is a staff with a palm fixed to its top, which is handed to the king at his coronation, 592. It signifies what is expressed by the formula accompanying the handing-over, ibid.

The *manutergium* is a cloth suitable for drying the hands, 495.

The *mappula* is the maniple that the bishop places on the left arm of each subdeacon, 496. Formerly the *mappula* was carried for wiping mucus from the eyes and nose, ibid.

Saint Marcellianus, martyr, 105, 700.

Saint Marcellinus, pope, 4. The feast of Saint Marcellinus the martyr on the fourth day before the Nones of July, 104, 699.

The baptistery of Saint Marcellinus, bishop of Embrun, is celebrated for an annual miracle, 399.

Saint Marcellus, bishop of Paris, while he was a subdeacon, assisted Saint Prudentius as he celebrated Mass, 563. The water he drew from the River Seine was changed into wine, ibid. Saint Prudentius ordered this wine to be poured into the sacred chalice, from which the Mass was celebrated and all received Communion, ibid.

The feast of Saint Marcellus the martyr on the Nones of October, 418.

The feast of Saint Marcellus, pope and martyr, is assigned to the seventeenth day before the Kalends of February, 19, 661, 662.

The feast of Saint Mark the Evangelist on the seventh day before the Kalends of May, 84, 390. Saint Mark was crowned with glorious martyrdom for the name of Christ, 84, 391.

Saint Mark, for whom the station of the second weekday in the third week of Lent is held, is the supreme pontiff and is commemorated on the seventh day of October, 48, 711. The feast of Saint Mark on the Nones of October, 135, 418.

The feast of Saint Mark the martyr on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of July, 105, 700.

The saying of Marcus Aurelius the emperor: “All things from above,” 443.

Marculus and Donatus, false martyrs among the Donatists, 285. The Donatists recited their names in their sacrifices, ibid.

The Nativity of the Virgin Saint Mary on the sixth day before the Ides of September, 127, 709, 821. The Blessed Virgin is called unmarried, that is, undefiled, 819. The Assumption of Saint Mary, 411, 707. Lust was overcome by the virginity of Saint Mary, 439. Saint Mary in the Octave of the Lord, 660. Mary is interpreted as “lady” or “enlightener,” 366.

The dedication of Saint Mary among the Martyrs, 392. Pope Boniface IV formerly instituted this feast when he converted the Roman Pantheon into a church of Saint Mary and All the Martyrs, 392.

The feast of Saints Mary and Martha, the sisters of Lazarus, is assigned to the fourteenth day before the Kalends of February, 304.

The feast of Saints Maris and Martha, husband and wife and martyrs, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of February, 304.

The name of Saint Martin of Tours, bishop, is recited in the canon of the Mass, 3, 4, 285. His humility is commended: he sat on a lowly chair in the church, 340. On the fourth day before the Nones of July: the translation of Saint Martin, his ordination, and the dedication of his basilica, 406. This is the church that Bishop Perpetuus built over Saint Martin’s tomb, ibid. The same Perpetuus transferred Saint Martin’s body from his tomb to the apse of the greater church, ibid. The feast of Saint Martin, with a vigil, on the third day before the Ides of November, 140, 422, 713. The Office of Saint Martin, 833. Saint Martin was healed by heavenly oil, 589. He divides his cloak with a poor man, 422. He is scourged by the Arians, ibid.

Saint Martinianus, 114, 703.

Martyrs were anointed and strengthened by the sacrament of Confirmation for suffering, 331.

On the twenty-second day of June is the feast of the 1,480 holy martyrs; their vigil is to be celebrated with silence and fasting, 404.

The reading of the Martyrology was scarcely in use before the time of Louis the Pious, 439. In the chapter, they are ordered to read the Martyrology, a rule, or a homily, ibid. The ancient formula for announcing a feast before Martyrologies were publicly read in church, ibid.

Males were separated from females during the exorcisms, 382. The males were placed on the right side, ibid.

A mathematician is called a magician who, by examining the hour of birth, investigates what is to come for each person, 473. He is called a *genethliacus*, ibid. What canonical penalty is due to a mathematician who has driven someone mad by invoking demons, 467.

Those who have entered into marriage with their father’s or brother’s widow are to separate first and then be judged, 468. Certain cases concerning impediments to marriage, 469, and concerning its indissoluble bond, ibid. The New Law brought the bonds of marriage to a more perfect state, 597.

Godmothers and godfathers are called sponsors and recipients, 357.

Mattathias is interpreted as “Given by the Lord” or “Gift of the Lord,” 601. Matthias is the same as Mattathias, with a syllable removed by syncope, ibid. Matthew is interpreted as “Given,” 601.

The feast of Matthew the apostle and evangelist on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October, with a vigil, 131, 710. The name of Saint Matthew is recited in the canon of the Mass, 3.

The name of Saint Matthias the apostle is recited in the canon of the Mass after the consecration, 4. The feast of Saint Matthias on the sixth day before the Kalends of March, 29.

Matthias Flacius Illyricus, a man of the Lutheran sect, published an ancient Mass from the Palatine Library, 570. The antiquity and importance of this Mass are examined, 571.

Maurice, bishop of Paris, was questioned by the bishop of Clermont about a certain baptismal formula, 354. His response was contrary to Stephen of Tournai’s opinion concerning the same formula, ibid.

The feast of Saint Maurice and his fellow martyrs on the tenth day before the Kalends of October, 416. His companions were Exuperius, Candidus, Victor, Innocent, Vitalis, and others, ibid. The feast of Saint Maurice, 710. The Office of him and his companions, 824.

The emperor Maurice and his wife Augusta were crowned by John, patriarch of Constantinople, on their wedding day, 584. At the request of Maurice, that same John blessed their marriage in the palace, 596.

Maurilius, archbishop of Rouen: in what year he died, 581. A summary account of his life, ibid.

Saint Maurus and seventy-two other martyrs, on the third day before the Kalends of December, 422.

The feast of Saint Maurus the abbot is assigned to the eighteenth day before the Kalends of February, 304.

The feast and Mass of Saint Maximus the martyr, 83.

The name of Saint Medard is recited in the canon of the Mass, 4, 285. The feast and Office of Saint Medard, on the sixth day before the Ides of June, 800.

What the honey and milk blessed and tasted by the newly baptized signify, 388.

Meltinus is an estate in Sicily where there is a baptismal spring famous for a miracle, 599.

The anointing of all the limbs in Confirmation, 361. The canonical penalty for one who cuts off one of his own limbs, 467. In sacred language, the virtues of the soul are generally understood by the limbs of the body, 366, 382.

According to ancient custom, the saints are commemorated in all liturgies, [Col. 1441] 285. A sacrifice cannot be offered except in communion with the saints, whose memory we share, ibid. After the consecration, a commemoration of the living and the dead is made together in the Greek liturgies, 567.

Menas, patriarch of Constantinople: according to what rites he celebrated the dedication of an oratory, 434.

The feast of Saint Menas the martyr, 140, 713.

The table of the emperor Justinian, made from every kind of precious material, 288.

The Mercians are a people of England, 587.

The “estimator of merit,” that is, of demerit or sin, 180, 290, 444.

Merolilanus, a Scot, Saint, a regional bishop—that is, consecrated without a title—484. His intact body, crowned with priestly insignia, was found in a tomb, ibid.

Triple immersion in baptism is performed according to the ancient custom of the Church, 352. Sometimes there is single immersion, ibid. The rite of triple immersion is included among the apostolic traditions, 353. What triple immersion and emersion signify, ibid. Who were the authors of single immersion, ibid. Those baptized by single immersion are ordered to be baptized again because they were baptized with an illegitimate form, ibid. Baptism conferred with single immersion and the legitimate formula is valid, ibid. In triple immersion the formula was spoken once, ibid. Among the Greeks it was sometimes customary for the formula itself to be pronounced three times together with triple immersion, 354. Immersion was performed so that the entire body, including the head, was submerged, 384.

*Μέθεξις*, that is, “participation,” the fifth grade of penitents, who, after completing their penance, were admitted to participation in the Eucharist, 461.

It belongs to the metropolitan to place the crown on the king, 591. Why the metropolitan did not crown Henry IV, king of the French, 592.

The dedication of the church of Saint Michael the archangel on the third day before the Kalends of October, 134. Mass in honor of Saint Michael, ibid., 711. The Office of Saint Michael, 825.

Micrologus wrongly said that the words “and to all the orthodox” are not part of the canon of the Mass, 284.

A minister is someone initiated into the minor orders, 241, 556.

*Ministerium* is used for a vessel, 432. The splendid equipment of the sacred ministry—that is, the Church’s gold and silver vessels, 433, 467, 474. *Ministerium* also means an *abacus*, that is, a marble table holding chalices, ibid. The term *ministerium* is also used for carpets, hangings, and similar church ornaments, ibid. Whoever defrauds or neglects anything belonging to the church’s equipment is punished by canonical penalties, 467, 474.

What minor cases are, 468.

Miracles concerning the Eucharist, 563, 579.

The celebration of Masses was called by the name of the sacraments, 274.

The singular word *Missa*, used for the liturgical sacrifice of Christ’s body and blood, was employed by Saint Ambrose, 275. This word is usually taken in the plural by the holy Fathers, ibid.

Formerly the Mass began with psalmody, preceded by the censing of the altar and choir, 275. Before Pope Celestine, the Mass began with the readings, 276. There was not one uniform practice among all Churches concerning the beginning of Mass, ibid.

The ancient custom of praying for the faithful departed in the liturgical sacrifice of the Mass, 289. Formerly Masses were held at the ninth hour on days of partial fasting, 293.
