On fast days, in the evening, 324. On other days, at the third hour, ibid. In the time of the primitive Church, solemn Masses were celebrated at night, ibid.

The pontiff sometimes celebrated two Masses and sometimes one, out of devotion, 405. Formerly one priest was permitted to sing several Masses, ibid. On the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul, the pope celebrated two Masses: one at Saint Peter’s and the other at Saint Paul’s, ibid. Saint Leo prohibited the celebration of Mass being repeated by the same person on the same day, ibid. Nevertheless, if, because of the church’s limited capacity, the whole people could not attend the sacrifice, repetition was permitted, ibid. When the pope celebrates two Masses in one day, he does not wash between them, except after the office, 111, 405.

What the three Masses on the feast of Saint John the Baptist are to be understood as celebrating, 404.

Formerly only one Mass per day was to be celebrated in one church, 405.

The Mass of Saint Augustine for the living or the dead, 486. The Mass to prevent [people] from [turning] to idols, 300. What the reason was for instituting this Mass, ibid.

The Chrism Mass on Maundy Thursday, 327. One Mass said simultaneously by the pontiff and priests, 336, 337. Three Masses on Maundy Thursday, 327. Sometimes only two Masses, ibid.

The Mass of the Presanctified among the Greeks, 333.

It is forbidden to offer Mass for evil things, 468.

Defects in the Mass, or accidents concerning the Eucharist: by what canonical penalties they are punished, 468.

The Mass properly begins with the offertory, 526. In the Mass for a sick person, the Introit, Gradual, Offertory, and Communion are doubled, 554.

According to ancient custom, the prayer in the Mass is said before the preface, 564. The Greeks recite the prayer before the offering, but the Latins do not, 562. Formerly the mystical prayer before the consecration was recited aloud, 577.

Formerly there was one prayer in the Mass before the Gospel, 278. Among the Greeks there are five prayers before the peace, ibid.; according to Saint John Chrysostom, three, ibid.

The prayer “for completion” is not a blessing, 297.

The prayer for kings and emperors in the canon of the Mass, 284.

The Mozarabic Mass has a double elevation of the host: the first immediately after the consecration, 565. According to ancient custom, after the pontiff had said “Through him and with him,” the archdeacon raised the chalice and held it by its handles, elevated before the pontiff, ibid. The elevation of the host and chalice immediately after the consecration is not an ancient rite, ibid. The Greeks raise Christ’s body after the Lord’s Prayer, immediately before Communion, ibid. When the pontiff raised the holy bread, he said, “Holy things for the holy,” and Communion took place, 566. With the host elevated, the priest made the sign of the cross three times, 567. What the elevation of the host with the threefold sign of the cross signifies, ibid. The commingling of the Lord’s body and blood: what is called consecration, 568.

It is asserted, against the error of Flacius Illyricus, that formerly there were Masses of saints and feasts, 570, 571.

The order of prayers is called the method of celebrating Mass, 572. The canon is called the text of the canonical prayer, ibid.

Nearly the whole sacred action of the Mass is thanksgiving, 609.

What Mass is to be understood as being offered for the dead who desired penance but did not attain it, 610.

Masses: of Saint Cyprian, 416; of the dedication of a church, 437; celebrated for eight days, 438; of the dead, 481, 572; of Saint Jerome, 417; of Saint Martin, 406; of Saint Maurice and his companions, 416; of Saint Remigius, 417; of Saint Vedastus, 418; for a sick person, 551; for a sick person who is near death, 552; for kings, 556; the Mass published by Illyricus, 570. Formerly there was no single uniform manner of celebrating Mass, ibid.

[Col. 1442] What it means to receive Communion with the mixed sacrifice, 569. Formerly prohibited, ibid. In what case it was permitted, ibid. To receive Communion with the dry sacrifice means that Christ’s body is given separately from the blood, ibid.

Mithra—that is, the devil, the ape of the divine mysteries—marks his soldiers on their foreheads, 361.

The mitre was woven of wool, gold, and purple, 441. In addition to the veil, virgins used to adorn their heads with a mitre or *mittella*, ibid. This indicated that, having rejected the men of the world, they had married Christ, 442. A mitre is a Phrygian cap protecting the head, ibid. The mitre of the ancients was a crown composed of bands and *oraria*, 558. The ancient bishops did not know the use of the mitre, 557. When its use began in the Church, ibid. By misuse, every crown is called a mitre, 558. The modern mitres of pontiffs differ from those of the ancients, ibid.

Saint Modestus, 402.

Monks receiving Communion on the solemnity of Good Friday, 342. Monks ought not to eat outside the hour prescribed by the Rule, 455. They ought to accept nothing without permission, ibid.

Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, departs far from the heresy of the Monophysites, 382.

Mormanus the Breton was restrained after rebelling against the emperor Louis the Pious, 319.

Our death was destroyed in the manner of Christ’s death, 388. If a dying person, having requested penance, immediately loses the use of speech and reason, what the priest who arrives ought to do, 609.

Anyone who eats carrion or an animal that has been strangled is subject to canonical penalties, 469, 478.

A pregnant woman may fast if she wishes, 469.

The gifts (*Τὸ munera*) in the canon of the Mass: how it is distinguished from *τὸ dona et sacrificia*, 283.

Gifts or offerings presented by the faithful at the dedication of a church were consecrated by the bishops for its use, 432.

Some attribute to Musaeus, a presbyter of Marseille, the canon prayer “Therefore, O Lord” (*Te igitur*), 283. Musaeus composed an excellent volume of the sacraments, 571.

Self-mutilation: by what canonical penalties it is prohibited, 467, 474.

The priestesses of Ceres were girded with a myrtle crown during sacred rites, 558.

## N
## N

The letter N, commonly used in place of a proper name: when this practice began, 572. Formerly the sign *ill.* with a transverse line was customarily used, ibid. The feast of Saint Nabor the martyr, 105, 700. The nostrils smeared with spittle during the scrutiny of catechumens, 381. The anointing of the nostrils in confirmation among the Greeks, 361. In extreme unction the nostrils are anointed, 538, 541, 549, 555. The nostrils are to be anointed at the top and underneath, in the form of a cross, 549. The feast of a saint was often celebrated on the day of the translation of his relics, 407, 418. The feast of Saint Nazarius the martyr, 105, 700. Νεφοδεῶκται, in Latin *tempestarii*, that is, those who unleash storms, 472. The canonical penalties by which they are to be punished, ibid. Those who assert that magicians can unleash storms are punished by the canons, ibid. The feast of Saints Nereus, Achilleus, and Pancratius, martyrs, 87, 392, 694. The name of Saint Nicasius is recited in the canon of the Mass, 4, 116, 285. The Council of Nicaea did not abolish, in its fourth canon, the customary election of bishops by clergy and people, 511. [Col. 1443] Nicholas Thuanus, bishop of Chartres, consecrated Henry IV, king of the Franks, 592. He composed a book on the coronation of Henry IV, 584. He anointed the king with a heavenly liquid that an angel had formerly brought to Saint Martin, 589. The feast of Saint Nicomedes on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of October, 129, 710. On the Kalends of June, at Rome, the dedication of the basilica of Saint Nicomedes, priest and martyr, 103, 402, 699. The feast of Nicostratus on the sixth day before the Ides of November, 139, 421, 608. The black garments of virgins, 440. Nilammon was elected bishop by the citizens of the city of Geras, 508, 512. When he refused to accept his election, Theophilus of Alexandria urged him to request ordination from him, ibid. The monastery of Nobiliacum in the territory of Arras, to which the translation of Saint Vedast took place, 418. “Us sinners also,” formerly found more frequently in the Mass, 577. Names were formerly commonly given to infants and children not at baptism itself but before it, 350. For infants who were baptized on the eighth day of their life, or earlier, names appear to have been given at baptism itself, ibid. Formerly among the Romans names were given to males on the ninth day after birth and to females on the eighth, ibid. The Greeks gave names to infants on the tenth day after birth, ibid. The Franks gave names on the ninth day, 351. Names already given were sometimes changed at baptism, 352. The names of the living recited in the Mass after the consecration, 567. A register of the names of those to be baptized was made, 351. An altar dedicated by the invocation of the name of God, 430. The ninth hour: see *Hour*. The Northumbrians are the people of England, 587. “We give thanks to you always,” etc. From these words of the Preface begins the thanksgiving for all benefits received from God, 280. The sign *ill.* with a transverse line, customarily written in manuscripts in place of a proper name, 572. Notes are signs, or abbreviations of words, produced by a rapid scribe whose speed outstrips that of the language, 343. The ancient practice of writing with shorthand signs, 613. Notaries are the bishop’s scribes, generally chosen from the college of readers, 70, 343. Notaries are called *exceptores* because they take down abbreviated notes, ibid. A writer, that is, a scribe or rapid copyist, is called a notary because of his use of abbreviated signs, ibid., 613. The heretic Novatus, when he offered the Eucharist with his followers, required them by oath never to go over to Cornelius’s party, 580. Why newly married people are joined after the blessing by the bond of life, 598. What is signified by a ribbon mingled with white and purple, ibid. The naked, wearing only a little tunic, were exorcised, 377. What the number six signifies, 301. What the number seven signifies, ibid., 371, 385; what the number eight signifies, 300, 301; the number twelve, 312; the number sixty, 314. The method of counting, ibid. “Now the Powers [of heaven]”: when the people among the Greeks began to sing this, 333. Nundina, the goddess of the Romans, so called from the ninth day of those being born, 350. The celebration of marriage takes place according to ancient custom amid the solemnities of the Mass, 595. The ancients devoutly celebrated the thirtieth day and the anniversary of a marriage, 596; on this day they held the celebration, ibid. *Nuptiae* and *nubere* are derived from clouds, 598. *Obnubere* means to cover the head, and *nuptiae* is derived from covering the head, ibid. This civil custom was transferred from the Romans to the Christians, ibid. The nuptial blessing [Col. 1443] is given in the Mass after the Lord’s Prayer, 596. This custom of blessing marriages is ancient in the Church, ibid. The condition of marriage, 597; its necessity, ibid.

## O

The offerings to be consecrated on the altar were small, according to ecclesiastical custom, 564; round and circular in form, ibid. Round loaves, which are called offerings, ibid. The offering blessed with the sign of the cross, 287. Formerly, at the Mass, the faithful—both clergy and laity—who were going to receive Communion brought their offering, that is, bread and wine, to the altar for their own Communion, 174, 443, 509, 563. To receive Communion without an offering means to communicate through prayer and supplication, by attending the entire Mass with the faithful without receiving the Eucharist, 474. The ordaining bishop hands the newly ordained bishop the entire offering, that is, the consecrated host from which he communicates, 518. The same is done by the bishop for the priest whom he has ordained, 519. Offerings were of two kinds: some were to be consecrated as the Body of the Lord, others to be blessed for the use of the poor, 564. The offering to be consecrated on the altar must be a whole loaf, clean and carefully prepared, ibid. The prayers to be said by those presenting their offerings and by the ministers receiving them, 574. A king crowned during the Mass offers bread and wine so that he may receive Communion, 594. *Obnubere* means the same as *operire*, “to cover,” 598. The eighth day signifies the final day of the Resurrection and eternal happiness, 300. One and the same day is called the eighth day, 301. The Greeks call the octave ἀπόλυσις, that is, departure, 300. *Octavas*, used for *octava*, is indeclinable according to ancient usage, 389, 401. The Octave of the Nativity of Christ, 300; of Saint Benedict, 407; of Pentecost, 401. It coincides with the feast of the Most Holy Trinity, ibid. Controversy concerning which feast should be celebrated, ibid. The feast of Saint Octavius at Thessalonica, on the Kalends of June, 402. The seven eyes in one stone in the prophet Zechariah: what they signify, 372. In extreme unction the eyes are to be anointed on the eyebrows and eyelashes, near the corners, 549. Why Oedipus cursed his sons, 590. The Offertory, or offering, is an antiphon, 582. It is so called because, while it was sung, the people offered their gifts on the altar, 279. Why the Offertory is not sung in the Mass of Holy Saturday, 388. In Africa, in the time of Saint Augustine, a psalm was sung before the Offertory, 562. At what hour the Office on the Lord’s Supper was formerly begun, 324. The Office of Holy Thursday at the Lord’s Supper, 336. The elements composing the Divine Office, established according to ancient usage and retained to the present day, 730. The Divine Office must be performed devoutly and humbly, 489. It was customarily recited before the sick person after extreme unction, 554. A codex containing the Divine Office is called an *officiale*, 730. The Divine Office is called the *cursus*, ibid. The oil of the sick is consecrated immediately before the words of the canon, “Through whom you make all these things,” etc., 328, 337. Oil for anointing both the sick and the possessed is to be blessed by the bishop and by all priests, according to apostolic tradition, 337. It is consecrated in the very rite of consecrating the Body and Blood of the Lord, ibid. The oil of catechumens is blessed according to ancient custom, 331. The rite of consecrating the oil of catechumens, 339. The Fathers often use “oil” to mean ointment, or chrism, 385. The oil of sanctification is consecrated oil, 587. Kings are anointed with sacred oil, [Col. 1444] 589. The kings of the Franks were anointed with sacred oil sent from heaven, 588. The oil sent from heaven was mixed with chrism, ibid. What the branch of the olive tree with which the dove returned to the ark signifies, 330, 331. *Omittere* means the same as *dimittere*, 389, 531. Ὁμολογία, that is, the profession of virgins, 441. Ὠμοφόριον is called *pallium* by the Greeks, 520. The form of the omophorion and that of the pallium are not altogether the same, ibid. The omophorion, or shoulder-cloth, is an ornament common to all bishops, whatever their rank; it resembles an oblong towel, 525. What it signifies among patriarchs and archbishops, ibid. What it signifies among bishops, ibid. What the crosses on the omophorion signify, ibid. The bishop’s woolen shoulder-cloth, not a linen one, signifies the skin of the wandering sheep which the Lord carried on his shoulders, ibid. *Optimum* means “good,” according to Greek usage, 443. Every good thing, at whatever level, belongs to God and comes from God, ibid. Christians pray with uncovered heads, 317. Pagans pray with covered heads, ibid. Those praying turn toward the East, 328. *Oraria* are certain oblong textiles, 558. An *orarium* is an oblong cloth, like the cloth laid beneath those who adore the cross, 340, 607. An *orarium* is what we commonly call a stole, 503, 607. A priest may not celebrate Mass or approach Communion without an *orarium* hanging from both shoulders, ibid. In his ordination the *orarium* is placed around the deacon’s left shoulder, 521. The Lord’s Prayer is recited over Christ’s Body according to ancient and apostolic custom, 291. According to ancient custom, after the commemoration of the dead in all liturgies, the Lord’s Prayer follows, ibid. What the priest formerly added to the Lord’s Prayer, ibid. The Lord’s Prayer contains the completeness of prayers, 365, and everything pertaining to the ordering of present and future life, ibid. Why the Lord’s Prayer is called perilous, 468, 476. With what reverence priests formerly recited the Lord’s Prayer in the Mass, ibid. The solemn prayers of Wednesday and Friday in Holy Week were formerly said some interval before Mass, 323, 606. At the eighth hour, that is, the second hour after noon, they enter for Mass, 64, 323. In the solemn prayer the bishop names the Apostolic See; priests name their own bishop, 69. The inclination to implore or pray is attributed by God, 179, 444. Without God’s grace no one can implore, ibid. A prayer is said in the Mass before the Preface, according to ancient custom, 564.

The Missal Prayer is the prayer that follows the Angelic Hymn in the Mass, 571. The order of prayers is the method of celebrating the Mass, 572. The Greeks recite a prayer before the offering; the Latins do not, 562. The mystical prayer before the consecration was formerly recited aloud, 577. The prayer of the laying on of hands, 464. The priest’s prayer before he receives the penitent, 463. Formerly there was only one prayer in the Mass before the Gospel, 278. The five prayers among the Greeks before the peace, ibid.; three according to Saint John Chrysostom, ibid. The Prayer at the Dismissal is not a blessing, 297. The prayer for kings and emperors in the canon, 284. The prayer for the empire of the Romans and Franks, 322. Prayers for imposing penance, 464. The seven prayers for the reconciliation of penitents, 458. The conclusion of a prayer, 295. The prayer to be said before extreme unction is administered, 548. The prayer said between the anointings, 555. The prayers to be said after the anointings have been completed, 556. The prayer of completion, to be said after the viaticum has been given, 551. The order for blessing the sacred orders, 219. Which ministers of the Church are ordained among the Latins, Greeks, Maronites, and others, ibid. Why all orders, both minor and major, are called sacred, 487. Long usage has established that some orders are called sacred and others not sacred, ibid. Formerly the major orders were conferred before the Gospel and the minor orders after Communion, 219. Today the minor orders are conferred first and the major orders afterward, 487. Formerly the minor orders could be conferred on Sundays, but this custom has long since fallen into disuse, ibid. The major orders were conferred on the Ember Saturdays—that is, at the beginning of Saturday evening, when Sunday begins—according to the ancient custom of the Church, ibid., and also on Sunday morning, with the Saturday fast continued, ibid. Sacred ordination should be conferred on those fasting, ibid. Why the sacred orders should be conferred on Sunday morning with the Saturday fast continued, 488. The present practice of conferring the major and minor orders together on the Ember Saturdays is ancient, ibid. The rite of conferring orders according to the Greeks, 521.

Sacred orders are not repeated when degraded persons receive the restoration of their instruments, 501. The essential matter of the sacred orders of the diaconate, priesthood, and episcopate is the laying on of hands alone, 504, 505. The handing over of the instruments is accessory, 506. This is the common opinion of the modern Parisian school, ibid. It does not conflict with the opinion of Pope Eugene IV in his decree to the Armenians, ibid. The Roman Church has never disapproved the sacred ordinations of the Greeks, which are performed by the laying on of hands alone, 504. Certain ordinations are invalidated in which the bishop laid on hands while the priest pronounced the blessing, that is, the form, 505. The consecrating bishop impresses the sign of the cross upon ministers being ordained to sacred orders, 515.

The conduct of those to be ordained was formerly examined carefully, 497. Their character and ability were investigated, ibid. They were ordained in the presence of the people, ibid. They were not ordained without a title, 496. The bishop is the priest of the first order; the presbyter of the second; the deacon of the third, 519.

The Roman Order that now exists is ancient, 458. Nevertheless, certain things have been removed from it, while others have been changed and added, ibid.

The order of prayers, 571. “Let us pray to the Lord” is customarily said among the Greeks, 321. It is sung by the deacon, not by the priest, ibid. On Wednesday and Friday of Holy Week the priest not only says “Let us pray,” but also announces for whom prayer is to be made, ibid. The practice of the Easterners in observing Lent, 315, 316. It is an ancient custom of the Church, derived from the apostles, that Christians praying should turn their faces toward the East, 328. Why Christians pray facing East, 329. Sacred buildings generally face East, ibid. The ancient orthography of certain Latin names that imitate the Greek language, and of others, 612–616. “Hosanna in the highest,” 2, 282. A kiss may be simple or seductive; it may be without defilement or with defilement, 468. What the canonical penalty for a seductive kiss is, ibid. It is not permitted to give the Eucharist or a kiss to the dead, 485. The pontiff, immediately before receiving Communion, gives the kiss of peace according to the rite of the Latin Church, 567. The Greeks give the kiss of peace before the Preface, ibid. At what point in the Mass the Spaniards formerly gave the kiss of peace, ibid. The metropolitan kisses the anointed king, 594. Henry IV kissed the pontiff and the peers of France, ibid. At the entrance of the Mass the pontiff kisses all, or at least the priests and deacons standing around him, 560. The priests and deacons kiss the pontiff’s hands, ibid. The doorkeepers: at what point in the Mass they are ordained, 487. The rite of ordaining doorkeepers, 219. Mention of doorkeepers in the ancient Fathers, 488. The duties of a doorkeeper, 489. The bishop of Ostia, according to ancient custom, consecrates the supreme pontiff, 517, as being closer to the Roman See, according to custom, ibid. The bishop of Ostia recites the third prayer in the consecration of the emperor, 586. He anoints the emperor’s left arm and the space between his shoulders, ibid. “For yours is the kingdom,” etc., added to the Lord’s Prayer, 291. Otto, archbishop of Bamberg, when near death, received the three sacraments in this order: penance, extreme unction, and finally the viaticum of the Lord’s Body, 536. The blessing of eggs, 565.

## P
### P

**To make peace**, in the canon of the Mass. We beseech God for the common peace of the Churches, 283.

The covenants made with God in baptism, both by those already baptized and by those preparing for baptism, must always be kept before their eyes, 368. How they are invalidated, ibid. These covenants are two, ibid. How they are to be observed, ibid.

The corporals, or corporal cloths, were formerly so large that they wrapped both Christ’s body and the chalice itself, 431. See *Chrismal*. The palls in the *substratorium* are cloths, or altar palls, 495. Some cloths are corporals, others altar cloths, ibid. The *substratorium* consists of coarser fabrics laid on the altar beneath the altar cloths, ibid. By whom and in what vessel the corporals are to be washed, 222, 495. Where the corporals have been washed, no other linen is to be washed, ibid.

Description of the pallium, 520. Among the Greeks it is called **ὠμοφόριον** (*omophorion*), ibid. The form of the pallium and the omophorion is not entirely the same, ibid. Formerly there were no crosses on the pallium, ibid.

The feast of Palms, 318. The Sunday of Palm Branches, 60. The solemnity of Palms is extremely ancient; in it a procession is made with blessed branches of trees, 318. The palm tree is a symbol of victory, 593. What the palm of the hand signifies, 592.

Pamelius published the book *Sacramenta*, Preface III, and *Liturgica*, ibid., and VI.

The Mass of Saint Pancratius the martyr, 87, 392, 694. Blessing of bread, 234, 533. Bread dipped in the chalice and given to the people in communion, 583. The elevation of the bread and chalice in the Mass, 565; in the form of a cross, 567. What kind of bread is required for the Eucharist, 564.

Saint Pantaleon, 116.

The Pantheon at Rome was converted by Pope Boniface IV into a church of Saint Mary and All the Martyrs, 392. This Pantheon had been built by Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa, ibid. Why it was called by this name, ibid. Formerly, in the village of Bethelia near Gaza in Palestine, there was also a temple called by this name, 393. Formerly at Athens there was a temple dedicated by the emperor Hadrian in common to all the gods, ibid.

The rite for ordaining popes, 517. The pope is ordained by the bishop of Ostia, as the one nearer to Rome, according to the custom of the Roman Church, 518. The *phrygium* is the pope’s tiara, 442. The pope is the primate of all [Col. 1446] priests throughout the world, 226, 518. The pope’s “birthday” is the day on which he was promoted to the pontificate, 520. The supreme pontiffs and bishops customarily celebrated this day solemnly every year, ibid. The pope’s name is ordered and customarily recited in the canon of the Mass, 577. When the pope celebrates two Masses in one day, 405.

What papyrus, customarily used for lamps, is, 346. Papyrus in candles, ibid.

The earthly Paradise is in the East, 329. *Parasceve* is the Friday of every week, 470. Washing the walls of a church, 342.

Saint Parmenas the deacon, 305.

The Parthenon Codex of Cales, Preface IV.

The apostles are called “partakers,” 398.

The annual, that is, anniversary, Pascha is so called because on that day of the following year after baptism the memory of baptism is solemnly celebrated with baptismal offerings, 390. This Pascha appears to have been celebrated after the Sunday *in albis*, ibid.

Paschal observance is the Lenten fast, 315. Why the fasts are called Paschal, ibid., 316. To fast Pascha—that is, Lent—ibid. The Paschal sacrament of Christ’s body and blood is called an eternal remedy, 317. “That we may possess the Paschal mystery perpetually,” 91, 393. Formerly the solemnity of Pascha began at sunset itself, that is, on the evening of Holy Saturday, 398.

The ancient custom of reading the Passion in church during Holy Week, 324.

Formula for the consecration of a paten, 151. The paten is consecrated with the sign of the cross, using holy oil or chrism, ibid.

Godparents answer the questions on behalf of infants who have not yet attained the use of reason, 352. Adults who have been baptized place their foot upon the foot of their godparent, 357. Godparents are those who present candidates for baptism and receive the baptized from the sacred font, ibid. They are called “receivers” and “sponsors,” ibid. What obligations they have toward their godchildren, ibid.

The name of Saint Paul the apostle is recited in the canon of the Mass, 3, 4. His Conversion and Mass, 22. It is said that Saint Paul’s name was changed on the day of his Conversion, 306. Saint Paul taught the whole world by his preaching, 305. “Thrown into chains seven times . . . he received the reward of patience,” ibid. “That radiance shone from Jerusalem . . . even to the ends of the earth,” ibid. The nativity of Saint Paul, the day before the Kalends of July, 113, 702, 808. Since formerly the two solemnities of the apostles Peter and Paul were celebrated together, Saint Gregory is said to have composed a Translation of Paul, 405.

—Saint Paul the martyr. See John.

—Saint Paul of Constantinople was first a lector and notary of that Church, 343.

Paul of Samosata, because he had established a lofty throne for himself in the church, was rebuked by the bishops for his vanity, 340.

**Peace be with you.** This is the formula used by the pontiff in greeting, especially in sacred rites, 326. Sometimes *Pax vobiscum*, “Peace be with you,” sometimes *Pax omnibus*, “Peace to all”; the latter formula is said to be the proper one, ibid. The former is the Latin formula, the latter the Greek, 327. Formerly the Spanish used the greeting formula *Dominus sit vobiscum*, “The Lord be with you,” ibid. A bishop says *Pax vobiscum* only on feast days, ibid. When the bishop greets the people with *Pax vobis*, “Peace be with you,” the people respond, *Et spiritui tuo*, “And with your spirit,” 387.

—The pontiff gives the kiss of peace immediately before receiving communion, according to the rite of the Latin Church, 567. The Greeks give the kiss of peace before the preface, the mystical prayers, and the consecration, ibid., 568. The ancient Church of Spain followed the Greek rite, 568. The kiss of peace signifies the benefit of our faith, 258.

[Col. 1447] To sin is one thing through sloth, another through malice, another knowingly, another ignorantly, another negligently, another arrogantly, 367. Why every sin can be called pride, 367. Whoever scorns repentance after sin plunges himself into the great abyss of pride, ibid. How sins committed after baptism are forgiven, 369.

—**Original sin** is called a transmitted fault, that is, one which passed from the first parent to his descendants, 426.

The customary striking of the breast upon hearing the words *Confiteor*, “I confess,” 559. Anointing of the breast in catechumens, 331; in extreme unction, 553; in confirmation among the Greeks, 361. The feet are to be anointed above and beneath the soles in extreme unction, making the sign of the cross, 549.

The Pelagians refuted from the Book of Sacraments, Preface VI. Decree of Pelagius II concerning the preface, 294.

Pentecost is so called as the feast of the fiftieth day, 400. According to the ancient institution of the Church, baptism was administered during the vigils of Pascha and Pentecost, 398. Formerly the day of Pentecost, like Pascha, began to be celebrated after Saturday evening, 400. There was formerly controversy in Gaul concerning the celebration of the eighth day of Pentecost, 401. In the vigil of Pentecost: the litany; then *Confitemini*, etc., 696.

“World without end.” This is an ancient formula of prayer among Christians, 294.

The various punishments of a striker, according to the circumstances of the person, 467, 474. Whoever, through anger or quarrelling, strikes someone and makes him disabled or disfigured is, besides paying damages and the physician’s expenses, subject to canonical penalties, ibid.

To be pardoned, that is, to be granted, 257, 584.

*Perennare* used transitively means the same as *perpetuare*, that is, to make something last forever, 531. Elsewhere it is used intransitively, ibid.

*Peripsema*, or *peripsima*, means metal filings, fruit peelings, household refuse, and scrapings of any object—in short, whatever is trampled under everyone’s feet, 527, 615.

Peristeria, a most illustrious woman of Alexandria, gave money for the relief of the poor and incense to be offered to God, 429.

The punishment prescribed by the canons for perjurers, 466.

To permit, that is, to let go, 148, 426.

The memory of Saints Perpetua and Felicity is made in the canon of the Mass after the consecration, 4. Their nativity is celebrated on the Nones of March, 310, 312.

Saint Perpetuus, bishop of Tours, built a church over the tomb of Saint Martin, 406.

To pertain, that is, to reach, 174, 444.

Stones were boundaries of fields, and formerly people worshiped them as boundary-gods, 311. Those who go to certain stones—who knows what stones—which do not belong to the Church are censured, ibid.

—**Πέτρος** (*Petros*) among the Greeks also means “rock,” 405. The Latin *Petrus* is correctly derived from the Greek, ibid.

The name of Saint Peter is recited in the canon of the Mass, 3, 4. In the vigil of Saints Peter and Paul, two Masses are assigned: one of Saint Leo, the other of the vigil, 405, 702. On the feast itself the pope also celebrated two Masses, one at Saint Peter’s and the other at Saint Paul’s, ibid. Office of the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul, 806. On the Kalends of August, at Saint Peter *ad Vincula*, 705. His chains are kissed on that day, 409. The Chair of Saint Peter, 29, 665. See *Chair*. The crown of Saint Peter, 449. “God granted Peter primacy in the citadel of the Roman name,” 605. “God entrusted to Peter the pontifical power of binding and loosing souls,” ibid. “Peter received primacy among the very leaders of the faith,” 637. Dedication of the church of Saint Peter *ad Vincula*, 409.

—Peter of Alexandria was chosen bishop in place of Saint Athanasius by the clergy and people, 512.

—The nativity of Saint Peter the martyr, 104, 699.

—Peter of Clermont, bishop, consulted Maurice of Paris and Stephen of Tournai, bishops, concerning the validity of a certain baptismal formula, 354.

—Peter the Fuller, a heretic, added to the *Trisagion*: “Who was crucified for us,” 282. By this he introduced a fourth person into the mystery of the most holy Trinity, or asserted that the Trinity was crucified for us, ibid.; he also maintained with the Manichaeans that the Holy Spirit had been crucified, ibid.

**Φαινόλης**, or **φελόνης**. The *phaenolium* is a type of pallium, a *paenula* or outer garment worn over the *sticharion*, that is, the close-fitting tunic, 523. The patriarch’s *phaenolium* was white and covered with many crosses, whence it was also called **Πολυσταύριον** (*polystaurion*), ibid.

The name of the apostle Philip is recited in the canon of the Mass, 3. The office of Saint Philip, in which this apostle appears to be confused with Philip the deacon, 795.

—Philip Augustus, king of the Franks, was consecrated with chrism by William, archbishop of Reims, 591. This metropolitan placed a golden crown on the king’s head, ibid.

Philo, bishop of Cyrene, did not validly ordain Siderius bishop of Palaebisca, 508.

*Philtra* are enchantments by which the love of women and boys is attracted, 472.

The *phrygium* is called the mitre or tiara of the supreme pontiff, 442. It is said to be an imperial ornament resembling a helmet and encircled by a golden band, ibid.

Phylacteries, or amulets and ligatures, worn on the arms, legs, and neck, 473.

Piety permits the person whom it has filled to overflow with works of mercy, 372. Piety is useless if it lacks the discernment of knowledge, ibid.

Pippin, king of the Franks, was crowned and covered with sacred anointing by Saint Boniface, bishop and martyr, 587. Pippin is called “Most Christian,” 591. Pippin and his two sons were anointed kings of the Franks by Pope Stephen III, ibid.

Formerly it was forbidden to eat a dead fish found in a river, 478.

**Πισσόκηρον** (*pissokeron*) is pitch mixed with wax, 426.

**Planet.** See *Chasuble*.

Plato was not unfamiliar with Hebrew matters, 301.

The fullness of the sacred gift is grace, which the Eucharist confers fully and abundantly, 33, 314.

Pluto was called the god Februus, 306.

The *podium*, or *pogium*, is a lectern or reading stand in the church, approached by steps, 785.

How penitents are to be received by bishops and priests, 462. A prayer is made for penitents after the catechumens have been dismissed, once they have received the laying on of hands, and they themselves depart, 278. Ashes are placed on the heads of penitents and they are purified with blessed water, according to ancient custom, 450. Penitents are clothed in sackcloth, ibid. Sackcloth is the garment of penitents, ibid. Penitents used to let their hair and beards grow, ibid. Why among the Goths a contrary rite was prescribed for penitents in a council, 451. Penitents are expelled from the Church while the clergy sing the responsory, “In sweat,” etc., according to ancient custom, ibid.

—[Col. 1448] By what rite penitents are reconciled on Holy Thursday, 457. At what part of the Mass absolution was formerly given to penitents, 458. Bishops and priests used to weep with weeping penitents, 463, 470. Fasts to be imposed on penitents as satisfaction, 463. They must add other fasts to those imposed upon them, whether tetrads or *parasceves*, that is, Wednesdays or Fridays, ibid. Penitents fasting throughout the week do not fast on Sunday at Rome, nor on Saturday among the Greeks, 464, 471. If one who has not repented wishes to receive communion while ill, holy communion is to be given to him, and he is to be instructed that, if he recovers his health, he must confess everything and then repent, 469. Penitents are excluded from the clergy, 491. If necessity compels, they may be admitted among the doorkeepers or readers, but in such a way that they may read neither the Apostle nor the Gospel, ibid. Formerly extreme unction was not administered to penitents, to whom no sacrament was given, 532. This practice was later changed, ibid. Bishops and priests, to whom the keys of the heavenly kingdom have been entrusted, alone ought to hear the cases of penitents, 629. If necessity arises in the absence of a priest, a deacon is to receive a penitent to holy Communion, 638.

The manner of imposing penance, 464. The order of penance, 463. What penance was, and how great a penance was imposed on competent catechumens, 369. Among the Greeks it lasted forty days, 380. These days appear to have begun somewhat before the Lenten fast, ibid. During these days the *competentes* confessed all the sins of their former life, 381. This confession was not sacramental, ibid. There was another penance for catechumens if they happened to have committed a capital crime during the period of their catechumenate, ibid.

The reason for undertaking public penance, 449. This undertaking of penance takes place through the laying on of hands on Wednesday morning at the beginning of Lent, ibid. Several orders for imposing penance and reconciling penitents, 214. The four celebrated stages of penance are weeping, hearing, prostration, and standing, 461. The duties of each of these stages, ibid.

The anointing of the sick was the sacrament of public penance in the time of Ivo of Chartres, 532. Pardon in penance is to be obtained through true contrition, 610. Neither Esau nor Antiochus obtained it, ibid.

The Penitential of Halitgar, 462. Formerly there was a great abundance of penitential books, 213. Through these the priestly rites of confession and absolution were taught, ibid. There were two Roman penitentials, 462. The penitential books of Theodore, bishop of the English, and of Bede, ibid. Among the many penitential books, the bishop should teach which one is to be followed, ibid.

The *pogium* is the place of the screens separating the sanctuary from the choir, ibid. The *pogium* is so called because it rises gradually by steps, ibid.

Anointing of the thumb takes place in the consecration of a bishop, 517.

**Πολυσταύριον** (*polystaurion*) is the garment covered with many crosses, such as the patriarch’s *phaenolium*, 523.

Polygamy is permitted, but polygamists are marked by irregularity, 476. Fasts are imposed upon them as penance, 469, 476. At Rome a surviving man who had survived twenty wives took as wife a surviving woman who had had twenty-two husbands, ibid.

Why Polynices and Eteocles were devoted to curses by their father Oedipus, 590.

The person being baptized renounces the pomps of Satan, [Col. 1449] 367. How the devil’s pomp is distinguished from his works, ibid. The pomps of the devil are ambition, arrogance, and similar vices proceeding from pride, ibid., 384. The pomps of the devil are interpreted as spectacles: the licentiousness of the theater, the cruelty of the amphitheater, and the shouting and madness of the circus, 383.

The Milvian Bridge should be understood by the name Bridge of Olbi, or Molbi, 391.

The pontiff does not pray for himself in the solemn prayers of Wednesday and Friday of Holy Week, 321. The pontiff’s ornaments, and how many they are, 573. While the pontiff is being vested in his ornaments, the clergy standing around him, or even the pontiff himself, sing the psalms “How lovely,” etc., ibid.

Supreme pontiffs were formerly called bishops, 502.

*Pontificium* means power or authority, 312, 405.

The people (*τὸ* “people”) sometimes means the whole assembly, whether ecclesiastical or lay, 277. Formerly the people prayed when *Flectamus genua*, “Let us bend the knees,” had been said, 321. The people’s right in the election of bishops, 511. What the people’s communion was like, 583. The people’s departure from Mass did not take place before the blessing, 297.

The bishop of Porto gives the second prayer at the consecration of the supreme pontiff, 517. At the emperor’s coronation he likewise delivers the second prayer, 586.

**Postcommunion**, or *postcommunionem*, also called the prayer *ad Complendum*, “for completion,” and *ad collectam*, “for the collect,” 604, 606. It resembles the prayer said over the people, ibid. This prayer is called the postcommunion because it is customarily said only for those who have received communion, 606.

The nativity of Saint Potentiana the virgin, 88, 695.

“Admonished by saving precepts,” etc. The antiquity of this formula preceding the Lord’s Prayer, 290.

The holy preachers are called “the heavens,” which declare the glory of God, 372.

The preface is a prayer, or thanksgiving, placed before the canon, 294. It is also called a *contestatio*, *contestada*, and *immolatio*, ibid. Pope Pelagius II selected nine prefaces from among many; two were later added, ibid. *Preface* is used in two ways: first, for the preface customarily placed before the canon of the Mass; second, for the invitation to prayer pronounced by the priest, 480. Preface of the Holy Trinity, 401; of Saint Augustine, 412.

Women formerly called *praeficae* were employed at funerals to weep, etc., 476. The *praeficae* were leaders of the lamentation, ibid. This madness was prohibited by Roman laws, 477.

Saint Praejectus, bishop, was slaughtered at Clermont together with Abbot Amarinus by the local nobles, 306. His feast and Mass coincide with the Conversion and Mass of Saint Paul, 23. His feast is a double feast in Gaul, ibid.

On Good Friday of Holy Week the priest uses the pre-sanctified gifts, both for himself and in giving communion to the whole people, 333. The Greeks use the pre-sanctified gifts throughout Lent, except on Sundays, Saturdays, and the feast of the Annunciation, ibid. They customarily transfer the birthdays of martyrs occurring during Lent to these days, ibid. Among the liturgies of the Greeks there is the liturgy of the Pre-sanctified, ibid. By what rite the pre-sanctified gifts are brought to the altar, ibid.

*Praesidium* means the property one possesses in movable goods, 466, 472. A household of both sexes, that is, male and female slaves, 472.

The nativity of Saint Praxedes, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of August, 116, 407, 704. In the first prayer of the Mass she is called a martyr, 407.

[Col. 1449] **Presbyter.** What a presbyter must know before he is ordained, 273. The concern and charity of the presbyter toward repentant sinners, 463. After hearing the penitent’s confession, he should immediately impose penance upon him, 463. The ordination of presbyters takes place immediately before the Epistle, 487. Formerly no wandering presbyters—that is, presbyters not assigned to a definite church—were ordained, 496. The rite for ordaining a presbyter, 224, 502. A presbyter is forbidden to celebrate Mass or receive communion without the stole hanging from his neck, 503. He receives this stole, called the *orarium*, at his ordination, ibid. He is vested with the *planeta*, or chasuble, at his ordination, 503. At their ordination presbyters’ hands are anointed with holy chrism, ibid. Formerly this anointing was done in the form of a cross, ibid. In some places the presbyter’s head was also anointed, 504. A presbyter is ordained through the laying on of hands, ibid., 522. In certain manuscripts the delivery of the paten with the host placed upon it, and of the chalice with wine and water, is ordered with this formula: “Receive,” etc., ibid. There is no mention of this delivery of the instruments in the holy Fathers, councils, Scriptures, or ancient manuscripts, ibid. The Eastern Church to this day knows nothing of the delivery of the instruments, ibid. Presbyters are consecrated by prayer, 509. The order of presbyteral ordination among the Greeks, 521.

—How a presbyter formerly announced the prayer, 321. How the presbyter’s feet and hands are anointed in extreme unction, 549. The dignity of the presbyterate, 499. Several presbyters employed in administering the sacrament of extreme unction, 540.

The nativity of Saints Primi and Felicianus, martyrs, on the fifth day before the Ides of June, 104, 699.

The ruler is anointed on the right arm and between the shoulders, 589.

The nativity of Saint Prisca the virgin, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February, 20, 662.

The nativity of Saint Priscus the martyr, on the Kalends of September, 413. This Saint Priscus the martyr was one of the seventy-two disciples of Christ and suffered at Capua, on the Via Aquaria, ibid.

“On behalf of whom we offer to you” (*Pro quibus tibi offerimus*) is not part of the ancient canon, 284. Custom prevailed that the missals should read, “On behalf of whom . . . or who offer to you,” ibid.

*Probabilis* means the same as *bonus*, “good,” 493.

*Procedere* means “to assemble at the church,” according to the ancient expression, 414. The reasons for processions among ancient Christians, ibid.

A procession is the assembly of clergy accompanying the pontiff himself to the altar and assisting him, 559, 563. *Processio* means the same as *collecta*, that is, the assembly of those proceeding when they have arrived at the church, 308, 345. “To the procession,” that is, to the *collecta*, synaxis, or assembly, 413. Processions, or solemn walks, purifications—commonly called supplications or rogations—were not practiced in the earliest centuries of the Church, 414. They began at Constantinople in the time of Saint Chrysostom, ibid. Procession with palms, 318.

Saint Processus, 114, 703.

Proclus, patriarch of Constantinople, was not the author of the singing of the victory hymn “Holy, Holy,” etc., in the sacred liturgy, 281. The same Proclus crowned Theodosius the Younger emperor, 583.

The profession of a virgin, called in Greek **ὁμολογία** (*homologia*), at what age it formerly took place, 441. The assumption of the veil is distinct from profession, ibid.

Profuturus, bishop of Barcelona. See Preface.

Projectus, Saint. See Praejectus.

The bishop’s promise, 510.

[Col. 1450] The pronunciation of certain Latin names following Greek usage, and of others, 612, 613, 614.

The anointing of prophets is mentioned in Holy Scripture, 331.

The prophetic reading preceding the reading of the Epistle, 561.

**Πρόῤῥησις** (*prorrhesis*), that is, preface or *contestada*, 294.

**Πρόσκλαυσις** (*prosklausis*), that is, weeping, the first stage of penitents, 461.

The feast of Saints Protasius and Gervasius is celebrated on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July, 108, 403, 700. The name Protasius is sometimes placed before the name Gervasius, 403.

The nativity of Saints Protus and Hyacinthus, on the third day before the Ides of September, 128, 415, 709.

What role the *protopapas* performs when the emperor of Constantinople washes the feet of twelve poor men on Maundy Thursday, 336. The *protopapas* is the defender, the first of the altar, and one holding the second rank after the high priest, 524. The emperor also had his own *protopapas*, ibid. Sometimes one *protopapas* presided over both clergy, ibid.

When Saint Prudentius the bishop was celebrating Mass, water was miraculously changed into wine, 563.

Many psalms are sung at the dedication of a church, according to ancient custom, 427. The nocturnal office of the dedication consists of twelve psalms, each with its antiphon, according to the rule of Saint Benedict, 145. These psalms are not taken from the weekday office but selected from different weekdays, ibid. From this the meaning of chapter 14 of the same rule becomes clear: “Except that the psalms,” etc., ibid., 744.

At the end of each psalm sung before the tomb during funeral rites, a prayer or collect is inserted, according to ancient custom, 486.

A psalm sung in place of the gradual, 561. Sung before the oblation, 562. Sung during communion, 570.

The ordination of a psalmist according to the Greeks, 521.

Formerly psalmody began the Mass, 275. Formerly an entire psalm was sung at the entrance of the Mass, ibid. The use of psalms before the oblation, and when it began at Carthage, 276.

The nativity of Saint Pudentiana the virgin, 88.

A boy, caught up into heaven, brought down the *Trisagion*, 282.

Boys who speak among themselves about catamite fornication and transgress the institutions of their elders are to be corrected by three “superpositions,” 468, 475.

Boys of good character are to be subjected to the ecclesiastical yoke through tonsure, 490.

*Pugillaria*, or *pugillares*, are wax or wooden tablets on which one writes with a stylus, 602. Some are called five-fold, or *pentatycha*; others three-fold, or *triptycha*, etc., ibid. A two-leaved writing tablet is called a diptych, ibid.

The pulpit of a church, or reading platform, is an elevated place from which lectors read and psalmists sang, 347.

A pure host in the canon of the Mass, 289.

The Purification of the Blessed Virgin Mary, which the Greeks call **ὑπαπάντη** or **ὑπαντή**, that is, “meeting,” 24, 306, 664. It is also called the feast of Simeon, ibid. According to ancient custom, why supplications or processions with burning candles are held on this feast, ibid., 307. When the Purification began to be celebrated at Byzantium, ibid. When it was instituted in the Church, ibid. This feast did not arise from the occasion of the Lupercalia, ibid. It was instituted on the occasion of the purification of the city that was performed at Rome, ibid. On this feast the responsory “Rejoice, Mary,” etc., is sung according to ancient usage, 730.

The king is vested in royal purple by the pontiff, 593. Pope Leo III vested Charlemagne in purple, ibid.

[Col. 1451] Q

The complete fast of Lent is enjoined, 314. Some did not observe the Saturday fast during Lent, ibid. In compensation for the Saturdays and Sundays, they began their fasts at Sexagesima, ibid. In the time of Saint Gregory the Great, Lent consisted of only thirty-six days of fasting to be observed, 315. Four days were later added by the Church to the Lenten fast, ibid. Nevertheless, Christians were always said in the Church to fast Lent. Among Eastern Christians, who did not fast on Sundays and Saturdays, they observed seven weeks and were said to fast Lent, ibid. Those among the Greeks who fasted forty complete days extended Lent over eight weeks, 316. Formerly the manner of the Lenten fast was not uniform either among Catholics or among heretics, ibid. How Lent was fasted at Constantinople in the time of Saint Chrysostom, ibid. The Lenten fast is called the Paschal observance, and to fast Pascha means to fast Lent, 315, 316.

Lent before the Nativity of the Lord, 445. The Lent of the catechumens, 380. The three Lents, called the three lawful fasts, enjoined during the year, 445. The later Greeks adopted a Lent before the Nativity of the Lord, 446. See *Advent*.

The fourfold mass of sins consists of the four principal sins, 55, 317.

Those married four times, marked by the canons, are barred from every ecclesiastical assembly and from entry into the temple, 476.

The Four Crowned Saints are Severus, Severianus, Victorinus, and Carpophorus, 139, 420, 421.

The number fifty as a mystical number, 386.

Except on the days of the fifty-day period—that is, from Pascha to Pentecost—it is permissible to impose an addition, that is, to add one fast to another, 475.

Why presbyters are forbidden to prescribe a sixtieth or fiftieth day, 314.

The nativity of Saint Quintus Paul, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of February, 304.

Saint Quintinus, 4, 831.

### R

Radulphus, count of Bayeux, whose son was John, bishop of Avranches, 581.

Radulphus, uterine brother of Richard the Elder, duke of Normandy, ibid.

*Ratum* in the canon of the Mass means “permanent with immovable firmness,” 286.

*Rationabilem* in the canon of the Mass means “full of reason and mystery,” 287.

The *rationale* is a certain episcopal breast ornament, like that formerly worn by the lawful priests, 557.

The reconciliation of penitents takes place on Holy Thursday, 324, 325. Reconciliation is the shorter form of administering extreme unction to a sick person who is near death, 550, 554. The prayers for reconciling a penitent at death are to be said by several priests, 548. The reconciliation of a sick person takes place after extreme unction and before communion, 550.

*Rectum* means the rectitude of the kingdom, 584.

The work of our redemption is performed as often as the memorial of the divine host is celebrated in the Mass, 175, 444.

Redemptus, a cleric of Saint Isidore, bishop of Seville, committed his confession to writing and, with death impending, made it public; it specified nothing in detail, 452.

*Reformare* means the same as “to restore,” 457.

The “refugee virtues” are apostate angels, or demons, 332.

[Col. 1451] Kings were established by anointing among the Israelites, 331. In common usage kings are anointed not with chrism but with sacred oil, 589. They are anointed on the crown of the head, ibid., in the form of a cross, ibid. Kings are crowned by metropolitans, 591. The kings of the Franks are anointed with chrism and heavenly liquid, 588. A prayer for kings, emperors, and princes exists in all liturgies according to ancient custom, 284. Antiphons and responsories for the reception of kings, 852.

The authority of the king in the election of bishops, 511.

*Regia* signifies “Janna,” 304.

The Codex of the Queen of Sweden containing the Book of Sacraments, Prefaces III and IV.

—The queen’s head is not anointed at her coronation, but her right arm is, 595. Queens Claudia, Eleanor, and Catherine de’ Medici were anointed on the head, ibid. What the queen’s role is in the kingdom, 595. By whom the queen ought to be crowned, ibid.

Reginald de Beaune, archbishop of Bourges and nominated by the king to the see of Sens: why he yielded to the bishop of Chartres the right to consecrate Henry IV, 592.

The increase of the heavenly kingdom, that is, of the honor and worship of God, by which God reigns in the faithful soul, 416.

Saint Regulus, bishop, 83.

Reinaldus, bishop of Langres, is not the author of the hymn *Gloria laus*, 320.

The rite for bringing relics into a new basilica, 434. The bishop and clergy keep vigil in the old church before the relics that are to be placed in the new one at its dedication, 423. The relics are transferred to the new church in solemn procession, ibid., 152, 434. It is an ancient institution of the Church to dedicate basilicas by the bringing in and placing of holy relics, 434. The basilica is sanctified by the presence of the relics, ibid. Whoever consecrated a church without holy relics is to be deposed as a bishop, as a transgressor of ecclesiastical traditions, ibid. It is an ancient custom to conceal the relics of the saints in the altar itself, 435. The place in which they are concealed is called a *confessio*, ibid. Within, this place is marked with a cross made of chrism at the four corners, 436. The Greeks pour sacred chrism over the holy relics as they deposit them, together with three portions of the Lord’s body and three portions of incense, ibid.

The name of Saint Remigius, archbishop of Reims, is recited in the canon of the Mass, 285. His vigil is on the day before the Kalends of October, 417. He is called Remegius, Remigius, and Remedius, ibid. The nativity of Saint Remigius is on the Kalends of October, ibid., 827. This day is not his nativity, or death, but his translation, 418. On the Kalends of October Saint Remigius was translated twice, but not in the same year, ibid. The day of his death is celebrated on the Ides of January, 418.

Anointing of the loins in extreme unction, 554. See *Extreme unction*.

The renunciation of the devil to be made by a catechumen, 382, 383, etc. See *Catechumen*.

The *Responsalis* is a codex containing the responsories to be sung in the divine office throughout the year, 733. See Preface VI.

The Resurrection of the Lord, according to all the Evangelists, is read in church during the seven days of the Octave of Pascha, 524, 561. On Easter Day itself the Gospel of the resurrection according to Matthew was formerly read in Africa, 561. On the second day, the Gospel according to Mark; on the third, according to Luke; and so forth, ibid.

Saint Revocatus is commemorated on the Nones of March, 312.

The history of the Church of Reims, by Flodoard, Preface V.

[Col. 1452] Richard the Elder, duke of Normandy, uterine brother of Radulphus, count of Bayeux, 581.

Riculphus, bishop of Soissons, decreed that the sick were to be anointed after confession and then given communion, 536. See *Extreme unction*.

In the time of Robert, king of France, what the formula for giving communion was, 580.

Robert, bishop of Le Mans, near death, sent his confession by letter to absent bishops; it specified no particular crime, 452.

Angelus Rocca. See his scholia on the Book of Sacraments, 599. He himself published the Preface III.

Rodradus the presbyter. See Preface.

The Rogations were instituted by Saint Mamertus, bishop of Vienne, 393. What the reason and necessity were for instituting these Rogation litanies, ibid. Three Masses were appointed for the three days of Rogations; elsewhere a single Mass was appointed, ibid. A fast was enjoined during this same three-day period of Rogations, contrary to the ancient custom of not fasting from Pascha to Pentecost, 395. The Rogations were not practiced in the Church in the time of Saints Ambrose and Augustine, 394, 395. See *Litany*.

Rogerius, bishop of Elne, built a wooden altar covered with silver and bearing a notable inscription, 309.

At Rome a purification was customarily performed in February according to an ancient superstition, 506, 307.

The dedication of the first church built and consecrated by Blessed Peter the apostle at Rome, 409.

The Romans received the custom of the Rogations from the Gauls, 395.

The custom of the Roman Church of consecrating the Eucharist on Maundy Thursday by the presbyters together with the pontiff, 337.

Roman virgins with their hair uncut, 442.

On the day on which they had been polluted, the Romans did not enter the church, 579.

The *phrygium*, or tiara, of the Roman pontiff, 442.

The Roman Pontifical book, 462.

Rotaldus, abbot of Corbie. See Preface.

The nativity of Saint Rufus the martyr near Capua, on the sixth day before the Kalends of September, 124, 412. He was a disciple of Saint Apollinaris, the disciple of Saint Peter the apostle, ibid.

Rufina and Secunda, holy sisters, are added to the sons of Saint Felicity, 407.

Ruth the Moabite, when she married Boaz, was blessed by the elders, 597.

### S
Sabanum is a rough, shaggy linen cloth, 355. Why the fast of Saturday is renewed in Lent, 314. Among the Easterners, on Holy Saturday before the cockcrow of Sunday, it was forbidden to break the fast, 315. The solemnity of Holy Saturday is described, 70. This begins at the eighth hour, that is, at two o’clock in the afternoon, ibid. The office of Holy Saturday looks toward the night of the Sunday Resurrection, 387. On Good Friday and Holy Saturday the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood is not celebrated, ibid. Holy Saturday has no vespers, 388. After the episcopal blessing, while the people are receiving Communion, the cantor begins “Alleluia,” “Laudate,” etc., ibid. Orders conferred on Saturday evening, 487. Why Ember Saturday is so called, 12. Ember Saturday “of the Lessons,” although only six lessons were then read at that time, 606.

The feast of Saint Sabina, Virgin and Martyr, 126, 708. Priests of the old law were consecrated by anointing, 331. The priest of the first order is the bishop; of the second, the presbyter; of the third, the deacon, 519. In former times several priests anointed the sick person, 237, 534, 543, 553. The priest’s prayer before hearing confession, 463. See Presbyter. Priests of the pagans crowned, 558.

The sacraments are spoken of in many ways, [Col. 1453] 1, 273, 274, 425. A sacrament is sometimes called a solemn feast in which some mystery of Christ is represented, 62, 298, 316, 320. “Sacrament” is used metonymically for sacramental grace, 316, 317, 389. A sacrament is called an arcane mystery, beneath whose covering something mystical lies hidden, 316. The two principal sacraments of the holy Church, signified by blood and water, flowed from Christ’s side as he slept upon the cross, 368, 384. Salt, customarily given to catechumens, is called a sacrament, 377. This sacrament is taken as that which is mystical, 378. In former times “sacraments” referred not only to the seven sacraments instituted by Christ, but to every rite in any way pertaining to sanctification, 425. “Sacraments,” that is, the solemn rites of the Mass, 431; and the prayers of the Mass, 599. Formerly three sacraments were given to the sick together, 536. In former times no sacrament was given to penitents, 532. Sacramentals are rites or things pertaining to a certain degree of sanctification, 425.

The distinction between sacramentaries and books of sacraments, 274, 340. See the preface. *Book of Sacraments*, *Sacramentary*, and *Book of the Sacramentary* are synonymous names, 599. The codex of Saint Gregory is more correctly entitled *Sacramentary*, ibid. It was first edited by Pope Gelasius and reformed and enlarged by Saint Gregory the Great, 600. See the preface. Pope Adrian sent Saint Gregory’s Book of Sacraments to Charlemagne, 617. Codices of the old Book of Sacraments. See Preface IV, V. The usefulness of the Book of Sacraments against heresies, Preface V, VI.

Sacrifices, that is, sacred acts: how they are distinguished from the gifts and offerings that precede them in the same prayer of the canon of the Mass, 283. A sacrifice cannot be offered except in the communion of the saints, whose memory we join in celebrating, 285. It is asserted from tradition that a sacrifice is to be offered for the faithful departed, 289. The saving sacrifice was foreshadowed by Melchizedek, who offered, in figure, the body and blood of the Lord, 373. Christ fulfilled this figure, ibid. He commanded his disciples to do the same in remembrance of him, ibid. The sacrifices of the old law receive their dignity from the Eucharistic sacrifice of the new law, 174, 443. Various defects concerning the sacrifice, to be corrected by canonical penalties, 468. No one except bishops and presbyters ought to offer sacrifice, 629. To communicate in a mixed sacrifice: what this means, 569. Formerly prohibited. In what case it was permitted, ibid.

Sacrilege is understood as a class of various dealings with the demon, 467, 472. By what canonical penalties those guilty of the different forms of this sacrilege are punished, ibid. A codex of the Book of Sacraments belonging to the Church of Sées, or Saliensis, in Normandy. See the preface.

Why those being baptized receive the salt of wisdom, 364. Salt is called the sacrament of catechumens, 377. The exorcism of salt for blessing water for the dedication of a church, 147. The blessing of salt, ibid. Salt is exorcised so that it may be mixed with blessed water, 533. Solomon’s temple facing west, 329. The salutation of newly prepared chrism, 338; and of the oil of catechumens, 339. Frequent mention is made of the salutation in the Greek rite for ordination, 526. This salutation is made with an embrace and as a token of friendship, ibid. By such a salutation sacred communion and the loving joy of minds in harmonious agreement are signified, ibid.

[Col. 1453] *Sancire*, that is, to sanctify, 174, 443. “Holy things for the holy” is said by the priest after the Lord’s Prayer, while he raises the consecrated bread, 566. *Sanctificare*, that is, to make something holy from an earthly substance, 290.

The feast of All Saints with the preceding vigil, 138, 712. Kalends of November. The feast of All Saints, 138, 832. This feast was instituted by Pope Gregory IV, 420. It was celebrated in Gaul under Louis the Pious, ibid. Under Charlemagne it was already celebrated in some places of Gaul, ibid. The memory of the saints in the canon of the Mass, 285. Also of the saint whose feast is being celebrated, ibid. And of the others who are celebrated throughout the world, ibid. He does injury to the saints who prays on their behalf, 607. How the prayer is to be understood: it asks that the offering may benefit such a saint for glory, ibid., 608. The adornment of all the saints rests upon the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, 372. Formerly it was permitted to name any saints after “Andrew” in the prayer that follows the Lord’s Prayer in the Mass, 292.

“Holy, holy,” etc., is called the victorious hymn, 281. The ancient use of this hymn in the sacred mysteries after the preface, 281. It is called the seraphic theology, ibid. This hymn is distinct from the Trisagion, ibid. Why it is called the Trisagion by Saint John of Damascus and in the Ambrosian liturgy, ibid. Alcuin and Leo of Ostia mention sandals, 556.

Only the blood of Christ was given to a very weak sick person, 554. The blood of Christ was formerly administered by deacons, 500, 569. “The blood of Christ, the cup of salvation”: an ancient formula of Communion, 580. The communicant responds “Amen,” ibid. What is signified by the blood and water that flowed from Christ’s side, 384.

—The eating of the blood of any animal was at one time forbidden in the Western Church, following the custom of the Eastern Church, 494. This custom was not universal in the West, ibid. Some interpret the passage in Acts 15 as referring to murder and the shedding of human blood, ibid.

To know (*sapere*) is different from to understand, 372. Wisdom is lesser if it lacks understanding, 372. Satisfaction is taken to mean excuse and purification, 526. These are called by one name, *Apologia*, ibid. What a penitent should do if, because of illness, he cannot fulfill the satisfaction imposed on him by the priest, 469. The priest should admit him to holy Communion, under the obligation of making satisfaction if he recovers his health, ibid.

The memory of Saint Saturninus the martyr is celebrated on the Nones of March, 312. Another Saturninus, a martyr who suffered at Rome, on the third day before the Kalends of December, 422. On the third day before the Kalends of December, the feast of Saint Saturninus, bishop and martyr of Toulouse, 142, 423. The Saxons, peoples of England, 587.

The anointing of the shoulders in catechumens, 331. In princes, anointing is performed between the shoulders, 589. Also in extreme unction, 553. The wicked and impious, according to the ancient custom of the Church, are excluded from the Church, the temple, sacred rites, and ordinary human society, 451. This too was practiced among the pagans, ibid. This custom also prevailed among the Gauls by the institution of the Druids, 452. Among them this was the most severe punishment, ibid. It also prevailed in Germany, ibid.

A scepter is called the emblem of royal majesty, 261. The handing over of the rod is distinguished from the presentation of the scepter, ibid., 592. The presentation of the scepter, 595. *Schola* is the college of singers, 323, and the choir of singers, 785. Saint Scholastica, virgin, on the fourth day before the Ides of February, 28. Knowledge drives away ignorance and, by its light, illumines the one whom it has filled, 372. Knowledge is nothing if it does not possess the usefulness of piety, ibid.

The sacred Scriptures were formerly kept by readers, 491. The announcement of the first scrutiny of the Elect, or catechumens, took place on Monday in the third week of Lent, 48. Catechumens of an age capable of understanding: who were to be scrutinized, 366, 379. Why the Church preserved this practice of scrutinizing those to be baptized at Easter, ibid. The Competentes gave their names on Palm Sunday and underwent the scrutiny, 379. The scrutiny was customarily performed by touching the nostrils and ears of the Competentes with saliva, 781, or without saliva, according to another usage, ibid. The Greeks did not observe this rite, ibid. In addition to this rite, insufflation, exorcism, renunciation, and the anointing of the shoulders and breast were rites of the scrutiny, ibid. There were seven scrutinies, ibid. The order in which they were customarily performed, ibid. During the scrutinies males were separated from females, 382.

The Mass of Saint Sebastian the martyr, distinct from the Mass of Saint Fabian, 20. See Fabian (Saint). The secret prayer in the Mass: why it is called “secret,” 293. It is also called the prayer over the offerings, ibid., 294. The mystical prayer “Te igitur,” etc., is also called the Secret, 252, 577. The Secrets of the Mass are recited jointly by the pontiff and the presbyter, 337. *Secretarium*, that is, *sacrarium*, 241, 556.

The sisters Saints Secunda and Rufina, 407. The memory of Saint Secundolus is celebrated on the Nones of March; he rested in prison, 312. The bishop’s seat in the church is higher than the others, 540. Formerly it was customary, once the consecration was completed, for the bishop to be solemnly placed in the episcopal chair, 520. The humility of Saint Martin sitting in the church on a lowly seat is commended, 340. The vanity of Paul of Samosata, sitting in a lofty throne in the church, is reproved by the bishops, ibid.

Semi-fasts, 293. Formerly, on semi-fast days, Masses were held at the ninth hour, ibid. *Sennes* in the nominative case—or the name according to each person’s preference, either declinable or indeclinable—409. His feast is celebrated on the third day before the Kalends of August, 116, 409, 704.

In the prayer we ask that we may not be left to our senses, that is, to our opinions, which are generally deceitful, 177, 444. And that our own sense may not be in us—that is, that we may not be anticipated or led by our own desires—ibid.

Burial in basilicas was formerly forbidden, 486. Later it was permitted, ibid. The feast of the seven brother martyrs, sons of Saint Felicity, on the sixth day before the Ides of July, 115, 407. What the seventh day signifies, 301. The number seven is sacred and mystical, ibid., 371, 385, 386. In it complete perfection is understood, 371. Either universality or the sevenfold grace of the Spirit is signified by the number seven in sacred Scripture, ibid. According to Aristotle, among the Greeks infants were given a name on the seventh day after birth, 350.

Septuagesima was formerly the beginning of the fast of ecclesiastical persons, 314. What civil and canonical laws impose as penalties upon violators of graves, 472. Formerly it was customary to bury treasures with the dead, ibid., 484. Why there are so many laws against violators of graves, ibid. The duty of burial, 480. The ancient burial rite, 478. See Exsequies. To which persons it was formerly granted to be buried within a church, [Col. 1455] 486. In the time of Saint Augustine it was permitted for Christians to be buried within the precincts of churches, ibid.

The old man Serapion, expelled from the church and a penitent, was reconciled at the point of death through a particle of the Eucharist sent to him by a presbyter and died in peace, 470. The feast of Saint Sergius the martyr, on the Nones of October, 418. The bishop’s sermon to penitents after the Gospel had been read, before the day of the feast of Easter, 457. The sale of another’s slaves and of a free man is punished by canonical penalties, 467, 474. Saints Severus and Severianus. See the Four Crowned Martyrs.

Why presbyters are forbidden to impose Sexagesima, 314. The number sixty is sacred, 314. What the sixtyfold fruit signifies, ibid. *Sēmeia* (Σημεῖα) are certain purple strips formerly sewn onto senators’ togas, 325. Siderius, bishop of Palebisca, was not lawfully appointed by Philo, bishop of Cyrene, 508, 513. Because he was ordained neither at Alexandria nor by three bishops, ibid.

Saint Sigismund the martyr and king of Burgundy, whose intercession is invoked for those suffering from fever, 615. The Lord’s seal is called the sacrament of confirmation, 359. The signing of the offering and of the chalice, 292. Of the offering alone, ibid. Of the chalice alone, ibid. The blessing of the sign, or bell, 438. The feast and Mass of Saint Pope Sylvester, 13, 660. See Sylvester. The feast of Saint Simeon, 664. The feast of the Purification is called Saint Simeon’s, 306. The opinion of Simeon of Thessalonica concerning the minister of extreme unction is rejected, 534.

The vigil of Saints Simon and Jude the apostles, on the sixth day before the Kalends of November, 137; and on the fifth day before the Kalends, their feast, ibid., 711, 712. Their memory is made in the canon of the Mass, 3. The feast of Saint Simplicius, on the fourth day before the Kalends of August, 408, 704. Another Saint Simplicius, a martyr, 139, 421, 608. The bodies of the dead were wrapped in a clean shroud, 484. Saint Sisinnius, a deacon and martyr who suffered at Rome under the Emperor Maximian, 423.

The name of Saint Pope Sixtus is recited in the canon of the Mass, 3. The feast of Saint Sixtus, or Xystus, pope, on the eighth day before the Ides of August, 117, 409, 705. This was not Xystus the Pythagorean, a pagan man, 409. Saint Smaragdus, 410.

*Sóleas* (Σωλέας), or *to soleon* (τὸ σωλέον), or *solea* (σωλέα), is the floor of the church before the doors of the sacrarium, between the choir and the sacrarium, where the altar is, 524. Among the ancient Romans, a *solidus* was a gold coin worth six thousand denarii, 471. The Frankish *solidus* was formerly worth forty denarii, ibid.; eventually it was reduced to the value of twelve denarii, ibid. Eight denarii, which make two hundred solidi, 472. The king’s throne, 593. What formula is pronounced while the king is placed upon the throne, ibid. The feast of Saint Soteris, virgin, on the fourth day before the Ides of February, 310.

“Species” signifies appearance or face, 400. To pass from hope to appearance—that is, to fruition or the clear vision of God—400. Whatever the Holy Spirit has touched is wholly sanctified and transformed, 309. Bread and wine are transformed into the body and blood of Christ through the descent of the Holy Spirit, ibid. Just as the Word of God was incarnate through the infusion of that same Holy Spirit, ibid. The Holy Spirit deigned to appear under a visible sign to holy men celebrating the sacred mysteries, ibid. A presbyter in Cilicia did not begin Mass until he saw the Holy Spirit overshadowing the altar, [Col. 1455] ibid.

The Holy Spirit is of one substance with the Father and the Son, 370. The Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son and is consubstantial with both, 365, 372, 379. One and the same Spirit is the source and principle of all virtues, ibid. The heavenly spirits are mentioned in the preface of the Mass, 280. Veiled brides, 598. See Marriage; Veiling. Sponsors at baptism, 357. See Godparents. Spittle used in the scrutinies, 366. See Ears; Catechumen; One to be Baptized; Scrutiny.

What the *statio* was among the ancients, 33. Collects and stations, which were formerly customarily held, 604, 664. *Staurophaneia* (Σταυροφάνεια), that is, manifestation of the cross, 415. The star appeared to the Magi; it was not one of many, or at least it followed a course unlike that of the others, 302. That which was formerly called a diadem is now called a *stemma*, 592. What a diadem is, ibid. A *stemma* is not altogether the same as a diadem, ibid.

Why Saint Stephen is placed before Saint Matthias in the latter part of the canon of the Mass, 4, 290. Saint Stephen is added to Saint Andrew in the prayer “Libera nos,” etc., which follows the Lord’s Prayer in the Mass, 4. The Nativity of Saint Stephen and his Mass, 9, 391. The deposition of Saint Stephen’s relics, 304.

—The feast of Saint Stephen, bishop and martyr, on the fourth day before the Nones of August, 117, 705. Two Masses are assigned, 705.

—Pope Stephen was received at Rheims by the Emperor Louis the Pious, while the various orders of the Church sang the *Te Deum*, 585.

—The response of Stephen of Tournai, and his opinion concerning the form of baptism, 354.

The *sticharion* is a close-fitting tunic, 521. The stole is called the *orarium*, with which the priest is ordained, celebrates Mass, and approaches Communion, 503. The shifting of the stole onto the presbyter’s right shoulder, 502. Strabo. His opinion concerning the author of the Book of Sacraments, Preface III.

*Stramenta* are carpets spread beneath, 424. In chapter 55 of Saint Benedict’s Rule, *stramenta* means bedding, ibid. Where subdeacons are ordained in the Mass, 487. The former distinct vestment of the subdeacon from that of the deacon, 325. The subdeacon is vested in a tunic, the deacon in a dalmatic, ibid. A subdeacon who has been married twice is relegated among the doorkeepers or readers, so that he does not read the Epistle or the Gospel, 491. An ancient mention of subdeacons occurs in the Church, 494. *Hypēretai* (Ὑπηρέται), that is, “ministers,” is what subdeacons are called, ibid. The subdiaconate formerly held a place among the minor orders, ibid. The subdiaconate was not a sacred order, ibid. Subdeacons were forbidden to touch the sacred vessels, ibid. A subdeacon is not ordained by the imposition of hands, 221, 505; he is ordained by the presentation of an empty chalice and an empty paten, ibid. Formerly the Book of the Epistles was not handed to the subdeacon at his ordination, 496. It did not belong to him to read at Mass, ibid. An unjustly degraded subdeacon is restored to his rank by means of the paten and chalice, 501. Among the Greeks, subdeacons are ordained by the imposition of hands, according to the Apostolic Constitutions, 521, 523. It is the duty of the subdeacon to guard the sacred doors, that is, the doors of the sacrarium’s screens, 523.

“To lie beneath for two years” signifies being in the third grade of penitents, in which they prostrate themselves before bishops who lay their hands upon them, 473. The raising of the emperor upon a shield, 583. “Subsequent grace” is called assisting grace, [Col. 1456] 318. See Grace. *Substratio* is the third grade of penitents, who prostrated themselves and placed their heads beneath the hands of the bishops, 461. A *substratorium* is that which is placed beneath something, 495. Coarser fabrics spread beneath the altar cloths are called *substratorium*, or *substratoria*, ibid.

The method of anointing the sick in the Church of Soissons, 554. The Codex of the monastery of Soissons of Blessed Mary, Preface V. Insufflation for making someone a catechumen, 376.
