What the triple insufflation of the bishop or priest at the blessing of baptismal water signifies, 349. *Synaxis* (Σύναξις), that is, collect, assembly, procession, and gathering: synonymous terms, 413. *Syntassesthai* (Συντάσσεσθαι), that is, to profess that one will serve Christ and adhere to him, 383.

Why the prayer “over the offerings” is called both *super oblata* and the Secret, 294. Man’s twofold pride against God, 368. The Greeks call the shoulder-vestment *omophorion* (ὠμοφόριον), 556. But this shoulder-vestment is not like the *omophorion*, as is clear from the *rationale* attached beneath it, ibid. See Omophorion. *Superpositio* is abstinence from food for the entire day, 475. See *Yperthetis*. Pagan superstition in the burial of the dead: they cut their own hair, tore their cheeks, or hired women to perform such acts for pay, 469, 476.

“Sursum corda”: these words of the preface of the Mass are of ancient institution and very famous among the Fathers, 279. Saint Susanna, 121, 410. *Suscipere*, that is, to honor or venerate, 416. *Systasis* (Σύστασις), that is, standing or established position: the fourth grade of penitents, 461. *Suxurium*, that is, a seat, 51, 69.

Pope Saint Sylvester instituted that the priest should anoint with chrism the one lifted from the water, 385. The Fathers who spoke of the anointing with chrism before Sylvester are to be understood as speaking of the anointing performed on the forehead by the bishop, ibid. See Silvester.

“Symbol” is interpreted as indication, sign, or contribution, 364. The Symbol is the complete and unshaken confession of the true faith, ibid. When and why the Symbol is delivered to the catechumen, ibid. Why the individual apostles, contributing their own statements, composed the Symbol—that is, the contribution of the whole faith—ibid. In twelve words the teaching of the twelve apostles is contained, 365. Explanation of the Symbol, ibid. The Symbol explained and to be retained and understood by those to be baptized, ibid. The Symbol was given to the catechumens who were Competentes on Palm Sunday, 378. The delivery of the Symbol is an exposition of the mysteries contained in it, ibid. The Symbol is said to have been composed by the apostles, ibid. After the renunciations have been made, the one to be baptized recites the Symbol according to ancient custom, 384. The Symbol is called the profession of the Holy Trinity, ibid. The Symbol is recited before the anointing of the sick, 548. The Nicene Symbol was not sung in the Mass of the Roman Church before the year 1014, 562. There was an opposite practice in the ancient churches of the Greeks, ibid. What caused this difference, ibid. The Spaniards began to sing it during the reign of Reccared, ibid. In the Mass of Illyricum the Nicene, or Constantinopolitan, Symbol is sung after the incensing of the offerings, 574.

Saint Symphorianus [or Symphonianus, Symphronianus, Sympronianus], martyr, 139, 421, 608. His office, 819. See Saint Timothy. *Synaxis*. See *Synaxis* (Σύναξις). The virgins of Syria were tonsured, 443.

[Col. 1457] T

* Tachygraphos* (Ταχυγράφος), that is, one who writes rapidly, or writes in shorthand, 343. Thaddeus, or Taddaeus, or Tatthaeus the apostle, is mentioned in the canon of the Mass, 3, 285. *Thathaeus* is formed by aphæresis, as though from *Mattathaeus* or *Mattathias*, 601. *Taddaeus* is interpreted in Latin as “praising,” or “confessing,” ibid.

Saint Audomar, bishop of the city of Thérouanne, and Saint Autbert of Cambrai transferred the body of Saint Vedast, 418. The *Te Deum laudamus* is sung according to ancient custom in public thanksgivings, 585. There is no mention of it before Saint Benedict and Teridius, a disciple of Saint Caesarius of Arles, 586. “Te igitur,” etc. This prayer is called mystical and secret, 252, 577. This prayer, together with the consecratory words, was formerly pronounced in certain places in a loud and clear voice, 577.

Pope Telesphorus is commonly said to have instituted the singing of the *Gloria in excelsis* at Mass, 277. Those who bring about storms: with what canonical penalty they are fined, 467. By the Latins these are called *tempestarii*, and by the Greeks *nephodioktai* (Νεφοδιῶκται), 472.

Temples generally face east, 329. The Jews pray turned toward the western region, 330. Pagan temples were generally turned toward the west, with their fronts facing east, 329. The temples of the ancient Greeks inclined toward the west, 330. The temple was anointed with chrism at its dedication, 430. See Dedication; Church; Basilica. The temples are anointed in extreme unction, 553.

The first Ember fast did not formerly always occur in the first week of Lent, 317. Nor did the fast of the fourth month always fall in Pentecost week, 400. The announcement of the Ember fasts, 105, 402. The fast of the first month formerly fell in the first week of March, 403. The fast of the fourth month likewise fell in the second week of June, ibid. By Gregory VII and Urban II these four Ember fasts were fixed as they are now, ibid. Let there be fasting on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday until the ninth hour, ibid. See Fast.

The pagans formerly called the Terminalia the feast of the Stone, that is, of the boundaries of fields. They were worshiped under the name of the god Terminus, 311. At the beginning of the year 1703 Rome and most of Italy were afflicted by earthquakes, 211. Prayers composed against these earthquakes by our most holy lord, Pope Clement XI, ibid. Earthly things are mentioned in the canon of the Mass, 281. *Tetras*, that is, the Wednesday of each week, 470.

The Theoderician codices, Preface IV. The feast of Saint Theodore the martyr, 139, 712. The edict of King Theoderic against violators of graves, 472. Pope Theodore restored the custom of blessing the Paschal candle, 347.

—The Jew Theodore was first baptized with sand and then with water, around the year 600, 355. The younger Theodosius, the first of the Constantinopolitan emperors, was crowned with solemn rite by the patriarch Proclus, 583. Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, did not compose the hymn “Gloria laus,” etc., 319. He was accused and condemned for conspiracy against the Emperor Louis the Pious, ibid. The emperor spared him and the other defendants accused of the same crime at Theodonis Villa, 320. The same Theodulf’s booklet on the order of baptism, 362. Theodulf was far removed from the heresy of the Monophysites, 382. Saint Theodulus, 693.

*Theophania*, that is, appearance of God, 301. The sacred days of the Theophany, ibid. The vigil of the Theophany is without a fast, 302. See Epiphany.

The patriarch Theophilus of Alexandria decreed that careful inquiry should be made into the morals and qualifications of clerics to be ordained, 497. His authorization was required for the ordination of Siderius, bishop of Palebisca, 508. His laying on of hands was necessary for the ordination of the bishop of Olbia, ibid. The Cappadocian Theophronius, a follower of Eunomius, 353. The author himself, together with Eutychius, [held the doctrine] of a single immersion in baptism, ibid.

Treasures were formerly buried with the dead, 472. See Violators of graves. The stricter discipline of the Thessalians concerning the time of baptism is rejected, 399. Saint Thomas the apostle, 144. His memory is made in the canon of the Mass, 3. His office, 842. Thomasius published the Gelasian Codex, Preface III.

The use of incense in the Church is ancient, 428. Frankincense was burned when entering the house of a sick person, 543. The Emperor Tiberius was crowned by Eutychius, patriarch of Constantinople, 584. The feast of Saint Tiburtius on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May, 83, 689.

—The feast of Saint Tiburtius the martyr, on the third day before the Ides of August, 121, 706, 815. John Tilius and the Tiliana Library. See the Preface.

*Timē* (Τιμή) of the episcopate, etc., that is, honor; this is the name by which the Greeks designate the three principal orders, the diaconate, etc., 499. While fear presses upon the mind, lest it grow proud of present things, it strengthens the mind concerning future things by the refreshment of hope, 372. Fear alone, without the other virtues, is useless for good action, ibid.

Timothy Aelurus, bishop of Alexandria, driven into exile, 512. Another Timothy was substituted for Aelurus by the votes of the citizens of Alexandria, 512. The feast of Saint Timothy, for which there are two Masses—the first of Saint Timothy, the other of Saint Symphorianus—412, 708.

A *tinnibulum* is a small vessel prepared for summoning the children of the Church, 146. Bells on the pontiff’s tunic, in imitation of the Aaronic priest, 557. Churches to which clerics are ordained are called titles, 496. In Rome they are called cardinal titles, to which deacons and presbyters are ordained and, as it were, incardinated—that is, established as fixed members, ibid. Formerly the custom had arisen that no clerics were ordained except for a definite church, shrine, or monastery, ibid.

Clerical tonsure is given among the Greeks at the ordination of a reader, 448. It is an ancient custom of the Roman Church that clerical dignity is conferred by cutting the hair, ibid. This is done before receiving any of the orders, ibid. That custom of the Greeks was not universal, because boys were admitted into the clergy who were not readers, ibid. Saint Peter the Apostle was the author of ecclesiastical tonsure, ibid. What clerical tonsure signifies, ibid. This is not a double tonsure but a single one, 449. The ancient crown of Saint Peter and of the early clerics represents Christ’s crown of thorns, ibid. See Clerical Dignity; Clerical Crown.

Cutting the hair at the death of parents is forbidden, 469. This was one of the pagan superstitions customarily practiced at funerals, 476. This madness is forbidden in the Law of the Twelve Tables, 477. This shaving of the hair was also customary among the Greeks as a sign of mourning, ibid. See Egyptians. Formerly a special prayer was said for the first cutting of children’s hair, 234, 533.

—Fallen virgins who were going to undertake penance were tonsured, 443. A professed virgin from Rome, having come to Bethlehem, was tonsured in order to preserve the custom of the people, ibid. If a woman cuts her hair on account of the monastic life, let her be excommunicated, ibid. In parts of Egypt and Syria, nuns were tonsured, ibid.

Pagans made water lustral by immersing in it a torch snatched from an altar, 348. On the day of the translation of the saints, it was formerly not the translation itself but the day of deposition that was celebrated, 407, 418. Men married three times were censured by the Church and subjected to canonical penalties, 476. What the thirtyfold fruit signifies, 314. The thirtieth day of marriage was devoutly celebrated by the ancients, 596. The number thirty is sacred, 314. “Thirty” (τὸ) refers to married women, just as sixty refers to widows, 314.

The one to be baptized makes a threefold profession, that is, recites the Symbol, 384. Triple immersion in baptism, 352. In the threefold name we believe one Majesty, without excluding the Persons, 6, 295. The profession of the Trinity is called the Symbol which those to be baptized “hand back,” that is, recite, 384. There was formerly controversy concerning the celebration of the feast of the Most Holy Trinity, 401. The preface of the Trinity, ibid. Sundays were assigned to the honor of the Most Holy Trinity, ibid. Why the Roman See formerly judged that no special day should be assigned to the solemnity of the Holy Trinity or of the Holy Unity, ibid. The office of the Most Holy Trinity composed by Albinus and Stephen of Liège, 725. It was rejected by the Apostolic See, 401. The feast of the Most Holy Trinity, formerly celebrated, was later discontinued and finally restored by the Roman pontiffs, ibid.

What the Trisagion is, and how it is distinguished from the victorious and seraphic hymn, 281. The Trisagion was not first instituted by Proclus of Constantinople to be sung in the sacred liturgy, ibid. A boy, carried up into heaven in the sight of everyone, heard this hymn being sung by the angels in heaven, 282. To this hymn Peter the Fuller added “Who was crucified for us,” thereby introducing a fourth Person into the Trinity, ibid. Certain words were added to the Trisagion in a Catholic sense by Calandion of Antioch, ibid. Other words were added by many provinces of Europe, ibid. Christ’s triumph signifies the cross, 391. *Troparion* (Τροπάριον), that is, a little verse, 570. When the Greeks sing this: “Let my mouth be filled with praise,” ibid.

Subdeacons are vested in a tunic by the pontiff, who says: “A stole of gladness,” etc., 496. The tunic that others call a dalmatic is put on the pontiff, 557. This tunic is furnished with rows of bells, 243. The beating of the breast was customarily performed at the words “I confess,” 559. To beat one’s breast is to accuse what lies hidden in the breast, ibid. Whoever beats his breast but is not corrected reinforces his sins rather than removing them, 560.

A tower was used for carrying the sacred ministry, 151. Formerly it was customary to carry Christ’s own body in a tower, 152. *Tutoare*, that is, to stumble or waver, 476. The quartan and quotidian type signifies the form or rule by which a fever, as though predetermined for itself, attacks a person, 616. Typical fevers, wandering fevers, ibid.

Anointing of the navel in extreme unction, 554. [Col. 1459] Anointing of priests, kings, and prophets in the Old Testament, 331, 515. Martyrs anointed and strengthened by the sacrament of confirmation, 331. It was an ancient custom that the baptized should immediately be anointed with chrism on the crown of the head by a presbyter, 355. What this anointing signifies, ibid. Anointing with chrism on the crown of the head must not be confused with anointing with chrism on the forehead, performed by a bishop, 385. The former is said to have been instituted by Pope Sylvester, ibid. All the Fathers who wrote about anointing with chrism before the time of Pope Sylvester are to be understood as referring to that performed on the forehead, ibid. The Greek Fathers, lacking the anointing performed on the crown of the head, must always be understood as referring to that performed on the forehead, ibid. The Latin Fathers sometimes speak of that performed on the forehead, sometimes of that performed on the crown of the head, and sometimes also of that by which certain heretics are reconciled, 385. Anointing on the crown of the head was not performed by a presbyter when chrismation on the forehead had preceded it, ibid. This happened whenever the bishop himself baptized, which occurred very frequently, ibid. The distinction between those two anointings, of the forehead and of the crown of the head, 386. The former is the ceremony of baptism; the latter is a sacrament distinct from baptism, 429.

—Double anointing of the head in the ordination of a bishop, 516. Anointing also of the thumb, ibid. The hands of bishops are anointed in ordination, 515, 516. The hands of presbyters are anointed in ordination, 503. The head of the same presbyter is also anointed, ibid. In ancient times in Gaul the hands of deacons were anointed with chrism in ordination, 501. The Greeks lack anointing in the ordinations of bishop and presbyter, 526. In these ordinations Saint Dionysius made no mention of anointing, ibid. Nevertheless, anointing appears once to have been in use among the Greeks, ibid.

—Anointing of kings, 589. Of queens, 595. Of princes, ibid. Anointing of an altar, 429. In the dedication of a church, crosses are drenched with anointing chrism, 430. Anointing of the relics that are placed in the altar, among the Greeks, 436. The *confessio* also—that is, the place in which the relics are deposited—is marked with chrism in the form of a cross at its four corners, ibid. Extreme unction. See *Extrema unctio*. The rite of extreme unction from the Codex of Ratoldus, 537. From the Codex Tilianus, 540. From the Codex of the monastery of Saint Remigius at Reims, 543. From the Codex of the Church of Soissons, 554. The bodies of the dead were to be anointed, according to a custom formerly practiced by many, 483. There was another anointing of the dead during the funeral rites themselves, while sacred hymns were being sung, ibid. Why this second anointing was performed, ibid. See *Defuncti*. *Exsequiae*. What the alabaster jar of ointment signifies, 366. The ointment of the Greeks used for confirmation, 326. What it means to anoint, or to anoint the feet of Jesus, 366. Claws are iron instruments, curved and pointed like a claw, suitable for tearing flesh, 477. Hooks, or claws, used in tortures or inquisitions, ibid. Martyrs were tortured with these by executioners, ibid. They are called *fidiculae* because they split, ibid. They were forked or bifid—that is, they had two curved points, ibid. The feast of Saint Urban, pope and martyr, on the eighth day before the Kalends of June, 88, 393, 696. —An *Apologia* published at the command of Pope Urban VIII, 530. See *Apologia*. Acolytes are ordained by the presentation of empty little vessels, 494. The canonical penalties imposed on usurers, 467, 474. Ripe grapes are blessed, in accordance with the institution of Pope Eutychianus, 234, 410. At Constantinople grapes are offered on the altar of the Church of Blachernae by the patriarch on the feast of the Dormition of Saint Mary, ibid.

## V

The heresy of Valentinus, who attributed a celestial body to Christ, is condemned, 299. —The feast of Saint Valentine, martyr, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of March, 28, 310, 665. The feast of Saint Valeria coincides with that of Saint Vitalis; and a Mass for several martyrs is celebrated, 391. The feast and Mass of Saint Valerian, martyr, 8, 689. It is not permitted to break church vessels except for the redemption of captives, 433. Altar vessels are customarily kept in the *sacrarium*, or *secretarium*, ibid. The altar pallia are to be washed in one vessel and the corporals, or corporal cloths, in another, 222, 495. A vessel of holy water at the doors of a church, 348. Contact with vessels is necessary in ordinations, 509. Whether this is so, and what kind of contact is required, ibid.

The feast of Saint Vedast at Arras, on the Kalends of October, 418. This day is the translation of his relics, ibid. This translation was made from the church of Saint Mary to the monastery of Nobiliacum, ibid. At Mass, it is not the day of the translation but the feast day that is celebrated, ibid. The feast of Saint Vedast on the eighth day before the Ides of February, 309. A Mass is celebrated for Saint Vedast on the eighth day before the Ides of February, 418. The Office of Saint Vedast, 827. The translation of Saint Vedast was carried out by Saint Aubert, bishop of Cambrai, and Saint Audomar, bishop of Thérouanne, 418.

*Vel*, the disjunctive particle, is often used in place of a copulative particle, etc., 284, 342, 427, 486. What the veil with which the heads of the newly reborn are covered signifies, 370, 386. The exorcized were veiled in the face, 377. The solemn veiling of virgins, 441. What the veiling of a virgin signifies, ibid. At what age a virgin is veiled, ibid. How veiling differs from a virgin’s profession, ibid. Why brides are veiled at weddings, 598. See *Nuptiae*. Formerly a veil was hung before the choir screen, where the clergy stood, 435. The mystical veil, 436.

Most people wish the “abbreviated word” prophesied by Isaiah to be understood in the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer, 365. When the divine Word assumed humanity, no confusion of the natures took place in the third person, 382. Who is meant by the statement that the Word assumed a human being, ibid. When the verse of the *κοινωνικόν* (“communion chant”) was customarily sung by the Greeks, 570. Why verses are recited after the offertory, 582. What the descending verses are, 730. Why they are so called, ibid.

Why the crown of the head is not anointed in the case of the sick, 553. On the crown of the head the presbyter anointed the baptized person with chrism, 358, 361, 371. This anointing was omitted when a bishop had baptized, 385. Anointing on the crown of the head had been instituted because of the absence of a bishop, who would immediately anoint on the forehead the neophyte whom he had baptized, ibid.

What the Vespers of Thursday in Holy Week, or the Lord’s Supper, were like, 333. In the choir itself, all the clergy or monks recite Vespers privately and silently on their knees, 343. Holy Saturday has no Vespers, 388. In the Codex of Ratoldus, the Vespers of this day are such as those now found in the Roman Breviary, 339. The evening synaxis included in the Mass of the Lord’s Supper and on Holy Saturday, 334.

A *vestiarium* is a place suitable for storing garments, 581. Properly, however, it is the place where the garments of a king or emperor are kept, ibid. The church *vestiarium* is the *sacrarium*, or *secretarium*, in which the sacred vessels and sacred vestments of the church are stored, ibid. The honor of a garment does not commend pontifical glory, 514. The black garment of virgins, 167, 440. Among the Romans, *vestes* are garments, 581. Why the Basilica of Saint John at Rome is called Saint John *ad Vestem*, 730, 731. The bodies of the dead dressed in precious garments, 483. Sacred vestments, 341, 556. *Ad vestem*—that is, the place where those to be baptized removed their clothing, or where the baptized put on the white garment, 785.

It is not permitted to practice *vetula* or *cervulus* on the Kalends of January, 472. What it means to engage in *vetula*. See *Cervulus*.

The viaticum was formerly given to the sick after extreme unction, 237, 536. The three sacraments of penance, extreme unction, and the Eucharist were conferred on the sick together, 536. Besides the formula of confession to be recited by the sick person, the sick person first made a secret confession of all sins, with their individual circumstances, 553. Because of imminent danger of death, the body dipped in the blood was offered to the sick person, 554. Those who were unable to swallow the body of Christ received communion by drinking the blood alone, ibid. A third part of the consecrated host is reserved as viaticum for the sick who are in danger, 583.

Saint Victor, 416. See Saint Maurice. Saint Victorinus, martyr, 139, 420. See the Four Crowned Martyrs. The widows for whom solemn prayer is offered on Good Friday are women who have professed widowhood by a solemn rite, 63, 322. The rite of a widow’s profession and clothing, 440. The calamities of Vienne on account of which Saint Mamertus instituted the Rogation days, 393.

One vigil is called a vigil at the ninth hour—that is, an all-night vigil—and another is a nocturnal vigil, 295. There is a twofold vigil on the feast of the holy apostles Peter and Paul: the first at the beginning of the night, the second at *maturitas*, that is, midnight, 405. The vigil of the feast of Saints Gervasius and Protasius, 108, 700. The vigil of Saint Remigius, 417. Nocturnal vigils in the old basilica before the dedication of the new one, 423.

The feast and Mass of Saint Vincent, martyr, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of February, 21, 663. Vincent the Victor is criticized because, while asserting corporeal members metaphorically of God, he asserted that the human soul possessed them literally, thereby making it corporeal, 382.

How wine in the chalice that has not been consecrated is sanctified through the consecrated species of bread mixed with it, 341. What *vinum de Graeco*, *de pactis*, *de procantu*, and *de procoma* are, 786. A man surviving twenty wives marries a woman surviving twenty-two husbands, 476.

The handing over of the rod is distinguished from the presentation of the scepter in the coronation of the kings of France, 592. The rod is what is called the hand of justice, ibid. See *Manus justitiae*.

The virgins for whom solemn prayer is offered on Good Friday are women devoted to God, or those who have professed virginity, 63, 322. After Christ, a virgin, came forth from the Virgin Mary, lust was conquered by the Virgin’s birth, 439. Consecrating virgins to God is an ancient custom of Christians, 410. It belongs to the bishop to consecrate virgins, ibid., 167. A presbyter must not consecrate virgins without consulting the bishop, ibid. On which days virgins are ordered to be consecrated, ibid. Formerly virgins consecrated to God wore a dark garment, ibid., 167. At what age the veiling of a virgin takes place, 441. In what year of age the profession of virginity takes place, ibid. Formerly virgins consecrated to God were veiled by a solemn rite, ibid., 168. The veiling of a virgin is her consecration and her strictest union with Christ the bridegroom, ibid. The vow of virginity and the taking of the veil are distinct, [Col. 1461] ibid. She wears on her head a mitre as though it were a crown of virginal glory, 442. A mitre is a Phrygian cap covering the head, such as is the head-dress of women devoted to God, ibid. The hair of virgins was spread out and unbound like that of brides, ibid. A fallen virgin is assigned the cutting of her hair as a penance, according to ancient custom, 443. A Roman virgin who had professed virginity, when she came to Bethlehem, was tonsured in order to preserve the custom of the country, ibid. Formerly in parts of Egypt and Syria, female religious—whether virgins or widows—were tonsured, ibid. Later, among the Latins and Greeks, the tonsure of female religious came into use, ibid.

The visitation, or anointing, of the sick, which is called extreme unction, is the last sacrament of the Christian law, 532. Its effects, ibid. Formerly Christians showed the greatest care in visiting the sick, ibid. The rite of visiting the sick, 232, 532. Prayers customarily recited formerly during the visitation of the sick, 235, 533. How great a concern priests formerly showed for the sick, 536, 537. See *Infirmi*, *Extrema unctio*.

The feast of Saint Vitalis, martyr, on the fourth day before the Kalends of March, 85, 391, 693. On the sixteenth day before the Kalends of March, the feast of Saint Vitalis, 28, 310. —Saint Vitalis, one of the companions of Saint Maurice, 416, 417. See *Mauricius (S.)*. The feast of Saint Vitus on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of July, 402. What the wedding ribbon signifies, 598.

“Long live the king!” This acclamation was customarily made at the coronation of a king, 594. It occurred at Solomon’s elevation to the kingship of the Jews, ibid. It is recorded as having occurred at the coronation of Justin the Younger, Philip Augustus, and others, ibid.

*Vivificas* (τὸ, “the [word] ‘you vivify’”) in the canon: that is, you change lifeless bread into the living body of Christ, 290. Some make Voconius Castellanus, bishop of a town in Mauretania, the author of the prayer with which the canon of the Mass begins: “Therefore, we beseech you,” etc., 283. What “their vows” signifies in the canon, 284. Vows are sacred prayers, even among the pagans, 285. A vow—that is, desire and will, 167, 441. A vow: a sacred and divine prayer, 231, 531. “Votive gifts” are called the sacraments of the body and blood of Christ, 12, 300, 317. Votive martyr-shrines—that is, devoted, offered, and consecrated to God, 410. A devout person—that is, one ready and eager for the worship of God—is called *votivus*, 439.

[Col. 1462] Walafridus Strabo. See *Strabo*.

## X

Xistus the Pythagorean. See *Sixtus*.

## Y

*Ὑπαπαντή*, or *Ὑπαντή*, that is, “meeting,” the name by which the Purification of the Blessed Virgin Mary is called, 306. *Ὑπηρέται*, that is, “ministers,” who are called subdeacons, 494. *Ὑπέρθεσις*, that is, “superimposition,” is abstinence from food for a complete and entire day, 475. It is also the superimposition, addition, and extension of a fast, ibid. *Ὑπερτιθέναι*, that is, “to superimpose,” and to add one fast onto another, 475. *Ὑπόπτωσις*, that is, “prostration,” the third degree of penitents, 461.

## Z

The feast of Saint Zeno on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of March, 28, 310. The Paschal proclamation customarily sung at the blessing of the candle is attributed to Pope Zosimus, 344, 347. The feast of Saint Zoticus on the fourth day before the Ides of February, 310.
